en: Oṃ Arhaṃ. Homage be to the ascetic, the Blessed One, Mahāvīra;
homage to the illustrious Antarikṣapārśvanātha.

The *Nayacakra*, consisting of twelve spokes, composed by the venerable teacher Śrī Mallavādi Kṣamāśramaṇa—the sovereign of the circle of logicians and a propagator of the [Jaina] scriptures—and adorned with the commentary (*vṛtti*) titled *Nyāyāgamānusāriṇī* compiled by the venerable Siṃhasūri Gaṇivādi Kṣamāśramaṇa; herein is presented the first spoke, "On Prescriptive Rules" (*vidhyara*), arranged according to the citations and references found within the commentary.
The *Nyāyāgamānusāriṇī*: A Commentary on the *Nayacakra*.
Oṃ! Homage to the One Free from Passion.
Aiṃ! Homage to the Root.

Pervading all, yet situated in one; infinite, yet appearing finite when placed within the proficiency of the intellect, but not so when there is delusion; the locus of the mind that perceives the expansion, emanation, and transformation of the universe;
transcending the reach of speech yet defined by speech; it is accessible, yet nowhere truly accessible.
Victorious is the exalted Jaina teaching through its categories of substance and modification;

victorious is the venerable teacher Mallavādi Sūri, who, having vanquished the entire circle of opposing doctrines with his Wheel of Reasoning (*Nayacakra*), is the sun in the firmament of the Jina’s word.

We shall now provide a detailed commentary on this treatise entitled *Nayacakra*, which expounds the great and true meaning established by him. That Blessed One, desiring to favor the fortunate people of this age who take delight in logical reasoning, was about to undertake the composition of the *Nayacakra* treatise in accordance with the teachings of the Arhat. For the sake of auspiciousness and to summarize the subject matter to be explained, he uttered the first verse beginning with "Pervading and situated in one" (*vyāpyekastham*).
It is called *vyāpi* because it pervades (*vyāpnoti*), or because its nature is to pervade; it is derived from the *uṇādi* suffixes or is used in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlika*).
What is to be pervaded? Since it is not specified, it is everything—entities such as atoms and so forth.
If it is asked how all this is pervaded by the Jaina teaching, [the answer is] from the perspective of the substantial (dravyārtha) point of view:

for example, a single atom is connected with its own inherent variations of color, odor, taste, and touch—whether present or past—as well as with dyads and so forth, which are conjunctive and extend up to great aggregates; and with those that are disintegrative and those produced by effort, such as the kārmaṇa-body and others.
As it has been said: "Whatever object-variants or verbal variants exist in a single substance, whether past, future, or present, to that extent is that substance"—this is from the *Sanmati*. (1)

31. Likewise, by means of the relative characteristics of motion, rest, spatial occupation, and duration—namely, the substances of dharma, adharma, ākāśa, and kāla—and by means of the inherent and adventitious characteristics of living beings such as consciousness (upayoga) and the body, there exists a state of identity (tādātmya) among all substances and modes.

This is because each respective entity, when considered from the perspective of its substantial nature (dravyārtha), does not deviate from its own essential form during those various modifications; and because those modifications are likewise non-different from that [substance], all substances and modes are indistinguishable in their existence.
Therefore, since it pervades each of them, it is called "all-pervading" (vyāpin).
The notes present the *Ṭippaṇa* (critical commentary) by Jambūvijaya:
"Having paid homage to the Siddhacakra and having fixed it within my heart..."
In this *Nayacakra-mahāśāstra*, a commentary (*ṭippaṇa*) is being composed by me.

The venerable and worshipful Śrī Mallavādi Kṣamāśramaṇas, desiring to explain the root *gāthā-sūtra*—which consists of a single verse to be stated later beginning with "vidhi-niyama-bhaṅga-vṛtti" and which is extremely concise in meaning—have composed this entire exposition (*vivaraṇa*) consisting of a commentary (*bhāṣya*).

Furthermore, because this commentary is exceedingly profound, fathomless in its realization, and like a great ocean difficult to traverse, the venerable Śrī Siṃhasūri Gaṇivādikṣamāśramaṇas composed a sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) following the principles of logic and scripture (*nyāyāgamānusāriṇī*), which serves as a boat for those wishing to cross it.

Thus, since this work of the sub-commentary is an explanatory exposition (*anuvyākhyāna*) upon the commentary (*vivaraṇa*) consisting of the *bhāṣya* composed by the venerable Śrī Mallavādikṣamāśramaṇa, the authors of the sub-commentary stated: "We shall provide an explanatory exposition."

The word *anu* is used in the sense of "subsequently" (*paścāt*); the intention is that the Blessed Mallavādī will provide the commentary (*vyākhyāsyati*), and this author of the sub-commentary (*ṭīkākṛt*) will provide the sub-commentary (*anuvyākhyāsyati*).
It appears here that there is an elision of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa-lopaḥ*) according to Pāṇini 6.1.135.
By this sūtra,

it is established that "the manifold alone is the ultimate reality" (anekānta eva paramārthaḥ); and because it is the proponent of that [reality], it will be stated later that the Jaina teaching alone is true—
this matter pervades what stands here.
*Vyāpi* (pervasive): *sthami* (Bhāṣya);
that which pervades (*vyāpnoti*) or whose nature it is to pervade (*vyāptuṃ śīlam*)—that which pervades is "pervasiveness" (*vyāpti*), whose nature it is to pervade (Bhāṣya).

The form *vyāpin* is established by the rule *supyajātau ṇinistācchīlye* (Pāṇini 3.2.78), which prescribes the suffix *ṇini* to express the sense of habit (*tācchīlya*) when it is intended to indicate that something has the nature of pervading (*vyāptuṃ śīlam asya*).
However, when denoting habitual action (*tācchīlya*), it is an *auṇādika* formation;
[as in] "by those who subsist on alms" (*praśrasikaiḥ*).
In that which is unique, whatever are the modifications of meaning or modifications of speech...

That which has been, is being, and will be [in a certain state] is called a substance (*dravya*) to that extent. — *Sanmati* 1.31. That which has been and will be [in a certain state] is a substance to that extent. — *Bhāṣya*.
In the absence of the measure of the arrow [i.e.,
the *iṣubhāga*],
there is neither the modification of the substance nor the non-modification of the substance.

This being the case, because the entity would be excessively indistinct, there would follow defects such as the absence of the linguistic expression and the cognition directed toward it, which have as their fruit the determination of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*). To prevent this, the perspective of synonyms (*paryāyādeśa*) is resorted to—namely, that [the entity] is "located in one" (*ekastha*). This is because entities, through their uncommon properties (*asādhāraṇadharma*), attain their own functional existence (*svavṛtti*) by virtue of having non-confused forms due to the complete presence [of those properties] in each [individual]. For no entity can exist in dependence upon anything else; rather, each and every entity is indeed singular.

Because of that dedication, the teaching is said to be "situated in one place"; yet because of its dedication individually and separately according to each [disciple], by virtue of the complete instruction regarding both its own and other forms, it is pervasive.
Thus, it is both pervasive and situated in one place, being truly one;
and this is likewise for the subsequent [teachings] as well.
Even though it exists,
it is deluded by the notion of "I" (satyapi tisanmugdha); it is indeed indeterminate regarding that which resides within the self (evātmasthasyaivāniścaya).
Due to the distinctness of each respective thing,
and by virtue of its own particular nature, that [reality] is both pervasive and indeed one.

In this context, the reading "and by virtue of the comprehensive standpoint (*samagrādeśa*), that very same [reality] is both all-pervading and situated in one place" is understood to be correct. By virtue of the substantial standpoint (*dravyārthādeśa*), it is all-pervading; by virtue of the modal standpoint (*paryāyārthādeśa*), it is situated in one place. The intended meaning is that by virtue of the comprehensive standpoint—that is, by virtue of the dual standpoint consisting of both the substantial and the modal—it is both all-pervading and situated in one place. Furthermore, it is both infinite and finite, because it is not differentiated and is also differentiated by the standpoints of substance, space, time, and mode (*dravya-kṣetra-kāla-bhāvādeśaiḥ*).
As it has been said:

"Thus, the twelve-fold collection of scriptures (*gaṇipiṭaka*), with respect to substance, is with beginning and with end when referring to a single person; it is without beginning and without end when referring to many persons.
With respect to space, it is with beginning and with end when referring to Bharata and Airāvata; it is without beginning and without end when referring to Mahāvideha."

With respect to time (*kāla*), [the teaching] is with beginning and with end (*sādyaṃ saparyavasitaṃ*) in relation to the *utsarpiṇī* and *avasarpiṇī* eras; with respect to [time] other than the *utsarpiṇī* and *avasarpiṇī*, it is without beginning and without end (*anādyaṃ aparyavasitam*).
With respect to state (*bhāva*), as stated in the *Nandisūtra* (42) and the *Ekabhāva*: "Those states proclaimed by the Jina at any given time," etc., it is indeed with beginning and with end.
In the same way, even further on, one should understand that in the manuscripts (prati) containing "ya," the reading "aṃ" is to be understood in place of "yaṃ.
The two time-cycles (kāla) are the *utsarpiṇī* and the *avasarpiṇī*. Bhā. [Note].
*sappi* (ghee), *pra* (prefix);
likewise hereafter, *sappiṇi-ṇusappi* according to the Bhāṣya.

Alternatively, it is "infinite" (ananta) because there is no end to it; it is "finite" (antavat) because there is an end to it—to what? Since nothing specific is mentioned, it refers to everything, as has been stated:—

“Blessed One, is this Jewel-Clarity Earth (*ratnaprabhā-pṛthivī*) eternal or non-eternal? “Gautama, it may be eternal; it may be non-eternal. “For what reason, Blessed One, is it said that ‘it may be eternal; it may be non-eternal’? “Gautama, in terms of its substantiality (*dravyārthatayā*), it is eternal; in terms of its modalities of color (*varṇaparyāyaiḥ*), modalities of odor (*gandhaparyāyaiḥ*), modalities of taste (*rasaparyāyaiḥ*), modalities of touch (*sparśaparyāyaiḥ*), and modalities of shape (*saṃsthānaparyāyaiḥ*), it is non-eternal. (Jīvābhigama Sūtra 3.1.78, etc.)
bhā॰ vinā'nyatra — ॰sayā goyamā sia vi॰ ॰sayā go siya pā॰ ḍe॰ līṃ॰ raṃ॰ hī॰ siaya॰.
Likewise, in the following [passages] as well:
"from the perspective of substance (dravyārthatas), they are eternal."

"Placed for the sake of proficiency" means it is placed— that is, deposited— as the cause for the proficiency of the intellects (*dhi*), which are the various types of *ābhinibodhika* [cognition], when that proficiency is to be achieved.

As it has been said: "Where there is sensory cognition (abhinibodhika-jñāna), there is scriptural cognition (śruta-jñāna); where there is scriptural cognition, there is sensory cognition" (Nandisūtra 24).

For those whose intellects are refined by the knowledge derived from scripture (*śrutajñāna*), [the doctrine of] "the jar and so forth is eternal," "it is non-eternal," or "it is inexpressible"—and other such one-sided views (*ekāntavāda*)—is refuted by demonstrating various defects: that if it were eternal, there would follow the consequence of the absence of the potter’s exertion and the like; that if it were non-eternal, there would follow the consequence of the absence of desire to act, memory, recognition, and preservation; and that if it were inexpressible because its own nature cannot be determined, there would follow the consequence of the cessation of all verbal discourse. Furthermore, since the statements "it is expressible" and "it is inexpressible" involve a contradiction with one's own words, it cannot be inexpressible. By thus avoiding these defects through the acceptance of non-absolutism (*anekānta*)—namely, "it may be eternal," "it may be non-eternal," and "it may be inexpressible"—and by establishing the distinction between attributes (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmī*) according to valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the true nature of things is demonstrated. Through this, the refutation of the positions of others and the concession of their validity lead to the reconciliation of mutual contradictions among disputants and the establishment of a single coherent discourse. Like an impartial witness, this [doctrine] becomes authoritative, for it is capable of bestowing proficiency in the awakening to reality even for those [disputants].

In the phrase "pāṭave," the locative case is used in the sense of a cause (*nimitta-saptamī*); therefore, the meaning is that [the aforementioned] is the cause of the clarity of cognitions (*dhiyām*).
Likewise, regarding the phrase "na vyāmohe" from the root text to be cited later, the meaning is that it is not the cause of delusion (*vyāmoha-hetu*). [This refers to] *ṇibodhika-ñāṇaṃ*.
Likewise, in what follows as well,
[it is] "the knowledge of the disciples" (suta-ñāṇaṃ);
likewise, in what follows as well.
"In this regard, wherever there is sensory cognition (*ābhinibodhika-jñāna*), there is scriptural cognition (*śruta-jñāna*); wherever there is scriptural cognition, there is sensory cognition;
these two are mutually interpenetrated"—such is the reading in the *Nandisūtra*.
The explanation of this is as follows: "jattha" and so forth;

in whichever person there is sensory-cognition (ābhinibodhika-jñāna), in that very person there is also scriptural-cognition (śruta-jñāna), and likewise, wherever there is scriptural-cognition, there is also sensory-cognition.

He asks: "When it is stated that 'where there is sensory cognition (ābhinibodhika-jñāna), there is scriptural cognition (śruta-jñāna),' it is already understood that 'where there is scriptural cognition, there is sensory cognition. Therefore, what is the purpose of this statement? It is replied: "It is not understood as a rule of necessity; therefore, this is stated for the sake of determining that rule. Thus, there is no fault. He clarifies this very determination of the rule: "Both of these—sensory cognition and scriptural cognition—are mutually concomitant and bound to one another" (*Nandisūtra-malaya-vṛtti*).
By the rule *iteḥ svarāt taśca dviḥprā* (Vyāsa 1.42), there is elision (*luk*) of the initial vowel *i* of the word *iti*; thus,
for those whose intellects are refined by scriptural knowledge (*śrutajñāna*), the connection of the phrase "of those" (*iti*) appears to be with the upcoming term "proponents" (*pravādinām*).

It might be argued: "But surely, for this very reason, [the doctrine] is also a cause of delusion—just like doubt or error regarding objects such as a post or a person—because it consists of one-sided conceptual constructions such as 'eternal' or 'non-eternal'; and because we observe the expansion and manifestation of the world through one-sided conceptualizations of causes such as time (*kāla*), necessity (*niyati*), inherent nature (*svabhāva*), the person (*puruṣa*), fate (*daiva*), the Lord (*īśvara*), or chance (*yadṛcchā*).
To this, it is replied: No; because it serves as the basis for a cognition that is free from error.

For the Jaina teaching—like the relationship between father and son in the case of a single man—transcends and turns back the one-sided paths of worldly distinctions such as time and so forth; by means of refuting mutual contradictions, it is the cause for establishing and reconciling the nature of manifoldness (*anekānta*); and it consists of a single realization that synthesizes both one-sided and manifold doctrines, precisely through the negation and affirmation of opposing views.

It is not time alone, nor is it destiny alone; for proponents of a single cause, just as there is existence of the cause, there is the fallacy of inconclusiveness regarding the existence of the effect. Furthermore, if the cause itself were to possess a cause, there would be the fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*), which leads to the consequence of multiple causes; yet, since multiple causality is established [by our reasoning], and because even in the case of multiple causes there is no lack of continuity due to the non-distinction of "being" (*sat*) and so forth, there are such faults as these. Thus, both time and destiny are excluded. Because faults are seen in the view of absolute unity (*ekānta*) and the absence of faults is demonstrated in the view of non-absolutism (*anekānta*), it accords with worldly discourse, as it has been said: "But not thus... (natvataya).
The reversal of the divine, the lord, the eye, the star, and the water.
In some places your words are understood as being heavy with partiality toward *niyati* (fate),

[stating] that living beings are determined by their own nature and proceed according to the constraints of time; in other places, they are understood as being heavy with partiality toward *svabhāva* (intrinsic nature).
In some cases [the soul] enjoys what it has created itself, and again it enjoys what was created by another;
yet, O you of clear speech, it is not stained by faults—oh, what a wonder! (Siddhadvātriṃśikā 3.8).
Thus, it does not possess the fault of taking [what is not given].

Thus, such a teaching is "mighty" (*ūrjita*): it is mighty because it is independent, because it is free from the weakness of subsisting upon the views of others, because it does not abandon its own well-established tenets when assailed by opponents, because it does not resort to alternative conceptualizations, and because it is untroubled;

or it is mighty because it is victorious through the reasons just mentioned; or it simply triumphs because it is endowed with the excellence of energy and power that follow one another, like the sovereignty of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) who possesses the established policy of merit.

Because of the abandonment of even the state of being well-accomplished (susiddhatā), that [reality] is accessible to yogins in every respect, since their wisdom has as its object that which is not within the range of those whose intellects are refined by the elaborations of all philosophical systems (sarvanaya-prapañca).

Because we and others perceive the majesty of only one part, the majesty of the remainder is understood through inference; it is not the case that [the Lord] is "not to be reached" (*agamya*) anywhere. Just as there might be accessibility elsewhere despite being unassailable in one particular region—as in the case of a king who rules over a fragmented territory—let it not be so [with the Lord]; thus, He is "not to be reached" (*agamya*) nowhere.
Alternatively, *gamya* means that which is to be approached, or that which is to be established [as the goal].

It is not something to be explained or demonstrated, because its categories are made clear by the adoption of *syādvāda*, which conforms to worldly conventional usage, and because once one part is understood, the remainder is easily grasped;
or else, it is not to be communicated with respect to unworthy persons, as stated in the *Aptamīmāṃsā-vivaraṇa*.

The meaning of the reading appears to be as follows: "Wisdom that follows after objects is 'wisdom conforming to objects' (*anuviṣayaprajñā*); however, the yogins possess 'wisdom not conforming to objects' (*ananuviṣayaprajñā*). For they do not understand the majesty of the remainder through inference based on seeing the majesty of only one part; thus, because their wisdom does not conform to [a single] object. Alternatively, it is possible that the reading here might instead be "because their wisdom has as its object that which is beyond inference" (*ananumānaviṣayaprajñatvāt*).
...by way of being [the object], ...by way of being [the object],
...by way of being [the object], ...by way of being [the object], ...of the destruction of the sphere of objects, so [it is said] in the Prajñā[pāramitā].
In this context, "object" means the place;
subtle meanings should not be explained to one of dull intellect, for failing to grasp them,
he would become mentally distressed or fall into false views due to his lack of transformation.

Otherwise, it would be false, contradictory, or inconsistent; or rather, one should never resort to alternative conceptual constructions for the sake of reconciling a previously stated meaning that was spoken without due consideration—

just as the Buddhists, having asserted the thesis that "everything is momentary," postulate the notion of a "continuum" (saṃtāna) in order to avoid the fault of the non-existence of memory, recognition, bondage, liberation, and so forth.
Having asserted the eternality of the Pradhāna, the Sāṃkhya (Kāpila) postulates its transformation into the form of the manifest;
[it is] like an action, possessing qualities, and the inherent cause, according to Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.1.

15. Having thus proposed the definition of substance in general, and in order to avoid the charge of non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) regarding the doctrines of absolute permanence or impermanence, Kaṇabhuj [Kaṇāda] formulated his categories by relying on the two standpoints of substance (*dravya*) and modification (*paryāya*): namely, that substance is of two kinds—non-substantial (*adravya*) and multi-substantial (*anekadravya*)—and that the essence of substance (*dravyatva*) is what is termed both a universal (*sāmānya*) and a particular (*viśeṣa*).

Likewise, having proposed the thesis that substance, quality, and action are distinct, one will prevail by subordinating the remaining teachings [of other systems] out of fear of the defect that absolute difference between them would result in the absence of linguistic conventions such as co-referentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) in cases like "blue lotus," as well as the relation of qualifier and qualified; therefore, that which is of such a nature must indeed be established as being of such a nature.

What, then, is to be established? It is the existence (*sattā*)—defined as that from which [the concept] "existent" arises for the sake of establishing the infinite variety of alternatives ranging from duality to infinity, such as substance-aspect (*dravyārtha*) and mode-aspect (*paryāyārtha*)—as stated in Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.2.7–8: "Existence is that which belongs to substance, quality, and action, and which is distinct from substance, quality, and action. Thus, under the guise of the categories (*padārtha*) accepted [by the Vaiśeṣikas], there is the recourse to substance-aspect and mode-aspect, as well as the postulation of generality (*sāmānya*) and ultimate particularity (*antyaviśeṣa*), for the purpose of avoiding the fault of confusion (*saṅkara*).

Regarding "bauddhe" (in the Buddhist [work]) in the Bhāṣya and Viṣama-pada sections, it appears that— in the absence of "bauddhau" (the two Buddhist [works]) in the Bhāṣya and Viṣama-pada sections— the reading "bauddhe" alone is appropriate here according to the context of the preceding and following passages, and it is the intended reading of the commentator.
The non-existence of [the self] in the aggregates;
the continuum of objects;
the non-existence of selfhood.
The manifest is caused, non-eternal, non-pervasive, active, manifold, dependent, indicative, composed of parts, and subordinate; the unmanifest is the opposite.

"The definition of substance (dravya) is that which possesses action and qualities and is an inherent cause"— this is the reading in the Vaiśeṣika Sūtra; elsewhere, however, it is read as "and the doctrine," according to the Bhāṣya and Pāṭha manuscripts.
And likewise, *ḍe*, *līṃ*, *raṃ*, *hī*, and *tam*—namely, the doctrine of manifoldness (*syādvāda*).
Without the doctrine of manifoldness, neither grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) nor the relationship between qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣyabhāva*) is possible;
for indeed, coreferentiality is the occurrence of two words with distinct bases of application (*pravṛttinimitta*) upon a single object.
Furthermore, if there were absolute difference between the two, as in the case of a jar and a cloth, they could not reside in the same locus;
nor could there be such residence if there were absolute non-difference, because this [residence] is dependent upon difference. Indeed, it does not occur that "blue is blue.
Moreover, if the object were understood from the word "blue" alone, it would follow that the word "lotus" (utpala) is redundant.
Likewise, when it is restricted that "one thing is existent alone," there would be an absence of the relationship between qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and qualified (*viśeṣya*).
A qualifier must be understood as being in some way a distinct entity from the qualified;
and here, existence (*astitva*) is the qualifier. Is its qualified object—the thing—identical to it, or is it something else? It cannot be identical, for a thing cannot be its own qualifier.

Furthermore, in the absence of a substantive (*viśeṣya*), there could be no qualifying attribute (*viśeṣaṇa*) either, because of the etymological derivation that "that by which a substantive is qualified is a qualifier.
If it were something else [than the substantive], then, since all things would be equally "other," everything would be a qualifier of everything.

Therefore, this [relationship] is not possible in absolute difference or absolute non-difference; thus, the *syādvāda* (the doctrine of manifoldness), characterized by difference-cum-non-difference, must be accepted even against one's will.
—Siddhahema° Laghunyāsa, p. 2— 1.
That which is of such a nature will surely conquer by means of subordinating all other teachings;
however, its being of such a nature must be demonstrated.

What, then, is to be established? It is that existence (*sattā*)—which possesses infinite conceptual variations from duality up to infinity due to its dual nature as both substance (*dravya*) and mode (*paryāya*)—exists in substances, qualities, and actions; and that this existence is an entity distinct from substances, qualities, and actions.
This is the reading in the *Vaiśeṣika-sūtra*: "Existence is [present] in substances, qualities, and actions; existence is an entity other than substances, qualities, and actions."
"Being" (*sattā*) is that [universal] on account of which there occurs, with respect to substances, qualities, and actions, the cognition "it is" (*sat*)—
the particle *iti* indicating the mode of both the cognition and its linguistic usage—

and likewise, that universal on account of which there arises, with respect to the three categories beginning with substance, the cognition characterized by the form "it is, it is" (*sat sat*), or the employment of words in the form "this is being, this is being" (*sad idam, sad idam*). That [universal] is existence (*sattā*).

[Objection: "But surely existence (*sattā*) is not experienced as distinct from substance, quality, and action; therefore, existence is simply one or another of these, such as substance. To this, he replies: "Existence is a different entity from substance, quality, and action.
Substances and the others are non-pervasive (*ananugata*), whereas existence is pervasive (*anugata*).
Thus, because their difference from them is established through the imposition of contradictory properties characterized by pervasiveness and non-pervasiveness, [existence is indeed distinct]."
—*Vaiśeṣika Sūtra Upaskāra*, p. 40:

"Transcending a portion of speech, it is called 'determined by speech' (*vāgviniyata*). This is because specific types of cognition (*mati*) are admitted among those very objects capable of being designated, depending on the particularities of the subsidence-cum-destruction (*kṣayopaśama*) through infinite, innumerable, and numerable divisions and multiples of increase and decrease; this applies only to those possessing the fourteen *pūrvas* in relation to one another, just like the excellence or deficiency of the sensory power of modern men.
And it has been said:
In the Samitiya school,
those who possess the fourteen pūrvas occupy six positions relative to one another. In the Caitya school, they are fourteen.
Of those [objects] expressible, that which is the scripture is an infinite-thousandth part of them; by that [scripture], it is infinite-thousandfold.
By that [karma], however, it is infinite;
by that, indeed, it is infinite — Viśeṣāvaśyaka-bhāṣya, Pañcama-prakaraṇa.
Likewise, even further on,
expressible entities constitute an infinite fraction of the inexpressible ones.
Furthermore, an infinite portion of those things that are expressible is bound to scripture (*sūtra-nibaddha*).
(Sūtra-bhāṣya;
Viśeṣāvaśyaka-bhāṣya)

In terms of the acquisition of syllables they are equal or slightly less; however, through distinctions of intelligence, they become superior. In terms of distinctions of intelligence, they become [superior]. Bhā. (Commentary).
Know that those specific distinctions of the intellect (*mativiśeṣa*) are also included within the scope of scriptural knowledge (*śrutajñāna*). (Viśeṣāvaśyaka-bhāṣya 63, 62, 64;
Āvaśyaka)
*mati-jñāna-bhāṣya*,
*śruta-jñāna-bhāṣya*
— Viśeṣāvaśyaka-bhāṣya.

"By subordinating all other teachings," and so forth—by means of this disparagement of the doctrines of others, he will certainly triumph; for through this praise, you have acknowledged his power. Indeed, you will demonstrate this: "Not by conforming to anyone else's views"—what is it that triumphs by the grace of someone? The intended meaning is that he triumphs by placing his foot upon the throat of the disputant.

That which is of such a nature: accessible in every way only to yogins and inaccessible to others anywhere; transcending the domain of speech and yet defined by speech; pervading all while remaining one, infinite yet appearing finite; established through the proficiency of the intellect, not through delusion; the firm ground for the mind that discerns the expansion, emanation, and transformation of the world; the formulation of the single sentence of the categories of reality according to the established rules of procedure; consisting of the components of all-encompassing knowledge; and having become a constituent part of the ocean of awakening—such indeed is this teaching.

What is there to be wondered at in the fact that "the firm, immovable abode and foundation, which is the reversal of the expansion and diffusion of the world, is victorious and powerful"? Rather, it is precisely this very nature—that is, the possession of qualities not shared by other doctrines—that must be established. The intention is that this [nature] is difficult to establish because of the absence of any possibility of contradictory attributes.
This is expressed in the passage beginning with "as if through subordination" (*nyagbhāvenaiva*), etc. (Bhāṣya).
Or, as you [have stated] in the passage beginning with "by being subordinate" (*nyagbhāvena*) and so forth— following that,

because of the formulation of the injunction for a single sentence consisting of the various categories of the prescribed rules, your teaching is of such a nature that it constitutes a part of the ocean of omniscience, being composed of all the components of knowledge.
"Because of the absence of possibility, it is difficult to understand;
because of the impossibility of possibility, it is difficult to understand.
Regarding this, the Teacher says: "Is there anything at all to be established in this way? That has indeed already been established."
Regarding the phrase "because of the substantial meaning and the modal meaning" (*dravyārthaparyāyārtha*), etc.:
the "substantial meaning" (*dravyārtha*) is that which has substance as its object; or, it is that for which substance is the object;

or, it is "substantialist" (*dravyārthika*). That for which substance alone is the object is this "substantial meaning" (*dravyārtha*); the suffix *ṭhan* is used here in its own sense to form "substantialist" (*dravyārthika*).
Thus, the meaning of a synonym, or that which seeks the meaning of a synonym, [is used] for an object not present, according to Pāṇini-vārttika 5.2.81.
If it is argued that, because of this statement, there must be only one proponent for both the plaintiff and the defendant, we say no; for there is no absence of their presence.
Alternatively, "āstika" means one who holds the view that "it exists"; thus, a "dravyāstika" is one who holds the view that substance exists.

There is no duality between these two, yet there are infinite variations beginning with those [two] and ending with the infinite. This is because the number of *nayās* (standpoints) is equal to the range of the paths of speech and equal to the number of other philosophical systems (*parasamaya*).
In this regard, the reading "the Teacher says" does not exist in the Ya manuscripts;
[is it] *kimavabhā*?
Is it indeed thus in Pā, Ḍe, and Līṃ?
From this [root], the suffixes *ini* and *ṭhan* are applied.
(Pāṇini 3.2.115)

It is conceivable that there might also be a reading here as "the state of those two is duality; there are infinite conceptual constructions beginning with that," yet according to the literal text, it should be understood with the intended meaning that "the state of those two is not merely duality alone; what then? There are infinite conceptual constructions beginning with that. (Note: This is to be reconciled with the intention of the meaning, as the variant *anantānnāvikalpāḥ* appears in the Bhāṣya and Vivaraṇa, excluding other versions).
Regarding the phrase *anantātrā vikalpāḥ* (Bhāskara’s commentary):

it is possible that the reading here might also be *anantā atra vikalpāḥ*; and if such a possibility is entertained, the root text itself should also be considered as *dvitvādyanantavikalpopakḷpta*. However, in the reading *anantāntāḥ*, the word *antaḥ* carries the senses of "intrinsic nature," "proximity," "limit," and "certainty" or "destruction."

Following the *Haimakośa*, which states "also in the sense of a part," the word *anta* may be understood as denoting either "essential nature" (*svarūpa*) or "part" (*avayava*), and [the verse] should be reconciled accordingly:
"Since the systems (*nayāḥ*) are equal, as many as are the paths of speech, so many indeed are the assertions of the systems (*nayavādāḥ*)."
...vatiyā bhā...; likewise in what follows:
vayaṇapadhābhā...
"As many as there are modes of discourse (*nayavāda*), so many indeed are the systems of other doctrines (*parasamaya*). — *Sanmati-tarka-prakaraṇa* 3.47.
*Vādābhāsa*.

The rule of a single sentence [is that which governs] the various categories of objects, which are distinguished by the methods of the web of conceptual constructions fashioned in such a manner; because of its formulation, all cognitions produced by every perspective (naya) are its constituent parts.

The teaching (*śāsana*) is that which has become an integral part of the ocean of awakening (*avabodhasamudra*) through non-differentiation; it is so because, like the ocean, it is a mine of jewels consisting of profound and unshakeable categories of reality (*padārtha*) that are difficult to fathom. Being of such a nature, it consists of the collection and expansion of the breaking waves of the various stated methods (*nayāḥ*). Because it illuminates all categories of reality without exception, it is like a multitude of suns, having created light from which there is no room for darkness. Because of its brilliance, like a thousand suns, it is unsurpassable. It is the indivisible manifestation of the support [of reality]. (Note: *avayavibhūtam* is corrected from the manuscript variants *avayavibhūtam*, *avayavibhūtaṃ*, and *avayavibhūtaṃ*.)
This reading in the Bhāṣya also appears entirely correct.

Furthermore, regarding this reading, the analysis (*vigraha*) should be understood as: "that in which the ocean of awakening itself has become the whole (*avayavin*) through non-difference, [thus] that which has become the whole consisting of the ocean of awakening. It should be noted that there is no flaw even in the absence of the long vowel *ī* for the suffix *cvī*, because the intention is not to express the transformation of one thing into another (*abhūtatadbhāva*). [The compound continues: "illuminating the manifestation of the objects of experience... (*padārthāvadyotamadyotamādanekā...*) in the Bhāṣya.
Because it illuminates the darkness [of ignorance] regarding the understanding of the categories of existence (*padārtha*),
and because it does not illuminate non-existent categories— excluding the *Bhāṣya*, *Raṅ*, and *Hī* [manuscripts]—

the words of other teachers are unable to inspire even a doubt as to their truthfulness, since they propound a misconception of the categories determined by perception and inference, like the words of one who asserts that sound is inaudible.
Even worldly convention does not hold sway in that regard;
thus, the knowledge of correctness [in such cases] is based on delusion.
Apart from that, there are the teachers—Kapila, Vyāsa, Kaṇāda, Śauddhodani, Maskari, and others—and their words [are the source].
Objects determined by perception and inference— such as form and so forth, jars and so forth, and fire and so forth—
have been presented by them in a contrary manner;
through that presentation in a contrary manner, their state of non-correspondence has been established.

How is that so? First, regarding those things perceived simultaneously, such as the objects of specific sense organs like jars and the like: they are not merely color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth, because there is no apprehension of them without a substratum such as a jar. Furthermore, since a jar and the like are not apprehended without the mediation of the apprehension of any one of their attributes—such as color-form—and since the absence of the jar follows from the absence of those attributes, they are not merely substance (*dravya*). Likewise, regarding those things that do not occur simultaneously, such as a lump of clay (*piṇḍa*) and a jar (*śivaka*) and so forth: they are not merely modes (*paryāya*), because the lump, the jar, and so forth are not apprehended when the clay is not apprehended, and because the absence of the lump, the jar, and so forth follows from the absence of the clay.
Since even clay is not perceived and does not exist except when it abides in some specific state such as a *śivaka* (a lump of clay), it is not a substance [independently].

By this, the conventional usage of the sign (*liṅga*) and the signified (*liṅgin*), such as fire and smoke, is explained. Furthermore, in the determination of inference from effect, the particulars (*viśeṣa*) alone are not [the object], because they lack a foundation, like a sky-flower;
nor is the universal (*sāmānya*) alone [the object], because it is not specified, like a sky-flower.

Therefore, regarding those objects determined by perception and inference that are well-known to all the world, the propounding of contrary views by the followers of other teachings—such as "form and so forth are the pot," "the pot is form and so forth," or "form and so forth and the pot are the quality and the whole" (meaning that form and so forth are the qualities and the pot is the composite whole), or "neither form and so forth nor the pot exist"—is like the statement of one who asserts a sound that cannot be heard; since this is an example of speech contradicting the sensory perceptions well-known to all the world, it is also cited as an example of contradiction with inference and so forth.

The meaning is that since they are not even capable of generating doubt regarding their truthfulness, their lack of truth is indeed beyond doubt; this is what has been stated in the *Nirukta*. (Note: *tambhā॰* appears to be a scribal error for *tadbhā॰*; *pra॰* likely refers to *prathamam*).
In these cases, there might also be the reading "ity api" here;
[the variants] are "ghaṭadyovārādṛte bhā" and "ghaṭadyovārādane ya".

The passage beginning from "etaccihnāntargataḥ ॰vasthānamantareṇa" up to "na viśeṣāḥ" does not exist in the manuscripts of manuscript Ya; furthermore, the reading "liṅgaṃ liṅgaṃ liṅgivyavahāraḥ" is also found in the *Mānaviniścaya*.
In all the world,
forms and so forth, as well as the pot, are contradicted by inference.
Furthermore— starting from "even worldly transaction" (*laukikavyavahāra*) and so forth, up until "the basis of delusion" (*vyāmohopanibandhana*).

Even by investigators possessing superior intellect, who follow the unsurpassed consensus of the world, the task must be undertaken of refuting specific doctrines of other schools and establishing the true reality; otherwise, such investigation would be as indeterminate in its object as a legal proceeding devoid of witnesses.

Indeed, even the unlearned are seen to employ worldly conventions while apprehending objects such as jars as having a manifold nature—being eternal, non-eternal, inexpressible, and so forth—and yet there arise extremist doctrines (ekāntavāda) intent on denying this, asserting that "the jar is exclusively eternal," "exclusively non-eternal," or "exclusively inexpressible."

In this regard, the meaning is that in the remaining scriptures, the deliberation "this is correct" or "that is correct" is itself the basis and cause of delusion; for there is no room for such deliberation, and because of contradiction, it has been said: "Where even worldly convention does not hold firm, the cognition of correctness therein is based solely on delusion."
Thus, this complete verse has been extracted from the *Uttarādhyayana-sūtra-bṛhadvṛtti*, folio 2–1, and from the *Pravacanasāroddhāra-ṭīkā*, folio 2–1; [the readings] are:
॰śayayuddhibhi॰ in the first edition (pra. and kāye in the second edition (pra.).
Even though [it] has arisen as something whose meaning is currently being spoken,
it exists from the perspective of conventional usage.
From the perspective of conventional usage,
that which proceeds as if it were a negation is indeed a proof.
As for the word *niba*, it is [the same as] *vyāmoha*;
[the word] *śibikā* is [the same as] *praśama*;
and so on for what follows.

Even when a matter is determined through worldly perception and other means, there may arise a lack of conviction due to contradictions with the remaining teachings; however, the Jina’s teaching establishes faith in even those utterly imperceptible objects by means of a conviction secured through the accomplishment of the two valid cognitions (*pramāṇa*).

To establish this point—the subject matter which transcends the scope of the doctrines of other teachers and serves as a proof for categories of reality—there is this concise sūtra in verse titled *Nayacakra*, which contains but a tiny fragment of a meaning that had slipped away from the waves of the ocean of scriptures brought forth as a gift by his sons:
"Because it is distinct from the modes (*vṛtti*) of the positive, the restrictive, and the negating standpoints (*bhaṅga*), it is like meaningless speech."
The heterogeneity [of other teachings] is that any teaching other than the Jaina is false;

this is certain even by means of worldly perception and so forth, how much more so in the case of objects beyond the senses? Furthermore, there is a conviction born from the contradictions of other teachings: "Because of the contradictions found in other teachings, our conviction in this Jina-teaching is that 'this is the most excellent'"; thus, the establishment of one's own position follows simply from the weakness of the opposing positions.

Alternatively, he states that there is also an inference based on the excellence of one's own position, beginning with the words "established by the two means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇadvayasaṃsiddhi*).

For worldly investigators (*laukikaparīkṣaka*), the validity of perception and inference is established through non-discrepancy (*avisaṃvāda*) according to the aforementioned principle; thus, by means of both—perception and inference—the two types of objects to be ascertained are thoroughly established through the two [causes]: the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*) consisting of the presence or absence of prior logic, and the configuration (*saṃsthāna*) such as being round-bottomed. In the Jaina system, the cognition produced by these is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). And for this very reason, faith (*śraddhāna*) is firmly established even regarding objects that are extremely beyond the senses (*atyantaparokṣa*), such as the measurements of Mount Meru, the continent of Uttarakuru, the oceans, celestial chariots (*vimāna*), abodes, and the expanse of the hells. This is what is celebrated as "this triumphant [system] prevails," for otherwise there would be a lack of validity.

As it has been said: "If the apprehension of the perceptible is established, then the apprehension of the imperceptible may be established; if that [apprehension of the perceptible] is not established, there is an absolute absence of possibility, because [the latter] would lack corroboration by perception, like the words of a madman.
This applies even in the case of the ascertainment of [perception] and so forth.
By means of the two instruments of action,
thus [it is] accomplished;
for the sake of valid cognition.
By the passage beginning with "The apprehension of what is beyond the senses is established" and continuing through "if that is not established,
this meaning [is not established]," up to the verse-sūtra, the connection and purpose for the commencement of the treatise are stated.

The connection [of the words] is as follows: it consists merely of fragments of meaning that have fallen away and then coalesced from the waves of the ocean of the *Naya-prabhṛta* (the "Gift of the Nayas") originating from the ancient great ocean; it is not spoken according to one's own fancy (*svamanīṣikā*). The meaning is that this has indeed come down through a succession of authoritative traditions (*pramāṇāgama-paramparā*).

The purpose is to establish the categories of objects that fall within a domain transcending the doctrines of other teachers (*anyatīrthakara*), because it would otherwise be impossible to favor the disciples. Therefore, the treatise named *Nayacakra* is to be commenced, since without it, that [purpose] cannot be accomplished.

Lest the disciple’s intellect, distracted by the proliferation of topics, fall into confusion, this verse-sūtra of summarized meaning is presented—beginning with "Prescription (vidhi), restriction (niyama)," and so forth.
This is a means for establishing the falsity of other teachings;

however, by implication (*arthāpatti*), it is understood that the Jaina word is true because it is endowed with the application of prescriptions, restrictions, and the breaking [of both], just like the utterance of pure words.
fallen from the path of the waves;
[the text] *prajñānābhya* [is] *bhā*;
[the text] *nṛtatvāpratipā* [is] *pra*.

And the author of the *Nayacakra-vṛtti* himself will clarify this at the end of the work: "Thus, by means of this entire treatise, the following has been stated: Because it is distinct from the modes of operation consisting of injunction (*vidhi*), restriction (*niyama*), and negation (*bhaṅga*), any teaching other than the Jaina is false, like meaningless speech; only the Jaina teaching is true, because its nature consists of the modes of operation of injunction, restriction, and negation, just like the word 'is' (*bhavati*) or like a 'pot' (*ghaṭa*). (*Nayacakra-vṛtti*, p.
568) [In this context: "Injunction" (*vidhi*) is conduct (*ācāra*), stability (*sthiti*), activity (*pravṛtti*), and the boundary (*maryādā*)...
...the rule...

Their divisions are: 1. *vidhi* (affirmation), 2. *vidhividhi* (affirmation of affirmation), 3. *vidher vidhi-niyamam* (affirmation-cum-negation of affirmation), 4. *vidherniyamaḥ* (negation of affirmation), 5. *vidhi-niyamam* (affirmation-cum-negation), 6. *vidhi-niyamasya vidhiḥ* (affirmation of affirmation-cum-negation), 7. *vidhi-niyamasya vidhi-niyamam* (affirmation-cum-negation of affirmation-cum-negation), 8. *vidhi-niyamasya niyamaḥ* (negation of affirmation-cum-negation), 9. *niyamaḥ* (negation), 10. *niyamasya vidhiḥ* (affirmation of negation), 11. *niyamasya vidhiniyamam* (affirmation-cum-negation of negation), 12. *niyamasya niyamaḥ* (negation of negation).
Their function (*vṛtti*) consists of the mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of objects by directing them toward their own respective domains;
however, the function that establishes the truth of the Jaina doctrine is the function [itself].
Explaining this, the Master, so that others might not think the terms *vidhi* (injunction) and *niyama* (restriction) are non-worldly, utters their synonyms: "Injunction is conduct," and so forth.
It is called *vidhi* because it is enjoined (*vidhīyate*); thus, it is a noun derived from the action (*bhāvasādhana*), with the agent implied.
That which enjoins is the agent; thus, [the term] has the sense of a substance (*dravyārtha*).
Who brings it about? Clay brings about the states of the lump, the small clod, and so forth; for by means of that clay, the small clods and other forms are produced.

However, from the perspective of its defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), "production" (*vidhi*) refers to the substantial aspect (*dravyārtha*) in which the distinctions of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) are not intended, because this is observed in the world.
Conduct (*ācāra*) is movement according to the limits of what is to be undertaken; it is the non-abandonment of one's own nature while being indifferent to the nature of others.
This should be applied analogously to abiding (*sthiti*) and the other [aspects of existence].

From the perspective of the meaning of synonyms (*paryāyārtha*), however, it is restraint (*niyama*). Restraint is the curbing of excess; it is characterized by the quality of existing as mutually distinct states, such as form and so forth, or objects like a *śivaka* stone and so on. It is a specific state determined at every moment, whether occurring simultaneously or non-simultaneously, such that whatever comes to be is precisely that very thing.
The meaning of all these remaining synonymous terms should also be applied according to their respective syllables:
*dhana* (wealth), *vyāhṛta* (utterance), *pra* (prefix), *ādāna* (taking), and *maryādayāya* (by way of limit).
The conduct that is one's own nature, the conduct that is one's own nature,
the manifestation arising from form and so forth.

*Śivakādiṃ* refers to *śibikā* (palanquin) and so forth, while *ya* refers to *yāna* (vehicle) and so forth; the analysis (*bhaṅga*) of these two consists of the rules such as "the rule of the rule" (*vidhividhi*) and so on.

In this context, a positive injunction (*vidhi*) is one whose operation does not depend on the functions of differentiation or exclusion. For example, the injunction "cow" is a positive injunction; however, when directed toward someone who asserts a restriction based on distinctions such as "white" and so forth, it operates to establish non-difference: "What is this so-called distinction of 'white' that is separate from cowness?

The restriction (*niyama*) of a positive injunction is the establishment of what is overly pervasive within a specific instance; for one whose primary focus is the positive injunction, it is the establishment of that very [positive] aspect, as in: "Bring the white cow."
That which consists of both is "prescription-and-restriction" (*vidhi-niyama*).

"Prescription-and-restriction" (*vidhi-niyama*) means both prescription (*vidhi*) and restriction (*niyama*); it is a singular collective form (*dvandvaikavadbhāva*). Prescription and restriction are of equal status when combined; thus, everything is of a dual nature.
The remaining permutations (*bhaṅga*s) are to be explained accordingly, following this interpretation as appropriate.

In general, however, the injunction (*vidhi*) is the cause, the restriction (*niyama*) is the effect, and both together constitute the injunction-restriction (*vidhi-niyama*). The remaining [categories] are merely variations of these two;
they are portions (*bhāga*) of those two.

The passage beginning from "etaccihnāntargato vidhividhistu" and ending with "ubhayam" does not exist in the Bhāṣya manuscript (bhā॰ pratau); [it is] excluded (vyāvṛttaḥ) in the Ya manuscript. [The terms] "vidhi" and "niyama" are [defined as follows].

Having thus established the permutations (*bhaṅga*) of injunction (*vidhi*), restriction (*niyama*), and negation (*bhaṅga*), the author, now desiring to explain their function (*vṛtti*), says: "The function of those [permutations]—injunction, restriction, and negation—is as follows; its definition is:

'the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of objects by causing them to fall within their own respective domains,' meaning that by which objects are cultivated after being brought down into each of their own respective domains."

For instance: "It is thus and not otherwise"—as in, "It is eternal precisely because it is uncreated, like space," or "It is impermanent precisely because it is created, like a jar. As it has been stated: "Naya is the determination of one specific nature out of the manifold nature of a substance, by means of bringing forward a single aspect. Thus, through perception and inference—as previously [explained]—there occurs a function characterized by the twelve aforementioned alternatives, based on the material causes of the configurations such as being stationary or non-stationary, having a broad base, and so forth; otherwise, there would be no such function at all, as will be explained later.
And that [reality] is to be understood through narratives whose forms consist of the individual functions of injunction and so forth.

Among these, first, the function of injunction is as follows: an object is exactly as it is grasped in the world; for since the categories of universal and particular are untenable with respect to being objects of themselves or of others, the effort at discernment in the treatises is not based on them.
For universals and particulars would have to be either objects of themselves or objects of others.

In this regard, first concerning the universal (*sāmānya*): if it were the entirety of one thing, there would be a contradiction with its being a universal; if it were a universal, then it would not be that very reality. Therefore, he says: "But the function [of the word] is the operation for establishing the truth of the Jaina [view], characterized by the twelve intended modalities (*vikalpa*). The meaning is that the explanation of reality consists in its being a single form through the synthesis of those [modalities], just as the explanation of the reality of an object consists in its being a single form through the synthesis of various related properties such as Devadatta’s being a father or a son.

The word "otherwise" (*anyathā*) is used here for the sake of exclusive determination (*ekāntāvadhāraṇa*); because the individual nature of each [element] is not determined, they would indeed be non-existent, as will be stated later. Thus, this very treatise would proceed; however, since their principles are mutually contradictory, they are simply non-existent—this is the meaning. If one desires to ascertain the principle of existence (*vṛtti-tattva*), that must be understood through the explanation of the individual modes of existence, such as injunction (*vidhi*) and so forth; therefore, that explanation must be provided.
What is the reason? Because that [existence] is the effect of their collective operation.
Having established [the definition] through its refutation,
the characteristic is for the sake of attaining the perfection of the object.
It is qualified by the twelve intended alternatives through the two [factors] previously established, otherwise there would be non-occurrence, as will be stated hereafter.
And that [reality] is to be understood through the narrative of the individual functions of the positive injunction (*vidhi*) and so forth.

Among these, first, the function of the positive injunction is as follows: an object is exactly as it is grasped in common worldly experience; for, since neither generality (*sāmānya*) nor particularity (*viśeṣa*) is tenable with respect to being the object of both self and other, the effort at discernment in the treatises is not based on such [dualities].
For indeed, would generality and particularity have their own objects or the objects of another?

In that regard, first concerning the universal (*sāmānya*): if it is its own object because of being one and all-pervasive, there is a contradiction with the nature of a universal; if it is a universal, then there is the [logical] consequence of both exclusion and inclusion (*vṛttānuvṛtti*).

Desiring to explain this matter in detail within the context of the relationship between the reality and its exposition, he introduces it as follows: "In that regard, the operation of the injunction," and so forth.

Regarding these aforementioned modes of function, beginning with the mode of injunction (*vidhi-vṛtti*): first, the mode of injunction is such that the object is grasped by the world exactly as it is grasped by the world;

"grasping" (*grāha*) is so called because it is like a [fish] catcher. Just as a fish-catching crocodile (*grāha*) draws other living beings toward itself, so too the world draws everything toward its own intention.

The phrase "whatever is the world's grasping, exactly as the world grasps" (using *yathālokagrāham*) is a restrictive emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*) meaning that the object does not transcend the intention of the world.

However, for the non-Buddhist outsiders who pride themselves on being investigators, since the categories of generality and particularity are untenable with respect to both self and other objects, their effort at discernment in the treatises is merely a departure from worldly consensus.

The word *iti* here signifies a reason: because we shall establish this point, the object exists exactly as it is grasped by the world; therefore, the effort at discernment apart from worldly consensus is useless. (Note: *prāyodviveka* is corrected to *prāyo viveka* based on the context.)

If it is asked how that is so, it is said: For the universal and the particular must either have themselves as their own objects or another thing as their object. Would the universal of an entity such as a jar reside within the nature of that very jar, or within the nature of another entity such as a cloth? Considering that there is a fault for the Sāṅkhyas and others in all four of these alternatives, the worldly person, wishing to refute them, adopts his own position supported by reasoning: "In that regard, first, since the primary universal is the 'allness' of a single thing, if it has itself as its object, then everything would be one and one would be everything. Why? Because of the manifold nature of the cause."
As it has been said:
"The state of being a partisan; the state of being corrupted."

If everything is one, and everything is of the nature of everything, then why is everything not perceived in one place, and the one everywhere? It is said in reply: because of the binding constraints of space, time, form, and causal conditions, there is no simultaneous manifestation of the Self.

We consider this manifold variety of taste and other qualities in water and earth to be transformative (*pāriṇāmika*): [it occurs] in the case of a stationary being that has attained the state of a mobile being, such as a plant that has been consumed by a mobile being and has undergone transformation into the body of that mobile being; and also in the case of a mobile being that has attained the state of a stationary being, having been consumed by a stationary being and transformed into its nature; likewise, in the case of a stationary being remaining stationary or a mobile being remaining mobile.
Therefore, everything consists of everything, through this manifold variety of taste and other qualities.
The similarity of taste and so forth, as it is conventionally designated,

is not the self, because a universal has multiple objects [as its referents]; if, on the other hand, it were the self, then it would not be a universal, because the self is a single entity— just like the case of an army and an elephant.
Now, it might be argued: "The self (ātman) itself is the universal;
the self of the jar and so forth is existence (sattva) and the like, for that is the effect of their aggregate.

Because one is everything and everything is one, the universal which is its own object resides within the self of the jar. Having thus presented the opponent's view, he states the refutation: "If this were so, there would be a contradiction of the universal (sāmānyavirodha)—that is, a contradiction of the universal, or a contradiction by means of the universal."

How so? It is said: if it were a universal (*sāmānya*), then it would not be the self (*ātman*), because a universal has multiple objects as its domain. Since a certain object becomes similar to another object by virtue of certain properties, a universal has multiple objects as its domain. Therefore, because a universal has multiple objects as its domain, it cannot be the own-nature (*svātmā*) of a real entity such as a jar, which is of a single form; for the self is one, whereas the universal is excluded from being a self and the self is excluded from being a universal. In the absence of a self, of what would it be the universal?

Now, if the self (*ātman*) is postulated so that this fault may not occur, even then there is no universal (*sāmānya*), because the self is a single entity; with what, then, could it have a universal? Thus, there is a contradiction between the self and a universal, for a universal is a state of being common (*samānabhāva*), as in the case of an "army" (*senā*) and an "elephant" (*hastin*). [The term] "army" demonstrates dependence upon multiple objects, as it is a collection of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry; whereas "elephant" demonstrates the state of being a single object. This is the nature of a universal entity.
Now, the phrase "it might be said" expresses the intention of the opponent who wishes to offer a rebuttal:
there would indeed be a contradiction if one were to admit a distinction between the self and its universality by asserting that "the self is its own [universal].

Although the distinction between owner and owned is established by the genitive case expressing separation (*vyatireka*), there is nonetheless no fault; for according to the principle of *vyapadeśivadbhāva* (treating a thing as if it were what it designates), we observe non-separative genitives such as "the head of Rāhu."
What then? We reply: here, however, the Self alone is the universal.
What is that? It is the existence (sattva) and so forth of the jar and other things, as it has been stated:

The internal distinctions consisting of effects—namely sound, touch, taste, form, and smell—which are established by the genitive case used in the sense of "intermixture," are merely the arrangement of the three [qualities]: pleasure, pain, and delusion.

Why? Because each set of five has a single common effect: for the five pleasant [objects]—sound, touch, taste, form, and smell—the effects are clarity, lightness, elation, attachment, exhilaration, and joy; for the five painful [objects], they are desiccation, burning, piercing, support, agitation, and aversion; and for the five deluding [objects], they are obstruction, depression, destruction, disgust, dejection, and heaviness.

Likewise, the eleven instruments consisting of the ear, skin, eye, tongue, nose, speech, hands, feet, anus, genitals, and mind, as well as the external distinctions belonging to the animal, human, and divine realms, are the effects of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, because their commonality (*samanvaya*) is observed.
Thus, earth and so forth, cows and so forth, and jars and so forth [are their effects];
therefore, *sattva* and the other *guṇas* are the essence (*ātman*) of the jar and the rest.
For that [self] is indeed the universal because it is the effect of the collection of those [particulars];
therefore, the self alone is the universal. Thus, there is no appearance of difference.
Regarding the reading *bhedāpastambho*,
it should be understood that although there may also be readings such as *bhedāpaṣṭambho*, *bhedāpastambho*, or *bhedāvaṣṭambho*,
we have adopted the former because the word *upaṣṭambha* or *upastambha* is observed to be used in almost all currently available texts that expound the Sāṃkhya doctrine.

It should be noted that in the *Ṭippaṇī* on the *Mudritanyāyakumudacandra*, on page 350, an alternative reading of "avaṣṭambha" is recorded in place of the word "upaṣṭambha" in the manuscripts *ba*, *ja*, *bhāṃ*, and *śra*. [The readings] are:
*tairyayona-bhā* and *tairyayauna-ya*.

Regarding the phrase *kāryasamanvaya* (in the Y and Bh commentaries), if the reading *kāryaṃ samanvayaḥ* is considered possible here, then it should be construed as follows: "And external diversities are the effect (*kārya*) of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, because of the observation of their pervasive presence (*samanvaya*)."

However, according to the reading of Ya, one should follow the preceding statement—that it is merely the arrangement (*sanniveśamātra*) of the three, namely pleasure, pain, and delusion—and construe it as follows: "And external differences are merely the arrangement of the three—pleasure, pain, and delusion—because we observe the persistence of the effects of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.
[The term *sāmānya* (generality) is used] because of its commonality (*sāmānyatvāt*).
This being the case, there would be a fragmentation of the self—the self would be pleasure, pleasure, and the collection of pleasure and so forth—because it would consist of those very things;
the same would apply to the remaining [qualities].
Consequently, the postulation of the transformation of the three *guṇas* as the cause [of the world] would be rendered useless.

If it is argued that [the world] is eternally composed of the three-fold nature, then because of its oneness and eternity, there would be no distinction between illumination (*prakāśa*), activity (*pravṛtti*), and restriction (*niyama*); consequently, there would be no origination, and both [the three qualities and their effects] would be non-existent.

Furthermore, just as in the state of the *pradhāna*, the connection with contradictory properties such as plurality and unity, as well as the undifferentiated uniformity of the single form of the three *guṇas*, is maintained—[if this were so], then due to the eternal unity of the three *guṇas*, there could never be a state of plurality.

To this we reply: if this were so, there would be a division of the self (*ātman*), because pleasure and the rest would be a single effect of a collective whole; thus, the desired generality (*sāmānya*)—namely, that pleasure and the rest are one—would be divided.
If it is asked how that is so, it is said: pleasure and pleasure, as well as the collection of pleasure and the rest, is *sattva* (purity); *rajas* (passion) is pain; *tamas* (darkness) is delusion.
Since those three have attained a state of identity, they become one; thus, the nature of pleasure and its status as a collection are established.
Why? Because they have that as their essence (*tadātmatvāt*). For the collection has pleasure and the rest as its essence, and pleasure has the collection as its essence;
the same applies to the remaining two, namely pain and delusion, which are extended by analogy (*atidiśati*).

If it is argued that there is no fault because suffering (duḥkha) consists of both suffering and the collection [of causes] beginning with suffering, and delusion (moha) consists of both delusion and the collection beginning with delusion; then, the postulation of a cause consisting of the transformation of the three qualities (*guṇas*) would be futile. Since you admit the identity of the three—each of which has the same collective effect—that single entity is a particular state of equilibrium of those [qualities]. And since there is no deviation from that particular state of equilibrium, how could there be any inequality among the qualities? In the absence of inequality, how could there be the causal relationship of prior and subsequent effects for *prakṛti*, such as the intellect (*mahat*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), the gross elements (*bhūta*), and the sense organs (*indriya*)?
"Indeed, it has already been established" (bhāṣya); and what is attained here?

[The following] is the doubt: if it is argued that "it is eternally triadic," then because it possesses the three *guṇas* even in its state as *pradhāna*, it is eternally—that is, at all times—triadic in nature, consisting of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. Therefore, the causes for the inequality of the *guṇas* and their transformation are logically consistent; and even though it consists of a collection of pleasure and the other [feelings], the fault of a distinction between selves (*ātman*) does not exist.

This too is no answer, as it is merely a matter of words; nevertheless, it is even more so the case that there is no commencement [of creation], because of oneness and permanence—due to the absence of distinctions in manifestation, activity, and restriction.
This means that because of oneness, or because of permanence through oneness, there is always oneness.

The distinction between the effects of illumination (*prakāśa*), activity (*pravṛtti*), and restriction (*niyamana*) attributed by you to *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*—likened respectively to a stage director, the wind, and a stone used to moor a boat—is untenable. For instance: a stage director establishes himself and his actress through acts such as raising his own hand, which are of the nature of illumination; the wind establishes itself and others through the movement of leaves and so forth, which is the setting both self and other into motion; and the stone that moors a boat establishes itself and others through the act of restraining them. It is not logical for *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* to function in this way, because since they are eternal and unitary at all times, there is an absence of plurality; consequently, there is no commencement of activity, as the qualities (*guṇas*) would, like in the state of primordial matter (*pradhāna*), never initiate any effect due to their lack of functional operation.

And there is the eradication of inequality; because of the absence of an undertaking, there is the non-existence of both—the cause and the state of being an effect—or alternatively, of the self and the universal. What would be the cause of pleasure and so forth, as well as their aggregate, namely the *pradhāna*? For if one of the two is not established, the other is not established either.
If it is asked, "How is that cultivated?", it is said: "Just as in the state of Pradhāna," and so forth, up to "by transcending triadness, unity, and so on.

The phrase "triadness, unity, and so on" refers back to what was previously mentioned; just as triadness and unity are held to be contradictory properties (*viruddha-dharmau*), so too are the part and the whole, the other and the non-other, the self and the non-self, the all and the non-all, and so forth—the inclusion of "and so on" (*ādi*) indicating the transcendence of subtlety, grossness, and the rest. Thus, in sound and the other [objects], there is both a single nature inseparable from the three qualities (*triguṇa*) and a connection with contradictory properties, because they are composed of those [qualities].

Furthermore, because everything would exist [simultaneously], there would be an absence of the restriction between cause and effect; since things would be mere chance, there would be a loss of the purpose of human effort as it has been accepted.

Moreover, because the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*) are related, if one is admitted, the other must necessarily be expected; thus, if the universal is admitted, one falls into the position of [the opponent's] restrictive view.
Even in the case of being the object of another, it is not a universal, because it does not abide in common.
What is the reason? Because it is not determined that substance (*dravya*) and the other categories are the sole cause;
therefore, by implication, the phrase "and gross" (*sthūlaṃ ca*) and so forth must be supplied.
This is the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

"Similarity always exists because of the unity of the three qualities"—this means that, just as in that case [of the Pradhāna], there is no deviation from its own essential nature consisting of the triad and the one; thus, while there is a connection with contradictory properties, the state of being a single form of the three inseparable qualities is intended. This is the description of the Pradhāna itself as the illustrative example.

"Likewise with sound and the rest" is the application (*upanaya*) to the subject of the illustration. The properties of being composed of the three *guṇas* without distinction and having a single nature, as well as the connection with contradictory attributes, must be attributed to the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) such as sound, to their effects—the gross elements (*bhūta*) such as space which possess an increase of one *guṇa* each, to their modifications such as cows and jars, and to the eleven organs such as the ear.
Why? Because they consist of that; for they are composed of the *guṇas* such as *sattva*.

Furthermore, because everything would exist [simultaneously], as in the state of primordial matter (*pradhāna*), there would be no restriction such that a specific thread or the like is the cause of a specific cloth or the like, nor that one is the effect of the other, nor that one is the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the other the object of knowledge (*prameya*). Consequently, activity everywhere would result in being purely accidental. Since it would be mere chance, there would be no fixed order of causes and effects, such as primordial matter, the Great Principle (*mahat*), and the ego-principle (*ahaṅkāra*).
And thus, because it is mere chance, there would be a loss of the purpose of the effort exerted for the sake of the goals of the person (*puruṣārtha*) as they have been accepted.

The *puruṣa* is of the nature of consciousness (*caitanya*). Its purpose (*artha*) is twofold: beginning with the perception of sound and so forth, and ending with the perception of the distinction between the *guṇas* and the *puruṣa*. Having accomplished that, [the *pradhāna*] ceases; thus, the effort of the *pradhāna* is for the sake of that *puruṣārtha*. The "purpose" (*artha*) of that effort is its motive. Since that [effort] may cease by chance, when it has ceased, there is also the cessation of the purpose of the scripture and the effort toward the thorough knowledge of the threefold conjunction of *pradhāna* and *puruṣa*. (Sarvabhāṣya)
Because it is necessarily [the object of] conventional usage, because it is the state of being a thing, because it is the state of being an entity, because it is the state of being reality.
The non-existence [of one] is the non-commencement of that;

and two contradictory properties (dharma) exist through the transgression of [their respective] natures and so forth. Likewise, in the case of sound and other objects, there is the state of being of a single nature inseparable from the three qualities (triguṇa), as well as the connection with contradictory properties, because they are composed of those [qualities].

Furthermore, because everything would exist [simultaneously], there would be an absence of the fixed relationship between cause and effect; since things would be mere accidents, there would be a loss of the purpose of human effort as it is conventionally accepted.

Moreover, because the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*) are related, if one of them is admitted, the other must necessarily be accepted; thus, if the universal is admitted, one falls into the position of determinism (*niyamapakṣa*).
Even if it were held that they occupy different domains, it would not be a universal, because they do not coexist in the same state.

What is the reason? Because it is not determined that substance and the other categories have either one [of these] as their cause, just as in the case of the transcendence of the principles such as triadness and oneness. (Praśastapādabhāṣya)

"Description alone [occurs] in the case of sound and so forth," thus [it is said]; in the case of jars and so forth, there are eleven [categories], beginning with the word "pada. (Pra. p. 10, Bhāṣya p. 10, Yaśomitra p. 10)
Whether it be the foot-soldiers and so forth,
the cause, or the effect,
it is a shrine (caitya).

"The activity of Pradhāna proceeds for the sake of the Puruṣa, and that purpose of the Puruṣa is twofold: beginning with the perception of sound and so forth, and ending with the perception of the distinction between the Guṇas and the Puruṣa" (Sāṅkhyakārikā, Māṭharavṛtti, p. 79).

In this context, the reading *tat kṛtvā* should be reconciled with the intention that the neuter gender is used in a general sense; otherwise, one would have to say *taṃ kṛtvā*. Furthermore, because the general and the particular are related to one another—and so on, up to the consequence of falling into the position of a restrictive rule—the general and the particular are mutually related, like "beginning" and "end," or like "father" and "son."

In that case, if a universal (*sāmānya*) is admitted, then because a universal necessarily depends upon particulars (*viśeṣa*), the particular must also be admitted—just as when fatherhood is admitted, sonship must also be admitted; and conversely, when a particular is admitted, the universal must be admitted just like it. Therefore, by force of logic, there is not only the consequence of adopting the position of the particular, but also the consequence of adopting the position of the restriction (*niyama*). By the word "also" (*api*), the previously mentioned faults are likewise implied.

Thus, first, the faults regarding the generality (*sāmānya*) having its own [particular] as its object have been stated; now the faults regarding the particular (*viśeṣa*) having the generality as its object will be stated.
Because it does not exist as something common even when there is a relation to another object, it is a non-universal (*asāmānya*);

for even among those things called "secondary universals," there is no commonality in their similar occurrence and exclusion. In that regard, substance (*dravya*)—characterized by the nature of being (*bhavana*)—is pervasive, functioning through clay, becoming, and ultimate forms such as color and shape, as well as through the successive states of a lump of clay and so forth, both simultaneously and non-simultaneously.
