Because the characteristics desired by others—those intended for other objects—are impossible, whereas the possibility of a universal (*sāmānya*) characterized by the common occurrence of what is desired by oneself exists, the worldly person will later conclude that what belongs to another is indeed not a universal. Having established that premise, he says: "It is a non-universal because it does not abide in what is not similar.

Furthermore, this refers to the objects of substance, space, time, and state; for those substances and so forth, which are desired by others as belonging to an entity such as a jar, are called "similar" in relation to that other existence, but not in relation to itself; thus, they have other objects as their domain.

But what is the reason that this [cause] is not common? To this he says: "Because no single one among them is determined to be the cause. That is to say, it is not determined that substance alone, space alone, time alone, or mode alone is the cause. If that were so, one might instead say "because of being the cause of only one [of these]. However, the suffixes *ḍatara* and *ḍatama* do not apply here. Why? Because Pāṇini 5.3.92 states: "The suffix *ḍatara* is used after *anya*, *kim*, *yat*, and *tad* when selecting one out of two; the suffix *ḍatama* is used when selecting one from many, or when asking about a genus. Since there are more than two [factors], the suffix *ḍatama* would be required, which is not the case here. Thus, the term *asāmānya* (uncommon) is used. Furthermore, it is not uncommon because it is not shared by other substances; nor is it uncommon because it is not shared by other modes (*bhāva*). This is because it is established that all four—substance, space, time, and mode—are causes. Therefore, it is called "uncommon" (*asāmānya*) because it is not shared with others, and yet it is not uncommon because it is not excluded from others. It is like the word *asādhāraṇa*. For example, although the word *asādhāraṇa* is formed with the suffix *anaṅ* and thus denotes something that is not shared, it is nevertheless not uncommon because it is not shared with other words such as *sādhāraṇa*. 3.91–92: Since the word *eka* is not listed [in this context] here, then in that case, the suffix *tarap* is used in the sense of excellence (*atiśāyika*).

For rivalry occurs among those with equal qualities; if it is argued that this is not the case here because of the absence of expressed qualities, we reply that there will certainly be a distinction based on the quality of being the cause (*kāraṇatva*).

If it is then argued that the suffix *-tama* [should be used] for such a case, we reply that there is no fault, as the suffix *-tarap* is used when one intends to express the excellence between two things (Pāṇini 5.3.57).
Alternatively, according to the rule *ekācca prācām* (Pāṇini 5.3.94) [the suffix *-tama* may be applied].
Thus, regarding the inquiry into genus (*jāti*), there is no fault in the rule that the suffix *-atar-* occurs [in interrogative compounds].

If it is asked, "By whom has it been determined that substance (*dravya*) and the other categories are the cause of either one [of the two]?"—it is said: by worldly people who prioritize the *vyavahāra-naya* (the conventional standpoint), and that [standpoint] is indeed just one part of the *ārhatas* (Jainas) system.

Furthermore, it is not as the authors of the treatises maintain— that they determine that only the universal, or only the particular, or any one among substance and so forth, is the cause or the effect; for even "substance," characterized by the process of becoming (*bhavana*), pervades all things— whether occurring simultaneously or non-simultaneously, whether in the form of clay or the ultimate reality of becoming, or in the form of a jar or a small lump— and extends to the color and other qualities residing in the *śivaka* (clay mold) and so forth, encompassing the objects of the highest [cognition] as desired by others.
According to the reading *parakīyasāmānyaṃ pra° ṣyate ya*, however, it will be concluded as follows.
It should be construed as follows: "Having established that [point] as being worldly, he says...
[The variants are: *mānādasthānādasāmānya* (Ya), *mānādasāmānya* (Bhā).
In this context, if the reading were *tadapekṣya* rather than *nātmānameva* in order to establish the connection, it would be excellent; however,
they do not take this [reading],
except for the editions of Bhāskara, Nirdhāra, Bhāskara-raṅga, and Hīra.
In the phrase *ina-ekaṃśa-bhāḥ*,
*ekaṃśa* [is read as] *ya-śāyikaḥ* according to the Bhāṣya.
Without that entity,
there is no effect or object of cognition.

"How is it determined whether the body is indeed [the cause], or rather whether substance (*dravya*) and so forth are the causes? It is said: first, regarding substance (*dravya*), it will be connected [in the text] as 'substance also,' characterized by existence (*bhavana*) and all-pervasive (*vyāpin*);
from the word 'also' (*api*), it follows that the field (*kṣetra*) is likewise."

Since it is stated in the established doctrine of all systems (*sarvatantrasiddhānta*) regarding grammar that "the term *bhavya* [is used] in the sense of a substance" (Pāṇini 5.3.104), a *dravya* is that which is called *bhavya*, meaning it is fit for becoming (*bhavana-yogya*).

It is called *dru* because it flows (*dravati*), will flow (*droṣyati*), or has flowed (*dudrāva*). A substance (*dravya*) is a modification or a part of that which flows. [The roots] *du* and *dru* signify "motion" (Pāṇini Dhātupāṭha 944–945). Because it is always characterized by motion, it is indeed of the nature of transformation;
for a substance is not, as the Pātañjala Mahābhāṣya (5.1) states, a mere collection of qualities (*guṇasandrāva*).
Or alternatively, the definition of substance is: "That which possesses action, possesses quality, and is an inherent cause" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.15).

If it is asked, "How does it come to be?"—it is as follows: *bheda* means that which is divided (*bhidyate*). That which has the nature of coming into being through division, or whose property is to exist well [through division], is called *bhedabhāvinī*, meaning "that which comes into being through division," referring to clay. The coming into being of that [clay] is *bhedabhāvimṛdbhavana*. That itself is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). What is it? It is form (*rūpa*) and so forth, and the small lumps (*śivaka*) and so forth. Furthermore, these, according to their respective order, are simultaneously and non-simultaneously the form, small lump, and so forth, which constitute the ultimate reality of the coming into being of clay through division; this is a compound of apposition (*samānādhikaraṇasamāsa*).

Furthermore, what is this "functioning" (*vṛtti*) of it [the substance], or its functioning within those [qualities]? This is the functioning of earth, becoming, ultimate reality, form, and so forth, as well as the jar and other objects, occurring both simultaneously and non-simultaneously.
What is that? It is *dravya* (substance).

It is called "pervasive" (*vyāpi*) because it pervades. The field (*kṣetra*) also has as its own nature the functioning of universal movement and abiding; it consists of the collective state of individual entities and objects. It is pervasive—comprising earth and jars established through the common location of form and so forth, and the neck and so forth—and it is the vibration of the states of form, the jar, and so forth, which occur simultaneously and non-simultaneously for the existent substance of the universe.
Nowhere does anything fail to arise;

just as forms, pillars, and so forth are merely the manifestation (*bhavana*) of clay, so too earth and the other elements existing simultaneously are, in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), merely the manifestation of substance (*dravya*).
Likewise, earth consists of stones, clods of mud, and so on; water consists of snow, hailstones, and so on; and fire consists of its own subdivisions such as flames, and so forth.

The sequence of rice—seed, sprout, leaf, stalk, stem, flower, fruit, awn, grain, and husk—and so forth, which occurs non-simultaneously, is the ultimate reality; thus, everything is merely the becoming of substance (*dravya*). Regarding the reading "dravyam atra tava" (the substance is yours here), this appears to be correct. Accordingly, the intention of the questioner seems to be: "In your position, how then is the causality of substance and so forth determined? In that regard, substance also... [is the cause].
And [it is] non-existence in a substance;
and that which is a substance,
indeed, as it is.

Ethical conduct (*śīla*) is its primordial field, the very nature of the dwelling and subsistence in all states of existence. It consists of the collective arrangement of the meaning of each individual entity, established through the unified state of form and so forth, and the neck and so forth. It pervades the entire universe—including earth, jars, and the like—which is manifested by the fluctuations of existing substances such as form and the like, whether they arise simultaneously or sequentially, from the subtle atom (*śivaka*) onwards.
It is the supreme, primordial [reality] of that which is to be transcended.
The substance is the state of becoming;
on the earth, there is stone and palm-leaf.
They become [such]— thus he says that "bhavya" means "substance" (dravya).

And regarding the word *bhavya*, it denotes that which is to be attained (*prāpya*), as stated in Pāṇini’s Dhātupāṭha (1845): "The root *bhū* is used in the ātmanepada sense in the meaning of 'attaining' (*prāpti*)."
"Thus, in this way, substances are either attained or they attain"— this is stated in the *Tattvārthabhāṣya* (1.1.5).
The root *bhū* is used in the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) when meaning "to obtain. According to some, the middle voice occurs only in conjunction with the causative suffix (*ṇic*), as in *bhāvayate*;
otherwise, it is *bhavati*.

—Pāṇini’s *Siddhāntakaumudī*: The field (*kṣetra*) is also established through the very process of the grammatical system; from the root *kṣi* in the sense of "dwelling" and "going" (Dhātupāṭha 1407), the true nature of all things as consisting of going and dwelling is established. "Going" (*gati*) means pervasion (*vyāpti*).

Since the abiding and persistence of all entities proceed by way of providing support for their attainment and maintenance, that which constitutes their mode of existence is their own essential nature;
for a field is indeed a specific arrangement of spatial locations (*pradeśa*).

It has the nature of being a collective assembly of the objects of each individual entity; that is to say, its essence (*ātman*)—its own fundamental reality—is the primary principle (*pradhāna*) existing as a unified state in the form of the broad base and so forth for each individual object such as a jar or a cloth. Why is this so? Because in the absence of the field (*kṣetra*), that [essence] does not exist, and because it exists only through the favor of the field. This is established respectively by the color-forms and so forth, and by the jars and so forth, which are determined by their existence as a single movement toward the neck and other parts.
According to their respective systems, for the Vaiśeṣikas and others, earth possesses color, taste,
smell, and touch (VS 2.1.1), or earth consists of sound, touch, color, taste, and smell, or it is characterized by solidity.

In this way, the pot (*ghaṭa*) too is a composite whole (*avayavin*), a mere collection of qualities (*guṇasamudayamātra*), or a conceptual existence (*prajñaptisat*); it is merely a mental construction.

However, according to the worldly perspective (*lokanaya*), it is indeed those very parts—form, neck, and so forth—which, being of a single nature as form and so on, and as neck and so on, situated in such and such a manner, establish the earth and so forth, as well as the pots and so forth. In that regard, what is the "earth-nature" (*pṛthivītva*) of the earth other than the fact that form and so forth are situated in a single state? Or what is the "pot-nature" (*ghaṭatva*) of the pot other than the fact that the neck and so forth are situated in a single state? Therefore, its own essence (*svatattva*) consists in the mode of abiding within all states of being.
"Pervading the universe," and so forth, up to "of the vibration":

it means that [the subject] simultaneously pervades the entire universe—which consists of existing substances—and the various manifestations of the vibration of forms, both those occurring simultaneously and those occurring sequentially, such as the states of Śiva, Śivaka, and so on, as well as the earth, water, and the like, and the collection of transformations such as jars and cloths. (From the *Prakriyā*).
It should be understood that in ancient scripts, the syllable *kakkha* was written as *rakka*; [the word] *niṣṭhuraḥ* means hard, harsh, cruel, rough, or coarse.
Firm, hard, rigid, tough...
—Thus, in the *Abhidhānacintāmaṇi*, verses 6.22–23:
"And what, O Great King, is the internal earth element? Whatever in this body is internal, solid, of a harsh nature, and appropriated."
What, then, is that? It is as follows: hair, body hair, nails, teeth, and so forth—this is called the internal earth element.

And what, O Great King, is the external earth element? Whatever is external, characterized by hardness, having the nature of solidity, and not appropriated (by consciousness)—this is called the external earth element. —Thus in the *Śikṣāsamuccaya*, p. 245.
In the *Satva* [tradition], there is the reading "ta eva" (those very ones); furthermore, in this [context], there may also be the reading "paṭādīṃśca bhāve."
O you who pervade all,
who are beyond duality, whose nature is light,
you who are the pervasive one.

Time (*kāla*) also has a function defined by entities whose own nature is both simultaneous and non-simultaneous time: it functions simultaneously with respect to the various categories (*astikāya*) such as earth and so forth, which have been described in their many divisions; yet it functions non-simultaneously with respect to the processes of bringing about rice-grains, boiled rice, and so on, which are accomplished by water through the acts of taking up, holding, ripening, and discarding.

Furthermore, even substances (*dravya*) and the like possess states that arise both simultaneously and non-simultaneously, such as color-form (*rūpa*) and the like, or the stages of a clay mold (*śivaka*), and so forth; it is exactly as previously stated.
"Time also," and so forth:
time also is a universal whose object is another;
indeed, time is action characterized by transformation (*pariṇāma*), for "time" (*kāla*) is derived from "reckoning" (*kalana*), or it is a collection of parts (*kalā*).
For example: "He sits for a month" (*māsam āste*) or "He sits while the cows are being milked" (*godoham āste*).
This refers to "subsistence" (*vartanam*) or "coming into being" (*bhavanam*), which are synonyms; or rather, it is the substance (*dravya*) characterized by subsistence (*vartanā-lakṣaṇa*).

And that [substance] has a mode of existence (*vṛtti*) defined by entities whose own-nature consists of time—both simultaneous and non-simultaneous—just like the aforementioned transformations (*pariṇati*) such as color-form (*rūpa*) and the clay figurine (*śivaka*), or like the earth produced from the water of the astikāyas, and the rice-grains, boiled rice, and so forth, which will be described later.

For example—beginning with "simultaneous occurrence is described as having many divisions," and so forth, up to "simultaneous occurrence is described according to the systems of the Sāṃkhyas and others"—those very *astikāyas* (existents), namely *dharma*, *adharma*, *ākāśa*, *pudgala*, and *jīva*, along with their subdivisions; or else, the *pṛthivī* (earth) and so forth are themselves the *astikāyas*, meaning existing bodies (*vidyamānakāya*). That wherein they exist simultaneously is simultaneous occurrence (*yugapadvṛtti*), which is time (*kāla*). And wherein there is non-simultaneous occurrence (*ayugapadvṛtti*) in activities such as taking up (*ādāna*), supporting (*dhāraṇa*), and so forth, up to the activity of cessation (*nirvṛtti*), [that is also time].
As it has been said: "Three months are for taking up, three months are for maintaining, three months are for ripening, and three months are for relinquishing."
The eastern, northern, and northeastern winds are providers [of moisture], while the remaining ones are desiccators.

Here too, as in the case of the sun’s heat—which absorbs, retains, ripens, and releases water—there is the taking up, retention, ripening, and release of the aggregate of smoke, light, water, and wind in the form of clouds; or alternatively, it is like the transformation of matter (*pudgala*) through natural decay (*visrasā*), such as its becoming cloud-like. Because matter is inseparable from them, even for divine beings and those with transformation-bodies (*vaikriya*), there is taking up through [the wind's] grasping, retention through holding, ripening through maturation, and release through emission.

The effects of released water consist of the liquefaction of the earth, the sprouting of trees, shrubs, and herbs, the growth of flowers and fruits, the nourishment of the bodies of living beings, and so forth;

furthermore, other effects include food, strength, physical vigor, health, and the production of jars, cloths, and the like—all such productions are effects. The non-simultaneous occurrence of these effects within their respective processes is time itself, because those entities are produced through its support.

The reading found in all manuscripts is *kālanaṃ kālaḥ kālasamūho vā pra° ṇatavadya° vrīhinaraudanādivadvā*; however, because the word *nara* (man) is irrelevant here, and because this section concerns the investigation of the true nature of entities existing simultaneously and those existing non-simultaneously— specifically intending to refer to the simultaneously occurring astikāyas such as earth (*pṛthivī*) and so forth, as well as the non-simultaneously occurring rice-grains, boiled rice, and so forth— we have conjectured the reading to be *vrīhikaṇaudanādivadvā*.

Alternatively, since the effects of released water— such as the softening of the earth, the sprouting of trees and herbs, the growth of flowers and fruits, and the nourishment of the bodies of living beings— are to be explained immediately hereafter, one should note that the reading here may also be "like the sprouting of rice and so forth," in accordance with that. Regarding the passage beginning with "color" (varṇa),
etc., the first three months are for taking up [the water], while the next three months are for retaining it.
Three months are for digestion; three months are for excretion;
[these] are for excretion, [these] are for giving away.
In accordance with this, the reading *ihāntyāḥ* might also be possible here;

however, in this reading, the meaning should be understood as follows: "in these four [categories], beginning with *ādānīya*, the final ones are the *visarjanas*, while the preceding, the succeeding, and both the preceding and succeeding are the *vāyavas*.
Furthermore, the reading *ihāpyāḥ* should also be considered here.
And furthermore, [the text] beginning with "pra-sthā-vādīni" and "pra-tyayaṃ cety-ādi-bhāṣyam."
"Only these three," and so forth;

as for that which is now called "existence" (bhāva), it has already been mentioned, since existence was previously defined as "the state of being" (bhavana) within the categories of substance and the rest.
Demonstrating this, he says: "But substance and so forth... and so on;
for it has been stated [in the *Tattvārthasūtra*]: "Substance possesses qualities and modes" (5.38).

Qualities (*guṇas*) are [attributes] such as color (*rūpa*) and so forth; modes (*paryāyas*) are [states] such as the "pot-sherd" (*śivaka*) and so forth. These exist either simultaneously or non-simultaneously.

These very states (*bhāvas*), as well as space (*kṣetra*) and time (*kāla*), are indeed substance (*dravya*); or rather, they are simply existence (*bhāva*) because of their commonality in the act of being (*bhavana*).

Therefore, those [categories] beginning with substance cannot exist by excluding the states that occur simultaneously or non-simultaneously, because they themselves possess the nature of being. Otherwise, substances and the rest would fall into the state of non-existence, like the son of a barren woman.
Existence (*bhāva*) also pervades the reality of all things;

therefore, even one who holds the position that the universal (*sāmānya*) is the essence of objects such as jars must necessarily depend upon these [categories], since they are of such a nature according to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). How much more so for one who maintains the position of the primary universal whose object is "the other" (*para*)? For, as has been stated, the commonality of the "other" manifests in various ways through direct perception itself, insofar as it exists as something similar to another in some respect. Thus, he extends the argument by analogy.
"Because they exist in that way"—this very existence functions as the cause;

otherwise, if there were an absence of the capacity for existence, substances (*dravya*) and the rest would fall into non-existence like the son of a barren woman. Since substances and the rest do not exist because they are devoid of existence, like the son of a barren woman—as indicated by the ablative case—[the author] states by way of contrast that existence is their cause through the method of *āvīta*.

And the non-existence of substances and so forth is not accepted; rather, these possess existence itself, and existence is that which is connected with the act of being (*bhavana*), as in the case of a jar;
therefore, substances and so forth are connected with the act of being.
Since existence (*bhāva*) pervades substances and so forth, it is said: "Existence also pervades the reality of all things. Thus, [it follows that] time and space are indeed substance (*dravya*).
Because they exist; otherwise, substances and the like would fall into non-existence, like the son of a barren woman.
Existence (*bhāva*), moreover, pervades the reality of all things.

Therefore, even one who holds the position that the universal is the very essence of objects such as jars must necessarily depend upon these [categories], since they exist as such through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). How much more so for one who maintains the position of the primary universal whose object is "the other" (*para*)? For, through direct perception itself, the "other" which is common [to many] exists in various ways; it exists as something common with others.
Because of their cultivation, [there is] their cultivation;
[the term] "son of a barren woman" etc. [is used].
Having stated "by that which possesses a cause" and "the state," [it says] "therefore these," and so forth, up to "are dependent."

By the force of the arguments established here, the categories beginning with substance (*dravya*) and ending with existence (*bhāva*), being primarily characterized by their process of becoming, are undeniable. Therefore, even by one who maintains the position that the universal (*sāmānya*) constitutes the very essence of objects such as a jar—meaning, by you who assert a universal within your own domain—the aforementioned [categories] must necessarily be accepted; the meaning is that you must seek out the essential core.
Why? Because they possess that nature [of becoming] through direct perception itself.
Indeed, even according to the method described, a commonality consisting in the occurrence of a single form—such as "substance" and so forth—is clearly perceived;

how much more so, then, for one who maintains the position of a primary universal (*mukhya-sāmānya*) directed toward external objects? Because substances and the like, though mutually distinct, possess a common mode of being, there exists a primary universal. Furthermore, worldly people are proponents of such a universal, because they follow the conventional standpoint (*vyavahāra-naya*);
it is not, however, like the similarity, exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), or the principle of reality (*tattva*) asserted by the Sāṅkhyas and others, which contradicts valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

And that [universal] ought to be metaphorical rather than primary, because in the world, universals (*sāmānya*) are understood through similarity and recurrence; thus, the definition of a universal as you describe it is not observed, whereas the worldly universal we accept is indeed observed. Therefore, he says: "Because a commonality regarding other objects occurs in such and such a way through direct perception (*pratyakṣataḥ*)," meaning that by various modes—in view of substance, space, time, and state—the commonality of entities occurring simultaneously or non-simultaneously, such as color-form and a small jar, occurs.

By means of grammar, which is established by the consensus of all systems and follows worldly usage, he states the etymological derivation (*nirukti*) that accords with reality: "It becomes equal to the other" (*pareṇa samānena bhūyate*). The meaning is "it becomes equal" (*samāno bhavati*).

"The state of being equal" (*samānabhāva*) is "universality" (*sāmānya*). That which all entities become is their "state of being" (*bhāva*); thus, the suffix *bhāva* is used in its own sense (*svārthika*).

Furthermore, here the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) characterized by the agent has the sense of an essential relation (*svabhāvasambandha*), as in the expression "the state of being of that" (*tasya bhāvaḥ*).
For example: "the body of a stone statue" (*śilāputrakasya śarīram*);
in this very manner, [expressions] such as "the beginning" (*anītyādi*) are intended to convey the predominance [of the primary referent].
And sounds, grasping,
and the objects of perception are to be understood as being dependent on conditions and devoid of intrinsic nature.
The world is indeed directly perceived as being of such a nature that it must not be reviled by Māra.
Now, one might object that, following the reading *sāṃkhyādīṣṭasādṛśyabhāvaḥ*,
there should also be a reading here as *sāṃkhyādīṣṭasādṛśyam*, since it will be stated immediately thereafter: "And because our desired [object], which is a worldly universal, is observed."
That [object] has been explained in the *Pramāṇaviniścaya* as being perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) alone.
*rūpāśivakādi pra*—
here, the reading *rūpaśivakādi* might also be possible;
this has been stated even by Niruktitattvādivādin.

And thus, for this entire world, there is a unity of qualification in various ways depending on substance and so forth, by virtue of both difference and relation—like a blossoming, fragrant blue lotus in autumn.

In that case, because there is an absence of any other similar object to be excluded (*apohya*), or of any identical reality (*tattva*) or commonality, the postulation of a universal (*sāmānya*) is untenable;
it is beset by the aforementioned defects, and due to the oneness of everything, it would result in the absurdity of everything being its own universal.

Having thus explained the general [principle], he now states the inference by way of a summary of its meaning: "And so," and so forth, up to "the unity of qualifiers" (*viśeṣaṇaikatā*). And so, having established that there is mutual differentiation and the attainment of oneness through mutual relation for this entire world, there occurs in each respective manner the unity of qualifiers with respect to substance, place, time, and state. Substance is qualified—distinguished—by place, time, and state; place and the others are qualified by substance; and likewise those [others] are qualified by one another.

Just as a finger is qualified—distinguished—by states occurring at different times, such as being curved or straight, by states occurring simultaneously, such as color and so forth, by location, and by other distinct substances, such that one says, "the finger is curved," "it is straight," "it exists in this part of space," "it is the index finger," "now," and so on; likewise, every single object, such as a jar or a cloth, is not unrelated to anything, but is qualified and distinguished in various ways through its particularity (*bheda*) and its relation (*sambandha*).

And the formal argument (*prayoga*) here is as follows: "The jar is related to its qualifiers such as substance and so forth, because, while being a distinct entity, it stands in a relation with them, like an autumn blue lotus that is blooming and fragrant.

In this example, "blooming," "closed," and so forth are qualifiers of the specific field (*kṣetra*); "fragrant" and "blue" and so forth are qualifiers of the states (*bhāva*) such as color and form which arise either simultaneously or successively; "autumn" is a qualifier of time (*kāla*);
and "lotus" is the substance (*dravya*). Even that [substance] is indeed a qualifier of those [other factors], because it serves to delimit them.
Through the expansion of that meaning,
because of the mutual distinction between the two,
there is mutual non-distinction.
It is possible that there is also a reading here: "distinguished by its state (bhāva), having become such through another place and other substances."
That which is distinguished by some particularity of thought is the state of non-difference from that.
The reading "due to the conjunction with specific substances and so forth,
[it is] autumn," which serves as a qualification of time, does not exist in the manuscripts of manuscript Ya.

Having thus established the absence of multiplicity and generality, he demonstrates that which was previously asserted: that for others, there is no generality because it does not abide in a common state even with respect to an external object. He shows this by stating: "In that case, since there is no similar other thing to be excluded, nor any common reality, the occurrence of a generality is untenable."

Thus, when the world—having been reduced to a state of mutual distinctness and unity—is nothing more than the singularity of a single jar, there is an absence of any other object (*arthāntara*). In this case, O learned one, from what source could there be a universal (*sāmānya*) as conceived by the modern Buddhists, which is defined as the exclusion of other objects (*arthāntarāpoha*)? Or, from what source could there be a universal defined as "similarity" (*sādṛśya*), based on the notion that "that which is seen as common is similar," and "the state of being similar is similarity"? For such a "similar thing" does not exist. Furthermore, from what source could there be "that-ness" (*tattva*)? "That-ness" (*tattva*) is the state of being that (*tasya bhāvaḥ*); its "that-ness" is *tattattva*. But that [universal] exists only in relation to distinct things, characterized by the persistence (*anuvṛtti*) through many common objects, such as existence (*sattva*), substantiality (*dravyatva*), quality-ness (*guṇatva*), and action-ness (*karmatva*).
The knowledge of joy (prītijñāna) is the cognition of the object of another (paraviṣayitā). Bhāṣya; Pratijñāna; Yā; Pra.
See page 14, line 6;
"sāmānyasya" [is the reading in] Bhāṣya; "parikliptam" [is the reading in] Bhāṣya.

Regarding the reading *asadṛśasyātasya* enclosed in the commentary: in this reading, one should understand the form *atasya* as a genitive case ending derived from forming a negative compound (*nañ-tatpuruṣa*)— namely, *na saḥ asau*— meaning "of that which is not like it" (i.e., different from it).
And thus, following the reading in the Bhāṣya, "because of the absence of another similar [entity]," the meaning is understood as follows:
it might be thought that the collection of those [individuals], precisely because they are mutually distinct yet identical, constitutes a universal (sāmānya) whose object is something external;

however, this is incorrect, and therefore he says: "Because of being a single 'all-ness' (sarvatva) bound by the aforementioned defects, there would either be the consequence of it being its own universal."

Regarding what was stated previously—that [the whole] is a universal because it is the effect of that collection—this being so, there would be a difference in essence (*ātmabheda*): pleasure and pleasure, as well as the aggregate of pleasure and so forth, would be distinct because they possess those respective essences.
Likewise for the remaining [categories]. Or, due to the difference in their state as aggregates, all objects would indeed be absolutely distinct, like a jar and a cloth;
for instance, a jar arises from atoms and so forth, or shards arise from a jar.
Alternatively, because all things are in a state of constant flux and lack stability, there is no simultaneous stabilization of objects such that their similarity could be determined.

Furthermore, without the attainment of form and the cognition of liberation, the establishment of distinct objects would be like [the case of] a staff [merely indicating a person]; and so on, up to the point that since both the universal and the particular are related to that [object], the acceptance of either one alone results in the fallacy of partiality regarding the rule.

The word "or" (*vā*) in the phrase "or the attainment of the generality of its own object" has the sense of an alternative; it is intended to demonstrate all the preceding and subsequent alternatives stated regarding the position of its own generality (*svasāmānya*). The entire collection of alternatives, such as "substance and substance," or "the aggregate of substance and so forth," should be applied here as well, according to what is possible; see page 12, line 3:
*kāyatvasāmānyasya*.
The state of being a body (kāyatva) is either identity or,
due to the difference in their composite state and persistence, it is indeed an absolute difference like that between a jar and a cloth;
for instance, a jar arises from atoms and so forth, or conversely, shards arise from a jar.
Or, because of its constant activity, there is no simultaneous stability of all objects in such a way that their similarity could be determined; otherwise,

the establishment of distinct objects— like a staff [indicating a person]— would have to be seen as occurring through the cognition of liberation and the attainment of form (rūpa), as noted on page 14, line 4.
Furthermore, O Venerable One,
whether by way of the distinction between the state of aggregation and [the individual], all objects are indeed absolutely distinct, like a jar and a cloth;

even if everything is one according to the perspective of the *saṅgraha-naya*, or if everything is distinct according to the perspective of the *ṛjusūtra-naya*, nevertheless, for those things existing in an aggregated state, there is absolute mutual difference from one another, like a jar and a cloth, and not oneness of all objects.

Now, it was indeed stated that [the pot] is one according to the perspective of the *saṅgraha-naya*; this is true, but the intention is that this is not tenable for things existing as an aggregate, because it contradicts what is perceived.

If one asks, "What follows from that?", it is as follows: having established this, what happens? Does the pot become the atoms and so forth, or do the shards belong to the pot? What is the relationship between father and son?
The phrase "the shards of the pot" demonstrates the lack of relationship even in the case of being produced by the destruction of that [pot].

By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), [it is implied that] for dyads (*dvyaṇuka*), triads (*tryaṇuka*), and so forth, as well as for necks and the like, their connection elsewhere is produced solely by their state of aggregation (*saṅghātasamavasthāna*) due to their differentiation from that [state]. And thus they become similar. The text contained within these brackets—from *sarvamekam* onwards up to *sarvārthānām na*—is not present in the manuscripts of the Ya lineage.

It might be thought by you, the commentator: "In this way, according to your own view, because objects that are mutually distinct would be separate, non-abiding (instability) would result; for there would be no collective coexistence (*saṅghāta-samavasthāna*) among those things divided by the distinctions of substance (*dravya*) and so forth, which are independent of one another.

To this it is replied: "Or, in the case of non-abiding, because all objects are in a state of constant flux, even for a single moment there is no such coexistence as would allow their similarity to be determined; the meaning is that they arise and perish independently of one another."
"Because of the non-existence of a locus," thus has the absence of a universal been stated regarding both the positions of total identity and total difference;
now, wishing to speak also regarding another position, he causes [the opponent] to understand: "Now, without the attainment of form," and so forth, up to "success is desired."

Without the attainment of either a single form or a differentiated form, there can be no expression or cognition [of a qualified object] by means of the words "like a staff-bearer" (*daṇḍivat*). For a cognition of the qualified does not arise without the apprehension of its qualifier; and because specific cognitions cannot be accidental, they must have a cause, just like the cognition and expression of a "staff-bearer" which is caused by the staff. Indeed, in the case of the expression "one who has a staff is a staff-bearer" (*daṇḍo 'syāsti iti daṇḍī*), the expression and cognition of "staff-bearer" with respect to Devadatta are seen to be caused by the conjunction with a staff. In the same way, the expression and cognition of "substance" (*dravya*) or "jar" (*ghaṭa*) and so forth must be caused by the inherence (*samavāya*) of specific universals (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*) such as "substanceness" (*dravyatva*) or "jarness" (*ghaṭatva*); otherwise, this would not be possible.

"The establishment of an object distinct from the individual is accepted" means that through expression and cognition, the establishment of an object such as "substance-ness" or "pot-ness," which is distinct from the individuals such as substances or pots, is indeed accepted;

likewise, for qualities and actions, the establishment of their respective essential objects as distinct from individuals such as number or upward motion must be accepted, because one observes expressions and cognitions of non-difference regarding objects that are actually distinct—
this is the existence of universals (*sāmānya*).
The conditions [are] like a staff;
thus, without *karma*, *go*, *aśva*, *bhāra*, *raṃha*, and *hīna*.
*Karma*, *go*, and *aśva* are without *bhāra*, *raṃha*, and *hīna*.
It is not contradicted, because those two are established even from other sources;

for they [the word and its meaning] pertain to some mere form and so forth, since the cognition of an object from a word is conventional, and because one's understanding arises from the usage of elders regarding that mere form and so forth.
To explain: it is said here—“That is not so; for those two are established through other means as well.
By the word “also” (api), he indicates that even names and so forth, which are established in common worldly usage, are causes of expression and cognition due to the absence of a restrictive rule.
Of what two is there accomplishment? Of speech and cognition.
He shows the absence of any fixed rule regarding them: for those two [operate] with respect to some mere form, or—by virtue of the inclusion of the word "etc."—with respect to a mere name.

The "form" (*ākāra*) is the mode of apprehension; whatever object is grasped by the intellect in a certain way, or designated by a name, that alone is its form, and it is no more than that, not exceeding it—just as, for example, [one might say] "space" or "Ḍittha. Whether it be one way or another, since space and so forth are unitary even in your own view, how can there be non-differentiated designation and cognition regarding things that are distinct? Or how can there be such notions as "the principles of space and so forth"? Yet, both expression and cognition are observed here as well;
therefore, the universal (*sāmānya*) does not exist.

If it is argued that the designation and cognition [of "pot"] with respect to those [atoms] occur through the metaphorical application (*upacāra*) of the universal "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) and so forth, we say no; for a primary universal is not established, and because there is an absence of commonality (*sādharmya*), there can be no metaphorical application. Furthermore, since there is no room for metaphorical application in the investigation of reality (*tattvaparīkṣā*), it would follow that the designation and cognition are false, as in the case of space (*ākāśa*) and other such entities. *Note: The text contains scribal variants: *natta anyato॰ya॰ nitta anyato॰ bhā॰*. These appear to be marginal or interlinear corrections or glosses, likely indicating a variant reading or a clarification regarding the source of the citation.*
Even the name and so forth are merely a verbal expression;
otherwise, [they would exist] in space and so on.

Furthermore, another point is observed: because the cognition of a meaning arises from a word through convention (*samaya*), the convention is its source; that which has convention as its purpose, or that which originates from convention, is "conventional" (*sāmayika*).
As it has been said: "The cognition of an object from a word is conventional" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 7.2.20); it is not caused by a universal (sāmānya).

And those two—the designation (*abhidhāna*) and the cognition (*pratyaya*)—consist of the linguistic usage of elders; having observed the usage of elders, designations and cognitions arise even for children who have not been trained in the usage of various technical treatises, solely from the usage of elders characterized by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
These do not result from the actual presence or absence of the real entity (*tattva*), because people lack knowledge of that specific reality;
it is precisely because they lack knowledge of that reality that [the designations and cognitions] occur for them.
The meaning of the word "icchā" is that you have been trained; you have been trained by the venerable ones.
It might be thought: "The act of naming is a mark of those superior to us, because the act of naming is preceded by perception" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 2.1.18–19);
thus it is stated in the treatise.

Therefore, Manu and others perceive the relationship between words and their meanings even when linguistic usage has been interrupted during intermediate and great cosmic dissolutions (*antarāla-pralaya* and *mahāpralaya*).

Consequently, the relation of inherence (*samavāya*) between a jar and "jar-ness" is also conventional (*sāmayika*), just as the convention that "this is the denoter of this" is grasped by a child in the form "this is a *panasa* fruit.

But this is incorrect, because it leads to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*): whatever word is used to establish a convention, that [word] would require another [convention] to be established; and if the meaning of the subsequent word is not understood, the convention for the former cannot be established.

That whose operation toward an object is natural and independent of convention is called "eternal" (*nitya*). This is stated because there is no interruption in the succession of the understanding of the relationship between word and meaning, its application, and its usage.
As Patañjali has said: "For that alone is not eternal which is fixed, immutable, unshakable, and free from loss, gain, modification, production, growth, or decay;
rather, that too is eternal in which the essential nature (*tattva*) is not destroyed."
"Reality (tattva) is the state of being that;
and reality is not lost even in the case of a generic form," as stated in Patañjali’s *Mahābhāṣya*, Paspaśāhnika 1.1.68.

Just as there is a rejection of the convention [regarding the suffix], there is an extension of the rejection of the demonstration [of the base]; this is not a fault because, according to the usage of the elders (*vṛddha*), comprehension occurs through the mere form [of the suffix] and so forth, and because it will be stated that [the cognition] does not arise from the word alone; [this applies to] *mān* and so on, which involve an intermediate cognition, just like the universals "jar-ness" and "cloth-ness."

This reality is endowed with non-duality, characterized by the absence of decrease, increase, arising,
and cessation.

If it is argued that, even in the absence of a substance that has begun its existence as the reality [of the object], the designation and cognition of "pot" are observed in cases such as a pot with a hole in its bottom because those two are produced there by superimposing the reality [onto the appearance], then it would follow that a post and a mirage would possess the nature of a man and water respectively, since the designation and cognition of those [man and water] exist in their case. [To avoid this,] let the designation and cognition of "man" and "water" not occur when the nature of man and water is not actually present.
However, if the verbal expression and the cognition were to arise from some real aspect (ākāra) that is not metaphorical,
then if a particularity (viśeṣa) were likewise its own object, there would be a contradiction regarding particularity.

If it is argued that there is a distinction [between the universal and the particular], then [the author], demonstrating that the application of both designation and cognition occurs even without a relation to an ultimate reality (tattva), says: "For thus, even without... and so forth; for the reality (tattva) inheres in the substance (dravya).
Substance (dravya) is of two kinds: non-substantial (adravya) and multibasic (anekadravya).
Regarding the non-substantial, such as space (ākāśa) and so forth, it is stated that even in the absence of [further] reality, there are still verbal designations and cognitions.
The multibasic substance is a produced substance (ārabdhadravya), and it is produced by inherent (samavāyi) and non-inherent (asamavāyi) causes.

The inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of a jar is its potsherds; the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) is their conjunction. The prefix *ā-* is used for the purpose of including injunctions, means, and limits. What is the injunction? [Substances] originate by themselves and within themselves. What is the means? [They originate] together with other instrumental causes such as conjunction. What is the limit? Substances originate another substance up to the final composite substance.
Destruction also occurs either from the disjunction of causes or from the destruction of causes.

In that case, when a jar has been produced with a hole at its base due to the disjunction of its causes, the name and cognition of "jar" are observed to persist even though the substance (the jar) initiated by conjunction no longer exists. Similarly, this is seen in the case of a jar painted on a wall—where there is an absence of both inherent and non-inherent causes—and in the case of children’s playthings such as clods of earth or stones, which are used for establishing the presence or absence [of a jar].

This might be argued: "But even in the case of a mere appearance (*ābhāsa*), that is to say, in the case of a mere form (*ākāra*), a mere configuration (*saṃsthāna*), or a mere similarity (*sādṛśya*), those two—namely, the verbal expression and the cognition—are produced there by the superimposition (*upanilayana*) of the reality (*tattva*), such as 'jar-ness' (*ghaṭatva*); thus they are accounted for. To this we reply: In that case, the absence of reality has already been stated. Furthermore, even if reality were present, we have already explained that verbal expressions and cognitions consist merely in form (*ākāramātra*). Moreover, if you maintain that the superimposition of reality occurs upon a mere appearance, then it would follow that a post (*sthāṇu*) and a mirage (*mṛgatṛṣṇikā*) possess the nature of a man (*nara*) and water (*salila*), because the corresponding verbal expressions and cognitions exist there, and because of the superimposition of that respective reality, just as a jar possesses its nature due to the superimposition of 'jar-ness'.

Let it not be that, in the absence of humanity in a tree stump and the absence of water in a mirage, there should be no cognitions or verbal designations of "man" and "water," yet these two are indeed observed. How can they be improper if the qualifiers [humanity and water] have not been apprehended? If it is asked, "In those cases, they are obtained through metaphorical usage (*upacāra*), but how can they be obtained here in the worldly method without metaphorical usage?"—the answer is: from some real form (*ākāra*) that is not merely metaphorical, the verbal designation and cognition of something [else] may arise and ought to arise, precisely because an incomplete form is perceived.
In your view, however, there is no such reality as "some [reality] is concealed" and "some is not concealed," for reality inheres in substance (bhāṣya);
and that which inheres in substance is [the whole]. Ya.
In the absence [of a universal], when there is no cognition of an individual,
the term *aneka* (many) is used here for the purpose of including the limits of the means and methods of injunction (*vidhyupāyamaryādā*).
The reading "ka" does not exist in the manuscripts;
[it appears as] "°dracunne pra°" and "°bhāgā utpanne pra°".
In playthings such as gourds, stones, and the like, there may be this [perception] merely due to that; in this alone, there may be that [perception] merely due to that.
In the case of clay, [it is so].
There may also be the reading "°mātroktipra°" or "°bhāsamātreya°" here.
The two [terms] "improper" (ayukta) and "unfit" (ayoga) are obtained by the removal of the word "pot" (ghaṭa).
Because it is somewhat merged within the [letter] *pra*, it exists as *ya*.
Thus, the universal (*sāmānya*) has been examined in two ways; now the particular (*viśeṣa*) is to be examined.

To this he replies: "In the same way, the particular (*viśeṣa*) also does not escape two alternatives—it must either have itself as its object or another thing as its object. In that regard, if it has itself as its object, there is a contradiction with its being a 'particular'."

There is a contradiction with the particular (*viśeṣa*), because it would result in the absence of the particular; there is a contradiction with the self (*ātman*) by means of the particular, because it would result in the absence of the self—is this not merely a matter of words? For the particular is distinct [from the self] either by way of quality (*guṇataḥ*) or by way of time (*kālataḥ*); otherwise, in the case of a jar and so forth, it would result in the status of a universal (*sāmānya*). If, on the other hand, it were the self, then it would not be a particular, because the self is one.

Now, it might be argued: "The faults of contradiction regarding identity and difference do not apply, because we maintain the thesis that the self itself is the particular, and thus there is no [need for] a separate substratum (apādāna) and so forth.

If the particular is dependent solely upon the self—such that the one is itself the other—then, because the self undergoes transformation, it would follow that it is non-self; and since the preceding and succeeding forms of the jar and its color and so forth would exist in the form of color and so forth, they would be non-existent, resulting in the non-existence of both.
[Is it] by means of three? It is said: no. If there were a particularity (*viśeṣa*), then the self (*ātman*) would not exist, because a particularity is something other [than the self].

There is indeed a contradiction between the self and a particularity. To demonstrate this: if a particularity such as form (*rūpa*) exists in the self with respect to its own object, then the self is not [that], because the particularity is other than it—being distinguished from others in terms of space, such as form and so forth; or in terms of quality (*guṇa*), or in terms of time, since form and so forth perish through the production of ever-new [states] at every moment, what then would be their self? Thus, there is an absence of self.

In the absence of that [self], of what would there be a particularity (*viśeṣa*)? Otherwise, there would be the consequence of [the collection] becoming a universal (*sāmānya*) in the case of a jar and so forth. "Otherwise" means: if one accepts the identity of the collection of form and the rest, then the position of particularity is abandoned and the acceptance of a universal follows; and in that case, the aforementioned faults easily arise—such as "pleasure, pleasure, and the collection of pleasure and so forth. These same faults apply here: "form, form, and the collection of form and so forth. Lest there be the fault of the non-existence of a self, and lest there be the fault of the non-existence of particularity in the absence of that self, one might adopt another position: "Now, the self possesses particularity; the self is indeed one, and it is precisely that which is non-different."

From that [Self], there can be no particularity (*viśeṣa*), because the Self is one; the meaning is that because the entity such as a jar is one with the Self, it shares its very essence, and thus no otherness exists. For a particularity cannot be "other" either in terms of quality (*guṇataḥ*) or in terms of time (*kālataḥ*); otherwise, the jar and so forth would fall into the category of the universal (*sāmānya*). Furthermore, from the Self, there can be no particularity, because the Self is one.

Now, it might be argued: "The faults of contradiction regarding identity and difference do not apply, because we maintain the thesis that the self itself is the particular (viśeṣa), and thus there is no [need for] a formal point of departure (apādāna) and so forth.

If the particular is dependent solely upon the self, then by being one and yet other, the self undergoes a change of state; consequently, it would lack the nature of a self, as it takes on forms such as color and so forth. Furthermore, since the preceding and succeeding forms of the pot and so forth would be non-existent, both [identity and difference] would be absent."

Regarding the phrase "specifically, as for contradiction, if [it occurs] in a jar or the like, specifically, as for contradiction, if [it occurs] in the self"—this reading appears duplicated in all manuscripts. [The variants are:
*ātmano'nyatvād* (Viśva, Yaśas) and *ātmāno'nyatvād* (Bhāṣya).
Having arisen from others,
and having arisen from non-others— among the perishable, the person (*puruṣa*), and so forth, who is their self (*ātman*)? What is the cause?
...by way of [logical] consequence, having accepted... and having grasped... and having attained... [Prasannapadā manuscript B; Yuktiṣaṣṭikāvṛtti manuscript Y; Prasannapadā manuscript A]

Line 1: To avoid this fault, if the opponent were to say— “The faults of contradiction regarding identity and difference do not apply to the self as a qualifier”—

then these two faults would arise either in the case of the use of the genitive or ablative cases for the relation and the substratum, or in the case of the use of the locative case of location (*adhikaraṇa-saptamī*) in the expression “the qualifier in the self.”

What then? Since it is asserted that the self itself is the particular (*viśeṣa*), and thus there is no [need for] a formal ablative case (*apādāna*) and so forth, the faults of contradiction regarding identity and difference do not apply to me. To this it is replied: if the particular is indeed dependent upon the self, then that is merely a reiteration of that [self]; the second alternative—that there is a contradiction regarding the particular—follows, and here too this fault remains: because the single [self] becomes other, it undergoes a change of state (*anyathābhāva*), and thus, by way of forms such as color and so on, it would become non-self (*anātmatva*).
Is it by mere words? No; he states the logical justification: "because of becoming otherwise" (*anyathābhavanāt*).
He demonstrates this: the preceding and succeeding forms of the jar and its qualities are non-existent.

How so? Since other and different forms and so forth arise, there is the non-existence of the jar. In the absence of that [jar], what could have a distinction? Or, if the jar itself becomes otherwise, there is the non-existence of the form and so forth.

Consequently, there is the absence of the later states such as the "pot-sherd" (*śivaka*) and so forth from the state of the "clod of earth" (*piṇḍa*), and the absence of the earlier states such as "earth-ness" (*mṛttva*) and so forth.

Alternatively, the nature of a cloth (*paṭatva*) is other than that of a jar; the nature of sound and so forth is other than that of form (*rūpa*). Because it becomes otherwise in that manner, there is the absence of the jar and the absence of form and so forth;

thus, there is the absence of both. There is the absence of the self (*ātman*) and the absence of the particular (*viśeṣa*). Or else, the absence of the self of the jar is brought about by the absence of form and so forth, and the absence of form and so forth is brought about by the absence of the self of the jar.
Or rather, in the explanation,
other forms [are mentioned] for the sake of mutual form.
The specific qualities themselves undergo transformation; this is the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa).
The two states, the absence of form and so forth,
and the nature of becoming through the attainment of water.
If, however, this [distinction] were undesirable, one would fall into the position of depending on another;

yet even so, there would be a difference in substance—for what dependence could a jar, whose existence is already established, have upon a cloth or other things, except for the assistance provided by its own occurrence? In that case, the self itself would be differentiated.

Alternatively, if it is argued that there is a requirement [for a universal] because of being earthy—just as a cloth is required by a jar because they belong to the same genus—then one might object: "In that case, since there is no distinction from heterogeneous things such as water and so forth, there must also be a requirement for the universal 'substance-ness' (dravyatva) in those cases. If it is then argued: "In those cases, there is no distinction from heterogeneous qualities and actions, and thus there too there is a requirement for existence (sattā)," [we reply: then how could there be a requirement for a universal from something entirely non-existent and heterogeneous, like a universal from a non-entity, or from an effect? Thus, there would be no distinction between existence and non-existence.
Nevertheless, there is the non-existence of both;
for if this [non-existence] were undesirable, one would fall into the position of dependence on another.

Since a jar or the like undergoes change from its own nature, it lacks selfhood (anātmatva); consequently, there is the non-existence of both the particular and the self. Thus, if one does not accept the aforementioned fault of contradiction, it follows that the position of dependence on another implies that the particular has another as its object and not itself as its object.
If it is asked, "What is the name of that fault?"—it is called "the abandonment of one's own position.

Furthermore, even if this [position] is accepted as a figurative designation (*upacāra*), there is this other fault: even so, there would be a difference in substance (*dravyabheda*). It would follow that a substance, such as a jar or the self, exists in a twofold nature by way of its own form and the form of another, because the particularity (*viśeṣa*) is dependent upon another.
One might think: "The jar consists precisely of the non-existence of cloth and so forth, and thus it is dependent upon cloth and so forth."

To this it is said: "No. For what dependence on cloth or other things could there be for a jar whose existence is already established, apart from assistance through its own functioning? "Assistance" (*sāhāyakam*) means the state of being an auxiliary (*sahāya-bhāva*). "Assistance through functioning" (*vṛtti-sāhāyakam*) means the state of being an auxiliary to the functioning. Aside from the state of being an auxiliary to the jar's functioning—which belongs to the cloth—what other dependence on cloth or other things could there be for the jar at a later time, since its own functioning is already established by itself even prior [to such dependence]? The meaning is that there is none at all. What is the reason? Because there is no purpose.

In that case, its very self would be divided; in that manner, the very nature of the jar would be divided, because it functions in dependence upon auxiliaries, like the function of the self in carrying a palanquin. Since there is the occurrence of dependence on another in that state, the nature of the self and the particularity [are not established].
The state of being composed of [the self], the bowing, the particularity, the accumulation, the assistance, and the primordial matter.
According to the Pāṇinian sūtra *yopadhād gurūpottamād vuñ* (Pāṇini 5.1.132), the form *sāhāyakam* alone is correct [for "assistance"];
alternatively, there is a dependence due to being a king (*pārthivatva*), as he says: "A jar has a dependence upon cloth and so forth."
What is that? It is a common genus;
because of the state of having a common genus, a cloth is related to a jar.
What is the common genus? It is earthiness.
If it is asked, "How is there a distinction? [the answer is: "The distinction of the cloth and so forth is due to their being of the nature of a jar.
To this it is replied: In that case, there would be an absence of distinction for water and so forth from things of a different genus;
for if a distinction is desired only in relation to things of the same genus, then it follows that a jar has no distinction from water and so forth, which are of a different genus.
And this is undesirable.

If it is argued that "in that case too, there is dependence upon substanceness (*dravyatva*)," meaning that by depending on the generality of substanceness, the jar will have a distinction from water and so forth—if this is claimed, then there would be no distinction [of the jar] from qualities and actions which are of a different genus (*vijātīya*). For qualities and actions of a different genus do not depend upon substanceness, yet a distinction of the jar from them is also desired.

If it is argued that even there [in the case of a universal], there is dependence upon existence (*sattā*), then it follows that there would be no distinction from something absolutely non-existent (*atyantāsata*) belonging to a different class.
Even so, there would be an absence of distinction from absolutely non-existent things such as a donkey's horn, because of the absence of anything to depend upon—
just as there is none for "non-genus" (*ajāti*) in relation to "genus" (*jāti*).

Furthermore, according to your own doctrine, for the universal "earth-ness" (pārthivatva), which is devoid of further universals, there is no dependence upon another universal; how then can it possess a distinction from other universals such as "water-ness" or from other individuals, given the absence of such dependence? Or, how could there be a distinction based on its effect? This question persists.

For in your doctrine, the effect—which previously did not exist—arises later upon the proximity of the inherent and non-inherent causes; since you accept the tenet that "the effect is non-existent because of the absence of activity, qualities, and designation," there can be no dependence [of the effect] on the causes while they are in the state of being causes, precisely because the effect is non-existent at that time. Furthermore, because it would be identical to earthiness and so forth, its nature would be the same as theirs. Thus, due to the fact that it would have to depend on them as such, the consequence follows that there is no distinction [between cause and effect].

Furthermore, when the effect has been produced and the causal operation has ceased, because the effect is already established, the causes lack the status of being causes; thus, there is no distinction between cause and effect.

The word "iti" serves to conclude the argument. Therefore, due to the sequence of reasons stated, there is no distinction between existence and non-existence. Just as, according to the method previously explained, there is no distinction because an existent thing does not depend on a non-existent one, so too there is no distinction because a non-existent thing likewise does not depend on an existent one.

Or rather, what dependence could a non-existent thing have? Since these two are thus indistinguishable, either non-existence must be existent like existence, or existence must be non-existent like non-existence.

Nevertheless, there is the absence of both; that is, the absence of existence and non-existence, or of universal and particular, or of self and attribute, in the case of a jar or the like—this is "substantiality" (*dravyatva*), which is a universal (*sāmānya*). Even in that case, there is dependence on [other] universals.

How can that [non-existence] belong to it, given that it is absolutely non-existent? (Yaśomitra) / How can that [non-existence] belong to it, given that it is absolutely non-existent? (Bhāṣya) / How can that [non-existence] belong to it? (Bhāṣya)
In that case, how could there be *raṃ* and *hīṃ* without *ya*; and since there is no dependence on *raṃ* and *hīṃ*, how could *raṃ* and *hīṃ* exist?

It arises from the five [elements], because it is equal to earthiness and so forth; likewise, its nature as that [element] exists because it must be considered as such—this is the discernment regarding the dependence on the existent and the non-existent. (Note: *pra* indicates a variant reading).
In consideration of that,
the reading "the very existence of non-existence" (satvamevābhāvasya) or even "the very existence of non-existence" (sattvamevābhāvasya) may also be possible here.

Thus, first of all, it is not logical for a jar or the like to depend upon its earthen nature (*pārthivatva*) and so forth. Even granting such dependence, because the jar is identical in its earthen nature with the cause, the clay, the effect—the jar—must possess that same nature as the cause. This is because the jar is equal to the clay in the respect of the attribute of being earthen; "like that" means that just as the jar has the nature of becoming a jar, so too does it have the nature of being clay, or, like the jar which has the nature of being earthen, it possesses that very nature.
What is the reason? Because it must be depended upon as that very reality (*tattattvena*).

"Reality" (*tattva*) is the state of being that; "being" (*bhāva*) is the process of becoming. Its reality is "that-reality" (*tattattva*). Because it must be depended upon as that very reality—just as the nature of earth (*pārthivatva*) is depended upon, like the becoming of a jar—it follows that the jar-ness (*ghaṭatva*) would possess the identity of that [earth-nature], because jar-ness is depended upon as having the jar as its essence, just as the jar itself has the nature of earth. The word "iti" is used in the sense of a reason. Therefore, due to that identity, there is a loss of the effort for discernment regarding that which is depended upon; that is, a loss of the effort to demonstrate the dependence on a specific object.

Regarding the term "non-distinction" (*aviśeṣa*): having established it in this way, that very non-distinction must be brought about—due to the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), because of the equality with [the categories] such as substantiality (*dravyatva*) and the equality with existence (*sattva*).
And likewise, it is because of that [equality]. (Bhāṣya)
Like the existence [of a jar] resulting from the contemplation of a jar,
because it does not depend on [anything else], it is indeed independent,
like the primordial matter (prakṛti).
For, in the case of independence from [other] causes, the reading "ghaṭatvam" does not exist in the manuscript of Bhāṣya; [the text reads] "tādātmyād apekṣya".

It may be thought that this is not a *viśeṣa* (particularity) at all, because generalities and particularities are relative and because "substance-ness," "quality-ness," and "action-ness" are merely figurative; for it is stated in the Vaiśeṣika Sūtra:
"Substance-ness, quality-ness, and action-ness are both generalities and particularities. (VS 1.2.4)
These have been stated; what then [remains] regarding "cowness," "jar-ness," and so forth? What, then, is the primary distinction?
The intention is that only the ultimate [particular] is the primary universal, and it is indeed a positive entity (*bhāva*).

Because, when atoms have reached or passed beyond a single point of space, there exists a final particularity (*antya-viśeṣa*) manifested by the power of cognition and designation of distinctness; for the expression and the cognition of distinctness are certainly not accidental. Therefore, this exists, and it is that very thing which is the primary particularity, as it has been said: "Except for the final particulars" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.2.6).

2.6 Thus, existence (*bhāva*) itself is the primary universal (*mukhya-sāmānya*), because it is that by virtue of which [the notions] "existent" apply to substances, qualities, and actions; that [existence] is a distinct entity from substances, qualities, and actions (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.2.4).
Because of this statement, since [qualities] such as substantiality (*dravyatva*) are merely figurative, it has been established that [substance] possesses a dual nature.
ākāśaveśātīya (Bhāṣya:
ākāśavetsātīya) is the form; it is the configuration.

All atoms whatsoever are spherical in shape; thus, there is equality of form among earthly atoms with all other earthly atoms. Furthermore, according to Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 5.2.13—"The first action of atoms and of the mind is caused by the unseen force (adṛṣṭa)"—the possession of motion produced by the unseen force is common to all of them. Therefore, their substratum is also a single location.

Therefore, from that same spatial location in space, one atom has moved away while another has arrived there at the very same time; in this case, even for the Supreme Sage, the cognition of "this is different from that" would not be without a cause,
yet such a cognition of difference is indeed observed.

"The cause of that other condition is the ultimate particular (*antyaviśeṣa*); therefore, it is distinct from that substance which is the atom. Such is the cognition of the Naigama-naya—see *Viśeṣāvaśyakabhāṣya-vṛtti* composed by Koṭṭāryavādigaṇimahattara, folio 155b2; see also page 6, note 1: *°katvāt tadvyātmatayo°*. (Prakrit text).

There would be a loss of effort and no distinction [between the stages], because even at the final stage, those [objects] are grasped through the progression of the distinctions of substance and so forth; otherwise, it would follow that yogins possess ignorance.
To this it is replied: "Because even at the final stage, those [objects] are grasped through the progression of the distinctions of substance and so forth."
The final state is the "end"; even in that final particularity, there is an absence of further particularity—this is how the word "api" (also/even) is connected [to the preceding].
What is the reason? Because it is graspable through the progression of the various divisions of substance and so forth.

Those of which substance is the first are "substance and the rest"—namely, substance, space, time, and mode. Their "division" is *tat-prabheda*; the "progression," "transformation," "functioning," or "modification" resulting from that division is observed in such a way that one can say, "the progression of this effect is such-and-such. Thus, because it is seen [in this manner], [there is no infinite regress].
By that movement, there is the state of being perceivable; of what? Of the ultimate particular (*antyaviśeṣa*).

Therefore, because it is perceivable through the movement belonging to the distinctions of substance and so forth, the ultimate particular should not be postulated, since it is not perceivable by either perception or inference apart from substance and the rest, and because it is perceivable only in its own form as those [substances, etc.].

For example: a yogi, perceiving a single atom through direct perception, sees it as fallen from the state of being a dyad; he sees another as fallen from the state of being a triad, another as inherent in a dyad, and another as inherent in a triad. He perceives those substances, such as atoms and so forth, as distinct by their very nature as substances; in that case, what is the use of "ultimate particularity" (*antyaviśeṣa*)? Likewise, even with respect to location (*kṣetra*), one [atom] is situated in the upper part of the field, while another is situated in the front part or the lower part.

Even from the perspective of time, there is indeed a diversity caused by substance (*dravya*), space (*kṣetra*), and state (*bhāva*) between one thing situated at the first moment and another situated at the second moment, or even between two things that have arrived simultaneously.

In terms of state (*bhāva*), one may be black while another is white; one may be fragrant while another is foul-smelling, or one bitter while another is pungent, and so forth. Alternatively, one may be black while another is blacker, or blackest, or even twice, thrice, numerable, innumerable, or infinitely many times blacker, and so on.
In this same way, the perception [of objects] by means of the remaining qualities—color, smell, taste, and touch, along with their subdivisions—must be explained.

Otherwise, if there were no specific distinctions among substances and so forth that differentiate one from another, it would follow that yogins possess ignorance because they would lack dependence on objects;
therefore, substances and the other categories must necessarily be accepted as being distinguished by their own nature.

If this were not so, it would follow that the yogin possesses false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*), because he would be perceiving an object as otherwise than it actually exists. Furthermore, regarding the ultimate particulars (*antyaviśeṣas*), another cause would have to be postulated for the occurrence of the verbal expression and cognition of their mutual distinction; or else, if they were distinct by themselves, the postulation of "ultimate particulars" should be abandoned. Why, then, is a similar independence from causes not accepted for atoms as well? If further causes were required even for these particulars, it would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*); consequently, the verbal expression and cognition of particulars would be impossible. Enough of this digression.
It is established— that there is no particularity regarding its own object—
except elsewhere [in the case of] "līṃ"; such-and-such substance and so forth (ya),
that substance and so forth (bhā).

The etymological explanation of the word *antya* (ultimate/particular) as "that which exists at the end" (*ante bhavaḥ*) or "that which exists among the ends" (*anteṣu bhavāḥ*), following the *Praśastapādabhāṣya*—as seen in the passage on page 168—is almost universally favored and accepted.

However, Śaṅkara Miśra, in his *Vaiśeṣikasūtropaskāra*, presents two views on this matter: "They are called *antya* because they exist at the end (*ante*) or in the finality (*avasāne*); for there is no further differentiator beyond them," so say the Teachers (*ācāryāḥ*).

The author of the *Vṛtti* explains: "They are called 'ultimate' (*antya*) because they exist at the end, that is, at the limit of production and destruction; those eternal substances in which they reside are the ultimate particulars (*viśeṣa*). — Vaiśeṣika Sūtra Upaskāra 1.2.6.
Regarding that distinction, namely:
"As for this body, such is its nature."
Just as for the body—
here, "of the body" means "of the physical frame"— it should be understood that if one prefers the meaning [as translated], the reading in the Bhāṣya exactly as heard is indeed correct;
[the term] *pracyutāśana* refers to a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*).
The *bhāṣya* on the *dvyaṇuka* [reads] "from which the fire has fallen away";
here, the reading "the *dvyaṇuka* from which the self has fallen away" (*pracyutātmānaṃ dvyaṇukaṃ*) is also possible, as it is equal in its three qualities. The *bhāṣya* [states] "equal."
In the *Ya* manuscript,
the reading "kṣetratopūrvabhāgasthitamekaparamavābhāga" appears; however, the word "ūrdha" is also found in lexicons as having the same meaning as the word "ūrdhva."
Furthermore, it should be noted that throughout this *Nayacakra-vṛtti*, the word *ūrdha* is generally seen in place of the word *ūrdhva*;
[the term] *avāgbhāga* means the lower part, the downward part, or the region below— [as stated in] *Kiñcitpra...* [etc.].
Even for those who have arrived, is there anything such as blackness or the like? Or perhaps...

This is the occasion for examining the specific nature of an external object; therefore, he says: "But in the case of having an external object, there is no distinction because the distinction does not persist. Now, was it not already stated previously that "there would be the consequence of falling into the position of dependence on another"? True; however, in that context, by means of abandoning what had been accepted and thereby producing a lack of core conviction, other points were introduced as a secondary consequence. Here, however, [the point is]: "In the case of having an external object, there is no distinction because the distinction does not persist. Because everything here is connected in relation to each substance and so forth, this entire world would become a qualifier of every single thing, just like the various states of qualities (guṇas) contained within a single jar.

In that case, because all objects are in constant flux, there is no fixed time (*samaya*) for their simultaneous existence (*samavasthāna*) upon which a specific object could be established as its substratum. The faults have already been stated [in the previous section] as being like those of the *ātman*; however, here the statement of the faults proceeds primarily by another method—namely, by establishing the lack of stability (*anavasthāna*), which is about to be proven, as a given fact, he says: "Because of the lack of stability, there is no distinction."

Just as previously, having begun with the statement that "because they do not exist in an identical state, there is no universal," the absence of a universal was established, so too here, by reversing that argument, the same section should be applied. Why?
