Because it has not been determined that they have a single effect, and so on—all of which is exactly the same [as before], up until: therefore, these [particulars] must necessarily be accepted even by one who holds the position that the self is a particular such as a jar, because the self is distinguished from others in various ways through direct perception itself; how much more so for one who maintains that the primary particular belongs to another object? For since the particular belonging to another object exists in various ways through direct perception itself, it is said that "it becomes distinguished by the other."

Regarding the term "here" (*iha*) in the sense of a specific object belonging to another: because everything here is related to substance (*dravya*) and the other categories, this entire world is a qualification for each individual thing without exception. Just as before, a substance depends upon other substances, space (*kṣetra*), time (*kāla*), and state (*bhāva*), as well as its own subdivisions and the subdivisions of others. Likewise, space, time, and state—all are interconnected with everything else. Therefore, because everything is interconnected, just as before, due to the coexistence of color, shape, and so forth, and the coexistence of the earth, barley, sprouts, and so on, there is a single mode of movement and coexistence for substances even from the perspective of space (*kṣetra*). Due to the coexistence of the various described divisions such as the *dharmāstikāya* and the taking up, holding, and supporting of water by the earth and so forth, there is also [coexistence] from the perspective of time (*kāla*). And due to the coexistence of the existence of substances and so forth, as well as color, shape, and the jar and so on, just as before, there is [coexistence] from the perspective of state (*bhāva*). Thus, it is "as if" a single jar were composed of various states of qualities.

As it has been said: "Indeed, substance itself, by existing in such a state, acquires the nature of color and so forth, just like the relationship between father and son in relation to a single person. For substance itself—designated as a 'jar'—does not transcend the status of being qualified by color, taste, smell, touch, number, configuration, white, blue, bitter, pungent, fragrant, soft, hard, whiter, or whitest, and so on.

These very things are the qualities (*guṇas*) and modes (*paryāyas*), which exist in various states, are mutually distinct, and serve as qualifiers both for one another and for the substance; indeed, substance itself is the qualities and the modes."
Likewise, other categories—substance, space, time, and mode—are also included along with their subdivisions.

By virtue of the term "syāt" (in a certain sense), it may further be said that this is so provided it is not contradicted by the fault about to be mentioned; therefore, he says: "In that regard, because all objects are eternally active, even for a moment," and so on, up to "that upon which the specific meaning depends would be established.
Thus, since all objects are eternally active through mutual qualification, there is not even a single moment of their remaining in a state of equilibrium.

For a distinction (*viśeṣa*) would be established only by having a basis in a common state (*samavasthāna*); since that [common state] is absent, how can there be a distinction? "Like something grasped" means like an entity that has arisen and perished in a moment apprehended at that time. If it is asked, "What follows from this?", [the answer is: because of the absence of a common state, the distinction lacks a basis and thus does not exist, like a flower in the sky. (Page 24, Line 1)
Whether they are appropriated or unappropriated, there is no distinction when they function as objects for another, because the specific characteristic does not persist.

In this case, because everything here is connected in relation to substance (*dravya*) and so forth, this entire world would be the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) of each [individual] without exception, like the various states of qualities (*guṇa*) inherent in a single jar. Since all things are constantly active therein, there is not even a moment when they exist in a state of equilibrium (*samavasthāna*) such that a specific object could be established as their substratum; see page 14, line 6.
Because of having a body that is less subject to obstruction (anavṛttikatarakāyatvāt);
see page 14, line 6.

See page 18, line 3: "Even by one who perceives [it], they must necessarily be expected; even by one who perceives through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), they must necessarily be expected. This reading has been doubled in the *Ya* manuscripts; this is the *Sāhityaprakāśa*.
It may be that [the text] is thus:
*utpattyavinaṣṭa* (produced and not destroyed), *ya*.

Regarding the absence of configuration (saṃsthāna), it might be thought: "The locus of relation is not refuted; it is disregarded. What does this mean? It means that while there may be no particularity (viśeṣa) because of a lack of support once one excludes the substances and so forth that constitute the locus of relation, why should there not be a particularity for jars, cloths, and the like which reside in those very loci of relation? To disregard the locus of relation is an arbitrary abandonment of what has been accepted, since it is equal [to the other categories] due to the admission of generality (sāmānya).

The distinction [of pure substances] consists precisely in their connection with the differences of color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth; this is not so, because if they were unconnected to anything else, they would lack color-form and the like, and thus pure substances would never exist anywhere. But is it not observed in the world that air is indeed a pure touch? Even there, the color-form and other qualities of the substance of the field (*kṣetra*) and so forth are not perceived due to their non-manifestation and subtlety; for the distinction [of the substance] is based upon that [touch], just as in the case of [other] substances and so forth. Thus [it is argued].
To this it is replied: "If there were disregard for the location of the relationship, there would be an abandonment of what has been accepted all of a sudden.
This being the case, there is an abandonment of the specific [quality] that was accepted all of a sudden.

If it is asked, "How is the universal (sāmānya) accepted, given the admission of the general? [the answer is: because of their equality; for those situated in the location of the relationship possess characteristics equal to the proximity of substance, space, time, and state, which is the very definition of the universal (*sāmānya*), that is, the state of being common (*samānabhāva*).

If there were indifference toward the location of the relationship with the atoms (*muvā pra°*), there would be an abandonment of what has been accepted [namely, the distinction between atoms] without cause, because [the atoms] are equal and because a universal is admitted;

for the specific distinction consists precisely in the connection with the differences of color-form (*rūpa*) and so on. This is not so, because if there were no connection with anything else, they would lack color-form and so on, and pure [atoms] do not exist anywhere at all.

Is it not observed in the world that the wind is indeed pure touch? For even there, the color-form (*rūpa*) and other qualities of the substance such as the field are not perceived, due to their non-manifestation and subtlety, just like [the qualities] of a substance and so forth. [The reading] *anabhivyaktisaukṣmyāt* is supported by the manuscript *mupāṃtyatyāgo* (which indicates the omission of the penultimate letter) and the variant *tasyabhā*.
Because of the equality of the moments of the final [moment] with those of the preceding [moments],
there is no difference in their existence.
Here it is said: "The very relation to the distinctions of form and so forth is the particularity.

Thus, the relation itself of color, taste, smell, touch, number, configuration, and so on—along with their subdivisions—is called the particularity; for these very things, being distinguished from one another, are designated as "particularities" (*viśeṣa*).
To this it is replied: that is not so, because if there were no relation to anything else, they would lack the nature of form and so forth.

If they were unconnected with other substances and so forth, it would follow that they lack the nature of color-form (*rūpa*) and the rest; for color-form and the others are indeed always, everywhere, and in every way connected by way of the inseparable division of substance, space, time, and state. What is the reason? Because pure [qualities] do not exist anywhere at all. As was stated previously, since there is an absence of the intrinsic nature of color-form and the rest in the absence of connection with substance and so forth—and because only those things connected with them are observed—it follows that in the absence of connection with substance and the rest along with their subdivisions, color-form and the others simply do not exist; thus, it follows that they lack the nature of color-form and the rest.

"Because they lack color and so forth, they have no connection with other substances and the like; because they lack color and so forth, they have no connection with other substances and the like"—this doubled reading is found within the brackets in all manuscripts. From "connected tastes" (*sambaddharasā*) up to "substances and the like" (*dravyādi*), this passage does not exist in the Bhāṣya manuscript; it is a pure interpolation.

The other says: "Is it not seen in the world that air is indeed pure touch? If there were no connection with substance, space, time, form, taste, and so forth, then the absence of form and the rest would be absolute; and there would be inference if it were not contradicted by what is perceived. And air is perceived as mere touch alone; for there is no means of knowledge more authoritative than perception. To this it is replied: Even in that case, form and the rest of the substance [of air] and its location are not perceived due to their non-manifestation and subtlety, just like [the qualities of] a substance and so forth by way of contrast.
Just as substances and other qualities are perceived by direct perception, so too color, taste, smell, and other qualities are not perceived in air due to their non-manifestation and subtlety.

What is the reason? Because of the absence of a transformation that makes them graspable by the sense organs such as the eye, and because of the absence of inferability through a logical mark (*liṅga*).
As it is stated in another *Saṅgraha*: "Why is the form of air not [perceived], and why is it not tasted or colored?"
Therefore, no one would be able to perceive those [qualities] with the sense organs;
thus,
fire and air possess smell, because they are corporeal, like earth.
Thus, fire and air possess taste because they are corporeal, like earth and water;
air possesses form because it is corporeal, like fire, earth, and water;
air, fire, water, and [the other elements] possess form, taste, smell, and touch because they are corporeal, like earth.

And here too, a corroborative instance based on similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) is stated: "They are not perceived, like the touch, taste, color, smell, and so forth of dust motes in a window. For in the case of those [dust motes] made manifest by the light of the sun's rays, it is their form alone that is perceptible. Regarding the phrase *vāyor rūpa* (the form of air) here—since *vāyoḥ* is in the genitive case, the reading in the Bhāṣya (*bhāṣya-pratipāṭha*) is indeed correct.
How is it that the form [of the wind] is not grasped? And how is it that the form is neither tasted nor manifested?
How is it perceived?
"Nor could it be perceived by the sense of touch; no one would be able to perceive that individuality through the senses. (Bhāṣya)
But that which, by means of the sense-faculties, [perceives] someone... [engaged in] the proximity of fire... [Bhāṣya]
...varttopagni... ya... ravikāro...
pra... Now, it might be argued: "There will be a distinction among objects due to their co-existence at the same time, for some thing indeed persists for some time."
Even so, because such a universal (*sāmānya*) is admitted, there would be no distinction at all;

and because of the co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of all [terms], even when one thing undergoes modification, a change in everything else would arise, since otherness resides in that alone, just as in the case of smell and water. If, however, it is argued that only that which is proximate to the cognition of them will be grasped as both the universal and the particular, then in that case, substances, qualities, and actions would possess neither a universal nor a particular, because they lack mutual proximity.

Regarding that cognition—it might be argued by the opponent: "If there is no distinction among objects due to their being situated in the same location as the relation, there will nevertheless be a distinction among objects due to their co-existence at the same time; for some thing persists for a certain duration, as in the case of a jar and a cloth situated one before the other.
[The author replies: Indeed, a specific cause for distinction ought to be stated here, yet this which has been raised is merely a general cause.

To this it is replied: "A particular is established by means of a universal; therefore, by the non-establishment of that [universal], the particular is not established"—this is to be understood everywhere.

On this point as well, the Teacher states the answer: "Even so, because such a universal is admitted, the very lack of distinction (aviśeṣatva) results in the opponent's own admission becoming the answer. For, since they exist at the same time, by admitting a temporal universal, there is an abandonment of what was previously accepted—just like the admission of a spatial universal—and because [the two cases] are equal, there is indeed a lack of distinction."
In place of *vasthānārthānāṃ pra° sthāne kakāla° ya° mādeśa* pra°, [the reading is as follows].
The abandonment of the example [is] as stated; see page 28, line 1.

Furthermore: because of the aforementioned method and because of the universal co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the specific essence (*viśeṣasvatattva*), and because entities are mutually dependent and thus differentiated, the entire world has a single substratum (*ekādhikaraṇa*). In that case, even when there is a modification (*vikāra*) in one thing, a change occurs in the rest—whether it be the remainder or the whole—since they are dependent upon it; for why else would such a transformation arise? It is because [the change] resides only in that [one thing].

What is the illustration? "Like the smell in air and water. Just as, by way of non-correspondence in number, a modification is observed through the state of being deficient or excessive—namely, that water is deficient in smell while earth is excessive in smell, such that water is devoid of smell and earth possesses it in excess—therefore, because of this lack of stability, there is no specific property (viśeṣa) that is without a substratum, like a sky-flower.
[The reading *viśeṣātva* is corrected to *viśeṣa* based on the manuscript *bhā.*]
Because of its distinctness,
there is the non-existence of even the remainder of that which was without remainder,
and the non-existence of even the remainder of the remainder.

In the section on transformation (*anyathātva*), [it is said that] there is no [change] because of the nature of existence, just as water and foam are not distinct from each other according to their respective order; nor is there smell for that which is not [existent].
Therefore, there is no excess.
This is a censure;
[in the manuscript] Bhā, it is an insertion.
However, if it is understood that "of the universal and the particular" refers to that which is proximate to that cognition, then [the objection is avoided].
The word *atha* (now) introduces a new topic;

the particle *tu* (but) serves as a qualification that distinguishes this section on proximity by cognition (*buddhyāsatti*) from the preceding section on proximity of place and time (*deśakālāsatti*).
"Proximate by cognition" means: *tadbuddhiḥ*—that is, the cognition that "this very first jar is the same as the second one. This is the cognition [of identity].

What is that? It is the cognition of conformity to reality (*tattvānuvṛttibuddhi*). Even the cognition of exclusion (*vyāvṛttibuddhi*)—which, through proximity to that [cognition of conformity], arises when the cognition of "substance-ness" has occurred, such as "this is not water, not sand, not a clod of earth, but a jar alone"—is as it has been stated: "The universal (*sāmānya*) is the cause of the cognition of conformity; the particular (*viśeṣa*) is the cause of the cognition of exclusion.
To this we reply: if that is so, then for substances, qualities, and actions, there would be neither a universal nor a particular.

What is the reason? Because there is no mutual inherence (*asatti*) among them, it is by that cognition of "existence" (*sattā*) that the inherence of a substance, a quality, or an action is apprehended. Is a quality or an action apprehended by the cognition of a substance? For by the cognition of a substance, it is indeed that very substance; for inherence belongs to a substance and to a substance alone. Therefore, the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*) would reside only there [in the substance], not in qualities or actions.
And thus, there is an absence of the universal of existence (*sattvasāmānya*) and the particulars such as the origination of a substance (*dravyārambha*) in those two.

Likewise, there is proximity between sand and a diamond; they would possess commonality and particularity, but not between earth and water. As long as a substance is apprehended as such due to its belonging to the same genus and its proximity [to other substances], only within that [substance] would commonality and particularity exist, and not in qualities or actions.

Why? Because the proximity of the cognition of "that" belongs to substance and substance, but not to substance and quality, nor to substance and action, nor to quality and action; thus, due to the absence of such a proximity of cognition, there is an absence of commonality and an absence of particularity.
And having established this, there is no distinction between those two [substance and quality] regarding their commonality as *sattva*, their being substances, or their origination, etc.;

for [if one applies the logic] by repetition—of substance and quality, of quality and action, of substance, quality, and action, and of those two and those two—the universal characterized as *sattva* would not exist.
Therefore, it is incorrect to say that "being" (*sat*) is indistinguishable among the three [categories].

Likewise, [the properties] "impermanent," "substantial," "effect," "cause," and "possessing generality and particularity" should not apply to generality itself; for it has been stated in your own treatise: "Existent, impermanent, substantial, effect, cause, and possessing generality and particularity—this is the common characteristic of substances, qualities, and actions" (VS 1.1.8). Thus, there is no distinction between substances, qualities, and actions regarding these properties.

If it is argued that, in that case, substances, qualities, and actions would consequently be non-distinct, the following distinction is stated: they are not indeed without distinction, because of the difference between initiating and not initiating [new entities]. Substances initiate another substance, and qualities initiate another quality;
however, there is no action that is to be accomplished by action. (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.8)

Furthermore, there is another [distinction]: due to the difference in their definitions (*lakṣaṇabheda*). "Possessing action, possessing qualities, and being an inherent cause" is the definition of substance (*dravya*); "residing in a substance, devoid of qualities, and not being a cause in conjunctions and disjunctions, being independent" is the definition of quality (*guṇa*); "residing in a single substance, devoid of qualities, and an independent cause in conjunctions and disjunctions" is the definition of action (*karman*) (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.15).

Likewise, based on the distinction between contradiction and non-contradiction: a substance is non-contradictory with respect to both its effect and its cause; a quality is [non-contradictory] in both ways; and an action is contradictory with respect to its effect. Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.8.

Furthermore, the entire collection of reasons for the diversity of substances, qualities, and actions— beginning with these [arguments]— would result in being purposeless due to the absence of *viśeṣa*.
Thus, in this way, there may be generalities and particularities of substance and substance, but not of quality and action. [Gṛhīta-satya-prakaraṇa]
Likewise, in the subsequent cases as well,
that which is proximate to the intellect— whether it be the agent or the object— is what is referred to by the term "it" (saḥ).
For "conjunction" (sannatā) belongs to substance and substance; only there could the general and particular properties exist, not in the case of quality and action.
Thus, there would be an absence of the general property of existence and the particular properties such as being the originator of a substance for those two [quality and action].

Likewise, there would be conjunction between sand and diamond, and for them there could be general and particular properties, but not for earth and water; this applies up to [the case of] things of the same genus.
In the case of a specific [object] being grasped, there would be two specificities;
they would abide as specificities.
And here the reading should be "karmaṇaśca"; [the text] reads "bhāvaṃ ca" in Prajñākaragupta’s commentary and "sattvaṃ" in Yaśovijaya’s commentary.
The passage beginning from "sāmānya" up to "sattvalakṣaṇam," which is contained within these brackets, does not exist in the Ya manuscripts;
[it begins with] "ārambhamārambhabhedātya" and "bhāgedyanapekṣaṃ pra."
And that which is opposed to its cause does not destroy the substance, neither the effect nor the cause— Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.10.

Its explanation is as follows: a substance does not destroy its own effect, nor does it destroy its own cause; the meaning is that there is no relationship of "slayer and slain" between two substances that have entered into the state of cause and effect, because the destruction of a substance occurs only through the destruction of its substratum or the destruction of the conjunctions that initiate it. This is the sense. The term *vadhate* (it destroys) is a Vedic (Sautra) usage—Vaiśeṣika Sūtra Upaskāra, p. 20.
The qualities—Vaiśeṣika Sūtra:

"The effect [is established] by the other. Another says: "Just as there is a proximity between two substances due to their connection with substanceness (*dravyatva*), so too will there be [a proximity] among substance, quality, and action due to their connection with existence (*sattā*)."

As it has been said: "That because of which there is the notion 'existent' (sat) with respect to substances, qualities, and actions, and which is a distinct entity from substances, qualities, and actions, is Being (sattā)" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.2.7–8).

To this we reply: Even regarding two substances, I have spoken to you out of compassion for you, with a mind softened by pity and in accordance with your own mental disposition; yet do not place your hope therein, for even that is not tenable. For you, who maintain that universals and particulars are produced by the proximity (*āsatti*) of the intellect, there can be no particularity in the absence of a universal. Such proximity exists between sand and diamond because they are both permeated by the universal of "earthiness" (*pārthivatva*); thus, sand, stones, clods of earth, diamonds, and the like would possess both universals and particulars. However, this is not the case for earth and water, because one of them lacks the universal of earthiness.

By that same causal sequence, there is such proximity between a lump of clay and a jar, but not between clay and sand; likewise, proceeding further and further, this applies only to two atoms possessing similar genus, quality, and action, but not even to those two [atoms] when their proximity is excluded by ultimate particularity (*antyaviśeṣa*) and inherence (*samavāya*).

Therefore, due to the absence of generality, there is an absence of particularity; in every case, both are absent. However, if proximity were defined as "contact with an object," then only earth, jars, colors, and so forth would possess the status of generality and particularity, and not other generalities and particulars.
The principle that "the universal and the particular must belong to two atoms of quality and action" continues to apply here.

Thus, there is such proximity between a jar and its shards, but not between a lump of clay and a jar; likewise between a shard and a fragment, but not between a jar and a fragment; between a fragment and a pebble, but not between a jar and a pebble; between a pebble and sand, but not between a fragment and sand; between sand and dust, but not between dust and a pebble; between dust and a minute particle (*truṭi*), but not between sand and a minute particle; between a minute particle and an atom (*paramāṇu*), but not between dust and an atom.
Alternatively, it applies between one jar and another jar, but not between a jar and a shard, and so forth.

[The relation] belongs only to those two atoms that are inherent in the white color of the earth-atom, and not to the blue and white colors, their states, their universals, their qualities, or their actions— such as those belonging to water and earth atoms—
and so on, up to "nor even to those two [atoms]," etc., until "of those whose proximity has been rejected."

Since the final *viśeṣas* (particularities) are characterized by the manifestation of the cognition of difference between two things that possess identical genus, quality, and action, and since their proximity (*pratyāsatti*) is likewise set aside—that is, removed—by the inherence (*samavāya*) of those [genus, etc. in them, how can there be a context for the cognition of those [final *viśeṣas*]? Therefore, due to the absence of universals (*sāmānya*), there is an absence of particulars (*viśeṣa*); thus, there is an absence of both in all cases. Consequently, from the point where it was stated that "substance, quality, and action have neither universal nor particular" up to the limit of "the two atoms," this sequence serves to remind us of the absence of universals and particulars as established through the force of the arguments presented in the intervening discussion.
Likewise, in the subsequent [passages] as well,
[the reading] *netrāpyāyana-vat-tva-ālatva-abhāvāt* is [to be understood].
The qualities and actions exist only in atoms, but not even in those two [atoms], because their proximity is already excluded by the inherence of ultimate particularity (*antyaviśeṣa*).

Therefore, due to the absence of universals (*sāmānya*), there is an absence of particulars (*viśeṣa*); thus, in all cases, both are absent. However, if proximity were defined as the "adherence of meaning" (*arthāśleṣa*), then the status of universal and particular would apply only to earth, jars, colors, and so forth, and not to other universals and particulars.
The two [terms] beginning with *araṇva* exist in the *pra*. *raṇavārevabhā* *raṇvādereva ya* *vartete pra*.
In the *Vimalaprabhā*, it is "of the two *vākalas*";
in the *Bhāṣya*, it is "of the two *tuṭis*"; likewise in what follows as well.
In the manuscripts of Ya, too, the word *tuṭi* is seen almost everywhere at the beginning;
[the reading] "of the two minute particles moving" (*vāyinoraṇvoḥ*) is found in Bhā,
while in Ya it is "of the two minute particles moving" (*vāyinoraṇvoḥ*).
The weapon of the intellect that severs [ignorance], p. 29, l.
Here he says: That proximity (*pratyāsatti*) is of two kinds—through connection with an object (*artha*) and through connection with a non-object (*anartha*).

Among these, that characterized as a non-object has been described as the apprehension of the inclusive cognition (*anuvṛttibuddhi*) regarding reality, substance, earth, clay, jar, and so forth; for generality, particularity, and inherence lack the status of being objects.
However, that characterized as an object consists in the connection with substances, qualities, and actions, because these are designated as "objects."
As it has been said: "The term 'object' (artha) refers to substances, qualities, and actions" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 8.2.3).
In this regard, the definition of substance (dravya) begins with "That which possesses activity" (vaiśeṣika-sūtra 1.1.15), and so forth.

And its definition according to those distinctions is as follows: earth possesses color, taste, smell, and touch; water possesses color, taste, and touch, and is liquid and cohesive; fire possesses color and touch; air possesses touch (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 2.1.1–4).

That which possesses the fourfold qualities beginning with color is earth; that which is devoid of smell and characterized by an abundance of liquidity and cohesion is water; fire is devoid of liquidity, cohesion, taste, and smell; air is devoid of color. A quality is defined as that which resides in a substance and so forth.
That object which is apprehended by the sense of hearing is sound; Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 2.2.21.
That object which is grasped by the eye is "form" (rūpa);
by such a fixed definition of the object, the universal and the particular would both exist—
this refers to the substance as the object of action (*karmavastu*).
"Substance has the definition: that which possesses action, possesses quality, and is an inherent cause"—*Vaiśeṣika Sūtra*.
"Moist"—*Vaiśeṣika Sūtra*.
"Air possesses touch"—*Vaiśeṣika Sūtra*.

That which inheres in a substance, is devoid of qualities, and is not a cause in conjunctions and disjunctions, being independent [of other causes], is the definition of a quality— Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.16.
"The object of apprehension is that word" (bhāṣya);
"the object of apprehension is the word" (yā).

To this it is replied: if proximity were defined merely as the connection with an object, then the status of being a universal or a particular would belong only to earth, jars, color, and so forth; the meaning is that [this distinction] would be established solely by the act of defining and specifying characteristics.

It follows that there is no "generality-and-particularity-ness" in other generalities and particulars; nevertheless, even so, there would be the occurrence of its own object as a generality and particular, and that [occurrence] is subject to the aforementioned defects.

Therefore, the Pradhāna, which is entirely internal, situated in its own form, established, and independent—[for it is not the case that] the characteristics of the cognitions of inclusion and exclusion, such as substantiality, earth-ness, quality-ness, or color-ness, would not exist for it.

Furthermore, the Vaiśeṣikas and those who maintain that substance is a collection of qualities (*guṇasamudāyadravyavādins*) accept that universals and particulars are characterized by similarity, persistence, and cessation. What is the intended meaning [of our critique]? The intention is this: if one accepts universals and particulars as being produced by a "presence" (*sattā*) characterized by the connection of objects (*arthāśleṣa*), then there would be no cognition or apprehension of the persistence and exclusion of reality (*tattvānuvṛttivyāvṛtti*). Conversely, if one accepts [universals and particulars] as being produced by the persistence and cessation of reality itself, then there would be an absence of the proximity (*pratyāsatti*) produced by the connection of objects. Thus, due to this contradiction, [the two positions] cannot be logically established. This is the intended meaning.
Nevertheless, it would follow that [the cause] assumes the general and particular forms of its own objects,
and that [consequence] has already been stated as a fault;
therefore, the Pradhāna remains established in its own form as the internal factor, independent in every respect— for indeed, it does not [depend on anything else].
Because it has the nature of qualities,
the cognition of continuity is conceptualized.

In this context, regarding the reading *prakalpete* in the Bhāṣya (bhā.), the meaning should be understood as "the universal and the particular are not conceptualized. However, regarding the reading *prakalpyate* in the Yaśomitra (ya.), the connection should be understood as "the state of being universal and particular is not conceptualized" (*na prakalpyate*).
Furthermore, even so, there is the occurrence of the universal and the particular within their own respective domains.

Even though there is no existence characterized by the connection of meaning (*arthāśleṣa*), the two previously mentioned conceptual constructions—that "the universal belongs only to its own object" and "the particular belongs only to its own object"—are incurred;

and that [non-existence] possesses the aforementioned defect. Furthermore, that occurrence of the universal and particular within their own objects is indeed subject to the aforementioned defect: if it belongs to its own object, there is a contradiction with being a universal;
if it is a universal, then it is not the self [of the particular], because a universal has multiple referents.
Now, the self (*ātman*) is therefore not the universal (*sāmānya*), because the self is a single entity.

Or, the self itself is the universal, since form (*rūpa*) and so forth constitute the nature (*ātman*) of the jar and other objects, being the effects of that collection [of qualities]. This being the case, there would be a division of the self—such as "form, form, and the collection of form and so forth," and so on—and the same applies to the particular (*viśeṣa*).
If it has itself as its object, there is a contradiction with its being a particular (*viśeṣa*):

if it is a particular, then it cannot be the self, because a particular is other [than the self] either by virtue of its qualities (*guṇa*) or by virtue of time (*kāla*); otherwise, it would follow that jars and the like would be universals (*sāmānya*).
If, on the other hand, it is the self, then it cannot be a particular, because the self is one.

Now, it might be argued: "The faults of contradiction regarding identity and difference do not apply, because it is asserted that the particular (*viśeṣa*) is nothing other than the Self itself; if the particular is dependent solely upon the Self, then since the one is the other, there is no 'becoming otherwise' of the Self, and thus the previously mentioned faults—such as its becoming a non-Self—do not attach. [This leads to] the consequence that the particular would become a universal with respect to its own object, as stated previously in the *Bhāṣya*, *Vikaraṇa*, *Dvaya*, *Līna*, *Pūrva-ukta*, *Vikaraṇa*, *Pāda*, *Raṃga*, and *Hīna*.
Thus it has been said; see Vikalpa-vinodini, page 11, line 6,
and page 22, line 6.
Without the phrase "doṣohī," there is only one [reading] in Bhāṣya.

Here, the proponent of the theory of inherence (saṃsargavādī) says: "If I were to say that the universal is the self and the particular is the self, then these same faults would apply to me as well, just as they do for the Sāṅkhyas and Buddhists."
Furthermore, I do not hold such a position;

rather, for me, the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*) are absolutely distinct from the categories of substance, quality, and action. For one who maintains that there is no cognition of a qualified object (*viśeṣya*) without the prior apprehension of its qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), and who thus asserts that something is "existent" due to its connection with existence (*sattva*), or a "substance" due to its connection with substantiality (*dravyatva*), and so forth—how could the faults belonging to the position of those who [accept] universals and particulars as their own objects apply? Even in this case, since the position of those who maintain universals and particulars as objects belonging to others has been refuted, what recourse remains? Enough of this digression.
°vāvīya °vartmyaretebhā °vatparete ya°

The phrase "completely distinct from actions" is intended to conclude the previously stated fault regarding the relationship between qualifier and qualified when the qualifier has not been apprehended; we shall connect this by stating that one must understand the object— such as a jar— to be entirely internal and free from these faults.

Having repeatedly investigated by every means and in every way that state—whether as a universal (*sāmānya*) or a particular (*viśeṣa*)—one must rely upon that very internal essence of the jar, which exists in a specific form capable of performing functions such as holding and carrying water, while being common to other objects; one should not rely on external factors such as existence (*sattva*), substantiality (*dravyatva*), or the universals and particulars pertaining to self and others, which depend on recurrence among other jars.

If it were so, then that [identity] would persist even in those [different times]; and consequently, due to total identity, it would be exactly the same thing, just as a single jar remains one and the same from the forenoon to the afternoon. This is because its essential nature and configuration remain unaltered—as it has been said: "Between an internal and an external rule, the internal rule is stronger."

That person who acts with foresight, having risen in the morning, performs his own duties first, then those of his relatives, then those of his friends, and finally those of others; Pāṇini, Mahābhāṣya 1.1.56.

Why is that [the jar] internal? Because it resides within its own form; its own form consists of the neck and so forth, and because it resides therein, and because the house—which is capable of fetching water and the like—is subordinate to it, that [jar] alone is what should be grasped.

Why is it primary? Because the general and the particular exist for the sake of it, like the clothing and ornaments intended for a bride; for the operation of conceptualizing generalities and particulars is indeed for the sake of the jar.
Because the universal and the particular are subordinate—like the husks and straw that accompany grain—they are to be discarded;

furthermore, it is precisely that manifestation as a jar (*ghaṭabhavana*) which is to be grasped, for it is established, being situated within the Self itself. It is not like those two, the universal and the particular, which are mobile, unstable, dependent on something else, and due to their instability are non-entities (*avastu*), like the son of a barren woman.

Where, then, do these two [the universal and the particular] migrate? They migrate among the real substances and so forth, because of their connection with the categories of real substance, earth, clay, and potness; for it has been stated by the Teacher that there arises in the pot the cognition: "It is a real substance, it is earthen, it is a clay pot.
But for one whose self is occupied with the fetching of water and other functions belonging to the existence of the pot, where could there be any further migration?
Whichever state of existence one has gone to, having gone to that very state and having conceptualized it in every way and by every means— [as stated in] the *Nayacakra-vṛtti*, p. 92—
one [remains within] the internal sphere of investigation.

If there were a dependence on persistence (*anuvṛtti*) regarding other jars, then that [persistence] would also persist in them; and consequently, because of the universal [nature of that persistence], it would be the very same [jar], just as, for example, it is one and the same jar in the forenoon and the afternoon.
The nature of that arrangement—

that a rule characterized by external factors (*bahiraṅga*) is unestablished with respect to a rule characterized by internal factors (*antaraṅga*)— is this maxim (*paribhāṣā*), which serves many purposes.
This must certainly be performed; and how is it that this [performance] is established by worldly convention? It is observed that the world conforms to each individual limb.
That alone is the state of being the primary cause; and because of that state of being the primary cause, O God, [it is] Yaṃ.
... *palādi* ...

*pra* ... because it is established within the self (*ātman*). Furthermore, the author of the *Nayacakravṛtti* will cite this statement of the Teacher (*ācāryīya*) again later in this way—as it was said: "Due to the connection with an existent substance (*sad-dravya*), such as earth, clay, or a jar, there arises the cognition regarding the jar that 'the substance is earthen' or 'the jar is made of clay'" (*Nayacakravṛtti*, p. 422-1).
And because of its independence, that very entity is what will be connected [to each term] everywhere;

for that manifestation as a jar does not depend on another substance such as a jar, or a cloth, or other substances like jars and cloths— just as, according to the doctrine of universals (*sāmānya*) characterized by inclusion and exclusion (*anuvṛtti-vyāvṛtti*), there is dependence on other objects like jars and cloths for that purpose, and according to the doctrine of particulars (*viśeṣa*) characterized by exclusion, there is dependence on other substances like cloths for that purpose.

However, according to the view that maintains worldly conventional discourse (*laukikānuvartivyavahāranayavāda*), because the manifestation of the nature of a jar occurs in close proximity and is self-dependent, there is no dependence upon others; this he demonstrates: "Indeed, it has no need for conformity (*anuvṛtti*) with respect to other jars, nor does it have a need for exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) with respect to other substances such as cloth and the like, by way of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). If it were to have such dependence, then that jar would conform even to those other jars."
Furthermore, there is no dependence [on other pots], because that nature of the pot is established by its own inherent capacity alone.
If a pot were to depend on other pots, it would persist within those other pots as well;

consequently, due to the persistence of that universal essence, it would be identical to them, and even another pot would become that very same pot, because of the persistence of that reality—just like the nature of a pot. Such would be the fault, even in the case of pots separated by space, just as with pots separated by time.
He demonstrates this as follows: for example, one and the same jar exists in both the forenoon and the afternoon.

Nor does the jar depend upon the persistence of its essence (*tattvānuvṛtti*), because if the nature of the jar itself is not established, the persistence of its essence cannot be established. For that very reason, it does not depend upon the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) from cloth and other things, since that [exclusion] would be contingent upon it. Therefore he says: "And because it depends on the nature of its own configuration (*sanniveśa*), its dependence on that [exclusion] is useless, as it would result in the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).
Likewise, there is no dependence on a particular (*viśeṣa*) either; for, as has been stated, it would not even exist [as such].

Just as previously established by worldly convention, independent of distinctions between prior and posterior, that which exists as "primordial nature" (*prakṛti*) or as "something else," being eternal and not subject to dissolution, exists as a real entity (*sat*); it should be understood that this very thing is the reality (*vastu*). What is the use of this [distinction]? Whether it be a cause, whether it be an effect, whether it be a universal (*sāmānya*), or whether it be a particular (*viśeṣa*), since it is dependent upon that [reality], its dependence on those [categories] is redundant.

The persistence [of the universal] in other jars and its exclusion from cloth and so forth depends upon the specific configuration of the parts of a jar; thus, it is logical that the persistence depends on the jar and the exclusion depends on the cloth and so forth.
However, for the jar itself, dependence on persistence and exclusion would be useless, because it is established by its own nature.
It might be argued: "Even the jar acquires its selfhood in dependence on 'jar-ness,' and the persistence of that [universal] also depends on the acquisition of the jar's selfhood."
And this is incorrect, because it incurs the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).

This conceptualization incurs the fault of mutual dependence between the persistence of the pot and the universal "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*); and effects that involve mutual dependence do not function, as it has been said: "A boat tied to another boat does not serve as a protection for either"—thus, the universal does not depend [on the individual].
Likewise, there is no dependence on a particular (viśeṣa) for this [the acquisition of the self-nature of a jar];

just as there is no dependence on a universal (sāmānya), so too there is none on a particular. By the method of the reason already stated, he extends [this principle] to the particular; and we have already applied it accordingly according to the sense.
The application according to the text is as follows: for indeed, that very thing would not exist, as has been stated;
for it has no requirement for exclusion from cloth and other such things—if it did, it would itself be excluded from them.

Furthermore, because it would be superior to everything, even the jar itself would not exist; and since that [universal] depends upon the nature of the arrangement of both the jar and the cloth—just as in the case of the jar and the cloth—the dependence upon it is useless, as it would result in the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). All of this should be extended by analogy.
*rāpekṣyā pra* (corrupt).
Having ceased from the state of being a jar,
one should look toward the jar as it exists in its own nature.
That which depends on cloth and so forth [depends] only on the generic part (sāmānyāṃśa), without [the specific].

Comparison: Furthermore, because [the object] would be superior to everything, that very [comparison] would not exist—*Nayacakravṛtti*, p. 34, l. 13. And since comparison depends on the nature of the thing to be compared (*śāsvarūpa*), its dependence [on comparison] is useless, as it would result in the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).

Likewise, it has no dependence even upon a particular (viśeṣa); for if it did, that very thing would not exist. As it has been said: "Just as previously established by worldly convention, that which exists—whether called 'primordial nature' (prakṛti) or something else—is independent of prior and posterior distinctions, eternal, and does not undergo dissolution; that existent entity is to be understood as the very reality (vastu). What does it matter whether it is a cause, an effect, a universal (sāmānya), or a particular (viśeṣa)?"
Exclusion alone; exclusion alone;
[it is] precisely in the exclusion of cloth and so forth.
The fault of [the word] *yatvāt* is to be supplied; except for Bhā and Hī, it is not elsewhere—except for Bhā; for the purpose of crossing over; Ḍe and Līṃ.
To avoid this circularity, [the opponent might argue that] the *pāda*, *viśeṣa*, *raṅga*, and *hīna* [are established first]; however, this results in mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*),
and mutually dependent effects cannot be logically established.
"Just as a boat tied to another boat does not serve as a means of rescue for the other"— thus it is stated in the *Patañjala-Mahābhāṣya* 1.1.1.
It might be like blood;
see page 32,
line 2, regarding "pada" and so forth.
Furthermore: because the becoming of the jar as a self precedes [the universal and the particular].
For the becoming of the jar exists prior to both the universal and the particular.
If it is asked how that is so, it is just as it is well-known in the world.

"World-renowned" (*lokaprasiddha*) means that which is well-known in the world; just as it is known in the world, so too is the existence of a jar, and it is known in the world that a jar is merely its form and other such qualities. That alone is "prior," because it does not depend on prior or posterior distinctions.

But what are these prior and posterior distinctions? For the Sāṅkhyas, the prior distinctions extend from the jar up to primordial nature (*prakṛti*); for the Vaiśeṣikas, they extend to "Being" (*sat*). The "other" distinctions extend up to the ultimate particularity (*antyaviśeṣa*), as imagined by the Sāṅkhyas and Vaiśeṣikas. Therefore, he says: "whether as primordial nature or as something else."

Or, according to the Buddhist, [the object] is entirely different [from its past state] because of its momentariness and because it exists in the present; for the root *vṛt* has the sense of "to exist," as stated in the rule: "The roots *as*, *bhū*, *vid*, *pad*, *pady*, and *vṛt*—these six when joined together—have the meaning of 'existence' (*sattā*).

For this very reason, [the object] is eternal, since jars, cloths, and so forth persist even during the past and future times, constantly participating in practical activities such as the carrying of water.

It does not undergo dissolution; it does not enter into its own self like water and waves, nor does it suffer absolute destruction like the flame of a lamp. It does not partake in either of these two types of dissolution, because a substance exists through its various modifications, and a modification is likewise inseparable from the substance. This is because the doctrines of the absolute arising of the non-existent and the absolute destruction of the existent lack both logical reason and illustrative examples, and because in the doctrine of absolute permanence, there can be no manifestation or concealment of attributes.

For that [reality] exists at all times in that form, because the root *vṛt* has the meaning of "existence" (*sattā*). He explains this very point: "Who indeed could be able to reach the end of arguments? And he says: "All viewpoints (*nayāḥ*) are true when their own subject matter is expressed; they are delusions (*moha*) when examining the subject matter of another. Furthermore, one who has not seen the time of the ultimate truth (*adṛṣṭasamaya*) might say, 'It is either true or false,' but the one of right intellect (*sanmati*) distinguishes between what is true and what is false. (Sanmati-tarka-prakaraṇa 1)
"Who indeed knows this? Or what is the use of knowing it?"—this shows that "existence" (*bhāva*) and "functioning" (*vṛtti*) are synonyms, as previously stated.
He concludes by reaffirming: "That which is this"—he points back to it—showing that one must understand that the very *bhāva* thus explained is that same reality and nothing else.
That reality is internal, primary, independent, prior, and present;

the word *iti* serves either to indicate completion or to signify restriction, meaning that this alone is the sufficient object, neither more nor less than this. As for those others who conceive of something else—whether as cause alone, effect alone, universal alone, particular alone, both together, one being subordinate while the other is primary, or that neither exists at all—[they are in error].

What is the harm in this? Whether it be the cause or the effect, what fault is there? For indeed, something is seen to be both cause and effect; for example, the atom (*paramāṇu*) is the cause of the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth, while the lump of clay (*mṛtpiṇḍa*), the pot-sherd (*śivaka*), and so forth, are the effects of that [lump], because they are produced from its differentiation.
In this way, even for dyads, triads, and so on, there exists the relationship of cause and effect through aggregation and differentiation.
This is because the generalities (*sāmānya*) of substance, space, time, and mode do not transcend their own and other modes of existence.
Because its nature consists of the manifestation of both self and other as distinct, it is indeed a "distinction" (*viśeṣa*).
Thus, both [self and other] exist as either subordinate or primary depending on the speaker's intention regarding their simultaneity, independence, or dependence;

yet neither exists in isolation, because a single, absolute form that is not mutually interdependent is unestablished, due to the experience of being free from such defects as non-establishment (*asiddhi*).

The term *pūrvaghaṭa* is well-known in the world; it appears in Prajñākaragupta, Lokānanda, Bhāsarvajña, and Vidyākaraśānti, but not elsewhere [in the other commentaries]. In Pātrasvāmin’s commentary, it reads *sattvārthāḥ*.
The seven meanings are: Ḍe, Līṃ, together with their own meanings; Vi, Raṃ, Hīṃ;
the state of the cloth; and Ya.
Without the manifestation of substances, there is no manifestation of the deity; in the doctrine [of their identity], they are not distinct.
...by way of discourse ... due to the non-existence of concealment and non-existence ... due to concealment ... līṃ.
Since existence proceeds by means of the king, who indeed could bring an end to these debates? And it is said:

"All viewpoints (*nayāḥ*) are true insofar as they are true according to their own verbal expression; however, through delusion (*moha*), they are false when analyzing another [viewpoint]. But one who has not seen the time [of the perfect teaching] again and again—having not seen the *samaya*—distinguishes [them] as either true or false.
(Sanmati-tarka-prakaraṇa 1.28) For who knows this? Or what is the use of knowing it?
This is the form of the root *mnā*, meaning "repeated practice" (Dhātupāṭha 929), preceded by the prefix *prati*;
it is neither less nor more than what precedes.

Having established this distinction, [the author] states that it is precisely he who, relying on the conventional perspective (*vyavahāranaya*), speaks as a worldly person: "Who indeed could bring an end to these doctrines?"—that is, who could effect their total cessation (*uccheda*)? This refers to those who hold extremist views (*ekāntavāda*).

What is the reason? For the reasons stated by the Sāṅkhyas—that the effect exists in the cause—such as "because that which is non-existent cannot be produced," "because there is the grasping of a material cause," "because not everything is possible from everything," "because the capable [cause] produces what is possible," and "because of the nature of the cause" (Sāṅkhya Kārikā 9), do not hold; nor do those stated by the Vaiśeṣikas—that the effect is non-existent because of the absence of action, quality, and designation (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 9).

1.1 Statements such as these, or those stated by the Buddhists—such as "pots and the like are momentary because their birth depends upon conditions"—can be refuted by one another, since the succession of intellectual excellence among the learned does not terminate in the unseen (adṛṣṭa). To provide proof for this point, he says: "And he says," meaning that I do not speak merely from my own imagination; rather, others also speak in this same way.

All viewpoints (nayās) are true when their own specific assertions are considered; they become delusions (mohas) when analyzing the perspective of another. However, one who has not seen the ultimate truth (samaya) may, through his own intellect, judge them as either true or false.
(Sanmati 1.1)

28. Because they are true with respect to their own objects, they are unshakable; therefore, attempts to shake them are futile, since [the opponents] lack an understanding of their nature as existing in a manifold state (anekānta). Thus, Master Siddhasena says that one who has not perceived this principle divides them [into categories], thinking "this is truly real" or "this is truly unreal," for the sake of the worldly person.

The effect exists [prior to its production], because (1) what is non-existent cannot be produced, (2) there is the grasping of a material cause, (3) there is no possibility of everything arising from everything, (4) the efficient cause produces only that for which it has the capacity, and (5) because of the nature of the cause. *Sāṅkhyakārikā* 9.

"Except for elsewhere—because it culminates in the unseen (adṛṣṭaniṣṭhatvāt). "Culmination" (niṣṭhā), "completion" (samāpti), and "end" (anta) are synonyms; thus, the meaning is "because it culminates in the unseen," that is, because its limit is the unseen.
We say:
all viewpoints (*nayas*) are true insofar as they express their own designated objects; however, they are delusions when used for the investigation of others.
Furthermore, one who has not seen the *samaya* (the ultimate truth) may regard them as either true or false. (Sanmati-tarka-prakaraṇa 1.28)

And thus, there is no fixed rule regarding the existence or non-existence of the effect in the cause; for even when the cause is present, the result may or may not occur due to the presence or absence of [auxiliary factors], and because the fruits of efforts such as service are not invariably certain when the cause is absent.
For example: the flower of the *vātakarkoṭakī* plant is seen to be non-existent [at the time it appears];
likewise, other things as well—even an object that has been inferred with great effort by skillful inferents [may later be found to be otherwise].
"By others who are more proficient, it is established in quite another way," as stated in *Vākyapadīya* 1.34.
The meaning is that if [the argument] were sublated by another inference, there would be an infinite regress of inferences; therefore, worldly consensus (*lokaprasiddhi*) alone is the authority.
By saying "Who indeed knows this?", he shows that its attainment is impossible; and by "What is the use of knowing this?", he shows the absence of purpose.

Since the proponents of the ten-membered syllogism (*daśāvayava-vādin*) hold that the result at the end is the removal of doubt—provided the thesis, reason, example, application, and conclusion are preceded by inquiry, doubt, the possibility of attainment, and purpose—it follows that worldly practice is established.

Therefore, let the definitions of logic (nyāya-lakṣaṇa) composed by those who are impoverished of the syllables of reason, who create deceptive fictions, and who fall into the errors of over-extension and under-extension regarding the present day, be abandoned.
For even an object that has been inferred with effort by skilled inferents is established in a completely different way by others who are more proficient. (Vākyapadīya 1.34).
Established as being without a basis, through knowledge. (Bhāṣya:
established as being without a basis; Yaśomitra:
through knowledge.)
The correct attainment of [the removal of] doubt consists of the five members:
the proposition (*pratijñā*), the reason (*hetu*), the example (*udāharaṇa*), the application (*upanaya*), and the conclusion (*nigamana*). (Nyāyasūtra 1.1.32)

Some Naiyāyikas declare that a formal argument (vākya) consists of ten members: inquiry (jijñāsā), doubt (saṃśaya), possibility of attainment (śakyaprāpti), purpose (prayojana), and the removal of doubt (saṃśayavyudāsa)— thus it is stated in the Nyāyasūtrabhāṣya, Book 1,
Chapter 1.
32. *Vyāpty-avyāpty-atiprasaṅga* (or *vyāpy-atiprasaṅga*), according to the Bhāṣya.

And thus, there is no fixed rule regarding the existence or non-existence of the effect in the cause. Having established this, by this same logic, just as there is no such restriction as "only the cause, not the effect"; "only the effect, not the cause"; "only the universal, not the particular"; "only the particular, not the universal"; "both"; "one subordinate to the other"; or "the absence of both"—according to the method already stated—likewise, there is also no restriction that the effect must either exist or not exist in the cause.
Why? If the effect exists, then the restriction "it is only the cause" does not hold, because the effect also exists.

How so? Because the status of being a cause and being an effect is dependent upon activity (*kriyā*), there is an absence of the effect when there is an absence of the cause, and an absence of the cause when there is an absence of the effect.
Thus, if the cause exists, then the effect cannot exist, because the cause itself exists.
This same reasoning should be applied to the cases where both the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*) are absent, whether one or the other is subordinate, or both are subordinate.

In this regard, the intention is that for those who assert that the effect is either existent, non-existent, or both existent and non-existent in the cause, a lack of restriction has been stated; indeed, the absence of both [extremes] when one or the other is subordinate has also already been stated. What is the reason for the lack of restriction—namely, that the effect is either existent or non-existent in the cause? The reasons are "only when the cause exists" and "by way of existence and non-existence," respectively, though these do not correspond to the order of the terms.

Because the effect exists only when the cause exists, there is no fixed rule that the effect must exist [only] when the cause exists; because the effect does not exist even when the cause exists, there is no fixed rule that it must exist [only] when the cause exists;
and because the existence or non-existence of the effect when the cause is absent is not fixed—why is this so? Because the results of efforts such as service and the like are not invariably certain.

For in the world, a lack of certainty regarding results is observed among farmers, merchants, royal servants, artisans, and others who are engaged in causes such as agriculture, trade, service, and craftsmanship;
this is seen both when the cause is present and when it is absent.

For example, even in the context of an inference—such as "the flower of the *vātakarkoṭakī* is a cause of fruit and thus possesses the effect [within itself], because it is a flower, like the mango flower"—it is nonetheless observed that the effect is non-existent [prior to its production].
The effect is non-existent because it is "that in which the fruit is non-existent"; thus it is called *asatkārya*.
Since its lack of fruit is observed, this inference contradicts what is perceived;
therefore, that [effect] is non-existent.
The non-abiding in the existence or non-existence of the effect;
[this is] the non-existence of the existence of the effect.
Even this, O Bhāratī, is non-existence. Liṅga.
In this context, there may also be the reading "or rather, non-existence itself" (*asattvam eva vā*); furthermore,
from the effect, [one infers] existence, and from that,
the state of being a cause (*kāraṇabhāva*).
By the two [terms] "non-creation" and "non-existence," according to their respective order, [it is established that] only when [the cause] exists [does the effect arise].
Because [the effect] exists only when [the cause] exists;
as in the case of the farmer and so forth, and likewise in what follows.
...of those engaged in crafts and so forth,
for the practice of crafts and so forth.
If it is argued that [the term] *vātakakkeṭikī* (Bhāṣya), *vātakakoṭika* (Yājñika), or [the word] is indistinct (*avyakta*).

It might be thought: "The fruits of the *vāta*, *karkoṭakī*, *vañjula*, *japākusuma*, and so forth, are unmanifest (*avyakta*). If this is argued, we say no; because the effect of the manifest would then be the effect of the unmanifest, it would be equivalent to non-existence. Consequently, even seeds and the like would lack causality altogether, since they do not produce [the fruit] at all times. Thus, the cause itself would be a non-cause, due to the absence of the invariable concomitance between cause and effect and the lack of a fixed rule regarding the existence or non-existence of the effect. Furthermore, since the operation of a sentence is directed toward an injunction for the sake of knowing what is unknown, at that stage [of the injunction], the object has not yet been produced; therefore, they are called "exceptions" (*apavāda*) as effects.
And this is incorrect, because the effect of manifestation is equivalent to non-existence due to being the effect of the unmanifest.
[Question: What is that which has manifestation as its effect? [Answer: It is the effect.

Because that effect has an unmanifested effect, it is equivalent to non-existence; its state [of being so] is "equivalence to non-existence. Therefore, due to this equivalence to non-existence, there is no such thing as an unmanifested effect. Alternatively, manifestation (*vyakti*) is the effect; thus, manifestation itself is the effect. That which has an unmanifested effect is an "unmanifested effect" (*avyaktakārya*). Because it has an unmanifested effect, it is equivalent to non-existence. Therefore, like the flowers and fruits of the *vātaka-karkoṭakī* and other such plants, it is non-existent; there is no such thing as an unmanifested effect.
(Note: *karkoṭikī*, as in the manuscript, is corrected to *karkoṭakī*.)

If it is argued that [the effect exists], we say no; because the effect of the manifest is identical to the effect of the unmanifest in its non-existence, even seeds and the like would lack causality since they do not produce [the effect] at certain times. Thus, even a cause is effectively a non-cause, due to the absence of an invariable relation between cause and effect and the lack of a fixed rule regarding the existence or non-existence of the effect. Furthermore, since the operation of a sentence is directed toward enjoining the knowledge of what is unknown, at that stage [of inquiry], there is no scope for an exception (*apavāda*) because the object has not yet been produced.

And here, "the unmanifest effect" (*tadavyakta-kārya*) refers to that unmanifest which is an effect; because it is an unmanifest effect, it is "equal to non-existence"—this is the construction of the sentence, and it appears that even the literal reading is entirely correct.
It might be argued: "that which acts is a cause."
As it has been said: "Bhāguri desires the lengthening of the vowel in the case of the roots *ṣṭhivu* and *ṣivu* when followed by a suffix with the marker *lyuṭ*;
and the followers of Śaunaka declare this [lengthening] for the root *kṛ* as well, in the sense of both the agent and the abstract state.
Therefore, because of the non-performance of its own function, there is indeed a lack of causality."
This also is not tenable, because it follows that even seeds and the like would have no causal efficiency at all, since they do not produce [their effects] at certain times;
the word "iti" here signifies a reason (*yasmāt*).

For even those seeds, when left for up to three years, lack the capacity to produce sprouts and so forth; by the inclusion of the word "ādi" (and the like), this applies to clay and other materials as well in the production of jars and the like.

In that case, what is the fault? Let even a cause be a non-cause, since there would be no invariable concomitance between cause and effect. This being so, farmers and others who have observed the causal relationship between seeds, sprouts, and so forth—even when that relationship has been seen only once—would not undertake activity for that purpose again; for in the absence of the instrument (the result), there would necessarily be an absence of the cause. And this is undesirable.

Furthermore, it arises again in the world—because there is no fixed rule regarding the existence or non-existence of the effect, even while the causality of the cause, such as the seed, remains present; for we observe the occasional production and non-production of the effect, such as cloth, even when the causes, such as the threads, are proximate. (Regarding the formation of the word *sthiti*: Bhāguri maintains that the vowel lengthening occurs before the suffix *lyuṭ* following the roots *ṣṭhiv* and *sīv*, as in *ṣṭhivasīvyor lyuṭpare dīrghatvaṃ vaṣṭi bhāguriḥ*.)

Regarding the rule *ṣṭhivsīvyor luṭparau* (Pāṇini 6.1.52): the roots *ṣṭhivu* (to spit) and *ṣivu* (to sew). — *ṣṭhivu* in the sense of "emitting" (Pāṇini’s Dhātupāṭha 560); *ṣivu* in the sense of "continuous weaving of thread" (Pāṇini’s Dhātupāṭha 1108).

"In the case of the roots *ṣṭhivu* and *ṣivu*, there is optionally a long vowel when the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied"— thus states Kṣīrasvāmī in his commentary on the Amarakośa; furthermore, the followers of Śākalya (the Saunāgas) declare that from the root *kṛ* there is the sense of both agent and state (*kartṛbhāva*), because [the suffix] *anaṭ* is used here in the sense of cause (*kāraṇatva*).
The state of being a non-cause for that [seed] is due to its being a non-cause; according to the Bhāṣya and Prajñapti,
the production of sprouts and so forth occurs after it has been stored for three years at most.
Even if they have been robbed for three years and lack the power to produce sprouts and so forth,
great merit arises for them through sacrifice performed according to the prescribed rite.
O Thousand-eyed One, sacrifice with seeds that have been stored for three years at most— Mahābhārata, Aśvamedha Parva 91.16.
Is the activity directed toward that [effect], such as a jar made of clay and so forth, characterized by the non-separation of cause and effect? [This is] the prima facie view.
In the absence of a cause, there is the non-determination of the existence or non-existence of the body. (Pra. kāyasadasadasattvāniyamabhā.
kāsaddasatvāniyamaya. (Ya.)

Regarding the instrument (*karaṇa*), it might be thought: "If there is no fixed rule as to whether the effect exists or does not exist in the cause, or whether it is produced or not produced, for what purpose is the etymological derivation of the word 'cause' (*kāraṇa*)—namely, 'that which acts' (*karoti')—resorted to?
To this, it is replied: "Because it makes known what was unknown," and so forth.

The purpose of this injunction is to make known what was unknown and to cause one to perceive what was not perceived; thus, an injunction has the purpose of making known the unknown, for it is with that as its primary aim that the sentence functions. In that state, because no [contrary] object has yet arisen, there can be no contact with an exception (*apavāda*). For at that time, in the case of "he makes" (*karoti*), which signifies a causal agent, only the prescription of causality is established. Since there is no qualification by specific place, time, and so forth, while its own object is non-existent, what object could an exception touch?—such as "Does he do this? Or does he not do it at some place or at some time? As for such contact, it is like the case of a blue lotus;
likewise, the fruit of the *nyagrodha* tree is seen to be a non-existent cause.

When the mango flower and fruit are seen as instances where the effect pre-exists in the cause (*satkāryakāraṇa*), then—since everything is of the nature of everything else and everything is the cause of everything—just as the entire complex of activities such as service is the cause for the attainment of the desired object, so too is it the cause for the attainment of affliction (*kleśa*).

If it is argued that "for this very reason, affliction must also occur," [we reply: if that were so, one would have to experience the desired [result] first, because its potentiality is present and has been declared [as such], just like the explanation given by any knower of all the scriptures.

Then the speaker considers: "Let this first be established—that 'it acts' is the cause. Once this is established and the status of being a cause is proven, then regarding the possible existence or non-existence of the effect, a qualification is resorted to by way of that specific mode of expression—such as "it certainly acts" or "it certainly does not act"—because a restriction is logically possible through the force of *vikalādeśa* (partial predication).
What is the example? A blue lotus.

For just as in the expression "it becomes a blue lotus," only the act of becoming is enjoined—without resorting to specific restrictions such as "only blue" or "only a lotus"—so too in the expression "it is a cause because it acts," only the production of the action is enjoined, without resorting to a restrictive rule such as "it necessarily acts" or "it does not."

Or, just as "blue" is said to be distinct [from other colors] without depending on specific qualities such as sesame or woolen cloth, and "lotus" is also said to be distinct [from other things] without depending on specific qualities such as redness, and both are thus described as mutually distinguished; likewise, "cause" (*kāraṇa*) is said to be merely the act of producing (*karoti*), independent of whether there is an obstruction or lack of obstruction to the effect in terms of place, time, and so forth. Alternatively, even though it possesses the variegated nature of a lotus, it is called a "blue lotus" without depending on its various distinct properties (*dharma-bheda*); similarly, action (*kriyā*) alone—without depending on the distinct properties of the presence or absence of the state of being an instrument—is called a "cause" (*kāraṇa*) when it is said that "it produces. [In this way,] there is no lack of restriction regarding the two [definitions].
Thus it is said that the touch is unknown; likewise, the fruit of the *nyagrodha* tree is seen to be without a real cause, like a blue lotus.

When the mango flower and fruit are seen as the cause and effect of the pre-existent effect (*satkārya*), then—since everything has everything as its essence and everything is the cause of everything—the entire collection of activities such as service is a cause for the attainment of the desired object; likewise, it must also be a cause for the attainment of affliction (*kleśa*).

If it is argued that "for this very reason, affliction also occurs," [we reply: if that were so, one would have to experience the desired [result] first, because its capacity is present and has been declared [as such], just like the explanation given by any knower of all the scriptures.

The word *sambhavataḥ* is a verbal usage ending in the suffix *-tas* in the sense of the ablative case; its meaning is "because of the possibility" (*sambhavāt*) of both the existence and non-existence of the effect.
[Regarding the phrase] *karoty eva vā na karoty eva*: the reading in the *pā* manuscript is *karoty eva na karoty eva*. The reading in the *raṃhī* manuscript is *karoty eva vā*.
In this context, there may also be the reading "it acts" or "it does not act at all," for the sake of [establishing] the nature of the cause;
likewise, [there is the example of] the fruit of the banyan tree (*nyagrodha*).

In that manner, just as previously stated, because there is no necessity regarding existence or non-existence, the cause’s status as a cause—whether it produces or does not produce—is established; likewise, because there is no necessity for the effect’s production or non-production, there is no necessity for the effect’s status as an effect.

For instance, since the fruits of the *vaṭa*, *nyagrodha*, *udumbara*, and other trees are effects, it would follow that one could infer they are produced from flowers; however, as before, this is fallacious, since we observe that an effect may exist even when its cause is absent.

Regarding the statement, "The mango flower and fruit are seen as cause and effect," this also demonstrates the very lack of restriction in the production or non-production of an existent or non-existent effect from a cause, because only occasional causes and effects are observed;
thus, as previously stated [in the *Yukti*],
and as previously stated [in the *Bhāṣya*].
pṛ॰ 37, paṃ॰ 3:
Here, the reading might also be "prāguktam" (as stated previously);
"dṛṣṭavat" means "as before. (Pra.)
The rule regarding the nature of cause and effect is not fixed.

Furthermore, there is no fixed rule regarding the existence or non-existence of cause and effect—because everything is of the nature of everything and everything is the cause of everything, and because we observe a manifold diversity (*vaiśvarūpya*) resulting from the transformation of the various forms such as sap, blood, and so forth, derived from the mutual consumption of stationary and moving beings; therefore, everything is of the nature of everything. Consequently, since everything is both the cause and the effect of everything, the entire range of activities such as service and the like, which are considered causes for the attainment of a desired object, are likewise conceived as causes for the attainment of suffering.
Furthermore, that result— such as the attainment of wealth or the cessation of afflictions— is also uncertain, because it deviates in both cases;
for [the result] occurs even without the perception of form,
due to its inherent nature.

The other says: "But surely, since affliction also arises only from the existence of the effect, it follows that the effect is necessarily present in the cause—if you think this is so, then in that case, there ought to be what is desired;
and what is that desired fruit? It is the attainment of wealth, not affliction for the servant."

What is the reason? Because it is expressed by that power which is present. This servant has that power present; he is one whose power for attaining the intended object is not departed. Or, service is present; that is its power, and thus it is "that which has that power present. Because it is expressed—that is, because it is manifested—by that [power], and because of the non-difference between the function and the possessor of the function (*vṛtti-vṛttimat*), the desired fruit is indeed not attained there, due to being bound by place, time, form, and cause, just as in the case of the explanation of knowledge (*jñāna-vyākhyāna*).

Now, what of space (*deśa*) and the rest? If they are effects, then because they are not causes [of everything], because they are not all-pervasive, and because they are not sovereign, they cannot be obstructors. Alternatively, if they are causes, then since they are the cause of everything and consist of everything, why does everything not become [manifest]? For they constitute the complete collection of causes, like a cloth produced from combined threads. Or rather, everything does not become manifest because space and the rest are unmanifest, just as the primary matter (*pradhāna*) remains in a state of equilibrium, or as two servants may have their bodies joined according to their will.
For it is logical that those two [the Buddha and the Teacher] should be endowed with the attainment of their desired goals, and not be subject to undesired afflictions;
what is the illustration? It is like the exposition of one who knows all the scriptures concerning any single one of them.
Just as a person who knows all the scriptures explains only that specific scripture—such as grammar—which he desires, so too is this case.
If you think that this [result] is indeed to be known,
