or that it is indeed attained there, then because it is bound by place, time, form, and cause, the desired fruit is not attained at all, just like the explanation of what is to be known (*jñeya*).
Now, what of space and the other [factors]? If they are effects, then because they are not causes, they are not all-pervasive, and because they lack independence, they cannot act as obstructions.

If, on the other hand, they are causes, then since they are the cause of everything and consist of everything, why does everything not become [manifest]—given that their causes are fully assembled, like a cloth from joined threads?
Or rather, everything does not become [manifest] because space and the others remain unmanifest, like the state of equilibrium of the *pradhāna*.

To this we reply: In that case, because it is bound by place, time, form, and cause, the desired fruit is not attained at all—just as [a servant] does not obtain [favor] even from a gracious king due to constraints such as his own city, treasury, and other lands; constraints of time such as "tomorrow morning"; constraints of form such as being inclined toward granting a favor; and constraints of causes such as the demonstration of a second capacity for action.

Since even in the case of an example cited by one learned in the scriptures, if such a kind of binding exists, there would likewise be no certainty regarding the result, as in the case of an unexplained [text]; therefore, he says: "like an unexplained [text]" (*jñāvyākhyānavat*). This means that even one who knows all the scriptures does not explain what is desired by means of these very bindings.
[Note: The text contains several scribal variants and fragments: *dheḥprabhātā* (pra.), *śāstrajñādṛṣṭāntasyāpiya* (ya).]
Even for the scripture,
there is the necessity of the doctrine of explanatory discourse;
[it is] for one who knows the scripture of the Omniscient One.
The worldly person says: "Now, what of space and the rest? His intention is that he will refute this by means of falling into one of two alternatives:
if those things such as space, which are considered to be obstructors, are desired to be effects, then because they would lack a cause, they would not be omnipresent.

For if everything were to exist because of its causal nature, then everything would consist of the nature of everything else; from the absence of that [causal relation], it follows that space and the other factors are not all-encompassing.
And because they are not all-encompassing, they lack sovereignty over those [effects], since nothing exists in dependence upon them.
Consequently, due to this lack of sovereignty, they also possess no obstructive power.
If you should say that those [factors], such as place and so forth, are the cause because the effect possesses their form—

If it is argued that [the cause] is the cause [of everything], then since it is the cause of all and the self-nature of all, why does everything not become [everything]? The meaning is that it indeed does so.
Why? Because the causes are assembled (*samuditakāraṇatvāt*). "Assembledness of causes" follows from its being the cause of all and its being the self-nature of all.
Here the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: everything should exist everywhere, because the causes are assembled, just like a cloth produced from combined threads.

Just as when threads are joined together, a cloth necessarily arises solely through the presence of its own causes, so too, when the state of being all causes and the state of being the self of all exist, what else could there be called a spatial or other kind of obstruction? Why, then, would everything not become [everything]? (mudhābhā॰ mucā ya॰)
Alternatively, the same worldly person raises this doubt, beginning with "everything does not exist," etc.:
"Now, it may be thought by you, the Sāṅkhya—why is it that everything, such as bodily affliction, pleasure, the attainment of goals, and misfortune, does not exist? Because it is unmanifest."

The root *añj* (Pāṇini-Dhātupāṭha 1459) is used in the senses of manifestation (*vyakti*) and smearing (*mrakṣaṇa*). That which is smeared (*mrakṣita*) is manifested (*abhivyakta*) or made clear; that which is not smeared is unmanifested (*anabhivyakta*) or unclear. Because the cause, such as space and so forth, is unmanifested, everything does not come into being.
What is the illustration? It is like the state of equilibrium (*sāmyāvasthāna*) of the primary matter (*pradhāna*).

Just as *pradhāna*—consisting of the three qualities (*guṇas*) of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*—though being the cause of all things, does not produce any entities such as jars or cloths while remaining in a state of equilibrium due to its unmanifest nature; yet, because it brings forth [all things], it is designated by names such as *prakṛti* (the source), *pradhāna* (that in which things are placed), and so on—and its unmanifestness is due to that state of equilibrium, like the neck and other parts contained within the fluid of a peacock's egg.

But surely, since space and so forth are all-pervasive and consist of everything, they exist only in a state of heterogeneity; thus, the nature of *prakṛti* is merely that of worldly materiality because it consists of everything.
Furthermore, its abiding in a state of uniform non-manifestation is untenable, as it would be purposeless—like indifference toward both accomplished and unaccomplished causal functions.
Consequently, one must either abandon *prakṛti* as the cause or admit another cause, or else a creator who arranges things in such a manner.
It might be argued that the cause, such as space and so forth, does not produce all its effects because it exists in a state of equilibrium, just like *pradhāna*.
A well-known worldly example for this is found in the case of the neck and other parts within the fluid of a peacock's egg.

Just as the various colors and the parts such as the neck remain unmanifest while in the state of the peacock's egg-fluid due to their existing in a state of equilibrium, therefore, everything does not manifest at once, just as those parts like the neck do not appear while in the state of the peacock's egg-fluid.
The root *añj* (pāṇinīya-dhātu-pāṭha 1459) is used in the senses of manifestation, smearing, and motion;
the root *añjau* (haima-dhātupāṭha 7.16) is used in the senses of manifestation, smearing, and motion.
Nor is it non-existent because of not being a thing; nor is it existent because of being all things,
like the neck and other parts contained within the fluid of a peacock's egg.

But surely, since space and so forth are all-encompassing and consist of everything, they exist only in a state of inequality; thus, by virtue of consisting of everything like space and so forth, the state of equilibrium is impossible for *prakṛti*, as it would lack purpose. Consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence that either the status of *prakṛti* as the cause must be abandoned—just as one remains indifferent toward causal efficiency whether it has been accomplished or not—or else another cause, or a creator of such a state, must be admitted.

"From the excellence of color and neck [of the peacock], everything does not arise from the fluid of the peacock's egg; from the fluid of the peacock's egg, everything does not arise, just as in the state of the peacock's egg.
To this it is said: "Do not think thus; for indeed... and so forth.
The word *nanu* is used here to seek permission; you too have accepted this—that "all" refers to space and so forth.

Therefore, because space and the rest constitute "all," they possess the nature of the All (*sarvātmakatva*). And because they possess the nature of the All, they are indeed in a state of inequality (*vaiṣamyāvasthā*).
The particle *iti* has the sense of a reason (*hetvartha*): because the very nature of the world is what is intended by the term "Prakṛti" in the well-spoken [scriptures].

How so? For just as the worldly *prakṛti*—consisting of space and so forth—is indeed in a state of inequality, yet is the essence of all causes and effects, both unequal and equal, manifest and unmanifest; in the same way, the *prakṛti* imagined by the Sāṅkhyas would also have to be so.

Why? Because it possesses the nature of everything (*sarvātmakatvāt*). The meaning is that, like space and so forth, or like the fluid within a peacock’s egg, it would exist only in a state of inequality;
or else, like the *prakṛti*, even space and so forth would exist only in a state of equilibrium, because they possess the nature of everything.
The comparison with the *Prakṛti* favored by the *Iṣṭasiddhi*:

"It is merely a dismantling of the meaning of the entire *tantra*; what, then, remains of the *Vārṣagaṇya-tantra*? This [system], though considered well-spoken, is to be abandoned as it consists of irrational assertions concerning imperceptible objects"—*Nayacakravṛtti*, p. 232.2. ...of the irregularity of the [directions] and so forth. *Pra.* (Prakaraṇapañcikā).

Furthermore, it is both inconsistent and manifest—what more can be said? These two conceptions are also untenable: namely, that there is a non-manifestation of space and so forth, and that Prakṛti remains in a state of equilibrium.
Why? Because it would serve no purpose.

For there is no purpose in the non-manifestation of space and the other [factors], since they proceed in a manifested form for the sake of the liberation of the *puruṣa*, and thus the goal of the *puruṣa* is accomplished; it is like the indifference toward the act of cooking once the rice is finished.

Nor is there any purpose for *prakṛti*—once its task is completed—to withdraw itself again and abide in a state of equilibrium, just as one who has finished cooking does not continue the activity of cooking for the sake of rice that is already prepared.
Alternatively, neither non-manifestation nor abiding in a state of equilibrium is appropriate for *prakṛti* alone, because it would serve no purpose.
The state of being purposeless [is untenable] because the object is either already accomplished or not yet accomplished.
If the object is already accomplished, then its remaining in a state of equilibrium is improper, like cooking rice that is already cooked.
If the Pradhāna has an unaccomplished object, then its remaining in a state of equilibrium is improper, like indifference toward rice that is not yet cooked.

Likewise, what is the cause for non-manifestation? It is because the purpose [of manifestation] is accomplished through the two—manifestation and its deficiency—when activity is directed toward illumination; for it is not accomplished without those two. Furthermore, since even the states of non-manifestation and equilibrium are specific forms of activity, it is untenable [to claim otherwise], as both cases would likewise lack a purpose.

Alternatively, non-manifestation would be purposeless because its object has already been accomplished; for what reason would the activity of the Self, manifested in the form of space and so forth, not be made manifest? Or for what reason would it remain in a state of equilibrium without having fulfilled all the purposes of the Puruṣa? For the Sāṅkhyas, the activity of Prakṛti is held to be for the sake of accomplishing these two kinds of Puruṣa-purposes; it is not accidental, as in the view of the proponents of chance, nor does it arise from other causes such as the nature of God or the like.
He shows two examples here according to their respective order: "like indifference toward an accomplished or unaccomplished purpose," meaning like [indifference] toward boiled or unboiled rice.

It might be thought: "That [evolution] occurs due to the power of one or another cause—such as time, necessity, chance, inherent nature, or God—while that primordial matter (prakṛti) remains in a state of equilibrium as the unmanifest.

But this is incorrect; for there is the fault of contradicting what has been accepted by abandoning the status of primordial matter as the cause. Indeed, the manifestation of a distinct self is the property of the Pradhāna, which is independent, whose object is knowledge, and which is all-pervasive and unimpeded.

Therefore, it must necessarily be eternally active, because that is its very nature (*svabhāva*). For instance, just as there is the occurrence of a related factor or of another cause (*kāraṇāntara*) that impels it in such a way—where "another cause" means a cause other than [the primary] cause, namely, a cause other than *prakṛti* which impels *prakṛti* in such a manner—it follows that one of these must exist: inherent nature (*svabhāva*), necessity (*niyati*), time (*kāla*), chance (*yadṛcchā*), the Lord (*īśvara*), or others. And this is undesirable for those who hold their respective positions. Thus ends the *Sthānāṅga-siddhi*. (Note: *bhā* refers to the Bhāṣya commentary).
In the case of non-cessation,
O Lord of Trees, regarding the action [of cooking], there is the boiling of rice and so forth.
If [the purpose] were for the sake of preparing rice and so forth, it would not exist without the two [factors] that have already engaged [in the activity].
The illuminator is the activity of the Self;

for the manifestation of another self by abandoning the state of being a cause is indeed the attribute of the Pradhāna, which is the object of knowledge, independent, and all-pervading without obstruction.

Therefore, it must necessarily be eternally active, because that is its very nature; for just as with primordial matter (*prakṛti*), it is contrary to reason for a cause that is independent of other causes not to produce its own effect. Thus he says: "For the manifestation of another self," and so forth, up to "is the property of the Pradhāna."

"Another self than the self" means another self (*ātmāntara*); its state is "otherness of self" (*ātmāntaratva*), which is the state of being distinct from one another in the various conditions such as *mahat*, *ahaṃkāra*, and so forth. The manifestation of that [is indicated by] the word *hi*, which has the sense of "because. Because it is the manifestation of the self as a mode of other states—which is the opposite of both non-manifestation and the state of equilibrium—this would be considered a property of *prakṛti*.
If it is thought that, due to ignorance of the means, it requires another cause endowed with the quality of assistance, this is incorrect, because [the purpose] is for the sake of knowledge.
And it has been said: "Virtue, knowledge, dispassion, and power are the qualities of the intellect (*buddhi*); likewise are non-virtue, ignorance, passion, and lack of power.

Of these eight, [the intellect] binds by means of seven and liberates by means of one. It might be thought that for this *pradhāna*, which exists in the state of transformation for the sake of knowledge, dependence on an associate would be improper; however, it does not require another assistant because it is independent. Since it is autonomous, it does not depend on another helper.
It might be thought: "In some cases the *pradhāna* is the cause, while in others it is something else, because of its lack of pervasiveness, like worldly causes such as time (*kāla*)";
however, this is incorrect, because it is unimpededly omnipresent and does not depend upon external means.
Because it does not beg for means,
it binds through the conjunction of knowledge, dispassion, and power.
In this way, Prakṛti binds herself by herself through seven forms; and she alone, for the sake of the Puruṣa's purpose, liberates herself by means of a single form.
(Sāṅkhyakārikā 63)

"By forms"—by which seven forms does Prakṛti bind herself? That is explained: virtue (dharma), vice (adharma), ignorance (ajñāna), non-detachment (avairāgya), detachment (vairāgya), power (aiśvarya), and lack of power (anaiśvarya). These are the seven forms;
by these seven forms she binds herself.
And that very [nature] liberates the human goal in a single form.
What is that single form? It is knowledge;
by means of that knowledge, one liberates the self from the person (puruṣa) through a single [means]—because of the lack of pervasion [of other means], according to the *Jainasāṅkhyakārikāvṛtti*.

Alternatively, "the manifestation of the state of being another self" means: the self is the *puruṣa*; another self than the self is "another self" (*ātmāntara*); its state is "the state of being another self" (*ātmāntaratva*). Pradhāna manifests its own self—which is distinct from the *puruṣa* and characterized by the three *guṇas*—to the *puruṣa*.

Or, "another person" means another self (*ātman*) distinct from [one's own] person; the state of being that is "otherness of self" (*ātmāntaratva*), which is "person-otherness" (*puruṣāntaratva*). For that person, [the intellect] reveals its own nature and reveals it to other persons. Or, "person-otherness" refers to the states of being situated within the pure and isolated consciousness-nature—which are mutually distinct—located in other persons. Even when these have been revealed in those other persons, [the intellect] reveals the "person-otherness" of yet other persons as being endowed with precisely those same qualities of consciousness and so forth.
Or rather, it is the manifestation of the insentient nature of *prakṛti* itself, which is of an insentient essence;
for this is the property of that *pradhāna*, which is independent, whose purpose is knowledge, and which is unimpeded and all-pervading,
[namely] the manifestation of another self.
The essential nature of the Self is luminosity (prakāśa). [Variant:
The essential nature of the Self is luminosity. It is not insentient (acetana). [Variant: It is not insentient.]

Having thus established its nature as a constituent principle (*svabhāvadharma*), he now infers the perpetual activity of the *pradhāna*, which serves as the counter-position to its state of non-manifestation and equilibrium: "Therefore, it must necessarily be perpetually active"—this is the formal proposition (*pratijñā*).

Therefore—meaning, because of the nature of *pradhāna* as just described—he says "in general" (*sāmānyataḥ*)—"because it has that as its inherent nature" (*tatsvabhāvatvāt*). That which has such an inherent nature (*svabhāva*) as its property is "that-which-has-that-as-its-inherent-nature" (*tatsvabhāva*), namely *pradhāna*, as qualified by the previously stated reasons; therefore, it must be eternally active.
In this world, whatever has a certain inherent nature, that thing acts accordingly: for example, fire is active in burning and illuminating.
[Objection: But surely even fire covered by ashes neither burns nor illuminates?

Now, how does it persist? How is it known that fire exists, if it neither burns nor illuminates its own substrate, such as a sheath and so forth, like a lamp in a house? Furthermore, the absence of concealment is observed in the Pradhāna by that very same nature, just as fire is observed to be engaged in burning and illuminating. That which is not perpetually active does not possess that nature, just as nothing else is seen to be so.
Whatever has a certain intrinsic nature (svabhāva), it functions by means of that very nature; fire, for instance, is engaged in burning and illuminating.
But surely, even fire covered by ashes neither burns nor illuminates?

Now, how does it live? How is it known that fire exists, if it neither burns nor illuminates its own locus, such as a sheath and so forth, like a lamp in a house? Furthermore, since there is no concealment [of the fire] when the primary [fuel] is burning, and because the nature of fire—consisting of burning and so on—is not seen to function in that way [in the case of the ash], the example suffers from the defect of lacking the property to be proven (*sādhyadharmavaikalya*). Demonstrating this, he says: "But surely even fire covered by ashes neither burns nor illuminates," because burning and heating are non-different.
To this, it is replied: "Then how does it live?"

The life of fire exists because it possesses consciousness; for consciousness is observed through the nourishment or decline resulting from the acquisition or non-acquisition of fuel, just as in the case of a human being.
That fire lives while burning its fuel, since "abiding" (sthiti) is a synonym for "living," and abiding is invariably concomitant with the burning of fuel.

Even granting its lack of sentience, since fire—which consists of abiding, illuminating, and burning fuel—is an object of perception and inference, if it were not apprehended by perception and inference in that manner, its existence could not be established by any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). How, then, would it be known as "fire"? For how long can it be called "fire" while not burning, not illuminating, or not illuminating another substance such as a cocoon and so forth, but [illuminating] only its own substrate? As for its dimension: if it does not illuminate even its own substrate, such as a cocoon, by means of its own dimension alone, how can it be called "fire"? A cocoon is called *kośaka*.
The illustration is that of a house-lamp:

a lamp ignited within a house is a "house-lamp. Just as if a house-lamp, though being of the nature of light, does not illuminate even a single grain of rice, it is understood that it is not a lamp; or else, there is the illustration based on the dissimilarity with fire—a house-lamp exists while illuminating the house, whereas if fire, despite being of the nature of light, does not likewise illuminate its own substrate, it is thereby understood that it does not exist.

Furthermore, there is also the absence of the analogy of fire covered by ashes for the *pradhāna*, because of the absence of any covering; therefore he says: "And there is an absence of covering for the *pradhāna*.

Since there is no concealment of the *prakṛti* as there is of fire by ashes, the *pradhāna* is not like fire covered by ashes. Therefore, we state the distinction: because its nature is like the burning and illuminating of an uncovered fire, it must necessarily be eternally active;
such is its state of eternal activity.
Consequently, the state of remaining in a condition of non-manifestation is untenable; for if it were insentient, it would not be sentient, and if it were sentient, it would not be [insentient].
In the case of illumination, you [assert] non-burning; in the case of burning, it is being illuminated; and in the case of transformation, [it is being transformed].
The suffix *vatup* is applied after the words *yad*, *tad*, and *etad* when expressing measure (Pāṇini 5.2.39).
Regarding the reading *atrapulikā* found here [in the text]—

and which is also found as *atrapulikā* in all the manuscripts including Bhāṣya— the exact meaning of this reading *atrapulikā* is not properly understood; nevertheless, considering that a particular type of vessel might be intended here, it is plausible that the reading should be *annapulikā*.

It should be understood that "atra" and "pulikā" are not two separate words here, for even later on there is the statement: "The house-lamp [is] merely a *pulikā* here" (Pañcāśaka 15). Furthermore, in that context, the word "atra" as a separate term is entirely unnecessary and inconsistent; thus it is read as "gṛhīdīpakaḥ."
[The term] *paka* [is explained as] *trapulikā*;
according to the variant reading *vaidharmya*, it is understood here that "fire is known," whereas according to the other reading, it is understood that "fire is not known."
Alternatively, there may also be the reading "or a dissimilar example" (vaidharmyadṛṣṭānto vā);
likewise, [the reading] "ashes" (bhasma) [should be understood] in what follows as well.
Agni is the beginning and the end.

It might be argued: "Even though the *pradhāna* proceeds toward the state of the *mahat* and so forth for the sake of manifesting its internal difference from the *puruṣa*, nevertheless, for the sake of some *puruṣas* and not others, it attains states of manifestation, non-manifestation, equilibrium, and disequilibrium over the course of time. Since this [process] belongs to that which is independent of other causes such as time, being autonomous and active for the sake of all *puruṣas*, once the knowledge of its own distinctness from the *puruṣas* has been imparted regarding every *puruṣa*, its purpose is fulfilled; therefore, what is the use of remaining in a state of equilibrium? And since its purpose is not yet fulfilled when [equilibrium] has not occurred, what is the point of withdrawing? Furthermore, because a state of non-manifestation and equilibrium is logically untenable, why is this world not accepted as having a nature consisting solely in the manifestation of various distinctions through perceptible causes, proceeding continuously and eternally? Is the activity of a lump of clay due to inherent nature (*svabhāva*), necessity (*niyati*), time (*kāla*), or chance (*yadṛcchā*)?"
This too is untenable, because [you claim] "independence from other causes such as time," and so forth;

for you have accepted that *pradhāna* (primordial matter) is the cause of the universe, independent of any one of the others—namely, necessity (*niyati*), time (*kāla*), inherent nature (*svabhāva*), God (*īśvara*), or chance (*yadṛcchā*)—and not as in the worldly view where sometimes time, or even necessity, and so on, are also [considered causes].

Furthermore, because it is independent in making known the distinction between the essential natures of *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, which is its own purpose; and because it is independent in bringing about the group of eleven organs beginning with the ear, which correspond to its own purpose; and because it is independent in producing the group of conceptualizations such as sound and cognition, as well as the group of objects such as sound, speech, grasping, movement, pleasure, and excretion, there is no dependence upon any other cause.

Furthermore, since [the *guṇas*] are active for the sake of all human goals, there is no purpose for their remaining in a state of equilibrium or for their cessation, respectively, for one who has accomplished his purpose and one who has not. Therefore, he says: "Once the knowledge of the Spirit's distinctness from itself has been communicated regarding the entire range of Spirits, what is the use of its remaining in a state of equilibrium for one who has accomplished his purpose? And even if it has not been communicated, since one has not accomplished his purpose, what is the use of its cessation? It would be like the cessation of a cook who has not yet prepared the rice. Thus, the lack of purpose remains as it was.

Here an objection is raised: "But was it not previously stated that 'the two states of non-manifestation and equality are untenable because they serve no purpose, just like indifference toward an action that has either already been accomplished or not yet been accomplished'? Therefore, this is a mere repetition.

To this we reply: No, for this [statement] is intended to negate the dependence on other causes; whereas that [previous statement] was intended merely to demonstrate that the *pradhāna* serves no purpose regarding engagement or withdrawal. Thus, there is no fault.

Since that [Primal Cause] is independent, being devoid of other causes such as time, and since it is engaged in the fulfillment of the purposes of all persons, once it has accomplished its task by making known its distinctness from the selves across the entire range of persons, what is the purpose of its remaining in a state of equilibrium? And even if it were not so accomplished, since there would be no completion of its task, what would be the point of its withdrawing? Furthermore, since a state of equilibrium characterized by non-manifestation is logically untenable, why is this world not accepted as having a nature that is the manifestation of various distinct effects through a cause that is eternally present and continuously active? Even the lump of clay [is not produced] by mere chance... [the rest of the sentence is fragmentary].
And when [the breath] has ceased,
it is joined with the wind (vāyu). (Praśna Upaniṣad 4.3)
"And because the state of equilibrium consisting of non-manifestation is untenable":

since the state of equilibrium consisting of non-manifestation is untenable due to reasons such as its lack of purpose, then—because that state of equilibrium consisting of non-manifestation is untenable—for what reason (*kiṃ kāraṇam*) is this world not understood to be of such a nature? This is the connection [of the text].

Regarding the phrase "with a continuous, ever-abiding, and constant activity" (*satatasamavasthitasamanupravṛtti*): "continuous" means at all times; "ever-abiding" means eternal and uninterrupted; and "constant activity" refers to the preeminent functioning whose essence consists in the activity of cause and effect—that is, this world is one whose activity is continuous, ever-abiding, and constant.

"Having as its nature the manifestation of the various distinctions of perceptible causes" means: those which are both perceptible and causes are "perceptible causes"—namely, for effects such as jars, the lump of clay, the staff, the wheel, water, the string, the potter, and so forth; for effects such as cloth, the threads, the shuttle, the loom, the weaver, and so forth—these are of various kinds. The "various distinctions of perceptible causes" are the specific differences among them, or the manifestations of those [causes] in the form of effects such as jars and cloth; that which has this very manifestation as its nature is "that which has as its nature the manifestation of the various distinctions of perceptible causes."

What is that? It is the world itself—this is the restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). What does it restrict? It restricts [the cause] to only those causes directly perceived, such as semen, blood, food, and so forth.
What is excluded by this? The unmanifest (*avyakta*) and other such unseen alternative causes.
Therefore, why is it not accepted that this world has as its very nature the manifestation of various differences through visible causes? Why is another cause, the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*), postulated?
Thus, first, the lack of certainty regarding the existence or non-existence of the effect in the cause has been stated; [now follows] the untenability [of the opponent's position].
The eternal,
uninterrupted activity [is] the manifestation of various distinctions and so forth, which are [the causes];
and those are perceived directly.
Thus they are determined, Bhā;
thus they are determined, Pā, Ḍe, Līṃ;
thus it is determined, Vi, Raṃ, Hī.
*Comparison*: The word "eva" (thus) is used for emphasis. What does it emphasize? It emphasizes the object in the world—[as stated in] *Nayacakra-vṛtti*, p.

39: "Without the unseen cause (*adṛṣṭa-kāraṇa*), there would be no emergence from the superimposition of indeterminate causes—whether existent or non-existent—such as the stone, the pedestal, the mold, the granary, the pot, the shards, the fragments, the gravel, the dust, the wind-blown particles, or the atoms that have reached infinity through re-accumulation; nor would there be the rootless nature of the effect, such as the lump of clay."

Therefore, let it be understood that no other fruit whatsoever is produced by that scripture; nor is there any lack of restriction regarding the performance of worldly transactions, for even such non-restriction is itself an effect, having as its cause specific factors such as time, whether real or unreal, and is indeed preceded by causes postulated by the authors of scriptures on the Pradhāna and so forth.

What is the reason? Because there is no observed example that conforms to such [a claim]. What then? This is the rule: that the effect is not released from the superimposition of the cause and is not uprooted from it; for this conforms to observed facts. This is because, following the series of examples beginning with "the lump of clay, the pot-sherd," and ending with "the dust and the lump of clay," it will be stated in the subsequent connection that there is a lack of release from the superimposition of causes—whether they be non-determined or real—and a state of being not uprooted from them.

The effect alone, whether it be existent or non-existent, has time and so forth as its cause; he provides an example to demonstrate the lack of fixed rule regarding this "cause with a beginning," stating: "the lump of clay, the small piece [śivaka]," and so on, up to "the dust and the lump of clay. Since these specific states of the lump of clay and so forth, ending with the window-dust, are observed in the world, those aggregates (*skandhas*) which attain infinity through further accumulation are called "aggregates that have attained infinity through further accumulation. Starting from the window-dust and proceeding by the sequence of further accumulation—namely, dust, lump of clay, small piece, *sthāsa*, *kosaka*, *kuśūla*, jar, potsherd, fragment, gravel, sand, and window-dust—an irregularity of cause and effect is thus observed in a cyclical manner.

Furthermore, even by way of transgression through the aggregation and disintegration [of parts], an absence of fixed rule regarding the existence or non-existence of cause and effect is observed: because a small lump (*śivaka*) is produced by crushing a large mass (*piṇḍa*), and a large mass is produced by crushing a small lump; and because even by crushing any particular specific state such as a stand (*sthāsaka*) and so forth, a large mass and the like are produced; and because, through the sequence of action and the fruit of action, a lack of fixed rule between cause and effect is sometimes seen. Thus, "having an indefinite beginning" (*aniyatādi*) means that its beginning is indefinite. This refers to the world (*jagat*). That very world has causes and effects whose existence and non-existence are indefinite; its cause is indefinite in its existence and non-existence. Its superimposition (*adhyāsa*)—or, by that cause, the superimposition—is the locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

Due to that superimposition upon the cause, there is non-liberation, which is non-abandonment; it is the inseparable concomitance with the generality of the cause, but not a state of being an effect characterized by absolute uprooting, origination, and destruction like a sky-flower, because such is observed in the world.
By means of that non-liberation, the non-uprootedness of the world—which is an effect—is [established], for the time and so forth are indeed effects of what is real.
Through the resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) of superimposition (*adhyāsa*),
[one attains] the finality of that very [state].
Or [the sequence] beginning with time, beginning with time; the vessel, the husk, the chaff, the grit, and the dust.

Because of that reason— namely, because there is no fixed rule regarding the existence or non-existence of perceived causes and effects, because a single unseen cause such as the *pradhāna* imagined by others is untenable, and because there is no inference for a single specific cause like Time (Kāla) and so forth, but rather only an inference for the mere generality of a cause— it should be understood that no other fruit whatsoever is produced by that scripture; the meaning is that scriptures are useless.
What is that? It is that which exists beyond the fruits of worldly transaction, and in dependence upon which the scriptures become meaningful.

Therefore, let it be understood: this world is merely as it is well-known in the world—a continuous succession of causes and effects with indefinite, unceasing, and finite beginnings and ends—and not as imagined by others: namely, that a *pradhāna* (primordial matter), having ceased its activity and being beyond the senses, creates the world again by becoming perceptible to the senses, and then, having withdrawn itself, remains with its activity ceased.
Nor is it the case that this [effect] is absolutely non-existent, or that it perishes as soon as it arises in a moment, or that it is devoid of a root;
the word "iti" here signifies a reason.
What is the reason? The futility of the treatise.
In what goal would it exist as something exceeding the fruit? Thus, the commencement of a treatise (*śāstra*) regarding such matters would be in vain;
however, in this case, the treatise would be purposeful—in the form: "One desiring this should do that.

For the instruction concerns action alone, as in the case of the *Citrā* sacrifice and others; it is not a deliberation regarding a merely worldly matter already grasped, such as "this is thus" or "this is not thus," or "it is not so."

Since, in this world, for one whose senses and mind are unimpaired, [the object] is perceptible through direct experience, the undertaking of a treatise would be useless in such cases; therefore, he says: "The undertaking of a treatise is thus useless.

If it is asked, "Where then would a treatise be purposeful?", [the answer is: regarding that which is beyond the senses—the relationship between the means and the end to be accomplished for the sake of human goals. To this he says: "But here a treatise would be purposeful"—namely, "one desiring this should do this."

By means of the word "this" (*idam*), a pronoun denoting generality, [the author] indicates all actions—those impelled by the desire for a fruit and serving as its means—such as: "One desiring heaven should offer the *agnihotra*," "One desiring a son should sacrifice," "One desiring cattle should sacrifice," "One desiring food should sacrifice," and so forth; for the connection between an action and its fruit is beyond the reach of the senses.
And it has been said: "The scripture is purposeful regarding that which is not [otherwise] attained" (*Mīmāṃsā-sūtra* 6.2).
The meaning is: that which is not to be apprehended by means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and other instruments of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Elsewhere, the fruit [is found] in the scriptures (*śāstra*).
The meaning of the reason (*hetu*) is that its function has been presented by what is seen at the beginning and end.
In this context, it appears that the reading "hetvarthe" (in the sense of a reason) is more appropriate;
for if [the scripture] were to exist beyond its fruit, the commencement of such a treatise would be in vain, whereas here the treatise becomes purposeful: "one who desires this should do this."
For the purposeful instruction concerns only the action, like [the instructions for] painting and so forth; it is not a deliberation— such as "this is thus" or "it is not thus"—
regarding an object already grasped in the world through unimpaired sensory and mental perception, as it exists in the world.
In this regard, the reading "°vācinā" appears to be more correct;
such are the actions [stated] in the Bhāṣya manuscript of Ya,
whereas in the manuscript of Bhā, following the reading "ityādyāḥ kriyāḥ," the entire passage ending with "arthādanapeto'rthyaḥ" is not present at all here.
Comparison: And by the sequence of action, the fruit of action, and so forth (p.
44, l. 15), it is like the instruction on the relationship between action, the fruit of action, and [their] connection (l. 15); because of this, [it is] red, to be attained... [dhaprāpyeya].

"But the attainment [of a result] is not according to the scripture; the scripture would not be a prescriber [if it were]. Therefore, it should be understood through the purpose, for the scripture is meaningful only where [the result] has not [otherwise] been attained"—this is the reading in the Mīmāṃsā-darśana composed by Jaimini.
Regarding the passage beginning with "arthyo hi," the term *arthya* means "not deviating from the purpose" (*artha*).

The particle *hi* is used in the sense of "because. Because it is precisely the teaching of action—along with its means and its connection to results and so forth—that is *arthya*, just as in the case of [the ritual] *citrā* and others.

By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), [the text implies that] just as in the case of paintings, book-illustrations, woodwork, and so forth, instruction regarding the arrangement of parts, their positions, the application of colors, their distinctions, and their specific functions is meaningful because it is useful for those things; whereas instruction regarding the nature of the wall, the pigments, or the painter themselves is not meaningful because it is useless for that purpose. In the same way, the description of principles such as permanence or momentariness, the description of how jars, cloths, and so on are preceded by the three *guṇas* as their cause, or the description of the world as being in constant flux, momentary, or ineffable, [is likewise meaningful].

It might be thought: "The undertaking of doctrines such as Primordial Matter (*pradhāna*), momentariness (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), and so forth, is purposeful because they concern objects that are not perceptible, just like the teaching on the relationship between action and its fruit.

This too is untenable; for the connection is this: when an object is being apprehended as something merely worldly, an investigation such as "is it thus or not thus? is indeed purposeful. This is because an investigation whose subject matter is already well-established results in the fault of infinite regress (*aniṣṭhā*).

"No" (*na*) is used in the sense of negation, and "but" (*tu*) is a particle of distinction. That which exists in the world is "worldly" (*laukika*). Regarding objects possessing form and so forth—which depend on specific distinctions of place, time, person, and action, and which are perceived directly as causes and effects such as clay lumps and jars—the inquiry as to whether "all this consists solely of the three qualities (*guṇas*) known as *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, and not otherwise," or whether it is "momentary, characterized by destruction and birth," or "neither this nor that"—what connection does such an inquiry have? What is its fruit? Or what is the utility of such thorough knowledge for achieving the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*)? Please reflect upon this yourselves.
Because the meaning is the purpose of the instruction;
the purpose of the instruction is the meaning. (bhāṣya)
°sambandhettyāḥ Ābhāḥ °sambandhatyāḥ Raṃ° Hī°;
without [the word] °sambandhevyāḥ Raṃ° Hī° Ya° [is missing].
*Raṃhī*: Description of the reality of the doctrine of momentariness;
*Ya*: [Description of the reality of the doctrine of momentariness] without *raṃhī*; *Bhā*:
Description of the reality of the doctrine of momentariness.
The connection between an action and its result is meaningful [only] when an object is being apprehended as it is in the world,
such that one grasps "this is thus" or "this is so";
for an object already thus apprehended, an investigation as to whether "this is thus" or "this is not thus" is not purposeful.

If, despite having four legs, a frog were to be hairy like a deer because of its ability to leap, then for that very reason a deer would have to be hairless like a frog; thus, a conclusion contrary to common consensus would be established, thereby rendering worldly experience invalid. Since this consequence would apply here as well, he says: "But it is not [the case] when only the worldly is grasped," and so forth, as in the previously mentioned illustration.

This will be stated in the *Nayacakravṛtti*, p. 98–2, because the object of [the critique] consists in the fault of being restricted [to a single perspective]. (Note: *bhā॰* indicates a correction or variant reading in the manuscript.)

Because the investigation of the object results in the fault of non-termination (*aniṣṭha*), "non-termination" here means *anavasthā* (infinite regress); thus, the meaning is: "because it possesses the fault of infinite regress.
This is the purpose of the qualification.
In this context,
regarding [objects] such as space and so forth, there is the non-existence of the three types of perception.
And it is not the case that what is thus established is not apprehended;

rather, a further statement there serves as a sublation of what is established by perception. Since the existence or non-existence of [the status of] restatement and so forth is already established, the commencement [of this rule] is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*), because this is observed in common worldly usage—that is, "it is not apprehended by the world in such-and-such a way."

If perception (*pratyakṣa*) is not accepted as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it would lead to the occurrence of all kinds of fallacies through reasoning (*tarka*). For instance: "A deer is hairless because, while being four-footed, it moves by leaping, like a frog;
and a frog is hairy for that very same reason, like a deer.
One might think: "The observation of the world is not a valid means of knowledge, because the perception of uneducated people is subject to error, just as in the case of a mirage and the like."
To this it is replied: If that were so, you must not think that perception—the eldest among the means of valid cognition—is being rendered invalid.
For while some perceptions, such as those of a mirage and the like, do deviate from reality, does it follow that all perception deviates?
On the contrary, let it be understood that perception by means of unimpaired sense organs and mind does not deviate.

In the world, such things as jars and cloths are indeed perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) exactly as they are established—by whatever mode and by whatever intrinsic nature—by those whose sense faculties and minds are healthy. Regarding such an object, a further statement such as "this is thus" or "it is not thus," or "it is not so," would constitute a sublation of what is established by direct perception, *if* that statement were a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
However, it is not a valid means of knowledge, because it is itself sublated by that very [perceptual] establishment.

A statement whose meaning is already established would not be a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) except as a restriction (*niyama*) or a restatement (*anuvāda*); therefore, he provides an indicator [of its status]: "Since a formulation is made when something is already established, whether there is the presence or absence of a restatement and so forth, that [formulation] is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*)," because such a technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) is observed in common usage. Furthermore, since even sciences such as grammar—which follow worldly convention—derive their authority from the world itself, one might ask: what kind of statement is this? To this he says: "Not in the way that this is grasped by the world.
The word *iti* is used in the sense of illustration; it is shown that this statement is intended to subvert common consensus (*prasiddhi*).

How so? "No" (na) is a negation; in whatever manner—that is, just as a jar produced by the activity of a lump of clay, a staff, a wheel, a string, water, and a potter, having the nature of a broad belly and so forth and being capable of fetching water and such, is perceived by people through their eyes and other senses—it is not of this very nature [that the effect exists prior to its production].

What then? As I say: because everything has everything as its essence, even that which takes the form of cloth, matting, chariots, and so forth—which is the substratum of qualities, actions, universals, particulars, and inherence, and is composed of atoms and other earthly substances that are not at all imperceptible to us—is a composite whole (*avayavin*) distinct from those [parts]. Just like the parts of a chariot, when analyzed by the intellect again and again, it does not reside in the atoms, nor in the [qualities] such as color, nor in mere cognition, because it would otherwise be indefinable; rather, it exists in such and such a manner.

It is rightly said that the statement of the learned experts in the treatises must not be rendered meaningless; thus, it serves as a refutation of common worldly usage, as it has been stated: "The means of valid cognition function with respect to their objects for all disputants;
however, those ascetics dispute only because of differences in terminology and intention."
Thus, "siddha-dvā-20-4"; therefore, the statement of the author of the treatise is not authoritative because it contradicts direct perception.
Do not think that [it occurs] only in cases such as *nagapramā* and *pra*. Do not think so.
Direct perception is knowledge; among those [types of knowledge], it is established as a means of valid cognition by means of mental [perception].
The negation regarding the negation in the world is [negated] by the eye.
Bound by the [notion of] parts such as wheels and so forth, it does not abide in the atoms, nor does it abide in the mere [collection of] atoms.
In this context, there may also be the reading: "it results in a sublation due to the establishment [of the object] through perception.
"The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) function with respect to an object for all proponents;
however, these poor fellows dispute because of differences in terminology and intention" (Siddhiviniścaya-dvātriṃśikā 20.4).

Or, if the authority of the words of the author of the treatise is accepted, what fault is there in the non-authority of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)? In that case, by means of reasoning (*tarka*), the subversion of everything would follow from the invalidation of direct perception; for it is possible to establish the subversion of all entities established by the authority of direct perception, as follows: "A deer is hairless, because, while possessing four legs, it moves by leaping, like a frog."
A frog is also hairy for that very same reason;
a louse is winged like a deer because it has six legs, like a bee;
a bee is wingless because it has six legs, like the earth; the earth is not the ground because it is a category of existence and a primary element, like space.

In this way, regarding the remaining categories as well, although there may be differences in examples, that which contradicts the determination of the scriptures is not invalid— such as the true nature of Hari and so forth— because it is free from exception,
unlike the case of a louse.
Likewise, earth is not the bearer of wealth (or: earth is not the earth), because it is an entity, like space;
furthermore, even by connection with its own specific properties, earth is not connected with the properties of color, taste, smell, and touch, because it is a primary element, like space.

It does not possess properties such as shape, weight, or roughness; for that very reason, likewise, in the Buddhist system as well, earth is not "ground" because it is a primary element (*mahābhūta*) and because it is form (*rūpa*), just like water; nor does it possess the properties of hardness and supporting, for that very reason, just like that [water].

In this same manner, the refutation of the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) is to be applied to the remaining categories of objects—such as water, fire, air, ether, the sense organs and so forth, the self and so forth—according to their respective systems and as far as applicable. Furthermore, when refuting their specific characteristics (*asādhāraṇadharma*), the proofs based on reasons such as "being a category," "being a great element" (*mahābhūta*), "having form" (*rūpatva*), and so forth, are to be employed. This applies to the intellect (*mahat*), the ego (*ahaṅkāra*), the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), the senses, sound and so forth; to the self; to substance, quality, action, generality, particularity, and inherence along with their subdivisions; to name and form (*nāmarūpa*); to perception, mental formation, feeling, and consciousness (*vijñāna-vedanā-saṃskāra*); to earth, water, fire, and wind; and to the eyes and other [senses], as well as to visible form (*rūpa*) and the rest.

"Because of the difference in examples": just as the earth has the example of space, so too the properties of space and so forth must be refuted by means of examples such as the earth and so forth; having made each one the example for the other, there is the consequence that [the argument] applies to all objects (sarvaviṣayāpatti). (Bhāṣya:
sarvaviṣayāpatti; Yāyavṛtti: sarvaviṣayāpatti)
Lomaśaśo?śo, or rather from this [source],
because of being a six-footed creature (ṣaṭpada), according to the Bhāṣya.

The earth is non-substantial (avasudhā), because it is a category of existence (padārtha) and because it is a primary element (mahābhūta), just like space; the same applies to the remaining categories of existence, according to their respective differences in illustration.

That which is contrary to the determination of the treatises is not non-authoritative, such as the true nature of a deer and so forth; this is not so, because it is free from contradiction, [as in the case of] earth, water, and fire.
*pṛthivy-avasudhā* bhā°; this portion of the text, from *pṛthivy-avasudhā* up to *na bhavati*, which is contained within these brackets, does not exist in the manuscripts of the *Ya* recension;
[it is found in] *karakaṭa* *Ya*.
See page 16, note 8.

In arguments such as "the earth does not have the nature of solidity because it is an element, just like wind," the non-establishment of the reason and so forth should be applied by oneself—*Mādhyamakavṛtti*, p. 33.
Regarding the phrase *asādhāraṇa-prakaraṇa*, there might also be a reading here: *svarūpa-nirākaraṇe asādhāraṇa-dharma-nirākaraṇe ca*.
The logician says: "That which is contrary to the determination of the treatise is invalid," and so forth.
"Exposition by means of scripture" (*śāstreṇa nirūpaṇam*) or "exposition within scripture" (*śāstre nirūpaṇam*) constitutes *śāstranirūpaṇam*.

For virtuous persons indeed expose a reality by means of scripture for the sake of favoring those whose intellects are characterized by doubt, error, or lack of proficiency—namely, toward their disciples who are to be favored. Whether it be [the doctrine that] there are only primordial nature and the spirit (*prakṛti-puruṣau*), momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅgaḥ*), consciousness-only (*vijñānamātram*), or substance and quality (*dravya-guṇādi*), because scripture functions as a corrective (*apavāda*), a reality stated in a manner contrary to what has been corrected by scripture is invalid. This is because scripture serves as a corrective for doubt and the like.

The nature of the deer and so forth is not invalid; in that regard, the function of the scripture is solely to remove delusion. Thus, the true nature of the deer and so forth remains beyond reproach. Because it is beyond reproach, it is indeed valid just as it is apprehended by the world—by the inclusion of the word "and so forth," this includes the true nature of the frog and so on—as well as its heat, like that of fire. This is because it is beyond reproach.
To this it is replied: No, because everything has been negated.

For just as the scripture, having provisionally assumed entities such as jars and the like, proceeds to negate them, so too does it negate even the nature of Hari and others, which are well-known in the world through direct perception; for that [scripture] is unrestrained.
If one asks how that is so, [the answer is: "Because they are exclusively characterized by distinctions created by space and time," and so forth.
For the sake of grasping that which has already arisen through the intellect, what is the use of a treatise? What is the purpose of the scripture?
In this context, according to the preceding and following textual connections, "kiṃsthāne hi" alone appears to be the correct reading;
since the letters *ka* and *ha* appear identical in ancient scripts, it seems that "hi" itself has undergone a corruption into "kiṃ," as evidenced by the existing manuscripts.
In this reading, however, the meaning would be that inferential valid cognition (*anumāna-pramāṇa*) regarding an object does not consist of *ūha* alone.
The apprehension of [objects] such as the triad [of time],
etc., occurs for everyone without exception, even without a real entity, by way of negating what is imagined by others.

The *bhā* manuscript reads: "the denial of the imagined nature of the entity" (*vastu parikalpāpavāda*), while the *ya* manuscript reads: "the one-sided [view] regarding the distinction of time" (*kālaviśeṣaikāntika*) and so forth.

Alternatively, it will be stated that what is contrary to the determination of the scriptures is invalid (*apramāṇa*), because it is subject to refutation. The determination of the scriptures consists of such things as "the earth possesses odor" or [the doctrines of] *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*. That which is established through reasoning (*tarka*) in opposition to this is invalid, because both perception (*pratyakṣa*) and reasoning refute every [position] that maintains an absolute distinction based on space and time.

In the absolute view that everything is of the nature of everything, even a frog is indeed hairy; however, in the absolute view of the plurality of universals and particulars regarding objects and non-objects, since the scripture does not have that as its nature and its object is not such [an absolute], by whom could the scripture be sublated? It follows that it is not invalid because its nature—such as being like a deer—is contrary [to reality]; to whom [is it invalid]? To one for whom it is established by perception;
why? Because it is subject to exception (*sāpavādatvāt*).
Indeed, that [notion] such as "having deer-hair" is invalid because it is being sublated by the fact of "having hair," which is established through perception;
thus the worldly person says: "No, for everything is indeed set aside.

For even in the scriptures, the very nature of the deer and so forth—which is established by perception—is indeed set aside. How then can the scriptures be free from contradiction? It would be better to propound a contrary nature to the deer and so forth based on reasoning, since that would only sublate a limited portion; however, the logicians claim that the scripture sublates everything—both cause and effect—that is well-known in the world through perception.

If it is asked how that is so: for one who holds the absolute view that distinctions are produced by place and time—where "distinctions produced by place and time" refers to a distinction made by place and a distinction made by time, and that very thing constitutes their absolute position—the proponent who maintains such a view asserts that everything is indeed distinct with respect to every place and every moment, and nothing at all is identical.

Therefore, since there is a distinction [of things] down to the level of atoms, down to the level of form and so forth, down to the level of mere consciousness, and down to the level of the indefinable, how can there be a "hare"? How could its hair and so forth remain? Thus, everything has been refuted; or rather, what has not been refuted? And here, what is perception and what is inference? [The categories such as] earth-ness, possessing-earth-ness, and so forth, are also [refuted] in the *Prakaraṇa*, *Vipañcitārthā*, and *Bhāṣya*.

Because everything has been negated, for one who maintains the absolute distinction between space and time, there would be the absolute identity of all things with everything; even a frog would be hairy. Furthermore, in the absolute view of the multiplicity of universals and particulars regarding objects and non-objects, the scripture would have no subject matter, because it would not consist of those very things.
Because the treatise has as its object that which is not within the scope of [ordinary] perception;
here, the reading "because the treatise has as its object the reversal of that [perception]" (*pratyakṣaviparyayārthatvāt*) is also possible,
since [the object] is established by direct perception.
Like [the state of] being without [duality],
in the region of the stainless,
the most excellent of all, without *līṃ*.
Furthermore, the reading "kiṃ vā nāpoditam" (or what has not been refuted? does not exist in the Bhāratī manuscript.

Likewise, in the extreme view that everything consists of everything (*sarvasarvātmakaikānta*), even a frog is hairy, because of the statement: "of the stationary having attained mobility, of the stationary [remaining] stationary, and of the mobile having attained stationariness.

If it is argued, "Surely everything has been established by that proponent; nothing has been refuted," we reply: if everything consists of everything, then due to the identity of all things, what is that "everything"? Thus, it has indeed been refuted, because the word "all" (*sarva*) denotes a collection of distinct objects.
Regarding the manifoldness and unity of the general and particular aspects of objects and non-objects:
the object-aspect is the general, and the object-aspect is also the particular;
for example, the object-aspect of a substance such as earth is its generality—namely, that "earth possesses color, taste, smell, and touch" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 2.1.1).

That which possesses these four qualities is earth; water consists of color, touch, taste, and viscidity; likewise, that which has color and touch is fire; and that which has touch alone is air—this is the general rule.
The specific distinction, however, arises from the mutual exclusion of their respective properties, such that they possess four, five, two, and one quality respectively.

The commonality of non-beneficiality (*anarthasāmānya*) among those very [substances] is "earth-ness" (*pṛthivītva*), because the cognition and designation of "earth" are obtained through connection with that [commonality]. Likewise, "water-ness," "fire-ness," and "air-ness" are [their respective] commonalities. And the particularities (*viśeṣa*) are those very [substances] as distinguished from one another, or the particularities are the specific divisions within their own commonalities.

These categories—substance, quality, action, universals, particulars, and the relation characterized by inherence—are distinct entities because their own-nature, purpose, definition, cognition, and designation differ, just as [they differ from] atoms, Hari, a frog, cause, effect, earth, conjunction, quality, jumping, action, existence, exclusion, and inherence. This is because substance and the other categories are not identical with one another, are absolutely different, lack a common root, and are entirely devoid of any real ontological status, like a sky-flower; otherwise, they would be like a child and a youth [who are essentially the same person].

For those who argue that [the world] arises from differentiation (*bheda*), since their position maintains the absolute distinctness of things, how could there be—given that they do not share a common nature—the following: the conjunction of atoms with the earth (which is the effect of deer and frogs), the quality of jumping, the action of leaping, and the inherence of existence and exclusion? By the term "atom" (*aṇu*), the substantial inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of the deer and the frog is understood according to the opponent's view;

by the mention of the "deer and frog," the effect-substance (*kāryadravya*) consisting of the composite whole (*avayavin*) produced through the completion of the initiation of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth, which are connected to the atoms, is understood.

The conjunction of that substance, such as a deer or a frog, with the earth is its quality (*guṇa*); its leaping is its action (*karman*); its existence (*bhavana*) is its state (*bhāva*), namely *sattā*; its exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) is its particularity (*viśeṣa*), being distinct from other existences; and their inherence (*tathāsamavāya*) is the relation (*sambandha*). Thus, these six categories do not exist, as will be shown by the example of a sky-flower.

What, then, is "existence" (*bhāvanā*)? There is no substance postulated by others, because it does not consist of quality, action, generality, or particularity, like a sky-flower; or rather, because its nature is absolutely different from those [categories].
Quality and action do not exist, because they lack the nature of a substance, just like a sky-flower.

Likewise, generality, particularity, and inherence do not exist as substances, because they lack the nature of quality and action, just like a sky-flower; and because they lack the nature of generality and particularity, just like a sky-flower.
Earth is not to be designated as "earth," because it is absolutely distinct from earthness, just like water.
Earthness is not to be designated as "earthness," because it is absolutely distinct from earth, just like water-ness.
Qualities, actions, universals, particulars, and inherence do not exist, because they lack the nature of a substance, just like a sky-flower.

In this way, even each single [entity] does not exist—like a sky-flower—because it is not of the nature of the others; or, like the nature of the others, it does not possess its own essential nature. This should be applied according to the distinctions among the examples of the remaining categories, as stated in the rule:
"The word *dravya* may be used in the sense of 'suitable' (*bhavya*)," Pāṇini 5.3.104. Thus, *dravya* is that which is suitable. And *dravya* is also [used] in the sense of "suitable" (Pāṇini 5.3).
According to the statement "it becomes," that which is capable of becoming (*bhavya*) is a substance (*dravya*), and the act of becoming is existence (*bhāva*).
Since they are distinct from the act of becoming, substances and the like do not exist at all, just like the son of a barren woman;
likewise, because the act of becoming is distinct from the substance, it too does not exist, just like the son of a barren woman.
Alternatively, it is not a substance (*dravya*), because it does not attain the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of being; it is just like the son of a barren woman.
Likewise, even "becoming" (*bhavana*) is not [a substance], because it does not attain the essential nature of a substance, for the same reason.
The same applies to qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth as well.
Thus, exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) and inherence (*samavāya*) [are established];
and regarding the object (*viṣaya*),
it is as stated in the *Praśastapādabhāṣya*.
The particularities are these; the others are the particulars. (Viśeṣāḥ, itarāṇi bhāṣye; viśeṣāḥ, itarāṇi yāskīye;
viśeṣāḥ, etāni yāskīye)
Qualities, actions, universals, inherence, and particularity—these are the categories. [The category of] substance is characterized by its own nature. *Praśastapādabhāṣya*.
In this context, there is a variation; there may also be the reading *svasvatattva*.
By examining the meaning as "mind" (*mati*) or "intellect" (*buddhi*), it is understood here that *matya* is the correct form.

Regarding the reading *anitya* as it appears in the text, if one prefers the reading *māna*, it should be understood through the etymology *mitir mānam* (measurement is knowledge), meaning that *mitiḥ* is valid cognition (*pramiti*), i.e., a cognition that accords with reality. For comparison: "Just as spatial and temporal distinctions, though distinct from the characteristics of the cognition of the designator, are not different from the real object itself, so too are qualities and the rest not different from the substance."
Viśeṣāvaśyaka-bhāṣya 2110:
"For this indeed is the 'particularity' (viśeṣatva) of particulars—that they are distinguished by others.

This alone is the definition of distinctions (bhedas), due to the difference in name, specific characteristic, own-nature, and purpose."—thus [it is stated] in the manuscript copy of the commentary on the Viśeṣāvaśyaka-bhāṣya composed by Koṭṭāryagaṇi Vādimahattara, folio 174–2.

Whence [could there be] the atom, the deer, the frog, the cause, the effect, the conjunction with the earth, the quality, the action of leaping, existence, and exclusion, as well as inherence? Because substances and so forth are not identical with one another, because they are absolutely distinct, because they are rootless, and because they entirely transcend the operation of reality (*tattva-vṛtti*), they are like a sky-flower. Otherwise, like a child and a youth, whence could there be the atom, the frog, the deer, the cause, the body, and the earth? *Note: Based on an examination of the preceding and following context, it is understood that the reading "kuto'ṇuhariṇamaṇḍūkakāraṇakāryadharaṇi" is indeed the correct one.*
Let it be seen: Paṃ. 22, vāya aṇu-bhā. (Vāyavya-aṇubhāṣya).
Or rather,
without the experience of the subtle connection with atoms, there would be no arising even of the non-existent.
In this context, there may also be the reading "they do not exist," following the example of the sky-flower (*khapuṣpa*) to be mentioned later.

This passage, starting from "like a sky-flower" (contained within such brackets) and ending with "because it lacks qualities and action, because it is like a sky-flower," does not appear in the manuscripts of the Ya lineage.
Furthermore, in this instance, there may also be the reading "because it lacks qualities and action" (*aguṇākarmatvāt*).

Comparison: Due to reasons such as being devoid of qualities and being actionless, as previously stated, there is indeed non-existence (pṛṣṭha 53, line 5); [the phrase] "of the nature of its own self" (svātmarūpa) [is used], and [the phrase] "to be joined with difference and so forth" (bhedādyojya) [is used]. (Bhāṣya).
"Substance is capable; substance is incapable like [an incapable thing]," according to the Bhāṣya;
"substance is incapable like [an incapable thing]," according to the Yāska-vṛtti.

Alternatively, it might be argued that because of the absence of action, quality, and designation, the effect is non-existent and arises later; that is not tenable, because it lacks a foundation, like a flower in the sky.

Qualities (*guṇa*), actions (*karman*), universals (*sāmānya*), particulars (*viśeṣa*), and inherence (*samavāya*) do not exist, because they are not substances (*adravyatvāt*), like a sky-flower. Likewise, [qualities] are distinct from qualities because they lack further qualities; [universals] are distinct from universals because they lack further universality; [particulars] are distinct from particulars because they lack further particularity; [inherence] is distinct from causes because it is not a cause; and [inherence] is distinct from effects because it is not an effect. For these reasons, how could there be atoms, Indra, frogs, causes, effects, the earth, conjunction, qualities, jumping, actions, existence, exclusion, or inherence? The meaning is that they do not exist.

Summing this up, it is said: "In every respect, its state (*bhāva*) is reality (*tattva*) because it transcends the functioning of reality (*tattva-vṛtti*). The functioning of reality is its operation through that which is not-reality (*atattva*) and through a nature other than its own nature. If it is argued that [the statement] is not so because, in the case of a statement contrary to the nature of Hari and others, there is a contradiction with established worldly consensus (*prasiddhi*) due to the proposition being opposed to what is well-known, we say no. This is because, as stated, the situation is equal; furthermore, since the world has been rendered non-authoritative [in this context], such a statement would contradict one's own accepted position (*abhyupagama-virodha*).

If it is argued that [the reason] is not a valid inference (*atarka*) because it occurs in both hairy and hairless *aikya* (identical) things, and because it neither occurs nor does not occur in similar and dissimilar instances, we say no. For the example is as follows: just as a substance (*dravya*) exists, so too do qualities such as color and taste, and actions such as staying and moving, exist through their occurrence and cessation; this is like the relationship between the properties of being father and son in a single person.

Since the six categories of existence, including atoms and substances, along with their conceptual determinations (*savikalpa*), have completely transcended that [kind of] occurrence, their non-existence is like that of a sky-flower; thus the final example is taught and should be understood to apply everywhere, as has been applied accordingly.

"Otherwise" means by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyeṇa*), as in the case of a child and a youth: that which exists does not transcend the reality of its own nature and what is other than it; for example, a child is indeed a youth, and a youth is indeed a child, yet they are distinct due to the difference in their states. Childhood is the basis for youthhood, and youthhood is different from childhood; thus, the functioning of reality consists of that which is both itself and other than itself. Without transcending that, one is neither merely a child nor merely a youth; and since he does not transcend the functioning of reality as such, he is known through the fivefold cognition (*pañcajñeyata*).
It is subsequently understood that the earth possesses the form of the effect of the hare-marked moon and the frog;
[the variant reading] *hariṇāmaṇḍūkākāraṇākāryādharaṇi* is in manuscript Bhā. and Ya.

If it is argued that [the proposition] is not so because it contradicts common consensus (*prasiddhi*) due to stating a nature contrary to that of the hare and other such things, we say no; for it is equal to what was stated before, and since the world has already been shown to be non-authoritative, there is a contradiction with one's own accepted position (*abhyupagama*) in speaking thus.

If it is further argued that when the hairy and the hairless are identical, the presence and absence [of the reason] in the similar and dissimilar instances (*sapakṣa* and *asapakṣa*) constitute a lack of logical reasoning (*atarka*), we say no; for this concerns the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
The stability of qualities (guṇāsthiti) [is] the state of abiding in qualities (guṇasthiti);
that is the activity (vṛtti).

Because of this [nature], the six categories—beginning with atoms (*aṇu*) and substances (*dravya*), as listed on page 49, line 1, such as the atom, Hari, the frog, cause, effect, earth, conjunction, quality, jumping, action, existence, exclusion, and inherence—are intended here; this should be understood.
[The term] *bālatva* is a corruption of *mūlatva*.
Childishness is the stain;
from the state of being other,
there are five.

If it is argued that the falsity [of the statement] regarding the nature of a deer and so forth arises precisely because the proposition contradicts common consensus (*prasiddhi-viruddha-pratijñatva*), then this objection is raised: the nature of a deer is its being hairy; a false statement regarding that is "the deer is hairless. In such a false statement, one whose proposition contradicts common consensus is "one whose proposition contradicts common consensus" (*prasiddhi-viruddha-pratijña*); the state of being such is *prasiddhi-viruddha-pratijñatva*, and from that alone comes the lack of truth.
To this, it is replied: No, because it is equal to what was stated previously.
"No"—this is a negation. This [position] is also not tenable.

In what way? "As stated above" (*uktavat*); that is, it is equal to what was stated: "That which is contrary to the determination of the scriptures is invalid because it is without exception. Therefore, this too is equal to that: in the case of a false statement regarding the nature of Hari and so forth, its lack of reality follows precisely from the fact that the proposition contradicts common consensus (*prasiddhi*). Here too, the same reasoning applies to the subsequent [objection].

If it is asked, "How so?", [the answer is] no, because everything has already been refuted, and so on—all that [applies] up to the point that it is like a sky-flower; otherwise, it would be like a child or a youth.

Furthermore, since the world has not been accepted as a valid authority (*apramāṇīkṛta*), how could there be a contradiction with worldly consensus (*prasiddhi*)? Or where is that consensus established?
Moreover, in stating this, there is a contradiction with one's own tenets (*abhyupagama-virodha*).

But surely, for you who maintain an extremist position (*ekāntavādin*), to charge us with the fault of making a proposition that contradicts worldly consensus while disregarding the world as a source of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*) results in a contradiction with your own tenets; therefore, it is improper to speak thus. [This] might be suspected, [but] it is not so. (pra. It may be argued: "The lion and the deer... (pra.)
The state of being a proposition (*pratijñātva*) arises even from that which is not suchness (*atathātathātva*).
...also arises;
what is it like? Like redness.
See page 47, line 3.
Because it is precisely due to its being a thesis (*pratijñā*);
see page 47, line 3;
see page 49, line 3.
In this context, it is conceivable that the reading should be "kutaḥ" [instead of "kṣa vā"], as it has been established by you; thus, it is well-known in the *Yati*.
bhā° without [the word] *anyatra* — thus in the Vana, Vi°, Ra°, Hī°; thus in the Cane, Pā°, Ḍe°, Lī°; [this is] the fault of the non-fulfillment of the promise, pra°.

Regarding the word *pādāna*, it might be thought: "I cannot establish the invalidity [of the argument] by way of a flaw in the thesis (*pratijñā*), because that would contradict what I myself have accepted; however, I am able to do so by way of a flaw in the reason (*hetu*). To this, he says: "If it is argued that when there is identity between the hairy and the hairless, there is no logical reasoning (*atarka*) regarding the presence or absence [of the reason] in similar and dissimilar instances."

Since both [the hare and the frog] possess four legs, yet the hare is hairless while the frog is hairy—both being established as objects of common worldly perception—it follows that for you, perception is not an authoritative means of knowledge; for if perception were authoritative here, then in all other cases as well, there would result the non-existence of the presence in similar instances (sapakṣa) and the absence from dissimilar instances (asapakṣa).

First, regarding the extreme of non-distinction (*aviśeṣaikānta*): how could there be another position or a counter-position? For if there were identity between the hairy and the hairless upon the occurrence of a property, then the reason "because of moving by leaping while possessing four feet" would result in being a contradictory reason (*viruddha-hetu*), since it does not occur in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*)—such as those with hair—where the probandum is "having deer-like hair," yet it occurs in the dissimilar instances (*asapakṣa*) which are hairy; or else, because it occurs in both similar and dissimilar instances, it would result in being a common inconclusive reason (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*). Alternatively, if there is identity between the hairy and the hairless, then due to the non-difference of the subject (*pakṣa*) and the non-difference of the property, the categories of similar and dissimilar instances would cease to exist, resulting in it being an uncommon inconclusive reason (*asādhāraṇānaikāntika*).
Therefore, this [position] is irrational.
