If there is the apprehension that because this [Reality] is beyond reasoning (*atarkya*), the presentation of its nature as being contrary to that of Hari and others is invalid, we reply: if you think thus, it is not so; for an example (*dṛṣṭānta*) has as its object what is established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Indeed, in the world, an example is an object such as a jar or a cloth, which is well-known through the means of valid perception. And the discernment of the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) has that [example] as its object; for the capacity of all inference and all its constituent members (*avayava*) to establish the probandum is established by virtue of that [example].
As it has been said: "The establishment of the members [of a syllogism] occurs by the force of the example (dṛṣṭānta), because all members depend upon it;
therefore, the true nature of the example is sought and investigated.
And because that [example] is perceptible, through it the understanding of the object will occur in the same way, so that your entire philosophical system (siddhānta-darśana) will be comprehended."

If the apprehension of the perceptible were established, then the apprehension of the imperceptible would be established; however, since that [apprehension of the perceptible] is not established, there is an absolute lack of possibility.
Consequently, that example is unestablished, because the world is not accepted as a valid authority.

Furthermore, in the absence of perception—which serves as the example—how can there be the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) between the probandum and the probans? Thus, if perception is rejected, reasoning (*tarka*) itself remains unestablished; how then can there be an investigation into what is or is not reasoning? Therefore, the fault of arriving at a conclusion contrary to the actual nature of things, such as the deer and so forth, remains exactly as it was.

By way of the faults of the thesis (*pratijñādoṣadvāreṇa*), [there are] its own nature (*svarūpa*) and so forth; by way of the faults of the reason (*hetudoṣadvāreṇa*), [there are] its own nature and so forth.
[The phrase] "due to the non-occurrence of the established rule" refers to the reason (*hetu*).
The reading "hetu...kṣavṛtti...gamanāt" does not exist in any of the manuscripts.

[The opponent argues: Because it is the object of worldly consensus established by perception (*pratyakṣa*), [the thesis] is not treated as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, since for you perception itself is non-existent here as well as everywhere else, there would follow the non-existence of both presence in similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and absence from dissimilar instances (*asapakṣa*);
thus, in the case of the extreme view of non-distinction (*aviśeṣaikānta*), how could there be another position or a dissimilar instance?
Having functioned as the basis for the commonality of non-existence, it is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the production [of that realization].
The proof has been established there;
in that regard,
[the following] is investigated.
The vision of that established doctrine will be understood thus: since there is an absence of even the possibility [of proof],
how can there be the state of being "bad reasoning" (sutarka) from the very fact that reasoning (tarka) is unestablished?

Furthermore: "In this very [case]" and so forth, up to "because it would result in non-existence. Just as whatever fault you attribute to me when refuting the true nature of a deer belongs to you alone—here the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*) is to be understood; that is, for you alone, the proponent of an extremist position (*ekāntavādin*). The word "only" (*eva*) is used for emphasis: just as there is no fault for me in this proof, but [the fault] is yours alone, this has been demonstrated in accordance with your own admission. It is not only here; rather, the meaning is that in all other cases as well—in the thesis (*pakṣa*), the reason (*hetu*), and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*)—the faults belong to you alone, not to me.

Because the world and direct perception have been rendered invalid—this being understood from the context—another reason is also stated: because it would result in the non-existence of presence and absence in similar and dissimilar instances.

If, as you maintain, the inference of an object is based on positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), and these two consist of presence and absence in similar and dissimilar instances, and the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) occurs through their force, then it follows that those very [concomitances] are non-existent.

Therefore, since it would follow that [the reason] does not exist in either the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) or the dissimilar instances (*asapakṣa*) respectively, this is merely a statement of the reason [intended] for you alone—whether you be a proponent of the doctrine of non-distinction (*aviśeṣaikāntavādin*), a proponent of the doctrine of distinction (*viśeṣaikāntavādin*), or a proponent of the doctrine of the manifoldness of both (*tadubhayānekatvaikāntavādin*).

This is now explained individually: first, in the case of the extreme view of non-distinction (*aviśeṣaikānta*), how can there be another position (*anyapakṣa*), a counter-position (*asapakṣa*), or exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*)? Non-distinction is the universal (*sāmānya*); the extreme view of non-distinction is that "everything is of the nature of everything. In such an extreme view of non-distinction, if you hold to this [view], how can there be another position—an "other-position" being the position of something else—or exclusion from it? For [in that view] reality is manifested as such [indistinguishably]. In the extreme view of distinction (*viśeṣaikānta*), how can there be that position, a similar position (*sapakṣa*), or the existence of that [property]? For things do not abide in such [a state of mutual distinction]. In the extreme view of the manifoldness of both (*ubhayānekatvaikānta*), how can there even be the properties to be proven (*sādhya*), the means of proof (*sādhana*), and the subject (*dharmin*)? For they would be unprecedented [in that context]. Furthermore, because there is no other disputant (*vādī*), and because for you too there is no distinction from anything else—due to the lack of distinction between the oneness of everything being of the nature of everything—[these categories are impossible].

Alternatively, because there is no other speech, or because all speech consists of your own speech, or because there is no distinction between your speech and the speech of others; or rather, what is the use of our resorting to harsh words that accept the non-existence of the speech of both ourselves and the opposing disputant? Let "another" (anya) and "position" (pakṣa) together constitute the meaning of "another-position" (anyapakṣa); from where would such a thing arise, given that everything is of one essence with your position due to the absolute lack of distinction among objects? Thus, for the proponent who says, "Sound is eternal, because it is unproduced, like space," there is an absence of the position, the speaker, the speech, and the object denoted regarding the position that sound is non-eternal.

In the same way, for the proponent of the doctrine of absolute permanence (*nityaikāntavādin*), there is no dissimilar instance (*asapakṣa*) because of the absence of things such as jars that are similar by virtue of sharing the common property of impermanence.
Due to the absence of that [dissimilar instance], there is an absence of exclusion (*vyāvṛttyabhāva*).

From the word "or" (*vā*), how could there be one's own position (*svapakṣa*), a similar instance (*sapakṣa*), or the subsistence [of the reason] therein? This is because of the very non-difference of the oneness in which everything is of the nature of everything. It might be argued: "Even for the proponent of non-distinction (*aviśeṣavādin*), impermanence and being produced (*kṛtakatva*) certainly exist, because manifestation and disappearance consist in coming into being after not having been, and ceasing to be after having been."
And this is incorrect; why? Because such manifestation occurs precisely within reality (*tattva*).
"Reality" means oneness; it is because such a manifestation occurs in that very way, precisely within that reality.

What is meant by this? Since the clay itself is non-different, and [the various forms] are merely its internal manifestation and concealment—just like the states of a finger being bent or straight—the specific state is simply manifested; what other clay is there in the states of the lump, the small piece, the jar, and so forth? Therefore, because it is manifested as such within the very reality (tattva) itself, how can there be a "different position" (anyapakṣa), which is the "opposite position" (asapakṣa), or the "exclusion from that," which is the "similar position" (sapakṣa), or the "existence therein"? Thus it is rightly said: for you alone, who maintains the doctrine of absolute non-distinction (aviśeṣaikāntavādin), there results the consequence of non-existence regarding the presence in the similar class and absence in the dissimilar class, just as in the case of proofs that result in the opposite of the nature of deer and other animals.
"In this very [text], Prajñākaragupta states:

'In this case, through examination of what precedes and follows, it appears that the reading "ihaiva" (in this very [place]) alone is correct. Comparing this with the statement—'It is rightly said: for you, who maintain the doctrine of absolute non-distinction, there arises the consequence of non-existence regarding the means of proof that establish the presence and absence [of a reason] in similar and dissimilar instances, just as in the case of the proofs establishing the contrary nature of lions and so forth' (p. 52, l. 13)—[it is clear]."
Likewise, O Hariṇapraśna, whatever fault Bhāva brings upon me, whatever fault he brings upon me— yaṃ yaṃ doṣaṃ yaṃ mamāpādayati bhā॰ yaṃ yaṃ doṣamāpādayati ya॰.
The proponents of the doctrine of alternation [state]:
"In that case,
there would be non-existence through mere negation."
The word *tasyāḥ* is in the ablative case;
its connection is with the phrase *asattvāpatter* ("because of the consequence of non-existence").
The reading *viśeṣaikāntavādinaḥ* does not appear in the Ya manuscripts.

Is there a deviation from your [proposition] at the end of the particularity of that friend, because it is manifested as such only in that reality? How can there be a thesis, a similar instance (*sapakṣa*), or the existence of that [reason] if there is an absolute monism of particularity, since it does not abide in that way? And how can there be the properties of the probandum, the probans, and the subject (*dharmin*) if there is an absolute monism of both [thesis and reason], since they would be unprecedented in that state due to the absence of anything else?
Why is the state of being a specific [word] not [the cause] for the composition of another [work]? (pra. bhā. (pra. racanayoḥ. ya. viśeṣāya vacanatvam. kim na para. 0.169b-0.170a.
...by means of harsh words such as the admission of non-existence, etc.; *pra* [is used];
"your position" (*tvatpakṣam*) by all; *pra*; here, there might also be the reading "in this position of yours" (*atra tvatpakṣe*).
Because it has the nature of being produced,
sound is impermanent;
and because there is no [eternal] existence, it is non-eternal.
The distinction [arises] from manifestation; in the case of the other position, there is no fixed status for the pot.
Absence from the similar class (sapakṣa); non-exclusion from the similar class in the dissimilar class (asapakṣa).
And these very [points] are to be seen at page 51, line 1,
by means of the occurrence and non-occurrence of the commentary (vṛtti).

Likewise, if there is an absolute extreme of particularity (*viśeṣaikānta*), how can there be a thesis (*pakṣa*), a similar instance (*sapakṣa*), or its presence (*tatsattva*)? In terms of space, because of distinctions such as [the division into] atoms, [the division into] form and so forth, [the division into] mere consciousness, and [the division into] the inexpressible; and in terms of time, because of not persisting beyond the absolutely subtle and ceased moment—how can there be a thesis? In this case too, whether that "thesis" refers to the proponent, the speaker’s statement, that very position, or even the meaning itself, it is impossible [to establish one], because of the impossibility of [distinguishing] the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*), or the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya*), as in the proposition "sound is impermanent."

Whence is there a similar instance (*sapakṣa*)? Because of the absence of a universal (*sāmānya*) connected with another entity; for if one were to admit a universal that is the absence of the property to be proven (*sādhyābhāva*), it would follow that there is no distinction between the similar and dissimilar instances.

Whence is there existence (*sattva*) therein? Because of its absence, and because of the absence of other conceptual properties such as "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth; because all phenomena (*dharmas*) consist merely of mutually distinct and inactive properties; and because of the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) of the ineffable (*nirupākhya*) emptiness (*śūnyatva*).
And as before, there is an absence of exclusion from the opponent's position and the similar instances, due to the word "or" (*vā*).
Having summarized as before, the reason for understanding that meaning is stated: "Because it does not exist in that manner" (*tathā'sthiteḥ*).

This means because no object exists in that way—namely, in the manner of being momentary, devoid of activity, and empty. Thus, even in the case of a specific [property], there is the consequence that the presence in the similar class (*sapakṣavṛtti*) and so forth would be non-existent everywhere; this is the meaning of the word "or" (*vā*) and what follows.
In the alternative view, see the rule "cāder ātaḥ paraḥ" (Pāṇini 8.1.58) and its commentary on page 26, note 7.
The speaker’s [intended] position (*pakṣa*), the speaker’s [intended] similar instance (*sapakṣa*) and dissimilar instance (*asapakṣa*), and the specificities thereof.

The meaning is as follows: just as previously—due to the word "or" (vā)—the absence of [the reason's] occurrence in one's own position (*svapakṣa*) and its similar instances (*sapakṣa*) was intended, so too here, due to the word "or," the absence of exclusion from the opponent’s position (*prativādipakṣa*) and its similar instances is intended; that is, there is no absence of [the reason's presence in] the opponent's position. Note: *pākhyaśūnyatva* is based on the Bhāṣya manuscript; *prativādipakṣavyāvṛttyabhāvo* is based on the Prajñā manuscript.
See Pañjikā 8;
as stated previously in the *Yukti*,
so too in the case of the absolute [position] of both being manifold and one.

"Both" refers to the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*). If one maintains the extreme view that these two are manifold and distinct from one another, then how can there even be the properties of the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*), or the subject (*dharmin*)? First of all, there would be an absence of the probandum, namely impermanence (*anityatva*); for by accepting a mere property (*dharmamātra*) as the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), one would be relying on perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*), which results in the fallacy of contradicting one's own thesis (*pratijñā-vyāghāta*) because it would then become a worldly matter (*lokatva*). If it is argued that it is not a worldly matter because it belongs to a treatise (*śāstra*), we say no; for those treatises rely upon the world, since those treatises are composed by superimposing the categories of universal, particular, cause, and effect everywhere.

Because it lacks a foundation, like a flower in the sky; likewise, the probans "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*)—wherein "produced" (*kṛtam*) is used in the sense of being pitiable, contemptible, or unknown—is itself without foundation because it is absolutely distinct from substance (*dravya*). Thus, there is an absence of both [the subject and the] property.
Even in the case of two substrata, such as sound and a jar, their non-existence [as one] is established by reasons such as their not being qualities or actions, as previously stated;

furthermore, the cause for their inclusion [under the same category] is said to be "being unprecedented" (*apūrvatva*). "Being unprecedented" means being without a basis, because substances, qualities, and so forth are absolutely distinct from one another.

Thus, first of all, because [your position] functions in the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and does not function in the dissimilar class (*asapakṣa*), or vice versa, the fault of being "non-reasoning" (*atarka*) belongs to you alone, since reasoning is established by the force of examples. Thus have been stated the faults in the doctrines of non-distinction (*aviśeṣa*), distinction (*viśeṣa*), both, manifoldness (*anekatva*), and monism (*ekānta*). [In the doctrine of] "both" as a monistic [position], [it is said that] the manifold is non-different.
If [the universal] were non-different from many [particulars], then there would be an absence of its unity;
for by accepting the example and thereby making perception the authoritative means of knowledge, it would result in the status of being a worldly convention, which would contradict your own thesis.

If it is argued that [the Vaiśeṣika system] is not worldly because it is a treatise (*śāstra*), we say no; for those treatises are dependent upon the world, since those treatises were composed by superimposing the categories of generalities, particularities, causes, and effects everywhere. Thus it has been stated in the *Vāda-nyāya*.

Furthermore, because the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is perception (*pratyakṣa*), because the reason (*hetu*) is inference (*anumāna*), because the application (*upanaya*) is analogy (*upamāna*), and because the proposition (*pratijñā*) is scripture (*āgama*), it follows that [the system] has accepted perception as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

And from that, it becomes worldly (*laukika*), since the purpose of the meaning of the treatise for logicians who approach it with their reasonings is to establish consistency with the example. As it has been said: "That object upon which there is a consensus of understanding among ordinary people and experts is the example" (Nyāyasūtra 1.1.25).
1.25 Thus, "the world" is the example; that which is stated in contradiction to it is "contrary to the example."
If it is asked, "What is the fault in that?"—the answer is: there is a contradiction with one's own thesis (*pratijñā-vyāghāta*).

What was the thesis? That "that which is contrary to the determination of the treatise (*śāstra*) is not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*)," whereas the nature of the deer and so forth is not [invalidated] because it is free from exception. That [thesis] is contradicted when the treatise is accepted as the authority, because worldly activity proceeds by the force of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), as stated in the *Laukika-prastāva* regarding the meaning of the commentary.
Just as the world [is], so is that which is expressed by words contrary to it; see page 47,
line 3.

If it is argued that the status of being a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is destroyed because [the subject matter] is not worldly due to its being scriptural (*śāstra*), then this might be the thought:

"Indeed, it has been stated that the authors of treatises, being skilled in explaining the objects they have perceived, explain the meanings of their treatises through arguments whose essence is illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*) for the sake of intellectual consensus; however, the meanings of the treatises cannot be made perceptible in the world."
"Therefore, the world does not rely on those treatises that express such [views]";

but that is not so, because those treatises are dependent upon the world. For the word "hi" has the sense of "because": because those treatises were composed by superimposing everywhere what is observed—namely, the mere universal among the universal, particular, cause, and effect (such as the cause of curd, or the observed particulars of oiliness and whiteness), and the mere particular consisting of the constant production and destruction of flames.

Having observed merely the configuration of the cause—such as milk, which possesses common properties like viscosity—and failing to see that this commonality does not persist in the absence of specific states such as curd and so forth, they superimpose upon everything the notion that "just as this is a mere configuration, neither an effect nor a particularity, so too all other objects such as jars and cloths are merely configurations of the primary cause consisting of the three *guṇas*. Thus, treatises were composed for that purpose, in the course of establishing the principle that the cause alone, the universal alone, exists everywhere.

Likewise, having observed the moment-by-moment arising, destruction, and distinctness of flames, and seeing that these are impossible without the existence of a common substrate such as color, taste, touch, smell, and form, [the proponents of this view] superimpose upon everything—just as this is merely a particularity, being neither a universal nor a cause—that other entities as well, such as the earth, mountains, rivers, oceans, islands, the sky, stars, constellations, planets, and the hosts of celestial bodies, are likewise so. Consequently, they have composed treatises for that purpose, which have become like an ocean of water with boundless waves consisting of the analytical breakdown of discourses and compositions intended to establish those [particularities].
To make [it] perceptible to the world (lokapratyakṣīkartum), Bhā° Vi°; without the scriptures, the world is otherwise, Pra°.
The cause of burning; here,
by superimposition (bhā),
and also by superimposition (ya).
There is no purpose for the qualities of one who is without purpose.

If it is argued that [the categories] have been established because they are superimpositions upon what is seen elsewhere, and thus lack worldly status just like the true nature of a jar, we say no; for delusion—like a mirage—is non-worldly, and consequently, the propositions (*pratijñā*) and so forth would likewise be untenable. If the object were not as it is apprehended by the world, then the proposition itself, being apprehended as it is, would not exist in that way due to the lack of distinction [between the two].

If it should be thought that, because of the superimposition (adhyāropa) elsewhere of what has been seen in one part, there is a lack of worldly nature (alaukikatva) like the reality of a jar—that is, "worldly" refers to what is perceivable by the senses, such as the form of a jar—then [we reply]: ... [the text continues with the refutation] ... [it would follow that] the nature of the jar and so forth would also be non-worldly. Therefore, this is not a valid argument. Furthermore, since the parts are indeed perceived through the senses, their non-worldliness cannot be established. Thus, the claim that the whole is non-worldly while the parts are worldly is untenable. Consequently, the distinction between the worldly and the non-worldly based on this reasoning is invalid.

Whatever is the essence of a jar here—namely, the specific form characterized by a broad belly, a narrow neck, and so forth—is superimposed upon another jar elsewhere; yet that [specificity] does not actually exist there. This superimposition occurs solely for the sake of communication with worldly consensus (*lokasaṃvāda*).

Likewise, the scriptures too possess their non-worldly character (*alaukikatva*) precisely through such superimposition. Thus, there is no fault of contradicting one's own thesis (*pratijñātavyāghāta*), as you believe would occur because of the consequence of becoming "worldly" (*lokatva*).

To this we reply: No; because delusion, like a mirage, is non-worldly (*alaukika*). That is true; it is indeed non-worldly in that manner because it is impure, like the cognition of a mirage and the like. However, it is not possible for a pure person, because that would entail the consequence that such delusion is invalid (*aprāmāṇya*), just like a mirage.
In a saline region, the rays of the sun, falling upon eyes scorched by the summer heat, rebound and appear from afar like water, causing delusion;

therefore, because it would follow that scriptural knowledge is invalid— just like the cognition of a mirage— the superimposition of what is seen elsewhere is an improper grasping and is non-worldly (*alaukika*).

When [it is said], "the jar is produced by the jar," even at the beginning of the sentence, a similar corrupt reading is seen as follows: "By the jar itself, the jar is made"—meaning that by means of the clay lump-jar (*mṛtpiṇḍaghaṭa*), the jar characterized by its upward neck, rounded lip, broad belly, base, and so forth, is made or manifested; for the root *kṛ* has the sense of manifesting (*prakāśa*). (Nayacakravṛtti, p. 215–2).

Following this [principle], it is probable that here too the reading is *pṛthukukṣyā* (having broad hips), whereas if one adheres strictly to what is heard [in the manuscript], the reading *vikukṣyā* must be assumed; its meaning should be understood as "one whose hips are large" (*viśālā kukṣir vikukṣiḥ pṛthukukṣiḥ*).
[The rest of the line] is *pādyevaya*.
See page 53,
line 1; *jaṭara-bhū-bhā-śāstra-vijñānasya* (in the Bhāṣya).

Furthermore: "And likewise, in that case, there is the impossibility of even the thesis (*pratijñā*) and the other members [of the syllogism], not merely the lack of authority of the knowledge of the scripture. What then? In that manner, and thus having done so, when that [scripture] exists as something non-worldly, like a mirage, there is the impossibility of even the members such as the thesis.
How so? If the thing is not as it is apprehended by the world."

The word "yadi" (if) indicates the opponent's admission: if your intention is that, by means of skill in exposition and as a mere agreement with the intellect of the expositor, you take up an example and establish that object through reasoning and scripture in such a way as I do it, but not in the way it is apprehended by the world—then, in that case, the thesis (*pratijñā*) as it has been stated would not be so, because there is no distinction [between the two ways].

First, in the doctrine of absolute non-distinction (*aviśeṣaikāntavāda*), because everything has everything as its essence, the proposition that "sound is eternal" cannot be apprehended by the auditory organ in the way it is [intended], for what reason? Because, on that view, it would also consist of color and other qualities apprehended by the eye and other organs.

Likewise, in the doctrine of absolute distinction (*viśeṣaikāntavāda*), the proposition that "sound is impermanent" could not be apprehended as it is, because the cognitions of the phonemes *a*, *kā*, *ra*, *na*, *ika*, etc.,—due to their absolute difference produced by space and time, their momentariness, their being non-existent, and their being indefinable—would lack mutual dependence, and in the absence of such dependence, all things would be non-existent. Thus, it could not be apprehended in the manner intended.

Thus, in the case of the absolute [position] of both being multiple or one, as before, because there is an absence of either of the two objects of apprehension when independent of the other side, the consequence [of non-existence] follows;
having established it thus.

...the occurrence [of contradiction]. "And therefore" (*tataśca*) means for that very reason; because that which is apprehended in the world is contrary [to the thesis], there is first a contradiction with perception (*pratyakṣavirodha*) regarding the extreme of non-distinction (*aviśeṣaikānta*). Regarding a "part" (*aṃśe*), that is, a portion: there is a contradiction with perception regarding the specific [nature] of that very object as it is perceived by perception, yet imagined by the proponent of the extreme of non-distinction. Regarding a "part," there is a contradiction with one's own words (*svavacanavirodha*), and regarding a "part," there is a contradiction with one's own tenet (*abhyupagamavirodha*), because of the acceptance of a form that is the opposite of what was stated by oneself.
If it is argued that "therefore, nothing is apprehended by the world in one way and then in another way,

as if it were the cognition of a madman," then, in that case, there is a contradiction with your own admission through your direct partiality for the worldly view; furthermore, because of the mention of "some things" being apprehended as they are and others being apprehended otherwise,
there is a contradiction with perception, since this implies a state of diversity.

In one respect, there is a contradiction with one's own words (*svavacanavirodha*), because at that time one desires specific words for the presentation [of the object]; in another respect, there is a contradiction with what has been accepted (*abhyupagamavirodha*), because the specific nature of the present subject and its properties contradicts the "all-pervasiveness" (omnipresence) previously accepted and well-known throughout one's own treatise, since this constitutes an acceptance that is the reverse of what was stated by oneself. At the end, the reason is stated: because perception, one's own words, and what is accepted do not differ in their status as forms of acceptance (*abhyupagama*).

Thus, in the case of the absolute particularity [of sound], there is a contradiction with perception because the sound grasped by the auditory faculty— which lasts for only that brief duration— lacks the designation of a relationship between preceding and succeeding phonemes, as well as the persistence of the cognition thereof, and yet it is perceived; likewise, since this is established by one's own words, the proposition that "sound is impermanent" is contradicted by one's own words,
and for this very reason, there is a contradiction with one's own tenet.

As before, that same reason applies here as well; thus, regarding the absolute [positions] of duality or non-duality, the very proofs previously stated should be applied here: "There is no impermanence because of being non-substantial, like the son of a barren woman"; "There is no such thing as sound," which is the absence of intrinsic nature;

and "The destruction of a quality that exists and is not perceptible by the eye is similar to [the destruction of] actions" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 2.2.31), because there is no mark [of existence] for that which exists.

At the time of its presentation for the purpose of explaining the reasons prescribed in the scriptures—such as "because it is an effect," "because of its cause," and "because of its transformation"—there is contradiction with perception (*pratyakṣavirodha*) because [the reason] lacks properties such as impermanence or being a sound (*śabdatva*), given that it is perceived [as permanent].
There is contradiction with one's own words (*svavacanavirodha*) because one accepts that the statement remains in that same state at that very time.

If there is a contradiction with what was previously accepted, then there is a "contradiction of acceptance" (*abhyupagama-virodha*) due to the contradiction with the present [position], as in the previous case; the reason for this in all instances is that it takes the form of accepting the opposite of what one has stated oneself.

Thus, in some respects there is a contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣa-virodha*), and in other respects there is a contradiction of one's own words (*svavacana-virodha*), while in yet other respects there is a contradiction of acceptance (*abhyupagama-virodha*), because of accepting the opposite of what one has stated oneself.

If it is argued that "therefore, nothing is apprehended by the world as it is, nor is anything otherwise, for [all] would be like the cognition of a madman," then, in that case, there is a contradiction with your own admission through the explicit adoption of the worldly position; for by stating "something" and by stating that it is "apprehended as it is" and "apprehended otherwise," you imply a distinction.
Because the complete cessation of sound is desired;
because [it exists] as the self of all,
now [it is established] as the self of all.

Now,
if others accept that it is "just so" in order to avoid these faults being based on falsity,
then it follows that what is apprehended by the world is not otherwise.
If it should be thought: "Because of the world's [conventional] acceptance, the contradiction of the thesis remains as it was;

thus, some things are as they are accepted and others are otherwise, like the assertions of a madman"—that is, some things such as the thesis and so forth remain exactly as grasped by the world, while others such as jars and the like are otherwise, because the world is not an investigator [of reality].
And as for the examiners who know words, sentences, and the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), their position is like that of a madman:

just as a madman, who is not an examiner and is ignorant of words, sentences, and the means of valid cognition, apprehends some things correctly and others incorrectly, and his apprehension is invalid because he makes no distinction between the existent and the non-existent and acts by mere chance; so too is the apprehension of worldly people.
To this it is replied: If that were so, there would be a contradiction with your own accepted position by directly siding with the worldly view.
How is it that you "directly" side with the worldly view? It is because [the world] perceives some things correctly, perceives others as they truly are, and perceives others otherwise.

Because it is "only something" (*kiñcit*), not everything is of the nature of everything; and the establishment of both "everything" and "not everything" occurs through the designation of distinction as "something.

Thus, in that manner, it is "so" (*tathā*); yet because it adopts other distinct categories of objects, it is also "not so" (*na tathā*). Consequently, there is a contradiction in the two assertions, and some property must be sought that serves as the basis for the designation of the mode in those two. When these three [aspects] are established, the term "so" (*tathā*) becomes logically consistent.

Likewise, even regarding "otherwise" (*anyathā*): [if one holds that] "this is other than that" and "that is other than this," then because the establishment of both "allness" and "non-allness" occurs, one merely falls into the position of worldly convention. Thus, within the extreme view of particularity (*viśeṣaikānta*), where there is absolute difference produced by space and time, and things are ineffable and void, how could there be anything at all? Having analyzed this, would one say that the unstable or the non-existent is "other" than that which is stable, or that it is "distinct"? In this way, neither "thus" (*tathā*) nor "otherwise" (*anyathā*) are tenable.

Thus, in the case of the absolute [assertion] of both unity and plurality, as previously stated, because substances and so forth lack mutual identity, or because the universal and the particular—or cause and effect—lack existence due to reasons such as being rootless, it is untenable for a real entity to be "in some respects thus and in other respects otherwise. Consequently, one falls into the position of common worldly opinion; and by that, the scriptural tenet that "everything consists of everything" is indeed contradicted. In this way, the thesis is first shown to be flawed.

Like the thesis, the reason and the example are also indeed defective, because they fail to prove that [thesis]. Furthermore, the example "one who is insane" (*unmatta*) cannot be established except by relying on worldly consensus; for the statement "insanity is excessive intoxication" is a designation made in relation to other forms of intoxication or in relation to being free from intoxication, and that [insanity] is purely worldly. Thus, those who, having accepted that [worldly convention], desire to refute it are themselves even more insane; this is the explicit acceptance of worldly censure.

In this context, the reading "sākṣāllokapakṣāpattyabhyupagama" (the acceptance of partiality toward the worldly view) is appropriate, because it is explained exactly thus in the commentary; see page 57, line 19,
due to the inclusion of the term "kathaṃcit."
And because it takes up distinct categories of entities that are the self of all, it is not so; thus, there is a contradiction with one's own renewed admission regarding some property.

Therefore, because of this worldly consensus, that which is accepted by the world as a valid authority—such as "something is something" or "it is otherwise"—is here [in this text] entirely devoid of meaning and inconsistent with one another. In this manuscript, the portion of the text from *asmāt* (line 17) up to *vilakṣāḥ* has been displaced from its original location on the following page (p. 57); it is completely useless, corrupt, and must be discarded.
Such, then, is the defect regarding the sentence.

Now, the subject of the single word (*ekapada*) is discussed: "And because it takes as its material cause (*upādāna*) both the differentiated and the non-differentiated referent (*padārtha*), it is not so [as previously stated]; thus, there is a renewed contradiction with one's own accepted doctrine.

That which possesses differentiation is "differentiated" (*bhedavān*); that which has no differentiation is "non-differentiated" (*abheda*). That which is both differentiated and non-differentiated is "the differentiated-non-differentiated" (*bhedavadabheda*). What is this? It is the referent (*padārtha*), such as a "tree" (*vṛkṣa*), which consists of the forms of the individual meaning (*svārtha*), substance (*dravya*), gender (*liṅga*), number (*saṅkhyā*), and case-role (*kāraka*) such as the object (*karman*).
As it was said in the *Kramayaugapadyacintā*: "Having denoted its own meaning, a word denotes the substance (*dravya*) inherent [in it] independently."
But when denoting that which is inherent [in a substance], having expressed its gender, number, and case-ending, that word— without requiring those specific qualifiers—
functions in such a way toward pleasant or contemptuous expressions as a whole, ending in a case-suffix.
According to the Pāṇini-Mahābhāṣya (5.3.74), this is the established doctrine in all systems of grammar.

In that context, "its own object" (*svārtha*) might be said to refer either to a genus (*jāti*) or to a form (*ākāra*). If it were "its own object" in the sense of being its very self, then because it would depend on something else, it would not be "its own" without that other thing; consequently, since substances and so forth would be established, the word-meaning (*padārtha*) would possess difference. Furthermore, if those very things—such as the "own object"—were absolutely distinct, they would lack mutual identity and thus be non-existent like a sky-flower. However, since non-difference is established through the perception of non-distinction in space, time, and so forth, the word-meaning is non-different. Therefore, even by a knower of the treatise who employs a word while advocating only the "own object," a word-meaning that possesses both difference and non-difference is thereby accepted.

Likewise, regarding substance (*dravya*), if the thesis (*pratijñā*) itself is the acceptance (*abhyupagama*), then because that [thesis] lacks worldly authority (*aprāmāṇya*), one must establish— just as in the world— that the meaning [of a statement] follows the worldly acceptance due to the employment of subjects (*pakṣa*) and so forth which do not exist in cases such as "non-distinction" (*aviśeṣa*). Having established this, whether applied sequentially or simultaneously to the word, the logical mark (*liṅga*), number, grammatical relation (*kāraka*), depreciation (*kutsā*), and other categories of meaning (*padārtha*),

when one who asserts non-distinction, distinction, or both-and-many asserts that very same thing [as previously stated] to be otherwise, there is a "new contradiction of acceptance" (*navo 'bhyupagamavirodhaḥ*).
"Nine" does not mean by way of accepting one's own [specific] treatise; what then? It means by way of acceptance at that particular time.
And that constitutes a contradiction of acceptance in every case—thus [it is said in the] Vākyapadīyabhāṣya.
In the phrase "the tree" (*vṛkṣa*) and so forth,

the "own object" (*svārtha*) here may also be read as "the universal of the tree" (*vṛkṣajāti*) and so forth; having denoted its own object, the word, being independent, denotes the substance (*dravya*) in which it inheres.
But when expressing that which is inherent, it expresses the gender, number,
and case-ending of that which is inherent;
and having expressed those specific features, while disregarding them, it expresses its entire self.
"Furthermore, this [word] ending in a case-suffix proceeds toward [the expression of] affection, censure, and so forth"—this is the reading in the Patañjala-Mahābhāṣya.

Having denoted those specific [meanings], it proceeds toward affection, censure, and so forth, as that [word] ending in a case-suffix, without regard for distinctions; thus [it is stated] in the Pātañjala-Mahābhāṣya on Pāṇini 5.3.74.
Except elsewhere in the Vyetasāra-bhāṣya and Bhāṣya, [the reading] is *na bhava* according to Pā.,
and *na bhū* according to Ḍe. and Līṃ.
Not "you" (na tvam), O Raṃ; not "I am" (hīṃ na-aham), O Viṣṇu; [not] others, nor self. Yaḥ.

Now, if "acceptance" (*abhyupagama*) is simply the thesis (*pratijñā*), then since that [thesis] lacks worldly validity (*lokāprāmāṇya*), [one might object]: "But surely, because of the inclusion of a non-existent subject (*pakṣa*) and so forth in cases such as 'non-distinction' (*aviśeṣa*), it is accepted by the world; and therefore, just like the world, the meaning is established. Having thus settled [the matter], [the author states: "The word [denotes] the simultaneous absence of the denotable..."

Alternatively, it must be stated that, by relying on the conventional arrangement of analytical abstraction (*apoddhāra-parikalpanā*), a word, having denoted its own primary meaning, denotes the substance (*dravya*) inherent within it independently; thus, one merely follows the rule of the sequence of comprehension.

For it is not possible for a word to function with respect to its own meaning and so forth in a sequential manner, pausing again and again, because it is uttered only once and is eternally inseparable from its meaning.
Indeed, this sequence of practice is not fixed for either the listener or the speaker;

for a thing qualified by all its attributes, having attained the status of being the object of a single cognition as a simultaneous collection of associated elements, is subsequently divided by other cognitions according to one's desire— thus it is stated in Bhartṛhari’s *Vākyapadīya-svavṛtti* 1.26.
There is no new attainment,
nor is there the destruction of treatises, nor the destruction of one's own treatises.

Now, it might be thought that the thesis (*pratijñā*) itself is the commitment (*abhyupagama*). For there is no commitment that is the object of the employment of individual words, because such a thing [as a word-meaning] does not exist; or because the word-meaning is merely an object of mental construction (*utprekṣā*), since it must be extracted from the sentence-meaning as a means for understanding that sentence-meaning and then explained.
Thus, the sentence alone is the word, and the meaning of that [sentence] alone is the meaning of the word.
Therefore, the thesis (*pratijñā*) itself is the commitment (*abhyupagama*), because the function of the remaining members of the sentence is for the sake of proving that [thesis].
Why? Because of the non-authoritativeness of the world (*lokāprāmāṇya*) with respect to it;
that is to say, by the force of that thesis which serves as the reason, since the non-authoritativeness of the world is thereby established.

Once it is established that sound is eternal because it is uncreated— like space— the world’s perception of a single entity as having multiple forms, such as being both eternal and non-eternal, becomes invalid by the force of that [logical proof]. This occurs even without the apprehension of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) or the grasping of the sentence-meaning.

To this it is replied: Indeed, because of the acceptance by the world that even in the absence of distinctions there is the adoption of a thesis (*pakṣa*) and so forth, when the absolute monism of non-distinction (*aviśeṣaikānta*)—namely, that "everything is of the nature of everything"—is accepted, then for the thesis "sound is eternal," as well as its reason and example, there is an absence [of validity] due to the previously stated reasons such as "being without distinction" (*nirviśeṣatva*). Likewise, in the case of the absolute monism of distinction (*viśeṣaikānta*), for the same previously stated reasons such as "being rootless" (*nirmūlatva*), there is an absence of the thesis and the other members of the syllogism.

It has been stated that even in the extreme view of both being identical or different, there would be an absence of universals, particulars, effects, and causes, which possess mutually distinct natures.

Therefore, since [the proponent] adopts things such as the thesis (*pakṣa*) which are non-existent in those [extreme views] but are established by worldly consensus, the world itself is once again accepted by these scholars of scripture who lack other means of recourse.

Therefore, by the very fact that you accept worldly conventions (*loka-abhyupagama*), the world has indeed been made authoritative (*pramāṇīkṛta*). Furthermore, because you accept mutually distinct usages such as "something is something" and "otherwise it is nothing," the invalidity of the world (*lokāprāmāṇya*) is not established. Thus, even if you go to the furthest extent, you, as experts in the scriptures (*śāstravidas*), ought to take refuge in the world itself. For the operation of the scriptures—whether concerning sentences or words—is not established without the observation of the world. Consequently, it has been stated that there is a contradiction with your own tenets due to your direct siding with the position of the world; [it is] not [a matter of] lack of distinction... [fragmentary].
The specific reality of the *viśeṣa* is the *vi-raṃ-hī*; it is the state of being the self-nature of all things (*sarvasarvātmakatva*),
which is the self-nature of all things, without exception.
The absence of [the cause] is the effect; [this is] beyond perception, etc.; [it is] the primary [cause]; [it is] the effect.
The world-renowned [authority],
the authority of the world, and the treatise of the Arhat.
In the same way, one should also understand that there is a contradiction with one's own words regarding that [subject].

Why? Because, having established that "the meaning is just like in common worldly usage" (*lokavat*), one employs the word; thus it "proceeds like the world" (*lokavat*). [The suffix] *vat* means "like the world" (*lokasyeva*) or "as in the world" (*loka iva*). The particle *eva* serves as a restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). What does it restrict? It restricts the meaning in the world, not the world in the meaning; for even those who know the treatises (*śāstra*) are part of the world.

Even if there is a distinction between the object (*artha*) and the world (*loka*), this particle *eva* (only/just) is to be understood in both cases: "the object is just like the world" and "the world is just like the object. This is because the two do not deviate from one another; for those learned in the scriptures, usage occurs even when there is a distinction between the world and the object, since their reality is established as such. However, regarding the word-meaning (*śabdārtha*), the claim that "it is not a thing as it is grasped by the world" would contradict one's own statement. Furthermore, contradiction with the world is precisely what is under discussion here, for [scriptural authority] does not function if it contradicts the world. Moreover, if the world were not authoritative, contradictions with perception and inference would arise everywhere, since those two [perception and inference] are grounded in the world.

And regarding the distinctness of worldly objects, the word *iti* is used in the sense of "manner" (*prakāra*), meaning "in this manner. Having thus established [the object] through the intellect and accepted it, one employs words for others in order to communicate the object as determined by oneself; therefore, even those authors of treatises accept that the conventional usage of employing words—whether delimited by the word (*pada*) or delimited by the sentence (*vākya*)—follows the world in this way.

And in that case, when the reality of the word-meaning is established in such a manner—that is, in the same way as the word "jar" is employed by the world with respect to an object characterized by a form of clay, a broad belly, and so forth—it is established as real. When this reality is thus established, those learned in the treatises who employ words in common worldly usage have effectively admitted the world's position; this is already stated by implication. Therefore, it would contradict [our position] to say, "The thing is not as it is grasped by the world. "Grasped by the world" (*lokagrāha*) means the world's apprehension; "grasping" (*grāha*) is used here in the sense of "like a grasp," meaning whatever is the world's apprehension is "as it is grasped by the world."

What is that? A proponent who asserts a thing exactly as it is well-known even to cowherds says, by his very own words, something contradictory: "Whatever word is employed by me, each and every one of those words shall not have such a meaning. By his own statement, each and every such statement would be contradicted; the optative suffix (*liṅ*) here is used in the sense of a wish (*āśaṃsā*), according to Pāṇini 3.3.173.
3.134. How can it be determined that verbal harshness is indeed contradictory? The Teacher shows his own courtesy by suggesting that it might somehow be contradictory;
thus, for now, there is a contradiction with one's own words.
Or else, as in the world,
because of the application of the term "separateness" (*pṛthaktva*) to an object,
its reality would be established; thus, it would contradict your own statement that the referent of a word is not a real entity as it is apprehended in the world.
But contradiction with the world (*lokavirodha*) is indeed the very subject at hand, because [the scripture] does not function when it contradicts that;
and if the world were not authoritative, contradictions with perception and inference would be present everywhere, since those two are established therein.

Even with [the suffixes] *li*, *luṅ*, *liṭ*, and *ktā*, [the forms] *raṃ*, *hī*, *satyasiddhe*, *pra*, and *āśaṃkāvacane* [are used]; *liṭ* is [used] in the sense of *pra*.

Contradiction with worldly convention (*lokavirodha*) is indeed the topic at hand; contradiction with established usage (*rūḍhivirodha*) is contradiction with the world, for [the scriptures] do not function when there is no such contradiction with that [usage], since the scriptures do not function when there is no contradiction with that worldly usage which is accepted simply through the employment of words. For, without establishing a contradiction with that established usage, the scriptures—which aim to demonstrate the non-differentiation, differentiation, both, manifoldness, and absoluteness—would fail to function.

How is there a lack of engagement? Do those [words] merely restate a meaning already established (*rūḍha*), or do they explain a meaning not yet established (*arūḍha*)? If they restate what is already established, they are redundant; if they explain what is not yet established—a meaning that contradicts conventional usage—they certainly conflict with worldly consensus beyond doubt. Thus it is rightly said: "In the absence of such non-contradiction, there is no engagement; therefore, contradiction with the world is precisely the issue at hand."
Or even if it has not arisen,
or if it has arisen,
it follows after.

Furthermore, if the world were not a valid authority, then for the authors of the treatises, contradictions with perception and inference would arise at every single step and in every single sentence.

Regarding that, it was previously stated that there is a contradiction with perception in that particular portion; now, however, the distinction is that a contradiction with perception must be asserted everywhere.

Or, if the contradiction with inference was not stated, it must be stated; furthermore, the statement regarding the contradiction with perception follows by association because inference is preceded by perception.
Since such is the activity of the author of the treatise, the contradictions with both perception and inference are indeed already present;
this is the meaning of the restriction "only," namely that they do not fail to occur, but rather certainly do occur.
What is the reason? Because they reside within that [world].
For the world is so called because it perceives; the multitude of living beings whose faculties and minds are unimpaired is called the "world.

Since perception and inference reside within that world, if the world itself were not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*), then perception and inference residing within the world would certainly be non-authoritative beforehand.
Alternatively, he himself is "established therein" (tatstha), according to the rule *supi sthaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.4); thus, it is the world itself that is established as the authority.

Where? In those two—perception and inference—it is that very world which [serves as their authority], because it is the substratum for the cognitions of perception and inference and because it assumes their form; thus, perception and inference [are valid]. Therefore, if those two were invalid, there would be invalidity for them; hence, the validity of perception and inference depends upon the validity of the world.

Or rather,

just as in the case of the treatises (*śāstra*), another definition must be postulated for those two as well— in order to conceive of them as being non-worldly (*alaukika*)— which would be consistent with the absolute [position] regarding universals (*sāmānya*) and particulars (*viśeṣa*).
Perception is free from conceptual construction regarding jars and the like; now, what is this "conceptual construction"? It is held by you to be the association with name, genus, and quality.
How then can perception, which is the eldest of the means of valid cognition, not be accepted as a valid authority? Thus [they ask].
In this regard, I offer you this deliberation: even that [liberation] must be conceived as being directly perceptible, just like the results of ritual action prescribed in the scriptures.

For even when the scripture is known, the desired fruit is accomplished through the performance of the actions enjoined therein; and since there is no deviation in the efficacy of those actions, it is as stated: "Though they know all the scriptures and cut through all doubts, they will not achieve that [liberation]; go to heaven, for you have no fear."

Thus, for this reason, knowledge is the unfailing cause of the fruit even for one who maintains that action is the means [to liberation]; how much more so, then, for one who maintains that knowledge alone is the means? Therefore, that very point is investigated, starting from the words "just as in the case of the scripture" up to "the collection of phonemes."

"As in the case of the treatise" means like that which is found in a treatise (*śāstravat*); just as the categories (*padārtha*) mentioned in a treatise are entirely distinct [from ordinary things], so too let perception (*pratyakṣa*) be distinct from worldly perception, and likewise let inference (*anumāna*) be so. For the purpose of conceiving the non-worldly nature of those two—that is, for the purpose of conceiving the non-worldly nature of both perception and inference—a different definition must be postulated.

What is that? It is that which accords with the absolute [positions] regarding universals and particulars (*sāmānyaviśeṣaikāntasaṃvādi*). "Universal and particular" means *sāmānyaviśeṣau*. Then, by the rule of *ekaśeṣa* (retaining one of identical forms), there is the form *sāmānyaviśeṣāḥ*, meaning either the universal alone and not the particular, or the particular alone and not the universal, or those two as mutually distinct. These very things are the "absolute positions" (*ekāntāḥ*), imagined in the treatises as distinct from worldly objects. That which has the habit of conforming to these is "that which accords with the absolute positions regarding universals and particulars."

Perception is to be understood as that which is excluded from conceptual construction—that is, from the conceptualization of jars and so forth—arising from the superimposition of jar-ness, existence, upward motion, number, and the like upon the jar. Therefore, perception is free from such conceptual construction.

There may be a doubt: "The view that perception is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*) belongs only to the proponent of the doctrine of absolute particularity (*viśeṣaikāntavādin*), not to the other two [schools]. How, then, can these [other views] be considered non-worldly (*alaukikatva*)? To this it is replied: First, that which is a mere particular, having the unique characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object and being inexpressible—that perception is non-worldly because it is free from conceptual construction; and since it does not consist of a universal (*sāmānya*), it is established as non-existent, like a sky-flower. Likewise, because it does not consist of a particular, a mere universal—which would be a reality free from conceptual construction wherein everything is the nature of everything—is non-existent, like a sky-flower; and because it is non-existent, the cognition of it is likewise [non-existent].
Likewise, because of their mutual non-substantiality in the case of an absolute dualism or monism, there would be non-existence like that of a sky-flower; thus, [the doctrine] is unworldly.

Even though the definition based on the universal and the particular has been stated—"Perception is the functioning of the ear and so forth" (Nyāyasūtra 1.1.4), and "That which arises from the contact of the self, the senses, the mind, and the object is another [kind of perception]" (Vaiśeṣikasūtra 3.1.18)—[it remains unworldly].

18. And so forth. Nevertheless, by the force of those who maintain the absolute distinction between the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*), that very [perception] results in being both free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*) and non-worldly (*alaukika*). If one accepts its dual nature, there is an abandonment of one's own thesis (*pratijñāhāni*); or rather, since it has been refuted by that very [dual nature], who will strike those two when they have already been struck? With this intention—that the girdle of argumentation is being tightened upon that very [position]—the Master, wishing first to refute the definition of perception as conceived by them, sets it forth; enough of this digression, let us proceed with the main topic.

As for this "thorough deliberation" (*saṃpracāraṃ ya*), it is as follows: in your own system, [the object] is merely imagined; what is the use of deliberation here? This will be stated at the end of the presentation of the opponent's view, right here in the *Nayacakravṛtti*, page 62, line 26:
"In the scripture, even in knowledge... (*śāstre jñāne'pi*).
And even regarding knowledge of the treatises, there is [the same] for the Bhāṣya.
And those who understand the non-deviation of the non-deviating [reasons], cutting through all treatises and all doubts.
"And they shall not do that to you; go to heaven, for there is no fear for you. Thus [spoke] the practitioner;
"it should be done," according to the Pāda-reading.
॰kāryati ḍe॰ līṃ॰ ॰kāryeti raṃ॰ hī॰ vi॰ [is] the supreme [state] beyond the objects of experience.

In the printed Vaiśeṣika Sūtra, the reading is *vāstu pratyakṣam ātmendriyārthasannikarṣāt*, but that is indeed a corrupt reading; compare [the correct version]: *ātmendriyamano'rthānāṃ sannikarṣāt pravartate*.
"That cognition which is manifest at that very moment is defined as perception"

The subject at hand is now stated: what is this "conceptual construction" (kalpanā) by which knowledge is said to be "devoid of" (*apoḍha*) it to be perception (*pratyakṣa*)? To this it is replied: conceptual construction consists in the recollection and determination of other entities that have assumed the forms of names, genera, qualities, actions, and substances. Knowledge that is devoid of such construction, which arises through the predominance of the sense organs, which has as its object a unique particular (*asādhāraṇārtha*), which transcends the range of verbal expression, and which is to be personally experienced within oneself—that is perception.
[This applies even to] the conceptual construction arising from the recollection and determination of other entities that have assumed the forms of eyes, actions, substances, and so forth.
"Then, *apoḍha* means removed;

name (*nāma*), designation (*saṃjñā*), and word (*śabda*) are synonymous. The conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) based on that is, in brief, of two kinds: arbitrary (*yādṛcchikī*) and based on a cause (*naimittikī*)."
That [cognition] arising from the apprehension of a name is arbitrary (*yādṛcchikī*), while that arising from the apprehension of genus (*jāti*) and so forth is causal (*naimittikī*).
A name is "arbitrary" when it is independent of a cause; for example, names such as *Ḍittha* or *Ḍavittha*.
Even though these function through the medium of words, their dependence on causes such as genus and so forth is distinct [from the former].

In that regard, in the case of [the cognition] "cow," by means of the genus (*jāti*), or in the case of "white," by means of the quality (*guṇa*)—either through the elision of the possessive suffix *matup* or through the metaphorical attribution of non-difference (*abhedopacāra*)—a thing other than that qualifier, having assumed the very form of the qualifier, is first determined by the mind through a conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) consisting of a relation of non-difference between those two, the qualifier and the qualified, and subsequently remembered. Likewise, in the case of names such as *Ḍittha*, there is a determination and subsequent recollection based on a relation of non-difference between two distinct entities—the object and its designation—expressed as "this belongs to him" or "he is this. This occurs because of the superimposition of non-difference upon the word and its object, which are distinct as cause (*nimitta*) and effect (*naimittika*).

In the case of verbal nouns such as *pācaka* (cook) and the like, there is no metaphorical identification (*abheda-upacāra*) because there is no difference in form between the action and the agent of the action; therefore, there is no [direct] determination (*nirūpaṇa*), but rather only recollection (*anusmaraṇa*). Furthermore, in all cases, both determination and recollection exist due to the metaphorical identification of word and object.
Likewise, in the case of substance-words such as *daṇḍin* (staff-bearer) and *viṣāṇin* (horned one), [the application occurs] on the basis of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or inherence (*samavāya*).

That consciousness, which is free from that conceptual construction and arises through the sovereignty of the sense-faculties, proceeds from form, light, attention, and the eye— just as fire arises from a gem, the rays of the sun, and cow dung.

Dependent upon the eye, visible form, and external light, and dependent upon the mind—designated as "immediately ceased"—which consists in providing an opportunity for another moment of consciousness, visual consciousness arises; for it is an established tenet that "mind and mental factors arise from four [causes]" (Abhidharmakośa 2.64).

Nevertheless, it is designated by its predominant cause as "visual consciousness," because of its being the uncommon cause, just as one speaks of a "barley sprout" despite the presence of a conjunction of seed, season, water, wind, and space.

Regarding the phrase "having as its object a unique particular" (*asādhāraṇārthaviṣaya*): because the cognitions of the eye and so forth have as their objects the non-conceptual unique particulars (*svalakṣaṇa*) of form and other qualities that are mutually distinct, they transcend the domain of verbal expression. Furthermore, because the mind has as its object things determined by mental construction, it too transcends the domain of verbal expression. Why? Because it is to be personally experienced within oneself (*pratyātmasaṃvedyatvāt*). "Within oneself" (*pratyātma*) means with respect to each individual self; it is experienced by oneself and cannot be described to another, just like the specific nature of a sensation such as a piercing pain.

Since the conceptualization "this is knowledge" is impossible elsewhere, the connection [of cognition] is perception (*pratyakṣa*), because it occurs in relation to each sense organ (*akṣam akṣam prati vṛttiḥ*). That which is born of the five senses consists of the conceptualization (*vikalpanā*) that follows from the investigation of another object which has assumed the nature of an action or a substance, as well as recollection.

Therefore, direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is that knowledge which has arisen from the sovereignty of the sense-faculties, which has as its object a unique particular (*asādhāraṇārtha*), which transcends the domain of verbal expression, and which is to be personally experienced within oneself; it is free from recollection and conceptualization.
They are non-conceptual with respect to the conceptualizations of investigation and recollection— Abhidharmakośa 1.33.

without that [nature], there is no other [existence] except through the conceptualization of the body (kāya) [in the various recensions such as] Pā., Ḍe., Lī., and Vi.

in Bhā, however, there is identity between word and meaning in all instances. Ya.
Visual consciousness arises from form, light, attention, and the eye, just as fire arises from a gem, the rays of the sun, and cow dung.
One who knows the external light and whose mind has ascended is a knower of You.

Regarding the phrase "bījartuvāribhā" (from the Bhāṣya) or "bījaṃ tu vāri" (from the Yaśomitra commentary): that which is the uncommon cause receives its designation [based on that]. For example, a sprout that emerges due to causes such as the season is not designated by the season and so forth, but rather it is designated by the uncommon cause, the seed, as a "barley sprout."
"So it is here as well; thus there is no fault"— Nyāyavārttika 1.1.1.
