11.23 The definition of a kalpa (ya)
Regarding the phrase "the conceptualization [of something] elsewhere," he says "perception," etc., in order to refute the misconception concerning its own nature.
"Pratyakṣa" means that which has returned to the senses;
its definition is: "this object of perception is free from conceptual construction."
Furthermore, because it is described as being "free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*), it is understood to have the nature of that [non-conceptual] cognition;
since the association with conceptual construction exists only in [ordinary] cognition, it is by the negation of that [association] that cognition itself is understood.
Just as in the command, "Let a cow without a calf be brought," by the negation of the calf, only a cow that is a *dhenu* (a milch-cow) is understood, and not any other.
—*Pramāṇasamuccaya-ṭīkā* 1.3:

And because [the object] is obtained through the capacity of cognition by means of the negation of conceptual construction (kalpanā), just as when it is said, "Let a cow without its calf be brought," the cow is understood through the negation of the calf—*Tattvasaṅgraha-pañjikā*, p. 367.

"One endowed with visual consciousness cognizes blue, but does not [cognize] 'it is blue. This is also stated in the *Abhidharma-āgama* and in the *Prakaraṇapāda*: "That which is called 'blue' is blue, yet it is not the referent of the word 'blue.
One who speaks of 'blue' while lacking the syllables [of that term] does not perceive the referent of 'blue.'"
The cultivation of this very meaning is as follows: one perceives the object as the object (*arthasaṃjñī*), but does not perceive the object as a phenomenon (*dharmasaṃjñī*).

Regarding the object—such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth—it is called "blue," yet that [blue] is not the blue-object; it is moreover beyond syllables (*anakṣara*). *Abhidharmapiṭaka* (Abhidharmapiṭaka).

"One who speaks of 'blue' does not perceive the object blue; one possessed of visual consciousness cognizes 'blue,' but not [the word] 'blue,'" so says the Abhidharma scripture as well. Thus, you have postulated that which is being conceptualized as distinct from worldly perception (*laukika-pratyakṣa*) with full confidence. You demonstrate that your own scripture is exactly the same: "one possessed of visual consciousness" (*cakṣurvijñānasamaṅgī*) refers to a continuum (*santāna*) associated with visual consciousness. According to the *Dhātupāṭha*, the roots *agi*, *ragi*, and *lagi* mean "to go. One is "possessed of visual consciousness" because it is his nature (*śīla*) to be endowed with visual consciousness. The same applies to those possessed of auditory consciousness and the others.

One perceives blue; one perceives the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of form as distinct from taste and so forth, but one does not perceive it as "blue. Since the word *iti* is a synonym for "word," one does not perceive that which is expressible by words, such as "this is that blue. Because sensory consciousness (*indriyavijñāna*) lacks clarity, how could it have the capacity to construct such a conceptualization? This is well-established in the *Lokabhāṣya*.
This is desired by the rule; here, the reading "viśvastametallokikaṃ laukikaṃ" might also be possible,
assuming a [scribal] error.

*kalpyamāna-cīkṛpaḥ* (Pāṇini’s Dhātupāṭha, excluding Bhāradvāja and Pāṇini): 128 *ukha*, 129 *ukhi*, 130 *vakha*, 131 *vakhi*, 132 *makha*, 133 *makhi*, 134 *ṇakha*, 135 *ṇakhi*, 136 *rakha*, 137 *rakhi*, 138 *lakha*, 139 *likhi*, 140 *ikha*, 141 *ikhi*, 142 *īkhi*, 143 *valga*, 144 *ragi*, 145 *lagi*, 146 *agi*, 147 *vagi*, 148 *magi*, 149 *tagi*, 150 *tvagi*, 151 *śragi*, 152 *ślāgi*, 153 *igi*, 154 *rigi*, 155 *ligi*. These [roots] have the meaning of "motion" (*gatyarthāḥ*).—Thus in Pāṇini’s Dhātupāṭha.

He shows that this has been stated even in the *Prakaraṇapāda*, and that it has also been expressed in another commentary on the Āgama accepted by you, which restates this same meaning. He says: "The *samaṅgila* [text] clearly understands... due to its clarity... and so forth.

The verse beginning with "That which is called 'blue' is not blue" means that this designation by name, such as "this is blue," is a conceptual construction (*nirūpaṇavikalpa*) consisting of the name "blue"; it is not the actual object blue. The ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) of the blue form—the entity that is the objective domain of the visual faculty—is, by its own nature, non-verbal; it is inexpressible by means of syllables, namely the sets of phonemes (*vyañjana*), phrases (*pada*), and names (*nāmakāya*).

And that person, whether at the time of investigation determining for himself, or at the time of recollection remembering, or desiring to explain it to another while uttering the words "it is blue," does not perceive the object blue—which is of an inexpressible nature—as being non-conceptual (avikalpa) like a portion of his own cognition; for at that time, both the non-conceptual cognition of the object blue whose domain is its true nature has ceased, and no other universal (sāmānya), which is expressible by the word "blue" and superimposed [upon it], has come within the range of the sense faculties.
And as for the scriptural authority (*śāstra*) mentioned—this refers to the *Abhidharma* treatise.
That [Abhidharma], together with its ancillaries...
others, however, explain that "the treatise" refers to the *Jñānaprasthāna*.
That [Abhidharma], which constitutes his very body, has six feet: the Prakaraṇapāda, the Vijñānakāya, the Dharmakāya, the Prajñaptiśāstra, the Dhātukāya, and the Saṃgītiparyāya;
therefore, that treatise also exists together with its attendants—*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-vyākhyā* 1.
In the *Abhidharmabhāṣya*, it is stated that the arrival of your company occurs within another [text] that restates a meaning not found there.
Without [the word] *antareṇa*, by means of that which restates its meaning, [it is said]:
"That indeed is blue," or "A small portion of this is blue. That indeed is blue; a small portion of this is blue. (nīlaṃ ti stokaḥ padetannīlaṃ bhāṣyam).
In this context, the reading "nirdeśe" may also be possible; however, the matter concerns the eye, the [visual] object, and the time.
Having desired to explain the blue [object], he explains the blue; having desired to explain the blue, he explains the blue. (Variant:
*śacavad* for *bhā*)

The cultivation of this very meaning is as follows: [it is] the conceptualization of the object as blue, which is to be expressed and established through superimposition. *Bhāṣya* reads "kalpanīlārtha," while *Praśasta* reads "lāpyasādhyāropi. The cultivation of this very meaning is as follows.

The word "tu" (but/however) serves to provide a qualification; it qualifies this very meaning by means of this cultivation (*bhāvanā*). This is the sense: that [cultivation] is the mental process by which one cultivates (*bhāvayati*) that being as "be! be! through an explanation;
what, then, is that cultivation? It is perceiving the object as an object, and not perceiving the object as a phenomenon (*dharma*).

A further explanation of this statement regarding cultivation (*bhāvanā*): with respect to an object such as form (*rūpa*) that is the domain of perceptual cognition (*pratyakṣavijñāna*), one who perceives its own nature (*svarūpasaṃjñin*) is associated with a non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) perception that takes as its objective support merely the specific characteristic of the object's own nature; this pertains to the continuum (*santāna*) of this [individual] with respect to the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
However, it is not the case that one perceives the name-designation (*saṃjñā*) by means of arbitrary names (*yadṛcchādināma*) with respect to the object such as form.
Thus it is stated in the Abhidharma: "Dharma" is said to mean the collection of names (*nāmakāya*), the collection of phrases (*padakāya*), and the collection of phonemes (*vyañjanakāya*).

Even this [conceptualization] is fruitless because it is non-worldly (*alaukika*); it is marred by contradictions that are difficult to resolve due to its dependence on its own words. [The term *rūpasaṃjñī* means: one who has the designation "form" (*rūpa*) with respect to that which is characterized by visible form, sound, odor, taste, and tangible objects; one who perceives merely visible forms and so forth. He is called "one who possesses perception" (*saṃjñī*) because he perceives (*saṃjānāti*), or because he possesses the perception of intrinsic nature (*svarūpa-saṃjñā*). Thus, he is "one who possesses the perception of intrinsic nature" (*svarūpasaṃjñī*).

What is the object (*ālambana*) of that perception (*saṃjñā*), or what is its essential nature (*svarūpa*), by which that non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*) mental state of form (*rūpa*) and so forth—being associated with that [perception] called a "concomitant factor" (*samprayuktaka-dharma*)—is designated as "possessing perception" (*saṃjñin*) through its association with perception, and thus its continuum is so called? To this he says: "associated with a non-conceptual perception whose object is solely the specific nature of the thing. This has already been explained in the commentary (*bhāṣya*).

That very [perception] has the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object; its own specific [nature] is the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), for it is characterized (*lakṣyate*). [The suffix -ana is used here according to] *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam* (Pāṇini 3.3.113).

173. Thus, the suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*). The meaning is that its object is the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and not anything else. "Of this continuum" refers to one who possesses visual consciousness. Just like visual consciousness, the five groups of consciousness beginning with the visual are explained in this way to demonstrate that they are free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*). Furthermore, it has been stated: "Knowledge whose nature is conceptual is not perception, because its object is not the specific characteristic of the thing (*arthasvalakṣaṇa*), just like the cognition of a horse in relation to a cow. This is the proof (*sādhana*).

Furthermore, determinate cognition such as "this is blue" is not perception because it involves the superimposition of qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇādhyāropa*), like the cognition of a fragrant lotus and so forth; this is the meaning of the conclusion, and thus the explanation of the phrase "one who perceives the object in the object" (*arthe 'rthasaṃjñī*) is finished. [This occurs] elsewhere except in the Ḍe-līṃ manuscript—where the word *tu* (but) appears after *bhāvanāt* in the Bhā, Pā, Vi, Raṃ, and Hī manuscripts.
The word "tu" (but/however) would serve the purpose of [indicating] the state (*bhāva*) through this meditation (*bhāvanā*).
Thus, this meaning is as follows:

it is that which possesses a perception of its own essential nature; it is associated with a non-conceptual perception that takes as its object only the specific qualities of the essential nature of the object; and it has the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its domain within this mental continuum—but it does not possess a perception of names, such as "form" (*rūpa*) and so forth, applied to the object through arbitrary convention or the like.
Thus it is stated in the Abhidharma: "Dharma" is said to be the collection of names (*nāmakāya*), the collection of phrases (*padakāya*), and the collection of phonemes (*vyañjanakāya*).

However, even this [designation] is merely conceptual; because it is not ultimate, it is fruitless and lacks worldly validity, as it is difficult to overcome due to contradictions arising from its dependence on its own linguistic expressions.
Just as there is an absence of the perception of a dharma associated with [the state of] being fully present.
"Without perception," "associated with," "dissociated," "with," "without," and "elsewhere"— thus it is shown in the *Viniścaya*.

The word *iti* is used here in the sense of "demonstration" (Pā., Ḍe., Lī., Raṃ., Hī.). Furthermore, the reading *ity api* might also be possible; [in that case] the meaning would be: "In this matter, the object is the designator" (Pra.).

The explanation of the phrase "but not perceiving the object as a phenomenon" (*na tvarthe dharmasaṃjñī*) is as follows: In the phrase "not [perceiving] the object," *na* functions as a negation; *tu* functions as a qualifier. It negates that specific object characterized by superimposition—that very object consisting of form and so forth—but it does not mean one who lacks the designation of arbitrary names (*yadṛcchā-nāma*). Since the word *dharma* is a synonym for the word *śabda*, "one who perceives the object as a phenomenon" means one who perceives it as a word; thus, the meaning is "one does not become a perceiver of words. *Yadṛcchā*, genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), action (*kriyā*), and substance (*dravya*) are the designations of words. Because the term *dharma* is a synonym for the term *śabda*, "one who perceives the object as a phenomenon" (*dharmasaṃjñī*) means one who perceives it as a word (*śabdasaṃjñī*); the sense is that he does not become such a perceiver of words.
This is not stated according to our own arbitrary fancy; what then? It is stated thus in the Abhidharma—that is, it is declared in the Abhidharma-piṭaka.
What is stated? "Dharma" is said to be the *nāmakāya* (name-group), and so forth.

A name itself is the *nāmakāya*, because like a physical body (*kāya*), it perishes moment by moment, and because it is an aggregate of the four primary elements; or else, because it is an aggregate of names such as consciousness and the rest, for it is accepted that even though individual words of designation are momentary, they arise and perish only when combined in an aggregate.
As it has been said: "Color, odor, taste, and touch—these four elements are inseparable; they arise together and perish together," according to the established tenet.
Words consist of nouns, verbs, prefixes, and particles; the collection of these is the "body of words" (*padakāya*).
Phonemes are the syllables; because they manifest the meaning, their collection is the "body of phonemes" (*vyañjanakāya*).

As stated in the Abhidharma-piṭaka:
"In this context, 'nāmakāya' (name-body) means that the name itself is the body; thus, there may also be the reading 'nāmaiva kāyo nāmakāyaḥ'."
And because it is a composite of the four elements,
color, odor, taste, and touch— these four elements as well—
are inseparable; they arise together and perish together.

These eight are indeed thus established according to your own doctrine; what is the use of deliberation on this point? Now, the ultimate reality (paramārtha) is being investigated: although this is "imagined" (kalpita), it is "fruitless" (aphala), meaning it has no fruit.

What is the reason? Because it is non-worldly (*alaukika*), like the conceptualization of the bluntness or sharpness of a donkey’s horn. If it is asked why it is non-worldly: it is because, like your own statement, this [conceptual cognition] is not a direct perception (*apratyakṣa*); because it consists of mental construction (*kalpanātmaka*); because it consists of conceptual differentiation (*nirūpaṇavikalpātmaka*); because it consists of an apprehension contrary to its objective support (*ālambanaviparītapratipattyātmaka*); because it consists of superimposition (*adhyāropātmaka*); because its object is of the nature of a universal (*sāmānyarūpaviṣayatva*); because it operates upon both that [object] and what is not that (*tadatadviṣayavṛttitva*); because it consists of the grasping of the identity between the existent and the non-existent (*sadasadabhedaparigrahātmaka*); and because its object is in every respect common [to all], and so forth—just like inferential and other types of cognition. It is excluded [from being a valid perception].

Because [this] is his own statement (*svavacana*)—namely, that of the monk Dignāga, who asserts the definition of perception—the term *svavacanavyapekṣā* means the dependence upon or consideration of one's own statement. That very thing constitutes an implication (*ākṣepa*). Since the removal of the contradiction is difficult to overcome by means of that implication, it is called "the removal of a contradiction difficult to overcome due to the implication of one's own statement. This is contradicted by this very statement of his own, when considered in its earlier and later parts, just like such statements as: "I am always observing a vow of silence" or "My father is a celibate from birth. However, this is not to be refuted in the same way as our own logical arguments; therefore, he provides an example for that purpose: "This is exactly like your own statement. Just as this statement of yours, being conceptual in nature, is not direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), so too is this [position of yours] not direct perception; such is the thesis (*pratijñā*).

In this context, the subject (*dharmin*) is cognition characterized by the definition of being free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*). What is the reason for proving it as qualified by the property of not being perception (*apratyakṣatva*)? [If you say] "because its nature is conceptual" (*kalpanātmakatvāt*), is this not unestablished (*asiddha*)? For that cognition is, by definition, free from conceptual construction.

In this regard, another property is stated for the purpose of proving that [point]: that [sensory cognition] consists of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), because it consists of the conceptualization of determination (*nirūpaṇa-vikalpa*). "Determination" (*nirūpaṇa*) is the knowledge that "this is thus"; that itself is conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). That perception consists of that [conceptual construction], just like the cognition of "pot-ness" and so forth. To this, [the opponent] says: "The fact that sensory cognition consists of the conceptualization of determination is also unestablished. To prove this, the Teacher says here: "Because it consists of a cognition contrary to its objective support (*ālambana*)."

In this context, the object (*ālambana*) consists of the substantially existent atoms (*paramāṇu*) such as blue and so forth, and not their aggregate which possesses forms such as blue or yellow; for that [aggregate] is only conventionally real (*saṃvṛtisat*).

Furthermore, because each of those forms—blue, yellow, and so on—possesses degrees of intensity, the object is not exactly as it is apprehended. Thus, it is of the nature of an apprehension contrary to the object.
That which is of the nature of an apprehension contrary to the object is not perception (*pratyakṣa*), just as the apprehension of a person in a tree-stump.

It might be thought: "Since atoms, which are substantially existent (*dravyasat*), possess forms such as blue, yellow, and so forth, there is no erroneous cognition. This, however, is incorrect, because a form consists of superimposition (*adhyāropa*), just like the superimposition of "lionhood" onto a young boy.
How is it known that this [form] is superimposed? Because its object is a universal (*sāmānya*);
and that universal, like "fireness" which does not depend on particular instances such as fire from cow-dung, fire from wood, fire from grass, or fire from leaves, [is common to all].
If it is argued that even this is unestablished, we reply: it is indeed established, because it functions with respect to both that [object] and what is not that.

"That and what is not that" refers to the object (*viṣaya*) which is both that and not-that; that cognition is "functioning with respect to that and what is not that" because it functions upon the collection and upon those [atoms] themselves. This is because it arises from a collection of multiple atoms, since it functions upon the collection and upon them [the atoms]. Since the collection is non-existent and only the atoms—which possess substantial existence (*dravyasat*)—are existent, and since cognition arises by grasping the form of blue and so forth through the non-difference of those two [the collection and the atoms], the non-existence of the collection is established, for when that [collection] is not grasped, there is no cognition of it, just as in the case of a row of cranes, a fist, a knot, and so forth.
And it is said in the *Ṣaṣṭitantra*: "The supreme form of the qualities does not come within the range of vision; that which has entered the range of vision is as utterly void as an illusion."

It has been stated in the Abhidharma itself: "The five groups of consciousness have accumulated objects as their support (*ālambana*). This is because a single, non-accumulated atom of form or other [sensory objects]—such as a jar or blue—cannot exist as an object; and even if such a thing were possible, it could not function as an object because atoms are beyond the reach of the senses. Therefore, for the visual and other consciousnesses, only an aggregate of atoms of form and so forth constitutes the object. Consequently, these individual atoms, which are ultimately real (*paramārtha-sat*), are not the actual objects of these [consciousnesses].

Therefore, because it consists in the apprehension of the non-difference between the existent and the non-existent, this [cognition] has both that and non-that as its object, like the cognition of hair-nets and the like by one suffering from ophthalmia;
furthermore, because its object is common in every respect,
the object of this cognition is common, and thus it is "common-objected" (*sādhāraṇārtha*).

The fact that these have a common object is due to reasons such as their consisting in the apprehension of non-difference, because of the inclusion of the word "etcetera," because they have as their object the meaning of positive and negative concomitance, and because they have as their object an entity consisting of both the universal and the particular;
for you yourself have cited examples [of this], namely: "erroneous cognition, conventional cognition, real cognition, inference, and that which is derived from inference."
"And that which consists of conventional desire is a semblance [of valid cognition] accompanied by obscurity," as stated in the *Pramāṇasamuccaya* 1.8.

Therefore, since its nature as being conceptual is established through a succession of reasons—or rather, from each individual reason stated—this cognition, characterized by the definition of being free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*), is not direct perception (*apratyakṣa*), just like inferential and other types of cognition. Just as inferential and other cognitions are not direct perception because they consist of conceptual construction, so too is sense-cognition intended by you [to be].

This necklace, like your own statement, is indeed not directly perceived (*apratyakṣa*), because it consists of conceptual construction (*kalpanātmakatva*), because it consists of the conceptualization of a description (*nirūpaṇavikalpātmakatva*), because it consists of a cognition contrary to its objective support (*ālambanaviparītapratipattyātmakatva*), because it consists of superimposition (*adhyāropātmakatva*), because its object is of the nature of a universal (*sāmānyarūpaviṣayatva*), because it operates upon both that [object] and what is not that (*tadatadviṣayavṛttitva*), because it consists of the grasping of non-difference between the existent and the non-existent (*sadasadabhedaparigrahātmakatva*), and because its meaning is in every respect common [to many], just like inferential and other types of cognition. Thus, this very statement of yours is refuted by itself.
That which is distinguished by [the state of] being [thus] is established;
what belongs to that?
The Teacher, however, established that [reading].

Here, regarding the passage enclosed within such marks—beginning with *tatrālambanam* and ending with *nīlapītādyākāratvān na*—in place of that, the following reading is found in all manuscripts of the Ya lineage: "If it be thought: 'It is due to the fact that only atoms existing as substantial entities (*dravyasat*) possess the forms of blue, yellow, and so forth; and because even that form of blue, yellow, and so forth possesses degrees of intensity in each individual case, it is according to how they are perceived'—it is not so. [End of passage].

This reading in manuscript Ya is disconnected due to being fragmentary, omitted, or in some places duplicated; therefore, it has been discarded, and instead, the reading from manuscript Sa-dā-dhy-ā-ro-pi-ta-pra (Sa) has been adopted as it is consistent with the context.
And that [reading] is indeed the correct one.
And that collection, being composed of both existent and non-existent [elements], is the supreme form of the qualities (*guṇas*), yet it does not come within the range of vision.

But that which has come within the range of vision is utterly void, like an illusion. (From the *Ṣaṣṭitantra*). "Utterly void" (*sutucchaka*) is the reading in the *Satasāhasrikā-vibhāṣā* and *Samutthaka-pāda*.

It has been stated in the Abhidharma itself: "The five groups of consciousness have accumulated objects as their support (*ālambana*). This is because a single, non-accumulated atom (*paramāṇu*) of form and so forth cannot exist as an object in things such as a jar or the color blue; and even if one were to imagine it so, it would be impossible for it to function as an object because atoms are beyond the reach of the senses. Therefore, for the visual and other consciousnesses, the support is exclusively a collection of atoms of form and so forth. Consequently, these atoms, which are ultimately real (*paramārtha-sat*), are not the individual objects of these [consciousnesses]."
*keśoṇḍuka* (in Ya and Bhā),
except for *āvigra* in Bhā and Vi.
In the same way, the cognitions have been illustrated:
the cognition of error, the cognition of conventional reality, inference, and that which is derived from inference.
*saṃjñāna* (cognition) is the reading of Prajñākaragupta.
"And that which is based on memory and that which is based on desire are pseudo-perception, accompanied by visual impairment" (Pramāṇasamuccaya 1.8). Thus,
that which is based on memory and that which is based on desire are pseudo-perceptions accompanied by visual impairment— (Pramāṇasamuccaya).

Do not think that our desired [reason] is unestablished because it consists of the conceptualization described here; for it has been stated by you yourselves in the Abhidharma— in the very Abhidharma-piṭaka within the Buddha’s word— that "the five groups of consciousness have accumulated [atoms] as their object."
Because they are constantly associated with conjoined factors such as attachment and so forth, the five consciousnesses—visual and the rest—are called "bodies" (*kāya*).

This is because a single atom of form (*rūpa*)—unaccumulated and unassociated with other atoms of the same kind—is absent as an object (*ālambana*), as a sensory domain (*viṣaya*), or as something graspable by the sense-faculties and cognition within those things commonly accepted as perceptible, such as jars, cloths, chariots, and the like; or within blue and other colors, tastes, smells, touches, and sounds, or their qualities, which exist only conventionally (*saṃvṛti-sat*). Therefore, it is only the accumulated atoms, appearing in the form of jars, blue, and so forth, that are grasped by the visual and other faculties.

Furthermore, in that state, subsistence as atoms is unestablished for the Ārhats, because the Vaiśeṣikas accept the occurrence of a transformation into another state; for the Sāṅkhyas, it is the constituents (guṇas), such as *sattva* and the rest, which have attained a specific state of equilibrium, [constituting] the composite substance (*avayavidravya*) originated from atoms.

For worldly people, however, there is merely a possibility of a subtle cause of the same class as inferred from its gross effect—namely, that "there exist certain many subtle things which serve as the cause of the gross, just as threads are for a cloth. Even when such a possibility is thus conceived, since those [subtle things] lack visibility and so forth in the absence of aggregation and transformation, they are like atoms (*aṇu*) pervading the world; therefore, because they are beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), it is impossible for them to be the objective support (*ālambana*).

Therefore, since it is impossible for atoms (*paramāṇu*) existing as substantial entities (*dravyasat*) to function as objects of cognition, this must be understood: for visual consciousness and the others, the object (*ālambana*) is precisely the aggregate (*saṅghāta*) of atoms of form (*rūpa*) and so forth;

by the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), it follows that the object is precisely the aggregate of atoms of taste (*rasa*), tangibility (*spraṣṭavya*), and circularity (*parimaṇḍala*), and so on.

If it is asked, "What follows from that?"—it follows that for each individual atom which serves as an object (*ālambana-paramāṇu*; i.e., atoms that are the objects of cognition), these [atoms], being ultimately real (*paramārtha-sat*), are the only things that are ultimately real; for neither the collection [of atoms] such as blue nor [objects] such as a jar are ultimately real, because they possess only conventional existence (*saṃvṛti-sattva*). Thus, according to your own tenet, atoms cannot be the objects [of cognition], and consequently, the reason [you have provided], namely "because of being an atom" (*paramāṇutvāt*), is unestablished (*asiddha*).
(Note: The text contains the repetition *°tvādihetusiddhi* twice, which appears to be a scribal error; it has been corrected to *°tvādihetu-asiddhi*.)
For those [atoms] are eternally associated; indeed, those atoms of form and so forth are of the same nature as that which is not aggregated.
That which is not accumulated by the elements, which is equal to space, which is beyond the domain of the senses, and which transcends the objects of the senses.
In this context, the reading "of the object of apprehension" (grāhyasya) is probable, [as it would otherwise result] in a different measure, pervasion, or atom.
Having understood the objective support such as [the nature of] being,
etc.,
one attains perfect awakening.

In that regard, concerning an aggregate of form (*rūpa-saṅghāta*) whose own nature is not distinct from other forms that are [themselves] distinct, and which is in contact with the sense faculty—this cognition which has as its object a blue form that is non-verbalizable and of a single nature, and which is contrary to the objective support (*ālambana*), is indeed verifiable by the communication of a reason; for it is verified by the communication of the apprehension of the collection, just as fire is apprehended by means of smoke. Therefore, there exists another, imagined, single universal, "blue form," by way of which [the cognition occurs].

In that regard, concerning that which has an undifferentiated intrinsic nature (*svatattva*) despite being differentiated from other forms: "other forms" (*rūpāntara*) refers to those forms that are individually distinct, either atom by atom or according to the distinctions of taste (*rasa*) and so forth; the "undifferentiated intrinsic nature" (*aviviktasvatattva*) is that which belongs to those very same other forms.

What is this? It is the aggregate of form (*rūpasaṅghāta*), or the aggregate of atoms belonging to the various divisions of the element of form (*rūpadhātu*), or the aggregate of forms intended as the objects of the eye under discussion.

When that aggregate of form (*rūpa-saṅghāta*), having come into contact with the sense organ, is presented facing its own object, this cognition—whether "this is blue" or "this is a jar"—which is contrary to the objective support (*ālambana*) in terms of ultimate reality, is erroneous; for when those [atoms] are not apprehended, that cognition does not occur, just like the cognition of a row in a flight of cranes. It has as its object a blue form (*nīla-rūpa*) that is non-designatable and of a single nature (*avyapadeśya-ekātman*). It is "non-designatable and of a single nature" because it is one single self-nature distinct from the objective supports consisting of many designatable atoms. What is that? It is the blue form. The intended cognition is thus described as "having as its object a blue form that is non-designatable and of a single nature. This is how the passage continues.

Or rather, that very cognition is "inexpressible" (*avyapadeśyā*) because its object is a single blue form that is distinct from the multiple blue forms of the individual atoms; for the purpose of explaining this, it is stated by you in the *Abhidharma-piṭaka*: "One cognizes blue, but not 'it is blue'";

thus, the intention is that such a cognition is indeed inexpressible. He demonstrates this [objection]: "But surely that [cognition] is expressible precisely through the indication of a cause (*hetvapadeśa*), since it has been said:
'Cause (*hetu*), indication (*apadeśa*), sign (*nimitta*), mark (*liṅga*), means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and reason (*kāraṇa*) are synonymous'" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 3.1.14).

2.4 Thus, it is not necessarily the case that only what is denoted by a word is "designatable" (vyapadeśya). What then? Whatever is apprehended through another object is designatable, because "another object" (arthāntara) is a synonym for "reason" (hetu), "designation" (apadeśa), "cause" (nimitta), and so forth.
Moreover, since even for you sensory cognition is held to be produced by another cause under the designation of "grasping a collection" (*sañcaya*), it must therefore be designated as such;
and thus it has been said: "The five groups of consciousness have the accumulated (*sañcita*) as their object" (*Abhidharmapiṭaka*), not that they have the collection (*sañcaya*) as their object.

To illustrate this point, he provides an example: "It is apprehended just as fire is by smoke. Just as it is observed that when knowledge arises—such as "there is fire here"—by means of smoke, which is a distinct entity, that knowledge is designated [as being caused by smoke], so too this visual consciousness and other cognitions whose objects are blue forms and the like are designated as being distinct from those [objects], because they are produced by atoms which are distinct entities, and so forth.

Therefore, just as it is designated—just as fire is [inferred] from smoke—that blue form is something other than those atoms which are ultimately real; it is a conceptualized unity, a universal derived from many particulars, which is not grasped directly by the senses without mediation. Rather, it is grasped only through mediation by other entities, namely the atoms; it is grasped by way of the atoms and not by itself. And that [is the nature] of what was stated in the *Pratibhāsa*.
One's own reality is one's own sovereignty,
which is explained as being self-dependent.
From the bases of apprehension regarding their own objects,
which are to be designated as distinct from one another, [the cognition arises].
Regarding *ekātmikāneka* (Ya),
*ekāneka* (Bh):

although the reading *ekātmikā* is found in the Ya manuscripts, nevertheless, since the singularity of the cognition (*pratipatti*) does not prove that the cognition is contrary to its object (*ālambana-viparīta-pratipatti*), and since it is precisely the fact that it has a single, unitary blue form as its object that proves this, it appears that the reading *ekātmakāneka* is the correct one here.
"Blue," "the opposite," "existence," "reason," "indication," "mark," "means of knowledge," "instrument"—these are synonyms. — Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 9.18;
Yadartha-Ḍe-līṃ-vi.
For my sake, O Raṅga-Hīna,
nevertheless,
I shall proclaim [it] again.

[Objection: But surely the collection [of causes] is designated as a *kāraka-hetu* (productive cause) because it is apprehended through perception, and not as a *jñāpaka-hetu* (informative cause) like smoke, [which makes known] a distinct entity such as fire, [whereas the collection] has a single form. [Response: Indeed, this very point was introduced by us for the purpose of demonstrating this meaning: if this were perception, it would arise from a productive cause alone—namely, its own object as a supporting cause—just like the experience of burning. This is because perception, being direct, consists of immediate apprehension; and because perception has the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object, it is non-superimpositional (*anadhyāropātmaka*). Such is the sense.
Here he says: "Now, [regarding] 'of the accumulation' and so forth, up to 'of the single nature of another object'.

The word *nanu* is used for seeking permission; the word *ca* (and) is used to collect together well-known distinctions. Indeed, this is well known: "The producer (*kāraka*) cause is one thing, and the indicator (*jñāpaka*) is another.

Therefore, because atoms and their accumulation are related to a producer [cause], while smoke and fire are related to an indicator [cause], there is a disparity between the cognitions of perception and inference. Consequently, the example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma-vaikalya*), and the reason (*hetu*) is contradictory (*viruddha*) because it subverts what is intended. This is the meaning of the sentence.
We do not elaborate on the fact that these syllables have a straightforward meaning; let it be seen [on this point] on page 77, line 2, where the single nature of the object is discussed.

For the sake of the cognition of smoke that is connected [to fire], and because it is understood from that [smoke] as the object to be understood, there is the conceptualization of the property (*dharma*) to be proven (*sādhya*).
Without [the word] *iṣṭa* (desired), the teacher, avoiding two faults here, says: "Indeed, this was introduced by us for the purpose of demonstrating this very point;

this is not undesirable to us, nor is there a deficiency in the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), since that which would lead to the consequence of the collection being a means of cognition (*jñāpaka*)—and thus cause those two faults to be leveled against us on account of perception (*pratyakṣa*)—does not apply."
But this is not so, because it is precisely this that we wish to demonstrate;

therefore it is said: if this [perception] were direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) according to your view, then the cognition of blue, yellow, and so forth—arising from the eye and other sense organs as the producers (*kāraka*)—would arise solely from the cause that serves as its objective support (*ālambana*), namely the "accumulation" (*sañcaya*) which is conventionally real (*saṃvṛtisat*), and not even from atoms (*aṇu*) and the like, which are ultimately real (*paramārthasat*). However, it does arise from those [atoms]; therefore, it is not direct perception, just like the cognition of fire which depends on smoke and the like as an indicator (*jñāpaka*); by way of contrast (*vaidharmyeṇa*), it is like the experience of burning.

Or it may have as its object only its own [intrinsic] meaning, because it is a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), like the experience of burning—as it has been said: "In one way, through a connection with burning, the burnt person conceives himself as burned;
in another way, by means of the word 'burning,' the meaning of burning is understood."
Vākyapadīya 2

Because perception consists in an unmediated apprehension, it is the very cause for the accumulation [of that knowledge]. Perception is observed to grasp an object that is not separated from another object, as in the case of the experience of burning; likewise, because its object is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), perception would be independent of other objects. However, this is not the case—meaning, because its object is the particular characteristic and it consists in non-superimposition (i.e., it is free from conceptual construction). What is meant is that, in every instance, no cognition arises by way of excluding other objects through the operation of superimposing other objects upon them. This is what is expressed by such statements as "because its object is the particular characteristic," "because it consists in unmediated apprehension," and "because it is perception."
Furthermore, it is observed that what is apprehended by means of a cause other than its own object is not perceptual, as for example, the cognition produced by the word "burning.
Thus, having first accepted the status of the aggregate as a causal factor (*kāraka*), the fault has been established; now it shall be further demonstrated.
It has indeed been established elsewhere by Yaśobhaga,
except for [the following]: "In this very way, of this alone" (pāda-viśeṣa),
"in this very way, of this alone" (ḍe-līṃ).
In this very manner, for this [mantra] itself, excluding *raṃ*, *hīṃ*, and *bhāḥ*, it would be otherwise: *syād akārakā* [is] *vi* *ḍe* *līṃ*;
*syād akārakā* [is] *raṃ* *hīṃ*.
Otherwise, due to its connection with burning, one who possesses cognition [but lacks the capacity for action] conceives himself as burnt by the burning.
In one way, a person who has been burned perceives the burning through contact with fire;
in another way, the meaning of "burning" and so forth is understood through the word "burning"—
*Vākyapadīya*.
Otherwise, the meaning of "burning" would not be understood by the word "burning. (Vākyapadīya 2.421) [The phrase] "because it is a superimposition" [is found in] manuscript Y;
[the phrase] "arisen from the state of being the object of that knowledge" [is found in] manuscript Y.
In the *Bhāṣya* [it is stated]: "The cognition that arises from the superimposition of another object is not knowledge.
Here, the meaning appears to be that a mental state (*vṛtti*) which functions by superimposing one object onto another, having arisen through the exclusion of the other object, is not knowledge.

The meaning is "by being abandoned through another object" (*arthāntaraheyatayā*), which is to say "by being understood through another object" (*arthāntaragamyatayā*). This is because the root *hi* (Pāṇini Dhātupāṭha 1258) has the sense of "going," and all roots with the sense of "going" have the sense of "knowing.
For comparison, [the author] says—summarizing those three meanings for the purpose of concluding the discussion on the cause and the thing to be abandoned—in the *Nayacakravṛtti*, p.
97–2: "And it will be stated that 'that which is to be grasped by means of another object as its cause is seen to be non-perceptual' (Pañcavastuka 23)."

Furthermore, because [the aggregate] is not perceived as distinct from its parts, it lacks causal efficacy (*kārakatā*); in ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), it is non-existent, like a firebrand-circle (*alātacakravat*), since it is merely the arrangement of individual parts.

In common worldly usage, a "designation" (*vyapadeśa*) is a specific instruction regarding a collection of entities that is distinct from the object to be grasped; by means of that designation, the object to be designated—the object of knowledge—is inferable and not perceptible, like fire inferred from smoke.

Now, wishing to refute its status as a causal agent (*kārakatā*) as well, he says: "The claim is that the collection has no causal agency whatsoever; the reason is that it does not exist in the ultimate sense;
the example is like a circle of fire [drawn by a whirling torch]."

In ultimate reality there is no existence, because it exists conventionally; according to your own view, like a jar—as it has been said: "That which, when broken, no longer evokes the cognition of itself, and that which [no longer evokes the cognition] when other [parts] are excluded by the intellect, is conventionally real, like a jar or water; otherwise, it is ultimately real."
As stated in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (6.4):

"Just as a firebrand being whirled appears like a wheel to one with a deluded vision, yet that wheel does not exist—because there is no continuity among the sparks of fire and because the wheel is ultimately non-existent—and thus the cognition of a wheel has no objective cause; likewise, because an accumulation exists only conventionally (*saṃvṛti*), the cognition of blue has no objective cause."

Likewise, because atoms and blue [color] are beyond the senses, the aggregate (*sañcaya*) is also not a causal agent; for it is merely the arrangement of each individual part. "Per part" (*pratyavayavam*) means with respect to each and every part. The parts are the atoms of blue and so forth; the aggregate is merely their collective arrangement in one place through mutual proximity, and it is not accepted by you as something distinct from them. Therefore, in ultimate reality, this so-called "aggregate" does not exist at all.
What agency can there be for that which is non-existent, like the horn of a donkey?

Regarding the phrase "when that is broken," the reading in the *Abhidharmakośa* is: "that [notion] does not occur when it is broken, and by the intellect's exclusion of other [factors], that [notion] occurs when that [other] is broken."

Regarding the passage "yat pra... atra tat" [in the verse] "anyāpohadhiyāya...", such is the reading in the *Abhidharmakośa*, and it was explained exactly in that way by Vasubandhu in his commentary (*bhāṣya*) on it.

The reading *tat* is also accepted by the authors of the *Nayacakravṛtti*, since they themselves will explain this verse at the time of its commentary as follows: "That jar which, when broken into its constituent parts, no longer gives rise to the cognition of it, is conventionally real (*saṃvṛtisat*), like a jar"—(Nayacakravṛtti, p.
66)—and [they cite]: "Conventionally real like a jar or water; ultimately real otherwise" (Abhidharmakośa 6.4), [with the variant *ambuvat* instead of *ambuvṛt*].
