Having understood [it] as blue due to its nature,
[one perceives] the state of each individual part with respect to each [constituent].
"Consolidated in one place"—
this refers to [the state of] "nothing whatsoever for me."

Even if one were to concede the existence of a composite whole (*sañcaya*), we shall state the fault: "But [it would be] like the world. Just as for the world—even for one who is unlearned—the whole (*avayavin*) exists as something distinct from its constituents; or whether it be a transformation (*pariṇāmāntara*) or that collection itself, let it be whatever it may be—it is accepted by others as existing once it has been explained, because distinctions such as cognition, capacity, function, designation, and number are observed in cases such as threads and cloth. Therefore, let it be understood that there is indeed a designation [of the whole] there, in accordance with the literal meaning of the words.
Furthermore, [the claim that] "the object of perception is inexpressible" and "perception itself is inexpressible" is false in both cases.

If one asks how so: the term *vyapadeśya* (inexpressible) implies a qualified designation (*viśiṣṭo 'padeśaḥ*). This shows that the prefix *vi-* has the sense of "qualified" (*viśiṣṭa*) and the word *apadeśa* has the sense of "reason" (*hetu*).
The meaning is that it is "distinct" (*anya*) from others.

If it is asked, "How so?", it is said: [it is] other than the object of apprehension (*grāhya*). The object of apprehension is blue and so forth; other than that is the aggregate (*sañcaya*), which is its designation (*vyapadeśa*). By means of that aggregate—that is, by means of that designation as a reason—it is to be designated. What is that? The object of cognition (*prameya*) such as blue, which is accessible through the means of perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*) as you intend.
What becomes of that form of blue and so forth? It follows that it is inferable (*anumeya*), because it is that which is designated by a designation; it is not [directly] perceptible.

For that very reason, the absence of perceptibility and the state of being inferable are established for that object of knowledge; likewise, the non-perceptibility and the state of being inferential are established for cognition.
What is the illustrative example? It is like fire inferred from smoke.
Just as fire, established by the designation "smoke," [is understood] in its capacity as either a causal agent or a non-agent of a thing—just as a father is [inferred] from smoke and so forth.
Furthermore, even if it were of a single nature consisting of both the denotation and the designatable, it would still not be so; for, like the inferred fire, blue has many objects.

Indeed, that determination of the form "blue" is a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Just as the inferable fire—produced from smoke—is not perceived, so too is the form "blue," which consists of many individual essences distinct from one another in each atom.

And just as the cognition of fire produced by taking smoke as its objective support is an inference and not perception, so too the cognition of blue is produced through conjunction [with mental factors] and is thus not perception.
Because of the difference in transformation,
those [atoms] produced from it possess a different magnitude, just like other magnitudes.
See that [passage] on page 64, line 19:
"sann evāsau bhāṣya".
...ṣṭasūtrākṣa... [should] be taken up by the Bhāṣya.
He demonstrates the sense of being a reason;
he demonstrates the sense of being a reason. Bhāṣya. anya. sañcaya. pra.
Immeasurable, because it is beyond all instruction.
Because it is an instruction;
that which belongs to the knowledge of that,
[belongs] to the knowledge of that.
Whether a thing is established as being a causal factor (*kāraka*) or not a causal factor— like a father or smoke—
it is certainly not [established] through identity with what is expressed or designated; for blue, like inferred fire, possesses multiple objects.
For that determination of the form blue is a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), [perceiving] a manifold blue form whose own nature is mutually distinct in each individual atom.

Furthermore, in every respect, that cognition of blue and so forth must be designated by means of that aggregate (*sañcaya*), because it is invariably concomitant (*avinābhāva*) with it; whether [the aggregate] acts as a causal factor or does not act as a causal factor, there is no difference regarding the establishment of the object's designatability.

Why? Precisely because it is caused by something else entirely, like a father or smoke. Just as a father is the progenitor of a son and the son is designated by that causal agent, or as fire is known by means of smoke which is its indicator—since the nature of the object is not different in these cases, and since the ground for being so designated is equal and equally capable of establishing non-perceptibility and inferential status—this investigation into whether [the cause] is a producer (*kāraka*) or an indicator (*jñāpaka*) is useless, as it obstructs what cannot be designated. This fault was stated even while accepting the status of being a producer.

Thus, first of all, the designation of this blue object as being "due to its object" (arthakṛta) is established; once that is established, it is proven that [the object] is not perceptible but inferable, and from that establishment, the inferential nature of the cognition of it is established. Furthermore, there would be no contradiction with the definition [of perception] characterized by being "inexpressible" (avyapadeśyatva) and so forth;
thus, for the time being, it is indeed expressible by virtue of its object.
Or,
by way of its being suchness, it is equal to reality as it is.
This is the mental means for the cessation of that [object];
it belongs to the knowledge of that.

Regarding that which is desired as the nature of that cognition—namely, that the form of blue atoms and so forth is not to be designated by a verbal expression, and that it is one because it is non-different from the aggregate of atoms—even these two properties of being unexpressible by a name and having a unitary nature do not exist at all for the form of blue; this is the proposition (*pratijñā*).

The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is "like the fire inferred [from smoke]," stated before the reason (*hetu*) for the sake of ease of comprehension, since the establishment of the members of the syllogism depends upon its force.

Since the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) serves the purpose of establishing the reason (*hetu*), what then is that reason? To this it is said: Because it has many objects, just as fire inferred from the cognition of smoke is grasped—even though it is distinguished by differences of place, time, and so forth, and is characterized by the exclusion of water and the like—as something designated by a name and possessing a manifold nature; in the same way, the object "blue" would also [be manifold], because its object consists of many atoms (*paramāṇu*), and the cognition [of it] would likewise [be manifold]. Thus says the *Praśastapādabhāṣya*.
The compound *tadbalāvayavasiddhiḥ*—meaning "the establishment of the members [of the syllogism] by the force of that"—accords with the reading as it is heard [in the text].
However, the reading *tadbalād avayavasiddheḥ* ("because of the establishment of the members by the force of that") would also be possible here; see page 51, line 9, where the text reads *°rapādi°*.

Now, wishing to demonstrate through inference—by means of the previously stated reasons such as its conceptual nature—that perception is inferior [to direct experience], he says: "For that is the determination of the form blue," and so forth.

The word "that" (tat) refers to the aforementioned conceptual nature; the particle "hi" (for) signifies "because. Because the determination of the form blue is seen to occur either by the designation of an object or by the designation of a word according to the logic already explained, and since that [determination] is nothing other than conceptualization, it lacks non-conceptuality (*avikalpakatva*). Therefore, the definition [of perception] as "free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*) is flawed with respect to both cognition and its object.

And its determination proceeds through superimposition (adhyāropa). If it is asked how that is so, it is said: "In every atom" (pratiparamāṇu)—that is, with respect to each and every atom—there are their own respective essences (tattva) which are mutually distinct.

Whatever is the nature (*bhāva*) of a thing, that is its reality (*tattva*); it does not exist elsewhere, for existence itself is indeed reality. Therefore, realities are distinct for every individual atom; each single atom has its own reality which is absolutely distinct from other atoms. Because it superimposes a single form upon the single reality of form without depending on any other entity, and because its object is the universal form of other forms, it functions with respect to both that and non-that, and because it does not exclude non-that—just like the inference of fire—it consists precisely of that universal. Since it consists in the non-differentiation between the apprehension of atoms and the aggregate established as conventional and ultimate, it is in every way a common object. It is not perception, because it is conceptual in nature, being a cognition of what is not actually perceived, just like the cognition of the inaudibility of sound.

Because they arise by their own inherent nature due to being both conventional and beyond the senses, and because the existence of entities is unique to each individual instance, the essential natures (*tattva*) of atoms are distinct;
likewise, the forms of those atoms, such as blue and so forth, are themselves manifold in form.

And by superimposing, respectively, a single reality and a single form upon those various realities—which possess multiple forms such as blue and so forth, and which are differentiated by one, two, three, or more qualities—and by superimposing a single reality upon all atomic realities, and by superimposing a single blue form upon all atomic forms, there occurs the conceptualization of them as a distinct object.

Furthermore, that superimposition (*adhyāropa*) has as its object a universal form (*sāmānya-rūpa*) which is a different form (*rūpāntara*). A "different form" is a form other than [the individual] form; the form of one atom is a different form from the form of another atom, and this applies to all forms of other atoms. That universal which is grasped by the intellect through non-differentiation as "this is blue" is the object of that superimposition. That universal is also called a "universal" because it subsists in both that [particular] and what is not that [particular]; and because that other thing is its object, it is so designated.
Therefore, in this case, there is no exclusion of anything else in perception (*pratyakṣa*), whereas in inference (*anumāna*) there is the exclusion of what is other than fire—that which is not fire.

Consequently, because it does not exclude that [other], perception has an undifferentiated object, since it functions without abandoning and without distinction between its own intended object and others; whereas inference does not function thus, as it functions only with respect to the universal (*sāmānya*) within its own object.
Thus, compared to inference, perception as conceived by others is more defective, because its object is more thoroughly mixed.

Therefore, "not like the inference of fire"—that [cognition] is not even equal to the inference of fire, because it lacks the capacity for the exclusion (*apoha*) of the object to be excluded. Consequently, the nature of generality belongs only to the inference of fire and not to perception; thus, for that object such as blue which is the domain of perception, and for the cognition thereof, there is that state of having a mixed form due to [the presence of] "whiteness" and so forth.
Because of being [so],
thus it is seen;
thus it is seen.
That which is to be seen is the imperishable, beyond the reach of thought.
[The cognition] is not [perception], because it does not attend to the mind; nor is it [perception], because it lacks the *raṃ* and *hīṃ*.

Since it superimposes a single essence and a single form onto form, its object is a common form of other forms; because it functions upon that and what is not that, and because it does not exclude what is not that, it consists precisely of that generality, like the inference of fire. Because it consists of the non-differentiation between the apprehension of the collection of atoms established as both conventional and ultimate reality, it has a completely common object. It is not perception because it is conceptual in nature, because it consists of a cognition that is not a [direct] cognition, like the cognition that sound is inaudible.
Because it is both conventional and beyond the senses, its own nature is indeed non-arising;
since it is the single object of expression for meditative cultivation, it is the state of being, and as such, it is the supreme state of being.

Because entities possess a unique mode of being (*asādhāraṇabhavanatva*) in each single instance; [the reading] *paramāṇūnām* is also likely to be found here according to the variant reading in manuscript Ya.

It appears that the use of the distributive repetition (*vīpsā*), "because of having a unique mode of being, because of having a unique mode of being," is intended to express that the intrinsic nature (*svatattva*) of all atoms is absolutely distinct in each individual case.

Alternatively, [the reading] "of entities" (bhāvānām) may be used; likewise, there might also be the reading here "because atoms possess a non-common mode of being" (asādhāraṇabhavanatvāt paramāṇūnām), in which case their existence would be [grasped] by a cognition of generality (sāmānyabuddhi).
Not even an atom of anything other than fire exists.

Just as perception does not have an undifferentiated object, so too inference does not have an undifferentiated object, because its operation occurs only with respect to the universal (*sāmānyamātra*) within its own domain; this appears to be the intended meaning here.
The reading *vadadi tatya* might also be *vadapi tat*.
Furthermore, another point: it is not possible for that cognition, nor for the blue form and so forth, to have as their object both that [the existent] and its opposite (atad).
Why? Because there is no relationship between the existent and the non-existent, just like a jar and a sky-flower.

Therefore, since that state of functioning upon both that [object] and what is not that object is indeed already implied, he says the following in order to demonstrate it: "Because it consists in the non-differentiation between the apprehension of the aggregate—which exists as a conceptual designation (*prajñapti*)—and the ultimate atoms which exist in the absolute sense (*paramārtha*), the aggregate is conventionally real (*prajñaptisat*); whereas the atoms existing in that manner are ultimately real (*paramārthasat*). Their apprehension consists in the non-differentiation between the existent and the non-existent. Consequently, because it consists in the non-differentiation between the apprehension of the existent and the non-existent, that state of functioning upon both that and what is not that object is, in every respect, a commonality of purpose; this is so in all respects regarding these aforementioned reasons."

Therefore, since its nature consists of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), that very [nature] has been established by these [reasons]; thus, it is not perception, nor does it have an unmixed object of its own like inference. For the sake of cultivating this meaning, those same reasons are employed again; each one should be applied to this point as before.
Furthermore, that cognition is not perception because its nature is that of a non-cognition, just like the cognition that sound is inaudible.

"Pratyaya" means cause or reason; "apratyaya" means that which does not possess such a cause. There is no causal status (pratyayatā) either in the atoms or in their aggregate with respect to that cognition [of the object].

Furthermore, inferential knowledge (*anumānajñāna*) is not fulfilled in that regard, because what was grasped as being connected [to the object] is cognized otherwise, just like the cognition of contradictory [reasons] and so forth.

Let it be for now; setting aside the acceptance of the rule that perception is established by direct observation, what is this "cognition" (pratyaya) that constitutes the state of being a perception whose object is merely the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa)? Cognition is consciousness (vijñāna), because the second occurrence of the word "cognition" has the meaning of "consciousness"; thus, it is stated that [perception] is a cognition that does not have a cause.

But how is that cognition devoid of a cause? Because, due to both being conventional (*saṃvṛti*) and being beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), atoms possess no causal efficacy toward the cognition of such [an object], either individually or in an aggregate, since they are not objects for that [cognition]. For atoms, being substantially real (*dravyasat*), are not causes of perceptual cognition precisely because they are beyond the senses; likewise, qualities such as blueness, being conventionally real (*saṃvṛtisat*), are non-existent in themselves, and thus their aggregate cannot be a cause.
Therefore, in both ways, that which is called "the cognition of blue color" is actually without a causal basis.

What is the illustration? Just as the cognition "sound is inaudible" is a non-cognition and is not perception, so too is this [case]. This is the end of the section on the distinction between apprehension and non-apprehension.
"Because of the absence of the nature of being an object," thus, by these [reasons], there is no causality either in atoms or in an aggregate with respect to such a cognition.

Furthermore, that inferential cognition is not fully established, because it apprehends something connected [with the object] in a manner other than [how it actually exists], like the cognition of contradictory [reasons] and so forth.

Let us set aside for now the acceptance of perception as a positive means of knowledge; rather, what is the cause of that cognition being a perception whose object is merely the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)?

Furthermore, it might be thought that if that cognition is conceptual (*bhāva*), then inferential knowledge would also be non-perceptual (*apratyakṣa*). [However,] due to reasons such as its being of the nature of conceptual construction (*kalpanātmaka*), inferential knowledge would then become a sensory consciousness (*cakṣurādivijñāna*) like that of the eyes and so forth.
To this it is replied: Even that inferential cognition (*anumānajñāna*) does not fulfill itself;

because the *ātmanepada* suffix and the *yak* affix—which require the agent to be the object—are prohibited, it does not fulfill itself. This is its nature: just as this rice, being spoiled, does not feed itself and is not eaten by itself—being like putrid meat—so too this cognition does not fulfill itself and is not fulfilled.
For what reason? Because it perceives otherwise than what was grasped through a [prior] connection.

The meaning is as follows: it is only when [an object] has been apprehended as connected that there can be a contrary apprehension of that which was apprehended as connected; for that cognition has as its object something connected that is being apprehended contrarily.
Any cognition that, while apprehending an object precisely as it is connected, apprehends that very object contrarily—that cognition does not even fully qualify as inference.
For example: a cognition of the contradictory and so forth.

Just as the cognition "sound is eternal because it is produced"—having grasped the knowledge of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) as being connected to jars and other things which are associated with non-eternality, yet leading one to understand sound as eternal—constitutes the cognition of a contradictory pseudo-reason (*viruddhahetvābhāsa*); and just as, by the inclusion of the word "etc.," the cognition of eternality regarding sound—which proceeds through the gateways of "knowability" (*prameyatva*) and "audibility" (*śrāvaṇatva*)—is likewise a pseudo-uncertain reason (*anaikāntikābhāsa*), so too this [present case] is not a complete inferential cognition, because of reasons such as [the fallacy of] "being" (*tattvādibhyaḥ*). In that regard, [one should] understand...

Regarding the rule for the application of *yaṅ* in the sense of the reflexive-passive (*prati-bhāva-karman*), there is an addition [to the rule] concerning the agent who is simultaneously the object (*karmakartṛ*)— Pāṇini-vārttika 3.1.87.
Pāṇini 3.1.87: Like the object, [the agent] has an action similar to that of the object.

87. An agent whose action is similar to that of the object by virtue of being situated in the same action as the object shall be treated like the object; this is an extension of grammatical operations (kāryātideśa). Consequently, the suffixes *yaK*, *ātmanepada*, *Ciṇ*, and *Ciṇvad-iṬ* shall apply.
Since the agent is already expressed [by the suffix], the nominative case (*prathamā*) is used.
"The rice is being cooked;
the wood is being split.
— Pāṇini Siddhāntakaumudī 3.1.87.
1.87 Taśvadamapi-bhāṣya (The Commentary on "Even That Which Is Not Tamed")
The cognition of a related object,
which has apprehended that which is related.
The phrase *sambaddham avārtham* is found in all manuscripts except Bhā, Ḍe, and Līṃ;
*gṛdbhuttām avārtham* is found in Bhā;
and *tajjñānam* is found in Bhā.

In the context of the connection [between sound and its cause], [the opponent argues that] sound is non-eternal like a jar and so forth; or rather, let us set aside for now [the argument] beginning with "let it be" up to the contradiction with the acceptance of [sound] being an object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Let it be for now that there is a contradiction with the status of being an object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa-viṣayatva*) due to the acceptance of a scriptural authority (*āgama*) situated at a distance;

rather, the meaning of the sentence is this very point previously cited in this context, beginning with "one who is endowed with visual consciousness" (*cakṣur-vijñāna-samaṅgī*), which does not cohere.

The "prescription of direct perception" (*pratyakṣasya vidhiḥ*) is the arising of direct perception; its "formulation" (*vidhāna*) is its explanation: "The five groups of consciousness have an accumulated [object] as their support" (*sañcitālambanāḥ pañca vijñānakāyāḥ*, Abhidharmapiṭaka). That very thing is the acceptance, namely, the acceptance of the formulation of the prescription of direct perception.

It is simply the state of being a perception whose object is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) alone; that which has only the particular characteristic as its object is "that which has the particular characteristic alone as its object. What is that? It is perception (*pratyakṣa*). The state of that is "the state of being a perception whose object is the particular characteristic alone. There is a contradiction with the rule for perception—that is, a contradiction with the acceptance of [perception] having an object—[in the case of the statement]: "The visual consciousness belonging to one who possesses blue-consciousness. Indeed, this very example of the definition of perception is not tenable.

Thus, since for you the aggregate is merely form (*rūpa-mātra*), and because that [aggregate] is perceived when it is grasped, the conceptualization of an "accumulated object" (*sañcitālambana*) is redundant. Furthermore, if it were not merely that [form], it would be a conventional existence (*saṃvṛti-sat*) and thus lack the nature of form; consequently, the eye would not truly be an "eye," as in either case it would fail to apprehend form—just like a jar or similar objects. This contradiction, established by the acceptance of such a definition, remains exactly as demonstrated in the immediately preceding text:
namely, that the notion of "visual consciousness possessing the cognition of blue" is simply untenable.
The word *tu* (but) is used for specification; what does it specify? It specifies that this scripture is less pure than the preceding definition-statement.

"Visual consciousness" (*cakṣurvijñāna*) is a distinguished cognition—either in the eye, or of the eye, or by means of the eye—which has a unique object. One who "possesses" (*samaṅgin*) that is, who is associated with—that [consciousness] is called "one possessing visual consciousness. Who is this? It is the continuum (*santāna*). Because the consciousness moves toward its specific object, the continuum of that [consciousness] is also said to be "associated" through that [consciousness]; thus, there is the blue-consciousness of one who possesses it.

The statement that "perception is itself free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*), inexpressible, and has the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object," and so forth, refers to the illustration of that which is defined by such [characteristics]; "demonstration" is the act of making it perceptually evident by saying, "this is that. For example, just as *āśvalāyana* is the illustration for that which is defined by the rule *vṛddhir ādaic* (Pāṇini 1.1.1).
Those two are respectively the past visual consciousness and the future visual consciousness.
That eye-consciousness... see page 60, line 2;
see page 64, line 1.

That which has as its object only the directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*)—this is *pratyakṣatva*. Likewise, there may also be a reading: "that which has as its object only the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
*tvan* [is the suffix].
There is a contradiction regarding its non-existence; that is, a contradiction with the admission that it is an object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
However, this very example for the definition of direct perception—namely, "the cognition of blue belonging to one possessed of visual consciousness"—is not tenable.

Thus, because the aggregate (*sañcaya*) is merely form (*rūpa*), and because it is perceived as such when grasped, the conceptualization of it as having an accumulated object would be useless; furthermore, if it were not merely that [form], it would be conventionally existent (*saṃvṛtisat*) and thus lack the nature of form. Consequently, the eye would not truly be an "eye," since in either case it would not grasp form—just like a jar or similar objects. However, the notion that "this is eye-consciousness" is indeed tenable, provided it is based on atoms (*paramāṇu*). (Pramāṇavārttika, Pratyakṣa-pariccheda)
The sage named Aśvalāyana belongs to that very lineage; his descendant is Āśvalāyana,
according to Pāṇini 4.1.99, which prescribes the suffix *phak* after words such as *naḍa*, because the word *aśvala* is included among those beginning with *naḍa*.
When the suffix *phak* is prescribed by the rule *iti sūtreṇa*, [the augment *yañ* is applied] to the first vowel among the vowels (*acāmādeḥ*) according to Pāṇini 7.2.117 (*taddhiteṣvacāmādeḥ*).
By this rule, according to Pāṇini 1.1.1 (*vṛddhir ādaic*),
the form *Āśvalāyanaḥ* is derived through the application of the *vṛddhi* vowel substitute.
How is it that this does not hold? To this he says: "In this way, for you, of the aggregate... and so on, up to "...because the conceptualization of an aggregate as an object would be futile.

This means: if, for you, the status of being an example is accepted [for atoms], then because the aggregate consists of nothing but form (*rūpa*), what happens? It will be connected [to the conclusion] that the conceptualization of an aggregate as an object would be rendered futile.

Why is the aggregate merely color-form (*rūpamātratva*)? Because when that [color-form] is apprehended, it is perceived directly (*pratyakṣatvāt*). When the perception of something occurs upon the apprehension of another, that [latter] is seen as being merely that much; just as when there is the perception of burning upon the apprehension of burning, one accepts nothing other than mere burning, so too, upon the apprehension of an aggregate, there is only the color-form blue. What follows from this? The uselessness of the conceptualization of an aggregate as an objective support (*ālambana*), because the aggregate does not exist;
the non-existence of the aggregate is due to its being merely color-form.

Furthermore, because the conceptualization of a composite object as a cognitive support (ālambana) would be futile, the illustrative example beginning with "one possessed of eye-consciousness" and so forth is indeed untenable; [the intended meaning is that] they are perceived merely as atoms (bhūta-mātra).

If [the aggregate] were not composed of those [atoms], it would be conventionally existent (*saṃvṛtisat*), and so forth, up to: "because in either case it does not grasp form, like a jar or similar objects.

Now, if one thinks, "Let this fault not occur," and thus maintains that the aggregate is not merely form, but rather that very [aggregate] is what is perceived, then—since the aggregate is conventionally existent—it would lack the nature of form (*arūpatva*), like a donkey's horn;
that conventional existence has been established previously.
Furthermore, because it would be formless (*arūpa*), that aggregate (*sañcaya*) could not be perceived by the eye, since it would be distinct from form (*rūpa*), like sound or like a sky-flower.
If you ask, "What is the fault in that?", it is said: the eye itself would no longer be the eye, because it would not be a grasper of form, like a jar, a tongue, or the skin, and so forth.

If you object, "How can it be said that the eye does not grasp form? This contradicts what is observed and established," then it is precisely you whom I am charging with contradicting what is observed and established.
What is the reason? Because it does not grasp form in either case.

If it were an aggregate (*sañcaya*), even then, as it has been stated that it would be non-existent and indeed no form at all, form would not be the object of the eye; therefore, because it does not grasp form, the eye would not be "the eye," just like the ear.

Alternatively, if the blue form of an atom (*paramāṇu*) is intended to be non-aggregated, even then, because it is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), form would not be the object of the eye; and thus, because it does not grasp form, the eye would not be "the eye," as previously stated. Therefore, it is well said: "In both ways, the eye does not grasp form."

Thus, first of all, regarding the phrase "one endowed with visual consciousness" (*cakṣurvijñānasamaṅgī*), the mention of the "eye" (*cakṣus*) is redundant because the eye itself is not the visual consciousness; furthermore,
it has already been stated that [visual consciousness] apprehends form and so forth only when the object is proximate.
Consciousness, too, would not be consciousness, because it would apprehend its object in a manner other than [its actual nature], like the cognition of a fire-brand circle (alātacakra) and the like;
nor does visual consciousness correspond [to its object], because it cannot occur apart from form (rūpa),
for a collection (sañcaya) is not form.
Furthermore, even though that form has that as its object, there is no conjunction with the visual consciousness because it is not its object, just like the objects of other sense faculties.

Even if it were an object consisting of an accumulation [of atoms], because it exists only conventionally (*saṃvṛtisattva*), like a sky-flower, it does not relate to the cognition of blue; the continuum of that [form] is not connected to it because there is no cause for the arising of a cognition possessing that aspect, just as one who has not been burned lacks the cognition of burning.
For this very reason, even the mention of "consciousness" (vijñāna) is useless; therefore, he says: "Consciousness, too, would not be consciousness," and so on, up to "like a flower in the sky."

Specific knowledge (*vijñāna*) is what you intend by "direct perception" (*pratyakṣa*); that primary *vijñāna* would not exist [in your view]. Otherwise, how could the venerable teacher Mallavādin have spoken of the contradiction with his own statement, "there would be no *vijñāna*," as Māyeya and Dinnā did? What, then, is the reason why that *vijñāna* would not exist? Because the object is apprehended otherwise: because a formless aggregate is apprehended as having form, or because mere form is apprehended as an aggregate.
What is the illustration for this? It is like the cognition of a fire-brand wheel (*alātacakra*) and so forth.

Just as one who perceives a mere spark from a firebrand as a wheel does not possess true cognition, so too— in accordance with the inclusion of the word "etcetera"— is the cognition of a person in a post and so forth;
thus, first of all, the dyad consisting of "the eye" and "cognition" has been refuted.

Desiring to refute even the state of "being endowed with" (*samaṅgitva*) in the expression "one who is endowed with visual consciousness" (*cakṣurvijñānasamaṅgī*), he says: "And visual consciousness does not go along [with the person]. He means that "going along" (*samaṅgana*) consists in the serial continuity (*saṃtāna*) called "person" proceeding by way of that [consciousness]; why then is its negation not [also] applied? [The answer is: because visual consciousness is impossible apart from visible form (*rūpa*), nor can its serial continuity exist elsewhere. For it has been said: "The relationship between qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) occurs when there is both possibility and deviation."

If it is argued that there is deviation because of the dependence on an accumulation [of atoms], and therefore [the term] is qualified [by "visible"], that is not so; for accumulation is not a form (*rūpa*), and due to its lack of form, there would be an absence of association with visual consciousness.

It might be thought: "Visual consciousness is said to be 'associated' precisely because it does not deviate from the blue form, as it moves toward that single [object]. But this is incorrect, because that [accumulation] is also beyond the senses (*atīndriya*) and, being outside the range of visual consciousness, lacks form.

Even granting your position, as for that which is "form" (*rūpa*): it is called "form" because it is "formed" (*rūpyate*) by way of its form; it is said, indeed, to be formed by visual consciousness. That which has this as its object is "having that as its object" (*tadviṣaya*). What is that? It is the single movement. Of what? Of visual consciousness. But even that does not exist.
Why? Because it lacks an object (*aviṣayatvāt*).
It lacks an object because it is beyond the senses (*atīndriyatvāt*), with respect to the visual perception under discussion.

It might be thought that, like the objects of other sense-faculties—just as sound, being the object of another faculty, is not conjoined with visual consciousness, so too that [aggregate] form [is not conjoined]—the aggregate would be fit for conjunction with visual consciousness. To this we reply: even regarding the aggregate as an object, there is no conjunction with visual consciousness; why? Because it lacks existence (*asattva*). It is like a flower in the sky (*khapuṣpa*); this is the example based on the common property of the absence of conjunction, since it exists only conventionally (*saṃvṛtisattva*).
Thus, first of all, form, the eye, consciousness, and the possessor [of these] have been refuted; next,
the knowledge of the qualifier [will be examined].
To the wisdom of the wheel,
to the wisdom of the pillar and the person, to the wisdom of the thunderbolt.
The eye does not go elsewhere than to forms and so forth; it does not proceed toward what is non-existent.
The reading *samaṅganā* might also occur here; however, the points "now blue" and "it cognizes" are what must be refuted.

Among these, "blue" has already been refuted from the perspective of its referent (*padārtha*), and "it cognizes" has likewise been refuted from the perspective of its referent, because the conjunction of form, the eye, and consciousness has also been refuted.

Lest the position of the [proponent] remain unrefuted, it is refuted even from the perspective of the meaning of the sentence: "That continuum does not possess a relation with blue-cognition, because there is no cause for the arising of a cognition having that form.

A cognition having that form (*tadākāra*) is a cognition whose form is blue (*nīlākāra*); the arising of such a cognition is "the arising of a cognition having that form," and its cause would have to be either the collection [of atoms] or the blue-form itself. Neither of these two exists according to the method already stated; therefore, due to the absence of a cause for the arising of a cognition having that form, [the continuum cannot be related to the cognition].

If it is argued that one will cognize both the blue and the collection because they are causes both individually and collectively, we say no; for simultaneous cognition is impossible, since cognition differs from action [in its non-simultaneity].

Since those two would be the object of a single cognition, if they were to be known as a single thing, they would be mutually identical, leading to the consequence of asserting that everything is of the nature of everything. For if the collection were grasped as a single blue, there would necessarily be the grasping of each individual blue.

Furthermore, what is the illustration for how, through this convergence (*sandrāva*), there is the unity of all that is blue? It is like the lack of knowledge regarding the burning of what has not been burned. Just as there is no experience or cognition of the burning of what has not been burned because of the absence of a cause for the arising of a cognition having that form, so too [the cognition] does not belong to the continuum of that [blue object];
thus the faults have been stated regarding the acceptance of either the blue form or its accumulation as the object.
(Astādhyāyī-prakaraṇa)

If it is argued that one will cognize both the blue and the collection because they are causes both individually and collectively, we say no; for simultaneous cognition is impossible, as cognition differs from action.

Since those two would be a single cognition and thus have a single object of knowledge, they would be identical to one another, resulting in the doctrine that everything is of the nature of everything. For if the blue and the collection were one, then upon the apprehension of the inherence [of color], there would necessarily be the apprehension of each individual instance of blue.

And therefore, the meaning is that just as here, due to the convergence [of perceptions], there is a unity of all blue, so too [it would follow] if one were to accept that [the cognition] has only one of the two as its object.

Now, wishing to state the fault in the view that both [the individual and the aggregate] are the single object, he presents an alternative position: "If it is argued that one will cognize both the blue and the collection because they are the causes individually and collectively, this might be the thought: 'For those very same blue atoms are the cause when taken individually—according to the analogy of carrying a palanquin—and when combined; yet each one alone is not the cause, nor does there exist a collection distinct from them. Thus, cognition has both as its cause, and therefore the non-establishment of the absence of a cause for the arising of cognition [remains a problem].'"

This is not so, because simultaneous cognition is impossible; for there is no single cognition of two objects simultaneously, nor is there a simultaneous cognition of each object individually, as it has been said: "Just as a single cognition does not cognize two objects, likewise, two cognitions do not cognize a single object."
If it should be thought— as stated in *Catuḥśataka* 268— that [the soul] might be like the hand grasping multiple objects such as jujube or myrobalan fruits,
this is incorrect, because cognition differs in nature from action.

And knowledge is said to be direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) does not deviate from [the nature of] knowledge; for it is stated in the *Nyāyapraveśa*: "Direct perception is that knowledge which is free from conceptual construction regarding an object such as color-form (*rūpa*).
Thus, there is no fault in the difference between the color-form and the collection of color-forms; this is the effort of the person.
...the efficacy of human effort (puruṣakāra)...
in the knowledge of the [correct] words... in one discourse... Bhāṣya.
"Consciousness cognizes one object, not two;
likewise, it cognizes one consciousness, not two. (Catuḥśataka 268).
See page 60, note 15.

However, for the purpose of establishing [knowledge] for oneself, there are only two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*): perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*). Among these, perception is that knowledge which is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*), being devoid of conceptualization regarding names, universals, and so forth, with respect to an object such as color-form (*rūpa*). It is called "perception" because it operates in relation to each sense-organ (*akṣa*). — *Nyāyapraveśaka*, p. 7.

Even if there were a single object of cognition (*ekajñeyatva*) for those two because they possess a single cognition (*ekajñānatva*)—that is, "a single cognition belonging to these two" constitutes *ekajñāna*; and because they possess that single cognition, their object of cognition would be one alone, and the state of being such is *ekajñeyatva*, like the experience of burning—if, while in that state of having a single object of cognition, there were mutual identity (*itaretaratva*), meaning they had attained each other's nature, how could there be the doctrine that everything is the nature of everything? For, since the aggregate is not distinct from its constituents, the aggregate itself is just form, like the nature of the aggregate; or else, the aggregate is just form, since it is not distinct from form, like the nature of form.

Thus, because things intended as distinct entities—such as the collection of taste and so forth, or the collection of form and so forth within a jar—are not actually different from one another, there follows the doctrine that everything has the nature of everything else.

Therefore, since all atoms of blue are not distinct from their aggregate, they constitute a unity; thus, when there is a perception of inherence (*samavāya*), and the collection of a young woman’s mass of hair is being perceived—where the word *hi* signifies "because"—since all blue is a single unity, therefore only a single blue form belonging to a single hair would be perceived. There would be a perception of each individual blue atom one by one. Furthermore, even upon perceiving a single blue hair, there would be a perception of the entire mass of blue hair, because the aggregate has the nature of that single blue.

And therefore, just as here [in the case of a blue object] there is oneness of all "blue" due to their coalescence (*sandrāva*), and a substance (*dravya*) is a coalescence of qualities (*guṇa*) that is not a separate entity because all the blue qualities have attained oneness by coalescing—so too, there would be oneness through the coalescence of the pentad of form and so forth, that is, the pentad of form, taste, smell, touch, and sound.
Why? Because they are qualities (*guṇatvāt*), meaning because they are attributes (*dharmatvāt*); for, unlike the Vaiśeṣikas, we do not maintain a distinction between substance and quality.

The illustration is like the oneness of blue (*nīlaikatva*): just as all blues are of the nature of a quality (*guṇa*) because they possess the property of being qualities, so too is the pentad beginning with form (*rūpa*), because it possesses the property of being qualities; thus, like the oneness of blue, earth and the other elements are in every respect substances consisting of a conglomeration of qualities (*guṇasandrāva-dravyatva*). Furthermore, since even those [elements] have form and the rest as their ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), there is the state of "everything having everything as its essence" (*sarvasarvātmakatva*).

However, this particular excellence of conglomeration is illusory (*māyeyīya*), because of the admission that the objective support (*ālambana*) is an accumulation [of atoms], whereas previously it was not admitted that the atoms of form and so forth exist either accumulated or unaccumulated.
Indeed, it has been stated in your own scripture (*āgama*): "Only aggregates touch aggregates because they possess parts.

In that context, when mutual contact is examined, there would be oneness of the entire self [of the aggregate], and likewise oneness of color, taste, and so forth. Therefore, if the conglomeration of qualities is established and color and the other qualities are one, what fault is there? It is replied: Because a substance (*dravya*) consists of the conglomeration of qualities (*guṇa*), a substance is merely the conglomeration of qualities. Consequently, earth and the others—earth, water, fire, air, and so forth—are in every respect one. Thus it stands.

What is the reason? That very oneness of form and so forth is the cause; therefore he says: "Because even for those [elements], form and so forth are the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Since form and the rest alone are the ultimate reality because they constitute substance (*dravya*) as a conglomeration of qualities (*guṇasandrāva*), and since there is oneness among them, it follows that all the world—earth, water, fire, air, jar, cloth, river, ocean, light, and so forth—attains oneness by having that [oneness of form] as its essence. Having thus summarized this, he says: "The state of everything being the self of everything.

Therefore, it is rightly said: "Even for one who maintains the doctrine of the absolute distinction [of things], the doctrine of the universal self-nature of all is exactly like that of one who maintains the doctrine of non-distinction."
Regarding the object of knowledge (jñeya),
in each and every instance, for each individual [being],
even for the ignorant... [text fragment].
Because of its existence, let it be seen; [see] page 15, line 20; having withdrawn, etc.

Just as the fivefold [group] consisting of smell, sound, and touch exists, so too does the fivefold [group] beginning with form exist, because they are all qualities (*guṇatvāt*), like the oneness of the color blue.

Furthermore, because earth and the other elements consist of a conglomeration of qualities (*guṇasandrāva*) and are substances, and because even those [qualities] have color and so forth as their ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), there follows the state of everything being of the nature of everything.

However, this particular excellence of conglomeration belongs to Māyā; for you accept that the object of cognition is an aggregate, whereas you previously did not accept that atoms of color and so forth exist either as aggregates or as non-aggregates.
Indeed, it has been stated by you in your own scripture: "Only aggregates touch aggregates, because they possess parts."
In that regard, when defining mutual contact, there is the existence of the entire self; this is also the case hereafter.
The [opponent’s] reading regarding the withdrawal (*saṃhṛti*) is indeed [correct];

moreover, the proponent of the doctrine of absolute particularity (*viśeṣaikāntavādin*) excels the proponent of the doctrine of absolute non-particularity (*aviśeṣaikāntavādin*). Desiring to explain that [point], he says "But this... and so forth, up to "...it is not possible without an accumulation," in order to establish that substance (*dravya*) consists of a confluence of qualities (*guṇasandrāva*).

The word *tu* (but) serves to distinguish; what does it distinguish? It distinguishes the following: for those who maintain that the non-distinct (*aviśeṣa*) [tanmātras] are absolute and who assert the commencement of ether and the other elements from the *ahaṅkārika* tanmātras of sound and so forth—which possess their own distinct natures prior to the attainment of unity with form and the rest—their process is that form and the others exist at times even as unaggregated (*asañcita*). However, for those who maintain that the distinct (*viśeṣa*) are absolute, there is only the attainment of unity through aggregation, because they do not admit the existence of form and the others as separate or unaggregated anywhere; thus, there is the extreme consequence of the doctrine that "everything consists of everything. This is what the commentator distinguishes by the phrase: "This is an extreme compression of the Māyeya school, due to their admission of the atoms of form and the rest as having aggregated objects."

In order to demonstrate the reason for that accumulation, he says: "Because [atoms] previously unaccumulated were not admitted [to exist prior to aggregation]; for it is not admitted by the followers of Māyāsūna that atoms, forms, and so forth, which were previously unaccumulated, later become accumulated and serve as objective supports (*ālambana*). This must necessarily be admitted by you in this very way. To demonstrate the validity of that point, the scripture itself has been cited: "For it has indeed been said to you. The word *hi* (for/indeed) signifies "because" (*yasmāt*). Because it has been stated in your own established doctrine (*siddhānta*), what was stated? It was stated: "Only aggregates touch aggregates, because they possess parts (*sāvayavatva*). Thus it was said.

Do atoms touch one another? Or do they not touch? Even if they do touch, do they touch part with part, or the whole [of each other], or do they touch an aggregate? And when aggregates touch aggregates, do they touch part with part or the whole? With such questions as the starting point for the investigation of mutual contact therein, and so forth, it has been determined by demonstrating the faults inherent in both the touching and non-touching of the entire self [of the atom]: "Aggregates touch aggregates only by means of a part, and only a part."

If one atom were to touch another atom, it would have to touch it with its entire self because there is no [other] part; consequently, through that penetration, the aggregate would become the size of a single atom, and its resistance (*sapratighatva*) would be lost.

Since the same applies to the composite mass, and since the faults of the aggregate becoming the size of an atom or the loss of resistance would follow from either touching or not touching, only "touching by way of location" is accepted; yet that is not possible apart from an accumulation [of atoms].

As for what was stated—that "it is not blue"—this alone is consistent, because there is never any cause for the arising of a cognition determined by the form of a blue atom (*nīlaparamāṇu*). Since the aggregate (*samudāya*) is not blue, even when one accepts the individual members of the aggregate as being intended to constitute the reality of difference, they are not blue because they possess mutual blueness; since they lack that [blue] nature, there is an absence of identity with the form of the universal (*jāti*) and so forth in every respect.
Even if there were no contact [with the universal], there would be an absence of resistance (*sapratighatva*).

Furthermore, since resistance (*pratighāta*) does not exist in individual atoms—just as there is no oil in sand—it would likewise not exist in their aggregate (*saṅghāta*). Yet, such resistance is observed in the aggregate; therefore, atoms and aggregates do not lack tangibility.
Consequently, it is the aggregates themselves that touch other aggregates by way of spatial location (*deśa*).

By including the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), one avoids the fault of the absence of obstruction to motion (*gati-pratibandhābhāva-doṣa*) for them; otherwise, due to the non-existence of aggregates, there would be an absence of objective supports (*ālambanābhāva*), and other such faults would follow. Thus, contact by way of spatial location alone is accepted.
Moreover, that tactile sensation cannot arise in any way without an accumulation; thus it is rightly said that "the excellence of condensation belongs to Māyā.
In this way, it has been stated that even the meaning of the sentence "one cognizes blue" is not tenable. *Nāyāvi* [refers to the source].
...not an accumulation... [according to Bhāṣya] ...by means of that alone... [according to Bhāṣya] ...therefore not... [according to Viśeṣa]
Therefore, indeed,
[it is] without the distinction of the proponents of the Vaiśeṣika and Vijñānavāda schools;
[this is] due to the unity of the accumulated [atoms].
The intention of the path of illusion is the beginning of the treatise.
...the state of being [a cognition] having a composite object as its support after the five [senses].
The reading "saṃghātaṃ vā" does not exist in the Bhāṣya manuscript; however, the Bhāṣya reads "paramāṇuḥ paramāṇuṃ spṛśet," while the Yaśomitra commentary reads "paramāṇuṃ spṛśet."
There would be the loss of the status of being "with-outflow" (sāsrava).
Here, one [element] is with-visible (sanidarśana), namely form (rūpa); ten are with-resistance (sapratigha);
eight are material (rūpin) and indeterminate (avyākṛta), namely those same [ten] excluding visible form and sound.

1.29 "The ten material [elements] are with resistance. The inclusion of the term "material" (rūpin) is for the purpose of excluding that which is non-material. "Forming" (rūpaṇa) is form (rūpa); those which possess this are material (rūpin).
"Ten" refers to the five elements beginning with the eye-element (cakṣurdhātu) and their five corresponding object-elements; thus, it is stated in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (1.29).

Because touching or not touching would entail defects such as the [atom] being merely a mass or a mere atom, or lacking resistance (*sapratighatva*), it is precisely the contact with a location (*deśasparśa*) that is accepted; and this is not possible without an accumulation (*sañcaya*).

As for what was said—that "it is not blue"—this alone is consistent, because there is never a cause for the arising of a cognition restricted to the form of a blue atom, since the aggregate (*samudāya*) is not blue.

Even if one accepts each individual or their aggregate as being intended to be the reality of difference, since they are not non-blue because of their mutual blueness, and because they lack that form [of difference], there would be either non-difference through the universal, the form, and so forth,
or else ignorance regarding them; and thus it has been explained.

This [statement], "it arises without [the object] being present" (dṛte saṃbhavati), accords in meaning with that definition and example of direct perception (*pratyakṣa-lakṣaṇodāharaṇa-vākya*) found in the Abhidharma.
In what sense? It refers to what was stated: "one does not cognize it as 'blue'. This is how it proceeds.

The particles *a*, *mā*, *na*, and *nā* function as negations; thus, the statement "he does not cognize blue" alone is consistent, and nothing else is. Why? Because there is never any cause for the arising of a cognition restricted to the form of a blue atom. As for those atoms which are called "blue," they have never been, are not, and will never be the cause for the arising of a cognition restricted to the form of blue, because they are beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriyatvāt*). Therefore, the statement that "one endowed with visual consciousness as you conceive it never cognizes blue" is a word whose logical justification is perfectly certain.

It might be thought: "Because the aggregate (*sañcaya*) is an object of the senses and because it consists of blue, one perceives blue. But this is incorrect, because the collection (*samudāya*) is not blue.

If there were blueness in the collection—which exists only as a conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*)—then this [perception] would be so; however, since non-existence has no blueness, one does not perceive blue. This alone is well said here:
"one perceives blue" (as found in the Pāṇḍulohitika, Laṅkāvatāra, Raṃgaśālā, and Hīnayāna versions).
One cognizes blue; [it is] determined by the aspect (*ākāra*).
It might be thought: "Of which... [the following applies].

Regarding this, the following might be the thought of that deity: "One would not perceive blue if one were to say that one sees each individual atom as being beyond the senses, or if one were to say it is their collection, which is like a flower in the sky. What then? One perceives those very atoms, distinct from one another individually, yet joined together and situated in a single place, like a heap of mustard seeds."
And this is incorrect, because [it would follow that] the reality of difference is intended, and so forth.

"Difference itself is the reality; thus, 'the reality of difference' (bhedatattva) means the state of being that [difference]. These very [differences], intended as such, constitute the aggregate individually, rather than the aggregate being primary. What then? The aggregate is primarily characterized by difference; that is the 'individual-aggregate. Even when that is accepted—that is, even when an aggregate consisting of mutually distinct individual forms of difference is accepted—even if there is no capacity in each individual part according to the analogy of those carrying a palanquin, let there be the capacity for the aggregate dominated by them to be the cause for the arising of the cognition of blue. Even when this position is adopted, because blue is absent [in the parts], one does not cognize blue.
Why? Because those [colors] are non-blue by virtue of being blue in relation to one another;

these instances of blueness are distinct for every atom and do not exist elsewhere than in their own supporting atoms. This is because entities possess an inherent arising and perishing, and because they lack connection with anything else.
Therefore, the blueness of one thing does not exist in the other, nor does the blueness of that [other] exist in the first.

What is the reason? Because it does not possess that nature (*atadrūpatvāt*), because the function of a hand is untenable, because its object is absolutely excluded [from being a substance], and because there is no apprehension of a real substantial form (*dravyasadrūpatva*), one does not cognize "blue. Therefore, this meaning follows for the statement prescribing the method of direct perception (*pratyakṣavidhi*): a continuum (*santāna*) associated with visual consciousness, having an accumulated [collection] as its objective support (*sañcitālambana*), cognizes blue—which is an accumulation existing only conventionally (*saṃvṛtisat*). Since that [accumulation] is non-existent, that very form is "of that nature" (*tadrūpa*) by means of the eye; yet it is not "of that nature" (*na tadrūpa*), which is to say it is "not of that nature" (*atadrūpa*). Its state is "the state of not being of that nature" (*atadrūpatva*). Therefore, because it is "not of that nature," that [blue] is certainly not the other [actual] blue form.
If it were [the same], then it would be that very thing, because it possesses that nature, like that [other blue]; but it is not so.

Or rather, its nature is "having that nature" (*tadrūpam asya*); since its nature is not that [other] nature, it is "not having that nature" (*atadrūpam*). By what form could this be? By the form of the universal (*jāti*), the configuration (*ākāra*), and so forth. For that [blue] is not the other blue by way of the universal characterized as blueness—which is the commonality—nor by way of the configuration, which is a particular shape such as circular or globular. Since, according to your own view, there is no possibility of anything that could effect the non-difference between those two atoms—whether by way of the form of the universal or the form of the configuration—it follows that they do not have that nature.
Therefore, blue does not exist as the form of another blue; likewise, another blue also does not exist as that [first] form.
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera," it is meant that what is seen in the first moment is not the form seen in the second moment, and that too is not the form of the other.
Thus, even spatially, what is seen in one location is not the form seen in another location.

Therefore, since the cause of non-difference is untenable, there is the state of being of a different nature; and because the cause of non-difference is untenable due to the objects being absolutely distinct, "object" (artha) refers to that which exists in the ultimate sense—the blue atom itself. And those atoms are absolutely distinct from one another, possessing unique, uncommon forms.

Why? Because it has the nature of substantial existence (*dravyasat*). For that which has the nature of substantial existence is precisely that which possesses a distinct, independent essential nature (*viviktasvarūpa*) not dependent on anything else. In this regard, just as it does not exist in the form of taste or in the form of smell because it has the nature of substantial existence, so too it does not exist in the form of another blue thing. Furthermore, just as a chariot does not exist in the absence of its parts such as the pole and so forth, or just as [the chariot] does not exist even when those [parts] are present if they lack the form of another blue thing, so too this [blue thing] does not exist at all in the absence of that [other blue thing], because it is devoid of blueness, like a different blue object that is not blue. And that other blue object is likewise not blue, just like that [first one].

Therefore, what could that blue be which might be cognized by the eye when it is possessed of visual consciousness? Because there is no such apprehension, one who possesses visual consciousness does not cognize "blue.

Furthermore, because of the absence of any factor—such as genus—that would establish identity, nor because of the absence of any apprehension of atoms—which are substantially real and utterly distinct—as being non-different [from one another] whether they be called "form" or "taste," one who possesses visual consciousness does not cognize "blue."

Alternatively, because mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*) is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), by the very logic already stated, there is no blue nor any other blue; since they do not possess a distinct nature, like color and taste, one does not cognize "blue"—this alone is consistent with what was well-said. This is so if [the object] is a single atom (*paramāṇu*) individually...
The sixth round:

the arising of the tone.

The reading "its blueness does not exist elsewhere" is not found in the manuscripts of Ya; because it is impossible for [the eye] to grasp [it], because its object is absolutely excluded, and because it is of the nature of a substantially real entity, one does not cognize it as blue due to the absence of apprehension.

For this very reason, the meaning resulting from the statement prescribing the method of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is as follows: a continuum (*santāna*) endowed with visual consciousness and having an accumulated object (*sañcitālambana*) cognizes as blue that accumulation which exists conventionally (*saṃvṛtisat*); yet, by means of the eye, that [accumulation] is non-existent.
That form is not its nature; otherwise,
it would be blue.
It may be that the two [versions] are non-authoritative;
it may be that, according to the opinion of Ya, they are non-authoritative.
Some are not like the sky;
others are not of such a nature.

In the absence of [the suffixes] māṇīya and so forth, [the form] is *asādhāraṇa* according to the Bhāṣya; it is *asādhāraṇī* according to the Raṅga and Hīna versions; according to Prajñāruci, it is *asādhāraṇī*.

Regarding *akṣāgrakīla*: it is the pin (*kīla*) at the tip (*agra*) of the axle (*akṣa*), which is the wooden shaft to be inserted into the nave (*nābhi*); it is for the purpose of binding there. It is called *aṇi* because it makes a sound (*aṇati śabdāyate*). Alternatively, it is derived from the root *aṇ* with the suffix *ṇidi*, according to the rule *kṛṣṝkuṭi uṇādi* 619; thus, *āṇiḥ*. (Abhidhānacintāmaṇi, Svaccha-svopajña-vṛtti 3.420).
The *īṣā* is a component of a chariot;
because there is no apprehension [of it] as being "possessing parts" (*saman-gin*), it is not blue. It is not "possessing parts," therefore it is blue. *Ya*.
"Let it be seen," [referring to] page 75, line 3.
Regarding the phrase "for this very reason" (*ata eva*) and so forth:

"for this very reason" (*ataḥ*) means because of the absence of the conjunction of the eye-consciousness with the object blue, which was just mentioned; "only" (*eva*) is used for emphasis. There is an implication (*arthāpatti*) regarding the meaning of the sentence that is about to be stated. From the rule of perception—that is, from the statement that establishes the arising of perception—this meaning follows: "but not 'it is blue'. In this context, since the word *iti* expresses a manner or form, it implies that the meaning of the sentence takes such a form.

In order to clarify which statement [is being referred to], he repeats the very statement concerning the example of the definition of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) that has been introduced, and demonstrates: "Visual consciousness," and so forth.

That same previously mentioned continuum (*santāna*) which is "endowed with visual consciousness" and has a "collected object" (*sañcitālambana*)—meaning one who possesses visual consciousness and for whom the collected is the object—is "one whose object is collected. It cognizes blue form, which is a collection and conventionally real; it knows that which is intended as blue, though it is a non-existent entity (*asadvastu*), and not some existent thing. This is the meaning that arises.

What is the reason? Because that collection of blue, being non-existent, is apprehended by the eye—that is, by the visual faculty—and yet the blue itself does not exist in that way, since its blueness consists of atoms that are ultimately real; however, there is a mental cultivation of it: perceiving an object where there is no object, and never at any time perceiving a phenomenon where there is an actual object.

Regarding a collection that exists conventionally but lacks ultimate reality, one perceives it as a substantial entity (dravyasat) and conceives of it as "blue," yet one does not perceive the actual object (artha) and conceive of it as such; nor does one perceive the object itself as a substantial entity and conceive of it as such, because that [object] is beyond the senses (atīndriya).
Furthermore, no one ever perceives an object and conceives of it as a "dharma" (phenomenon), because it is entirely and at all times ungraspable due to its being beyond the senses.

Thus, one conceives of what is not an object as a "dharma," and even conceives of names and so forth as "dharmas" when they do not exist as objects, because collections and names and so forth are of the nature of conceptual construction (kalpanā), and conceptual construction cannot be excluded.

Because of its apprehension, it is not the case that "blue" is thus; that is to say, blue does not exist as such an unreal form. For although that blue is indeed existent, it does not know [itself as] ultimately real. If one asks what the reason is for that blue not being [ultimately] blue, it is because the ultimate reality consists of the blueness of atoms (*paramāṇu*). For only atoms that are ultimately real are blue, not the aggregate (*sañcaya*).
Therefore, one who possesses eye-consciousness does not cognize blue; rather,
it is the mind that cognizes the object.
Because other consciousnesses do not apprehend it, blue does not exist [in that way], since [blue] is the blueness of atoms that are ultimately real (*paramārthasat*).
As for its cultivation: one perceives what is non-beneficial as beneficial; yet never does anyone perceive what is beneficial as a [real] dharma.

One perceives a collection—which is conventionally existent and non-beneficial—as a substantially existent blue object, but one does not perceive what is beneficial as beneficial in that way. Nor does one ever perceive what is beneficial as a [real] dharma, because it is beyond the senses and is therefore absolutely ungraspable at all times.

One who perceives a phenomenon (*dharma*) in what is actually non-existent, and likewise perceives phenomena such as names (*nāman*) in what is non-existent—since the accumulation [of aggregates] and names and so forth are of the nature of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), and since there can be no removal of that construction—the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) you have described is untenable by the very force of the arguments already stated. As it says in the *Abhidharmapiṭaka*: "One perceives an object (*artha*) as an object, but one does not perceive a phenomenon in what is not an object."

How, then, is this consistent? To this he says: "But his cultivation [consists in] perceiving what is not an object as an object, and never perceiving anything that is an object as a dharma. He explains this: with regard to a collection that is not an object but exists conventionally (*saṃvṛtisat*), for that collection is not an object because it exists only conventionally; since when that [collection] is not grasped, the cognition of it does not arise, as it has been said: "That which, when broken, no longer produces the cognition of itself" (Abhidharmakośa 6).

This verse [is explained as follows]: "Like a row and so forth"—according to your own view, regarding that collection characterized by non-existence, one who perceives a substance as "blue" is one who perceives a blue atom as ultimately real; because those [atoms] alone are the object, this is obtained as implied by the meaning from the sentence of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanāvākya*)—"one who perceives an object in what is not an object"—and not [simply] "one who perceives an object in an object."
He explains this: "But it is not the object itself that is designated as 'substance' when it exists as a mere atom, such as a blue atom;
why? Because that object is beyond the senses (*atīndriyatva*). He shows that this reason is sufficient for the statement of our proposed cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
If it were so, one might think that the designation "dharma" applies to the object; but it is said, "No," for never at any time does anyone designate the object as "dharma."
Since the aggregate as a whole alone is the object of the senses, at the time of its perception—or at any other time—it cannot exist as an object designated by the term "dharma.

Alternatively, whether at the time of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) or at the time of inference (*anumāna*), what is the reason? Because it is beyond the senses (*atīndriyatvāt*). The word "at any time" (*kadācit*) is an explanation of "always" (*atyantam*); that is, because it is never apprehended.
Of what? Of an atom, a blue [color], and so forth.
From that, it follows by implication: "one who perceives phenomena (dharma-saṃjñin) is in fact without an object.
He explains this: even when there is no object, one is merely a perceiver of phenomena such as names and so on.

What is the reason? Because the aggregate (*sañcaya*) and [the categories] such as name (*nāman*) are conceptual in nature, one perceives what is not an object as an object; that is to say, within the aggregate—which is conceptual and not a real object—one perceives the characteristics (*dharma*) of sound and so forth, which consist of the conceptualization of what is not an object. Why? Because the exclusion of conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoha*) is impossible, whether with respect to the collection as a whole or to the names and so forth that serve as its basis. Furthermore, conceptual construction is the association of name, genus (*jāti*), and so forth; the exclusion of that [construction] is simply impossible for that cognition which has the imagined collection and its names and so forth as its objects. Therefore, this meditation (*bhāvanā*) as described by us is logically consistent.

Alternatively, this meaning is expressed by your own words: "One who perceives an object as an object" means that one does not perceive an object—such as blue and so forth—as ultimate reality, because such an object is beyond the senses;

the word *tu* (but) serves as a qualification. The phrase "one who perceives an object as a phenomenon (*dharma*)" follows. Since he is first of all one who does not perceive an object as an object, how could he perceive an object as a phenomenon? This is the distinction indicated by the word *tu*.
By implication, as before, it follows that he perceives what is not an object as an object, and he perceives that very thing as a phenomenon.
