In the passage "°kāle'ttaittara°" (Bhā) and "°kālettaitvara°" (Ya),
there may also be a reading "°kāle uttarakāle vā".
In the sense of making known (*saṃjñāpya*),
[it is] *pra° saṃjñapi*;
in the sense of non-benefit (*anartha*), [it is] *anartha*, up to *yāvatya*.
Therefore, because its object is non-existent—being like the production of a "void-void"—it is merely true as a rootless conceptual construction.

Furthermore, as it has been stated in the *Abhidharmakośa*: "Regarding this sense-field of form (*rūpāyatana*) which is divided into many types, what arises from it when [perceived] by a single [atom] at any time? Even the collection of faults, such as having a non-existent object like the production of a "void-void," belongs to that conceptual construction.

Just as when zero is multiplied by zero, the result is simply zero, so too is this [your argument] a conceptualization concerning a non-existent object, intended for the purpose of training the intellect of students—a practice common among mathematicians.

Consequently, because its object is non-existent, its truth consists merely in being a rootless conceptualization; the conceptualization of its arising is seedless, and the conceptualization of its properties is likewise. Both conceptualizations are rootless, yet they are taken as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for this [subject]; thus, that alone is true, and nothing else whatsoever is true in the "perception" imagined by you.

Therefore, because they are true only as rootless mere conceptualizations, your two conceptualizations of perception and inference are even more wretched than the conceptualizations of worldly things such as water, seeds, or mirages; for the sake of establishing the void, you have established the void itself.
In this context, *pratyutpādanā* means multiplication;
likewise,
from the seedless (*nirbīja*), there is the emergence of the aggregate (*samudaya*).

And as for what was stated in the *Abhidharmakośa*: "That which is divided into many kinds," and so forth, up to: "When one perceives a substance possessing various colors and shapes, visual consciousness is produced by that [substance] when there is a delimitation of its specific types, such as blue and so on; sometimes it is produced by many [atoms] when there is no such delimitation of its specific types, as for example, when one perceives from a distance a cluster of jewels possessing various colors and shapes."

Regarding this as well, he introduces [the following] in order to demonstrate that the Buddha’s statement, "How is it divided into many types?"—which follows as a consequence of the definition of direct perception—is indeed not tenable, just like the illustrative sentence concerning the cognition of blue for one possessed of visual consciousness:
"This, moreover, is the Buddha’s word which is authoritative," as shown in the *Abhidharmakośa*; that must be examined.
In that context, "many types" (*aneka-prakāra*) means a preeminent mode (*prakṛṣṭaḥ kāraḥ*); what is that? It is mutual dissimilarity.
In what manner is the sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) differentiated? It is differentiated by types such as blue, yellow, and so forth.
Within that sense-sphere of form, which is differentiated by many types, sometimes visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) is produced by a single substance.

But when is it produced by a single substance? When there is a delimitation of its specific type, such as blue and so forth—when there is a delimitation to a single type, such as "this is blue only, not yellow," or "this is yellow only, not blue"—then visual consciousness is produced by a single substance.

Sometimes by many [atoms], and when again by many? When there is no exclusion of its specific mode—that is, when there is no exclusion of modes such as blue—then visual consciousness is produced by many substances.
Regarding this point, he provides an illustration: "For example, from afar, a cluster of jewels," and so forth.

One who sees a cluster of jewels situated at a remote location—which possesses many colors and shapes, meaning it has a configuration (*saṃsthāna*) consisting of many colors—is seeing that which has many colors and shapes; or rather, one is seeing many colors and many shapes.

When a person sees a collection of jewels—such as diamonds, sapphires, emeralds, cat's-eyes, topazes, rubies, and crystals—which possess many colors like blue and yellow and many shapes like circular and triangular, and which are divided into many varieties, there is no discernment of them from a distance; however, from nearby, discernment occurs, such that one thinks, "This is a sapphire, or perhaps one of the others, like a diamond.
Since both the *Abhidharmakośa* and its commentary (*bhāṣya*) were composed by Vasubandhu, the term *Abhidharmakośa* here is intended to refer specifically to the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*.

And therein, from the manuscript of the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* obtained through the efforts of the eminent scholar Śrī Vāsudeva Viśvanātha Gokhale, with the assistance of the venerable Bhadanta Śrī Śānti Bhikṣu, and by the kindness of the eminent scholar Śrī Prahlāda Pradhāna, the reading is as follows:
"Form is twofold, twentyfold; sound is eightfold; taste is sixfold;
odor is fourfold; and the tangible consists of eleven types."
1.10 The five faculties have been explained.
Five objects are to be explained;
among them, form (rūpa) is twofold—color (varṇa) and shape (saṃsthāna). Therein, color is fourfold, beginning with blue, while the others are its subdivisions.
Shape (*saṃsthāna*) is of seven kinds, beginning with long and ending with irregular (*visāta*).

That same sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) is further said to be of twenty kinds, namely: 1. blue, 2. yellow, 3. red, 4. white, 5. long, 6. short, 7. square, 8. circular, 9. high, 10. low, 11. even, 12. uneven, 13. cloud, 14. smoke, 15. dust, 16. mist, 17. shadow, 18. glare, 19. light, and 20. darkness.
Some recite twenty-one [kinds], adding "the sky" as a single color.

In this context, "even" (*sāta*) refers to a regular shape, while "uneven" (*visāta*) refers to an irregular shape. "Mist" (*mahikā*) is frost or haze. "Heat" (*ātapa*) is the radiance of the sun. "Light" (*āloka*) is the radiance of the moon, stars, fire, medicinal herbs, and jewels. "Shadow" (*chāyā*) is that wherein forms are visible; by contrast, "darkness" (*andhakāra*) is the opposite.

The remainder is not explained here because it is easily understood. Thus, the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) exists by way of color (*varṇa*), but not by way of shape (*saṃsthāna*); it is known as blue, yellow, red, white, shadow, heat, light, and darkness.
There is a portion of long and so forth that exists by way of shape (*saṃsthāna*) but not by way of color (*varṇa*), which has the nature of bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*).

There is another portion that exists in both ways; as for the remaining sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*), others maintain that only sunlight and light exist by way of color, for the demarcation of long and so forth is indeed seen in blue and other colors.
But how can a single substance exist in both ways? Because both are perceived therein; for this root *vid* has the sense of "knowing," not the sense of "existing.
[Objection: In that case, it would follow that bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) is also [form]. [Response: It has already been stated that this refers to the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*).
Sound is of eight kinds; it is first fourfold, being caused by appropriated or non-appropriated great elements and designated as pertaining to sentient beings or non-sentient things.
This, in turn, becomes eightfold through the division into pleasant and unpleasant.
Among these, that which is caused by appropriated great elements is, for example, the sound of hands or speech.
That which has non-appropriated great elements as its cause is, for example, the sound of wind, trees, or rivers;
that which is designated as "sentient" is the sound of vocal intimation, while the other is designated as "non-sentient."

Others maintain that there is also sound caused by both appropriated (*upātta*) and unappropriated (*anupātta*) primary elements (*mahābhūta*), such as that produced by the conjunction of a hand and a drum;

however, just as a single-colored atom is not accepted as being derived from two sets of four primary elements, so too [this sound] should not be so desired. Sound has been explained. Taste is of six kinds, distinguished as sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter, and astringent.
Odor is of four kinds, because fragrant and foul odors each possess both even and uneven qualities;
however, in the treatise it is said to be of three kinds: fragrant, foul, and even odor.
The tangible consists of eleven aspects; the tangible has the nature of eleven substances: the four great elements, smoothness, roughness, heaviness, lightness, cold, hunger, and thirst.
Among those, we shall explain the primary elements later; here [we mention] smoothness, softness, roughness, and hardness.
Heaviness is that by which things are weighed; lightness is the opposite;
coldness is that which produces a desire for warmth.

Hunger is that which produces a desire for food; this is a case of applying the name of the effect to the cause, as in the expressions: "The birth of the Buddhas is blissful, the teaching of the Dharma is blissful, the harmony of the Saṅgha is blissful, and the austerity of those who are united is blissful."
In that realm of form (rūpadhātu), hunger and thirst do not exist; the rest, however, does exist.
Although garments there are not weighed individually, they are weighed when accumulated.
While harmful cold is absent, it is said that beneficial cold does exist.

Regarding this manifold form that has been described as manifold, visual consciousness sometimes arises from a single substance when there is a discernment of its specific type, and sometimes it arises from many substances when there is no such discernment; for example, as when one sees from a distance an array of troops with various colors and shapes, or an array of jewels.
In the same way, auditory consciousness and the others are to be understood.
However, some maintain that body-consciousness arises from at most five tangibles: the four great elements and one [quality] such as smoothness;
others hold that it arises from all eleven.

But if this were so, would it not follow that the five groups of consciousness have general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) as their objects because they take a collection [of dharmas] as their objective support, rather than having specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) as their objects?

These [cognitions] are held to have the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the sense-field (*āyatana*) as their object, not the specific characteristic of the substance (*dravya*); thus there is no fault. This is now investigated: when the objects of the body and tongue faculties are reached simultaneously, which consciousness arises first? Whichever has the more intense object; however, when the objects are equally reached, the tongue-consciousness arises first, because the continuum is inclined toward the desire to eat.
The five sense objects have been described, as well as the manner in which they are apprehended. 1.10

Visual consciousness is produced by a substance when there is a delimitation of its specific mode, such as blue and so forth; sometimes it is produced by many substances when there is no delimitation of that specific mode, as for example when one sees from a distance a cluster of jewels possessing many colors and shapes.
Even in this case, how is it that one does not see [the object] as differentiated by multiple modes?
In this [passage], "bhā" reads "ṣyan," though there may also be the reading "ṣyan paṭhati";
in the "tanenaika" [manuscript], "pra" [is found].
How again? Without [the specific cause], how again?
When that mode [of cognition] occurs.
The flow of activity,
having been released from the senses, brings about existence.

In this context, as an incidental discussion arising from the objection regarding the definition of perception (*pratyakṣa*) as having the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*), it was asked: "If that [perception] does not conceptualize [the object] as a single unit, then how is it that 'the five groups of consciousness have an accumulated [object] as their objective support' (*abhidharmapiṭaka*)? Furthermore, when it was stated that [perception] is a cognition produced by many distinct substances—both single and multiple—it was objected that this entails the consequence of its being conceptual in nature and the consequence of its not having the particular characteristic as its object. To resolve these points, it is said: "These [five consciousnesses] have the particular characteristic of the sense-field (*āyatana*) as their object, not the particular characteristic of the substance (*dravya*). (Abhidharmakośabhāṣya 1.10)
10. Thus, how is it that [the object] is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpetam*)? An investigation will be undertaken on this point.
First, let us examine this very word of the Buddha: "Sometimes cognition is produced by a single substance, sometimes by many.

Here too, it must be explained: since the five bodies of consciousness (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*) are taught to have the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as their object, how can they have as their object that which consists of the nature of a sense-field (*āyatana*) existing as a commonality (*sāmānya*), when that sense-field exists as a commonality divided into many modes, and for one who perceives that sense-field, it is indeed its object?

And how so? If [the object] has a composite as its objective support (*sañcitālambana*), then because it consists of a collection existing in an undifferentiated state, there would be a delimitation by a single type [of atom], like the color and shape permeated by the luster of a cluster of jewels. Furthermore, since a single substance is never perceived, how could visual consciousness be produced by a single substance? It would be like the lack of knowledge regarding the taste of something when one has not tasted it.

If, however, the production of the cognition of a single substance were admitted, then the postulation of a composite objective support would be entirely pointless; this would contradict the very acceptance [of that postulate].
This must be stated until [the atoms] are enumerated.
The connection is: "How should it be stated?"

The term *anekaprakārabhinnasāmānyavṛttirūpāyatana* refers to the sense-field of form (*rūpāyatana*) which functions upon a generality (*sāmānya*) that is divided into many types. Its state is "the condition of being such a sense-field of form" (*tādṛgrūpāyatanatā*). When that condition exists—that is, when there is the condition of the sense-field of form functioning upon a generality divided into many types—for one who perceives that sense-field of form, how could it be logical for that visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) to have a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object? For that [consciousness] consists of a composite whole because it takes that [generality] as its objective support (*ālambana*), and because its object is a sense-field of form consisting of a composite whole termed a "generality. Likewise, since all five groups of consciousness (*pañcavijñānakāya*)—beginning with form—are merely examples of the sense-field of form and its corresponding consciousness, one must state the resolution here: how can the five groups of consciousness be taught to have particular characteristics as their objects?

The meaning is that because an *āyatana* (sense base) is of a general nature, it does not possess a specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). Thus, perception as being free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*) is established. This is also stated in the Abhidharma: "One endowed with visual consciousness cognizes blue, but does not [cognize] 'it is blue'; one perceives the object as an object, but does not perceive a phenomenon (*dharma*) within the object."

If that is so, how is it that the five groups of consciousness have "accumulated" (*sañcita*) as their object, as stated in the *Abhidharmapiṭaka*? For if they do not conceptualize that [object] as a single unit, how can this be? Furthermore, regarding what was said—that these [consciousnesses] have the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the sense-field (*āyatana*) as their object, and thus have the specific characteristic as their object but not the specific characteristic of a substantial entity (*dravya-svalakṣaṇa*), according to the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (1.10)—how is that to be understood? To this, the answer is: because it is produced by multiple objects, it is said to have a universal (*sāmānya*) as its range with respect to its own object;

because it is generated by multiple substances, it is said to have a universal as its range within its own sense-field (*svāyatana*). This is not, however, due to the conceptualization of non-difference among things that are actually distinct.

Thus has this objection, along with its refutation and so forth, been stated in the *Svavṛtti* on the *Pramāṇasamuccaya* composed by Dignāga. 1.4. "They [perceive]... as found in the *Ubbhā* [manuscript].
And that which [he] diminishes,
and that which [is] knowledge— herein,
this much is the limit.

It must be stated how it is that the five bodies of consciousness (vijñānakāya) are taught to have specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) as their objects, given that for one who perceives that form-base (rūpāyatana) as having the nature of a common occurrence (sāmānyavṛtti), that [base] is its object.

How so? Because, insofar as they take a collection as their objective support (sañcitālambanatā), they consist of an aggregate existing in an undifferentiated state; thus, there is no distinction of individual types, like the color and shape permeated by the light of a cluster of jewels. Furthermore, since a single substance is never perceived at any time, how could visual consciousness be produced by a single substance? It would be like the lack of knowledge regarding taste when the flavor has not been tasted.

However, regarding the production of a cognition of a single substance, the postulation of a composite (sañcita) as the objective support is indeed purposeless; moreover, this would contradict the acceptance of that [composite].
In this context, there may also be a reading: "divided into many kinds" (*anekaprakārabhinne*).
Because it is the state of being that which is to be purified (pavyamānatva), and because it is the state of being the characteristic,
it is that which possesses the characteristic (tallakṣaṇa).
"How so? and so forth, up to "the delimitation by a single mode."

"How" (*katham*) expresses an inquiry regarding the cause; "and" (*ca*) is used to aggregate the faults. By what cause, in that case, could there be a basis (*āyatana*) consisting of a universal (*sāmānya*) divided into many types? The word "thus" (*iti*) denotes a manner. For one who perceives the visual object-field (*rūpāyatana*) in this way as having various forms, since it has the nature of a collection whose objective support is an accumulation, and because that collection—whose state is one of non-distinction—is essentially a mass where [parts] have attained unity through non-distinction, how could there be a restriction to a single type for the visual object-field? The meaning is: it is not possible.

What is it like? It is like the color and configuration permeated by the luster of a collection of jewels; just as in a collection of jewels of various colors, when their luster permeates the color and configuration, there is no restriction to a single type, so too there is an absence of restriction to a single substance. (See *Prakārasāmānya*, Pañjikā 9).

Furthermore, because a single substance is sometimes not perceived, and because a single substance—an atom—is never perceived as it is beyond the senses, how could visual consciousness be produced by a single substance? The meaning is that it is never produced in any way whatsoever.

Therefore, when knowledge is produced by a single substance at some time—namely, when there is a delimitation of a specific mode such as "blue"—one must consider: is this a word of the Buddha or a non-Buddhist statement? Reflect upon this.

If it is asked, "Why, moreover, is visual consciousness not produced at times due to the non-apprehension of a single substance? it is said: like the lack of knowledge of taste when there is no tasting of flavor. Just as the cognition of taste does not arise when a flavor has not been tasted by the gustatory faculty (*rasanendriya*), so too visual consciousness does not exist when an object is not apprehended by the eye. Furthermore, if for the sake of establishing that this word of the Buddha is indeed the word of the Buddha, one were to admit that cognition is produced by a single substance, then the conceptualization of an aggregate as the objective support (*sañcitālambana*) would be entirely purposeless in the production of the cognition of a single substance.
And when the visual object-status of atoms is thus asserted individually, then this other word of the Buddha becomes a non-Buddha-word and meaningless.
Which [word]? "The five bodies of consciousness have an accumulated [object] as their objective support" (Abhidharmapiṭaka).

If that [latter statement] is true, then the unreality of the former is established; thus, there is a contradiction between the two statements regarding their respective objects due to mutual incompatibility. Therefore, he says: "contradiction with that acceptance."
See page 78,
line 2: "grahaṇacakṣu" is stated as "sānāsvādana" in the manuscript (pra.).
Regarding this, it is said that there may also be a reading *rasanānāsvādane*;
this is stated except for [the editions] *Anupamavijaya* and *Vinā*.
Furthermore,

cognitions of being differentiated by multiple modes— whether through the exclusion or non-exclusion of a single mode— would also not exist, because the sense-field of form (*rūpāyatana*) consists only of what is aggregated (*sañcita*), like Narasiṃha.

For even though the lion-man (*narasiṃha*) has a manifold mode of being, this is because manhood and lionhood were previously perceived as distinct; however, when there is no such aggregation, there is not even the apprehension of those modes within the atoms that constitute that substance, since an unaggregated [entity] is never observed. How much less, then, could there be its exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) and so forth? Because of the expression "by many," the five groups of consciousness have as their objects a conceptualization of a commonality (*sāmānya*) that exists only conventionally (*saṃvṛtisat*).

Furthermore—starting from "the delimitation of aspects" (*prakārāvaccheda*) and so forth, up to "because it pertains only to the accumulated" (*sañcitagater eva*)—aspects (*prakāra*), delimitation (*avaccheda*), non-delimitation (*anavaccheda*), and being differentiated by multiple aspects (*anekaprakārabhinnatva*): these too ought to be cognitions.
Why? Because the sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) pertains only to the accumulated; for it is only the accumulated that is perceived as the sense-sphere of form, not the unaccumulated.

Therefore, the cognition of a "mode" (*prakāra*) is not tenable. A mode is a preeminent cause (*prakṛṣṭaḥ kāraḥ*), such as "blue" or "yellow," [implying] "this is distinguished from that. Since there is no absolute difference between things, there is an absence of modes; for when non-difference is apprehended in a universal, the cognition of a mode is not possible. Likewise, there is no delimitation (*avaccheda*) of one thing by another, because of the dilemma of whether it is different or non-different. Similarly, there is no non-delimitation, because [the object] is not manifold. And since it is said to be "differentiated by many modes," there would be an apprehension of non-difference among things that are [otherwise] different.

Because of the non-differentiation of the collection and the non-differentiation of the [individual] forms, cognitions of the parts and so forth cannot possibly be non-conceptual and have particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) as their objects.

Why? Like "Narasiṃha. Just as the lower part is the form of a man and the upper part is the form of a lion, and because of the cognition of the non-difference between those two, it is called "Narasiṃha," so too the cognitions of the parts and so forth must arise from the conceptualization of non-difference among things that are distinct, and not otherwise. If it is argued that this is not a valid example—because in the case of a man and a lion, there is no cognition of non-difference between two distinct entities—[we reply]: No, for it is precisely the two collections that possess the nature of non-difference.

"Even though the lion-man has various modes of movement," and so forth; for although each of those two—namely "man" and "lion"—is distinct, there is nevertheless a mode of movement consisting of the collection of the states of being human and being a lion. Since substances such as blue atoms and the like were previously perceived as distinct, it is logical that there is a cognition of difference characterized by the conceptualization of non-difference; however, it is not understood in that same way regarding the uncollected [atoms].
Because of the state of manifestation,
it is called Narasiṃha; thus it is said.
Even having accepted that [the soul] is joined with the body through its prior division,
and that it follows the mode of Narasiṃha (the Man-Lion), [it is argued that] there is no accumulation [of parts] in those atoms which constitute that substance, and so forth.

Having forgotten what you previously stated—that the five groups of consciousness have accumulated objects as their focal points—you have now said this: that regarding this sense-field of form (*rūpāyatana*), which is divided into many varieties, knowledge is sometimes produced by means of a single substance.

"One who possesses visual consciousness perceives blue, but not 'it is blue'"; this too was said while forgetting that sometimes there is no exclusion [of other colors] when there are many [objects], such as when one sees a collection of jewels with various colors and shapes. For if one were to admit the simultaneous apprehension of multiple forms such as blue, yellow, and so on, it would contradict the cognition of a single form, such as blue. Enough of this digression; the subject at hand is stated: among atoms existing as substances, there is no apprehension of modes such as blue or yellow; what is the reason for this? Because that which is not aggregated is not perceived.
It has been stated that there is no perception of unaggregated [atoms] because they are beyond the senses;

how, then, could there be the exclusion of them and so forth? For if perception were present, cognitions of their differentiation, non-differentiation, and their distinct modes might be possible; but in the absence of perception, these would not exist from afar.
Thus, for now, the claim that [the whole is produced] by a single substance is untenable.
"Having undertaken," etc., see *Narabhāṣya*, *Narayana*, p.
See page 78, line 2;
see page 61, line 1;
see page 79, line 1.
This has been explained in the *Vyākhyā* [of Prajñākaragupta].

Furthermore, as for what was stated—that knowledge is sometimes produced by multiple substances—because of that expression "by multiple," those multiple substances possess a conventional existence (*saṃvṛtisattva*). Due to this commonality, they are a conceptual construction of the unreal (*asatkalpana*). The five groups of consciousness (*vijñānakāya*) have that as their object; because they have an unreal conceptualization as their object, like inferential knowledge and its fallacious counterparts, they are not direct perception (*apratyakṣa*) or are non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*), being like the sight of a cluster of jewels from a distance. Thus, they do not have the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as their object, even though a single consciousness may have multiple objects.
Furthermore, that which was said by the Buddha: "The arising of consciousness occurs in dependence upon a duality.
In dependence upon what duality? In dependence upon the eye and visible forms, visual consciousness arises;
in dependence upon the ear and sounds, auditory consciousness arises."
Dependent upon the nose and odors, olfactory consciousness arises;
dependent upon the tongue and tastes, gustatory consciousness arises;
dependent upon the body and tangibles, tactile consciousness arises.
Dependent upon the mind and mental objects, mind-consciousness arises.
In this case as well, if the teaching is intended with respect to individual instances for the sake of expressing a collection, then this very same fault applies;
however, if it is stated for the sake of denoting a substantial entity, then there is a contradiction with what has been accepted here.
Furthermore, cognition and the like would also be perceptible by the senses because they are supersensible, just as color is;
and whatever contradiction exists here is equal [to the following]: there is a contradiction with inference because atoms are supersensible, yet [you claim] they are perceptible by the senses.
It does not follow that [cognitions] have specific individuality (*svalakṣaṇa*) as their object;

nor is it only the fact of not having specific individuality as their object that constitutes a fault. What then? Even the state of a single cognition having multiple objects—as in the case of seeing from a distance—is likewise [faulty]. See page 79, line 1.

Because that [cognition] is a conceptual construction (*saṃvṛti*) consisting of multiple substances, its objects are not particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*); furthermore, there is the state of a single cognition having multiple objects.
And as for what was said by the Buddha—that the arising of cognition occurs in dependence upon a duality—
Depending on what duality? Depending on the eye and forms, visual consciousness arises;
depending on the ear and sounds, auditory consciousness arises;
depending on the nose and odors, olfactory consciousness arises.
Dependent upon the tongue and tastes, tongue-consciousness arises; dependent upon the body and tangibles, body-consciousness arises;
and dependent upon the mind and mental phenomena, mind-consciousness arises.
In this case as well, if the designation is made with reference to individual instances for the purpose of expressing a collection, then this very same fault [of non-existence] follows.
If, however, it is for the sake of denoting a substance (*dravya*), then there is a contradiction with your own tenet here;
for even cognition and so forth would be perceptible by the senses, because they are not beyond the senses (*atīndriyatvāt*), just like color-form (*rūpavat*).

And whatever contradiction exists here is equal [to that previously mentioned]: since atoms are supersensible (*atīndriya*), there is a contradiction with inference regarding their being sensible (*aindriyaka*); this applies solely to the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
In this context, there may also be the reading *kevalaṃ svalakṣaṇam*.

This has been introduced here in connection with demonstrating the inconsistency of the Buddha’s words— starting from "And as for that which was spoken by the Buddha" up to "mental consciousness arises toward phenomena"— with the thought that it is indeed nothing but a [mere] perception (*darśanam eva*).

The connection [of the argument] is as follows: if cognition were produced by multiple substances, it would contradict what was directly stated by the Buddha, namely, "depending upon a duality," and so forth.

Having stated that the arising of consciousness occurs depending upon a duality—the internal sense-field (*āyatana*) and the external—one then asks a question and provides the answer oneself: "Depending upon which duality? The detailed explanation—"depending upon the eye and depending upon visible forms," and so forth—is already understood from the meaning.
This is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*): that the sixfold group of consciousnesses arises from the sixfold group of dualities.
And so it has been said: "The two [aspects] of the self and the object of cognition... [and so forth].
The eye does not cognize two objects simultaneously as a single consciousness does;
likewise, it does not cognize a single object with two consciousnesses. (Catuḥśataka 268)

To this, he states the following reply: "In this case as well, 'dependent upon the eye and dependent upon visible forms, the arising of visual consciousness occurs'—there are two possible interpretations for the use of the plural number. Is it based on a collection [of atoms], such that even though visible forms are beyond the senses, they are treated as individual entities? Or is it according to Pāṇini 1.2.58: 'The plural may optionally be used for a single thing when it denotes a genus'?"

Is this [the term "atom"] based on the category (jāti) as the referent? In that case, if the designation is made with reference to individual instances (*vyakti*) for the sake of expressing a collection, then there is the fault that these five groups of consciousness (*vijñānakāya*) would have as their objects a conceptualization of a commonality (*sāmānya*) that exists only conventionally (*saṃvṛtisat*), and not the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).

Alternatively, if it is for the sake of denoting the substance (*dravya*), then all atoms of that same kind must be designated by a single form; thus, the use of the plural for a singular entity would contradict your own position, for you have accepted that atoms are beyond the senses (*atīndriya*). Therefore, there is a contradiction.
Furthermore, in accepting this position, another undesirable consequence is stated: even cognition and the like would be perceptible by the senses;

because they are supersensible, [it follows that] qualities such as cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and feeling—which are postulated by you—would be visible, since they are supersensible, just like color.
Or else, color itself would not be graspable by the eye, because it is supersensible, just like cognition and the like.
You might say: "But surely being beyond the senses (*atīndriyatva*) and being perceptible to the eye (*cakṣurgrāhyatva*) are mutually contradictory.
Do not think so; for this formal argument (*prayoga*) is intended solely to produce an undesirable consequence for you and has as its fruit the overturning of your own understanding.

Furthermore, whatever contradiction might be suspected here is equal to that which exists regarding the sensory perceptibility of atoms (*paramāṇu*); an atom is "the ultimate particle" (*paramo 'ṇuḥ*), and, as in the aforementioned reasoning, there is even a contradiction with one's own words (*svavacanavirodha*).
And thus, we take refuge in the Supreme Lord of Debate; yet there is no contradiction between us and him, for he is the Lord of the World,
the protector and savior of the true nature of the world when it is being subverted, by means of preserving the reality of all the various systems of debate.
If it is asked how there is a basis [for this], it is because of the acceptance of the sense-bases (*āyatana*) as having a nature consisting of multiple entities.

The word *aṇu* (atom) is a synonym for "subtle," and the word *parama* (ultimate) expresses its excellence; this [excellence] is consistent with being beyond the senses (*atīndriyatva*). Just as it is contradictory for that which is beyond the senses to possess sensory perceptibility—specifically visual perceptibility (*cākṣuṣatva*)—so too is this sensory perceptibility of cognition (*buddhi*) and so forth equal [in contradiction]. Thus, let there be the pointing out of contradiction due to the equality of the fault; what is the harm? Furthermore, [it is stated]: "Visual consciousness arises depending on the eye and depending on forms. This contradicts inference because of their being beyond the senses. Since gross things are preceded by subtle ones, atoms are established through the inference of the effect. Therefore, if one accepts that those [atoms], which are eternally inferable, are objects of the eye, both statements contradict inference.

Furthermore—there is also a contradiction with one's own words (*svavacanavirodha*) as in the case of the aforementioned cultivation (*uktabhāvanā*). "The aforementioned cultivation" means *uktā bhāvanā* (the cultivation that has been stated); "as in the case of that" means *tadvad uktabhāvanāvat*. Because it is equal to this very cultivation of the contradiction in inference—that "the atom (*paramāṇu*), being beyond the senses (*atīndriyatva*), is visible (*cākṣuṣa*)"—there is a contradiction with one's own words for one who asserts that "the atom, though considered beyond the senses, comes within the range of the eye. [This applies] to both those things which possess form (*rūpa*) and those which lack form (*arūpa*), for the purpose of refuting the accumulation [of atoms]... from that... [fragmentary].

Just as in the case of the aforementioned meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), there is likewise no contradiction with our own words,
and there is indeed reliance upon the Supreme Lord of Discourse (*vādaparameśvara*).
Furthermore, we have no contradiction with him, because he is the Protector of the World (*lokanātha*).

If it is asked how he can be a refuge— he being the protector of the true nature of the world that is being subverted, since he preserves the reality of the distinctions between all doctrines— the answer is: because he accepts that the sense-bases (*āyatana*) consist of multiple natures,
and because of his statements that [the self] is both beyond the senses and visible to the eye.
Here, "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*) has been mentioned; there may also be a reading, "just like the cultivation that was mentioned" (*tadvad-uktabhāvanāvat*).
[Regarding the variants: *yac-cākṣuṣa* (Bhā), *yatvākṣuṣa* (Raṃ), *hī*.

And thus, by the statement of the opponent, you who rely on the Supreme Lord of Non-absolutism (Syādvāda-parameśvara) and who were previously proponents of absolutism (ekāntavādin), become adherents of non-absolutism (anekāntavāda) through the abandonment of that [absolutist] position.

All doctrines indeed rule over the world because they are capable of making the world their own; yet, among all of them—even those that are one-sided—the doctrine of non-absolutism (anekāntavāda) is the Supreme Lord, for it rules over those who abide under its authority.

For those seekers of victory (*vijigīṣu*), who—though capable of advancing their own interests—are yet possessed of the defect of mutual contradiction, and who rely on one or another of the six political measures (*ṣāḍguṇya*) such as alliance (*sandhi*) like a neutral or intermediate king, the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), namely Syādvāda, serves as the support for the quality of seeking refuge (*saṃśraya*), which is characterized by entrusting oneself to another. This is because they obtain their own function only by relying upon it; for if they do not rely upon it, their respective functions would perish and they themselves would be destroyed.
Regarding this, the worldly method of conventional discourse (*vyavahāranaya*) says: "And we have no contradiction with him.
Why? Because he is the Lord of the World (*lokanātha*)."
For the world is the system of conventional discourse; because it observes the views of that [world] by being subject to its influence, the Syādvāda is called the "Lord of the World" (*lokanātha*).

Why? Because it is the protector, the one whose nature is to protect, whose characteristic is protection, or the one who effectively provides refuge for the reality of the world and the essence of the world—the jewel of right vision—which is being plundered here and there by the proponents of extremist doctrines.

If it is asked, "How is he the protector? [the answer is] "The diversity of all doctrines," and so forth. The diversities of all doctrines—which have become worldly—are the various one-sided views such as permanence and impermanence (*nityānityādyekāntāḥ*). Their "truths" are their actual states of being, which consist in the support of their own respective objects. He is called the "protector" because he causes these to be accepted through conformity with worldly consensus and because he protects them by establishing a state of mutual compatibility among them.
[He is also the source of] the circle of the sixfold policy (*ṣāḍguṇya*), which is his natural sphere of activity (*prakṛtimaṇḍala*).
"Peace, war, sitting neutral, marching, seeking shelter, and duplicity—these are the six measures of policy (*ṣāḍguṇya*), according to the teachers...

...In this regard: 1) peace (*sandhi*) is the making of a treaty; 2) war (*vigraha*) is the infliction of injury; 3) sitting neutral (*āsana*) is indifference; 4) marching (*yāna*) is the pursuit of superiority; 5) seeking shelter (*saṃśraya*) is surrendering to another; and 6) duplicity (*dvaidhībhāva*) is the simultaneous adoption of both peace and war. These are the six measures of policy.

1. One who is declining relative to another should make peace; 2. one who is gaining the upper hand should wage war; 3. one should remain seated [in neutrality] thinking, "The other is not capable of harming me, nor am I capable of harming the other."
One endowed with superior qualities should march forth;
one lacking power should seek refuge;
and in a matter that can only be accomplished through allies, one should adopt a double policy—thus is the establishment of the strategic qualities.
— Thus ends the seventh chapter, sections 98–99, on the "Suppression of the Body" in the *Arthaśāstra* of Kauṭilya.
The *Kāryāvaloka* by Bhāskara,
composed for those who speak in the Kali age.
O Father, O Father,
O Blessed One, according to the true meaning.
Having caused those who speak appropriately and with capability to grasp the meaning, another [person]... [is] supreme.
By means of this [synthetic] protection, there is preservation from the other [extreme views]. Another asks: "How is there recourse [to the Lord of Doctrine]?

It may be granted that Syādvāda is the Supreme Lord of Doctrine because it protects the world; for the protection of the world comes from establishing the mutual non-contradiction of those [views] and from their unification. But how can there be recourse to the Supreme Lord of Doctrine for those who hold extremist (ekānta) doctrines? To this it is replied: Because of the acceptance of a substratum (āyatana) whose nature consists of multiple aspects.

That which possesses many natures is "multitudinous-natured" (*anekātmaka*). This refers to the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*). Here, by the word "therein" (*tatra*), the very sense-base of form just previously mentioned is spoken of as the substratum for that single [perception]. Thus, its dual nature is once again demonstrated;

in this way, it possesses both unity and multiplicity. Since cognition arises through that which is essentially undifferentiated, it follows that the sense-base of form may be one, and the sense-base of form may be many, according to the reasons already stated.

Knowledge is sometimes produced by a single substance and sometimes by many; this is due to its being either excluded or not excluded [from other substances]. Since this is accepted, one relies upon *syādvāda* (the doctrine of manifold aspects), while the *nayās* (standpoints) are merely partial aspects of *syādvāda* and constitute one-sided doctrines (*ekāntavāda*). As it has been said: "Blessed is the right view... (*Sanmati-tarka*, 3.59).

These are not mere products of one's own imagination; the definition of the *nayās* is likewise [as follows]. For it has been said: "A *naya* is the exclusive adoption of one particular aspect of a substance that possesses multiple natures. It is called a *naya* because it leads (*nayana*) toward an object by means of its own predominance. Furthermore, it is a false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) because it is a contrary apprehension of an object that has multiple forms. The *syādvāda*, however, possesses truthfulness because it is the apprehension of a reality that consists of multiple natures."

If it is asked, "How then are the proponents of extremist views (ekāntavādins) refuted by the conventional method (vyavahāranaya), which is itself worldly? [the answer is: Because they rely upon the Lord of the World (lokanātha), their very reliance on the side of the Lord of the World constitutes the acceptance of the opponent's position; thus, at the very moment of that acceptance, the debate ends in a point of defeat (nigrahasthāna) for the extremists. Here, by the word *tatra* ("therein"), the sense-field of form (*rūpāyatana*)—which was just indicated—is mentioned as the substratum for the single form; its dual nature is then shown once again. And here, because it is the support for the single form-sense-field, the word *tatra* refers precisely to the form-sense-field just mentioned, and its dual nature is further demonstrated.
And thus, for that very [object], there would be both unity and multiplicity, because cognition arises through its undivided reality;
consequently, the sense-field of form (rūpāyatana) might be one, and it might also be many— let this be seen as per the stated reason, page 78, line 2.
Just as it is in reality,
so it is grasped by those who speak according to reality.
They are grasped by those who maintain such a doctrine;
regarding this doctrine, it is said here: "by way of having a single form-base as their support," and so forth.

By you as well, the doctrine of non-absolutism (*anekāntavāda*)—which maintains that a single entity possesses multiple natures and is both one and many, as accepted by the *syādvādin*—is indeed accepted. For, in the statement beginning with "divided into various modes" and ending with "one who sees [it] as having multiple colors and shapes," it is intended that the single sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) alone is the basis for cognition; since that very sense-sphere of form is expressed by the word "therein" (*tatra*), which ends in a locative suffix and functions as a container, referring back to what was just mentioned without distinction or difference from that entity.

Furthermore, by asserting that knowledge is produced sometimes by a single substance and sometimes by many, and thus demonstrating its dual nature, how can one who does not admit that the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*) itself can be designated as having either a singular or plural number manage to establish its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "there"? If that [base] were neither one nor many, then it would be possible to say "there" in reference to the sense-base of form or elsewhere; however, this is not the case—see page 78, line 2.
Thus, see page 78, line 2, for "itiṣṭaṃ raṃ hī" and "imiṣṭaṃ raṃ hī" without [the intervening text].
Because it is precisely that which has the nature of having a form beyond form,
it appears that the reading here should be "tasyaivorūparūparūpatāyāṃ tasyaivorūparūparūpatā bhāvyam upapādayituṃ śakyate."
"Therefore, in this way," and so forth;
thus, by the method already stated, there is both unity and multiplicity of that very single sense-field of form (*rūpāyatana*) which was spoken of by you yourself.
Why is this? Because it is "undivided," and so on, as you have stated.

In that manner, "thus" (*tathā*); "undivided reality" (*avibhaktatattva*) refers to that whose nature is such an undivided reality; its state is "reality," meaning the reality of an entity that is undivided in terms of oneness, multiplicity, and so forth. For what probandum is the reason "because of the arising of cognition from that undivided reality"? It is for the sake of proving the very same thing's oneness and multiplicity. For it is observed that the very same sense-field of form (*rūpāyatana*) is both one and many: it is one as a collection of atoms (*paramāṇu*), and many as those atoms themselves. Thus, there is the arising of cognition.

The example, "one sees from afar a collection of jewels of many colors and shapes," likewise serves as a homogeneous illustration (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) for proving that a substance can consist of both a single and multiple forms within the sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*), provided that the object is the basis of visual consciousness. It does not, however, prove an absolute oneness or multiplicity. Consequently, this point necessarily follows: there may be a single sphere of visible form, and there may be multiple spheres of visible form.

Why? Because it becomes one through the transformation of the union resulting from smoothness (*snigdhatva*) and roughness (*rūkṣatva*), it is one insofar as it is graspable as a collection of those [atoms]. It is manifold because of the distinction between atoms whose individual natures are different, due to their persistence as substantial entities (*dravyārtha*).

For that very reason, it is a substance (*dravya*); yet, because it undergoes transformation into qualities (*guṇa*) and modes (*paryāya*) such as color and so forth, it is a non-substance (*adravya*).
With respect to its own unique transformations of color and so forth, it has its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object.

Because it undergoes a transformation into visuality (*cākṣuṣatva*) and so forth, which depend upon a collection of differences that have become common [to many], it has a universal (*sāmānya*) as its object. Now, [an opponent might argue] that the word "sometimes" (*kadācit*) refers to a different time; [we reply: no, because both forms exist at one and the same time. It would be "that" and it would not be "that," because its meaning is qualified by the designation of its apprehension. This is like the form of a gem consisting of many colors, or like a single person's being both father and son. Therefore, the refutation of non-absolutism (*anekānta*) falls back upon an unacknowledged admission of one's own position, whose capacity has not been demonstrated. As it has been said: "Visual objects [arise] from both difference and aggregation" (Tattvārtha-sūtra 5.32).

28. Thus, "because of the stated reason," just as there arises a cognition of non-distinct reality, so too, like the arising of a cognition consisting of both difference and non-difference, this entity also consists of both difference and non-difference; such is its "reality" (vastutva). (Bhāṣya)

"And from both [the qualities of] smoothness and roughness, there is union through transformation"— Tattvārthasūtra 5.32.

And [the claim that] "visual [perception] depends on [other factors]"—is it not the case that sometimes the word [“visual”] refers to a different time? No; because both forms exist at one and the same time, it would be both that and not that, since its meaning is qualified by the designation of apprehension. This is like the form of a gem with many colors, or like a single person being both father and son.
Therefore, the refutation of non-absolutism (anekānta) results in a flaw that disregards one's own accepted position.

And because its capacity [to produce cognition] has not been previously manifested, it is visual; thus, even in the case of a word, the object consists of a distinction. (Bhāṣya and Praśastapādabhāṣya)
The other says: "But surely the word 'kadācit' (at some time) refers to a different time;

for regarding that very same object, at one time (kadācit) knowledge arises with a single form, while at another time (kadācit) it arises with multiple forms. Since it is knowledge itself that possesses forms, this occurs on the view that external objects are formless.
To this it is replied: No, because both forms exist at the very same time.

For it is observed that at one and the same time, a cognition having the form of an aggregate of blue atoms possesses the nature of both difference and non-difference; therefore, it is not correctly stated that the word "sometimes" refers to a different time. Consequently, it is not the case that a cognition arises with a single form at one time and with multiple forms at another time regarding that very same object. Rather, because it possesses both forms at one and the same time, it would be both that [the whole] and not that [the whole]: it would be that [the whole] because it is non-different from the aggregate of atomic substances, and it would not be that [the whole] because of the difference in the transformations of color and so forth.

Another reason is also stated here: "Because it has an object qualified by apprehension and designation. Apprehension (*grahaṇa*) is cognition (*jñāna*); cognition itself is the designation (*apadeśa*), which is the reason (*hetu*). That which is qualified by that reason is "qualified by apprehension and designation" (*grahaṇāpadeśaviśiṣṭa*). And that is the "object" (*artha*). The state of being such is "having an object qualified by apprehension and designation" (*grahaṇāpadeśaviśiṣṭārthatva*).

Since the object, form (*rūpa*), which consists of both the aggregate and its constituents, is apprehended as something qualified by the cause that is visual consciousness, therefore that entity is manifold in nature.

What is the illustration? It is like the form of a gem with many colors; or like the form of a single gem, such as a sapphire or rock crystal; or like the form of a collection of gems of various colors.

Just as that [collection] is distinguished by its perception and designation and is determined by cognition to have distinct forms, so too is the object intended as the domain of the eye—like a single person who is both father and son—and this is another illustrative example based on the common characteristic of being distinguished by perception and designation.

Just as a single person receives designations such as "father," "son," "nephew," or "maternal uncle" in relation to various relatives, yet no faults of contradiction, confusion, or infinite regress apply because these are distinguished by specific objects of cognition; in the same way, an object cognizable by visual consciousness is to be understood as being distinguished by its specific time, color,
and mode of apprehension.
...for the sake of [attaining] the goal;
the wheel consisting of the nature of bestowing [blessings]; [made of] crystal...
The cognition qualified by [the object] is delimited and possesses a distinct form;
therefore, it is "independent," and so forth.

For this very reason, those who raise the objection here—asking how mutually contradictory things can possibly exist in one place—fall into a refutation of non-absolutism (*anekānta*) that disregards their own accepted tenets. "One's own accepted tenet" (*svābhyupagama*) means one's own position; a refutation that does not take that into account is a "refutation of non-absolutism that disregards one's own accepted tenets."

For example: why is there a refutation of the non-absolute (anekānta) by those who assert that "everything is of the nature of everything" and is undifferentiated, while disregarding the explanation of the distinction between transformations; or by those who assert that things are absolutely distinct due to differences in space and time, while disregarding the explanation of the lack of distinction in their continuity; or by those who assert the production of an effect from what was previously non-existent, while disregarding the rule regarding the commencement of other substances and qualities of a similar class? It is because the proponents of absolute views (ekāntavādins) have not demonstrated the validity of their prior assertions.

The object whose nature has been described as non-absolute (anekānta) is "thus-object" (*evamartha*); the state of being such is "thus-ness" (*evamarthya*). Since those [proponents] have not realized this thus-ness and their own prior admissions, there is no specific fault for the proponents of absolutism (*ekāntavādin*) regarding any of the bases (*āyatana*).

These [cognitions] have the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as their object with respect to the base-characteristic (*āyatanasvalakṣaṇa*), but not with respect to the substance-characteristic (*dravyasvalakṣaṇa*)—this very point you have already established as a fault that was previously raised in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, chapter 1, verse 10.

As for the argument that a cognition whose object is a composite whole would result in having a universal as its object rather than a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)—this has already been established;
however, this specific defect remains: the consequence of [the cognition] being non-cognition (*ajñānatva*) is even more evident.

...How, then, can there be direct perception (*pratyakṣatva*)? Furthermore, when it is objected that if [perception] has an aggregate as its object (*sañcitālambanatā*), it follows that perception is conceptual (*kalpanātmakatva*) because of the construction of a single form, and that it would follow that its object is not the particular characteristic (*asvalakṣaṇaviṣayatva*), the following resolution is stated to avoid the fault of [it not being] a particular characteristic: "Because it is produced by multiple objects, it has a universal (*sāmānya*) as its range with respect to its own object; because it is generated by multiple substances, it is said to have a universal as its range within its own domain (*svāyatana*). This is not, however, because of the construction of non-difference among things that are distinct (as stated in *Pramāṇasamuccayavṛtti* 1.4), for there is no separate apprehension of each of those [atoms].

For just as all these proponents of one-sided views (ekāntavādins) have previously accepted [the validity of their own positions] while failing to realize their true nature—like leaves on a śamī tree—because they fail to realize their true nature due to having previously accepted [their own views], their refutation of non-absolutism (anekānta) disregards their own prior admissions, like the confused, the deluded, or the intoxicated.

Therefore, whom among us should we single out to say that he alone is deluded, confused, or insane, and thus charge him with fault? You all are equally corrupted by such faults; what has been wronged by this poor fellow, the partisan of particularism (*viśeṣaikāntavādin*), who strives to destroy the reality of the world protected by the Supreme Lord of Debate? For this reason, he says: "It was previously stated [in our own accepted system] that there is no fault of particularity for anyone," because [we] do not depend [on such particulars]. (svābhyupagama-pramāṇa-nirapekṣataḥ)
That which does not depend [on anything] at that time is independent;
thus it is "without dependence."
Thus,
because they accept that the object of cognition (*artha*) is manifested (*prabhāta*) by consciousness, there is no fault of distinction whatsoever for the proponents of monism.

"These [cognitions] have the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the sense-fields (*āyatana*) as their object, not the particular characteristic of a substance (*dravya*)," as stated in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (1.10).
By this, you have merely reaffirmed the very fault previously raised:

namely, that a cognition which has a composite (*samasta*) as its objective support (*ālambana*) would result in having a universal (*sāmānya*) as its object, rather than a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object; this point has already been established.
But this is a specific flaw: the consequence of its being ignorance is even more evident...
...from what [source] would it possess the status of direct perception?

Furthermore, when it is objected that if perception has a "collected" (*sañcita*) object, it would follow that perception is conceptual (*kalpanātmaka*) due to the construction of a single form, and that it would consequently have the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object; the resolution is stated as follows, which avoids the fault of [perception] not being a particular characteristic: "Because it is produced by multiple objects, it has a universal (*sāmānya*) as its range regarding its own object;

because it is generated by multiple substances, it is said to have a universal as its range within its own domain (*svāyatana*), but not because of the construction of non-difference among distinct things, since they are not perceived individually therein. (Pramāṇasamuccayavṛtti 1.4).

For just as [the cognition] regarding the leaves on a branch of the *śamī* tree, because it is produced by many diverse factors, has a universal (*sāmānya*) as its object with respect to its own referent; thus, [the reason] "being produced by many" is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Those who perceive faults; [the reading] *doṣadraṣṭāraḥ* is in Bhāṣya, while *doṣadraṣṭā* is in Yajñavalkya; [the reading] *paratvam* is in Yajñavalkya.

O Supreme Lord of Debaters, please observe: on page 83, line 2, without stating a refutation of the objection that [the cognition] would result in being conceptual in nature due to its connection [with the object], you have offered a rebuttal by accepting that very point. Having first articulated the explanation—"These [cognitions] have the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the sense-field (*āyatana*) as their object, not the specific characteristic of a substance (*dravya-svalakṣaṇa*)"—you have shaken off the fault previously raised and established [your position]; that is to say, you have made it firm.
As for the passage beginning with "that which has a composite object" and ending with "this has already been established," this is the distinction:
what other fault is there besides the fault of being conceptual in nature? It is the consequence of [the cognition] being non-cognition (*ajñānatva*).

For example—starting from "more clearly manifest" and so forth, up to "from what [source] does perceptibility arise"—this has been demonstrated; the meaning is thus understood. (See *Tattvasaṅgraha-pañjikā*, page 79, line 24).
Let it be seen on page 79, line 23;
and this objection beginning with "yo 'pi caikākāra... is restated up until the point concerning the state of having a composite as its objective support (*sañcitālambanatā*).

This is what is meant: if one does not conceptualize that [object] as a single unit, how can there be a collective object of cognition (*sañcitālambanatā*)? For this [collective state] is invariably concomitant with conceptualization and cannot exist without it. When this objection is raised, the resolution to be stated later is expressed; indeed, that very [resolution] is intended as the remedy for the fault of [cognition] not being a particular characteristic (*asvalakṣaṇatva*), because this statement does not contradict its denoting two meanings. He restates that [resolution] along with its explanation: "Because it is produced by multiple objects, it has a universal (*sāmānya*) as its scope regarding its own object," and so on, up to "because there is no separate apprehension of each among them"—the meaning of which is already explained.

The summary of the meaning is as follows: Although cognition does not have a universal (sāmānya) as its object in reality because it is produced by an aggregate of atoms, nevertheless, whether it be color or taste, its own object is that which is unassociated with anything else; for if one were to postulate another object [such as a universal], that cognition would lack clarity. Furthermore, atoms are capable of producing that cognition only when acting in concert, like those carrying a palanquin, and not otherwise. Thus, let there be the status of having a universal as its object; what is the harm?

If that [cognition] were to arise by conceiving non-difference among things that are different, then it would be a conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), a cognition arising through a lack of discrimination regarding its object. Yet, there is no such thing as a single composite (*saṅghāta*) because the effect characterized by [the composite] has not been produced from those [parts]. This same flaw applies even in the case of atoms, because it destroys the very meaning that has been accepted. Like the Vaiśeṣika who proceeds to establish the manifestation of sound—which is unproduced—as being something created, [this cognition] claims its own objective domain and then concludes by referring to a universal (*sāmānya*) that is neither that nor not-that. Is it not therefore the case that this is not perception, because its object is a universal within its own domain, just like inference?
Alternatively, inference is not of that nature [i.e., not based on a real universal], for it does not arise from the conceptual construction of a single form of non-difference among distinct things;
this is the meaning of the illustration: "just as, indeed, in the case of the leaves on the branches of a *śamī* tree," and so forth.

Just as the cognition that takes all leaves as its object arises through the non-differentiation of the end, beginning, and middle, it might be thought that direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) would likewise function in the same way. That is to say, apart from those [individual parts], there would be a cognition of the leaf and the aggregate that is direct perception;
however, this is incorrect. For there is no such thing as a single composite whole (*saṅghāta*), because it does not possess the characteristic of an effect produced by those [parts].

For the aggregate does not exist separately like the effect-substance (kāryadravya) imagined by the Vaiśeṣikas, nor has it undergone a different transformation; because those constituent causes are momentary, there is no persistence through distinct stages of time such as the beginning and the completion [of the process]. Thus, he demonstrates the application of the example to the case of atoms as well.

bhavatābhā॰ ॰nantarī॰ pra॰.
Because it expresses the meaning of the two suffixes *mat* and *artha*;
[the reading] *vākasya* is in manuscript *ya*, while *vāvasya* is in manuscript *bhā*.

The object of cognition arises as non-different from the atoms, O Venerable One; for cognition arises without distinction from the support of the parts, and there is no single composite entity whatsoever because their effect, characterized by being unproduced, does not exist— this is likewise the case with atoms.

This is indeed not a valid means of knowledge (*asamādhi*), because it destroys the very object it has accepted, like the Vaiśeṣika who proceeds to establish that sound is manifested rather than produced; having first asserted its own subject-matter, he then concludes with a focus on a universal (*sāmānya*) that is neither that [particular] nor its opposite.
Is it not for this very reason that it is not perception, since it has a universal as its object regarding its own referent, like inference?
Or rather, even inference would not be [valid].

(Kāśmīra manuscript, Prayāga manuscript).

Regarding this objection, the following answer is stated: Why is this not a valid resolution (*samādhi*)? Because this matter, like an old hut, lacks the capacity to withstand being torn asunder; thus, this so-called resolution for the fault previously pointed out arising from your statement is actually no resolution at all, because it destroys the very point you have accepted, just like a Vaiśeṣika who proceeds to establish the manifestation of sound’s non-produced nature [only to undermine his own premise].

Just as in the case of a Vaiśeṣika [proponent], "like a Vaiśeṣika" (*vaiśeṣikavat*): there is a similarity with actions regarding the cessation (*apavarga*) of a quality that exists but is not perceptible to the eye; and because there is an absence of a mark for its existence, according to Vaiśeṣika Sūtras 2.2.25–26, its non-eternality is established through such reasons as "being an effect" (*kāryatvāt*), as well as its being produced (*kṛtakatva*) due to its being a specific property (*vaiśeṣikatvāt*). Thus, for one who has set out to establish the manifestation of that [quality], there is the loss of the accepted position, just as in the case of the Vaiśeṣika. Likewise, there is a fault in both the object and the statement [of the definition]: "because it is produced by multiple objects, it has the universal as its scope regarding its own object."

He explains that: if it is asked, "Whence does that similarity [with inference] arise?", it is said: having first established its own object, because of the synthesis (*upasaṃhāra*) of that and what is not that—which has as its domain a universal (*sāmānya*) that is both that and not that—it is "that-and-not-that-object" (*tadatadviṣaya*). Its state of being such is "the state of having that-and-not-that as its object" (*tadatadviṣayatā*). That which is both that and not that is the universal; that is the domain, the object, of this synthesis. Therefore, from that synthesis...

That universal has both that [particular] and another as its objects; therefore, it does not apply to either one exclusively, because it is not observed in either one alone. According to your own view, since entities are restricted to their respective identities, that universal cannot even possess a single form; it does not subsist in that [particular], nor does it subsist elsewhere. Because it does not subsist in that, it is not that; because it does not subsist elsewhere, it is not other than that. Thus, that universal—which is neither that nor other—is now being made by you the object of this synthesis (upasaṃhāra) through its having both that and other things as its domain.

Therefore, because it synthesizes a domain of unreal universals by taking both that [particular] and its opposite as its objects, perception is admitted to be destroyed; to this he says: "But for this very reason, it is not perception, because with respect to its own object it has a universal as its domain, like inference. Regarding its own object—that is, the thing to be grasped by itself—any cognition that has a universal as its domain with respect to the thing to be grasped is observed to be non-perceptual, just like inference. Or rather, it would not even be inference, because with respect to its own object it has a universal as its domain, just like perception.
The prefix *pra-* [is used] with the root *rudh* in the sense of "obstruction"; here the meaning appears to be "due to the inability to endure obstruction.
This is the *pra-* of *pratipeṣa*.
Because it is of the nature of [the] body;
see page 55, line 12:
"The absence of that is the non-cognition of that and the other."
That which is both that and not that,
established in that which has become both that and not that.
In that regard,
the reading "that which is not perception with respect to the object to be grasped by itself" does not exist in the manuscripts designated as Ya.

Because it operates upon that [object], this cognition contradicts its own statement, just like the words of a father who claims to be a lifelong celibate (*kumārabrahmacārin*). This is because it has a universal (*sāmānya*) as its range regarding its own object—a specific object characterized by its own nature in the form of color (*rūpa*) and so forth. For the two terms "object" (*artha*) and "range" (*viṣaya*) are used here precisely in the sense of defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*); indeed, you yourself have stated: "Perception and inference are the two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), since the objects of knowledge (*prameya*) are of two kinds."

For there is no object of cognition other than the particular (svalakṣaṇa) and the universal (sāmānyalakṣaṇa); perception is restricted to the particular as its object, while [inference] has the universal as its domain. To claim that [perception] has the universal as its object is a contradiction of one's own words.

What is it like? It is like the statement of a man who is a lifelong celibate (kumārabrahmacārin) regarding his father. For instance, if someone were to say, "My father is a lifelong celibate," that statement contradicts itself by its very nature: if he is a father, how can he be a lifelong celibate? Or if he is a lifelong celibate, how can he be a father? In the same way, if that cognition has its own particular object (svārtha), how can it have a universal as its domain? Or if it has a universal as its domain, how can it have its own particular object? Furthermore, when you define "its own object" (svārtha) by relying on the distinction that it is the object of the eye or some other sense organ, what do you mean? You are not referring to a specific object; rather, you are stating that the object of knowledge (prameya) is the thing-in-itself (svalakṣaṇa) as a universal (sāmānyataḥ). This is what is meant by "its own object."
Likewise, the "universal characteristic" (sāmānyalakṣaṇa) is not merely the fire to be inferred from smoke; rather, it is everything that is cognizable through a logical mark (liṅga).

In order to establish this point, he speaks while defining the very nature of "one's own object" (*svārtha*): "in that which is distinguished from what is not one's own object. One's own object is *svārtha*; that which is not one's own object is *asvārtha*, meaning something other than one's own object. It is distinguished from that [non-own-object], and thus it is "one's own object" (*svārtha*). Regarding that very object, he expresses it by way of synonyms: "in its own domain" (*svaviṣaye*). What is meant? [It means] in a single mode, such as a preeminent form, color, taste, or another [quality]; [it refers to] that which has the universal (*sāmānya*) as its range. And the claim that "cognition has the universal as its object" and "cognition has one's own object as its object"—these two are mutually contradictory.

Since the words "object" (*artha*) and "word" (*śabda*) have the sense of "definition" (*lakṣaṇa*), being synonyms for the term "definition," it follows that what you intend to say is: "one's own object" (*svārtha*), "one's own domain" (*svaviṣaya*), and "one's own specific characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇa*). Having forgotten this, it is not appropriate for you, in your confusion, to state a rebuttal based on the conceptual distinction between the generality (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*bheda*) of the object grasped by the senses.

Why? Because the words "one's own object," "one's own specific characteristic," and "one's own domain" are the subject matter of the explanation of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). [In the case of] a contradiction with the statement... [text fragment].
The general characteristic is perceived;
it occurs in that single [entity] which has fallen into [the state of] being.
In the *Sārthavāha*,
it is stated that "the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is the object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)," and this is opposed by conceptual construction (*parikalpanā*).
The passage beginning with "pratyakṣa" within these brackets and ending with "tvayaiva" does not exist in the Bhāratīya manuscript;

do not think, however, that this is so— that it is not the case— because you yourself have stated in the determination of the number of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that there are two means of valid cognition, perception and inference,

and so forth, thereby establishing the duality of the means of valid cognition due to the duality of the objects of cognition (*prameya*), just as the duality of measures such as the *prastha* and the balance is necessarily determined by the duality of the things to be measured (*parimeya*).

He demonstrates this: since it might be thought that there are two types of objects of cognition (*prameya*)— namely, another object of cognition characterized by both its own specific nature (*svalakṣaṇa*) and its general nature (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), and that because of this there would have to be another means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) corresponding to it—

he says, in order to preclude that, "Indeed, there is no object of cognition other than the particular and the universal, because it is not apprehended by perception and inference, like the horn of a donkey."

It might be thought: "In those very two objects, the operation of the means of valid cognition—perception, inference, scripture, and so forth—will occur through the modes of conceptualization, conjunction, and the relationship of subordinate and principal parts. That is not so, because it has been stated that perception is restricted to the object that is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), while inference is restricted to the object that is the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).

But how is the word *lakṣaṇa* a synonym for "object" (*artha*)? It is an "object" (*artha*) because it is sought after (*aryate*) or understood; likewise, it is a "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) because it is characterized (*lakṣyate*). This is because the word *lakṣaṇa* functions as a passive derivative (*karmasādhana*).

And that characteristic (lakṣaṇa) is synonymous with entity (vastu), intrinsic nature (svabhāva), essential form (svarūpa), object (artha), and the object of cognition (prameya). Furthermore, it is of two kinds because it is to be determined by two means of valid cognition (pramāṇa); the meaning is that the means of valid cognition is the determiner and the object of cognition is that which is to be determined.
Inference is necessarily [one of these]. (Pramāṇasamuccayavṛtti 1)
For a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) has as its purpose the comprehension of an object of knowledge (prameya),
and this [cognition] does not have an unperceived object.

Furthermore, since there is no confusion of objects between the two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and because the object to be apprehended is twofold, it is established that the cause for its apprehension must likewise be of two forms. Consequently, [the object] must be its own object (*svārtha*) as something excluded from the domain of the universal (*sāmānya*).
Therefore, the claim that "it has the universal as its domain within its own object" is contradictory;
for if perceptual knowledge (*pratyakṣajñāna*) arises with respect to its own object, that very universal would be its own object, and the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) would not exist.

Therefore, since these two characteristics do not exist, the conceptualization that restricts the objects of cognition (*prameya*) and the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) to a duality is futile; or else, a confusion of the objects of the two means of cognition would result, or even perception (*pratyakṣa*) would be nothing but a variety of inference (*anumāna*), because it would grasp aspects such as color and so forth whose object is a universal (*sāmānya*) produced by multiple things—just like smoke or a crane, which serve as marks (*liṅga*). This is because the word "for" (*hi*) has the sense of a reason: for in the world, a means of cognition is observed to be the cause for the apprehension of an object of cognition, since a means of cognition is indeed the cause for the apprehension of an object of cognition.
