Nor is this [inference] like scriptural injunctions such as "one desiring heaven should perform the Agnihotra" or "one desiring merit should give a gift," which have an unseen purpose; rather, this has a purpose seen through direct perception, because it brings about the apprehension of its object, and that object is seen to be of two kinds.

Nor is there a confusion of objects between the two means of valid cognition (pramāṇa); thus, the word "iti" indicates the demonstration of the distinctness of their respective objects according to the reasoning stated previously.
This much is the meaning here in brief; by saying "the elaboration of that is another work," he indicates that the full treatment is found elsewhere.
Regarding the phrase "naitadevaṃ na bhavati," there might also be a reading here as "naitadevaṃ saṃbhavati";
however, in the Bhāṣya manuscript, this entire passage is not present at all.
Perception and inference are the only two means of valid cognition,
because the objects of cognition possess only two characteristics;
for there exists no object of cognition other than the particular (svalakṣaṇa) and the universal (sāmānyalakṣaṇa).
For perception has the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object, whereas inference has the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) as its object— *Pramāṇasamuccayavṛtti* 1.2;
[the object of inference is] of a different nature, namely duality.
By means of the relationship between parts and whole (*aṅgāṅgībhāva*),
it is "proceeded toward" (*prāryate*);
from the verbal root *ṛ*, meaning "to go" (*gatau*) according to Pāṇini’s Dhātupāṭha, the form *aryate* (or *prāryate*) is derived.
That which is sought after (*aryate*) is the *artha*— Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya, Sthiramati’s commentary, 2.106. svābhyām bhāṣye.
Inference is necessarily [a means of valid cognition]. *Pramāṇasamuccayavṛtti* 1.2:
For a means of valid cognition is that which has the apprehension of an object of knowledge as its purpose.

This [cognition] does not have an unperceived object, nor is there a confusion of the objects of the two means of valid cognition; thus, since the object to be apprehended is twofold, it is established that the cause for its apprehension is twofold in form. Consequently, it must have its own object as something excluded from the domain of the universal;
therefore, the claim that "it has the universal as its domain within its own object" is contradictory.
If it is argued that perceptual knowledge arises with respect to the universal as its own object, then the universal alone would be the object, and the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) would not exist;

consequently, because these two characteristics are absent, the conceptualization of a fixed duality of objects of cognition (*prameya*) and means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) is useless. Alternatively, a confusion of the objects of the two means of cognition would result, or else perception itself would be merely a variety of inference, since it would grasp aspects such as color and so forth—the universal produced by multiple objects—just like the inferential signs of smoke or a crane.

Regarding the phrase *dṛṣṭārthaṃ* (perceived object) in *pratyakṣaṃ dṛṣṭārthaṃ*, [the author] now states this sentence for the purpose of summarizing the established meaning: "Since that which is to be apprehended is twofold, the means of its apprehension is of two forms. When the definition has been thus established, the word *lakṣaṇa* (definition) is used as a synonym for "object" (*artha*) and does not refer to the specific objects grasped by the senses; this being the case, the faults of the absence of the essential nature of perception and inference, as well as the contradiction with one's own statement, apply to one who asserts that [inference] has the universal as its object in its own domain, according to the method previously explained. This is settled.
Furthermore, there is a fault here: this being the case, the object of the universal must be its own object by virtue of being excluded from other objects;

what then is the fault? It is that [the claim] "the universal has its own object as its domain" is contradictory, for such a relation of universality does not exist in the object itself, nor does the universal have a relation to its own object. (Prakaraṇa-pradīpa)
In this context, there may also be the reading *pravṛtta*; furthermore, [the word] *pra* must have the sense of *vṛtta*.

If it is argued that this fault does not apply to its own object, and thus perceptual cognition arises with respect to that very universal as its own object and domain, then for that reason the universal alone would be the object of its own domain and the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) would not exist.

Consequently, since the specifically defined unique particular (*asādhāraṇasvalakṣaṇa*)—which is the object [of perception]—would be absent under such a supposition, the two-fold definition [of the objects of knowledge] would not exist; there would be only the single definition of the universal. And because of the absence of these two, inference would become the only means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), having that [universal] as its sole object.

Consequently, the conceptualization that restricts the objects of cognition (*prameya*) and the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) to two each would be futile; lest such restriction be rendered meaningless, it would follow either that perception operates upon both its own particular object and the universal, and inference likewise [operates on both], resulting in a confusion of the domains of the two means of cognition;
or, by virtue of the word "or" (*vā*), a single cognition would have two objects; or else even perception, as conceived by others, would be nothing but a variety of inference.
For what reason? Because it apprehends the various types of objects such as color and so forth, which have a universal as their domain and are produced by multiple things.

Lest you think this reason is unestablished (*asiddha*), for you yourself have stated: "In that case, because it is produced by multiple things, it has a universal as its domain with respect to its own object" (Pramāṇasamuccaya 1).

Thus, the cognition that arises by apprehending a single, undifferentiated universal form—such as "color" (*rūpa*) or "taste" (*rasa*)—through various distinct objects is produced by those [objects]. Therefore, since that cognition apprehends a universal object produced by multiple things in the form of color and so forth, what is its illustration? It is like the cognition produced by smoke.

If it is argued that the object [of cognition] possesses the nature of a particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) in both cases—since there is no occurrence of either multiplicity or unity, and that very object is a particular which is the domain of the universal (*sāmānya*)—we say no. This is because [the object] consists of a universal that is not itself a universal, [yet] whose mode of existence is distinct from the beginning, end, middle, color, dimension, and shape; and because there is no such thing as a "composite" (*saṅghāta*), since its characteristic effect has not been produced by those [parts].

The same applies to atoms. Just like the cognition produced by the mark of a crane, there is no difference in the essential nature of the inferential cognitions of fire and water produced from the marks of smoke and cranes—namely, "there is fire here because of smoke" and "there is water here because of cranes. Likewise, there is no difference in the inferential nature of those cognitions of color-form and so forth which are considered to be perception; for this very reason, they have non-specific (asvalakṣaṇa) objects. Perception has non-specific objects because it grasps aspects such as color-form that consist of universals produced by multiple entities, just like inference.

By the phrase "in both cases," it is meant that even in inference there is the state of having the non-particular (*asvalakṣaṇa*) as its object, for that very same reason, just like the perception that occurs immediately thereafter.
Alternatively, "in both cases" means that in both the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) and the universal (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), there is the state of having the non-particular as the object.
How so? That which is intended to be the particular is actually a non-particular, because of the unification of the many, just like a collection (*samudāya*).

If it is argued that even that universal (*sāmānya*) is not a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) for this very reason—that its status as a non-particular characteristic is established and proven just like the aggregate mentioned immediately above—it is not so; because [the opponent] accepts it as being for one's own sake (*svārtha*), according to the statement that "it has the universal as its object. Moreover, this must necessarily be accepted, since a host of defects—such as its being non-perceptual, non-inferential, non-authoritative, having a non-particular characteristic as its object, and the confusion of objects—has been clearly demonstrated by the example of the observation of the undifferentiated mass of leaves on the branches of a *śamī* tree.

"Because it is produced by many objects, [perception] has the universal as its object regarding its own referent. (Pramāṇasamuccaya 1.4) Thus [it is said]. Regarding the two characteristics, the retention [of the object] therein... [is established].
If it is argued that, like [cognition] produced by sensory contact,

both [types of cognition] have the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) as their object— since there is no occurrence of either multiplicity or unity, and this very object is the particular which is the domain of the universal (*sāmānya*)— we say no. This is because [the object] consists of a universal that is not itself a universal, having as its objects particulars whose existence is distinct from [attributes such as] color, dimension, shape, and state, from the beginning to the end and the middle.
Nor does any composite (saṅghāta) exist, because its effect, characterized by being unproduced, [does not arise] from them; the same applies to atoms as well.
[Note: *vipratya* is corrected to *vipratipatti* based on context.]
And [it is] one's own [position];
and in the case of [the view that it is] for one's own sake, [it is] accepted.

Regarding the reading *anumānatva* (being inference), although the reading *anumānatva*—which appears in all manuscripts—is appropriate here according to the statement on page 89, line 7, "Or even perception would be merely a variety of inference," nevertheless, the reading *ananumānatva* (not being inference) appears to be more correct. This is because immediately after the example of the undifferentiated mass of leaves on a Śamī branch, it is stated: "But for this very reason, that is not perception, because its object is a generality regarding its own referent, like inference;
or else, inference too [is not perception], as stated on page 87, line 4. Thus, the reading *ananumānatva* seems preferable in this context.

If it should be thought: "The object of perception is indeed the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) which has as its domain the universal (*sāmānya*) consisting in the attainment of unity among many;

for 'the universal' is the attainment of unity among many, and that very thing is its domain—thus it is 'that which has as its domain the universal consisting in the attainment of unity among many'—and that alone is the particular characteristic, and that alone is the object of perception," [we reply: no, this is not tenable, because from the far end to the near end and so forth, up to the point that it would have the nature of a universal whose objects are particulars existing in mutually distinct states such as prior and posterior.
This is because it would possess the nature of a universal whose objects are particulars existing in mutually distinct states such as prior and posterior.

The near end (*ārānta*), the far end (*parānta*), the middle (*madhya*), color such as the excellence of blue (*nīlaprakarṣādi*), measurement such as shortness, length, smallness, and largeness (*hrasvadīrghālpamahattvādi*), and shape (*saṃsthāna*) such as circularity (*vṛtta*); those particular leaves whose functions (*vṛtti*) and states (*avasthā*) are distinguished by these [factors] are "those with functions and states distinguished by them" (*tairviviktavṛttyavasthapatraviśeṣāḥ*). These alone are the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*). This universal (*sāmānya*) has that as its object; thus it is "that which has the specific characteristic as its object" (*svalakṣaṇaviṣaya*). Its essence (*ātman*) or intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) is this; the state of being that is "having a universal as its essence" (*sāmānyātmakatva*). Therefore, because of having a universal as its essence...

This is what is meant: it is the particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) themselves—extremely distinct by way of place, form, color, magnitude, configuration, and so forth—that possess the nature of the universal (*sāmānya*); there is no other universal. Therefore, it is untenable [to claim] that the object is a particular characteristic which is the domain of a universal resulting from the convergence of the many and the one. As for the objection that "it was stated [by you] that it is the domain of a universal resulting from the convergence of the many and the one," that is not so; because, according to your own view, there is no such thing as a composite (*saṅghāta*), nor (as indicated by the word *ca*) a whole (*avayavin*), nor any other transformation (*pariṇāmāntara*) distinct from those [particulars].

For what reason? Because that [object] is not produced from multiple substances, nor does it exist as some kind of accumulation; for this very reason, it is not logical for it to be the objective support (*ālambana*) of cognition. And because it lacks an objective support, even the object appearing therein does not exist, just as the son of a barren woman’s son does not appear.
Indeed, only that which produces a representation manifesting its own appearance is logically fit to be an objective support.

Since this [object] lacks self-nature and is not a substantial entity (*adravyatva*), how could there be the manifestation of a representation? However, atoms themselves are incapable of producing a manifestation because they are beyond the senses;

thus, perceptual knowledge does not arise, because it would lack a supporting object (*nirālambanatva*), like a sky-flower, since those petals do not constitute an effect characterized by being produced from causes.

For there is no distinct effect produced by the specific leaves; rather, those very specific leaves, which are characterized by not having begun as something else, become the effect through being assembled. Therefore, there is no other universal (sāmānya) in them.
It is the same with atoms; even among atoms, there is likewise no universal whatsoever.
Consequently, that cognition does not have a universal as its object in relation to its own referent.
The passage beginning with "anekaikatvā" and ending with "asyeti," located within these brackets, does not exist in the Ya manuscripts. [The text reads: "anyaṃ gocaraḥ pra° kṣaṇa sāmā° ya°."
If there were a beginning,
there would be a subsequent limit; thus,
there would be a prior and a posterior state.
*avasthāpanna-vibhāga*,
*avasthāpanna-viśeṣa*, *dīrghābhyam ahaḥ* (or *dīrghābhyam ahaḥ*) [in] *ya*.
The moments remaining as mere fragments; the moments whose own objects have perished.
That object is the color-form of the two [types of] formative activity; it is the color-form of the two [types of] formative activity. (Bhāṣya)

Regarding the [cognition] whose object is the universal-of-universals (*sāmānyasāmānya*): it is not produced by multiple substances, nor does any accumulation (*sañcaya*) exist; therefore, it is not logical for it to have an objective support (*ālambana*). And because it lacks an objective support, even the object that appears (*ābhāsārtha*) does not exist therein, just as the son of a barren woman’s son does not appear.
An object is logically established as a basis (ālambana) only when it generates a representation (vijñapti) that bears its own image;

however, since this [object] lacks self-nature and is not a substantial entity, how could there be the manifestation of an image? As for the atoms themselves, they are incapable of producing an image because they are beyond the reach of the senses;
thus, direct perceptual knowledge does not arise, because of the absence of a basis, like a flower in the sky.

Because [the former] has a body whose characteristic is already commenced (*ārabdha-svalakṣaṇa-kāyatvāt*), whereas [the latter]— as for their comparison— has an effect whose characteristic is not yet commenced (*anārabdha-lakṣaṇa-kāryatvāt*). (Page 87,
Line 1) For they are indeed unconditioned (*anābhoga*).
Having become corporeal, [the sense-cognition] occurs without that knowledge.

Furthermore, it has been stated: "Because it is produced by multiple substances, it is said to have the universal as its object within its own sphere, and not because of the conceptualization of non-difference among distinct things. (Pramāṇasamuccayavṛtti 1).

Thus, even that "objectivity of a universal" (sāmānyagocaratā) which you desire is not tenable; for it is not produced from multiple substances—how then is it produced? [If you say] from an accumulation (sañcaya), an accumulation is not a universal. Therefore, there exists no such thing as an "accumulation of color and so forth" distinct from color and the other [sensory qualities].

For this very reason, it is not logical for the cognition to have an objective support (ālambana). Why? Because cognition is [itself] consciousness; what is the reason? Because it is non-existent, like the son of a barren woman.

One might raise the following objection: "Even though the collection [of causes] is not the cause, it will serve as the objective support because it gives rise to a cognition that bears its own reflection."

Why is this so? Since there is an absence of being an object (*ālambanatva*) precisely because of the lack of a cause, what hope can there be for the appearance of an object? To this he says: "And because it is not an object, even the appearing object does not exist therein;
how so? Like the non-appearance of the son of a barren woman's son.
For just as the son of a barren woman is not an object due to his non-existence, and because he is not an object he does not appear, so too is the accumulation (*sañcaya*).
Let it be seen on page 86, line 10;
see also page 79, note 7:
"syād aṃśakāya."
"O noble lady, O daughter, [it is] one's own manifestation," and so forth.

For an object (*viṣaya*) is that whose nature is determined by cognition (Ālambanaparīkṣāvṛtti 1). Thus, the very argument you have stated is applied here. But why is that? Because it lacks selfhood (*asvatva*) and lacks self-nature (*anātmakatva*). What logic is there to claim that what is unestablished by way of its own self or intrinsic nature could be an object of cognition? Since it lacks selfhood, it is not a substance (*adravyatva*), and thus, due to the absence of ultimate existence (*paramārthasattva*), how can there be the making known of an appearance (*ābhāsa-vijñāpana*) according to the terminology of others? For "making known," "representation" (*vijñapti*), and "cognition" (*buddhi*) are synonyms; the meaning is that such representation does not exist even from afar.

If that is so, then let the atoms themselves be the self and let them become the object; this is denied. They are not capable of producing an appearance because they are beyond the senses (*atīndriya*).
Their being beyond the senses is due to their lack of appearance, like space.

The word "iti" marks the conclusion. Thus, it is established that perception lacks an objective support (*anālambana*)—both with respect to the collection [of atoms] and the atoms themselves. Therefore, perceptual cognition does not arise, because it lacks an objective support, like a sky-flower.

Therefore, since perception that is without an objective basis (*nirālambana*) cannot arise—just like a sky-flower—according to the method of proof already stated; and since, if the absence of a cognition of perception that is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*) and possesses an object were established, an unavoidable contradiction would arise due to the implication of one's own words; this definition, "perception is free from conceptual construction," would be meaningless because of the non-existence of the thing to be defined (*lakṣya*), just like determining whether a donkey’s horn is blunt or sharp. For [the opponent] holds that "one's own appearance is indeed devoid of its own nature. (Hīnayana, Bhāṣya)

"Instruction on intrinsic nature" (*svabhāvovavāya*) refers to that which is without consciousness (*vijñāna*), according to Yaśomitra; it is the making known (*vijñapana*), according to Bhāṣya and Raṅ 'byung; it is without [consciousness], according to Hīnayāna.
In the absence of the manifestation of the knowledge of the self, [there is] non-apprehension of the word "self" and so forth.

Even if it were admitted that [the cognition] has a composite (*sañcita*) as its objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), it still could not be considered direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). This is because it is a mere appearance of that [composite], because it consists of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), and because it is a form of erroneous cognition (*bhrānti-jñāna*) due to the misrepresentation of name (*saṃjñā*), shape (*saṃsthāna*), number (*saṅkhyā*), and color (*varṇa*). It is like the cognition of a mirage, the cognition of a fire-brand circle (*alātacakra*), the cognition of two moons, or the cognition of a yellow form by one whose eyes are afflicted by jaundice;

therefore, this is not direct perception at all, because it consists in the superimposition (*adhyāropa*) of an object that does not exist in that way—just like an error or a conventional (*saṃvṛti-sat*) cognition—as in the case of the cowherd...
[etc.]
...likewise in conventional reality...
As it has been said:

"That which, when broken, no longer produces the cognition of that thing, and which [no longer produces that cognition] when other [parts] are excluded by the mind—such as a jar or water—is conventionally real (*saṃvṛtisat*); otherwise, it is ultimately real (*paramārthasat*). (Abhidharmakośa 6.4)
Even if the object is accepted [as the cause], there is a fault;
and even if that object is admitted, it must be conceived as an aggregate (*sañcaya*) alone, not as atoms, because atoms are beyond the reach of the senses.

That aggregate is the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) of cognition. Even if this status of having an aggregate as its objective condition is accepted, its nature as direct perception (*pratyakṣatā*) is not established according to your own view, because it would merely be an appearance thereof (*tad-ābhāsatvāt*).
Its nature as an appearance [of that object] is due to its being conceptual in nature; and conceptual nature has already been explained.

Both of these are of the nature of erroneous cognition because they involve a misrepresentation of name, shape, number, and color—namely, through the misrepresentation of name, shape, number, and color, or by means of those [factors].
In this context, "conceptualization" (kalpanā) is intended as nothing other than a misapprehension (*anyathāpratipatti*).

The examples are, respectively: like the cognition of a mirage due to the misapprehension of name, shape, number, and color; like the cognition of a fire-brand circle; like the cognition of two moons; and like the cognition of a yellow form by one whose eyes are afflicted by jaundice. These are the examples corresponding to the [four] reasons when the probandum (*sādhya*) is that [the cognition] consists of erroneous knowledge. Furthermore, the subsequent passage is for the purpose of establishing the absence of perceptuality (*pratyakṣatva*) as the probandum.

To that end, the proof is summarized at the conclusion: therefore, this [perception of atoms] is not direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) because it consists in the superimposition of an object that is not as it appears, like an error. This is like the single error of action—namely, the seeing of trees on a bank running by one who is aboard a boat—excluding that, it is like the fourfold types of error previously mentioned.

As for the application (*upanaya*), it is because the apprehension of the blueness of atoms, which is established in common worldly usage, shares the common property of being a cognition of an object that is not as it is in every respect.
Alternatively, for that very reason, it is not direct perception, like the cognition of a conventionally real (*saṃvṛtisat*) entity.

The explanation of that is as follows: having established the example with the words "Just as [in the case of] Gopāla," etc., the application of the example (*dārṣṭāntika*) is established by the words "In the same way, though existing conventionally," etc.
[The compound *saṃjñā-saṃkhyā-saṃsthāna-varṇā* means] name (*saṃjñā*), shape (*saṃsthāna*), and color (*varṇa*). [The word *pra* refers to] the prefix *pra*.
...because of [the word] *kalpanā* (imagination),
*dṛṣṭāntaḥ* (example), or *hetor vā bhrāntiḥ* (or the error of the reason).
Having set aside error, he states the evidence for the true characteristic of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti-sallakṣaṇa*): "That which, when broken...

[referring to] a jar. When that jar is broken into the state of potsherds, fragments, gravel, and so forth—wherein other things intended as the jar have been removed, such as the potsherds and the rest—the cognition of a "jar" no longer exists, because in the absence of the apprehension of those [parts], that cognition is absent. This is like the cognition of a "snake" in a rope on a fingertip, which becomes useless once the rope is seen.

In that perception of its parts, there too occurs the delusion of a rope regarding a snake, just as in the case of [perceiving] a hair on the hand. As for what was said—that "these [sensory cognitions] have the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the sense-base (*āyatana*) as their object with respect to their own object, but not the specific characteristic of the substance (*dravya*)," if one asks how that is so: it is because they are produced by multiple objects that they are said to have a universal (*sāmānya*) as their range regarding their own object;

and because they are produced by multiple substances, they are said to have a universal as their range regarding their own sense-base. It is not, however, because of the conceptual construction of a single undifferentiated form among distinct things. (Pramāṇasamuccaya-vṛtti 1)

Here too, because it is a single cognition whose object consists of multiple things, and because it has the nature of a generality, it does not have the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object; like the cognition of a "fist," just as there is no fist apart from the fingers, so too there is no jar apart from the shards and so forth—thus, the jar exists only conventionally (*saṃvṛti*).

Thus, when exclusion (*apoha*) occurs through action where such action is possible, even in cases where exclusion by action is not possible, there too it occurs through cognition (*dhī*). For example, regarding a jar, that cognition [of "jar"] does not exist apart from the collection of other things such as color-form (*rūpa*);

and regarding the collection of color-form and so on, that cognition does not exist once the atoms of color-form and so forth have been excluded. This is the illustration: like water. Since the cognition of "water" is observed even in a single drop of water, whereas the cognition of "water" no longer exists when color-form and the rest are mentally excluded, this is the definition of that which exists conventionally (*saṃvṛtisat*).

Alternatively, that which, when broken into its constituent parts, no longer produces the cognition of it—as in the case of a jar—is conventionally real (*saṃvṛtisat*). Furthermore, where the cognition [of water] does not persist upon the exclusion of other objects through the notion of "water"—because there is no intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) to the entity consisting of the exclusion of other things, being merely the absence of fire, air, and so forth, like the "water" established in common usage—that too is conventionally real.

Ultimate reality (*paramārthasat*) is otherwise; it possesses a nature distinct from this [conventional] definition, being by its very nature differentiated [from others], such as form (*rūpa*), taste (*rasa*), and so on. That is ultimate reality, which is the object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
See page 67, line 7:
"The four truths were taught by the Blessed One, as well as two truths—the conventional truth (saṃvṛtisatya) and the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya).
What is the definition of these two? That which, when broken, no longer produces the cognition of that thing, and which [no longer produces the cognition] when other factors are mentally excluded."
That which is conventionally real is like a jar or water; that which is ultimately real is otherwise.

That which, when broken down into its constituent parts, no longer gives rise to the cognition of that thing, is conventionally real (*saṃvṛtisat*); for example, a jar, for when it is broken into shards, the cognition of a "jar" no longer occurs.
Furthermore, that which no longer gives rise to the cognition of that thing when other properties are mentally excluded is also to be understood as conventionally real; for example, water.

For in that case, when one excludes the dharmas such as form (rūpa) by means of the intellect, the cognition of "water" no longer occurs; yet, since that conventional designation (saṃvṛti-saṃjñā) has been applied to those very [dharmas], those who say "the jar exists" and "the water exists" by virtue of convention speak the truth and not a falsehood. This is conventional reality (saṃvṛti-sat). Other than this is ultimate reality (paramārtha-sat): that which, even when broken, still gives rise to its own cognition, and which, even when other dharmas are excluded by the intellect, still gives rise to its cognition—that is ultimately real. For example: form (rūpa).

For when an object is broken down into its atoms, and even qualities such as taste are mentally excluded, the cognition of the intrinsic nature of form still persists; the same should be understood for sensation and the other aggregates.
Because these exist in the ultimate sense, they are called ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).

The former masters have stated that ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) is that which is apprehended by supramundane knowledge (*lokottara-jñāna*) or by the mundane knowledge subsequently attained (*tatpṛṣṭhalabdha-laukika*), whereas conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*) is that which is apprehended by other [forms of] knowledge. Thus it has been said in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (Chapter 6), graciously provided by the eminent scholar Śrī Prahlādapradhana Mahodaya.
The cognition "this is a snake" with respect to a rope is useless once the rope has been seen.
Even in that perception of its parts, there is the delusion of a rope regarding what is [actually] a snake.

As for what was said—that these [sensory cognitions] have the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the sense-base (*āyatana*) as their object, and not the specific characteristic of the substance (*dravya*)—if one asks how that is so: it is because they are produced by multiple objects that they are said to have the universal (*sāmānya*) as their domain with respect to their own object;

and because they are produced by multiple substances, they are said to have the universal as their domain with respect to their own sense-base. It is not, however, due to the conceptual construction of a single, non-different form among distinct things. (Pramāṇasamuccayavṛtti 1)

Here too, because it is a single cognition whose object consists of multiple things, and because its nature is that of a universal (*sāmānya*), it does not have the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object;
rather, since it is produced by multiple objects, it has the universal as its domain with respect to its own object.
When [the universal] is excluded,
the designations "pot" and so forth exist as mere conventional designations.

Even this [snake], though intended as ultimately real (*paramārthasat*), is indeed non-existent because it does not transcend the characteristics of conventional reality (*saṃvṛtisat*). According to the method already stated, everything is merely conventionally real; regarding this point as well, an illustrative example that confirms it has been stated: "the cognition of a snake in a rope. To that extent, there exists the erroneous cognition (*viparyayajñāna*) of a snake in the rope only so long as one does not perceive specific signs such as its lack of movement. However, specifically, when there is the perception of those specific [features] through ascertainment, the previous vision of the snake becomes useless.

When that cognition of a rope is seen in its parts, it is as useless as the cognition "this is a snake"; thus, it is likewise useless. Therefore he says: "Upon seeing those parts, even there, the delusion of a rope is like [the delusion of] a snake. In this way, by such a conceptualization, it is rightly stated that all cognitions of composite objects have only conventionally real things as their objects: "The visual and other sensory consciousnesses of the Śākya-putrīyas, which have blue and so forth as their objects, are non-perceptual and like a delusion."

Thus, first of all, the fault—along with its attendant implications—has been stated regarding the statement that "the object of its own generality is produced by multiple [atoms]," which was intended as a rebuttal to the objection arising from the contradiction with the textual passage on the five groups of consciousness having aggregated objects while being free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*).
[The text contains the corrupt reading] *daspaṃdaspaṃdādi* (Bhāṣya);
it should be *tadadṛṣṭau* (Y).

Now, regarding what was stated as a response consisting of conceptual construction— introduced by way of the objection in the text beginning with "this [form] which is divided into many types"— namely, that "these have the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the sense-fields (*āyatana*) as their object, not the specific characteristic of a substance (*dravya*)," the Master [Vasubandhu], wishing to state the fault in that statement intended as a rebuttal, first restates the opponent's position and explains it by writing down exactly what was written by the author of the *Ṭīkā*, up to the point "because of the conceptualization of a single form," the meaning of which has already been explained.

But the rebuttal here is as follows: because of the word "also" (*api*), those faults already explained regarding the previous alternative interpretation of the meaning are possible here as well. If one asks how that is so, it is because of the nature of being a single cognition whose object is multiple things (*anekārthaviṣayaikapratyayatva*). Multiple things are the atoms; a single cognition having them as its object is "a single cognition whose object is multiple things. Because of that state—namely, because of the nature of being a single cognition whose object is multiple things—[the fault remains].

And regarding the proof that perception is not [itself] perceptible, two arguments have been briefly suggested by you yourself: "The perception accepted by you is non-perceptual because it is produced by multiple objects, like inference;
for even inference is produced by multiple objects such as the property of the subject (pakṣadharma) and so forth.

If it is argued that "a reason is that which makes known," then [we reply] that it is also produced from multiple objects acting as causes, provided it possesses the necessary concomitance between the property to be proven and the proving property.
No, because [the cognition] arises from many objects that are not aggregated (*asañcita*).

But surely, even smoke and the like are perceived only as aggregates; for there is no cognition regarding those atoms—whether they are each individually beyond the senses, or whether they are combined or uncombined—except for that single cognition whose object is the many things within that collection. This is because it is accepted that a cognition resembling them arises with that aggregate as its objective support (*ālambana*).
Furthermore, if one accepts a cognition whose object is a distinction between different things, it would contradict such statements as: "Cognition does not cognize" (Vijñānakāya 4.268).
Therefore, a single cognition has multiple objects as its domain while appearing as a single object;

for that very reason, it takes the form of a universal (*sāmānya*). Because its domain consists of both that and not-that, it has as its range a universal that is neither real nor unreal. Consequently, it does not have the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its domain; for only those atoms are the particular characteristic, and not their aggregate, because the latter is a universal.

For this very reason, it is conventional (saṃvṛti) and, because its object is not the specific characteristic (asvalakṣaṇa), it consists of conceptual construction (kalpanātmaka) and is expressible; thus, that which we previously introduced has been fully elucidated by you yourself when you offered the rebuttal: "Because it is produced by multiple objects, it has the universal as its domain with respect to its own object" (*Pramāṇasamuccaya* 1.4).
See page 78, line 2;
see page 79, line 24;
page 79, note 7.

And you yourself have, by implication, provided two arguments for establishing that perception is non-perceptual: namely, that your own accepted perception is non-perceptual because it is produced by multiple objects, just like inference;
for inference, too, is produced by multiple objects such as the property residing in the subject (pakṣadharma) and so forth.

If it is argued that this reason is merely indicative (*jñāpaka*), [we reply: it is not so, because it arises from multiple causal factors (*kāraka*) that possess the necessary concomitance (*anvaya*) between the property to be proven (*sādhya*) and the proving property (*sādhana*). For in inference, it is indeed the case that smoke and the like are perceived only as a collection (*sañcaya*) of many atoms; thus, since it is produced by a non-aggregated plurality of things, it cannot be a mere indicator.
Because of the admission of [its] arising;
see page 73, line 13.
The object of the characteristic. *prabhṛti* (or similar term).

...the accumulation of delusion; therefore, that accumulation [is abandoned] by him. ...the accumulation; therefore, that accumulation [is abandoned] by him. Vi. mūḍhasāmānya-prasaṃcaya sa tasmāt pāḍe līṃ raṃ hī saṃcayaḥ sa tasmāt.

Furthermore, two reasons for establishing that your accepted perception is not actually perception have been briefly indicated by you yourself, lest the fault of contradicting your own tenets be exposed; these are accessible to the reasoning of wise people, yet they are not explicitly clear.
Which two? They are: "because it is produced by multiple objects" and "because its object is a generality (sāmānya) regarding its own object.
Of these, first is the initial proof: your accepted perception is non-perceptual, because it is produced by multiple objects, like inference.

Do not think that it is unestablished (*asiddha*) that inference (*anumāna*) is produced by multiple objects in the case of the example; for inference itself is produced by multiple objects, such as the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), its presence in similar instances (*sapakṣānugama*), and its exclusion from dissimilar instances (*vipakṣavyāvṛtti*). Just as the inferential cognition of fire, impermanence, and so forth is produced by these multiple factors, so too this perception is produced by multiple objects in the form of atoms (*paramāṇu*);
thus, [the opponent argues], that reason is a prover (*jñāpaka*).

It might be thought: "In inference, although there are multiple factors such as the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and so forth—such as smoke or being produced—they are not the *kāraka* (producing cause) for the cognition of fire or impermanence. What then? They merely cause one to remember the previously established, inseparable relation; thus, that reason (*hetu*) is a *jñāpaka* (indicator). On the other hand, the object is the *kāraka* of perceptual cognition; therefore, because of this difference in nature (*vaidharmya*), there is no illustrative example. This is incorrect, because the same logic applies here as well, starting from the phrase "even from a producing cause" (*kārakād api*). The term "inference also" (*anumānam api*) carries over [from the previous context]: inference regarding one's own purpose (*svārtha*) also arises from multiple objects that are producing causes.

Why is this so? Because [the reason] possesses the property of being concomitant with the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) and is exclusive; it possesses the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), follows along with similar instances (*sapakṣa*), and is excluded from dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*). It is because of its exclusivity that there is indeed a "productive reason" (*kārakahetu*) even in inference. When the object of that [reason] is indicated even slightly, it is called "inference" (*anumāna*). Thus ends the section on the exclusion [of other types].
It is understood that [the object] is not manifest;
here, there may also be a reading "na gamye te, na sphuṭe," which would be intended by him. *Pra.* (Prakaraṇa) notes this.
...from fire and so forth, they proceed; from what [do they proceed]? From Prakṛti.

Regarding "because of being smoke," the other says: No; this similarity does not hold for inference because it is produced by multiple non-aggregated objects, whereas perception is produced by multiple aggregated objects. Why? Because inference is produced by multiple non-aggregated objects, while perception is produced by multiple aggregated objects.
Inference has as its object things that are separated by space and time, whether they are present or absent, whereas perception has an object that is the opposite of that.
To this it is replied: But surely even smoke and the like, when apprehended as a mere collection, causes one to infer fire and so forth, just as atoms do;

if you argue that this is a causal cognition (*hetupratyaya*) and not a dominant cognition (*adhipatipratyaya*) consisting of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), [we reply] that it arises from multiple causal factors (*kāraka*), being endowed with the necessary concomitance (*anvaya*) of the property to be proven (*sādhya*) and the proving property (*sādhana*).
Now, how is this [conceptual cognition] not a dominant condition (*anadhipati*)? Because it is not an object of the sense faculties.
But then, would not the causal condition consisting of the synthesis (*sañcaya*) also be a non-dominant condition because it is not an object of the sense faculties?
Likewise, with respect to its own object, it is not direct perception (*apratyakṣa*), like inference, because its range is that of a universal (*sāmānya*).

Alternatively, inference would be perception, because it is produced by multiple objects, because its object is the universal regarding its own referent, and because both of these [inference and perception] are one and the same, like perception,
due to having a single defining characteristic; thus it makes known [objects] such as fire and so forth, just as atoms do.

The word "nanu" is used here to acknowledge what is well-known: Is it not the case that smoke—which is a property of a location qualified by the presence of fire, which is a composite of the four elements, and which is accompanied by positive and negative concomitance—produces the cognition of the presence of fire in that location, just as a collection of atoms produces the cognition of color? Since this causal condition (hetupratyaya) leads one to understand [the fire] by producing that cognition, it functions as a cause without deviation in both cases, just as it leads one to understand the atoms of fire and so forth. If it is argued that it is not an "overlord-condition" (adhipatipratyaya) because it is a conceptual construction (kalpanā), [we reply: even from multiple causes, a single object arises, provided it possesses the positive concomitance of the property to be proven (sādhya) and the proving property (sādhana).
Now, how is this [conceptual cognition] not a dominant condition (*anadhipati*)? Because it is not an object of the sense faculties (*indriya*).
But then, is not the causal condition consisting of the collection (*sañcaya-hetu-pratyaya*) also not a dominant condition because it is not an object of the sense faculties?
Likewise, because its object is a universal (*sāmānya*) with respect to its own referent, it is non-perceptual (*apratyakṣa*), like inference (*anumāna*).

Alternatively, inference would be perception because it is produced by multiple objects and because its object is the universal regarding its own referent; thus, both of these are one and the same, like perception, because they possess a single defining characteristic. [Otherwise,] it would not produce knowledge of fire. *Praśastapādabhāṣya*.

It might be thought: "The phrase 'causal condition' (*hetupratyaya*) and so forth means that the cause (*hetu*), the condition (*pratyaya*), and the motive (*nimitta*) are without an objective support (*anālambana*). This smoke is the motive for inference, but it is not a dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*); for while non-conceptual cognition is a dominant condition—being direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)—inference is not so. Therefore, because of this difference in nature (*vaidharmya*), it cannot serve as an example. If you think thus:
In this context, there may also be the reading "hetu-pratyaya" (cause-condition);
and here, there may also be the reading "nimittaṃ nālambanam" (the sign is not the object).
Desiring to have the opponent state the answer himself, he says: "Now, how so? and so forth.
You must be asked this: "How can this smoke be without a dominant cause (*anadhipati*)? which means it would be without an objective support (*anālambana*).
The other replies: "Because the object characterized as fire and so forth, which is the causal correlate (*pratyeya*), is not an object of the senses."
The Teacher says: But surely, even the causal condition consisting of an accumulation (*sañcaya*) is not a dominant factor (*anadhipati*), because it is not an object of the sense faculties;

indeed, even in the case of direct perception, the accumulation of atoms itself is not a dominant factor for that very reason—that it is not an object of the sense faculties—since an accumulation distinct from the atoms does not exist. This has been explained at length previously;
therefore, both are in every respect equal in their status as causal factors (*kāraka*).

Likewise, regarding the proof that [perception] is not direct (apratyakṣa) because its object is a universal even when directed toward its own particular object—just like inference—the detailed exposition intended to demonstrate the status of the reason as a causal factor (*kāraka-hetu*) is identical; thus he extends [the argument] by stating: "This is to be seen as unestablished (*asiddha*); how so? Because smoke is dependent on the means of proof (*sādhana-adhīna*). (Bhāṣya). "This is to be seen as unestablished; how so? Because smoke is dependent on the means of proof" (Yāyavṛtti).
Because it is not an object of the [mental] consciousness that accumulates [the latent impressions],
even direct perception is non-existent [for that consciousness].

Regarding the phrase "or inference" (*anumānaṃ vā*) and so forth, the word "or" (*vā*) has the sense of an alternative. If this—inference—has been established by me through the force of reasoning as being [in fact] perception according to your own accepted view, yet you, whose mind is colored by dogmatic attachment and who do not follow the conventions of your own school, do not accept it as such but instead insist that it is indeed perception, then for that reason, by virtue of its similarity [to perception], it would be either inference or perception. Because it is produced from multiple objects and because its object is a universal with respect to its own referent, these two proofs are also slightly suggested by these very same reasons, though they are not explicitly stated, just like the case of perception.

Furthermore, because these two reasons result in the identity of the object, there is an identity of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); therefore, he says: "Both of these are indeed one, because they possess a single defining characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇatvāt*)."

Since it has been established by the aforementioned method that the object of these two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is in fact a single entity characterized by both its own specific nature (*svalakṣaṇa*) and its general nature (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), there would follow either that perception alone is the single means of valid cognition—because [the object] is the domain of a single generality produced from multiple objects, just as the variety of perceptions arising through the doors of the eye and so forth is nonetheless perception—or else that inference alone is the means of valid cognition for that very same reason, just as the inferential cognition of fire, impermanence, and so forth is produced from smoke, the quality of being produced (*kṛtakatva*), and so on. (Praśastapāda-bhāṣya) *Note: The text contains the corrupt sequence "agnyamityādi" which has been corrected to "agnyādy-anityādi" based on the context.*

Furthermore, because it is produced by multiple objects, when cognition arises with respect to them having the generality of its own object as its domain, those [atoms] appear in that way; thus they constitute the objective support (*ālambana*), since the form of each individual atom does not enter into the cognition, but rather the cognition appears as such due to being produced by the collection [of atoms].
This being the case, that cognition which arises toward the sense faculty from the contact with the object is [the one under discussion].

Now, regarding the reply given by Dignāga—whose mind was possessed by envy for the virtues of his rival and whose heart was utterly indifferent toward the investigation of reality—to Vasubandhu’s own teacher, who stated that "from that object, consciousness is direct perception" (*vādavi*): [Dignāga] has merely presented his own view with some particular intention while refuting Vasubandhu’s definition of perception. As for the meaning of that [statement], let it be what it may; what is it to us? Let this much suffice: the meaning of "object" (*ālambana*) in relation to form and so forth must be explained (*pra-samu-vṛ-1*).

Having thus formulated these two alternatives, the author of the *Nayacakra*, wishing to demonstrate that the collection of faults arising from those two definitions applies equally to you as well, states—along with specific reasons for the contradiction of their own view—the fault produced by their own words: "And because it is produced by multiple objects, [the word] has as its domain the generality of its own object," and so forth; for the answer is the same for both the student and the teacher.

"Own object" (*svārtha*) refers to blue and so forth; this very thing, it is said, is the universal (*sāmānya*) because it is produced by multiple objects. Multiple objects are atoms; the perception whose object is blue is produced by them. Therefore, since the sense organ has its own object as its domain, and because it is produced by multiple objects, when a cognition arises toward those [atoms] with a certain appearance while having the universal of its own object as its range, those [atoms]—form and so forth—are the objective support (*ālambana*). It is accepted that they are the objective support exactly as they appear, namely, in their nature as blue, yellow, and so on.

If it is asked what the reason is for those very atoms of blue and so forth not being the object (*ālambana*), it is said: because the form of each individual atom does not enter into the cognition (*buddhi*). Since the form of each atom—blue and so forth—is beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*) with respect to each [atom] individually, it does not enter into the cognition. What, then, follows from this? It follows that the object is that which appears as such through being produced by a collection (*samudaya*), because the form of blue and so forth consists of that collection.
From that object, cognition is direct perception; this definition of direct perception was stated by the Buddhist master Vasubandhu in the *Vādavidhi*.
Dinna, the disciple of Vasubandhu—Dinna being another name for Diṅnāga himself—[stated as follows].

In the *Pramāṇasamuccaya* and its commentary (*vṛtti*), Vasubandhu’s own teacher Dignāga—who wished to refute the definition of perception (*pratyakṣa*)—proceeded at length as follows: "In the [verse] *tato 'rthād vijñānaṃ pratyakṣam* (Vādavidhi), if by the phrase *tato 'rthāt* (from that object) all [causes] were meant, then [the cognition] would not arise from that alone;

for if by this [phrase] every condition (*pratyaya*) were expressed—such that whatever cognition arises from whichever object is designated as such—it would not arise from that [object] alone, since cognition does not arise from the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) alone; rather, 'mind and mental factors arise from four [conditions]' (*caturbhiś cittacaittāḥ*, Abhidharmakośa 2.64)."
64. According to this established conclusion (siddhānta), if memory and other cognitions have an objective support (ālambana), they do not depend on anything else.

If, by the phrase "from that object," one means merely the objective domain, then even cognitions such as memory, inference, and desire do not require another objective support; for indeed, the cognition of fire does not have smoke and so forth as its objective support.

The meaning of "object" (*ālambana*) with respect to form and the other [sensory objects] must be stated: do they constitute an object in the sense that cognition arises toward them bearing their appearance, or rather, in the sense that they exist as causes for a cognition even though it bears the appearance of something else? If one asks what follows from this: if they constitute an object in the sense that cognition arises toward them bearing their appearance, then—since the five groups of consciousness have a composite (*sañcita*) as their object—it is accepted that the object is only conventionally real (*saṃvṛtisat*). Consequently, in cognitions that bear the appearance of blue and so forth, the status of being direct perception (*pratyakṣatva*) would follow from the fact that the cognition arises from that object; for in those cases, even though there is a superimposition of a collection upon them, a form that is substantially real (*dravyasat*) is obtained.

Even the forms of substance, number, and so forth will be obtained, for those very things appear as substance and the rest. Now, if it were the case that existing things serve as causes for a cognition even when there is no appearance of them, then the fault of the consequence of [actual] substance and so forth would not exist; however, because they do not exist in that way, the designation "that by which [the cognition] is designated" cannot be established. Furthermore, they are individually the cause when combined, but the collection itself is not, because it lacks conventional reality.
He says this very thing: "That which appears is not [the cause]; therefore, the pentad has consciousness as its support."
Since, from the perspective of ultimate reality, that [designation] is not predicated of that [object] therein— this is the transitional verse (avasara-kārikā).

There would also be the undesirable consequence that the eye and other sense organs would likewise be objects of cognition (*ālambana*), for even they, existing otherwise from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), serve as causes for cognitions appearing as blue and so forth, or appearing as two moons and so forth— *Pramāṇasamuccayavṛtti* 1.15–16.
This is the reason [given] because it contradicts their own doctrine.
Thus,
each one individually, in its entirety, possesses manifold meanings.

And this being the case, if [the object] were the objective support (*ālambana*) by virtue of appearing as a collection of atoms (*paramāṇu*) such as blue and so forth, then perception would arise only with respect to an object in the following manner: "That cognition which arises toward the sense faculty (*akṣa*) due to contact with an object is perception. In this way, the cognition is qualified by the object; however, that [definition of] perception—[that it is] "perception because of the contact of the sense faculty with the object"—is not tenable, because that object does not exist.
Nor is the collection the object, because it exists only conventionally (*saṃvṛtisat*).

Therefore, since this [cognition] is not accepted as having origination as its condition, there is an abandonment of the admission of both "cognitiveness" (*jñānatva*) and "perceptuality" (*pratyakṣatva*), due to the absence of a qualifier-qualified relationship. Consequently, because there is no object of cognition (*prameya*) distinct from its own appearance within cognitions such as those of the eye and so forth, the perceptuality [of such cognitions] is refuted by means of what is well-established as non-perceptual—namely, the cognition of the non-existent as existent; thus, there is a contradiction with inference.

Furthermore, just as in this case, that which arises from sense organs produced by similar or multiple objects, or from the sense-object itself, is also a cognition arising from a defect such as ophthalmia; and since it functions toward the sense organ, it would be "perceptual," whereby the object's status as a qualifier in cognition [is undermined].

Alternatively, an object that exists in proximity to a sense organ (*akṣa*) is "perceptible" (*pratyakṣa*); because it occurs in relation to the sense organ due to the contact between the object and the sense organ, the object—being the thing measured—is designated by the sense organ through a figurative application of the term. To this, the following answer is given: that is not tenable, because that [composite] object does not exist.
Having stated "this being so," he refutes [the opponent's position] by leading them to accept the consequence that a collection (*sañcaya*) would follow, for the object is not a collection.

If it is asked what the reason is that an object (*artha*) is not considered a collection, it is because it exists only conventionally (*saṃvṛtisattva*); or because its conventional existence lacks substantial reality (*adravyatva*), like the son of a barren woman.

For this reason, it is not accepted as a causal condition for arising; "causal condition for arising" means an objective support-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*), and since that [object] does not exist, it is not accepted.

The word "iti" has the sense of a reason; for this reason, that object is not qualified by the qualifier. Therefore, due to the absence of the relationship between qualifier and qualified, there is a loss of the accepted [status] of being both cognition and perception. Since it is accepted that "cognition is perception," and because of the non-existence of both the qualifier and the qualified object, what would the cognition and perception have as their object? Thus, the [position] is lost. (See Pramāṇavārttika, p. 76, l.
This direct perception is distinguished [from others],
yet it is not tenable, because that object does not exist.
Furthermore, the object [of cognition] is not an accumulation, because it exists only conventionally;

therefore, that [accumulation] is not accepted as a causal condition for arising. Consequently, due to the absence of a relationship between qualifier and qualified, there is a loss of the admission of [the cognition's] nature as knowledge and its status as perception.

Thus, since there is no object of comprehension distinct from the self-manifestation [of the cognition] in visual and other types of cognitions, the status of perception is refuted by the well-established fact that [such a cognition] is not perception because it apprehends what is non-existent as existent; this constitutes a contradiction with inference.
And just as in this case, that which arises from the sense-object and so forth produced by multiple similar objects is also considered to be like [the vision of] one with ophthalmia; thus,
even the scripture is not subject to refutation.
There is no arising of the non-existent, nor is there the destruction of the existent. (Bhāṣya: It will not be despised. (Vivaraṇa)
Furthermore: "In the cognitions of the eye and so forth," and so on, up to "contradiction by inference":

the cognitions of the sense-faculties such as the eye have as their nature only the appearance of their own objects, because they are cognitions, because they are real entities, and because they exist, like the cognitions of those with ophthalmia and the like;
therefore, in the cognitions of the eye and so forth, there is no object of cognition distinct from its own appearance.

Furthermore, just as a person suffering from ophthalmia perceives hair-nets, mosquitoes, flies, double moons, and so forth, that [cognition] is indeed the apprehension of the non-existent as existent—the apprehension of a non-existent thing as an existent thing.

For this reason, because it is an apprehension of the non-existent as existent and is thus a mistaken apprehension, the non-perceptual nature of that cognition is established, just like the cognition of a fire-brand wheel (*alātacakra*) and the like. By means of that well-established non-perceptual nature, your asserted perceptuality is refuted; and by virtue of that refutation, there is a contradiction with inference (*anumāna-virodha*).

[Objection: "But since this is a refutation of perception (*pratyakṣa*), how can it be a contradiction with inference (*anumāna*)? To this it is replied: According to your own view, because conceptualization (*vikalpa*), which is the property of perception, is refuted by the aforementioned inference, there is an absence of non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka-pratyakṣa*). Therefore, what is that perception which would be refuted, or what [perception] would refute? Consequently, this is indeed a contradiction with inference. [This applies] to cognitions regarding [objects] such as the self (*ātman*), etc., because they are established through [inferential] comprehension. Thus it is.
Because there is an absence of the status of being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) for a conceptualization that is not real,
and because there is an absence of the status of being a property of the subject for a counter-example (*vipakṣa*) that is not real.

Furthermore, there is another point: it would follow that cognitions of forms such as the number of a jar, its upward motion, existence, and its nature as a jar (*ghaṭatva*) would also be [considered] perception (*pratyakṣa*).
If one asks how this is so, it is said: "And just as... and so forth; setting aside the illustrative example itself, he describes the analogy and its commonality with the subject at hand.

Furthermore, according to your own view, the sensory object (*indriyārtha*) is produced from multiple common objects (*samānānekārtha*); that is, the sensory object is produced by multiple objects characterized as an aggregate of atoms (*paramāṇusaṅghāta*) which possess the common quality of blue color. It is not the unique (*asādhāraṇa*) object intended as the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). Why? Because, having abandoned that [specific characteristic], the cognition regarding its own object has a universal (*sāmānya*) as its domain, since it is produced from multiple objects. (Pramāṇasamuccaya 1)

Because of this statement, since a different kind of object is intended as its own referent (*svārtha*), the following occurs: from such a self-referent, a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) arises; from a collection of blue and so forth—which is a conventional reality (*prajñaptisat*) consisting of multiple identical objects that do not exist in that way—an aspect of ultimate reality (*paramārthasat*) is obtained. For it is those very atoms that appear as blue and so forth; thus, the cognition having them as its object is accepted as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). In the same way, from the aspects of a jar, number, and so forth—[aspects] which share the properties of the objects that produce direct perceptual cognition, being produced by sense faculties from multiple identical objects, and being multiple identical objects that do not exist in that way—an aspect of ultimate reality would be obtained. Consequently, the cognition of a jar and so forth would also be direct perception, because it would have a conventionally real object (*saṃvṛtisat*) as its support, just like the cognition of blue and so forth.
Alternatively, the cognition of blue and so forth would not be direct perception, just like the cognition of a jar and so forth;
for it is those very atoms that appear [in both cases].

Since the capacity to produce [cognition] is equal in both instances, why is this: that the cognition appearing as blue and so forth is direct perception, while the cognition appearing as a jar and so forth is not?

For just as those very atoms appear in the collection of atomic parts, so too in cognitions of jars and the like, it is those very same [atoms] appearing in combination that manifest; and upon such [atoms] alone does the cognition of a "jar" proceed and its designation [arise]. Likewise, upon such [atoms] alone does the cognition of forms such as blue proceed and its designation [arise].

It will be connected with the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*). And that too is invalid, like [the vision] of one suffering from ophthalmia; "taimira" means that which arises from *timira* (a visual disorder). Just as the perception of two moons is invalid, so too is the variegated sensory object produced by a collection of many-colored gems, even if they are uniform; the knowledge arising from that is also invalid, like the vision of one suffering from ophthalmia.

Why? Because from a collection of blue and so forth—which consists of many similar objects and thus has an object that is not [ultimately] real—cognition arises. Its state of having an unreal object is its conventional existence (*saṃvṛtisattva*); therefore, he says: "From a collection of blue and so forth, which consists of many similar objects and has an unreal object, and which is a conventionally existent (*prajñaptisat*) support, a form such as blue is obtained that is conventionally existent. Since those very atoms, which are ultimately real (*paramārthasat*), appear as blue and so forth, cognition whose object is that [collection] is accepted as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of blue and so forth."

If it is asked: "In what respect are they similar to those [forms] which have been excluded from being perception—namely, the forms of the jar's number, its upward motion, its existence, its jar-ness, and so forth, which possess the same properties as the objects that generate perceptual cognition? It is replied: They are similar in that they are produced by the sense organ acting upon its own object together with multiple common factors (*sāmānya*). Thus, they are similar in these respects.

What is meant by this? From causes that are common to many objects and which do not exist as such [in reality], a form that is ultimately real would be obtained, just like a collection of blue and other colors; therefore, having set that aside, he states the proof: "The cognition 'the jar is conjoined,' 'it is disjoined,' 'it is another,' 'it is not another,' 'it moves,' and so forth, would be perception, and its object would also be perceptual, because it has a conventionally real entity as its objective support, like the cognition of blue and so on.
Alternatively, the cognition of blue and its object would not be perception, because they possess only conventional existence, like the cognition and object of a jar."

Because the word "or" (*vā*) has the sense of an alternative, and because there is no difference in the object that produces cognition in both cases, he establishes this: for those very same atoms which appear as a jar and so forth are the very same ones which appear as blue and so forth.

Thus, since the capacity to produce both cognitions—of blue and so forth, and of a jar and so forth—is equal, how can it be that the cognition appearing as blue and so forth is perception (*pratyakṣa*), while the one appearing as a jar and so forth is not? The meaning is that there is no reason other than mere personal preference.
Having stated the illustrative example (*dārṣṭāntika*), [the text] says:
"equal, unequal, many... (*samānāsamānānekā*);
here, there may also be a reading of *tantyaktvā*.
The universal of its own referent.

[Objection: A valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) [is established as follows]: from a collection of blue and so forth—which is a conceptual existence (*prajñaptisat*) consisting of multiple identical objects that do not exist as such [in reality]—an aspect of ultimate existence (*paramārthasat*) is obtained; for it is those very atoms that appear as blue and so forth. Therefore, the cognition having that as its object is accepted as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Likewise, from aspects such as "pot" and "number"—which possess the same properties as the objects that generate perceptual cognition, being produced by sense-faculties from multiple identical objects, and being multiple identical objects that do not exist as such—an aspect of ultimate existence will be obtained. Thus, the cognition of a pot and so forth would be direct perception, because its objective support (*ālambana*) is a conventional existence (*saṃvṛtisat*), just like the cognition of blue and so forth.
Alternatively, cognition of blue and so forth would not be perception, just like cognition of a jar and so forth;
for it is those very atoms that appear [in both cases].
Since the capacity to produce [cognition] is equal for both, why is this the case—that cognition appearing as blue and so forth is perception, while cognition appearing as a jar and so forth is not?

For just as in a collection of atomic parts those very [parts] appear, so too in cognitions of jars and the like, those very [parts] appear when aggregated; and it is with respect to things existing in that state alone that the cognition of a "jar" arises and its designation occurs. Likewise, it is with respect to things existing in that state alone that the cognition of forms such as blue arises and its designation occurs. Just as [in the case of] a forest... just as [in the case of] a forest... [repeated].
Therefore, that which arises from a collection of causes—
whether homogeneous or heterogeneous, and whether multiple or single—
is produced as a real entity, such as a jar.
By means of the commonality with a pot produced by [human] effort,
[the subject] is [established as] manifold through both similar and dissimilar [instances].
Whether they are identical, non-identical, or manifold,

[the text] from "just as indeed" (*yathaiva hi*) up to "those very things appear when combined" (*samuditāsta evābhāsante*) demonstrates precisely the lack of distinction in the producing cause (*janakahetu*), because there is no difference in their capacity to appear within the cognition (*buddhi*).

And here, just as in the collection of parts of an atom those very [parts] appear in general as the form and configuration of cognition because they manifest as blue, so too in cognitions of jars and the like, those very [parts] appear as aggregated under a specific form; there is no other thing called a "jar" that could manifest in such a way. Thus, it is only among the visible forms and so forth existing in their respective states that a jar exists. If it should be argued: "In the collection of blue and the rest, a substantially real form exists; since it consists of atoms and exists in that manner, its perceptibility is logical."
But the form of a jar and so forth does not [exist], because it lacks the nature of atoms and because it is non-existent in that way;
and this is equal in both cases without distinction.

Just as in that case there is no form of a jar and so forth because it lacks atomhood and is non-existent in that way, so too the form of color and so forth has no [intrinsic] form, because that which is accumulated is perceptible by the senses and serves as an objective support (*ālambana*), whereas [the individual atoms] lack atomhood and are non-existent in that way; otherwise, they would not be objects, would not serve as objective supports, and would not be perceptible.

And thus there is the admission of another position: that those [atoms] exist in such a way that they are the objective support (*ālambana*), and that the cognition and designation proceed with respect to each one as previously stated. In this same way, it is precisely regarding atoms situated thus that the cognition and designation of blue and other forms proceed; therefore, everything is equal in both cases.
[The cognition of blue arises from the collection... *pratyaya*... *pra*.
Thus they appear.

Now, it might be argued: within the aggregate of blue and other [colors], there exists a form that is substantially real; because it consists of atoms and exists in that manner, its perceptibility is logical, whereas the form of a jar and so forth is not, because it does not consist of those atoms and does not exist in that manner.
And this is equal in both cases because there is no distinction:

just as that [consciousness] lacks the form of a jar and so forth because those are not atoms and because they do not exist, so too the form of color and so forth lacks form [in that consciousness], because the accumulated [atoms] are what is perceived by the senses, because they are the objective support (*ālambana*), because they are not atoms, and because they do not exist; otherwise, they would not be objects, would not be objective supports, and would not be perceptible, which would result in the acceptance of another position, namely, that "those things exist in the manner in which they are the objective support."

And as it has been stated here by the opponent, for the purpose of demonstrating the dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) between the two individually, it might be argued: "In the aggregate of blue and so forth," and so on, up to "because it consists of atoms (*aṇu*) and because it exists in that manner.
[The opponent's position is: in the aggregate of blue and so forth, there exists the form of the substance blue and so forth, which is a form existing in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*).

What is the reason? Because those [objects] such as blue and so forth consist of atoms (*aṇu*); because they consist of atoms, and because atoms possess substantial existence (*dravyasattva*), it is logical (*nyāyya*)—meaning consistent with reason (*nyāya*) or appropriate—that they are perceptible. Furthermore, the perceptibility of the cognition whose object is that [blue] is "perceptibility of that" (*tatpratyakṣatva*). However, there is no form such as a jar, nor does the form of a jar’s number, its upward motion, and so forth exist; this is because they do not consist of atoms (*atatparamāṇutvāt*). "Consisting of atoms" (*tatparamāṇutva*) means the atom-ness of that form; "not consisting of atoms" (*atatparamāṇutva*) means the absence of that atom-ness. Therefore, it is because they do not consist of atoms.

What follows from that? Because they are non-existent in that manner; because those forms of jars and so forth do not exist as atoms. [Regarding the passage beginning with] "the collection," etc., the Teacher here gives the reply: "And this is equal in both cases, because there is no distinction; for it is precisely because they are produced from atoms that the direct perceptions of blue and so forth, and of jars and so forth, are alike."

Just as in that collection of form and so forth there is the absence of the form of a jar and the like because it is not composed of atoms, and as that form of a jar and the like is itself formless because that form is not atomic, so too, due to non-existence—that is, due to the non-existence of the form of a jar and the like by way of being non-atomic, and due to its non-existence precisely by way of being atomic.

In this way, the formless nature of the aspect of color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth follows from the reason just stated: because that which is accumulated is perceptible by the senses; because the aggregate of atoms is perceptible by the senses; and because only that [aggregate] is the objective support (*ālambana*). Because that which is not accumulated is beyond the senses, for that very reason it is not an objective support. Because it is not an atom—since that accumulated, sensible objective support is not an atom—and because it is non-existent precisely due to its not being an atom; otherwise, it would not be an object, as it would not be an object in the sense of being an atom. Precisely because it is not an object, it is not an objective support, and for that very reason it is not directly perceived. [Therefore,] it exists only as an atom. (Note: *bhā* refers to the commentary).

Furthermore, because it would follow that [the object] is sensory (aindriyikatva), and moreover, this would entail the acceptance of an alternative position. *Bhāṣya*: "And furthermore—thus there is the consequence of another alternative."

If one abandons the position that "the object of cognition is that which appears in the cognition arising with respect to those [atoms]" (*Prakaraṇasamuccayavṛtti* 1.15), and instead adopts the position that "the object of cognition is how those [atoms] actually exist," then by shifting to another position, the debate would come to an end. Furthermore, even in this position, the same faults that you yourself have directed against Vasubandhu would apply to you as well.

If it is asked how this very position has been accepted by you as well, he shows it: "And just as it was stated for the purpose of producing the seed for the arising of perception— that 'they [the sense organs], when combined, are the cause'—
in that case, because it is produced from multiple objects, it has the universal as its object regarding its own referent" (Pramāṇasamuccaya 1).
