In the commentary on this [verse], the same point was formulated by one wishing to refute Punarvasubandhu: "Do form and the other [sensory objects] serve as the objective support (*ālambana*) for direct perception in the same way that existing things are the cause even for a cognition that has another appearance?
Since these two statements have the same meaning, you have accepted this position as well; therefore, what are those [atoms] combined that constitute the cause? (PSPVṛ 1).

Even so, those [objects] are not the objective support (*ālambana*), because they are beyond the senses (*atīndriya*). Furthermore, if such and such a state of being an objective support were possible, then smoke would become the objective support for a perceptual cognition of fire; for even though it exists [only as smoke], it serves as the cause for a cognition that appears otherwise, just like the objective support of the perception you have described.

If it is argued that even the eye and so forth would then be the object (*ālambana*), and that there is no fault in blue atoms being the object of the visual consciousness of blue and so forth—[we reply: even so, those atoms are not the object because they are beyond the senses (*atīndriyatvāt*). Since they transcend the range of the sense faculties, like space, atoms do not become the object of sensory cognition. (See page 96, line 25).
For the explanation of this,
see the commentary on page 96, line 26.

And even when combined, they are not the cause [of cognition], because [the object] is beyond the senses (*atīndriyatvāt*). Thus it is stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda* (Pra-samu-vṛ), chapter 1, verse 15. Even so, those [atoms] do not constitute the objective support (*ālambana*), because they are beyond the reach of the senses.

Furthermore, if such a state of having that as its objective support were the case, then smoke would become the objective support for the perceptual cognition of fire; for even though it exists [elsewhere], it acts as the cause for a cognition that appears otherwise. Consequently, just like the objective support of the perception you have described, the eyes and other sense organs would also become objective supports.
Moreover, the atoms of blue and so forth—which are the objects of the cognition of the eye and other senses—would not be the objective supports of the apprehended blue and other objects.

Furthermore, another fault is stated: even if one were to admit such a nature of the objective support (*ālambanatā*), as expressed in the passage beginning with "and so forth" up to "like the objective support of the perception you have described," then smoke would become the objective support for the perceptual cognition of fire. This is because, if atoms exist in that manner—existing as beyond the reach of the senses—they would nonetheless serve as the cause for a cognition in which a composite whole appears; thus, while such a nature of the objective support exists, smoke would [absurdly] be the objective support for the direct perception of fire, since it acts as the cause for a cognition that appears otherwise than its actual state of existence.

It is observed that smoke existing as smoke becomes the cause of a cognition that manifests as fire, as another manifestation, or as its own manifestation; thus, it possesses the property of being a characteristic of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), just like the objective support of the perception you have described—this demonstrates its presence in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) within the example.

Just as, according to your view, atoms—which exist otherwise, namely as existing in their state as atoms—become the cause of a cognition appearing as a collection [of them] by serving as the objective support (*ālambana*) of perception; so too, smoke, by virtue of that similarity, establishes for itself the status of being an objective support of perception, because it is pervaded by being the objective support of the perception of fire, which is the objective support of the cognition produced by it. Alternatively, the cognition of fire caused by smoke would itself be a perception, because its object is a thing existing in such a way that it generates a cognition appearing as something else, just like the perception described by you.

Or rather, by virtue of that very same similarity, the perception described by you would be non-perceptual with respect to its object, just like the cognition of fire produced from smoke; or else, by virtue of that very same similarity, [it would follow that] what was stated by you [is not perception].
In other places, [the reading] is *sahāt* with the sense of "together" (*sahārthena*),
*vi*sahāt with the sense of "self-together" (*sahātmahārthena*),
and *satāt* with the sense of "being-together" (*satātmahārthena*) according to the Bhāṣya, Viṣṇu-purāṇa, Pādma-purāṇa, and Ḍer̤ha-līṅga-purāṇa.
Furthermore, this reading "raṃ hī" does not even exist;

moreover, for that very reason, even the eye and so forth would become the objective support (ālambana). Thus, there is this fault of an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) for one who speaks thus: if the cause of consciousness is accepted as its objective support, even though it appears as something else, then the sense organs such as the eye would be the objective supports of the visual consciousness and so forth. Otherwise, because it becomes the cause of a consciousness appearing as something else despite being present [as a different thing], the visual organ would be the objective support of the visual consciousness, just like the atoms of form (rūpa) and so forth.

Alternatively, that cognition would have the sense-faculty as its objective support, because, while being produced by it, it appears as something else— just like the visual consciousness produced by atoms.
This fault has been stated by assuming that cognitions such as those of the ear and so forth have atoms as their objective supports.
...even more than that, ...the appearance of ... the object of focus is accepted... Yaśomitra.
And as for the phrase "of the object of apprehension, such as blue," and so forth:

the "object" (*viṣaya*) refers to the range of perception consisting of a collection of blue and so on, which is apprehended by the eyes and other senses; the "related" (*sambandhi*) refers to the visual consciousness and so on. The atoms of blue and so on are not the objective support (*ālambana*) of that [consciousness], because otherwise they would exist in an ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*).

"Otherwise" means that they appear as something other than their own appearance; thus, they do not exist in that way from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). In fact, even though they exist as specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) from the perspective of ultimate reality, they are ungraspable. Therefore, because they exist otherwise in terms of ultimate reality, atoms do not serve as the objective supports (*ālambana*) for cognitions that grasp objects such as blue, just like the eyes and other sense organs. Just as the sense organs, such as the eyes, exist in one way from the perspective of ultimate reality—as consisting of atoms that are not blue—and yet assume the state of being causes for the arising of cognitions of blue and so forth without being [direct] objective supports, so it is with atoms.
Furthermore, the atom cannot be the objective support (*ālambana*), because otherwise it would exist in an ultimate sense, or because it would be its own unique object, like the cognition of taste.

[Objection: But when they are gathered together, each one individually is the cause; thus, atoms in that state of being gathered are the objective support because they are the cause for the arising of visual and other cognitions, since their power to produce cognition is manifested in that condition, just as in the case of the atoms of the eye and so forth.

For neither a single sensory atom nor a single object-atom is capable of producing consciousness, nor is their collection so, because that collection exists only as a conceptual designation (*prajñaptisat*). However, when atoms function as individual causes, the power of vision is manifested within the collection, just like the power of carrying possessed by a group of palanquin bearers. Or rather, visual consciousness arises because it differs from the lack of vision in each individual member—like a row of blind people—or because its object is unique; for visual consciousness has a unique object. Thus, because its object is unique, it is visual consciousness.

Since each individual blue atom is its unique object, it possesses the quality of having a unique object (*asādhāraṇaviṣayatva*); and this is established by the statement [in the *Prakaraṇasamuccayavṛtti*]: "Each of those, when combined, is the cause" (1.15).

Therefore, because it has a unique object, like the cognition of taste—just as the cognition of taste, due to having a unique object, does not have a blue atom as its objective support (*ālambana*), so too is visual consciousness.

Because of the word "or" (*vā*), those blue atoms are not objects of the eye, because they are uncommon objects (*asādhāraṇaviṣayatvāt*). They are both uncommon and objects, like the cognition of taste (*rasajñānavat*)—that is, just as in the case of the cognition of taste. Just as, according to your own view, an object characterized as taste is not an object of visual consciousness because it is an uncommon object, so too are the blue atoms. [The passage beginning with] "otherwise" (*anyathā*) and ending with "because of being a means of knowledge" (*pramāṇatvāt*) is not present in the manuscripts *ya*; however, it is found in manuscript *bhā*. This is not so, because otherwise they would exist ultimately (*paramārthataḥ*), or because they would have a non-common object (*asādhāraṇaviṣaya*), like the cognition of taste.

But surely, it is only when combined that they are the cause; thus, atoms in such a combined state are the objective support (*ālambana*) because they are the cause for the arising of visual and other cognitions, since their capacity to produce cognition is manifested in that state, just like the atoms of the eye and so forth.

For neither a single atom of the sense organ nor a single atom of the object is capable of producing consciousness, yet neither is their collection [capable], because it exists only as a conceptual construct (*prajñaptisat*).

In the case of atoms, while each possesses causal capacity individually, the power of perception is manifested in their aggregate, just as the power of carrying is manifested in the aggregate of palanquin bearers; this is distinct from the lack of visibility in each individual atom, like a row of blind men— as may be seen in the Sādhana-paddhati, page 96, line 30.

The other says: "But surely, even when combined, they are each individually the cause," and so on, up to "like a row of blind men, because of their difference from individual non-perception. Now, I have already specified this: "even when combined, they are each individually the cause. What does this mean? It means that those very atoms, existing as such in their ultimate reality (*paramārtha-sat*), are the objective support (*ālambana*) because, when combined as atoms, they are the cause for the arising of visual and other cognitions.

What is the reason? Because the capacity for producing cognition is manifested when they are in that state. "Those in that state" (*tadavasthāḥ*) refers to those whose states constitute a collection (*samudāya*). For it is only when they are in that state that they are capable of producing cognition. Indeed, although that capacity for producing cognition exists in each [atom] individually, it is not manifested; it is manifested only in the collection. What is the illustration? Just as in the case of the atoms of the eye and so forth, even though each possesses the capacity to see form, that capacity is not manifested individually, but is manifested in the collection. It is the same for the atoms that serve as the objective support (*ālambana*).

He demonstrates that the absence of causal capacity is equal for each individual atom of the object and the sense-faculty, as well as for their respective powers when not yet aggregated: for neither is a single atom of the sense-faculty nor a single atom of the object capable of producing consciousness, and thus their collection is incapable because it exists only as a conceptual designation (*prajñaptisat*); nor is the collection of those atoms of the sense-faculty and the object capable of producing consciousness, because they exist only as conceptual designations and are non-existent from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). This is the meaning.

Therefore, the state of being a cause with respect to each individual is "individual causality" (*pratyekakāraṇatā*). When that individual causality exists, the manifestation of the power of vision occurs in the collection of atoms;

how so? Like the power of carrying in the case of a group of palanquin-bearers. Just as the power of carrying, which exists in each individual palanquin-bearer, is manifested in their collective assembly, so too is the power of seeing and being seen in the atoms of the sense organs and their objects.

By way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyeṇa*), [the example is] a row of blind people, due to their difference from individual vision. Just as the manifestation of the power of seeing—which does not exist in each individual blind person—will not exist even in their row, so too here the powers of the sense organs, objects, the seer, and the seen would not exist; yet they do exist.

Therefore, the atoms of the sense organs and objects possess powers that exist individually, and these powers become manifested in the aggregate, just as in the case of the row of blind people where [vision] is absent individually.
And to whatever extent the individual [manifestations] are manifested within the row of atoms,
that power of vision is perceived.
Likewise, regarding the sense faculties:

indeed, this establishment of perception has as its result the refutation of what was previously accepted, because it relies upon unaggregated atoms as its objective support, because it demonstrates the capacity for perceiving each [atom] individually, because there is no deviation in the causal factors, and because there is no such thing as an aggregate—just like the initial thesis. Thus, by reaffirming that the object is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), this constitutes a refutation of the view that [perception] has as its domain a universal (*sāmānya*) of its own object produced by multiple things.
Alternatively, it is stated here by way of a summary that follows the prior examination and consideration:
"But surely, this establishment of perception has as its result the refutation of what was accepted;

for it was accepted [in the Abhidharmapiṭaka] that 'the five collections of consciousness have an accumulated [object] as their support' (Abhidharmapiṭaka), and the refutation of that accepted position is the result of this establishment of perception."

Why? Because it relies on the premise that the atoms are not accumulated (*asañcita*) as the objective support (*ālambana*). In this conceptualization—that there is a manifestation of the power of seeing in the atoms of the sense-object and the sense-faculty, each of which possesses the individual power of seeing—it follows that unaccumulated atoms are capable of producing visual consciousness. This implies that the five groups of consciousness have unaccumulated things as their objective supports; yet this reliance on an alternative conceptualization contradicts the accepted principle that they have accumulated things as their objective supports.

What is the reason? It is because the capacity for vision is manifested in each individual, due to their similarity to the carriers of a palanquin. For it might be thought: "Indeed, it has been stated that the manifestation of that capacity occurs only when those who possess the capacity individually are gathered together."

The Teacher says: "True, this has been said; it is incorrect. Why? Because there is no difference from the producers. For it has already been explained in detail that there is no aggregate distinct from the atoms which are the producers of cognition. Therefore, since there is no difference from the producers and no such aggregate exists, this attempt to establish perception as the manifestation of the power of vision in each [atom] results only in the refutation of what was previously accepted."

Alternatively, "otherwise" (*anyathā*) refers to a state different from that of the producers; its negation is "the non-otherwise-ness of the producers. Therefore, because there is no establishment of perceptibility for the producers—the atoms—which are beyond the senses due to their non-otherwise-ness, and because there is no such thing as a "collection" (*sañcaya*) existing as a distinct entity, the recourse to unaggregated atoms as the objective support remains as it was.

The power of giving,
cessation,

This state of hanging down is real; this has been stated. However, the reading "but what was stated is improper" might also be possible here, because there is no other way [to understand it].
Regarding "nanyatvātya" and "vyaktapratyakṣa," the reading "vyakteḥ pratyakṣa" might be possible here.
Otherwise, otherwise-being; otherwise;
due to being perceptible by the senses.
Or rather,

this conceptualization should be adopted by you, because it is consistent with the proposition that perception has the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object; for one who wishes to fulfill that [proposition].
Because each of them, when combined, is the cause—*Pramāṇasamuccayavṛtti* 1.1.1.

15. This statement, which establishes the object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), functions as being equivalent to the initial proposition (*pratijñā*); thus, it is "like the initial proposition," meaning it conforms to the initial proposition. For that initial proposition—that direct perception has the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object—is fulfilled by this statement. Since this fulfillment is achieved through the resolution regarding the particular characteristic as the object, one must state that direct perception has the particular characteristic as its object; for having first proposed that "direct perception has the particular characteristic as its object," and then asserting that "those [atoms], when combined, are the cause," one must explain the relationship between the means and the end established by examining the sequence [of atoms], because atoms possess the nature of particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).

"Ah, excellent! But furthermore, O Devānāmpriya, what is the collection of faults here? It is the rejection of [the definition] that 'it has as its object a generality regarding its own referent, being produced by multiple meanings' (Praśastapādabhāṣya 1.4). By adopting the position of the response to this objection, this concluding statement—which aims at the excellence of the consistency between preceding and following parts—is thereby rejected."

Now, lest this fault should arise, one might attempt to avoid it by refuting the previously examined, subsequent, and initially asserted propositions; yet, like the doctrine of non-absolutism (*anekāntavāda*), one must abide in both extremes. One must abide in the state of individuality, as in the case of fire and water, even though that is impossible in their aggregate, because [the aggregate] would possess the reality you have described directly, and because of the inclusion of the collection of meanings such as "many," "one," "bearing," and "swift motion.
Otherwise, there would be no aggregate of these at all, since they do not exist individually, like the son of a barren woman.

It should be observed (p. 96, l. 30) that this [position] is inconsistent with the Buddhists' own admission of the momentariness and impermanence of conditioned phenomena distinct from the three [categories]; or else, by accepting each individual conclusion, the meaning of the initial thesis is refuted;

or, because the word "or" (*vā*) implies an alternative, either the fact that perception has the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object is refuted, or the fact that it has the generality of its own object produced by multiple things as its domain, or both are refuted.
See page 96,
line 30: *pratyavekṣitapyorthoparyasādhya* (Bhāṣya) / *pratyavekṣitavyorthoparyasādhya* (Yaśomitra).

Having examined the state of things as they truly are, the refutation of the initial thesis regarding stability is as follows: one must abide in two extremes characterized by non-absolutism (anekānta)—one must abide in individuality, like fire and water, in a collection where each possesses its own impossible power; for this is the reality you have directly stated, and because it involves the thorough comprehension of a collection whose meanings consist of both multiplicity and unity.
Furthermore, their collection would not even exist, because each individual member lacks such existence, like the son of a barren woman;

this [position] is inconsistent with the Buddhist admission of the momentary impermanence of conditioned phenomena as distinct from the three [other categories], because it is characterized by being distinct from each [of those]. *Svalakṣaṇa*.

Furthermore, because of the statement that "they, whether individually or combined, are the cause," it follows by implication that they must exist separately; he recalls this very point again through other defects: "Just as in the case of non-absolutism (anekānta), one must abide in two extremes. Two extremes mean two locations; in those two locations, there must be an abiding by those atoms, whether individually or combined. What is the result? It would be like the case of non-absolutism."

It exists as manifold (anekāntavat) because it exists in a non-exclusive manner; just as atoms, while abiding in both the state of being distinct substances and the state of being ultimate modifications, are designated as "those very atoms" and also as "their aggregate," so too must they abide in both individuality and [the aggregate]. The word "and" (*ca*) indicates a conjunction, showing the similarity to manifoldness. What does it conjoin? It conjoins the subsequent [state], namely that they must abide both in individuality and in the aggregate.

And just as in the case of fire and water, that collection possesses both the possible and the impossible; for fire, burning and so forth are possible, while refreshing and moistening and so forth are impossible; whereas for water, moistening and refreshing and so forth are possible, while burning and so forth are impossible. Thus, the collection is capable of what is impossible for each individual member—that is, it is "capable of the impossible. Now, as for the meaning of the sentence: even atoms, though they pervade the world, become objects of visual perception and the like only in dependence upon aggregation, division, and transformation, and not otherwise. Therefore, you have arrived at the very same position as the Jains, who maintain the doctrine of the non-abandonment of both extremes.

Why? Because it is the reality explicitly stated by you yourself; for you have explicitly stated that the reality of these atoms is such that individually they are not capable of producing visual consciousness, whereas collectively they are capable. Thus, first of all, there is an explicit acceptance of non-absolutism (*anekānta*), or it is accepted through logical implication (*arthāpatti*), because of the inclusion of the collective sense of the verbal root *sam-ud-i* as "to go together" or "to assemble" into a multitude of unities.

The prefix *sam* signifies unification (*ekībhāva*), and that unification belongs to the manifold (*aneka*). From the root *iṇ* (to go) [Pāṇini Dhātupāṭha 1045], *ayana*, *gamana*, *gati*, and *āya* are synonyms. *Udāya* means intense movement (*utkaṭāya*). Thus, *samudāya* refers to a collection (*saṅgata*) of intense movements; by including that term, the meaning is established as "those [factors] taken individually, when combined, constitute an intense movement of the manifold unified. Therefore, let the acceptance of the doctrine of non-absolutism (*anekāntavāda*) be observed [see page 96, line 30].
Thus it is. [Yaśovijaya]
It causes one to remember the sequence of the two internal states.
In this state,
there is both the presence and the absence of fire, and likewise the absence of fire.
Regarding the consideration of measure,
there is the abandonment of both;
because that very [measure] is the reality explicitly stated therein, it is by that alone [that they are abandoned].
Capable even without a husband,
O lady of noble lineage.

Furthermore, there would be no collection (*samudāya*) of these [atoms] even in another sense—that is, even according to logic; this is the proposition that there could be no collection at all because they do not exist individually, like the son of a barren woman—this is the reasoning. Just as there is no collection of sons of barren women who do not exist individually, so too there is none of atoms.

If it is argued that this is illogical because the non-existence of atoms individually has not been established, we say: no. This is inconsistent with the very position of the Buddhists themselves, who accept a conditioned momentary impermanence distinct from the three [other types of impermanence];
for since [the atom] perishes immediately after reaching [its state], its attainment of individuality is likewise impossible, due to its non-existence, like the son of a barren woman.

If it is argued that there is no fault because they arise simultaneously, we say no, for the same difficulty applies: of what is there simultaneity? Of that which has already come into being, or of that which has not yet come into being? If it is of that which has already come into being, how can there be simultaneity, given that it perishes immediately after arising, as its non-existence would follow as previously stated? As it is said in your own established doctrine: "That which is cognizable by the intellect, other than the three [unconditioned things], is conditioned and momentary."

That which is other than the triad known as space (*ākāśa*), analytical cessation (*pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*), and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*) is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) because it is produced by conditions; and because it is conditioned, it is momentary and impermanent. It is "momentary" (*kṣaṇika*) because it possesses a moment (*kṣaṇa*); its duration is only a single moment and not beyond that, and thus it is exclusively momentary and impermanent, lacking the kind of impermanence that persists over a period of time like the jar and other things favored by worldly people. According to this tenet, there is no consistency with the claim that those [factors] together, each individually, constitute the cause.

What is the reason? Because they perish immediately after attaining individuality; since each individual atom perishes at the very moment it acquires its own nature, what collective whole could there be? Or rather, what is the individual existence of those things which, due to their absolute difference in form and other qualities across space, necessarily differ in such a way that they remain inexpressible as they are? Thus, it is established that individuality is non-existent, because no other state is reached either spatially or temporally.

Furthermore, the attainment of individuality does not exist in this way either; even that attainment of individuality which belongs to atoms is likewise non-existent according to the method described above. This is because, due to their lack of duration in space and time and their perishability, they lack existence as mere attainment of intrinsic nature, just like the son of a barren woman. Just as there is no attainment of individuality for the sons of barren women, so too there is no attainment of individuality for those things considered atoms, because they do not persist and are non-existent;
thus, they perish immediately after [the supposed] attainment.

Furthermore, the attainment of individuality is likewise impossible because of non-existence, like the son of a barren woman. If it is argued that there is no fault because they arise simultaneously, we say no; for the same logic applies: of what is there simultaneity—of that which has come into being, or of that which has not? If it is of that which has come into being, since it perishes immediately after its arising, how can there be simultaneity? For, as already stated, this results in the very same consequence of non-existence.
"That which is to be cognized by the intellect, other than the triad, is conditioned and momentary.
Furthermore, the Nihilists (Vaināśikas) postulate: "That which is to be cognized by the intellect, other than the triad, is conditioned and momentary."
Furthermore, they call those three "cessation through deliberation" (*pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*), "cessation not through deliberation" (*apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*), and "space" (*ākāśa*).
They consider all three of these to be non-entities (*avastu*), mere non-existence (*abhāva-mātra*), and indefinable (*nirupākhyam*).

Indeed, it is said that the destruction of entities preceded by intelligence is called "cessation through deliberation"; its opposite is "cessation not through deliberation"; and space is merely the absence of obstruction—*Brahmasūtra-Śāṅkarabhāṣya* 4.2.12.
The manifestation of space is the non-limitation of space.
See page 96, line 30, regarding the readings *trayā* (in the Prajñāpāramitā) and *pratiṣṭhāpya* (in the Niḥsvabhāvaprakaraṇa).
*prāptānantabhā.* (Bhāṣya) *prānantabhā.* (Yaśomitra); each [term] is combined with *samu.* (Yaśomitra).
The state of abiding;
that which abides;
awaiting non-existence.

If it is argued that there is no fault because they arise simultaneously, the non-existence of those atoms remains unproven; for even those [entities] that do not persist [as a single whole] are admitted to arise simultaneously by virtue of occupying the same location and the same time. Therefore, the state of being a discrete individual is established.

And this is not so, because of the equality [of the two cases]; for the non-existence of atoms is equal to the non-existence of simultaneous production, since there is no production distinguished by difference of place or time. Since simultaneity is not established in either of the two alternatives, you must be asked: "Of what is there simultaneity—of that which has come into being, or of that which has not? Since these two alternatives are unavoidable, one who intends to state the answer that this question is untenable in both ways says:

The other says: "The conceptual construction that 'the non-existent co-exists' is illogical; for who would say that the non-existent, like a sky-flower, co-exists with the existent or the non-existent, such that this conceptual construction is put forward as a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*)? Therefore, we say that 'the existent co-exists. To this, the Teacher says: 'You yourself, while stating these two alternatives—that atoms are the cause either in their individual states or when combined—consider this: who has ever said such a thing?'"

What is the point of this? Let whoever says it say it: if there is simultaneous arising of what has already come into being, then since it perishes immediately after arising, how can there be simultaneity in the doctrine of momentariness? The meaning is that there is no cause for the simultaneity of anything with anything else, as stated previously. By the principle of extension (*atideśa*), it has been said that when there is absolute difference in terms of place and time, those things whose intrinsic nature is inexpressible cannot even attain individuality; likewise, because they would consequently fall into non-existence, how could there be simultaneity among atoms? This is the connection [of the argument].

Furthermore, you speak of the arising of that which has already been attained; however, in that case, even the collection of a barren woman’s son would exist, because it is non-existent and lacks stability, just like a collection of atoms or a continuum.
If this is argued, then that [collection] is exactly the same.
Now, if it should be said: "All this contradiction and affliction is produced solely by the conceptualization of the intrinsic nature of external objects."
"This triple world is consciousness-only;

there exists nothing distinct from it by way of substantial reality or conventional truth—surely, O beloved of the gods! this undertaking is for the very purpose of demolishing the doctrine of consciousness-only, just like your own view."
Concomitance (*sahatva*) means simultaneity (*yaugapadya*); since this has not been attained, it would result in non-existence.
Therefore, the claim that there is no fault because of simultaneous arising is not a valid defense.
Furthermore, if the arising of what has not yet come into being is intended to be simultaneous, even that concomitance is not tenable, as it leads to an undesirable consequence.

What is the undesirable consequence? It would follow that even a collection of the sons of barren women would exist; why is this undesirable? Because it is non-existent and lacks stability, just like a collection of atoms—this is the direct demonstration of the undesirable consequence. Furthermore, even a collection of atoms would not exist, because it is non-existent and lacks stability, just like a collection of the sons of barren women.

The two reasons—non-existence (*abhūtatva*) and non-abiding (*asthitatva*)—are stated because they are established for both the proponent of emptiness (*śūnyavādin*) and the proponent of momentariness (*kṣaṇikavādin*).

If it is argued that [the fault does not apply] "because of the continuum" (*santānāt*), the thought might be: "Although non-existence and non-abiding are accepted by them, nevertheless, because there is no interruption in the continuum of birth and destruction, there is abiding; therefore, since they arise together, there is no fault."

And this is incorrect, because that [series] is likewise [subject to the same analysis]: would that series be existent or non-existent? If it is existent, how can there be a series, since—as already stated—there is no series other than those things that perish immediately after arising? If it exists as something distinct from them, being different in character and eternal, then the thesis of universal momentariness is abandoned. If, on the other hand, it is non-existent, then it is subject to the very same faults previously mentioned, such as being like the son of a barren woman; thus, the fault of [the series] not arising remains.
It should be understood that [the text] is accompanied by [the word] *saha* and *oḍya*,
as established in the Bhāṣya and the Ya manuscript.
This [is] the activity;
thus it is explained.
By this, [the refutation of] the doctrine of primordial existence (*prāgvāda*) and so forth [is established].
(Bhāṣya: *vādaḥ*; Yaśomitra: *vādaḥ*)

If it is argued that because atoms do not arise [as a collection], even a collection of the sons of barren women would exist— on account of their being non-existent and non-located, just like a collection of atoms due to the continuity [of the series]— then that too is exactly the same.
Now, it might be argued: "This entire affliction of contradiction is produced by the apprehension of the true nature of external objects;
this triple world is consciousness-only (*vijñānamātra*), and there exists nothing distinct from it, such as substantiality or conventional reality."

O beloved of the gods! Is it not the case that this undertaking is precisely for the purpose of demolishing the doctrine of consciousness (*vijñānavāda*), just like your own view? This is the fault [of your argument].
[The rest of the text is] for the sake of the one accompanied by... [corrupt].
dāyāpiya (Bhāṣya) / dāpi (Syāt) / ato tvādasthita (Praśasti)
The reality of that [is] the exclusion of what is to be accomplished by the continuum;
it is youthful.

As stated with its reason, [the opponent might argue]: "The eternal [nature] is not logical," and it may be said: "Because of the intrinsic nature of external objects," and so forth, up to "therefore there exists something distinct from that."

Now, "atha" (now) marks a new topic. Now, in the view that cognition has as its object a collection [of atoms], the various arguments put forward are rendered fruitless and fallacious; therefore, having abandoned that position, this is said: "All this confusion regarding contradiction is produced by the apprehension of the reality of external objects. This confusion arises when there is the apprehension that 'the reality of an object exists external to consciousness.'"

If atoms were the objective support (*ālambana*), then there would be a contradiction with the accepted doctrine that they are beyond the senses (*atīndriya*) and that [cognition] has a composite object as its support. If, on the other hand, it is the aggregate (*samudāya*), then because it is non-existent, like a sky-flower, it could not be an objective support at all. Whether they are taken individually or collectively, the aforementioned logical principles lead to faults such as self-contradiction. Why, then, should we be afflicted by the mental distress born from raising such contradictions? Rather, let us resort to this alternative conception which is free from all defects: that these three worlds are mere consciousness (*vijñānamātra*).

As it has been said: "The earth, wind, ether, oceans, rivers, and the directions exist as if external, though they are actually portions of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇatattva). — Vākyapadīya 3.7.102.

7.41 Thus, there is no such thing as substantial conventional reality (*dravya-saṃvṛti*) and so forth; nor, within this conceptualization, does such defilement exist as would belong to those who maintain that the various categories of objects—conceived as "this is conventionally real," "this is ultimately real," "this is sensory," or "this is supersensory"—are distinct from consciousness. For they do not exist as something separate from it.
Therefore, the investigation is useless,
except for the purpose of [establishing] the meaning of sentences, the substance of statements, and the collection of words.
May the earth, wind, ether, oceans, rivers, and the directions, together with the lords of speech, protect us. May they grant us forgiveness.
The ocean,
the sky, the earth, the wind, the sun, the oceans, the rivers,
and the directions are the external manifestations of the components of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa-tattva).
—Thus is the reading in the printed *Vākyapadīya*:
"The parts of the principle of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇatattva*) exist as if situated externally. (*Vākyapadīya* 3.7.41).
According to the *Nabhā*, substance (*dravya*) consists of concealment (*saṃvṛti*) and so forth.
"By way of substantial convention (*dravyasaṃvṛti*), there is no [self] here"—here too, the reading might be "there is this.
To this it is replied: "But, O Beloved of the Gods (*devānāmpriya*), this undertaking is indeed for the purpose of demolishing the doctrine of Idealism (*vijñānavāda*), just like your own view."

As for this: let it be for now that in the absence of external objects there is an absence of being an object of cognition (*vijñeya*), and in the absence of being an object of cognition there is an absence of consciousness (*vijñāna*).
For consciousness consists of direct perception and so forth;
therein, what is this "all" of the three realms that is said to be "consciousness-only"? It cannot be merely direct perceptual consciousness, because it exists in such a state [of being dependent].

It is not merely inferential cognition, because that too is preceded by [sensory perception]; since it would be unestablished if that were unestablished—just as there is no cloth without threads—this undertaking of mine is for the purpose of refuting both your doctrine that "perception is free from conceptual construction" (kalpanāpoḍha) and the word of the Buddha which accords with it, as well as for the purpose of refuting the doctrine of consciousness-only (vijñānamātra), because that too was propounded by you, a teacher of a rival school.

Alternatively, one might argue that because that [emptiness] is the ultimate reality and because all Buddhist teachings are intended to demonstrate it, this undertaking is solely for the purpose of refuting it; however, this too should be understood as incorrect due to the absence of valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, since the absence of objects of cognition (*prameya*) follows from the absence of means of cognition, that very fault remains. To show this, he says: "Let it be for now," and so forth.

And intending to demonstrate that by means of a logical method, he says: "In the absence of external objects, there is an absence of being an object of cognition, because that [external object] consists of nothing but consciousness."

And in the absence of being an object of cognition (*vijñeyatva*), its status as consciousness (*vijñānatva*) also does not exist; for it is called "consciousness" because it cognizes. What does it cognize in the absence of an object of cognition? Consequently, due to the absence of being an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*), there is an absence of being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatva*) for perception. Thus, what is this so-called "perception" that is distinct from the object of knowledge, the act of knowing, the means of knowledge, and the state of being an object of knowledge—like a flower in the sky? This fault is difficult to avoid. Let that remain for now; rather, let us consider this further by way of accepting its existence, starting with the words "For consciousness... and so forth.

The word *hi* is used in the sense of providing an illustration; for it is observed in the world that "cognition" (*vijñāna*) refers to perception and so forth. Perception and inference are the two valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), while by the inclusion of the term "and so forth," cognitions characterized by doubt, error, and indecision—which are considered pseudo-means of knowledge (*pramāṇābhāsa*)—are also included.

Regarding this, you must be questioned: having determined among those [cognitions], which one alone constitutes this entire triple-world (*traidhātuka*)? The intention is that not even a single cognition is "mere-cognition" (*vijñānamātra*).

You might say: "It is merely perceptual cognition. That is not so; it is not merely perceptual cognition because it exists in such a state. This state of that very perceptual cognition is as we have explained: it is neither an object consisting of form and so forth, nor an object consisting of a collection, nor is it caused by the eye and so forth, whether conventionally or ultimately; thus, it cannot be merely perceptual cognition.
You might think: "It is merely inferential cognition.
That too is not merely inferential cognition.

What is the reason? Because that too is preceded by that; because that inference is also preceded by that—namely, preceded by perception. For inference, which consists of conceptualization arising subsequent to one's own direct experience and is born immediately after non-conceptual knowledge, is held to be mental and sensory, and thus necessarily preceded by the mental perception of a yogin. If that very perception is not established, how can inference be established? Therefore, it is not merely inference [that fails]; hence he says: "If that is unestablished, there is no establishment, like a cloth without threads."
Just as a cloth preceded by threads is not established when the threads are not established—because it is preceded by them—so too inference is not established when perception is not established;
thus, for now, there is no proof that [the world] consists solely of the cognition of the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

If that is the case, then let there be only the cognition consisting of the conceptualization of doubt, error, and so forth; yet even that is not merely the cognition consisting of the conceptualization of doubt, error, and so forth—meaning it is neither doubt alone nor error alone (the term "and so forth" including neither the mere imitation of experiences encountered in dreams nor the mere appearance of hair-nets and the like seen by one with ophthalmia)—because all of this, being conceptual in nature, is a fallacy of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāsa*), and precisely because it is preceded by perception, it remains unestablished in the absence of that [perception]; therefore, it is also not merely non-determination (*anadhyavasāya*), since the latter is characterized by a lack of apprehension (*anavagrahātmakatva*).

Therefore, it is not mere consciousness; enough with this overly expansive discussion. And by this very same line of reasoning, there is a refutation based on one's own words even for the proponent of the doctrine of non-distinction (*aviśeṣaikāntavādin*), who asserts that "in the state where everything is of the nature of everything, the function of hearing and so forth is direct perception" (Ṣaṣṭitantra). This is because, due to the absence of conceptualization and the consequent lack of differentiation, [his own assertion] is established [as self-contradictory].
It might be thought: "Let it be mere non-determination (anadhyavasāya).
But even that is not mere non-determination; the meaning is that it is not a state whose nature consists of unperceived and unmanifest pleasure, pain, and so forth.
What is the reason? Because its essence is not one of grasping (anavagraha); for there is no such thing as knowledge that is absolutely unperceived.

Even if there is an unmanifest cognition, because it is indistinct, it does not consist of the apprehension of its object; therefore, it is not even a cognition at all, since cognition is defined as that which "cognizes" (*vijānāti*). And since such [indistinct cognition] does not cognize anything, it is not merely a cognition lacking determinate judgment (*anadhyavasāya*). Therefore, it is not mere cognition, because it is not included within the categories of valid cognition, fallacious cognition, or cognition in general. What, then, is this "mere cognition" (*vijñānamātra*) of which you speak? Since there is no other cognition apart from these aforementioned types of cognition, this so-called "mere cognition" is nothing at all.

Thus, enough with this overly prolix discussion; he concludes by summarizing, because the definition of perception has been refuted in every respect. Otherwise, there would still be scope for many further elaborations of refutation.

In this way, first of all, the perception postulated by the proponents of the doctrine of absolute particularity (*viśeṣaikāntavādin*)—which is distinct from worldly perception—is not tenable, because it involves contradictions that are difficult to overcome due to its dependence on its own words. Let alone the absence of being an object of cognition (*vijñeyatva*) when external objects do not exist, and the absence of consciousness (*vijñānatva*) when there is an absence of being an object of cognition.
For consciousness consists of direct perception and so forth;

therein, what is this "consciousness-only" (vijñānamātra) that comprises all three realms? It cannot be mere direct perceptual consciousness, because such consciousness exists only in that specific state [of sensory engagement].

Nor can it be mere inferential consciousness, because inference is preceded by that [direct perception], and if the latter is unestablished, the former is likewise unestablished—just as there is no cloth without threads.
For the Buddhists, there is no consciousness consisting of conceptual constructions such as doubt or error that is not struck down by [the aforementioned arguments].
In the passage "gamenaivānyathā pra...",
there may also be the reading "gamenaivānyathā"; [this refers to] the *vijñāna* portion of the *bhāṣya*.
...the consciousness of one who is intoxicated by [the pride of] "I," which is the state of being thus situated within all the three realms... O humble one!
This state would be such;
this state would be such, because [it] is preceded by that, being preceded by direct perception.
Because [inference] is preceded by perception (pratyakṣapūrvakatvāt), [it arises] from the sensory cognition (indriyapratyayaṃ) [of the mark].
Even if that [non-existence] were established by means of [the absence of] perception,
that too would be merely a conceptual construction such as doubt or error; [this applies] to the end [of the argument].
Or rather, for this very reason, it is not merely non-determination (*anadhyavasāya*), because that [non-determination] lacks the nature of apprehension (*anavagraha*);
therefore, it is not mere consciousness (*vijñānamātra*). Enough with this overly expansive discussion.

And by this very same method, for the proponent of the non-distinct monism (*aviśeṣaikāntavādin*) who asserts that "everything has everything as its nature" and claims that "the operation of the ear and other senses is perception (*pratyakṣa*) [and] the sixty [categories]," there is an implication (*ākṣepa*) based solely on his own words: because it is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*), there is an absence of differentiation,
and thus it is unmanifest (*avyakta*) and cannot be cognized.
For that [object] of hers is not entirely unperceived;
here, there may also be the reading "yadapy" instead of "yadapya". It is a valid means of knowledge.
In the future cognition,
there is no appearance of the object;
even though it is distinct, there is no appearance.
And by this very same direction, it should be understood that "implication (*ākṣepa*) consists precisely in the dependence on one's own words"—this is the remainder of the sentence.
To whom does this extension (*atideśa*) apply? It applies even to the proponent of non-distinction (*aviśeṣaikāntavādin*);

by the word "even" (*api*), it includes the proponent of distinction (*viśeṣavādin*) mentioned immediately prior, as well as the proponent of both (*ubhayavādin*), since [the argument] is impossible for them.

In this regard, the collection of faults previously stated against the proponent of particularity—who maintains that perception is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*)—is now to be addressed in reverse order. Having established through a series of reasons that [such perception] would result in being conceptual by nature, non-perceptual, inferential, a unity of both, a confusion, non-existent, expressible, lacking its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), and further, being designatable by words due to the lack of distinction between the producer (*kāraka*) and the indicator (*jñāpaka*); and subsequently, even having accepted the absence of conceptual construction, [the faults such as] the non-existence of the eye, of form, and of the cognition thereof due to the absence of the definitions of both the particular and the universal; all these are to be explained now in reverse sequence. He indicates the direction of this [explanation] with the passage beginning "If everything were of the nature of everything" and continuing until "it would not be a sense-faculty."

Thus, by extension of the refutation of the definition: for the Sāṅkhya as well, who maintains the non-distinction that "everything is of the nature of everything," there can be no conceptual differentiation—whether by distinctions of form, taste, and so forth, or by distinctions of the auditory organ and so forth—of a single entity that is of the nature of all things; consequently, like the proponent of the absolute particular (viśeṣaikāntavādin), his [doctrine] is devoid of conceptualization due to its similarity to the ultimate atom, which is non-conceptual in its ultimate reality.

Because of its non-conceptual nature (*avikalpakatva*), just as there were previously stated faults in the definition and example of perception (*pratyakṣa*)—such as "the eye is not truly the eye," "form is not truly form," and "consciousness is not truly consciousness"—so too [are there faults] regarding the function of the ear and other senses. For one who asserts that perception is the function of the ear and so forth—that is, the function presided over by the mind (*manas*) belonging to the ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose, operating respectively in the apprehension of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell, and constituting the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) called perception—if everything is of the nature of everything (*sarvasarvātmakatva*), then due to the absence of conceptualization and the consequent lack of distinction, what is the ear that is distinct from the skin and the rest? And what is the non-ear (skin, etc. that is distinct from the ear? Furthermore, regarding what was said, "the ear and so forth" (*śrotrādi*): since all things are a single entity whose nature is everything, what is the ear? What is the non-ear? What is the beginning (*ādi*)? What is the non-beginning? What is the function (*vṛtti*)? Or what is the non-function? With respect to what? Or with respect to what not? What is the sense-organ (*akṣa*)? What is the non-sense-organ? And so forth? For in both the world and the scriptures, perception is the direct realization of the true nature of an object.

But that [perception] is not characterized as such by you, for its nature as non-conceptual is unestablished, since it possesses the nature of conceptual construction and so forth, like error and the like.

Regarding the state of having a "collected" (*sañcita*) object: as stated previously, since a single [atom] such as form (*rūpa*) is not a "collected" object—just as it is not a non-collected one—there is an absence of mutual dependence and division, such as that between a jar or its first, second, and subsequent parts. What, then, is the beginning, middle, or end? What is the "activity" (*vṛtti*) of those [senses] such as hearing, which did not function previously but function later, being distinguished by difference in time and by a different state? Or what is "non-activity," characterized by the cessation of activity, precisely because of the absence of division? With reference to what, and what other entity, is something called "perceptual" (*pratyakṣa*) in relation to that? Because the neuter gender is a domain of doubt regarding unmanifest qualities, the question is: "With reference to what? (*kiṃ prati*)?

What is "non-sense" (*aprati*)? If there is a unity consisting of the essence of everything (*sarvasarvātmakaikatva*), what would not depend upon what? Is "sense" (*akṣa*) that which is distinct from its object, such as the ear and so forth, or mutually distinct [from one another]? Or is "non-sense" (*anakṣa*) that which is distinct from the senses, such as the objects like form (*rūpa*) and so forth, or mutually distinct [from one another]? In demonstrating this, since there is no such division, the formulation of definitions through division involves an insurmountable contradiction due to the requirement of one's own words;
Without the occurrence of both existence and non-existence, and without the agent of origination, [there is] non-existence.
See page 71, line 4 for "ityādi" and so forth;
and [there is] the non-existence of this, according to the Bhāṣya.
The non-existence of that very [thing], Ya, folio 72, line 1; consisting of a single self, Ya.
See the kalpaka section, page 71, line 4:

What is the ear? What is not the ear? What is the beginning? What is without beginning? What is function? Or what is non-function? What is directed toward? What is not directed toward? What is the sense organ? What is not the sense organ? And so forth.

In both the world and in the treatises, direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is indeed the immediate realization of the true nature of an object; however, according to your view, perception does not have such a definition, because its non-conceptual nature (*nirvikalpatva*) is unestablished, since it consists of conceptual construction (*kalpanātmaka*) and so forth, like error and the like. Furthermore, regarding the position that [perception] has an aggregate as its objective support (*ālambana*), as stated previously, a single entity such as form (*rūpa*) is not an aggregate, just as a jar [is not a single atom].
An entity exists in dependence upon another entity; since all entities are of the nature of being mutually dependent, what single thing is not dependent upon another?
In the case of the identity of being composed of [the self] and oneness, each one is not required;
[this is] difficult to overcome due to mutual dependence,
such as the grasping of wealth and so forth.
Furthermore, according to your own view, the definition of perception is untenable;

for both in the world and in the treatises, perception is defined as the direct apprehension of the intrinsic nature (*svatattva*) of an object. The "intrinsic nature" of an object is its own unique, specific form; that apprehension of it which is not mediated [by anything else] is perception.

However, that [perception] does not possess the characteristics of perception as you define it, just like your own position (*tvanmatavat*). Just as it was stated in your view—wherein everything is of the nature of everything—that the functioning of the auditory organ and so forth is impossible because the functioning of the ear and other senses would have as its object only a portion of a thing that consists of all things (such as sound), and because there is no differentiation since the true essence of a thing is a single totality; in the same way, the definition of perception—whether worldly (*laukika*) or conventional (*sāmayika*)—which is intended to be the direct apprehension of the true essence of that non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*) reality, is untenable. This is because its non-conceptuality is unestablished. Indeed, that perception is not non-conceptual, because its object is the conceptual differentiation of distinctions such as sound and so forth. Furthermore, the true essence of a thing, which is undivided and wherein everything is of the nature of everything, is not its object; therefore, it is of the nature of conceptual construction (*kalpanātmaka*). Because it is of the nature of conceptual construction, because it consists of the conceptualization of determination, because it consists of an apprehension contrary to the objective support, because it consists of superimposition (*adhyāropa*), because its object is not of the nature of a universal, because it functions upon both that and what is not that, because it consists of the grasping of the identity between existence and non-existence, and because its object is in every respect common [to all], it is not perception—just like erroneous cognition, doubt, inference, and so forth. This is the conclusion. *Note: The term *sarvasarvātmakatva* refers to the monistic doctrine that everything is identical with everything else.*
That which is stated in worldly treatises as being outside [of this]— namely, elsewhere than in the *Pratyabhijñā-hṛdaya*— is indeed [mere] perception (*pratyakṣa*).

[The proof] is direct perception (pratyakṣa), because [the probandum] is established by the exclusion of what is other than your own position (tan-mata-raṃhī-tvāt). Proof (pra°). Pā॰ ḍe॰ līṃ॰ vi॰ bhā॰. Tanu. Tvan-mata-raṃhī-tvāt-siddheḥ. Pra°.
...because it possesses the state of being an object of cognition, like that which consists of [the self]... Ya.
Let it be seen (pṛṣṭha 63, line 1):

"As stated in the section on the object as a collection" (*sañcitālambanasthāna*), and so forth, up to "because [the universal] does not exist in the blue and other [colors]"—by this, he demonstrates the direction of the means for contemplating the meaning of the extended passage, lest there be confusion.

Just as we stated in the section on the object as a collection—that the collection of atoms, blue and so forth, is a universal and is non-existent because it is a conventional reality (*saṃvṛtisattva*)—here, however, the opposite is the case: the collection is the ultimate reality (*paramārthatva*), while the blue and so forth are conventional realities.

Since [the whole] is absent in blue and other [parts], and even if it were possible [to conceive of it], it would be beyond the senses (*atīndriya*) and thus unfit to be an objective support (*ālambana*), it follows that the objective support of visual and other consciousnesses is the aggregate (*saṅghāta*) of form and so forth.

Furthermore, since those [parts] do not exist as ultimate realities (*paramārthataḥ*) individually, they cannot be its objects; all such points should be applied here in full according to their respective parts by means of establishing the distinction between difference and non-difference, and between the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) and the ultimate (*paramārtha*).
Thus, blue and the rest are conventionally existent and are accessible to the senses, but the aggregate is not ultimately real.

What is the reason? Because it consists of form (*rūpa*) and so forth; and because even though form and the rest—which constitute a single part of that [whole]—are not ultimately real, they exist in an undivided state. A single, non-universal (i.e., partial) object of cognition, such as form, taste, or sound, is never an object of perception in the way that unaggregated atoms were held to be non-sensory in the previous theory. Thus, in this present theory, since such [partial objects] are absent from jars and the like, or from blue and the like—which are accepted as being perceptible through worldly and supramundane conventional usage—the knowledge whose object is that [whole] is not perception. This is the connection [of the argument].
What is meant? Form (*rūpa*) and the other [sensory objects] exist only as having a single, universal nature (*sarvaikātmarūpa*), and not as having separate individual natures (*pṛthaksvarūpa*).
Therefore, the cognition whose object they are is not a direct perception (*apratyakṣa*) because its object is non-existent, just like a cognition whose object is the son of a barren woman.

Following this line of reasoning, the entire detailed argument previously stated against the proponent of the doctrine of particularity (*viśeṣaikāntavādin*)—namely, that "that which appears in a direct perception does not exist as an object, and that which exists does not appear in a direct perception," and so forth—should be applied here as well.

Regarding the phrase "even if such a possibility were granted," and so forth: even if one were to grant the possibility that a single entity such as *rūpa* (form) could be the substance called *pradhāna*, characterized by the state of equilibrium among the qualities (*guṇas*) of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, that state of equilibrium—which consists in the absence of the differentiation of all things into sound and so forth—can never be established. Furthermore, even if that unmanifest (*avyakta*) were granted, because that unmanifest is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), it cannot logically serve as an objective support (*ālambana*); therefore, it follows that the objective support for visual and other sensory cognitions is the aggregate of form and the other [sensory objects].

Furthermore, those [objects] such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth are each non-existent from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). The word "iti" is used in the sense of a reason; therefore, for this reason—namely, because they have a collection of form and so forth as their objective support (*ālambana*), and because they lack individual ultimate existence—they do not possess the status of being objects.
Form and the others are not the objects of the eye and so forth, because they are non-existent ultimately, like the son of a barren woman.
Alternatively, perception does not have form and the others as its object, because its object is non-existent ultimately, like the cognition of the son of a barren woman.

Therefore, that entity which is designated by synonyms such as *yoni*, *bīja*, *prakṛti*, *bahudhānaka*, *pradhāna*, and *avyakta* is imperceptible because it is beyond the senses; whereas that which is an object of the senses—such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth within a composite of various transformations—is not ultimately real (*paramārthasat*).

Thus, one should apply this according to each respective part, following the same logic for every part as it applies to the doctrine of absolute particularity (*viśeṣaikāntavāda*), and conversely, for the doctrine of absolute generality (*aviśeṣaikāntavāda*), wherever something is applicable, it should be applied accordingly. This recalls the meaning of the preceding text.

He states this even for the purpose of merely indicating the direction of that method of application: "By means of the systematic establishment of the positions of difference and non-difference, the conventional and the ultimate.

In that [system], those atoms which are of the nature of difference and are ultimately real (*paramārthasat*) are here conventionally real (*saṃvṛtisat*), according to the doctrine of the ultimate wherein everything has everything as its essence; whereas that which is there the non-difference, namely the collection of atoms, is conventionally real but is here ultimately real (*paramārthasat*). This is to be applied by means of this systematic establishment; see page 64, line 1.

Since [the whole] is absent in the blue and other [parts], and even if it were possible [to conceive of it] in that way, it would be beyond the senses (*atīndriya*) and thus cannot function as an objective support (*ālambana*); therefore, it follows that for visual and other cognitions, the objective support is the aggregate (*saṅghāta*) of form and so forth.

And since those [parts] are individually non-existent from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), they are not its objects. All of this, beginning with these points, should be applied here according to their respective parts, by means of establishing the distinction between difference and non-difference, and the positions of conventional and ultimate reality. (Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya)
...also for that which is in the state of non-manifestation,
the word "pra" [is used] according to its [proper] application.
anuṣṭhityaya Bhā., anuṣvatya Pra.;
for the sake of attainment.
...antaḥ tatra bhāraṃ pā antaḥ tatra ḍe līṃ vi hīṃ...
The text should be joined again with the subsequent passage beginning with *satṛ*, *sotraya*, *sa*, *śautra*, and *bhā*.

For example: when a collection of form (*rūpa*) and so forth, or sentient beings (*sattva*) and so forth—which possesses a single nature that is not distinct from the internal essence consisting of the totality of all things—is in contact with the senses, this cognition arises which has as its object a blue form that is manifold in its designations yet appears as a single nature contrary to the objective reality; and this [cognition] is not un-designatable because it is designated by the apprehension of the "all-encompassing" nature, just as fire is apprehended through smoke by way of its general characteristic (*sāmānya*), and not as something whose form is indefinable.

Even in the doctrine of absolute manifoldness (*nānātvaikāntavāda*), that which is produced from the contact of the self, the sense organ, the mind, and the object is something distinct [from them], according to Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 3.1.4.1.

Since substances and so forth lack any foundational reality, what is the self and so on? Thus, it is not perceived directly. What is the reason? It is because [the self] is imagined as a single form distinct from that [perceived reality]. Is it not the case that everything is designated as a causal factor (*kāraka-hetu*) based on direct perception, rather than being designated as an indicative cause (*jñāpaka-hetu*)—like smoke for fire—for the sake of establishing another entity characterized by multiple forms?

Indeed, this was introduced by us precisely to demonstrate this very point: if this [cognition] were a perception (*pratyakṣa*), it would arise from the causal factor itself—the objective support (*ālambana*)—just like the experience of burning; for perception consists in immediate apprehension, has the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object, and is non-superimpositional (*anadhyāropātmaka*).

Furthermore, even the status of being a causal factor does not belong to everything therein, because, like a second moon, it is ultimately non-existent and exists merely as a conventional determination of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*).

In common worldly usage, "designation" (*vyapadeśa*) refers to a specific instruction regarding all sentient beings that is distinct from the object itself; by means of that designation, the object of cognition (*prameya*) is designated and inferred, not perceived directly—just like fire inferred from smoke—whether the entity functions as a causal agent or not, as in the case of a father or smoke [as a designation for the son or the fire].

1.18 Since [the self] is devoid of a basis such as substance and so forth, how could there be a self? Thus, it is not perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because it is conceptually constructed (*kalpita*) based on the distinct causes for the existence of substances, forms, and other qualities.
Compare page 66, line 1;

Furthermore, even though it is comparable [to a universal] on page 68, line 1, and is both denotable and non-denotable, and although it possesses a manifold nature, blue is nevertheless not [a universal], because— just like fire inferred [by smoke]— its object is both unitary and manifold.

For that determination of the form "blue" is indeed a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). It is either because it superimposes a single essence onto multiple forms—each atom having its own distinct intrinsic nature—or because it superimposes multiple forms, such as color, onto a single entity that is essentially identical to everything; or because its object is a universal form of another color; or because it functions with respect to both that and what is not that; or because it is non-exclusion (*anapoha*) or exclusion (*apoha*), like the inference of fire. Its very nature as a universal consists in the grasping of the distinction between blue atoms and the conventional designation of an aggregate established in ultimate reality. Because it is of the nature of a conceptualization that discriminates a common object, it is not direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), since it is of the nature of a cognition that lacks [sensory] causal conditions, just like the cognition that a word is inaudible.

Because [the object] is both conventional and beyond the senses, causality does not exist in the case of blue and other such [colors], nor in their collection, with respect to the cognition that apprehends them as such.

Furthermore, inferential knowledge does not fulfill that [cognition], because it apprehends something connected [to the object] in a manner different from how it is actually perceived, just like the cognition of contradictory [reasons] and so forth; this is the same [in all cases].
Therefore, setting aside whatever else may fall under that same process according to its possibility, everything that is common to both [types of cognition] should be applied here.

Thus, it has been stated that the perception postulated by those who maintain the one-sided views of either distinction (*viśeṣa*) or non-distinction (*aviśeṣa*) is improper—even if imagined—because it is distinct from worldly perception and because it is riddled with contradictions resulting from its dependence on its own words. Furthermore, it follows that even in the doctrine of absolute difference (*nānātvaikāntavāda*), perception regarding the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*) is untenable; this is what is understood [from the context].

What is that perception like, or how is it untenable? [The opponent claims: "That which arises from the contact of the self, the sense organ, the mind, and the object is distinct; perception arises from the contact of four, three, or two [of these]—namely, the self with the mind, the mind with the sense organ, and the sense organ with the object. This view of those who maintain the doctrine of absolute manifoldness (*anekāntavāda*) is also not perception, because its foundational categories such as substance (*dravya*) and so forth lack a basis. What is this "self" and so on? It is not perception. Those things of which substance is the first are "substance and the rest"—namely, substance, quality (*guṇa*), action (*karman*), generality (*sāmānya*), particularity (*viśeṣa*), and inherence (*samavāya*). Because they are not substances, they would not exist as distinct from substances, just like a sky-flower. Likewise, they could not be distinct from qualities because they lack qualities; they could not be distinct from actions because they lack action; they could not be distinct from generalities because they lack generality; they could not be distinct from particulars because they lack particularity; and they could not be distinct from inherence because they lack inherence. Furthermore, because they lack a foundation, all of them are like a sky-flower.
Its lack of foundation is due to its being unchanging, like the son of a barren woman;

therefore, since the self and so forth do not exist, in the absence of a self, mind, sense-faculties, and objects, what is this "self" etc., from whose contact with [objects] cognition would arise? Whose would it be, given the absence of the substance *ātman*? What is it, given the absence of qualities (*guṇa*)? The word "iti" has the sense of a reason, as in the expression "I am the king’s man, therefore I am not afraid. Thus, it is not perception; the meaning is that there is no perception because of the non-existence of substances such as the *ātman* and qualities such as cognition.

He explains that very point previously stated—that because of the superimposition of something else upon those [entities] such as the self (*ātman*) which exist in reality as manifold-natured (*anekāntātmaka*), and because of reasons such as being of the nature of conceptual construction (*kalpanātmakatva*), it is not perception, just like error and so forth—by means of the passage beginning with "the substance, form, etc. and ending with "because of conceptual construction":

"from the conceptual construction of any one of the manifold natures of the entities that are the effect and its non-effect, due to the nature of conceptual construction and so forth, it is like error and so forth."

Therefore, just as worldly consensus accepts the existence of generalities (*sāmānya*) and particularities (*viśeṣa*) as objects such as jars in accordance with reality that is not contradicted by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), this positive injunction holds: even those who follow the Vedic doctrine rely upon this worldly authority (*lokapramāṇaka*) of the theory of omniscience (*ājñānikavāda*). By this [theory], through the apprehension of substance (*dravya*), there is the apprehension of earth and the others, as well as all their imagined qualities; through the apprehension of quality (*guṇa*), the apprehension of existence (*bhāva*); through the apprehension of being (*sattā*), the apprehension of the universal "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth, down to the ultimate particularity (*antyaviśeṣa*); and through the apprehension of the cause, there is the apprehension of constituent substances such as parts, as well as qualities like conjunction (*saṃyoga*), actions (*karman*), and so on.
By the mention of "effects" (*kārya*), there is the inclusion of composite substances such as dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth, as well as qualities such as variegated color (*citra*) and the like.

In that regard, the categories just mentioned—substance and the rest—are, in the ultimate sense, non-exclusive (*anekānta*); their own nature (*svatattva*) consists of being substance, form and so forth, existence (*bhavana*), particularity (*viśeṣa*), cause, and effect.

To conceive of any one of these as absolute is to fall into unreality (*atattva*), [holding] that it is substance alone, quality alone, action alone, existence alone, or particularity alone, and not its other inherent natures.
Therefore, its nature as conceptual construction (kalpanātmakatva) is established;
consequently, due to this nature as conceptual construction and other such factors, it is not direct perception (apratyakṣa), just like error and so forth.

These factors—nature as conceptual construction and the rest—are characterized by being cognitions contrary to the object of apprehension (ālambana) which consists of the previously mentioned superimposition (adhyāropa).

Therefore, by the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*), he concludes what was previously asserted—that a thing exists exactly as it is apprehended in the world—along with its supporting arguments: that it exists precisely as accepted by the world, which is established in a state of conventional practice regarding reality that is consistent with all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and accompanied by supporting arguments. The "reality" (*tattva*) of each respective thing is its mode of being (*bhāva*), which is non-contradictory; it is not determined by the means of valid cognition—perception, inference, or scripture—as having the nature of cause, effect, both, or neither. "Conventional practice regarding reality" (*tattvavyavahāra*) refers to the activity of reality through reality. The "state of establishment" (*samavasthā*) is that of the world (*loka*) which abides in that [conventional practice]. The "acceptance by that world" (*lokaparigraha*) is the acceptance by such a world. Thus, "that which exists like that" (*tadvat*) means it exists in a manner equal to that [worldly acceptance].

The word "eva" (only) serves as a restriction: the universal and the particular are exactly like that worldly apprehension; they are neither merely the universal nor merely the particular, nor are they mutually distinct or non-distinct, as they are postulated in the technical treatises.

Alternatively, "the world" refers to that which is established in a reality and conventional practice (*tattva-vyavahāra*) that is non-contradictory to all means of valid cognition (*sarva-pramāṇāvirodhin*); for such a world, generality and particularity exist only as its constituent elements and not otherwise, as it has been demonstrated that they have *ghaṭa* (pot) and so forth as their objects. Just as in the world, the very existence (*bhavana*) of a pot and so forth is both the general and the particular; through the aforementioned method, by way of the non-distinction of existence in the forms of substance, space, time, and state (*dravya-kṣetra-kāla-bhāva*), or by the distinction of cause and effect, they are determined everywhere, yet not by fixed boundaries, and thus their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is not definitively restricted.
