In brief, there are four types of proponents [of doctrines], as declared in the fourth section of the *Sthānāṅga Sūtra*: namely, the proponent of action (*kiriyāvāī*), the proponent of non-action (*akiriyāvāī*), the proponent of ignorance (*aṇṇāṇiyavāī*), and the proponent of fate (*veṇaiyavāī*).
Another classification is that this entire world, beginning with the earth and so forth, is bound solely by ignorance.

The sense organs as well are composed of that [intellect] alone and are insentient, because they are its instruments. Regarding that object which is in contact with the senses, there exists a unique nature distinct from other substances; yet, because this nature—such as that of the self (*ātman*) and so forth—is supersensible (*atīndriya*), it has never been perceived at any time or place. Consequently, there is no means of defining it as "this is that. By "definition" (*nirūpaṇa*), we mean a determinative cognition (*niścaya-jñāna*).

Why is there no means of definition such as "this is that"? It is said: because its perception is impossible either individually or in a collection. Since that unique form is unprecedented (*apūrva*), precisely because of its unprecedented nature, its perception is impossible, and thus its determination is impossible.

To begin with, individually, each single jar is not perceived in its own nature as having a black or other color, because it is unprecedented [in that state]. For that very reason, how can there be a determination of those whose natures are not determined individually within a collection? It is like the absence of oil being determined in a collection of sands when it has not been determined in each individual grain. Determination (*nirūpaṇa*) is the act of ascertaining through form; since the means for that is absent, everything is indeed obstructed by ignorance. Thus it was well said: "The ignorant person does not perceive even while perceiving; the wise person perceives. *Bhāṣya* and *Yaśastilaka*.

For that many [means] are indeed not possible, because such a view is untenable.
Through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), there occur unperceived actions such as breathing, ingestion, digestion, sleeping, moving, scratching, twitching, smelling, and tasting;
thus, because neither purely constructed nor purely non-constructed cognitions are logically possible, every cognition is permeated by ignorance (*ajñāna*),
and the function of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consists solely in the act of determination (*pariccheda*).

In this case, there is no such determination [of the object], yet it is not a lack of knowledge; thus, there is no contradiction with what was previously stated. This is because, like the designation "Rādhaka-Pūrṇaka-mother" (where the mother is the primary referent despite the dual name), there is no definitive ascertainment due to the predominance of the substantive [the self] over the qualifiers. Furthermore, since there is no distinction between knowledge and ignorance [in this state], and because the terms *saṃśaya* (doubt), *viparyaya* (error), *anadhyavasāya* (indefinite cognition), *nirṇaya* (ascertainment), *avagama* (comprehension), and *avabodha* (awareness) all share the same essential meaning, it might be argued: "If there is no determination by the experiencer of external objects as 'this is this,' then why should there not be a determination of internal self-awareness regarding pleasure, pain, and so forth?"

It is said: [the claim that] "by self-awareness one performs inhalation, ingestion, digestion," and so forth, does not hold because it is subject to deviation. For every person performs these actions while remaining entirely unconscious of the vital breaths (prāṇa and apāna). Even while transforming what has been ingested into the state of chyle-essence (khalarasa) and into blood and other constituents, one is not conscious of it oneself.
Likewise, in those who are asleep and the like, who perform actions such as moving, scratching, and throbbing, those actions are seen to occur even while they remain unconscious.
Thus, those who are asleep, intoxicated, swooning, or in the womb are examples of those who are "asacetayamāna" (unconscious).

Likewise, for those whose minds are directed elsewhere, there occurs the unperceived sensation of movement, itching, or the touch of mosquitoes and gadflies; the cognition of odors and so forth; and for those who are asleep and the like, the tasting of sour substances—an unperceived tasting by the tongue, which is the meaning of "tasting.
By the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (ādi), hunger, yawning, sneezing, and other such states are also included.

Just as these actions are unperceived, so too is self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*); for in this way, neither a conceptualized nor a non-conceptualized cognition of such a nature is possible. To begin with, a conceptualized cognition cannot be a cognition of such a nature precisely because it is conceptualized. Nor is a non-conceptualized cognition possible in the manner described above; that is to say, a pure cognition of such a nature is not established. Therefore, since a conceptualized, non-conceptualized, or such-like cognition is impossible, all cognition is permeated by ignorance.

Furthermore, the function of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consists in the determination of an object; for it is held that a means of valid cognition, when operating, functions for the sake of determining an object as it truly is. Since such a determination does not exist in this case [of the non-existent], he demonstrates the dissimilarity [between the non-existent and the object of a valid cognition].

Why? Because of the predominance of the substantive (*viśeṣya*) and the absence of restrictive determination (*anavadhāraṇāt*). What is meant by "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*)? For example, when only one mother of either Rādhaka or Pūrṇaka is intended to be expressed, she may be qualified by Rādhaka as "Rādhaka’s mother," or by Pūrṇaka as "Pūrṇaka’s mother," or by both as "the mother of Rādhaka and Pūrṇaka. In every case, there is no restrictive determination that she is the mother of Rādhaka alone or Pūrṇaka alone, because of the predominance of the substantive. Likewise, that very same entity is qualified by knowledge and ignorance; thus, due to the predominance of the substantive, there is no contradiction in the statement, since there is no distinction between knowledge and ignorance [in their relation to the substantive].
But it is not as in the case of "the blue lotus," where there is a restriction due to the predominance of the qualifier;

therefore, because their meaning is the same—namely, "awakening" (avabodha)—both "knowledge" (jñāna) and "non-knowledge" (ajñāna) are indistinguishable in this respect. Demonstrating this, he says: "Because [the roots] *gam*, *sṛp* (Pāṇini Dhātupāṭha 982–983), and *ava-gam* have 'awakening' as their meaning. *Gam* and *sṛp* mean "to go"; *ava-gama* is "complete going" (*pūrṇa-gamana*). And *ava-gama* is "awakening" (*avabodha*), according to the rule: "The root *budh* is used in the sense of awakening" (Pāṇini Dhātupāṭha 858, 1172).
Since all doubt, error, certainty, and non-ascertainment have understanding as their purpose, and since understanding is synonymous with awakening (*avabodha*), what else [remains] here?
In whatever way this [was done] by the wisdom of Rādhakapūrṇaka...
Because this [position] is subject to sublation (*bādha*), the meaning of a word remains unknown within this system of the destruction of the three-fold [criterion].
As they have said: "The meaning 'it exists' (*asti-artha*) is the defining characteristic of what is to be communicated by all words."
In the *Vākyapadīya* (2.121), it is stated that words such as "cow" are spoken of together with words denoting unseen forces (*apūrva*) and deities;
furthermore, all words constitute the meaning of the sentence.

"All words possess a referent (*astyartha*); this is the defining characteristic of what is signified, as they say in the case of words such as 'cow' and others, which are equal to words for *apūrva* (the unseen force) and deities. (Vākyapadīya 2.121).
Furthermore, because it is the locus of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), it has the nature of a substance (*dravya*).

The word *dravya* (substance), the word *dravya*—in the sense of a part of a tree (*dru*), or "going" (*gati*), or "conduct" (*yātrā*), or "worldly transaction" (*vyavahāra*)—therefore, in this perspective (*nayabhaṅga*), the meaning of a word remains unknown [in isolation].

The mention of "perspective" (*bhaṅga*) is for the purpose of indicating other perspectives, because perspectives that function independently of one another are false, whereas their opposite is true; and since these [perspectives] constitute the "perspectives" (*bhaṅga*) precisely within the categories of affirmation (*vidhi*) and restriction (*niyama*).

Therefore, within this very system (*nayabhaṅga*), there is an unknown meaning for a word, whereas in other systems there are various different meanings; he states the indicator (*jñāpaka*) of this view as follows: "And as they say"—the verse "The meaning of 'existence' belongs to all words"—means that the mere state of being (*sattāmātra*) is the meaning of all words. Every word has some meaning; no word is devoid of meaning. Yet, that meaning cannot be defined as "this" or "that"; such is the definition of what is to be communicated (*pratyāyyalakṣaṇa*).

In this regard, the examples are the meanings of the words *apūrva*, *devatā*, and *svarga*; for, since these are absolutely unperceived, we cannot comprehend them through definition, such that we might say, "The *apūrva* is like this," or "Heaven is like this," or "The deity is like this. In the same way, the meanings of words such as *go* (cow) must also be similar to those; for there is no specific form of meaning established in the acts of going, speaking, or bellowing, nor is there any such thing as a [definitive] meaning. This much alone is to be understood in this very analysis of the method (*nayabhaṅga*), wherein all words constitute the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*).

For example: "Devadatta! Bring the cow, white, with a staff. In this case, the words—which possess mixed forms due to their mutual non-distinction—are directed toward a single meaning; through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), they express a unified meaning alone, not one that is separate [from them].
Therefore, all words belong to the sentence, and the sentence-meaning is the words themselves; it is neither each individual word nor something distinct from them.
As it has been said: "A sentence is one because of the unity of its meaning, provided that if it were divided, there would be mutual expectancy" (Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 2.1.46).
1.46 Thus it is not as it is imagined by others in another way: that the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta-śabda*), the aggregate (*saṅghāta*), or the genus (*jāti*) residing in the aggregate [is the denoter].

Regarding the definition of a sentence (*vākya*), the views of those who perceive logical principles are manifold: some hold that a sentence is a single, partless sound; others that it is a sequence synthesized by the intellect; some that it is the first word; others that every word is distinct; and still others that a sentence consists of words that are mutually dependent.
As stated in Vākyapadīya 2.1–2: "Because they are non-worldly (alaukika), and because they are either impossible to attain or fruitless, [the parts] are mutually independent."
Their opposites are as follows:
"much," "seen by others," and so forth.

Even regarding the meaning of that [word], there are various different etymological explanations by some scholars, derived from the roots *gṛ* (to swallow), *garj* (to roar), and *gam* (to go). Furthermore, there is the going and coming to and from assemblies of those equal to him.
Whether derived from the root *gavati* or *gadati*, the word *gauḥ* has been demonstrated here. (2.175)

For just as the act of going (*gamikriyā*) is absolutely distinct from other acts of going that inhere in the same object despite being of different types, yet when its uniform nature is established, it is designated by the word *gami* itself and adopted as the basis for the etymological derivation of the word "cow" (*go*), so too are these common specific actions— such as swallowing (*girati*), roaring (*garjati*), and speaking (*gadati*)— which are based on general terms, accepted by various teachers in the process of deriving the word "cow," according to the *Vākyapadīya-svavṛtti* (2.175).

"A cow (go) is so called because it goes (gacchati), speaks (gadati), or bellow (garjati)"—this is to be understood from that very [passage] in the *Vṛtti* named *Tripādī*, composed by Bhartṛhari on the *Pātañjala-Mahābhāṣya*. (The variant readings are:

In the reading of the *Yaśomitra-bhāṣya*, however, there is the fourth [case ending] according to Pāṇini 2.3.13: *tadarthārthabalihitasukharakṣitaiḥ*. This is because the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*) is either like the meanings of the individual words (*padārtha*), or the words themselves constitute the meaning of the sentence.

Sound is a single, partless entity; sequence is a mental synthesis [or conventional construction].

"Every word is distinct [from its referent], and every word is dependent [on others]; thus, regarding the sentence, the views of those who perceive the principles (*nyāya*) are manifold. (Vākyapadīya 2.1–2) But where is this method (*naya*) included? Is it within the division of the substance-view (*dravyanaya*) or the mode-view (*paryāyanaya*)? It is said: because it pertains to the domain of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), it has the nature of substance (*dravyārthatā*). Conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) is that which is similar to worldly practice, primarily consisting of metaphorical application (*upacāra*), and whose objects are extensive. (Tattvārthabhāṣya 1)
Because of this statement, each of its parts (*avayava*) is a single portion (*ekadeśa*) that does not function as a whole, since it functions otherwise;

for in the world, the state of functioning as a single portion belongs to clay, jars, and so forth, which are [examples of] generalities (*sāmānya*), particularities (*viśeṣa*), and substances (*dravya*). This is the direction of the argument. Therefore, [the universal] is not a real entity (*avastu*), because it is non-worldly (*alaukika*), like a sky-flower; whereas, by contrast, it is like a jar.
And regarding its basis: "Is the self, O Venerable One, knowledge or ignorance? "O Gautama, the self is necessarily knowledge; but the self may be either knowledge or ignorance.
(Bhagavatī Sūtra 12.3)
Because of the distinction between the substantial and the modal aspects.

For "conventional usage" (*vyavahāra*) is the domain of worldly discourse, and "the method of injunction" (*vidhinaya*) is a portion thereof; therefore, there is a distinction regarding the substantial object (*dravyārtha*). As it is said: "The perspective of the substance-view (*dravyārthika-naya*) is pure, being the object of the comprehensive description (*saṃgraha-prarūpaṇā*); however, its conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) is the determination of the meaning of words according to their specific forms."

In the *Sanmati-tarka-prakaraṇa* (1.4), for the purpose of demonstrating the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) of the meaning of the word, it says: "the word *dravya*. This is because it has been etymologically derived as "a part (*avayava*) of a tree (*dru*). Now, what is a "tree" (*dru*)? [The root] *du* or *dru* [is used] in the sense of "motion" (*gati*) (Pāṇini Dhātupāṭha 944, 945). Alternatively, there is an un-derived nominal stem (*prātipadika*) with that same meaning. [According to Pāṇini 5.2.108: "The suffix *ma* [is added] after *dyu* and *dru*. (Pāṇini 5.2.108).
Because [the term] is thus established as a nipāta, its meaning is "the way of life (yātrā) or the conduct (vyavahāra) of the world";
the explanation of its sense is that it is a "part" (avayava), meaning a single portion of that way of life.

If one asks what that single portion is, it is said: the single portion is "partial engagement" (asamastavṛtti) because it is an engagement of a different kind; the meaning is that it is "wrong view" (mithyādṛṣṭi) because it is an engagement contrary to the conduct of the entire world.
If it is asked, "From what is this partial application (*ekadeśavṛttitā*) of that systematic operation determined? the meaning is that it is determined from common worldly experience itself.

For in the world, the partial application of those [categories]—such as the universal-particular relationship between clay and pot, or substance-ness—is evident: clay is the universal, the pot is the particular; substance-ness is the universal of clay, while the particularity of the pot consists of its having a hole in the bottom, a broken rim, being complete, or being red, black, and so forth.

This entire range of objects must not be discarded; rather, in the case of the comprehensive application (*samastavṛtti*), all these aspects are to be established according to their respective nayas and by the force of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Since this [view] is permeated by ignorance and is subject to the faults that will be stated hereafter, it is illogical even for the worldly person;
thus concludes the section on the hundredfold divisions of the method of injunction (*vidhinaya*), which is a synonym for "direction" (*dig*).

From the perspective of substantial reality (*dravyārthatas*), a single part (*avayava*) or portion (*ekadeśa*) of that [universal] does not have a complete occurrence (*asamastavṛtti*), because its mode of occurrence is otherwise;

for in the world, the state of occurring in only one part belongs to the generalities and particularities such as clay, jar, and so forth, as well as to substantiality (*dravyatva*). This is the direction of the argument.

Therefore, that which is other [than the self] is not a real entity, because it is non-worldly (alaukika), like a sky-flower; whereas, in the case of its opposite, it is like a jar. And the basis for this is stated in the *Bhagavatīsūtra* 12: "Is the soul, O Venerable One, knowledge or ignorance? Gautama! The soul is necessarily knowledge; the soul, however, may be knowledge or it may be ignorance."

Due to the distinction between the substantial and the modal aspects, the pure perspective of the substance-standpoint (*dravyārthika-naya*) is the domain for the exposition of the comprehensive standpoint (*saṃgraha*).
The nature [of things] is the description; however, the conventional usage regarding that is the determination of the meaning of words. *Sanmati* 1.4.

other than those, it is non-existent because it is not of the world, like a flower in the sky— this has already been explained.

The intended meaning is as follows: that person considers the world’s absolute transcendence (alaukikaikānta) as postulated by the Sāṅkhya and others to be a non-entity, because it is distinct [from what is real], like a jar. Whatever is a real entity is necessarily worldly (laukika), such as a jar—whether it be an effect, a cause, a universal, or a particular; whatever it may be, it exists according to worldly consensus, through the aforementioned existence of universals and particulars characterized by broad bases and so forth, and thus it is worldly. This is stated in contrast to the dissimilar case (vaidharmye).
The world-cherished effect or cause [is known] through meditation.

In this reading, however, one should reconcile the text by intending the meaning "because [the self] is cultivated," since all the *nayās* have their basis solely in the teaching of the Jina. If it is asked, "What is its basis?", it is said: its basis is [the answer to the question]—"O Venerable One! Is the self knowledge (*jñāna*) or ignorance (*ajñāna*)? When the Lord was thus questioned by the venerable Gautama, he explained: "O Gautama! The self is necessarily knowledge. Knowledge is necessarily the self, because no functioning of knowledge is observed apart from the self.

The self, moreover, may be knowledge and may be ignorance; it may be knowledge because it is subject to the karma that obscures knowledge (*jñānāvaraṇīya-karma*), and it may also be ignorance due to the abundance of doubt, error, and lack of discernment. From this sūtra, this [doctrine of] false view emerges, which possesses a resolution to the contradiction regarding the statement of ignorance:
"O Venerable One, is the self knowledge or ignorance?

It is as follows: the mode of activity that establishes the truth of the Jaina doctrine—attained through the modes of injunction and restriction (*vidhiniyamavṛtti*), which consist of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) directed toward their respective objects and have ascertained the individual reality of each—is intended as a single mode characterized by twelve specific alternatives. Since even the aforementioned mode of injunction, when taken individually, constitutes a false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), this absolute adherence to the mode of injunction must also be abandoned.
Why? Because it is illogical. Illogicality arises from contradiction (*vipratiṣedha*);

"contradiction" means a contradictory negation. If it is asked, "How is there a contradiction [in this]?"—it is said: As for what was stated by you, that all cognition (*jñāna*) is indeed permeated by ignorance (*ajñāna*), and that there is no distinction whatsoever between knowledge and ignorance because doubt (*saṃśaya*), error (*viparyaya*), non-determination (*anadhyavasāya*), and ascertainment (*nirṇaya*) have the single purpose of being cognitions; and that the true nature of the world cannot be known, and the effort toward discrimination (*viveka*) in the scriptures is therefore fruitless.

If, therefore, the reality of the world (*lokatattva*) is indeed unknowable, then the refutation of the reality of the world as established by all the scriptures would likewise be untrustworthy, because it would be impossible to attain and would be fruitless; furthermore, since a negation must have as its object the knowledge of the very nature of that which is to be negated, did you yourself—whether knowing it or not—refute the categories of universal and particular, whether they belong to your own domain or another's, and so forth, as these categories of worldly reality are imagined and then criticized in other treatises? If you refute them while knowing them, then that [opponent’s] doctrine was not unknown to you.

Now, if [the object] is not known, how can it be said to be "refuted"? Thus, in either case, a negation is not tenable because it would be contradictory; for it would be a laughable position to claim that while the negation is being performed, the object to be negated is not known.

It might be thought: "The object to be negated is indeed known, because that entity is conceived in many ways—as consisting of the three qualities such as *sattva*, as having the nature of a momentary existence, or as consisting of the six categories such as substance (*dravya*) and so forth—and such [conceptions] are untenable."

This too is contradictory: for regarding those doctrines which fall within the scope of worldly reality, is their status as false prescriptions known or unknown? Since this dilemma applies equally to both cases, if it were known, the effort to prohibit them would be futile; furthermore, the justification for teaching ritual action would likewise collapse, because such teachings lack the discernment of the transformation that conforms to the true nature of the object to be cultivated—like the prescription of unwholesome medicine or the instruction of a child to seize a venomous snake—and even if it were known, one would not be freed from that very fault.

It has been explained at length that it is not tenable for a universal (*sāmānya*)—whether regarding its own object or another's object—to be "thus" or "otherwise," and the same applies to a particular (*viśeṣa*). If all this is unknown, then because there is no cognition (*apratyayatvāt*), no negation is possible; this has already been stated.

If, on the other hand, it is known, how can the reality of the world (*lokatattva*) be impossible to know? Thus, because you yourself have failed to examine the relationship between words and their referents, your speech is like that of a madman. It has been said that the reality of the world cannot be attained [by such means], because of contradiction (*vipratiṣedhāt*).

As for what was said—that because the true nature of reality cannot be attained, it is only logical to teach action (*kriyā*) itself, since the attainment of happiness is preceded by that—it is here replied: even the acceptance of the logic of teaching action would thus be undermined. How can you speak so harshly, saying "it is indeed undermined"? When we say "it would be undermined," we do so out of consideration for the possibility [of its being so], out of courtesy and knowledge of the world. What is the reason for its being undermined? It is because of the absence of the discernment (*vijñāna*) of the transformation that conforms to the own-nature (*svatattva*) of the object to be cultivated.

The word *sam* means unification; the true nature (*svatattva*) of an object such as food—which is being consumed through identification with oneself and which consists of sound, touch, taste, form, and smell—is that which brings about the pacification or aggravation of the bodily humors (vāta, etc.), as well as their increase or dissolution. As stated in the *Caraka Saṃhitā* (Sūtrasthāna 6.15): "A decoction of *nāgara*, *ativiṣā*, and *mustā* serves to digest undigested matter (*āmadoṣa*)."

98. Thus, "transformation" (pariṇāma) is that which conforms to those respective realities; its nature is to conform to them. What is meant? It is the ripening (vipāka) of an object being cultivated through its very activity, by way of conforming to its own essential nature;
it is the state of being devoid of cognition thereof.

This cognition that "such a ripening leads to pleasure" or "leads to pain" is for the purpose of attaining what is beneficial and avoiding what is harmful; yet, according to you, that [cognition] simply does not exist.

Therefore, because of being devoid of that [knowledge], even the instruction of ritual action—such as "one desiring heaven should offer the *agnihotra* sacrifice" or "one desiring to eat should cook rice"—which has both seen and unseen purposes, is not tenable. This is because it would be a transformation based on an object of practice whose true nature is unknown, like the instruction for an unlearned physician regarding medicine. If it is argued that, just as for someone who does not know the specific qualities of a substance—its taste, potency, post-digestive effect, power, constituent parts, and their combinations—an application of knowledge arises simply from an instruction in a particular place, we say no. For in either case, since it would be a human composition, the instruction for medicine by one ignorant of the characteristics of the patient's constitution, suitability, digestive fire, strength or weakness, and the causes and origins of diseases such as wind (*vāta*), is not tenable; likewise, the instruction "one desiring heaven should offer the *agnihotra* sacrifice" and so forth is not tenable.

Alternatively, since all instructions have the purpose of attaining the beneficial and avoiding the harmful, in the absence of that [purpose], let it be mere play; thus, for one devoid of knowledge of that [reality], hearing, grasping, retaining, reasoning about, and practicing such instructions would result only in misfortune, like the grasping of a snake by a child. If it is argued that the yoga of knowledge arises from instruction alone, we say no; for in either case, it would be dependent on a human source, and thus [the authority of] the Veda would be undermined. Furthermore, [this contradicts the view of one who is] an expert in the [Vedic] tradition.

If it be thought that the yoga of knowledge does not arise from instruction alone—for that yoga of knowledge arises from instruction alone—[we reply:

this may be so, because a person lacks the power to perceive supersensuous objects; thus, regarding the knowledge of the connection between heaven and unseen merit (*apūrva-karma*), there is an absence of the causes for prior cognition, just like a barren woman’s recollection of her grandson.
One might suppose that the knowledge of substance, quality, taste, potency, post-digestive transformation, and so forth, has prior cognition as its cause through inference;
therefore, the knowledge regarding the connection between the *agnihotra* rite and its fruit of heaven arises solely from instruction (*upadeśa*).

This is incorrect, because in either case there is human authorship (*pauruṣeyatva*). This is because the knowledge of the instruction—whether its purpose be visible or invisible—is itself of human origin; or rather, because it depends upon a person both in terms of the cognition and the verbal expression. Just as you consider that for objects beyond the senses (*atīndriya*) there is an absence of a prior cause for cognition, and thus the cognitions and words of a person regarding such objects, along with their subjects, lack authority due to the person's connection with passion and other defects; likewise, since every instruction, the instructor’s cognition, and the cognitions and words of the listener do not transcend being human by virtue of being cognitions and words, they lack authority, just like the *Mahābhārata*, the *Rāmāyaṇa*, and so forth.

Just as there is validity in the instruction on the Agnihotra and other rites concerning supersensible objects, so too there might be validity in the Sāṅkhya and other systems' instructions on supersensible objects;

however, such knowledge of reality would be limited to some particular subject for a certain person—like the knowledge of the "monkey-root" and so forth—and not a single person's knowledge encompassing all medicinal herbs and the like. Therefore, even in the case of medical science and similar fields, there is an absence of any prior cause for such knowledge.

Just as there is a single person’s cognition regarding those objects, the acceptance of a single person’s cognition whose objects include all things—whether beyond the senses or perceivable by the senses—is necessarily required. Why? Because the two [terms] "Veda" and "vacana" would otherwise be inexplicable. "Veda" means knowledge (*vedana*) without a person; the meaning is that it is cognition. And "vacana" (speech) is the statement of what has been known for the purpose of communicating it to others. Both of these—cognition and communication—are not possible without a person, because they both inhere in a person.
And it has been said: "Form, composition, connection, authority, cognition, and action."

Furthermore, for you, the impossibility of instruction would likewise follow from the untenability of the two statements: "The knowledge of sound is dependent on the person" and "Knowledge is not other than the self," because no instruction whatsoever is possible without the investigation of the principles of the world, just as in the case of the instructions of the Sāṅkhya and others.

Furthermore, if that [instruction] were also not established, then the instruction regarding the *agnihotra* and so forth would be as much a lack of knowledge as the instruction regarding medicine; or else, like the knowledge of that [medicine], it too would be cognizable through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Thus, having for the time being accepted the instruction regarding action, the fault has been stated.
[This is because] there is no perception [of such an agent].

Otherwise, the reading would have been: "Because of the absence of a cause for prior cognition, like the memory of a barren woman’s grandson, [Dharma] would be non-authoritative, as Dharma is rooted in verbal testimony (*śabda*). Thus, anything not based on verbal testimony would be disregarded.

Furthermore, for you, there would be the impossibility of any instruction whatsoever, because no instruction—just like the instructions of the Sāṅkhyas and others—is possible without an investigation into the reality of the world;
and that [investigation] too, in turn, would lack a final foundation.

Furthermore, even without accepting [the opponent's position], the impossibility of instruction for you occurs precisely according to your own view—this is the remainder of the sentence—because no instruction whatsoever is possible apart from an investigation into the reality of the world, just like the instructions of the Sāṅkhya and others; "instruction" (upadeśa) means explanation (vyākhyā), and this explanation concerns words, sentences, means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), or the objects that are their referents, as formulated by the Vedas, grammar, Sāṅkhya, and other treatises through their respective methods of exposition.

In this regard, just as the reality of things such as jars cannot be understood through the systems of the Sāṅkhya and others without an exposition devoted to investigating the nature of worldly reality, it is therefore explained in that manner; likewise, the Agnihotra and other rites are explained by establishing the relationship between names and the things named. Furthermore, whether concerning words, sentences, or means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is impossible to comprehend them—through the analysis of roots and suffixes, or through direct perception, inference, scriptural authority, sublation, corroboration, doubt, and the relationship between primary and subordinate factors—without investigating the nature of worldly reality. Thus, every instruction proceeds with the aim of investigating that reality.

In this regard, just as there is the impossibility of attaining the goals taught by the Sāṅkhya and other schools, as well as the futility of their teachings, so too it is with the teachings of the Vedas, grammar, Mīmāṃsā, and so forth; thus, the teachings are not established.

Now, for those intent on investigating the reality of the world, if the instructions regarding the attainment of what is possible and the fruitfulness of such instruction are indeed possible, then why is there such hostility toward the positions accepted by others? Here too, just as the determination of the reality of jars, cloths, and so forth—accessible through perception and inference—is possible based on common worldly experience, so too is the determination of words, sentences, and means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) possible. This is because, from the very world, the non-deviation of the relationship between signifier and signified, determined by the sequence of phonemes and so forth, is well-established in the case of words such as "jar" with respect to the objects of verbal meaning and cognition;
the same should be applied to sentences and means of valid cognition.
And it has been said: "The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) function [in relation to] the objects of cognition (*prameya*) for all disputants;
however, those poor ascetics dispute due to differences in terminology and intention.
(Siddhadvātriṃśikā 20)

Thus, according to your own view, the lack of authority of all these instructions is established; for, while being intent on investigating the nature of the world, they are accepted as having unattainable goals and no fruit, like the instructions of the authors of the Sāṅkhya and other treatises. Consequently, because there would follow the futility of explaining the scope of words, sentences, and means of valid cognition regarding the performance of actions with visible or invisible purposes, the validity of the Vedic scriptures cannot be established, since they do not transcend the intent to investigate the nature of the world; or else, there must be the fruitfulness of the knowledge resulting from the investigation of the nature of the world as expressed in the treatises on logic (*tarka*).

If instruction (*upadeśa*) is not established, the status of being an investigator (*parīkṣaka*) is lost, because investigation consists in the knowledge of non-erroneous objects regarding words, sentences, and means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, investigation itself is instruction, since investigation and exposition are not different in meaning.
Moreover, according to your own view, that instruction does not stand as such, because it consists in the search for the true nature of the world (*lokatattva*).

It might be thought: "Just as in the investigation of the reality of the world—such as jars and so forth—consisting of universals, particulars, and the like, there is a lack of finality regarding words, sentences, and means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because if these means of valid cognition themselves were to be apprehended by other means of valid cognition, the fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*) would follow.

To this it is replied: First of all, there is no infinite regress of means of valid cognition, because means of valid cognition illuminate both themselves and others, like the moon, the sun, jewels, lamps, and so forth.

Even granting [the existence of] words and so forth, he points out the infinite regress according to your own view: even the scripture that prescribes the action for that [word] would not be established; thus, there would be an absence of merit and so forth resulting from it. This is because, like the injunction "One desiring heaven should perform the Agnihotra," since it would prescribe an object whose meaning is unestablished, it would be unfit for practical use, and consequently, there would be no connection between the action prescribed by it and its fruit—just as in the case of saying to one who desires health, "Eat ḍittha."

Now, it might be argued: "By prescribing the manner of performance (*itikartavyatā*) after prescribing what is to be done (*kartavyatā*), it will become established that the ritual named *agnihotra* is of this very nature; thus, by not investigating other matters, there will be no infinite regress. [To this we reply: Even a scripture that prescribes action would not be established, because it too would not transcend the nature of an investigation into worldly reality and would therefore lack authority (*apramāṇatva*).

The word *iti* has the sense of a reason (*hetu*); this reason is "because the scripture that enjoins action does not exist. Therefore, there is an absence of merit and so forth resulting from that [action]; the meaning is that there is an absence of the *apūrva* (unseen potency) manifested by the actions taught in the scripture that enjoins action. But what, then, is that scripture which enjoins action? It is said: for example, "One desiring heaven should perform the *agnihotra* sacrifice"—this is the scripture.
Now, is this [scripture] an injunction (*vidhi*), a restatement (*anuvāda*), or an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*)? It is said: it is an injunction (*vidhi*).
How is an injunction (*vidhi*) characterized? It is characterized by its function of enjoining an object that is not already established.

Here, an oblation (*havana*) to Agni as the recipient—which was previously unestablished—is enjoined. Since the agent’s desire for heaven—whether understood as the name "bliss" (*sukha*), or as the attainment thereof based on a specific location, or as the longing for it—is already established, the oblation to Agni is the means (*upāya*) for attaining heaven. Because this means is something new (*apūrva*), how can there be an absence of the *apūrva* manifested by that action? [It cannot,] because according to your own view, it has been stated as above.

Furthermore, because that injunction does not depend on knowledge of the nature of reality produced by reasoning (*tarka*), it is not fit for practical application (*asaṃvyavahāryatva*). Due to its lack of practical applicability, there is no connection between the action enjoined by it and its fruit. The illustration is like the statement "Eat Ḍittha" addressed to one seeking health; just as such a statement and the action toward a person seeking health are fruitless precisely because they are unestablished, so too your stated action has an object that cannot be attained. Thus, you also share the same status as those who exert effort in the discrimination [of principles] characteristic of the Sāṅkhya and other schools, which are likewise characterized by having unattainable goals and so forth. [The word *anāvasthā* appears in the source text.]

Even a scripture that prescribes an action would not be established [as authoritative], and thus there would be an absence of merit and so forth resulting from its practice; for example, the injunction "one desiring heaven should perform the *agnihotra* sacrifice" would lack a connection between the prescribed action and its fruit because it prescribes a subject matter whose meaning is unestablished (*aprasiddhārtha*) and is therefore not fit for worldly transaction (*asaṃvyavahāryatva*), like the statement that one seeking health should eat *ḍittha*.

If it were argued: "Having prescribed the duty (*kartavyatā*), by prescribing the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), it will become well-known that the ritual named *agnihotra* is of such a nature"—this is not so, because it is understood through the investigation of other meanings.

Here he says: Do not think that this [system] is equal to the efforts of the Sāṅkhya and other schools. What is the reason? Because of the difference in nature (*vaidharmya*). For example: after prescribing what is to be done (*kartavyatā*), one prescribes the procedure (*itikartavyatā*). In that regard, "one should offer the *agnihotra*"—by this, the *agnihotra* is prescribed as something to be performed; subsequently, further on, the specific procedure is prescribed, stating, "that very *agnihotra* is to be performed in such and such a manner," characterized by specific forms such as the *agniṣṭoma*, and by specific details of substance, quality, deity, agent, desire, time, place, and so forth, as in: "A Brāhmaṇa should sacrifice in spring; a Rājanya in summer; a Vaiśya with the *vājapeya* in autumn."
The Holākā is [performed] by those of the East, while the sacrifice of the bull (udvṛṣabhayajña) is [performed] by those of the North.

Now, even in this case, the comprehension of what ought to be done (*kartavyatā*) arises precisely from following the reality of worldly duties and so forth. Once the injunction of what ought to be done has been established, there follows the occasion for the procedure (*itikartavyatā*); just as when the duty to make a jar has been enjoined by saying "Make a jar," there subsequently follows the sequence of the procedure—so too [one should think], "In this manner, one should accomplish it."

But the word *agnihotra* is not like the word *ghaṭa* (pot); rather, you will understand [it] from such passages as: "One desiring prosperity should sacrifice a white animal to Vāyu; Vāyu is indeed the swiftest deity; he approaches Vāyu with his own share; he bestows prosperity upon him" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.1.1). Thus he instructs the disciple.

Thereafter, the fact that there exists a ritual action called *agnihotra* of this very kind will become well-established for that disciple through the power of understanding the meaning of the specific injunction; this occurs by virtue of his distinction from the efforts toward the discrimination [of principles] found in the Sāṃkhya and other systems, and by not investigating other matters—namely, by not investigating the nature of causes and effects such as pots and atoms, nor universals and particulars—and thus he should offer oblations into the fire. (Praśastapādabhāṣya, Puruṣottama-vivaraṇa-pāda-ramaṇa-hīna)

Regarding the phrase "the state of being a duty" (*kartavyatā*): that realization of duty concerning the *agnihotra* and other such rites is, by virtue of being a realization, nothing other than a pursuit of the reality of worldly duties and so forth. Realization (*pratipatti*) is the act of taking hold of each [object] individually; it is twofold—internal (*ādhyātmikī*) and external (*bāhyā*). Among these, the internal is simply the intellect itself, consisting of thoughts such as "this ought to be done" and "this ought not to be done. The external, however, is the act of appropriation (*mamīkriyā*) for the sake of bipeds, quadrupeds, wealth, grain, and so on.

Both of these [types of knowledge] must follow only an object that is well-known in the world, not one that is unknown; therefore, even the understanding of the *agnihotra* and other rites proceeds solely from following the reality of worldly convention, and not otherwise.

Otherwise, what would be its object, and what would it not be the object of? It would be like the absence of the understanding of a cow-dhen for an old man born on Coconut Island. He shows this: "After the prescription of what is to be done (*kartavyatā*), there is the occasion for the manner of performance (*itikartavyatā*); [this occurs] precisely through following the reality of the objects of worldly duties and so forth. This is how the text continues.

The principle that "the occasion for the understanding of the well-known *itikartavyatā* (procedure) follows immediately after the understanding of the well-known *kartavyatā* (duty)" is untenable; for both [of these] are non-worldly (*alaukika*), since the general form of the *agnihotra*, its specific forms such as the *agniṣṭoma*, and its constituent elements—consisting of substances, mantras, deities, officiating priests, and restrictive rules—are themselves not well-known (*aprasiddha*). Furthermore, there is another point: the impossibility of that principle.

To exclude that [misconception], he says the following, demonstrating the difference between the well-known *kartavyatā* (the "what is to be done") and the *itikartavyatā* (the "manner of doing"): "Just as when the *kartavyatā* of making a jar is enjoined by saying 'Make a jar,' there follows subsequently the sequence of the *itikartavyatā*—he shows this by indicating the manner (*prakāra*) as follows: 'Having placed a lump of clay upon the wheel, having spun it with a rod, one should fashion it through the specific sequence of forms such as the *śivaka* and so forth with both hands'—this subsequent injunction of the well-known *itikartavyatā* regarding objects such as jars is appropriate because its meaning is well-established. However, there is no such established knowledge for the *kartavyatā* of the *agnihotra* or for the *itikartavyatā* consisting of animal slaughter and the like; for since the word *agnihotra* is not well-established [in this sense], it is incapable of expressing any *itikartavyatā* or *kartavyatā*. Therefore he says: 'But unlike a jar, the word *agnihotra* does not express any *kartavyatā* at all'—by the inclusion of the word 'also' (*api*), he implies 'nor even the *itikartavyatā*'."

What is the reason? Because words intended to express distinct meanings do not recur to the meaning of another word.

To this, he says: Since this suffix has arisen after the verbal root *hu*, how could it abandon that which is to be performed by it and proceed toward what is to be performed by another word? For the learned have established the paribhāṣā: "The mention of a suffix [includes] both the base and the suffix, as they express the meaning of the suffix together" (Pāṇini-Mahābhāṣya 3.1.67).

The opponent might think: "Now, if it were the case that they are one and the same— such that what is the *agnihotra* is the very same as the *havana*, and what is the *havana* is the very same as the *agnihotra*— then this identity of purpose between these two would contradict established convention, because it is well known that nouns (*nāman*) and verbs (*ākhyāta*) have distinct meanings."

Even if one were to admit that these two words express the same meaning, for the sake of avoiding redundancy and for the sake of brevity, let it simply be "juhuyāt" (one should sacrifice); what is the purpose of the word "agnihotram"?
The other [author] says, beginning with "In the case of an action to be performed by another word," etc., in order to avoid the objections of unfamiliarity and redundancy;
the word "tāvat" is used in the sense of sequence. First, as for what was asked—"How would one proceed in the case of an action to be performed by another word?"—this is the response.

The intention is that when this resolution has been stated, the defects of tautology and lack of established meaning, which pertain to that very position—that "it is that same thing"—are also already resolved.

In that context, the act of offering (*havana*) requires another word [to complete its meaning]. By what principle? By the principle of the sentence (*vākya-nyāya*). What is the principle of the sentence? It is a relationship based on mutual expectancy through either distinction (*bheda*) or conjunction (*saṃsarga*). By virtue of that expectancy, a word functions toward the meaning of another word. For example, when it is said, "He studies together with a fellow-student" (*sabrahmacāriṇā sahādhīte*), there arises an expectancy—by implication—that he is identical to that very person who is a fellow-student (*sabrahmacārī*) with whom he studies, and not with anyone else;
such is the meaning of "requiring capacity" (*sāmarthya*).

But it is not as when an object has been delimited by a word, such as "jar," where no further object is required; rather, that requirement [of a further word] is like the jar itself, or like the word "jar. Because they are designated without distinction, the word "jar" is spoken of as having the meaning of the jar. Just as the word "jar" is accepted as being meaningful, so too the word "agnihotra" is intended to be meaningful; otherwise, the word "agnihotra" would be meaningless. Let there be no such meaninglessness; therefore, it would follow that the word "agnihotra" was recited through negligence.

From this, the explicit meaning of the statement would be: "One should perform the oblation known as the Agnihotra. This is like saying, when it is stated, "One should make a pot," that one should perform the act of making a pot.
However, this is incorrect because the analogy is dissimilar;

for there is no well-known oblation called "Agnihotra" established in the same way as a pot, which could be referred to by restatement (anuvāda) such that "one should perform that oblation named Agnihotra. Nor can it mean "the oblation which one should perform is that which is called Agnihotra," because it is not established by any other sentence or any other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
Therefore, both [the word *agnihotra* and the word *juhuyāt*] will be required;

for if it were not so, there would be a fault. But if the word *agnihotra* were independent and applied solely to the meaning of the verbal root *hu* (to sacrifice), what fault would there be? In that case, the word *agnihotra* would have to be considered a mistaken reading (*pramādādhīta*), and the word *agni* would have no separate meaning at all, since its meaning would be exhausted merely by the root *hu*. Consequently, like parts of a verse such as "ten pomegranates" (*daśadāḍima*), it would be a mistaken reading because it would lack expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣatvāt*); however, this is not what is intended.

Therefore, the explicit formulation of the statement is as follows: "One should perform the oblation called Agnihotra; one should perform the oblation that requires the action designated as Agnihotra. Why is this so? Just as when it is said, "one should make a jar," the general injunction would be meaningless without a connection to a specific [material], lest that happen, the explicit formulation becomes "one should make a jar" or "one should perform the action of making a jar"; likewise, "one should offer the Agnihotra" is the other [specific] formulation.
The meaning of the sequence proceeds elsewhere; [it is] in Bhā, Pā, Ḍe, Līṃ;
it proceeds elsewhere in Vi.

The Teacher says: This is incorrect because of the disparity between the examples and the lack of proof for a difference in meaning. Even granting a difference in meaning produced by expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), there is a disparity with the established example of the pot, since such a distinction is not well-known in the case of the *agnihotra* and the act of offering (*havana*). He demonstrates this: "For there is no such thing as an 'agnihotra' that is an offering well-known like a pot, which could be referred to [by a prior mention] before being enjoined. Just as one might refer to a pot well-known in the world and then enjoin an action regarding it by saying 'make a pot,' such a reference is not possible here because the *agnihotra* and the act of offering are not well-known. Nor is there a unity produced by expectancy; he shows this through a contrast: 'One should perform that offering which is named the *agnihotra*. Only if the *agnihotra* and the act of offering were established as identical could an injunction regarding them be formulated."

Nor is it logical to enjoin the act of offering (*havana*) as being identical with that which is called the *agnihotra* by first restating the act of offering—namely, "one should perform the offering"—because neither the *agnihotra* nor the act of offering has been previously enjoined by another sentence, nor are they established through other means of knowledge in common worldly usage or in other scriptures; how, then, can there be an injunction by way of restatement?
This is what was meant [by the phrase]: "the object desired... etc.

For this very reason, both are impossible;

that is to say, because of the reason just mentioned—that neither is perceived through another statement or another means of valid cognition—both are impossible: namely, the qualifier and the qualified, the primary and the subordinate, the injunction and the restatement, the subsidiary and the principal, and the general rule and the exception, since the meaning of neither is apprehended.

Is *agnihotra* the qualifier and the act of offering (*havana*) the qualified? Or is the act of offering the qualifier and *agnihotra* the qualified? In this way, regarding the relations of injunction and restatement, primary and subordinate, general rule and exception, and part and whole, [to claim] it is "improper"—like a sky-flower or a donkey's horn—is impossible even with the word "but" (*tu*), if one were indeed to qualify it thus: "one should perform the offering, and that is called *agnihotra*," or "the *agnihotra* is the offering. This is improper, because if both were the objects of an injunction and a restatement, it would result in a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*).

Nor is there any action well-known—such as [the action] in the case of "that which is to be made" (kartavyatā) regarding a jar or the like—by means of which the status of being called *agnihotra* could be extended to the act of offering (*havana*), or the status of being called *havana* to the *agnihotra*, when the word *karoti* is used as a qualifier;
for, as already stated, its being a qualifier and so forth is not possible, and thus he specifies [it].

If it is asked how this is impossible, he shows: "If it were to be qualified, it should be qualified in this way"—namely, that one should perform the *havana* (offering), and that it is called *agnihotra*. Thus, either the *agnihotra* would be qualified by the act of offering as "the *agnihotra* is the *havana*," or the *havana* would be qualified by the *agnihotra* as "that which is the *agnihotra* is the *havana* ritual. In demonstrating this, if there were necessarily a purpose for such a relationship of qualifier and qualified, that could not be possible in this manner, because the meaning [of the terms] is not established.

As for what was said—that either the *agnihotra* is restated (*anūdyate*) and the act of offering (*havana*) is enjoined, or the offering is restated and the *agnihotra* is enjoined—this is incorrect because it results in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). To this he says: "Because a syntactical split would result from [one being] the object of a restatement and [the other] the object of an injunction. In that case, one part would be a restatement and the other an injunction; whichever of these two you prefer, a syntactical split follows for these two because they have distinct meanings. For example, having restated a well-known fact in "This Devadatta is to be known as skillful," the act of bringing him is enjoined in "Bring him"; or, having enjoined the bringing of Devadatta in "Bring Devadatta," there is a restatement for one who does not know [which one is better] in "Of these two, he who is more skillful"—thus there are two sentences regarding the objects of restatement and injunction involving a known and an unknown meaning. Likewise, if one is a restatement and the other is an injunction, a syntactical split results. Therefore, this path of interpretation is also not sound.

In the [passage] beginning with *śeṣībhāvādiṣu*, there might also be the reading *śeṣibhāva* and *khapuṣpa*; this is because the word *eva* has the same meaning [as *eva* used for emphasis], according to the Viśeṣeṇapāṭha, Ḍe, Līṃ, and Vi. manuscripts.

If the particle *eva* has the sense of a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), it is impossible [to establish] a single meaning; if it were to qualify, it would have to be qualified thus: "one should perform the offering, and that is named *agnihotra*," or "the *agnihotra* is the offering. This is incorrect, because if it were both a restatement (*anuvāda*) and the object of an injunction (*vidhi*), it would result in a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*).

Nor is there any action well-known— such as [the action] in the case of "the pot is to be made"— by which the status of being called *agnihotra* might be extended to the act of offering (*havana*), or the status of being called "offering" extended to the *agnihotra*, through the excellence of that act of offering.

3.1 Thus, for this reason, it is the very act of offering (*havana*) directed toward Agni that is enjoined. Consequently, there is no disparity with the illustrative example, because a substance cannot be either enjoined or prohibited—[one does not say] "one should make a jar" or "one should not make [it]," but rather "one should perform the action of making a jar. Likewise, [one says] "one should perform the offering" or "one should perform the *agnihotra*"; therefore, it is logical that the injunction applies to the acts of offering and the *agnihotra*.
To this it is replied: "Nor [is there such a thing] as the 'to-be-done-ness' (kartavyatā) regarding a jar and so forth," and so on.

Just as in the world the "to-be-done-ness" concerning a jar and the like is well-known to consist of a sequence beginning with the fetching and kneading of clay, no such thing as a "to-be-done-ness" called *agnihavana*—consisting of a sequence of ritual actions preceded by mantras beginning with the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), the spreading of sacrificial grass (*barhirāstaraṇa*), and the pouring of clarified butter (*ājyaprakṣepa*)—is well-known, such that one "to-be-done-ness" might be extended (*atidiśyeta*) to the other by the name *havana*, or the name *agnihotra* to the name *havana*.
