Now, regarding the passage beginning with "atha punaḥ" (then again):

the word "atha" introduces a new topic (*adhikārāntara*), which is an alternative position (*pakṣāntara*). This alternative position is that the previously mentioned procedure does not hold; thus, one should perform the *havana*—one should offer oblations. In this sense, within the injunction for *havana*, there is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the *agnihotra*. Because this meaning is not well-known [in common usage], and because there is an absence of the relationship between qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣyatā*) and so forth, the sentence [is problematic]. If it were argued that, since it cannot be carried out in this way, one should simply not perform the *havana* at all—this being one position—what then? Another position is adopted: that one should perform the *agnihotra*. This is because the root *juhoti* is already indicated by the word *agnihotra*, and the suffix [denoting] the agent is applied to the root *kṛ* (to do).

Even so, by observing the agentive suffix *kṛt* [in the word *yajati*], there is an abandonment of the meaning of the root *hu* (to sacrifice) due to the difference [from the root *yaj*]; just as there is a difference in the abandonment of the meaning of *hu*, there follows the consequence of abandoning all specific meanings of verbal roots because they are abandoned. Since a generality exists only when there is no distinction [between its instances]—for a generality without a substratum does not exist—and since there would be a loss of differentiation, if one were to enjoin either a substance or an action, it would be impossible to fulfill [the injunction]. Therefore, the opponent might say: "One should certainly not perform the offering (*havana*)," and so forth; thus, he considers the resolution to consist in abandoning the status of the sentence as an injunction of what is to be done (*kartavyatā*).

Regarding the adoption of another alternative position—one that is both supported by reasoning and free from defects—what, then, is this other alternative? To this he says: "What then? One should perform the *agnihotra*.

This is the alternative position adopted here, and the supporting reasoning is as follows: because the root *hu* (to sacrifice) is shown to have its meaning in the word *agnihotra*, and because the suffix denoting the agent (*kartṛ*) is shown to have its meaning in the root *kṛ* (to do/make).

For this [expression] "one should sacrifice" (*juhuyāt*) consists of the root *hu* followed by the optative suffix (*liṅ*). And that *liṅ* is prescribed for the agent; according to Pāṇini 3.4.67, "The suffixes *kṛt* are applied in the sense of the agent and the object."

Thus [it is said], "4.67, 69. Furthermore, the word *kartṛ* (agent) is derived from the root *kṛ* with the suffix *tṛc*; and since the suffixes *kṛt* and the verbal endings (*lakāra*) occur when the meaning to be expressed is the agent—that is, the one who brings about the action—it follows that even when the *kṛt* suffix or the verbal ending is prescribed for the object (*karman*), it does not deviate from the sense of the root *kṛ*.
However, since the suffix prescribed for the sense of "being" (bhāva) has as its sole purpose the expression of action, it refers precisely to the meaning of the root *kṛ* (to do).

This is because, when asking "What does he do?"—which serves as a question for a qualifier regarding all specific actions such as "he cooks" (*pacati*) and so on—it is understood that "he should sacrifice" (*juhuyāt*) means simply "he should do. Likewise, even in the case of intransitive verbs such as "Devadatta is being" (*bhūyate devadattena*) or "Devadatta sleeps" (*supyate devadattena*), one says "he sleeps" or "it comes to be. Furthermore, by the word *agnihotra*, the specific meaning of the root *hu* (to sacrifice), which constitutes a particular instance of that general action, is already expressed. Therefore, the meaning of the injunction is: "One should perform the Agnihotra."
*antaropakṣāntara* (Bhāṣya) / *antarāpekṣāntara* (Ya).

Now, if it were further argued that this [interpretation] is untenable and the position is that one should not perform the *havana* at all—what then? Another position is adopted, namely that one should perform the *agnihotra*. This is because the root *juhoti* is already shown to have its meaning expressed by the word *agnihotra*, and the agentive suffix is likewise shown by the root *kṛ*. Even so, through the observation of the agentive suffix and the root *kṛ*, there occurs the abandonment of the meaning of *juhoti*; and just as there is a distinction between the abandonment and non-abandonment of the meaning of *juhoti*, there follows the abandonment of the specific meanings of all verbal roots. Since a general property cannot exist without a basis when its particulars are absent, [the action] would be devoid of activity.
In the case of *pattike*, [the reading] *pra* is [correct]; in the case of *juhoti*, the root is *hu*; in the case of *dhātoḥ*, it is *bhāḥ*; in the case of *kucchoya*, it is *ku*.
This [form] *juhuyāt* is derived from the root *hu*,
in the *liṭ* (perfect) tense, *pra* (parasmaipada), active voice (*kartari*), and formed with a *kṛt* suffix.
Or [the following words] may optionally take the suffix *ya*: *bhavya*, *geya*, *pravacanīya*, *upasthānīya*, *janya*, *āplāvya*, and *āpātya*.
4.1.68: *laḥ* [are used] in the sense of the object (*karman*) and in the sense of the state (*bhāva*) after intransitive verbs (*akarmaka*).
thus in the Pāṇinian grammar.
The suffixes *ṇvul* and *tṛc* are applied after roots ending in *as*, *an*, and *kvasu*.
(Pāṇini 3.1.133)
*Kṛtsna* [is used] in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) in the *bhāva* [vibhakti].
For the sense of the agent (kartr-artha): Pāṇini; for the sense of the agent: Vyākaraṇa; for the sense of the agent: Raṅgashashtri; Hīnayāna.

Regarding the meaning of *katra*: *ḍe* [is used] in the sense of *viśeṣeṇa* (specifically), while *bhā* [is used] here in the sense of *aviśeṣeṇa* (generally); there may also be a reading *aviśeṣeṇa*.
To this it is replied: even so, he restates what was said by the opponent, namely, "because [the root] *kṛ* is seen with an agentive suffix."

"In this way, one should now perform the *agnihotra*"; this is another alternative view. You have stated that the root *hu* (to sacrifice) has the meaning of "offering" as expressed by the word *hotra*, and also the meaning of the verbal root *kṛ* (to do/make) ending in the agentive suffix (*kartṛ-pratyaya*). Although I have accepted this along with its reasoning, nevertheless, there is both an abandonment of the meaning of *juhoti* and a difference in meaning. First, regarding the abandonment of the meaning of *juhoti*: you have accepted that it denotes merely the general action qualified by an agent, whereas *juhoti* itself refers to a specific action; and since the general and the specific are distinct from one another, you yourself have abandoned [the original sense] because of your statement that "the word *juhuyāt* expresses the meaning of the word *kuryāt*," since the meaning has already been shown by the word *hotra*. Thus, *juhoti* is rendered redundant.

Furthermore, [the opponent might argue] that the word *juhuyāt* (one should sacrifice) expresses the meaning of the word *hotra*, and the word *hotra* also expresses the meaning of the word *juhuyāt*; thus, because both the noun (*nāman*) and the verb (*ākhyāta*) each possess two meanings, there would be a distinction: the word *hotra* denotes both action (*kriyā*) and a name (*nāman*), and likewise the word *juhuyāt*.

This being the case, a confusion of word-meanings (*śabdārtha-saṅkara*) and a contradiction with established usage (*prasiddhi-virodha*) arise; as it has been stated in the *Nirukta*: "One expresses a process consisting of prior and posterior stages by means of a verb, such as 'he goes' (*vrajati*) or 'he cooks' (*pacati*)—[this refers to] a concrete entity (*mūrta-sattva*) from its commencement until its completion—whereas one expresses [such things] by names, such as 'going' (*vrajyā*) or 'cooking' (*pakti*). (Nirukta 1.1).

And if it is argued that [the injunction] does not apply because of the two reasons—the difference in the meaning of the root *hu* (to sacrifice) and the abandonment [of the original context]—due to the fact that the duty of performing the *agnihotra* is heard in close proximity [in another text], we say: no, because the meaning of the root *hu* is heard in even closer proximity [here].

Furthermore, even when another object is enjoined, because [the root *juhoti*] functions solely as the *hotra* (offering) heard from the other word, one must abandon the mere meaning of "offering" (*juhoti*) itself; thus, there is an abandonment of all specific verbal roots (*dhātu*), just as there is an abandonment of the distinction between the meaning of the root and the suffix. Just as the root *juhoti* expresses the meaning of the verbal base *kṛ* (to do) ending in a suffix denoting the agent, so too all roots such as *pacati* (cooks), *paṭhati* (reads), and others, by virtue of being verbal roots, express that same [general sense]. Therefore, all specific meanings of the verbal roots are abandoned. Since the word "specific" (*viśeṣa*) signifies "distinction" (*bheda*) and applies to both nouns and verbs, there is a difference in meaning, just like the previously mentioned meaning of the root *kṛ*.

Furthermore, because of the abandonment of the specificities of all verbal root meanings, there follows the abandonment of that [root] as well; for even that meaning of the root *kṛ* (to do), which constitutes the generality of all root meanings, would result in being abandoned.

Why? Because in the absence of specificities, a generality cannot exist without a substratum. When "he does" (*karoti*) is said, one asks "What does he do?"—for without resorting to specificities such as "he offers oblations" (*juhoti*), "he cooks" (*pacati*), or "he reads" (*paṭhati*), the meaning of the root *kṛ* is non-existent.
Moreover, by the word "also" (*api*), there are the faults of confusion (*saṅkara*), contradiction with established usage (*prasiddhi-virodha*), and tautology (*paunaruktya*).
The root *kṛt* is seen [in the sense of an agent]; *pra* [is a prefix]; *juhoti* is the verbal form;
thus is the meaning of the word.
Prajātibhāṇḍe līṃ pāṃ prejati viṃ paraṃjati raṃ hīṃ.
A *patti* (line) is a *paṅkti* (row).

According to the reading in Yāska’s *Nirukta*: "One expresses a state consisting of a temporal sequence by means of a verb—as in 'he goes' (*vrajati*) or 'he cooks' (*pacati*)—[denoting] that which begins with the commencement and ends with the completion; whereas [one expresses] that which is embodied and substantial by means of nouns denoting substances—as in 'the act of going' (*vrajyā*) or 'the act of cooking' (*pakti*)."

If it is argued that this is not the case because the performance of the *agnihotra* has been heard of as being proximate [in the preceding text], we say no; for that would involve abandoning the meaning of the root *hu-* (to sacrifice), which is even more proximately heard,
and since the injunction pertains to another object, the term *juhuyāt* (he should sacrifice) must refer solely to the act of sacrificing itself, as indicated by the other words in the sentence.
...like the abandonment of distinctions through abandonment;
[the text] reads *kṛtsnaprabhā* and *tatsarvapra* in the Ya manuscript.
Or rather,
thus [it is] for all;
the previously mentioned fault [applies].
If it be thought that [the word-meaning] is not [determined by the context] because the performance of the *agnihotra* has been recently heard [as a duty], it may be argued:

"The exclusion of the word-meaning from other possibilities occurs through the capacity [of the word] as distinguished by association and so forth, and through specific indicative marks (*liṅga*), just as it has been said:
'Association, dissociation, concomitance, and opposition...'"
The meaning, the context, the indicative mark, the proximity of another word, the capacity, propriety, place, time, gender, and accents—
these are the causes for the recollection of specific meanings when there is ambiguity regarding the meaning of a word.
As stated in *Vākyapadīya* 2.317–318,

the capacity known as "proximity to the word *yat*" (*yacchabdasannidhi*) which serves as the cause of exclusion exists here as well; for example, when the word *agnihotra* is heard in close proximity, it is connected precisely with the duty enjoined by that [word].

Therefore, the meaning of the root *hu* (to sacrifice) is not abandoned; for even when there is the perception of the meaning of the verb *kṛ* (to do) as the agent of that [action], in the injunction "one should perform the *agnihotra*," only the performance (*karaṇa*) whose object is the offering (*havana*) is prescribed.

Regarding the doubt expressed by "if" (*ced*): if you think this [is the case], that too is not so, because it involves abandoning the meaning of the immediately proximate verbal root *juhoti*. If you consider it right to adopt the meaning of that [root] due to its proximity to the immediately proximate mention of the *agnihotra*, then why do you not consider it even more right to adopt the meaning of the immediately more proximate verbal root *juhoti*? Furthermore, that meaning has been abandoned by you; and even if it were adopted, defects such as being unestablished (*aprasiddhatā*) would remain as they were. It has already been stated: "How could [the word] function for the meaning of another word while abandoning its own word-meaning?
(Śruta-agni-pāda-vivaraṇa, Śrutagni-raṃ-hī-ḍe-līṃ).
*argābheda* (Ya);
*icchapṛcchabdārtha* (Ḍe); *līṃ* (Līṃ);
*icchabdapṛdvabdārtha* (Pā).

The word *praśna* (question) has the sense of "asking" (*pṛcchā*). [The word] *viyukta* has the sense of "separated" (*viyukta*). *Raṃ* and *hīṃ* [are used for] conjunction (*saṃsarga*) and disjunction (*viprayoga*), as well as association (*sāhacarya*) and opposition (*virodhitā*).
Meaning, context, indicative mark, proximity of another word, capability, propriety, place, time, gender, accent, and so forth— [these are the factors that determine the specific sense].
(Vyaktiviveka 1.3)

"In the exclusion of the meaning of a word, [the phonemes] are the causes for the recollection of the specific [meaning]. (Vākyapadīya 2.317–318). [The reading is: "of this meaning... by hearing... [with variants:
*arthasya-vya* (Ya), *śrutāgni* (Pā), *ḍe* (Līṃ)].
The sounds *śruta-agni-raṃ-hī-śabda-staccodya-tyakta-satkartṛ-bhā* [are present].
॰staktasātkartṛ ḍe līṃ ॰staktastatkartṛ vi ॰staktatkartṛ raṃ hīṃ.
In every philosophical system,
it proceeds according to proximity.
See page 123, line 2.

Even granting the expression of the meaning of another word, the fault is stated as follows: "Even when there is the prescription of the meaning of another word, because it functions solely toward what is heard from the other words, one should perform only the mere act of offering (*juhuyāt*); thus, the adoption of the meaning is non-differentiating."

In the other word, *agnihotra*, it is well-known—that is, fully understood—that what is signified is merely the act of offering (*hotramātra*); no other distinct meaning apart from that is perceived. Therefore, the word should function solely within the meaning of the term "one should offer" (*juhuyāt*). The particle *iti* here signifies a reason: for this reason, because it consists of nothing more than the meaning of the word "one should offer," one should perform the act of offering; thus, the inclusion of the object [of the action] does not differentiate it, since the meaning of the verbal root has merged with the meaning of the verbal suffix (*tiṅ-pratyaya*), and there is no presence of a compound with *agni*. Furthermore, in this sense, this [usage of the word *agnihotra*] would be a grammatical error (*apaśabda*).
Its inclusion is non-differentiating; "non-differentiating" (*abhedaka*) means that there is no difference in this [term], i.e., it has an undivided meaning.
If it is asked, "Why does it not have a divided meaning?", [the answer is: because of the sentence-meaning "one should perform the oblation," therefore those same faults [apply].
It might be thought: "The application of the term *mātra* (only) is not established because [the word] is a compound qualified by the word 'fire' (*agni*);

for it is not merely the act of offering (*hotra*) that is heard [in the injunction], but rather, what then? It is the act of offering to Agni, in Agni, or for Agni—namely, the *agnihotra*. Therefore, one should perform that," and thus the meaning is distinct.

This, however, is incorrect; because the meaning of the verbal root is unified with the meaning of the verbal suffix (*tiṅ-pratyaya*), it is already established that the term refers exclusively to the act of offering (*hotra*). This is the sense.

Where the meaning of the verbal root has merged with the meaning of the verbal suffix (*tiṅ-pratyaya*), there the operation is observed to apply to the meaning of the root alone; for example, in "he hangs down" (*pralambate*) or "he approaches" (*adhyāgacchati*).

If it is argued that—by way of contrast with such cases—the compound *agni-hotram* (fire-oblation) must have a specific meaning because it is a compound, just like *kumbhakāra* ("potter") or *kāṇḍalāva* ("reed-cutter"), this too is untenable. This is because there is no such thing as a compound with a verbal suffix (*tiṅ-samāsa*); for indeed, there is no compounding of the word *agni* with the word *hotra* when the latter is dependent on the meaning of a verbal suffix. As stated in Pāṇini’s Mahābhāṣya: "A case-inflected word (*sup*) is compounded with another case-inflected word (*sup*) that is semantically compatible. (Pāṇini 2.1.4).

If it is argued that there is no fault because of the statement "1.4" and because compounds such as *astikṣīrā* ("having milk"), *aśnītapibata* ("eat and drink"), and so forth are seen with finite verbs (*tiṅanta*), we say no; for [compounding] does not occur outside of those specifically enumerated cases, and because these words are either indeclinables (*nipāta*) resembling finite verbs or nominal stems (*subanta*). (Pāṇini 2.2.6: *asti-nāsti-diṣṭa-mati-...*)
Thus, like a nominal stem (*prātipadika*),
otherwise even in the case of "Devadatta cooks" (*devadattaḥ pacati*), there would be a compound (*samāsa*), but it does not occur.

Furthermore, a compound is untenable due to a lack of semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*), because of the governing rule: "A grammatical operation concerning words applies only when they possess semantic capacity" (Pāṇini 2.1.1).

Furthermore, there is a lack of capacity [for composition] because of dependence, just as in the case of "look at the piece with the mallet" (*paśya śaṅkulayā khaṇḍaḥ*), where the compound is not possible due to the opposition between the mallet and the piece; it is not the same as "Devadatta’s teacher’s family" (*devadattasya gurukulam*), for in that case, because of the predominance [of the teacher], the compound does occur—as it has been said:
"For a predominant word, even when dependent, a compound does indeed occur" (Pāṇini-Mahābhāṣya 2.1.1).

Thus, in this context, neither the word *agni* nor the word *hotra* possesses primacy; rather, primacy belongs to the verbal form ending in a *tiṅ*-suffix—such as *kuryāt* or *juhuyāt*—because it denotes the action (*kriyā*), and because the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) function solely for the sake of achieving that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
Indeed, what is called an *apaśabda* (corrupt word) is so designated because, while intending to convey a specific meaning, it deviates from the form that expresses that meaning;
for example, the word *goṇī* is an *apaśabda* when used in the sense of "that which possesses a dewlap" (*sāsnādimat*), yet it is a correct word (*śabda*) in the sense of "a sack" (*āvapana*).
Similarly, the word *gāvī* is incapable of denoting the object "cow" (*gavya*), but it is a correct word in the sense of "the word *gāvī*" itself.

And thus it has been said: "But he who, being skilled, employs words according to their specific distinctions as they are used in correct linguistic practice, attains infinite victory in the hereafter; however, one who knows the application of speech is defiled by corrupt words" (Pāṇini-Mahābhāṣya 1.1.1).

Therefore, it has been well said: "In this context, one should employ even an incorrect word (*apaśabda*), provided that the inclusion of the meaning does not cause a distinction [in the sense intended]," and so forth. *Pra.* (Prakaraṇa-pañcikā) 1.1.1.
In the phrase *parapadāntarapariśruta*,
there may also be the reading *parapadārthābhidhāne 'pi*;
[this refers to] merely the *hotṛ*.
Because of this [nature], one should not perform [it];

one should rather undertake the inclusion of the meaning as non-distinctive, since the meaning of the verbal suffix (*tiṅ-pratyaya*) has become unified with the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), and because there is no existence of a compound with *agni*. Furthermore, this is a corrupt word (*apaśabda*) in this sense; [its] establishment is from the root *ṇā*.
This very [state] is the manifestation of the suffix *tip* belonging solely to the root *hu*.
Or the occurrence is seen for the sake of the object of perception; come to the support,
because of the non-existence of a composite entity.
Because it is a compound (samāsa), [the rule] "ya-ṭi-pra-saha-supā" [applies].

...the analysis of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) will be performed as follows: "The word *saha* is compounded with a word ending in the *sup* case-suffix; with what? With a word that is semantically related (*samarthena*)," as in the example *anuvyacalat*.
Then [the suffix] *sup* entered; and *sup* is compounded with *sup*—this is the reading in the Patañjala Mahābhāṣya. 2.
1.4 "There is milk; let those who wish to drink it do so. (Bhāṣya)
There is salt; there is the drinking of hot [liquids];
and because of the elision of *ya*, there is *ḍe*;
and because it ends in a *su*-affix, there is *bhā*.
And because of being unattainable, [it is] Pā॰ Vi॰;
and because of being unattainable, Raṃ॰ Hī॰ Saṃkulā॰ Pra॰.

"And there occurs a compound of a principal word even when it is dependent [on another], provided that the dependence is not obscured by another factor"— this is the reading in the *Patañjala-Mahābhāṣya* (2.1).
The word "api" (also/even) indeed has the sense of a noun;
in the sense of "existence," it is the very word [denoting] that which is to be established.

"One who employs words with skill regarding their specific distinctions as they are used in correct linguistic practice attains infinite victory in the hereafter; however, one who knows the application of speech is defiled by corrupt words. (Pāṇini-Mahābhāṣya 1.1.1)
The word *śabda* [is used] in Ya;
and the words *cāraṃ* and *hī* are without [the suffix] *pada*; *pra*... [is used].

However, if one accepts the agenthood of the *juhoti* (the act of offering) as something already abandoned, then because it would be an agent devoid of action, there would be an absence of purpose (*arthābhāva*), and consequently, the application of the term *juhoti* would be non-existent due to its being something to be abandoned—just like a disease.

Furthermore, through the abandonment of its own function and the adoption [of another], there would be a distinction between the verbal root (*dhātu*) and the nominal stem (*prakṛti*), rather than merely a distinction of words (*padabheda*), since that would pertain to a different word; or rather, it would be a distinction of sentences (*vākyabheda*), because the previously unknown *agnihotra* is restated (*anuvāda*) as a qualifier of the action.

But if one were to adopt the meaning of the agent while abandoning the act of offering (*juhoti*), then because the agent would be devoid of action, there would be an absence of purpose for the injunction "one should do" (*kuryāt*). Now, if you should say: "For fear of this defect, having abandoned the meaning of offering, we grasp only the agent devoid of action; thus, 'one should do' (*kuryāt*) has the sense of an injunction regarding the mere manner of performance (*kartavyatā*)."

This being the case, if one were to adopt the meaning of the agent (*kartr-artha*) while abandoning the meaning of the root *hu* (to sacrifice), the particle *tu* serves as a qualification; it qualifies [the agent] by means of the absolute absence of an object. For words such as *karoti* (he does) and *kuryāt* (he should do)—which are derived from the verbal root *kṛ*—what would be their meaning if they lacked a reference to an object such as a pot, since their meaning remains undetermined in the form "what should he do? or "what might he do? In the absence of the meaning of the root *kṛ*, there would be no agency for the agent, as his function would be devoid of anything to be accomplished (*niḥsādhya*).

Therefore, the word would be meaningless, because its own primary meaning has been abandoned; for we have never observed the usage of such forms—those ending in suffixes like *yāt* and so on—which are devoid of roots such as *kṛ*, *bhū*, and the like. Even granting such usage for the sake of argument, we maintain that the usage of *juhoti* is non-existent. "Non-existence" here means "unacceptability. Why? Because it must be rejected. It must be rejected because you yourself have abandoned it, and according to our view, it lacks a referent (*artha*).
And the absence of a referent is already established by the reasoning stated above.

Therefore, because it is to be abandoned, one should offer that which is non-existent; this is the illustration for the application [of the term], like a disease. Just as a disease is undesirable because it is to be abandoned, so too the word *juhoti* (he offers) possesses a meaning. Furthermore, there is another point: "in the functions of the names of actions," and so forth.

An *ākhyāta* (verb), which is conventionally established as having action (*kriyā*) as its meaning, abandons its own primary sense—the dispersed collection of its constituent parts—and adopts the sense of a unified, existing entity (*sattva*). Yet, even after adopting that, it does not remain fixed there; rather, it again abandons the sense of an existing entity and adopts the sense of action. In the same way, a noun (*nāman*) also abandons its own inherent function of denoting an existing entity and adopts the sense of action; then, having abandoned the sense of action, it adopts the sense of an existing entity.

And by means of those very two—renunciation (*tyāga*) and taking up (*upādāna*)—one should perform both the acts expressed by the words "should do" (*kuryāt*) and "should offer" (*juhuyāt*). Although these two words possess general and specific meanings, they function through mutual implication; thus, there is a distinction between them based on the power of their own roots (*prakṛti*), due to the gathering together and the scattering apart [of the elements].

Just as there is a distinction between those two [actions] by virtue of that [distinction in the roots], so too there is a distinction between the two roots that express them, by means of those two [operations of] renunciation and taking up.

If it is asked, "Of which two bases? [the answer is] "of the verbal root (*dhātu*) and the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Therefore, he says: "Even the distinction between the bases of verbal roots and nominal stems is not merely a distinction of words. If it is asked, "Whence does that distinction of words arise? [the answer is] "Because its object is another word. That word—whether a verb (*ākhyāta*) or a noun (*nāman*)—has another word as its object; because of that state of having another word as its object, [one understands] "one should do" (*kuryāt*) or "one should offer" (*juhuyāt*).

Alternatively, for the Mīmāṃsaka, whose primary concern is the investigation of the meaning of sentences, that which was stated previously—namely, that there would be a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*) because of the consequence of one part being an injunction (*vidhi*) and the other a restatement (*anuvāda*)—is not merely a split of the sentence nor even a split of the word (*padabheda*); rather, it is connected with the idea that there is also a split of the verbal root (*dhātu*) and the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). If it is asked what the reason for this is, [the answer is: because the unknown *agnihotra* is restated as a qualifier of the action; and thus, there is an absence of that comprehension of the meaning of the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) which occurs when the object is already known.

And because that [meaning] is abandoned according to the logic of restating one's own individual reflection (*svapratyavekṣā*), and because the meaning of a word is established by the force of understanding meanings such as an agent, human cognition alone is made the authority.
If this is so, then just as with the *agnihotra*, even the act of offering (*dhavana*) will be accepted according to the literal scriptural statement;
but surely, it is impossible for two distinct meanings to be enjoined by a single sentence.

[The author] presents as a supporting argument the point previously stated: "Injunction (*vidhi*) is that which has an unknown object; restatement (*anuvāda*) is that which has a known object. By the very abandonment and adoption of the self-referential functions of the names of the actions indicated immediately after "in this way"—namely, by the word-hearing (*pada-śruti*) "one should sacrifice" (*juhuyāt*), whose meaning is the injunction of the act of offering, namely "one should sacrifice, one should perform the offering"—there is the absence of that [injunction]; it does not exist, because the meaning is understood otherwise. "What the word says is our authority" (Pāṇini-Mahābhāṣya 2.1).

And thus it is abandoned, due to the faults of discarding or adopting the distinct meanings of nouns and verbs, and because of the lack of fixedness in words; for the status of word and meaning is established merely by the power of human intellect. Why? Because of the abandonment of that [scriptural authority] according to the principle of personal investigation and restatement. Having personally investigated whether "this is the word for this meaning" or "is it not so," one concludes—on account of its being faulty—that "this must be discarded" and on account of its being virtuous—that "this must be adopted. Consequently, by abandoning that [position], and by establishing the meaning of words through the apprehension of meanings such as the "agent" (kartṛ) and so forth, it is the cognition of the person (*puruṣa*) alone that has been made the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it is that [cognition] itself which is restated as being established like the meaning of an injunction (*vidhi*).

And therefore, for you, there is the point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) known as "abandoning the thesis" (*pratijñātyāga*) and "shifting to another thesis" (*pratijñāntaragamana*), because, by relying on the validity of human cognition, you fail to accept the validity of the instructional sentence regarding action (*kriyopadeśavākya*), which constitutes the conclusion of your argument.

In one case, the act of offering (*havana*) is described as being characterized by fire as its recipient (*sampradāna*), while in another, it is described as being characterized by its own specific agent (*kartṛ*).

To this, it is replied: "Indeed, it is impossible for a single sentence to enjoin two distinct meanings—namely, an offering that has fire as its recipient and the agency characterized by that [offering]—just as a sentence regarding the giving of an oblation to a Brāhmaṇa cannot simultaneously enjoin the bringing of a white cow."

The offering (havana) is not enjoined at all; what then? By the word "agnihotra," the offering already enjoined is restated—that is, it is restated as something already established by another sentence—or else, that which is not yet established is enjoined.
However, there is no prior establishment of the offering, because it has not been previously enjoined.
If it is argued that the *agnihotra* is merely an offering (*havana*), then it would be a tautology, because there is no distinction between these two;

for an "anuvāda" (reiteration) is the restatement of what has already been enjoined by an injunction, and since the *agnihotra* is itself the object of the injunction regarding the offering, it is unfit to be a reiteration.
If, however, the restatement were to occur by mere whim in any way whatsoever, then there would simply be no fault of tautology;
for it has been said: "There is no repetition in cases of restatement, respect, repetition (vīpsā), intensity, purpose, cause, envy, slightness, agitation, wonder, counting, and recollection."

But this [particle *tu*] is incapable of being a mere restatement (*anuvāda*), because it is something being enjoined (*vidhīyamānatvāt*), like the "scholarship" (*paṇḍitatva*) that is being described; for the particle *tu* is employed in the sense of an injunction, a restatement, disregard, repetition, intensity, application, cause, or censure.

Another, considering [the situation] with slight agitation, wonder, calculation, and recollection, says that [the objection] is not redundant: "The oblation (*havana*) is certainly not enjoined," and so forth.

By the word *juhuyāt*, the oblation is indeed not enjoined; what then? The oblation already enjoined by the term *agnihotra* is being restated (*anūdyate*), because injunction (*vidhi*) and restatement (*anuvāda*) have distinct characteristics.

If it is asked what the characteristics of these two are, it is said: that which has already been established is restated by another sentence, as in "the scholar stands," where the standing is a restatement of the scholarship already enjoined by another sentence—since "scholar" means one who knows the scriptures.

And that which is not yet established is enjoined; that which has not been obtained by another sentence, being unknown through any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), is enjoined, such as "one desiring heaven should sacrifice.

To this it is replied: if these are the characteristics of injunction (*vidhi*) and restatement (*anuvāda*), then a restatement of the act of sacrificing (*havana*) is not appropriate, because there is no prior establishment of the sacrifice, since it has not been previously enjoined.

The other says: "There is indeed an injunction for the *havana*, because the *agnihotra* is a *havana* and that [injunction] has been prescribed. To this he replies: "If that *agnihotra* is merely a *havana*, then it is a tautology; for in that case, there would be no distinction between these two injunctions—the *agnihotra* and the *havana*. And this is a semantic tautology; moreover, what is a tautology is not a restatement (*anuvāda*), like the speech of a madman."

And he demonstrates the absence of the defining characteristic of restatement (anuvāda) for this [passage]: "For restatement is the subsequent mention of that which has been enjoined by an injunction. The word *hi* means "because"; because a restatement (*anuvāda*) is a subsequent statement intended to convey a specific detail regarding a matter already enjoined by an injunctive sentence (*vidhivākya*), that definition does not apply here. This is because the *agnihotra* and the *havana* (offering) are themselves what are to be enjoined, as the *agnihotra* and the *havana* are enjoined as a single unified entity. He concludes: "therefore, it is unfit to be a restatement."

The commentary on the Vivaraṇa (Viva-bhā) states that the injunction (*vidhāna*) has been explained; thus, it shows that the exception to the rule against tautology (*punarukta-apavāda*) depends upon a specific purpose, as there is respect for the restatement (*anuvāda*).
When it is said, "Bring the scholar," the statement "The scholar is Devadatta" is a restatement (*anuvāda*) and not a tautology (*punarukta*).
Likewise, in the case of emphasis, as in "Master! Master! (*svāmin svāmin*), or in the sense of repetition, as in "Every village is delightful" (*grāmo grāmo ramaṇīyaḥ*).
Rather, that very [act] is restated for the purpose of prescribing a specific detail;
yet, no specific detail is produced here by the repetition of the word *juhoti*, and consequently, it remains exactly as it was previously established.

In every respect, what is superior [to this] that is free from the fault of tautology? Since the suffix *liṅ* has the sense of an agent (*kartṛ*), it is not a mere restatement (*anuvāda*), because it lacks connection with a subsequent qualification, just like the "learnedness" (*paṇḍitatva*) being enjoined.

Or, if it should be argued: when the meaning of the suffix as an agent remains and must necessarily be expressed, there is the intensive force (*bhṛśārtha*) following the verbal root, such as "firmly, firmly," "softly, softly," or "gradually, gradually."
In the sense of application (*viniyoga*): "Make a jar, make a jar"; in the sense of cause (*hetu*): "The jar is impermanent because it is produced; therefore, because it is produced";
in the sense of envy (*asūyā*): "He smiles, he smiles, having turned his face away."
"Little by little," "bit by bit"—this is used in agitation;
"welcome, welcome"—this is used in astonishment;
"vidyādhara, vidyādhara"—this is used in wonder.

In counting, one says "one, two," and in recollection, "Ah! he is known, he is known; he was seen in Pāṭaliputra, he was seen"—since there is no such distinction of meaning, if this is not a restatement (*anuvāda*), then its repetition would necessarily constitute the fault of tautology (*paunaruktya*).
The meaning is that in the absence of tautology, there is no status as a restatement (*anuvāda*);
therefore, this [word] is incapable of being a restatement and is unfit for such a role. Which word? This word "juhuyāt" (one should sacrifice).

Why? Because it is something being enjoined (*vidhīyamāna*). Whatever matter is being enjoined is not restated, just like the state of being learned when it is being described—for example, in the case of "This Devadatta is learned," Devadatta, whose learning is being enjoined, is not restated. Likewise, "juhuyāt" is also not a restatement because it is an instruction on what was previously unknown (*apūrvopadeśa*), and because it lacks the characteristics of a restatement due to its difference from the nature of a restatement.

If it is asked what that characteristic is: it is precisely that which has already been enjoined and is then restated for the purpose of enjoining a specific detail—just as in the cases, "Devadatta is clever," or "Feed him with milk.

Why [is it not so]? Because in the absence of such a characteristic, there is no restatement; rather, because it is a previously unestablished injunction (*apūrva-vidhāna*), where no specific detail is enjoined, that is merely the original injunction itself.
It is indeed restated for the purpose of enjoining a specific detail.
And no distinction whatsoever is produced here by the repetition of the word *juhoti*; therefore, that which was already established remains exactly as it was.
In every respect, what is added that is free from the fault of tautology? The optative suffix (*liṅ*) expresses the agent.
Therefore, it is not a restatement (*anuvāda*), because it lacks connection with a subsequent qualification, like the "learnedness" (*paṇḍitatva*) being enjoined.

The point is that the *liṅ* suffix in the injunctive sense remains unrefuted only insofar as its meaning is restricted to the agent (*kartṛ*)—that is, when the *liṅ* suffix prescribed for an injunction denotes merely the agent—and everything else is indeed afflicted by faults such as tautology. Therefore, it is not a restatement (*anuvāda*), because it would be subject to the faults already mentioned; this is the meaning.

"If you were to say—the meaning of the suffix [in *juhuyāt*], namely the agent (*kartṛ*), remains as the unexpressed residue; and this must necessarily be expressed. However, its meaning is not intended to be expressed, because its purpose has already been fulfilled."

In that case, it would be even better to employ the verbal root *kṛ* (to do/make) in its proximate, non-intended sense, because a word exists for the purpose of conveying the meaning it has been employed to convey; and that [root] also, like what was said before, maintains a state where the expressed meaning is set aside.

However, if this principle were completely disregarded, even the doctrine of the instruction of action (*kriyopadeśavāda*) would be abandoned just like the doctrine of reality (*tattvavāda*), since in that case too one would be resorting to mere arbitrariness.

"Who indeed knows this?"—this is like the idle chatter of children. The fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) is used here in the sense of "purpose" (*hetvarthe*), according to Pāṇini’s *Mahābhāṣya* (Pāṇini-Mahābhāṣya 3.1.92): "A suffix (*pratyaya*) should be employed after a base (*prakṛti*)."

Such is the established rule (*vyavasthā*). For the sake of that rule, its limit, and its stability, the employment of a verbal root (*prakṛti-upādāna*) is necessary. When that necessary employment of a root has been reached, one deliberates: "Which root is fit to be employed?"—and it occurs to him: "This is suitable for me. It is better that a proximate root be employed; however, its meaning is not intended to be expressed because its purpose is already understood. Therefore, although its meaning is not intended, since a proximate root must necessarily be employed, it should be understood that, having abandoned another dissimilar [root], the *juhoti* root itself—which is non-dissimilar—is employed. The actual application (*prayoga*) is: "One should offer the *agnihotra*. (*agnihotraṃ juhuyāt*)

To this it is replied: "If you think that it is thus 'even better' (*varatarakam*) and so forth—that the employment of a proximate verbal root (*prakṛti*) is better because it is indispensable—then I myself shall provide you with an even better assistance for the intellect: namely, that the verbal root *kṛñ* (to do/make) has been employed [in the sūtra] as something whose meaning is not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣitārthā*), whose meaning is already stated (*uktārthā*), and which is more proximate than the agentive suffix (*kartṛpratyaya*) for the sake of avoiding redundancy."

What is the reason? Because speech exists for the purpose of communicating a meaning already grasped; for a word is clearly communicated by the verbal root *kṛ* (to do) ending in a suffix denoting an agent, as in the thought "I shall communicate the meaning. Therefore, let it simply be "one should perform the Agnihotra.
The other replies: "Let it be exactly so, since you yourself have established this."

The Teacher says: This might be so if that established state of meaning were also faultless; however, as previously stated, even that established state of meaning has its expressed meaning rejected by the very same arguments—namely, through the distinction between the meanings of "one who sacrifices" (*juhoti*) and "one who does not sacrifice" (*ajuhoti*), and so forth. As explained before, because of defects such as the absence of the literal meaning and because it would entail [the scripture] being of human origin, this statement, when examined by means of logic characterized by human reasoning, is not tenable as something to be expressed.

In the case of the *sthāyin* [suffixes] in the *āvaśyaka* [sense], although the employment of the root (*prakṛti*) would have been required, it is better that the proximate root has been employed; however, its meaning is not intended to be expressed because the sense is already understood. If that is so, then it is even better that the root *kṛñ*, which is more proximate and whose meaning is not intended to be expressed, has been employed, since the purpose of a word is to convey the meaning that has been employed [as a substitute]. And this [root *kṛñ*] also has its status as a directly expressed meaning set aside, as previously stated.

But if this principle were transgressed, even the doctrine of the instruction on ritual action (*kriyopadeśavāda*) would be abandoned just like the doctrine of ultimate reality (*tattvavādavāda*), because there too one would be accepting things by mere whim. For it is said in the *Pātañjala-Mahābhāṣya*: "Who indeed knows this? It should be established like the prattle of a child that the suffix alone must be employed, with the base being subordinate."
The term "pratyupāya" is explained as having its meaning already understood from the preceding context.

In this context, one should understand that there might also be the reading "one should offer the *agnihotra* in the ritual application," and it is stated as "iti" in Bhāṣya and also stated as "iti" in Yāska.
You think it is "bha," you think it is "ya," O best of the best, O protector.
In the Ya manuscript it reads "samārthā," while in the Bhā,
Kṛtsnaprakṛti, and Pra manuscripts it reads "asamarthā."
In this regard, it appears as though some portion of the text has been omitted; for comparison: "The employment of a word is for the sake of conveying meaning;
a word is employed with the thought, 'I shall cause the meaning to be understood.'"

"In that case, since that meaning has already been expressed by one [word], there should be no employment of a second; for 'that which has already expressed its meaning is not employed'— thus it is stated in the Patañjala Mahābhāṣya on 1.1.44."
By you alone [is] the meaning of the words of the Ācārya’s *Prakaraṇa* to be spoken.

Even though it is accepted that the Vedic teaching of ritual action—which is non-human, eternal, and called "Veda"—is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it transcends the logic (*nyāya*) characterized by human reasoning and is free from the causes for suspecting defects such as passion inherent in persons; and whereas human-made statements are invalid because they belong to persons inseparable from ignorance, passion, and so forth, and deal with subjects such as the nature of things like the fruitless, the impossible-to-attain, the eternal, and the non-eternal, whereas the Vedic doctrine is superior because it teaches the performance of beneficial means for a person to attain fruitful and possible results—even so, if this very logic is transgressed merely on your word, then the teaching of ritual action would have to be abandoned just like the teaching of ultimate reality (*tattva*).

What is the reason? Because even in that case, it is accepted as being accidental; because all persons—including both the speaker and the listener—are inseparable from ignorance (*avidyā*), passion (*rāga*), and so forth, and because the tradition of instruction depends upon such persons, there is no instruction whatsoever preceded by conscious wisdom (*buddhi*). Therefore, is this not like the incoherent chatter of one who is asleep or intoxicated—uttered by chance? What is the use of knowing this, when those who claim to be wise have spoken thus [regarding the Unmanifest], whether out of ignorance or out of hatred and the like? Who indeed says that this is the word of a wise person? If, due to the presence of doubt and other defects, one who is not wise is not an authority, then this [tradition] is likewise not authoritative, because it was spoken by one who is not wise, like the speech of a madman.
Since it is insentient, how can it possess authority? How can there be its speech? Just like the word "wood," if it is thus insentient, the authority of the Vedic sentences is not tenable;
for the Vedas are accepted as authoritative by the followers of the Veda (Vaidikas).
Consequently, this follows: who indeed knows whether this sentence, "One desiring heaven should offer the Agnihotra," is meaningful or meaningless?

How could it not be known? It is like the prattle of children; for just as that which is uttered by children—whose connection between action and its factors is indeterminate—is impossible to understand because it is not preceded by conscious intent, in what sense would it be meaningful for the purpose of communicating a meaning? Thus [it is meaningless].

What is the reason? Because it deviates from established convention (*vyavasthā*). For the employment of words is for the purpose of communicating meaning; it consists of a fixed sequence of phonemes capable of conveying a meaning ascertained by oneself, wherein the relationship between the signifier and the signified is required. This is the established convention of the world and the treatises. Therefore, the speech of those such as Brahmā and all other proponents of the Vedas—who are not free from ignorance, passion, and so forth—deviates from this [convention]. Consequently, the realization of the meaning of sentences such as the injunction to offer oblations into fire is impossible for them to attain.

Therefore, who indeed knows this which has been established and proclaimed like the prattle of children? Furthermore, it is fruitless; thus he says: "What is the use of knowing this? Those who know this—the knowers of the Vedas and knowers of the Agnihotra ritual—have spoken thus: "One should offer the Agnihotra. This sentence is unmanifest (*avyakta*), meaning its sense is unmanifest and its meaning is unclear. Because they possess only unmanifest knowledge due to their human nature and connection with ignorance (*avidyā*), he demonstrates their connection with ignorance, just like those who recite verses such as "Ten pomegranates" (*daśadāḍima*).
He shows the connection with ignorance by the phrase "if through lack of knowledge," and he shows the connection with passion and so forth by the phrase "if through hatred and so forth."
...iti... pra... ṣaṃ pra... prāmāṇyāni pra...
The entity such as attainment, permanence, and so forth;
the instruction on the purpose of action;
the statement regarding that.
Is this [the truth] established by their word? Or what is the point of knowing this, given that those who claim to be knowers have spoken thus—whether out of ignorance, or out of hatred and the like?

Who indeed says that this is the word of a knower? If, due to the presence of doubt and other such flaws, one who is not a knower is not an authority, then this [scripture] is likewise unauthoritative because it was spoken by one who is not a knower, like the speech of a madman.
Since it is insentient, how can it possess authority? How can there be its speech? Like the word "wood," even though it is thus insentient, the authority of the Vedic sentences is not tenable.
What indeed is known [to be the case]? It is said to be connected with a conscious agent.
In this context, there may also be the reading "it was stated that the kāraka is unconnected," as in the case of *pratyupeya* and *yadetajñā*.

If the other says that this [effort] toward knowledge is fruitless and results in an undesirable consequence for you because it is a mere admission, who indeed has said that "this is the word of a knower"? For was it not previously stated that even certainty (nirṇaya) is nothing but ignorance (ajñāna), since it is permeated by doubt, error, and indecision?

Alternatively, who indeed says that this is the word of a "knower" (*jña*), given the absence of any person who is a knower and serves as a valid authority (*pramāṇa*) in all matters? What then? It is because the word itself is free from defect.

To this, the Teacher says: "If a knower is not an authority due to being subject to doubt and other such defects, then [the Veda] would be like the speech of a madman because it was uttered by one who is not a knower; so consider where the doctrine of the efficacy of the instruction on action goes.
Thus, first of all, the utterance of words through the sequence of phonemes such as 'a' and so forth, when preceded by conscious intent, is equal to the cawing of a crow or the shouting of a man.
Now, you might say: "Just like the insentient sound produced by the clashing of wood, stone, and so forth, everything is insentient.
Nevertheless, because it is insentient, how can it possess authority (*prāmāṇya*)? Because it is insentient, like space;

and proceeding thus, because it is insentient, how can there be its speech? For it is accepted by you [in the *Pātañjala-mahābhāṣya*] that 'that which the word says is our authority'; since the word *vacana* is derived from the sense of an action (*bhāvasādhana*), speaking, uttering, or the pronunciation of a word, the meaning is that because it is insentient, it lacks the capacity to be a speaker."

How so? Because it was uttered by one who is ignorant, this [Veda] lacks the status of being "speech" (vacana), for that [status] is preceded by the intention to communicate a meaning to be expressed; in the absence of that, it is not spoken. Therefore he says: "Like the word 'wood' (kāṣṭha)," thus, even though it is insentient, the authority of the Vedic sentence is not established. See page 113, line 6; [the text is] perfumed (vāsita) in the Bhāṣya.

note 4; here, there may also be the reading "bhavatām" (of you), followed by "tat-pūrvaṃ".

In the *Bhāṣya* it is stated: "In the case of [the word] *bhāva*, it is said... In this regard, he says: as for what was stated previously—"Who indeed says that this is the word of a knower?"—we do not maintain the second alternative, namely, that the words of all speakers are invalid, because of the fault of contradicting one's own statement (*svavacanavirodha*).

What then? It is because of the absence of an omniscient and dispassionate author that the treatise—which has as its object the intrinsic nature of all things—is not authoritative; it is not, however, because of the speaker who is without beginning or end and who belongs to a lineage of speakers, since there is authority in both the speaker and the speech in some cases.
Thus, just as with the original speaker, there is an equal lack of confidence in the words of a wise person spoken by a subsequent speaker, similar to the case of *vātika* mantras and the like.

Furthermore, it is observed that in some cases, even when a meaning exists, the non-intentionality (*avivakṣā*) of that meaning is logically justified. Where, among those two [types of words], has it been seen that they possess meaningfulness through the existence of a meaning and yet lack intentionality toward that meaning? Therefore, this statement—that there is usage of a word whose meaning is not intended because it is inseparable [from the form]—is improper, as it would entail the consequence that a word so employed lacks meaning altogether. For if the application of words were subject to no restriction regarding intentionality or non-intentionality, and if non-intentionality were purposeless, then there would be no distinction in the absence of non-intentionality regarding fire and so forth. To this, it is replied: It is the same for the subsequent speaker as it was for the original speaker.

Just as the original speakers of treatises concerning the nature of all things are untrustworthy because they lack authoritative knowledge due to being non-omniscient and not free from passion—being devoid of both true knowledge and truthful speech—likewise, the students of treatises that are established as having a beginning or as being beginningless are also devoid of true knowledge and truthful speech; therefore, the lack of confidence in the incorrectness of the knowledge and speech of both groups is equal.

What is it like? It is like the statements of quacks and [pseudo-]mantras; for example, the cognitions and mantra-utterances of quacks concerning the humors (*dhātu*), objects, and powers, are unreliable because they are mostly deceptive. By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), one should understand cases such as mantras and yogic practices for subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*).

Therefore he says: "Just as with the original speaker, so too with the subsequent speaker, there is an equal lack of reliability in the words of the knower, like the statements of quacks and [pseudo-]mantras. There may also be a reading here: "enough with this overly prolix discussion regarding the second alternative"; see Pañjikā, pp. 16–17.
Just as with the original speaker, so too with the subsequent speaker, there is an equal lack of confidence in the words of Jina, similar to the *vātika* mantras and the like.

Furthermore, it is observed that in some cases, even when a meaning exists, there is a non-intention to express that meaning; for what is seen to possess meaning in those two [cases], and where is their meaningfulness seen through the non-intention to express that meaning? Therefore, this statement—that "there is usage because the meaning is not intended to be expressed" (*avivakṣitārtha*) due to its being an inseparable concomitant—is improper, because it would entail the consequence that what is used is devoid of meaning. Since there would be no restriction regarding intention or non-intention in the application of words, and since non-intention would be purposeless, there would be no distinction in the absence of non-intention regarding fire and so forth.
Even for one who speaks fourfold,
may you shine forth;
thus indeed, O one free from pride.
Of you two, who are as they truly are, [the power] of those such as the Pradhānika and the Vādika, by means of [their] power and so forth... Ya.
...of those who [hold] views such as nihilism (yāvalādivādin), according to the Bhāṣya;
[the reading] "without a seat" (nāsthāsanāni) is found in the Bhāṣya except for [one manuscript];
[the reading] "like" (vat) is according to the Prajñaptiśāstra.

Furthermore, as for what was said—that the verbal root *juhoti* is employed even when its meaning is not intended to be expressed, yet it assists the agentive suffix—this too is incorrect because it contradicts logical principle (*nyāya*). How so? [As stated in the verse beginning with] "In some cases... and so forth.

The phrase "in some cases" (*kvacit*) means not in all cases; for example: "Having seen a star, they utter words," or "Which is Devadatta’s house? That one where that crow is. In these instances, although the words "star" and "crow" have already served their purpose in the act of seeing the star and perceiving the bird, it is observed—without departing from logic—that there is no intention to express the literal meaning of the star-sight or the crow when they function as indicators (*upalakṣaṇa*) for time and the house respectively. This is logical and seen to be so. But how could such a thing be seen in the case of those two—the *agnihotra* oblation and the word *juhuyāt*—which are themselves seen to possess meaning, and whose meaningfulness is established precisely through the non-intentionality of their literal sense? Therefore, what was said—that the root *hu* is employed because its meaning is unintended due to its being an inseparable concomitant—is contrary to logic.

What is the reason? Because it would follow that there is no lack of meaning for a word that has been employed. If this rule were not fixed regarding the employment of words, then even when used by necessity, there would be correctness alone; consequently, whether used through negligence or non-negligence, there would be no absence of meaning for the word employed, and there would be no distinction between a negligent and a non-negligent speaker. But such is not the case, because that would contradict what is observed, the tradition of the learned, and what is desired.

It might be thought: "If there is an intention to express a specific distinction for the purpose of secondary indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) and so forth, what is the use of this non-intention to express its own primary meaning? Since every employment of a word is preceded by the speaker’s intention, whether one proceeds with intention or without intention [is the same]. This is incorrect. If the application of words were to occur without restriction regarding intention and non-intention, and if non-intention were purposeless, then even in the absence of non-intention regarding fire and so forth, a specific reason for the distinction must be stated. Furthermore, since the use of the word "fire" is as inseparable as the employment of the verbal root *juhoti*, it follows that its meaning is not intended to be expressed.
And therefore, one should offer the *bhasma-hotra* sacrifice; the reason must be stated.

However, it is more appropriate—and indeed most appropriate—to not intend that [literal meaning], because, as will be shown by the logic to be presented, that [intention] depends upon the true nature of the matter.
Thus, for the time being, this [statement] lacks the power to convey meaning, because it expresses the reality of the object without due consideration, like the prattle of a child.

However, even if one accepts the Agnihotra as qualified by the restatement of the oblation (*havana-anuvāda*) according to your intention, the instrument (*karaṇa*) remains unestablished because the nature of the Agnihotra is not well-known, just like the reality of the self (*ātman*) and other such entities.
Now, it might be argued: its establishment occurs through the style of enjoining another injunction (*vidhyantara-vidhāna*), as in "he cuts the sacrificial post" (*yūpaṃ chinatti*).

...then by what reason is it to be determined that this sentence "one should offer the Agnihotra" is more correct? Furthermore, why is that non-intentionality—the non-intentionality regarding fire and so forth—more logical? Because of the observation of the principle to be stated hereafter; for you will see this principle in the section on injunctions (*vidhinaya*) when it is stated: "The Person alone is all this" (Ṛgveda 10.90).

90. And so forth. Because of that [realization], since conceptual constructions such as "fire" and so on do not exist, there is no *agnihotra* and no "offerer"; thus, due to the very absence of an object (*arthābhāva*), it is logical that there is no intention to speak [of them]. What is the reason? Because that [intention] is dependent upon the reality of the object; for intention or non-intention to speak must arise by the power of the object, and not otherwise. Furthermore, it has been said [in the *Prakaraṇa*]:
In the constellation Nakṣatra, [the bird] Icchāṇa is joined with Pra, joined with Bhā,
and joined with Vo. Ya.
Furthermore, it will be explained that [the scripture] possesses purpose by virtue of its meaningfulness; however,
for those who lack the capacity, it is devoid of purpose.

there may also be a reading *prakṛter* instead of *anantarīyakatvāt*, because [the latter] would not intend that meaning in the present context.
Because it is preceded by the knowledge of the Tathāgata and the speaker of the application, [it is] the *pratyakṣa*.

"By intention," thus [it is said] in the Vivakṣā; "by that which intends," thus [it is said] in the Bhāṣya; [this occurs] in the context of the non-conventionality of words, as stated in the Prajñāpradīpa.
In this context, there may also be the reading "in the application of words" (*śabdānāṃ vṛttau*), following the sequence: *pratyupādāya*,
*jñāya*, *pra*.

however, it is more appropriate—and indeed most appropriate—not to intend [to provide one], because that [intention] depends upon the reality of the matter, as will be seen from the logic to be explained later.
Thus, for now, this [statement] is non-communicative, because it expresses the nature of things without having examined their true state, like the prattle of a child.

However, even if one accepts the Agnihotra as qualified by the restatement of the offering according to your intention, there is a failure to establish the instrument (*karaṇāsiddhi*), because the essential nature of the Agnihotra is unestablished, just like the reality of the self and other such entities.
Now, it might be argued: its establishment occurs through the style of enjoining another injunction, as in "he cuts the sacrificial post" (*yūpaṃ chinatti*).
to be cut off, to be severed, [in] the world.
Either the intention to speak must arise from the desire [to speak], or the desire to speak must arise from the capacity [to speak].
Having summarized that, he says: "In this way, first," and so forth.

By the method of reasoning just mentioned, one should perform the *agnihavana*; because faults have been shown regarding this meaning, or rather, because faults have been shown regarding such meanings as "one should perform the *agnihotra*," "one should offer the *agnihotra*," "one should perform the *havana*," "one should perform the *agnihotra-havana*," or "one should offer"—the word *tāvat* (first/in this way) has the sense of sequence. Furthermore, there will be the statement of other faults as well; thus, "this, first of all, is the fault."

This sentence lacks communicative power. Why? Because it expresses a matter whose true nature has not been examined, like the babbling of a child. "Yāthātathya" means being exactly as it is; "arthayāthātathya" is the true nature of the object. Regarding that unexamined object—without having investigated what the nature of this object is, whether it is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), an object of valid cognition (*prameya*), or in what form it is a means of valid cognition or an object of valid cognition—the statement of that unexamined object, whether it be the word or its meaning, is made without having examined the nature of that which communicates; therefore, it lacks communicative power.

Furthermore, because it possesses a referent (*arthatva*), a word or its denoted object conveys [its meaning] only by means of an utterance whose reality has been examined, just like [the teachings on] *pradhāna* and so forth; this is by way of contrast (*vaidharmyeṇa*).

Therefore, since it is an utterance whose reality has not been examined, it is established that it is non-conveying, whether by way of the word or by way of the referent—in both cases it lacks the capacity to convey. Consequently, due to this lack of conveying power, it is non-instructive, just like the babble of a child;
such is the meaning of the passage beginning with "tāvat" and so forth.
...considering the object as it truly is... [the state] of this... the means of valid cognition and the object of valid cognition...
...to be depended upon;
...the denotable object;
...or of the mountain...
Furthermore, regarding the statement "one should perform the Agnihotra sacrifice," we shall state another defect in this very point just mentioned: "according to your own intention," and so forth.

"Equal to your intention" means like your intention, or possessing your intention; for example, regarding the matter "one should perform the offering of the Agnihotra" as intended by you, if one were to accept the Agnihotra as qualified by that reference to the act of offering (havana), then—just as the Agnihotra, which is your desired ritual action, is difficult to know because it is extraordinary (*alaukika*), unestablished, and its nature is unknown due to being conceived by the Sāṃkhya and others as the reality of the Self and so forth—the performance of that act of offering would not be established, since it is impossible to carry out what is not understood. This is the meaning.

*abhipretāgnihotraṃ pra* (Prakaraṇa).
Regarding the *agnihotra* intended [by the Veda]—

which is otherwise imagined by the Sāṃkhya and other schools— an opponent might here state the following rebuttal: its establishment is achieved through the stylistic method of enjoining another injunction (*vidhyantara-vidhāna*).
A different injunction from the injunction "one should offer the Agnihotra" is another injunction, such as "he cuts the sacrificial post" and so forth;
the formulation of that [latter] injunction— whether its determination is unintended, or whether it occurs before or after—
is as follows...
... "The sacrificial post [should be] made of *pālāśa* wood and eight-cornered," and so forth—this too is not [the case], because of the disparity.

First, with respect to time: at the very moment of the act of cutting, it is not yet a sacrificial post (*yūpa*); rather, it will become a sacrificial post once it has been consecrated by the acts of cutting and so on. Therefore, while it does not yet possess the status of a sacrificial post at that time, it is appropriate for its future sacrificial form—which is to be realized at a later time—to be disregarded; however, this is not the case for the *agnihotra*, which exists at that very moment.

But surely its status as a word for that [post] arises from being for that purpose; just as a pillar intended for Indra is called "Indra," so too the act of cutting would not be established as a consecration (*saṃskāra*) because the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) has already been brought into existence. And if there were no status as a consecration, the act of cutting would have an unintended meaning, as it would be defined merely by its necessity of performance. [The opponent replies: It is a matter of style (*śailī*), which is the inherent nature [of the text]. From the observation of this style, and because it possesses the character of an injunction, the establishment of this [act of cutting] occurs through inference, namely: "This too is a rule (*vidhi*), for such is the style of this [text]."

In what other injunction (*vidhi*) has the establishment [of a rule] been seen through the stylistic method of prescribing another injunction? For example, from "he cuts the sacrificial post" (*yūpaṃ chinatti*) up to "it is made of *pālāśa* wood and eight-cornered" (*pālāśamaṣṭāśrim*). He provides this as an illustration for the inference regarding the style:

just as here, first the duty (*kartavyatā*) was enjoined with a determination that did not intend to specify [the material], and later it is established in its specific form by the injunction of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) such as "eight-cornered, made of *pālāśa* or *bailva* wood," so too here the Teacher says: "This also is not [the case], because of the disparity; because of the disparity in style between the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*)."
That discrepancy [in the meaning] arises from three perspectives: time, established usage, and restrictive determination.

Regarding these, first, from the perspective of time: it is not the case that the post (*yūpa*) exists at the very moment of the act of cutting; this is the completion of the sentence [implied by the objection], because it would otherwise follow that acts such as cutting are purposeless.
What then? It will become a post once it has been consecrated by the acts of cutting and so forth.

Thus, it is appropriate for that piece of wood—which does not yet exist as a sacrificial post (*yūpa*) at that time—to disregard its future sacrificial-post form which is to be realized at a later time; however, there is a disparity [in the case] of the *agnihotra*, which exists at that very moment and is independent of any further consecration (*saṃskāra*), such that it cannot disregard an object to be realized at a later time.
(Navi-vya) ...
"...made of *pālāśa* wood, eight-sided," and so forth—
this too is not [correct], because of the inconsistency.

First, with respect to time: the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) does not exist at the very moment of the act of cutting; rather, having been consecrated by the acts of cutting and so forth, it will become a sacrificial post. Since it is not yet a sacrificial post at that time, it is logical that its essential nature as a post—which is to be realized at a later time—should be disregarded [in the initial injunction]. This is not the case for the *agnihotra*, which exists at that very moment. For instance, in the statement "he cuts the sacrificial post," there is first a description where the specific form is not intended (the mere act of cutting), followed by a description through the constituent procedures (*itikartavyatā*), such as "it is made of *bilva* wood, or *pālāśa* wood, eight-cornered," and so on. This is the basis for the possibility here. Now, as for its being designated by the word "that" (*tat-śabda-tā*), it is because it is for the sake of that (*tad-arthatvāt*); just as a pillar intended for Indra is called "Indra."

The character of being a consecratory act (*saṃskāra*) would not be prescribed for the cutting, because the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) has already been brought into existence; and in the absence of its being a consecratory act, the cutting would have no intended meaning, resulting in the non-existence of the injunction.
According to the rule,
the carpenter goes to the sacrificial post, taking the remainder of the clarified butter.
One made of *pālāśa* wood, with abundant leaves, its tip and base unwithered, its branches upright and split, its top and base tapering, and free from blemishes.
In their absence, [one may use] khadira, bilva, and rauhitaka.
He makes it eight-sided, with the exception of the upper part.
1.26. Thus, in the Kātyāyana Śrautasūtra, the trees suitable for sacrificial posts (yūpa) are the palāśa, khadira, bilva, and rauhitaka.
It has eight facets, is well-proportioned, and is narrower at the front; its Agniṣṭha facet is clearly defined, being neither too thick nor too thin.
Thus, the nature of the sacrificial post (yūpa) has been described in detail in the Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra;
this is to be understood by me.
Furthermore, impelled by that, [the syllables] pāṃ, ḍe, līṃ, raṃ, hīṃ, tā;
subsequently, bhā, palāśaṃ, ya.

*yūpatvenāmato* (pṛ॰) / *yūpatvanāmato* (ya॰) / *yūpatvanāmato* (bhā॰).
The other [opponent] says: "Is it not the case that [the designation] is based on that word (*tacchabdya*), and so forth, up to 'the pillar Indra' (*sthūṇendra*)?

Just as in those cases the designation is based on that word because of being for the sake of that (*tādarthya*), so too wood intended for a sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is called a 'sacrificial post' (*yūpa*) because of being at that same time (*tatkālatva*)."

To this it is replied: The act of cutting would not be established as a *saṃskāra* (purificatory rite) because the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) has already ceased to exist; for the rite of cutting exists for the purpose of bringing that [post] into being. And if that status as a *saṃskāra* were absent, the act of cutting would have no intended meaning; the sense is that if it were not for the sake of a *saṃskāra*, the act of cutting would be entirely purposeless.

Therefore, the moment one accepts the wood as a sacrificial post—that is, appropriates it as one's own—it is said that one "cuts" it, because the act of cutting lacks any other purpose than to serve as a *saṃskāra*.

It is not restricted to the act of cutting alone, because if it were so restricted, it would follow that the making of the eight-sided shape and other such rites would not be preparatory acts (*saṃskāra*). Rather, it is restricted to the sense that "one indeed performs [the rite]. This [restriction] cannot be adopted here, because such a restriction is impossible; for one performs the *agnihotra* by means of the oblation (*havana*), not by means of renunciation (*pravrajyā*) and so forth, nor is it restricted to the sense that "one performs it [only]," since in the absence of a desire for heaven and the like, there is no performance of the rite.

For this very reason, there is also a disparity in established usage (*prasiddhi-vaiṣamya*); because that [term] is unestablished, it is merely a name for the intended object consisting of a collection of ritual actions.

Furthermore, since its status as a style (*śailī*) is not authoritative—and because the ritual action regarding the sacrificial post (*yūpa-kriyā*) is not in accordance with reality—there is also a disparity in the determination (*avadhāraṇa-vaiṣamya*), as indicated by the words "this" (*iyam*) and so forth.

Regarding this very cultivation (bhāvanā) just mentioned: by means of this cultivation alone, I shall also cultivate the differentiation of restriction (*avadhāraṇa-vaiṣamya*). Therefore, he says: "In that context, the cultivation [consists in] 'it cuts the sacrificial post' and 'by cutting it, it appropriates the sacrificial post,'" because it has been stated that when there is no refinement (*saṃskāra*), the root *chid* signifies the appropriation of the sacrificial post.
And in that case, how is it restricted? It is said: it is not restricted to "cutting alone," for the word "does" (*karoti*) is understood to follow.

If it is asked, "What is the fault in that?"—the restriction applies to something other than that which follows the word *eva*; this would result in the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the making of the eight-sided shape and so forth are not acts of consecration (*saṃskāra*). That [consequence] is what is entailed here, but it is not accepted; rather, it is restricted by the phrase "he certainly performs" (*karoty eva*) for the purpose of negating only the non-appropriation [of the wood] as one's own.
This is the intended force of the restriction regarding the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).
In this sentence concerning the procedure for offering (*havana-vidhi-vākya*), it is not possible to rely on such a restriction.

If one asks, "Why is it impossible?"—because a restrictive determination (*avadhāraṇa*) is untenable. How, then, is it untenable? Because while one performs the *agnihotra* by means of the offering, one does not do so by means of renunciation (*pravrajyā*) and the like; yet it cannot be restricted to the sense that "one performs it [only] by means of the offering," because in the absence of a desire for heaven and other rewards, the performance would not occur. Thus, there is an inconsistency in the restrictive determination.
