Therefore, having summarized those three points, he speaks for the purpose of concluding the argument regarding the reason and the thing to be abandoned: "And because of the lack of correspondence between the ritual procedure (*śailī*) and the act of making a sacrificial post (*yūpakriyā*) when its ritual procedure is accepted as authoritative. When the ritual procedure (*śailī*) is relied upon as authoritative, then, by the very method already stated, there is a lack of correspondence (*ayāthārthya*) between this *agnihotra* ritual and the act of making a sacrificial post (*yūpakriyā*). "Correspondence" (*yāthārthya*) is the state of being according to the facts; the absence of correspondence is "lack of correspondence" (*ayāthārthya*). Therefore, due to this lack of correspondence, there is no similarity in ritual procedure (*śailīsāmya*) between the act of making a sacrificial post and the act of the *agnihotra*.

Therefore, it is not correct [to claim] that its establishment occurs through the style of enjoining another injunction, as in the case of the cutting of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and so forth; or rather, "style" (*śailī*) refers to the authority of style, which is an inference from style. And if the authority of style were accepted, then by the style of the *agnihotra*, would it not follow—just like the act of service—that it is merely an action, and thus its realization would be derived from the procedural requirements (*itikartavyatā*)? No; for if service is understood in the sense of devotion, those [requirements] serve the purpose of service.
Otherwise, there would be the consequence of distinctness for every individual action.
Even here, there is no inequality because [the acts] have giving and so forth as their purpose, and because they consist merely of subsequent actions.

This also is not the case, because it would result in [the sacrifice] being merely a procedure connected to the purpose of giving and so forth as known in the world, which would contradict the fact that Agni is the recipient (*sampradāna*). Furthermore, how could there be an identical established usage for both the injunction and the style of another injunction, given that the worldly [practice] is not the true reality (*ayāthārthya*)? Moreover, since it is non-worldly (*alaukika*), inference is impossible; for in the world, what is seen is inferred, but the making of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) in the form of having eight corners and so forth is not known to exist as something distinct from the nature of the *agnihotra* ritual itself, from which one might infer the style of the *agnihotra* offering by analogy with that style.

Therefore, if the style [of the text] were the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then the establishment of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) through that style would be entirely improper, because it is not in accordance with reality.

Furthermore, even though there is a difference between the act of offering (*havana*) and the *agnihotra*, since the injunction for the *agnihotra* is qualified by a reference to the offering, there is no inference based on style due to the dissimilarity of the example according to the aforementioned logic. For the root *gati* (to go) is listed as number 1258 in the *Dhātupāṭha*; since all roots meaning "to go" have the sense of "to know," the term *hetu* (cause/reason) means "that which makes one understand" (*hinoti gamayati*). Thus, its meaning is "that which is to be abandoned, understood, or established" (*heyaṃ gamyaṃ sādhyam*).

Even though there is a disparity in style—such as the cutting of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and so forth—between the mere performance of the *agnihotra* and other rites, nevertheless, it will be just like the act of service (*sevā*) and the like.

For instance, "service" consists of attendance, joining the palms in salutation, and following the master’s commands; it is essentially one thing, characterized by compliance with the master’s mind, and comprises various specific movements of mind, speech, and body. In the same way, the single action called *agnihotra* does not exist as something distinct from the collection of its own constituent parts.
Therefore, those very acts—the immolation of the animal, the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), and so forth—are designated as "the *agnihotra*" through non-difference.

Because of the inclusion of the word "etcetera," just as in the case of mere activities such as agriculture or trade, there is comprehension through their own inherent procedures (*itikartavyatā*), so too should it be seen here [in this case]— see page 109, line 1: *°mātratva pra*.

To this it is replied: that is not so; for when devotion is known as the purpose of service, those [acts] are for the sake of service. The connection here is that there is a disparity between the example and the thing exemplified.

He demonstrates this: "Devotion" (bhajana) is *bhakti*; since that itself is the purpose of service, service has devotion as its purpose (*bhajanārthā sevā*). When that service is known, those acts—such as standing nearby, joining the palms, and so forth—which are considered parts of it, serve the purpose of service. This is because if they were unknown, they would not convey that purpose. Indeed, only when they are known do they produce the realization that "these are indeed services," and not otherwise.

But the constituent actions of the Agnihotra are not known in that way; therefore, there is a disparity, and this must necessarily be so. Otherwise, there would be the consequence of distinctness for each individual action, just as there is mutual distinctness between agriculture and service, and between their respective constituent actions, precisely because they are not known as being parts of one another. In the same way, there would be such [distinctness] between the Agnihotra and its constituent actions; however, this is not the case, because [the Agnihotra] is not known as having the status of a part of the Agniṣṭoma and other rites—see page 137, line 1.
He states the rebuttal: "Even here, there is no inequality because [the acts] have giving and so forth as their purpose.

What is the reason? Because here too, according to the root *hu* (to give) in the sense of 'giving and so forth' (Pāṇini Dhātupāṭha 1083), the acts such as *havana* (offering oblations) are known to have giving and so forth as their purpose; therefore, since the Agnihotra sacrifice also consists of actions whose constituent parts (*aṅga*) include known acts of giving and so forth, it is indeed equal to service and the like."

Furthermore: because it is merely a subsequent action (*uttarakriyāmātratvāt*). Just as standing nearby (*upasthāna*) and so forth are merely subsequent actions to service (*sevā*), so too are the *agnihotra* and the *agniṣṭoma* procedures merely subsequent actions [to something else].

This too is not correct, because it would result in [the ritual] having as its sole purpose the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) connected to the meanings of giving (*dāna*) and so forth already known in the world.

Even so, it would fall into the state of having as its sole purpose that meaning which belongs to the procedure connected with the meanings of giving and so forth known in the world—just like the view expressed in the passage beginning with "when [the fire] is being grasped" (*gṛhyamāṇe*).

That act of offering (*havana*) does not have such a real object; likewise, the doctrine of *pradhāna* and so forth is invalid because it appears as that [object], since its established reality is contrary to the actual state of things.
Or rather, just like the Vedic doctrines, the Vedic doctrines themselves are invalid for the same reason.

If, on the other hand, it were assumed that the statement "Now, the Agnihotra" is intended solely to denote a specific transcendental result (*apūrva*), then what purpose would be served by denoting such a transcendental result? The meaning [of the Agnihotra] is this: "He who desires heaven should bring about heaven through the act of offering. This is the meaning of the Agnihotra.

For in the world, giving (*dāna*) is the relinquishing of one's own property for the sake of benefiting others; that which is given with affection upon meeting is *sampradāna*. Giving is such a renunciation where there is benefit for both oneself and others; it is not the mere relinquishing of material substance anywhere—like the voiding of urine and excrement—or like the pouring of clarified butter into ashes.

Therefore, every offering of clarified butter and the like into the fire should be solely for the purpose of assisting oneself and others; nor is this [latter kind] desired or observed [as true giving].

What is the reason? Because of the contradiction with the status of the recipient (*sampradāna*). Since fire—being of the nature of burning and the destroyer of all substances—is incompatible with being a recipient, it is like a man whose hand has been severed giving a gift of safety to a fish, or like a robbed man granting immunity from thieves. Because the specific mention of "to Agni" implies a similarity to worldly sacrifices, when the meaning is understood as purely worldly, an inquiry as to whether "this is thus" or "not thus" is not meaningful. If it were [meaningful], then by disregarding worldly authority, one might conclude that because a frog moves by leaping while possessing four feet, it must therefore be hairy like a deer; or conversely, that a deer, though possessing four feet, must be hairless like a frog. Such a conclusion would contradict established consensus. Since this same fallacy would apply here as well, he says: "But not when the worldly [meaning] alone is accepted," and so forth, as seen in the previously cited example.

"Indeed, it is not [an act of giving]," and so forth; here too, the proof establishes an undesirable consequence: that sacrificial act (*havana-kriyā*) is not truly of such a nature because it merely appears as such. Its appearance as such is due to its being taken as "giving" when, in the ultimate sense, it is not of the nature of giving, since there is no actual bestowal.

And this is established just as in the case of games played by children or acts involving the perception of delicious food and the like, where the mutual acts of giving and eating are merely appearances of those things; likewise, this "giving" which consists of throwing [the oblation] into the fire is also [merely an appearance].

And here is the demonstration of an undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭāpādana*): the validity of doctrines such as the *Pradhāna* (Primordial Matter) would be contrary to common consensus (*prasiddhi*), and so forth. "Contrary to consensus" means that its reality (*tattva*) is the opposite of what is commonly accepted; its state is "reality," and the object of this doctrine is established upon a reality contrary to consensus. Because of that—that is, because its object is established upon a reality contrary to consensus—it would follow that these doctrines, such as those concerning the *Pradhāna*, conjunction (*saṃsarga*), momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhanga*), and so on, would be valid, just like the Vedic doctrine (*vedavāda*).

Alternatively, just as the invalidity of the doctrines of the *Pradhāna* and so forth is accepted, by the same reason stated, there would be the invalidity of the Vedic doctrine. Thus, in both cases, an undesirable consequence is demonstrated.

Because of the specific terms, the *apūrva*s—which are to be manifested by the sacrificial sessions (*yajñasaṃsthā*) such as the *agniṣṭoma* and by the *iṣṭi*s that are mutually distinguished—are themselves distinguished. [If one were to say] "it would be produced by the substance," what has been diminished from the doctrine of the *apūrva*? As soon as it is said, "one desiring heaven should sacrifice," it is simultaneously said, "one desiring heaven should bring about the *apūrva* by sacrificing. Since the meaning is already conveyed by the productive operation (*bhāvanā*), the *apūrva* is not directly perceived such that one could begin its definition—namely, that "the sacrifice by which the *apūrva* is accomplished is to be performed."

Let it not be that the designation "sacrifice" (yajña) refers only to ritual action as distinguished by mantras, deities, and so forth—as is explained by certain Mīmāṃsakas [regarding the verse]: "The gods sacrificed with sacrifice; those were the first dharmas" (Ṛgveda 10.90).

Because, with respect to that object, one does not perceive through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) a connection between the fruit and an action that is impermanent, and because it would entail the fault of the action being rendered futile. Therefore, it is said that "Dharma" is the *Agnihotra*, which is manifested by the action; for the cause is figuratively applied to the effect, such that what is manifested by the *Agnihotra* is called "the *Agnihotra*."

Then, in order to clarify the meaning of the statement that "one who desires heaven should offer the *agnihotra* sacrifice" or "should cultivate [it] as a duty"—and that this meaning is faultless—the *vidhinaya* asks: "If that were so, what would be accomplished by denoting the *apūrva*? Since the word *artha* is seen to denote both 'purpose' and 'meaning,' what purpose (*artha*) would be achieved, what objective would be fulfilled, or what subject matter (*abhidheya*) would be established? The *vidhinaya* replies: "The meaning that would be accomplished, achieved, and established is this: 'He who desires heaven should bring about heaven through the oblation (*havani*) characterized by its specific procedure (*itikartavyatā*). This is the sense."

The method of injunction (vidhinaya) says: Since the employment of words is for the purpose of producing the knowledge of reality that is synonymous with *vidyā* and for the purpose of dispelling *avidyā*, what has been diminished by this *arthāvidyā*? The intended meaning is: nothing at all has been diminished.

He supports that [point] with the words "yāvadeva" and so forth. What is meant is this: when it is said, "one who desires heaven should sacrifice," what is actually stated is, "one who desires heaven should sacrifice the *apūrva* (the unseen potency). No additional meaning beyond the *apūrva* is obtained by the word "Agnihotra," because that [unseen potency] is manifested by the act of offering (*havana*) itself; for the sense is already conveyed by the mere statement, "one who desires heaven should sacrifice. In the expression of the sentence-meaning, "one who desires heaven should sacrifice—that is, should bring about (*bhāvayet*) merit (*dharma*)"—what purpose is served by the words "agni" and "hotra"? To this he says: "Because the bringing-about (*bhāvana*) is already understood. Since the act of bringing about—which consists of the verbal root-meaning (*dhātvartha*) characterized by the cause, the agent, the means, and the goal—is already understood from the very use of the word "juhuyāt" (should sacrifice), there is no further purpose served by the phrase "agnihotram."

Thus, for the time being, the employment of the word *agnihotra* is meaningless.
Furthermore, this conceptualization contradicts common experience, for neither in the world nor in the Veda does such a thing exist, as its referent is non-existent.

Even granting the designation of a specific *apūrva*, we maintain that its determination through the act of offering (*havana*) is untenable because it is imperceptible. This is due to the difference in the nature of determination: for in this world, when an object such as a jar has been previously perceived through direct observation during the process of bringing clay, kneading it, and so forth, it is designated by means of those actions as "the jar is produced by this action," "this is its effect," or "this is its cause. This is because there exists a relationship between cause and effect that is based on what is observed.

But it is never [the case that there is inference] regarding something previously unperceived, because in the absence of a supporting example based on similarity, there can be no inference. Therefore, he says: "And that [fire] is not perceptible as something new, such that an investigation could be undertaken by means of it—namely, the investigation that 'this is the effect of that [fuel]' and 'this is the cause of this [fire]'; the meaning is that this is the explanation."

If it is asked how this is explained, it is said: by means of that oblation (*havana*), which possesses the power to bring about an unseen potency (*apūrva*) not previously seen, the unseen potency called *agnihotra* is brought into being. Or, if it were argued: "First, there will be the establishment of this attainment; and because it is connected to that, the 'how-to-be-done' (*itikartavyatā*) itself constitutes the 'what-is-to-be-done' (*kartavyatā*)," then one would have to say, "one should not sacrifice again."

Furthermore, by adopting an object reached through an investigation that avoids successive contradictions, reasoning (*tarka*)—which has the person as its authority—is brought to completion; thus, "you must perform that oblation, just as the acts of fetching clay and so forth are for the purpose of producing a jar.
But that is not tenable, because these two [the oblation and the jar] have an absolutely imperceptible relationship between cause and effect.
Because of its nature as [the object] of determination,
it is "that which has attained the state of being determined";
"determination" is the word to be supplied.
The example based on similarity is for the sake of [establishing] similarity; the example based on dissimilarity is for the sake of [establishing] dissimilarity.

In that case, one would not have to say "one should sacrifice again" (*na tarhi punar juhuyāt*).

Furthermore, by thus adopting the meaning obtained through an investigation that resolves successive contradictions, reasoning (*tarka*) becomes a means of knowledge for the person (*puruṣapramāṇaka*).

Even having formulated this [argument] through mere assumption (*sambhāvanā*), those faults which were stated—namely, that even what is expressed by means of conceptualization (*kalpanā*) is not possible—are disregarded by the opponent. [This refers to the attainment] "of the attainment" (*prāpteḥ*), according to Pāṇini 3.3.94: *striyāṃ ktin*.

In this regard, it must be stated that "and [the suffixes] āP and so forth" (ābādīnāṃ ca) applies; for otherwise, by the rule *gurośca halaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.103), which prescribes the suffix aP as an exception (*apavāda*), the form *bādha* would not occur. Thus, there will be an established usage (*prasiddhi*) obtained through another sentence, because [otherwise] the application [of the suffix] would be precluded.

The term *agnihotra* is a dative compound meaning "the oblation for Agni"; its formal derivation and the establishment of its conventional meaning are achieved either through the rule of *yogavibhāga* (separation of grammatical rules) or by the addition of examples such as *aśvaghāsa*. Consequently, it is entirely logical that the instrument [of the sacrifice] and its connection to the result belong to the agent.

If one asks, "From which sentence is this conventional meaning established? [the answer is: from another sentence to be cited later: "That which one offers in the evening to Agni and to Prajāpati" (*MaiSaṃ* 1.8).

Thus, [the statement] "one should offer with ghee, milk, and curd" implies that because of its connection to that [primary injunction], the *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance) itself constitutes the *kartavyatā* (the duty to be performed). Because of the connection—that is, the relationship—of that [manner of performance] which has been obtained from another sentence, and because its expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) remains unfulfilled, all subsequent *itikartavyatās* are themselves the duties to be performed.
And the establishment of those *itikartavyatās* is the establishment of the *agnihotra*, since [the *agnihotra*] consists of them.

To this it is replied: In that case, one should not say "one should sacrifice again," because by the word *agnihotra* itself, the meaning has already been expressed—including the recipients such as Agni and Prajāpati, the act of sacrificing (*juhoti*), and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*). Thus, the very same expansion of faults previously mentioned in the passage beginning with "for there is no one who sacrifices again" by means of the repeated statement stands here too in this path of interpretation. Here, the reading might also be *prasiddhimātra*, while *prāpti* would be the *pra*.
Regarding the rule *ktin* in the context of *apādīnām pra...* and *striyām ktin*, it should be stated in the Patañjali Mahābhāṣya (3.3) that [the suffix applies] "after *āp* and the others."

If it is argued that a modification [is formed] from the base form (*prakṛti*) by means of [the suffix] *aśvamādyupa* (as in *pra*), then an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be made for words such as *aśvaghāsa*. Thus it is stated in the Patañjali Mahābhāṣya, Book 2.

furthermore, why does the consequence of [the doctrine] that the person (*puruṣa*) is the authority (*pramāṇaka*) arise here as well? Because one resorts to a mutual contradiction between successive [positions], just as in the case of the absolute [view] regarding objects such as the universal (*sāmānya*).
And that [position] is untenable, because after having accepted the theory of the non-existence of the effect (asatkāryavāda) due to the fault of tautology and so forth, one subsequently abandons it.

Furthermore, because one prescribes the adherence to the notion that fire and other things are distinct entities whose prior and posterior natures are severed by a mere difference in state, and because one accepts the absolute non-existence of the effect in the cause—thereby adopting a meaning reached through an investigation into the avoidance [of contradictions] regarding the existence of the effect as pervading the cause—the contradiction [alleged] in the case of the *agnihotra* and the act of offering (*havana*) due to the fault of redundancy is resolved as follows: it is not so, because these are [respectively] restatements (*anuvāda*) and injunctions (*vidhi*). When it is further argued that there is a contradiction because [the meaning] is not established, the resolution is reached through investigations such as: "the word 'should do' (*kuryāt*) has the sense of 'should offer' (*juhuyāt*)," and so forth; thus, you have adopted a meaning reached through such deliberations. Consequently, by relying on the authority of your own intellect, you have resorted to reasoning (*tarka*) which takes the person as its authority. And the definition of reasoning is: "Reasoning (*tarka*) is a conjecture (*ūha*) for the sake of knowing the truth of an object whose true nature is unknown, based on the logical possibility of the causes" (Nyāya Sūtra 1.1.40).

1.40 What is this like? It is just like the one-sided views regarding universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth. For instance, when one adheres to the one-sided view that there is only the universal, or only particulars (*viśeṣa*), or both the universal and the particulars, the goal—attained through the avoidance of contradictions between preceding and succeeding statements according to the method previously described—is impossible to attain and fruitless, because it depends on human authority. Such is this [opponent's] reasoning as well.
And that [reasoning] is undesirable; moreover, if reasoning were not incomplete, it would be resorted to, but why is it incomplete? Because of the three defects.
Which three defects? From tautology and so forth, from the acceptance of the theory of the non-existence of the effect (*asatkāryavāda*), and from subsequently abandoning that [theory].
One should offer oblations as previously stated; otherwise, faults such as tautology would arise, just as in the case of those who maintain the absolute oneness of the universal and so forth—
a position that is undesirable because it involves first accepting the doctrine of the non-existence of the effect in the cause (*asatkāryavāda*) and then subsequently abandoning it.

Furthermore, because one would be enjoined to produce [an effect] by means of a superimposition of the distinctness of entities— such as fire and so forth— which are differentiated only by their preceding and succeeding states, this is due to the absolute admission that the effect is non-existent in the cause; therefore, let it be seen that [this view] applies to the doctrine of the all-pervasive existence of the effect in the cause (satkāryavāda), page 124, line 2,
and again in the Prasiddhiviniścaya.
Furthermore, see again Prasannapadā, page 126, line 2, and also Aniṣṭa-prasaṅga.
The meaning of "incomplete" (*aniṣṭha*) is that its finality or fullness does not exist;

however, in order to demonstrate the acceptance of the theory that the effect is non-existent (*asatkāryavāda*), he says: "separated by only one state," and so on, up to "it would produce," because of the absolute acceptance of the non-existence of the effect within the cause.

And because of the imposition of an adherence to the state of being distinct entities—such as fire and so forth—wherein the prior and posterior realities are separated by a mere single state; and because of the word "and" (*ca*), which implies the injunction "one should sacrifice" (*juhuyāt*); A "single state" (*ekāvasthā*) is that which is both one and a state. Its measure is "mere single state," which is uninterrupted like the water of a still lake. Yet, its reality is again interrupted, as in the case of the prior and posterior fuel and so forth, or fire and so forth, or ashes and so forth, or jars and cloths, according to the view of those who maintain a universal commonality regarding external objects. There is an adherence to—that is, an acceptance of—the fact that what exists as having attained total unity, such as fire and so forth, is a distinct entity. Thus, while it is merely a succession of interrupted states—fire, ashes, fragments, atoms, and so on, produced from the conjunction of earth, water, and so forth, arising from trees, which in turn arise from dyads and atoms of fire—it is called "fire" due to the acceptance of a gradual distinction in transformation (*pariṇāma*). Because of the imposition of this [distinction], the performance of the act of offering, the heaven desired as its fruit, and the relationship between the two would not be tenable, as they would be mutually disjointed within the two prior and posterior acceptances.

If it is asked what the reason for this "dissolution" (vighaṭitatva) is, it is said: it is because one accepts the absolute non-existence of the effect in the cause; such is the demonstration of dissolution.

For in this way, when the cause—such as clarified butter (*ghṛta*)—is present, the performance of the ritual act of offering into the fire (*agnihotra*), which is its effect, and the result thereof, such as heaven (*svarga*), becomes possible; yet that [performance] would not be possible if [the cause] were already established [like] cooking rice that is already done. Furthermore, it is possible only when one accepts a specific state such as the single fire (*ekāgni*), which is contrary to the acceptance of the universal identity of all things consisting of causes such as the *puruṣa*; it is not possible otherwise. Therefore, he says: "Because, if the causal operation of the existent effect were omnipresent, there would be no object for the injunction of differentiation. The single cause called *puruṣa* is omnipresent, whether sequentially through the states of sleep, deep sleep, waking, and the fourth (*turīya*), or simultaneously. And that is the existent effect (*satkārya*). Because there is no object for the injunction of differentiation, that [activity] is enjoined as being truly existent through the proximity of all things, brought about by the relationship that establishes differentiation. Subsequently, it is performed through the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) consisting of the arrangement of the various constituent factors (*kāraka*).
Therefore, that [effect] did not exist previously, because it is accepted as being something produced (*kāryatva*), like a substance that is exclusively particular;
and this argument is incomplete, because its reason is unestablished and it is sublated by a counter-argument.

However, the reality (*tattva*) of a thing is not such that its effect is non-existent, because it is manifest (*vyaṅgyatva*), like a jar at the time of the lump of clay; for that reality is all-pervading and is both the existent effect and the cause, according to the analysis of the term. Furthermore, according to the perspective of the *vidhi-vidhi-naya* to be explained later, if [the cause] were merely the occurrence of that [reality], then the injunction "one should perform the Agnihotra" would lack a subject matter due to the absence of fire and so forth, because of the nature of the injunction regarding distinctions.

because difference and injunction have no objective referent (*nirviṣayatva*), that [injunction] is established as being truly existent through the presence of all things, as something to be accomplished by means of a connection that effects differentiation; subsequently, it is performed through a procedure (*itikartavyatā*) consisting in the arrangement of the factors of action (*kāraka*) according to their respective parts.
Therefore, it did not exist previously, because it is grasped as an effect (*kāryatva*), like a thing that is exclusively particular (*viśeṣaikānti*).
And that reasoning is incomplete, because its reason is unestablished and it is sublated by a counter-reasoning; however,

the reality of the thing is not such that the effect is non-existent [prior to its production], because it is manifested, like a jar at the time of the lump of clay, and because that reality exists therein, as in the case of the Agnihotra.

The method for attaining the state beyond becoming is not through ritual action, nor through progeny, nor through wealth; some have attained immortality through renunciation alone—not through ritual action, progeny, or wealth, but through renunciation alone. They have attained immortality.
"Beyond the sky, it is placed in a secret cave; it shines brilliantly, that which the ascetics enter. (Kaivalya Upaniṣad 3).

"Therefore, in the presence of all things," etc. Even though that act of offering (*havana*) exists as a reality only in the presence of all things, its specific forms are the means (*sādhana*). Such differentiated acts—as in "one should offer with ghee" or "with milk"—are indeed the means for the act of offering into the fire, because without them that [act] would not exist. Thus, it is enjoined as something to be accomplished through a connection with means. By whom? By the instructor, through speech directed toward a person desiring heaven, enjoining: "This must be performed by you."

Subsequently, the performer also accepts that [the action] is to be accomplished by means of the specific instruments (sādhana) prescribed for it; thus, that procedure (*itikartavyatā*) which consists in the arrangement of the various factors (*kāraka*) according to their respective parts—namely, the manner of seizing the cow, pouring the clarified butter (*ājya*), and so forth—is performed by that procedure. Why, then, is it not held that this [procedure] did not exist previously? Because it is grasped as something to be produced (*kārya*); for, by such injunctions as "one should act" (*kuryāt*) or "one should offer" (*juhuyāt*), it is indeed grasped as something to be brought into being through production.

The example is "like an entity that is exclusively a particular" (*viśeṣaikāntivastuvat*). Just as an advocate of the doctrine of exclusive particulars (*viśeṣaikāntavādin*) maintains that there is only the effect and not the cause—because he accepts that an entity consists of arising and perishing at every moment, and thus did not exist previously—and since you have accepted this by accepting [the existence of] activity, the example is endowed with both the property to be proven (*sādhya*) and the proving property (*sādhana*) for your sake; and because I too have stated it after having accepted that, it is a proof of the property to be proven.
Thus, by this reasoning, you have accepted the doctrine that the effect is non-existent (*asatkāryavāda*).
And that reasoning is incomplete, because its reason is unestablished and because it is sublated by a counter-argument:
"The Person alone is all this—whatever has been and whatever is to be;

But this is not the true nature of the thing, namely that the effect is non-existent [prior to production]. Why? Because it is manifested (*vyaṅgya*). For that action is indeed manifested, not produced; it is manifested as a property of substances such as clarified butter (*ghṛta*) and so forth, whether considered individually or collectively, though these were not previously intended [to be expressed].

What is the illustration? It is like a jar at the time of the lump of clay (*piṇḍakālaghaṭavat*). Just as a jar, although existing even at the time of the lump of clay, is not perceived because its manifestation depends on other means—just as [the embryo] is not perceived in the state of semen and blood—so too [the action] is not perceived because it has not yet attained its own nature as a jar.

For this very reason, this [cause] is merely the cause even when accompanied by its effect, because it is identical with it and because the effect is produced from it—just as clay is the cause of a jar—or because, while being a distinct state of that [cause], it is perceivable at a later time, like Devadatta; or else, simply because it is an effect, just as a jar is manifested, since the act of manifestation itself is what is called "causing.
Otherwise, even the son of a barren woman could be produced, because he would be a non-existent effect, just like a jar.

If it is argued that, in this case, the manifestation and non-manifestation of the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*—just like their state of equilibrium and disequilibrium—would contradict the doctrine of a single cause, we say: no. Why? Because there is no such thing as "being otherwise" (*atathābhūti*) within the reality itself (*tattva*). Indeed, there is no such thing as a separate state called the "unmanifest"; rather, it is simply the reality itself existing in a different manner. "Reality" (*tattva*) means the state of being that very thing; since it becomes otherwise precisely while remaining in that state of reality, it is that same entity which becomes otherwise while still in its own essential state (*svarūpa-avasthā*). For if something other were to become otherwise, then even a lump of clay would become a cloth, but that does not happen.
And the corroborative instance based on similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) is "like the pot's own self":

just as a pot, while remaining within its own self as a pot, arises from a new state into an old state, so too that very same lump of clay becomes another [state], namely a pot. There is no such thing as a "manifestation" (*avyaktatā*) as postulated by the Sāṅkhyas. For if that very same pot did not become another through the transition from new to old, it would not be old; it would remain merely new, or else something else, such as a cloth, would become the old pot, or perhaps nothing at all would exist. Therefore, since there is no such transformation within the reality itself, there is no such thing as a state of non-manifestation.

Here he says: The example "like the jar's own self" is appropriate because one experiences the state of being old immediately after the state of being new; however, the example "like a lump of clay and a jar" is not tenable, because there is no change of essence (tattva). For after the lump, a "śivaka" (a preliminary stage of the pot) occurs, and not a jar, nor a *stūpaka*, *chatraka*, *sthālaka*, *kośaka*, or *kuśūlaka*.

To this it is replied: because the proximity [of the cause] is equal, just as a jar arises from a granary, so too does the granary from its husk, the husk from its sheath, the sheath from its bowl, the bowl from its mold, the mold from its core, the core from its lump, and the lump from clay; thus, it is from clay alone that these various forms come to be.

Alternatively, what is the use of this adherence to the Sāṅkhya account of the sequence of creation? Accept that the jar exists even in that very state of the lump of clay; for, like waves in the water of a still lake, there is no sequence here either, since it is the reality itself that undergoes transformation. To demonstrate this, he says: "like the jar at the time of the lump of clay."

Alternatively, there is the reading *tattva eva tathābhūteḥ*, meaning "because it exists in that very way when that state [of reality] alone exists," since it manifests in various modes; that is, even while being a mere lump (*piṇḍa*) whose nature consists of form and so forth, it manifests as a *śivaka* (a small clay model) and so on, and as blue, red, and so forth. [The opposite case is:
"because it does not exist in that way," like the self-nature of a jar (*ghaṭasvātmavat*).

For this very reason, it is merely the cause even when accompanied by its fruit, because it is identical with that [fruit] and because it is produced from that; just as a jar is [identical to] the state of clay. Let it be done: let the effect be non-existent, or let it be existent. (Pāda-vibhāga)
By action, [it is] non-existent; by existence, action is existent. Thus it is in the Ḍe and Līṃ traditions, and likewise in the Ya tradition.

from the state of alteration, from the state of transformation, from the state of the absence of the sheath and the spike.
From the granary and the storehouse; from the small vessel and the large vessel; from the small measure and the large measure.
See page 144, line 5. *lavavatta* *pā* *ḍe* *līṃ* *dupaprada* *ya*.

Because it exists in that manner, for this very reason it is merely the cause; since it does not exist as such [prior to the effect] or exists as such [afterwards] in reality, this act of oblation (*havana*) is not distinct from its causes, such as clarified butter (*ghṛta*). For the reason stated—namely, the non-existence of the pre-existent effect (*asatkārya*)—it must necessarily be understood that this action is merely the cause.

Not only is the action itself merely the cause, but together with its fruit, it is merely the cause; even its fruit, known as heaven (*svarga*), consisting of pleasure and so forth, is merely the transformation of the causes, such as the clarified butter.

In this context, the two reasons for accumulation (*upacaya*) have already been established, because [the effect] has that as its nature (*tadātmatva*) and is produced from that (*tannirvṛttatva*). "Having that as its nature" means either that it is the self of that, or that it has that as its self; thus, it is produced by that, in that, of that, or it is that very thing which is produced. The state of being produced from that and having that as its nature constitute the reason. Therefore, because of having that as its nature and being produced from that—just like the "clay-ness of a jar" (*ghaṭamṛttva*): the jar’s clay-ness is simply that the jar is clay, or that clay is the jar. As has been explained, due to the inherent nature of the doctrine of non-duality (*ekāntavāda*), and because of the acceptance of the performance or non-performance of duties through the connection between preceding and succeeding states, there results the acceptance of cause and effect as being merely different in configuration (*saṃsthāna*), like the coiling, expansion, budding, and spreading of a snake, or like the thread, the cord, and the cloth of a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*). Consequently, the abandonment of the status of being an effect follows; since this contradicts the intended meaning regarding the scope of the implication of the word itself, there is a contradiction of the intended distinction.

If the *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance) produces [the action], then it cannot be produced by that [action], because it is the producer, being the cause; for such a thing cannot be both the producer and the produced, whether it be of such a nature or otherwise.
Therefore, the action itself is the cause and the fruit of the action.

Thus, the argument remains incomplete: first, because the action did not previously exist as something to be accomplished (*kārya*), and second, because the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*) and is sublated by a counter-argument (*pratitarka*). This is well said.

However, because of the acceptance of the performance of duties (*itikartavyatā*) and non-performance [of duties] due to the nature of absolute monism (*ekāntavāda*), there follows—due to the connection between prior and subsequent states—an acceptance of the relation of cause and effect as being merely a difference in configuration (*saṃsthāna*), like the expansion of a snake’s hood and its contraction, or like the state of a thread and the state of a cloth in a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*). Thus, there is an abandonment of the [status of being a] product (*kārya*). This constitutes a contradiction of the intended meaning (*vivakṣābhedavyāghāta*), because it results in a meaning contrary to the scope of the implication of its own words (*svaśabdārthāpatti-viṣaya-viparītārthatva*).
For if the performance of duties produces [the result], then it is not produced by that [result], because it is the producer, that is, the cause. (See page 144, lines 3–4).

Furthermore, it is incomplete precisely because it has been abandoned by you yourself. Why? Because of the inherent nature of extremist doctrines (*ekāntavāda*). For such is the nature of extremist doctrines, just like the doctrine that everything spoken is false. By stating—as you have stated—that "the 'how-to' (*itikartavyatā*) itself is the 'what-is-to-be-done' (*kartavyatā*)," you have accepted the existence of the effect within the cause and abandoned its non-existence. Therefore, we say: "Because of the acceptance of the 'how-to' and the 'what-is-to-be-done,'" and so forth.

Because the word *iti* denotes a manner (*prakāra*), "that which is to be done in this way or that way"—such as "one should offer with clarified butter" or "one should offer with milk"—is *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance). That very *kartavyatā* (duty to be performed) is the cause; those very actions such as sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and so forth are accepted as being the *agnihotra*. Because there is no [entity] whatsoever whose prior and posterior states are severed due to the connection of prior and posterior states, the cause itself is the effect—just like the expansion of a snake's hood, its opening of its mouth, and its coiling, or like the thread, the state of being a sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*), and the state of being a cloth. Just as the thread itself receives the name "sacrificial thread" because of its particular arrangement, so too the threads themselves are the cloth; likewise, the position is reached that the cause itself, when differentiated merely by its configuration (*saṃsthāna*), is the effect. The word *iti* here has the sense of a reason (*hetu*). For this reason—that the consequence of accepting that the cause and effect are differentiated merely by configuration leads to the abandonment of the effect—the term "abandonment of the effect" (*kāryatyāga*) applies. Indeed, the word "one should do" (*kuryāt*) is meaningful only when there is an effect to be accomplished, and not otherwise.

The word "again" (*punar*) has the sense of a reason (*hetu*). Consequently, by abandoning the literal meaning [of the injunction], there would be a contradiction of the intended meaning (*vivakṣābheda*) and a logical inconsistency (*vyāghāta*), because the resulting implied meaning would be the opposite of the meaning of the words themselves. By the very words of the injunction "one should perform the *agnihotra*," the doctrine that the effect does not pre-exist in the cause (*asatkāryavāda*) is accepted. Yet, through the necessary implication (*arthāpatti*) that the "how-to" (*itikartavyatā*)—which is invariably connected to that [action]—is itself the "what-is-to-be-done" (*kartavyatā*), the doctrine that the effect exists in the nature of its cause (*kāraṇātmakakāryavāda*) is accepted. Since these two are mutually contradictory and opposed in meaning, there is a difference in the intended meaning and a logical inconsistency.

First, there is a difference in intention (*vivakṣābheda*): because [the proponent] accepts that a word expressing the theory of the non-existent effect (*asatkāryavāda*) denotes an effect whose nature is that of its cause, and [the opponent] accepts that a word expressing an effect whose nature is that of its cause denotes a non-existent effect;
and for this very reason, because they are mutually contradictory, these two [positions] involve a logical inconsistency (*vyāghāta*).

Alternatively, because two meanings—one falling within the scope of the word itself and the other within the scope of presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*)—are accepted, there is this difference in intended meaning (*vivakṣābheda*). This difference in intended meaning contradicts the non-personal authority (*apauruṣeya-prāmāṇya*) of the Vedic doctrine by virtue of the influence of human intellect; thus, it is a "contradiction of intended meaning. And this [contradiction] is not perceived by you, who, out of hatred for the investigation of the reality of things, fail to see the fault of disregarding the true nature of reality. For even though one disregards the essential nature of cause and effect, this doctrine of the reality of cause and effect is forcibly imposed as being of a manifold nature (*anekāntarūpa*), since it is identical with the thing itself. Thus, even if it is not taken into account, it contradicts your own position. Therefore, there is no need to perform any further refutation.

Even if it is accepted that [the *kārya*] has the nature of a cause (*kāraṇa*), if it is maintained that the *itikartavyatā* (the "how-to") produces it, then that *kartavyatā* (the "what-is-to-be-done") would not be produced, because it is primary, prescriptive, like clarified butter (*ghṛta*) and so forth, and like the word for "mother.

Alternatively, if it is produced, then it is not the producer, because it is itself produced, like a son and so forth; and since the *itikartavyatā* is the completion of the *kartavyatā*, there is no commencement of another *itikartavyatā*.

However, since each individual [factor] is incomplete and lacks the status of being a cause, the collection as a whole is likewise not such [a cause]. As has been stated, there is no action whatsoever that exists apart from the causes and the procedural requirements (*itikartavyatā*); therefore, that action is not produced by them. The meaning is that it does not produce itself by means of itself.

Why? Because it is a producer, because it is a cause, because it is prior, and because it is an enjoiner—just like a mother. Just as a mother does not produce herself, but rather produces another, her daughter, so too this *itikartavyatā* (procedure), being a producer, is to be explained as such by virtue of its being a cause, its priority, and its nature as an enjoiner.

Regarding the phrase "like a word" (*vacanavat*): just as a word does not produce itself, but rather produces another cognition whose object is the thing signified (*vācyaviṣaya*), so too is the *itikartavyatā*.

Now, lest this fault should arise, it might be argued that its status as a *janaka* (producer) is unestablished because it is itself produced (*janya*), for it is indeed produced; to this, it is replied: if it is produced, then in that case it is not a producer, nor is it a cause, because of such reasons as being produced, being an effect, being unprecedented (*apūrva*), and being something to be enjoined (*vidheya*). Like a son and so forth—the inclusion of "and so forth" (in the compound *putrādi*)—implies [the example of] the knowledge of the meaning of what is expressed.

Therefore, since the faults previously stated apply whether it is considered produced or a producer, and since one cannot escape these defects, the statement that "the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) itself is the duty (*kartavyatā*) because of its connection with that [result]" is incorrect.
Because it is prior and because it is prescriptive, like the word "mother";

yet if it were produced [by another], then it would not be a producer, due to its being produced and so forth, like a son or similar entities; and regarding the "manner of performance" (itikartavyatā), once the performance is completed, there is no commencement of another manner of performance.
But since each [individual] is incomplete and lacks the status of being a cause, it is not so [i.e.,
not a cause]; and because the aggregate is nothing more than those [individuals], as has been stated, it is likewise not produced.
See the discussion on the meaning of the sentence, which is appropriate, on page 142, line 1.

Furthermore, if [the action] were merely the cause, would the "to-be-done-ness" (*kartavyatā*) be completed within the "means-of-performance" (*itikartavyatā*), or would it remain incomplete? In that regard, first, if the "to-be-done-ness" were completed in each individual means-of-performance, then because the "to-be-done-ness" would be finished with the "means-of-performance" itself, there would be no undertaking of further means-of-performance. This is because the "to-be-done-ness," which is completed by that alone, would have been accomplished by this very means-of-performance—"one should offer with clarified butter" (*ghṛtena juhuyāt*)—and thus the undertaking of other means-of-performance, such as "with milk" (*payasā*) or "with curd" (*dadhnā*), would result in being purposeless.

Alternatively, there would be no undertaking at all, because even that [action] would be a mere cause; for you yourself have admitted that "the manner of performance (*itikartavyatā*) is itself the duty to be performed" (*kartavyatā*), and because it has been logically established that an action is merely a substance such as clarified butter which serves as its cause—thus, like the cooking of already-prepared rice, the result would be the non-undertaking of the action itself.
Such, then, is the defect if [the action] were completed in each individual part.

But individually, because they are incomplete and lack the status of being a cause, there is "non-suchness" (*atathātā*). Even if the duty (*kartavyatā*) were incomplete in each individual instance—just as in the case of the bearers of a palanquin (*śibikāvāhaka*)—it would still not be a cause, because of the absence of causality in each individual part, like oil from sand.

This is because the word *iti* has the sense of "thus," and the word *evaṃ* has the sense of "manner"; thus, that which is to be done is "thus-to-be-done" (*itikartavya*). The nature of the duty consisting in the pouring of ghee and so forth is "suchness" (*tathātā*); the absence of suchness is "non-suchness. And because it does not attain that state of being "thus" due to the absence of causality in each individual part, there is "non-suchness."

[Objection: But was it not said that, just as there is a capacity for carrying in the bearers of a palanquin, so too the capacity for the performance of the ritual procedure (*itika-tavyatā-śakti*) resides in the aggregate? [Response: To this it is said: because the aggregate is nothing other than those [parts], and because it is merely the parts themselves, as has been stated. For it has been stated that [the capacity] exists either in the reality itself or in that which is not so; indeed, it is only the parts that are seen becoming an aggregate. Otherwise, just as there is no oil in sand, there would likewise be no oil in an aggregate of sesame seeds.

sirs, there would otherwise follow the fault of contradiction between the injunction (*vidhi*) and the restatement (*anuvāda*) of what is intended;

for, since the act of offering has as its sole purpose the oblation itself— just like clarified butter (*ghṛta*) and so forth— it would possess the character of an injunction, while clarified butter and the like would possess the character of a restatement, because they function merely as the material cause, just like the act of offering.

And thus it would lack the status of being a sentence, because it would neither be a restatement (*anuvāda*) nor an injunction (*vidhi*); it would be like a word whose meaning is disconnected, or like the cawing of a crow, and because there would be no distinction between what is known and what is unknown, just as in the case of the cognition of a jar, where there is a simultaneous occurrence of injunction, restatement, and the objects known and unknown.
Furthermore, there would follow the fault of the reversal of the intended injunction and restatement.

In that regard, in sentences such as "one should offer with ghee" or "one should offer with milk," since ghee and the like—which are intended to be the objects of injunction—are merely the causes for the act of offering, and because that act of offering has no other purpose than to serve as the very procedure (*itikartavyatā*) for those [substances] themselves, there is no lack of reference to the offering already heard in the sentence "one should perform the *agnihotra*. This is because there exists no offering distinct from ghee and the like.

Consequently, just like the injunctions regarding ghee and so forth, the sentence concerning the offering—which is intended to convey a matter already known—would possess only injunctive force (*vidhāyakatā*), and not the status of a restatement (*anuvādatā*).

And there is the status of restatement (*anuvādatā*) for substances such as clarified butter (*ghṛta*), even though they are intended to enjoin an unknown object, because they function solely with respect to the cause, just like the act of offering (*havana*). "Functioning solely with respect to the cause" means that its operation is restricted to the cause; thus, both clarified butter and the act of offering function solely with respect to the cause. Since the absence of an effect [independent of the cause] has been established by the aforementioned method, therefore, due to functioning solely with respect to the cause, substances such as clarified butter have the status of restatement just like the offering, and the act of offering has the character of an injunction just like clarified butter.

And thus, because injunction (*vidhi*) and restatement (*anuvāda*) would lack a fixed nature due to the mutual confusion of their respective essences, there would be neither injunction nor restatement. Therefore, in the manner described, there is a lack of sentential status (*avākyatva*), because, being neither a restatement nor an injunction, it lacks the required meaning—just as a single word with a detached meaning, such as "cow" (*gām*), is not a sentence precisely because it lacks an object of expectation through its connection with other relevant word-meanings. Likewise, [sentences such as] "One desiring heaven should offer the Agnihotra," or "One should offer with ghee and milk," and so forth, [would fail to be sentences].
For one for whom the referent (padārtha) does not exist at all, the analogy is "like the cawing of a crow" (kākaruta).

Just as the cawing of a crow—being devoid of any expectation of another meaning—is not a sentence because it is neither an injunction nor a restatement, so too should this [case] be regarded; see page 142, note 9.
The effect of that which possesses [qualities] such as [grossness] is other; its effect is not composed of those [subtle elements].
(Ḍe, Līṃ)
The non-existence of the act of offering, the non-existence of the offering,
[the non-existence] of the clarified butter and so forth for the offering,
and the state of being a speaker of falsehood.

Likewise, because there would be no distinction between what is known and what is unknown— just as in the case of the cognition of a jar—

it would follow that if one accepts that [correctness] arises solely from its cause, then correctness would be established; however, in the case of correct forms such as the word *gauḥ* or sentences such as *agnihotraṃ juhuyāt*, their status as injunctions (*vidhi*) or restatements (*anuvāda*) would not be tenable.

For a word is employed either when its meaning is already known or when its meaning is unknown. When the meaning is known, it is employed for the purpose of restating (*anuvāda*) that which is known in order to enjoin (*vidhāna*) something unknown. Furthermore, that known meaning may be employed when the object is known through its own nature by means of perception (*pratyakṣa*) or other valid means of knowledge, or when the object has been made known by another through a different sentence. For example, in the case of "This is Devadatta," because the word "this" denotes an object perceived through direct observation, it restates [the person] and then enjoins his being Devadatta. Or, having restated words whose meanings have been understood from another sentence, the act of driving toward is enjoined, as in: "Devadatta! Drive the white cow toward me. Thus, it is observed that for all words and sentences deemed correct, whether individually or collectively, there is a twofold function consisting of the expression of both a known and an unknown meaning.
What is the illustration? It is like the cognition of a jar.

Just as the parts of a jar that are proximate are perceived by the eye and other senses and thus known, while the further parts such as the base and so forth are not known—this well-known worldly distinction between the known and the unknown would not be possible in this theory of the effect being identical with its cause regarding words such as *pada* and *vākya*. This is because, if everything were of a single nature, the distinction between the known and the unknown would be untenable; or else, for a single entity, both [the known and the unknown] would be absent, as it has already been stated that there can be no status of injunction (*vidhi*) or restatement (*anuvāda*), just as in the case of the cawing of a crow and the like.

Nor does the charge of grammatical incorrectness (*asādhutā*) apply, as it would involve faults such as syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) or pointlessness (*anarthakya*). This is because, in the theory that the effect is of the nature of the cause (*kāraṇātmaka-kāryavāda*), there is no distinct entity; thus, the fabrication of faults like syntactical split—arising from the simultaneous intended application of injunction, restatement, or reference to objects known and unknown—is rendered utterly baseless. Even the difference in verbal forms (*śruti-bheda*) is likewise useless regarding correctness or incorrectness, since they share a single meaning, just as the words *ghaṭa* and *kuṭa* do.
Furthermore, even though this [truth] was unknown to you, you have demonstrated it to one who discerns reality in this manner, like a worm carving out a letter by chance (*ghuṇākṣara*).

Now, it might be argued: "The charge of 'sentence-splitting' (*vākyabheda*)—which consists in the simultaneous desire to express two meanings (*yugapadvivakṣā*), the occurrence of that desire in a single sense, and the resulting dual-purpose nature of the sentence (*dvyarthatā*)—is baseless and discarded here; therefore, the formulation is loose. For instance, an *anuvāda* (restatement) has a known object, while a *vidhi* (injunction) has an unknown object. When there is a simultaneous desire to express these two purposes, and that desire applies to a single [syntactical] meaning, this dual-purpose nature constitutes the fault of sentence-splitting. However, the conceptualization of this fault of sentence-splitting—which arises from the impossibility of a single word having the power to denote two meanings simultaneously—is entirely baseless in this case, because there is no actual difference in meaning. [This is the argument presented by the opponent.]
Therefore, there is no such thing as incorrectness of words; for it follows that all words would be either correct or incorrect.
(Jñātāvibhāga, Jñātājñātavibhaṅga)
Having established [the state of] being subject to injunction,
[the text reads] *vidheyatva* (in Bhāṣya and Ya; *ṇapite* in Bhā, Pā, Ḍe,
Līṃ).
In the case of the cognition of a jar,
this [non-existence] is the absence of other [cognitions].
The looseness resulting from the fabrication of faults such as the occurrence of [the term] *pattiḥ*, the mention of *asya*, and the division of the sentence (*vākya-bheda*).

Even the difference in Vedic recensions (śrutibheda) is likewise useless, whether in terms of correctness (sādhutva) or incorrectness (asādhutva), because they possess the same meaning, just like the words *ghaṭa* and *kuṭa*.
Furthermore, although this [distinction] remains unknown, it has been demonstrated by you to one who seeks the truth like a "gnawed-through" letter (*ghuṇākṣara*).
Now, it might be argued: "The observation here of the mere cause and its effect is a succession of verbal compositions whose ritual actions have been uprooted and discarded."
Yet this is the state of being one;
if this is the power of one, it is the *līṃ* of the *ḍe*;
this effort is the *vi* of one.

Furthermore, regarding the sacrifice of one [deity], not only is there the fault of syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), but also the fault of non-distinction (*bhedābhāva*) consisting of a non-entity; thus, even the distinction of Vedic revelation (*śrutibheda*) becomes entirely useless through such correctness and incorrectness.

Having thus extended by analogy what was stated in the manner of accepting the doctrine that the effect is of the nature of the cause, he states the proof in brief along with an example: "Because they have the same referent, like *ghaṭa* and *kuṭa*. Just as between the words *ghaṭa* and *kuṭa*, which are understood to have the same referent, the use of either one is redundant since both are intended to be correct; or likewise, because the word *go* alone—whether intended to be incorrect or used simultaneously for objects such as speech (*vāc*), direction (*diś*), and the dewlap (*sāsnā*)—has the same referent, the suspicion of the fault of difference in meaning remains loose (i.e., does not apply).

Therefore, since there is no distinction between the correctness and incorrectness of words and sentences, there is likewise no distinction between the linguistic usage of the learned and that of others. Thus, it has been stated that [the opponent's position] possesses defective reasoning because it involves redundancy and self-contradiction in the statement "one should sacrifice in this way," the abandonment of the doctrine of the non-existence of the effect (asatkāryavāda) as expressed by its own words, and the acceptance of the doctrine of the existence of the effect in the cause (satkāryavāda). This concludes the section on the *ātmakaśruti* from the *pāḍe* of the *līṃvi* commentary.
vācādisāgnādimadarthepāḍeḷīṃviḥ vācādisāgnādiyamadārthe bhāḥ vācādignāditamadārthe raṃ hīḥ.
And because that which is not employed simultaneously has a single meaning (bhāṣya);

and because that which is not employed simultaneously has a single meaning (pāda); and because that which is not employed simultaneously has a single meaning (ḍe); and because that which is not employed simultaneously has a single meaning (līṃ);
and because that which is not employed simultaneously has a single meaning (raṃ); and because that which is not employed simultaneously has a single meaning (hī).
And because they are applied simultaneously and have a single purpose, [this is] from the *Vivaraṇa-prameya-saṃgraha*.

Furthermore, as for this doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect within the cause (*satkāryavāda*) which you have accepted, it too was stated without reflection and without prior deliberation; therefore, in order to demonstrate that, he says: "And although this is unknown to you, you have presented this very reality to one who discerns it in this manner, like the accidental carving of a letter by a wood-boring insect."

Just as a wood-boring insect, while gnawing through wood, might by chance carve even a line in the shape of a letter, so too have you demonstrated this very principle of the pre-existence of the effect in its cause (*satkāryavāda*) by stating that "the manner of performance (*itikartavyatā*) is itself the duty to be performed (*kartavyatā*). This was shown specifically for the sake of a discerning person—one who knows how to distinguish between the nature of the means and the object of expression—thinking, "In this way the effect is non-existent (*asatkārya*), and in this way it is existent (*satkārya*). It was not shown for those whose intellects are equal to your own; for although you yourself demonstrate such a distinction, you do not desire that they should discern it.
Even though [it is] from the effect, it is quickly [realized as] the self-existence.

Now, it might be argued: "The observation here is merely that the effect exists in the cause," and so on, up to "through a quibble of words.
If you were to say this: "I do not accept the absolute necessity of observing the effect in the mere cause, such that these faults you have leveled against me would apply;
rather, I accept that the non-existent effect is intended [to be produced], because it has not yet acquired its own activity, like a sky-flower."
That is of two kinds: consisting of non-procedure (*anitkartavyatātmaka*) and consisting of procedure (*itikartavyatātmaka*).
Among these, that which consists of non-procedure includes things such as a jar (*ghaṭa*) and a sacrificial post (*yūpa*);
whereas that which consists of procedure is that which accords with attainment (*prāpti-saṃvādi*), such as service (*sevā*) and the like.

And that [cause] is not merely a cause; for, since you accept that what is to be produced exists at the beginning, middle, and end—thereby refuting the doctrine of the non-existent effect (*asatkāryavāda*)—the collection of faults you have alleged applies only through a quibble of words (*vacanacchala*).

This is because, without investigating the true nature of reality and without adopting an absolute position (*ekānta*), you assert that "it is neither cause alone, nor effect alone, nor both, nor neither," while in fact you accept it as being either the cause, the effect, both, or neither.

In the sentence, "One desiring heaven should offer the Agnihotra," that which is merely a demonstration of cause and effect—though it exists here in this system of injunctions, it is neither adopted nor rejected—is that in which the continuity of action and the continuity of sentences are both rootless and discarded; that is to say, it is that wherein the continuity of action and the continuity of sentences are rootless and cast aside.

The word *iti* has the sense of a reason (*hetu*); because the continuity of the sequence of actions and statements is uprooted and discarded, therefore, for the sake of avoiding that fault, the view of "merely the cause" regarding the effect is intended—that is, it is desired to be expressed—since it is a view whose certainty has not been determined. Having abandoned the state of being "merely the cause," that very non-existence of the effect is what is intended and accepted in the statement "one should perform the *agnihotra* sacrifice," namely, the perception of the effect as merely the cause, wherein the effect is [regarded as] both existent and non-existent.

What is the reason? Because its function has not been attained. That whose function has not been attained is "unattained-function," namely the effect (*kārya*). Therefore, because its function has not been attained, like a sky-flower—just as a sky-flower is non-existent because its function has not been attained—so too the effect, such as heaven or the unseen force (*apūrva*), is non-existent because its function has not been attained. If its function were already attained, one would not be enjoined with "one should perform" or "one should offer"; it would be like the lack of an injunction such as "one should cook for the sake of already-cooked rice. Therefore, having apprehended the non-existent effect, such as heaven, action is resorted to for the sake of attaining it, as in the injunction: "One should perform the *agnihotra*."

That [result] is of two kinds, and that result is twofold: consisting of non-procedure (*anitikatavyatātmaka*) and consisting of procedure (*itikartavyatātmaka*). Among these, the result consisting of non-procedure is seen in both the world and the Veda, such as a jar or a sacrificial post (*yūpa*). A result called a "jar" does not consist of procedures such as bringing clay, kneading it, taking up the stick, and spinning the wheel; for even when those [procedures] have ceased, the jar is perceived separately. Likewise, the sacrificial post does not consist of procedures such as making it eight-cornered.

Furthermore, the task consisting of the "how-to" (itikartavyatā) is that which accords with attainment; "accordant with attainment" means having the nature of being in agreement with attainment, such as service and so forth, because service—consisting of attendance, joining the palms in salutation, and the like—is not perceived as distinct from those [attainments].

Furthermore, that effect is neither the mere cause nor is it of the nature of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), like a jar or a sacrificial post; for [the injunction] "one should perform" (*kuryāt*) would follow from the doctrine of the non-existent effect (*asatkāryavāda*). From the word "should perform" as presented in the statement "one should perform the *agnihotra*," this sentence—just like the sentence "one should make a jar" which presents the jar as a non-existent effect—is even more clearly one whose meaning is a non-existent effect.

What is the reason? Because it is accepted that [the effect] is to be brought about in the beginning, middle, and end; therefore, since the theory of the non-existent effect (*asatkāryavāda*) is accepted throughout the specific actions from the commencement until the final completion, the entire mass of faults you have alleged—such as "the fault arises from your own words," "the 'to-be-done-ness' (*kartavyatā*) is merely the 'procedure-to-be-followed' (*itikartavyatā*) obtained through verbal instruction," and "consequently, the effect would be a mere modification of the cause, leading to the impossibility of injunctions"—does not apply. Thus, the non-existent effect is intended here because it has not yet acquired its functional activity, like a flower in the sky.
That [object] is of two kinds: consisting of non-procedure (*anitikatavyatātmaka*) and consisting of procedure (*itikartavyatātmaka*).
Among these, that which consists of non-procedure includes things such as a jar and a sacrificial post;
whereas that which consists of procedure is that which accords with attainment (*prāpti*), such as service and the like.

And that [cause] is not merely a cause; for, since you accept the necessity of action in the beginning, middle, and end, it would follow [the consequence of] the theory of the non-existent effect (*asatkāryavāda*) which was previously refuted. As for the collection of faults stated by you, they are merely a result of verbal quibbling (*vacanacchala*). (Note:

This also is not tenable, because of the doctrine that [the effect] is merely the cause, as will be established in the exposition of the Vidhi-vidhi-naya; for even if one were to accept the statement of the theory of the non-existent effect (*asatkāryavāda*), this [sentence] would still not constitute a complete sentence, since its establishment depends on the establishment of the "how-to" sentence (*itikartavyatāvākya*), and its establishment occurs only when that is established.
The sentence concerning the *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance) is not a true sentence (*avākyam*), because it is not a restatement (*ananuvādatvāt*), like the ravings of a madman.

Just as in the case of "one should sacrifice" (*juhuyāt*), upon examining all applications, there is an absence of meaning; thus, even through the cognition of the sentence regarding the *itikartavyatā*, there is no comprehension of what is to be done. Where, then, is this expressed by "one should sacrifice"? Even if one speaks of the doctrine of the effect (*kāryavāda*) regarding the primary *agnihotra* scripture as having the purpose of bringing about the unseen potency (*apūrva*) of the sacrifice, this [sentence] does not possess the status of a sentence. For a sentence—whether its purpose is the *itikartavyatā* obtained through the connection with attainment (*prāpti-anubandha*) or whether its purpose is the performance of the *agnihotra* sacrifice—does not attain the status of a sentence [in this context].

Why? Because if the sentence regarding the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is not established, that [sentence prescribing the act] is not established; but if that is established, then it is established. Furthermore, that is the sentence regarding the procedure. If that were not a sentence, then the sentence regarding the duty established by its force would also not be a sentence.

In this regard, first of all, the sentence "one should offer with clarified butter" is not a sentence regarding the procedure, because it is not a restatement (*ananuvāda*), like the prattle of a madman.

Just as in the case of one intoxicated by passion, the delusion of seeing a bird results in a confused outburst such as "O beloved! O beloved!", which is not a [valid] sentence because it lacks the restatement of a well-known meaning; likewise, because that [restatement] is absent in the case of "one should offer with ghee," there is an absence of a sentence enjoining its performance.

Furthermore, this [statement] is not a restatement (anuvāda) because it is an injunctive sentence (vidhi-vākya) that enjoins an oblation (havana) where ghee is the object of the offering (sampradāna); and between an injunction and a restatement, which are mutually independent, the absence of one entails the absence of the other.

It might be thought: "Since it is observed that for a mere injunction the word 'door' [is used], and for a mere restatement the word 'let it be opened,' one need not have recourse [to other means of proof]. No; even in those cases, there is indeed a requirement [for other means], because that [meaning] is established through external factors such as context (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth.

Therefore, since it is stated here that "the manner of performance (*itikartavyatā*) itself is the duty to be performed (*kartavyatā*)," the very sentence expressing the duty to be performed remains unestablished. Consequently, because the sentence "one should offer oblation with clarified butter" (*ghṛtena juhuyāt*) lacks the status of a restatement (*anuvāda*) of an already established meaning, it does not constitute a valid sentence. Due to its lack of sentential status, there is no establishment of the injunctive sentence that prescribes the duty to perform the *agnihotra* offering based on its authority. To this, he says: "of the word 'juhuyāt' [it is] just as has been stated," and so forth. One might think: "one should offer oblation" (*juhuyāt*), "one should perform the *agnihotra*" (*agnihotraṃ kuryāt*), "one should perform the offering" (*havanaṃ kuryāt*), "one should perform the *agnihotra*-offering" (*agnihotraṃ havanaṃ kuryāt*), or "one should perform the *agnihotra*, which consists of the manner of performance such as clarified butter obtained through the connection with attainment" (*prāptyanubandhaprāpitaghṛtādītikartavyatātmakakartavyatāgnihotraṃ kuryāt*), or "one should perform the *agnihotra*, which is the unprecedented" (*agnihotram apūrvaṃ kuryāt*). However, among these aforementioned alternatives, because of the connection with the previously mentioned defects, upon examination of the application (*prayoga*) through all these modes, it is found to be baseless in meaning due to being outside the scope [of valid cognition]. It is outside the scope because its meaning is unprecedented (*apūrva*). It is unprecedented because its meaning was unknown. Its meaning was unknown because it was not previously enjoined by another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) or by another sentence.
Having summarized that, he says: Even if there is a cognition of the "sentence of procedure" (*itikartavyatāvākya*), there is no comprehension of the "thing to be done" (*kartavyatā*);

furthermore, even when the theory of the non-existence of the effect in the cause (*asatkāryavāda*) is stated, this does not constitute a sentence at all. Since the "sentence of procedure" is unestablished, that [comprehension] is unestablished; since it is established when that is established, the "sentence of procedure" is not a sentence, because it is not a restatement (*ananuvāda*), like the prattle of a madman.

Regarding the injunction "one should sacrifice" (*juhuyāt*), just as has been stated, since there is no [independent] purpose in the examination of all ritual applications, even the cognition derived from the injunctive suffix of the *itikartavyatā* (procedural) sentence cannot convey the sense of something to be performed.

Where, then, is this expressed by the word "one should sacrifice"? It is for the sake of establishing that the primary Agnihotra mentioned in the Veda is subordinate to the apūrva (unseen potency) resulting from the act of offering.
