If [the term *agnihotra*] were established by its etymological derivation (*śailī*), then because it would consist of the act of offering (*havana*) into the fire, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that it would not be the [well-known] *agnihotra*. Therefore, what is the purpose of restating the meaning of the root *juhoti* (to offer), which is not connected with the primary desire for heaven? Because it would lead to the fault of [redundancy], and because there is no [other] meaning, the phrase "and so forth" (*ityādi*) is connected [to the objection]. The presentation of two alternative interpretations (*vikalpa*) by skipping over the sequence is due to their having equal responses: [namely,] "one should perform the offering" and "one should perform the *apūrva* called *agnihotra*. In these two alternative meanings, there would follow the abandonment of the primary word *agnihotra* and its referent.

In cases such as "one should offer with ghee," for the purpose of making the restatement (anuvāda) fruitful, the word *juhuyāt* (should offer) in the sentence "one should perform the Agnihotra" retains its own primary meaning; however, the word *agnihotram* would then become redundant and thus meaningless due to tautology.

If, on the other hand, because the Agnihotra is the principal element, one were to accept that the word *juhuyāt* is meaningless so that the word *agnihotra* does not become meaningless, then, due to the meaninglessness of the word *juhuyāt*, the performance of the rite would not be possible; for in the absence of a prescribed meaning, there can be no status as a restatement (anuvāda).

Furthermore, the primacy of the Agnihotra is established because it is enjoined as a direct means for achieving desired human goals such as heaven; if the *juhoti* (the act of offering) were primary, that [primacy] would be untenable.

And here, the entire passage beginning with "But the word *agnihotra*, unlike the word 'jar', does not enjoin any duty whatsoever" should be applied according to the context of the prima facie (*pūrva-pakṣa*) and the final conclusion (*uttara-pakṣa*), up until: "Nor is there any well-known action—such as those found in the case of the duty to make a jar—by which the name 'offering' (*havana*) could be extended to what is called the *agnihotra*, or the name 'Agnihotra' extended to the offering. Thus, the alternative interpretation of the meaning, namely "one should perform the offering," has already been answered.

Even in the view that [the word] denotes an *apūrva* (unprecedented result), since the words "agnihotra" and "juhuyāt" (one should sacrifice) have the same meaning, there would be the abandonment of the word "agnihotra," which denotes the primary *apūrva*.

Furthermore, the specific distinction—that the phrase "atha agnihotram" is assumed to denote a specific *apūrva*—must be addressed; and if that were so, one must apply the passage beginning with "What is the purpose of denoting an *apūrva*? up to "it is to be performed.
By the inclusion of the word "etc.," other defects such as [the Veda] being measured by human authority and the abandonment of the authority of the Word (*śabda*) are also to be understood.

Regarding the point established by the style [of the text], such as "like a hole" (*chidivat*): just as in the case of a "hole," there is only the visible, worldly result of a mere post (*yūpa*), and not the invisible, non-worldly nature of the *agnihotra* consisting of an oblation, so too, by that very same style, the statement "one should perform the *agnihotra*" refers to the *agnihotra* as consisting of an oblation. Since the use of the verb *juhoti* (to sacrifice) is well-established in the context of the *agnihotra*—which is already established as the object to be attained—it cannot, by obstructing the well-known meanings of "giving" and so forth, enjoin the act of burning alone. Thus, because it is not something previously unestablished, it is not injunctive; how then could it be a restatement (*anuvāda*)? Furthermore, if one were to accept such a meaning, the established practice would be set aside, because the use of the word *juhoti* is employed by those who are not careless, just like the syllable-knowledge in the mantra "For food, thee! (*iṣe tvā*).

Furthermore, because it consists of the *āhavana* [offering] which is the essence of the *agnihotra*, the consequence follows that it is not an *agnihotra*, just as the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is not established by the act of cutting wood.

In this regard, the passage beginning with "this too is not so, because of the disparity" should be applied, up until the point: "and since its style is authoritative, the ritual action regarding the sacrificial post is not literal according to that style."

Furthermore, because it would follow that [the act] is not an *agnihotra*, and since the primary element—which is intended as the means for attaining heaven—is defined merely as "that which is an offering (*hotra*) to Agni," it would therefore not be an *agnihotra*. What, then, is the purpose of this restatement (*anuvāda*), "one should offer with clarified butter" (*ghṛtena juhuyāt*), which is a restatement of the meaning of the root *hu* (to sacrifice) as connected to the primary desire for heaven? What use is that procedure (*itikartavyatā*) without the primary agent who desires heaven? As it has been said: "Fill the coward with courage, and the fool with a thousand insights."

Regarding the phrase *prāptipratipādyaprasiddhāvagnihotre*: "establishment through an injunction" (*prāptipratipādyaprasiddhi*) refers to that which is established by means of an injunction (*prāpti*) as something to be conveyed (*pratipādya*). In that case of "establishment through an injunction," specifically in the context of the *agnihotra*, where there is the establishment [of the meaning] through the injunction, "When one offers [oblations] to Agni and Prajāpati in the evening," the use of the term *juhoti* (offers) must first be prescribed in the sense of "burning" (*dāhana*), setting aside its conventional meanings such as "giving" (*dāna*) and so forth. The word *tāvat* is used for the sake of indicating sequence. This verbal root *hu* does not have the conventionally known meaning of giving or eating; rather, it is said that one should cause substances such as clarified butter (*ghṛta*) to be burned by means of fire—that is, "one should perform the *agnihotra* offering. Having thus reflected on this, and subsequently, based on the well-known act of burning, the rule for the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) will be appropriate once the meaning is understood through the following expressions: "one should offer with clarified butter," "one should burn the clarified butter with fire," "one should cause the clarified butter to be burned by fire," or "fire should burn the clarified butter. This is because it is taught in opposition to worldly convention; it would not be so otherwise.

Otherwise, since burning and such acts are not observed in common worldly practice, how could the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) regarding clarified butter and so forth be enjoined by restating the act of burning? Thus, because [burning] is not established in that way, [the word *juhuyāt*] is not an injunction at all; how then could there be a restatement (*anuvāda*) of it? The word *iti* has the sense of a reason (*hetu*). For this reason—that is, because it is not established as having the purpose of burning in that manner—the word *juhuyāt* in the sentence "one should offer the *agnihotra*" is not even an injunction for burning, let alone a restatement.

In this very context, one should apply the passage beginning with "Surely, the understanding of the duty [to act] arises from the procedural rules (*itikartavyatā*) just as [the duty to perform] service and so forth," up until "or else, like that, the Vedic injunctions would be invalid" (p.
142, n. 8). Thus, one should observe the inappropriateness [of the argument] either because the word *juhuyāt* does not have the meaning of "burning," or because of the word *hotra*.

Regarding the phrase "and in the acceptance of such a meaning": even having accepted that "giving" (*dāna*) consists solely of the act of burning, we state the following fault: what is this? It is the rejection of the established rule (*prāpti*). What is this established rule? It is the rule that "one offers in the evening to Agni and Prajāpati," by which it is established that "giving" is the throwing [of the oblation] into the fire; there is a rejection of that established rule. Why? Because of the use of the verb *juhoti* ("he offers") in the injunction "one should offer with clarified butter. Otherwise, if it were merely a restatement of an already established rule, one might object: "In that case, the word *juhoti* is a restatement (*anuvāda*) occurring within the sentence that establishes the rule. We say no, because the application of the injunctive optative (*liṅ*) in that context has not been previously known.

If it is argued that its object [the clarified butter] is established through transposition (*vyatyaya*), we say no; because it is not a restatement (*anuvāda*) precisely since it is unknown, and because its meaning is already conveyed by the *juhoti* mentioned in the *kośa*-text, it would be redundant (*paunaruktya*) as it would be unfit for further employment. However, this term is indeed employed; therefore, it is understood that the *juhoti* mentioned in the source-text is purposeless.
Consequently, the *juhoti* is employed to exclude what has been obtained [by other means].

Or rather, when it is employed in the form "if one should offer with clarified butter" (*yadā vāyaṃ ghṛtena juhuyāt*), then it should be understood that its meaning is not yet conveyed, provided its meaning has not been expressed by another word.

What is the reason? Because it is produced by one who is free from negligence (*apramatta*). For, according to your view, this [word] is produced by the Veda—which is distinct from a negligent person and devoid of attachment, ignorance, and so forth—while according to our view, it is produced by a worldly person who is knowledgeable and free from negligence. Let it not be that words are invalid simply because they are perceived as dependent upon persons; for if all persons were invalid, words would necessarily be invalid as well.

For in the statement "one should offer this with clarified butter," the word *juhoti* (he offers) is employed by one who is not careless; it is not like a formula used by anyone at random—such as those used by children or cowherds—or like a formula such as "the cawing of a crow.

To what is it comparable? It is like the mantra "For food thee" (*iṣe tvā*) and so forth, as in: "For food thee, for strength thee; you are winds, you are helpful winds; may the god Savitṛ impel you toward the most excellent work" (Yajurveda 1).

Words such as these are understood to have a meaning not yet conveyed; likewise, in the sentence "one should sacrifice with clarified butter," the act of sacrificing (*juhoti*) would be understood as having a meaning not yet conveyed because it is employed by one who is attentive, and not otherwise.

Or else, it is like the knowledge of the syllables (*akṣara-vidyā*): as it is said, "Two sciences are to be known—the higher and the lower. Now, the higher is that by which that Imperishable (*akṣara*) is attained, which is invisible, ungraspable, without lineage, without color, without eyes or ears, and without hands or feet."

"The wise perceive that eternal, all-pervading, omnipresent, ancient Person, the Self of all, who is imperishable and the source of all beings" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.6). Thus, this knowledge of the Imperishable (akṣaravidyā) is understood not to have its meaning already established elsewhere, because it is employed with great care; so too is this use of the verb *juhoti*. It cannot be otherwise. If, in the passage "one should offer the Agnihotra," the word *hotra* or the word *juhoti* itself were intended to convey the act of giving as already established by the rule of application (*prāpti*), then the verb *juhoti* would not be used again in the subsequent injunction "one should offer [it] with ghee. Yet it is indeed used. Therefore, the rule of application is set aside.

If it is argued that, in this case, the word *juhoti* (he offers) is a restatement (*anuvāda*) occurring within the injunctive sentence, we say no; for in that context, the repetition of the subject matter of the injunctive optative (*vidhiliṅ*) is not known [from elsewhere].
If it is argued that, due to a transposition (*vyatyaya*), this [word] has that as its subject matter, we say no; because precisely due to being unknown, it cannot be a restatement. [End of] Kośa...

ungraspable, without lineage, without color, devoid of eyes and ears, without hands or feet, eternal, all-pervading, omnipresent, exceedingly subtle, and immutable— that [the wise enter]..."— such is the reading in the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad.
If it is argued that, in that case, the word *juhoti* is a restatement (*anuvāda*) occurring within the context of the sentence concerning attainment (*prāpti-vākya*), [we reply:]...

It might be thought: "This [statement] 'one should offer with ghee' is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the root *juhoti*—which is heard in the injunction regarding attainment (*prāptivākya*) as 'he offers to Agni' (*agnaye juhoti*) and has the sense of giving with Agni as the recipient"—but this is not so, because in that case, the repetition of what is the object of the injunctive optative (*vidhiliṅ*) would be unknown.

This is not tenable either; for in that sentence of attainment (*prāptivākya*), the word *juhoti*—which employs the verbal root *hu* (to sacrifice) in the sense of giving by an agent who is not being prompted—is incapable of functioning in the sense of prompting within the scope of the injunctive optative (*vidhiliṅ*). Furthermore, since this word *juhuyāt*, which falls under the scope of the injunctive optative and has the meaning of a mandate (*niyoga*), does not recur in the meaning of the word *juhoti* which is devoid of a mandate, its purpose as an injunction is simply not understood there. Therefore, because it is unknown, it is unfit to be a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the meaning of *juhoti* occurring in the sentence of attainment, according to the principle that "what is already attained is restated, while what is not attained is enjoined."

Therefore, because it is unfit to be a restatement (anuvāda), it was incorrectly stated that "the word *juhoti* occurring in the injunction of attainment (*prāptivākya*) is a restatement"; for [in this case], the word *juhoti* is not a restatement of anything whose meaning is "taking" (*ādāna*). Thus ends the section on the non-application of the rule.

If it be thought that its objectivity [is established] through transposition—
should the opinion be held that "transposition occurs frequently" (Pāṇini 3.1.85) is stated in the science of grammatical definitions— then [we reply]: no.

And because [the suffix] has the sense of "being caused to drink" (pāna-pratyāyyārthatvāt), and because of the offering (havana), the efficient force (bhāvanā) would remain uncomprehended regarding what is intended;

for since the nature of the Agnihotra—established by its own acquisition—is already accomplished, there is the statement that it is the object of the action of one who desires heaven (svargakāma-karmatva). Because of this, there is the teaching of an action corresponding to that desire, and through that, the understanding of a specific action of that kind arises. Furthermore, since the desire is to be attained through action, [this applies to] the case where the person is understood from the blind man's staff (andhalakā), as well as to the verbal roots (su), the personal endings (tiṅ), the upagraha (voice), the gender (liṅga), the number (nara), the tense (kāla), the hal (consonant), the svarita accent (svara), the agent (kartṛ), and the yaṅ suffix.
The author of the treatise intends a transposition of these [suffixes], and that too is established by the rule of "generality" (bāhulaka).
(Pāṇini-Mahābhāṣya 3.1.85)

85. Therefore, because the word *juhuyāt* is employed in the sense of *juhoti*, it merely restates what is already established; and since this [word] has that very [act] as its object, [one might argue] this too is so.

But this is not correct, because it is not a restatement precisely because the meaning is unknown. Furthermore, since we observe words whose purpose lies in having an operation (*savyāpāraṇa*), it is not logical to understand them as having no operation (*nirvyāpāraṇa*), for that would lead to the undesirable consequence of destroying the established distinction between them.

Therefore, because its meaning is not already known, it cannot be a restatement (*anuvāda*); and because it is not a restatement, this [interpretation] is also not tenable. Furthermore, since its meaning must be established by the *kośapāna* (drinking from the vessel) ordeal: "This matter must be proven by you through the drinking from the vessel of the presiding deity, for in the absence of any specific indicative mark (*liṅga*), how could it be known whether the word *juhuyāt* is used in the sense of the root *juhoti*, or whether *juhoti* is used in the sense of *juhuyāt*? Therefore, because its meaning is not already known, it possesses the character of an injunction (*vidhi*); and because it is an injunction, it is not a restatement; and because it is not a restatement, even this [interpretation] is not tenable.

Even granting that the word *juhuyāt* functions in the sense of "one should offer," we state the following fault: through such an offering, the intended efficient force (*bhāvanā*) would remain entirely uncomprehended.

In the absence of an injunctive meaning (*vidhyartha*), the person would not even be enjoined to the act of offering (*havana*). Consequently, this sentence—which was uttered for a specific purpose—would fail to convey the *bhāvanā* (productive operation) directed toward a desired object, namely, heaven characterized by a particular kind of pleasure, or a specific location that serves as the means for such pleasure. For this very sentence, "One should offer the Agnihotra," was uttered with the intention: "I shall enjoin the person to the act of Agnihotra, which is the means for attaining the fruit called heaven. If there were no communication of that purpose—that "heaven is brought about by this very act, therefore do this"—then what would be the use of this sentence, which merely says "one offers, one offers"?

Because of the non-existence [of the result] due to the transgression of the injunction for knowledge (*vidyā-vidhi*), because of the non-existence [of the result] due to the transgression of the injunction [for the sacrifice], and because the meaning is not to be brought about by drinking, the production (*bhāvana*) intended would remain uncomprehended despite the act of offering (*havana*).

Since the nature of the *agnihotra* sacrifice is established by its attainment, and because it is designated as an action for one who desires heaven (*svargakāma*), it is understood that the action prescribed conforms to that desire; thus, from the statement of such an action, the specific ritual procedure is known. Furthermore, since desire is to be attained through action, the author of the grammatical treatise intends a transposition (*vyatyaya*) of the following elements: person (*puruṣa*), tense (*kāla*), suffixes ending in *hal*, vowels (*svara*), agent (*kartṛ*), and the *yaṅ* affix—just as in the case of the blind man’s discovery of the sleeping woman, where the verbal endings (*sup* and *tiṅ*), voice (*upagraha*), gender (*liṅga*), and person (*puruṣa*) are transposed. And this [transposition] is also established by the principle of diversity (*bāhulaka*). (Pāṇini-Mahābhāṣya 3.1.85)

...by that very [word] *uttama*... by that very *uttama*... *ḍe*... *līṃ*... *vi*... *raṃ*... *hī*.

Here he says: this explanation of the meaning is adopted for the purpose of avoiding the faults found in the alternative interpretations of the meaning of the previously mentioned sentence concerning the performance of the *agnihotra*, starting with the words, "because the essential nature of the *agnihotra* as enjoined has been established."

This much is established: the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the Agnihotra is established by the injunction contained in the text, "One offers to Agni and Prajāpati in the evening. Since the essential nature of the Agnihotra is thus established by what is prescribed through that injunction, and since it is heard [in scripture] as an action (*karman*), for whom? For the agent who desires heaven, because it is designated as the object of his action.

If it is asked, "What follows from that?"—it is stated that because one hears a word expressing desire for a specific object denoted by the word "heaven," it follows that the action called *agnihotra* must also be specifically distinguished as corresponding to that [desire]. Therefore, since the mention of the "one desiring heaven" implies the performance of an action suited to that desire, and because the action mentioned is precisely that which accords with the desire made known by the term "one desiring heaven," it is understood that the specific nature of such an action is established. Consequently, the person who desires a specific result is the agent; the action is also specifically distinguished because it corresponds to that [desire]; and the action itself is likewise of that specific kind. Just as an action related to a desire for an unestablished result is itself unestablished, so too the specific mode of its performance is understood to be equally unestablished and distinct.

What is the reason? Precisely from that word, because there is no other sentence [to provide] the understanding of that specific action or movement, there is an understanding of its particularity; therefore, because the specific action is understood and because desire (*kāma*) is attained through action, this interpretation—that it is a restatement of a meaning already implied by the sense, such as "one should offer oblations like the *kāmaraṭana* bird"—is logical, even if it involves abandoning the primary direct statement (*śruti*) in the initial sentence and relying on a subordinate quality. If this is argued, it is not so. Because it would be a redundant repetition of the word’s own meaning already established by the sense, there is a means for the attainment of desire through an injunction (*vidhi*), since that meaning is understood either through action or through the word. Just as in the case of a blind man fallen in the middle of a road who, stretching out his hand, cries out repeatedly, "Give me a cowrie! Give me a cowrie, sir!", his desire is understood either through action or through the word due to the connection with a specific context. And that action is not accomplished without an instruction. Just as in the case of the blind man’s crying out of desire, when it is said, "One desiring heaven should perform the *agnihotra*," the injunctive meaning—namely, "he should do it"—is implied by the sense because the desire has been made known, just as the purpose of that blind man was the act of begging.

And that specific relationship arises through the logic of syntactical connection (*vākya-nyāya*). For example, in the expression "studied together with a fellow-student" (*sabrahmacāriṇā sahādhītaḥ*), [the meaning is] "he studied together with a fellow-student"; with what commonality is he a "fellow"? It is understood to be by virtue of the commonality of the qualifying factor of the context—namely, "by one who performs the act of study under discussion. In this same way, this sentence also [is understood]: by this logic of syntactical connection, it is understood that this [sentence] teaches the performance of the ritual action in accordance with the injunction for the *agnihotra* rite intended for one desiring heaven (*svargakāma*) as presented in the context. Therefore, the passage beginning with "of the *agnihotra*, whose nature is established by the rule of attainment" and continuing up to "one should sacrifice" (*juhuyāt*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the sense already implied; for the purpose is already conveyed by the sentence consisting of the mere words "one desiring heaven [should perform] the *agnihotra*" along with its remaining portion.

If it is argued that this explanation—that one should offer oblations like the "kāmaraṭana" sound—is the correct one because it restates a meaning already established by implication (arthāpanna), and because it does not abandon the primary scriptural statement (*pradhānaśruti*) while still accounting for the subordinate quality (*guṇa*)—that is not so; for such a restatement would be redundant, as it merely repeats the meaning of a word already established by implication. Thus, [the objection] is refuted.
Because of that state of being blind, the purpose of the request for the blind man; because of that state of being blind, the purpose of the request for the blind man; [he] studies the *Ahā* [text].
That which is studied by [someone] is not a restatement of what has already been said.

Thus, the interpretation that "one should sacrifice in this manner" (*juhuyāt*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*) and not an injunction (*vidhi*) is the correct one; for it is to be understood as correct because its meaning is clearly established and because it is free from the defects arising from the alternative interpretations previously mentioned. This is because, regarding the initial sentence, it does not involve the abandonment of the primary sense of the Vedic word (*pradhānaśruti*), even though it functions as a subordinate element (*guṇakṛt*). As was stated previously, in the alternative interpretation of the sentence "One should sacrifice the Agnihotra" (*agnihotraṃ juhuyāt*) as "One should perform the Agnihotra" (*agnihotraṃ kuryāt*), there would be an abandonment of the primary sense of the root *hu* (to sacrifice) which is intended to express the injunctive meaning; consequently, the authority would depend on human cognition. Alternatively, if that [primary sense] were not abandoned, there would be the contingency of a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) and a host of other defects such as tautology (*paunaruktya*). However, none of that applies here, precisely because the word *juhuyāt* is a restatement. Even in the case of the phrase "one should perform the offering" (*havanaṃ kuryāt*), the aforementioned host of defects—such as the abandonment of the primacy of the Agnihotra—is likewise absent. Therefore, this interpretation is correct because it does not involve the abandonment of the primary sense of the Vedic word in the initial sentence, since that root *hu*, being a restatement, is free from tautology, abandonment, and syntactical split.

If one should raise this doubt—meaning, "if you think thus"—the Teacher, having questioned the opponent in this manner, gives the reply: "That is not so; [the explanation] beginning with 'implied by the sense' (*arthāpanna*) is also untenable. Why? Because of the fault of *punarukta* (redundancy). Due to redundancy, there is an unfitness for formal application (*prayoga*), and consequently, the impossibility of it being a restatement (*anuvāda*). Therefore, because a restatement is impossible, the connection is "that is not so" (*tan na*). Furthermore, this is redundant in the context of the category of points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) characterized as redundancy, which consists in the repetition of a word whose meaning is already established by implication.

Furthermore, repetition as a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) is of two kinds, namely: repetition of the word and its meaning, and repetition by one's own words of that which is already implied by the sense (Nyāya Sūtra 5.2.14–15).

Therefore, this is a restatement of what is already implied by the sense; for there would be no tautology in the case of "one should offer with ghee," because that which is implied by the sense is here uttered by its own word, since it prescribes an oblation qualified by ghee. Without such a specific prescription, the meaning would not be established.

In this case, however, since it has already been accepted that the function of the instruction (*upadeśavṛtti*) consists in the purpose of enjoining specific ritual acts corresponding to the desire for heaven and corresponding to the [prescribed] action, and since the status of *juhuyāt* as a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the injunction of an oblation qualified by clarified butter is impossible given its occurrence in the root sentence; and since one would have to abandon the directly heard injunction *juhuyāt* and instead assume a *juhuyāt* that is not heard but merely implied by the sense and restated; and since this involves restating a sentence-meaning that is itself being enjoined, thereby accepting the faults of syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) and tautology (*punarukta*); and because a restatement of a restatement must concern an object that is a qualifying attribute already established or a subordinate element; and because its meaning would thus be remote from the actual subject matter of the injunction.
Thus, since the purpose is not accomplished, this is indeed not a restatement (*anuvāda*).

Furthermore, why is this interpretation even more inferior? Because it abandons the injunction (*vidhi*) directly heard in the text—namely, "one should sacrifice" (*juhuyāt*)—and instead postulates a "one should sacrifice" that is neither heard nor restated, but merely implied by the sense; thus, one incurs both the fault of relying on human authority (*puruṣapramāṇakatva*) and the fault of the non-authoritativeness of the word (*śabdāprāmāṇya*).

Having abandoned the direct hearing—that is, the perceptual hearing—of the verbal root *juhuyāt*, which is a term denoting action (*kriyāśabda*) and expresses an injunction (*vidhi*), one would then [be forced to] assume that very word *juhuyāt* as being intended as a restatement (*anuvāda*). This is because of the assumption of a restatement (*anuvādakalpanā*) regarding that unhearing word whose meaning is already implied by the context (*arthāpannārtha*). The phrase "that is not so" (*tan na*) carries over from the previous argument.

Furthermore, because it is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of that which has the sentence-meaning currently being enjoined as its object: "the sentence-meaning being enjoined" is *vidhīyamāna-vākyārtha*; that which has this as its object is "that which has the sentence-meaning being enjoined as its object" (*vidhīyamāna-vākyārtha-viṣaya*). That very word *juhuyāt* (he should sacrifice) is what has this as its object; the restatement of that very [word] is "that very restatement. Therefore, what follows from this restatement of that which has the sentence-meaning being enjoined as its object? It results in the acceptance of both a split of the sentence (*vākya-bheda*) and a redundancy (*punarukta*). For this single sentence cannot simultaneously enjoin the *agnihotra* connected with one desiring heaven and also restate it, since the performance of the *agnihotra* rite by one desiring heaven has not been established by another sentence.

Just as in the expression "this Devadatta," it is not the case that Devadatta alone is both referred to (*anūdita*) and enjoined (*vidhīyate*); rather, the object of the demonstrative pronoun *idam*, which is established by direct perception, is what is referred to. Likewise here, one must rely on a meaning that is already well-known; however, such a meaning does not exist [in this context].

Therefore, because it is impossible for a single sentence to have two distinct meanings—or rather, because of the assumption of two separate meanings—there arises the fault of syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).

However, there is redundancy because no specific injunction is provided; for a restatement (*anuvāda*) is appropriate only when intended for the sake of a specific injunction, as in "This is Devadatta," where one restates the meaning already established by direct perception through the word "this" and then enjoins "Devadatta. But here, no such specific thing is enjoined; therefore, because nothing specific is expressed, there is redundancy.

Therefore, because the sentence "one should offer the Agnihotra" is the first [in the context] and because these two—the injunction and the restatement—belong to a single syntactical unit (*ekavākya*), if the act of Agnihotra were understood as being enjoined by implication while the verb *juhoti* ("he offers") were treated as a restatement, one would have to accept the faults of "splitting the sentence" (*vākyabheda*) and "redundancy" (*punarukti*); thus, [the word *agnihotram*] is necessarily connected with "not" (*na*).

In this way, first of all, the word *juhuyāt* in the phrase "one should offer the Agnihotra" cannot be a restatement. Nor can the phrase "one desiring heaven [should perform] the Agnihotra" be an injunction. Furthermore, a restatement of a restatement has as its purpose the qualification of what is already established, or the sense of something intended for another.

For the nature of a restatement (*anuvāda*) is for the purpose of [confirming] a subject matter already established; as in the case of "This is Devadatta," the referent of the word "this" is already established, while the referent of "Devadatta" is not yet established and must now be brought to mind.

Thus, by virtue of being well-known or unknown, there is a distinction between the qualifier and the qualified. These two are respectively the subordinate (*parārtha*) and the principal (*svārtha*) by way of being the benefactor and the beneficiary.

However, in the case of "One should offer the *agnihotra* sacrifice," the words "agnihotra" and "should offer" do not have as their object a qualifier that is already established or something subordinate. Therefore, because the qualifier is not already established and because they are not subordinate, there is no similarity [to a restatement], and thus there is an absence of the status of a restatement.

Even granting [the existence of] "attainment" (*prāpti*) and so forth, the fault is stated: as for what was said later—that it is for the sake of establishing "what is to be done" (*kartavyatā*)—the sentence expressing "what is to be done," namely "one should sacrifice with clarified butter" (*ghṛtena juhuyāt*), becomes remote from the scope of the injunction (*vidhi*). Since the word *juhuyāt* is intended to be a restatement (*anuvāda*), you—who exert yourself to resolve that very point through a complex and disjointed reconciliation—have, by your own medical treatment, produced a pustule on top of a boil.

This supreme restatement (*anuvāda*) would have to concern only the subject matter of the instruction regarding the performance of the worldly act of *juhoti*; yet that instruction, intended for a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*), is untenable because it does not exceed the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) already established by prior attainment, nor the name of the sacrificial act (*havana-kriyā*). Why? Because a restatement has as its object a specific attribute already established for the sake of another, whereas an injunction (*vidhi*) has as its object a substantive meaning not yet established. Thus, first of all, the word *juhuyāt* occurring in the opening sentence cannot be a restatement, as there is no prior attainment (*prāptatva*) and so forth. However, a restatement of that [act] would be acceptable in the case of the word *juhuyāt* in the phrase "one should offer with clarified butter" (*ghṛtena juhuyāt*), where its meaning is like a mere echo (*pratiśabdaka*) of the original. But this is not the case here, because the meaning is remote from the scope of the injunction, as it concerns an unestablished attribute for the sake of another.

Furthermore, because it concerns an object that is remote from the scope of an injunction (*vidhi*), the *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance) cannot have "what is to be done" (*kartavyatā*) as its object, just like the parts of the verse beginning with "ten pomegranates" (*daśadāḍima*). Moreover, by stating "thus, having been joined and disjoined," and so forth, you have brought about a "boil upon a boil."

The word *iti* has the sense of a reason (*hetu*); because there is this collection of defects—such as the remoteness of the *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance) from the object of what is to be done (*kartavya*), and so forth—due to the absence of both injunction (*vidhi*) and restatement (*anuvāda*), therefore [the position] is "joined and disjoined. Previously, it was somewhat joined in the notion that the *itikartavyatā* itself is the *kartavyatā*, like [the sequence of] service and so on; yet even that is disjoined by this conceptualization beginning with "because the established nature [of the act] is accomplished through this attainment" (*prāpti*). Consequently, in that which requires correction, one incurs an even more contradictory defect, because its meaning has become remote from the scope of the injunction.

Furthermore, since that very sentence which was supposed to be remedied lacks the status of a restatement (*anuvāda*) and is thus vitiated by defects such as being a non-sentence (*avākya*), you—who have exerted yourself to remedy it—alas, like a most learned physician, have by your very treatment produced a pustule upon a boil, disregarding the sequence of prior and subsequent actions and their results.
Therefore, because its meaning is not established, neither the original *juhoti* nor the subsequent one can be considered a restatement; rather, they must be injunctions (*vidhi*).

If it is intended that "one who offers oblations with ghee [is liberated]" is a restatement (*anuvāda*), then I shall provide you with an analysis of the intellect; listen: this supreme restatement would only be applicable if its subject were an instruction regarding the performance of the worldly meaning of the root *hu* (to sacrifice). For the root *juhoti* has the worldly sense of giving and eating; if its subject were an instruction regarding the performance of that meaning, then since those meanings are well-established, it would be appropriate as a restatement of that subject, or else as an injunction such as "he should give" or "he should eat."

If one were to give anything whatsoever to anyone, one should offer that very thing as an oblation; if one were to eat, one should offer it with clarified butter—it is in this sense that the restatement (anuvāda) is appropriate.

Furthermore, that instruction, whose restrictive rule is untenable, has been explained by me to you by harmonizing the meaning of this word; nevertheless, it nonetheless results in a meaning contrary to what you desire, because we observe in the world that instructions with untenable rules serve a purpose, since diverse acts of giving and eating are causes of satisfaction for both oneself and others—just as one should eat according to what is appropriate with ghee, milk, curd, and molasses, and give those very same things to one who is hungry.
But it is not as in the science of ophthalmology, where one should consume triphalā with ghee alone and not with jaggery, because jaggery is detrimental to the eyes—
as it has been said: [Bhāvaprakāśa].
It becomes [the state of] being naturally composed.
