he should give that... he should not give... yaḥ.
"Molasses produces an abundance of worms, marrow, blood, fat, and flesh" (Caraka Saṃhitā 1.27.238).
"The eye consists of light; it has a particular fear of phlegm" (Caraka Saṃhitā 1.5.16);
thus [it is stated] in the Caraka Saṃhitā as "from phlegm in particular."

Its meaning is merely that [of the root *kṛ*], because it consists of only that much; for, by connecting it to the context, one must demonstrate its status as the agent (*kartṛ*) of the verbal root *kṛ*, setting aside the abundance of uses of the verb *juhoti*—namely, that "one who desires heaven should perform [the act] with ghee and so forth at evening for Agni and Prajāpati," according to your statement. Furthermore, it would be possible to suspect that this is a source of invalid restrictive rules and is non-instructive even for a discerning person, because its meaning has not been examined, because its sequence lacks logical connection, and because it destroys established and accepted injunctions, like the speech of a madman.
Furthermore, one should offer this Agnihotra sacrifice; for when one offers it to Agni and Prajāpati in the evening, [it is so stated in] the Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā 6.7 and the Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā 1.8.5.1.8.
One should offer with clarified butter (Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā 6.3.5);
one offers with a winnowing basket, for by it food is prepared (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 1).

Thus, the root *juhoti* (to sacrifice), as heard in sentences consisting of injunctions (*vidhi*), restatements (*anuvāda*), or explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), serves merely to name the act of offering (*havana*)—which is not distinct from the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) already established by other means—just as [the term] serves merely to name the act of service (*sevana*) which is not distinct from the procedure of "approaching" (*upasthāna*) and so forth. Its meaning is the action itself, whose constituent parts are scattered and which exists in an unestablished form (*asiddharūpa*), and not in an established form (*siddharūpa*), unlike [the names of objects such as] a sacrificial post (*yūpa*) or a jar (*ghaṭa*).

Because that action consists of nothing more than that [the mere form], and because it is connected to the context, the speaker, by connecting it through the context, says, and the listener understands: "This word must necessarily express a mere action"—this much alone is enjoined.

Therefore, because it is a mere action (*kriyāmātra*) and because it is connected to the context (*prakaraṇa*), one must set aside—that is, abandon—the abundance of *juhoti* usages, including all instances of the *juhoti* verb. Since the root *kṛ* (to do/make) must be demonstrated as having the same nature of action, verbal suffix, and agent when the mere action is to be expressed—as that [action] is invariably concomitant with it—for the purpose of demonstrating that, this [root *kṛ*] would indeed have the status of the intended sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) when it is so conceived.

He demonstrates this: "When one offers to Agni and Prajāpati in the evening, one who desires heaven should do so with clarified butter and other substances. Since the meaning is thus easily understood, the frequent use of the verb *juhoti* (he offers) is merely a conventional repetition; otherwise, one might offer here and there [repeatedly], as seen in the phrase *juhoti* and so forth in the *Agnipurāṇa*, page 123, note 3.
See page 142, note 8;
see page 142, note 9;
by Sūrya, pra.
Having abandoned [the notion of] being the agent, and having again demonstrated elsewhere the state of being the offerer, one performs the oblation.
Furthermore, according to your statement, it would follow that this [scripture] is a non-authoritative source of rules and lacks instructional value even for a discerning person.

For even a discerning person— one capable of inferring the meaning of words employed by the ignorant, and who is an expert in the criteria of words, sentences, and means of valid cognition— this employment of the sentence remains a non-authoritative source of rules and lacks instructional value,
because its content does not accord with what is established by perception and inference.
"But because it does not convey [the truth], it is non-instructive (*anupadeśaka*);

however, I consider that this might indeed be so. Do not think that it is being stated with harshness by definitively concluding that 'scripture lacking the restriction of valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*) is non-instructive.

Why? Because its meaning has not been examined, because its meaning is disconnected due to the lack of connection between preceding and succeeding parts, and because it destroys what has been established and accepted."

The lack of consideration for the meaning [of the text] consists in its being devoid of connection between preceding and following parts due to the pointlessness of performing numerous *juhoti* offerings and so forth; it is the destruction of what has been constructed because there is no supplementary relationship (*śeṣabhāva*) among those things intended to have separate meanings, such as injunctions and the like;

and it is the destruction of what has been accepted as constructed, on the grounds that "the manner of performance (*itikartavyatā*) is itself the duty (*kartavyatā*)," since one accepts the restatement (*anuvāda*) of the *juhoti* occurring in the opening sentence of the constructed whole.

For these reasons, this application of speech—which lacks a restriction on its means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*) and is non-instructive—is like the prattle of a madman. Just as the speech uttered by a madman or similar person, though appearing to be a valid statement due to the commonality of being sound produced by a person, lacks a restriction on its means of valid cognition and is non-informative; for example: "The conch is in the plantain tree, and the plantain tree is in the drum; and in that drum is a very great celestial chariot (*vimāna*); that conch, drum, plantain, and chariot became like the mad Gaṅgā."

It is like idle chatter, because both critical examination (*pratyavekṣā*) and validity (*prāmāṇya*) are objects of cognition; moreover, according to your own view, the Veda is not cognition, and therefore it is necessarily non-authoritative and non-instructive due to its insentience (*acetanatva*), like space. Furthermore, as for your forceful assertion that the effect is non-existent within its causes—like a sky-flower—that is also entirely unreasonable, since you yourself maintain that this so-called "non-existence" is something distinct from the cause; likewise, this [Veda] is also incapable of conveying meaning even to a discerning person.
When this statement is examined in this way, it is not liberated from its defects.

Or rather, this is not a defect at all, nor is this [notion of] apprehension (*udgrāha*) subject to such investigation; for it is cognition (*jñāna*) that is investigated and scrutinized as to whether it is a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) or not, because validity (*prāmāṇya*) is primary therein. Indeed, validity is not accepted here in the same manner as the validity [of perception] attributed to the eye and other senses.

Therefore, since both critical investigation (*pratyavekṣā*) and validity (*prāmāṇya*) are objects of knowledge, according to your own view the Veda is admitted to be non-knowledge; consequently, neither investigation nor the status of being a means of valid cognition applies to it, because the Veda is non-knowledge.
For you have already stated previously: "Indeed, no knowledge whatsoever is certain or pure, because for everyone [knowledge] is permeated by ignorance such as doubt and the like."

Demonstrating this, he says: "But according to your view, the Veda is not knowledge, nor is it produced from knowledge. This means that, unlike [the self], which—because it is the effect of knowledge—is of the nature of knowledge, even though the consciousness of the word employed by the self is an effect; for one may metaphorically designate the cause as the effect, just as the vital breaths (prāṇas), being effects of food, are called "food.
If it is asked, "What follows from this?", [the answer is: the Veda is restricted to non-authoritativeness and is not an instructor, because it is insentient (*acetana*), like space (*ākāśa*).

Just as space, due to its insentience and its immutable eternity, is not authoritative and does not possess speech like [a sentient being], so too is the Veda; thus, there is an absence of both authority and instruction.
*mati-vi-pra-tyapekṣitā juhoti*; see page 142,
line 1.
The conch was upon the plantain tree, the plantain tree was upon the drum, and upon that drum was a vast celestial palace;

thus, that palace of the conch, drum, and plantain tree became like the mad Gaṅgā, resembling incoherent chatter. This is because both critical examination (*pratyavekṣā*) and validity (*prāmāṇya*) are objects of knowledge. According to your own view, however, the Veda is not knowledge; therefore, its restriction to being a means of valid cognition is untenable, and it is non-instructive because it is insentient, like space.
Furthermore, as for the claim that the effect is non-existent within its causes— like a flower in the sky— such an absolute assertion is also entirely illogical;
for this so-called "non-existence" which you conceive of in some cases must be distinct from the effect, since [the effect] is perceived [as existing] in relation to [its causes].
Because [the two] lack an objective referent (*nirviṣayatva*),
there might also be a reading here such as *kuḍyādivat*.
See the Pratyakṣa section of the Vedānta-jñāna-nyāya, page 113, line 6.
According to your view, that which is known by you is neither knowledge nor the knower; it is not so,
for according to your view, that [object] is not knowledge, nor is it the knower,
because it is conditioned by the nature of ignorance.
Even that which begins with "prasahya" (by force), etc., [is not so] if one breathes while bowing, as stated in the Bhāṣya.

Having forcibly and by compulsion disregarded another person, you—who consider yourself a solitary hero—have attacked and insulted our doctrine. Furthermore, regarding the statement "one should offer the *agnihotra*," you assert that among the causal factors such as clarified butter (*ghṛta*) which constitute the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), the result such as heaven is non-existent like a sky-flower; and you maintain this even in the beginning, middle, and end of all such procedures. Moreover, you claim that this non-existence is absolute, such that there is not even a trace of existence for the effect and so forth, independent of any other position, and that it is simply "non-existent in every way. This too is utterly unreasonable.

Since this so-called "non-existence" (asattva) is conceived by you in some respect—[the word] "nāma" [meaning] it is merely a false conceptualization—that which you consider to be non-existent in some respect independently of existence, how then is that non-existence unjustified?
If you ask, "By what reasoning is it sublated? we reply: "Because it is sublated by reasoning.
If you ask, "What is that reasoning? then we say this: "The effect is other than that; the meaning is that it is other than the non-existent."

Why? Because it possesses an ineffective conceptualization (*tadasamarthavikalpatvāt*). An "ineffective conceptualization" is a conceptualization whose object is disconnected, ineffective, or incoherent; thus, an effect that possesses such an incoherent conceptualization relative to that which is non-existent is called "one with an ineffective conceptualization. Because that effect possesses an ineffective conceptualization, it is distinct from that [non-existent cause].

Like what? Like a jar and a cloth. Just as the conceptual constructs (vikalpa) of a jar—such as its broad base and upward-pointing neck—are unconnected with the conceptual constructs of a cloth—such as its softness and four-sided shape—and conversely, the conceptual constructs of a cloth are unconnected with those of the jar, so too are the jar and the cloth distinct from one another; in the same way, the effect is unconnected with unreal conceptual constructs, and therefore it is other than them. Thus [it is] understood. (Source: Vīramati-prakaraṇa).
The suffix *khaś* is applied after [the root] *mān* when preceded by *ātma*.
(Pāṇini 3.2.82)

The suffix *khaś* (which becomes *kāś*) is applied after the root *man*, when it occurs with a word ending in a case-suffix (*sup*) denoting its own object (*svakarmaka*), and the suffix *ṇini* may optionally also be applied.
One who considers himself a scholar is "one who fancies himself a scholar" (paṇḍitamanya);
[this is] not possible in any way according to the Siddhāntakaumudī.
See the commentary on that [passage], page 478;
by means of conceptual construction (vikalpataḥ), it is thus... [Ya].
The pot does not exist in the atoms because it is a conceptual construction lacking [real] capacity, like a pot and a cloth;
and the lack of capacity in conceptual constructions regarding non-existent effects is already established.

Regarding the four alternatives, there would be two possibilities: either that both the effect and the sky-flower are non-existent, or that only the effect is non-existent; for there can be no debate regarding the acceptance of their opposites—namely, the existence of both or the existence of the effect—since such a position is untenable.

Therefore, if it were first the case that both are non-existent, then because there is no distinction between them in their non-existence, just as the effect manifests, the sky-flower would also manifest in the future, being equally non-existent.

Now, if it is certain that the manifestation of a sky-flower is like the manifestation of an effect, and that the effect is non-existent, then the sky-flower is not non-existent because of its dissimilarity to that [effect]; for it is distinct from both the existent and the non-existent, like a jar—or rather, like the flower of the *udumbara* tree.
[Objection: But is not the non-existence of a jar distinct from the non-existence of a cloth? [Reply: No, because it is distinct from the existent.

It might be thought that the impossibility of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) regarding a non-existent effect is unestablished; that is not so, for it is indeed established. Understand that the incapacity of conceptual construction with respect to both the non-existent cause and the non-existent effect is already proven, because [of the four possible alternatives], only two are possible.

The non-existent is the sky-flower (*khapuṣpa*); the effect is the sprout and so forth. Regarding these two, there are four conceptual alternatives: 1) the sky-flower is non-existent and the effect is also non-existent; 2) the sky-flower is existent and the effect is non-existent; 3) the sky-flower is non-existent and the effect is existent; 4) the sky-flower is existent and the effect is also existent. Among these four alternatives, there would be—i.e., it is possible for—only these two alternatives: that both the effect and the sky-flower are non-existent, or that only the effect is non-existent.

What is the reason? It is because the acceptance of the counter-thesis (*pratipakṣa*) for both the existence of the cause and the existence of the effect is precisely this: the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) is the counter-thesis to the doctrine of the non-existence of the effect (*asatkāryavāda*). The word "iti" has the sense of a reason; for this reason, there is an absence of debate (*vādābhāva*). Therefore, due to the absence of debate, only the two alternatives of the non-existence of both [cause and effect] or the non-existence of the effect would be possible, and not the other two. Thus, [it is established that] only the existence [of the cause] is [true]. This is the end of the investigation. *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
Let it be seen (pṛ.
305–2): only the two [alternatives] consisting in the non-existence of the conceptual construction (*kalpa*) and the non-existence [of the effect] would be possible, and not the other.

And thus, between those two—the non-existence of both and the alternative of the non-existence of the effect—if first there were the non-existence of both, then, precisely because of the lack of distinction in their non-existence, there would be no distinction between a sky-flower and an effect. Since there is no distinction due to the lack of distinction in their non-existence, the manifestation of a sky-flower would also occur in the future, just like the manifestation of the effect; that is, in a future time, at another moment than this present moment, it would come into being.

The illustration is: like an effect that is non-existent [prior to its production], or like a sprout from a seed. And this manifestation of a sky-flower is neither observed nor accepted. Now, if you should attempt to avoid this fault of an undesirable consequence by retorting—due to the contradiction with what is observed and accepted—that "the manifestation of a sky-flower is not accepted as being like the manifestation of an effect, for it is certain that the effect is non-existent," [we reply:]...

If it is asked, "What is the fault in that? it is replied: Because of its difference from that [non-existent effect], the sky-flower is not non-existent; because of its difference from a non-existent effect, the sky-flower is not currently non-existent, but rather it follows that it is existent.

The difference of the sky-flower from a non-existent effect is its non-manifestation in the future. Therefore, because of its difference from a non-existent effect—namely, its non-manifestation in the future—the sky-flower is not non-existent; what then? It is existent. What is the reason? Because it is different from the non-existent, that is, because it is different from a non-existent effect.

The example is like a jar (*ghaṭavat*). Just as a jar is indeed existent because it is distinct from the non-existent, so too a donkey’s horn would follow as being existent because it is distinct from the effect that will manifest in the future; "the other" refers to the example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), namely the flower of the *udumbara* tree. [The argument is: that which is non-existent does not possess the characteristic of being distinct from the non-existent, just like the *udumbara* flower. This is for the purpose of establishing an undesirable consequence for the opponent—that the sky-flower (*khapuṣpa*) possesses the property of being distinct from the non-existent.
[Objection: But surely the non-existence of a jar is distinct from the non-existence of a cloth?

It might be thought: "Even if there is such a distinction between the jar and the sky-flower, the certainty of the non-existence of the sky-flower does not cease; and that [non-existence] consists in non-manifestation. If that is so, then an effect would not be non-existent because it consists in manifestation, like a jar that has been produced.
If it were non-existent, it would not manifest in the future, because of its non-existence, like a sky-flower.
The remainder is exactly as before, but by way of the reverse argument.

If it is argued that there is an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*) of the reason because we observe the existence of a difference from the non-existent—even while [the things themselves] exist—since the existence of a cloth as a cloth and the non-existence of a cloth as a pot are observed to have a mutual absence (*itaretarābhāva*) as their characteristic of non-existence and a mutual difference, and yet both that pot and that cloth are existent;
to this it is replied: No, there is no inconclusiveness of this reason because it is a difference from what is existent.

Because it is a difference from the existent, the difference belongs only to the existent; for that difference, which consists of mutual absence, belongs only to the existent, not to the non-existent.

Therefore, it does not have a distinction from the non-existent; what then? It also has a distinction from the existent, because even that [non-existence] is, in relation to something else, non-existent in its own form. However, this manifestation of the effect in the future is absolutely distinct from the non-existent sky-flower due to its non-manifestation, whereas the non-existence of the sky-flower is [distinct] from the effect. Thus, there is no distinction from the existent, because it is a specific attribute of the existent, just as there is no distinction from specific attributes such as color and so forth.
Or rather, because it is not distinct from the existent (*sato 'vailakṣaṇyāt*). Because it is not distinct from the existent.

However, for existent things such as a jar, there is no difference whatsoever from a cloth and so forth, because there is no distinction in their commonality of existence (*sattva*), since the mere distinctions of place, time, form, and so on do not constitute a true difference—just as there is no difference in space as qualified by a finger and so forth. (Note: *viśiṣṭa* is corrected from *viśeṣa*; *viruddha* is corrected from *viruddhāda*; *abhā* is corrected from *abhāḥ*; *itare* is corrected from *pra*.)

[The opponent argues: "Even if there is such a difference [between the two], the certainty that a sky-flower is non-existent does not cease; moreover, it (the effect) consists in non-manifestation. Therefore, because it consists in manifestation, the effect is not non-existent, like a finished jar."
A non-existent entity would not manifest in the future, because it is non-existent, like a flower in the sky;
the rest is exactly as before, [stated] by way of the opposite [inference], namely,
the absolute beginninglessness [of saṃsāra].
Because there is no absolute certainty without [the cause],
there is no absolute certainty without that; without that, there is no existence, [and thus] it is dissolved.
Tatsatam pāṃ, tadakṣam raṃ, hīṃ,
tatsattvam viṃ.
...extremely devoid of activity,
[yet] existent by virtue of its effect; thus, the existent is indeed the existent.
Either it possesses the specific quality of being a brick, or it does not possess the specific quality of ending with "brick"; otherwise, it would not be non-existent like a sky-flower.

For what reason? Because it is distinct from both the existent and the non-existent; that is, because it differs from both the existent (*sat*) and the non-existent (*asat*). Furthermore, the existent is of two kinds: that which is of a similar class, such as a jar for a jar, and that which is of a dissimilar class, such as a cloth and so forth.
The non-existent is the effect, such as a sprout and so forth, because it does not exist in the future.

Because of its absolute non-manifestation, the sky-flower (*khapuṣpa*) is distinct from the non-existent effect; and according to your own view, it is distinct from existent things such as jars and cloths—by way of mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*), whether they be of the same class or of a different class—just as there is mutual distinction among existing entities. The example is "like a jar": just as a jar is seen to be distinct from other jars of the same class and from cloths and so forth of a different class, both being existent, and yet it is also distinct from the non-existent sky-flower and the like; and since it is existent, it is not non-existent. The meaning is that it is indeed existent, on the principle that "a double negation leads back to the original state."

The other [example], like the *udumbara* flower: that which is non-existent is not distinct from both the existent and the non-existent, just as the *udumbara* flower [is]. However, according to your own view, this too is a dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*). Since there is no difference in the non-existence of the sky-flower, the donkey’s horn, the *udumbara* flower, and so forth, they are identical in their capacity to lead to an undesired conclusion; therefore, they fall within the scope of the probandum (*sādhya*). Consequently, there is no purpose in using a dissimilar instance.

In that case, let it be that [the effect] is distinct from the existent (*sad-vilakṣaṇa*) because it depends upon mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*). If it is asked, "How can a sky-flower be distinct from the non-existent (*asat-vilakṣaṇa*)?", [we reply: you yourself have already admitted its distinction from the non-existent effect that is to manifest in the future; since this effort is for the purpose of refuting your own position, there is no fault on our part. (Note:
Although the reading *asaccara kāryaṃ pra° atulyajātīyena* does not appear in any manuscripts, it appears necessary.)
And from those virtuous ones who have seen the example... [the teaching] was spoken.
(Variant readings: *dṛṣṭāntobhāvi* [Bhā], *dṛṣṭānto pā* [Pā], *ḍe*, *līṃ*, *raṃ*, *hī*;
*sadbhyoya* [Ya]).
The meaning is: "only by means of non-existence" (annasatya);
that which is non-existent is distinct from the existent; it perishes.
In this context, there may also be the reading "because of being included within the probandum" (*sādhyāntar-pātitvāt*).
[The phrase] "for the purpose of investigating that" (*tad-vicāraṇārtham*) is in the Bhāṣya.
Now, even so, etc. (*athaivam apīty-ādi*).

Now, even though there is a difference between the effect and a sky-flower regarding their manifestation and non-manifestation, this certainty that "the sky-flower is non-existent" does not cease—even when one attempts to turn it back by the logic that "it must be existent because it differs from the non-existent, like a jar. Furthermore, the fact that the sky-flower consists of non-manifestation is precisely what constitutes the difference [between it and the effect]. [The prefixes] *prāduḥ* and *āviḥ* signify visibility and birth; therefore, the effect is existent because its nature is manifestation, like a finished jar; whereas, by way of contrast, it is like a jar in space [which is non-existent].
The sky-flower (*khapuṣpa*) is non-existent because it lacks the nature of manifestation, like a pot in the sky; by contrast, [it is like] a finished pot.

Or, if they were equal in their non-existence, a distinction must be stated; for if there were no distinction, a difference in character would be untenable, just as between a pot and the pot’s own self. [An entity] manifests, becomes visible, is apprehended, is known, arises, or is born—thus it "manifests. And so, since the sky-flower lacks the nature of manifestation, its non-existence follows as a matter of course: therefore, an effect is not non-existent because it possesses the nature of manifestation; rather, it is existent. This is the meaning.

What is the illustration? It is like a finished jar (*nirvṛttaghaṭavat*). Just as a finished jar is indeed existent because its nature is manifestation and its nature is luminosity, so too the effect is existent. And because this *arthāpatti* (presumption) is conclusive, it does not constitute a futile rejoinder (*jātyuttara*). For example, when Devadatta is absent from the house, the inference of his presence outside by one who knows he exists is established through presumption; because it is conclusive, it is not a fallacious argument.

Our intention here, however, is this: that which exists is sometimes perceived or produced, but never that which is absolutely non-existent; and perception and non-perception apply to what exists, not to what is absolutely non-existent. We shall demonstrate this later, as it is the fruit of this very inquiry.

Now, even if you do not accept the existence of the effect in this way, then if the effect were non-existent, it would not manifest in the future because of its non-existence, like a sky-flower. Yet it does manifest; therefore, it exists.
The remainder is as before, and he extends [the argument] by way of the opposite through the preceding text.
"By way of reversal" means that, both in terms of meaning and in terms of words, this [argument] should be applied by reversing those two.

For example: "Now, if it is certain that the non-manifestation of an effect is not like the non-manifestation of a sky-flower, and that the effect is non-existent, then the effect is not non-existent; rather, it is existent, because it is distinct from the non-existent, like a jar. Otherwise, it would be like the flower of the *udumbara* tree.
[Objection: "But surely the non-existence of a jar is distinct from the non-existence of a cloth. [Reply: No, because it is distinct from the existent.

Now, even given such a difference in characteristics, if the certainty that the effect is non-existent does not cease, and yet that [effect] consists of manifestation, then the effect cannot be non-existent because it consists of manifestation, like a finished jar. If it were non-existent, it would not manifest in the future due to its non-existence, like a sky-flower. Therefore, the effect is existent because it consists of manifestation, like a finished jar. By way of contrast (vaidharmya), it is like a jar in space; and the sky-flower is non-existent because it does not consist of manifestation, like a jar in the sky; by way of contrast, it is like a finished jar.

Or, if their non-existence is equal, a distinction must be stated; for if there is no distinction, a difference [between them] is untenable, as in the case of a jar and the self-luminosity of the jar itself. Thus it is said.
Even so,
O Supreme Goddess, within those very [beings],
there is the splendor of one's own innate flower.
Because it is understood that the nature of things is dependent origination,
there is no cognition whose object is absolutely non-existent.

For the purpose of summarizing this, he says: "Therefore, the effect exists, because it consists of manifestation, like a finished jar; by way of contrast, like a 'space-jar' (ākāśaghaṭa)—that is, either space itself or a jar within space—which does not exist because it does not consist of manifestation, whereas the effect does not lack manifestation; therefore, it exists."

Non-existence is like a sky-flower because it lacks the nature of manifestation, just like a pot in the sky; by contrast, it is like a finished pot—this demonstrates the distinction between those two, the existent and the non-existent, namely the effect and the sky-flower.
[Variant readings: *°tvāttvaghaṭavat* (Bhāṣya);
*°tvāt ghaṭavat* (Yaśomitra)].

If, according to your view, the non-existence of the effect and a sky-flower is indeed equal, then a distinction must be stated regarding that equality—namely, that for this specific reason, although both are equally non-existent, the effect manifests while the sky-flower does not. If such a specific reason is not stated, there would be no distinction between the two; and if there is no distinction, a difference in nature is untenable, just as there is none between a sky-flower and a donkey’s horn, both being non-existent. Yet, a difference is observed through their manifestation or non-manifestation in the future; however, that difference is not possible if there is no distinction between the two.

Therefore, because there would be no distinction [between them] due to the lack of difference in their cause, there could be no disparity between them, just as in the case of a jar and the jar’s own self; for just as the jar itself is the jar’s own self, there would be no disparity between the two precisely because they are non-distinct. However, this is not the case, since manifestation and non-manifestation are both observed and have been explained.
Therefore, existence and non-existence must necessarily be accepted for those two respectively.
The other [opponent] says: "There is indeed no non-distinction even for that which is non-existent... [The suffix] *vat*...
Even when a specific distinction is inferred, because that distinction must always have a real substratum, its existence is like that of a jar; thus, it is indeed a generality (*sāmānya*).

Now, if this similarity [between the two] were to result from the non-existence of both, let it not be so; rather, let there be the non-existence of one or the other. By rejecting the acceptance of the existence of the effect, one might claim that the effect alone is non-existent. In this context, the particle *eva* (only) is placed immediately after "effect" (*kārya*), establishing a restriction regarding the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) elsewhere: non-existence resides in the effect *alone* and not elsewhere.
Consequently, a sky-flower is not non-existent [in the same sense as the effect].

And thus it is for one who holds [the view]: "Because non-existence is admitted to be fourfold—namely, prior, posterior, mutual, and absolute—with respect to a jar, just as in the case of a lump of clay, potsherds, cloth, or a donkey’s horn.
To this it is replied: Even when a specific distinction is being inferred, existence must belong to that which is the substratum of the distinction, just as it does to the jar.

The word "api" (even/also) indicates non-acceptance [of your position]: according to your own view, there is no mutual distinction between non-existents—such as a donkey’s horn or the son of a barren woman—because they are all non-entities; however, according to our view, even some forms of non-existence possess substantiality because they share properties such as being objects of knowledge (*prameyatva*), possessing general and particular characteristics, and so forth, for reasons accepted by you as well as by us, just like positive entities (*bhāva*). Therefore, according to your own view, there is ultimately no distinction between non-existence and existence.

Even granting your position, we say this: even if one were to establish a distinction by some means or other, that fourfold non-existence (abhāva) imagined by you must have existence as its substrate because it is a "distinction" (*viśeṣa*), just like color-form (*rūpa*) or a jar (*ghaṭa*).

Consequently, since a distinction has existence as its substrate, it possesses existence, just like a jar; for just as a jar exists by depending on an existent object such as earth, or exists by depending on its own self, so too does this distinction exist because it has existence as its substrate.

The word *iti* is used here for the purpose of stating the reason, the example, the application to the subject, and the conclusion: namely, that there is only a commonality between existence and non-existence, and not a distinction.
Thus, first of all, the equality has been established according to your own view—that both the effect and the sky-flower are equally non-existent.
In this context, there may also be the reading "bhavanmate" (in your view); [the text] reads "kāryatve" (if it were an effect) in the Prajñāpāramitā, but that [reading] is in the Bhāṣya.
When that [power] manifests,
it is like the manifestation of light and so forth.
Even when a specific distinction is inferred, because that distinction must always have a substratum, its existence is like that of a jar; thus, it is indeed a generality (*sāmānya*).

Now, if one were to say, "Let there not be this parity [between cause and effect] due to the non-existence of both," and instead assert the non-existence of one of the two—thereby abandoning the acceptance of the existence of the effect and claiming that the effect alone is non-existent—here the particle *eva* (only) is placed in proximity to "effect. This establishes a restriction regarding the counter-correlate elsewhere: namely, that non-existence belongs to the effect *alone* and not to anything else.
Consequently, a sky-flower is not non-existent.
And likewise, for that which exists, let its perceptibility [be considered], as stated previously at page 167, line 26: "prior, posterior, other, and absolute... [etc. from the *Praśastapādabhāṣya*.
Its particularity [is not established] because it is a non-entity;
due to the absence of existence,
there is an absence of a substratum.
This very second alternative, "svasvī," is now examined—beginning with the words "Now, this equality... and so forth.

Now, for one who does not accept this [proposed] generality, because he rejects the existence of the effect and accepts the non-existence of both, this non-existence of either one follows; namely, that which is distinct from the opposing view and characterized by either of the two previously mentioned [alternatives]. What is that? It is the claim that "the effect alone is non-existent. Since one must necessarily accept one of the two, a restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) results. And that restriction is established because it has been defined in the treatises and observed in common usage that "the restriction applies to what is other than where the particle *eva* occurs," and because the sentence has the result of restriction. This is appropriate because the particle *eva* is placed immediately next to the word "effect"—thus, "the effect alone is non-existent"—due to the placement of *eva* immediately after the word "effect. Furthermore, the word "iti" has the sense of a reason (*hetu*). There is a restriction regarding the non-existence of the opposite counterpart; however, there is no restriction regarding the meaning expressed by the word "non-existent," such as a sky-flower and so forth, because the particle *eva* is absent there, and not in the sense of the word "effect."

Just as in the case of "the tree is a mango," the mango is necessarily a tree, whereas a tree may or may not be a mango—there being no such restriction—so too here, it is only the effect (*kārya*) that is non-existent (*asat*), not things like a sky-flower which are non-effects (*akārya*). Why so? Because they are existent (*sat*). It is not restricted that only the effect is non-existent; if even the effect were existent, what harm would there be? He shows this: non-existence belongs to the effect alone and not elsewhere, namely, not to non-effects such as a sky-flower.
The word *iti* has the sense of a reason (*hetvartha*); the meaning is: "for this reason of such a restriction."

If it is asked, "What is the fault in this being so?", it is replied: Consequently, it would follow that a sky-flower is not non-existent; the meaning is that the existence of a sky-flower would be established, which contradicts both perception and accepted doctrine. To designate a non-existent thing as "existent" is like [calling] the non-existence of an effect identical to the non-existence of a donkey’s horn and other such things; there would be a discrepancy merely in name. Furthermore, by abandoning the absolute negation of the existence of the effect, one falls into contradiction with one's own words and so forth. If, however, the particle *eva* is attached to "non-existent" (*asat*), then since the non-existence is not definitively established, the same fault as before remains.

Now, it might be argued: "Because they are both non-existent, there is no distinction between them at the time of the cause; that which is thus perceived [is merely a difference in name]," and so on, up to "there is only a disagreement regarding names.
And having established this, one would apply the designation "existent" to an effect that is non-existent like a donkey’s horn, and the designation "non-existent" to that which is existent.

"Non-existence of the effect" means that it is equal to the non-existence of things such as jars which have arisen as the opposites of a donkey’s horn; the non-existence of the effect is merely a name for something that is actually existent, being the opposite of [absolute] non-existence, like the name "Agni" (Fire) given to Maṅgala (Mars). There is no contradiction regarding the existence of the object here in saying "the effect is non-existent.
Furthermore, by abandoning the absolute negation of the existence of the effect, there arises a contradiction with one's own words and so forth.

The cessation of the existence of the effect is the non-existence of the effect; the ascertainment of that is the "one-sided view" (ekānta). The abandonment of the one-sided view that "the effect is indeed non-existent"—which was obtained through the method just described—is [the point at issue]. Furthermore, from the abandonment of this one-sided view regarding the cessation of the existence of the effect, there arises the consequence of contradiction with one's own words and so forth.

First, regarding the contradiction with one's own words: having stated that "that very effect is non-existent," by the force of the word "only" (eva), one brings about its existence; thus, for one who says "that very thing is existent, that very thing is non-existent," there is a contradiction.

Alternatively, if it is an effect, how can it be non-existent? Or if it is non-existent, how can it be an effect? For you will state that "the pot is produced" means it is manifested as a pot by the action, like [an object] by a lamp;
thus, there is a contradiction with your own tenets due to such an admission, and a contradiction with the world because it is so well-known in common experience.
There is a contradiction with inference because such a state of affairs does not exist in reality;
likewise, there is a contradiction with perception because we observe the cause-and-effect relationship between a lump of clay and a jar, and so forth.
Thus, the restriction that "only the effect is non-existent, but not things like a sky-flower" is flawed.
Now, let that very equality be seen: page 167, line 26; 306–2;
*icchata* (emended from *pra*).

Regarding the phrase *satvabhyupa*bhā* (in the manuscript *bhā*), here, when there is the intention to express the positive concomitance (*anvaya*)—namely, "this [consequence] has been brought about for one who does not accept a universal, because he accepts the non-existence of both by way of rejecting the existence of the effect"—the reading in manuscript *Ya*, *ubhayāsattvābhyupagamāt*, is indeed correct. However, when the intention is to express the positive concomitance as "this non-existence of either one follows from rejecting the existence of the effect, because of the acceptance of the non-existence of both," then the reading *ubhayāsattvānabhyupagamāt* must be supplied here; and it should be understood that this alone is the pure [correct] reading.
In the phrase "the remaining tree," the effect, which is the earth and water, exists as that very reality even before its manifestation.

The designation "existent" is applied even to that which is non-existent; the non-existence of the effect is equal to the non-existence of things such as a pot, which is the opposite of a donkey's horn. There is a discrepancy merely in name, and by abandoning the absolute negation of the existence of the effect, there arises a contradiction with one's own words and so forth. However, if the particle "eva" (only) is used [in the phrase "the effect is non-existent only"], then because the non-existence is not definitively established, the same fault as before remains.
Now, it might be argued: "Precisely because they are non-existent, there is no distinction whatsoever between those two at the time of their cause;
let that which is seen for the sake of conjunction be observed" (see page 509).
And this is the first existence of the causal condition.
First,
let it be observed that even without the agent (*kartṛ*), there is indeed action (*kriyā*) alone;
see page 124–1.
The meaning is that there is a fault resulting from the restrictive particle *eva*; cf. p. 166, l. 9.

If one were to maintain the restriction that "only the effect is non-existent, not the cause," this would entail the position of an opposing doctrine; therefore, it is restricted in this way: "the effect is indeed non-existent."

In that case as well, according to the principle that "the restriction applies to what is other than that from which the particle *eva* [is used]," the effect is restricted by the particle *eva* placed near the word "non-existent" (asat) to being non-existent; thus, the effect is necessarily non-existent. However, whether the effect is non-existent or something like a sky-flower, since the non-existence of the effect has not been specifically determined by the particle *eva*, the same fault remains as previously stated—namely, that because non-existence is indistinguishable, there would be no distinction between the effect and a sky-flower based on their manifestation or non-manifestation in the future. Thus, the fault of the loss of distinction (*aviśeṣāpatti*) mentioned before applies here as well.
[The text fragment reads: *kāryanayamāsadatbhā° kāryanayamāsat ya*.
See page 161, line 4.
Now, it might be argued, etc.

In order to avoid the fault of the consequence of non-distinction (*aviśeṣāpatti*), you might say [the following], thus anticipating the opponent’s view: "How so? Precisely because of their non-existence, no distinction between those two—the effect and the sky-flower—is possible at the time of the cause. Just as the sky-flower is non-existent, so too the effect is non-existent at the time of the cause; thus there is no distinction whatsoever between these two. For a non-existent, indefinable sky-flower does not possess specific features such as a stalk, fruit, or filaments, nor fragrance and the like, which would have characteristics distinct from the bluntness or sharpness of a donkey’s horn; this is because both are non-entities and indefinable. Therefore, the non-existence of the effect is itself the non-existence of the sky-flower. Consequently, there is neither the fault resulting from the restriction [of the term 'non-existent' to the effect alone] nor the previous fault of the consequence of equality, since equality pertains to multiple objects."
Even so, because of their identity, there would be an absence of distinction;

for just as a sky-flower is without material cause, not established by cognition, and devoid of both universal and particular, likewise the effect would lack a material cause, establishment by cognition, and possession of universals and particulars.

Now, if it is maintained that the existence or non-existence of the effect and the sky-flower is established by the presence or absence of the cognition that apprehends them as possessing universals and particulars—such that even though it does not exist like a sky-flower, it is nonetheless non-existent, and likewise, even when it has been produced, it is non-existent because it possesses universals and particulars, and because there is no difference from the cause; and if it is argued that the non-existence of the effect at the time of the cause is identical to the non-existence of the sky-flower, and therefore nothing has been avoided—if this is asked, [we reply]: the fault is not caused by the restriction (avadhāraṇa); thus the fault of restriction is avoided.

If it is determined that "the effect alone is non-existent" or "the effect is indeed non-existent," then two faults arise: the existence of a sky-flower and the lack of distinction between the effect and a sky-flower; these two do not apply because we admit there is no distinction between them.

Furthermore, the first fault—the consequence of equality—is also absent, for there is no lack of distinction: the effect’s non-manifestation in the future is its non-existence, whereas a sky-flower’s non-manifestation is likewise its non-existence.

There is also an absence of the fault of the consequence of [the object] being identical, because there is no distinction in what is non-existent, and because identity has multiple objects; for identity is observed to have multiple objects, as in "this is equal to that," "these two are equal to these," or "these are equal to those. Indeed, it is not seen that something is identical to itself—see page 163, line 7 and page 168, line 5.
Here it is said, etc., [referring to] *saviśeṣā*... *ya*.
Regarding this, it is said: "With qualifications," as seen on page 306; and [it is] said here:
"by you," as in the Bhāṣya.

If it is argued that "the ultimate reality (paramārtha) is what is meant by you," then the non-existence of the effect is itself the non-existence of the sky-flower; thus, there is no fault arising from the restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇa*), nor is there the aforementioned fault of falling into parity, because parity applies to multiple objects.

Even so, because of their identity, there would be no distinction; for just as a sky-flower is without material cause (*anupādāna*), not established by cognition (*abuddhisiddha*), and devoid of both universals (*sāmānya*) and particulars (*viśeṣa*), so too the effect would lack a material cause, would not be established by cognition, and would be devoid of universals and particulars. If, however, you maintain that the existence or non-existence of the universal, the particular, the material cause, and establishment by cognition belong respectively to the effect and the sky-flower—such that, like the sky-flower, it [the effect] is non-existent even while coming into being, and likewise non-existent even when produced because it possesses universals and particulars—then [the cause] must also be non-existent.
See page 162, line 2;
see page 161, line 5;
[the word] *tulyasya* in the manuscript.

Regarding the point raised [in the *Pādābuddhi*]: "Even so, because of their oneness, there is no distinction," you yourself have admitted that there is no distinction between an effect and a sky-flower in terms of their non-existence, since both are non-entities (avastu) of a single nature; thus, the fault of non-distinction remains exactly as it was.
Now, in order to demonstrate that very same fault of non-distinction, another undesirable consequence is formulated: "For just as... and so forth.

Just as the material cause (*upādāna*) of a sky-flower—which is established in the intellect through what was previously seen, heard, or experienced—is not possessed of specific forms such as "A" and so forth, and thus the sky-flower itself lacks a material cause and is not established in the intellect; what follows from this? Because it lacks a material cause and is not established in the intellect, it is proven to be devoid of both generality (*sāmānya*) and particularity (*viśeṣa*). In the same way, the material cause of an effect such as a jar—clay and the like—would not possess establishment in the intellect, nor would it possess generality and particularity. Yet, that very clay, by the manner in which it comes into being, is a generality because it remains the same despite the differences in the jar (such as place, time, newness, oldness, blackness, redness, etc.), and it is a particularity in relation to cloth and other things.

And that [effect] would possess both the status of being established by the cognition of its material cause and the possession of general and particular properties, because both [the effect and the sky-flower] are equally indefinable;
however, this is not accepted.
Therefore, since there is a distinction between these two, the effect exists [prior to its production].
In the phrase "pādābuddhi," there is a variant reading "viśeṣatvaṃ ca pra-"; furthermore, the reading "tenākāreṇa" might also occur here.

O Vatsa, here [the argument is]: "And that would entail the existence of a material cause for a sky-flower (*khapuṣpa*), as well as its being established by cognition and its possessing general and particular properties"—this might also be the reading.

Now, if you maintain that the presence or absence of the material cause, general and particular properties, and establishment by cognition are the specific distinctions between an effect and a sky-flower, then even though it does not come into being like a sky-flower, that [effect] is nonetheless non-existent.

The phrase "like a sky-flower" means that just as a sky-flower does not exist and does not arise, so too this effect—though it exists in one way and arises in another, and though it is sometimes seen arising—is nonetheless held to be non-existent (*asat*) by virtue of its mode of being established through the cognition of its material cause (*upādāna*), and its possession of universals and particulars. And this being the case, there is this further fault: even when it has come into being, the effect remains non-existent, despite the presence of its establishment through the cognition of its material cause.

Why? Because it possesses both universals (*sāmānya*) and particulars (*viśeṣa*), like the effect at the time of its cause. Just as, according to your own view, the effect at the time of its cause is non-existent yet possesses universals and particulars, has a material cause (*upādāna*), and is established by cognition (*buddhisiddha*); likewise, the sky-flower—though not existing like the effect at a subsequent time and though not being an effect—would not be non-existent because it lacks both universals and particulars, [whereas the effect] does possess them. Or, because it differs from the non-existence of the effect, it would be like the cause.

Alternatively, if you argue that the sky-flower does not possess a material cause and so forth like the effect's material cause, etc., and that the effect is determined to be non-existent, then the same two-fold circular reasoning (*cakraka*) as before would ensue.

The distinction created by the qualification of possessing the beginning of appropriation (*upādāna*) and so forth would mean that even when it has ceased, that [entity] would be non-existent, just like the time of its cause; and conversely, like the effect, even though it has not come into being, the sky-flower would not be non-existent. For even if it has not come into being in the manner of the manifestation of an effect, it would nonetheless attain existence in that specific mode of non-existence, because the sky-flower lacks both generality (*sāmānya*) and particularity (*viśeṣa*). Indeed, it is established that this sky-flower is without generality and without particularity; therefore, due to its lack of generality and particularity, it would possess existence.

What is the example? "Like a universal-particular (sāmānya-viśeṣa) that possesses an effect"—this is stated by resorting to the Vaiśeṣika doctrine. By means of this example of a universal-particular, it is shown through irony (*kāku*) that for those who maintain that universals and particulars are devoid of both universals and particulars, their status as real entities (*vastutva*) is equivalent to a sky-flower. As for the application (*upanaya*) to the subject at hand: just as a universal-particular such as "pot-ness" is established as being real while being devoid of further universals and devoid of particulars, so too would a sky-flower be real.
Furthermore, because it differs from the non-existence of the effect, the sky-flower would not be non-existent, just like the cause; this is understood [from the context].

Since the sky-flower differs from the non-existence of effects such as jars—in terms of its lack of manifestation, lack of material cause (*upādāna*), lack of being established by cognition (*buddhisiddhatva*), and lack of common or specific characteristics—the sky-flower too would be existent, just like the cause.
By these various modes, the difference from the non-existence of the effect is indeed established, and thus the logical reason (*hetu*) is proven.
Since the cause is established as distinct [from the effect] by way of its being produced and so forth, the similarity between the cause and a sky-flower [is undermined];

for either the cause would be non-existent like a sky-flower due to the distinction of the non-existence of the effect, or the non-existence of the effect must be abandoned. This is the intended meaning.
[The existence of] production and existence [belong] to the effect...

Just as [the non-existent] is like the effect of time and like an effect, even though the sky-flower is non-existent, it would not be non-existent because it possesses a universal and particularity, being like other things that possess universals and particulars; or else, because it differs from the non-existence of an effect, it should be seen as being like a cause (see page 168, line 5).

Now, if it is certain that even a sky-flower possesses material cause (*upādāna*) and so forth— just as an effect does— and yet the effect is non-existent, then the same two-fold circle of reasoning (*cakraka*) proceeds as before;
the only distinction being the qualification "possessing a material cause and so forth," which applies to the generality of the objective support (*ālambana-sāmānya*).
[The opponent says: "Now, [it is] not like having a cause, material cause, and so forth... etc.

Now, for fear of the fault of the consequence that a sky-flower would possess existence (*sattva*), you do not accept even the presentation of logical reasons—just as [you do not accept] having a cause, material cause, and so forth—for the sky-flower; by the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), you do not accept its possessing a universal or particular established by cognition (*buddhisiddha-sāmānya-viśeṣavattva*). You thus accept this lack of commonality (*asādharmya*) between the effect and the sky-flower, and it is certain that the effect is non-existent (*asat*). By saying "and so forth," he refers back to the same text concerning the operation of the two circles of reasoning (*cakraka*) as before.

How, then, is it cultivated? If, like the possession of material causes and so forth by an effect, the possession of material causes and so forth by a sky-flower is not admitted, and it is certain that the effect is non-existent, then—due to its dissimilarity to that [effect], namely due to its dissimilarity to having no material cause and so forth—the sky-flower is not non-existent; for it is distinct from both the existent and the non-existent, like a jar.
[Objection: But is not the non-existence of a jar distinct from the non-existence of a cloth? [Reply: No, because it is distinct from the existent.

Now, even given such a difference in characteristics, the certainty regarding the non-existence of a sky-flower does not cease, because it lacks a material cause (*upādāna*) and so forth. If that is so, then an effect is not non-existent simply because it possesses a material cause; for if it were non-existent, it could not possess a material cause, like a sky-flower. This is a circle of contrapositives (*viparyaya-cakraka*). The remainder is exactly as before, but in reverse order: therefore, the effect exists because it possesses a material cause, like a finished jar; by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), it is like a jar in space, and so forth, up to "because it has existence as its locus, it exists, like a jar. This is precisely that same circle of contrapositives. Thus, [the argument] regarding the non-existence of both [cause and effect]...

But if one were to say that this parity [of the argument] should not occur because both are non-existent, and thus one asserts the non-existence of the other while avoiding the admission of the existence of the effect—claiming that "the effect itself is non-existent"—then regarding this point, from the phrase "in proximity to the effect" up to "contradiction with one's own words," the effect must be existent, just like its cause.

Now, [an objection may be raised]: even if it exists, does it not follow that it should be perceptible, just like the cause? No; because it is unmanifest, like an elephant in a pit before it has been dug out, or like the scent of the earth before the digging begins.

And for this very reason, there arises an investigation into the context: Is the effect, such as a jar, existent or non-existent? Since non-perceptibility is observed both in the case of the existent and the non-existent, it is inconclusive; furthermore, if the particle *eva* (only) is applied to "non-existent," then because the non-existence remains undetermined, the aforementioned fault recurs.

Now, regarding the passage beginning with "athocyate" and ending with "or, because of its distinction from the non-existence of the effect, like the cause," that very same text [states] that the distinction is produced by the qualification of having material causes (*upādāna*) and so forth. Therefore, the effect is existent because it possesses material causes and so forth, like the nature of the cause itself; by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), like space or a jar. Furthermore, the non-existent is like a sky-flower because it lacks material causes, like a jar in the sky; whereas the other [the existent] is like a finished jar.
Likewise, the effect exists [prior to its production] because it is established by cognition, like a finished jar; the other [non-existent thing] is like a jar in the sky.
And the non-existent is like a sky-flower because it is not established by cognition, like a jar in the sky; the other [existent thing] is exactly like a finished jar.
This should be applied in the same way to both the general and the particular.
Therefore, the meaning is that the effect exists like its cause, but not like a sky-flower;
[this is] the proof of the existence of the effect.
Therefore, that which is non-existent is seen as an effect;
[see page 161, line 7];
"my effect is non-existent" (Bhāṣya).
The intention is that this [passage] beginning with "etadapi paryāya-pra... is also a textual source; see page 164, line 1.
See page 164, line 2:
"Therefore, the effect exists, like its cause.

[Objection: But if it exists, does it not follow that it must be perceptible, just like the cause? [Reply: No, because of its unmanifest state (*avyaktatva*), like an elephant in a pit before it has been dug out, or like the scent of the earth before the digging.

And for this very reason, there arises an inquiry into the subject matter: Is an effect such as a jar existent or non-existent? Since non-perceptibility is observed both when something exists and when it does not, the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). [See page 165, line 3].
Then it is said, etc. (Yaśomitra).
In this context, the reading should be "athocyeta" and so forth; see page 165, line 4,
and see page 167, line 2.

Because of this [reason], the proponent of the jar (ghaṭavādin) says: "But surely, even if it exists, the consequence follows that it would be perceptible, just like its cause; the effect called 'jar,' as conceived by you, would be perceptible in the state of the lump of clay, because of its existence, just like the cause—that is, like the lump of clay."

To this it is replied: No; this fault does not apply because of its unmanifest state. Why? Because of its unmanifest state. For in that stage of being a lump of clay, the jar is not perceived by the senses due to its lack of manifestation, just as an elephant previously buried in a trench is not seen before it is dug up. Indeed, those very same clay particles existing within the wall [of the lump] even prior to the digging acquire the designation "elephant" after the digging has taken place; yet, they do not cease to exist simply because they were unperceived prior to their manifestation.

Alternatively, even when an effect exists, it may be imperceptible due to its unmanifest state, like the scent of the earth. Just as the scent of the earth, though present, does not come within the range of the sense of smell because it is unmanifest, yet is perceived later once it has been manifested by being sprinkled with water; so too, a jar, though imperceptible in its state as clay, is perceived later once it has been manifested by the causes of the potter’s effort, the staff, the wheel, the string, and so forth. Therefore, what fault is there in its becoming perceptible? For this very reason, the "investigation of the context" (*prakaraṇacintā*) constitutes the fallacy of the "neutralized" (*prakaraṇasama*), because of its inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*); thus, the inconclusiveness of this reason has been stated.
That very point for which an investigation has been undertaken, when it is adduced for the purpose of reaching a conclusion, is the "neutralized" (prakaraṇasama) [pseudo-reason], Nyāya Sūtra 1.2.6.

7. For here, precisely because the effect such as a jar (*ghaṭa*) is imperceptible, the following inquiry arises: "Is the effect such as a jar existent or non-existent? Since two of the four logical alternatives result in the fallacy of opposing positions, they must be abandoned; thus, there would have to be either the existence of both or the existence of one.

If, first of all, there were the existence of both, then due to the lack of distinction in their existence, there would be no distinction between universality and particularity; and just as there is oneness of the effect, there would likewise be oneness of the cause.

Now, if it is not certain that the cause is one just as the effect is one—given that the effect is existent (*sat*)—then, because of its dissimilarity to that [existence], the cause is not existent; it is non-existent (*asat*), because it is dissimilar to existence, like the flower of the *udumbara* tree, whereas the other [the existent] is like a finished jar.

In this regard, among the four alternatives—(1) the cause being existent and the effect being existent; (2) the cause being existent and the effect being non-existent; (3) the cause being non-existent and the effect being existent; and (4) the cause being non-existent and the effect being non-existent—one must abandon two of them because they result in the opponent's position as before. Likewise, there are conformity (*anuvṛtti*) and exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*). Conformity is the notion "clay, clay" with respect to the lump, the small ball, and so forth; exclusion is the notion "pot," "jar," and so on. Through such investigation, the two-fold circle [of reasoning] proceeds as before. However, it is not merely a summary [of the previous argument], because it is unestablished (*asiddhatvāt*). For if the pot were different from the lump of clay, then just like that [pot], the lump and the rest would also lack the nature of being the whole (*asarvatvam*).

Therefore, if both [cause and effect] possess existence (*sattva*), then because there is no distinction in their existence, just as there is no exclusion of the effect, there would likewise be no exclusion of the cause; for by virtue of its existence, the cause would be like a jar.

Now, if it is certain that the effect is existent and yet there is no exclusion of the cause—just as there is an exclusion of the effect—then the cause is not "existent," but rather "non-existent" (*asat*), because it is distinct from existence, like the flower of the *udumbara* tree; whereas the other [the effect] is like a finished jar.
But surely the existence of a jar is distinct from the existence of a cloth? No, because it is distinct from non-existence.

Now, even if there is such a difference in nature (*vailakṣaṇya*), if the determination of the existence of the cause does not cease, and that [cause] is of the nature of persistence (*anuvṛttyātmaka*), then the effect cannot be existent by virtue of being of the nature of exclusion (*vyāvṛttyātmakatva*). If it were existent, it would not exclude [the cause], because of its existence, just like the cause. This is the second circle [of reasoning]. The remainder follows the previous pattern, but with the reverse order. Now, if the persistence of the effect is not like the persistence of the cause, yet the cause is determined to be existent, then the effect is not existent due to its difference from that [cause]; it is non-existent (*asat*), because it is different in nature from the existent, like the flower of the *udumbara* tree, whereas the other [the cause] is like a jar.

[Objection: "But surely the existence of a jar is distinct from the existence of a cloth. [Reply: No, because it is distinct from non-existence (*asat*). First, there is a circularity (*cakraka*) consisting of a reversal:

even if there is such a distinction, the ascertainment of its existence does not cease, and that existence is of the nature of persistence (*anuvṛtti*). If that is so, then the effect is not existent by virtue of being of the nature of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), for if it were existent, it would not be excluded from existence, just like the cause. This is the second circularity, by way of reversal: therefore, the effect is other than the persisting existent cause, because it is excluded, just as one [person] is other than a row [of people].

Furthermore, the cause is distinct from the effect which possesses discrete existence because it is continuous; however, this is not a valid conclusion, because— as in the previous analysis of the two circles— the application of the same reasoning leads to a circular argument, and [the reason] is unestablished (*asiddha*).

For if the jar were other than the lump of clay, then, just like that [lump], it would follow that the lump and so forth are not all-encompassing (*asarvatva*), and its existence would be impossible. Otherwise, its existence would be non-existent.
The other [wheel] is described as having the form of a wheel with spokes. Thus it is said.

This is not tenable; your proof for your own position is no more valid than our proof for ours. Why? Because the reasons such as "non-universality" (*asarvatva*) and so forth are unestablished (*asiddha*). Since, for us, everything is indeed the universal (*anuvṛtti*), the cause, the material substrate (*upādāna*), and established by cognition (*buddhisiddha*), because it is distinct from all else—therefore, since everything is non-universal, there is an absence of the fourfold destruction of universality and unity, and likewise, for that very reason, there is no absence of the universal and so forth.

Furthermore, if an effect were non-existent, how could it be subject to contradictions with one's own statements and so forth? Conversely, if it is non-existent, how can it be an effect? For it is clay itself that is made into a jar; it is merely manifested as a jar through action, just as [an object] is revealed by a lamp.
And thus, there is likewise no lack of proof regarding the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified.

Thus, because [the reasons] such as "not being everything" are unestablished (*asiddha*), and because there is an absence of their conceptual alternatives (*vikalpa*), the proof of that [reason] being an ineffective alternative is not established;
for that reason, the claim that "the effect is other than the cause" is not proven.

Once non-universality has been established as unproven there, the non-establishment of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) and so forth will necessarily follow as well; therefore, in order to demonstrate the very absence of non-universality, he says: "For if a jar, which is intended to be a non-universal effect, is held to be other than the lump of clay which is intended to exist, then—just like that [lump], and just like the jar, and just like any effect—the non-universality of the lump and so forth would also apply even to what is remote, let alone to what is proximate, such as the *śivaka* stage, because of being other than everything, just like the jar."

Therefore, just as each individual thing lacks "allness" (*asarvatva*), because everything [taken individually] lacks allness, there is an absence of the fourfold collapse of "allness" and "oneness. For this very reason, the state of being an ineffective conceptual construction (*asamartha-vikalpatva*) does not exist; likewise, the absence of persistence (*anuvṛtti*) and so forth does not exist for that same reason. Just as there is an absence of the persistence of clay in a single jar, so too is there an absence in all jars, and likewise in the *śivaka* and other stages; thus, due to the absence of persistence, there is also an absence of conceptual constructions based on persistence and exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*).

In this way, by means of the fourfold alternatives involving the generalities established through the cognition of causes and materials— which possess their respective counter-theses— one must demonstrate both the non-establishment of those [alternatives] and the non-establishment of the alternative that they are incapable [of producing the effect].
Consequently, the claim that "the effect is other than its cause" is not established, because it would follow that [the effect] is other than everything.

Therefore, since everything is non-universal, there is an absence of the fourfold set of fallacies regarding universality and unity; likewise, for that very reason, there is no recurrence [of those fallacies], nor is there any contradiction with one's own statements and so forth.

If it is an effect, how can it be non-existent? Or if it is non-existent, how can it be an effect? For it is clay itself that is made into a jar; it is manifested as a jar by the action, just as [an object] is [manifested] by a lamp.
And thus, even the non-establishment of the qualifier and the qualified follows from the existence [of the effect].

Regarding that which you have undertaken as an exposition—namely, the demonstration with great effort, through the exclusion of various positions regarding objections and their resolutions, that "the 'how-to' (itikartavyatā) itself is the 'what-is-to-be-done' (kartavyatā)"—one need not undergo the exhaustion of explaining action by means of action.

Why? Because the exhaustion of investigating entities such as universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth results in a lack of stability regarding ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), and this contradicts the accepted position that it is logical to teach only action for everyone.
Thus, first, the contradiction with one's own words has been stated regarding the position that teaches action preceded by knowledge.

Even in that case where there is no reliance on the instruction of actions such as "one should offer the *agnihotra*," and [the opponent claims] that everything is exclusively bound by ignorance (*ajñāna*), there is a contradiction with one's own words regarding this exclusivity of being bound by ignorance. If it is said, "This was stated knowing that the effect is non-existent," then it is not the case that everything is exclusively bound by ignorance, because this [fact] is established through knowledge. Alternatively, if it was stated without knowing it, how could it be an expounder or a proof? Thus, there is a contradiction with one's own words.

Since you also have stated this after determining and accepting it to be so, there is a contradiction with that [prior] acceptance which was obstructed by ignorance; because of the understanding that "it is thus," a contradiction with your own acceptance has been established.

Furthermore, since worldly practice proceeds from knowledge, there is a contradiction with that; for worldly practice is preceded by knowledge, and therefore, because your acceptance—which is obstructed by ignorance—is not perceived [as such], there is a contradiction with worldly convention (*lokarūḍhi*).

The contradiction with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is indeed the subject at hand. First, there is the contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because it is observed thus in the world: that an effect such as a jar, which is manifested by an action, is perceived as already existing, just like [the object] by means of a lamp. There is a contradiction with inference (*anumāna*) because [the opponent’s position] serves as a means of making known; this is a "contradiction regarding a specific feature" (*viśeṣavirodha*), since the statement "the effect is non-existent" is intended to function as a specific means of making something known. Among the contradictions with perception, one's own words, and so forth, "contradiction regarding a specific feature" consists in the establishment of the opposite of a specific property (*dharmaviśeṣa*).

Because this would lead to the consequence that no application [of means] is possible toward those very things, and because it negates the nature of the property (*dharma*) intended to be established, there is indeed a contradiction regarding the nature of the property;

likewise, contradictions regarding the nature of the substratum (*dharmin*), as well as contradictions regarding the natures of both, should be applied as appropriate. Enough with this overly prolix discussion.

Therefore, the theory of the non-existent effect (*asatkāryavāda*) is untenable. Furthermore, the opponent has accepted that "one should perform the *agnihotra* sacrifice" refers to the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) itself as the duty to be performed, and that one "should act."
