[Objection: But was this very view—that the self (*ātman*) itself is the universal—not already refuted previously through the detailed expansion of the preceding and subsequent arguments, such as "pleasure, pleasure, and the collection of pleasure and so forth"? [Response: To this it is said: No; because the word *ātman* is a synonym for *puruṣa* (the Person), and since no constituent parts are admitted, this universal *puruṣa*—which possesses states and is non-different from those states—subsists in its own essential nature by avoiding the doctrine of a mere aggregate. Because of its difference from that [aggregate], it is called "self" (*ātman*); here, the term is not a synonym for the essential nature of a material object, like the jar, which exists in a state of both difference and non-difference from its neck, form, color, and so forth.
And when conceived in this way, it is conceived without transgressing the fundamental secret of the "all-in-all" nature and the pre-existence of the effect (satkāryavāda);

and even though it is not [yet] investigated, it is logical by relying on the identity [of all things] in reality. This is the injunction for that sequence of activity, because it is not obstructed by ignorance; such is the meaning of "activity" (pravṛtti).

It is not grasped as being "produced by a rite" (*vidhinā bhavati*); rather, it is called the *ātman* because it "continually moves" (*atati*) through various specific states without abandoning its own essential nature. That very [ātman] is the universal (*sāmānya*), characterized by consciousness.

If this is so, then in the absence of particulars (*viśeṣa*), of what would it be the universal? Thus, there follows the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the non-existence of the universal. To avoid this, the particulars must be stated.

It is said: [the universal is] the *puruṣa* because it "lies in the city" (*puri śayanāt*); the particulars, however, are the states belonging to that very [ātman] which possesses states—namely, those called waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth (*turīya*).

If it is asked what the illustration is for the claim that the person (*puruṣa*) is the commonality (*sāmānya*) of its own states (*svāvasthā*), it is like the case of the difference and non-difference of the states of a jar’s neck and so forth, or its color and so forth, or its newness and so forth. Just as a jar has gross states such as the neck, the base, and the middle, as well as subtle states such as color and the rest—which are distinguished by differences of place and distinguished by differences of time, such as the states of being new or old—and yet there is a state of non-difference among those very different states which is the jar; in the same way, the self (*ātman*) alone is the commonality of its own states.

And when conceived in this way, it is conceived without transgressing the fundamental secret of the "all-in-all" (sarvasarvātmakatva) and the pre-existence of the effect (satkāryatva); thus, a merit exists here. For in this manner, the fundamental secret—that everything consists of everything and that the effect is real—is not transgressed; because everything has the Puruṣa as its essence, and because all differences are merely its transformations, they dissolve back into and emerge from that very source, just as the various color-patterns of a chameleon are seen within the chameleon itself.

"Law (vidhi), stability (sthiti), conduct (ācāra), activity (pravṛtti), and boundary (maryādā)"—this is precisely the law, conduct, stability, and so forth, of this system of law (vidhinaya); such is the meaning of "activity. Furthermore, that activity which consists of the nature of the conscious self is the law of law; he explains this very point, [stating] that the previous notion of "law" is not tenable because of the passage beginning with "by means of law," and so on.

The term *bhāva* means "it comes into being"; it has *bhū* as its root and expresses the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*), according to the statement in Pāṇini’s Mahābhāṣya (3.1.67): "The root and the suffix together express the meaning of the suffix."

If it is argued that *bhāva* is so called because the suffix *ghañ* is prescribed in the sense of a state (*bhāve*), such that "it is being" (*bhūyate*) is *bhāva*, whereas "it does not come into being" (*na bhavati*) refers to the agent (*kartṛ*); even in that case, since it is established that the agent is the commonality—by which one "becomes" (as in the rule *bhuvaścopasaṅkhyānam* in the section on *ṇa*), where the commonality is the *bhāva*—then, while the *bhāva* is universal across all systems, it is analyzed as "there is no non-existence of the becoming-thing" amidst diversity and non-diversity. Yet, it is not so analyzed;

thus, the prescriptive nature of the injunction (*vidhi*) does not truly exist. Because of the injunction "as in the world," the injunction is merely a general rule (*utsarga*), and it does not exist in this way [as a specific prescription].
The rule is established that it must be stated how something comes to be both as it is and otherwise; thus, the injunction is set forth.

According to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) of grammar, there is no [independent] existence (*bhāva*) in the following systems due to their respective defects, because of the absence of a "becomer" (*bhavitṛ*), and consequently, due to the absence of an agent who constitutes the primary sense of that [root] *bhū*: 1. In the doctrine of the Buddhists (*bauddha-mata*), which asserts only particularity (*viśeṣamātra-vāda*), where there is a process of becoming characterized by mutual distinction between substances, space, and time, and distinctness in substance, space, time, and state, as well as non-distinction in the mere act of becoming as substance and so forth; 2. In the doctrine of the Sāṅkhyas (*sāṅkhya-mata*), which asserts a plurality of existences (*nānā-bhāva*); 3. In the doctrine of the Vaiśeṣikas (*vaiśeṣika-mata*), which asserts the manifoldness of difference and non-difference (*bhedābhedanānātā*) regarding universals (*sāmānya*) and particulars (*viśeṣa*). The word *iti* here has the sense of a reason (*hetu*); thus, instead of employing the ablative case, it is stated as "due to the absence of a becomer" (*bhavitur-abhāvāt*), according to the logic previously explained, because of the absence of a becomer.

The term *bhāva* (being) refers to things such as a jar (*ghaṭa*) and so forth; this is established by the etymological meaning according to the perspective of grammar. It is analyzed through the method of affirmation (*vidhi*) by means of similarity and dissimilarity:

because of similarity, it is asserted that "it becomes the same," and thus it is posited as distinct. Since faults have been stated regarding those conceptual alternatives (*vikalpa*), and because of the statement regarding "being" as being free from faults, it is analyzed by way of affirmation. Is it analyzed in this manner alone? No, it is said: "It is neither analyzed nor unanalyzed. Furthermore, that proposition was indeed made as unanalyzed, based on the statement: "Who indeed knows this? Or what is the use of knowing this?"

This very [position] is not a valid injunction (*vidhi*), because it prescribes a meaning that is being analyzed, because it suffers from the fault of contradicting its own statement, and because there is both partial analysis and non-analysis.

Even where there is partial analysis, regarding the very portion being analyzed, just as it has been stated by you, the proponent of the system of injunction (*vidhinaya-vādin*), so too it is both analyzed and not analyzed—due to the refutation of the opponent's view and the establishment of one's own view. Thus, an entity such as a jar is both analyzed and not analyzed; likewise, the nature of an injunction does not exist at all. The intended meaning is that an injunction is not truly an injunction in the sense of "it is enjoined thus."

If it is asked, "How, then, is it prescribed? [the answer is: "Like the world" (*lokavat*). "Like the world" means as in the world; because of this prescription of being "like the world," if it is prescribed exactly like the world, then the prescription is merely a general rule (*utsarga*). If one asks, "Why is it not so? What is the reason for this?"—if it is not analyzed, then even the thesis (*pratijñā*) should not be made by way of its parts, and so forth. Because it is prescribed without such deliberation, it is not [merely] that. Rather, through the excellence of what has been stated, the prescription as a general rule is established by virtue of its being the self of all (*sarvātmakatva*). For example: "As it is, so it is otherwise," and so on.

Alternatively, as is observed in the world, such is the rule for the rule of the Creator (vidhi). But how is there a rule for the rule in the world? It is said: "Thus is the rule," and so forth. "Thus" means that the rule which is about to be described immediately hereafter becomes the rule in the world; [as it is said] "as it is, so it is otherwise," and so forth. That it becomes "as it is" through the manner of the lump of clay, the small pot, and so on, and "otherwise" likewise, must be explained accordingly. And that it becomes "this" and "that" according to the reasoning by which it occurs, must be explained accordingly. This is the rule for the rule.

Thus, that [positive entity], with exclusions not intended to be expressed, with distinctions not admitted, and with particulars set aside, becomes a positive injunction (vidhi) that is indeed devoid of exclusion; it is designated as "the general" (utsarga). By means of this synonymous term, "the general" (utsarga) is [shown to be] the "positive injunction" (vidhi); he demonstrates this definition of the positive injunction everywhere, [as in the passages]: "The injunction of that is the injunction of the injunction, which is stability," and "The injunction of that is stability. (Yaśomitra and Bhāṣya).
Let it be seen on page 10, line 1: "An entity exists without the operation of a creator" (vidher vidhiṃ vinā bhavati bhāvaḥ).
[Variant readings: vidheḥ vidhir iha vinā bhavati bhāvaḥ; vidheḥ vidhir iha vinā bhavati bhāvaḥ].
The term *bhāva* (existence/being) [is used] without the *pāṭha* "bhā";
it has the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) when derived from the verbal root *bhū*.
According to Pāṇini 3.3.16, the suffix *ghañ* is optionally applied [to roots ending in long vowels].
1.143 This is an option fixed by rule (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*),
which he clarifies with the words "this water-dweller" (*etaj jalacara*) and so forth.
It should be stated that "of the root *bhū* as well";
this means that for the root *bhū*, the suffix *ṇa* optionally occurs, and this form must be explained.
This explanation, however, should be carried out by means of a *yogavibhāga* (splitting the rule) using the term "optionally" (*vibhāṣā*).

Thus, in the *Kāśikāvṛtti* on Pāṇini’s grammar composed by Jinendrabuddhi and Vāmana, it is analyzed that "the state of being (*bhāva*) exists within the various distinctions and non-distinctions; there is no state of being for that which does not exist. And yet, it is not so analyzed;

likewise, the prescriptive nature (*vidhitva*) of an injunction (*vidhi*) does not truly exist. Because it is prescribed as being "like the world," an injunction is merely a general rule (*utsarga*), and thus it does not exist [as an absolute].
It should be stated that it exists both as it is and otherwise; thus, the rule is prescribed and abandoned.
It is distinguished by similarity and dissimilarity; "by similarity" means it becomes equal.
Herein, it is analyzed by way of similarity and dissimilarity.
The reading "samāno bhavati" might also exist; see page 35, line 4.
And because of the lack of discernment even with respect to a portion—wherever there is discernment even with respect to a portion, [that is] in the Pāṇḍu, Ḍe, Līṃ, and Vi manuscripts.
And because of partial discernment; where there is partial discernment, there [is] Raṃ Hīṃ; where there is non-discernment, there [is] Bhā;
here, and because of partial discernment.
Even where there is partial discrimination, there too the reading might be "tatra" (there); thus it is said in the *Bhāṣya* on the *Loka-vārttika*.
Thus, let it be seen: page 34, line 4; "taddarśadvārikā" is the reading in the manuscript.
The rule of the rule, the rule of the primordial rule;
the rule of the rule, the rule of the manifestation.

The ritual procedure (vidhi) is that which is to be performed; the ritual procedure is the manifestation of the ritual procedure; the ritual procedure is the path; the ritual procedure is the lineage (līṃ).
Raṃ Hīṃ Vidhiḥ Vidhiḥ Bhāḥ Vidhividhiḥ Yaḥ.
...thus it is emitted,
thus it is protected;
for example— a person is indeed a knower, because he consists of knowledge.
The sense is that because all this is composed of that, and because of the oneness of that and the oneness of all, what comes into being? Who is the agent?
Who is the agent? He who is independent.
Who is independent? It is the Knower.

But surely the essence of milk and so forth is the agent of curds and the like, yet it is not a knower? No; because that [essence] is subordinate to its own activity, just as the state of being milk or curds is subordinate to the activity of the cow; or because it is subordinate to the Knower, just as the rotation of the wheel [is subordinate to the potter]. But in the case of the rotation of the wheel, upon the inquiry "who is the bringer-about?", just as in the conventional usage of the "becoming of a jar," [the answer is] the clay.

If it is asked, "Who is he? Let him be pointed out," it is said: "For instance, the word *puruṣa* has been explained [as follows]: The word *hi* means "because"; because he is a knower (*jñātṛ*), characterized by knowledge (*jñānaśīla*), possessing the attribute of knowledge (*jñānadharmā*), or one who rightly knows (*sādhujñāyī*), he is indeed a *puruṣa*.

And his state of being a knower arises from being composed of knowledge (*jñānamayatvāt*). He is "composed of knowledge" (*jñānamaya*) either as a constituent part of knowledge or as a modification of knowledge, because his defining characteristic is cognitive application (*upayoga*).

If it is asked, "What follows from that?"—it is this: this entire world, differentiated by the distinctions of gods, humans, animals, hell-beings, the earth, and so forth, as well as jars and other objects, is composed of that [Purusha]. Because of its oneness—that is, because that Purusha is one and is the ultimate reality—there is the oneness of all, just like His oneness. And due to this oneness of all, He is both the One and the entire world; such is the meaning. It does not exist through the differentiation of jars, cloths, and so forth, because its essence is the Purusha consisting of consciousness (*jñānamaya*); the sense is that whatever exists is He alone. He is the Self itself, the universal, for He is common to all.

The text proceeds by way of questions and answers for the sake of determining that [point]: "Who is it that exists? and so forth, until the meaning is exhausted with the question, "Who is independent? [The answer is: "He who is the knower. This is because one who is ignorant lacks independence, and therefore lacks agency, just like wood and other materials used in the process of cooking. For example, in the statement, "Devadatta cooks rice in a pot with wood," Devadatta alone is the accomplisher of the act of cooking because he is the knower, not the wood and other materials; likewise, the sense is that the *puruṣa* (Spirit) alone exists. The word "yasmāt" (because) does not appear in the manuscripts. [The passage continues from] "ityādi" to "pra".
Because of the absence of an agent, [the opponent says] "wood and so forth" [are the cause].
To this, another says: "But surely the essence of milk and so forth is the agent of curds and the like."
From milk, curd arises; from juice, molasses. Yet, that milk or juice is not itself the conscious agent; thus, the agency of a conscious being is not an inconclusive reason.

This is not so, because it is a remainder of that very activity. Since it is a remainder of the ongoing activity of that same conscious being while his activity is not yet completed, the distinction created by the difference in the sequence of time is not precluded.
As it has been said: "The juice extracted by the teeth possesses a potency equal to sugar;
that which is pressed by the teeth is superior, whereas that produced by a machine causes burning."

It is like the remainder of the milk, curd, and so forth from the activity of a cow; just as when the activity of a cow, such as a milch-cow, has not yet ceased, there remains a residue consisting of the production of milk, curd, fresh butter, clarified butter, and so on, so too the world is merely the residue of the activity of the Puruṣa.
Alternatively, because it is a residue for the sake of the Knower, it is like the rotation of a potter’s wheel.

Or what is this "activity" (*pravṛtti*), distinct from the active person, since everything is subordinate to the Knower? The example is the whirling of a wheel: just as when a wheel is spun by the effort of a potter, its whirling is subordinate to the potter's activity—and thus subordinate to the Knower—so too is curd and the like subordinate to the Knower. The cow is subordinate to the Knower, and the curd is subordinate to that cow; for there is no becoming of milk, curd, and so forth, from the grass and other food consumed by the cow and transformed into chyle, blood, and so on, without the Knower. [The reading *jñād akartuṇaḥ* (from the Knower, not from a non-agent) is supported by Bhāṣya, Vi., Ḍe., and Līṃ.]
The juice extracted by chewing has a potency equal to sugar; it refreshes the mouth and brings joy. The juice extracted by chewing [is] the agent of knowledge, Raṃ Hīṃ.
The guru is known to cause burning sensations and constipation, whereas the yāntrika is proclaimed [to have the opposite qualities].
Thus reads the text in the printed Suśruta-saṃhitā; however, in Jejjaṭa’s commentary on it, the reading is: "But the juice squeezed from the teeth has a potency equal to sugar."
Thus the reading is:

"That which is squeezed by the teeth is best; however, that produced by a machine causes burning. Here, the word *nanu* is used for requesting permission. Then, in response to the expectation or inquiry—"What will become of it even during the rotation of the wheel?"—that very thing which exists as the fundamental cause (*mūlabhavitr*) is [the answer].
Otherwise, that [state] would not exist at all, because there would be no one to become [awake];

for the state of sleep belongs only to a conscious being, since it is a state [of consciousness], and because the instruments such as the wheel and the staff are inactive—just as curd is [inactive] compared to milk—and because the state of sleep is a state belonging to the remainder of the conscious being.

For just as form and the other [sensory objects], without abandoning their subtle state due to being formless (*amūrta*), assume gross forms through various divisions such as earth and so forth by superimposing themselves upon atoms whose materiality is bound by the power of their own activity—just as clay is required for the conventional usage of the "production of a jar," where clay alone is the primary entity in the process of a jar's production through the sequence of stages such as the lump and the handle—so too here, because it is a process of production within the rotation of the wheel, one must depend upon a fundamental producing substance; for even further and further back, that which becomes and that which is becoming is precisely that, meaning that very thing is the root cause.

Therefore, just as clay is required for the production of a jar, the potter is required for the production of delusion; and just as everything remains as the potter's [tools], so too everything remains as the residue of the Knower (*jña*). Otherwise, he would not exist at all, because of the absence of anything that could come into being, due to his being rootless like the son of a barren woman—this is the meaning.
That by which one comes into being is precisely that;
otherwise, he would not exist at all, because of the absence of anything that could become manifest.

Because it is a state belonging to the conscious one (jña) during sleep, and because it is a state [of being], and because the instruments such as the wheel and the staff are inactive— just as curds [arise] from milk— and because it is a state of sleep remaining as a residue of the conscious one; for just as form and other qualities, without abandoning their subtle mode of existence due to their immateriality, come to possess gross forms through various distinctions such as earth by superimposing themselves upon atoms whose material nature is bound by the power of their own activity,
so too it might be thought that since movement is observed even in insentient things like clouds, the activity of the staff and other instruments occurs without the application of a conscious agent.

This is incorrect, because the state of sleep belongs only to the conscious knower; nor do the wheel, the rod, and other instruments function by themselves, since instruments are devoid of activity. Being instruments, they are inactive; being inactive, they cannot exist by themselves without the effort of the knower, or at least without that effort as their prerequisite. Therefore, in the state of sleep, the wheel, the rod, and so forth must become motionless and insentient, which is indeed the state of sleep for that very knower.

Therefore, that state of sleep must also be an activity of the conscious knower alone, just as curd is [an activity] of milk; for just as curd is a state of milk, so too the staff, wheel, and other tools belong to the conscious potter alone. By this, the production of curd and the like is also explained as being the manifestation of the knower. Since it is a state that is a remainder of the knower's sleep, and because it is a state—just as the wheel, staff, and so forth are remainders of the potter's effort—the absence of activity without the effort of the knower (or the effort remaining from the knower) means that it consists solely of the activity of the knower. This is the meaning.
(Vasthātbhā°)
If the state of another [entity] were conscious,
then the state of that other would be non-conscious,
because it is a state.
To illustrate this point for the sake of its cultivation (*bhāvanā*), he states the example beginning with "just as indeed" (*yathaiva hi*), etc.

"Just as form, taste, smell, touch, and sound do not abandon their subtle state by virtue of being incorporeal," and so forth. Since the gross is preceded by the subtle, having first described subtlety, he now describes grossness. For those [qualities] such as form and the rest are not accepted by anyone as being corporeal or gross, since their own nature is manifested by the specific cognitions of the eye and other senses; therefore, they are incorporeal (*amūrta*). Their state is incorporeality (*amūrtatva*); by that incorporeality there is a "state" (*vṛtti*), and that very state is subtle. Not abandoning—that is, not relinquishing—that subtle state, [they remain] as atoms whose "course toward corporeality" (*mūrtatvaprakrama*) is bound by their own activity and power (*svapravṛttiprabhāvāvabaddha*). The course toward corporeality is bound for the atoms, along with their divisions, by the respective activity of form and the rest. By saying "having superposed those atoms," he shows the sequence of creation by way of an illustration.

Thereafter, gross forms consisting of various distinct varieties of earth and the other elements arise; these are the very forms such as color and so forth, appearing as the specific varieties of earth such as stones, clods of earth, sand, and diamonds; of water, such as snow and hailstones; of fire, such as flames, embers, and glowing coals; of wind, such as gusts, whirlwinds, whistling sounds, and storms; of plants, such as trees, shrubs, creepers, climbing vines, spreading plants, and grasses; and of mobile beings, such as worms, ants, bees, humans, gods, and denizens of hell—this is an illustration of their manifestation.
For power (prabhāva) is indeed inconceivable; because power is inconceivable, there arises from the formless the manifestation of form.

Furthermore, taste, potency, post-digestive transformation, and power are the modifications of a substance as it proceeds [through its stages]. In this regard, there is an illustration: the *citraka* is pungent in its post-digestive transformation (*pāka*), hot in its potency (*vīrya*), and pungent in its taste (*rasa*);
likewise is the *dantī*. Yet, by virtue of its power (*prabhāva*), the *dantī* causes a person to purge.
Carakasamhitā 1.26.68.

Just as these [elements] such as earth and the rest—being subtle—are preceded by subtle forms that are both material and immaterial due to their grossness, like a cloth preceded by threads; even beyond that, there is something further, and even beyond that, a cause which attains the state of form and so forth. That which is thus differentiated by form and the rest, yet whose own essential nature (*svatattva*) is undifferentiated—that indeed is the Reality (*tattva*).

What is that? Is it not the case that the Self, whose true nature is consciousness (*jñāna*), has already been defined by [the categories of] form and so forth? For that "formation" (*rūpaṇa*) is form (*rūpa*), which is indeed consciousness itself, whether differentiated or undifferentiated; it is simply the act of grasping. It is not "form" in the sense of being formed (*rūpyate*) by something else, or as existing within that [object], and so on. This is because form does not persist as something distinct from the collection of qualities such as taste, nor from the substance itself—just as [the quality of] being a son is distinct from the person [who is the father].

Even though matter (*rūpa*) is of an undifferentiated essential nature in both ways, one must understand that among things other than matter—such as taste and so forth—there exists another cause, distinct from matter and the rest, which is "further" (*apara*), "beyond" (*para*), most excellent (*variṣṭha*), and primary (*pradhāna*), and which attains the state of matter and the rest. And that "further" cause is that which proceeds by dividing itself into the form of immaterial and subtle matter and so forth, as well as into the form of gross, material atoms, aggregates of two spatial units (*dvipradeśa*) and so on, earth and so forth.

Furthermore, regarding this form and so forth which are thus divided, what indeed is their own essence (*svatattva*), given that they possess an undivided own-essence within the atoms, dyads, and the like, just as the earth and other elements possess an undivided reality of their own nature? "Essence" (*tattva*) is the state of being (*bhāva*); here the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) is used in its own sense. He demonstrates this: that which exists is itself the essence;

and it is "own" (*sva*) in relation to its own particular manifestations. It is designated as "own-essence" (*svatattva*) because it is followed by reality (*tattvatā*), and because it is distinguished from the absence of any other essence (*paratattvābhāva*) in relation to the perspective of others.
Citraka is unmanifest in its form yet manifest [in its effects]; it is pungent in digestion, hot in potency, and pungent in taste;
Citraka is considered pungent in digestion, pungent in taste, and hot in potency.
Thus is the reading in the Caraka-saṃhitā:

"Likewise, dantī causes a person to purge by its specific power (prabhāva)" (Caraka-saṃhitā 1.26.68). In this way, that which is the further cause beyond even that, which attains the state of form and so forth—that which is both differentiated as form and so on, and yet possesses an undifferentiated own-nature (svatattva)—that alone is reality (tattva).

What is that? Is it not indeed the case that the Self, whose essential nature is knowledge (*jñāna-svatattva*), has been defined by means of form (*rūpa*) and the other [sensory objects]? For that "form-ness" (*rūpaṇa*) is form; it is knowledge itself, whether differentiated or undifferentiated, and it is simply the act of grasping (*grahaṇa*). It is not "form" in the sense of being "that which is formed" (*rūpyate*) by it, or "in that," and so forth. Because form does not persist as something distinct from the collection of qualities such as taste or from substance—just like the state of being a son, which is distinct from the person—in both ways, even though form consists of an undifferentiated reality, there is that which is perceived directly regarding tastes and the others as distinct from form.
"Or rather, it might even be 'independent' (*svatantram*) here"; to this, the other replies: "In that case, it must be investigated what [it means] by that."

The Teacher says: But surely it has been defined by means of form and the other [sensory qualities] that the Self is the very essence of knowledge, and that the Self is the supreme cause; yet that [Self], which is the very essence of knowledge, is again defined by means of form and the others. [In the root *rūp* (Pāṇini-Dhātupāṭha 1934), the sense is] "to form"; "formed" (*rūpitam*) means determined or known. Determination (*nirṇaya*) and forming (*rūpaṇa*) have the same meaning.
For that forming is "form" (*rūpa*), because forming and form have the same meaning.

By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the tongue is the instrument of tasting and taste is the object; likewise for the remaining [senses]. Because they obtain their own nature through the act of "coloring" (*rūpaṇa*), there is "the state of being colored" (*rūpaṇatā*). Since "knowledge" (*jñāna*) is a synonym for "coloring," it is knowledge itself. Apprehension is both differentiated and undifferentiated: apprehension as differentiated consists of the cognitions of form, taste, smell, sound, and touch; apprehension as undifferentiated is simply "form" (*rūpa*) common to all. Both of these types of apprehension are indeed "form" (*rūpa*), because the word *rūpa* functions as an abstract noun (*bhāvasādhana*).

But "form" (*rūpa*) is not defined as that which is transformed by it, or that in which [transformation occurs], and so forth; nor does it consist in its being established as the object, the agent, the instrument, or the locus. By the inclusion of the word "and so forth," it follows that form cannot be defined through the distinctions of the other *kārakas*, such as the recipient (*sampradāna*) or the point of departure (*apādāna*), in the sense of "form for that" or "form from that."

What is the reason? Because even such things as "being tasted" or "being touched" are observed in that very same [substratum]. For a real entity whose nature is cognition (*jñānātman*) and which is characterized by "form-ification" (*rūpaṇa*), there is no separate existence apart from the collection of qualities such as taste, or apart from the substance (*dravya*) which is distinct from the collection of qualities. This is like the case of a son being non-different from his father: just as the attributes of fatherhood, sonship, brotherhood, nephewhood, unclehood, and so forth—which belong to a single person who possesses multiple relations—do not exist separately from that person, so too form, which consists of form-ification, does not exist in ultimate reality apart from qualities such as taste, nor apart from substances such as atoms which are distinct from those qualities.

Therefore, the distinctions such as taste, atoms, and earth—which consist of a reality whose nature is indivisible form—are [in fact] their own true forms. [Note: This phrase "nirṇītaṃ ya pratiṣu nāsti" indicates that this specific reading does not exist in the manuscripts consulted.]

Alternatively, by including the word "etc. (*ādi*), the status of being an instrument (*sādhana*)—consisting of object (*karman*), agent (*kartṛ*), instrument (*karaṇa*), and locus (*adhikaraṇa*)—is [implied]; thus, even the reading as heard in the text, "for that [purpose], from that [source], form" (*tasmai tasmād rūpam iti*), should be reconciled by intending the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the word "not" (*na tu*). [This is] with respect to form (*rūpeṇa*)...

[the one] to be praised for his multitude of virtues (*guṇagaṇya*). *Note: The text contains several scribal errors (e.g., *o॰ pra॰ ॰rguṇagaṇya dra॰ pra॰*), which have been interpreted based on the context of the commentary.*
By way of connection, in the form of... [incomplete]... ya.

If it is argued: "In that case, since their essence is undivided from the nature of being manifested (rūpaṇā), there would have to be a perception of them as undivided from form by the eye alone; and since they are seen to be perceived by the tongue and other senses, this conceptualization contradicts direct perception," we reply: No. This is because that reality is admitted to be manifold in nature. Thus, even though form has an undivided essential nature—whether through the non-difference of taste and so forth, or through the non-difference of the substance—it can be said, up to the point of "from the substance, taste and so forth. It can be said that "it is form alone, not taste and so forth" based on observation; yet it cannot be said that "this is a single substance distinct from form and the rest," because nothing is observed apart from form and the other qualities.
However, if there is a perception of [consciousness] as undivided from the reality of the self (*ātmatattva*), then there is no contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Consciousness is indeed one; although it appears divided by forms and so forth, it is undivided, because we observe experience to be thus.

Furthermore, since a distinction [between subject and object] is untenable, that very consciousness must be accepted as being the very nature of the self of cognition, serving as both the grasped and the grasper, just like the realization of the intended self.

The subtle and gross nature of intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth, as well as form (*rūpa*) and so on, is like the established distinction of the extremely imperceptible essence in milk and other substances; for even though they are a single reality, they are perceived through direct perception as distinct entities such as "form" and "taste. Since it has been stated that the various divisions of this manifold entity—which is bound by the power of its own activity—have been explained, it follows that there is no separate collection of qualities such as taste and the rest apart from one another, nor are those others [the substrates] anything other than the specific differences in the nature of their manifestation as form and so forth. Thus it has been said.

It might be thought: "A single substance is distinct from color and the other [sensory qualities], because it is perceived separately. But this cannot be asserted—that "this is one single substance distinct from color and the others"—for what reason? Because nothing distinct from color and the rest is observed. In the previous case, since tastes and other qualities are perceived by direct perception as being other than color, it can be asserted that "it is color alone, not tastes and so forth. However, in the present case, since no substance distinct from color and the others is observed through direct perception, such an assertion is impossible.
Regarding the reading *yāvad-dravyādīti*: although this reading is found in all the manuscripts, it appears that if the reading were *yāvad-rasādīti*, it would be more appropriate;
see page 178, line 11.
Alternatively, it appears that some portion of the text here is missing;

for while one can say that "there is only form (rūpa) and not taste (rasa) and so forth," one cannot say that "this is a single substance distinct from form and the rest," because nothing is observed apart from form and the other qualities.
However, if [the object] is apprehended as inseparable from the reality of the self (ātmatattva), there is no contradiction with direct perception (pratyakṣa).
Consciousness is indeed one; though divided by forms and so forth, it remains undivided, for such is observed in its experience.

Since any distinction [between subject and object] is untenable, that very consciousness, being the essential nature of knowledge itself, must be accepted as both the grasped and the grasper—just like the realization of the intended Self.

This is because the subtle and gross natures of the intellect, forms, and so on, exist within the reality itself, just as the arrangement of the distinctions between milk and other substances exists within their true essence, even when those distinctions are not perceived.
There is no other [reality] than substance itself.

In which conceptualization, then, is there no contradiction with perception? It is said: there is no contradiction with perception when there is a cognition that is not differentiated from the reality of the self (ātmatattva).

How is that so? It is explained as follows: Consciousness (*caitanya*) is indeed one; though differentiated by form and the like, it remains undifferentiated because it is inseparable from consciousness and persists through it. Due to its unity, it is undifferentiated in its general nature of manifestation (*rūpaṇa*); yet, although it is differentiated through the distinct apprehension of forms and so forth, it remains that very same one because it possesses a manifold nature. Thus, the perceptual observation of the differentiation of taste and other qualities, as well as the non-differentiation of the nature of manifestation, is not contradictory, since consciousness itself consists of the forms of color and the rest.

And because, insofar as [the object] is conceptualized by others as being distinct—wherein form (*rūpa*) and so forth are distinct from consciousness (*caitanya*), and where an external entity consisting of a collection of qualities such as form, taste, and so on, or an entity consisting of the substance that is their substratum, could exist—such a thing would indeed contradict perception; however, when that very same form and so forth are apprehended as non-different from the reality of the nature of consciousness, they do not contradict perception, since consciousness itself possesses both a differentiated and a non-differentiated nature, and because one perceives it to be experienced in that way, no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is possible for its own determination.

What then? Since the existence of an object distinct from cognition is untenable due to the impossibility of its separation [from it], the object of apprehension and the apprehender must be accepted as being of the very nature of cognition itself, just like the realization of one's own self. Just as your own accepted self—which, though perceiving the self as distinct from the body and so forth in each individual body, perceives external objects such as the body and the like—is both the object of apprehension and the apprehender because there is no other means of knowledge for the realization of its own self; so too, cognition itself revolves through its own variations in the form of color and so on, and in the form of pleasure, pain, and so on.

The contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣavirodha*) is not present in the Bhāṣya manuscript (Bhā), whereas the contradiction with observation (*darśanāvirodha*) is present in the Prajñākaragupta manuscript (Pra).
Without the determination of its own nature, the existence of this [object] is impossible; thus it is designated as "non-existent."

He also states an illustration—beginning with "intellect, etc."—whereby intellect (*buddhi*), pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, time, space, direction, self, and so forth are called "subtle" because they are formless (*amūrta*); whereas color-form (*rūpa*) and the rest are indeed "gross" because they are perceptible. Furthermore, their subtlety and grossness, respectively, will be connected to the very nature (*tattva*) of those [categories], namely intellect and the rest, as well as color-form and the rest. Regarding the phrase "the nature of milk and so forth being entirely unperceived," it means that at the stage of milk, those properties (*dharma*) which arise simultaneously are entirely unperceived; and thus, omniscience is obtained without effort, since everything has the self of the Person (*puruṣa*) as its essence.

Knowledge itself, when it reaches its ultimate limit of excellence through degrees of intensity—like the height of a mountain or the measurement of a field—is essentially characterized by the nature of a perceiver, just as the light emitted by fireflies and other sources varies in degree. Now, one might object that since qualities such as "being a speaker" are invariably concomitant with non-omniscience, [the Lord] must be non-omniscient; but this is not so, for even the quality of being a speaker is observed only within the context of that very [ultimate] reality. For example: "The juice is liquid," "curd is solid," "the root is hard," and "whey is indeed liquid."

By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), milk is also included as something entirely unperceived [in its causal state] as being the cow. Just as the specific sequence of transformations of the juices, blood, and so forth residing in the cow—which are entirely unperceived in the grass consumed by the cow and in the cow itself—results in the flow of milk and other products established through differentiation at the very moment of their reality; likewise, there is a simultaneous establishment of the entire world, both sentient and insentient, which is entirely unperceived [as such], within the conscious Self, the Puruṣa.

And just as other qualities such as sweetness, sourness, and so forth arise sequentially in that very [substance], so too do the modes (*paryāya*) exist within that very reality which is of the nature of knowledge, and these are its states.

These are not spoken of out of one's own imagination; rather, they are indeed drops from the ocean of the Jina’s words, as follows: "What is a substantial atom (*bhāvaparamāṇu*)? A substantial atom possesses color, possesses smell, possesses taste, and possesses touch" (Bhagavatī Sūtra 20.5).

6. Thus, because the elements such as color (varṇa) exist within the reality (tattva) itself—which is manifold in nature—as being of that very essence; and because the intellect (buddhi) and so forth, as well as form (rūpa) and so forth, exist within the reality of taste (rasa-tattva) [according to the Bhāṣya], and within the reality of pleasure (rata-tattva) [according to the Yaśas commentary].
And thus, omniscience is obtained without effort because everything has the nature of the Person (*puruṣa*);

for knowledge itself, when reaching its ultimate limit of excellence due to a gradation—just like the height of mountains or the measurement of fields—is realized as having the nature of a cognizer, just as light exists in a gradation ranging from fireflies and so forth. [Objection: But since the capacity to speak and other such qualities are never found apart from non-omniscience, there is only non-omniscience; [Reply: No, for even the capacity to speak has a gradation...
The root text reads *tattvabhā* and *maduḥbhā*, except for the manuscript vi,
which reads *pratibhā*.
In that state, they exist as possessing [qualities].

Regarding the *praśnavyākaraṇas*, it is said: "O Lord, how many kinds of ultimate atoms (*bhāvaparamāṇu*) are taught? O Gautama, four kinds are taught, namely: possessing color (*vaṇṇamaṃte*), possessing smell (*gaṃdhamaṃte*), possessing taste (*rasamaṃte*), and possessing touch (*phāsamaṃte*). This is the reading in the *Bhagavatīsūtra*.

In this doctrine—which asserts that all distinctions are merely manifestations (*vivarta*) of a single cause consisting of consciousness—the state of omniscience is effortlessly attained through other lines of reasoning, because everything has the *puruṣa* as its essence. For there is no *puruṣa* whatsoever who does not know himself; just as the nature of curd, though entirely unperceived in grass and such things, is of the same essence as them because it is their causal material, so too is omniscience his.

What is this omniscience? It is simply the state of being a knower (*jñatva*) existing at the ultimate limit of excellence. That very state of being a knower reaches its unsurpassed culmination somewhere, because of gradation (*tāratamya*). Gradation is the state of being more or less; it is a distinction of excellence relative to one another, such as "more knowing" or "most knowing. Since it is characterized by such gradation, it cannot exist without reaching that ultimate limit which is unsurpassed.

Like the height of mountains: just as the height of mountains—such as the Vindhya, Sahya, Ujjayanta, Pāriyātra, Indrapada, Malaya, Mahendra, Himavat, Kailāśa, and so forth—is not possible without an unsurpassed height that has reached the ultimate limit of excellence through a gradation of degrees, so too is omniscience.

Even for one who does not go to Kailāsa or Mandara, since there exists a field (kṣetra) consisting of earth and other elements that is capable of providing space for that void and which is infinite on all sides, we observe therein an unsurpassed excellence of measurement—being great, greater, and greatest; thus, "like the measurement of a field" is the illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta).

Within this very proposition, there is another reason: because it consists of the nature of "making known" (*pratyavagamaka*). That which makes known is "making known," and that is itself knowledge (*jñatva*). Therefore, its state of reaching the limit of unsurpassed excellence is the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), like the light (*uddyota*) found in a range of gradations starting from a firefly. Just as light is seen to reach the limit of unsurpassed excellence in the sun because it exists in a state of gradation among fireflies, gems, lamps, stars, and so forth, so too does knowledge [reach such a limit] in some [supreme being]. (Note: *utka* and *pra* appear to be scribal fragments or abbreviations for *utkarṣa-prakarṣa*.)
Just as the height of mountains is seen even by fire, so too is it seen by the wise.
The other says: "But surely, because of [the properties] such as being a speaker... and so forth.
Surely, since properties such as being a speaker, possessing a body, having a name, and possessing a genus do not deviate from non-omniscience, there is indeed non-omniscience.

Furthermore, in this very case, because we observe excellence and deficiency in the scope of sensory perception and inference, and because there is a progression toward excellence, an object characterized by a measurable degree of excellence must have a counter-correlative, since it is a specific entity, like a jar.

The state of not being an omniscient speaker must be the opposite of [the state of] speaking what is entirely true, because it is a state of non-omniscience, or alternatively, a state of being a speaker who is not omniscient; for it is a real entity (*vastu*) and a specific property (*viśeṣa*), like the states of knowing and not knowing, or like the states of being a blue lotus and a red lotus, or even like the states of possessing smoke and possessing fire. Therefore, in reality, why would there be any doubt? This is certainly established; thus, it must also exist in reality.

However, because the self (*ātman*) consists of knowledge and because speech is a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) manifested by that [self], it is logical that the speaking belongs to the person (*puruṣa*) himself; and since it has been stated that this [person] is indeed omniscient, [the opponent objects]: "This is not so, for since the quality of being a speaker also possesses degrees of excellence, there must be a corresponding decline in the opposite case. To this we reply: We maintain that omniscience follows precisely from the status of being a speaker. There is a progressive series of excellence—speaker, better speaker, best speaker—and because this series culminates in the unsurpassed, one must necessarily accept that he is the speaker of everything and of what is true.

Furthermore, because he is the speaker of all that is true, he is "one who knows that"; since the excellence of omniscience is established by the very fact of his being a speaker, the denial of his omniscience is untenable.

As for the argument regarding the gradation of excellence concerning the objects of the senses and the objects of inference based on them, that too is not a fault, as it shares the same nature as the example of space, which is eternally inferable and possesses great magnitude.

It might be thought: "Because space is unestablished, there is no example [for the argument]. But this is incorrect, because inference does exist: "An entity possessing a finite dimension is accompanied by its opposite (i.e., something infinite), because it is a particular kind of existent, like a jar. This inference is stated from the perspective of those who maintain that categories are distinct; however, in the doctrine of differentiation arising from the transformation of a single undifferentiated cause, he will state the absence of any further excellence (the ultimate limit).

Because [the argument] is endowed with a gradation of degrees, he speaks in order to introduce the future point to be established, following the sense of what has already been proven: "The opposite must hold true for those who do not speak exclusively of truth, because non-omniscience—whether as the state of being a speaker or as the state of not being omniscient—is a condition; or because non-omniscience, which is invariably concomitant with the state of being a speaker, exists in the form of a statement as an inference, while the other is accepted as a mere word-meaning; thus both types of non-omniscience are indeed a condition, since they possess the nature of a real entity (*vastu*) and the nature of a specific attribute (*viśeṣa*)," and so forth, thereby demonstrating the ease of finding logical reasons.

The illustration is like the states of knowing and not-knowing: that which knows is the sentient being, whether stationary or moving; that which does not know is forest wood and the like. Similarly, according to the perspective of the *vidhi-naya*, there are the states of waking and deep sleep. This illustration concerns the meaning of the words (*padārtha*), while the illustration concerning the sentence (*vākya*) is like the distinction between a blue lotus and a red lotus.

Just as the wise man does not exist without the ignorant, nor the ignorant without the wise; and just as a blue lotus does not exist without what is non-blue or non-lotus—such as a red lotus—or their opposites, so too, by the meaning of that statement, omniscience does not exist without non-omniscience, nor does non-omniscience exist without omniscience.

Therefore, because it functions as a progressive excellence, an entity characterized by a measurable degree of intensity must possess its opposite, since it is a particular state of being, like a jar.

The state of not speaking all truths must be the opposite [of the state of speaking all truths], because it is a state of non-omniscience or a state of being a speaker who is not omniscient, and because it is a real entity (vastu) and a specific property (viśeṣa), like the states of knowledge and ignorance, or like the states of being a blue lotus and a red lotus. Likewise, there must also be a reversal of the states of possessing smoke and possessing fire; what doubt can there be regarding this in reality? This is indeed certain; therefore, that too must exist in reality.

However, because the Self consists of knowledge and because speech is a conceptual construction manifested by it, it is logical that its expression belongs to the Person (puruṣa) alone; the meaning is that, since this has already been stated, there is no need for further examples. This concludes the section on the opposing view.
The state of being [that] due to the gradation of existence;
see page 179, line 2;
by way of its essential nature.
In reality,
that which is stationary or moving, ignorant and insentient— such as forest wood and the like— is produced by that same method;
likewise, through omniscience, non-omniscience is eliminated.
Likewise, [the reading] "omniscience does not exist without non-omniscience" (sārvajñonāsarvajñaṃ vinā bhavati) is acceptable;

here, the reading "likewise, omniscience does not exist without non-omniscience" (tathā'sārvajñyena sārvajñyaṃ vinā na bhavati) may also somehow be consistent. The other [opponent] says: "In that case, there must also be a reversal of the states of possessing smoke and possessing fire in reality; for smoke, which is an effect consisting of a state and which is never found without fire, is never seen in the absence of fire at any place or time—thus, its being a 'state' is the cause of doubt. This is the intended meaning.
The Teacher says: What is the deliberation? The meaning is that this is certainly established: even one who is not fire indeed becomes so.

By that [reasoning], it must also exist as reality through its opposite; for is this not precisely what is under discussion—the demonstration that the single cause, whose nature is knowledge (*jñāna*), consists of its own states such as fire, non-fire, and so forth? In this way we shall demonstrate the deviation regarding fire. First, let us establish the meaning of the proposition according to the opponent's view—starting with "by that, however," and so on: because the Self is of the nature of knowledge, and because speech is a conceptual construction manifested by that [Self], it is said: "Whatever word says, that is our authority" (Pātañjala Mahābhāṣya 2.1).
Thus, like grammar, [the Veda] would be of human origin, because everything consists of that [speech], because it is merely a state of that, and because it is a real entity;
otherwise, it would not exist at all.
But surely, for that very same single entity, both being fire and not being fire would contradict perception and other means of valid cognition.

If it is argued: "Is it not the case that through direct perception itself, a single entity such as rice (*vrīhi*) exists at one and the same time as earth, water, and so forth? Since rice consists of all things, its non-perception at that time is due to its not being perceived in that [total] manner. [Response: Then there would be a total lack of perception at all times;

for an object is not perceived by the senses in exactly the way it exists. This is because visual perception of rice and the like functions only by grasping specific forms such as the husk and the grain, whereas the perception of form and other qualities functions only by grasping those respective forms and qualities.

That sound, too, cannot come into being or be spoken without the activity of a person; therefore, it is logical that its utterance belongs only to the nature of a person and not otherwise. Regarding this point, he states the reason: "Because it has been spoken, because it is speech, like grammar, it is of human origin. By this, he demonstrates that everything consists of the person. Furthermore, by the phrase "even because it is a real entity," he shows the availability of reasons for this point, since everything is of that [person's] nature and is merely a state of that [person], and so forth—all such reasons apply to this matter.
Otherwise, it would not be speech at all, because as a non-human (apauruṣeya) sound, it would be like a donkey’s horn;
or rather, by this [definition], would it be speech or not speech? Or else, it would not exist at all, because it lacks a human nature, like the son of a barren woman.
See page 130, note 4.
Like grammar, [the Veda] is of human origin because everything has that as its nature, because it is merely a state of that, and also because it is a real entity;
otherwise, it would not exist at all.
But surely, for that single entity, both being fire and not being fire would contradict perception and other means of valid cognition?

If it is argued that rice and other grains are indeed perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as a single entity existing at one and the same time as earth, water, and so forth—since the rice consists of all these elements—and yet they are not perceived as such because they are not grasped in that way at that time, [we reply: then there would be a total lack of perception at all times;

for an object is not perceived by the senses in exactly the form in which it exists. This is because visual perception of rice and the like functions only by grasping limited aspects such as the husk, the grain, and so on, whereas the perception of color and other qualities functions only by grasping those specific qualities.
The reading enclosed within these marks does not exist in the Bhāṣya manuscript; it is obtainable as *yāvad aprastutatvāt* in the Ḍe, Līṃ, Raṃ, and Hī manuscripts,
while it is obtainable as *vayovad vastutvāt* in the Pā manuscript.
"It is not possible [to know] the reality as it truly is" (yathāvadvastutva);
furthermore,
he says "But surely," and so forth.

As for what you have stated—that at one and the same time there is both fire-ness and non-fire-ness in that very same single object—that is contradicted by perception and other means of knowledge, because [fire-ness] is absent in its totality; and by the inclusion of the word "etcetera," it is also contradicted by inference, scripture, and worldly convention. To this, the Teacher says: "But from perception," and so forth. From perception itself—the foremost of all means of knowledge—[we see that] rice and the like (the inclusion of "and the like" referring to mangoes, rose-apples, and so on) are a single object even at the time of its state as rice, [consisting of] earth, water, and so on, because the rice possesses the nature of all things.

What is this rice (*vrīhi*) apart from the transformation of the qualities (*dharma*) such as color, smell, taste, and touch residing in the earth, water, seed, and so forth? Thus, because the earth and other elements mutually assume one another’s qualities, they possess the nature of all things (*sarvātmakatva*). Because they possess the nature of all things, the rice—which consists of them—also possesses the nature of all things, just like water and the rest. Therefore, water and the rest are indeed the rice, because [rice] does not exist without them and because it arises in that manner, just like its own self-nature.
Therefore, there is no contradiction with perception and so forth. [Variant readings:
*°gata-varṇa°* (Pāda-mañjarī), *°bhāga°* (Bhāṣya)].

If it should be thought that "it is not perceived because it is not grasped in that manner at that time"—that is, since at the time of rice (*vrīhi*) the object consisting of earth, water, and so forth is not grasped in its mode as earth, water, and so forth, then that object would not be perceptible; for that object is not merely rice alone—it is replied:

"In that case, there would be non-perceptibility of everything at all times," and so on; because there is no grasping of any object at any time in its entirety as its own essential nature (*ātmasvarūpa*), nothing whatsoever would be perceptible.
He demonstrates this: "For it is not the case that whatever exists in whatever manner [is perceived by the senses]," and so forth.

Even a grain of rice (*vrīhi*) does not possess perceptibility in its entirety, because it is not grasped by the senses in the way that it actually exists; for one perceives only the husk with the sense organ, yet that alone is not the rice, since the kernel and other parts are not seen, and even the kernel alone is not the rice, since the broken grains (*kuṇḍaka*) and so forth are not seen, and so on—because only one among form, taste, smell, or touch is the object of the sense organ. Therefore, he says: "Because the visual and other sensory perceptions of rice and the like function by grasping only the form and other qualities of the husk, the kernel, and so forth."

It might be thought: "Since form is merely form, it must therefore be perceptible. But this is incorrect, because the perception of form and so forth functions only as long as there is the grasping of form. Furthermore, its states—form, taste, smell, sound, and touch—are fourfold, known by their literal names as waking (*jāgrat*), sleeping (*supta*), deep sleep (*suṣupta*), and the fourth (*turīya*).
These exist in many ways:

as pleasure, pain, delusion, and purity; as the liberation from *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*; as the divisions of the worlds above, across, and below; or as the states of being conscious, unconscious, and insentient.
These [states] are indeed fixed by the sequence of liberation;

or, omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) is the fourth [state], which is unobscured, free from the obstacle of delusion, and the absolute cessation of sleep—the very nature of the Self (*ātmasvatattva*) that is distinct from states such as waking associated with sleep;
that alone is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).

Form and the other [sensory objects] exist in a state of mutual inseparability; how, then, could the apprehension of form alone among them be a perception that corresponds to reality? Thus, there is no such thing as perception.
Therefore, this is established: everything consists of everything else, being merely the manifestation of the single cause that is the essential nature of consciousness.
Thus ends the section on the earth and the other elements.
On the earth,
on the earth, or in water;
likewise, the sense organs.

And its four states—waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth—are named according to their literal meanings; these states manifest in many ways as pleasure, pain, delusion, and purity; as the predominance of *sattva*, *rajas*, *tamas*, or liberation; as the distinctions of the worlds above, across, and below; or as the conditions of being conscious, unconscious, or insentient.
These are indeed fixed by way of the sequence of liberation;

or rather, omniscience is the fourth state, free from the obstacles of obscuration and delusion, the absolute cessation of sleep, the true nature of the Self which is distinct from states such as waking that are connected with sleep;
that alone is the Supreme Self.

Now, for the purpose of demonstrating its very nature, it is said: "And its four states. These are the four states—waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth (turīya)—of that reality of consciousness (caitanya-tattva) just described, which possess names corresponding to their meanings. They are the waking state, the dreaming state, the deep sleep state, and the fourth state; and these are indeed meaningful. Furthermore, they are established in many ways, because, with the exception of the fourth state, each of the three possesses numerous subdivisions due to differences in technical systems (saṃjñā) and differences in worldly usage.

The fourth [category], however, is of a single nature due to its purity; or rather, by the power of its own nature, it also manifests in manifold ways through its entire self. As it is said: "Whatever substance undergoes transformation through application (*prayoga*) or spontaneous change (*visrasā*), the Jina knows that exactly as it is; there is no knowledge of that which lacks a mode (*aparyaya*).
(Āvaśyaka-niryukti 794). What are these? They are said to be: pleasure, pain, delusion, and purity; those known as the liberation from *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.

And the functions of these three [qualities] are as follows, according to their respective order: serenity, lightness, procreation, attachment, exhilaration, and joy; suffering, emaciation, burning, piercing, paralysis, agitation, aversion, obstruction, depression, destruction, disgust, dejection, and heaviness.
But for the fourth [quality], it is pure consciousness, which illumines all states of being within the entire manifold of its own transformations.

Alternatively, they may be the divisions of the worlds above, across, and below, respectively: the world above is the waking state, the world across is the dreaming state, the world below is the deep sleep state, and the undivided state is the fourth state (turiya).

Or, there are the states of being with perception, without perception, and without consciousness: those with perception and possessing mind—gods, humans, hell-beings, five-sensed animals—are awake; those without perception who are asleep include the earth, water, fire, air, plants, and two-, three-, four-, and five-sensed beings lacking mind; and those in deep sleep include wood, walls, and so forth. Existence (*bhāva*) is mere becoming; it is the fourth state (*turīyāvasthā*), undifferentiated everywhere.
Thus, its four [states] are of one and the same nature.
Alternatively, whatever substance transforms into whatever various states through application (*prayoga*) or spontaneous evolution (*visrasā*), it is [defined by] that application.
The Jina knows that [object] in such a way; there is no cognition of the non-particular (aparyaya). (Āvaśyaka-niryukti 794;
see p.
12, l. 19; *lokā avibhāgā*, manuscript reading).
The states of consciousness, unconsciousness, volition, and the state [beyond them]...

Here it is argued: "Since that very Self, whose nature is indivisible, possesses four states, and since there is no distinction of time, all four—named the first, second, third, and fourth—would be simultaneous. This is incorrect, because these states are fixed according to the sequence of liberation; or rather, omniscience is the fourth. The state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), in which consciousness has become stable, is the second state, called "sleep" (*supta*), because its impurities have been liberated. The third consists of false vision (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and so forth. The third [in this context] consists of right vision, knowledge, and conduct (*samyag-darśana-jñāna-cāritra*), due to its proximity to liberation. Omniscience is the fourth.

Furthermore, that fourth [state] is characterized by the removal of the obstacles of delusion and obscuration (*nirāvaraṇamohavighna*). It is called *nirāvaraṇamohavighna* because the obstacles of the veils of knowledge and perception (*jñānadarśanāvaraṇa*) and delusion (*moha*) have departed from it. This is because delusion itself is like a great sleep; thus, in those with only one sense-faculty and so forth, consciousness—which arises based on the sense-faculties as both the physical form (*nirvṛtti*) and the instruments (*upakaraṇa*)—is in a waking state due to its nature of investigating through perception and other means. It consists of the instrument and the conscious self, like a substantial person (*dravyapuruṣa*). And because the object is likewise of such a true nature, it is indeed knowledge itself.

Likewise, even the state of sleep is indeed knowledge; for doubt and so forth are states of slight sleep because they consist of such-and-such [partial] reality. Similarly, error is also indeed knowledge because it consists of such-and-such [partial] reality. Sleep is particularly [characterized] by the arising of *styānarddhi* (torpor), but in a general sense, it is the sleep of all deluded living beings who possess false view and lack right conduct. As it has been said: "The non-munis are always asleep; the munis are always awake" (*Ācārāṅga Sūtra* 1.3).

Thus, that fourth state is absolute liberation (*kaivalya*), free from the obstacles of veiling and delusion; it is a vision distinct from the obstructions of passion, hatred, and delusion—a pure and perfect unity. If one asks what its nature is, it is the absolute cessation of sleep.

The explanation of that [verse] is as follows: the true nature (*svatattva*) of the Self is distinct from the states such as waking and so forth associated with sleep. There are three states associated with sleep, known as waking, dreaming, and deep sleep; the Self's own true nature, which is distinct from each of those, is pure consciousness (*caitanya*).
By means of this alternative explanation, it should be understood that the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), being liberated and omniscient, is thus explained.
Here, [the author] says: *vibhāgā*... [fragmentary].
The state of deep sleep is the second because of its nature of non-duality; it is the second because of its being beyond the second. (Variant readings: *dvitīyāt* and *dvitīyā*).
In this context, because it is free from impurities, it is the second [state]; there may also be a reading stating that the second consists of false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and so forth.

For the sake of all beings, through the power of the subsidence and destruction (*kṣayopaśama*) of the great sleep of delusion, consciousness (*caitanya*)—which has as its conditions the sense organs of the body and its accessories—is the waking state, because its nature consists in the examination of perception and other means of knowledge. It is of the nature of the instrument (*karaṇa*) and of the conscious self (*cetana*), like the substantial person (*dravyapuruṣa*); and because the object exists in such and such a way according to reality, it is indeed knowledge itself.

Likewise, even the state of sleep is indeed cognition, because the object is perceived in such and such a way through slight sleep; similarly, even error is indeed cognition, because it consists of the object being perceived in such and such a way.
Thus, [it is] always manifest.
The nature of that which always exists is indeed [realized] by another means.

We shall explain the nature of the instrument (*karaṇātman*) and the nature of the effect (*kāryātman*). Regarding that, first, starting from "great delusion" (*mahāmoha*) up to "the nature of the instrument": because living beings who possess wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and lack right conduct (*acāritra*) are asleep when there is the arising of delusion regarding vision and conduct (*darśana-cāritramoha*), therefore great delusion itself is sleep. When that [delusion] arises, there is slumber; when it ceases, there is awakening.
As it has been said: "But when the mind is exhausted, the selves of the intellect (*buddhyātman*) are possessed by fatigue..."
When [the senses] turn away from their objects, then the person sleeps. (Carakasamhitā 1.21)
35. Thus.

The subsidence-cum-destruction (*kṣayopaśama*) of that sleep occurs through the destruction of those eighteen types of destructive karma (*ghātikarman*) that have arisen and attained the state of human transformation, and through the subsidence of those that have not yet arisen; from this, the power of attainment (*labdhiśakti*) arises within that very person, consisting of the various modalities of knowledge, perception, and energy. By means of that power of the subsidence-cum-destruction of destructive karma, the eyes are produced in the form of a black antelope's pupil with variegated eyelashes, and the remaining sense organs are produced according to their respective forms. These same organs are further assisted as instruments (*upakaraṇa*) by various shapes such as the *masūraka* (lentil-shaped), the *kṣurapra* (razor-shaped), the *atimuktaka* (creeper-bud-shaped), the *candraka* (moon-shaped), and the *yavanālikā* (barley-stalk-shaped). Consequently, consciousness (*caitanya*), which is the functional activity (*upayoga*), arises conditioned by that—conditioned by the senses produced by attainment and the instrumental organs. Attainment and functional activity constitute the "substantial sense organ" (*bhāvendriya*). (Tattvārtha-sūtra 2.17)

Because of this statement, and because it consists of the examination of perception and so forth—by the inclusion of "and so forth," it consists of inference and scripture—it is the waking state. That very state, consisting of the instruments [of cognition], is the intermediate state between the states of deep sleep and waking; it is the "sleeping-waking" state, wherein the vision of dreams occurs.
As it has been said: "One does not see a dream while asleep; one sees a dream while engaged in wakefulness amidst sleep" (Bhagavatī Sūtra 16.5.577).

And that [state] as well, being conscious by nature, is indeed knowledge—just like a waking state—even though there is no discernment due to sleep, as in the case of a physical object or a person; for it is a specific kind of sleep. Because it possesses the nature of consciousness, it is consciousness itself, just like the waking state; since the self is conscious by nature, it is consciousness alone, because that very object [of experience] has the nature of awakening. This is like the states of doubt and so forth, or like sleep, which are designated as having the instruments [of cognition] as their nature, yet are essentially consciousness by nature. This is because that very object has the nature of being awake.

It is like the case of a "substance-person" (*dravyapuruṣa*): just as one who has been or will be a king is called simply "the king"—because of the observation of marks such as the lines of wheels and lotuses on his hands and feet—so too, that very body which has experienced or will experience kingship is the king; likewise, the instruments (*karaṇa*), whether sleeping or waking, are essentially the conscious self (*cetana-ātman*).

Or, the substance-person (*dravyapuruṣa*) is non-engaged; because it is not engaged with that object of knowledge, just as a substance-person who is non-engaged with boiled rice—though transformed into the state of "not-self"—is not transformed into the cognition of the nature of the self, and is thus merely the substance-self (*dravyātman*); likewise, even when devoid of the application of knowledge (*jñānopayoga*), the instrumental-self (*karaṇātman*) is indeed the conscious-self (*cetanātman*).

If it is argued that, in this case, because the Supreme Self consists of pure consciousness and is the self of all, its state as possessing organs (karaṇātman) is untenable, we say: no. Even though consciousness is the self of all, the state of waking is that knowledge which belongs to one who has arisen from sleep while still having residual sleep, like one who has not fully awakened; whereas the state of omniscience is like that of one whose sleep has completely vanished. This is the distinction between these two states: that of the Supreme Self and that of possessing organs.

It might be thought that because the nature of the object is not grasped, the state of the instrument (the senses) is utterly dissimilar to the Supreme Self; but this is incorrect. Why? Because the object, by its very nature, is nothing but cognition. For that object, since it has been established that the creation of the Puruṣa possesses manifold forms, is itself a transformation of the single Self and thus consists of many forms, as it exists in various ways according to its respective modes—being "such and such" in its essence. Therefore, even that cognition of the instrument is indeed cognition, or rather, the instrument itself is cognition, because it is a transformation of cognition.
Thus, first, the waking state consists of the instruments (karaṇātman).

As for knowledge itself, when the mind is fatigued, the intellects (buddhyātman) become possessed of weariness, and the agents of action (karmātman) become possessed of exhaustion; such is the reading in the Caraka-saṃhitā.
"When [the senses] turn away from their objects, then the person sleeps" (Caraka-saṃhitā 1.21.35). [The text reads] *annāṣṭavidha* in both the Bhāṣya and the Ya manuscript.

Regarding the eighteen-fold nature of the state arising from destruction-cum-subsidence (*kṣayopaśamika*) which was previously mentioned, he speaks in order to define its divisions: "The acquisitions of knowledge, non-knowledge, and vision have four, three, and five varieties respectively; as do right belief, conduct, restraint, and non-restraint. (2.5)

"...the four cognitions (*jñāna*), the three non-cognitions (*ajñāna*), the three visions (*darśana*), and the five attainments (*labdhi*)— [these arise] from the destruction of the rise of all-pervading (*sarvaghāti*) *spardhakas*, and from the subsidence of those very same [all-pervading ones], while there is the rise of partial (*deśaghāti*) *spardhakas*, it is called 'subsidence-cum-destruction' (*kṣāyopaśamika*). Thus it is stated in the *Sarvārthasiddhi* commentary on the *Tattvārthādhigamasūtra*, composed by the venerable teacher Devanandin, at [sūtra] 2.5.
Energy, non-conceptuality,
right regard,
and the practice of wakefulness through the sutras.

"Venerable Sir, does one see a dream while asleep? Does one see a dream while awake? Or does one see a dream while both asleep and awake? "Gautama, one does not see a dream while asleep; one does not see a dream while awake; one sees a dream while both asleep and awake. This is the reading in the *Bhagavatīsūtra*. [The opponent argues: The conscious self, because it is asleep, is like a material person (*dravyapuruṣa*);

likewise, even non-determination (*anadhyavasāya*) is a specific sleep and is merely knowledge, because it possesses the nature of consciousness, just like the waking state. [The author replies: It is like the state of being both conscious and unconscious, such as doubt and the like, or like the state of being asleep.
Volition alone is the self; volition indeed is the nature of the self,
just as [it is said] regarding the king’s own self.
Because of the [scriptural] statement, the Self alone is joined with contraction and expansion; it is not joined with non-Selfhood,
for the individual soul is not joined with non-Selfhood.
Of him alone, O Lord, of him alone, O Great Sage, [is] the self... [of] the Vaiśeṣika.

Just as this [dream] is knowledge, so too is the entire waking state; the mere onset of the sleeping state is the sleeping state itself, and that too is indeed knowledge. Slight sleep consists of doubt and the like, and this [state]—being of the nature of the instruments—is also knowledge consisting of doubt and so forth. By the inclusion of "and the like," error and non-apprehension are also meant. And even though it is the sleeping state, slight sleep is indeed knowledge, because, as before, the object possesses its reality in such and such a way within the totality of all things.

"Could it be a post? Could it be a person?"—because the commonality of verticality is a real entity (*vastu*). If it is a post due to specific features such as being a hollow abode for birds, and if it is a person due to specific features such as rising, sitting, moving the hands and feet, then in both cases that entity is such and such by virtue of its reality as either a post or a person.

Likewise, error (*viparyaya*) is also simply a form of cognition, occurring when an object is perceived in a manner contrary to its true nature—such as through the misapprehension of a post as a person; this is explained by the commentator in the same way. The proof is: "The conscious self exists because it possesses sleep, like a material person.
