The explanation is exactly as before: the state of sleeping or waking belongs only to that which is conscious, never to anything unconscious.

Just as this [state] is knowledge (*jñāna*), so too is non-determination (*anadhyavasāya*). Non-determination is not determination; it is unmanifest cognition (*anabhivyakta-bodha*). This, being distinguished from doubt (*saṃśaya*) and error (*viparyaya*), is sleep; because of its state of being asleep, it is indeed knowledge, since it consists of consciousness (*cetanā-ātmakatva*), just like the waking state. Just as the waking state is indeed knowledge because it consists of consciousness, so too is non-determination.

From "consciousness and unconsciousness" (*cetanācetanāt*): because that very same thing is both conscious and unconscious, due to its having much consciousness and little consciousness; and by the analysis (*vigraha*) of the compound as "that which is conscious is also unconscious," it follows from either consciousness or unconsciousness, just like doubt and so forth. By the inclusion of "and so forth" (*ādi*), error (*viparyaya*) and certainty (*nirṇaya*) are included; just as in those cases, so too from consciousness and unconsciousness, knowledge arises. Likewise, even non-determination (*anadhyavasāya*)—such as the physical sense-organ, earth, and so on—is indeed knowledge in its causal nature, because it consists of the state of deep sleep, like one who has fallen into a sleep induced by drinking wine mixed with *hālāhala* poison, which is like non-determination.

That which is the Puruṣa is indeed that [intellect], because it has been transformed into the nature of the Self (*ātmatva*) by Him, due to its being of the same substance as Him, just as the earth, water, and so forth [become] rice; because it is His effect, like cloth and threads; and because it did not exist without Him, there is no determination [of the intellect] apart from Him—or rather, it is like one who is asleep. For just as one who is asleep, though possessing indistinct consciousness during activities such as inhalation and exhalation, is nonetheless a knower, so too this non-determination is simply the instrument-aspect of the Self, being a more manifest state of sleep; the meaning is that it is a specific kind of sleep. Thus, the instrument-aspect (*karaṇātman*) has been explained.
In this reading, its inherent appropriateness (*svārasya*) should be understood to mean that "it too has the nature of an instrument" (*karaṇātmā*).
[The variants are: *valanādi* (Bhāṣya), *ḍe* (Ḍe), *līṃ* (Lī), *raṃ* (Raṃ), *hī* (Hī).
bahucetanabhāṣya,
bahucetanayā,
from [the word ending in] ṇa, modification, Prakrit.

And just as this is so, even non-determination (*anadhyavasāya*)—such as the physical sense-organ (*dravyendriya*), earth, and so forth—is indeed knowledge in its causal nature, because it consists of the state of deep sleep (*suṣuptāvasthā*). It is like the sleep induced by drinking liquor mixed with *hālāhala* poison; it is non-determination because that very person has been transformed into that [state] by virtue of being the self, since it is the substance thereof, just as the earth, water, and so forth [are the substance] of rice; because it is the effect thereof, just as cloth is the effect of threads; and because it did not exist without that, just as [there is no cloth] apart from [the threads].
(In this context, there may also be the reading *nidrāsuṣuptavat*.)
Now, the nature of the effect (*kāryātman*) is explained: "Just as this," and so forth.

Just as this aforementioned cognition—consisting of non-determination (*anadhyavasāya*), error (*viparyaya*), doubt (*saṃśaya*), and non-erroneous perception (*avitatha-pratyakṣa*)—is consciousness (*caitanya*), so too is the matter of the sense organs (*dravyendriya*) such as earth and the rest, which is intended to be insentient (*acetana*) and devoid of determination (*apagatādhyavasāya*), the effect-natured self (*ātman*). This is because it has been transformed into the state of selfhood by the self itself; such reasons will be stated hereafter.

And that state of sleep is the material sense-organ (*dravyendriya*); the structural (*nirvṛtti*) and instrumental (*upakaraṇa*) material sense-organs were explained previously, and they are transformed by the person as his own self;
whereas the functional sense-organ (*bhāvendriya*) is the self itself, when it is possessed of attainment (*labdhi*) or engaged in its operation (*upayukta*).

Earth and the other elements, having undergone transformation through the process of evolution, consist of earth, water, fire, air, plants, and beings with two sense-faculties; this state of being their effect is the state of deep sleep (*suṣuptāvasthā*). This too is essentially of the nature of consciousness (*jñānātmaka*), because it is the very essence of the state of deep sleep, just like one who has fallen into a deep sleep induced by drinking wine infused with *hālāhala* poison. Just as a person, having drunk wine infused with the *hālāhala* poison that kills instantly, falls under the power of the sleep induced by it and, while remaining conscious, perceives nothing at all during deep sleep—in the same way, the earth and other elements, which are the effects of the material sense-faculties (*dravyendriya*), are of the nature of deep sleep.

Alternatively, it is like non-apprehension (*anadhyavasāya*): just as the state called non-apprehension, which is distinct from the previously explained states such as waking and so forth, is indeed cognition, so too the state consisting of the effect—the substance-faculties, earth, and so on—is indeed cognition.

Just as there is a specific degree of unconsciousness resulting from the progressive intensification of the distinctions among the sub-types of *nidrā-nidrā*, *nidrā*, *pracalā-pracalā*, *pracalā*, and *styānarddhi-vedanīya*—which obscure the power of knowledge—or just as omniscience is attained at the limit of the excellence of consciousness-purity brought about by the removal of specific obscurations, so too the earth and other elements, having reached the limit of the intensity of the obscuration of consciousness, are indeed knowledge itself. Since the eightfold karma with its subdivisions attains identity with the transformation of the person (*puruṣa-pariṇāma*), they possess the nature of knowledge; thus, consciousness alone is the [nature] of the earth and other elements. This is the "consciousness of the insentient" (*sāyacetanā*). *Praśastapādabhāṣya*.
See page 185,
line 3; here, there may also be the reading "like sleep and deep slumber" (*nidrā-suṣuptavat*), even without the qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*).
Specifically,
as in [the case of] *nidrā-nidrā*, *pracalā-pracalā*, *styāna-ṛddhi-vīrya-āhāra-āvaraṇa-bheda*.
In this context, there may also be the reading "ṣaṣṭhatathāvaraṇā," or perhaps "sārvajñavad vā pra°.
Therefore, he says: "That which is the *puruṣa* is precisely that substance, such as the sense organs and the earth, because it has been transformed into the nature of the self (*ātmatva*)."

"What, then, is the difference here between the transformer (*pariṇāmaka*) and the transformed (*pariṇamya*)? To this he says: "Because of being that substance" (*taddravyatvāt*). That very [substance] is the substance; "that-substance" refers to action (*karman*) along with its various modifications. Because of being that substance—just as in the case of earth, water, and so forth, and rice (*vrīhi*)—just as earth, water, and so forth are indeed the rice because they have been transformed into the state of rice, and because of being that substance, rice is indeed earth and so forth because it has been transformed into the nature of earth and so forth by means of earth and so forth, and rice is indeed earth and so forth; likewise, earth and the other elements are the Person (*puruṣa*) himself, who consists of consciousness.

Furthermore, that which is the Person (puruṣa) is indeed that [earth and so forth], because it is its effect; for whatever is the effect of something is indeed that very thing, like a cloth and its threads. Just as a cloth is the threads themselves because it is their effect, so too earth and the rest are the Person itself, since it has already been established that they are preceded by the Person. Moreover, because [the world] does not exist without Him, that which does not exist without something else is indeed that very thing; this is because of its existence and because it occupies the same location, just as a jar is identical to its own nature, its color, and so on.

The Self, being consciousness, through its reversal from the state of deep sleep within earth and the other elements, becomes engaged with passion and the like; by means of its own independence of application (*upayoga*), it binds itself to itself and renders itself dependent. Through the bondage of karma, it repeatedly assumes the state of possessing form and so forth, and repeatedly attains the state of possessing form and so forth in the form of subtle and gross bodies. Just as form and the rest are indeed earth and the rest, and earth and the rest are indeed form and the rest—since they do not exist apart from one another, they are mutually identical—so too is the Person (*puruṣa*) indeed even wood and such.

Furthermore, because it does not exist apart from that; for whatever does not exist apart from something else is indeed that very thing, just as, for example, the nature of a jar consists of its own essence and its location.

"Its location" (*tad-deśa*) means the location belonging to it; the location of that person is his own constituent part, his very self, just like the street, the person, the hand, and so forth, belonging to a person on the road. The reason is that the creation has that [person] as its antecedent, which constitutes its being located in that place.

Whatever occupies a particular location is of that very same essential nature (*svatattva*). How so? Just as the states of being new, young, middle-aged, or old belong to the jar’s own essential nature; likewise, even the insentient [elements] such as earth are nothing but the essential nature of the sentient Puruṣa. As it has been stated and established through reasoning: "The transformation of earth and the other elements is merely the transformation of the Puruṣa—just like the transformation from the formless, subtle, and imperceptible causal state into the formed, gross, and perceptible state, which possesses shape, color, and other qualities. (Bhūmyapādi-prakaraṇa).

Just as [the word] "bahuvrīhi" itself, by virtue of being a *bahuvrīhi* compound, does not require [another] *bahuvrīhi* operation upon it— because that [operation] would be redundant (*prabhāvāt*) and because it occupies that very position— so too is the case with the self-nature (*svatattva*) of a jar, such as its being newly perceived (*pratyagrāditva*).

The self, being distinct from consciousness, functions in a manner contrary to its state of deep sleep; through the application of passion and other afflictions, it binds itself by means of its own volitional agency and renders itself dependent. Through the bondage of karma, it repeatedly assumes a state of possessing form and so forth, beginninglessly and endlessly;
it attains the state of possessing form and so forth in the form of subtle and gross bodies, beginninglessly and endlessly, [just as] one perceives the nature of a jar and so on.
See the state of being a person in the Madhyapurāṇa, page 176, line 3.
Regarding the "knower of the subtle" (*sūkṣmajña*),

it is further introduced in that very same [text] for the purpose of establishing the existence of *saṃsāra* through reasoning, beginning with "The self [is] from consciousness" (*caitanyād ātmā*) and continuing up to "possessing an infinity of revolutions" (*viparivartānantyavat*).

The state of consciousness is *caitanya*; therefore, the self (*ātman*) exists in a state opposite to that of earth and the other elements during deep sleep. Consequently, it is in a slightly purified state. This is because consciousness undergoes transformations such as passion (*rāga*); since passion and the like are the causes of bondage, [the self] is "engaged" (*upayukta*) through the independence of its engagement (*upayoga-svātantrya*). For engagement is indeed consciousness; its independence consists in its being the agent (*kartṛtva*). False view, lack of restraint, negligence, passions, and activity are the causes of bondage (Tattvārtha Sūtra 8).

Because of this statement, since false view (*mithyādarśana*) and the other [passions] consist of the impurities (*kaṣāya*) such as attachment (*rāga*), the soul binds itself by means of its own independence and thereby renders itself dependent. And by that very bondage created by itself, it is rendered dependent, just as a drunkard is rendered dependent by the liquor he himself has drunk; or like a person spun around on a swing whose momentum has been filled by himself, one is whirled about by the swing of karma. Through the bondage of karma, one undergoes the state of possessing form and so forth, beginninglessly and endlessly.

Thus, both of these are beginningless and endless in terms of their continuity (*santati*), yet they exist as substantial entities (*dravyārthatayā*). As it has been said: "O Venerable One! Is the hen first, or the egg? Is the egg first, or the hen? Roha! From where does that which is the hen come? From the egg. And from where does that which is the egg come? From the hen. Thus, Roha! Both of these exist before and after; both of these are eternal states (*bhāva*). This, O Roha, is a non-successive sequence (*aṇāṇupuvvī*)," so says the *Bhagavatīsūtra*. 1.

6.53 "Venerable Sir, do all living beings [in the past] serve one another as mother, father, brother, wife, son, or daughter? "Gautama, [it is] not once, or rather, an infinite number of times. (Bhagavatī Sūtra 12)
7.458 And that [object] is twofold: form and so forth, both subtle and gross.

Karma and so forth are subtle; by the inclusion of "and so forth," this refers to inhalation, exhalation, speech, mind, and the like, as well as the kārmaṇa, taijasa, and āhāraka bodies. These are subtle by virtue of being of the nature of that [karma]. On the other hand, gross matter such as earth and so forth, as well as the physical (audārika) and transformational (vaikriya) bodies and consciousness, are gross because they are of the nature of effects. This is like the infinite transformations of a substance, such as clay, a pot, potsherds, fragments, gravel, dust, powder, atoms, and subatomic particles, or the sequence of form and so forth.

Now, if it is thus beginningless and endless, and if the lack of discrimination (*aviveka*) is equal for both that which possesses the nature of consciousness and that which possesses form and so forth, for what reason is it said that everything consists of knowledge (*jñāna*), and why is it not said that everything consists of form and so forth? There is no fault even in accepting the latter; rather, this very point is precisely what one intends to establish. For instance: since the coming-to-be (*bhavana*) is possible only for that which is conscious, and because of its persistence therein, the coming-to-be is established by means of space and time.
However, if one were to accept [the existence of] objects distinct from that [consciousness], the coming-to-be of a jar would not be established.

Since consciousness possesses the nature of the body by virtue of its identity with it, this has already been established through the very process [of analysis]; nevertheless, it is stated as a formal proposition for the sake of easy comprehension: "Consciousness assumes the form of beginningless and endless subtle and gross bodies, etc., and possesses qualities such as form."

Why? Because it has the nature of an effect (*kāryātmatvāt*). And its having the nature of an effect is established because its transformation into the various forms of earth and so forth, such as color and so forth, has already been proven; here, however, it is being proven that this [transformation] occurs without beginning or end. Whatever has the nature of an effect is seen to undergo transformation without beginning or end, just as in the case of clay and a jar, and so forth: the substance becomes clay, clay becomes a jar, the jar becomes shards, and from there, in sequence, fragments, gravel, dust, powder, atoms, and then color and so forth; and from color and so forth, again in reverse order, atoms and so forth, until the endless cycle of transformation back to the state of substance and so forth.

Because of the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), this same kind of becoming—which, like transformation (*viparivarta*), consists in the non-abandonment of its own genus through qualities, actions, existence, and so forth—cannot be established otherwise than as previously stated. This is because, if one were to admit an absolute distinction between space and time, the faults that will be mentioned immediately below would ensue; therefore, it must be understood that it is not otherwise. Why? [From the *Prakaraṇa*].

"Venerable Sir, was the egg first and the hen later? Or was the hen first and the egg later? "Rohā! From what did that egg come? "Venerable Sir, from the hen. "From what did that hen come? "Venerable Sir, from the egg.

"In this very way, Rohā, both that egg and that hen were previously existent, and they are existent later; these two entities are eternal. This, Rohā, is a non-succession," so says the reading in the *Bhagavatī-sūtra*.
Whence [comes] the hen? And [how] is it eternal?
See page 4, note 2.

"By way of being a father, by way of being a mother, by way of being a brother... O Venerable One! Has this soul (jīva) previously been born as a mother, a father, a brother, a sister, a wife, a son, a daughter, or a daughter-in-law to all other souls? Yes, Gautama! [It has been so] up to infinite times," such is the reading in the *Bhagavatīsūtra*.

Consciousness, because it possesses the nature of an effect, is like the infinite transformations of clay, jars, potsherds, fragments, gravel, dust, particles, atoms, and so forth, including the substances such as form and other atoms.

Now, if it is thus both beginningless and endless, and if there is no distinction between consciousness and the possession of form and other qualities—since they are equal in this regard—why is it said that everything is "of the nature of knowledge" (*jñānātmaka*), and why is it not said that everything is "of the nature of form and other qualities"? There is no fault even in accepting [the latter], because it is precisely this point that one intends to establish.

For it is thus: since the coming-into-being (*bhavana*) belongs only to that which is known, and because [the effect] follows from that [cause], the coming-into-being is established through space and time;
however, if one were to grasp an entity distinct from that [cause], the coming-into-being of a jar would not be established, due to the absence of its own attainment.
Because of its nature as the self;
see page 188, line 1 of the Bhāṣya on the Tuṭi.
Here the opponent says: "But if this is so," and so forth.

But if this is so—given that [the relationship] is beginningless like that of a hen and its egg, and given its endlessness, and given that the word *kukkuṭi* (hen) signifies a "wretched hutch" (*kutsitā kuṭiḥ*) while the word *kukkuṭi* is also explained as meaning "body"—then since there is no distinction for one who is liberated, as both the transformation into the cognition of objects such as form and the possession of the nature of consciousness and form are equal, for what purpose is it said that [the soul] consists of knowledge (*jñānātmaka*), and what is the reason that it is not said that everything consists of form and so forth? Or rather, the specific cause [for the distinction] should be stated. Showing this, the opponent says: "But if this is so, even though it is beginningless and endless," and so on; the meaning has already been explained.

The Teacher says: "Even in this manner of acceptance, there is no fault whatsoever. Why? Because it is precisely this meaning that is intended to be established, since He consists of four states; for that very reason, He is called by such forms as 'form' (*rūpa*), 'substance' (*dravya*), 'senses' (*indriya*), and 'earth' (*pṛthivī*). And since this was stated prior to the creation, [one might ask]: 'Is it not thus? [To which] he replies: 'Because of the beginninglessness [of the relationship]. Furthermore, since the present topic concerns the bringing about of unity between the conscious and the unconscious, why is the term 'knower' (*jña*) used as a qualifier, and why is the term 'independent' (*svatantra*) used? [The Teacher continues: "The knower is the Person (*puruṣa*); and if this [universe] consists of Him, then He alone is independent. Thus, for what purpose is the mention of the 'knower' as a qualifier and the mention of 'independence'?
The Teacher says: "For instance," and so forth.

It has been stated that "existence" (*bhāva*) is that which "comes to be" (*bhavati*). However, in order to demonstrate the essential nature of existence, the term "knower" (*jña*) is employed to indicate that "that which comes to be" is what is to be expressed. This too is explained by the passage beginning with "for instance. And having established this, the previously mentioned objection—that there would be the fault of the absence of coming-to-be (*bhavana*) due to the difference in space and time, as will be discussed—is refuted. Since the coming-to-be of the knower alone is logically tenable, and because of its continuity through the presence of all places, times, and selves, coming-to-be is established by means of space and time. For indeed, it is possible to say, "the object comes to be."

Regarding the phrase "different from that" (*tadbhinna*) and so forth: if one were to include as [the meaning of] "entity" (*padārtha*) things that are distinct from earth and the other elements due to differences in space and time, then otherwise, even this manifestation of a jar—which is well-established through direct perception—would not be established as an entity (*bhāva*).
See page 14.
...due to the fault of the non-existence of the cultivation of differentiation; it would pervade the self,
it would pervade the self.
First, by means of the cognition of spatial distinction, there is no existence of a jar when there is a distinction of its parts such as the neck;
nor is there clay when there is only a single part such as whiteness; nor is there earth when there is a distinction of [its constituent] stones and so forth.

Existence (*sattva*) is not a single substance because of the distinctions of earth and so forth, nor is it a single [entity] because of the distinctions of qualities and actions, or because of the distinctions among substances and so on.

Even by virtue of the cognition of temporal distinction, since there is an indefinable becoming at every moment, which one is the "becoming of the jar"? For when there is a difference in states distinguished by time—such as clay having become rice, water, and so forth—the clay no longer exists; subsequently, too, there is the becoming of shards, dust, rice, and so forth.

Since there is no single existence (*sattva*) that consists of all things such as jars and so forth, and since individuality itself consists of mutual non-existence (*itaretarāsattva*), how could there be the becoming of an entity such as a jar?
For it is by means of distinctions such as color and so forth—extending to the limit of all possible distinctions—that one establishes that there is only consciousness (*vijñānamātra*).

How so? First, regarding the cognition of spatial differentiation (*deśabheda*), and so forth: since there is a difference between the neck, back, belly, base, lips, and so on—which are distinct in location—and the shards of the pot and other fragments, down to their ultimate atoms (*paramāṇu*), their qualities such as color-form (*rūpa*), and even their state of being indefinable (*nirupākhya*), the existence of the jar as a whole is not established; this is the sense.
Likewise, when there is no single part such as "white" or "yellow," earth does not exist as a distinct entity from stones and the like.

[The opponent argues: "It is not a substance (*dravya*) because of the distinctions of earth, water, fire, air, and so forth, nor because of the distinctions of qualities (*guṇa*) and actions (*karman*). For that very same substance, due to the distinctions of qualities such as color and actions such as motion, up to the distinction of being indefinable (*nirupākhya*), and because of the absence of a collection and the lack of connection, it is not a substance.
Furthermore, because of the distinctions among substances and so forth, and because of the plurality of substances, qualities, and actions, existence (*sattva*) is not one.
Thus, insofar as there is a difference in location, the existence of a jar would not occur, since substances and the rest are untenable."
Substance [is established] through its connection with [other categories].

Even by means of the cognition of a difference in time, since there is an indescribable becoming at every moment, which [of these] could be the "becoming of a jar"? For it is impossible for it to consist of form and so forth that are like iron rods utterly unconnected from moment to moment. What is the reason? Because when there is a difference in states distinguished by time—such as rice and the like having become clay, or water and the like—the state of being clay does not exist [according to your view]. According to our doctrine, rice and the like that have become clay, as well as water and the like, remain as one and the same entity throughout the duration of different times, and thus their transformation is logically possible. But according to your doctrine, due to the difference in states distinguished by time, because there is no connection with any new object at every moment, there would be a difference in states such that the rice itself perishes and does not become clay, nor does the water and the like perish and become clay; thus, due to the absence of a seed, the state of being clay would not exist.

And if clay were non-existent, what would the pot be? Or what would the process of becoming (*bhavana*) be? For us, however, because of the persistence of the universal (*sāmānyānvaya*), it is logical that rice and so forth, or water and so forth, become clay, or that a pot becomes [clay], and so on; for even after the pot, there is the becoming of shards, dust, rice, and so forth. Even after the becoming of the pot, the pot itself becomes the shards and so forth; even after the shards and so forth, until they become gravel; and even after the dust and so forth, until they become rice and so forth.
Therefore, the pot and all such things consist of the nature of everything (*sarvātmaka*).

If such a process of becoming (*bhavana*) is not accepted, then—since there is no single existence (*sattva*) according to your own view that consists of everything (such as pots and so forth) and pervades space and time, and since the desired "oneness" is, for you, essentially the non-existence of one thing in another—how could there be a becoming of an entity such as a pot? A pot does not exist in the nature of a cloth, and a cloth does not exist in the nature of a pot; thus, whether spatially or temporally, whether before or after, it is not the same thing. Consequently, neither the cloth nor the pot exists. Since all entities would be individually distinct [from one another], and thus non-existent, what is the pot? Or what is becoming?
The state of water and so forth, the state of dust and so forth, and the state of rice and so forth arise from the state of the earth.
The passage beginning with "ceṣṭasya" is not found in the manuscripts;
however, as for the section starting with "rūpādīti" and so forth, up until the point where it is stated exactly as we have described it:

those who maintain that consciousness-only (vijñānamātratva) exists argue that a jar, being differentiated by spatial distinctions, is differentiated through the differentiation of its form and other qualities, and so on, until it reaches the level of the indefinable (nirupākhyatā); and being differentiated by temporal distinctions, it is differentiated down to the level of the indefinable arising and perishing of the most subtle moment (paramāṇu-kṣaṇa). By thus establishing differentiation even unto the limit of all possible distinctions, they have nevertheless stated, just as we have described, that it is indeed nothing but consciousness-only.

Furthermore, if one were to admit the non-existence of cognition (*jñāna*), then because the seeds for the negation of form and so forth—such as the investigation [of their nature]—would be rootless, there would be contradictions with perception and other means of valid knowledge.

For this very reason, as previously stated, the functioning of cognition occurs everywhere through direct contact, proximity, or remote influence, in relation to the self, the intellect, the senses, light, form, jars, medicinal herbs, food, and so on.
And it is said: "The Person alone is all this—that which has been and that which is to be."
Furthermore, it is established that [the Self] is the lord of immortality, for there is nothing else whatsoever that surpasses it by means of food (Śukla Yajurveda Saṃhitā 31.2).

However, the way in which that [consciousness] is established is as follows: it has been stated, in accordance with our own explanation, that consciousness is a single, undifferentiated unity. Consequently, because it consists of the manifold diversity of the universe—such as form, taste, and so forth, or pots, cloths, and the like—if form and the other qualities were mutually distinct, there would be no continuity within that consciousness; thus, the conceptualization of the distinctions between form, taste, and so forth would be absent, as would the conceptualization of its parts, and the conceptualization of its lack of designation (nirupākhyatva) would be absent. Therefore, it is stated that the state of "consciousness-only" (*vijñānamātratā*) does not hold, exactly as we have described.

Furthermore, if one accepts the non-existence of cognition (*jñāna*), then because the investigation into the seeds for the denial of form and so forth would be rootless, there would be contradictions with perception and other means of knowledge.

For this very reason, as previously stated, the functioning of cognition occurs in relation to the self, the intellect, the sense organs, light, form, the jar, medicinal herbs, food, and so on, through their being either proximate, remote, or acting from afar.
And it has been said:
The Person alone is all this—whatever has been and whatever is to be;
moreover, he is the lord of immortality, that which grows by means of food. (Śukla Yajurveda Saṃhitā 31.2)

Now, if someone were to say: "That cognition (*vijñāna*) is also non-existent because all things are empty," this is incorrect. For if one admits the non-existence of cognition as well, then the refutation of form (*rūpa*) and so forth would lack any basis, such as the investigation [of its nature], and there would be contradictions with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and other means of knowledge. Since the investigation that serves as the basis for the refutation—namely, the claim that "form and so forth do not exist"—itself does not exist, the negation of form and so forth cannot be established. Furthermore, through one's own direct experience, the investigation of form is perceived individually; by the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the experiences of tasting, smelling, touching, and hearing are also perceived. Therefore, there is a contradiction with direct perception.

Because there is contradiction with inference due to the observation of recollection—and by the inclusion of the word "etcetera" [other reasons are implied]—for recollection belongs to an object previously experienced by oneself, not one never experienced;

therefore, it is established that the Self (*ātman*) is the cause, being of the nature of consciousness, unitary, pervading all entities, persisting through changing states. Thus ends the *Vijñānasatyatā*.
Therefore, it is said "as previously stated," and so forth.

Precisely for this reason—because the cause is established through its pervasion of the self and its reversal—the [distinction] is "like what was stated. Because form and the other [objects] consist of that very reality (*tattva*), because they are of the nature of being formed (*rūpaṇātmaka*), and because they are merely particular states of the self whose nature is cognition, this distinction is to be seen everywhere in all entities as something other than the specific benefits derived from that very causal entity: namely, that the intellect (*buddhi*) is the directly and immediately proximate factor for the self in the enjoyment of the specific transformations of entities, both its own and those of others; whereas the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*) is the self itself, [enjoying] both itself and others.

The sense organs (*indriya*) are proximate because they are instruments; illuminations and the like are remote as they are the benefactors of the sense organs; forms and the like are more remote; jars and the like are most remote; and foods—such as medicinal herbs, condiments, ointments, and so forth—are the enhancers that support them by generating acuity in the sense organs through the relationship of the benefited and the benefactor. This applies to all cognitive functions (*jñānavṛtti*) pertaining to all objects; therefore, he says: "In all cases, the cognitive function occurs with respect to the self, the intellect, the sense organs, light, form, jars, medicinal herbs, food, and so forth, due to the causes of proximity, remoteness, and the state of being a benefactor. This is established because of the reason [previously stated]. *Note: The final portion of the sentence appears to be a scribal corruption or a fragment of a commentary on the logical reason.*

The statement "he recites [the mantras] for medicines, ointments, and so forth" is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of this meaning; for this purpose, the Jains cite the previously mentioned very same [text], which serves as an indicator for what is to be stated: "I am one, yet I am many" (Bhagavatīsūtra 18.10).
And so forth. For this reason as well, the worldly person, following that [scriptural tradition], says:

"The Person alone is all this," and so on. The word "eva" (alone) is used for emphasis; because there is no other entity to become, and because it is he himself who becomes as previously described, the term "this" refers to the visible, the tangible, and so on—the objects of the senses. Precisely because of his universal manifestation, he is designated by names such as "Self" (*ātman*) and so forth. Just as a jar, a pot, and the like do not transcend the clay, since everything is non-distinct from the root meanings of "to be" (*bhū*), "to exist" (*as"), and so on, he is the Self of all, meaning his own nature and reality.

He indicates the entire range—whether understood through signs or otherwise—as "all" without exception; for even though its general and particular divisions and sub-divisions are infinite, it is all comprehended by the intellect.
And this is a demonstration by way of location: "all this."

In terms of time, "what has been" and "what is to be" is a demonstration of the past, future, and present, since the word *bhūta* denotes both the present and the past; or [it means] "behold," "look upon.

He is the lord (*īśāna*), the sovereign power over immortality—that is, imperishability—for he is that inexhaustible, undecaying, immortal Person (*puruṣa*) because of the indestructibility of knowledge; the meaning is that he experiences that state of imperishability.
As it has been said: "An infinite fraction of the [conscious] syllable (akṣara) is eternally uncovered in all living beings" (Nandisūtra 42).
And as an illustration of its explanation: "If even that were to be covered, then the soul would become a non-soul;
for even during the dense gathering of clouds, the light of the moon and sun still remains."
*Nandīsūtra* 42:

"Thus" (*iti*) means for the reason that [the soul] grows by means of food (*anna*). Food is that which is eaten, consumed, or ingested; it is the substance of matter (*pudgaladravya*). Because it has been transformed [by the soul] as its very own self (*ātman*) countless times since beginningless time, the soul grows, increases, and accumulates by means of that food, just as a child does through the consumption of butter due to its own nature. This is because one observes the support of knowledge and action [through food], and because of the growth of the instruments (senses) and the body.

As it has been said: "Food is indeed the vital breaths; for this person (*puruṣa*) consists of food. He is called *puruṣa* because he lies within the city (*puri*). None of this is possible for one who lacks knowledge; it 'overgrows'—it grows excessively. Regarding this, [Somila] asks: "Are you one? Are you two? Are you imperishable? Are you indestructible? Are you stable? Are you one who possesses the states of many beings? The reading in the *Bhagavatīsūtra* (Śataka 18) is: "O Somila! I am one, yet I am also that which possesses the states of many beings."

"Are you one? Are you two? Are you many? Are you indestructible? Are you unchanging? Are you immutable? Are you also one who has become manifold through various states of being? "O Śruta! I am one, I am two, and so on, up to being one who has become manifold through various states of being."

For this very reason, through the universal establishment of that [Self], it is designated as "Ātman" and so forth; just as a jar, a pot, and the like are not distinct from clay, because it is the unsurpassed source of everything—starting from the meanings of the roots *bhū* (to be) and *as* (to exist)—it is the Self, the essential nature, and the reality of all things.
See page 4, note 2.
Even if that [space] were to be obstructed by it, then the soul would become a non-soul.
"Even when there is a dense gathering of clouds, the light of the moon and sun still shines. (Nandisūtra 42;
see page 4, note 2).
"Because of the reversal of the seasons, [the sacrifice] is supported by food;
the moon is indeed food, and the vital breaths are food; he approaches both for the sake of non-repetition," as stated in the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.10.9.1.

Nor is there anything else [to be said]. Furthermore, for this very reason—as expressed in the passage beginning with "for this very reason"—there is the establishment of his omniscience (*sarvatva*) as the essential nature of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna-svarūpa*); and by means of that well-established omniscience, he possesses the designation of "Self" (*ātman*) and so forth.

The *ātman* is so called because it constantly moves (*atati*), goes, knows, and transforms; *sattva* is the state of being (*bhāva*) of that which exists (*sat*). The meaning is that it itself becomes existent, or alternatively, that it always exists as it truly is.
The *puruṣa* (Person) is so called because he dwells (*śayana*) within the body or the world, which consists of conceptual constructions manifested by himself.

He is a *pudgala* because of filling (*pūraṇa*) and dissolving (*galana*); or alternatively, a *pudgala* because he swallows (*gilati*) the person (*pumāṃs*). This means that, by dividing [the self] into the soul and the body, through the relationship of enjoyer and enjoyed, and through increase and decrease, or arising and destruction—that is, through filling and dissolving—he is born with various states; thus he is a *jantu* (living being).

Because it sustains the ten vital breaths (prāṇas)—namely, the five faculties, mind, speech, body, strength, life-span, inhalation, and exhalation—it is called a "possessor of breath" (prāṇin) and a "living being" (jīva); such designations as these are applicable to everything, since there is no contradiction in its being designated by this or that particular attribute.

Just as jars, pots, and the like do not transcend clay—meaning that jars, pots, and so forth do not emerge from such verbal roots as *bhū*, *as*, and *vṛt* (in the sense of "becoming," "existing," and "abiding") because they do not transcend their state of being (*bhavana*)—and since all verbal roots have the sense of "becoming" and so forth as their primary meaning, in the same way, the agent whose nature is knowledge exists, is, and abides, because he does not transcend his state of being as the nature of knowledge.

Therefore he says: "Because it is the unsurpassed essence of everything, starting with those whose meaning is 'to be' (bhū-asti-artha). The roots *as*, *bhū*, *vid*, *pad*, and *vṛt*—with *sat* as the sixth—are those whose meaning is existence (*sattārtha*). Furthermore, all verbal roots beginning with *bhū* do not transcend that meaning; the sense is that whatever arises, perishes, or remains established, this [Being] is the self, the essential nature, and the reality of all that. Thus, by means of synonyms, there is the introduction of the essential nature (*svarūpopanaya*).
And the self...
[omitted] ...without the state of being the object of enjoyment (*bhojyabhāva*).
See page 34, line 20, from the word *uttārāt*.

[Objection]: It might be thought that because of the contradiction of something acting upon itself (*svātmani vṛttivirodha*), how can He create and withdraw Himself, or be bound and liberated? For indeed, the tip of a finger does not touch its own tip, nor does a sword cut itself. [Response]: This is incorrect, because the distinction between the causal factors (*kāraka*) is established through the differentiation of powers (*śaktibheda*). Just as in the case of a weaver, a shuttle, and a silkworm, these processes of withdrawal, emission, bondage, and liberation are essentially of the same nature as that [Self].
And just as sparks issue forth from a well-kindled fire...
That very [principle] is time (kāla) because of its reckoning, primordial nature (prakṛti) because of its manifestation,
and necessity (niyati) because of its regulation of forms and so forth.

Because it exists by its own nature (*svena rūpeṇa bhavanāt*), it is *svabhāva*. Just like a silkworm, that which must proceed—by what means, where, how, from what cause, at what time, and for what purpose—is of that very same nature as those processes of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*), emission (*visarga*), bondage (*bandha*), and liberation (*mokṣa*). Just as a silkworm weaves out and withdraws its thread by means of the saliva produced from its own body, and not from anything else whatsoever, so too are the withdrawal and emission [of the universe] from the Self alone.
For it has been said: "As a spider emits and reabsorbs [its web], and as herbs arise upon the earth..."
Just as hair and body hair arise from an existing man, or as sparks arise from a well-blazing fire, so does the universe originate here from the Imperishable (Muṇḍakopaniṣad).

Thus, bondage and liberation also belong to the Self alone and not to anything else; just as a silkworm encloses itself with a cocoon produced from its own body and later dissolves back into that very same place, while another pierces the cocoon and emerges, so too are the bondage and liberation of the Self.

Furthermore, as in the passage beginning "as from a well-blazing fire," this example also serves to demonstrate the similarity between the Puruṣa and fire, because it arises from the nature of fire itself without deviating from its own essence. As he has stated: "As from a well-blazing fire...
and so forth; thus far it has been said that the Puruṣa alone is everything—[as in the verse] "He touches the tip of his finger... (Pātañjala Bhāṣya).

Just as a weaver or a silkworm is identical in nature to the cloth or the cocoon it produces, so too are these processes of withdrawal, emission, bondage, and liberation identical in nature to that [Self].
And just as sparks arise from a well-kindled fire...
here, just as sparks arise from a well-kindled fire, so does this entire universe originate from the Imperishable.
Thus, that very [principle] is conceived as the root; through its reckoning it is time (kāla),
and by context it is primordial nature (prakṛti).
*Niyati* (destiny) is so called because of the determination of transformation and so forth;
*svabhāva* (intrinsic nature) is so called because of existing by means of its own form.
That by which, where, how, from what cause, when, and for what purpose one must proceed [is determined].
Or space,
or the navel;
then, O Prajñā.
As a spider emits and reabsorbs [its web], as herbs arise from the earth,
and as hair and body-hair grow from a living person, so does this entire universe emerge from the Imperishable.
1.7 ...This is the truth: just as from a well-kindled fire thousands of sparks of similar form emanate, so it is.
In the same way, my dear, various beings are born from the Imperishable, and into it they also merge.
Thus reads the text in the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad:
"And just as sparks fly forth from a well-kindled fire, so from the Imperishable (Akṣara) the universe originates here."
Thus,
the root is considered to be "non-returning" (anivṛtti), "formless" (arūpa),
"unreal" (anartha), and "non-existent" (abhāva).
As it has been said by Prajāpati:
"Just as a spider emits and reabsorbs [its web], just as herbs arise from the earth,
and just as hair and body-hair grow from a living person, so does this entire universe arise from the Imperishable."
...This is the truth: just as from a well-kindled fire thousands of sparks of the same nature emerge, even so, my dear, various beings are born from the Imperishable and into it they also dissolve.
Thus reads the text in the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad.

That very [Prakṛti] is also called "Time" (kāla). Because it knows and because it calculates, it is Time; for the root *kal* (Pāṇini Dhātupāṭha 497, 1866) means "to count. Counting (*kalana*) here signifies knowledge (*jñāna*), meaning reckoning. As some have said in the verse, "Time cooks all beings," by virtue of the context, it is that same Prakṛti who is meant.

Prakṛti is so called because it brings about the guṇas—sattva, rajas, and tamas—which have as their respective natures illumination, activity, and restraint, and which serve the purpose of the experiencer by creating conceptual distinctions within its own nature. As some say: "The one unborn [Prakṛti], red, white, and black, producing many offspring of similar form;
the one unborn [Puruṣa] lies beside her, enjoying her, while another unborn [Puruṣa] abandons her once she has been fully enjoyed" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.5).

1.55 Thus, *niyati* (restriction) arises from the restriction of [sensory] manifestation and so forth; for instance, due to the restriction of manifestation, the object of the eye is form alone and not taste or other [objects], and due to the restriction of tasting, the object of the tongue is taste and not form or other [objects]. It is from such restrictions that *niyati* arises.
Intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is so called because it exists by itself, through its own very form;
as some have said: "Having known the [sixteen] digits... (*jñātvā kalaṃ...*) [and so forth].
Just as [it is said]: "The one unborn, red, white, and black, producing many offspring of similar form"— as stated in the *Bahu-eka-prakāśa-vṛtti*.

"Of black and white, manifold, and formless; for the one unborn (aja) enjoys and lies along with her, while another unborn (aja) leaves her once her enjoyments have been experienced. Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.5.55.

In the manuscripts *Ya*, in place of the reading enclosed within these marks, the text reads: "Who creates the sharpness of thorns, and the diverse nature of beasts and birds? [The reading *dinniya* is a variant; *pra* refers to the primary text.]
"All this proceeds by way of its own nature; there is no acting according to one's own will, so how could there be effort?
Thus, Time ripens all beings; Time destroys and withdraws all creatures;
Time remains awake while others sleep; for Time is indeed insurmountable."
Thus is the complete verse.
By this [verse], there is activity directed toward that [object] in that manner, from that [source], at that time, and for that purpose;

yet it exists only within that [reality] and is not distinct from it, for that very [reality] is this world—both evolved and unevolved, manifold, and consisting of the various distinctions of sentient and insentient beings.
And he quotes:
"Now others say that consciousness is both manifest and unmanifest, and manifold.
(This is from Bhartṛhari’s *Vākyapadīya-vṛtti*, 1.)
It moves, and it does not move; it is far away, and it is near.
Furthermore, others say that consciousness is manifold, both manifest and unmanifest.
Thus, in the *Vākyapadīyavṛtti* composed by Bhartṛhari, 1.8:
"That [Brahman] is within all this, and it is outside of all this. (*Śuklayajurvedasaṃhitā* 40.5).

Due to the excellence of his supreme purity, as indicated by such qualities as being worthy of worship (*arhaṇa*) and awakening (*bodhana*), it is even possible that he is a deity himself, up to the point that he may become an Arhat;
this is true because becoming (*bhavana*) belongs to the agent, since becoming is an action (*kriyā*), just like the act of cooking (*pacati*).

As for the statement "he is a knower" (*sa jña*): by whatever cause, in whatever field, in whatever manner, from whatever basis or substance, at whatever time, and for whatever purpose—that is, aiming toward whatever objective—one must act; accordingly, one acts there, in that way, from that, at that time, and for that purpose. For example: a cook commanded by a king takes rice from a granary and, having brought it to a pot, cooks soft, pure rice preceded by a thin gruel (*peyā*) for the sake of quenching hunger.
Furthermore, that manifestation occurs within that very Person and is not distinct from or external to him;

for he alone is this, that same Person from whom this entire world has proceeded and issued forth, evolving through various diversities. And yet, because it does not abandon its own essential nature, it remains unevolved as well, being the manifold source—the support—of many things.

That which has as its form the various distinctions such as sentient and insentient is "that whose form consists of the various distinctions of the sentient and insentient. That which is sentient—such as humans, animals, gods, and hell-beings—and their various subdivisions, as well as that which is insentient—such as wood, walls, pots, and cloths—together with their subdivisions, is its form.
Likewise, there is the term *pravṛtti* (activity) here; alternatively, the reading might also be *yathā rājñājñaptaḥ* (just as commanded by the king).
Having made it into the shape of rice grains, soft and clear;
*taṇḍulaviśada* [is the reading in] Bhāṣya; here, the reading *peyāpūrvakam* is likely intended.
In the various manuscripts, there is no mention of the name of the person who composed this prescription;
it is based on many [authoritative] sources.
The meaning is that [the statement] "that which is manifold, that which is non-substantial, and that which is conscious" is made precisely in accordance with the Jaina doctrine.
It moves, it stirs, it vibrates; yet it does not move, it does not stir, it does not vibrate.
It is far away—in the world of the animals, in the lower worlds, and in the world beyond;
yet it is near at hand, right here in this very place, as that which is seen, touched, and so forth.

Because there is no obstruction to the transformation of the Self—which is characterized by the application of both form and formlessness—into all things within it, such as jars and cloths, therefore that [Self] is "outside" (bāhyataḥ) of all this; for it exists even in the non-light (aloka). By the phrase "of all this," there is a reference to the entities contained within the world (loka); thus, in the passage "its outside is non-light" (tasya bāhyamaloka), the reading in the *Yajurveda* is *tadvantike*. Likewise, in this *Nayacakravṛtti*, there may also be the reading *tadu cāntike*.
Therefore, when one [thing] is perceived, all [things] are perceived; when one is obstructed, all are obstructed.

Due to the excellence of his supreme purity—beginning with his being worthy of honor (*arhaṇa*) and awakened (*bodhana*)—he is indeed the deity himself. He is called an *Arhat* because he is worthy of the worship that transcends all the world; a *Buddha* because he awakens; a *Brahmā* because of his increasing (*vardhana*) or greatness (*bṛhattva*), or because he is ever-increasing (*vardhamāna*); a *Viṣṇu* because he pervades (*vyāpnoti*) all objects through the nature of his knowledge; and an *Īśvara* because of his lordship (*īśana*). Furthermore, due to these distinctions in the excellence of his purity of knowledge and because he has reached their ultimate limit, it is possible that he may even become an *Arhat*; this is stated as a possibility because the state of an *Arhat* is difficult to attain, whereas the attainment of the remaining stages is easily achieved. Indeed, it is he alone who is capable of attaining even that most difficult-to-reach state of omniscience, which is supremely pure and known by the name of the Supreme Sage (*paramarṣi*).
Thus ends the conceptualization of the *vidhi-vidhi-naya* (the method of the doctrine of agency), which is the doctrine of the Person (*puruṣavāda*).

Now, the doctrine of Necessity (*niyativāda*), which relies upon the perspective of the *vidhi-vidhi-naya*, is being stated: "It is true; that 'existence belongs to the agent' and so forth—this which you have said is indeed correct. Therefore, the independence (*svātantrya*) of yours, which is being perceived, cannot be denied, just as [one cannot deny] the act of cooking.
What is the reason? This must be carefully considered:
if he were a knower and independent, he would not bring about his own harm or what is undesirable, like a wise king;

but this is not so, because during the occurrence of the state of sleep, there is a lack of independence on the part of the person itself, like a man who has fallen from a cliff due to the force with which he was propelled.

Is it not the case that this very lack of propriety regarding his being omniscient and so forth is what is being established? For even if [the opponent] considers it to be proper, this same rule serves to bring about another agent as the creator...
[the creator].

...it also becomes insentient, because its becoming is an action performed by that which causes it to become; for whatever is an action belongs only to the agent—whether it be a jar or the like, or an atom or the like—just as the act of cooking belongs only to the independent cook.
Furthermore, becoming is itself an action, and being an action, it does not occur without an agent, just like the act of cooking.
He will be the agent, and the agent is independent; precisely because he is an agent, he is not brought into being or caused to act by anyone, owing to his independence and agency.

As for the point that he is "cognizant," this must be carefully considered by you: regarding the assertion that the agent is necessarily cognizant due to his independence, you must deliberate and investigate whether it is improper to maintain that he is indeed omniscient. This is the intended meaning.

What is the reason it is illogical? Because faults are observed even when the existence of an omniscient being is admitted. Let there be independence due to being a creator; who can prevent that? If he is held to be endowed with both qualities—being both wise and independent—then, being wise and yet independent, he would not bring about his own disadvantage or what is undesirable, because he possesses independence while possessing wisdom.

What is the illustration? It is like a wise king. For just as a king who understands the course of fate and human effort, who is endowed with place, time, allies, and means, and who possesses valor, does not bring about his own harm or undesirable [consequences] such as death or defeat—so too this [soul], if it were a knower, would not bring about its own harm or what is undesirable. Yet this harm and what is undesirable are observed: physical [afflictions] such as birth, old age, death, disease, cold, and heat; and mental [afflictions] such as grief, fear, despair, envy, and malice. Therefore, one must consider that its being a knower is untenable.
If he were both cognizant and independent, he would not inflict harm or what is undesirable upon himself, as a wise king does not;

however, this is not so, because his state of being a person (*puruṣatā*) lacks independence due to its occurrence within the states [of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep], like a man who has fallen from a cliff with accumulated momentum.

But surely it is precisely this lack of propriety—his being cognizant and so forth—that is being established; for even if it were intended to be proper, this very same rule would lead to the conclusion that there must be another agent.
It becomes an agent;
even though it is insentient, it becomes so.
Is that which effects the restriction caused to perform an action, or is it not? [Abhāva-mata-prakaraṇa]
The readings *vapyaya* and *vapyā bhā* are not correct, because [the mind] functions in states similar to those of sleep, and so forth.

This is not tenable, namely, that "the occurrence of undesirable and harmful states is impossible for the conscious Self. Why? Because its functioning occurs in a state like sleep; "a state like sleep" means a state possessing sleep; "functioning in such a state" means functioning by means of that state. This is because that functioning, being the very nature of the person (*puruṣatā*), lacks independence; for even the conscious one lacks independence due to the force of functioning in a state like sleep brought about by itself.

"Like one who has fallen into a ravine due to a momentum he himself initiated": just as a certain man, having himself generated a momentum, falls into a ravine because he is unable to turn back that momentum, so too that supreme cause—though independent and wise—might bring about misfortune and harm undesirable to itself. What is the fault here? If there is curiosity regarding this fault, we shall explain: "Indeed, because of its wisdom," and so forth. By asserting thus—that due to the influence of the state and activity like that of sleep, there occurs a fall into a ravine due to a momentum initiated [by itself] because of a lack of independence, leading to undesirable harm—you are actually supporting the very inconsistency of its being "wise" and so on. For if it were unknown [that such a fall would follow], then the fall into the ravine would occur through this momentum-filled action of rapid movement; but if it *were* known, then for one who is independent, such a fall into a ravine is not possible. That, then, is the fault.
Therefore, that state remains illogical;
[it] occurs in the state of flowing,
O one who falls.
Regarding the phrase "even though it is accepted as being joined with the state of being a branch," and so forth:

although you consider that this entire [world] consists of the Self alone, augmented by the power of existence which is inseparable from sovereignty and omniscience, nevertheless, the remainder of the sentence is: "this very [principle of] necessity serves to bring about the status of being another agent."

If it is asked how that is cultivated, it is said: [The opponent] repeats the very logic of the literal meaning previously stated, beginning with "he becomes the agent" and ending with "even the insentient becomes so. By speaking thus, you yourself have established the existence of some other cause for these various states. For, just as in the act of cooking, we observe fixed powers—such as those of the knower and the ignorant, the independent and the dependent, or the specific roles of agent, instrument, locus, object, and so forth—belonging to Devadatta, the wood, the pot, the rice, the water, and the like; since these things do not exist otherwise than in their fixed nature, there must necessarily be a cause for them. Thus, Niyati (Fate/Restriction) alone is the agent.
For in that [series], there is never, in any way, an appearance of a form other than its own object that would contradict its unity;
and it is said: "Whatever object is to be attained by relying on the power of necessity, whether auspicious or inauspicious for men, that necessarily comes to pass.
Even when a great effort is made by living beings, that which is not destined to be does not happen, and that which is destined to be cannot be destroyed."

Furthermore, because it has the singular nature of establishing the reality of all things—whether differentiated or undifferentiated, such as the formed and the formless—it must necessarily have a cause that acts with fixed determination.

What is the reason? It is because they lack both suchness (*tathābhāva*) and otherwiseness (*anyathābhāva*). Devadatta possesses a fixed independence regarding his own operations, such as placing [the pot] on the fire, pouring water, sowing rice, adding fuel, and removing it; however, he does not possess independence regarding operations such as burning, arising, supporting, or softening. Likewise, for the remaining factors such as wood and so forth, there is a restriction of independence regarding their own respective operations as instruments (*karaṇa*) and the like; this is "suchness. Conversely, when those very same causal factors (*kāraka*) possess powers contrary to their own operations due to mutual interaction, that is "otherwiseness."

This means that because of the absence of these two—remaining as they are (*tathābhāva*) and changing (*anyathābhāva*)—there would follow the consequence of non-existence. Since these two, remaining as they are and changing, are observed, entities must necessarily depend upon a regulating cause due to their necessity; and that cause cannot be anything other than *niyati* (fate). Therefore, he says: "Thus, *niyati* alone is the agent. The word "thus" (*iti*) has the sense of a reason; for this reason, because the regulation of entities is inseparable from a regulating cause, let it be accepted that *niyati* alone is the faultless conceptualization of the agent.

How so? Because, in the doctrine that [the world] has a single cause consisting of consciousness (*jñāna*), there is never, in any way, a contradiction of their unity through the appearance of those objects as something other than themselves; nor is there a contradiction in the case of insentient things like earth and so forth being dissimilar to their cause, even when all four possible states are postulated, since it is admitted that effects are preceded by a cause.
Indeed, there is no contradiction in the diversity of similarity and dissimilarity among entities, even given the existence of a creator who is merely the regulator of necessity (*niyati*).
The term "kadācit" (at some time) refers even to other states, and "kathañcit" (in some way) refers even to other modes;

therefore, since it is capable of avoiding the fault of dissimilarity even when the cause is one, the postulation of *niyati* (destiny/fixity) as the cause is superior. He says "and so forth," and this too is a restatement of the Jina’s teaching, serving as an indicator as before.

"Whatever is to be attained is by the power of destiny," and so forth. Since one observes the failure of an effect despite effort being exerted, and the attainment of results such as finding a treasure even without effort, there must exist a quality corresponding to the cause that is capable of resolving the contradiction regarding the dissimilarity of the effect;
see page 175, line 2, where the reading should likely be "taṇḍulaudana-ādīnām."
There must necessarily be a cause for their being thus or otherwise, because of the absence of [change] in that state; therefore, destiny alone is the agent.
For in it, there is never, in any way, a transformation of its purpose or form that would contradict its unity.
And he says: "Whatever object is to be attained by relying on the power of destiny, whether auspicious or inauspicious, that necessarily comes to pass for men."
For even when beings exert great effort, that which is not destined to be does not come to pass, nor is there the destruction of what is destined to be.
Because it possesses the singular nature of establishing the reality of all things— whether manifest or unmanifest, differentiated or undifferentiated— in their true state,
whatever object is to be attained by the power of necessity through the force of destiny, whether auspicious or inauspicious, that necessarily comes to pass for human beings.
For even when a great effort is made by beings, that which is not destined to be does not come to be, and there is no destruction of that which is destined to be.

What is this distinct action (*kriyābheda*) among cooking and the like that serves as its counteragent? The act of placing [the pot] on the fire, pouring water, adding rice, and removing the fuel constitutes "cooking" for the primary agent;
it is precisely while performing these acts—placing on the fire, pouring water, adding rice, and removing the fuel—that Devadatta is said to "cook."
In that case, the following meaning occurs: "This is the cooking of the primary agent";
this is the agency of the primary agent.

In the expressions "he cooks a *droṇa*" (*droṇaṃ pacati*) and "he cooks an *āḍhaka*" (*āḍhakaṃ pacati*), the act of cooking consists of the acts of containing and supporting the substratum (*adhikaraṇa*). When the pot performs the act of containing—that is, the act of grasping—and the act of supporting, it is said that "the pot cooks" (*sthālī pacati*); in that case, the verbal root *pac* (to cook) is operative.
This is the ripening of the locus; this is the agency of the act of placing [the pot] on the fire;
"the fuel will cook" means they will burn until the softening [of the food]; thus, the ripening belongs to the action of burning, which serves as the instrument.
"The fuel-sticks will cook" means "they will burn until they are softened"; thus, while performing the action of burning, the wood-sticks are said to "cook.
In that case, the root *pac* (to cook) is applied [to them];
this is the agency (*kartṛtva*) of the instrument (*karaṇa*).
Thus [ends the section] in the Patañjala-Mahābhāṣya on [Pāṇini] 1.4.23.
The phrase "anniyatatvāt" does not exist in the Bhā manuscript;
[the reading] "cid iti vyavasthā" is in the Ya manuscript;
[the reading] "jīvinam e" is in the Pra manuscript.
In this context, the reading should be "the quality of being formless" (arūpyaguṇa).
Is this the only quality? Or is there another as well? It is said that there is;

which one is it? It is the quality of being established without effort (ayatnapratipādyatāguṇa), and that occurs by avoiding the occurrence of contradictory properties such as being corporeal or incorporeal. He demonstrates this with the passage beginning "nor [is there] corporeal or incorporeal... and ending with "...there is no need for effortful establishment."
The proof for this is as follows: "In both ways, divided in such and such a manner," and so on, up to "by necessity.

By that and that mode—whether as embodied or unembodied, conscious or unconscious, subtle or gross, through sovereignty or poverty, and so forth—all objects are divided; and by the statement "all things to be known are real entities" and so on, all undivided objects likewise possess their state of being "as-it-is-ness" (*yathātathābhāva*), which is to be established with effort.

In matters to be accomplished through effort and even in those things produced by human action, because the fruit of the activity directed toward them is likewise determined, the universality of *niyati* (destiny) as the cause is established.

This is because, in the ultimate sense (*paramārthatas*), there is no difference [between the cause and its effects]. Even when a cognition of difference arises, it is due to this ultimate non-difference—just as in the case of "childhood" and "manhood," which are distinct yet ultimately one.

How so? Because even when there is the appearance of a cognition of non-difference, non-difference is admitted; and precisely because non-difference is admitted even when there is the appearance of a cognition of difference, just as in the case of a post and a man that are perceived as distinct.

This is true; therefore, because that very reality (*yāthātathya*)—which exists as the necessary determination (*niyama*) of every respective object—is the motivator (*prayojaka*), the causal agency (*hetu-kartṛtva*), and the establishing factor (*sthāpana*), and because that [agency] is of a single uniform form (*ekarūpa*) throughout that necessity (*niyati*), there is no need now to exert any effort to establish the causality of necessity, which has the sole function of mere restriction (*niyamana-mātra-eka-vyāpārā*).
[The reading *mūrtādyayukta* is incorrect;
it should be *tathāpravi* as in the manuscript.]

The state of being brought about by effort exists in both things accomplished through effort and in created things, because the result of the action directed toward those objects is likewise determined; thus, the causality of *niyati* (fate) is all-pervasive.

In the ultimate sense, this is not a cause of the world that is distinct [from it], because even when a cognition of difference arises, there is ultimately no difference—just as, for example, the various states of childhood and so forth do not differ from the essential nature of a person.

How so? Because non-difference is admitted even when there is the appearance of a cognition of difference, and because non-difference is admitted precisely even when there is the appearance of a cognition of difference— just as in the case of a post or a person whose specific identity has been excluded—
and that which causes this [cognition] is the logical reason (*hetu*).
4.55 The instigator of an agent shall be designated as a *hetu* (cause) and also as a *kartṛ* (agent).

Thus, in the Siddhāntakaumudī of Pāṇini’s grammar, [it is stated] that regarding objects achieved through effort— even those produced by human action— the pervasiveness of the necessity of the result of the action directed toward them is due to the causality of necessity (*niyatikāraṇatva*).

It might be thought that because all things are bound by necessity (*niyati*), there is no fixed rule regarding action and the fruit of action; however, that is not so. For in the case of an object such as a jar, where the means are the lump of clay, the staff, the wheel, and so forth, and the fruit of the action consists in the accomplishment of the jar’s own nature through effort—since it is determined in that specific manner, necessity itself is the cause here.
Now, the nature of that necessity is considered: is necessity said to be the distinct, individual form of each of those very things, differing from one thing to another, or is it non-different?

In this regard, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), this non-differentiation (*abheda*) is the cause of the world; it is not its differentiation. Why is it "non-differentiated"? Because even when a cognition of differentiation arises, it remains non-differentiated from the standpoint of ultimate reality. Or rather, what indeed is this so-called "differentiation," even in the case of necessity (*niyati*)? If it is argued that "necessity" consists in the nature of things as being objects either accomplished or unaccomplished by action, then even while cognitions such as "sentient" or "insentient" arise, there is still only necessity from the standpoint of ultimate reality. Thus, because they are non-distinct, they are "non-differentiated. The cognition of differentiation, however, depends merely upon the existence of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) regarding them.

What is it like? It is like the state of being a person despite the differences between childhood and so forth; just as the nature of being a person remains entirely undivided even when cognitions arise that distinguish the different stages of infancy, youth, maturity, and middle age, so too *niyati* (the principle of necessity) remains undivided amidst the various distinctions such as the cognition of action, non-action, and the distinction of fixed results.
Thus, its own nature (*sva-svarūpa*)—its very essence—is [unchanging].
The essential nature: Raṃ Hīṃ.
[The sequence of] action, that which is to be accomplished, and the object to be accomplished;
[the sequence of] action, that which is to be accomplished, and the object to be accomplished; Vināyaka.

In the absence of [that], apart from [the state of] *pra-vi-raṃ-hī*, elsewhere there is the restriction of action and non-action; [this is] the restriction of action in the manuscripts Pā., Ḍe., Līṃ., Ya.,
and Bhā.

He asks: "How is it that, even while there is the appearance of the cognition of difference, there is no difference in reality? For, since the appearance of the cognition of difference is being perceived, why is one thing accomplished by action and another not; or why is one [established] from itself and another from another? Or rather, let there indeed be difference in reality, even though there is the appearance of the cognition of non-difference? To this twofold objection, the Teacher provides the following resolution, beginning with "How... and so forth.

If difference is intended there, how can there be difference in the ultimate sense? For even when there is the appearance of a cognition of non-difference, you yourself have admitted non-difference, [saying] that "it is difference itself that appears as non-difference. Alternatively, if non-difference is desired, how can there be non-difference? Precisely because you have admitted non-difference even when there is the appearance of a cognition of difference.

If, according to your view, the cognition of absolute unity has the ultimate reality as its object, then—since you admit non-difference even from that which appears as dual—it would follow that it is neither proximate to nor distant from "that" and "not-that. This is because it would be differentiated by the various states of substance, location, and so forth, which are bound up with being proximate to or distant from "that" and "not-that. Consequently, there would be no non-existence of what is to be, no destruction of what is to be, and no such diverse regularity regarding time and other factors; for even during the rainy season and nights, there are instances where things proceed contrary to the seasons.

Nor can it arise from intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); for if the states of childhood, youth, adulthood, and old age were all [identical] intrinsic natures, they would have to exist simultaneously. Since we observe that states arise with distinct characteristics and in a fixed sequence, intrinsic nature is not the cause.
Rather, let it be understood that such a thing exists as a specific determination (*tathāniyati*) of objects, and that this is what constitutes their differentiation.

What is it like? It is like the exclusion of "stump-ness" and "person-ness. Just as when an object has been definitively determined—either as a stump alone or as a person alone—the non-difference of the universal of verticality (ūrdhvatāsāmānya) is perceived through its appearance, so too is there non-difference among all destinies (*niyati*) consisting of action and the fruit of action. Thus, according to the view that [the manifestation] has the ultimate reality as its object, those manifestations are of two kinds at each respective time.
According to his view, regarding the object of ultimate reality, that which appears as "that" and "not-that" is twofold;

and it is both proximate to and distant from "that" and "not-that," due to its differentiation based on various states—such as substance, location, and so forth—which are either proximate or distant from "that" and "not-that. Like the interior of a cloud, there is neither the non-existence of what is to be, nor the destruction of what is to be.
This diversity of restriction is not caused by time and so forth, because even during the rainy season, winter, and other such periods, things sometimes proceed contrary to the season.

Nor is it due to intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), for if it were, the stages of childhood, youth, adulthood, and old age would all occur simultaneously, since they would all possess that same intrinsic nature. Since we observe the arising of states restricted by specific differences and sequences, intrinsic nature is not the cause; rather, it is *niyati* (destiny/fixity) that determines the thing in such a way.
"Thus," [it is said].
Furthermore, that *niyati* (necessity) consists of both difference and non-difference. Why? Its definition, along with its cause, is stated as follows: "And that," and so forth.
And that *niyati* is precisely that very thing, because there is no distinction between it and all other instances of *niyati*.

And thus, it is "near" because of its distinctness from [the categories of] action, non-action, necessity, and so forth; it is "not near" because of its distance in the case of objects perceivable by direct perception, since it is restricted by proximity,
and in the case of those accessible through inference from effects or scripture.

And here, as well as in the case of heaven and so forth, what is the cause for this lack of uniformity regarding proximity and non-proximity? It is because of the differentiation of that very *niyati* (destiny) due to its being bound by various states of substances, locations, and so forth—whether proximate or not. "Proximate and non-proximate" refers to those various states which are either proximate or not; "bound by those" means bound by those substances, locations, and so forth. Through the differentiation of that very *niyati* bound by these—as indicated by the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*)—it is determined by way of substance, as well as by time and state (*bhāva*).

That very necessity (niyati), in terms of substance, becomes that [necessity] in the form of a jar; it is "not that" in the form of a cloth, being proximate to another jar through proximity of form, yet not proximate in the form of a cloth.

Regarding space (*kṣetra*): it is fixed to that very point on the top of the wheel where it is performed, or to whichever region of the ground it stands upon, or to the neck and so forth; it is not elsewhere. Regarding time (*kāla*): the duration for which it is produced, or the length of time for which it remains, is the determination of time (*kāla-niyati*). Regarding state (*bhāva*): the determination (*niyati*) is that it occurs exactly with whatever colors, shapes, and so forth it possesses. Thus, although the arrangement of things is a single unity in its nature as *niyati*, it is differentiated by its connection to substance, location, and other factors.

What is it like? It is like the interior of a cloud.
