Just as clouds, when taking up their "womb" (garbha), take up water of a certain quality and quantity, and release it in exactly that same way in substance; in space, they release it in the very same region where they took it up; in time, they release what was taken up in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa in Vaiśākha, and so forth; and in state, they release it with the same qualities as taken up—such as salty, sweet, and so on—as factors that cause the drying up or nourishing of living beings, medicinal herbs, and forest trees.
He summarizes that: "There is no non-existence of what is to be, nor destruction of what is to be"—this has already been explained by the preceding verse. [The text continues:
"...due to the distinction from difference, the form of non-difference... without action and non-action... [prāṇa].
Except for *baṃdha* (Bhāṣya, Vṛtti) and *badha* (Bhāṣya, Vṛtti), this [reading] does not exist in the manuscripts (*prati*).
Only when [the fire] has been kindled...
at that very place, according to the time, by means of the *bhāṣā-pāda-raṅga-ḍe* [mantra], thus says Prajñākaragupta.
See page 194, line 3.

It might be thought: "This rule [of succession] arises from time, because time is called 'sequence' and because entities possess transformations determined by the temporal sequence of prior, posterior, and so forth.
But this is not so; this diverse rule does not arise from time.
Why? Because even during the rainy season, winter, and so forth, there is sometimes an occurrence that does not correspond to the season;

for we observe a deviation among plants and other beings regarding the emergence of sprouts, shoots, leaves, flowers, fruits, and internal embryos. This is seen both naturally and through human application: in the rains, autumn, early winter, late winter, spring, and summer, there is observed a failure to act at their own natural times of transformation, and conversely, an occurrence at non-own-times. Therefore, the previous [argument] is not established.

Regarding the phrase "because of the fourfold occurrence," if one should think that [the states] arise from intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), that is not so; for from intrinsic nature, etc., up to the contradiction with one’s own tenet (*abhyupagamavirodha*).

Since the states of childhood, youth, adulthood, and old age in a tree, a sentient being, or the like, are all its own state—that is, its intrinsic nature—then if one does not admit those [states] at the time of childhood and so forth, there would be a contradiction with one’s own tenet, because in the absence of all distinctions, the intrinsic nature of the states and so forth would be non-existent.

Just as in the world, there is the apprehension of forms such as mountains within a single unity, and just as cognition, though being one, possesses the forms of many objects—since otherwise the very nature of cognition could not be established—so too, because it is of the nature of necessity (*niyama*), that [seed] becomes both one and many, such as the sprout and so forth, within a single entity like rice. If it is argued that the cause is non-necessity (*aniyatika*) because irregularities are observed in portents and the like, and because abnormalities in germination and so forth are indeed seen, we say no; for even in those cases, it is by the power of necessity (*niyati*) that... [it occurs].
...the transgression of properties such as production is observed;
the states of youth and so forth would have to exist simultaneously, yet they do not.

Therefore, since it is seen that those states—youth and the rest—are restricted by a sequence of differentiation, and because their arising, persistence, and passing away occur only at the time of childhood and so on, intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is not the cause.

What then? Destiny alone must be accepted as the cause. For it is by that cause, in that manner, and according to the fixed order of the sequence of different states such as birth and so forth that are observed, that the entity is determined by destiny in such a way. If that were not accepted—if all distinctions were denied and all states were admitted to be without distinction, or if intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and the like were accepted [as the cause]—then those states would not exist; nor would those natures consisting of the states, such as childhood and so forth, or sleep and so forth, belong to Devadatta and others. Consequently, due to the absence of states, natures, and the like, the very intrinsic nature that was accepted would cease to exist.
Consequently, a contradiction with your own tenets arises for the proponent of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvavādin*).

By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), there is a contradiction with the tenet because of the non-existence of the intrinsic nature of parts such as the hand that coexist with those respective states, or the intrinsic nature of external qualities such as color-form (*rūpa*), or the intrinsic nature of internal qualities such as acuity or dullness. Alternatively, by the inclusion of "etcetera," there is a contradiction with the tenet even for one who holds time to be the cause, because—according to the previously stated reasoning—time also lacks simultaneous existence.
Therefore, this must be accepted: that its restriction does not arise from anything other than necessity (niyati). See page 206, line 14.
If this were not accepted, there would be a contradiction with [your own] tenets, because in a state of total non-differentiation, the nature of states and so forth would be absent.

Just as in the world there is the apprehension of forms such as mountains within a single unity, and just as cognition, though being one, possesses multiple forms of the objects to be known—since otherwise the very nature of cognition could not be attained—so too, because it is of the nature of necessity (*niyama*), that [seed] becomes both one and many, such as the sprout and so forth, within a single entity like rice. If it is argued that the cause is non-necessity (*aniyatikāraṇatva*) because irregularities are observed in cases such as portents, and because abnormalities in germination and the like are indeed seen, we say: no; for even in this case, it is by the power of necessity (*niyati*) that... [it occurs].
...a transgression of properties such as production is perceived;
they would not exist without *avaśyambhāvitva* (necessity),
nor would they [exist] otherwise.
In the *Bhāṣya* and *Vivaraṇa*, [the reading] "lyādau ya" and "lyādoḥ" is absent.
And because of non-existence, it does not abide as something else; it abides as something else. (Bhāṣya, Viśva, Raṅga, Hīna)
...it remains as such (pāṭha: ḍe, līṃ).

To resolve the contradiction regarding the unity and multiplicity of that very *niyati*, he provides an illustration: "Just as in the world," where there is only oneness, yet there is the apprehension of forms such as mountains;

just as the single world, being perceived through various forms such as rivers, oceans, earth, mountains, villages, and gardens, appears divided, so too does *niyati* exist in the form of both difference and non-difference. This is the external example.
As for the internal [process]: how is it that cognition, despite being a single entity, possesses the forms of multiple objects of knowledge?
What is the reason? Because otherwise, there would be no attainment of the very nature of cognition apart from the forms of jars, cloths, and so forth.

Regarding this illustrated point, the following contemplation on the nature of difference and non-difference is stated: "Because it consists of necessity," and so on, up to "the sprout and so forth come into being."
That *niyati* (determinative necessity) is "rice" (*vrīhi*)—in a single entity, it is non-different as "sprout" despite the differences in its roots and so forth;
it is different due to the differences in states such as sprout, leaf, stalk, and so on, or it is different due to the differences in color, taste, and so forth.

Furthermore, regarding a manifold object consisting of the nature of earth, water, wind, and so on, because the earth and the other elements themselves attain that state [of rice], it is non-different due to the unity of being "rice."
Even though it is one, it appears as divided; even though it is manifold, it does not become divided, by virtue of its various determined objects.

Thus, within the Brahman that is the essence of speech (*śabdatattva*), there exist combined powers (*śaktayaḥ*) which, though contradictory, are non-contradictory with respect to unity and constitute its very self.

For example: when there is a single perception consisting merely of the manifestation of distinct objects, there appear manifestations of the forms of objects such as "the world is earth" and "the world is not earth."

For the apprehension of forms such as trees, which reside within the object of knowledge, is not contradicted by the unity of cognition; nor does there exist a difference in essence between that [cognition] and its form, because they do not transcend the single reality of cognition—
thus it is stated in the *Vākyapadīya-vṛtti* composed by Bhartṛhari, 1.2.

In this context, there is a division; there may also be a reading: "this is an external illustration of necessity (niyati) in the form of both difference and non-difference," [where the reading] *niyatātmaka* appears in manuscript Bhā.
In the case of form and objects,
when form exists within the object, it is distinct from the object.

Because irregularities are observed regarding substance, place, time, and state in cases such as portents, non-fate (aniyati) is established as the cause; for indeed, abnormalities in procreation and so forth are seen—the term "and so forth" including abnormalities in birth, dwelling, feeding, activity, and natural constitution. Among humans and animals, there is a reversal of number, form, color, and limbs, as well as a deviation from the inherent nature of things, all occurring solely by the power of fate (niyati). Thus, some things that exist are incurable, some that do not exist are incurable, some that do not exist are curable, and some that exist are curable; yet even that which exists, such as the fragrance of the earth, may remain unmanifested—just as a jar in deep darkness remains unperceived until it is revealed by a lamp or similar means.

But this [case] is strictly impossible, like the son of a barren woman, because it is contrary to the established order of things. For an action, while operating upon the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), enters into an existing object that is to be accomplished (*sādhya*), since the application of the means is restricted to specific objects. Since the son of a barren woman and such do not exist, what could the action of sexual union enter? Furthermore, this non-existent object to be accomplished—such as a jar—which previously did not exist in that state, [is the subject of actions];

likewise, there is the eating of what is forbidden to eat by those born in villages, forests, water, or on land, and by those who frequent them, as well as the reversal of their respective dwellings and so forth.

The reversal of ethical conduct, such as the substitution of anger for forbearance; the reversal of physical state, such as the appearance of grey hair; and the reversal of intrinsic nature, such as changes in color, fragrance, and so forth.

If it is argued that because of such observations of irregularity (*vaikṛta*), destiny (*niyati*) alone is not the cause, we say: no. For even here, by the force of such destiny—and so on, up to the point where a transgression is perceived—that very same kind of destiny is the cause.
Thus, the state of having a restricted cause (*niyatakāraṇabhāva*) and the transgression of the inherent nature of things (*vastusvabhāva*) occur solely by the power of destiny.

Some things are existent and incapable of being accomplished; some are non-existent and incapable of being accomplished; some are non-existent and capable of being accomplished; and some are existent and capable of being accomplished.
Furthermore, even though space exists, it is not overwhelmed—just as a jar in deep darkness is not perceived by a lamp and the like—and thus it remains unmanifested.

But this [case], which is a fixed destiny contrary to that established order, such as the son of a barren woman and so forth, is simply unachievable. For activity, while operating upon the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), enters into an object that is already existent and is being accomplished, because the application of the means is restricted to each respective object. Since the son of a barren woman and the like do not exist, what could the act of sexual union enter? Furthermore, this non-existent object to be accomplished, such as a jar, did not previously exist in that manner—this [is the point].

In this context, the reading *abhakṣyabhakṣyatvam* appears correct, as it is well known that "the village pig is not to be eaten" and "five five-nailed animals are edible," or else the meaning should be understood as "humans are not to be eaten, while animals are edible. This reading within the brackets is not found in the Ya manuscripts. Furthermore, it is not only the transgression of natural laws such as birth and so forth, but rather, by the power of necessity (*niyati*), there is also a transgression of the inherent nature of things.

The fourfold logical alternative (*caturbhaṅgī*) beginning with "some things are both existent and unachievable" is not explained here because its meaning is clear; it has been indicated and will be further described.
Thus, a person perceives the achievability or unachievability of things precisely because they function according to destiny (*niyati*).

In this regard, the illustration for that which is both existent and unachievable is as follows: even though space exists, it is "unovercome" (*anabhibhava*), like the fragrance of the earth, in the sense that it cannot be overcome—meaning it cannot be altered by anything such as the sprinkling of water.

Like a jar covered in deep darkness [is revealed] by a lamp or the like, that which is unmanifest—what is it? Space and so forth. Since it exists (*sattvāt*), it is to be established (*sādhya*) just like the scent of the earth; such being the position, it is nonetheless not to be established.

However, this [unmanifest] is established through the union of male and female, like the son of a barren woman; such being the position, there is a fixed rule contrary to that determination: the son of a barren woman and the like are simply not to be established, because they are non-existent (*asattvāt*) by the very power of necessity (*niyati*).
Therefore, that which is existent by necessity cannot be established, and that which is non-existent by necessity alone does not deserve to be established.

What is the reason? Because things to be accomplished (*sādhya*) are to be accomplished by an action permeated by means (*sādhana*), there is no permeation therein of an action that is itself permeated by means; for those [means] lack the power to serve as means.

Therefore, the son of a barren woman and the like are "unattainable" (*asādhya*) because they are determined by the fact that even the act of sexual union between a man and a woman cannot bring them about; and since there is an absence of an object to be accomplished (*sādhya*), the means of accomplishment lack the status of being means. He demonstrates this with the words beginning "for action" (*kriyā hi*): the word *hi* has the sense of "because. Because action, while residing in the means such as wood and so forth, enters into an existing object to be accomplished—an object consisting of the transformation of rice grains into boiled rice through the process of softening—since it is restricted to each specific object due to the application of means such as wood for the purpose of placing [fuel] in fire and so on; therefore, in the absence of an object to be accomplished, what could that act of sexual union enter into, such as the son of a barren woman? Consequently, the son of a barren woman and the like are unattainable, as their determination is contrary to the established order of things.
Not present in the Cabhā manuscript; "seneva" in Pra;
"ndhaditi" in Pra.
Is it because there is no manifestation of this [object] as something deficient that it is "non-deficient" (avyaṅga),
[implying] it is non-existent due to necessity? Or is it because of the [object's] being perceived therein?
In the *Pra* manuscript, there is the reading *kriyāyāḥ*; in the *Bhā* manuscript, there is *ādima-artha-*. Here, there may also be the reading *nidhānādy-artheṣu*.
Because of the absence of that which is unprovable (asādhyasyābhāvāt). [Variant readings:
*asādhyatvābhāvāt* (Pā., Vi., Raṃ., Hī.), *sādhyatvābhāvāt* (Ḍe., Līṃ.).]

Regarding the opposite of that, [the text] begins with "But this," and so forth. The opponent says: "If the object to be established (*sādhya*)—such as a jar—is non-existent, how can it be established? Like a sky-flower, that which is said to be non-existent is not perceived; whereas that which is existent is invariably perceived, like a staff used as a means of proof for straightness. Or rather, the existent is established through its specific differentiation, such as a jar produced from clay-substance through a sequence of states like being upright, or like a person established by the removal of the possibility of him being a post."

And this [result] being accomplished is accomplished by this very action; and these alone are its causal factors (*kāraka*s). Thus, although the status of the causal factors remains fixed and equal in their respective positions, the person acts accordingly, because he does not transcend the various conceptualizations of the result for each specific object.

To this it is replied: This is not a fault, because we adopt a position where affirmation and negation apply to things other than what exists—that is, "the non-existent is other than the existent. Since this is a conceptual distinction regarding the nature of substance (*dravyārtha*), there is no absence of necessity (*niyati*). Therefore, he says: "Previously, it was not so manifested"—meaning it had not manifested in that manner as a jar-form, because the word "existent" (*sat*) implies manifestation (*vṛtti*). According to the statement, "The words *asti*, *bhavati*, *vidyati*, *padyati*, *vartate*, with *sannipāta* as the sixth, all have the sense of 'being' (*sattā*"), the meaning of "non-existent" is "not manifested. At the time of its state as a lump of clay and so forth, it is determined by its non-manifestation at that time as the effect to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera," [the list includes] cloth, mats, and so forth. This [subject] is determined by its perception or non-perception according to the difference in time.

That which is invariably perceived at all times is established as distinct—just as a staff is established as straight—or as being produced through a sequence such as the upward orientation of a clay substance, like a jar; or else, that which is to be proven is a person and so forth, by means of the exclusion of the apprehension of a post and the like.

And this [result] being accomplished is accomplished by this very action; and these alone are the causal factors (*kāraka*) of this [action]. Thus, even when there is an equality in the presence of other causal factors due to the fixed state of necessity (*niyati*), let it be seen that the person acts accordingly toward each object. (p. 34, l.
20; *avyaktyabhā*...)

"This other [example], 'that which is invariably perceived at all times,' and so forth—likewise, this [subject] is to be connected as follows: 'this existent is to be proven as being invariably unmanifest.

Like what? Like the proof of a staff by means of its straightness; for a staff, while already existing through its constituent parts, is proven to exist as having a particular configuration—that is, it is proven to be straight."

This is another [example] where that which is already constantly perceived as existent is to be proven as being a clay substance through its attainment of the state of a jar via the sequence of stages such as the "upward-facing" form (*ūrdhvāditva*). The distinction from the previous example is that in the former there was a slight difference in shape, whereas here there is a difference in an entirely distinct form; showing this, he says: "The existent is to be proven either by means of the difference consisting in the state of clay, the upward-facing form, and so on, or else by means of difference alone. Here, the phrase "and this is another" is understood to carry over.

That which is accomplished by cognition alone, and not by action consisting of physical movement—such as [the case where] a person and so forth, though already existing, are established by removing the grasping of them as a post and so forth, through the removal of the grasping of doubt and error regarding that object; here, nothing such as a person is produced, but rather that which is already existing but unperceived is established by means of perception. However, this *niyati* (determinism) consists solely of the nature of knowledge, and is thus distinct from the previous [types of causes]. What is that? [End of fragment.]

The state of being the head and so forth [of the body] exists only through the distinction of being a jar; likewise, [the state of being the head and so forth] exists only through the distinction of being a jar. Vi. [Note: The text appears to be a repetitive commentary on the ontological status of the body's parts as distinct from their conventional designations.]

In this context, there may also be a reading: "by means of the very distinction consisting of the soft, the upward [direction], and so forth, as the skin and the jar"; something is withdrawn from this [text].
This is the *niyati* [kalā] of the *pramātṛ*.
Regarding the indeterminacy of these [actions], he says—"And this being accomplished," etc.—in order to demonstrate that these actions and their results are produced by necessity (*niyati*).

This action of cooking has rice as its object and is distinct from actions having jars or other things as their objects. Furthermore, even while this rice and so forth are being accomplished, they are accomplished by this very action of cooking—which is distinct from actions such as going elsewhere—and not by any other; thus, it is accomplished through the necessity of action (*kriyā-niyati*).

And for this act of cooking, these very things such as wood and so forth are the causal factors (*kāraka*), and not a lump of clay, a staff, and so forth; such is the restriction of the relationship between the goal and its means, as expressed by the words "in this way" and so on.

And having established this, just as there is a fixed state (*sthiti*) or arrangement (*vyavasthā*) of necessity (*niyati*) manifested by the specific rule governing the relationship between the object and the particular means of accomplishment, so too—on the basis of that state and because the causal precedence of the qualities of the cause is well-established through inference—one understands through the intellect that even though there is equality in the co-presence of other causal factors (*kāraka*), such as the staff and others, in the co-presence that brings about the accomplishment of the goal, yet by the very force of the established necessity, in conjunction with the co-presence of the act of cooking (*pacikriyā*), the person acts upon each respective factor according to its own purpose. This is the meaning.

And those causal factors (*kāraka*) are restricted to that very restricted action according to the rule of application; for whatever the rule of application may be, one employs the causal factors as restricted according to that rule of application, functioning through a single mutual friction and operating by manifesting a mutual, restricted assistance.
For there is no other way to achieve that [action] than through the accomplishment of its means.
For success is necessarily the manifestation, through its own necessity (*niyati*), of those [factors] that were previously unmanifest and merged;
and that [success], he [the agent], and they [the factors] proceed from necessity alone, or else do not.
Thus are seen the failures and non-occurrences of actions.

Therefore, even that which has been performed is as if unperformed because it remains within the sphere of prior destiny (*pūrva-niyati*); likewise, even that which has perished is as if not perished because it likewise remains within the sphere of destiny. However, it would perish in this way if [the actions] were applied to their respective objects characterized by specific place and time; such is the meaning.

Engaged in a single friction—that is, proceeding with a single purpose, through a non-attachment, and by means of an operation that is mutually dependent—they proceed by manifesting a fixed mutual assistance based on their reciprocal dependence; therefore it is said: "they function by manifesting a fixed mutual assistance. They accomplish the object to be achieved by the activity directed toward their own respective domains; their functioning is their domain, and all of that—their activity, their domain, and their fruit—is strictly determined. Consequently, necessity (*niyati*) alone is the cause of everything.

But there is no way for that [result] to be accomplished other than through the accomplishment of its specific means; for example, boiled rice—which is to be produced by the act of cooking accomplished by means such as firewood and flames—cannot be accomplished by means such as the rotation of a staff and a wheel, nor does an object such as a jar have as its means of accomplishment things like firewood and flames.
[The phrase] "sādhyārthaiḥ" (by means of the objects to be accomplished) means "this is the object to be accomplished by those [means]. [Note: *tāni* refers to the aforementioned means.]

In this context, there may also be the reading "yathāsvasādhyārthopāyam" (the means for each respective goal to be accomplished). [The agent] employs the causal factors (*kāraka*) in their proper sequence, according to the rules of application; they proceed toward a single consummation (*ekavimarda*), acting in mutual dependence through a fixed mutual assistance.

But there is no accomplishment of that [result] otherwise than through the accomplishment of its means; for accomplishment is necessarily the manifestation, according to its own necessity (*svaniyati*), of those [factors] that were previously unmanifested and merged together. And that [means], he [the agent], and those [factors] proceed only from necessity, or else they do not.

And thus, the failures and non-occurrences of actions are observed; therefore, even that which is done is as if undone because it remains within prior necessity, and even that which is destroyed is as if not destroyed because it likewise remains within necessity. It would only be destroyed in this way if it were subject to its own specific objects.
In its own object, by means of a single application that is mutually dependent; by means of a single application that is mutually dependent. Ya.
"arisen from manifestation" (yathābhāvamavṛttāni) according to Y; "functioning through manifestation" (yathābhāvanavṛttīni) according to Bhā;
"perfected by destruction" (pacinirvṛttāni) according to Bhā.
If it is asked, "What then is *siddhi* (accomplishment)? it is said: *Siddhir hi* and so forth.

By the rule of the aforementioned definition, the manifestation (*abhivyakti*) of forms and other qualities—which exist in a state of seed, whose functions are unmanifest and unevolved, which have arisen and persist through their mutual integration (*sammūrcchita*), and which are produced by the very necessity of their own nature (*svaniyati*) according to the necessity of color, shape, and so on—is what is called *siddhi*. This refers to the manifestation of those things previously unmanifest.
In this regard, there arises in the person this false conceit (*mithyābhimāna*): "This was done by me."

He said: "What is the reason? Is it not a false conceit that 'the jar was made by me'? Since the birth of the jar is established as being inseparable from that action, such a conceit is indeed appropriate."

To this it is replied: "That [effect] and he [the agent]," and so forth. This is because we observe deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding both the occurrence and non-occurrence of those [effects], as well as their accomplishment and non-accomplishment. That effect, such as a jar, and that agent, the potter, and those instruments, such as the staff and so on, proceed—or do not proceed—only by necessity (*niyati*). Sometimes the desire to act arises in him, sometimes it does not; even when desiring to act, he may proceed due to laziness or other factors, or he may not; even having proceeded, he may turn back without having made the jar at all, or he may make something else, or an obstacle may arise for him.

In the same way, other causal factors (*kāraka*) should also be mentioned; and that effect is sometimes accomplished and sometimes not. When one thing is undertaken for the sake of another, that other thing may or may not be accomplished. Thus, he demonstrates the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) well-known in the world—that there are failures and non-occurrences of actions—as seen in the phrase *anudbheda* (non-emergence).

In that regard, even that which is falsely perceived as "done" is, by worldly convention, "not done," because it was previously established by necessity (*niyati*); for it was already situated in such a state by necessity. Likewise, even that which is "destroyed" is "not destroyed," because it subsequently exists in the form of shards and so forth due to necessity; for the jar is destroyed only in its state as a jar, whereas it is not destroyed in its state as threads and so forth.

Regarding the passage beginning with "In this way, however, it would perish," etc.: if that [pot], having fallen apart, being falling apart, or already fallen apart, does not undergo that necessity consisting in the destruction of the pot in the form of a sequence of shards and so forth, then it would either become an absolute non-entity like a donkey's horn, or it would not perish at all but would remain precisely as a pot; only then could it be said to perish. But such is not the case; therefore, there is no destruction.
For destruction is alteration according to its characteristic; and since that [alteration] consists in the state of existing as shards and so forth, it cannot bypass necessity (*niyati*).
Likewise, origination also does not exist, because there is no destruction of non-existence.

In the manuscripts of Ya, however, this reading does not exist at all: "He does not fall into that [state of] dissolution; rather, the sprouts and so forth of the mango seed proceed with their previous forms already established through a sequence that provides space for their arrangement, like the banners of a magician. Having finally experienced the state of the fruit produced by the operation of necessity, they return once more to the very seed; and from that seed again, it proceeds in the same way."
Furthermore, the processes of manifestation for barley, sesame, ashes, and so forth occur in various ways;
and these cannot be bypassed even by human effort,
since the time of ripening is seen to be fixed— for example, sixty-day rice ripens in sixty nights.
And since the object is established in this very way, everything is indeed determined by the manifestation of that very unmanifest object; therefore,
the conceit "this was created by me" from an object that is eternally established through its own manifestation is a false presumption,
for there is nothing at all that is not determined.
And likewise, regarding the phrase "the mango seed" and so forth, the word "are seen" is understood to carry over.

For those things—root, sprout, leaf, stalk, trunk, branch, sub-branch, stem, flower, and so on—which are latent through their own necessity (*niyati*), their activity proceeds according to a sequence of arrangement and spatial opportunity, with their prior forms already established. This applies to the colors such as red and dark-green of the mango fruit, as well as to the tastes such as astringent, sour, and *ṣāḍava*; for in each respective state, whatever other [qualities] arise, they are only those specific ones that were already present and determined.

What is it like? It is like a magician’s banner. Just as a magician, having transformed his banner into the form of a pill or similar object, gradually draws forth from his mouth various colors and various forms that were previously swallowed, so too here, in the case of the mango seed: after experiencing the state of the fruit produced by the activity of *niyati* (destiny) at the end, it returns once more to the seed itself; and from that seed again, in the very same way, the previously mentioned process of the sprout and so forth proceeds.
Thus, let this established continuity of *niyati*, which is beginningless and endless, be observed (pṛ. 20, l. 4).

If it be thought that, because the sprout and so forth never manifest once the seed has been burnt, there is an inconsistency regarding the manifestation and disappearance brought about by *niyati* (destiny), according to the sequence of the [sixfold] path (*ṣaḍadhvakrama*).

To this it is replied: even when the necessity for burning arises, that [necessity] is strictly determined; otherwise, they are seen to appear in such a way. What are these? They are the modes of manifestation occurring in various ways. Of what things? Of barley, sesame, ashes, and so forth. For the ash of barley is of one kind, the ash of sesame is of another, and the ash of sesame is yet another; here too, the modes of manifestation and disappearance are strictly determined.
And these are unassailable even by human effort (*puruṣakāra*); some are established through a different principle, while others are established without human effort.

What is the reason? Because the time of ripening is also seen to be determined; examples such as "the sixty-day rice ripens in sixty nights" have their meaning already explained, since the observation of ripening and so forth occurs through the very determination of place, time, agent, instrument, and so on, and is seen otherwise and otherwise—see page 20, line 4.
In the Ya,
Ṇa, Siddha, Pā, Ḍe, Līṃ, and Bhā manuscripts, however, the reading "tattvāntareṇa siddhāḥ" (established by another principle) does not exist at all.

And thus he applies [the example]: by this aforementioned method, since the object is indeed established, everything regarding that specific manifestation of the unmanifested object is necessarily determined as such.

For that person who maintains the notion of a distinction from its own manifestation, there arises at all times a false conceit regarding a fixed object that is already established—such as "a jar has been made by me out of clay," or "the sixty-day rice and so forth have been cooked by the method of preparing the field and so on. This is because, in reality, nothing is produced; rather, everything that exists is merely manifested, either through action or without action, being supported by time and necessity (*niyati*), though it was previously latent. *Note: The variants provided for the phrase *svavyaktervyatirekamatiḥ* are as follows:
bhā॰vi॰raṃ॰hī॰ reads *svavyaktervyatirekamatiḥ*;
pā॰ ḍe॰ līṃ॰ reads *svavyaktirvyatirikamatiḥ*.*

[The opponent asks: "How can there be ripening from the seed's own causal necessity (*bījaniyati*) alone when it does not occur without earth, water, and so forth? Furthermore, how can there be ripening without time? [The response is: Ripening occurs due to time, heat, wind, and so on; yet we observe ripening of fruits and the like even before the [expected] time has arrived, due to such acts as digging the earth. Moreover, ripening does not occur even when the time has arrived, due to factors such as the stabilization [of the process] through contact with other substances.

Furthermore, in accordance with the will of the knower, there is a transgression of the fixed nature of things, such as the inversion of the color, shape, and other qualities of flowers and so forth; and from sources such as the *Yoniprābhṛta*, it is shown that births in all wombs occur in a manner entirely different [from natural law], thus there is an absence of determinism.
Due to this absence of determinism, there is an absence of necessity (niyati) because of their being produced and impermanent.
No, because [the causal capacity] is not fixed in that way;
for it is the very determination of the seed and so forth that operates upon the water and other factors.
Regarding this, he says: "How does it exist? and so on, up to "the absence of necessity."

As for what you said—that everything exists within the fixed law (*niyati*)—how can that be so when the ripening of a mango fruit and the like do not occur from the fixed law of the seed alone, but rather in dependence upon earth, water, and so forth? By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), earth, water, wind, sunlight, and time are included; these are the factors such as earth, water, and so on. He explains this: ripening results from time, sunlight, wind, and other such factors. Therefore, because it depends upon earth, water, time, wind, sunlight, and the rest, the sprout and so forth, as well as the ripening of its fruit, do not exist within the fixed law of the seed alone.

Likewise, even at an improper time, a deviation from the determination of time is observed; for instance, through such means as digging up the ground, the ripening of fruits and the like is seen to occur even before the [proper] time has arrived. By the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (ādi), [other causes] such as wrapping *kodrava* grains in straw or inflicting wounds [upon them] are intended.

And even when the time has arrived—that is, even when the time for cooking has been reached—cooking does not occur for things that have been solidified by contact with another substance; for example, when a branch is bound according to the prescriptions of *vṛkṣāyurveda*, [the fruit] is prevented from ripening due to that very contact with another substance, or because of liquefaction, as in the case of tender mangoes at the stage where the fragrance has developed, which turn into oil for the purpose of extracting mango oil (*sahakārataila*); and by the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), [it refers to] consumption of birds such as sparrows and the like.

"Furthermore," and so forth: it is not only because of the non-abandonment of the self's own nature that cooking does not occur; what then? Furthermore, in various ways—just as the knowing person himself desires—by following the will of that knower, there occurs a reversal of color, shape, and so forth in objects, transcending their inherent necessity. For example, redness on one side and blueness on the other in a lotus; or the red color of a citron fruit and the seeds infused by it; likewise, the pot-like shape of a pumpkin fruit that has been raised in a pot.

Furthermore, the production from all types of wombs (*yoni*) occurs in entirely different ways than those described in the *Yoniprābhṛta* and other such texts. In the *Yoniprābhṛta*, two kinds of wombs are taught: the sentient (*sacitta*) and the insentient (*acitta*).
Among these, by mixing substances from a sentient womb and burying them in the ground, one is born into the species of humans, snakes, and so forth that lack teeth.
And through the application of substances from an insentient womb according to the prescribed rule, there is the production of gold, silver, pearls, coral, and the like.

Thus, there is an absence of necessity (*niyamābhāva*). In this way, whether cooking occurs at the [proper] time or not at the time, because it depends on other factors and follows the will and effort of a person, there is an absence of necessity. Due to the absence of necessity, cooking and the like are produced (*kṛtaka*); and because they are produced, they are impermanent (*anitya*)—the meaning being that they exist after having not existed, and cease to exist after having existed.
And by these two [properties], there is an absence of fixed order (*niyatyabhāva*).
This concludes the argument.
This is the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa):
[if it is argued that] "earthness" and so forth [are the causes], Bhāṣya, Prakarana, and Prakaraṇapada.
And in the non-dual branch: Bhāṣya; and in the non-dual branch: Pāda, Ḍe, Ya, Lī, Vi.
In the *Śākhā* [recension], on the branch of the *Āmra* [tree], there is the syllable *raṃ* and *hī*;
as for the *pra* of *Yathola*, there is an absence of rule (*niyamābhāva*). This is not present in the *Bhā* manuscript.

To this it is replied: It is not so, because of the necessity [of destiny] (*niyati*). As you have stated, there is an absence of destiny (*niyatyabhāva*) due to the necessity of being dependent, the necessity of non-occurrence in time, and the necessity of occurrence outside of time. He demonstrates this with the words "For the necessity of the seed and so forth," and so on. The word *hi* has the sense of "because" (*yasmāt*); because the activity of all those things is indeed determined by obstruction.
For thus he said: "The water that falls is either possessed of its own nature (*sabhāvaka*) or devoid of its own nature (*nirbhāvaka*)."

For when the determination of the seed is present, then its location—specifically that situated in water—is said to be "conducive" (*sabhāvaka*) toward the production of a sprout; with respect to that aspect of its existence, even the water is said to be "conducive. At other times, however, the opposite is true. In the same way, regarding the earth, wind, time, and so forth, their states of being conducive or non-conducive, as well as whether a person is "busy" (*vyagra*) or "unbusy" (*avyagra*), and so on, depend solely upon *niyati* (determination).

Regarding the capacity or incapacity and the proximity of the instruments (*karaṇa*) and so forth, that very same necessity (*niyati*)—which is singular—resides in the seed and other factors, as well as in water and the rest, in time, in wind, in heat, and in the person, as well as in his will and effort; by the inclusion of "and so forth" (*ādi*), the necessity of water and the rest also resides in the seed and the rest through mutual interaction. For, in accordance with that necessity—that is, in accordance with their mutual necessity—the word "hi" signifies "because" (*yasmāt*); because such is the necessity of all these, therefore the activity of all of them is determined by their mutual necessity due to their inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*), meaning they proceed in exactly that manner.
Because of its necessity,
[the effect] is dependent on the cause;
the state of necessity is the essence of necessity.
Existence occurs through necessity (niyati), for by the obstruction of that [necessity], the activity of all those things is determined;
thus it is said: "The water has fallen, whether possessing its own nature or devoid of its own nature."

For when the determination of the seed is present, then its location, being situated in water and active in the production of the sprout, is called "possessing the capacity" (*sabhāvaka*); with respect to that aspect of its existence, even the water is called "possessing the capacity. At other times, however, the opposite is true. In the same way, regarding the earth, wind, time, and so forth, their states of possessing or not possessing the capacity [to produce] depend on *niyati* (destiny/fate) alone, as in the cases of a person being "busy" or "not busy," and so on.
The non-operation of destiny [is due] to the presence or absence of the capacity or incapacity of the instruments and so forth;
thus he shows the proof established in the world by saying "for it is said."
That which exists together with an entity is "with-entity" (sabhāvaka); that from which an entity has departed is "without-entity" (nirbhāvaka). What is that? It is water that has fallen.

Regarding its cultivation (*tadbhāvanā*): when the seed’s necessity (*bījaniyati*) is oriented toward the manifestation of the sprout—that is, when the seed’s necessity has become imminent—then a certain location, portion, part, or constituent of that necessity, while still situated in the water, is said to be "possessing the capacity" (*sabhāvaka*) as it proceeds toward the production of the sprout. In relation to that portion of the capacity, even the water is said to be "possessing the capacity. This is because, when a distinction is intended, one may resort to a *bahuvrīhi* compound, or omit the possessive suffix (*matup*), or employ a metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*) such that the water itself is the capacity.

And that existence (*bhāva*) belongs to plants, herbs, and the like, such as sprouts; furthermore, the use of the possessive suffix *-mat* is justified by way of distinction, as follows: "there is in this [water], or this has its existence, namely the existence of a sprout (*aṅkurabhāva*), or the sprout itself in that water"; therefore, it is said to be "possessing that existence" (*sabhāvaka*).

At other times, however, there is the opposite: because sprouts and the like do not exist in alkaline or sour water, there is a reversal due to this necessity; therefore, that water is called "lacking that existence" (*abhāvaka*). Thus ends the *Praśastapādabhāṣya*.
...having become the enemy of [the world] through the power of manifestation,
[there is] the piercing of the distinctions...

In this way, regarding the presence and absence of specific conditions in soil, wind, time, and so forth: on saline soil there is the absence of crops and the like, while there is the presence of softness of the feet and the like; or, in well-plowed fields and the like, there is the presence of sprouts and the like from all seeds, whereas in the aforementioned wind there is the absence of sprouts and the like, but the presence of the production of buffalo-hides, cotton, and so forth. Furthermore, there is the absence for humans of certain flowers, fruits, and so forth, as it has been said: "One should avoid sleeping during the day, dew, and the eastern wind in this regard."
In the case of crops, there is no growth when the wind blows from the north; there is growth when they are sown in the rainy season; and there is no growth in Vaiśākha and other such months.

By the inclusion of the word "etcetera," it is meant that there is no growth in excessive heat or when the soil is too hard or too sharp. There is growth when conditions are balanced, and even in the absence of heat, there is simply no growth.
Thus, the principle of necessity (*niyati*) has been stated regarding non-intelligent things such as time and sprouts, which function without conscious intent.
In this condition, one should avoid sleeping during the day, exposure to dew, and the eastern wind; furthermore,
one should avoid alkaline substances, curd, daytime sleep, and the eastern wind.
Thus, in the Caraka Saṃhitā, [chapter] 1.7.451.
Even among the wise, destiny alone prevails.

As for what was stated by you previously—that there is a subversion of the fixed order of things (*vastuniyati*) due to the conscious person (*puruṣa*) acting according to his own will—that is not tenable, because even in that case, the cause is indeed fixed necessity (*niyati*).
Why? Because whether a person is distracted or undistracted occurs solely through fixed necessity; and since that [distraction] is relative, it is likewise fixed necessity.
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the fact that a person is skillful or unskillful is also due to fixed necessity alone.
Thus, in the case of things that are unapplied—that is, those whose activity proceeds independently without depending on the direction of another—there is *niyati* (destiny/fate);

and even in the case of things that are applied, there is *niyati* alone. Whether the production or non-production of a sprout occurs due to the proximity of instruments and so forth, *niyati* alone is the cause.
By this, defects such as those in cooking and the like are refuted.

And even the Omniscient One, perceiving that very single principle of necessity—which is without beginning, middle, or end; which does not undergo transformation in its essential nature; which is both one and manifold; and which is subtle as the process of bondage and liberation—concludes that "it is from necessity alone [all things arise]. Thus, he observes the capacity and incapacity of the instrument, locus, agent, object, recipient, and point of departure—that is, their fitness for and unfitness for the accomplishment of those respective actions. As it has been said: "This is the capacity of the axe, that it cuts wood and not grass" (Pātañjala Yoga Sūtra 4.3).
23. Thus, by the inclusion of the word "etcetera," [it is meant that] the presence of those very factors is their attainment (*prāpti*), and their absence is non-attainment (*aprāpti*);

and because of the inclusion of the word "etcetera," there are obstacles even for those instruments and so forth that have been attained. For these reasons, such as the production or non-production of a sprout and the like, destiny (*niyati*) alone is the cause, because things are determined in such a way.

By this, defects such as [the problem of] cooking and so forth are refuted and denied. As for what was stated by you—that there are defects such as "there is no cooking at the [proper] time" or "cooking at the wrong time"—that too is likewise due to fixed necessity (*niyati*). It is not a defect because, through non-cooking at the [wrong] time and cooking at the [right] time, those various entities are determined by necessity; that very necessity occurs in such and such a way as it is fixed. See page 202, line 4:
"In the production or non-production of a sprout and so forth from the presence [of conditions] and so on, necessity alone is the cause."
By this, defects such as the [alleged] imperfection of digestion are refuted;

for even an omniscient being, perceiving that very single, manifold, beginningless, middleless, and endless determination of things—which is by its nature unchanging and subtle in its process of bondage and liberation—acts solely through that determination. Thus, the acts of raising and lowering [the axe], or the act of cutting, belong to the agent [only as governed by] necessity (*niyati*). (Pāṭha-vārttika)
Even while performing the acts of raising and bringing down [the axe], Devadatta is said to "cut"; in that case, the verb *chid* (to cut) applies to him,
for this is the cutting performed by the primary agent.
This is the agency of the primary agent:
that which is not the cutting of grass by an axe (Pāṇini-vārttika).
That which occurs when, the exertion and the felling being equal, it is the axe that cuts and not the grass—that is the cutting by the axe.
And this must necessarily be understood in this way;
for otherwise, there would be no distinction in the cutting of a sword and a blade of grass.

For one who thinks that "one cuts" occurs solely from the raising and lowering [of the instrument], there would be no distinction in the cutting of a sword and a blade of grass; what is cut by a sword would likewise be cut by a blade of grass.
Thus, in the *Patañjala-Mahābhāṣya* upon the *Vārttika*s composed by Kātyāyana for Pāṇini’s *Vyākaraṇa*, [Adhyāya] 1,
[Pāda] 4,
[Āhnika] 23.

likewise, it is necessarily [the case] in the Bhāṣya.

Furthermore, as for the statement beginning with "even the omniscient one," and your belief that omniscience is achieved through human effort by means of right vision, knowledge, conduct, and austerity, resulting in the destruction of all karma such as the veil of knowledge (*jñānāvaraṇa*) and the attainment of absolute knowledge (*kevalajñāna*)—you should not hold that view either, because it cannot exist without destiny (*niyati*).
How, then, should it be understood? Omniscience arises from destiny alone; he becomes omniscient by perceiving that very entire destiny, and by that destiny alone, and not otherwise.

For he [the Lord] perceives that *vastuniyati* (the fixed order of things)—which exists in all three times as non-arisen and indestructible; which is non-transformable by its own nature and whose essence does not deviate from the stability of the world; which consists of the distinct transformations of movement, station, immersion, duration, form, taste, color, body, speech, mind, breath, and so forth in persons distinguished as capable (*bhavya*), incapable (*abhavya*), perfected (*siddha*), and others; which is a single unity undifferentiated across all these distinctions yet appears manifold because it is restricted to those specific forms in each particular case; which is subtle due to the fixed order of the processes of bondage and liberation; and which constitutes the beginningless connection between the soul and karma through their mutual relationship of cause and effect via *mithyādarśana* (false view) and other factors—by the force of *niyati*, there arises in the case of the capable (*bhavya*) a continuous, beginningless bondage. Furthermore, through the transformation (*vivarta*) of the states of right view and so forth, which are capable of overturning that bondage, there occurs liberation, defined as the abiding of the soul’s own nature—consisting of knowledge, vision, vigor, bliss, and so forth, which is immaterial by nature—within itself. Thus, the process of bondage, with its many divisions and sub-divisions such as the bound, the binder, the object to be bound, and the method of binding, is perceived. Consequently, it is established that, according to the very contemplation you have described, Time alone is the agent, since it functions toward its determined objects both simultaneously and non-simultaneously.

In this world, no entities such as a jar, its form, and so forth—which exist simultaneously—can be differentiated as distinct things without a time characterized by the manifestation of simultaneous occurrence;

for it is through such an occurrence that the jar exists as its neck and other parts, as clay exists as a lump and so forth, as earth exists as clay and so forth, as substance exists as earth and so forth, and as existence exists as substance and so forth.

Beholding the process of liberation—which consists of non-simultaneous existence, contemplation, victory over the afflictions, conduct, and self-restraint; which involves the shedding of karma through the performance of twelve kinds of austerity; which is to be explained by means of [the analysis of] field, time, state of existence, gender, ford-maker, self-enlightened one, and enlightened-by-others, as well as knowledge, immersion, interval, number, and relative magnitude; and which is characterized by the absolute, exclusive, and unimpeded bliss resulting from the total destruction of all karma—he remains for infinite time in unimpeded bliss.

This process of bondage and liberation has been shown merely by way of direction; because it is extremely subtle and involves much that remains to be said, it cannot be fully explained here at the time of this investigation, as it has been stated: "In this world, the contemplation of the soul is difficult to fathom even for one who has mastered all scriptures; yet the contemplation regarding bondage and liberation is even more difficult to grasp."
This marks the conclusion; thus, the doctrine of necessity (*niyativāda*) is completed. [End of] the section on divisions. [End of] the inquiry. [End of] the treatise.
The assistance provided by dharma and adharma consists in the grasping of the movement and stationing of the soul and the mind.
The accommodation of space;
bodies, speech, mind, and the out-breath and in-breath belong to the *pudgalas*.
And [the notions of] pleasure, pain, life, death, and grasping; 20. [And the notion of] self.
There is mutual assistance among living beings; duration, transformation, activity, and priority and posteriority belong to time.
Persons (pudgala) possess touch, taste, smell, and color.
Thus, in the fifth chapter of the Tattvārthādhigama-sūtra:
"The vow consists of abstaining from violence, falsehood, theft, unchastity, and possessiveness.
Restraint is the cessation of the outflows.

He [proceeds] by means of the restraints (gupti), the careful conducts (samiti), the duties (dharma), the reflections (anuprekṣā), the conquest of the hardships (parīṣahajaya), and the conduct (cāritra).
Through austerity, there is also shedding (nirjarā).

They are to be established by way of field, time, destiny, gender, place of birth, conduct, the awakening of a pratyekabuddha, the awakening of a buddha, the penetration of knowledge, internal distinctions, numerical enumeration, and relative magnitude.
Liberation is the total destruction of karma.
Thus, in the *Tattvārthādhigamasūtra*,

it is thereby demonstrated that time itself exists as the occurrence of determined objects, whether simultaneously or non-simultaneously, precisely through the process of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) you have described.

In this world, no things such as the form of a jar (*ghaṭa-rūpa*) and so forth, which exist simultaneously, can be distinguished as distinct entities without a time characterized by the manifestation of simultaneous occurrence; for it is through such occurrence and such becoming that the jar exists as its neck and other parts, as clay and lump, as earth and soil, as substance and earth, and as substance and so forth— these being states (*bhāva*) that do not exist simultaneously.
In this world, the inquiry into the nature of the soul is difficult to grasp according to all the scriptures;
yet even more difficult to comprehend than that is the inquiry into bondage and liberation.

Another proponent of the substantialist perspective (*dravyārtha*), namely the variety of the *vidhi-naya*, says: "Even this doctrine of necessity (*niyati-vāda*) is not entirely satisfying; therefore, it is as follows," and so forth.

As for this which was stated—that whether [an entity] is conscious or unconscious, independent or dependent, it cannot be merely unconscious—what then? This [world] is determined by *niyati* (necessity) alone as having a causal relationship characterized by manifold actions, whether simultaneous or non-simultaneous. By means of this very conception expressed by you, since the desired objects such as seeds and sprouts, with their simultaneous or non-simultaneous and fixed forms and so forth, are established, it follows that it is not *niyati* itself that exists; rather, it is *kāla* (time) that exists. For "the other being prior or posterior, simultaneous or non-simultaneous, long or quick" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 2.2.6) are indeed the marks (*liṅga*) of time.

Because of the statement, "Since existence (*vṛtti*) consists of the occurrence of objects that are determined as simultaneous or non-simultaneous, and since 'occurring' (*vartana*) is the definition of time," he says the following for the purpose of explaining that:
"In this world, do the form and other qualities of a jar, which exist simultaneously, come into being by their own nature through mutual distinction, or rather through the power of time?"

First, it is considered in terms of its substantial form (*vasturūpa*): the ellipsis of the sentence is that, therein, there are not even any [entities] existing through a differentiation of substance; for, whether by way of differentiation from color, taste, smell, touch, and sound—that is, by way of distinction or through such a differentiated form—it does not arise from a cause, because even though it is perceived together with them, it does not exist apart from them.

Furthermore, because they are perceivable by distinct sense organs, their lack of unity establishes both their simultaneity and their plurality; for there is no simultaneity for that which is non-different. Just as the simultaneous falling of two yokes occurs upon two shoulders, so too elsewhere simultaneity has multiple substrates. Therefore, the manifestation of their "occurrence" (vṛtti)—namely, that color-forms and the rest exist simultaneously—is observed both in fact and in word. For "occurrence" (vṛtti) is precisely what is meant by existing, being reckoned, being enumerated, being spread out, or being determined by means of the intellect or by speech.

Therefore, according to the literal meaning of the word *kāla* as "that which calculates" (*kalana*), time is "occurrence" (*vartana*). Without that essence of time—which consists of the manifestation of simultaneous occurrence—those forms and other qualities could not possibly exist simultaneously. Thus, the fact that forms and so forth exist simultaneously is due solely to the power of time. In this way, subtle forms and so forth have been described; likewise, gross objects such as a jar and its neck are also [manifested] through such simultaneous occurrence. Of what? Of the very essence of time itself.
And since "functioning" (*vṛtti*) means "coming into being" (*bhavana*), he says: "because of existing in such a way.
This refers to clay, clods of earth, and so forth; for "clay" means that clods of earth and the like exist simultaneously.
Since there is no possibility of anything else occurring apart from the functioning of one who desires to become clay and so forth, it follows that [the world] has the nature of time (*kālātmakatā*).

But since *niyati* (the principle of necessity) possesses the nature of all things, everything would always possess all forms; for in the absence of time, there would be no distinction between the past, the future, and the present.

Furthermore, even so, it has been observed that there is indeed no transgression of time, because things continue to exist in such a manner—just as clay, clods of earth, diamonds, stones, sand, and so forth [retain their respective natures].
Thus, substance (*dravya*) consists of earth and the others; earth, water, fire, air, ether, and so forth, existing simultaneously, are substance.
Substance and the rest are existence (*bhāva*); "existence" is the designation for substances, qualities, and actions along with their subdivisions, because they exist simultaneously.
In this way, it has been demonstrated that time alone is that which exists through simultaneous occurrence.
The mode of existence is characterized by mutual penetration.
And their unity, and not their unity; see Bhāṣya, page 158–1.

Thus, even for one who desires to exist, since there is no possibility of anything whatsoever occurring apart from the process of becoming (*vartanā*), there would follow the consequence that everything would always possess all forms due to the nature of time;

for if time were absent, there would be no distinction between the past, the future, and the present. This is because *niyati* (the principle of necessity) consists of the essence of time and therefore possesses the nature of all things.
Moreover, even so, there is indeed no transgression of time;

thus, it is contemplated that even the necessity of sequential occurrence is itself time. Therefore, he says: "Even those things which do not occur simultaneously," and so on, up to the point of "attainment."

That which has the nature of arising not simultaneously is "non-simultaneous-arising" (*ayugapadbhāvin*). If, for such a thing that desires to arise and is oriented toward becoming—such as a seed, a sprout, or other entities—the temporal existence consisting of "occurrence" (*vṛtti*) is not admitted, then it follows that nothing at all could be established apart from occurrence, because in the absence of occurrence they would be like the son of a barren woman.
Since this consequence of non-establishment arises, and since their establishment occurs when time exists in the form of occurrence, [time] must therefore have the nature of time.
Thus, it has been stated that the acceptance of a fixed object does not occur without time; therefore, time itself consists of simultaneous and non-simultaneous operations.
[This occurs] when there is the state of being about to become, becoming, having become, and existing.
Regarding the phrase *padvyāvṛttyā* (in the Bhāṣya),
there may also be a reading here as *padvā vṛttyā*.
Now, the fault of the proponents of necessity (*niyativādin*) is stated, beginning with "But of necessity" (*niyatestu*) and continuing up to "always for everyone" (*sadā sarvasya*).

The very same objection that you raised against the proponent of *svabhāva*—namely, that for Devadatta and others, the states of childhood, youth, adulthood, middle age, and so forth would exist simultaneously because of the nature of possessing all forms (*sarvākāra-svabhāvatva*), and that for rice and other plants, the states of sprout, leaf, stalk, and so forth would likewise exist simultaneously—that same objection applies equally to you, the proponent of *niyati*. This is because *niyati* is the essence of everything; why then does it not consist exclusively of every form? If this were so, there would always, at all times, be every single thing, whatever it may be. For if time did not exist, there would be no distinction between the past, the future, and the present. Yet, we do observe the absence of past and future forms and the presence of present forms. Since there is no time characterized by sequential activity (*vṛtti*) and since *niyati* is undifferentiated, there would have to be an absence of present forms just as there is an absence of past and future forms, or conversely, there would have to be past and future forms just as there are present forms. However, neither the presence of past and future forms nor the absence of present forms is ever observed.
As it has been stated [in the *Prakaraṇa*], see page 196, line 4:
"the state of having attained the form... (*°gatākāratā*).

It might be thought: "The past and future forms exist in the same way as the present form within the determined [entity], but they are not perceived because they are concealed; whereas the present form is perceived because it is manifested. Since this has already been addressed, it is not a valid rebuttal. To this, we reply: furthermore, even so, there is still no transcendence of time.

Even so, this threefold nature occurring simultaneously, as well as its manifestation and disappearance in succession—designated as "past" and "future"—all this would not be possible without a reckoning (*kalana*), a proceeding (*vartana*), or an becoming (*bhavana*) established by the inherent power of the meaning of words denoting time; therefore, because time is unavoidable, [the term] "immediately after" (*anantaram*) is used. If one asks: "Why is that? [it is because... [The text here appears to contain scribal corruption.]
"Thus, even though it has been well-examined," and so forth—

by this method, even when thoroughly investigated, no cause other than time (kāla) is observed that sequentially establishes states such as childhood and so on, or sprouts and so on, nor one that simultaneously establishes forms and so on.

Therefore, although you have accepted time as a specific, non-specific, and immediate manifestation, by rejecting it due to the fault of grasping at mere necessity (niyati), you deprive yourself of those qualities resulting from your partiality toward the position of time as possessing attributes.

If the activity of things were produced solely by necessity (*niyati*), then it would not be logical to say "this first, this later," "this now, this simultaneously," because necessity is present in all things, such as seeds and so forth.
If you argue that [the sequence] is due to necessity itself, we say no, because [such a claim] is purposeless.

What is the use here of "prior" and so forth? Time has already been accepted through the very manifestation of such alternative conceptualizations as: "for seven days it becomes *kalala*, then for seven days an *arbuda*, and likewise a *peśī* and a *ghana*," and so on. In this sequence within the womb and elsewhere, the subsequent state is manifested immediately following the preceding state; thus, time has been accepted precisely through this regulated manifestation. Yet, because of the fault of grasping at mere necessity (*niyati*) and out of attachment to your own position, you—who do not wish to accept it—deprive yourself of those qualities resulting from your partiality toward the side of time, which possesses such qualities.

When it is said, "Let there be no *grāha*," because of its extreme harshness it causes mental pain; thus, by the figurative term explained previously, it is called *grāha* as if it were a crocodile (*grāha*).

Alternatively, *grāha* means intention (*abhiprāya*); it is called *grāha* because it causes one to grasp (*grāhayati*). By the fault of that intention, not seeing even the time you yourself have accepted, you deprive yourself of the multitude of virtues such as fame and the quality of speaking the truth regarding time (*kālatattvavāditva*), and so forth. The "emergence" (*samuddhāta*) of a Kevalin is the "Kevali-samuddhāta."

At the time of performing that [process], the Blessed One, the Kevalin, performs *āvarjīkaraṇa*—an activity consisting of the projection of karma into the *udīraṇāvalikā* for a period of one *antarmuhūrta*; thereafter, he enters *samuddhāta*. Its sequence is as follows: first, in the initial moment, by means of the expansion of his omniscience (*kevalajñānābhoga*), he forms a "staff" (*daṇḍa*) composed of an aggregate of soul-units (*jīvapradeśa*), which possesses the same width and thickness as his own body and extends from the top to the bottom of the world. In the second moment, he transforms that very staff into a "door-panel" (*kapāṭa*) by expanding it toward the two directions of east and west, reaching to the edge of the transverse world (*tiryagloka*). In the third moment, he transforms that very door-panel into a "churning-stick" (*manthāna*) by expanding it toward the two directions of south and north, likewise reaching to the edge of the transverse world. In this way, most of the world is filled; however, the spaces within the churning-stick remain unfilled because the soul-units move along their respective linear paths (*anuśreṇi*).
In the fourth moment, those [rays] also fill the world-enclosures (lokaniṣkuṭa), and thus the entire world becomes filled.

One might object: "When a Kevalin situated in the middle of the world performs the *samudghāta*, then even in the third moment the world is indeed filled; so what is the purpose of filling the intermediate spaces in the fourth moment? Furthermore, it should be reflected upon that when he performs the *samudghāta* elsewhere, the intermediate spaces are indeed cleared away in the third moment.

Immediately thereafter, in the fifth moment, he withdraws the internal churning-sticks (*manthāntara*) in reverse order according to the aforementioned sequence; the meaning is that he contracts the extended soul-units (*jīvapradeśa*).
In the sixth moment, he withdraws the churning-stick (*manthāna*), and in the seventh moment, he contracts the door-panels (*kapāṭa*).
