"Indeterminate sentience and insentience," and so forth, up to "time is the act of reckoning": it is precisely the contemplation of the identity between the essential nature [of consciousness] and its manifestations that exists.
Sentience is indeterminate because, in the form of the modes of cognition (*upayoga*), it is employed as the nature of form and so on;
likewise, insentience is also indeterminate because it is employed through the attainment of the application of sentience.

Alternatively, when grass and other substances are consumed by cattle and so forth, they undergo the state of being endowed with consciousness such as pleasure and pain; and when matter undergoes the acquisition of vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so on, there occurs the state of the destruction of the vital breaths of that substance. Due to the force of transformation occurring through the sequence of time, and because living beings (*jīva*) and matter (*pudgala*) have functioned through the states of subsidence, destruction, destruction-cum-subsidence, and manifestation in an infinite succession from beginningless time, their form—which is characterized by calculation—repeatedly undergoes transformation, even though it possesses all the characteristics of permanence, such as stability and so forth.

Therefore, for those who are not omniscient, such as ourselves, the reckoning of the process of the manifestation of all conceptual constructions is accessible only through inference and remains undifferentiated; however, for the omniscient one, time is the reckoning of the differentiated process, like grain in a vast, full, and clearly defined granary.

By means of such a sense of "reckoning" (*kalana*), it continues its very process of existence (*vartanā*) without abandoning its general nature, being past, present, or future. Not only does this operation consist of the mutual transformation of the conscious and the unconscious, but how so? Even for the unconscious, such as the earth and other elements, it is likewise. For example: because *pudgalas* belong to a single genus, their operation—consisting of transformations revolving through the states of earth, water, fire, wind, vegetation, and so forth—is a process that occurs infinitely and without beginning or end. Those atoms whose own essence (*ātman*) or intrinsic reality (*svatattva*) consists of such an operation without beginning or end are "atoms. Of these atoms, whose intrinsic reality is an operation without beginning or end, the form consisting of reckoning revolves and recurs again and again. This recurrence occurs through the transformation of distinctions such as color, taste, and so on; or even through the distinction of qualities (*guṇa*), such as by decreasing or increasing in one, two, three, numerable, innumerable, or infinite degrees, or by degrees of blackness, whiteness, and so forth. Even for a single part—an atom of the most subtle state of form and so on—there is recurrence without beginning or end.

Therefore, that which consists of the past, future, and present—unitary, immutable, immovable, free from loss, birth, and modification, and not subject to increase or decay (the inclusion of "and so forth" [ādi] refers to all such characteristics of eternity, such as being fixed)—this alone is logically established as the cause consisting of *kalana* (temporalization); the eternity of atoms, the *puruṣa*, *niyati*, and so on, is not. For, since no beginning, middle, or end is perceived in this kind of eternity—which is essentially the temporalization of the cyclical process (*viparivarta*) consisting of prior and posterior states—the term *kāla* (time) shall be understood as the *kalana* of the unfolding of the manifold conceptualizations of the universe.

And that reckoning is of two kinds: for those who are not omniscient, such as ourselves, it is accessible only through inference; it is an undifferentiated grasping of the mere generality of all things, like the reckoning of grain in an immeasurable, full granary. Just as grain, having been measured, is filled into a granary and grasped by way of a general indication—thinking, "It is some quantity such as hundreds of thousands of jars"—in the same way, we and others grasp the reckoning of the processes of the past, future, and present merely by way of a general indication.

And regarding the Omniscient One, that time consists of the calculation and reckoning of the isolated progression (*vartanā*) occurring at every moment during the period of supreme cessation (*paramaniruddha-kāla*). This is understood from the root *kala* in the sense of "reckoning" (Pāṇini Dhātupāṭha 497, 1866), as it has been said: "In whatever manner and in whatever state a substance transforms through application (*prayoga*) or spontaneous change (*visrasā*), the Jina knows it exactly thus; there is no cognition of a non-existent mode (*aparyaya*)."

Thus, this determination of the time of the true nature of persistence [is established] because it is not of the same essence as the nature of time itself. (Āvaśyakaniryukti 794) [End of] Chapter on Time.
The form beginning with *ga*, etc., [is] *vi*, *ḍe*, *līṃ*, *raṃ*, *hī*;
[it is] also attained as the form beginning with *ga* and *pā*.

The nature of time (*kāla*), which consists of sequential calculation (*kalana*), revolves again and again as the defining characteristic of all eternal things, beginning with the Pole Star (*dhruva*).

Therefore, for those who are not omniscient, such as ourselves, the calculation of the process of the manifestation of universal conceptualization is accessible only through inference and remains undifferentiated—like grain in an immeasurable, full granary. However, for the Omniscient One, time is the calculation of a process that is clearly differentiated.

In that manner, by way of the sense of reckoning, while not abandoning the commonality of mere occurrence (*vartanā*) itself, it is past, it is present, and it will be future; for occurrence is indeed occurrence,
and occurrence is indeed occurrence.
The conduct is indeed dead; [the syllable] Raṃ, Hīṃ, [is] the form consisting of the self;
[it is] not that quality, Pra.
Regarding "possessing neither increase nor decrease" (*avṛddhyavyayayogī*):
it appears that the reading *avṛddhyavyayayogī* etc., as found on page 21, line 22, is correct.

Alternatively, this is not the sole definition of the eternal; rather, that which is constant (*dhruva*), immovable (*kūṭastha*), unshakable, and free from loss, gain, modification, production, increase, and decrease—that is the eternal.
"That too is eternal, in which reality is not destroyed;
what then is reality? Reality is the state of being that [thing] (*tadbhāvaḥ*)," as stated in the *Paspaśāhnika* of Patañjali’s *Mahābhāṣya*.
*Oṃ kaṣaṭkāra-bhāḥ kaḥ ṣaṭkāra-pāḥ ḍe līṃ raṃ hīṃ kaṣaṭkāraka-viḥ*
The term *vikalpa* does not appear in the *prati* manuscripts;
furthermore, *pratibhā* appears in all [manuscripts],
whereas *prati* appears in all except *ya*.

"Whatever substances transform into whatever states through effort (*prayoga*) or spontaneous change (*visrasā*), the Jina knows them exactly as they are; there is no knowledge of that which lacks a substance (*aparyava*). (Āvaśyaka-niryukti 794). Thus ends the section on negation (*natthiya*).
"Thus," and so forth:

that very Time, by means of its mode of existing (*vartanā*)—which has the sense of "reckoning" (*kalana*) as its essential nature and serves as the substratum for that [reckoning]—does not abandon that very existence (*vartanā*) which is common and undifferentiated, yet it receives the designation of particularities such as "past," "present," and "future. No other entity whatsoever, such as Necessity (*niyati*) and the like, possesses this character of reckoning, because they lack existence. Rather, that very reality characterized by reckoning is divided into three ways, because it has that [existence] as its substratum and because its nature is existence, just like a jar; it is not something with a different substratum. That which is past, present, or future, if it were a non-time with a different substratum, would simply not be of that nature at all.
Thus it receives its specific designation;
yet that very [reality] is divided into three ways, for otherwise nothing else would exist.
It exists by measuring itself through its own persistence, it is measured by itself, and [it acts] by means of itself, for itself, and through itself, and so forth.

In this very way, that [entity] is perceived as being oriented toward the designation of an effect within the causal states of both the present and the past—clouds and so forth in one case, cloth and so forth in another; and just as it is perceived, so too is it produced by that same activity (*vṛtti*), for it is conceived through action. Why? Because otherwise there would be no other [state], for here one thing does not become something else: just as a flower does not become a sky-flower, nor a sky-flower a flower; or a jar does not become cloth, nor cloth a jar.

What then? That very thing becomes that; the flower itself remains the flower, yet it also becomes otherwise, as when the very same flower appears through states such as being a bud, half-blossomed, fully blossomed, withered, or faded.
Thus far, existence (*bhavana*) has been explained as non-different from time—that is, as "time itself.

Furthermore, by means of the differentiation of causes, that very same [time] exists as it differentiates [objects] in such a way; thus, by "acting" (*kalayatīti*), it experiences the agency of differentiation (*kalana*). The meaning is that "differentiation occurs."

The meaning is that it itself is "kalita" (conceived), "kriyate" (performed), or "bhavati" (becomes), due to the causal relationship between preceding and succeeding states. Furthermore, through the differentiation of the powers (*śaktibheda*) of that very same *kalana* (process of conceptualization/construction), there arises the status of instrument (*karaṇatā*) in the sense of "it is performed by that," the status of recipient (*sampradānatā*) in the sense of "it is performed for that," and—by the inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*)—the statuses of ablative (*apādāna*) and locus (*adhikaraṇa*) as well, in the senses of "from that" and "in that."
Present by means of the present,
consisting of the present.
Thus it receives the designation of a specific distinction;
yet that very [reality] is divided threefold, for otherwise there would be nothing else.
It exists by fashioning itself in such a way: it fashions through its own activity, it is fashioned by itself, and so forth—by it, for it, and from it.

In this very way, that [entity] is apprehended in its causal state—whether present or past—with a tendency toward being designated as an effect: in one case as a cloud and so forth, in another as a cloth and so forth;

and just as it is apprehended, so too is it produced by such activity, being conceived through the action [of its manifestation], as when a jar comes to be as a cloth [in the process of weaving]. (Pātañjala Yogaśāstra Bhāṣya)
It does not exist as clothness or as potness; the sky of the jar exists as clothness. (Note: This sentence is absent in the Rañjanā, Hīnayāna, and Bhāratīya manuscripts.)

The meaning is that this is also [the case] through the distinction of the grammatical factors (kāraka); [this is] by means of conceptualization (kalanayā) regarding the prior and the subsequent. *Prakaraṇa*.
And for that [person],
even though there is the state of being an instrument (*karaṇa*) and an agent (*kāraka*), it is not [the case]... [text fragment].

Now, in order to demonstrate that even this time, though divided threefold, is non-different, its unity through knowledge and action is stated: "In this very way," and so forth. First, unity is perceived through knowledge as long as [the divisions] such as clouds and so on are seen in one place.

"Even so" means that just as time remains undivided despite the differences in the powers of the agent, the object, the instrument, and so forth, likewise, this locative case ending (*saptamyanta*) refers to the two causal states of the present and the past. It is understood by way of being oriented toward what is called the "effect" (*kāryākhyā*), through the acceptance of the effect, by virtue of its predominance, and indeed through identity with it. That same time is grasped as being oriented toward the effect in its present state, and as being oriented toward the subsequent state in its past state. What is meant? It is measured (*kalyate*) and known (*jñāyate*).
According to their respective order, in one case there is a cloth and so forth, while in another case there is a cloud and so forth; specifically, a cloth in the present and a cloud in the past.

For example, a person seeing a cloth in the forenoon thinks that even in the afternoon it is this very same cloth, and likewise tomorrow, the day after, and the next day as well—it is the cloth; thus, he considers it to be the cloth both in the present time and in the future time.

As soon as a cloud rises and begins to rain, one thinks, "It rains," and then this [seed] rains; from that, the seed of the *pralaho* plant arises, followed by the root, the sprout, and so forth; then the stalk of the *pralaho*, then the cotton, then the thread, and then the cloth. Thus, regarding the very past time, one conceives of the future cloth; therefore, that same time—whether past or present—is perceived without distinction through its orientation toward the manifestation of the effect. Consequently, it is indeed non-different.

Having thus established unity through cognition, he establishes unity through action as well, by means of an extended application (*atideśa*): "And like the act of grasping, that very [action] is performed."

What is the reason? Because it functions in that way; for such is its mode of being. Indeed, that very action is performed in the same manner as it is perceived, since it is not distinct from it. Thus, he demonstrates the meaning of the *kāraka* (the factor of action): "it is fashioned by the action.

In this way, first, there is an identity between the past and present causes through their grasping and instrumentality directed toward what is called the effect. The word *ākhyā* (designation) [is used] because of the distinction made merely by the word itself.

Even regarding those two in the future: when those two causes are in the future while the effect is past or present, the state of being reckoned as "causes" is observed by virtue of their orientation toward the designation of cause; this is seen, for example, in the case of conjunction, threads, and so forth, through the processes of producing a water-filled loom-shuttle and cooking, resulting in the state of being cloth.

For this very reason, it is *kalana* (reckoning) alone that is capable of revolving as the sole function of both cause and effect—being devoid of personal effort (*apuruṣakāra*), lacking inherent nature (*asvabhāva*), independent of necessity (*aniyati*), and belonging to transmigratory existence (*saṃsārin*) from beginningless time.

For one who maintains that the person (*puruṣa*) exists as a temporal occurrence, it is logical that the acquisition of sequential order arises through the very power of time, based on the fourth statement concerning the purpose of the sequence of liberation;

furthermore, the process of the bondage of karma is established through false views and the like, as well as through the concealment of its defects and so forth, whereby the beginninglessness of *saṃsāra* is tenable due to the non-interruption of the continuum. However, for the proponent of the person who holds that the supreme self (*paramātman*) is eternally pure, *saṃsāra* is not tenable because of the absence of bondage.

The absence of bondage is observed to be conceived as identical to the instrument of perception, just as the cause directed toward the manifestation of the effect [is conceived as identical to the effect]; therefore, there is indeed identity.

For example, it is like the state of being a cloth resulting from the conjunction of threads and so forth, through the processes of sowing, ripening, and weaving. Just as, having seen the conjunction of threads, the activities of sowing water, ripening, and supporting the seeds of *ruta*, cotton, *pralahī*, and *poṇḍa* plants, as well as their sprouts and so forth, and the formation of clouds, have occurred and are likewise performed—those very processes are accepted as the cloth; thus, the cloth is indeed [the result]. In this way, because the weaver is engaged through the acts of grasping and making, the state of being a present or past cloth is observed; therefore, there is identity between the two.
(Note: *tadātmanena* is according to the readings of Pā., Raṃ., Hī., Bhā., and Ya.)

In these two as well, a state of being prepared for the future is observed through their orientation toward what is called the "cause," just as [the sequence] from the conjunction of threads and so forth, to the production of the water-filled [loom], to the cooking, to the weaving, and finally to the state of being cloth.

For this very reason, it is *kalana* (the act of measuring/time) alone that is capable of revolving through the functions of cause and effect; it is devoid of human agency (*apuruṣakāra*), lacks inherent nature (*asvabhāva*), and is not subject to fixed necessity (*aniyati*). It belongs to the transmigrating world (*saṃsārin*) and has existed since beginningless time. Precisely because of the power of Time, the attainment of sequence is possible solely through the fourth word—the meaning of the stages of liberation taught by the proponents of the Puruṣa.

The beginninglessness of saṃsāra is logical for one who maintains the doctrine of the person (puruṣavādin), because the process of karmic bondage is established through false views and the like, as well as through the corruption and concealment of that [knowledge] and so forth; however, it is not logical for the pure supreme self (paramātman) of those who maintain its existence, because of the absence of bondage,
and there is an absence of bondage.
In the *Graha-karaṇa*, in the chapter on the calculation of the planets (*praśna-paṭala*), it is said: "The body [of the planet] is calculated... [End of fragment].
This is a designation ending in the locative case;
for this very reason, it says "and so forth."

For this very reason, because its activity is unobstructed and because it is all-pervasive, it has no dependence on other causes. Indeed, *kalanā* (the act of reckoning) alone—being singular and having no other means—is capable of revolving by itself through the functioning of cause and effect. It is devoid of human effort (*apuruṣakāra*), because there is no distinction in its activity among sentient and insentient things; it is without intrinsic nature (*asvabhāva*), because it is incessant in its unfolding through the sequence of transformations consisting of the living (*jīva*) and the non-living (*ajīva*); it is without fixed necessity (*aniyati*), precisely because its essence consists in the revolving transformation of becoming otherwise; and it is characterized by transmigration (*saṃsāra*), because transmigration consists in the transition from one nature to another through the revolving transformations of the embodied soul’s forms, such as dyads and triads, earth, water, rice, and so forth, up to food, sap, blood, and the like. Therefore, it is beginningless (*anādi*). By virtue of this beginninglessness, any dependence on other causes such as necessity (*niyati*) and the rest is cast far away by this *kalanā*.

Therefore, because it is beginningless, there is the operation of Time (*kāla*). It is solely from this very operation of Time, independent of any other cause, that even what is asserted by the proponent of the Person (*puruṣavādin*)—namely, that "everything arises from the activity of the Person alone"—occurs; it does not arise from human effort (*puruṣakāra*). This is because things that are beginningless exist simultaneously, whereas things with a beginning possess an operation characterized by succession (*paurvāparya*), and both of these are indeed Time, since Time was established by that very proponent of the Person himself. For this reason, he says: precisely from the fourth statement regarding the sequence of liberation as taught by the proponent of the Person—"The state of deep sleep (*suṣupta*), becoming purified, becomes the state of dreamless sleep (*supta*); the state of dreamless sleep becomes the waking state (*jāgrat*); and the waking state, when purified, becomes the fourth state (*turīya*), the state of liberation"—the acquisition of succession through the power of Time is logically established. Therefore, the establishment of the specific states such as deep sleep and so forth, which consists in their operation throughout beginningless time, is possible only in our own doctrine regarding the reality of the Supreme Self’s manifestation (*vartana-tattva*), and not in the doctrine of the Person, because in that [latter] doctrine there is no possibility of the conceptualization of succession or non-succession.

Otherwise, among these four states—which are [allegedly] of one and the same nature as all-pervading, eternal, and non-sequential—what state would be the first, the second, the third, or the fourth? Furthermore, because the relationship of cause and effect is established between the two states of cause and effect brought about by the sequence of functional activity (*vṛtti*), and because the process of the bondage of karma is established through general causes such as false views and specific causes such as the denial of those defects, the beginninglessness of *saṃsāra* is maintained due to the absence of any cause for the interruption of the continuum. Moreover, due to the absence of a body and the absence of instruments, there is an absence of defects (*pradoṣa*), and consequently, an absence of karma.

...the beginninglessness of saṃsāra does not belong to that *niyati* either, because it is not the ultimate reality (*atattva*). Whatever is not the ultimate reality is not seen to possess *niyati*, like a jar or a cloth.

In the same way, because time has as its nature a beginningless continuity, it is logical that there is a continuous process of the emergence and disappearance of earth and so forth, as well as rice and so forth.

Furthermore, for those who maintain that the Puruṣa is the Supreme Self—pure, immutable, eternal, and constant—it is not logical that both cause and effect [belong to Him], because there is no transmigratory existence (saṃsāra) due to the absence of bondage. There is an absence of bondage because of the absence of a cause, owing to being bodiless and lacking instruments; by the word "and" (ca), other reasons such as omnipresence, oneness, and eternity are also implied. Just as there is an absence of passion (pradoṣa) when the causes of passion and so forth are absent, there is an absence of karma; this has already been explained up to the point where the beginninglessness of saṃsāra is established through its non-recurrence.
The existence of the turning [of the wheel]...
by the very first person... of those who possess birth and so forth.
False view, non-restraint, negligence, passions, and activities are the causes of bondage. (8.1)
Thus ends the first chapter, "Yoga as the Activity of Body, Speech, and Mind," in the *Tattvārthādhigama-sūtra*.
That influx is auspicious for merit.
The unwholesome [is the cause] of evil.
Defamation, concealment, envy, obstruction, striking, and injury belong to the karma of knowledge-obscuring and perception-obscuring [subtypes].
Suffering, grief, torment, lamentation, killing, and wailing— whether residing in oneself, in others, or in both— belong to the karma of unpleasant sensation (*asātavedya*).
Compassion for living beings and those observing vows, charity, restraint from passion and the like, patience, and purity— these constitute the experience of pleasant karma (sadvedya). 13.
Speaking ill of the Kevalins, the scriptures, the Saṅgha, the Dharma, and the Devas is the cause of the delusion of vision (darśanamoha);
and an intense state of self-modification resulting from the arousal of the kaṣāyas is the cause of the delusion of conduct (cāritramoha).
And having many undertakings and possessions [is a cause] for the lifespan of a hell-being.
Deceit is the nature of animals;
for humans, it is having few undertakings and possessions, as well as gentleness and straightforwardness by nature.
And the state of being devoid of moral precepts and vows for all [beings].
Passion, restraint-cum-non-restraint, non-restraint, involuntary shedding of karma, and foolish austerity belong to the celestial [status] name-karma;
crookedness of yoga and deception belong to the inauspicious name-karma.
The opposite of the auspicious.

Purity of vision, perfection in discipline, non-transgression regarding vows and observances, constant application of knowledge and spiritual agitation, renunciation and austerity according to one's capacity, service to the Saṅgha, the virtuous, and meditation, devotion to the Arhats, the teachers, the learned, and the scriptures, non-neglect of the essential duties, glorification of the path, and affection for the teachings— these constitute the cause of the status of a Tīrthaṅkara.
(23) Self-reproach and praise of others, and the concealment or manifestation respectively of real and unreal qualities, constitute the cause of the low family-determining karma (*nīcairgotra*).
The opposite of that [is the first], and humility and lack of arrogance are the two [factors] for the latter.
"Causing obstacles is an obstruction," according to the sixth chapter of the *Tattvārthādhigama-sūtra*.
Due to the absence of causes, due to being bodiless, and due to the absence of instruments, there is an absence of fault; consequently, there is an absence of karma.

...the beginninglessness of saṃsāra does not belong to that *niyati* either, because it is not the ultimate reality (*atattva*). Whatever is not the ultimate reality is not seen to possess *niyati*, like a jar or a cloth.

In this very way, because time has as its nature a continuous process that has existed without beginning, it effects the series of occurrences and cessations of the earth and so forth, as well as rice and so forth.

Regarding this, the proponent of necessity (niyativādin) says: "Because that very cycle of existence (saṃsāra) is thus determined, the cycle of existence occurs for both the person (puruṣa) and the individual (pudgala)."

To this we reply: nor does that *niyati* (destiny) possess the beginninglessness of *saṃsāra*. For what reason? Because it is not the ultimate reality (*atattva*). That which exists as such is reality (*tattva*); what is not reality is non-reality (*atattva*). Therefore, because that *niyati* is non-reality, *saṃsāra* does not arise from it. Furthermore, this *saṃsāra* is non-reality because its cessation is admitted in certain cases. To demonstrate that the probandum is invariably concomitant with its own cause, he says: "Whatever is non-reality, that is not seen to be the *niyati* of that [reality]; for example, a jar is not the *niyati* of a cloth, nor is a cloth the *niyati* of a jar. Therefore, like a jar or a cloth, because it is non-reality, it is not the *niyati* of that [reality]. Thus it has been well said.
Furthermore,
if one were to say that its beginninglessness in saṃsāra is due to its very nature (*svabhāva*), this too cannot be due to its nature, because it is not the true reality (*atattva*).
That it is not the true reality is established as before, since the state of liberation is admitted for it.

Whatever is non-eternal does not possess that [eternal] nature, like a jar or a cloth; thus it has been stated that, in the doctrines of Niyati and so forth, beginningless transmigratory existence is not tenable without Time (kāla). [End of citation from] Pātañjala.
And for him, there is no [cessation] of saṃsāra.
Now, the proof of its occurrence is described in the doctrine of time (*kālavāda*)—from the words "therefore, because it consists of beginningless progression" up to "it is not illogical.
The word "therefore" connects to the idea that the beginninglessness of saṃsāra is not illogical, based on the aforementioned time.

The word *tu* (but) serves as a qualification. This [notion of] beginninglessness of transmigratory existence (*anādi-saṃsāritva*) is only logical as a discourse on time (*kāla-vāda*), because "beginninglessness" is synonymous with "simultaneity," and simultaneity is invariably concomitant with the power of time; furthermore, time is synonymous with the function of reckoning (*kalana*). To demonstrate this, he states the reason: "because time consists of a beginningless process of persistence. For time indeed consists of a simultaneous, beginningless process of persistence.

If it is argued that this contradicts what was stated previously—namely, that there is no simultaneity because the functions of "prior," "posterior," "prior-and-posterior," and so forth, do not occur at once—the answer is no, because the process of *vartana* (the act of abiding) is simultaneous. For example, the series of illustrations begins with: "the functioning of the earth and so forth, [and] the functioning of rice and so forth."

Just as the earth possesses its own activity regarding its own self—namely, bondage and transmigration—so too, for the *jīva* and the *pudgala*, whose intrinsic natures consist in non-differentiated existence (*vartanā*), the activity of bondage and the activity of transmigration occur by their very nature. Through the differentiation of existence and the differentiation of form, the activity within the self-nature of time itself, or within that which is not the self-nature, establishes bondage and transmigration simultaneously; thus, the beginninglessness of bondage and transmigration is not illogical. Consequently, through the sequence of prior and posterior moments in the differentiation of beginningless existence, various states are attained in succession: the conjunction with earth, water, and so forth, the sprouting of the seed, the root, the shoot, and so on.
...rice cooked with *kuṇḍaka* and *tandula* grains;
existence itself, through the distinction between the subsistence and transformation of living beings and *pudgala*s, constitutes the commencement, engagement, and completion [of action];
for that very existence [is characterized] by transformation and non-transformation.

Earth, water, air, space, spirit (*puruṣa*), and so forth, having come together simultaneously and being designated as the "world" (*loka*), are beginningless. These very same entities exist simultaneously in the form of rice, barley, wheat, mango, jackfruit, and so on, as well as in the form of women, men, buffaloes, goats, cattle, gayals, and so forth. Through the uninterrupted continuity of such manifestation (*vṛtti*) and withdrawal (*vivṛtti*)—that is, through earth and so forth becoming rice and so forth—their own self (*ātman*) is the object of this activity. This activity, which has the nature of their own essence as its object, occurs through the continuous process of manifestation and withdrawal of those [substances] such as rice and earth; and that itself is bondage, because of their mutual cohesion through the qualities of smoothness (*snigdha*) and roughness (*rūkṣa*). Transmigration (*saṃsaraṇa*) is the assumption of various different forms; and that, too, is seen to be beginningless, with both bondage and transmigration occurring simultaneously. Thus, for the soul (*jīva*) and matter (*pudgala*), whose essential natures consist in non-differentiated persistence (*vartana*), there occurs—just as in the case of earth, rice, and so forth from their respective causes—an activity of bondage and an activity of transmigration arising spontaneously from their own causal factors (which are themselves the means to their ends) consisting in mutual cohesion. This is explained by means of examples well-known in the world, through the distinction of persistence and the distinction of form.

The explanation according to the Dārṣṭāntikas, however, is as follows: whether the activity of time occurs within its own self or within that which is not its own self—since time possesses the essential nature of non-differentiated progression (*abhinnavartana-svatattva*)—just as there is the binding and transmigration (*saṃsaraṇa*) of earth and so forth, or rice and so forth, so too does activity occur simultaneously within its own self in the form of the *jīva*, or within that which is not its own self in the form of the *pudgala*. This activity is established as binding and transmigrating, and is produced by time because there is no other creator. This very state of being a transmigrant (*saṃsāritā*), consisting of a simultaneous, non-differentiated, beginningless progression, is the beginninglessness of the binding and transmigrating of the *jīva* and *pudgala* through their mutual activities of self-nature and other-nature; it is not illogical, for there is no contradiction—this is the intended meaning.

Thus, first of all, the beginninglessness of saṃsāra is established by the evidence of simultaneity and by the fact that it is not produced by time, because [the relationship between cause and effect] is characterized by invariable concomitance (avinābhāvitva).
The manifestation of time,
having unfolded in the light of the day,
is seen as the light of existence.

Just as the bondage and transmigration of one’s own self are [inherent], so too, for the *jīva* and the *pudgala*, whose essential natures consist in their non-differentiated existence (*vartanā*), the act of bondage and the act of transmigration occur spontaneously. Through the differentiation of *vartanā* and the differentiation of form, the action of time occurs within its own self or within what is not its own self; thus, the simultaneous occurrence of bondage and transmigration, established through bondage and transmigration from beginningless time, is not untenable.

Consequently, through the sequence of prior and posterior stages in the differentiation of beginningless *vartanā*, various other states are attained in succession: the conjunction with earth, water, and so forth, the sprouting of the seed, the root, the shoot, and so on.
...rice cooked with *kuṇḍaka* husks;

subsistence itself—through the distinctions of the activity and transformation of living beings—is the commencement, the engagement, and the completion; for that very subsistence exists within both transformations and non-transformations.
Bondage occurs through the very nature of the soul itself, due to the qualities of smoothness and roughness. (Tattvārthasūtra 5.32)
Forms are mutually distinct; forms are distinct from one another.

Just as [the case of] divatva-saṃ°, even the beginninglessness of saṃsāra—which is established by temporal distinctions such as "prior" and "subsequent" based on marks such as "before" and "after"—is not at all contradicted in this system. Therefore, he says: "Thus, the various divisions of beginningless progression," and so forth.

The meaning of the word *iti* here is "in this manner. These very divisions of progression, whose beginninglessness has been thus established, consist of the sequence of "prior," "subsequent," and so on; these are themselves the various states (bhāva) attained in succession.

If one asks what those are: they are the contact with earth, water, and so forth; the sprouting of the seed; the root, the shoot, and so on—the meaning of which is understood—up to the rice-gruel made from husked grains.

Even from boiled rice that has been consumed, there arises everything from its essence (*rasa*) up to the physical body (*kaḍevaram*); from the body, earth; from earth, a lump of clay; from the lump of clay, a small clod; and again, up to the state of being earth and so forth, as aggregates of atoms, dyads, and so on. Through the differentiation of the transformations of the functions of the *jīva* and *pudgala*, there occurs only "existence" (*vartanā*), which begins, proceeds, and concludes—thus are the "beginning," "proceeding," and "conclusion. Furthermore, "transformation" (*vipariṇāma*) is the manifestation in another form; that is the beginning. "Proceeding" is persistence (*sthiti*). "Conclusion" is disappearance (*tirodhāna*). This [process] is an uninterrupted wheel of the three properties (*dharma*), whether occurring non-simultaneously or simultaneously. Just like the previously mentioned bondage and transmigration, arising, persistence, and destruction are also the very self-nature of existence. Indeed, that very existence [occurs] in both transformations and non-transformations; thus, he demonstrates the lack of contradiction in the doctrine of time as the cause.

To demonstrate its well-known status, he says: "Indeed, indeed, even by farmers and others, the time of the mango sprout is worshipped in such and such ways; it has not yet manifested, and from that very [time]—which is understood through its nature as substance (*dravya*), location (*kṣetra*), and state (*bhāva*)—various states (*bhāvabheda*) consisting of distinctions such as excellence arise. Due to the power and pervasiveness of time, even within a single year, distinctions of state such as abundance and famine occur."...

For this very reason, he is attended upon even by farmers and others—how much more so by the learned? This is the meaning. And since the postulation of other causes is thus rendered useless when the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is accepted, he says: "And likewise, in the case of intrinsic nature, all... and so forth, up to "who are they? Intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is that which has its own being (*bhavana*), its own self (*ātman*), for every entity; it is the "self-being of all entities" (*sarvasvabhavanātmā*). When such an intrinsic nature exists—that is, when it exists as the independent agent (*kartṛ*) and experiencer of being (*bhavana*)—or when it is established as the agent of the verb *bhū* (to be), being established independently of any other object (*arthāntara*), who are those [other causes]? In this very way, because it does not transcend the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of the person (*puruṣa*) and so forth in each respective case, the non-differentiated unity of all things is described precisely because it possesses that same nature. Thus, *prakṛti* (primordial nature) is the essence of everything without exception; and since the existence of the person and so forth is not excluded from their own-being (*sattva*), time alone—being the self-nature of becoming—is equal [to them], whereas the person and so forth are not [independent]. Therefore, nothing is established apart from *svabhāva*.

Since that which is already established cannot be further proven—just like cooked rice—when [the nature of things] has been demonstrated by those very arguments independently of any other object, who are these "persons" (puruṣa) and so forth? It might be thought: "Their own state is their 'own-nature' (sva-bhāva), and thus it depends upon them. If this is so, it follows that each respective entity is its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and thus intrinsic nature is indeed mutually distinct; for it is by their very own selves that they are established as such.

Otherwise, if their state of being those [entities] were not established through their own natures, then they would not be those very things at all, because they would lack self-nature (*anātmatva*), like a jar and a cloth. Just as a jar does not become a cloth because it lacks the nature of a cloth, and a cloth does not become a jar because it lacks the nature of a jar, so too persons and other entities would not be selves because they lack self-nature; or rather, they would not exist at all due to their lack of self-nature, like a flower in the sky.

In order to demonstrate the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of that [principle] of intrinsic nature as the cause, he says: "In this very way," and so forth. This is indeed exactly so; necessarily, just as here in the doctrine of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvavāda*), because there is no deviation from intrinsic nature, it is described as being nothing but intrinsic nature—since there is no object distinct from intrinsic nature and because that [intrinsic nature] is non-different—likewise, in those various doctrines of the Person (*puruṣa*), Necessity (*niyati*), Time (*kāla*), and so forth, because they do not deviate from the intrinsic nature of the Person and the rest according to the stated method, the non-different oneness of all things is described precisely because they possess that state of being. For whether it be the becoming of consciousness, the becoming of necessity, the becoming of duration, or any other, it is described solely through its respective intrinsic nature.

The word *iti* has the sense of a reason; for this stated reason, [He] is the self-nature (*svabhāva*), the primordial nature (*prakṛti*), the womb (*yoni*), the seed (*bīja*), the source (*prabhava*), and the cause (*kāraṇa*)—this is the meaning.
Here, there may also be the reading *sarvabhāvasya*.

Since the meaning is established independently of any other referent, what are those [entities]? For even their "own-ness" (*svatva*) is brought about solely by their own nature (*svabhāva*); otherwise, they would not be themselves because they would lack selfhood (*anātmatva*), like a jar or a cloth.

In this very way, because it does not transcend the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of the person (*puruṣa*) and so forth in each respective case, the oneness of all things is described as undifferentiated precisely because they possess that being. Thus, *svabhāva* is the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) of everything, including the person and the rest; since existence is not excluded from their own-being, time alone is the essence of becoming, and not the person and so forth. Therefore, the supreme manifestation is not established apart from *svabhāva*.
The state of being, etc.; the syllable *pra*; the syllable *ṣa*; the syllable *syapa*; the syllable *ḍe*; the syllable *līṃ*; the syllable *vi*; the syllable *ṣsya*; the syllable *bhā*.
The other’s *raṃ* and *hīṃ* are right here;
in this very discourse, one’s own [nature] is [revealed].

Furthermore, regarding the statement "the selfhood of the person (*puruṣa*) and so forth," since the substance-aspect (*dravyārtha*) functions without abandoning anything, and because the subsequent [standpoints] follow from the preceding ones despite their mutual opposition, he first demonstrates the functioning of time by not abandoning the person and so forth. In the doctrine of time (*kālavāda*), the selfhood of the person and so forth exists because existence (*sattva*) is not excluded. How is existence not excluded? Because one accepts that transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) is beginningless, there is the nature of the person (*puruṣatva*).

At that very same time, even destiny (*niyati*) has the nature of the self because existence is not excluded; and the non-exclusion of existence is due to the acceptance of destined objects as both simultaneous and non-simultaneous.

Thus, in the doctrine of Time (*kālavāda*), there is the acceptance of the existence (*sattva*) of both Destiny (*niyati*) and the Person (*puruṣa*); likewise, in the doctrine of the Person (*puruṣavāda*), there is the selfhood (*ātmatva*) of both Destiny and Time because their existence is not excluded. How is their existence not excluded? Because the sequence of liberation is accepted, there is no exclusion of the existence of Time; because the restriction of states is accepted, there is no exclusion of the existence of Destiny, and so forth. Similarly, in the doctrine of Destiny (*niyativāda*), there is the selfhood of both Time and the Person because their existence is not excluded. There is no exclusion of the existence of Time because the Destiny that is without beginning, middle, or end is accepted; and there is the acceptance of the existence of the Person because [it is said] that "one who perceives that [Destiny] correctly is omniscient."

This constitutes the thesis that "existence" (*sattva*) is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of substance (*dravyārtha*), because it exists everywhere and in all things. In this regard, since existence is not excluded [from them], and while existence is common [to all], it is time alone that has the nature of becoming (*bhavana*), and not persons (*puruṣa*) and so forth—this is not incorrect, because existence is not uniform. This is because only time, like a grain of rice (*vrīhi*), undergoes such-and-such becoming, whereas persons and the rest undergo becoming as distinct, separate, and individually different entities.

[Objection: Even so, by stating "of time alone and not of anything else," is it not the case that an intrinsic nature is being exclusively appropriated? And thus, due to the restriction of cause and effect for persons and the rest...

If it is argued that because time itself is the ultimate reality, there is no distinction between cause and effect, and consequently no conventional usage of "universal" and "particular," even so, that very nature [of the object] is established as being devoid of time—which is obtained through conventions such as "prior" and so forth—because its own essential nature is inseparable from existence, apart from this non-prior nature. As for the example of time, since the doctrines of those who propound Puruṣa and others are also refuted by the refutation of time, and are thus to be demonstrated just like the demonstration of time, it has been said: [as follows].
Regarding *satattvānām*, there may also be the reading *puruṣasvatvam* here;
[the word] *anapohya*...
See page 204, line 2;
see page 204, line 2.
Here, the reading might also be *svatve*.

No, because existence (*sattva*) is not comparable; for it is time alone that exists in such and such ways like a grain of rice, whereas the person (*puruṣa*) and other entities exist as distinct, separate, and individually differentiated states. If it is argued: "Even so, by saying 'of time alone and not of anything else,' one merely accepts its inherent nature (*svabhāva*); and thus, since the restriction of cause and effect belongs to time alone—which is the reality—and there is consequently no distinction between cause and effect, there would be an absence of the conventional usage of generalities and particulars," even if this were the case, it remains that very same inherent nature.

And thus there is an absence of time as established by conventions such as "prior" and so forth: those that are unprecedented, immediate, and conformable; those opposed to the prior; and those in which residual tendencies have ceased.
This is the cessation of residual tendencies (*nivṛtti-niranuśaya*).

The proponent of Time (Kālavādin) says: No, because of the inequality of existence (*sattva*). Since the existence of Time and the existence of the Person (*puruṣa*) are mutually unequal, how so? Because Time alone, like a grain of rice (*vrīhi*), comes into being in such and such ways; whereas the Person and others come into being as distinct, separate entities possessing different natures. Just as a single grain of rice comes into being through the states of root, sprout, and so forth, so too Time alone comes into being as the nature of successive occurrence (*vartanā*) in such and such ways—just like a grain of rice appearing as root, sprout, and so on—but the Person and others do not do so, because they come into being as distinct natures.

To this it is replied: even so, by the statement that "it belongs to time alone and not to anything else," and that "the becoming belongs to time alone and not to the *puruṣa* and so forth," it follows all the more clearly that this essence of becoming is simply the very nature (*svabhāva*) of time itself.

And just as you state that there is an equality of existence regarding time—just as rice and the like [arise] from seeds, and as persons and the like come into being [from causes]—so too, because of the fixed rule of cause and effect for persons and the like, time is of such a nature: it is the cause, like the rice and the like, and persons and the like are the effects, like the sprouts and the like. Because of this necessity, "that is its specific nature," and thus that very nature is what is accepted by others.

The distinction is this: in the former case, there is the cultivation [of the concept] of existence (*sattva*)—which is intended as the cause—as being inseparable from existence; whereas here, there is the cultivation of the establishment of the conventional usage of "universal" and "particular" regarding that which is already established as existing and residing non-differently within its own particulars. Thus, it is by way of its being so... [the self-nature] of that... [is its... *pra*...? *tasya pra*.

If it be your opinion that [the distinction between cause and effect] is merely the absence [of such a distinction], because time itself is the reality—since time is eternally uniform throughout the three periods of time, and in the doctrine of time there is no division into cause and effect, resulting in the absence of the conventional usage of "universal" and "particular," and because this convention is false since its object is non-existent—even so, the ellipsis of the sentence is "that very same nature exists. For it is the very nature of time that "it (the effect) comes to be"; thus is the nature [of time] established.

Furthermore, in the rejection of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), there is the fault of rejecting the previously stated inference for the existence of time. For example: "Time does not exist because it lacks the status of being 'prior' and so forth, just like necessity (*niyati*).

Just as it is said that necessity does not exist because of the absence of the conventional usage of cause and effect such as "prior" and "subsequent," so too it follows that time does not exist due to the absence of that [conventional usage].

Furthermore, even that inference regarding time (*kālānumāna*) which is spoken of in terms of the simultaneous or non-simultaneous occurrence of the color-forms of jars and the like, or of rice-sprouts and the like, turns out to be nothing other than an inference of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānumāna*). This is because there is nothing whatsoever distinct from "simultaneous" or "non-simultaneous" occurrence, since these are simply the simultaneous or successive functioning [of things]. The examples of jar-colors and rice-sprouts are cited for the purpose of defining that very subject (*uddeśya*), namely time; for it is precisely by virtue of the fact that the entity being defined exists as this or that specific mode of being that its particular intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is accepted—this is shown for the sake of demonstration.
Regarding "turviśeṣaṇaivabhā," here "turviśeṣaṇe" [is the reading]; there may also be the reading "viśeṣeṇaiva. [This is] from the *Gama-pra*.

Because it is so stated, and because— just as in the case of necessity— it is observed that the pot, its color and other qualities, and the rice-sprout and so forth, arise in such and such a manner both simultaneously and non-simultaneously, their intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is thus accepted;
and indeed, it is seen by direct perception that even when the earth, water, and other factors are identical, the thorn and such possess a distinct individuality.
That very thing becomes sharp and so forth, whereas flowers and the like do not possess such qualities;
furthermore, that [sharpness] belongs only to trees and the like,
just as it does to a peacock's egg.
...and he recites various [ornaments] such as the plumage of peacocks and other birds—
Who creates the sharpness of thorns, and the diverse nature of beasts and birds? Observe:
all this proceeds from its own inherent nature (*svabhāva*); there is no exercise of will (*kāmacāra*), so how could there be any effort (*prayatna*)?

By what are the eyes of the female deer anointed? Who creates the beautiful plumage of the peacocks? Who arranges the multitude of petals in the lotuses? Or who instills discipline in men born of noble families?

If intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) alone is the cause, why does the production of thorns and such not occur from intrinsic nature alone, independent of substances such as the earth? Why would it not be otherwise? For what purpose does the thorn pierce?

Alternatively, this inherent nature (*svabhāvahetutva*) is not accessible through reasoning; for it is observed that even when the causes—such as earth, water, and so forth—are identical, things like thorns possess distinct natures (*bhinnātmabhāva*) by direct perception itself: the thorn has a body that is long, tapering from the base, and lacking symmetry, while by the inclusion of the word "etcetera," its leaves, sprouts, configuration, color, and so forth are likewise of a distinct nature.

Furthermore, that very same thorn and so forth becomes sharp, sharper, blunt, blunter, poisonous, or non-poisonous; whereas flowers and the like do not possess such qualities, being instead characterized by delicacy and the like, or by fragrance and foul odor and the like—and these [qualities] belong only to trees and the like.

Moreover, those thorns and so forth belong only to trees, creepers, shrubs, and the like; even among them, they belong only to species such as the *varvala* and not to species such as the *nyagrodha*.
Furthermore, this peacock-eye pattern and the like belongs only to trees and the like, and thorns and the like do not belong to birds such as peacocks or pigeons.

Likewise, regarding the passage beginning with "peacock eggs" and so forth, up to "variegated," it is the peacock feathers and such that possess the five colors, not water and the like; furthermore, it is specifically the feathers of peacocks and the like that are variegated, not the feathers of parrots and the like.

This is stated in accordance with the previous [verse] following the words of the Jina, as in the verse beginning with "Who [made] the thorns... and ending with "By whom were they painted...," the meaning of which has already been explained.

In the *Mayūrāṅgakaprakaraṇa*, the root text is likely intended here to convey the following meaning: "Even though the origin from the fluid of a peacock's egg is the same, only the plumage and so forth possess the five colors, and only the plumage of the peacock and other such birds are variegated. [The reading *vaicitryāṇi* is supported by the Viramitrodaya.]
Furthermore, another [opponent] says: "If intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) alone were the cause," and so forth, up to "it is not even a little bit.
Because production is observed to depend upon other factors (*arthāntara*), intrinsic nature alone is not the cause, just as the casting of a morsel into the mouth [depends on other factors].
Moreover, the production of thorns and the like is observed to depend precisely upon the formation of substances such as the earth, and that [dependence] cannot be denied;

yet, that production which depends on the formation of substances such as the earth would not exist if it arose from intrinsic nature alone, because intrinsic nature is a cause that is independent of any other entity.

If intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) alone were the cause, for what reason would the production of thorns and the like not occur solely from intrinsic nature, independent of the material substances such as the earth? Furthermore, for what reason would it not be otherwise? Why would the production of a thorn not occur without the earth and other such factors? Or why would there not be softness in a thorn or sharpness in a flower? For what purpose does that very thorn exist, and for what purpose does it sometimes pierce? Why does it pierce only certain things and not others? [Objection: But surely, by the power of the restriction of intrinsic nature—such as that of portents and the like—the production of thorns and the like is indeed observed even without depending on material substances, time, and so forth.

Moreover, by asserting that the production of a thorn depends precisely upon the production of substances such as the earth, you yourself describe the establishment of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), since you are describing its nature by stating that the thorn arises from the earth and other such elements alone.

Just as the very nature of the earth and so forth consists in piercing with thorns and the like, does the quality of being a piercing agent likewise exist for other things? Why does a flower not pierce? And for what reason does it pierce only at certain times? Even though its nature is sharp and piercing, why does a thorn not pierce at all times? For what reason does it pierce only some things and not everything? Furthermore, why does it pierce only in a specific location and not everywhere? To these questions, a specific cause must be stated.

Moreover, this observed rule is seen to depend upon other factors; however, that [rule] is not tenable in the case of an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), because an intrinsic nature is independent of other factors.

For what reason, then, does it sometimes pierce? And for what reason does it pierce only certain things and not others? [Objection: But surely, even without depending on substances, time, and so forth, the growth of thorns and the like is observed by virtue of the restrictive power of their own intrinsic nature, such as that of portents (*utpāta*).

Moreover, by asserting that the production of a thorn depends precisely upon the production of substances such as the earth, you yourself describe the establishment of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), because you describe the thorn as having that very nature insofar as it arises from the earth and other elements.
Just as the nature of the earth and so forth is established in its various ways, so too must the causality of causal conditions be determined.
Having emerged from that state,
he also manifests slightly in some place.

To this it is replied: As for the statement beginning with "Now, regarding the nature of portents and so forth," up until "it is observed that production is indeed seen to depend upon the manifestation of substances such as the earth"—this must be understood as being simply a matter of essential nature (*svabhāva*), because we observe production occurring independently [of external causes] and because there is no deviation from essential nature.

For example, among portents and the like, thorns are seen on trees that are naturally thornless, and the absence of thorns is seen on those that are thorny; these are observed as signs indicating the presence of hidden treasures and so forth.
As it has been said: "Thornless trees become thorny, and thorny ones likewise become thornless; they appear thus in reverse order, indicating the presence of a treasure."

Thus, even when substances such as the earth exist, thorns may be absent; and even when the existence of these substances, time, and so forth is absent, thorns may still be seen. Therefore, there is no dependence [on external factors] for intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Rather, by the force of the necessity of an intrinsic nature—such as that of a portentous event—the production of thorns and the like is observed even without depending on substances, time, and so forth. However, that production does not occur apart from that specific intrinsic nature. Consequently, because it is non-deviant and all-pervasive, intrinsic nature alone must be accepted as the cause.
Furthermore, "moreover," and so forth.

Moreover, by asserting that earth and other substances arise as trees, thorns, and sharpness only in dependence upon the production of earth and other substances, and that the production of thorns depends upon their conjunction with those [substances], you are in fact describing nothing other than the establishment of intrinsic nature (svabhāva-siddhi) itself.

What is the reason? It is because the thorn is described as having that very nature (*svabhāva*)—that it arises from earth, water, soil, seed, sprout, and so forth, which are the substances from which the thorn is produced. Otherwise, what other cause could possibly be stated here? That "the thorn arises only from earth, water, soil, seed, sprout, and so forth, and not from a lump of clay or similar things" is simply their *svabhāva*; thus, even that [explanation] is merely a support for *svabhāva* itself, since those things arise due to their respective natures. (Note: The text contains several scribal errors and fragments such as "apekṣovotpa° bhā° vi° vinā °pekṣocotpa° bhā°", which appear to be corruptions of the phrase *nirapekṣotpāda* or *nirapekṣotpatti*, meaning "arising without dependence [on external causes]").
"By nature, thornless trees become thorny, and even thorny ones become thornless; they are seen in reverse order—this, they say, is the characteristic sign of a treasure. Thus it is said.
Furthermore, regarding the state of being a tree, there is the thorn;
moreover, as stated in the passage beginning with "just as earth and so forth," up to the point that even the causality of causes is inherent by nature.

Just as this thorn and so forth—which is produced through the sequence of seed, sprout, and so on, in every way, in all respects, and in manifold manners, having the earth and other elements as its nature—comes about without effort and independent of human exertion; or alternatively, since it is admitted that the very nature of the earth and other elements [manifests] as trees, jars, and so forth according to the logic previously stated, it is simply their inherent nature (svabhāva)—so too, regarding the causality of the causes such as the lump of clay, staff, wheel, string, water, and potter in the production of jars, cloth, and the like, which are considered to be accomplished by human effort, that causality is also inherent. Therefore, there is nothing whatsoever apart from inherent nature.

And thus, since everything possesses its own inherent nature (*svabhāva*), how could there even be an origination [of that nature]? For every entity, this very nature is like [the sequence of] age, milk, and so forth;
if it were not present, it would certainly not exist later either, because it would have been non-existent, like the son of a barren woman.

Thus, for jars and the like which already exist within clay and other materials, their origination consists precisely in the manifestation of their nature dependent upon instrumental causes (*nimitta*); this is not the case for space and such things.
If it is argued that the production (*utpatti*) of action in jars and the like is observed, we say no; because [the action] was previously unmanifest.

If it is asked why it is not perceived even when it exists, provided there is no cause for its non-perception, [we reply: it is simply due to its own nature (*svabhāva*). Furthermore, how could there be even a production of that which is either too close or too distant to be perceived? As for what you previously stated—that production depends upon the manifestation of substances such as earth—that itself is from where? There is no cause at all; therefore, that [production] does not exist, precisely because it remains in a latent state (*līnāvasthā*) prior to its manifestation.

Therefore, this "origination" (sotpatti) is simply the own-nature (svabhāva) of each individual thing. By the etymological definition (*nirukti*) that "own-nature" (*svabhāva*) means "the nature belonging to each thing" (*prati-vastu svo bhāvaḥ*), it expresses the specific nature inherent in each respective object. The examples are like "age," "milk," and so forth. Just as the stages of age such as childhood and youth manifest as they were previously established, and just as the states of milk, curd, whey, butter, clarified butter, and so on [manifest], so too do jars and other things manifest with natures that have been fashioned as manifestations dependent upon causal natures. And if that [nature] were not so... [and so on] up to "...like the son of a barren woman."

And if this nature of origination (*utpatti-svabhāva*) which we have described were not [existent], then it would not exist at all even subsequently, just as it did not in its prior state, because it would be non-existent, like the son of a barren woman.
To cultivate this very point, he says: "In this way, regarding clay and so forth," and so on, the meaning of which is understood up to the words "not in space and so forth...
the thorns and so forth."
bhā° without [it], elsewhere; °diśvabhāvaḥ pā°;
°diścabhāvaḥ ḍe° līṃ° vi° raṃ° hī°; °tnaka eva ya°
Since it is inherent, how could there even be an arising? This very nature belongs to each individual thing, like the age or the milk [of a cow] and so forth;
if that nature were not present, then it would certainly not exist later either, because of its non-existence, just like the son of a barren woman.
Thus, for jars and other things existing within clay and so forth, their arising has as its very nature a dependence upon instrumental causes (*nimitta*), but this is not the case for space and such.
If it is argued that the production of action in jars and other objects is observed (see page 14), we say no, because [the action] was previously unmanifest.

If it is asked why it is not perceived when it exists provided there is no cause for its non-apprehension, [the answer is] simply due to its own nature, as in the case of what is too near or too far away.
In the case of its non-existence there,
its non-existence here has no cause whatsoever; therefore, the reading "it does not exist" (*nāsti*) might also be [the correct one].
°apekṣyābhivyaṅgya° Bhāṣya;
°apekṣyābhivyañjya° Pāda; Ḍe; Līṃ; Raṃ; Hī;
Vāsā; Pra.

If it be thought that the production of jars and the like is seen to arise from action— should you think: "What you have stated contradicts perception, namely, that the production of existing jars and the like has as its very nature a dependence upon instrumental causes, since we observe that the object such as a jar arises from the action of the potter alone."

And this is not so, because [the action] was previously unmanifest; its production exists prior to the action, but being unmanifest, it is manifested by the action—just as a jar in a room is manifested by a lamp—and is not produced [anew]; thus there is no fault.

If you ask, "Why does that [non-apprehension] occur when the causes of non-apprehension are absent?"—that is, if you think: "When there is an object and there is an absence of the causes of non-apprehension—namely, extreme proximity, excessive distance, being obstructed, confusion with similar objects, suppression, subtlety, weakness of the sense organ, distraction of the mind, impairment by bile, and so forth—why does it still occur?"—we reply here: "It is due to its very nature," and so on, up to:
"collyrium, Mount Mandara, and the like are not apprehended by the eye and other senses; just as that is their nature, so too is this."
Likewise, there are certain things, such as the self (*ātman*) and so forth, whose very nature is absolute non-apprehension;
nothing at all is produced from them through human will, effort, or exertion.

In that case, how could there be for anyone who desires something any undertaking, action, or accomplishment, whether it be in accordance with their aim or even its opposite? Thus they say: "The *citraka* is considered pungent, pungent in its digestion, and hot in its potency."
In the same way, the elephant [root] purges a person by its potency; thus says Caraka (Saṃhitā 1.26).

But it is not only we who must say this: that even when the causes for non-perception are absent, the very nature of an existing object is the cause for its non-manifestation; indeed, its own nature alone is the cause.

Why? Because you yourself have accepted this. When asked, "By what cause do you understand that the visual faculty does not perceive form at all when it is extremely close, extremely distant, or obstructed—such as collyrium or Mount Mandara?"—you must necessarily reply, "It is due to its inherent nature (svabhāva). For this is the inherent nature of the eye: that it does not see what is too close, such as collyrium, nor what is too distant, such as Mount Meru. Likewise, for the other sense faculties as well, the non-perception of what is too distant and so forth, as well as the restriction to their own respective objects, occurs solely by way of their inherent nature.

Furthermore, just as that [non-perception] is its inherent nature (*svabhāva*), so too is this; for just as it is the inherent nature of the sense organs, such as the eye, not to perceive what is extremely close to the self, so too why is it not accepted that non-perception of the unmanifested is their inherent nature?

[The reasons for non-perception are: from excessive distance, from proximity, from injury to the sense organ, from instability of the mind, from subtlety, from obstruction, from being overwhelmed, and from blending with similar things.

Here, the non-perception of an existing object due to extreme distance is observed; for example, when a bird situated on a remote path is not perceived, one does not conclude from its non-perception that it does not exist, because it is simply not perceived due to extreme distance.

Here it is asked: Why is that which is not very far away not perceived? To this it is replied: Because of extreme proximity (*sāmīpyāt*). When Devadatta does not perceive the collyrium located in his own eye, is that because it does not exist? Here it is asked: Why is that which is neither too far nor too near not perceived? To this it is replied: Because of the impairment of the sense organ (*indriyaghātāt*). Just as a deaf person does not hear sound and a blind person does not see form, is it that those sounds and forms do not exist? Here it is asked: Why does one whose sense organ is unimpaired not perceive it? To this it is replied: Because of the instability of the mind (*mano'navasthānāt*). One whose mind is unsettled does not see an elephant walking about, even though it is there; people say, "It was not noticed because the mind was distracted."

Why does he whose mind is undistracted not perceive [the Self]? To this it is replied: because of subtlety (*saukṣmyāt*). Smoke, heat, and mist, when situated in the sky, are not perceived; does that mean they do not exist? To this he says: why are those things which are not extremely subtle not perceived? To this it is replied: because of obstruction (*vyavadhānāt*); jars and other objects are obstructed by a wall.

And why are those [subtle elements] that are not obstructed by others not perceived? Because they are overwhelmed (*abhibhava*), just as the lights of the planets, lunar mansions, moon, and stars are not perceived because they are overwhelmed by the light of the sun; does this mean they do not exist? To this he says: Why are those which are not overwhelmed not perceived? To this he replies: And because of their being mixed with similar things (*samānābhihāra*). "Similar" means alike; their "mixing" is a collection (*rāśi*). Therefore... Thus, there is an eightfold non-perception of existing objects.
(Jain Sāṅkhyakārikā)

Here it is asked: Why are those things which are not overwhelmed not perceived? To this it is replied: "And because of being mixed with similar things" (*samānābhihārāt*). "Similar" (*samāna*) means "like. For example, when beans are thrown into a heap of beans, or lentils into a heap of lentils, or a pigeon into the midst of a flock of pigeons—do those beans and so forth not exist? They are not perceived because of being mixed with similar things. Thus, there are eight kinds of non-perception even of objects that do exist.
Just as collyrium, Mount Mandara, and so forth are not perceived by the eye and other senses, so too is this [self];
likewise, the self and such things possess a nature that is absolutely unperceivable.
Therefore, nothing at all is produced there from human effort, desire, exertion, and so forth;
how then could there be for anyone who desires it the accomplishment of an undertaking, whether in this way or its opposite? Thus they say:
"The *citraka* is considered pungent in taste, pungent in digestion, and hot in potency."
See page 256, line 1; page 176, note 6.
Likewise: "The elephant [is so called], but by its power it causes a man to purge. *Carakasamhitā* 1.26.68 (without Bhāṣya;
not in Casma, Pā, Raṃ, Hī).

Furthermore, there is another point: just as this [is so], so too some things, such as the self (*ātman*) and so forth, have the nature of being absolutely unperceivable. Entities such as the self, space, time, and direction are always to be inferred solely from their effects; because of their subtlety, they are not objects of the external senses, yet they possess that very nature.

In this regard, the Śākyas and others, being ignorant of the distinction of inherent nature (*svabhāva*), argue in vain that there is no self, no time, and that objects such as merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*), space, and the directions do not exist.

Therefore, as for what you say—that a jar or the like is produced from action—that is not so; for nothing at all is produced from the independent activity or effort of a person. The meaning is that [production arises] from the person, from his desire, from his engagement, and from his effort—*vīrya*;
by the inclusion of "and so forth" (*ādi*), it is meant that it does not arise from his intellect, nor from the commands of a master, because deviation is observed in every case.

What then? Even a jar, which possesses the nature of being manifested or unmanifested as earth, water, and so forth, or as a rice-sprout, a clay-pot, and so forth, is indeed of the very nature of earth and the other elements, because it is a real entity (*vastu*) and because it has that [earth, etc. as its essence. Just as in such cases as "water is fluid," "earth is stable," "air is mobile," "space is formless," and "fire is hot," these are merely its inherent natures (*svabhāva*), there can be no undertaking, activity, or completion for anyone seeking anything regarding them—whether in this way or the opposite. For even a person who desires, "May water be fluid," "May earth be stable," "May air be mobile," "May fire be hot," or "May space be formless," there is no undertaking, no effort, and no completion; nor would there be any undertaking, activity, or completion in the opposite case, such as "May water not be fluid," "May earth be stable," "May air be mobile," "May fire be hot," or "May space be formless," because it is impossible to alter an inherent nature.

In this same way, the inherent nature [of the cognition] should also be applied to jars and other objects, because that cognition arises from them; however, on the earth, it is due to [the presence of] "earth-ness" and so forth.
And thus they say; this states the proof for [the quality] being inherent.

Citraka has a pungent taste, a pungent post-digestive effect (vipāka), and a hot potency (vīrya); likewise, Dantī has a pungent taste, a pungent post-digestive effect, and a hot potency. However, its distinction from Citraka is that it causes purgation by its *prabhāva* (specific power). Since *prabhāva* is a synonym for *svabhāva* (intrinsic nature), and since it is the intrinsic nature of the taste and other qualities as well, it is described in various ways through both general and specific characteristics. Therefore, regarding what you said—that the production of a jar and so forth arises from action—in that case, because the jar-nature is something to be attained through a sequence of stages such as earth, a lump of clay, and a small mound, there is no stability of the jar-nature [as a pre-existent entity]. Thus, how could the production of a jar and so forth be possible? It is simply the inherent nature (*svabhāva*) of the active particles of earth.
Therefore, since activities are established as being in accordance with the nature of their results, effort is useless;
things proceed from their own nature alone, acting without deliberation, like the blinking of an eye, the elements, or thorns,
because destruction has already been explained as its cause.

The word "iti" has the sense of a reason; for this reason, how could the production of a jar and so forth be possible? By the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (ādi), it is asked: how could even destruction and transformation—which will be discussed later—be possible? The meaning is that those three are not at all possible. See p. 256, l. 1; see p. 176, n. 6; see p. 224, l. 4.

Thus, how can the production of a jar and so forth be conceived? It is simply the inherent nature (*svabhāva*) of the clay and other materials that their activities correspond to the nature of the result; therefore, such activities are established as they are. Effort is useless, for things proceed from their very nature alone. Things proceed without deliberation, just like the blinking of an eye, the elements, or thorns.

The reason for the absence of arising and destruction has been stated previously; see page 224, line 1. It might be thought: "Since we observe that the potter’s exertion, the operation of the staff, wheel, string, water, clay, and so forth, are connected with results such as the arising, destruction, and transformation of jars and other objects in accordance with the human intention, it cannot be [due to] nature alone. This is incorrect, because that very nature belongs to the activity and the clay, as was stated earlier: "The causality of causes is inherent. Therefore, it is indeed nature alone.

Furthermore, activities are established in accordance with the nature of their results; indeed, it is solely by the power of their inherent nature that a jar is produced from a lump of clay, a staff, and so forth. Knowing this, one places the lump of clay upon the wheel and performs the operations of grasping the staff and spinning the wheel; these actions conducive to the result of a jar are established as being conformable to that end.

Likewise, the means such as the shuttle, loom, and needles, along with the actions of taking up the thread, weaving the strands together, stretching, and sewing, are established as being conformable to the nature of the result, which is a cloth.

Thus, in the world, activities such as agriculture, service, trade, and wandering mendicancy are seen established as supporting their own nature alone as the cause; there is neither any excellence nor any deficiency in these, for activities are commensurate with their fruits and fruits are commensurate with those activities—this state of activities having fixed fruits arises from nature itself. (The word *saṃbadhya* is supplied from the Bhāṣya.)
Connecting [this] with Ya,
folio 223, line 5:
*santānānantapāya* (the end of the continuum, the destruction of the endless).

In this context, when weavers, having driven two stakes on both sides, stretch out the threads in a state of tension, that is *tananam* (stretching).
