Furthermore, when the threads are stretched and arranged on both sides by means of a rod (*nalaka*) in the space between the lower and upper series of tensioned threads, that is *vitananam* (spreading).
And when a cloth is pressed through a *khalikā* by means of a brush (*kūrcika*), that is *pāyanam* (pressing)—according to the *Bṛhatkalpasūtra*, Bhābhāṣya manuscript, Gāthā 625.

It might be thought: "If an entity possesses a nature whose activity results in a fixed outcome, then human effort is useless. This is true; effort is indeed useless. Just as you say—that because the success or failure of an action's result arises solely from the power of its own nature, effort is useless—this very position, though considered flawed by you, is not abandoned by me for fear of falling away from the discourse on reality. Thus, although this effort is useless, it nonetheless exists for the person; it truly exists by virtue of nature alone.
As it has been said: "He who sees that things proceed by their own nature and cease by their own nature, seeing that 'I am not the agent,' he truly sees.

For this very independence of nature (*svabhāva-svātantrya*) belongs to things in their engagement and withdrawal, since it has been stated that "that which is their own nature (*svo bhāvaḥ*) is the self (*ātman*) of entities once they have ceased [to act]."

If it is argued that, given the pointlessness of both engagement (*pravṛtti*) and withdrawal (*nivṛtti*), what causes or what fruit could there be for engagement? Therefore, there is a contradiction with the proposition that engagement follows its own nature—[we reply] there is no contradiction. Because things engage precisely due to their own inherent nature (*svābhāvya*); they engage simply as "one must engage," without deliberation (*apratarkataḥ*). "Deliberation" (*pratarka*) is [the process of] reasoning; *tarka* is the inquiry (*ūha*) as to how an object is accomplished by this means or that. "Non-deliberation" (*apratarka*) is the absence of such inquiry. Things engage simply as "one must engage," solely due to their own nature, just like the blinking of an eye, the movement of elements, thorns, and so forth. Just as the closing and opening of the eyes occur, so too, whether a jar, a thorn, or other things arise from a cause or without a cause, in both cases there is no transgression of their inherent nature.
The self-nature (*ātmabhāva*) has been functioning since beginningless time as the cause of the world.

Thus, if there were arising, destruction, or transformation therein through a reversal of that beginninglessly functioning nature, then—due to the alteration of the nature of the beginninglessly functioning cause—the treatises intended for the attainment of the beneficial and the avoidance of the harmful would be rendered useless for a person, because his action and its fruit would likewise lack such a nature. Otherwise, from arising, destruction, and transformation, it would follow that when efforts are made for the sake of a jar, a cloth would arise; when efforts are made for its destruction, there would be no destruction; and when efforts are made for its transformation, there would be no transformation.

Therefore, for the sake of making the treatise meaningful, it is better to accept this very cause: that the various activities of a person—such as the division [of food] into its constituent parts of essence, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, semen, and so forth, which occur even without prior deliberation, as well as the sharpness of thorns, and likewise activities corresponding to the inherent natures of jars and other fruits—all proceed from nature alone;
for activity proceeds from nature, and cessation proceeds from nature. (Bhāṣya-vivaraṇa)

"He who perceives that 'I am not the agent' of entities— of things that have ceased— thus he sees," so it is said; "of things" (vastūnām) is stated in the Ya manuscript, while "of entities" (bhāvānām) is stated in the Bhā manuscript.
In this context, since it has been stated that "of things that have proceeded and ceased," there may also be the reading:
"they proceed by their own nature, beyond reasoning" (*pravartante svabhāvapratarkataḥ*).
Furthermore, there may also be the reading here: "they proceed from their very nature, beyond reasoning" (*pravartante svabhāvādevāpratarkataḥ*).
It is indeed beyond reasoning;
it is just so, as follows:
[as stated] in the Prajñāpāramitā.
And thus, whether from a cause or without a cause, in both cases a jar, a thorn, or any such thing does not transcend its own nature (*svabhāva*).
Self-existence is the beginningless activity that serves as the cause of the world.

And so, if there were therein an arising, destruction, or transformation by way of a reversal of that beginningless inherent nature, then—due to the alteration of the nature of the beginningless cause—the treatises intended for the attainment of the beneficial and the avoidance of the harmful would be rendered useless; for the person, their action, and its fruit would likewise lack such a nature.

Otherwise, while those engaged in producing a jar would instead produce a cloth, while those engaged in destroying it would instead achieve non-destruction, and while those engaged in transforming it would instead achieve non-transformation;
therefore, for the sake of making the treatise meaningful, it is better that this very cause is its own existence—
thus, "and so forth."

And having established this, whether by way of a cause or without a cause—according to worldly convention—whatever may be intended as produced with or without prior cognition, such as a jar or a thorn, in either case there is no deviation from its own intrinsic nature (svabhāva).

In this way, this self-nature (*ātmabhāva*), which has functioned without beginning, is the cause of the world; it should be understood as being one and eternal, appearing and disappearing in the form of solidity, fluidity, and so forth, in earth, water, seeds, sprouts, and the like, neither arising nor perishing, nor undergoing transformation. This is because arising, perishing, and transformation are opposed to a cause whose nature has functioned without beginning.
Thus, the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*)—from "in that regard, [it is] a nature functioning without beginning" up to "or transformation"—has its meaning made clear.

The counter-argument, however, is as follows: if there were a reversal of the nature of causes that have been functioning since beginningless time—occurring at every moment of utterance and with the consequent overturning of one's own existence—then there would be a fault; the treatises intended for the attainment of the beneficial and the avoidance of the harmful would become useless, and the scriptures composed for the purpose of prescribing the means to attain the fruits of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, as well as those intended to avoid their opposites, would all be rendered futile.

What is the reason? It is because the person (*puruṣa*), the action (*kriyā*), and the fruit (*phala*) do not possess such a nature; that is to say, the means—such as the agent, the instrument, and the object—as well as the action perfected by its constituent parts, and the fruit thereof, whether it be dharma, artha, kāma, or mokṣa, are not of the same nature as one another.

The meaning is that if their mutual correspondence is not admitted, there would be production in one way, destruction in another, and transformation in yet another, all occurring through a lack of correspondence.

The phrase "because [the result] arises otherwise than through production, destruction, and transformation" thus establishes the selflessness (*anātmatva*) of the fruits of actions that have the person (*puruṣa*) and so forth as their means. For instance, when those engaged for the sake of a jar proceed toward the production of a jar, a cloth is produced instead; when those engaged for its destruction proceed toward its destruction, there is no destruction; and when those engaged for its transformation proceed toward its transformation, there is no transformation. Because there is no fixed nature (*svabhāva*), production, destruction, and transformation do not exist. If they were to exist, they would be contrary to what is intended, due to the lack of a fixed nature. Thus, if one does not accept a fixed nature, the meaningfulness of the scriptures is not tenable.

Therefore, since established treatises cannot be disregarded and because [the doctrine of] purposelessness is undesirable, one must seek a cause for things such as jars in order to establish the meaningfulness of the treatises. And when that cause is sought for the sake of establishing the meaningfulness of the treatises, this very "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*) is the best cause; there is nothing else more worthy of being investigated than this.

Whence else could there be anything? That which is the cause is its own, its very self, or its own state (*bhāva*). What is this? Briefly stated, it exists in two ways according to each respective object, abiding as the living (*jīva*) and the non-living (*ajīva*). That which exists is *bhāva*; that which is the self (*ātman*) is *bhāva*, the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). And though it is one, it acquires a diversity of causal factors solely through the diversity of its own powers. It alone experiences; it alone is experienced;
by virtue of its inherent nature of conjunction with and separation from its own substance, it alone comes to be—thus, both saṃsāra and liberation arise from its own nature.

It exists in two ways with respect to each entity, like the living (jīva) and the non-living (ajīva). That which exists is "being" (bhāva); that which is the self (ātman) is "being," and it is called "intrinsic nature" (svabhāva) for the purpose of excluding extrinsic nature (parabhāva).

As it has been said: "What is this, O Venerable One, that is called 'it exists' (atthi)? Gautama! Sentient beings (jīva) and non-sentient things (ajīva). (Sthānāṅga Sūtra). Likewise: "What is this, O Venerable One, that is called 'equanimity' (sama)? Gautama! Sentient beings and non-sentient things. (Sthānāṅga Sūtra). In this same manner, the categories of time—such as āvalikā, exhalation and inhalation, prāṇa, stoka, lava, muhūrta, day and night—as well as the earths beginning with Ratnaprabhā, the continents, the oceans, the mountains, and so forth, are to be understood [as existing].
[Note: The word *vat* does not appear in the manuscripts.]

And in this context, there might also be the reading "paṭa utpadyeta" (a cloth would arise). [The commentary states: "Without *abhipreta*, *asyuḥ*, *bhā*, *vi*, or *vinā*, it exists in two ways for each respective object, like the living (*jīva*) and the non-living (*ajīva*); that which exists is *bhāva*; that which is the self (*ātman*) is *bhāva*; it is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)."

And although it is one, it acquires a diversity of causal factors solely through the diversity of its own powers; it is that very self which experiences, it is that which is experienced, and by virtue of its inherent nature of conjunction with and separation from its own substance, it is that which comes to be—thus, both saṃsāra and liberation exist by its very nature.

Whatever exists in this world, all that is twofold, namely: living beings (*jīva*) and non-living beings (*ajīva*); mobile beings (*tasa*) and immobile beings (*thāvara*); those with a womb (*sajoṇiya*) and those without a womb (*ajoṇiya*); those with a life-span (*sāuya*) and those without a life-span (*aṇāuya*); those with sense organs (*saïndiya*) and those without sense organs (*aṇindie*); those with gender (*saveyaga*) and those without gender (*aveyaga*); those with form (*sarūvi*) and those without form (*arūvi*); those with matter (*sapoggala*) and those without matter (*apoggala*); those involved in the cycle of existence (*saṃsārasamāvannaga*) and those not involved in the cycle of existence (*asaṃsārasamāvannaga*); eternal (*sāsaya*) and non-eternal (*asāsaya*); space (*āgāsa*) and non-space (*no āgāsa*); the principle of motion (*dhamma*) and the principle of rest (*adhamma*); bondage (*baṃdha*) and liberation (*mokkha*); merit (*puṇṇa*) and demerit (*pāva*); influx (*āsava*) and restraint (*saṃvara*); feeling (*veyaṇā*) and shedding (*ṇijjarā*).
Thus, in the Sthānāṅga Sūtra, 2.1.57–59.

Whether it be called a *samaya*, or a *āvaliya*, it is designated as either "living" (*jīva*) or "non-living" (*ajīva*); whether it be called a breath-in or breath-out (*āṇāpāṇu*), or a *thova*, it is designated as either "living" or "non-living"; whether it be called a *khaṇa*, or a *lava*, it is designated as either "living" or "non-living. In the same way, whether it be called a *muhutta*, or a day and night (*ahoratta*), or a fortnight (*pakkha*), or a month (*māsa*), or a season (*utu*), or a half-year (*ayaṇa*), or a year (*saṃvacchara*)... or an *usappiṇī* (descending cycle) or an *osappiṇī* (ascending cycle), it is designated as either "living" or "non-living."

"...whether it be called a village or a city... whether it be called earth or ocean... whether it be called an island or a sea... whether it be called a continent or a mountain range... whether it be called a peak or a peaked-roofed house... whether it be called a victory-hall or a royal capital—it is designated as either a soul (jīva) or a non-soul (ajīva).
Thus it is stated in the *Sthānāṅga Sūtra*, 2.4.
"Venerable sir, why is this called 'east'? "Gautama, it is because of both living beings and non-living beings.
(Bhagavatīsūtra 10)

And that single nature, although endowed with the characteristics of absolute eternity as previously described, acquires the distinctions of the factors of action (*kāraka*)—such as agent, object, and instrument—precisely through the differentiation of its own powers. For example: from the very nature of its specific means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), a distinction arises; it is that [nature] which experiences, and it is that which is experienced. These two examples are provided for the sake of explanation in order to demonstrate that the remaining *kārakas* are indeed nothing other than variations of the agent and the object *kārakas*.
"He experiences" means that having performed [an action], he experiences the fruit; he "enjoys the fruit of karma.
He "is experienced" by his own nature through differentiation; he is also enjoyed by himself.
To explain how it is that he both experiences and is experienced, he says: "By one's own substance," and so forth.

The substances themselves—the very Self—are by their own nature the agents and objects of action; they unite and disunite. It is through the differentiation of the natures of those very substances that conjunction and disjunction occur, which constitute bondage and liberation, with the distinctions of being partial or total. In the diversity of pleasure and pain, birth and death, resulting from those variations, it is by virtue of its own inherent nature (*svābhāvyena*) that the Self becomes that [which it appears to be]; thus, transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) and liberation are due to its own nature. Just as a grain of rice, by experiencing itself as the state of a sprout and so forth, both experiences and is experienced.

Although the self-nature of the disease fluctuates through the reciprocal conjunctions and disjunctions of karma and the possessor of karma, it remains established everywhere—within both the categories of those capable of liberation (*bhavya*) and those incapable (*abhavya*)—because it does not abandon its own nature and because it is non-dual, just as the dual forms of curability and incurability do not abandon their own respective natures.

What is the illustration? Just as gold exists in two ways within a gold-bearing stone—its nature being manifested through both action and non-action, and its nature being that in some cases there is no gold at all—so too, for some, the manifestation of the soul's purity occurs through its own spontaneous departure even without alchemy (*dhātuvāda*), just as gold is manifested; likewise, for fortunate souls (*bhavyajīva*), the manifestation of the Self occurs simply through the inherent nature of the separation from karma. However, through action preceded by right vision and knowledge, the attainment of liberation (*kaivalya*) occurs predominantly, just as the production of gold occurs through the process of alchemy; whereas for others, there is no manifestation at all due to the inherent nature of the non-separation from karma.
And thus, because of that description of the intrinsic nature of both [the soul and karma], [there is no connection] between the soul incapable of liberation and karma...
[etc.]
But for one who is capable, there is purification...

If another cause were to be sought for this [beginningless state], it would follow that this too is beginningless; because it is beginningless, like space, it would be endless. Alternatively, if it were to have an end despite being beginningless—just as the karma of one destined for liberation (bhavya) has an end—then why would there not likewise be a beginning for the continuum of perfected karma? Thus, its own nature (*svabhāva*) alone is the refuge; liberation is the nature of the means to that [nature].

Thus, regarding all such objections concerning how isolation (*kaivalya*) occurs—as in the cases of Bharata, Marudevi, and others—it is said by way of illustration: just as the manifestation of gold occurs even without alchemy (*dhātuvāda*), so too the manifestation of the Self for fortunate souls (*bhavyajīva*) occurs simply through the inherent nature of the discernment of karma (*karmaviveka*). However, the attainment of isolation through action preceded by right vision and knowledge occurs predominantly like the production of gold through the process of alchemy; this is due solely to the diversity of inherent natures. Likewise, the non-manifestation [of the Self] experienced by some is likewise due solely to the inherent nature of the non-discernment of karma. Thus ends the [Yogabindu].
Having performed [an action], one experiences its fruit; there is no self among beings, yet it is as if there were a self.
The hunter [attains] the non-duality of the attainable; the hunter [attains] the non-duality of the attainable and unattainable. ...
from the self... pure... primordial.

Just as the manifestation of gold occurs even without alchemy (*dhātuvāda*), so too does the manifestation of the self occur for worthy souls (*bhavyajīva*) simply through the inherent nature of the discernment of karma; however, through action preceded by right vision and knowledge, the attainment of liberation (*kaivalya*) occurs abundantly, just like the production of gold through the process of alchemy. For some, however, there is no manifestation at all due to the inherent nature of the non-discernment of karma.
Thus, by describing the nature of both these factors, [the distinction between] the unworthy soul (*abhavyajīva*) and karma is established.
...but for one who is capable, there is purification...
...if another cause were sought for that [cause], then there would be an infinite regress for it as well, because of its beginninglessness, like space; or,
if it had an end, then space too would have an end, because of its beginninglessness, like the karma of one destined for liberation.

Furthermore, if there is no cause for its end despite its beginninglessness, why then is there not a beginning for the established continuum of karma? In such cases, one's own nature (*svabhāva*) is the only refuge; liberation is the very nature of the means to that [end].
Thus, in all such objections, the non-interruption of the beginningless continuum of the insentient (*abhavya*) soul and its karma is due to nature alone.

However, it is certainly possible that there is some underlying basis here for the intention that the cessation of the beginningless stream of karma occurs precisely through the pure nature of the *bhavya* (the one capable of liberation).

And thus, with regard to the passage beginning "And so," and likewise, having established this, living beings (*jīva*) are declared to be of two kinds by the power of the method of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-naya*): those destined for liberation (*bhavasiddhika*) and those not destined for liberation (*abhavasiddhika*). This is because both of these natures are described; thus, the two statements beginning with "of the non-bhavya and karma" and "but of the bhavya, [there is] purification," etc., have already been explained.

The cessation or non-cessation of the beginningless continuum of the jīva’s karma occurs by its very nature (*svabhāva*); therefore, no cause other than nature can be stated here for either the finitude of the continuum of those capable of liberation (*bhavya*) or the infinity of the continuum of those incapable of liberation (*abhavya*).
If another cause were sought, then even this [continuum] would possess infinity. Of what? Even the continuum of the karma of the capable would be infinite.

Why? Because it is beginningless, like space. Those who do not accept intrinsic nature must necessarily admit "beginninglessness" as the cause; that [beginninglessness], however, serves to prove an undesired infinity.

Now, even though the reason of beginninglessness exists, if one were to accept its having an end, it would follow that space also has an end; therefore, he says: "If it [the soul] were to have an end, then space too would have an end, because of its beginninglessness, like the karma of a *bhavya* (one capable of liberation). Thus, intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) alone is the cause for having an end; no other cause exists when sought through the logic of causal reasoning.

Furthermore, even if this potential cycle of existence (*bhavya-saṃsāra*) is beginningless, if its end were to occur without a cause—that is, if an end were accepted as being causeless or having a causeless cause—then one must state the specific reason here for why, just as there is an end to this beginningless cycle of existence that is causeless, the stream of karma of a potential being (*bhavya-karma-santāna*) does not likewise possess an end that is causeless or has a causeless cause, whereas the stream of karma of a perfected being (*siddha-karma-santāna*) does. For me, however, who am a proponent of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vādin*), intrinsic nature alone is the cause everywhere, because of its all-pervasiveness.

The word "iti" signifies a reason; for this reason, for those who maintain the doctrine of causality, intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) alone is the refuge. How so? Because liberation has the nature of that means—namely, liberation has the nature of the absolute cessation of the continuum of karma in a worthy being (*bhavya*) who is endowed with the means consisting of the Three Jewels, such as right view.

Thus, when the doctrine of causality has been urged regarding both the cessation of the cycle of existence for the worthy and the non-cessation of the cycle of existence for the unworthy (*abhavya*), the rebuttal has been stated by resorting to intrinsic nature.

Thus, if one does not accept intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), there can be neither proof nor refutation, because one would be speaking of parts whose meaning is devoid of intrinsic nature; therefore, you suffer a defeat in debate.
All this effort of yours serves only to refute your own position by adopting a nature distinct from others.
For instance, in the doctrine of the Person (*puruṣavāda*), he is composed of consciousness and not composed of form and the like, because form and the like do not consist of him.

The phrase "to be applied in all objections" is an extension [of the principle]. Just as when it was objected that a specific cause must be stated for the distinction between those capable of liberation (*bhavya*) and those incapable (*abhavya*), or between the cessation and non-cessation of *saṃsāra*, the established position was stated to be "from intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) alone"—so too, when it is objected as to why there are distinctions such as the nature of sentient beings (*jīva*) and insentient matter (*ajīva*), or the possession of form and lack of form, or activity and inactivity, the established position must necessarily be resorted to as being from intrinsic nature alone;
thus, the non-interruption of the beginningless continuum between the incapable soul and its karma is due to intrinsic nature alone.

However, it is conceivable that there may be some underlying basis here for the intention that, for one who is capable of liberation (*bhavya*), there is a severance of the beginningless stream of karma precisely because of its nature as purity; [otherwise], there would be no beginning to the continuity that is endless. (Pra.
Now, regarding the beginninglessness... (Pra.)
In this context, there may also be the reading: "even though the cause of beginninglessness exists.
(pra. kathahe)
The [view] beginning with "without cause," etc., is mine. (Bhāṣya, Ṭīkā, Yaśomitra, Prajñākaragupta)

But if you do not admit an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then there can be neither proof nor refutation, because [your position] asserts that the meaning of the members [of a syllogism] is devoid of intrinsic nature; thus, you suffer a defeat in debate.
All this effort of yours serves only to refute your own intended view by means of adopting a nature distinct from others.
In the doctrine of the Person (*puruṣavāda*), for instance, [the Person] consists of consciousness and not of form and so forth, because form and the rest are composed of that [consciousness].
There is a distinction between the cessation of an effect and [the cessation] of non-existence, because of the presence or absence of activity. (Bhāṣya)

Because they possess activity, they are specific [entities]; [this applies] to those things that will necessarily be explained later. However, if one does not admit an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then [the consequences] beginning with "but... lead to the defeat of your argument.

If intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is not admitted, then there would be an absence of proof and refutation, and consequently, the abandonment of debate. For instance: a proof consists of the thesis (*pakṣa*), the reason (*hetu*), the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), and so forth, when they are established by their own nature (*svena bhāvena*). The thesis is that which is intended to be proven, provided it is not contradicted by opposing facts. The reason is a property of the thesis (*pakṣadharma*) that exists in similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and is excluded from dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*). The example is the demonstration of the presence of the reason where the probandum (*sādhya*) is present, and the demonstration of the absence of the reason where the probandum is absent;
its opposite constitutes a fallacy (*tadābhāsa*). Thus, a proof, along with its fallacies, exists by virtue of its own nature.

Having accepted that "refutation" (*dūṣaṇa*) is the pointing out of defects in a proof (*sādhana*), and that what is stated otherwise is a "pseudo-refutation" (*dūṣaṇābhāsa*), you have become one who wishes to debate both proof and refutation along with their fallacies. Otherwise, there would be neither proof nor refutation, because you would be speaking of parts whose meanings have deviated from their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); thus, you would be forced to abandon all discourse.
Therefore, it is intrinsic nature alone—by virtue of its power and pervasiveness—that is the cause of the world;
such, then, is the doctrine of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvavāda*).

By this direction [of reasoning], this world is merely an illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) consisting of the differentiation and conjunction of the forms of the reality of the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahma-tattva*).

As it has been said: "Brahman, which is without beginning or end, is the reality of speech, the imperishable syllable; from it proceeds the evolution of the world, through its manifestation as objects. (Vākyapadīya 1)
1. Thus, theories concerning causes differ due to distinctions such as terminology and so forth.

Furthermore, all of these [theories] proceed without even touching the essential nature of the ultimate substantial reality (*paramārtha-dravyārtha*) of the *vidhi-naya*. This is because, in brief, this entire effort is undertaken solely by means of assuming entities distinct from [the intended subject] in order to refute one's own position. For example, when those who propound the doctrines of the Person (*puruṣa*), Necessity (*niyati*), Time (*kāla*), and Nature (*svabhāva*) say: "That which is other than the Person is a non-entity (*avastu*) because it lacks the nature of the Person, like the son of a barren woman; likewise, that which is other than Necessity is non-existent because it lacks necessity; that which is other than Time is non-existent because it lacks time; and that which is other than Nature is non-existent because it lacks nature, like the son of a barren woman"—then, for those proponents who strive to establish the attributes of the self, the substantial reality, the ultimate truth, and the principles such as the oneness of all things, their permanence, their being the sole cause, and their omnipresence, the demonstration of [their doctrine] occurs only through the acceptance of objects inherently different from [the self], and not otherwise. Thus, this effort aimed at demonstrating [those attributes] does not exist without the assumption of forms distinct from [the self]; therefore, that effort serves only to refute the very objects (the Person, etc. they themselves intend to establish, precisely because they accept objects distinct from [the intended subject].

Brahman, which is without beginning or end, is the reality of speech, the imperishable syllable; from it proceeds the evolution of the world, as it manifests in the form of objects. (Vākyapadīya 1.1) [Variant reading:
*vartanāt*]

"How so?"—he demonstrates this: first, in the doctrine of the Puruṣa, [the world] consists of consciousness (*jñānamaya*) and not of form and the like (*rūpādimaya*), because form and the like—which are considered to be merely the state of deep sleep—are identical with that [Puruṣa], since they consist of the Puruṣa whose nature is consciousness;

and those forms and the like are of the nature of effects (*kāryātmānaḥ*). If things that are of the nature of effects were identical with that [Puruṣa], then being an effect, multiplicity, impermanence, and non-universality would necessarily accrue to the Puruṣa himself.
And just as there is a distinction of states (*avasthā*), so too in the cases of "prior" (*pūrva*) and so forth, and in [the categories of] necessity (*niyatya*) and so forth;

however, in the doctrine of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvavāda*), this is a further refinement (*atiśaya*), because it assumes a distinction from the very beginning. This is due to the acceptance of the occurrence of non-deviation (*avyabhicāra-vṛtti*) as if it were possible, and because of the employment of the word "own" (*sva*) as a qualifier of the entity (*bhāva*), and because the object is defined in that very way:
namely, that this is what "comes into being" (*bhavati*) or "by which one comes into being" (*bhūyate*). Thus, it is called *bhāva*.

The word "own" (sva) is for the purpose of excluding what is not its own; [it refers to] those whose nature consists solely of mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*). If these [elements] were identical with that [Pradhāna], being of the nature of a single cause which is consciousness, then the properties of being an effect, multiplicity, impermanence, and non-universality would accrue to the Puruṣa alone, because of his identity with them and because they are each fully present in him, as well as because they are perceived through direct perception.

Therefore, the [doctrines] of the person (*puruṣa*) being the sole cause, eternal, and omnipresent are refuted, because it has been stated that the various states—which consist of causes and effects—are composed of the person; thus, the effort to establish that the person is the essential nature [of all things] serves to refute the erroneous adherence to the oneness of all things as substantial entities. By resorting to these "states," he demonstrates the refutation of his own [opponents'] adherence even regarding necessity (*niyati*), time (*kāla*), and inherent nature (*svabhāva*), by means of an extension (*atideśa*) based on the analogy of the "states" and their prior [conditions]. Thus, he shows that those [theories] are likewise to be rejected.

And "like the states" (*avasthāvad*): just as in the doctrine of the Puruṣa it is stated that the refutation of one's own position occurs precisely through the assumption of different forms distinguished by the differences in the states of deep sleep, dreamless sleep, waking, and liberation, so too—in the case of selves being identical with those states—the refutation of one's own position regarding necessity (*niyati*) and so forth occurs simply by accepting the distinctions of nature and so on in the earlier and later states such as childhood and the rest.
If the selves were identical with those states, then for the Puruṣa alone would follow [the properties of] being an effect, multiplicity, impermanence, and non-omnipresence;
and this applies likewise to necessity and the other [categories] in their prior and subsequent states.

In the theory of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvavāda*), however, there is this further distinction: because the distinction [between existence and non-existence] is adopted from the very beginning, and because the term "existence" (*bhāva*) is employed as a qualifier for an entity by way of admitting the occurrence of both possibility and non-deviation, and because the object is thus defined—

namely, that which "comes to be" (*bhavati*) or "by which one comes to be" (*bhūyate*)— the word "own" (*sva*) is used for the purpose of excluding what is not itself, having as its scope the mere mutual absence (*itaretarābhāva*).

In this context, there may also be the reading "svaḥ asvavyāvartanārthaḥ" (the word *sva* is for the purpose of excluding what is not-self). Regarding the doctrine of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvavāda*), however—the word *tu* (however) serves as a qualification; the distinction here is that this [doctrine] possesses a superiority over the fault of refuting its own position.

What is the reason? Because [the first view] adopts distinction from the very beginning, whereas the others, having gone far by way of demonstrating creation, adopt distinction only afterwards; furthermore, the proponent of the theory of inherent nature (svabhāvavādin) adopts distinction at the very moment of arising—this is the distinction.

If it is asked, "From where does this adoption of distinction come? [The answer is: because of the adoption of the word "itself" (*sva*) as a qualifier of the entity, in accordance with the acceptance of a non-deviating occurrence similar to possibility (*sambhava*).

A qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is employed when there is both possibility (*sambhava*) and deviation (*vyabhicāra*), as in the case of "blue lotus" (*nīlotpalam*). If blueness is possible in a lotus but also deviates from it—since that same lotus is sometimes seen as red, and blueness is also seen in bees and so forth—it therefore becomes a qualifier such that "it is both blue and a lotus. Thus, since there can be no employment of a qualifier without admitting a mode of existence based on distinction (*bhedavṛtti*), so too here, the employment of its own word (*svaśabda*) for the sake of qualifying the object denoted by the word *bhāva* is accompanied by the admission of a mode of existence based on deviation, just as [the admission of] distinction is the basis for possibility. Just as there is no qualifier without the admission of possibility, likewise there is no qualifier without deviation either.
In that regard, the deviation is contradicted because of the unity of the doctrine of substantial reality (dravyārthavāda); such is the intended meaning.

"And likewise because of the determination of the meaning (*tathaiva cārthasya nirūpaṇāt*). It is not only by the mere employment of its own word that a distinction is admitted; rather, the object (*artha*) itself is also determined as such, by way of being "earth" and so forth, or "thorns" and so forth, through the subsequent portion of the text which establishes distinction as the primary principle. Thus, the object is also fit to be employed as a qualifier in its distinct form, as follows: "That this comes to be," and so on. In that regard, between the etymological derivation of the meaning for the word "own" (*sva*) and the word "being" (*bhāva*), the etymological derivation of the meaning for the word "being" is indeed the same for both of us—the proponent of existence (*bhāvavādin*) and the proponent of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvavādin*). The etymological derivation of the word "being" is identical: it is "being" (*bhāva*) because it "comes to be" (*bhavati*), or it is "being" because "it is brought about by this" (*bhūyate 'nena*). And since there is this equality, there is no disagreement whatsoever.

Whether it be the word "self" (*sva*) or its referent (*artha*) that functions as a qualifier, this must be considered: such a term would function to exclude what is not-self (*asva*), having the purpose of negating the non-existence of self; however, because its capacity is exhausted in that exclusion, it cannot be the cause for the existence of self. Furthermore, this exclusion of the non-existence of self does not even belong to the word "self," because that which is not-self has never come into being, and what has not come into being cannot be excluded.

Now, if it is already of such a nature, then it is that very entity; what is the use of a useless exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*)? For that would entail the consequence of it being that [excluded] entity itself—just as when one says "non-Brahmin," Brahminhood is [implied]. Furthermore, that which is excluded would also necessarily exist, because the non-existent cannot be the subject of a logical connection (*aprasakta*), and what is not connected cannot be excluded, like a sky-flower. There is no purpose [in saying] "its own nature is not a non-own-nature"; thus, the exclusion of the non-own is its meaning. And the word "own" (*sva*) denotes the self-same nature of the entity. Therefore, by virtue of being a qualifier, it results in the exclusion of the non-own.

And because its purpose is that [negation], its object is merely mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*); namely, "the self is not the other," and "the other is also not the self. Thus, from the negation of self and other, there is mutual non-existence, which is to say the absence of an object, or the absence of an entity. Consequently, since its purpose is the absence of an object, it functions in the non-becoming of "self" (*asvābhavana*). "It is not non-self"—this arises as its primary meaning, and not the presentation of the nature of an entity. Therefore, because it does not touch upon the meaning of an entity, nothing specific is established by this.
It exists;
[this is] because it is not subject to deviation from what is possible, having been made non-existent by the primary cause.
Because it is made non-existent, there is no means [of attainment] due to its non-existence; because of its non-arising, there is no existence.
In the reading *pattobhā* and *ya*, the phrase *svaśabdārtho ya* might also be read as *atra svo 'svavyāvartanārthaḥ*.

If, by way of distinction, that which has the meaning of "non-existence" were to function as "not being its own nature," it would not be the cause for its own existence because its capacity would have been exhausted therein.
Furthermore, this exclusion of "not being its own nature" does not even belong to the word *sva* (self), because that which is "not-self" (*asva*) has never come into being.
And that which is unreal cannot be excluded;

rather, it would remain exactly as it is. Therefore, that thing would indeed exist—what is the use of a useless exclusion? For it would follow that it possesses the nature of that [excluded] entity, just as the state of being a Brahmin is attributed when speaking of one who is not a Brahmin.

Furthermore, even that which is excluded would necessarily exist, because what is non-existent is not applicable [as an object of exclusion], and what is not applicable cannot be excluded, like a sky-flower.

If it should be thought that there is an absence of the referent (*arthābhāva*) [of the word], and that one might say "express even the existence [of the object]," this is incorrect. Why? Because, since its capacity is exhausted there [in the exclusion], it is not the motivator (*prayojaka*) of its own existence. For it would be an excessive burden for a single word, uttered only once, to simultaneously effect both the exclusion of other existences and the communication of its own existence. Therefore, the meaning is that it is neither the motivator nor the designator (*vācaka*). Or rather, the referent of this word does not motivate the word itself, because that would contradict the function of words.
Therefore, the meaning is precisely the exclusion of the absence of intrinsic nature (*asvabhāvatva-vyāvartanam*).
Furthermore, this exclusion of the absence of intrinsic nature does not actually belong to the word "own" (*sva*);
rather, this has been investigated by accepting it for the sake of understanding the meaning.

If it is asked why [the term "self"] does not exist, it is said: because the non-self has never come into being, and because only the self has come into being; that is to say, because only an existent entity (*bhāva*) has come into being.
Since the referent of the word "self" is absent, one does not employ the word "self," just as one does not employ it for the son of a barren woman.

Because of that absence, even the word "self"—which is intended to have as its object a meaning distinct from the word "existent entity"—does not exist. Therefore, he says: "And that which has not come into being is not capable of effecting exclusion"; this is the completion of the sentence, because of its non-existence, like the son of a barren woman.
To be recited by both;
[this is] the commentary on the *Vṛttavibhūṣaṇa-prakaraṇa*.

Since the non-existence of an entity is itself non-existent, that object is indeed existent as it truly is; therefore, that [object] is simply an entity. Just like the referent of the word "existence," what is the use of a useless exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) for that referent denoted by its own term? Thus, because there is no object to be excluded for its own term, exclusion is useless; and the absence of an object to be excluded is stated to be due to its being an entity, just like existence itself.

It might be thought: "Because that which is to be excluded does not exist, there is both the state of being excluded and the meaningfulness of the qualifier. But this is incorrect, because it would entail the existence of that [non-existent thing]. For there can be no entailment (*prasaṅga*) of what is non-existent; and for that which is not entailed, there is no state of being excluded, just as in the expression "non-Brāhmaṇa" (*abrāhmaṇa*), [the Brāhmaṇa-hood] is not excluded. For in the expression "non-Brāhmaṇa," a Brāhmaṇa who is not [otherwise] entailed is not excluded. As it has been said: "When *nañ* or *iva* are joined [to a word], the understanding of the meaning proceeds by way of something else similar to it" (Pāṇini-Vārttika 3.1.12).

For the sake of deriving the meaning of the word *bhāva* (existence), because the agent is employed [in the definition], this statement of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the word *bhāva*—namely, "this which becomes" (*yadayaṃ bhavati*)—is qualified by the word "this" (*ayam*); thus, even the word "own" (*sva*) is redundant. Therefore, whatever it may be—whether due to being a thing (*vastu*), an object (*artha*), and so forth—it is like "self" (*sva*).

Furthermore, is this intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) pervasive (*vyāpin*) or does it terminate with each individual thing? If it were pervasive, it would have abandoned its own and other qualifications (*sva-paraviśeṣaṇa*).
If it pertains to each individual object, what is the use of that imagined [entity] which yields no different result from common worldly discourse?

Furthermore, since a thing such as a jar exists only as an individual entity, and because it is defined by its mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*) with respect to other things like jars, how and where could that "own-being" (*svabhāva*) exist? For if "own-being" consists in the state of being a distinct entity within the sphere of existent things, then there is nothing else that could be called "own. What, then, is accomplished here by distinguishing a jar from a cloth or other entities? If that [distinction] is itself an existent thing, what is it that is excluded? That too would certainly be an existent thing because it is something to be excluded, just like a "non-Brahmin" (who is actually a person). It is not non-existent in this sense of being a negation of a different nature; why? Because the non-existent is never applicable [to a subject], and what is not applicable cannot be excluded, like a sky-flower.

It has been stated [in the *Pāṇini-vārttika*]: "When a negative particle (*nañ*) or the word 'like' (*iva*) is joined [to a term], the operation applies to something else that is similar; for such is the understanding of the meaning. Whatever is seen here joined with a negative particle or joined with the word 'like,' the operation is understood to apply to something else that resembles it; for such is the meaning grasped. When it is said, "Bring a non-Brahmin" (*abrāhmaṇam ānaya*), one brings someone who is similar to a Brahmin; one does not become satisfied by bringing a clod of earth.
Thus is the reading in the Patañjala-Mahābhāṣya, 3.1.12.
Because it possesses some degree of existence, because it is a real entity (*vastu*), because it is an object (*artha*), and so forth, it is like [the universal] itself.

Furthermore, is this intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) pervasive (*vyāpin*) or does it terminate with each individual thing? If it were pervasive, it would be devoid of its own and others' specific distinctions.
If it terminates with each individual thing, what is the use of postulating that which yields no distinct result from mere worldly convention?

Furthermore, since an entity such as a jar exists only as a particular [individual], and because it is the mutual absence of other things like jars, it does not possess the nature of others; how and where could such a nature exist? Since "selfhood" (svatva) is a single property whose object is existence (bhāva), there is nothing else that can be called "self. What, then, is accomplished here by distinguishing [entities] such as jars from entities such as cloths? If even that [distinction] is merely existence itself, what is this [distinction] that is being excluded? If that too is excluded, then that too is existence.
In this context, there might also be a reading such as "like a Brahmin" (*brāhmaṇavat*) because of the need for exclusion.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "and this intrinsic nature" (*ayaṃ ca svabhāvaḥ*) and so forth:

this "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*), which you intend to be a "being" (*bhāva*) qualified by the word "own" (*sva*), is it all-pervasive or is it complete within each individual thing? If it were all-pervasive—that is, if it were a single entity existing everywhere—then, due to that pervasiveness, it would be devoid of the qualifications of "self" and "other. Because it would possess a single form and lack any other form, the employment of the words "own" (*sva*) and "other" (*para*) would be entirely meaningless.

Now, since [the universal] is fully contained within each individual thing (*vastu*), it exists as a "thing-per-thing" (*prativastu*). Therefore, what is the use of postulating such a [universal] which has no distinct fruit from worldly convention (*lokavāda*)? For it is heard in worldly convention that the very nature of a jar is "jar-ness" and nothing else, and the very nature of a cloth is "cloth" and nothing else; there is no single entity whatsoever existing apart from the jar and so forth.
If it is postulated as such for every individual thing, then there is no purpose served by postulating it, as its fruit is no different from worldly convention.
Consequently, no single intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is established in the manner previously described by the proponent of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvavādin*).
What then? It is established as merely worldly.

Furthermore, the non-existence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) itself follows as a consequence. For example: a thing that exists only as an individual instance, such as a jar and so forth, is simply "jar" and so forth; a jar is only a jar, and a cloth is only a cloth. Since a jar does not exist in a cloth, nor a cloth in a jar, through mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*), there is an acceptance of their mutual lack of intrinsic nature. Therefore, because of this acceptance of mutual lack of intrinsic nature, from where and in what could that intrinsic nature possibly exist? If the object [is established] by way of logical proof, then this is the door of proof for it: in the case of a single entity which is the locus of existence, existence is not other than its own-being (*svatva*); that which is existence is itself the own-being. Thus, these two are indeed not different in meaning. It is true that there is nothing else called "own-being. The word "iti" is used here in the sense of a reason. Consequently, what is accomplished here by means of a distinction such as "jar" and so forth, characterized by the existence of "cloth" and so forth? Because the essential nature of the substantial object (*dravyārtha-svarūpa*) is non-different.

When it is stated through differentiation that "this is a jar," it is for the purpose of excluding other entities such as cloth; thus, one says, "the existence of the jar is not that of the cloth," or "its own nature is not the nature of another. This is like the doctrine of the *puruṣa* (primordial spirit) and other such views, which rely on differentiation. Therefore, what is the use of postulating this basis of differentiation, which contradicts the essential nature of the substantial entity (*dravyārtha*)? Furthermore, regarding the phrase "if that too": if that jar or whatever else is differentiated is indeed an "existent" (*bhāva*), then because it exists, it is simply an existent; the so-called "differentiation" would be non-different from the very nature of the existent. Or is the jar or other such thing, called "differentiation," distinct from the existent? If it does not exist, then its very existence is negated.

Is it not the case that "the existence of a jar" is simply the jar itself, distinct from cloth and other things? No; for it is the very state of being (*bhāva*) that manifests in various ways. Indeed, when Devadatta moves his hand or performs an action, he does not cease to be, nor does he cease to act.
Therefore, whether in the state of being or non-being, there is no such distinction as "jar" and so forth.

That which all verbal roots (*dhātu*) express as the meaning of "being" (*bhū*) is a state of becoming (*bhavana*) in which every particular attribute has been set aside; it is the womb of all things, the universal commonality of all forms, and the undivided seed.

For that very becoming—whether it be rice and the like, or clay and the like—is the goal and the means, one and the same, not to be discarded, and never falling away. Therefore, what is this so-called "difference," such that a jar or other object would be distinct from existence? Thus, the non-existence of difference has been stated by you yourself.

Now, if there is no distinction, then it is not an entity (*bhāva*), nor does it experience becoming (*bhavana*), nor is existence itself even admitted; we do not admit its very existence because, due to its non-becoming, it is like the nature of a donkey’s horn—it is nothing at all. Therefore, [the claim that] "its prior nature... [is untenable].
In the Vastusaṃgrahaṇī manuscripts, the passage beginning with "pra" and ending with "bhedāvāraṃ" is not found; what is the purpose of this fabrication? Pra.

Whether it be a positive entity (*bhāva*) or a negative non-entity (*abhāva*), if there is such a thing as a distinction (*bheda*), is this so-called distinction— such as a pot and so forth— separate from the entity? Or, if it does not exist [as something separate], then its very existence is not established.

Is it not the case that "the existence of a jar" is simply the jar itself, distinct from cloth and other things? No; for it is the very state of being (bhāva) that manifests in various ways. Indeed, when Devadatta moves or acts with his hands and so forth, he does not cease to exist or cease to act.
Therefore, whether in the state of being or non-being, there is no such distinction as "jar" and so forth.

That which all verbal roots (dhātus) denote as the object of "becoming" (bhū) is that very becoming—a state in which every particular attribute has been set aside without remainder; it is the womb of all things, the universal commonality of all forms, and the undivided seed.
For that very becoming—whether it be rice and the like, or clay and the like—is the goal and the means, one, not to be discarded, and never falling away.
Regarding that, it does not exist in the manuscripts;

another says: "But surely, because it is designated by a non-distinctive genitive case as 'the existence of the jar,' the jar itself exists through an existence that is not separate from itself; therefore, the jar alone is the agent of existence through its distinction from cloth and other things."

To this it is replied: No, because it is the single entity (*bhāva*) itself that manifests in such and such ways. We do not say that there is no designation of difference—such as "the manifestation of a jar" and not "the manifestation of a cloth"—but rather that such [distinctions] are figurative (*upacarita*), because it is the one single entity, which is non-different from the jar and so forth, that manifests in various ways as the jar, the cloth, and so on. Otherwise, it has been stated that cloths and the like would not manifest at all, because they would be distinct from manifestation itself.

For that very same entity—the jar, the cloth, and so forth—becomes [the agent] through the hands and other instruments, just as a person becomes [an agent] through the hands and other instruments; this is because jars and the like are not distinct from the being of the person, just as the hands and other instruments are not distinct from the person who acts.

He demonstrates this: "Indeed, when the hands and so forth become or act, Devadatta does not fail to become or act; for when the hands and other instruments assume the agency of becoming and acting, the agency of their aggregate is necessarily attained, since there is no difference between the aggregate and its constituent parts."
He summarizes this: "Therefore, whether it be existence or non-existence, there is no difference at all between [the essence of] a jar and so forth.

Since the topic under discussion is *bhavana* (coming-into-being), for what purpose is the term *karoti* (he does/acts) employed? It is for the purpose of demonstrating that all verbal roots (*dhātu*) have the sense of *bhavana*. Therefore he says: "All verbal roots express that which is the meaning of the root *bhū*";
from this state of being (*bhāva*), the jar and so forth are not distinct.

Thus, in the *Vyatipātadevlīṃvi*, that "becoming" (*bhavana*) is one in which all particularizing attributes have completely subsided. All particularizing attributes—whether "self" or "other," or "pot," "cloth," and so forth—have been submerged, dissolved, and completely set aside within that very state of being.
And that [state] contains the womb of all things; that very becoming is the fundamental substrate of all entities.

The "universal archetype" (*sarvabimbasāmānya*) is the commonality of those self-forms—which, though differentiated according to the logic of a seal and its impression, appear in manifold ways like crystal—and which serve as both the original models (*bimba*) and the reflections (*pratibimba*). Descriptions of its essential nature, such as "the undivided seed" (*abhinnaṃ bījam*), are of this kind; they are conceptualizations of parts even within that which is without differentiation. If it is asked, "How is that cultivated? it is said: "That very becoming is the rice-seed," and so forth, up to "the means is a single becoming. Becoming itself is the rice-seed; by the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), water, soil, time, and so on, or the sprout and so forth, are included.

And that very clay and so forth—clay, clods of earth, diamonds, stones, sand, and the like—is indeed "becoming" (*bhavana*); it functions as both the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) and the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*). According to the logic of the proponents of the *puruṣa*, the universe itself exists as the primordial source; just as in that case, the agent, instrument, and so forth are non-different from it, they are always both the means and the goal. Just as for the *puruṣa* alone there is the becoming of elephants and so forth from clay and so forth, there is no difference in the non-becoming of things such as jars, because their difference is non-existent. This is because they are distinct from being (*bhāva*), like the horn of a donkey; and because, due to their lack of jar-ness, they do not exist as selves, like a cloth.
For conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) occurs through differentiation, conjunction, or transformation;

yet for this [Being], there is neither differentiation, nor conjunction, nor transformation, because its essence consists of a single reality (*ekatattva*), like individual selfhood (*pratisvatva*). Furthermore, by means of conceptual construction, it is indeed existence (*bhāva*) and not non-existence. Thus, manifestation itself—which is non-different from the Self—is both the means (*sādhana*) and the end (*sādhya*), being one and the same in each respective way. This manifestation alone is that which is not to be abandoned or relinquished, even amidst the infinity of conceptual constructions such as rice and so forth; it remains in that very state, never falling away from its own nature as manifestation, at all times and for all eternity.

What is the illustration? It is like an elephant and so forth, up to a house. Just as an actor, who is a person engaged in dramatic performance (*abhinaya*), represents through his acting (*abhinayati*) the manifold variety (*prapañca*) of elephants, horses, mountains, rivers, oceans, and so on—creating them himself and withdrawing them according to the various modes of his performance—and yet those elephants and so forth do not exist as anything other than him in a state of difference; rather, it is the person himself who, through the manifold variety of the elephant and so forth, becomes the elephant and so forth, and through clay and so forth (the word "and so forth" including paintings, plasterwork, wood, and cloth), becomes those things; likewise, the very act of becoming (*bhavana*) itself becomes earth, water, clay, and so on. There is no difference whatsoever between the act of becoming and the jar or other objects. Why is this? Because the purpose is fulfilled in that single [act] alone.

The non-existence of the non-becoming of a jar and the like—which is their difference [from existence]—is indeed non-existent, because it is distinct from existence, just like a donkey’s horn. If it is argued that even though the jar is distinct from existence, it nevertheless comes into being, then the son of a barren woman would also come into being. This is because [the jar's non-existence] is merely a direction [of negation], because it is not a jar, and because it lacks the nature of a jar, just like a cloth. For the becoming of a jar is the jar; its absence is the non-existence of existence, which is "not-a-jar. Therefore, because it is not a jar and because it lacks the nature of a jar, [it does not exist].

He explains this very point: "Because of non-existence through its own self," or rather, "because of existence through another self," as in the case of a cloth. Just as a cloth, by not existing through the nature of a jar, does not become a jar, so too a jar, by not existing through its own nature as a jar, should not be a jar; and this non-existence through its own nature as a jar is established because it is admitted to be distinct from existence. If this were not the case, then even the son of a barren woman would be a jar, since he too does not exist through the nature of a jar, like a cloth.

Or rather, just like a jar, because of its existence [as such], there is no difference; and because there is no difference from the jar and so forth, it is precisely this non-conceptual existence that is real here. That very [reality] is the manifestation of all things, such as jars and cloths.

Always, through the manifold display of elephants and so forth, just as a person alone becomes an elephant or clay and so forth, there is simply the non-existence of difference—the non-becoming of a jar and such—because it is distinct from being, like the horn of a donkey; because, not being a jar, it lacks existence through its own nature, like a cloth;
for conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) indeed occurs through differentiation, conjunction, and transformation.
And for this [reality], there is no division, no conjunction, and no transformation, because its nature consists of a single principle (*ekatattva*); like individual ownership (*pratisvatva*),
it exists as a positive entity through conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*), and not as a non-entity— thus,
it is not to be abandoned.
From the hand up to the jar,
from the hand up to the jar and so forth.
A jar and so forth; if it were sentient, [it would be] like an elephant, etc.; [this is] a refutation of the elephant, etc.; a refutation of the non-existence of the elephant, etc.
...from clay, etc.;
...arises, O Bhā [viveka];
[the existence] of a jar, etc., O Pra [jñākaragupta].
The non-existence of the pot and so forth; of that non-existence, which is the absence of the existence and the difference [of the pot and so forth];
of that non-existence, which is the difference of the non-existence of the pot and so forth—this is the meaning of the *Praśastapādabhāṣya*.
Existence arises from the state of differentiation; and because of the state of differentiation such as that of jars and so forth,
existence arises from the state of differentiation.

Now, intending to refute the direction of the argument regarding the causes of differentiation, he says: "For conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is not real," and so forth. If it were real, it would exist through these three causes: differentiation (*bheda*), conjunction (*saṃsarga*), and transformation (*pariṇāma*).
Among these, by means of differentiation, the shards are perceived as distinct from one another, being differentiated from the jar.
Through the conjunction of threads and their aggregation, a cloth is produced as something other than the threads;

through transformation, milk is transformed into the state of curd, and curd is other than milk. Furthermore, the distinctness of these [entities] is well-known in the world due to differences in their purposes for expression and so forth. These arguments of the proponent of difference (*bhedavādin*) might thus be applicable; however, in this case, there is neither difference, nor conjunction, nor transformation—these three propositions are established by a single reason.

What is this reason? It is stated: because of its nature as a single reality (*ekatattvātmakatva*). "Reality" (*tattva*) is the state of being that; "single reality" (*ekaṃ tattvam*) means non-different. That very thing is its essence (*ātmā*), hence it is "of the nature of a single reality. Because of that state—namely, because of its nature as a single reality—it is like "each its own" (*pratisvatva*). Just as, according to your own view, for things that are distinct, there is an uncommon self-nature (*svātmā*) relative to each individual which is simply their "state of being," so too, due to being of the nature of a single reality, there is no [transformation consisting of] difference or conjunction, because such things as a "sky-flower" are non-existent.

Thus, since this is the very nature of reality (*tattva*), how can there be any conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) here? [Objection: But surely difference (*bheda*) is apprehended through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) itself, because things are distinguished by their spatial and temporal relations—such as east and west, or by their arising and perishing; whereas non-difference (*abheda*) is not so apprehended, because apart from the mere existence of "something," there is no such distinction of space, time, arising, or perishing as "east," "west," and so forth. For that [distinction] indeed exists otherwise, like the occurrence of portents, water, or fire; but it is not so with existence (*bhāva*). Therefore, there is no conceptual construction regarding existence.

Furthermore, it might be argued that this conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) occurs according to our own view alone, and not through the admission of actual difference. To this he says: "And by means of conceptual construction, there is only existence (*bhāva*), not non-existence (*abhāva*), because [non-existence] such as a sky-flower lacks reality. Thus, like existence itself, this [conceptualized entity] is an existence possessing attributes such as oneness, permanence, and omnipresence; its manifestation is simply as a jar, a cloth, and so forth, and it has no difference whatsoever. It has been stated that difference is non-existence because it does not have the nature of existence. Therefore, because it is non-existent, this difference should not be conceptually constructed, just like a sky-flower.

Therefore, even in your own view, it is precisely the nature that is being conceived as possible; since that entity is also [of the same] reality, according to the previously stated mode of reasoning, and because that reality is indeed one, how could there be conceptual differentiation regarding this entity?
(nārātya) [variant:
nārātya bhā].
The self, cultivate...
thus indeed one... bhā... pā... ḍe... līṃ... thus indeed one... raṃ... hī...
