because [entities such as] a sky-flower and so forth lack existence (*asattvāt*).
Thus, since this is the very nature of reality (*tattva*), how can there be any conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) here? [Objection:

But surely difference (*bheda*) is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) itself, because things are distinguished by direction (such as east and west), time, origination, and destruction; whereas non-difference (*abheda*) is not perceived, because apart from the mere existence of "something," there is no distinction of direction, time, origination, or destruction such as "east" or "west. For that very thing, like a meteor or water and fire, while existing in one way, indeed exists in another way as well. It is not so.
And it is not that non-existence itself is non-existence; rather,
when its own intrinsic nature is being considered, it is indeed existence— this might also be the reading here.
The other says: "But surely, difference is [known] through perception," and so on, up until "and non-difference is not grasped."

A jar or similar object is perceived as "this is to the east" or "this is to the north" through spatial distinction; by the inclusion of the word "etcetera," it is also perceived through distinctions such as above, below, south, and west. Likewise, it is perceived through arising and destruction, as in "it has arisen" or "it has perished. Furthermore, in terms of its actual nature, there is a distinction between a jar and a cloth, or between their respective forms, tastes, and so forth, as in "black," "red," "fragment," or "piece. Since objects are thus divided by these causes and are perceived with distinctness, how can there be an absence of difference? By the words "east" and "north," the sequences of space, time, and transformation are also included.
Thus, while the diversity of things is apprehended through direct perception, it follows that non-difference is not apprehended through direct perception itself;
to this, it is replied: "There is something," and so forth.

Having established the absence of distinctions such as "prior" and "subsequent," and intending to establish the absence of perceptibility as well, he first speaks in order to demonstrate that absence of distinction: "There is nothing whatsoever"—neither prior nor subsequent—existing apart from Being (bhāva), because of the reasons previously stated. Therefore, what is that "unprecedented" thing which is produced, or what is that "prior" thing which perishes? Since prior and subsequent do not exist at all, production and destruction do not exist; for that very reason, even the differentiation of entities does not exist.

Therefore, since there is no differentiation of directions such as east and west, nor of time, nor of objects arising or perishing, what is it that is differentiated, has been differentiated, or will be differentiated? That which possesses such characteristics does not exist at all. Thus, there is no "prior" (pūrva) distinct from the "being" (bhāva), nor are there "subsequent" (uttara) and so forth. Consequently, non-existence (abhāva) is not a differentiation (bheda).

If it is asked, "How then is differentiation perceived? it is said: "For that very [non-existence] exists in another way, just as the nature of water or fire [is perceived] during portents (utpāta)," and so on, up until the end of the passage.

Just as in a portent there is the appearance of fire from water, which possesses qualities such as coldness and fluidity—that observed difference arises because the water has acquired the property of fire, which is its opposite; or else, it is the occurrence of something existing in one way appearing otherwise.
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera," there is the occurrence of earth, water, and so forth through their differentiation, such as by being a sign of hidden treasure.
As it has been said: "Heat occurs at ten thousand [years], smoke at a hundred thousand, and blazing fire at ten million, once the Great Time has arrived."

Thus, that very same entity (bhāva) exists in the form of various distinctions such as painting, laughing, weeping, moving from one place to another, and so forth; therefore, there is no real difference.

For an object that undergoes differentiation differentiates itself from its own nature through a process of reversal, provided that non-existence were to become existence. However, since it does not differ in any way—whether through becoming increased or diminished—there can be no state characterized by divisions of beginning and end, such as a pot of curd.
If such were the case, even the state of a sky-flower would possess the properties of a functional entity, because it would be excluded from everything else, just like a pot of curd.

Alternatively, the pot would be devoid of the distinction between beginning and end; for that very reason, like a sky-flower, both the great earth and space would possess the distinction of having a beginning and an end, because of their mutual non-existence, just like the pot;
or else, the pot too would be without beginning or end, for that very reason, like space and the great earth.

There is no apprehension of difference whatsoever, precisely because difference does not exist; for, like the apprehension of a sky-flower, the apprehension of spatial and temporal difference consists of a conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) and is of the nature of a false superimposition (*asadadhyāropa*), since spatial and temporal differences do not exist—just like a sky-flower. Even the notion "I am distinct" is, in some sense, a non-existence; for non-existence is distinct from existence, or rather, it is existence that has increased or decreased. Thus, that very existence does not become distinct; the connection is that it exists as something that has increased or decreased only in some sense. To the extent that it must exist, that existence remains neither deficient nor excessive.

The word *iti* has the sense of a reason (*hetvartha*). The reason is that when there is no existence of accumulated or non-accumulated states of being, one observes the absence of the distinction between beginning and end in the states of curd, jars, and so forth. To demonstrate this, he says: "Thus, no state such as curd or a jar possesses the distinction of beginning and end. Here, "beginning" (*ādi*) is the arising of what previously did not exist; "end" (*nidhana*) is the destruction of what exists; and "distinction" (*vibhāga*) is alterity. These distinctions of beginning, end, and division do not exist for the states of curd, jars, and so forth, because it has already been established that there is an absence of the distinction between entities characterized by prior arising and subsequent destruction.

Therefore, due to the absence of that [distinction], this entity neither increases nor decreases, because the process of becoming remains uniform across states such as milk and curd, just as it does across states such as a lump of clay and a jar.

Avoiding the charge that this reason is unestablished (*asiddhi*), he proves it by demonstrating an undesirable consequence for the opponent's position, beginning with "yadi syāt" and so forth: If that state of curd, jar, and so forth were to possess a distinction between beginning and end, then even the state of a sky-flower would possess the properties belonging to that [state of curd, jar, etc. therein, because it would be excluded from everything, just like the curd-jar; and the exclusion from everything is established because the difference between the jar and the states of curd, jar, and so forth is admitted. Thus, for one who does not accept this, the two proofs—which result in the attribution of the properties of a sky-flower to the jar by way of the opposite conclusion—have their meaning already explained.

The great earth and space would either possess the distinctions of beginning and end, because they are mutually non-existent like a jar; or else, even the jar would be without beginning or end and devoid of distinctions, precisely because of that mutual non-existence, as in the case of space and the great earth. Thus, by the very admission of the difference between the jar and [the other], this proof results in an undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭāpādana*).
In this way, there is first of all an absence of distinction between what is accumulated and what is diminished.
Nor is there even a reflection from that; nor is there even a reflection from that. (Bhāṣya, Pāda, Praśna)

The heat that has passed into the Great Time (mahākāla) is devoid of [dualistic] manifestation; the heat that has passed into the Great Time is the state of being (bhāva). If non-being were to become being, it would be a state of being.
If non-existence were existence, then existence would become existence;
or if it were differentiated in some way through being accumulated or diminished, then no state such as that of a curd-pot could possess a distinction between beginning and end.
If that were so, even the state of a sky-flower would possess the properties of a causal continuum (*tantra*), because it would be excluded from everything, just like a curd-pot.

Either the pot would be devoid of the distinction between beginning and end; for that very reason, like a sky-flower, both the great earth and space would possess the distinction of having a beginning and an end, because of their mutual non-existence, like a pot;
or else, the pot too would be without beginning or end, for that very reason, like space and the great earth.
There is no apprehension of difference at all, precisely because difference does not exist; for, like the apprehension of a sky-flower, it consists of mere conceptual construction.

The apprehension of difference in space and time is of the nature of a false superimposition, since there is an absence of difference in space and time, just like a sky-flower; [the thought] "I am distinct" is likewise.
Previously [it was] "abhidya" (pra°); "pra°sthādyekarū°" (pra°);
there, that triad (tatra tat traya°) [is established] by the *Pāda* and *Ḍe* [commentaries]. *Līṃ*.
In this regard, there might even be a reading such as: "O Vatsa, in that case, even the state of a sky-flower would possess the properties of those three.

Furthermore, as for what was said—that difference is apprehended through direct perception itself—that apprehension is not at all of difference, precisely because difference does not exist, just like the apprehension of a sky-flower.

Non-existence is conceptual in nature because of that [difference]; since the identity of existence has been established, difference is conceptual in nature; and that which is conceptual in nature is unreal, because it is other than the actual thing.

Furthermore, that conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) must arise either from the imputation of non-difference among objects that are distinct by way of place, time, or intrinsic nature, or from the imputation of difference where there is no distinction of place, time, and so forth. In both cases, however, conceptual construction lacks any real objective basis (*asadrūpatvāt*). In this context, according to your own view, there is no non-distinction by way of place or time; rather, there is only distinction. This is because an entity—such as a jar—which is divided into shards and so forth, lacks non-distinction due to its distinction down to the level of atoms, its distinction in terms of color-form (*rūpa*) and other qualities, and its distinction in terms of ineffability. Moreover, there is no non-distinction by way of time, because [the entity] is different at every moment (*kṣaṇe kṣaṇe'nyatvāt*).

Therefore, the apprehension of an entity whose ultimate reality is inexpressible as "a pot" or "form and so forth" consists of a false superimposition (*asadadhyāropa*), because it lacks distinctions of space and time, like a flower in the sky. On the contrary, non-difference alone is apprehended through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because the entity is non-different and that which is being apprehended is the entity itself. Now, why is the entity not apprehended in its entirety? Or, in the case of the position of difference, why is the entire pot not apprehended? This objection is not to be raised, as the fault is equal in both cases.

This might be rightly said by one who perceives a distinction within their own position; however, for a position that is characterized by non-perception everywhere, that very non-perception ceases right here and not elsewhere.

For when there is non-difference here—whether in the case of existence or non-existence—the grasping of a single part of it is the grasping of that [whole] itself, because of its non-difference from it and because it is of the nature of that, just like the location's own self.
For even a single instance of that [non-existence] is as non-existent as a sky-flower; like a sky-flower, it is merely a semblance of perception—this is the meaning.
As for what is also said, "And non-difference is not apprehended through perception," that too is not correct, because it is indeed non-difference that is apprehended through perception.
What is the reason? Because an entity is non-different, and that which is being apprehended is an entity; since a non-entity, such as a sky-flower and the like, is never apprehended.

Non-difference alone is apprehended through perception, because the entity (*bhāva*) is non-different and that which is being apprehended is an entity. Now, why is the entire entity not apprehended? Or, in the case of difference, why is the entire pot not apprehended? This is not a valid objection, as the fault is equal [in both cases]; this would be appropriate to say if one perceived a distinction in one's own position, but not for a position that is subject to non-perception everywhere.
That non-perception ceases precisely here and not elsewhere;

for when there is no difference here between being and non-being, upon the apprehension of one part of it, there is the apprehension of that very thing itself, because of its non-difference and because it constitutes its nature, just like the spatial location itself;
for even a single [part] is its manifestation.
Look at page 236, line 3.

You might say: "Why then is the entire object not perceived? To this we shall respond with reasons regarding the perception of the whole; however, first, in order to turn back your [erroneous] grasp, we ask you something: an ignorant person does not remain with his mouth unopened. Now, according to your view that there is a distinction [between parts], when you see a jar, why is the entire jar not perceived? Are the parts such as the far end and so forth not perceptible? Or are only the near parts perceptible? Tell us the specific reason for this.

Furthermore, this objection is not to be raised because the fault is equal for both sides; for one does not raise an objection against oneself when the fault is common to both—namely, that the fault of a universal entity being imperceptible does not apply to me.
This might be appropriate to say for one who perceives the specific qualities of difference, such as perceptibility, in their own position, [thinking]: "It is thus, and it is not otherwise."

This too is stated by way of possibility; however, the meaning is that for you, whose position is characterized by non-perception everywhere, it is simply not tenable. That is to say, perceptibility is not tenable anywhere—not in a jar, nor in form and so forth, nor in anything at all.
Alternatively, it means in every respect regarding both one's own and the opponent's positions.

This is what is meant: thus, being possessed by attachment to your own position, you do not see your own fault due to malice toward others, like a bird that does not see the snare caught in its own foot but sees only the bait placed there for its purpose; for in your view, because the absolute non-perception [of objects] is impossible, there is no lack of perceptibility for jars and the like.

line 18; it says "pra° .tvādi viśeṣaṃ ḍe° līṃ°."
Because of [the word] *tvāt*, the manuscripts Bhā., Pā., Vi., Raṃ., and Hī. read *viśeṣam*.

Now, he says this in order to demonstrate what was stated previously—that perception is possible only in the case of non-difference (*abhedapakṣa*) and not elsewhere: "But that is non-perception" (*tattu adarśanam*).

"But" (*tu*) indicates a distinction (*viśeṣa*); by this distinction, it is here, specifically in the case of non-difference alone, that [perception] ceases, and not elsewhere—that is, not in the case of difference (*bhedapakṣa*), up until the point where there is the splendor of ineffability (*nirabhilāpyatvaśobhā*) due to difference, as has been stated.

How, then, is perception [possible]? He explains this: here, in the case of an entity (*bhāva*) that is non-different, all this is indeed that very entity because of its non-difference. When there is the apprehension of a single part of that non-different entity—namely, the jar—in the apprehension of the jar, there is the apprehension of that very [entity]; that is, the apprehension of the entire entity itself.
Why? Because of non-difference from it; that is, because the jar is non-different from the entity, or because the entity is non-different from the jar.

He explains this: "Because it is that very being" (*tadbhāvatvāt*). This means either because that [entity] is also a being (*bhāva*), or by way of another synonym, it is a different reason: even a jar is indeed a being, because there is no difference between them. Whatever is a being is apprehended when that [universal] is apprehended.

The example is: with respect to a location, a location is not excluded from possessing all forms (*sārvarūpyam*), because its nature consists in existing as an undifferentiated whole. Furthermore, there is no limitation whatsoever—whether above, below, across, or in any direction—of this [universal], such as the distinctions found in the various limbs of a physical manifestation which are considered to be one.

Thus, that *dhruva* (the eternal) is immovable, unshakable, without loss or addition, immutable, without origination, without growth, and undecaying—just as it has been described and as it is its own self. The "own" (*sva*) of a location is the state of being its own self; because it is non-different from its own nature (*bhāva*), it is perceived through that nature, just like the nature itself. Likewise, when a location is perceived, the entire nature is perceived because of its identity with that nature. This is the perception of both that and not-that. (Bhāṣya)
Let that one part be examined (pra-dṛśyatām):

every location, because its nature consists in the occurrence within the undivided whole, does not transcend its possession of all forms; nor is there any limitation of it anywhere—in the directions above, below, or across—such as the differentiation found in the limbs of a physical manifestation that is conceived as a unity.

Thus, that *dhruva* (the eternal) is immovable, unshakable, without loss or addition, changeless, without birth, without growth, and imperishable; as has been stated, it is the [nature] of that region.

To explain the purpose of this meditation, he says: "For even a single part of that, with respect to its manifestation... The word *hi* (for) is used in the sense of *yasmāt* (because). Because even a single part of that [Reality], by virtue of having as its essence the function of being undivided from all existence (*sarvāvibhaktabhavanavṛttyātmakatvāt*), experiences its own nature as a single function—namely, "being" (*bhavanam*)—undivided from every (*sarveṇa*) whole (*samastena*) state of being; therefore, that part too has the nature of all states of being (*sarvabhāvātmā*). This is like the case of the Puruṣa, whose limbs such as those "with hands" and "without hands" have been previously mentioned. Therefore, he says: "For even a single part of that, with respect to its manifestation, does not transcend its universal form (*sārvarūpyam*), because it has as its essence the function of being undivided from all existence."

Therefore, by this reasoning, since the apprehension of the whole occurs upon the apprehension of the location (*deśa*), the vision [of the object] belongs only to the position of non-difference and not otherwise. If it is argued that "it is contradictory for the location to be one and the same as that [the object]," that is not so; for it was stated with reference to the state of being perceived. According to your own view, even that which is partless appears as if it were possessed of parts; thus I spoke in that manner. However, in the ultimate sense, it is said—and will be further explained—to be indeed without division.
Alternatively, *prathana* means expansion; because that entity is expansive, its manifestation (*prathana*) occurs in relation to the location (*deśa*), and thus there is no fault.
Therefore, it is said to be "undivided"; hence he says:

"And for this [Being], there exists no limitation anywhere—whether above, below, across, or in any direction—due to a division among the limbs of its manifested forms as conceived in their unity, even in the case of the southern and northern Mathurās, much less in the case of a jar and a cloth, because they are not limited by being manifestations of the single form of the world-Being."

Just as for a corporeal entity such as a jar—which is conceived as a unity—the various manifestations or divisions (vibhāgas) appearing as parts of its body through the directions of up, down, and across are not something other [than that unity], but rather, being perceived as individual limbs like the hands of a person, they appear as shards and so forth; thus, there is a single ultimate non-difference which, because it is a unity, is indivisible and is held to be perceptible by the eyes and other senses. In the same way, because the individual limbs of the manifestations of existence are one with that [existence], they are indivisible.
Therefore, because of its unity, there is no delimitation of an entity anywhere—whether as a jar or the like, or as color and so forth—in the manner of the distinctions you yourself accept.

The word *iti* has the sense of a reason (*hetu*). Because there is an absence of division or limitation, that entity (*bhāva*) is constant (*dhruva*) throughout all three times; it is immovable (*kūṭastha*), like a single bean situated within a heap of beans, being entirely one with everything; it is unshakable (*avicālī*), for it does not migrate from one place to another; it is without loss or gain (*anapāyopajana*), for there is no exit or entry—no loss or gain—of the entity, as in the case of grain in a granary; it is changeless (*avikāry*), because even while remaining in its own place, there is an absence of modification, unlike the movement of a dancer’s eyebrows; it is without origination (*anutpatti*), because there is no arising after having previously been non-existent, as in the case of a jar or similar object; it is imperishable (*avyaya*), because there is no decay, as in the case of the falling off of leaves or the breaking of branches of a tree.

For these qualifiers of permanence apply only to *bhāva* (Being) and not to the *puruṣa* (Spirit) and so forth; here, the connection with the characteristics of "constant" (*dhruva*) and "eternal" (*nitya*) regarding *bhāva* is explained by its possessing properties that are impossible for the distinctions imagined by others, because there is no illustration [of such distinctions] in terms of its own nature, as has been stated. The establishment of this [non-cognition] as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) occurs right here; elsewhere it is merely inference, because its nature consists in the cognition of a part of a relation and the establishment of the remainder. How, then, could there even be inference? Since two related things are sometimes not apprehended, if [inference] were preceded by perception, that [inference] would be possible; but in the absence of that [perception], since it is not established, how could there even be non-cognition (*ajñāna*)? [Inference] is preceded by perception—

Furthermore, the establishment of this [entity] through the means of valid cognition of direct perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*) occurs right here: because the entity is non-different [from its parts], direct perception is established as the means of valid cognition for the entity, as has been stated. As it was said: "For even a single part, in its manifestation, does not transcend the state of possessing all forms (*sārvarūpya*), because its nature consists in the functioning of all undivided existents. Therefore, since it is that very entity and is non-different from it, when one part is apprehended, that [entity] itself is apprehended, just like the spatial location of its own self. Thus, the direct perceptibility of the entity is established.
Therefore, the establishment of perception as the eldest among all means of valid cognition occurs here alone, because its object is a real entity as it truly is;

elsewhere, it is merely inference. In any position other than that of a single positive entity (*bhāva-eka-vastu*), even that which is considered perception is nothing but inference, given the position of difference (*bheda-pakṣa*).

What is the reason? Because its nature consists in the establishment of the remainder through the perception of one part of a relationship and the cognition thereof; for when two things are related, if one part of that relationship is perceived and there is a cognition of it, the establishment of the remainder is the essence (*ātman*) of inference, and thus inference is of that nature. Alternatively, the reading is *sambaddhaikadeśa* (one part of the related). As it has been stated: "Inference is the establishment of the remainder from the perception of one [part] of what is related"—meaning that some object, by way of the relationship of owner and owned (*svasvāmibhāva*) and so forth among the sevenfold types of relations, becomes perceptible to a certain sense organ.

Therefore, inference (*anumāna*) is that establishment of a remaining object which is not currently perceived through sensory perception; for example, the cognition "there is fire" arising from the sight of smoke.

Likewise, in this case, it is only the threefold [inference] characterized as *pūrvavat* and so forth that is possible—namely, that which is preceded by the contact of the self, the sense organ, the mind, and the object.

This is because the apprehension of a single part, having as its object a distant portion, does not touch the entirety of that thing; thus, the apprehension of the remainder by means of the apprehension of one part is indeed inference.

Even if that [perception] were an inference, do not form a fixed conviction [regarding its validity]; therefore, he says: "How can there even be inferential status? Because, according to the logic already stated, perceptuality is unestablished.

If it is asked why, it is because the two related things are never perceived together. To this it is replied: we do not say that they are non-conveyors [of meaning].

What then? We say that they are not denoters [of meaning]. However, their status as communicators—by way of indicating [an object] through the power of the conventions of the cognizer—is not contradicted, for their domain is the object as it appears in conceptual construction (*vikalpātman*). This is because, like the cry of a peacock, they follow worldly usage (*vyavahāra*) based on convention. Just as the cry of a peacock, having been previously heard in association with a specific state such as fear, intoxication, joy, or movement, produces a corresponding cognition in a person who has established a connection [between the sound and that state] at a later time; in the same way, a person, by uttering words such as "pot" or "cloth," conveys his own intention to another person by virtue of prior convention. Thus, there is no contradiction with established usage or worldly practice. Likewise, even in the case of insentient sounds, such as the thundering of clouds at the right or wrong time, the discernment of auspicious or inauspicious results is seen to arise solely from convention.

Or rather, what is the use of this laborious effort to avoid contradictions with established usage? Is it not the case that this very [explanation] is both well-connected and comprehensive? It is as follows: all those words have as their referent (*lakṣaṇārtha*) none other than that single Brahman, according to whichever one of the various methods of injunction—such as "person" (*puruṣa*) and so forth—has been demonstrated by you and accepted; for they are parts of that [Brahman], just like the previously mentioned establishment through perception (*pratyakṣasiddhi*).

Just as in the case of "the cow has horns, a hump, a tail-tip, and a dewlap," these words such as "horns" and so forth—because they denote specific parts of the cow—are intended as indicators (*upalakṣaṇa*) of it; yet, by virtue of well-established convention (*prasiddhasaṅketa*), they are denoters of the cow itself, precisely because those parts are non-different from it. In the same way, since all words do not exist apart from its parts, they are denoters of that very Brahman alone. Thus, even in their capacity as denoters, there is no contradiction with established usage and common practice.

Regarding the fact that all words have the undivided, single, non-dual Brahman as their implied object (*upalakṣaṇa*), he states a proof that accords with the consensus of those who know the definition of words: "And having established it thus, those who know the definition of words say..."—this is the completion of the sentence—"all verbal roots express the meaning of *bhū* (to be). Even for them, according to this very view, roots such as *kṛ* (to do) possess the meaning of existence (*sattā*). Thus, that one partless word is the meaning of the sentence;
however, because it is the locus of synthesis (*saṅgraha*), its nature is that of a substance (*dravya*).

That which comes into being (*bhavati*) is "becoming" (*bhavana*), and that which exists as such is "existence" (*bhāva*). That which flows (*dravati*) is "substance" (*dravya*); neither modification nor part [can be so called], for the verbal root *bhū* (to exist) would then lack its primary meaning. Thus the meaning of the words has been stated.

Thus, in the fourth quarter of the *Uṇādi* section of Pāṇini’s grammar, the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*) is now stated: that single, partless word is the sentence-meaning; the sentence and the sentence-meaning together are the "sentence-meaning" (*vākyārtha*); the meaning joined with the sentence is the sentence-meaning; the meaning related to the sentence, derived from the sentence, or belonging to the sentence itself is the sentence-meaning. As they have said: "The verbal form (*ākhyāta-śabda*), the aggregate (*saṅghāta*), the genus (*jāti*) residing in the aggregate..."

The views of those who perceive the principles of logic regarding the sentence (*vākya*) are manifold: some hold that the word is a single, partless entity; others that it is a sequence synthesized by the intellect; some that the first word is the sentence; others that every word is distinct; and still others maintain that a word is a sentence only when it is semantically expectant (*sākāṅkṣa*).

Its scriptural basis is found in the response given by the Blessed One to the question of the Brahmin Somila—beginning with "O Somila, am I one? and so forth—which states: "O Somila, I am indeed one, I am also two, I am also undecaying, I am also imperishable, I am also unchanging, and I am also that which has been, is becoming, and will become in manifold ways," and so on. Thus says the *Eka-prakaraṇa*.
Thus, the second chapter on the method of injunctions (*vidhi-vidhyara*), which includes conceptualization (*savikalpa*), from the *Nayacakra* is completed.
Oṃ Arhaṃ.
Now begins the third section, the Investigation of Both [Views].

Now, regarding these various states (*avasthā*) described by you for each respective doctrine such as that of the *puruṣa*: is the reality (*tattva*) of the *puruṣa* and so forth characterized by those states, or are those states characterized by the *puruṣa* and so forth?

If the *puruṣa* and so forth are merely the self of the states, and the states are not the self of the *puruṣa* and so forth, then there is no such thing as a "puruṣa" distinct from the four states, because you would be accepting a mere collection of the constituents (*samudāyin*), just like the collection of form (*rūpa*) and the other aggregates.
May the Blessed Lady Śrutadevatā— the one with large eyes like lotus petals, whose face is a lotus, who is as fair as the interior of a lotus,
and who dwells within a lotus— grant success now;
for this is the occasion for the practice of both piercing and drawing.

If this state (*bhāva*) described by the method of injunction (*vidhi-naya*) were faultless, then the undertaking of another alternative would be purposeless; however, since that [state] is indeed faulty, having reached the opportunity to state its defect, and desiring to point out hereafter the "injunction-and-both" (*vidhyubhayāra*), he first speaks for the sake of stating the aforementioned defect, beginning with: "Now, what do you... and so forth.

Here, the word *atha* (now) is used to introduce a new topic (*adhikāra*), specifically to introduce the section concerning the refutation of the previously mentioned doctrines of the Person (*puruṣa*) and so on.

The word *kiṃ* (what) is used here in the sense of a question. Regarding the aforementioned categories—Person (*puruṣa*), Destiny (*niyati*), Time (*kāla*), Nature (*svabhāva*), and Being (*bhāva*)—each is grasped as being identical with itself in its respective manner and through its respective mode: 1. The Person (*puruṣa*) consists of the four states beginning with sleep; 2. Destiny (*niyati*) consists of the fixed states such as prior and subsequent actions and non-actions; 3. Time (*kāla*) consists of the reality of the distinctions of sequence and simultaneity, and of the past, present, and future; 4. Nature (*svabhāva*) consists of the reality of the various manifestations of existence, which are distinguished solely by the internal differentiation of the Self; 5. Being (*bhāva*) consists of the reality of the world, which is the specific state of objects, words, and cognitions that are unadorned and pervaded by pure existence alone, free from the conceptual constructions of ignorance regarding "one's own" or "not one's own. These states, which are individually and exhaustively the pervasive functions of entities such as rice-sprouts, jars, and cloth, have been mentioned for the purpose of demonstrating the pervasiveness of each respective view of the Person and the others. Among these, is the reality of the Person and so forth merely a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) defined by those states? Or are those [states] the characteristic of that [reality]? There is no such thing existing apart from them, just as a jar is nothing other than its color and other qualities.

Or are they characterized by the person (*puruṣa*) and so forth? Is it that only the person and so forth are real, and those states do not exist at all—just as the pot itself is the color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth, and there are no such things as "color-form" apart from the pot? One of these two alternatives must be determined; for [otherwise] there would be a contradiction with the meaning of the other [position]. (Bhavataraṃhīnyāsorthebhā)
The meaning is as follows: because of the state that will arise from that, [it is] from that state which will arise. (bhā) *nyāsortho* ya *dbhāvivivasthāttataḥ* ya *dbhāvivṛvasthāttataḥ bhā.
The reading enclosed within these marks— *prativivaktya-svanaśeṣaḥ pra*— is not present in the Ya manuscripts.
What follows from this? If [it is argued that] the self exists in the various states, and so forth, up to the point where it is said: "this is merely another doctrine of origination."

If there is no such thing as the *puruṣa* (the person) and so forth, and if the self (*ātman*) itself, characterized by those states, is that [reality], then it follows that only those states are real, and not the states that constitute the nature of the *puruṣa*—that is, those states do not possess the essential nature of the *puruṣa*. Consequently, this amounts to yet another form of the doctrine of the mere aggregate (*samudāyamātravāda*), according to which there is no such thing as a "person" distinct from the four states. Furthermore, because the states occur sequentially rather than simultaneously, it is like the doctrine of momentariness (*kṣaṇikavāda*). Since it is accepted for the sake of establishing the state of the Fourth (*turīyatva*) through the sequence of liberation, it is like the example of clothing. Because it consists of only the four cognitions, it is a doctrine of the emptiness of objects external to consciousness (*vijñānavyatiriktārthaśūnyavāda*), wherein only conceptual cognition is real, and nothing exists outside the appearance of that cognition, just as in a dream.
This very inconceivable is being contemplated:

whether above, below, or across, the Puruṣa is established as the one and only reality; for he consists of the nature of that which is to be joined with the non-distinct higher and lower, like a tree that has fallen.

Having begun with the general statement "the person and so forth," the specific denial of the person's existence in the words "there is no such thing as a person" is because the person is the first among the options of the systems of injunction and non-injunction, and because [the denial] is to be extended by analogy through the refutation of that [person].

If it is asked, "When the doctrine of the *puruṣa* (the Person) is introduced, how can it be established that the *puruṣa* does not exist at all? we reply: Because this other [doctrine] is merely a theory of a collection, since it accepts only the collection of its constituent parts—just like a collection of form (*rūpa*) and so forth—it is simply this very same collection of the aggregates (*skandha*) of form, sensation, consciousness, mental formations, and perception as conceived by the Buddhists. Like a fist made of fingers, a row of cranes, or a chariot consisting of axles, wheels, a framework, spokes, yokes, and poles, this theory of a collection appears as something else while actually resulting in the negation of the *puruṣa*, much like a rooster smeared slightly with ink; for it is distinguished only by the different designations of the states of deep sleep, dreamless sleep, waking, and the fourth (*turiya*).

The theory that the collection of four states exists simultaneously is equivalent to the theory of a collection of qualities such as form (rūpa) and so forth existing simultaneously; it is thus comparable to the theory of a collection of forms and so forth located in different places.

This [theory] is not at all like the doctrine of the simultaneous arising of form and other qualities that differ according to location; rather, it is like the doctrine of *nāmarūpa* (name-and-form), which consists of a continuous succession of births and deaths occurring non-simultaneously and distinguished by temporal differences. The momentary doctrine (*kṣaṇikavāda*) is so called because it maintains a sequence of liberation for the purpose of establishing the state of the Fourth (*turīya*), involving the occurrence of successive states rather than simultaneity. This is due to the acceptance of a sequence of purification through the states of deep sleep, dream, waking, and the supreme state beyond sleep (*paramavinidrā*), as well as their contrary occurrences. Since there is a destruction of these states, "alteration" (*anyathātva*) occurs. Furthermore, because destruction is observed at the end, destruction at the beginning must be inferred for these states; thus, it is the momentary doctrine.
What is the illustration? It is like clothing: just as a garment, decaying and wearing out moment by moment, finally falls apart, so too are the states [of existence].

It is not only the doctrines of the momentariness of the aggregate (*samudaya*) and so forth, but what then? Even the doctrine of emptiness (*śūnyavāda*). For example: "Of the four [states], there is no knowledge," and so on. Just as by the proponents of the *puruṣa* (Sāṃkhya), the four states are separately grasped and even within them it is established that knowledge alone exists—because of being asleep like a sleeping person, because of being in deep sleep like one intoxicated by wine, and so forth; and likewise, by you yourself, through the transformation of form and so forth from the formless into the formed, it has been demonstrated in many ways that "form" is so called because it is a formation, and that the creation of form, taste, jars, and so forth, does not deviate from the nature of consciousness which is the essence of knowledge. And that [creation] is conceptual knowledge; only that is real, and not form and so forth which exist outside of the knowledge appearing as such, just as in a dream. Just as in a dream there is only the knowledge appearing as a lion and so forth, and no lion or such thing exists external to it, so too waking-consciousness is merely knowledge; it is merely the knowledge of forms such as villages, gardens, women, and men, and is devoid of any object distinct from it, just like the dream-consciousness. This is the conclusion reached.

Therefore, [the view that] reality consists merely of conceptual cognition is the doctrine of the emptiness of objects external to consciousness; for even the doctrine of consciousness-only, which relies on the state of non-conceptuality that transcends the dualistic discrimination of grasped and grasper, would result in the consequence of being empty—what more could be said than this?

This is yet another doctrine of mere aggregation (*samudāyamātravāda*); like the sequence of liberation accepted for the purpose of demonstrating the state of the Fourth (*turīyatva*), it is a doctrine of momentariness (*kṣaṇikavāda*) because states occur non-simultaneously, like clothing. Because it consists of only four cognitions, the truth is merely conceptual cognition (*kalpanājñāna*); nothing exists outside of that appearing cognition, like a dream—this is the doctrine of the emptiness of objects distinct from consciousness (*vijñānavyatiriktārthaśūnyavāda*).
This very inconceivable [reality] is thus contemplated:
"Above, below, and across, the Puruṣa alone is established everywhere; he is not composed of higher or lower, nor of subtle or gross forms, like a tree."

Abiding for as long as the world lasts? Equal to the four [immeasurables], momentary, primordial, and at the end, leading to destruction.
The state of the inference of destruction;
likewise,
such-and-such a certain external existence.
Is something external empty? Or is it also [empty] of this [internal] nature?

The proponent of the Puruṣa says: This criticism—that "this which is being thought of is indeed inconceivable," and so forth—is an incoherent refutation arising from a failure to understand my statement. For I have stated, with the restrictive particle *eva*, that "this [world] is indeed the Puruṣa"; I did not say, "only this is the Puruṣa," referring specifically to the perceptible states such as deep sleep and the rest.

Here, [the opponent objects]: "But surely he has established that [the Puruṣa] possesses the essential nature of only a single state, because you describe him as never transcending consciousness (*caitanya*)."

And since that [waking state] is not other than the state of being awake, the Puruṣa is characterized solely by the state of being awake, because he is defined by the absolute departure from sleep, just like the state of being awake itself. For this [Puruṣa] does not consist of the other states, as that would entail the abandonment of his own nature;
however, if he were limited to that alone, then the Puruṣa, like those states, would not consist of the waking and other states, and thus would lack omnipresence.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: **Thesis:** The Puruṣa alone is established everywhere—above, below, and across. **Reason:** Because he consists of the nature of that which is not different from, nor superior to, nor inferior to, nor more extensive than [anything else]. **Example:** Like a tree. As it has been said: "Than whom there is nothing higher, than whom there is nothing smaller or greater;
like a tree, He stands alone, firm in heaven; by Him, this entire universe is pervaded by the Puruṣa. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.9)
9. Thus, because there is nothing else superior to it, the meaning is that there is only non-duality (*ananya-advaita*).

Alternatively, because there is nothing else—whether superior (*para*), meaning preeminent, or inferior (*apara*), meaning not preeminent, or anything other—due to the absence of distinctions such as above, below, or across, and because it exists as an undivided self.

There is nothing smaller or greater, because there is no division between the subtle and the gross; for even though it remains undivided in that very nature, it persists as such—this is the remainder of the meaning already explained.
Now, one might object: has this not been established as having only a single state as its essential nature, since it was described as never transcending consciousness?

And since that [awakened state] is not other than the state of being awake, the Puruṣa is characterized solely by the state of being awake, because it is defined by the absolute departure from sleep, just like the self-nature of the state of being awake.
For this [state] does not consist of anything else, as that would entail the abandonment of its own function;
but if it were merely that [state], then the Puruṣa, like it, would not consist of the states of waking and so forth, and thus would lack omnipresence.

"Than whom there is nothing further, than whom nothing smaller or greater exists; like a tree standing firm, He alone dwells in heaven; by that Puruṣa all this is filled. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.9). Thus, there is no non-dualism other than this.
There is nothing else;
because of the absence of division into self and other,
it exists as the nature of the division of space.

Regarding this, it is said [in the *Abhāsa*]: "Now, this... and so forth. Indeed, by means of describing the nature of the four states, you have established that this Person (*puruṣa*), without transcending his state-nature, has as his very essence only a single state; for since he is defined through that very description, he consists essentially of those states. Furthermore, specifically, his essential nature is that of a single state alone—the reality of the fourth state (*turyāvasthā*). This is the meaning.

If it is asked why this is so, it is because of the description of the non-deviation from consciousness (*caitanya*). Having asserted the proposition that "this Puruṣa consists of knowledge everywhere," and for the purpose of demonstrating its pervasiveness, it was described that trees, grass, walls, men, and so forth, are nothing but consciousness—because of being asleep, because of being in deep sleep, and because of being awake, like a man who is asleep and so on—and that very consciousness is not different from the state of being without sleep (*vinidrāvasthā*); and that consciousness is indeed the state of being without sleep. As it has been said: "For the Puruṣa there is no mere emergence [of states], and even bound souls (*paśu*) do not cease to be non-mere [consciousness]."

"And even though you alone are the Lord, your way of being should not be thought of as inconceivable, for it is established that 'the movement of the perfected one is inconceivable' (Dvādaśamukhaśāstra 4.22)."

The word "iti" has the sense of a reason; for this reason, the person (puruṣa) is characterized solely by the state of being without sleep (vinidrāvasthā); this alone is its characteristic, because of the statement [in the Tattvārthasūtra]: "Upayoga is the characteristic [of the soul]" (2.8).
This, however, is merely a proposition.

The reason for this is stated here: because it is defined by the nature of the absolute cessation of sleep. "Absolute" (*atyanta*) means that which has transcended all limits at all times and in all places; that which exists therein is the "absolute" (*ātyantika*), namely the cessation of sleep. That itself is the "form" (*rūpa*), meaning the essential reality (*tattva*). Because it is defined by that reality—just as it has been defined by the proponent of the Puruṣa that everything, everywhere, always, and in every way is of the nature of consciousness—the reason is established.

What is the illustration? It is like the self in the state of wakefulness (*vinidrāvasthā*). Just as the Person (*puruṣa*) does not transcend the fourth state of pure consciousness—the state of wakefulness—because it is defined by the aforementioned nature, so too in the remaining states, he does not transcend the possession of those attributes. Thus, this very state of wakefulness is established everywhere; for it is not of the nature of the others. Just as the states of deep sleep and so forth are actually the fourth state itself, so that [fourth state] is not of the nature of them.

Why? Because it would entail the abandonment of its own function. If that state of wakefulness were also the state of sleep and so forth, then by that [latter state] the state of purity would have abandoned its own function; however, there is no such abandonment of its own function, due to defects such as the confusion of states and the impossibility of determining their distinct natures.

Therefore, that [state] is merely the state of being without sleep (*tanmātra*); and since it is merely the state of being without sleep, the *puruṣa* must also be merely that state. Consequently, he is merely the state of being without sleep. Likewise, although the *puruṣa* consists of states such as waking and so forth, and is characterized by the state of being without sleep, he is not merely the state of being without sleep because he is everything (*sarvatva*). Furthermore, the state of being without sleep, while being essentially the state of being without sleep, cannot be merely the state of being without sleep because it is everything; for it is characterized by the state of being without sleep, just like the very nature of the *puruṣa*.

Furthermore, since that very [consciousness] constitutes the nature of all states, even grass and such would be omnipresent; what then is the use of postulating the oneness of the Person (*puruṣa*)? Alternatively, because the waking state lacks those characteristics [of the other states], it would be non-existent; and consequently, there would be an absence of a Person who is the nature of all things across the four states of reality.

Now, even if a person who possesses characteristics contrary to those of one without sleep is still indeed a "person" due to a difference in the specific determination (*avadhāraṇabheda*), there is the state of being "without sleep. Because that [state] consists of states such as waking and so forth, and because it is merely the state of being without sleep, it does not function during the remaining states perceived while asleep and so on; thus, there is the fault of non-pervasiveness (*avyāpitva*) for the doctrine of the Person as the cause, since [the definition] does not apply to trees, stones, walls, and so forth.
"Let it be seen (pṛṣṭha 183, 184):

'For the Puruṣa there is not only [the state of] emergence, nor are the bound souls (paśus) those from whom isolation (kaivalya) has not yet ceased; and even though isolation exists, the Lord is like one whose course is inconceivable to you, as if he were inconceivable. —Siddhāntadvādaśikā 4.22."

Now, even though the *puruṣa* is characterized by the state of being awake (*vinidrāvasthā*), because he is everything (*sarvatvāt*), he would not be merely the state of being awake; and the state of being awake, while consisting of the state of being awake, because it is everything, would likewise not be merely the state of being awake, since it possesses the characteristic of the state of being awake, just like the *puruṣa*'s own self."

Furthermore, since that very [state] is the self of all in every state, even grass and such would be omnipresent; so what is the use of postulating a single Puruṣa? It has been observed that these states lack all-pervasiveness because they do not function [therein].
Now, [the verse beginning with] "vinidrā" and so forth...

Lest there be the fault of the Puruṣa being non-omnipresent, it is maintained that although the Puruṣa is characterized by the waking state, because he is omnipresent (*sarvatva*), he is not merely the waking state alone; rather, he is also the states of sleep and so forth. Consequently, even the waking state, while being essentially the waking state, would—due to that very omnipresence—not be merely the waking state alone, but would also be the states of sleep and so forth. This is the meaning.

The reason is that, because it is characterized by the state of being without sleep, it is like the self-nature of the Puruṣa; just as the Puruṣa is held to be all-pervading because he is characterized by the state of being without sleep, so too the state of being without sleep must reside within the Self and be all-pervading, for it is indeed characterized by the state of being without sleep.

Regarding the passage beginning with "tataśca" and so forth: this being the case, there is yet another fault. For every state (*pratyavastham*), the activity of the waking state (*vinidrāvasthāvṛtti*) persists; since that very waking state is omnipresent (*sarvagatatvāt*) without distinction even in the states of deep sleep (*suṣupta*), dreamless sleep (*susupta*), and waking (*jāgrat*), the state of deep sleep would also have to be omnipresent—just like grass and other things—because it consists of everything (*sarvātmakatvāt*), in the same way as the waking state. Its consisting of everything has been stated [previously] because its characteristic is the waking state, just like the person (*puruṣavat*).

Therefore, since even grass and such are omnipresent, what is the use of postulating the oneness of the Puruṣa? What is this prideful attachment to the specific doctrine of the Puruṣa? Why is it not recited that "all this, whatever has been and whatever will be, is indeed only grass; for there is nothing whatsoever beyond it," and so forth, or "all this is filled by this grass"? [Note: This appears to be a critique of the textual variants regarding the reading of the *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad*].
Furthermore, it is said: "Because it does not possess that characteristic," and so forth.

A characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is that which, having distinguished its qualificand from other objects, establishes it in its own nature, as in the case of a blue lotus. However, because it does not abide within itself, there is no characteristic; this is because [the universal] exists in all things throughout every state.
Consequently, due to the absence of those characteristics, or because it does not abide in its own nature, the state of being sleepless would be non-existent, like a flower in the sky.

And therefore, regarding that very reality (*tattva*): the reality of those four states is that same [reality]; in that reality, there is the absence of the four states; and those [states] themselves are everything, so from their absence, there is the absence of everything. From the absence of everything, there is also the absence of the Puruṣa, who consists of all things and whose nature is that [everything]. Therefore he says: "And therefore, there is the absence of that reality, the four states, everything, and the Puruṣa. For consciousness alone is the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of both the Puruṣa and the states. In its absence—when there is the absence of the Puruṣa and the states—what remains? [The text reads] *sthāsarvā* [in the Bhāṣya].
Now, regarding the passage beginning with "the characteristic of being sleepless" (*vinidrālakṣaṇa*), etc.:

if it is your view that by avoiding the two defects—the absence of the person in the state of sleeplessness and [the defect of] the state itself—all defects are avoided, and that this occurs through the reversal of the restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), then it is as follows: the Person (*puruṣa*) is indeed the Person alone, even though he is the opposite of the characteristics of the state of sleeplessness. What is the reason? Because there is a distinction (*bheda*) in the restriction.

How is there a distinction in the restriction (*avadhāraṇa*)? It is said: when the state of wakefulness is restricted within the Self, the state of wakefulness alone is the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of that Self; however, in the case of the Person (*puruṣa*), it is merely a characteristic because he does not exclude the other states either. For he is not manifold like a variegated painting (*mecaka*), as such a distinction in restriction would be improper according to what was stated before, and because it would contradict the initial proposition, like [the claim that] a jar is identical with its form and so forth. The nature of the Person was previously described in terms of the states; now, however, those states are spoken of as distinct from the Self. Thus, the reality of the Person is like a jar being distinct from its form and other qualities.

And when their very essence consists of that [state of wakefulness], then the state of being awake alone is their defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), and no other state whatsoever exists; thus, it is certain that the state is the defining characteristic of one’s own self. However, because that same state also serves as the defining characteristic of other states, it is not restricted [to them]; therefore, there is at least no absence of the state of being awake.

There is no absence of the *puruṣa* either; however, because of the restriction that "in the *puruṣa* there is only the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*)," the state of wakefulness is indeed a characteristic of the *puruṣa*, not a non-characteristic. Thus, the *puruṣa* is not restricted to being characterized by [the state of wakefulness] alone, since it is characterized by other states as well. Because he does not abandon the other states either, they too serve as characteristics of the *puruṣa*; therefore, this is a restrictive determination made through differentiation. For that *puruṣa* is of manifold forms, like a variegated gem (*mecaka*). A variegated gem is indeed a mixture of colors; it is blue, yellow, and also of all other colors. In the same way, the *puruṣa* possesses the characteristic of the state of wakefulness, yet he also possesses the characteristics of any one of the other states, such as sleep and so forth.
This reading enclosed within the brackets does not exist in the Ya manuscripts;
is it due to a difference in emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*)? That which is being emphasized is the Bhāṣya.

The defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) within its own self is indeed the state of being awake; however, in the case of the *puruṣa*, it is merely a characteristic because the other states are not abandoned [by it]. For he is not manifold like a variegated painting (*mecaka*), as that would be improper due to the distinction of restriction (*avadhāraṇabheda*) mentioned previously, and because it would contradict the initial proposition, like the nature of a jar or form and so forth. It was stated previously that these states belong to the *puruṣa*; now, however, those states are spoken of as distinct from his own self. Thus, the reality (*tattva*) of the *puruṣa* is like the jar-nature of form and so forth;
and when they [the states] themselves are that reality, then for them—

To this it is replied: No; [the objection] beginning with "as has been stated" and so forth is not tenable, because, as has been stated, a distinction in restriction (*avadhāraṇabheda*) is improper. "As has been stated" (*uktavat*) means equal to what was stated; by that very [statement], in the manner previously explained and by that very same reasoning, there is no occasion at all for a distinction in restriction. That which is not devoid of reason is "proper" (*nyāyya*); that which is not proper is "improper" (*anyāyya*).

Why? Because of the contradiction with the initial proposition (*pratijñā-vyāghāta*). If the restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) is taken to refer to distinct objects, then the proposition that "all this consists of the one Person whose nature is consciousness" is abandoned. On the other hand, if the proposition that "it consists of the one Person" is maintained, then the logical possibility of a restriction based on distinct objects is shattered. How so? Like the case of the jar and its form, etc. Just as in the position that "the jar itself is the form and so forth," there are no such things as form and so forth existing as entities distinct from the jar; in that case, for the nature of form, the state of being form alone is the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), not the state of being taste and so forth, whereas for the nature of the jar, the state of being form is indeed a defining characteristic because it does not exclude the others—what would be the point [of the restriction] since form and the rest would be non-existent? Likewise here too, since there is no object distinct from the Person characterized by the single state of wakefulness, and consequently the other states such as sleep do not exist, what room is there for the meaning of a restriction? Thus he demonstrates both the absence of restriction and the contradiction with the proposition: "The state of being the Person was previously stated [as applying] to the states, but now those states are said to be separate from their own self"; therefore, as before, the distinction of restriction is improper and there is a contradiction with the proposition.

Thus, for this reason—because of the contradiction of the proposition and because the restriction [of identity] would be improper—the reality is in both cases the opposite of what was intended: that the state (*avasthātva*) belongs to the person (*puruṣa*), or that the states alone are the person, and not that the person alone is the states. This follows, like the case of "the jar-ness of color and so forth" (*rūpādighaṭatva*). Just as in the position that "the jar is nothing but its color and so forth," the meaning is that there is no such thing as a "jar" apart from them; in that case, a restriction such as "it is color itself, not taste" is appropriate because they refer to distinct objects. Similarly, if it were said that "the states alone are the person," then a restriction would be logical—namely, the restriction of one state in the absence of a person, for the purpose of excluding other distinct states. However, that is not logical, because it contradicts the proposition that there is a single person whose nature is consciousness (*caitanya*).
How can there be a refutation when [the opponent's] position has fallen apart?
A counter-objection such as "refutation" and so forth is not possible.
Furthermore, regarding the passage beginning with "And when their very essence... up to "...the attainment of essence is just as in the world":

when their existence is their essence, they are indeed that essence; they exist as nothing other than themselves. Because it is determined through differentiation, the waking state itself is the defining characteristic within the waking state's own self. However, in the case of the *puruṣa*, that [waking state] is merely a characteristic; it is not the *puruṣa* itself that is the characteristic, because the *puruṣa* does not relinquish the fact that all other states also possess that same characteristic.

In that very way, because of the mutual absence within each other's essences, due to the distinction of determinations, and because they possess distinct and separate meanings, is it not the case that this itself constitutes both all-pervasiveness and non-all-pervasiveness? Thus, there is an attainment of reality just as it appears in the world.

Now, [it may be argued that] because the meaning of the word "non-conceptual" (*avikalpa*) is the absence of characteristics (*alakṣaṇa*), it is not [so] because its true nature (*tattva*) is unknown. How then can there be a description of its four states and the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) of its manifold and all-pervading nature? If each of its individual states does not exist [independently], then, due to their non-existence, how could it possess the state of being non-conceptual, which consists in the attainment of their unity? For it is not the case that when they do not function separately, they are absent from one another’s essences, since there is a distinction in their specific determination (*avadhāraṇa*).

From the statement "in such and such a way," it follows that even for the successive distinctions, there is no existence within one another's selves. For example: in the self of the state of form (*rūpāvasthā*), the state of form alone is the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*); however, in the self of the jar (*ghaṭa*), the state of form is merely a characteristic, because it does not abandon its status as a characteristic for the states of taste (*rasa*) and so forth. Likewise, because earth, clods of earth, and the like do not exist within one another's selves, when determining the self of the state of a clod, the state of a clod alone is the self of the state of a clod; but when determining the self of earth, that [state of a clod] is merely a characteristic, for it does not abandon its nature even in the case of diamonds (*vajra*) and the like. Thus, in every case, there is a distinction in the application of restrictive determination (*avadhāraṇabheda*).

Therefore, due to the distinction in determinations (*avadhāraṇa*) as you have stated, there is a mutual absence among the various selves; because of this distinction in determinations, their referents are absolutely distinct. Consequently, because their referents are each distinct, there is an absence of a universal (*sāmānya*). Due to the absence of a universal, everything consists merely of a state of many distinct and separate particulars; thus it follows that everything is non-pervasive (*asarvagata*): "A jar is only a jar," "Form is only form," "Taste is only taste," "A cloth is only a cloth," and so forth.

Consequently, does this not lead to the very same view that was stated: "An object exists exactly as it is grasped by worldly convention; therefore, the effort to discern [its nature] in the treatises is useless," and so forth? By refuting generalities and particulars regarding the objects of self and others, the view arises that an object is merely its worldly manifestation according to substance, place, time, and state—that alone is reality—and thus one arrives at a reality that is identical to the worldly view. This is precisely what was stated in the *Pramāṇaviniścaya*.

"...is its own self," etc. Thus, because of the absence [of one] in the various mutual selves, due to the distinction of determinations (*avadhāraṇa*), and because of having distinct and separate referents, is it not the case that this very thing constitutes both "all-pervasiveness" and "non-all-pervasiveness"? Consequently, there would be a lapse into [the error of] worldly convention (*lokavat*). Alternatively, if it is argued that because the meaning of the word is non-conceptual (*avikalpa*), it is indeed without defining characteristics (*alakṣaṇa*), and not because its reality is unknown—then how can there be a description of four states (*caturavasthā*) and the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) of all-pervasiveness consisting of multiple natures? If each individual state does not belong to this [reality] separately, then, due to its non-existence [as such], how could it possess that non-conceptual form which consists in the attainment of oneness? For [oneness] does not exist when things function separately.
See pages 201–2;
*jñānādī* (Ya);
*trāsvāvadhāraṇa* (Pra).
See page 11, line 3:
"Now, it is indeed without definition because the word lacks a referent in non-conceptual [cognition], and not because its true nature is unknown."

How could there be a definition, or how could there be a state, for that reality which is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*), undivided (*avibhāga*), devoid of conjunction, differentiation, or transformation; which transcends the sphere of words such as the rumbling of clouds; which cannot be characterized by words—whether following conventional usage like the cry of a peacock or based on social convention—just as a cow cannot be defined by its horns and so forth; and which consists of the conceptualization of an identification between word and object that is differentiated merely by its own internal parts? For it is not, as in the worldly view, of a nature consisting of an investigation into the established distinction between the unknown universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*). How, then, could there be a definition? How could there be a state? Thus [it is asked].

And this is illogical because of the description of four states; for if those four states were indeed non-existent, how could that description be tenable, like a description of the fragrance of a sky-flower? Furthermore, it would entail the consequence of the absence of the contemplation of omnipresence. Demonstrating this, he says: "And how can there be the contemplation of an omnipresent self consisting of many parts? [the phrase] "how" continues from the previous context.

"Everything has gone, [therefore] it is all-pervading (*sarvagata*). According to the *Dhātupāṭha*, the root *sṛ* (935, 1095) means "to go. This very word *sarva* expresses the action characterized by reaching another location, which is the meaning of "going"; that which is "this" and "that other" constitutes the entirety, which is "everything" (*sarvam*). Consequently, that entire thing having gone is "all-pervading" (*sarvagatam*). Its state is "all-pervasiveness," which is inseparable from having multiple natures. For everything indeed possesses multiple natures; "all-pervading" means having gone to the entirety of objects as they appear in various distinct conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*). This contemplation is not tenable if there were a single nature devoid of conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*).
But that [is] the state of not knowing reality (Bhāṣya); the state of knowing reality (Yājñavalkya)—
see page 243, line 11–24.
The meditator,
the object of meditation, and the act of meditating— if these are distinct from one another...

Furthermore, it would follow that there is an absence of non-conceptuality (*nirvikalpatva*). If, for this [Puruṣa], each individual state—beginning with "each one" up to "in the variegated nature"—were not complete in every single instance, such as sleep and so forth, then, because each one would be absent, those states would simply not exist. Given their non-existence, how could the two forms of unity and diversity belonging to those very distinct states occur within the variegated nature of this Puruṣa-principle?
Indeed, he would be non-existent in this way, because, being without stability, he would lack a fourfold nature, like a sky-flower.

And precisely because of what you have said, that [reality] is neither a characteristic (*lakṣya*), nor an object (*artha*), nor a thing (*vastu*), because it lacks characteristics, like a sky-flower. Furthermore, since it is improper to either accept or reject one or the other of these [categories], its very inexpressibility (*avācyatā*) follows; likewise, it cannot be of the nature of "not this" (*neti*). Thus, would there not be a state of non-conceptuality (*avikalpatā*) in the sense that the single, non-conceptual reality of the Person (*puruṣatattva*) is such? No, for the nature of non-conceptuality consists in the cessation of distinct conceptualizations. From where, then, could that non-conceptual nature arise? The meaning is that it simply does not exist.

What is the illustration? It is like the absence of a variegated color (*mecaka-varṇa*), which consists in the merging of distinct colors such as white and black; for in the absence of separately established colors, there can be no variegated color. He demonstrates this: "Indeed, two forms, white and black, existing separately, do not become variegated by their own nature, because there is an absence of that single merging which is inseparable from the acquisition of their distinct identities. In the same way, even these states, being unestablished in their own separate natures, cannot exist as a single form devoid of conceptual differentiation (*nirvikalpa*).

Thus, first of all, in the absence of states, there are the defects of describing four states, of the non-existence of the cultivation of being manifold and omnipresent, and of the absence of a non-conceptual nature;
these two [defects] occur in a form that is variegated in nature.

But this [object] is indeed non-existent in this way; because it lacks stability and lacks a fourfold nature, like a sky-flower, it is neither a definable [object], nor a referent, nor a real entity, due to its lack of defining characteristics, like a sky-flower. Furthermore, for this reason, since it is illogical to either accept or reject either of these two [positions], its very inexpressibility is established.
Likewise, he is not seen at all, because of his nature as [the self] (pṛṣṭha 201–2). [The manuscript reads:
*°tmikatvā*]. Prakaraṇa.

Is it by contemplating [the self] alone, or by falling away from one's wife? Or is it by casting arrows at its side and following the practice of inciting fear? We shall refute that very person as follows: "But he is indeed non-existent," because of the non-existence of such states; why? Because of being non-abiding (*anavasthātva*), because of being other than a state (*avasthāto 'nyatvāt*), because of having the nature of non-abiding (*anavasthātmakatvāt*), and because of the absence of the nature of a state (*avasthātvābhāvāt*); the person is like the son of a barren woman.

It might be thought: "Just as there is the existence of a jar—which possesses states—despite being devoid of the nature of its specific states such as color and so forth, so too there is the existence of the Puruṣa, who possesses the four states beginning with sleep, despite being devoid of the nature of those states such as sleep. This, however, is incorrect; for if it were devoid of states, it would lack the nature of the four states.
Since the fourfold state is absent, the absence of that fourfold nature in what is devoid of states is established.
Therefore, in order to eliminate the suspicion of inconclusiveness, he says: "Because, in the case of being devoid of states, it lacks the nature of the four states."
The example "like a flower in the sky" has its meaning already explained.

Alternatively, what is the use of this exertion in establishing its non-existence through further arguments? Is it not the case that, by your own statement, that Puruṣa postulated by you is not even a definable object; he is not a definable object because he lacks defining characteristics (*alakṣaṇatvāt*)?

If it is argued that [the Self] is not an object of definition because it is desired [as the ultimate goal], and thus cannot be established as such, we reply: no, because the negation of its being an object of definition is for the purpose of negating the [conventional] object itself; we say it is not an "object" (artha) because, while an object is that which is "attained" (aryate), this [Self] is not denotable by words or cognizable by knowledge due to its lack of defining characteristics. Consequently, it would be either a state of sleep or a state of wakefulness, but it is not the Puruṣa, because it lacks the characteristics of both.

If you argue that because it is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*), the object (*artha*) does not exist either, then accept this very point: that just like non-conceptual knowledge, its status as a real entity (*vastutva*) also does not exist; for the purpose of establishing this, [it is said]: "That reality (*tattva*) which you desire is indeed a non-entity (*avastu*), because it lacks the defining characteristics (*alakṣaṇatvāt*), like a sky-flower. [End of fragment].
In reality, it is characterized by impermanence.
In meaning,
it is characterized by the absence of other [states], or it is "without sleep" (vinidrā),
or it is "awakened" (vinidrā).

[Regarding the section] beginning with "atha ata" and ending with "asyāvācyataiva": if you were to say—"From this," meaning from the person (*puruṣa*), and "from this," meaning from the state (*avasthā*); therefore, the absolute abandonment of either the person or the states is not logical. For if the states are abandoned, there would be an absence of defining characteristics, which entails the consequence of the non-existence of the person; or if the person who possesses the states is abandoned, there would be the consequence of the non-existence of the states themselves.

Furthermore, it is not logical to accept only one [of the two], because if one were accepted while the other were absent, it would follow that the former could not exist; it would also follow that there is no description of states and the possessor of states, that there is no freedom from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpatva*), and that there is no omnipresence (*sarvagatatva*), which would contradict your own thesis.
Therefore, since it is improper to either accept or reject one of the two, it cannot be said of this *puruṣa* that its nature consists of states, nor can it be said that states do not exist.
What then? That *puruṣa* is inexpressible in terms of having those characteristics or not having them.

And this is incorrect because, in that case, it would not exist at all; for it would be impossible to state whether it is identical to or different from the waking state, like a sky-flower, since it cannot be described as either one or the other due to its lack of definable characteristics (*nirupākhyatva*).
Whatever exists, however, must be stated as being either identical to or different from the waking state—just as the waking state itself is, or as the self-natures of the waking and other states are.

For this very reason, because it is illogical to either abandon or adopt one [of the two], and because it must be admitted that both are joined in being expressible—just as in the case of a father and son—even if the state is indeed the very self of the person (*puruṣa*), it is nevertheless not so, because it would lack stability, like a sky-flower. Even under this conceptualization, that person is non-existent. Why? Because regarding identity with or difference from the waking state, he is "inexpressible" (*avacanīya*); like a sky-flower, since the person characterized by the waking state or the person not characterized by the waking state cannot be expressed in terms of either difference or non-difference, the person is non-existent.
