A sky-flower cannot be described as being either identical to or different from the state of being sleepless; why is this so? First, it cannot be called "identical" because of its non-existence. Nor can it be called "different," because even while possessing the state of being sleepless, its non-existence renders it indefinable (*nirupākhya*), and thus it transcends the domain of speech and cognition. This demonstrates, by means of the example of the sky-flower, the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāvitva*) of the reason with the probandum.

As for the statement, "That which exists [is shown] by the waking state," etc., this is a dissimilar example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) intended to demonstrate the absence of the reason where the probandum is absent. Do not think that there is an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*) because we observe an inexpressibility (*avacanīyatā*) when the self exists in its collective states as we maintain; rather, it demonstrates the waking state and other states of the self in contrast to the waking state, because they are expressible in terms of being either different or non-different—just as the waking state is non-different from the self of the waking state but different from the selves of the dreaming state and so forth, and likewise those [other states] are different from it [the waking state] but non-different from their own selves and are real—whereas the *puruṣa* is not so; therefore, it is non-existent.
The person (puruṣa) [is] beyond the states from here; like the states, the color [is]... [omitted].
The non-existence of [intrinsic] nature,
by virtue of both its definition and its manifestation,
is established.

It may be so; for since [the state of being awake] cannot be described as either identical to or different from the state of being sleepless—just like a sky-flower—it cannot be said to be either one or the other because it lacks any defining characteristic (*nirupākhya*).

Whatever exists, however, can be described as being either identical to or different from the state of being sleepless, such as the state of being sleepless itself, or the states of waking and so forth.

For this very reason, because it is illogical to either abandon or adopt one [of the two], and because it is indeed accepted that both are joined through expressibility— just like the case of father and son—
even if the state is nothing other than the self-nature of the person (*puruṣa*), it is nevertheless not non-existent, for it would otherwise be non-substantial, like a sky-flower.
See pages 201–2.

Furthermore, for this very reason—that it is illogical to either abandon or adopt one of the two based on the cause you have stated—it must indeed be admitted that both [states] are applicable and expressible, just as in the case of a father and son. For example, a single person is both a father and a son; he does not experience fatherhood toward his own son without [simultaneously] possessing sonship toward his own father. Thus, he neither abandons sonship nor adopts only sonship, nor does he adopt only fatherhood. Therefore, he must be called both "father" and "son," and is observed to be endowed with both those properties. Likewise, that person, precisely because it is illogical to abandon or adopt either of the two characteristics—sleeplessness and non-sleeplessness—must necessarily be endowed with both those properties (the characterized and the non-characterized) and must necessarily be expressible by both those terms, because the illogicality of abandoning or adopting either is invariably concomitant with that [dual nature].

Thus, first of all, the claim that the person itself is the states is incorrect, because in the absence of distinct states, numerous logical faults would follow, such as [the confusion of] the state of father and son,
and so forth.

Even if one were to concede that this [Puruṣa] is indeed the self of the Puruṣa, we shall state the fault of the non-existence of the Puruṣa regarding the four states— beginning with "Even if it were so," and so forth.

And although the four states are indeed the very self of the person (*puruṣa*), nevertheless, it is not the case that the person does not exist now; for he would be "without state" (*anavastha*). He is "without state" because he does not possess those states; the condition of being so is "statelessness" (*anavasthatva*). Therefore, due to this statelessness—because of being distinct from the nature of the states and because of being devoid of them—he is like a flower in the sky (*khapuṣpa*).

Alternatively, there is no "non-state" (anavasthā); the person (puruṣa) does not become a state. That which does not become a state does not exist, like a sky-flower. Furthermore, you have accepted that there are states—specifically four states—which, through the description of their various conditions, consist of the conceptualization of being manifold, omnipresent, and unitary, and by virtue of accepting them as having the nature of both difference and non-difference in each individual state; therefore, anything other than these [states] is equivalent to a sky-flower.

Previously, it was stated that even if one accepts the existence of the states themselves, there is no fault because they lack a fourfold nature due to being non-terminal (*anavasthātva*). Now, however, having accepted the *puruṣa* itself as being non-terminal in nature, this fault is stated regarding the positions imagined by others. Even if one accepts the *puruṣa*, the oneness of all four states would follow, because they share the *puruṣa*'s own nature, just like the *puruṣa* itself; thus, since the state of "all" is impossible, the *puruṣa* lacks pervasion over all [states].
For the waking state is indeed the sleepless state, because it has the sleepless state as its own nature, just like the sleepless state; and so it is for the others as well.

The waking state itself is the sleepless state, because it has the waking state as its own nature, just like the waking state; likewise, the others are also so. The sleeping state itself is the sleepless state, because it has the sleeping state as its own nature, just like the sleeping state; likewise, the others are also so. The deep-sleep state itself is the sleepless state, because it has the deep-sleep state as its own nature, just like the deep-sleep state; likewise, the others are also so.

The distinction between the two explanations is that "whatever state is one, that very same [state] is also the other. Thus, the person (puruṣa) is non-existent because of his lack of stability, like a sky-flower; for even if such an unstable person were admitted, there would result an identity among all four of his states.

Why? Because they are the very self of the Puruṣa. For you have stated that the states are indeed the self of the Puruṣa and nothing else; therefore, their identity follows from being his self, just like the Puruṣa himself. Just as the Puruṣa is one because he is the self of the Puruṣa, so too those states are one because they are his self. Consequently, since there is no plurality, the expression "four states" is untenable due to the impossibility of a plural number.

Furthermore, because of his oneness, the Puruṣa cannot be conceived as being "all" in every respect; for according to the roots *sṛ* (in the sense of "going," Pāṇini-Dhātupāṭha 935, 1095), "allness" (*sarvatva*) must have multiple substrates. Therefore, when it is said that "the Puruṣa alone is all," upon what basis is this stated? What is the substrate of that "all" by whose mention the Puruṣa's pervasiveness over everything is described? To this he says: "Because of the absence of the possibility of being 'all,' the non-pervasiveness of the Puruṣa follows, which is contradictory to the intended pervasiveness over all."
The meaning is that this is because one accepts a non-conceptual form (*avikalparūpa*) which consists in the non-differentiation of the various distinct states.
See page 252, line 1. [Objection: Even if this is accepted, there would be unity among all four states, because they have the nature of the *puruṣa*, just like the *puruṣa* itself.
Because there is no possibility of non-existence for anything whatsoever, the person (puruṣa) is all-pervasive;

for the waking state is indeed the sleepless state, because it has the sleepless state as its own nature, just like the sleepless state itself. Likewise, the others [the other states] are also the waking state, because they have the waking state as their own nature, just like the waking state itself; and so too are the others.

The state of sleep itself is the state of being awake, because the state of sleep has the nature of the Self, just like the state of sleep; likewise, the others as well—the state of deep sleep itself is the state of being awake, because the state of deep sleep has the nature of the Self, just like the state of deep sleep—and so it is with the others too:
whatever one state is, that indeed is the other.
The person, because of being a state,
[is] the absence of the fourfold [set] in all cases.

That oneness which exists everywhere is established as the essential nature of those states, because they have the state of wakefulness (*vinidrāvasthā*) as their own self, and because they have the *puruṣa* as their own self, they are also established as being identical with one another. This is now to be contemplated: for the waking state is indeed the state of wakefulness, because it has the state of wakefulness as its own self, just like the state of wakefulness itself.

Just as the state of wakefulness is indeed the state of wakefulness because it has the state of wakefulness as its own nature (*svātmatva*), so too the waking state is indeed the state of wakefulness because it has the state of wakefulness as its own nature; thus, the identity of the waking state with the state of wakefulness and the fact that all states have the person (*puruṣa*) as their own nature have been accepted by you yourself.

The same applies to the others as well: the waking state is indeed the sleepless state, because it has the sleepless state as its own nature, just like the sleepless state; the deep-sleep state is indeed the sleepless state, because it has the sleepless state as its own nature, just like the sleepless state;
likewise, the waking state is indeed the sleepless state, because it has the sleepless state as its own nature, just like the waking state. Its explanation is also to be understood as before;
thus, the identity of the sleepless state with the waking state is to be explained.

"Likewise, the others as well"—this is the extension [of the argument]. The waking state itself is the sleeping state, because it has the waking state as its own nature, just like the waking state; the waking state itself is the deep-sleep state, because it has the waking state as its own nature, just like the waking state; likewise, the sleeping state itself is the dreamless state, because it has the sleeping state as its own nature, just like the sleeping state.
"Likewise, the others as well"—this is the extension: the sleeping state itself is the waking and deep-sleep states, because it has the sleeping state as its own nature, just like the sleeping state.

Likewise, the state of deep sleep (*suṣuptāvasthā*) itself is the state of wakefulness (*vinidrāvasthā*), because the state of deep sleep has its own nature as the Self (*svātmatva*), just like the state of deep sleep;

this is an extension (*atideśa*) to the other states as well. Thus, the state of deep sleep itself is both the waking and sleeping states, because they have their own nature as the Self of deep sleep, just like the state of deep sleep.

In this way, having meditated upon the identity of each of these states with one another through their specific distinctions, it is stated by way of a general summary of all of them: whatever is one state, that is indeed the other as well, because they are of a single nature.

Because they possess a single self-nature (*ekasvātmatva*), there is no extension (*atideśa*) such as "she is like this" or "the Puruṣa alone is all this," due to the absence of difference. However, through the confusion and intermixture of forms that are distinct in their descriptions, these [states] are not thus [identical], and because he possesses their respective self-natures, there is an absence of fixed distinction between the states of the Puruṣa. Alternatively, if one accepts a fixed distinction as previously stated, there is an extension to the Puruṣa. Or else, by establishing the mutual identity among the individual differences of the states themselves, unity should be inferred among humans, animals, gods, and so forth, as well as among jars, cloths, grass, and so on: "The other consists of the other, because it has the nature of the other, just like its own self."

Thus, from the passage beginning with "the Puruṣa alone" up to "due to the absence of difference," for this reason—namely, because of oneness and because of the impossibility of imagining any "allness"—it was stated that the Puruṣa does not pervade everything. This [text] brings that forward: "The Puruṣa alone is all this. The "absence of extension" (atideśābhāva) is due to the absence of difference;
"extension" (atideśa) means bestowal (*atisarjana*), which is to say, the explanation of the nature of the Puruṣa and the cultivation of that realization.

Either by means of the person who is not perceived, there is an extension (*atideśa*) of that which is perceived and denoted by the word "this" [to that which is not perceived]; or else, by means of this [perceived thing], there is an extension of that which is not perceived, such that "all of it is composed of that.
This reading enclosed within these brackets does not exist in the Ya manuscripts; likewise in the Ava and Ya manuscripts.
And as for the other [scriptural passages],

because there is no difference [between them and the Self] due to their being of one essence even without the word "tu" (but) or the particle "pra," there is an absence of such extended application (*atideśa*) as "that is like this," or "the Person alone is all this," because of the non-existence of any distinction.

However, due to the confusion arising from the blending of differentiated forms through description, these [states] lack such [distinct] reality, and this [Puruṣa] lacks their respective natures; thus, there is no fixed determination of the states of the Puruṣa.
Or, if one accepts a fixed determination as previously stated, let the extension of the nature of the Puruṣa [to these states] be observed, as on page 202.
See page 254, line 2.
Furthermore, regarding the passage beginning with "upavarṇanā" and ending with "vyavasthābhāva eva":

the prefix *upa* signifies proximity; thus, "upavarṇana" (description) means a description by way of proximity, that is, by means of specific attributes (*viśeṣadharma*) and not by means of general attributes (*sāmānyadharma*), because a general attribute is remote.
For example: "This is a person, because he has risen and sat down, because his hands and other limbs move, and because he scratches his head"—it is not [inferred] from mere height.

By such descriptions, their forms are differentiated through the specific characterization of states such as wakefulness without sleep, waking, dreaming, and deep sleep; and by means of those differentiated forms, there arises a confusion and a commingling of these states, since they have thus been described as having attained unity.

There would be a confusion of identities: the identity of the self in the waking state with the self in the dreamless sleep state, and the identity of the self in the dreamless sleep state with the self in the waking state; likewise for the other two states as well. Furthermore, there would be the attainment of each other's identities between these two states.

Consequently, one would attain hell through specific acts of generosity, ethical discipline, and austerity, while attaining heaven through violence and the like; one would experience suffering in heaven and experience pleasure in hell; and liberation would result from ignorance of the true nature of the Puruṣa.

"Confusion (*saṅkara*), however, consists in the state of being indistinguishable from one's own nature, like the mixing of milk and water; thus, these two—interchange (*vyatikara*) and confusion—are established. And due to those two causes, interchange and confusion, there is 'not-being-that,' meaning that the waking state is not the waking state, and likewise for the remaining states, they possess a non-corresponding nature because they are its own nature—that is to say, because they are the self-nature of the *puruṣa*, since the waking and other states are non-different from the self-nature of the *puruṣa*. He states that very oneness as the cause, saying 'because they are its own nature'; in this way, their lack of being themselves has been explained."

And for this person (*puruṣa*) as well, there is likewise the state of not being such, namely the state of non-personhood (*apuruṣatva*), because it is his own self (*svātman*), just like his own self; thus it follows.
[In this way] there is the attainment of that self, and the attainment of this self of those two.
"...like the nature of the self" (Bhāṣya).

He concludes this point: "Thus, there is an absence of the determination of the states of the person. In this way, the "determination of the states of the person"—meaning the definition (*vyākhyā*) consisting of the establishment (*vyavasthā*) [of those states] by ascertaining them through their specific, unique characteristics—is absent because there is no establishment of their own-nature (*svarūpa*).

Lest this fault arise—the absence of a fixed order for both the Puruṣa and its states—if you maintain a separate distinction for each as previously stated, then since the Puruṣa pervades all states and the states are differentiated by the manifestation and concealment of consciousness, and by variations in intensity and degree as explained earlier regarding creation; and if, as stated, such a fixed order is accepted, then the extension [of identity] to the Puruṣa must be abandoned. For if one accepts the distinct natures and fixed orders of the Puruṣa and its states individually, the doctrine that "all this is indeed the Puruṣa" and the proclamation of the oneness of the Puruṣa must be relinquished, and the theory of the Puruṣa as the sole cause must be abandoned.

If that [distinction] is not abandoned, then there is the very non-establishment of that for the sake of which this extension (*atideśa*) was intended—the absolute oneness of non-duality (*advaitaikānta*).

Even that single Puruṣa who is postulated would thus result in being manifold; for if states whose characteristics are non-distinct from his own nature are spoken of without difference, then that Puruṣa, because he is pervaded by those states, would be a Puruṣa whose essence of established oneness is unstable. Consequently, he would be subject to the same extension as the states, since he is identical with them, or else, if they were objects of direct perception like "this," there would be a contradiction regarding their being composed of the *māyā* principle.

Lest this fault should arise, if that [distinction] were not abandoned, for what purpose was this extension (*atideśa*)—this relinquishment (*atisarga*) previously explained as "Puruṣa alone is all this"—formulated? If you ask, "For what purpose is this extension?", it is for the sake of the absolute non-duality (*advaitaikānta*); that is, for the purpose of establishing that "this consists of the one Puruṣa. But why is there a failure to establish that very absolute non-duality? Because this admission of a single Puruṣa actually brings about the non-establishment of a single Puruṣa;
for the state of Puruṣa is indeterminate (*avyavasthā*). (The reading *ittham api* might also occur here.)
See page 189, line 5:
it must be abandoned;
for if it is not abandoned, that very purpose for which this extension (*atideśa*) exists—the absolute non-duality (*advaitaikānta*)—remains unestablished.

Even for that single Puruṣa who is postulated, multiplicity would likewise result; for if states whose characteristics are non-different from his own nature are spoken of without distinction, then that Puruṣa—being pervaded by [other] Puruṣas—would be a Puruṣa whose established nature of oneness is not fixed, and thus he would be subject to the same logical extension as the states, since he is the very self of the Puruṣa. Or else, if there were the state of being an object of direct perception regarding this thing, then what is the object? [The original text ends here.]
If it is asked, "How so?"—even that single person who is postulated by you would likewise result in being manifold.

This is because of the non-duality [implied] by the extension of the Self of the Person (*puruṣātma-atideśa*) through your very statement "thus. What, then, is the underlying contemplation (*bhāvanā*)? It is stated: "That which is the essential nature... and so on, up to "...possessing states."

"Whose nature is what?"—whose nature? Of the *puruṣa*. What is its nature? Its eternality, omnipresence, being the self of all, causality, and so forth. These states have as their defining characteristic that which is non-different from him; they have as their defining characteristic that which is non-different from his own nature, the *puruṣa*. Yet they are spoken of by you as distinct [from one another]. Therefore, the meaning is that they are indeed declared to be non-different from that *puruṣa*. For example: "The *puruṣa* alone is the states," and "The states alone are not the *puruṣa*. By this very restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) and by the demonstration of difference, difference is admitted. From that very [restriction], the plurality of him [the *puruṣa*] over against them [the states], and the plurality of them [the states] over against him, is established solely from your own statement. Just as a jar is characterized by having a neck turned upward and so forth, and the jar alone consists of the neck turned upward and so forth—it is not a cloth, nor is it the squareness of a cloth and so forth—so too, through the restriction and non-restriction of him with respect to them, and of them with respect to him, difference itself is established.

However, in the case of non-difference, there is no distinction in the restriction [of identity], as in the case where "the jar is indeed its own self," but it is not the case that "the jar's own self is only the jar. Therefore, the difference between the states—such as wakefulness and the rest—and the person who possesses those states follows from your own statement alone. Furthermore, regarding the passage beginning with "that person also... and so forth: this being the case, since the extension of the principle of consisting of a single person has been abandoned, it follows that even that person is pervaded by another person, because he is the self-nature of a person, just like the states.

Just as states such as wakefulness and the like are pervaded by the Puruṣa because they are not essentially different from the very nature of the Puruṣa, so too the Puruṣa—being the very nature of the Puruṣa and being inseparable from it—would have to be pervaded by another Puruṣa. Likewise, that other Puruṣa, being the very nature of the Puruṣa, would be the same; thus there would be a plurality of Puruṣas. And since the same would apply to that [other Puruṣa] as well, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Consequently, it follows that the Puruṣa, being pervaded by [another] Puruṣa, would lack a stable foundation for its unity; that is, this Puruṣa would be one whose establishment in unity is unstable. Because it is the very nature of the Puruṣa, it would be like the states themselves: just as the states, being the very nature of the Puruṣa, lack a stable foundation for their unity, so too would the Puruṣa be.

Likewise, there would be one whose stability in reality (*tattva*) is unsettled. "Reality" (*tattva*) refers to its state, namely the nature of the self (*ātmasvarūpa*). One whose stability (*pratiṣṭhā*) in reality or in the [true] principle is unsettled is "one whose stability in reality is unsettled. The person (*puruṣa*) would not be established in his own nature; for, like the states (*avasthā*), the person is the self of those states. Just as the states—though they are the very establishment of the person’s own nature—are held to have their stability only in that [person], and not in their own selves, so too would the person be.
Furthermore, the Puruṣa would have to be transferable to another Puruṣa, because he is the self-nature of the Puruṣa, just like the various states.

Just as these states—such as deep sleep and so forth—are designated as "the Puruṣa alone is all this" because they are the self-nature of the Puruṣa, so too the Puruṣa, being the self-nature of the Puruṣa, would have to be transferable to another Puruṣa, [which is] not [the case]. For...
Thus,
[the opponent asserts] that the ultimate reality consists of objects such as the insentient, the manifest, the embodied, and the non-eternal, as well as the Puruṣa.

The states must necessarily be distinct from the person, because they are multiple; for it is undesirable that the person should undergo their nature, just as [the person is not identical] to its other states. Since its identity with the states is not admitted—because, by the extension of the term "person," no distinction based on subject or object can exist, and since it is impossible for anything else to arise in any way whatsoever—the states, like the attainment of distinctness itself, are each individually the person.
Let it be seen (pṛ. 201202–2):

It might be thought that, out of fear of this defect, one accepts a Person distinct from the perceptible object denoted by the word "this," and then—by attributing these very states to the Person—through the objective reference of the perceptible "this," the phrase "the Person alone is all this" is extended to the visible, the tangible, and so forth; just as in the case of "This is indeed Devadatta," where Devadatta, who is denoted by the word "this," remains the same whether he is perceived or not, so too [is it] with "the Person alone is this."

This is incorrect because, if this state of having the manifest object as its domain were to exist, it would follow that the ultimate reality of the Person (puruṣa) would consist of objects characterized by being insentient, unmanifest, material, impermanent, and so forth; by the inclusion of "and so forth," it would also follow that the ultimate reality of the Person would consist of objects characterized by being non-omnipresent, effectual, manifold, and so on; nor would there be the ultimate reality of the Person consisting of a cause that is sentient, unmanifest, immaterial, eternal, omnipresent, and unitary. Thus, this fault has been adduced as a logical consequence (*prasaṅga*). In this way, first, by not abandoning the Person's own nature, the difference in states has been described through that [manifestation], stating that the Person is manifold.
See page 189, line 26.

Now, by means of the very difference in states (*avasthānyatva*), we shall state the plurality of the *puruṣa* just as you have said—this is a statement introducing a distinction in order to refute the claim that "the *puruṣa* is indeed one despite the difference in states. The meaning is that this is an introduction for the sake of investigation by way of reminding one of that statement. As for the states, the *puruṣa* exists only when there is difference and plurality; since the nature of the self (*ātmatva*) is accepted for the *puruṣa* with respect to the states, he is therefore manifold due to their difference, or [alternatively] he is distinct from them and thus manifold.

If it is asked how that is so: by your own statement, it is necessarily established that those other states—such as wakefulness and the rest—are distinct from the Person (*puruṣa*), and that he is distinct from them; thus, a mutual distinctness is proven. The reason for this is "because of the undesirability of their assuming each other’s nature. The fact that the state and the possessor of the state do not admit of such an exchange of natures is already established. Otherwise, if one were to attempt to prove the distinctness of the specific states while treating the Person as separate [from them], the reason would suffer from the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*), or else the "undesirability of assuming each other’s nature" might be suspected of being unestablished.

Alternatively, the meaning is that both entities as conceived by the opponent—namely, "the person" and "the states"—are established in a general sense as being distinct from one another without further qualification, because it is undesirable for one to assume the nature of the other; this undesirability of assuming the nature of the other is brought about through the distinction of their respective determinations (*avadhāraṇa*).
How so? Like other states: just as the waking state is not desired when it assumes the form of the sleeping state, so too [the person] is not desired as being other than itself.

Do not think that the proof of the undesirability of the Self’s undergoing such a transformation is unestablished; therefore, he says: because the identity of this Puruṣa with these states is not admitted, since the Puruṣa is undesirable [as being] through the assumption of the form of these states, the difference and multiplicity of the Puruṣa and the states is established by way of the states. And in your own statement, this has been demonstrated: "Is the difference [of the Puruṣa] due to Prakṛti? Or is the difference due to its [the Puruṣa's] own statement? They are distinct. [Prakṛti]... [The rest of the fragment is incomplete].
But because of the extension [of the term] to the person (*puruṣātideśāt*), there is the phrase "again," and so forth.

In the statement "The Person alone is all this," since there is an extension (*atideśa*) of the state of being the Person, any otherness (*anyatva*) is simply impossible. Why? Because otherness could only occur through the door of distinctions created by one's own objects or by the objects of another; yet such otherness is not possible here. Distinction created by one's own objects refers to the difference between the form and other qualities of a jar, or between the *sattva* and other *guṇas* of primordial matter (*pradhāna*), which are merely attributes belonging to a single entity. Distinction created by the objects of another, however, refers to the difference of those very same entities from other things, such as a cloth or from the Person itself. It is through these two types of distinction that otherness might be conceived;
but that [otherness] is not admitted here, because both types of distinction are impossible.

Consequently, the non-establishment of the otherness of any entity whatsoever follows; for, by no means—that is, not in any manner such as its form (*rūpa*) or its existence (*sattva*)—is that [otherness] accepted through those [attributes]. Therefore, there is no otherness from that *puruṣa*. Now, if even the sleepless state, though characterized by the *puruṣa*, is not the *puruṣa* itself, then the *puruṣa* is likewise not the *puruṣa*, because it possesses the characteristics of the *puruṣa*, just like the sleepless state.
The same applies to the remaining states as well.

Thus, there is simply an absence of the *puruṣa*; how, then, can it possess omnipresence? Indeed, it is your own intended position that is being established by this very absence, through the refutation of what was claimed to be its essential nature—just as the non-existence of fire is established by the refutation of its heat. As for the fact that you have so laboriously asserted its lack of defining characteristics (*alakṣaṇatva*), you have, in effect, clarified its non-existence yourself. For if all these [theories] were logically tenable, then those four states, like the attainment of otherness, would each be a distinct *puruṣa*, resulting in four different types of *puruṣas*.

This too is just like what you have said; how so? That is explained as follows: just as by some manner of reasoning even a non-existent difference might be asserted, so too those states, having their difference brought about through conceptualization (*sambhāvanā*), would each be distinct.

Consequently, because they are the very self of the Puruṣa and yet differ from one another, the Puruṣas would be distinct from one another; the state of wakefulness would be a separate Puruṣa for each, and likewise the remaining states would each be a separate Puruṣa. By what manner of reasoning, then, is there this difference? Precisely from the difference in their determinations (*avadhāraṇa*).

Thus, by the extension [of the nature] of the Puruṣa, there is a multiplicity of Puruṣas, because the states such as sleeplessness and so forth are the very self-nature of the Puruṣa. [This is established] through the non-acceptance of the identity [of the Puruṣa with those states].

Now, if even the state of wakefulness, which possesses the characteristics of a person, is not the person, then the person himself is likewise not the person because he possesses the characteristics of a person, just like the state of wakefulness;
and so it is for the remaining states as well.

Thus, there is simply an absence of a person; how, then, can his omnipresence be established? Indeed, it is your own intended position that is being demonstrated by this very absence, through the refutation of that which is claimed to be his essence, just as the non-existence of fire is demonstrated by the refutation of its heat.
See page 202–1.

As for that which was stated with effort regarding the absence of defining characteristics (*alakṣaṇatva*), indeed, by what you yourself have said, the non-existence of all that is visible has been made clear; see page 202–1.
If it is said that there might also be a reading here as "anyathāpatti-prabhedā bhāvaḥ," then [it would mean] "the various divisions of the state of becoming otherwise."
Regarding the passage beginning with "atha" and so forth:

Now, even the waking state, which possesses the characteristics of a person (*puruṣa*), is not the person itself. If, having observed the faults of both individual personhood and the plurality [of such states], one does not accept that the waking state—even though it possesses the characteristics of a person—is the person, then in that case, let the person also not be the person, because it possesses the characteristics of a person, just like the waking state.

The same applies to the remaining states as well. Just as the state of wakefulness was established as being distinct from the Person (puruṣa), and for the sake of refuting that, the objection was raised that "even while possessing the characteristics of a Person, it is not the Person," and thus it was established that the wakeful state is not the Person; so too, each of the sleeping and other states should be established as the Person. Then, for the sake of refuting that, one should raise the objection that "even while possessing the characteristics of a Person, it is not the Person," and thus establish that—just like those states—the Person, whose nature is the Self, is also not the Person. Consequently, there would be an absence of the Person; in this way, the non-existence of the Person itself follows as a logical consequence.
Whence is its omnipresence? For it would be necessary to investigate whether that which exists possesses universality or non-universality, or omnipresence or non-omnipresence;
or rather, this demonstration of its absence is precisely according to your own intended view, not our own, by means of this method [of yours].

Why? Because of the refutation of that which is intended to be its very nature. Whenever a proponent refutes an object that is intended to be of a certain nature, he is seen to be refuting that very object itself; for example, one who says "fire is not hot" refutes fire itself, which is inseparable from heat and whose very essence is heat. Similarly here, having stated that the person is characterized by states such as wakefulness and so forth, you then deny those states by saying "these do not exist as distinct from the person. Thus, in refuting their identity with it, you refute the person itself. Therefore, this absence of the person is nothing other than your own intended conclusion.
Thus, for now, your intention as characterized by its manifestation has been explained;
likewise here too, is it not their very own self?

Non-existence does not follow from mere intention alone; rather, you have stated quite explicitly that "the person (puruṣa) does not exist," as in the passage beginning with "that which [is said] with effort," and so forth.

This principle is introduced in a general sense, but its specific cultivation (*bhāvanā*) must be stated—just as in the case of "the person is characterized by states" or "states are characterized by the person. Regarding those things being extended [by analogy], there would be conceptual alternatives (*vikalpa*) such as their mutual identity, difference, inexpressibility, or non-existence, provided they were subject to conceptualization (*savikalpatve*). However, these do not exist, because they are beyond the scope of imagination and because they are the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), which is free from conceptualization (*nirvikalpa*) and transcends conceptual thought. Furthermore, you yourself previously stated that they are "without characteristics" (*alakṣaṇatva*); therefore, by your very words, you have clarified and intended to establish the non-existence of everything, not merely of the *puruṣa*. We too say: how could there be the manifestation of this [person] through arising? Because it has not come into being as a distinct entity, and because it has not come into being through transformation (*pariṇāmitva*), it is like the son of a barren woman.

For we also maintain that the state of difference—the non-deviation from multiplicity and unity—is the very nature of both the states and the person who possesses those states; it is not only on the basis of your own words that the person (*puruṣa*) is non-existent. Rather, in order to support your own position, we declare that everything you desire is likewise non-existent.

Why? Because in your view, nothing exists at all. Indeed, there are two kinds of existence which I shall describe: existence as the functioning of duality through mutual dependence (*itaretarāpekṣadvaitavṛtti*), and existence as adventitious occurrence (*sannidhibhavana*) or as actualization (*āpattibhavana*).

In the absence of the state of falling into transgression (*āpatti-bhāva*), the state of proximity (*sannidhi-bhāva*) cannot exist. Let alone the state of proximity, from where could this state of falling into transgression for a person come? Why does it not exist? Because it has never existed as a distinct entity (*bhedatva*) and because it has never existed as a transformation (*pariṇāmitva*), like the son of a barren woman (*vandhyā-putra*). Just as the son of a barren woman does not exist because he has never existed either as a distinct entity or as a transformation, so too that which you desire—namely, that [the self] experiences all transgressions—is non-existent.

For what purpose is it thus qualified by way of distinction or as "being untransformed" (*abhūtatvāt*), rather than being stated as "because of non-distinction" (*abhedatvāt*) or "because of being untransformed" (*apariṇāmitvāt*)? It is said in reply: "Non-distinction" (*abheda*) might mean either that difference does not exist, or that it is something other than difference; likewise, "untransformed" (*apariṇāmī*) might mean [the same]. Alternatively, it may be a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning: "non-distinction" because it has no difference, and "untransformed" because it has no state of transformation, [and thus] "because of non-distinction" and "because of being untransformed."

To begin with, a *bahuvrīhi* compound is not possible at all, because there is no other referent (*anyapadārtha*) for another meaning to exist; therefore, there is a lack of coordination (*samanvaya*). Due to this lack of coordination, that [compound] is absent.

A *tatpuruṣa* compound is also not possible under the view of absolute negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*), because the negative particle (*nañ*) is incapable when connected with a verbal action. Therefore, it must be an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) in the sense of "other than difference. And since that is identical in meaning to a *bahuvrīhi*, it has been stated [as such] for the sake of easy comprehension and to dispel doubt, namely: "because it has not come into being as difference" and "because it has not come into being through transformation (*pariṇāma*)."

For "universality" (sarvatva) belongs to distinct entities that have attained an unerring unity, but not to that single, undivided entity you desire; he explains this as follows: "unerring," etc., up to "the state of being all.

That which possesses an unerring multiplicity is a "single [entity] with unerring multiplicity" (*avyabhicaritānekatvamekam*). Its "course" (*gati*) is its transformation (*pariṇāma*), which is its attainment of that [unity]. This attainment of unity does not occur without the manifold, just as in the case of semen, blood, and so forth—the manifold internal factors that have attained unity.
As it has been said: "The soul, having first taken as food that which is mixed from the mother’s blood and the father’s semen—a mixture that is turbid and impure—descends into the state of an embryo.
For seven days it becomes *kalala*; for seven days it becomes *abbuda*;
from *abbuda* is born the *pesī*; from *pesī* is born the *ghana*."
As stated in the *Tandulavaikṛtika* (17) and other texts,

the "universality" (*sarvatva*) of the body, the senses, and so forth arises from the unification of food and other substances that were initially distinct and transformed unequally upon their contact with semen and blood;

likewise, external universality is also observed, for the "universality" of objects such as earth, water, rice, oceans, place, and time— which are distinct and have undergone unequal transformation— is seen to result from their attainment of unity, and not otherwise.

The word *hi* has the sense of "because"; because "allness" (*sarvatva*) is thus the non-deviating single state of distinct objects—that is, that state of being all is indeed the state of difference—therefore, no undifferentiated unity can possess allness. Consequently, due to the absence of allness, it is incorrect to say, "This all is indeed the Person alone. (Nāvi-pra.)

And we too say: how could there be the existence of this [difference], since it has not come into being as a difference and has not come into being as a transformation, like the son of a barren woman?
For the state of difference is invariably characterized by both multiplicity and unity; thus, your words lead us to meaninglessness. We are the ones who speak thus.
The reading *bhedatvena* might also occur here; [it is] "becoming non-different" (*abheda-bhava*), according to the *Gatipariśuddhi*.
Then,
having first consumed that impure, foul, and putrid mixture of the mother’s blood and the father’s semen, the *jīva* enters into the state of the womb;
[it takes] the vitality (*teja*) of the mother and the [semen] of the father.

Indeed, this soul, upon the union of mother and father, having first taken as its nutriment that which is the mother’s blood and the father’s semen—both combined, turbid, and impure—enters into the state of an embryo.
For seven days it becomes a *kalala*; for seven days it becomes an *abbuya*;
from the *abbuya* arises the *pesī*; and from the *pesī* it becomes a solid mass (*ghana*).
Thus is the reading in the *Tandulavaicārika-prakīrṇaka*:

"Bhante, when a living being is entering the womb, what does it consume as its very first food? Gautama, it consumes as its very first food the mother’s blood, the father’s semen, and that which is mixed from both, which is turbid and impure."
Thus is the reading in the Bhagavatī-sūtra, 1.8.61.
For seven days it is a *kalala*, for seven days it is an *abbuda*;
from the *abbuda* the *pesī* is born, and from the *pesī* the *ghana* is born. (From the *Tandulavaikṛtika-sūtra* 17, etc.)—this statement is also [found] in the *Praśna-vyākaraṇa*.

The "universality" (*sarvatva*) of earth, water, and so forth, or of rice—[if this refers to] the "single universality" you have asserted, then there are contradictions with perception, inference, one's own words, and worldly consensus; contradictions with both the specific nature of the property (*dharma*) and the locus (*dharmin*) as accepted from a non-conceptual word-meaning; the status of reasons (*hetu*) such as being unestablished (*asiddha*); and faults of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), such as the non-establishment of the property to be proven (*sādhya*), the probans (*sādhana*), or both the property and the locus.

And just as it is with the person (*puruṣa*), so too should this be applied individually to the objects consisting of other substances: non-dual unity (*abhedaikatva*) in the place of the waking state is the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), while succession, simultaneity, and so forth, are the specific characteristics (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*), just like sleep and the rest—having explained this, what else?
Regarding "in your asserted single-allness" (*tvaduktaikasarvatāyām*) and so on:

in this "single-allness" (*ekasarvatā*), or according to the reading "all-oneness" (*sarvaikatā*), which means the state of being composed of a single person for everything, there is a contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣavirodha*), because one perceives through direct perception itself the manifoldness of distinct individuals within that single-allness.

There is a contradiction with inference because of the difference in apprehension; for when there is a difference in apprehension, a difference in the object apprehended is logically required. Alternatively, there is a contradiction with inference because, in the absence of states such as difference and transformation, there would follow the consequence of everything being one, or the non-existence of becoming. There is a contradiction with one's own words and admissions because you admit a difference between what you have said and what we have said, despite their being identical in meaning. And there is a contradiction with common worldly experience because the world perceives differences such as those between a jar and a cloth.

Regarding the passage beginning with "from the non-conceptual referent of words" (*avikalpa-śabdārthāt*): there is a contradiction with one's own tenets because, having accepted that the referent of words is non-conceptual, one nevertheless accepts conceptual linguistic usage. Furthermore, by asserting that "everything is one," one negates the intended object—both as a property (*dharma*) and as a substratum (*dharmin*), and by both its specificities—precisely through that very acceptance; thus, there is a contradiction with the nature of the property, the substratum, and both their specificities as they were originally accepted for the non-conceptual referent of words.

Furthermore, the reasons (hetus) are unestablished (*asiddha*) and so forth, because [the subject] consists of forms that are not distinct from one another—such as "that which is to be joined with the higher and lower"—due to the non-difference from the single Puruṣa asserted by you and by us, according to the logic already stated. Since there is no Puruṣa, the substratum (*dharmin*) is unestablished; thus, there is the fallacy of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*). According to your view, since there is no other object (*arthāntara*), the reason is over-exclusive (*asādhāraṇa*); according to our view, because it exists only in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), it is contradictory (*viruddha*) or else it is an inconclusive common (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*) reason. Or, if you accept a similar instance (*sapakṣa*), then due to the difference in states such as a jar, and in the absence of a difference in states such as a tree distinct from the Puruṣa—as in the example "it is a tree"—there are faults of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadoṣa*), namely the non-establishment of the property to be proven (*sādhya*), the probans (*sādhana*), both properties, or the substratum. By the inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*), one should apply the faults of the example based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) after making the appropriate conceptual constructions as the case may be.
"Sentient beings alone are non-contradictory in the world;
let this be seen," page 247, line 5.
Or is it that [the cognition] is not capable of being a jar, a tree, or the like?

The fallacious example (dṛṣṭāntābhāsa) is of two kinds: by similarity (sādharmya) and by dissimilarity (vaidharmya). Among these, the fallacious example by similarity is first of five types, namely: (1) that in which the property of the probans (sādhana-dharma) is unestablished; (2) that in which the property to be proved (sādhya-dharma) is unestablished; (3) that in which both properties are unestablished; (4) that lacking positive concomitance (ananvaya); and (5) that with inverted concomitance (viparītānvaya).

...Furthermore, there are five types of fallacious examples by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), namely: (1) that from which the probandum (*sādhya*) is not excluded, (2) that from which the probans (*sādhana*) is not excluded, (3) that from which both are not excluded, (4) the lack of negative concomitance (*avyatireka*), and (5) the inverted negative concomitance (*viparītavyatireka*);
thus it is stated in the *Nyāyapraveśa*.
Thus far it has been stated that the theory of the "person" (puruṣamayatva) as the cause of everything is untenable;

now, by means of extension (atideśa), he states those very same defects regarding the doctrines of necessity (niyati) and so forth: "And as it is with the person, so it is with the other categories of substance"—this [critique] should be applied individually to each one, namely to necessity, time, inherent nature (svabhāva), and destiny (bhāva).

He explains that method of extension (*atideśopāya*) as follows: "In the place of the state of wakefulness, there is non-dual unity. This means that the state of wakefulness is the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of the Person (*puruṣa*) in the discourse on the Person (*puruṣavāda*), because it pervades states such as sleep; and the states of sleep and so forth are its particular characteristics (*viśeṣa*), because they are of the same nature as it—just as has been explained. In the same way, one must explain non-dual unity in the case of Necessity (*niyati*) and the rest: Necessity and the others are the general characteristic, while the past, future, and present, as well as childhood, youth, old age, succession, simultaneity, and so forth, are the particular characteristics, just like sleep and the other states. Having thus explained this, the refutation of the two alternatives (*vikalpadvaya*) should be performed in exactly the same manner: "Now, are these very states Necessity and the rest? Or are Necessity and the rest themselves the states? If it were the former—that these very states are Necessity and the rest—then there would be the doctrine of aggregation (*samudayavāda*), the doctrine of momentariness (*kṣaṇikavāda*), the doctrine of consciousness-only (*vijñānamātratāvāda*), the doctrine of emptiness (*śūnyatāvāda*), and so forth.

Now, if Niyati and the others are themselves the states (avasthās), then since they are characterized by non-differentiation, unity, and statehood, that very [Prakṛti] is the manifestation (prapañca). Therefore, the principle is consistent insofar as it is said: "That which comes into being is its essence (bhāva). Because it is all-pervasive, eternal, and undivided by space and time, that which comes into being must be considered the agent itself; for the roots *as*, *bhū*, *vid*, *pad*, *vṛt*, and *asti*—the latter six being joined with *san*—all have "existence" (sattā) as their meaning, since the root *bhū* possesses the dual sense of both proximity (*sannidhi*) and coming into being (*āpatti*).

The existence [denoted by] "is" and so forth functions merely as a presence, distinct from the actualization of the action; that which is its substrate is what is designated here—[as stated in] Patañjali’s Mahābhāṣya (2.3.1): "The verb 'to be' (asti), when followed by forms of the present tense (bhavantī) in the third person, is understood even if not explicitly employed; for example, when one says 'tree,' it is understood that 'it exists.'"
Therefore, from this [point] onward, the reality (*tattva*) corresponds; however, the remainder of what you have said does not correspond at all.

If one asks, "Which part corresponds?", it is this which corresponds: "that which becomes is its state of being" (*yad ayam bhavati so 'sya bhāvaḥ*). Its state of being is its reality (*tattvam*); that by which one becomes, that which becomes—that alone is the state of being (*bhāvaḥ*). Having formed a genitive case characterized by the agent (*kartṛ-lakṣaṇām ṣaṣṭhīm*), [the phrase] "its state of being" means "that state of being. This is what corresponds with our own philosophical system.

What is the reason? Because of its omnipresence and eternity, there is no distinction [of it] by place or time; that is, because of its omnipresence and eternity, there is respectively no distinction of it from place and time. For that existence (*bhavana*) is not non-existent in any particular place, and thus it is non-distinct due to its omnipresence; it exists constantly throughout time and is never non-existent, and thus it is non-distinct due to its eternity.
Therefore, because of this non-distinction, this [property] is accepted even in cases such as "it is" (*asti*), and so forth.
In this context, there may also be the reading *abhedaikatvam*; compare pp. 246, l. 3–pp. 247, l.
4 [of the work on] Śūnyavāda.
Therefore, first of all, this principle is consistent: that which "comes to be" (bhavati) is its "being" (bhāva), because [the latter] is omnipresent, eternal, and undifferentiated by space and time;

however, it must be considered that "he who comes to be" is indeed the agent (*kartṛ*), since the root *bhū* has two meanings—proximity and coming-into-being—and because the group of six verbs consisting of *as*, *bhū*, *vid*, *pad*, *vṛt*, and *asti* all have "existence" (*sattā*) as their primary meaning.

The existence [denoted by] "is" and so forth is a mere presence that functions as something distinct from the actualization of the action; this is what is called the "substratum" (upādāna). As stated in the *Pāṇinīya-Mahābhāṣya* (2.3.1): "The verb 'to be' (*asti*), when followed by a form of the present tense (*bhavantī*) in the third person (*prathamapuruṣa*), is understood even if it is not explicitly employed; for example, when one says 'tree,' it is understood as 'the tree exists.'"
See page 34, line 20:
"The verb *as* (to be), when followed by a form of *bhū*, is understood even when not explicitly employed in the third person;
for example, from 'the tree is a *plakṣa*,' it is understood that 'it exists.'"
Thus is the reading in the Patañjala-Mahābhāṣya; however, in some places it does not occur in the *pramāṇa* [section], hence *pra*.

Furthermore, we do not yet accept this [definition], because it requires further deliberation; rather, that which "comes into being" (*bhavati*) must be deliberated upon as the agent itself. For agency does not follow merely from hearing the word *bhavati*, which ends in the suffix *tip* prescribed for the agent. This is because even non-agents such as space (*ākāśa*) "come into being," since "coming into being" (*bhavana*) signifies existence merely as the exclusion of non-existence. Moreover, the root *kṛ* (to do/make) is a synonym for cause; thus, even an effect that lacks a cause "comes into being," because the root *bhū* has two meanings: proximity (*sannidhi*) and attainment (*āpatti*). Furthermore, since the group of six verbs—*asti*, *bhavati*, *vidyati*, *padyati*, *vartati*, and *sannipāta*—have existence as their common meaning, the author states here the cause for the coming into being of even that which is dependent and inactive.

The root *bhū* has the sense of "becoming through proximity" (*sannidhi-bhavana*), while the roots *as*, *vid*, and *sad* have the sense of "becoming as mere presence" (*sannidhi-mātra-bhavana*), and the roots *pad* and *vṛt* have the sense of "becoming through attainment" (*āpatti-bhavana*). This distinction arises because the three [latter] possess activity (*savyāpāra*) while *bhū* is devoid of activity (*nirvyāpāra*), and because *bhū* denotes general becoming (*sāmānya-bhavana*). Furthermore, there is a distinction based on being unchanging (*apariṇāmin*) versus changing (*pariṇāmin*), and being a non-agent (*akartṛ*) versus an agent (*kartṛ*).

Since there is no becoming (*bhavana*) of that which is non-existent, the becoming of "being" (*asti-bhavana*) exists only as a function of mere presence (*sannidhi-mātra-vṛtti*). That which has mere presence as its function is "functioning as mere presence"; this becoming-as-being is distinct from the becoming-of-attainment (*āpatti-bhavana*), meaning it is other than that, slightly different, and inactive—this might be the thought. [But] this independent becoming is contradicted by grammar, the established doctrine of all systems (*sarvatantra-siddhānta*), because the root *bhū* ends in the suffix *tip*, which designates an agent.

And this is incorrect, because it has already been admitted in that very [context] where it was stated, "that which is grasped is called *upādāna*," and so forth. However, this was stated by taking up the mere existence (*bhavana*) that functions through proximity; for even where another verb is not heard, there the verb *as* (to be) with the present tense suffix is understood, even if it is not explicitly used in the first person.

The term "present" (*bhavantī*) refers to the current tense, which is designated as *laṭ* by the ancient teachers. The verb *as* follows that [suffix]; *as* is the verbal root according to Pāṇini’s Dhātupāṭha 1065 (*as bhuvi*). The rule *ikśtipau dhātunirdeśe* (Pāṇini Vārttika 3.3.108) indicates that the suffix *ik* is used here to denote the verbal root.

In the first person, neither the middle nor the highest [persons] are used; yet, even when not explicitly employed, they are understood because the meaning exists through an inseparable connection with the object.
He illustrates this: in the word "tree" (*vṛkṣa*), it is understood that "it exists. What is meant? The sense is that it "exists," "is," or "is present.
Since the state of being present is indicated for both [the subject and the verb], it is placed at the beginning because they share the same grammatical characteristic.
Even for that which is not excluded [from the class],
let it be seen [in the commentary on] page 233; the reading "because both possess activity" (*dvayoḥ savyāpāratvāt*) is also possible here.
Because of being non-agent (*akartṛtva*) and because of the absence of agency (*akartṛtva*), there is a distinction; [the text] is not excluded from the middle. (Bhāṣya, Raṃga, Hīna, Pra.)

Thus, the state of attaining [the effect] is indeed the state of its existence, because the effect exists within the cause as something present and functioning in that manner; for example, "the jar comes into being," "is produced," or "is attained.
And this is established as a presence within the duality of the enjoyer and the enjoyed, since there is no deviation [from this principle] whether there be deficiency or excess.

There is no state of being a knower in the absence of an object of knowledge, because of the non-existence of the object of knowledge, like the cognition of a sky-flower; by way of dissimilarity, it is like the cognition of other flowers.
Thus, the state of being a knower belongs to the knower, but [the knower] does not depend upon...

But "the becoming of occurrence" (*āpatti-bhavana*), "the becoming of existence" (*asti-bhavana*), and so forth, up to "that which occurs"—this too is merely a slightly different way of describing the "becoming of presence" (*sannidhi-bhavana*) as it functions in that manner; for the "becoming of occurrence" is simply the functioning of that which is present in such a way.

Alternatively, "tathāvṛtti" means having such a mode of existence (*vṛtti*); and that which is both present (*sannihita*) and possesses such a mode of existence is "present-tathāvṛtti. What is that? It is the becoming of the effect (*āpattibhavana*). Why is it said to exist as such precisely when it is present? It is said: because the effect exists within the cause. For an effect, such as a sprout and so forth, exists already present within the seed and so forth, and thus manifests or remains unmanifested in various ways according to the influence of place, time, form, and causal conditions.

He demonstrates this: "Just as 'the jar comes into being' (ghaṭo bhavati). The meaning is that the coming-into-being of the jar, which was previously perceived in the clay as non-jar-ness, is now clearly manifest in the very clay that is present. This is a statement of its synonyms: "it is accomplished" (nirvartate) means "it undergoes attainment" (āpadyate). It is said that the very process of being present becomes an attainment; thus, the "coming-into-being through attainment" has been explained.
The reading *vṛttiḥ ā* might also occur here. The establishment of these two [the subject and object] in a form that is neither deficient nor excessive is stated as follows: "And that," etc.

Because it is a generality (*sāmānyatvāt*), there is first the establishment of their presence (*sannidhibhavana*). That is to say, it is the establishment of presence within the state of duality consisting of the enjoyer and the enjoyed; this is the establishment of presence. For that presence is established when there is duality, not when there is non-duality, because of the faults already shown such as the impossibility of a single enjoyer and enjoyed. Nor is there establishment in deficiency or excess relative to duality, because a third possibility does not exist.

He states the reason for the impossibility of deficiency or excess: "because of the absence of distinction" (*vyatirekābhāvāt*). Distinction (*vyatireka*) is the occurrence of one thing as separate from another; even in the absence of such separation, existence persists.

Therefore, in the case of deficiency, there is no proof [of its existence], because it would lack that [separate] existence—just as a servant cannot exist without a master, nor a master without a servant.

Furthermore, even in the case of excess, there is no distinction, just as there is nothing distinct from existence itself. Thus, in this case, because there is an absence of distinction between the enjoyer and the enjoyed, [neither deficiency nor excess is possible].
Therefore, because there is an absence of deficiency or excess, the manifestation of proximity is established in that duality, but not in non-duality, triad-ness, and so forth;
for in these [latter cases], there is no deficiency or excess among the enjoyers and the rest.
Because of the state of being [a] statement;
[the reading] *pṛthaktvena ekasya eva* is superior in the manuscripts *Pā*, *Ḍe*, *Lī*, *Raṃ*, *Hī*, and *Ya*.

Regarding the phrase "in the duality of the *vāt*," there may also be a reading of "in the duality of the *vāt*. To establish that point, the following reasoning is stated: There is no state of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*) without an object of knowledge (*jñeya*). Since that which is to be enjoyed is an object of knowledge, and since the perception of the two—the qualities such as sound and the like, and the Puruṣa—is for the sake of the Puruṣa’s experience, that [perception] constitutes the manifestation of the object of knowledge. Without that, there is no state of being a knower for the knower.

Why? If it is argued that the reason is unestablished because the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) does not exist—due to the lack of co-referentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) in the statement "because of the non-existence of the object of knowledge" since [non-existence] is a property of the object of knowledge rather than the knower (*jña*)—we say no. This is because the two things to be proven—the knower and the object of knowledge—are related as correlates; therefore, their non-existence is indeed a property [of that relation]. Alternatively, at the time of the formal argument, the meaning is explained as follows: "Knower-ship is untenable because the object of knowledge is non-existent," and that [untenability] is due to the object of knowledge being non-existent, i.e., because its status as an object of knowledge has not been apprehended.

The illustration is like the knowledge of a sky-flower: just as the state of being a knower with respect to a sky-flower is untenable because the object of knowledge is non-existent, so too is the state of being a knower [with respect to] a non-existent object of knowledge.

By way of contrast (*vaidharmyeṇa*), it is like the knowledge of flowers other than [certain specific ones]. Just as the knowledge of flowers other than the "sky-flowers" (non-existent things) such as mango blossoms is possible because they are real objects of knowledge (*sajjñeyatvāt*), so too the knowledge of non-duality (*advaitajñatva*) as you intend it would only be possible if duality existed. However, since this [alleged non-duality] lacks any distinction between knower and known, it is included within that [very duality]; thus, its status as an object of knowledge (*jñeyatva*) cannot exist without a seer, because the knower is non-existent—just as the "pot-ness" of a pot known by the son of a barren woman is impossible, whereas by way of contrast, the "pot-ness" of a pot known by another's son is possible. For in this very way does the knowability of an object of knowledge arise.

There can be no state of being an enjoyer (bhoktṛtva) without an object of enjoyment (bhogya), because the enjoyer would be non-existent, like a bee for the nectar of a sky-flower; by way of contrast, it is like a bee for the nectar of an actual flower. Likewise, there can be no object of enjoyment without an enjoyer, because the enjoyer would be non-existent, like a young man raised by the son of a barren woman; by way of contrast, it is like a young man raised by an actual son.
In this very way, the state of being an object of enjoyment (*bhogya*) belongs to that which is enjoyed because of its relation to the enjoyer;
furthermore, even that existence (*sattva*) which consists in the various modes of abiding or becoming within form and so forth does not arise from a single, unchanging cause.

Alternatively, there is a separate proof: the status of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*) is established because of the knowability of existing objects (*sad-jñeyatva*), just as one possesses the knowledge of other flowers [only by virtue of their existence].
By way of dissimilarity, [the opponent's position] is untenable because it is non-existent, like the cognition of a sky-flower;
for such is the knower's status as a knower: he who knows an existent object of knowledge is a primary knower, just as one who knows water is water;
whereas he who cognizes a non-existent object of knowledge is not a knower, just as one who perceives a mirage as water.

Thus, the view that "only the knower exists, not the object of knowledge"—which is non-dualism (advaita)—has been refuted. Now, the view that "only the object of knowledge exists, not the knower" is being refuted with the words beginning "not the knower" (*na jñātāram*). He shows a synonym for that [knower] by saying "the witness" (*upadraṣṭāram*). Without a knower, there can be no state of being an object of knowledge, because the knower would be non-existent. Here too, as before, the reason is either "because the knower is non-existent" or the logical reason based on similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) is "the state of being a pot known by the son of a barren woman," while the logical reason based on difference (*vaidharmya*) is "the state of being a pot known by another's son."

Alternatively, as before, there are two proofs by way of contrapositive; or else, the reason should be stated so as to avoid the fallacy of non-co-referentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) by establishing that the knower and the known are mutually dependent.

For in this very way the knowability of an object is possible: if it is known by some cognition whose sense faculties are unimpaired, just like a jar known by a person whose intellect and sense faculties are unimpaired; or just like the proof is known by a neutral, wise cognizer who is skilled in reasoning and scripture.

Likewise, there can be no state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*) without an object of enjoyment (*bhogya*), because of the non-existence of an object of enjoyment, like a bee [seeking] nectar from a sky-flower; or, by way of contrast (*vaidharmya*), there is the state of being an enjoyer because of the existence of an object of enjoyment, like a bee [seeking] nectar from an actual flower. Or, by way of similarity (*sādharmya*), [there is the state of being an enjoyer] like a bee [seeking] a sky-flower. Alternatively, as before, the proof of the states of enjoyer and object of enjoyment is mutually dependent.
In this case as well, the text should be understood as: "In this very way, the state of being an enjoyer belongs to the enjoyer."

Likewise, there can be no object of enjoyment (*bhogya*) without an enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*), because [otherwise] it would lack the state of being enjoyed, like the "youthful growth" of the son of a barren woman; conversely, that which has an existing enjoyer possesses the state of being an object of enjoyment, like the "youthful growth" of another's son. The explanation here is exactly as before: the very nature of an object of enjoyment is such that it exists simultaneously with, or in mutual connection to, the enjoyer, because they possess a relationship of mutual dependence. This is the reason for demonstrating the meaning; however, the reason for the formal argument (*prayoga*) is simply "because of their relationship."

Just as a relative, such as a brother, does not exist without another relative—neither the younger without the elder nor the elder without the younger—so too are the enjoyer and the enjoyed. Through such examples as a couple adorned with ornaments, it is established that the relationship between the enjoyer and the enjoyed is characterized by mutual inseparability; thus, as previously stated, the state of "being in proximity" (sannidhibhavana) is only possible when duality exists.
This is what is to be known. (jñeya-bhā° ta°; jñeya-ya° ya°)
Because of its nature, it is not an object of knowledge; because of its nature, that is the object of knowledge,
as it is undifferentiated.
...due to the application of [the suffix] -tva, etc.; *pra* (prefix);
that which is intended by it (*tad-abhimata*);
*pra*; ...would follow; *raṃ*; *hī*.

In this regard, its status as an object of knowledge (*jñeyatva*) cannot exist without a knower (*draṣṭṛ*), because of the non-existence of a knower; it is like the pot-ness of a pot known by the son of a barren woman. By way of contrast (*vaidharmyeṇa*), it is like the pot-ness of a pot known by another's son.
For such indeed is the knowability of an object of knowledge.

There can be no state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*) without an object of enjoyment (*bhogya*), because the enjoyer would be non-existent, like a bee for the nectar of a sky-flower; by way of contrast, it is like a bee for the nectar of an actual flower. Likewise, there can be no object of enjoyment without an enjoyer, because the enjoyer would be non-existent, like a youthfulness-increased son of a barren woman; by way of contrast, it is like a youthfulness-increased son of another woman.

In this very way, the state of being an object of enjoyment belongs to that which is enjoyed because of its connection to it; furthermore, even that existence or becoming in various ways within form and so forth does not arise from each individual [cause] alone, nor from that which is unchanging, just as in the case of a sprout, according to the Bhāṣya.
Like a flower;
the state of being a knower of the knower;
the son of Bhāma. Ya.

Now, as for the other [case]: that which is the existence, becoming, or manifestation in such and such a manner within form and so forth—in various ways and in diverse manners—consisting of the occurrence and transformation of the entire world within form, taste, smell, touch, earth and the rest, cows and the like, and jars and the like; even that does not arise from each individual thing. For "each one" refers to a single entity such as a person or the like; it does not arise from each of those individuals.
What then? It arises from that which is both manifold and one—from a single manifold [cause] through mere proximity, because it is an occurrence, just like rice.
Nor is it the case that there is no purposelessness in non-duality;
rather, because they are composite in nature, like a house, a jar, or the earth, they exist for the sake of another.
Thus, the internal organs such as the eye and so forth are for the sake of another, as are all things from the eye onwards up to the dyads of form and the rest.

And this [cause] must be of the nature of differentiation because it is a cause, like threads and so forth; and it must exist for the sake of another because its purpose is the perception of sound and other objects—for what cause has ever been seen that is both unitary and for its own sake? Or, [it might be argued that it exists] as something unchanging merely by virtue of its proximity; [the answer is] "no," [this] being understood from the context.
What then? It arises precisely from that which is subject to transformation (*pariṇāmin*) and capable of becoming the state of occurrence;

why? Because it is an occurrence, because it is the process of becoming an occurrence, like rice. Just as for each individual grain of rice there is the occurrence of the sprout and so forth from the aggregate of atoms, dyads, and so on—consisting of form, taste, and other qualities—or as there is the occurrence of rice from the aggregate of earth, water, place, time, and so forth belonging to the sprout and so forth, so too this single entity, which consists of many factors, undergoes the process of becoming an occurrence.

Nor does it occur in non-duality (*advaita*). Thus, while there may be the occurrence of an undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) when there is duality within one's own domain, this [consequence] is said to occur only when there is duality in the domain of another—[but] even in non-duality, where there is an absence of duality in the domain of another, there is no occurrence of an undesirable consequence; for precisely because there is no occurrence of an undesirable consequence that is purposeless, there is nothing to be done for the sake of any purpose by that single, non-dual entity.

However, the connection is that because they consist of composite aggregates (*saṅghāta*), they exist for the sake of another (*pārārthya*). Their being-for-the-sake-of-another arises from their nature as composites; for those things that act through combination exist for the sake of another, not without purpose, nor for their own sake, nor for each other’s sake. The sole illustration is like a house, a jar, the earth, and so forth. Just as a house, a jar, the earth, and the like—which are composite in nature—exist for the sake of the Puruṣa who is distinct from themselves, and are neither purposeless, nor for their own sake, nor for each other’s sake, yet are for each other’s sake only for the sake of the Puruṣa, like ornaments intended for the beauty of a woman.

Likewise, by means of the abundance of examples—such as the internal [elements] like the eye—he demonstrates their pervasiveness for the sake of another (*parārtha*). Thus, from the phrase "of the eye and so forth," even the subtle internal [elements] such as the eye must be analyzed as being for the sake of another, as must [the objects] such as the dyads of form (*rūpa-dvyaṇuka*) and so on; how much more so, then, [the case of] gross things such as houses, jars, and the earth, or villages, gardens, and the like? Furthermore, if... [text fragment].
There is no contradiction [in our position], because [the world] exists merely by way of proximity; for it is a manifestation, like rice.
Nor is there non-duality, because there is no occurrence of what is purposeless.
However, because they consist of composite aggregates, like a house, a jar, or the earth, they must exist for the sake of another;
likewise, the internal sense organs such as the eye and so forth also exist for the sake of another. This applies from the eye onwards, up to the dyads of form and other elements.

Furthermore, this [composite] must be of a divisible nature because it possesses causality, like threads and the like; and it exists for the sake of another in the sense that its purpose is the perception of sound and other objects.
For what reason is it that form and so forth, when perceived as a single [entity], are for their own sake?
[It is] because of the aggregate of the eye and so forth. (Note: This phrase is absent from the Bhāṣya manuscript.)
Furthermore, as for that which is desired as a single internal, subtle cause, such as the *puruṣa* and so forth— that we do not accept.

Even according to your own view, if some single entity is accepted as the cause of being for another, we maintain that it must necessarily consist of a plurality of parts; because it is a cause, like threads and so forth. For threads, potsherds, and the like, by virtue of being causes, are seen to assume the state of causality while consisting of a plurality of parts—such as the collection of color-forms (*rūpa*) and so on, or atoms (*tuṭi*) and so on—with respect to their effects, such as cloth or jars. It is not otherwise. Therefore, that cause which you desire must likewise consist of a plurality of parts.

And it follows that [the cause] must exist for the sake of another; "for another" (*parasmai*) means *parārtha*. That cause which has a purpose or effect for another—that cause, having the effect of serving another's purpose, must exist because it is a cause, just like threads and so forth. For example, just as threads have the effect of being a cloth for the purpose of Devadatta’s protection from cold and the like, so too must that cause intended by you exist.
