If it is asked, "What is that object? it is said: Because its purpose is the apprehension of sound and so forth—the word "and so forth" (ādi) being used because the apprehension of sound and so forth is the beginning and the apprehension of the distinction between the *guṇas* and the *puruṣa* is the end—these two ends of experience constitute the object of the *puruṣa*. That [apprehension] is the purpose for which this manifestation of the world exists; therefore, because its purpose is the apprehension of sound and so forth, it must exist by virtue of that purpose which serves another.

"What indeed is the reason that form (*rūpa*) and so forth are perceived as manifold, [yet] singular and for their own sake? By this, he demonstrates the inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) between the cause and its multiplicity, its singularity, and its being for the sake of another (*pārārthya*), as well as the absence of being for one's own sake (*svārthaikya*). The intention is that there is no such thing as a counter-example (*vipakṣa*).

The mention of "form and so forth" (*rūpādi*), however, because they constitute the subject of the proposition (*pakṣa*), shows their distinction from mere proximity and existence through their being composite, being for the sake of another, and being subject to transformation (*pariṇāmitva*).
[The suffix -ti is derived from] *uṇ* etc., by the rule *nāmyupāntya* (Uṇādi Sūtra 609); *kidi* means the suffix *-tuṭ*.

Thus, in the case of dualism, since primordial nature (*prakṛti*) consists of multiple constituents, the objects such as sound and so forth—which are produced by the selves through the successive transformations of pleasure, pain, and delusion—are themselves of that same nature; for they are effects whose nature is manifested by that [primordial nature], just as the shards and other products of a lump of clay possess the nature of clay.

Furthermore, for those [objects] such as sound that consist of pleasure (*sukha*), their effects are clarity, lightness, buoyancy, productivity, attachment, exhilaration, and joy; for those consisting of pain (*duḥkha*), they are desiccation, burning, piercing, obstruction, agitation, and aversion; and for those consisting of delusion (*moha*), they are covering, depression, destruction, loathsomeness, dejection, and heaviness. Therefore, the effect manifested as the nature of pleasure and so forth belongs to these [objects] such as sound.
Let it be observed that the internal bodies and other things composed of these [elements] are seen [to possess these qualities]. (Page 12, Line 19)
Thus, with the passage beginning "In this way, in the case of duality...

and continuing with "for the sake of the enjoyment of the two kinds of puruṣas, [it arises] from prakṛti, which consists of many natures," there is a description of the nature of the process by which that [transformation] occurs.

It is called *prakṛti* because modifications (*vikāra*) are produced from it; it is called *pradhāna* because the Great Principle (*mahat*) and the others are deposited within it; it is called *bahudhānaka* because it contains many things; and it is called *amṛta* because it is immortal and indestructible. Of this *prakṛti*, which possesses these etymological names and consists of multiple natures, there is a manifestation through its own selves—pleasure, pain, and delusion—which consist of illumination, activity, and restraint. As previously stated by the Teacher, like wind and stone, it acts as a dancer for both itself and others, and like the perception, movement, and support of a boat, a leaf, and a stone respectively.

For those qualities (*guṇas*)—characterized by *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion, and having the nature of illumination, activity, and restraint—are called "Prakṛti" when they are in a state of equilibrium. However, when they fall into a state of disequilibrium and undergo a sequence of transformations, functioning inseparably from one another through the relationship of primary and secondary factors (*aṅga-aṅgibhāva*), they transform and give rise to sound and the other objects. Sound and the rest, being produced by that sequence of transformations beginning with the Great Principle (*mahat*), are themselves of that same nature. He will explain the sequence of transformations of sound and the rest himself through the application of proofs; for now, their being of that nature is established. Sound and the rest are indeed of the nature of pleasure and so forth, because they are effects manifested as being of that nature. "That-nature" (*tadātmā*) means pleasure and the rest are the self (*ātman*) [of them]; the state of being that is "being of that nature" (*tadātmakatva*), which is the state of being of the nature of pleasure and so forth. Those whose effects are manifested as being of that nature are "those whose effects are manifested as being of that nature," namely sound and the rest. This is because of that state: because they are effects manifested as being of that nature. It is like the clay-ness of a lump of clay, a small pot-sherd (*śivaka*), and so on. Whatever object has an effect manifested as being of a certain nature is seen to be of that very nature; for example, the lump is the effect of clay, its effect is the pot-sherd, and thus in sequence the pedestal, the jar, and so on, up to the pot or the shards—all these effects are of the nature of clay. Since there is no subsequent effect without the nature of the original cause, the state of being clay is seen at the beginning, in the middle, and at the end. In the same way, sound and the rest are the effects of pleasure and so forth, while the effects of sound and the rest are ether (*ākāśa*) and so on, and their effects are cows, pots, and so forth. All of these must be understood as being of that nature, manifested as being of the nature of pleasure and so forth.

If it is asked how sound and the other objects are manifested as effects consisting of pleasure and so forth, [the author] demonstrates this with the passage beginning, "Because of the perception of pleasure, and because they consist of pleasure," and so on, up to the point that "the effect of these sounds and so forth is manifested as having the nature of the self (*ātman*). Thus, it has already been explained that sound and the others are composed of the *ahaṅkāra* of the element-class (*bhūtādi*).
See page 13, line 20; here, the reading might also be *dhāraṇakāraṇaiḥ*.
From the *vaikṛta* ego (*ahaṅkāra*), the elevenfold group of *sāttvika* [faculties] proceeds.
From the *bhūtādi* arises the subtle element (*tanmātra*), which is *tāmasa*; from the *taijasa*, both [the subtle element and the sense organ] arise.
(Sāṅkhyakārikā 25)

And everything consists of pleasure (*sukha*), pain (*duḥkha*), and delusion (*moha*), because they are initiated by those [qualities], and so on, up to the point that they are composed of pleasure and the rest. By means of the sequence of transformation, he demonstrates that the elements, beginning with space (*ākāśa*), are initiated by sound and the other qualities which consist of pleasure and the rest. In that context, "corporeal and so forth" refers to internal things; the bodies are composed of the elements, while the sense organs—beginning with *bhūta* and *vaikārika*—are initiated by sound and the rest. These are specific arrangements of the three—pleasure, pain, and delusion—and thus consist of pleasure and the rest. Likewise, earth and the other elements consist of these, because they are initiated by causes composed of them.
Whatever is composed of certain causes is itself composed of those causes, like a cotton cloth.
Furthermore, bodies and the like are composed of the elements, yet they are like tents woven from cloth because they are produced through a succession [of parts];

thus, the body is preceded by multiple constituents because it possesses modifications that persist [through change], like a piece of sandalwood. It is not preceded by a single constituent, nor is it without a prior cause, because its parts are interconnected.

And he recites: "The one unborn female, red, white, and black, producing many offspring of similar form—the one unborn male lies beside her, delighting in her; another unborn male abandons her after she has been enjoyed. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.5)

The elements and so forth, as well as the eleven organs beginning with the ear—which consist of the elements, are composed of the three *guṇas*, and are originated from the *vaikārika* [sattva]—are all indeed specific arrangements of the three: pleasure, pain, and delusion.

Consequently, external objects such as jars and the like are "composed of those" (*tanmaya*), because they are aggregates of form and other qualities, and because those qualities are essentially pleasure and so forth;

likewise, earth and the other elements are "composed of those" because they are originated by causes that are themselves composed of those [qualities]. Thus, since the entire range of transformations—from *mahat* onwards, and the entire world from Brahmā down to a blade of grass—is originated by causes consisting of pleasure and the rest, it is composed of them.
"That which consists of this" is the application (*upanaya*); "therefore, it consists of that" is the conclusion (*nigamana*).

The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is "like a cotton cloth. Just as a cloth, though begun by threads which are modifications of cotton, is called "cotton," so too the elements (*bhūta*), being begun by pleasure and so forth, and begun by sound and so forth, consist of the nature of pleasure and so forth.

Furthermore, bodies and the like—where the phrase "and the like" includes jars and so forth—are composed of the primary elements (*bhūta*). Because they are produced through a succession [of causes], just as a hut made of cloth is called "made of cotton" because it is produced from cloth which itself was produced from cotton threads; likewise, the earth and other elements, cows and other animals, jars and the like, rivers, oceans, Mount Mandara, and so forth, are also of that same nature, being produced by pleasure and the like, produced by sound and the like, and produced by the primary elements and so on.

The elements and the sense organs, which are produced from the *vaikārika* [sattva], are specific configurations of the three—pleasure, pain, and delusion—and are thus composed of pleasure and the rest. Likewise, earth and the other elements are composed of those [qualities] because they are produced from causes consisting of them;
for whatever is produced from causes composed of certain things is itself composed of those things, just like a cotton cloth.
Furthermore, bodies and so forth, which are produced by the elements, are composed of those [qualities] because they are produced through a succession [of causes], like a tent made of cloth.

The body is preceded by that which is manifold and unitary, because it possesses both persistence and transformation, like a piece of sandalwood; it is not preceded by the unitary nor is it without a prior cause, because it is characterized by persistence.
And the scripture declares:
"The one unborn female, red, white, and black, producing many offspring of similar form."
"For one unborn, indeed, remains attached while enjoying [her]; another unborn leaves her once her enjoyment has been experienced. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.5;
see page 257–265, note 4, Brahmāstava-prakaraṇa).

Regarding the proposition that "the body is preceded by a single entity consisting of multiple constituents," what is the reason for formulating this proposition in such a manner? It is for the purpose of refuting the previously mentioned view that it is preceded by a single cause such as the *puruṣa*, and for the purpose of refuting the views that will be discussed later which hold it to be preceded by causes such as *Īśvara*.

What is the reason? Because it possesses modifications that are concomitant (*anvitavikāratvāt*). That which has concomitant modifications is "possessing concomitant modifications. Modifications such as the contraction and expansion of the hands, the raising and lowering of the fingers, the stepping forward of the feet, and the turning of the limbs, as well as the body-parts themselves, are concomitant with pleasure and so forth, and with sound and so forth. Therefore, because it possesses concomitant modifications, like a piece of sandalwood (*candanaśakalavat*). Just as pieces of sandalwood—which possess various modifications such as softness, fragrance, coldness, green, red, white, and so forth, as well as touch, taste, color, and smell—are concomitant with pleasure and the like, and are preceded by a single sandalwood tree composed of many parts such as atoms (*paramāṇu*) and dyads (*dvyaṇuka*); likewise, this body too is preceded by a single cause composed of many elements such as pleasure, and is not preceded by each [part] individually, as in the case of the person (*puruṣa*) alone, and so forth; nor is it without a prior cause, nor causeless, nor preceded by non-existence, as is maintained by the Nihilists (*vaināśika*) and others. This is for the purpose of specifying the objects to be excluded from this proof. Or, the phrase "because it possesses [concomitants]" (*anvitatvāt*) may serve as the conclusion (*nigamana*) for what was stated generally above. Alternatively, it may be a separate proof for the refutation of the theory that [the body] is preceded by each [part] individually, and so forth.

"He recites [the mantra]," as before;

"unborn" (*ajā*) means she is not born (*na jāyate*), thus she is eternal. Alternatively, according to Pāṇini’s Dhātupāṭha (2.30), the root *aja* signifies "to move" or "to cast"; thus, because she moves swiftly, she is the "unborn" (*ajā*). This *prakṛti* is called the "unborn" (*ajā*) because of her similarity to swift transformation and movement, or because of her similarity to prolific birth;
she is one, without a second, and all-pervading.

Lest it be [produced] one by one, there arise many infinite progenies—each consisting of multiple natures, composed of red, white, and black, and made of *rajas*, *sattva*, and *tamas* (the qualities of passion, purity, and darkness). They are called "progenies" (*prajā*) because they are born forth. By means of this [Prakṛti], one experiences pleasure, pain, and latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) in turn;
therein, those three who are distinct enter various wombs, while the Unborn (*aja*), however, is pure and possesses the wisdom that transcends birth.

Two birds, companions, inseparable and with beautiful wings, nestle upon the same tree; of these two, one eats the sweet fruit of the fig, while the other looks on without eating. (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.1)

1.1 Gradually creating—that is, producing—all beings from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, she is of the same nature as them, consisting of pleasure and so forth, and identical in form to the Self; for she is reckoned as the Unborn (Ajā), the Primal Nature (Pradhānī), who brings forth offspring in many forms that are identical in essence to her own self.

The unborn (aja) indeed, being alone—meaning enjoying, serving, and taking pleasure in her—is called "unborn" because he is eternal; he is "one" because his presence is undivided, uniform, and all-pervading. Enjoying her alone, he lies down with her (anuśete); that is to say, he does not release her bond or attachment and pursues her, just as a calf pursues its mother goat; in this same way, the Puruṣa [pursues] that Prakṛti.

Another unborn one abandons her once her enjoyments have been experienced; that very person becomes "other" to her, having ceased [from union] because he has experienced the objects of perception, has known the distinction between the Self and the non-Self, and recognizes the difference between Nature (prakṛti) and Spirit (puruṣa). Like a spectator observing the external movements of a dancer—such as the casting of eyebrows, the sequence of steps, and the turning of limbs—he perceives these modifications as causes of latent attachment, arising from the internal organ, the body, and so forth, yet as being non-self. Like a mendicant, through the contemplation of his own true nature, he becomes dispassionate, thinking: "I have been vainly afflicted by this one, who is pure neither externally nor internally. Thus he desists. She too, having displayed her modifications and thinking, "I have been seen by him," withdraws as if out of shame.
In the same way, the second verse, which is connected to this meaning, has already been explained: "He experiences pleasure, pain, and latent tendency by turns;
there, those three who are distinct enter the womb, while the Unborn, being pure and possessing intelligence, does not."

"Both both": from the substitution of *ḍa* for the case endings, "both" refers to two friends who are joined together with one another; by virtue of their pervasiveness (*vibhutva*) and eternity (*nityatva*), they are "united" (*sayujā*), and as before, from the substitution of *ḍa*, they are "equally united" (*samānayujau*), due to the substitution of *sa* for *samāna*.

"Along with two leaves" means having two leaves, or having two wings; "the pure and impure sides," or alternatively, the reading is "suyujau suparṇau," meaning well-yoked or exceedingly joined, being always joined without division due to their omnipresence, and possessing beautiful wings—that is, wings consisting of the various colors of pleasure and pain produced by the attainment of mutual union. They have embraced a single tree, the world-renowned *aśvattha*; it is called a "tree" (*vṛkṣa*) because of its rootedness and immovability, sharing the characteristics of an *aśvattha* tree. They have embraced it, having become entwined around it.

Of those two birds embracing a single tree, only one bird is capable of enjoyment; he eats, consumes, and partakes of the *pippala*—the fruit of the *pippala* tree—which is sweet, a specific modification of an object of enjoyment, and possesses manifold flavors. Only the *Puruṣa*, by virtue of being the enjoyer and the knower, [does this]. The other, known as *Prakṛti*, does not eat; remaining unenjoying, it shines intensely toward that [fruit]. Because the subject introduced is a bird, the masculine gender is used: "it shines" (*abhicākaśīti*). It is the active *prakṛti*.
Having a nature characterized by the single essence of existence,
he experiences pleasure, pain, and latent tendencies in turn, here and there.

Because even a fragment of pleasure is pervaded by that [suffering], as long as this mark [of conditioned existence] does not cease, there must necessarily be suffering; for due to the power of the formative forces (*saṃskāra*), one is reborn in another world in turn.
Thus he says: "For pleasure, pain, and doubt, he experiences in turn here and there.

Now, why is space (*viyat*) accepted as having the single quality of sound immediately after the refutation of a single cause? It would not function at all in this way, because it is non-concrete (*asandruta*), like the *puruṣa* or like the son of a barren woman.

If you maintain that a single cause can possess multiple natures, then why—immediately after refuting the doctrine of a single cause, and without even waiting for the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by that refutation to fade—do you assert that space (*viyat*) arises with sound as its sole quality? Granted, in the case of the creation of form and so forth, since these qualities observed in the world—such as touch, taste, smell, and others—are seen to follow worldly usage and consist of two, three, or more components, let there indeed be a creation of air and the other elements consisting of such [multiple] natures; this is consistent with your own view. However, it is not tenable for space to arise with sound as its sole quality. And the formal argument (*prayoga*) here is as follows: it would not function in this way; that is to say, it would not be space characterized by the single quality of sound, because of its non-concretion (*asandruti*). For the definition [of substance] is "substance is a concretion of qualities" (Pāṇini-Mahābhāṣya 5.1.119). Concretion (*sandruti*) is the coming together or unification of many qualities; the absence of that is non-concretion (*asandruti*). Therefore, due to this non-concretion, it would not function, like a person or like the son of a barren woman—this is the undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭāpādana*).
From those [five subtle elements] arise the five gross elements...

therein, from the subtle element of sound (śabda-tanmātra) comes space (ākāśa); from the subtle element of touch (sparśa-tanmātra) comes air (vāyu); from the subtle element of form (rūpa-tanmātra) comes fire (tejas); from the subtle element of taste (rasa-tanmātra) comes water (āpas); and from the subtle element of smell (gandha-tanmātra) comes earth (pṛthivī).

Although it could have been stated simply that "the gross elements arise from them," the expression "from each of the five" is used to indicate that their production occurs in equal numbers; by this, it is established that from each individual subtle element, one specific gross element is produced.

Consequently, the view held by other teachers—that from the *tanmātras*, which possess a single characteristic each, the specific elements (*viśeṣas*) are produced one after another through mutual interpenetration—is refuted.

What then? Even without the interpenetration of the *tanmātras*, there is the production of specific elemental derivatives one after another from the primary elements; therein, from the *tanmātra* of sound, which has sound as its quality, arises space, which possesses that single quality.
From the subtle element of touch (*sparśa-tanmātra*), which has the qualities of sound and touch, wind arises with two qualities;
from the subtle element of form (*rūpa-tanmātra*), which has the qualities of sound, touch, and form, fire arises with three qualities;
and from the subtle element of taste (*rasa-tanmātra*), which has the qualities of sound, touch, form, and taste, water arises with four qualities.
From the subtle element of smell (*gandha-tanmātra*), which possesses the qualities of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell, arises the fivefold earth;

Thus, from the five subtle elements (tanmātras), the five gross elements (bhūtas) arise;

Because it has the nature of a single pleasure, it is non-distinct from that; its state is its "essence" (*tattva*), and that pleasure possesses an essence non-distinct from its single self-nature. And light (*prakāśa*) and the rest are the self of that essence, because there is no state of difference anywhere. Therefore, by way of having light and the rest as its self, may it not proceed—that is, may it not undergo the occurrence of transformation—because it is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇatva*), because it does not consist of a confluence of qualities, because it is one, because its oneness is not manifold in nature, and because transformation is impossible due to the impossibility of inequality. For it would be through the occurrence of inequality that there could be transformation; however, in the state of equilibrium (*sāmyāvasthā*) of the qualities, since that [inequality] is absent, there is no possibility of inequality, and therefore there is no transformation.

Because it is not of the nature of non-transgression, and because it is not of the nature of attaining another form; for in that very state, existence (*sattva*) of such a nature serves as the example, like the *puruṣa*. Furthermore, sound and the other [qualities], being of a single nature and so forth—being devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), one, equal, and unchanging—would, by virtue of their undergoing transformation (*āpadyamānatva*) and proceeding from the state of *pradhāna*, incur the opposite properties such as having a manifold nature, just like pleasure and the rest; this has already been explained.

Therefore, let them not proceed as consisting of light and the others, because they would be devoid of qualities, being one, because inequality is impossible, because they are unchanging, and because they do not consist of transformation, just like the *puruṣa*.

He says: "But surely, because it is of the nature of light," and so forth. To this it is replied: If fire were non-existent in that state because it has not yet begun its activity, then this very fact leads to the conclusion we desire—namely, its lack of luminosity. Since its activity as a manifestation of its own nature is absent at that time, it is therefore non-existent, like the son of a barren woman. The same applies to pleasure because it has not yet begun its activity. Thus, in the phrase "for in this way," etc.: the existence of the effect in the cause would indeed be possible only if that existence were to proceed by way of the nature of manifestation, because otherwise there would be no commencement.

Otherwise, because it would involve the commencement of a connection with something else, this too would become a theory of the non-existent effect (*asatkāryavāda*). As the proponents of *asatkāryavāda* say: "Because of the absence of action, quality, and designation, [the effect] is non-existent; when there is a connection with the inherent and non-inherent causes, substances produce another substance. Thus, the doctrine of origination (*ārambhavāda*) would follow, and that is undesirable.

Therefore, because there is no beginning (*anārambha*), existence (*sattva*) proceeds by way of manifestation. Since the effect exists within the cause in this manner, if existence proceeds—that is, if it comes forth—what is the reason? It is "because there is no beginning," meaning because of the abandonment of the theory of origination (*ārambhavāda*).

If it is asked how it is that "it proceeds" or "it comes forth"—these being synonymous terms—it is said in reply: because the root *vṛt* has the sense of "to exist"; for "it proceeds," "it exists," "it comes into being," and "it comes forth" are synonyms.

Just as a seed assisted by water undergoes the activity of swelling and sprouting, so too the *sattva* assisted by *rajas* has an activity directed toward creation, or indeed, that very creation itself is what is intended here.

See page 207–1.

Regarding the passage beginning with "But thus" (*evaṃ tu*): there is no mutual assistance between these two, *sattva* and *rajas*, because they possess a power that is to be aroused by assistance (*utthāpyasāhāyakaśaktitvāt*). Assistance is the state of being a helper; the power consists in that state, or rather, in that very act. Those two entities have such a power which is to be aroused at that very moment; because of that state, or because of possessing a power whose assistance is to be aroused, they are like two boats struck by the wind. Just as two boats tied together on the water are not for the protection of one another, so it is with *sattva* and *rajas*.

If it is asked, "Could there not be mutual assistance [between the qualities], like that of the bearers of a palanquin?"—the answer is no, because of the qualification regarding being raised up. For this very example is like that of the bearers of a palanquin who are ill: just as one who is ill cannot carry [the load] unless he is raised up, because his capacity for assistance requires being raised up, so too, when *sattva* and *rajas* are not raised up, they are unable to activate one another, as they have not yet attained their own nature. Thus, there is an absence of intense activity (*prakṛṣṭavṛtti*). Due to the absence of intense activity, there is an incompleteness of power; therefore, he says: "Or, incompleteness of power is non-intensity. In this way, there would be no causality at all for that *sattva*, because of its incomplete power, like a damaged seed. Just as a damaged seed is not a cause at all because it lacks the power to produce a complete sprout, so too would *sattva* be.

Even if one were to concede that *sattva* possesses causality during its state of equilibrium, its own essential manifestation does not arise from anything else—such as the principles of *rajas* and *tamas*, the *puruṣa*, or any other source—due to reasons such as "the non-production of what is non-existent" (*asadakaraṇāt*). The excellence of the nature of illumination belonging to that *sattva* does not originate from *rajas*, *tamas*, the *puruṣa*, or anywhere else, for the reasons beginning with "the non-production of what is non-existent. For example: because of the non-production of what is non-existent, just as an effect such as a jar—which already exists in a potential form within the clay—is produced from the clay, but things like a sky-flower are not; and just as that excellence in the manifestation of the jar’s own nature, which is restricted to the clay itself, does not arise from any other cause of production such as the *puruṣa* or the threads [of a cloth], but rather arises from itself alone; in the same way, the excellence in the manifestation of the nature of *sattva* does not arise from anything else, but rather from itself alone.

Thus, from these reasons— "because of the grasping of the material cause," "because of the non-occurrence of everything from everything," "because the capable [cause] produces the possible," and "because of the nature of the cause" (Sāṅkhyakārikā 9)— it must be understood that the quality of *sattva* is the excellence of the manifestation of its own nature independently of anything else.
In this way, the illumination of *sattva* is to be joined with *tamas*, and the instigation of *rajas*.
The meaning is that they are bound to one another; see page 34, note 5. ... [the state] in which causality exists... *pra*.

The effect exists [prior to its production] because (1) that which is non-existent cannot be produced, (2) there is the grasping of a material cause, (3) there is no possibility of everything arising from everything, (4) the efficient cause produces only that for which it has the capacity, and (5) because of the nature of the cause. 9.
—Sāṅkhyakārikā 9:
Because that which is non-existent cannot be produced, because there is the grasping of a material cause, and because everything is not possible from everything... [pradhāna].
Because the capable [cause] produces what is possible for it, and because of the existence of the cause, the effect exists [even prior to its manifestation]—
Sāṅkhyakārikā 9.
Furthermore, as stated in the passage beginning with "and when [one goes] even very far," and ending with "because of being transformative":

even if one travels a very long distance along the path of inquiry, there can be no excellence—avoiding the doctrine of the non-existent effect (*asatkāryavāda*)—without the theory of transformation (*pariṇāmavāda*). Therefore, transformation must be sought as the cause of excellence through the process of manifestation.

And when this is the case, then by accepting the theory of transformation (pariṇāma), this very same point follows once again: [the activity] resides in the self alone because of its being a transformation, just like youthfulness; for a transformation occurring in one thing does not produce a transformation in another. A transformation occurring in Jinadatta does not initiate childhood or youth in Sādhudatta; what then? It produces these in Jinadatta himself. Just as that which occurs in one thing does not make another thing otherwise, so too no other [agent] could cause activity in a sentient being (sattva); rather, it would have to proceed from itself alone.
And what else? Even by means of this very [method],
it is so.
See *paribhāṣā* ॰dādṛtenaḥ pari॰;
see *ya* ॰dādatena pari॰ on page 207–1.

As before, from the very example [given], pleasure consists in non-activity (*apravṛttyātmakatva*). For what distinction is there—apart from the incitement of *rajas*—between that which was previously inactive and that which subsequently becomes active, like the transformation of milk into curds? No; for transformation has already been explained in that very context. Activity is essentially luminosity (*prakāśa*). Otherwise, that luminosity would not be such, because it would be inactive and would not have become so, like a jar or a cloth.
And that which is activity is itself luminosity, because it functions in that manner, like the jar and the nature of the jar. See page 207–1.

If it is argued that [the Self] does not act like a breeze on a sprout because it is the instigator of what is to be set in motion, we say no; for it is that very essence which acts, since it does not instigate as before by mere proximity alone.
That which is the luminous nature of the sentient being (*sattva*) is the instigator;
let this be seen—p. 207–2.

Thus, having first introduced the argument concerning the example of light that does not belong to fire by means of the negation of activity in that which has not yet begun to act, he says—"From the very example of the prior state," and so on, up to "it has not yet acted"—intending to raise an objection regarding the example as before: "But surely this has been accepted by you, that the subsequent state is distinguished precisely from the example of the prior state;

for otherwise, what difference would there be between the prior and subsequent states apart from the setting in motion of the *rajas*? Therefore, that distinction arises solely from the setting in motion of the *rajas*."

What is the illustration? It is like the time of the transformation of milk into curd. Just as the state of being curd is distinct from the state of milk—where it is observed that previously, at the time of milk, there was no curd, but later it came into being—and just as this distinction does not exist without a process of excellence (prakarṣavṛtti), so too is that [distinction in the case of pleasure]—this is not correct, because transformation has already been explained in that very context. This distinction is not established by something external. Why? Because we have stated that transformation is accepted in that very pleasure.

Since the modification (*vṛtti*) is of the very nature of light, that which is the self-nature of light is itself the modification; and time is the modification of light alone, and it is non-different from that [light], because the states of the transformations of milk and curd are designated as "time," for the attainment of the state of being milk or curd occurs through a distinction of time. And since that transformation has happiness as its own nature, no other cause need be sought, as the transformation proceeds from its own self.

Otherwise, that would not be manifestation; if that very manifestation were not a specific activity, it would be of another nature, and thus it would not be that very self which is manifestation, because it would be inactive—meaning, because it would be inactive in the manner of being the self of manifestation. Expressing this by way of a synonym, he says: "because it has not become such.

The illustration is like a pot and a cloth: just as a pot is not a cloth because it has not become such in that manner, and a cloth is also not a pot, so too that manifestation would be non-manifestation itself.

The proof of its essential nature by means of the contrapositive is stated as follows: the proposition is that "whatever is activity is precisely that manifestation, and no other object exists," because it exists in that manner, meaning because it proceeds in that manner—just like the jar and the jar's own self. Just as the jar itself is the jar's own self because it exists in the very form of the jar and nothing else, so too activity is precisely manifestation.
(See page 270, line 5).
Having caused [it] to enter, let it be seen; see page 270, line 4 of the previous manuscript. Corrected from *pūrvakṣī*. Corrected from *pra*.

If it be argued that [the pot and the cloth] do not [arise from the same source] because of the relationship between the impelled and the impeller, like a sprout and the wind—this might be the thought: "That which is the activity is itself the manifestation; this is incorrect because of the difference between the impelled and the impeller. For *sattva* is the impelled and *rajas* is the impeller; therefore, due to the relationship of impelled and impeller, there is a difference between them, like a sprout and the wind. Just as a sprout and the wind, being the impelled and the impeller respectively, are distinct from one another, so too are *sattva* and *rajas*."

And this is not so, because it proceeds from that very self; "tadātmanaḥ" means from that which has itself as its essence, since it proceeds from the light-self alone. Because the distinction between *sattva* and *rajas* is unestablished, and because there is no similarity of difference—as in the case of a leaf and the wind—this example is improper, as he will state later. To explain that, he says: "By mere proximity, as before, [the Unmanifest] does not possess the nature of an active manifestation; rather, by such activity, through the production of the nature of *rajas*-activity and the production of the other [nature] accordingly, it is like *rajas*."

For what else does *rajas* do, other than bringing about the other [qualities] into a state contrary to their own nature? And in this way, *rajas* itself becomes like a sprout; since activity (*pravṛtti*) is thus a manifestation (*prakāśa*), or because its essential nature is not distinct from such a manifestation, how can there be a similarity with the distinction between a sprout and the wind? For [the similarity] is appropriate in the case of a sprout due to its being set in motion; but here, although *rajas* is present, it is not a motivator merely by virtue of its presence, as it is itself inactive because its activity is dependent upon *sattva*. Rather, it is that which is to be set in motion, because it does not motivate itself.
What, then, is the instigator? It is said: it is that very self of the sentient being which is the Light (*prakāśa*).

If one asks "How so?", it is said: it is the nature of the individual manifestation (*vyakti*) as it is to be instigated; that is, the Light, whose nature is the manifestation to be instigated in various ways—namely, in the manner of being brought about by sound and so forth—is the instigator, just as a dance master is the instigator when he acts upon a dancer through the manifestation of movements such as the twitching of eyebrows.

What is the reason? Because of its functioning in that manner; for it is by the functioning of *rajas* as it proceeds in the form of manifestation that *rajas* is set in motion. Indeed, it is *sattva* alone, proceeding in the form of illumination, that sets *rajas* in motion. Therefore, since the nature of *sattva* is illumination, and because it functions in that way toward *rajas*, there arises the very opposite of the "instigator-ship" you intend for *rajas*. This is because *rajas* is what is set in motion, its activity is dependent upon *sattva*, and thus *sattva* alone is the instigator; consequently, there is a contradiction with the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*).

And that capacity of *sattva* to set [the world] in motion arises from its imparting to *rajas* a form whose essence is activity; for activity is the very nature of *rajas*. That which has activity as its essence is "the form whose essence is *rajas*-activity," and this is what is imparted by *sattva*, because there is no activity where *sattva* has not manifested itself. Thus, *rajas*—having been imparted by *sattva* a form whose essence is activity—is therefore set in motion by *sattva* through the imparting of that form whose essence is *rajas*-activity, just as *rajas* [sets others in motion] by imparting such a form.

"Even *rajas*," and so forth. For even the capacity of *rajas* to impel is only thus logically consistent; for according to your own view, what else does *rajas* do when it acts, other than bringing about such a nature in the other two, *sattva* and *tamas*? It is accepted that it is an impeller only by bringing about the very form of activity, and not otherwise.

Just as it was previously established that it is an impeller only because it impels those two—which were inactive due to their natures of illumination (*prakāśa*) and restraint (*niyama*)—so too let *sattva* be an impeller by bringing about such a nature in the other; what fault is there?
See page 274, line 4.
Its nature consists of being set into motion; for it is through such activity—by bringing about the nature of the other [the Sattva] through the impulse of Rajas—that Rajas acts.
Indeed, like Rajas itself, what else does Rajas do other than bring about that nature of the other?
And thus, Rajas becomes like a sprout, because the Light (Sattva) is that which is to be set into motion.

Alternatively, since activity (*pravṛtti*) has as its essential nature a reality that is not distinct from such manifestation (*prakāśa*), how could it share the common characteristic of being differentiated by a slight breeze like a leaf? For it is indeed appropriate [to say] that the leaf is visible;
[but] regarding the instigator of the ongoing activity... [text fragment].
The initiator of [the world] is the self of that [world];
because of its nature as a self, it exists as such.
Everything is impermanent;
otherwise,
the self would be impermanent.

And thus, just as in the case of a leaf, it follows that only the dust is set in motion; and this being so, according to the stated method, it results that only the dust, which occupies the position of the leaf, is that which is set in motion, while the mover is not; and only the *sattva*, which occupies the position of the wind, is the mover, while it is not that which is set in motion.

What is the reason? Because activity is set in motion by illumination (*prakāśa*). Since activity is produced in *rajas* by means of that illumination, the meaning is: "because *rajas* is set in motion by illumination. For it has been said: "Activity is the very nature of *rajas*; illumination brings this about, because without being illuminated, *rajas* does not act. Therefore, since *rajas* is thus set in motion by illumination, it is rightly stated: "because it proceeds as having that [illumination] as its essence."

Thus, having first accepted the distinction between *sattva* and *rajas*, the non-establishment of the reason (*hetu*) was stated by way of its opposite; nor do we admit that *rajas* exists apart from *sattva*. Therefore, he says: "Or, because activity (*pravṛtti*) has as its essential nature (*tattvarūpa*) nothing other than such illumination (*prakāśa*). There is no nature of activity apart from the essence of illumination in the manner already explained. For that very reason, how can there be a similarity to the distinction between a sprout and the wind? Since *sattva* and *rajas* are not distinct, whereas the sprout and the wind are distinct. The wind, having an essential nature distinct [from the sprout], sets the sprout in motion; however, activity does not exist with an essential nature distinct from such illumination.

If it is argued that [the Self] does not possess that nature because it does not function as such, we say no; for it functions precisely as that very essence, just as the activity of *rajas* is its own inherent activity. Otherwise, as it has been stated, it would not manifest; for otherwise, there would be an absence of activity.
Thus, it may be thought: "Manifestation (*prakāśana*) is shining forth pre-eminently (*pra-kāśana*)."...
...not like the process [of manifestation], because existence (*sattva*), like passion (*rajas*), is of an incomplete nature;
and because it has been stated that the absence of an impeller is insufficient.

And thus, [the opponent's argument] revolves like a wheel of logical refutations: "Activity is the Pradhāna, because it is a single state, just as the state of being awake is the person; therefore, that [Pradhāna] is merely activity itself, because it is defined by the occurrence of activity, just like the nature of activity itself," and so forth. This demonstrates the disparity between the example and the subject of the illustration: "Just as in this world wind, characterized by motion, is seen to be distinct from a leaf, and a leaf is seen to be distinct from wind; for it is logical that the wind, whose essence is a reality distinct from the leaf, sets the leaf in motion by striking it, and the leaf, struck by it, is set in motion as a reality distinct from it—yet there is no such activity whose essence is a reality distinct from Light (prakāśa), because both have as their sole fruit the manifestation of sound and the other objects. Therefore, there is a disparity."

Since the rule *kṛtyānāṃ kartari vā* (Pāṇini 2.3.71) renders both the genitive and the instrumental case endings equally valid, there is no fault even if the author of the Vṛtti explains this word as "by means of its manifestation."
See page 208, line 2:
˚śitarajaso˚; see page 273, line 6: raṃ hī.

If it is argued that just as the wind—which is a reality distinct from dust—causes the leaf to move, there is no such activity (pravṛtti) that is a reality distinct from illumination (prakāśa), and thus it does not possess that nature because it does not function as such;

we say no, because, like the inherent activity of dust itself, activity proceeds from that very self-nature of illumination. For otherwise, as it has been stated, it would not manifest at all; otherwise, indeed, there would be an absence of activity.
Let it be seen (pṛ. 209–1):
It might be thought—manifestation (*prakāśana*) is shining forth pre-eminently (*prakarṣeṇa kāśanam*)...
[etc.]
...not [like] activity, because existence (sattva) also lacks a completed form, just like passion (rajas),
and because it has been stated that the absence of an impeller is insufficient.
See page 209–1:

And thus, just as the state of being awake is one and the same as the person, so too is the *pravṛtti* (activity) identical to the *pradhāna* (primordial matter). It is merely that [the *pradhāna*], because it is defined by its manifestation as the occurrence of activity, like the very nature of activity itself; such is the revolving wheel of arguments.
See page 209–2.

If it is argued that "it does not possess that nature because it does not subsist in that," [the response is: the wind has the form of a sprout, the sprout has the form of the wind, and the wind has the form of the sprout.
(Variants: *pallavamābhāḍe līṃ*, *pallavamā pā vi raṃ hī*).
If you say that it lacks that nature because it does not function as such...

It might be thought: "The function of *sattva* is mere illumination, whereas the function of *rajas* is instigation; therefore, because *sattva* does not instigate and does not consist of that activity, it does not have the nature of activity."

And this is not so, because its activity proceeds from that very self, just as the inherent activity of *rajas*. Just as the inherent activity of *rajas*, though previously non-existent, subsequently proceeds by itself from the very nature of *rajas*—because it is inseparable from *rajas*, because it functions without abandoning it, because it is dependent upon it, and because it proceeds as that very form from that very self—so too the activity of *rajas* is not something other than the reality consisting of the manifestation and activity of *sattva*; for it is dependent on manifestation, inseparable from it, functions without abandoning it, and thus proceeds as that very self.

Furthermore, because it has been stated that "otherwise it would not manifest," it was said previously that existence (*sattva*) would not manifest because it is inactive, like the *puruṣa* or like light without fire; or because its own nature is inactive, like a eunuch. It is exactly so. Otherwise, however, due to the absence of activity, there would be no manifestation, and since passion (*rajas*) does not act where there is no manifestation, it follows that for passion as well, there is no activity otherwise than through manifestation. Thus, it might be thought that manifestation is indeed activity—namely, shining forth pre-eminently—and so on, up to the point that it is just like activity. This is incidental [to the main argument].

And in that case as well, because the nature of the sentient being (*sattva*) is likewise incomplete, like dust, and so forth—by means of such substitutions of terms as appropriate—one should explain [the argument] up to "because it lacks the power of assistance for arising, like two boats struck by the wind," and "like a carrier of a palanquin who is ill," and up to "like a damaged seed.
Therefore, this is intended as an explanation, since it has been stated that the absence of an impeller (*pravartaka*) is insufficient. (Note:
*°ttinirvartanaṃ* is read as *°ttinirvartanaṃ* in manuscript Bhā.)
°ttinivartanaṃ Ya; °ttādi Pra; °vadagni Pra.
See page 270, line 5;
see page 271, line 2;
see page 271, line 5, and pages 209–1.

And thus, just as the state of wakefulness is identical with the nature of the person (*puruṣatva*), activity (*pravṛtti*) is the *pradhāna*; therefore, it is that alone. Having established this, since the state of wakefulness is the *pradhāna* by virtue of being identical with the nature of the person, activity alone is that *pradhāna*, being merely activity.

What is the reason? Because it is defined by its occurrence in the form of activity, just like the very self-nature of activity; such is the revolving wheel of arguments. Thus, he extends [the argument] by analogy of meaning to the passage concerning the reduction of the state of wakefulness to the nature of the person.

For example: just as a person whose sole characteristic is the state of being awake is not distinct from the absolute departure from sleep, or just as the self is not distinct from its own activity, so too the three [states] are merely states of the person because they are defined by the form of the person, like the nature of the waking state; likewise, the *pradhāna* has activity alone as its characteristic because it is defined by the form of the attainment of activity, like the nature of activity itself. For this [activity] cannot have another nature, as that would entail the abandonment of its own function;
but if it were merely that [activity], then the *pradhāna*—like that [activity]—would lack the nature of illumination and so forth, and thus would not be all-pervading (*asarvagata*).
And see each individual [verse] on page 209–2;
see page 248, line 2.
Alternatively, the three [guṇas] are the very self of activity (*pravṛtti*), just as in the case of the states of the *puruṣa*. (Note:
This passage enclosed within these brackets does not appear in the Ya manuscripts.

Now, even that which is characterized by activity is not merely activity alone, because it is "all" (*sarva*); nor is it all [the guṇas] taken together, because "all-ness" belongs to a single entity. Furthermore, since activity itself is "all," being of the nature of activity, it is not merely activity alone, because it possesses the characteristic of activity, just like the very self of the *pradhāna*.

Furthermore, since she (Prakṛti) consists of all things according to each respective quality (*guṇa*), even grass and such are omnipresent; so what is the point of the conceptualization that the Pradhāna is a single entity? Alternatively, because it does not possess those characteristics, there is an absence of the qualities of activity (*pravṛtti-guṇa*); consequently, there is an absence of a Pradhāna that is composed of the three qualities and is the self of all things.
See page 249, line 1; this sentence is also seen on page 244, line 12.
Because of its state of non-activity...

[omitted] ...Now, even though *pradhāna* is the opposite of the characteristic of activity (*pravṛtti*), it is still designated as *pradhāna* due to a difference in emphasis (*avadhāraṇabheda*). For instance, there is the emphasis that "in the nature of the *guṇas*, the *guṇa* itself is the characteristic"; whereas in the case of *pradhāna*, the emphasis is that "activity is indeed the characteristic," since the other two characteristics are not excluded. For that [pradhāna] possesses multiple forms, like a variegated [object].

No, because—as previously stated—the restriction [of the term "only"] is improper, as it contradicts the initial proposition, just like the case of [asserting] that a jar is identical to its color and other qualities. Previously, the primacy (*pradhānatva*) of the qualities was asserted in such passages as "the one unborn [Prakṛti], red, white, and black"; yet now they are described as having separate selves. Thus, the reality (*tattva*) belongs to the Pradhāna, not to them [the qualities], just like the position that a jar is identical to its color and so forth.

And when their very nature is [the Pradhāna], then because they do not exist within each other's natures in those respective ways—and because the restriction implies distinct meanings—surely that itself constitutes the state of being both all-pervading and non-all-pervading; thus, the consequence is that [the Pradhāna] would be subject to the same ontological status as worldly objects.
See page 249, line 6;
see page 266, line 6.

Now, since [the Absolute] consists of the nature of all things and is the object of non-conceptual words, it is indeed without characteristics (*alakṣaṇa*). How then can there be a description of its three qualities (*triguṇa*) and the contemplation of its manifold nature and omnipresence? If each individual quality does not belong to it separately, then how could it possess that non-conceptual form which consists in the attainment of unity through the absence of those [qualities]? For two forms characterized by a variegated nature (*mecakātman*) do not exist when they do not function separately.

But that [object] is indeed non-existent in this way, because, lacking qualities, it lacks a triple nature; and by your own statement, it is like a sky-flower: it is neither an object of definition, nor an object, nor a real entity, because it lacks defining characteristics, like a sky-flower.
(Note: *tvālakṣa* is corrected to *tvālakṣaṇa* based on the variant reading *bhā.*)
Because of its nature as a characteristic (lakṣaṇa), see page 251,
line 3;
and it is directed toward non-existence (abhāvaga).

Now, therefore, because it is illogical to either accept or reject one [of these two] over the other, and because it lacks their defining characteristics, this [reality] is indeed inexpressible. Likewise, it cannot be that [it is expressible], because its identity with or difference from activity (*pravṛtti*) is unanswerable. It cannot be said to be either identical or different, because it is indefinable (*nirupākhya*).

That which exists, however, can be answered as being either identical to or different from activity—just as, for example, the nature of activity itself, or the natures of illumination and restriction. Furthermore, since it is illogical to either adopt or reject one of the two, the very admission of expressibility through the conjunction of both [identity and difference] would result in a situation like that of a father and a son; thus, it remains inexpressible.
Let it be seen that [the word] *syad-eva* is indeed [correct]; see page 252, line 3; [the reading] *nanu rūpa-yu* is incorrect.
Or, the very self of the activity itself possesses the state of being the three, just like the state of being a son; for just as if the self of the person were the states,

then it would not be the person because, lacking those states, it would be like a sky-flower, so too if the self of the *pradhāna* were the *guṇas*, then it would not be the *pradhāna* because, lacking the *guṇas*, it would be like a sky-flower.

Even if the Pradhāna is admitted [to exist], the three Guṇas must also be one, because they have the nature of the Pradhāna, just like the Pradhāna itself; thus, due to the impossibility of their being distinct from everything, there is no pervasion of all things. For the quality of activity (pravṛtti) is indeed the quality of illumination (prakāśa), because it has the nature of activity, just like activity itself; likewise, the other is also just illumination, for activity has the nature of illumination, just like illumination itself—and so too for the remaining one.

Furthermore, activity is indeed restriction (niyama), because its very nature is restriction, just like restriction itself; likewise, the other [quality] is also that which is another quality, because it has a single nature, just like that [other quality]. Thus, since all this is merely primordial matter (prakṛti), there is no application of a rule of extension (atideśa) due to the absence of difference. If that is so... [text fragment ends].
See page 253, line 6;
the [term] "sthātvāt" does not exist in the Bhāṣya manuscripts (bhā॰) or the A manuscript (a॰).

In all cases, due to the confusion arising from the intermixture of forms distinct from the description [of the Pradhāna], these [qualities] and this [Pradhāna] lack such a nature because each possesses its own specific self-nature. Thus, since the doctrine of the Pradhāna as the primary cause necessarily results in [the admission of] a single [cause] preceded by each [individual quality], what is the point of postulating a single entity that is manifold in nature? Since its non-sentience has been established through arguments such as the "existence for the sake of another" (*saṅghātapārārthya*), and since its difference from the sentient is settled, the absence of the established nature previously stated—namely, non-sentience, unity, and transformability—is proven. Alternatively, if one accepts the aforementioned establishment, the extension of the properties of the Pradhāna must be abandoned.

If that [principle] is not abandoned, then the very purpose for which this extension (*atideśa*) was made—to establish the absolute non-duality (*advaitaikānta*)—remains unproven. For even that *pradhāna* which is conceived as being "one" would, in this way, result in being manifold; since the *guṇas*, whose characteristics are non-distinct from its own nature, are spoken of without distinction, that *pradhāna* too—because it is pervaded by the *pradhāna*—would lack a foundation in a stable, unitary reality, and thus the *pradhāna* would itself become subject to the same extension (*atideśya*), just like the *guṇas*, because it is the very self-nature of the *pradhāna*.

Alternatively, if it were an object within the scope of direct perception, then the ultimate reality (*paramārthatā*) of the *pradhāna* would consist of objects characterized by being manifest, having form, impermanent, and so forth.
Therefore, let it be seen that [the self] is as described on page 255, line 2.

And since this leads to the consequence that each [entity] must be preceded by a single [cause], what is the point of postulating a single entity composed of multiple parts? Since its distinctness from consciousness has been established through arguments such as its being for the sake of another (*saṅghātapārārthyāt*), its non-consciousness, unity, and transformability have been established as stated. Its mode of existence—[namely, its nature as] a self—has thus been established.
Even if it were so,

the qualities (*guṇas*) would necessarily be distinct and manifold from that primary matter (*pradhāna*), because it is undesirable for them to assume its nature, just as they are distinct from one another.
Since its nature as being identical with the qualities (*guṇa*) is not accepted,

and because of the extension [of the definition] from the primary cause (*pradhāna*), if one does not admit the distinction created by the objects of self and other, then since it is impossible for anything else to exist in any way whatsoever, those [qualities] would also— just like the attainment of otherness— each be a separate *pradhāna*.

Alternatively, if the activity characterized as the *pradhāna* is not the *pradhāna*, then the *pradhāna* itself is likewise not the *pradhāna*, because it possesses the characteristics of the *pradhāna*, just like the activity.

In this way, the same applies to the remaining [qualities] as well; thus, there is simply an absence of the primary [quality]. How, then, could it possess omnipresence? It is precisely its absence that you intend to establish in this manner, by refuting what is claimed to be its essence—just as the absence of fire is established by refuting its heat.
See Guṇastava, p. 257, l. 2.
...not necessarily...

[as corrected by] the proof (*pra*)... "produced by its own object" (*svaviṣayakṛta*) [as corrected by] the proof (*pra*)... "only existence (*bhāva*)," yet by you, this very intention (*abhiprāya*) has been stated thus.
See the state of being thus; see page 258, line 3.

The cycle of refutations has been completed, and it has been established that this [world] is preceded by a single [cause], not by many; thus he says: "And so, because of the consequence of the doctrine of a single preceding cause"—the word *eva* (only/just) being used for the sake of emphasis—it follows that the postulation of a primary cause (*pradhāna*) consisting of the three qualities (*triguṇa*) is useless. To this he replies: "What is the use of postulating a single entity that is manifold in nature? If the primary cause itself, characterized by activity (*pravṛtti*), proceeds as a single entity in the form of manifestation, restriction, and activity—or if activity alone, though one, consists of the three qualities—then in either case there is simply the doctrine of a single cause. Therefore, the explanation of a cause consisting of three qualities with distinct natures is nothing but a waste of effort."

Therefore, each single entity, being of a unitary nature, becomes manifold in form for the sake of producing thousands of other individual manifestations; let that very thing which was previously described as the cause of the creation of the world with its infinite divisions—beginning with the Puruṣa and so forth—and which is capable of such production, be itself the manifold one. What is the use of this [designation] "consisting of the three guṇas"? Thus ends the *Ākhyā* commentary on the *Prakaraṇapañcikā*.

Furthermore, even if it were established by the reasons you have stated— such as the fact that a composite must exist for the sake of another— that the Puruṣa is distinct from Prakṛti, on the grounds that "because a composite exists for the sake of another," "because there is a reversal of the three guṇas and so forth," "because there is a presiding presence," "because there is the state of being an enjoyer," and "because there is activity for the sake of liberation"; yet...

[Sāṅkhyakārikā 17]. Nevertheless, these essential natures remain established precisely because that cause is distinct from consciousness (*cetana*). Since the non-conscious (*acetana*) acts for the sake of another—the conscious—and since it is the experiencer (*bhoktṛ*), and because it is non-conscious by virtue of undergoing transformation (*pariṇāmin*) such as into form (*rūpa*) and so forth, its unity is established through that very non-consciousness; for there is no difference within non-consciousness. Its state of being subject to transformation is likewise established for that same reason, because the process of becoming (*āpattibhavana*)—which consists of form and so forth—is called "transformation," and because that [process] is distinct from mere proximity (*sannidhibhavana*). As it has been said: "Those very same particles (*pudgala*) transform into a pleasant odor, and those very same particles transform into a foul odor. Because it functions according to its own nature (*svatattva-pravṛtti*), why is it not perceived by me? Or why is it not spoken of? Suffering is indeed non-different from pleasure. This is because, in the absence of a self (*anātmatva*), it consists of obscuration (*āvaraṇa*) and so forth. By this restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), the absence of a counter-example (*vipakṣābhāva*) is indicated, since any difference would be excluded by the other proofs to be stated later, just like the nature of pleasure itself, owing to the non-existence of anything else.

If it is argued that there is a difference [between the self and matter], that will be refuted because [matter] consists of the nature of obscuration and so forth; for how could there be any difference? [The Jñātādharmakathā Sūtra states: "They transform.

Thus, since it exists as something other than consciousness due to its being a composite and existing for the sake of another, its functions—namely, its state of being non-conscious, its unity, and its capacity for transformation—are established. This very cause possesses the functions of being non-conscious, unitary, and subject to transformation; and that [cause] is either pleasure, or pain, or delusion, or atoms, or simply "the cause" itself.

"Uktavat" means "like what was said. Just as it was stated [in the passage] beginning with "But if there were a distinct nature [of the self], existence would not manifest because [the cognition] has not occurred," and continuing up to this limit, [it follows that] it is exactly as stated, because its activity proceeds from a self-nature established by the self-nature itself—since its activity is established by the self-nature—why is this not understood by you, as in the proof to be stated later: "Pleasure and pain are non-different"? Is it due to attachment to your own position or out of delusion? Or why do I not state it myself? When a discussion on reality is underway, why resort to such persistence, whether out of fear of the destruction of future prospects or for some other reason?

If it is asked, "What, then, is that proof? [the answer is: Suffering is indeed non-different from pleasure, because, while being non-self (*anātmatva*), it consists of the qualities beginning with *avaraṇa* (obscuration). *Varaṇa*, *sadana*, *apadhvaṃsana*, *baibhatsya*, *dainya*, and *gaurava* are the qualities beginning with *varaṇa*. *Tamas* is that which has these qualities as its essence—that is, its effect—and is thus characterized by *varaṇa* and the rest; it is not characterized by *varaṇa* and the rest, but rather by the absence thereof (*avaraṇa*). What is that? It is suffering. Since it is non-self and yet consists of the absence of *varaṇa* and the rest, it is precisely non-different from pleasure.

Why, then, is it emphasized that [delusion] is "non-different from pleasure" (*ananyadeva*)? It is said: By this emphasis—namely, "non-different from pleasure"—the absence of a counter-example (*vipakṣābhāva*) is indicated, wherein any otherness set aside by the proof (*sādhana*) to be stated later is excluded. The proof to be stated is: "Delusion (*moha*) is indeed non-different from pleasure. Since otherness is thereby excluded even for darkness (*tamas*), there is an absence of a counter-example. However, the *puruṣa* (Spirit) might be a counter-example because of its difference from pleasure; therefore, the qualification "while being non-self" (*anātmatve sati*) is added in order to exclude it. "Like the self-nature of pleasure" (*sukhasvātmavat*) is the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

Just as pleasure (*sukha*), being of the nature of obscuration and so forth, is not other than its own self, so too suffering (*duḥkha*), being of the nature of obscuration and so forth, is not other than pleasure; this is the explanation of the non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) of the reason, based on the absence of anything else. When suffering is to be proven as non-different from pleasure, once the Self (*ātman*) has been excluded by the qualification "non-self" (*anātmatva*), and once it has been excluded by other means of proof, there is nothing other than pleasure apart from darkness (*tamas*). Therefore, because of the absence of any other thing, there is no counter-example (*vipakṣa*) at all;
and due to the very absence of a counter-example, this reason does not occur in what is not the similar class (*asapakṣa*), and thus it is a non-deviant reason.
"Because the composite is for the sake of another; because of the reversal of the three qualities and so forth; because of superintendence;
because of the state of being an enjoyer; and because of activity for the sake of isolation, the Puruṣa exists. (Sāṅkhyakārikā 17). [Variant readings: *kaivalyārthapra°* in A and B.]

...for the sake of the meaning; according to the printed Sāṅkhyakārikā, "the conscious is indeed the enjoyer of the unconscious," and thus the status of the conscious as the enjoyer of the unconscious is entirely unimpeded.
And because of that, by it... [text fragment]...ya.
Having been spoken by him, those very *pudgalas* transform for you; that which was spoken by him, those very *pudgalas* transform for you. And... [ya].
