Because it functions as its own essential nature (*svatattva*), why is it not perceived by me, or why is it not spoken of? Suffering is indeed non-different from pleasure, because, insofar as it lacks selfhood (*anātmatva*), its nature consists of obscuration and so forth. By means of this restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), the absence of a counter-example (*vipakṣābhāva*) is indicated—whereby any otherness [of suffering] that might be excluded by other proofs to be stated later is precluded—just like the very essence of pleasure itself, since no other [entity] exists.
If it is argued that there is a difference [between them] due to delusion, that will be refuted because they consist of the nature of obscuration and so forth; how could there be any difference?
Indeed, O Master! even pleasant-sounding matter-particles transform into unpleasant sounds, and even unpleasant-sounding matter-particles transform into pleasant sounds.
Even beautiful matter-particles transform into ugliness; even ugly matter-particles transform into beauty.

Even fragrant matter-particles transform into foulness; even foul-smelling matter-particles transform into fragrance. Even delicious matter-particles transform into bad taste; even bitter-tasting matter-particles transform into deliciousness.
"Substances with pleasant touch transform into unpleasant touch, and substances with unpleasant touch also transform into pleasant touch;
furthermore, O Lord, substances are declared to be transformed through the power of application (prayoga) and transformation (pariṇāma).
This is the reading in the *Jñātādharmakathā-sūtra*, section 12.
See page 4, note 2;
regarding the word *°nā*, it should be read as *°neya*.
In the state of non-existence,
because of the non-existence of the oneness of the [mental] continuum and its subsistence...
[text fragment].
See page 270,
line 4;
see pages 209–2.

If it is argued that "otherness" belongs to something else [and not to consciousness], and that this otherness exists within delusion (*moha*), we shall refute that; furthermore, for the sake of clarifying the meaning already explained, the objection and its response are understood from the context and are not further elaborated.

If it is asked, "Since [moha] consists of *āvaraṇa* (concealment) and so forth, how can there be the cessation of its otherness?"—the thought might be: "The cessation of moha consists of *varaṇa* (covering) and so forth. This is not so, because the word *āvaraṇādyātmaka* (consisting of concealment, etc. functions as a *paryudāsa* (exclusion) primarily characterized by affirmation (*vidhi*). Just as in the case of the neuter suffix *suṭ* being non-prohibitive, where the status of being a *sarvanāmasthāna* applies; or just as in the case of *taṭas*, *taṭam*, and *taṭī*, which denote male, female, and neuter respectively, and thus exhibit all three genders within a single entity; so too would this be the case here, since we observe all three genders even while [moha] consists of *āvaraṇa* and so forth. Precisely because it is non-prohibitive despite consisting of *āvaraṇa* and so forth, the distinctness of *moha*—which is the object to be negated—from *sattva* and *rajas*, which consist of *āvaraṇa* and so forth, is established. Therefore, there is no cessation of that distinctness.

And this is not so, because it consists of obscuration and so forth; for the word "consisting of obscuration and so forth" has the nature of an exclusion (paryudāsa) that is primarily affirmative (vidhi-pradhāna).

For the negative particle (*nañ*) has two possible functions: absolute negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*) and relative exclusion (*paryudāsa*). For example, in the case of "he is not a Brāhmaṇa" (*abrāhmaṇa*), there is absolute negation when the primary intent is the cessation of the Brāhmaṇa; whereas there is relative exclusion when the primary intent is the prescription of something other than a Brāhmaṇa, such as a Kṣatriya or others, as in "one other than a Brāhmaṇa is a non-Brāhmaṇa. Similarly here, because [the subject] consists of non-obscuration and so forth, that which is other than delusion—which consists of obscuration and so forth—is prescribed as being non-obscuration and so forth, consisting of clarity such as drying up and the like. However, regarding the state of consisting of obscuration and so forth, there is neither a prescription nor a negation, because it is of the nature of relative exclusion (*paryudāsa*); it is not an absolute negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*).

To establish that point, he provides an example: "Just as, when there is no prohibition due to the absence of the neuter gender, the *suṭ* [augment] following a non-neuter word is designated as a *sarvanāmasthāna*; for instance, since the *suṭ* is prescribed as having the designation *sarvanāmasthāna* for feminine and masculine words—according to the rule *napuṃsakād anyatra suṭ sarvanāmasthānasaṃjño bhavati* (Pāṇini 1.1.43)—whereas for the neuter, the *śi* [suffix] is the *sarvanāmasthāna* (Pāṇini 1.1.42)."

Thus, in the case of *suṭ* prescribed by another rule, its status as a *sarvanāmasthāna* is neither enjoined nor prohibited; likewise here too, there is neither an injunction nor a prohibition regarding its consisting of *varaṇa* and so forth, because its consisting of *śoṣa*, *prasāda*, and so forth is what is enjoined—so it is said in the *Pra* [commentary] on the passage beginning with *yādau*.

If it is argued that [the word] signifies cessation (*nivṛtti*), we say no; for a word whose nature consists of "non-obscuration" (*an-āvaraṇa*) and so forth is essentially a *paryudāsa* (exclusion) dominated by a positive injunction (*vidhi*). Just as when the neuter suffix (*suṭ*) is not applied in the case of a non-neuter, the status of being a *sarvanāmasthāna* is maintained, so too would this be the case—just as *taṭas*, *taṭam*, and *taṭī* exhibit the three genders despite being masculine, neuter, and feminine respectively—even though its nature consists of non-obscuration and so forth, it would possess the nature of the letter *a*. (Note: The manuscript variants *ana-ṇātmakam* and *a-ṇātmakam* refer to the same grammatical point regarding the initial vowel.)
However, in the Viśeṣa-prakaraṇa-vacanāpratividhi manuscript (Ya), as well as in the Bhāṣya manuscript (Bhā), the reading contained within these brackets does not exist at all.
śi is a *sarvanāmasthāna* [suffix]. 1.1.42.
*suṭ* is applied before a neuter [stem]. (Pāṇini 7.1.72)

1.42 ...If it is argued that "a *sarvanāmasthāna* [ending] is marked with *suṭ* except for the neuter," then a prohibition of *śi* would follow in the case of *jas*, as in *kuṇḍāni tiṣṭhanti* and *vanāni tiṣṭhanti*.

As for what was said—"If [the rule] *śi sarvanāmasthānaṃ suḍ anapuṃsakasya* is stated, then there must be a prohibition regarding *śi* in the case of *jas*"—that is not so, because there is no prohibition. This is not a prohibitive negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*) such that "it does not apply to the neuter"; rather, this is an exclusionary negation (*paryudāsa*), meaning "whatever is other than the neuter. Thus, the neuter has no operation [in this context]; if something were to apply by some [other rule], it would take effect by that, and it does indeed apply by the preceding rule.
Thus, in the Patañjala-Mahābhāṣya,
[the rule] "jaśśasoḥ śiḥ" (Pāṇini 7.1.20).

It might be argued: "This is not a valid example because of the disparity; for while the designation 'sarvanāmasthāna' would be appropriate for the suffix *su*—the relatum—since there is no contradiction in its application to both neuter and non-neuter bases, for the object [the base], however, just as there is a contradiction between being neuter and non-neuter, it is impossible for it to possess the nature of both 'covering' (*varaṇa*) and 'not covering' (*avaraṇa*)."

Moreover, this does not constitute an inconsistency, for here too the same principle applies. This would be like the case of *taṭaḥ*, *taṭam*, and *taṭī*, which denote a riverbank in the masculine, neuter, and feminine genders respectively; for all three genders are observed in a single entity. Indeed, the three genders are seen in a single bank: *taṭam*, *taṭaḥ*, and *taṭī*. When it is in the neuter gender, it is neither feminine nor masculine; when in the masculine, it is neither femininity nor neuterness; and when in the feminine, it lacks the other two. Thus, let there likewise be the nature of both being and non-being (obstruction and non-obstruction) and so forth—what fault is there? As for the failure to form a *sarūpa-ekaśeṣa* (a single remainder of similar forms), there is no fault, because it is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) intended to manifest the three genders.
...nābha... equal... bhāra... hīna... not equal... pāda... ḍe... līṃ... vi...
The state of being female, male, or neuter; the state of being neither female nor male; the nature of being characterized by choice and so forth.

If it is argued that, in that case, since pleasure and pain also consist of covering (*varaṇa*) and so forth, their lack of consisting of covering and so forth is not established; or, even if they were established as consisting of non-covering and so forth, their non-difference [from the Self] would not be established—[we reply]: No. Even though [the Self] consists of non-covering and so forth, because it is non-different from that which consists of covering and so forth, pleasure and pain—even while consisting of non-covering and so forth—are non-different from that which consists of covering and so forth. Therefore, although there is a difference in effects such as clarity (*prasāda*) and desiccation (*śoṣa*), [pleasure and pain] are indeed non-different and consist precisely of covering and so forth, because they possess the nature of being causes, having no self-nature (*anātmatva*), and undergoing transformation (*pariṇāmitva*).

What is it like? It is like the nature of delusion consisting in non-obstruction, non-seating, and so forth; just as, because of its non-difference from the nature of obstruction and so forth, there is the nature of non-obstruction, non-seating, and so forth—just as will be explained later—and since even when there is the nature of obstruction and so forth, the nature of non-obstruction and so forth is established due to non-difference, this [argument] is not a proof, because everything would be equal, and because it would lead to the absurdity of proving what is contradicted by common consensus.

For one could indeed say: "A jar is non-different from a mat, because it does not have threads as its nature, just like the mat's own self," using the method of difference (*vaidharmya*) with a cloth as the example.

The other [passions] such as *sādana* (depression) and so forth, which are of the nature of delusion (*moha*), though they consist of both obstruction (*varaṇa*) and delusion, are nonetheless not of the nature of obstruction alone; just as delusion itself, although characterized by depression, destruction, loathsomeness, dejection, and pride—which are distinct from obstruction—is nevertheless of the nature of obstruction. This is because there is no difference between cause and effect, and yet there is a distinction; otherwise, there would be the faults of redundancy and meaninglessness in the text, as well as the fault of the absence of a designation for that which is to be designated. Since these are not accepted, it must be admitted that delusion consists of both obstruction and non-obstruction, and that the same applies to depression and the others.
Just as this is so, pleasure and pain, as well as clarity, dryness, and so forth, would consist of the nature of being obstructed or unobstructed;
therefore, there is no dissimilar instance (*asapakṣa*) to demonstrate the deviation of the reason for the non-difference between pleasure and pain.

Furthermore, as will be explained later, even though darkness (*tamas*) has the nature of covering (*varaṇa*) and so forth, it is established that it does not have the nature of non-covering and so forth, because it is non-different from them; for it will be stated that "darkness is non-different from pleasure" and "restriction (*niyama*) is non-different from light (*prakāśa*). In that regard, since darkness has the nature of covering and so forth, its non-difference from pleasure alone will be proven on the basis of effects such as clarity (*prasāda*) and drying (*śoṣa*). Therefore, because darkness is non-different from those [qualities], although it has the nature of covering and so forth, darkness—like *sattva* and *rajas*—also possesses the nature of non-covering and so forth.

Furthermore, because the nature of being characterized by obstruction and so forth is established immediately following [the discussion of] that which consists of obstruction itself, and because it will be explained in that manner [later].
[The reading] "obstruction and so forth" (varaṇādi) is the correct one; [the variants] "varaṇādyātmakatvasya" (Ya), "varaṇādyātmakatvasya" (Bhā), and "varaṇādyātmakatvasya" (Bhā) are incorrect.
Even though pleasure and pain consist of the nature of [the self],
[the suffix] vaś is a sarvanāmasthāna [only] when it follows a word ending in the feminine suffix ṅīp.
The substitution of *suṭ* occurs before a neuter [stem].

42. ...If it is argued that "the [suffixes] *su* and so forth are *sarvanāmasthāna* except for the neuter," then a prohibition of *śi* would follow in the case of *jas*, as in *kuṇḍāni tiṣṭhanti* or *vanāni tiṣṭhanti*.

Regarding what was stated [in the *Mahābhāṣya*]: "If it is argued that because of the rule *śi sarvanāmasthānaṃ suḍ anapuṃsakasya*, there would be a prohibition of *śi* in the case of *jas*, [we reply] no, because there is no prohibition;

this is not a prohibitive negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*) such as 'it does not apply to the neuter,' but rather an exclusionary negation (*paryudāsa*), namely 'that which is other than the neuter. Thus, the neuter has no operation [here]; if something is applicable by some [rule], it will take place by that. And since it is applicable by the preceding rule, [the suffix *suṭ* applies].
— from the *Patañjala-Mahābhāṣya*.
The suffix *śi* replaces the dual endings *jas* and *śas*.
(Pāṇini 7.1.20)

Because [the nature of] being characterized by veiling (varaṇa) and so forth is non-different [from the nature of] being characterized by non-veiling, non-seating, and so forth— just as [the nature of] being characterized by delusion [is non-different from its opposite]— and because, even if it were characterized by veiling and so forth, it would follow that it is non-different [from its opposite] due to what will be stated hereafter,
this [argument] is not a valid proof; for it applies equally to all cases, and it would lead to the over-extension (atiprasaṅga) of proving what is contradicted by common consensus.
For it can indeed be stated: "A jar is non-different from a mat, because it does not have threads as its nature, just like the mat's own self; [this is] by way of dissimilarity, like a cloth.
[The elements] such as earth consist of covering and so forth.
Let it be seen on page 205–2;
or else, what else? (Bhāṣya)

The other says: This is no proof, because it applies equally to all cases, and because it leads to the over-extension of proving things that contradict common consensus (*prasiddhi-viruddha*). If this were so, it would follow that even objects contrary to common consensus could be proven; for by the exclusion of the attributes of other things, one thing is reduced to the nature of another. For example, one could indeed say: "A jar is non-different from a mat, because it does not have threads as its essence (*tantvanātmakatvāt*); whatever does not have threads as its essence is non-different from a mat, like the mat's own self; and whatever is different from a mat does not lack threads as its essence, like a cloth"—thus it has been stated by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), using the cloth as an example.

The Teacher says: "Now, how can universal equality be a fault—whether from one's own perspective or from the perspective of another? This is the question of one who considers that there is no fault in either case.

If there is a fault in your own position, then the attachment to the fault of contradicting what is commonly established (*prasiddhi-virodha*) is indeed desired by me; for I, as your opponent, desire the establishment of the non-difference of all things, just as in the case of the category of existence (*bhāva*). Just as in the doctrine of the method of affirmation (*vidhi-naya*), which was just discussed, the non-difference of all things is accepted, this being merely an illustration—so too, in the reverse order, the positions of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), time (*kāla*), necessity (*niyati*), and the person (*puruṣa*), as well as the method of affirmation and restriction (*vidhi-niyama*) to be explained later, are each desired according to their respective [proponents].
Thus, for the time being, the attachment to faults in your position is accepted on account of the intention of the opposing disputant.

This is not only because of the views of others; rather, even in our own system, everything is non-different from all else, since everything consists merely of the persistence of pleasure and so forth. Is not a jar non-different from a mat? For you, who maintain that this world—consisting of external and internal distinctions—is permeated by pleasure, pain, and delusion, everything must indeed be of the nature of everything else, as there is no deviation from the persistence of the three *guṇas*. Since nothing exists apart from *sattva* and the other two, if there were anything distinct from *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, then the fault of the doctrine that "everything is of the nature of everything" would arise; but such a thing does not exist. Therefore, the fault belongs to you alone.
The jar is its own self;
without the power of the [supreme] principle,
it is the all-in-all of everything.

Now, how can this universal equality be a fault—whether from one's own perspective or that of another? Your attachment to the fault is indeed intended for your opponent; for even in your own view, everything consists merely of the association with pleasure and so forth, just like the position of [the existence of] entities (*bhāvapakṣa*). Is not a jar non-different from its matting? For what is there apart from existence (*sattva*) and so on? Or else, there would be an abandonment of the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*), because since it is absent therein, it would result in the doctrine of the collection, momentariness, and emptiness. Furthermore, since form and the other [sensory objects] are also non-different according to this same logic, you have no counter-example at all.
Likewise, even "restriction" (*niyama*) is non-different from manifestation;
for that restriction is precisely the attainment of the nature of manifestation itself, which is non-otherness from manifestation.

If it were of a different nature, existence would not truly be existence, nor would manifestation truly be manifestation, because it would be indeterminate, and otherwise there would be no manifestation at all—just as in the case of *rajas* or activity (*pravṛtti*).
Let it be seen from the very beginning: page 270, line 4;
page 286, line 10.
It might be thought: "The pot does not exist on the mat even though it consists of the three *guṇas*;

therefore, either the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) is abandoned because [the effect] is non-existent there, or—if the mat and so forth were not present in the clay and so forth which possess the *guṇas* such as *sattva*—then the pot, though consisting of the three *guṇas*, should likewise not exist. Consequently, the pot would be non-existent and produced later, having previously been absent; thus, the doctrine of the non-existence of the effect (*asatkāryavāda*) and the abandonment of the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect would follow.

Furthermore, because you accept a collection of *guṇas* whose essential nature is distinct from light and so forth, this too is merely a doctrine of a collection of aggregates (*skandhas*) such as form, since it is nothing more than a collection of *guṇas* that are spatially distinct, simultaneous, and indescribable."

Furthermore, the doctrine of momentariness [is untenable] because it consists merely of indeterminate, non-conceptual objects that cannot be designated as "lumps," "potsherds," and so forth, even though they arise sequentially;
for this very reason, it results in the fallacy of nihilism (*śūnyavāda*), since its nature is indefinable, like a flower in the sky.

If you should suspect that there exists a counter-example (the *vipakṣa*)—namely, that color, taste, smell, touch, number, shape, and so forth, which are observed in jars and other things, are distinct [from the object itself]—then even in that case, by the argument beginning with "of color and the rest also by this... and so on, up until the point where you reach the absence of any counter-example, your position fails.

"Form is not distinct from taste, because it does not have the nature of smell and so forth, just like the very nature of form"—such arguments lead to the fallacy of proving what is already established by common consensus (*prasiddhiviruddha-siddhi-atiprasaṅga*). Furthermore, those faults you attribute to your opponent are actually intended [by us] as well; thus, the argument applies equally to the position that [form] exists (*bhāvapakṣa*). Moreover, even in our own system, the discussion is identical up to the point where it results in the undesirable consequence of a doctrine of momentariness, emptiness, and the aggregate [of atoms], starting from the premise that "it consists merely of the persistence of pleasure and so forth. In this way, it has been established that suffering is not other than pleasure; now it must be established that darkness is not other [than light]. Furthermore, just as activity is non-different from light, so too is the cosmic law (niyama) non-different from light.

In order to demonstrate that [the object] is not distinct from Light, he states the definition of restriction (*niyama*): "Indeed, its restriction is precisely the attainment of its own nature as Light; for the self-nature of Light is manifestation itself, and its state is 'being the self-nature of Light. Indeed, its attainment is precisely the acquisition of its own essence—that is its restriction. Whether it be form or flavor, the manifestation of the manifestable nature is the restriction. For there is no such thing as a restriction existing without a support, like a sky devoid of clouds. To state its synonyms: restriction is non-difference from Light, it is merely the very nature of Light. This is defined as the definition of restriction; there is no other restriction distinct from Light, because faults would be seen in such a case."

If it is asked, "What is the fault? it is replied: If there were a state of distinct natures, then because restriction would exist in relation to light (*prakāśa*), it would follow that *sattva* could not be *sattva* itself, or that light could not be light itself—this is the position—because of such lack of restriction. The meaning is that this is because *sattva*, which is devoid of assuming the nature of another quality, and light, which is devoid of the nature of another quality, are incapable of assuming the nature of another quality. For sound, while manifesting as sound, manifests as restricted precisely by its own nature, which is excluded from the nature of form and so forth; otherwise, there would be no manifestation at all, which means there would be no individualization (*vyakti*).

The two examples are given respectively: [the claim] that it is like dust or that it is light would not hold, because of its lack of necessity; for instance, like the son of a barren woman, or like a person. Now, if it is argued that because *sattva* is of the nature of light, it is restricted by darkness—such as walls and the like—just as fire is, and thus possesses a non-deviant occurrence, then if it were unrestricted, it would not exist; for due to its lack of necessity, it would be like the son of a barren woman.

For in this way, if the effect exists in the cause, it must be invariably present there and not otherwise; since the root *vṛt* in the sense of "being present" (*sannidhi*) has the meaning of "existence" (*sattā*), it is not [merely] because of its presence, but rather because it is not constrained by anything else— this "constraint" (*yama*) being due to the influence of darkness (*tamas*)— it takes on a form that is not otherwise manifested.

Just as in the case of activity (*pravṛtti*): since it is not restricted by the nature of illumination (*prakāśa*), rajas is not sattva, and activity is not illumination; likewise, sattva would not be sattva, and illumination would not be illumination.

It is not merely that there is no attainment of its own self for that which is devoid of the acquisition of other qualities; rather, its very existence from the root onwards would not even be "being" (sattva), nor would it be "manifestation" (prakāśa). Thus, its very existence is negated because of its lack of necessity. If that [being] were itself non-necessary, then that being does not exist, like the son of a barren woman; nor is it of the nature of manifestation, like the Puruṣa. These two examples correspond respectively to the preceding [arguments], as found in the *Ātmaprakāśa* and *Prakāmyasvarūpa*.
How can a restriction be established regarding the nature of the power of acting according to one's will? This is explained in the Bhāṣya.
That which is not subject to cessation would not be called "manifestation," because it would lack determinacy, like the son of a barren woman or [the nature of] a person;

Now, since existence consists precisely of luminosity, it must be constrained by darkness—such as walls and the like—just as fire is, and thus its non-deviation [from its nature] is established.
If it were unconstrained, it would not exist; for, being unconstrained, it would be like the son of a barren woman.

For in this way, if the effect exists in the cause, it must exist there invariably, not occurring otherwise; for the root *vṛt* in the sense of "to exist" implies being present there (see page 271, line 1, 2).
This is not so, because [the cause] does not function with such predominance.

The other [author] says, beginning with "But surely" (*nanu*) and continuing up to "the state of not functioning otherwise" (*ananyathāvṛttatā*), [arguing that] there is a distinction [between the two] because of the favoring of darkness (*tamonugraha*), which consists in the form of manifestation being non-otherwise.

The word *nanu* is used here for the purpose of seeking permission. Since existence (*sattva*) is by its very nature luminous, like a lamp, it possesses an unrestricted light directed toward all directions. When this light is oriented toward objects such as the Great Principle (*mahat*), the ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and so forth—whether in the form of touch, color, or other qualities, or in the form of a mass, a clod of earth, or various preceding and succeeding individual manifestations—it is subject to regulation by an obstructing factor, such as a wall, just as fire is regulated by a wall or similar barrier. Alternatively, it is regulated by darkness (*tamas*), which, like a heavy anchor-stone that prevents a boat from moving in all directions, obstructs its movement to other locations; thus, the regulation of light is observed to be like that of a boat. And this regulation consists in the restriction of its activity to a specific manner: "It must proceed only in this way, and not otherwise."
Furthermore, because their distinction as the governed and the governor is directly perceived, it cannot be denied;
therefore, the restriction is distinct from the light. Thus [ends the section]. *Diyatāni* (pra.).

Is this view indeed [the same] as that?

To this it is replied: If that manifestation were non-existent because it is indeterminate, and if it were itself an indeterminate light, then, being indeterminate, it would be like a barren woman’s son.

Thus, the explanation of the phrase "for in this way" and so forth must be made by way of demonstrating an undesirable consequence: the view that "the effect exists in the cause" is only tenable if that [effect] is determinate therein. What is meant? It means "not occurring otherwise"; it occurs exactly as it ought to occur and not otherwise; it occurs by its own self and is not caused to occur by anything else.

And that [effect] exists in the cause as having a non-alterable mode of being; thus, this effect can be accepted as existing in the cause in a non-alterable manner. Why? Because in that context, the root *vṛt* has the sense of existence (*sattā*), for "it exists" (*vartate*) in the cause means "it exists in the sense of being present" (*sannihita-vartate*). Regarding the statement, "The roots *as*, *bhū*, *pad*, *vid*, *vid*, and *vṛt*—the latter being the sixth—are six roots whose meaning is existence," since *vṛt* here signifies the act of being present, "it exists" (*vartate*) means it is invariably present, i.e., it exists in a state of constant presence. Thus ends the section on the constant presence.

The other says: No; because it is not merely a matter of proximity, since the prefix *ni-* has the sense of "excess," *niyama* here is intended to mean "an excessive restraint" (*adhiko yamaḥ*), and not that which functions as mere proximity.

Who is this Yama that is superior? It is that which arises from the favoring of *tamas*; and that consists in the state of being non-otherwise (*ananyathā-vyakti-rūpatā*). For *sattva* favored by *tamas*, there is the state of functioning as nothing else—namely, the cessation of other forms such as taste and so on, while appearing in the form of sound, such that one thinks, "This is sound, not taste, nor smell. Since *tamas* also, like *sattva*, does not have a distinct or complete form, its manifestation likewise occurs through the favoring of *sattva*, whose nature is luminosity (*prakāśa*); for even the manifestation of *tamas* is called "manifestation" (*vyakti*) because it is a form of luminosity. Furthermore, how could that which is itself unrestricted proceed toward the restriction of another? Such is the text, as before, up to the point where it is said that transformation (*pariṇāma*) is taught in that very context.
But the very nature of manifestation is indeed restriction;
otherwise, that would not be manifestation, because it would be unrestricted and would not have occurred as such—just like a jar and a person, or a jar and a cloth.
That which is restriction is itself manifestation, because it is restricted in that way and proceeds in that way—just like a jar and its own self-nature.

"Form is neither non-space nor the like; therefore, *sattva* manifests in such a way when assisted by *tamas*, and not by itself alone. Thus, there is a restriction [of manifestation] other than [the nature of] light. This is incorrect, because *tamas*—like *sattva*—is also incomplete in its form when considered separately. Since it requires the manifestation of *sattva* for its own manifestation, according to your own view, *tamas* is likewise incomplete, just like *sattva*, whose nature is light only insofar as it depends on the restriction imposed by *tamas*.

The explanation of that is as follows: "For even *tamas*," and so forth. *Tamas* would bring about the manifestation of *sattva* in its form of luminosity, which is a manifestation whose specific nature (*tathā-niyati*) has been acquired through the illumination of *sattva*; it would not [bring about] a manifestation whose specific nature has not yet been illuminated. Why? Because such a manifestation is acquired through the illumination of *sattva*.

Because manifestation (*vyakti*) is defined as illumination (*prakāśana*) in that manner—the word "iti" here having the sense of a reason—illumination of *tamas* by means of its capacity for restraint is indeed the manifestation of *sattva*. And this occurs through the favor of *sattva*, which is of the nature of light, and not otherwise; thus, it consists in the incomplete state of restraining *tamas* when it has not been illuminated by *sattva*, since, in the absence of the favor of light, there is no restraint.

And one who is himself uncontrolled is not capable of controlling another, like the son of a barren woman; therefore he says: "How could that which is itself uncontrolled proceed toward the control of another? and so forth. Consequently, there follows an extension (*atideśa*) of the preceding section, consisting of a detailed exposition of the prima facie (*pūrva-pakṣa*) and final (*uttara-pak�ṣa*) positions beginning with "But this is not the case for these two," and continuing until [the conclusion] where transformation (*pariṇāma*) has already been explained therein.

For example: "But this is not the case for these two, because they do not mutually assist one another, since their power is to be activated by an external stimulus, like two boats struck by the wind, or like the carriers of a palanquin who are exhausted."

"Imperfect power" (*asampūrṇaśaktitā*) means "lack of excellence" (*aprakarṣa*), which is to say "lack of necessity" (*aniyama*). Thus, due to its imperfect power, it would not even be a cause, like a damaged seed; and for reasons such as "the non-production of what is non-existent" (*asadakaraṇa*), there can be no excellence of its own nature from anything else. Furthermore, if one goes to the furthest extent possible so that the effect is not non-existent prior to its manifestation, then excellence must arise solely from transformation (*pariṇāma*). Since a transformation occurring in one thing does not produce a transformation in another—just as youthfulness resides only in the self—it is the case that what occurs in one thing does not alter another, because [the cause] is itself subject to transformation.

If that is so, then, as before, from the very example [given], the non-activity-nature of pleasure means its state of being non-activity by necessity; for what distinction is there—apart from the instigation of *tamas*—in saying that it did not act previously and acts afterwards, like the time of the transformation of milk into curd? No, because transformation has already been explained in that very context; this passage is the same here as well, and furthermore, its manifestation is not otherwise.

No, because even *tamas* (darkness/inertia), like *sattva*, does not possess a distinct or complete form; for even the manifestation of *tamas* occurs through the assistance of *sattva*, which is of the nature of light (*prakāśa*), as manifestation is defined as such. Furthermore, how could that which is itself unregulated function to regulate another? Such arguments follow as before, up to the point where it is stated that transformation (*pariṇāma*) is explained in that very context; see page 271, line 14 to page 273, line 5. otherwise, that which is unrestricted and has not become so would not be manifestation, like a jar and a person, or like a jar and a cloth.

From this point onward, although the subsequent text follows a similar sequence in meaning, it is written down with specific qualifications for the sake of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), because the qualifications are not identical; namely: "The restriction (*niyama*) is indeed of the nature of manifestation (*prakāśātman*); otherwise, that manifestation would not be itself, because of its lack of restriction and because it would not have become so"—this is a restatement of the very same meaning as in the previous commentary.

Light must be light because it illuminates objects determined by their own nature, such as form and so forth; otherwise, it would not be light, according to your own view, just like a jar and a person. That which is not thus determined is not light, just as a jar is not necessarily present in a person, nor is a person necessarily present in a jar. Whatever is light is necessarily determined in that way, just as form, taste, and so on are, or as the worldly examples of a jar and a cloth are.

If it is argued that, in this way, there is no restriction [of the self] due to the relationship between the restricted and the restrictor—like a blue object and its supporting stone—it is not so; for it is precisely that very self which is thus restricted, since, as before, there is no restriction by mere proximity alone.

That very light which is the self of the being is the regulator (*niyāmaka*), because of the rule of such regulation, just like any other agent. Since the nature of darkness consists in the imposition of limitation, the statement that [light] has the nature of limitation is made by demonstrating that there is no manifestation of anything else without a limitation consisting in the exclusion of other forms. Now, it is established that these two are non-different: that which is limitation is itself light. This is because of its being regulated in that way—that is, because it is regulated in that manner; since light is regulated by the exclusion of the nature of taste and so forth through the manifestation of form, it is regulated in that way. Furthermore, this explains the meaning of the phrase "because it functions in that way," since "function" (*vṛtti*), "limitation" (*niyati*), and "manifestation" (*vyakti*) have the same referent, just as a jar and the jar's own self are identical. That which is regulated in that way, that which functions in that way, and that which is manifested in that way is precisely that [itself], just as a jar is indeed the jar's own self.

If it is argued that what is not itself [the agent] is neither thus determined, nor thus active, nor thus manifest—just as the *puruṣa* is not [determined by the intellect] because of the relationship between the governed and the governor, like a stone supporting a pillar—[we reply: no, because that very self (*ātman*) is thus determined; for, through mere proximity, there is no determination as before. That which is the luminosity (*prakāśa*) of the *sattva*-nature is the governor, because of the rule of such determination, like the action of another agent, since it brings about the form of the governance of *tamas* and the other [qualities].

If it be thought that there is no [oneness] because of the relationship between the governed (*niyamya*) and the governor (*niyāmaka*), like a boat and a stabilizing stone—such might be the opinion: the principle of *sattva* is the governed, while *tamas* is the governor;

therefore, due to the distinction between the governed and the governor, there is no oneness of *sattva* and *tamas*, just as in the case of a boat and a stabilizing stone. For example, a boat moving forward is governed by a stabilizing stone which acts as its governor, and these two are distinct; so too it is with *sattva* and *tamas*.

And this is not so, because that very self is thus restricted; for "that-self" (*tadātman*) means either that which has that as its self, or that which is itself the self, since it is precisely that luminous self (*prakāśātman*) which is restricted. Because it is restricted by that very self, and because there is no distinction between *sattva* and *tamas*, the example [of a stone] is improper due to the absence of any commonality of difference, like a stone used as a support for the perception of blue; this will be explained later.

To explain this, he says: "By mere proximity, as before, there is no restriction. Here, although *tamas* is present, it is not a restrictor by mere proximity alone, because it is itself unrestricted and its restriction depends upon *sattva*. Rather, it is restricted by that which is to be restricted (*niyamyamaniyamāt*). If one asks, "What then is the restrictor?"—it is said: that very light (*prakāśa*) which is the self of *sattva* is the restrictor. If one asks, "How so?"—it is said: because it has the nature of manifesting the specific forms of those things to be restricted in such a way; thus, it is that very light which has the nature of manifesting the restriction of sound and the other objects in their respective modes.

Why? Because of the injunction of restriction (*niyamavidhi*). For that is the injunction of restriction in such a manner: namely, the restricted manifestation of a word—which manifests through its own verbal form—as something not having form and so forth as its essence; for that reason, manifestation itself is the restriction.

The example is "like other agents," such as a potter and the like. Just as the material substance of clay, being manifested through various states such as a lump or a small mound, is brought forth (*nirvartyate*), regulated (*niyamyate*), and established in a fixed form by the regulating agent—the potter—who makes it manifest; for, according to the acceptance of the theory of the pre-existent effect (*satkāryavāda*) and the force of reasons such as "the non-production of the non-existent" (*asadakaraṇāt*), it cannot be produced while remaining unmanifest or inactive. Therefore, that agent stands in the place of light as the regulator of the regulated objects, such as the lump and the mound; likewise, light is the regulator of darkness.

Why? Because [Sattva] brings about the nature of restriction for Tamas. For it is by Sattva alone, as it manifests in various ways, that the form of restriction is imposed upon Tamas—just as a potter, while manifesting clay in such a way, brings about its attainment of that specific form—because [Sattva] is the cause of Tamas attaining that nature. Consequently, there arises the opposite of the "restrictive agency" you intend; since Tamas is restricted, and its determination is dependent on Sattva, it follows that Sattva alone is the restrictor. Thus, the nature of restriction brought about by Sattva—which is the very property of the subject (pakṣadharma)—is established as the contrary of your position, because there is no restriction where Tamas is not manifested by Sattva.

For the nature of *tamas* is indeed brought about by *sattva* through its restrictive function; therefore, because it brings about the nature of the restriction of *tamas*, *sattva* is the restrictor, just as *tamas* is [the restrictor] because it brings about a corresponding form.

For what else does darkness do but produce the other [the boat] as having a different nature? And thus, it follows that darkness itself becomes the boat; likewise, because restriction (*niyama*) is either subject to illumination or its essential nature is not distinct from such illumination, how can there be a similarity with the "supporting stone" (*ālambana-pāṣāṇa*) that breaks the boat? It is logical that, in the case of a difference, the supporting stone holds back the boat; however, there is no delusion (*moha*) that acts as a restrictor which has an essential nature distinct from such illumination. If you argue that it cannot have that nature because it does not function in that way, we say: no, for just as darkness is restricted by its own nature, so too is that very self-nature restricted.

For it has been stated that otherwise, *sattva* would not truly be *sattva*; however, in the absence of such a restrictive principle (*niyati*), even *tamas*—as expressed in the phrase "for even *tamas*" and so forth—would likewise be logically capable of acting as a restrictor in your own system, provided it could bring about the essential nature of the other two, *sattva* and *rajas*. Otherwise, apart from bringing about their respective essential natures, what else does *tamas* do? For it is precisely the bringing about of the essential nature of those two, *sattva* and *rajas*, that constitutes being a restrictor when one brings about their essential nature.

Just as darkness is a regulator because it regulates the two—sattva and rajas—which were previously unregulated by the activity of light, so too let sattva be a regulator by imparting its own regulated nature to the other; what is the fault? (Note:

In this way, it would follow that there is only darkness;
and since, according to the stated method, it is *sattva* alone that acts as the regulator, then *tamas*— standing in the place of the boat— would be the regulated object,
while *sattva*— standing in the place of the anchor-stone— would not be the regulator, but rather the regulated object.

What is the reason? Because illumination (*prakāśa*) is that which regulates; since delusion (*moha*) is regulated by that illumination in the manner described, the meaning is that it is regulated by *sattva*. Therefore, because there is an absence of regulation for *tamas* when it is not illuminated, and because *tamas* is regulated by illumination in that way, it is rightly stated that it is regulated precisely as its own nature.

Thus, having first accepted the distinction between *sattva* and *tamas*, the non-establishment (*asiddhi*) of the reason "because of the relationship of regulator and regulated" due to the occurrence of the opposite has been explained.

Or rather, we do not admit that *tamas* is distinct from *sattva*; therefore, he says: "Because the nature of the restriction (*niyama*) is not distinct from the nature of illumination (*prakāśa*). Since the restriction—which manifests through the mode of sound as well as through the modes of form and so forth—is by its very essence not distinct from that illumination, how can there be a similarity between it and the distinction between a boat and a stone anchor? A "boat" is not a "non-boat"; what is it? It is a "stone anchor. The "distinction of the boat" refers to its difference [from the anchor]; the "similarity to the distinction between the boat and the stone anchor" means its resemblance to that. But why is there such a similarity to the distinction between *sattva* and *tamas*? The meaning is: because there is no distinction [between them].

Then, showing the disparity [between the two cases] by pointing out that the lack of similarity between the example and the thing exemplified makes [the opponent's argument] untenable, he says: "When there is a distinction, it is logical that a heavy stone, being of a different nature from the boat, obstructs the moving boat; however, there is no such regulator as 'delusion' (moha) whose nature is a reality distinct from light (prakāśa), because these two [light and objectivity] have as their sole fruit the manifestation of sound and so forth. Therefore, it is not tenable. See page 274, note 9.

It might be thought: "The function of *sattva* is mere illumination, whereas that of *tamas* is restriction; therefore, because *sattva* lacks restriction, because it does not possess that function, and because their functions are distinct, there is a difference between them such that restriction does not belong to *sattva* and illumination does not belong to *tamas*."

And this is not so; for, just like the self-limitation of darkness (*tamaḥ-svaniyama*), it is restricted to that very nature [of *sattva*]. Just as the self-limitation of darkness—which did not exist previously—arises later from the very nature of darkness itself, because it did not exist without darkness, because it functions without abandoning that [darkness], because it is dependent upon it, and because it is of the same form as it, since it has proceeded from that very nature; in the same way, the limitation of *tamas*, whose essential form is not distinct from the manifestation and activity of *sattva*, would be non-different from *sattva* and would be a manifestation (*prakāśa*). It might be thought: "Manifestation (*prakāśana*) is shining forth intensely...
[and] like activity (*pravṛtti*).

No, because the *sattva* (the quality of purity) also lacks a fully completed form, like *tamas* (darkness), and because it has been stated that the absence of a determiner (*niyāmaka*) is insufficient; and thus, just as the state of being a person who is awake is a single determination, so too the *pradhāna* is merely that [determination], since it is defined by the nature of the occurrence of determination, like the self-nature of determination— and so on, with the revolving wheel of arguments— [it follows that] either the self-nature of determination alone constitutes all three [qualities], or, as in the states of the person, suffering is not other than pleasure.

But here, delusion (*moha*) is indeed non-different from pleasure (*sukha*), because in its state of being non-self (*anātmatva*), it consists of [the qualities] such as softness (*aśauṣya*) and so forth, just like the very nature of pleasure; this and other points—including the objections and their refutations—should be understood as before. Having established the rule regarding the locus of activity (*pravṛtti-sthāna*), it is not the case that reality (*tattva*) exists as a single unity alone, because of the relationship between the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*); rather, reality would exist as a single unity [only if that were the case].
Because [the one] is dependent on the other, because it is inseparable from it, because activity proceeds without abandoning it, and because activity is thus of that very nature;

furthermore, as for the phrase "otherwise, existence" and so forth: if there were no inherent restriction, then existence would not be existence alone, or manifestation would not be manifestation alone. Because of such lack of restriction, like passion (*rajas*) or like activity, it would not fundamentally be that manifestation at all due to its lack of restriction, just as it has been stated that it would be like the son of a barren woman or like the *puruṣa*. Thus it is.

Otherwise, however, because there would be an absence of restriction (*niyati*), and since darkness has no restriction regarding what is illuminated or not illuminated—and because that which is unrestricted does not exist—illumination itself would be the restriction. This might be the thought [of the opponent]: "Illumination (*prakāśana*) is shining forth preeminently (*prakarṣeṇa kāśanam*)."... [Śavṛtti, Abhāṣya]... [The text continues: ...it might be thought: "Illumination is shining forth preeminently..."
...not like the process of manifestation, because existence (*sattva*), like darkness (*tamas*), is also incomplete in its form...

...and because the absence of a restrictor (*niyāmaka*) has been stated to be insufficient, see page 275, line 5 to page 276, line 1. And thus, just as in the case of a person in a waking state, the restrictor alone is the primary [principle]; that [primary] is merely that [restrictor], because it is defined by the nature of the occurrence of restriction, like the very self of the restriction; such is the revolving cycle of arguments. Or rather, all three are simply the self of the restriction, just as in the case of the states of the person, until finally suffering is not other than pleasure.

In this case, however, delusion (*moha*) is indeed non-different from pleasure (*sukha*), because, while being non-self (*anātmatva*), it consists of [the qualities] such as *aśoṣa* (non-drying), just like the very nature of pleasure; thus, having established the rule regarding the locus of activity as before, including the objection and its refutation, let it be seen on page 275, line 5 to page 276, line 1, and let it be seen on page 278, line 1.

"Nor is this reality [established] through identity alone, because of the existence of the relationship between universal and particular; it might be established through identity alone [if that were the case]."
Page 281, line 7:

Vācaspati-prabhṛti says: It might be thought that [the objection] starting from "manifestation is a shining forth with excellence" and so on, up to "like activity," is merely incidental; and the response to that—starting from "because even *sattva*, like *tamas*, has an incomplete form" and so on—is also to be stated by rearranging the syllables and presenting the words as appropriate, up to "because it lacks the power of assistance to be aroused, like two boats struck by the wind, like a palanquin-bearer who is ill," and up to "like a damaged seed. Therefore, this [objection] is for the purpose of explaining [the opponent's position], because it was stated that the absence of a regulator (*niyāmaka*) is insufficient.

And thus, the previously mentioned wheel of refutations (*bhaṅgacakra*)—beginning with "in this way, [the cause] is one alone, like the state of being a person in the waking condition," and so on up to the turning of the wheel of refutations—is to be explained by revolving that very wheel; he extends that [analysis] here because it is similar.

However, in that case, activity (*pravṛtti*) alone was the primary [subject], because it is defined as the occurrence of activity, just like the nature of activity itself; thus, the wheel of refutations regarding the primary subject was revolved in its state as mere activity. But here, having substituted "restriction" (*niyama*) for the place of "activity," and having placed the primary [subject] itself in the place of the primary [subject], the turning of the wheel of refutations must be performed in exactly the same manner.

Furthermore, just as in the case of the states of the *puruṣa*, a second cycle of the wheel of permutations (*bhaṅgacakrāvartana*) has been written wherein all three [qualities] are identical with the self of the restriction (*niyama*). Just as the threefold nature of activity (*pravṛtti*) was written there, so too should the threefold nature of restriction (*niyama*) be understood as written here.
He also states the extent of the rotation of the permutation-text: "As far as suffering is not other than pleasure"—this is how far it extends.

However, the distinction here is that the proposition (*pratijñā*) is: "Delusion (*moha*) is not other than pleasure"; the reason (*hetu*) is: "because, while being non-self, it consists of the nature of non-drying up (*aśoṣa*) and so forth"; and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is: "like the self-nature of pleasure."

With the phrase "and so forth," the inclusion of objections and their refutations is indicated as before; by the restrictive particle *iti*, the absence of a counter-example (*vipakṣābhāva*) is signaled, since other means of proof have been set aside due to [the subject's] distinctness. This is an extension of the detailed explanation of everything that has passed [before], and this is merely a demonstration of the direction for the method of explaining it—namely, "having established a rule at the point of engagement" (as in the *Candrakrama*).

Nor is this reality (*tattva*) from one side alone; such is the connection with the subsequent section that raises the alternative view.

It was stated that reality consists in the non-difference between pleasure, pain, and delusion. Reality is manifold because of the relationship of universal and particular (*sāmānyaviśeṣabhāva*), due to the distinction between universals and particulars. For example, "tree" is the universal and "kadamba" is the particular. Just as in this case, a *kadamba* is necessarily a tree, but a tree may be a *kadamba* or something else; thus, while reality might seem to be from one side, it is actually from both sides because of their non-difference, identity, and oneness.
...the state of being the existence of a proximate offense would be non-conformable to reality...
If this is not accepted, then the following must be examined: "The Pradhāna exists because of the causal relationship between effects and their causes.

How is this to be examined? The postulation of a cause consisting of multiple natures is merely a false doctrine (*asadvāda*), because its proposed alternatives are untenable in meaning—just like the position that everything spoken by others is false because the truthfulness of what they have said is untenable.

Furthermore, if there were a relationship of generality and particularity (*sāmānyaviśeṣabhāva*) [among the gunas], then reality would consist of only one [principle]; however, such a relationship of generality and particularity does not exist here among pleasure, pain, and delusion.

However, because they are non-different from both, undivided, and one—through such arguments as these, for the purpose of establishing the oneness of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*—the entire preceding section, with its various introductory variations, is to be understood in the same manner through that very text, by means of the process characterized by illumination and the process characterized by delusion; and since this has been well-written in the Bhāṣya itself, it is not further explained here.

However, there is this distinction: the sense that "existence" (*sattā*) means "being present" (*sannihita*) would be incorrect; for the "becoming" (*bhavana*) of an occurrence (*āpatti*) is only logical if it is inseparable from the "being present" (*sannidhi*), and not otherwise. If that form and so forth were not present in the seed, then the consequence would be the non-existence of the sprout. Furthermore, the twofold nature of becoming—namely, that the effect exists [already] in the cause—is only thus logically consistent, based on the distinction between occurrence and non-occurrence. The rest is as before.

When the cultivation [of the mind] has been performed with both *sattva* and *tamas*, and likewise again with *tamas* and *sattva*, and similarly with *rajas*, the entire manual of cultivation has been written by the Teacher himself; therefore, we shall not explain it here, as that very work is what must be followed.

If it is argued that in all instances where a distinction is challenged, there is no [independent agency] because one is the impeller and the other is the impelled—like a leaf and the wind—it is not so; for [the Sāṃkhya replies] "it is of that very nature," and so forth. This applies even in the conjunction of *sattva* and *rajas*. If it is argued that there is a distinction between the illuminator and the object of illumination, like a dancer and a dance instructor, it is not so; for [the Sāṃkhya replies] "it is of that very nature," and so forth. This applies to the conjunction of *sattva* and *rajas*, as well as the conjunction of *sattva* and *tamas*. If it is argued that there is no [independent agency] because of the relationship of the regulated and the regulator, like a stone and its support, it is not so; for [the Sāṃkhya replies] "it is of that very nature," and so forth. This applies to the conjunction of *sattva* and *tamas*, and the conjunction of *rajas* and *tamas*. In those cases, the terms "illumination," "impelling," and "regulating" should be applied according to their respective logical consistency.

"How can there be a similarity between a sprout and the wind? How can there be a similarity between a dancer and a dance instructor? How can there be a similarity between a blue lotus and a stone?"—having thus raised these objections regarding the application of examples (*upanaya*), each pair [of qualities] must be refuted on the grounds that two [qualities] are possible for each of the two [categories]. In this way, we have rightly declared: "Because pleasure, pain, and delusion—which consist of manifestation, activity, and restraint—are not distinct from one another, they must be preceded by a single cause consisting of a single essence.
Thus ends the *Vāpī-prakaraṇa*.
...or else it is manifold; however, because it is not other than both, because it is non-different, and because it is one...

How is this to be examined? The postulation of a cause consisting of multiple natures is merely a false doctrine (*asadvāda*), because its proposed alternatives are untenable, just like the position that everything stated by [certain opponents] is false while what they have asserted as true is untenable.
As before, the entire matter is [untenable].

Thus, since a single essence or a single cause is not admitted, the Sāṅkhyas must explain this: what is it? That which they have asserted while adopting a state of difference in their discourse on cause and effect: "Pradhāna exists because of the causal relationship between differences; for a causal relationship is observed among internal and external differences. We shall explain how the three—sattva, rajas, and tamas—which constitute the internal effects, abide as the nature of sound and so forth, and perform functions for one another," and so on. How is this to be explained? The intention is that, regarding the various arguments to be presented, however they are stated, there is simply no logical consistency; thus, because the word *iti* here signifies a reason, the meaning is that there is a total lack of a valid explanation.

To introduce the investigation of that [position], he states the proof: "The postulation of a cause consisting of multiple natures is indeed a false doctrine (*asadvāda*), because its possible alternatives are untenable; that is to say, because its possible alternatives are untenable. He will explain later that the alternatives which are possible here have untenable meanings; therefore, this is a false doctrine by way of analogy—just like the position that everything stated by others is false, where the truthfulness of what was stated by him is untenable. By that very [analogy], the position stated by him—that "everything is false"—is what is meant by "stated by him" (*tadukta*). Or rather, it is simply "stated by him" (*tadukta*).

If it is true that what is said—that the three qualities, *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, abiding in the forms of sound and the other [objects], perform their functions for one another—is so, then *sattva*, having manifested its activity as sound and abiding in the form of sound, makes manifest the activity of *rajas* and *tamas* toward the state of being the nature of sound.

In this context, is manifestation (*vyakti*)—which is the activity for the sake of attaining the nature of sound—proclaimed by *sattva*, which consists of luminosity, as something that abides in the form of sound while [engaging] with *rajas* and *tamas*, both of which also consist of luminosity; or rather, [is it proclaimed] as something belonging to those two which do not consist of luminosity? If *rajas* and *tamas*, being non-luminous, are proclaimed for the sake of attaining the nature of sound, then *sattva* will likewise proclaim the activity of the *puruṣa* for the sake of attaining the nature of sound, and will impel him toward the state of sound; for even he, though non-luminous, must act for the sake of becoming sound, since there is the presence of a causal agent of illumination, just as in the case of *rajas* and *tamas*.

In that case, it is not true that everything spoken is false, because this [statement] is true and because it is included within "everything spoken. Alternatively, if this is false, then the falsity of everything spoken is not established by this falsehood, since this falsehood lacks authoritative validity (*apramāṇatva*). Thus, in both ways, it is a false doctrine (*asadvāda*), and likewise, because there is no third alternative, the conception of a single cause that is manifold in nature—namely, "this [world] also has a single cause consisting of the three qualities" (*triguṇam ekam kāraṇam*)—is a false doctrine. Thus, *tvam* is not [the case], and *na* is not [the case]. *Bhāṣya*.
Let it be observed that regarding each individual self (pṛ॰ 288, l.

1), it is said that the three—sattva, rajas, and tamas—while abiding as the nature of sound and the other [objects], perform their functions for one another's sake. Sattva, having manifested its activity as the effect of sound, while abiding as the nature of sound, makes manifest the *pravṛtti* (activity) of rajas and tamas toward the state of being the nature of sound.

In this context, by means of *sattva*, which consists of luminosity (*prakāśa*), is the activity of *rajas* and *tamas*—both of which also consist of luminosity—manifested as manifestation (*vyakti*) for the sake of attaining the nature of sound (*śabda-ātmatva*), while they abide in the form of sound? Or [is it manifested] for those two which do not consist of luminosity? If *rajas* and *tamas*, being non-luminous, are manifested for the sake of attaining the nature of sound, then *sattva* will likewise manifest the activity of the *puruṣa* for the sake of attaining the nature of sound; it will impel him toward the state of sound, because even he, though non-luminous, must proceed toward the state of sound through that [agency], since the presence of a luminous causal factor is established, just as in the case of *rajas* and *tamas*.
