What, then, is that speech? Demonstrating this, he says: [the statement] "Sattva, rajas, and tamas... up to "...they perform each other's functions" is the *uddesa-vākya* (propositional statement); and the *nirdeśa-vākya* (explanatory statement) beginning with "Sattva has sound as its effect" up to "it manifests activity"—this is the sentence taken as the subject (*pakṣa*) according to the principle of the false doctrine (*asadvāda*).

Here, two possibilities are conceivable, since a third does not exist; he shows them: "[By that which is] of the nature of illumination," and so on, up to "is manifested"—this is the first alternative.

Sattva, being luminous by nature, establishes itself as sound through the very Rajas and Tamas that are of its own essence; thus, while establishing itself as sound and benefiting them through that form, it makes manifest their activity toward the state of being sound. What is this "activity" (pravṛtti) that is made manifest? It is "manifestation" (vyakti)—this is the explanation of the meaning.

Wishing to clarify precisely this point—that "it makes manifest the activity"—the author explains it by reversing the case ending, stating "the activity is made manifest," because the object is expressed by the verb and thus takes the nominative case.

This is the first alternative of the question. The second, however, is as follows: "Or rather, [does] that *sattva*, having manifested its effect as sound while abiding in the form of sound, manifest an activity for the sake of becoming the nature of sound, [out of] the two—*rajas* and *tamas*—which are non-luminous (*aprakāśātmaka*)? This is the question. The alternative "of the two which are luminous" (*prakāśātmaka*) is simply not tenable, because it is accepted that *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* belong to different classes (*jātyantara*), due to their distinctness in terms of being the effects of luminosity, activity, and restraint, and due to their distinctness as consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion; thus, *rajas* and *tamas* are not luminous.
The reading here might also be "and because of the distinction consisting of [their] nature.

To this it is replied: "If, beginning with 'if unmanifest' and ending with 'like rajas and tamas'—if rajas and tamas, being unmanifest in nature, are made known for the sake of becoming the essence of sound, then likewise sattva will also manifest an activity for the sake of the Puruṣa becoming the essence of sound. The explanation of its meaning is as follows: it will set him (the Puruṣa) into motion toward the state of being sound; the meaning is that it will cause him to undergo transformation through the transformation into the state of being sound.

The *puruṣa* is impelled toward the state of being the essence of sound (*śabdātmabhāva*), is manifested, and is established by means of *sattva*, which manifests as the effect of sound and abides as the essence of sound; for it is of a non-luminous nature. Whatever is of a non-luminous nature is observed to be impelled toward the state of being the essence of sound, to be manifested, and to be established by means of *sattva*, which manifests as the effect of sound and abides as the essence of sound—just as *rajas* and *tamas* are. Since there is no counter-example (*vipakṣa*), its exclusion [from such cases] need not be stated.

By way of explaining that proof, or by way of presenting another argument, the text begins with "the [Self] is of a non-luminous nature," and so forth, up to: "Now it might be argued: 'Because of its non-luminosity, it is not possible to establish [its existence] definitively; the Puruṣa does not shine because of its being *sattva* (pure quality), since it lacks the capacity for illumination. However, space (*viyat*) is illuminated by a lamp despite its lack of luminosity, because it acts as a proximate cause for illumination; likewise, *rajas* and *tamas* are also illuminated, because they lack luminosity, just like the earth is illuminated by a lamp.'"
The Puruṣa is non-luminous, while rajas and tamas are indeed luminous;
thus, because it constitutes the fallacy of "balancing the alternative" (vikalpasama-jāti), [your argument] is simply no answer.

Furthermore, space is certainly not non-luminous, because non-luminosity is not possible in the case of earth and the other elements—which, though distinct from form and so forth, undergo distinct transformations—just as it is not possible in the case of the intellect (bodhya) due to rajas and tamas.

By the inclusion of the word "also" (api), it follows that by the qualities of *rajas* and *tamas*, and also by that *puruṣa* whose nature is non-luminous (*aprakāśātmaka*), there must be activity for the sake of sound, illumination, and restraint; these—activity, illumination, and restraint—are the functions of the *puruṣa*. The meaning is that he acts, illuminates, restrains, and transforms.
Why? Because of the logical necessity of a luminous agent (*prakāśakāraka*); the meaning is that since he is not himself luminous, the existence of a luminous agent is required.

Whatever, while not being self-luminous, is established as an instrument of illumination, by that very thing [the intellect] must be illuminated, set in motion, and established for the sake of the manifestation of sound; just as by *rajas* and *tamas*, or alternatively, just as *rajas* and *tamas* proceed—and so forth—it should be explained in accordance with the meaning thus manifested. This is what is to be expressed (*vyañjyam*).
The two [terms] beginning with "pra" and "tyādi" are to be expressed as "jyaṃ" and "bhā".
Now, it might be argued: "Because it is not luminous, it is impossible to establish [the soul] as being exclusively [of the nature of consciousness];
for the *puruṣa* does not shine by virtue of its existence (*sattva*). Since it is non-luminous, it acts as a cause of illumination for what is present, just as the sky is illuminated by a lamp;
and likewise, *rajas* and *tamas* are illuminated because they are non-luminous, just as the earth is illuminated by a lamp."
The person (*puruṣa*) is non-luminous, whereas *rajas* and *tamas* are indeed luminous;
thus, for the time being, [your argument] is simply no answer because it is a futile rejoinder (*vikalpasama-jāti*).

Furthermore, space (*viyat*) is certainly not non-luminous, because non-luminosity is not possible in the case of earth and the other elements, which are distinct from form (*rūpa*) and so forth and undergo distinct transformations—this must be understood.

In order to demonstrate the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) of this proof, he anticipates the opponent's view by means of another argument and says: "Now, it might be argued—'Because of its lack of luminosity (*aprakāśatva*), it is not conclusive,' and so forth. This refers to the demonstration of the proof regarding manifestation and non-manifestation, including the conclusion and the reasons, up to the point where it says: "'Because of its lack of luminosity, it cannot be made conclusive'; that is, this reason cannot be established as certain, because one can also say in this way: 'The Person (*puruṣa*) does not manifest, nor is he revealed, because he possesses existence (*sattva*')."

Why? Because, despite being non-luminous, it acts as a manifestor of what is proximate. Whatever is non-luminous yet acts as a manifestor of what is proximate is seen to be non-shining itself; for example, just as the sky and the qualities of *rajas* and *tamas* are manifested by a lamp, so too is the earth manifested by the lamp. This point has already been explained by the previous argument—that it exists because it acts as a manifestor of what is proximate—and thus it is not further qualified [by the term "non-luminous"].

And just as, although the sky and the earth share the common property of being non-luminous, luminosity and non-luminosity are nevertheless observed [respectively] when causal factors are present—so too, even though the *puruṣa* is of a non-luminous nature, let there be this distinction: that non-luminosity belongs to *rajas* and *tamas*, while luminosity belongs to *sattva*. Thus it might be argued. (Prakāśabhāṣya)
It is said:
because it is incapable of being manifested,
it is possible for it to exist as a single entity.
[It is] seen that [space is] non-manifesting;

regarding this, it is said: first of all, this is not a valid reply at all because it is a futile rejoinder (*vikalpasama-jāti*) based on the following: even while both [the pot and space] are equally produced immediately after effort (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*), there would be a distinction between them—such as being manifest or unmanifest, and so forth—just as there is a distinction between the words "pot" and "sound," namely that one is impermanent and the other is permanent.
Furthermore, according to your own view, this non-manifestation of space does not even exist, because it is manifested in the form of sound.

Furthermore, as for the non-manifestation of the object-form (*rūpa*) within earth and the other elements, even this non-manifestation is not tenable; because, starting from "form and so forth" up to "there is manifestation in the absence of non-manifestation."

The word "because" (*yasmāt*) indicates the reason for the meaning to be stated hereafter; the thesis (*sādhya*) is that non-manifestation is not possible. Regarding "form and so forth" (*rūpādi*): these refer to form, taste, and smell within fire, water, and earth. Space and air, which are distinct from those [three], consist of sound and touch respectively. In those elements—earth and the others—that are distinct from space and air (which are themselves distinct from form and so forth), and in which there is a transformation distinct [from them], the manifestation consisting of luminosity (*prakāśaka-prakāśa*), though existing within them, is internally transformed and concealed. However, the manifestation of the illuminated (*prakāśya-prakāśa*) exists because it is manifest; therefore, they possess only the state of being illuminated.

In some cases, because they are completely obscured, there is no manifestation [of them] while they remain unmanifest, even though they stand in the relation of cause and effect—just as in the case of a lamp that reveals objects to be revealed by human agents. Or, let it be granted that those two alone (rajas and tamas) function, just as the specific manifestations of space and earth occur, and not the Puruṣa. If that is so, then rajas and tamas must be of the nature of light (*prakāśātmake*), because they proceed toward the manifestation of sound, just like *sattva*; otherwise, by contrast, they would be like the Puruṣa.

The doctrine of the non-existence of the effect in the cause (*asatkāryavāda*) is indeed very clear, because you admit that the activity and restriction [of the Self] toward existence—which were previously non-existent—are established as the nature of sound; and because illumination, which is an effect belonging to a different genus and was previously non-existent in *rajas* and *tamas*, is observed even in diamonds and other such things. Therefore, the luminosity found in hard earth and the like is simply the state of being a possessor of existing illumination, resulting from a transformation of the luminosity inherent within itself, just like the relationship between the knower and the known or the illuminator and the illuminated in the case of a human being. For it is observed that a human being, whose nature is knowledge, is luminous by essence, being both the illuminated and the illuminator, as well as the knower and the known; whereas a wall or similar object is insentient and not so. The same applies to earth and the other elements.
The mention of "human" is because this very person on the street is to be cited as the example.

One might think: "Since there is a cause-and-effect relationship between the awakener and the one to be awakened, it is not the case that both properties belong to both; thus, there is a disparity between the illustration and the thing illustrated.

This, however, is incorrect, because even though they stand in a cause-and-effect relationship, for both of them—the teacher and the disciple—there is an illumination of each individually despite their prior lack of illumination.

Therefore, since even space (*viyat*) and earth (*pṛthivī*) share the common quality of being illuminators, there is no illustrative example [to distinguish them]; consequently, the establishment of a distinction between the *puruṣa* and *rajas-tamas* is unproven. Even if, out of deference to you, we were to admit the possibility of a distinction between space and earth—such that the *puruṣa* lacks illumination while *rajas* and *tamas* possess activity and so forth—even then, just as in the case of the established distinction between space and earth, let it be granted that it is those very two, *rajas* and *tamas*, that act and not the *puruṣa*. This is the intended meaning: [the distinction] does not exist at all.

However, another undesirable fault follows for you: namely, that *rajas* and *tamas* would then be of the nature of illumination (*prakāśātman*), and thus not distinct from *sattva*. Why? Because they proceed toward the manifestation of sound (*śabdabhāvāya pravṛtteḥ*), just like *sattva*. Whatever proceeds toward the manifestation of sound is observed to be of the nature of illumination, as is *sattva*; by way of contrast, like the *puruṣa*. Conversely, whatever is not of the nature of illumination does not proceed toward the manifestation of sound, as is your *puruṣa*.

The "balancing by alternative" (*vikalpasama*) occurs when, based on an alternative regarding another property in an example that possesses the property of the probans (*sādhanadharma*), one implies an alternative regarding the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*).

For instance: "Some things possess action due to the quality [of gravity], while others are heavy, such as a clod of earth; and some are light, such as air. Likewise, some thing possessing the quality that is the cause of action might have action, like a clod of earth, while another might be without action, like the self (*ātman*); or else, a distinction must be stated."
Thus [it is stated] in the Nyāyabhāṣya 5.1.4.
Just as in the case of the welcome [greeting] and the subsequent awakening, where there is the relationship of the illuminated and the illuminator manifested by a human being,
so too, despite the relationship of cause and effect between those two, there is no manifestation if they themselves are not luminous.

Granted that those two [rajas and tamas] alone function, just as the specific emergence of ether and earth occurs, and not the Puruṣa; however, in that case, rajas and tamas must be of the nature of light (prakāśātmake), because they proceed toward the manifestation of sound, just like sattva. By contrast, this would be like the Puruṣa. Furthermore, the doctrine of the non-existence of the effect in the cause (asatkāryavāda) becomes exceedingly clear, because you admit that the functions of activity (pravṛtti) and restriction (niyama)—which were previously non-existent—attain the state of being the essence of sound within sattva. Thus, for rajas and tamas, there is the manifestation of a light-natured effect (prakāśana) which was previously non-existent and belongs to a different genus.

Therefore, it does not proceed in the manner of a non-existent thing (*aviyat*), nor does it proceed in the manner of that very same thing (*ta eva*).
It proceeds in the manner of a thing (*bhāva*).
The non-existence of the year.

Furthermore, if this [Sāṃkhya position] were not accepted, the doctrine of the non-existence of the effect in the cause (*asatkāryavāda*) would follow as an utterly undesirable consequence; and that doctrine of the non-existence of the effect is indeed very clear. How so? Because it is accepted that activity (*pravṛtti*) and restriction (*niyama*), which are non-existent, belong to *sattva* at the time of its establishment as the nature of sound (*śabdātma*). For the effect of *sattva* is held to be manifestation (*prakāśa*) alone, and not activity or restriction, because those two are effects of *rajas* and *tamas*, which are of a different genus (*jātyantara*). Yet, those two, being non-existent therein, are nevertheless accepted as its effects. Why? Because of the statement regarding "establishment": by saying that *sattva*, having manifested as the effect of sound, remains established in the form of sound, this is what is accepted.

In that case, if that *sattva* were inactive or undetermined—as previously stated—then, due to its inactivity and indeterminacy, it would not manifest such an activity consisting of sound, or it would simply not exist at all, as it has been said that [an inactive entity] is like the son of a barren woman. Furthermore, since the establishment (*vyavasthāna*) consisting of manifestation, activity, and determination—which was previously non-existent—is admitted to arise during the state of origination, which is distinct from the state of equilibrium, the admission of *sattva* for the sake of activity and determination that were previously non-existent is extremely clear.

Furthermore, from the passage beginning with "of rajas and tamas" up to "because of the admission of illumination," it follows that the doctrine of the non-existence of the effect in the cause (*asatkāryavāda*) is extremely clear;

for [the Sāṃkhya] admits that the assistance [rendered] consists in the establishment of the nature of illumination belonging to *sattva*, since manifestation occurs by relying on causes that are distinct principles, just like a cloth produced by relying on threads as accepted by the Vaiśeṣikas.

Just as those [elements] such as light and so forth—which exist without a cause—have begun their respective effects, these effects too are mere illusion. Precisely by the force of the reason you have stated, because they are begun by that [which is itself unreal], they are indeed unreal in nature. This is like a cloth made of cotton threads being of the nature of cotton;

and that which is composed of what is composed of that is also unreal in nature, because it is begun by what is composed of what is composed of that, just as a tent made of cotton cloth is of the nature of cotton, or as [the world] consists of form and so forth, or pleasure and so forth.

Because the statement "in speech, it makes manifest the activity of *rajas* and *tamas* for the sake of the manifestation of sound" implies that when those two—*rajas* and *tamas*—manifest a light (*prakāśa*) that was previously non-existent and constitutes an effect of a different genus, one must therefore admit either the manifestation or the production of what was non-existent. For if those two, *rajas* and *tamas*, were to thus perceive, remain fixed, or proceed [toward that light], then they would be illuminated by *sattva*, just as a dancer is illuminated by a teacher who has not yet perceived her, nor set her in motion, nor established her [in a particular posture].
Therefore, since even their manifestation was non-existent prior and arises subsequently, this constitutes the doctrine of asatkāryavāda (the theory that the effect is non-existent in the cause).

Now, it is considered that [this view] is similar to the Vaiśeṣika position because of its doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*)—in the passage beginning with "the distinct reality" (*pṛthagbhūtatattva*). That which has as its nature a distinct reality—the self (*ātman*)—is the quality (*guṇa*) whose essence is such; that very [quality] is both the substratum and the cause. Just as the effect, such as a cloth imagined by the Vaiśeṣikas, arises within its respective qualities—sattva, rajas, and tamas—while being non-existent in the threads and so forth which depend upon mutual conjunction, so too is the arising or coming into being of the effects—illumination, activity, and restraint—described as occurring within sattva and the others, which depend upon one another for their operation: namely, the arising of illumination and restraint where activity and restraint are non-existent in *sattva*; and the arising of activity and illumination where they are non-existent in *rajas*; and the arising of illumination and restraint where they are non-existent in *tamas*.

Understand that manifestation, activity, and restriction, which were previously non-existent, arise at the time of the commencement of sound and other phenomena, because they are manifested by relying on causes consisting of distinct principles— just as a cloth arises by relying on threads accepted by the Vaiśeṣikas. This [process] proceeds until the very end.

For instance, a cloth woven from cotton threads is of the nature of cotton;

Furthermore, this [view] is even more wretched than the effect (kārya) asserted by the Vaiśeṣikas— such as "according to their respective [causes]" and so forth— because it is mere delusion.

By the logic already stated, those qualities such as *prakāśa* (illumination) do not exist within their causes, such as *sattva* and the others. "Yathāsvam" means according to each respective [cause]: illumination does not exist in *sattva*, yet it arises in dependence upon the others; the same applies to the other two. Therefore, it follows that the manifest (*vyakta*), active (*pravṛtta*), and determinate (*niyata*) effect—the three-fold sound and so forth—which is commenced by those *prakāśa* and other qualities that do not pre-exist in the causes, is merely an illusion like a whirling firebrand (*alātacakravat*) and does not exist in ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Precisely because of the force of the reasons you have stated, that [effect] is essentially non-existent (*asadātmaka*), since it is commenced by things consisting of those [non-existent causes]. For you yourself have stated: "Whatever is commenced by things consisting of X, that is of the nature of X. This applies to the fact that sound and the rest consist of pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth, as well as to the elements (*bhūta*) commenced by sound and the rest, and to bodies, jars, and so forth commenced by the elements. Therefore, we too say the same: sound and the rest are essentially non-existent because they are commenced by things consisting of them, just as a cloth made from cotton threads is called "cotton" because it is commenced by cotton threads. Just as a cloth commenced by cotton threads is called "cotton," so too sound and the rest are essentially non-existent because they are commenced by *prakāśa* and the others which [themselves] consist of those [non-existent causes].

Furthermore, whatever consists of that [sound], consists of that [sound], and likewise all things such as the elements, the body, and jars—which are of the nature of non-existence because they are composed of that which consists of that—just as a cotton cloth or a tent is "cotton-like" because it is composed of cotton;
this is indeed an example well-known in the scriptures.

Just as there is the state of consisting of form, pleasure, and so forth, when the fact that sound consists of non-existence is to be proven, "consisting of form, pleasure, and so forth" is the example; and in the same way, the fact that forms and so forth consist of non-existence is to be established by means of the illustration of their consisting of sound, pleasure, and so forth.
See page 266, line 2.

Now, it might be argued: "In this very way, there is its causality and the existence of effects such as sound therein, just as the rope—which consists of white, red, and black threads—is the effect for which the threads are the cause."
Now, if it is as we have stated, then even *rajas* and *tamas* would be nothing but *sattva*, because they are causes of illumination, just like the nature of *sattva* itself.

Alternatively, according to your own view, since the two effects consisting of illumination and so forth are previously non-existent for each respective quality (*guṇa*), despite pervading all manifest entities, there would be the doctrine of the non-existence of the effect (*asatkāryavāda*).
This is either like the Buddhist position, because of the production of a thing from no prior basis, or like a jar produced in the second moment.
Now, it might be argued: "In this very way its causality [is established]; the causality of those [qualities], such as *sattva* and the others, is indeed logical in this very manner."

And in that regard, it is likewise logical that the existence of effects such as sound resides within those causes such as *sattva* and the others; for each individual effect, such as light and so forth, [arises] just as a rope—which is an effect composed of white, red, and black threads—has the threads as its cause. Just as each of the three threads, possessing qualities such as whiteness, does not transcend causality when they produce a single rope consisting of the three *guṇas*, because the threefold nature (*traiguṇya*) already exists within them and merely manifests, so too the rope is a pre-existent effect (*satkārya*). In the same way, the causality of *sattva* and the others, and the pre-existence of effects such as sound, is likewise logical.
Regarding the question, "How do they not perish?", it is said here: "But if this were so," and so forth, up to "like the self of a sentient being."

"In the same way"—this statement has two possible interpretations. First, it may be understood according to our own position, namely, that there is a single cause which undergoes transformations into manifold forms, just like the *puruṣa*; he shows this with its underlying reason: "Just as we have stated, unity [belongs to the cause]; even *rajas* and *tamas* are indeed *sattva*, and their status as causes of illumination is established as previously explained. Therefore, in that interpretation, the very same fault applies: the acceptance of a doctrine of a single cause, such as the *puruṣa* or others.
But if, according to your view, by accepting that the three—pleasure and so forth—are effects consisting of their causes which are of a different genus, then this is simply the same conclusion.

The other says: "Let this be the case; what is the fault? To this, if there is curiosity regarding the fault, we shall explain: "Pervading all manifest things," and so forth. For that very state of being an unexistent effect (*asatkāryatva*) is established here through another mode of contemplation. That which has the nature of pervading all manifest things—such as sound and the rest, or threads and cloth—is that state of being an unexistent effect, "pervading all manifest things. For what reason? Because, with respect to each *guṇa*, the two effects consisting of manifestation and the rest were previously non-existent. With respect to each *guṇa* (*pratiguṇam*), in *sattva*, because the two effects consisting of activity and restriction were previously non-existent; likewise, in *rajas*, because the two effects consisting of manifestation and restriction were non-existent; and in *tamas*, because the two effects consisting of manifestation and activity were non-existent. This is because it is accepted [by the opponent] that there is a statement of the establishment and a statement of the manifestation of the production of effects—which were previously non-existent—in one place by means of the causes and effects belonging to other *guṇas*.
Therefore, like the effect [of the] Vaiśeṣikas, the effect is non-existent; or rather, as it is said in our own [text], "whether it exists" and so forth.
...at the end of the *pra* [mantra], elsewhere *pra*...

Not only like the Vaiśeṣika, but rather like the Buddhist, is there the doctrine of the non-existence of the effect (*asatkāryatva*). For it is better to have a state of non-existence of the effect similar to that of the Vaiśeṣika, since they maintain that the effect remains with its causes for some time.

This has resulted in exactly the same position as the Buddhist doctrine of *asatkāryavāda* (the theory that the effect is non-existent in the cause). Why? Because there is the rootless production of an entity that has already come into being (*tathābhūtavastu*). An entity that has already come into being in such a manner—such as sound, form, and so forth—is produced without a root; because of that state, there is the "rootless production of an entity that has already come into being."

But for what purpose, when [the point] is already established by the phrase "because of arising without a root" (*nirmūlotpattitvāt*), is there the mention of "such a thing" (*tathābhūtavastu*)? It is for the purpose of demonstrating two points by means of two examples, namely: like a jar in the second moment. Just as a moment, without having arisen in another moment, ceases in the subsequent one while the next arises immediately after it, being rootless—like the rising and falling of the ends of a balance scale—so too are sound and the rest non-existent as effects (*asatkārya*). This is because they possess causality, like the pleasure, activity, and so forth that consist of the qualities of other [elements], or like the causes of pleasure and so forth consisting of the three [qualities] such as light (*prakāśa*), which exist without being assisted by others.

Alternatively, pleasure and the other qualities (*sukhādi*) each perform their own function through the triad of illumination (*prakāśa*) and so forth, which exist independently of one another; for they possess causality, like sound and the rest, or like threads and the like.

Or, if it is held that *sattva* alone establishes itself for the manifestation of sound within *rajas* and *tamas*, both of which are essentially luminous (*prakāśātmaka*), then there would be a single cause consisting of a single essence; and that is not accepted.
Therefore, just as a jar is produced by a jar because the effect exists within the cause—as it has been stated regarding the manifestation of its own nature—[so too must the effect pre-exist].

And since it is accepted that an object such as a jar, which co-exists with that [cause], arises—each subsequent one arising only when the preceding one has ceased—it is like an arising from no root; thus both [the cause and the effect] serve as the example, and both are the probandum (*sādhya*). Due to this similarity, this Sāṃkhya doctrine regarding sound and so forth—which holds that effects such as existence and manifestation [arise from a cause]—should be understood accordingly.
Therefore, because of the similarity to an arising from no root, it is equivalent to the Buddhist theory of the non-existence of the effect (*asatkāryavāda*); is that not so?
This is an indication ending in the locative case [of the reason] with the word *hetunā*.

Sound and the other [objects] do not have their effects pre-existent [in the cause], because they possess causality, like pleasure, activity, and so forth, which consist of qualities belonging to another; or like the causes of pleasure and the rest, such as light and the other three, which exist without being assisted by anything else.

Alternatively, pleasure and the other [qualities] each perform their own function as a manifest illumination that is not assisted by the others, because they possess causality, like sound and so forth, or like threads and so forth.

Or, if it is held that sattva alone establishes itself for the manifestation of sound while rajas and tamas are essentially of the nature of illumination, then there would be a single cause consisting of a single essence; and that is not accepted (see p.
Therefore, just as an effect exists within its cause and thus a jar is produced by a jar itself, so too is the analogy of the person [to be understood] through the manifestation of its own nature.

Thus, once it is established that light and the other [qualities] have non-existent effects, the proof for the non-existence of the effects of all manifest entities is as follows: sound and the rest have non-existent effects because they are causes; whatever is a cause is seen to have a non-existent effect, like pleasure, activity, and so forth, which consist of the qualities of others. "Another quality" refers to *rajas* [passion], distinct from *sattva*; its essence is pleasure (*sukha*). And that [pleasure], though existing as an effect consisting solely of light during its state of equilibrium, is accepted as being of the nature of activity—an effect of *rajas* belonging to a different genus—during its state of manifestation, because of the statement regarding the establishment of the self-nature of sound and the rest as consisting of the three [qualities]. Likewise, it is also of the nature of restriction, by virtue of the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*).

Therefore, pleasure (*sukha*), which is a quality of *sattva*, is seen to be non-existent prior to its activity and to be the effect of a restrictive cause; subsequently, that effect is observed, and the cause is likewise [non-existent prior to the effect]. Thus, sound and the other [objects] are effects non-existent in their causes (*asatkārya*), yet they bear the nature of being causes. In this same way, by taking each one as an example—just as with the restriction of the manifestation of the qualities of *rajas* (pain) and *tamas* (delusion)—and just as with the activity of the manifestation of the qualities of *rajas* and *tamas*, the argument should be applied.

To clarify this point, he says: "Like the three—illumination and the rest—which, when unaided by others, are the causes of pleasure and so forth. This means that activity and restriction, which previously did not exist because they were unaided by the other [factors], namely *rajas* and *tamas*, are later seen to be the causes of pleasure when produced by their assistance; by the inclusion of the word "and the rest" (*ādi*), it follows that likewise in the case of pain, illumination and restriction—which previously did not exist being unaided by others—are produced by their assistance, and the same applies to delusion as well.

If this is not accepted, then pleasure and the other qualities must each individually produce their own effects—namely, illumination and the rest—while existing independently of the others, because they possess causality, like sound and so forth, or like threads and so forth. By the use of the word "own" (*sva*), it follows that all three—illumination and the rest—are the very effects belonging to the single quality of *sattva*, as well as those belonging to the other two; thus, this is merely the doctrine of the Puruṣa and so forth, differing only in terminology. In this way, the faults have been stated regarding the manifestation of the nature of *sattva* by means of the manifestation of sound—which is the nature of *sattva*—while *rajas* and *tamas*, which are non-luminous by nature, remain subordinate to it.
[The reading] *ātmakāryam api bhā* within these brackets does not exist in the manuscripts Ya;

and if this alternative is not accepted for fear of the consequence that the theory of the pre-existent effect (*satkāryavāda*) would have its roots uprooted, and for fear of the consequence that the theory of the non-existent effect (*asatkāryavāda*) would become firmly established—if [one argues] "of those whose nature is non-luminous," then let it be "of those whose nature is luminous. Desiring to state the fault even in that case, he says: "Now, of those whose nature is luminous," and so on, up to "is not accepted," the meaning of which has already been explained.
And thus,
let it be seen in the commentary on the two [verses] beginning with "pra," page 295, note 3.
Then, with the words "just as" and so forth, he first describes the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) that is well-established through conventional practice.

Because the effect exists within the cause, it is said that "the jar is made by the jar itself. By means of the lump of clay as the jar, the jar—characterized by its upward neck, rounded rim, broad belly, and flat base—is produced, which here means it is manifested (*prakāśyate*), since the root *kṛ* (to make) has the sense of manifestation. For example, one says, "make a back," or "make feet"; and this act of making means purification or manifestation. Since the effect is manifested only while already existing within the cause—just as a snake manifests through the expansion of its hood or the budding of its coils, or through the state of being long and coiled—so too here, due to the entry into a specific sequence of its own causal factors, the jar as the effect is revealed by the jar as the cause. Because the clay itself becomes the jar through the attainment of grossness via such a power of manifestation, existence (*sattva*) is manifested by means of existence itself. Likewise, space and other elements, whose essence is inseparable from light and so forth, are manifested through the manifestation of sound and the rest; they are set in motion and regulated by the activity and the fixed laws of sound and the other qualities.

By means of existence and manifestation that are non-different from reality itself, and by means of active existence, the jar is produced from the clay as its wide-bellied form and so forth, without dependence on anything else; for one thing cannot be produced by another that is absolutely distinct from it.

Furthermore, because of the entry into the sequence of its own specific means of manifestation, there is the manifestation of the nature of the jar—the perception after it was previously unperceived—due to the fact that its own specific factors such as the potter, the rod, and so forth, as well as their sequence, serve as the means known as "time. This means that they function sequentially while operating according to their respective states in the forms of the lump, the shaped mass, and so on.
He demonstrates this by saying: "the jar as effect is manifested by the jar as cause."

If it is asked how [the effect] is manifested, it is said: through the attainment of grossness by the power of manifestation existing in that manner. When the power of manifestation in this clay—which possesses that power—passes from its subtle state and, subsequently, through the removal of the constraints of space, time, and so forth, attains grossness, it becomes perceptible to the senses. Thus, like the perception of the nature of a polished mirror, the very object which is the action (*karman*) becomes the agent (*kartṛ*). This is because the pot is nothing but the clay; for it is the clay itself that becomes the pot. By means of itself, it makes itself—the pot—characterized merely by a different state, since it is accepted that the agent itself is the object.

If it is argued that the potter’s staff and other tools lack the status of being instruments because clay itself is admitted to be both the agent and the object—since the pot alone [is the result]—we say no. Precisely for this reason they are instruments; for, by such reasons as "that which is not produced from non-existence" (*asadakaraṇāt*) and "because it is not produced from things like *vīraṇa* grass," the potter, the wheel, the staff, and so forth, manifest the pot which already exists in the clay. Thus, they acquire the status of agent, instrument, recipient, point of departure, and locus, but only with respect to that [pot], not with respect to *vīraṇa* grass or threads. Because they enter into a sequence of their own specific means, determined by the power of manifestation inherent in the nature of that [clay], these causes, possessing the power to accomplish an effect mutually generated among themselves, proceeding in a single continuous stream, are called "factors of action" (*kāraka*). They do not have other things as their objects.
Therefore, since the status of being an agent and so forth is established for the potter and others in exactly the same way, it has been well said: "A jar is made by the jar itself.
(See *Athikukṣi-bhāṣya*, page 171, note 9).

Because of the entry into the sequence of its own fixed means of proof, the effect-pot is manifested by the cause-pot; since the clay itself becomes the pot through the attainment of grossness by the power of such a manifestation, existence (*sattva*) alone is thus manifested by means of existence. By the manifestation of sound and so forth, space and other elements—whose essence consists of manifestation and the rest that are non-different from it—are manifested; and by the activity of sound and so forth, they are set in motion and regulated according to the laws of sound and the rest.
By means of existence as non-different from reality itself, through manifestation as the existence of activity, and without dependence, having cast off the power of clay— prabhṛti, nirmita, ya.
Having cleansed the state of the self (or the states of the selves).
Bound by the assumption of agency, [one perceives] causes as being governed [by that agency].

Having thus established that the example demonstrates by itself how it illuminates and acts upon itself, he now sets forth the application of the example (dārṣṭāntika), beginning with the words "in the same way, by means of existence," and so forth.

Just as it was stated that because the effect exists within the cause, a jar is produced by the jar itself, so too, because the effect exists within the cause, that very *sattva*—which consists of the nature of the cause such as pleasure and light—is manifested through its existence (*sattvena*). This is like the state of clay and the jar. He demonstrates this: "By the manifestation of sound and the rest, the reality (*tattva*) of manifestation and so forth, which is non-different from them, [is manifested]. What is that? It is space and the rest. Just as when clay—which has a reality non-different from form and the rest—is present in a jar, there is the manifestation of the jar and so forth, whose reality is non-different from that [clay]; likewise, the reality that is non-different from manifestation is manifested by that which is non-different from manifestation. The meaning is that even activity (*pravṛtti*) and restriction (*niyama*) are indeed non-different from manifestation. He demonstrates this: "By the activity of sound and the rest, and by the restriction of sound and the rest. That too, such as space and the rest, is both manifested and set into motion and restricted in the same way that it is manifested due to its non-difference from manifestation.

He develops this in detail through an explanation of synonymous terms, beginning with "by means of the non-distinct reality," and so forth. By the very fact of its being a non-distinct reality, he demonstrates the identity of manifestation (*prakāśa*) and activity (*pravṛtti*) through that existence which is manifestation; and by the restrictive particle *eva*, he shows the absence of any object separate from it. For this very reason, he says: "independence" means manifestation through one's own power (*svaśakti*); and by "manifestation," which is activity, he shows that independence is precisely the manifestation of one's own nature through the existence of activity—that is, activity itself.

Thus, by means of the independent existence of *niyama* (restriction), through its own power (*svaśakti*), manifestation (*āvirbhāva*), and its own necessity (*svaniyati*), it is precisely *niyamasattva* that is independence; its own manifestation is light itself, as is activity (*pravṛtti*) and restriction (*niyama*). Activity alone is the other two, and restriction alone is the other two.

Therefore, because these are the very essence of a single reality—just as a single person possesses dark eyes, long arms, and so forth—they possess a mode of being that is non-differentiated and functions as a single occurrence.

The existence of *sattva* is manifested by the very existence of *sattva*; it becomes manifest through the transformation of the individual [state], as stated by its own power (*svaśakti*). What is meant by the synonyms "by *sattva* which is not separate from light" and so forth is this: by means of the active *sattva* (*pravṛttisattva*), through its own power of activity, there is manifestation (*vyakti*), that is, appearance. The root *janī* (Pāṇini Dhātupāṭha 1149) signifies "becoming manifest," while *prāduḥ* signifies "visibility"; thus, "light" (*prakāśa*), "birth" (*janman*), and "manifestation" (*abhivyakti*) are synonymous. Because of the statement that "rajas and tamas are of the nature of light itself," the reality that is non-separate from light and the other qualities is independent of any other object.

Just as it has been shown that manifestation itself is activity (*pravṛtti*), so too he shows that activity itself is manifestation: "By manifestation, by activity, [and] by the existence of activity, its own self-manifestation is independent of the existence of activity; the meaning is that its own self-revelation is independent of any rule regarding a light distinct from itself.
This is a statement of synonyms: manifestation is activity.

Thus, by means of the passage beginning with "by the existence of restriction (*niyama*) independently," [the author] explains that restriction itself—which is not distinct from manifestation (*prakāśa*) and activity (*pravṛtti*)—is *sattva* and *rajas*. To this he says: "By the manifestation of its own power, through its own restriction (*svaniyatyā*). And what is that? It is the very manifestation of the restriction of *sattva* itself, which is independent; its own manifestation, as before, is its own activity and its own restriction. This has one and the same meaning, because it was established previously that manifestation itself is activity and restriction, since an object, while being manifested, is active and restricted.

In this way, activity itself is the other two [aspects], because that which is active shines forth and is restricted; restriction itself is the other two, for a restricted object shines forth and acts. Therefore, let it be seen that here too, that very identity is what has been contemplated (p.
293, l. 6: *°gbhūtatvaghaṭā* in the manuscript).

By its own power, there is manifestation (*vyakti*), which is appearance (*āvirbhāva*). Through this appearance, there is activity (*pravṛtti*); through the existence of activity, there is indeed non-dependence upon the existence of activity; [thus] activity is the manifestation of its own manifestation.

Thus, by the very existence of *niyama* (restriction), which is independent and manifests through its own power (*svaśakti*) and its own necessity (*svaniyati*), there is the manifestation of *niyama*-existence itself as independence; its own manifestation is indeed luminosity (*prakāśa*), and activity (*pravṛtti*) is restriction (*niyama*). Activity itself is the other two [luminosity and restriction], and restriction itself is the other two.

Therefore, because these are the very self-nature of a single reality—just as a person possesses dark eyes, long arms, and so forth—they possess a mode of being that is non-differentiated and functions as a single occurrence.

How then does a single [reality] come to possess the distinct notions and designations of manifestation (*prakāśa*), activity (*pravṛtti*), and restriction (*niyama*)? This marks the conclusion. Thus far, it has been stated that for *sattva* and the other qualities—which have attained unity through this very cultivation—the functioning as agent and object occurs precisely by virtue of their being the self-nature of *sattva*, having accepted their difference through the mutual assumption of each other's essential forms.

That which is *sattva* is indeed *sattva* alone; it does not become *rajas* or *tamas*. That is *sattva-sattva*, and by that very *sattva-sattva* it is illuminated and manifested. By means of the existence of *rajas* within *sattva*, there is the existence of *sattva*; it is stated that manifestation occurs through manifestation itself by way of the transformation of active engagement.

By means of the existence of *tamas* within *sattva*, there is the existence of *sattva*; it is stated that manifestation occurs through manifestation itself by way of the transformation of restriction.

In this very way, the manifestation of *sattva* is manifested by the manifestation of *sattva*, as well as the manifestations of *rajas* and *tamas* by the manifestation of *rajas* through its own transformation; for it is only that which exists (*sat*) which transforms into *sattva*, not that which does not exist (*asat*), as it has been said: "Existence transforms into existence" (Bhagavatī Sūtra 1.3.32).
What is meant by "it becomes manifest" is this: the essence of *sattva* is revealed by the essence of *sattva*.

Furthermore, the qualification "the essence of *sattva*" [is made] in relation to the essences of *rajas* and *tamas*; for even though there is a difference between those two according to your own doctrine, as we have stated, they are indeed non-different because their results are identical, and thus they must be treated as one.

What is the reason? For that [reality], while evolving, does not depend on anything else; thus, [it proceeds] by means of the existence-of-existence that is independent of any restriction on its activity.
