Thus, the failure to establish that pleasure (*sukha*), pain (*duḥkha*), and delusion (*moha*) constitute distinct classes has been demonstrated; and for that very reason, the inference that [objects] such as those characterized by *vīta* and *avīta* reasons are preceded by the three qualities (*traiguṇya*)—namely, pleasure and so forth—is a fallacious inference (*anumānābhāsa*). Therefore, he says: "Because the concomitance (*samanvaya*) regarding the three... and so on, up to "...of the *vīta* [reasons]," and "because of the lack of such reality (*atathārthatva*) of the *avīta* [reasons], which are intended to determine the status of being a cause," starting from "well-established in common usage (*vyavahārasamprasiddha*)" and so forth.

The definition of those *vīta* and *āvīta* [arguments] is as follows: Having previously explained inference (*anumāna*) along with its divisions, that which was described as "generally observed" (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*) or "the remainder" (*śeṣavat*)—this being the means for the comprehension of supersensible entities—possesses a twofold division due to specific differences in its application and usage: namely, *vīta* and *āvīta*. Generally speaking, the establishment of the *vīta* occurs from its essential nature; specifically, when a reason is stated for the establishment of an effect by its own form alone, without depending on the opponent's position, it is then termed *vīta*.

The establishment of the *āvīta* [inference] occurs by way of elimination (*pariśeṣa*). When it is determined that "this cannot be otherwise than this, and yet this exists; therefore, by elimination, this is indeed the cause," and it is then stated for the sake of establishing the effect, it is called *āvīta*. This is the definition of its formal application (*prayoga*). Its specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), however, is the act of adopting one's own position through the refutation of the opponent's position;

thus, *āvīta* is the state of *āvīta*, or the state of the argumentative discourse (*vākya-bhāva*) consisting of five members: the proposition (*pratijñā*), the reason (*hetu*), the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), the application (*upasaṃhāra*), and the conclusion (*nigamana*).

In this regard, they consider it logical to employ the *vīta* [syllogism] first and the *āvīta* [syllogism] afterwards: the determination of the probandum is the *pratijñā* (thesis); the concise statement of the means of proof is the *hetu* (reason); the illustration of that is the *dṛṣṭānta* (example); the application of a single operation to both the probandum and the example is the *upasaṃhāra*; and the repetition of the thesis is the *nigamana* (conclusion). Thus, "the *vīta*...
[is used] first, and the *āvīta* afterwards.
Let it be seen (pṛṣṭha 232–1):

Sāṅkhyakārikā:
Therefore, it is established that the comprehension of supersensuous objects is achieved through inference based on general observation (sāmānyato dṛṣṭa).

Its twofold nature arises solely from the difference in its application—as *vīta* and *avīta*. They state their definitions as follows: when a reason (*hetu*) is employed in its own essential form for the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*), it is *vīta*; the other, which excludes other possibilities, is *avīta* by means of elimination (*pariśeṣa*).
The nature of a probans (*sādhana*) is indeed twofold: common (*sādhāraṇa*) and uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*).
Among these, the common [probans] is that which coexists with the probandum (*sādhya*).
Furthermore, the uncommon [reasons] are "measure," "homogeneity," "being for the sake of another in an aggregate," and so forth.

In that regard, when a reason is stated for the establishment of the probandum by its actual nature, independent of the opponent's position, it is called *vīta*. However, when it is stated for the establishment of the probandum through elimination (*pariśeṣataḥ*)—having set aside incidental [possibilities] that are distinct from the object of one's own probandum—it is called *avīta*.

For example: if the origin of the world is not possible from atoms, the person (puruṣa), the Lord (īśvara), karma, fate (daiva), time (kāla), inherent nature (svabhāva), or chance (yadṛcchā), then by process of elimination it must be from primordial matter (pradhāna); in that case, it is called *avīta*. Therein, when the *vīta* reason is brought into the form of a statement, then a sentence consisting of constituent parts (*avayava*) is constructed.
Furthermore, its members are as follows:
the determination of the thesis is the proposition (*pratijñā*);
the concise statement of the means of proof is the reason (*hetu*).

That by which something is established is the *sādhana* (means of proof), namely the logical mark (*liṅga*). A *samāsa* (compound) is a concise formulation; thus, "the concise statement of the means of proof" (*sādhanasamāsavacana*) refers to a brief expression of the proof.
The inclusion of the term *sādhana* is for the purpose of excluding fallacious proofs (*tadābhāsa*), for those are not true means of proof because they are causes of doubt or error.
The inclusion of the term *samāsa* is for the purpose of providing room for the other members of the syllogism.

The mere indication of the mark (*liṅga*) is the reason (*hetu*); however, its elaboration, characterized by its coexistence with that which is to be proven (*sādhya*), is said to consist of the other members [of the syllogism]. As for the example (*udāharaṇa*) here: it is the demonstration of the coexistence of that means of proof with the object to be proven; that is to say, the demonstration of the coexistence of that probans with the probandum is the example, as follows: "It is observed that things acting in combination exist for the sake of another, such as beds, seats, chariots, and wheels."

The application (*upanaya*) is the unification through a single function of both the probandum (*sādhya*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). Regarding the probandum—characterized by the eyes and so forth being for the sake of another—and the example, such as a bed and so forth, their unification through a single function is not possible in a direct sense because the probandum and the example are distinct entities; since one cannot be demonstrated by means of the other, the unification through a single function is applied figuratively on the basis of a commonality of properties (*dharmasāmānya*), in the form "as this is, so is that. For instance, just as beds and the like are for the sake of another because they are composite, so too must the eyes and so forth be for the sake of another.
That which is the "other" (para) is the Puruṣa;
by virtue of that [Puruṣa], the restatement of the proposition is the conclusion (*nigamana*).
Furthermore, the restatement with regard to the application of the reason and the example is that conclusion. For example: "Therefore, the Puruṣa exists."
Thus, it is extended [by analogy] that a sentence is a collection of these constituent parts (*avayava*) possessing a specific meaning.
The teachers consider it logical to employ the *avīta* [reasoning] first;

for what reason? Because it does not contradict the definition of the *avīta*. For the definition of the *avīta* is the confirmation of the probandum by means of elimination (*pariśeṣataḥ*). In that case, if a conclusion were made merely through the negation of the opponent's position regarding the subject (*dharmin*), whose essential nature has not been apprehended through positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and so forth, then the definition of elimination would be subverted.

Why? Because here, at the outset, a mere negation is stated; by that, just as it can be inferred that the manifest does not arise from atoms and so forth due to a contradiction with the reason (*hetu*), so too it can be inferred that it does not arise from the Pradhāna either due to the absence of a reason. Therefore, its exclusion is also understood through the *avyatireka* (negative-only) inference. This being the case, what would remain as the alternative (*pariśeṣa*)? When the subject (*dharmin*) has been determined by its own nature, the application of the conclusion is appropriately possible: "If it does not arise from atoms and so forth, then by way of elimination (*pariśeṣataḥ*), the manifest arises from the Pradhāna alone."
"By elimination" (pariśeṣa) means [it is] from among those [reasons] previously mentioned, such as positive concomitance (anvaya) and so forth;
therefore, it is established that the application of the *vīta* [inference] occurs first,
and thus the comprehension of supersensuous objects (*atīndriya-artha*) is achieved through inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa*).
Thus, in the Yuktidīpikā commentary on the Sāṅkhyakārikā, verse 6: "If it is argued that [the self] depends [on something else], then it is not so in its own form..."

Although the term *avīta* alone is generally observed in use throughout the texts of the Sāṅkhya and other systems, whereas in the *Nayacakravṛtti* the term *āvīta* is found everywhere, nevertheless the usage of the word *āvīta* appears to be the correct one, because the term *āvīta* alone is also employed in the *Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika* composed by Kumārila Bhaṭṭa; for example: "Therefore, [the reason] is inconclusive even by means of *āvīta* reasons," as he states in a half-verse exceeding four syllables: "When one makes all [things] the subject (*pakṣa*), then too [it is inconclusive] by means of *āvīta* reasons."
Regarding the term *anaikānta* (inconclusive):

those who establish their point solely through exclusion from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) are here called *avīta* reasons. The meaning is that, for example, vital functions (*prāṇa*) and so forth, being observed in a living body and excluded from soulless things such as jars, lead to the understanding of the presence of a soul precisely by means of that exclusion;
thus it is stated in the *Śarkarikā-ṭīkā* on the *Apohavāda* chapter (verse 166) of Jayamiśra Bhaṭṭa’s commentary on the *Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*.

And the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: Primal Matter (*pradhāna*) exists, because of the observation of a commonality among diverse things; for it is observed that the internal diverse things, consisting of cause and effect, possess a commonality of a single genus (*ekajātisamanvaya*). He will state the example of sandalwood fragments and so forth in the passage beginning with "of diverse things preceded by a universal" (*sāmānyapūrvakāṇāṃ ca bhedānām*), etc., for the purpose of demonstrating the commonality of a single genus. Taking as the subject (*pakṣa*) the fact that those things consisting of effects possess the specific nature of being particular arrangements of that [Primal Matter], he states the reason (*hetu*): "because they have a single effect. Furthermore, from the subsequent summary in the passage beginning with "of each group of five," he demonstrates the pervasion (*vyāpti*) through the distributive repetition (*vīpsā*).

Likewise, this [world] consisting of the effects of the instruments (the senses)—characterized by functions such as clarity, drying, and covering—is observed to be endowed with a single genus common to the three *guṇas*.

The elements beginning with space (*ākāśa*), which are composed of those [instruments], possess an increase of one additional quality each; because they are the effects of those [instruments] and because they are endowed with their properties, they are preceded by them.
Likewise, for external objects—whether belonging to the animal, human, or divine realms—their nature is preceded by that [triple-guṇa state];

therefore, because they are endowed with the three guṇas, these diverse objects are preceded by the triple-guṇa state, just like pieces of sandalwood and so forth, or like fragments, potsherds, amulets, ornaments, and the like. This abundance of examples for the proof is intended to demonstrate the pervasion (*vyāpti*).
"The expansion of proofs [is as follows]: 'The uniformity of a single genus is observed among internal entities and those consisting of cause and effect,' and so forth.
See *Yuktidīpikā* on the *Sāṅkhyakārikā*, verse 6, page 49, line 11; see also page 12, line 17.
Because of the finite magnitude of differentiated objects, because of their commonality, because of their activity proceeding from power,
because of the distinction between cause and effect, and because of the non-differentiation of the manifold universe.
Furthermore, [it is established] by way of concomitance (samanvaya):
here, the existence of that by which differences are pervaded is observed,
just as, for example, jars and other objects [are pervaded] by clay.
And this concomitance of sound and the other objects with pleasure, pain, and delusion exists;
therefore,
those [qualities] which are pleasure and so forth, when their specific distinctions have subsided, constitute the Unmanifest (avyakta).
Therefore, the unmanifest exists...

Here, when sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are present, cognitions arise in living beings in the forms of pleasure, pain, and delusion due to their connection with specific latent impressions (*saṃskāra*); and whatever [object] produces a cognition of a certain kind, it is endowed with that [quality].

For example: "Just as [fragrant] chips and so forth [arise] from sandalwood and the like" (Sāṅkhyakārikā 15); and from this [it follows that] there exists [a primal cause], because of the observation of homogeneity (Yuktidīpikā).

Through the inherence of what? Through the inherence of the very parts themselves; for this reason, from that same prior cause, one demonstrates by means of their true nature the inherence of shards, potsherds, ornaments, and gold upon seeing such things as jewelry.

In common worldly practice, it is observed that diverse things possess a connection with a single genus; their connection consists in their properties (*dharma*). Therefore, from this observation of such connection (*samanvaya*), we see that the Pradhāna exists.
(Sāṅkhyakārikā-vṛtti, B, Kārikā 15; the same is stated in Māṭhara-vṛtti with a slight variation in reading.)
For this reason as well, Pradhāna exists because of the finite measure of differentiated things.
The finite measure of internal things, consisting of causes and effects, is observed:

generally, there are three—pleasure, pain, and delusion; and specifically, in terms of effects and instruments, there are sixteen entities, namely the five gross elements and the eleven organs, and so forth; such is the measurement of form.

The measure of activity (*pravṛttiparimāṇa*) is twofold, because it serves the purpose of attaining the beneficial and avoiding the harmful; it is fourfold, because it has *dharma* and so forth as its purpose; and it is fivefold, because it has as its purposes sustenance (*dhṛti*), virtuous conduct (*sadācāra*), sensual pleasure (*kāmasukha*), curiosity (*kutūhala*), and cessation (*vinivṛtti*), as well as being characterized by the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so on.
The measure of the fruit (*phalaparimāṇa*) is twofold: the seen (*dṛṣṭa*) and the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*).

The unseen is twofold: the capacity of the body and the organs (*kāryakaraṇasāmarthya*), which is the power of mastery (*prabhuśakti*), and the proximity of the means (*sādhanasānnidhya*), which is the pervasive power (*vibhuśakti*).
Thus, incapacity is the opposite of that; capacity is twofold:

gods, gandharvas, yakṣas, rakṣasas, pitṛs, and piśācas [are of the nature of] capacity, while humans, domestic animals, wild beasts, birds, reptiles, and stationary beings [are of the nature of] incapacity.
The cause of the body is capacity, whereas the causes of birth are the womb, the egg, moisture, and spontaneous generation, which result from incapacity.

From the parents come the womb-born and the egg-born; that consists of six sheaths (*ṣaṭkośika*). From the earth comes the sprout-born (*udbhijja*); from the condensation of earth and water comes the sweat-born (*saṃśokaja*). Thus is the measure of the unseen fruit (*adṛṣṭaphala*).
As for the measure of the seen fruit (*dṛṣṭaphala*), the organs, while operating, at the conclusion of their activity, generally produce one of the four conditions, beginning with power (*śakti*);
thus power has been described.

The eight perfections (*siddhi*) are as follows: *tāraka* through the practice of the form of accomplishment (*siddhirūha*); *sutāra* by means of sound (*śabda*); *tārayantam* by means of study (*adhyayana*); *pramoda* through the action of transcending internal obstacles such as wind (*vāta*) by means of any one of the three—*tāraka*, *sutāra*, or *tārayantam*; *pramudita* through the transcendence of external obstacles such as humans (*mānuṣa*) by means of any one of those three; *modamāna* through the transcendence of celestial obstacles such as cold (*śīta*) by means of any one of those three; *ramyaka* through the reliance on what is associated with the wholesome (*kuśala*), the transcendence of doubt, and any one of those [other] three; and *sadāpramudita* through the transcendence of misfortune (*daurbhāgya*). These are the eight perfections.

Contentment (*tuṣṭi*) is the cessation of one who desires an object that is less than what was intended, due to satisfaction with an object at hand; it is of nine kinds because it possesses nine forms, based on whether the means are present or absent.

These arise from the failure to discern the difference between the Self (*puruṣa*) and the causes consisting of primordial nature (*prakṛti*), material cause (*upādāna*), time (*kāla*), and fortune (*bhāgya*); they consist of the attainment of indifference and are named Ambhaḥ, Salila, Ogha, and Vṛṣṭi. Furthermore, there are four internal contentments (*ādhyātmika-tuṣṭi*) which have as their means the body, the embodied soul, specific qualities, and the instruments.

Furthermore, there are five external contentments (*tuṣṭi*) born from detachment toward sense objects, arising from perceiving the defects in the acquisition, preservation, decay, attachment, and injury associated with sense objects; these are named *sutāra*, *supāra*, *sunetra*, *sumārīcī*, and *uttamābhayā*. Thus, there are nine contentments in total.

There are eleven impairments of the faculties (*indriyavadha*): deafness, blindness, loss of smell, muteness, idiocy, insanity, mutilation of the hands, leprosy, impotence, upward-moving wind (*udāvarta*), and lameness.
There are eight non-attainments (*asiddhi*), which are the opposites of the previously mentioned means of attainment (*siddhyupāya*).

Likewise, there are nine forms of discontent (atuṣṭi), such as the "lack of water" (anāmbhasikī) and others, which are the opposites of contentment; thus, incapacity (aśakti) is of twenty-eight kinds.

Furthermore, there are five errors (viparyaya): non-beneficial activity, egoism, possessiveness, anger, and death, along with despondency, darkness (tamas), delusion (moha), great delusion (mahāmoha), gloom (tāmisra), and utter darkness (andhatāmisra). This is the enumeration of the results seen in this world.

In this manner, the enumeration of the results of activity among the internal divisions consisting of causes and effects has been specified; by this, it should be understood that the same applies to the animal, human, and divine realms, including their various manifestations.

Therefore, because they are finite, particular entities are preceded by a state of conjunction, just as in the case of rice, there are states such as root, sprout, leaf, stalk, stem, panicle, husk, awn, flower, pericarp, grain, and kernel which are conjoined; or as, from the conjunction of semen and blood, there arise the stages of the embryo (kalala), the vesicle (arbuda), the fleshy mass (peśī), the formation of the body, and the states of infancy, childhood, youth, and old age.
See especially the cause [discussed] on page 298, note 3.
In that regard, the characteristic of the fruit of the evolution of form is manifest form.

Furthermore, form consists generally of the Great Principle (mahat), the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), the five subtle elements (tanmātra), the eleven organs, and the five gross elements. Evolution is twofold: that which has the purpose of seeking what is beneficial, and that which has the purpose of avoiding what is harmful.
Specifically, there are five sources of action (karmayoni), namely the five beginning with *dhṛti* and the five vital airs (*vāyu*) beginning with *prāṇa*.
The fruit is twofold: seen and unseen.
Among these, the seen fruit is characterized by success (*siddhi*), contentment (*tuṣṭi*), incapacity (*aśakti*), and their opposites.

"In the *Yuktidīpikā*, a commentary on the *Sāṅkhyakārikā* (verse 2), it is stated in the *vṛtti*: 'The acquisition of karma within the cycle of existence, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, is unperceived; this is the manifest.

In the Sāṅkhya texts, in the context of defining the cause of the functions such as *prāṇa* and so forth, a description of *dhṛti* and the others is found under slightly different names—namely, the five winds beginning with *prāṇa*."
...the five vital breaths, beginning with prāṇa—namely prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna—[are mentioned].
But from what does this activity of prāṇa and the others proceed? It is said: it proceeds from the wombs of karma.

For when one has fallen from the Great One (mahat), there arise five wombs of action that constitute the locus for the modified egg (vikṛta-aṇḍa)— namely, steadfastness (dhṛti), faith (śraddhā), happiness (sukhā), the desire to know (vividiṣā), and the lack of desire to know (avividiṣā).
Their characteristics, objects, true nature, and endowment with qualities are as follows: first, the characteristic—fortitude (*dhṛti*) is non-deviation from resolve;
faith (*śraddhā*) is the state of being a seed for the sense of necessity regarding actions prescribed in the scriptures, without aiming for their fruits.
For the mental application (*ābhoga*) of the intellect (*buddhi*), which is mediated by the desire for the fruits of what is seen or heard,
is the wish to know (*vividiṣā*);
the cessation of that is the absence of the wish to know (*avividiṣā*).

...this, first of all, states the true nature of the defining characteristic [of fortitude], and it says: "He who indeed guards his promise in speech, in action, and in resolve—he is devoted to that and firm in that promise; for this is the characteristic of fortitude."
Freedom from envy, celibacy, performing sacrifices, officiating at sacrifices, austerity,
giving gifts, receiving gifts, and purity are recorded as the characteristics of faith.
But he who, desiring happiness, practices knowledge, ritual action, or austerities,
and is constantly intent on expiation— he indeed abides in happiness.

Duality, unity, and separateness; the eternal and the non-eternal; the conscious and the unconscious; the subtle; the existent effect and the non-existent effect; that which is to be desired by those desiring to know, and that which is to be known through the desire to know.
Like one who has drunk poison, fallen asleep, or is intoxicated, the lack of desire to know is always the source for meditators;
this natural course of existence is declared to be that which causes the destruction of both the body and the instruments of action.

Furthermore, the true nature of the objects [of these states] is as follows: *dhṛti* (fortitude) has all things as its object; *śraddhā* (faith) has the stages of life (*āśrama*) as its object; *sukhā* (pleasure) has both perceived and scriptural objects as its object; *vividiṣā* (the desire to know) has the manifest (*vyakta*) as its object; and *avividiṣā* (the lack of desire to know) has the unmanifest (*avyakta*) as its object.

As for the conjunction of the qualities (*guṇas*), *dhṛti* abounds in *rajas* and *tamas*; *śraddhā* abounds in *sattva* and *rajas*; *sukhā* abounds in *sattva* and *tamas*; *vividiṣā* abounds in *rajas*; and *avividiṣā* abounds in *tamas*.

Thus, in the Yuktidīpikā, a commentary on the Sāṅkhyakārikā, verse 29: "...and because of [the word] 'cause' (kāraṇa). (Note: Correcting the manuscript readings *pra* to *ṇāceti* and *pra* to *kāraṇa*).
The divine creation is of eight kinds, that of the animals is fivefold, and the human is of one kind; such, in brief, is the elemental creation. 53.
The meaning is that it is eightfold, consisting of eight types or eight divisions;
namely: Brahmā, Prajāpati, Indra, Pitṛs, Gandharvas, Nāgas, Rakṣasas, and Piśācas.
The animal realm is fivefold: domestic animals, wild beasts, birds, reptiles, and immobile beings;
and the human realm is of one kind, because there is no occurrence of intermediate births—thus it is stated in the Yuktidīpikā commentary on the Sāṅkhyakārikā.
The subtle [elements], those born of mother and father, and those that are abundant—thus there are three kinds of distinctions.
In that regard, the subtle [body], which is based on activity, consists of the eight vital breaths (*prāṇas*) and it transmigrates;
whereas those born of mother and father are of two kinds— viviparous and oviparous—
and their sheaths (*kośas*), which are brought forth by a covering, are characterized by hair, blood, flesh, bone, sinew, and semen.
In that regard, hair, blood, and flesh originate from the mother;
bone, sinew, and semen originate from the father;
and in that very context, others explain eight sheaths (kośa) together with what is eaten and drunk.
But how do these possess the nature of a "sheath" (kośa)? Because of their capacity for enveloping;
just as a silkworm, enveloped by its cocoon, becomes dependent, so too the subtle body, together with the vital breaths, being enveloped by these, becomes dependent and accumulates various karmas.
However, those born from sprouts and those born from sweat are numerous.
but for humans, it is the womb-born (jarāyuja).
...For animals as well, there are four types: the womb-born, such as cows and others; the egg-born, such as birds;
the soil-born, such as grass and the like; and the sweat-born, which is known to belong to small creatures.
Thus, the three kinds of distinctions have been explained—[as stated] in the *Sāṅkhyakārikā* and the *Yuktidīpikā*.
Furthermore, the learned say: "The external body consists of six sheaths."
In other texts, however, the reading *ṣāṭkauśika* is found;
[the word] *udbhidya* is the original.
And this is conceived as the form of the manifest and its activity;
now we shall speak of the fruit.
He asks: "What, then, is that fruit?"
It is said: "That which is indeed this creation of cognition (pratyayasarga), known as error, incapacity, contentment, and attainment—'its fruit' is the completion of the sentence.
The word "this" (eṣa) is used for the purpose of bringing to mind that which is about to be described.
Regarding the term *pratyayasarga*: "pratyaya," "padārtha" (category), and "lakṣaṇa" (characteristic) are synonyms.
Thus, the creation of these *pratyayas* is the *pratyayasarga*, meaning the creation of categories or the creation of characteristics.

Alternatively, "pratyaya" means intellect (*buddhi*), determination (*niścaya*), or resolve (*adhyavasāya*)—these are synonyms. This creation belongs to that [intellect], and is therefore the *pratyayasarga*; it means the effect of the intellect, or the activity of the intellect.
Alternatively, *pratyayasarga* is a creation preceded by cognition; it is said to be preceded by the intellect (*buddhi*).
It consists of that which is called error (viparyaya), that which is called incapacity (aśakti), that which is called contentment (tuṣṭi), and that which is called attainment (siddhi).
Among these, error is the designation of what is not beneficial as being beneficial;
incapacity is the lack of capability due to deficiency.
Contentment (tuṣṭi) is desisting from what one intends to do with the thought that it is insufficient;
attainment (siddhi) is the accomplishment of what is desired—
Sāṅkhyakārikā with Yuktidīpikā, verse 46.

He said: "It was previously stated that perfection (siddhi) is eightfold; let that now be explained. It is replied: "Reasoning (ūha), oral instruction (śabda), study (adhyayana), the three types of removal of suffering (duḥkhavighāta), acquisition of a friend (suhṛtprāpti), and charity (dāna)—these are the eight perfections.

Among these, 'reasoning' (ūha) is when one realizes a desired object through the power of inquiry alone, even apart from perception, inference, and scripture; that is the first perfection, designated as 'the Savior' (tāraka)—it is called 'the Savior' because it carries one across the ocean of saṃsāra."

But when one, being hindered in personal realization, realizes through the instruction of a teacher, that is the second attainment, designated as "Easy Crossing" (*sutāra*); how so? Because by means of this, even in the present time, they cross easily over the perils of existence. But when one is incapable of realizing even through the instruction of another and accomplishes it through study, that is the third attainment, designated as "Causing to Cross" (*tārayanta*).
Although this [Buddha] is the basis for the act of delivering, because he is non-exclusive and possesses a vast range of objects, he is designated as "the Deliverer.
These three [refuges], by means of the methods of practice, enable living beings up to the level of Brahmā to attain their intended goal.
...but for the sake of negating the adversaries of these means of accomplishment, there are three types of affliction by suffering;
the sufferings are threefold, beginning with the internal.

In that regard, having eliminated through the application of medical treatments from the *Āyurveda* those internal [obstacles] such as wind (*vāta*) and so forth which are contrary to success, one accomplishes [the goal] by means of any one of the previous three; this fourth accomplishment is called *pramoda*.
Why? Because living beings, being freed from disease, rejoice (*pramodante*).

When, however, one overcomes obstacles to success arising from external beings (*ādhibhautika*)—such as those caused by humans and so forth—by means of conciliation (*sāma*) or other methods consistent with the duties of an ascetic (*yatidharma*), using any one of the first three [means], that is the fifth attainment (*siddhi*), called "The Joyful" (*pramudita*).
Why? Because one who is undisturbed is indeed joyful.

When, however, one overcomes obstacles to success arising from divine forces (*ādhidaivika*)—such as cold and other dualities (*dvandva*)—in accordance with one's own duty (*svadharma*), by means of any one of the first three [means], that is the sixth attainment, called "The Exultant" (*modamāna*).

How so? Because living beings rejoice when they are not afflicted by the pairs of opposites (*dvandva*), there is the attainment of friends (*suhṛtprāpti*). However, when one, having touched upon what is wholesome, relies upon a true friend and attains the cessation of doubt, that is designated as the seventh perfection, *Ramyakam*.
For in the world, contact with a true friend is delightful; thus, from the name for that [delight], *ramya*, it becomes *ramyakam*.

Regarding *dāna* (giving): when one overcomes misfortune through giving and accomplishes [the goal] by means of any one of the first three, that is the eighth accomplishment (*siddhi*), which is called "Always Joyful" (*sadāpramudita*). For one who is fortunate indeed becomes always joyful; therefore, the cessation of misfortune is "Always Joyful.
Thus, these eight accomplishments have been explained.

Since one accomplishes the desired goal by relying upon these [means], one who wishes to ascend the path transmitted by the ancient teachers should be inclined toward it; thus [it is said] in the Yuktidīpikā on Sāṅkhyakārikā 51:
"by means of the transcendence of [the afflictions] such as [mental] suffering and [physical] materiality..."
Suffering... is internal and twofold: bodily and mental.
Bodily suffering, first of all, is caused by the imbalance of wind (vāta), bile (pitta), and phlegm (śleṣman);
likewise, mental suffering is caused by desire, anger, greed, delusion, despondency, fear, envy, discontent, and the perception of distinctions.
The *ādhibhautika* [suffering] has its cause in humans, domestic animals, wild beasts, birds, reptiles, and stationary beings;
the *ādhidaivika* [suffering] has its cause in cold, heat, wind, rain, lightning, frost, and possession by spirits (*Sāṅkhyakārikā*,
Yuktidīpikā, Kārikā 1).

Contentment (*tuṣṭi*) is the cessation of desire for an object that one intends to acquire due to satisfaction with what is already present; in general, it is one, yet it is infinite with respect to each particular object—as in "satisfied with a hundred" or "satisfied with a thousand. In the scripture, however, there are nine contentments, characterized by specific conditions regarding the attainment or loss of external and internal objects of pleasure, pain, and delusion, because they possess distinct means (*upāya*).

Of these—there are four internal [contentments] known as nature (prakṛti), means (upādāna), time (kāla), and fortune (bhāgya). They are called "internal" because they relate to the body and the embodied soul. When a yogin, desiring to perceive the distinction between the body and the embodied soul, establishes the notion of "self" in what is not the self, that indeed is internal perfection, contentment, satisfaction; the meaning is security. (*Sāṃkhyakārikā*, *Yuktidīpikā*, Kārikā 50).
The four internal [contentments] are known as those consisting of nature, means, time, and fortune;
the five external ones consist of the cessation of objects. Thus, nine contentments are recognized.

They are called "internal" (*ādhyātmika*) because they cause one to know the internal self. There are four types of contentment known as internal: those termed *prakṛti* (nature), *upādāna* (means), *kāla* (time), and *bhāgya* (fortune).

For example, suppose someone knows only the *prakṛti* (primordial nature) but does not know whether it is eternal or non-eternal, conscious or unconscious, possessed of qualities (*saguṇa*) or devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), or all-pervading (*sarvagata*) or non-all-pervading; that is, he does not know these attributes. He is merely satisfied with its mere existence and has renounced the world. For him, there is no liberation. This is the contentment termed *prakṛti*.

The second contentment, called "appropriation" (*upādāna*), is as follows: just as someone, having taken up a triple staff, a water-pot, a mendicant’s bowl, a black antelope skin, a rosary, and so forth, declares, "Liberation will come to me," yet remains satisfied and does not pursue the acquisition of knowledge—there is no liberation for him; this is the second contentment called appropriation. The third contentment, called "time" (*kāla*), is as follows: someone who has not realized the truth says, "Liberation will come in time," and thus does not pursue the acquisition of knowledge, asking, "What is the use of knowledge? For one who is satisfied in this way, there is no liberation; this is the third contentment called time.

The one called "Fortune" (bhāgya) is as follows: someone who has not realized the truth says, "Liberation will come through fortune," and does not pursue the acquisition of knowledge, asking, "What is the use of knowledge? For one who is satisfied in this way, there is no liberation; this is the fourth contentment called "Fortune. Thus, these are the four internal contentments—Jaina Sāṅkhyakārikāvṛtti B.
In the *Yuktidīpikā* on the *Sāṅkhyakārikā*, however, the internal contentments (*ādhyātmika-tuṣṭi*) are explained differently:
"The first contentment is called 'Ambhas' (Water).
Why? Because the principle of *pradhāna* appears as immeasurable (*amita*), being the seed of the universe."
The second contentment is called "water" (salila).
But why is this called water? Because when there is a material cause (upādāna), the modification (vikāra) dissolves into it.
The third contentment is designated as "the flood" (ogha).
But why is this time called a "flood"? Because, like a torrent of water, it carries everything away.
The fourth contentment is called "rain" (*vṛṣṭi*).
Why, then, is it called rain? Because it nourishes all sentient beings.
For just as even withered grasses, creepers, and the like are replenished upon receiving rain, so too is there a replenishment for all living beings through the transformation of their fortune;
therefore, because of this similarity to rain, contentment called "fortune" (bhāgya) is designated as "rain" (vṛṣṭi)—
Sāṅkhyakārikā with Yuktidīpikā, verse 50.
There are five external contentments, which will be explained;
and there are also five cessations from external objects.

And these are as follows—the defects of acquisition (*arjana*), preservation (*rakṣaṇa*), destruction (*kṣaya*), lack of contentment (*atṛpti*), and injury (*hiṃsā*). Among these, "acquisition" refers to engaging in agriculture, cattle-rearing, trade, and so forth, taking the objects of the senses—sound, touch, form, taste, and smell—as the motive. Regarding this, one desists from sense-objects upon realizing that the pain of exertion and toil involved in acquiring them is suffering; having desisted, one attains contentment. This is the fifth contentment.

The suffering of protection (*rakṣaṇa-duḥkha*) is as follows: the guarding of acquired wealth and grain from kings, thieves, and so forth is itself a form of suffering; by desisting from this, one attains contentment—this is the sixth contentment.

The suffering of depletion (*kṣaya-duḥkha*) is as follows: even when guarding has been performed, one realizes that things being consumed are depleted; thinking thus, one desists and attains contentment—this is the seventh contentment.

Having reflected that even when remedies have been applied for the acquisition, preservation, and depletion [of objects], there is no cessation of thirst (*vaitṛṣṇya*) regarding the sense organs, one desists from sense-objects; having desisted, one attains contentment. This is the eighth contentment.

Even when remedies have been applied for acquisition, preservation, depletion, and lack of satisfaction, sense-objects cannot be acquired without injury, without violence, and without obstructing living beings through the activities of acquisition and so forth; therefore, having desisted from sense-objects, one attains contentment—this is the ninth contentment.
Thus, by these contentments, there is no liberation from ignorance; rather, contentment arises through dispassion alone.
In this way, these nine contentments have been explained—four internal and five external.
Regarding these nine contentments, there are the following designations here: *ambhaḥ*, *salila*, *ogha*, *vṛṣṭi*, *sutāra*, *supāra*, *sunetra*, *marīcika*, and *uttamāmbhasika*.
Yoga-sāṅkhya-kārikā-vṛtti, Chapter 50: *kṣayāsaṅga* (detachment from decay).
One who has withdrawn from sound, touch, form, taste, and smell does so because of observing [the faults of] acquisition, preservation, decay, attachment, and violence.
"...when attachment to the enjoyment of sense objects occurs, there is no tranquility of the senses; this is the fault of attachment" (Sāṅkhyakārikā, Gauḍapādabhāṣya, Kārikā 50).
[The commentary] is called *Sutāra*, *Supāra*, *Sunetra*, and *Mārīcottamā*. Primary source.

And for one who has set out for the sake of happiness, there is mostly only suffering; from this insight, one attains equanimity. This is the fifth contentment (*tuṣṭi*), which is called "Easy Crossing" (*sutāra*). Why, then, is it called "Easy Crossing"? Because by means of this method, they cross over the straits of sense-objects; thus it is "Easy Crossing. The sixth contentment is called "Good Crossing" (*supāra*).
How, then, is it called *supāram*? Because by means of this, one goes happily to the further shore (*pāra*) of the ocean of sense-objects;
thus, the seventh contentment is called *sunetram*.
How, then, is it called *sunetram*? Because by means of this, one leads oneself happily to the state of absolute liberation (*kaivalya*); thus, it is *sunetram*.

The eighth contentment is called *sumārīca*. Why is it called *sumārīca*? Because of the root *arca*, meaning "to worship," there occurs for the yogin who has withdrawn from attachment to sense objects a state that is beautifully honored (*sumarcitam*). The ninth contentment is designated as *uttamābhaya*.

How so? For among all fears for living beings, the fear of injury (*hiṃsā*) is indeed the greatest; therefore, because that has been removed, it is called "supreme security" (*uttamābhaya*), according to the *Yuktidīpikā* on Sāṅkhya Kārikā 50.
Furthermore, incapacity (*aśakti*) is defined as the eleven impairments of the sense organs together with the impairments of the intellect (*buddhi*).
There are seventeen types of "slaughter" (vadha) of the intellect due to the perversions of contentment and power.
...The incapacity of the sense organs to grasp their own respective objects is called "slaughter," as it is like being slain.

In this world, a certain Devadatta, seized by dispassion, calls out to Yajñadatta and says: "O Yajñadatta, I am suffering; what shall I do? He is told by him: "Acquire the knowledge of Sāṅkhya; you will go to the end of suffering."

Thus addressed by Yajñadatta, Devadatta replied: "I am unable to attain the knowledge of Sāṅkhya because I am deaf and cannot hear my teacher’s words; being incapable of service, how shall I attain knowledge? In this same way, defects such as blindness, muteness, and insanity—which are impairments of the senses—should be understood as being incapable of grasping their respective objects. Thus, these eleven types of sensory impairment are called *aśakti* (incapacity); incapacity is defined together with the defects of the intellect (*buddhi*).
The "destructions of the intellect" (*buddhivadhāḥ*) are the destructions of the intellect; by these destructions of the intellect, incapacity is indicated here.

To this, he asks: what are those destructions of the intellect, and how many are they? There are seventeen destructions of the intellect, which arise from the inversion of contentment (*tuṣṭi*) and perfection (*siddhi*).
These seventeen destructions will be explained when contentment and perfection are being explained.
Deafness, blindness, loss of smell, muteness, and dullness; insanity, hoarseness, leprosy, impotence, upward movement of wind (udāvarta), and lameness. (Sāṅkhyakārikā-vṛtti B, Kārikā 49)

In that regard, deafness is the impairment of the ear, blindness of the eye, loss of smell of the nose, muteness of speech, numbness of the tongue, insanity of the mind, skin disease of the skin, lameness of the hand, impotence of the generative organ, upward movement of wind (constipation) of the anus, and lameness of the feet; thus there are these eleven impairments of the sense organs (*indriyavadha*),
according to the *Yuktidīpikā* on Sāṅkhya Kārikā 49.
And incapacity (*aśakti*), due to the impairment of the instruments (*karaṇa*), becomes twenty-eight-fold; this [phrase] continues [from the previous verse].

Among these, the impairment of the external instruments, together with the mind, is of eleven kinds, while the impairment of the intellect (*buddhi*) is of seventeen kinds. These are the varieties of incapacity, according to the *Yuktidīpikā* on Sāṅkhya Kārikā 47.

There are five varieties of error: *tamas*, *moha*, *mahāmoha*, *tāmisra*, and *andhatāmisra*. Among these, the first error, called *tamas*, is the conceit of superiority regarding an inferior object of cognition for one who is engaged in what is not the highest good. It is the grasping of a self in material forms such as the head, hands, and so forth—thinking, "I am he who has broad shoulders, white teeth, copper-colored eyes, and long arms."

Likewise, regarding the functions of the instruments characterized by hearing, touch, tasting, smelling, speaking, grasping, moving, excreting, enjoying, volition, self-identification, and determination, the initial grasp occurring at the first moment—such as "I am the hearer," "I am the seer," and so forth—is called the secondary delusion (*moha*) compared to the former. Furthermore, the attachment to external objects in the form of "this is mine" is the secondary one compared to the former; it is called great delusion (*mahāmoha*).
Anger is the fourth inversion; it is the secondary one compared to the former and is designated as darkness (*tāmisra*).

...the fifth perversion is despair at death, which is inferior to the former; it is designated as *andhatāmisra*. (Sāṅkhyakārikā, Yuktidīpikā, Kārikā 47) [The hells] are *tāmisra* and *andhatāmisra*. (Praśastapādabhāṣya)

The point is this: since conjunction presupposes conjunction, it is impossible for it to exist in that which is one and non-dual; therefore, one must postulate multiple causes for that which inheres in a single object despite its manifold nature, and those [causes] are none other than *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.

2.1 Likewise, having observed that limited differentiated entities such as roots and sprouts are preceded by a combination [of causes], one who infers that external and internal differentiated entities must also be preceded by a combination because they are limited, faces the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* are preceded by a combination, since there is no difference in their being objects of inference.
— Thus, in the Śaṅkara-bhāṣya on the Brahmasūtras, 2.2.1.

Because of the finite measure of differentiated effects, that which is finite is seen to have an origin; for example—the root, sprout, leaf, stalk, stem, husk, chaff, awn, flower, milk, rice-grain, and kernel are finite.

Likewise, the differentiated effects characterized by the Great Principle (mahat), ego-consciousness (ahaṅkāra), the senses, the subtle elements (tanmātra), and the gross elements are finite; therefore, they must be preceded by a cause.
That which is their cause is the unmanifest (avyakta);
furthermore, the embryo and so forth reside within the effect.

When the subtle body enters the mother’s womb at the time of birth, the mother’s blood and the father’s semen effect its growth; the stages of the embryo—*kalala*, *arbuda*, *ghana*, *peśī*, *māṃsa*, *peśī*, *garbha*, childhood, youth, old age, and so forth—are produced by means of the essence of food and drink from the mother. Therefore it is said: "And the *kalala* and other stages reside in the effect" (*Jaina Sāṅkhyakārikāvṛtti*, Kārikā 43). *Peśī* (variant reading).
For this reason as well, the Pradhāna exists because differentiated entities stand in a cause-and-effect relationship:
Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas, which exist in the form of sound and so forth, perform their functions for one another through illumination, activity, and restraint.
Sattva, existing in the form of sound and so forth, manifests the activity of the other two for its own sake; likewise, Rajas impels them, and Tamas restrains them.

The earth and other elements, originated from sound and the rest, perform their mutual purposes through support, cohesion, digestion, expansion, and the granting of space, respectively, according to the order of their origination;
the sense organs likewise assist one another by cooperating in the perception of each other's objects.
That which makes an object known to another, acquires it for it, protects it, refines it, or deposits it within it is the cause, while the other is the effect.

The effect (the body) performs its function for the sake of the instruments (the senses) by means of providing a locus, accomplishing [purposes], self-manifestation, and enjoyment; the instrument (the sense organ), in turn, performs its function for the sake of the effect through the healing of growths, wounds, and fractures, as well as through contraction, protection, and maintenance.

Thus, there is mutual assistance among external and internal things—whether divine, human, or animal—including their manifold varieties. Such distinctions, such as those of caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*), are to be understood as having a single agent, characterized by actions like protection, gathering, service, worship, nourishment, stability, and attendance, because they stand in a relationship of mutual assistance and being assisted, just like a bed and so forth.
Therefore, the Pradhāna exists; this is the existence [of the Pradhāna] established through the sequence of the existence of beings.

pṛ. 260–268, note 1: Having set aside the sequence of the commencement of creation described therein, the reading *ārambhotkrameṇa* (by a sequence of commencement) appears more appropriate here, since the earth is taken up at the beginning. However, if this seems unsatisfactory, the reading *ārambhāt krameṇa* (in sequence from the commencement) should be adopted; and it should be construed with the phrase *dhṛtisaṅgrahapaktivyūhāvakāśadānaiḥ* (through support, cohesion, digestion, expansion, and providing space), according to the Vṛtti-saṃgraha-prakaraṇa.

However, their mutual assistance when existing together is not denied; for example, that of earth and the other elements through supporting, cohesion, maturation, structuring, and providing space—[as stated in] the *Yuktidīpikā* on Sāṅkhya Kārikā 15, p. 80, l.
26: "Earth itself is the earth-element (*pṛthivīdhātu*), because it maintains properties such as supporting."
— *Nayacakravṛtti*, p.

267–1: The five great elements (mahābhūta) are established as follows: space (*ākāśa*) for providing room; earth (*bhūmi*) for movement; water (*āpaḥ*) for cohesion and purification; fire (*agni*) for the digestion of food; and wind (*vāyu*) for expansion. (*Jaina Sāṅkhya-kārikā-vṛtti B*, Kārikā 39).
He asks: "What, then, is the mutual relationship of cause and effect among the manifest?

It is said: First, regarding the qualities (*guṇas*)—namely *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*—the manner in which they function through mutual assistance by means of their characteristics of illumination, activity, and restraint has been explained in the Sāṅkhya Kārikā (verse 12), beginning with "consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion.
Likewise, the fact that sound and the other objects reside together in a single substratum for the sake of one another within earth and the other elements [is also established].

The mutual acquisition, preservation, and refinement of the ears and other [senses] belong to the instrument from the perspective of the effect; the acquisition of the site, the means of accomplishment, and the manifestation of the effect belong to the effect from the perspective of the instrument. For the elements such as earth, there are growth, injury, breaking, healing, drying, and protection through support, cohesion, digestion, differentiation, and the provision of space. The state of being cattle and so forth belongs to gods, humans, and animals through seasonal ordainment, sacrifice, nourishment, and consumption. Among the social classes (varṇas), there is mutual study, worldly transaction, legal procedure, and engagement in their respective duties and spheres of activity.
Furthermore, other matters should be understood from the world as they may occur;
see Sāṅkhyakārikā Yuktidīpikā, verse 15, commentary.
See page 298, note 3.
Because it is the cause of the body's growth, healing of wounds and fractures, and so forth, [the *Praśastapādabhāṣya*] states "of the body.
Growth (*vṛddhi*) is the accumulation of parts; the healing (*saṃrohaṇa*) of fractures and wounds refers to the rejoining of broken and separated portions of bone, skin, and flesh.
Thus, let it be seen in the *Praśastapādabhāṣya-Ātmanirūpaṇa* of the *Kiraṇāvalī*, note 2:
"The animal, human, and divine [bodies] exist for the sake of one another."
Vyāsabhāṣya: "Because they serve each other's purpose."

The human body is indeed sustained by the consumption of animals, birds, wild beasts, reptiles, and immobile beings; likewise, the body of a tiger and such is sustained by the consumption of humans, domestic animals, wild beasts, and so forth; similarly, the bodies of animals, birds, wild beasts, and others are sustained by the consumption of immobile beings and the like; likewise, even a celestial body, when being worshipped with goats, deer, *kapiñjala* birds, meat, clarified butter, sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*), mango branches, bundles of grass, and other offerings presented by humans, is sustained by that consumption; and in this way, even a deity sustains humans and others through the granting of boons, rain, and so forth—thus, the meaning is that there is a mutual dependence for the sake of one another.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth [sūtra] in the *Tattvavaiśāradī*, the commentary on the *Pātañjalayogadarśana* composed by Vyāsa, written by Vācaspatimiśra.
What are the [eight] limbs?
...sprinkling, worship, and nourishment...
[of] the various conceptualizations of the beginningless [stream], such as the support and the supported... [and so forth].

The duties of the social classes (varṇas)—namely Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas—and the stages of life (āśramas)—namely the student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and the ascetic—are described in Praśastapāda’s commentary on the Vaiśeṣika-sūtra; they are also found in the Dharmaśāstras such as the Smṛtis, which define dharma. Furthermore, this is so because powers (śaktis) consist merely of states of potentiality.
The potencies of causes and effects—whether presided over by a conscious agent or not—remain capable of producing their respective effects throughout the three periods of time.

For instance: the existence of potency prior to activity is inferred from the observation of activity; its existence at the time of activity is known from the perception of the completion [of the effect]; and its existence subsequent to activity is known from the observation that it persists even after the activity has ceased.

Thus, having perceived the manifest as possessing a beginning and an end, there exists a state of the power of the manifest; for that which has an unstable power lacks both a beginning and an end, like a flower in the sky, whereas that which possesses a stable power necessarily exists in those states, just as clay exists in the form of a lump and so forth.
Therefore, because the activity of the power of the manifest is perceived, the Pradhāna exists—so it is said in the *Abhāva* [section].
Alternatively, the reading here might also be "vā" (or);
furthermore, because activity proceeds from power,
whatever activity whatsoever is observed here in the world, all of that proceeds from power.

For example: just as a potter’s engagement in the making of a jar occurs due to the presence of a power characterized by the arrangement of instruments such as the rod, and since this [engagement] of the manifest exists because it is an effect, its activity occurs through that state;
therefore, that [manifest] must also possess a power, and that which is this power is the unmanifest.
He said: Prior to activity, there is an absence of capacity, because activity is not perceived.
To this we reply: No, because it is unestablished.
Therefore, the power exists prior to its manifestation.
Furthermore, regarding what was said—that [the cause] perishes at that very moment—we reply: No, because we observe the completion of the effect.
If destruction were to occur at the very same time as the activity, the effect would not reach its completion, because the effect is caused by that [activity].
Therefore, there is no destruction of the potencies at the time of their activity.
Why does it not exist even after the time of activity? Because activity is observed again.
Therefore, the powers abide throughout the three times—
Sāṅkhyakārikā with Yuktidīpikā, verse 15.

For this reason as well, the Pradhāna exists: because the attainment of non-differentiation of manifold forms (vaiśvarūpya) occurs through the proximity of place, time, measure, power, and form; and because cessation occurs through the necessity of either their destruction or non-destruction.

The transformational variety of tastes and other qualities of water and earth is observed in stationary things; likewise, [the variety] of stationary things in mobile ones, of mobile things in stationary ones, of stationary things in stationary ones, and of mobile things in mobile ones.

By reason of the non-interruption of the genus, everything is of the nature of all things; however, due to the constraints of place, time, form, and cause, their self-manifestation does not occur simultaneously. We consider this manifold variety of tastes and so forth to be a transformational state of water and earth, while for other elements it is a transformation of something else. Thus, there must necessarily be a state of non-differentiation (avibhāga) wherein one thing becomes another;

and that wherein there is non-differentiation is the Pradhāna, because this manifold variety is preceded by a cause of non-differentiation, just as the variegation of a peacock's plumage is preceded by the essence within its egg.

Therefore, Pradhāna exists. By these five reasons—known as *samanvaya* (homogeneity), *parimāṇa* (measurement), *upakāra* (assistance), *śakti* (power), and *pravṛtti-vaiśvarūpya* (the diversity of activity)—Pradhāna is established as that which is designated by the names *sāmānya* (commonality), *saṃsarga* (conjunction), *ekakartṛ* (single agent), *śaktimat* (possessing power), and *śaktyavibhāga* (non-distinction of powers). For this very reason, it possesses unity and purposefulness. It exists for the sake of another, because things that act in combination exist for the sake of another, like beds and so forth. From this, the existence of Puruṣa, its distinctness [from Pradhāna], and the plurality of Puruṣas are established.

The cessation of the Pradhāna occurs after it has accomplished its purpose for the Puruṣa from beginning to end—either like water flowing through rice or like a dancer finishing her performance; such is the nature of the conjunction and disjunction of the Pradhāna and the Puruṣa, and this much is the fruit of the knowledge resulting from this scripture.
Furthermore: "From the non-separation [of the Puruṣa], the manifoldness of forms [is explained]."

In this world, the non-distinction of that which possesses manifold forms is observed; for example, water and the like [merge] into earth and water, and the Great Principle (mahat) and the others possess manifold forms. Therefore, these too must exist in a state of non-distinction.
That which is this non-distinction is the Unmanifest (avyakta);
therefore, the Unmanifest exists.

He asks: "What, then, is this *vaiśvarūpya* (multiformity), or who is the *viśvarūpa* (the multiform one)? It is said in reply: by *vaiśvarūpya*, we mean a specific state (*viśiṣṭam avasthānam*), namely the absence of distinction (*astamitaviśeṣatva*) or non-differentiation (*avibhāga*).

Since a particular (*viśeṣa*) is preceded by a universal (*sāmānya*), this is what is meant by the statement [in the Sāṅkhya Kārikā]: "from the non-differentiation of the multiform" (*avibhāgād vaiśvarūpyasya*). (Sāṅkhya Kārikā with Yuktidīpikā, Kārikā 15).
See page 11, line 27, regarding [the discussion on] non-interruption and interruption:
"Just as this manifold variety of tastes and so forth exists even in water and earth, so too does it exist in stationary beings within moving ones, and in moving beings within stationary ones."

Thus, because birth is not subject to annihilation, we consider that everything is of the nature of everything else; there exists the Pradhāna, wherein the subtle mark (liṅga) consisting of Mahat and the rest goes to dissolution. Thus, this dissolution is inevitable; that wherein dissolution occurs is the Pradhāna.
Therefore, the Pradhāna exists;
thus it is stated in the *Jainasāṅkhyakārikāvṛtti* (B), and with a slight variation in terminology in the *Māṭharavṛtti*, on verse 15:
"Everything has everything as its essence."

Regarding this, it has been said in the *Vyāsabhāṣya*: "The transformational diversity of taste and other qualities in water and earth is observed in stationary things; likewise, [the qualities] of stationary things [are seen] in moving things, and those of moving things in stationary things.
Thus, without the destruction of their respective classes, everything is of the nature of everything.
However, due to the constraints of place, time, form, and cause, there is no simultaneous manifestation of these natures."
He demonstrates that very point— namely, "everything has everything as its essence"— with the verse beginning with "of water and earth."

For it is observed that water—possessing taste, form, touch, and sound—and earth—possessing smell, taste, form, touch, and sound—undergo transformation (*pāriṇāmika*) into the manifold variety of tastes and other qualities found in the roots, fruits, flowers, and sprouts of trees, creepers, shrubs, and the like.
This [variety] cannot be a transformation of earth which is not of such a nature, nor of water which is not of such a nature; for it has been established that "what is non-existent does not arise.
Likewise, a diversity of tastes and other qualities is observed among stationary beings within mobile ones, such as humans, cattle, wild animals, and so forth.
For while they consume fruits and the like, they indeed obtain a perfection consisting of various forms and qualities;

thus, the transformative (pāriṇāmika) nature seen in mobile beings is observed in stationary ones as well—namely, that it is said that by the sprinkling of blood, the fruits of the pomegranate tree become as large as palm fruits.
He concludes with the word "thus" (evam).
Thus, everything such as water, earth, and so forth, consists of all tastes and other qualities;
he states the reason for this: "by way of the non-interruption of the genus," meaning that because the genus of water-ness, earth-ness, and so on, is recognized everywhere, it is not interrupted.

Now, if everything consists of the nature of all things, alas! since everything is present at all times, in all places, and in every way, it would follow that there must be the manifestation of all entities simultaneously; for indeed, an effect whose complete causes are present ought not to be delayed. To this, he says: "Space, time... [and so forth].

Although every cause contains everything within its nature, nevertheless, that which is the specific location for a particular effect—such as Kashmir being the location for saffron—even though [the potential for] those [other effects] exists there, they do not manifest in places such as Pañcāla; thus, saffron is not manifested in Pañcāla and so forth. Likewise, during the summer, the rainy season does not manifest, and therefore rice does not [ripen] then. Similarly, a doe does not give birth to a human, because the manifestation of a human form does not occur in her. In this way, one who lacks merit does not experience happiness, because the manifestation of the cause of merit does not occur in him.
Therefore, because of the obstruction caused by place, time, form, and causal conditions, and due to their removal, there is no simultaneous manifestation of the self-natures of entities;
thus ends the third chapter, verse 14, in the *Tattvavaiśāradī*, a commentary on Vyāsa’s *Bhāṣya* on Patañjali’s *Yoga-sūtra*, composed by Vācaspatimiśra.
It appears that the indeclinable *te* functions in the sense of *tataḥ* (from that/thence); see page 11, line 27.
The usage of the indeclinable *te* in the sense of *tataḥ* is seen frequently even in the Pātañjala-Mahābhāṣya, as for example: "He says 'Brahmadatta' when it is not Brahmadatta;
we think that he [is] like Brahmadatta."
Pāṇini-Mahābhāṣya 1.1.22,

Through their respective concomitances, the ten root-meanings are established: through commonality, there is universality (*sāmānya*); through dimension, conjunction (*saṃsarga*); through benefit, a single agent; from the activity of power, the power of the possessor of power (*śaktimat-śakti*); and through the comprehension of manifold forms, non-differentiation (*avibhāga*). They are as follows: existence, oneness, purposefulness, subservience to another, otherness, and cessation.
Union, separation, plurality of spirits, the persistence of the body, and the subsistence of the remainder—
by these five affirmative reasons, namely "because of the finite measure of differences" (Sāṅkhya Kārikā 15), the existence, unity, and purposiveness of the Pradhāna are established.
From the Sūtra "Because the aggregate is for the sake of another" (Kārikā 17), its being for the sake of another is established;
and from the Sūtra "The Spirit is likewise the opposite of that" (Kārikā 11), the distinctness of the Pradhāna and the Puruṣa is established;
and from the Sūtra "Having shown the spectacle to the stage" (Kārikā 59), [the Spirit's] cessation is established.
The conjunction [of the self with the body] is established by the sūtra "for the purpose of the Puruṣa's perception" (Ka.
21); the disjunction [from the body] is established by the sūtra "when the separation from the body has occurred" (Ka.
68); and the plurality of Puruṣas is established by the sūtra "of births, deaths, and instruments" (Ka. 18).
"The residual activity is established like the whirling of a potter's wheel" (Sāṅkhyakārikā 67);
thus it is stated in the *Jeṣṭha Sāṅkhya-kārikā-vṛtti* (B), and likewise in the *Māṭhara-vṛtti* on verse 72:
"The existence of the Pradhāna, its unity, its purposiveness, and its distinctness..."
Existence for the sake of another, as well as non-unity, disjunction, conjunction, the state of being a remnant, subsistence, and non-agency— these are remembered as the ten root-meanings. (Verse 2)
therein, existence and oneness are established by five reasons.
Possession of purpose consists in the relationship of cause and effect;
it is the state of being for the sake of another, because those things that act in combination exist for the sake of another;
and for this very reason, there is a distinctness from the three guṇas in the power of consciousness.
The plurality of Puruṣas is established by such [sūtras] as "of birth, death, and the instruments" (Kārikā 18);

the conjunction [of Puruṣa and Prakṛti] is for the sake of the Puruṣa's seeing [Prakṛti], as stated in "for the sake of the Puruṣa's seeing" (Kārikā 21); and the disjunction [of Puruṣa and Prakṛti] occurs when the body has been separated, as stated in "when the body has been separated" (Kārikā 68).

"From the attainment of right knowledge" (Sāṅkhyakārikā 67)—this is the remaining [portion of the] commentary; and "from that [state of] error" (Sāṅkhyakārikā 19)—thus the non-agency of the *puruṣa*. These are the ten root topics according to the *Yuktidīpikā* on the *Sāṅkhyakārikā*, page 5.
Oneness, purposefulness, and being for the sake of another are stated with reference to the Pradhāna;
distinctness, non-agency, and multiplicity are stated with reference to the Puruṣa;
and existence, disjunction, and conjunction are stated with reference to both.

"Functioning (vṛtti) and persistence (sthiti) refer to the gross and the subtle," as stated in the *Sāṅkhyatattvakaumudī* on verse 72. [The text appears to contain a scribal corruption regarding the term *upalakṣaṇāt*].

The activity of *pradhāna* is for the sake of the *puruṣa*; and that purpose is twofold: beginning with the perception of sound and so forth, and ending with the perception of the distinction between the *guṇas* and the *puruṣa*. (Sāṅkhyakārikā-vṛtti, Māṭhara-vṛtti, Kārikā 66; Raṅganātha’s commentary).
Just as a dancer, having exhibited herself to the audience, desists from her dance,
so does Nature (prakṛti), having manifested herself to the Spirit (puruṣa), desist.
— from the *Sāṅkhyakārikā*,

the result of measurement [is established] because of the well-known nature of worldly convention, and so forth; this should be understood as explained up to the point concerning "those that are reversed" (*āvītānām*).

For the sake of purifying these very five *vītas*, there are exactly five *āvītas*. Thus, having established the grasp of the *pradhāna* by means of these five *vītas*, we shall now do so again by means of the *āvītas*.
It was previously stated that an *āvīta* is the act of establishing one's own position through the refutation of the opposing position.

The counter-arguments to this [doctrine] are all the extremist theories concerning the Person (puruṣa), the Lord (īśvara), and the atom (aṇu), as well as the theories of transformation (vikāra-puruṣa) and the nihilists (vaināśika).

Among these, we shall first state the refutation of the nihilists. Why? Because some nihilists hold [the following view], starting from the point where it is said: "Because of non-perception, it does not exist. Having reached the consequence of deviation—namely, that there is no arising of a second head which is unaccepted and non-existent—[the argument continues]: "It will not exist even in the future time," as seen on page 314, line 3.

Furthermore, his opponents— those who propound a Supreme Person (Puruṣeśvara) and atoms, as well as the Nihilists (Vaināśikas), those who maintain primordial matter (Prākṛtikas), and those who maintain the transformation of the Person— are refuted first.

"In order to obstruct their desires, the teachers of subtle intellect have composed difficult logical tangles within their own treatises," as stated in the opening verses of the Yuktidīpikā commentary on the Sāṅkhyakārikā.

Furthermore, as counter-arguments against that proponent of the Lord of Men (Puruṣeśa) and the atom (anu), there are the nihilists (vaināśika), those who hold to primordial matter (prākṛtika), and likewise those who hold to the soul as a transformation (vikārapuruṣa); for the sake of refuting their views, the teachers of subtle intellect [have composed this work].
"Difficult and dense with logic have been composed by opponents within their own systems"—
thus it is stated in the opening verses of the *Yuktidīpikā* commentary on the *Sāṅkhyakārikā*. Furthermore,
those opponents of his [the Sāṅkhya] are proponents of the doctrines of Puruṣa, Īśvara, and atoms.
The nihilists, the proponents of primordial matter, and likewise the proponents of the transformation-self—
so that their desires might be thwarted, the teachers of subtle intellect have composed,
within their own treatises, difficult arguments that are like dense thickets of logic.
Thus, in the *Yuktidīpikā* commentary on the *Sāṅkhyakārikā*, regarding the opening verses, Hītakarapāda says:

"Furthermore, if the manifestation of what was previously non-existent were possible, then those seeking wealth would make pearls, gems, silver, and gold out of grass, dust, and sand. Why? Because the production of a non-entity is laborious, whereas the production of an entity is easy."

But this is not done; therefore, [the objection] beginning with "it is improper" is incorrect, because the answer has already been stated, and the procedure is flawed. Furthermore, if there is the production of a manifest entity from what is non-existent due to the absence of a source (yoni), the consequence would be its being a single unity. Because of the absence of *pradhāna*, it would follow that this manifest world is merely a generality (*sāmānya*) devoid of particularity (*viśeṣa*). Why? Because particulars are preceded by a generality. For in the world, particulars are observed to be preceded by a generality; for example, the states of curd, whey, clots, butter, clarified butter, *ariṣṭa*, *kilāṭa*, and *kūrcikā* are all preceded by milk.
But there is no entity whatsoever that exists when [the cause] is non-existent, such that specific manifestations could be preceded by it;
therefore, this manifest world is merely a generality, devoid of particularity. However, this is not so [in the case of the effect], and thus this manifest world does not arise from the non-existent.
Furthermore, since this [world] does not arise from that which already exists,
by the method of elimination it is logical that this manifest world arises from Pradhāna alone;
therefore, Pradhāna exists.
This is the *avīta* [form] of the *anvaya-vīta*:
"Milk transforms quickly into the states of curd, whey, buttermilk, fresh butter, clarified butter, *ariṣṭa*, *kilāṭa*, and *kūrcikā*."
YDhSāṅkhKāVṛ A, Māṭharavṛ, Kā 16:
"Is it not this [that is] 'this'? No, it is not this; Bhāṣya.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "and what else," etc., it means that there would be the consequence of an infinite regress because of the absence of a source (*yoni*); this is because dimension (*parimāṇa*) is invariably concomitant with being preceded by conjunction (*saṃsarga*).

Because of the absence of a primary cause (pradhāna), it would follow that this manifest world is without measure and lacks stability; why so? For in the world, a measure of existing things is observed through scales, weights, cubits, fathoms, ropes, and bodily dimensions. However, there is no such thing as an entity that exists in the absence [of a cause] which, being apprehended, could abide within a measure.
Therefore, it would follow that this [world] is without measure and unstable; but since this is not the case, this manifest world does not arise from non-existence.
And this does not arise from that which already exists;
by process of elimination, it arises from the Pradhāna alone;
therefore, that [Pradhāna] exists.
"A *vyāma* is the distance between the tips of the two outstretched arms," according to the *Amarakośa*, chapter 2.
6.87 Without attachment,
[he is] liberated.

Furthermore, because it would follow that there is no continuity of a single genus (*ekajātisamanvaya*), that very specific example—such as "the pot in the cooking-pot" and so forth—is stated here for the purpose of establishing the universal-particular (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*) relationship.

Here, the opponent might say: "Since only the particular is observed, there is the arising of what was previously non-existent; for instance, due to the distinction between properties such as shape, weight, and so on."

The answer to that is as follows: there is no fault because there is assistance through that very nature (*tādrūpyeṇa*). This is because, by means of the transformation of the distinction between properties (*dharmabheda-pariṇati*), one brings about the worldly course of events; thus, by demonstrating the distinction in assistance, it touches upon even a slight trace of the "non-erroneous" (*avīta*) character of the "non-erroneous" (*vīta*) relation of cause and effect. This is to be understood from that very text, as explained previously, namely: "Animals, humans, and gods would not act for the sake of one another."

In this regard, as for what was stated—that because of the exclusion of both the elements (*bhūta*) and their aggregates, this manifest world is merely a particularity, and therefore it arises from the non-existent (*asat*)—that is incorrect. Having thus dispelled the doubt regarding the continuity of the non-existent (*asatsamanvaya*), the Teacher has explained at length, up until the point where he says, "Therefore, this is logical: because of the absence of a womb (source), there would be the consequence of [unbridled] differentiation," that this is an *āvīta* (reductio ad absurdum) argument based on positive concomitance (*anvaya*).

He has established it in exactly that manner when he said, "Because of the continuity of a similar genus, etc. By the inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*), the remaining three types of *āvīta* arguments are also indicated in that same sequence.
Except in the *Vāprabhā*, elsewhere it is *°sthāpa* (pā);
*°svāpa* (ḍe; līṃ).
The letter Ā has the nature of water; it possesses weight, roughness, obstruction, stability,
persistence, divisibility, endurance, a dark luster, and universal enjoyability.
Thus have these duties pertaining to the earth been described; now learn of those others, even more distinguished,
which pervade water, fire, air, and space.
Moisture, subtlety, radiance, whiteness, softness, weight,
coolness, protection, purity, and refreshing clarity are the qualities of water.
The upward-moving light is burning, cooking, light, radiant, perishable, and powerful;
it is distinct from the two preceding elements.
Moving horizontally, purity, projection, impelling, strength,
roughness, lack of shadow, and coldness— these are the various attributes of wind.
Sarvatogati, Avyūha, and Viṣkambha— these three should be known as space-like phenomena that are contrary to the aforementioned phenomena.
But that which is the common effect of those things joined together— such as cows and the like—
is distinct from their mutual properties; of this there is no doubt.

In this regard, the earth benefits the world and other primary elements through its qualities such as shape (ākāra) and so forth. First, by way of shape: it brings about the formation of the shapes of cows, jars, and the like; and through its heaviness (gaurava), it provides them with stability.
From its roughness comes the cohesion of water and clarity; from its capacity for obstruction comes the veiling of undesirable things;
from its stability comes the maintenance of the livelihood, sustenance, and stability of living beings and other elements.

From stability (*sthiti*) comes the assistance provided by the proximity of the *mātrās* and so forth; from differentiation (*bheda*) comes the production of jars and other objects, as well as the arrangement (*vyūha*) of the constituent parts;
and from forbearance (*kṣānti*) comes fitness for experience and the accomplishment of effects such as shade, like the excellence of night due to its dark shadow.
Because it is the object of enjoyment for all, there is indeed favor toward all beings;
thus, benefit is rendered to the world through moisture and other qualities, as well as to other elements:
through moisture, there is the excellence of form; through [moisture], there is the counteracting of wind and the quenching of fire, and the cohesion of the earth.
Due to its subtlety, there is penetration;
due to its whiteness, the manifestation of the moon and so forth; due to its softness, bathing and immersion occur as a single action, and hard objects are bent down.
Out of reverence and because of his lineage, for the sake of favoring living beings, he is a stream; through his coolness, he is the remedy for heat;
and by means of protection, he brings peace to the terrible calamities among the people.
Due to its purity, there is an accumulation of merit; there is the rule of purification even when no [visible] injury occurs, and because it is continuous, there is a collection of substances.
Likewise, through its upward movement and other qualities, it benefits the world and other elements even by means of its mere nature as a property (*dharmamātra*).

From its upward movement comes the accomplishment of digestion and illumination; from its nature as fire comes the purification of substances, and from its power to burn comes the production of alkali, the counteracting of cold, and the heat of the atmosphere for the purpose of producing sound.
From its nature as a digester comes the sweating of those to be sweated and the cooking of food.
The capacity for action in the constituent parts of the earth, as well as the internal and external transformation of chyle, blood, flesh, sinews, bone, marrow, and semen;
