the overcoming of combustibility due to lightness; and the illumination of other substances due to luminosity.
Because it has been destroyed and its ripening burnt away, there is the enjoyment of the vital essence (*ojas*) and the protection of progeny;
likewise, through qualities such as moving horizontally and so forth, benefit is rendered to the world by the wind, as well as to other elements.
From its transverse fall comes the diversion of sight and the carrying away of odors;
because of its purity, it purifies foul substances;

through attraction and repulsion, it brings about excellence; it causes the spreading of sweat and water, the arrangement of the bodily constituents such as the *rasas* and other *dhātus*, the blowing of fire, and the striking of space.
By its force it agitates all the bodily humors;
by its dryness it causes desiccation;
and because it lacks shade, the distinction between day and night is established.
Just as coldness serves as a remedy for heat,

so too does space (nabhas) provide benefit to the world through its qualities such as omnipresence; and because it pervades everywhere, it allows for the simultaneous hearing from all directions of those sounds originating from the same location.
It has been stated that earth and the other elements provide space for all things through their non-expansion and non-obstruction (*avyūha-viṣkambha*)—

as found in the *Yuktidīpikā* commentary on Sāṅkhya Kārikā 38. These very same [qualities], such as form (*ākāra*), heaviness (*gaurava*), and dryness (*raukṣya*), are found with slight variations in reading in the first, third, fourth, fifth, and sixth verses of the *Tattvavaiśāradī* (the commentary by Vācaspati Miśra) on the *Pātañjalayogadarśana*, as well as in the *Yogavārttika* composed by Vijñānabhikṣu.

In this regard, concerning the *kāryakāraṇavīta*, the *āvīta* is as follows: furthermore, having divided this manifest [world] into two parts—namely, the aggregate of effects and the aggregate of causes—the remaining part of the statement is that "the arising of the non-existent is not possible," because of the impossibility of the occurrence of sequence or simultaneity, and because of the mutual dependence for the acquisition of their own nature between cause and effect, there is an absence of reciprocal conformity in the acquisition of their nature;
therefore, for the proponent of non-existence (*asadvādin*), there is an absence of sequential occurrence, like a wheel and its axle.

Likewise, even if they were simultaneous, since two things that are non-existent or already destroyed are independent of one another—like a donkey’s horn—there can be no commencement of activity at the beginning, middle, or end, precisely because of their non-existence.
It is observed in the world that "what is begun is performed and reaches completion," and this is not possible without mutual dependence, as has been stated in the analogy of the wheel and the axle;
therefore, due to the impossibility of activity occurring either successively or simultaneously, it follows that there can be no relationship of cause and effect.
This manifest world exists in a state of cause and effect;
therefore, it does not arise from what is non-existent.

By the method of elimination (*pariśeṣataḥ*), this [world] arises only from the Pradhāna. This is the *āvīta* form of the argument concerning the relationship between cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇavīta*).

Furthermore, if that which is without a seed were to arise spontaneously, then the manifest would arise as unconnected because the various distinctions occupy multiple locations; yet it arises as connected. Therefore, this is not non-existent. This is the *āvīta* argument against the *śaktivīta*.

The remainder, however, concerns the investigation of what follows from what has been discussed: that "configuration" (*saṃsthāna*) is merely a beginningless property of sound and the other elements, both perishable and imperishable; likewise, "mark" (*liṅga*) is merely a beginningless property of *sattva* and the other *guṇas*, both perishable and imperishable. It is with respect to this [mark] that the designation "modification" (*vikāra*) is used. In this regard, what was stated—that because modification is perishable, primordial matter (*pradhāna*) must also be perishable—is incorrect. This is because there is no cause for the activity of the *guṇas* apart from the *guṇas* themselves, and because there can be no activity that is accidental. Thus, by means of such arguments as recognition, causal efficiency, and the necessity of effects, the entire section—both the *vīta* and *avīta*—should be understood as intended to refute the production and destruction of that which is absolutely non-existent, and as establishing the non-differentiation of the manifold forms of nature.

Thus, for the sake of establishing their existence as the primary principle, their oneness, and so forth, there are *vīta* arguments; and for the sake of determining that the three-natured source must necessarily be the cause—either by demonstrating the impossibility of manifestation otherwise or by showing the existence of that [source]—there are also *avīta* arguments. Furthermore, another says: "It is not logical to accept that everything is of the nature of everything else, because otherwise, due to the acceptance of the dual nature of becoming, the absolute positions (*ekānta*) of both the affirmative (*vidhi*) and the dualistic (*ubhaya*) standpoints would be established.

For proximity (*sannidhi*) does not exist merely as a state of proximity, because it has not yet arrived, because it has not yet manifested, because it has not yet begun to function, and because it is not fixed."

Because they have not entered [into existence] and so forth, there is no presence [of these categories], just like the son of a barren woman; for *sattā* (Being) functions precisely as the meaning of "to go" (*padyati*) and "to persist" (*vartati*).

Indeed, unlike the specific existences of substance (*dravya*) and so on, "going" and "persisting" are not employed as specific varieties of *sattā*. Since it is stated without distinction that "the meanings are *sattā*," their lack of such a meaning has been demonstrated by the aforementioned method. Furthermore, there is unity and, like the *puruṣa*, the absence of transformation (*apariṇāmitva*) regarding pleasure (*sukha*) and the other qualities.

Furthermore, because it is a single entity, like the *puruṣa*, it is unchanging and thus does not possess the capacity for such [transformation]. Therefore, due to this lack of correspondence with reality (*atathārthatva*) and because they are fallacious inferences, these propositions are untenable—namely: that there is a distinction of qualities (*bhinnaguṇatva*), that there is a nature of inequality (*vaiṣamyātmakatva*), that there is transformation (*vipariṇāma*), and that there is a return to equilibrium (*sāmyāpatti*).
Since these are untenable, the conceptualization of the creation and dissolution of the world is baseless, as the *pradhāna* does not exist.

Because that [world] is rootless, the claim that activity is impelled by the goal of human life (*puruṣārtha*) as its cause is also false. Since that is false, the cognition regarding it is also merely ignorance. Because it is ignorance, there is an absence of the goal of human life to be attained through knowledge; thus, the entire purpose of that system is shattered. What remains, then, in the Vārṣagaṇya doctrine? This doctrine, which is considered well-spoken but consists of irrational assertions concerning imperceptible matters, must be abandoned. If even an imperceptible matter were logically consistent, we would accept it; but it is not consistent.
Therefore, the acceptance of the principle that "everything is the essence of everything" alone is logical.
And what is non-existence? And what is the state of non-existence? Or rather, [what is] existence?
Primary matter.

However, the entire remaining text should be understood as both *vīta* and *avīta* regarding the process of the non-differentiation of the manifold forms (*vaiśvarūpya*), as will be explained in the following connection: "Just as configuration (*saṃsthāna*) is a perishable and imperishable mere property (*dharmamātra*) of sound and the rest, so too the subtle body (*liṅga*) is a perishable and imperishable mere property of the qualities (*guṇa*) such as *sattva* and the rest;
in that [subtle body] lies the designation 'modification' (*vikāra*)."
Thus, in the commentary composed by Vyāsa on the *Pātañjalayogadarśana*, at [sūtra] 3.13,
this sentence also appears as if it has been extracted from some other work.

The commentary composed by Vācaspatimiśra on this [verse] demonstrates that the very diversity of *vimarda* (dissolution) is the cause for the diversity of transformations (*vikāra*) in both the primal nature (*prakṛti*) and its evolutes (*vikṛti*). He says "just as":

just as the configuration (*saṃsthāna*), characterized as the transformation of earth and the other elements, is a mere property (*dharma-mātra*) that has a beginning, is perishable, and subject to disappearance; [the text] shows that this applies to sound and the rest—that is, to the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell—which, with respect to their own effects, are imperishable and non-disappearing within the primal nature (*prakṛti*). He concludes: "In the same way, the *liṅga* [is]."
The meaning is that while there is the notion of modification in that [object], the power of consciousness (citiśakti) is not thus possessed of modification— *Tattvavaiśāradī*.

In the commentary known as the *Yogavārttika*, composed by the monk Vijñāna, it is explained as follows: "Even though the *guṇas* are eternal, he illustrates their transformation (*vimarda*) with the word 'just as' (*yathā*); this is not a mere example (*dṛṣṭānta*), but rather an illustration (*udāharaṇa*). Regarding the term 'configuration' (*saṃsthāna*): the meaning is that the configuration of the five elements—which is the form of the sound-tanmātras and the rest, which are themselves imperishable despite the destruction of their objects—is merely a property (*dharma*) that has a beginning; therefore, it is perishable. The passage beginning with 'in the same way' (*evam*) should also be explained in this manner."

It should be understood that the *liṅga* (the subtle body), the principle of *mahat*, as well as the *ahaṅkāra* and so forth, and even objects such as jars, are merely attributes (*dharmamātra*) of imperishable causes; they are perishable through their own destruction.
The meaning is that in that dharma there is the notion of modification (*vikāra*) and the notion of transformation (*pariṇāma*).
Thus it is said in the *Yogavārttika*: "That which has arisen previously, is unattached, and is constant—the Great One (*mahat*) and the rest, ending with the subtle elements (*sūkṣma*)."
"The *liṅga* transmigrates, devoid of enjoyment, permeated by the dispositions" (SK 40).

Thus, in Māṭhara’s commentary on the *Sāṅkhyakārikā*, as well as in the *Sāṅkhyatattvakaumudī* and other works, the eighteenfold *liṅga*—consisting of the five organs of action, the five organs of cognition, the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*), mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), and ego (*ahaṅkāra*)—is described as comprising everything from the Great Principle (*mahat*) down to the subtle body. However, in commentaries such as the *Yuktidīpikā*, this verse is explained differently.
See *pratyakṣa*, p. 320, note 6;
[the reading] *anarthābhāsa* is correct.

Regarding the objects [of knowledge], another, however, says: "It is not logical to accept that everything possesses the nature of everything else; otherwise, because one would be accepting the existence of duality, the absolute positions of the positive (vidhi) and both (ubhaya) standpoints would be established.
For proximity does not exist as a mere presence, because it has not been attained, because it has not manifested, because it has not functioned, and because it is not determinate."

Because it has not been predicated (*anāpanna*) and so forth, there is no presence [of the action] like that of the son of a barren woman; for existence (*sattā*) functions precisely as the meaning of "to go" (*padati*) and "to persist" (*vartati*). Indeed, unlike the various distinctions of existence such as substance (*dravya*) and so on, "to go" and "to persist" are not employed as specific types of existence, since they are stated without distinction as having existence as their meaning. (The reading within these brackets does not exist in the manuscripts of the *Ya* recension.)

The purpose of the Spirit (*puruṣārtha*) alone is the cause; no instrument is set in motion by anything else. (Sāṅkhyakārikā 31) "The activity of the *guṇas* proceeds because the purpose of the Spirit must be accomplished.
(Jayamaṅgalā on Sāṅkhyakārikā)

Furthermore, the phrase "another [view], however," and so forth, indicates that it is not logical to maintain that everything is of the nature of everything else; otherwise, by accepting the duality of existence (*bhāva-dvaita*), the absolute positions of the affirmative (*vidhi*) and dual (*ubhaya*) standpoints would be established.

In that regard, there exists the duality of existence, and the establishment of existence occurs through the two distinctions of a thing being either the object of becoming (*bhāvya*) or the agent of becoming (*bhavitṛ*); this will be demonstrated later.
But it is not as has just been refuted—the duality of proximity (*sannidhi*) and the state of falling into manifestation (*āpatti*).

In that regard, that which is "proximity" does not exist merely as proximity. Why? Because it has not yet fallen [into manifestation]. "Falling" (*āpatti*) is the manifestation of what was unmanifest; therefore, he says: "because it is unmanifest. Non-manifestation is non-activation, and non-activation is non-restriction (*aniyama*).

Alternatively, *āpatti* is transformation (*vipariṇāma*), apprehension through a change of state; *āvirbhāva* is manifestation (*vyakti*); *pravṛtti* is a continuous stream of transformations; and *niyatasvarūpatva* is the persistence of the substantial entity (*dravyārtha*) in its unaltered state. The opposites of these are "non-attainment" (*anāpannatva*) and so forth. Due to these reasons—namely, the nature of non-attainment and the rest, including [the inclusion of] non-activity, non-manifestation, lack of determination, and so on—there is no presence (*sannidhi*), just as there is none for the son of a barren woman. Since "presence" is a synonym for existence, there is an absence of the becoming of presence.

Now, it was indeed stated: "Among the verbs *asti*, *bhavati*, and so forth, *asti* and *vartati* express proximity; *bhavati* and *vidyati* express general existence (*sāmānyabhavana*); and *padyati* expresses the occurrence of attainment (*āpattibhavana*). This is true as it was stated, yet what was stated is incorrect. For all these verbs—*asti* and the others, six in number including *sannipāti*—express the meaning of existence (*sattā*) without distinction, and that existence is one and the same in meaning as *padyati* and *vartati*. Therefore, he says: "Precisely because existence functions with the same meaning as *padyati* and *vartati*..."

It might be thought: "Just as with substance, quality, and action, which are specific instances of existence (*sattā*), the term 'existence' (*vartate*) and 'occurrence' (*padyate*) are employed as specific forms of existence.

But this is incorrect, because—as in the passage beginning "for there is no distinction of existence in substances, etc. and ending with "the employment [of the term]"—the meaning has already been explained.
What, then, is the employment? It is said: by virtue of having the same meaning as "is" (*asti*) and so forth.

If it is asked, "How is this known? [the answer is: because they are stated without distinction as having the sense of existence (*sattārtha*). For Siddhasena Sūri stated without distinction that "the roots *asti*, *bhavati*, *vidyati*, *padyati*, and *vartati*, with *sanni* as the sixth, have the sense of existence" (Sarvāsarvātmaprakaraṇa, Bhavyabhavatṛtīya-bhāṣya).
You should examine this yourself; furthermore, it should be noted that a difference from the preceding description is observed here at page 261, line 18.
And regarding the phrase "in the sense of becoming" (*bhavanārthe*), see page 34, line 21.

Although it might be argued that the description of "becoming" (*āpatti*) is indeed primary because [the world] becomes through the transformation (*vikāra*) into the Great One (*mahat*) and so forth—on the grounds that "by that, it is indeed brought into being"—that too is not correct. This is because that [transformation] itself is something yet to be produced (*bhāvyamānatva*), and since it cannot occur without a producer (*bhāvayitṛ*), and because that which has not yet undergone transformation lacks existence; furthermore, it is not independent, just like sound and other such objects.

He who is independent is the agent, because he functions by instigating [others] and because he functions by coming into being; this is like the case of the threads and the cloth. Thus, first of all, there is no such thing as "coming into being through proximity," because its definition is untenable. Nor is there "coming into being through occurrence. If one asks how so, the remainder of the sentence is: "because even that definition of 'coming into being through occurrence' which is formulated by the Sāṅkhyas [is untenable]."

Pradhāna itself becomes [the world] through the assumption of modifications such as Mahat and the rest; for it is said that "by it, indeed, it is produced. Because the word *iti* has the sense of a reason, it means: for this reason—that it assumes the state of Mahat and the rest—it is Pradhāna itself that exists. It is by that very thing that the universe is produced, because it consists of *sattva* and the other qualities. The word *kila* is used in the sense of censure, meaning: "such, indeed, is their opinion. And that censure is due to the fact that [their view] is untenable.

If it is asked how this is so, it is said: that too is not the case, because even that [object] is something to be brought about (*bhāvyamāna*), and since being brought about is impossible without one who brings it about (*bhāvayitr*), the meaning is that it does not exist by itself. Furthermore, its status as something to be brought about is established because it possesses the logical justification (*upapatti*) that will be stated later. And if that [object] is occupied with one [activity], it cannot proceed without another, more intensely occupied [agent], because it has not yet attained [its state]; and for that which has not yet attained [its state], mere proximity does not establish its existence.
Therefore, since for one who has not fallen [into a state of transgression] there is an absence of falling by its very nature, the existence of that aforementioned falling is not tenable.

If you ask, "What is the reason why it is untenable? it is because of its lack of independence (*asvatantratvāt*). For that which is called *pradhāna* is dependent on another, owing to its insentience (*acetanatvāt*). What is the illustration? It is like sound and so forth. Just as sound and the other qualities, being composed of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, are not independent and are brought into manifestation by the *pradhāna* which consists of those [qualities], even though they are themselves active, they are made to act by another who impels them; so too is the *pradhāna*.
"Arising from cultivation," "cultivation," and so forth;
that which arises from cultivation is indeed existence. [Prakaraṇa] Yaśomitra.
Excluded (vyāvṛtta) [in] Pra.,
excluded (vyāvṛta) [in] Bhā.,
excluded (vyāvṛtta) [in] Ya.
The reading here might also be *asya pādi* (pra. or *vāttvaduktā* (pra.); [it] should be studied according to the *tantra*. (pra.)
Likewise,
[the words] *pra°*, *°tvāsvata°*, *pra°*, and *vyāvṛtā* are corrected.
Therefore, there exists another who is primary;
who is he? He who is the agent.
Who is the agent? To this he says: he who is independent.

Why? Because it functions as an instigator (*pravartana-vṛttatvāt*). "Instigation" (*pravartana*) is the activity of one who instigates; the meaning is that it functions by way of being an instigator.

For a cause, while instigating, attains the state of being that [effect]; according to your own view, for example, the cause characterized by *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* attains the state of sound and so forth while instigating them.

Because it exists by way of being set in motion; that is, because it comes into being through that form by which it is set in motion, and because it does not exist—i.e., because it has not come into being—without a setter-in-motion, like the case of threads and cloth. Just as threads, while setting cloth in motion, are called the cause of the cloth, and the cloth is the effect of the threads because it is set in motion by them.

Now, it may be argued that these examples—the threads and so forth for the primary cause (*pradhāna*), and the cloth and so forth—support the doctrine of non-duality (*advaitavāda*). To this, we reply: they are presented as distinct illustrations by accepting [the analogy] on the sole basis of the common property of being a "causer" (*pravartayitṛtva*). Otherwise, if non-duality were accepted [in the absolute sense], there would be no possibility of the emergence of either injunctions or prohibitions, as in the case of the *puruṣa* (the Spirit). Furthermore, because the distinction between the producer and the produced is well-established, and because that which is not yet produced lacks existence—like the son of a barren woman—even atoms, qualities, and so forth, would only exist when being produced. It is on the basis of this common property that sound and the other elements serve as examples;
let this be seen on page 243.1.
Because of its being set in motion,
[there are] examples of the heterodox; bhā° [reads] "examples of the heterodox," while ya° [reads] "examples."

If it is argued that since merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), atoms, or the like are already established as causes for what is under discussion, what is the use of postulating an inferred cause? We say no. Even in the case of merit, demerit, atoms, and so forth, there must be a cause that possesses a specific intelligence, is independent, and acts through its own intention, because they are set in motion by one who exercises sovereignty over them—just as threads and fibers are directed by a weaver. This is because such a being alone possesses sovereignty over the engagement, withdrawal, and application of those things that possess causal power, just like a master cook over the ingredients at his disposal.

Because of its sovereignty over the operations of containing, supporting, heating, moistening, and pervading, as well as over the engagement and withdrawal of pots, wood, rice, and so forth, it is said: "Devadatta himself cooks," "it is cooked by him," "he cooks," or "the act of cooking is performed by him. This is because the action exists solely for the sake of the agent, whether directly—as in the case of the one who comes into being—or indirectly, like the threads [of a cloth]. And just as this is stated regarding the operations of containing and supporting, so it applies to merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), atoms, and so on, just as it does to the threads and fibers, and so forth, up to the point of specific cognition.

Just as a cloth is preceded by threads, threads are preceded by filaments, and filaments are preceded by minute particles (*tuṭi*), and it is inferred from sound and other evidence that there exist prior causes capable of setting even those *tuṭis* in motion—descending through dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and atoms (*paramāṇu*) up to the primordial matter (*pradhāna*)—so too, merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) are the movers of insentient things such as atoms;
by the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), time, inherent nature (*svabhāva*), necessity (*niyati*), and other factors imagined by rival schools are also included.

Thus, by virtue of the relative gradation of powers in each preceding stage, the Lord exists as one whose power is present for the respective arrangement of dharma, adharma, atoms, and so forth, as well as the primary matter (pradhāna), sound, and the rest, in their various corresponding ways. He is that one in whom such power resides.

If it is asked, "What is that primary power of his for the placement of such [entities] here?", it is said: it is a distinct cognition (*prativiśiṣṭā buddhiḥ*). Therefore, this distinct cognition, because of its knowledge and sovereignty over the engagement, withdrawal, and application of the placement by each agent—even compared to specific cognitions belonging to architects, potters, and the like—rules over those entities; they do not rule over him, nor over themselves, nor even among themselves, due to their lack of knowledge and lack of sovereignty.
But he, owing to his distinguished intellect, is independent; by his very intention alone, dharma, adharma, atoms, and so forth, undergo their respective activities.

Furthermore, because it functions through the operation of His intention (*abhiprāya*), He does not act merely by His mere proximity; therefore, He is their instigator (*pravartayitṛ*). Because He is the instigator, He alone is the cause, possessing the power (*śaktimat*) [to bring them forth]. Even for those who possess power, there is a lack of independence (*asvātantrya*) due to their being objects to be brought into being (*bhāvya*); for He alone possesses independence in the application of their activity and cessation throughout the creation, maintenance, intermediate dissolution, and great dissolution of the universe. "Instigation" (*pravartana*) refers to the setting in motion of *dharma* and the other principles which previously existed in a state of indifference until creation. "Cessation" (*nivartana*) refers to their withdrawal once they have been set in motion, through subsequent reabsorption. "Application" (*viniyoga*) refers to the arrangement and distribution of the various parts of bodies and instruments, such as gods, humans, animals, rivers, and oceans. This is because even authorized persons (*adhikṛta-puruṣa*) such as Viṣṇu and Manu proceed only in accordance with the intention of the Supreme Lord here, just like subordinate officials such as kings who act under the direction of a sovereign. Thus, He alone is the true instigator.

Therefore, in order to demonstrate its similarity [to that], he says— "like the appointed cook"— and for the purpose of explaining that, he states "possessing the powers of bringing together and supporting," and so forth, up to "because action has as its sole purpose the fulfillment of a specific aim.

For just as a cook appointed by a king becomes the very essence of each respective function through his autonomy in the activities of bringing together, supporting, igniting, and softening the pot, the wood, the rice, and so on, during their engagement, withdrawal, and application, so too is the Lord.

Alternatively, with respect to each factor (*kāraka*)—namely the agent, object, instrument, locus, recipient, and point of departure—the various actions such as "cooking" (*pacati*) are distinct; thus, by virtue of their respective capacities and independence, they are all agents. For example, the pot, which serves as the locus, is said to "cook" (*pacati*) because it performs the acts of containing and supporting [the rice], which are merely illustrative instances. Likewise, the pieces of wood are said to "cook" (*pacanti*) because they perform the act of burning. Furthermore, the earth, water, and so forth, being capable of such functions as placing [the pot] on the fire, pouring water, sowing the rice grains, and the rising of the fuel, likewise come into being and exist; thus, the rice is born and it exists.

Even though *sattva* possesses the qualities of illumination, restraint, and activity, it is shown through a multiplicity of examples—such as the case of *rajas* becoming active—that it acts as an instigator; this is for the purpose of demonstrating that the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) and other factors, as observed by those holding opposing doctrines, are the true instigators.

When Devadatta performs actions such as plowing and so forth, he is said to "cook"; and so on. Although each individual factor (*kāraka*) possesses independence (*svātantrya*), because Devadatta alone possesses independence throughout the entire sequence of actions—from their commencement until their completion—and because he is perceived as the agent even when [the action] is possible [through other means], it is said that "Devadatta alone cooks," even though the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) and other factors also possess the capacity to cook. This is because the others lack sovereignty (*anīśvaratva*).

He demonstrates that primary power of agency: "By him it is cooked" (*tena pacyate*) with the instrumental case prescribed for the agent, or "he cooks" (*sa pacati*) with the nominative case prescribed therein due to its coreferentiality with the *tip* suffix;
then, for the sake of further clarification, he says: "By him the act of cooking is performed"—to the extent that this is said, so much is said by "by him it is cooked" or "he cooks."

Why? Because action exists solely for the sake of a purpose, and the purpose here is the causing of another to act. Actions such as placing on the fire and igniting are for the purpose of the operation of moistening; and since all of these depend upon Devadatta, it is said that "he cooks" or "it is cooked by him."

Furthermore, even in the case of atoms of merit and demerit (*dharmādharmāṇu*) and so forth, there exists a cause that possesses a specific cognition and is independent, because it initiates activity through its own intention—just as threads [initiate the cloth]—due to the presence of a corresponding capacity in each preceding stage according to a gradation of power; for it possesses independence in the application of the activity and cessation of those possessing capacity, like a designated cook.

Because of his autonomy in the operations of containing, supporting, heating, moistening, and pervading—namely, in the application of activity and cessation regarding the pot, the wood, the rice, and so forth—it is said: "Devadatta himself cooks," "it is cooked by him," "he cooks," or "the act of cooking is performed by him. This is because action has as its sole purpose the [agent's] objective, whether directly or like the subject of becoming (*bhavitṛ*); and this is seen in the operations of containing, supporting, and seeing...

He provides another illustration for the sake of clarification and to demonstrate pervasiveness: "Or [the description is] like that of the agent itself" (*sākṣādvā bhavitṛvat tadvarṇanam*). And as in the passage beginning with "and just as it comes into being," etc., up to "it becomes and it exists": agency (*prayojyatva*) is not restricted solely to external actions such as cooking; rather, it is also applicable to internal actions such as the coming-into-being of rice and so forth.
Thus, while the earth, water, and other external things "come into being," the rice is born and comes into being as an internal process of becoming.

The earth is capable of supporting; water is capable of causing growth; by the inclusion of the word "etcetera," wind, time, and so forth are understood as being capable of causing development. Even though the arising of rice (*vrīhi*) brought about by these factors is perceptible, it is said that "the rice is born" or "it comes into being" because of the internal inherence of independence within that very Lord (*īśvara*), who is the impeller. Thus, even the very process of becoming occurs only as it becomes, meaning that even the mere acquisition of its own nature (*svarūpa-mātra-lābha*) is due to His power.
(Note: *tvāmbhā* and *tvāt* are corrected to *tvāt* based on context).

Or rather, this illustration— beginning with "sattva-tamas-prakāśa" and ending with "or like the production of rajas"— is established by those who maintain that the primary cause (pradhāna) is the subject under discussion, even without [the specific terms] *vananādya*, *ḍe*, *līṃ*, *vartana*, or *ya*.

It has been stated that, respectively, there is indeed the activity of illumination (*prakāśa*) for *sattva* and the activity of restriction (*niyama*) for *tamas*. In the passage beginning with "sattva proceeding as the nature of sound," which describes their mutual assistance, it is said that the activity of *sattva*, characterized by illumination and so forth, and the activity of *tamas*, characterized by heaviness and obstruction, "make known" and "establish" [their functions] respectively for the other two.

However, *rajas* is specifically intended as the instigator, being characterized solely by activity (*pravṛtti*), because of the statement: "even though activity is common to all, it acts and causes [others] to act."

Likewise, even though the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), atoms (*aṇu*), primordial matter (*pradhāna*), time (*kāla*), and so forth, are active as general causes, it is God alone who is the cause because He is the instigator; this abundance of examples is shown for the purpose of demonstrating that God is the instigator of even those things—such as the unseen force, atoms, and Viṣṇu—that are postulated in various systems (*pratisiddhānta*) and observed through inference in those respective Vaiśeṣika and other doctrines. This is because of the application of the example (*dārṣṭāntika-upanaya*) which concludes: "God is the instigator of all these. (Navyanyāyabhāṣya)

Thus, he alone exists, because his nature consists in the activity of all individual manifestations; and for this very reason, he is described as having eight forms (*aṣṭamūrti*).
Otherwise, there would be no excellence or deficiency in the results of activity arising from unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), atoms (*aṇu*), primordial matter (*pradhāna*), and so forth.
And since these two [the self and the body] are thus perceived,
there exists no cause capable of effecting their destruction except for the arbitrary will of a Lord; therefore,

the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), atoms, primordial matter (*pradhāna*), and so forth— which are engaged in the production of bodies, organs, and the world— must be presided over by a specific conscious being.

What, then, is the reasoning for God’s being the cause? This reasoning is stated as follows: "Primal matter (pradhāna), atoms, and karma proceed toward activity only when presided over by an intelligent cause, because they are insentient, like an axe or similar tools.

Just as an axe or other such tools proceed toward activity because they are insentient and are presided over by an intelligent carpenter, so too do primal matter, atoms, and karma—being insentient—proceed toward activity;
therefore, they too must be presided over by an intelligent cause.

In this regard, those who hold the Pradhāna to be the primary cause describe it as having the purpose of the Puruṣa as its supervisor; they maintain that the Pradhāna proceeds when impelled by the purpose of the Puruṣa. And the purpose of the Puruṣa is twofold: the perception of sound and other objects, and the discernment of the difference between the Guṇas and the Puruṣa. [The opponent argues: "Neither of these two occurs without the activity of the Pradhāna"—[but we reply:
no, because they do not exist prior to that activity.

As long as the *pradhāna* does not undergo transformation into the form of the Great One (*mahat*) and the rest, there is no perception of sound and the other objects, nor is there perception of the distinction between the *guṇas* and the *puruṣa*. Therefore, because of the absence of a cause, the activity of the *pradhāna* is illogical.

If, on the other hand, it does exist [in a latent state], then it follows that "the non-existent does not come into being, and the existent is not destroyed. This being the case, if it is argued that the existing purpose of the *puruṣa* impels the *pradhāna*, then the activity of the *pradhāna* is not for the sake of that purpose;
for in the world, when something already belongs to someone, that person does not strive for it again.

Furthermore, it would follow that there is constant activity because the cause is ever-present. Since the purpose of the Puruṣa (puruṣārtha) is the cause of activity, and since that purpose is eternal, there ought to be constant activity.
Now, if [Prakṛti], despite the presence of the purpose, does not act, then the purpose of the Puruṣa is not the cause.
That in the absence of which the Pradhāna does not act, and in the presence of which it acts—that alone is the cause.
...when you describe *prakṛti* as the state of equilibrium among the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, it must be explained from what this [equilibrium] ceases;
for as long as the state of equilibrium has not ceased, it is impossible for there to be disequilibrium.

If it is argued that there is an inequality because the relationship between the parts and the whole is not fixed, we question you on this point as well: how can that which exists in a state of equilibrium become both superior and inferior? For there is no acquisition of what was previously non-existent, nor is there a loss of what was previously present... Thus, the more this doctrine of Pradhāna is examined, the more it contradicts the operation of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Regarding those who describe atoms as the cause of the world, presided over by the karma of a person (Puruṣa), this is said in response: [If] atoms were to proceed [of their own accord], they would have to be in a state of constant activity.
Or, if they proceed in dependence on a specific time, then time is explained by means of the atoms;
for just as atoms, being insentient, require an intelligent supervisor, so too must time, since its insentience does not cease in that case.

If it is argued that there is activity even in that which is insentient, as in the case of milk and the like, that is not tenable because it is equivalent to the point yet to be proven (*sādhyasama*).
Just as it remains to be proven that atoms function independently, so too it would remain to be proven that insentient things like milk function independently.

If milk and the like were to function independently, they would continue to function even after [the cow] has died; however, they do not so function. Therefore, it is understood that even these are presided over by an intelligent cause.
And this reason does not cease [to apply] to that;

thus, as long as anything proceeds without consciousness, all of it is presided over by consciousness—this is another reason: the manifest world, consisting of the great elements and so forth, which serves as the cause of pleasure, pain, and the like, is presided over by an intelligent cause because it possesses form and other qualities, just like a chariot and such.
Thus ends [the section] in the Nyāyavārttika composed by Uddyotakara, 4.1.21.

Uddyotakara, however, offers this proof: "The causes of the world—namely *pradhāna*, atoms, and *adṛṣṭa*—require a supervisor possessing superior intelligence for the production of their own effects, because they act after having remained inactive, like threads, a shuttle, and so forth.
This is found in the *Tattvasaṅgrahapañjikā* composed by the Buddhist master Kamalaśīla, verse 50.
Thus, it is he alone who exists; in this way, it is Īśvara himself who exists in the ultimate sense.

Because it has the nature of the activity of all individual manifestations (*vyakti*); for its self consists of the activities of all individuals, it is "that which has the nature of the activity of all individuals" (*sarvavyaktipravṛttyātmaka*). This is because they (the individual manifestations) consist of the descent (*āvāsa*) of the power of consciousness (*buddhiśakti*) characterized by that [Self]. In this very way, its eightfold form (*aṣṭamūrtitā*) is described; namely, its state as having the eight forms known as earth, water, wind, fire, the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), ether, the moon, and the sun, because they consist of the descent of its own power. Within those [forms], He alone exists, and each of them is indeed He. See his *Prakaraṇapañcikā*, page 243–2.

Furthermore, because it would follow that there is no excellence or deficiency in the results of activity, God alone is the cause, and not the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) or primordial matter (*pradhāna*) and so forth; therefore, he says "otherwise," etc., up to "and they are seen."

If the activities or fruits of actions—whether they proceed from atoms (*aṇu*) and so forth, or from primordial matter (*pradhāna*) and so forth—are impelled by the fruits of previously performed karma, then because the fruits correspond to that [karma] and the karma corresponds to the fruits that impel it, only those things whose nature is softness (*mārdava*), which are to be accomplished by humans, proceed; for they act together toward a single purpose, like the collection of wooden parts of a chariot presided over by a carpenter.
Likewise, because they are insentient, they proceed after having first come to rest, like a loom and such tools.

If it is argued that [the reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), like milk, curd, clouds, and so forth, which are not presided over by volition (*cetanā*), we say no; for there is no deviation from the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*) concerning objects whose agent is unperceived, just as the impermanence of the sound of the ocean is included within the proposition when proving the impermanence of sound.

Having performed actions leading to human birth, one might become a human again; let it not be that there is a connection with actions that produce the state of gods through passion-restrained self-control (*sāra-gasaṃyama*) and so forth, resulting in the excellence of obtaining a corresponding transformation-body (*vaikriya-śarīra*) and other acquisitions. Likewise, let it not be that one partakes in karma that produces hellish lifespan through extensive violence and possession (*ārambha-parigraha*), thereby experiencing the inferior fruit of being a hell-being whose sole essence is suffering. Just as there is a continuous succession of cause and effect characterized by mutual conformity—such as the seed and sprout of a *śāli* rice plant—it cannot be due to an unseen force (*adṛṣ�ṭa*) or from *pradhāna* (primordial matter) and the like. This is because there is an absence of impelling by a specific, specific intelligence acting as an independent cause, and because we must admit the capacity for a continuous bond between causes and effects that correspond to themselves. Furthermore, inequality (*vaiṣamya*) is observed in the acquisition or non-acquisition of study, knowledge, and sacred scriptures; apart from the arbitrary will of a Lord (*īśvara-kāmacāra*), there is no other cause capable of accounting for this excellence or deficiency. "Arbitrary will" (*kāmacāra*) is the operation of an unimpeded intention. By means of that, the impelling of entities is their setting into motion: the connection of even those of good conduct with undesirable fruits, and the connection of those of evil conduct with desirable fruits. Therefore, everything proceeds as set in motion by the Lord, and not otherwise.

The proposition is that atoms, impelled by unseen forces (*adṛṣṭa*) presiding over bodies, senses, and the world according to their respective processes—as held by the Vaiśeṣikas; or the *sattva* and other qualities (*guṇas*) set in motion by *pradhāna*, as held by the Sāṅkhyas; or the elements presided over by time, inherent nature (*svabhāva*), necessity (*niyati*), and so forth, as accepted by others—all these objects to be set in motion, along with their movers, proceed only when presided over by a specific conscious being.

The reason is "because they act together toward a single purpose. Their acting together is established by the statement of the inference regarding the cause of the progressive gradation of capacities in each preceding stage. Atoms, *sattva*, and so forth, are observed to exist as bodies and the like by acting together; by acting together with one another, they perform effects such as movement, ingestion, the experience of pleasure and pain, the perception of color-form, and the state of being a substratum for the quality of *sattva*. Thus, their acting together toward a single purpose is proven.

Like a collection of wooden parts for a chariot presided over by a carpenter: "the collection of wooden parts for a chariot" refers to the assemblage of wood intended for a chariot; that [collection], being presided over by a carpenter who possesses a specific consciousness, acts in such a way.

Because these [other things] are likewise insentient, the phrase "because of their insentiency" in that same proposition (*pratijñā*) serves as the corroborative reason (*upacayahetu*). That very collection of wooden parts for a chariot is the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), or alternatively, as will be stated later, "like the shuttle and so forth.
Thus, the insentiency of the body, the instruments, and the worlds is established.

Alternatively, [the world] proceeds after having remained [in a state of latency], like a shuttle and so forth; just as a shuttle, a loom, a shuttle-pin, a reed, a cord, a shuttle-rod, a thread, and so on—having remained for some time without proceeding—proceed when presided over by the intellect of a skilled weaver for the purpose of producing cloth, so too are the body, the instruments, and the worlds. If it should be thought that [the reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because of the case of milk, curd, clouds, and so forth— which, like those [mountains], exist and function without being presided over by consciousness—

then the following might be the opinion: since milk, curd, clouds, and the like are seen to perform a single purpose through their collective action even without being presided over by someone possessing a specific intellect, the property of existing, functioning, and acting while remaining stationary is inconclusive and thus a cause for doubt.

And this is not so, because it does not differ from the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*) whose subject has an unperceived agent. This proposition has an unperceived agent as its subject; that is, it is a proposition whose subject consists of the body, the instruments, and the world, and which has as its property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) the state of being presided over by a distinct intelligence. Since this [example]—consisting of subjects such as milk, curd, and clouds—is not separate from that proposition, it falls within the scope of the proposition itself. Thus, in the absence of a dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), there is no deviation of the reason (*hetu*). If it is argued that [the reason is] inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) like God, who exists yet does not act without being presided over by a conscious being, or like the non-presiding of a conscious being [over something], then there would be an infinite regress: either God himself is presided over by a conscious being, or he too is presided over by another.
No, because the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is that of functioning under the direction of a conscious being.
In that case, Devadatta and others would function without being directed by a conscious God; yet that very God would likewise have to be directed by another conscious being.

Furthermore, you yourself state, in order to refute the doctrine of the Self (*puruṣavāda*), that even conscious beings are directed by God: "This ignorant creature is not its own master over its pleasure and pain."
"Impelled by God, one may go either to heaven or even into a pit" (Mahābhārata, Vanaparvan 30.28).

It is not an inconclusive (*anekānta*) argument, because it is like the inclusion of the ocean’s sound within the proposition when proving the impermanence of sound. For instance, when the proposition "sound is impermanent" is stated, the objection that it is inconclusive because the property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) is observed in the ocean’s sound—which is continuous across space and time—and in the sounds of *sāman* chants, which vary according to different persons, is a mere challenge to a fallacious argument. This is because even the sounds of the ocean and *sāman* chants, though differentiated by their respective material causes (*upādāna*), do not transcend the category of "sound" (*śabdatva*) since they are all equally apprehended by the auditory organ; thus, they are included within the subject (*pakṣa*) of the proposition. Furthermore, the impermanence of sound follows from the fact that no eternal thing is ever observed to be produced, and because the property of being produced is invariably concomitant (*avinābhāvin*) with impermanence. Moreover, this is a futile rejoinder (*jāti-uttara*), for although there is no difference in the nature of the property as perceived, there is a distinction based on differences of place, time, and material cause, and because the individual instances of sound (*śabda-vyakti*) serve as the locus (*dharmin*). Therefore, this is not a valid rebuttal.

If it is argued that [the argument] is inconclusive because of the case of God, who exists yet whose consciousness does not exercise superintendence over activity—then [we reply]: Is God himself superintended by consciousness? And is that [consciousness] also superintended by another? This would lead to an infinite regress.
No, for the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is "functioning through being superintended by consciousness.
In that case, Devadatta and others function without being superintended by a conscious God; likewise, that God too must be superintended by another conscious being.
And you yourself have stated, for the purpose of refuting the doctrine of the Puruṣa, that even sentient beings are under the governance of Īśvara:
"This ignorant creature is not its own master over pleasure and pain;
impelled by Īśvara, it may go either to heaven or indeed to hell" (Mahābhārata, Vanaparvan 30.28).

If it is argued that [the argument] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because there are cases such as water and so forth which, having been set in motion by a conscious being, are not presided over by a Lord (*īśvara*).

It might be thought: "Just as the Lord himself, though previously inactive, begins to act while remaining uninstigated by another conscious being, so too the body and other things may begin to act after having been inactive; thus, there is no inconclusiveness (anaikāntika) regarding the Lord being instigated by a conscious being," and so forth. Alternatively, if one does not accept this inconclusiveness, then it follows that this Lord must be instigated by a conscious being because he acts after having been inactive, like the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), atoms, or *pradhāna*. Consequently, there would be another Lord who instigates him, just as a man or woman is instigated by a planet, and for that instigator as well, there would be an instigator by another, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

And this is not so; there is no such fault because the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is "having activity presided over by a conscious being" (*cetanādhiṣṭhitapravṛttitva*). For it is this state of having activity presided over by a conscious being that is established as the property; and since that [property] has as its locus only non-conscious things (*acetana*), and since conscious beings are already established [as such], and because there would be no purpose [in proving them again], the non-conscious entities—the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), atoms (*aṇu*), primordial matter (*pradhāna*), and so forth—which are the means for accomplishing the body, organs, and the world, are indeed the subjects (*dharmin*) qualified by the property of being presided over by a conscious being. Thus, because there is no lack of understanding regarding the subject of the proposition (*pratijñāviṣaya*), there is no fault. (Vṛtti, Y)

[The opponent objects: "In the passage beginning with 'presided over' (*adhiṣṭhita*), etc., [it is stated that] Devadatta and others proceed without being presided over by a conscious Lord (*cetaneśvara*). Therefore, since the capacity [of the argument] establishes that the presiding over by a conscious being applies to insentient subjects, the scope of the thesis (*pratijñā*) is restricted; consequently, it does not follow that conscious beings such as Devadatta are themselves presided over by a conscious Lord. Thus, there is an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) regarding the atoms, *pradhāna*, and so forth, which—like Devadatta and others—are not presided over by a conscious being, yet serve as the means for producing bodies and other effects through unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*)."
It follows that this Lord, too, must likewise be presided over by another conscious being;
yet you say—and indeed you yourself accept—that even conscious beings are presided over by the Lord, as it is said: "This ignorant creature is not its own master over pleasure and pain;
impelled by the Lord, it goes either to heaven or to the pit."

In the *Mahābhārata*, *Vanaparvan* 30.28, he states the purpose of the verse regarding the refutation of the doctrine that the Person (*puruṣa*) is the cause: "Let there be no consequence of the doctrine that the Person is the cause—that [the world] consists merely of those states, such as the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), primordial matter (*pradhāna*), or atoms (*aṇu*). No; because [the existence of] a conscious being with superior intelligence has not been previously established, and because this [alleged creator] possesses superior intelligence only by virtue of being the arranger of objects according to their fitness for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), [it follows that] bodies and so forth were not created by a being of superior intelligence, unlike the lotus-stalk, the thorn, the peacock's eye, and the like.

the specific sequence of lightness, illumination, heaviness, and obstruction is preceded by a particular cognition, because they mutually oppose one another yet act together toward a single purpose, like fire, water, and rice being presided over by a cook;
and because they function through mutual suppression and conjunction and undergo transformation—if this is argued, we say no, because transformation itself is an effect.

The reading in the *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad* is "bliss is eternal for [the self], not for others. To demonstrate the lack of necessity (*anaikāntikatā*) [in the opponent's argument], he says: "the body and so forth," up to "like the stalk of a lotus, the thorns, and the eye-spots on a peacock's tail. For indeed, the stalk of a lotus—which possesses praiseworthy color, fragrance, taste, and touch; which is the abode of beauty; and which serves as an ornament for a body of water—was not made with thorns by anyone out of malice, thinking, "Let no one grasp it, hold it, or enjoy it. This would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) even to the stalks of blue lotuses and the like.

Furthermore, the variegated colors of the eye-spots on a peacock's feathers—which rival the hues of Indra’s bow—were not created by anyone possessing superior intelligence upon walls and such surfaces, like a painter; for if they were, it would follow that there would be no need to pay wages to painters and so forth.

To this, it is replied: No, because the answer has already been stated. Just as in the case of milk, curd, clouds, and the like, the same response applies here. Since the lotus stalks, thorns, peacock eye-spots, and so forth, like the body [of the universe], do not deviate from the subject of the proposition—that they have an unseen creator—there is no lack of certainty (anaikāntikatva); thus, this matter has already been answered. (Padmanālabhāṣya)

Thus, first, the state of being preceded by a specific cognition has been stated in general; and with reference to the currently under discussion Sāṃkhya doctrine, the proposition is formulated as follows: "Light, luminosity," and so forth, up to "like fire, water, and rice-gruel prepared when presided over by a cook."

Just as fire and water, though mutually antagonistic, are seen to accomplish the preparation of rice when presided over by a skilled cook who establishes their non-antagonism toward that end—since they act in concert under the influence of his intellect—so too, although lightness and heaviness, illumination and obstruction, and activity and restraint are mutually contradictory, they nevertheless act for a single purpose in the form of the *mahat* and the rest by acting in concert; therefore, it follows that this is preceded by a specific intelligence, because they function through mutual suppression, pairing, and transformation. If this is argued:

It might be thought: "The relationship of subordinate and principal among sattva, rajas, and tamas proceeds with a view toward the purpose of the Puruṣa, resulting from their transformation into an imbalance [of qualities], giving rise to the Great Principle (mahat) and the rest. And it is said: "The one controller of the many who are inactive, who makes the single seed manifold—those wise ones who perceive Him abiding within themselves, theirs is eternal peace, and not that of others" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.12).

12. [The opponent claims: "The proof [of a creator] is not that there is no other agent. But this is not so, because transformation (*pariṇāma*) is also an effect. Therefore, it is incorrect [to say] that the *sattva* and other qualities transform by themselves alone. (Note: *kayopratya* is a scribal error for *kāryapratyaya*; *pra* is a scribal error for *pratyaya*; *tvapari* is a scribal error for *tattvapari*.)

"Those wise ones who perceive Him as abiding within themselves attain eternal peace, and not others. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.12).
The reading in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad is: "They [attain] that supreme, eternal bliss, and not others. From these... [prabhṛti].
In this context, there may also be the reading "dharmāntara" and so forth; furthermore,
there may be the reading "niṣedhān na dharmā" (because of the negation, not the dharmas) in the Prajñāpāramitā, and here there may also be the reading "nirodho dharmā" (the cessation of dharmas).
And he recites [the following] in accordance with the doctrine of the Jina:

"He is one, without a second, or preeminent; he is the controller (*vaśī*) by virtue of his knowledge and sovereignty over those who are inactive, ignorant, and not independent. For even those who possess knowledge but are dependent on others are indeed inactive.

He is called the 'controller' because he is capable of setting in motion and bringing under his own control many infinite things—such as primordial matter (*pradhāna*), atoms (*aṇu*), and so forth—which possess the infinite powers of object (*karman*), instrument (*karaṇa*), recipient (*sampradāna*), source (*apādāna*), locus (*adhikaraṇa*), and preeminence (*pradhāna*)."

Those who perceive that Lord—who, as the single primordial seed (*pradhāna*), brings about, creates, presides over, and establishes through its own volition the manifold world—divided into infinite distinctions from Brahmā down to a blade of grass by means of the transformation of the Great Principle (*mahat*) and the rest; who is the cause of the manifestation of all things distinct from Himself, designated as *pradhāna* and so forth; who resides within the Self; and who is omnipresent as the eightfold form beginning with Earth, because those [eight] exist everywhere—they perceive Him solely through His grace, following that knowledge by means of the gradual process of purification through the practice of yoga.
Who perceive this? The wise ones, whose minds are steady through the concentration of yoga.
What is yoga? Withdrawal of the senses, as well as meditation, breath control, fixation, reflection, and absorption—this is said to be the six-limbed yoga.
Amṛtanādopaniṣad 6: Therein, *pratyāhāra* is the withdrawal of the senses from their objects and of the mind [from its fluctuations].
*Prāṇāyāma* is threefold: *recaka*, *kumbhaka*, and *pūraka*.
Among these, *recaka* expels the internal air outwards through the nostrils.
Pūraka is that which fills by drawing the external [air] inside; kumbhaka is that which causes the air to remain motionless nearby, like a full jar;
dhyāna is the contemplation of one's chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā).

Dhāraṇā is the stabilization of the mind in specific locations such as the heart and so forth, according to one's practice; for example, first at the navel, then in the heart, the throat, the tip of the nose, between the eyebrows, on the forehead, and finally on the crown of the head.

*Tarka* (reasoning) is as follows: one should reason, "When I meditate in a secluded place such as an empty house or a mountain cave, in a clean location, with the body held straight, the tips of the teeth joined by the tip of the tongue, and having assumed a posture such as *paryaṅka*, *svastika*, or *vīrāsana*, or a standing position with feet even, then concentration (*samādhi*) arises for me. By means of this specific performance of action—such as particular modes of eating, moving about, and recitation—meditative concentration arises; such deliberation regarding the means is *ūha*, which is *tarka*. Delight in the yoga of meditation is *samādhi*. This is the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅga-yoga*).

By this yoga, having perceived the Lord in the form of earth and the other elements everywhere, one whose self is subsequently purified beholds Him as residing within one's own self: "That which is solid in this body of mine is earth, the form of the Supreme Lord; that which is liquid is water; heat is fire; that which moves is air; the void is ether; and that which is consciousness is the Sacrificer (Yajamāna); the eye is the Sun; the tongue is Soma—this [body] partakes of both [the microcosmic and macrocosmic orders]."

The rule (*vidhi*) has been explained as the operation of worldly non-exclusion (*anapavāda*); it is established by way of general application (*utsarga*), and because everything is the self of everything, the restriction (*niyama*) operates without exclusion.

Since those two [the restricted and the restrictor] do not operate when one is present and the other is absent—because the absent would then possess existence—the meaning of a word is the generality of similarity (*sādṛśya-sāmānya*). Furthermore, even though everything is the self of everything, there is no lack of conceptual differentiation (*avikalpa*), because the purpose of creation remains effective.
Moreover, every sentence consists of distinct words; therefore, because everything has the nature of all else,

those wise ones who perceive the differentiation of substances (dravyārthabheda) as applicable even among other components— be it the mind or otherwise— attain eternal peace, which means union with that very Lord, Nirvāṇa, or liberation.
The others—Pradhāna, Puruṣa, Niyati, and so forth—are not the causes. Thus, [the sequence is]:
withdrawal (pratyāhāra), as well as meditation (dhyāna), breath control (prāṇāyāma), and then concentration (dhāraṇā).

"Reasoning (tarka) and meditative absorption (samādhi)—this is called the six-limbed yoga. This verse, "And reasoning as well as meditative absorption," exists in the *Amṛtanāda Upaniṣad* and in the third quarter of a verse in the *Atri-smṛti*. It is also found in the *Atri-smṛti*.
In the phrase "kuṃbhakadhāraka" (the holder of the kumbhaka),
it is not understood what the purpose of the word "vā" (or) is; since its inclusion appears meaningful, it is probable that some portion of the text has been omitted here.

Now, meditation (dhyāna) is of two kinds: with attributes (saguṇa) and without attributes (nirguṇa). That with attributes is meditation on the Form (mūrtidhyāna); that without attributes is the true nature of the Self (ātmayāthātmya).
Thus, in the Śāṇḍilya Upaniṣad,
[it is taught] regarding the forehead, the navel-center, the middle of the heart, the root of the throat, and the palate.
"One should hold [the mind] between the eyebrows, on the forehead, and likewise on the crown of the head," thus it is said in the Jābāladarśana Upaniṣad, 7.12.
If it is argued that this injunction partakes of both [the general rule and the exception],

then the injunction has been explained as proceeding without exception, just as in the world; because of its universal application, it is established by way of a general rule (*utsarga*), and since everything is of the nature of everything, it indeed proceeds without exception.

The restriction [of a word's meaning] is due to the non-occurrence of two things when they are present but not being employed; because those two exist as non-existent [in that context], the meaning of a word is the universal of similarity (*sādṛśya-sāmānya*). Furthermore, although everything has everything as its essence, there is no lack of conceptual differentiation (*avikalpa*) because the purpose of creation remains effective.
Moreover, even a sentence is a distinct word for every [part]; therefore, precisely because everything has everything as its essence, [the system holds].
The meaning is the distinction between the substantial (dravya) and the modal (artha).

To explain the nature of the *nayas*, he says: "This [substantial view] partakes of both. It partakes of both—namely, affirmation (*vidhi*) and restriction (*niyama*)—thus it is called "partaking of both.
He recalls what was stated previously: "Affirmation has been explained as being like the worldly [convention]."

He explains again in brief: "The operation [of this doctrine] is without exception. It does not deny any object whatsoever, whether it be a universal (*sāmānya*) or a particular (*viśeṣa*), and so forth. Because that rule is established through its general application (*utsarga*), that rule is indeed prescribed. Why? Because everything has everything as its essence (*sarvasarvātmakatvāt*), it proceeds without exception; it proceeds and is never obstructed anywhere. For this *naya* maintains that "everything has everything as its essence," which was previously indicated in the explanation of "proximity" (*sannidhi*) and "occurrence" (*āpatti*), and that very point will be stated here as well. As for the restriction: because of the non-operation of both "proximity" (*sannidhi*) and "the prompted" (*prayojya*). These two, which were just mentioned—namely, "proximity," which consists of occurrence and its accompaniment, or that which is set in motion by God (*īśvara*); and "the prompted," which is an entity such as primordial matter (*pradhāna*), unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*), atoms (*aṇu*), and so forth—their non-existence follows from the non-operation of both of them.

What is the reason? Because those two [negation and affirmation] are non-existent while existence is real; for both of them are called "existent" only when they are actually non-existent, since they arise only from an independent, knowing agent. That which is different from that [agent], being devoid of existence, inactive, and non-existent like a sky-flower, cannot function.
Therefore, there is a restriction (*niyama*); it is both enjoined (*vidhīyate*) and restricted (*niyamyate*). Consequently, this [agent] possesses both parts of the injunction (*vidhi*).

As it was indicated in the Ya[panīya] [tradition], as it was indicated by Ka in the Bhā[drabāhu] [tradition]: "The Lord (Īśvara) is the companion for the occurrence of transgressions. [This is according to] Pra[bhava].
The procedure is seen in the *Prakaraṇapañcikā*, p. 9.

Now, regarding the meaning of words: similarity (*sādṛśya*) is the meaning of a word; since the meaning of a sentence will be discussed later, it is understood here as the meaning of a word (*padārtha*).

It is called "similar" (*samāna*) because it is measured by means of its similar configuration and magnitude; that which is "similar" (*sadṛśa*) is that wherein there is a commonality of appearance (*dṛktva*) for observers. "Similar" (*sadṛśa*) is the same as "common" (*samāna*); the state of being common is "universality" (*sāmānya*). It is [the basis] for the cognition and designation of the genus (*jāti*), the mark (*liṅga*), and the conceptual content (*pratyaya*). It is neither the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), nor a reality distinct from common entities, such as a "that-ness" (*tattva*) and so forth, because those are untenable. This universality is the meaning of the word.

If it is argued that there is the consequence of the previous position—that the universal (*sāmānya*), such as the *puruṣa* or *niyati*, is non-conceptual (*avikalpātmaka*) because everything is of the nature of everything—[we reply]: no. Even though everything is of the nature of everything, because the purpose of creation exists, and because this system has its purpose in the pervasiveness of the general rule (*utsarga*) characterized by the creation of the world, it follows that [the universal] is not non-conceptual; thus the meaning of the word under discussion is connected. According to the stated logic, since the conceptual cognition (*vikalpapratyaya*) arising from words such as "existence" (*sattva*) and so forth regarding the body (*tanu*) and so on possesses a true object, whereas the cognition of non-duality (*advaitapratyaya*) lacks a true object, the meaning of the term [non-conceptual] has been explained.

Now, regarding the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*): according to the view that "the sentence consists of all its words taken individually," because it is easier to determine the meaning once the sentence has been established, among the various definitions of a sentence—such as "the verb (*ākhyātaśabda*)," "the collection [of words]," "the genus (*jāti*)," or "that which resides in the collection" (Vākyapadīya 2.1)—this particular perspective holds that the sentence is each individual word separately, and the sentence-meaning is the meaning of each individual word separately. For example, in the sentence "O Devadatta, drive the white cow hither," each single word, by virtue of being a locus of synthesis (*saṅgraha*), possesses the nature of substance (*dravyārtha*).

Substance (*dravya*) is also a confluence of qualities (*guṇa*); it is so called because it flows through the unification of qualities, and because [the soul] has mastery over it. Its exposition is twofold: the exposition of souls (*jīva*) and the exposition of non-souls (*ajīva*). (Prajñāpanā Sūtra 1.9)

"Venerable Sir, what is this that is called 'the world' (loka)? "Gautama, it is both living beings (jīva) and non-living things (ajīva). Likewise [it includes] the Jewel-Luster [hell], up to the Īṣatprāgbhāra [mountain], or [units of time such as] the moment (samaya) and the minute (avalikā). What is the reason? Because of the fact that everything has everything as its essence (sarvasarvātmakatva). Since even Devadatta possesses the nature of a cow and the nature of driving [cattle], because he functions in those ways and thus attains those states; and since those [others] are likewise so, therefore, due to the fact that everything has everything as its essence, every individual term is a sentence in itself.

The meaning of this dual method of injunction (*vidhi*) is the distinction of substance (*dravyārtha*); because it is not contradictory to what preceded, it is distinguished from the method of injunction (*vidhinaya*), which has a non-conceptual meaning, by virtue of having a conceptual meaning and the nature of substance.

Into which [of the categories] are the *nayās* spoken by the Ṛṣis included? To this he says: "The *dravyārthika* [is so called] because it is a portion (*deśa*) of the *saṅgraha*. Its explanation: *sam* means "in a state of unity," and *dru* (Dhātupāṭha 945) means "to move. Therefore, it is the flowing together (*dravaṇa*) of the qualities through their unification. Since the effect exists within the cause, there is the transformation of the soul (*jīva*) and matter (*pudgala*) due to the attainment of oneness by pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth, or by color (*rūpa*) and so forth, which, though existing separately, come together. He states that this "coming together" (*saṅgamana*) occurs because of the dual nature of the injunctions and the principles: because of the distinctness of the Lord (*Īśvara*), who possesses such inherent powers, and because each atom and so forth is the essence of all things, let there be unification among them; but let there be no [such unification] for the Lord.

This is not so; for even by that [individual soul], because it is under His control—even while its own power remains present—there is no manifestation of that power otherwise than through union with the Lord.
For this very reason, there is a distinction between this system and the doctrine of non-duality (advaitavāda), as stated in the *Arthasamgraha*.
