the point is that there is no rising [of an objection] because one is not satisfied with this view, just as before.

Now, as for the word "nanu" used here to seek permission: surely the arguments you have stated each individually establish that every living being is the Lord. This is because the world consists merely of external and internal pleasure, pain, and delusion; because the various distinctions of objects to be experienced as existent or non-existent, and those characterized by delusion or obstruction, do not transcend the ripening results of the triad of pleasure and so forth; and because karma is defined by its being cognizable through its own self. Indeed, karma, which is the cause, is indicated and inferred by the very experience of pleasure and so forth—its effect—just as the motion of the sun is inferred from its reaching another location by means of the general inference (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭānumāna*).

Therefore, because the effect exists within the cause, and by metaphorically designating the cause as the effect, pleasure and the like are "karma. Just as food is called "life-breath" (*anna-prāṇa*), that which is desired by others as the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*)—known as merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*)—is indeed karma. The self (*ātman*) is also karma. How so? That unseen force, having attained the state of karma through the transformation of application (*prayoga-pariṇāma*) in the self—which is in the state of transformation as the ripening of the karma of passion and so forth—leads again from pleasure to passion and so forth; from that, again, karma; and from that, the fruit, which is pleasure and so forth.

And that [object] is indeed a collection of atoms suitable for the *kārmāṇa* body, which has been assimilated by the soul through its own transformation; it resides within the soul and becomes one with it. As it has been said: "By means of yogas, being embodied, it simultaneously takes up an external object through its own yoga;
and there is the experiencing of what has been taken up, which, in relation to bondage, is not different from the agent, and that is the object of cognition because it is cognized by the agent."

Therefore, because action (*karman*) has the characteristic of being experienced (*saṃvedya*), it will be connected with the state of being the Lord of all (*sarveśvaratā*). For action, which is restricted to a specific agent for every living being, is to be experienced as its own ripening in the form of pleasure and so forth. Thus, "experience" (*saṃvedana*) is the experiencing by the selves (*ātman*)—who have attained the transformation into the state of action—through their identity with the atoms (*aṇu*). And because they are employed in that manner by that Person (*puruṣa*), they possess agency. Therefore, he says that even the atoms of unseen merit and demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) such as pleasure and so forth are indeed action.

For it has already been established that through the conjunctions of dyads, triads, and so forth, there is a transformation of earth, water, rice, sprouts, and the like; thus, both the Self and those [entities] possess unity and the state of being the self-nature of all things.
Therefore, the very arguments you have stated actually prove that the activity of the world is caused by karma.

Furthermore, the world is preceded by karma, because the activity of all living beings is admitted to be dependent on karma; for it is solely by the power of karma that living beings experience the excellence or deficiency of auspicious or inauspicious birth, lineage, physical form, and so on.
As it has been said:
"O future one, O present one; indeed, O you..."
From passion and the like arises fruit, and from that fruit again,
through the application of one's own yoga, the embodied self repeatedly takes up external objects by means of its own yogic powers.
Indeed,
the meaning of "being" (satva) is that which begins with "sa";
and the experience of what has been grasped (ātta) with respect to bondage— that too is not different from that [meaning].

Therefore, because he is the agent of all living beings, and because it is accepted that the agent alone is the one who comes into being, and because he is the purpose for that very one who comes into being, his status as the Lord of All follows.

But regarding the initiation of action by the Lord, does it proceed from what is existent or from what is non-existent? If it proceeds from that which has not yet come into being, then there is non-duality, because even that [action] is of the same nature as him.

If it is argued that [the effect] exists [prior to its production], then it must exist even before; and since it is of the very nature of God, it follows that it arises as such and functions as such. Even so, non-duality is all the more established, precisely because it is of the nature of that [God]. Furthermore, in whatever manner it is impelled toward whatever end, it becomes so by virtue of that [impulsion], for God acts in that way. Therefore, when He impels it, this person is born entirely bound by his own karma; it is God alone who is the Lord.
It is brought about by him in such a way that it does not follow his own desire;
just as food, through the sequence of its specific transformation over time when consumed at the proper hour, produces pleasure when wholesome for embodied beings and pain when unwholesome.
Likewise, how can those whose intellects are wounded by the force of the poison of sense-objects not be led to listen even to a discourse that is free from doubt regarding dharma and adharma?
These [are not...].
Furthermore, it continues [from the previous argument]: "Because living beings are agents.

This is stated so that defects such as the arrival of results for what was not done (*akṛtābhyāgama*), the loss of results for what was done (*kṛtapraṇāśa*), and the transfer of fruits to another agent (*kartṛantaraphalasaṅkrānti*) may not occur. Therefore, one must accept that living beings themselves—possessing good and bad conduct—are both the agents and the enjoyers; otherwise, there would follow the futility of the scriptures intended for the attainment of the beneficial and the avoidance of the harmful.
Consequently, because the state of being the experiencer is accepted as belonging to the agent alone, [the self is established].

Who is the agent? It is he who is independent. If it is thought that "only he who is to become [something] would be the agent," we say no; for even the Lord is an agent only because he is one who becomes. Every living being, as an individual who is to become, impels himself by himself, urged by the qualities of passion, hatred, fear, pride, and so forth, which consist in the ripening of the karma performed by himself.

As it has been said: "These popular sayings among the faithful regarding the sun and other celestial bodies— that this [fortune] is born of another birth or of mere effort— are for those who perceive that prosperity attends the man who strives, even while destiny is being accomplished."

Therefore, although the subtle body (*tanu*) and other [constituents] exist as primary atoms (*aṇu*) and so forth among those things to be set in motion, because it is precisely those living beings who have become one with karma who are the agents of existence, and because all living beings attain their respective states through their own autonomy—continually coming into being by means of the relationship between cause and effect impelled by the power of karma—it is rightly said that each individual who acts in such a way possesses the nature of all things and thus possesses universal lordship (*sarveśvaratā*).
This is the very effort of one's own self; these [notions of] the sun and so forth being born from another birth are merely the rumors of the credulous.
"For Fortune favors the man who is energetic while he is still perceiving the accomplishment of destiny.
Now, however, the faults in your doctrine that God is the cause are stated—beginning with "From God... and so forth.

This must be considered: does the initiation of action by God occur from an existing action or a non-existing one? And what follows from this? If God is the initiator of an action that has not yet come into being, then non-duality (advaita) results, just as in the doctrine of the Primordial Person (puruṣa), because that [action] would then consist of Him; since action also consists of the nature of God, it would arise as nothing other than God Himself.

If it is argued that [the world] arises from God as an already existing effect (*bhūta*), then this follows: that action (*karman*) exists even prior [to its manifestation], because the effect exists within the cause; and since that [action] is identical with the very self of God, it is like the future state of the body, organs, and so forth, due to such an existence, such an operation, and the attainment of those respective states—by such arguments as these. Nevertheless, non-duality (*advaita*) is all the more established precisely because of that identity, just as in the case of the state of the Person (*puruṣa*), or like the becoming of atoms and so forth which are identical with God as their future state. Or else, for what purpose is it set in motion, and in what manner?

Then you might say: "That action is not of the nature of the Lord; what then? Rather, it is of the nature of that particular living being for whom—whether auspicious or inauspicious—it is set in motion by the Lord in whatever manner, in the various forms of human, hell-being, animal, or god."

To this it is replied: Therefore, that [result] is of such a nature; the meaning is that each living being becomes such and such due to its respective cause. Now, even that which is produced by those [causes] proceeds in dependence upon God, just like human effort or royal favor. Insofar as its production is concerned, His independence is established; for it is action performed by Him alone that produces divine favor, just as the performance of service depending on the five factors—substance and so forth—is directly perceived to yield its fruit.

If, however, the Lord accepted by you acts independently and without regard for karma, then—given the absence of karma as the regulator for each individual—this world would lack the distinctions of place, body, sense organs, enjoyment, prosperity, adversity, liberation, and so forth, because the cause would be uniform, just like the case of a cloth and its threads.

Because the Lord acts in that manner under the influence of that [karma], therefore, when He impels him, that very being is the Lord; for by acting thus according to his own will, that particular living being possesses lordship as you intend it. But this does not apply to the Lord Himself, because He is one who is impelled in such a way, and thus, like a servant, He is logically established as an object of action (karman). [This is concluded] by these arguments. (Bhāṣya)

[Objection: Even that which is produced by human effort (puruṣakāra) proceeds in dependence upon God, just like [the favor of] a king. [Response: Insofar as its being "produced" is concerned, its independence is established for that [human effort] alone; for it is the very action performed by him that produces the favor of God, just as the fruit of an action such as service—which depends on the five factors beginning with the substance—is perceived.

But if the Lord as conceived by you acts independently and without regard for karma, then—given the absence of karma which determines each individual—this world would lack the distinctions of place, body, sense organs, enjoyment, prosperity, adversity, and liberation; for all things would have the same cause, just as the state of being a cloth or a blanket [would be indistinguishable]. Thus it is refuted. (Bhāṣya on Sūtra 4.1.20)
Now, even that which is performed by human effort proceeds depending upon God, just like [the favor of] a king.
If it is thought: "Even the action performed by living beings is indeed performed by God, because it proceeds under the control of God;

for example, when two men possess equal human effort, the king is pleased with only one and not the other. Thus, the result is seen to depend on the king's will and not on the power of the man's own action; likewise, the engagement in that action depends on the power of God."

To this it is replied: first of all, his sovereignty with respect to the act of creation is established, because the grace that arises from the conviction regarding the ritual actions to be performed by living beings is produced by him alone, the Lord who is pleased by the vital breaths; and in that regard, the king is merely the instrumental cause.

Just as a king’s favor is produced by the action performed by one particular person, so too the Lord’s favor arises based on the action performed by one particular person; thus, there is independence regarding karma. For it is the very action performed by that specific individual—not by another—that produces the Lord’s favor, because the Lord’s favor, which is conditioned by the action of one particular person, is produced by that [action] alone. Therefore, since the activity of the Lord is dependent upon human karma, karma is primary both in regard to his activity and its fruit.
It might be thought: "Just as with a king, since God must be depended upon for the initiation of karma and the granting of its fruit, He is the primary cause.

But this is not so; because, as stated in the passage beginning with "the pentad of substance, etc.," the initiation of karmas is observed to occur only by depending on substance (*dravya*), space (*kṣetra*), time (*kāla*), state (*bhāva*), and destiny (*bhava*), and the fruit of those performed karmas is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
That very person is the agent; the substance is that which is given, or the substance to be given, such as clothing, gold, and so forth;
the field is that place where the fruit is obtained, such as a village, a city, a forest, or a wilderness tract;
and the time is at a certain time—by day or by night, in the forenoon or the afternoon, immediately or after a long interval.
The state [of mind] being serene, angry, and so forth,
as well as the giving of food, ornaments, and the like appropriate to the bodies of elephants and their mahouts—

herein lies the formal argument (*prayoga*): even in other cases, the fruit produced by a living being depends upon specific substances and so on, because it is the fruit of an action such as pleasure, just like the fruit of service which depends upon the fivefold set beginning with substance.

Therefore, even though action depends upon the five categories beginning with substance (*dravya*), it is the primary factor in the bestowing of results because it determines the independent living being; nor does God depend on action, since He is not dependent [on anything else]. (Isvarapratyabhijñākārikā 2.1.15) *Bhāṣya* ad loc. says "na ceśvaraḥ".
...dādīśva॰ ya॰ by Praṇinoṣiteśvara; here, there may also be the reading *pra॰ atra prāṇino vineśvareṇa*.
Is it "veśva-pra" and so forth?
It is independent (svatantra).
Is the living being independent?
As for your [proposed] "Lord" (īśvara) and so forth...

Let it be granted for now that God possesses sovereignty and independence in setting in motion the *pradhāna* and other principles for the sake of creating the world; however, the fault in the view that the actions (*karman*) of living beings are not the cause—and thus are independent of them—is stated as follows: "Therefore, with respect to each individual person," and so forth. If there were no action that determines [the state] for each and every person (*puruṣa*) by means of the fivefold categories beginning with substance (*dravya*), then God alone would be the undifferentiated cause. Because the cause called "God" would be without distinction, there would be no differentiation.
Of what? Of the multitude of living beings known as divine, human, and animal.

If it is asked, "What kind of distinction [would there be]? it is replied: There would be no distinction characterized by place, body, sense organs, and experience. Why? Because of the independence from the cause of that distinction. And is this [independence] with respect to an existing action or a non-existing one? If it were with respect to a non-existing one, what [would follow]? There would be the abolition of activity.
And it has been stated in your own scripture: "One who intends to accomplish yoga..."
...and he would be free from sleep, drowsiness, negligence, and laziness; and so forth.
Furthermore, since living beings would be eternally liberated due to the absence of karma, the creation of bodies and so on by the Lord would be purposeless.
Consequently, because of the absence of the distinction between the producer and the produced, the conceptualization of duality would be rendered rootless.

But if [the Lord] were not to depend upon merit and demerit even though they exist, then the two defects of "attaining what was not done" (*akṛtābhyāgama*) and "losing what was done" (*kṛtapraṇāśa*) would ensue; for in that case, the Lord would be identical to those who have neither been liberated from the bondage of the accumulation of karmic impressions (*karmāśaya*) nor have exhausted them.

However, that distinction [of the Lord] would exist when there is a specific ripening (*vipāka*) of karma—determined by the dependence on substance (*dravya*), place (*kṣetra*), time (*kāla*), state (*bhāva*), and destiny (*bhava*)—which acts as the regulator for each individual soul.

And that [Lord] is observed to be logical in His sovereignty over the multitude of living beings whose karma ripens as specific substances and so forth desired by us—namely, the prosperity of some, the adversity of others, and the liberation of some.

Here is the formal argument (*prayoga*): This world would lack the distinctions of place, body, sense-faculties, enjoyment, prosperity, adversity, liberation, and so forth, because its causes are identical, just as cloth is made of threads. Just as cloth—due to the non-distinction of its causal threads—is made of threads and is not made of clay or gold, and thus remains undifferentiated in terms of genus, configuration, color, and so on; so too would this world be. But it is not so;
therefore, [the claim that a single cause produces all diversity] is untenable.

Alternatively, this world is preceded by a single Lord as its cause, whose maturation depends upon specific substances and other factors, because it possesses distinct genera, forms, colors, and so forth, like jars, cloths, chariots, and the like;
therefore, the state of being a Lord for all living beings is dependent upon their karma. [This argument does not appear in the Prajñāpradīpa manuscripts.]

If [the self] were independent in its status as the cause of action—that is, in its causality—would it be independent of action while it exists, or while it does not exist? If it were [independent] precisely while it does not exist, what would follow? The abolition of action.
And it has been stated to you in the scripture: "One who intends to accomplish yoga... should be free from sleep, lethargy, negligence, and laziness," and so forth.
Furthermore, if there were an absence of karma for living beings, they would be eternally liberated; consequently, the Lord's creation of bodies and the like would be purposeless.
Furthermore, because there would be no distinction between the object to be produced and the producer, the conceptualization of duality would be rendered rootless.

Moreover, if merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) were already existent and did not depend [on action], then the two faults of "attaining what was not done" (*akṛtābhyāgama*) and "the loss of what was done" (*kṛtapraṇāśa*) would ensue. [This is so] because of the bondage and liberation from the accumulation of karma that has neither been exhausted nor arisen; and it is for this reason that the arising, destruction, subsidence, and suppression of karma have been explained.
"Having reached substance, space, time, existence,
and state," thus [it is said] in the *Viśeṣāvaśyaka-bhāṣya* (verse 575).
The genus (*jāti*) is "cloth-ness" (*paṭatva*); the configuration (*ākṛti*) is the shape; the color (*varṇa*) is blue and so forth.
Even having accepted [the view that] there is no dependence on action (*karman*) therein, we state the fault: "And [if there were] independence," and so forth.
Is this independence of God [due to] his action, characterized by merit and demerit, being existent or non-existent?

What follows from this? If there is no dependence [on anything else] for *dharma* and *adharma*, which are simply non-existent, why is there a question? If you ask, "What follows from that?", it is said: there would be the abolition of all action (*kriyā-vilopa*). For if those two are non-existent—like a sky-flower or a donkey's horn—what dependence could there be? Consequently, all actions intended for the attainment of the beneficial and the avoidance of the harmful would be abolished; yet these are desired. This is because it has been stated in your own scripture: "One who intends to accomplish yoga," and so forth—the meaning of which has already been explained—up to "he should be free from sleep, lethargy, negligence, and laziness," etc.; thus, this is a reminder of the texts prescribing right conduct.

Furthermore, regarding the passage beginning with "And moreover, in the absence of karma" and ending with "rootlessness": because living beings would be devoid of action, they would be eternally liberated;
consequently, they would not possess bodies associated with sense objects, and thus the Lord's creation of bodies and so forth would be purposeless.

Consequently, there is an absence of distinction between the object to be produced and the producer; therefore, due to this absence of distinction between the object to be produced and the producer, the conceptualization of duality—such as God, karma, primordial matter (*pradhāna*), atoms, and so forth—is utterly groundless.
Thus, in the first place, it is not logical for an action that is non-existent to be independent.

But if you think that although merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) exist, the Lord does not depend upon them for the performance of actions leading to worldly prosperity, misfortune, or the supreme good—because of His absolute independence and because He has no need for those two, just as one who knows [how to plow] does not require oxen for the acts of explaining and so forth—then there would be the faults of "attainment of what was not done" (*akṛtābhyāgama*) and "loss of what was done" (*kṛtanāśa*). How so? Through the bondage and liberation resulting from the persistence and exhaustion of the accumulation of karma (*karmāśaya*), respectively.

Furthermore, even for one whose karma is exhausted, there would be the arrival of what was not done (*akṛtābhyāgama*), consisting of the connection with bondage, prosperity, or misfortune; why? Because of independence from merit and demerit (*dharmādharmanirapekṣatvāt*), as in the systems of those who maintain that [the world arises from] primordial nature (*svabhāva*), the person (*puruṣa*), and so forth.

Likewise, even for a hell-being or the like who has accumulated an extremely non-virtuous store of karma, there would be the destruction of what was done (*kṛtapraṇāśa*), consisting of the connection with liberation or prosperity, because of independence from merit and demerit, just like the systems of those who maintain the person, primordial nature, and so forth. And this is undesirable.
Thus, the Lord’s independence from karma is untenable due to the occurrence of such undesirable consequences.
"Herein," says Ācārya Prajñākara, "that from which the attainment of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) results is Dharma.
Vaiśeṣika Sūtra
"Adharma also is a quality of the self, being the cause of harm and transgression for the agent"—thus it is stated in the *Praśastapādabhāṣya*.
Furthermore, [adharma] proceeds depending upon karma; therefore, those very karmas are sovereign, because He (the Lord) acts as their instigator in that manner.

He does not bring those [causes] into being in that manner, because they are brought into being in such a way that they do not exist when unproduced, like the horn of a donkey; and because he is not independent, like sound and so forth,
for an agent is independent, since he acts by setting [them] in motion, like threads and cloth—
let this be observed (pṛṣṭha 325, line 3).

Furthermore, since even the Lord acts in accordance with karma, every person possesses a corresponding power inherent within them; their actions are validated by a specific intelligence, and they are independent, because such activity would otherwise result in the Lord himself being the instigator down to the level of the individual.
If, in order to avoid this undesirable consequence, you think that he acts only in dependence upon karma, then those very karmas must be the agents, the independent ones, and the lords.

For what reason? Because those [actions] bring about that [Lord] as well in such a manner; for it is those very actions which bring about even that Lord in various ways, and not he who brings about those actions in that way. Why? Because they are brought about by him in that manner, just like sound and so forth, according to the example to be stated later regarding the primary cause (*pradhāna*).

And just as rice alone, even while depending on earth, water, and so forth, transforms them into itself because it attains that state, whereas earth and the rest do not because they do not attain that state; so too, actions alone are sovereign because they are the transformers, and not the "Lord" (Īśvara) you desire, because he is merely that which is to be transformed—this might be your thought:
that even earth, water, and so forth certainly transform rice into its nature as rice, even though they have not themselves attained the state of being rice.

And this is incorrect because they do not exist; and their non-existence is due to the fact that what has not undergone transformation does not exist, like a donkey’s horn. Thus, he demonstrates the very same reasoning already introduced in the refutation of existence through proximity.

"Because of its lack of independence, like sound and so forth"—this is the example adduced in every case by way of similarity with the Pradhāna for the sake of the followers of Kapila. Just as [the example] implies that the Pradhāna possesses causality due to its independence, while it implies that sound and the rest lack the status of being primary causes because they lack independence; and just as you yourself have stated that neither "the unmanifest" nor "the manifest" constitutes the state of being the Pradhāna, in the very same way, God—due to His lack of independence and His dependence upon karma—is not the cause, and it is implied by those very arguments you have put forward that those [karmas] alone are the causes.
Therefore, as for what was said—that the very arguments you have stated prove that all living beings are lords—it is well;

reflecting upon that, he says: "He becomes the agent," and so forth. These phrases, whose meanings have already been explained, share a single sense up to the point of the example "like threads and cloth.
Just as it is the threads themselves that become the causes of the cloth through the process of its production because they function in that manner, so too are the persons themselves the agents.
And likewise,
[the state of] rice is not unpleasing by way of being rice;
nor is it unmanifest, just as the unmanifest itself is not.
"Neither as the unmanifest nor as the manifest"—
here the reading might also be "that which is not manifest is the unmanifest," or alternatively,
the reading might also be "neither as 'not unmanifest' nor as 'manifest'."
See page 335,
line 2: *°tyekadyekārtha* (Bhāṣya) / *°tyekadyikārtha* (Yaśomitra).
The passage beginning with "Even for the Lord" (*īśvarasyāpi ca*) and so forth, by means of this text, contemplates the orientation of those very arguments toward this [conclusion].

Just as you previously established by stating that a specific cognition is characterized by the proximity of such a capacity according to the relative gradation of preceding capacities, so too here, by those very same arguments and with those same examples of the threads, fibers, and so forth, because activity resides in action—that is, because it is grounded in action—and because the excellence of the preeminence of creation belongs to actions which constitute the nature of the Person (*puruṣa*), every person indeed possesses the proximity of such a capacity and has his actions validated by a specific cognition. Those actions have been validated by that specific-cognitioned Lord, by other authors of scriptures who are all-seeing, and even by those who possess established scriptures; for the purpose of thoroughly understanding the fruits of those actions, the authors of scriptures and others are beyond suspicion.

And that [agency] would be independent, because it would entail activity in that manner; for just as there is activity on the part of the agent and the living being, so too would activity entail [the agency] of the Lord (*īśvara*). Because he is the instigator from the Lord—meaning, as long as there is the state of being an instigator up to the Lord—he is the cause, since we observe the activity and non-activity of one who possesses power, like a cook and others. Furthermore, because his "allness" is exactly thus, there is also the state of having all forms.
Moreover, because we observe excellence and deficiency, [there must be] the experience of activity and its fruit;
for excellence and deficiency do not arise from the mere whim of a seedless Lord, since there is no activity at all apart from the Person (*puruṣa*).

If it is argued that even though [the Lord] depends upon karma, the Lord is not rendered redundant because there would be no activity in his absence—just as a carpenter requires wood and other materials—we say no, for the same logic applies to the other case as well.

For instance: even though [the Lord] depends upon the Lord, karma is not rendered redundant for that very same reason; and since the Lord is the initiator, just as the wood of a chariot depends on a carpenter, so too is karma the initiator of action. Since the person is the source of karma, the person alone is the Lord.
In this way, the consequence of [Ishvara] being subject to obstruction also applies to Ishvara, because his activity is dependent [on other factors], like a chariot-maker;

for just as in the case of a chariot-maker, there is the possibility of deficiency in the capacity of his materials and tools, so too, since Ishvara is something to be set in motion, all persons are the causes.

"Because of the activity of those who possess power," and so forth; for even in the case of the Lord (Īśvara), one observes activity and non-activity based on the presence or absence of the totality of the powers of those very persons who possess power. Thus, he recalls that same collection of arguments up to the phrase "like a cook, etc."; by the inclusion of "etc.," [the examples] such as "like the *rajas* quality" and "like activity" are intended. He extends the application of the text just as before: "In this very way, because of His being everything (*sarvatva*), there is His having all forms (*sarvamūrtitā*); and in this very way, His eightfold form consisting of earth and the rest is taught"—from this point onward, the entire subsequent text is to be understood through those same arguments regarding the Lordship over all living beings, just as in that previous case.

Furthermore, the section beginning with "and because of the observation of increase and decrease" and so forth is intended to establish the creation of Īśvara; likewise, the section beginning with "activity, experience, and fruit" and so forth, up until "because there is no activity without a Puruṣa," establishes that action (*karman*) is the cause, since increase and decrease do not occur through the arbitrary will of a seedless Īśvara.

Therefore, because it depends upon action and because everything has everything as its essence, there is the state of being the Lord of All (*sarveśvaratā*). [This is] the two-fold [nature], according to the Bhāṣya.
See page 326, line 1, note 5: *tadvividha* (Bhāṣya);
see page 326, line 1, note 5.

The cause [of the world] is that which possesses the fruit [of action], because we observe the activity and non-activity of that which possesses power, as in the case of a cook and others; furthermore, since it is exactly thus for this [cause] in its entirety, it also possesses all forms;
moreover, because we observe increase and decrease, there is the fruit experienced through activity.

...because [the world] does not proceed without a Person (puruṣa), there is indeed an increase and decrease [of merit and demerit], and not from the arbitrary will of a seedless Lord; see page 328, line 1;
see page 328, line 3.

If it is argued that even though [the Lord] depends upon karma, the Lord is not rendered redundant because there is no activity in its absence—just as a chariot-maker depends on wood and so forth—we say no, for the same logic applies to the other case as well. For instance: even though [the Lord] depends upon the Lord, karma is not rendered redundant for that very same reason; and since the Lord is the impeller, just as the wood of a chariot depends on the chariot-maker, so too is karma the impeller and the person is the impeller of karma; thus, the person alone is the Lord.
In this way, the consequence of being subject to obstruction also applies to Īśvara, because his activity is dependent [on other factors], just as in the case of a chariot-maker,
who acts when there is the presence or absence of the capacity and deficiency of the materials and tools required for the chariot.
See page 327, line 2;
and [the text] instructs: "pra॰ ॰smādaverārā॰ pra॰" [is to be read as] "pra॰ smād averārā॰ pra॰".

If it be thought— as expressed in the passage beginning with "if [the Lord's] activity depends upon karma" and ending with "like a chariot-maker"— that even though His activity depends upon karma, the causality of the Lord is not purposeless, because in the absence of that [karma], there would be no activity;

If you think that where there is an absence of activity in the absence of something, the existence of that [thing] as the motivator is seen not to be useless—as for example, the dependence on wood and so forth for the sake of a chariot when a chariot-maker is active—that is not so, because the same applies elsewhere as well.

If you ask how that is so, the proof of the contrary is shown by the very application [of the argument]: even if there is dependence on God, karma is not useless, for that very reason, like the wood required for a chariot when a chariot-maker is present; thus, [your argument] is a contradictory and non-conclusive [reason].
(Note: *kāratvavaditi* is corrected from *kāratvavaditi ya*.)
Having also [addressed] the lack of partiality regarding the wood used for the purpose of the chariot,
and having concluded that discussion, he says: "And because the Lord is the initiator," and so forth, up to "the Person alone is the Lord."

For God is the instigator, just as a master is to a servant; and that quality of being an instigator is established for action by the method already stated, while the state of being instigated belongs to God. Likewise, action is the instigator; it is understood from the context that "the person acts through action. The word *iti* has the sense of a reason (*hetu*); therefore, the person alone is the Lord of all. Furthermore, this sovereignty of action will be further elaborated upon later.

Since it has been stated that every person possesses the status of a Lord, there follows the consequence of contradiction and so forth; furthermore, the Lord as conceived by you is contradicted because his activity is dependent [on other factors], like a chariot-maker.

The explanation of this proof is as follows: "just as a chariot-maker," and so forth. The material cause (*upādāna*) is wood; the instruments (*upakaraṇa*) are the axe and so on. Their "inefficacy" (*asāmarthya*) is their deficiency (*vaiguṇya*), which is either the incompleteness of those [materials and tools] that already exist or simply the absence of one of them. In that case, an obstruction is observed—this is the completion of the sentence.

Regarding the passage beginning with "tathā" (so it is): likewise, for one who desires to favor those whose merit is diminished and who desires to strike down those whose merit is accumulated, if there were no obstruction [to his will], he would possess independence; however, this is not the case, because we observe that the activity of the Lord is obstructed by the causal condition of karma performed by persons.

As for what is said—that at the beginning of creation, having produced bodies and so forth by the power of His own unimpeded capacity, He teaches the boundaries of dharma and adharma to awakened beings; that in the intermediate period, He bestows favor through desired or undesired fruits according to their adherence to those boundaries—this very favor is like the release from a debt for them, and He leads those who follow the path of liberation to *sāyojya* (union); and that at the time of dissolution, having withdrawn the bodies, senses, elements, as well as the wholesome and unwholesome, He puts them to sleep during the night of cosmic dissolution—and furthermore, that His omniscience and His status as the ultimate agent are required: the application [of the analogy] should be made to the chariot-maker (*rathakāra*) by following the similarity of acting with dependence; however, He shows the dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) by saying, "desiring to favor one whose merit has been diminished," and so forth.

If that Lord, who desires to favor a person whose auspicious karma has been diminished and desires to harm one whose karma is the opposite, were unimpeded, he would possess independence; however, this is not the case. For we observe that the activity of the Lord is impeded by the influence of the karma to be considered—that is, by the power of the individual's own performed actions.
If this were not accepted, then he would join the performer of auspicious karma with suffering and the other with happiness;

and in that case, there would be the fallacies of "attaining what was not done" (*akṛtābhyāgama*) and "the destruction of what was done" (*kṛtapraṇāśa*), as has already been stated, which is not desired.

Therefore, there is an obstruction to the activity of the Lord by virtue of the conditions of human karma; and because his activity is obstructed, he lacks sovereignty, since he is subject to obstruction like an ordinary person. Thus, how can he be called a "mover"? If there were no obstruction for him when he desires to favor one whose merit is diminished or to strike down one whose merit is accumulated, he would possess independence; but this is not the case, for we observe that the activity of the Lord is obstructed by the condition of karma performed by persons.

As for what is said—that at the beginning of creation, by the power of His own unimpeded capacity, He produces bodies and so forth and instructs conscious beings in the boundaries of dharma and adharma; that in the intermediate period, He bestows favor through desired or undesired fruits according to their adherence to those boundaries—this very favor is like the release from a debt for them, and He leads those who follow the path to liberation to *sāyojya* (union); and that at the time of the end, having withdrawn the bodies, senses, and elements along with the wholesome and unwholesome, He puts them to sleep during the night of dissolution; and furthermore, His omniscience and His status as the creator of all are required [as attributes].

line 5: As for what is said [in the passage] beginning with "yattu ucyate" and ending with "svāpayati," since both positions— the one involving dependent activity and the one involving independent activity— are accepted according to the distinction of time, there is no fault because activity is established in both ways and thus cannot be obstructed.

For example—at the beginning of creation—he produces bodies, senses, and objects independently, solely by virtue of his own unimpeded power for those who are devoid of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*). Having produced these, he instructs the awakened ones who have arisen from sleep regarding the boundaries of merit and demerit, saying: "Perform austerity, charity, sacrifice, and so forth; do not commit violence, falsehood, theft, illicit sexual intercourse, and the like. And by means of instruction, he establishes the fixed order and the limits of those two, merit and demerit, through the demarcation of their boundaries.

And when, during the intermediate period (*madhyakāla*), He bestows favor upon those living beings—consisting of the enjoyment of objects characterized by either desired or undesired fruits—in accordance with the merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*) they observe according to their respective limits and in accordance with their performance, then it may be thought: "Favor through the enjoyment of the desired fruit of the performance of dharma is appropriate; but how is it appropriate that [He] is joined with an undesired [fruit] through the enjoyment of the fruit of the performance of adharma? To this it is replied: This very [undesired fruit] is indeed a favor for them, because it releases them from that [debt].
Furthermore, he leads those who have set out upon the path to liberation taught by Him and who follow that path to *sāyojya*.
What is this path to liberation? It is the method of Yoga belonging to Maheśvara.

Because it unites (*yuñjate*) them with Himself, it is called *sayuk*; the state of being that is *sāyojya*, which is their becoming one with God (*īśvara-sādbhāva*). He leads them to that; He conducts them there.
In the midst of this, sovereignty is dependent.

Furthermore, at the time of dissolution (*antakāla*), just as he withdraws the body, the sense organs, and the elements—namely, the objects designated as "elements"—so too, having withdrawn from them both merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), which constitute their wholesome and unwholesome [actions], he causes all persons to sleep during the night of dissolution. Just as a father, when his sons are overcome by the exhaustion of daytime exertion, gathers his little children who have been wandering through the day and puts them to bed, so too [the Lord] withdraws the merit and demerit that are the causes of *saṃsāra* and puts all persons to sleep during the night of dissolution. [Objection: Even so, [the Lord] is not indifferent [to the results of actions], because [he acts] out of independence. [Response: That is not the case either, because his engagement in teaching merit and demerit shares the same nature as the activity of ignorant people who act for the sake of what is harmful; thus, it has as its object that which is harmful. This is like the activity of children and others who engage in actions that result in what is harmful.
That in the absence of which something else is absent, and in the presence of which that other thing is invariably present, is the cause; the other is the effect.
However, there is no absence of the body and so forth upon the absence of merit (*dharma*) and the like, because the production of the body and so forth is admitted at the beginning of creation;

nor is the existence of the body and so forth invariably tied to the presence of merit and the like, since at the time of death, even accumulated wholesome and unwholesome actions whose fruits have not yet been experienced are withdrawn.

Just as there is a lack of independent agency for Him regarding the act of instruction, so too is there a lack of independent agency for Him regarding the act of bestowing grace upon living beings; for it is precisely when He is thus deprived of autonomy that He is intended [as the agent].

Therefore, since His sovereignty is established both ways—whether by depending on or not depending on [auxiliaries]—there is no fault at all. The fault you have raised was merely an illusion of a fault; such is the refutation of the opposing position.
See the edition by Sāyapatī, page 344, line 14;
[the reading] is *hataḥ* in the manuscript (*pra*).
Do not commit violence; having set aside both dharma and adharma...?

That too is not at all [the case], because the engagement in the instruction of dharma and adharma shares the same nature as the activity of ignorant persons—such as children—who engage in activities that result in meaningless ends; therefore, it has as its object that which is meaningless. (See page 344, line 14).

That whose absence constitutes the absence of something else, and whose presence constitutes the certain presence of that other thing, is the cause; the other is the effect. Furthermore, there is no necessary absence of the body and so forth upon the absence of *dharma* and the like, because the production of the body and so forth is admitted at the beginning of a cosmic cycle (*sarga*).

Nor is there the certain presence of the body and so forth upon the presence of *dharma* and the like, because at the time of death, there is the withdrawal of wholesome and unwholesome actions whose fruits have not yet been experienced.
And once his status as the creator of all things is established, his omniscience is proven effortlessly;
for a creator must be one who perceives the nature, form, and other qualities of the effects he produces.

Now, one might ask: "How is his omniscience established, by virtue of which he becomes an object of devotion for those desiring both ultimate liberation (*niḥśreyasa*) and worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*)? To this he says: "And when his status as the creator of all is established," and so forth.

Likewise, Praśastamati and others have said: "His omniscience is established precisely because he is the cause of the entire universe; for a creator must possess thorough knowledge of the effect, its material cause, its instruments, its purpose, and its recipient."

For in this world, whoever is the creator of something knows its material cause and so forth; as it is well known that the potter, being the creator of jars and the like, knows their material cause—the lump of clay—as well as the instruments such as the wheel, the purpose such as the fetching of water, and the recipient, namely the householder; in the same way, God, being the creator of all worlds, must know their material causes characterized by atoms and the like, their instruments such as merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), space, and time, the instruments of worldly transaction characterized by generality (*sāmānya*), particularity (*viśeṣa*), and inherence (*samavāya*), and the persons designated as recipients.
"Therefore, his omniscience is established"—
see page 43–44 of the *Tattvasaṅgrahapañjikā* composed by Kamalaśīla, page 345, line 19.

Just as he lacks knowledge regarding the instructions [of the scriptures], so too does he lack the capacity for the act of bestowing grace upon living beings. Furthermore, when we say here that "he possesses knowledge because he performs those actions," even that omniscience which is sought after would not exist; for if his activity were independent of karma, it would be obstructed by it, resulting in a lack of sovereignty (*anaiśvarya*). Moreover, during the time of the created world’s cycle of existence, as well as at its beginning and end, defects such as the arrival of what was not earned (*akṛtābhyāgama*) and the loss of what was earned (*kṛtapraṇāśa*) remain exactly as they are. Thus, since these defects have not been removed, this [position] is of no consequence.

There is yet another fault: even that which is desired—namely, his omniscience—is untenable because of his being an "all-doer. Since the instrument [of action] is invariably concomitant with knowledge, if he performs everything, he must necessarily know everything; thus, it is argued that he is omniscient because he is an all-doer. But this too is not logically consistent. Because his activity regarding harmful matters shares the same nature as the ignorant actions of children and the like, you are, by this very assumption, effectively perceiving before our eyes that he is ignorant, like a child, due to acting without deliberation. Why? Because his engagement in teaching dharma and adharma has for its object that which is harmful; for dharma and adharma are indeed harmful objects for this teaching of the boundaries of dharma and adharma.

Furthermore, those two—merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*)—do not possess the status of being the cause of the body and so forth; for it is accepted that at the beginning of creation, the bodies and other things are produced by the Lord’s own emission even without the operation of merit and demerit, and it is also accepted that during the period of dissolution, the absence of bodies and such occurs precisely when the operation of merit and demerit exists.
Therefore, because they lack the definition of a cause, these two do not have causality.
If it is asked, "What is that definition of a cause?", it is said: "In the absence of which... and so on, the meaning of which has already been explained, up to the phrase "the other effect."

If it is asked, "How is that [the body] impossible? it is said: by the passage beginning with "And there is no absence of dharma and so forth," he demonstrates that even in the absence of those two which are considered the causes, the effect—the body and so forth—exists; and conversely, even when they exist, the effect does not exist; and he shows their lack of understanding regarding the fruitfulness of instruction, up until the point where, at the time of death, there is the withdrawal of wholesome and unwholesome actions whose fruits have not yet been given. Since the meaning has already been explained, the words are not further analyzed. Because of the absence of knowledge... [text fragment].
"...thus necessarily...

Furthermore, regarding the passage beginning with "And just as the instruction... and continuing up to "...the lack of knowledge even regarding action," it is not only that he lacks knowledge of the instruction;
rather, he also lacks knowledge of the activity of benefiting living beings. This is what is being extended [by analogy] here.
So how is it that this [power] is, through sheer delusion alone... what...
achieved by the exceedingly weighty act of distributing enjoyments and bestowing favors? Thus, sovereignty is said to be nothing other than absolute dependence on others.
Even grace (*anugraha*) is described as its opposite, by virtue of being the cause of suffering and having the nature of suffering, just like the affliction of eating food prepared with poison;
and this remains true even when attaining union (*sāyojya*) with it.

Furthermore, as for what you have suspected—that because God is predominant even in the middle [of existence], if activity proceeds solely under the power of God, there would be the consequence of a confusion of fruits; that such a consequence would lead to the collapse of ritual action (*kriyā*); and that from that, there would follow either universal liberation or universal non-liberation—[that objection is invalid].

If it is argued that [this is] "cultivated" (*bhāvyate*), it is said: when this section on cultivation begins with "Because of sheer delusion... and continues until "...by the exceedingly weighty act of distributing enjoyment," why does it proceed thus? For at that time, since the activity of living beings proceeds like that of a blind man, it is the Lord alone who produces their bodies and so forth for them, establishes the boundaries of *dharma* and *adharma*, impels them therein, binds them with the fruits thereof, and—having distributed the desired and undesired enjoyment according to those fruits—favors those living beings. Such is the act of favoring; and for one who is afflicted by that act of favoring, there is extreme exhaustion, like that of a hired laborer common to many men, women, and eunuchs.

Thus, in the sense of "because," it follows that since it involves excessive affliction and absolute dependence on others, sovereignty (*aiśvarya*)—which is denoted by synonymous terms such as *śītalikā*—is said to be like a spider (*lūtā*);
therefore, this [notion] is due solely to delusion...
what [else could it be]?
"...by means of the act of bestowing enjoyment, distribution, and favor that is exceedingly weighty? Thus, sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) is said to be absolute dependence;

even "favor" (*anugraha*) is described by its opposite, because [the world] consists of suffering both as a cause of suffering and as suffering in itself, like the distress of eating food prepared with poison—even in attaining union (*sāyojya*) with Him, it is the same.

And thus, that which you suspect is indeed correct: since God is predominant even in the middle [of the process], if activity proceeds solely by the power of God, there would be the consequence of a confusion of results; if that were to occur, there would be the abolition of ritual action, and from that, either universal liberation or universal non-liberation. Thus, while you are thus deluded, this [following] is your delusion.
The activity which is an act of favor;
the affliction of that [activity].
Regarding "yallatā," Hemacandra Sūri states: "But *lūtā* refers to a disease, an ant, and a spider."
Furthermore, even what is called "favor" is stated to be the opposite; that is, it is actually non-favor while being called favor.

What is the reason? It is because of its being both a cause of suffering and having the nature of suffering. For the enjoyment of desired objects—which consists of violence and so forth—is a cause of suffering due to the defects of acquisition, preservation, decay, and attachment; and the enjoyment of undesired objects is of the nature of suffering. And because it is of the nature of suffering, this [so-called favor] is indeed non-favor.

The illustration is as follows: it is like the suffering caused by eating food prepared with poison. For instance, suppose some cruel and foolish king were to feed his own servants food mixed with poison, saying, "I am favoring you. Your proposed Lord would be just like that. Furthermore, as for the claim that even suffering is a favor—like the release from a debt—that too is incorrect. It would lead to the absurd conclusion that beings killed by those who liberate others from saṃsāra, such as hunters, butchers, or outcasts, would be favored; and because it involves bringing about one's own downfall through the defilement of the multitude of living beings, it would result in ignorance, just like the so-called "favor" toward beings which actually leads to their lack of knowledge.

The same applies even regarding the attainment of union (*sāyojya*) with Him. For liberation is supposedly union with the Lord; yet, by leading the multitude of living beings to union with Himself, He makes them merely vessels for excessive suffering. Since the state of being a Lord—characterized as described above and afflicted by the created cycle of existence—is denoted by the term "non-liberation," what is the use of such sovereignty or liberation? It consists essentially of the exhaustion of bearing the burden of all human activities at all times. Therefore, even a state of wretchedness, in which one is independent and acts according to one's own will, is better than [such] servitude. Thus he says: "Better even poverty... and so forth.

[the text] "cāṇḍālāya" [is found there]; by this, the violation of the command... [is shown].

page 342, line 11.
Is it *kliṣṭasaṃprayukta*?
The reading *asya mokṣaḥ* might also occur here.

And thus, regarding what you have suspected through the passage beginning with "like that which has a beginning and an end," and so forth—namely, that these faults indeed exist even with an *Īśvara*, and they arise in exactly the same way even when an *Īśvara* is accepted—he says, "It is quite correct," and so on. The meaning has already been explained; by means of the sequence establishing the relationship between cause and effect, [the argument proceeds] until the consequence that, if that were the case, there would be a collapse of all action (*kriyāvilopa*).

Why? Because of the predominance of God and because of the faults mentioned immediately above, the actions of merit and demerit of living beings would not exist due to the absence of results, since the results [of those actions] would be mixed up at the beginning, end, and middle by the power of God alone; consequently, there would be either the liberation of all living beings—meaning universal liberation—by His power alone, or the non-liberation of all, as previously stated. Thus ends the first section.
See page 338, line 1;
here, the reading might also be "prasaktaḥ."

However, in order to avoid the total abolition of the ritual activities prescribed by all the scriptures, when the primacy of the Lord is taught with karma and other factors as subordinate, He Himself first directly intervenes through His own power to produce bodies and the like, and establishes the boundaries of dharma and adharma. Subsequently, having generated merit through meditation, He appoints the presiding deities, such as Brahmā and others, as the guardians of those boundaries of dharma and adharma. Finally, having withdrawn both dharma and adharma, He causes [the soul] to sleep, purified from the stains of the latent impressions of wholesome and unwholesome deeds, just like the body and its adjuncts.

This is grasped in one way: dualism arises from the admission of a primary and secondary relationship between God (*īśvara*) and karma; however, it is cultivated in another way through the contemplation of the meaning of non-duality, based on the restriction that "He alone [acts] by His own power. Thus, even this cultivation—for the sake of the direct restraint of someone who has no other motive—is concluded with the thought: "Having produced merit through meditation upon Him" (*tadanudhyānāt*). Yet, having abandoned both dualism and non-dualism, [one reaches the goal].
First, there would be the abandonment of non-duality by virtue of the statement establishing the boundaries of dharma and adharma.
A "boundary" (maryādā) is a place that is not to be transgressed; it is the limit of the occurrence of pleasure and pain.

Consequently, at the beginning of creation, pleasure and pain—which consist of states [such as heaven and hell]—would also not exist, because their objects would be unrestricted, just as in the case of cosmic dissolution (pralaya).
And [the two] would exist beforehand; as for the statement "in all treatises," etc., [it refers to] the state of being seen indeterminately (aniyata-dṛśyatā). Pañjikā 8.

To avoid this fault, [the author] explains in the subsequent text how it is that Īśvara is taught to be the primary cause while karma and other factors are subordinate: "In the beginning, He alone, by His own power... and so on, up to "...He causes [them] to sleep, purified of the stains of latent impressions (āśaya) of wholesome and unwholesome [karma], like a body. This concludes the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).
The distinction is that [Īśvara] appoints the presiding deities (*adhikārika*), such as Brahmā and others, who maintain the boundaries of dharma and adharma.
Regarding this, the Teacher states the following rebuttal: "This is being presented quite differently," and so forth.

To begin with, the proposition is stated otherwise, since duality is accepted through the admission of the primary and subordinate relationship between the Lord and karma; however, the explanation of the probandum and the reason is formulated in a different manner.

If you ask how this is so: because of the restriction that "He alone, by His own power, is independent of anything else," through the cultivation of the meaning of non-duality (*advaita*), one excludes unseen forces (*adṛṣṭa*) and other such powers as being inherently distinct from Him; thus, by restricting [the cause] to "directly and solely by His own power" without employing any other instrument for anyone, you cultivate nothing but non-duality. Furthermore, he says: "for the sake of such a regulation"—this cultivation is also for the sake of regulating non-duality.
If it is asked, "What is that cultivation? [the answer is: "Having generated merit from meditation thereafter"—this too is precisely the cultivation of non-duality (*advaitabhāvanā*).
Thus, first, duality has been asserted; it was stated that non-duality has been cultivated. (Sthāpanā-prakaraṇa)
This is the remainder; [the readings] "divā" and "kiñcida" are from the manuscript (pra).

However, it is withdrawn by abandoning both duality and non-duality; for one who has cultivated what was promised, having abandoned even duality and non-duality, the abandonment of non-duality is first accomplished by the statement establishing the boundaries of *dharma* and *adharma*—this is the remainder of the sentence.
What is that boundary? It is said: the definition of a boundary (*maryādā*) is "the place where there is no transgression. Thus he states the characteristic of a boundary.

Regarding the object (*viṣaya*), however, it is the boundary (*sīmā*) for the occurrence of pleasure and pain. Thus, there is the establishment of the respective limits of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) according to the principle that "pleasure extends this far" and "pain extends this far. This is the division of boundaries (*sīmāvibhāga*), characterized by the cessation of the occurrence of pleasure through merit and the cessation of the occurrence of pain through demerit, such that "this is distinct from that" and "this is distinct from the other. If one asks, "What follows from that?"—from that, at the beginning of creation, [there would be] "place and so forth" (*sthānādi*). By "and so forth," place, body, sense organs, and objects are meant; even pleasure and pain, which consist of those [factors], would not exist.

Why? Because their objects are indeterminate. For at that time, the objects of pleasure and pain would be indeterminate, because [the soul] does not exist as a substrate and because merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) do not exist. The illustration is: "like the dissolution" (*pralaya*). Just as during the dissolution, pleasure and pain have indeterminate objects precisely due to the absence of merit and demerit, and thus they are non-existent, so too would they be at the beginning of creation. Furthermore, it follows that pleasure and pain would also exist at the end. (The phrase "pleasure and pain would exist" is understood to carry over.)
Why? Because it has an object, or because its objects are restricted; otherwise, like the middle, these two would not exist in the middle, or like the end.

Or, it might be argued: for this very reason, the boundary of dharma and adharma does not consist in the instigation toward pleasure and so forth; what then? It is simply "this is dharma" and "this is adharma."

This too is equal to what was stated previously: since there is no such thing as "dharma" in the sense of being something that exists, is maintained, or is abandoned, how can it be dharma? Or, how can its opposite be adharma? Furthermore, if pleasure or pain arises solely from one's own inclination (*ruci*), then the teaching on the boundaries of dharma and adharma is purposeless; for anything could be established in any way whatsoever, solely by the power of the Lord (*īśvara-śakti*), because [such a system] would lack fixed objects, like something that has a beginning and an end. Moreover, there would be no restriction of objects at the time of withdrawal, due to the absence of the fivefold nature of form and so forth, just as in the intermediate state.

Alternatively, because they possess fixed objects and because the boundaries of dharma and adharma have been established, pleasure and pain at that time would have fixed objects; therefore, they should exist then just as they do during the intermediate period and the period after creation—this is the meaning. Or, the proof may be formulated by way of its opposite: "Or pleasure and pain would not exist in the interim, because they have fixed objects," [the reason] being "like the end" (*antavat*), due to the absence of dharma. (Praśastapāda-bhāṣya)
Because they have objects, or because their objects are restricted, the two [dharma and adharma] would not exist in the middle, just as they do not exist at the end;

or rather, it might be argued: for this very reason, the boundary of dharma and adharma does not consist in the instigation toward pleasure and so forth; what then? It is simply "this is dharma" and "this is adharma."

This too is equal to the previous [argument]: since there is no such thing as "dharma" in the sense of being that which is held (dhāraṇa) or that which causes one to fall away (dhāna), how can it be dharma? And how can its opposite be adharma?

Furthermore, if pleasure or pain arises solely from one's own desire (*ruci*), then the statement defining the boundaries of dharma and adharma is useless; for anything could be established in any way whatsoever at all times, simply by the power of the Lord (*īśvara-śakti*) alone, just as in the case of things that have a beginning and an end.
Regarding "°vatvātya°," there may also be a reading here as "niyataviṣayatvāt"; see page 16.
Then, from "athocyeta" onwards, up to "this is dharma, this is adharma."

It might be thought: "Precisely because God alone is the cause, the boundary of dharma and adharma—which consists in the instigation of pleasure and so forth—is neither capable of nor incapable of supporting that [divine action]; for since God alone is the instigator of pleasure and pain, if that boundary does not instigate them, for what purpose does He establish it? To this it is replied: He establishes the definition and designation of those two for the sake of worldly convention; therefore he says: "What then? It is merely by way of instruction that 'this is dharma' and 'this is adharma'."

Regarding this, the Teacher states the following reply: "This too is equal to the previous [argument], because of non-existence. At the beginning of creation, the two would not exist, because their objects are indeterminate; or at the end, they would exist, because their objects are determinate, like the middle; or else, in the middle, they would not exist, like the end. Thus, this very same web of defects is incurred.

What is the reason? According to the etymological derivation (*nirukti*) that "dharma" means either "that which upholds" (*dhāraṇāt*) or "that which causes to fall away" (*dhānāt*): if it upholds the boundaries of living beings and sustains them in happiness, then in the absence of this meaning, how could it be called "dharma"? Or conversely, in the absence of the opposite meaning, how could its opposite be called "adharma"? Therefore, dharma is so called because it upholds states such as happiness; for that which is the unfailing cause of happiness is intended [as dharma]. When the absence of one thing results in the absence of another, and the presence of one thing results in the certain presence of another, the former is the cause and the latter is the effect. Thus, there is an unfailing relationship between the cause, dharma, and the effect, happiness.
In the same way, an explanation regarding non-dharma (*adharma*) must also be made with a reversed meaning;
therefore, it is incorrect [to claim] that "the boundary is seen merely by the application of a name" (p. 344, l. 10).

Now, as for the passage beginning with "But if," it might be thought: "Pleasure or pain [for beings] arises solely from the will—that is, the desire—of that Lord, and not from *dharma* consisting of the performance of retention and so forth, nor from anything else.

To this it is replied: the statement regarding the boundaries of *dharma* and *adharma* is purposeless. That which was said—that after teaching the boundaries of *dharma* and *adharma* to conscious living beings, [the Lord acts] subsequently in accordance with their adherence to those boundaries, and so forth—all of that has become purposeless.
To establish that point, he states the reason along with an illustration: "Always," and so forth, up to "the accomplishment of anyone, like the beginning and end [of creation].

This means that at the beginning, middle, and end of creation, at all times, solely by the power of Īśvara and in the absence of any other cause, in whatever manner or by whatever means, there occurs the unregulated attainment of pleasure or pain, and of desirable or undesirable bodies and so forth, for anyone—whether a killer or a non-violent person—due to which it follows that merit and demerit are not the causes [of such results].
Since that [limitation] lacks a cause, it would be like having a beginning and an end— as in the case of the initial and final times— and thus the statement of its boundaries would be meaningless;
in this way, there is first of all the abandonment of non-duality (advaita) by that very Lord.
"...of that which possesses such qualities... of his statement... See page 341, line 4.
In the manuscripts Bhā and Ya,
the reading is *nānuṣyeṇa*; here, there may also be the reading *nānurūpeṇa*.
See page 341,
line 5; for [the word] *hiṃsā* [is used], and likewise even duality (*dvaita*) is abandoned because of the statement regarding direct activity (*sākṣād-vyāpāra*).

For direct agency (*sākṣād-vyāpāra*) is indeed sovereignty; therefore, for one whose activity is unimpeded, what need is there for merit (*dharma*) and so forth, or for those [entities] belonging to the sphere of authority (*ādhikārika*)? If, on the other hand, his power were obstructed without them, then, because his power would be obstructed, he would likewise lack sovereignty like any other being. [Objection: Surely, since there is a thesis regarding the duality of primary and subordinate factors (*pradhāna-upasarjana*), direct agency at the beginning of creation is stated for the sake of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) in accordance with that [thesis]. For the primary factor proceeds even without the subordinate factor, just as a master painter proceeds even without a pupil; likewise, [agency occurs] for the Lord even in the absence of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) and so forth.

No, because the first creator possesses agency; "the beginning" (ādi) refers to the manifestation of a mode that was previously unmanifested, due to its being the source (ādāna), just as the rising of the sun is the source [of light], since the state of being an existent (bhavitṛtva) has as its ultimate reality its purposeful activity.
It is not only non-duality that is abandoned; what then? Duality is also abandoned.
Why? Because of the statement regarding direct activity, and so forth, up to the question: "What [is the purpose] of those who hold office?"

Sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) is indeed direct activity; he explains this: "Therefore, because its functioning is unobstructed"—that is, its functioning is unimpeded in every respect, at all times, and in all places. Therefore, since its functioning is unobstructed, what is the use of merit (*dharma*) and so forth? By the inclusion of "and so forth" (*ādi*), he asks: what is the use of demerit (*adharma*)? Or what is accomplished by the abodes, bodies, senses, and objects which are the bases of pleasure and pain for living beings, or by the living beings themselves? The intention is that nothing at all is accomplished. Nor is there any need for those appointed to office—such as Brahmā, Manu, Viṣṇu, and others—who are employed for the purpose of maintaining the boundaries of dharma and adharma.

Now, if you think that without them the power of that Īśvara is obstructed, then, because his power is thus obstructed, he would indeed lack the status of a Lord (anīśvaratā) due to his inability to produce other effects or due to exhaustion, just like others—that is, like ordinary people (pṛthagjana). This is because [the reason] is excluded from that [class of objects] by the property of being a probans (liṅga-dharma). Pra... [fragmentary].

[The opponent asks: "Is it not the case that [the text] from 'pradhānopasarjana... up to 'tathā'dṛṣṭādyabhāve'pīśvarasya' has presented, cultivated, and concluded with duality itself? How could there be a presentation, cultivation, and conclusion otherwise? [The author replies:

Duality—consisting of the primary and the subordinate—was indeed proposed; and for the sake of reinforcing that very point through corroboration, it is stated that at the beginning of creation, the Lord himself directly exerts his activity by means of his own power, in order to cultivate the idea that the Lord is the primary cause and not karma.
Why? Because the primary element functions even without the subordinate element, just as a master painter functions even without his pupil.

Just as a master painter proceeds in his work—whether with or without a disciple who is subordinate and unskilled in painting—precisely because of his own primacy, since he is the one who causes activity regardless of the presence or absence of the disciple; so too does the Lord proceed regardless of the presence or absence of the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) and other factors, because of His primacy. Since this is to be understood as a summary consisting of a meditative cultivation corresponding to the duality already introduced, there is no fault whatsoever. Thus it is concluded in the *Pratyakṣasamuccaya-upanibandhana*.
See page 344, line 2:
"Or, having caused [the body] to grasp the form, this life-force is led by that...
because it is to be cultivated (*bhāvyatvāt*), [it is] because it is to be cultivated (*bhāvyatvāt*). (The manuscript reads *bhāvyatvāditi bhāvyatvā*.)
And this is not so, because the "originator" (*ādikara*) is the agent;

one who performs the beginning is an "originator," and he alone is the agent. If it is asked, "What is that beginning? it is said: the beginning is the manifestation of a mode that was previously unmanifested. It is the manifestation, by some particular mode, of an existent object that was previously unmanifested.

Why? Because of "taking up" (*ādāna*). He states the etymological derivation of the word as "the beginning (*ādi*) is taking up (*ādāna*"), and provides both the reason and the illustration: "like the rising of the sun and so forth. Just as the divisions of the day that already exist become manifest through the modes of the sun's rising, midday, and setting, so too, because it is the ultimate purpose (*prayojana-paramārtha*) of the state of being (becoming), he who causes that purpose to be realized in the ultimate sense is the agent, the one who comes into being, and the primordial creator (*ādikara*). This is just as it is conceived in the case of rice: for what was not previously rice—such as clay or other materials—is made into rice by him, and thus he is the primordial creator of rice.

Likewise, just as earth and the other elements were the original causes in the past, they remain so even later; because rice is preceded by those [elements], and because its manifestation is conditioned by them, why is rice not itself earth? Or who says that rice is not earth and water and so forth, or that rice and the like are not earth and the like? Because it is conditioned by them, and because it consists of their essence and is non-different from them, that [rice] is indeed that [earth].

Because the roots *bhū* and *kṛ* encompass the meaning of all verbal roots, there is no need for an external agent (*prayojya*). For this reason, that which is the first cause (*ādikara*) is the agent (*kartṛ*), and that which is the agent becomes [the first cause], because *bhū* and *kṛ* pervade the meaning of all roots.

This is what is meant: since a thing comes into being as the first cause of another state of existence by manifesting itself through a different mode, each single entity possesses the nature of everything; yet everything does not possess the nature of one, because they are the first causes by manifesting themselves in mutual dependence.
Thus, "it acts" (*karoti*)...?

And just as the status of being the "first-maker" (ādikaratva) is possible in the case of rice—since earth and other materials that were not previously rice become rice through its first production—so too was there a first production of earth and the other elements previously, and so it remains afterwards; because rice is the beginning of that [series], and because it is manifested as such and is governed by that [cause], why is it not simply earth? Or who says that earth and water and so forth have not become rice, or that rice and so forth have not become earth and so forth? Because it is governed by that [cause], and because it consists of that very essence and is non-different from it, that is indeed that.
"Conquering the end of existence" (bhavānta) [variant: conquering the end of non-existence] (avānta).
And regarding this point, he states a pervasive example for the sake of clarification: "And just as the status of being the first originator is possible in the case of rice."

The explanation of that is as follows: "Because it is the primary cause (*ādikara*) by virtue of being rice, even though it is not rice, such as clay and so forth. By bringing about the manifestation of non-rice—namely earth, water, air, and space—in the form of rice, rice is the "primary cause" (*ādikara*). Having established this meaning as the logical reason, he employs it through the ablative case [in the compound] *vrīhitvenādikaratvāt* ("because of being the primary cause by virtue of being rice").

"Likewise, before," and so forth. Having established this, because of its nature as rice (*vrīhitvāt*), even before [its manifestation], earth, water, air, and space are also the primary causes (*ādikaratva*) of it, and likewise after [its manifestation] in that same manner, just like the rice itself; for the rice is their beginning, meaning that earth and the others are its beginning both before and after [the rice], and thus they possess the status of being its primary causes due to being manifested in that manner. Furthermore, because the rice is impelled by them, for they are indeed its impellers; whoever is the impeller of something is its agent, just as the rising of the sun [is the cause] of daybreak. Therefore, he says: "The rice is impelled by them... and so on. Thus, *pra*... [text fragment].
Thus addressed, he said:

"Why is it that the rice-grain (*vrīhi*) is not itself the primary element (*bhūta*), nor is earth itself, water itself, air itself, or space itself? Is it not because [the grain] is conditioned by those [elements], being their primary cause, just as the rising of the sun and so forth [are conditioned by the elements]?"
