To this it is replied: Who indeed says—either that "the earth is not an element, and water and so forth are rice," because [rice] is conditioned by them; or that "rice and so forth are not earth and so forth," because they are conditioned by those? Rice also consists of earth, water, air, space, and so on; and earth, water, air, space, and so on also consist of rice, beans, mangoes, rose-apples, and so on. That which is made from their food also consists of earth and so on, as well as rice and so on; and earth and so on also consist of that which is made from their food. Furthermore, the body, senses, intellect, and so on produced by that food, as well as humans, animals, hell-beings, gods, and so on produced by them, and the rice, earth, and so on that constitute the food for those produced by them—all of these consist of one another's essence, because they are conditioned by one another, because they are manifested as such, because they are the causes of one another, and for other such reasons.
How much more could be cited? Since this principle is all-pervasive, everything is indeed an illustration of it;

however, he says "from this and from that" for the purpose of showing just a direction and to demonstrate its pervasiveness. If rice comes from rice, or if earth and so forth come from earth and so forth, those very cases are the illustrations.
This should be understood likewise regarding the food, body, senses, and so on produced by them, because every single thing consists of the nature of all things.

To this he says: "Because it has that as its nature, because it is not distinct from it, therefore it is that very thing"—thus, earth and so forth themselves are the cause and the illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta) for each respective mode. Is it not precisely this? [The manuscript reading is *tatpra*...].
...precisely that, by means of such causes as its luminosity and so forth... [as found in] Prajñāpāramitā and Tattvasaṃgraha.
...by means of such causes as its luminosity and so forth, [as found in] Prajñāpāramitā.
The reading enclosed within these marks does not exist in the Ya manuscripts:
"In the case of human actions as well, it is exactly the same;

the person is the primary agent (*ādikara*) with respect to the karma of those individuals (*pudgala*) who are fit for action, because the state of being an experiencer (*bhavitṛtva*) has as its ultimate purpose the attainment of such a mode of application (*upayoga*)."
Furthermore, that action (*karman*) is the primary cause; even external things such as pots and the like are likewise primary causes.

Having thus established the doctrine that "everything consists of everything" by means of this illustrated logic, [the author] now states the application of the example—the doctrine of human action—to refute the view of God as the cause: "In the case of human actions also, it is exactly the same," and so forth.
The person (*puruṣa*) is the agent; he is the primary cause who transforms the *pudgala* particles suitable for action into the state of being action (*karman*).

Which *pudgala*s are fit for action? It is said: the atom-group (*paramāṇu-vargaṇā*), the non-graspable group (*agrahaṇa-vargaṇā*), and the two-partite group (*dvipradeśa-vargaṇā*). In this manner, there are groups consisting of ten parts and so on, up to groups with numerable parts.
A "group" (*vargaṇā*) is a collection of homogeneous [atoms] established individually by the intellect, like a herd of cows of the same color belonging to Kucikarṇaka and the cowherd Ābhīra.
Among the infinite-partite groups as well, some are fit for grasping and some are unfit for grasping.

The suitability or unsuitability for perception is due to being excessively gross or subtle, like atoms or sugar granules [which cannot be perceived] by sweat; whereas those of medium dimension are suitable. Among these, the *pudgala*-groups (*vargaṇās*) that are suitable for perception constitute, in terms of measure, an infinite-thousandth part of the perfected beings (*siddhas*), and are infinitely greater than the number of those who will never attain perfection (*abhavyasiddhis*).
This, then, is the rule for the smallest [unit] suitable for the gross body.

When one atom is added above that, the second [unit] also becomes fit for the coarse; thus, by increasing one by one, there are infinite-infinite stages that are fit to be grasped as causes of coarseness. From the lowest to the highest stage, it is an incalculable multiple (*asaṅkhyeyaguṇa*). Because, through successive comparison (*paramparopanidhā*), starting from the first stage, there is a doubling at each of those various infinite stages, it is therefore an incalculable multiple or a calculable multiple (*saṅkhyeyaguṇa*); however, through immediate comparison (*anantaropanidhā*), it is simply greater by one unit of form (*rūpa*).
When that most excellent, coarse, and suitable matter (dravya) is added to the form (rūpa), it becomes the lowest [degree] of the transformation body (vaikriya-śarīra), which is unfit for grasping;

thus, through an increase exceeding that form, those [levels] also become infinite-infinite places as before. From the lowest to the highest, it is an innumerable-fold (asaṅkhyeya-guṇa) increase. What is the multiplier (guṇakāra)? It is an innumerable part of a line (śreṇi).
Above those [levels] unfit for grasping lies the lowest degree of the transformation body that is fit for grasping.

Those locations as well, as before, are infinite-infinite; furthermore, there are locations for the non-grasping of *āhāraka* [bodies], and likewise above those, locations suitable for grasping them. Just so, compared to those suitable for gross (*audārika*) bodies, those suitable for transformational (*vaikriya*) bodies are innumerable times more numerous; from those, those suitable for *āhāraka* bodies are innumerable times more numerous. Thus, the instances of grasping and non-grasping are innumerable times more numerous than each preceding one.

Above that, when the maximum [amount] of matter (*rūpa*) is added to the minimum [amount] of the luminous body (*taijasa*), the minimum [intensity] of the luminous body results; the maximum is infinite times the minimum. What is the multiplier? It is the infinite-th part of the perfected beings (*siddhas*), multiplied by an infinity greater than that of the incapable beings (*abhavyas*). Above that, when more matter is added, the minimum suitable for the luminous body results; the maximum is infinite times the minimum. What is the multiplier? It is the infinite-th part of the perfected beings, multiplied by an infinity greater than that of the incapable beings.

By this method, for the subsequent [types of matter] suitable for speech, respiration, inhalation, exhalation, and mental activity—which are separated by non-grasping and are subject to grasping—their quantities should be understood as increasing infinitely at each successive stage.

Regarding the interval between the lowest and highest [quantities] of those subject to grasping, it is everywhere "specifically greater" (viśeṣādhika). What is this specific difference? It is an infinite part of that very [total].

However, for those not subject to grasping, the highest is infinitely greater than the lowest. What is the multiplier? It is an infinite part of the Siddhas, and infinitely greater than that of the incapable (abhavyas).

By means of such individuals, having transformed [the matter] throughout the entire world—which is densely packed and deeply immersed—into the state of *karman*, a person, through his own vigor known as *yoga*, grasps with the body-yoga (*kāyayoga*) those three types of yoga characterized by body, speech, and mind that are appropriate for it; he transforms it into the form of the *kārmaṇa* body by that very [body-yoga]. Having transformed it into the state of speech, mind, *prāṇa*, and *apāna*, and having taken hold of it as speech, mind, *prāṇa*, and *apāna* by means of the body-yoga alone, he emits it, as it has been said: "Having grasped it, he transforms it into the five bodies according to its suitability by means of the yogas."
In the *Karmaprajñapti*, verse 17, it is stated that speech consists of an infinite number of aggregates (*skandhas*).

Furthermore: "The transformation of energy (*vīryapariṇāma*) within the soul (*jīva*) itself, when the soul is engaged with mind, speech, or body—that indeed is designated as 'yoga' by the Victors (*Jinas*)."

Just as a jar undergoes a transformation such as redness through its connection with light, so too does the self undergo a transformation in the form of potency (vīrya) through the application of the soul's instruments.

What is the reason? It is because of the occurrence of such a type of activity (*upayoga*); that is to say, it is because the person undergoes a transformation consisting of an exertion (*prayoga*) directed toward the grasping of matter (*pudgala-dravya*) that has reached a state of modification suitable for bondage. As it has been said: "Just as a lamp, possessing the quality of heat, takes up oil by means of a wick, and having taken it up, transforms that oil into the form of its body."

Just as the self is the original agent (*ādikara*) of non-actions by virtue of their being actions, so too is the self the original agent of actions because they are manifested by it and are dependent upon it.

Why then is the self alone not [regarded as] the object of action (*karmabhūta*)? Who says that this [self] is not the object of action and that actions are not identical with the self? For it is through its engagement in such a state that [actions] are dependent upon it.

Because the action and the agent act as mutual causes for one another, there is the state of everything being the self-nature of everything; [this occurs] through the non-conscious knowledge-obscuration...
...because it possesses the nature of a person who protects and fulfills [the body],
in that same way, the self-lamp— whose qualities are passion and so forth— takes up the aggregates by means of the wick of yoga; having taken them up, it transforms them into the state of karma.
Just as dust and dirt adhere to the body of one anointed with oil,
so too does karma cling to one anointed with the oil of passion, hatred, and attachment;
indeed, the face of a man who is angry becomes parched, while that of a man who is enamored becomes moist.
Indeed, even this gross body undergoes transformation by virtue of its constituent states;

therefore, the Self is the agent, endowed with instruments, acting as the primary cause through the state of being an object of action, because—as before—the ultimate reality consists of purposeful existence.

Is the self alone the primary cause? No, it is said; that karma is also the primary cause. Furthermore, that karma—consisting of the obscuring karmas such as knowledge-obscuring (jñānāvaraṇa) and so forth, which is fit for grasping and has its maturation (*vipāka*) in the various types of bodies such as the gross (*audārika*) body—is a *pudgala*. What does it become? It becomes the primary cause of all bodies of the self and of the selves associated with them, encompassing the various states of existence as humans, hell-beings, gods, and animals, as well as the many subdivisions such as those dwelling in the subterranean realms (*bhavanavāsin*), and so forth. As it has been said: "Matter-molecules (*pudgalas*) transform into the state of karma by being the cause of the soul’s transformation;
likewise, the soul transforms by having matter-karma as its cause."

Thus, it is not only the internal that is "initially formative" (ādikara); rather, external things such as jars and so forth are also initially formative. All that is initially formative is called "pudgalas fit for action. (Bhāṣya)

Those individuals who are fit for [the teaching of] karma are called those who, by means of the analogy of distinguishing various types of cows, illustrate the aggregate of matter (pudgala-kāya) to their disciples through the classifications of substance and so forth.

He asks: "For what purpose, then, are these *vargaṇās* (groupings) described? It is said: For the sake of the non-confusion of those to be instructed (*vineyas*), by means of the illustration and example of the cows of Kucikarṇa, the lord of the cattle-herds, and the discernment—that is, the thorough knowledge—of their mutual distinctions; thus, by means of the *vargaṇās* of substance (*dravya*) and so forth—the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) including the *vargaṇās* of space (*kṣetra*), time (*kāla*), and state (*bhāva*)—the Tīrthaṅkaras, Gaṇadharas, and others demonstrate the entire *pudgala-astikāya* (mass of matter) after having divided it. This is the literal meaning of the verse.
Now the meaning of the story is told: Here, in the land of Magadha within the region of Bharata-kṣetra, there was a householder named Kucikarṇa who was the owner of a vast herd of cattle.
Because those cows were so numerous—numbering in the thousands and more—he appointed many cowherds for the purpose of looking after them individually.
However, when those cows mingled together, the cowherds, being unable to properly distinguish their own respective animals from one another, constantly engaged in quarrels.

Having observed them thus disputing with one another, he— for the sake of their non-delusion and to terminate the quarrel—established distinct groups (*vargaṇā*) consisting of homogeneous collections of cows, differentiated by categories such as white, black, red, and brindled, for each respective cowherd. This is the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*).

Now the application (*upanaya*) is stated: here, the Tīrthaṅkara, who is like the lord of the herd of cows, has described the category of matter (*pudgalāstikāya*), which is like the herd of cows, to his disciples who are like the cowherds, by means of divisions into groups starting from the atom (*paramāṇu*), so that they may not be deluded regarding it.
Thus, in the *Viśeṣāvaśyakabhāṣya-ṭīkā* composed by the illustrious Maladhārin Hemacandrasūri, page 328: "There was a village named Sughoṣa in the midst of the Magadha region,
and there a leader named Kucikarṇa was renowned."
Hundreds of thousands of cattle were born to him in succession;
indeed, alas, the lake was filled drop by drop.
Then he entrusted the cows to the cowherds for their protection;
they fought outside, saying, "These are ours, those are not ours."
Kucikarṇa divided them and assigned them: the white ones to one,
the black ones to another, the red ones to yet another, and the yellow ones to someone else.
He established separate herds of cattle in various forests,
and while consuming curd and milk, he dwelt among them in succession.
Day after day he increased his wealth of cattle in every pen,
insatiable for curds and milk like one intoxicated by liquor.
Then, his food became undigested, with its essence flowing both downward and upward; a great burning arose within him, like that of one who has fallen into a blazing fire.
"Alas, my cows! Alas, my young calves! Alas, my Śākvara songs! Where and when shall I find them again?
Having died while still unsated with such wealth of cattle, he has now entered the state of an animal."
Thus ends [the section] 2.112 in the autocommentary on the *Yogaśāstra* composed by Hemacandrasūri, the omniscient one of the Kali age.
Sweat itself is the primary [element],
and it is the primary [element] by virtue of its gross form.

In this context, there may also be the reading "by way of having a gross body. In those places, [there is] *dviya* (twice-born), *vagāḍha* (deeply entered), *nicita* (accumulated), *ḍe* (O Goddess), *līṃ*, *raṃ*, *hīṃ*.
Deeply immersed, firmly established, and densely packed within the abyss of karma—
speech, mind, and breath are restrained.

Then, having taken up [the matter], the yogins transform it into a form corresponding to that [new body] by means of yogic activities; and through those same yogic activities, they bind the suitable aggregates of speech and mind to the five bodies. (Karmaprakṛti, Gāthā 17)
Comparison: "In this world, living beings transform matter (daliya) according to their yoga; they take up [matter] suitable for speech, breath, and mind, and rely upon it as substance.
(Pañcasaṃgraha 6)

In this world, souls continuously take up the karmic matter corresponding to their own yoga, which is present here, and transform it by unifying it with their own spatial units (pradeśas); the meaning is that they establish it within themselves, just as particles of clay absorb water and the ancient particles therein, or as [milk] establishes itself in the form of clarified butter and the like.

The *yogas* (vibratory activities) take hold of speech, respiration, and mind, as well as the appropriate collection of matter (*dravyajāta*) in the form of *vargaṇās*, strictly according to their respective nature. What is meant by this? By taking hold of matter suitable for speech, the soul emits that speech through its own spatial units (*pradeśas*). It is just as one of weak strength might walk by leaning on a staff with his hand, or cross a river by holding onto a gourd or similar object, or climb out of a well by grasping a rope.

In the same way, even regarding inhalation and exhalation (*ānapāna*), the soul (*jīva*), supported by those [respiratory] substances, emits [them] through its own spatial units (*pradeśa*) in accordance with its own activity (*yoga*). Relying upon substances suitable for the mind (*manas*), it then cogitates through its own spatial units in accordance with its own power. This is the meaning of the verse.

Thus, in the *Svopajñapañcasaṃgrahavṛtti* composed by the great sage Candraprabha, [it is stated that] there is a transformation of energy (*vīryapariṇāma*) for one who is engaged with the mind, speech, or body.
And it is said: "The transformation of energy (vīryapariṇāma) belonging to a soul that is engaged through mind, speech, or body—whatever that is, it is designated as 'yoga' by the Jina.

Just as through a particular conjunction there is a transformation of a jar into redness and so forth, so too, through the effort of the soul's instruments, there is likewise a transformation of energy (vīrya).

Thus, for the *jīva* endowed with the instrument of the mind (*manas*), "yoga" is a synonym for energy (*vīrya*); mental yoga (*manoyoga*) acts as a support for the weak, like a staff, and the same applies to vocal yoga (*vāgyoga*) and bodily yoga (*kāyayoga*).
(From the *Sthānāṅgasūtra-ṭīkā* composed by Abhayadevasūri, section 3).
That which indeed exists within the self of the soul is designated as "yoga" by the Jinas.
This verse has been extracted from the *Tattvārthasūtra-ṭīkā* composed by the master Siddhasena, Chapter 7,

page 70: "Just as the transformation of a jar into redness and so forth occurs through contact with fire, so too, when there is the application of the soul's instruments, vigor (*vīrya*) is likewise a transformation of the self."
Just as a lamp, possessing the quality of heat, draws up oil through its wick and,
once ignited, transforms that oil into the form of its own body; so too does it act.

Or rather, just as the self is the primary agent (*ādikara*) of non-actions by way of being their object (*karmatvena*), so too is it the primary agent of actions because they are manifested [by it] and are dependent upon it.

Why then is the self alone not [considered] the object? Who says that it is not the object and that actions are not identical with the self? For it is established through such a mode of application (*upayoga*) that [actions] are dependent upon it.

Because the action and the agent act as mutual causes for one another, there is the state of everything being the self of everything; [this applies even to] insentient matter and the veil of knowledge...
because it possesses the nature of a person who protects and fulfills [the senses],
in that same way, the lamp of the self, whose qualities are passion and so forth, takes up [objects] by means of the wick of yoga.
The reading in this verse, as cited by the venerable Siddhasena Sūri in his commentary on the *Tattvārtha-sūtra* (Aṅga 5, p. 343), is "svayogavartyā. [It states:
"Having taken up the aggregates (*skandha*), he transforms them into karma;
or else, like dust clinging to a limb smeared with oil, they become impurity (*mala*)."
Just as the body of one whose limbs are smeared with oil becomes coated with dust,
so too does the bondage of karma occur for one who is moistened by passion and hatred.
Thus, in this *Praśamarati*,
for a man anointed with the oil of passion, hatred, and attachment, his karma becomes coarse when he is angry; indeed, his face becomes oily when he is lustful.
"Indeed, even this gross body transforms according to one's state of being;
thus, even a gross body transforms by the power of one's state of being"—
this is the reading of this verse as cited by the venerable Malayagiri in his commentary on the *Prajñāpanā-sūtra*, page 455.
See page 346, line 7;
*pudgala-pra°* [is] by one who asserts [it] as a person (*pudgala*). Primary source (*pra°*).
"Substances transform into karma by way of being the cause for the soul's transformation;
substances transform into the state of karma by way of being the cause for the soul's transformation"—
this is the reading found in this verse-cum-commentary cited by the venerable Malayagiri Sūri in his commentary on the *Prajñāpanā-sūtra*, page 455.
The soul likewise transforms itself according to the characteristics of matter and karma;
thus it is said in the *Mantītiya* and the *Mattīti*.

The reading here might also be "the jar and so forth are the makers of all. Desiring to demonstrate this even by way of the reverse [argument], he says: "And just as in the self, of those who are without action," and so forth, as before. This has already been explained, including the objections and their refutations, up to the point where it is asked: "Who indeed says that he is not the locus of action, or that actions are not identical with the self? This is because [actions] are produced by that [self] through its attainment of such a state of application (*upayoga*), and for other reasons such as these. Therefore, since everything is of the nature of everything, who else could be the Lord (*īśvara*)? Or what else could be *prakṛti*? Thus [he concludes].
Furthermore,
because the agent and the object of action act as causes for one another and so forth, all things possess the nature of being identical with everything else.

He states the reason: "Non-conscious [karmas], such as knowledge-obscuring," and so forth. Non-conscious karmas—namely those known as knowledge-obscuring (*jñānāvaraṇa*), perception-obscuring (*darśanāvaraṇa*), feeling-producing (*vedya*), deluding (*moha*), life-span (*āyus*), name (*nāma*), status (*gotra*), and obstructive (*antarāya*)—along with their subdivisions, consist of matter (*pudgala*). Even when these are intensely active (*atyudīrṇa*), they do not obscure even an infinitesimal fraction (*akṣarānantatama-bhāga*) of the self due to the self's inherent nature of consciousness (*upayoga-svābhāvya*). They obscure the remainder for some, such as those with a single sense-organ, those in the *nigoda* state, and subtle, undeveloped (*aparyāptaka*) beings, due to the diversity of the subsidence-cum-destruction (*kṣayopaśama*) of karmas.

Now, if this is not accepted, then the self would neither be bound by karma nor joined with the body and so forth that constitute its fruit; because it would be inactive, like one who is liberated, it would neither be bound nor joined with the body and so forth due to the power of creation by primordial matter (prakṛti), God, or others. Furthermore, because it is formless, like space, [it would follow that] even for all living beings, an infinite-thousandth part of the syllable [of consciousness] is eternally unobstructed.
If even that [space] were obstructed by it, then the soul would attain the state of being non-living;
for even when there is a great accumulation of clouds, the light of the moon and sun remains—Nandīsūtra 42.
Likewise, even a small amount of dust makes the sky turbid, yet the powerful Rāhu swallows the moon, and the moon [remains].
Mud destroys the excellence of the qualities of water; faults [destroy] the nature of the momentary impulse; and powerful inherent nature [destroys] both.
Therefore, there is a mutual causal relationship between karma and the agent.

As for the *kevalin* (the omniscient one), although the movement of such a cognitive application (*upayoga*) is not established—because all obstructions, hindrances, and delusions have vanished and thus there is an absence of any obscuration to that application—nevertheless, because of the existence of causes here, namely the fourfold karmas of feeling (*vedya*), lifespan (*āyus*), name (*nāma*), and lineage (*gotra*), which are impelled by those [other karmas], their mutual causal relationship is established.

Furthermore, the Siddhas possess the status of being "first-causers" (ādikara) with respect to their liberation from karma, their unassailable transformational and ultimate bliss, their destruction-based right conviction, knowledge, perception, vigor, and acquisitions.

Now, one might object that there is a contradiction in one's own statement, because the very mention of the identity between the self and the *pudgala* implies a recognition of difference [between them].

This is not so; why? Because of the nature of "protecting" (*pālana*) and "filling" (*pūraṇa*). [The root] *pṛ* is used in the sense of protecting and filling (Dhātupāṭha 1086). A *puruṣa* is so called because he protects various individuals from the ripening of pleasure, pain, and so forth by means of his own self-nature (*ātmabhāva*), or because he is protected by them through such a mode of application. Alternatively, a *puruṣa* is so called because he fills those [beings] with those [qualities], or because he is filled by them. A *pudgala* is so called because he swallows (*gilati*) a male (*pumāṃsam*), or because he is swallowed by a male. Although there is a difference in etymological derivation (*nirukti*)—whether from "filling" (*pūraṇa*) or "dissolving" (*galana*)—there is no fault, because the meaning is identical. Since the words *puruṣa* and *pudgala* have the same referent, like *Indra* and *Śakra*, there is no inconsistency. [The text continues: ...due to the state of being a producer of [the qualities beginning with] *tādi*...

Now, if it is not accepted in this way, then the self would neither be bound by karma nor joined with the body and so forth that constitute its fruit; because it would be inactive, like one who is liberated, it would neither be bound nor joined with the body and so forth, due to its formlessness, like space. Furthermore, for all living beings, an infinite-thousandth part of the imperishable [self] is eternally uncovered.
Knowledge, however, is imperishable because it never decays;
indeed, an infinite portion of that [knowledge] within the soul is never obstructed by any living beings.
For the reason that this knowledge never at any time flows away from or falls away from the soul, for that reason knowledge is called "indestructible" (*akṣara*).

How is it determined that knowledge never flows away from the soul? To this he says: even by the most powerful arising of the veil of knowledge (*jñānāvaraṇa-udaya*), not even an infinite fraction of that indestructible [knowledge] is obscured for all souls residing in *saṃsāra*.
And it has been said: "Even for all souls, an infinite fraction of the indestructible [knowledge] is eternally uncovered" (Nandīsūtra 42).
"Perpetually open" means eternally uncovered.

(72) But by what is it covered, such that only an infinite fraction of knowledge remains eternally uncovered? To this he says: "Each individual soul-surface is indeed [covered] by infinite [karmic particles] of the knowledge-obscuring karma. (73)
Except for the Jinas, all other living beings are covered by infinite indivisible units of the knowledge-obscuring karma.

(73) Excluding the Jinas—those possessed of *kevalajñāna*—each individual soul-point (*jīvapradeśa*) of all remaining living beings is covered by infinite *avibhāgas*, which are indivisible portions of the knowledge-obscuring (*jñānāvaraṇīya*) karma. Those portions for which it is impossible to further divide them into smaller parts are called *avibhāgaparicchedas*. By these [units] they are covered.
If this is so, how is it that an infinite portion of knowledge is eternally unobscured? To this he says: "But if even that [infinite portion] were obscured, then the soul would become a non-soul;
for even when there is a dense mass of clouds, the light of the moon and sun still remains."

Just as the light of the moon and sun remains [unobstructed] even when a mass of clouds arises most intensely, because it is their very nature—as is perceived through direct observation—so too, although each individual soul-unit (*jīvapradeśa*) is covered by infinite indivisible portions of the veil of knowledge (*jñānāvaraṇa*), an infinite portion of knowledge remains eternally uncovered because it is its very nature. If that [portion] were also covered, then, due to being entirely devoid of consciousness, the soul would become a non-soul (*ajīva*), i.e., it would cease to be a living being, like a jar.
74. Thus, in the *Bṛhatkalpabhāṣya-vṛtti* composed by the master Malayagiri:
"If even that [space] were to be obstructed, then the soul would attain the state of being non-living (*ajīvatva*)."
May it quickly come to pass; may it quickly be accomplished.

Even when a great mass of clouds has gathered, the light of the moon and sun still shines forth. (Nandīsūtra 42) For even a tiny speck of dust makes the sky turbid, yet the powerful Rāhu swallows the moon;
the mud destroys the excellence of the water's qualities, yet the powerful nature [of the water] overcomes these faults in an instant.
Without the excellence of the qualities of water,
or without the non-excellence of the qualities of water—
[is it] water, or the excellence of qualities?
The ritual for the attainment of the state beyond exhaustion, for the proponent, for the practitioner, for the enjoyment, for the practitioner.
Persons (pudgalāḥ) [are] persons (pudgalā);
from [the word] "person" (pudgala), the two words "person" (pudgala-śabdau) [arise]. Corrected.

Now, if it is not accepted as I have stated—that action and the agent are mutually dependent—and if it is instead maintained that the diversity of saṃsāra arises from some other cause such as the will of God, inherent nature, primordial matter (prakṛti), or the like, then the self would not be bound by action, which is the seed of saṃsāra, whether auspicious or inauspicious. Consequently, it would not be joined with the auspicious or inauspicious bodies, senses, stations, and objects that constitute the fruits of that action, because it would be devoid of action, like one who is liberated.

If this Lord were to exist even in the absence of the unseen (adṛṣṭa), then He would create bodies and so forth for the liberated souls as well, because He is the Lord, just as in the case of creation and so on.
For this very reason, the arguments regarding acting in concert, insentience, persistence, and activity lack the property of being attributes of the subject (apakṣadharmatā).
Having established this, all that which those who maintain the absolute primacy of karma as the cause have said is likewise incoherent.

They say this: "If human effort (*puruṣakāra*) were the cause by virtue of being the initiator [of bondage], then one who is liberated from *pradhāna* would become bound again for that very reason, and likewise, the conceptual distinction between the liberated and the unliberated would be impossible. This is because, in ultimate reality, the arrangement of creation proceeds by the power of [the creator].

This too is not tenable; for precisely by the power of the creation of *prakṛti*, Īśvara*, and so forth, one would not be bound by the body, organs, and so on, nor would one be joined with the world, due to being formless like space (*ākāśa*). *Note: The term *pradhāna* refers to primordial matter in Sāṃkhya philosophy, while *Īśvara* refers to the Lord in various theistic systems.*

Or else, space itself would be bound and joined with bodies and so forth for that very reason; and likewise, undesirable consequences such as these would accrue to you, just as they do to the *puruṣa* you yourself accept.

Furthermore, if this Lord exists even in the absence of your own unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), then He would produce bodies and so forth for your liberated souls as well, because He is the Lord, just as He does at the beginning of creation.

For this very reason, because of their acting in combination, their lack of consciousness, and their remaining inactive, [the arguments for] these [qualities] lack the property of being attributes of the subject (*apakṣadharmatā*).
And having established this, all that which those who maintain exclusively that action is the cause have said is also incoherent;
they speak as follows: "If human effort were the cause by virtue of its being the initiator, then [the role of] primordial matter (*pradhāna*) and the intermediate [factors]..."
See page 256–2:
*muktamuktavi* (Y),
*muktavi* (Bh).
Furthermore, regarding the passage beginning "even in the absence of *adṛṣṭa*," etc.:

first, I have stated that [the Lord] is the sovereign of all persons who have attained the state of having karma called *adṛṣṭa*, because He is the maker of their bodies and so forth. If you do not accept such agency as the maker of these things, then even though you follow me by accepting the absence of karma called *adṛṣṭa*, I shall state a fault: this Lord would then create bodies, organs, and worlds even for those liberated beings who lack such causes and are without karma, because He is the Lord, just as in the case of the creation and so forth.

Likewise, he should act toward all [beings] even at the time of universal dissolution (pralaya) for that very reason; or else, he should not act even in the interim, because of his lordship (īśvaratva), as in the case of the time of dissolution—
and this latter course is undesirable.
And from this undesirable [consequence], because the self is one with action and because everything has everything as its essence, there would be the state of being the Lord of all;
thus it has been explained regarding the actions of those who have offered [themselves].
In this context, there may also be a reading "of those whose actions are similar" (*°tulyakarmaṇām*);
likewise, for this very reason, etc.

By virtue of the identity of the self with action (*karmātmaikya*) and the state of being the Lord of all (*sarveśvaratva*), [it must be accepted that] atoms alone are action; those very [atoms] are pleasure and so forth;

and from that unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), creation proceeds—whether as creation from *pradhāna*, or as creation from atoms distinct [from it], or as creation impelled by the unseen force. Having abandoned such alternative conceptualizations, the acceptance of the identity of the self with action and the state of being the Lord of all, who is the self of everything, is inevitable.
Therefore, the properties you have stated—conjoint action, insentience, remaining stationary, and lack of activity—are not attributes of the subject (*apakṣadharma*).

Since [the body] is a single entity, with what second thing could it act together to produce a single effect? Is that insentient matter separate from consciousness? Furthermore, because its nature consists of constant processes such as filling, maintaining, wasting away, and growing, how can there be "activity after having remained stationary"? Thus, because the meaning is unestablished, the claim that bodies and so forth are presided over by a specific consciousness cannot be proven.

As for the specific reason stated—that they act together toward a single purpose despite being mutually opposed—that too is non-existent, as was already explained previously by the verse beginning with *ṇicchayato savvalahum*.
Therefore, creation is not preceded by a single Lord, but rather it should be understood as preceded by many Lords; see page 335, line 8;
see page 331, line 5.
See page 301, line 4:
"anekaikaiśvara" (pra.);
see page 338, line 12.
And by stating "having done thus," and so forth,

it should be understood that by this revelation of the faults in the doctrine of an absolute primordial Lord (ekānta-īśvara-pūrvaka-vāda), the revelation of the faults in the doctrine of absolute action (karma-ekānta-vāda) is also accomplished, because that doctrine of absolute action is likewise incoherent.

But how do those who maintain the doctrine of the absolute efficacy of action (karmaikāntavādins) speak? Or how is that [the doctrine of human effort] inconsistent with it? To demonstrate this, he first shows their arguments by presenting the way they establish *karman* while refuting human effort (*puruṣakāra*), saying: "If you think that human effort alone is the cause—and not even *karman*—on the grounds that it is the instigator, then this undesirable consequence follows for you who hold to the absolute view that human effort is the sole cause. Thus he demonstrates their logical justifications. As it is said: if human effort were the cause because of its capacity to initiate action, then one implies the absolute position that human effort alone is the cause and not *karman* as well; consequently, this following undesirable result accrues to those who maintain the absolute view that human effort is the cause.

What is the undesirable consequence? It is said: the various successes (*siddhi*) or failures (*asiddhi*) differentiated by superior, middling, and inferior [levels] would not exist, because the cause for those seeking excellence is one, and because the human effort (*puruṣakāra*) of those seeking excellence is one.

Thus, the various types of successes and failures distinguished by superior, middling, and inferior grades would not exist as distinct varieties, because their cause is non-differentiated, like cloth produced from identical threads.
Since there is a multiplicity of effects, there must be a multiplicity of causes; thus, it is karma alone that impels [beings],
and it is twofold...
for the other [cause], however,
there is no entry whatsoever of the operation of the personal effort (puruṣakāra) as you have postulated, because it is incapable of imparting its own power.

For human effort (*puruṣakāra*) has volition alone as its essence and power; yet, while existing in the state of a bound soul (*paśu*), it would not result in various successes or failures distinguished as middling or inferior, if they were not [produced by that effort]. And these are observed; for there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) more weighty than what is perceived.

If it is asked why there would not be diversity, it is said: because of the oneness of the cause for the sake of excellence. One might suspect the doctrine of the absolute causality of human effort (*puruṣakāra*), holding that the person seeking self-excellence alone is the cause, and even karma is not a cause. "Oneness of human effort" means the oneness of the effort of the person seeking excellence. Since the action of the person seeking excellence is a single cause, the various forms of human effort well-known in the world—which are distinguished as superior, middling, and inferior, and produced by the two alternatives of good conduct and bad conduct—would not be established; rather, only one person would attain excellence.

Consequently, even for those results to be accomplished—which are themselves of superior, middling, and inferior grades, and are either auspicious or inauspicious—distinctions would not obtain; rather, only one supreme accomplishment (siddhi) would result, and there would be no middling or inferior accomplishments with their respective distinctions.

Furthermore, human efforts would not result in failures, yet such failures are observed; therefore, having summarized that point, he states the proof: "Those successes and failures, along with their various subdivisions, would not be of diverse kinds because they would have an identical cause, like cloth produced from identical threads. For you, who maintain the doctrine of the absolute efficacy of human effort (*puruṣakāra*), since human effort alone is the cause and there is no cause distinct from it, successes or failures—being non-different from that [effort]—would not be diverse, because the cause for the purpose of excellence is one and the same.
Because human effort (puruṣakāra) would be identical for one who seeks excellence, various types of human efforts—distinguished as superior, middling, and inferior—would not be established;

consequently, those successes and failures, along with their subdivisions, would not exist as distinct varieties, because the cause would be non-differentiated, like cloth produced from identical threads.
However, since there is a difference in the effects, there must be a difference in the causes; therefore, karma alone is the instigator.
And it is twofold... [text missing] ...twofold.
But for the other [the animal],
there is no entry whatsoever for the operation of the human effort (puruṣakāra) you desire, because it is incapable of imparting its own power;
for human effort has consciousness alone as its essence, and that [consciousness] does not exist in one who is in the state of a beast.

It is likely that the original reading here was intended to convey the following intention: "And activity is of two kinds—that which is achievable and that which is unachievable by the exertion of one person, [but not] by the other. Compare—page 366, line 14.
Those things distinct from the property [of being a cause]—
see page 365, line 17—
have a single cause. Ya.

In this context, there may also be a reading stating that "there is only one cause. Having thus stated the defect in the opponent's position, he states the proof for his own position: "But because of the diversity of effects, there must be a diversity of causes; therefore, karma alone is the instigator. The word "iti" has the sense of a reason. Because effects—whether they be various types of successes or failures—are mutually distinct, there must necessarily be a diversity of causes. And that cause must be understood as karma alone, which is the instigator—that is, the mover—of the person (puruṣa) as you conceive him, and which possesses manifold distinctions.

The designation "action" (*karma*) is applied to that general cause which is inferred from the diversity of effects; for the [notions of] human effort (*puruṣakāra*) and other such causes have already been refuted. The inference of this [cause] is derived from the mark (*liṅga*) of its effects, which differ according to whether they are established or unestablished, just as the motion of the sun is inferred from its arrival at another location. The passage beginning with "and it is of two kinds" up to "of the other" is intended to avoid the charge that its mark is unestablished (*asiddhi*); the meaning is that the mark is well-known (*prasiddha*).

Regarding the passage beginning with "tatra" and so forth: in this case, regarding this effect which serves as the inferential mark for the diversity of causes, there is no entry whatsoever for the operation of the "Person" (puruṣa) you desire; this is well-established for both of us, just as it is for the world at large. He demonstrates that while the effect as a logical mark is established, the cause favored by you is impossible, whereas the cause according to our own view is indeed possible.
Why? Because [the Person] lacks the capacity to impart its own power.
If it is asked, "Whose own power is it?"—it belongs to the conscious Person.

For human effort (*puruṣakāra*) has volition alone as its essence; the word *hi* (for) is used in the sense of "because. Because this is his power, and because he is unable to instill it while existing in the state of a beast within the desired human condition, [the author] demonstrates his incapacity to instill his own power with the words beginning "And not he... Even though consciousness exists, he is not capable of instilling that power of his own consciousness into a base animal body dragged down by the force of karma; being a human, he does not possess that knowledge in an animal, since even for an animal, [knowledge] is obtainable through karma. Rather, [it is obtained] from the current of the Gaṅgā...
Furthermore, whatever person there may be is not independent, because he is subject to the power of karma, like a corpse possessed by a vetāla;
from the moment of conception, he may even lose his life-breaths.

Therefore, just as in the involuntary actions such as the ingestion of specific foods and the digestion of their juices, the person—who is not independent regarding them—fancies "these were done by me" when they were actually performed by karma; for if those actions were dependent on him, there would be no time when they were not performed, and the consequence would be immortality in this very life. Likewise, even in the production of the body and the senses, there would be no undesirable bodies or senses; rather, due to his independence, only desirable ones would be produced.
Therefore, all of that is indeed the result of karma alone.

Apart from that, who could conceive of a self? One existing in the state of animal-like ignorance and incapacity is not able to establish a distinguished and desired human consciousness; conversely, being a human, one is likewise unable to instill that knowledge into an animal. Thus it stands.

That which you have conjectured to be the true nature (*svatattva*) of that self cannot be deposited by one who is under the sway of *karman* in another birth-class (*yonijāti*), situated within one birth-class, into yet another; why? Because even that [nature] is obtainable through *karman*. Whether it be an animal or a human, the state of consciousness arises precisely through the power of *karman*; the meaning is that one becomes a human or an animal solely through the emergence of the *karman* named after its own birth-class, since the causes for that emergence are difficult to ward off by any other means.

Regarding this, he provides an illustration: "Even so, [in the case] of the Gaṅgā," and so forth. This is stated by way of possibility; moreover, this is possible—that through a divine transformation, a portentous event, or the like, the course of the Gaṅgā's stream might change, and thus the activity [of the water] proceeds otherwise.
Thus, having for the time being accepted an independent conscious agent and human effort, that which was stated regarding the [river's] flow... [the rest of the sentence is incomplete in the source].
In the *Bhā* manuscript, it reads "pravartamāne" for "pravartayituḥ pravartamāne," and in the *Ya* manuscripts,
it reads "pravartyamāne" for "pravartayituḥ pravartyamāne";
the reading enclosed within these brackets does not exist in the *Ya* manuscripts.

He alone is capable of instilling the power of his own consciousness into these [beings]; being a human, he does not bestow that knowledge upon an animal, because even for that [human], it is obtainable through action;
rather, [it is obtained] from the current of the Gaṅgā...
Furthermore,
whatever person there may be is not independent, because he is subject to the power of karma, like a corpse possessed by a vetāla from the moment of birth onwards.
...and one might even give up one's life;

therefore, just as in the involuntary actions of ingesting specific foods, the separation of the *khala* and *rasa*, and so forth, a person—being devoid of autonomy—fancies "these are performed by me" when they are actually performed by *karman*. For if those actions were dependent on him, there would be no occasion for their non-performance, which would result in the absurdity of attaining immortality even in this very world. Likewise, in the production of the body and the senses, there would never be undesirable bodies or senses; rather, due to his autonomy, only desirable ones would be produced.
Therefore, all of that is indeed the work of *karman* alone.
Apart from that, who could perceive a self?

We do not accept at all this notion of a "divine activity" (devakriyā) as being anything distinct from karma. Why? Because in the investigation of reality, no cause exists apart from karma; this he demonstrates with the passage beginning "And even... and ending with "...like a corpse possessed by a vetāla."

For a person possessed by the vetāla of karma is indeed not independent; because of being under the control of another, his activity toward the desirable and the undesirable is equal. From the beginning of the undertaking [of life]—and so forth, up to the point where it says "he should abandon"—the meaning is to demonstrate the absence of that person’s independence, starting from the opening of the eyes until the conclusion at death and liberation. This has already been explained. Furthermore—from the passage beginning with "therefore, according to the specific food" up to "the consequence of immortality right here"—[it follows].

The mother’s *ojas* and the father’s *śukra* constitute the first food; from that, for seven days, it becomes the *kalala*, and so on according to the sequence beginning with "like a grain of rice" (*tandulavaiṣayika*). Thus, there is the food that serves as the cause for the body, senses, and so forth, which is capable of sustaining the life-process such as breathing. Furthermore, there is the differentiation of that [food] into the states of waste (*khala*), essence (*rasa*), and so on. In these and other unperceived, unmanifest activities, the fetus is entirely dependent and remains as if asleep.
Yet, those very activities—though produced by karma—the person conceives of as "done by me," because they appear to him in that way.

For if those activities were indeed the result of human effort—that is, the result of personal exertion—then because there would never be a failure to perform them, and because the causes for the maintenance of life would never cease, there would be no death; consequently, the fault of contradicting both what is observed and what is desired would follow, namely that one could attain immortality right here. Likewise, even in the production of the body and the senses, undesirable bodies, senses, and so forth—such as being one-eyed, lame, or deaf—would not occur; rather, one would possess only perfectly developed senses, caste, physical form, and constitution.

Furthermore, in the accomplishment of human effort (*puruṣakāra*), such as in the performance of dharma and so forth or in the enjoyment of objects, there would be the production of only what is desired due to [the soul's] independence;
yet action (*karman*) would be a non-cause because it depends on auxiliaries, like the lifting of a load.

This too should not be thought: "Action is a non-cause because it depends on auxiliaries," for in order to bring about the fruit, both the master’s exertion and the constituent elements such as ministers must be depended upon. This is because even those [elements] are bound by the ropes of the master’s dharma and adharma, owing to their dependence on him and their being his objects of experience.
...like threads and cloth;
if they were not bound by the ropes of their master’s merit (dharma) and demerit (adharma), then the consequence would be that all things would be indistinguishable.
Furthermore, even the master’s human effort is itself merely karma, because it is a fruit of demerit and because it is an affliction (kleśa), like a fever.

Therefore, all that [variety] is due solely to the cause of action (*karman*), not to the self (*ātman*). Since the word "action" (*karmaṇaḥ*) is used in the ablative case to signify a cause, who could conceive of anything apart from that [action] as existing in the self? Thus, what wise person, knowing this, would accept such an untenable thing as existing in the self independently of action? The intention is that the wise person certainly does not accept it. Therefore, the person is not the cause, nor is he the agent thereof.
See page 259, note 6;
[the reading] "garttādiṣu" (in pits, etc. is found in manuscript Ya, while "gatārthādiṣu" (in those whose purpose has been understood, etc. is found in manuscript Bhā.
See page 113, line 12:
"kalpateti" in the Prabhākara [edition];
"kāryendriya" in the Prabhākara [edition].

If it is argued that action (*karman*) is not without a cause because it depends upon auxiliary factors (*sahāya*), like the lifting of a load—this too should not be considered [a valid objection]. For although action is without a [prior] cause, it requires both the master’s exertion and the constituent elements such as ministers for the production of its fruit; yet even these [auxiliaries] are bound by the ropes of the master’s merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*), because they are dependent upon him and are his objects of experience.
...like a cloth made of threads;

for if they were not bound by the ropes of their own merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), then the consequence would follow that there is no distinction between them at all— [just as there is no distinction] in the case of [objects] tied to a rope?
Even that which is the exertion of the master’s men is itself merely karma, because it is the fruit of unwholesome action (adharma) and because it is an affliction (kleśa), like a fever;
therefore, all of that is indeed [the result] of that very karma.
Thus, one who knows this might think: "Even though action is not the cause, it depends upon assistance;
even though action is not the cause, it requires assistance, just like the act of placing food into the mouth."
As it has been said: "He who, due to laziness, lacks enthusiasm does not obtain even the slightest fruit;

and the drinking of breast milk and so forth is not distinct from human effort, just like the lifting of a weight. Just as a man carrying a load is unable to carry it by himself without an assistant to lift it or someone to set it down, so too action [cannot exist] without human effort (puruṣakāra). Thus, that which is a cause is seen to be a non-cause."

He who, due to laziness, lacks enthusiasm does not obtain even the slightest fruit; moreover, the drinking of breast milk and the like is not distinct from human effort (*pauruṣa*), such as the lifting of a burden.
See page 363, line 20:
"The cause of the cause" (kāraṇakāraṇaṃ).
Furthermore, by the words "and this also should not be thought of as being without a cause," etc., he explains that very same prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa).

If it is asked, "In this case, what kind of assistance is required by the action, similar to how one who intends to lift a load requires a carrier for that load? it is said: "For the sake of bringing forth the fruit," and so on. For an action that is about to bring forth its fruit, the internal efforts of the agent who is its master—the application of policy (*naya*) and exertion (*udyoga*)—are required, as well as external factors such as the constituent elements of sovereignty like ministers (*amātya*) and so forth.

But what is the reason that one should not think in this way? It is said: because those [ministers and others] are likewise bound by the ropes of their master’s merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), and so forth—up until the point where, by means of a sentence containing a logical reason and an example like "as in the case of threads and cloth," the fact that ministers and others are the effects of merit and demerit is established; thereby, by determining that action (*karman*) is the cause, he refutes human effort (*puruṣakāra*). Furthermore, he demonstrates the ease of establishing the reason through such statements as "because they are dependent on that" and "because they are to be experienced by that," using the example "like threads and cloth"—meaning, just as cloth is dependent on threads, it is the threads themselves that are to be experienced as the cloth.
"If those [elements]... and so forth; thus, by not accepting this, there follows the undesirable consequence (aniṣṭāpādana) that everything would be without distinction.
[The six constituents are: sovereign, minister, friend, treasury, territory, and fortresses, as well as the army.
"The constituent elements of the state are the subjects and the guilds of the citizens," according to Amarakośa 2.8.
[The section on] the rope as a counter-example;
[the section on] the example with a cause.
By means of the cloth-sentence,
[it is said] "all without remainder" (pra° sarvāśeṣa° ya°) and "always without remainder" (bhā°).
Regarding the passage beginning with "yo 'pi" and so forth:

as for what was stated—that both the master and human effort (*puruṣakāra*) must be relied upon—that "master-effort" (*svāmipuruṣakāra*) is also merely *karman* because it is the fruit of unwholesome action (*adharma*). This supports the previously asserted thesis for the sake of determination: that there is no such thing as "human effort" distinct from *karman*. Because it is an affliction (*kleśa*), for affliction consists of anxiety and exertion, having the nature of mental and physical fatigue, like a fever;
let this be seen [in Pañjikā 2].

[The opponent says: "If you do not accept that this [suffering] is the fruit of unrighteousness (*adharma*), then it follows that suffering is not the fruit of unrighteousness. Consequently, it would follow that from actions such as the taking of life, there is the attainment of the fruit of righteousness (*dharma*)—that is, the attainment of what is desired. Furthermore, because of this reversal of the fruits of righteousness and unrighteousness, human effort (*puruṣakāra*) would be rendered useless."
And if that [activity] were causeless, it would belong even to those who are liberated;
if it were caused, it must be caused by action alone, since no other cause can withstand logical scrutiny.

Furthermore, when the person possesses no agency in its engagement [with activity], then "substance" (*dravya*)—derived from the sense of "that which flows" (*dravati*)—cannot function as an agentive instrument.

The specific nature of the appropriation of karma, however, is as follows: "substance" (*dravya*) is that which is moved (*druyate*) or approached; thus, by means of the object of experience, the person of karma (*karmapuruṣa*), and so forth.

Now, if you do not accept that this human effort (*puruṣakāra*) which is a defilement is the fruit of unwholesome action (*adharma*), because it is desired as something praiseworthy for one endowed with wisdom and energy in the world, then it follows that suffering such as headaches and the like is not the fruit of unwholesome action, since it is a defilement, just like the human effort of exertion and endeavor. As it has been said: "Having studied the 'wisdom' of misfortune, constantly suspicious of his sons and wife, he stays awake at night and harms his kinsmen; homage be to kingship! Poverty is better."
Thus.

Now, if, out of fear of the fault of contradicting common consensus (*prasiddhi*), you concede that suffering is the fruit of unrighteousness (*adharma*), then—since acts such as violence, which act as auxiliaries to that [unrighteousness], have become means for producing suffering—it follows that from the cause of that action, namely the taking of life (*prāṇātipāta*) and so forth, there would be the attainment of the fruit of righteousness (*dharma*). What is this? It is the attainment of desired bodies, sense organs, objects, pleasure, right knowledge, health, and so on; for this is what has been reached, since you admit that the fruits of the auspicious and inauspicious are the opposites of the desired and undesired, and because it was stated that "from righteousness come policy and effort, or else suffering. Therefore, it follows that happiness is the fruit of righteousness, arising from the suffering that is the fruit of unrighteousness.
What is that? To indicate its general direction, he says: "the attainment of the desired. This means the attainment of the desired body, sense organs, and so forth; this has been established.

What is the reason? Because of the reversal of the fruits of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*). Consequently, human effort (*puruṣakāra*) would be useless, as there would be no distinction from mere chance. Therefore, the position that action alone is the cause—since even human effort is itself a fruit of action—is the superior view.
As it has been said:
"Having studied the 'Wisdom of Futility' (Anarthapaṇḍitya) from the *Śaddharma-puṇḍarīka*, one remains constantly apprehensive regarding one's children and wife."
"He stays awake at night and destroys his kinsmen; let there be salutation to sovereignty! Poverty is better.
Thus [it is said]. Why? Because of the manifestation of the individual self (*vyakti*), and because of the state of having reached the nature of that action.
Because that [result] has arrived through the very nature of that action,
there is for both [the agent and the experiencer] the reversal of what was desired;
just as the fruit of previously performed karma approaches, as if it were a treasure stored away.

In that very manner, the intellect proceeds according to its prior dispositions, like a lamp held in the hand; yet, even while conceding the existence of human effort (*puruṣakāra*), we point out a flaw: would that effort be without a cause or with a cause? What follows from this? If that human effort were without a cause, it would exist even for those who are liberated, characterized by exertion and activity, which is not desired by you in their case.

Now, lest this fault arise, one might say that [the result] occurs "with a cause. If that were so, then since action itself is insentient, it would follow that even from auspicious human effort such as service and the like, misfortune is obtained; and even from inauspicious acts such as the taking of life, prosperity is obtained. Because of the aforementioned confusion between the fruits of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), it can be inferred that this diversity of auspicious and inauspicious results arises solely through the power of insentient action that is not preceded by conscious intention.

What is the reason? Because there is no other cause capable of withstanding logical reasoning, and because other causes such as the Person (puruṣa), necessity (niyati), time (kāla), and inherent nature (svabhāva) have been refuted through investigation; therefore, there is no other cause here capable of withstanding scrutiny than this very karma known as destiny (daiva). Thus it is stated in the *Iśvarapratyabhijñākārikā-vimarśinī* by Abhinavagupta.

Regarding the statement "When [it is] thus," etc., at the time when it is established that there is no agency (*kartṛtva*) on the part of the person (*puruṣa*) in the activity to be accomplished— since it has been established that [agency belongs] to action alone— at that time, that which "flows" is a substance (*dravya*); it does not function as an agent (*kartṛ-sādhana*), because an independent agent is logically untenable.

Regarding the specific nature of the appropriation of karma: the word "but" (*tu*) serves to emphasize this distinction. That which accomplishes karma is a substance whose purpose is established; it is "substance" (*dravya*) because it is worn away (*druyate*) or produced. A "karma-person" (*karmapuruṣa*) is produced by a karma-person alone, just as rice is produced by rice itself. Just as the rice of the sprout is produced by the rice-seed through its very effect, so too all that those who maintain the absolute primacy of human effort (*puruṣakāra*) as the cause say is entirely incoherent.

They speak thus: "Since action is characterized by its being an effect, and according to the literal meaning of the word, there exists an agent distinct from the action, just as a potter is distinct from a jar.
[Objection: "Surely the action itself will perform it.

[Reply: "Indeed, even if one goes very far, because rice (vrīhi) possesses the capacity for reversion and because there is a difference in essential nature, and according to the literal meaning of the word, since action is indisputably something produced, the existence of an agent alone follows from that power of the action."
Thus, this specific distinction is determined;
he demonstrates its etymological analysis: "it is sounded" (drūyate), "it is understood" (gamyate), and so forth.
This is now being defined: by that "object-of-enjoyment," namely the *karmapuruṣa*, the substance (*dravya*) is produced.

What is meant? It is said that the "action-person" (karmapuruṣa) is produced by the "action-person" itself; in this regard, there is an illustration: "just as rice is produced by rice alone"—that is, the sprout-rice is produced by the seed-rice which is its effect. This is the explanation. Thus, by means of this restriction, the status of an agent has been refuted, and the doctrine of the absolute primacy of action (karmaikāntavāda) has been established. Furthermore, because of the identity of the conscious and the unconscious, and because everything is of the nature of everything else, it is illogical to posit a separate Lord (Īśvara) as the cause.

In the case of accomplishment, a substance is produced by a substance; a person of action is produced by a person of action alone, just as rice is produced by rice itself, or as the rice-sprout is produced by the rice-seed which is its cause.

See Pañjikā 19, page 365, line 13. Furthermore, that which those who maintain the absolute view that human effort (*puruṣakāra*) is the sole cause say is also entirely incoherent. They speak as follows: "According to such proponents, because action (*karman*) is characterized by its effect and based on the literal meaning of the term, there exists a doer distinct from the action, just as a potter exists for a jar."
See page 359, line 17:
"But surely it will be accomplished by action alone.

Indeed, even going to the furthest extent, because even a grain of rice possesses the quality of returning [to its source], and because of the difference in essential nature (*svarūpa-bheda*) and the literal meaning of the word, action is without dispute something produced; therefore, existence belongs to the agent alone, as that is the power of the action.
See page 358, line 24;
see page 358, line 24:
*sarvāsarvātma* (Bhāṣya).

Regarding the passage beginning with "And also," it is not only the fault [found] in the agentive derivation (*kartṛ-sādhana*); what then? The doctrine of the absolute [nature] of the object (*karma-ekānta-vāda*) is also untenable.

To demonstrate this, he says: "Furthermore, for you who speak thus, because action (*karman*) is characterized as an effect (*kārya-lakṣaṇatvāt*), action is an effect; that which is performed is action; 'the object is that which is most desired by the agent' (Pāṇini 1.4.49)."
Thus, from the definition and the literal meaning of the word, the agent is to be inferred;

therefore, since there would be no action in the absence of an agent distinct from that action— one separate from the action— just as a potter is necessarily required for a jar, so too must an agent be admitted.
And the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: "The action desired by you has a conscious agent distinct from itself, because it is an effect, because it is being produced, like a jar.

[This is] the opponent's objection: "But surely it will be done by the action itself; it was stated previously that the action is performed by the action itself, not by an agent distinct from it. In the example, I said that a rice plant is produced by the rice plant itself—that the rice plant which is the effect is produced by the rice seed which is the cause. Thus he reminds [the proponent] of what was said.

The other says: "But even having gone very far," and so forth. Even after investigating again and again, you, who maintain the doctrine of *karman*, must also admit this—namely, that there exists a person (*puruṣa*) as an agent distinct from *karman*—because *karman* is invariably concomitant with a person distinct from itself. Why? Because even the rice grain is a repeater [of its own kind]; for this example of the rice grain consists in its recurrence through earth, water, space, wind, sprouts, and so forth, and since these possess differences in their essential natures, it is established that *karman* is invariably concomitant with an agent that is inherently separate from it. Therefore, [your argument] proves the opposite of what you intend.

Furthermore, from the literal meaning of the word: "it is done" (kriyate) is *karman*; according to Pāṇini 1.4.49, "the object (*karman*) is that which is most desired by the agent"—this is the literal meaning of the word *karman*.

Therefore, its being produced (*kṛtakatva*) is beyond dispute; and from that indisputable state of being produced, the existence of the agent alone as an independent entity follows, and thus it is the Person (*puruṣa*) himself who exists. Alternatively, because of the use of the ablative case in the statement "everything arises from the agent alone" (*kartureva bhāvaḥ sarvasya*), everything arises from the Person alone as its cause.

And in this way, by the very reason you have stated, the existence of a Person distinct from action is established, and since action is established as distinct from him, it is logical to determine that action is produced and that it is a different entity from the agent—just as in the case of the dissimilarity with a weaver.

Why? Because of its power; for it is from that very agent, the person, that the action possesses the power of being produced, or the agent, the person, possesses the power of instrumentality—not as rice [is the cause] of rice by way of revolving [the wheel], as it were. (See Pañjikā 1, *kartṛ-vi*.)
Because it is the agent, [the term] "agent" is redundant; [the reading] "kartravyarthāntarabhāvaḥ" or "kartravyarthāntaraḥ" [is correct].
Or is it something other than the agent?

No, for it does not exist as something being produced; since the object (karman) lacks independence, it has not yet attained its own mode of existence and thus does not come into being, just like Devadatta [before he is born].
Let it be seen that, as in Pañjikā 24,

there is the refutation of the scripture, and likewise the refutation of actions such as your own instruction, because both the comprehension and non-comprehension of that [scripture] consist merely in the engagement with ritual action;
let it be seen in Pañjikā 23.
Because the meaning of the scripture and our own acts of instruction and so forth consist merely in the engagement of action,
[the author] elaborates on that very point in the passage beginning with "for that is not being done" and ending with "like Devadatta until the end of the world":
the power of that action is not independent, because its own functioning has not yet been attained.

And since there is no independence, how can there be coming-into-being? The illustration: Devadatta, while in the state of being in the womb, is not independent because he has not yet attained self-functioning for the sake of action; due to this lack of independence, he is not an agent; and due to his non-agency, he does not come into being apart from the state of being an effect, just like [the case of] Devadatta. Likewise, in the state of being an effect, even the object (*karman*) being acted upon would not come into being. This is undesirable even to you; therefore, the object does not come into being [without an agent], and since that [coming-into-being] does not occur without the coming-into-being of a distinct Person (*puruṣa*), the Person exists. (Śaktye-sva-bhā)
And because [the world] is the manifestation of the power of [consciousness], which has as its essence the activity of the subject.
Furthermore, if human effort (*puruṣakāra*) were rejected, there would be the consequence that all treatises (*śāstra*) would be rendered useless.

How so? The purpose of all treatises is, respectively, the attainment of the beneficial and the avoidance of the harmful. And it is because they fulfill these purposes—the attainment of the beneficial and the avoidance of the harmful—that treatises such as medicine are established as true through their consistency with other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For example: "The *citraka* is considered pungent in taste, pungent in its post-digestive effect (*pāka*), and hot in potency (*vīrya*); likewise is the *dantī*, yet by its specific power (*prabhāva*), it causes a person to purge."
A decoction of ginger (nāgara), ativiṣā, and mustā serves as a digestive for undigested matter (āma).

In this way, passages such as Carakasamhitā 6.15.98 would be refuted under the extreme view that action is solely caused by the object (*karman*), given the absence of both the person (*puruṣa*) and his activity (*kriyā*).

The refutation of that [position] is not accepted, because we observe the validity of certain scriptures that correspond with other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and because the refutation of your own teachings and other such actions—which have perceptible purposes—proceeds in the same manner. Furthermore, in the view that karma alone is the cause, since there would be no independent person (*puruṣa*) nor any action by him, the act of uttering words endowed with power for the purpose of instructing others could not occur, as all activity would proceed from karma alone.

By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), actions such as joining the mouth to the rice would also not occur; for the engagement in action depends solely on the [subject's] comprehension or non-comprehension of that [object], and according to your teaching, the comprehension of the object by another arises from the action itself. He may comprehend it even without instruction, or he may not comprehend it even when the instruction is present.
As it is said: "The *citraka* is considered pungent, pungent in digestion, and hot in potency" (see p.

Likewise, the *dantī* plant, by its potency, causes a person to purge. (Caraka Saṃhitā 1.26.68) A decoction of *nāgara*, *ativiṣā*, and *mustā* serves as a digestive for undigested matter (*āma*). (Caraka Saṃhitā 6.15.98) [Regarding] the application of that... (Praśastapāda)
If it is argued that [the world] exists because it is merely the engagement in action (*karmapravṛtti*), and so forth, up to "because it is precisely action," then...

It might be thought: "If action lacks independence, then the refutation of the scriptures as well as the refutation of your own teachings and so forth—being unable to establish their own existence—would fail to come into being, like the case of Devadatta [who does not exist]. Since they are clearly produced, the existence of the agent alone follows from his power; and since even rice undergoes transformation due to a difference in its essential nature, it is the person alone who acts, and so forth—all this would be untenable. Rather, it is tenable that everything arises from action alone, because it is merely the operation of action. Thus, regarding the meaning of the scriptures and our own teachings and other activities, whether they are understood or not understood, they are merely the operation of action, just like the understanding of a wise man and the lack of understanding by a bullock, etc."

Therefore, all these [states] arise solely from the cause of karma, according to the logic previously stated regarding the attainment and non-attainment of physical conditions such as reflection and exertion; if you say that all these arise solely from karma, then from where does that initial karma come? You might say: "Oṃ, it comes from the person (puruṣa) alone.

But it does not come from karma alone, because—unlike rice—it lacks an agent, like the self (ātman) and so forth. It is not like the act of lifting [an object], for how could it be unrelated [to a cause]? Because there is nothing whatsoever, whether auspicious or inauspicious, such as form and so on, that is exclusively a cause of the desired or a cause of the undesired.

If there is the doubt that "that very same [action] is both auspicious and inauspicious, being the cause of the desirable and the cause of the undesirable, because its fruit is solely mental affliction," and if you think this, then you must first be asked this: "In that case, from where does that primordial action arise?"

My intention is as follows: since action is produced, you—who do not accept that it arises from the Person (puruṣa) alone—must be asked: "Whence does that primordial action (ādikarman) come, from which all this [subsequent action], including the exertion of engagement and non-engagement, proceeds? This question is intended to draw out your own position: is even that [primordial action] from action itself, or from the Person?

You might say: "Let it be 'from the Puruṣa alone'—what is the harm? Since there is no other alternative, the intention must be that it arises from action alone. To this we reply: No; because, unlike rice (*vrīhi*), it lacks an agent. Even in the case of rice, its status as an agent is attained through its own recurrence; therefore, that rice is not unproduced, for it lacks an agent. Consequently, since it is not being produced, the status of being an "action" (*karman*) is not tenable for that primordial action (*ādi-karman*).

What is it like? It is like the Self (*ātman*) and so forth. Just as the Self, space, time, direction, and so on, are not produced by anyone and are thus non-actions (*akarmāṇi*), so too would the primordial action be.

"Not like throwing upwards" is the demonstration of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*); let it be seen that just as the action of throwing upwards does not occur without a thrower distinct from it, so too is this [the case]. (Pañjikā 3) [From the Prakaraṇa]...

If it is argued that all these [distinctions] between correct and incorrect practice arise solely from karma, then from what does that initial karma itself arise? You might say: "It arises from the person alone. But it does not arise from karma alone, because—unlike rice—it lacks an agent, just like the self (*ātman*) and other such things. Why is this not inconsistent with the example of "throwing upwards" (*utkṣepaṇa*)? Because there is nothing whatsoever, whether pleasant or unpleasant, such as form (*rūpa*) and so on, that is exclusively a cause of the desirable or a cause of the undesirable.
That very same [mind] is both auspicious and inauspicious, the cause of the desirable and the cause of the undesirable; it is one and the same.
*praśamarati* 19.3.
See page 357, line 6:
*tamovātaḥ* [is] *pra*.
Thus, the proponent of human effort (*puruṣakāra*) has refuted the proponent of karma (*karmavādin*), and previously, the proponent of karma [refuted] the proponent of human effort.

Therefore, wishing now to demonstrate that both [positions]—that which those who maintain karma as the sole cause have said, and that which those who maintain human effort (*puruṣakāra*) as the sole cause have said—are equally incoherent because they are mutually refuted, he asks: "How are they incoherent?
