Since these two are identical according to both the opponent's statement and his own statement, they are incoherent precisely because there is no separate existence of karma and human effort. Wishing to demonstrate this, he says: "Because neither the auspicious nor the inauspicious... and so on, up to "...the body."
For now, let this visible body be considered a "person," whichever you prefer; I have no partiality here.

And why? Because there is nothing here—whether pure or impure—that is external to the body and yet accepted as distinct from it, such as form and so forth, which are held to be the causes of desired pleasure (like variegated peacocks, garlands, sandalwood, or the song of bees), or the causes of undesired suffering (like extremely discolored, misshapen forms, thorns, or the howling of jackals).

Understand that all this—whether it be a cause of the desired or a cause of the undesired, auspicious or inauspicious—is perceived as having states that are fragrant, sweet, pleasant to the touch, beautiful in form, or otherwise, due to the attainment of specific transformations based on particular combinations of substance, place, time, state, and other persons; just like a sweetmeat that has been eaten or not eaten, a mango fruit that is ripe or unripe, a lotus filament or its stalk, wine that is produced, unproduced, spoiled, or unspoiled, and the songs and cries of men and women who are healthy or unhealthy.

As it is stated in the *Ārṣa*: "Those very same *pudgalas* transform into a state of pleasant fragrance, and those very same *pudgalas* transform into a state of unpleasant fragrance" (*Jñātādharmakathā*, etc.).

Therefore, there is nothing that is exclusively pure or impure by its very nature; rather, that which is pure becomes impure, and vice versa. Consequently, the very same thing may serve as a desirable cause or an undesirable cause, just as a medicinal confection (*modaka*) that cures the three *doṣas* [can be beneficial or harmful depending on the context]. For this body of *pudgalas* is indeed subject to measurement [and transformation].

Because its mode of existence consists in the transformation of the nature of the enjoyer and the enjoyed, it follows that—like food—it possesses the quality of being auspicious or inauspicious, etc., due to its being the enjoyer and the enjoyed. [Objection: But surely the auspiciousness or inauspiciousness of food and drink is caused by their connection with specific superior or inferior substances. Likewise, this very person-body (*pudgalakāya*) is as follows: "person" (*pudgala*) has the etymology already stated; "body" (*kāya*) means the physical frame, or that which is accumulated, or the dwelling place for sufferings such as disease. Thus, every external or internal collection of material substances is a "body" because it is a collection of form and so forth.
Even in the case of a single atom, it is a "body" of a "person" (*pudgala*), or rather, it is a "body" in the same sense as a "person"—such is the analysis (*vigraha*) and the compound (*samāsa*).

Alternatively, what is the use of this separate conceptualization? Whether it be the physical body called the *pudgala-kāya*, which is considered direct perception by the senses and consists of self-cognized knowledge, or the *ātma-kāya*, inferred through signs such as activity, these two are indeed one; for no notion of difference should be maintained here, since this perspective of the *naya* shows that they attain oneness through the transformation of bondage. Having established the similarity of the body—the subject to be proven—as being like the example of food to be mentioned later, he states its commonality with that as the reason: "because it functions through transformations consisting of the enjoyer and the enjoyed."

If, according to the view of those who maintain the doctrine of the person (*puruṣakāra*), there is an enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*), or even according to the view of those who maintain the doctrine of karma, there is that which is enjoyed (*bhogya*), therefore the body consists of both the enjoyer and the enjoyed. Its modification (*vipariṇāma*) is its function; thus the term "body" is connected as "the modification of either the enjoyed or the enjoyer. Semen and blood, as well as the essence of food taken by the mother and so forth, are the primary and subsequent causes of this body. Both of these are the enjoyer and the enjoyed because they have attained a state of mutual interdependence. Likewise, the fourfold food—eating and so on—is both the enjoyer and the enjoyed due to the relationship between the consumer and the consumed. And that [food] is indeed the cause of the auspicious and inauspicious, the desirable and undesirable. Thus, it is established that for the body and consciousness which have undergone a single transformation (*vaikalyapariṇāma*), there exists the functioning of the modification of the enjoyer and the enjoyed. Therefore, like food, this [body] possesses the nature of being auspicious, inauspicious, and so forth. Just as food is seen to be both auspicious and inauspicious, refined or unrefined—the refined being inauspicious precisely because the food being refined is inherently impure, and because even desired perfumes such as camphor are seen to become foul-smelling after some time—and just as all *pudgalas* (material entities) are both auspicious and inauspicious according to the previously stated method due to their nature as *pudgalas*, so too is the body.

Alternatively, because of the transformation into oneness of the conscious and unconscious—the self and the body—that very same entity is both the enjoyer and the enjoyed; thus, by means of this very example of food, he shows that these two properties are established even individually. Therefore, he says: "Because of being the enjoyer and because of being the enjoyed.
In the same way, because of being the agent and because of being the object, the body is both auspicious and inauspicious, just like food.

And individuals transform themselves through false view and so forth; they cause the self to undergo transformation into the states of false view, non-restraint, negligence, passions, and the arising, destruction, or subsidence of yoga, pleasure, and pain. Because this dyad of action (*karman*) and the agent of action (*karmin*) undergoes mutual transformation, they are beginningless and indeed one. He says: What you have stated—that there is oneness between insentient things such as camphor-water and their transforming substratum due to the relationship of transformer and transformed, and likewise between the sentient and the insentient, namely the soul and karma—is not tenable.

we shall explain both the essence of form and the like, as well as the Self itself.

If it is asked, "How can the object such as form have the nature of *upayoga*? it is said: because its form is obtained through non-distinction from that [upayoga]. Otherwise, there would be no determination of the object's own nature.

Therefore, because its form is obtained as non-different from that [consciousness], the object such as color-and-form (*rūpa*) consists of cognitive activity (*upayoga*). Whatever consists of cognitive activity, that has as its very essence the nature of that [activity] itself; for example, the various types of cognition such as sensory perception (*mati*) and visual intuition (*cakṣurdarśana*), which are cognitive activities, are of the same nature as consciousness—just as camphor and so forth [are of the same nature as fragrance]. *Note:* The fragment "karpūrādekādya" appears to be a corrupt reading; it likely refers to the analogy of camphor (*karpūra*) and other substances being identical in nature to their fragrance. When that location is divided down to its atoms, neither form, nor taste, nor smell is perceived; however, they are perceived through their connection with the location, for when the absolute difference from the location is grasped, those [qualities] cease to exist.

Likewise, if it is held that in the distinction of moments there is one form in the first moment and another in the second moment, then "form" (rūpa) would not be anything at all; for time, which is dependent upon that [form], would lack the connection that serves as the basis for the apprehension of form. Consequently, because it would be characterized by non-existence rather than existence, it would result in its being a non-entity. Therefore, it is substance (*dravya*) alone—characterized by existing in such and such ways—that is real, appearing through the application of designations such as "visual cognition" and so forth, just as a single real person is designated by various titles such as "nephew" and so on.

Furthermore, that which constitutes the essential nature of cognition (*upayoga*), such as sensory perception (*mati*) and the rest, is also the essential nature of the person (*pudgala*), because it consists of matter (*rūpa*) and other qualities, just like atoms and the like. The self, characterized by cognition, when engaged with material entities consisting of form and so forth, becomes itself composed of form and the rest; for if it were to grasp [the object] in its entirety, being identical with the cognition, it would become insentient—just as a lump of clay becomes a small pillar (*śivaka*) and so on—or like a jar that is not currently functioning within a cloth. Moreover, the self is indeed of the same essential nature as matter, because its state is inseparable from the activity of the manifestation (*udaya*) of karmic veils such as the obscuration of knowledge (*jñānāvaraṇa*).

Furthermore, since it would otherwise follow that there is no real entity at all, this must be understood: only substance (*dravya*), characterized by its becoming in such and such ways, is real; there are no such things as "form" (*rūpa*) and so forth.

It is real because it becomes "in such and such ways"—that is, in the manner of color, taste, and so on, as well as in the manner of its specific variations such as dark or red. And substance is [defined] as that which is capable of becoming (Pāṇini 5.3.104).

If it is asked, "How can that substance (*dravya*), while remaining undivided, come to exist through the differentiation of form (*rūpa*) and so forth?"—it is said: it exists by way of the designation of the application of conditions such as the eye (*cakṣus*).

These "conditions" (*pratyaya*) are the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*), the object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*), the causal condition (*hetupratyaya*), and the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*). These are the causes for this application known as cognition and vision (*jñānadarśana*). This is the "application of conditions such as the eye. As it has been said: "Consciousness arises from form, light, mental attention, and the eye, just as fire arises from a jewel, the rays of the sun, and cow dung."

Because it consists of becoming (*bhāvanātmakatva*) and because it would otherwise result in the absence of any real entity (*nirvastutva*), substance (*dravya*) alone—characterized by becoming in such and such ways—is real. Furthermore, that which is the essential nature of cognitive application (*upayoga-svatattva*), such as sensory cognition (*mati*) and the rest, is also of the nature of *pudgala*, because its essence consists of form (*rūpa*) and other qualities, like atoms (*aṇu*) and the like.

The self, characterized by consciousness (*upayoga*), when engaged with *pudgalas* consisting of form and other qualities, would itself consist of form and other qualities; for if it were to grasp [the object] in its entirety, it would—like a lump of clay becoming a small jar and so forth—be devoid of consciousness, just as a cloth does not possess the nature of a pot that is not currently functioning within it. Furthermore, the self would become identical to the very nature of the *pudgala*, because its state would be inseparable from the manifestation of the arising of the veils of knowledge and perception regarding the true nature of the self.
[This is] not the case among the wise.

"Consciousness [arises] from the eye, light, space, attention, and form, just as fire [arises] from a jewel, the rays of the sun, and cow dung.

Thus, in the *Pudgala-prajñapti* of the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, the nature of the *pudgala* as consisting of functional utility (*upayoga*) has been explained through its various divisions such as color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth.

Now, the material nature of even consciousness (upayoga) is stated: the position is that whatever constitutes the essential nature of consciousness, such as sensory cognition (mati) and so forth, is also of the nature of matter (pudgala).
Why? Because it consists of form and other qualities, just like atoms and the like.

For that self, characterized by cognitive engagement (*upayoga*), is engaged with, operates upon, and is pervaded by its entire being within *pudgalas*—such as atoms (*paramāṇu*), dyads (*dvyaṇuka*), triads (*tryaṇuka*), and so forth—which consist of form and other qualities; "engaged" means fully occupied or completed. It consists precisely of form and the rest, because of its engagement with and transformation into those [qualities], just like a *pudgala* with non-spatial, numerable, innumerable, or infinite spatial units (*pradeśa*), and according to the previously stated principle that "that very thing is that."

If the self is not admitted to have the nature of form and so forth, then even though it consists of innumerable spatial units (*asaṃkhyāta-pradeśa*), when there is the application of consciousness (*upayoga*) toward a single substance possessing form and so forth, it would attain identity with that object of perception. Consequently, even though it has innumerable spatial units, would it not thus become a *pudgala* (matter) itself? For that which consists of consciousness would then possess the nature of matter; how, then, could it have the nature of form and so forth? No, because it consists precisely of the nature of consciousness, even form and the rest [are understood] as stated above. By this, the entire doctrine of those who maintain that karma alone is the cause, as well as the doctrine of those who maintain that human effort (*puruṣakāra*) alone is the cause, should be understood as incoherent, because they lack mutual identity.

If a substance were to be grasped by all its parts through its entire self—that is, through its universal nature—it would, while not attaining its functional capacity (*upayoga*), remain devoid of such capacity; thus, being non-functional, it would necessarily be insentient (*acetana*), just like a jar that is not currently serving the purpose of a cloth. This is how the argument will be connected.

How, then, could it undergo application? It would be like a lump of clay [in its transformation] into a small jar (*śivaka*) and so forth. Just as a lump of clay, in its entirety, undergoes activity through its total identity (*sārvātmyena*) in the state of becoming a small jar and so on, if the Self did not likewise undergo [application] toward the object of perception (*grāhya*), then, failing to attain identity with it, it would remain merely insentient, like a pot that is not being applied to a cloth. These are, respectively, the examples by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) and similarity (*sādharmya*).

For consciousness is characterized by functional application (*upayoga*); in the absence of that, it would be unconscious. This fault would arise if the self were devoid of the nature of form and so forth, since the self is characterized by functional application.
Therefore, it is established that the self possesses the nature of form and so forth, because its essence is functional application.
Consequently, it is well said that the very intrinsic nature of the *pudgala* consists of cognition (*mati*) and the rest.

For this reason as well, the self (*ātman*) is precisely the intrinsic nature (*svatattva*) of the person (*pudgala*), because its intrinsic nature as a self and so forth [is established], up to and including the fact that its form is not distinct from existence (*bhāva*).

The self's own true nature (*svatattva*) is the emergent state (*audayika-bhāva*). "Emergent" (*audayika*) means that which exists in emergence (*udaye bhavaḥ*). Of what? Of all eight kinds of karma, such as knowledge-obscuring (*jñānāvaraṇīya*) and the rest. And that state is non-distinct and inseparable from the activity of its emergence; it is the self's own true nature. Furthermore, the self is of a form inseparable from that [emergence]. Therefore, because the self is of a form inseparable from the activity of the emergence of the self’s own true nature—the knowledge-obscuring karma and so forth—the self is indeed the very nature of the *pudgala* (matter), due to the realization of identity (*tādātmya*), just like atoms whose nature consists of color-form and so forth. This is the meaning. [Note: The variants *aśvādi* and *andhādi* appear in the manuscripts.]

[Objection: If the self (*ātman*) is thus [defined as] the object of apprehension (*grāhya*), then it follows that the person (*pudgala*) itself is the self, because that which consists of cognition (*upayoga*) is the person. How, then, can this [person] have the nature of matter (*rūpa*) and so forth? [Reply: No, precisely because it consists of cognition, matter and the rest are also [the self], as has been stated.

By this, the entire doctrine of those who maintain that action (*karman*) alone is the cause, as well as the doctrine of those who maintain that human effort (*puruṣakāra*) alone is the cause, must be understood as incoherent, because they are mutually identical in nature.
Those which arise from the primordial source through their own essential nature.
Is it a nature not distinct from the stated state? [The text reads] *tāvadātmya* in both *ya* and *bhā*.
The meaning is "because it consists of subtle [atoms]";
see page 363, line 23.
Is the meaning "because it has the nature of subtle [atoms]"?
Here he says: "But surely, in this way," and so on, up to "how can it have the nature of form and the rest?

Indeed, sir! By this very method you have stated, it follows that the *pudgala* itself is the self, because that which consists of cognition (*upayoga*) has the nature of a *pudgala*. This cognition of a *pudgala*—consisting of knowledge such as "form" or "taste"—is precisely the cognition of the self, since there is no form and so forth apart from cognition, and because cognition has the nature of form and the rest, and form and the rest have the nature of cognition.

Therefore, from where could this self possess the nature of form and so forth? This inquiry negates the view that the instruments of cognition, such as sensory perception (*mati*), are of the nature of matter (*pudgala*).

To this it is replied: this is not so; because they are of the nature of cognitive engagement (*upayoga*), there is no fault in the aforementioned [position]. For the self possesses the nature of form and so forth, while form and so forth possess the nature of cognitive engagement.
Since it has just been stated that even form and the other [sensory objects] consist of cognition (*upayoga*),

therefore, because form and the others also consist of cognition, as previously explained, the person (*pudgala*) is the self (*ātman*) and the self is indeed the person; thus, the fact that the self consists of form and the others is not a fault for the person.

By this [statement], "all of this as well," and so forth, up to "because they are mutually identical in nature"—and having established this, since the *puruṣa* consists of the *pudgala* which possesses form and other qualities, and the *pudgala* also consists of the *puruṣa* whose nature is cognition—it is stated that "karma alone is the cause" and "human effort alone is the cause. One should understand that both of these definitive assertions fall into one-sided extremes and are incoherent; this is the statement of the defects common to both positions.
As for what is said:
"Let it be seen," see page 352, line 4; page 357, line 3.

However, because it initiates the cultivation of individual responses and so forth, the Person (*puruṣa*) is the cause; and since, as stated, he alone is everything, action (*karman*) also belongs to him alone, as does its state of being an object (*karmatā*). Furthermore, the various successes and failures of human efforts and their results would indeed be manifold, because the Person himself is the non-distinct yet differentiated cause, just like the expansion and contraction of a snake’s coils.
See page 368, line 7:
Likewise, because there is neither non-excess nor excess [of agency], karma is also the instigator;
for that very person is both conscious and unconscious, due to being engaged in the performance of desired and undesired actions.
Now, if this is not accepted, then that [person] would be like an animal even in terms of being human.

Now, regarding the direction of the individual refutation concerning cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and so forth—the word "but" (*tu*) serves a restrictive purpose—the direction of the individual refutation is distinguished from the direction of the simultaneous refutation.

First, as for the direction of the refutation of the doctrine of absolute action (*karmaikāntavāda*): because of his status as an instigator, the person is the cause, seeking excellence; and by the word "and" (*ca*), it is implied that action (*karman*) is also [a cause], since the refutation of absolutism will be stated hereafter.

One who seeks elevation is "one who desires elevation" (*utkarṣārthī*). Alternatively, it means that elevation itself is his object (*artha*). The suffix *ini* is applied here according to Pāṇini’s rule *arthāccāsannihite vā* (Pā. 5.2.135). This elevation consists of external prosperity, such as wealth, grain, friends, and land, as well as internal prosperity, such as health, knowledge, and so forth. For one who has already achieved his purpose, since he has ceased the undertaking for the sake of that [elevation], he is called "one who desires an object not yet present" (*asannihitārthārthī*).

If it is asked why the *puruṣa* is the cause, it is said: because, as stated previously, he alone is everything; thus, according to the logic expressed in such passages as "rice is produced from rice itself," this very *puruṣa*—who possesses breath and so forth—is both conscious and action (*karman*). By the use of the word "also" (*api*), non-action (*nokarman*) is also included; that is, the *pudgalas* consisting of breath, exhalation, speech, mind, and matter, whether internal or external, such as the *pudgalas* of form and so forth, are conscious. Since this is so, he alone is the instigator.

Since, in this very view, everything—including action and so forth—is that [single reality] itself, what other action could there be? Thus, even its status as "action" exists; and by the force of the word "also" (*api*), its status as "person" (*puruṣatā*) and its status as "individual" (*pudgalatā*) should also be seen (see p.

358, l. 1). Therefore, what was stated—that the superior, middling, and inferior human efforts, as well as their successes and failures, would not be diverse, being [all] superior, middling, and inferior—is incorrect.
The successes and failures of human efforts and their respective results must indeed be manifold; they cannot but be so.
Why? Because, even though the succession of excellence has many divisions, up until liberation, it is the Person alone who is the non-distinct yet distinct cause.

He alone is the non-distinct and distinct cause, because he himself consists of all the various divisions. Furthermore, those *pudgala* entities—distinguished by karma, non-karma, external form, and so forth—are non-distinct from him, because they consist of the very nature of the Person’s conscious experience (*upayoga*).
Therefore, there would indeed be a diversity of human efforts, as well as a diversity of successes and failures achieved through them; yet that [Puruṣa] alone would remain the sole cause.

What is the illustration? It is like the expansion and contraction of a snake’s body. Just as a snake—though distinct from its qualities such as form and so forth, which exist either simultaneously or non-simultaneously, such as when it spreads out its hood or coils itself into a circle—is nevertheless not separate from its true nature as a snake because it is the cause of that non-distinct state, and thus acts as their agent; likewise, the person (puruṣa), whose essence is consciousness (upayoga) and who dwells together with the aggregate of hands and other limbs, desiring the excellence of movement and so forth, is seen to be the person alone as the reality amidst those things that occur simultaneously or non-simultaneously. (See Tattvārtha-bhāṣya, p. 352, l. 5).
External to action;
see Pañjikā, p.
14, for the purpose of making [it] real.
Is it *uktabhinnā*?
Regarding the phrase *yugapadbhāveṣu ya*, there might also be a reading here: *yugapadayugapadbhāvibhāveṣu*.

In this very way, action (*karman*) is also the initiator [of existence], because it neither exceeds nor falls short [of the self]. Just as the person (*puruṣa*), though divided by the distinctions of *pudgala*, self, action, and qualities (*dharma*), is nonetheless the initiator as something non-distinct [from them], so too is action the initiator, because its causality is neither distinct from nor separate from that [self].

Furthermore, because the person (puruṣa) is ultimately both conscious and unconscious, his activity regarding the attainment of the desired and the avoidance of the undesired belongs to him alone; for that very person is both conscious and unconscious. Why? Because, in this way, within the undivided dual nature [of the self], the continuous flow of activity known as human effort (*puruṣakāra*)—termed "action" (*karman*)—is twofold: achievable and unachievable. This is due to the accumulation [of results] through the cultivation of causes such as intensity or mildness, like diseases that are curable or incurable. It is movable or immovable, like a tree with loose roots or one with firm roots, and characterized by having parts that are either consolidated or not, like a bundle of iron rods.

Because he is engaged in the performance of injunctions regarding the desirable and the undesirable— which are characterized by excellence and deficiency— their injunction consists of the means for attaining them, namely heedfulness and heedlessness; and since these two are observed,
this person is both conscious and unconscious, because he is engaged in the performance of injunctions regarding the desirable and the undesirable through heedfulness and heedlessness.
Therefore, because the influence of insentient *karman* is perceived and the influence of the sentient person (*puruṣa*) is also perceived, that [person] is the ultimate reality of those two;
and for that reason, even *karman* is set in motion [by him].

Now, if this is not accepted by you, and if the person is held to be merely the power of sentience, then he would be like an animal—just as an animal lacks discrimination regarding what is to be approached or avoided, or what is edible or inedible, so too would he be in his human state, possessing only limited sentience.
Furthermore, if a human being possessed the power of articulating sounds capable of conveying meaning through distinct phonemes, words, and sentences, then even an animal would be such;

likewise, a human would be as inert as a worm, and a worm would be as wise as a human. Therefore, it must be understood that action is sentient and the person is insentient, and these two are inseparable.

Thus, in this state of being an undivided dual nature, the continuous stream of activity of the human effort known as *karman* is twofold: that which is achievable and that which is unachievable, due to being accumulated through the cultivation of causes such as intensity or mildness, like curable and incurable diseases; it is movable or immovable, due to having roots that are either bound or unbound, like a tree or a *haṭa* (a type of grass); and it is characterized by parts that are either consolidated or not consolidated, like a bundle of iron rods. Thus [it is said].
This very power is proclaimed as that which is exceedingly insentient (atijaḍa). [Variant readings: *yaṣyo* (Bhā., Ḍe., Līṃ., Vi.);
*ṣyomijaḍaḥ* (Pā., Raṃ., Hī.)]

And having established this, when there exists for that very [Pradhāna] a dual nature consisting of the non-differentiated unity of the conscious and the unconscious—just as it has arisen—there follows a twofold continuity of activity: a continuity of the transformation of results, which is both achievable and unachievable by the human effort known as past karma, due to the twofold nature of the material cause and the temporal transformation that serve as the causes for its accumulation.

He demonstrates this by stating: "Because it is accumulated through the cultivation of causes such as intensity and mildness. Karma accumulated through intense transformation of yoga (yogapariṇāma) is bound, nourished, and consolidated with intense fruition, duration, and spatial extent; because its fruit of pleasure or pain cannot be brought forward [prematurely], it is incurable and necessarily ripens. However, that which is accumulated through mild means has mild fruition and so forth, and because it can be brought forward, it is curable.

It is like the distinction between curable and incurable diseases; just as a disease such as fever or dysentery becomes curable or incurable depending on whether its cause is mild or intense, so too is the continuous stream of human effort known as *karman*.
The explanation of their curable and incurable natures is as follows: they are respectively movable or immovable, and bound or unbound at the root, like a tree and a stone.
Correspondingly, that which is curable is to be moved, while the other is immovable and cannot be shaken.

The first [type of karma] is firmly rooted like a tree; the second is unrooted like a clod of earth, meaning it is separable from suffering or separable from pleasure, because its constituent parts are either consolidated (*nikācita*) or not consolidated (*anikācita*). Furthermore, the transformation of karma is sometimes within the scope of human effort (*puruṣakāra*) and sometimes not, because it exists in states where transformation has not yet occurred or where it has already occurred, just like flowers or firm fruits. And thus, having acted in this way, it yields fruit both with the assistance of action and alone, because its power is either dependent or independent, like the lifting of a load by a person whose nature is karma and who acts with exertion.

...or like the burning of grass, so too are accumulated portions of karma [destroyed] by an intense transformation of unwholesome states such as anger, whereas non-accumulated karma is destroyed by a mild transformation. What is it like? It is like a bundle of iron rods: just as iron rods held together merely by a thread all fall apart with the effort of pulling out a single rod, whereas those that are heated, joined, and struck together cannot be separated without friction—such is the nature of karma.

In the eighth chapter, the *Karmapravāda-pūrva*, of that very [scripture] consisting of fourteen parts (*caturdaśapūrvātmaka*), karma is explained; namely, how the bondage of the soul (*jīva*) and karma occurs. Regarding this, they say: it is bound (*baddha*), touched (*puṭṭha*), and accumulated (*nikāiya*).

Just as a flock of cotton is bound, just as it is pressed by a dense, continuous hammering, and just as it is condensed by being heated and beaten—so too does the soul first bind karma through passion and aversion; subsequently, not abandoning that state of transformation, it makes it "pressed" (puṭṭha); and by that same defiled transformation, not abandoning it, it makes some of it "condensed" (nikāīya), which is without external mitigation and can only be exhausted by its own fruition, otherwise it cannot be exhausted.

Thus, in the commentary on the *Uttarādhyayana-sūtra* composed by Śāntisūri, in the third chapter concerning the heresy of Goṣṭhāmāhila; this very same reading is also found in the *Uttarādhyayana-sūtra-vṛtti* composed by Nemicandrasūri, though there the specific reading is: "bound like a silk-worm [in its cocoon], touched like [iron] with rust, made dense and continuous"—(variants:
˚rātīsā˚, bhā˚, ˚calyaśca, pra˚).
Haṭṭhapāda said:
"If you will entertain such a disposition toward whatever woman you see,
you will become like a puppet tossed by the wind— a mere skeleton of a soul."
Uttarādhyayana 22.44:

"If you harbor a disposition—by context, one of longing for sensual enjoyments—toward whichever women you see, what will happen? To this he says: you will become like a *haṭha* tree, a specific kind of forest plant, blown about by the wind; that is, your mind will be unsteady."
Thus, in the commentary on the *Uttarādhyayana-sūtra* composed by Ācārya Nemicandra, [this concludes] the chapter on the *haṭṭa*.

Furthermore, the transformation of karma is both within the scope of human effort (*puruṣakāra*) and, in some cases, not within its scope, because it exists in states of transformation where what was unobtained is obtained— just like a flower, a tender fruit, or a firm fruit.

And having established this, such karma yields its fruit both as an auxiliary to action and by itself, due to its power being either dependent or independent, like the lifting of a load by a self whose nature is karma through the agency of the person.
...or like the burning of grass,
there is also transformation (*pariṇāma*), and so forth, up to being like a flower that yields firm fruit.

Furthermore, that previous karma—accumulated through the cultivation of causes such as intensity or mildness—is both the object and the non-object of human effort (*puruṣakāra*) consisting of the performance of agriculture, study, service, trade, and so forth in this life. This is because it exists in two states: the state of having reached maturation and the state of not yet having reached it. Respectively: 1. That which has itself not yet reached the state of maturation is matured by human effort; it is brought into the state of being an object and is raised up (*udīryate*) by the instrument of raising (*udīraṇākaraṇa*). 2. However, that which has already reached the state of maturation is not made an object by human effort, is not matured by human effort, and is not raised up, because it would be futile; it has already matured of its own accord.
What is it like? It is like a flower and a firm fruit; these two—namely, the flower and the firm fruit—are the examples respectively.
Just as a firm fruit ripens by itself and is not ripened by human effort, whereas a flower is ripened according to the methods of the science of tree-life (vṛkṣāyurveda).

Alternatively, just as when a flower has arisen, one knows that a firm fruit will surely come of it, so too a "firm-fruit" arises with such a power that it belongs only to that [seed] and not to one devoid of that power. Thus, a fruit such as that of the plantain or the mango, which has not yet reached the time of ripening, is made to ripen by being wrapped in the husks of *kodrava* grain or buried, or by means of smoke applied to its sides; whereas another [fruit] would necessarily perish [without such treatment].

Alternatively, when the fruit is in a state where it has not yet reached maturity or undergone transformation, it does not ripen even through artificial application because of its extreme tenderness and its unsuitability for ripening; instead, it either rots or dissolves. However, a firm fruit, being suitable for ripening because the proper time has arrived, does indeed ripen. The word *toka* is derived from the root *tu*, as stated in Hemacandra’s *Dhātupārāyaṇa*: "The suffix *ka* is applied after the roots *bhī*, *ṇśali*, *vali*, *kali*, *yati*, *mṛc*, *mṛj*, *ku*, *stu*, *dā*, *dhā*, *rā*, *trā*, *kāp*, *ani*, *hā*, *nañ*, and *śubh*. *Tuka* is likewise formed from the same root.
The suffix *ka* occurs after these [roots]...
...in the sense of injury, livelihood, and fulfillment; *toka* means offspring...
