Therein, the substance (*dravya*) is the seed, which is free from all distinctions through its state of being fully condensed; activity (*kriyā*) is the manifestation of the reality of proximity that is inseparable from such becoming; activity is the process (*pravṛtti*), which is existence (*bhāva*). Just as in the case of the continuous series of banners of a magician, which consist of forms and dimensions with a fixed sequence located in the mouth [of the magician], so too, from the substance—earth and the rest—which is characterized by non-arising and non-perishing like a magician, there arise roots and other parts; these, like a garland of banners, are essentially activity and are not [separate] substances.

Therefore, it is not the case that everything is one according to the perspective of the immediate method (*anantaranaya*); nor is everything one according to the perspective of the method of rules regarding the conceptual constructions of the Person (*puruṣa*), necessity (*niyati*), and so forth; nor is this [reality] the dualistic view of both [cause and effect], consisting of an agent and a non-agent, namely Nature (*prakṛti*) and the Person (*puruṣa*); nor is it the view of a Lord as the cause, wherein the substrate (*adhiṣṭhātṛ*) and the object to be acted upon (*adhiṣṭheya*) exist in a relationship of primary and subordinate, as previously indicated. What then? Both are the agents of becoming, because their powers are equal; thus, by way of generality, "this being comes into existence. To the question, "What, then, are those two? he says: "Substance (*dravya*) and state (*bhāva*)."
In this context, the word *bhāva* denotes action (*kriyā*), according to the definition: "Action is *bhāva*; [it is] the verbal root" (Pāṇini-Vārttika 1.3.1).
The verbal root (dhātu) expresses the agent as well as the act;
the verbal root expresses the state of being (bhāva).
Thus, in the *Pāṇinīya-vārttika* on 1.3.1.
Therefore, every duality—such as a pot, a cloth, and so forth—comes into being like [the process of] cooking and the like.

In this context, "that in which all distinctions are coalesced and undifferentiated" means that all distinctions—such as wings, feathers, arms, legs, vehicles, seats, beds, and so forth, as well as blackness, whiteness, unevenness, shortness, length, and so on—are coalesced (*sammūrchita*), meaning mixed together (*saṃsṛṣṭa*) without separation. That which possesses such coalesced distinctions is "that in which all distinctions are coalesced. Furthermore, because it abides in its own essential nature (*svarūpa*) everywhere, it is "undifferentiated" (*nirbheda*), like the water of a lake in which distinctions such as waves have not been grasped. This—that which is their seed (*bīja*), substratum (*āśraya*), and substance (*dravya*)—is the definition of substance (*dravya-lakṣaṇa*).

Action (*kriyā*) is the manifestation of the substantiality (*vastutva*) of an object whose presence is inseparable from its becoming in such a manner. "Becoming in such a manner" (*tathābhavana*) refers to becoming by way of such modes as cooking, reading, or going. An "object whose presence is inseparable from that becoming" (*tathābhavanavinābhūtasannidhivastu*) is an entity whose presence—its state as a mere possessor of power—is inseparable from that becoming, meaning its power is not yet manifested. The "substantiality" (*vastutva*) of that is its being an entity; the manifestation of that is the manifestation of the entity's power, which is action. This is the definition of action.
Furthermore, "activity" (*pravṛtti*), "action" (*kriyā*), and "becoming" (*bhāva*) are synonyms. [The commentary] states: "All substance (*dravya*) is twofold... [Yaśovijaya].
The entire duality is non-dual; this [reality] is indivisible, accessible through yoga, beginning with the unborn and the unperishing.

This passage does not exist in the Bhāratīya manuscript; its appearance there is due to the manifestation of its substantiality (*vastutva*), that is, the manifestation of the power of the entity (*vastuśaktyabhivyakti*). (Pā., Ḍe., Līṃ.)

This is the illustration of that independent duality—beginning with "situated on the face" and ending with "like the timeless"—referring to those whose forms, shapes, and dimensions are established as a sequence upon the face of the illusionist; they are the banners of the illusionist, and their continuum is like the timeless.

In order to explain the distinct natures of these two, he says: "Just as from a magician (māyākāraka) [arise] roots and so forth from a substance (dravya) that is characterized by non-origination and non-destruction, such as earth and the rest—thus equating the world, which is the subject of the illustration (dārṣṭāntika), with the example (dṛṣṭānta) of the magician, he explains 'substance' and 'action' as being of the nature of action, like a series of banners according to their respective [forms]."

Just as various individual garlands of flags—blue, yellow, and other colors; of fixed dimensions such as short or long, thin or thick—emerge one after another in a regular sequence from their respective sources, so too do actions such as "cooking" or "going" proceed from substances such as Devadatta.

These [actions] are distinct from him, yet they do not exist without him, nor does he exist without them. Furthermore, these [actions] possess fixed forms, appearances, and dimensions, while he is the individual manifestation resulting from their transformation; thus, both exist, and their separateness is established.
In this context, there may also be a reading "and separately from those two";

thus, because [the categories] are included within that very entity consisting of substance and action, the postulation of them as separate categories is useless, since categories such as qualities and so forth are merely actions.

Furthermore, the conceptualization of a distinction between substances and their generic classes would be futile, because all substances possess activity. To demonstrate this, he says: "The conjunction and disjunction of substances, upward motion, downward motion, and other such specific modes of becoming, as well as inherence and so forth, are simply *bhavana* (becoming). It flows (*dravati*), knows, desires, hates, sounds, exerts effort, joins, disjoins, and becomes white (*śvetate*), and so on."

Without the occurrence of conjunction and disjunction, lifting and lowering, such transformations, particularization, inherence, and so forth, beginning with earth and ending with the ultimate substance (*antyadravya*), no distinct substances can exist; likewise, without earth and the other elements, there can be no conjunction, disjunction, lifting, lowering, such transformations, particularization, inherence, and so forth, nor the state of being roots and so on—thus is the inclusion of the existence of substances established.

And having established this, it was said: "Indeed, nothing whatsoever remains even for a moment in its own self, as long as there is the conjunction of non-substantial [qualities], substantial [qualities], and substances," and so forth. It was previously stated that qualities and the like are merely action; now it is further stated by way of that [action] that there is no difference in genus [between them].
For substance is of two kinds: non-substantial and multi-substantial.
That which has no substance as its inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) is called "non-substantial"; it consists of the self, space, time, direction, and atoms.

Substance, however, like [the category of] substance itself, consists of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) up to the great earth; there is no difference in genus between these two kinds of substance. This is because conjunction (*saṃyojana*), which is attainment (*prāpti*), is characterized by action (*kriyā*) and transformation (*pariṇati*); that very [action] is the quality (*guṇa*) of atoms, space, and so forth, since even the self and space possess the action of transformation, and as stated, that which lacks action is non-existent. Likewise, disjunction (*viyojana*) is separation (*vibhāga*), which is mere action and not a quality.

Likewise, it is called *rūpa* because it is perceived by the eyes; *rasa* because it is tasted by the tongue. In the same way, smell, touch, sound, and others such as number (*saṅkhyā*) and so forth are to be understood through the intellect, because they are being enumerated.

"Throwing upwards," "throwing downwards," and so on—these actions such as upward throwing are properties of substance (*dravyadharma*), a differentiation of substance, and its becoming in such a manner.
This is the generality of existence (*sattāsāmānya*), which is the common becoming of the substance itself—that which is experienced as common.

"Qualification" (*viśeṣaṇa*) means "distinction" (*viśeṣa*). That by which a substance becomes qualified—namely, through a specific action such as "blue" or "going"—that distinction is "inherence" (*samavāya*), which is a relation. That too is simply a form of conjunction (*saṃyoga*). "Inherence" (*samavāya*) refers to the state of parts, such as threads and the like, abiding in a state of oneness (*ekībhāva*) as a whole, such as a cloth; it is the unification of cause and effect in the sense that "it is here.

By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), he shows that there is an infinity of inherences due to the diversity of all substances that possess inherence, and that there is no fixed limit to the six categories because of the infinity of the properties of transformation and the infinity of categories such as action and quality.

"Existence" (*bhavana*) itself is "being" (*bhāva*) and indeed "action" (*kriyā*); qualities and so forth do not exist [independently]. Thus, by the word "existence," he demonstrates action. Now, desiring to demonstrate substance (*dravya*), he says: "it flows," and so on, up to "it whitens," and so on. This is because the agent—expressed by the *l*-suffix which denotes the agent—is used to denote those specific actions to be accomplished (*sādhya*) such as *dru*, *jñā*, *iṣ*, *dviṣ*, *dhvan*, *yat*, *saṃyuj*, *viyuj*, and *śvit*, all of which possess an agent.

The conjunction and disjunction of substances and non-substances, upward motion, downward motion, and other such specific modes of becoming, as well as inherence and so forth, are simply *bhavana* (becoming); for it is *bhavana* alone that flows, knows, desires, hates, sounds, exerts itself, conjoins, disjoins, becomes white, and so on.

Without the occurrence of conjunction and disjunction, throwing upward and downward, such becoming, particularization, inherence, and so forth, the various substances do not exist, up to the ultimate substance; and without earth and the other elements, there is no conjunction, disjunction, throwing upward and downward, such becoming, particularization, inherence, and so forth, nor the state of being roots and so on. Thus, there is the inclusion of the existence of substance. And having established this, it was said: "Indeed, nothing remains in its own self even for a moment, as long as it is said to increase by this [process] and so forth. (Praśastapāda-bhāṣya)
The word *yāvat* is used in the sense of limitation (*avadhāraṇa*).
"As many verses as there are, so many prostrations to Acyuta"— this is the rule "yāvacchlokam" according to the *Siddhāntakaumudī*.
Regarding the absence of transformation (*pariṇāmābhāva*),
see *Dravyatattvopadeśa*, page 126, note 7.

The following passage—beginning with "the conjunction of earth and so forth" and extending up to "the inclusion of substance and state"—is intended to demonstrate the non-existence of substance and action when they are mutually devoid of one another.

First of all, without *bhāva*, which is action, there can be no distinct substances such as earth and so forth, down to the final substance, the atomic substance (*paramāṇu-dravya*). Having stated that without the aforementioned distinct substances—starting from earth and so forth and ending with the state of roots and so on—there are no distinct actions such as conjunction and the rest, he thereby presents an undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭāpādana*).
Therefore, he introduces [the argument] that the apprehension of both substance and state is logical, because the word *iti* has the sense of a reason;
the reading contained within these brackets does not exist in the Ya manuscripts,
as there is an absence of action (*kriyā*).

And having established it thus, etc., up to "or it is joined with *apāya*," this explanatory passage (*jñāpaka-grantha*) was cited by the author of the Bhāṣya from the Sāṅkhya school; [the sūtra] states: "It should be augmented, or it is joined with *apāya*" (Pāṇini-Mahābhāṣya 1.2).

For no entity whatsoever remains for even a moment as a substance within its own self, which is undifferentiated and indefinable; by the force of the word "even," it does not remain for even a single moment. It increases as much as it is to increase by this [process], and it undergoes decrease for exactly as long as it is to depart by this [process], because it is joined with manifesting factors that are in close proximity.

If, however, substance were exclusively non-active, then it would not exist; for it exists either before, at that time, or after. This is consistent only with this doctrine of a reality consisting of both substance and activity, and not with the rival doctrines of absolute substance, transformation, or the doctrine of constant flux.

He explains that [passage]: "For no object whatsoever is a substance; for nothing at all"—this is the meaning of the general neuter reference [of the pronoun *kiñcit*], which is then explained by specifying it with the masculine gender as "no object. As it has been said in the *Pātañjala Mahābhāṣya* (1.2.69): "When there is doubt regarding the qualities (*guṇa*) of an unmanifest thing, the neuter gender should be employed; for when something is born, only two things are born—a male or a female. Nevertheless, speakers say: 'What has been born to him?'"* *Note: This refers to the grammatical rule Pāṇini 1.2.69, which prescribes the use of the neuter gender for an unknown or indeterminate object.*

Furthermore, he states a synonym for the word "object" (*artha*): "substance" (*dravya*), according to the opinion of the author of the *Bhāṣya*. This means "in its own self," that is, in the nature of substance. It is devoid of differentiation and lacks any defining description, being free from distinctions such as going, moving, closing, or opening the eyes; for that which is devoid of differentiation cannot be described, as it lacks any defining characteristic (*upākhyā*). Since it would be impossible to describe it, it would be non-existent; therefore, it does not persist even for a moment, being devoid of the activity of transformation (*pariṇati*).

He explains this: by the word "even" (*api*), it means that [the breath] does not remain even for the duration of a *samaya*—that is, through the loss of the sequence of inhalation and exhalation consisting of even a small fraction of a *nālikā* or a *lava*. Beyond that, there is no subtler time.

By this statement regarding non-abiding in one's own self, everything is shown to consist of the constant occurrence of increase and decrease; thus, the very existence of substance (*dravya*) is rejected.

Furthermore, by stating "it increases as much as it ought to increase," and by specifying its measure as "as much as this [is]," he demonstrates that the growth of lotuses and other such things—which has a fixed limit—is never found beyond a thousand yojanas; thus, it is shown that growth is merely a particular state (*avasthā-viśeṣa*) of that very substance which remains constant.

Likewise, regarding "deprivation" (*apāya*): one contemplates the meaning of the word "as long as" (*yāvat*) with reference to the fact that for as long as one must be deprived [of certain capacities], for that long one remains associated with deprivation. For example, in the case of a soul in a subtle *nigoda* state that is not yet fully developed (*aparyāptaka*), which possesses the nature of yoga and upayoga produced by the subsidence-cum-destruction (*kṣayopaśama*) of the veils and obstructions, there necessarily persists a loss of yoga and upayoga caused by the affliction arising from the operation (*udaya*) of the veils of knowledge and vision and the obstruction of energy (*vīryāntarāya*). Beyond that point, it does not suffer further loss; otherwise, it would follow that such a being lacks the very quality of being a living soul (*jīvatva*).

Therefore, according to the statement, it is the substance itself that persists while increasing or decreasing; and this is not the case even when there is a state of remaining established devoid of increase or decrease—such is the meaning of this text.
Consequently, it must be understood that this text can only be interpreted through the perspective of the dual nature [of the soul], and not otherwise.

What is the reason? Because it is connected with a manifest individuality (*vyakti*). Manifestation is the appearance of that which is already present and possesses established power, just as the fragrance of the earth appears through the sprinkling of water. Since it is connected with that manifestation, it must be understood that "it becomes both substance and action. Otherwise, because such a connection would be impossible, there would follow the doctrine of the non-existence of the effect in the cause (*asatkāryavāda*), and [the effect] would have to be either produced from nothing or perish; thus it is joined with [the principle of] increase or decrease (Pātañjala Mahābhāṣya 1.2).

Indeed, no object whatsoever remains as a substance even for a moment within its own self, which is undifferentiated and indefinable; by the force of the word "even," it does not remain even for an instant. It increases as much as it is to increase, and it is joined with decrease for as long as it is to depart; this is because it is associated with manifesting particulars. See pp. 284–2, 285–1.
Furthermore, activity is indeed eternal;
for no one remains even for a moment within their own self, but rather increases as long as there is growth to be achieved, or undergoes diminution,
and both of these states are present everywhere.
Thus is the reading in the *Patañjala-Mahābhāṣya*:
"If, however, 'substance' (dravya) were to be exclusively non-active, then it would not exist; let it be observed either before that [activity], or at that time, or after" (p. 242, note 4).
Without *niśvāsa*, *pra*, *saṃvṛtti*, *pra*, *vi*, and *pastyākṣa*.
The reading *paścāt tv akṣa-vi-sapibhā-theti* is to be understood as *pra*.
The logical inconsistency of these two positions—that it is "only substance" (*dravya*) and that it is "only action" (*kriyā*)—is now stated.

First, the position that "it is only substance" is not tenable; how so? If "substance" were indeed a non-action, a non-becoming, devoid of increase and decrease, and of an exclusively unchanging nature, then it would follow that it "would not have come into being. This is the *liṅ* (conditional) used in the sense of the non-occurrence of an action (*kriyātipatti*). The meaning is that it does not even undergo becoming; it simply does not exist, because it lacks activity, like a sky-flower. Action is becoming, which is engagement; since there is no engagement [in the case of a static substance], it is like a sky-flower.
For that which has come into being must indeed exist, otherwise even a sky-flower would have existed, because it would be something that has come into being from non-existence, like a substance;
and the self and so forth are also already active, because they possess substantiality, like a thread or like a seed.

And thus, although the self and other entities share the same status as substances, they possess characteristics such as consciousness because of their capacity for the activity of becoming in that specific way.

The meaning is as follows: if activity (*pravṛtti*) itself were non-substantial (*adravya*), then it could not exist either before, after, or at that [present] time, because of its lack of substantiality. If it were not to engage in activity—that is, if it were not to undergo transformation (*pariṇāma*)—then there would be no action (*kriyā*) either. A substance (*dravya*) which was previously inactive in some manner such as moving and so forth, or which is inactive "at that time"—by the word expressing general time—refers even to the present moment of description; thus, it would not exist later in the future time either, because it is inactive.
What is meant by this? It did not exist previously, and because it is inactive now, it is like a sky-flower (*khapuṣpa*).

Now, it would not exist [in the past] because it had not yet come into operation, like a sky-flower; nor will it exist [in the future] because it is not currently operating, just like a sky-flower. Thus, that substance (*dravya*) would be non-existent, in the sense that it is devoid of activity (*kriyā*), devoid of transformation (*pariṇāma*), and inactive. For only that which *is* comes into being; only that which is currently operating comes into being through some attribute, like clay through the form of a *śivaka* (a lump of clay); it is not something that is indefinable (*nirupākhya*).

If even that which is indefinable were to exist, then even a sky-flower would exist; or else, a sky-flower would have existed, does exist, and will exist—just like the substance you assert—because of its having been, existing, and being about to exist, meaning because of its existence as a non-action. [This refers to the rule: "The conditional (liṅ) is used for the past tense (kriyātipatti) when there is a condition involving the conditional (liṅ). (Pāṇini 3.3.139).
3.139 Because it does not function, like a sky-flower.
For that which has come into being must indeed exist, even a sky-flower would have existed because it was coming into being from non-existence, like a substance;
and the self and so forth are also already active, because they possess substantiality, like a thread or a seed.

And likewise, although the self and other entities possess the same status as substances, they are characterized by consciousness and so forth due to their capacity for the activity of becoming such [entities];

yet, since it is precisely this activity that constitutes non-substantiality, that [characteristic] could not exist either before, after, or at the same time [as the substance], because there would be no transformation [without activity]. (Bhāṣya)
That very [cause] would proceed as a transformation; thus [it is said] in the *Prakaraṇapāda* and the *Vibhāṣā*.

In this context, there might also be the reading "paścādvai" (or "paścādvai"). It might be thought: "This [reason] is inconclusive—because of the coming-into-being of what was not previously existing, even a sky-flower would become a substance; and a substance, too, might not exist because of its lack of activity, like a sky-flower. Why? Because we observe the existence of things such as the self and space, which come into being without activity, meaning they do not undergo transformation (*apariṇāmitvāt*).

This is incorrect, because their being the opposite of that [non-existence] is not established; for even the self (*ātman*) and so forth are indeed active, since they possess substantiality (*dravyatva*), like a thread or like a seed.

Just as threads exist precisely because they are active both in the state of being threads and in the state of being a cloth, so too do the self and the rest. Likewise, the seed itself is active in its various states such as the sprout and so forth, and the same applies to the self and the rest. By employing these two examples, it is demonstrated that the principle is all-pervasive, as it has been said: "The verbs *asti*, *bhavati*, *vidyati*, *padyati*, and *vartate*—with *sannipāta* as the sixth—are six terms whose meaning is existence (*sattā*)."

Therefore, it is said that a thing comes into being (*bhavati*) as it transforms and proceeds in various ways; and since it exists and transforms according to its own specific mode of transformation, the author states the reason for this [distinction]—namely, "and thus, characterized by consciousness and so forth," and so on, up to: "even though there is equality, that is, an equality in their substantiality (*dravyatva*), there indeed exists a distinction in the manner of being (*bhavana-viśeṣa*) between soul-substances (*jīva-dravya*) and non-soul-substances (*ajīva-dravya*)."

For example: the capacity for the occurrence of such states in the substance *jīva*—such as consciousness (*caitanya*), energy (*vīrya*), formlessness (*amūrti*), and its existence within an innumerable number of spatial points (*asaṅkhyātapradeśāvagāha*)—as well as the capacity for the occurrence of such states in non-living substances (*ajīvadravya*), namely the color, taste, and so forth of *pudgala* particles, and their karmic defects and karmic matter; and likewise, the capacities for the occurrence of such states in *dharma*, *adharma*, *ākāśa*, and *kāla*, which are respectively the movement (*gati*), stability (*sthiti*), accommodation (*avagāha*), and temporal change (*vartanā*). Therefore, although the self (*ātman*) and other substances are equal in their status as substances (*dravyatva*), it is indeed established that they possess specific characteristics such as consciousness due to their respective capacities for the occurrence of such states. (This passage does not appear in the Ya manuscripts.)

or *°karmādi* (Vi.).
...the turning [of the wheel] and likewise ... the primordial wisdom ...

Thus far, the non-existence of a substance devoid of action has been stated; by that same logic, it follows that action also lacks existence without a substance. Therefore, he says: "But if activity (*pravṛtti*) is indeed origination (*bhūti*), then it is without substance. This means that origination, characterized by the cessation of activity at every moment, is simply this: the word "indeed" (*eva*) serves as a restriction, meaning that action itself is without substance, i.e., devoid of a substance. Consequently, it would not exist at all—either before, after, or at that very time—just like the previous case, because, being without substance, it is unoriginated, like a sky-flower. This should be explained in the same way through synonyms such as "being seedless" (*nirbījatva*) and "not being established" (*asthitatva*); for [action] is unoriginated, seedless, and not established across all three times.
...for that which exists would indeed be like a sky-flower from the perspective of substantial reality;
or else, even a sky-flower would be like an existent thing because of its lack of substantiality.
For activity arises solely from the power of the actual state of things;
even qualities and so forth are indeed substances because they function like threads and the like,
and likewise, action does not exist without a substance.
That which comes into being is "bhāva" (an entity); since it comes into being, it is "bhavana" (the process of becoming).
For this very reason, there is a restriction regarding both: a suffix must be employed only after a stem, and a stem must be followed only by a suffix.
The distinction is that [the agent] is "engaging" (*yojayadbhiḥ*).
For it is established that "only that which exists exists as a substantial entity" (*dravyārthataḥ*); thus, he explains the existence of a substance as having the nature of stability (*sthitirūpa*).

For one who does not accept this, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭāpādana*) that even a sky-flower might exist as a substance and possess activity—just like an existent thing (*bhāva*)—because it would share the common property of existing without stability (*asthitabhavana*). This is an undesired conclusion.

For activity proceeds solely from the efficacy of the real object (*bhūtārtha*); since activity—that is, action—proceeds solely from the efficacy of the substantial object (*dravyārtha*), it is not without a seed. Here too, as before, there is the suspicion of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*): "Is it not observed that the activity of qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth occurs without a seed? To this he gives the reply: "The qualities and so forth are also indeed substance (*dravya*) because they function [as such], like threads and the like; like the seeds of threads, clay, and so forth," as previously explained. However, the distinction here is that after demonstrating the absence of activity without the becoming of substance (*dravyabhavana*), the conclusion must be drawn.

In the same way, it should be observed—according to the very logic already stated—that action also does not exist without a substance, because it is non-existent [prior to its arising], because it is seedless, and because it is unstable... (p. 380, l. 5).
...for that which exists would indeed be like a sky-flower from the perspective of substantial reality;
or else, even a sky-flower might exist like a real entity because it lacks substantiality.
For activity proceeds solely from the power of the actual object;
even qualities and so forth are indeed substances because they function like threads and the like,
and likewise, action does not exist without a substance.
That which comes into being is "bhāva"; since it is that which comes into being, it is "bhavana.
For this very reason, there is a restriction of both: the suffix must be employed only after the stem, and the stem must be followed only by the suffix.

Is this a restriction on the suffix (*pratyayaniyama*)—that a suffix must be employed only when preceded by a stem (*prakṛti*) and not otherwise—or rather is it a restriction on the stem (*prakṛtiniyama*)—that a stem must be employed only when followed by a suffix and not otherwise?

And what is the distinction here? In that case, if there is a restriction on the suffix, there would be an absence of restriction on the stem; for if there is a restriction on the suffix, no restriction applies to the stem, and the employment of a stem without a suffix would result.

Let it be, then, that there is a restriction regarding the base (*prakṛti*). When there is a restriction regarding the base, there is no restriction regarding the suffix (*pratyaya*); for while the base is restricted, a restriction on the suffix does not follow, [and thus] the employment of a suffix without a base would result.
However, [the desired outcome] is established through the restriction of both.

This is established; how so? Because of the restriction of both. This is the restriction of both: "A suffix must be employed only after a stem, and a stem must be followed only by a suffix"—thus it is stated in the *Patañjala-Mahābhāṣya* 3.1.1.
For activity [occurs] precisely through the capacity of the substantial object; indeed, activity occurs precisely through the capacity of the substantial object.

Having thus stated the duality characterized by substance and action, and wishing to demonstrate it also through the logic of the literal meaning (*akṣarārtha*), he says: "That which becomes is *bhāva*. Regarding this, some say that the suffix *ṇa* is applied to the root *bhū* in the sense of the agent according to the rule *bhuvaśca*; however, here [the suffix] *ghañ* is applied in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*) because it is that which is "become" (*bhūyate*). And since that [suffix] implies by the force of the meaning that "that by which one becomes is *bhāva*," it is connected precisely to that which "is" (*yo bhavati*); thus it is said, "that which becomes is *bhāva*."

And that [agent] is the agent, and the agent is a substance; therefore, a word denoting "being" (bhāva) denotes a substance. It is called "being" (bhāva) because it comes into being (bhavati); for whatever reason, in whatever manner, and by whatever property or from whatever property it comes into being—that substance is its "being. Since the word "iti" has the sense of a cause, that from which it comes into being—namely, "it becomes"—is action (kriyā).

How, then, does it "become" (bhavati)? It is called "becoming" (bhavati) because of its connection with the process of becoming; that is the state (bhāva) of that substance. Therefore, that becoming is the "existent" (bhāva); it means action, activity, or the process of coming into being. See page 173, line 25, note 9:
*vibhāṣā grahaḥ*.

Or rather, this is an optionally fixed rule (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*) regarding the vowel *ac*; therefore, *grāhaḥ* [is used] for an aquatic animal, while *grahaḥ* [is used] for a celestial body (*jyotiṣ*), according to the *Kāśikā*. Furthermore, *bhavaḥ* means both "the god" and "saṃsāra," while *bhāvāḥ* means "entities" (*padārthāḥ*).

According to the view of the Bhāṣya, however, the suffix *ac* is added in the sense of "attainment" (*prāpti*) to the causative form of the root *cur*; thus, it is established in the *Siddhāntakaumudī* that [the word] also denotes the act of speaking (*vācītva*).
That which becomes is an existent; that which is an existent is that which becomes—
thus it is called "becoming."

The passage beginning with "ata eva" (for this very reason) serves to strengthen the demonstration that [the word] has both meanings, up until the point where it is stated that "the base (*prakṛti*) alone is subordinate to the suffix. This is because, when the *kvip* suffix is applied, one observes the use of the base alone in the nominative singular of words such as *cit*; furthermore, in cases such as "adhunā," one hears only the suffix. To demonstrate that it possesses both meanings, [the author asks]: "What is this so-called 'being' (*bhāva*)? It is that which is brought about by something, yet it is not expressed [as a separate entity]. For that which "becomes" (*bhavati*) is some [entity], since being (*bhāva*) is established through the employment of its own word.

Of what is there the state? If it is argued that [the suffix] deviates, then for that very reason—since both usages are observed elsewhere in the comprehension of its meaning—it is inferred that it has two meanings. Furthermore, if one asks: "Why are the derivation of the base-meaning and the derivation of the affix-meaning performed separately in the grammatical treatise through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)? [The answer is: "It is for the purpose of demonstrating that both possess meaning," and so on, up to the words "even someone."

"What is this so-called 'being' (bhāva)?"—starting with such a question, action (kriyā) is explained. Since it is prescribed that the verbal suffix (*lakāra*) denotes the state of being (*bhāva*) in the expression "it is being" (*bhūyate*), and since the term "that which" (*yat tat*) points specifically to the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛtyartha*)—namely, the act of becoming itself—it does not refer to the agent who becomes, as in the question "Who is this that becomes? Nor is the agent—the one by whom it is being, who is the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*)—mentioned in that question.
Therefore, the explanation in this manner is directed solely toward the meaning of the verbal root.

What is the reason? Because existence (*bhāva*) has its state established through the employment of a term other than its own (*asvaśabdopādāna*), following what we have stated. As others have said in demonstrating the distinction between substance (*dravya*) and existence (*bhāva*) regarding their definitions as "utterance" (*ukti*) and "action" (*kriyā*): "Existence (*sattva*) is that whose state is established through the employment of its own term; existence (*bhāva*) is that whose state is to be accomplished through the employment of a term other than its own. This distinctness of existence and being (*sattva-bhāva*) based on utterance and action is indeed well-known in the world and in the scriptures—as it is said: "The verb (*ākhyāta*) expresses action, while the noun (*nāman*) denotes substance"; for substance is established by its own nature, whereas action is brought into being (*bhāvyate*). (Pāṇini-Mahābhāṣya 1.3.1)

3.1 Likewise, one expresses a state of being consisting of a prior and posterior sequence by means of a verb (*ākhyāta*), from its commencement until its completion; whereas one expresses a completed, embodied entity by means of a noun (*nāman*). As it is said in the *Nirukta* (1.1): "One goes, he cooks; going, cooking. Thus, [the former] corresponds to action, while the latter corresponds to substance.

Therefore, words such as "jar" and "cloth" are the specific designators (*svaśabda*) of substances; words such as "cooks" and "goes" are the designators of action (*kriyā*); and the word for "being" (*bhāvaśabda*) is seen to apply to both.

In this context, when a substance that is not its own specific designator—such as a jar or Devadatta—is employed, the "being" (*bhāva*) that is to be accomplished is its "state of being accomplished" (*sādhyatva*). This action, which is accessible through inference and cannot be shown separately from its means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), is like a fetus that is not yet fully extracted; it acquires its identity only through those external means of accomplishment. Thus, even in its verbal expression, the "being" is that whose state of being accomplished is established by the employment of what is not its own specific designator; this is the meaning of "action" (*kriyā*).

Because that [non-existence] exists, and because the existence characterized by activity is established through the employment of the term "non-self" (asvaśabda), the establishment of the question and answer occurs in this manner.
If it is argued that all [words] are distinct, then in the case of *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one), the perception of distinct case-endings occurs because they are based upon that [retained word].
If it is argued that [the suffixes] are distinct for all [the stems], then in the case of *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one), the perception of distinct case-endings would result.

Why is it said that "in *ekaśeṣa*, there is the perception of distinct case-endings"? For a convention has been established that neither a base (*prakṛti*) alone nor an affix (*pratyaya*) alone should be used; since [the base] depends on that [affix], [distinct endings] would follow. Indeed, where the cessation of the affix is caused by the base, there the base is used without an affix—just as in the examples *agnicit* and *somasut*.

And where there is the cessation of the base (prakṛti) due to the cause of an affix (pratyaya), there the employment of an affix occurs even for that which lacks a base— as in "iyān" for "idānīm," according to the Pātañjala Mahābhāṣya 1.2.1.2.
Now,
The suffix *adhunā* occurs in its own sense after the word *idam*, provided it ends in the locative case and denotes time.
The suffix *iś* [is applied], and by Pāṇini 6.4.184 (*yasya*), there is elision; thus, *adhunā*.

Thus, in the Pāṇinian Siddhāntakaumudī, for the purpose of demonstrating that both [the agent and the object] possess meaning: what is this so-called *bhāva* (action/state)? It is that which is experienced by someone but is not expressed; since it is a state (*bhāva*) whose realization is achieved through the employment of no specific word, one asks:
"Whose is this state? (i.e., whose action or state is it?).
In this context, the reading "for the purpose of demonstrating both meanings" appears correct; see page 382, line 9.
A discussion with a similar meaning is found in the *Patañjala-Mahābhāṣya* as follows: "And an addition must be made for cases where the verb is elided, such as *niṣkauśāmbiḥ*, *nirvārāṇasiḥ*, etc."

but it is established [that *pra* and other prefixes do not govern the case of the following noun] because of the statement regarding the extreme difficulty [of the compound] in *kvāṅsu*, or because of the understanding of that meaning through the rule *prādayaḥ ktārthe*.
Alternatively, this [meaning] is established through the understanding of that object (*tadarthagati*).

What is this "understanding of that object"? That which is the object of it is "that object" (*tadartha*); the understanding of that object is "understanding of that object" (*tadarthagati*). By the phrase "through the understanding of that object," that meaning which possesses the capacity for Kauśāmbī is expressed by the *niṣṭhā* suffix. Or else, that which is the object is "that object" (*tadartha*); the understanding of that object is "understanding of that object" (*tadarthagati*). By the phrase "through the understanding of that object," that meaning which is capable with respect to Kauśāmbī is expressed by the *niṣṭhā* suffix.
Pāṇini-Mahābhāṣya 2.1.1

But how is it known that "this is the meaning of the base" (*prakṛti*) and "this is the meaning of the suffix" (*pratyaya*)? It is established by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). What, then, is this positive concomitance and what is negative concomitance? Here, when "he cooks" (*pacati*) is uttered, certain words are heard: the word *pac*, ending in the letter *c*, and the suffix *ati*.

A certain meaning is also understood: when "he reads" (*paṭhati*) is said, something is lost, something arises, and something persists. The word *pac* is lost, the word *paṭh* arises, and the word *ati* persists.

As for the meaning as well, something is lost, something arises, and something persists: the act of cooking (*viklitti*) is lost, the act of reading (*paṭhikriyā*) arises, and agency (*kartṛtva*) and oneness (*ekatva*) persist.

We consider that the meaning which is lost belongs to the word which is lost; the meaning which arises belongs to the word which arises; and the meaning which persists belongs to the word which persists—thus it is stated in the *Pātañjala-Mahābhāṣya* 1.3.9.
Here, the reading "in order to demonstrate that it serves both purposes" appears correct; see page 382, line 9;
see page 125, line 7.
In that case, it will be a *karmasādhana* [derivation]: "that which is brought into being (*bhāvyate*) is *bhāva*";
for it is indeed action (*kriyā*) that is brought into being, whereas a substance (*dravya*) is established by its own nature (*svabhāvasiddha*).
This is the reading in the *Patañjala-Mahābhāṣya*.

See page 126, line 24: "In that regard, this so-called 'action' (kriyā) is absolutely imperceptible; it is impossible to demonstrate action as a solidified mass, just as a fetus cannot be extracted [from the womb]."
That [action] is to be known through inference.
What is this inference? Here, when all the means [of cooking] are present, sometimes the thought "he cooks" occurs and sometimes it does not;
that action is surely that [cause] for which, when the means are present, the thought "he cooks" occurs.
