thus it is stated in the *Patañjala-Mahābhāṣya* 1.3.1.

Regarding that which exists, it is not said [to be non-existent]— for that which is spoken of by anyone [is existent], because existence is established through the employment of its own term (*svaśabda*).
Substance possesses gender and so forth; action is devoid of them.
Because they respectively possess or lack gender and so forth, both "being" (bhavana) and "becoming" (bhava) are indeed existence (bhāva).
From substance, which possesses gender and number, there arises the cognition of its substantiality and unity; [whereas] action is [the locus of] becoming.

Conversely, however, when the question and answer regarding the state of being as a substance (*dravyabhāva*) are observed at the time of exposition—for example, the question "Whose is the state of being? or "Whose is the activity (*pravṛtti*)?"—one employs the genitive case in reference to the agent (*kartṛ*). Accordingly, the corresponding answer is also given: "He who is that which becomes," meaning he who is the one about to become, or rather, the very agent characterized as a substance (*dravyalakṣaṇa*), is what is being spoken of.

It is not said: "That which comes into being is indeed becoming; what is it that comes into being? Is it not [something] that is brought about by anyone? For the general state of being (*bhāvasāmānya*) itself is without a specified agent, because being is non-different from the act of being.

What is the reason? Because existence is established as a state of being through its own term. Thus, it is asked by means of its own term: "Whose is the state of being? The meaning is: "Who is it that becomes?"
It is not asked: "Does anyone exist, or does no one exist?

And the reply is likewise stated: "He who is 'somebody' (ko'pi) exists"—it is not said that "his state of being exists" or "by him it is existed. That which is expressed as "it is existed by someone" is an indistinct mere becoming (*bhavanamātra*) and is not analyzed, because it was not asked.

What is the reason? Because the manner of answering questions is seen to be the opposite of the exposition of existence characterized by activity; because the establishment of the meaning is exactly thus; and because the application of words expressing that [meaning] is also conformable to it. (The portion "na bhūyate" does not exist in the Bhāṣya manuscript; the word "śabdam" is in the Prajñāpāramitā manuscript.)
Furthermore, regarding the passage beginning with "possessing gender and so forth" up to "both are indeed existence," substance (*dravya*) is that which is connected with gender,
number, time, and case-role (*kāraka*), whereas action (*kriyā*) is devoid of those.

Because of having gender and so forth (*liṅgādimattva*) and because of not having gender and so forth (*aliṅgādimattva*), the entity (*dravya*) and the process of becoming (*bhavana*) are, respectively, distinct entities consisting of "being" and "becoming," and are thus twofold.
Therefore, on the basis of these two entities, it is established by reasoning that there is a single [reality]; hence it is asserted: "Of that which possesses gender and number," and so forth.

"Oneness as an entity" (*vastutvenaikatva*) means the oneness of the state of being an entity (*vastutvaikatva*). Its "attainment" (*gati*) or "realization" (*āpatti*) is such that the action, having attained oneness as an entity, is indeed other than its own [mere] form; the meaning is that there is a single entity distinct from the individual natures of substance and action.
Why? Because it is devoid of gender and number (*aliṅgasaṅkhyatvāt*). That which lacks gender and number is "devoid of gender and number," namely *bhāva* (being).

For that [Being], having attained oneness as a reality (*vastutvena*), although it is non-different from substance (*dravya*), is indeed different; this is the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*) established by the reason (*hetu*) "because it is devoid of gender and number."

The example: the meaning [of a word] refers to a single related object even when there are distinct objects, as in "the *plakṣa* and the *dhava*. Here, although the word *ca* (and) conjoins two different things—the *plakṣa* and the *dhava*—it functions by taking a single related entity as its object; thus, despite their non-difference [in being a single conjunction], it expresses a distinct meaning. Similarly, in the case of "substance, action, essence, unity, and difference," [one might argue]. To this, he replies: if the very act of conjunction is cited as the example for action—which has been proposed as the subject because it is distinct from substance—that is not a valid example, because it is itself the very thing to be proven (*sādhya*).

Now, if a collection of distinct substances (*dravyāntara-samuccaya*) is cited as an example so that this fault may not arise, even then there is an abandonment of the "substance-meaning" (*dravyārtha*). This is because the meaning of the collection of *plakṣa* and *dhava* trees—which is intended to include all existent things (*sattārtha*)—is ontologically different from the individual [trees], since it lacks gender and number; furthermore, the referent of the substance-meaning is the single related object (*ekasambandhiviṣaya*) of distinct entities such as the *plakṣa* and others. If, on the other hand, one maintains that only a single [substance] is intended so as not to abandon the substance-meaning, then once again there is an absence of an example, because there exists no other entity distinct from the substance itself.
To this it is replied: because of the inclusion of the term "of word-meanings" (*padārthānām*), this fault does not arise;

for it is the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) that is connected with the action due to the action's internal nature (*antaraṅgatva*), and not the "word-meaning" (*padārtha*) itself due to its external nature (*bahiraṅgatva*). Just as in the case of *putrīyati* ("he desires a son"), the accusative ending expresses an external object because the son is connected with the root *iṣ* ("to desire") which is internal; and it has been said: "The connections of nominal stems are brought about by action" (Pāṇini-Mahābhāṣya 2.3.1).

3.50 Thus, this connection of Devadatta, the seeker, is with his son, not with the word-meaning as a suffix-terminated element; however, upon the proximity of another word, that manifestation is the specific activity of the *kārakas*, which is action (*kriyā*). (Pāṇini-Mahābhāṣya 1.2.45)

Because of this statement, [a word] attains the status of being an object (*karman*) and so forth only after having entered into a relationship with an action; thus, the relationship with the action occurs first.

Furthermore, if the relationship with conjunction (*samuccaya*) and the like were to occur at the very stage of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), just as it does with the relationship to an action, then—because it would exceed the meaning of the nominal stem—the nominative case would have to be prescribed by a separate effort, just like the vocative, and the accusative and other cases would not occur, for those cases are prescribed when the meaning of the nominal stem is exceeded by the object (*karman*) and so forth.

If, however, because there is an action (*karman*) and so forth when there is an addition such as conjunction (*samuccaya*), the accusative and other cases were to occur, then even when there is an addition of an object and so forth, since the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) still exists, the nominative alone would have to occur. Therefore, since the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) arises subsequent to the word-meanings (*padārtha*), and the particles such as *ca* ("and") assist in that [sentence-meaning], they are connected with the words; hence it is said: "of distinct word-meanings" (*bhinna-padārthānām*), in order to exclude connection with a [single] action (*kriyā*).
And that conjunction has as its object a single related entity (*ekasambandhiviṣaya*).

Who is this single related entity? It is the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), namely the state of being a part of the same whole as the *plakṣa*, *dhava*, and so on; or, in the case of *anvācaya* and *samuccaya*, it is the bringing, leading, and so forth.
And it has been said: "The *dvandva* compound occurs in the sense of *ca* (and)" (Pāṇini 2.2.29).

And what is the meaning of *ca*? The meanings are conjunction (*samuccaya*), subsequent mention (*anvācaya*), collective aggregate (*samāhāra*), and mutual connection (*itaretarayoga*), which occur subsequent to the meaning of the word. Among these, conjunction is illustrated by: "Vaivasvata, leading a cow, a horse, a man, a bird, and an animal day after day, is not satiated, like one intoxicated with wine. Subsequent mention is, for example: "O Devadatta, go for alms, and bring Yajñadatta as well."
The terms *pāṇipādam*, "brāhmaṇa-kṣatriya-viṭ-śūdrāḥ", and "rāma-keśavau" are examples of collective (samāhāra) and distributive (itaretara-yoga) compounds, respectively.

Furthermore, those things which are perceived as substances, qualities, and actions—such as "a jar" and "a cloth," "form" and "taste," or "he laughs," "he stands," "he enjoys," and so forth—which arise subsequent to the primary categories and consist of conjunctions, disjunctions, and the like—are neither substance, nor action, nor quality. Rather, because action is indeed the very nature of the substance, these properties (dharmas) partake of the same reality and oneness as the substance itself, just as the qualifier and the qualified in the case of a "heroic man" are non-different from one another; thus it is well established that activity alone is the essence. Consequently, the three genders found in words such as *devadatta* do not exist in the act of "being" (*bhavana*), nor do the various numbers exist when one, two, or many things are in the state of "becoming."

However, according to the established rule of the supreme nature of the suffix (*pratyaya*), it appears in the nominative singular; and because there is no reason for deviation, it is neuter, since the process of becoming (*bhavana*) is unmanifest, as in the expression "something is seen. Thus, existence (*bhāva*) is distinct from the substance (*dravya*) which has the three times as its object, yet without that [existence], there would be no agent (*kāraka*) nor a connection with the three times.

Just as here the word *vīra* (hero) attains oneness as a real entity through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *puruṣa* (person), so too the word *puruṣa* attains oneness through coreferentiality with the word *vīra*; otherwise, due to lack of coreferentiality, there would be defects such as a lack of connection, as in the case of "pot" and "cloth."

Moreover, the hero is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the person is the qualified (*viśeṣya*); thus, these two have distinct meanings from one another. Otherwise, due to their grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), there would be faults such as identity or tautology. Yet, their oneness is observed through coreferentiality, while their difference is established by the relation of qualifier and qualified.

Thus, when the illustration is complete by means of the words *plakṣa* and so forth, there is non-difference (*ananyatva*) in the sense that the object existing at a later time has as its domain a single related entity—that is, it is the scope of a single conjunction (*samuccaya*) denoted by *plakṣa*, *dhava*, and so on. Difference (*anyatva*), however, consists in the fact that this conjunction belongs specifically to the *plakṣa* and the *dhava*. Likewise, in the case of the statement "from substance [arises] existence (*bhāva*), which is devoid of gender and number; the cognition of 'thing-ness' (*vastutva*) and 'oneness' (*ekatva*) is non-different and different," if explained in this way, the faults—namely, the absolute difference (*anyatvaikānta*), the abandonment of the substantial meaning (*dravyārtha*), and the abandonment of the underlying persistence (*anvaya*)—are avoided. Furthermore, because it possesses gender and so forth... [the word *pra*].
Having established that [the world] has become that [Brahman], and because it is indeed so in reality;
here there might also be the reading: "Therefore both are the reality, and that is one."

It appears that the word "and" (*ca*) is intended here as an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) for the purpose of demonstrating the concomitance (*anugama*) with the probandum (*sādhya*), based on the reason "because it lacks gender and number," just like the *plakṣa* tree and others.
See page 385, line 13; furthermore,
there is a *dvandva* compound in the sense of "and" (*ca*).
And "artha" is stated [as the final member]; since "ca" is an indeclinable (avyaya), by that [rule], the designation of an indeclinable would apply to the compound.
This is not a fault; the designation of *avyaya* (indeclinable) is established by explicit recitation (*pāṭha*), and a compound is not recited therein.
Even when the designation of *avyaya* is established by recitation, the gender and number follow those of the expressed meaning (*abhidheya-vat*);
however, the meaning expressed here has no connection with gender or number.

This is not something established by explicit rule (*vācanika*)—namely, that there is an absence of gender or number—but rather it is inherent (*svābhāvika*). For example: among those who exert equal effort and study equally, some are endowed with meaning while others are not. Now, it is not possible for someone to become meaningful simply because everyone else is meaningful, nor can anyone become meaningless simply because everyone else is meaningless.
In this regard, what can we do? It is an inherent fact that prior to compound formation there is no connection with gender and number, whereas in the compound such a connection does occur.
Thus, in the Patañjala-Mahābhāṣya, 2.2.29.

Is "conjunction" (*samuccaya*) a distinct substance? It is not, because it does not exist as a separate entity; rather, it is simply another form [of the referents themselves], since it lacks gender and number. Furthermore, its meaning is the single object of relation belonging to multiple distinct entities, such as *plakṣa* trees and others.
I shall not abandon the substantial meaning (dravyārtha),
because of its inherent connection.

From nominal stems (prātipadika), distinctions produced by action arise, and from those [distinctions] the designations (ākhyā) emerge— namely, object (karman), instrument (karaṇa), point of departure (apādāna), recipient (sampradāna), and locus (adhikaraṇa).
Thus, in the *Patañjala-Mahābhāṣya*, we do not say that the factors of action (*kāraka*) are the action;
rather, what is it? Action is a specific mode of activity of the factors of action.
Thus, in the Pātañjala-Mahābhāṣya: "The first case ending occurs when there is mere denotation of the nominal stem-meaning, gender, measure, and number, as well as in address."
Pāṇini 2.3.46–47
Let it be seen in the Pātañjala Mahābhāṣya, 2.3.46.
For him, there arises [the state of] accumulation; the purpose of that accumulation is [this].
Day after day leading away cattle, horses, men, and livestock,
Vaivasvata is not satiated, like a drunkard with wine.
Thus [ends] the second [chapter] of the Patañjala Mahābhāṣya.
And why [is it said], "having bowed down, according to the rule," and so forth?
If [the categories] beginning with [substance] are not substance, then they are qualities.

An addition must be made for co-referential (samānādhikaraṇa) compounds because of their lack of syntactic independence (asamarthatva). An addition must be made for co-referential compounds, as in *vīraḥ puruṣaḥ* → *vīrapuruṣaḥ*.
But what is the reason that it is not established? Because of their lack of syntactic independence.

How is there a lack of capacity? If it is argued that the referent of a word is a substance (*dravya*), then if the referent of a word is a substance, there is no capacity because of the absence of distinction.
On the other hand, if the referent of a word is a quality (*guṇa*), then there is capacity.
For heroism (*vīratva*) is one quality (*guṇa*), while manhood (*puruṣatva*) is another;

there is no difference [between them] such that there would be capacity [in the former] but not in the latter. For Devadatta is one thing, and cows and horses are another; yet he does not possess capacity merely by virtue of this distinction.

Or rather, what is the specific difference such that capacity would exist in a quality as a category (*padārtha*) but not in a substance (*dravya*)? This is the difference: they have a single substratum (*adhikaraṇa*), yet heroism is one quality and manhood is another.
Thus, in the Patañjala Mahābhāṣya, 2.1.1.

It is correct that in the case of *devadatta* and so forth, that which possesses the three genders does not exist in the sense of "becoming" (*bhavana*). Likewise, when one, two, or many things are in the state of "becoming," those numbers do not [apply] because of the established rule regarding the suffix and the base (*pratyaya-paraprakṛti-vyavasthā*), specifically in the nominative singular; for there is no reason to bypass this.
And it is neuter because of the unmanifested nature of existence (*bhavana*); something is seen,

and thus existence (*bhāva*) is distinct from the substance (*dravya*) which has the three times as its object, yet without that [existence], there is no agent (*kāraka*), as established by the term "three times."
The word *pada*, by that [means],
[is] the prefix *upa* for *dhava* and so forth;
*pra* and *ca*.

From this point onward, the subsequent portion of the text serves well to establish that [the word *sādhu*] is devoid of gender and number, beginning with the statement "it is well" (*sādhu bhavati*) and continuing until "those numbers which exist in you do not exist.

This means that in a single instance—whether there be one, two, or many agents such as Devadatta and others who possess differences of gender and number—that which possesses the three genders and the numbers such as singularity and so forth does not exist; rather, in the case of the act of becoming (*bhavane*), only the neuter gender and the singular number are inferred. Furthermore, when used as an adjective for that [agent], it is heard in the form "Look at the well-becoming one" (*sādhu bhavantaṃ paśya*), and so on, even in the absence of [specific] grammatical relations (*kāraka*s) and the like.

Therefore, one might think that there should be a different gender (*bhavana*) for "you" (*bhavadbhyaḥ*) as compared to [words like] *devadatta*, even though they possess the same ontological unity (*vastutva-ekatva*) by their very nature. To this it is replied: the nominative singular case ending is used due to the rule governing the base (*prakṛti*) followed by the suffix (*pratyaya*). What is the reason? Because there is no cause for transgression, and the base must necessarily be employed followed by a suffix. [As stated in Pāṇini 2.3.46: "The first case ending occurs merely to express the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), its gender, its measure, and its number."

2.46. Thus, since the nominative case is prescribed even for the mere sense of existence (*sattāmātra*), and because there is no possible meaning beyond that, and because there is no purpose in bypassing the nominative, and because the word is invariably [associated with it], and because it functions as the cause for the sense of mere existence, and because there is no other cause— since a deviation from that [rule] would only occur due to another cause— and furthermore, because "becoming" (*bhavana*) is indistinct, and when there is doubt regarding a quality in what is indistinct, the neuter gender should be employed.

If it is asked, "What is seen in the world in such a manner?", it is said: "Something is seen. For example, having seen a collection of elephants, horses, men, and so forth, people say, "Something is seen. The word "iti" is used in the sense of illustration; this very sentence is presented as an example. [The text continues: "...the object possesses three genders... or "...only the following... [Note: The provided fragment appears to be a corrupted portion of a commentary].
...nam evānu...
bhā... sthāyāya... sya vacanānta... pra...
See page 242, line 4, beginning with "tathā" (in that manner), etc. Just as in the previous proof, another reason (*hetu*) is stated by way of addition regarding that very same subject (*pakṣa*).

In that same manner—that is, just as previously it was established by taking as the subject [the proposition] "being a real entity (*vastutva*), oneness, movement, non-difference, and difference"—so too here the subject is: "An entity (*bhāva*) is different from the substance (*dravya*) which is the object of the three times, and yet there is no agent (*kāraka*) without it. The meaning is: an entity is not itself an agent without the substance; even though there is difference, its activity is necessarily concomitant with that [substance].

Because [substance] has the three times as its object, while action, however, pertains to the three times—just like the act of going and the goer—there is a threefold temporal relation regarding the act of going even when Devadatta, the goer, exists only in the present: "he went," "he goes," and "he will go"; likewise, "it was," "it is," and "it will be."

If it is argued that because existence (*bhāva*) is to be proven as being both distinct from substance (*dravya*) and non-separate from it, and because "existence" and "going" have the same meaning, the example is a part of what is to be proven (*sādhyaikadeśa*), [we reply]: no, because a distinction between Devadatta and his going is established through their being simultaneous or non-simultaneous, and the same applies to substance and existence, like a jar and its form (*tattva*) which exist either simultaneously or not.

Now, since this [existence] is characterized by the distinction of substantial reality (*dravyārtha*), how can it possess this threefold temporal nature consisting of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and posterior non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*)? Why? Because it possesses the three times (*trikālatvāt*). That which has three times is "three-timed" (*trikāla*). What is that? It is existence (*bhāva*), characterized by action (*kriyā*). Because it is presented as having been, being, and about to be, and because existence is seen to be connected with all three times through their distinctions, its possession of the three times is established; thus, it serves as the logical reason (*hetu*).

"Substance has the three times as its object": although the mode (*bhāva*) is divided into three distinct times, substance—which remains in a single form—encompasses those three times by virtue of being present; thus it is said to "have the three times as its object. The meaning is that it remains that very same thing throughout all three times. It is stated that while substance is beyond time yet has the three times as its object, action (*kriyā*), however, belongs to the three times and has the present as its object;
the illustration for this is "like the act of going and the goer."
He explains this: "While Devadatta, the goer, is indeed present"—the word *eva* (indeed) serves for emphasis—and it emphasizes that the goer exists only at one time among the three times;
[it refers to] the three times of going (*gatitraikālya*). All three times of the act of going (*gamana*) are observed as not having a single, determined form.
He demonstrates this by saying: "he went," "he goes," and "he will go"; likewise, the application (*upanaya*) beginning with "it was so" has its meaning already explained.

Because [substance] has the three times as its object, while action belongs to the three times—just like the act of going and the goer—there is the threefold temporality of the act of going even when Devadatta, the goer, exists only in the present: "he went," "he goes," and "he will go"; likewise, "it was," "it is," and "it will be."

If it is argued that because existence (*bhāva*) is established as being both different from substance (*dravya*) and non-separate from it, and because "existence" and "going" have the same referent, the example is a part of the thesis (*sādhyaikadeśa*), [we reply: no, for the difference between Devadatta and his going is established by their being simultaneous and non-simultaneous respectively; and since this is the case for substance and existence as well—like a jar and its parts, or like the sky and its parts—[they differ] through simultaneity and non-simultaneity. Now, if [existence] is distinct from the substance-aspect (*dravyārtha*), how can it possess this threefold temporal nature (*traikālya*) consisting of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and non-existence after destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*)?
See page 2, line 15.
...in the blind, gone to the three realms of existence, gone to the three realms of existence, feminine? ...ya...
"By such being," etc.,
see Pañjikā 2.8;
"of an entity," etc., is a suspicion regarding the position of another.

It might be thought: since existence (*bhāva*) is established as being both different from substance (*dravya*) and not separate from it, and since "existence" and "going" have the same meaning, just as the difference between existence and substance is not established, so too the difference between the goer and going is not established; thus, the example is one that lacks a part of the probandum (*sādhyaikadeśa*). If this doubt arises as to how there can be a proof, it is said in reply: because the difference between Devadatta and going is established through their being simultaneous and non-simultaneous, it is likewise for substance and existence. Since the general and the particular are intended here in terms of the probandum and the probans, there is no fault; for even in that doubt, the principle is the same. The example is "like the reality of a jar and the sky": *tattva* means its state of being, i.e., the fact that it simply is.

Now, was it not said that when there is a difference in substance (*dravya*), there is an abandonment of the substantial aspect (*dravyārtha*); and if there is no abandonment, there is an absence of concomitance (*anvaya*)? This is not a fault. Because of the simultaneous and non-simultaneous qualification of reality (*tattva*), there is simultaneity of reality due to the identity of all things such as the self (*ātman*) and so forth; or, because of the non-difference between the substance-aspect (*dravyārtha*) and the self, the ether (*kha*) and so forth are the very self of the substance, or the jar is the non-simultaneous reality. Thus, regarding the difference and non-difference of substances and modes (*bhāva*) across the three times and the non-three-times, the distinction between the three times is equalized through simultaneity.
See page 384, line 24, and page 386, line 6;
and [the passage beginning] "atha," etc.

Now, it might be thought: since this *naya* (perspective) pertains to the substantial aspect (*dravyārtha*) and the substantial aspect is eternal, how can this threefold temporal framework—consisting of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), posterior non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), and so forth—be logical? This is the remainder of the sentence.

That which did not exist previously but exists now is called "present"; and that was non-existent previously. That which has perished, being past and destroyed, is "non-existent. That which will come to be is also non-existent previously because of its current absence, as seen in the case of the sprout, the pot, the shards, and so forth.

And that [duality] is not tenable for a permanent entity because of its equality between prior and subsequent times; nor is it [tenable] by the suffix *tyap* in the sense of "fixed" (*dhruva*), because its activity is permanent. Furthermore, even for permanence, there is a duality:
the fixity (*dhrauvya*) and the immutability (*kauṭasthya*) of a substance that remains eternally fixed while experiencing its respective self-nature.
But for the other [the substance], which is manifested in such and such ways, there is non-eternality (*akauṭasthya*) and eternality (*nityatva*) consisting in constant activity;
for this very reason, it possesses both the state of being existent and non-existent. This establishes the point that "being" (*bhāva*) is something other than the substance (*dravya*).

Because they possess the states of transcending and not transcending [their prior form], the states of action (*kriyā*) and substance (*dravya*) are distinct. For example: "The mat was made by Devadatta," and "A separation was made by the action."
The action (kriyā) undergoes transgression, while the disjunction (vibhāga) and the action (karman) do not undergo transgression, because the meaning of the word is a unified whole;
furthermore, transgression and non-transgression cannot possibly be without a cause.
And it is observed that when there is no transgression of the action and the disjunction, there is a transgression of the instrument (karaṇa), which is the object of the disjunction.

In that regard, according to the etymological derivation (*nirukti*) of the term "eternal" (*nitya*), the threefold temporal existence of an entity (*bhāva*) is unestablished; for, by accepting the substantial aspect (*dravyārtha*), one accepts temporality only for the substance (*dravya*).
Alternatively, if one were to accept temporality for the substance itself, it would entail the abandonment of the doctrine of the substantial aspect regarding the entity.

To this it is replied: there is no fault, because activity (*pravṛtti*) is eternal. Even here, there is no abandonment of the nature of substance (*dravyārthatva*), because activity is eternal. "Becoming" (*bhāva*) means the activity of coming into being; and since that activity is eternal—because the entity is always active—the state of being (*bhāva*) is also indeed eternal. Thus, there is no abandonment of the nature of substance, nor is there a restriction to the three times (*aikālya*). This is the specific meaning of the sentence. (Praśastapādabhāṣya, *pratyakṣanitya* section).
The suffix *tyap* is applied after an indeclinable (*avyaya*).
... ityab nerdhruve ityab nerdhruve should be stated.
"It is eternal" is not [stated] in the Patañjala-Mahābhāṣya, because activity is eternal.
Even eternity is twofold:
the immutability and persistence of an immutable substance as it experiences its respective self, and,
for another [type of substance], eternity in the form of continuous activity, which is non-immutable since it is manifested in various ways.
For this very reason, the proof for the proposition that "existence (*bhāva*) is distinct from substance (*dravya*)"—namely, that it possesses both actuality and non-actuality—is as follows:

action and the state of substance are distinct because they possess the qualities of transcending and not transcending [the object]. For example: "The mat was made by Devadatta. Here, the action (*kriyā*) transcends the object (*karman*), whereas the object and the action do not transcend one another, because the meaning of the word is presented in its integrated form.
Furthermore, transgression and non-transgression cannot be without a cause;
for it is observed that when there is no transgression regarding the two divisions of action, there is nevertheless a transgression of the instrument with respect to the object of division.
In that case:
"Is the abandonment of objects the state of being, or is it activity, or is it existence?
The other replied: "How can there be duality in eternity?"

To this it is replied: because the entity, consisting of both substance (*dravya*) and becoming (*bhāva*), is itself twofold, the duality of its permanence (*nityatva*) is also established, as previously described. For it is not the case that "only that [substance] is permanent," and so on, up to: "for that too is permanent in which its true nature (*tattva*) is not destroyed" (Pātañjala Mahābhāṣya 1.1).

Since it has been stated [in the *Paspaśā*] that "it is so said," the duality of that [substance] is now demonstrated—beginning with the words "of the immutable" (*kūṭasthasya*). For substance (*dravya*) is indeed immutable and eternal because of its equality between prior and subsequent times. Of that immutable substance—which is the seed of all distinctions and non-distinctions, which exists as the essence of all things such as motion and station, and which experiences this or that particular self—it is logical that there be both persistence (*dhrauvya*) and immutability (*kauṭasthya*), precisely because its nature consists in that very experience of itself.

But for the other state—that state which is manifested in such and such a way, which is being experienced, and which consists of a continuous process whether sequentially or simultaneously—there is non-eternality due to its activity, and eternality consisting of uninterrupted existence in the form of constant engagement. Thus, it is rightly said that there is a twofold nature even to eternality; see also page 21, line 22, and footnote 4 on page 212.
*Dravya-kauṭika-bhāṣya*,
*Dravya-kauṭika-yaśas*;
"for this very reason," and so forth.

For this very reason, apart from [the reasons] such as permanence and duality, this other cause—namely, the state of participating in both the existent and the non-existent—is the proof for the fact that this activity is different from substance, establishing the point that "the state [of activity] is distinct from substance. The meaning is that it serves as the logical reason (*hetu*) for the proposition that "the state is characterized differently from substance.
An action may be past or future, whereas a substance exists only as something present; likewise, an action may have occurred or be occurring, whereas a substance simply exists. This is the meaning.

Alternatively, the existent is the substance (*dravya*) and the non-existent is the instrument (*karaṇa*); likewise, that which is "stayed" and that which is "gone" correspond respectively to these two. Because they partake in the states of being transcended and not transcended [by action], the states of action (*kriyā*) and substance (*dravya*) are distinct. For example: "The mat was made by Devadatta. At the time of making the mat and even when the act of making has ceased, the mat remains of one and the same form; however, the action—remaining untranscended during the state of contact with the *vīraṇa* grass—is transcended in the state subsequent to the completion of the mat.

Thus, the second example is that "the division is produced by action" (*karmaṇā vibhāgaḥ kṛtaḥ*), because action inheres in both the agent and the object, as in the cases of the verbal roots *pac* (to cook) and *bhid* (to split). According to the established tenet of the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇasiddhānta*), "the object is that which is most desired by the agent" (*kartur īpsitatamaṃ karma*, Pāṇini 1.4.49); however, for the Vaiśeṣika, it is action itself. Here, without distinction, action is the cause of division, and division [occurs] through the uninterrupted activity characterized as an instrument, due to the non-cessation of the series [of moments], whether in the substance Devadatta or in the action; and that [activity] has the nature of becoming that and not-becoming-that.

Just as action (*karma*), which has conjunction and disjunction as its fruit, is a distinct category (*padārtha*) from the mover, and without a connection to that [mover] there would be no "going," so too going and the like do not exist without a connection to an instrument (*karaṇa*). Otherwise, it would not be an action (*karman*) distinct from anything else—either from its own essence (*svatattva*) or from substance (*dravya*); or, even if it were such, it would not produce the designation "it has been done" due to the absence of a connection with an instrument, like space (*ākāśa*) and so forth.
And thus, being a cause of both the existent and the non-existent, it would be eternal.

What is intended by him is that [the substance] remains as a substance (*dravyavat*). Disjunction (*vibhāga*) is the most desired object (*īpsitatama*) of the agent of separation, which consists of the action (*karman*) of motion; thus, it is said that "the substance is produced by the action of motion which causes it to reach another location. Therefore, that action (*kriyā*) passes away, but neither disjunction nor the action itself pass away. This is because the meaning of the word is condensed and possesses the nature of a noun (*nāman*); furthermore, passing away and not passing away cannot be without a cause.

Furthermore, it is observed that when two substances—one the object and the other the agent—are present, there is no deviation from their respective roles of action and instrument, provided there is no deviation regarding the object of the separation [produced by the action].

Yet, in a single entity, both deviation and non-deviation cannot occur simultaneously due to contradiction, except through dependence on another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, this must be inferred: in that case, with respect to the substance Devadatta—whether he is the agent of the mat or the object of the action—and with respect to the movement which is the agent or the mat which is the object, there must be an uninterrupted activity characterized by the function of an instrument.

And that activity (*pravṛtti*) is action (*kriyā*), whose essential nature consists in becoming that [substance] or not-becoming that [substance]. The nature of this activity is its becoming in that substance and in what is not that instrument; and it must necessarily be of a dual form—consisting of transgression and non-transgression, uninterrupted, non-static, and having the essence of becoming through activity.
Thus, the distinction between action and the state of the substance is seen... (see page 283–2).

In the case of Devadatta, whether as a substance (*dravya*) or as an object (*karman*), there must be an uninterrupted activity characterized by instrumentality (*karaṇa*). And that [activity] consists in the nature of becoming that [substance] or not-becoming that [substance]. Just as motion (*gamana*), which has conjunction and disjunction as its result, is a distinct category (*padārthāntara*) from the mover, and motion does not occur without a relation to that [mover], so too motion and the like do not occur without a relation to an instrument. Otherwise, it would not be an action (*karman*) distinct from anything else, nor would it exist as a substance with its own essential nature. Thus, it would not be an action at all.

Likewise, it would not give rise to the designation "it was done by you," because of the absence of a connection with an agent; like space and so forth, and thus being an existent cause of both the existent and the non-existent, it would be eternal. Furthermore, [the opponent might argue that] action is the agent.

Therefore, indeed, by means of that very reality,
[it is] through the state of being the Lord of Reality.

"And just as in conjunction," and so forth.

Now, with the intention of stating the faults that arise if—as previously mentioned—one does not accept the distinction between the mover and the act of moving (the example) and the existent and the process of becoming (the application), it is said:

"Conjunctions and disjunctions are the common effect of actions; upward throwing is the common cause [produced] by gravity, effort, and conjunction" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra). According to this statement, the action of upward throwing—which is produced by gravity and other factors—initiates both the conjunction of the substance with another location and its disjunction from another location, which constitute the action of going.

Therefore, motion (*gamana*), which has conjunction and disjunction as its result, is a distinct category (*padārthāntara*) from the goer. Since those two—conjunction and disjunction—and their cause, motion, exist or do not exist as long as the substance exists, they possess the status of a distinct category according to the Vaiśeṣika doctrine. When that status as a distinct category exists, there is a relation between the goer and the motion; and without that relation, motion does not occur. For it is observed that "Devadatta goes" [only] because of his connection with motion. Furthermore, one who has transcended motion is said to have "gone. Therefore, without that transcendence, there is no such thing as "having gone."
This rule is observed regarding specific actions in the context of motion;

likewise, since even motion and so forth do not occur without a connection to an instrument (*karaṇa*), action is established. [If it were otherwise,] because it would be distinct from other things, the substratum of the essence of action—whether by virtue of its own nature (*svatattva*), its status as an object (*karman*), or as a substance (*dravya*)—would not exist, and thus it would not be "action. For it is an action precisely because it is being performed when an instrument exists; and if there were a deviation from the instrument, it would be "done" rather than "being done," and thus it would not be an action. However, in the case of an action that is distinct from a substance or from its own nature, it would indeed be so.

If it is argued that even though an instrument (*karaṇa*) exists, it would not produce the designation "it has been made" without transcending its own relation to becoming—and yet such [a designation] is observed—what is the reason for this not being the case? Just as an object (*karman*) does not exist without an action (*kriyā*), so too an instrument would not exist at all without the manifestation of becoming. Likewise, without transcending its relation to becoming, it could not be called "produced" (*bhūta*), because each preceding [factor] serves as the cause for each succeeding effect.

Furthermore, there is no such thing as "prior" (prāc) and so forth without qualification, because there is no deviation from the relation of becoming (*bhavana*), just like a sky-flower; or else, because it lacks an existent cause, since there is no deviation from the relation of the becoming of what was previously non-existent.
And this deviation [is observed] in cases such as grass and action, when there is the actualization of the separation of a mat and so forth;
for in that state, both substance and action are present, due to the absence of a lack of connection.
What is it like? It is like space (*ākāśa*) and so forth.

What would follow from that? Furthermore, since that [effect] exists as an action (*karman*), and because it lacks a connection to a cause, it would have both existent and non-existent causes; thus, it would be eternal, due to its possession of the characteristics of the eternal.
If one asks, "What are the characteristics of the eternal?", it is said: "That which is existent and without a cause is eternal" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 4.1.1).
Thus, according to the Vaiśeṣika school, this is the definition of the eternal;
in this way, it has been established that action, such as going and so forth, arises from its connection with the instrument.
Just as in the case of the conjunction of tastes,
among substance, quality, and action, substance is the common cause. 1.

Just as an action does not exist without an activity (*kriyā*), so too an instrument (*karaṇa*) would not exist without the manifestation of becoming (*bhavanavyakti*); likewise, "it has come into being" (*bhūtam*) would not occur without a deviation from the connection with becoming. Thus, each preceding [factor exists] by way of being the cause for each succeeding effect.

Furthermore, that which is devoid of qualifiers such as "prior" and so forth does not exist, because there is no deviation from the relation of coming-into-being, like a sky-flower; or because it lacks an existent cause, since there is no deviation from the relation of the coming-into-being of what was previously non-existent.

And this deviation [is observed] in cases such as the action of grass [producing] a mat, where both substance and action constitute the state of having become what was previously the separation [of parts].

And as for the phrase "just as action," etc.:

just as action such as going does not exist without an act, according to the method already stated, so too an instrument (*karaṇa*) would not exist at all without the manifestation of the act of becoming—that is to say, it could not possibly come into being. Likewise, without the occurrence of a connection with the process of becoming, there could be no such thing as "having become" (*bhūta*); when that connection exists, one says "it becomes" (*bhavati*), and upon the completion of that connection, one says "it has become" (*bhūta*).

The phrase "each preceding [is related] to each succeeding through the relation of cause and effect" demonstrates a continuous stream of connection between actions. Consequently, regarding the statement "prior and so forth, without distinction," etc., if there were no connection with "becoming" (*bhavana*) and no transgression thereof, then—due to the absence of prior, posterior, mutual, potential, conjunctive, and so forth, as well as their non-existence—there would be no differentiation within non-existence. Thus, "non-existence is not distinct from non-being" is a synonymous expression. Because there is no transgression of the connection with becoming, non-existence would be a single, undifferentiated absolute non-existence, like a sky-flower. Just as a sky-flower does not exist because it lacks a connection with becoming and lacks any transgression thereof, so too everything, such as a jar and the like, would likewise not exist.

Or, because it lacks a real cause; for in that case, since that connection with an agent and connection with the process of becoming—which constitutes the cause of a thing’s existence—does not exist, or there is a transgression of it, then due to the absence of a real cause and the state of being causeless, everything such as a jar and so forth would be an absolute non-entity, like a sky-flower.

Having summarized that, he states the reason: "Because of the transcendence of the connection with the coming-into-being of what was previously non-existent" (*abhūtabhavana-sambandha-vyatikramatvāt*). This means that because there exists a transcendence of the connection with the process of becoming the instruments of motion, stability, and so forth, the entity Devadatta—who consists of the manifested individuals that have gone, stayed, acted, and come into being—is perceived as existing while moving, staying, acting, and becoming; it is not otherwise. Thus, it may be thought that there is no transcendence of the "becoming" (*bhavana*) which is constantly and continuously active.

To this it is replied: "And there is a transgression [of the rule] in the case of the action of grass (*tṛṇakarma*) and so forth. The action of grass and its fibers is *tṛṇakarma*; by the inclusion of "and so forth" (*ādi*), conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is also included. Correspondingly, in the case of the becoming and having-become of a mat (*kaṭa*) and its disjunction (*vibhāga*), etc.—here too, by the inclusion of "and so forth," the disjunction and conjunction of the cloth (*paṭa*) and so on are understood—in the becoming and having-become of such a process as this, there occurs a transgression: "the grass becomes a mat," "the action becomes disjunction," and "conjunction would be with another. It might be asked: "How can it be said that 'the grass becomes a mat' or 'the action becomes disjunction'? To this it is said: [as follows].

To this it is replied: here too, has it not already been stated—that all this is nothing but substance and action? Since conjunction and so forth are all established as being either qualities or actions, there is a departure from the state of "becoming" (bhavana) for that which has already come into being (bhūtatā).
And thus, all this is precisely the basis for the states of object and so forth among the factors of action (kārakas), which are rooted in the activity of becoming.

If action were the reality of a thing just as substance is, then a thing would not exist at all without that action, because it would be identical to it—just like Devadatta’s childhood or like the color and form of a jar.
However, this is observed to be the case: even without the action of going and so forth, the entity called "Devadatta" exists;
indeed, the thing exists even in the absence of action. Therefore, it is distinct from action, because it can exist without it, just like a jar or a cloth.
For it is observed that while Devadatta is walking, Yajñadatta experiences agitation;
if action were as ultimately real as a substance, then because it possesses the nature of action like "going," even "staying" would likewise be ultimately real, and so forth.
Having established this, [it follows that] the substratum of the action of being (*bhāva-kriyā*) is being itself; for being is indeed action—this is "the action of being."

Substance (*dravya*) is existence (*bhāva*), and that itself is action (*kriyā*); or rather, action belongs to substance, and this state of the factors of action (*kāraka*) as object (*karman*) and so forth—the state of being an object, instrument (*karaṇa*), and so on—is based upon the becoming of substance, that is, based upon the becoming of the substance. It is not of a fixed form, because it arises from its connection with the occurrence of various diverse actions. This is seen, for example, in such instances as: "Devadatta cooks rice with wood in a pot," "the rice comes into being," "the wood blazes and kindles," "the pot holds [it]," or "it is placed upon the fire," and so forth.

For there is nothing that, by virtue of being associated with a specific genus—such as the association with "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth—is restricted to being exclusively an object (*karman*), an instrument (*karaṇa*), or a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) due to its association with the nature of an object, instrument, or locus, such that it could never be anything else.

What then? It has an indefinite range of capacities (*aniyata-śakti-viṣaya*), because the factors of action (*kāraka*) consist of capacities. Indeed, that same substance becomes the object in one action, as in "he wipes his eyes" (*netre pramārṣṭi*); in another, it is the instrument, as in "he sees with his eyes" (*netreṇa paśyati*); and in yet another, it is the locus, as in "the collyrium stays in the eyes" (*netre añjanaṃ tiṣṭhati*), and so forth.
Therefore, the seed, the entity, the substance, and the reality is that which is free from all differentiation; its manifestation as differentiated existence is action (*kriyā*),
which demonstrates the continuity of the sequence of connections.
Does this [text] demonstrate the connection, the continuity, and the sequence?
Would it be thus, [if there were] no distinction and only one-sidedness? Bhā. [asks].
Regarding the phrase "kāraṇa-pra-asatkāraṇābhāvāya," in reality, the reading *asatkāraṇabhāvā* appears correct here; the meaning is "because of the state of having no unreal cause."
In all [manuscripts], it is *pra* [not *prati*];
*itibhā* [is the reading] in the Bhāṣya;
*anyatheti* [is the reading] in the Yaśomitra commentary.
Of this [world], which is pervaded by the excellence of all virtues, all this is [empty].
In this very way, the status of the factors of action (kārakas) as objects (karman) and so forth depends upon the activity of becoming (bhāva-kriyā).

If activity, like substance, were the reality of an entity, then the entity could not exist without that activity, because it would be identical to it—just as Devadatta cannot exist apart from his childhood and so forth, or as a jar cannot exist apart from its color and other qualities.
Yet, this is observed to be the case: the entity called "Devadatta" exists even without the activity of walking and so forth.
However, an entity indeed exists even without action; therefore, it is distinct from that [action], because it exists even in its absence, like a jar or a cloth.
For it is observed that while Devadatta is walking, Yajñadatta experiences distress.
If action were as ultimately real as substance, then standing would also be ultimately real, because it possesses the nature of action, just like walking.
The phrase "yogādi" does not exist in the Bhāṣya manuscript.

Regarding the passage beginning with "yadi" (*if*, etc.): this is the fault for one who does not accept [this]. If action (*kriyā*) were also the reality, the self, or the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of an entity, just like its substance (*dravya*), then the entity would simply not exist without that action. This is because it is the reality, because it is the self, and because it is the essential nature. Whatever is the reality, the self, or the essential nature of something cannot exist without it—just as, for example, Devadatta’s childhood and other states. Just as Devadatta’s reality consists of various states such as childhood, which occur sequentially and do not exist without him, so too this entity would not exist without action. The distinction is that it would be like the form and other qualities of a jar; just as the reality of a jar consists of form and so forth, which arise simultaneously and do not exist without it, so too the entity would not exist without action. Thus is the specific point.
Moreover, this is observed: the entity called Devadatta exists even without actions such as going; thus, this [opponent's] argument leads to an undesirable consequence.

Furthermore, because one observes defects [in the opponent's position], he states a proof for the purpose of establishing that an entity exists: "But an entity indeed exists even without action; therefore, since one observes defects in its non-existence, it must be understood that the entity is other than action—that is, distinct from action."

It is not only because of the observation of defects [in the opponent's position]; what then? There is also a reason based on difference (*anyatva*). Therefore, he says: "Because it exists even without that. Whatever exists even without something else is different from that, like a jar and a cloth. Just as a jar, existing without a cloth, is different from the cloth, and a cloth, existing even without a jar, is different from it; so too, an entity existing even without action is different from it.
To provide another illustration, which serves as a basis for further investigation, he says: "For it is observed that while Devadatta is walking, Yajñadatta experiences distress (*adhṛti*)."

In this context, the cause of Yajñadatta’s lack of composure is his departure from the object named Devadatta, which is distinct [from the object itself]; for since the lack of composure occurs even when that object remains the same in its prior and subsequent states, therefore action is not the true nature (*tattva*) of the object.
Regarding the phrase "that which is the self" (*ya ātmā*), there may also be the reading "of whom the self" (*yasyātmā*).
Do not go [to that conclusion].
The passage contained within these words, beginning with "yadi dravyapāramārthyavad" and so forth, does not exist in the manuscripts designated as Ya.

If, just as the substance (*dravya*) of the entity named Devadatta exists in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), so too were action (*kriyā*) to exist [ultimately], then—since standing is an action just like going—standing would also be ultimately real. Consequently, because of that very act of standing which is opposed to going, Devadatta could never go; for he would be confined to a space already occupied by himself, just like Yajñadatta.

Now, even if Devadatta is accepted as being identical with the act of going itself, since Devadatta would then be the ultimate reality of the action of going, there could be no standing still at all. Thus, due to the absence of both going and standing, there would be either constant motion or constant lack of motion, as before. Furthermore, just as there is a lack of stability for him while Devadatta is going, so too—because they are of the same nature—there would be the undesirable consequence of a lack of stability extending as long as Devadatta exists, just like that specific moment, since Devadatta himself would be the cause of this instability.
Or, because its nature is stability, even while Devadatta is moving, Yajñadatta’s maintenance [of the body] would always be exactly like when he is stationary, as in the case of Yajñadatta...
[etc.]
whether there be steadfastness or lack of steadfastness,
he would be obstructed.

Furthermore, because that place is occupied by Devadatta, Devadatta’s movement would never occur; the meaning is that Devadatta would never go there at any time, just as in the case of Yajñadatta in a place occupied by Devadatta. Just as the entity named Devadatta is already determined as being Devadatta, and thus there is no room for the contradictory state of being Yajñadatta—so that the state of being Yajñadatta can never occur there—likewise, when the location is occupied by Devadatta, movement [into it] can never occur.

Now, even if it were granted that Devadatta is accepted as being essentially identical with his act of going—lest there be an absence of Devadatta’s going, which is the cause of Yajñadatta’s lack of steadiness—even so, because Devadatta would be [merely] the ultimate reality of the act of going, he could never stand still; for Devadatta would be occupied by the act of going, just as Devadatta who is occupied by his own nature cannot possess the nature of Yajñadatta.

The word *iti* has the sense of a reason (*hetu*). Consequently, because of that reason, there is an absence of both going and staying. First, regarding the absence of going: just as previously there was no stability because motion was non-existent prior to the arising of motion, so too, even while Devadatta is going, Yajñadatta would lack stability because of Devadatta’s existence; for just as Yajñadatta possesses stability when there is an absence of motion, he would likewise possess constant instability [if motion were present]. The same logic applies to the absence of staying: stability and instability would both occur [absurdly] by this same reasoning.

"So be it"—in that manner, by the mode of non-existence attained through the sequence of logical arguments as stated; "of going and staying"—thus, for him, there would be no going at all, just as Yajñadatta does not exist in a place occupied by Devadatta.

Even if Devadatta is accepted as the very essence of going, nevertheless, because Devadatta is in reality the action of going, there could be no staying. Since both going and staying are absent, as before, there would be either constant motion or constant rest; and so it is.

Likewise, even when [Devadatta] exists, just as Devadatta possesses instability while walking, so too—because of his identity with that [instability]—there would be the consequence of instability extending as far as Devadatta exists, just as it exists at that specific time. Alternatively, since Devadatta alone is the cause of this instability, then because of his nature as a stable entity, Yajñadatta would always possess stability even while Devadatta is walking, just as he does at the time of standing still.
Yajñadatta...
steadfastness or lack of steadfastness.
Its state of being obstructed is [the obstruction] of that [consciousness],
O Deva.
As in the case of [the absence of] functioning due to non-existence,
so too there is an absence of functioning due to the non-existence of that which has arisen.
Just as it is with "being," so it is also with "becoming," and so forth;
or rather, let there be "going" or "staying"— even while accepting this, a fault is stated.

Regarding that movement: first, just as there is instability (*adhṛti*) in Devadatta while he is moving, so too—because [the self] has that [movement] as its nature—there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of instability persisting as long as Devadatta exists. Just as at the time of Devadatta’s movement, Yajñadatta’s cause of instability is Devadatta because Devadatta has movement as his nature, so too for as long as life lasts, the self would be the very cause of Yajñadatta’s instability for as long as his lifespan endures, because it has movement as its nature, just like at that specific time. This is because for that Devadatta, movement is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), and because the entity persists; and because Devadatta, whose nature is movement, remains identical in both prior and subsequent times.

Therefore, in order to explain that, he says: "Devadatta himself is the cause of his lack of steadiness"—here the word *iti* signifies a reason (*hetu*). Since Devadatta is essentially of the nature of motion (*gamanātman*), there follows the consequence of constant lack of steadiness.

Thus, first of all, this fault has been stated regarding the existence of motion, which is opposed to staying. Or rather, if it were the existence of staying itself—which is opposed to motion—it would follow that even while Devadatta is moving, Yajñadatta’s steadiness would always exist, because Devadatta exists [for Yajñadatta] just as he does during the time of staying, since [Yajñadatta] consists of the essence of staying.
Whether it be existence or non-existence,
whether it be becoming or non-becoming,
that which is beyond the conditioned and unappropriated.
Thus, first, the faults have been stated by way of examining Yajñadatta’s exertion regarding Devadatta’s movement and staying; now,
the examination regarding Yajñadatta’s exertion itself must likewise be carried out.

In this context as well, the passage beginning with "just as the ultimate reality of substance" (*dravyapāramārthyavat*) should be applied, as appropriate, by uttering the words *dhṛti*, *adhṛti*, and *Yajñadatta*;

furthermore, in another manner, from the words "but Yajñadatta... up to "...neither persistence nor non-persistence is the substantiality of Yajñadatta," [it is shown that] because the permanence of activity—which consists in the uninterrupted process of becoming that and not that—is not immutable, this very becoming is what constitutes motion, persistence, stability, and so forth.

However, the distinction between cognitions and linguistic usage arises from conformity with the reality of the differentiation of words and substances; for the word is the very nature of the object, and the actions of supporting and non-supporting are not distinct from it.

Consequently, since Devadatta’s going and staying are also not distinct from Devadatta, then—just as in the case of Yajñadatta’s true nature—his going or staying would be nothing but supporting or nothing but non-supporting, because, as before, there is no other contradictory action present.

Therefore, he says that this [objection] also applies to action because of its permanence: "No, because the permanence of activity—which consists in the uninterrupted succession of being that and not being that—is not immutable. Here, "being that and not being that" (*tadatadbhavana*) is formed by a *sarūpa-ekaśeṣa* (retention of one term from identical forms): namely, "being that" (*tadbhavana*) and "not being that" (*atadbhavana*). "Being that" refers to the domain of verbs such as *asti* (is) and *bhavati* (becomes), in the sense that it "continually comes into being. "Not being that" refers to moving from standing to walking, and from walking to standing.
The states of being that and not that, along with the act of becoming, are those very things—namely, staying and going, as well as steadiness and lack of steadiness.

The non-interruption (*aviccheda*) is its essence; that activity which has non-interruption as its essence is "activity characterized by the non-interruption of becoming this and not-becoming-that. Its permanence (*nityatva*) is not immutable (*akūṭastha*), being distinct from the permanence of an immutable substance (*kūṭasthadravyanityatva*). Because of that state—since the permanence of activity characterized by the non-interruption of becoming this and not-becoming-that is non-immutable—this very process of becoming consists of going, supporting, staying, and so forth. These mutually contradictory actions, such as moving, standing, supporting, and not-supporting, are indeed nothing but becoming, because their nature consists in a state of constant, continuous activity. Thus, they are distinct from [the concepts of] "being" and "not-being," and are simply the eternal activity of mere becoming—an undivided unity of pure action.

Therefore, it might be thought that both substance and action are eternal entities; however, because there would be no difference in action, there would be an absence of differentiated cognition and linguistic usage, yet differentiated cognition and differentiated usage are both observed.

And this is incorrect; therefore, both the cognition of difference and linguistic usage—such as "he goes," "he stands," "he exerts effort," or "he does not exert effort"—proceed in accordance with the reality of the operation of substance characterized by verbal differentiation. "Verbal differentiation" (*śabdabheda*) refers to that operation of substance (*dravyapravṛtti*) for which the word is the differentiator; the word is not something other than the substance. Furthermore, it has been stated previously that "operation" (*pravṛtti*) is action (*kriyā*), and even a quality (*guṇa*) is a form of action.

The manifestation of distinctions in sound is distinct from the manifestation of the distinctions of form, taste, smell, and touch. Its reality consists of its nature as phonemes (*varṇa*) and so forth; and in accordance with that—that is, in accordance with the reality of the manifestation of distinctions in sound—the cognition of distinction and the linguistic usage of distinction arise.
The powers of a potent substance, such as form, taste, and so forth, are simultaneous; however, actions such as moving and staying are successive.
As it has been said: "Of the universe, whose wondrous deeds are beyond measure, which is accompanied by nothing but its own potencies..."
Because everything exists in every way at all times, something or other is intended to be expressed [in speech].
(Vākyapadīya 3.7)

Thus, because the powers [of words] function by conveying their respective objects in accordance with their specific capacities, and because designations—which are characterized by an adherence to specific portions of an entity through a sequence of eternal activity—are incapable of expressing the entire nature of an entity.

Just as in the expression "Devadatta goes," the word *devadatta*—because its power is restricted to the objective domain of the substance (*dravya*)—neither includes nor excludes going and so forth; likewise, the verb (*ākhyāta*) also neither includes nor excludes Devadatta, because its power is restricted to the objective domain of action (*kriyā*). Since the noun (*nāman*) and the verb are each fixed upon their respective restricted portions of the entity, this cognition of difference follows from that [restriction].

In the same way, the conventional distinctions between going, staying, supporting, not supporting, and so on, exist for the purpose of experiencing all such differences, because they are eternally active.
The movement is indeed already acquired by means of the substance Devadatta, because it has that as its essence, just as heat is [acquired] by fire.

The intention (*vivakṣā*) is also expressed by the word "goes" (*gacchati*), because those word-powers function to convey their respective objects in accordance with [the speaker's] intent; for even though the substance-aspect perspective (*dravyārthanaya*) maintains that everything possesses the nature of everything else, the power of the word "jar" consisting of phonemes functions restrictively toward the cognition of the form of a broad belly, a vertical neck, and so forth, and not elsewhere. Just as there is perceptibility by specific sense organs due to the restriction of the operation of the powers of substances such as color-form (*rūpa*), so too, through the distinct operations of word-powers, there arise the cognition of difference and linguistic usage. This is the meaning.

He explains this with the passage beginning "nityapravṛtti" and so forth: because it is impossible for words—namely, designations that are intent upon a specific portion of reality distinguished by its sequential occurrence due to constant activity—to express the entire nature of an object, he demonstrates this with the example "Devadatta goes," and so on, up to "or does not exclude," the meaning of which has already been explained.

The passage beginning with "likewise even when so-called" (*tathākhyātam api*) has its meaning already explained in the same manner as before, up to the point: "because [the two] have fixed capacities regarding the objects of the action-portion (*kriyāṃśa*). This is for the very reason that nouns (*nāman*) and verbs (*ākhyāta*) are characterized by their adherence to fixed portions of reality (*vastubhāga*). He concludes: "this cognition of difference follows that [adherence]. The meaning is that the cognition of difference follows the application of words which are restricted to specific portions of the power of substances (*dravyaśaktyaṃśa*).

In the same way, conventional designations such as going, staying, supporting, and not supporting exist for the purpose of experiencing all distinctions, because they are eternally active. That which is this constant activity proceeds with the thought, "I am the substance that experiences all these various states of being, such as going and so forth. If the substance did not experience those various actions, then they would not exist, because they would not be experienced by it—just like a flower in the sky. Therefore, the substance is asserted to be the seed of all distinctions, itself devoid of distinction.

Or else, that substance would not exist, because its various modifications (bhedas) are not experienced, like a sky-flower. Thus, that substance would be a seed only if it were to experience those modifications; however, as seen on page 391, line 6, this is not the case. Because its activity—which consists in the uninterrupted succession of being and non-being—is not eternal in the sense of being unchanging, this very process of becoming constitutes its movement, support, persistence, and so forth.

However, differentiation-cognition and linguistic usage [occur] in accordance with the reality of the application of distinct words and substances, just as [the application of] words [occurs] in accordance with reality. (Is it "śabdatattvavat" or "pravṛttatvavat"?)
See page 395, line 10.

Regarding "tadatadbhavanaṃ ca," it is [understood] through *sarūpaikaśeṣa* (the retention of one form among similar items); thus, "tadatadbhavanaṃ" refers first to that which is both that and not that... [text fragment].
What is that...? [text fragment]. Primary source.
For that [non-existence] as well,
there is the manifestation of existence, just like the manifestation of existence,
because of what?
Sound is not a substance;
because it is seen as a substance, sound is not [a substance]; [it consists of] phonemes and non-phonemes. Primary.

"Because the universe, which possesses wondrous activities and has nothing other than mere powers (*śakti*) as its companions, exists in every way and at all times, something or another is intended to be expressed [as the primary factor] in a particular context. (Vākyapadīya 3.7.2).

Having raised the doubt, "How, then, is it understood that power (*śakti*) is the means (*sādhana*), and not the substance (*dravya*)?", he says: "[Because] the universe, which consists of a collection of mere powers and possesses manifold properties..."
Because everything exists in every way at all times, something specific is intended to be expressed in a particular instance.
(Vākyapadīya 3.7)
Entities such as jars are denoted by the word "universe" (viśva); they consist of a collection of powers capable of accomplishing their respective functions, such as carrying water.
Therefore, those powers are the "measures" (mātrā) or constituent parts therein; thus, jars and the like are merely a collection of powers.

And these powers are of many kinds: some arise from their own causes alone by destiny and do not perish even when considering the destruction of their substratum, such as the powers of illumination in consciousness-lamps; some, though residing within human effort, are obstructed in their substratum, such as the powers of poison and so forth; for those are produced through repeated practice and the application of observed substances, while others, though existing, are destroyed by the exertion of another person, such as the lethal power of poison or the sprout-producing power of a seed.
Others are transformed by one possessing extraordinary power, such as when a yogi effects a transformation of the form of all things;
some are manifested through the lapse of time, such as the capacity of merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*) in the yielding of their fruits. In this way, many varieties are to be inferred.

Thus, since the collection of powers possesses manifold natures, when there is a diverse effect, the occurrence of specific causal factors is established according to the intended distinction of their respective capacities.
The meaning is that if a substance (*dravya*) were the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), then because it possesses a single uniform nature, there would be no diversity of effects;
as it has been stated in the Bhāṣya: "The collection of qualities (*guṇasamudāya*) is the means of accomplishment."

Since the principal action (*pradhānakriyā*) cannot be accomplished by each individual power (*śakti*) alone, there is a reference to the collection (*samudāya*). However, with respect to the subordinate actions (*guṇakriyā*), each [power] possesses the status of a means (*sādhanatā*) individually; and because of the diversity of that [means] in relation to the principal action—whether it takes the form of an object (*karman*), a non-object (*akarma*), and so forth—there is a reference to the collection even though each is a means individually, for the purpose of explaining how the difference in effects (*kāryabheda*) of a single [agent] is possible through the differentiation of these powers acting as means.

Therefore, even though an entity possesses multiple powers (*śakti*), when it exists in its actual state, a particular power is intended to be manifested in a specific context; thus, the status of [an object] as an *karman* (object), *karaṇa* (instrument), and so forth—as in "see the jar," "bring water with the jar," or "place water in the jar"—is established by necessity, and there is no risk of confusion among the *kārakas*.

However, since a substance (*dravya*) has a single nature, its status as an object, instrument, and so on would not otherwise be possible; therefore, this power must be understood as being implicitly contained within the power itself when that power functions as a means of accomplishment (*sādhana*).
Thus, in the *Sādhanasamuddeśa* of the third book of the *Vākyapadīya*, in the commentary composed by Helārāja:

because powers (*śakti*) function in a manner restricted to the communication of specific objects according to their respective correspondences, and because designations—which are intent upon those portions of reality characterized by the attainment of an eternally active sequence—are incapable of expressing the entire nature of a thing.

Just as in the expression "Devadatta goes," the word "Devadatta"—because its power is restricted to the object consisting of the substance (dravya)—neither includes nor excludes going and so forth; likewise, the verb also neither includes nor excludes Devadatta, because its power is restricted to the object consisting of the action (kriyā). Since the noun and the verb are each intent upon their own restricted portion of the reality, the cognition of difference that follows them is exactly like that. Thus, the linguistic usages of distinctions such as going, staying, supporting, and not supporting exist for the purpose of experiencing all possible distinctions, due to their eternal operation. Let this be seen! (Pañjikā 21)

Bhāravi says: Just as it was stated immediately above—that the word *devadatta* neither assumes nor excludes motion and so forth because the powers of words are restricted to specific parts [of their referents] and because they function [in that way]—is it the case that motion and so forth are likewise not assumed and not excluded by the entity *devadatta*? No, it is said; there is a distinction: "by the entity *devadatta*" and so on. For even though motion is not assumed by the word *devadatta*, it is indeed assumed by that entity, due to the absence of restriction to specific parts and due to the cause of the particularity [of the entity].

If it is asked what the specific reason for this is, it is said: because they have that as their essence (*tadātmatvāt*). For Devadatta has movement and so forth as his essence, since he experiences them; whatever has something as its essence is appropriated by that thing, just as heat is appropriated by fire. Just as heat is the essence of fire and is therefore appropriated by fire, so too should it be seen that movement is [the essence] of Devadatta, and thus Devadatta is appropriated [by it]; for sound has as its essence the activity of experiencing the distinctions of substances.
However, because speech is dependent upon its meaning, even by the word *devadatta*, motion and so forth are not excluded; for, like the meaning itself, it exists for the sake of that [meaning].

Indeed, the word *devadatta*—being inseparable from the accusative case and so on—is employed only with reference to the agent alone. And since the agent is the means (*sādhana*) of an action, as he functions in various ways within those actions, the word likewise denotes those respective meanings. As they say at the end [of the Mahābhāṣya]: "The verb *as* (to be), followed by the present tense (*bhavantī*), in the third person, is understood to exist even when not explicitly used; [for example], in 'the tree,' it is understood that 'it exists'" (Pāṇini-Mahābhāṣya 2.3.1).
3.1 See page 261, line 6, note 2.
Thus far, the distinction has been stated that movement (*gati*) is conveyed by the object "Devadatta" and not by the word "Devadatta.

Now, it is asked: is the referent Devadatta conveyed by the word "goes" (*gacchati*) and by the meaning of "going"? To this it is replied: "And Devadatta is conveyed by the word 'goes. Because of its connection with Devadatta, the word takes the masculine gender;

and if the referent is conveyed by the word, then the referent Devadatta is indeed conveyed by the meaning characterized as "going," because [the meaning] is identical to that [referent]. This is the distinction.
