Just as [in the case of movement], because the continuity of activity—consisting of the non-interruption of being that which is both this and not-that—is not immutable, this very "becoming" (bhavana) is what constitutes going, staying, supporting, and so forth; thus, by means of the becoming of the activity of the object of motion (the path), the becoming of the agent is already included. Since a real entity possesses a dual nature consisting of substance and action, it is said that "Devadatta and others, being taken up by the object [the path], cause [himself] to go," because action consists in the experience of the distinction from the substance. This same rule applies to the word as well: "by the word 'goes'" and so forth; for Devadatta is taken up by the word "goes" because, as stated, he is a dual-natured entity, since prior to the word's activity, its nature consists in the experience of the distinction from the substance.
See page 393, line 1:
"...by means of this, not becoming...
[variants: bhā॰ gaṃtvādyu॰vi॰ḍe॰līṃ॰]
Having gone [to the city], today, quickly,

secretly, thus— so far, because of the substance-aspect view (dravyārthanaya) which consists of the nature of all things, the cognition of difference and linguistic usage have been explained by relying on imagined differences that do not exist; however, from the perspective of ultimate reality, since speech arises from the presence of the object,
even by the word "Devadatta," going and so forth are not excluded, but are indeed included, just like the object itself.

Why? Because its meaning is that coming-into-being (bhavana). "Its coming-into-being" (tadbhavana) means that the very coming-into-being of motion and so forth is the meaning of the word "Devadatta. Therefore, understand that the meaning of motion and so forth is already included by the meaning of Devadatta; do not suspect that "having that coming-into-being as its meaning" is unestablished. To this, he says: "For the word 'Devadatta,' etc."

When the established doctrine (siddhānta) holds that a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) expresses its own meaning, substance, gender, number, object (*karman*), and so forth; that case-endings (*vibhakti*) are the manifesters of these; and that specific grammatical relations (*kāraka*) are adopted by virtue of the speaker’s intention—since objects and the like are also *kārakas*, agency (*kartṛtva*) is indeed intended—then, even when no such specific relation is intended, the word "Devadatta," though invariably accompanied by the second case ending and others, is employed to denote the agent alone. And since an agent is a means (*sādhana*) for an action, he does not exist without an action; and actions consist of sitting, lying down, standing, and so forth. While acting as an agent himself in various ways within those respective actions, the word likewise denotes those respective meanings.

As they say, "in the end" serves as an indicator; at the conclusion of their investigation, the grammarians have determined this: "the root *as* [is used] with the present tense (*bhavantī*)," and so forth—here, the present tense (*laṭ*) is called *bhavantī*, while the rest is self-evident.

A verb may indeed occur at the beginning, middle, or end [of a sentence], and even elsewhere; for there is no fixed rule regarding its position, as seen from examples such as "you are," "I am," "he stands," "you stand," and "I stand. The only rule is that [a sentence] does not exist without a verb (see *Abhyarthe dravya*, p.
...from verbal roots and nominal stems; [the suffix] *ka* is applied to words denoting those who are attached,
even when they are the objects of reliance.
In those [manuscripts], let it be seen by oneself; see page 261, line 5: "bhatyeva" (pra.).
Thus you remain [in this position]:

the word "Devadatta" does not exist without its referent; it is neither for the purpose of conveying the meaning of Devadatta as the agent, nor is it meaningless, because the employment of speech is for the purpose of conveying meaning.

When the referent Devadatta is already being cognized by means of the word "Devadatta," it is restated (*anūdyate*) for the purpose of enjoining [the action] "he goes" (*sa gacchati*). The injunction of going is intended to demonstrate a movement performed by Devadatta as its agent, which is the opposite of his staying—expressed in the form "he who goes is Devadatta," or "that very person who is there goes. In this way, what appears to be meaninglessness or redundancy serves to distinguish between the injunctive and the restating portions. For the speaker, the second word functions to clarify the meaning proximate to the first word’s employment; for the listener, it provides assistance through that mere proximity alone, and not for anyone else.

This very word "Devadatta," having assumed the sense of the action [of going], does not exist for the purpose of conveying the agent Devadatta, nor is it meaningless; this is understood in the context of "correct reflection. Because the engagement of speech has the purpose of conveying meaning—speech is engaged with the thought, "I shall convey the meaning"—it is therefore not meaningless, since it is the utterance of one who acts with deliberation.

Furthermore, because Devadatta is perceived through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the word "Devadatta" does not denote him; rather, the meaning of Devadatta, being already understood by the word "Devadatta," is merely restated (*anūdyate*). For a restatement concerns an object already known, as it serves as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) to an injunction (*vidhi*).

If it is asked, "For what purpose is there this restatement?", it is for the sake of enjoining "he goes"; that is, for the sake of enjoining the act of going as qualified by Devadatta. Indeed, the act of going is enjoined because its specific nature is not yet known, [namely] as having Devadatta as its agent.

Let it be that the mention of Devadatta is for the purpose of prescribing motion. If it is asked, "For what purpose is the prescription of motion?", it is said: [the phrase] beginning with "contrary to the place" intends a movement contrary to the place, accomplished by the agent Devadatta who has been superimposed [upon the action]. To explain that, one employs the expression, "I cause Devadatta—who was not previously the agent of motion—to be superimposed as the agent of motion."

He demonstrates this: "He who goes is Devadatta," and likewise, "That which is [Devadatta] goes. Thus, Devadatta is the agent (*kartṛ*) of the action of going. This is because there is an injunction (*vidhāna*) by means of a known referent (*jñātārtha*) restating an unknown referent (*ajñātārtha*), and because, in reality, that which expresses a substance (*dravya*) and that which expresses an action (*kriyā*) have the same referent (*abhinnārthatva*). Furthermore, in view of the fact that [the action] exists in dependence on the substance... [text fragment].
Let it be seen in the Patañjala-Mahābhāṣya 2.1.1.
See page 133, note 11;
*kārayukti* (as in the manuscript); *rītītyādi* (as in the manuscript).
If it is argued that there is redundancy because that which goes has the nature of heat, we accept that it is so, and thus [the following] applies.

And having established this, when "Devadatta" is uttered, because there is a designation of an agent characterized by a specific action, the word "goes" (gacchati) is redundant since the going has already been [conveyed]; furthermore, it is a tautology. Likewise, since the act of going with its specific agent is expressed by the word "goes" alone, the word "Devadatta" is also [redundant], as the meaning of Devadatta is already understood.

Furthermore, those two defects—pointlessness (*ānarthakya*) and tautology (*paunaruktya*)—do not apply to either the speaker or the listener when the purpose is to distinguish between injunction (*vidhi*) and restatement (*anuvāda*). To whom, then, do they apply? It is said: they apply to the speaker and the listener who fail to distinguish between injunction and restatement. One might think, "This word is an injunction because its meaning is unknown," or "This is a restatement because its meaning is already known and because it serves as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) to the injunction. Having encountered such a speaker or listener who lacks discrimination, one of these two—either pointlessness or tautology—would indeed occur for one of them. However, having encountered a speaker or listener who *does* possess discrimination, neither pointlessness nor tautology would occur for either of them, since they correctly understand that these two have the respective purposes of injunction and restatement.
From the word "abdāt" [comes] "viśiṣṭa"; from the word "abdāt" [comes] "viśiṣṭa";
for the purpose of the discussion.

What would be the thought of one who speaks? It might be thought: "Let there be a statement directed toward the speaker for the purpose of enjoining or restating a single entity consisting of substance and action as determined by himself; but how [could it be] for the listener? If this is asked, it is replied: "For him too, starting from 'the employment of the first word' and so forth, up to 'it is beneficial to the listener.'"
In this context, the first word—such as "Devadatta" or "goes"—is employed according to the speaker's intention;

that which takes up this first word constitutes its meaning, and thus it is "that whose meaning is conveyed by the first word. The second word serves solely to convey the meaning already expressed by the first word, because its purpose is to elaborate upon the meaning that has been introduced, like a commentary (*bhāṣya*). It is not, from the very beginning, the cause for the cognition of that meaning, because it merely clarifies what has already been made manifest, like a lamp.

And that which is intended to be denoted by the second word is "present" (*sannihita*); the word "manifestation" (*vyañjana*) is the second word. By its mere presence, by its mere employment, that very meaning previously apprehended is manifested by it—this is the sense. Likewise, for the "perceiver"—that is, the listener who is capable of inferring the speaker's intention, meaning one who has grasped the linguistic convention—it is "beneficial," meaning capable of producing comprehension, and not for anyone else, such as one for whom the rule and its restatement are undifferentiated, or one who has not grasped the convention.
It is not a fault of the word that one does not understand its meaning, just as it is not a fault of the sun that the owl does not see it.

Therefore, even though they have the same referent, these two [words] have distinct functions—one being the injunction (*vidhi*) and the other the restatement (*anuvāda*). Because the second word serves to clarify the meaning already presented by the first word, it is like the text of a commentary (*bhāṣya*); it is not the cause for the initial cognition of that meaning, because it merely makes manifest what was already expressed, like a lamp.
Is the phoneme (*vyañjana*) the word (*śabda*)? [Answer: No; this consists of two words.

Here is the formal application (*prayoga*): the second word has precisely the same meaning as that conveyed by the first word, because its purpose is to explain the meaning already introduced (*udgrāhita*). Devadatta is introduced as being connected with the acts of going and existing; the word "goes" (*gacchati*) serves to explain him. For it has been stated that when "Devadatta" is mentioned alone, his movement is not understood by another person even if he has already grasped it.

A word intended for the purpose of explaining a meaning already grasped is seen to convey exactly the same meaning as the preceding word, just like the text of a *bhāṣya*; for example, in the *bhāṣya* on the sūtra *vṛddhir ādaic* (Pāṇini 1.1.1), the words explain the meaning already conveyed by that very sūtra: "The technical term *vṛddhi* applies to the vowels *ā*, *ai*, and *au*," because this is already contained within the sūtra itself by virtue of its being a treatise instructing on what is correct (*sādhu*).
And so it has been said:
"The vowels beginning with *a* and *ā*, and the consonants beginning with *s*, *d*, *y*, and *n*."
For all that which is in the *vṛtti* and that which is in the *vārttika* is indeed contained within the *sūtras*.
Indeed, one does not grasp the words solely from the *sūtras*;
rather, [one grasps them] from the commentary (*vyākhyāna*).
This has already been addressed: that very aphorism (*sūtra*), when analyzed, constitutes the commentary (*vyākhyāna*).

But was it not said—that a commentary is not merely the words of the discussion (*carcāpada*) such as "vṛddhi," "āt," and "aij"—but rather, that the example (*udāharaṇa*), the counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*), and the supplying of ellipsis (*vākyādhyāhāra*), all taken together, constitute the commentary?
"This occurs for one who does not understand thus:
'one understands words from the sūtra itself,'" as stated in the *Paspaśāhnika* of the *Pātañjala-Mahābhāṣya*.
Following this, in Kaiyaṭa’s *Bhāṣyapradīpodyota*, only the first half of this verse is seen to have been cited:
"The example [is for] the meaning, the counter-example for the animal," thus [concerning] the root *maṃth* with the prefix *pra*.

It might be thought: "If the meaning were already contained in the first word, it would have assisted the listener—the cognizer—at the very moment the first word was uttered, because [the meaning] would have been manifested by that alone."

To this it is replied: For some, it becomes a cause for the cognition of that meaning even when [the action] exists; for others, from the very beginning, because it is a manifester (*vyañjaka*) of what is already manifested (*tathāvyakta*). "Manifested in that manner" means *tathāvyakta*. By the mere utterance of the word "Devadatta," there is first of all deposited in the intellect of the hearer the notion: "Devadatta is the agent whose object is a specific action. Therefore, it is *tathāvyakta*. The word "goes" (*gacchati*) is its manifestor; it does not state anything new, because it is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of that. Thus, because it is a manifestor of what is already manifested in that manner—just like a lamp: just as a lamp manifests a jar situated in a room that was previously unmanifested, and thus is not a cause for the cognition of its meaning from the very beginning, so too is the word "goes" in this sentence.

Alternatively, according to the doctrine of substantial reality (*dravyārthavāda*), even a potter merely manifests a jar that already exists; he does not produce something non-existent, just like a lamp.

Therefore, since the potter also acts as a manifester of what is to be manifested, the jar is indeed manifest even during its stages as a lump of clay and so forth, because it is perceived through the manifestation of a sequence of actions, like a jar manifested by a lamp. Likewise, in the case of "Devadatta goes," because the agent manifests what is to be manifested, the cognition of that object is not caused [by the action] from the very beginning.

The passage beginning from "etaccihnāntargataḥ ॰va tathā pratipattuḥ" up to "śroturapi bhavantī dṛṣṭā ta॰ pṛ॰ 399 paṃ॰ 10" is found in the Ya manuscripts; furthermore, the passage following "itaścāsiddhiḥ svavi॰ pṛ॰ 40॰ paṃ॰ 18" up to "paṃ॰ 23" (contained within these markers) is not present in the Bhā manuscript.
The jar is not other than the pillar;
the jar is indeed that very thing.

And likewise, even in the absence of the presence of such a word, the function belongs only to the meaning conveyed by the previously heard word, because it is restricted in that manner; just as in the case of the command "Enter, [eat] the cake," when the speaker’s intention is otherwise, the utterance would be purposeless, and because the meaning is established through context and so forth, it is observed that at the end, the comprehension of the noun's agency occurs for the listener as well. Therefore, the comprehension of the listener is just like that of the speaker.
Or else, it is because of the employment of a portion of a sentence;
for indeed, people are seen employing portions of sentences within full sentences, and portions of words within words.
For example, in the case of sentences, they employ such portions as "enter," "the ball of rice," "enter," or "refreshment."
Just as Devadatta is called Datta and Satyabhāmā is called Bhāmā— using a part of a word for the whole—

so too here, in place of the full sentence "of that which is produced from a semivowel (saṃprasāraṇa) [which itself was] produced from a semivowel," the phrase "from a semivowel (saṃprasāraṇa) [to] a semivowel" is employed as a part of that sentence; thus we shall understand the rule to apply to that which is produced from what has been produced from a semivowel.
Thus in the Patañjala Mahābhāṣya, 1.1.44.

The explanation of this is as follows: the verb "enter" implies an action suitable for the object of entry; since entry into a *piṇḍī* (a small mound) is impossible, it leads to the understanding of a "house.

Similarly, the object "the *piṇḍī*" implies an action suitable for it, which, by virtue of the context, conveys the act of eating. Likewise, the word "from the *saṃprasāraṇa*" will imply that which has been produced from it. This is the meaning.

And how the use of a single part of a word [is justified] has been explained in the section beginning with "siddhe śabdārthasaṃbandhe" (when the relationship between word and meaning is established) in the *Pradīpa*, the commentary on Patañjali’s *Mahābhāṣya* composed by Kaiyaṭa, 1.1.1.
The explanation of this is as follows: "In sentences" means when sentences are to be employed for the purpose of communicating their own meaning.
Since activities such as perception and so forth are also [means of] fitness, he says: "By the context...

At the time of grasping the expressive power (*śakti*) of a particular sentence toward its sentential meaning, there is also the grasping of the expressive power of each of its constituent parts toward that same sentential meaning—just as with a word-part toward the word-meaning. Thus, comprehension occurs through expressive power itself.
In the previous refutation, the term *saṃprasāraṇa* was used metaphorically (*upacāra*) for the phoneme produced by it.
In this case, however, the distinction is that the comprehension of that meaning occurs through a portion [of the word] by means of its power; thus he says:
"it will imply," for here "implication" (ākṣepa) is simply "making known" (bodhana).

Regarding the phrase "in the sense of this sentence" (*bhāṣye ityetasya vākyasyārthe*) [in the commentary], the word *vākya* here refers to a collection of words (*padasamudāya*). Thus, the meaning is: "in the sense of this"—that is, of that which has the meaning "from that which is produced by *saṃprasāraṇa*"; and also "in the sense of the sentence" "of that which is the grammatical operation (*kārya*) resulting from *saṃprasāraṇa*."
Thus ends [the commentary] on Pāṇini 1.1.44 in the Uddyota, the commentary on the Pradīpa on Patañjali’s Mahābhāṣya, composed by Nāgeśabhaṭṭa.

And do not think that this is merely stated as a logical necessity—that the second word expresses the meaning already contained in the first word—but rather, since such usage is observed even in worldly convention, he says "and likewise, even without... and so on, up to "...enter the grove," in order to demonstrate that.

And this being the case, even in the absence of the proximity of a word whose meaning differs only by way of being a mere restatement (*anuvāda*) of what has already occurred, there is indeed the occurrence (*vṛtti*) of the meaning conveyed by the previously heard word, because its application is thus restricted. For the application of that word is restricted in such a way that, even when a second word is not heard in some instances, it becomes the cause for the cognition of the object denoted by that word; and indeed, speakers are observed to act accordingly. For example, in the case of "Enter the *piṇḍī*," upon hearing the word "enter," one understands through context and other factors that the object of the action (*karman*) here must be something hollow like a house or the like, which is suitable for entering; and upon hearing the object-word "*piṇḍī*," since what was just mentioned [entering] is impossible [in relation to a ball of food], they understand it as the object of the act of eating, which is the action appropriate to it.
Therefore, it is rightly said that the second word (*pada*) is the manifestation (*vyañjana*) of the meaning conveyed by the first word;

just as the word *gacchati* expresses the meaning conveyed by the word *Devadatta*, so too the agent (*kartṛ*) is indeed conveyed by the suffix *tip* in the form *gacchati*. What is the reason? Because *tip* is a substitute for the *lakāra* prescribed for the agent according to the rule *laḥ kartari ca*.
If one asks, "Who is this agent?", it is replied: it is precisely Devadatta as qualified [by the action], because the intention is to express the act of going as having a specific agent.

Alternatively, the verbal root *gam* (to go) has as its object only that meaning which is grasped by its own constituent parts (*svāṃśa*), because its essential nature is established by that [root]. Whatever word has its essential nature established by a particular term is observed to have as its object only the meaning grasped by its own constituent parts, just as, for example, the word "pot" has as its object properties such as verticality which are established by that term; this is according to the commentary (*vṛtti*). Indeed, this is not found in the Bhāṣya manuscript.
Even in the word?
Thus enter, Pra...
just as you enter?
Because of the impossibility of entry;
see page 126, note 7.
"Give what is appropriate," as in the *Prakaraṇa* [commentary on] Ślokavārttika 1.1.5;

thus, the fault is stated for one who does not accept this: "Because of the pointlessness of speaking otherwise than what the speaker intends. For if a speaker, desiring to communicate the motion whose agent is Devadatta, employs the verb *gacchati* (he goes), and if that word did not express that very meaning, what would be the purpose of the utterance? Thus, it follows that the utterance is pointless (*ānarthakya*).

Furthermore, because of the introduction of meaning, context, and so forth—namely, conjunction (*saṃsarga*), disjunction (*viprayoga*), association (*sāhacarya*), opposition (*virodha*), meaning (*artha*), context (*prakaraṇa*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), and word (*śabda*)—through this process of the comprehension of the meaning of words, this very "becoming" (*bhavana*), which is of a single nature, comes to possess distinctions such as Devadatta or distinctions such as motion (*gati*) and staying (*sthiti*). Thus, it is said that "it becomes in such a way.
Now, action (*kriyā*) is indeed a specific manifestation of the causal factors (*kāraka*);

since manifestation is possible everywhere, the inclusion of the term "specific" (*viśeṣa*) is for the purpose of selecting that [manifestation] which possesses causal factors with a view toward a particular result.

For in all entities, there is an activity consisting of appearance and disappearance, occurring in conjunction with both coexistent and non-coexistent qualifiers at each substratum. It is observed that this activity involves the determination of a meaning—which is not inherently perceived—by commentators who follow the intention of the speaker, through various distinctions such as proximity, suitability, place, time, individuality, accent, and so forth. And this [determination] is possible only if the meaning is already contained within that very word, and not otherwise.

Likewise, even though the listener has not heard [the name] "he," when it is said, "He goes," [the question arises] "Who goes? and at the end, upon the conclusion of the name, the understanding of agency occurs—namely, "Devadatta. Although the agency is expressed by the verbal suffix (*tip*), nevertheless, it is observed that the listener also arrives at the understanding that the agent is precisely the referent of the nominal word, having reached whatever state [of cognition] it may be. For this reason, from that observed understanding, just as with the speaker (*vaktṛvat*)—that is, just as with the speaker (*vaktṛvat*)—just as the understanding previously arisen in the speaker was "I am employing the verb 'goes' with Devadatta as its agent," so too is it for the listener.

Thus it has been rightly stated that the words "noun" (*nāman*) and "verb" (*ākhyāta*) denote respectively substance and action which are mutually interconnected. In this way, through another supporting argument, it has been demonstrated by the speaker that the meaning of a word also has as its object a reality consisting of substance and action.
Or [it may be] other than the statement of the speaker; see page 127, line 11 of the Bhāṣya, Pāda, Ḍe, Līṃ manuscripts.
Please see *Vākyapadīya* 2.317 and 318.
In the printed edition, there is a footnote reference, but no corresponding note is provided.

The state of being the object of manifestation (*pratipādaviṣayatā*) belongs to the *ya* [suffix]; and through this cultivation of the movement of word and meaning, this very becoming (*bhavana*)—which is of a single nature—comes to possess distinctions such as Devadatta, or distinctions such as motion and stability; thus, it "becomes" (*bhūyate*) in that manner.
Is it not the case that action (*kriyā*) is a specific activity (*pravṛttiviśeṣa*) of the causal factors (*kāraka*)?
Since activity is possible in all cases, the term "specific" (*viśeṣa*) is employed for the purpose of selecting that [activity] which possesses causal factors with a view toward a particular result.
For indeed, in all entities there exists activity—consisting of manifestation and disappearance—which occurs in each substratum accompanied by both coexistent and non-coexistent specific qualities.
It has been seen; for this reason, therefore,
without *dṛ*, *bhā*, *vi*, and *dvata*, from that *dṛ* and *ya*.
...from this [it follows that] ...
the substance of the connection ... is produced.
Immediately after [the word] "pra...
[comes] "anayā ca" and so forth.

By this very cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of the meaning of words as explained by us—which is observed in the world—this becoming (*bhavana*) itself, being of a single nature, comes into existence everywhere as a manifestation (*vyakti*), whether it be the distinction of Devadatta, the distinction of motion, the distinction of stability, or the distinctions of support, lack of support, laughing, speaking, and so forth; it exists as a manifestation in all cases.

Because it becomes such by that [process], the word "iti" (thus) has the sense of a reason; because the single process of becoming—which takes the form of the substance Devadatta and the forms of actions such as going and staying—becomes by means of each of those respective forms, there is nothing else whatsoever that is devoid of becoming; for it is said in the *Abhava-prakaraṇa*: "Becoming itself becomes. It exists (*bhavati*) according to the *Yāska* commentary.
Does it become manifest? Does it exist as a manifestation? Does it become manifest?
[The answer is: "Indeed, [it is] of the causal factors," and so forth.

When it has been established that "action" (kriyā) is simply the undifferentiated state of being (bhāvana) everywhere, the Grammarian, unable to tolerate this, states the following definition of action: "Action is a specific manifestation of activity" (*pravṛttiviśeṣaḥ*). This is the superior definition of action, not merely constant ongoing activity.

In that regard, regarding the phrase "of the factors of action" (*tatra kārakāṇām*), the explanation is as follows: by using the word *udbhūta* ("manifested"), it is intended that you should not understand the agency itself to be the action; rather, let it be grasped as something distinct from the factors of action. Thus, the genitive case is used for the purpose of showing their distinction.

If it is asked, "For what purpose, then, is the mention of 'distinction' (*viśeṣa*) made?", he says in response: "Because activity is possible everywhere," and so forth. By the phrase "with a view toward some result," a conventional result such as boiled rice (*odana*) and the like is intended. By the phrase "possessing causal factors" (*kārakavatī*), the meaning is "possessing means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) such as instruments (*karaṇa*) that are distinct from its own substratum. For every action must either reside in the agent (*kartṛ-samavāyinī*) or reside in the object (*karman-samavāyinī*), and thus be fruitful—just like the actions of cooking (*pacati*) or splitting (*bhinatti*). The mention of "distinction" is for the sake of including verbs such as *pac*, *paṭh*, and *gam*, as well as [verbs] like *bhid*. The remainder [of the commentary] is as follows... [text fragment].
...by way of a single function...

Regarding the acceptance of mere activity (*pravṛtti*) alone in your position, the following fault is stated: "For there is activity in all entities," and so forth. That activity is indeed joined with, or associated with, each respective substrate—be it a thing or another thing—along with specific qualities such as color-form (*rūpa*) and the like, which coexist, or motion, stability, and the like, which do not. Its nature is described as consisting of manifestation and disappearance; its result is said to be accumulation and depletion, for the author of the Commentary (*Bhāṣyakāra*) stated regarding action: "It has accumulation and depletion as its fruit. Because everything does not remain stable even for a moment, what would be the worldly fruit? However, the specific qualities (*viśeṣa*) that arise depend upon other causal factors (*kāraka*) distinct from their own substrate, just as the softening (*vikleda*) residing in rice grains depends upon firewood and the like.
In that case, whatever activity there is does not constitute a factor of worldly convention;
therefore, it is not established that action is a specific kind of activity rather than activity in general,
nor that existence is action.

How can there be the status of "action" (*kriyātva*) for the general category of activity (*pravṛttisāmānya*), given the absence of a connection between a factor of action (*kāraka*) and an intended result? Alternatively, its nature as something pervading [the states of] "going" and so forth is not established because it is merely a particular instance of activity, just like the factors of action themselves. Furthermore, it possesses a difference [from them], just like their distinctions; likewise, the general category of activity cannot even be accompanied by a substance (*dravya*), because it is non-existent, like a sky-flower. Its non-existence follows from the fact that, while not being a substance, it lacks the nature of "going" and so forth, just like a sky-flower.

Having cited the statement "so it was said by the Commentator," he connects the text as follows: this was stated in order to demonstrate the existence of the essential nature and the fruit of that [action], which is possible in every case regarding an entity. Since everything does not persist even for a moment, what mundane or conventional fruit could there be? Thus, he demonstrates its incapacity for practical transaction (*vyavahāra*).

Furthermore, due to their capacity for grasping specific distinctions, particular actions such as *pac* (to cook) arise and, being causes for other fruits such as boiled rice (*odana*), require other factors (*kāraka*) distinct from their own substratum.

He demonstrates this: just as the softening [of rice] which resides in the grain depends upon wood and other such factors, he brings that analogy forward with the words "the activity therein," and so forth, up to the point "not a general activity.
Thus, the fruitfulness of employing the term "particular" is explained, as well as the fact that a general activity is not an action.

Regarding the phrase "having accumulation and non-accumulation as its fruit," the author of the Bhāṣya has stated that this refers to the activity of an effect (*kārya-sāpravṛtti*): "Since everything does not persist for even a moment, what worldly result [could there be]? However, specific qualities (*viśeṣa*) that are arising depend upon other causal factors (*kāraka*) apart from their own substratum; for example, the softening (*vikleda*) residing in rice grains depends upon firewood and so forth. In that case, such activity is not a constituent part of worldly transaction (*lokavyavahārānaṅga*)."
Therefore, action is a specific kind of activity, not activity in general;
see page 379, line 8; see page 380, note 1, line 29;
Furthermore, the claim that "existence (*bhāva*) is action" is not established.

How could there be the nature of action (*kriyātva*) in the general state of activity (*pravṛttisāmānya*), given the absence of a connection with factors of action (*kāraka*) directed toward a result? Alternatively, its pervasive form—such as "he goes"—is not [action] because it is a specific instance of activity (*pravṛttiviśeṣa*) and thus has not yet come into being, just like a factor of action; it possesses a different character (*vaidharmya*) from that [action], like its various subdivisions.
Likewise, the general state of activity cannot even be accompanied by a substance (*dravya*), because it is non-existent, like a sky-flower.
And non-existence [is established] because, while lacking substantiality, it lacks motion and so forth, like a sky-flower;
let this be seen on page 285–2,
as stated in the *Viśeṣabhāṣya*.

"Existence (*bhāva*) is action (*kriyā*)," and so forth, up to: "How can it have the nature of action? Because there is an absence of the relationship between a factor of action (*kāraka*) and an intended result (*phala*). The meaning is that what you assert on the strength of logic—that existence consists of both substance (*dravya*) and action (*kriyā*), such that existence is of the nature of substance and action—is not established, because the existence of action as you intend it is unproven.
Furthermore, it is unestablished because it does not pervade its own particulars; thus, "action" is not a universal activity (*pravṛtti-sāmānya*).
To demonstrate this, he says: "Or, [if it were] a form pervading 'going' (*gacchati*) and so forth, how [could it be so]?"—the word "how" (*kutaḥ*) carries over from the previous context.

The activity characterized as "general operation" (pravṛtti-sāmānya-lakṣaṇā) as you define it does not pervade [the categories of] going and so forth, because it has not existed as a specific operation (pravṛtti-viśeṣa). Whatever has not existed as a specific operation does not pervade going and so forth, just as a causal factor (kāraka) does not pervade them—since a causal factor has not existed as a specific operation and is thus non-action (akriyā), and the status of being non-action is established for both of us; this is the example by way of similarity (sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta).

The dissimilarity is that [the universal] possesses those particular instances: whatever is an action (*kriyā*), it exists as a specific instance of activity (*pravṛttiviśeṣa*), just like the various actions of going, standing, and so forth, or the various types of movement such as running, falling, crawling, and gliding.

Therefore, because it does not pervade [all] instances such as "going," the universal of activity (*pravṛttisāmānya*) is non-action, just like a *kāraka* (grammatical factor), since it is that which is "acted upon" (*kriyate*).
See Bhāṣya on *kṛcchra*, page 397,
note 7; [is this] in the case of dissimilarity (*vaidharmye*)?

Thus, there is a distinction between substance and action (*tyākriyābheda*). Furthermore, regarding the statement "in this way, substance and action are two entities (*bhāva*)," such that action is the second entity of the entity that is substance—this too is untenable for one who maintains that action is a general activity (*pravṛttisāmānyakriyāvādin*), because that action which you propose does not exist, being like a sky-flower. Just as a sky-flower, due to its non-existence, cannot be the second [entity] of a substance, so too is the case with the general activity.

If it is argued that the non-existence of the universal "activity" (*pravṛtti-sāmānya*) is unproven, [we reply]: it is non-existent because, while not being a substance, it lacks motion and so forth, like a sky-flower; and its lack of motion and so forth is due to its not pervading those [entities].
Therefore, action (*kriyā*) is a particular kind of activity, not the universal activity; such is the position of the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*). See page 40, line 3.

First, it is admitted—as is our own view—that the activity of entities has as its object all things; for it has been stated that the "self" (ātman) of entities functions in a manner undivided from the causal relationship between causes and other effects.

Due to the proximity of the two specificities just mentioned, and because they are the causes of other effects, those very [entities], just as specificities depend upon other causal factors (*kāraka*) for the production of an effect, likewise require other causal factors for the production of the effect that is the jar from the state of being clay. The potter is the agent of this [jar], who, by means of a staff and so forth, brings water and other materials and thus makes the jar in the workshop.
In the city of Mālava, for seven hundred years, the jar was indeed [unbroken]; here, in this year, it is said:
"Granted that, as we maintain, [the jar] is accepted as such," and so forth.

Indeed, even by you, who assert that action consists in a specific activity (*pravṛtti-viśeṣa*), it has been accepted—just as we maintain—that action is simply the general state of activity (*pravṛtti-sāmānya*).

How so? He demonstrates this: "The activity (*pravṛtti*) directed toward all entities is the very self (*ātman*) of those entities. First of all, you yourself have already accepted this by stating that "nothing whatsoever remains in its own nature for even a moment; rather, it either increases as long as it is to increase, or it is joined with diminution. Thus, you have asserted that the constant activity (*satatasampravṛtti*) is the self, the essential nature (*svarūpa*), of all entities. And that acceptance, because it accords with our own view, establishes the fact that activity is a universal function (*kriyātva*). What is the reason? Because it has been stated that "the functioning (*vṛtti*) in all entities is undivided from the causal relation (*hetu-hetubhāva*) consisting of further effects (*phalāntara*). The "effect" (*phala*) refers to the sprout and so forth, which result from the activity of the seed and other causes. "Further effects" (*phalāntarāṇi*) are the subsequent fruits arising in connection with that, such as leaves, stalks, stems, husks, awns, milk, rice grains, and so on, occurring in succession. The "causes" (*hetavaḥ*) are the preceding ones, each according to its own nature; furthermore, the preceding ones relative to those are the "causes of causes" (*hetuhetavaḥ*). Those very entities are of the nature of action (*kriyātmānaḥ*). Since it has been stated that the "functioning" (*vartana*)—that is, the constant activity—is undivided from those very things across all entities, [activity is established].

How was this stated? It was stated regarding all entities—such as seeds, sprouts, and lumps of clay—in the passage beginning with "for nothing [exists] in itself," and that refers to the general nature of activity (*pravṛtti-sāmānya*), because even the softening of rice grains and so forth does not transcend that very nature.

Furthermore, as for what was said by someone else—that "the specific activity of the causal factors (*kāraka*) is directed toward a result"—that specific activity consists of co-existent qualities such as color and so forth, as well as non-co-existent states such as moving or staying; and since these are joined to each respective substratum and constitute its essence, by this statement as well, it is shown that action-ness (*kriyātva*) belongs precisely to the general nature of activity.

What is the reason? Because of the proximity of the two specificities (viśeṣa) just mentioned, and because those very specificities—which consist of general activity—take the form of the intended fruits such as boiled rice; and because of their proximity, they are the cause of other fruits. Indeed, it is those alone that are the causes of other fruits like boiled rice, and nothing else whatsoever. Therefore, even though it consists of a specific activity, it is precisely that same general activity. (See Pravṛtti-vāda, p. 379, l.
The sprout and so forth of that which has come into being;
all [are] from the prior;
the prior [is] the cause.
See page 379, line 8;
see page 399, line 3.
The passage beginning with "bhavatiya" does not exist in the manuscripts;

furthermore, as for what was said starting from "the particularities (*viśeṣa*), however, being produced... and so forth, up until the text just mentioned ending with "...because activity in general (*pravṛtti-sāmānya*) is not a constituent of worldly convention," it is here replied: "In this case too, there is no fault because it is of a similar nature, and the inclusion of the term 'particularity' is useless in the opponent's position. Therefore, he says: "And just as the particularities... and so forth; the text concerning the lack of distinction between the two actions characterized as the particularity of activity and generality has already been explained.

Just as in the accomplishment of the result of cooked rice there is a dependence on other causal factors (*kāraka*), so too in the becoming of clay [into] a jar there is a dependence on other causal factors; the meaning is that in all stages such as the lump of clay and so forth, it is the very process of becoming that depends on the potter and other causal factors distinct from the clay.

He illustrates these: "The potter is its agent," and so forth—namely, the agent (*kartṛ*), instrument (*karaṇa*), recipient (*sampradāna*), point of departure (*apādāna*), and locus (*adhikaraṇa*), consisting of the potter, the staff, water, the bringing [of materials], and the workshop.

Showing that time (*kāla*) is also a causal factor for some [entities], he says: "In the city of Mālava, for seven hundred years... There, a jar made of clay (*āmaghaṭa*) is repeatedly displayed and concealed during the milking of cows or at ponds and the like. Even its non-abiding for a single moment when thrown into water is established as a specific activity; thus, its non-existence (*abhūtatva*) and its lack of proof (*asiddhatā*) have already been stated.
Furthermore, because it is not something that has gone away (*agatyāditvāt*), it is not non-existent (*asattva*).

If it is argued that space (*ākāśa*) is indeed the locus of non-going, and that the absence of motion constitutes non-activity or the cessation of motion—thereby serving as the cause for doubt—then it follows that this locus is merely an indefinable absence of motion. Because it is a non-entity and inactive, it would be like a sky-flower;

yet it is concealed for the purpose of indicating that substances whose essence has been hidden are preserved, as in the case of a cow-milking vat or a pond, where even raw grain thrown into water does not remain there for even a moment. This demonstrates the dependence upon specific causal factors (*kāraka-viśeṣa*).
See page 40, line 2; "of the hall" (iti) is shown in the manuscript (pra. from the year [blank].
It is shown and then concealed during the milking of cows or at a pond and so forth; for that very thing, there is not even a moment’s persistence once it has been cast into the water.
Because it does not exist as a specific activity (*pravṛtti-viśeṣa*), its lack of establishment (*asiddhatā*) is likewise stated;
and because it is due to necessity (*agatyāditva*), it is not non-existence (*asattva*).

If it is argued that space is indeed the locus of non-going, and that this absence of motion constitutes the cause of doubt—being defined as non-activity or the cessation of motion—then it follows that such a locus would be utterly indefinable, being merely the absence of motion; for, due to its nature as an absence and its lack of activity, it would be like a sky-flower or like the burning of a cow in a pond. It is exactly so.

The meaning of that very [passage] is as follows: as for what was stated—that because it has not come into being as a particular activity (*pravṛttiviśeṣa*), the commonality of activity (*pravṛttisāmānya*) does not pervade [the domain of] "goes" and so forth, just like a *kāraka*—that too is not a valid inference, because the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*).

The non-existence of the general activity (*pravṛtti-sāmānya*) as a particular activity (*pravṛtti-viśeṣa*) is unproven, precisely because it is of the very nature of a particular activity. Furthermore, that general activity is of the nature of a particular activity because existence (*bhavana*) is uninterrupted everywhere, and because particular activities such as motion (*gati*) and so forth are inseparable from it, just like the self-nature of existence itself. Recalling this principle, he says: "And thus, the unproven status [of the reason] due to its not being a particular activity has already been stated;
by the inclusion of the word 'etcetera' (*ādi*), the states of contradiction and non-contradiction between substance and action have likewise been stated."

As for what was also stated—"Because it does not exist, even its being accompanied by a substance is impossible; and the non-existence of the universal of activity is like that of a sky-flower because it lacks movement and so forth"—to this it is replied: "And it is not non-existent because of the lack of movement and so forth, since the reason is unestablished (asiddha) for the very reason already stated, namely that constant becoming has the nature of movement and so forth. See page 40, line 6.

In place of the reading contained within these brackets, there appears a doubled passage in the manuscripts: "Because it is of the nature of a specific activity, its non-existence as a specific activity is unestablished; because the universal is of the nature of a specific activity, its non-existence as a specific activity is unestablished" (p.

40, l. 7). Even granting the establishment of the reasons such as "non-going" (*agati*) and so forth due to the lack of any other recourse, we state that they are inconclusive (*anaikāntika*): "Is not space the locus of non-going? Space is indeed both non-going and stationary."

In this regard, one might think that there is a cause for doubt as to whether [space] is non-existent because it is "without motion" (*agati*), like a sky-flower, or whether it is existent like space itself. One might argue: "Let it be without motion; how can space be 'without location' (*asthāna*)? For it exists eternally. Therefore, while "because it is without motion" may be a cause for doubt, "because it is without location" is incorrect. To this, it is replied: even this [space] is indeed "without location," because it is recited in the *Pāṇini Dhātupāṭha* (928): *ṣṭhā gatinivṛttau* ("the root *sthā* means the cessation of motion"). That which is the cessation or obstruction of motion already set in motion is "staying" (*sthiti*), as will be explained later.

Nor can there ever be an obstruction to the movement of this space, like the turning back of Devadatta’s movement once it has already set out; furthermore, "non-abiding" (*asthāna*) refers to movement and so forth other than staying, not the absolute non-existence of staying. Therefore, since space is also a non-abiding movement and yet exists, the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) of these two reasons remains exactly as it was. [Objection: But surely space is non-movement... *Note: The sentence fragment at the end appears to be an objection or a point of transition regarding the nature of space.*

Is it not the case that space is non-going and non-abiding? Is it not the case that space is non-abiding and non-going? As for the statement "non-abiding like the cessation of motion," this is [a point] to be considered.

If it should be thought: "The absence of motion is non-activity, which is the cessation of motion; therefore, because staying is merely the absence of motion, it is a non-entity, and thus space is not a locus of staying, nor does it possess staying, precisely because motion itself is absent"—to this it is replied: "Now, [if you say] it is indeed indefinable," and so forth.

A designation (*saṃjñā*) is a figurative expression (*upākhyā*); that which is devoid of such a designation is "without designation" (*nirupākhya*). It reaches a state that consists merely of the absence of the mode of existence you have imagined.

Because it is a non-entity (*abhāva*), and its status as a non-entity arises from its lack of activity—like a sky-flower—we shall explain later that while space and so forth are active, this [unmanifest] is a non-place despite being a place.
In the Bhāgavata, the reading is "bhāvagate";
in the Ya manuscript, it is "sthānatadeva."
Or rather, it has proceeded;
for that which has proceeded is non-existent.

If it is argued that [the distinction between] the active and the inactive arises from the capacity of the qualification of motion (*gativiśeṣaṇa*), then this very point we desire is established: the existence of the state (*sthāna*) is proven through its connection with the qualification of motion, which is the absence of motion.

This is because the reality of subsequent states, such as stability (*sthiti*), is brought about by the capacity of the qualification of motion. For this very reason, by relying on the essential nature of existence (*bhavana-svatattva*) which comprises all things, existence (*bhāva*) consists in the manifestation of one of the preceding or succeeding states and the non-manifestation of the other, due to that inherent nature.

For when a contrary state manifests, there is the cessation of another state, precisely because that very state is the manifestation of a contrary state; just as sleep is dispelled by waking, for no other action arises here while some other action is being undertaken. And in this case as well, the manifestation of the state of standing does not occur while the state of going is being undertaken.

If it be argued that this is due to the force of the qualification "of motion," the thought might be as follows: if one were to say simply that "staying" (sthāna) is cessation or non-existence without qualifying it, it would be indefinable (nirupākhya), like a sky-flower. What then? We say that staying qualified by motion is the cessation of motion;
therefore, the absence of motion is something definable (sopākhya).

To this it is replied: This very thing is what we have intended—the reality of "staying" (sthāna), which, like the reality of "going" (gamana) despite the absence of "coming" (gati) and the absence of "staying," is established as contrary to your own view due to its connection with the qualification of "going. And when that "staying" is established, it is likewise proven that all verbal expressions denoting action—such as "going," "staying," and so forth—are indeed real entities (bhāva) and not non-existent. Furthermore, because the reality of subsequent states such as "staying" is brought about by the power of the qualification of "going," for this very reason [it is said] "consisting of all things" and so on, up to "existence is the entity" (bhavanaṃ bhāvaḥ).

As for this etymological derivation—that "existence" (*bhāva*) is "becoming" (*bhavana*)—it too, for this very reason, relies upon the essential nature of becoming as being entirely composed of movement, stillness, and so forth. Without abandoning that [nature], because of its inherent character and because its very essence consists in the experience of various such becomings, "existence" is defined as "becoming" through the manifestation of one and the non-manifestation of the other, as the case may be—whether it be the prior state of movement and the subsequent state of stillness, or the prior state of stillness and the subsequent state of movement—according to the sequence intended by the speaker and according to the sequence of transformation, as far as possible.
Is it that, in the absence of the *tattva*, *ya*, and *raṃ* [of this], there is respectively *e* and *pra*, and [in the other case] *e* not according to the respective order?

It might be thought: "The destruction of motion occurs through the manifestation of a subsequent opposing state, such as rest; or, upon the manifestation of motion, there is the cessation of rest. And that destruction is a non-existence, like the production of [qualities] born of baking.

To this it is replied: Even that destruction which is considered a non-existence—and which is indeed desired as the cessation of one entity upon the manifestation of a contrary entity—is actually the non-manifestation of another entity. That is, it is simply the existence of another state, such as rest, in place of motion, or the existence of motion in place of rest; it is not a non-existence, precisely because it is the manifestation of a contrary entity.
Just as a dream is brought to an end by waking; what is meant by this? It is said that it is brought to an end, which means it is led to non-manifestation.

Just as a dream is brought to non-manifestation by waking, so too is waking [brought to non-manifestation] by a dream; for even in one who is awake, there is observed a consciousness that is faint, fainter, and faintest, like that of one asleep, while in one who is asleep, there is observed a dream that is manifest, more manifest, and most manifest, like that of one who is awake. Indeed, that very same consciousness is seen to possess distinctions such as sleep, drowsiness, and physical agitation, depending on the rise and subsidence of intense or mild veils, and to possess distinctions such as sharp, sharper, and sharpest faculties.

Therefore, dreaming and waking consist merely in the manifestation and non-manifestation of a single reality, because one arises by the suppression of the other, just as a snake may assume the states of a coiled mass or a loop.
Hence he says: "For no other action is suppressed," and so forth; the meaning has already been explained up to the point "whatever is here. This is the description of the illustration.

And here too, the passage beginning with "the becoming of a state of existence" (*gatibhavanam*) has its meaning already explained; the description of the illustrative example (*dārṣṭāntika-varṇana*) is likewise [established].
Therefore, when another action manifests, there is the cessation of the prior cultivation (*pūrvabhāvanivṛtti*), and not its non-existence; thus, it is called "destruction" (*vināśa*).
