And this would be the case for the non-existence of the object as well. It might be argued: "Just as the activity of eating ceases when it culminates in the result of satiety—because in the absence of a purpose there is no further connection with the causal factors, and thus the cessation of the act of eating occurs rather than being obstructed by another action—so too would this [cessation] be."
To this it is replied: even here, the result is satisfaction (*tṛpti*). There is indeed another action:
for eating proceeds by subduing hunger, and satisfaction proceeds by subduing eating; these are cycles of actions.
If "stability" were intended as a non-substantial designation, there would be the undesirable consequence of the non-occurrence of both intention and speech.

Now, if stability were merely the substance itself, it would exist even during motion because there is no contradiction between substance and motion; however, since the status of things as expressed in speech depends on the relationship between the contradictory and the non-contradictory, therefore stability—which is contradictory to motion—exists only when it is not distinct from becoming (*bhavana*).
Here [the opponent] says: "It might be so," and so forth, up to "this too might be so."

Just as the cessation of the act of eating terminates in the result of satisfaction—since the causal factors (kārakas) are activated with that purpose in view—and once that purpose has been accomplished the causal factors no longer operate, therefore the cessation of the act of eating results from the non-connection of the causal factors, not from the sublation of another action; in the same way, motion also terminates in the result of reaching its destination, and in the absence of a purpose it ceases due to the non-connection of the causal factors, not from the sublation of another action.

Therefore, we have a doubt: Is it that, as in the case of dreaming and waking, when one action is subordinated to another, the emergence of the other action occurs only upon their identity (*tādātmya*)? Or is it rather an absolute cessation, like the act of eating which concludes with its result? To this it is replied: Do not think here too that the cessation of eating is a mere non-existence; what then? The result is satisfaction, because activity itself is an action. For, as stated in the passage beginning with "having overcome hunger," these are indeed cycles of actions.

This is what is meant: there is no cessation of an action without the manifestation of another action, nor is there the manifestation of another action without the suppression of the previous action; for, like the cycle of actions consisting of hunger, eating, and satiety, where each subsequent one arises through the sublation of each preceding one, this case is the same.
Therefore, the cessation of motion is not a non-entity (*abhāva*); rather, it is indeed an entity (*bhāva*), namely, rest (*sthiti*). Thus [it is said].
Is it not simply the engagement with the objects of the senses?
The fault of one who does not accept this is stated as follows: "If [it is argued that] there is such a thing as stability," and so forth.

If one does not admit that "stability" (sthiti) is an entity (bhāva), there are only two possible courses for the word "stability," since a third alternative is impossible: either the designation "stability" refers to a non-entity (avastuka), or it must have as its object mere substance (dravyamātra). What follows from this? From this, the following collection of faults arises: if it were a non-entity, there would be the undesirable consequence that neither the speaker's intention (vivakṣā) nor the word would function. For if the expression of the word "stability" were to have a non-entity as its object, the desire to speak (vivakṣā)—which arises with the thought "I shall make known to another the object determined by myself"—would not occur, because of the absence of an object.

And thus it is said: "Abhidhāna" (designation) is that by which something is designated, namely the word for "staying" (sthiti); its non-existence would follow from the non-existence of its referent, or else it would be meaningless, like the expression "crow-sitting" (*kākavāsitā*).
Such, then, is the fault in the case of the absence of a real entity (*avastukatva*).

Now, if "staying" (sthiti) were merely the substance itself, then because the substance is not contradicted even during motion, the designation would apply even while moving. Just as in the case of "Devadatta goes," where the designation "Devadatta" applies because Devadatta exists and because his going is not contradictory, so too the designations "Devadatta stays" and "Devadatta goes" would both apply; for in both cases, only the substance exists and there is no distinction between them.
Since this fault is observed, staying is not merely the absence of motion.

Regarding the passage beginning with "yatastu khalu" and so forth: the state of being contradictory or non-contradictory is the actual status of the object to be expressed; because motion and stability are mutually contradictory, yet [both] are non-contradictory with respect to the substance *devadatta*, both motion and stability are indeed states (*bhāva*) like the substance itself. The text has already explained that as long as there is non-difference from becoming (*bhavanā*), stability—which is the opposite of motion—is non-different from becoming; thus, motion or stability is not other than the becoming of the substance. He concludes the discussion as it was introduced: "non-contradiction between the contradictory and the non-contradictory. (pra.)
Because of the non-existence of entities, there is no established state of things; the non-existence of entities is the non-establishment of things. (Vi. Pā. Ḍe. Līṃ. Raṃ.)

[Objection: It might be argued as follows: Just as there is a contradiction with "existence" (*sthiti*), there is also a contradiction with "non-existence," such as a sky-flower, by way of the absence of motion (*gatyabhāva*). Since there is a contradiction in that case, and because [the two] are invariably concomitant (*avinābhāvitva*) due to being contradictory, why is this [contradiction] restricted only to the domain of existence, or why is it restricted only to the domain of non-existence? If both existence and non-existence are contradicted by existence or by non-existence respectively, then both are indeed existences; therefore, because they are contradictory, like any other pair, the designation "state" (*sthāna*)—which refers to the destruction of a substance that is invariably concomitant with the occurrence of a single entity consisting of motion and rest—would apply to the cessation of motion during a state of non-arising.
Therefore, [it is] characterized by the absence of motion...

Thus, one might think that words expressing the non-existence of things such as "sky-flowers" possess positive referents (*bhāvārthatva*), just like [the words] "he stands" or "he cooks. To this we reply: this is not so, because the argument is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to the consequence that they would also be non-existent (*abhāvatva*). This is because [your reason] is contradictory.

The absence of motion is contradicted by motion, just as light is contradicted by darkness, which is the absence of light. Now, according to your own view, it has been stated that motion itself, when rendered unmanifest by the emergence of another action, is indeed a positive entity (*bhāva*). In that case, just as there is a contradiction with "staying" (*sthiti*), there would also be a contradiction with the absence of motion (*gatyabhāva*), such as a sky-flower and the like, because of its opposition to that [motion]. Since it is invariably concomitant (*avinābhāvitva*) with that which it opposes, motion would be invariably concomitant with the absence of motion, because of its opposition to it. And whatever is opposed to something else is seen to be invariably concomitant with it; for example, motion is [opposed to] staying.
Alternatively, even a sky-flower and the like would have to possess the nature of an existent (bhāva), because of the contradiction with its motion, just as with its staying;

for if there is such an invariable concomitance (avinābhāvitva), why is this designation "staying" restricted only to the domain of existents? Or why is it that [the term] "sky-flower and the like" is restricted only to the domain of non-existents (abhāva)? Or rather, a distinction must be stated here.
Thus [it was said] by him.
Regarding the passage beginning with "if even non-existence" (*yadyabhāvo’pi*) and so forth, we say this here: [concerning the reading] *bhāvatvebhā* / *bhāvatte ya*.
By taking the sky-flower and so forth as the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), there is no undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭāpādana*) because [the subject] possesses existence (*bhāvatva*).

What is the point of stating a specific qualification? The intention is that just as the argument for the non-existence of persistence (*sthiti*) applies, so too does it apply to the sky-flower and so forth.

How, then, is that cultivated? This is explained: if non-existence is contradicted by existence, or existence by non-existence, then both that which is contradicted and that by which it is contradicted are indeed existences, because they possess the quality of contradiction. Thus he demonstrates the ease of finding examples: "like the snake and the mongoose," "like the jar and the cloth," or "like the jar and its shards. Since contradiction characterized by non-coexistence is observed everywhere—whether spatially or temporally—it follows that even a sky-flower and the like are existences; therefore, we say there is no undesirable consequence. (Bhāṣya)
This passage is not present in the Bhāratīya manuscript; it exists only in the Bhāva manuscript, specifically in the Viśeṣa and Vinaya sections.
From seeing [it]... [he] gave...

Furthermore, as for your view that the designation "stability" (sthiti) has non-existence as its object, this following reasoning would apply to that as well: namely, that stability which does not arise has as its object merely the absence of motion, such that it is the cessation of motion. And when stability is thus conceived as the cessation of motion, then existence—which is a single entity consisting of motion, stability, and so forth—is subject to the previously stated logic; the substance is inseparable from that [existence], and its destruction is absolute non-existence. Thus, the designation "staying" would have that [non-existence] as its object. However, this cannot be the case, because the substance is eternally immutable (*kūṭastha-nityatvāt*).

And for that very reason, out of fear of that which is undesirable, one must understand this: "stability" (sthiti) is the cessation of movement, not non-existence; likewise, it is like a sky-flower and so forth.
He concludes this with the words "therefore, characterized by the absence of movement," etc., the meaning of which has already been explained.
[In the case of] the state being raised while being measured, O Yaśas... without effort (pāda-vinā-mānāyām-udyamāna-sthitau).

In the state of being unproduced while being produced (*anudyamānasthiti*), as stated immediately following [the discussion of] the sky-flower and so forth—which was mentioned by way of a logical consequence (*prasaṅga*)—even that which is considered non-existence (*abhāva*) is not called a non-entity (*apadārtha*). What then? Because the negative particle (*nañ*) has the sense of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), it is a particular kind of entity (*bhāvaviśeṣa*), namely an entity other than an entity, just like "non-Brahmin" refers to a Kṣatriya and so forth.

Thus, words expressing the non-existence of things such as "sky-flowers" possess a positive (bhāva) meaning; likewise, even regarding those things considered to have non-existent being, they have existence as their object. This is the principle of "becoming otherwise" (*anyathābhavana*). For instance, in cases such as "it perishes," there is indeed for sky-flowers and the like a "not becoming thus" (*tathā-abhavana*); however, it is not a case of "not becoming at all" (*na tu abhavanam*), because "becoming otherwise" consists precisely in a change of state or a different mode of persistence. This applies equally to sky-flowers and the like, because the various modes of being are necessarily restricted to what exists.

And thus, this single entity, existing as a sequence of prior and posterior states, is called "activity" (*pravṛtti*); and that very same entity, because its own internal distinctions are included within it, is called a "particularization of activity," just like a particularization of eating. For example, eating itself demonstrates the pervasion of substance and space; and an illustration of this principle of extension (*atideśa*) will be stated later.

Now, this subject at hand is being examined: how it is that [verbs such as] *tiṣṭhati* (he stands) and *pacati* (he cooks) denote "becoming otherwise. That is to say, when a substance, having been transformed through one mode—such as vibration (*parispanda*)—comes to exist in another mode, namely a non-vibratory mode of transformation, this is expressed by *tiṣṭhati*, *āste*, *śete*, and so forth; likewise, the softening of a hard substance such as rice and the like is expressed by *pacati* and similar verbs.

Just as these actions, though distinguished merely by their different modes of becoming, do not transcend the commonality of activity (*pravṛtti-sāmānya*) which is "becoming" (*bhavana*), so too such modes of becoming as "perishing," "being destroyed," and "coming to rest" likewise do not transcend the commonality of activity or the state of being (*bhāvatva*).
In this way, the fact that the meaning expressed by a verb (*kriyāpada*) consists merely in "becoming otherwise" (*anyathābhavanamātra*) has been explained.

Even those things considered to be absolute non-existents (atyantābhāva), which are denoted by terms such as "sky-flower" (khapuṣpa) and the like—surely even for them there is "not-becoming" in that manner; it is not a non-becoming in any other way, but rather a becoming, meaning that there is no absolute non-becoming. How so? It is "the stationing of non-motion" (agati-sthiti); "stationing of non-motion" is a stationing other than motion, not merely the absence of motion. Just as motion itself is a different mode [of being] and thus constitutes a stationing, so too is it a becoming otherwise; likewise, the sky-flower and so forth are also a becoming otherwise.

What is the reason? Because modes exist as necessary; since it is a mode, even a "sky-flower" and the like must exist. Whatever is a mode exists, just as the cessation of motion, which is called "stasis," exists by the logic already stated.

If it is asked, "How can there be a mode-of-being (*prakāratā*) for things such as a sky-flower?", it is said: because the sky-flower is unmanifest in its form as an inherent relation (*samavāya*), yet manifest in the mode of an *aśoka* flower and so forth, it does not transcend the status of being a mode. Since substance and action possess the nature of everything, within this division of the substantial standpoint (*dravyārthika-naya*), everything is both substance and action—such as going and so forth. Because, as stated, there is no difference between the two modes of becoming (*bhavana*) for the various substances and the various actions of going and so forth, what is the "sky" and what else is the "blooming of flowers"? Thus, like the two modes of becoming in Devadatta’s act of going, even that [sky-flower] is an existent entity (*bhāva*).
The non-becoming of things such as sky-flowers, and likewise their perishing— surely this non-becoming applies to sky-flowers and the like as well; otherwise, there would be no non-becoming at all.
Coming, staying, and changing—these apply even to things like a sky-flower, because the various modes [of existence] are necessarily restricted to what is real.

Thus, this single entity, existing as a temporal sequence of prior and posterior states, is called "activity" (*pravṛtti*); and because its own internal subdivisions are included within it, it is also called a "particularization of activity," just like a particularization of eating. For example, just as eating itself is included within the categories of substance and location. (Note: This passage is not found in the Bhāratī manuscript.)
He perseveres;
[this is] the state of abiding in conduct, according to the *Prakaraṇa* and the *Abhāva-vibhaṅga*.
And thus, etc.:

by adopting this view, even for actions occurring in a sequence such as going, standing, and so forth, because they do not transcend their identity with a continuous flow, a single entity consisting of a prior and posterior state is called "activity" (*pravṛtti*). And it is precisely in this way that what was stated in the *Nirukta*—that "one expresses a prior and posteriorly ordered entity by means of a verb, as in 'he goes' or 'he cooks'"—is logically established. (Nirukta 1)

Regarding the phrase "and so forth" (*ityādi*): since the identity of all roots (*sarvadhātvaikārthya*) will be established immediately hereafter, why is that state called "activity" (*pravṛtti*)? We reply: because it proceeds with excellence (*prakarṣeṇa vartanāt*).

And that excellence consists in the constant experience of all its own particular manifestations; and because it includes those very particular manifestations within itself, it is called a "particularization of activity" (*pravṛttiviśeṣa*). An entity, while existing as characterized by the general act of becoming (*bhavan*), includes within itself its own particular manifestations such as the perception of form and so forth. This is because, among particular entities, there is both difference and non-difference from one another, due to their being permeated by the universal. However, it is not like the "particularization of activity" of causal factors (*kāraka*) as you conceive it—something distinct from the general activity—as an illustration: "like a particularization of eating."
The explanation of that is as follows: "Just as the two arms," and so forth, up to "only the mode differs.

By means of the distinction between substances such as food, drink, chewables, and tastables, and by means of the distinction between time and state, only the mode differs; likewise, whether it be movement and stillness, or birth and death, all of this is exactly the same.

...and thus action alone possesses such pervasiveness across all states of being, including the movements, postures, and successions of serpents; for even in the case of [verbs such as] *bhāṣati* (speaks), *jānāti* (knows), and *śvetati* (becomes white), there is a unity of existence through the manifestation and non-manifestation of preceding and succeeding stages.

Whether in a bronze vessel, in the hand, or in a bowl—distinguished by the difference of receptacle; or by the first, second, and subsequent mouthfuls, or by day and night, or by morning and evening meals—distinguished by the difference of time; and by the state of intense or mild hunger, fatigue, medicine, or one's own elixirs, it is distinguished merely by its mode (*prakāra*), not by its nature as eating (*bhuji-tva*).
For among those various modes, there is nothing that is not eating, nor is there any absence of action (*akriyā*).

However, all of this is indeed "being" (*bhūti*), because it does not transcend the nature of being; yet, they are distinguished from one another merely by their different modes. Thus, a particular activity is nothing but the universal activity, because the root *vṛt* (to exist/be) consists of various distinctions such as going, staying, and so forth.

In this way, even the emergence of opposing states—such as going and staying, or existing and dying—is merely the vibration of the universal becoming (*bhavana*) itself, which is differentiated only by its modes. He concludes this point: "Or rather, all of this is [the universal]"; that is to say, it is nothing but action (*kriyā*).

Therefore, since the roots *asti*, *bhavati*, *vidyati*, *padyati*, and *vartati* have the same meaning and yet differ in their modes of expression, there is no lack of generality in their specific activity; this is like the specific instances of "eating" (*bhujiviśeṣa*) which, though distinct in mode, are not different from the general category of "eating" (*bhujisāmānya*).
See page 126, line 24:
*°māpāyāntarbhāvidayiṣya°* (in manuscript *ya*).
And that very state of ultimate limit— that indeed is the limit?
O Bhavabhedavid!
What would be the specific distinction between the states of Bhairava, Bhairavī, and Liṅga? Ya.
Because difference is not accepted [as real], Yaśomitra says:
"By means of the difference of time and state, only the mode differs; thus it is the same for going and staying, or for living and dying."
All this is indeed nothing but action.

And in this way, the pervasiveness of all states applies likewise to the movement, stationing, and alignment of serpents and so forth; for even [the actions of] speaking, knowing, and shining possess a unity of being through the manifestation and non-manifestation of preceding and succeeding moments.
[Note: This passage does not appear in the *Rātra*, *Pra*, *Sāyamprātarāśādi*, or *Nāya* manuscripts.]
The *svarasāyanā* [is] from its own *svara*; the *bhā* [is] other than that, being common to all *svara*s.
Is it different from other universals (sāmānya), or is it non-different from them? Furthermore, "and moreover, thus... and so forth.

It is not only verbs such as *asti* (to be) that serve as examples for the cultivation of the state of being a mere general activity due to their pervasion of the meanings of all verbal roots; what then? Even [verbs] such as *bhuj* (to eat), *gam* (to go), *sthā* (to stand), and *pac* (to cook) likewise possess a pervasion of all states of being. For instance, in the case of *bhuj*, which has the meaning of "eating" (*abhyavaharaṇa*), it is synonymous with "utilization" (*upayoga*); "utilization" has the meaning of "attainment" (*āpatti*); "attainment" has the meaning of "transformation" (*pariṇāma*); and "transformation" has the meaning of "occurrence," "existence," and "becoming" (*vṛtti-sattā-bhavana*).

Likewise, motion (*gati*) also pervades all existents, because "going," "moving," "trembling," and "transforming" share a single meaning. That which flows (*dravati*), will flow (*droṣyati*), or has flowed (*dudrāva*) is *dru*; a modification of wood (*dru*) is *dravya*. According to Pāṇini 5.3.104, *dravya* refers to that which is capable of becoming (*bhavya*). Thus, the meaning is that a substance (*dravya*) is eternally characterized by motion and characterized by transformation.

As it is stated in the *Ārṣa* [tradition]: "O Blessed One, does an atom (*paramāṇu-pudgala*) move, vibrate, shake, quiver, tremble, fluctuate, and transform into this or that state? Yes, O Gautama; it is exactly so, up to 'it transforms. (Bhagavatī Sūtra 5.7.212).
"Abiding" (*sthiti*) also means that [the substance] remains, persists, exists, does not abandon its own nature, and transforms in such and such a way.

Verbs such as *pacati* (cooks), *kṛṣati* (plows), and *likhati* (writes) denote "cooking" and so forth; yet even these acts of cooking and the like are not distinct from "existence" (*asti*) and so on, because cooking is the fruit of an action, and an action is an undivided transformation consisting of both cause and fruit. This is because they share the same meaning, as seen in such expressions as: "it is cooked," "it cooks itself," "the seed becomes a sprout," "it is born," "it exists," and "it transforms."

Just as a ploughshare, while furrowing the earth, reveals its own edge, so too does [the mind] scratch at the itch of the activity of all states of being; these and other such expressions have the same meaning.

It might be thought: "Let it be that [verbs] such as *bhuj* (to eat) possess pervasiveness across all states (*sarvabhāvavyāpitā*), because they do not transcend movement, stability, existence, transformation, and so forth; but how can this be the case for [verbs] such as *paṭh* (to read), *has* (to laugh), *vid* (to know), *śvit* (to be white), and *gaḍ* (to swell)? To this it is replied: Even for [verbs] such as *bhāṣ* (to speak), *jñā* (to know), and *śvet* (to be white), there is indeed unity in their becoming through the manifestation and non-manifestation of preceding and succeeding states. And thus, if one fails to understand the perspective of the *naigama-naya*—which begins with [the observation of] such [states]—and instead proceeds to define the nature of stability (*sthiti*) as falling under the previous [categories of the *saṅgraha-naya*], then that [stability] must be understood as a particular state of the substance (*dravyāvasthāviśeṣa*), just like movement (*gati*). In this regard as well, the abandonment of the distinction between action and its object, which was previously established with effort, follows from the fact that [stability] is an unmanifest state of the substance.
The action is non-different from that substance because it is its very state, just as [the states of] Devadatta as a child, a youth,
and so forth; and thus there is a contradiction with your own tenet regarding the pervasiveness of all entities.

The roots *bhāṣ* (to speak) in the sense of articulate speech (Pāṇini-Dhātupāṭha 612), *jñā* (to know) in the sense of comprehension (Pāṇini-Dhātupāṭha 1508), *śvitā* (to be of a certain color) (Pāṇini-Dhātupāṭha 742), and *gaḍi* (to speak) in the sense of a part of the face (Pāṇini-Dhātupāṭha 65, 361)—and so forth—are all one and the same "being" (*bhavana*) characterized by manifestation and non-manifestation occurring in a prior and posterior sequence.
For it has been stated that "being," like going, staying, and so on, is a single entity consisting of a prior and posterior sequence because it possesses the nature of action (*kriyā*).

Likewise, since roots such as *bhāṣ* do not transcend the nature of action characterized by manifestation and non-manifestation in a prior and posterior sequence within a single "being," they possess the quality of pervading all states of being.

Just as one who was previously silent speaks later—whether walking, standing, or remaining indifferent—the same analysis applies to seeing, knowing, desiring, hating, exerting effort, remembering, and so forth.

Therefore, there is no such thing as a "new" action (*apūrvā*) that exists as a temporal sequence; and because it is an action, the meaning of every verbal root (*dhātu*) pervades the meaning of all verbal roots. Thus it is rightly said:
*bhuja* [is used] in the senses of protecting and eating (*pālanābhyavahārayoḥ*). (Pāṇini Dhātupāṭha 1455).

"O Blessed One, does an atom (paramāṇu-pudgala) move, vibrate, and so forth, until it transforms into this or that state? O Goyama! Sometimes it moves, vibrates, and so forth, until it transforms; sometimes it does not move, vibrate, and so forth, until it does not transform.
This is the reading in the *Bhagavatī-sūtra*, and so on, for the purpose of [pointing out] such faults.
Because it has the sense of "fault" (doṣa), [the root] *bhā* [is used]; from the root *kṛṣ* in the sense of "scratching" (*vilekhana*), Pāṇini Dhātupāṭha 990; *°khati*, Praśasti.
Likewise, is "sarva-bhā-vi-raṃ" [an abbreviation for] *ādy-ekārthya*, and "pra" [an abbreviation for] *ādy-ekārthya*?

Furthermore, if—without understanding the perspective of the *naigama-naya*—one proceeds to define the nature of persistence (*sthiti*) as falling under the previous [substance] (*pūrva-naya*), that [persistence] must be understood as a particular state (*avasthā-viśeṣa*) of the substance, just like motion (*gati*). In this case as well, one must abandon the previously established argument for the distinctness of action;

for since it is an unmanifest state of the substance, action is non-different from that substance, because it is its very state, just as in the case of Devadatta’s states as a child, a youth, and so forth.
Thus, there is a contradiction with your own accepted tenet.

[Objection: Previously, it was stated that activity (*pravṛtti*) in its general sense alone is action (*kriyā*), while activity in its specific sense is [the object of] action; now, another definition must be examined. Therefore, he says: "That which is measured by many means of knowledge (*māna*) through many ways—that is *naigama*; this is its etymological derivation (*nirukti*). (*yadapyādinaigama...
ṇegehiṃ miṇati māṇehiṃ ṇegamo esa tassa ṇeruttī*).

The *naigama* [view] is so called based on its etymological derivation (*nirukti*) as "the scripture (*gama*) that is manifold (*aneka*) in its duality (*dvitva*) and so forth, consisting of substance (*dravya*) and activity (*kriyā*), summarized (*saṃgaha*) and condensed (*piṇḍita*) in meaning through concise statements (*saṃgahavayaṇa*)," according to the characteristics of the method beginning with Āvaśyaka-niryukti 755. Thus, the first *naigama* view is the doctrine of an entity (*vastu*) consisting of the duality of substance and activity; since views concerning triads and so forth constitute the second *naigama* and subsequent views, this particular view—failing to comprehend this [distinction] and having the disposition to fall into the *saṃgraha* [view] which follows the preceding method—is now described as a determination of the nature of persistence (*sthiti*), following the *saṃgraha* view.

Those previous standpoints (*pūrva-naya*) that have passed away, being opposed to the first standpoint—the method of injunction (*vidhi-bhaṅga*) or the empirical standpoint (*vyavahāra-naya*)—are the varieties of the standpoint of synthesis (*saṅgraha-naya*). Regarding that which follows them, the subsequent [standpoint] characterized by action (*kriyā*), which is stated by way of the example of persistence (*sthiti*), is expressed for the purpose of defining its own nature by those who do not discern the distinctions between the objects of the standpoints they themselves do not know. But how is the definition of the nature of persistence performed by them? It is said: "That [persistence], however, is to be understood as a particular state of a substance (*dravyāvasthā-viśeṣa*), just like motion (*gati*). In this manner it is defined.
Just as motion (*gati*) is a particular state of a substance (*dravya*)—like [the stages of] childhood, youth, and so on—and is not different from the substance, so too is stability (*sthiti*);
and just as there are motion and stability, so too are all actions (*kriyā*).

To this, a fault in another definition is stated: if it is asked, "What [is the fault] in the case of the non-conceptualized [definition]?", it is said: it is the abandonment of the fact that action is a distinct entity established through effort. Previously, by your own effort, you established through the designation of the characteristics of the action of the entity called "liberation" (*ukti-vastu-kriyā*) that action is a distinct entity from the substance; the abandonment of that [position] is the fault.

What is the reason? Because it is the state of a substance in its unmanifest form. For here, by the word "state" (*avasthā*), the manifest properties (*dharma*) such as childhood, youth, and so forth—which occur sequentially—are said to be merely parts (*aṃśa*) of the very substance, such as Devadatta; and since those parts are non-different from it because they are its constituents, it follows that [the action] is not a separate entity from it. And this entails the fault of abandoning the category of action (*kriyā-padārtha*) which was accepted as being a distinct entity from the substance.

This [negama-naya] is manifested through its very application—that which is that substance, from which it is non-different, and so forth—the meaning of which has already been explained up to the point of "contradiction with one's own tenets" (abhyupagama-virodha).
"By means of many measures, one measures; this is the negama [naya].

Its etymological derivation is as follows: the word 'saṃgraha' refers to the meaning of what is gathered and condensed; thus, the statement of the saṃgraha [naya] is by way of summary. (Āvaśyaka-niryukti 755)
Because it measures by means of many standpoints (*naya*), it is called *naigama*; this is the etymological derivation (*nirukti*) of *naigama*.
Now listen, for I shall explain the defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the remaining viewpoints as well.
They speak of the "collective statement" (saṃgrahavacana) in brief for the purpose of grouping together the summarized points.
such is the reading in the *Āvaśyakaniyukti*.
...the various scriptures state that [it is] "imagined as one," except in the *Prabhākarī* and *Vinānya*, where it reads *praktyapekṣayā*.
Therefore, because it is designated as "other than that," there is a contradiction with one's own words and so forth, whether [the term] is understood etymologically or not.
First, regarding the state of non-understanding: the state is other than that [entity], because it is denotable by words whose objects are its own [properties] and so forth, like Devadatta’s horse.

If it is argued that [the self] does not [act] because it is like the body of a stone statue (*śilāputraka*), we say no; for in that case, the application of the terms "state" (*avasthā*) and "body" (*śarīra*) would be purposeless. Here too, since there is the state of being an action belonging to the state of the body, even in the case of etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*), this genitive case is used in the sense of the agent, as in "the state of the substance. That state, which is the object of the substance's agency, shows itself to be of the nature of a non-action because the self is inactive; it is a state consisting of the prevention of movement and displacement from that [original] location. This is so whether one accepts such a designation through etymological derivation or not, and so forth.

In this context, two possible interpretations of the term *dravyāvasthā* may be conceived: either as an unanalyzed compound (*avyutpatti*) like the word *rājavṛkṣa*, or as an analyzed compound (*vyutpatti*) like the word *rājapuruṣa*.
In either case, there is a contradiction with one's own statement.

He explains this as follows: First, regarding the state (*avasthā*) when there is no [prior] linguistic convention (*avyutpatti*), it is distinct from that substance (*dravya*); the state is other than the substance because it is denotable by words whose objects are "its own" (*tat-sva*) and so forth. The substance is denotable by the word "state," which has the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*)—indicating relations such as owner and owned—as its object; otherwise, either the word "substance" or the word "state" would be meaningless. In this case, one must necessarily admit that even for a word denoting a particular, its denoted object is something else, just like "Devadatta’s horse. For example, when it is said "Devadatta’s horse," the horse is Devadatta’s property and he is its owner; since Devadatta is denotable by that word "horse" which has the owner as its object, their distinctness is clearly observed. Thus it is with "the substance and the state."
In the case of *vyutpatti*, [the reading] *ve* or *pra* is [preferred]; or rather, in the case of *vyutpattiḥ*, [the reading] *pra* is [preferred];
[and in the case of] *āditi-viṣa*, [the reading] *pra* is [preferred].
In this context, [the reading] *ṣaṣṭhyaviṣayeṇa* (from Bhā) is superior to *ṣaṣṭhyaviṣayiṇo* (from Ya),
and *dviśeṣa* (from Bhā) is superior [to other variants].
Is it a distinction here? Is it a distinction of that here?
By that which is poisonous, belonging to the master, in the domain of "svādi" and so forth?

If it should be thought: "It is like the body of a stone statue (*śilāputraka*)," that is to say, just as in the expression "the body of a stone statue," even though the body is not other than the stone statue, we observe that it is denotable by words whose objects are [qualities] such as "own" (*sva*) and so forth; therefore, [your reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

And this is not so, because the employment of both the words "state" (*avasthā*) and "body" (*śarīra*) would be purposeless. If the body of the stone-son (*śilāputraka*) were non-different from the stone-son himself—such that "the stone-son is the body" and "the body is the stone-son"—then, like the words "jar" (*ghaṭa*) and "pot" (*kuṭa*), they would be mere synonyms. Consequently, for a listener who already understands the referent, the employment of either one would be redundant due to the meaning already being conveyed. Likewise, since the state is nothing but the substance (*dravya*), the expression "the substance's state" would render one of the two terms redundant. Therefore, because one of the two would be redundant, this [position] is not tenable; thus, the argument regarding the stone-son’s body is not inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

Furthermore, here too, [the claim that] it is an action (*kriyā*) due to being a state of the body (*śarīrāvasthā*) is incorrect. Have we not already established that every entity consists of both substance (*dravya*) and action?

Therefore, in this case as well—[when one says] "it is worn away by the *śilāputraka* (grinding stone)," or "it is a body (*śarīra*) because of its perishability (*śarārutva*), thus it becomes perishable," or "it is made perishable by that which is perishable"—this does not transcend the designation of substance and action.

Likewise, in the cases "the state of the substance" (*dravyāvasthā*), "the substance abides" (*dravyam avatiṣṭhate*), or "one abides by means of the substance" (*dravyeṇa avasthīyate*), since abiding does not transcend the nature of action, it is therefore simply something other [than the substance].
Thus, first, regarding the lack of etymological derivation:
from "son" (*putraka*), [the term] *śilāputraka* (stone-son) [is derived]; the body of the stone-son is indeed just a body.

In the case of the word *śilāputrakasya śarīram* (the body of a stone-son), even when analyzed as *śilāputraka eva śarīram*, *śarīram eva bhāvaḥ*, and so forth, because it is a compound word (*sāmāsikapada*), and because the compound is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), and because the genitive is prescribed [to denote] the agent (*kartṛ*), this genitive refers to the agent; thus, "this is the state of the substance" (*dravyasyāvasthā*) or "the substance abides" (*dravyam avatiṣṭhate*), and so on, as explained previously.

The passage beginning with "sā yadviṣayam" and so forth, up to "tadanyagativicalanapratibandhātmikāmavasthāṃ darśayati," shows that this sixth [category]—the substance whose agency (*kartṛtva*) has a particular object and which, as a means (*sādhana*), accomplishes a particular action—indicates that state (*avasthā*) which consists in the prevention of movement toward anything other than that [object]. This is how it will be connected: it indicates that state-action (*avasthānakriyā*) which is a distinct entity from that substance.

What is the reason? Because the self is devoid of action; since that substance (*dravya*) is itself inactive, and because there can be no agency on the part of an agent without action, the genitive case would not apply to the agent. Therefore, "movement elsewhere than from that substance" means the movement of something other [than the substance], a displacement from the substance. This follows by the force of your own mental construction, due to the necessity of the meaning of the word *dravya* as a reality that cannot be abandoned. Consequently, there arises the consequence of movement, stability, and so forth, as actions distinct from the substance; or else, the substance is "becoming" (*bhavati bhavanam*), and thus its establishment as both substance and action is proven through the etymological derivation of root and suffix according to their respective meanings, owing to the difference between the agent and the process of becoming (*bhāvanā*).

Furthermore, as for that which was stated—that "staying" (sthiti) is a conjunction with a location that is non-distinct [from its prior state]—that is not tenable, except for the word "or" (vā), because there is no contradiction between two [explanations].

The modification of motion (parispanda-pariṇati) is the departure from the previous state of indifference (audāsīnya-avasthā), or rather, it is the obstruction of those two—the movement of another and the displacement—from the state of being a different action.
This is the nature of the action of staying; it consists in the obstruction of the movement and displacement caused by another. He demonstrates this by means of the sixth case.
Alternatively, "movement to that or another" means movement—that is, motion—necessarily toward either that [original place] or another. The rest is as before.

In the previous explanation, there was a distinction between these two: "movement" was the reaching of another location, while "motion" was activity even within one's own field; here, however, the distinction is that there is no such difference.

Therefore, if it is a substance (*dravya*) both when there is manifestation (*vyutpatti*) and when there is non-manifestation (*avyutpatti*), then it contradicts [the claim] that it is a state (*avasthā*); if it is a state, then it contradicts [the claim] that it is a substance.
Because this is observed to be so in the world, as indicated by the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), there is a contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Likewise, because it is an object of inference, there is a contradiction with inference; and because it is conventionally established as such, there is a contradiction with conventional usage.
Thus, the definition of action as "a particular state of a substance" is untenable due to contradictions with accepted tenets and other such factors.

Since the [definitions] "that which accomplishes time" (*kālasādhana*) and "the state of being" (*bhāva*) do not cover cases such as those beginning with *krī*, they have been rejected by those very [authorities] as being non-definitive; thus,
the genitive case would apply in [the phrase] *anyām anyatra*.

However, due to the adherence to your own mental conception (*manoratha*), by the force of the very principle that [a substance] is not to be abandoned and is considered as such, there follows the occurrence of actions such as motion and persistence, which are distinct from the substance itself—this being because of the etymological derivation of the meanings of roots and suffixes according to the rule that "a substance (*dravya*) is that which is to become (*bhavya*) or the act of becoming (*bhavana*"), whereby both substance and action are established through the difference between the agent (*kartṛ*) and the process of becoming (*bhāvanā*).
As for what was further stated—that "persistence is a conjunction with an unchanging location"—that is not tenable, except for the word *vā* (or), because there is no contradiction between the two;
for how could that [persistence] be other than motion?

The two definitions intended here for action (*kriyā*) are: "existence (*bhāva*) as connected with the times of past, future, and present," and "existence as connected with the factors of action (*sādhana*), such as agent (*kartṛ*) and object (*karman*).
[This is stated] because of the persistence of your own mental construction, and so forth.

Action is merely a state of the substance and not a separate entity; this desire of yours, who follow the Sāṅkhya doctrine, to convince others—that such is the case—is untenable, because, as has been stated, there is everywhere the occurrence of the substance’s attainment of the nature of action.

Furthermore, even though we have turned our attention toward the mere substance (*dravya*) in accordance with your own desire, and even though we have set aside the term "state" (*avasthā*) despite it being heard, and even though—our hearts having been melted by compassion for you—we say nothing [against you], nevertheless, by the force of logic itself, and by virtue of the meaning of the word *dravya* as that reality which you hold to be non-abandonable, the following occurs: for you, the Sāṅkhya, the reality (*tattva*) held to be worthy of not being abandoned is indeed the object (*artha*) of *dravya*; and by the power of the word *dravya* which denotes that, and by the power of its meaning, there follows once again the occurrence of actions such as going (*gati*) and staying (*sthiti*), which are distinct from the substance. That action having occurred, why? Because [the definition] "it becomes" (*bhavati*) or "the state of becoming" (*bhavanam*) is the object of what is to be produced (*bhavya*); and according to Pāṇini 5.3.104, *dravya* [is used] in the sense of *bhavya*.
3.104. Whether the word *bhavya* denotes the agent (*kartṛ*) or the action/state (*bhāva*), the same applies to the word *dravya*.

Since the word *dravya* has the sense of "that which is to be" (*bhavya*), the etymological derivation of the meaning of the base and the suffix is necessarily required. Consequently, from this derivation of the meanings of the base and the suffix, the distinction between substance (*dravya*) and action (*kriyā*) is established: because the meaning of the base is action, and the meaning of the suffix is substance.

If it is asked how this derivation occurs, it is said: due to the distinction between the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*). That which is brought about is action (*kriyā*); that which comes into being is substance (*dravya*). That which is brought about by that becoming entity is the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛtyartha*), namely *bhāva* (becoming); that which comes into being is the agent (*kartṛ*). Therefore, because of the multiplicity of agent and becoming, and because of the multiplicity of substance and action, duality is established—otherwise it would not be. Thus, it has been rightly stated that duality is established by the force of the subject matter arising from the perspective (*naya*), by virtue of the meaning of the word "substance" (*dravya-śabda*), and by virtue of words such as "that which is to be" (*bhavya*) and "that which becomes" (*bhavati*).

Furthermore, as for this definition stated—that "stasis" (sthiti) is conjunction with a location that is non-distinct [from its prior state]—that is not tenable, even when excluding the word "or" (vā). In that case as well, the word "or" is redundant because there is no possibility of it having the sense of an alternative (vikalpa). Why, then, is it untenable? Because of two reasons. Furthermore, as for the second purpose for employing the term "particularity" (viśeṣa)—namely, that since all entities are always associated with activity, even the entity called "Devadatta" is not devoid of activity; however, because it conforms to the connection with all distinctions, this is not a "particularity," and therefore it is not "action"—for this reason the term "particularity" is employed.
This too is an abandonment of the position arising from the [literal] meaning of the substance (*dravya*);

for just as in that case [of the *vṛtti*] there was the inclusion of a specific term for the sake of excluding general activity, so here too, for the sake of excluding [the application of] verbal roots such as *devadatta*, there is no contradiction because of the view that "action is a different entity from substance," and because there is no contradiction with the previously stated reasoning concerning the basis of substance and action, characterized by the expression, the thing, and the action. Thus it should be stated.
With the exception of [the word] *bhā* and *pa*,
see page 406, line 7.
See page 409, line 1.

Furthermore, as for the second purpose of mentioning "particularity" (*viśeṣa*) which is stated—namely, that because all entities are always associated with activity, even the [term] "Devadatta" does not refer to a thing devoid of activity; however, this is not a "particularity" because it conforms to the connection with all [other] differences, and therefore it is not "action"—the mention of "particularity" for this purpose also arises from having abandoned the category of substance (*dravyārtha*).

Just as in that case [of the *bhūvādi* sūtra], where the mention of a specific term was for the purpose of excluding general activity (*pravṛtti-sāmānya*), so too here, the mention of a specific term is for the purpose of excluding the status of being a verbal root (*dhātu*) in the case of "Devadatta" and so on. Thus far, the fault has been stated regarding the purpose of mentioning a specific term for the sake of excluding general activity—that is, the state of being an action (*kriyātva*). Now, this purpose of mentioning a specific term is also refuted: as for the second purpose of mentioning a specific term which is stated as "at all times" (*sarvadā*) and so forth—the word "at all times" demonstrates the non-cessation of activity.

How is there pervasion (vyāpti) regarding "all entities" (sarvabhāvānām)? It is because of the reason of "concomitance with activity" (pravṛttisamanvaya). Even the word "Devadatta" does not denote an object that is without activity or devoid of action; rather, it denotes precisely that which possesses activity. Just as words such as "cooks" (pacati) have the nature of expressing action, so too even words like "Devadatta," which are considered to denote substances (dravya), possess a concomitance with the expressed object's activity—that is, its existence (sattā) consisting of all modes of being such as going (gati) and so forth.

Consequently, like [the words] *pacati* and so forth, words such as *devadatta* would also be denoters of action; therefore, by the rule "a verbal root is that which denotes action" (Pāṇini 1.3.1), they too would receive the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of 'verbal root' (*dhātu*). However, this is precluded because the inclusion of the specific term ['action'] has the force of excluding such cases, whereby no such distinction [of being a root] occurs.

But why is it said that [terms] such as "Devadatta" are not *viśeṣas* (particulars)? It is because this is not a *viśeṣa* due to its conformity with the relation to all differences (*sarvabhedasambandhānuguṇyāt*). For, through its connection with all differences—such as being a lion, a paṭhi, or a gami—the application of the term "Devadatta" conforms to them; thus, this is merely a general application (*pravṛttisāmānya*), just like the word "existence" (*bhavana*). This remains so even though there exists a particularity of the states of "being" and "not being," because the particle *tu* has the sense of emphasizing a distinction (*viśeṣārthatvāt*).

Therefore, he concludes that Devadatta and others are not "action" (*kriyā*) because the word *iti* signifies completion; the inclusion of the term "particular" (*viśeṣa*) is for this purpose, serving as a summary of the subject at hand: action is a particular activity (*pravṛtti-viśeṣa*), not activity in general. Thus, neither mere existence (*bhavana-mātra*) nor Devadatta himself is action—this is the meaning of the conclusion. Now, the defectiveness of this inclusion of the term "particular" is stated: even this [argument] is an emergence based on abandoning the objective reality of substance (*dravyārtha*); for this very explanation of the purpose of including the term "particular" effects the abandonment of the objective reality of substance precisely at the moment of its emergence.

By the word "api" (also/even), the author recalls that the mention of "particularity" (*viśeṣa*) at the end is for the purpose of excluding the previously mentioned general action of "becoming" (*bhavana*). This is shown by the statement of the reason—"because all entities are always associated with activity"—and by the statement regarding the nature of the referent of the name, "Devadatta is not without activity. Through this second explanation of the purpose of mentioning "particularity," it is established that this [name] is merely activity and not a substance; thus, the substance-aspect (*dravyārtha*), which was previously accepted, is abandoned. This is accomplished by this second statement concerning the purpose of the mention of "particularity."
Others, however, understand the universal (sāmānya) as that which conforms to all particularities; it assumes the form of a particular through its association with other entities— Vākyapadīya 2.124.

It is not only the abandonment of the substantial aspect (*dravyārtha*) that constitutes a fault; rather, this [abandonment] is also accompanied by the same defects as those associated with grasping at specificities (*viśeṣa*), which were explained previously.

If it is asked how this is so, it is said: by the passage beginning with "Just as there," once the [previous] section has been concluded, he establishes the very objection as the answer, through the attachment to the fault.

The author of the Bhāṣya, having established that action (*kriyā*) is that which possesses a causal factor (*kāraka*) and aims at a result (*phala*), concludes: "Therefore, action is a specific kind of activity (*pravṛtti-viśeṣa*), not activity in general (*pravṛtti-sāmānya*). To this, an objection is raised: if action is a specific kind of activity, then verbal roots (*dhātu*) such as *pravartate*, *īhate*, and *ceṣṭate* would not receive the designation of "verbal root" (*dhātusaṃjñā*), because only those denoting action are verbal roots, and these [words] are not actions since they denote a specific kind of activity. Just as the inclusion of the term "specific" (*viśeṣa*) there was intended to exclude activity in general, so too here, if the inclusion of "specific" were intended to exclude Devadatta and others from being verbal roots, then verbal roots such as *vṛt* (to exist) and so forth would never receive the designation of "verbal root," because they would not denote action, just like the word "Devadatta. Furthermore, the statement defining [action] by means of its accomplishment through the employment of its own words and the like would become meaningless.

And as it is said there: "This is not a fault. Wherein do you have confidence regarding 'particularity' (*viśeṣa*)? If [it is that] when something is being employed it excludes another, then in this case, even roots such as *vṛt* (to turn) exclude particularities when they are being employed; and so it has been stated: 'Just as a universal is a particular, so too [is a particular]' (Pāṇini-Mahābhāṣya 2.2.6)."
24. Consequently, the designation "root" (*dhātu*) is established for these [words].
Similarly here as well, when there is a specific apprehension of meaning, the designation "root" does not apply to *vṛta* and so forth.

What is the reason? Because they do not express an action (*akriyāvacanatvāt*), like the word "Devadatta. Since their referent is not an action, they do not express an action; and the fact that their referent is not an action is due to its compatibility with all types of distinctions.
Alternatively, that Devadatta would be the action itself, because he conforms to the relationship with all its various modifications, just like the verb *vṛt* and so on; and this is undesirable.

Furthermore, if one were to employ the term "particular" (*viśeṣa*) for the purpose of excluding general activity and for the purpose of excluding substances such as Devadatta, then in either case, the statement defining the state of being accomplished through the employment of words other than "self" (*asva-śabda*) and so forth would be rendered meaningless.

As for what was stated—that "existence" (*bhāva*) is defined by the characteristic of being that which is to be accomplished through the employment of its own word (*asvaśabdopādānasādhyabhāva*), while "substance" (*sattva*) is defined by the characteristic of being established through the employment of its own word (*svaśabdopādānasiddhabhāva*) because of the inclusion of "existence" and so forth—and thus they are distinct even from the mere statement [of their definitions]; in reality, too, the distinction between the two consists in [substance] possessing gender and number while existence lacks them, as well as [their difference in] having or not having the three times as their object, and so on—such statements regarding the characteristics of their distinction are purposeless, since both are essentially action (*kriyā*). This has been refuted; see page 40, line 3.

If [the term *kriyā*] were to be understood as "that which is expressed by a verbal root" (*prakṛtivācyatvāt*), then the designation of "verbal root" (*dhātusaṃjñā*) would not apply at all to words such as *vṛta* when they denote a specific state (*viśeṣagrahaṇe*), because they do not express action (*akriyāvacanatvāt*), just like the word *Devadatta*; furthermore, the statement defining [roots] as expressing states (*bhāva*) and so forth that are to be accomplished through the employment of their own words (*asvaśabdopādāna*) would be rendered meaningless.

And as it is said there: "This is not a fault; for what is your understanding of 'particularity' (*viśeṣa*)? If it is that which, when employed, excludes another, then in this case, actions such as *vṛt* (to exist) also, when employed, exclude particularities. And thus it has been stated: "Just as a universal (*sāmānya*) is a particular, so too [is the action]" (Pāṇini-Mahābhāṣya 2.2).
24. Consequently, the designation "element" (dhātu) is established for these;
likewise here, it is established for [the factors] such as the "counter-reversion" (pratyu-vṛtta).
The statement regarding liberation for those who have completed their conduct,
as seen in the Yaśas and Prajñāpāramitā sūtras.

see page 384, line 1; and regarding the number of two and their separateness, see the Prakrit [text].

And as it is said there—"This is not a fault," and so forth—when the fault has been stated, you might think, "I shall avoid the fault regarding the purpose of grasping a specific [term] for the sake of excluding general activity. To this, beginning with the question, "In what sense do you understand 'specific'?", the proponent of the fault will be made to state the rebuttal; for the proponent of the fault would indeed say: "That which, when employed, excludes the other."

An opponent might say: "If that is so, then even [verbs] such as *vṛt* (to exist), when employed, exclude specific actions; for by them, specific actions such as 'going' are excluded, as in: 'He does not go, he does not lie down, he does not eat; he simply exists, he is, he is present. Therefore, like [verbs] such as *tiṣṭhati* (he stands), [verbs] such as *vṛt* exclude specific actions such as 'going' when they are employed."

And so it was said by the author of the Bhāṣya: "The fact that even a universal (sāmānya) is like a particular (viśeṣa) is an indicator [of this principle]. Thus, in the case where *vartati* and so forth are employed as particulars, they serve as the cause for the exclusion of other particulars, just as *gacchati* and so forth are the cause for the exclusion of *tiṣṭhati* and so forth.

Consequently, the designation *dhātu* is established for *vṛt* and the others. Just as this is the solution when a particular is mentioned for the sake of excluding the application of a universal, so too here, a solution should be stated when a particular is mentioned for the sake of excluding a substance (*dravya*). This solution should indeed be stated.

Since all entities are always associated with activity (*pravṛtti*), even that which is called "Devadatta" is not an entity devoid of activity. Therefore, in order to exclude that [notion], and because this [term] conforms to the connection with all distinctions (*bheda*), if one were to include the word "particularity" (*viśeṣa*) for the sake of the meaning "this is not a particularity," then Devadatta would have the status of an action (*kriyātva*). Alternatively, since substances like ghee (*vṛta*) are likewise non-actions, they would not receive the designation of *dhātu*; furthermore, the mention of "established by its own term" (*svaśabdopādāna-siddha*) and so forth would be rendered useless. When such faults have been raised, you offer this very rebuttal: "In what sense do you understand the word 'particularity' (*viśeṣa*)? and so on, up until the point where the designation of *dhātu* is established.
The conduct... is explained... is explained.
See page 411, line 2:
...because of [the absence of] the nature of a designation... (saṃjñābhā°) ...because of [the absence of] the nature of a designation (saṃjñā ya°).
If there were faults... [pra]... here, there might also be the reading "cetidoṣā" (or "ce ti doṣā"); see page 412, line 3.

If it is argued in this way, [we reply]: "Is it not seen right here in our own hearts? Indeed, we too have stated that activity itself is a specific kind of activity; and having established this, [the objection applies] to mere activity..."
...both of these two alternative explanations are useless;
nor are they fruitless, for they would also produce an undesirable consequence:

in this way, even Devadatta’s [mere] existence would have the status of an action (*kriyātva*), because it possesses the specific quality of engaging in the exclusion of others, just like the roots *pac* (to cook) and *vṛt* (to exist).

Verbal roots such as *vṛt* (to turn) would also be non-actions, and those words would consequently lack the designation of "verbal root" (*dhātu*), because they possess specific qualities suitable for connection with all various distinctions, just like [the name] Devadatta.
And having established this, since mere activity is itself a specific kind of activity, the mention of "specificity" (*viśeṣa*) would be redundant in both alternative interpretations;
thus, the original reading of the root text here must have been intended with this underlying thought.
Furthermore, regarding what is said— that we do not claim the cessation of non-coexistence (*asahabhāvatā*) with respect to the object, but rather that when one says "he cooks...
he cooks," the word "cooks" produces a cognition of the exclusion of other actions, and this property is no different even for boiled rice and the like—
it is possible that the underlying reading (*mūlapāṭha*) here had such an intention.
Thus, this same response is stated for both defenses: "If this is being said, then indeed [it was] seen right in our own heart.

Here, *nanu* is used for the purpose of seeking consent; you have indeed granted this consent, that the fruit of the seed of the teaching (*darśana-bīja*) sown in the field of our hearts has been manifested by the watering of your words.

He explains this while reminding [the reader]: "Now, we too have stated that activity itself is a particular kind of activity. As for the claim that a general term such as 'vṛt' (to turn), when employed, excludes particulars such as 'gati' (going)—that would be tenable if a particular like going existed apart from the generality of turning; however, it has already been said that it is indeed the generality itself.
Therefore, since there is no distinct particular, a generality cannot, when employed, exclude particulars, just as one cannot exclude particulars such as 'sky-flowers'."

Therefore, since there is no distinction in the nature of their activity (*pravṛtti*), the faults regarding the lack of purpose in the inclusion of the term "distinction" (*viśeṣa*) in the refutation of both positions—namely, that [the verb] would be the action of Devadatta or the action of *vṛta* and so forth—remain exactly as they were. He concludes this: "And having established it thus, 'of mere activity' and so forth" has already been explained; up to the point where it says "thus the answer is the same for both alternative explanations," this response is identical.
[In the case of] *vṛtta* etc., [the reading] *pra* [is used]. [The reading] *°ṇārthakya* [is used].

Thus, first of all, the inclusion of the term "particular" (*viśeṣa*) is purposeless; moreover, it is not merely purposeless—what then? It is even for the sake of something harmful. Therefore, he says: "And it is not without fruit; it also brings about what is undesirable."

That [action] brings about what is undesirable is demonstrated by the very proof: "In this way, Devadatta would be an action, because he is a specific activity characterized by the exclusion of others, like the act of cooking or the act of moving. However, it is incorrect [to say this] because there is no entity other than substance—namely, a specific activity that is distinct from the general category of activity and separate from it. Even granting [the premise], there is a fault: Devadatta would be an action because, while excluding others, he is a specific activity; for he excludes specific activities such as "he goes" and excludes specific activities such as "Yajñadatta," due to his being a general [agent], and because he is a specific activity while being something that is undertaken and excludes others.

Consequently, like the verbs *pacati* and so forth, and like *vartate* and so forth, there is action (*kriyā*). Because it is action, the word expressing it receives the designation "root" (*dhātu*). According to the sequence of reasoning previously established, just as with *paca* and so forth, so too with *vṛti* and so forth; and just as with those, so too with Devadatta and so forth. Thus, it follows that everything is merely action, which is undesirable for both of us. Therefore, even these [states] such as *vṛta* and so forth are not actions; consequently, the words for them do not receive the designation "root," and so on, because they possess specific qualities suitable for connection with all [other] distinctions, just like Devadatta himself.

Furthermore, since it has already been established that roots such as *pac* pervade all verbal root meanings, including "going" (*gamana*) and so forth, this proof is even more sound because the reason is proven; and because they are indicated by the word "ca" (and), and because words denoting the two kinds of actions just mentioned are the subject at hand, they would also possess the status of being pronouns (*sarvanāman*), as stated [in the rule] "or because of that very fact" (*vādeve*).
Are not *pra*, *vṛt*, and so on [also such]?
Regarding the phrase beginning with "yat punar" up to "and this property is not distinct even for *vṛt* and the others":

when it is stated that "because they exclude specific [roots] such as *pac*, *vṛt* and the others receive the designation *dhātu*," a doubt might arise in the opponent: "Do *vṛt* and the others not indeed exclude *pac* and the others? Furthermore, since *pac* and the others are included within *vṛt* and the others, there is no contradiction; therefore, because they lack the exclusion of specific [roots], *vṛt* and the others would not have the designation *dhātu*. To this, [the author replies]: "And this property is not distinct even for *vṛt* and the others."

Substance (*dravya*) is also a means of establishing an entity (*bhāva*).

Anticipating this objection, the following resolution is stated: We do not assert that cessation (*nivṛtti*) is the non-coexistence (*asahabhāva*) of real entities (*vastu*). Here, cessation as conceived by us is not intended as a property of the object (*arthadharma*); rather, it is intended as a property of the word (*śabdadharma*). For cessation pertaining to an object is produced by non-coexistence, since [contradictory properties] such as a jar and a cloth cannot exist together in one place; however, cessation pertaining to a word is produced merely by the engagement and withdrawal of cognition. Even though Devadatta is connected with all properties—such as presence, substantiality, motion, location, activity, and non-activity—the word "goes" (*gacchati*), when uttered regarding him, excludes the entire complex of actions such as "stands," "sits," or "lies down," and connects Devadatta solely with the act of going. This is because the word serves as the cause for establishing a single cognition directed toward that specific [action]. Such cessation is not possible in the case of a real entity, because Devadatta consists of all properties that are eternally present [within him].

He illustrates this: "What then?"—the sense of "he cooks" (*pacati*) and so forth is already explained; the illustrative point (*dārṣṭāntika-artha*) corresponds to the meaning of the example: and this property (*dharma*) is no different even for words such as *vṛta* ("turned") and so on. Even words such as "exists," "exerts effort," and "strives" possess the property of instilling a cognition that excludes other actions, yet they are not capable of negating properties inherent in the object itself, because words have mastery over the activity and cessation of mental cognition (*buddhi*), but do not operate upon the actual activity and cessation of the thing-in-itself (*vastu*). Furthermore, where there is an absence of any part or limb [of the action], such as "turned" and so forth... [text fragment].
And this dharma is no different even for those who have turned away from worldly activity;
to this we reply: regarding the engagement with an object...
by way of dissimilarity;
thus is this twofold method.
Because it expresses a general location, this is a term denoting substance (*dravyārtha*);
furthermore, "substance" (*dravya*) is here derived in the sense of a state (*bhāva-sādhana*), and this indication is in the locative case.
The manifestation regarding the object arises from the possibility [of its existence], and so forth,
through the subsequent manifestation.

To this we reply: the statement beginning with "in the activity of a real entity" and ending with "by way of dissimilarity" has its purpose already established, because you yourself have admitted and cultivated the very notion that the activity of a real entity is necessarily accompanied by all specific types of activity; for it was not merely a possibility, but rather that the activity of a real entity consists of all specific activities—a point which has been fully demonstrated at length in our previous investigations.

How so? Since you yourself have eloquently stated that "linguistic usage involving distinctions does not apply to a reality whose nature is absolute non-differentiation, because its scope is the engagement with or withdrawal from other distinctions," what need is there for us to say whether the designation *dhātu* applies to roots such as *vṛt* or *pac* and so forth? Since all roots do not transcend our accepted expression of a common activity (*pravṛtti-sāmānya-kriyā*), nothing whatsoever fails to be established, whether in the context of objective reality or linguistic convention.

But you, on the other hand, have established that the cognition of words has an unreal object as its domain because it is a delusive cognition, since it does not touch the real entity; enough with this digression. [Note: *abhyajñāta*, *pra*, *sabhāva* are corrections of the manuscript readings *ajñāta*, *pra*, and *svabhāva* respectively.]

The subject at hand is now stated: thus, this is that "dual method" (*ubhayanaya*) which was previously indicated by me as being of the nature of both injunction (*vidhi*) and restriction (*niyama*). Both injunction and restriction—namely substance (*dravya*) and activity (*kriyā*) everywhere—constitute the "injunction-restriction," due to the singular form used for a copulative compound (*dvandvaikavadbhāva*). This very [method] has been pointed out and made manifest to you.

Now, as to the question: "Of which of the scripturally proclaimed methods (*nayāḥ*) is this a subdivision?"—it is said here: because it is a partial view (*deśatva*) of the Naigama, this is the "substance-view" (*dravyārtha*), not the "modification-view" (*paryāyārtha*).

Among the many varieties subsumed under substance (*dravya*) and mode (*paryāya*), this is a single part of that *naigama* which possesses multiple divisions within the *dravyārthika-naya* categories of *naigama*, *saṅgraha*, and *vyavahāra*; the meaning is that it is a specific variety thereof.
This is because of the statement: "Each one [of these] is sevenfold; thus there are seven hundred *nayas*. (Āvaśyaka Niryukti 226).
The reading contained herein is not found in the manuscripts designated as *ya*.

"Each one [of the standpoints] is of a hundred kinds; likewise, there are seven hundred standpoints, and yet another [set]."
As stated previously, the meaning of a word consists of two aspects:
the substance and the action;
a sentence is a verb.
To that end, the aphorism on the emergence of the method that partakes of both has been stated: "Existence transforms into existence," Bhagavatī-sūtra 1.3.

If it is asked, "In this context, what kind of derivation (*sādhana*) for the word *dravya* is intended?", it is said: *Dravya* is also derived from the sense of "being" (*bhāva*). That which is being flowed through (*druyate*) by something, that which flows, goes, and constantly proceeds—that which is its flowing, its going, its constant proceeding, is the "being" (*bhāva*), that is, its coming-into-being (*bhavana*). The word *dravya* is derived from that [being]. Because an explanation of the derivation from "being"—which is inseparable from the derivation from the "agent" (*kartṛ*)—has been provided at length with supporting arguments, that same twofold nature has already been stated. This twofold nature, consisting of substance (*dravya*) and action (*kriyā*), is mutually inseparable, because instruments and so forth do not have a nature distinct from that [substance], and because the identity of all things has been well-established everywhere, in jars, cloths, seeds, sprouts, and so on.
The statement "the categories of meaning are substance and action" continues [from the previous rule].

A sentence is defined as "an expression consisting of a verb," or "a sentence is a single verbal form together with indeclinables, kārakas, and sentences," or "a sentence is a single finite verb together with indeclinables, kārakas, and qualifiers" (Pāṇini-Vārttika 2.1.1).

Thus, the statement has been explained, and its meaning—the meaning of the sentence—has been stated. This meaning of the sentence partakes of both, as it possesses the nature of a reality consisting of both substance and action; this has been explained in detail by this [text] through the breaking down of injunctions and restrictions, according to the Naigama standpoint and the perspective of substance.
