regarding this, it is said: "Now, [the objection] beginning with 'But by us also' and ending with 'whence could there be arising and so forth?'—[our response is] 'Indeed, for us those very things are not tenable,' which connects with the terms 'manifestation' and 'non-manifestation'; likewise, whether there is manifestation or non-manifestation of the state of a substance that partakes in an indefinite becoming."
Why? Because of non-difference and because everything has everything as its self-nature.

Furthermore, that [substance] is indeed a non-different substance, and its persistence, origination, and destruction are non-different from it. What is the reason? Because the persistence and so forth you have accepted are merely states of the substance itself; for you have adopted this position that persistence and the others are simply the states of the substance and are non-different from one another, out of fear that if persistence and the others were mutually distinct yet still states of the substance, it would destroy the meaning of all your positions.
Therefore, because they are states of the substance itself, there is no contradiction among stability and the other [phases]; it is not as there is a contradiction between dreaming and waking.
Thus, because they are states of the substance itself, there is no contradiction;
and due to this lack of contradiction, these [states] are non-different from it.

Furthermore, because they are non-different, there is no sequence such that "this is prior" and "this is subsequent. Consequently, in the absence of priority and posteriority, which one could be overcome by which so that existence (*sthiti*) and the other states might attain unity? And from what [reason] could it be said, "This state is manifested by this action"? Because their distinctness does not exist; for the attainment of unity occurs only among things established as separate, provided there is no contradiction, as in the case of threads and cloth.

Therefore, since there is no occurrence of a single state of overcoming [the distinction between states], and because of the absence of a prior and subsequent [state], and because there is no contradiction in its being a state of the substance itself, and because it is non-different [from the substance], the manifestation and non-manifestation of anything are not possible; and since these are impossible, how could there be a distinction such as origination and so forth based on the states of manifestation and non-manifestation of a portion of the entity that occurs in a fixed manner? Thus, the same fault remains regarding origination and so forth.
Let it be seen: paṃ 25; °padyate bhā°; °padyate ya°.
Furthermore,
[the phrase] "api ca" and so forth [is used] because of the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) and because manifestation and non-manifestation must be distinguished.

Having granted [the opponent's position], we state that in the case where there is the consequence of the identity of non-different objects, there is an absence of production and so forth, because the manifest and the unmanifest are contrary to the properties of manifestation as recognized in common worldly experience.

For in the world, a manifestor is well-known to be something other than the prior existence [of the object], such as the contact with water, collyrium, or a lamp, which are respectively the causes for the manifestation of the power of the earth-fragrance, the sense of sight, and the perception of a jar. Furthermore, since the conjunction (*yoga*) is the means for the action of joining (*yujikriyā*), and because [the opponent] denies the distinction between substances while accepting only the substance itself, they must abandon the properties of manifestation; thus, there is an absence of a cause for manifestation.
Or, if manifestation occurs without a cause, then non-manifestation would likewise be without a cause; thus, everything—whether manifest or unmanifest—would be eternal.

If you argue that this is not so because of transformation (*pariṇāma*), we say no, for the same fault applies. A collection of substances such as earth and water is perceived, but it is not perceived as something distinct from those substances. That which arises is precisely what perishes; therefore, by asserting that a substance is inseparable from its own states, you do not admit a conjunction or a conjoined entity other than that [substance], since arising and the rest are merely the substance's own states, being non-different from the substance and its activity.

What is the reason? Because we have refuted both the position that origination and so forth are the internal states (*svāvasthā*) of an action (*kriyā*), and the position that they are states of a substance (*dravya*) that are mutually distinct; for we have done so because of faults such as the [substance] being devoid of a basis (*nirmūla*).
Therefore, you have accepted that nothing exists apart from the substance;
and by that acceptance, the property of being a particular (*vyakti*) is abandoned, since you accept a mere substance (*dravyamātra*) characterized by the opposite of that [particularity].
And because of the abandonment of that [manifestation], manifestation is indeed *anuttara* (unsurpassed), due to the absence of a cause for manifestation;
this is because [the opponent] denies the distinction between substances, accepts only substance, abandons the property of manifestation, and thus lacks a cause for manifestation. (Bhujiyaya)
Or, if manifestation occurs without a cause, then non-manifestation would likewise be so; thus, everything—whether manifest or unmanifest—would be eternal.
If it is argued that this is not the case because of transformation (*pariṇāma*), we say no, for that is equal to the fault already stated, as it is distinct from mere motion (*parispanda*).
The *bhāṣya* states that there is a substance distinct from the qualities; the *yā* [manuscript] states that there is a substance distinct from the qualities.
The *bhāṣya* states that there is a substance distinct from the qualities.

It might be thought: manifestation or non-manifestation is a property of substance, an inherent nature (*svabhāva*) that is without cause, as it has been said: "Even after pursuing the matter to its furthest extent, when all logical proofs have been exhausted, no one can deny at the end [the existence of] inherent nature or scripture."

This is incorrect; for if manifestation were without cause, then non-manifestation would likewise possess that same nature. "Tadvat" means "possessing that"; "tadbhāva" means the state of possessing that, which signifies the state of being like manifestation.
How so? Just as manifestation is without cause, so too is non-manifestation without cause.

If it is asked, "What follows from that?", it is said: thus, manifestation (*vyakti*) or non-manifestation (*avyakti*) would be eternal for everything, because of being causeless. Just as there is non-manifestation of a jar in its state as clay, there would be non-manifestation of the jar even in its state as a jar; or, just as there is manifestation of the jar in its state as a jar, there would be manifestation [of it] even in its state as clay. Or, just as there is manifestation of the jar in a lump of clay, it would exist even in space; or, just as there is non-manifestation in space, there would be non-manifestation even in clay, and so forth. Thus, even when one pursues the matter to its furthest extent, the logical grounds for [distinguishing] attributes within a substance are utterly exhausted.
Even after traveling very far and establishing numerous logical arguments here,
who would not finally take refuge in intrinsic nature and scripture?
Thus is the reading in the *Śāstravārtāsamuccaya* composed by the master Haribhadra, in the collected verses:

"No one fails to accept [the existence of] either intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) or scripture (*āgama*) at the end. Or, as in the *Vyākhyā*: "Even for the unmanifest, there is no [failure to accept it]."
Or is it that even for the individual [entity], without [the cause],
the effect is likewise [produced];
and for you, likewise, the effect is likewise [produced]?

If it be argued that "it is not so because of transformation" (pariṇāma), the thought might be: "It cannot be as you have stated, because transformation is admitted. Transformation is the occurrence of another property upon the cessation of a previous property in a persisting substance; therefore, through the transformations of the lump of clay, the pot-sherd, and so forth, there will be persistence, origination, and destruction, and these are not without cause.
For this very reason of transformation, manifestation and non-manifestation also exist."
This also is not [the case], because the faults are equal to those already stated.

Those very faults which were stated by us regarding the two alternatives of identity and difference—namely, the alternative that [change] is a state of the entity (*bhāva*) and the alternative that it is a state of the substance (*dravya*)—are to be seen as equally applicable to the alternative of transformation (*pariṇāma*) as well. This is because there is only a verbal distinction between "transformation" and "state," since [transformation] is the manifestation of arising and the cessation of destruction, and because the word "of the persisting" (*avasthitasya*) itself explicitly expresses stability, while the utterance of "transformation" [implies its opposite]. Thus, the entire passage from the beginning—"In this way, both would be non-entities," etc.—is to be applied up to this very limit.
Therefore, transformation (*pariṇāma*) is not a [valid] refutation here; there may also be a reading "origination" (*utpatti*),
as seen on page 423, line 23.

Comparison— Now, what is this transformation (*pariṇāma*)? "The emergence of another property upon the cessation of a previous property of a persisting substance is transformation," as stated in the Vaiyāsika-bhāṣya on Patañjali’s Yoga-sūtra 3.13.
See page 20, line 2;
see page 416, line 2.

Now, because a fault is seen in [the claim of] co-occurrence with destruction, [it is argued that] "that very thing arises, and that very thing persists. To this we reply: if it persists in that manner or in every respect, how can there be arising? Or, if it is arising, how can there be persistence? Thus, as before, there are contradictions with one's own words and so forth.
Let it be seen (p. 303–2):
like threads and cloth accepted as its own pervasive essence, the prior and subsequent states of an extended substance, such as seedness and sproutness, are to be observed (p.

Thus, first of all, this analysis regarding the conjunction of arising and destruction has been stated, along with its attendant objections and refutations. In the same way, the same analysis should be understood to apply to the conjunctions of arising, persistence, and destruction that will be discussed hereafter—namely, the conjunction of arising and persistence, the conjunction of persistence and arising, the conjunction of persistence and destruction, the conjunction of destruction and arising, the conjunction of destruction and persistence, and the conjunctions of three [factors] and so forth—as long as this limit holds, starting from the point where it is said, "that which arises is the very same thing that perishes. This will be applied through the structural arrangement of the text; see page 1, and see pages 303–2.
See page 304–1;
see page 303–1;
see page 303–2.

See page 304, line 2; there may also be the reading "the discussion of the similar [case] is to be seen," the intention being that "the discussion of the similar [case] is an alternative. See page 418, line 1.

Now, because faults are seen in the case of production and destruction having a single locus—as expressed in the phrase "in the case of co-occurrence with destruction" and so forth—an alternative conceptualization is resorted to, thinking that this [position] is faultless: "that very same thing arises, and that very same thing persists."

In this case as well, we say that it is not entirely free from fault. For here too there are two possible alternatives: either (1) that which remains in the mode of arising, or rather that which remains by means of arising itself, is said to "arise" and "perish"—that very same thing both arises and perishes; or (2) that which remains in every way through the modes of stability, arising, and destruction is said to "arise" and "perish. If it is said that it arises and perishes while remaining by means of arising itself, then since it already exists by virtue of arising, why does it arise again? Or, if it is said that it arises while remaining in every way, then how can that which possesses a threefold nature (stability, arising, and destruction) arise? Furthermore, since the form of arising itself is already present, it does not arise; thus, in both ways, how could there be arising? The meaning is that it is impossible.
And there is the question: "How can there be arising, or how can there be persistence while it is arising?

If it arises, how does it persist? If it persists, how does it arise? Thus, as before, there is a contradiction with one's own words; just as in the example of the co-location of the arising and destruction of a sprout, there were contradictions such as those with one's own words, so too here, these should be applied to the co-location of arising and persistence.
The meaning is that this conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is perceived;
O God, it is perceived [by] Deva. It is perceived by Vina. Ya.
*sthityutpatti* (the reading within these brackets is not found in the Ya manuscripts); *utpattir vidhāpi* (Pra).
Let it be seen on page 418, line 4, from "vyāpī" onwards up to "prakalpa":

it might be thought that [the Lord] is "all-pervading" (vyāpī) because he pervades like the threads and fibers accepted as his own essence; for since no specific pervaded effect is distinguished, the cause that pervades all effects is called "all-pervading."

Even by you, who rely on the *dravyārthavāda* (the doctrine that substance is real), it is accepted that "the part (*aṃśu*) is indeed its own pervasive essence," or rather, the analysis of the compound is "its own pervasive essence. And that part, which is accepted as its own pervasive essence, is the very thread (*tantu*) that is pervaded, because the effect consists of the cause.

What is being said? Just as the thread consists of the part, and therefore the part is indeed the thread—whether one says "the part is the thread" or "the thread is the part"—so too is the illustrative example: the sprout consists of the seed, and thus the seed is indeed the sprout, whether one says "the sprout is the seed" or "the seed is the sprout. This is the point of the illustration.

He describes that [objection] with the words "of an exceedingly long substance," and so forth: for a substance of extreme length, such as Mount Meru, its states of abiding, arising, and perishing—existing as prior and posterior—are [the same as] the seed, sprout, and so on, which are accepted as having a pervasive intrinsic nature (*svatattva*). In this conceptualization, because of the principle that "that very thing arises" and "that very thing perishes," since the atoms of the seed or the seed itself are unproduced and indestructible—and thus eternal—the emergence of the sprout or the thread is simply impossible. Those very same contradictions [apply], or else, due to the permanence of the previous pillar, the seed is impossible.

Because the production of a seed from a pillar [is impossible], and because production is distinct from persistence—just like a sprout—everything that has the nature of a substance is impermanent and lacks pervasiveness; or else, due to the absence of prior [existence] and so forth, there would be no distinction at all. Now, if it should be argued: "That which is produced is the very same thing that persists," this amounts to saying that persistence is merely the form of production itself; thus it is stated in this way simply to distinguish it from a sky-flower.

This being the case, since that which arises is the very same thing that persists, there are no contradictions with one's own statements or other authorities regarding the coreferentiality of arising and abiding; for that entity—which is distinct merely by its states—is itself abiding, and thus its arising is simply the manifestation of what was already present and neither previously unarisen nor subsequently destroyed.

To this it is replied: Even in this alternative, because the seed—which is the subject of the illustration—or the threads which serve as the examples, or by the word "or" (*vā*), any other entity whatsoever, being long-lasting, is neither produced nor destroyed; therefore, due to its permanence, there is only persistence and no production or destruction. How then could a sprout arise from a seed? How could a thread arise from threads? Consequently, the production of the sprout and the thread is simply impossible. If one asks, "What follows from that?", these are precisely the same contradictions as before: since there is no production, the contradictions with one's own words and so forth remain exactly as they were.

"Because of the permanence of the original pillar, or because of the impossibility of a seed—those same contradictions [apply]," so it continues. Indeed, by the very logic you have stated, since the original pillar possesses the nature of being pervasive and is accepted as having the status of a seed, and since it exists as an extended substance, its permanence follows from the fact that the original pillar is neither produced nor destroyed; and because of this permanence, the impossibility of a seed follows. Therefore, the refutation—"that very thing arises, that very thing persists"—demonstrates the pervasiveness of the logic [by showing] the contradiction with one's own words and so forth.
(The reading *anunātāṃśu* is for *pra-anunātāṃśu*, and *pra-ṇo* is for *pra-ṇo*).

In the case of the [proposition] "of this [seed]," according to the *prakalpa* (conceptual construction), since the parts (*aṃśu*) or the atoms (*bīja*) are unproduced and indestructible, they are eternal; consequently, the production of a sprout or a thread is simply impossible. These are the very same contradictions: either because the previous pillar is eternal, the seed is impossible;

or because the subsequent seed arises from the pillar, its production is distinct from its persistence—just like the sprout—and thus everything that has the nature of a substance would be non-eternal and non-pervasive, or else there would be a total absence of the prior [state] due to the lack of distinction.

Now, it might be argued: what is meant by the statement that "whatever arises is itself that which persists" is that persistence is of the very nature of arising; this is stated precisely to distinguish [existence] from a sky-flower.
This being the case, [the opponent asks]: "Is it then that whatever arises is known? [Thus ends the objection.]

Now, regarding the logic of the refutation: if it is maintained that seeds arise after the stalk so that these faults may not occur, then because of the arising of the seed subsequent to the stalk, [the seed] must be distinct from its substrate, just like a sprout.

Just as a sprout arising from a seed arises as something other than what was previously established, and because of the fear of the aforementioned faults, the seed likewise arises as something distinct from the prior stalk; thus, everything arises as distinct from its state of stability. Therefore, because everything arises as distinct from its state of stability, all things in their substantial nature are impermanent and non-pervasive.

Just as a sprout produced from a seed or similar source is impermanent and non-pervasive, so too would that which you accept as having the nature of a long-lasting substance likewise be impermanent and non-pervasive.

Furthermore, because there is no distinction [between them], either the very non-existence of "prior" and so forth occurs, or else the non-existence of this [distinction]—namely, that "this is the prior seed and so forth" and "this is the subsequent sprout and so forth"—occurs. Why? Because there is no distinction. For that entity, the substance (*dravya*), is undifferentiated and not an action (*kriyā*); since the manifestation of the pervasive essence as seed, sprout, and so forth, falls within the domain of action, the conceptualization of its length or shortness is an error. Consequently, the discourse regarding the establishment and arising of "prior" and "subsequent"—asking "what is prior? and "what is subsequent?"—is untenable. And thus, it is precisely in this way... [the text is fragmentary].
In your own [system], there is the absence of the *pāda*, *ḍe*, *vi*, *raṃ*, and *cā*; elsewhere, there is no substance (*dravya*) without action (*kriyā*).
[Objection: "Substance is without activity" (*dravyam akriyam*).

Now, if it were argued [as follows], starting from the words "it might be said" (*athocyeta*) up to "it is stated precisely thus by way of its distinction from a sky-flower" (*khapuṣpavailakṣaṇyenaivamevocyate*), there would be the following doubt regarding the explanation of the intended refutation: "What is meant by this statement that 'that very thing arises' and 'that very thing persists'? To explain that, he says: "The meaning expressed by this statement is that what is said to arise is precisely what persists; that is what is meant by this statement. This is the sense he conveys.
Furthermore, this matter is stated as follows: "Abiding is nothing other than the very form of arising.

If that which is intended to abide were not to arise, it would not abide; therefore, since that very thing abides, it follows that arising itself is abiding, because of the abandonment of the previously stated [doctrine of] stability. Consequently, momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) results. Alternatively, if one intends not to abandon either [position], the consequence is indeterminacy (*anekānta*). Or, if it should be argued: "Let these faults not occur by making arising the priority; rather, that very same thing perishes and that very same thing arises," [then the following applies].

In this case as well, since that very seed which perishes is itself what arises, it follows that the sprout would never manifest; thus, as before, there are contradictions with one’s own words and so forth. Furthermore, by negating the preceding leaf and other parts, there are contradictions with common worldly experience and so forth. To say "that very thing perishes" and "that very thing arises" implies an excellence of the doctrine of momentariness and so on, because [the seed] has the nature of arising, as previously explained.

Therefore, that which is unarisen and non-abiding, such as a sky-flower, is distinct from that [which arises]; whatever arises is precisely what abides, whereas that which is unarisen does not abide. Consequently, the stability of a substance is merely inferred from its arising.
To this, it is replied: "If this were so," and so forth, up to "the consequence of momentariness."

In that case, this interpretation follows: the word *yad* (in *yadeva*) has the sense of *yasmāt* (because), owing to its indeclinable nature; thus, "from whatever [cause] it arises, from that very same [cause] it persists. Consequently, just as there was previously the identity of the producer and the locus (*utpattṛ-sthātr-aikya*), there now results the identity of arising and persisting (*utpatti-sthity-ekyāpatti*). Therefore, it follows that arising itself is persistence. Why? Because of the abandonment of the stated [notion of] persistence. By one who infers that "arising itself is persistence," persistence is reduced to arising alone; thus, that which was previously stated—namely, that persistence is the prior and subsequent states of an extended substance, like a thread in a cloth, and is accepted as being all-pervasive and independent—that would be abandoned. Due to that abandonment, arising itself is persistence, and not some distinct persistence at all; hence, the consequence of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) follows. It is thereby stated that "everything is momentary," in the sense that "it arises, it arises, and nothing whatsoever persists."

It might be thought: "Let there not be the fault of momentariness; therefore, let it be accepted that [an entity] persists in one way and arises in another. Consequently, if you intend not to abandon either [position], you fall into the error of non-absolutism (*anekānta*). If you do not relinquish both persistence and arising, then your own system of Syādvāda—which maintains the reality of non-absolutist entities—would result in a contradiction of your own tenets. This is precisely what is being stated.

The passage beginning from "etaccihnāntargataḥ ॰rthavyākhyā॰" and ending with "athocyeta utpādavināśapūrvatāyāmityā॰" (p. 427, l. 18) is not present in the Vi., Raṃ., and Hī. manuscripts; the passage enclosed within these brackets is also not present in the Ya. manuscripts. [mukimuktaṃ bhā.]

If it is argued that "that which does not arise remains," then it follows that arising itself is remaining; this is because the stated [definition of] stability has been abandoned. Consequently, momentariness would result. Alternatively, if one intends to avoid abandoning both [arising and remaining], then the consequence of non-absolutism (anekānta) follows, and the root [of the argument] would be that arising itself results in momentariness. See commentary 7.

Now, it might be argued: "Let these faults not arise if [the seed] precedes its production; rather, that very thing perishes and that very thing arises. To this we reply: even here, if that very seed which perishes is the same as that which arises, it follows that the sprout would never appear—just as before, there are contradictions with one's own words and so forth. Furthermore, by the exclusion of the preceding leaf and other parts, there are contradictions with worldly experience and so forth. And the claim that "that very thing perishes and that very thing arises" entails an excessive degree of momentariness (kṣaṇikavāda), as previously explained.
It has been established; therefore, as before, there would also be contradictions with one's own words and so forth—this too would be the root [of the argument]. See page 418, line 4:
*°kyātpattiḥ* (Bhā).
The origin of the [word] *kya*— see page 424, line 4 of manuscript Ya; and regarding the arising of the word *kācit*, see manuscript Ya.
In the *Bhāṣya*, there is the reading "kācid ity ataś ca"; here, the reading might also be "kācid ity utpatteś ca.
Now, it might be argued: "These faults apply if [the effect] exists prior to its production," and so forth.

"That which arises is the very same that perishes; that which arises is the very same that persists"—regarding these two primary conceptual alternatives (*vikalpa*) concerning origination, he restates their unavoidable defects and, having assented to them, abandons those two conceptualizations. Then, considering another conceptualization to be faultless, he might resort to one characterized by destruction. In that regard, first there is the initial conceptualization: "that which perishes is the very same that arises.

Even with respect to this conceptualization, a defect is stated: in the world, it is well-established through perception and other means of knowledge that the seed perishes upon the arising of the sprout.

Furthermore, for you, that which perishes is the very seed itself, and not the sprout; thus, the non-appearance of the sprout would necessarily follow, because the word "iti" here signifies the reason (hetu). Consequently, as before, there are contradictions with one's own words and so forth. Moreover, by the negation of the preceding leaf and other parts, there are contradictions with the world and so forth. Just as the sprout is denied, so too—due to the absence of the sprout—are the subsequent parts such as the leaf, stalk, stem, flower, fruit, and awn, which are well-established in the world through means of valid cognition like direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Thus, by denying these, there are contradictions with the world and so forth. As previously stated, the faults are expressed by way of both one's own words and common worldly experience. This is what might be suspected. (*Praśastamati*)
See page 419, line 5, regarding the variants *sūkādī* (Bhā) and *sūkṣmaikādī* (Ya).

Regarding the passage beginning with "tadeva" and so forth: by the statement "that very thing perishes, that very thing arises," the excellence of the doctrine of momentariness (*kṣaṇikavāda*) is shown, as before, because both destruction and arising occur at one and the same time for that which is not distinct [from itself]. For the doctrine of momentariness consists in destruction and arising occurring at different times; and this [doctrine] surpasses it.

By the inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*), it should be observed (p. 419, l. 3) that because [the seed] would be neither destroyed nor arisen and would lack duration, there would be an absence of the sprout from the seed, like a flower in the sky.
In the Bhāṣya it says *tavyasya*,
while in the Ya[panīya] version it says *navyasya*;
here, there may also be a reading *tasya*.

Now, since a fault is seen in the case of production and subsistence having the same locus—namely, that "that very thing perishes and that very thing subsists"—whether it subsists in this manner or in any other way, how could there be destruction if it subsists, or subsistence if there is destruction? Thus, those same contradictions with one's own words and so forth, as well as the superiority of the theory of momentariness and so on, should be observed as before (p. 424, l. 2).

Now, it might be argued: "Let these faults not arise from [the view that] the state of being preceded by production and destruction; therefore, let it be said that 'that very same thing persists' and 'that very same thing arises. Even in this case, whether it arises in that manner or in every respect, how can there be persistence while it is arising? Or how can there be arising while it is persisting? Thus, those same contradictions with one's own words and so forth remain; why then is this called an excellence of the doctrine of momentariness?

Now, if that which persists is itself that which perishes, then in this case too, it either perishes in that same manner or in every way; how then can there be persistence? Or, if there is persistence, how can there be destruction? As before, there are contradictions with one's own statements and so forth. Whether it be the doctrine of momentariness, its intensification, or emptiness, [the argument] remains:
"that which persists" is the positive concomitance (*anvaya*), and "it perishes" is the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).

And because only the negative concomitance is perceived within the scope of non-positive concomitance, the claims that "that very thing persists" and "that very thing perishes" entail the same aforementioned contradictions with one's own statements and so forth.
By accepting the destruction of an object that remains [in existence], there would be the annihilation of all members of the proof (*sādhana*);
and what about the positive concomitance (*anvaya*)?
See page 427, note 13.

Now, regarding the second alternative beginning with "if [destruction] has the same locus as arising" (*athotpādaikādhikaraṇya*), even though the position that stability is primarily characterized by destruction was just presented, the faults are exactly as previously stated; however, they should be applied here by substituting the term "abiding" (*sthāna*) for "arising. To demonstrate how this application is made: one must consider the alternatives—either it would perish in the manner of "stability," or it would perish in the manner of "arising, stability, and destruction."

Just as the faults were stated regarding the alternatives where origination is primary, here too, when [the entity] is conjoined with duration through the predominance of destruction—whether it perishes in that manner while abiding, or whether it perishes in every respect—how can there be destruction while it is abiding? Or, if there is destruction, how can there be abiding? Thus, those same contradictions with one's own words and so forth, as well as the [absurdities of] excelling over the Kṣaṇikavāda and so on, apply exactly as before.
In this way, the faults have been stated for the alternatives of origination preceded by [destruction], and of destruction preceded by origination and duration. (Vināśādi-tibhāṣya)
The reading "vināśāviti" (as seen on page 424, line 2) should also be applied here; thus, that reading might also exist in this place.

Now, it might be argued: having recited the passage beginning with "if [the entity] were prior to its arising and destruction," and having admitted the faults while abandoning even those four alternatives, one might resort to these two alternatives as being faultless.

In that case, first of all, the statement "that very same [entity] remains" and "that very same [entity] arises," and so forth—up to the point where the superiority of the theory of momentariness is established—should be explained here just as before; however, it should be applied by reciting the word "remaining. See page 425, note 7.
Is it said that "having abandoned the [view] considered as such," and so forth;
or is it said that "it is called *ya*," and so forth?
In this context, the word *granthaḥ* (text) is to be understood as the ellipsis [of the preceding phrase];
however, if the intended meaning is an explanation (*vyākhyā*), then the reading *yojyāḥ* (to be applied) alone should be considered the correct one.

Now, regarding the second alternative concerning persistence—that "whatever persists is precisely what perishes"—the same explanation should be applied, up to the point where the doctrine of momentariness is surpassed, as the meaning has already been explained. Alternatively, regarding the alternative that "it is emptiness," he speaks—beginning with "or the continuity persists" and ending with "contradiction with one's own words and so forth"—with the intent of pointing out further faults: "having non-continuity as its object," and so on. Here, "persistence" (*avasthāna*) is "continuity" (*anvaya*), and "cessation" (*vināśa*) is "exclusion" (*vyatireka*). "Non-continuity" (*ananvaya*) is simply exclusion devoid of continuity; that very "object" (*gocara*) is exclusion, which means it is cessation devoid of any real entity.

Furthermore, because there is the perception of only those [specific] components, even in the case of seeds, sprouts, leaves, and so forth, such designations as "that very thing persists" or "that very thing perishes" are not possible; thus, as before, these same contradictions apply by this method as well. In this way, the faults of the thesis have been stated.

But it is not only the faults of the thesis that are intended; rather, by this acceptance of the destruction of a persisting entity, all the members of your proof (*sādhana*) are likewise destroyed due to their lack of stable establishment.

For it would indeed be a similar instance (*sapakṣa*) only if there were no destruction of that very state of being established, as in the case "there is fire here because of smoke"; since destruction consists in functioning in a manner contrary to the state of being established,
in this way, even in the cases of the breakdown of the conjunctions of the triad and so forth, they are destroyed according to their respective conjunctions.

What is the reason? Because its establishment would be destroyed in that case. Just as one might say, "A donkey's horn is sharp because its back is cracked," like the bursting of space—by way of this contrast, he demonstrates the proper establishment of the proof: for it is only when there is no destruction of the established state that even the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) would exist; indeed, that proof, in order to be a proof, must exist only when the object established along with the thesis (*pakṣa*) remains undestroyed, not when it is destroyed.

What is it like? It is like "there is fire here because of smoke. For just as smoke, established in its own form as smoke, [indicates] fire as being established in that very place along with its possession [of that place], so too—whether the probandum consists in the meaning of the aggregate supported by the exclusion of both [subject and predicate], or whether the probandum consists in the locus (dharmin) qualified by the property (dharma)—in every case, the portion of smoke which is the pervaded (*vyāpya*) of an entity established [as existing], being pervaded (*vyāpta*) by the portion of fire which is the pervader (*vyāpaka*), makes that established portion known as something established; thus, the non-perished [smoke] would be the means of proof (*sādhana*) and the non-perished [fire] the object of proof (*sādhya*).

In your view, however, since destruction consists of various forms—such as non-perception, absolute non-existence, or the arising of something else—and is thus of a contrary nature, this part called "smoke" must necessarily perish according to its intended state; because it functions in a manner contrary to that state and consists of a transformation (anyathābhavana), its status as a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) is unestablished.
Consequently, because the location (*pradeśa*) itself has undergone a change or has ceased to exist, there is a lack of a locus for the reason (*āśrayāsiddhi*).

There is also contradiction due to contrary occurrence (*viparītavṛtti*): having accepted that smoke exists as smoke—which is the property of the subject (*pakṣadharman*)—the existence of fire in the form of fire is otherwise; or rather, because its occurrence is contrary to its state of existence. According to your view, there is contradiction in this way; however, in agreement with my own view, all your reasons are contradictory.

You have accepted that fire consists of two aspects: subsistence and destruction. To the extent that it touches the aspect of the subsistence of "fire-ness," it is observed in other fires and in similar instances (sapakṣa). To the extent that it touches the aspect of destruction, it is observed in the absence of the subsistence of "fire-ness" or in its opposite, the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa). Therefore, because it is inconclusive (anaikāntika), these are defects of the logical reason (hetu-doṣa).

Since one observes only the portion consisting of the state of persistence and destruction of that very fire, and the portion consisting of the location possessing it, the probans—like sleep in the case of the sentience of trees—is a property of the subject that is non-pervasive; thus, both its presence and absence [in the example] are subject to the faults of the unestablished nature of the property to be proven (*sādhya*), the probans (*sādhana*), and the subject (*dharmin*), as well as the faults of its non-exclusion from the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), and so forth.
This has been explained.

That very point has already been explained [in the Bhāṣya] starting from "ityādi" up to "svavacanavirodhā" in the Yaśomitra commentary, meaning the contradictions such as those mentioned in the Bhāṣya.
...and so forth; 2. the state of being established (avasthā);
2. the state of not being established (anavasthā); [the sequence] seed-sprout, etc., as in the *Prakaraṇa*.

For if there were destruction of that state as it was established, then even that [subject] would be a similar instance (*sapakṣa*), just as in the case "there is fire here because of smoke," provided there is no destruction of the state as it was established; for [the reason] functions in a manner contrary to the state [of being a similar instance] when there is destruction.
Thus it is also in the cases of the breakdown of the conjunctions of the triad and so forth, up to the point of the conjunction itself.
The non-existence of the destruction of two;
the nature of phenomena is non-existence.

And regarding the property (*dharma*), even if it is excluded from non-trees, the word "tree" would be incapable of [establishing] its own object through inference or verbal expression; this is the meaning of "it does not prevail," because it exists only in a single part of that. Its nature is to exist in a single part of its own object—the locus (*dharmin*), the subject (*pakṣa*), the inferable (*anumeya*), or the denotable (*abhidheya*)—or its occurrence therein is correct; thus it is "existing in a single part. What is meant? Because it is a property of the subject that is non-pervasive, meaning it does not occur throughout the entirety of the inferable.

It is for the purpose of establishing consciousness as excluded from non-trees, like the case of sleep. For instance, in the proposition "trees are conscious," the reason "because of sleep," although it exists in one part of the subject—trees—such as the *śirīṣa* tree, does not suffice to infer consciousness in *tāla* trees and others because it does not pervade them due to its lack of universal application; likewise, the word "tree" (*vṛkṣa*), while excluding non-trees, functions only with respect to a portion of the tree's own meaning and is thus incapable of either inference or denotation.
This will be explained in the eighth chapter of the *Nayacakravṛtti*, pp. 666–667; see p. 260, note 7.
Thus, regarding the breakdowns of combinations starting from three [elements] up to the full combination,

these six faults mentioned in the case of the breakdowns of combinations of pairs are to be stated likewise for the breakdowns of combinations starting from three; he extends this rule because those alternatives also fall within the same direction as what has been stated.

In that regard, there is one triadic conjunction: first, that which arises is itself that which persists and perishes; second, that which arises is itself that which perishes and persists. Thus, there are two triadic conjunctions primarily characterized by arising, as well as those primarily characterized by perishing and persisting.

Alternatively, in order to avoid the fault of non-arising—that "whatever arises is that very same thing which perishes"—one might conceptualize the nature of arising as being co-referential with destruction, and apply this likewise to the remaining [characteristics]. In this position, however, these faults arise: namely, that one thing arises while another perishes, and so forth. Just as in the case of the seed and sprout, karma and its result, or the self and its attributes, and the atom and gross earth, one must establish a threefold conjunction for each pair of dharmas.

Because destruction is overcome by arising, and because persistence co-exists with the manifestation of arising, the qualities known as *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* function through mutual overcoming, emergence, and pairing; thus they come to be designated as arising, destruction, and persistence.
In this manner, the combinations of four, five, and six [qualities] are to be understood as occurring.

The phrase "as far as possible" (*yāvadyogam*) means that there are as many *bhaṅgas* (propositional permutations) as there are means of all the instruments [of cognition]; or rather, it means that as many philosophical views (*darśanas*) as are possible in terms of their actual meaning, one should formulate that many *bhaṅgas* in accordance with those views. He shows the method by which one should explain [the system] while increasing the number of faults by resorting to an increase in the number of *bhaṅgas*, following the direction of the fault of the impossibility of the stated grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). In this view, these faults arise: "one thing is produced, another perishes," and so forth—just like the seed and sprout, karma and its results, or the self, its attributes, atoms, and gross earth, etc.
And the qualities (guṇas) function through mutual suppression, support, production, and companionship.
(Sāṅkhyakārikā 12)

In this position—that "according to possibility" (*saṃbhavato-bhāva*), "the whole" (*saṃkala*), and "existence" (*bhāva*) refer to the mere states of a substance, and that stability and the other [phases] are not distinct from one another—these faults arise. Therefore, let the opposite be the case; he concludes this by stating: "thus, one thing arises and another perishes," and so forth.

By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (ādi), other possible permutations are to be understood, such as: one thing perishes while another arises; one thing arises while another persists; one thing perishes while another persists; one thing persists while another arises; and one thing persists while another perishes. These and similar logical alternatives are to be grasped.

Just as in the case of the seed and the sprout, action and so forth, the self, qualities, atoms, and gross objects such as earth; that which is a thing is "as-it-is": one thing perishes while another substance arises, such as the sprout arising while the seed perishes; action arises while stationariness perishes; by the inclusion of "and so forth," a quality such as the cognition of certainty arises while the cognition of doubt and so forth perish; substances such as the self, space, time, direction, and mind do not arise nor do they perish, but remain constant; likewise atoms also [remain]; a gross object such as a cloth arises while a mass and so forth perishes; a quality such as merit (*dharma*) produced by acts like consecration arises, as do qualities such as latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) and effort (*prayatna*), and these perish due to the destruction of their causes and so forth, but omnipresence (*vibhutva*) and the like do not [perish].
"One thing arises, another perishes, and another persists" (Bhāṣya);
"another perishes, another arises, and another persists" (Yājñavalkya).

Having thus stated that Dharma arises from the injunctions of Śruti and Smṛti, he now describes the specific manner in which these [sources] establish Dharma; for instance: "The application of those things seen to have visible purposes, in the absence of such visible purposes, leads to spiritual prosperity" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 9.6).

When the performance of acts such as bathing, which are prescribed by Śruti and Smṛti, is undertaken without aiming at their visible results—such as the removal of physical impurity—it leads to spiritual prosperity (*abhyudaya*).

What are these acts? They are: ritual ablutions (*abhiṣecana*), fasting (*upavāsa*), celibacy (*brahmacarya*), residence in the teacher’s house (*gurukulavāsa*), the life of a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), householdership (*gārhasthya*), sacrifice (*yajña*), giving (*dāna*), sprinkling with water (*prokṣaṇa*), as well as regulations regarding direction (*diś*), stars (*nakṣatra*), mantras (*mantra*), and time (*kāla*)—all for the sake of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*). (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 9.6)

Bathing (*snāna*) is the contact of the body with water that depends upon specific place and time; fasting (*upavāsa*) consists of abstaining from food according to a rule, such as wearing or not wearing clothing during the day and night.

By the word *brahma*, the Self (*ātman*) is meant. "Moving in the Brahman" (*brahmacarya*) refers to the union of the self and the mind within the Brahman, characterized by the avoidance of women and other such objects. "Residence in the teacher's house" (*gurukulavāsa*) is the dwelling in the teacher’s home by one who is intent on serving the teacher and seeks knowledge (*jñāna*), higher knowledge (*vijñāna*), and so forth.

One who has departed from the village according to the scriptural injunctions and has not yet returned, or who has set out for the forest, is a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*); his duty is the state of a forest-dweller (*vānaprasthāśrama*).
Sacrifices refer to the *pākayajña* and others;
giving refers to the gift of gold and so forth, as well as the gift of fearlessness (*abhayadāna*); and sprinkling refers to the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) and similar rites.

There are other specific rules, such as the rule regarding direction: "One should eat food facing the east"; the rule regarding constellations: "One should establish the sacred fires under the constellation Kṛttikā"; the rule regarding mantras: "With the mantra 'devasya tvā,' one pours out [the grain]"; and the rule regarding time: "A Brāhmaṇa should establish the sacred fires in the spring.
All of this, when performed while setting aside any visible purpose, conduces to *dharma*.

Thus, in the oldest manuscript of the *Vaiśeṣikasūtravṛtti* composed by Candrānanda, obtained from the venerable and illustrious monk Puṇyavijaya of meritorious fame, on folio 24A2, such a discussion concerning the existence and non-existence of the effect (*sadasatkārya*) is found; this same discussion appears on pages 160–171 in the first chapter (Āhnik), pages 478–479 in the ninth chapter, and pages 506–509 in the tenth chapter.
That discussion, too, should be consulted here for determining the original text, understanding the meaning, and correcting the readings.

That effect which is other than that [cause] which exists is not [identical] to it, because of their unequal conceptualization (*atulyavikalpatvāt*), like a jar and a cloth. How is there an inequality of conceptualization? Here, regarding the two—the cause and the effect—there would be these two alternatives: either both exist, or the effect alone does not exist. This is because the other two alternatives are rejected by what has already been accepted, and thus no debate [could occur].
That effect which is other than that which exists... [is not identical to it].
See page 435, line 15; page 434, line 5; and 506–2. For comparison, see page 160, line 4; and 478–2.
It appears that the reading here might also be "that which exists, its effect is other than that"; see page 161, line 2.

Therefore, if both [cause and effect] exist, then, since the existence of the effect would be indistinguishable from the nature of the cause once it has reached the conditions for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptatva*), the manifestation of the effect would have to be eternal, just like the manifestation of the cause itself.
Otherwise, the cause would not be visible. (Page 434, Line 7)
See page 170, lines 15–22.

Here, an inference is stated regarding the diversity between cause and effect: that which is existent is other than its effect, because its conceptualization is not identical [to that of the effect], like a jar and a cloth. The intention is that the effect—such as the body, the world, or a sprout—is other than its causes—such as the seed or the *puruṣa*—whereas the position (*pakṣa*) being established is that the effect is other than that entity which you consider to be "existent."

The specific reason (*viśeṣahetu*) is: "because it has a conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*) unlike that [of Being]. This refers to the effect (*kārya*), which is connected as follows: "that effect has a conceptual differentiation unlike that Being. Since you maintain that the effect is non-different from its cause, there is no fault of the reason being unestablished in its locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*). The example is "like a jar and a cloth. Just as in the world a jar is seen to have a conceptual differentiation unlike a cloth—having a conceptual differentiation such as a broad belly, base, rounded body, and upright neck, whereas a cloth has a conceptual differentiation such as a square or long shape—so too the effect is other than Being. That which is other than Being is the effect. *Praśastapādabhāṣya*.
See page 435, line 15; page 434, line 5; and 506–2. For comparison, see page 160, line 4; and 478–2.
It appears that the reading here might also be "that which exists, its effect is other than that";
regarding this, he asks: "How can there be an unequal alternative? The intention of the objector is that the state of having an unequal alternative is unestablished.

In this regard, four logical alternatives (bhaṅga) are conceivable: either that the cause exists and the effect exists; or that the cause exists and the effect does not exist; or that the effect exists and the cause does not exist; or that the effect does not exist and the cause does not exist. Among these, only two are possible, and not the other two. That is to say, there would be these two alternatives: both cause and effect exist, or only the effect exists. Thus, the two alternatives—"the cause exists and the effect exists" and "the cause does not exist and the effect exists"—are the ones that can occur, and not the others.

Why? Because for the other two [positions], since their counter-arguments have been accepted, there is an absence of debate (*vādābhāva*). That [position] in which, or by which, a proponent has accepted a counter-argument is one where a conceptual alternative (*vikalpa*) or the proponent himself has accepted a counter-argument; because of that state, it is "one in which a counter-argument has been accepted. What happens? There is an absence of debate because the purpose has already been concluded. If the opponent accepts [the point], why would a debate be conducted? And those two conceptual alternatives are: "the cause exists, the effect does not exist" and "the cause does not exist, the effect does not exist. If you accept these, then my purpose would be concluded; therefore, due to the absence of debate, these two conceptual alternatives would stand.
Is it *vyāsrūḥ*, or *yo vābhā*, or *vyāstu*, or *yo vā ya*, or *sambhāvyāste*, or *yo vā*, or *sambhāvyāstrayo vā*?
The state of mind, O mind, purify yourself;
elsewhere, what great joy is there? Therefore, [attain] the state of liberation through the teaching.

[From] the *Mahāvādabhāṣya*: What follows from this? It is said: First, let us examine the alternative that both exist—that is, the existence of the effect and the existence of the cause—leaving aside for now the alternative that the cause is non-existent and the effect is existent.

In this context, the meaning of the thesis is connected as follows: if both [cause and effect] exist, then just as there is the manifestation of the cause, there should likewise be the manifestation of the effect; because, while meeting the conditions for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptatve*), it is not distinct from the existence that constitutes its nature, just like the nature of the cause itself. For example, when the causes of non-perception—such as concealment, excessive distance, or extreme proximity—are absent, the cause, which consists of existence, such as clay and so forth, manifests eternally; likewise, when the causes of non-perception are absent, the effect, which is not distinct from the existence that constitutes its nature, would manifest eternally. *Note:* Regarding the variants: *°virbhāvavasatkāryā°* (Pā., Ḍe., Vi. and *°virbhāvasatkāryā°* (Raṃ.).
Like its own self, which is a specific cause; see page 434, line 7. [Regarding] the existence of the cause... [pratiṣedha].
"Then," and so forth.

By this, even though [the cause] exists, a distinction between cause and effect is established based on manifestation (*āvirbhāva*) and non-manifestation (*anāvirbhāva*). Consequently, if the manifestation of the effect is eternal—just like the existence of the [cause] itself—and the effect is established as being existent, then because of that distinction, the cause is not "existent"; rather, it is "non-existent," because it is distinct from existence, like a sky-flower.
[Objection: But surely the existence of a jar is distinct from the existence of a cloth. [Reply: No, because their distinction consists merely in their mutual non-existence (*itaretarāsattva*).

Now, even if there is such a difference in nature, if the certainty regarding the existence of the cause does not cease, and that [cause] is of the nature of manifestation, then the effect cannot be existent by virtue of being non-manifest, like a sky-flower;

for otherwise, it would manifest eternally because of its existence, just like the cause. Or else, the cause itself would not manifest, since it is not distinguished from the non-manifest existence of the effect.

Now, if it is determined that the manifestation of the cause does not occur like the manifestation of an impermanent effect, and that the cause is existent, then the effect is not existent, because it is dissimilar to that [cause]; it is non-existent, because it is dissimilar to the existent, like a sky-flower. Alternatively, the other [the cause] would be existent like a sky-flower, because its manifestation is not perceived, just like the effect. [Objection: But surely the existence of a jar is dissimilar to the existence of a cloth. [Reply: No, because their dissimilarity consists in their mutual non-existence.

Now, even if there is such a difference in character (*vailakṣaṇya*), the certainty of the existence of the effect does not cease; and since that [effect] consists of the manifestation of the impermanent, then the cause is not existent by virtue of being a manifestation. But this is not the case; therefore, the cause is existent because it is a manifester when there is perceptibility, just like a produced thing. And the produced thing is also existent, like the cause, because it is a manifester when there is perceptibility, just like the cause itself.
But the effect is not existent; for, if it were perceptible, its nature would consist in the non-perception of its manifestation, like a sky-flower.
Or, if it were existent, a distinction [from the cause] must be stated, since no difference is possible in the absence of a distinction.

Even if a distinction is inferred, because that distinction would have a non-existent locus, it is simply other than that [cause]; in that case, it is simply non-existent, like a pot and a cloth [which are distinct from one another].
Because it possesses characteristics (*lakṣaṇatvāt*), the non-existent would follow as being a cause, which contradicts both your own tenets and direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth.
As for the objection regarding its inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*): "Is it not the case that the existence of a jar is distinct from the existence of a cloth?

For a cloth is indeed distinct from an existent jar, yet it is seen to be existent; whereas a sky-flower is non-existent. Regarding this, there is a doubt: would the effect be non-existent like a sky-flower, or would it be existent like a cloth which is distinct from the jar?"

To this it is replied: No, because their distinction lies in their mutual non-existence (*itaretarāsattva*). A jar does not exist in the form of a cloth, and a cloth likewise does not exist in the form of a jar; thus, the distinction between these two consists solely in their portions of non-existence. Therefore, since the opposite case (*vipakṣa*) is unestablished, and [the reason] exists only in the similar case (*sapakṣa*), the remaining portion of the text is not inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). This follows the same logic as the refutation of the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*); it should be inferred according to what has been stated, up to the point where, because it is not distinguished from existence that prevents manifestation, it would follow that the effect exists [even before its production]—this constitutes the first cycle of reasoning.

Just as manifestation is eternal, it is certain that the effect is existent (*sat*) because its manifestation occurs; however, since the cause is distinct from that [effect], the cause cannot then be existent. It must be non-existent (*asat*), because it is distinct from existence, like a sky-flower.
[Objection: But is not the existence of a jar distinct from the existence of a cloth? [Reply: No, because their distinction consists merely in their mutual non-existence (*itaretarāsattva*).

[Objection: Even if there is such a distinction, the certainty that the cause is existent does not cease. [Reply: Furthermore, if that [cause] were of the nature of manifestation, then the effect could not be existent due to its being of a non-manifest nature, like a sky-flower.

Otherwise, [the effect] would manifest eternally because of its existence, just like the cause; or else, the cause would not manifest at all, because it is indistinguishable from non-manifesting existence, just like the effect.

Now, if the manifestation of the cause is not like the non-eternal manifestation of the effect, yet the cause is determined to exist, then the effect is not existent, because it is different from that [cause], being non-existent like a sky-flower. Alternatively, the other [the cause] would be like a sky-flower, or even the sky-flower itself would be existent, because no manifestation is perceived, just like the effect.

[Objection: Is it not the case that the existence of a jar (*ghaṭasattva*) is distinct from the existence of a cloth (*paṭasattva*)? [Reply: No, because they are distinct only through their mutual non-existence (*itaretarāsattva*). [Objection: Even if there is such a distinction, the determination of the existence of the effect does not cease; moreover, that [existence] consists in a manifestation that is impermanent (*anityāvirbhāvātmaka*). [Reply: In that case, the cause would not be existent by virtue of being a manifestation; but this is not so. Therefore, the cause is existent, because it is perceivable and because it brings about manifestation, like an action (*kṛtavat*).

Even that which is produced exists as something possessing a cause, because it manifests when it is perceptible; whereas the effect does not exist in the same way as its cause, because when it is perceptible, its nature consists in the non-perception of manifestation, like a sky-flower.
Otherwise, if they were both equally existent, a distinction must be stated, for without such a distinction, their difference would be untenable.

Even when a particularity is inferred, because that particularity has a non-existent locus, it is indeed other than that [locus]; its non-existence therein should be seen as being like that of a non-pot or a cloth (pṛ. 434, l.
14). There is doubt regarding the authenticity of the reading enclosed within these marks.
See page 434, line 18;
see page 434, line 19; page 163, line 4;
[it] will exist, Bhāṣya.
...let it be as follows; see page 162, line 1.

Now, the second circle of consequences regarding the existence of the cause, beginning with "not like the manifestation of an impermanent effect" and so forth, extends up to the concluding passage: "Therefore, the cause is existent, because it brings about manifestation while being perceptible, just like a produced [object], that is, like a produced jar. This is the meaning.
It might be thought: "The effect, such as a jar, has been produced; it is other than and distinct from the unproduced cause; therefore, it is non-existent.

But this is not so. Even though it is produced as something specific, it exists like its cause, because it is manifest when there is the possibility of perception, just like the cause itself. Thus, the qualification "being perceptible" serves to demonstrate the manifestation [of the effect] through the absence of veils and so forth.

The remainder of the argument follows the same course as the second cycle of the previously mentioned *satkāryavāda*, up to the point where it concludes that [the effect] is indeed nothing other than [the cause].
What is meant there? To explain that, he says: "In that case, it is simply non-existence, like a non-pot or a cloth.

Just as the absence of a pot is itself the cloth—the non-pot—so too, even if a particularity (*viśeṣa*) is postulated, it would have to exist by way of its aspect of non-existence and not otherwise; thus, because there is no distinction, the impossibility of differentiation [is established]. This concludes the second cycle of reasoning, the "Cycle of the Refutation of the Consequence" (*prasaṅgabhaṅgacakraka*).
