*kalpamā* (for *kalpyamāna*).

Now, lest this similarity [of the two] result from the existence of both, [the opponent might argue] that there is the existence of only one of the two, by rejecting the admission of the non-existence of the effect and asserting that "only the effect exists."

In this context, the particle *eva* (only) is used in proximity to the effect (*kārya*). Thus, there is a restriction regarding the existence [of the cause] elsewhere, namely that existence is restricted to the effect alone, such that nothing else exists. Consequently, the cause is not existent; and so, the name "non-existent" is applied to what is existent, and the name "existent" is applied to what is non-existent. The existence of the effect is equivalent to the existence of a donkey’s horn and the like; there is a contradiction merely in the names, and because of the absolute abandonment of the cessation of the non-existence of the effect, there is a contradiction with one's own tenets and contradictions with one's own words and so forth. However, if the particle *eva* is attached to "existent" (*sat*), then since existence is not determined, the same faults as before remain.
See page 508–2, line 12;
see page 509–1, line 4;
see page 509–1, line 2, and page 168, line 5.

Now, it might be argued: "Since existence is in every way identical, there is no distinction whatsoever; that which is the existence of the effect at the time of the cause is itself the existence of the cause. Thus, there is no fault arising from the restriction [of identity], nor is there the aforementioned fault of the consequence of total equality. Even so, because of this oneness, there is an absence of distinction. Therefore, just as the cause is established without dependence [on external conditions]—being a universal (*sāmānya*) whose nature consists of the existence of all particulars (*viśeṣa*) included within it—so too, since the effect is established without dependence, being a universal and thus having a nature consisting of the existence of all particulars included within it, the effect, like the cause, would likewise be devoid of temporal succession (*akrama*)."
See page 165,
line 4: "Now, regarding this 'similarity' and so forth— if,

by avoiding the previous fault, one accepts the existence of either [the cause or the effect], then for one who does not desire that the effect be non-existent, there would necessarily be the position of the restriction that the effect alone is existent."

And this [refutation] should be stated here as well—just as in the case of the statement refuting the cause along with its respect—as an expression of faults through the inversion [of that position], up until the point where there is disagreement regarding mere names.

This being so, because of the abandonment of the absolute [position] that the non-existence of the effect is negated, there is a contradiction with one's own tenet (*abhyupagama-virodha*), and so forth; the meaning is already understood in the same way. Now, if it is argued that these faults apply when it is determined that "the effect alone exists," and that existence is not thus determined because it is accepted that "the effect exists and the cause also exists," then the very same previous faults arise due to the lack of distinction and other such reasons.
And let it be seen that [this] is due to the lack of respect for the refutation of the theory of the non-existent effect (*asatkāryapratiṣedhavāda*) at page 164, line 2.

Now, it might be argued: in order to avoid the faults stated in both positions—beginning with "because of existing in every way" and ending with "because of the equality [of the cause] due to having multiple objects"—one might conceive it thus: because of existing in every way, there is a single causality due to the non-difference between the various distinctions such as lumps of clay (*piṇḍa*), small pots (*śivaka*), and jars (*ghaṭa*). By that [single causality], no distinction exists; just as in the case of a single snake, which remains non-different whether it is coiled (*saṃvarta*) or uncoiled (*vivarta*), for its causality belongs to the single, undivided cause, and the coiled or uncoiled states are not separate from the snake since they exist as merely its own particular conditions; nor is it the case that the snake does not become coiled or uncoiled. Thus [the objection is answered].

He explains that [point] with the passage beginning "Whatever is the cause... and ending with "...even the existence of the cause," which constitutes the application (*upanaya*) because the word "iti" has the sense of a reason (*hetu*). If it were said that "only the effect exists" or "only the cause exists," or if it were said that "both cause and effect exist as real," then in every case there would be no fault arising from such restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), because that cause possesses a single nature consisting of both its own dissolution and manifestation; for even the restriction is made in relation to the views of others.

Nor does the defect of [the cause and effect] becoming identical apply to the former [position], nor is there the defect of the lack of distinction between cause and effect regarding the manifestation or non-manifestation of that which is distinct from non-existent things like a sky-flower; for if there were multiplicity, it would be either similar or dissimilar—such as "this, a jar or a cloth, is similar to that"—but when the effect is of a nature in which prior and posterior states have been discarded, what indeed could be called a distinct cause? Or, since the effect exists as the very essence of the cause, what could possibly be the cause? Thus [it is concluded].
But there is no difference; therefore, there is no fault— thus [it is said] because of the non-difference of all these various divisions.
And because of the non-difference from the various manifestations, by virtue of having a single cause;
[the world] is not different from the transformation (vivarta).
See the previous edition, page 166,
line 1: *°kāryāvilakṣaṇadoṣo* (pra.).

To this it is replied: Even so, since there is oneness, the absence of distinction that you have just stated—what follows from that? From that [oneness], just as before; for if, in order to avoid this fault, it were accepted that the effect exists in the cause simultaneously (without succession), like fire, then if the cause such as firewood were to possess succession, it would not exist [as a cause] because of its successive nature, like a sky-flower.

Therefore, everything is indeed without succession, precisely because it is a cause, just like the very nature of a cause. Furthermore, although it does not exist as a distinct entity, it must be existent; otherwise, even a sky-flower would be existent and a cause, since it is unperceived, just like an effect.
Or else, a cause would be non-existent and an effect likewise, because they are unperceived, just like a sky-flower.

If, however, just as the cause is not established without a material basis (*anupādāna*), the effect were also not established without a material basis, and the certainty that it exists does not cease—then, because of its dissimilarity [to the cause], the cause would not be existent, nor non-existent, since it would be distinct from existence; for it would follow, up to the point of being non-sequential, that the cause of a sky-flower is without a material basis, and so forth.

Because there is no distinction [between them], the effect—like the cause—is established as being without a material substrate (*anupādāna-siddha*). Because it is established without a material substrate, it is a universal (*sāmānya*); and because it is a universal, its very nature consists of all particularities (*viśeṣa*) subsumed within it. Since that effect is a universal, is established without a material substrate, and its nature consists of all particularities such as the lump, the jar-fragment, the pot-sherd, the unbaked vessel, the baked jar, and so forth, subsumed within it, the effect too—just like the cause—would be devoid of succession (*akrama*). Yet, it is perceived in a sequence: first the lump, then the jar-fragment, and so on.
Now, lest this fault should arise, it is maintained that the effect exists in the cause without succession (*akrama*), because of its presence [in the cause], like fire.
If the cause, such as fire, were to possess succession, it would not exist, because of its successive nature, like a sky-flower.

Therefore, everything is indeed without succession, precisely because it is a cause, just like the very nature of the cause itself. Likewise, even though it does not exist as a distinct entity, it is nonetheless existent.
In that case, even a sky-flower would be existent and possess a cause, because it is unperceived, just like an effect;
or else, the cause would be non-existent and the effect likewise, because they are unperceived in the same way as a sky-flower. (p. 166, l. 7)

But if, unlike the case where the cause is established without being grasped [as a substrate], the effect were not established without being grasped [as a substrate] and the certainty that it exists did not cease, then—due to its dissimilarity [to the cause]—the cause would not be existent; it would be non-existent, because it is distinct from existence, like a sky-flower (see p. 167, l. 3).
*°sthāsakāśakuśūla°* (Y), *°sthāsakakuśūla°* (Bhā); now,
[the passage] beginning with "lest it be so" up to "only Being" (*sadeva*).

It might be thought: "A non-sequential cause is indeed accepted, because, as in the case of fire, the dissolution (*saṃvarta*) and evolution (*vivarta*) exist [simultaneously], since the effect is already present within the cause.

If the cause, such as fire, were to possess sequence, it would not [be a cause], because of its sequential nature and the consequent absence of non-sequentially; this is the meaning. Since it is utterly distinct from a non-sequential cause, like a sky-flower, the cause is held to be fire and so forth, possessing all properties simultaneously present. Otherwise, dissolution and evolution would occur even in space, just as they do in fire, because both are equal in their lack of sequence."

Therefore, in the sky, along with non-existent [phenomena] such as the dissolution and evolution of the serpent-like world, the serpent itself exists simultaneously through its own essential nature; for that reason, because it is the cause, everything exists simultaneously, just like the Self which is the cause of the earth and all else.

If it is asked: "For what reason, then, are the differences not perceived separately at that very time, just as the cause [is perceived]? It is said: Precisely because it is the cause, like the very nature of the cause itself. Just as a serpent, although not existing through distinctions such as contraction (*saṃvarta*) or expansion (*vivarta*), exists and is indeed perceived as being due to its existence—existing in the form of a non-sequential unity by virtue of being the cause—the meaning is that the cause itself is perceived in this way or that way. To this, it is replied: This too is incorrect, because it contradicts other inferences; for then even a sky-flower would have to be existent, since it is unperceivable, just like the effect.
Furthermore, the cause would be like a sky-flower because it is unperceived, just as the effect is;
or, if it were a cause, it would not have come into being through such distinction [from the effect], and thus the sky-flower would be existent like the effect.

If this is not accepted—namely, that the cause is non-existent while the effect is existent as you assert—it follows that [the cause] is like a sky-flower precisely because of its unperceivability through a distinct sequential process, such as the modes of cosmic dissolution (*saṃvarta*) and evolution (*vivarta*). This is the meaning.

And this is not what is intended; therefore, the meaning that appears here is that the cause, being established through non-appropriation (*anupādāna*), is existent, while the effect, being established through appropriation (*upādāna*), is non-existent yet becomes existent—thus the cause is indeed without sequence (*akrama*).
Here, there may also be a reading: *akramamevāherā*.
Is it indeed non-sequential?
Here, there might also be the reading "sannevāsti" (it exists as being). "nohisaṃvarta" [is] the manuscript reading.
The reason [that] "the effect is not established by way of its material cause" is unproven.

If, however, [you argue] that just as the cause is established as being without a material cause because of its existence (*sattvāt*), so too the effect is established as being without a material cause because of its existence—this is not accepted; rather, it is accepted that [both] are indeed established by way of their material causes, for fear of falling into non-existence. Furthermore, since your certainty that "[it] exists" does not waver, then, because of its difference from that—that is, because of its difference from being established by way of a material cause—the cause is not [then] existent.

Why? Because it lacks the nature of being derived from causes (*anupādānāditvāt*) and because it is a universal (*sāmānyatvāt*), as previously stated; thus, the two cycles of reasoning proceed as before.
Therefore, the effect is non-existent.
[Objection: But if it is thus non-existent, then like a sky-flower, the effect would not manifest even in the future.

No, because [the non-existent] possesses qualifiers; because it consists of all existents whose qualifiers are included within it; because it is non-existent due to its difference from effects, like a sky-flower, and so forth—this should be understood as the operation of the two cycles of reasoning as before, through statements such as "being distinct from material cause and non-material cause," just like the statement "consisting of manifestation and non-manifestation. The phrase "due to its difference from that" (*tadvailakṣaṇyāt*) and so forth should be understood as the operation of the two cycles of reasoning as before.

Therefore, let it be seen that the effect is non-existent [prior to its production] (p. 168, l. 1). But if this is so, then because of its non-existence, the effect would not manifest even in the future, like a sky-flower.
No, because [the reason] is qualified by non-existence;
see page 168, line 1:
"tāśeṣasattvā" (pra.).
See page 432, line 11:
...tvādisatkārya... in the manuscript;
is it ...tvāt, asat, satkārya...?
The reading enclosed within these marks does not exist in the Ya manuscripts; [it is as follows]:
"That which exists is real, and that which is other than it must be an effect, because its conceptualization is not identical [to the existent], like a jar and a cloth, or like substance and action."

What is the state of incomparable conceptualization (*atulyavikalpatā*)? In this context, there would be two possible conceptual alternatives: either that both cause and effect exist, or that only the effect exists. Since the other [positions] involve the acceptance of a counter-thesis, they lack the status of a formal debate.

Now, if first of all both exist, then because they are not distinct from the existence that constitutes their very nature, just as the cause—despite meeting the conditions for perception—is not perceived as having a material cause (*upādāna*), so too would the effect be unperceived.

Now, if it is certain that the effect is non-appropriating (anupādāna) just as the cause is non-appropriating, and yet the effect is existent (*sat*), then—because of its dissimilarity [to the cause]—the cause is not existent; it is non-existent because it is dissimilar to the existent, like a sky-flower. [Objection: But is not the existence of a jar dissimilar to the existence of a cloth? [Reply: No, because their dissimilarity consists in their mutual non-existence (*itaretarāsattva*). If, even with such dissimilarity, the certainty that the cause is existent does not cease, and if that [cause] is non-appropriating by nature, then the effect cannot be existent because it is non-appropriating by nature, like a sky-flower.

Otherwise, [the cause] would necessarily be appropriated because of its existence, just like a cause; or the cause would be like the material cause (upādāna), because it is not distinguished from that which has an apprehended existence, just like the effect—thus is the first circle.
See page 430, line 1, and page 435, line 15;
here there might also be the reading: "that which is existent, other than that, is the effect."
See the equality [of this] on page 430, line 2;
"it is precisely the effect" is the reading of the manuscript (pra).
See page 430, line 2 of the Upādeya-prakaraṇa.

Now, if the cause does not have a material cause (upādāna) like the material cause of an impermanent effect, and it is certain that the cause is existent, then the effect is not existent because of its dissimilarity to that [cause]; rather, it is non-existent, because of being dissimilar to the existent, like a sky-flower; otherwise, it would be like the cause.

"Even a sky-flower must be existent, because it is not perceived without a material cause (*anupādāna*), just like an effect"—this is the objection beginning with "nanu," and so forth. To this, the reply is: "Even if there is such a difference, the certainty of the existence of the effect does not cease; and if that [effect] consists of a material cause, then it is not the case that the cause is non-existent simply because it lacks the nature of a material cause, as in the case of a city of Gandharvas. It is not so; therefore, the cause is existent, because if it were perceivable, it would lack the nature of a material cause, just like an action (*kṛta*); or rather, even an action is like a cause."
But it is not an effect, because its nature is the non-apprehension of a material cause (*anupādāna-anupalabdhi*), like a sky-flower;
or, if it were existent, a distinction [from other existents] must be stated, for if there were no distinction, a difference in character (*vailakṣaṇya*) would be impossible.

Even if a distinction is inferred, since that distinction would have a non-existent locus, it is simply other than that [existent]; in that case, it is simply non-existent, like a non-pot or a cloth. Thus, the second cycle of reasoning has been set in motion.
See page 431, line 6;
see page 431, line 8;
see page 431, line 9.
The ellipsis of the sentence is "existent" (sat), but the intention is not that the effect is existent;
therefore, when it is concluded that "the effect is non-existent," he says: "But if this is so," and so forth.

If, on the other hand, an effect that is non-existent were to arise, then because of its non-existence, even at a later time—following the period when the seed, the lump of clay, and so forth exist—the sprout would not manifest; nor would effects such as the *śivaka* stage or the jar manifest, due to their non-existence, like a sky-flower. Alternatively, the sky-flower itself might manifest at a later time because of its non-existence, just like the sprout or the jar. This undesirable consequence follows, yet it does not occur.
Therefore, the effect exists within the cause.

And this is not so, because it lacks a qualification. This reason—"because of non-existence"—which was stated for the purpose of establishing an undesirable consequence, is unestablished (*asiddha*). According to the statement in the *Vaiśeṣika Sūtra* (9.1.9), "that which has not come into being does not exist" (*abhūtaṃ nāsti*), there is no difference in meaning; thus, it refers only to that which is absolutely non-existent, just like [the claim] that there is no second moon.

For this very reason, there arises an inquiry into the context: does the effect, such as a jar, manifest while being non-existent like a fire-brand wheel (*alātacakra*), or does it manifest while already existent like other wheels? Because [the reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntikatva*), one might then say: "That which is non-existent is other than the effect, because it lacks the capacity for that conceptualization, just like a jar and a cloth," and so forth; yet no such answer can be given here.

If this is so, I too shall speak; for it is proper to state that even the proofs for the pre-existence of the effect (*satkārya*), when presented with their formal logical applications (*upanaya*) and in full detail, are impossible to refute, because such [arguments] do exist.

Just as in the case of "non-otherness" regarding the moon and so forth—for example, when it is said "there is no other moon," the moon is negated in its general sense as being "non-other" than this very one due to the absence of a second moon—likewise, non-existences such as "the jar does not exist in the house," or "in the lump of clay," or "in the state of potsherds," and others, are qualified by [the presence of] specific conditions and are indicated by the illustration of "non-otherness" regarding the moon and so forth. And because these things, while existing, are seen to manifest in the future despite being non-existent [at present], "that which has not come to be" (*abhūtam*) and "that which does not exist" (*nāsti*) are not different in meaning. (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 9.1)

9. That which is of the nature of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), such as a hare’s horn, is "non-existent" (*abhūta*); it is expressed by the two synonymous terms (*paryāyaśabda*) "is not" (*nāsti*) as being non-distinct from them. Its distinctness from the meaning of these synonymous terms is not asserted; therefore, its definition is its presentation by those very synonymous terms. There is no negation of [its existence] in terms of space, time, and so forth.
However, in other cases—such as "the jar does not exist in the house"—there is a negation of the connection with the house of an existing jar. (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 9.1)

10. The negation of a jar in this place or at this time is a negation of the jar with respect to its location and so forth; it is not a negation of the jar in terms of its own essential nature (*svarūpa*).
Thus, the statement "there is no other moon" is a negation of [the existence of] another moon in general. Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 9.1.10.

Regarding the statement "there is no second moon," since the moon is excluded by the negation of number based on the generality known as "moon-ness" (*candratva*), it follows that what is being said is that the generality "moon-ness" does not exist.

They explain that in the absence of the limiting conditions (*upādhi*) of place, time, state, and capacity, there is an absolute non-existence; thus, the negation of the generality "moon-ness" is merely a specific instance [of that non-existence].
(Candrānanda’s *Vaiśeṣikasūtravṛtti*, p. 31)
It is not otherwise, just as [the moon] is not other than the moon and so forth;

for this very reason, there arises a deliberation regarding the context: does the effect, such as a jar, manifest while being non-existent like a fire-brand wheel (*alātacakra*), or does it manifest while being existent like the other [actual] wheels? Because of this very inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*), I too am able to say: that which is non-existent is other than the effect, because it lacks the capacity for those conceptual distinctions, just like a jar or a cloth, and so forth.

It is impossible to state a further reply here; for if this is so, I too am able to refute the proofs for the pre-existence of the effect (*satkārya*), since it is appropriate to state them along with their logical applications (*upanaya*) and detailed elaborations (*prapañca*).
Thus—
See page 169, line 1:
*°candrādityavat pra*.
Here, the reading might also be *ananyacandrādivat*; see page 320–1.
*Ānanyacandrāsattvanidarśanabhāṣya*:
*Ānanyacandrāsattvanidarśana* (Ya).
Here, there may also be a reading: *anyacandrāsattvanidarśanasūcitāni*.
Therefore, [it is said] "investigation of the context" and so forth;
because it is an investigation of the context, that which is stated for the sake of a definitive conclusion is the *prakaraṇasama* (the equal-to-the-context), Nyāya Sūtra 1.2.7.

7. Thus, because manifestation is observed to be of two kinds—namely, both the non-existent (*asat*) and the existent (*sat*)—as for example, the non-existent such as a fire-brand circle (*alātacakra*), and the existent such as a wheel of a chariot and so forth; in this regard, there arises a doubt: "Does an effect such as a jar manifest as something non-existent like a fire-brand circle, or does it manifest as something existent like the other [real] wheels? Since the conclusion cannot be reached from that very source of doubt, for it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*);
for a logical reason (*hetu*) must be conclusive (*aikāntika*), just as fire is inferred here from smoke.
Thus, the effect is indeed non-existent;
for that [reason] for which there is an investigation of the matter, stated for the sake of a definitive conclusion, is the "neutralized" (prakaraṇasama) [fallacy], according to Nyāya Sūtra 1.2.7.

When the two sides—the proponent's position and the opponent's counter-position—are not yet determined due to doubt, that is a *prakaraṇa* (a formal debate). The investigation of that [debate], from the onset of doubt until before reaching a conclusion, is *jijñāsā* (the desire for knowledge). That [investigation] which is employed for the sake of a conclusion, because it remains balanced between both sides, does not transcend the *prakaraṇa*; thus, it is called *prakaraṇasama* (equal to the debate) and is not capable of leading to a conclusion.

However, the demonstration is as follows: "Sound is non-eternal, because its eternal properties are not perceived. For that which lacks perceived eternal properties is seen to be non-eternal, such as a cooking pot and the like.

Where a common property (*samāna-dharma*) is presented as a reason (*hetu*) for doubt, that is the "equal-to-doubt" (*saṃśaya-sama*) fallacy, which is indeed nothing other than the "inconclusive" (*savyabhicāra*). However, when there is a requirement for a distinction in the deliberation (*vimarśa*) and no distinction between the two sides is perceived, that gives rise to a "point of controversy" (*prakaraṇa*). How so? Because the point of controversy ceases upon the opposite [determination]. If a property of the eternal were perceived in sound, the controversy would not exist;
thus, this reason, by setting both sides in motion, is not capable of leading to the determination of either one.
Thus, in the *Nyāyabhāṣya*, regarding the section on "non-unique" (*anekānta*), there may also be the reading: "For the reason would have to be unique (*aikāntika*). See page 168, line 4.

"In that case," and so forth—the proponent of the theory of the pre-existent effect (*satkāryavādin*), desiring to employ a "non-deviant contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*) argument against the proofs for the pre-existent effect previously stated, says: "In that case, it is also possible for me to say as follows: 'That which is non-existent is other than the effect, because it lacks the capacity for its modification, like a jar or a cloth'—the extensive elaboration of proofs for the pre-existent effect mentioned above should be seen here. This is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*). The reply here is that it is impossible to state [a definitive conclusion], for just as the proofs for the non-existent effect (*asatkārya*) cannot be overturned, so too are the proofs for the pre-existent effect (*satkāryavāda*) [unassailable].
[The text reads] *tāsatkārya* in the Bhāṣya.

If this is so—that is, if you speak thus—having repeated those words, he says: "I too say this: even so, the proofs for the theory that the effect exists [in the cause] (*satkāryavāda*) cannot be refuted, because it is proper to state them along with their applications (*upanaya*) and in detail, just as you have stated them with applications and counter-objections (*pratyavasthāna*) in the course of the preceding and following positions. If it is your view that the justification for both the theories of the existence of the effect and the non-existence of the effect is equal, then both theories are established; for there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the negation of either one of the two."

Indeed, since the reality of objects exists in this way, one has resorted to non-absolutism (*anekāntavāda*), the lord of all doctrines, because it possesses the capacity to account for both that [reality] and its opposite, just as a single person may be both father and son;
nor is there any contradiction with anything else. Therefore, he is to be honored and taken as a refuge.

That which is expressed by the term *dravya* (substance) is its universal rule (*utsarga*), namely its omnipresence and eternity; while the distinction between its manifested (*bhūta*) and unmanifested (*abhūta*) states constitutes its exception (*apavāda*). And the prescription (*vidhāna*) regarding that [substance]—this is not a case of two separate rules.

The establishment of the doctrine of fearlessness is the establishment of both the doctrines of *satkāryavāda* (the pre-existence of the effect) and *asatkāryavāda* (the non-existence of the effect), because it is impossible to refute them.
It might be thought: "Since these two doctrines mutually exclude one another, neither is established; therefore, it is better to resort to the doctrine of non-existence (*asadvāda*).

But this is incorrect, because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to negate either one of the two, since the two means of valid cognition—namely, cognition (*jñāna*) and verbal designation (*abhidhāna*)—have as their object things possessing dual aspects, and that which has a non-existent object lacks validity.

Therefore, the establishment of the truth of the existence of objects as possessing both natures is necessarily the proof of the doctrine of fearlessness (*bhayavāda*), because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the negation of either one of the two or of both.

[Objection: If this is so, then by virtue of the truth of the existence of objects in that manner, one has resorted to the non-absolutist doctrine (*anekāntavāda*), which is the lord of all doctrines, because it possesses the conceptual constructions capable of establishing both that and its opposite, like the case of a single person being both father and son.
And there is no contradiction with anyone regarding that; therefore, let this [principle] be honored and regarded as a refuge (pṛ॰ 83, paṃ॰ 2).

That which is said to exist as a substance has "all-pervasiveness" and "eternality" as its general rule (utsarga), while its distinction into "manifested" and "unmanifested" constitutes its exception (apavāda). And the prescription of that [exception]—this is not a twofold prescription.

If it is asked, "What follows from that?", it is said: "In this way, because the state of things (*arthasthiti*) is thus established as true, you have resorted to non-absolutism (*anekāntavāda*), the sovereign of all doctrines"—this is the ellipsis of the sentence.

For non-absolutism is the leader of all doctrines, because it is capable of both punishing and favoring through its capacity for contradiction and non-contradiction with all other doctrines, like a neutral king among enemies, conquerors, and so forth.
And it is as follows: "In some sense, the effect is different from the cause; in some sense, it is not different," and so on.

Why? Because it possesses the capacity for both that [identity] and its opposite; that is, because it has the capacity for the conceptualization (*vikalpa*) of both "in that" and "not in that. Whether one takes the position that the effect exists [identically with] the cause or that it is non-existent [as something distinct], this reason—which consists of the synthesis of the two previously mentioned types of partial predication (*vikalādeśa*)—is capable of proving both positions.

What is the illustration? It is like the case of one person being a father, a son, and so forth. Just as a single person, through various specific perspectives, becomes this or that—such as a father, son, brother, nephew, maternal uncle, and so on—and is both different and non-different from those [roles] in their respective ways; likewise, he is existent and non-existent, and is to be presented through the categories (*paryāya*) of cause and effect, permanent and impermanent, and so on.
The realization of this reason is to be understood from the two previously stated proofs alone; it has indeed been explained by means of the refutations of alternative positions (*vikalpa-bhaṅga*).
The establishment of non-absolutism (*anekānta*) follows precisely from the power of the reasons presented by both the proponents of existence and non-existence.

Furthermore, there is no contradiction with anyone regarding this [teaching]. Therefore, those who have abandoned attachment to their own positions, who are free from dogmatic adherence, and who seek their own welfare—since otherwise the attainment of welfare is impossible—should recognize that this [teaching] is to be relied upon and honored as a refuge. Because it consists of a collection of methods, it should be sought by those desiring victory, just as the Universal Monarch Bharata, who possessed uncommon energy, sovereign power, and the power of counsel, was relied upon.

If he is to be honored by all and is the refuge of disputants (*vādānām*), for what reason does he engage in conflict with other disputants? Furthermore, dispute is observed; therefore, because of being a disputant, like other disputants, he is not to be honored and is not a refuge even for you, as seen from your own perspective. To this it is replied: There is indeed no contradiction between me and him, nor for you either; however, we speak because the absolute reality (*ekāntavastu*) asserted by you is untenable. We are your instructors for the sake of favoring you; thus there is no fault. (Note: *tvādaraviji* is corrected to *tvādaraviṇi* based on context).
And because they are mutually renowned as being established.
And [it] is derived from *pra* and *naya*.
Is it *ca naḥ nayaḥ*?
It is derived from *pra*.
The meaning here is that a dispute is raised;
nevertheless,
the intention is that even for you [the opponent], a contradiction with that [position] is observed.

Now, the proponent of the *naigama-naya*, desiring to state the nature of his own doctrine which involves both types of affirmation (*ubhayavidhi*), restates the opponent’s position that was previously refuted and concludes as follows: "That which becomes... and so forth.

That which exists by means of that which becomes—namely, the substance (dravya) by which one comes into being—possesses a universal state of being (*bhavana-sāmānya*) characterized by omnipresence in terms of space (*kṣetra*) and eternity in terms of time (*kāla*). This universal nature of that [substance] is its "prescription" (*vidhāna*), and that very [prescription] is the previously mentioned "rule" (*vidhi*). Subsequently, the second [type of rule], consisting of the distinction between the actualized (*pravṛttyātmaka*) and the unactualized (*bhūtābhūta-bheda*), is an exception (*apavāda*) to that very [universal]. And the prescription of that [exception]—this "twofold rule" (*ubhayavidhi*)—is certainly not what you intend here;
for there is also a reading, *°sāmānyasya* [instead of *°sāmānya*].
Thus, it is not the case that there is no rule at all;

rather, the general principle (*utsarga*) is that existence (*sattā*), substantiality (*dravyatva*), and so forth, as well as the omnipresence (*sarvagatatva*) of space (*gagana*) and the like, and the eternality (*nityatva*) of atoms (*aṇu*) and so forth, are established.

Because substances, qualities, and actions that have begun [to exist] are impermanent, there is an exception (*apavāda*) stating that the aforementioned substances, qualities, and actions are distinct from one another, from their own specific sub-classifications, and by virtue of being cause and effect;
this is the rule (*vidhi*) for those two, which is a rule of restriction (*vidhi-niyama-vidhi*).

If it is asked, "What then is the general rule (*utsarga*)?", it is the existence of being (*sattā*), substantiality (*dravyatva*), and so forth, up to permanence (*nityatva*). This is the general rule.

Existence (*sattā*) is the highest generality (*mahāsāmānya*); substantiality (*dravyatva*) is the generality within earth and the other [substances]; by the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there are also the generalities of quality-ness (*guṇatva*) and action-ness (*karmatva*) within [the categories of] color and the like, and motion and the like. The specific generalities (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*) are its subdivisions, such as ether and the rest—the substances of space, self, direction, and time—which are distinct and all-pervading. These substances possess universal pervasiveness (*sarvagatatva*), and along with atoms and the like, they possess eternality; thus, the eternality of those substances and of the atoms consists in their persistence throughout time, as do the four types of atomic substances beginning with the earthly.

By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), it is meant that they are accompanied by mind (*manas*) and substance (*dravya*); that is to say, they are accompanied by qualities (*guṇa*) such as omnipresence (*vibhutva*) and sphericality (*parimaṇḍalatva*). And the meaning is that those qualities and those substances are eternal.
This is the general rule (*utsarga*), the universal injunction.
[The source is] *Dravyādi* (Praśastapādabhāṣya).
In this context, the reading should be "omnipresent due to pervasiveness" (*vibhutvāt sarvagatāni*);
[this applies] from the passage beginning with "a substance already commenced" (*ārabdhadravya*) up until the exception (*apavāda*).

By means of four kinds of atoms—earthy, watery, fiery, and airy—which depend upon conjunction and are of the same class, dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and subsequent compounds up to the magnitude of the great earth and so forth are produced; these substances, whether two or many, produce other substances of the same fourfold nature. According to the statement that "in a product-substance produced by those very [atoms] which possess the capacity for such production, the qualities inhering therein necessarily produce another quality," variegated colors and the like are qualities produced [by the atoms]. Because both of these—the produced substances and the produced qualities—are impermanent, they differ from those previously mentioned; the same applies to action along with its subdivisions.

Thus, first of all, there is difference based on the distinction between eternal and non-eternal, and all-pervasive and non-all-pervasive. Furthermore, there is mutual difference among substance, quality, and action: qualities and actions from substances; substances and actions from qualities; and substances and qualities from actions. There is also difference from within their own respective classes: for instance, the class of substance differs mutually among earth, water, and so forth; water differs from earth and the others; and likewise, fire, air, ether, direction, time, self, and mind differ from the rest. There is also difference from existence (*sattā*), inherence (*samavāya*), generality (*sāmānya*), particularity (*viśeṣa*), and ultimate particularities (*antyaviśeṣa*), as well as the difference of non-eternal things from eternal ones—this constitutes the exception (*apavāda*). Likewise, there is difference by way of cause and effect; for among substance, quality, and action, substance is the cause of generality (*sāmānya*) [Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.2.8].
1.17 Conjunctions and disjunctions are the effects of actions; Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.6.

28. And so forth; the "exception" (apavāda) is that difference [of things] arises from the diversity of cause and effect. The "rule" (vidhi) regarding these two—the general rule and the exception, or the general and the particular—is what is meant by "the rule of rules" (vidhiniyamavidhi); it is not the former one imagined by you.
In this context, the reading might also be: "The substances that have begun [to combine] are two or many substances" (vaiśeṣika-sūtra 1).
Substances indeed originate another substance. (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.8)
1.8. Regarding the analysis of the compound *dravye ca dravyāṇi ca* (both substance and substances): a single [substance] is non-initiating;

rather, substances that are inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*) initiate a resultant substance distinct from themselves. However, ultimate composite substances such as space (*ākāśa*) do not initiate [other] substances, because it is only two or more causes—belonging to the same genus and possessing corporeality, motion, color, and so forth—that initiate an effect.

Furthermore, such things as space and so forth cannot be the material cause of substances because the mind is intangible; nor can they be the cause of ultimate composite substances because such substances are not observed [to exist];
and qualities do not produce other qualities (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.10).

"And qualities [produce] qualities," as before; for example, the color and other qualities of a thread do not produce color and other qualities—which are distinct from themselves—in a cloth-substance inherent in its own substrate.
(From Candrānanda’s *Vaiśeṣikasūtravṛtti*, p. 7b).
Let it be seen, let it be seen (p. 271, l. 14; p.

314–2). And [the phrase] "other than those that are eternal" is an exception (*apavāda*) regarding both eternal and non-eternal things. Furthermore, there is another point of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) between those two due to their being cause and effect: "Substance is the cause of substances, qualities, and actions; generality [is the cause] of substances" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.8).

The word *sāmānya* (common) is a synonym for *samāna* (equal). Earth and the other [elements] are the common cause of the three [qualities]. Although ether (*ākāśa*) and the others are causes solely of qualities, because each one possesses multiple qualities, ether and the others are a common cause with respect to the qualities. Likewise, the mind is [the cause] of qualities and actions in the substance that is the ultimate atom; and similarly, a quality [is the cause] of another quality. Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.17.
1.18: Substance is the result of conjunctions.
25. Thus, [action arises] from conjunction with fire due to the manifestation of a different quality.
7.1.5, 6. Thus, action in the hand [arises] from both conjunction with the self and effort. 5.

1.1 From these statements, it follows that conjunction alone is the common cause of substances, qualities, and actions, and no other quality is so; for instance—through the conjunction of a mass of cotton with a swift-moving tuft of cotton, action [is produced], resulting in a substance consisting of two tufts of cotton, and therein a large dimension (*mahat*) arises, as do other qualities according to their respective applications, [as well as] conjunctions and disjunctions; [this is] action. Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.6.

1.19. Having separated its own substrate from one thing, it joins it with another substrate; therefore, action is the common cause of conjunctions and disjunctions, but not of substances, because of their difference [from them]. Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.9.

1.20. If action were indeed the cause of substance, then even after producing conjunction, it would not cease; however, since we perceive the conjunction alone once the action has ceased, we consider that action is not the cause of substance, because it possesses characteristics different from those of qualities. (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.6)

Gravity, fluidity, propulsion, impact, and conjunction with that which is conjoined are causes of action both in their own substratum and in another substratum. However, effort and the unseen force (adṛṣṭa) cause action only in another substratum;
in those cases, action is not a cause of action in its own substratum, because it would otherwise follow that motionless substances could never be perceived.
Nor does it [motion] reside in another substratum, because it is brought to cessation by that very conjunction;

therefore, due to these qualities which are the causes of action being of a different nature (vaidharmya), action is not the cause of action. Another difference in nature is stated: "The effect of substances is substance" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.8).
1.22. Among homogeneous substances, whether two or many, the substance [as a whole] is the common effect, just as a cloth is the effect of threads;
likewise, numbers beginning with duality, separateness, conjunction, and disjunction [arise from them]. (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.6)
In two substances, duality is the commonality (sāmānya) as its effect; likewise, in three, there is triplicity, and so forth, as well as dual separateness (dvipṛthaktva) and the rest.
Conjunction is the state of two substances being conjoined; disjunction is the state of those being separated.
Because these [qualities] reside in many [substances], they are similar;
because they do not [inhere] in a common substratum, there is no commonality of action as an effect. Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.16.

1.24. Because the inherence of a single action in multiple substances is prohibited, there is no common effect of action for two or more substances; [rather], substance is the result of conjunctions. Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.15.

A substance is the common effect of two or many non-inherent causes (asamavāyikāraṇa), such as a cloth [being the effect] of the conjunctions of threads, or color [being the effect] of colors. Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.25.

When two or many causes in the form of qualities possess a common quality residing in the substance that is their effect, that [common quality] is the "effect" [of those causes]; for example, the color of a jar is the effect of the colors of its shards. Likewise, [the effects] of taste and so forth, as well as heaviness, effort, and conjunction, are upward throwing (*utkṣepaṇa*). Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.6.

Because the rays of the sun lack heaviness (*gurutva*), because there is likewise an absence of such effort (*prayatna*) in the case of a mountain, and because a clod of earth is not in conjunction with the hand, it is not lifted up; thus, lifting is a common effect of heaviness and the other [qualities], while conjunctions and disjunctions are the effects of actions (*karman*). Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.6.
1.28. Those conjunctions and disjunctions produced by both [types of] action constitute the common effect of actions.
Regarding the similarity of causes, it has been stated in the Vaiśeṣika Sūtra (1.1.15) that action is not a cause for substances or actions.

1.29. Thus, in this section where the common cause of substances and so forth has been described, since it was stated that action is not a cause for substances and actions within that general category of causes, it follows that these [substances and actions] also do not constitute its common effect.
In this way, it is established that substances, qualities, and actions are distinct.
"Thus ends the first Āhnika of the first Adhyāya," as seen on page 8 B–9 B of the *Vaiśeṣikasūtravṛtti* composed by Candrānanda; see page 389, line 17, note 6.

For action, which has the purpose of producing what was previously non-existent, occurs when there is a multiplicity of substances; [thus] motion arises in atoms by the power of the unseen force (adṛṣṭa).

As for what you have said—that action (*kriyā*) is the manifestation of the power of a substance present in its true state, and that substance is the seed which, despite the non-difference of substances, is devoid of distinctions through all its various divisions—that is not so. For action has the purpose of accomplishing what was previously non-existent. And at the time of the dissolution of the world (*jagatpralaya*), what action characterized by your desired "activity" could there be, given that the motion inherent in atoms impelled by my desired *adṛṣṭa* (unseen force) is absent? For that [action] would be produced by the motion of atoms impelled by *adṛṣṭa*, having the purpose of accomplishing *dharma* and the purpose of creating the world. Moreover, for us, action is simply *karman* (motion); it does not proceed pointlessly to accomplish what is already accomplished, nor does it act with the thought, "Let it be played with."

And that [quality of magnitude] occurs when there is a multiplicity of substances; furthermore, this multiplicity of substances cannot exist without the motion of atoms impelled by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*). Why? Because motion arises in atoms by virtue of the unseen force, from which the production of dyads and other multicomponent substances follows, and because of their inherence therein, all worldly effects—such as the upward flaming of fire produced by many atoms and the maintenance of the world—are established. Therefore, no single eternal entity, such as space, possesses action.

Nor does this world provide any assistance toward the manifestation of the power of the substance that is the mere seed of differentiation; for what reason? Because it has been stated: "The initial action of atoms and the mind is caused by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*)," Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 5.2.14.

If this is not accepted—that is, if it is not admitted that when atoms are governed by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), motion cannot arise [in them] and thus the production of multiple substances such as dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth does not occur—then, because that single substance would be devoid of motion due to its unity, it could not initiate anything; consequently, motion itself would not exist at all, and since the production of multiple substances like dyads would not take place, action would simply have no object.

Furthermore, even if [action] were to originate from substances that have already begun [to exist], it would lack its defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) due to their absence. At that time, being a single substance like the motionless sky, it would not originate anything because of its lack of activity; and since there is no origination, action itself would not exist. For action is conceived as having origination as its very nature; since that nature is absent, action is non-existent like a flower in the sky. Due to its non-existence, the various substances such as dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth would not be substances. Because they do not exist, action would be devoid of an object. If it does not have multiple substances as its object, then—precisely because of the impossibility of multiplicity due to the absence of origination—it also cannot have a single substance such as an atom or space as its object, even though you claim it does. That [action] desired by you, which is distinct from the action we accept, would be like the eternal, single, and motionless sky, because there is no origination in them. Since qualities originate from a substance that possesses no qualities, and according to our view qualities and actions are without qualities and without activity, yet according to your view qualities and the rest are themselves actions, and since action—which is primary to a substance—is itself inactive, it is rightly said that action is devoid of an object.
