Just as motion (*karman*) arises in earth due to pushing, striking, conjunction, or conjunction with what is conjoined, as well as from the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), so too it arises in fire and air; this is non-restricted motion (*aniyata-karman*).

But these are restricted: the upward flaming of fire, the horizontal blowing of air, and the initial action of atoms and the mind—these indeed are caused by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*). Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 5.2.18.

14. If fire were to remain stationary or move horizontally, there would be no burning of what is being cooked, nor would there be cooking by water. Likewise, if air did not move horizontally, there would be no blowing of substances being purified, and no ignition of fire. Furthermore, at the beginning of creation, there would be no initial action of mutual approach among the atoms of earth and other elements for souls whose bodies have perished. Similarly, at the beginning of creation, there would be no initial action of the mind for yogins who have attained mastery over the earth and, at the end of the kalpa, having separated the mind from the body through effort and intent, remain [in that state], unless it were due to *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit).

Therefore, the upward flaming of fire, the horizontal blowing of air, the movement of atoms toward [other atoms], and the initial movement of the mind—these are produced by the unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) of living beings.
The action of the mind has been explained by means of the action of the hand. Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 5.2.18.

15. Just as there is motion in the hand due to both conjunction with the self and effort, so too there is motion of the mind due to conjunction with the self and the mind and due to effort; this is the action of one possessing a body. In that regard, for one who is awake, [the action arises] from effort preceded by desire and aversion, whereas at the time of awakening [from sleep], it arises from that which is preceded by the life-force (*jīvana*). Since conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is *yoga*, and that is the effect of action, therefore action is a limb of *yoga*. Furthermore, *yoga* and *mokṣa* are discussed even within the context of the authority over action: "Pleasure and pain arise from the contact of the self, the senses, the mind, and objects; the non-undertaking thereof [is the means to liberation]. Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 5.2.18.

16. Because the conjunction of the self, the senses, the mind, and the objects produces pleasure and pain by being the cause of cognition, therefore there is the non-commencement of that; the "non-commencement" of that conjunction is said to be its non-arising.
For instance: when the mind is situated in the self, there is an absence of pleasure and pain in the body; that is *yoga*. Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 5.2.18.

17. For when the mind is established in the self (*ātman*) and not in the senses, then, because the fourfold contact [of sense-organ, object, self, and mind] does not commence, there is an absence of pleasure and pain—which are its effects. This conjunction of the self with the mind, which exists in one whose body is still present and which depends upon the restraint of the vital air (*vāyu*), is *yoga*. Why has the practice of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), a limb of *yoga*, not been mentioned? By the action of the body, the action of the self is explained (VS 5.2.18). Here, by the word "self" (*ātman*), the vital air is meant; just as there is action in the hand due to the conjunction of the self and effort, so too there is the action of breath control due to the conjunction of the self and the vital air, and from effort.
Going away, coming toward, the conjunction of what has been eaten and drunk, and conjunctions with other effects—these are caused by the unseen force (adṛṣṭa). Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 5.2.18.

19. At the time of death, the departure or exit of the mind from the previous body is *apasarpaṇa*; the connection of the mind with another body is *upasarpaṇa*. The connection of the mind, situated in the womb, with the food and drink consumed by the mother that enters through the channels starting from the semen and blood is the "conjunction with what is eaten and drunk" (*aśitapīta-saṃyoga*). Those connections within a single cycle of existence, such as the stages of the embryo—*kalala*, *arbuda*, *māṃsa*, *peśī*, *ghana*, and so forth—are "internal conjunctions for the sake of an effect" (*kāryārthā antarasaṃyogāḥ*). These, beginning with *apasarpaṇa* and the others, are brought about solely by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), not by volitional effort (*prayatna*).
"In the absence of that, there is the absence of conjunction; its non-manifestation is liberation" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 5.2.20).

Thus, in the absence of *adṛṣṭa*—which has beginningless descent (*apasarpaṇa*) and so forth as its cause—there is the absence of the conjunction of the self and the mind known as "life," and the non-manifestation of another body; this is liberation.

Because darkness is the cause of the non-arising of all cognition due to its being an activity of *tamas*, it is a mere absence (*abhāvamātra*). Regarding this absence as darkness, Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 5.2.21 states: "Darkness is not a substance, because it possesses characteristics different from substances, qualities, and actions; nor is it a quality or an action, because no substratum for it is perceived. Darkness is not a substance, because it differs from eternal substances by virtue of being perishable, and it differs from impermanent substances by virtue of being formless, intangible, and opposed to light. Nor is it a quality or an action, because no substratum [for such qualities or actions] is perceived.
Therefore, how can it be said that darkness is merely the absence of light? [It is not so] because light is obstructed by another substance; Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 5.2.18.

22. Since light—such as the radiance of the sun—is present externally, yet absent in mountain caves and other locations when covered by another substance, we consider that darkness is merely the absence of light;
it is external and removable by lamps and the like, whereas that which consists of ignorance is removed by the light of knowledge. Thus it is said: "Yoga and liberation [are attained].
(Candrānanda’s *Vaiśeṣikasūtravṛtti*, pp. 21B–22B).

Because of the possibility of the production of multiple substances such as dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth; if this is not accepted, then that single substance, being unitary and inactive, would not initiate anything at all, and consequently, even action (*karman*) itself would not exist, since there would be no production of multiple substances such as dyads, and thus action would simply lack an object. Furthermore, even when a substance has been initiated, because of the absence of that [action], its definition— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly with "lakṣaṇā-", indicating the sentence is incomplete.*
Because it arises from multiple substances such as [the threads] and so forth? For action indeed exists as the commencement [of the effect]. (Bhāṣya) [Prakaraṇa]... [incomplete fragment]
[If] it were not a substance, [it would be] just a state (bhāva).
Thus, it has first been stated that action does not initiate a substance; now, however, [we shall consider] the substance as you have proposed. (Pātañjala Yogaśāstra 5)

3.104 Furthermore, because of the distinction between being commenced (*ārambha*) and not being commenced (*anārambha*), there is indeed a difference [between substance and its qualities]; for qualities and actions do not exist as that [substance], they are distinct from substances. To claim that "it becomes a substance" is incorrect, as we shall explain how so.

Even granting that a substance is commenced, since the effect does not exist in the cause—just like the arguments already described—the effects (the substances) are different from the causal substances; for it is not the case that that very same substance becomes [something else].

Alternatively, this is also a rule of exception: even though they have begun as substances, because the effects are distinct from their prior causal substances—either by virtue of being qualities or actions, or because that very substance no longer exists—and furthermore, because of the difference between the commencement and non-commencement of defining characteristics, there is indeed distinctness due to that very [difference], as stated in the Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.6: "That which possesses motion is a substance."

"Thus begins the definition of substance (*dravya*); 'that which resides in substance' (VS 1.1.15) and so forth is the definition of quality (*guṇa*); and 'residing in a single substance' and so forth is the definition of action (*karman*). Thus, due to these distinct definitions, substance, quality, and action are indeed different."

Even among substances, there is a diversity between those that do not initiate [effects], such as space (*ākāśa*), and those that initiate [effects], such as earth; likewise, among qualities, there is a diversity between those that initiate [effects], such as conjunction, disjunction, and color, and those that do not initiate [effects] due to their omnipresence (*vibhutva*); and there is a distinction of action from those that do not initiate [effects], because it initiates conjunctions and disjunctions of composite substances. Due to the absence of such [initiating capacity], there is a diversity among them based on contradiction or non-contradiction, causes and effects, and context—this being indicated by the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*).

Because qualities and actions do not possess that [existence], only substance becomes substance, and neither qualities nor actions do; for qualities lack qualities and lack action, and action lacks qualities and lacks action, thus they are distinct from substances.

Furthermore, because sound is unproduced (*anārabhya*), it is distinct from others. Consequently, the existence of the nature and definition of substance as stated by you is untenable, and thus both [substance and its properties] are non-existent.
The nature (*bhāva*) of the sixfold division beginning with substance (*dravya*), along with its sub-divisions, is as follows:

that which is said to be "this thing exists by itself" or "that by which it comes to be," that indeed is its nature; yet this is not the only nature, for it comes to be through another [factor], and that other factor is also its nature, as is the means by which it comes to be.
Even regarding existence (*bhāva*), there is duality because both [types] are excluded; for existence is indeed twofold: intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and relation (*saṃbandha*).

Furthermore, sound, as a quality of space, is distinguished from others, as are universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth. This is because the universal, the particular universals (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*), and the ultimate particulars (*antyaviśeṣa*) are not produced [by causes], whereas inherence (*samavāya*), despite being a substratum, is distinct from others due to its being the cause of producing a corresponding cognition in its own substratum and in relation to itself. Because such specific reasons exist, everything is indeed different [from one another].

Furthermore, there is distinctness [of qualities and actions] precisely because of their distinctness from substances, such as through the difference between *rambhā* (the plantain tree) and *anārambha* (non-commencement). Qualities and actions are distinguished from substances because they do not possess that [substantial] nature; this is the comparison. (Page 313–2, *apavāda*)
Or, because of the absence [of these properties] in the case of non-existence,
another dissimilarity is established: "that which possesses action, possesses quality, and is an inherent cause" is the definition of substance (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.15).

Action (*karma*), such as upward throwing (*utkṣepaṇa*) and so forth, is that in which action exists by way of inherence (*samavāya*) according to possibility; it is "possessing action" (*kriyāvat*). This excludes space, time, direction, and the self.

Quality (*guṇa*), such as color (*rūpa*) and so forth, is that in which qualities exist according to possibility; it is "possessing quality" (*guṇavat*). Inherence (*samavāya*) is that from which [the cognition] "here" arises with respect to things that are inseparable (*ayutasiddha*) and stand in the relation of the supported and the support. That which possesses this [inherence] is "possessing inherence" (*samavāyi*). And that is precisely the cause; or rather, it is the cause of the effect that possesses inherence.

In that regard, earth and the other [elements] are the inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of the three—substance, quality, and action; ether and the others are the inherent causes of qualities; and the mind is the inherent cause of qualities and actions in its final composite substance.
"That which resides in a substance, is devoid of qualities, and is not a cause in conjunctions and disjunctions, being independent," is the definition of a quality (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.15).

15. That which rests upon substance is "substance-dependent" (*dravyāśrayī*); that which is devoid of qualities is "qualityless" (*nirguṇa*). Being "non-causal with respect to conjunctions and disjunctions" means it is not a dependent cause; for instance, the conjunction of two fingers, when producing the conjunction of the space between them, depends upon the production of those two fingers. Likewise, the mutual disjunction of the two fingers, with respect to the disjunction from the intervening space, depends upon the destruction of the effect [the prior conjunction]. Thus, a quality characterized by conjunction, disjunction, or disjunction itself is a dependent cause in relation to conjunctions and disjunctions.

"Action is that which has a single substance as its locus, is devoid of qualities, and is an independent cause with respect to conjunctions and disjunctions" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.16). This means: this action has one substance as its substratum (*āśraya*), not two; or rather, it exists in only one substance, thus it is "single-substance-located" (*ekadravya*). It is "devoid of qualities" (*aguṇa*) because it possesses no qualities. With respect to its effects—conjunctions and disjunctions—it is an "independent cause" (*anapekṣaṃ kāraṇam*) because, having separated its own substratum from one thing and conjoined it with another substratum, it acts without dependence on anything else from the moment of its production until its destruction. Thus, it is an independent cause with respect to conjunctions and disjunctions.
Thus, in the *Vaiśeṣikasūtravṛtti* composed by Candrānanda, page 8,
he states another point of dissimilarity: "Substance is non-opposed to its effect and non-opposed to its cause" (VS 1.1.1).

11. Destruction is opposition (virodha), which is a form of obstruction (pratibandha). In some cases, an effect such as a substance does not oppose its cause-substance, nor its inherent (samavāyi) and non-inherent (asamavāyi) causes. For example: a finger-substance, which is the effect about to produce a two-finger [length], is not opposed by the action intended for that purpose, nor by the conjunction produced by that action, nor by the resulting two-finger [length]; nor is it opposed by its inherent and non-inherent causes, namely the joints and their conjunctions. Likewise, the mind and ultimate composite substances are not opposed by their effects—qualities and actions; nor are ether and the like opposed by their qualities. Because these are eternal, there is no opposition with respect to their causes. Is there not [opposition] with respect to their effects? [No, because they are eternal.]
In both ways, there is indeed a merit. Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.1.

12. With respect to atoms, dyads, and other ultimate composite substances, color and the other qualities are non-contradictory with their causes, yet they are also contradictory [to one another]. Color, taste, smell, and touch—when they are neither cause nor effect—are non-contradictory [with each other], but initial, middle, and final sounds are mutually contradictory. Unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) is contradictory with its effect; speed and effort are contradictory with conjunction with a substance possessing touch; conjunction and disjunction, as well as pleasure and pain and desire and aversion, are mutually contradictory when they are not related as cause and effect. Knowledge is contradictory with the counter-agents of the stream of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), and mental impression is contradictory with knowledge, pleasure, pain, and so forth. This should be understood according to the specific circumstances of each case.
Action is indeed opposed by its effect (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.13).

Among the effects— namely conjunction, disjunction, and impression— it is only by conjunction that action is opposed, not by disjunction or impression, because [if it were opposed by them] it would follow that conjunction could never arise.
Thus, in the *Vaiśeṣikasūtravṛtti* composed by Candrānanda, see page 7b–8a; page 437, note 8:
"anyārabhya" (the manuscript reads "pra").

Furthermore, because sound is not produced [by conjunction or disjunction], it is distinct from the others; and since generalities (sāmānya) and so forth likewise [lack such production], the existence of the nature of substance as characterized by you is untenable. Thus, there is the non-existence of both [the categories and their definitions], and only the existence of the sixfold division of substance and the rest, along with their subdivisions.

As for what is said—that "whatever this [entity] becomes by itself, or whatever it is produced as by means of something else, that alone is its state (bhāva)"—this is not the case; rather, it is produced by one thing after another, and that [successive thing] is indeed its state, as is that by which it is produced. See page 383, line 1.
Even in the case of *bhāva* (existence), there is duality because both [types] are abandoned; for *bhāva* is indeed twofold—namely, intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and relation (*saṃbandha*).

And this [relation] is a category distinct from substance and the others, due to the difference in its defining characteristics, just as *bhāva* [is distinct] from substance-ness (*dravyatva*) and so on. Just as *bhāva*, substance-ness, and the rest, by producing cognitions corresponding to themselves in their own substrates, exist as entities distinct from their own supports and from one another, so too does inherence (*samavāya*), because the cognition "here" is observed in the five categories; therefore, it is a distinct category from them. Thus it is stated in the *Praśastapādabhāṣya* in the section defining inherence.

What follows from this? It follows that the existence (*bhavana*) characterized by the nature of the substance (*dravya*) as you have described it is untenable. For you define a substance as a seed (*bīja*) that is devoid of all distinctions, and existence (*bhāva*) as the manifestation of such inherent power (*sannihita-śakti*) within that very substance. However, such an existence is untenable because qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth—whether they be other substances distinct from the substance-existence, or categories dependent on existence such as inherence (*sattā-samavāya*)—are by nature existences distinct from the existence of the substance itself.

The word *iti* has the sense of a reason; therefore, for that reason, there is an absence of both: the universal (*sāmānya*), which is the substance-existence (*dravya-bhavana*) of a single form as the general rule (*utsarga*), and the action-existence (*kriyā-bhavana*) as the exception (*apavāda*), along with the distinction between the real and the unreal, and so forth.

If it is asked, "How then is the existence of those two [established]? it is said: let it be seen that their existence consists precisely in the sixfold division beginning with substance (*dravya*), including its sub-divisions, each having its own distinct essential nature and possessing specific attributes (see page 378, line 1).

"Being dependent (*āśritatva*) [is defined] as being other than eternal substances," [states] Praśastapāda’s *Bhāṣya*. "And being dependent is apprehension through dependence on another; it is not an occurrence characterized by inherence (*samavāya*), because that [inherence] is absent in inherence itself.
Furthermore, since this state of being dependent does not exist in the four kinds of atoms, nor in ether, time, space, self, and mind, he says: "other than eternal substances.
This is from the section on Similarity and Dissimilarity in the *Kandalī*, a commentary on Praśastapāda’s *Bhāṣya*.
The non-existence of that very thing which possesses the property of being undifferentiated;
here, even the reading "the existence of that very thing which possesses the property of being undifferentiated" is to be considered.
[Furthermore,] the six categories possess existence, nameability, and cognizability.
Thus, in the *Praśastapādabhāṣya*:

"Furthermore, even that which is its own mere existence (*svasat-mātra*), its essential being (*svarūpa-sattva*), does not exist by itself alone. As it is said: 'That which exists here by itself, independent of other objects and autonomous'—this very point he clarifies through another case-ending when he says, 'that by which this [thing] comes into being. The meaning is 'essential relation' (*svabhāva-sambandha*). This is what you intend when you say, 'that indeed is its existence (*bhāva*). But this [existence] does not come into being by itself; what then? It comes into being by means of something else, in dependence upon another, and thus, being distinct from that, it is precisely that other thing which is its existence."

What is this? It is *sattā* (existence), the great universal (*mahāsāmānya*). That by which something exists is its *bhāva* (state of being). Even for a substance (*dravya*) or other category that is already existent and thus fit to be designated as "existent," there is a further state of being; it is not merely existence itself. Because of its connection with this [existence], the thing comes to be; thus, that existence (*sattā*) is also a *bhāva*. And the substance and so forth become "existent" (*sat*)—this is the meaning. (Sva-tathā-pra.)

And here, there might also be the reading "tathā"; likewise, the reading "anyāpekṣeṇa anyāpekṣeṇa ca tathā" should also be considered; that too [is found] in the Viśeṣāvaśyaka-bhāṣya, and it concerns substance (dravya) and so forth.
And is that [universal] a substance and so forth?

Even in the case of existence (*bhāva*), there is duality because both are abandoned; even in the case of *sattā* (being), there is duality as both universal and particular, for it is both abandoned and restricted—it is abandoned insofar as existence is all-pervading, and it is restricted insofar as it pertains only to its own locus.

If existence were not independent of its connection with other entities, there would be no end to the series of relations; for existence is twofold: every entity has two distinct natures—a general nature consisting of its own essential existence (*svarūpasattā*), and a relational nature consisting of its connection (*sambandhasattā*). It is through this connection that substances, qualities, and actions come to be called "existent" (*sat*);

however, an entity does not exist simply by virtue of being an existent thing (*bhāvaḥ san*), because it lacks the inherence of the universal "existence" (*sattā*) as found in substances, qualities, and actions.

Just like a staff [which serves as a qualifier], because they depend on other entities, universals (*sāmānya*) and the rest serve as the causes for cognitions corresponding to their connection with existence (*sattā*) and so forth in substances, qualities, and actions. However, a cognition does not proceed toward a qualified object when the qualifier has not been apprehended;
rather, [the author] demonstrates them as having distinct and separate forms.

The explanation of this—beginning with "intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and relation (*sambandha*)" and so on—is already understood up to the point where it says: "In substances, qualities, and actions, there is 'existent' (*sat*). The meaning is that while intrinsic existence (*svarūpasattā*) does not depend on another entity, relational existence (*sambandhasattā*) does depend on one.

"Manifesting," "emitting," and "relinquishing" refer to existence as intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and existence as essential form (*svarūpasattā*). "Relation" refers to existence as relation (*sambandhasattā*), through which [the notion] "existent" arises with respect to substances, qualities, and actions.
But an entity does not exist as an existent in itself, because it lacks the inherence of existence (*sattā*), unlike substance, quality, and action;

rather, like a staff, it depends on something else. It is through their connection with existence and so forth that universals and the rest become the causes of cognitions corresponding to those connections in the case of substances, qualities, and actions; for a cognition of the qualified does not proceed when the qualifier has not been apprehended.

Just like a staff, because qualifiers are the cause of cognitions corresponding to their connection with other objects, universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth are the causes of cognitions corresponding to their connection with existence (*sattā*) and the like. Furthermore, the reading "the cognition does not proceed toward the qualified object when the qualifier has not been apprehended" is also possible; and as for the passage beginning with "intrinsic relation" (*svabhāvasambandha*), etc., [it refers to] the intrinsic relation, etc. (Yaśomitra).
"But it does not exist as such," and so forth;

that is, existence (*bhāva*) is not a being (*sattā*), nor is it existent (*san*) like substance, quality, or action. Even within the generality of existence (*sadbhāvasāmānya*), there is a difference in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of individual entities. Because it possesses a character distinct from the existence of substances, qualities, and actions, it is "not existent"—meaning it is not a substance, nor is it a jar or the like. The meaning is that, unlike a substance or a jar which is connected with the generalities of substantiality (*dravyatva*) or jarhood (*ghaṭatva*), this [existence] does not become a substance or the like.

What is the reason? Because there is no inherence of existence (*sattā*) in its own essence, nor is there inherence of existence in the specific essences such as substantiality (*dravyatva*), quality-ness (*guṇatva*), action-ness (*karmatva*), or pot-ness (*ghaṭatva*). For it is precisely because those entities—substance and so forth—inhere in their own specific essences along with existence that they become fit for the designations "existent substance" (*sat-dravya*), "existent pot" (*sat-ghaṭa*), and so on.

If it is asked: "What is the reason for this distinction—that substance and the rest become 'existent' (*sat*) through inherence in existence (*sattā*), which is their own essence (*svatattva*), whereas existence and the rest do not become substance and the rest through inherence in substance and the rest, which are their own essences? It is said in reply: Even though universals (*sāmānya*), particulars (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*), and inherence (*samavāya*) exist by virtue of their own essential existence (*svarūpasattā*), they lack existence [in the sense of being perceived as such] because they are devoid of the reality of their own being. Therefore, the distinction of existence and the rest from other things consists in their being empty of the reality of a relation, whereas that [distinction] exists for substances and the rest, which are related. This is shown by the passage beginning with "But like a staff, in another object... and so on, until "the cognition follows into the qualified object," the meaning of which has already been explained.

Because qualifiers serve as the cause for the cognition of the specific nature [of the qualified], they function as the cause of cognitions corresponding to their connection with existence (*sattā*) and so forth; this applies to universals (*sāmānya*) and the like regarding their own substrates, just as the staff serves as the cause for the cognition of "one who possesses a staff" (*daṇḍin*). However, this does not apply when the qualifier has not been apprehended, such as in the case of a specific cognition of whiteness and so forth. For in this very way, there is a rule for both [substance and quality] to have mutual predominance; but this is not the case for substance and action, because of the absence of mutual predominance. Since proximity has as its object an entity of that nature, even the manifestation (*vyakti*) is dependent upon that coming-into-being (*tadbhavana*).

"Just as there is non-existence in things such as space that are unrelated to it," so too, the affirmation of both—wherein both are equally predominant—is possible exactly as we have stated; likewise, the affirmation of both the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*) is possible, because the distinctions among the six categories of entities consist of absolute particularity. Thus, the affirmation of both the universal and the particular can occur, but not in the manner favored by previous systems regarding substance (*dravya*) and action (*kriyā*), because in those cases there is an absence of mutual predominance, and in the absence of independence, there is an absence of agency (*kartṛtva*).

Even though we have accepted agency on your behalf, since the substance alone possesses primacy—consisting of independent existence—and because agency is not established as belonging to the action due to its lack of such primacy, it follows by this reasoning that the substance would be the agent by virtue of its independence, whereas the action would not be so because it lacks primacy. Thus, even if agency were granted to both out of compassion for you, it could not be the case, because there is no primacy in both simultaneously; this is the meaning.

If it is asked, "What is the reason that there is no primacy for both? it is said: because proximity has as its object an entity already existing in such a state; for a substance is held to be that which is already present (*sannihita-bhavana*). This is like a house where jars and other things are already present and facing toward becoming this or that state, or like a jar already situated within a house. Since it is accepted that all those things intended to be manifested by action are already present within the substance—just as jars and other items already present in a house require no further purpose from the action of a lamp—even if a purpose were conceivable, it would be merely a matter of manifestation. Since even that manifestation is dependent upon the coming-into-being of those things, and since manifestation serves only as an auxiliary to the primary coming-into-being of the substance, manifestation itself lacks primacy.

This, however, is the rule where both [the general and the particular] are predominant. The distinction arises from the difference in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of substances that have been initiated and those not yet initiated; for the existence of a state (*bhāvasattva*) undergoes transformation due to the absolute independence of its manifestation (*vyañjana*).
[The elements are] earth, water, fire, air, and space. "This, however, is the rule where both are predominant" is the conclusion.

The word "however" (*tu*) is for the purpose of specification (*viśeṣaṇa*); for in this way, without abandoning the scope of the qualified meaning, it is the rule for both the general and the particular.

If one asks what this is like, the author demonstrates it with the passage beginning "ārabdhānārabdha" (produced and unproduced), etc., a text intended to show the mutual distinctness of the six categories along with their subdivisions, up until the point: "But in the case of action, [the distinction arises] from the existence of both essential nature and relation. Although the meaning is for the most part already understood, something further is stated here: even among those things produced, such as the atoms of earth and so forth, and dyads, there is multiplicity due to the difference in their essential natures, despite the non-difference of space and time; and the same applies to unproduced things, such as atoms and space. Furthermore, although there is non-difference manifested by the relation of being, there is a distinction between produced things—because they are occasional—and others, because they are eternal.

There is a distinction between the existence of an entity (*bhāva*) and the existence of a sentient being (*sattva*), even though both possess intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Why? Because of the absolute independence of its manifestation (*atyantavyañjana-svātantryāt*); while others are manifested by it, it itself manifests [others].
This is because it exists in a different manner (*anyathābhūti*); thus, by existing in this other way, it becomes present everywhere, and because it does not exist otherwise, there is a distinction.

If this were so, then existence (*sattā*) would not exist at all even when there is independence of both the entity (*bhāva*) and its manifestor (*vyañjana*), because it would be devoid of any relation, like a sky-flower. For an entity (*bhāva*) would indeed not exist—like a sky-flower—due to the absence of independence between the existent state (*sadbhāva*) and its existent manifestor (*sadvyañjana*). Thus, these substances such as earth, water, and so forth, do not exist even as mutually non-existent entities (*itaretarābhāvātmanā*). Since the substances of time, space, self, and mind are themselves non-existent and mutually non-existent, their "otherness" (*anyatā*) arises in various ways through their connection with existence (*bhāva*) and so forth; and it is precisely in the absence of such otherness that existence (*sattva*) occurs.
The same applies to qualities and actions;

nor do their designations and cognitions as "existent" arise from anything else, because they possess the nature of self-illuminating causes like a lamp. Their non-existence while being existent by virtue of their own being is impossible due to the absence of any relation [to another]; just as a quality cannot be a non-quality.
Thus, a universal is simply a universal.

The intrinsic existence (*svabhāvasadbhāva*) of effect-substances and so forth does not exist; rather, something indeed exists. It exists precisely because of its connection with atoms (*paramāṇu*), space (*ākāśa*), time (*kāla*), direction (*diś*), self (*ātman*), mind (*manas*), and existence (*sattā*). Through the connection with "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*), it becomes a substance. Furthermore, from existence, from substance-ness, and from their mutual relation, there is distinctness (*anyatā*) in various ways. Only in distinctness do entities possess non-existence in relation to one another (*itaretarāsattā*) through their connection with being and so forth; only in distinctness does existence reside. Thus, it is only in distinctness that existence occurs.

The same applies to qualities (*guṇa*) and actions (*karman*): through their connection with existence (*bhāva*), quality-ness (*guṇatva*), action-ness (*karmatva*), and so forth—which are themselves non-existent (*asat*) in relation to one another—the states of being existent qualities and actions arise.

Thus it has been stated that existence (*sattva*) produces the existence of substances (*dravya*) and the rest by means of its connection with what is non-existent. Now, is the connection of this existence produced by something else? No; to this it is replied: "And not of this," and so forth.

For existence (*sattā*) itself, through its connection with others, is the cause for the application of the term and cognition "existent" (*sad-abhidhāna-pratyaya*); it does not derive those two from anything else, because it is the cause for illuminating both itself and others, like a lamp. Indeed, a lamp, though capable of illuminating jars and other objects, does not depend upon those jars and so forth for its own illumination; existence is likewise.

Therefore, its non-existence [in relation to something else] arises only from the absence of the presence of a connection, not from mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*). For example, a quality (*guṇa*) is called "without qualities" (*aguṇa*) because it has no further qualities, not because it is not a quality at all.
Why? Because of the absence of connection with other qualities, and not because it is itself devoid of qualities;

thus, the point that "the universal is indeed a universal" has already been explained. In this way, for the time being, existence (*bhāva*) is by its very nature independent of any other existence (*sattā*).

Furthermore, as for that inherent existence (*svabhāvasadbhāva*) of effects, substances, and so forth, which is said to be "non-existent" because it is to be established through a relation to an external entity—it is not [non-existent] in that sense. Rather, it certainly exists in the sense that "it does not become what it was not. Because an effect comes into being after having not been, and ceases to be after having been, it becomes existent while being non-existent by virtue of its own inherent existence, and even while existent, it becomes non-existent. Thus, there is a dual nature (*dvairūpya*)—existence and non-existence—of that inherent existence of the effect, due to its capacity for both being that and not being that, just as in the case of a single person being both father and son; this has already been explained.

Therefore, everything is in every way of the nature of both the universal and the particular; however, some things—such as this [entity]—indeed exist as they are, solely by virtue of their own inherent existence (*svasadbhāva*), and not by having previously been non-existent or through a connection with "Being" (*sattā*). This applies to substances such as atoms, space, time, direction, self, and mind; by the inclusion of the word "etcetera," it also includes inherence (*samavāya*) and the categories beginning with substance.

Even regarding a particular, there is a twofold nature [as a substance and a mode] by virtue of being both a general property and an ultimate particular; however, regarding an action, it is so by virtue of its own-nature and the existence of a relation.
And this [view] is a *dravyāstika* because it is a portion of the *naigama* standpoint.

Substance (*dravya*) is also a genus (*jāti*) due to its connection with substantiality (*dravyatva*); likewise, qualities such as all-pervasive dimension (*vibhu-parimāṇa*) and spherical dimension (*parimaṇḍala-parimāṇa*) are genera.
Particularity (*viśeṣa*) consists in the mutual non-existence and difference found everywhere; generality (*sāmānya*), however, is existence by intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-sattva*).

Regarding "in both cases even in the case of a particular": general particulars (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*) are such as substantiality, quality-ness, and action-ness; ultimate particulars (*antyaviśeṣa*) are those which effect the differentiation of atoms situated in the same location of space for yogins.
As for action, however, there is both difference and non-difference from others by virtue of the existence of its own nature and the existence of its relation to action-ness.

Thus, because of the existence of the relationship between substance and quality with respect to substantiality and qualitiness, and because of the existence of their own-nature (*svabhāva*), and so forth—through such similarities and differences regarding the six categories (*padārtha*)—it is precisely the "particularities" (*viśeṣa*) that constitute the Vaiśeṣika, or the Vaiśeṣika is that which has particularity as its purpose. Therefore, among the rules of affirmation and restriction, the rule of affirmation (*vidhi*) is established; however, it is not a rule of affirmation-restriction for a single entity as you desire. [This applies to] that which possesses existent substances, qualities, and actions, and the substances and so forth related to jars and the like.
In this context, there might also be the reading "na saddravyādi" (not existing as substance, etc.);
[the meaning is] that they do not exist as substance and so forth.
Here, "adhikaḥ" (excessive) is not present.

"Existence (sattā) is the particularity (viśeṣa); however, that [particularity] exists for substances and so forth because of their relation"—this is the meaning here. Alternatively, there may also be the reading: "However, that relation exists for substances and so forth."
Specifically,
[the application] of conciliation and so forth,
beginning with "one's own" and so on.
Now, cognition (*buddhi*) is being examined: "Knowledge regarding substances has been explained" (VS 8.1).
Among the six categories, knowledge has been explained as occurring only with respect to substances; it arises from contact in that way, but not so with respect to qualities and the rest.
Its [instruments] are the mind and the self (VS 8.2).
The mind and the self have been explained as the causes of knowledge;
now he describes the knowledge [that arises] regarding qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth. In the *Vaiśeṣika Sūtra* (8.3), under the heading of "knowledge," the production of knowledge was stated;
since the production of knowledge through the contact of the sense organs with qualities and so forth has been stated, [he now addresses this].

Because, regarding qualities and actions which are not in direct contact [with the senses], substance is the cause and the cause of the cause for the production of cognition (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 8.4). Since substance is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of qualities and actions, when they are not in direct contact with the sense organ, that very substance is the cause of the contact—which is the cause for the production of cognition—and not the qualities or actions themselves. Therefore, cognition regarding qualities and actions arises through "inherence in what is conjoined" (*saṃyuktasamavāya*). The word "and" (*ca*) indicates the reason.
Regarding universals and particulars, since there is no further universal or particular, cognition arises from that very same [substance] (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 8).

5. In the case of universals such as existence (*sattā*) and in the case of ultimate particularities (*antyaviśeṣa*), for those who perceive them, cognition arises from the mere contact of the substance with the sense organ, and not from the universals or particularities themselves, because they are absent in those [ultimate particulars].

But elsewhere, in the case of substances, qualities, and actions, [cognition] depends upon universals and particularities (VS 8.6). In substances, qualities, and actions, from the contact of the substance with the sense organ, and from the universal such as existence (*sattā*), and from the universal-particular such as substantiality (*dravyatva*), cognition arises in the form "it exists" or "it is a substance," and so forth.
In this sūtra, "generality" (sāmānya) refers to existence (sattā), while "particularities" (viśeṣa) refer to substantiality (dravyatva) and so forth; in the previous sūtra, however, it was otherwise.
There too, regarding substance, [the cognition] arises in dependence upon substance, quality, and action (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 8.7):

from the contact of the eye with a substance, there arises a cognition in dependence upon generality and particularity such as "it has horns," in dependence upon quality such as "it is white," and in dependence upon action such as "it moves."

Furthermore, because substance (*dravya*) and the other categories serve as qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*), they are apprehended first; therefore, the cognition of the qualifier is the cause and the cognition of the qualified (*viśeṣya*) is the effect.

Regarding qualities (*guṇa*) and actions (*karman*), [the rule] "there is no [cognition] dependent on qualities or actions" (VS 8.8) applies, because qualities and actions are absent in qualities and actions respectively;
thus, there is no cognition of qualities or actions caused by qualities or actions within qualities and actions.

Regarding the prior arising of cognition with respect to substance and so forth, there is no fixed rule; for example, from the whiteness inherent in a substrate (*samavāyin*) arises the cognition of whiteness, and from that cognition of whiteness arises the cognition of the white object—these two being related as cause and effect (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 8.9). From the generality (*sāmānya*) of whiteness inherent in the quality of white, and from the cognition of that generality of whiteness, the cognition of the quality of white is produced. The relationship between the generality and the quality should also be understood. Thus, the cognition of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is the cause, and the cognition of the qualified (*viśeṣya*) is the effect. However, in the absence of the relationship between qualifier and qualified, substances do not stand in a mutual causal relation because their causes do not arise simultaneously (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 8.10).

10. Because the mind is atomic (aṇu), there is no simultaneity; and even if there were succession, there is no relationship of cause and effect between the cognitions of a jar and a cloth, because they cannot stand in the relation of qualifier and qualified. Likewise, among substances, qualities, and actions, there is no such relationship due to the lack of distinction in their causes (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 8.11). Furthermore, in the case of "the white cow goes," even though the cognitions of substance, quality, and action arise successively, there is no relationship of cause and effect, because—as stated previously—the reason for this is the same: the absence of the relation of qualifier and qualified.

Therefore, the cognition of a substance (*dravyajñāna*) is not the cause of the cognitions of qualities (*guṇa*) and actions (*karman*), nor are the cognitions of qualities and actions the causes of another [cognition], in the absence of the principle of qualification (*viśeṣaṇanyāya*). However, according to the Vaiśeṣika Sūtra (8.1.2), "This was done by you; feed him," there is a dependence upon cognition: "this" (*ayam*) is the notion regarding what is proximate, and "that" (*eṣaḥ*) is the notion regarding what is somewhat remote; "done by you" (*kṛtaṃ tvayā*) consists of the notions of object (*karman*) and agent (*kartṛ*); and "feed him" (*bhojayainam*) consists of the notions of agent and object.

The cognition of "remote" is dependent upon the "near"; the cognition "done" is dependent upon the object (*karman*) with respect to the agent (*kartṛ*); and "feed! is dependent upon the agent with respect to the object.
If it is asked, "Why are they dependent? [the answer is: because they exist when [the objects] are perceived and do not exist when they are not perceived (VS 8.1.3).

Since cognitions such as "remote" arise only when proximate things and so forth are actually perceived, and not when they are unperceived, they are therefore dependent; yet, despite being dependent, they do not stand in a causal relationship, because they lack the connection of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣyatva*).
Thus, in the *Vaiśeṣikasūtravṛtti* composed by Candrānanda (p. 29):

"In this very way, there is indeed a rule for both [substance and action] having mutual predominance; however, it does not apply to substance and action [individually], because they lack mutual predominance, since proximity has as its object such [mutually predominant] entities, and because even manifestation is dependent upon that coming-into-being. (*svataḥ* is the reading in the manuscript).
In this very way, today both [parts]; in this very way, today both;
according to the rule, as before.
In the *Bhāṣya* on the *Pāṇinīya-vyākaraṇa*, it is stated in the introduction to Pāṇini’s sūtra 1.4.54 that "the agent is independent" (*svatantraḥ kartā*).
And since substance alone possesses primacy, the meaning appears to be that, according to the two preceding systems, an injunction regarding both substance and action cannot be possible.

Let it be seen [in Pañjikā 5]: "The face is present... This, however, is the rule where both [factors] are predominant—the distinction arises from the difference in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of substances, whether they have been commenced or not, because the existence of the state (*bhāvasattva*) undergoes transformation due to the absolute independence of its manifestation (*vyañjana*).
If there were independence regarding the manifestation of the objects of earth, water, fire, wind, space, and form, it would not exist.
The meaning shines forth as "only when it exists";
now, therefore, we shall explain Dharma. (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1)

1. To a certain Brahmin, whose impurities had been removed through the practice of the Vedas, this Vedic statement appeared: "Verily, pleasure and pain do not touch one who is bodiless" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.1). Having reflected upon this statement, he approached Kaṇabhakṣa.
Then he said: "Venerable sir! By this statement, it is said that there is a means for the well-being of one whose body has been destroyed; therefore, let it be told—what is the means?
Then the sage replied: "It is Dharma.
Thereupon the Brāhmaṇa asked: "What is Dharma? What are its characteristics? What are its means? What is its purpose, and whom does it benefit?"

Therefore, immediately following these questions, in the formal promise to explain the Dharma (*dharmavyākhyānapratijñā*), the word *atha* denotes immediate succession (*ānantarya*). The word *ataḥ* also teaches that the perfection of the disciple’s qualities—such as the ripening of dispassion (*vairāgya*) and wisdom (*prajñā*)—is the cause [for this teaching]. Since this disciple is endowed with such a perfection of qualities, we shall therefore explain the Dharma to him immediately after these questions.
What is Dharma? It says: "That from which the attainment of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) results is Dharma" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.1).

2. Prosperity is the attainment of a desired body in the worlds of Brahmā and others, as well as the cessation of misfortune;
the supreme good is liberation (*mokṣa*), which consists in the absence of the specific qualities (*vaiśeṣika-guṇa*) of the self.

If it is asked, "How is a dharma characterized in this way known? [the answer is: its authority derives from tradition (āmnāya). To explain how that is so, he says: "The authority of tradition [is established] because of his word" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.3).
3. The word "that" (tad) refers to Hiraṇyagarbha; however, because he possesses golden seed (hiraṇya-retas), it is the Lord Maheśvara himself who is being spoken of.

Furthermore, God (Īśvara) has been established through the inference that the body, the world, and so forth, being effects like a pot, must have an intelligent agent as their creator.

The nature of dharma and its characteristics have been stated; now we shall describe its means of accomplishment, namely the substances. Among these, earth, water, fire, air, ether, time, space, self, and mind are the substances (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.4).

4. "Substances" [are so called] because of their connection with substantiality (dravyatva); they are no more than these—this is the meaning of the word "iti" (thus). Having thus enumerated the substances, he asks: "What, then, are the qualities? He says: Form, taste, smell, touch, number, size, separateness, conjunction and disjunction, priority and posteriority, cognitions, pleasure and pain, desire and aversion, and effort are the qualities. Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.6.

These seventeen qualities—form and the rest explicitly mentioned, as well as heaviness, fluidity, viscidity, momentum, merit, demerit, and sound, which are included by the word "and"—will be discussed in their proper place later on.
Now, as to what the actions are, he says: "Throwing upward, throwing downward, contraction, expansion, and locomotion are the actions" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.6).

1.6. These same five actions are to be understood; by the mention of "going," "whirling," "shaking," and so forth are included. Thus, having enumerated substance, quality, and action, the categories of generality, particularity, and inherence will also be discussed as a consequence thereof.

Thus, the thorough knowledge of the similarities and differences among the six categories, by way of perceiving the defects in sense-objects, becomes the cause of *dharma* when dispassion has arisen for the sake of attaining the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*).

Furthermore, their status as causes of *dharma* for the sake of attaining worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) is seen in such injunctions as "one should sacrifice with [the element] earth" (*same yajeta*), "one leads water" (*apo nayati*), and so forth for the other substances;
and regarding qualities, such as "one should sacrifice a black [animal]" (*kṛṣṇam ālabheta*), and so forth.
Regarding actions, however, there is the example "one threshes rice grains" and so forth;

Since qualities and so forth inhere in substance, he explains inherence: because the cognition "here" arises with respect to cause and effect—such as "the cloth is here in the threads," "color and so forth are here in the jar," or "action is here in the jar"—that is inherence.

Because the mention of "cause and effect" is illustrative, it is stated that there is inherence (samavāya) of universals (jāti), individuals (vyakti), and particularities (viśeṣa) in eternal substances;

however, regarding an action, it is twofold by way of its own nature and the existence of its relation.

1.26. The dimension of the atom is spherical; it is eternal. Its non-perception is the mark of its perception. Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 7.1.26.

27. The absolute impossibility of a substance devoid of dimension is the mark (*liṅga*) for the existence of atoms and their atomic dimension; non-existence is ignorance (*avidyā*), while existence is knowledge (*vidyā*). Space is greater than pervasiveness (*vibhava*). Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 7.1.27.

1.28. From the conjunction of material substances that have come together and then depart due to their dissolution, it is understood that space possesses supreme magnitude; likewise [it is understood] for the self. Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 7.1.28.

(VS 1.2.5) Because there is a recurring cognition (*anuvṛttabuddhi*) that "this is a substance, this is a substance" with respect to earth and the other [substances], and because there are cognitions that "this is a quality, this is a quality" with respect to color and so forth, and "this is an action, this is an action" with respect to throwing upwards and so forth, these—substance-ness, quality-ness, and action-ness—are generalities; and because they exclude one another, they are particularities.
"Except for the ultimate particularities" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.2.6).

Existing by way of inherence in eternal substances such as atoms and space, and residing in those things that possess identical shapes and qualities, they are the causes of the cognition of absolute distinction—such as "this is different from that" and "that is different from this"—for those who perceive them; they are called *viśeṣas* (particularities) because they serve as the differentiators for observers.
"Thus the particularities have been explained," as seen on page 9 of the *Vaiśeṣikasūtravṛtti* composed by Candrānanda (see page 25, note 12).

Here it is asked: "Is this a variety of the *dravyāstika* or a variety of the *paryāyāstika*? It is replied: It is the *dravyāstika* because it is a partial aspect (*ekadeśa*) of the *naigama* [view]. Its cognition is that "substance exists" (*dravyam asti*). The word *naigama* has a distinction in its etymological meaning (*nirukta-artha*). Among those [views], [the *dravyāstika* holds] that "it is also substance," and so forth; it is "substance" (*dravya*) due to its connection with the general property (*sāmānya*) of substantiality and its specific qualities (*viśeṣa*).
