"The universal (jāti) is the meaning of a word" means that all words denote only universals; even for [words such as] "space" (ākāśa) and so forth, the meaning of the word is the universal, because [space, etc. possess a universal.
Furthermore, the final word is the sentence-meaning by way of metaphorical designation;

for the final word is the sentence-meaning because, as in the example "Devadatta cooks rice in a pot with firewood," the meaning— characterized by mutual relation and possessing positive and negative concomitance— is fully realized through its connection with the final word, "cooks" (*pacati*), which is manifested [by the other words].

And that sentence-meaning arises from the cognition of the final word, depending upon the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) deposited by the cognitions of the preceding words. For the cognitions produced by each individual word, which have their own respective parts as objects, deposit mental impressions. Therefore, the cognition of the final word—by virtue of the maturation of the impressions from the cognitions of the preceding words—arises as having as its object the mutual connection [of the parts] while excluding other related things. This is the aphorism for its emergence: "Venerable Sir, is this Jewel-Lustre Earth eternal or non-eternal? Gautama! It may be eternal, and it may be non-eternal."

"For what reason, O Blessed One, is it said: 'It may be eternal, it may be non-eternal'? "O Gotama! From the perspective of substantiality (*dravyārthatā*), it is eternal; from the perspective of the modifications of color, smell, taste, touch, and shape, it is non-eternal. Regarding the meaning of a sentence as the manifestation of individual word-meanings through their presence and absence (*anvaya-vyatireka*), or as the collective sense of the words, it is as stated: "In the intellect, whose seeds have been sown by the preceding sounds and whose maturation has been completed, the word-sound is apprehended together with the final sound."
As stated in *Vākyapadīya* 1.84,

that sentence-meaning or word-meaning is the cause of cognition for a person who has already established a linguistic convention (*saṅgīti*) and knows the meaning of words such as "pada" and so forth, but not for one who has not established such a convention, just like the failure to understand the meaning of words used by barbarians (*mleccha*).

Thus, having demonstrated the extraction of words (*padāpoddhāra*), he speaks in order to show the nature—according to different philosophical views—of their extracted meaning, which possesses two forms: that which is already established (*siddha*) and that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*). "In the extraction of word-meanings, for all words, the word-meanings are described as being either the universal (*jāti*) or the substance (*dravya*), and both are indeed eternal. (Vākyapadīya 3)

1.2. Since a word is examined by way of its meaning, there first follows an analysis of the meanings of words as extracted [from sentences] according to different philosophical views. To illustrate: for all words in the form of *pada*s—whether they are *nāman*s, *ākhyāta*s, or otherwise—in the view that maintains the reality of universals (*jāti*), the meaning is exclusively the universal (*jāti*), not the substance (*dravya*).
In the view of the Dravyavādins, however, it is the substance itself and not the genus;
by the second word "or" (vā), another category of meaning is indicated—namely, that there is the denotation of a substance qualified by a genus.
For this very reason, it has been made clear that those two together, in the form of a synthesis, constitute the "category of meaning" (padārtha).
Otherwise, this conclusion regarding the meaning would not be tenable when a different meaning had been introduced;

however, if it is expressed in that manner, the expression itself is indeed common to both. Since a word lacks a function after it has ceased its operation, the relationship of subordinate and predominant between the genus (*jāti*) and the substance (*dravya*) pertains to the meaning.

Alternatively, this is the position stated here as "the two word-meanings" (*padārthau*): that in the system of Pāṇini, primarily and by virtue of having distinct objects, the universal (*jāti*) and the substance (*dravya*) are denoted by the word.

In that regard, since a universal—such as that of "cowness" (*gotva*) in a noun like *gauḥ*—is untenable if it were not supported by a substratum and were to denote only its state of being a qualifier for a specific number inherent in a single object (the means) whose activity is restricted to that universal, the substance is understood by implication (*sāmarthyāt*).

Likewise, the denotative power (*vācaka-śakti*) of a verb (*ākhyāta-pada*) directly concerns the action-universal (*kriyā-jāti*), which is the cause of the cognition and designation of non-difference inhering in the various momentary instances of action.
In this context, however, the universal of the factors of action (*kāraka-jāti*) is subordinate;

furthermore, the action-universal residing in the verb becomes conjoined with the universal of the factors of action residing in the noun (*nāman-pada*) by means of their respective individual instances (*vyakti*).

The substance-genus (*dravyajāti*), however, through its inherent power as a means (*sādhanaśaktidvāreṇa*) and by virtue of inhering in a single object (*ekārthasamavāyāt*), undergoes connection with action; likewise, the number-genus (*saṅkhyājāti*) also, through inhering in a single object and by way of its own manifestation, enters into connection with action precisely via its power. Thus, when the coordination of all word-meanings is established, the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*) is rendered possible. Or, just as the genus "throwing upwards" (*utkṣepaṇatva*) is manifested through repetition by the various moments of throwing upwards that occur at different times, so too will it be examined how the genus of the action "cooks" (*pacati*) is manifested by the various moments of action such as placing [the pot] on the fire (*adhiśrayaṇa*).
And although this [universal] is eternal, its status as something to be accomplished (sādhya) is established by way of individual instances.

Furthermore, in this context, prefixes and the like—which coexist with nouns and verbs—serve to illuminate specific features of their meaning; for it is only when the universal as the word-meaning is determined as resting upon a particular that the particular is apprehended. Likewise, even a *karmapravacanīya* (prepositional particle) is grounded solely in the universal of relation.
Even for quality-words such as "white" (*śukla*), the denoted object is the universal of quality (*guṇajāti*);
and even for proper names such as "Ḍittha," it will be established that they denote a universal.
Thus, according to the view of the teacher Vājapyāyana, the systematic arrangement of the universal as the word-meaning is established as being universally applicable.

According to the view of Vyāḍi, however, the meaning of all words is the substance (*dravya*), because it alone can directly be connected with action, and because, as a constituent of the sentence-meaning, it is the object of the injunction (*codanā*). As he says: "And because it is the starting point in the injunctions.
Furthermore, the convention (*saṅketa*) is established here by virtue of the connection with a single universal (*jāti*);
even though not explicitly denoted, the universal serves as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the word-meaning, just as a crow and so forth serve as indicators for a house and so forth.

This [distinction] holds even in the case of verbal forms (*ākhyāta*). According to the view of Vyāḍi, there is a predominance of the substance (*dravya*) which serves as the locus of the action (*bhāvanā*); for instance, in "Devadatta cooks" (*devadattaḥ pacati*), grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the substance itself is directly established. Here, the action is subordinate; for the meaning of a verbal form is a substance permeated by activity (*vyāpāra*), and it is this substance that is capable of being referred to by pronouns such as "this" or "that. This is a universal rule, and thus he will state later: "But when the referent is a substance, the entire meaning is expressed as possessing the properties of a substance" (*Vākyapadīya* 3.1).
13. Thus, for this very reason, it is established that even white and other qualities are substances (*dravya*).
Alternatively, Brahman itself—delimited by various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*)—is denoted by the word "substance" and is the referent of all words; this will indeed be stated later.

Or else, the word "substance" is synonymous with "individual" (*vyakti*); thus, through the alternative of being either a genus (*jāti*) or an individual, it is the referent of all words. This is because of the expression "of all words."

Even when words are further analyzed into their constituent parts, such as stems and suffixes, the referents of these analytically extracted elements—whether action, grammatical relation, number, and so forth—are traditionally taught according to their respective applications, distinguished by whether they are universals (*jāti*) or individuals (*vyakti*).

Alternatively, since both [the stem and the suffix] are understood from the word, both together constitute the referent (*padārtha*); the various alternative views merely rely on differences in the status of the subordinate (*guṇa*) and the primary (*pradhāna*).
Furthermore, the description of the eternity [of the word] is based on the established fact that the relationship between word and meaning is eternal (Pāṇini-Mahābhāṣya 1.1.1).
In this regard, the commentary (bhāṣya) on Pāṇini’s *Mahābhāṣya* 1.1.1 states: "That in which the true nature [of the word] is not obstructed..."

1. Thus, even the eternity of the substance [is established] by way of the eternity of its stream, because it is always perceived from the word; so it is stated in the commentary on the *Vākyapadīya* composed by Puṇyarāja. 3.1.1.
The meaning of a word is the [meaning of] the final member, and the meaning of a sentence is the [meaning of] the final word.

Since time, space, and direction are unitary and lack distinctions of state due to their eternity, how can there be a genus (*jāti*) by which pervasion (*vyāpti*) could be established? To this, he says: "When a location is conceptually constructed through the distinction of properties belonging to that which is conjoined [with it], the universal (*sāmānya*) exists even in the case of space within those locations" (Vākyapadīya 3).

1.15. Just as for universals and particulars, non-difference consists in the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of a recurring property (anvayidharma), so too for space, difference consists in the limiting adjunct of conjunction (saṃyoga). This is a cumulative statement (samuccaya) with reference to the subject at hand: those substrates of space, such as jars and the like, which possess conjunction with space, are "conjoined" (saṃyogin).
For space is the substratum of all material things;
it is called "space" (ākāśa) precisely because it provides room (avakāśa).
Material entities, however, are mutually obstructive; therefore, they do not provide room for one another.

The difference in properties among conjoined things is established by means of valid cognition such as perception; or, by virtue of that [difference], there is the state of being restricted to a limited space, which is well-known in the world. For that region in which a conjunction is fully present constitutes a "limited space" (*pradeśa*) of space, as it is manifold; for according to the etymological definition, a "space" (*deśa*) with respect to an effect is a "limited space" (*pradeśa*).

Furthermore, while some qualities—such as color and so forth—are all-pervading (*vyāpyavṛtti*), conjunction, however, resides only in objects delimited by corporeal form, and thus it always resides only in a limited space.

Therefore, because conjunction occupies a restricted location, the conjoined entities also exist in restricted locations; thus, through the distinction of the properties of the conjoined, a distinction of space arises as produced by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), but not inherently.
As it has been said: "And when a location is postulated...
and because of the difference in location, a universal (*sāmānya*) exists even for space.

Therefore, because the uniform recurrence of non-distinct denotation and cognition—namely, "this is space" and "that is space"—exists in every location, there is indeed a universal of space (*ākāśasāmānya*) which is the referent of the word "space.
By the same logic, a universal must likewise be described for time and the other categories through the conceptualization of their locations.
For instance, although time is divided by its conjunction with Yudhiṣṭhira and others, there exists an undivided universal of time (*kālasāmānya*) which is the denotation of the word "time."

In this way, as the sun revolves clockwise around Mount Meru, there arise conjunctions with specific regions held by the world-protectors (*lokapāla*). When these conjunctions occur between the sun and the directions through such limiting conditions (*upādhi*), one must postulate a non-differentiated universal of direction (*diksāmānya*) denoted by the word "direction," despite the apparent difference.
However, since the self (*ātman*) is indeed distinct in each body, the universal of selfhood (*ātmatvasāmānya*) exists there as well.
Similarly, although inherence (*samavāya*) appears to be manifold due to the diversity of its relata, a universal must be postulated because the cognition of "here" (*ihabuddhi*) persists everywhere.

But is it not the case that by attributing spatial divisions to space through the locations of its conjuncts, there arises a mutual dependence between the conjuncts themselves? This is not so; for the very nature of the sun and other luminaries as being mutually distinct, due to their corporeality, makes known their limited dimensions. However, the spatial divisions of space, which are conceptually constructed and well-known in common worldly usage, indicate the limited spatial extent inherent in the substances with which they are conjoined.

In general, regarding the spatial location of the sun and other celestial bodies, their all-pervasiveness—which contradicts the nature established by perception and other means of valid cognition—is superimposed; this is refuted by their own inherent finitude through the conceptualization of space as consisting of discrete locations.

If spatial locations (*deśa*) are thus imagined, how could they—being based on a distinction of space—produce in the inherently partless ether an effect characterized by the conceptualization of a genus (*jāti*) or the characteristic of a genus-word (*jāti-śabda*), by means of which the genus residing therein might be denoted? It is replied: just as in the non-dualistic philosophy (*advaita-darśana*) the unreality of spatial locations—which stand in the place of individual manifestations (*vyakti*)—will be stated [in Vākyapadīya 3.1.28], "Unreal individual manifestations are recorded," so too here, even while the ether remains real, there is no contradiction regarding the individual manifestations.

Alternatively, he states that the regions of space are indeed primary, just like those of jars and other objects: "Just as there are regions belonging to jars and other things which have no [inherent] regions, so too there are regions of space— which itself has no regions— namely, its conjuncts" (Vākyapadīya 3).

1.16. Here, "place" (*deśa*) is said to mean a part (*avayava*). Pots and the like are wholes (*avayavin*), which are themselves partless in their own nature; for those parts that constitute them, such as potsherds and so forth, are distinct originating causes (*ārambhaka-kāraṇa*) related to them by the relation of inherence (*samavāya*). Similarly, space (*ākāśa*) also, because it is not originated by anything, is formless, all-pervading, and partless. Since there is no place that constitutes its own nature, the sun and other luminaries are merely its points of conjunction (*saṃyogin*); thus, due to the distinction between those [conjunctions], there is a distinction in space. Furthermore, because the uniform cognition of "space" follows everywhere, it must be postulated as a universal (*jāti*).

For objects that delimit space become its "locations" (deśa), and space, being delimited by them, also becomes their "location" because it attains the status of a substratum; thus there is a mutual relationship of location between the two.
However, among material and immaterial things, material things—which are non-pervasive—do not act as mutual delimiters; rather, for these [material things], the location is simply their substratum.
Thus, in this way, the pervasion of the category of "genus" (jāti) has been established by relying upon the Vaiśeṣika system.
Thus ends the section on *jāti* (universal) in the third book (*kāṇḍa*) of the *Vākyapadīya-vṛtti* composed by Helārāja.
Because it precedes [the subsequent sections], [this concludes] the first part.

In this manner, the nature and other characteristics of the word (*śabda*), together with its purpose, have been briefly determined; and its capacity as a signifier (*vācakatva*) and non-signifier (*avācakatva*) has been established in a general sense.

Now, because for some the word (*pada*) is the expressive unit while for others it is the sentence (*vākya*), the second book begins in order to explain in detail the nature of the sentence as the essence of expression.

Therein, based on the differing opinions of the teachers, he states the definition of the sentence: "The verbal form (*ākhyāta-śabda*), the aggregate (*saṅghāta*), the genus (*jāti*) residing in the aggregate, the single partless word (*eko 'navayavaḥ śabdaḥ*), the sequence (*krama*), and the mental synthesis (*buddhyanusaṃhṛti*)."

"The first word is a *pada*; every word is distinct; and even a sentence is that which has expectancy"—thus is the opinion of those who perceive the principles of logic (*nyāya*) regarding the sentence manifoldly.
(Vākyapadīya 2)
1, 2. These eight alternative views on sentences belong to various teachers.

Among them, according to the indivisible (akhaṇḍa) position, there are three definitions: the sentence as a genus (jāti) residing in a collection, the sentence as a single partless word (śabda), and the sentence as a mental synthesis (buddhyanusaṃhṛti).

However, according to the divisible (khaṇḍa) position, there are five definitions: the sentence as a verb (ākhyātaśabda), the sentence as a sequence (krama), the sentence as a collection (saṅghāta), the sentence as the first word, and the sentence as all words taken separately yet mutually expectant (sākāṅkṣa).

In this regard also, there is a distinction: according to the *abhihitānvaya* (expression of related meanings) position, there are two definitions—namely "conjunction" (*saṅghāta*) and "sequence" (*krama*)—and one definition, namely "the verb-word" (*ākhyāta-śabda*). According to the *anvitābhidhāna* (expression of related words) position, there are three definitions: "the first word," "every word separately," and "that which is expectant" (*sākāṅkṣa*). Furthermore, here the *Ṛk-prātiśākhya* states that "the *saṃhitā* is the source (*prakṛti*) of the words. In that context, the term *padaprakṛtiḥ saṃhitā* ("the *saṃhitā* is the source of the words") represents the indivisible (*akhaṇḍa*) position; whereas the term "that of which the words are the source" (*padāni prakṛtiryasyāḥ*) arises as the divisible (*khaṇḍa*) position.

In this regard, he will demonstrate later in the section on the determination of word and meaning that "a sentence is a verbal form" (*ākhyātaśabda*), as follows: "Where a verbal form is present and a specific means (*sādhana*) is understood, even if it is not explicitly stated,
that too is called a single sentence whose meaning is complete" (Vākyapadīya 2).
With the verse beginning with "Thus,
by a single word alone the meaning [is conveyed]" (Vākyapadīya 2.41) and continuing through eight verses, he will demonstrate that a sentence is a collection [of words].

Just as [it was stated] by the passage beginning with *vākyapadīya* 2.7, "Just as a single [word] has all meanings," and ending with *vākyapadīya* 2.14, "In that same way, Devadatta and others would be meaningless in a sentence," so too [is the case for] the unmanifest (*avyakta*) and sequential [sentence], *vākyapadīya* 2...
By the passage beginning with "19" and ending with "vyāvṛttabhedo yenārthaḥ," it is demonstrated that the word, characterized as *sphoṭa* and being entirely indivisible (*akhaṇḍa*), is the sentence.

And it has been said [in the Pāṇinīya-mahābhāṣya]: "That which, when uttered, causes the form of an object—such as a dewlap, tail, hooves, hump, and horns—to be understood, is the word" (Pāṇinīya-mahābhāṣya 1.1).
1. Likewise, "the word is the sphoṭa; sound (dhvani) is a quality of the word" (Pāṇini-vārttika 1.1.70).
Sphoṭa is of two kinds: external and internal.

The external is also twofold, distinguished by genus (*jāti*) and individual (*vyakti*). Among these, the definition of the genus-sphoṭa is "that which resides in a collection" (*saṅghātavartinī*); the definition of the individual-sphoṭa is "the single, partless word" (*eko 'navayavaḥ śabdaḥ*); and the definition of the internal [sphoṭa] is "the synthesis by the intellect" (*buddhyanusaṃhṛtiḥ*); such is the enumeration.

In that regard, the nature of the external [word] characterized by genus (*jāti*) and individual manifestation (*vyakti*) has been stated by the passage beginning with "Just as one alone" (*vākyapadīya* 2.7) and further by the section beginning with "Unmanifested and possessing sequence" (*vākyapadīya* 2.19).
By the four verses beginning with *yadantaḥ śabdatattvam* (Vākyapadīya 2.30), the nature of the internal [word] has been described;
those very particulars (*viśeṣāḥ*) which... (Vākyapadīya 2).
By this five-verse section beginning with "Thus, etc. and ending with *vākyapadīya* 2.53, [the author] will demonstrate that the sentence (*vākya*) is the sequence [of words],
according to the principle that "the probandum is necessarily [established] by the means of proof" (*vākyapadīya* 2).

And by these two verses, he will explain two definitions [of a sentence]: that "the first word" [is a sentence] and that "each individual word is expectant. Furthermore, there is another technical definition of a sentence in the treatise provided by the author of the Vārttika: "A sentence consists of a verb together with its indeclinables, kārakas, and qualifiers; it contains a single finite verb" (Pāṇini-vārttika 2).
And thus,

as stated by the aged Mīmāṃsaka, there is also a worldly principle: "A sentence is one because of its unity of meaning, provided that it remains expectant [of completion] when divided"— Mīmāṃsāsūtra 2.1.46.
1.46 Thus, these two are included within the category of the aggregate (saṅghāta).
These two will also be examined first, for the purpose of establishing the rules regarding the *nighāta* accent and so forth, in the passage beginning with *vākyapadīya* 2.3;
thus, it should be understood that there are exactly eight variations of the sentence according to different opinions.

Furthermore, as for what was stated by this Bhartṛhari in the *Vṛtti*—"this is merely an illustration; he will show other definitions of sentences as well"—that should be understood as being made without regard for the inclusion of the definitions of sentences provided by the author of the *Vārttika* and others.

And regarding the definitions of sentences already mentioned, he will reveal their true nature in due order through the *Kārikās* themselves according to the established arrangement; therefore, there is no purpose here in demonstrating them again.
Furthermore, in connection with the definition of the sentence, he will likewise demonstrate the various doctrinal differences concerning the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*) and its relations.

In that regard, according to the view that the sentence is indivisible (*akhaṇḍapakṣa*), the meaning of the sentence is *pratibhā* (intuition) across all three definitions; as he will show: "When there is no apprehension of the divisions [of words], a distinct *pratibhā* arises as the meaning of the sentence;
they call that the sentence-meaning" (*Vākyapadīya* 2.144).

Among the remaining five characteristics, according to the position that "the sentence is the word whose meaning is expressed," the action (*kriyā*) is the sentence-meaning; as he will state: "Action is distinct from other actions" (Vākyapadīya 2.417), and so forth, and just as intuition (*pratibhā*) has a vast range of meanings upon which performance depends.
"Since that action from which the fruit is produced is the scope of the sentence"—
thus,

according to both the view of a composite whole (*saṅghāta*) and the view of succession (*krama*), the meaning of the sentence is a conjunction (*saṃsarga*); and when that connection exists, whatever further excellence (*ādhikya*) arises [is also included].
This meaning of a sentence, which rests upon multiple words, will be demonstrated by [the author] starting with VP 2.42: "They have declared this... and so forth.

Likewise, when the view that the meaning is connected [within the sentence] (*abhihitānvaya*) is being established by means of another method— starting from *Vākyapadīya* 2.44, which states that "in the very view of the aggregate (*saṅghāta*), there is conformity with all distinctions"— it is said: "In that case, its nature, which is a relation inferable from the effect (*kāryānumeya*), does not exist" (*Vākyapadīya* 2).

By this verse, it is indicated that the meaning of the sentence is the meaning of the words themselves as they rest upon their specific distinctions; however, in these two positions—that the first word is independent and that every word is expectant of others—the meaning of the sentence proceeds primarily through their very combination, as he will explain: "But for them, the entire meaning of the sentence is completed with each individual part" (Vākyapadīya 2.1).
18. Just as the supreme Self follows along with preceding meanings, so too does the subsequent connection alone proceed; thus it is with the primary objects of meaning, Vākyapadīya 2.2.18.
Thus, by the statement in the *Vākyapadīya* (2.114),

"The meaning of a word is the denotable object (*abhidheya*), while the purpose (*prayojana*) is the meaning of the sentence," the purpose is presented as the meaning of the sentence; since this [purpose] is common to all definitions according to the view of some, the purpose is not separately categorized within the definitions of sentences.

Thus, six types of sentence-meaning (vākyārtha) have been demonstrated here: intuition (pratibhā), relation (saṃsarga), the word-meaning itself as established in its particularity through the force of relation and being free from expectancy, the related meaning (saṃsṛṣṭa evārthaḥ), action (kriyā), and purpose (prayojana).

Among these, the theory of "expression of the related" (abhihitānvaya) applies when the sentence-meaning is either the relation or the word-meaning established in its particularity through the force of relation;
whereas the theory of "expression of the related" (anvitābhidhāna) applies when the sentence-meaning is the related meaning or the action.
In the case of *pratibhā* (intuitive flash), however, the comprehension is of a single flavor; thus, no discussion regarding the "connection of what is expressed" (*abhihitānvaya*) applies there.

As for the purpose [of the sentence], it is indeed the "connection of what is expressed" (*abhihitānvaya*), though the designations of injunction (*vidhi*), mandate (*niyoga*), and productive activity (*bhāvanā*) as the meanings of sentences have not been definitively established. This is because the synonymy of *bhāvanā* and "action" (*kriyā*) is generally observed; the dispute between the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*) and the Mīmāṃsakas here concerns only whether these belong to the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛti*) or the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*).

Furthermore, since *bhāvanā* is both transitive (*sakarmika*) and intransitive (*akarmikā*), and is thus a "kriyā" (action), there is no difference between these two despite their distinction, because they are equally that which is to be accomplished (*sādhyatva*).

Just as the action consisting of the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is exclusively something to be accomplished, so too is *bhāvanā*; how then could there be a difference between these two based on a mere internal distinction? As for *vidhi* (injunction) and *niyoga* (mandate), since these are meanings found only in sentences ending in optative (*liṅ*), imperative (*loṭ*), or gerundive (*kṛtya*) suffixes, they are not accepted here because they do not apply to all cases; therefore, they have not been demonstrated in this context.

The meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*) for the Śākyas is as follows: it is a form projected as having an external nature, which is indeed indivisible, yet which is delineated by a particular conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). This form appears as if variegated by word-meanings (*padārtha*) that—though non-sequential—are superimposed as if they were sequential through an external form. These word-meanings arise from the awakening of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) instilled by various conceptualizations of sentence-meanings since beginningless time. Thus, this [sentence-meaning] should generally be understood as residing within the very interior of the mental appearance (*pratibhāsa*).

A sentence, too, arises from the awakening of latent impressions (vāsanā) deposited by various beginningless conceptualizations of sentences; though its constituent words are sequential, it appears as if variegated by non-sequential words. Being superimposed as an external form and delineated by a specific conceptualization (*viśiṣṭa-vikalpa*), it is merely a particular form superimposed as an external reality. Thus, it is essentially identical to the "synthesis by the intellect" (*buddhyanusaṃhṛti*); therefore, one should understand that there is no omission here of the sentence and the sentence-meaning according to that [Bhartṛhari’s] doctrine.

For the Naiyāyikas and others, however, just as the final phoneme—assisted by the memory of each preceding phoneme—is the word when it is made the object of an experience occurring in its state of perishing, so too the very last word—assisted by the memory of each preceding word—is the sentence when it is made the object of an experience occurring in its state of perishing; thus, this view generally falls within the category of the "aggregate" (saṅghāta) theory.

Likewise, since the cognition produced by the final word, assisted by the recollection of each preceding word-meaning, constitutes the sentence-meaning, this [sentence-meaning] is for the most part included within the *saṃsarga* (relation) view; therefore, one should not claim that there is an *avyāpti* (lack of pervasion) here due to its non-inclusion in that [other category]. Alternatively, if the sentence is considered to be a single, partless entity consisting of *sphoṭa*, and the sentence-meaning is characterized as *pratibhā* (intuition), then the relationship between the sentence and the sentence-meaning is one of superimposition (*adhyāsa*). As he will state: "The function of that which resides in the sentence [occurs] with respect to the sentence-meaning" (*Vākyapadīya* 2.263), and so forth.

Among the remaining positions, from the perspective of the Mīmāṃsakas, the relationship between word and meaning is exclusively that characterized as "fitness" (*yogyatā*), defined by the relation of signifier and signified (*vācyavācakabhāva*).

However, according to the Buddhist view, following the method of the Vijñānavāda, this relationship is everywhere one of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) within the mental [representation of] the word and meaning; whereas, in the theory of external objects (*bāhyārthavāda*), it should be understood as being characterized by convention (*saṅketa*).
Furthermore, according to the Naiyāyikas and others, it is precisely characterized by convention.

Thus, in this context, the nature of sentences, sentence-meanings, and their relations should be understood in brief. Among these relations, the author will demonstrate only *adhyāsa* (superimposition) here; however, he will explain all [the relations] in the section on words (*padakāṇḍa*). Therein, the commentator—who is intent upon refuting the positions of those who maintain that words are real—establishes that for the Grammarian (*vaiyākaraṇa*), the sentence is a single, indivisible, partless word characterized as *sphoṭa*, that the sentence-meaning is *pratibhā* (intuitive flash), and that the relation is *adhyāsa*. This is the summary of this section.
Thus, in the commentary on the *Vākyapadīya* composed by Puṇyarāja, [verse] 2.1.2.
The scriptural passage concerning its emergence is as follows: "Venerable Sir, is this Jewel-Luster Earth eternal or non-eternal? Gautama, it may be eternal and it may be non-eternal.

For what reason, Venerable Sir, is it said that it may be eternal and it may be non-eternal? Gautama, in terms of substantiality (*dravyārthatayā*) it is eternal; [but] in terms of modalities of color, modalities of odor, modalities of taste, modalities of touch, and modalities of shape, it is non-eternal."

The root text cited here has been indicated in accordance with the reading of the *Jīvājīvābhigama-sūtra* mentioned previously on page 3, line 14–16 by the author of the *Nayacakra-vṛtti*. However, since this is the sūtra from which this perspective (*naya*) emerges, and because the reading "imā ṇaṃ bhaṃte rayaṇappabhetyādi yāvat saṃṭhāṇapajjavehiṃ" is seen in the *Nayacakra-vṛtti*, the reading might also have been: "davvaṭṭhayāe sāsatā, asāsatā vaṇṇapajjavehiṃ gaṃdhapajjavehiṃ rasapajjavehiṃ phāsapajjavehiṃ saṃṭhāṇapajjavehiṃ."
In the intellect, which has had seeds sown by the preceding sounds, the final sound—

together with those preceding sounds— manifests the nature of the word and deposits seeds of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) and mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) that are conducive to the discernment of the manifest [word], each succeeding one being superior to the last.

Thereupon, that final particular sound, through its assistance, causes the form of the word’s own nature to be established in the intellect, whose capacity for maturation has been reached through the attainment of the activity of the seeds of latent impressions and mental cultivation for discernment.

Thus, in the *Svavṛtti* on the *Vākyapadīya* composed by Bhartṛhari, regarding the phrase "by means of sounds" (*nādaiḥ*), the ellipsis is "by means of the resonances (*dhvanibhiḥ*) which illuminate the *sphoṭa*.
Regarding the phrase "in that upon which the seeds have been sown" (*āhitabījāyām*), "seeds" (*bījāni*) are powers (*śaktayaḥ*); they are deposited in that [intellect] by way of those powers.
The connection is: "together with the resonance (dhvani)," meaning that at that time the word-sound (śabda) is apprehended.

Regarding the phrase "whose maturation has been repeated" (āvṛttaparipākāyām), it means that of which the maturation (paripāka) has been repeated; and "maturation" is a specific attainment of its own nature toward the production of an effect, and this [maturation] exists even in the case of seeds.

Because the manifestation of that [subtle form] occurs through the specific cognition of the distinction between the primary sound and its echo due to their simultaneous presence, and because it persists until the time of the final sound, there is also the appearance of duration over an interval of time.
However, this ripening of the seeds is not the ripening of the intellect itself; rather, since the seeds are not distinct from the intellect, they are treated as being related to the intellect alone.
The analysis of the compound is: "that in which maturation has reached its completion.

Regarding the term *vyaktapariccheda* (distinct determination): it means the ascertainment of a specific nature; or, the distinct determination of the manifest is the cultivation of latent impressions (*saṃskāra-bhāvanā*). It is precisely the capacities (*śaktayaḥ*) that are deposited, and these are designated by terms such as "latent impressions" and so forth.

For instance: the potencies (*śaktayaḥ*) which refine the mind and produce a specific [result] are designated by the term "impression" (*saṃskāra*); and the cultivation of that form is "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*), because they cultivate it through a conscious aspect as seeds by way of generating a subsequent specific cognition.
Therefore, it is a coordinate compound (*samānādhikaraṇa-samāsa*): it is both an impression, a cultivation, and a seed.

"Delimitation" (*pariccheda*) refers to the impressions (*saṃskāra*) and other factors which are the means for delimiting the *sphoṭa*. Their "attainment of activity" (*vṛttilābha*) means that they have reached a state directed toward a specific effect;
here, "maturation" (*paripāka*) is simply this capacity (*yogyatā*). The meaning is that this [capacity] has been attained by which [the intellect] becomes capable of delimiting the *sphoṭa*.
Thus it is stated in the commentary on the *Svavṛtti* of the *Vākyapadīya* composed by Vṛṣabhadeva.
"In that [intellect] in which the seed has been deposited by sounds and resonances" means that in which the seed of cultivation (*bhāvanā-bīja*) has been placed;

"whose maturation has been repeated" means that whose maturation has been practiced. Although a certain seed of cultivation is deposited by the first resonance and a certain maturation—a specific capacity for producing an effect—is produced by it, and likewise by the second, and thus the maturations are distinct, nevertheless, the expression "repeated" is justified by recourse to the genus (*jāti*), just as one says, "the Brahmins have eaten eight times."

There is another explanation for the term *āvṛtta*: it refers to that [cognition] in which there is the ripening (*paripāka*)—that is, the maturation—of the afflictions (*kaṣāya*) such as passion, which had been an obstacle to ascertainment (*avadhāraṇa*). Alternatively, it means that in which the ripening of the afflictions occurs through repetition (*āvṛtti*).
In some places, however, the reading is *āvṛtti*.

The meaning is that the word is ascertained within the intellect, the internal organ; when the final sound is ascertained along with the preceding sounds, then the word "cow" (*gauḥ*) itself is also ascertained.
The Sāṅkhyas maintain that even knowledge, which is a synonym for ascertainment (*avadhāraṇā*), has as its locus the internal organ known as the intellect (*buddhi*).
Regarding this ascertainment, the followers of the Vārttikakāra consider it to be a "variegated cognition" (*citrabuddhi*).

Alternatively, when the seeds have been deposited in the intellect by the preceding sounds along with the final sound, the word is ascertained immediately after the last sound as "the word 'cow' is one"; they call this ascertainment, which has all the phonemes as its object, "recollection" (*smaraṇa*).

"But from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), this is indeed perceptual knowledge (*pratyakṣajñāna*), because it is produced by the auditory faculty refined by sound; for otherwise, a clear manifestation would not be possible.
Thus it is stated in the *Gopālikā*, a commentary on Maṇḍana Miśra’s *Sphoṭasiddhi* composed by Rāmacandra, page 132:
"The word is apprehended in the intellect when it has reached maturity through repeated practice" (*Vākyapadīya* 1.84).

These are not stated as mere personal inventions; rather, they are the "sūtra of origin" for this perspective (*naya*), from which it emerges. The author of the *Nayacakra* states that this very scripture—beginning with "O Venerable One, these [worlds] of Ratnaprabhā... and continuing up to "...in terms of the varieties of shape"—is the reason, because it speaks of differentiation (*bheda*). Thus, [the text says]: "The living and non-living beings are impermanent... (Jīvājīvābhigama Sūtra 3.1).

78. Because of this statement regarding differentiation, [the term] *varṇa* [is used] for *varṇa*, *paryava*, and so forth; it will exist everywhere (*samantād bhavitā*) because they form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyabhāvāt*). Furthermore, because it exists and moves all around (*parito bhavanād gamanācca*) the *varṇas*, he explains [it] as being from the *varṇas*:
"In *varṇa*, *paryāya*, and so forth," and so on.

Because the term *paryāya* is understood as having the sense of "encompassing" (*parigamana*), and because the word *paryava*—which denotes a state of being—is taken [in this sense], it refers to that in which there is an encompassing of color (*varṇa*) and so forth, or where there is a state of being on all sides (*samantato bhāva*). Alternatively, since the root *ava* is listed in the Dhātupāṭha with the meaning of "protection" (*rakṣaṇa*), the term *paryava* may be a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "the *paryāyas* themselves are the *paryavas*," due to the application of the rule for identical forms (*sarūpaikaśeṣa*) and the inclusion of both types of compounds. Furthermore, because the *paryāyas* and *paryavas* involve movement on all sides and a state of being on all sides, the same etymological derivation applies to both meanings of *paryāya* and *paryava*. Anticipating the question, "By what meaning does the explanation of one apply to the second when either *paryāya* or *paryava* is mentioned? he says: "Color (*varṇa*) is the *paryava*, because it exists and moves on all sides. This is because they form a single sentence; that is, because substances, qualities, and actions—including their subdivisions—which are primarily related through the connection of inherence (*samavāya*) with existence (*sattā*), exist in a combined form, they constitute a single sentence. Thus, he demonstrates the *bahuvrīhi* [interpretation]: "because of the existence and movement of color itself on all sides."
The reading "ratappabhe" found within this [passage] does not exist in the Ya manuscripts;

Because of the statement regarding differentiation: "The living and the non-living are impermanent" (Tattvārthasūtra 3.1.78).

Regarding the sequence beginning with "color" (*varṇa*) and so forth: because it forms a single syntactical unit, "color" (*varṇa*) is [also] "paryava," meaning it exists (*bhavitā*) everywhere (*samantāt*). This is because color itself exists (*parito bhavana*) and moves (*gamana*) all around.

"Bhante, is this Jewel-Lustre Earth (Ratnaprabhā-pṛthivī) eternal or non-eternal? Goyama! It is sometimes eternal and sometimes non-eternal. For what reason, Bhante, is it said that it is sometimes eternal and sometimes non-eternal? Goyama! Thus [ends] the third chapter, first section, seventy-eighth [sūtra] in the Jīvājīvābhigama Sūtra.
The explanation of this [passage] beginning with "Imāṃ ṇaṃ bhaṃte" is as follows:

"O Venerable One! Is this Ratnaprabhā earth eternal or non-eternal? The Blessed One replied: "Gautama! It may be eternal in some way—that is to say, according to the intention of a certain philosophical standpoint (naya)—and it may be non-eternal in some other way."
Desiring to know this very point in detail, he asks: "Se keṇaṭṭheṇam" and so forth.

The word *se* has the meaning of the word *atha* (now/then), and it is used here in the sense of an inquiry: "For what purpose, for what reason, O Venerable One, is it said that [the soul] might be eternal or might be non-eternal? The Blessed One replied: "Gautama! By way of substantial reality (*dravyārthatayā*), it is eternal," and so forth.

In this context, "substance" (*dravya*) is everywhere called the "universal" (*sāmānya*). Based on the etymological derivation that "it flows toward" (*dravati*) or "goes toward" (*gacchati*) those various modes (*paryāya*) or particularities (*viśeṣa*), substance alone is the real object; that [view] for which the categories of existence are substance and not the modes is the "substance-view" (*dravyārtha*). A specific perspective (*nayaviśeṣa*) that establishes the existence of mere substance is the "substance-view"; its state is "substantiality" (*dravyārthatā*). By this—that is, by the intention of the perspective that establishes the existence of mere substance—it is "eternal" (*śāśvatī*), because when one reflects upon the doctrine of the substantialist perspective, such a form of the earth, such as the "Jewel-Luster" (*ratnaprabhā*), exists at all times.

It is impermanent and non-eternal by virtue of the modalities of color such as black and so forth, the modalities of odor such as fragrant and so forth, the modalities of taste such as bitter and so forth, and the modalities of touch such as hardness and so forth; for these [qualities] such as color undergo alteration either moment by moment or after some period of time, and it is this lack of persistence in its own state that constitutes impermanence.

Nor is it the case that permanence and impermanence reside in different substrata, because we accept both difference and non-difference between substance (*dravya*) and mode (*paryāya*); otherwise, both would result in non-existence. For it can be argued: the substance postulated by others is non-existent, because it is distinct from its modes, like the son of a barren woman who lacks modes such as childhood; likewise, the modes postulated by others are non-existent, because they are distinct from substance, like the modes of childhood and so forth belonging to the son of a barren woman. And it has been said: "Substance devoid of modes, and modes devoid of substance [are non-existent]."
