"One who desires a detailed exposition should consult the *Dharmasaṅgrahaṇī-ṭīkā*," as it will be stated in the *Nayacakravṛtti* at the conclusion of the ninth chapter, based on the fact that [the root *ava*] is listed among the meanings of "protection, motion, splendor, affection, satisfaction, understanding, entry, hearing, ownership, begging, action, desire, radiance, attainment, embracing, injury, burning, state, and increase" in the *Jīvājīvābhigamasūtra-vṛtti* composed by the venerable teacher Malayagiri.

In the *Haimadhātupāṭha* as well, the reading is: "489. *ava* [is used] in nineteen senses: protection, motion, splendor, affection, satisfaction, understanding, entry, hearing, ownership, requesting, action, desire, radiance, attainment, embracing, injury, burning, state, and increase. However, in the printed *Pāṇinīyadhātupāṭha*, the reading found is: "601. *ava* [is used] in [twenty-one senses]: protection, motion, splendor, affection, satisfaction, understanding, entry, hearing, ownership, requesting, action, desire, radiance, attainment, embracing, injury, giving, portion, and increase. (Pāṇini 1.2.64: *sarūpāṇām ekaśeṣa ekavibhaktau*—"Of similar forms, only one remains when they are in the same case ending").
2.64 Because there is a single denotation. *pra* (is understood).

But how is there that encompassing (*parigamana*) and pervading (*paryavana*)? To demonstrate this with reasoning and illustration, he says: "From the colors themselves," and so on, up to "are perceived. From the colors themselves—namely, from qualities such as form (*rūpa*) and the rest—a distinct quality (*guṇāntara*), such as a variegated color (*citravarṇa*) consisting of red, dark, pale, and so forth, arises in earth and the other elements; it is indeed another color (*varṇāntara*). This occurs precisely because of the rule governing its origination, and it either exists [therein] or extends everywhere (*samantād gacchati*).

These [qualities] are understood as consisting of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*). Therefore, by means of those ultimate constituents (*paryava*) such as color and so forth, [the earth] is non-eternal. Furthermore, "color" itself is an ultimate constituent (*paryava*), a quality (*guṇa*), such as blackness and so on, as far as possible, as well as conjunction, disjunction, separateness, priority, posteriority, and so forth; or it is produced by heating (*pākaja*), precisely because of the rule governing its origination. As it has been said: "Those for whom the capacity for origination is authorized," [and] in the case of earth and the other elements, another color arises or it moves everywhere.

Those [entities], whether they be the ultimate constituents (*paryava*) or modes (*paryāya*) such as color and so forth, or substances such as jars and the like, are themselves composed of others; and by those [latter] are further understood substances composed of yet others—namely, states such as the lump of clay and so forth, which consist of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*), and which lack the nature of color and so forth, such as jars and potsherds.

Therefore, the meaning is that [the world] consists of these impermanent causes and effects, which are the ultimate constituents of color and so forth, and which constitute the very essence of jars and other things, yet are characterized by prior non-existence and destruction.

In a *karmadhāraya* compound, [the term] "color" (*varṇa*) alone, as well as "perfection" (*paryava*), "quality" (*guṇa*), and so forth, apply as far as possible. These are the qualities; by them, [the substance] is "non-eternal. This connects with the phrase "by means of color and the other perfections. As far as possible, certain qualities such as blackness and the like reside in substances that have been produced or not yet produced; some reside in the fourfold [atoms] that have not yet begun to form a composite, while in other substances produced from them, they are preceded by the qualities of their causes within the fourfold [categories]. Among earthy substances alone, redness and the like are produced by heating (*pākaja*). Furthermore, it is eternal in terms of the substantial reality (*dravyārthataḥ*) by way of smell and the other [qualities].
Thus ends the sixth chapter on injunctions, prohibitions, and further injunctions.

Conjunction and disjunction exist in things possessing activity; separateness exists in all substances; priority and posteriority depend upon direction, place, and time, and these are their indicative marks. By the inclusion of the word "etcetera," the specific qualities such as odor, sound, and cognition belong respectively to earth, space, the self, and so forth. Numbers such as unity and so on are common to all substances. Because of the use of the instrumental case in the phrase "by means of odor etc.," it is understood that by these [qualities], whether non-eternal or eternal, the substance is called "Ratnaprabhā" (Jewel-Light) from the perspective of its substantial nature (*dravyārthataḥ*), through its general properties such as form, configuration, and shape.
A single variegated color (*citra-rūpa*) arises from blue and other colors as a single form;

for just as whiteness and so forth are specific qualities of color, so too is variegation itself a specific quality of color. Even though it is not designated by terms such as "white" and so on, its existence is established because it is designated by its own term.
Now, one might ask: how can contradictory elements like blue and so forth give rise to a single form? [The answer is: just as in the case of white [threads].

Just as it is observed that many white forms produce a single white form, so too, because it is seen that blue and other colors likewise produce a variegated form (*citrarūpa*), this must be accepted;
thus, in the *Vyomavatī* commentary on Praśastapāda’s *Bhāṣya*, in the section defining earth,

it is stated that sometimes even in a single individual object there is the coexistence of multiple types of color, where a composite whole (*avayavin*) is produced by constituent parts (*avayava*) that are related to various kinds of colors.

If it is asked, "How is this so?", it is said: Just as a composite whole (*avayavin*) is produced from its parts (*avayava*), so too must color be produced in the composite by means of the colors of the parts. In the parts, there is not only white color nor only black; rather, there are black, white, green, and so forth.
Nor is there any rule that one of these alone produces the color of the whole while the others do not, for each of them is observed to possess the capacity [to produce color] individually elsewhere.

Nor is it logical to claim that because they are mutually contradictory, none of them initiate [the effect] at all; for a composite whole (*avayavin*) possessing a variegated form (*citrarūpa*) is perceived, and a substance devoid of form lacks perceptibility.

Furthermore, it is not the case that the colors of the parts, when aggregated, are perceived here by the variegated cognition such that the composite whole is perceived through them alone—this would render the conceptual construction invalid. For if that were so, the same would apply elsewhere, resulting in the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the total abolition of the form of the composite whole.

Therefore, it is produced by them acting together; and being so produced, because it conforms to the natures of its various constituent causes, it must consist of black, white, and green [parts], and is thus designated as "variegated" (*citram*).

This is stated in the *Kandalī*, a commentary on Praśastapāda’s *Bhāṣya*, in the section defining earth, where it says that another color arises in earth and the other elements precisely due to the rule of their production, or that it goes everywhere.

These are understood as consisting of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*); therefore, by means of those ultimate limits (*paryava*) such as color (*varṇa*), it is impermanent. Furthermore, the color itself is the ultimate limit, the quality (*guṇa*), such as blackness and so forth, as well as conjunction (*saṃyoga*), disjunction (*vibhāga*), separateness (*pṛthaktva*), priority (*paratva*), posteriority (*aparatva*), and so on, according to their possibility. By these [qualities], let it be seen that [the object] is produced by the dominant influence (*adhipattikṛta*). (See Ṭīkā 8). *pra*. (Prakaraṇa)
See page 437, line 12, etc.?
...by them also another [thing] is begun;
how should I maintain [it], O Prajñā?
...and so forth.
Now he states the [objects of] form and so on: "The qualities have been stated" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 7.1).
1. This means they have been indicated by the *rūpādi-sūtra*; furthermore, the definition of the qualities (*guṇa*) has been stated in Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 7.1.
The meaning is that its dissimilarity to substance and action has been stated by [the sūtra] "2.1.15: [Quality] resides in a substance," and so forth.
And it has been stated [in the Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 7.1.3]: "This possesses such qualities; this possesses such qualities.
Likewise, it has been said: "Earth possesses color, taste, smell, and touch. (VS 2.1.1)
1.1 In that regard, on earth, color, taste, smell, and touch are impermanent because their substance is impermanent; Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 7.1.1.

1.4: Due to the destruction of an earthen object such as a jar, there is also the destruction of the color and other qualities residing therein, because of the destruction of their substrate and due to contact with fire (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 7).

Furthermore, due to conjunction with fire (*agni-saṃyoga*), there is the destruction of color and other qualities in the atoms (*paramāṇu*) composed of earth; however, for those qualities inherent in the effect (*kārya*), destruction occurs solely from the destruction of their substratum.
But why [is it that] in the atoms [destruction occurs] specifically from conjunction with fire? Because of the manifestation of another quality (*guṇāntara-prādurbhāva*). Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 7.1.5.

1.6. Since another quality distinct from qualities such as blackness arises, the previous qualities of the atoms have perished, because qualities do not originate in that which already possesses qualities; by this, the non-eternality of eternal things is stated. Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 7.1.6.

By this [statement] regarding the manifestation of other qualities, the impermanence of color and other [sensory qualities] in eternal atoms has been explained specifically with respect to those of the earth; for [it is held that] in water, fire, and air, these qualities are eternal because the substance is eternal (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 7.1).

8. Water, fire, air, atoms, color-form, and so forth are eternal because their substrata are eternal and because there is no manifestation of another contradictory quality; therefore, there is no destruction by contact with fire.
In the case of non-eternal [substances], they are non-eternal because the substance itself is non-eternal. Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 7.1.8–9.

9. In impermanent things such as water and the like, qualities such as color (rūpa) are impermanent because they perish when their substratum perishes; furthermore, on earth, they are preceded by the qualities of their causes and are produced by heat (pākaja). Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 7.1.9.

In non-eternal earth, which exists in the form of an effect, qualities such as color and so forth arise preceded by the qualities of their causes; however, in eternal earth, which has the nature of atoms (*paramāṇu*), those qualities produced by heating (*pākaja*)—arising from heating through contact with fire—are found.
In water, fire, and air, qualities produced by heating do not exist, being preceded by the qualities of their causes. Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 7.1.10.

11. In the effect, such as a composite substance consisting of water and other elements, qualities such as color (*rūpa*) and so forth are originated by way of their inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*). However, qualities produced by heating (*pākaja*) do not exist at all in the atoms of water and the like, because there is an absence of any other opposing quality; for a substance devoid of qualities cannot originate further qualities (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 7.1.7).

12. Qualities are produced by the qualities of the causes only in a substance that has been produced while devoid of qualities, but not in qualities or actions, because [qualities and actions] lack co-inherence in a single object with the qualities of all their constituent parts, just like action-ness (*karmatva*). By this, those qualities produced by heating (*pākaja*) are explained. Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 7.1.12.

13. If it is argued that when the dark [color] and other qualities cease due to contact with fire, qualities produced by baking (*pākaja*) arise, and thus they too are established as being in a substance devoid of qualities— just as conjunction is initiated in a substance possessing conjunction, and qualities produced by baking are in a substance possessing qualities— [the answer is] no, because [a substance] possesses only one quality at a time (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 7.1.7).

14. Those qualities produced by heating (*pākaja*) possess a single substance (*ekadravyavantaḥ*); how could they be initiated in that very same [substance], given their mutual contradiction? However, the initiation of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) in that which already possesses conjunction is not faulty, because it possesses multiple substances (*anekadravyatva*).
Thus it is stated in Candrānanda’s *Vaiśeṣikasūtravṛtti*, p. 25, regarding odors and so forth.
"Permanence exists from the perspective of substantiality"—thus ends the sixth section on the rules of injunction and restriction.
Now, time is described: "The marks of time are 'the other,' 'the further,' 'simultaneous,' 'non-simultaneous,' 'long,' and 'quick'" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 2.2.6).
2.6. These—namely, the notions of remoteness (*paratva*), proximity (*aparatva*), and so forth—are the marks (*liṅga*) of time (*kāla*).

In this regard, when a cognition of remoteness arises with respect to a young man conjoined with a distant spatial region, and a cognition of proximity arises with respect to an old man conjoined with a proximate spatial region, that causal factor by which—through the consideration of such traits as black hair in the young man and wrinkles or grey hair in the old man—the cognition of proximity arises in the young man and the cognition of remoteness arises in the old man, is time.

Likewise, time (*kāla*) is that from which the cognition arises when agents performing equal actions do so simultaneously or non-simultaneously. Similarly, with respect to the single result of an action known as boiled rice (*odana*), when a series of many actions such as placing the pot on the fire proceeds with a single agent, time is that from which the cognitions "it was done long ago" and "it was done recently today" arise.
Its qualities are number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, and disjunction.
That from which [the cognition] "this is here" arises is the indicative mark of space; Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 2.2.10.
Taking a corporeal substance as a limit, that from which there arises the cognition "this is to the east of that" and so forth is the indicative mark (liṅga) of space (diś).
Its qualities are number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, and disjunction.
Thus, in the Vaiśeṣika-sūtra-vṛtti composed by Candrānanda (p. 13):
"Odor is the quality apprehended by the sense of smell;
it is of two kinds—fragrant and foul."
Functioning solely upon the earth...
Sound is a quality perceivable by the ear, residing solely in space.
...Buddhi is the cognition that is the cause of all worldly transactions;

sukha is that which is experienced as agreeable by all; duḥkha is that which is experienced as disagreeable by all; kāma is desire; dveṣa is aversion; prayatna is effort; dharma is that produced by enjoined action; adharma is that produced by prohibited action; these eight—beginning with buddhi—are the specific qualities (viśeṣaguṇa) belonging exclusively to the self (ātman).
Thus ends the *Tarkasaṅgraha* composed by Annambhaṭṭa.

Now he begins [the discussion of] number and the other qualities. Number is the cause of the conventional usage of difference (*bhedavyavahāra*). To show that it is distinct from color and the other [qualities], he says: "On account of its being distinct from color, taste, smell, and touch, oneness is a different entity; likewise is separateness" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 7.2).
1. This cognition, such as "this is one," does not have color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth as its cause, because it is distinct from the cognition of those [objects].
For if color-form and so forth were the cause, the cognition would be "possessing color-form" (*rūpavān*) and so on;
therefore, it must have a different object as its cause.
In effects, oneness and single separateness are preceded by the qualities of their causes;

duality and so forth are produced from unities accompanied by a cognition whose object is multiple; likewise, double separateness and so forth are produced from [single] separatenesses. However, there is no lower generality (aparasāmānya) for single separateness and the like.
The eternality and non-eternality of those two [unity and separateness] are explained by the eternality and non-eternality of the color and touch of fire (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 7.2.2):

just as the color and touch of a fire-atom are eternal because the substance is eternal, so too unity and separateness residing in an eternal substance are eternal; and just as color and touch are non-eternal in non-eternal fire because the substance is non-eternal, so too unity and separateness residing in an effect are non-eternal.
"Retraction, evolution, and accomplishment" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 7.2.3):
and just as in the case of fire, which is an effect, the production of color and touch is preceded by the qualities of the cause, so too it is with unity and separateness.
"Thus [is the treatment] of heaviness, fluidity, and viscidity," according to the *Vaiśeṣikasūtravṛtti* composed by Candrānanda on page 27.

Thus ends the sixth method (*naya*), the variety of *naigama*, which falls within the scope of *dravyāstika*. The word "iti" serves the purpose of indicating completion; this is the designation of the chapter titled "The Chapter on Prescriptive and Restrictive Rules" (*vidhiniyamavidhyara*), arranged as a division of the *Nayacakra*, where the syllable "ra" is like a spoke (*ara*) of a wheel.
The word "iti" [is used] in the Ya[panīya] recension;
the word "iti" [is used] in the Bhā[draka] recension;
[the particle] "ca" [is used] in the Pra[tyeka] recension.
"Priority and posteriority [arise] from two things that are proximate and remote in terms of both space and time" (VS 7.2.25).

Two masses situated in the same direction are the cause of priority and posteriority produced by space; two [masses] existing at the same time, being connected with the present time, are the cause of priority and posteriority produced by time.
And those two [substances] are the cause of the notions of "near" and "distant" respectively,
because of their priority as causes and their posteriority as causes, according to Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 7.2.10.

26. Conjunction with spatial points (dik-pradeśa) that are distant or near is the non-inherent cause [of distance]; likewise, conjunctions with temporal points (kāla-pradeśa) that are distant or near [are the causes].

Due to the conjunction with spatial and temporal points, in relation to two objects—one proximate and one remote—and depending upon the cognitions of proximity and remoteness, "remoteness" (paratva) arises in the remote object and "nearness" (aparatva) arises in the proximate one.
Thus, in the *Vaiśeṣikasūtravṛtti* composed by Candrānanda (p.
28), this sixfold *dravyāstika* has been described;
and among these, the word *paryava* denotes "state" (*bhāva*), while the word *paryāya* denotes "movement everywhere" (*samantādgati*).

Specifically, however, one should understand the distinctions in the nature of each—such as injunctions (*vidhi*) and so forth—as they have been explained according to their respective observations, without abandoning the commonality of all categories.
The meaning of the word *dravya* (substance) has already been explained in various places;
here, moreover, it is called *paryava* because it exists everywhere (*samantād bhavanāt*), and *paryāya* because it moves everywhere (*samantād gamanāt*).
This reading may also be found; see page 451, line 3.

Having combined these five past [categories] with this sixth, there are six divisions in brief for one three-hundred-fold division. Among them: 1) *vidhi* (affirmation), 2) *vidhividhi* (affirmation of affirmation), 3) *vidhividhiniyama* (affirmation of affirmation and restriction), 4) *vidhiniyama* (affirmation and restriction), 5) *vidhiniyama* (affirmation and restriction), and this sixth, 6) *vidhiniyamavidhi* (affirmation of affirmation-restriction). Thus, the *dravyāstika* (substantialist) is described as having six divisions; the meaning is that all these six divisions belong exclusively to the *dravyāstika*.

And among these six principles (*naya*), the word *paryava* expresses existence (*bhāva*); it is *paryava* because of existing everywhere (*samantād bhavanāt*), that is, because of existing in its entirety (*sarvātmanā bhavanāt*).

The word *paryāya* expresses movement everywhere; it is *paryāya* because of moving everywhere (*samantād gamanāt*), since a substance (*dravya*) moves all around through its nature as color and so forth.

And this meaning of the analysis (vigraha) is to be understood generally for all six [categories]; however, specifically, one should follow the distinctions in their essential natures as they have been explained individually regarding injunctions (vidhi) and so forth, according to how they appear, without abandoning the commonality of being present in all states of existence. This is because everything has everything as its nature, because the One has everything as its nature, because each single thing has everything as its nature, and because everything has each single thing as its nature; thus, he speaks of the universal presence exactly as it appears.

The meaning of the term *dravya* has already been explained in various places according to the [textual] evidence, due to the predominance of substance (*dravya*) and the subordination of mode (*paryāya*). Here at the end, the term *paryāya* is explained as "the six substances" (*ṣaḍ-dravyaḥ*), [as stated in] Prajñāpanā 176 and Paryāya-samgrahaṇī 176.
Thus end the variations of the substantial-objective standpoint (dravyārthika-naya).
Oṃ Arhaṃ.
Now begins the seventh [chapter], the "Both-and-both" standpoint (ubhayobhayāra).
If a non-existent effect were not produced because it lacks a proximate bringer-into-being, like a sky-flower;
or if even a sky-flower were produced because it lacks a proximate bringer-into-being, like an effect;
[if you argue] that there is no basis for the existence of a sky-flower—[we reply: no, for the same applies to the other case as well.

Since the jar is not identical with the clay, there is no substratum for the existence of the jar and so forth either, because that which is yet to arise is non-existent and thus cannot possess inherence of being (*sattā-samavāya*).

Now, with the desire to demonstrate the first limb of the *paryāya-naya* (the mode of perspective), and wishing to refute the two-fold method of the Vaiśeṣika mentioned immediately prior, [the author] speaks the following verse—beginning with "If it were non-existent"—in order to follow the sequence, because it is contrary to the preceding [view], and because among the *nayas* there is no lingering trace of the former once it has been set aside; he speaks specifically to refute the doctrine that the effect is non-existent (*asatkāryavāda*).

Let our own position rest for a moment; rather, we say that this view of yours is untenable even according to the perspective of the former school (the *pūrva-naya*), because the proponents of the substantialist standpoint (*dravyārthika-naya*) accept that an entity comes into being only when its potential agent is present. Therefore, an effect that is non-existent cannot arise, because it lacks a present agent, just like a sky-flower.
Alternatively, a sky-flower would also have to arise, because it lacks a present agent, just like the effect.

Since the doctrine of the conjunction of the six categories proceeds by virtue of existence (*sattā*) and inherence (*samavāya*), this discussion on existence and inherence is undertaken with the intention that by uprooting existence and inherence, the entire system itself is uprooted. [Note: *avidhi* and *ruddhānnivṛtta* appear as variants in the manuscripts.]
See *nivṛtti* from *ruddha*,
page 221, line 8;
see page 317–2, line 2.
Let it be produced; see page 323–1.
Or perhaps the reading here should be "let it be produced because it has a non-proximate agent" (*asannihitabhavitṛkatvāt*); compare page 351–2.

If it should be thought that the sky-flower lacks a substratum—on the grounds that while effects arise later, having previously been non-existent, through inherence in existence (sattā) when their causal substances exist as a substratum, the sky-flower will not arise because it lacks a substratum and thus differs in nature from an effect—this is not so, for the same logic applies to the other case as well; for even an effect, being non-existent, is likewise without a substratum like the sky-flower. Therefore, there is no distinction whatsoever between an effect and a sky-flower.

What is the reason? Because the effect, the jar, is not the reality of the clay; for in your view, the substance of clay—which undergoes transformation into forms such as a lump—is not the reality of those effects, since the lump and so forth are non-existent. Therefore, there is no substratum at all for the existence of the jar and other such things, just like the existence of a sky-flower and the like.

According to your own view, an effect such as a lump of clay or a jar, which is about to arise, is non-existent (*asat*) because it lacks inherence in existence (*niḥsattāsamavāya*); yet you admit its inherence in existence, for it is your established tenet that "inherent properties such as existence inhere in a substrate only after that substrate has arisen. In that state, even without inhering in a substrate, the effect arises by its own very existence and becomes a substrate, unlike a sky-flower. If this is so, what is the purpose of postulating a connection with an existence distinct from itself for that which already exists by its own nature? Or else, there would be no distinction between an effect and a sky-flower regarding their lack of a substrate.

If that which is non-existent becomes existent, a specific reason must be stated: why does a sky-flower not arise? Why do jars and the like arise? If it is argued that, due to the distinction between having a cause and lacking a cause—that which lacks a cause does not arise, whereas that which is called "person" (puruṣa) arises—then it would follow that an effect never arises at all, and only a cause arises; thus, the very doctrine of causation (kāraṇavāda) would be accepted.

Now, as for the recourse to the *bahuvrīhi* compound [to explain "existence"], that is not tenable because its cause does not exist, like a jar; for that which is itself non-existent lacks the capacity to serve as a substratum—how, alas, can you be so subservient to the views of others as to claim that "the sky-flower has arisen and serves as the substratum for its own attributes"? Furthermore, if there is no inherence (*samavāya*) of existence, how can there be the production of an effect? Thus, [the opponent claims] that "from the non-existent, the existent arises. (Bhāṣya)

Now, if it is argued that even without inherence in a substratum (*āśrayasamavāya*), an effect, having arisen by its own very existence, becomes a substratum—by contrast with a sky-flower—then what is the purpose of postulating a connection with a separate existence (*sattā*) for that which already exists by itself? Or, if the non-existent were to become existent, there would be no distinction between an effect and a sky-flower created by a substratum; thus, the reason for this distinction must be stated: why does the sky-flower not arise, while the jar and so forth do arise? If it is said that it is due to the distinction between having a cause and lacking a cause, like the case of causes [themselves]...

If that which is without a cause does not arise, then what is called "person" (puruṣa) would not arise at all as an effect; rather, it would be the cause itself that arises, and thus the doctrine of causality (kāraṇavāda) alone would be accepted. Alternatively, if one resorts to a *bahuvrīhi* compound [interpreting it as "that for which a cause does not exist"], then it does not arise because its cause is non-existent, like a jar; [the text continues: "they resort to the substratum... (*āśrayanty āśrayiṇaḥ*).
What is the state of being a servant? It is the state of being a servant to another's doctrine;
it is the state of being a servant to existence.
Now, regarding the passage beginning with "athāśrayī" and so forth:

if, for fear of the defect of falling into the state of being like a sky-flower, it is maintained that the effect—which is existent even without inherence in an existent substratum—is produced as a substratum by its own existence, that is, by its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-sattā*), because it is different from a sky-flower which will never be produced; then, as for the passage beginning with "tata evaṃ tarhi," this very point is indeed accepted by us—that it is existent by its own majesty—but not by you.

And if you maintain this view, just as we do, then for that effect—which is already existent in its own right and distinct from non-existent things such as a donkey’s horn—what purpose is served by postulating a connection with an additional "existence" (*sattā*)? The meaning is that nothing at all is gained by such a postulation; thus, the connection with existence is useless. Consequently, the doctrine of the inherence (*samavāya*) of all substances, qualities, actions, and so forth, in their causes and effects, is refuted for that very reason.

If you do not accept that undesirable consequence, then as I stated previously regarding the effect (*kārya*) and the sky-flower (*khapuṣpa*), there is no difference in their lack of a substratum; since both are equally non-existent, what is the specific reason why only the effect arises and the sky-flower does not? That manifestation—namely, "if [it] were non-existent," and so forth—is already explained up to the point: "why then does the jar and so forth arise? Therefore, the fault of there being no distinction between the effect and the sky-flower remains as it was.
Is it from that [cause], or rather from this [cause]?
If [the two cases] are equal, there is victory for the opponent; if they are equal, there is defeat for the opponent?

Now, if it is argued that this fault is avoided by stating that there is a distinction between having a cause and lacking a cause—just as, respectively, a jar and the like have a cause while a sky-flower lacks a cause, such that a distinction exists—and that jars and the like are connected with causes, namely inherent and non-inherent causes, whereas sky-flowers and the like are not.

He himself clarifies his own intention: "If that which is not produced is called 'akāraṇa' (non-cause), then it does not follow that it is a cause; thus, if a *tatpuruṣa* compound is intended, then the effect would never be produced at all, but rather only the cause would be produced. Since, according to the ancient systems such as the *vidhi-vidhyādi*, that very thing is produced as an effect, the doctrine of causality (*kāraṇavāda*) itself would be accepted. And that is not desired by me;
therefore, no investigation should be made regarding the *tatpuruṣa* [compound]."

Now, as for the recourse to the *bahuvrīhi* compound in the sense that "that which has no cause is 'causeless' (*akāraṇa*"), under that conception of a *bahuvrīhi*, the effect does not arise because its cause is non-existent, like a sky-flower; this is the point of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), for it is not the case that the effect arises in the same manner as a jar.

What follows from this? From that [non-existence], because they have not yet arisen, there is no substratum for existence (*sattā*); and because there is no substratum for existence, there is an absence of its relation [to them]. If that is so, then it follows that everything is non-existent. Since atoms (*paramāṇu*) and the like are not causes, they have not arisen; and since they have not arisen, they lack a substratum, and thus there is an absence of inherence (*samavāya*) with existence. For it is accepted that inherence with existence occurs only when they serve as a substratum. Consequently, due to the absence of inherence with existence, the causes—atoms and the like—are absent; and because of the absence of these causes, there is no distinction between the effect and things inherent in the effect (such as qualities) and a sky-flower. Thus, everything is void, which entails all contradictions.

Now, it might be argued: "Because they are eternally produced, atoms, space, and so forth exist by their very own presence; for only effects—substances, qualities, and actions—possess existence through inherence in *sattā* (Being). If this were the case, then because [space, atoms, etc. do not undergo any modification of their essential nature and because they are non-different from the Self (*ātman*), there would be no connection between them and *sattā*.

And in the absence of such a connection, just as *sattā* exists—as it is a category (*padārtha*) and possesses its own essential presence—so too would those substances, qualities, and actions exist by virtue of their own essential presence, even without *sattā*. Thus, the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) would be established.

To this it is replied: "In that case, there would follow the consequence of the non-existence of all things," and so on, up to "the voidness of all things" and "all contradictions. [The argument is as follows: atoms do not arise because they lack a cause, and ether and the other elements likewise do not arise. Because they have not arisen, they provide no substratum for existence (*sattā*). Since they lack such a substratum, there is an absence of the inherence (*samavāya*) of existence in them; for it is accepted that the inherence of existence occurs only when those [atoms and elements] serve as its substratum. Thus, he demonstrates their dissimilarity [to the case where existence does inhere].

Furthermore, due to the absence of inherence in existence (*sattā-samavāya*), there is a non-existence of causes such as atoms, like a sky-flower. Because of that non-existence, where could the effect—inhering in nothing and lacking a cause—possibly inhere? Therefore, because it does not inhere in a cause, there is no distinction between that [effect] and a sky-flower; thus, the previously mentioned fault of non-distinction remains exactly as it was. Moreover, by you yourself, the effect has now been brought together with the atoms that are the substrata of the effect, according to another analysis of the compound: "of those qualities such as color, etc., and of the pot-ness, etc., and of the upward motions, etc., which inhere in the effect and have the effect as their substratum."

If it is asked, "What follows from that?", it is replied: By asserting "thus there is the voidness of all," and saying "thus all entities do not exist," you become a proponent of the ultimate void; for the word *iti* serves the purpose of a conclusion, [it implies] "thus there are contradictions to everything. In this way, for one who asserts that everything is non-existent, there are contradictions with one's own words, with what is accepted, with perception, with inference, and with common usage, because of the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Since the sūtras defining cause and non-cause, effect and non-effect, opposition and non-opposition, as well as the sūtra on the non-distinction of existence and so forth, all arise from the inherence of existence (*sattā-samavāya*), what would remain of the Vaiśeṣika system—which is intended to establish their manifoldness—given that there is no distinction between effects and causes, or between [existent things] and a sky-flower? [Note: The text contains several scribal errors and abbreviations (e.g., *samba॰pā॰ḍe॰ bhā॰* and *samba॰ raṃ॰ vi॰*) which appear to be marginalia or citations from other works; these have been omitted from the translation as they do not form part of the philosophical argument.]
...ṭādi abhisamba°?
...vācyam, thus [it is said] in the Bhāṣya;
"vācya" [is said] in the Ya[śomitra-ṭīkā].
Is it "in the sentence" (*vākye*)? Or is it "the recourse to the sentence" (*vākyasamāśrayaṇa*)? See page 320.1.

If that were the case, it would follow that all things are non-existent. Since atoms and the like are not causes, they are unproduced; and because they lack a substratum (*anāśrayatva*), there is no inherence of existence (*sattā-samavāya*) in them. For it is accepted that the inherence of existence occurs only when those [atoms] serve as a substratum. Consequently, due to the absence of the inherence of existence, and thus the absence of causes such as atoms, there would be no distinction between an effect or its inherent properties and a sky-flower. Thus, everything would be empty, which contradicts all established principles.

Now, it might be argued: "Because they are eternally arisen, atoms, space, and so forth exist by their very own presence; for existence belongs only to effect-substances, qualities, and actions through their inherence in existence (*sattā*).

If this is so, then because [existence] does not descend into space, atoms, and the like, and because there is no difference in essence (*ātmābheda*) between them, it would have no connection with anything.

And in the absence of such a connection, just as existence itself is existent because it is a category (*padārtha*) and because of its own essential presence, so too would those substances, qualities, and actions be.
Because of [its] non-existence, it is not a substratum;
because of its non-substantiality,
there is no existence.
See *Sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*, *Kāryasama*, and *Pāka* in the first *āhnika* of the first chapter of the *Vaiśeṣikadarśana*.
See page 437, note 5, 8; page 440, note 5, 6:
*sattāsattāsamavāya* (see Bhāṣya);
see page 455, line 11.
Thus, lest there be no distinction between an effect that previously did not exist and a causal one and a sky-flower, it might be argued: "Because they are eternally produced," and so forth;

[namely,] the substances—earth and the other four types of atoms, space, time, direction, self, and mind—exist by their own very being, as do existence (*sattā*) and inherence (*samavāya*), and qualities such as omnipresence (*vibhu*) and sphericality (*parimaṇḍala*).
However, it is only through the inherence of existence in effects—whether substance, quality, or action—that these possess existence.

To this it is replied: "In that case," and so forth, up to "like the nature of the referent of the word *tat*. Just as this existence (*sattā*) does not have the habit of falling upon [inhering in] space, atoms, and so on, so too, because its very nature is existence, it does not fall upon effect-substances, qualities, or actions; and because its nature is not one of falling upon them, it lacks non-difference from itself. And because it lacks non-difference from itself with respect to all things such as atoms and space, it would have no connection whatsoever with any of those entities like space.

Furthermore, if there is no relation, then just as existence (*sattā*)—despite the absence of relations with existence, substantiality (*dravyatva*), quality-ness (*guṇatva*), and so forth—is of such a nature that it imparts its own essential form to itself within itself because it is a category (*padārtha*) and because of its own intrinsic being, so too let those effects—substances, qualities, and actions—exist even without inherence in existence and the like, just like space, atoms, and the like, and just like existence itself. Why, then, postulate an inherence in existence, substantiality, and so forth, distinct from them? Therefore, let actions be devoid of cause and effect, just like the status of being a category; thus, the claim that "substances and the like exist because of their relation to existence" is untenable.

Therefore, because the inherence of existence (*sattā-samavāya*) is logically untenable, it is improper to designate specific properties—such as non-distinction, distinction, contradiction, non-contradiction, origination, or non-origination—based on the relationship between existence and categories such as substance, quality, action, and form, resulting in the claim that "substance, quality, action, form, and so forth exist. This would lead to the non-existence [of these categories], just as all statements would be false, because existence and its inherence would be like a sky-flower.

Thus, the claim that "substances and so forth exist due to their connection with existence" is incorrect; consequently, it is improper to say that "substance exists, quality exists, and action exists" by virtue of their connection with existence.

Because of the inclusion of the word "etcetera," it is incorrect to say that earth and the other elements are substances due to their connection with "substanceness" (*dravyatva*), that color and the others are qualities due to their connection with "qualityness" (*guṇatva*), and that going and the others are actions due to their connection with "actionness" (*karmatva*). This is because the word "iti" serves the purpose of a conclusion; thus, we have already established—according to the perspective of the previous system—that the effect is non-existent because it lacks a presently existing producer, like a sky-flower. Furthermore, it is incorrect to claim that substances and the rest exist because of their connection with "existence" (*sattā*), on the grounds that actions such as going would likewise exist simply by virtue of being included within the category of "categories" (*padārtha*).

Therefore, because the inherence of existence (*sattā-samavāya*) is logically untenable as a conceptual construction, it is improper to designate specific properties—such as non-contradiction or contradiction, commencement or non-commencement, and so forth—based on the relationship between existence and [the categories of] substance, quality, action, form, and so on, resulting in the designation of "existent substances, qualities, actions, forms," etc.; for this would be like the falsity of all statements, since [existence] lacks [any such] distinction. *Note: The text contains several scribal errors (e.g., *pra॰* for *prati*, *sanni॰* for *sannidhi*). The translation reflects the intended philosophical argument.*

See page 455, line 1 onwards. Following this very logic, he states—in order to support precisely that which was proposed as the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣita*) in the *Kaṭaṇḍī* commentary and elsewhere—the introductory statement beginning with "Therefore, because the alternatives are untenable," etc.:

"They exist due to their connection with existence (*sattā*); they are substances due to substantiality (*dravyatva*); qualities due to quality-ness (*guṇatva*); actions due to action-ness (*karmatva*); color due to color-ness (*rūpatva*); by the inclusion of 'etcetera,' earth and so forth [are established] from earth-ness (*pṛthivītva*) and so on; tastes and so forth from taste-ness (*rasatva*) and so on; motions and so forth from motion-ness (*gamanatva*) and so on. And so forth.
The definition of substance (*dravya*) is that which possesses action, possesses qualities, and is an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*).
The definition of quality (*guṇa*) is that which resides in a substance, is devoid of qualities, and is not a cause in conjunctions or disjunctions, being independent [of other causes].
The definition of action (*karman*) is that which resides in a single substance, is devoid of qualities, and is an independent cause in conjunctions and disjunctions. Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.15–17.

1.14–16. By such [statements], the manifoldness of substances and the rest is established through their mutual opposition or non-opposition, their being producers or non-producers, and their being effects or causes; and furthermore, through the three [attributes] beginning with existence (*sattā*), there is no distinction between substance, quality, and action, as they all share the common characteristics of being existent, non-eternal, possessing substance, being an effect, being a cause, and possessing both generality and particularity (VS 1.1).

7. Thus, this statement of a distinction by way of six non-distinctions is the seed for [proving] existence (*sattā*) and inherence (*samavāya*). To say that all of this is improper—why? Because the alternatives are untenable, just as in the case of "all statements are false. For instance, if someone were to say, "All my statements, yours, and those of others are false," would his own statement be true, false, or both true and false? In no way is it tenable.

If that statement is either false or both true and false, then it is incapable of establishing the falsity of all statements because it is itself not a valid means of knowledge; its lack of validity follows from its being untrue.

Now, if that [universal] is real, then not everything is unreal; for since it is included within "everything," by its being real, the remainder must also be real. Thus, the statement [of yours] is entirely untenable. Furthermore, there is a contradiction with the definition of non-distinction regarding "being" (sat) and so forth, such as "it is 'being' due to the inherence of existence" (*sattā-samavāyāt sat*). Does existence (*sattā*) make substances and the like—which may be existent, non-existent, or both existent and non-existent—existent prior to their connection with existence? It cannot first make non-existent things existent, because that would entail the absurdity of even a hare's horn becoming existent. Nor can it make already existent things existent, because they are already accomplished, just as it is useless to illuminate what is already illuminated.
Furthermore, since existence belongs to existent things, there would be the consequence of an infinite regress;
therefore, prior to its connection with existence, one must determine its essential nature by asking, "What is its nature? Otherwise, it would be non-existent.
Nor can it belong to both the existent and the non-existent, because a single identity is impossible, as in the case of a jar and a sky-flower.

Furthermore, because both faults would follow: that which is non-existent is like the horn of a donkey, and for that which is existent, the connection with existence is redundant; since there is a difference between the existent and the non-existent, as stated in the Vaiśeṣika Sūtra (9.1.12), "Existence and non-existence do not belong to an effect," this alternative [of yours] results only in the logical inconsistency of your own doctrine.

Therefore, since conceptual construction is untenable, the connection with existence (*sattā*) is not the cause of verbal designation or cognition; nor are sentences that introduce specific properties (*viśeṣadharma*) tenable. This is because all Vaiśeṣika categories consist essentially of particularity (*viśeṣa*) rooted in inherence with existence (*sattā-samavāya*), and because it is precisely this that is investigated in the context of analyzing the production of effects such as substance (*dravya*) and so forth, since the Vaiśeṣika system has that [existence] as its vital breath. — *Pakṣistambha* (Fragment).
The alternative reading "the side [of the argument] that here the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) is the definition of substance" might also exist; see page 440, note 5.
[This is] independent of...
See page 440, note 5;
see page 457, note 5.

Since substances (*dravya*) and the other categories, whose similarities and differences have been understood, are the causes of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), [the author] first states their similarity: "Existence, non-eternality, possession of substance, being an effect, being a cause, and possessing generality and particularity" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.8) constitute the common characteristics of substances, qualities (*guṇa*), and actions (*karman*).

1.7: Substance is existent, quality is existent, and action is existent; thus, existence (*sattā*) is a common characteristic of these three. Likewise, impermanence—except for space and the like—and the possession of an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), like substance, are common characteristics [of qualities and actions], with the exception of atoms, space, and so forth.
The state of being an effect is the coming into existence after not having existed; this is likewise the case for all things except for eternal substances.

The state of being a cause (*kāraṇatva*) consists in the production of an effect, and this is common to all three categories [substance, quality, and action]. Earth and the other substances are the inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of substances, qualities, and actions; ether and the others are the inherent causes of qualities; the mind and the ultimate composite substance are the inherent causes of qualities and actions; as for qualities, color, taste, smell, non-hot touch, number, dimension, singleness, separateness, viscidity, and sound are non-inherent causes (*asamavāyikāraṇa*); cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, and mental impression (*bhāvanā*) are efficient causes (*nimittakāraṇa*); conjunction, disjunction, heat, gravity, fluidity, and speed are causes in both ways [inherent and efficient]; while priority, posteriority, duality, dual separateness, spherical dimension, and so forth, are not causes; and actions are non-inherent causes of conjunctions and disjunctions.

"Those [categories] are both universals (sāmānya), such as substantiality (dravyatva) and so forth, and particulars (viśeṣa); thus they are 'universal-particulars' (sāmānyaviśeṣa). The possession of these [universals and particulars] is common to the three [substances, qualities, and motions].
This is found on page 7 of the *Vaiśeṣikasūtravṛtti* composed by Candrānanda. True. Proof.
In this context, there may also be a reading such as "contradiction, non-contradiction, commencement, and non-commencement," etc.

Here, does existence (*sattā*) make existent those substances and so forth that are already existent prior to their connection with existence—whether they be existent, non-existent, or both existent and non-existent? First of all, existence does not make non-existent things existent, because that would entail the absurd consequence that even things like a rabbit's horn would be made existent by it.
Nor does it make existent things existent, because they are already in being; it would be as futile as illuminating what has already been illuminated.
Furthermore, since existence belongs to existent things, there would be the consequence of an infinite regress;
therefore, prior to its connection with existence, one must determine its essential nature by asking, "What is its own-being? Otherwise, it would be non-existent.
Nor can it belong to both the existent and the non-existent, because a single identity is impossible, as in the case of a jar and a sky-flower.

Furthermore, because both faults would follow: that which is non-existent is like the horn of a donkey, and for that which is existent, the connection with "existence" (sattā) is redundant; since there is a difference between the existent and the non-existent, as stated in the Vaiśeṣika Sūtra (9.1.12), "Existence and non-existence do not belong to an effect," this alternative [of yours] results precisely in the untenability of your own doctrine.
Therefore, since conceptual construction is untenable, the connection with existence is not the cause of the word and its cognition; see page 461, line 9;
see page 461, line 14.
"And the Vaiśeṣika doctrine belongs to him" (Bhāṣya); "and the Vaiśeṣika doctrine is his" (Yāyāvara).

If it should be thought: "But how is it that the inherence of existence (*sattā-samavāya*) possesses an untenable set of alternatives?"—to this it is replied: Here, the presentation of the three alternatives—"of things already existent prior to their connection with existence," and so forth—is already explained; such would be your [Vaiśeṣika] position.

The response to that is as follows: first, regarding the statement "not of non-existent things" and so forth, because it is concise, the refutation of the designation and cognition of "existent" prior to the connection of existence with non-existent things is established by reversing the order;
nor is the statement "not of existent things" redundant, as its meaning is already understood from the analogy of "existence," since [the thing] is already present.

The second example, "like the uselessness of illuminating what is already illuminated," is presented as distinct from the scripturally established example of existence (*sattā*); this is the difference.

It is not merely the fault of uselessness in this alternative view; rather, it is because there would be the consequence of infinite regress (*anavasthā*) due to existent things possessing existence again by way of a connection with *sattā*. For if one accepts that only existing things possess existence through a further connection with *sattā*, then since *sattā* itself must also possess existence—being the cause of the designation and cognition of its own existence—it would require another connection with *sattā* for its own existence, and that too would likewise require another, resulting in an infinite regress.
Furthermore, regarding the passage beginning with "prior to its connection with existence" and ending with "otherwise it would be non-existent":

one must first determine the essential nature of that substance and so forth prior to its connection with existence. Since it is devoid of connection with existence at that stage, it does not exist at all, because its nature has not been determined, like a flower in the sky.
Because it would otherwise be non-existent; for if its nature were not determined, it would lack existence— thus, as previously stated, there is no prior existence (prāk-sattā).

In this context, there might also be the reading "prior existence" (*prāk sattā*); if that were the case, then even the root [of the inquiry] would have to be conceived as: "What is its nature prior to its connection with existence? And what about "prior existence" itself?
Nor is it the case that it belongs to both the existent and the non-existent; this is the answer to the third alternative.

"Because a single nature is untenable": this is because the acceptance of the doctrine of manifoldness (*anekāntavāda*) contradicts the previously accepted [doctrine of oneness]. Alternatively, "because a single nature is untenable" means that according to the non-Arhat system, there is an absolute difference between existence and non-existence, like light and darkness; for existence is characterized by designation (*sopākhyam*) while non-existence is devoid of designation (*nirupākhyam*). Due to this difference between existence and non-existence, it is not logical for both existence and non-existence to reside in one place, just as with a jar and a sky-flower. A jar is characterized by designation because of its existence, whereas a sky-flower is devoid of designation because of its non-existence. Thus, due to their difference, there is no unity between them; likewise, it is incorrect to say that an effect consists of both existence and non-existence.

Furthermore, because both faults would follow, he explains it thus: "That which is non-existent is like the horn of a donkey," and so on, up to "this conceptual construction is simply the impossibility of establishing your own position.

In the case of the non-existent alternative, there is no distinction from a sky-flower; in the case of the existent alternative, there is a connection with existence (*sattā*). Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that, as in the example of qualities and the like, the connection with *sattā* is denied for substances and so forth, but their own essential existence (*svarūpasadbhāva*) is not? Therefore, *sattā* does not at all make non-existent things existent."
If you argue that this alternative is untenable, then you yourself have already established [our point].

Even so, this is not at all the case; for by means of demonstrating the non-existence of an effect whose intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is already existent prior to its connection with *sattā*, this very inquiry has been introduced. [Objection: But surely, if it were to make what is previously non-existent into something existent, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that it would likewise make things such as a rabbit’s horn existent; that situation remains unchanged. Furthermore, if substances (*dravya*) and so forth exist by themselves, the connection with *sattā* would be useless. Therefore, *sattā* merely makes the non-existent existent. [Response: This is useless, because of the difference in nature (*vaidharmya*) between the existent and the non-existent; "the existence or non-existence of an effect [is not determined] by the existence or non-existence of its cause" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 9).
And thus, the very impossibility [of the relation] is contrary to your own doctrine;
therefore, because conceptual construction is untenable, the connection with *sattā* (existence) is not the cause of denotation and cognition— this is the conclusion.
Is it *tacchaviṣā*? Or *tacchaśaviṣā*?
[It is] a specific [instance] such as *viṣpa*.
[Regarding] the specific differences [of substances], etc.:

[Objection: But surely, just as in the case of qualities and so forth, the connection with *sattā* (existence) is denied for substances and the rest, but not their existence by way of their own nature (*svarūpasadbhāva*). Therefore, *sattā* does not at all make non-existent things existent;
thus, this alternative [of yours] is untenable. [Reply: In that case, you yourself have already established [the point].

Even so, this is not at all the case. Indeed, this very inquiry has been introduced by way of demonstrating that an effect, though existing as its own nature prior to its connection with *sattā* (existence), is nonetheless non-existent. Now, [the opponent objects]: "If it makes what was previously non-existent existent, then the consequence follows that it would likewise make a rabbit’s horn and such things existent; that situation remains unchanged. Furthermore, if substances and so forth exist by their own nature, the connection with *sattā* would be redundant; therefore, *sattā* merely makes the non-existent existent. Moreover, because an effect is not perceived in the cause—such as the non-arising of curds from sand and the arising of curds from milk—it follows that the effect is both existent and non-existent in the cause."
Because of the difference in nature between the existent and the non-existent, there is indeed neither existence nor non-existence in the effect (Sūtra 9.1.12).
Since existence and non-existence are contradictory simultaneously, the effect is neither existent nor non-existent in the cause; therefore, it is simply non-existent.
Thus, in the *Vaiśeṣikasūtravṛtti* composed by Candrānanda, page 31:
"It is neither non-existent, nor existent, nor both existent and non-existent, because of the difference in nature between the existent and the non-existent" (*Nyāyasūtra* 4.1.47).

48. Prior to its production, that which possesses the nature of being produced is not non-existent, because of the restriction of the material cause (*upādāna-niyama*). A specific material cause is to be employed for the production of a specific effect; it is not the case that everything is the cause of everything. Thus, if [the effect] were non-existent, such a restriction would not be possible. Nor is it existent, because the production of something already existing prior to its arising is untenable. Therefore, it is neither existent nor non-existent, due to the difference in nature (*vaidharmya*) between existence and non-existence. "Existent" implies the affirmation of an object, while "non-existent" implies the negation of an object. These two are contradictory, which constitutes their difference in nature. Because of this contradiction, their non-distinction (identity) is untenable.
Thus, in the Nyāyabhāṣya,
is it the very inconsistency that contradicts your own position,
or is it the inconsistency that is already established by your own position?
He said: "Indeed, [as stated] in the passage beginning with 'not from the qualityless,' etc., up to 'the non-existent does not make the existent'."

Let it be granted, then, that existence (*sattā*) is the maker of existent things alone, and not of non-existent things, just as the previously mentioned example of the "quality" (*guṇa*) was intended to demonstrate the reality of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Just as a quality, being existent by virtue of its own intrinsic nature, is called "non-qualified" (*aguṇa*) even while it is indeed a quality, so too an entity (*bhāva*), though existent by virtue of its own intrinsic nature, is called "non-existent" (*asan*) because it does not possess [the universal] existence (*san*), and not because it is itself non-existent. Likewise, substance (*dravya*) and the other categories are also existent; however, their connection with [the universal] existence is denied, but not their own essential reality. Therefore, existence is not the maker of non-existent things; rather, it is the maker of existent things alone.

"Therefore, since we do not admit a relation of existence (*sattā*) with non-existent things, there is no fault"—let this be seen [as stated] on page 445, line 3. To this it is replied: "This alternative is untenable"—by saying this yourself, you have indeed done what we were to establish; for by speaking thus, you yourself have carried out our point that "existence does not make non-existent things existent. Consequently, since this is proven, we have become certain in this matter.

Moreover— even though I have stated "not even this" and so forth for the purpose of demonstrating your ignorance— this claim that "there is no connection between non-existents and existence" is not correct either.
However, one must investigate whether the connection with *sattā* (existence) can belong to things that are non-existent or not.

If one asks what the reason for this is, it is said: because there is the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even things like a rabbit’s horn would become existent through their connection with *sattā*.

Regarding the doubt as to whether the effect—such as a substance (*dravya*) and so forth—which is the object of that [connection], is existent by its own nature (*svabhāva*) prior to the connection with *sattā*, or whether it becomes existent through the connection with *sattā*: since this very investigation has been introduced by way of demonstrating the non-existence of an effect that is already existent by its own nature, how could a resolution that abandons the subject under discussion be appropriate? This is the intended meaning.

Moreover, is it not the case that the objection we previously raised—beginning with the words "Furthermore, that [existence] would first have an object," and following with the argumentative passage starting from "If the non-existent becomes existent"—which established that there is an absence of existence itself (sattā) in the same way that there is an absence of qualities in a qualityless substrate; and which intended to lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that if existence, being itself non-existent, were to make an existent object such as substance and so forth, then the son of a barren woman and the like would likewise make the horn of a hare and the like existent—that consequence remains just as it was?

For one who does not accept this, the connection with *sattā* (existence) would be purposeless if substances and the like existed by their own nature; or rather, this is the fault: that the connection with *sattā* would lack an object. Furthermore, it is undesirable and likewise untenable that [the universal] makes the non-existent existent.
Moreover, even that final alternative regarding the analysis of the meaning of the word's components is untenable, because it lacks a connection with the probandum (*sādhya*).
...either the lack of proof or a qualification of the thesis...
...the distinctness of substances and so forth...

If it is argued that their non-existence is unproven because they do exist as substances and so forth prior to their production, this is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), since at that time [prior to production] their connection with existence (*sattā*) is not admitted.
Existence is not connected with that which is non-existent, because it is a qualifier, like a staff;
just as there is no connection between a qualifier, such as a staff, and one who does not possess it (the staff-bearer), so too it is for existence.

If, on the other hand, it were connected, then by the very power of existence itself, that which possesses existence—namely substance and so forth—would become its substratum, and this is what is observed.
Therefore, since existence consists precisely in making the non-existent existent, this alone must be the conceptual alternative;
yet even that "making the non-existent existent" is untenable according to the method already examined. He concludes [this point] at page 456, line 3, and page 459, line 2.

And that [existence] being thus situated is likewise untenable; furthermore, the capacity of the non-existent to produce the existent is untenable.
Moreover, even that final analysis of the meaning of the components within the various etymological options is likewise untenable.
No, because it lacks a necessary connection with the probandum; therefore,
it is not a valid means of proof.
Or, it is a specific qualification of the proposition, namely,
its distinctiveness.
Now, as for the non-existence of substances and so forth... their non-existence is unestablished, because they do exist when substances and so forth are admitted.

If it is argued that [the relation exists] prior to production, this is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), because at that time you do not admit a connection with existence (*sattā*) for those [entities].
Existence does not connect with what is non-existent, because it is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), just like a staff;
for just as a staff, being a qualifier, has no connection with a person who does not possess the staff, so too it is with existence.
Now, if it is connected [to the word], then by the very power of existence (sattā), that which is existent—such as substance and so forth—becomes its substratum;
and as for the meaning of the parts, and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "because the conceptualization is untenable" (*anupapannavikalpatvāt*), the meaning of the components of this proof consists of the following alternatives: that existence (*sattā*) makes existent, non-existent, or both existent and non-existent categories such as substance (*dravya*) and the rest existent. Among these, the proofs that were formulated to establish the alternative that "existence does not make non-existent things existent," and which were subsequently refuted by taking them as the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), include a final conceptualization of the establishment that was intended as the ultimate refutation of the prima facie view. However, since even that is shown to be untenable through investigation, and because all investigation becomes as futile as threshing chaff when the final response is itself untenable, the intention is that the prima facie position itself becomes the final position (*uttarapakṣa*).
See page 458, line 2;

See page 458, line 10.

Regarding what was stated—starting from "not of non-existent things" (*nāsatām*) as the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), up to "because it would entail the consequence of being a producer of existent things" (*satkaratvaprasaṅgāt*)—here, Praśastamati introduces the following: [The objection] "no, because of the lack of connection with the probandum" (*sādhyenānabhisaṃbandhāt*) is the response, up to "the state of not being a means of proof" (*asādhanatvam*). This is the first alternative analysis (*vyutpattivikalpa*).

The second, beginning with "or a qualification of the thesis" (*pratijñāviśeṣo vā*), has its meaning already explained, along with its subsequent parts, up to "being specifically distinguished" (*prativiśiṣṭatvam*).

Now, the third [section] beginning with "of substance and so forth" follows along with its refutation, up until: "their non-existence is unproven, because they exist when substances and so forth are admitted.
Herein lies the objection: "If you say 'prior to production,' then prior to production substances and so forth do not exist; therefore, their non-existence is proven.
To this, the reply is: "This is proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), because at that time the connection with existence (*sattā*) for them is not admitted."
See the correct reading on page 459,
line 2: [it was] not by one who is deceitful in mind.
By one whose mind is not destroyed by another;
by one whose mind is not destroyed by another.
(pā., ḍe., vi.)
By means of the probandum (*sādhya*) consisting of [the quality of] being so-minded,
the first [reason], such as "being a sentient being" (*sattva*), etc., is established.

Among these three alternative explanations, existence (*sattā*) is not connected with non-existence (*asat*) by virtue of the understanding that [non-existence] lacks essence, because it is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), like a staff;
this is the explanation of the proof (*sādhana*) beginning with "like a qualifier" and continuing up to "even for existence."

Now, beginning with the words "atha sambadhyate" (then it is connected) and continuing up to "tadavasthaḥ" (that state remains), the author provides the response by first raising an objection from the perspective of the opponent (*pūrvapakṣika*). [The opponent says: "If your view is that even a non-existent entity such as substance (*dravya*) and so forth is connected [to existence] because its nature is to receive existence (*sattā*), and because existence is what is to be established therein—then, since existence itself is the cause, it would follow that it could also be connected with things like a hare’s horn. Consequently, the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even hare’s horns and the like would possess existence would remain unavoidable.
[The author replies: No, for we do not admit that effect-substances, qualities, and actions are absolutely devoid of essence (*atyanta-nirātmakatva*) in the same manner as a hare’s horn.

[Objection: But since the negative particle (*nañ*) in the term "non-existent" (*asat*) serves to exclude the referent of the subsequent word and has the sense of negating existence, how can this [entity] possess a self? [Reply: No, because of the lack of exclusivity (*anekāntāt*). It is like a "sonless Brahmin" (*aputra-brāhmaṇa*) or a "quality-less quality" (*aguṇa-guṇa*). Just as a Brahmin is called "sonless" when he has no son, and a quality is called "quality-less" when it has no quality, so too here, "non-existent" means that it does not have existence.

Yet even that is not devoid of a self (*nirātmaka*), like a hare’s horn; for even without a connection to the category of existence (*sattā*), it may possess a self, just as in the opponent's own system the *pradhāna* and other principles possess a self.
If it is argued that there is an absence of an illustrative example (*d� substance*) in your position, [we reply:

"or like universals and so forth" (*sāmānyādivadvā*). Just as in the case of universals and so forth, by implication (*sāmarthyāt*), that [existence] has "existent substance" (*sad-dravya*) and so on as its substratum;
this too is not tenable, because—as in the case of the horns of a hare and so forth—the meaning has already been explained.

Having thus set forth the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), Praśastamati states the following reply: "Because absolute selflessness (*atyanta-nirātmakatva*)—like that of a rabbit's horn—is not admitted [of what?], [namely] of effect-substances (*kārya-dravya*), qualities (*guṇa*), and actions (*karman*). For existence (*bhāva*) has been stated to be twofold: existence as intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-sadbhāva*) and existence as relation (*sambandha-sadbhāva*). This is because those things which are non-existent in relation to one another are indeed possessed of a self (*sātmaka*), due to their non-existence being qualified [by something else], unlike the 'non-other' moon and so forth," and so on, as previously explained.

Therefore, only things such as a hare’s horn, which are absolutely non-existent (*atyantāsant*), possess non-existence; whereas things that are non-existent in other ways—such as prior non-existence, posterior non-existence, mutual non-existence, and so forth—are not devoid of self-nature (*anātmaka*).

Consequently, substance (*dravya*) and the rest are existent; moreover, they are indeed real entities (*vastu*) inhering in their own causes. Even when devoid of a connection with the universal "existence" (*sattā*), they are still possessed of self-nature (*sātmaka*); they are not devoid of self-nature (*nirātmaka*) like a donkey’s horn.
Therefore, a connection with the universal "existence" is logical for substances and the rest, but not for things such as a sky-flower.
If it were so,
then it would also be connected with things such as a hare’s horn; thus, the consequence that even a hare’s horn and the like possess existence remains unavoidable.
No, because we do not admit that effects—substances, qualities, and actions—are absolutely devoid of self-nature (*nirātmaka*), like the horns of a hare and so forth.

[Objection: But in the term *asat* (non-existent), since the negative particle (*nañ*) serves to exclude what is denoted by the subsequent word and has the sense of negating existence (*sat*), how can this [effect] possess self-nature? [Response: No, because [the application of the negative] is not absolute; it is like "a Brahmin without a son" or "a quality without a quality.

Just as one is called a "sonless Brahmin" (*aputra*) because he has no son, or a "quality-less quality" (*aguṇa*) because it has no further quality, so too here, it is "non-existent" (*asat*) because it does not possess [an eternal] existence.

Nor is that [the self] devoid of selfhood like the horn of a hare; for even without a connection to existence (*sattā*), just as there is "possession of self" (*sātmakatva*) for the *pradhāna* and other categories in the opponent's position, so it would be here as well.
If you argue, "Look! On your own side, there is an absence of an example,"...
Or like universals and so forth; indeed, just like universals and so forth, it becomes their substratum (see page 441,
line 5).
See page 434, line 2.

Here he says: "Now, [the objection] beginning with 'nanu asat' and ending with 'how can this possess a self? is a passage whose meaning has already been explained, intended to establish that substance and so forth are devoid of a self (*nirātmaka*). Because it negates what is denoted by the latter term, it has the sense of a negation of existence (*sat-pratiṣedha*); and because its purpose is the negation of existence, [it concludes] 'it is without a self' (*anātmaka*)."

To this, the following reply is given: No, because of non-exceptionality (*anaikāntāt*), and so forth, up to "likewise here too. This passage—using the two examples from common and technical usage, namely "existent" and "non-existent," and employing a *bahuvrīhi* compound to show the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) by means of the expressions "like a Brāhmaṇa without a son" and "like that which has no quality" (*aguṇavat*)—has already been explained. Thus, since its lack of self-nature (*anātmakatva*) is established, the deviation of that [reason] is stated: "And yet that is not devoid of self-nature," and so forth; [this is shown] by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyeṇa*) with the horn of a hare.

If it were argued that [the self] is soulless because it lacks a connection with existence (*sattā*), like a donkey’s horn—just as the *pradhāna* and *puruṣa* imagined by the Sāṅkhya and the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) imagined by the Buddhists—or conversely, if it were said that it possesses a self because of its connection with existence, then [the reason] would lack pervasion (*avyāpti*), since the state of possessing a self is observed even in the absence of a connection with existence, as in the case of the *pradhāna* and so forth; the same would apply here as well.
Thus, [the opponent claims] it possesses a self. [End of fragment].
The intention [of the author] in the passage "the word *asat* [is not a compound]" is that the negative particle (*nañ*) negates the denotation of the subsequent member [of the compound];
see page 324–2.
Laukaśāstrī:
*pra*. Here, there might also be the reading "evam ananātmakatve sthite" (thus, while its non-cognition-nature is established);
in this case, the meaning of "tasyāḥ" would be "of existence" (*sattāyāḥ*).
If there is a lack of appropriateness here, then the reading "tasya" (of that) should be postulated;

Having raised the prima facie objection (pūrvapakṣa) beginning with "If it be argued that there is an absence of an illustrative example (dṛṣṭāntābhāva) in your position," the following is the response: starting from "Or like universals and so forth" up to "or like universals and so forth, it is endowed with a self (sātmaka), not endowed with a self like a jar," this section of the text—including the explanation of the word "or" (vā) as having a restrictive sense—is intended to show that when the Vaiśeṣika position is challenged by the absence of an illustrative example of something "endowed with a self" that is devoid of the relation to existence (sattā), [the answer is] that it would be like universals, particulars, and inherence in being endowed with a self; thus, it is "endowed with a self, not endowed with a self like a jar."

If it is argued that the possession of a self (sātmakatva) by universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth is unestablished, we say no; because, while being distinct in their own nature (*svarūpa*), they are the objects of non-distinct verbal and cognitive usage.
