For the sake of accomplishing various enjoyments—such as holding water, protection from cold, and covering by means of distinct objects like jars, cloths, and mats; for the sake of establishing the linguistic usage of identical designations and cognitions regarding distinct jars and the like which are similar in kind through place, time, and other factors, and which possess a common universal (*sāmānya*) characterized by existence (*sattva*); and for the sake of illuminating that which already possesses meaning, just as the light of a lamp illuminates a jar already made manifest by speech, without the fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*) because the state [of being illuminated] is already present—this proposed alternative solution (*pratisamādhāna-vikalpa*) is also untenable, and so on, up to the point where it says "like the illumination of a lamp and so forth."

If it is asked why this is untenable, it is said: because of the non-existence of the state and the example. This very example of the lamp, which is intended to possess states, does not actually possess states, because it is inconclusive (*anekāntatvāt*). For an example must be a determined object that possesses a single, uniform nature; however, illumination does not invariably follow from the futility of your proposed point. If the illumination of a lamp by another illumination were futile, then a "state" would exist therein; but such a state does not exist.

Because, like a lamp that illuminates the light of speech, even the light of a lamp is perceptible by the sense organ; for even a lamp is illuminated by the sense organ—just as the lamp that illuminates the light of speech—and because the various enjoyments of objects such as jars cannot be established for one who has not perceived or grasped them through the sense organ.

What state could belong to the sense organ? It is said: "No," because that [organ] too is made manifest by many varieties of auxiliary means (*upakaraṇa*). For that sense organ is manifested by the matter-substance (*pudgaladravya*) known as the *indriya-paryāpti* (the capacity for the completion of the sense organ), which consists of both the physical formation (*nirvṛtti*) and the auxiliary means; it is manifested by external substances such as collyrium, foot-unguents, nasal drops, wholesome food, lamps, and so forth; and it is manifested by the self whose nature is knowledge.

For even those—the substances of the body, its accessories, and the appropriate capacities for completion, as well as external substances such as collyrium and the like—are manifested by the attainment (*labdhi*) dependent upon the destruction or subsidence of the knowledge-obscuring, perception-obscuring, and energy-obstructing karmas, along with the rise of the primary and secondary bodily parts (*aṅga-upāṅga-nāma-karma*) that have arisen, been destroyed, or subsided within the self. Therefore, because they too are manifested by attainment, there is no infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

That attainment (*labdhi*) as well, when the impurities such as the veil of knowledge (*jñānāvaraṇa*) have been removed by the vigor known as one's own resolve (*praṇidhāna-vīrya*), is merely the clarity of the soul characterized by consciousness (*upayoga*); it is manifested by that consciousness, because even attainment—which has consciousness as its fruit—is manifested by that [consciousness]. Furthermore, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) because that [attainment] too is manifested by the application of external, useful substances; and because everything from the application of sensory-cognition (*mati-jñāna*) up to the application of omniscience (*kevala-upayoga*) is manifested by the application of external, useful substances, there would be an infinite regress.

For he, the Jina, knows whatever substance undergoes transformation through application (*prayoga*) or natural evolution (*visrasā*), exactly as it is; there is no cognition of that which lacks its own manifestation (*aparyaya*).

(Āvaśyaka-niryukti 794) Thus, because the cognitive activity (*upayoga*) is manifested in accordance with the transformations of external objects due to its engagement with them, to say further [that it is so] would be redundant. This is because the object of manifestation and the manifesting agent are distinct, since the object is apprehended through states that do not possess the nature of the manifestor itself.

Furthermore, existence (*sattā*) is manifested by a cognition that does not possess the form of the substance (*dravya*) and so forth, just as a lamp or similar light reveals an object made known by the manifestation of speech.

Primordial matter (*pradhāna*) would likewise be such [a manifestation], because your postulated existence has the purpose of bringing about the experience of the manifold forms [of the world] and thus serves the aim of the *puruṣa*; it would be like the three *guṇas*.

Moreover, for you, the effect would also have to exist even prior [to its production], because it is being superimposed as an existent despite being incapable [of existing as such], and because it is being made existent, just like a substance and so forth immediately upon its arising.
Alternatively, that [light] is not made manifest or brought into being by any other entity, because it is already existent, like existence itself (*sattā*).

Its own existence does not depend upon another existence, as that would result in the fallacy of a circularity (*cakraka*) regarding the nature of existence. Therefore, light is self-manifesting; even the light of a lamp is not manifested by another light, because it is apprehended through entities that do not possess its own form. This concludes the demonstration that the examples cited for the state [of dependence] lack reality.

In order to bring about the same infinite regress (*anavasthā*) regarding existence (*sattā*) as well—on account of its similarity to that which is manifested by what is not of its own nature—he says, with reference to the subject at hand: "And existence also," and so forth.

Existence also acquires its own self through a cognition of its substratum, such as substance (*dravya*), which is not of its own nature; it is manifested by that [cognition], just as an object made known by speech is manifested by a lamp or similar means, and not by itself alone. Thus, the fault of infinite regress remains here as well.
(Praśastapādabhāṣya-vyākhyā) *prayogakriyā* (or *prayogakriyā-prasaṅga*).
And for the sake of the house, and for the sake of the house; in the cause... [pra]...?
[pra]... in the cause.

"The connection [of the word] with the specific entity (sattvaviśeṣaṇa) is purposeful, like rice that is incapable of remedying hunger, for the sake of accomplishing various enjoyments, and for the sake of establishing the linguistic usage of non-differentiated names and cognitions regarding differentiated things—just as in the case of the state of manifesting a meaningful object. This alternative response is also untenable, because the example of "state" (avasthā) is non-existent and because [the argument] is inconclusive (anekāntatvāt).

Just as a lamp illuminates speech, the illumination of that lamp is also made manifest by the sense organs; those [organs] too are made manifest by their respective acquisitions (*labdhi*); and since acquisition has the fruit of functional application (*upayoga*), it should be regarded as being like the state of the soul itself (see page 332).
"By means of place, time, non-time, and so forth.
Here, there may also be the reading "by means of place, time, form, and so forth" (see page 468, line 17).
[This is] for the sake of the accomplishment of one's own commonality... [bhāṣya/vṛtti].
For the sake of accomplishing one’s own common [aim], O beloved one...
[variant readings: *siddhyartha* (ḍe), *siddhyarthe* (pā., raṃ.); *svasāmā* (ḍe), *svasāmā* (pā., raṃ.); *kāntātbhā* (ḍe)]
In this context, even the single word "syāt" would suffice;
the reading contained within this [passage] does not exist in the manuscripts of the Yaṅ tradition, as it is like a lamp illuminating [the darkness]. Bhāṣya.
Is it even of light? Is it even of a lamp? A certain difference of opinion regarding the nature of the sense organs as instruments for the accomplishment of perception is observed in the treatises.
For instance—the nature of these has already been described according to the opinion of the author of the *Nayacakra-vṛtti*; see page 183, lines 19–20, and page 372, lines 19–21.
[According to] Tattvārtha-sūtra 2.16, "The senses are of two kinds: the material senses (*dravyendriya*) and the functional senses (*bhāvendriya*)."
The material sense organ (*dravyendriya*) consists of the "organ as manifestation" (*nirvṛtti*) and the "organ as equipment" (*upakaraṇa*) (Tattvārthasūtra 2.17).
Therein, the material sense organ is twofold: the organ as manifestation and the organ as equipment.

The "organ as manifestation" refers to the gateways of the senses produced by the *nāma*-karma known as "limbs and minor limbs" (*aṅgopāṅga*); it means specific regions of the body conditioned by particular karma, which constitute the production of the primary qualities based on the causal conditions of the "limbs and minor limbs" produced by the *nirmāṇa-nāma* [karma].

"The external and internal instruments (upakaraṇa) are beneficial to that which has been produced [the sense-organ] through non-injury and assistance"—this is from the *Tattvārthabhāṣya* composed by the eminent teacher Śrī Umāsvāti.

Regarding this, the commentary (*vyākhyā*) composed by Siddhasena Gaṇin states: "In general, the sense-faculties (*indriya*) are of two kinds: those consisting of substance (*dravya*), which are material (*dravyātmaka*), are the 'substance-sense-faculties' (*dravyendriya*); whereas the 'mode-sense-faculties' (*bhāvendriya*) consist of modes (*bhāva*) and take the form of transformations of the self (*ātmapariṇati*)."

And here, it is the substance of the person (*pudgaladravya*) itself—consisting of an infinite number of spatial units (*anantapradeśa*) and depending upon the activity of the self—that extends [to form the senses] in the form of the physical organ (*nirvṛtti*) and the accessory (*upakaraṇa*). All the sense organs consist of infinite spatial units and are presided over by innumerable spatial units of the self; thus they are substantial (*dravyātmaka*). In the other two cases, it has been stated that the modification of the self (*ātmapariṇāma*) is the state (*bhāva*), and that effort (*prayatna*) is established therein. Thus, the sense organ is said to be twofold according to the distinction between substance and state. Now, desiring to define it according to its essential nature, he says: "Therein, the physical organ and the accessory constitute the substantial sense organ" (Tattvārthasūtra 2.17).

17. By the word "therein" (tatra), the commentator connects the sūtra. Therein, within the twofold [classification], the material sense-organ (*dravyendriya*) is first determined by way of its essential nature and its distinctions.
*Nirvṛtti* means production; it is the arising of a specific configuration. *Upakaraṇa* is that by which something is assisted.
The sense-organ as manifestation (*nirvṛtti-indriya*) is indeed the manifestation itself;
the instrumental sense-organ (*upakaraṇa-indriya*) is likewise.

Although both of these consist of the transformation of the person (*pudgala-pariṇāma*), they receive the designation "sense-organ" because they serve as the cause for the employment of the functional sense-organ (*bhāva-indriya*), since their cooperation leads precisely to the manifestation of that functional state.

That substance which, by way of being an auxiliary, is capable of bringing about the future transformation of the self (ātmabhāva) is here to be understood as the material sense-organ (dravyendriya), like the wood for a cart.

Regarding that, the commentator reveals the nature of the "formation" (nirvṛtti) and the "accessory" (upakaraṇa) through the commentary itself, beginning with the words: "Formation is the name of the primary and secondary limbs," and so forth.

The *nirmāṇa-nāma* is a specific variety of *nāma-karma* included within the category of *nāma-karma*, which is comparable to a carpenter; it possesses skill in the construction of the specific arrangement of parts such as the ear-cavity (*karṇa-śaṣkulī*). Similarly, there is a specific variety of *nāma-karma* known as the *aṅgopāṅga-nāma* pertaining to the three bodies—the gross (*audārika*) and so forth—by the arising of which the limbs (*aṅga*) and minor members (*upāṅga*), such as the head and fingers, are produced. These two types of karma strive to bring about the formation of the two kinds of material sense organs (*dravyendriya*).
The commentary should be meditated upon in this way: "What is the nature of *nirvṛtti* (formation)? To this, he says: "The limbs... [and so on].
The doors of the sense organs (*indriyadvārāṇi*)—that is, the apertures of the sense organs—are produced, generated, and formed by a specific variety of karma known as *aṅgopāṅga*.

Here, by the term "sense organ" (*indriya*), the functional sense organ (*bhāvendriya*) in the form of cognitive application (*upayoga*) is intended; the doors of that sense organ are the various paths for the directing of attention, such as the shape of a conch-shell and so forth, which are perceived externally as their manifested form. One manifestation is this external one, while the other is the internal manifestation.

The body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) is of various forms because it possesses innumerable divisions; regarding its internal and external distinctions, there is generally no single [fixed] shape, though it is often described as being shaped like a long, triangular weapon of the Karṇāṭakas, namely a crescent-headed arrow (*kṣurapra*). The tongue-faculty (*rasanendriya*) has the shape of the petal of an *atimuktaka* flower or a moon-motif (*candraka*), while the nose-faculty (*ghrāṇendriya*) is somewhat circular with filaments, slightly curved in the middle.
The organ of sight should be understood as being slightly elevated in the middle and circular in shape like a lentil (*masūra*);
the organ of hearing is shaped like a barley-stalk container for provisions (*pātheyabhāṇḍaka-yavanālikā*), and the organ of smell is to be known as having the form of a *nālikā* flower.

Among these, the first (the organ of sight) is equal in size to its own body and consists of material atoms; the remaining organs are each one-inconceivable-numberth part of a finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) in measure for all living beings.
And thus says the scripture: "O Venerable One, what is the shape of the sense-organ of touch declared to be? O Gautama, it is declared to be of various shapes.
O Venerable One, what is the shape of the sense-organ of taste declared to be? O Gautama, it is declared to be shaped like a razor.
O Venerable One, what is the shape of the sense-organ of smell declared to be? O Gautama, it is declared to be shaped like an *atimuktaka* flower or the moon."

"Venerable sir, what is the shape of the eye-faculty said to be? Gautama, it is said to be shaped like a lentil seed (*masūra*). Venerable sir, what is the shape of the ear-faculty said to be? Gautama, it is said to be shaped like a *kalaṃbu* flower. (Prajñāpanā-sūtra 191). All these sūtras have been recited with reference to the internal formation (*nirvṛtti*).

Furthermore, external manifestation cannot be fixed because it possesses diverse forms; for example, the ear of a human is level with the eyebrows on both sides of the eyes, whereas that of a horse is above the eyes on the head with a sharp tip, and so forth, due to the many kinds of forms resulting from differences in species.

To clarify this very meaning of the commentary (*bhāṣya*) which was already passed over, the author of the commentary (*bhāṣyakāra*) states by way of another synonym: "regions of the body conditioned by specific karma," or rather, in the previous commentary, only the name "limbs and minor limbs" (*aṅgopāṅga*) was employed, but not the "formative karma" (*nirmāṇakarma*); therefore, this is said for the purpose of including that: "by specific karma," and so forth.

The specific type of karma is *nāmakarma*; its further subdivisions are *aṅgopāṅganāma* (the name for major and minor limbs) and *nirmāṇakarma* (the name for creative manifestation). By means of these two specific types of karma, the portions of the three kinds of bodies—the gross (*audārika*) and so forth—are refined, produced, and brought into existence through a distinct arrangement of their constituent parts. These specific locations, such as the ear-cavity and so on, are particular regions [of the body].

Because one whose intellect is utterly deluded by hearing the designations of these specific karmas remains in a state of confusion regarding them, [the author] speaks again for the sake of clarifying that understanding: "The production of the primary qualities is conditioned by the *nirmāṇa*, *nāma*, and *aṅgopāṅga* [karmas]"—this is the meaning.

He states the specific types of karma by name: "nirmāṇa-nāma" (name of the creation) and "aṅgopāṅga" (limbs and minor limbs), thus "nirmāṇa-nāmāṅgopāṅga. The word "nāma," situated in the middle, implies both as the objects to be qualified. That completion for which those two [types of] karma are the condition (*pratyaya*), the cause (*kāraṇa*), or the motive (*nimitta*) is "nirmāṇa-nāmāṅgopāṅga-pratyayā. This refers to the accomplishment of the primary qualities (*mūlaguṇa*) with respect to the accomplishment of the secondary qualities (*uttaraguṇa*).

For the production of secondary qualities (*uttaraguṇa-nirvartanā*) consists of piercing the ears, causing them to hang down, enhancing the eyes and nose with collyrium and nasal ointments, removing the dullness of the tongue through the administration of medicines, and making the skin pure through various powders, perfumes, unguents, and fragrant pastes.

Thus, the term "thus" (*iti-śabda*) refers to the meaning of "in this way" (*evam-śabdārtha*): it denotes the production of qualities established as primary causes by means of groups of material aggregates (*dravya-vargaṇā*) suitable for the gross body and so forth, which function according to their arising and are independent of such various specific [external] conditions. This is the meaning explained by those learned in the sacred teachings (*pravacana*).

Now, in order to explain the nature of the auxiliary sense-organ (*upakaraṇendriya*), he says: "The auxiliary is both external and internal; it is that which assists by means of non-injury and favor toward what has been produced. Once the "production" (*nirvṛtti*)—which stands in the place of a sword—is present, the auxiliary sense-organ must necessarily be relied upon. And that [auxiliary] is endowed with the power to grasp its own object, just as the edge of a sword is capable of cutting. Even when production is present, another sense-organ in the form of that power does not grasp the object due to injuries to that power.

Therefore, when the *nirvṛtti-indriya* (the physical organ) designated as "hearing" and so forth has been produced, that which assists [the soul] through its presence—by means of non-obstruction and support for the self—is the *upakaraṇa-indriya* (the functional organ).
And this is both external and internal; its twofold nature is also made known in relation to the *nirvṛtti-dravya-indriya*.

It is stated that wherever the *nirvṛtti-dravya-indriya* is located, the *upakaraṇa-indriya* is not situated in a different place from it, because that capacity for grasping its own object resides within the *nirvṛtti* itself.

He clarifies this very point: the wise determine that the instrument-faculty (*upakaraṇendriya*) is that which, having been produced—that is, brought into existence—assists [the soul] by means of non-obstruction and favor through the division of its own parts, being constructed from a network of extremely pure *pudgala* matter.
However, in the scripture (*āgama*), there is no distinction between internal and external regarding the instrument; this is simply a tradition of the Teacher (*ācārya*) derived from some source.

The naming [of the faculties] at the beginning of their manifestation is for the purpose of explaining the sequence of birth, for if that were absent, the instrument would exist [without them], like the power of a weapon.

Thus, in the *Tattvārthabhāṣyavyākhyā* composed by Siddhasena Gaṇin, follows this commentary composed by Haribhadra Sūri: The collective meaning of the sūtra is that all five sense organs just mentioned are of two kinds.
As for the meaning of the individual components, he says with the words beginning "of two kinds," etc.

The collective meaning of the sutra is that the material faculty (*dravyendriya*) consists of the produced organ (*nirvṛtti*) and its accessory (*upakaraṇa*), both of which are composed of a person (*pudgalamaya*).
He states the meaning of the individual parts, however, with the words beginning "the produced faculty" (*nirvṛttīndriya*).

*Nirvartana* (formation) is *nirvṛtti* (evolution), which is the production of a specific configuration; that itself is the *nirvṛttīndriya* (evolved sense organ). *Upakaraṇa* (the instrument) is that by which [the evolved organ] is assisted; this very same sense organ is also the *upakaraṇendriya* (instrumental sense organ). The word "and" (*ca*) is used in the sense of conjunction. Thus, this *dravyendriya* (substantial sense organ) is of two kinds, because it consists of both the instrumental sense organ and the substantial nature of the sense organ.
He states the definition of *nirvṛtti* with the words beginning "nirvṛtti," etc.

Here, the *aṅgopāṅga-nāman* is that which brings about the limbs and sub-limbs of the three types of bodies, such as the gross body (*audārika*), from whose arising the limbs and sub-limbs—such as the head, fingers, and so forth—are produced. Furthermore, the teachers maintain that the *nirmāṇa-nāman* here stands in the place of a carpenter, possessing skill in the specific arrangement and construction of parts such as the ear-cavity.

Thus, these gateways of the sense organs—the apertures of the senses, which are the gateways for the application of the functional senses (*bhāvendriya*)—are produced and generated by specific karmas known as *aṅga* and *upāṅga*.
These possess various shapes and so forth; and thus says the scripture: "O Venerable One, what is the shape of the organ of touch (*phāsiṃdia*) declared to be?"...
[and so on].

"...it is described as being shaped like a *kalaṃbuā* flower" (Prajñāpanā-sūtra 191). All these sūtras have been recited with reference to the internal formation (*nirvṛtti*). However, the external formation cannot be precisely defined because it possesses diverse shapes, such as those of horses, humans, and so forth, due to the differences in their external ears and other features.
To clarify this very meaning of the commentary (*bhāṣya*) by means of another synonym, he says: "Karma," and so on.

Regarding the phrase "refined by specific karma" (*karmaviśeṣasaṃskṛtā*): "specific karma" refers to the karma of name (*nāmakarma*). This [name-karma] further consists of the karma of the primary and secondary limbs (*aṅgopāṅganāma*) and the karma of transformation (*nirmāṇakarma*). Refined by these two—meaning produced through a particular arrangement of parts—the specific regions of the body, such as the ear-cavities and so forth, are the distinct locations of the three [types of bodies], the gross (*audārika*) and the rest.
To dispel the delusion of those with dull intellects, he says: "transformation," and so forth.

"Transformation" (*nirmāṇa*) refers to the primary and secondary limbs (*aṅgopāṅga*); that which has these as its conditions or causes is "the production of the primary qualities" (*mūlaguṇanirvartanā*). This is the conclusion; it does not refer to the production of the secondary qualities (*uttaraguṇanirvartanā*). For the latter consists of: the piercing and elongation of the ears; the benefit to the eyes and nose through collyrium and nasal drops; and the making of the tongue pure from touch, smell, and so forth, through the application of *brāhmī* and other herbs—such is the meaning declared by those learned in the scriptures. Thus is explained the "production" (*nirvṛtti*).
Now he describes the instruments (upakaraṇa): "The instrument is both external and internal.
An instrument is that by which something is assisted; the external instrument consists of [objects] such as fried cakes and the like.

In this context, the internal [organ] is like the edge of a sword relative to the manifestation (*nirvṛtti*), which is produced by a network of extremely pure *pudgala* atoms and occupies the same location as that [manifestation], being comparable to the power of its blade. With reference to this, it says: "of that which has been manifested," and so forth; that is to say, of the sense-organ (*indriya*) that has been manifested or produced through the differentiation of its own constituent parts. It is "beneficial" by way of non-injury and assistance; that which benefits by means of non-harming and supporting is the instrument-organ (*upakaraṇendriya*).

For instance: even when [the internal organ] is intact, there is no apprehension of an object if there is an impairment of the capacity; and when external instruments are impaired, there is necessarily an impairment of the capacity. Therefore, due to their predominance, he says that [the organs] are both external and internal.

Thus, in the *Tattvārthabhāṣyavyākhyā* composed by the venerable Haribhadra Sūri, regarding the purpose of the [senses] for the experiencing self which consists in the perception of desirable and undesirable objects, he speaks as follows—in order to establish the individual distinctions among those senses whose specific capacities have been described and which fall under different categories—he says: "They are of two kinds" (Tattvārtha-sūtra 2.16).

16. Regarding the inclusion of the word *vidha* as signifying "kind": this word *vidha* is taken here as signifying "kind"; since the words *vidha*, *yukta*, *gata*, and *prakāra* are synonymous, the meaning of "those which have two *vidhas*" is "those which are of two kinds" (*dvividhāni*), that is, "of two types" (*dviprakārāṇi*).
And what are the two types? They are the substantial sense-organ (*dravyendriya*) and the functional sense-organ (*bhāvendriya*).

Regarding these, in order to explain the nature of the substantial sense-organ, he says: "The substantial sense-organ consists of the *nirvṛtti* (the physical organ) and the *upakaraṇa* (its auxiliary parts)" (Tattvārtha-sūtra 2.17).
That which is produced (*nirvartyate*) is called *nirvṛtti*.
That which is brought about or accomplished by action is taught as "nirvṛtti" (accomplishment).

It is twofold due to the distinction between the external and the internal; that accomplishment is twofold because of the distinction between the external and the internal. Why? Because of the distinction between the external and the internal.

In that context, the internal formation (*ābhyantarā nirvṛtti*) is the manifestation of pure self-spatial units (*ātmapradeśa*); it is the manifestation of pure self-spatial units, measured by an incalculable fraction of an *utsedhāṅgula*, which are situated according to the specific dimensions of the respective sense organs such as the eye.
Therein, the external formation (*bāhyā nirvṛtti*) is an accumulation of matter (*pudgalapracaya*) characterized by a particular state produced through the emergence of name-karma (*nāmakarmodaya*).

Among those spatial units of the self (*ātmapradeśa*), that accumulation of matter (*pudgalapracaya*) which possesses a specific configuration, receives the designation of a sense organ (*indriya*), and has its particular state produced by the emergence of name-karma (*nāmakarmodaya*), is the "external formation" (*bāhyā nirvṛtti*).
That by which this formation is assisted is the "instrument" (*upakaraṇa*);
that which provides assistance to the formation is the instrument.
That is twofold as previously described;
its two types of accessories are likewise twofold, distinguished as external and internal.
Among these, the internal consists of the white and black circles [of the eye], while the external consists of the eyelids, the two rows of eyelashes, and so forth.
In this same way, it should be understood regarding the remaining sense-faculties as well;
thus [it is stated] in the *Tattvārtharājavārtika* composed by Akalaṅkadeva. (Reference:
ṇātadyo॰bhā॰pā॰ḍe॰)
"From that [arise] attainment and application; these two are the functional sense-faculties" (Tattvārthasūtra 2.18).
Attainment and application constitute the functional sense-faculty.

That which is called *labdhi* (attainment) arises for the soul through the subsidence-cum-destruction (*kṣayopaśama*) of the karma that obscures it, as well as through the manifestation (*udaya*) of karma that produces the basis of the sense organs; it is generated by the *nāmakarma* (name-karma) pertaining to the types of migratory states (*gati*), birth (*jāti*), and so forth.

It is fivefold, namely: the attainment of the sense organ of touch (*sparśanendriya-labdhi*), the attainment of the sense organ of taste (*rasanendriya-labdhi*), the attainment of the sense organ of smell (*ghrāṇendriya-labdhi*), the attainment of the sense organ of sight (*cakṣurindriya-labdhi*), and the attainment of the sense organ of hearing (*śrotrendriya-labdhi*).
[The resulting] *upayoga* (active engagement) occurs with respect to touch and the other objects. (Tattvārthasūtra 2.18–19)
19. This means that there is the application of sensory cognition (*matijñāna*) with respect to touch and the other [objects of the senses].
This has been stated: "Application (*upayoga*) is the defining characteristic" (Tattvārthasūtra 2.8).

*Upayoga* is *praṇidhāna*; *āyoga* is its state of being, meaning *pariṇāma*. When these [three] are present, there arise *nirvṛtti*, *upakaraṇa*, and *upayoga*. Furthermore, when *labdhi* (attainment) is present, there arise *nirvṛtti*, *upakaraṇa*, and *upayoga*. For even if any one of *nirvṛtti* and the others is absent, the perception of objects does not occur—so it is stated in the *Tattvārthabhāṣya* composed by the eminent teacher Śrī Umāsvāti.
Regarding this, there is the commentary composed by Siddhasena Gaṇi: "The faculties of attainment (*labdhi*) and application (*upayoga*) constitute the internal faculty (*bhāvendriya*).

Attainment is the subsidence-cum-destruction (*kṣayopaśama*) of the respective obscuration of each sense-organ; application is the directed activity toward its own object, which is effort (*vīrya*). Both of these constitute the internal faculty, characterized as a transformation of the self.
On this point, the Teacher speaks in order to describe the nature of attainment, beginning with the commentary: 'Attainment is called... etc.

"Lābha" means gain, acquisition, or attainment; the word "nāma" is used for the purpose of poetic ornamentation. Alternatively, regarding this term "labdhi," its meaning is as follows: it is called "attainment" because it is produced by *nāmakarma* (name-karma) such as the karma pertaining to the destinies (*gati*) and the types of birth (*jāti*).

That which has "gati" (destiny) and "jāti" (birth) as its beginning is called *gatijātyādi*; that which is both *gatijātyādi* and *nāmakarma* (name-karma) is *gatijātyādināmakarma*. Produced and brought about by this—such as being a human through the rise (*udaya*) of the *manuṣyagati-nāma* [karma], and likewise being five-sensed through the rise of the *pañcendriyajāti-nāma* [karma]—the subsidence-cum-destruction (*kṣayopaśama*) of the respective obstructing karma is produced upon the attainment of humanity, five-sensedness, and so forth. Since name-karma such as destiny and birth is the cause of that subsidence-cum-destruction, it was pointed out by the Teacher.

By the inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*), everything that is invariably concomitant with this [attainment], such as the body and so forth—which falls under the category of the name-karma (*nāma-karma*) acquired through the subsidence-cum-destruction (*kṣayopaśama*)—is included.
Others, however, declare even the life-span (*āyuṣka*) to be a cause, because it is the substratum for that subsidence-cum-destruction.

Having thus pointed out a remote cause, he now reveals another, more proximate cause: "and it is produced by the subsidence-cum-destruction of the karma that obscures it" (*tadāvaraṇīya-karma-kṣayopaśama-janitā*).

Indeed, for that transformation consisting of the grasping of form and so forth, there exists an obscuring, veiling, and covering factor; the derivation [of the term] is in the active sense (*kartari*) due to its frequent occurrence. That which is to be obscured is *āvaraṇīya*, and it is also *karman* (karma); thus, it is *āvaraṇīyakarman*. The meaning is "the karma that obscures sensory cognition and intuition" (*matijñāna-darśanāvaraṇakarman*).

The subsidence-cum-destruction (*kṣayopaśama*) of both of these is characterized as previously described. The word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "produced by that" (*tajjanitā*)—meaning "accomplished by that"—conjoins it with the aforementioned cause.

But surely, it has been stated that *kṣayopaśama* (subsidence-cum-destruction) itself is *labdhi* (attainment); therefore, what other attainment could there be produced by it? It is replied: the presence of knowledge (*jñāna-sadbhāva*) which arises from the state of the subsidence-cum-destruction of the veils of sensory cognition and intuition (*mati-jñāna-darśanāvaraṇa-kṣayopaśama-avasthā-nirvṛtti*) is here called *labdhi*. How was it previously stated that *kṣayopaśama* is *labdhi*? By resorting to a metaphorical designation of the cause as the effect (*kāraṇe kāryopacāra*), just as water in a reed-thicket is called "foot-disease" (*pādaroga*). Therefore, there is no fault.

Others, however, say: "The capacity for the cognition of objects through the senses, which depends upon the destruction or subsidence of obstructive karma (*antarāyakarma*), is called 'attainment' (*labdhi*).

Furthermore, desiring to point out the most proximate cause, the author of the Commentary expands the text, stating: "And it arises in the soul as produced by the emergence of karma that has the senses as its substratum."

The sense organs (*indriya*) are the substratum (*āśraya*) or the locus (*avakāśa*) for those actions (*karman*) which are "dependent on the sense organs" (*indriyāśraya*). Whatever [actions] there may be—such as the primary and secondary limbs of a transformation (*nirmāṇa*)—without which those [actions] would not be accomplished, through their arising, through that fruition (*vipāka*), the attainment (*labdhi*) of the self (*ātman*) is produced and brought forth. For a reflection arises upon the surface of a clear mirror, not upon one that is soiled; likewise, the sense organs, fashioned from extremely pure matter (*pudgaladravya*) suitable for that purpose, provide incomparable strength to that attainment resulting from the subsidence of karmic destruction (*kṣayopaśama-labdhi*), assuming the role of its cause.
This very attainment (*labdhi*), depending upon three causes, becomes fivefold;
namely—as stated in the commentary: "attainment of the senses through touch," and so forth—the manner in which it is fivefold is now demonstrated.

*Spṛṣṭiḥ* means touching (*sparśanam*). That which is both touching and a sense organ is the tactile sense organ (*sparśanendriya*). This very [organ] is "attainment" (*labdhi*), meaning the unmanifest capacity for the thorough cognition of touches such as cold and heat, which exists in the form of functional application (*upayoga*); the same should be said for the attainments of the gustatory sense organ and the others.
Thus, the word [in the original text] indicates the extent of attainment;
attainment has been explained, and now functional application (*upayoga*) is being discussed.

If the application [of knowledge] occurs through the sequence of acquisition, manifestation, and instrumental aids, then there would be an absence of application regarding that which is beyond the senses, because of the absence of dependence on manifestation and so forth.
What is meant by this is that, since avadhi and the other types of knowledge are beyond the senses, their absolute non-existence— or at least a specific distinction [from the others]— must be stated.

It is said: Indeed, not every *upayoga* (active engagement) is produced by the *labdhi*, *nirvṛtti*, *upakaraṇa*, and the sense organs (*indriya*). What then? That very [consciousness] alone is the cause of the triad; therefore, he says: "Upayoga" is understood as the operation in the form of apprehension regarding touch and so forth—namely, touch, taste, smell, color, and sound—which has the tactile organ (*sparśanendriya*) and the others as its cause; it does not refer to the *upayoga* of *avadhi* (clairvoyance) and the rest.
Clarifying this very point, the author of the Bhāṣya says: "The meaning is that there is the *upayoga* of sensory cognition (*matijñāna*) regarding touch and the other [objects]."

The operation of sensory cognition (*matijñāna*) has as its object touch and so forth; "perception" (*upalambhana*) is the experience of specifically determined objects. By this, he demonstrates the exclusion of the remaining types of knowledge (*jñāna*), for it is only the application of sensory cognition (*matijñānopayoga*) that proceeds in dependence upon the *labdhi*, *nirvṛtti*, and *upakaraṇa* [faculties], and not the others. Here, someone objects, focusing on the denial of the general term "application" (*upayoga*): "It was stated that the application which has touch and so forth as its object is an operation that reaches completion; and this is also observed in the case of atoms, dyads, and so on."

For even a single atom is utilized in its entirety during the transformation into aggregates such as dyads (dvyaṇuka) and so forth; consequently, it too would attain the definition of "activity" (upayoga). Therefore, the author of the Bhāṣya says: "This has been stated—that activity is the defining characteristic.
Alternatively, the author of the Bhāṣya, wishing to elaborate upon the specific nature of activity, says: "This has been stated," and so forth.

This means that activity, which is a modification of consciousness, is the specific characteristic of the soul (jīva); what possible connection could there be here with atoms and the like? There is no connection whatsoever.
He explains that very same *upayoga* (active engagement) through synonyms by means of a specific exposition: "Upayoga," and so forth.
Upayoga is twofold consciousness: characterized by cognition (*saṃvijñāna*) and characterized by experience (*anubhavana*).
Among these, the perception of jars and other objects is characterized by cognition; the sensing of pleasure, pain, and so forth is characterized by experience.
Both of these are included by the mention of "application" (*upayoga*);

it proclaims this [distinction]: for the application of sensory cognition (*matijñāna*) is clearly necessarily accompanied by mental application and depends upon the physical sense organs (*dravyendriya*) and so forth, whereas the application of clairvoyance (*avadhi*) and the other types of knowledge is not like that.

"Āyoga" refers to the arising of cognition—born from the sense organ of touch and so forth—which manifests as the distinct perception of objects such as touch according to the limits of its own domain;

this is what is meant by "tadbhāva" (the state of that). A living being is characterized by this application (*upayoga*), and it is he who is denoted by the word "tat. His "state" (*bhāva*) is the cognition born through the doors of touch and so forth, which is the manifestation or emergence of the self; in other words, it is a transformation (*pariṇāma*) of the self itself, characterized by that state, and not characterized by the appearance of something external. This means that cognition caused by touch and so forth is essentially a modification of the self.
Now, establishing the rule of sequence regarding their activity (*pravṛtti*), he says: "Of these," and so forth, in the commentary.

"Of these" refers to the sense organs (*indriya*) whose natures have been explained—namely, those consisting of the physical organ (*nirvṛtti*), the auxiliary (*upakaraṇa*), the attainment (*labdhi*), and the functional application (*upayoga*). This is the sequence of their activity: first the physical organ (*nirvṛtti*); when that exists, there is the auxiliary (*upakaraṇa*) and the functional application (*upayoga*), because the auxiliary has the physical organ as its substratum and the functional application arises through the medium of that [auxiliary].

And this demonstrates that the triad beginning with *nirvṛtti* (the physical organ) is preceded by *labdhi* (the capacity): when there is the attainment (*labdhi*) of the subsidence-cum-destruction (*kṣayopaśama*) of the ear and so forth, there arises the *nirvṛtti*, such as the ear-drum (*śaṣkulī*) and other parts. However, for a living being who lacks such an attainment, the ear-drum and other constituent parts are certainly not produced. Therefore, all four—beginning with *labdhi*—when combined, bring about the discernment of objects such as sound and thus receive the designation "sense-organ" (*indriya*). An organ lacking even a single part is not called a sense-organ, nor is it capable of grasping its own object.
He demonstrates this point by means of the commentary: "Of completion, etc. This is stated while accepting the sequence presented in the aphorism.

If there is the absence of even one among completion, instruments, attainment, and application—that is, when the aggregate is deficient by even a single limb—there can never be for the self a cognition of the nature of objects such as sound and so forth, because the instruments are incomplete.

Some say that "the employment [of the senses] is in touch and so forth" is not a sūtra; rather, some study this as a commentary (bhāṣya) having turned it into a sūtra. This is incorrect, because it is established as a sūtra by its being studied among the sūtras without dispute, by its being understood through the tradition of specific teachers, and by its being a formal exposition.
Thus, in the commentary on the *Tattvārthabhāṣya* composed by Gaṇi Siddhasena,
the internal sense-faculty (*bhāvendriya*) is described: "The internal sense-faculty consists of both attainment and application" (Tattvārtha-sūtra 2.18).

Acquisition (*labdhi*) is a specific subsidence-cum-destruction (*kṣayopaśama-viśeṣa*) that serves as the cause for the manifestation of the sense organs; it is understood as that specific subsidence-cum-destruction of the knowledge-obscuring karma (*jñānāvaraṇa*) by whose presence the self (*ātman*) exerts itself toward the manifestation of the material sense organs (*dravyendriya*).
The specific modification resulting from that cause is *upayoga*.
As it has been said: "The modification of the self arising in dependence upon a cause is taught as *upayoga*.
Both of these constitute the *bhāvendriya* (psychic sense-organ).
Thus, in the *Tattvārtharājavārtika* composed by Akalaṅkadeva,
because that [knowledge] is made manifest by it, and because that too is made manifest by the utilization of external substances suitable for use, there would be an infinite regress;
therefore—
"Whatever and whichever substances transform through effort (*prayoga*) or natural state (*visrasā*)...

And having heard this exposition of the various conceptualizations of the *nayas*, the student, becoming perplexed, said: "O Blessed One! What is the truth here? Therefore, it is stated according to the *siddhānta*: "Whatever..."

794. Thereupon the Guru says: "O gentle-faced one! That which the Jina knows is the truth. But what does the Jina know? It is said: Whatever substance there is, and whatever states there may be—that substance transforms into all those states, and every substance is subject to transformation into all states. As it has been stated: "One state possesses the nature of all states; all states possess the nature of all states.
By whomsoever one state is seen in its true essence, by him all states are seen in their true essence."

Regarding the power of application and disintegration (*payoga-vīsasa-tti*): some states transform through application (*paogato*), while others do so spontaneously (*vīsāsā*). One knows that transforming substance (*pariṇāmi-vatthu*) in its entirety through all modes of transformation; however, as for that which is non-terminating (*apajjavanta*), there is no cognition thereof.
Thus, the doctrine of the Jina is the synthesis of all viewpoints (*savva-naya-samūha-mataṃ*).
Thus, in the *Āvaśyakacūrṇi* composed by the great elder Jinadāsagaṇi (p.

435), and likewise now, for the purpose of supporting the perspective of the substantialist (*dravyārthika*), the author of the *Niryukti* says: "Whatever states... and so forth. Whatever entities such as jars and the like the substance transforms through application (*prayoga*) or spontaneous evolution (*visrasā*)—therein, through application, it becomes jars and the like; through spontaneous evolution, clouds, rainbows, and so forth. It is the substance itself that possesses the imagined mode (*paryāya*), just as gold is fit to be designated by various terms such as bracelets, armlets, and anklets.

Moreover, the Jina knows and discerns each respective [substance] precisely as it is, with its primary mode (anvaya) and secondary modes (paryāya). Regarding "there is no knowledge of the non-mode" (*apajjave jāṇaṇā ṇatthi*): this means that in the non-mode—which is formless and devoid of such transformation—there is no comprehensive cognition (*parijñā*). Furthermore, those modes do not exist there as real entities; rather, it is the substance alone that possesses those forms.
And therefore, "that very [reality] is existent because it is apprehended even by the Kevalin, just like his own pure self," as stated in the *Viśeṣāvaśyakabhāṣyavyākhyā* composed by Koṭyācārya (p.
755). To support this very doctrine of the Dravyārthika-naya, the author of the *Niryukti* also says: "jaṃ jaṃ... (whatever...).
*Prayoga* (effort/application) is the activity of a conscious being; *visrasā* (spontaneity) is its inherent nature. A substance produced by these two is called a *prayogavisrasā-dravya*.
Among these, that produced by effort is such things as jars and cloths, while that produced by spontaneity is such things as clouds and rainbows.

In this regard, the substance (*dravya*), acting as the agent through its functional application (*prayoga*) and natural transformation (*visrasā*), undergoes and attains various states or modes (*bhāva-paryāya*), such as blackness, redness, yellowness, whiteness, and so forth. Because the instruction is characterized by repetition—expressed as "that and that"—the Jina, the Kevalin, knows that very substance as it transforms in each respective form; he does not, however, perceive modes as something distinct from that substance. This is because those modes exist merely as mental constructs (*utprekṣā*). Indeed, even in states such as the snake’s expanded hood, contracted hood, or coiled position, no mode whatsoever is observed to be separate from the inherent nature of the substance, such as the snake itself, since it is only the substance—the snake—that is perceived as possessing an unchanging nature across all its conditions.

If modes (paryāyas) do not exist, then how can it be said that "it transforms into whatever state"? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In the absence of modes, there is no cognition. We maintain that in the case of an object devoid of modes—that is, an object lacking its modifications—there is no thorough knowledge for the Kevalins and others; those modes exist merely as mental constructs (utprekṣā), and they do not exist as any real entities distinct from the substance (dravya).
Therefore, the substance alone is ultimately real. This is the meaning of the *Niryukti* verse.
Thus, in the *Viśeṣāvaśyakabhāṣyavyākhyā* composed by the venerable Maladhārin Hemacandrasūri, on page 1060, the Dravyārthika says: "Whatever [is perceived]...

Whatever object—such as clay or the like—transforms into various states or modes, such as consciousness or a jar, and thereby attains their nature, whether through application (*prayoga*) or by natural evolution (*visrasā*);
therein, "application" refers to the activity of a conscious agent, while "natural evolution" refers to its inherent nature (*svabhāva*).

All that consists of various modes (*paryāya*) is indeed the substance (*dravya*) itself, just like the substance of a serpent which is endowed with modes such as having its hood expanded, contracted, or coiled. For instance, there are no modes such as "having the hood expanded" and so forth that exist apart from the substance of the serpent, because they are not perceived by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), just like the modes of being curled up or half-curled up belonging to a sky-flower.
Therefore, it is that very substance which exists in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha-sat*) therein;
furthermore, the Blessed Lord Jina, the Kevalin, knows and discerns that substance exactly in that way, with the modes of persistence (*anvaya-paryāya*) as subordinate.
Why does one know [an object] with its modes (*paryāya*) as subordinate, and not devoid of modes? To this he says: "In the absence of modes, there is no cognition" (*apajjave jāṇaṇā natthi*).

Since even for those such as the Kevalins, thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) does not exist when there is an absence of modes—that is, when [the object] is devoid of modes—they are designated by mere conceptualization (*utprekṣā*), but they do not exist in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*). Therefore, substance alone is real.
Thus it is stated in the *Āvaśyaka-niryukti-vyākhyā* composed by Malayagiri.

The detailed meaning of this *Āvaśyaka-niryukti* verse is to be understood from the following verses of the *Viśeṣāvaśyaka-bhāṣya* composed by Jinabhadra Gaṇi Kṣamāśramaṇa: "When a substance transforms into a particular state at a particular time, the Jina-knowledge perceives that [state] as non-different from that [substance], for it is the substance itself, distinguished merely by its transformation.
Gold does not become something other than gold, nor do earrings; that very same substance, having reached that particular form, receives that designation, being non-different from its own nature.

Or, if qualities and so forth were different from the substance, there would certainly be a plurality of spatial locations, or else there would be the perception of color and other qualities in distinct locations.

If a modification of state (paryāyopacāra) is applied to that which consists merely of the transformation of latent impressions (laya-prakāśa-pariṇāma-mātra), it is merely a name; it does not become a substance distinct from the object itself.
A mode is merely the transformation of a substance; and that [transformation] does not belong to a donkey's horn.
Since knowledge has the knowable as its object, that which is not a knowable is not known.

The commentary on these verses is to be understood from the commentaries composed by Koṣṭhācārya, Maladhārī Hemacandrācārya, and others: "In that same way, the Jina knows [them]; there is no cognition regarding the non-paryāyas. (Āvaśyaka-niryukti 794)

Light is that which is to be manifested, because it is apprehended through entities that do not possess its own nature; even existence (*sattā*) is manifested by a cognition that does not have the nature of substance (*dravya*) and so forth, just as light from a lamp or similar sources manifests objects made known by the light of speech.

Furthermore, the Primal Nature (*pradhāna*) would likewise be [existence], for the existence postulated by you has the purpose of effecting the experience of universal forms, and thus serves the purpose of the Spirit (*puruṣārtha*), just like the three *guṇas*.

The effect also must be existent even prior [to its production], because it is superposed as being either incapable or capable, and because it is being made existent, like a substance that has just been produced; or else, it is not made existent nor brought into being by any other entity, because it is already real, like existence itself (*sattā*),
for the existence of that which is of the nature of existence does not depend upon another existence.
Furthermore, "the locus is not of that nature," etc., and also "the Pradhāna is likewise," and so forth.

The *pradhāna*—the cause of the entire world, synonymous with terms such as *prakṛti*—as postulated by the Sāṅkhya, would be identical to the *sattā* (Being) postulated by you, the Vaiśeṣika. This is because, like the three *guṇas*, it exists for the sake of the *puruṣa* (spirit), namely for the purpose of providing the experience of the manifold forms of the universe. Just as that which is called *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* proceeds for the sake of the *puruṣa*—proceeding specifically as the *pradhāna* in order to provide the *puruṣa* with the experience of the manifold forms of the universe—and there is nothing else distinct from it because it is merely its transformation (*vikāra*), so too would *sattā* be nothing other than the *pradhāna*. And this is undesirable [to you]. [End of fragment] *puruṣārtha pra*.
...because of its very nature, there is indeed no injunction regarding [the status of] devas and sentient beings;
furthermore, "the effect also belongs to them," and so forth, up to "like substance (*dravya*) and the rest."
It follows that even your "effect," such as a substance (*dravya*) and so forth, must exist prior to the time of its birth; this too is an undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭāpādana*).

How could causes such as threads be related to their own selves—which are intended to exist at a later time—even prior [to that]? The reasons beginning with "because they are superimposed as being either incapable or existent" up to "because they are being produced while already existing" have already been explained. The illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is "like a substance and so forth immediately upon its arising."
See page 473,
line 7: "Because it is being superimposed as existent upon that which is incapable of being either existent or non-existent"?
"Or else," and so forth:

if it is not accepted that [the effect] is thus [produced], then it is not treated as real, nor is it produced merely from substance (*dravya*) and so on, nor is it brought about by any other distinct entity, because it already exists, like "existence" (*sattā*) and so forth. By the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), it is meant that [it is like] substance-ness (*dravyatva*) and other generalities (*sāmānya*), particularities (*viśeṣa*), inherence (*samavāya*), and like "cowness" (*gotva*), which possesses existence that is eternally pervasive.
Furthermore, the existence of that which is non-existent cannot be imparted elsewhere for that very reason, just like its own [intrinsic] existence.

If it does not exist by itself even when inherent in its cause, then it must be non-existent; for, being inherently indefinable, incapable of designation, and thus indistinguishable [from nothingness], the effect would be non-existent—just like a sky-flower—even prior to its production, for these same reasons, just like a substance as soon as it has been produced.

That existence (*sattā*) does not depend upon another existence. The meaning is as follows: the essential existence (*svabhāva-sattā*) of substances (*dravya*) and so forth that have already arisen does not depend upon the existence of a correlate (*sambandhi-sattā*), because even in the absence of a connection with [the universal] Existence (*sattā*), they possess the nature of existence; this is like the Great Universal (*mahāsāmānya*), which possesses an existence that is eternally inherent. Regarding "existence of non-entities" (*anartha-sattā*): since the term "entity" (*artha*) is restricted by convention to substances, qualities, and actions, the Universals, Particulars, and Inherence are "non-entities" (*anartha*). The existence belonging to those non-entities is likewise not to be imposed elsewhere and is not dependent; for that very reason, it is like their own individual existence (*svasattā*). These are the logical arguments (*sādhana*) for establishing what is undesirable [to the opponent].
Because it is produced,
the existence of the effect is necessarily non-existent elsewhere [prior to production], just like the existence of a sentient being that has not yet arisen; for that very reason,

if it were not existent by its own nature while inhering in its cause— just like its own existence— then it would be non-existent, because it would be devoid of intrinsic character (*nirupākhyatva*), indefinable (*avyapadeśyatva*), and thus indistinguishable from a sky-flower, which is likewise non-existent.

Or perhaps the effect (*kārya*) also exists prior to its production from these very [causes], just like a substance and so forth immediately upon being produced. Even though cognitions depend upon both objects and sense organs, the "object" (*artha*) is first discussed: "The term 'object' (*artha*) applies to substances, qualities, and actions" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 8.14). Even without the general property (*sāmānya*) of "object-ness," the word "object" is established—meaning it is well-known, or used for the sake of establishing—precisely with respect to those three, substances and so forth; thus the word "object" is defined for the purpose of such establishment.

Where indeed? Just as in the case of generalities and particulars—such as "existence" (*sattā*) and the like—there is a cognition of "generality, generality" even without another generality; and just as in the case of particulars, there is for those who perceive them a cognition of "particular, particular" despite the absence of another particular; so too, in the case of substances and the rest, the term "object" (*artha*) is used conventionally even without an objective referent, and it refers to the sense organs. And these are not composed of five elements, because in the case of substances, that which is composed of five has already been refuted (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 8).

15. Since, among the substances that are to be produced, the five gross elements do not exist as the initiators [of those specific effects], but rather those which initiate them—such as water—initiate their own respective species, so too the sense organs have specific gross elements as their causal effects. For instance: "Due to the predominance [of earth] and its possession of smell, earth [is the cause] in the cognition of smell" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 8.16). The cognition of smell is the olfactory organ; in the production of that, earth is the cause due to its predominance, and this predominance is relative to the body.

Furthermore, earth predominates in the sense of smell (*ghrāṇa*), because there is no perception of odor by means of the feet and other such parts, and because it possesses odor; and since the olfactory organ manifests odor through the odor inherent in itself, its cause is therefore earth alone, which possesses odor. The other elements, however, being merely conjoined and present in small quantities, are not so. Likewise, in the cognitions of taste, color, and touch—namely, in the specific tastes, colors, and touches [of water, fire, and air]—[the respective element predominates], according to Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 8.1.4.

17. Thus, because the tongue, the eye, and the sense of touch manifest taste, color, and touch respectively through a sweet taste produced by post-origination transformation (*apākaja*) inherent in themselves, a white and brilliant color, and a touch that is neither hot nor cold and produced by post-origination transformation; and because, due to their possession of taste, color, and touch, they are not overwhelmed by other elements as instrumental causes and possess a predominance [of these qualities], water, fire, and air should be understood as the inherent causes (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*) of the three sense organs respectively.
Space itself is the auditory organ (*śrotra*), delimited by the ear-cavity; it is not primordial matter (*prakṛti*), because the latter does not initiate [sensory functions].
Thus has perception been explained.
This is the eighth chapter.
Thus, in Candrānanda’s commentary on the *Vaiśeṣikasūtra*, page 30, the same fault is stated again by way of another formulation: "If it is inherent in its causes," and so forth.

If the effect, merely by being inherent in its causes, does not exist in itself, but becomes existent through its connection with existence (*sattā*), [then] even though it is [already] existent, it is not yet existent as such—as in the case of qualities and the category of quality (*guṇatva*)—and thus it would also be non-existent; if this is accepted, then it follows that it is indeed non-existent.

Why? Because it is devoid of any designation (*nirupākhyatva*) by its own nature; the qualification "by its own nature" (*svataḥ*) is added because, although [the subject] is devoid of designation, there exist feelings (*vedanā*) and so forth which are self-cognized and yet possess existence. Thus, this [reason] may not be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

For that [subject], although it is devoid of designation in its specific form (*asādhāraṇarūpa*) such as feeling and so on, is nonetheless possessed of a designation (*sopākhyam*) by its very own nature as a real entity (*vastu*), namely through its aspect as a universal (*sāmānyātman*) and through its other aspect which is excluded from the nature of others.

Likewise, "vyapadeśya" means that which can be designated as diverse or specific; "na vyapadeśya" means it cannot be designated in any other way, such as [the categories of] sensation (*vedanā*) and so forth. The meaning is that, unlike a sky-flower, it is not non-distinct [from existence]. For by the qualifier "existent" (*sat*) and so forth, a real entity (*vastu*) alone—such as sensation—is connected with aspects like generality (*sāmānya*), and not a non-entity. Thus, due to this similarity, it would follow that it is non-existent like a sky-flower; the point has already been explained.

If this is not accepted, then even the effect must exist prior to its production for these very reasons, such as "because it is by nature indefinable," and so forth, like a substance immediately after it has been produced. If the reading is "it exists" (*sadeva*) and then "it exists" (*sadeva*) repeated somehow, then the reading appears to be correct: "it becomes existent through connection with existence; it is not merely existent [by itself], and it is also non-existent, like the absence of qualities or the absence of the nature of being a quality. (Note: *aguṇatvādi* in the Bhāṣya and Hīṃ editions).
Regarding "sato pra... vasvātmanaiva," there may also be a reading here as "svātmanaiva."
In such a manner,
prior to its arising, [it exists] without [the distinction of] "thus-qualified" (tathāviśiṣṭa).
Prior to its production—
before the production of the effect—

even though one has established the self-nature [of the effect] as being merely the entity produced by the operation of causal factors such as the agent, which is devoid of all specific attributes and inherent in the cause, it was argued that because the mere entity is without distinction, the restriction of its connection with attributes such as "existence" (sattva) is untenable; and this is indeed so, for since there is no distinction among all effects inherent in the cause due to the absence of a connection with existence and the like, the restriction of the connection with attributes such as "existence" is simply untenable.

As for what is replied: No; because there is a distinction in the causal totality (*kāraṇasāmagrī*), that which is an effect consisting merely of a thing (*vastumātra*) produced from parts of a similar class is connected with substantiality (*dravyatva*), whereas that which is an effect consisting merely of a thing produced from the qualities of its causes is connected with quality-ness (*guṇatva*).
Furthermore, that which [is produced] by weight and so forth, either in its own substratum or together with the conjunction of its own substratum,
as well as that which pertains to the agent and so forth.

The activity of the causal factors (*kārakas*)—such as the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth, whether they be inherent (*samavāyin*) like clay or non-inherent (*asamavāyin*) like Devadatta or the stick—which, having come together, initiates its own effect, has as its fruit the mere entity that is the produced effect, such as a jar. Its "ascertainment of self" (*ātmāvadhāraṇa*) is its function; therefore, in order to eliminate the expectation regarding the object previously raised, he says: "That which is devoid of all qualifiers"—meaning devoid of all qualifiers such as existence (*sattva*), substantiality (*dravyatva*), quality-ness (*guṇatva*), action-ness (*karmatva*), and so on, being empty of the presence of relations and consisting merely of the existence of its own nature—that is called "inherent in the cause. Having thus established the ascertainment of the self, he himself raises the following objection: because the mere entity is without distinction (*niratiśaya*), a restriction regarding its connection with qualifiers such as existence, substantiality, and so on, is untenable. For in that state, there is no cause for a restriction on the subsistence of substantiality, such that one could say, "This is substance; it must reside here specifically as substantiality, and not as quality or action-ness," precisely because of the absence of any distinction.
Likewise, regarding the [universals] *guṇatva* and *karmatva* in relation to qualities (*guṇa*) and actions (*karman*), the same applies;
thus, the very reason you stated—beginning with "that is exactly so"—is precisely what he articulates up until the point where it becomes untenable:

because of the inclusion of *sattā* (existence) and so forth, there is no excellence of connection produced by the particularities of *sattā*, *dravyatva*, *guṇatva*, *karmatva*, *ghaṭatva*, *rūpatva*, *gamanatva*, and so on, which would otherwise link all effects such as substances, qualities, and actions inhering in their causes.
...non-inherence... [Prakaraṇa] ...quality-action... [Prakaraṇa] ...presence of fuel... [Prakaraṇa]

Regarding "satvādi" (existence, etc.): for in that state, there is no such restriction as "this is a substance; it must be lodged here specifically as a substance, and not as a quality or an action. Thus, there would be no cause for a restrictive rule regarding the lodging of substantiality (*dravyatva*). This reading might also exist [in some versions], except for Viśālāmalavatī, where it says "there is no cause."
See Ṭīkā 5.

Regarding the objection "in the effect [there is no difference]," that which is stated in response to its refutation is: "No, because of the existence of a specific distinction within the causal complex."

The explanation of that is as follows: from the passage beginning with "composed of parts of a similar class" up to "is connected with substantiality," the rule regarding the subsistence of substantiality (*dravyatva*) means that substantiality subsists in a composite effect-substance (*avayavidravyakārya*) which is initiated by two or more atoms of earth, water, fire, or air—of a similar class and depending upon their own conjunctions. This is the meaning.

As for the passage beginning with "the qualities of the cause" (*kāraṇaguṇa*), it is because of the statement that when a substance as an effect is produced by those [causes], the qualities residing therein necessarily produce another quality; thus, since there is a restriction to "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*) regarding the other quality produced as an effect, it is connected by way of being a quality. Furthermore, regarding gravity and so forth: wherever gravity is inherent in its own substrate, if there is an absence of conjunction, the action of falling is initiated there. By the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), effort, impulsion, impact, conjunction, and velocity initiate action.

Or, [the action is initiated] by those very qualities such as gravity (*gurutva*) together with their conjunction with their own substratum. By these same [qualities], action is initiated in the substratum itself and in another substratum; that mere entity (*vastumātra*), being the effect, is connected with the state of being an action (*karmatva*). Thus, there is a distinction (*atiśaya*). This is merely an illustration, for in all cases, because of the presence of the determining causal complex (*kāraṇasāmagrī*), action is indeed restricted to specific instances. For example, when action is initiated by gravity in the fruit of a *kapittha* tree and its stalk, a falling motion is initiated in the insect conjoined with it. That initiated action in the other substratum—the mere entity which is the effect—is distinguished from the others and is connected with the state of being an action.
By showing that "there is thus a superiority," he brings about the non-establishment of the state of being without superiority.

From the words "this is merely an illustration" up to "is to be seen," one should see everywhere the relationship between the universal and the particular, such as pot-ness, cow-ness, and so forth, with respect to form-ness and the like.
By this, it is made clear that whatever entity has arisen is distinguished from others by its very nature;
thus, the existence of particularity (*viśeṣa*) is directly admitted for the drum, and through the description of that [particularity], non-particularity (*aviśeṣa*) is also [established].

Even in cases such as "non-disappearance" and so forth, by this same reasoning, one should see that the relationship is strictly restricted, because among generalities and particularities there exists a superior, regulating causal totality (*kāraṇasāmagrī*).
But as for that which [is stated] in the *Praśastapādabhāṣya* regarding "that which is similar to its own class" (*yattulyajātīyāvayava*) and so forth,
it refers to the absence of connection (*saṃgābhāva*).

In this context, regarding the statement "it initiates [action]," it should be understood that if one intends to express its agency (*kartṛtva*), the reading exactly as heard— namely, "it initiates" (*ārabhate*)— is indeed correct;
see the *Karmanirūpaṇa* in Praśastapādabhāṣya.
When these substances have been thus described, [the author], without omitting their qualities, states the actions [of the hand] because they require fewer words to explain:
"In that regard, action in the hand arises from conjunction with the self and from effort" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 5.1.6).
1. Because effort depends upon its own substratum’s conjunction, the conjunction between the self and the hand is the cause of the action at the commencement of movement;
since conjunction is a dependent cause, effort is also a cause. Therefore, the action in the hand arises from both.

Likewise, "the action of the pestle [arises] from the conjunction with the hand" (VS 5.1.2). The word "likewise" (tathā) is an extension by way of number alone; therefore, the conjunction of the hand and the pestle is the cause of the action of the pestle, as is the effort previously under discussion.

However, the conjunction of the self with the hand is not the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) of the action of the pestle, because that [action] is established solely from the conjunction of the hand with that which is conjoined to the self;
furthermore, in the case of the pestle's action produced by impact (*abhighāta*), the conjunction of the hand is not a cause due to its absence [therein]. Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 5.1.1.

3. Impact (*abhighāta*) is the conjunction with a substance possessing velocity. In the act of upward motion produced in the pestle due to impact from the mortar, the conjunction between the hand and the pestle is not the cause, because the prior effort has been destroyed by the impact; because there is an absence of the desire "let the pestle-substance fly up," there is an absence of any further effort; and since conjunction is a dependent cause for the initiation of action, the conjunction of the hand and pestle devoid of effort is not the cause of the upward motion.
Likewise, the conjunction with the self [is not the cause] in the action of the hand and pestle (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 5.1.6).

4. Just as the conjunction of the hand and the pestle is not the cause for the action of the pestle’s upward motion, so too the conjunction of the self and the hand is not the cause for the action of the hand’s upward motion. If it is asked, "Since conjunction is a dependent cause, and since there is no intention such as 'let the hand fly up together with the pestle' and there is an absence of effort, how can there be an upward motion of those two? [The answer is: "But from the impact of the pestle, through the conjunction with the pestle, there is indeed action in the hand" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 5.1.6).
5. The impact on the mortar is the cause of the action of the pestle’s upward flight;

however, the conjunction of the hand and the pestle, depending on the velocity inherent in the pestle, is the cause of the action of the hand. Impact [of the mortar] is not the cause, because it does not reside in the same substrate [as the effect].
Likewise, the action of the self [is caused] by the conjunction with the hand. (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 5.1.6–7)

1.6. "Ātman" refers to a single part of the body. Just as there is non-conscious action in both the hand and the club, so too, due to the conjunction with a part of the hand and depending on the momentum residing in the hand, at the time of the hand's upward movement, non-conscious action arises in that specific part. In the absence of conjunction, falling occurs due to gravity. Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 5.1.6.
1.7. When the conjunction between the hand and the mace has ceased due to disjunction, falling occurs because of gravity;
because of the absence of any specific impulse, there is no upward or horizontal motion. Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 5.1.7.

*Nodanam* (impulsion) is that by which something is impelled; it is a specific kind of conjunction dependent upon velocity and effort. In the absence of the effort of the impeller, there is an absence of impulsion; therefore, due to gravity alone, no upward or horizontal motion occurs in objects such as a pestle.
Whence then comes the specific impulsion? Specific impulsion arises from specific effort. (*Vaiśeṣika Sūtra* 5).

Herein, the effort (*prayatna*) produced by a specific desire, [expressed as] "I shall throw this," arises and generates a conjunction of a substance such as the hand with another substance, which is termed "impulsion" (*nodana*). From a specific impulsion, a specific upward motion (*udāsana*) arises. Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 5.2.1.1.9.

A specific impulse produced by an effort characterized by the desire to project [an object] to a distant place causes its projection to that distant place; the action of a child [is explained] by means of the action of the hand. Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 5.1.10.

That action of the embryo, such as throbbing and so forth, occurs with a cause (*sapratyaya*), arising from the conjunction of the self and a part of the body in dependence upon an effort preceded by life. The action of the embryo approaching the mother's place of excrement is without a [perceptible] cause (*apratyaya*), arising from the conjunction of the self and the body in dependence upon the unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*).
Likewise, the bursting of a burnt [wound]... (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 5).

Even that movement of the hand or other limbs of one who is burned while the mind is distracted occurs from the conjunction of the self and the hand, which depends upon effort preceded by life; thus it is not a non-causal instance.
In the absence of effort, the falling of one who is asleep occurs due to gravity. Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 5.1.12.

1.13. In the absence of the effort that sustains the body, the limbs of one who is asleep fall due to gravity because of the absence of volition; or, as in the case of grass, motion arises from contact with the wind. Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 5.1.13.

1.14. Or, from the conjunction of air and grass due to momentum, there is motion in the grass and so forth; since they lack effort, the movement of the gem and the gliding toward the needle are caused by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*). Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 5.1.14.
1.15. The meaning is that the movement of gems toward a thief, or of needles toward a magnet, is caused by merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*).
In the case of an arrow, the cause for the difference in its actions at non-simultaneous moments is due to specific conjunctions (*saṃyoga-viśeṣa*); Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 5.2.17.
From the initial impulse (nodana), the first action arises; from that momentum (saṃskāra), many subsequent actions arise in the arrow.

For if there were only one action, it would be destroyed by the very first conjunction with space, and thus subsequent conjunctions and disjunctions could not be produced by that action. Therefore, there must be multiple actions in the arrow.

"From impulsion comes the first action of the arrow; from the momentum produced by that action, subsequent actions arise, and likewise each subsequent one. (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 5.1.17) Impulsion (*nodana*) is the conjunction of the bowstring and the arrow, depending either on effort or on the velocity inherent in the bowstring. From that arises the first action of the arrow, which, depending on the impulsion, produces a momentum (*saṃskāra*); however, independent [of further causes], it produces conjunctions and disjunctions.

Then, when the action [of throwing] has ceased due to the destruction of the conjunction, and the impulsion has ceased due to the disjunction, the momentum produced by the initial action produces a subsequent action in the arrow; likewise, subsequent actions follow one after another repeatedly—this is the meaning.
In the absence of momentum, falling occurs due to gravity. Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 5.1.8.
18. Due to the destruction of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) caused by contact with a substance possessing tangibility, gravity produces the action of falling.

Having explained the actions among internal [objects] and those ignited by connection therewith, [the author] now explains the actions of the great elements: "Action in earth arises from pushing and so forth, from impact, and from conjunction with that which is conjoined" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 5.2.1).

That particular kind of conjunction which, independent of gravity, fluidity, momentum, and effort, is the cause of an action that is the cause of disjunction from *nodana* (pushing); that is *nodana*. To illustrate: when the earth, known as mud, is being pushed by feet and the like, an action arises;
