[furthermore], the conjunction that, depending on momentum, is the cause of an action that is the cause of disjunction from an impact (*abhighāta*) is *abhighāta*. To illustrate: an action is observed in certain parts of the earth due to an impact from chariots and the like.
And from conjunction with what is conjoined, as well as from that which is being pushed and that which is being struck, actions arise in the conjoined objects;
this [action] is specifically caused by the unseen force (adṛṣṭa). Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 5.2.18.

2. That action, such as trembling, which arises in the entire earth due to conjunction with air possessing contrary motion, for the purpose of indicating the auspicious or inauspicious [destiny] of living beings, is caused by the *adṛṣṭa* (unseen force) of all beings specifically because it indicates their auspicious or inauspicious [karma];
whereas falling occurs due to gravity (*gurutva*) in the absence of conjunction with water. Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 5.2.2.

3. In the absence of the conjunction of the supporting wind and clouds, the action of falling occurs due to the heaviness of water; this is specifically caused by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*). Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 5.2.10.
The action of falling produced by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) for the sake of the abundance or destruction of crops, or for all living beings, is called "caused by the unseen" (*adṛṣṭakārita*);
[and] flowing occurs due to fluidity (*dravatva*). Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 5.2.1.
5. Due to the absence of a restraining force, the downward movement of water occurs because of its fluidity;
however, its upward ascent occurs through the channel due to contact with air. Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 5.2.10.
6. "Nāḍī" means a ray; the sun has two rays—the *śuci* and the *śukra*.
By the *śuci*, it takes up water; by the *śukra*, it effects growth.
By means of the channel called *śuci*, which is conjoined with the wind and depends upon the effort of the sun, there is an upward ascent.
"From impulsion, from pressure, and from conjunction with that which is conjoined" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 5.2.7).

From impulsion, there is climbing by means of variegated poles and the like; from pressure, by means of garments and the like; and [action arises] in that which is conjoined with both the object being pressed and the object being impelled.
"Creeping toward a tree is caused by the unseen force (adṛṣṭa)," Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 5.2.8;
that is, the upward movement of water poured at the root of a tree to the top of the tree is brought about by the unseen force.
"The solidification of water and the melting of fire result from conjunction" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 5.2.9).
Solidification of water—that is, hardness—results from conjunction with celestial heat; however, melting results from both celestial and terrestrial heat.
Regarding this, the Vaiśeṣika Sūtra (5.2.10) states: "In that case, thunder is the mark.
This means that in the statement "there is heat in divine waters," the mark for the existence of heat is the emission of thunder from the clouds.
And the Vedic passage, *Vai. Sū.* 5.2.11,
"They, desiring splendor, have conceived Agni as their embryo," is a Vedic statement that serves as an indicative mark (*liṅga*) of fire within the celestial waters.
"From the conjunction and disjunction of waters arises thunder" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 5.2.12); "thunder" (stanayitnu) refers to the sound of clouds and lightning.
Sound arises from the conjunction known as mutual impact among water particles that have become waves and are being propelled by two winds moving in opposite directions;
sound also arises from the disjunction of water particles when they are separated by even a single agitated wind.
By this, the action of fire and the action of air are explained through the action of earth. (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 5)
Just as action occurs in earth due to impulsion, impact, conjunction-with-conjunction, and the unseen force (adṛṣṭa), so too does it occur in fire and air; this is non-uniform action.
Thus, in the *Vaiśeṣikasūtravṛtti* composed by Candrānanda (pp. 19–21):
"Action is initiated in another substratum; that mere substance, as the effect, becomes connected with the nature of action—thus there is a specific excellence (*atiśaya*).
This is merely an illustration, for in every case, due to the presence of the determining causal totality (*kāraṇasāmagrī*), [the result] is strictly determined."
The relationship between the universal and the particular is to be understood as follows:
by this [statement], it is made clear that whatever mere entity has arisen is, by its very nature, distinguished from others through mutual differentiation.
First, the existence of the particular is directly admitted by [the opponent] regarding the drum; and by way of describing that, the non-particular (the universal) is also [established].
Because it does not convey [the intended meaning], etc.;
[this applies] to one who maintains [such a view].
When the objection was raised, "By what [reasoning]? and "By the reasoning 'raṃ'," the author of the present treatise says: "By this," and so forth.

By this very statement of yours regarding the resolution [of the objection], it has been made clear that the effect which has arisen—that which is considered to be a mere entity—is itself distinguished from others solely through the excellence of the causal complex (*kāraṇasāmagrī*), and does not depend upon a connection with existence (*sattā*), substantiality (*dravyatva*), and so forth; for by that very distinct manifestation of the entity, the function of connecting it with qualifiers such as "existence" and so on—which serves as the cause for the non-distinct cognition and designation of the particular—has been secured. *Note: The text contains scribal corruptions at the end (°bhavanena ? °ṣeṇasa° ya°), which have been interpreted based on the context as part of the preceding argument concerning the manifestation (*bhavana*) and qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*).*

Regarding the statement "the non-distinction between the qualifier and the qualified" (in the Bhāṣya): therein, the existence of the particular (*viśeṣa*) has indeed been explicitly accepted [by the opponent], because [he argues that] a specific relation between the universal and the particular is observed everywhere due to the presence of a non-restrictive causal complex (*kāraṇasāmagrī*). Thus, by means of this concluding statement, it follows that the non-distinction (*aviśeṣa*) has also been accepted through the description of that [particular].

You yourself have already demonstrated that even when the lack of distinction—consisting in being an effect produced by a conjunction of homogeneous constituents—is described through the qualification of the locus of substance-ness (*dravyatva*), or through the description of quality-ness (*guṇatva*) as residing in another quality produced by qualities, or through the description of action-ness (*karmatva*) as residing in an action inherent in another substratum produced by gravity (*gurutva*) and so forth, it does not become devoid of its remaining specific qualifications. For, by demonstrating the true nature of an entity as qualified by distinctions such as the conjunction of homogeneous parts, there exists [this specific character]...
and not otherwise, nor in anything else.

Furthermore, because the causal complex is applied without distinction, even in the case of water and the other elements, substantiality (*dravyatva*) is established through the conjunction of constituent parts belonging to the same genus;
by this, the substantiality of that which is distinct from earth and the other [elements] has been explained.

Furthermore, even when there is a difference in genus (*jāti*), it should be understood that a thing (*vastu*) is not devoid of both the non-specific (*aviśeṣa*) and the specific (*viśeṣa*). This is because of the statement "in two or in many," and because, by way of their concealment (*nilayana*), all substances, qualities, and actions are described as having specific objects and belonging to their own respective genera; thus, the non-specific (*aviśeṣa*) is also explicitly accepted as a distinct category (*bheda*).

Therefore, the establishment of the connection with the specific and non-specific qualifiers residing in the effect is due solely to the excellence (*atiśaya*) produced by the specific and non-specific qualifiers residing in the cause.
Thus, it has been stated by way of describing the qualifiers; let it be seen on page 482, line 2,
or in the *Avi* and *Ya* [manuscripts].

Furthermore, you yourself have already demonstrated that [the object] does not even become devoid of its remaining specific qualities; for, by showing the true nature of a thing as qualified by specificities distinct from the conjunctions of homogeneous parts and so forth, there exists [this reality],
and not otherwise, nor in anything else.
For there is indeed a mutual distinction among substances and the other categories; therefore, the intention appears to be that "one is not [identical] to the other.

Furthermore, because they are joined without distinction by the causal totality (*kāraṇasāmagrī*), even in the case of water and so forth, the nature of substance (*dravyatva*) is manifested through the conjunction of parts belonging to the same class.
By this, [the nature of substance] is distinguished from earth and the others...
...the nature of substance (*dravyatva*) has been stated;

for even substances distinct from earth and the others possess the nature of substance because there is no difference in their being originated by the conjunction of homogeneous parts, etc.—this appears to be the intended meaning.
Furthermore, even when there is a difference in genus, a thing is not devoid of both the general and the particular, as indicated by the statement "in two or in many."

Is it stated by way of describing specific qualifiers? Or is it stated by way of describing specific [objects]? Furthermore, regarding the passage beginning with "without distinction" (*aviśeṣa*), you yourself have already demonstrated that it is not even devoid of specific qualifiers.
For example: "distinguished by the conjunctions of parts of a similar class," and so forth.

Parts that are of a similar class (*tulyajātīya*) are those of a similar type; from the conjunctions of such parts—such as the earthy elements characterized by the possession of odor and other qualities—the earthy substance (*dravya*) arises as an effect. By the inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*), the previously mentioned fact that qualities (*guṇa*) and actions (*karman*) also possess a specific mode of proximity to their own causes is implied.

Even though there is a distinction [in the cause] due to those conjunctions and so forth, you have demonstrated the true nature (*svatattva*) of the entity as being non-distinct—that is, distinguished from others—by means of this "non-distinction" (*aviśeṣa*) regarding substances and the rest.
Therefore, the concluding passage beginning with "For it exists" (*tasmāt tatpradarśanād asti hi*) has its meaning already explained, up to the point where it says "not the other,
not the other," [referring to] the effect of earth being distinct from water and so forth.

Is it "without distinction, distinguished by distinction" (nāviśeṣeṇa viśeṣeṇa viśiṣṭa), or "without distinction, distinguished by a qualifier" (nāviśeṣeṇa viśeṣaṇena viśiṣṭa)? [Note: Variants include *vinā* and *viśeṣaṇaviśiṣṭa*].
"Not the other, not the other here" (bhāṣya);
"not the other, not there" (yājñavalkya).
Furthermore, "and again," and so forth.
In the case of earth-particles possessing color, taste, smell, and touch that have conjoined, no distinction has been shown;

yet this is not the only distinction you have clarified as residing within the homogeneous. What then? Even among heterogeneous substances, substantiality (*dravyatva*) is manifested through the non-distinctive connection with the causal totality (*kāraṇasāmagrī*). This is because, even in the case of water and other elements, the causal totality is identical, and substantiality is produced from the conjunction of parts belonging to similar classes, since there is no distinction in the conjunction of parts belonging to a similar class.

By the inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*), it is meant that [the production of a whole] also occurs from the conjunction of parts of fire and air; for it has been stated that there is no distinction in the commencement of a conjunction of similar kinds even among things of dissimilar kinds. Thus, the qualification of "non-distinction" has been clarified.

Therefore, he extends [this principle] by saying: "By this, [it is shown that] earth and so forth are distinct," and so on, until the nature of substance (*dravyatva*) has been explained; this is the meaning of the non-qualification (*aviśeṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, as stated in the passage beginning with "even in the case of similar species" (*tulyajātibhede’pi ca*) and ending with "whether in two or in many" (*dvayor bahuṣu vā*),

even when there exists this intermediate genus termed "pot-ness," "cloth-ness," and so forth— which is a sub-division of the genus "earth-ness"— the entity remains inseparable from its general and specific qualifiers.
Why? Because it has been stated that an effect-substance (*kāryadravya*) arises from the conjunction of two, three, four, or more [atoms].

Thus, it has been explained that the relationship between a qualifier and the qualified (*viśeṣaṇasambandha*) is established in the mere entity (*vastumātra*) itself, independent of any other related factor. Even so... [the text continues with *pra*].
The relationship between the qualified and the qualifier [is] primordial (pra°), [as stated in] the *Iṣṭasiddhi*,
the *Bhāṣya*,
the *Atiśaya*, and the *Yukti*.

And as it has been stated regarding the conceptualization of genus (*jāti*), that which is manifested as a mere thing (*vastumātra*) is connected with the universal-particular (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*) by way of being a regulator, merely through its function as a non-distinct particular. From this, the following is established: the thing, existing by itself, is connected with such notions as "substance" and so forth;
for that very reason, it is also the illuminator of the universal, because the universal, the particular, and so on, have that [thing] as their substratum.

Therefore, because the accomplishment of various activities of enjoyment arises from the connection with differentiated objects, and because the conventional usage of non-difference is established even among distinct things, a relation with a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) need not be postulated.

This is merely an illustration; however, in all cases—even regarding [universals] such as "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*)—the reality [of the universal] exists simply due to the presence of the causal complex that determines it.
Furthermore, it is like the conceptualization of a genus (*jāti*), and so forth.

Just as birth, by its very nature, manifests itself through a manifestation that functions upon the mere entity (vastu) without requiring anything else, so too, for the purpose of demonstrating the point that "substance and the rest are inherent in their causes," it was stated: "the mere entity has become manifest. As previously stated, by way of being the regulator (*niyāmaka*), because the causal complex (*kāraṇasāmagrī*) exists as the regulator everywhere, the entity—being determined by its own majesty according to this stated logic—is connected with qualifiers such as "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*).

And that [category], such as substantiality (*dravyatva*) and so forth, which exists merely as both the non-specific and the specific, is the "particular universal" (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*). That which has its occurrence through the previously mentioned non-specific [universal] and through the specific is this "occurring as both non-specific and specific," namely substantiality and so forth; its measure is merely that, and thus every mere entity (*vastumātra*) is connected with that particular universal which exists merely as both non-specific and specific, and it is manifested thereby.

If it is asked, "What follows from that?", it follows from this: an object that has arisen by itself becomes connected with such notions as "substance" and so forth; the qualifier, being established independently of anything external, manifests by itself alone—it is said that there is no need for another manifestation. Furthermore, for the very reason stated above—beginning with the words "But from that very [object]"—that which manifests is simply the bare object (*vastumātra*), which reveals even the universal (*sāmānya*), because the universal, the particular (*viśeṣa*), and so forth have that [object] as their substratum.
The passage from "nyānyānākāṅkṣābhā" to "dṛśyatāṃ pṛ॰ 481 paṃ॰ 1" has been duplicated in the manuscripts.
And [the term] "particular" (viśeṣaṇa) is connected with substance and so forth; why is that? Because of the [word] "only" (eva).

As for what was also stated—that the connection with existence (*sattā*), substantiality (*dravyatva*), and so forth is postulated for the sake of establishing the performance of various acts of enjoyment—that too has been refuted by this very [argument]. Like a lamp, from a primary entity (*vastu*) that is independent of any other illumination, there arises a connection with a distinct object (*pravibhaktaviṣayānvaya*). This "distinct object" refers to the specific causal complex of substantiality, such as the conjunction of homogeneous parts and the sequence beginning with the qualities of the causes, produced by qualities that initiate action in their own substratum and further substrates. Because of the distinction [of the effect] from its cause and so forth, and because of the connection with non-distinct qualifiers such as "existent" and "non-eternal," it is through such a connection with a distinct object that the establishment of the performance of various acts of enjoyment occurs from that very entity, and the establishment of the conventional usage of non-difference among things that are actually different. Thus, he demonstrates the two-fold purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*).

And since these two human goals are established by their very nature as already stated, no connection with qualifiers need be postulated; for it is not reasonable to postulate a connection with qualifiers such as "existence" (sattā) or "substantiality" (dravyatva), because it would be purposeless—see page 474, line 1;
see page 481, line 5.
That which is without cause (takāraṇa) is the cause of that (tatkāraṇa);
[this is] the state of being afflicted by suffering (viṣāyādhaccabhāva).
The phrase "as far as...
in reality" does not exist in the manuscripts;

this is merely an illustration. By the logic already stated, the conceptualization of a relation for its various sub-divisions is also purposeless. Therefore, he extends the argument: "But in all cases—even in the case of 'jar-ness' (ghaṭatva) and so forth—the word 'and so forth' including 'cow-ness' (gotva), 'human-ness' (manuṣyatva), and the rest—their very essence as jar-ness, cow-ness, human-ness, etc., exists by itself alone, and not from a universal-particular (sāmānya-viśeṣa) as imagined by you. Thus, by your own statement, everything you desire is established as being real in itself, and not through a connection with some other entity.
And it is established that this very [cognition] is also the illuminator of the qualifier, such as existence (*sattā*);
see page 482, line 3;
see page 482, line 2.

However, to show that you yourself have accepted this very entity—which possesses a more manifest manifestation of the connection with qualifiers—in order to establish the necessity of that connection, the statement was made: "Alternatively, even without a connection with qualifiers, there exists a mutual excellence (*atiśaya*) among mere entities; by means of that, the restriction of the connection with qualifiers is established.

This refutation of the objection also demonstrates our aforementioned position as being well-known. If it is asked, "How can there be a mutual excellence?", [the answer is: how could there be excellence previously? No, because of the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
Just as there is a superiority in the opposing position, so too would it be here.
The example from one's own system (*svasamaya*) also confirms this very point, as it is said: "Or, like universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth...
it would exist eternally. [The opponent asks:

"How could there be a mutual distinction among substances, qualities, and actions prior to their connection with *sattā* (existence)? [The author replies: "No, because of the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*); for just as in the opposing view (*parapakṣa*) there is a mutual distinction among *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* even without a connection to *sattā*, so too it would be here. This appears to be the intended meaning.
See page 462, line 7;
see page 462, line 8.

The underlying intention here appears to be that just as universals and so forth exist by themselves, independent of a relation to other entities, so too would substances and so forth exist by themselves.

Substances and the like are not self-luminous by virtue of being "located" (anyādheya); nor do they possess existence and so forth as something "located" (ādheya), nor do they possess an incomplete existence and so forth, because they are existent.
Furthermore, this is even more evident:

a thing is called "the manifestation of the relation with qualifiers" (*viśeṣaṇasambandhaprakāśa*) because the manifestation of the relation with qualifiers—such as existence, substantiality, and so forth—is present within it.

The statement is introduced to demonstrate that it is the object itself which manifests the qualifier, and thus that very object is the manifestation; furthermore, no connection with the universal is required by that object, for you yourself have accepted that it is the universal alone that requires a connection with the object, in order to establish the rule for that connection.

What is the statement being introduced? It is said: regarding what was stated—that when the nature of an entity is determined, there is an absence of distinction due to the lack of any excellence—and when this objection was raised, the response given by means of an alternative conceptualization is that the entity itself, even more clearly, manifests its own qualifiers independently of any other object.

For example—regarding what was said: "Alternatively, even in the absence of a connection with qualifiers, there exists a mutual distinction among mere entities; by this, the restriction regarding the connection with qualifiers is established"—let it be seen that this statement has its life-breath in the logic of the distinction or non-distinction of the presence of the totality of causes as previously described (see p. 481, l.
2). This also includes the objection and its refutation, and so forth.

Regarding the objection raised in this context—"If it is asked how there can be a mutual excellence"—its explanation is as follows: "How, previously... and so forth, which has already been explained up to the point where "there would be excellence.

This is the resolution of that objection; furthermore, it demonstrates the very renown of what we have stated. What is that resolution? It is said: "No, because of the illustrative example (dṛṣṭāntāt)."

The explanation of that is as follows: from "just as in the case of another’s position" up to "so too here there would be an excellence," the meaning is already understood. It has been stated [in the *Prakaraṇa*]:

"If, according to the other’s view, there is a mutual excellence among *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, what of yours? To refute this doubt, the author provides an example from his own system (*svasamaya*) to further solidify this very point. This is the demonstration of his own statement: "As it is said, 'like universals and so forth,'" along with its commentary, which has already been explained, including the application (*upanaya*), up to the conclusion: "it would exist by itself alone."

Thus, the *Aśaṅkā* (Bhāṣya) confirms this very point; so says the *Pra*. Here are the formal arguments (*prayoga*s): The thesis (*pakṣa*) is that substance (*dravya*) and the rest are not self-luminous by virtue of being dependent on another, nor is the manifestation (*prakāśa*) of this substance and the rest dependent on another. Alternatively, the thesis is that substance and the rest do not have the qualification of "existence" (*sattva*) as something dependent, nor do they have the qualification of existence as something incomplete. This is because of their existence (*sattvāt*). Whatever exists is not seen to be self-luminous by virtue of being dependent on another, nor to have existence as something dependent, nor to have existence as something incomplete—just like universals (*sāmānya*) and the like. For example, a universal, because it possesses a self-nature (*sātmakatvāt*), because it exists in each instance (*pratyekaṃ sattvāt*), and because its own nature is truly existent (*svabhāvasadbhūtatvāt*), is like a universal and the like [in not being dependent for its manifestation].

Or rather, it would be non-existent itself, because its existence is obtained through inherence in existence (*sattva-samavāya*), just like an effect; therefore, it has been rightly stated that even for substances and so forth which are already existent, existence does not make them existent, because it would be redundant. Nor does existence make existent those things that are both existent and non-existent, because such a thing has never occurred; for according to your own view, the nature of being both existent and non-existent is like a sky-flower.

As for the argument you stated—that the identity of being and non-being is untenable—that is not a valid argument; for according to your own view, the identity of being and non-being is indeed tenable because they are not absolutely contradictory. An effect consists of both being and non-being even prior to its connection with existence (*sattā*), just as universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth, or substances (*dravya*) and so forth, are both existent and non-existent in relation to themselves and others;
thus, universals and the like exist by their own nature...

...even while abiding, they do not possess specific inherences; they are not existent by means of another's manifestation, nor do they have existence as something to be imparted, nor do they have incomplete existence, and the same applies to substances and the other categories.

Thus, the reasons—"because it possesses a self," "because it exists individually," and "because its intrinsic nature is real"—are merely synonyms for the fundamental reason. If this were not accepted, [the effect] would be non-existent, because its existence is obtained only through inherence in existence (*sattvasamavāya*); that is, its existence is obtained by means of inherence in existence. This refers to the triad [of substance, quality, and action] immediately upon its production. The phrase "like an effect" (*kāryavat*) refers to the effect in its causal state, which serves as the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

If it is argued that, in this way, the effect does not exist in that state because its existence is obtainable only through inherence in existence (*sattva*), we say no; for you yourself have already avoided this by admitting that completion (*niṣṭhā*) and relation (*sambandha*) are simultaneous.

[Furthermore,] because it possesses a self (*sātmakatva*), because each [constituent] exists, and because it is existent by its own nature (*svabhāva-sadbhūtatva*), like a universal (*sāmānya*) and so forth, it would either be non-existent, since its existence is obtainable only through inherence in existence, just like the effect.
Therefore, it has been rightly stated that existence (*sattā*) does not make existent things such as substance (*dravya*) existent, because it would be purposeless;

nor does existence make existent-and-non-existent things existent, because such a nature (being both existent and non-existent) is non-existent according to your own view, like a sky-flower. As for the argument you offered—that the identity of the existent and the non-existent is untenable—that is not a valid argument, because according to your own view, the identity of the existent and the non-existent is indeed tenable.

Because they are not absolutely contradictory, the effect is of the nature of both being and non-being even prior to its connection with existence (*sattā*), just as universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth, or substances (*dravya*) and so forth, are both existent and non-existent in relation to themselves and others;
likewise, universals and the rest [are so] by their own nature...

The intention appears to be this: even while existing, universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth do not exist by way of their own nature; they exist [only] through the existence of a relation (*sambandha*), and thus they do not exist [independently]. Likewise, effects such as substances (*dravya*), having just arisen, do not exist even while existing.
Is this not [the doctrine of] self-luminosity (*svaprakāśa*) wherein [existence] is not something to be imposed upon another?
In the Prajñā (pra) [manuscript], there is "prakāśanādheya";
in the Ya [manuscript], there is "yo nāpratipūrṇasattvāda". This does not exist in the Prati manuscripts. If one accepts it in this way, [it is found] in the Prajñā.

Regarding the objection raised against those [categories] beginning with substance—namely, "Is this 'cow' connected with cowness, or is it a non-cow?"—that is not worthy of a rebuttal, because the completion [of the object] and its connection [with a universal] occur at the same time. As stated in the *Vyomavatī*, a commentary on Praśastapāda’s *Bhāṣya* during the examination of action: "The very acquisition of its own nature by the individual (piṇḍa) is its connection with its own causes, such as existence (*sattā*) and so forth; prior to that, it has neither the form of a cow nor the form of a non-cow. Therefore, it is rightly said that "existence does not make existent even substances and the rest that already exist, because it would be redundant"; this concludes the justification for stating the fault under discussion.

Thus, it has been stated that existence (*sattā*) does not bring about the state of being existent for non-existent things, nor for existent things such as substance (*dravya*) and the rest (see page 459, line 3; page 473, line 7). Furthermore, existence does not bring about the state of being existent for things that are both existent and non-existent. For the opponent’s intended position might be that substance and the rest are "existent-and-non-existent" (*sadasat*), meaning they possess a dual nature; and that existence would then produce the designation and cognition of "existent" for those things that are both existent and non-existent. But even that is not tenable.

Why? Because, according to your own view, its nature as both existent and non-existent is unreal, like a sky-flower. Prior to its connection with *sattā* (Being), the effect—such as substance (*dravya*) and so on—is neither existent-nor-non-existent; rather, it is simply non-existent, because by nature it lacks any designation (*nirupākhyatva*), and for other reasons such as those previously stated, it acquires existence only through its connection with *sattā*. Furthermore, if it were said that the effect exists even independently of its connection with *sattā*, then the connection with *sattā* would be redundant.
Therefore, in either case, the conceptual alternative of being both existent and non-existent does not hold.
Therefore, because it is non-existent like a sky-flower, it is not connected with existence according to your own view; nor does it exist even according to our view,
because it is a past [entity],
and that which is past is non-existent.
See page 480, line 2;
see page 460, line 6;
[the reading] "sattādyābhā" [is to be adopted].

As for the argument you stated—that the unity of being and non-being is untenable because existence and non-existence cannot coexist—that is not a valid argument; for according to your own view, the unity of being and non-being is indeed tenable, as there is no absolute contradiction between the two. Because they are not absolutely contradictory, the effect consists of both being and non-being even prior to its connection with existence (*sattā*).

For example: [the category of] "general property" (*sāmānya*) and so forth, as well as substance (*dravya*) and the rest, possess both thatness and otherness, existence and non-existence. Now, regarding what is called "generality," "particularity," and "inherence"—if it is argued that because these are not perceived prior to their manifestation, they are simply non-existent (*abhūtatva*), like the distinction of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*); then one must ask: is this non-existence of something already existent (*bhūta*) or of something non-existent (*abhūta*)? If it is of something existent, then the identity of existence and non-existence is established. If, however, it is of something non-existent, then the cause for the non-existence of substance and the rest must be stated;
for if there is no arising from a cause, then, just as in the case of the realization of momentariness or emptiness, there would be absolute non-existence.
If this is not the case, then, as before, the very possibility of the identity of being and non-being arises:

the triad of entities exists as real by its own nature (*svabhāvasat*), and thus it "is"; yet, because it does not exist through the existence of a [permanent] relation, it is "not" (non-existent). Since being and non-being are not at all contradictory according to your own view, it is established that the three effects known as substance, quality, and action, as soon as they are produced, are both existent and non-existent—just like universals and the rest. Thus, according to your own doctrine, they are proven to be "existent and non-existent."

The explanation of these two examples, beginning with "generalities and so forth, by their own nature," has its meaning already explained in sequence, up until the point where it says "even though they exist, they do not exist.

Therefore, according to your own view, since the identity of existence and non-existence is untenable, non-existence does not [absolutely] not exist; rather, existence is established precisely because of that very tenability.
But how then is that non-existence? It is said: "Because it has not come into being"—this has been well stated.
See page 459,
line 5: *prākprattāsamba* (Ya) / *prākpravṛttāsamba* (Bhā).

[Objection]: But if this is so, then because it is not treated as such [prior to its manifestation], it is simply non-existent (*abhūtatva*), just like the difference between prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and other absences. Now, is this non-existence that of something already existent (*bhūta*) or of something non-existent (*abhūta*)? If it belongs to what is already existent, then there is the consequence of the identity of existence and non-existence (*sadasadaikātmya*).
If, on the other hand, it belongs to what is non-existent, then a cause for the non-existence of substance and the rest must be stated.

If it is argued that there is no non-existence at all— just as in the case of the realization of momentariness, emptiness, and so forth— despite the absence of a cause, then, as before, the identity of existence and non-existence would necessarily follow; therefore,
this [position] is incorrect.
See page 487, line 4.

The other [opponent] says: "But in that case, because it is not yet being treated as such, it is simply non-existent (*abhūtatva*), just like the various types of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva-bheda*). For example, just as a substance such as a jar, immediately after its production, lacks the practical function (*vyavahāra*) of fetching water and so forth due to its prior states of being in the granary, the husk, the lump, the pot-sherd, or the clay-clod—which are themselves varieties of prior non-existence—and thus the jar is non-existent in those cases; likewise, before its connection with existence (*sattā-sambandha*), the effect, which consists of both the existent and the non-existent, is simply non-existent because it is not yet being treated as such. What is the fault in this?"

In this regard, the following must be considered: Now, as for the question introduced by the presentation of the two alternatives beginning with "that which is non-existent" (*abhūtatva*), its meaning has already been explained; the answer to that is as follows: If it is maintained that "non-existence" belongs to an existent thing such as a substance (*dravya*) immediately after its production because it is not yet subject to linguistic usage (*avyavahāra*), then that very same real entity is "existent" in its own nature and "non-existent" in its aspect of not being subject to linguistic usage. Therefore, since existence and non-existence are not contradictory, the identity of the existent and the non-existent (*sadasadaikātmya*) is indeed established.

Now, if you maintain that the effect is "non-existent" (abhūta) so that its oneness with [the cause]—which contradicts your own admission—may not be the case, then you must state the reason why the substance and other factors are absent from the effect. For by what reason is that non-existent effect, having merely arisen as inherent in its own causes, considered "non-existent" despite being existent, according to our stated non-contradictory reason, namely because it is unfit for conventional usage? It might be thought: "It is non-existent precisely because it lacks a cause; in the absence of a cause, it is like a sky-flower."

And this is incorrect because, if there were no arising from a cause—that is, if there were non-existence without a reason—then, as in the case of the conceptualization of momentariness, emptiness, and so forth, there would be absolute non-existence; this is the completion of the sentence.

Just as it follows that the subsequent thing arising after a prior thing has ceased would be without a cause, thereby resulting in the doctrine of momentariness, and since even that which has arisen is expected to perish precisely without a cause, it would—due to its lack of substantiality and lack of seed—be an absolute non-entity like a sky-flower; and this too would be the case here, which is undesirable.

Or, just as through the analysis of non-establishment, illogicality, non-arising, the collection of causes, perception, and non-perception, everything might be void— due to the commonality of lacking causeless arising, abiding, and destruction, like a flower in the sky;
and by the inclusion of "etcetera," [it would be] like the analysis of dependent origination, aggregates, continua, and conventional reality—

if this were not the case, as before, then in order to avoid the fault of absolute non-existence, by accepting that effects possess causes and are not non-existent, it follows that our own position regarding the identity of being and non-being is indeed established.

Thus, it has first been established that the effect is both existent and non-existent prior to its connection with existence (*sattā*), without [the distinction between] the prior non-difference of being and the difference of being,
or without [the distinction between] the prior non-difference of being and the non-difference of being.
Whether there are sentient beings or not,
it is without cause.
It might be thought that there is no causal basis;
it might be thought that it does not exist by way of causality.
*pra* [is corrected to] *yad*.
...would have considered it to be without cause;
or as [it would be] through unestablished reasoning, or as [it would be] through unestablished reasoning.

Alternatively, [regarding] "non-establishment, illogicality, and non-arising" (asiddhyayuktyanutpāda)—here is the inquiry into the proof: "Now, how is there the absence of self, other, and both? We reply: "From these reasons—namely, from the observation and non-observation of the causal complex for non-establishment, illogicality, and non-arising"—this will be explained in detail in the twelfth chapter (*ara*) of the *Nayacakravṛtti* within the discourse on emptiness (*śūnyavāda*).
The manifestation of seeing and so forth has arisen; this is the nature of these [faculties].

Even when it is connected with existence (*sattā*), according to your own view, that effect which is connected with existence is designated as "existent"; indeed, it is existent by its own existence, not by the existence of *sattā*.

Furthermore, *sattā* itself is manifested only as existent upon obtaining a substratum, due to the distinctions of cause and effect, non-cause and non-effect, permanent and impermanent, related and unrelated, and possessing a genus (*jāti*) and lacking a genus—just like the inherence (*samavāya*) in threads.
And through descriptions such as mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*) and so forth, there is everywhere merely a detailed exposition of the identity of existence and non-existence;
therefore, having attained and proclaimed this very sovereignty of the Jina, it is concealed from those whose intellects lack discernment.

Furthermore, let alone the question of whether an effect is existent or non-existent prior to its connection with existence (*sattā*); even when it is connected with existence, according to your own view, it remains both existent and non-existent. For instance: that effect which is connected with existence is designated as "existent" because it is qualified by existence acting as a qualifier, just as a man is qualified by a staff to become "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍin*), since it is the object of qualification. Now, is it not the case that it is "existent" by its own existence (*svasattā*) alone, having already attained its self-nature, like Devadatta distinguished by a staff? It is not made existent by the existence of [the universal] *sattā*; for Devadatta is not made non-existent or existent by his connection with a staff. What then? He is already existent by his own existence, but he becomes the locus of the designation "staff-bearer" through the existence of the staff. Thus, being existent by its own existence and non-existent by the existence of the staff, it is both existent and non-existent.

Likewise, according to the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*), an effect is already existent at the time of its connection with existence (*sattā*), because it differs from non-entities such as a sky-flower by virtue of its own existence.
Similarly, even existence itself is not made existent by the existence of the entity; rather, it is manifested through the acquisition of a substratum while already being existent.

Thus, both of these—the universal "existence" and so forth, as well as the substance and so forth—are existent by way of their own substantial existence, yet they do not exist by way of the existence of their related correlates; this is the meaning.
Why? Because of the reasons beginning with "cause and effect" up to "difference":

substance and so forth are both effects and causes, whereas existence (*sattā*) is neither an effect nor a cause; existence is eternal, while substance and so forth are non-eternal; substance and so forth possess relations, whereas existence is unrelated; substance and so forth possess genus (*jāti*), whereas existence is without genus—it is because of these differences that [existence] is distinct, like the inherence in threads (*tantu-samavāya*). Just as the threads possess the properties of being causes and so forth, so do substance and the rest; just as inherence possesses the properties of not being a cause and so forth, so does existence.

Furthermore, the application of existence and non-existence to both the example and the exemplified must be performed by means of the existence of an essential nature and its relation [to that nature];
therefore, the establishment of the identity of existence and non-existence remains always valid.
Neither by way of non-existence,
nor by way of existence, nor by way of being.
Is Devadatta [the result] from the connection with *bhā*,
or is Devadatta [the result] from the connection with *ya*,
or is Devadatta [the result] solely from the connection with *eva*?

But furthermore, Bhāṣya: moreover, by your very descriptions of mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*) and so forth, you have everywhere merely provided a detailed exposition of the single-naturedness of being and non-being; this is the completion of the sentence [from] Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 9: "Being is non-being. (saccāsat).

1.4 Thus, regarding the description of mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*): "A jar exists as its own self, but not as the self of a cloth and so forth. Now, having taken up this very debate, what is being said here specifically directed at you, who follow the *Sāṃkhya* doctrine, is as follows: "Because the restriction of material causes is observed, the effect exists [prior to production], like oil in sesame seeds; therefore, due to the absence of its activity and so forth, it does not exist [as a manifest entity]."
Likewise, according to the Vaiśeṣika Sūtra (9.1.1), "that which is non-existent is characterized by the absence of action, quality, and designation"; thus,
it is called "non-existent" because it is not perceived as a present reality, yet there is a perception of its opposite through the memory of its prior existence.

And there is also the description of antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and non-existence through destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) in Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 9.1.6–7: "Because [the effect] does not exist when [the cause] exists in such a state."

In every case, existence and non-existence alone have been described, with the sole exception of absolute non-existence (atyantābhāva), because an absolute lack of self-nature (ekāntanirātmakatva) like that of a hare’s horn and so forth is not admitted.

Therefore, having established this very status of being the Lord of the Jains (jainendra)—namely, the doctrine of being both existent and non-existent—and having explained it in many ways, you thus conceal and hide [this truth] from those of undiscriminating intellect, lest there be respect for the Jains alone among simple people of unrefined wisdom who might think, "They are knowers of reality," while I am thought to be "one who does not know reality."
Now, desiring to explain inference (anumāna), he shows its object: "Because of the absence of action, quality, and designation, [the effect] is non-existent" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 9.1.1).
To begin with, the effect is not perceived by direct perception prior to its production.

Nor can it be established by inference, because inference exists only when there is a mark (liṅga), and there is an absence of such a mark because its action and quality are not perceived; nor is there any other mark indicated by the word "designation" (vyapadeśa). Therefore, [the effect] is non-existent prior to its production, and existent-subsequent-to-being-non-existent (sadasat) after its production. (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 9.1)

Furthermore, even an existing entity is designated as "non-existent" by way of negating its being something else— for instance, "a cow is not a horse"— or by its failure to perform a function, as in "this cow does not carry [the load]," or "it is non-existent.
And whatever else is distinct from the existent, that too is non-existent (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 9.1).

5. Furthermore, that which is other than an existent entity—namely, that which consists of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), such as a hare’s horn, which is not the object of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) or non-existence through destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*)—is also simply non-existent (*asat*), because there is no distinction among non-existent things. If it is asked: "How is it that the activity of causal factors (*kāraka*) occurs with respect to what was previously non-existent, and not elsewhere? The answer is: No, because of the perception of a specific distinction (*viśeṣagrahaṇāt*). For in that case (with respect to a hare’s horn, etc.), there is an absence of the cognition "it exists" (*asad iti bhūtapratyayābhāvāt*), an absence of the direct perception of its existence (*bhūtapratyakṣābhāvāt*), an absence of memory of its having existed (*bhūtasmṛter-abhāvāt*), and because there is the perception of something contradictory (*virodhipratyakṣatvāt*). [Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 9.1]

6. What is non-existence through destruction (*pradhvaṃsāsati*)? It is the cognition "it is non-existent" regarding an existing object that arises by postulating its destruction—due to the absence of perception of that existing object now, as it was before; due to the recollection of that existing object; and due to the perception of a contradictory factor such as the potsherds. Otherwise, how could it not be perceived, since its nature remains unchanged? But in the case of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), [the cognition arises] because of the perceptibility of the entity when it exists, and because of the perceptibility of the entity when it does not exist [in that way]. Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 9.1. (Note: The final portion of the sūtra text provided appears to be a corrupted repetition of the reasoning regarding the perceptibility of existence and non-existence.)

7. In the state of the lump of clay, prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) existed and no perceptual cognition regarding the jar had arisen; now, however, a contrary cognition regarding the jar has arisen, and the state of non-existence is remembered. Therefore, one arrives at the certain cognition that "this entity has now come into being, whereas previously it was indeed non-existent. By this, the cases of "non-jar," "non-cow," and "non-dharma" are explained. Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 9.1.7.

8. Just as for one who has the cognition "a jar in a pot," there arises a correct cognition mediated by another cause—namely, "this is not a jar; this is the pot"—which is to be understood from the absence of the cognition of "jar," from the recollection of that [prior cognition], and from the perception of the contradictory object such as the pot; so too, when the possibility of dharma is conceived for night-bathing and the like based on general observation, the cognition "this is non-dharma" arises. Thus, there are three examples according to the distinction between sentient, insentient, and supersensible objects.
Thus, in the *Vaiśeṣika-sūtra-vṛtti* composed by Candrānanda, pages 30B–31A.
Now, [the opponent objects]: "But surely I have engaged here in debate precisely against you, who follow the Siddhārthīya school;

for it is said by the Siddhārthīyas: 'Because a restriction regarding the material cause is observed, the effect exists [in the cause], like oil in sesame seeds; because of the non-existence of its production and so forth...'"

Regarding the phrase "asaditi" (the cognition "it does not exist"): in the *Vaiśeṣikasūtra* accompanied by the commentary composed by Candrānanda, the reading is "jñānam" [cognition], based on the absence of the cognition of existence (*bhūtapratyayābhāvāt*), the recollection of existence (*bhūtasmṛteḥ*), and the perception of the contrary (*virodhipratyakṣatvāt*). However, in the manuscript containing only the root *Vaiśeṣikasūtra*, the reading is "jñānam," based on the absence of the perception of existence (*bhūtapratyakṣābhāvāt*), the recollection of existence (*bhūtasmṛteḥ*), and the perception of the contrary (*virodhipratyakṣatvāt*). See page 489, note 6.

In the *Vaiśeṣikasūtra* accompanied by the *Upaskāra* composed by Śaṅkaramiśra, however, the reading is: "It is non-existent because there is no perception of it as having come into being, just as there is perception of its opposite despite the memory of its prior existence"; likewise, [the reading] is "tathābhāvāt" in the manuscript "bhū", and "tathābhāvabhāvāt" in the manuscript "bhā".
Regarding the phrase "because it exists when there is such an absence," this appears correct;

however, in the *Vaiśeṣikasūtra* accompanied by the commentary (*vṛtti*) composed by Candrānanda, as well as in the manuscript containing the root *Vaiśeṣikasūtra* alone, the reading is "tathābhāve bhāvapratyakṣatvācca" (and because there is perception of existence when there is such an absence). See page 489, note 6.
In the *Vaiśeṣikasūtra* accompanied by the *Upaskāra* composed by Śaṅkara Miśra, however, the reading is "tathābhāve bhāvapratyakṣatvācca" (*Vaiśeṣikasūtra* 9).

Although this term "non-existence" (abhāva) is used in a general sense, by virtue of the context it refers specifically to prior non-existence (prāgabhāva). Just as there is perceptual knowledge regarding destruction (pradhvaṃsa), so too is there such knowledge regarding prior non-existence. Why? Because of the perceptibility of the entity (bhāva); that is, because the entity—such as the vīraṇa grass being arranged [into a mat]—is perceptible, meaning it is made an object of perception.
Alternatively, it means because the locus (adhikaraṇa), the counter-positive (pratiyogin), and the entity itself are perceptible, that is, they possess the requisite capacity for perception.

Since the fitness of the locus (*adhikaraṇa-yogyatā*) and the fitness of the counter-positive (*pratiyogi-yogyatā*) are necessary conditions for the apprehension of a relational non-existence (*saṃsargābhāva*),
the word "and" (*ca*) indicates that the recollection of the counter-positive is also required; thus, it combines this with the previously mentioned reasoning (*tarka*).
"This very state of being the Lord of Jinas is the state of being both existent and non-existent," [the author] says here.
To this, he replies: "I do not accept the state of being the Lord of Jinas, nor do I conceal it from those of undiscriminating intellect.

Indeed, I have already refuted this in the debate here, because of the difference in nature between the existent and the non-existent: 'In an effect, there is neither existence nor non-existence' (Sūtra 9)."
By this sūtra,
that further discussion is directed specifically at you, who follow the doctrine of Siddhārtha’s son and who maintain the theory of the identity of existence and non-existence.

The passage beginning with "yaducyate" and so forth is a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) intended to demonstrate the view of the Saiddhārthīyas. For those Saiddhārthīyas, desiring that a real entity possesses the nature of both existence and non-existence, would state the following justification: "The effect exists [prior to its production], because we observe a restriction regarding its material cause (*upādāna*), like oil in sesame seeds; yet it does not exist [in that state], because we observe the absence of its activity and other functions, like a jar in grass or even in clay. Otherwise, in the doctrine of an absolutely non-existent effect (*atyantāsatkāryavāda*), there would be no restriction of the material cause, just as there is none for a sky-flower. Furthermore, since the cloth is perceived while the threads are still in their state [of being threads], it is non-existent [in that state]; for such is what is observed.
otherwise, there would be no distinction between threads, dust, and so forth, and there would be an absence of activity even prior [to production]; yet, activity is indeed observed.

"...because faults are seen in both extremes, the extreme view that 'it is only existent' or 'it is only non-existent' is improper; for since the effect consists of both existence and non-existence, the restriction of its material cause and its production are logical"—this is not so, because the alternatives are untenable.

Is it "only existent" [that becomes non-existent], or is it "existent and non-existent," or is it "existent by its own nature and non-existent by another nature"? Is it non-existent in the form of a jar? First of all, it is not the former...
[and so on].
...and non-existence is the counteragent to existence;
existence is that which has a designation, while non-existence is that which lacks a designation.
The meaning is that there is no such thing as "being both existent and non-existent.

Here, the claim that existence has non-existence as its counter-correlative is unestablished, because [non-existence] is a constituent part of it, identical with it, and proceeds from it; otherwise, the weaver’s activity for the sake of a cloth would not be directed toward the upper part of a jar.

The restriction of the material cause and the operation for its sake are the causes of the effect’s existence and non-existence; he supports this with the words beginning "It is observed, first of all," and so forth.

And it brings about an undesirable consequence: for one who does not so desire, there would be no distinction between threads, dust, and so forth, such that what is a material cause (*upādāna*) would be non-material, or conversely; and just as there is an absence of the operation of causal factors (*kāraka*) once their own nature has been attained, there would likewise be an absence of operation even prior [to that attainment]. Thus, he concludes by way of correspondence according to possibility with the words "but action is observed," etc., because faults are seen in both extreme positions (*ekānta*), namely, that [the effect] is either existent alone or non-existent alone.

The absolute position that "it is either existent or non-existent" is untenable, because an effect possesses the nature of both existence and non-existence. To claim that, based on the position of existence (*satpakṣa*), the restriction of material causes is logical, while based on the position of non-existence (*asatpakṣa*), causal activity is logical—this is the doctrine of the Siddhārthikas, and it is not correct because such conceptual alternatives (*vikalpa*) are untenable. Thus, regarding the repeated statements "it is existent," "it is non-existent," or "it is both existent and non-existent," in brief, through these two alternatives and with supporting reasoning, [the object] is existent by its own nature and non-existent by another nature; for example, it is existent as a jar, yet non-existent as something else.
"Having engaged in debate" means with the desire for victory, not with the desire to know the truth— Nyāyabhāṣya 4.2.51.
See page 460, note 1:
"Siddhārtha by name was a lord of men; his son was the Śramaṇa, the Blessed One Mahāvīra, also known by the name Vardhamāna. 'A Jaina' means one who follows his doctrine. (vīraṇoṣvivadvaṭobhā॰)
Like a pillar of *vīraṇa* grass [supporting] the ocean—thus in the Pā., Ḍe., and Vi.
recensions; like a pillar of *vīraṇa* and the ocean—thus in the Raṃ. recension.
It is non-existent because it is perceived; for it is indeed seen that...
[otherwise], there would be no distinction between threads, dust, and so forth, and there would also be an absence of activity even prior [to production]; however, activity is indeed observed.

because faults are seen in both extremes, the one-sided view that 'it is only existent' or 'only non-existent' is improper; for since the effect consists of both existence and non-existence, the restriction of its material cause and its production are logical"—this is not so, because the alternatives are untenable.

Is it existent and yet non-existent? Is it existent and non-existent by its own nature? Or is it existent [by one nature] and non-existent by another nature, as in the case of a jar? First of all, it is not the former...
...and existence is the antidote to non-existence;
existence is that which has a designation, while non-existence is that which lacks a designation.
...the meaning is that existence does not constitute non-existence.

Here, the fact that existence has non-existence as its counter-correlative is unestablished, because [non-existence] is a constituent part of it, because it is of the same nature as it, because it functions as it, like the upper part of a jar—

First, it is observed that when there is a desire for a cloth, only the threads are taken up as the material cause, and not dust or other such things; likewise, the activity of the weaver is seen to be for the sake of the cloth. Thus, the intention appears to be: "The action is observed to be for the sake of the cloth, and the material cause is indeed the threads; therefore, by virtue of the restriction regarding the material cause and the activity directed toward that purpose, the effect is both existent and non-existent."

In this regard, the intention of the two alternatives appears to be: "Is that which exists by one nature also non-existent by that very same nature? Or is existence and non-existence relative, such that an effect like a jar, which was previously existent in the form of clay or other materials, is non-existent in its own form as a jar?

First, it cannot be that it is non-existent by the very same nature through which it is existent, because of the difference in characteristics (*vaidharmya*) between the existent and the non-existent, as it has been stated:
"Due to the difference in characteristics between the existent and the non-existent, there is indeed no simultaneous existence and non-existence in the effect" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 4.1.9).

The meaning appears to be that existence (*sattva*) is the counter-correlate of non-existence (*asattva*), and non-existence is the counter-correlate of existence; existence is that which has a designation (*sopākhyam*), while non-existence is that which lacks a designation (*nirupākhyam*). Due to the difference between these two, existence and non-existence cannot coexist in a single effect—this is the intended sense.
If [the words] end in the nominative case, this very construction of the sentence is correct;
however, if they end in the accusative case, the connection should be understood as "he supports the two reasons" (hetū samarthayati). Thus it is seen. *Prakaraṇa*.
And the reasoning concerning existence and non-existence is not logical.

First, having established the initial alternative, he states the refutation by means of the aphorism along with its commentary and detailed exposition, up to the point where it says, "and existence is the counter-correlate of non-existence"—the meaning of which has already been explained. [One might think:
"The opposition between the existent and the non-existent is their state of being counter-correlates (*prātipakṣya*), and this very difference (*vaidharmya*) is the reason;

do not suppose that this [reason] is unestablished (*asiddha*). Therefore, in order to demonstrate that, he says, "The existent is characterized by description," and so forth, up to the clarification of the difference, the meaning of which is well-explained as: "existence does not constitute non-existence."
To understand the nature of the second alternative, its refutation, and the response thereto, please see pages 499 and 500,
as well as the description of the *suvarṇana* and the *pra* position.

On this point, the Teacher states the following reply: "In this proof of yours, the fact that the existent lacks a counter-proposition (*asatpratipakṣatva*), its contradiction (*virodha*), and its dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) are unestablished (*asiddha*).

Why? Because they are its constituent parts (*aṅgatvāt*). A 'part' (*aṅga*) is a limb or a portion thereof; that which is a part of something cannot be its counter-proposition. For example, the state of having an upward neck and so forth is not a counter-proposition to the state of having a neck and so forth."

Being existent, it becomes [the object] for the sake of the cognition of the specific nature of each individual thing; it consists of existence and non-existence through engagement with that and exclusion from what is not that; it is by its own nature an experience of a function that is absolutely undivided; it is distinct from a sky-flower which is non-existent; it is distinct from momentary destruction which is a different entity; and it performs a single action of being and non-being across the past, future, and present, just like space.

Likewise, even a thread or a cloth is both existent and non-existent as they occur sequentially; likewise, even space is both existent and non-existent as it occurs simultaneously, such that one perceives "it is here" and "it is there."

Furthermore, it is not the case that the counter-positive (pratipakṣa) is [the negation], because it has that as its nature (*tadātmakatvāt*). That which is the self of this entity is the non-existence whose nature is that [negation]; because of being that, it is "because of having that as its nature. It is just like the pot’s having a neck and so forth.

Furthermore, because it is the activity of that (*tatpravṛttitvāt*): that very non-existence is the activity of this existent; the meaning is that the entity proceeds by way of the form of non-existence.

Thus, a single object—in the manner of a pot—proceeds as the existence and non-existence of properties occurring simultaneously or non-simultaneously, such as the forms of a lump of clay, a small pot-sherd, and so forth.

Alternatively, if one explains that the limb (*aṅga*) is the self (*ātman*), and the self is activity (*pravṛtti*), such that they possess the same referent (*aikārthya*); then, being the state of being an "existent" (*bhavan*) like the neck and other parts [of a body], it exists as the very nature of each individual thing. It is characterized by the exclusion of what is not that activity, and consists of both the existent and non-existent. It is, by its own nature, an experience of an entirely undivided function; it is distinct from a non-existent sky-flower, and distinct from momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) as a separate entity. Like space, it performs a single action consisting of the past, future, and present, as well as the differentiated existences of the existent and non-existent.

Likewise, even things such as threads and cloth, which arise sequentially, are both existent and non-existent; likewise, even space, which arises simultaneously, [is so]. Let this also be seen from here and there. (Note: This passage does not exist in the Bhāṣya manuscript on page 493, line 13.)
Regarding the simultaneous occurrence of dharmas:

existence (*sattva*) belongs only to that which exists as it comes into being, not to that which does not exist. Furthermore, the self (*ātman*) is that which proceeds into manifestation (*pravṛtti*).

And what is the nature of this cultivation? It is permeated by non-existence (*abhāva*); he demonstrates this with the verse beginning "each individual object" (*pratyekavastu*) and continuing through the *daṇḍaka* meter up to "consisting of existence and non-existence" (*sadasadātmaka*). With respect to each individual thing, for the purpose of apprehending the specific nature (*svarūpa*) of every single object, there arises that which is called a "pot"—distinguished from the *śivaka* (the unbaked clay lump) and distinguished from the cloth and so forth. Therefore, that very thing called a pot exists as the essence of a pot, while it does not exist as the essence of a cloth, a *śivaka*, or the like;
thus, it consists of both existence and non-existence.
Therefore, non-existence is a constituent part of existence; its very nature is existence, and it is indeed the manifestation of existence.

Thus, while that jar exists even through the simultaneous presence of form and other qualities, it does not exist without non-existence, which constitutes the nature of its own functional activity as a constituent part. This has been stated with reference to substance and space;

now it is stated with reference to time and state: that very jar, the subject of becoming, whose experience consists of an activity entirely inseparable from itself, experiences that activity of its own throughout—both before and after.

Therefore, because it is of the nature of becoming (*bhavana*), it is distinct from a non-existent sky-flower, since a sky-flower does not exist in any form whatsoever, whereas a jar exists through its prior, subsequent, and present forms; and it is also distinct from momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) which is a different entity, because becoming—the process of coming into existence—is absolutely non-different from the substance (*dravya*) perspective across the past, future, and present, whereas in the doctrine of momentary flux, difference is admitted at every single moment. Thus, it is distinct from that [momentary flux].

[Objection: "In that case, since there is no difference between the becoming of a substance (*dravyārthabhavana*) and its non-becoming, non-becoming would have no place at all; yet this is not so. To this, he says: "[The substance] has a single action consisting of past, future, and present distinct becomings, whether existent or non-existent. Those becomings which are past and those which are future are distinct from the present becoming due to differences in place, time, form, cause, and so forth; and the present becoming is [distinct] from them. Furthermore, because they are mutually dissimilar, they do not exist in each other's form; nevertheless, the single action of becoming is predicated of all of them.

How so? Like space (*ākāśa*). Just as for you [the Vaiśeṣika], space—which is a single, uninterrupted existence (*bhavana*)—serves as the substratum for things inherent in it such as sound, and for things conjoined with it such as jars; yet, because it appears differentiated by virtue of being the substratum for the existence of those various jars, cloths, sounds, and so forth, it must be accepted as both existent and non-existent through the categories of difference and non-difference. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the confusion (*saṅkara*) of those jars, sounds, and other entities. Likewise, according to our view as well, although [space] exists as a general location (*avagāhasāmānya*), it is nonetheless non-existent in its particularity due to the differences in the locations occupied by fingers, jars, and so on. Thus, a jar is an "existent occurrence" (*bhāvana*), a substance (*dravya*), and an effect (*kārya*).

Just as space, so too are threads, cloth, and the like, because they are real; otherwise, they would not be entities at all, due to their unprecedented nature, like a sky-flower. By way of contrast, [they are real] like a *campaka* flower, because they are other, because they are non-different, or because they are present—unlike a barren woman's son or the doctrine of momentariness.

Therefore, there is no opposition between existence and non-existence, nor is there identity, because affirmation and negation have the same object, just as in the case of the cultivated notions of identity regarding sentience and insentience.

Furthermore, the claim that "the existent is with a defining characteristic (*sopākhyam*) and the non-existent is without a defining characteristic (*nirupākhyam*)" is also untenable, because even the existent lacks a defining characteristic.
For who is able to define the existent in every individual object at every moment by its existence? Because it is unique (*asādhāraṇatvāt*), the existent is non-existent in its successive occurrence;

and just as that [existent] such as thread or cloth occurs successively, so too space, though occurring simultaneously, is both existent and non-existent, and both different and non-different—thus, its dual nature is demonstrated from this perspective and from that.
Meditation (bhāvanā) is directed toward each individual object;
that is, toward every single thing.
And is the jar existing as non-existence? See page 492, line 10: "svatātyantāvi... (its own absolute non-existence).
The destruction of the characteristic of being [produced] from itself, from another, from both, or without cause.
The true characteristic (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is the destruction (*bhaṅga*).
For the sake of knowing the essential nature of place, time, and so forth, see page 320, lines 4, 18, and 26; [this is] the arising (*bhavana*). Ya.
De. Ya. Bhavane-ya.

Otherwise, the entity would not exist at all because of its unprecedented nature, like a sky-flower; by way of contrast, [it would be] like a campaka flower. Or, because of being other, because of non-difference, or because of non-existence, it would be like the son of a barren woman or like the doctrine of momentariness.
Therefore, there is no opposition between existence and non-existence.

There is no identity [between existence and non-existence], because they have mutually exclusive domains of application, just like the consciousness of being sentient and insentient when cultivated as identical.

Furthermore, the claim that "the existent is with designation (sopākhyam) and the non-existent is without designation (nirupākhyam)" is also untenable, because even the existent is without designation;
for who is able to designate the existent with respect to every individual thing at every moment? This is because it is unique (asādhāraṇatvāt).
The state of being existent is demonstrated by existence.
The demonstration of the state of being [a single entity] in the Vi[ṣṇu-purāṇa],
whereas in the Pādma and Rāmāyaṇa it is otherwise,
as expressed by "not at all" and so forth.

Thus, for you who do not accept that an entity consists of both existence and non-existence, there can be no entity at all, because it would be unprecedented (*apūrva*) and seedless. This is so whether one takes the *bahuvrīhi* compound "that which has nothing prior" (*na pūrvam apūrvam*), meaning it did not exist previously, or the *tatpuruṣa* compound "that which is not prior," meaning it was non-existent before—just like a sky-flower as a point of contrast, whereas a *campaka* flower is not. For a *campaka* tree, which already exists, becomes a flower through the process of its roots, sprouts, and so forth;
and thus, that *campaka* blossom consists of both existence and non-existence.

In the same way, this should be applied to posteriority (*aparattva*), supremacy (*anuttarattva*), and non-differentiation (*abhedattva*). Therefore, that which is present would not exist; and consequently, because it would also be non-present, it would likewise not exist—just like a barren woman’s son or according to the doctrine of momentariness (*kṣaṇikavāda*). These two examples are introduced to demonstrate the distinction from the "momentary destruction of a sky-flower" (*khapuṣpa-kṣaṇabhaṅga*). He concludes this by stating: "Therefore, there is no opposition between the existent and the non-existent."
Of the very same *caṃpaka* tree: Bhā°, Pā°, Ḍe°, Vi°,
Raṃ°.
See page 492, line 2.

Furthermore, there is no identity between existence and non-existence; indeed, their identity would result from a double negation. Why? Because affirmation and negation have a single object. Affirmation is *anvaya* (inclusion), and negation is *vyatireka* (exclusion). That both of these have a single object is established by such statements as: "It consists of existence and non-existence, characterized by the engagement with and withdrawal from that and not-that for the sake of apprehending the nature of each individual thing"; and "The experience of an undivided nature which performs the single function of existence and non-existence across past, future, and present diverse manifestations. Thus, it is proven.

Therefore, existence and non-existence constitute a single identity (aikātmya), just as consciousness and unconsciousness have been shown to constitute a single identity. And just as it was stated that "the conscious is the unconscious" by contemplating the conscious and the unconscious as having the same object through affirmation and negation, so too here, because substance and so forth consist of the single identity of existence and non-existence, there is no opposition between existence and non-existence. (See *Āptamīmāṃsā*, p. 492, l. 2).
See page 372, line 7.
Furthermore, as for the statement beginning with "And even though...

and so forth—where you state a difference in nature (*vaidharmya*) for the purpose of cultivating the realization that existence and non-existence are opposites, namely that "the existent has a designation (*sopākhyam*) while the non-existent lacks a designation (*nirupākhyam*)"—that too is untenable, because even the existent lacks a designation.

"Ko hi" and so forth: regarding each and every entity, such as form, taste, and the like, whatever its unique nature (*asādhāraṇa ātmā*) may be—which is distinct in the preceding moment and distinct in the succeeding moment—the state of being (*bhāvaḥ*), that is, its existence (*sattvam*), by virtue of that existence, and by virtue of its existence at every entity and at every moment, that existent thing cannot be described by anyone. This is because it is unique; for that which is unique cannot be described, just like the personal experience of one's own pleasure and so forth.
Therefore, the view that "whatever exists must necessarily be describable" is not an absolute rule.
We do not say that "whatever exists is necessarily describable," since an exception to this is stated.
What then? Is it existent, possessing a designation (*sopākhya*), or is it non-designatable (*nirupākhya*), like the experience of one's own pleasure and so forth?
Moreover, even in the case of being non-designatable, it is certainly not non-existent, because it possesses the general property of having a designation;
furthermore, this is also [admitted] by you...

...the connection with a qualifier must be postulated; yet it is not non-existent, because it lacks a defining characteristic (*nirupākhya*). Rather, both the existent and the non-existent possess a universal, because they respectively have and lack a defining characteristic (*sopākhya* and *nirupākhya*). Furthermore, both the qualified and the unqualified possess a universal, because they respectively exist and do not exist. Thus, while a universal exists in itself, it does not exist as a universal in the same way that a real entity (*vastu*) exists; therefore, the universal is existent yet non-existent.

Because it bestows designations based on the cognition of itself and others, it is "with designation" (*sopākhya*); and because it is like a non-entity, it is also "without designation" (*nirupākhya*). Thus, that which is "without designation" is indeed "with designation," while for a real entity (*vastu*), the reverse is true.

Therefore, by virtue of being established as both "with designation" and "without designation," it must be either existent or non-existent, like a universal (*sāmānya*) or a substance (*dravya*) respectively. However, that which is "without designation" is simply non-existent; it does not share any commonality with the existent.

This too is not tenable because of the fallacy of deviation; therefore, he says: "And yet, even in the case of being indefinable (*nirupākhya*), it is not non-existent, because it possesses a general definition (*sāmānya-sopākhyatva*). "Upa" means proximity; "upākhyā" means a definition through proximity—that is, by way of nearness. "Sopākhyam" means that which is accompanied by a definition.
