Even that which is specific, such as the experience of pleasure and so forth, is defined in a general sense—as "some kind of pleasure," "some kind of pain," and so on. Therefore, since existence is observed even for that which is indefinable, what was said is incorrect: namely, that "the non-existent is indefinable, while the existent is definable."

Therefore, since the non-existent exists in some respect and is indeed expressible, there is no difference between the existent and the non-existent; or rather, because the universal is expressible, just as the universal is expressible by its own nature through its own existence, and not by way of a particular or another universal—unlike a substance or other entity—it is observed that the existent is expressible while the non-existent is inexpressible. Thus, for you alone, there is no opposition between the existent and the non-existent in a single locus;
see page 491, line 6.
Let it be seen on page 491, line 6: "of which two [is there] the uncommon...
and "which object?"
It might be thought: we say that [the cognition] is direct, like the experience of one's own pleasure and so forth?
And yet, even in the case of being indefinable (*nirupākhyatā*), that [entity] is not non-existent, because it possesses the definability of a universal (*sāmānya-sopākhyatva*);
moreover, this has been stated by you as well...

...the connection with the qualifier must be postulated; yet it is not non-existent, because it lacks a defining characteristic (*nirupākhyatvāt*). Rather, it is both existent and non-existent, like a universal (*sāmānya*), because it possesses a defining characteristic and lacks one. Being both existent and non-existent, it is a universal like a universal;

it is existent in itself but not existent as a universal, unlike a real entity (*vastu*). Thus, the universal is existent yet non-existent; it is "possessing a defining characteristic" because it provides the basis for cognition and designation of both itself and others, and it is "lacking a defining characteristic" because it is like a real entity. Thus, that which possesses a defining characteristic is itself lacking one; there is a reversal in the case of a real entity.

Therefore, because it has been established as being both with designation (*sopākhya*) and without designation (*nirupākhya*), non-existence (*abhāva*)— like [the categories of] generality (*sāmānya*) and so forth, or substance (*dravya*) and so forth— is indeed both existent and non-existent;
such is the meaning of "proximity" (*pratyāsatti*).
The meaning is "proximate. [The text] beginning with "abhāvāt" is joined with "pra° dayuktam bhā° raṃ°."
See page 491, line 6:
"Is it with designation or without designation?"

Furthermore, regarding the passage beginning with "Moreover, by you as well," this is stated in order to demonstrate that "existent" and "non-existent" are merely your own conceptual constructs. This section has already been explained in its meaning up to the point where it says "the connection with qualifiers must be imagined"; however, it is introduced here specifically to demonstrate the point that even before the connection with qualifiers, that which is [claimed to be] non-existent is actually desired by you to be something that exists, albeit "devoid of description" (*nirupākhya*). Therefore, he says: "And yet, that is not non-existent because it is devoid of description. By this, a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is pointed out, since being "devoid of description" is observed in things that do exist.
In that state, it is non-existent because of the absence of its connection [to existence]; yet at a subsequent time, it possesses a designation (*sopākhya*) because of its connection with existence.

Having thus established the lack of contradiction between being designated and being non-designated, the Teacher states the proof for the lack of contradiction between the existence and non-existence of the effect under discussion: "But it is both existent and non-existent, because it possesses a designation and lacks a designation, like a universal (*sāmānya*)."

Alternatively, since both the named (*sopākhya*) and the nameless (*nirupākhya*) possess existence and non-existence, they are like a universal (*sāmānya*); thus, when the identity of existence and non-existence is to be proven, "being named and being nameless" is the reason (*hetu*), because you yourself have accepted—by the logic already stated—that existence and non-existence reside in that which is both named and nameless (p. 474, l. 2).
This is the intended meaning.
Is it imagined? Let it be seen that [this is] because of the existence of a relation (sambandhasattāt), page 485, line 18.

In this context, there may also be the reading "because of the absence of the existence of a relation" (atra sambandhasattābhāvāt). The term "nirupākhya" does not appear in the manuscripts *ya* and *pra*, while "nirūpyam" appears in manuscript *pra*.

He demonstrates that the universal (*sāmānya*) possesses the identity of being both existent and non-existent, with designation and without designation: "The universal is existent by its own existence (*svasat*); it is not existent as a thing (*vastu*) through the existence of a relation (*sambandhasattā*).

This means that, according to your own view, a thing called substance, quality, or action is held to be existent through its relation to the universal; however, the universal is not so [existent], because there is no relation of one universal to another universal. Thus, it is existent yet non-existent. As for what was said [previously] regarding the greater fault of the prior defect, [it is not so].
For example: "In that [case], indeed...

there is an absence of the restriction of cause, material, and action; but in this case, on the side of the effect being both existent and non-existent, the state of having two defects is more evil. This is not so, because the previous defect has been avoided by the universal (*sāmānya*), since the word *iti* has the sense of a reason; thus, the universal possesses the single nature of being both existent and non-existent.

And that very [existence] is "definable" (sopākhya) because it bestows cognition and designation upon itself and its correlates; for while existing, it imparts both cognition and designation to itself and to the entities related to it, such that one says, "Being exists," or "Substance, quality, and action exist"—thus it is a universal (sāmānya). Yet that same [existence] is also "undefinable" (nirupākhya), for it has no definition like a [particular] entity; just as with a particular entity, there is no definition for the universal and so forth through a further universal related to it, because there is no other universal belonging to a universal.
Thus, the "definable" is indeed the "undefinable. In this manner, according to the logic stated, there is no difference between being definable and being undefinable.

Regarding "error with respect to the entity": within the triad of entities beginning with substance (*dravya*), there is by its own nature a lack of designation (*nirupākhyatā*) as a universal, while there is a possession of designation (*sopākhyatā*); furthermore, its own inherent non-existence and its existence derived from another related factor are the opposites of *sattā* (Being).
What is this identity of essence and identity of referent?

As for what was said— that because it is more wicked than the previous fault, it is not [acceptable], for in that case there is an absence of the determination of cause, material, and action, whereas in this position of the effect being both existent and non-existent, there is a more wicked state of having two faults— that is not so, because the previous fault has been avoided.

For in that regard, since there would be the consequence of an absence of restriction regarding the material cause (*upādāna*) in the position that the effect is absolutely non-existent (*atyantāsat*), and an absence of activity (*kriyā*) in the position that the effect is absolutely existent (*atyantasat*), the intention appears to be that there is an absence of restriction regarding the cause, the material cause, and the activity in both the positions of the effect being existent and non-existent; thus [the author] composes the *Prakaraṇapañcikā*.
Is it self-existence and the absence of another related entity?
Or is it existence through another related entity and the absence of self-existence?
Or is it non-existence by itself and existence through another related entity?

Therefore, in the passage beginning with "established," the inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) between the property to be proven—which has reached the single extreme of existence or non-existence—and the reason-property—which has been rendered into the single extreme of being both with and without a designation, as illustrated by the explained examples—is here summarized.

Therefore, let Your Honor establish that those two properties are indeed distinct and contradictory, based on the very fact of being "denotable" (*sopākhya*) and "inexpressible" (*nirupākhya*), like the categories of generality (*sāmānya*) and the substances (*dravya*), etc. Here, "generality and so forth" refers to generality, particularity, and inherence; "substances and so forth" refers to substance, quality, and action. Just as these—generality and so forth, and substances and so forth—both exist and do not exist, and are both denotable and inexpressible, thus the state of being both denotable and inexpressible is the reason for their identity as both existent and non-existent. Furthermore, according to your own view, the state of being both existent and non-existent is likewise the reason for their identity as both denotable and inexpressible.
However, since you yourself have accepted the inclusion of substances and so forth as examples in the application (*upanaya*),
here too— in the case of the identity of existence and non-existence, and the identity of the expressible and the inexpressible— there is undoubtedly no counter-example (*avipakṣa*).
(Kāṣṭhī-prakaraṇa)
Now, wishing to refute the objections raised by others against the *syādvāda*, [the author] says: "As for what was stated," etc.

In the commentary on Praśastamati’s work, two faults were stated against the proponent of *syādvāda* regarding the statement "no," because those faults are even more grievous than the previous ones. Therein, with respect to the positions of the Sāṅkhya and Vaiśeṣika schools—which respectively maintain that the effect is existent (*sat*) or non-existent (*asat*)—there are, in due order, the faults of the impossibility of action (*kriyānupapatti*) and the absence of a restriction regarding the material cause (*upādānaniyamābhāva*).

As it has been said: "Because of the consequence that there would be an absence of action whether the material cause (*upādāna*) exists or does not exist, the Jaina who asserts that the effect is both existent and non-existent incurs a second fault; indeed, this is stated to be even more wicked than the previous fault" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra, Praśastamati’s Commentary). This is as follows: "In that case," and so forth. The passage demonstrating each individual fault according to their respective order is self-evident, up to the point where there is an absence of the restriction of causes, material causes, and action. Causes are the staff and so forth for a jar; the material cause is the clay; and the action is the activity of the potter.

Furthermore, regarding this position that the effect is both existent and non-existent (*sadasat-kāryapakṣa*), there is a more grievous twofold fault than the single faults of the positions of existence and non-existence respectively: because of its existence, there would be an absence of activity for the sake of the jar; because of its non-existence, there would be an absence of restriction regarding the material cause. Due to these two faults, this position is more grievous. To this, the Teacher says: "That is not so, because the previous faults have been avoided. In this position where the effect is of a dual nature—both existent and non-existent—the previously mentioned faults of the absence of activity and the absence of restriction regarding the material cause have been avoided. Thus, the fault is complete [in the opponent's view]. (Note: *pūrṇadoṣa* is corrected from *pra.* based on context).
Is this presentation in the ablative case [intended to mean] "due to the absence of giving"?

For in that regard, what contradiction would there be for action in the view that the effect pre-exists (*satkāryapakṣa*)? Since the Sāṅkhya asserts that this jar is absolutely existent, action is not possible for that which is already accomplished, because there is nothing further to be done—just as with what has already been made. Thus, the fault of the absence of action arises for him, but not for the proponent of the doctrine of manifoldness (*syādvādin*).

If, however, that [injunction] were to prescribe even the duty to act by means of an initial [impulse], then who could speak against it in such a way? Even in the view that the effect is non-existent (*asatkāryapakṣa*), why would the restriction regarding the material cause (*upādānaniyama*) be contradicted? If one were to speak with contempt toward an object that—though existing within the causes and materials—is manifested through action, because that object is absolutely non-existent; for such a person, there would be no restriction on taking threads as the material cause when there is a desire for a cloth.

The opponent himself causes [the objection] to be voiced by means of a preliminary question: "In that case, regarding the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*), with what reason is action contradicted? The Sāṅkhya replies: "Because it is absolutely so," and so on, up to "as if it were already made.
For, from the perspective of substance (*dravyārtha*), the jar exists in the lump of clay, but not from the perspective of mode (*paryāya*).

The Sāṅkhya, however, asserts that the pot is already existent even prior to its state as an effect; therefore, for him, action and the instrument of action are not tenable for that which is already accomplished and exists in every respect, because there is nothing further to be done, just like a pot already produced. Thus, this proponent of *satkāryavāda* (the doctrine that the effect pre-exists) falls into the fault of the absence of action. This, however, does not apply to the Syādvādin (proponent of the doctrine of manifoldness), who maintains the substance-aspect (*dravyārthika-naya*) wherein the required state of being to-be-done is acknowledged. For one who says, "The pot is indeed existent in the lump of clay, though it is non-existent in a certain respect," the aforementioned fault of the extremist *satkāryavāda* is avoided.

If, however, that Sāṅkhya were also to employ a qualification expressing non-absolutism (anekānta)—such as "in some way" or "from some cause"—stating that "the effect is existent in some respect," just like the Syādvādin, then who could say this of him? What proponent, even one who has carefully examined the merits and defects of speech, would be able to say of another proponent—whether that other proponent be the Sāṅkhya who has avoided the aforementioned defect by accepting non-absolutism, or anyone else—that "the defect of the absence of action applies to you because of the absence of 'that which is to be done' (kartavyatva)," as if he were a mere agent?
Who would thus address or cause another to address [him]?
From a different perspective, [the views of] those who maintain that the effect exists [in the cause] (satkāryavādins) [are as follows]: Bhāṣya-satkāryavādins; Yaśas-satkāryavādins.

In this context, the reading "satkāryaikāntavādinaḥ" (proponents of the absolute doctrine that the effect pre-exists in the cause) also appears correct; [this applies] even to the Sāṃkhya, who are proponents of that [doctrine]. Regarding the [variant] "vācinaḥ," [it is found in] Ya; [and] "tasau" [is found in] Pra.

"Even in the view that the effect is non-existent (*asatkāryapakṣa*)," and so forth; he introduces the inquiry as before, asking: "Does this fault—the absence of a restriction regarding the material cause (*upādānaniyamābhāva*)—which was stated against the Vaiśeṣika who maintains the theory of the non-existent effect (*asatkāryavādin*), constitute a contradiction? Thus he speaks.

Regarding the passage beginning with "When he [asserts] exclusively," etc.: when that Vaiśeṣika, relying on the perspective of the modal aspect (*paryāyārtha*), asserts that the effect is non-existent because of the absence of activity, qualities, and designations, and thus speaks with contempt—disregarding—that cloth-named object which is present yet unmanifest within its causes such as the shuttle and the loom, and within its material causes such as the threads, and which is to be manifested by activity; for him, the restriction to the threads as the material cause when there is a desire for cloth is not tenable, because it is non-existent therein, just like grass and the like. Just as taking grass and such as a material cause is not appropriate when there is a desire for cloth because it is non-existent therein, so too is the case with taking threads as a material cause. Thus, even in the doctrine of the absolute non-existence of the effect (*asatkāryaikāntavāda*), there is the fault of the absence of a restriction regarding the material cause. This fault does not exist in the doctrine of non-absolutism (*anekāntavāda*) characterized by the "syāt" formula and the like, for one who asserts that "the effect may be non-existent," thereby allowing room for its existence.

Likewise, if even a Vaiśeṣika were to state the qualified [object], who could say anything against him? For that proponent, whose established position consists of a qualified subject and its properties characterized by positive and negative concomitance, there would not be even a hundredth part of a sesame husk remaining to be said.
And it has been said: [Yuktidīpikā 1.46]...

The intention [of the objection] is: "How is this restriction regarding the material cause (*upādāna*) contradicted?"— [this is stated] so as not to disregard the cloth that is to be manifested (*vyaṅgya*).

Even in the case of a [logical] debate (*vāda*), what is the means (*upāya*)? When the opponent turns back from the verbal expression (*vacanīya*) presented as the object of the reason (*hetu-viṣaya*).
If trade were as [the merchants] give it to others, who would live? (Sanmati-tarka-prakaraṇa 3.58).
Even while giving, [they do not give] enough.
In the *Sanmatiprakaraṇa* (as found in the Jitanta edition), the reading is *jivvaṃto*.

Demonstrating that the very thing which is accepted as the object of inference (*sādhya*)—wherein there is no room for the opponent who offers refutations—is precisely what must be accepted as the object of the reason (*hetu*), he says: "Just as the opponent turns back [the argument] regarding the verbal expression (*vayaṇijja*) brought forward as the object of the reason."
If he were giving it away in that manner beforehand, by whom could he be defeated?

The object characterized as the subject of the probandum (*sādhyadharmin*), which has been brought forward and presented by the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*) as "sound is impermanent," is refuted by the opponent, the proponent of the critique (*dūṣaṇavādin*), through the adducing of faults such as proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*) or lack of concomitance (*ananugama*). This is because that which is stated categorically and is not accompanied by other properties can be refuted due to being vitiated by numerous defects; for if it were to be pervaded by a second property, the aforementioned proponent of the prima facie view would have demonstrated it through the application of the term "sound," and thus he would not have been defeated by anyone at all.

Furthermore, because he fails to demonstrate the subject (*sādhyadharmin*) as it actually exists, and because that which is demonstrated is of an exclusively [one-sided] nature and thus non-existent, he—being a proponent of that [position]—is worthy of defeat due to his untruthfulness;
so it is stated in the *Sanmativṛtti* composed by Abhayadevasūri, written at Jesalmer, page 226:

"In that case, since it is non-existent, like grass and such, there is the fault of the absence of a restrictive rule regarding the material cause (*upādānaniyamābhāva*), but not for the advocate of *syādvāda*."
Likewise, if even a Vaiśeṣika were to state the qualified object (*viśeṣya*), who could say anything against him? Thus, this initial apprehension is for the sake of establishing priority;

however, as for what is further asserted—that the restriction of the appropriation of the existent portion and the activity of the non-existent portion are logical, and that both indeed exist in the entity—this is not so, because it would entail the opposite consequence.
Since there is no specific reason for a single entity to possess a dual nature, how can this be?
"...the former fault is indeed more grievous"—
this too is nothing, precisely because it is an effect.
Regarding the effect, both the material cause (*upādāna*) and the action (*kriyā*) are restricted to their own respective objects; they are indeed existent entities.

Why is this so? Because there is a restriction of the material cause to that which possesses an existent portion (*sadbhāga*), and the action belongs to that which possesses a non-existent portion (*asadbhāga*), rather than both being non-existent. Therefore, the intention here appears to be that [the opponent's view] is merely more grievous than the previously mentioned fault.

Therefore, for the proponent of *syādvāda*, those two previous faults do not exist; how then could there be a state of being worse? Or rather, it is precisely better than them. To this he says: "In this way, this [statement] has the sense of being better than the former. The state of being better than the two previous doctrines is "being better than the former" (*pūrvaśreyastvam*); that itself is the meaning of this initial proposition (*udgrāha*). Thus, this first proposition—the statement of the thesis—has the sense of being better than the former, and it leaves no room for the mention of faults. In that first proposition, the declaration of the thesis, I have already shown: "The effect may exist; the effect may not exist."
Furthermore, this was not understood by you either due to attachment to your own side or due to aversion toward us. [Therefore] explain it.

As for the passage beginning with "But this... and so forth, it is the opponent's prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), up to the point where it is shown that the previous fault is indeed even more grievous.

The Jaina, who maintains the doctrine of both existent and non-existent effects (*sadasatkāryavāda*), has offered this rebuttal regarding the gravity of the aforementioned fault: "There is a restriction of the material cause for the existent portion; because the jar exists in the clay, there is a restriction that the jar must have clay as its material cause. Furthermore, action is possible for that non-existent portion of the jar, based on either one of the two parts—the existent or the non-existent. And these two parts certainly exist within the entity. Anticipating this Jaina rebuttal with the words "If you think thus," he states the following response: "And this is not so, because it leads to the opposite consequence (*viparyayaprasaṅga*). The 'opposite consequence' consists in the consequence of action being based on the existent portion, and the consequence of the restriction of the material cause being based on the non-existent portion. These two are undesirable for the Jaina. Since a single entity cannot possess both natures without a specific reason, there would be an absence of the restriction of the material cause in the case of the existent, and an absence of action in the case of the non-existent. Thus, because these two reasons—each excluded from the other part—are absent, they lack the property of the subject (*apakṣadharmatā*)."

For how could a single entity be both real and unreal? Regarding that which possesses this dual nature, the application of the consequence of the opposite [view]—beginning with "whence is this? and so forth—is already explained; for there is no specific reason [to favor one over the other], and there is no fixed rule regarding cause and what is to be abandoned, since that very portion which is non-existent cannot possibly exist without the Ārhata system.
The reading enclosed within these brackets does not exist in the Ya manuscripts;
see page 495, line 20.
The entity is real (sadbhāva).
In this context, there may also be a reading stating that "the entity is both existent and non-existent";
see page 138, note 9.
Regarding this, the Teacher says: "This too is nothing at all," meaning that even the slightest scent of a valid response is absent.

Why? Precisely because it is an effect (*kārya*). For that which is produced is called an effect. In that effect, both the material cause (*upādāna*) and the action (*kriyā*) have existence (*bhāva*) as their respective objects (*svaviṣaya*), not non-existence (*abhāva*). "One's own object" means one's own specific domain. The restriction of the material cause applies only to what exists, because its restriction is fixed upon that; therefore, existence is its object. On the other hand, the object of the action is precisely what does not exist, because its nature consists of fear (or destruction). This is like the relationship of father and son, which is restricted to a single person;
for it is not [possible] for one [person alone...]
...but not the absence of both; thus...
Moreover, even if the consequence of the opposite [view] were to follow, it would still result in precisely this kind of state of affairs:

by relying on the aspect of non-existence (*asadbhāga*), there would be an absence of restriction regarding appropriation (*upādāna*), because the nature of existence, substance, and so forth is obtained through the generality of being without appropriation;

and by relying on the aspect of existence (*sadbhāga*), there would be an absence of action (*kriyā*) for everything, because everything would have the nature of everything due to such being the case, since that which is absolutely non-existent does not exist at all.
As for what is said— "Because of the difference in nature between the existent and the non-existent, there is neither existence nor non-existence in the effect" (VS 9.1.12)—
it follows from the fixed meanings of the words "existent" and "non-existent" that non-existence is the object, as previously stated.

And how is it known that these two activities of appropriation (*upādāna*) are restricted to their respective objects? Because a single thing possesses a dual nature; for I have accepted, and you [have also accepted] with the intent of pointing out a fault, that a single effect consists of both existence and non-existence. Therefore, because a single thing has a dual nature—since whatever is a single thing possessing a dual nature is observed to be restricted to its own object, like the relationship of father and son which is restricted to a single person—the explanation of the example beginning with "not of one" continues until "but not the absence of both."

The passage beginning with "evam" (thus) and so forth is an explanation of the illustrative example (*dārṣṭāntika*). It demonstrates the commonality of the absence of lack of restriction (*aniyamābhāva*) and demonstrates the absence of defects.
Furthermore, the specific reason (*viśeṣahetu*) is precisely the unity of both; because that [unity] is restricted to its own object, there is no possibility of the opposite consequence.
Therefore, it is indeed superior to the two preceding [cases].
Because it consists of fear, just as the relationship of father and son is restricted to a single person;
for it does not belong to one [alone]...
...but not the absence of both; thus...
Moreover, even if the consequence of the opposite were to follow, it would still result in this very same state of affairs:

by relying on the aspect of non-existence (*asadbhāga*), there would simply be an absence of restriction regarding appropriation (*upādāna*), because the nature of existence, substance, and so forth is obtained through the generality of being an entity that lacks appropriation;

and by relying on the aspect of existence (*sadbhāga*), there would simply be an absence of activity, because everything would consist of everything due to such a state of being, since that which is absolutely non-existent does not exist at all.

For there is no lack of a fixed rule regarding the status of father and son for a single person; relative to his own son he is a father, and relative to his own father he is a son, yet this does not entail the absence of both roles simultaneously.

Likewise here, because a single entity possesses both natures, and because the acts of taking up (upādāna) and acting (kriyā) are restricted to their own respective objects, there is no contingency of contradiction—this is the intended meaning that appears here.
As for what is said— "Because of the difference in nature between the existent and the non-existent, there is neither existence nor non-existence in the effect" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 9.1.12)—
this concerns the meanings of the words "existent" and "non-existent."

Furthermore, even if one were to admit the consequence of the opposite [view], such a consequence would still result in precisely this kind of meaning, because non-absolutism (*anekānta*) is established; thus, there is not even a trace of fault. For, with respect to that aspect of non-existence which constitutes the modal-reality (*paryāyārtha*) of an entity that is by nature both existent and non-existent—such as the absence of a jar in clay—why would there be no restriction regarding its material cause (*upādāna*)? This is because the nature of the existent substance and so forth is obtained through the universal (*sāmānya*) of existence and other properties, even when they are not currently functioning as material causes.

Prior to its production, the effect is non-existent; it arises upon the proximity of the inherent (samavāyi) and non-inherent (asamavāyi) causes. It has no purpose whatsoever with respect to its material cause (upādāna). Once produced, that which is called substance, quality, or action becomes connected with existence (sattā)—that is, as a substance through the universal "substanceness," as a quality through "qualitiness," and as an action through "actionness. Since its own nature is thus obtained through these entities known as universals, there is no fixed necessity for the effect to depend on a material cause; thus, the doctrine of non-absolutism (anekānta) is established.

Furthermore, based on the true nature [of reality], there is indeed an absence of action. For one who desires the very existence of an effect, such as a jar, from the perspective of substantial reality (*dravyārtha*), there is no purpose whatsoever for action; thus, action does not exist at all.

Why is this so? Because, according to that proponent, everything consists of everything else; for a lump of clay possesses the nature of all dharmas, both those that occur simultaneously and those that occur sequentially.

In that manner—that is, by way of the substantialist standpoint (*dravyārthavāda*)—suchness (*tathātva*) consists in the state of being thus (*tathābhāva*), which is the fact that everything has everything as its essence. Because of that suchness, there is nothing whatsoever called "non-existent. Therefore, since the absolutely non-existent does not exist, when one intends to express a particular standpoint (*naya*), one relies on one [aspect] because the other is absent; for here, the object itself is not [established] by means of a specific cause, and so forth. That [object] exists as the nature of the existent (*sadātman*).
And that [state] of the ten-fold self is the obtainable essential nature of the vessel; thus reads the manuscript (ya),
while the manuscripts (pā, raṃ, vi) read "the obtainable essential nature of the vessel."

1.12—This too is nothing [new]: for within each single object, which is of the nature of reality (*tattva*), the world consists of both mutually existent and non-existent realities. When one contemplates the substantial aspect (*dravyārtha*) as undivided from the modal aspects (*paryāyārtha*)—namely, their occurrence and non-occurrence—is it not the case that even what is existent is non-existent within its own self, which must be brought into being through the mutual dependence of both?
And so...

as for what was also said—that existence and non-existence are relative; that before its production, the effect exists in the form of clay but does not exist in the form of a jar; that even when the jar is produced, because the nature of clay is observed, clay is established as the material cause (*upādāna*); and that because it does not exist in the form of a jar, its functional efficacy (*arthakriyā*) as a jar is established—this is indeed what the Jaina says.

To this, the reply is: No, because the non-existence of the effect (*asatkāryatva*) is thereby established. For, in that case, since there is nothing to be produced in the form of clay, while there is something to be produced in the form of a jar, the effect is simply non-existent [prior to production].
Therefore, according to the *Vaiśeṣika Sūtra* and the *Kaṭaṇḍī*, the effect is neither existent nor non-existent prior to its production.

Regarding this [sūtra], what is meant by the phrase "because of the difference in nature between the existent and the non-existent"? It means that because they are mutually contradictory, it is impossible for the same thing to be both existent and non-existent prior to production through the relation of coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇabhāva*). Since there is a contradiction between the referents of the words "existent" and "non-existent," how could existence belong to the very same effect prior to production? What then? It is simply non-existence. Thus, there is no usage of the words "existent" and "non-existent" with reference to a single substratum.

He explains this: there is no synthesis [of the ideas] that "the existent is the non-existent" because they do not exist as having a single substratum; since that is absent, the application [of such a statement] is untenable.

This meaning is shown by the use of the locative case in the phrase "in the effect, there is neither existence nor non-existence. Otherwise, for the sake of brevity, he would have said "the effect is both existent and non-existent.
This point remains as it was stated earlier, up until the passage beginning with "this too is nothing," and so on, within its own context.

In each and every object, such as a jar or a cloth, within its own essential nature, the world consists of the reality of both the existent and the non-existent in relation to one another: the jar exists in the form of a jar, but does not exist in the form of a cloth; and the cloth likewise exists in its own form but does not exist in the form of the other. Thus, existence and non-existence are relative to their own respective natures. Therefore, he demonstrates the pervasiveness [of this principle] by stating that the world is the reality of both the existent and the non-existent—not only the effect (kārya) alone that is both being and non-being.

Likewise, the substance-aspect (*dravyārtha*) is one and undivided by means of the two successive states—existence and non-existence—which correspond respectively to the stages of the lump (*piṇḍa*) and the figurine (*śivaka*). The cultivation of this [aspect] is as follows: "The clay-lump itself becomes the figurine; the figurine itself becomes the bowl," and so on, until the jar, and even down to the dust and the atom. In these various states, [the substance] exists as the lump but does not exist as the figurine and so forth; thus the lump consists of both existence and non-existence. Similarly, the figurine exists as the figurine but does not exist as the lump, and likewise in all subsequent states. By way of its own positive nature and by way of the mutual non-existence of the other, it is both existent and non-existent; for existence is non-existence. (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 9)

Because of this statement, in the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) of the substance-aspect (*dravyārtha*) which is undivided from the mode-aspect (*paryāyārtha*) regarding the occurrence and non-occurrence of the entire world, that which is existent is indeed non-existent.

"Is it both? and so forth. Furthermore, with respect to what entity (*vastu*) its own nature (*svātman*) is to be conceived—whether that entity consists of successive states (*paryāya*) occurring simultaneously, such as form, taste, and so on, or those occurring non-simultaneously, such as a *śivaka* (a small clay model) and so on—is it then to be conceived as "existent" and also "non-existent"? The meaning is that, without any doubt, it is both existent and non-existent at that time.

He concludes this with "And thus" (*tathā ca*), the sense of which has already been explained; he demonstrates this by means of the sevenfold predication (*saptabhaṅgī*). *Pra.* [refers to the *Prasannapadā*].

*Kaṭandī* is the name of a certain ancient commentary on the *Vaiśeṣika-sūtras* composed by Kaṇāda. "Ho there, Lakṣmaṇa! I am wandering about, conquering the world as a scholar of the *Vaiśeṣika-kaṭandī*.
Where is that Rāma? I wish to debate with him."

Thus, in the fifth act of the *Anargharāghava* Nāṭaka composed by the poet Murāri, regarding Rāvaṇa’s speech: there is no employment of the words "existent" (*sat*) and "non-existent" (*asat*) with reference to a single object through a relation of coreferentiality (*ekādhikaraṇabhāva*); nor is there the conceptual synthesis "the existent itself is non-existent" through a relation of coreferentiality. This is demonstrated by the mention of the locative case in the *Vaiyākaraṇasūtravṛtti Kaṭaṇḍī*, 9.1.

12—This too is nothing; for within each individual object, which is of the nature of reality (*tattva*), the world consists of both mutually existent and non-existent realities. And thus...

As for what was said—that existence and non-existence are relative, that prior to its production the effect exists in the form of clay but does not exist in the form of a jar, that the clay is established as the material cause because clay is seen even when the jar is finished, and that the purposeful activity of the jar is possible because it is non-existent in the form of a jar—this is indeed what the Jaina says.

To this, the answer is: No, because the non-existence of the effect is thereby established. If that is so, then since there is nothing to be produced in the form of clay and something to be produced in the form of a jar, the effect is simply non-existent; therefore, prior to its production, the effect is neither existent nor non-existent. (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra Kaṭandī).

As for what was stated beginning with "it is relative," etc., this is the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*): the proponent of the theory of manifoldness (*syādvādī*) indeed establishes existence and non-existence in this way—namely, that the jar exists prior to its production in the form of clay, because even after its completion, it is seen to be clay; and since it has that as its essence, the clay is logically established as its material cause (*upādāna*).

Regarding the argument that the causal efficiency of a jar is possible because it is non-existent in the form of a jar, the author of the *Kaṭandī* indeed offers this rebuttal: "No; since the theory of the non-existence of the effect (*asatkāryavāda*) has been established, the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is not a valid rejoinder (*uttarapakṣa*). For what proponent of non-absolutism (*anekāntavādin*) would even say: 'The effect exists in the form of clay prior to its production, but does not exist in the form of a jar'? For if that were the case, clay itself would be a non-product..."
What is the difference? By the mere utterance of the preceding word expressing "arising after having not existed," there is an explicit admission of absolute non-existence.

One who asserts that [the jar] exists by means of another nature, such as that of clay, but does not exist by its own nature as a jar, would be like a drunkard or a madman, contradicting perception and other means of valid cognition.
Since this consists merely of two modes characterized by differences of space and time, it would be nothing but a doctrine of non-existence (*asadvāda*).

"In that case, then," and so forth, is the explanation: because the clay-nature itself cannot be something to be produced (*kārya*), for it is that which "is being made" (*kriyate*) which is called an effect (*kārya*). Now, the clay is not what is being made; rather, it is the jar that is being made, and that [jar] is non-existent [prior to production]. Thus he brings forward this [conclusion]: "Therefore, prior to its origination, the effect is neither existent nor non-existent."

The prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is not the correct conclusion (*siddhānta*), for who indeed among those who profess non-absolutism (*anekāntavādin*) would say: "Before its production, the effect exists in the form of clay but does not exist in the form of a jar"? For if the clay were not the cause [of the jar], what difference would there be? By merely uttering the word "prior" (*prāk*), which denotes arising after having not existed, one directly accepts the absolute non-existence [of the effect];

yet to say that it exists in another form—that of clay—and does not exist in its own form—that of a jar—is to speak in contradiction to perception and other means of knowledge, like one who is intoxicated or insane.
Since this [position] consists merely of two aspects characterized by the distinction of place and time, it would indeed be a false doctrine (*asadvāda*).

For in this way, if clay were not a product, what difference would there be from the Vaiśeṣika or the Buddhist, given the abandonment of the non-absolutist view (*anekāntavāda*) and the acceptance of an absolutist view (*ekāntavāda*)?
This appears to be the intended meaning.

And so forth.

He demonstrates that if one were to say it, there would be an abandonment of non-absolutism and an acceptance of absolutism: "For in this way, if the clay were not the cause of the effect," and so forth; the meaning has already been explained up to "what is the difference?"—for he would be either a Vaiśeṣika or a Buddhist, or even a Jaina.

for the word *prāk* (prior) indeed expresses the meaning of having arisen after not having existed, because it denotes the state prior to the state of the jar.

Furthermore, this [position] does not even equal that of an extremist (ekāntavādin) who speaks without any critical reflection; for if one were to say that a jar is absolutely different from the nature of the clay that is other than the jar, yet is not different from its own nature as a jar, such a person—speaking in contradiction to perception and other means of valid cognition—would be like one intoxicated or insane. Moreover, even that extremist avoids certain things that contradict perception and the rest.
Furthermore, [the verse says] "space, time," and so forth.

There is a distinction of form-color (*rūpa*) and taste (*rasa*) etc. by way of space (*deśataḥ*); there is a distinction of a lump (*piṇḍa*), a small ball (*śivaka*), and so forth, by way of time (*kālataḥ*). That distinction is the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of these two types of modalities (*paryāya*)—those that exist together and those that do not. These are the modalities characterized by spatial and temporal distinctions. Their measure is merely the modalities characterized by spatial and temporal distinctions. Because of that state, because it is merely that, in this manner, this would be a doctrine of non-existence (*asadvāda*) alone: "Form is other than taste"; and that [form], when further divided, is black; and again, it is a single-fold blackness, and so on, until through division down to the level of atoms, form is simply non-existent. The same applies to taste and the rest, as well as to the lump and so forth. In this way, who could be a proponent of non-absolutism (*anekāntavādin*) who would speak thus, like a proponent of non-existence, regarding the relative existence of the nature of clay?

However, because it is qualified by the attribute of "existence" which is relatively mild, this [statement] is indeed a designation of non-existence, since it is necessarily fixed on the negation of the thing’s own true nature, like the designation of fire as "not hot. But if that [negation] were not excluded, then it would exist even as a pot, because it possesses that very state;

therefore, in order to directly perceive the reality of an entity as being both existent and non-existent, the Jains describe the one ultimate Self as having the dual characteristic of substantiality (*dravyārtha*) and modal transformation (*paryāyārtha*), for otherwise it would be impossible, like a sky-flower.

And as for the claim that even the word "substance" (dravya) is a doctrine of non-existence (asadvāda), how could a proponent of non-absolutism (anekāntavādī) speak in the same manner as this proponent of non-existence—who asserts that "form does not exist in the nature of taste, taste does not exist in the nature of form, and blackness, etc., do not exist in the nature of whiteness, etc."? He would certainly not say such a thing. Why? Because clay and the like, as well as jars and the like, consist of earth and the other elements characterized by supporting, cohesion, maturation, expansion, and providing space; therefore, who among the wise would, like the proponent of non-existence, assert the relative existence of the nature of clay by saying that "clay exists only in its own nature" with reference to a single instance of clay? This is how the passage is to be connected.

The formal argument here is as follows: because it is qualified by "existence" whose nature is relative to clay, this expression "non-existent" is indeed a designation for that which exists in its nature as clay but does not exist in its nature as a jar; thus, the statement is: "it exists as clay, but it is non-existent as a jar."

Why? Because this statement is necessarily restricted to the negation of the very nature (*svatattva*) of the denoted object. The "own nature" of the denoted object—the lump of clay—consists of spatial distinctions such as different forms, tastes, and configurations; temporal distinctions such as the form, taste, and stages like the *śivaka* (the initial stage of the pot) or the dust-particles; and elemental distinctions such as earth characterized by solidity and so forth. Since the pot exists only as the essence of clay and not through its own natures as form, taste, the *śivaka*, water, and so on, those very natures of its must be negated. This is because this sentence is necessarily restricted to that negation.

Whatever statement is invariably intent upon negating the essential nature of its own subject is observed to be an expression of what is non-existent; for instance, the utterance "fire is not hot. Do not think that the negation of the essential nature of the subject is unestablished; it is indeed established, because it excludes [the subject] from being of the nature of a non-contradictory entity, due to the difference in its defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇabheda*). (Sahābhāṣya-pāda-deśa)
The difference in characteristics is simultaneous;
that which possesses the state of being that [is] like that state of being.

it appears that the prefix *āṅ* is used in the sense of inclusion (*abhividhi*); therefore, the meaning is "as far as [the division] down to the level of atoms."

In this context, there might also be a reading such as "ā para" following "ā mityādi. However, how could a proponent of non-absolutism (anekāntavādī) speak in this manner? [He would say: "The existence of the nature of clay is relative, like that of a non-existent thing.

But if there were no exclusion [of the one from the other], then even by way of its nature as a jar, it would exist precisely because it possesses that state; therefore,

for the sake of directly perceiving the reality of an entity that consists of both existence and non-existence, the Jains describe the single ultimate self as having the dual characteristic of substance-aspect (dravyārtha) and mode-aspect (paryāyārtha), since otherwise it would be impossible— just like a sky-flower—
and they employ the term "substance" (dravya).
