[The opponent] might think: "We do not say that it exists only as the nature of clay and not as anything else; what then? If the jar exists as the nature of clay, let it also exist as the nature of form, mass, potsherd, water-jar, and so forth—since it possesses those natures, what is the harm?"

To this we reply: If it is not excluded, then even as a jar, it exists precisely because it possesses that nature (*tadbhāvatvāt*). Those entities—such as the *śivaka* (the first stage of the clay lump), the *ābā* (the second stage), the rice-grains, and so forth, as well as the jars and the like—are the manifestations of this clay; "possessing that nature" means having the state of being that [clay]. Therefore, because it possesses that nature, the effect exists even prior to its production as a jar, since it has that identity—that is, the identity of a jar. Furthermore, by the word "also" (*api*), it exists even as the *śivaka*, the dog, the rice-grains, and so forth, because it is the self-nature of all things.
Thus, one who speaks in this way does not merely avoid stating that the effect is non-existent; rather, he has indeed stated that the effect is existent (*satkāryavāda*).

Therefore, the proponents of non-absolutism (syādvādins) do not speak in this manner— disregarding what precedes and follows like the proponents of absolutism (ekāntavādins)— just as [one does not speak] regarding a lump of clay, a small pot, or a large jar.
If it is asked, "How then do they say [this]?"— to this he replies: "Consisting of both being and non-being," and so forth.

In order to directly realize the fact that the reality of an entity consists of two natures, the Jains, who uphold the doctrine of *syādvāda*, describe the single ultimate self as possessing the characteristics of both [existence and non-existence]. This is because it has been established that such an entity exists; otherwise, it would be impossible—like a sky-flower—due to the absence of a single identity consisting of both forms. For if there were only a single form, whether of the nature of substance (*dravyārtha*) or of the nature of modification (*paryāyārtha*), it would be devoid of differentiation. Consequently, being seedless, it would result in non-existence like a sky-flower. Therefore, the self of an entity is indeed of the nature of both existence and non-existence.

Explanation of the term *dravya* (substance): It continues that they describe the word *dravya* as having the meaning of identity and difference regarding the past, future, and present states of clay and so forth, as well as form and so forth. For instance, from clay there arise sequentially the lump, the pot-sherd, and so on; and simultaneously, there exist distinct qualities such as color, taste, and the like. Among these three—the clay and so forth, the form and so forth, and the distinctions of past, future, and present—the term *paryāya* (mode) refers to the meaning of both universal non-difference and particular difference. Thus, the self-nature of clay is the substance-aspect (*dravyārtha*) and the mode-aspect (*paryāyārtha*), while the self-nature of the jar is likewise the substance-aspect and the mode-aspect;
for indeed, it is the *dravya*.
...the substance-aspect jar is absolutely existent, whereas the mode-aspect is...
non-existent.
And from where does this [conclusion] come that there is only the perception of clay, and not, as in the case of support (*dhṛti*) and so forth, the perception of cohesion (*saṅgraha*) and so forth?

And why is it "indescribable"? From what [reason] do you derive this: that because the effect is non-existent in the form of a jar, it is only non-existent; whereas, on the contrary, because the jar exists within the reality of the clay, its existence is indeed attained through the sequence of experience, just like the existence of the jar's own novelty (*pratyag-ādi*)? Furthermore, as for what is said—"No, because the theory of the non-existence of the effect (*asatkāryatva*) is established"—[that is incorrect].

In that case, since the clay-nature has no need to be produced, the clay and so forth existing at the time of the jar, as well as qualities such as redness and shapes such as globularity that have already occurred, are both distinct and non-distinct from it because they do not transcend their own material form (*mūrti*). Thus, they describe the word "substance" (*dravya*) as having the meaning of both difference and non-difference, and the word "mode" (*paryāya*) as having the meaning of both total non-difference and difference; they describe "universal" (*jāti*) as that which differentiates among those very things existing in all three times and those existing in the present time.
Therefore, both terms possess the meaning of both.

The dual nature [of the object] does not arise merely from the verbal description of its meaning; rather, the essential nature of the thing itself is also determined. For example, it is connected as follows: "They describe the essence of the clay as consisting of both substantial and modal aspects," and likewise, "the essence of the jar as consisting of both substantial and modal aspects."

The explanation of these two follows their respective order: "Substance indeed," and so forth, regarding the substantial standpoint (*dravyārtha*), up to "the pot as a substance is absolutely existent. This has already been explained previously—that the prior and subsequent states of the pot itself become clay and so forth, or rice seeds and so forth, and roots and so forth. Regarding the modal standpoint (*paryāyārtha*), "But the mode," and so forth, up to "it is non-existent"; this is understood by the reverse of the former case.
And just as the essence of the pot is also clay, so too is a real entity (*vastu*) [constituted] by both the substantial and modal standpoints. (Bhāṣya)
In reality, what is it?

It is the substance (*dravya*)—the essence of clay—which, for the sake of expressing the distinctions and non-distinctions of the past, future, and present forms such as color and so forth, employs synonymous terms; and which, for the sake of expressing all non-distinction and distinction, constitutes both the self-nature of the clay and the self-nature of the jar, in terms of both substantial aspect (*dravyārtha*) and modal aspect (*paryāyārtha*).
...the substance-aspect of the jar is absolutely existent, whereas its mode-aspect is...
non-existent.
Moreover, from where does this [conclusion] come that there is only the perception of clay, and not the perception of cohesion and so forth as in the case of support and the rest?

And why is it "indescribable"? Why is it said that the effect is non-existent because it is non-existent in the form of a jar? Is it not rather the case that, because the reality of the clay exists within the jar, the reality of the jar is indeed attained through the sequence of experience—just as the jar's existence is like its own immediate manifestation (*pratyagrāditva*)?

And as for what is further said—"No, because the theory that the effect is non-existent [in the cause] is established"—if that were so, then since the nature of the clay would not be something to be produced, let the jar be seen [as such]. (p. 499, l. 7)
Regarding those very three, even the manifestation of their own nature at the three times— this too, from where does it arise? And so forth.

As for what is said—that because the nature of clay is observed even when a jar has been produced, clay is the material cause (*upādāna*)—how can this be a definitive conclusion based on the observation of a specific type of earth-nature? For [the jar] consists of earth characterized by the properties of support (*dhṛti*) and so forth, through the exclusion of water, fire, air, and space, which possess the properties of cohesion (*saṅgraha*), maturation (*pakti*), expansion (*vyūha*), and providing space (*avakāśadāna*). He demonstrates this: "But there is no observation of cohesion and so forth as there is of support and so forth," and so on, up to "all the properties existing in that object are observable, yet it remains inexpressible."

Therefore, it is not the case that there is perception of the clay alone in both ways— namely, either the perception of the nature of clay in the clay, or the perception of the nature of clay in the jar (see page 499,
line 6).
Furthermore, as for what is said— that because [the jar] does not exist in the form of a jar, action is possible— it is indeed the Jaina who says this.

To the question "Why is this so? and so forth, he does not reply in this manner—that the effect is non-existent because it does not exist as the nature of a jar; rather, he says that the jar exists, because the essence of the clay exists as the jar.

He demonstrates this: "Because it does not exist as the nature of the jar—how can this be so? Is it not rather because of the existence of the jar within the essence of clay? Furthermore, that existence of the jar is attained through the sequence of experience precisely within the essence of clay; the experience of the successive states (*paryāya*) of the jar, which arise in succession, is attained gradually within the reality (*tattva*)—the substance (*dravya*) existing in its own established form called "clay"—just like its states of being new, slightly used, middle-aged, old, and so forth. Just as these conditions of the jar belong to that very jar established in the essence of the jar, in the same way, the existence of the jar is attained through the sequence of experience precisely within the essence of clay.
Therefore, due to a failure to understand the statement of the Arhat, what has been said is incorrect;
see *Ātmakriyā*, page 499, line 6.

Furthermore, the passage beginning with "yadapi ca" and so forth is stated with the intention of providing a response to this prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*): "No, because the non-existence of the effect (*asatkāryatva*) is established," since the effect is indeed non-existent because it is something yet to be produced by the self (*ātman*).

"Therefore, prior to its production, the effect is neither existent nor non-existent"— this [view] from the *Vaiśeṣika-sūtra* commentary *Kaṭaṇḍī* is also not correct, because the establishment of the existence of the effect (*satkāryatva*) is just as certain as the establishment of the non-existence of the effect (*asatkāryatva*). Thus,
there is the existence of the effect.
For there is no absence of the essence of clay within the state of being a jar;

the very self of the clay is the self of the jar, because if that [essence] were abandoned, its own nature would be untenable—just as the clay exists as a reality whose nature consists in the superimposition of various past, future, and present particulars, or just as the jar exists as a reality whose nature consists in the superimposition of various past, future, and present particulars. By this, all of his non-dualism (advaita) is refuted.

Since it has already been established that the effect is neither existent nor non-existent prior to its production, the Teacher provides the following response: "This too is not so; for just as the non-existence of the effect is established, so too is the existence of the effect established," beginning with this and proceeding through the contemplation up until the point where the existence of the effect is fully demonstrated.

Just as you accept that a jar—which has not fallen away from its state as clay, and which is neither produced nor destroyed by that state of clay—is "non-existent" because it is intended to be made for the sake of being a jar, why do you not likewise accept that the effect is "existent"? For the reality of clay—which is eternally non-fallen from itself and uncreated, and whose nature consists of the jar, the lump of clay, and so forth—is not intended to be made when one intends to speak of the reality of clay; since it is not to be made, the effect is existent. Therefore, the effect is neither existent nor non-existent prior to its production (*Vaiśeṣika Sūtra Kaṭandī*).

— This too is not so, for just as the theory of the non-existence of the effect in the cause (asatkāryavāda) is established, so too is the theory of the existence of the effect in the cause (satkāryavāda) established...
Indeed, the existence of the effect in the cause does not mean that the nature of clay ceases to exist when it takes the form of a jar.

The self-nature of the clay is indeed the self-nature of the jar, because if that [clay] were abandoned, its own essential nature could not be established— just as there is the real existence of "clay-ness" whose nature consists in the superimposition of various specific states past, future, and present, or just as there is the real existence of the "jar" whose nature consists in the superimposition of various specific states past, future, and present.
By this, his entire doctrine of non-duality (*advaitavāda*), concerning the status of the effect as being existent, non-existent, or both existent and non-existent, is refuted.
See page 50, note 3;
[the word] *bhāvānām* is the reading,
and likewise *kartavyam* is the reading.

Regarding the passage beginning with "not indeed in the state of being a jar" (*na hi ghaṭatāyām*): if the jar were to exist in the absence of the clay-reality (*mṛttattva*), as in the case of the *śivaka* and other stages, then the jar would be non-existent prior [to its manifestation] and would arise later; however, that is not the case, because the very self of the clay is the self of the jar.

Why? Because its own nature cannot be established upon the abandonment of that [quality]; for when the abandonment of something results in the impossibility of a thing's own nature, that [thing abandoned] is the very self of that [thing].

"Past, future," and so forth, up to "like the nature of clay": just as the nature of a lump of clay—which has as its own-nature (*tatsvabhāva*) those various specific qualities such as coldness, heat, and so on, as well as wetness, dryness, broken fragments, and the like, throughout the times of past, future, and present—that very existence (*sadbhāva*) is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). That ultimate reality, which is the actual essence of clay (*mṛttattva*), does not function apart from those specific qualities, and they too are that [clay]. Thus, that alone is the self (*ātman*) of the specific qualities and of the state of being clay; likewise, the self of the jar is the very self of the clay.
Alternatively, the second example is: "like a real jar whose nature is superimposed with various distinctions of past, future, and present. This is the same explanation;

for that very reason and by this same illustration, it is asserted in two ways: "the self of the clay is the self of the jar" and "the self of the jar is the self of the clay"—thus [ends] the section on the nature of clay.
Of what essential nature is the clay of the cosmic egg (or the fragment of clay)?
The ultimate reality (paramārtha) does not exist in the manuscripts;
[it is] the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of that very [reality],
which is pervasive (vyāpaka).
By this, the entire doctrine of non-absolutism (syādvāda) has been refuted.

It should be understood that by means of the effort consisting in the demonstration of a single reality whose nature comprises both the existent and the non-existent, and by means of the negation of its absolute [one-sided] character, all dogmatic doctrines of eternalism, non-eternalism, and so forth, are refuted. Because action is impossible both in the absence and in the presence of a material cause (*upādāna*), this non-dual doctrine (*advāda*)—which maintains that the cause and effect are simultaneously eternal and non-eternal, one and manifold, and both particular and universal—is established.

Eternal nature is sublated by non-eternal nature, and non-eternal nature is sublated by eternal nature; both are of an absolute form [only when taken in isolation], yet everything is established as being relative. For example: eternality exists because of perpetual existence, and perpetual existence exists from the perspective of substance (*dravyārtha*); therefore, there is no absolute non-eternality. Furthermore, non-eternality exists because of perpetual non-existence, and perpetual non-existence exists from the perspective of modification (*paryāyārtha*); therefore, there is no absolute eternality. Thus, all this is the doctrine of non-absolutism (*anekāntavāda*).
See page 495, line 20.

Furthermore, regarding the subsequent argument intended to negate the existence of a restriction on the material cause (*upādāna*): "The taking up of a substance already established as capable of activity is the cause of the action, not the cause of the existence of the effect;
[if that were so], from what would its restriction of activity arise?"...
...it is not established [as such] prior to its production; for that which possesses the nature of being produced is not non-existent, because of the necessity of the material cause (*upādāna*).

"In the *Nyāyabhāṣya* (4.1.21), it is stated: 'Nothing is to be taken up for the production of anything; everything is not [the cause] of everything. Thus, a restriction regarding non-existence is not tenable.'"
If it is argued that "it" [the cause] exists because one who is capable undertakes the performance of an action, then even for one who is capable of performing the effect...
the effect is indeed non-existent.
Because that which has attained a state of identity possesses efficacy, the effect must exist [prior to its production];

and because only that which is efficacious is entitled to undertake the performance of an action, there is a restriction regarding the material cause. Therefore, the intention appears to be that the effect is indeed non-existent [prior to its production].
See page 504, note 15.
Furthermore, regarding the statement beginning with "the subsequent [explanation] is for the purpose of negating the existence of a restriction of material causes," and so forth:

the terms *kartṛ* (agent) and *kāraṇa* (cause), as well as *karman* (object) and *kārya* (effect), are words based on action (*kriyā*). In that context, the taking up of a substance (*dravya*) that is already established and capable of activity is what is based on action; it is not based on the existence of the effect.

Here, the proponent of *syādvāda* (the doctrine of manifoldness) indeed asks: "Now, from what does this restriction of its activity arise? and so forth, until: "That which possesses the property of being produced cannot exist prior to its production; because of the restriction of the material cause (*upādāna*), something specific is to be taken as the material for the production of a particular thing, and not everything for everything—thus, if [the effect] were non-existent, such a restriction would not be logical."
Thus [it is stated] in the Nyāyabhāṣya 4.1.48.

As for what was stated previously— that before its production, the effect does not exist because of the restriction of its material cause (NS 4.1.49)— that [effect] is non-existent only insofar as it is established by the intellect (NS 4.1.50).

This is because, prior to production, the effect is determined by its specific cause— namely, that "this [cause] is capable of producing this [effect], and not everything"— as is established by the intellect through the observation of the restriction of production.
Therefore, the restriction of the material cause is logically established;
however, if the effect already exists, there is no production at all prior to its arising—
thus it is stated in the *Nyāyabhāṣya* composed by Vātsyāyana.

As for the argument that "this is not so, because there is a restriction regarding the material cause," [the reply is: "But that which is established by the intellect is non-existent" (Nyāyasūtra 4.1.50). This restriction of the material cause does not arise from existence, but rather from causal capacity.

Having established that an effect is conceptually determined such that "this can be produced by this" and "this cannot be produced by this," whatever is capable of producing something is taken as its material cause (*upādāna*), and not everything for everything; nor is it observed that everything is produced from everything. Thus, one establishes the restriction between cause and effect through the restriction of production and the restriction of the effect. Even so, the meaning of the words "cause" (*kāraṇa*) and "effect" (*kārya*) must be stated: what is meant by "cause," and what is meant by "effect"?
Is it not the case that a "cause" is that which acts (*karoti*), and an "effect" is that which is acted upon (*kriyate*)?
If manifestation [is the object], then the same consequence as before follows.

If you think that the meaning of "doing" (*karoti*) is observed even with respect to things already existing—just as one says, "make the hair," or "make the back"—that is not so; for in those cases, a particular arrangement of what already exists is produced later, and in the case of the back, it is the removal of dirt that was previously non-existent. Thus, we never observe the sense of "causing to exist" (*kāraṇārtha*) in regard to what is already existent.
Therefore, this [argument] is invalid.

Regarding what was stated by Uddyotakara in the *Nyāyavārttika*— namely, "because of the restriction of the material cause" (*upādānaniyamāt*)— if there is a restriction of the material cause for the person such that one seeking a cloth takes up only threads and not *vīraṇa* grass, and one seeking a mat takes up *vīraṇa*, then this is because of the thorough knowledge of the capacity (*sāmarthya*) of those respective materials for their respective effects.
And that capacity is inferential;
thus it is said: "But that which is established by cognition is non-existent" (Nyāya Sūtra 4.1.50).

50. Thus, the meaning is that this effect, which was previously non-existent, is produced by this very cause and not by another; this is established through inference (*anumāna*). Now, if you argue that under the theory of the non-existence of the effect (*asatkāryapakṣa*), there would be no such restriction as that "the threads alone are the material cause (*upādāna*) of the cloth, and not the *vīraṇa* grass," etc., that is incorrect. For even though [all things] are equally non-existent [prior to production], it is possible—due to a specific inherent nature (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*)—that only a certain thing produced from its own cause is capable of generating a certain effect, while others are not. This concludes the section on "The Occasional Causes" (*naimittika*) in the *Nyāyavārtikatātparyaṭīkā* composed by Vācaspatimiśra.
Regarding this meaning:
here, the Vaiśeṣika position is raised as an objection— namely, "If it is argued that [the Lord] is such because he possesses the authority for the performance of what is capable."

The explanation of this is as follows: the passage beginning with "only that which is capable performs an action" and so forth, which serves as an illustration of the cause, has its meaning already explained up to the point where it says "the effect is indeed non-existent. This, indeed, is the response of the proponent of the theory of the non-existence of the effect (*asatkāryavādin*), given by way of the reason for the restriction of the material cause (*upādānaniyama*).

To this, the Teacher provides the following reply: Because that which has attained a state of identity possesses efficacy, it follows that the effect pre-exists (satkāryavāda). Indeed, by you yourself, when asserting that "the restriction of the material cause arises from the agent's undertaking of an office in producing what is efficacious," the pre-existence of the effect was already supported. That which is "efficacious" (samartha) is that whose purpose is consistent; that object which has attained identity with the means of accomplishment—being designated as the "instrument"—is efficacious. Because of its being such, since that object which has attained identity possesses efficacy, the effect must indeed pre-exist. For no efficacy whatsoever can be established between what is non-existent, such as a donkey’s horn, and anything else, nor can it belong to that [non-existent thing] through anything.

The reading enclosed within these brackets does not exist in the Ya manuscripts; its meaning is untenable. Now, why is it that only the threads, the shuttle, and so forth are accepted as the material cause (*upādāna*) for the production of a cloth, and not sand, a loom, or other such things? Because they alone possess the capacity (*sāmarthya*). In this way, the effect, such as a cloth, exists in the threads; likewise in the fibers (*aṃśu*); likewise in the filaments (*pakṣman*), the weft-threads (*tuṭi*), and the atoms (*paramāṇu*); and likewise in the shuttle and so forth, and even in the sand and so forth, because they are the causes of the cause, just like the atom (*aṇu*).

Because there is doubt regarding the textual corruption of the *Nayacakravṛtti*, there is uncertainty here concerning the root text (*mūla*). However, if the reading of the *Nayacakravṛtti* were correct, the root text would also include here the following: "Now, why are only the threads, the shuttle, and so forth the causes for the production of a cloth, and not dust, a loom, and so forth? Furthermore, that which is the cause of accumulation [is stated]: 'Before its production, the effect is non-existent, because of the absence of action, qualities, and designation, like a sky-flower...'"

The explanation of this is as follows: Now, how is it that [the opponent], by asking about the threads, the shuttle, and so forth—up to the point where they are the cause of the cause—regarding them as being specifically Vaiśeṣika like atoms (aṇu), causes him to explain by means of that very same [argument]?

Only the shuttle and so forth are taken as the material cause (*upādāna*) for the production of a cloth, and not the dust or the loom; this is because, by virtue of being included within the category of instruments (*karaṇa*), the effect pre-exists in that [material cause] alone, since it is that which possesses the capacity in such and such a manner—that is, because it possesses the specific power inherent to each respective object. Thus, the effect, such as a cloth, exists within the threads, and likewise within the fibers which are the causes of the threads, as they bear the causal nature of the cloth in various ways. Similarly, even down to the eyelashes, moments, particles, and atoms, the cloth exists in those respective substrates through a continuous succession, because they serve as the causes of the cloth in their own particular ways according to their respective capacities, being manifested by inherence (*samavāya*) in it and being of its very nature.

The cloth, though a non-inherent cause (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*), is nonetheless manifested by conjunction; since conjunction is non-different from the substances that possess it, and because it is non-different from the substance transformed into the state of conjunction with infinite spatial points—such as dyads, triads, and so forth—those very atoms are the cloth. Just as the nature of "cloth" exists in the constituent parts of the cloth (the conjuncts) due to their being of that same essence, so too does it exist in the atoms that are its causes.

This applies likewise to the shuttle and other tools; for the shuttle, loom, pegs, needles, combs, and so forth, when their operations are aroused by the effort of the weaver, they possess the nature of "cloth" due to their being of that same essence and being non-different from the substance.

Furthermore, even in the case of dust and such, the nature of being a cloth (*paṭatva*) is established because it consists of cotton produced through the conjunction of earth, water, air, fire, space, and seed; for it is the cause of the causes of that [cloth], just like an atom (*paramāṇu*).

Thus, for now, the negation of the existence or non-existence of the effect is not established, because the reason for the negation is untenable and because the demonstration of the firmness of the proof for the identity of existence and non-existence has been shown. Therefore, the effect is indeed both existent and non-existent.
Here, there may also be a reading beginning with "of the shuttle and so forth" (*turyāderityādi*).
Is it from the threads, the loom, and so forth?
Likewise by that [means], likewise by that [state], likewise by that sleep.

Likewise, in the case of "in the threads" (*tantuṣu*), because the word *ādi* (beginning) and the word *anta* (end) are mutually connected with the phrase "having infinite ends" (*anantāntapradeśa*), one should understand that the reading in the Bhāṣya is indeed correct when the intention is that the word *ādi* refers to "dvy-aṇuka, try-aṇuka, etc. in this context, and the word *anta* follows immediately after "infinite" (*ananta*) in the phrase "infinite-end" (*anantānta*). Thus, it should be noted that the Bhāṣya's recension is perfectly valid.

Regarding conjunctions, the substantial cause (dravyakāraṇa) is twofold: the cause consisting of that very substance (taddravyakāraṇa) and the cause consisting of another substance (anyadravyakāraṇa).
The lump of clay is the cause consisting of that very substance for a jar; the wheel, staff, string, water, and human effort are the causes consisting of other substances.
Alternatively, the substantial cause (*dravyakāraṇa*) is twofold: the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) and the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*).
The threads are the inherent cause of the cloth, because the cloth inheres in the threads.
The shuttle, the loom, the weaver’s knife, the comb, and so forth are the non-inherent causes.

Alternatively, there is the instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) and the efficient cause (*naimittikakāraṇa*); for example, straw is the instrumental cause of a mat, while the efficient causes are human effort, rope, pegs, and so forth;
the same applies to jars, cloth, and other things—thus it is stated in the *Āvaśyakacūrṇi*, composed by Jinadāsagaṇimahattara, verse 736, page 372.

Furthermore, regarding the passage beginning with "that which is also a cause of accumulation" (*upacaya-hetu*), it is said that after having negated both existence and non-existence, the cause of accumulation was stated for the purpose of proving the non-existence of the effect. For example: "How [can there be an effect] since the effect does not exist prior to its production?
To this it is replied: "Because of the absence of action (*kriyā*), quality (*guṇa*), and designation (*vyapadeśa*)."

Activity (*kriyā*), such as weaving and so forth, as well as qualities (*guṇa*) such as conjunction and transformation, and designations (*vyapadeśa*), which are either distinct words or logical marks (*liṅga*), do not exist in the state of the threads prior to the cloth. Therefore, because of the absence of activity, quality, and designation, the effect is non-existent before its production, like a sky-flower. To this [argument], the reply is: "This too is subject to refutation. The effect exists [in essence] even before [its manifestation], because it lacks activity, quality, and designation that were previously non-existent, just like a substance (*dravya*) and other categories that are unrelated to the universal "existence" (*sattā*).

Furthermore, there is the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*), because these [features] are observed in the three types of effects—namely, those that are non-existent (like a sky-flower), those that are existent, and those that are just born.
"Is it not the case that there is an inconclusiveness [of the reason] due to the example of a sky-flower? No, because that contingency has already been rejected by the preceding qualification.
Is it not the case that substance is indeed existent, and not an effect?"
But is it not [the case that] accomplishment...
for the word "accomplishment" (niṣpatti) indeed...

...the threefold accomplishment of *prabhūta* is certain, fixed, or superior; indeed, "becoming" (*bhavana*) itself is the contradictory nature of the reason, as the Teacher has stated. This very [reason] of yours for accumulation is for proving the opponent’s position: "The effect exists, it comes into being, it is manifested, it arises, because it possesses the designation of action and quality prior to its non-existence, like a substance that is not connected with existence (*sattā*). This is the proof of your own position, provided with its qualification.

Just as, according to your own view, the three types of effects known as substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and action (*karman*) exist by their very nature (*svabhāvasat*), yet do not participate in the designations of action or quality until they are connected with existence (*sattā*); nevertheless, they do exist merely as inherent (*samaveta*) in their own causes—so too is our position established that this [effect] is an inherent effect. Furthermore, the reason "because of the absence of the designations of action and quality" is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because it is observed both in the case of non-existent things like a sky-flower and in the case of the three types of effects immediately upon their birth. Thus, the claim that "it is non-existent" is doubtful.
(The reading enclosed within these brackets is not present in manuscript *ya*).

[The reason] "because it exists" is also contradictory; for the effect exists [only] as something that comes into being, because it lacks prior designation by action or quality, like a substance (dravya) etc. that is not connected with existence (sattā).

Furthermore, there is inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatā), because [the property of coming into being] is observed in non-existent things such as a sky-flower, and in existent things such as the three types of effects immediately upon their birth.
Is it not the case that there is an inconclusiveness [of the reason] due to the example of a sky-flower? No, because that contingency was already ruled out by the preceding qualification.
Is it not the case that... substance is indeed existent, not an effect?
Is it not the case that "accomplishment" (niṣpatti) [is meant]?
For the word "accomplishment" indeed...
...the threefold accomplishment of the abundant [cause] is certain, fixed, or superior; indeed, it is simply existence itself.

Was it not previously stated by me that "before its accomplishment, the effect is non-existent because of the absence of action, qualities, and designation"? However, the substance is existent, not the effect.
Indeed, such is the root [of the matter] that appears here:
production (*niṣpatti*) is arising (*utpatti*), which is existence after having been non-existent; it is stated that what was unmanifestly existent becomes manifestly existent.
And the triad of substance and so forth, being not yet merged with existence (*sattva*), becomes "existent" (*sat*) by means of the universal of existence (*sattāsāmānya*) as soon as it is born.

The intention appears to be that the word *niṣpatti* (accomplishment) is a denoter of *bhavana* (coming-into-being) or *sattā* (existence); thus, this [word] would be connected with existence (*sattā*). (Note: *pra.* and *cedamya.* appear to be manuscript variants or scribal marks).
He experiences connection,
he experiences pleasure,
and he experiences delight.

The other says: "But surely there is an inconclusiveness (anaikānta) like that of a sky-flower; since the effect is non-existent prior to its production because of the absence of designations for action and quality as they have not yet come into being, it would be like a sky-flower [non-existent], whereas it would be existent like a substance etc. that has just been produced. Thus, even your proof causes doubt.
To this we say: no, because the contingency has already been rejected by the qualification "prior" (prāk).

This undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) would indeed arise if I were to state merely that "the effect exists" because of the absence of designations for action and quality without qualification. What, then, have I stated? I have qualified it by saying: "because of the prior non-existence of designations for action and quality. That for which the designation of action and quality was previously non-existent but will exist later is indeed existent, just like that very substance and so forth as soon as it has arisen. However, this does not apply to things like a sky-flower, whose non-existence is characterized by the lack of any temporal distinction between "before" and "after. Therefore, one might say that prior to this qualification, the charge of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) against this reason (*hetu*) is avoided. Thus says the opponent (*pra*).
Is it thus [as you claim], or is it yours alone?
To this he replies: "But surely," and so forth, up to "but substance is indeed existent, not an effect."

I previously stated the proposition that "the effect is non-existent prior to its production," meaning that as long as it has not arisen, it does not exist as qualified by time; then I stated the reason, "because of the absence of action and so forth. However, that [reason] does not apply to a substance that has already been produced. Therefore, because the property of the probans is deficient, the example is invalid.

To this we reply: "But [regarding] 'production,' etc."—for even when it is said "prior to production," since "production" (niṣpatti) has the same meaning as "arising" (utpatti), "coming into being after not having been" (abhūtvābhāva), and so on, what is meant is that the unmanifestly existent becomes manifestly existent.

For example: that triad of substance and so forth, being "uninhabited by existence" (*anupanilīnasattva*)—that is, prior to its completion because it has not yet been inhabited by existence—is "existent" (*sat*) through the universal of existence (*sattāsāmānya*), and it becomes "manifestly existent" (*vyaktasat*) through the inherence of existence (*sattāsamavāya*). This is the meaning of the word "completion" (*niṣpatti*).

Therefore, he says: "The word 'completion'... and so forth, which is its explanation: there is a threefold completion of that which is abundant and has begun to come into being; namely, it is either determined (*niyatā*), certain (*niścitā*), or predominant (*adhikā*).

What is that [distinction]? Just as for you, in the case of substances and so forth, the production of an effect is determined and certain solely through its connection with existence (*sattā*), because existence is distinguished from other forms of being; and further, because it is produced repeatedly, it is superior. Likewise, here too, the accomplishment of an action is determined by the operation of the agent through the restriction of the material cause and the necessity of its own existence—just like the winnowing of rice—and it is superior due to its occurrence simultaneously, non-simultaneously, or in a sequential order.
Therefore, since action and quality exist both as being and non-being, the designations "action" and "quality" apply precisely to what is both existent and non-existent.

Otherwise, there would be the consequence of [the cognition] being a mere verbal designation of the causes, potencies, and material substrates, since they are indistinguishable in their lack of existence;
however, for one for whom the object is indeed existent...

Because these objects do not exist [prior to their production], there would follow the consequence that they are mere designations, since there is no distinction between that which is produced and that which produces;
therefore, the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) is indeed untenable.
Why? Because the root *pad* has the meaning of "existence" (*sattā*), and that [existence] is threefold for you alone; namely:

it is restricted to effects such as substance (*dravya*) precisely through its connection with pure existence (*sattā*), because the inherence in the cause (*kāraṇasamavāya*) and the universal (*sāmānya*) are eternal; it is determined because existence is distinct from other existences such as substantiality (*dravyatva*), quality-ness (*guṇatva*), action-ness (*karmatva*), pot-ness (*ghaṭatva*), form-ness (*rūpatva*), and upward-thrusting (*utkṣepaṇa*); and it is "additional" (*adhika*) because of the coming-to-be of the effect, since according to your own doctrine, birth is admitted to occur in the inherence in the cause.
Thus, the threefold production of the triad of the example—consisting of the effect-substance and so forth—has been explained.

Now, regarding the effect according to the Dārṣṭāntikas: it is determined by its material cause and determined by its own existence. By the restriction of material causes such as clay, the existence of a jar and so forth is established; it is determined by that existence because the production of the jar occurs only from clay. In reality, this [jar] is ascertained as being a jar through the exclusion of being a cloth and so forth. This is, for example, like the selection of rice grains (*taṇḍulavicaya*). Just as rice grains are selected—meaning they are ascertained by the removal of chaff and the like and by the grasping of their own form—the production of the jar is ascertained and distinguished from non-production through the activity (*vyāpāra*) or motion (*parispanda*) of the action, by means of the grasping of its own form. This is the meaning.

"Exceeding" (*adhika*) means existing through the occurrence of successive states (*paryāya*)—whether simultaneous or non-simultaneous—in such a manner. Those states which previously existed simultaneously, such as the modes (*paryāya*) of color and so forth, or the lump, the clay-rod, and so on; and those which exist non-simultaneously, such as newness, mediocrity, and antiquity—they occur in succession through the process of being fashioned into a clay-rod and so forth. Because it comes into being in that specific way, there is an "exceeding" production here as well.

Therefore, just like the production of the three types of effects (the material cause and so forth) which serve as the illustrative examples, that which was unmanifest exists and then becomes manifest; thus, it is established that the effect exists in its material cause. This incidental discussion is concluded.
The existence and non-existence of the effect previously mentioned has been explained by you,
O Lord of Speech.

Just as in the case of a product such as a substance, existence (*sattā*) is determined and fixed solely through its connection with [the universal] Existence (*sattā*), because Existence is distinguished from other existences and is further augmented by its repeated occurrence; likewise, here too, the accomplishment of an action is determined by the operation of the action—just like the sifting of rice—and it is augmented by the simultaneous, non-simultaneous, sequential, and such-like manifestation, being restricted by its own existence and the restriction of its material cause (*upādāna*). Is this not the operation of the action? (The text appears to repeat "operation of the action" due to a scribal error).
Therefore, because action and quality exist both in the existent and the non-existent, the designations of action and quality apply only to that which is both existent and non-existent;
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of causes, potencies, and materials being mere verbal designations, since there would be no distinction from non-existence.
But for one for whom the object is indeed already present...

Because these [three] objects do not exist, there would follow the consequence that there is mere verbal designation, since there is no distinction between that which is to be produced and that which produces;
therefore, the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (satkāryavāda) is indeed untenable.
The three [factors] beginning with the object (*kārya*) are to be understood through the removal of the [three] beginning with the agent (*kartṛ*).
Is it that action is the manifestation of activity? Or is it that prior to the manifestation of activity, there is the non-existence [of action]?
Those which do not exist prior to their arising and do not exist simultaneously [with it],

therefore, actions and qualities belong only to that which both exists and does not exist; because of that state— namely, because of being an action or quality belonging to that which both exists and does not exist— the designations "action" and "quality" apply only to that which both exists and does not exist.

Otherwise, there would be the consequence that the mention of causes, potencies, and material causes (*upādāna*) would be mere words. If the effect were indeed non-existent, then the statements regarding the stick and other tools being fit for the action of crushing (the *hetu*), the potency (*śakti*), and the clay as the material cause (*upādāna*)—specifically, that clay alone is employed for a jar and not thread or the like—all of this would be nothing more than empty talk. Since these [causes] would be non-existent like a donkey’s horn, such claims as "this stick is the cause of this [jar]," "this softness and so forth is the potency of the clay substance," and "clay alone is the material cause of the jar" would have no actual referent. This is because, like the absence of causal efficiency or causes for the production of a sky-flower and the like, there is no distinction in their state of non-existence.
Is the staff and so forth the cause?

If, however, the effect were already existent [prior to its production], that same fault would apply there as well; therefore he says: "But for whom the object is indeed already existing," and so on, the meaning of which is understood up to: "Because these objects do not exist, there would follow the consequence of mere verbal designation, since there is no distinction between that which is to be produced and that which is not produced. Therefore, since both extreme positions are untenable, it is logical that what is both existent and non-existent manifests at first.

Furthermore, as for what was said—that there is no fault because conceptualization is untenable due to not resorting to three alternatives and resorting to another alternative—that is not a fault, because the completion (*niṣṭhā*) and the connection [with the cause] occur at the same time. Completion is the jar resulting from the operation of the causal complex; the producers are the potter, the stick, and so forth. Since the jar exists just as the potter, clay, stick, and so forth exist, what is produced by a cause such as the stick, or is it not? The power of softness and so forth belongs to the clay alone, not to the diamond and so forth. Clay alone is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the jar because the jar is yet unproduced, and not the already produced jar; thus, there is no distinction, since there is no difference in their existence (*sattva*).
This concludes the incidental discussion; he summarizes it as follows: "Therefore, the theory that the effect pre-exists (satkāryavāda) is indeed untenable.
What follows from this? This follows: just as the theory that the effect does not pre-exist (asatkāryavāda) is untenable, so too is the absolute theory of satkāryavāda untenable.
Therefore, since both absolute positions are untenable, it is logical that what was previously both existent and non-existent manifests [into being].

Furthermore, as for what was said— that because one does not resort to the three alternatives and yet resorts to another alternative, a conceptual construction (vikalpa) is untenable, and thus there is no fault— this is incorrect, because the completion [of the effect] and its connection [with the cause] are simultaneous,
and completion is the operation of the causal complex.
Therefore, since those two absolute positions are illogical, the Syādvādins conclude that it is correct to understand that what is both existent and non-existent manifests first.

Because faults are seen in the positions of absolute unity and absolute difference, whereas no fault is seen in the position of non-absolutism (anekānta), it is established that an effect—which is both existent and non-existent—is non-manifestly existent and becomes manifestly existent. This being so, as for what was said [previously] beginning with "because the threefold conceptualization is untenable, the effect is not connected with existence," etc.—if you argue that by resorting to another conceptualization intended to be faultless, which avoids these three conceptual positions, [the objection] "because the conceptualization is untenable" does not constitute a fault; for [in our view], there is no reliance on those three conceptualizations and instead recourse is taken to a different conceptualization.

If it is asked, "From which other conceptual construction [does this arise]?", [the answer is: since the completion (*niṣṭhā*) and the relation (*sambandha*) occur at the same time, what is completion? To this he says: "Completion is the state of a thing coming into existence after not having existed previously; it is the reaching of its end.
... "Relation is inherence (*samavāya*) with the existence of its own cause."

The two [the effect and its properties] are simultaneous; the very moment of connection with the existence (*sattā*) of its own cause is the moment of completion (*niṣṭhākāla*). Why? Because inherence (*samavāya*) is one. At the very time the effect reaches full completion and becomes connected with its causes by way of the relation of inherence—which is the cause of their inseparable existence (*ayutasiddhi*)—at that same time it is also connected with existence and so forth. Therefore, because there is no distinction prior to the production of the effect, the conceptualization of "non-existent" or "existent" and so on is groundless.

This too is not correct, because such conceptualizations are untenable, due to the lack of a relationship [between the effect and its properties] and because [the unproduced effect] is not a real entity.
And how could there be a connection between a non-entity and causes, or with existence itself? If such a thing were possible, then even a sky-flower would have its time of causal operation.

This refers to the time when the collection of causes—namely, the inherent (*samavāyin*), non-inherent (*asamavāyin*), and instrumental (*nimitta*) causes such as threads, their conjunctions, the stick, and so forth—is active; that is to say, the time when the operation of the shuttle and other tools has ceased during the production of a cloth.

He explains this very point: "the becoming of an entity that previously did not exist" (*prāgasato vastubhāvaḥ*), which is synonymous with the birth of an entity such as a cloth, its coming into being (*niṣṭhāna*), or its completion (*samāpti*).

What is this relation? To this he says: the relation is inherence (*samavāya*) with the existence (*sattā*) of its own cause; that is, the inherence of the effect, the cloth, with its causes, the threads, and the simultaneity of these two relations of inherence residing in those two [substrata].

He demonstrates this: "The very connection with the existence of its own causes is the time of completion. Having proposed that the connection of the effect with its own causes and with existence is itself the time of completion, he asks for the reason—"Why?"—and states the reason: "Because inherence is one. For inherence is a relation, and it is one for both [the cause and the effect]; therefore, the effect is indeed completed through the connection with the causes, existence, and so forth.

He demonstrates this: at the very same time that the effect—attaining its own nature and called "cloth"—is connected with its causes, such as the threads, by means of the relation known as inherence (*samavāya*), which is the cause of non-separability (*ayutasiddhi*), he shows the distinction of this from conjunction (*saṃyoga*), which is the cause of separability (*yutasiddhi*); at that very same time, it is also connected with existence (*sattā*) and the like. This implies that the very same inherence which is the relation of the effect to its causes is also the single inherence shared with existence, substantiality (*dravyatva*), and so forth, because there is no difference in time.

Therefore, there is no distinction [of time]; for since there is no temporal distinction here between the completion (*niṣṭhā*) and the relation, the very expression "prior" is not tenable. Since the effect is non-existent at its production, the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) regarding its being existent, non-existent, or both is groundless. Because there is no objective basis for a relation of existence with an effect that is existent, non-existent, or both existent and non-existent, what could be the support for such a conceptual construction? Thus, without relying on those three conceptual constructions, let the conceptual construction of the simultaneity of completion and relation be accepted as faultless.
How, then, does "cowness" subsist in cows...

If it is argued that this is because there is no occurrence [of the universal] in either the cow or the non-cow—meaning, if you think: "Is this 'cowness' (*gotva*), which is the cause of the inclusive cognition (*anuvṛttipratyaya*) among cows, present in the cow or in the non-cow? If it is present in the cow, then since it is already a cow prior to its connection with cowness, cowness is redundant.
If, on the other hand, it is present in the non-cow, then even a horse or the like would become a cow through its connection with cowness;
and there is no other alternative."

Therefore, it is not the case that the cognition of recurrence does not arise from "cowness," for we do not accept such an alternative [view]: cowness exists neither in the cow nor in the non-cow; prior to its connection with cowness, this entity is neither a cow nor a non-cow.

What is the reason? Both of these are cognitions of a qualified object (*viśeṣya*), and they do not occur without a connection to a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). Furthermore, prior to its connection with "cowness" (*gotva*), the entity does not exist; nor can that which is non-existent be designated as either "cow" or "non-cow. At the very moment the entity exists, it is simultaneously connected with "cowness"; thus, this conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is without foundation. By this, the dilemma regarding the existence or non-existence of the connection with "Being" (*sattā*) is explained: there is no connection with "Being" for that which already exists, nor for that which does not exist. Since the entity is connected with "Being" at the very moment it exists, the fault of relying on both existence and non-existence is untenable.
Therefore, birth is established;
thus [it is stated] in the *Nyāyavārttika* composed by Uddyotakara, 2.2.10.

Now, let it be granted that the cognition "existent, existent" is figurative with respect to universals (*sāmānya*) and the like, while primary with respect to substances (*dravya*) and the like; however, the connection with existence (*sattā*) is still subject to doubt: does existence belong to things that are already existent, or to those that are non-existent?
If it belongs to those that are already existent, then is their existence prior to the connection with existence, or is it [existent] even without the connection with existence?

If you argue that when the relation with existence (*sattā*) is accepted, this same dilemma applies there as well, and thus there is no infinite regress (*anavasthā*), then what is the use of existence? Alternatively, if you claim that non-existent things become existent through their relation with existence, then that existence would be merely conventional (*apāramārthika*), because it depends upon an external adjunct (*upādhi*). Furthermore, if non-existent things were made existent by their relation with existence, then even things like a donkey’s horn would possess existence, since they are equally non-existent. Likewise, if existence itself were non-existent, then by its connection with that [non-existent] existence, there would be no existence in substances and the like. If, on the other hand, existence exists by its own nature (*svarūpeṇa*), then the same undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) would apply to substances and the like; and if it exists through a relation with existence, there is an infinite regress.
Therefore, the Śākyas maintain that existence consists in causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*),
while others hold it to consist in connection with the present time.

Regarding this, what we previously asked— whether existence belongs to things already existent through their connection with "existence" (*sattā*), or to things non-existent— is untenable, because the completion [of the entity] and its connection [with existence] are simultaneous.

For instance: the "origination" of entities is simply their connection with the existence of their own causes; it is not existence prior [to that connection], because the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) has been refuted.

Nor does the admission of a connection with the existence of their own causes for non-existent things entail the absurd consequence of such a state existing for things like a donkey's horn, since the absence of that [connection] is ascertained precisely by the absence of its cause of origination.
Furthermore, in the case of eternal things, since a temporal sequence of priority and posteriority is impossible, the conceptual alternative [of origination] is untenable.
Nor is existence non-ultimate, because the connection with existence is ultimate (pṛ.

...Now, what is this so-called "being an effect" (*kāryatva*)? It is the relation with the existence of its own cause, because of the conventional usage that "it is an effect by virtue of being connected with that [existence]."

Some maintain that it is "coming into being after not having existed. Even in this case, as stated on page 129, "coming into being after not having existed" is simply the subsequent connection with its own causes and with existence (*sattā*).

...As for the objection, "Is this cow connected with cowness, or is it a non-cow?", that is not worthy of a resolution because the completion [of the object] and its connection [with properties] occur at the same time; for the very acquisition of the individual's (piṇḍa) self-nature consists in its connection with its own causes, such as existence (sattā) and so forth. Prior to that, there is neither the state of being a cow nor the state of being a non-cow for it, because its very existence would be impossible.
(p. 690) — Thus in the *Vyomavatī*, a commentary on Praśastapāda’s *Bhāṣya* composed by Ācārya Vyomaśiva.
Time is the state of a thing’s existence when it was previously non-existent; "completion" (niṣṭhā) means termination or conclusion.

"Relation" (sambandha) is the inherence (samavāya) with the existence of its own cause; the simultaneity of these two is such that the very relation with the existence of its own cause is the time of completion. Why? Because inherence is one. At the very same time that the effect, reaching its final completion, becomes related to its causes by way of the relation of inherence—which is the cause of their inseparable connection—it is also related at that same time to existence and the other categories. Therefore, because there is no distinction [between these relations], prior to the production of the effect, the conceptualization of a non-existent thing as having existence and so forth is groundless.
—This too is not [the case], because its conceptualization is untenable, because it lacks connection, and because it is a non-entity (*avastu*).

Furthermore, how can there be a connection between a non-entity and causes, or with existence? If such a connection were possible for it, it would also exist for a sky-flower; yet that [connection] is one and the same.
But that one is [so] because of that;
therefore...
Regarding the production of an effect, it is not dependent upon [the destruction of] the cause;
to this, it is replied: this too is not so, because the alternatives proposed are untenable.
This alternative [view] is also untenable; since it is untenable, no resolution of the fault has been achieved.

If one asks, "In what way is this alternative untenable? it is because there is no relation [between cause and effect]. There is no relation because [the effect] is a non-entity (*avastu*). Just as a sky-flower, being a non-entity, has no relation with anything, so too an effect that is non-existent prior to its production has no relation [to its cause].

Furthermore, since that effect, while reaching its final completion, is non-existent, it lacks substantial reality (*avastutva*). And how can there be a connection between a non-substantial entity and its causes or with existence? That which "reaches its final completion" is the effect as it is being produced; because it has not yet acquired its own nature, it is non-existent. At that stage, that effect is not connected with its own causes or with existence, because of its lack of substantial reality, just like a flower in the sky.

If that [effect] were to exist, then even a sky-flower would exist; for if an effect, while reaching its final completion, being unproduced and non-existent, were to be connected with causes and with existence, then a sky-flower, upon reaching its final completion, would likewise be connected with its own causes and with existence because of its lack of substantiality, just like the effect. Therefore, this alternative—that "the non-existent is connected with existence"—is included within that very same category of alternatives. Thus it is stated in the *Udyotana-bhāṣya*.

In this context, there may also be the reading "ity ucyamānaḥ" (being so called), because at the time of connection it exists as a real entity like a thread; and it is precisely while existing that it connects, since the time of its completion and the time of its connection are one and the same.
Therefore, connection belongs to the real entity itself, which is the effect.

Furthermore, this remains in that very same state; for in the world, existence is observed in things that are being related, but the state of being related is never observed in the case of a rabbit's horn. Nor does existence arise from the relation of an already established entity; if it did, then even a rabbit's horn, upon reaching completion, would enter into a relation, or else the effect itself would not enter into a relation at all.

If it is argued that [the objection does not apply] because of equality, since the non-perception of a relation is equal whether [the effect] exists or does not exist: just as a non-existent thing such as a sky-flower is not seen to be related by means of the two kinds of inherence (samavāya) with its own causes, such as existence (*sattā*) and so forth, in the same way, an existent thing is also not seen to be related; for what is being related here is not something indistinct, since at the time of the relation it possesses substantial reality (*vastubhāva*), like the threads [in the case of a cloth].
It might be thought: "Surely at the time of the relation the effect exists, for it is a real entity in the very process of arising, just as the threads are the cause of the cloth."

And while coming to its final completion (*pariniṣṭhā*), the entity becomes related, because the time of completion and the time of relation are one and the same; "completed" and "related" refer to a single moment, as there is no division of time.

Therefore, it has been stated that relation belongs only to a real entity (*vastu*) and not to a non-entity, but it is not a conjunction (*saṃyoga*) between cause and effect, because they are inseparable (*ayutasiddha*).

"Separate existence" (*yutasiddhi*) is the state of existing as unconnected; however, an effect does not exist unconnected to its cause. Rather, the notions "it has been produced" and "it is connected" refer to the same moment.
Therefore, the cause and the effect are not conjoined (*saṃyukta*).
(Nyāyavārttika 2, composed by Uddyotakara)

1.33 To this it is replied: This remains in the very same state; because the state of being produced (*niṣpadyamāna*) precedes the actual arising, and because the effect is non-existent prior to its arising, how can there be a connection for that which is non-existent, such as a sky-flower? If not, then in that state the effect would have to be existent already, since it is connected with its own causes and with existence, just like an already accomplished effect.
For in the world, existence is observed in things that are being related; this is the example by similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).

Indeed, the state of being related is not observed in the case of a rabbit’s horn; this is the example by dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*). Thus, there is either an inference that establishes an undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭāpādana-anumāna*), namely: "At that time, the effect is not related because it is non-existent, like a sky-flower"; for neither final accomplishment (*pariniṣṭhā*) nor relation constitutes existence. For neither final accomplishment nor relation—though they are seen elsewhere—can produce existence for what is non-existent, such as a sky-flower; for it is only that which is already existent that is seen to have final accomplishment and relation.

If existence were to arise from the completion [of its causes] or from a relation, then even a rabbit’s horn would, upon reaching completion, become related and thus exist as something completed and related;

however, because it is non-existent, like an effect, the effect itself would not be related to its own causes or to existence while reaching its final completion, because it is non-existent, like a flower in the sky.

And regarding the word "then" (*tadā*): if, as you have stated, one accepts that the completion (*niṣṭhā*) and the relation [to an effect] occur at the same time, then even for a non-effect such as a sky-flower, there would likewise be completion and relation with its own causes and with existence (*sattā*) at that same time; this is the undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭāpādana*).
This is so because, in this way and that, even for an effect such as a sky-flower... [the same would apply].

If it is argued that [the objection] does not apply because of the similarity [of the case], the following might be thought: "This undesirable consequence (aniṣṭāpādana) is not tenable. Why? Because the non-perception of a relation is equal whether [the thing] exists or does not exist.

The explanation of this is as follows: from the words "just as of the non-existent" up to the point where the subject under discussion is introduced. Just as the state of being related through the relation of inherence (samavāya)—which is twofold, consisting of the relation to its own cause and the relation to existence (sattā)—is not observed in the case of non-existent things such as a sky-flower; and by the inclusion of the word "etc.," [it is implied] that it is also not observed in relation to categories such as substantiality (dravyatva), quality-ness (guṇatva), and action-ness (karmatva). This is the illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta).

The illustrative application beginning with "in that same way" has already been explained; for it is not just anything unrelated or undifferentiated that is under discussion here, because of the mention of its own cause, its own existence, and so forth—
as in the case of an existent thing [arising] from its own cause, its own existence, and so on.
To this we reply: that very relation does not exist at all, because it has not come into being while its relata already exist, like the horn of a hare.
It must necessarily have an existing object, because it is a relation, like the conjunction of two fingers.

If, however, the threads—the causes for the existence of the self and what belongs to the self, as well as the cloth and the dyed color—were to be related to that cloth, [only then could such a relation exist].
But that is not so;
for those very threads, while reaching their final completion, become connected—thus there is no division of time regarding the connection between the existence of cause and effect.
Therefore, if they are merely "threads" at that time, this doctrine would be like the doctrine of a mere primal cause such as *puruṣa*.

Even the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) would not be fulfilled; for, like a coil of thread, because the states before and after are identical, the relation [between cause and effect] would be purposeless, and there would be no distinction between being established and not being established. If it is argued that the cloth [is already present], we reply: that is not a relation at all, because it does not come into being among existing things, like the horn of a hare. Thus, by means of this argument establishing an undesirable consequence, the inequality of the relation between the non-existent and the existent is demonstrated.

The relation of the effect with its own causes and its own existence exists even prior [to the production of the effect]; this is the proof for that point: it must be by means of that very relation of inherence (*samavāya*) which has an existing object as its domain, because it is a relation; just as conjunction (*saṃyoga*), being denotable by the word "relation," takes two existing fingers as its objects, so too inherence takes the cause and the effect as its objects only when they exist, because its occurrence is dependent on two factors. Therefore, wishing to state the fault in this very context by way of the linguistic usage of words and their meanings, he says: "If, however, the self... and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "their own causes are their own existence" (*svakāraṇāni svasattā*), the word *sva*—which has synonyms such as "self," "one's own," and "wealth"—here functions with reference to either the self or what belongs to the self, according to the speaker's intention. Now, that effect—the object [of causality]—must exist; for if those two, the cloth and the manifestation, were present, the causal threads would be connected to that cloth by way of performing the action of producing the cloth. But that cloth does not exist. In its absence, what could be the object of the agency of the causes? This is the meaning.

Those very threads, being devoid of the existence of qualities (*vyañjana*) and the agency of acting, reach their final completion; they are connected while being independent of cause and effect, like a flower in the sky. Thus, it follows that there is no temporal distinction for the relationship between the existence of cause and effect.
If you ask, "What is the fault in this?", it has already been stated that there can be no connection with what is non-existent.

Furthermore, it is said as follows: if, at that time, those threads—being devoid of causal activity due to the absence of an effect—are merely "threads" and this doctrine were to become like the assertion that "this is merely the primal cause, such as the Puruṣa," then how could there be the theory of the non-existence of the effect (*asatkāryavāda*)? Even the theory of the existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) favored by the Sāṅkhyas—that modifications are latent within primordial nature (*prakṛti*)—would not be fulfilled, because you accept a doctrine of a cause that is entirely inactive, like the water of a still lake or like the sky; thus it would not be fulfilled. I do not say it is not fulfilled, for that would be harsh; rather, it is stated with conciliation.

What is it like? It is like coiled threads (*tantvākuṇḍalana*). Just as threads that are coiled—that is, gathered together—lack causality when they are independent of actions such as being stretched by a weaver, being moistened, being spread out, and being woven, because the effect, namely the cloth, is not seen there at all; for indeed, the cloth is not perceived while the threads are coiled. Thus, this mere cause is a "satkārya" (pre-existent effect) that is incomplete, because it remains identical in its state before and after [the action]. In this way, when there is only the state of the mere threads, which are devoid of activity and identical in their prior and subsequent states, there is not even a trace of the effect called "cloth. Therefore, the connection of the causal threads with that [effect] is as purposeless as [the connection] with a sky-flower.

Furthermore, there is the distinction between the completed and the uncompleted, as well as the accumulation of defects; consequently, the effect would be like a flower in the sky, for if one does not resort to the non-exclusive [reason], there can be no connection with the existence of its own cause, nor the co-operation of the two—the threads and the cloth.

And for the purpose of avoiding an unreal connection, [the author] explains this very sentence along with its commentary (*sabhāṣya*) in another way, as Praśasta [Mitra] does: "The two connections" (*sambandhau*) refers to both the connection and the connection [itself]; because the state of completion (*niṣṭhā*) is absolutely non-existent, and because the temporal sequence of causes is exactly the same whether prior or posterior—like space—how could anything remain as something fully completed? It does not remain fully completed. For everything must at all times and in every way be either completely established or not established; there is no distinction [between them].

Thus, the defects of asserting that the cause consists only of the effect-in-process (*asampūrṇasatkāryakāraṇamātravāditva*), the pointlessness of relations (*sambandhānarthakya*), and the lack of distinction between the final and non-final states (*niṣṭhāniṣṭhāviśe�șa*) contradict their own established tenets. *svaḥ* refers to one’s own kinsman (*jñāti*) or oneself (*ātmani*); it is *sva* in three genders when meaning "one's own" (*ātmīya*); and *sva* in the non-feminine gender means wealth (*dhane*).
Thus, in the Amarakośa, [it is said]: "It should be fulfilled from this point," as noted in the Prajñāpāramitā-pañjikā.
