Therefore, Praśasta explains this very sentence along with its commentary in a different way—stating that "the two relations" (*sambandhau*) refers to the relation with its own cause and the relation with existence (*sattā*), supported by the two instances of the cloth and the threads—and that this is for the sake of avoiding the fallacy of non-exclusion (*anekānta*) and for the purpose of excluding a relation with the non-existent; furthermore, because the two relations of completion (*niṣṭhā*) occur at the same time. There might also be a reading here: "the completion (*niṣṭhā*) both culminates (*parinitiṣṭhati*) and does not culminate."
The reading enclosed within these marks does not exist in the Bhāratīya manuscript;
furthermore, there is also a cloth [painting].

Now, lest these faults arise, if one were to accept—by some logic—that even the cloth exists in the threads, then for you, who are an extremist (*ekāntavādin*), this acceptance of non-absolutism (*anekāntavāda*) results in a contradiction of your own tenet. Therefore, he says: "Therefore, the co-existence of the two—the connection with its own cause and existence, and the pair consisting of the threads and the cloth—is not possible without resorting to non-absolutism. There are two connections for the effect, the cloth: its connection with its own causes, the threads, and its connection with its own existence. These two are themselves the two entities: the effect and the causes. Thus, there is that very tetrad. The cloth, being unmanifestly existent (*avyaktasan*) in the state of the threads, is connected with its own causes, the threads, and with its own existence; subsequently, through the operation of causal agents such as the weaver, it becomes manifestly existent (*vyaktasan*) by way of transformation into the nature of a cloth. This power of expression is obtainable only through the influence of taking refuge in the Supreme Lord of Non-dualism (*advaita*), which consists of substance and mode (*dravyaparyāyātmaka*); it is not otherwise.
Therefore, this conceptual construction (vikalpa) as well is corrupted by the defect of connection with the non-existent; thus,
the cloth is like an illusion,
for it does not rely on multiple [causes].
Is it not because of not relying on the Lord who is non-absolute?
And for the sake of avoiding a connection with what is non-existent in the relation between one's own effects and causes, and so forth.

Because the completion (*niṣṭhā*) and the relation (*sambandha*) occur at the same time—explaining this very statement along with its commentary while wishing to avoid the fault of connecting [the two] as non-existent—the learned author provides another interpretation: "The relation and the relation are 'the two relations' (*sambandhau*); the two relations of the completion are 'the completion-and-relations' (*niṣṭhāsambandhau*), not 'the completion and the relation.
Because those two, the completion and the relation, occur at the same time, they are 'the two relations of the completion,' because those two occur at the same time."

"Completed" (*niṣṭhita*) means "completion" (*niṣṭhā*). An effect that has attained the state of a real entity through the movement of its causal factors, which now possesses an indefinable substratum, is called "completed" or "completion. Its two relations—namely, with its own causes and with existence (*sattā*)—occur simultaneously.

Furthermore, the *Bhāṣya* demonstrates this meaning by using the expression "reaching completion" (*pariniṣṭhāṃ gacchat*) as equivalent to "having reached" (*gatam*), according to Pāṇini 3.3.131: "In the vicinity of the present tense, one may use the present tense."

131. Thus, just as another factor (*kāraka*) is seen arising through the operation of causal factors, attaining the state of a real entity (*vastu*), becoming established upon an inexpressible substratum, and then—once accomplished—becoming connected with its own causes and with existence (*sattā*); so too is that [entity] called "cloth" not [the case], because it contradicts the status of being an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), and because it contradicts both one's own words and one's own tenets.

Furthermore, the relation between a finished effect and its causes, as well as with existence (*sattā*), is a relation of separate establishment (*yutasiddha-sambandha*). This is because the effect is established elsewhere than in its causes;
"niṣṭhita" means "niṣṭhā" (completion), and "niṣṭhāṃ gacchat" (going toward completion) and "gata" (gone/completed) have the same meaning.

When the causal factors such as the agent (kartṛ) and others—the weaver, the shuttle, the loom, and so forth—have attained the state of being an entity (*vastubhāva*), that is, have reached the state of becoming an entity (*vastubhavana*) and are thus produced, there arises the effect called "cloth," which has an indefinable substratum (*avyapadeśyādhāra*). Its indefinable substratum is the inherent cause (*samavāyi-hetu*), such as the threads, which serves as the basis for the relation of inherence (*samavāya-sambandha*) that causes the cognition and designation "the cloth is here in these threads. This established effect is called "completion" (*niṣṭhā*).
For that completed [effect], two simultaneous relations occur: with its own causes and with existence (*sattā*).
See page 508, line 3.
This, however, must be considered: it is not fully known by whom and when this *Vākya* and this *Bhāṣya* were composed.

It appears from an examination of the preceding and following texts that there was once a certain work named *Vākya*, which was a concise commentary on the *Vaiśeṣika-sūtras* composed by Kaṇāda; upon that there was a *Bhāṣya* composed by someone else; and upon that there was a certain *Ṭīkā* composed by Praśastamati. See page 517, line 9.
All three of these are no longer found anywhere today.
However, this discussion is not found in the Praśastapādabhāṣya that is currently available; therefore, this Bhāṣya must certainly be distinct from the Praśastapādabhāṣya.
Furthermore, the Praśastapādabhāṣya is not a direct commentary on the Vaiśeṣika Sūtras, but rather an independent treatise.

In ancient works such as the *Tattvasaṅgrahapañjikā*, the *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, and the *Nyāyakumudacandra*, it is mentioned by the name *Padārthapraveśaka* alone; however, in the *Syādvādaratnākara* composed by Vādidevasūri (p. 920), it is also referred to by the name *Praśastakarabhāṣya*. In other texts, it is mentioned simply by the name *Bhāṣya*, whereas at present, it is most commonly known by the name *Praśastapādabhāṣya*.
Thus, many names such as Praśasta, Praśastakara, Praśastadeva, Praśastakaradeva, and Praśastapāda are found for the author of the *Praśastapādabhāṣya*;
furthermore, it appears that *Praśastamati* may also be another name for the same person.

However, this should be noted: in the *Tattvasaṅgrahapañjikā*, the *Sanmatitarkavṛtti*, the *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, the *Nyāyakumudacandra*, and other works, numerous statements by Praśastamati are seen to have been cited; yet, among those, only that which is cited in the *Tattvasaṅgrahapañjikā* within the "Examination of Particularity" (*viśeṣaparīkṣā*) and the "Examination of Inherence" (*samavāyaparīkṣā*) is found word-for-word in the *Praśastapādabhāṣya*. Other statements of Praśastamati, however, are not found at all in the *Praśastapādabhāṣya*.

Therefore, it may be inferred as follows: first, a work consisting of an exposition of the Vaiśeṣika Sūtras along with their commentary was composed by Praśastamati; second, it should be understood that he also composed an independent treatise devoted to describing the Vaiśeṣika doctrine, which is now universally known by the name *Praśastapādabhāṣya*.
(Note: Correct the manuscript readings *ṣyamatsa*, *ya*, *ṣyasatsa* to *ṣyamat sa*, *ya*, *ṣyasa tsa* respectively.)
The two relations—the relation with the agent (*praśasta*) and the relation with the substrate (*niṣṭhā*)—are simultaneous because they occur at one and the same time.

"Niṣṭhita" means "niṣṭhā. When an effect has attained the state of being a real entity (*vastubhāva*) through the movement of its causal factors (*kāraka-parispanda*), and it is a product that cannot yet be designated as having a specific substratum, it is called "niṣṭhita" or "niṣṭhā. Its two relations—with its own causes and with existence (*sattā*)—occur simultaneously.

The commentary (*bhāṣya*) also demonstrates this meaning— that [the action] has reached its completion— even while being expressed by means of the present tense, according to the rule *vartamānasāmīpye vartamānavadvā* (Pāṇini 3.3.131).

Just as another factor (kāraka) is seen arising through the operation of causal factors, attaining the state of a real entity (*vastu-bhāva*), being produced with an indefinable substratum, and then becoming connected with its own causes and with existence (*sattā*); so too it is not the case for that which is called a "cloth," because this contradicts its status as an inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*) and contradicts both its own words and its accepted tenets. Furthermore, the connection of an already completed effect with its causes and with existence is a connection of separate existence (*yuta-siddha-sambandha*), since the effect is established elsewhere than in its causes.
The phrase "the commentary also" indicates that this explanatory text for the sentence also demonstrates the meaning of "has gone," which is the state of having reached completion.

But by what characteristic is it said that, while being "gone," it is "going"? We reply: according to Pāṇini 3.3.131, "or [the present tense is used] like the present when there is proximity to the present."

131. To the question "What is this like?", he provides an illustration: "Just as another causal factor (*kāraka*) is seen arising. This means that another causal factor, distinct from [the original] causal factor, is produced—that is, it has arisen. Why? Because of the reference to an object that has entered the range of vision by the word "seen" (*dṛṣṭa*). Otherwise, it would not be "seen," for if that which is arising were unarisen, its entry into the range of vision would be impossible.

What, then, is that? Having attained the state of a real entity—the acquisition of its own self-nature—through the operation of causal factors, namely the activity of Devadatta, the pot, the wood, and so forth; having come into being as something previously unnameable and supported [by its causes]; and being called "rice-gruel" (*odana*) and the like, it becomes connected with its own causes, such as the rice grains, and with existence (*sattā*), just as that which is called a "cloth" (*paṭa*) does.

Regarding this, we say: that too is not correct. For one who speaks thus, there are two faults: a contradiction with one's own words and a contradiction with one's own accepted tenets, due to the incompatibility with the status of being an inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*).

Substance has been described as that which possesses action, possesses qualities, and is an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), because it initiates another substance, as well as qualities and actions, through inherence. However, if the effect—consisting of the triad beginning with substance—once it has attained the state of being a real entity (*vastubhāva*), were to be connected with its causes and with existence (*sattā*), then the causal substances such as threads would be non-initiators and non-causes. Consequently, both your own statement and your formal commitment—that "substance is the inherent cause of effects"—would be subverted, [as shown] from the words "for what reason...
up to "...because of their being already established."

These two, moreover, involve contradictions with one's own statements and accepted tenets. For it has been stated and accepted that the relation of inherence (*samavāya*) is an inseparable connection (*ayutasiddha*) among effect and cause, quality and possessor of quality, individual and form; yet now, a connection of an already established effect with its causes and with existence (*sattā*) is accepted. But that is a connection of separable entities (*yutasiddha*), because the effect is already fully established elsewhere than in its causes, like a jar and space (see *Guṇasamavāyin*, p.
The reading here might also be: "This substance [is] the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa). This is not [the case]. Bhāṣya.

If it is argued that this [inherence] is now [the cause], and that what is stated— namely, the cessation of the status of being an inherent cause— is intended, we say no, because there is no inherence elsewhere.

If it is argued that there is no fault because [the cause] is praised by Praśastamati (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra), that too is not a valid rebuttal; for it is a mere assertion, it contradicts the logical proof stated by oneself, it is irrelevant to the point at hand, it is established elsewhere, it does not function there— just as a jar [does not function] in its threads— and it does not originate there, since its production is unconnected to that [substratum].

As for what is said—"No; because of non-inherence elsewhere"—there might also be the reading "yadi tasyānyatra samavāyo 'bhyupagamyeta syād ayaṃ doṣaḥ," meaning that this fault would arise if its inherence in something else were admitted, but it is not so admitted; therefore, there is no fault. This appears to be the intended sense here. Furthermore, like the production of an effect, a sky-flower ought to be produced, because it is unconnected with causes.
If you argue that [the effect does not arise] because there is no cause, then cloth and other such things would also not arise because they lack a cause, like a sky-flower;
or else, this reading might also be applied here: "Or rather, let the sky-flower arise just as the effect arises—why does the sky-flower not arise?
Just as threads and the like are not causes for an effect—whether that effect exists in them or does not exist—so too would everything everywhere be a cause.

As for the passage beginning with "But as for what is said" and ending with "therefore there is no fault," which sets forth the rebuttal of the objection regarding the cessation of [the self's] being an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of substance—having raised the doubt, "If it is argued that this means the cessation of being an inherent cause," [the author replies]: "No, because it does not inhere elsewhere.
Since the explanation of that [passage], beginning with "If it were its... and so on, has already been well-written, it is not further elaborated here.

That too is not a valid rebuttal because it is merely a matter of wishful thinking. Your statement—that the description of a finished effect as being related to its causes is a way of speaking about inherence elsewhere—is contradicted by the subsequent sentence, "because there is no inherence elsewhere. That [subsequent sentence] contradicts the former; therefore, since it is untenable and its meaning is contradictory, your words are mere wishful thinking and not a rebuttal. To this he says: "Because its meaning is contradicted by the proof stated by yourself. Its meaning is contradictory because the effect is unrelated to those causes. It is unrelated because it is already fully established elsewhere. How so? Just as a pot is in the threads. Just as a pot, because it is not established in the threads but is established elsewhere in the shards, is indeed unrelated to the threads, so it is with the effect consisting of substance and the rest.
If it is argued that this is unestablished, we say no; for [the cloth] does not operate there, just as a jar [does not operate] in its threads—this is the sense.

There is non-operation there and operation elsewhere because it does not originate there; and there is no origination there because it originates unconnected with those [threads], since you yourself accept the origination of the cloth as something unconnected with those causes. Thus, the commencement, operation, and completion of the cloth do not exist in the threads, just as they do not exist in a jar, or in space, or in a sky-flower.
Or, generally speaking, the single reason is simply "because it originates unconnected with them."
Anticipating this objection,
[the author] begins that statement right there, even though it is unconnected to that [preceding point].
Because of the production of what is desired [in one place] and the non-perception of it in that very same place.

And here, the undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭāpādana*) regarding the jar itself, space itself, and the [Self] itself— as stated in the *Bhāraṅhī* and *Pra*— is as follows: "and of the effect," and so forth.

If it is argued: "Let the sky-flower arise, because it is unconnected with causes, like the effect you yourself accept; for it is without a cause," [we reply: "The sky-flower is without a cause, whereas cloth and such things have causes; therefore, because there is a disparity between the example and the subject of the example, this undesirable consequence is illogical. To this it is said: "Cloth and such too," etc. Even cloth and such effects should not arise, because they are without a cause, like the sky-flower;
and its being without a cause follows from its being unconnected with a cause, just like space.

"Let that [non-existent effect] arise"—this is like the arising of an effect that is unconnected to its cause; it has already been stated that "let the sky-flower arise," because it lacks a cause, just as in the case of threads and so forth. Threads and the like possess causality only through their connection with an effect; therefore, what is non-existent in them cannot, according to the circumstances, be its own effect, nor can it be the effect of something else, because there is no connection.
Consequently, the connection exists even prior [to the production of the effect].
This meaning of the terms "relation" (*sambandha*) and "inherence" (*samavāya*) also fits in this very way:

relation is bondage through unification; because [the cause] is the self of all things in their manifoldness, there is movement toward unification, which is "binding" (*aya*). Inherence is comprehension (*avagati*), characterized by the identity of the cause and the existent effect.
Out of fear of such a logical fallacy, you maintain this refutation of the "unnameable substratum" (avyapadeśyādhāratva):

namely, that this unnameable substratum is the locus of effects such as substance (dravya) which are nameable, and that it is inherent in its own causes even prior [to their manifestation], because it is eternally established, like all-pervading space (vibhu), the spherical atom (parimaṇḍala), or the ether (viyat).

He introduces the following [conclusion], which was stated [previously]: that even for an existing effect, there are no causes for something absolutely non-existent—such as a sky-flower—or for a pot, which is to be accomplished by other causes: "In all cases, the cause... and so forth. The term *kāraṇa* (cause) is derived from the agentive sense of the root *kṛ* ("to do/make"); thus, it is a causal instrument. A sky-flower or the like, or a pot, is not made by threads; therefore, in those cases, they are not causes. However, a cloth is made; therefore, they are its causes. Whatever connection (*yoga*) exists according to its proper application belongs only to its own specific effect: threads for a cloth, potsherds for a pot, and so on. It does not belong to what is non-existent, nor to another effect. Why? Because of the lack of relation (*asambandha*). The relationship of cause and effect occurs only when there is a state of relatedness; therefore, there must be a relation even prior to the production of the effect, and thus it has a relation with its causes beforehand.

How could that effect be established by its causes if it were unconnected to them? Therefore, it is inferred that the effect exists in an unmanifest state and becomes manifest while always being connected to its own causes;
this applies appropriately to its own effect, and not to what is non-existent or to another's effect, because there would be no connection.
Thus, the connection exists even prior [to manifestation].
This very meaning of the terms "relation" (*sambandha*) and "inherence" (*samavāya*) is established in this same way:
relation is bondage through oneness, because [the cause] possesses the nature of all things;
inherence is movement through oneness, which is "going" (*ayaḥ*), and it is inherence by virtue of comprehension (*avagatyā*), characterized by the identity of the cause and the existent effect.

Out of fear of such a logical fallacy, you perform this "crushing of the heterodox path," namely: that this [substratum] which cannot be designated [as a substance] is the substratum for that which can be designated—such as substances and their effects—which are inherent in their own causes even prior [to their production], because they are already established, like space, which is all-pervading and spherical. This is precisely what is being refuted.
The transcendence of all, and all in the dative, and all in the genitive.
That yoga which is in the *pralāda* and other [states],
what is it?
The meanings of the words *sambandha* (relation) and *samavāya* (inherence) are also established in this very way and not otherwise; therefore, he says "yo 'yam" and so forth.

The prefix *sam* denotes the state of becoming one (*ekārthībhāva*). *Sambandha* is a binding (*bandha*) through unification (*ekībhāvena*). It expresses that object wherein a manifold thing called a "cause" becomes indeed one when it is called an "effect," and is thereby bound together with one another. Because it consists of the nature of the manifold as a whole, there occurs a transformation (*pariṇati*) of the manifold—such as threads and the like—without each abandoning its own individual self, by way of becoming a single composite whole known as an effect such as a cloth.

"Motion (*gati*) is the transformation of movement (*gamana-pariṇati*), characterized by *ava*, which means 'departure' (*apagamana*); through this departure—that is, by the abandonment of prior attributes such as shape and so forth—there occurs a transformation into the state of a cloth (*paṭatva-pariṇāma*) by way of substance and modification (*dravya-paryāyābhyām*), without abandoning the nature of the threads (*tantutva*). Having thus explained the meaning according to the literal sense of the words, he speaks in order to clarify the reality: "characterized by the oneness of the effect existing in the cause. This is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) of the relationship: that while the causes are scattered, the pre-existing effect attains oneness and, becoming the cloth, reaches manifestation.
[This is stated] for fear of falling into that [opposite] view, and so forth.

Out of a sudden fear arising from attachment to one's own position and aversion toward the positions of others—fearing "I shall not attain the ultimate doctrine of non-dualism, which consists of both substance and modification"—you thus perform this crushing of the wrong path at an inappropriate time, which serves only to exhaust your power.

If it is asked, "What is this crushing of the wrong path? it is replied: that which was previously explained as being the "inexpressible substratum" (avyapadeśyādhāratva)—why is that undertaken again here? Because, according to the Vaiśeṣika Sūtra (7), that inherence (samavāya) exists between cause and effect.

2.29 Thus, inherence (*samavāya*) is inferred from the notions and designations "here" pertaining to cause and effect; however, that is not possible here because the effect is non-existent. Therefore, this construction of a relationship between an effect and an unnameable substratum is a laborious deviation from the path and is purposeless; moreover, it is merely a false designation.

Do not think that the effects such as substance (*dravya*) exist prior to their production without a designatable substratum or without being inherent (*asamaveta*) in their causes; rather, let it be considered that they exist in those very [causes], and thus it should be understood: the effects such as substance possess a designatable substratum and are inherent in their own causes even prior to their manifestation, because according to your own view they are already fully established (*pariniṣṭhita*). Furthermore, as for the rebuttal that was stated—"No, because there is no conjunction (*asaṃyoga*); for there is no conjunction of the effect with those things connected to the cause" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra, Praśastamati)—that too is not a valid rebuttal, because as previously stated, the absence of conjunction is unestablished (*asiddha*).

The view of many is that, because of the concealment of reality, there is a subsequent connection with existence for an entity already inherent in its cause, for the purpose of designating it as "existent" and so forth.

The intention of the author of the *Vākya* (Bhartṛhari) is followed here in the phrase "at the very time of the production of the object," because [the effect] has attained the state of being a real entity (*vastubhāva*), like space and so forth which possess all-pervasive spherical dimension (*vibhu-parimaṇḍala*). Just as the substances—space, time, direction, and the self—which possess the quality of all-pervasiveness, are established as such and are designated as the substrata for the quality of pervasiveness; likewise is the case with effects such as substances. Similarly, atoms possessing spherical dimension (*parimaṇḍala-parimāṇa*) are inherent in their own sphericity and are designated as the substrata for dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and other effects. Thus, it is established that just as space and atoms—the respective substrata of the qualities of pervasiveness and sphericity—are the designated substrata and the inherent loci for dyads and the like, so too is the case for effects such as substances.

Thus, for one who asserts that the two [substances] already possess an established relation, the attempt to avoid the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the cessation of the substance’s status as an inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇatva) is ineffective;
[this is shown by the passage beginning with] "because of the absence of production" (*utpattirūpābhāvāt*), etc. (Praśastapāda-bhāṣya).
Thus?

"It appears correctly that it is merely a false conceit"; even before this,
there might also be the reading "prāgapīti" (even previously).

As for the rebuttal that was stated—"No, because there is no conjunction of this [effect] with [the cause]," for "there is indeed no conjunction of the effect with those things related to the cause" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra, Praśastamati)—that too is not a valid rebuttal, because, as already explained, the non-existence of conjunction is unestablished.

For many hold the view that, following the merging into the ultimate principles (*tattva*), a thing inherent in its cause subsequently enters into a relation with *sattā* (Being) for the sake of being designated by terms such as "existent";
however, the intention of the author of the *Vākya* (Praśastapāda) follows the view that this occurs at the very moment of the object's production.

Regarding the passage beginning with "even in the case of dyads and so forth" and "the removal of the defect of the separateness of cause and effect as stated by us"— [we reply: no, because there is no conjunction between these.

He explains this: "Indeed, there is no conjunction of the effect with those things that are related to its cause, as in the case of two fingers being joined in space—where there is a conjunction of the two fingers which are the causes of the conjunction with space, yet those [fingers] are separately established (yutasiddha). It is not so for the effect, such as a substance, that there is a conjunction with any things related to its cause, by virtue of which the fault of separate establishment would follow, as it does for two things that are independently established. Therefore, because there is no conjunction—that is, because of the difference from conjunction—there is an absence of separate establishment. Therefore, conjunction is [of three kinds]: that produced by the action of one, that produced by the action of both, and that produced by another conjunction. Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 7.2.10.
11. Conjunction produced by the action of one [of two things] occurs, for example, through the approaching action of a hawk toward a post;
conjunction produced by both occurs through the approaching of two wrestlers;

and conjunction produced by conjunction occurs when, from the conjunction of a cause and a non-cause, a conjunction arises between an effect and a non-effect, such as the conjunction of two fingers with space resulting from the two conjunctions of the individual fingers with space.
By this, disjunction is explained:
"Disjunction produced by the action of one [of two things] occurs from the moving away of a hawk" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 7.2.12).
That produced by the action of both [substances] arises from the moving apart of two rams.

That produced by disjunction, however, occurs when, immediately upon the destruction of the two fingers due to their mutual disjunction, there is a disjunction between the finger and space; or, from the disjunction between the cause and the non-cause—such as between the hand and space—there is a disjunction between the body and space.
The absence of conjunction and disjunction [in the case of atoms] is explained by [the discussion of] minuteness and magnitude. Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 7.1.23–25.
The meaning is that those two do not exist because of the absence of separate establishment;
actions [are established] by actions, and qualities by qualities. Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 7.1.28.
2.14. The meaning is that they do not possess conjunction or disjunction because of the absence of separate existence (yutasiddhi).
Due to the absence of separate existence, conjunction and disjunction do not exist between cause and effect; Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 7.1.6.

There is no mutual conjunction or disjunction between cause and effect, as in the case of a jar and its shards, because of the absence of separate existence (*yutasiddhi*). Separate existence consists in either both or one of two things possessing distinct motion; this applies to eternal things. Alternatively, for non-eternal things, it consists in inherence in different substrates, as in the case of the tactile sense-organ and the earthly body.

"Furthermore, there is no inherence in a common substratum between the jar and its shards, because the jar inheres in those very [shards] themselves"—this is stated in Candrānanda’s *Vaiśeṣikasūtravṛtti*, pp. 27 B–28 A.
To this it is replied: even that is not a solution, because, as previously stated, the absence of conjunction remains unestablished.

If [the cloth] has been fully established, set in motion, and begun there [in the threads], how could it be unconnected with them? By such elaboration, it is stated that they are indeed connected; this is further confirmed by the explanation of the meanings of the words "connection" (*sambandha*) and "inherence" (*samavāya*).

Therefore, as stated, because non-conjunction (*asaṃyoga*) is unestablished, the [opponent's] rebuttal fails. If, however, the production [of the cloth] therein and so forth were unestablished, and its connection were likewise unestablished, then non-conjunction would exist, and consequently, the fault of "separate establishment" (*yutasiddhi*) would be avoided.
Thus, this alternative explanation is likewise untenable;
for if only the words "so 'pi na" were the root citation (pratīka), then the reading "so 'pi na, na parihāraḥ" found in the Bhāṣya would also be consistent.

See page 514, line 3; see page 515, line 3. Now, having gathered together the views of the authors of the Vākya, Bhāṣya, and Ṭīkā who support the position of the Sūtrakāra, [the author] says the following to refute the view of the Sūtrakāra—since the others follow the principal one—in this manner: "Because of its dissolution into reality (tattva), for the purpose of denoting 'Being' and so forth, the subsequent Bhāṣyakāras [state that] the entity inherent in the cause..."
The intention of the Prāśastamatas is that there is a relationship between an established entity, its own causes, and its own existence;
however, all three of these are unreal because their meanings are mutually contradictory, like [the simultaneous claims of] being a celibate youth, a father, and [a son].
This very example is cited elsewhere as well.
Likewise, since [the speaker] follows the lead of everyone, it might also be argued that the speaker or the author of the treatise is himself untrustworthy or a liar;
furthermore, the impossibility of the conceptual alternatives regarding "existence" (*sat*) and so forth remains exactly as previously stated.

As for the claim that substances and the like are by their very nature the objects of verbal expression and cognition because they possess existence (*sattva*), just like "existence" (*sattā*) itself—[this is untenable].

Just as the designation and cognition of "existent" (sat) apply to *sattā* and the like by their own nature and not through a connection with another *sattā*, so too the designation and cognition of "existent" apply to substances (*dravya*) and the rest by their own nature and not through a connection with *sattā*. To this objection, it is replied: This is not so, because substances and the like are not identical to *sattā* and thus lack its essential nature; therefore, the designation "existent" and so forth are caused by *sattā*, just as the status of being "possessed of a staff" is caused by a staff. It is the opinion of many that the connection with *sattā* occurs at the time [of the object's existence], whereas the intention of the author of the *Vākya* (Vātsyāyana), followed by the authors of the *Bhāṣya*, is that it occurs at the very moment of the object's production.

The intention of the venerable [author]—that is, our own intention—is that there is a relationship between an established entity, its own causes, and its own existence. Why is it that all three of these are unreal?
Because they involve mutually contradictory meanings.

What is the contradiction in meaning that has been shown? It is like [the case of] being both a celibate student from childhood (*kumārabrahmacārin*) and a father. If he is a father, how can he be a celibate student from childhood? Or, if he is a celibate student from childhood, how can he be a father? This very example applies elsewhere as well; since there is a contradiction with one's own stated reasoning and accepted tenets, this same example should be cited for those cases as well—such as when [the fault applies] to the speaker, and so forth.

Since all authors of *vākya*, *bhāṣya*, and *ṭīkā* follow the views of the original author of the treatise (*śāstrakāra*), it might also be thought that he alone is untrustworthy or a speaker of falsehood; thus, in accordance with worldly convention, this is stated as if with suspicion. This is done so that there may be no quarrel with those devoted to him who—having their minds drawn by respect for the Teacher (*tīrthakara*)—are provoked by such harsh words as "he is indeed untrustworthy," lest they engage in dispute with others. (Viśeṣāvaśyaka-bhāṣya, verse 147). Because of the absence of faults such as [the aforementioned defects]... (praśasta) ...because of the absence of faults... (viśeṣa).
The meaning is that this is the intention of Praśastamati regarding the two types of aversion.

The commentators have asserted that an established entity has a relationship with its own causes and with its own existence; therefore, their intention is that all three of these are unreal because they involve mutually contradictory meanings, like [the claims] that one is a celibate student from childhood and yet a father.

This very same example applies elsewhere as well; for if the speaker or the author of a treatise were [the sole authority], then because everyone would have to follow him, it would follow that he alone is untrustworthy or a liar,
and the impossibility of the alternatives regarding existence and so forth remains exactly as previously stated.
Existence is the relation with existence.

Furthermore, as for the claim that substances and so forth are by their very nature the objects of the designation and cognition "existent" because they possess existence—just as existence and the like are by their very nature the objects of the designations and cognitions "existent," and not due to a connection with [another] existence—likewise, substances and so forth also have the designations and cognitions "existent" by their very nature, and not due to a connection with existence: to this it is replied—it is not so, because there is no identity (atādātmya).

Since substances and so forth do not have existence as their intrinsic nature, the designation "existent" and so on is caused by *sattā* (existence), just as the state of being a staff-bearer is caused by a staff; [this] *sattā* is the relation with *sattā*. (Praśastapādabhāṣya)
The contradiction shown by Praśasta [is] to be seen on page 514, line 2.

Furthermore, as previously stated, the impossibility of conceptualizing [the effect] as existent and so forth remains exactly as it was; for even by one who asserts that the time of the completion (*niṣṭhā*) and the relation are identical, the question remains: is the relation of the effect with existence [of] something existent, non-existent, or both existent and non-existent? Thus, the self has not been liberated from this critique.

For example: is the relation of the effect with existence [of] something already completed, uncompleted, or both completed and uncompleted? Since the underlying reasoning is the same, the fault cannot be avoided merely by uttering different words.
Let it be seen: page 508, line 3; "sattāyāḥ" [in] the manuscript "pra°"; "pravartaca°" [in] the manuscript "ya°".

Regarding the passage beginning with "Furthermore, as for substances and so forth," the meaning is that substances and so forth are, by their very nature, the objects of verbal designation and cognition because they exist— that is, because they exist inherently, which means they exist by way of their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

What is it like? It is "like existence (*sattā*) and so forth," etc., which is a proof for establishing an undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭāpādanasādhana*) directed against the Vaiśe�ṣika, its meaning having been explained up to the point where it is said, "because of the connection with existence. Then, the following rebuttal is indeed stated by the followers of Kaṇāda (*Kāṇāda*): "This is not so, because of the lack of identity (*atādātmyāt*). That which has that as its essence is "identical" (*tadātman*), such as existence and so forth; the state of being that is "identity" (*tādātmya*). Because substances and the rest possess a different nature from that, they are "not identical" (*atādātmya*). The explanation of this, up to the words "designation and so forth," has already been covered.

The analogy is: "like the state of being a staff-bearer (daṇḍitva) for one who was not previously a staff-bearer, caused by the staff. Just as one who possesses a staff is called a "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍī*), so the state of being a staff-bearer—which belongs to one who was not previously a staff-bearer—is caused solely by the staff; likewise, for a substance (*dravya*) and so forth, which are non-existent in their own nature, the designation "existent" (*sat*) and so on is caused by existence (*sattā*). [Note: *pra.* refers to the commentary. *daṇḍanimittādaṇḍadaṇḍitvavaditi dṛṣṭāntaḥ, yathā daṇḍo'syāstīti daṇḍī iti daṇḍitvamadaṇḍadaṇḍino daṇḍanimittamevaṃ dravyāderasadātmanaḥ sattānimittaṃ sadabhidhānādīti* // [End of fragment] *...vadi savyākhyāna pra॰ ॰tvasaṃdaṃḍādaṃḍinobhā॰* [Fragmentary notation of the source text].

Regarding the statement, "The one who possesses the staff [is known] from the staff, which is non-existent in itself," we deliberate upon this: how is this identity [established]? Is it because of the existence of that which is existent, or because of its making [something] existent? If, first of all, it is an existence by itself, then it has been stated that everything that exists exists by itself alone.
Now, as for the argument regarding "being honored" (*satkāra*), that has already been refuted previously.

Just as in the case of *sattā* (existence), the designation and cognition of "existent" (*sat*) occur by its own nature because they are identical with it, so too in the case of substance (*dravya*) and the like, or substantiality (*dravyatva*) and the like, their identity with existence is the cause of the designation and cognition of "existent" everywhere.

Furthermore, since the designation and cognition of "staff" (*daṇḍa*) are established even when the staff exists merely through identity with it, the designation and cognition of "the man with a staff" (*daṇḍin*) occur by their own nature; they do not occur without such identity.

The intention might be that just as the staff exists by itself through identity (*tādātmya*), like existence (*sattā*), so too does the possessor of the staff (*daṇḍin*); or alternatively, the intention might be that just as existence exists by itself through identity, so too does the staff.
Now, it might be argued: "The staff also, by virtue of the universal 'staffness' (*daṇḍatva*) which is distinct from the staff, is the locus of the designation and cognition of 'staff'."

In that case, "the man with a staff" (*daṇḍin*) would be a non-example; for [you claim] there is no state of being a staff (*daṇḍya-bhāva*) in the staff, since it is only from a staff established as such by its "staff-ness" (*daṇḍatva*) that one becomes "the man with a staff.

Here we deliberate with you: how is this identity (*tādātmya*)? Is it because of the existence of what exists—that which comes into being is the identity of that existent, its acquisition of self, its experience of its own nature—or is it the act of making something existent?

If, first of all, existence (*bhavana*) belongs to that which already exists, then it has been stated that everything that exists—whether as "existence" (*sattā*) and so forth, or as "substance" (*dravya*) and so forth—is established by itself alone.
Alternatively, if it is argued that something becomes existent because it is made existent (*satkaraṇāt*) due to identity (*tādātmya*), that has already been refuted previously:

for existence does not make substance and the like existent when they are already self-established, because that would be redundant; nor can what is non-existent become existent, because it lacks existence, like a sky-flower; nor is there any possibility of both being existent and non-existent, as has been stated.
And just as, for the sake of meditation,

the verbal designation and cognition of "existent" apply to substance and so forth, and to substantiality and so forth, by their very own nature because they have that as their essence— just like existence (*sattā*)— and since substance and so forth have that as their essence, namely the essence of the existent; in this same way, the verbal designation and cognition of "existent" apply even to universals (*sāmānya*), which are eternal, single, omnipresent, such as substantiality, quality-ness, and existence, and which are devoid of both universals and particulars.
"Existing everywhere" demonstrates the universal pervasiveness of this principle. Furthermore,
"and even in the staff," and so forth, [shows that] existence is not distinct from the one [reality].

As for the example "just as [the cognition] 'staff-bearer'," that too occurs precisely through identity (*tādātmya*), because the staff itself is the very nature of its existence. Since the designation and cognition of "staff" are established through this identity, they produce the designation and cognition "Devadatta is staff-bearing" in the person Devadatta who possesses the staff, by virtue of their own nature. These two—the designation and the cognition—do not occur without this meaning of identity; therefore, it establishes the point we desire. Otherwise, there would be no distinction between one who has a staff and one who has earrings.

And the proof here is as follows: even the staff (*daṇḍa*) itself produces its own designation and cognition by its very nature, because of its identity (*tādātmya*), just like existence (*sattā*); likewise, the person with the staff (*daṇḍin*) [is established] for that very reason in the same way, as in the passage beginning "and just as... This being the case, it is established that the staff exists by its very nature, independent of the universal-particular (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*) of "staff-ness" (*daṇḍatva*), because of its identity, just like existence.
The logical connection (*anvaya*) is that this [staff] also proves the point we desire.
"Kurvaṃti" means "they perform"; it is a word ending in the locative case (*saptamyanta*),
as in the phrase "tathā ca" and so forth.
Now, [the author] says "athocyeta" and so forth.

The Vaiśeṣika considers even a staff to be distinct from "staffness," yet the Teacher states that it is the bearer of the name and cognition "staff. [The opponent replies: "In that case, 'the man with a staff' (daṇḍin) is not an example, because the state of being the possessor of a staff (daṇḍitva) does not exist apart from the staff itself."

Since the staff (*daṇḍa*) is not established in itself, the person with the staff (*daṇḍin*) is not established. If it is argued that the "person with the staff" is cited for the sake of establishing existence through another [factor], then from what would its establishment come, given that the staff is unestablished? If this is so, this is a case of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*): the establishment of the staff comes from the reality of "staff-ness" (*daṇḍatva*), and the establishment of the person with the staff—established by the qualification of the staff—again results in the establishment of the reality of "staff-ness. Furthermore, it must be determined how there can even be such a thing as a "person with a staff."
If it is argued that [the cognition] is established from the staff alone—which is established by itself—then let it be so;

however, if it is from "staff-ness" (*daṇḍatva*), then let there be "possessor-of-staff-ness" (*daṇḍatvī*), but not "possessor-of-staff" (*daṇḍī*). Furthermore, in this way, there would be a transition to another self (or substrate).
But we say: it exists by itself; for in its absence, everything would consist of nothing but a non-universal nature.
Just as in the case of the staff, so it is even though [the self] exists...

As for what was also said: "Since substances and so forth do not possess that nature [of being *sat*], their designation and cognition as 'existent' (*sat*) result from their connection with *sattā* (Being), and not from a staff-bearer (*daṇḍin*) being established by the staffness (*daṇḍatva*) of the staff. If you say this, we reply: the staff is established through the universal-particular (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*) of staffness; from the staff comes the staff-bearer. Thus, the example is established because the qualified (*viśeṣya*) is established precisely through the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). If you think this, then the following consequence follows: the staff is established from the reality of staffness (*daṇḍatvatattva*), and the reality of staffness is established from the establishment of the state of being a staff-bearer (*daṇḍitva*) which is itself proven by the qualifier "staff. This results in a circular argument (*itaretarāśraya*). And circular arguments are not tenable; as the saying goes, "A boat tied to another boat does not save either. To demonstrate this, the text begins with "itaretara... and continues until "tattvasiddhiḥ," the meaning of which has already been explained.

If you say that the staff is not established [prior to the person], this results in mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*): the establishment of the staff occurs because of the reality of "staff-ness" (*daṇḍatva*), and the establishment of the staff-bearer—established through the qualification of the staff—results in the establishment of the reality of "staff-ness. Furthermore, it must be determined how the term "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍin*) is even possible.
If [the cognition] is established from the staff alone, it has been said that it is established by its own nature (*svataḥ*).

Now, if it is from "staff-ness" (*daṇḍatva*), let there be "possessor-of-staff-ness" (*daṇḍatvī*); let there not be "possessor-of-staff" (*daṇḵī*). Furthermore, in this way, there would be a transition into another self (*ātmāntara*).
But we say: it exists by its own nature; for in the absence of that, everything would be merely of the nature of a non-universal (*asāmānyātmaka*).
Just as in the case of the staff, so it is even when [the cause] exists...
[etc.]
Regarding the statement:

"Even though it was said that because substances and so forth do not have that [existence] as their essence, the designation and cognition of them as 'existent' arise from their connection with existence (sattā), this is not so, because the qualified [entity] is established. (Bhāṣya)
Regarding the passage beginning with "daṇḍī" in the Bhāṣya: it must be determined how Devadatta is "staff-bearer" (daṇḍin)—is it because of the staff-ness (daṇḍatva) or because of the staff (daṇḍa)?
[The answer is: Devadatta is "staff-bearer" because he possesses a staff (daṇḍo 'syāsti).

If it is said that he is established by the staff alone, being established through its own inherent existence, then let him be "possessing-staffness" (*daṇḍatvī*) because he has "staffness" (*daṇḍatva*), but let him not be "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍī*). It is indeed logical that one is a staff-bearer by virtue of the staff, but not by virtue of staffness; moreover, he would be a staff-bearer even by himself. Furthermore, there would be a transition to another self in this way: from staffness, the staff and the staff-bearer would be distinct selves; from the staff, staffness and the staff-bearer [would arise]; and from the staff-bearer, the staff and staffness [would arise]. In that case, the staff, having come into being by itself, becomes that very self by virtue of staffness; and the same applies to the staff-bearer as well.

We, however, say this: that which exists as a staff possesses the very nature of being a staff; whatever becomes a staff, that alone becomes a staff and attains its own identity as something distinct from other entities. That very process of becoming is "staff-ness," and it does not arise from anything separate from it, nor from a reality called "staff-ness" existing apart from it. In the same way, the self-experience of Devadatta who possesses the staff is his true nature.

In the absence of that [universal], everything would necessarily be of a non-universal nature. If that individual—such as a staff or a staff-bearer—does not exist by itself, but exists only through such categories as existence (*sattā*), substantiality (*dravyatva*), staff-ness (*daṇḍatva*), and staff-bearer-ness (*daṇḍitva*), then, since it does not exist by itself, it is non-existent like a sky-flower.

Consequently, existence and the other categories would themselves be non-universals; and that is undesirable, because for something that exists by itself, there is no commonality, and thus a universal would not even be a universal.
Therefore, the staff exists by itself, and likewise the designation and cognition of "existent" occur by themselves, not through connection with existence (*sattā*).
Just as in the case of the staff, so it is with "even though it exists" and so forth; the proof is already explained.

Thus, first of all, it is incorrect [to claim] that because of identity there is the designation "existent" and so forth in respect to existence (*sattā*) and the like, since [existence] is not a staff-ness.
Since he possesses a staff and is a staff-bearer, how is it that you, being a staff-bearer, are called "the one who possesses a staff"?
Because of [the nature of] punishment as described in the Bhāṣya and the Yājñavalkya-smṛti,
Devadatta becomes that [state]. Praśna.
In this context, even the reading "Devadatta does not exist" would be intended to indicate the distinction from other entities;
thus, what is intended to be expressed is that "the staff is a staff, but it is not Devadatta.

Furthermore, regarding what was stated—"because it is not of that nature," etc.—it means that because substance, quality, and action are non-existent in their own right, the designation and cognition of them as "existent" arise from their connection with *sattā* (existence), and not inherently.

That too is not [the case], because it does not have that as its nature (*atadātmakatvāt*), and so forth; the passage beginning with "because of being inconclusive" (*anaikāntikatvāt*) and extending up to "like substanceness and so forth" (*dravyatvādivat*) is intended to demonstrate inconclusiveness. Its explanation is as follows: "Even though substanceness, qualityness, actionness, and potness do not have identity with [the substance] by their own nature," that too is not [the case], because it does not have that as its nature, just like substanceness and so forth.

If it is argued that—given their non-identity with substantiality (*dravyatva*) and so forth—the designation and cognition of "existent" (*sat*) would occur intrinsically [in substances] because they are unitary, like the self (*ātman*); and just as the designation "existent" is observed to apply intrinsically to existence (*sattā*) which resides in substantiality and the rest, so too the designation and cognition of "existent" would apply to substances and the rest even in the absence of a connection with existence, just as the single designation and cognition applies to the quality-ness (*guṇatva*) and action-ness (*karmatva*) despite their being non-numerical; and thus these two would be merely figurative (*aupacārika*) in the case of substantiality and the rest—[we reply: they would be figurative in the case of substances and the rest as well, since the reasoning is identical.

If it is argued that this is not so because, like the case of being a "lion among men" and the like, such [an identity] is not directly possible, then you are merely attributing a fault to your own position;
for if... [the argument continues].
Furthermore, he himself must be asked this:

if it is argued that [the universal] is established within existence (*sattā*), then it is not logical for the self to act upon itself. For if universals and particulars such as "form" (*rūpa*) and "upward motion" (*utkṣepaṇa*) were non-existent by nature, their own designations and cognitions as "existent" would arise from themselves, and not from existence (*sattā*).
Why? Because of oneness:

there is only one substance-ness (*dravyatva*) in all substances, since a second substance-ness is not admitted; therefore, the connection with existence (*sattā*) is not admitted therein, because of the absence of further recurrence (*anupravṛtti*). Nevertheless, it is designated as "existent" (*sat*) and is so cognized. The same applies to quality-ness (*guṇatva*) and the rest.

Therefore, because of their oneness, they possess existence by themselves (*svataḥ-sattvam*), meaning they possess *sattā* like the Self (*ātmavat*). And that example is described as follows regarding its own inherent existence as a substance (*dravyatva*) and so forth: "It is observed that among the distinct [categories] such as substance-ness (*dravyatva*) and the rest, there is the designation 'existent' for the single *sattā* which exists by itself; in the same way, it is established by this proof that substances and the rest also [exist] by themselves alone. See page 517, line 7.

"Because [the property] such as 'substance-ness' (dravyatva) is not non-eternal," or "because it is intrinsic (svataḥ)"— that too is not [correct], because it does not have that nature, just like substance-ness and so forth.

The intention appears to be as follows: "If substance-ness (*dravyatva*) and so forth were not identical [to existence], then the designation and cognition of 'existent' would occur intrinsically [in them] because they are each single [entities], just like the Self (*ātman*); for in substance-ness and so forth, the designation 'existent' is observed to belong to existence itself intrinsically; likewise, substance and so forth would also [possess it] intrinsically because they are not of that nature. This [argument] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because we observe the designation and cognition of 'existent' occurring intrinsically even when there is no identity of nature, as in the case of substance-ness and so forth.

If it is argued that even in the absence of a connection with existence (*sattā*), just as there is a single denotation and cognition for quality-ness (*guṇatva*) and action-ness (*karmatva*) despite their being non-numerical, so too the denotation and cognition of "being" (*sat*) in substance-ness (*dravyatva*) and the like would be figurative (*aupacārika*), [we reply: they would likewise be figurative in substance and the rest, since the case is the same, like [the expression] "lion-man" and so forth. If you say, "No, because it is not possible in the primary sense," then you are merely attributing a fault to your own position.
But if...
Furthermore, he himself must be asked this.

Furthermore, as for what is said—"If it is argued that [the universal] is established in existence... it is not logical for [existence] to [establish] itself by itself"—just as in the case of a staff, even though this is so, the name and cognition of "existent" arise from its own nature due to identity (*tādātmya*), and not from a connection with existence (*sattā-yoga*); such appears to be the intention. To this, he says: "The connection with existence," and so forth.

The single designation and cognition—"oneness" as a quality (*guṇatva*) and "oneness" as an action (*karmatva*)—are seen to be figurative (*aupacārika*) even in the case of the two [entities] that lack number, namely quality-ness and action-ness. Similarly, what is the fault if the designation and cognition of "existence" (*sat*) were also figurative in the case of substantiality (*dravyatva*) and so forth? To this it is replied: the objection beginning with "even in the case of substances, etc. is already answered by the fact that it results in [the same] parity through their being figurative.

He says: "If you argue that it is not so because it is not directly applicable, as in the case of 'man-lion' (manuṣyasiṃha) and the like—just as the qualities of bravery and ferocity, being established as primary in a lion, can be metaphorically applied to a man but cannot be so when unestablished—likewise, if the designation and cognition of 'existent' were established elsewhere in a primary sense, they could then be metaphorically applied to substance and the rest; but those two are not established anywhere [else], and there is no figurative usage without a primary one; therefore, they must be primary in substance and the rest themselves"—if you think thus, then you are merely attributing a fault to your own position.

He explains this with the words "If, however," and so forth; the intended meaning is that even in the case of [the categories] such as *sattā* (existence), direct [perception] and [inference] are unestablished. Furthermore, he says, "This must be asked of him alone": for those who do not accept the designation and cognition of "existent" as being dependent upon an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-sattā*), what is the use of postulating a connection with *sattā*? But for you, who desire a connection with *sattā* and who assert an identity [of the object] distinct from the existence of the entity itself, it is difficult to establish. Therefore, you yourself are the one who must be questioned.

The argument "because it does not have that as its nature" is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because even when something does not have that as its nature, we observe the occurrence of its own inherent designation and cognition, just as in the case of "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) and so forth; such is the intention [of the author], as seen in the *Sato* [text], where it is stated that [the property] exists directly (*vāñjasā*).

Regarding what is further stated—"If it is argued that [existence] is established in existence"—this, along with its commentary, has already been explained. Against whom, however, is this objection appropriate? It is directed at one who maintains that existence, which is distinct from substance and the other categories, is established by itself and constitutes their very nature; for he is none other than the Vaiśeṣika, and it is against him that one should fear [to speak].
[it is] for the purpose of that connection; or when...
"...[it is] for the purpose of that connection; but surely this latter [position] is also untenable."

How can the primary application of the designation and cognition of "existence" to substances and other categories— which are non-existent in their own nature— be logical? It would be like a mere wishful thought.
But it is not at all the case that,

like the state of being the punisher and the state of being the punishment, [the self] exists as something real by its own nature; rather, because it is connected to those [attributes], it exists through their existence, and thus, like existence itself, it is truly existent in its own right.

Therefore, since there is no absence of identity (*atādātmya*) for anything that exists, everything is of the very nature of existence (*sadātman*); thus, there is no possibility of [existence] being figurative (*bhākta*), and like [the categories of] "Being" (*sattā*) and so forth, it possesses existence by its own nature (*svataḥ*). Since this is so, the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) of existence as "the state of being existent" (*sato bhāvaḥ sattā*) refers precisely to an existence that is not distinct from substance (*dravya*) and the other categories; therefore, it is not proper to challenge [this view] by saying "it is not joined to itself by itself. Thus, the section of the *Uddhaṭṭana* commentary beginning with "or when... and extending up to "the cause of conjunction with that" has already been explained. This is the *Uddhaṭṭana* passage of that kind which stands at the beginning.

Now, is not this subsequent [objection] also improper? It is not so; for the statement to be made later—that "the establishment [of existence] occurs directly in substances and so forth"—would be incoherent, because a cognition of existence (*sat-pratyaya*) cannot arise from a cause that does not have that [existence] as its essence. How could the primary designation and cognition of "existent" be appropriate for substances and so forth, which are by nature non-existent? This statement of the Teacher (Ācārya) has fallen into the midst of the opponent's argument in order to expose the opponent's lack of skill; it is like a mere wishful thought. For the Vaiśeṣika, the idea that "existence is distinct from substance and so forth" is nothing more than a wishful thought. If it were the case, then in his own system, the preceding and succeeding positions would indeed be explained [as contradictory].

When the Vaiśeṣika has stated that there are two faults—namely, the negation of the status of being a possessor of substance (*dravyādibhāktatva*) and the contradiction of the statement that "existence is inherent (*svataḥ sattva*)," just like [the universal] *sattā* and so forth—the Teacher says: "Not at all," and so on. Just as "stick-ness" (*daṇḍitva*) and "stick-ness-as-a-universal" (*daṇḍatva*) exist inherently because they are connected to that [the stick], meaning they are connected to existence (*sattā*); likewise, existence itself exists inherently because it exists through existence—that is, because it exists by its own nature (*ātmatva*), meaning it possesses inherent existence (*svataḥ sattva*).

Such is the logical principle: namely, that only the existent is existent, and existence itself is the existent; there is no existence apart from the existent, nor is there an existent other than existence.

Therefore, for everything that exists, there is no non-identity with existence—that is, no nature of non-existence. Because of the absence of that [non-existence], everything is of the very nature of the existent; thus, there is no lack of [the application of] figurative status (*bhāktatva*) and so forth. This is the meaning: "and like existence and so on, there is intrinsic existence (*svataḥ-sattva*)," where the phrase "and so on" includes [intrinsic existence] like substantiality (*dravyatva*), quality-ness (*guṇatva*), and action-ness (*karmatva*), which are used as distinct designations.
[it is] for the purpose of that connection; or when...
[it is] for the purpose of that connection—surely this latter [position] also is untenable.
How can the primary designations and cognitions of "existent" be appropriate for substances and other categories that are non-existent in their own right, like a mere fantasy?
And when?
But certainly not...

The underlying intention appears to be as follows: [the opponent argues that] just as the state of being punished and the act of punishing exist inherently, so too, because they are connected to existence (*sattva*), they exist by virtue of that existence; thus, like existence itself, the existent is truly existent. Therefore, since there is no lack of identity (*atādātmya*) between everything that exists and existence, everything has existence as its very essence. Consequently, there is no absence of figurative usage (*bhāktatva*) and so forth. Furthermore, just like existence (*sattā*) and the like, there is inherent existence, but not the absence of figurative usage regarding substance (*dravya*) and the rest. To claim otherwise would contradict the statement: "Inherent existence is like existence and the like. These constitute the two-fold fault. This is the intended meaning.
Is everything indeed existent?

Since this is so, therefore the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) of "existence" (*sattā*) as "the state of being existent" (*sato bhāvaḥ*) refers precisely to existence that is not distinct from substance (*dravya*) and the other categories; thus [ends] the first section of the *Praśastapādabhāṣya*.
The section on the gift of the *udyuddhaṭṭa* manuscript?
Starting from "yadā vā" and so forth; starting from "pra...
and so forth; and starting from "yadā ca" and so forth?

Is it for the sake of lifting up, or because [the result] is directly established in substances and so forth? (The reading *uddhahanāya* is not in Bhāsarvajña’s commentary; the reading *uddhahadānā* is in Bhāsarvajña’s commentary.)
There may also be a reading here: *ity api pāṭho 'tra syāt* [of this statement] "itasya pra°" [following] "lasyākhyāpa°".
In whatever way, so [it is]; as it is, so [it is].

Just as prior to the connection with a staff, the "staff-bearer" exists because he is established by his own nature through characteristics such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth; and just as prior to the connection with the staff-bearer, the staff also exists because it is established by its own nature through characteristics such as roundness and length—therefore, it is logical that one is called a "staff-bearer" due to the conjunction with a staff—so too, it is logical that a cloth or other object is "blue" due to its conjunction with the substance blue. Likewise, since prior to fire there is no other specific characteristic to manifest its existence, fire is non-existent [prior to its heat]; and for heat as well, there is non-existence prior to its conjunction with fire, because a quality cannot exist without a substratum.
Furthermore, no connection between two non-existent things is observed or accepted;
thus it is stated in the *Tattvārtharājavārtika* composed by Akalaṅka (1.1).
Is all this accompanied by a self? No, it is without a self. (svatvādi) 6.19a evam bhāṣyam.

Regarding this, [the text says] "And because it is thus," and so forth. Since the existence (*sattā*) of substances and the like is logically established as being inherent (*svata eva*), therefore that etymological derivation of the word *sattā*—namely, "the state of being (*bhāva*) of that which exists (*sat*)"—which is intended to introduce a genitive case expressing distinction (*bhedapaṣṭhī*), is understood to have as its object an existence that is non-different from the substance and so forth. Why? Because the genitive case functions in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). Thus, "the state of being of existing things" means that existence is not distinct from those things that exist.
That which is spoken of by the wise as "existent" is the cause of the designation and cognition "existent" everywhere.
Therefore, this apprehension of [existence] without a cause—
that is,
the claim that existence is intrinsic— is also untenable.
For here, when it is said "like existence (*sattā*) and so forth," it is stated according to your own position, not mine.
For me, there is no such thing as "existence" distinct from substance (*dravya*) and the rest;

otherwise, the fallacy would follow that substances and so forth lack a cause and the like. So how has this inconsistency fallen upon me? As for me, however, because substance and the rest are one, there is no inconsistency.

Whether by an agent (*kartṛ*) or a non-agent (*akartṛ*), that which exists as a factor of action (*kāraka*) is itself the state (*bhāva*), the universal (*sāmānya*); it is itself the particular (*viśeṣa*) when independent of the existence of others, being the agent due to its own becoming and ceasing; it is itself the substance (*dravya*), the quality (*guṇa*), and the action (*kriyā*); and it is itself the particular because it is distinguished from other states of being. Furthermore, as will be explained later, it is itself inherence (*samavāya*);
thus, the absence of a relation is refuted along with its non-existence, for there is neither non-conjunction (*asaṃyoga*) nor non-inherence (*asamavāya*).
The suffix *ṇam* [is applied] after those two? It occurs in the sense of the agent (*kartari*), as indicated by the genitive case;

its explanation is as follows: the passage beginning with "that which is by the wise" has already been explained, up to the point where it says "that which is the cause of the designation and cognition as 'existent' everywhere"—[this is stated] for the purpose of providing the basis for the genitive case.
Is it for the purpose of excluding the genitive case (bhāṣya: *ṣaṣṭhyapavādārthā*), or for the purpose of employing the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhyupādānārthā*)?
[The latter], because the genitive occurs in the sense of the agent (*kartari*).
That which is referred to by the wise as "Being" (sat) is the cause of the designation and cognition of "Being" everywhere.

That which is spoken of by the wise, that which the wise become—that is *sattā* (Being); it is the cause of the designation and cognition "existent" (*sat*) everywhere. This is the intended meaning that appears here;
therefore, this too is a grasping based on non-cognition—...
[end of fragment]
...the claim that existence is intrinsic is untenable; for here, when it is said "like existence and so forth," it is stated according to your own position,
not mine, as I do not maintain that there is any existence whatsoever distinct from substance and the other categories.

If it is argued: "Since the faults such as [substances] being non-causes would otherwise follow, why has this inconsistency fallen upon me? For me, however, because substances and so forth are one, there is no inconsistency; substances and so forth possess existence intrinsically (*svataḥ*), like *sattā* and the like, and not through connection with *sattā*," we reply: No. If substances and so forth possessed existence intrinsically like *sattā* and the like, it would follow that they are devoid of genus (*ajātimat*), due to the impossibility of their being related to causes or being eternal.
Therefore, the claim that substances and so forth possess existence intrinsically is untenable.
Thus, the intention appears:

whether by an agent (*kartṛ*) or a non-agent, whatever exists as a factor of action (*kāraka*), that alone is *bhāva* (being), which is the universal; that alone is the particular (*viśeṣa*), because it is the agent independent of the becoming of anything else due to its own becoming and non-becoming; that alone is substance (*dravya*) and quality (*guṇa*); that alone is action (*kriyā*); and that alone is the particular (*viśeṣa*), because it is distinguished from other states of being. Furthermore, according to what will be explained later, that alone is inherence (*samavāya*);
in this very way, the absence of relation is rejected along with [the notion of] non-existence.
There is no non-conjunction (*asaṃyoga*), nor is there non-inherence (*asamavāya*);

apart from those two, there are no categories such as quality (*guṇa*), action (*karman*), generality (*sāmānya*), particularity (*viśeṣa*), or inherence (*samavāya*) other than substance (*dravya*). Rather, it is the transformation (*pariṇāma*) of substance itself—dependent upon the causes for both types of transformation—that occurs under various synonymous designations such as quality, action, generality, particularity, inherence, and so forth.

Thus, in the *Tattvārtharājavārtika* (1.1), the preceding and following positions along with their commentaries—beginning with "Therefore, this also... and so forth—are understood up to the application (*upanaya*) belonging specifically to the Vaiśeṣika. Regarding that which was stated [by the opponent], namely "existence by itself" (*svataḥ sattvam*), the Teacher says the following—"In this case, like existence (*sattā*) and so forth"—in order to show how this [objection] is a mere grasping of what is not a valid cognition (*apratyaya*).

"All this is stated in order to establish you by following your own position; there is no existence (*sattā*) of mine whatsoever that is distinct from substance (*dravya*) and the rest, because it has been said that the genitive case [is used] for the agent, and thus the defects such as the lack of causality in substances and so forth would follow, making it untenable. [Response: "From where has this untenability fallen upon me through that consequence? It has come upon me through your own doctrine, since you have accepted existence and then, like existence itself, have applied an undesirable consequence to substances and the rest. But for me, since substance, quality, action, generality, particularity, and inherence are one, there is no untenability."
The meaning is that it would follow as a logical flaw that substances and so forth would lack causality and other such properties.
And [the question] "Is it due to unity, or not due to diversity? Is it unity, or not due to diversity?"— he explains that with the words "by agents or non-agents," and so forth.

The term *bhāva* [is derived] as "that which exists" (*bhavati*) in the sense of the agent (*kartari*), or "the act of existing" (*bhavanam*) in the sense of the action (*bhāve*); thus, when there is an intention to express such grammatical relations (*kāraka*), that very thing which exists is the *bhāva*, the universal (*sāmānya*), because its nature as "existing" remains identical despite differences in place, time, and so forth.

That very particularity (*viśeṣa*), independent of other existents, is the agent; as stated, the genitive case is used for the agent. Thus, from the act of becoming (*bhavana*), that which becomes is simply "becoming" (*bhavat*). That very substance (*dravya*) is "to-be-become" (*bhavya*) precisely because of its becoming and being. "Calculation" (*kalana*), "multiplication" (*guṇana*), and "quality" (*guṇa*) [are so called] because of its becoming through simultaneous and non-simultaneous modes (*paryāya*). That itself is existence (*bhāva*), action (*kriyā*), becoming (*bhavana*), and "being" (*bhāva*). That very particularity is distinguished from other states of being because it is independent of anything else, because it consists of both the existent and the non-existent, and because it is distinguished by both existence and non-existence. And as will be explained later, the identity of cause and non-cause will be discussed immediately hereafter; that itself is inherence (*samavāya*).

"In this very way," [it means that] by virtue of being the agent (*kartṛ*), it alone possesses causality; and because it attains the state of being an effect through the process of unification with that [agent], the absence of a relation has been rejected by the method already set forth, due to the explanation of inherence (*samavāya*). By the phrase "along with non-existence" (*sahāsattvena*), non-existence itself is established as possessing a relation; thus, both eternality and non-existence do not exist [as unrelated entities].
Furthermore, it is precisely what is being demonstrated that [substances and so forth] are devoid of birth (*ajātimant*);

or rather, substances and the like are without cause, eternal, without relation, and without birth, because they possess intrinsic existence (*svataḥ sattvāt*), just like universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth.

The cause and so forth, as well as the universal and so forth, exist inherently because they possess existence by their own nature, like substance and the rest; and because they are identical in essence to that [existence], both substance and the rest, as well as the universal and the rest, exist inherently, like existence (sattā), due to their being real entities (vastu).

Furthermore, as for what was urged—that if there were a single inherence (samavāya) of substances, qualities, and actions with their qualifiers such as substantiality, quality-ness, and action-ness, that too is rejected; because it consists of both the existent and the non-existent, and because it is an agent, it is indeed conjoined with its effect, so there is no lack of conjunction; because it establishes cause and effect, there is no lack of inherence; and because it possesses a relationship through those two—conjunction and inherence—neither eternality nor non-existence exists [in it], and it is precisely established that it is devoid of genus (ajātimat), since it is intended to be denied as something distinct from substance.

Thus, first of all, the state of being the cause and so forth of substance and the rest arises from manifestation (bhāvanā), because of their coming into being and ceasing to be; is that itself [what we call] "conception" (kalana)?
In the Guṇanirṇaya and Bhāṣya commentaries, [the term] does not appear;
furthermore, because it possesses a relation, its eternality and non-existence do not exist,
and it is indeed established that it is devoid of birth (*ajātimat*).
Alternatively, substances and so forth are not produced and are not related to causes because they are eternal; this is because they exist by themselves, like universals (*sāmānya*) and so on.
And causes and so forth are universals and so on, because they exist by themselves, like substances and so on.
