Because it has that very nature, existence exists by itself, like the universal "existence" (*sattā*).
Both [categories], namely substance and so forth, as well as generality and so forth, are real entities because they possess the nature of being a thing (*vastutva*).

Furthermore, as for what was raised: "If inherence (*samavāya*) is one, let it be perceived along with the qualifiers such as substantiality, quality-ness, and action-ness in relation to substances, qualities, and actions" (p. 524, n. 3, l. 18).
Even though the relation is non-eternal, it does not possess the same kind of non-eternality as conjunction, because, like existence (*bhāva*), it is without a cause;
just as it has been stated that existence is eternal because no cause for it is perceived through any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), so too is inherence (*samavāya*),
for no cause for it is perceived through any means of valid cognition.

Furthermore, by what mode of existence does inherence (samavāya) subsist in substances and the like? It cannot be conjunction (saṃyoga), because that, being a quality (guṇa), must reside in a substance;
nor can it be inherence itself, because inherence is one;
and there is no other mode of existence.
No, because of identity (*tādātmya*).

Just as for substances, qualities, and actions—which are of the nature of being (*sadātmaka*)—there is no other connection with existence (*sattā*), so too for that which is inherent (*samavāyin*) and consists of an inseparable occurrence (*vṛttyātmaka*), there is no other occurrence; therefore, its occurrence is within its own self.

Thus, in the *Praśastapādabhāṣya*, within the exposition on inherence (*samavāya*), there is a mention of an entity that lacks connection through either conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or inherence (*samavāya*), which is eternal and devoid of existence (*sattā*), cited as an example.
Here, "entity" (*bhāva*) means "existence" (*sattā*).

Regarding this *Praśastapādabhāṣya*, the *Nyāyakandalī* commentary states: "But what is this [inherence]—is it non-eternal or rather eternal? Having raised this doubt, he says: "Even though the related things are non-eternal... (referring to the phrase *sambandhy-anityatve 'pi*).

Just as the conjunction [of two things] is impermanent when the related entities are impermanent, so it is not the case that inherence is impermanent when the inherent entities are impermanent, because—like existence—it is causeless;
he explains this with the words "just as" and so forth.
For the destruction of a conjunction is indeed logical upon the destruction of the related entities, because those related entities are the inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*) for its production.
The two relata, however, are not the cause of inherence, because they are merely the relata;
and how they are not the cause has already been demonstrated.
Therefore, even upon the destruction of the relata, inherence does not perish, because it is recognized as persisting in another substratum, just like existence (*sattā*).

Is inherence (*samavāya*) unrelated that it connects two related things, or is it itself related? First of all, it is not logical for that which is unrelated to possess the capacity to connect, because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Furthermore, its connection cannot be of the nature of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), because conjunction resides only in substances;
nor can it be inherence itself, because inherence is a single entity.

And since there is no mode of existence other than conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and inherence (*samavāya*), how does this [inherence] exist? He says: "By what mode of existence, then, does inherence exist in substances and so forth?
The intention of the opponent is that it does not exist because of the absence of a mode of existence.
He explains:

"No"—it is not the case that [the Self] does not function because of the absence of a mental modification (*vṛtti*), for, due to identity (*tādātmya*)—that is, because its nature consists of modification—it is itself inherently a modification.
Indeed, conjunction is something produced; even for that which consists of modification, there exists another modification, since the inherence in a cause is the defining characteristic of an effect.

"Inherence has no other mode of existence; therefore, its existence is by its own self, that is, by its very nature, and not through another mode of existence— this is the meaning," as stated in the *Nyāyakandalī*,
because it possesses a relation (*saṃbandhavattvāt*).
The meaning is that because it is a relation, [it cannot be] a universal (jāti) distinct from substance and so forth;
this applies to [universals] such as substantiality (dravyatva).

Alternatively, and so forth: because they possess existence by their own nature as previously stated, substances (*dravya*) and the like are not characterized by being caused, impermanent, related, or born—just like universals (*sāmānya*) and the like.

Conversely, universals, particulars (*viśeṣa*), and inherence (*samavāya*) possess being caused, being impermanent, being related, and being born, because they possess existence by their own nature, just like substances and the like; that is to say, because they exist in themselves.
Because they have that as their essence: it has been stated that whatever has something as its essence exists by itself, like existence (*sattā*) and so forth;

thus, both [categories]—namely, the properties of being cause or non-cause, eternal or non-eternal, related or unrelated, possessing a genus (*jāti*) or not possessing a genus, and so on, belonging to substances and the rest as well as to universals (*sāmānya*) and the rest—possess a dual nature because everything is a real entity (*vastu*), since there is no distinction in their becoming one through mutual form. [The word *jātimat* in the phrase *jātimadajātimattvāni* is corrected to *sāmānya* in the Bhāṣya.]
Regarding the passage beginning with "svatvād dravyā...

and so forth, which aims to demonstrate that the time of the completion (*niṣṭhā*) and the time of the relation are simultaneous; [the opponent argues] that because inherence (*samavāya*) is one, and because the relation is one, there follows the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the confusion (*saṅkara*) of categories. That [consequence] remains exactly as it was, because many related entities possess a single relation, and because—just like the designations "cow" and so forth for [individuals] such as Vāgā and others—there is no fixed distinction, such that everything would have the time of everything. Having stated this, the fault of the undesirable consequence of confusion (*saṅkaraprasaṅga*) which was raised here remains exactly as it was, difficult to avoid.

The reason is that many related entities possess the state of being related to a single [entity]. For indeed, many related entities become related to one and the same thing; consequently, there is a confusion among them, as in the case of the denotations "cow" and so forth. Just as when "cow" (*go*) is uttered, because the word "cow" is a synonym for words such as "speech," "direction," "earth," and "rays"—since it is identical with each of those and conveys their respective meanings due to its relation to them—it is impossible to determine and establish definitively that "this is the related entity of this one alone. Thus, just as all ten [categories] accept *samavāya* (inherence) as the substratum of cause and effect, so too would the qualities of quality-ness (*guṇatva*) and action-ness (*karmatva*) be [the substrata] in the same way as substance-ness (*dravyatva*). (Note: This page consists merely of footnotes.)

There would be [confusion] regarding both the designation and the cognition, because there would be no established distinction between the characteristics of the categories; or else, how could there be the exclusion of the six categories? Since inherence (*samavāya*) is one, and because quality (*guṇa*) and action (*karman*) are related to substance (*dravya*) by way of being substances, they would lose their status as quality and action.
For their distinction would arise from the difference in their specific defining properties (*tattvaviśeṣaṇa*), just as in the case of a person with an umbrella and a staff.

Furthermore, since there is no distinction in the evidence (*liṅga*) for its connection with [substances, qualities, and actions] here, and because there is an absence of any specific evidence [to differentiate it], inherence (*samavāya*) is one. Therefore, just as the cognition of "substance" arises toward a substance due to its connection with the universal "substanceness" (*dravyatva*), it would likewise produce the cognition of "substance" toward qualities and actions. Consequently, all things would be denoted by all names and give rise to all cognitions; thus, the fault of confusion (*saṅkara*) has been stated by way of generality.

If it is argued that "because the relation is one, there would be the undesirable consequence of a confusion of word-meanings," that objection remains exactly as it was; for since many related things possess a single relation, there is no fixed distinction—just as in the case of the words *vāk* and so on denoting *go* and so on—and thus everything would be everything:
a cow in water, in sight, in heaven, in a direction, in an animal, in a ray, in a thunderbolt, in the earth, and in poison.
(Hemacandrācārya, *Anekārthasaṅgraha*, verse 6).
Please see page 709, line 7.

Even in the context of the refutation of *sattā* (existence), the Master Śrī Mallavādin has already introduced *samavāya* (inherence) as a point of occasion; hereafter, it is refuted through an extensive discussion.

Furthermore, by examining the preceding and following contexts, it appears that this debate was composed by the author of the work directed toward Praśastamati, with the opponent acting as the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).

This kind of argument concerning the relation of inherence (*samavāya*), preceded by the mention of the name Praśastamati, was also cited by Kamalaśīla in the *Tattvasaṅgrahapañjikā* during the examination of inherence (*samavāyaparīkṣā*).

However, this much is the distinction: the passage concerning the relation of inherence (*samavāya*) that is cited by name from Praśastamati’s *Tattvasaṅgrahapañjikā* is found in its entirety within the section defining inherence in Praśastapāda’s *Bhāṣya*. This will become clear upon comparing the readings of the *Praśastapādabhāṣya* and the *Tattvasaṅgrahapañjikā* provided below in these very notes;

furthermore, it should be noted that the prima facie arguments (*pūrvapakṣa*) cited extensively in the *Tattvasaṅgraha* during the examination of the six categories (*ṣaṭpadārtha*) favored by the Vaiśeṣikas are also seen in the *Praśastapādabhāṣya*.

However, a certain portion of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) extracted in the *Nayacakra* during the examination of inherence (*samavāya*) is found in the *Praśastapādabhāṣya*, while another portion is not. Therefore, it is conjectured as follows: Mallavādin may have extracted the prima facie argument from a commentary (*ṭīkā*) on the *Vaiśeṣikasūtra* composed by Praśastamati—which is now mostly lost—whereas [the argument] in the *Tattvasaṅgraha* was taken from the *Praśastapādabhāṣya*.
This should be examined by those desiring detailed knowledge; see page 512, note 7.

Nor is there plurality [of inherence] as there is of conjunction; for, like existence (*bhāva*), its defining marks are non-distinct and there is an absence of any specific marks [to differentiate it].
Therefore, like existence, inherence is one everywhere.

If it is argued that if inherence were one, then because the relation with the qualifiers—substance-ness, quality-ness, action-ness, and so forth—is identical for substances, qualities, and actions, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of a confusion of categories (*padārtha-saṅkara*), we say: no, because of the restriction of the locus and the located (*ādhārādheya-niyama*).
Although inherence (*samavāya*) is one and independent everywhere, there is nevertheless a restriction regarding the locus and the located.

How so? Why is it that substantiality (*dravyatva*) exists only in substances, quality-ness (*guṇatva*) only in qualities, and action-ness (*karmatva*) only in actions, and so forth? It is because of the observation of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
Because the cognition whose cause is inherence (*samavāya*) is observed to occur concomitantly (*anvaya*) here [in all cases], it is understood that inherence is one and the same everywhere.
Because cognitions caused by "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) and so forth are observed to be non-concomitant (*vyatireka*), their specific restriction is known.

Just as, despite the oneness of the conjunction (*saṃyoga*) between a bowl and curd, there is a restriction regarding the relationship of substratum and superstratum, so too, although inherence is one and the same for "substance-ness" and the rest, there is a restriction regarding the container and the contained due to the difference in the powers of the manifestor and the manifested.

Thus ends the *Nyāyakandalī* commentary on the section defining inherence (*samavāya*) in Praśastapāda’s *Bhāṣya*, composed by Śrīdhara Bhaṭṭa. Regarding the question of whether this [inherence] is one or many, he says: "And it is not manifold like conjunction.
That is to say, whereas conjunction is manifold, inherence is not so.
Why is this so? To this he says: "Because there is no distinction in the mark [of existence] as in the case of positive entities, and because there is an absence of a specific mark.

Just as, since the definition of the cognition "existent, existent" is everywhere without distinction—that is, without difference—and because there is an absence of a specific mark or means of proof for any particularity or division, there is one single "existence" (bhāva) everywhere; likewise, here too, since the definition of the cognition "this" is everywhere without difference and there is an absence of proof for any division, there is one single inherence (samavāya) everywhere.
He concludes: "Therefore..."

He objects: If inherence is one—given that inherence is a single entity—then the very same connection that subsists between substanceness (*dravyatva*) and earth and the other substances must also subsist between qualityness (*guṇatva*) and qualities, and between actionness (*karmatva*) and actions.

In that case, just as the connection of substanceness exists in earth and the others, such that they possess substanceness, so too, since that same connection is possible for qualities and the rest, they too would possess substanceness.

Just as the connection with "quality-ness" (guṇatva) exists in color and so forth, such that color and the rest possess quality-ness, so too, because that same connection is possible for substances and actions, they too would possess quality-ness; and the same would apply to actions [being qualities]. Thus, one must demonstrate the confusion of categories. He provides the resolution: "No."
Nor is there any confusion among categories;
why? Because of the restriction between the locus and the located.

Substantiality does not exist merely through the presence of inherence, but rather through the inherence of substantiality. And the inherence of substantiality occurs only in substances, not in qualities or actions; therefore, those two do not possess substantiality.
This summary statement should be explained in the same way regarding qualities (*guṇa*) and actions (*karman*).

He elucidates it with the words "although inherence is one," etc., up to "it is independent" (*svatantra*); the meaning is that, unlike conjunction (*saṃyoga*), it does not exist by means of another relation.
He raises another objection, clearly stating: "Why is it so?"—the meaning is:
why do you know that substanceness (dravyatva) resides only in substances, quality-ness (guṇatva) only in qualities, and action-ness (karmatva) only in actions, and so forth?
He states the answer: "Because of the observation of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
This means that the cognition caused by the universal *dravyatva* (substanceness) occurs in substances (*anvaya*) and is absent from qualities and actions (*vyatireka*);
likewise, the cognition caused by the universal *guṇatva* (qualityness) occurs in qualities (*anvaya*) and is absent from substances and actions (*vyatireka*).
Likewise, the connection of the suffix denoting the cause of "objectness" (karmatva) with the object, and its exclusion from substances and qualities, is observed;
therefore, from this observation of positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), the restriction of "substanceness" (dravyatva) and so forth is known.
The explanation of this is easy to understand.

If inherence (*samavāya*) is indeed one and the same, how can this restriction be established—that inherence of "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) occurs only in earth and the other substances, inherence of "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*) only in color and the like, and inherence of "action-ness" (*karmatva*) only in upward throwing and so forth, and not elsewhere? To this, he says: "Just as...

Even though conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is one, a restriction regarding the relationship between container and contained (*āśrayāśrayibhāva*) is observed between a bowl and curd due to the restriction of their capacities; the bowl alone is the container and the curd alone is the contained, such that the bowl is not the contained nor the curd the container. Likewise, even though inherence is one, there is a restriction regarding the container and the contained for substance-ness and the others, due to the distinction in the capacities of the manifested (*vyaṅgya*) and the manifestor (*vyañjaka*).
What is meant? The power that manifests substantiality belongs to substances alone; therefore, substantiality inheres in substances alone and not elsewhere.
This should be explained in the same way for qualities and actions as well—so it is stated in the *Nyāyakandalī*.
Now, the discussion found in the *Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā* is cited: "And because there is no difference in the cognition 'here,' this [universal] is not divided like a conjunction;
rather, it is perceived as one and the same throughout all existing things. (825)
Thus, according to the view of the Vaiśeṣikas, inherence (*samavāya*) is inferable from the mark of the cognition "here";

however, according to the view of the Naiyāyikas, it is indeed directly perceivable through the cognition "here. For they declare that it is perceptual because, when the operation of the senses is present, there arises the cognition, for example, "the cloth is here in these threads. Furthermore, this inherence does not differ among its related entities as conjunction (*saṃyoga*) does; rather, like existence (*sattā*), it is one and the same everywhere, because its mark is non-distinct and there is no specific mark [to differentiate it].
"Like a yogi" is an example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).

Regarding what was stated previously, beginning with "because there is no difference in the cognition here," he says: "If inherence were one and the same in all things, then even in the case of potsherds and the like, the cognition 'cloth' and so forth would result.
It follows that the nature of "cowness" and so forth also exists in elephants and other such beings;
therefore, these possess the form of a cow and so on, just like a brindled cow (śābaleya).
If it is argued that the cloth exists in its threads because it is perceived through inherence (samavāya),
and since that same [inherence] exists in the potsherds, why is it not the case that [the pot] exists there in that same way?
If it is argued that [the jar] does not reside in the potsherds, then surely it is accepted that [it] resides even in the threads;
yet why is it not the case that it also lacks inherence (samavāya) in the potsherds?
For that very inherence which is said to belong to the cloth in its threads would, by that same logic, be perceived without limit in the pot's shards. (839)

In this way, that very same inherence of elephant-ness and so forth which exists in elephants and other such things [belongs] to the various universals such as cow-ness, even with respect to their own substrata. (840)
"If it were one," and so forth:

if there were a single inherence (*samavāya*) in the three worlds, then cognitions such as "the cloth is in the potsherds" would also arise; furthermore, it would follow that "cowness" and the like exist in horses and other animals.
Consequently, just as there is a cognition of "cow" in brindled cows and others, there would likewise be a cognition of "cow" in elephants and the like.

For instance: that inherence (*samavāya*) by virtue of which the cognition "the cloth is in the threads" is described, that same inherence exists in the potsherds and so forth with respect to that cloth; why, then, does such a cognition not occur?
It might be argued: "The cloth is not dependent upon the potsherd, therefore no such cognition arises.
This too is false.

Since it is described that the cloth is inherent even in the threads by virtue of the force of inherence (*samavāya*), why does that same inherence not exist in the potsherds, such that the cognition "the cloth exists there" would not arise in them as it does in the threads?

But that very inherence which is designated as the inherence of the cloth in the threads is the same as the inherence of the cloth in the potsherds; how then would there not be a confusion [of categories]? Therefore, the cognition (*dhī*) would be "without limit" (*anavadhi*), meaning devoid of any restriction; and consequently, because the relation of substances, qualities, and actions with their qualifiers—such as substanceness (*dravyatva*), qualitiness (*guṇatva*), and actionness (*karmatva*)—would be one and the same, the division into five categories (*pañcapadārtha*) would not exist.
With the words "in this way" (*evam*) and so forth, he establishes the consequence that the cognition of a cow and so on would arise even in respect to elephants and the like;
for even if the relation is one, the rule regarding the container and the contained (*ādhārādheya-niyama*) still exists.
"For that universal [of substance] resides only in substances, and the state of being an action resides only in actions.
With the words "the substratum," etc., he anticipates the response of Praśastamati to this objection.
For he says: "Even though inherence (*samavāya*) is one, there is nevertheless no confusion among the five categories, because of the restriction between the locus and the located.
For instance: substantiality (*dravyatva*) exists only in substances, quality-ness (*guṇatva*) only in qualities, and action-ness (*karmatva*) only in actions.
Thus, the cognition of substantiality and the other categories arises through the delimitation of their respective fixed loci."

If this were so, it would follow that inherence (samavāya) is distinct for each individual object; therefore, he says: because we observe the persistence of the cognition arising from inherence in the form "it is here," it is understood that this inherence is one and the same everywhere.
Because the exclusion of the causes such as substantiality is observed in cognitions,
the restriction of the universals such as substance is determined by the intellect.
Regarding the passage beginning with "here" (*iha*):

because the cognition based on inherence (*samavāya*) is observed to have a uniform form everywhere through its positive concomitance (*anvaya*), it is understood that inherence is one and the same in all cases.

Furthermore, although it is unitary, since cognitions based on causes such as "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) arise only in relation to their respective specific substrates, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—characterized by non-occurrence—is observed; thus, the distinctness of the universals such as substance-ness is known. Consequently, there is no confusion among the five categories.

But how is it that, even though the relationship is not distinct, this specific determination of container and contained is logical for these [categories]? To this he says: "Just as, for example, although the conjunction between a bowl and curd is one and the same, a restriction of container and contained is observed; so too is the restriction held to be here.

If it is argued that there is no contradiction because, although inherence is a single entity across categories such as substance and the rest, there is a distinction in the capacities of the manifested and the manifestor;
"Namely," and so forth:

for just as there is a specific determination of the locus and the located (āśraya-āśrayi-pratiniyama) between a bowl and curd even though their conjunction is one, so too, although inherence (samavāya) is one with respect to substance-ness and the like, there is a specific determination of the container and the contained due to the difference in the powers of the manifestor and the manifested; this is what is meant by "that," namely, the rule of the container and the contained.

He provides a rebuttal with the verse beginning "the relation of substratum and superstratum" (ādhārādheya): "Surely, if this [universal] were one, the restriction of substratum and superstratum would be difficult to establish;
the nature of being a substance (dravyatva) is held to reside only in a substance—how could that be due to inherence (samavāya)? (846)
And that inherence of his also exists in qualities and so forth; for this [inherence] is indeed one and the same for both, due to its connection with qualities, universals, and so on. (847)

For us, a restriction regarding the inherence of "form-ness" (*rūpatva*) and so forth within form and the like is not established; rather, it is you yourselves—who assert that inherence (*samavāya*) is one and the same everywhere—who face this difficulty. Thus, we present the following reductio ad absurdum: the restriction that "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) resides only in substance is maintained solely by the power of inherence; yet that very same inherence which belongs to "substance-ness" and the like also exists in qualities and so forth, because those [qualities] are related to the genus "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*) and the rest.

Even if there were such a relation, how is it determined that inherence (*samavāya*) alone exists therein? To this he says: "The same one," and so forth; "of those two" refers to the universals (*jāti*) such as substantiality (*dravyatva*) and quality-ness (*guṇatva*).
Thus, because they would have a single cause, the consequence of their confusion (*saṅkara*) would be unavoidable—this is the sense.
Otherwise, this [Self] would indeed be differentiated by qualities, universals, and so forth, just as yoga is differentiated for each individual according to the differences among yogis. (848)

"Otherwise" means: if the inherence (*samavāya*) of "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) in a substance were not the very same as the inherence of "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*) and so forth in qualities and the like, then—inherence being distinct for each substratum, just like conjunction (*saṃyoga*)—the argument previously stated regarding "the causes of [cognitions such as] substance-ness," etc., would fail. To this he replies: "The exclusion of the cognitions caused by substance-ness and the like is not tenable, because their cause exists; therefore, even their restriction [to specific objects] does not hold."

Regarding the phrase "because of substantiality, etc.": for when the cause is unimpaired, it is not logical for there to be an absence or non-existence of the effect, as that would entail the consequence that it is not its effect.
Consequently, since an absence of [specific] cognitions is impossible, a restriction regarding that relationship of container and contained is also not tenable.

[Objection: Surely, the restriction will be established by such designations as "substantiality is supported by and resides in substance alone. [Reply: He says: "Its being supported by that, its residing therein, and so forth, are designated as proceeding from that very inherence; therefore, this is not a valid regulator of that [restriction]. (850)

Regarding the passage beginning with "because it depends on that" (*tadāśritatvāt*), you indeed describe the determination of dependence and so forth as being due to that very inherence (*samavāya*). Since that [inherence] is indistinguishable everywhere, how can this restriction be justified?

Therefore, even this [property of] dependence and so forth is not logically a regulator of that relationship between locus and located (*ādhārādheyabhāva*), because these [properties] share the same fate as the relationship between locus and located itself.

If it is argued that the restriction [of the relationship] will then arise from the specific determination of the powers of the manifested and the manifestor, he says: "Even the distinction between the capacities of the manifested and the manifestor arises from inherence (samavāya), and not from anything else, because production is impossible for eternal things.

Regarding the phrase "manifested" (*vyaṅgya*) and so forth: when it is said that substances and the like possess the quality of manifesting universals such as "substanceness" (*dravyatva*), this occurs solely by the power of inherence (*samavāya*).
For instance, precisely because "substanceness" is inherent in a substance, for that very reason it is said to be manifested by that [substance].

"From another" means from the production of a nature capable of generating cognition as described by the Buddhists, since [the Buddhists] accept that even eternal entities such as *sattā* (existence) possess inherence (*samavāya*); and the production of eternal things is not logical, which he supports with the words "for indeed... etc.: "For these [entities] do not arise from the mere presence of lamps and the like."

Likewise, the universals such as "jar" and so forth, which are capable of producing cognition, as well as the conjunction of the curd and the bowl that was cited as an example, are also unestablished for us; he demonstrates this by stating: "And the single conjunction of the bowl and the curd has already been refuted."

And that [relation] is not fixed; therefore, it is not logical [to claim a relation between them], because it would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga), as in the case of the pot and the curd, and so forth. 853.

Regarding the phrase "previously," he shows that even if conjunction (*saṃyoga*) were granted as a single category during the refutation of the category of conjunction, the same undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) would still apply—starting with the words "And not this... and so on.

Therefore, from that conjunction, there would be the undesirable consequence of the cognition "the bowl is in the curd" and so forth; this is an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), because the cause, namely conjunction, is indistinguishable [in all cases].

Thus, in the *Tattvasaṅgrahapañjikā*, a commentary on the *Tattvasaṅgraha* composed by Kamalaśīla, [the following appears] from the *Anekārthasaṅgraha* composed by the master Hemacandra, verse 6: "The word *gaura* [is used] for water, sight, heaven, a direction, an animal, a ray, a thunderbolt, the earth, poison, and a mountain."

In the *Anekārthasaṃgraha* composed by Ācārya Hemacandra, verse 6, it is stated: "The word *gaur* [is used] for water, vision, heaven, direction, animal, ray, thunderbolt, earth, poison, and mountain.

Since there is no fixed determination of the characteristics of categories (*padārtha*), either the names and the cognitions [of objects] would [be indeterminate], or else the system of the six categories (*ṣaṭpadārtha*) would cease to exist.

How so? Because inherence (samavāya) is one, there is a relation between substance and quality-action; thus, there would be the state of being a substance and the loss of the states of being a quality or an action.
For their distinction would arise from a difference in their specific characteristics (tattvaviśeṣaṇa), like [the distinction between] a man with an umbrella and a staff.
However, because the general characteristic of "being" (sat-liṅga) is not different and there is an absence of any specific characteristic, existence (bhāva) is one. (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.2.18)
2.18 Thus, by the word "one" (eka), non-difference is expressed; however, it is not a number.

A "mark" (liṅga) is so called because existence is indicated (liṅgyate) by it—that is, by the cognition (pratyaya). Since that existence which is cognized by the cognition "it exists, it exists" is undifferentiated everywhere, and since there is no distinct cognition [of it], existence is non-different.
The negation of substanceness and qualityness is explained by means of existence (bhāva), Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 7.2.10. p. 10...

30. Just as existence (*bhāva*) is not a substance because it possesses a single substance, and is neither action nor quality because it exists in qualities and actions, so too is inherence (*samavāya*); and this is its true nature. Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 7.2.30.

31. Thus, just as there is one entity because its characteristic marks are non-distinct, so too here, because its characteristic marks are non-distinct, inherence is one, devoid of occurrence, eternal, and partless. Thus ends the seventh chapter. (See Candrānanda’s *Vaiśeṣikasūtravṛtti*, p. 29; cf. p. 524, l. 17).
The second type of confusion begins with the words "padārtha" and so forth;
because there is no established definition for the six categories (padārthas), beginning with substance (dravya), all six categories are negated.
The explanation of how this occurs and so on follows.

Because inherence (samavāya) is one, there would be the defect that substances (dravya) possess the nature of substance (dravyabhāva) through their connection with quality (guṇa) and action (karman) by way of [the universal] substantiality (dravyatva), just as [individuals] possess substantiality; furthermore, there would be the defect of the loss of the intrinsic nature of those two, namely quality-ness (guṇatva) and action-ness (karmatva). For their distinction [from the universal] would arise from the distinction of their specific attributes (tattvaviśeṣaṇa), like a person with an umbrella and a staff—this is a counter-example (vaidharmyadṛṣṭānta). A person with an umbrella is distinguished by the umbrella, and a person with a staff is distinguished by the staff; it is not so here, for no distinction of substantiality is observed anywhere. See page 529, line 4.

In this context, it is possible that the reading is *dravyabhāvo dravyavat* (the state of being a substance is like a substance), or alternatively, the reading might be *dravyabhāvo dravyatvaṃ dravyavat* (the state of being a substance is substantiality, which is like a substance). If it is argued that those two [qualities and actions] will exist because of their causal relationship, their relationship as substratum and superstratum, and their inherence [in substance], then—given the cessation of the state of being qualities and actions in those two [qualities and actions] while they are connected to the state of being a substance—the substance would cease to be a substance, because qualities and actions would no longer have a substratum.

Because the relations of cause and effect, substratum and superstratum, and inherence are unitary, and because qualities and actions have become substances, when the state of being a quality or an action ceases, qualities and actions lack a substratum; thus, substance does not possess the characteristics such as "possessing action," nor do qualities and actions possess those characteristics. Consequently, there is the cessation of the state of being a substance even for [what was considered] substance, and likewise for substance and qualities...
The mutual exclusion of the six categories;
see page 440, note 5.

Likewise, since there is an absence of substances, qualities, and actions—which possess fixed definitions—once they have ceased to exist, categories such as "substanceness," "qualitiness," and "actionness" are also untenable due to the absence of their substrata.
Because of this mutual confusion, there is no established distinction between the definitions of the categories; thus, the intention appears to be that the six categories themselves cease to exist.

If you think that—starting from the phrase "cause and effect" and so forth—the cause is the substratum (*ādhāra*) and the substance (*dravya*), while the effect is the superstratum (*ādheya*) consisting of quality (*guṇa*) and action (*karman*), and that those two states of quality and action will come to be through the inherence (*samavāya*) of those distinct cause and effect, or substratum and superstratum—if you think this, do not think so. Here is the response: the passage beginning with "of those two, quality and action" and ending with "the cessation of the state of being a primary substance" is the instructional statement; the subsequent text is its commentary. By means of the cessation of the state of being quality and action, the cessation of the state of being a substance for the substance itself is explained.

For example: since that which was described as the relation of cause and effect, substratum and superstratum, and inherence is itself one, the inherence of quality and action within a substance as its constituent parts is one; because of its connection with that substance, those qualities and actions make the substance itself appear as one. Consequently, the qualities and actions cease to exist. Upon their cessation, the substance—lacking its support—is no longer a substratum, nor is it a cause, because of the absence of the inherent qualities and actions. Therefore, the substance lacks the definition of a substance, namely: "that which possesses motion, possesses qualities, and is the inherent cause" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.15).
14. Thus, because it lacks action and qualities, it is not a substance.

In that same manner, the relation between inseparable things (*ayutasiddha*) which stand in the relationship of the supported and the support, and which is the cause of the cognition "it is here," is inherence (*samavāya*).

It is the relation called inherence from which the cognition "this is here" arises with respect to substances, qualities, actions, universals, and particulars—whether they stand in a causal relationship or not—as long as they exist in an inseparable state of being the supported and the support; and it is that relation by virtue of which there is non-separation (*aviṣvagbhāva*) among non-pervasive things whose distinctness has been apprehended.

How so? Just as the cognition "curd is in this bowl" is observed when a relation exists, so too are there observed such cognitions as: "the cloth is in these threads," "the mat is in these vīraṇa-grass fibers," "quality and action are in this substance," "existence is in this substance, quality, and action," "substance-ness is in this substance," "quality-ness is in this quality," "action-ness is in this action," and "ultimate particularities are in this eternal substance. From the observation of these cognitions, it is known that a relation exists between them; thus it is stated in Praśastapāda’s *Bhāṣya* in the section defining inherence (*samavāya*).

The *Nyāyakandalī* commentary on this [verse]: "Salutations to You, Śambhu, who destroys worldly existence, the cause of the dissolution and creation of the universe, whose body is pure knowledge, and who is accompanied by Umā.

Now, for the purpose of defining inherence (*samavāya*), he says: "Inherence is that relation between things that are inseparably established (*ayutasiddha*) and stand in the relationship of the supported and the support, which is the cause of the cognition 'it is here' (*iha-pratyaya*)."
This has already been explained during the section on the enumeration [of categories].

To address the question—"Which are those inseparably established (ayutasiddha) things whose relation is inherence (samavāya)?"—it is said: "Of substances, qualities, actions, universals, and particulars.
This is stated without restriction, whether they stand in a cause-and-effect relationship or not.

The rule is that inherence (*samavāya*) occurs between parts and wholes; between impermanent substances and their qualities; between eternal substances and the impermanent qualities inherent in them; and between actions and their possessors when they stand in a cause-and-effect relationship.

Furthermore, there is a rule that inherence occurs between eternal substances and their eternal qualities, as well as between universals and their possessors, and between ultimate particulars (*antyaviśeṣa*) and their possessors—provided these are not related as cause and effect—and that this inherence pertains to things that are inseparable (*ayutasiddha*).
This is also a rule regarding those things that exist in the relation of the supported and the support.

Inherence (*samavāya*) is that cause from which the cognition "this is here" arises, and by virtue of which there is the non-separation (*aviṣvagbhāva*), the non-distinctness (*apṛthagbhāva*), and the lack of independence (*asvātantrya*) of things that are not all-pervading, which abide in fixed locations, whose difference has been apprehended, and whose distinction of essential nature has been apprehended; for we observe that the mutual contact of two distinct things is brought about by a relation.
He establishes this very point through a series of questions beginning with "How so? and so forth.

Just as the cognition "curd is in this bowl" is observed when there is a relationship between the bowl and the curd, so too, because cognitions such as "the cloth is in these threads" are observed, it is known that there exists a relationship between these [entities] such as the threads and the cloth.

This is stated in the *Nyāyakandalī*: "Cognitions such as 'the cloth is in these threads' are caused by a relationship, because they are uncontradicted cognitions of the form 'it is here,' like the cognition 'curd is in this bowl.'"
Because of its very oneness;
here, there may also be the reading "because of its oneness" (*tasyaikatvāt*),
from which follows the definition of substance (*dravyalakṣaṇam*).
See page 440, note 5:

"Qualities and actions do not possess such characteristics. The word *iti* is used in the sense of a reason (*hetu*); because there are no qualities or actions with such characteristics due to the absence of their substrates—the inherent [substances]—when those [substrates] cease, the substantiality of the substance also ceases, just like its qualities. And as for the statement: "No, because of the oneness of many," meaning that there is a single inherence (*samavāya*) for many [categories] such as substances and so forth, but not for each pair of two.

...the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) must be either a substance possessing action or a substance composed of multiple substances; however, in this case, it is impossible for it to be neither a non-substance nor a substance composed of multiple substances.

Therefore, when the state of being a quality or an action ceases for qualities and actions, and there is a connection with the state of being a substance, because qualities and actions lack a substratum, the state of being a substance ceases for the substance; thus, the cessation of the category of substance has been described.

Alternatively, if there were a connection with *dravyatva* (substanceness), which according to your view is omnipresent, then a quality (*guṇa*) or an action (*karman*) would possess the state of being a substance (*dravyībhāva*), because it would be connected to a substance by way of *dravyatva*. Due to that state [of being a substance], qualities and actions would not reside in a substance; consequently, the definition of a substance would be untenable, and the status of being a substance would be excluded. If one asks, "What is the definition of a substance? it is stated: "That which possesses motion, possesses qualities, and is an inherent cause" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.15).

14. Thus, because the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇa*), the relation between locus and located (*ādhārādheya*), and inherence (*samavāya*) are unitary, and because qualities (*guṇa*) and actions (*karman*) have become substances (*dravya*), they do not possess the characteristics such as "possessing motion" (*kriyāvat*). This is because qualities and actions do not have such characteristics; for a quality has the characteristic of depending on a substance (*dravyāśrayin*), and an action has the characteristic of existing in a single substance (*ekadravya*).

Therefore, with respect to the absence of their own specific characteristics, the cessation of the state of being a substance for a substance follows from the fact that the definitions of quality and action are not applicable to it.

And then, regarding the passage beginning with "of substance as well," etc., having established the non-existence of qualities and actions due to the absence of a substratum, it follows that when there is no substrate, there is also the absence of the substance which is the substrate; thus, the meaning is already understood.
In this way, for qualities and actions as well, the cessation of the state of being qualities and actions should be understood as stated, because their defining characteristics cannot be established.
Thus, first of all, there is the cessation of substance, quality, and action due to the absence of established definitions.
And as for the statement: "No, because of the oneness of many;
there is a single inherence (*samavāya*) of many substances and so forth, but not [an inherence] of each pair..."
...Inherence is one for many substances and so forth,
but it is not as with conjunction, which occurs between each pair; inherence does not occur between each pair.

Therefore, the intention appears to be that there is no impermanence of inherence (samavāya), because it is not connected as a substance; thus, there is an absence of substantiality. *Praśastapādabhāṣya* 1.9.12.
See page 440, note 5; see page 440, note 5.
*vyābhūta* (variant reading:
*ya*). See page 440, note 5.
See the definition of *avadalaksana* on page 440, note 5;
see page 440, note 5.
Likewise, regarding the phrase "substance, quality," and so forth,

there is an impossibility [of their existence] because of the absence of a substratum for substance-ness, quality-ness, action-ness, and the like; by the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (ādi), the universal "existence" (sattā) is also intended.
He explains that [passage]: from "mutually," etc., up to "the cessation of the six categories," the meaning is already explained. Regarding the phrase "and that which," etc.:

having raised the prima facie objection (*pūrvapakṣa*) that since inherence (*samavāya*) exists in two things—just like conjunction (*saṃyoga*)—because there is a distinction between the locus and the located, it would therefore be non-eternal, the Vaiśeṣika offers the rebuttal: "No, because many are one. This description of its essential nature—that there is a single inherence of many [categories] such as substance and so forth—is for the purpose of refuting [the charge of] existing in two things.

"But [the claim that] 'inherence is distinct from conjunction because it does not occur between pairs [of substances]'— by this too, the consequence of confusion remains exactly as before, since one accepts the inherence of many [qualities] in a single [substance];
thus all six categories are undermined,
up to the point of the definition of inherence."
The Teacher says: "By this also," and so forth.

By this very statement regarding the avoidance of impermanence, the consequence of confusion (*saṅkara*) is reinforced; for since there is no general distinction, if everything were to reside in everything, there would be a confusion of all designations and cognitions. Furthermore, because it is impossible to establish the definition of the categories (*padārtha*) as qualified entities, the exclusion of the six categories and so forth has been stated. Since you accept the inherence (*samavāya*) of many things in one, the aforementioned confusion persists. Consequently, due to that confusion, all six categories are excluded. When they are excluded, inherence itself ceases to exist due to the absence of anything to which it belongs. Therefore, being non-existent like a sky-flower, how could it possess either permanence or impermanence?
Regarding the passage beginning with "yat tu" and so forth:
what is this "twofold occurrence"?
The intention appears to be that if inherence (samavāya) were to reside in two things, it would follow that it is non-eternal—just like conjunction (saṃyoga)—upon the destruction of its relata;
see page 524, note 3.
[However,] even if the relata are non-eternal, inherence is not non-eternal like conjunction, because it is not produced by causes, just like an existent entity (bhāva).
Just as it was stated that an entity is eternal because its cause is not perceived through valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), so too is the case with inherence (*samavāya*);
for no cause of this [inherence] is perceived through any valid means of cognition.
Thus, the eternality of inherence is established in the *Praśastapādabhāṣya*.
The commentary on this, *Nyāyakandalī*, is to be found at page 523, note 2.

The refutation of this doctrine of Praśastapāda’s *Bhāṣya* is stated in the *Tattvasaṅgrahapañjikā* as follows: "As for what was said—that inherence (*samavāya*) is eternal because its cause is not perceived—he replies: 'If it were eternal, then all things, such as jars and the like, would necessarily be eternal, because they would always abide in their own substrata due to [their] inherence therein.'"
Regarding the phrase "by way of permanence" and so forth:
for if inherence (*samavāya*) were eternal, it would follow that jars and other such things would also be eternal, because they would exist at all times within their own substrates.

For instance: it is maintained that these [qualities] abide in their own substrates solely because of the existence of inherence (*samavāya*), and since that inherence is eternal, why would these not always remain?

With the words "by the disjunction of their own constituent parts" (*svārambhaka-vibhāgāt*) and so forth, the opponent anticipates the following answer: "They perish either through the disjunction of their own constituent parts or through their destruction;
and [qualities] such as motion (*kriyā*) perish through conjunction (*yoga*) and so forth. If this is argued, it is not so.
For their inherence in their own substratum is also always held [to exist];
however, if those [substrata] were subject to destruction, then its [inherence’s] perishability would also be certain.

It might be argued as follows: the destruction of jars and the like occurs through the disjunction or the destruction of their own constituent parts; just as, in the states of unfolding and baking, the actions and other qualities of a jar perish due to contact with substances possessing touch, as it has been stated: "Action is destroyed by contact with a substance possessing touch."
And action is opposed to its own effect, according to Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.13.
Likewise, the destruction of one cognition by another cognition, or of one sound by another sound, is the system of the opponent.

Therefore, even though *samavāya* exists as the cause of subsistence, because of the absence of other auxiliary causes and due to the encounter with a contrary condition, there is no consequence of permanence for jars and the like; such is the intention of the opponent.
[The author] refutes this with the words "not that," and so forth.

This is not tenable, because even for those [products], such as the potsherds which are their own constituent parts, there is inherence (*samavāya*) in other constituent parts that originate them; and for those too, there is inherence in yet others, continuing until only the atom (*paramāṇu*) remains.
Since that atom is eternal, it possesses no change of state;
therefore, since the inherence of all things in their own constituent parts exists at all times, how could there be destruction or disjunction?
By the word "also" (api), he indicates that this applies not only to the substances initiated by it, but also to actions and so forth.
However, if the destruction of its own constituent parts were admitted, then the destruction of this inherence (samavāya) would necessarily follow.
Why? He says: for when the related entities have ceased to exist, it is impossible for the relation to remain.
For conjunction does not persist even when the conjoined things are destroyed,
whereas the conjoined things do persist as long as the conjunction exists.
If inherence were to exist, it would likewise be so for the inherent things;
for [it is said] "upon the cessation of the related thing," and so forth.
Explaining this very point, he says: "For not," and so forth.
Consequently, because its relata have perished, inherence would result in being non-eternal—just like a conjunction whose conjuncts have perished;
or else, it follows that the relata themselves must persist, because their relation has not perished, just like two substances whose conjunction has not ceased.

"Otherwise, the loss of the very nature of that relation would follow for both [relata] even upon the destruction of one related member," with these words the opponent objects: "Inherence persists even upon the destruction of one related member because of the existence of the other related member; if you say this is not so because of their difference, [we reply: no."

He thinks as follows: If, in the first reason, the intended meaning of the reason (*hetvartha*) is "because all relations have been destroyed," then the reason suffers from the fallacy of being unestablished with respect to a portion of the subject (*pakṣaikadeśāsiddha*).
For the destruction of all related things never occurs anywhere, since even at the time of cosmic dissolution (*pralaya*), atoms and so forth remain.
Now, if the reason is stated with reference to a relationship whose connection has somehow perished, then it is inconclusive (*anaikāntikatā*).
For even if one related member has perished somewhere, its persistence may still be based on another related member.

Anticipating the objection that "by this same logic, conjunction (*saṃyoga*) would also result in being eternal," the opponent provides the following rebuttal: "Not due to difference" (*na bhedataḥ*).

For conjunction (*saṃyoga*) differs according to its correlates; therefore, its impermanence is logical. Inherence (*samavāya*), however, is one and the same throughout the world because the basis for the notion of "herein" (*ihapratyaya*) is non-different. Therefore, its impermanence is illogical, since it is perceived even in other relations elsewhere.

He refutes this with the words "If it were so," etc.: "If it were so, then that inherence which is postulated as consisting of the subsistence (*vṛtti*) of those inherent things such as jars and the like that perish—"
Would that very [relation] itself persist because it resides in other related entities, or is the relation something else entirely, like the multiplicity of conjunctions and so forth?
If inherence, which is characterized by that very subsistence,
were to remain established, then jars and other such objects would necessarily follow as being established exactly as they were before.
If these [qualities] do not persist, how could their inherence— which consists in their functioning— persist? Or else, it would exist merely as a name.
Therefore, since they exist even prior to that [state], those [characteristics] would not reside in the substratum,
just as they do not afterwards; for such is the nature of these characteristics, being devoid of substantial reality.

For instance: when those things such as jars that perish—which are inherent in their own causes—do so, is that very inherence (samavāya) which was postulated as consisting in their subsistence within their own causes still present among those other related entities once they have perished? Or is it something else entirely, just as conjunction or plurality differs with respect to each individual conjunct?
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), disjunction and so forth are included.

In that regard, if the first position is held, then because their activity has not ceased—just as it was in their prior state—it follows that jars and other such things must remain exactly as they were. Alternatively, if those jars and other things do not remain stable, then because their activity is unstable, it follows that the inherence (*samavāya*) itself cannot remain stable; otherwise, it would not consist of "subsistence" (*vṛtti*).

And if one were to apply the name "inherence" to something of such a nature—that is, something independent and providing no assistance—then it would be a mere matter of nomenclature, and there would be no actual reality corresponding to that designation.

"Thus" (*tathā*) means "consisting of that function" (*tad-vṛtti-ātmaka*). From this, there arises the fault of [the relation] being a mere convention of names (*saṃjñā-mātra-anvaya*). He demonstrates this with the words "Therefore," and so forth.

Even before the destruction of the relata—that is, even in the state where the relata have not yet perished—the jars and other such things would not be established by virtue of the existence of that inherence (*samavāya*), due to the power of its presence. This is because, just as later on when the inherent cause has perished, there is in reality no functioning [of inherence];
he demonstrates the meaning of this reason with the words "For instance" (*tathā hi*), and so forth.
Alternatively, inherence (samavāya) persists upon the existence of another related entity, just as conjunction, disjunction, plurality, and so forth do. 865
For in this way, like conjunction and so forth, there would indeed be a multiplicity of this [cause]; if such a primary entity existed, many things would become inconsistent. (866)
If the second position—that [the inherence] is indeed something else—is maintained, then, like conjunction and so forth, there would follow a multiplicity of inherences;
consequently, there would be a loss of the accepted tenet that "inherence is not differentiated.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "and so on" (*evam-ādi*), [other such consequences are implied].

"...the acceptance of another fault," as stated in the *Tattvasaṅgrahapañjikā* located at Jaisalmer, during the examination of the category of inherence (*samavāya*). Here, the reading indicated by the bold typeface is to be understood according to the manuscript copy from Jaisalmer.

Regarding the phrase "of inherence" (*samavāyasya*) on page 703 of the *Sanmatitarka-vṛtti*: by this [argument] as well, the consequence of confusion (*saṅkara*) remains exactly as it was, because many [categories] are admitted to have a single inherence;
consequently, all six categories are subverted.
See page 524, line 2, and page 526, line 1.
As for what was stated—[namely], "No, because of the restriction of locus and located;
although inherence (samavāya) is one and independent everywhere, nevertheless there is a restriction of locus and located"—[this is the response].
How so? [The view that] "substantiality exists only in substances, quality-ness only in qualities, and action-ness only in actions" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra, Praśastamati)—
this too has been refuted.
...be seen as specifically determined (see page 524, line 19; page 525, line 25).

This too has been refuted, because if inherence (*samavāya*) were one and the same everywhere, there would be no restriction regarding the locus and the located; for it is only when [inherence] resides in two things that properties such as "substanceness" (*dravyatva*) are specifically determined within substances and so forth.
The intention behind what is said—

"Let it first be understood that even if inherence (*samavāya*) were one, there would still be a restriction between locus and located"— is merely a path established by one's own doctrine as a response.
But it is not so... [text missing] ...so.

In all cases, first of all, there is a dual occurrence (dvivṛttitva) in the inherence of substance and substanceness and so forth, because it produces denotations and cognitions qualified by both related entities, just like the conjunction of a bowl and curds in the case of a substance and a quality.
And thus...
impermanence itself.
Let it be understood, first of all, from the observation of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*):
because the cognition whose cause is inherence (*samavāya*) is observed to occur here [in the case of "this is a substance"], it is understood that inherence is one and the same everywhere;
whereas, because the cognitions caused by substanceness (*dravyatva*) and so forth are observed to be absent [elsewhere], their specific restriction is known.

The intention appears to be this: just as there is a restriction regarding the relationship between substratum and superstratum when the conjunction between a bowl and curd is one, so too there would be a restriction regarding the container and the contained even if inherence (*samavāya*) were one for substance-ness (*dravyatva*) and the other categories. See page 524, note 3.
However, such an absence of confusion (*saṅkara*) is not tenable;

for if inherence, being of the nature of all [categories], were the single substratum of substance and the rest, why then would there not be confusion? Furthermore, the intention appears to be that there is no cessation of inherence’s occurrence in two [relata].

The naming and cognition— "inherence exists between substance and quality, between substance and action, between substance and substanceness, between quality and qualitiness, and between action and actionness"— are observed;

and thus, since there is a distinction based on the relationship of container and contained, inherence, like conjunction, would necessarily be non-eternal due to its subsisting in two things— this appears to be the intended meaning.
See page 528, note 8.

As for the passage beginning with "But as for what was replied," etc., which states the answer to the charge of the fault of confusion (*saṅkara*)— namely, "No, because of the restriction of the container and the contained"—

and the subsequent explanation starting with "Even though it is one," etc., up to "the quality of being an object [inherence] exists only in objects," the Vaiśeṣika maintains that by this statement— "In all cases, inherence is one"— both the lack of permanence and the difficulty of its occurring in two substrates are avoided.

The Teacher says: "This too has been refuted," and so forth; the meaning of this has already been explained up to the point where he will state that these [categories] are restricted and that this [inherence] possesses only a dual occurrence.

As for what was said—"Let it first be understood," and so forth—this is his entire life-force for avoiding the fault, namely, his contemplation that there is no lack of restriction nor any over-extension through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), up to the point where he argues that even if inherence were one, there would still be a restriction between the locus and the located.

Regarding this, the Teacher says: "This too," and so forth. You yourself have provided the answer to this statement by explaining the definition of inherence (*samavāya*) in the passage beginning with "here, O Vaiśeṣika, O Sūtrakāra, O Praśastamati," since inherence is characterized by the cognition of the relationship between the locus and the located (*ādhārādheya*). Furthermore, because the cause and effect stand in the relation of locus and located, and because this point is well-established by the example of the bowl and the curd, we say [in response] "but not in that way," and so forth. In that manner, the absence of confusion (*saṅkara*) is not tenable according to the latter method. If, in the example of the conjunction of the bowl and the curd, the bowl as the locus becomes conjoined with many located things such as curd, honey, water, and so on, then why is there no confusion? Likewise, if inherence—which is of a single nature—is the sole locus for substance, quality, action, substantiality, quality-ness, action-ness, existence (*sattā*), and so forth, then why would there not be confusion? Nor is there an exclusion of inherence from residing in two things, which you assert as its distinction from conjunction in the passage beginning with "between each pair," and so forth.

The proof for this is as follows: First of all, you yourself have described "subsistence in two" (*dvivṛttitva*) in the case of inherence (*samavāya*) with respect to substance, substanceness, and so forth. And we shall prove this subsistence in two by means of the following: [Inherence possesses] subsistence in two because it is the cause of denotation and cognition qualified by a pair of related entities, like the conjunction of a bowl and curds. Just as in the case of the conjunction of a bowl and curds, where a denotation and a cognition caused by that [conjunction] are observed—either "the curd-bowl" or "the bowl-curds"—and thus that subsistence in two exists, so too does it exist in the case of inherence between substance and quality, and so forth; such is the description of subsistence in two.

Therefore, the attachment of the faults you previously asserted remains in the case of *samavāya* (inherence); to this he says: "And thus," and so forth, up to "only non-eternality," the meaning of which has already been explained. [The reading] *aṅgabhāvabhāvagataṃ* is found in the Pāṭhāvalī and Viśeṣa manuscripts.
See the state of being a limb in Ḍe-raṃ, page 527, note 2;
the example is in Pra.
See page 528, line 17:
*vāvaddravya* (variant:
*sambandhe dvaya*) in the manuscript.
Are they observed?

Indeed, the designation and cognition—"inherence exists between substance and quality, between substance and action, between substance and substanceness, between quality and qualitiness, and between action and actionness"—are observed.

Furthermore, since inherence, like conjunction, would subsist in two things due to the relationship of container and contained (ādhārādheyabhāva) within a state of difference, it would necessarily follow that inherence is non-eternal.
Such is the intention that appears;
see page 528, note 8,
regarding the description of its twofold occurrence.

See page 528, line 17: as for this passage beginning with "jñānam" and so forth, by this you are raising an objection regarding contradiction with perception (*pratyakṣa*) against your own position; for indeed...

...In this way, if inherence (*samavāya*) were a single entity, there would also be cognition of qualities (*guṇa*) regarding substances (*dravya*), because inherence is the cause of the cognition of qualities, just like the quality itself.

As for what is stated—that due to the restriction by substance-ness (*dravyatva*) and other [universals] which are mutually distinct from one another, the cognition of a substance occurs only with respect to substances, and so forth—it appears that you are, by this, raising an objection based on contradiction with perception (*pratyakṣa-virodha*) against your own position. This is the intended meaning.

For if inherence (*samavāya*) were one, there would be no distinction, and thus neither differentiation nor restriction would exist; consequently, the cognition of a substance would not occur in relation to substances alone.
This appears to be the intended meaning:
since the very same relationship that exists between a substance and its status as a substance also exists for a quality, the substance itself would possess the nature of a quality.
And because of its connection with the state of being a quality (guṇatva), there is a loss of its status as a substance; thus,
its [substantial] nature ceases.

Because it is connected with that substance as a subordinate element (*guṇabhāva*), because it has become subordinate, and because it is not the substratum of qualities, it is called "non-existence" [in the sense of being non-substantial]; thus there is the cessation of the state of being a quality, since the definition of a quality does not apply to it.
The definition of substance (*dravya*) is: "that which possesses action, possesses qualities, and is an inherent cause" (VS 1.1.14).
The definition of quality (*guṇa*) is: "that which resides in substance, is devoid of qualities, and is independent in not being a cause of conjunctions and disjunctions" (VS 1.1.15).
1 14–15 And then...
What is the reason? ...

Because that substance is connected as a subordinate factor (guṇabhāvena), there is the cessation of the state of being a substance [in the quality]; this appears to be the intended meaning—see page 440, note 5.

As for the passage beginning with "yattvidam" and so forth, he refers by extension to the very text stated by the opponent, namely the section beginning with "yāvajjñānam" and so forth; [it means that] there is a restriction of the substrata, such as substances and the like, by their respective superstrata, such as substanceness and the like, which are mutually distinct qualifiers, because of the arising of cognitions corresponding to their own essential nature.

To this it is replied: How do you raise the objection of contradiction with perception against our own position? He explains this with the words "for not," etc.; the word *hi* has the sense of a reason (*hetu*). Since inherence (*samavāya*) is one, there is no distinction [between categories] due to its being non-distinct from substance and so forth, as well as from substanceness and so forth; consequently, there would be neither differentiation (*vyatireka*) nor restriction (*niyama*). Therefore, the cognition "substance" would not occur only with respect to substances. The explanation of that is as follows: "In this way," etc. Thus, for you, if inherence were one, the cognition of a quality would occur even with respect to substances because of non-distinction, just as it does with respect to qualities.

By virtue of the word "also" (api), [the question arises: what is the reason [that inherence is not a cause] even with respect to actions? It is because inherence is the cause of the cognition of qualities (*guṇa*). How so? Like that which possesses qualities (*guṇavat*); that is, just as in the case of qualities, so it is for that which possesses qualities.
[The proof for this—"like that which possesses qualities"—is not found in the Bhāṣya manuscript.]
He explains that very point: "In the case of identity, this which is 'this'... and so on, up to "...the quality-ness of even a substance."

If, when curd, honey, water, and so forth are mixed in a vessel, it is impossible to determine with certainty that "this is the nature of this very thing" because of the lack of distinction—since the conjunction is one and thus connected to everything such that one cannot say "this is the curd-vessel," "this is the honey-vessel," or "this is the water-vessel"—then likewise here too, since the relation by way of substance is the very same as that of the quality, for this reason it follows that the state of being a quality belongs to the substance as well; the meaning is that the substance itself becomes a quality.

Furthermore, due to its connection with the state of being a quality (*guṇatva*), there is a loss of its status as a substance (*dravyabhāva*); thus, when it attains the state of a quality, its status as a substance is lost. By inducing a foreign form (*pararūpatā*), it brings about the abandonment of its own nature (*svarūpa*). The phrase "of that" (*tasya*) and so forth is the means of explanation up until the point of cessation; because the substance is connected with the state of being a quality, it has abandoned its status as a substance and is thus like a quality.

In this way, first of all, there is the consequence that a substance would become a quality and abandon its status as a substance; would there not also be the same [consequence] for a quality in the case of non-abiding? Primary Text: "pra" (the word *anavasthāne* is repeated).
The meaning is that there are two types of instability: the attainment of the state of a quality (*guṇatva*) and the abandonment of the state of a substance (*dravyatva*).
Regarding the phrase "of that substance" and so forth:

since that substance is connected by way of being a quality, it has become subordinate (*guṇībhūta*) and is no longer a substratum for another quality. Furthermore, there is no quality that does not reside in a substance; consequently, there is also no substance that does not serve as a substratum for qualities. Due to the absence of that [substance], when a substance does not exist, of what would there be a quality? Thus, the status of being a quality ceases, because the defining characteristic of a quality is untenable in its absence.
By the two sūtras beginning with "possessing action" (*kriyāvat*), he demonstrates the definition;
then, by the passage beginning with "and therefore," he applies the previously mentioned subject matter.

Why is this? Following such a question regarding the cause, here too—as in the previous case—there are two instances of instability: the consequence of [the substance] becoming a substance and the abandonment of its quality-ness.
Is it that when a quality becomes a substance,
there is both the attainment of substantiality and the non-abandonment of quality;
and when a substance becomes a quality, there is both the attainment of quality and the abandonment of substantiality?
Likewise, as for this [quality] being the object of an action...
neither quality nor action possess such characteristics;
because they lack those characteristics and do not exist, there is an absence of a substance that could serve as their substratum or be indicated by them.
Due to the absence of that [substratum], there is likewise the absence of the properties residing in it, such as substantiality (*dravyatva*) and so forth.
In this way, through combinations of pairs, twenty-four infinite regressions (*anavasthā*) and circularities (*cakraka*) arise; the same applies to cause and effect.

Regarding the passage beginning with "of the quality" (*guṇasya*), one might object: "Since inherence (*samavāya*) is all-pervading, the reality [of the quality] is established because it is connected even by its own nature.
To this we reply: "Indeed, for that very reason, a confusion (*saṅkara*) is asserted, since it is also connected by the nature of another, and thus lacks reality [as such]."

And thus, since the principles (tattvas) pertaining to their own respective objects are all-pervading by virtue of inherence (samavāya) being both all-pervading and unitary, they [the principles] become all-pervading;
therefore, [there would follow] the cognition of action within substances, qualities, and actions.

Therefore, since substances (*dravya*), qualities (*guṇa*), and actions (*karman*) are not established [as distinct entities], there arises the implication that there can be no cognition of substance among substances, no cognition of quality among qualities, and no cognition of action among actions. Likewise, regarding the passage beginning with "this [quality] being treated as an action," the two instances of instability—the assumption of another form and the abandonment of one's own form—are explained through the door of the impossibility of defining them; this has already been understood up to the point where it is established that qualities and actions do not possess such characteristics, thereby demonstrating the absence of a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).

Because those two lack defining characteristics, they are non-existent; since those two—quality (*guṇa*) and action (*karman*)—lack defining characteristics, they are non-existent like a sky-flower. Due to their non-existence, there is an absence of the substance (*dravya*) that is characterized as their substratum (*āśraya*). Because of the absence of the substrata—the qualities and actions which serve as the defining characteristics—there is no substance as a substratum, just as there is no fire in the absence of heat, or like a sky-flower due to the absence of defining characteristics. And when that substance is absent, because qualities and actions—which lack a substratum—are non-existent, and because the substance itself is non-existent, there is also the non-existence of "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) and the other categories which depend upon it. For it has been said: "Dependents (*āśrayin*) resort to a substrate (*āśraya*) once it has arisen."
See page 455, line 18.

Thus, by way of pairwise combinations, there are two [cases] for a substance together with a quality and an action; two for a quality together with a substance and an action; and two for an action together with a substance and a quality—making six cycles.

Furthermore, there are two for a quality by way of its being a substance and an action; two for a substance by way of its being a quality and an action; and two for a substance by way of its being an action and a quality—making another six.

Thus, there are twelve cycles (*cakraka*). Specifically, there are six cycles for substantiality (*dravyatva*) with respect to action and quality (*guṇa*); for quality-ness (*guṇatva*) with respect to substance and action; and for action-ness (*karmatva*) with respect to substance and quality. There are another six cycles for substance with respect to quality and action; for quality with respect to substance and action; and for action with respect to substance and quality. These also total twelve.
In this way, through the combination of pairs, there are twenty-four infinite regress cycles (*anavasthā-cakraka*).
Why? Because [the argument] beginning with "likewise, of cause and effect" up to "of the quality" and so forth, presents the reason already explained;
it applies the [reason] by means of substance and quality.
The wheels are wheels; they exist as substantial entities characterized by their qualities.
"...and so forth"— this is the explanation of the reason (hetu) alone, excluding the explanations found in the Uv, Vi, Hī, Khyāna, Ma, and Ḍe.
He says: "But surely," and so forth;

because inherence (*samavāya*) is all-pervading, there is also a relation by way of its own nature (*svatattva*). For a substance, its own nature is "substanceness" (*dravyatva*); likewise for the remaining two [categories], each has its own pair. Since inherence exists with everything, and because there is a relation even by way of its own nature, the state of being that [nature]—whether it be the state of being a substance, the state of being a quality, or the state of being an action—is established. "State" (*tattva*) means the condition of being that; thus, the state of being a substance, the state of being a quality, or the state of being an action is accomplished.
