To this it is replied: "Is it not precisely for this reason that confusion (*saṅkara*) is asserted—that because there is a connection even with the Supreme Reality (*paratattva*), [an entity] is also 'not-that' (*atattva*)? This is used in the sense of a reason; since there is a connection even with the Supreme Reality, therefore there is both its state (*tadbhāva*) and the state of not being that (*atadbhāva*). Thus, one is not released from the fault of confusion. Furthermore, by the word 'also' (*api*), which you yourself have employed, [this fault] is established; moreover, there is an accumulation of defects. This is what was stated.

that too is not the case; for since the pot, the curd, the relation of container and contained, and inherence are all one, there is no differentiation—just as it is established in common worldly experience—due to the reality that is the cause of inherence, precisely because it acquires its own subsistence. Rather, the restriction of container and contained between the pot and the curd arises solely from the causal power (*kāraka-śakti*), even though their conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is one.

Regarding the passage beginning with "and just as [the categories] have their own objects," etc.: for it is held that the principles (tattvas) are all-pervading; since inherence (samavāya) is both all-pervading and unitary, those [principles] now become all-pervading [by virtue of inhering in it]. Consequently, a contradiction arises with one's own tenets. Thus, the absence of the remaining categories is stated. Therefore, the previous section of the text beginning with "of substance, quality, and action" continues up to "the knowledge of action regarding actions."

In that [previous case], the refutation was by way of the absence of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), on the grounds that "there is an absence of those things possessing established characteristics"; here, however, the distinction is that the refutation is because "there is an absence of those things established," since they have been refuted along with their realities (*tattva*) and characteristics. Furthermore, it is also by way of refuting the restriction of the causes for the differentiation of the cognitions to be contained [within them], as has been stated... [end of quote].
...that too is not the case, because even the pot, the curd, the relation of container and contained, and inherence are one;

for, due to the unity of the principle that is the cause of inherence, there is an absence of difference just as it is established in common worldly experience through the very acquisition of its own subsistence. Rather, the restriction of container and contained between the pot and the curd arises solely from the causal power (*kāraka-śakti*), even though their conjunction is one, just as in the following example:

As for what was also said—that just as there is a restriction regarding the locus and the located despite the unity of the conjunction between a bowl and curd, so too there is a restriction regarding the relationship of locus and located among substance and the other categories despite the unity of inherence—this also is certainly not the case;
such appears to be the intention.
See page 524, note 3.

"Even though universals (*sāmānya*) have unlimited spatial extension, nevertheless, due to the restriction of their indicators (*upalakṣaṇa*) and the restriction of the causal complex (*kāraṇasāmagrī*), they are omnipresent within their own respective domains; and because the modes of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and inherence (*samavāya*) do not exist in the intervening space, they are not designated [there]. This is the explanation of this passage in Praśastapāda’s *Bhāṣya* on the definition of universals: he states the reason for what was previously asserted—that a universal inheres everywhere within its own domain and nowhere else—with the words "even though."

Although universals, because they are related to the individual (piṇḍa) arising here or there, are unconfined in space and have no fixed location, nevertheless—due to the restriction of the specific configuration of parts which serves as the defining characteristic and the manifestor, and due to the restriction of the causal complex that produces the individual—they inhere everywhere within their own proper domain and nowhere else.

This is what is meant: the specific configuration of the dewlap and so forth is the manifestor of "cowness" (gotva); the specific configuration of the mane and so forth is that of "horseness" (aśvatva); and the specific configuration of the particular neck and so forth is that of "potness" (ghaṭatva), because of the necessity of their cognition.
Furthermore, these specific configurations are not common to all individual objects (piṇḍa), but rather they occur only in their respective restricted instances.

In this regard, although every universal is capable of being connected with another individual—just as it is with its own [manifesting] object—even when that other individual is arising—nevertheless, the inherence (*samavāya*) of a universal occurs only in that individual where its manifestor is possible, and not elsewhere.
Thus, the restriction regarding the connection of a universal follows from the restriction of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*).
For this is the very nature of causes such as threads, that when a substance is produced by them, only "cloth-ness" (*paṭatva*) inheres therein, and nothing else.

For this is the greatness of the lump of clay and so forth: that when a substance is being produced by them, it is pot-ness alone that inheres in it, and nothing else. A universal does not come from elsewhere and become connected [to the object], because it is devoid of motion. Furthermore, if it did not previously exist there, then its connection with the lump being produced would be impossible; yet, in all cases, a connection with the produced lump is observed. Therefore, in order to refute the view of some who hold that "everything exists everywhere," he says: "Because of the absence of the modes of conjunction and inherence in the intermediate state, they are inexpressible."

The "intervening space" (*antarāla*) may be ether (*ākāśa*), the substance of direction (*dig-dravya*), still air, or the absence of corporeal substances. In these, there is neither conjunction (*saṃyoga*) nor inherence (*samavāya*) of universals such as "cowness" (*gotva*). Furthermore, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for their existence while remaining unconnected. Therefore, universals are not designated as being in the intervening space; the meaning is that they do not exist [there]. How, then, are they connected with the individual (*piṇḍa*) arising therein? It is through the causal capacity (*kāraṇa-sāmarthya*).

For conjunction (*saṃyoga*) occurs either for that which has come from elsewhere or for that which is already situated right there; however, inherence (*samavāya*) is of a different nature, because wherever the causes operate toward the production of an aggregate, it occurs in that very same place within the aggregate—neither having come from elsewhere nor being situated [previously]—due to the efficacy of the causes, since the power of things cannot be questioned. Thus it is stated in the *Nyāyakandalī* regarding "having come" and "not having come."
See page 526,
line 1, or read "veti" (or rather) in the manuscript;
as for the passage beginning with "yadapi" (even though), etc.

As for what has been stated by another—that just as in the conjunction of a bowl and curd, there is a restriction such that the curd alone is the contained (*ādheya*) and the bowl alone is the container (*ādhāra*), so too substance alone is the container and quality, action, etc., are the contained; and substance, quality, and action alone are the containers, while substanceness, qualitiness, and actionness are the contained—this too is not correct. This is because the bowl, the curd, the relation of container and contained, and inherence (*samavāya*) are all one. Furthermore, according to your own view, since the inherences of the two containers (the bowl and the curd), the two contained (bowl-ness and curd-ness), their respective essences, and the essences such as substanceness are all one—and since those whose distinctness is merely figurative due to the difference of their substrates are in fact one in a primary sense—the fault of confusion (*saṅkara*) remains exactly as previously described by the aforementioned method.
Regarding the doubling of the syllable *ta* in the word *yosta*, the reading *tvayostattvayoḥ* is also correct.

As for the phrase *vāyabhedo ya*, if its meaning is intended to be non-confused and restricted, we ourselves shall explain it more clearly, as follows: "of that which has conjunction as its cause," and so forth.

Whatever is the cause of inherence—the potness of the pot and the curd-ness of the curd in the case of a pot and its contents—is acquired by those [qualities] through their own nature; and you yourself have stated that this occurs for those two just as it is established in common worldly experience, not because of any similarity [between them]. Likewise here too, the answer is the same: even though inherence is one, the distinction in restriction arises solely from the power of the causal factors (*kāraka*).

As for what is said— that there is no contingency of confusion regarding the manifested (*vyaṅgya*) and the manifestor (*vyañjaka*)— this [distinction] between the manifested and the manifestor would indeed remain unconfused in this way.
Of inherence...
likewise, if that very [same thing]...
...the cessation of qualities, actions, and states—thus all conceptual proliferation (prapañca) regarding every mental construction should be explained according to its own respective meaning.

Difference arises precisely from the acquisition of their own respective functions; for even in your own view, the difference between curd and a bowl, as recognized by the world, is not due to some external factor. Therefore, lest we speak in contradiction to the world, we maintain that difference is established through the very capacity of the causal factors (*kāraka-śakti*), just as it is established in worldly experience. Even though there is an underlying unity produced by conjunction and transformation, we disregard that and declare an unmixed rule: that although the conjunction is one, the bowl possesses the capacity of the substratum (*ādhāra-śakti*) and the curd possesses the capacity of the contained (*ādheya-śakti*).
The commentary on this point, up to the rule regarding the relationship between the locus and the located (*ādhārādheya-niyama*), has its meaning already explained.

And this must necessarily be so: even if you were to postulate an inherence (*samavāya*), you would still have to accept exactly this [conclusion]; for, by the very authority of your own words, you yourself have stated that even though conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is a single entity, the specific restriction of locus and located between the bowl and the curd is distinct due solely to the causal capacities (*kāraka-śakti*). This is the answer you have given.

If it is asked, "What is that answer? it is said: "No, because of equality. Thus, here too, the answer is the same: even though inherence (*samavāya*) is one, the distinction in restriction arises solely from the power of the causal factors (*kāraka-śakti*). The explanation of that has already been understood up to the point where you yourself stated, "only in some [case]," because of equality; thus, here too, the answer is the same—namely, that even though inherence is one, the distinction in restriction arises solely from the power of the causal factors.
...in some [place] indeed.

Even though inherence (*samavāya*) is a single entity, the restriction between the locus and the located depends solely upon the capacity of the causal factors (*kāraka-śakti*); thus, the property of "substanceness" (*dravyatva*) and so forth does not inhere in all substances and the like, but only in some. This appears to be the intended meaning when it is said: "There is no consequence of confusion (*saṅkara*) regarding the manifested and the manifestor. And this non-confusion of the manifested and the manifestor would indeed be established in this way.
Of inherence...
likewise, if that very [same thing]...
"...the cessation of the state of qualities and actions"—thus all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) regarding every [category] should be explained according to its own specific meaning.

As for what is said—that there is a distinction between substance (*dravya*) and substanceness (*dravyatva*) and so forth due to the difference between the manifested (*vyaṅgya*) and the manifestor (*vyañjaka*), like a jar and a lamp—the intention appears to be that there is no consequence of confusion (*saṅkara*) because of the restrictive rule of the distinction between locus (*ādhāra*) and located (*ādheya*); see page 524, note 3.

Furthermore, this relationship of the manifested (*vyaṅgya*) and the manifestor (*vyañjaka*) could only exist if substance (*dravya*), substantiality (*dravyatva*), and so forth were established as distinct entities; however, they are not so established. For if that [distinction] were established, there would also be a fixed rule regarding the distinction between the locus (*ādhāra*) and the located (*ādheya*), and thus there would indeed be no confusion (*asaṅkara*). Such appears to be the intention [of the opponent]. However, since inherence (*samavāya*) is unitary, just like the conjunction of a bowl and curd, there is an absence of a fixed rule regarding the distinction between locus and located; therefore, the undesirable consequence of confusion remains exactly as it was. This appears to be the intended meaning. Thus ends that section.
Having established the proof of difference, [there is] the proof of that statement. *pra* [is] the beginning.

Regarding the phrase "as in the case of... and what is said—namely, that "the distinction between substance and substanceness, etc., arises from the difference between the manifested (*vyaṅgya*) and the manifestor (*vyañjaka*), like a jar and a lamp"—this other refutation has its meaning already explained up to the point where there is no risk of confusion (*saṅkara*). This is the position of the Vaiśeṣika.

As for the Master’s statement beginning with "the manifested and the manifestor," this would be so if the relationship of manifested and manifestor between the substance and substantiality and so forth were established as separate—like the example of a lamp and a jar—but rather, a rule of difference in essence has not been established; for if that were established, there would also be a rule of difference between the locus and the located, and thus, until that purpose is clarified, there would indeed be no non-confusion.

And in order to demonstrate the non-establishment of that reason, he says: "of inherence," and so forth. This has already been answered; because it is equal in its lack of a restrictive rule regarding the distinction between locus and located, it does not share the common characteristics of the example. Since this point was explained at length previously, he merely recalls it: "Likewise, if it were the very same... and so on, up to "...the cessation of the state of qualities and actions. All conceptual proliferation must be elaborated; this is an extension of the previously stated argument.
If one asks, "Up to what point? it is said: up to this limit of the text.

"According to their respective objects" (*yathāsvārtham*) means that whatever is its own object, it is explained according to that object; thus, substance, quality, action, substantiality, qualitiness, actionness, conjunction, and non-existence are to be explained exactly as before, in their respective cycles.
Furthermore, as for this objection raised—that the oneness of inherence (*samavāya*) contradicts the conventional usage of "fivefold"—it is precisely so.
Moreover, this is answered: "No, because of the distinction of substrata, just like existence (*bhāva*)."

"...so too, even if inherence (*samavāya*) were one..."—this is utterly baseless. Since there is no fixed rule regarding either the manifested (*vyaṅgya*) or its substratum (*ādhāra*), how could there be a manifested object or a manifesting agent (*vyañjaka*)? Or how could there be a diversity of substrata? Because inherence is one, like the moon in water, and because an entity (*bhāva*) lacks any commonality with the moon in water, how can there be a metaphorical attribution of multiplicity? And how, then, could there be an entity at all?

Just as a single entity may be metaphorically designated as manifold due to its specific substrata—like the moon reflected in water—so too, although inherence (*samavāya*) is one, the conventional usage of "fivefold" will occur due to the distinction between the manifested and the manifestor, the restriction of container and contained, and the specificity of its substrata; this appears to be the intended meaning. Thus, both of these share in the nature of the universal (*sāmānya*) and the existent (*bhāva*), which is the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛti*); that by which something exists is *sattā*, and the particular (*viśeṣa*) is also the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*).

Furthermore, regarding this doubt you raised—that the oneness of inherence (*samavāya*) contradicts the conventional usage of "fiveness"—that very point appears to me exactly as it does to you: that it indeed does contradict. As for the response given by the Vaiśeṣika to that doubt—"No, because of the distinction of substrates, just like existence" (*bhāva*)—the three existences of substance and so forth are the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), and the moon reflected in water is the counter-example (*pratidṛṣṭānta*). Thus, the application to the subject (*dārṣṭāntika*) beginning with "even though inherence is one," and so forth, has its meaning already explained, up until the word "will be."

The Teacher states the following reply: This [objection] is entirely baseless. Since there is no fixed rule regarding either the manifested (*vyaṅgya*) or its substratum (*ādhāra*), the very locus (*āśraya*) you desire—whether as the manifester (*vyañjaka*) or the manifested (*vyaṅgya*)—is unestablished; how then could the object to be superimposed, which is manifested by that [locus], be established? Or how could there be a diversity of substrata, given that the cessation of the six categories (*ṣaṭpadārtha*) is well-established when inherence (*samavāya*) is one? Since inherence is unitary—like the moon in the sky—and since the entity called "existence" (*sattā*) lacks any commonality with the moon in the water, how can there be a metaphorical attribution of multiplicity? Furthermore, because the moon in the water is a mere reflection, or because it is not manifold, how could there even be an "entity"? Even an "entity" does not exist as a single thing distinct from substance (*dravya*) and the other categories, for this dispute is rooted in that [very notion]. Enough of this overly prolix discussion.
And [he who is] water-drinker and [he who is] non-water-drinker.
From the state of being sustained (*dhāraṇīyatva*), from the state of being sustained,
there would be water.
...of his water?
...of his much... Pāhīḥ.
In the edition of Viśvanātha (vi), there is the reading *bahu-ḍe-raṃ-vi-tvād vidasya pra-*,
whereas here, the reading might also be *tvād vādasya*.
See Kāśikā, page 107, note 6.

Thus, by means of this detailed refutation of the Vaiśeṣika position—which asserts that there is a real distinction between the existence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the existence of relation (*sambandha*), and the existence of the entity itself—it follows that this [conclusion] is reached; he demonstrates that as follows: "In this way, both... and so forth. The nature of this principle—that "both possess both"—is that whatever is a universal (*sāmānya*) is both affirmed and regulated, and whatever is a particular (*viśeṣa*) is likewise both affirmed and regulated.

He explains that by demonstrating the meaning of the phonemes through the meanings of the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*): "The universal (*sāmānya*) is the state (*bhāva*), which is the meaning of the base. He shows this: "That which exists by means of that [universal] is *sattā* (existence)," because the root *bhū* is listed in the *Dhātupāṭha* as "in the sense of existence" (*bhū sattāyām*). Thus, it is the universal. Is that merely the meaning of the base? No, it is said; the particular (*viśeṣa*) is also the meaning of the suffix, because it is the meaning of the suffix expressing the state of being that very [universal's] possessor. Therefore, it is stated that the same thing is both the meaning of the base and the meaning of the suffix.

That which is the meaning of the suffix denoting the agent is a particular; yet it is also a universal, because it is existence (*sattā*), being, or the nature of becoming (*bhāva*). For without the universal of becoming, that [agent] would not be an agent, as it would lack the capacity to exist. Thus, that very meaning of the suffix functions without overstepping the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*); therefore, it is said to be "denoting the state of being" (*tvāvācin*) and also "the meaning of the suffix" (*pratyayārtha*).
Is the meaning "that which is to be accomplished" (kāryārtha) also logical?
[It is so, for] the universal (sāmānya), the activity (pravṛtti), the injunction (vidhi), the existent (bhāva), and the particular (viśeṣa) are also [included].
...the restriction and the absence [of it]—
both these, without attaining oneness as before, become the universal and the particular;
[this applies to] engagement and withdrawal...
...by which... as...
...for by which...
...if this...
...is like a flower in the sky.

The underlying intention appears to be that "universal" (sāmānya) is "activity" (pravṛtti), "substance" (dravya) is "continuity" (anvaya), "possessor of attributes" (dharmī) is "affirmation" (vidhi) or "existence" (bhāva); while "particular" (viśeṣa) is "cessation" (nivṛtti), "synonym" (paryāya) is "exclusion" (vyatireka), "attribute" (dharma) is "otherness" (anyatva), and "restriction" (niyama) is "non-existence" (abhāva). See page 371.

The underlying intention appears to be as follows: "Universal" (sāmānya) is activity (pravṛtti), substance (dravya) is continuity (anvaya), the substratum (dharmī) is affirmation (vidhi) or existence (bhāva); "particular" (viśeṣa) is cessation (nivṛtti), synonym (paryāya) is exclusion (vyatireka), attribute (dharma) is otherness (anyatva), and restriction (niyama) is non-existence (abhāva). See page 371–1.
In this way, the existence and non-existence of substance, field, and so forth [is established].

Every individual object, such as a jar, depends upon its own cause, such as clay; for if it were devoid of specific distinctions, it could not exist. Thus, its existence or non-existence consists in its occurrence within the various parts of its own constituents. A jar is therefore characterized by the presence or absence of these states. In this manner, through substance (*dravya*), space (*kṣetra*), time (*kāla*), and mode (*bhāva*), there is existence and non-existence based on the jar, the cloth, another jar, its own space, another space, its own time, another time, its own mode, and another mode. This constitutes its existence and non-existence.
The intention shines forth thus:

"The throat exists as its own self and not as the self of the skull and so forth; the skulls exist as their own selves and not as the self of the throat and so forth"—thus there is a mode of existence characterized by presence and absence among its own constituent parts; this is the shining intention.

It might be thought: "Just as in the view of the Vidhi-naya, the attainment of unity between the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*) is accepted, so too by the logic you have stated, this attainment of unity [of the two] would also follow; let it not be so. Desiring to state the definition of the particular for these two—distinguishing them from each other through synonyms and the like, while setting aside the unity consisting of the existence of all conceptual constructions—he says: "The universal is activity," and so on, up to "the positive is existence"; likewise, "the particular is also," and so on, up to "the restrictive is non-existence. These two, existence and non-existence, differ according to their synonyms.

Both of these, as previously explained in the context of the doctrines of injunction (*vidhi*), the object of injunction (*vidhyartha*), conceptualization (*vikalpa*), the person (*puruṣa*), and so forth—without falling into such a state of being a single entity—are such that the universal (*sāmānya*) remains both universal and particular, and the particular (*viśeṣa*) likewise remains both particular and universal.
This should be understood according to the rule; the nature of the *vidhividhi-naya* is to be seen in the second chapter (*ara*).
He demonstrates this, starting with "In activity, there is cessation," and so forth; the meaning is that both are mutually inseparable, and "bhāva" refers to a real entity (*vastu*).

Existence (*bhavana*) consists of being and non-being; it is a real entity (*sat vastu*). The state of that which exists is "existence" (*sattā*), because that which is existent persists through constant necessity. Thus, for both the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*), both necessity and injunction apply.

He demonstrates those two [meanings] by means of "by which" (*yena*) for the sake of the suffix-meaning (*pratyayārtha*), and "just as" (*yathā*) for the sake of the stem-meaning (*prakṛtyartha*). By the words "by which indeed," etc., he states that existence (*bhavana*) is restricted by a restricted agent (*kartṛ*) in an action.

The passage beginning with "if this... and ending with "like a sky-flower" is the production of an undesired consequence (*aniṣṭāpādana*); it has been stated that the acquisition of self-nature (*ātmalābha*) occurs through the restriction of existence. Consequently, the acquisition of the self-nature of existence occurs through the restriction of the existent (*bhavitṛ*) by means of an obstruction (*āvaraṇa*). Thus, both of these—prescription (*vidhi*) and restriction (*niyama*)—have been stated in general terms for both cases;
he will also state them specifically later.
In both meanings, there is a restriction for both; [this is] the reading in the *Upāyaviśuddhi-bhāṣya*.
In the *Ḍe* and *Raṃ* manuscripts, the reading here might also be "there is a restriction for both meanings."
If it is argued that "one's own nature" (niyaṃ bhavana) and so forth [is the cause],
then what follows from its non-performance?
Thus, regarding the passage beginning with "substance, field," and so on, up to "existence and non-existence":

in terms of substance (*dravyataḥ*), a jar exists by way of its own persistence (*ātmanuvṛtti*), while it exists as both being and non-being through its exclusion from cloth and the like, and its exclusion from other jars.
In terms of field (*kṣetrataḥ*), a jar exists in the house and not outside; is it not so? Thus, existing in its own field and not existing in another's field or in a different field, it exists.

In terms of time, existing in the present time and not existing in the two other times—the past and the future—it is said that "it exists as a *śivaka*," even though it does not exist as such through its prior states such as the lump (*piṇḍa*) and the mound (*stūpaka*), nor through its subsequent states such as the potsherd (*kapāla*), or even while in the state of a *śivaka* itself, because it does not exist as such through its prior and subsequent [states].

Alternatively, existence and non-existence consist in the fact that an entity exists by way of its own nature (*bhāva*) through attributes such as "white" (*śivaka*) and so forth which are present, and through those occurring simultaneously—such as color, taste, and so forth—and yet does not exist by way of other states (*bhāvāntara*) such as "utility" (*upayoga*) and so forth; thus all entities possess the nature of both existence and non-existence. This is the intended meaning. *Sasattva-prameya-mīmāṃsā-vivaraṇa*.
Regarding "saṃnaya," there should be the reading "atra maṇḍape" (in this pavilion) here, or perhaps "madhye" (in the middle);
[this is] by means of the *piṇḍaka* and the *stūpaka*. (Bhāṣya)
By means of [cognitions] that arise simultaneously and [those] that arise sequentially;
here, there may also be the reading "by means of [cognitions] that arise simultaneously and...
In the absence of that, it does not occur, and rather, it occurs as the very existence of non-existence.

Likewise, even when there is totality (sāmastya) with respect to the existence of a jar, cloth, and so forth— whether in terms of substance, space, time, state, presence, or absence— there is no distinction whatsoever, because they are all equally real entities (vastu), just like [the case of] non-totality (asāmastya).
Just as...

...this distinction between the two [categories] arises from the intention to speak of the differences in the manifestation or non-manifestation of qualities, since both possess that same essential nature.

Thus, a jar certainly exists because it possesses action, quality, and designation, just like a cloth or a chariot; yet, because there is no inherence of everything in everything, inherence occurs only of a capable thing in capable things, as a jar inheres in its color, and this should be understood to apply to taste and the other qualities as well.
Alternatively, since practice proceeds toward an object, does it function with respect to each individual object?

Every individual object, such as a jar, depends upon its own cause, such as clay; by the inclusion of the word "etcetera," it is implied that cloth and other things depend upon threads and so forth. Regarding the state of being "without distinction": because it does not depend on any other cause and yet depends on its own cause, there is no distinction between existence and non-existence. The neck exists in its own nature but does not exist in the nature of the potsherds; the potsherds exist in their own nature but do not exist in the nature of the neck and so forth. Because they function toward each instance of difference—whether in the presence or absence of existence and non-existence—in relation to one another, there is a functioning characterized by existence and non-existence among the differences within its own constituent parts.

The cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of that meaning is as follows: "A jar consists of the presence and absence [of its causes]"; thus, in their absence, it does not exist; when there is no absence of presence and absence, it does not exist; and only when there is the presence of presence and absence does it exist, which means it exists only through their presence.
This is because the engagement with an object follows from the cognition [of it], and the cessation of an object follows from the cessation of the cognition of the object.
It appears that this reading is either corrupt or incomplete.

Is it because of its occurrence with respect to each individual thing— that is, its functioning upon every single object— or is it because of its occurrence as an engagement with objects, like the act of comprehension, that there is a cessation from objects?
Or is it because it has occurred in dependence on the limit of [the parts], [functioning] through each of its own constituent parts?
"Existence, non-existence, and non-existence itself; existence, non-existence, and existence itself.

To cultivate this very meaning, he states the proof: "Likewise, even when a jar is present, there is no distinction whatsoever in the existence of the substance, location, time, and state—whether as presence or absence—of the jar and other things"; this is the proposition.

The fourfold nature of the objects described in the *daṇḍaka*—beginning with "pot," "cloth," and "within a pot"—has been demonstrated to be non-existent in its entirety; the meaning of the thesis (*sādhya*) is that it is likewise [non-existent] even in its totality.
"Because it is a real entity" (*vastutvāt*) is the logical reason (*hetu*);
"like that which is not in its entirety" (*asāmastyavat*) is the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

The description of the fourfold illustrations beginning with "just as" (*yathaiva*) has its meaning already explained, up to the distinction between the manifestation (*āvṛtti*) and non-manifestation (*anāvṛtti*) of qualities. In this context, "manifestation" refers to being twice or thrice as white or black, and so forth; "non-manifestation" refers to simply being white or black. Among these, the manifestation of the quality of *sattva* (purity) is the non-manifestation of the two [other] qualities; the manifestation of the two qualities is the non-manifestation of the one quality. Likewise, the manifestation of whiteness is the non-manifestation of blackness, and the manifestation of blackness is the non-manifestation of whiteness, and so on.
See page 536, note 2:
"asāmānyavat" in the manuscript; "śukla-kṛṣṇa" in the manuscript.

If it is asked, "Since there is no difference between being of the nature of existence and non-existence, what is the distinction between totality and partiality? it is said: this distinction between both totality and partiality is due to the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*).

Why? Because of its true nature (*tattva*). True nature is the state of being that [nature], namely, the state of being both existence and non-existence (*bhāvābhāvatva*). From that true nature, due to the specific intention of the speaker (*vivakṣāviśeṣa*) alone, this distinction arises: "this is a complete jar," or "these are the neck, the shards, and so forth"—the aforementioned fourfold nature (*cāturātmya*), by virtue of the comprehensive mode of predication (*sakalādeśa*) and the partial mode of predication (*vikalādeśa*), serves as the means of demonstration. Thus, the fact that everything consists of both existence and non-existence has been established through the comprehensive mode; we shall now establish it individually through the partial mode. Why? Because of that respective true nature. *Pra.* [1/4]

In that regard, first, as for its nature as a positive entity (*bhāvātmakatva*): a jar certainly exists, because it possesses activity (*kriyā*), qualities (*guṇa*), and designations (*vyapadeśa*). Activity is the fetching of water and so forth; quality is color and so forth; designation refers to a mark (*liṅga*), a reason (*hetu*), or a term such as "mark" (*liṅga*); or it may refer to words such as "like a cloth" or "like a chariot. This is the illustration for its nature as a positive entity, by way of its distinction from a sky-flower (*khapuṣpa*).

By way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyeṇa*), the reason for the contemplation is that there is no inherence of everything in everything; for indeed, everything does not inhere everywhere—a jar does not inhere in threads, nor does a cloth in shards. Therefore, because there is no inherence of everything in everything, but rather inherence occurs only of the capable in the capable, [the effect] exists in each [cause].
If, on the other hand, it were not thus, then it would follow that it is non-existent, like oil in sand.
Yet, such being the case, the jar is not non-existent, since the jar exists in its form and color.
But surely the earth of a jar and so forth is also clay and the like; otherwise, it would be without a root.

And thus, because they consist of a single existence (*ekabhavanātmakatvāt*), like a pot and the pot’s own self, the particularity is indeed a particularity and not a non-existence; for while the generality of earth exists, qualities such as height and breadth certainly exist. This is just as, according to the view that a pot is a collection of qualities (*guṇasamudāyavāda*), one says "the pot is in color" or "color [is in the pot]"; or, according to the view that it is merely the qualities (*guṇamātravāda*), or the view that it is the substratum (*tadādhāra*) [of the qualities] (the view of the whole, *avayavivāda*), one says "the pot is certainly in color," and so forth. Likewise, this should be understood for taste and the other [qualities] as well, because each [quality] resides in a single [substance].
(Note: *°tvādyudakā* is a scribal error for *°tvādy udakā*.)
Cause (hetu), indication (apadeśa), mark (liṅga), sign (nimitta), means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), and reason (kāraṇa) are synonymous.
Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 9.2.1.
See page 489, note 6:
˚ṇānapekṣa˚ (for ˚ṇāpekṣa˚). The reading in the manuscript is ˚ṇānapekṣa˚.
Because each [quality] exists individually;
otherwise, if it were not so, then that [pot] would follow as being non-existent, like oil in sand.
Yet, while remaining thus, the pot does not cease to exist, because the pot exists in its color and taste.
But surely the earth is also [composed of] clay and so forth, like a jar; otherwise, it would be without a foundation.

And thus, because they consist of a single existence, just like a jar and the jar's own nature, that very particularity is indeed a positive entity (bhāva) and not an absence; for [qualities] such as height and breadth exist only while the universal "earth" exists. Now, the intention appears to be this: just as the particularities of a jar, such as its color and so forth, are particularities of a positive entity, so too is earth, clay, and the like; otherwise, [those particulars] would be rootless.
See page 539, line 17.

Thus, color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth, as well as clay and so forth, are indeed specific states (*bhāvaviśeṣa*) of the jar and of the earth, because they consist in a single existence (*ekabhavanātmakatva*), like the jar and the jar’s own self.

And yet, it is not the case that there is no distinction; for that very distinction—such as height, breadth, and so on—exists only while the generality of earth (*pṛthivīsāmānya*) exists. Such a root [of the argument] would also be present here.

Furthermore, if it were not thus—namely, by virtue of its similarity to cloth, chariots, and so forth, and its distinction from a sky-flower—then, like oil in sesame seeds, [the pot] would exist only in each individual [constituent]. Consequently, it would follow that it is non-existent. Why? Just as oil does not exist in sand either individually or in the aggregate, so too the pot, because of its non-existence in each individual constituent such as form (rūpa) and the rest, would become non-existent; and this is an undesirable conclusion.

Thus, the existence of a jar or the like is established in its totality because of the individual existence of its form and other qualities; otherwise, just as form [is form], taste would also be form due to the absence of its own specific nature. Yet, taste does not become form like form, nor does form become taste like taste, because that would contradict what is perceived.
Since form is indeed form and taste is indeed taste, and each does not assume the state of the other, therefore form and the rest exist, and this constitutes the existence of the jar and so forth.

If that were the case, one might suspect that because it consists merely of form and so forth, there is no "jar" at all; let such a doubt not arise. It is not the case that the jar ceases to exist when it abides in such a state, just as form and the other qualities exist even though they possess mutually exclusive natures. Such being the established state of affairs, the jar likewise exists; it does not fail to exist. Since the jar is present in both color and taste—and since the jar-ness belongs precisely to those two when they are not separate from one another, or else since the jar-ness belongs to those two which serve as its substrates—it leads to this conclusion: either collectively, the jar is indeed of the nature of both existence and non-existence.
It might be space;
that [space] is non-existence (*abhāva*), or it is established as being of the nature of existence (*bhāva*).

Now, the Vaiśeṣika, asserting that the particular (*viśeṣa*) is indeed positive in nature and rejecting the particular as being negative in nature, says: "Is it not the case that [the term] 'pot'... and so forth.

Just as a jar exists in its substrata such as form and so forth, or according to other philosophical systems, the jar is established as being nothing but form and so forth—thus not being without foundation—so too is the earth [established] as clay and so on. Within clay, stone, sand, clods of earth, diamonds, trees, shrubs, creepers, climbing plants, and spreading vines, the earth is their very essence; these are merely its particular manifestations (*viśeṣa*), just as form and so forth are of the jar. A non-entity (*abhāva*) is not a particular manifestation; otherwise, if it were a particular manifestation of a non-entity due to being without foundation, then like a sky-flower, the jar and its forms would result in non-existence, which is not desired.

Thus, by this reasoning, it has been stated that form (*rūpa*) and so forth, as well as clay and so forth, are the specific states (*viśeṣa-bhāva*) of the jar and the earth respectively. Furthermore, the passage beginning with "and likewise" and continuing through the section on the cultivation of the nature of being a specific state of existence, up to "extensiveness and so forth," presents the reason: "because its essence consists in a single becoming. The analysis of the compound is as follows: either "a single becoming" (*ekam eva bhavanam*), or "that whose essence is the becoming of one thing alone" (*ekasyaiva vā bhavanam ātmā asya*). Whatever has a single becoming as its essence is not a specific state of non-existence (*abhāva-viśeṣa*).
The illustration is: like a jar and the jar’s own self. Just as the jar itself is the jar’s own self, and nothing else—such as a sky-flower or the non-existent—could be so considered;

[if you object that] then a lack of distinction would follow, such that even the element of earth would not consist of a single being because it too possesses the nature of both existence and non-existence;
[we reply: surely even earth does not become water and so forth.
[Objection: No, because [the term] "substance" (dravya) occurs through the process of becoming (*bhāvanā*), just like the aforementioned examples. [Reply:
But does it not follow that substance is also a quality (*guṇa*)? [Objection:
No, because [the term] "existent" (*sat*) occurs through the process of becoming.
If it is simply "existent," for what specific reason is everything considered "only existent" and not "only substance"? Because...
[as in the case of] a cloth in its threads.

If this is so, then even when "it exists" (*bhavati*) is said, it amounts to saying "it does not exist," because clay, form, and so forth, possess the nature of being one with the jar, just as the jar is one with its own self; and this is undesirable.

To this, it is replied: there is no such lack of distinction, because we observe specific states of existence within the very self of the jar itself, which possesses distinctions of place, time, form, and so on.
Therefore, he says: "The distinction is precisely that [specific state], not non-existence."

If it is asked, "What is this particularity (*viśeṣa*) of earth and so forth?", it is said: while the generality (*sāmānya*) of earth exists, there is no absence of particularities such as height or breadth; likewise, a jar (*ghaṭa*) is also a particular form consisting of the single becoming of clay, and is thus a positive entity (*bhāva*), not the absence of cloth or other things. This is just as in the case of desired objects, where "spreading" (*avatāna*) refers to branches—such as those of the *ketakī*, citron, and so forth—that extend downward. (*Pra. avatanvantītyavatānā nāma viṭapāḥ ketakībījapūrādayaḥ*)
Thus, in the *Nyāyakandalī* commentary on Praśastapāda’s *Bhāṣya*, regarding the definition of earth,
it is stated that the nature of the earth-element is not merely the state of being a single entity, because that too consists of both existence and non-existence;
indeed, even earth does not become water and so forth.
No; for [the term] "substance" arises from the act of becoming (*bhavana*) in the same manner as the aforementioned examples.
But does it not follow that substance is also a quality?
No; for [the term] "substance" arises from the act of being existent (*sat*).
If it is simply "existent," for what specific reason does everything become "only existent" and not "only substance"? Since, however...
[as in] the cloth in the threads.
If this is so, then even when "it exists" (bhavati) is said, it amounts to saying that "there is no object," because such existence [is understood] as being other than [true] existence.

[Regarding the reading] *°tmakakākāra* [or] *°tmaka ākāra*? Here the Teacher says: Even for the element of earth (*pṛthivībhūta*), the state of consisting of multiple existences (*anekabhavana*)—which you maintain—is not possible; how much less so for the jar and the jar’s own self? Why? Because even that element of earth consists of both existence and non-existence (*bhāvābhāvātmakatvāt*) with respect to its becoming as ground (*bhūmibhavana*).

He demonstrates this with the words "But surely," and so forth: the becoming of earth is the non-becoming of water, fire, and so on; this very thing is its root, namely the becoming of a specific absence. Since it has that as its root, why should there be the consequence of its non-existence? The intention is that, in the establishment of a specific entity devoid of a specific absence, there is no illustrative example for me [to cite].
Mā pra°.

The opponent says: No; because [the term] "substance" (dravya) arises as a presentation of what has been stated, earth exists only through its inseparable connection with the existence of substance, or else earth, water, and so forth exist as substance within earth, water, and so forth; otherwise, there would be a lack of foundation—and thus that very same passage should be recited as appropriate.

To this, the reply is: Observe that even "substance" does not exist as a quality; therefore, the statement regarding existence is one whose existence is inseparable from non-existence (see page 538, line 3).

"No," says the proponent of non-existence (*abhāvavādin*), following the previous argument that "existence" is a qualification of an entity because of its pervasive presence in the manifestation of being. He states: "If [it is] 'existent,' etc. This is an argument for the doctrine of non-existence by way of demonstrating an undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭāpādana*).

If it exists simply as "existent," then because existence is non-distinct and because substance, quality, and action are not separate from it, they would be mere modalities (*paryāya*); by what specific cause, then, does everything exist as "existent" alone, rather than as "substance" alone? Moreover, this is observed: it is not merely substance, since existence (*sadbhāva*) belongs to qualities and actions as well.
"Because of the absence of qualities and actions, a substance is 'existent' (*sat*); and because of the absence of that [substance], qualities and actions are 'existent.

Since it has been stated that there is no such thing as 'existence' apart from substance and so forth, you are stating something contrary to what is observed. To this we reply: your argument beginning with "because of that," which establishes the existence of things as being inseparable from non-existence—just as a cloth exists in its threads—is already refuted.
The phrase "incapable of [understanding] the two" is found in the Bhāṣya;
furthermore, this example is found in the Ya manuscript, while "caṭamarka" is found in the Bhāṣya.

Thus far, existence accompanied by non-existence has been explained by way of refuting the position of absolute existence. Hereafter, it will be demonstrated that non-existence accompanied by existence is established by way of refuting the position of absolute non-existence—beginning with the words "If it were so," and so forth. The proponent of absolute existence addresses the proponent of absolute non-existence: because of the absence of existence on all sides, [non-existence] is like a sky-flower.
Now, does a mat not indeed come into being only by not existing on all sides within cloth and other such things?
Surely, by the expression "on all sides," its own non-existence as well is stated.
Likewise...

non-existence is the property of the subject (pakṣadharma) in the case of absolute non-beneficiality; a cloth is neither a mat nor is it color and so forth—surely even its non-existence on all sides establishes its existence as well.
Even a mat, while being a mat, does not become a pot or a cloth; yet,
because it does not cease to be [itself],
is it not the case that even a quality, while being a quality, does not become a mat or a cloth?
No, because [the word] "substance" does not occur;
if [it] were not at all,
then [the word] "jar" would occur.
But surely, in this way...
[it is] like two boats tied together.

No, because its nature is that of a fixed benefactor; [the opponent] objects: "If, when it is said 'a jar exists,' what is actually expressed is only non-existence—namely, 'it is not a cloth'—then it follows that even when it is said 'it exists,' the meaning is simply 'it does not exist. Thus, the proof [of its existence] is also refuted here, because there is an absence of existence anywhere, like a sky-flower."

It might be thought: "But surely, since the mat is not produced at all while [the cloth] exists on all sides, [your reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). If this is argued, we say no, because there is no counter-example (*vipakṣa*). As for the phrase "by the word 'on all sides' (*paritas*)", and so forth: the expression "on all sides" means "everywhere"; by that, its non-production even within its own self is stated. Therefore, there is no inconclusiveness.

The passage beginning with "tathā" (so it is) is a *daṇḍaka* (a series of examples) intended to demonstrate the application of this logical principle, extending as far as the statement: "the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) being non-existent is necessarily [the reason for] its lack of purpose," the meaning of which was explained previously. The example is: "a cloth is neither a mat nor color and so forth," and this is undesirable because [the cloth] consists of existent entities (*bhāvātmakatvāt*).

Because of its non-existence everywhere, [the mat] is like a sky-flower; indeed, by not existing at all in the cloth and so forth on every side, the mat is established as non-existent. Surely, by the expression "on every side," its own non-existence is also stated.
Likewise...
non-existence (*asattva*) is a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) in the case of absolute non-beneficiality; for a cloth is neither a mat nor is it color and so forth.
But does not even its non-existence on all sides establish its existence?
Even a mat, while being "mat," does not become a jar or a cloth; yet,
because it does not cease to be [itself],
is it not the case that even a quality, while being "quality," does not become a mat or a cloth?
No, because it does not exist as a substance;
if it were not at all,
then [the cognition] "it is a jar" would not occur.
But in this way...
[it would be] like two boats tied together.
No, because their nature as benefactors is fixed; however, [an objection arises]:

"In that case, since earth and the other elements would be mutually bound, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) due to their unfixed nature, like two boats tied together"—this appears to be the intention [of the opponent]. [This objection] does not occur elsewhere except in the *Rahasya-hṛdaya* (*raṃhīṃ*); therefore, it is not found in the *Pārameśvara*, *Ḍe*, or *Vijñāna-bhairava*.
In that case,
the object is not then designated as non-existent.
Daṇḍaka...
[the meaning] has been explained previously.
Of that, pra...

On this point, the proponent of existence and non-existence (bhāvābhāvavādī) offers the following reply: "Surely even 'not becoming anything else' establishes what you have stated, namely our desired existence as well; for example, while a mat (*kaṭa*) is indeed a mat, it is not a jar or a cloth. The absence of jar-ness, cloth-ness, and so forth is inseparable from the mat’s own being as a mat; thus, it is not released from its becoming as an existent. The other replies: "It is not [merely] becoming, because it is 'non-becoming' in the sense of not being a quality (*guṇa*). Here too, the existence of the mat is permeated by the absence of qualities, since it does not become a quality."

Now, as for the passage beginning with "nanu guṇo'pi" and so forth: [the opponent argues that] a quality (*guṇa*), while existing through the affirmation (*vidhi*) of being a quality, does not exist as a mat (*kaṭa*) because it is excluded by a specific restriction (*niyama*); thus, the proponent of existence (*bhāvavādī*) states that the quality exists.
That is not so.

The opponent says: "No, because [the word] does not signify 'substance'. To this it is replied: even here, the state of being a quality (guṇabhāva) as intended by you is permeated by the absence of substance. Herein it is said: by means of the "sparrow-and-monkey" logic (*caṭakamarkaṭikā*), having established that substance and quality are respectively non-existence and existence, one establishes that a specific substance such as a mat (*kaṭa*) is [also] a substance, according to the maxim of "going and returning. Consequently, even for a pot, as long as it exists as "a pot," it remains a substance.
In this way, the two objections raised by the proponents of absolute existence and non-existence against one another are resolved.

Precisely in this manner, the resolution of those objections must also be applied—by means of the opposite perspective—to the doctrines of the proponents of absolute existence and non-existence, as well as to the systems of the Ekāntavādins such as the Naiyāyikas and others.

Alternatively, there is no room at all for such an objection here, because even by that [objection], all proponents of absolute positions are effectively refuted through the dual application of both perspectives (nayavāda), since the nature of both existence and non-existence is established through the complete (sakala) and partial (vikala) modes of predication (deśa).
The objection raised against those who maintain that the wheel and the sun [move] is refuted.
Because it is not subject to transformation (*avartitvāt*).

Now, regarding the passage beginning with "But if this were so" (*nanvevam*), etc.: this is another objection; in the context of the theory of partial predication (*vikalādeśapakṣa*), it is the demonstration of an undesirable consequence for the proponent of both [views]. This has already been explained by the proof: even though earth and the other elements are impermanent—like the states of the world such as stability and so forth—their established capacity to provide assistance is proven because there is no interruption in the manifestation of their purpose (*arthabhavana*), and thus there is no lack of continuity. Likewise, this applies to selfhood and otherness, as well as to existence and non-existence.

If, however, existence and non-existence were not mutually bound, then in the absence of a cloth, there would be both the existence and the non-existence of a jar, because existence [in that case] would be equivalent to non-existence, just like the cloth;
or else...
...Is it not the case that its non-existence is directly [evident] on both sides?
Is it not for this very reason that this [is so]?

...and if this cloth were not [constituted] by its being a substance and so forth—that is, if it did not exist through the two properties of clothness and substantiality—it would not be a cloth, just as [two boats] tied together by ropes do not function as one. This is the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*). To this, it is replied: "That is not so; because its nature is established as that which provides assistance, just like the state of the world consisting of the functions of support and so forth. By this proof, the fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā-doṣa*) is avoided.

If earth and the other elements were eternal, their stability and mutual assistance would be established through the functions of supporting, cohesion, maturation, structuring, and providing space; therefore, since there would be no instability at all, what need would there be for concern? However, even in the case of non-eternality, because the manifestation of objects is uninterrupted—due to the continuity of constant becoming—their nature as mutually assisting entities established in their respective states is proven. Thus, earth assists others and itself through supporting; water through cohesion; fire through maturation; air through structuring; and space through providing room for all. Therefore, their nature as mutually assisting entities established in their respective states is established, and there is no instability. This literal meaning has been explained in the commentary (*bhāṣya*). Regarding the phrase "by way of self-nature and other-nature" (*svatvaparatvābhyām*): when their own-natures and other-natures are established, and they are bound together with one another, there is no instability. The same applies to existence and non-existence: that which becomes a jar does not become a cloth; that which becomes a cloth does not become a jar. While becoming a jar, it does not become a cloth; while becoming a cloth, it does not become a jar. Likewise, it should be understood that "it both exists and does not exist. Because their nature consists of mutually bound and established assistance, there is no instability.

Just as the states of the world—such as persistence (*dhṛti*) and so forth—are established despite the impermanence of the earth and other elements, because the continuity of the manifestation of objects (*arthabhavana*) is uninterrupted, their capacity for assistance is proven and there is no lack of stability. This is likewise the case with existence and non-existence through the categories of selfhood and otherness (*svatva-paratva*). However, if existence and non-existence were not mutually bound, then upon the non-existence of a cloth, there would be the non-existence of the existence of a jar; it would indeed be existence, because it would be equivalent to non-existence, just like the cloth.

In the absence of the cloth, the non-existence of the existence of the jar would result in the subversion of what you desire; what is that? It is existence itself. Why? Because it is equal to non-existence, just like the cloth—this is the fault in the position of absolute non-existence (*abhāvaikāntapakṣa*).

Furthermore, in the position of absolute existence (*bhāvaikāntapakṣa*) as well, if [it were so], and so forth, there would be the fault of the confusion of jars, cloths, and so on; for the existence of the jar would be... non-existence.

Regarding the reading "ko'sau bhāva eva" in this *Nayacakra-vṛtti*, if the intended meaning is "What is that very existence? None at all is existence," then one should note that even in the root text (*mūla*), the reading should be: "In the absence of the cloth, there is the absence of the existence of the jar, because of its equality with non-existence, like the cloth"—provided this is not found in the Bhāṣya manuscript.

Thus, the nature of being both existent and non-existent [in a jar] arises through the mediation of the universals and particulars such as "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) and "existence-ness" (*sattva*), and not by means of those [universals] alone. Why is that? Is it not the case that its non-existence is direct on both counts: because, in a general sense, the jar does not exist as "substance-ness," and in a specific sense, it does not exist as the "substance-ness" belonging to another substance, nor as the "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*) residing in a cloth; and likewise for the cloth by way of the reverse. Furthermore, because there is a distinction between the "substance-nesses" residing in the cloth and the jar, and because there is no "substance-ness" distinct from those [two], [the jar's non-existence is established].

Indeed, by the passage beginning with "Therefore, this... and ending with "...as substance and so forth," [the author] demonstrates that a jar does not exist directly as a quality (*guṇa*) nor as the substance of a cloth (*paṭa-dravya*), but exists as the substance of a jar (*ghaṭa-dravya*);

whereas a cloth exists directly as the substance of a cloth, but does not exist directly as a quality or as the substance of a jar. Thus, these two possess the nature of both existence and non-existence, because the jar comes into being [in one way and not in the other].

If, however, [the opponent] accepts the proof for establishing an undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭāpādana*), [the argument is as follows]: if this cloth were not produced by its "cloth-ness" (*paṭatva*) and its "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*), it would not be a cloth because it lacks the property of being produced, like a jar or like a quality (*guṇa*).
But since it is indeed produced, it must therefore be produced by those two [universals], just like a blue lotus and so forth.

even with respect to time...

"It is not as worldly convention says" means that the world, not knowing the true nature of things, speaks falsely; this is an example by contrast (*vaidharmyodāharaṇa*), such as "fire burns the straw. He explains that this is a statement contradicted by one's own words, inference, and perception—namely, "if it were indeed being burned," and so on, up to "because its reduction to ashes would be impossible, as before, at the time of the straw," since the opponent might think there is a solution because he accepts that time is distinct: "the location of the straw is burned, and that [location] is simply the straw itself."

The reply to that is: "Even so," and so forth, which has already been explained up to the point, "because the reduction of even a location to ashes is untenable. Now, regarding the passage beginning with "If it is argued that [it is] distinct from space," etc.: it might be thought that, according to the perspective of the *dravyārthika-naya* (substantialist standpoint), because there is no difference [between things], and since burning occurs only within material substances such as straw, it is the straw itself—not space and other immaterial substances—that is burned. To this, [the author replies]: "That too is not so," and so forth. The suffix *-cvī* is used in the sense of "becoming what one was not"; by means of the word *bhasmīkaraṇa* ending in that suffix, a different kind of burning is indicated, and the straw is something else. Since the meanings are distinct, the objection is not resolved.

A thing existing in the present time is "straight" because it abides in its own essential nature; that alone is what threads together or delimits [an object], whereas the past and future are not, because they are crooked due to their non-existence.
The expression for that is a word (*pada*) or a sentence (*vākya*); its "delimitation" (*viccheda*) means its end or boundary (*sīman*).
Furthermore,

when he explains that which is solitary through its various preceding and succeeding modes as being merely a single mode, his speech is interrupted, because a single mode does not touch upon other modes.
And it has been stated by those elucidating that doctrine: "Fire does not burn straw, nor is a mountain ever burned;
one who is unrestrained does not go forth [into the religious life], and a sentient being capable of liberation does not attain perfection.

This is because the state of being straw is absolutely distinct from the state of the presence of fire: whatever is straw is not burned, and whatever undergoes the state of becoming ash is not the state of being straw.
Thus, in the *Sammatitīkā* composed by Abhayadevasūri, [chapter] 1.5:

"Therein, the *ṛjusūtra*—by excluding that which is crooked, past, and future—straightens out (*ṛju sūtrayati*) the mere existence of a thing delimited by the present moment; it distinguishes [the object] from others, like the casting of a measuring line."
For neither the past nor the future exists;

if the past and future did exist, then a young woman whose son has died would not weep for her son, nor would a woman desiring a son perform sacrifices such as the *aupayājika* in the presence of specific deities.

For that entity exists only during its present moment; it never thereafter experiences existence, nor does anything that has acquired its self-nature in past time persist therein. Having arisen upon the proximity of the totality of its own causes, all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāras) resort to a state of natural fragility, subsisting for only a single moment.

This being the case, how could those verbal expressions of action that are employed in proximity to nouns denoting a substance acting as an agent—such as "Devadatta cooks," "he reads," or "he goes"—or in proximity to nouns denoting a substance as an object—such as "the jar is broken" or "he breaks the jar"—not be non-conformable to reality? For it is because a noun denotes a substance in its unmodified state, whereas a verbal expression conveys a modification; and there can be no co-referentiality (*aikādhikaraṇya*) between a modification and its absence, since they are contradictory.

For a word employed to convey a specific meaning does not produce valid knowledge when it communicates a contradictory meaning, because it is non-conformable to reality, like the word "water" used for a mirage; and a verse expressing this point was sung by one who knew the past: "Fire does not burn straw; a jar is never broken [by mere words];
one who is unrestrained does not become a renunciant; and one who is unfit does not attain perfection."

The conventional statement "the straw is burning" is contradicted in this context when one analyzes the meaning of the sentence for the sake of understanding its constituent parts. At that time, the word *palāla* (straw) is a name denoting a substance with a specific form; for as long as that substance exists in that very form, it is expressible by the word *palāla*.
However, at other times, it lacks the status of being "straw" because it does not exist in that state, just like a cloth [which is not straw].

Therefore, by the word "palāla," a substance is indicated as being stable in form, inactive, indifferent, and unchanging. How could that very same thing be said to be "burnt" by this word? For a word denoting an action signifies a modification (*vikāra*). Indeed, it is impossible for that same object to be both a modification and non-modification. If it is that *palāla*, then it cannot be that which is burnt, because it has not undergone transformation, just like its prior state.
And that which is undergoing transformation is no longer merely *palāla*, because the word "transformation" denotes a different state of being.

"Therefore, as long as that straw exists, it is not burned; when it is burned, it is no longer straw. Consequently, these two [words] are not the cause for generating correct knowledge regarding a single object, because they cannot tolerate the occurrence of another word [in their place]; thus, these two are merely the songs of the intoxicated.
In this manner, the contemplation of examples such as 'pot' and so forth should be applied.
Thus ends the fifth [section] in the *Tattvārthabhāṣyavyākhyā* composed by the venerable Siddhasena Gaṇi.

And regarding the statement "the decoction (kaṣāya) is the medicine," here the decoction that has already acquired its flavor is the medicine; the initial decoction is not its object because its flavor is slight and unmanifest.
That which is being cooked is "cooked" [in a figurative sense], whereas that which is actually cooked may be either currently undergoing the process of cooking or one whose cooking has ceased.

In this same manner, the categories of "being done" and "done," "being enjoyed" and "enjoyed," "being bound" and "bound," "being accomplished" and "accomplished," and so forth, are to be applied accordingly. Furthermore, a "prastha" (a measure of capacity) is that in which things are established; yet, at the very moment one is measuring, there can be no past or future measurement of grain, and thus no potter could exist [to create it]. Moreover, when the successive stages such as the *śivaka* (the initial lump) are being produced, the designation "pot" does not yet apply; and at the time of the stage of the "pot," it has already been brought into existence from its own constituent parts alone.

And in the context of the inquiry into the one who is established [in Brahman], when asked, "From where do you come today?", he thinks, "From nowhere," because there is an absence of the transformation of action at that time;
therefore, there is an absence of burning by straw and the like, due to the apprehension of a specific [transcendental] time.

For in this system, the undivided present moment is the object; since the connection with fire, its kindling, its blazing, and its burning occupy an interval of incalculable moments, there is an absence of burning [in any single moment].
Furthermore, at the time when there is burning, there is no straw, because the ash has already been produced; and at the time when there is straw, there is no burning.
If it is argued that "it burns the straw," this is not so, because [the action] would have a remainder.

If it is argued that there is no fault because we observe words denoting a whole functioning with respect to its parts, we say: no, for the situation remains as it was; since it has already been stated that there is no burning of a single part, it is impossible for the whole to be burned without remainder. If this is further argued, we say: no, because it contradicts the statement [of the opponent] and because the situation remains as it was.

First, there is a contradiction in your own statement: if the burning of the entire straw is impossible, then the burning of the straw due to the burning of one part is not "burning" at all. Indeed, since your statement lacks the capacity to refute the opponent’s position in its entirety, it refutes only a portion of that position; therefore, because it refutes only a single part, it lacks the power to establish that "this [statement] as a whole is indeed a refutation. Thus, it remains in its original state, for it has been stated that there is no burning at a single moment.

If there were multiplicity of parts, then if burning occurred in one part, would there not be burning everywhere because of the other parts? Or, if there is no burning at all, then if burning occurs everywhere, why does it not fail to burn? Therefore, there is no burning;
likewise, there would be an absence of activities such as drinking and eating.

If it is argued that "the white does not become black because the two exist at different times, and since there is no connection with the sequential state (*paryāya*) that has ceased in the present object,

all worldly transaction (*saṃvyavahāra*) would be lost," we say: no, for the establishment of worldly transaction occurs through the demonstration of the mere object, as was previously stated in the [first] method (*naya*).
Thus, in the *Tattvārtharājavārtika* (1.33),
it is stated that one who is not restrained in their inner disposition does not truly go forth into the religious life.

In the same way, one who is destined [for liberation] does not attain it at the very moment of experiencing the first lifespan as a hell-being; rather, the designation "hell-being" occurs only then, according to the perspective of the *ṛjusūtra* standpoint.
For this reason, those learned in the systems (*naya*) who define the nature of the *ṛjusūtra* have said: "Fire does not burn straw; a jar is never broken."
There is no exit from emptiness here, nor is emptiness entered;
and one who is distinct from the denizens of hell is not reborn in hell.
"And no one among the denizens of hell shall be liberated from that hell," and so forth.
Thus ends [the commentary on] the fourteenth chapter, the tenth uddeśaka, verse 174, in the Bhagavatīsūtra-vṛtti composed by Abhayadevasūri.
Then, at the very first moment of experiencing the lifespan as a hell-being and so forth, one receives the designation "hell-being" and so on;
this is the perspective of the *ṛjusūtra* standpoint (*nayadarśana*).
