"From hell, no one among those in hell is liberated," and so forth.
Thus, in the commentary on the *Prajñāpanā-sūtra* composed by Malayagiri, [it is stated]:

"The straight (*ṛju*) is the object existing in the present time because it abides in its own nature; that alone is what the sūtra expresses and delimits, not the past or the future, because of their crookedness due to non-existence."
His word, phrase, or sentence; its interruption is its end, that is to say, its limit.

Furthermore, when one explains that which is devoid of preceding and succeeding modes (*paryāya*) as being only a single mode, one's speech is cut off, because a single mode does not touch upon other modes.
And it has been said by those who explain the meaning of that doctrine: "Fire does not burn straw; a mountain is never burned."

A living being who is unrestrained does not go forth [into the religious life] nor does he attain perfection, because the state of being straw is absolutely distinct from the state of the presence of fire; for whatever is straw, that is not burned, and whatever undergoes the state of ashes, that is not the state of straw— thus it is stated in the *Sammatitarka-vṛtti* composed by Abhayadevasūri, [chapter] 1.

Among these, the *ṛjusūtra* (straight-thread) perspective delineates the mere existence of a thing as delimited by the present moment, excluding that which is crooked—namely, the past and the future. It distinguishes [the object] from others like a line drawn with a thread;
for neither the past nor the future exists.

If the past and the future were to exist [in the same way as the present], then a young woman whose son has died would not weep for her son, nor would a woman desiring a son perform sacrifices such as the *aupayājika* in the presence of specific deities; for that object exists only while abiding in the present moment, never experiencing existence beyond that. Furthermore, nothing that has acquired its own nature (*ātmalābha*) in a past time persists there; all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), having arisen upon the proximity of their own collection of causes, assume a state of natural fragility and depend upon that single moment alone.

This being the case, how could those verbal expressions of action that are employed in proximity to nouns denoting a substance acting as an agent—such as "Devadatta cooks," "reads," or "goes"—or in proximity to nouns denoting a substance as an object—such as "the jar is broken" or "he breaks the jar"—not be non-conformable to reality? For a noun denotes a substance whose form is unmodified, whereas a verbal expression conveys a modification; and there can be no co-referentiality (*aikādhikaraṇya*) between a modification and its absence, because they are contradictory.

For a word employed to convey a specific meaning does not produce valid knowledge when it communicates a contradictory meaning, because it is non-conformable to reality, like the word "water" used for a mirage; and a verse expressing this very point was sung by one who knows the ancient lore: "Fire does not burn straw; a jar is never broken [by mere words];
one who is unrestrained does not become a renunciant; and one who is unfit does not attain perfection."

The conventional statement "the straw is burning" is contradicted here; for at the time when the words are analyzed in order to understand the meaning of the sentence, the word "straw" (*palāla*) is a name denoting a substance with a specific form. That substance is denotable by the word "straw" only as long as it exists in that very form; otherwise, however, it lacks existence in the state of being straw, because it does not exist in that state, just like a cloth [does not exist when it is straw].

Therefore, by the word "palāla," an entity is indicated as being stable in form, inactive, indifferent, and unchanging. How could that very same thing be expressed by the word "is burned" (*dahyate*), since a verb denotes a modification? For it is not possible for that same object to be both a modification and non-modification.
If it were that *palāla*, then it would not be that very same thing which is burned, because it has not undergone transformation, just like its prior state.
And that which is undergoing transformation is no longer merely *palāla*, because the word "transformation" (*vipariṇāma*) signifies the emergence of a different state of being.

"Therefore, as long as that straw exists, it is not burned; when it is burned, it is no longer straw. Consequently, these two [words] are not the cause for generating correct knowledge regarding a single object, because they cannot tolerate the occurrence of another word [in their place]; thus, these two are merely the songs of the intoxicated.
In this way, the application of the example of the jar and so forth should be contemplated.
Thus ends the fifth [section] in the *Tattvārthabhāṣyavyākhyā* composed by the monk Siddhasena.
Fire does not burn straw; a jar is never broken [by fire];
one who is unrestrained does not go forth [into homelessness]; and one who is unfit does not achieve success.
Thus, in the *Nayopadeśa* composed by the preceptor Yaśovijaya,
the *Ṛjusūtra* [naya] is [described], being straight like the laying down of a measuring line.
...only for a moment is this intended to be pointed out.

Regarding the statement "decoction is medicine," here decoction as medicine refers to that which has already acquired its flavor; it does not refer to the initial decoction, because this [initial stage] is slight and its flavor is unmanifest. As for the object [of the term], there may be that which is being cooked (*pacyamāna*), that which is cooked (*pakva*), and that which has ceased from cooking (*uparata-pāka*).

In this same manner, the categories of "being made" and "made," "being enjoyed" and "enjoyed," "being bound" and "bound," "being accomplished" and "accomplished," and so forth, are to be applied accordingly. Furthermore, a "plate" (*prastha*) is so called because things rest within it; yet at the very moment one measures [the grain], since past and future quantities of grain cannot exist [simultaneously], the potter would be non-existent. Moreover, when the successive stages such as the *śivaka* (the initial lump) are being produced, that specific designation [of "plate"] does not yet exist; and at the time of the stage of the "pot" (*kumbha*), the object is already fully realized from its own constituent parts alone.

And in the context of the question regarding one who is established [in Brahman], when asked, "From where do you come today?", he thinks, "From nowhere," because there is an absence of the transformation of time-action at that moment...
therefore, there is an absence of burning by straw and the like, due to the apprehension of a specific, transcendent time.

For in this system, the undivided present moment is the object; since burning, igniting, blazing, and consuming have intervals of incalculable moments, there is an absence of burning [in any single moment].
Furthermore, at the time when there is burning, there is no straw, because the production of ashes has already occurred; and at the time when there is straw, there is no burning.
If it is argued that "it burns that which is straw," we say no, because there would be a remainder.

If it is argued that there is no fault because we observe words denoting a whole functioning with respect to its parts, we say no; for the situation remains the same, as it has already been stated that there is no burning of a single part, since a complete burning without remainder is impossible.
If it is argued [again] that this is not so, we say no, because it contradicts the statement and because the situation remains the same.

First, there is a contradiction in your own statement: if the burning of the entire straw is impossible, then the burning of the straw due to the burning of one part would not be "burning" at all. Now, since your statement lacks the capacity to refute the opponent's position in its entirety, it refutes only a portion of that position; therefore, because it refutes only a single part, it lacks the power to establish the claim that "this [statement] as a whole is indeed a refuter. Thus, the same state of affairs persists, for it has already been stated that there is no burning at a single moment.
If there were multiplicity of parts, then if burning occurs in one part, would there be burning everywhere? Or, if burning occurs in another part, would there not be a total absence of burning?
Alternatively, if burning occurs everywhere, why does it not fail to burn? Therefore, there is no burning at all;
likewise, there would be an absence of such activities as drinking and eating.

If it is argued that "the white does not become black because the two exist at different times, and since there is no connection with the category of 'ceased' (nivṛtta) regarding a present object, all worldly transaction (*saṃvyavahāra*) would be lost," we say: no; for the establishment of worldly transaction occurs through the indication of the mere object, as explained in the previous method (*pūrvanaya*).
Thus, in the *Tattvārtharājavārtika*,
[it is stated that] action is for the sake of liberation.

Regarding the phrase "ṇārthasvā kriyā," there might also be the reading "ṇārthamvā kriyā" here; and thus, for the purpose of strengthening the cultivation (bhāvanā), it could also be "kriyā" [followed by] "gatabhāva" [in the manuscript].

Regarding the statement "empty from the perspective of the field" (*kṣetrataḥ śūnyam*) and so forth, the impossibility of entry, departure, or staying has already been explained. As a secondary illustration, by way of the opposite of staying and going:
at the very moment of the first experience of the lifespan of a hell-being and so forth, the designation "hell-being" and so on occurs according to the view of the *ṛjusūtra* standpoint.
For this reason, those learned in the standpoints (*nayavid*), while defining the nature of the *ṛjusūtra*, have said: "Fire does not burn straw; a jar is never broken."
There is no exit from emptiness here, nor is emptiness entered;
and one who is distinct from the denizens of hell is not reborn in hell.
"And no one among those in hell is released from it," and so forth.
Thus ends [the commentary on] the fourteenth chapter, the tenth section, verse 174, in the Bhagavatīsūtra-vṛtti composed by Abhayadevasūri.
Consequently, at the very first moment of experiencing the lifespan of a hell-being and so forth, one receives the designation "hell-being" and so on;
this is the perspective of the *ṛjusūtra* standpoint (*naya*).
Thus, those learned in the standpoints, while defining the *ṛjusūtra* standpoint, have stated: "Fire does not burn straw, nor is a jar ever broken."
There is no departure from what is not empty, nor from the empty; nor is the empty entered. Furthermore, one who is distinct from the denizens of hell does not arise within hell.
"And no one among those in hell is liberated from it," and so forth.
Thus, in the commentary on the *Prajñāpanā-sūtra* composed by Malayagiri, [it is stated]:

"The straight (*ṛju*) is the object existing in the present time, because it abides in its own essential nature; that alone is expressed and determined by the sūtra, and not the past or future, because they are crooked due to their non-existence."
His word, phrase, or sentence; its interruption, end, or limit— so to speak.

Furthermore, for one who explains that which is devoid of preceding and succeeding modalities (*paryāya*) as being only a single modality, their speech is interrupted, because a single modality does not touch upon other modalities.
And it has been said by those elucidating the meaning of that doctrine: "Fire does not burn straw; a mountain is never burned."

A living being who is unrestrained does not go forth [into the religious life] nor does he attain perfection, because the state of being straw is absolutely distinct from the state of the presence of fire; for whatever is straw is not burned, and that which undergoes the state of ashes is no longer the state of straw— thus it is stated in the *Sammatitarka-vṛtti* composed by Abhayadevasūri (1).

Among these, the *ṛjusūtra* (straight-thread) perspective, by excluding that which is crooked—namely, the past and the future—depicts (*sūtrayati*) the mere existence of a thing delimited by the present moment as straight (*ṛju*). It distinguishes [the object] from others, like the casting of a thread;
for neither the past nor the future exists.

If the past and the future were to exist [in the same way as the present], then a young woman whose son has died would not weep for her son, nor would a woman desiring a son perform sacrifices such as the *aupayājika* in the presence of specific deities;

for that object exists only during the moment of its present state and never experiences existence beyond that. Furthermore, nothing that has acquired its own nature in a past time persists therein; all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), having arisen upon the convergence of their own collection of causes, assume a fragility inherent in their very nature and depend upon that single moment alone.

This being the case, how could those verbal expressions used in proximity to nouns denoting a substance acting as an agent—such as "Devadatta cooks," "reads," or "goes"—or in proximity to nouns denoting a substance as an object—such as "the jar is broken" or "he breaks the jar"—not be non-conformable to reality? For, by a noun (nāman), a substance in its unmodified form is denoted, whereas by a verbal expression (ākhyāta), a modification is conveyed; and there can be no co-referentiality (aikādhikaraṇya) between that which is modified and that which is unmodified, because they are contradictory.

For a word employed to convey a meaning does not produce correct knowledge when it communicates a contradictory sense, because it is non-conformable to reality, like the word "water" applied to a mirage; and a verse expressing this very point was sung by one who knew the past: "Fire does not burn straw; a jar is never broken [by mere words]; one who is unrestrained does not become a wandering ascetic; and one who is unfit does not attain perfection."
The conventional statement "the straw is burning" is contradicted [by this analysis].

At the time of analyzing the word-meanings for the sake of understanding the sentence-meaning in this sentence, the word *palāla* (straw) is a name denoting a substance with a specific form. That substance is denotable by the word *palāla* only as long as it exists in that very form;
at other times, however, it lacks existence precisely in the state of being straw, because it does not exist in that state, just like a cloth [when it has ceased to be a cloth].

Therefore, by the word "palāla" (straw), an entity is indicated as having a stable form, inactive, indifferent, and unchanging. How could that very same thing be said to be "burned" by this word, since a word denoting an action expresses a modification? For it is not possible for that same object to be both a modification and non-modification. If it is that straw, then it cannot be burned, because it has not undergone change, remaining as it was in its prior state.
And if it is undergoing transformation, it is no longer that very straw, because the word "transformation" denotes a different state of being.

"Therefore, as long as that straw exists, it is not being burned; when it is being burned, it is no longer straw. Consequently, these two [words] are not the cause for generating correct knowledge regarding a single object, because they cannot tolerate the occurrence of another word [in their place]; thus, these two are merely the songs of the intoxicated.
In this way, one should apply the reflection on the examples of the jar and so forth.
Thus ends the fifth [section] in the *Tattvārthabhāṣyavyākhyā* composed by the monk Siddhasena.
Fire does not burn straw; a jar is never broken [by fire];
one who is unrestrained does not go forth [into homelessness]; and one who is unfit does not attain success.
Thus ends the section on the *Ṛjusūtra* [viewpoint], characterized by its straightforwardness like the laying down of a foundation line, in the *Nayopadeśa* composed by the preceptor Yaśovijaya.
...only for a moment is this intended to be pointed out.

Regarding the statement "the decoction is the medicine," here the decoction that has already acquired its flavor is the medicine; the initial decoction is not its object because its flavor is slight and unmanifest.
That which is being cooked is "cooked" [in a figurative sense], whereas that which is already cooked may be either currently cooking or one whose cooking has ceased.

In this same manner, the categories of "being made" (*kriyamāṇa*) and "made" (*kṛta*), "being enjoyed" (*bhujyamāna*) and "enjoyed" (*bhukta*), "being bound" (*badhyamāna*) and "bound" (*baddha*), "being accomplished" (*sidhyat*) and "accomplished" (*siddha*), and so forth, are to be applied accordingly.

Likewise, a "plate" (*prastha*) is that in which things are established; at the very moment it measures [the grain], there can be no past or future measurement of grain, and thus there is an absence of a potter [as an agent]. Furthermore, when the successive stages (*paryāya*) such as the *śivaka* (the initial lump) are being produced, those specific names do not yet exist; and at the time of the stage of the "pot" (*kumbha*), it is produced from its own constituent parts alone.
And in the inquiry regarding one who is established [in the Self], when asked, "Whence do you come today?", he thinks, "From nowhere," because there is no modification of action at that time...
therefore, there is an absence of burning by straw and so forth, due to the apprehension of a specific time.

For in this system, the undivided present moment is the object; since there are countless intervening moments between the contact with fire, the kindling, the blazing, and the burning, there is consequently an absence of burning [in any single moment].
Furthermore, at the time when there is burning, there is no straw, because the ash has already been produced; and at the time when there is straw, there is no burning.
If it is argued that "it burns the straw," this is not so, because [the action] would have a remainder [of unburnt parts].

If it is argued that there is no fault because we observe words denoting a whole functioning with respect to its parts, [we reply: no, because the situation remains the same; for it has already been stated that there is no burning of a single part, since a complete burning without remainder is impossible. If it is argued that this is not so, [we reply: no, because it contradicts the statement and because the situation remains the same.

First, there is a contradiction in your own statement: if the burning of the entire straw is impossible, then the burning of the straw due to the burning of one part is not [true] burning. Now, since your statement lacks the capacity to refute the opponent's position in its entirety, it only refutes a portion of that position; therefore, because it refutes only a single part, it lacks the power to establish the claim that "this [statement] as a whole is indeed a refuter," and thus it remains in that same state [of deficiency]. Furthermore, it has already been stated that burning does not occur at a single moment.

If there were multiplicity of parts, then if burning occurred in one part, would there be burning everywhere because of the burning of that part? Or, if there were burning in another part, would there not be an absence of burning everywhere?
Alternatively, if there is burning everywhere, why is there no non-burning? Therefore, there is no burning at all;
likewise, there would be an absence of such activities as drinking and eating.
If it is argued that "the white does not become black because the two exist at different times, and since there is no connection with the sequence of cessation regarding a present object,

all worldly transaction (*saṃvyavahāra*) would be lost," we say: no, for the establishment of worldly transaction occurs through the demonstration of the mere object, as explained in the previous method (*pūrvanaya*).
Thus [ends] the commentary on the *Tattvārtharājavārtika*, chapter 1, verse 33,
by Tiṣya-gaṇi-bhadrabāhu.

"From the perspective of internal state (*bhāva*), he is un-restrained," and so forth. Since renunciation (*pravrajyā*) is the departure from non-abstinence—which arises from the manifestation of deluding karma related to vision and conduct (*darśana-cāritra-mohanīya*) bound since beginningless time—and since abstinence (*virati*) is the supreme advancement [toward restraint], how can that [abstinence] be possible for one who is un-restrained? In this very way, following the context of the discussion regarding how a single entity can consist of both existence and non-existence, he provides an illustration showing that [the claim] is untenable due to the distinction between the times of being a perfected soul (*siddha*) and a candidate for liberation (*bhavya*):

"At the very moment of the first experience of the life-span (*āyuḥ*) of a hell-being and so forth, the designation 'hell-being' and so on occurs, according to the perspective of the *ṛjusūtra-naya*."
For it has been said by those learned in the methods (*nayavid*) while defining the nature of the *ṛjusūtra* [view]: "Fire does not burn straw; a jar is never broken;
there is no exit from emptiness here, nor is emptiness entered.
And one who is distinct from a hell-being is not reborn in hell;
nor is any hell-being whatsoever ever released from hell.
And so forth;
thus [ends] the commentary on the Bhagavatī-sūtra composed by Abhayadevasūri, [chapter] 4, [section] 10.
Then, at the very first moment of experiencing the lifespan of a hell-being and so forth, one receives the designation "hell-being" and so on;
and this is the perspective of the *ṛjusūtra* standpoint (*nayadarśana*).
And likewise, by those who know the methods (*naya*), while defining the *ṛjusūtra* perspective, this was said: "Fire does not burn straw; a jar is never broken;
there is no exit from the non-empty nor from the empty; and one does not enter the empty."
And one who is distinct from a hell-being is not reborn in hell;
nor is any hell-being whatsoever ever released from hell.
And so forth;
thus [ends] the seventeenth [chapter], section three, in the commentary on the *Prajñāpanā-sūtra* composed by Malayagiri.

An object existing in the present time is "straight" (*ṛju*) because it abides in its own essential nature; that very [object] is what threads together (*sūtrayati*) and delimits, but not the past or the future, because they are crooked due to their non-existence.
Its expression—whether a word (*pada*) or a sentence (*vākya*)—is its "delimitation" (*viccheda*), which is to say its end or boundary (*anta-sīmā*).
Furthermore,

for one who explains that which is empty of prior and subsequent sequences as being merely a single sequence, their speech is interrupted, because a single sequence does not touch upon other sequences.
And it has been stated by those elucidating that doctrine: "Fire does not burn straw, nor is a mountain ever burned;
one who is unrestrained does not go forth [into the religious life], and a soul capable of liberation (bhavyajīva) does not attain perfection.

This is because the state of being straw is absolutely distinct from the state of the presence of fire: whatever is straw is not burned, and whatever undergoes the state of ash is not the state of straw.
Thus, in the *Sammatitīkā* composed by Abhayadevasūri, [chapter] 1, verse 5:

"Therein, the *ṛjusūtra*—avoiding that which is crooked, past, and future—straightens out (*ṛju sūtrayati*) the mere existence of a thing delimited by the present moment; it distinguishes [the object] from others, like the casting of a measuring line."
For neither the past nor the future exists;

if the past and future were to exist, then a young woman whose son has died would not weep for her son, nor would a woman desiring a son perform sacrifices such as the *aupayājika* in the presence of specific deities.

For that entity exists only during its present moment; it never thereafter experiences existence, nor does anything that has acquired its own nature in past time persist therein. Having arisen when the collection of its own causes is present, all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāras) rely upon their own inherent fragility and depend only upon that single moment.

This being the case, how could those action-words (*kriyāśabda*) which are employed in proximity to substance-words denoting an agent—such as "Devadatta cooks," "he reads," or "he goes"—or in proximity to substance-words denoting an object—such as "the jar is broken" or "he breaks the jar"—not be non-conformable to reality? For a substance whose form is unmodified is denoted by a noun (*nāmaśabda*), whereas modification is what is conveyed by an action-word; and there can be no co-referentiality (*aikādhikaraṇya*) between that which is modified and that which is unmodified, because they are contradictory.

For a word employed to convey a specific meaning, if it communicates a contradictory meaning, does not produce valid knowledge because it is non-conformable to reality, just like the word "water" used for a mirage;
and a verse in accordance with this stated meaning was sung by one who knows the past: "Fire does not burn straw; a jar is never broken [by mere words];
one who is unrestrained does not become a renunciant; and one who is unfit does not attain perfection."

The statement "the straw is burning," which is a sentence of conventional usage, is contradicted at the time of analyzing the word-meanings for the sake of understanding the meaning of that sentence. In this context, the word *palāla* (straw) is a name denoting a substance with a specific form; for as long as that substance exists in that very form, it is denotable by the word *palāla*.
However, at other times, its existence as straw ceases to be, because it lacks the state of being straw, just like a cloth [which is no longer a cloth when it has changed form].

Therefore, by the word "straw" (*palāla*), an entity is indicated as being stable in form, inactive, indifferent, and unchanging. How could that very same thing be expressed by the word "is burned," since a verb denotes a modification? For it is not possible for that same object to be both a modification and non-modification.
If it is that straw, then it is not that very same thing which is burned, because it has not undergone transformation, just like its prior state.
And that which is undergoing transformation is no longer merely "straw," because the word "transformation" denotes a different state of being.

"Therefore, as long as that straw exists, it is not being burned; when it is being burned, it is no longer straw. Consequently, these two [words] are not the cause for producing correct knowledge regarding a single object, because they cannot tolerate the occurrence of another word; thus, these two are merely the songs of the intoxicated.
In this way, the application of the examples of the jar and so forth should be contemplated.
Thus ends the fifth [section] in the *Tattvārthabhāṣyavyākhyā* composed by the venerable Siddhasena Gaṇin.
Fire does not burn straw; a jar is never broken [by fire];
one who is unrestrained does not go forth [into homelessness]; and one who is unfit does not attain success.
Thus ends the section on the *Ṛjusūtra* [standpoint], characterized by its straightness like the laying down of a foundation line, in the *Nayopadeśa* composed by the preceptor Yaśovijaya.
...only for a moment is this intended to be pointed out.

In this same manner, the categories of "being made" (*kriyamāṇa*) and "made" (*kṛta*), "being enjoyed" (*bhujyamāna*) and "enjoyed" (*bhukta*), "being bound" (*badhyamāna*) and "bound" (*baddha*), "being accomplished" (*sidhyat*) and "accomplished" (*siddha*), and so forth, are to be applied accordingly. therefore, there is an absence of burning by straw and so forth, due to the grasping of a specific [transcendent] time.

For in this system, the undivided present moment is the object; since burning, igniting, blazing, and combustion have intervals of innumerable moments, there is an absence of burning [in any single moment].
Furthermore, at the time when there is burning, there is no straw, because the production of ash has occurred; and at the time when there is straw, there is no burning.
If it is argued that "it burns that which is straw," [we reply] no, because there is a remainder [of the causal sequence].

If this is argued, we say: no, because it contradicts the statement [of the opponent] and because the situation remains as it was.

If there were multiplicity of parts, then if burning occurred due to the burning of one part, there would be burning everywhere; however, because other parts are not burned, there is indeed an absence of universal burning.
Or, if burning occurs everywhere, why is there no non-burning? Therefore, there is no burning at all.
In this way, there would be an absence of everyday activities such as drinking and eating.

all worldly transaction (*saṃvyavahāra*) would be lost," we say no; for worldly transactions are established by the mere indication of the object, as explained in the previous method (*pūrvanaya*).
Thus, according to the *Tattvārtharājavārtika* (1.33),
from the very moment of the first experience of the life-span of a hell-being and so forth, the designation "hell-being" and so on occurs, according to the perspective of the *ṛjusūtra* standpoint.
For it has been said by those learned in the *nayas*, while defining the nature of the *ṛjusūtra*: "Fire does not burn straw; a jar is never broken;
there is no exit from emptiness here, nor is emptiness entered.
And one who is distinct from a hell-being is not reborn in hell;
nor is any hell-being whatsoever ever released from hell.
And so forth;
thus [ends] the commentary on the Bhagavatī-sūtra composed by Abhayadevasūri, [chapter] 4, [section] 10.
Then, at the very first moment of experiencing the lifespan of a hell-being and so forth, one receives the designation "hell-being" and so on;
and this is the perspective of the *ṛjusūtra* standpoint (*nayadarśana*).
And likewise, those who are experts in the methods (naya) have stated this while defining the *ṛjusūtra* method: "Fire does not burn straw; a jar is never broken;
there is no exit from the non-empty nor from the empty; and one does not enter the empty."
And one who is distinct from a hell-being is not reborn in hell;
nor is any hell-being whatsoever ever released from hell.
And so forth;
thus [ends] the seventeenth [chapter], section three, in the commentary on the *Prajñāpanā-sūtra* composed by Malayagiri.

The expression for that [present] is a word (*pada*) or a sentence (*vākya*); its "delimitation" (*viccheda*) means its end or boundary (*sīman*).

Having arisen upon the proximity of the totality of their own causes, all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāras) resort to a fragility inherent in their own nature, subsisting for only a single moment.

For a word denoting action signifies a modification (*vikāra*). Indeed, it is impossible for that same object to be both a modification and non-modification. If it is that straw, then it is not that very same thing which is burnt, because it has not undergone transformation, just like its prior state.

"Therefore, as long as that straw exists, it is not being burned; when it is burned, it is no longer straw. In this manner, the application of the examples of the jar and so forth should be contemplated.
Thus ends the fifth [section] in the *Tattvārthabhāṣyavyākhyā* composed by the venerable Siddhasena Gaṇi.

Thus ends the section on the *Ṛjusūtra* [standpoint], characterized by its directness like the laying down of a foundation line, in the *Nayopadeśa* composed by the preceptor Yaśovijaya.

That which is being cooked is "cooked" [in the sense of the process], whereas that which is "cooked" may be either currently undergoing cooking or one whose cooking has ceased.

In this same manner, the categories of "being made" and "made," "being enjoyed" and "enjoyed," "being bound" and "bound," "being accomplished" and "accomplished," and so forth, are to be applied accordingly.

Furthermore, a "plate" (*prastha*) is so called because things rest within it; yet at the very moment one measures [the grain], since past and future measurements of grain are impossible, there is an absence of the potter.

This is because when the successive stages such as the *śivaka* (the initial lump) are being produced, that designation [of "plate"] does not exist, and at the time of the stage of the "pot," it is produced from its own constituent parts alone.

And in the context of the question regarding one who is established [in the Self], when asked, "From where do you come today?", he thinks, "From nowhere," because there is an absence of transformation through the passage of time at that moment...
therefore, there is an absence of burning by straw and so forth, due to the apprehension of a specific [transcendental] time.

For in this system, the undivided present moment is the object; since the connection with fire, the kindling, the blazing, and the burning occupy an interval of innumerable moments, there is an absence of burning [in any single moment].
Furthermore, at the moment when there is burning, there is no straw, because the production of ash has occurred; and at the moment when there is straw, there is no burning.
If it is argued that "it burns that which is straw," we say no, because [the straw] would still have a remainder.

If it is argued that there is no fault because we observe words denoting a whole functioning with respect to its parts, [we reply: no, because the situation remains the same; for it has already been stated that there is no burning of a single part, since a complete burning without remainder is impossible. If it is further argued that this is not so because of a contradiction in the statement and because the situation remains the same, [we reply: no, because of the contradiction in the statement and because the situation remains the same.

First, there is a contradiction in your own statement: if the burning of the entire straw is impossible because it is impossible to burn it without remainder, then the burning of the straw through the burning of one part is not "burning" at all. Indeed, since your statement lacks the capacity to refute the opponent's position in its entirety, it only refutes a portion of that position; therefore, because it refutes only a single part, it lacks the power to establish the claim that "this [statement] is a refuter of the whole. If there were multiplicity of parts, then if burning occurred in one part, would there be burning everywhere because of the burning of that part? Or, if burning occurs in another part, would there not be a total absence of burning?
Alternatively, if burning occurs everywhere, why is there no non-burning? Therefore, there is no burning at all;
likewise, there would be an absence of activities such as drinking and eating.

If it is argued that "the white does not become black because the two exist at different times, and since there is no connection with the category of 'ceased' regarding a present object, all worldly transaction (*saṃvyavahāra*) would be lost," we say: no; for the establishment of worldly transaction occurs through the mere indication of the object, as has been explained in the previous method (*pūrvanaya*).
Thus, in the *Tattvārtharājavārtika* (1.33),
it is stated even at the outset: "He makes a jar."
It is not tenable in that way:

Or rather, [the author] states that even a single example applies to the fourfold nature of substance and so forth: he says "he makes a pot" and so on; even at the time of kneading the clay, the potter says "I am making a pot. Now, it might be argued: "True, it was previously non-existent, now it is being produced, and while being produced, it comes into existence. To this we reply:

even in this case, if it is non-existent (*abhūta*), then that jar is not being produced; and even if it were already existent (*bhūtatva*), it is not being produced because the act of making what is already made would be futile.
Now, if even a non-existent jar is said [to exist], then it follows that the earth itself would be a jar for you;
and consequently, there would be an absence of action,
for [the jar] does not exist in any state whatsoever.

...how then is that jar produced without being made? Who says it is "produced," given that its birth and destruction are identical to those of the substance (*dravya*) and other factors? Is it possible to say, "It is not born"? Yes, it is.

Now, it might be argued that, considering the two aforementioned positions untenable, one resorts to another alternative, thinking: "Truly, it did not exist previously but is now being produced; and while being produced, it comes into existence. Even here, one does not escape the two-fold dilemma of whether it is already existent or non-existent. If it is non-existent, then it is not a jar, because—like a cloth or other things—it has not yet attained the state of being a jar; thus it is neither being produced nor can it be called a jar.
On the other hand, if it is already existent, then like a cloth or other things, its production is useless since it is already present; therefore, it is not being produced.

Now, even if a lump of clay or the like is not [yet] a jar, it might be called a "jar" within one's own school out of attachment or in conformity with worldly usage; however, for you, it would follow that the earth itself is a jar, because it is equally non-existent as a jar, just like a jar being made by you.

Consequently, there would be an absence of action, and just as the purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*) of the earth would be futile, there would be an absence of the purposeful activity of a jar. He demonstrates this [in the passage] beginning with "And in no state whatsoever... up to "...action."

From the perspective of substance (*dravyataḥ*), there is no action because [the jar] is already contained within a single atom, as it consists of all spatial points; nor is there action from the perspective of another substance, because of its non-existence therein. From the perspective of space (*kṣetrataḥ*), since it is said to occupy a space encompassed by parts such as the base, middle, and top, which jar is being made? From the perspective of time (*kālataḥ*), because of the containment of the vibration of various distinct points at every moment, what is being made? From the perspective of state (*bhāvataḥ*), since the jar consists of a collection of all forms, colors, and so forth, and because each state is distinct from every other state, what action is there? Therefore, it is only that which is already being made that is made—such as the fetching of clay—and thus this is an illustration in four ways.

Because of its pervasiveness;

Another says: "How then is that pot produced while not being made? Since there is an absence of action, it follows that because it is not being made—and due to this state of not being made—the pot is produced like a sky-flower; and this is undesirable, as it contradicts worldly consensus."

To this it is replied: Who indeed says that [an entity] is "born"? I consider only the common world to be speaking improperly, because birth and destruction are identical in terms of substance and so forth—wherever, whenever, and however something is born, it is exactly the same thing that is destroyed. Thus, existence (*bhāva*) is the becoming (*bhavana*) of both presence and absence; that very becoming of presence and absence is the real entity (*vastu*), which consists of both being and non-being. Because it is a real entity, the prior absence of this lump of clay and so forth is its "existence" (*bhāva*); the absence of that prior state is "destruction" (*vināśa*). That very subsequent state is "birth. Such is the definition of birth and destruction, and they are equal in terms of substance and so forth.

Is it possible to say that this object, consisting of both being and non-being, is not born? Yes, it is said: "It is not born" because it is subject to destruction; yet, as before, it is also possible to say "it does not perish" because it is subject to birth, as in the case of what follows.

This is the illustration regarding actions whose objects are *nirvartya* (produced) or *vikārya* (transformed); this same principle applies to all such actions, and even to some actions whose objects are *prāpya* (attained).
Thus far, it has been shown that words denoting produced entities would be rendered devoid of referents.

Since all entities consist of both existence and non-existence, even in the case of words denoting substances (*dravyaśabda*), how could there be speech that accords with reality? Why can it not be said that, like the raising of eyebrows and so forth, such speech is made by those who have established conventions as a means of indicating their own intention? Because of its state of perishing; for the state of a jar is indeed its birth, and according to the logic already stated, that very state is one of perishing, just like the subsequent state of a non-jar as you yourself accept.

It cannot even be said that "it does not perish," because it is currently coming into being, like a subsequent [moment] or like the state of a jar; or rather, because it is both being acted upon and not being acted upon, like a pot [in the process of being made]. Or, because it is both being produced and not being produced, it is a jar.
Because of being made into a debate?

Here, regarding "because of being made into a debate," there might also be a reading such as "from where [is it] because of being made into a debate? or even "from where [is it] because of not being made into a debate?"—substantially.
And that very abode of accumulation is always of the nature of both existence and non-existence.
The prior state consisting of existence is destruction; the definition of these two [existence and destruction] is based on their identity with substance and so forth.
An entity that consists of existence perishes because it is subject to destruction, as in the previous case;
yet it can also be said that it does not perish because it is currently arising, as in the subsequent case.

This is the illustration regarding actions whose objects are *nirvartya* (produced) or *vikārya* (transformed); this same principle applies to all such [actions], as well as to certain actions whose objects are *prāpya* (attained).
Thus, for the time being, there is a lack of referential object (*nirviṣayatā*) for words that have already come into existence.

Since all entities consist of both existence and non-existence, even in the case of words denoting substances, how could there be speech that accords with reality? Rather, like the raising of eyebrows and so forth, it is employed by those who have established conventions to indicate their own intended meaning—
just as [in the cases of] *datviṣṭa*, *datviṣṭā*, *pā*,
and *ḍe*, [as opposed to] *ratviṣṭa* and *ratviṣṭā*.

This illustration applies to all actions: to those such as cooking, which have instruments (*karaṇa*) and involve objects that are produced (*nirvartya*), like a jar; and to those such as burning, which involve objects that are modified (*vikārya*), like straw. The same principle holds for all of them—there is no such thing as "action" [independently].

If one asks how this applies to actions involving objects that are merely reached (*prāpyakarma*), such as "he goes to the village," the answer is that it has already been explained in the case of certain actions with reached objects, such as "going" (*gacchati*) and "renouncing" (*pravrajati*). However, in some cases, such as hearing or seeing the Himalayas or the sun, this principle does not apply; yet in the case of hearing or seeing words or jars, this very principle does indeed hold.

Furthermore, regarding the actions expressed by words such as *kṛta* (made), *dagdha* (burnt), and *gata* (gone)—which end in the suffix *kta*—since these actions are already completed and since the suffix *kta* is prescribed for the past tense, it is impossible for the object, such as clay or straw, to be both partially completed and partially uncompleted. Therefore, because the state of being "partly done and partly undone" (*kṛtākṛtatva*) is untenable, the application [of the term "object"] is all the more absent. Thus it is well said: "As the world speaks, so it does not happen. This is stated in the *Vākyapadīya*, verse 3.7, concerning the nature of the three kinds of objects, beginning with the "object to be produced" (*nirvartya*).

Action (karman) is threefold: that which is to be produced (nirvartya), that which is to be modified (vikārya), or that which is to be attained (prāpya); it is the fruit of action, consisting of visible or invisible refinement (saṃskāra), which is desired by the agent.

In this case as well, [the suffix] would not occur: "he sees the sun," "he hears the Himalayas," "he goes to the village" ...

Thus, in the Patañjala-Mahābhāṣya,

Thus, for now, it has been shown that verbal roots expressing action, verbal suffixes (*ākhyāta*), nouns such as *pācaka* (cook), and words denoting qualities such as *śukla* (white) are devoid of an object; that is to say, they are meaningless.

"Even in the case of words denoting substances," and so forth, up to "the statement"—this has been explained in detail that all entities consist of both existence and non-existence. Since, according to the reasoning already stated, words intended to denote those [entities] do not touch upon them, how could there be for any [word] the nature (*śīla*), the property (*dharma*), or the capacity for correct action (*sādhukāritā*) to apply to a reality that consists of existence and non-existence? [The suffix *ṇini* is used here in the sense of "having that as its nature," "having that as its property," or "acting correctly in that regard. (Pāṇini 3.2.134).

If it is argued that, in that case, there would be an abandonment of the conventional usage of words and their meanings, we say: no; there does exist the conventional usage of words and their meanings, wherein the relationship between the designation (*saṃjñā*) and the designated (*saṃjñin*) holds, and it is the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) that constitutes the meaning of the word.

For it has been said: "A word, while performing the exclusion (*apoha*) of the meanings of other words with respect to its own object, is said to 'denote' (*abhidhatte*). This [process] consists in the establishment of a relationship.

Just as among those who have established a convention, one's own intention is indicated by means of bodily gestures such as the knitting of eyebrows, the winking of eyes, or the movement of hands—since these actions are merely synonyms for the intended meaning—so too, because the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) of a word is merely a synonym for the object intended to be denoted, the word is a means for the comprehension of that object, just like the knitting of eyebrows and so forth.
A designation (*saṃjñā*) is merely a designation because it causes one to recognize;

it is not the expressive word itself. For those who have established a convention, it is a means of comprehension; however, for those who have not established a convention, it serves only as a cause for the cognition of a mere verbal tumor (*śabdagaḍu*).
As it has been said: "Words have their origin in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), and conceptual constructions have their origin in words."
"There is no absolute connection between them; words do not even touch objects.

Thus, because a thing consisting of both existence and non-existence is inexpressible, a word does not denote the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*); however, with respect to conventional reality (*saṃvṛtisat*), the word serves as a mere indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), appearing as if it were a denoter of conventional usage.
And here, the meaning of a word is the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*).
For it has been said: "A verbal expression (*śruti*) is said to 'denote' when it effects the exclusion of the meanings of other words with respect to its own object.
This is like the raising of an eyebrow.

Uddyotakara, however, offers this proof: "The cognitions of Devadatta regarding color, taste, smell, and touch have a single and multiple cause, because they are synthesized by the cognition 'by me,' just like the simultaneous cognitions of many men regarding a single movement of a dancer's eyebrows when a signal has been given."

The meaning of this is as follows: Just as, for instance, among many people who have made an agreement that "the garments must be cast aside immediately after the dancer’s brow-frown," various cognitions produced by different agents—though distinct from one another—are synthesized as "it was seen by me, it was seen by me" because the cause, the brow-frown, is a single entity; so too here, cognitions directed toward various objects will be synthesized because their cause is a single entity, and that which is the single cause is the Self.
(Tattvasaṅgrahapañjikā, verses 180–181)
"Indeed, even without the employment of words, many meanings are understood through the winking of eyes and the movements of hands," as stated in the Patañjala Mahābhāṣya, 2.1.58.

As it has been said: "Words have their origin in conceptual construction; conceptual constructions have their origin in words."

Commentary: As stated by Bhadanta Dinna—“Words have conceptual construction as their source; conceptual constructions are words and conceptual constructions; they have words as their source,” etc. (p.
1, 337)—thus [it is said] in the *Anekāntajayapatākā* composed by Ācārya Haribhadra, together with his own commentary (*svopajñavyākhyā*).

It should be understood that the name Bhadanta Dinna belongs to the Buddhist master Diṅnāga himself; see note 9. Regarding the statement "there is no absolute connection [between them]; words do not even touch objects," it means that words do not [touch] objects.
Words do not have [external] objects as their referents; see Bhāṣya, page 498, line 1.
The word *bhūta* [is used here]. (Pra.)

In this context, having determined the nature of the object and the relationship between word and meaning according to the principles of the *Naya* system, the meaning of the word is now ascertained. Here, in the analysis of affirmation (*vidhi*), negation (*niyama*), and the combination of both (*vidhiniyama-bhaṅga*), the meaning of the word is "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*).

For it has been said: "The meaning of other words," and so forth. Words other than a given word are "other words"; the word "jar" excludes the meanings of those [other] words, such as "cloth" and so on, because they are naturally distinct from it and do not participate in its conventional usage.

By the statement "The scripture (śruti) expresses its own meaning," it is said that it "shows" or "denotes" an object consisting of both being and non-being; however, it does not denote [it] in the ultimate sense, because the nature of an object is inexpressible and because names are merely conventional. Rather, it appears as if it denotes by indicating the object through the power of linguistic convention. This is the meaning of the word, and intuition (pratibhā) is the meaning of the sentence.

What, then, is the meaning of a sentence? It is said: the meaning of a sentence is *pratibhā* (intuition). This *pratibhā*, produced by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) resulting from the repeated practice of words, arises from sentences regarding objects; it is determined by one's own species and follows the pattern of one's own cognition, as in the case of the brave and the cowardly. Because this [doctrine] belongs to the *Ṛjusūtra* perspective, it is a follower of the *Paryāyāstika* (the aspect of successive states).

One should understand, accordingly, that it serves as the cause for anger, joy, fear, and so forth, upon hearing words such as "tiger," and so on, in accordance with the repeated experience of animals and humans.

The meaning of a word (*padārtha*), which is a means for the comprehension of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), is explained by being extracted from the sentence through conceptual construction (*utprekṣā*), even though it does not exist [independently].

In the Buddhist view, it is understood that the meaning of a word is *apoha* (exclusion), while the sentence-meaning is *pratibhā* (intuition). For instance, *apoha*, conceived as the meaning of a word, is intended as the meaning of a word that has been conceptually extracted from the sentence.
The meaning of a sentence, however, is characterized solely as *pratibhā* (intuition), as it has been said: "When a word is extracted from a sentence, this [isolated] meaning is analyzed;
yet this meaning of the sentence, known as *pratibhā*, is produced first."
Thus,
this is the statement of the Buddhist master Diṅnāga, as found on page 294 of the *Tattvasaṅgrahapañjikā*.

*Dinna*, *dinnaka*, and *dattaka* are also alternative names for Diṅnāga; in the Sanskrit language, the forms are *datta* and *dattaka*, which correspondingly become *dinna* and *dinnaka* in the Prākṛta language. This is found in ancient Jaina texts, such as the *Nayacakravṛtti* on page 63, line 5; page 96, line 6; page 545, note 1; and the *Anekāntajayapatākāvyākhyā* on page 1.

In such places as these, he is referred to as *Dinna*; in Siddhasena Gaṇi’s commentary on the *Tattvārthabhāṣya* (5.24), as *Dattaka*; and in many other locations, as *Diṅnāga*. Thus, three forms of his name are observed. Furthermore, in ancient Chinese texts, the name of Diṅnāga appears both as *Dinna* and *Dinnaka*. See Thomas Watters, *On Yuan Chwang’s Travels in India*, Part II.

Therefore, regarding what was stated by Uddyotakara concerning the teacher Diṅnāga— namely, that if the exclusion (*apoha*) of other words is the denoted meaning (*abhidheya-artha*), then its own meaning (*svārtha*) must be stated as distinct from that denoted meaning; or, if that [exclusion] itself is its own meaning, then this statement is contradicted, for it is said that "the word denotes while effecting the exclusion of the meanings of other words in its own meaning"— [this is the point].
For the meaning of this statement at that time is: "while expressing, it expresses," as stated in the *Nyāyavārttika* (2.2.67).
"This was stated because of a failure to understand the meaning of the sentence," as noted in the *Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā* on verse 1016 (Sanmativṛtti, p. 204).

Nor is the meaning of a word merely the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), because an absence (*vyatireka*) independent of a positive injunction (*vidhi*) is unestablished, and a presence (*anvaya*) devoid of absence is never perceived; for in all cases, the comprehension of an object occurs through both presence and absence which are mutually dependent. Thus, it is incorrect to claim that absence alone is predominant. As the monk Dattaka himself has said: "A word is said to 'denote' when, while effecting the exclusion of other objects, it operates upon its own referent."

The word *hi* has the sense of "because. Just as it is said that the word "tree" (*vṛkṣa*), while effecting the exclusion of the word "non-tree" (*avṛkṣa*) within its own referent, conveys its own referent—the characteristic of being a tree—so too the object qualified by exclusion is the meaning of the word, not exclusion alone. Exclusion alone would indeed be indefinable, because it is a non-entity, like a description of the sharpness or dullness of a donkey's horn.

Furthermore, in this case, one does not first grasp the jar through a positive injunction and subsequently perform the exclusion of others; nor does one perform the exclusion of others and subsequently grasp the jar at a different time.
For if apprehension occurs sequentially, it is not logical for sound and cognition to perform two operations simultaneously, because all entities are extremely subtle and momentary.
If it is argued that this is possible through a continuum (*santāna*), that is incorrect, because a continuum is not a real entity.

In that case, the apprehension of a jar and its exclusion of others are both established simultaneously, just as at the rising of the sun, the dispelling of darkness and the manifestation of its own nature occur by its very nature.

This being the case, even one who maintains that the meaning of a word is the exclusion of others (anyāpoha) must necessarily admit that both the universal and the particular are denotable, because positive concomitance (anvaya) and negative concomitance (vyatireka) are of equal status. Let both be primary; for when two objects are presented simultaneously—like a *dhava* tree and a *khadira* tree—it is not better to conceive of one as subordinate.

Now, if the primacy of positive concomitance were accepted, then the property of "being produced immediately after effort" (prayatnānantarīyakatva), being non-pervasive of the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), would certainly not lead to the cognition of impermanence.

By whom was it said that "that which pervades the similar instances (sapakṣa) makes [the object] known, while that which does not pervade the similar instances does not"? This much is merely stated: negative concomitance (vyatireka) does not make [the object] known if independent of positive concomitance (anvaya), nor does positive concomitance convey the meaning if independent of negative concomitance. When there is mutual dependence, as in the case of those carrying a palanquin, there is predominance in every instance; or, by the force of the speaker's intention, one or the other may be conceived as secondary or primary. As it is said in the *Dvādaśaśatikā*: "Furthermore, as for what was asked—'Why is there a negation of that which is not even suspected?'—this is not stated as a mere negation; rather, some part of that entity is understood in the world through the exclusion of other things, just as [one knows] 'he is not a horse because he has horns.'"
Nor is the particular implied by the object [of the general], because it is directly denoted;

for just as the universal is expressed, so too is the particular. Thus, both are the primary denotable content here, and therefore the denotable object consists precisely of the universal and the particular—so it is stated in the *Tattvārthabhāṣyavyākhyā* composed by Siddhasena Gaṇi. 5.
And this very distinction, which appears as having a common form, has been pointed out by the Master Diṅnāga.

How so? He says: "By means of the exclusion of other objects (*arthāntaravyāvṛtti*), some part of that entity is understood," and likewise, "The word denotes entities as qualified precisely by the exclusion of other objects," and so forth.

By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of such [positions] as "the auditory perception (*śruti*), while effecting the exclusion (*apoha*) of other word-meanings, denotes its own object" is intended. On page 251, the Master Diṅnāga says:
"...the auditory perception, while effecting the exclusion of other word-meanings, denotes its own object."
Page 253. Thus, in the commentary on the *Pramāṇavārttikasvavṛtti* composed by Karṇakagomin [at verse 1.129]:
"Is apoha the denotable object, or is it non-denotable?"

If it is expressible, then the meaning of a word—the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*)—is indeterminate, or else there is an infinite regress; for if *apoha* is expressed in the form of the exclusion of what is not-apoha, then that too would require another [exclusion], leading to an infinite regress.
Alternatively, if it is inexpressible, then the claim that "it effects the exclusion of other word-meanings" is contradictory.
Furthermore, if the exclusion (apoha) of other words is not the denoted meaning of a word, then its own meaning must be stated as distinct from the denoted meaning;

yet if that [exclusion] itself is its own meaning, then the statement that "the auditory cognition (śruti), while effecting the exclusion of the meanings of other words within its own meaning, denotes [it]" becomes contradictory.
In that case, the meaning of that sentence would be: "it denotes while not denoting anything else."
Thus [ends the section] in the Nyāyavārttika composed by Uddyotakara, 2.2.67.
And let it be seen that *pratibhā* (intuitive flash) is the meaning of a sentence (see page 547, note 8).

In ultimate reality, however, the meaning of a sentence is one alone; since every word is a cause for *pratibhā* itself, he now introduces its nature, saying: "By others, it is held that every word is a cause of *pratibhā* through repeated practice (*abhyāsa*)."

Regarding the communication of meaning to children and animals, other teachers have stated that every word whatsoever is a cause of *pratibhā* (intuitive flash). He says "of children," etc., to show that even for the dull-witted, it is a cause of *pratibhā*. (Vākyapadīya 2.118)
Let alone one who knows the convention—could this not be the cause of his intuition?

Even for those infants, or those nearly insentient animals, who do not know the linguistic conventions, it is observed that words are understood to convey their meaning due to the force of beginningless predispositions (*vāsanā*).
Thus, even for insentient beings, a word uttered with a fixed sequence is used for the purpose of addressing them.

Therefore, by following a specific innate disposition (*pratiniyata-jāti*), a particular intuition (*pratibhā*) is awakened as a matter of necessity; thus, every one of their various activities is rooted in that very [intuition]. By this it is meant: if this intuition—which is experienced by all living beings, caused by words, the foundation of all worldly activity, and undeniable—is denied, then one is merely deceiving oneself.
Therefore, the acceptance of *pratibhā* (intuitive flash) must necessarily be resorted to;
it has been stated that *pratibhā* is the cause [of cognition] arising from repeated practice (*abhyāsa*).

Regarding this, one might wonder whether this practice (*abhyāsa*) belongs to the present life or to another birth, and what its essential nature (*svarūpa*) is; anticipating this doubt, he says: "And that practice, which is without scripture (*anāgama*), is held by some to be the convention (*samaya*). This practice, being without scripture, does not belong to the present life—for it was certainly not taught to a child at that very moment by anyone. Thus, it is held to belong only to another birth. Furthermore, since this is intended to be the nature of the convention (*saṅketa*), he speaks in order to clarify its essential nature: "That which demonstrates, 'This is to be done immediately after this.'"
Vākyapadīya 2.119:
And that [pratibhā] has the nature of indicating that "this is the effect immediately following";

just as horses gallop immediately after the mere stroke of a whip, and elephants [respond] to the strike of a goad, so too other living beings, impelled by the force of the practice of beginningless latent impressions (vāsanā), perform appropriate worldly transactions as they arise through pratibhā, thereby maintaining the course of worldly life—this is established.
Thus, it has been established that the sentence is indeed indivisible and that the meaning of the sentence is *pratibhā* (intuitive flash);

by relying on this, the extraction of individual words and word-meanings will be possible for the sake of secondary application, the postulation of substitutes, and the maintenance of logical principles such as *prāsaṅgika*.
Now, following up on the very nature of *pratibhā* (intuition) previously introduced, he says: "When the [individual] objects are perceived as discrete, a distinct intuition (*pratibhā*) arises;
they call that 'the meaning of the sentence' (*vākyārtha*), which is brought about by the meanings of the words."

Vākyapadīya 2.144: When the meanings of words such as "Devadatta" are apprehended through their very separation from the distinct words, at the moment of cognition, a single intuition (*pratibhā*) arises which is indeed non-different from the meaning of the word; and the Grammarians call that the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*).
He states what the means for that [realization] is: "brought forth by categories" (*padārthairupapāditām*),
meaning brought forth— that is, manifested— by categories which, though unreal, serve as limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
Thus,
in the *Vākyapadīya-ṭīkā* composed by Puṇyarāja, it is stated that,
in brief, every word is a cause of *pratibhā* (intuitive flash) through repeated practice.
And just as in the case of conveying meaning to children and animals;

others, however, say: "Due to habituation, a word is the cause of intuition (*pratibhā*), but it does not convey an external object. He demonstrates this with the words beginning "due to habituation" (*abhyāsāt*).
*Abhyāsa* (repetition) is the observation of the repeated application of a word toward a particular object.

*Pratibhā* (intuition) is the wisdom conducive to the comprehension of an action as delimited by its specific means; it is produced by a word accompanied by the repeated observation of its usage. This intuition varies with every sentence and for every person.
However, because its divisions are immeasurable due to the infinity of linguistic usage (*śabdavyavahāra*), it is impossible to define them all; therefore, he says "in brief" (*samāsataḥ*).
Here he provides an illustration: "of children and of animals," and so forth.

For just as the striking of a goad and other such means become causes for *pratibhā* (intuitive flash) when the comprehension of meaning is being produced in elephants and the like, so too all words accepted as meaningful—such as "tree" (*vṛkṣa*) and others—become causes for the convergence of mere *pratibhā* according to habituation, but they do not directly convey an external object.

Otherwise, how could the various divisions of the teachings, which are mutually contradictory, as well as the compositions of fictional narratives—which manifest distinctions between categories of objects constructed by one's own conceptualization—exist?
(Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā). In brief, every word is a cause for intuitive insight (*pratibhā*) through repeated practice.
And regarding the method for conveying the meaning to children and animals,
he refers to the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) produced by repeated practice with the word "practice" (*abhyāsa*), employing the term for the cause in place of the effect.
The understanding of meaning from a word is not dependent upon its denotation, but rather upon repeated practice (*abhyāsa*).

For just as the strikes of a whip or a goad, though not denotative, produce through habituation a flash of intuition (*pratibhā*)—which manifests as the appearance of an object that serves as the cause for the spontaneous engagement or withdrawal of horses, elephants, and the like—and thus act as instigators or deterrents; so too, in brief, every word acts in this way for those who are proficient and those who are not in this very life.

An example is: "O Venerable One, do hell-beings possess the bodies of one-sensed beings? This is the discourse; in this manner, these viewpoints have been explained by way of illustration.

Commentary: Since the soul (*ātman*) is the subject under discussion, and because states such as those of *ratnaprabhā* (the first hell) are considered to be the nature of the soul and so forth, he says: "O Venerable One, is it the soul? and so on. That which moves (*atati*) constantly through various successive states (*paryāya*) is the soul (*ātman*). Therefore, the soul is earth in its form of existence (*sadrūpa*); "non-soul" (*anātman*) means that which is in the form of non-existence (*asadrūpa*). "It may be the soul, it may be the non-soul" (*siya āyā siya no āyā*) means it may be existent, it may be non-existent. "It may be inexpressible" (*siya avattavvaṃ*) means the entity which cannot be designated as either soul or non-soul; this is the sense. To the question "In what way is it inexpressible?", he says: it is impossible to say "it is the soul" and "it is the non-soul"—this is the meaning.

"Appaṇo āiṭṭhe" means when there is an instruction (ādeśa) regarding one's own self—that is, regarding Ratnaprabhā herself—by means of its various attributes such as color and so forth; the meaning is that she is designated by those [attributes]. "Noātmā" means "anātman" (non-self); the meaning is that she is non-existent with respect to a different form.

Regarding the statement "both [of these] are designated as 'inexpressible'": *tadubhaya* means both of those two, namely self and other; or rather, that very thing which is both is *tadubhaya*. When there is a designation (*ādiṣṭe*) by means of its modes (*paryāyaiḥ*), the meaning is that it is designated by the modes of both; thus, the entity would be "inexpressible" (*avaktavya*), that is, unspeakable. To explain: it cannot be called "self," because with respect to the modes of the other, it is non-self;
nor can it be called "non-self," because with respect to its own modes, it is self.

And its "inexpressibility" is only with respect to the words *ātman* and *anātman*, but not in every respect, because it is expressed by the very word "inexpressible"; for even things that are inexpressible [by other means] are expressible by such words as "existence," "category," "entity," and so forth, or by the word "inexpressible" itself. Thus is the sūtra on the atom [to be understood]. — From the *Bhagavatīsūtravṛtti* composed by Abhayadevasūri.

10 469 Its explanation: there are six permutations (bhaṅga) in the sūtra concerning two spatial units (dvipradeśika).
Among those, the first three refer to the totality of aggregates (*skandha*) and are exactly as previously described; however, the other three refer to partial portions (*deśa*).

This is explained starting from the word *goyam* (O Gautama): "of oneself" (*appaṇo*) means by its own modalities (*paryāyaiḥ*); "designated" (*ādiṭṭhe*) means when there is a designation (*ādeśe*), that is, when it has been designated—this refers to the self of a two-portion aggregate (*dvipradeśika-skandha*). 1.
Likewise, that which is designated by the modalities of another is the non-self (*anātman*). 2.

That which is designated by means of the synonyms for both—that characterized as a two-partite aggregate and that characterized as an aggregate other than it—would be an inexpressible entity. How so? As "self" and as "non-self. (3)

Likewise, because it consists of two spatial units (*pradeśa*), one of its parts is designated as "existent" (*sad-bhāva*); that which possesses modalities (*paryāya*) characterized by existence and following from the category of being is called "existent modality" (*sad-bhāva-paryāya*). Alternatively, this is the third case plural, meaning "by its own modalities. However, the second part is designated as "non-existent modality" (*asad-bhāva-paryāya*), meaning "by other modalities" (*para-paryāyaiḥ*). These other modalities are either those connected to its second part or those connected to other entities.
Consequently, this aggregate (*skandha*) of two spatial units is, in sequence, both "self" (*ātman*) and "not-self" (*anātman*). 4.

Likewise, when one part of it is designated as having the quality of existence (*sadbhāva*) and the other part as having both qualities, then it would be "self" and "inexpressible" (5). Likewise, when one part of that very same thing is designated as having the quality of non-existence (*asadbhāva*) and the other part as having both qualities, then it would be "not self" and "inexpressible" (6).
However, the seventh type—consisting of "self," "not self," and "inexpressible"—does not exist in a two-part entity, because such an entity possesses only two aspects.
In the case of a triadic [skandha] and so forth, however, there would be the sevenfold predication (saptabhaṅgī);
but in the case of a triadic skandha, there are thirteen predications.
"...twenty-three [atoms] in a six-part [space]," as seen on page 551, note 1, in the *Bhagavatīsūtravṛtti* composed by Abhayadevasūri.
Thus ends the seventh spoke, "The Refutation of Both [Views]," in the *Nayacakra-ṭīkā*.
Oṃ Arhaṃ.
Salutations to the true gurus.
Now, the eighth [section], on the restriction of both:

regarding the contemplation of existence and non-existence, if existence is the positive [nature] and non-existence is the qualification (*viśeṣa*), and that [non-existence] is intended as the non-existence of another (*parābhāva*) rather than a qualification of its own nature alone, then in the absence of that [other], selfhood and otherness would be undetermined, because they would be equivalent to the qualification of the non-existence of otherness.

Consequently, since both would result in having each other's nature, there would be no occurrence of existence and non-existence as distinct entities in the absence of the distinction between self and other; thus, there would be non-existence even from itself, and existence from another.

This must be considered here: are both these two—existence and non-existence—equally primary? Is existence primary and the particularity subordinate, or is the particularity primary and existence subordinate, or are both subordinate? If both were equally primary, there could be no relationship of principal and subordinate between them, because they would be independent of one another, not subserving each other's purposes, and being primary like two rival contenders;
for instance, a jar exists by its own nature as a jar, and not by way of being a cloth or as non-existence.

In this section concerning the demonstration of the truth of all modes of existence through the breaking of rules and restrictions, the subsequent *naya* is undertaken because of dissatisfaction with the perspective of the preceding *naya*. For instance: "In the contemplation of existence and non-existence," and so forth.

If a thing consists of both existence and non-existence—wherein existence is the general rule (*vidhi*) and non-existence is the particularity (*viśeṣa*), and that [non-existence] is intended as the negation of another rather than a particularity of the existent thing itself as a restriction (*niyama*)—then, in the absence of that [particularity], namely the absence of its own internal particularity, even for another thing, since its own internal particularity is absent, its status as "self" (*svatva*) and "other" (*paratva*) remains undetermined, due to the equality of the particularity consisting in the absence of otherness.

Each thing is not itself because it is a particular instance of the absence of another, just like another thing; and it possesses the state of being a particular instance of the absence of another because it is a real entity, just like itself. Furthermore, another thing is not "another" because it is devoid of its own specific nature, just like itself; and it possesses the state of being a particular instance of the absence of another as previously stated. Thus, the property [of being distinct] is established in the thesis.
Consequently, since both self and other would result in having each other's identity, there is no distinction such that one is "selfhood" for the self and "otherness" for the other.
And since there is an absence of distinction between self and other, there would be no occurrence of existence and non-existence as distinct from the universal and the particular;
this is understood through the possibility that [otherwise] one might speak harshly to the face,
and thus there is the consequence of their identity.

It is not merely a logical fallacy (ekāpatti), but what then? It is also a confusion (saṅkara). Therefore, he says: "Non-existence even by itself" is precisely for the sake of what will be explained; because of the word "also" (api), non-existence through another (parataḥ) is indeed already accepted by you, and existence through another would follow, which is undesirable. See page 536, line 1: "existence" (sattvam). Pra. [text].

Furthermore, there is another point here that must be deliberated upon: are both these two—existence and non-existence—equally primary, like two rivals seeking victory and independent of one another; or is existence primary while particularity is subordinate, or is particularity primary while existence is subordinate, or are both subordinate? Thus it should be considered.
Having set aside three of the four possible alternatives, we shall now support the view of this system, which subordinates the existence [of the parts] and prioritizes the particular [whole].
In that regard, first, the demonstration of the undesired consequence regarding the predominance of both— starting from "if both" and so forth, up to "like one desiring victory"—
applies to the cloth in exactly the same way.

If it is argued that there is a relationship of principal (aṅgin) and subordinate (aṅga) among objects of equal power, like the carriers of a palanquin, we say no; for, unlike the case of the palanquin carriers, there is no other primary agent who impels both the general and the particular.

If it is argued that the subsequent state acts as the impeller, we say no; because that [subsequent state] did not exist at that time, and even when it has arisen, it is of the same nature [as the previous], and thus, like the palanquin carriers, it lacks independence.

An auxiliary (aṅga), when functioning to accomplish the purpose of another—the principal (pradhāna)—requires that principal; likewise, the principal requires the auxiliary. This is the relationship of auxiliary and principal (aṅgāṅgibhāva). That [relationship] would not exist because the two are independent of one another. Their mutual independence arises from their not being for the sake of another (aparārthatva); their not being for the sake of another arises from their being principal. Consequently, due to this contradiction, there is no engagement with a single object, and thus it should be understood that a real entity cannot consist of both existence and non-existence (pṛ. 555, l. 7).

If it is argued that the cloth is likewise [the cause], just as in the case of the bearers of a palanquin—where there is a relationship of principal and subordinate among things of equal capacity—the answer is no. This is because, unlike the bearers of a palanquin, there is no other primary entity that acts as the instigator (*prayojayitr*) of the universal and the particular.

If it is argued that a subsequent state acts as the instigator, we say no; for at that time [the prior state] has ceased to exist, and even when the subsequent state has arisen, it is of the same nature [as the former], and thus, like the bearers of a palanquin, it lacks independence.

If it is asked, "How then does it come to be?", [the answer is: a jar comes to be as a jar by its own nature, through the predominance of its own being; it does not come to be as a cloth or other things, for fear of the aforementioned faults of confusion and the non-existence of distinctions; nor does it come to be as a non-entity, whether that of a cloth or of itself, precisely because of those same faults.
