A cloth likewise comes to be in this very same way: it comes to be as a cloth by its own nature, and not as a jar or as a non-entity; here, the predominance of the cloth... [text fragment].
If it should be thought that— due to the very fault stated by the Self [in the passage] beginning with "the carrier of the palanquin" and ending with "and this"—

the reason [stated as] "because of mutual independence" and so forth is unestablished (*asiddha*), since we observe a relationship of subordinate and principal (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*) even among things of equal power, just as in the case of the carriers of a palanquin.

And this is not so; [the argument] beginning with "like the carriers of a palanquin" and ending with "due to the absence of an instigator" does not constitute a failure of the reason (*hetvasiddhi*). For just as there exists a principal Lord who acts as the instigator of the palanquin-carriers—who act in combination as the cause of the relationship between parts and the whole (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*)—in the act of carrying, there is no such other principal instigator for the universal and the particular, nor for the jar and its like, nor for the lump of clay and the pot-sherd and so forth. Therefore, because of this dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), this rebuttal is based on an improper example.
Page 553, line 8.

If you argue that the subsequent state (*uttarabhāva*) is the motivator (*prayojayitṛ*), [we reply: the subsequent state of the lump of clay (*piṇḍa*) is the small piece (*śivaka*), which is the primary motivator; yet for that too, there is a subsequent state such as the *sthāsaka*, the *kośaka*, the *kuśūlaka*, and so on, until finally the jar (*ghaṭa*). If you think this way, even that is not correct, because at that time the subsequent state has not yet come into being. Since it is unproduced at that moment, it is non-existent (*asat*); and since that which is non-existent lacks the capacity to motivate, how can it possess primacy? It would be like a flower in the sky (*khapuṣpa*). Furthermore, even granting its production, since the subsequent states—such as the *sthāsaka* and so forth—are of the same nature as the lump of clay, they are non-different from their own cause (*svabīja*). Therefore, the subsequent is simply the prior; how then can it motivate itself? Even if one grants a difference between them, they lack independence, like bearers of a palanquin (*śibikāvāhaka*), because they exist under the control of another. Thus, whether distinct in space or time, the prior and subsequent states, being respectively existence and non-existence, lack primacy, just like bearers of a palanquin who are not impelled by a lord (*īśvara*).
Thus, first of all, there is no activity of the two primary principles, the general and the particular,
[as stated in the *Sakoshaka-bhāṣya* and other works].

[The opponent objects: "Now, regarding the phrase 'like two good friends' (*sanmitravat*) and so forth, [the author] raises the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) that there is no distinction between the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*), because one or the other may function as subordinate (*upasarjana*) or primary (*pradhāna*).

If you think that—just as in the case of two good friends acting in concert who follow each other's lead, one becomes subordinate and the other primary due to the force of the objective (*arthavaśāt*)—this is not so, because of what will be stated later, up to the point where it says 'due to non-existence' (*abhāvāt*)."

It will be stated that the view of this system is that the meaningfulness of the word *bhāva* (existence) arises through the restriction of both— that the specific (*viśeṣa*) which is about to come into being has primacy, while the general (*sāmānya*) act of becoming (*bhavana*) itself is secondary— and not otherwise;
therefore, there is no meaningfulness [of the term] through a restriction where one or the other is either subordinate or primary.

[Page 555, Line 7] Now, if it is argued that—just as in the case of a good friend—the generality and the particular are non-distinct due to one being subordinate and the other primary, we say no; for, unlike the doctrine of the "mutual restriction" (*ubhayaniyama-naya*) which will be discussed later, there is an absence of such a state where one is subordinate and the other primary.

Furthermore, if existence and non-existence themselves were merely subordinate, then there would necessarily have to be another primary entity to set them in motion, because in its absence there could be no activity.
There is no object that exists apart from existence and non-existence;

nor is there a subordinate element without a principal one, nor is the operation of things such as the enjoyer, the object of enjoyment, the body, and food ever observed without the relationship of principal and subordinate. Therefore, these two alone possess the nature of the principal and the subordinate.
Thus, the restriction of both is stated: existence (*bhāva*) is primary, while non-existence (*abhāva*) becomes secondary (*upasarjana*), which is the distinction.

Alternatively, if both existence and non-existence are indeed secondary, then there must necessarily be another primary [element] for them, a powerful substratum, just as two men—a king’s servant and his subordinate—are set in motion by a sovereign king; for in the absence of that [primary], their activity would not occur.
For it is observed that activity [proceeds] from two weak things by relying on one that is strong.

And this activity, occurring between the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*), would have to be of such a nature; yet it is in every respect untenable, because existence (*bhāva*) and non-existence (*abhāva*) are merely synonyms, since there is no separate entity for properties such as identity and difference. Existence, the universal, activity, substance, affirmation, and continuity are synonyms; non-existence, the particular, difference, cessation, exclusion, restriction, and property are synonyms. Even in conceptual constructions such as quality and qualificand (*guṇa-guṇin*), since no object distinct from existence and non-existence is possible, it must be only twofold.

If this object, when examined in these four ways, is found to be untenable, then it might be thought: "Since there is no entity distinct from existence and non-existence, the two secondary factors (upasarjana) do not function";
however, the two secondary factors will indeed function even without the primary factor (pradhāna).
And even that [is not so], because it continues [to be understood] that "there is no subordinate without a principal," just as a servant and the like [do not exist] without a master;
therefore, this conceptualization is also [unfounded].
In this regard, according to the literal reading, the word-division should be made as "by the powerful one who serves as the substratum" (*balavatā āśrayabhūtena*).
In this context, there may also be the reading *balavadāśrayabhūtena*; see Ṭippaṇī 2,
which reads *vatāśrayābhā*.

Likewise, if it should be thought here that "a thing exists even without the relationship of beneficiary and benefactor," this too is not so; [this applies] from the phrase "not by way of the relationship of primary and subordinate" up to "the functioning of things."

The enjoyer is the Pradhāna; for its sake, the object of enjoyment is subordinate, just as boiled rice is subordinate to the eater. For the self consisting of the body and so forth, the body itself is the enjoyer presided over by consciousness; for its sake, food and such are subordinate. By the use of the word "and so forth" (ādi), clothing, bedding, seats, houses, and the like are included. For the sake of food there is rice and such; for the sake of rice there is water and such.
Just as this relationship between the enjoyer and the enjoyed proceeds solely through the state of being primary and subordinate, and not without it.

Furthermore, the activity of an entity is observed in this manner as being directly perceived; thus, between those two—existence and non-existence—there is a relationship of primary and subordinate, or a relationship of quality and principal, because there is no third entity [to serve as a basis for such a distinction].
[The word division is: "the body and so forth are [beneficial] to the self" (kāropakārātmaka-śarīrādy-ātmanaḥ).

In the phrase *guṇadhāna* (the source of qualities), because the word *iti* has the sense of a reason, when things are established in this way for that cause, the dual restriction is stated as to which [element] is determined in what manner; namely: the suffix-meaning (*pratyayārtha*) is the agent-instrument (*kartṛsādhana*) "being" (*bhavat*), while the base-meaning (*prakṛtyartha*) is the subordinate "becoming" (*bhāva*), which is the action-instrument (*bhāvasādhana*).

If it is asked, "What is it that becomes?", it is said: there is a particularity; that very thing which becomes is called "becoming" (*bhāva*) by means of a word ending in the suffix *ṇa* that denotes the agent, just as in the explanation of the previous method (*naya*).

Even when there is an intention to express the meaning of the root (*prakṛtyartha*) from the perspective of the actual sense, because the agent (*kartṛ*) is predominant, it is expressed as having the agent as its meaning even though it is established as a state (*bhāvasādhana*). Therefore, to demonstrate this, he says: "that by which one becomes" (*yat tena bhūyate*). If it is asked, "What is meant by this?", it is said: "That he becomes, that he undergoes becoming, that he experiences the action of becoming; while his own nature is being attained, the object revolves, assuming the status of an action as a subordinate factor. Thus it is said: "that by which one becomes," "that he becomes"—just like a dancer [who assumes] the ultimate reality of being a king.
It is the *bhavitṛ* (the agent of becoming) that becomes, not the act of becoming (*bhavana*) itself;
for if it were the act of becoming that became, even a sky-flower would exist, since the act of becoming would then entail being a substance (*dravya*).

Yet, nowhere is an undifferentiated act of becoming observed to exist; rather, it is always observed as governed by a specific agent of becoming (*bhavitṛ*), as seen in the distinction between the action, the pot, the rice, and Devadatta, or between the instrument, the form, the root, and the boy, and so forth.

Thus, both are restricted here: the particular (viśeṣa) is the primary existence (bhāva), while the universal (sāmānya) is subordinate, like the relationship between the carriers of a palanquin and the master of the vehicle; indeed, the coming-into-being of the particular alone constitutes the coming-into-being of existence.

What is this like? It is like the case of an actor and the state of being a king in its ultimate sense (*paramārtha*). Just as an actor, while being essentially an actor, assumes the guise of a king and engages in royal activities such as issuing commands, yet remains primarily an actor whose ultimate reality is that specific role; so too, a particular entity called a "jar" (*ghaṭa*), while engaged in functions such as holding water, remains primarily a jar whose ultimate reality is that specific nature. Thus, the jar is the "becomer" (*bhavitṛ*) and the agent (*kartṛ*); by means of that agent-becomer, it "is" (*bhūyate*), and it is that very thing which becomes the process of becoming (*bhavanībhavati*). It is not the case that the process of becoming is effected by the agent, nor does the jar become the process of becoming. Because it is subordinate, the agent is unable to become [the process].

If that which is non-existent were to become existent, then even a sky-flower would become existent; for if that which is non-existent were to become existent, existence would be experienced by the non-existent, and thus it would be experienced by a sky-flower as well.
Indeed, because it is non-existent, a sky-flower does not experience existence; likewise, because existence is non-existent, it is not experienced. This is the meaning.

If it is asked why existence does not experience [itself as] "existence," it is said: because existence would entail the status of being a substance (*dravya*). Since the word *dravya* ends in an agentive suffix—according to the rule "the suffixes *kṛtya*, *lyuṭ*, and others are frequently used in the sense of the agent" (*Pāṇini* 3.3.113)—that which "comes into being" (*bhavati*) would be a substance (*dravya*), or something to be produced (*bhavya*).
And this is undesirable; let this be observed (see page 377).
See page 173, line 20; see page 382, line 13;
see page 536, lines 13–14:
"That which he becomes, that he is, like an actor who is essentially a king."
It is the *bhavitṛ* (the agent of becoming) that comes into being, not the act of becoming (*bhavana*) itself.
If it were the act of becoming that came into being, then even a sky-flower would exist, because the act of becoming would then result in being a substance (*dravya*).

However, nowhere is an undifferentiated act of becoming seen to exist; rather, it is always seen as governed by a specific agent of becoming. Indeed, in cases such as an action, a jar, rice, or Devadatta, a distinction is clearly observed based on the factors of action (*kāraka*), form, roots, children, and so forth.

Thus, both are restricted here: the particular (viśeṣa) is the primary existence (bhāva), while the universal (sāmānya) is subordinate, like the carriers of a palanquin and the movement of the master in the vehicle; let it be seen that the coming-into-being of the particular itself is the coming-into-being of existence (bhāvabhavana). See page 377–2.
Let it be seen on page 377–2:
*bhavatābhā* in Bhā, *bhāvatā* in Ya.
Regarding *bhāvanā*:
since it is said "it becomes by means of becoming," the reading *bhā* also fits here in the sense of the fundamental being (*mūlasattva*).
Existence and non-existence, existence and non-existence, and cultivation.
In the case of the root *as* (to be), as in "bhavatā bhūyate," even the reading *bhā* here is consistent with the form *bhavati-bhavati*.
If it is argued that the agent is the "becoming" (bhavana),
[we reply] that the substance (dravya) exists in the state of being-become (bhavya).

The word *dravya* is derived as an irregular form (*nipātita*) when the meaning "capable" (*bhavya*) is to be expressed; the suffix *yat* is irregularly applied to the root *dru* (as in the sense of "to run toward"), resulting in *dravya*.
One who is capable—that is, self-possessed—is called a *dravya*, meaning one who has become a worthy recipient (*pātrabhūta*) for desired objects.
"This prince is a substance;
this young student is a substance"—
Pāṇini’s *Kāśikā*.
The suffixes *kṛtya* and *lyuṭ* are used diversely (to form nouns).
Pāṇini 3.3.113.
The rule "in the sense of a state (bhāva) and when not denoting an agent (akartari) among the kārakas" is no longer applicable;
the affixes designated as kṛtya and the affix lyuṭ occur abundantly (bahulam) in various senses, and they occur even in cases other than those for which they are specifically prescribed.

The *kṛtya* suffixes prescribed for the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*) also occur with other *kārakas*. The suffix *lyuṭ* occurs in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*), the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), and the abstract action (*bhāva*), and it also occurs elsewhere.
Because of the mention of the term "variously" (*bahulam*), other *kṛt* suffixes as well deviate from their assigned denotations according to specific requirements.
—Pā. Kāśikā:
In that case, it follows that even the "becoming" (*bhavana*) would not exist as something "becoming," like a sky-flower; thus, the undesired consequence is equal.

Just as there is no "becoming" without a "becomer" (*bhavitṛ*), since it is observed to be qualified by that [comer], so too there is no "becomer" without "becoming," since he is observed to be qualified by that [becoming].

Furthermore, this [existence] is not observed anywhere as a mere generality of becoming devoid of particularity; rather, it is observed as governed by a specific entity that comes into being. This is true; we too do not say that "becoming" does not exist at all. What then? It is observed as having the particularity as primary and itself as secondary. If it is asked, "Where is their equality seen? it is said: "In the case of 'the jar of action' (kriyā-ghaṭa), etc."

In an action, the agent is the *kāraka*; in a jar, there are color and so forth; in rice, there are the roots and so forth; in Devadatta and others, there are childhood and so forth. That universal of existence (*bhavanasāmānya*) which possesses these as its distinctions is seen in the world as predominated by difference, with the general nature subordinated by the specific. Indeed, both types of existence are predominant.
Regarding the two [statements] "brūtaḥ" and "brūvo yaḥ":

for this reason, both injunction (*vidhi*) and restriction (*niyama*) are regulated; namely, that the general is merely subordinate while the particular is primary. Thus, injunction and restriction are fixed. It is not as in the previous case where, according to both views, there is freedom of choice such that either the injunction is enjoined and restricted, or the restriction is enjoined and restricted, making them of equal status. Rather, like the immediately preceding principle, both are both: even "existence" (*bhāva*) is existence because it is a distinction within its own modal perspective (*paryāyanaya*), and its opposite is the manifestation of all substantial objects (*sarvadravyārtha*).
First, regarding the contemplation on name and substance: the name is the cause and the substance is the effect, because it consists of becoming (*bhavana*).
For instance, the consciousness of the potter is the cause of a jar; it is not the formless self, because that is not an instrument of action.
And all of this is indeed nothing but name.

For the potter exists within himself as both being and non-being; even non-being becomes both non-being and being. Due to the fault of confusion (*saṅkara*), in this system, the pot is the specific form (*svarūpa*) and the particularity (*viśeṣa*); it is not the absence of cloth or other things that constitutes that very particularity.
That [pot] is the primary being (*bhāva*), while the universal (*sāmānya*)—the act of becoming (*bhavana*)—is the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛtyartha*), subordinate and secondary.

What is this like? It is like the carriage of a palanquin-bearer and the carriage of a lord. Just as the carriage of the palanquin-bearers is subordinate because it exists for the sake of the lord’s carriage, and therefore it is not said that "the palanquin-bearers go," but rather that "the lord, being carried by them, goes" because he is the primary agent; likewise, although you [the opponent] generally maintain that the pot is merely a subordinate becoming (*bhavana*), it is said that "the pot itself comes into being" because of its primacy.
Therefore, does the example bring forward the nature of the determined entity—that the becoming of the particular is indeed the becoming of the entity—or does it establish both meanings?
Because this is a distinction within the method of perspectives (paryāyanaya), the cultivation of all substantial entities (dravyārtha) is the counter-position.
First, regarding the cultivation of names as substantial entities: the name is the cause and the substance is the effect, because it has the nature of becoming (bhavana).
For instance, the consciousness of the potter is the cause of a jar; the formless self (amūrtātman) is not [the cause], because it lacks agency (akaraṇa).
And all of this is merely a name;
for the potter is indeed the self.
There may also be a reading here: "even non-existence becomes existence, and existence [becomes] non-existence."
Just as there is no difference between the two [types of] vehicles (*yāna*),
here too the reading might be "in this vehicle, like the vehicle of Īśvara";
thus, this is a distinction of synonymous methods (*paryāya-naya-bheda*).
Since this system is a division of the mode of conditional predication (*paryāyanaya*), the manifestation of all substantial objects (*dravyārtha*) constitutes its counter-position (*pratipakṣa*).

Within that context, the various manifestations of substantial objects—such as injunction (*vidhi*) and so forth—have been explained and refuted; they follow immediately in sequence, are consistent with what precedes them, and, being contrary to what was previously established, are now ceased and free from latent tendencies (*niranuśaya*). Thus, by the order of logic, those are the divisions of substantial objects.
Having provided an explanation for *nāma* (name) and *sthāpanā* (representation), which were not previously explained, he will now refute them.

Regarding that, first, the existence (*bhavana*) of the objects of name and substance: by its own nature, it bends (*namayati*) and inclines everything toward itself; thus it is called *nāma*. It acts as a cause (*kāraṇaṃ karoti*), thus it is *dravya*; the meaning of *dravya* has been explained previously.
Alternatively, that which is the very process of becoming (*bhavana*) is *dravya*, the cause, which is called *nāma*.

It indeed exists, for it remains as the cause of the universe, being one and the same like the previously mentioned causes such as Puruṣa and others. As for the word "cause" (kāraṇa), it is said that it is so called because it "acts" (karoti). [The opponent asks: Since there is no effect, what could possibly be done? How could that which acts be a cause? Therefore, due to the absence of an effect, there is an absence of causality; and due to the absence of causality, there is an absence of its own characteristic, making it non-existent like a sky-flower. To this it is replied: That very thing is both effect and cause; the effect is not non-existent.
Why? Because its nature is existence (bhavanātmakatvāt).
For the cessation [of this], see page 221, line 8; page 455, line 7;
and tippanī page 72, line 7.
What are the distinctions between substance and substantial object?
They are precisely those that persist, precisely those that endure.
Substance is the cause;
[the terms] "substance" and "name" are used in the sense of "existence" (bhāva). Thus it is said in the Prajñapti.
In order to define this aforementioned relationship of cause and effect, he begins with the example of a jar, stating "for of the jar," and so forth.
For the conscious potter, accompanied by a body capable of making jars, is the cause of the jar which is the effect; for that which is devoid of consciousness is not a maker.
If it is argued, "Then let the Self be the cause, because it possesses consciousness," that is not so, because the formless Self is not a maker.

What follows from this? Since the potter’s body possesses agency, is corporeal, and consists of clay and other materials, it might be considered the cause of the jar; or, since the jar consists of clay, water, and so forth, it might be considered that clay, water, and the like alone are its cause. Be that as it may regarding the effect and the cause, in every way, because it is impossible for a material substance devoid of consciousness—even if it belongs to the same genus as the jar—or for a conscious being devoid of materiality, to be the cause of a jar belonging to a different genus, the potter, who is both material and conscious, comes into being under the name "potter" through the combination of earth, water, fire, air, and ether.

And all this is indeed only name, only sound; the world—consisting of the distinctions and subdivisions of the formed and the formless, such as earth, the self, and so forth—is merely a transformation of the single Śabdabrahman.
Regarding the intended meaning of "without cause" (*akāraṇāt*), the reading *akāraṇatvāt* (due to being without cause) is also correct according to the literal text.

Regarding the reading *akāraṇāt*: when there is a desire to express the meaning "because of being causeless," the reading *akāraṇāt* as heard in the text is also correct. Because its nature is consciousness associated with the words that are arranged [in the mind], it consists of sound; its activities, which conform to that [nature], are also of that same essence, and they do not proceed in the absence of that, like a weaver [without threads].
Indeed, there is no consciousness whatsoever that is devoid of sound;

even those immobile and mobile beings whose consciousness is unmanifest possess an internal consciousness corresponding to their own nature, produced by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the repeated practice of sound, because they engage in activity toward what is beneficial and desist from what is harmful, just like a potter [acting under the influence of the Blessed Arhat].

Another says: "Space is the very essence of sound, or sound is a quality of space, because that object which is grasped by the ear is designated as 'sound'"; thus some have understood it. By what reasoning is this stated—that "sound alone is everything"? To this it is replied: "For the potter... and so forth.

The word *hi* signifies a reason. First of all, the potter is essentially composed of sound (*śabdātmaka*), because his nature consists of consciousness (*caitanya*) bound to internal sounds. The activities as well—consisting of the sequential operations upon the lump, the clay-spike (*śivaka*), and so forth—are of that same nature, being impelled by consciousness bound to internal sounds corresponding to them. This is because they proceed from that [consciousness], just like a jar which proceeds from the activity of clay; for [the jar] exists when that [consciousness] exists, and does not exist when it does not. By way of contrast, it does not [proceed] in the absence of that; it does not proceed in the absence of consciousness bound to internal sounds corresponding to it, just like a weaver [who does not produce a cloth without the appropriate internal intention].

It might be thought: "Let it be that activity has the nature of consciousness corresponding to it, because activity is inseparable from consciousness; however, its having the nature of sound remains to be proven.

To this it is replied: What is to be proven here? This is already established. For there is no consciousness whatsoever that is devoid of sound, because consciousness is permeated by the habitual practice of the usage of sound operating since beginningless time. Indeed, consciousness itself is called the cause for the arising of the two states of *madhyamā* and *vaikharī*, which exist in the state of *paśyantī*; for effects have the nature of their cause.
As it has been said: "This is the wondrous form of Vaikharī, Madhyamā, and Paśyantī" (Vākyapadīya 1.142), and so forth;
[this is] the wondrous [form] of Vaikharī, Madhyamā, and Paśyantī.
The supreme state of the threefold speech, which has many divisions of paths (tīrtha),
is the basis for all words; thus he says, "of Vaikharī" [Vākyapadīya 1.142].
The connection is as follows: "this" refers to grammar (*vyākaraṇa*); "the supreme state" is the marvelous and wonderful;
it is a wonder that this is the foundation and the support for the multitude of words consisting of many sections.
By the phrase "of the one divided into many paths," he expresses the state of being differentiated into the various paths of *vaikharī*, *madhyamā*, and *paśyantī*.

Regarding the term *trayī*: it is called *trayī* because its three constituent parts are *vaikharī* and the others; it is "supreme" (*param*) because it is the highest state (*padam*), as it constitutes their essence.

Thus, in the commentary on the *Vākyapadīya* composed by Vṛṣabhadeva: Vaikharī is that speech which is perceivable by others through its specific nature as an object of the sense of hearing; it consists of the utterance of distinct phonemes (*śliṣṭā vyaktavarṇasamuccāraṇā*), is well-known for its correctness (*prasiddhasādhubhāvā*), and may be either grammatically refined (*bhraṣṭasaṃskārā*) or otherwise; furthermore, it possesses immeasurable varieties, such as that which exists in the human voice, in a drum, in a flute, or in a lute.

The *madhyamā*, however, is situated within [the body] as if grasping a sequence; it consists of the material cause of cognition alone, yet it follows the subtle activity of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Even when the state of sequential withdrawal occurs, for some it still maintains the grasp of the manifest vital breath.
Although there is no difference [between the stages], the *paśyantī* possesses the power of sequence already inherent within it, even when the sequence has been withdrawn.

It is both moving and unmoving; it has attained meditative composure; it is both veiled and pure; it is established in the forms of the objects of knowledge, yet possesses a withdrawn form and is formless; it manifests as distinct objects, as blended objects, and as the manifestation of all objects in perfect tranquility—thus its divisions are immeasurable...
likewise, illustrative examples are found in the Itihāsas—...

And he said further: "When the vital air (vāyu) is held in its [respective] places, the articulate speech (vaikharī vāk), which assumes the form of phonemes, arises for speakers, being bound to the activity of the breath."
Taking the intellect as its substrate and following the form of sequential succession,
the intermediate speech (madhyamā-vāk) proceeds by transcending the activity of the vital breath (prāṇa).
But Paśyantī is undivided, with all succession withdrawn;
she is the light of her own nature within, the subtle, imperishable Speech.

3—Thus, in the *Vākyapadīya-vṛtti* composed by Bhartṛhari, it may be thought: "If [the argument] is subject to deviation because activity induced by cognition is possible even among those with indistinct consciousness who are unacquainted with linguistic usage," we reply: "No," as in the passage beginning, "Even those whose consciousness is indistinct... and so forth.

It is asserted that even for mobile beings such as worms and ants, and for stationary beings such as creepers, tin, lead, and the *citaka* plant, there exists an internal consciousness corresponding to themselves, produced by the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the practice of sound; this is because they engage in and desist from what is beneficial and harmful, just like a potter. Here, "on account of engaging in and desisting from what is beneficial and harmful" (*hitāhitapravṛttivyāvṛttivṛttatvāt*) may be understood either as a locative of cause (*nimitta-saptamī*) or a genitive of relation (*sambandha-ṣaṣṭhī*), or as an instrumental denoting a characteristic state (*itthambhūtalakṣaṇā tṛtīyā*). Thus it is heard [in scripture]: "For all living beings, moreover, an infinite fraction of the syllable is eternally uncovered" (Nandīsūtra 42).

Therefore, just as the state of being a jar—which is endowed with a form produced by the superimposition of the varying degrees of activity in the potter’s hands, tools, sounds, and volitions—manifests directly from the name [of "jar"], so too does the body of the potter, the clay, and so forth, manifest through the application of words and the resulting variations in their usage, such as being crooked or straight. Because these consist in the construction of objects possessing form and other qualities, they are established as causes even in the case of trees, by way of exclusion and inclusion: namely, the tendency to approach a support such as a pillar due to the exclusion of other possibilities; the tendency toward beneficial activity; and the tendency to avoid harmful things, such as moving away from pits, fire, and the like due to fear. Thus, the logical reason is proven.

In the case of worms and the like, however, activities such as trembling, paralysis, wandering, fleeing, coming and going, and so forth, which are invariably concomitant with fear and other states, are already established; therefore, the occurrence of engagement with the beneficial and avoidance of the harmful exists as being invariably concomitant with consciousness permeated by sound (*śabdānuviddhacaitanya*), just as in the case of a potter. Consequently, in both [categories of beings], it is established [that this is the case]; moreover, in mobile beings such as those asleep or burned, the evidence of activity—such as the flapping of wings—is manifest. By that, since it is invariably concomitant, consciousness itself is established, while its state of being permeated by sound is what remains to be proven.

This is not merely by the force of our own intended logical arguments; rather, the command of the Blessed Arhat is also heard in this regard: in the exposition of scriptural knowledge (*śrutajñāna*) through the divisions of "syllables" (*akṣara*), "non-syllables" (*anakṣara*), "scripture" (*sūtra*), and so forth, it is stated in the Sūtra—and likewise in the Bhāṣya—that [knowledge] belongs to the masters who are one-sensed beings (*ekendriya*) and others, beginning with the words "for all living beings" (*sarvajīvāṇaṃ*).

"Vallī, vratatī, and latā" [are synonyms for creeper] according to the *Amarakośa*; [the term *sīsakarṇikā*] is used in the sense of a "cause" (*nimitta*) in connection with an action (karmayoga)— according to Pāṇini’s *Vārttika* 2 on *bhāṣya*.
"The sixth [case-ending] is used for the remainder"— Pāṇini 2.3.50.

Furthermore, it is declared and likewise heard: "Of all living beings (*sarvajīva*), even an infinite fraction (*anantabhāga*) of a single syllable (*akṣara*) is eternally uncovered (*nityodghāṭita*). (Nandīsūtra 42)

Therefore, just as the state of being a jar—which has acquired its form through the superimposition of the varying degrees of activity in the potter’s actions, sounds, and consciousness—manifests directly from the name, so too does the body of the potter, the clay, and so forth, which originate from that very [name], manifest through the crookedness or straightness of the application of sounds and their functions, because they consist in the construction of objects possessing form and other qualities;
let this be seen on page 378.
(Note: *vṛttitvaṃ* in the manuscript).
The root *kram* and others: bhā॰, mubhā॰, mū, ya॰.
See page 190, line 7; page 351, line 4; and footnote page 67, line 7:
"Even if that [karma] were to obstruct it, the soul would not become non-living;
for even when there is a dense mass of clouds, there is still light from the moon and the sun. (Nandīsūtra 42)
The verse beginning with "°daye hoi pahāya" is currently found mixed within the *Nandīsūtra*; however,
it appears that for the author of the *Nayacakravṛtti*, this was accepted as a verse from the *Nandīsūtra-bhāṣya*.
See footnote 68, lines 2–7.

Therefore, the series of examples beginning with "just as" (*yathaiva*) and so forth—which serves as a summary of the aforementioned meaning—continues until it reaches the point "in such and such a manner" (*tathā tathā*), where it becomes manifest.

The potter consists of consciousness permeated by sound; his action also consists of that same [consciousness], though it appears as a variety of movements toward objects such as the lump of clay (*piṇḍa*) and the shaped lump (*śivaka*). This is nothing other than consciousness-as-sound itself. Through its diverse functioning, there occurs a superimposition (*adhyāsa*) via a gradation of excellence in successive stages. The form of this "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatā*) is thus fully endowed with that [superimposition]. That "pot-ness"—whose form is fully endowed with the superimposition resulting from the gradation of the functioning of the potter’s diverse consciousness-as-sound—is the pot-ness itself. It becomes manifest through the name directly, and likewise in those various ways through forms such as the lump, the shaped lump, and so forth, characterized by broad bases and the like. This is the illustration.

Now, the illustrative meaning: likewise, that which originates from that—namely, originating from sound-consciousness (*śabda-cetanā*)—is the human body of a potter and so forth, as well as the bodies of animals belonging to the earth-body (*pṛthivī-kāya*), such as clay, sand, clods of earth, diamond, stone, and rock; by the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), one contemplates the bodies of animals belonging to the water, fire, wind, and plant realms, as well as the bodies of gods and those of hell-beings—this is expressed in the passage beginning with "through the application of sound," and so on.

Cognitive application (*upayoga*) consisting of sound is *śruta-jñāna* (scriptural knowledge), which is both manifest and unmanifest. Due to its connection with that [knowledge], the bodily, vocal, and mental activities of karma—whether auspicious or inauspicious—are *āsrava* (influx) for merit (*puṇya*) and demerit (*pāpa*). Crookedness of yoga and deception lead to the name-karma (*nāma-karma*) of the one-sensed beings and so forth, as well as the sub-class of animals. Conversely, straightness of yoga and non-deception lead to the auspicious name-karma of humans, gods, five-sensed beings, and so forth. By the inclusion of "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of non-deception;
and by the use of the ablative case in "from the beginning" (*ādeḥ*), the meaning is "due to the cause."

Just as the clay and other materials of a potter’s body are produced from that very source, so it is stated according to the logic of the process; however, if you argue that this is not established by a formal reason (*hetu*) but rather that the nature of consciousness is permeated by sound (*śabda*), then we reply: because it consists of the arrangement of objects possessing form and other qualities—just like the work of a potter consisting of form, taste, smell, sound, and touch—and because the "pot-ness" of a jar arises solely from the power of its name (*nāman*), it does not depend on any external cause.

For instance—even when the causes for [the names] Skanda and so forth are not established, a designation is applied to a living being or a non-living thing independently of any cause, such as "Skanda," "Rudra," or "Indra.

This is because they are perceived directly and because they are denoted by words well-known to all the world. Furthermore, those who have become such [beings], like cowherds and others, are spoken of in a primary sense; therefore, they are indeed those very [entities].

Number, shape, and so forth, as well as color and so forth—whatever possesses these is an "object possessing color and other qualities" (*rūpādimadartha*). Its "construction" (*viracanā*) is its formation through mutual correspondence; that very [construction] is the "self" (*ātman*), which constitutes the essential nature of things such as humans, animals, limbs, minor parts, names, completed objects, potters, bodies, and clay. This is connected as the subject (*dharmin*).

The analogy is "like the work of a potter. For just as jars, bowls, and the like—which are the work of a potter—are produced by the potter's activity permeated by internalized sound through various methods such as kneading the clay; and because they consist of the arrangement of objects possessing form and so forth, they originate from him and are of his nature, being essentially the potter’s activity—likewise, even the potter’s body, clay, and other materials are essentially the activity of consciousness permeated by internalized sound. Therefore, through that connection, [the body] is [of that nature]. (kāya-bhā) [Note: The repetition in the source text *kāya॰ya॰ tatsambandha kāya॰ bhā॰* appears to be a scribal error for *kāya-bhā* or *tatsambandhāt kāya-bhā*].
There may also be a reading here: "the application of the actions of body, speech, and mind connected thereto";
that application of the actions of body, speech, and mind is *āśrava*.
The fruit of merit is auspicious, and that of sin is inauspicious—
Tattvārtha Sūtra 6.
Crookedness of yoga and deception belong to the inauspicious name-karma;
the opposite belongs to the auspicious.
— Tattvārthasūtra 6.21–22:
"In such and such a way, it exists in that very manner."
Just as the nature of a jar is due to the power of its name alone, like the work of a potter, and does not depend on external causes— for instance,
even when causes such as the act of falling (skandana) are absent, names such as Skanda, Rudra, or Indra are applied to a living being or a non-living thing independently of any cause.

Because they are perceptible and because they are denoted by words well-known to all the world, those who have become such [entities]—cowherds and others—are spoken of in their primary sense; therefore, it is they alone who are meant here. To this, he says: "Since a jar is not produced even when the external causes such as a staff are present, how is it determined that it arises directly from the name and not from the staff and so forth? To this, it is replied: "And from the name alone," and so on.

Since even existing things such as the staff and so forth are ineffective [in producing the effect], it is solely through the power of the consciousness of the word that the reality of the entity called "pot"—which is produced by the movement of effort impelled by that [consciousness]—is obtained from the majesty of the name itself, and not in dependence upon external causes.

Since even the operations of those [entities]—which are enjoined by the consciousness of words—attain their own existence at various stages, they possess that nature (the nature of being the word). Otherwise, if they did not possess that nature, the very operation of their own form would be difficult to achieve; how then could there be "pot-ness" or "reality" in a pot? Therefore, even when all other causal factors are present, if the agent is indifferent or absent, there is an absence of action and its result, such as a jar, cooked rice, cloth, or speech. Consequently, the entire world originates from the power of the Word (*śabda*);
thus, he explains this with the words "tathā hi" and so forth.

The word *hi* is used here as an illustration. And having established this, [we see that] Skanda, Rudra, and Indra—[derived from] *skandi* (to dry up), *rudir* (to shed tears), and *idi* (supreme sovereignty) according to the Pāṇinian Dhātupāṭha—are designated as "Skanda" by reason of drying up, "Rudra" by reason of weeping, and "Indra" by reason of ruling. Even though these specific causes are absent, names such as "Skanda," "Rudra," and "Indra" are applied to a cowherd, a shepherd, or even to a soul (*jīva*) or a non-soul (*ajīva*) such as wood, a wall, or a stone, independently of any such cause. It is simply through the power of superimposition (*samadhyāropa*) that cowherds and others are addressed by those respective words.

It might be thought: "Existence" (*bhava*) is so called because it exists; "Rudra" because he weeps; "Indra" because he rules. Thus, there exist specific deities who possess objects that serve as their causes, though they are imperceptible and established in other systems of convention (*samaya*). Therefore, the metaphorical application (*upacāra*) of these names to other things will occur based on their primary usage. This, however, is incorrect, because [the objects] are perceptible, and so forth, up to: "they are those very same things."

Those such as Bhava, Kārtikeya, and others are imperceptible; they are accessible only through words conceptualized according to the conventions of other systems, and are not denotable by words well-known to all the world—unlike cowherds and the like, who are perceptible and denotable by words well-known to all the world. Therefore, their existence and their identity with those words are imperceptible and accessible only through metaphorical usage. For these reasons, those who have become those [deities]—that is, those who have become the words "Skanda" and so forth—are both perceptible and spoken of in a primary sense, like cowherds and the like. Consequently, they are indeed those very persons: cowherds and the like are themselves Skanda and the others; there are no such beings as they are conceptualized in other systems.

Therefore, by the very power of the capacity of words, even those designations such as Skanda, Rudra, and Indra that are imagined through different conventions—since the grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) exist for each of the other names within even a single one of them—all three would be expressible by one another’s names.

Now, if it is held that the reality is merely any one of these grounds [of application] according to the speaker's desire to express a particular intended object, then, in this case, because of the linguistic usage directed toward the intended object desired by the speaker, the practice of designation is accepted as being caused by consciousness (*caitanya*) which is internally connected with words; however, an external ground [of application] is abandoned.

When perception (*saṃjñā*) proceeds by means of a causal sign (*nimitta-pratyaya*), and when the application of names occurs as far as possible, then even [the suffixes] *bhāvaka* and so forth are obtained. And thus, whatever is grasped by the cause of becoming (*bhavana*), for all of that, Indra, Skanda, and so forth, are the referents (*artha*), because they are the meaning of all verbal roots (*dhātu*). Furthermore, there is synonymy (*paryāya*), just like the words *ghaṭa* and *kuṭa*, because [all things] consist of the act of combining (*ghaṭana*) and the act of scattering (*skandana*) that is possible [in them], and therefore everything is everything.
The arrangement [of names] does not arise from any other cause.

Even granting the existence of the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth as imagined by other systems, the fault of the absence of a restrictive cause for the application of names is stated: "And those who... and so on.

For even in the case of *skanda*, both "weeping" (*rodana*) and "crushing" (*indana*) exist; therefore, why would he not be Rudra or Indra? Likewise, in the case of Rudra there are "flowing" (*skandana*) and "crushing" (*indana*), and in the case of Indra there are "weeping" (*rodana*) and "flowing" (*skandana*); therefore, why would he not be the one or the other? Indeed, the cause for the application of both alternative designations exists within a single entity.
Therefore, all three would also be mutually designated by one another's names through confusion.

Now, lest this fault arise, one might maintain that a single reality is accepted as a specific cause—such as Skanda alone, and not Rudra or Indra—for the sake of unconfused linguistic usage, with the intention of expressing a desired object. If that is so, then since linguistic usage regarding the intended object is carried out by means of a name determined solely as a particular cause, you have admitted that the cause of linguistic usage is consciousness associated with an internal word; thus, the external cause is abandoned. This is the fault. By the word "but" (*tu*), he distinguishes between the acceptance of the undesirable and the abandonment of the desired.

Is the "thing-ness" (vastutva) of the entity called a jar due to the completion (nirvṛtti)—that is, the accomplishment (niṣpatti)—of the jar? Is that thing-ness of the entity called a jar its jar-ness (ghaṭatva)?
[The word *ghaṭatvam* does not appear in the middle of the Bhāṣya.]
The word "mahimnaḥ" ends in the fifth case (genitive); [the words] "sthāne," "śabda," and "svasvarūpa" end in the seventh case (locative).
*skand* in the sense of drying up; *rudir* in the sense of shedding tears; *idi* in the sense of supreme sovereignty—these are [the roots] from the Pāṇinian Dhātupāṭha. [Is it] *kuṣṭya*?
"He weeps"—thus they are directly perceived in them (Pra.); "those very [beings]"—thus they are directly perceived in them (Bh.); "those very [beings]"—thus they are directly perceived in them (Ya.).

Furthermore, regarding those [beings] such as Skanda, Rudra, and Indra who are imagined by other systems of doctrine (*samaya*), since the grounds for the application (*pravṛtti-nimitta*) of even one name among them exist in the others, all three would be designatable by one another's names.

Now, if it is maintained that reality (*tattva*) consists merely in any one of these grounds, then—by the very desire to express a specific intended object—it follows that the linguistic usage of names is accepted as being caused by consciousness (*caitanya*) associated with internal words, arising from the practical activity directed toward the intended object; thus, the external ground is abandoned.

When conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) proceeds by means of a causal sign (*nimitta-pratyaya*), and when conceptualization is established as far as possible, then even [grammatical suffixes] such as the *bhāvakā* (agentive) are attained. Thus, whatever is grasped by the cause of "becoming" (*bhavana*), for all of that, Indra, Skanda, and so forth, are the referents (*artha*), because they possess the meaning of all verbal roots (*dhātu*). Furthermore, like the words *ghaṭa* and *kuṭa*, they are synonyms (*paryāya*), because they consist of the "clustering" (*skandana*) and so forth of everything that is capable of being "joined" (*ghaṭana*) and so forth; hence, there is the state of "all being all."
The reading contained within this [passage] does not exist in the middle of manuscript Ya; what is the purpose of the other [reading], pra°? miṣyatābhā°?
Furthermore, [the opponent argues that] the external object (*bahirnimitta*) is directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*);
moreover, [it is argued] by means of the cognition of the object (*nimityapratyayena*), and so forth.

If the activity of perception (*saṃjñā*) proceeds by means of conditions characterized by crying and so forth, then, as long as they are possible and as many as there are—namely, the conditions consisting of standing, sitting, lying down, speaking, walking, turning, transforming, and so on—if perception were established through all those conditions, then because he would possess all such designations (such as being "Rudra" from crying, "Bhava" from existing, "Bhāvaka" from causing to exist, and "Kāraka" from acting), it follows that he would also be [designated] as a "Bhāvaka" and so forth.

And then, regarding the passage beginning with "tathā ca yāvad" and so forth: the meaning is that whatever its measure may be—"yāvat" meaning as much as there is—everything whatsoever that is seized by the cause of becoming (*bhava-nimitta*), all of that, such as pots and cloths, has Indra, Skanda, and others as its referent (*artha*). This is because the meaning of all verbal roots is the sense of "becoming" (*bhvarthatva*); therefore, these are synonyms (*paryāya*). And what are the synonymous words that denote them? They are just like the words "ghaṭa" and "kuṭa."

Everything would indeed be everything: a jar is Skanda, a cloth is Skanda, and even the physician Skanda is simply Skanda; likewise, Rudra, Indra, and so forth [would be Skanda], and Skanda too would be a jar, a cloth, and so on—this consequence follows.

Thus, first of all, because it has the sense of "all elements" (*sarvadhātu*), there is "all-inclusiveness" (*sarvasarvatva*) due to the absence of distinction. Furthermore, there is "all-inclusiveness" even in a specific sense, because it involves the occurrence of [actions] such as joining and the formation of aggregates (*skandana*). This is because it has the sense of movement (*parispanda*) preceded by intention or non-intention regarding activities such as stretching or contracting. Even so, since the employment of words is for the purpose of conveying meaning, one must accept that the nature of aggregates and so forth is established merely as a designation (*saṃjñāmātra*), independent of external causes, in order to avoid the lack of systematic arrangement characterized by the denotation of everything as everything.

For since the relationship between word and meaning consists merely of convention (*saṅketa*), it is established without effort that all regional languages possess primary meanings; for this very reason, the following traditional teaching of the learned is also appropriate: "Verbal roots have multiple meanings..."
...let it be seen that this is called the "manifestor" (bhāvaka) of this entire world, including its distinction between the sentient and the insentient.

Since the substance (*dravya*) of a jar is common to all [roots] whose meanings involve cognition, motion, and so forth—namely, all roots whose meanings such as *skandana* (leaping), *śoṣaṇa* (drying), *visaraṇa* (spreading), *rodana* (weeping), *indana* (impelling), *sadana* (sitting), *stambhana* (paralyzing), and others are possible within that same referent (*artha*), each of those has that very meaning; thus there is "all-in-all" (*sarvasarvatva*).

Furthermore, because the meanings of *vasana* (dwelling) are the same as those of *vastu* and *vāstu*, and because the synonyms for the cessation of motion (*gati-nivṛtti*) and the remaining verbal roots do not transcend the meaning of "substance" (*vastu*), which substance would not be denoted by which [root] through what cause? Therefore, there is "all-in-all," because [the usage] is figurative (*bhākta*).
Because it serves its purpose, let it be seen; page 244, line 3;
"paṭaḥ skandaḥ" does not exist in the middle of the Bhāṣya.

The reading "skandavadyo 'pi" (or "skandavad yo 'pi") may also be possible here; its intended meaning should be understood as: "A jar is a *skanda*, a cloth is a *skanda*—like a *skanda*; whatever is a *skanda*, that is a *skanda*. [This is] because the verbal root [√*skand*] has the sense of "to go" (*artha*), [and thus] the possibility of its application is not obstructed.

Even though the nature of everything is thus established as "all-in-all," nevertheless, since the employment of words is for the purpose of conveying meaning, one must accept that categories such as "aggregate" (*skandha*) are established merely by convention, independent of external causes, in order to avoid the lack of regulation characterized by every word denoting everything.
For in this way, because the relationship between word and meaning is based on mere convention, it follows effortlessly that all regional languages possess primary referents.
For this very reason, the following traditional teaching of the learned is also appropriate: "Verbal roots have multiple meanings...
[and so forth].
"Let it be seen":
this refers to that which brings into being this entire world, including the distinction between sentient and insentient things— the substance of a jar, for instance.
The construction here might also be "let it be seen as the distinction between the sentient and the insentient," and the reading "viśaraṇa" (dissolution) might also occur here.
The root *tul* (ṣadḷ) is used in the senses of weighing, perishing, moving, and sinking (*avasādaneṣu*)—Pāṇini Dhātupāṭha 854, 1428;
the form *sadana* does not exist in the middle [of the list] in the Yajurveda recension; the root *sthā* is used in the sense of cessation of motion (*gatinivṛttau*)—Pāṇini Dhātupāṭha 928.

It might be thought: "In that case, by way of bringing about an even greater over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), you yourself have established that everything depends upon external causes; moreover, in your own position as well, the over-extension whereby everything could denote everything remains difficult to avoid."

And this is incorrect for the very reason already stated; for even if one were to maintain [the existence of a self] as previously argued—since the employment of words is intended to convey the specific object one wishes to communicate—it would follow that because everything is everything, the lack of restriction characterized by the denotation of all things by all words would necessarily result. To prevent this, it follows that words such as "aggregate" (*skandha*) are established as mere designations (*saṃjñāmātra*) with respect to some particular object, independent of external causes, and thus denote that specific object by necessity. Otherwise, if everything were everything, the lack of restriction regarding the denotation of all things would be inevitable.

Therefore, because it is merely a conventional designation (*saṃjñā-sanniveśa*), there is no fault whatsoever for me; thus, this objection is fallacious because it commits the same error. (The reading *saṅgopādāna* is found in the manuscript.)
"In every case, for all [words], in all respects"—this phrase beginning with "for thus" (*evaṃ hi*) demonstrates the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of this logical principle.

And having established this, since the relationship between word and meaning is merely conventional (*saṅketamātratvāt*), it follows without effort that the primary meanings of words in all regional languages are established; for instance, *ghaṭaḥ*, *kuṭaḥ*, *kumbhaḥ*; *kṣīram*, *payaḥ*, *pāli*, *dugdham*; *agniḥ*, *āturaḥ*, *kiñcu*, *maṅgalaḥ*, and so forth. By virtue of convention, these various words are established as denoting a single intended object, because convention is independent of fixed [etymological] constraints and because those respective words are capable of conveying their own intended application, just like the name *Ḍittha* and others.

For this very reason, the recollection of the learned is also justified, and not otherwise. As it has been said: "Roots have multiple meanings"—let this be understood as far as the passage beginning with "conscious and unconscious" extends.

In this manner, that which was stated—that the name is the bringer-forth (*bhāvaka*) of this entire world, consisting of the distinction between the conscious and the unconscious, such as the potter and the jar, down to earth and so forth, humans, hell-beings, animals, perfected beings (*siddhas*), atoms, time, and space—it is thus established that the entire world arises from the Name (*nāman*).

Therefore, it becomes a jar; the substance (*dravya*) is the cause of the jar; it is called "it brings about the jar" (*ghaṭaṃ bhāvayati*); from that [substance] comes the name of the jar, because the jar comes into being from that. Just as the jar comes into being through this [substance], like clay, so too does the jar come into being through its name. Or rather, the state of being the essence of the action of "jar-making" (*bhāvakatva*)—which is the coming-into-being through the application of form and so forth—is bound to the internalized word and consists of that word.
Therefore, the very non-subordinate status of the name-substance (nāmadravya) constitutes this "doctrine of the meaning of name and substance" (nāmadravyārthanaya);
this too has its own restrictive rule.
It is intended as a subordinate element (upasarjana), not as the primary element;
for since the employment of words is for the sake of meaning, the meaning is primary, not the word.
Furthermore, because even the meaning serves as the cause for the arising of cognition, cognition alone is primary.
For a jar or the like does not arise from a name;
rather, from that [name], only an impact upon the auditory organ is produced.
And thus, if a jar were to possess substantiality (*dravyatva*) in its production from a name, then those seeking a jar would say, "Let there be a jar! simply by uttering those words.

Therefore, because it has been established that the cause of engagement and withdrawal for those who seek an object and those who seek its absence is the state arising from the subsidence-cum-destruction (*kṣayopaśama*)—since it arises from that—the reason is proven.

For whatever arises from something is seen to be the cause of that, just as clay is the cause of a jar which arises from clay; thus, the term "name" (*nāma*) functions as the application (*upanaya*) to show that it is the cause of the jar.
The phrase "by this," etc., means that just as clay is the substance (*dravya*) of the jar, so too is the name.

The term "being the bringer-into-being" (*bhāvakatva*) refers to the name's nature as the act of making a jar; the word attains the state of a substance because its essence is the making of a jar, as previously stated. Therefore, the name brings the jar into being; the meaning is that "the jar becomes from the name. (See *Kiccupabhāṣya*, Tippanī p. 63, l. 20).
Are they fixed? Because they are independent of causes;
[this refers] to those words.
How does the root *añc* also function in the sense of "to go"? Roots can have multiple meanings—
Pāṇini-Mahābhāṣya 8.2.48.
"Let it be seen," [referring to] "sentient and insentient" and so forth;
here, "let it be seen" means:
One might also apply the interpretation beginning with "intentional and unintentional" (*cetanācetanā*), because the jar arises from that [name], just as [a jar arises] from clay;

for in this way, the jar comes to be by means of its name, or rather, its state of being a jar consists in its nature as the action of being a jar (*ghaṭakriyātmakatva*). Its state of being a bringer-into-existence (*bhāvakatva*) is likewise established.
The manifestation of the utilization of form and so forth is bound to an internally situated word and is of the nature of that word;
therefore, the substance of the name (nāmadravya) possesses precisely the status of being non-subordinate—
this is the Nāmadravyārtha-naya.
For this [word] as well, restriction is intended by virtue of its being subordinate (upasarjana), not by virtue of its being primary;
for since the employment of a word is for the sake of the meaning, the meaning is primary, not the word.
Since the object is also a cause for the arising of cognition, cognition alone is primary;
for a jar or similar object does not arise from a name,
but rather, from that [name], only an impact upon the auditory organ is produced.

And likewise, if name were indeed the substantiality (*dravyatva*) in the production of a jar, then those seeking a jar might say, "Let there be a jar," and those seeking its presence or seeking its absence might say, "Let there not be one. Such a basis would thus be possible here; therefore, for those seeking an object and those seeking its absence, the cause of engagement and withdrawal must be that which arises from the subsidence-cum-destruction (*kṣayopaśamika*) [of karma].
"Through the application to form and so forth," etc., means:

alternatively, the application to form and so forth is the cognition of form and so forth. Its existence is bound to the internally present word and consists of that word. According to the definitions—"it is form because it is formed," "it is taste because it is tasted," "it is smell because it is smelled," and "sound is that which is grasped by the ear"—since that application consists of sound and form and the rest consist of that [same] nature, sound is also form and so forth.
Therefore, the meaning is that for the name-substance (*nāma-dravya*), there is indeed no subordination, but rather primacy alone.

This is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the perspective of name and substance (*nāmadravyārthanaya*). Here, the perspective of speech (*śabdanaya*), which functions as the refutation by breaking the restriction of both, will state: "Of this too there is a restriction," and so forth.

This state of name and substance is also held to be restricted as being subordinate (*upasarjana*), not as primary; however, it has been stated that the particularity (*viśeṣa*) is restricted as the primary element.
We do not say that sound, being occupied merely as a cause, does not assist cognition;

rather, it functions as an auxiliary to cognition itself and is brought forth by cognition alone. Since the employment of sound is for the purpose of conveying meaning, and because the employment of sound is for the sake of the object, the object is primary and not the sound, for the sound is not itself the meaning.
Since the object also serves as a cause for the arising of cognition, cognition alone is primary;
yet there is no identity between cognition and the word [denoting it], due to both direct perception and contradiction.

For, through direct perception itself, a jar or the like does not arise from a name—that is, from a sound—which causes an impact on the ear; nor is sound the cause of a jar, because the jar is not produced from it.

From that sound, however, only an impact upon the auditory organ arises; therefore, sound is the cause for the impact upon the auditory organ, but it is excluded from [being the cause of] the jar or the cognition, as previously stated.
Because [the consequence] is untenable—starting from "and likewise" up to "they would say"—this is the demonstration of an undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭāpādana*).

If sound were a substance (*dravyatva*) at the time of the production of a jar, then those seeking a jar would say, "Let there be a jar!"; and kings who desire the destruction of their enemies and wish for victory would not maintain elephants and horses, or they would say, "May it not come upon the enemy's army!"
And that enemy force was neither seen nor desired by me;

therefore, for those seeking an object and for those not seeking its absence, the cause of engagement and withdrawal is the state arising from the subsidence-cum-destruction (*kṣayopaśamika*) [of karma]. The meaning is that knowledge has as its cause the subsidence-cum-destruction of the veil of knowledge (*jñānāvaraṇa*); this is precisely because engagement and withdrawal are observed [to follow] from that very [state].
That too, having abandoned substantiality, becomes a mode; that mode also, having abandoned substantiality,
exists as nothing other than a particular.

For that scripture (*āgama*) is the scripture of existence (*bhāvāgama*), whereas this is the scripture of substance (*dravyāgama*); for thus they say: "One should know the scriptural learning (*suta*) associated with the [spiritual] atom (*aṇu*) by means of scripture (*āgama*)."
Knowledge alone is primary;
from it alone arise its production and its activity, for the sake of that [knowledge], just as the carrying of a palanquin depends on the master of the vehicle.

Therefore, as you have stated, the predominance of the arising of specific modifications (*upayoga-viśeṣa*) occurs because sound is its effect and [the soul] is its cause; thus, the state arising from the subsidence-cum-destruction (*kṣayopaśamika-bhāva*), due to its momentary nature and its change from moment to moment, sets aside the substantial perspective (*dravyārthatā*) and exists as a particularity alone—it becomes a particularity itself, and the etymological derivation of the word "sound" as previously mentioned comes to pass. Having begun with the statement "existence (*bhava*) is the primary sense of 'being' (*bhāva*"), the literal meaning is established up to the point where the various distinctions such as "child" and so forth are indeed perceived.

And it has been explained from the perspective of substantiality (*vastu*): the universal is subordinate and the particular is primary; this is the state of being (*bhāva*), like the relationship between the carriers of a palanquin and the lord of the vehicle.
That [state of being] also comes into existence by relinquishing its status as substantiality (*dravyārthatā*).
By that very distinction, it becomes so;
for that word is the source of existence, the source of substance.
For thus they have said: "One should know scriptural learning (śruta) as being associated with the self through scripture.

What is that substance-essential act (dravyāvaśyaka)? It is declared to be of two kinds, namely: from the perspective of scripture (āgama) and from the perspective of non-scripture (noāgama). (Sūtra 12)

What is the *dravyāvaśyaka* from the perspective of scripture (*āgama*)? It is one for whom the word *āvaśyaka* has been learned, mastered, conquered, measured, and fully internalized; who possesses it with the same name, the same phonation, with no missing syllables, no extra syllables, no inverted syllables, without stumbling, without blurring, without confusion, complete, with a complete phonation, uttered from the throat and lips, and received through the oral instruction of a teacher. Why is such a person not [considered] engaged in the actual practice (*anuprekṣā*) there, despite being involved in reciting, questioning, rehearsing, and preaching the Dharma? Because it is said: "Non-application (*anupayoga*) is substance (*dravya*). (Sūtra 13)
Thus, that is the essential practice (āvaśyaka) as substance from the perspective of scripture...
Sūtra 14.

What, then, is scriptural knowledge (*śruta*) from the perspective of substance (*dravya*)? It is that for which the word "scripture" has been learned, mastered, and internalized, yet [the meaning] has not reached the stage of contemplation (*anuprekṣā*).

"Why? Because it is 'substance' (dravya) due to its lack of application (anupayoga)... This is the reading found in the *Anuyogadvārasūtra* [sūtra 33] regarding scriptural knowledge as substance from the perspective of scripture (āgama)."
Knowledge alone is primary;
from it alone arises its production and its activity, for the sake of that [knowledge], just as in the case of the bearers of a palanquin and the owner of the vehicle.

Therefore, as you have stated, the predominance of the arising of specific utility belongs to the word because it is its effect, and [the predominance] of arising belongs to it because it is its cause; see page 8555,
line 7.
See page 555, line 7;
see page 556, line 5.

For that is the "approach through disposition" (*bhāvāgama*); since knowledge, which is a state resulting from the subsidence-cum-destruction (*kṣayopaśama*) of karma, is called the approach through disposition, it is therefore primary. "Approach" (*āgama*) means comprehension, whether by way of exclusion (*maryādā*) or inclusion (*abhividhi*). Thus, the word possesses the nature of an approach (*āgamatva*). Consequently, the word is brought forth from knowledge.
Therefore, sound is the arrival of a substance;

for they say "thus indeed they have said," which is the scriptural authority (*ārṣa*) indicating that sound is the arrival of a substance: "One should know through scripture that the substance-hearing (*dravya-śruta*) is not associated with [the mere] atom.

Furthermore, knowledge alone is primary, because its very production arises from that; the production of sound arises from knowledge itself, since it is instigated by the speaker's knowledge. Thus, knowledge alone is the cause of sound.

Even though sound is active, it is dependent because its purpose is knowledge; it is dependent because its function is to produce knowledge in the listener. Therefore, he says: "And activity [is subordinate] because it exists for that purpose, both by virtue of being rooted in that [knowledge] and by virtue of having that as its goal. Regarding these two points—that knowledge is primary—the illustration is: "like the carriage of the carriers and the carriage of the master. The carriage of wage-earners, though set in motion by the master's journey, exists for the sake of the master’s journey; thus, in both ways, just as the master is primary, so too is knowledge primary. This was stated by the author of the *Vākya-padīya*.
For the purpose of grasping the dependent nature through ignorance (paratantrājñānopādānārtham),
and for the purpose of grasping the dependent nature through knowledge (paratantrajñānopādānārtham) [as stated in the Bhāṣya],
therefore, it is as you have said, and so forth.

Application (*upayoga*) is conjunction through proximity with the whole self; it is the orientation of all the soul's spatial units (*pradeśa*) toward objects such as form when they are in close proximity. The crookedness or straightness of the application of the self toward sound occurs respectively as clay and so forth, or as a potter and so forth, produced by the *nāma-karma* of animals and humans, because it consists in the arrangement of objects possessing form and other qualities, like the work of a potter; [it is said]: "The self, having empowered the objects by means of the intellect, joins the mind through the desire to speak."

Pāṭha-śikṣā 6 and all such [arguments] establish the predominance of the arising of specific functions (*upayoga-viśeṣa-bhavana*), because sound is an effect thereof. Now, if it should be argued: "The universal (*sāmānya*) is non-distinctive, because there is no distinction between the two in terms of their mutual causality;

therefore, why does *upayoga* itself not attain the status of being a 'name' (*nāmatva*)?"—[the answer is: because a name attains the state of *upayoga*, it possesses the predominance of specific [functions] everywhere.

Alternatively, regarding that very word "name" (*nāma-śabda*), by [the rule] beginning with "chest" (*uraḥ-prabhṛti*), having set aside the meaning of a name-substance (*nāma-dravya-artha*), the meaning of a substance-substance (*dravya-dravya-artha*) is accepted, due to the admission of material substances (*mūrta-dravya*).
A material substance cannot be the [cause] of that which is immaterial;

the word "name" (nāma) is the word for conjunction (yoga), and it is the effect of that very [conjunction], which is the cause of the functional capacity (upayoga) such as the potter’s body and so forth. Thus, you yourself have previously elaborated in detail that "it is the cause of that"—see page 559, line 4.
The self, having empowered the objects through the intellect, joins the mind with the desire to speak. (Pāṇini Śikṣā 6) Having come together with the objects—(Pāṇini Śikṣā).
Now it might be said: [the term] "general" (*sāmānya*) is non-specific (*aviśeṣa*), because there is no distinction between the two in terms of their being mutual causes.

Now, why does only *upayoga* (conscious activity) attain the status of being a "name" (*nāman*)? Because for a name that has attained the state of *upayoga*, there is a predominance of its specific quality in all cases;

or else, in the case of the word "name" itself—as in the rule beginning with "chest, etc. (*uraḥ-prabhṛti*)—having set aside the meaning of "named substance" (*nāmadravya*), the meaning of "substance-substance" (*dravyadravya*) is accepted because of the admission of material substances (*mūrtadravya*).
A material thing cannot be the substance of an immaterial thing.
Let the word "nāma" be seen on page 559,
line 4. The prima facie argument beginning with "athocyeta" and so forth, up to the point "because there is no distinction," has already been explained.

The universal (*sāmānya*) is the non-distinct; the fact that it consists merely in being (*bhavanamātratva*) results in its not being a particular (*viśeṣa*). Thus, the meaning has been established: because there is no distinction between the two in terms of their mutual causality. This is the established meaning. Here follows the response, beginning with "Now, why? and continuing up to "everywhere there is a predominance of the particular."

"Only *upayoga* (active engagement) attains the state of being a *nāma* (name)," thus the particularity of *upayoga* holds primacy because it is that which achieves the status of *upayoga*, while the *nāman* (the name-word) is secondary—or rather, the word "name" (*nāmaśabda*) itself is distinguished from sounds such as those of the lute, flute, and cymbals, because it is the subject under discussion and because it is instrumental [to cognition]. By the passage beginning with "chest, etc.," you have abandoned the objective of the substance-as-name (*nāmadravyārtha*) and accepted instead the objective of the substance-as-substance (*dravyadravyārtha*). As it has been said: "The self, through the intellect, makes objects capable; the mind then engages them with the desire to speak.
The mind strikes the bodily fire, and that [fire] impels the vital air (*māruta*)."
But the wind, moving above, produces a deep and resonant sound.
By stating "the training of speech" (*pāṭha-śikṣā*) and so forth, you accept [it] as a material substance (*mūrtadravya*);

thus, even the scriptural authority (*ārṣa*) serves as a proof. Non-scriptural substance (*noāgama-dravya*) has been described as the body, as in: "Aha! By means of this collection of bodies, the term 'equanimity' (*sāmāyika*) has been made known, explained," and so forth.
Therefore, by abandoning the status of being the cause of sound and accepting the status of being the cause of a material substance, your position falls into contradiction.
Therefore he says: "A material thing cannot be the transformative cause (*pariṇāmikāraṇa*) of an immaterial one; this is the meaning.

Just as it is accepted that a material thing cannot be the cause of an immaterial one, so too, because the word "name" (*nāma-śabda*) is material, its being the cause of the immaterial *upayoga* (conscious activity) is not tenable, primarily because of its material nature.
Following the sequence of predominance:
the Self, having empowered the objects through the intellect, joins the mind with the desire to speak, as in the case of a lute, a player, and rhythmic beats.
In his own commentary (*vṛtti*) on *Vākyapadīya* 1.116, Bhartṛhari also cites this verse with the reading *samarthyārthān*,
whereas the *Śikṣā* reads *sametyārthān*.
The mind strikes the fire of the body, and it impels the vital air (māruta). The vital air, moving upward, produces a deep sound. (Pāṇinīya Śikṣā:
"The vital air, moving in the chest, produces a deep tone.")

...by way of non-scriptural authority (noāgamato), what is that non-scriptural substance-essential (davvāvassaya)? It is declared to be threefold, namely: substance-essential as the body of the knower (jāṇayasarīra-davvāvassaya), substance-essential as the body of the potential being (bhaviya-sarīra-davvāvassaya), and substance-essential distinct from the body of the knower and the body of the potential being (jāṇayasarīra-bhaviya-sarīra-vatiritta-davvāvassaya). Sūtra 15.

What is the substance-essential-activity (*jñāyakaśarīra-dravyāvaśyaka*)? It is as follows: when someone sees the body of one who knows the subject matter of the term *āvaśyaka*—a body from which life has departed, which is dead, cast off, abandoned, and devoid of soul, whether lying on a bed, on a mat, in a place of rest (*naiṣedhika*), or upon the surface of the Siddha-stone—and says: "Aha! By means of this aggregate of a body and through dispositions seen by the Jina, the word *āvaśyaka* was proclaimed, explained, demonstrated, shown, and illustrated. What is the illustration? "This was a pot of honey; this was a pot of ghee. That is the substance-essential-activity of the knowing-body. (Sūtra 16)
Regarding the *sāmāyika* derived from names, it is briefly of four kinds, namely: *nāma-sāmāyika*, *ṭhavaṇā-sāmāyika*, *dravya-sāmāyika*, and *bhāva-sāmāyika*.
"Name and designation were mentioned previously; the same applies to substance-right-conduct (dravyasāmāyika)," as stated in the *Anuyogadvārasūtra*, Sūtra 150.

It might be thought: "How can sound be corporeal, since it would otherwise not be the cause of incorporeal cognition? To this we reply: Sound is corporeal because its movement is obstructed by walls and the like, just like a clod of earth; therefore, that which is called 'name' (nāma) is a substance of utility because of its corporeality, just like clay.
