For it has been said: "Indeed, that which is corporeal does not become incorporeal, nor does that which is incorporeal attain corporeality;
a substance does not deviate from its own nature throughout the three periods of time.

Now, one might object: since their essential natures are mutually interpenetrated, as in the case of the substances consisting of the body, the instruments, the senses, cognition, and the self, how can a corporeal substance [be the locus] of incorporeal cognition?

The material sense-organ (*dravyendriya*) is material; it is the material cause for immaterial cognition, and likewise the body and other instruments are the material causes for the self of another birth. Furthermore, let it be understood that a jar is material in relation to the space within the jar, because its movement is obstructed by walls and such. That whose movement is obstructed by walls and the like is observed to be material, just as a clod of earth or similar objects are.
Regarding the phrase "that name [does not belong] to the activity" (*upayoga*), etc., the proof for demonstrating the meaning is as follows:

activity (*upayoga*) is not caused by material substances (*mūrtadravya*), because it is formless (*amūrtatva*), like space (*ākāśa*). For space is not the effect of material substances such as clay or a staff; this is the example based on similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*). By way of contrast (*vaidharmya*), [the argument is]: that which is caused by material substances is not formless, just like clay.
Alternatively, the word "substance" (dravya) does not apply to that which is formless (amūrta), because it possesses form (mūrtatva), like clay;
for that which is the substance of something formless, such as spatial extension (avagāha), is not itself formless, just as space (ākāśa) [is not the substance of its own extension].
Thus, he states the supporting evidence beginning with the words "for it has been said."

For a material substance (*pudgala-dravya*) possessing form, color, and so forth, being material does not turn into immateriality—that is, while remaining material, it does not become characterized by the absence of color and so forth, nor does it transform in such a way as to attain the nature of soul (*jīva*), space (*ākāśa*), merit (*dharma*), or demerit (*adharma*). Likewise, the immaterial does not attain materiality; nor does an immaterial substance such as space ever attain materiality throughout all three times—past, future, and present—the meaning being "never. This is because it never abandons its own nature (*ātmabhāva*); that property which exists as long as the substance itself is its "own nature," and a substance never relinquishes that own nature.
Regarding "embodied cognition" (*mūrtijñāna*):

[the opponent argues that] because it has a corporeal form (*mūrta*), its movement would be obstructed by walls and the like, just like a clod of earth; therefore, that which is called cognition cannot be a substance (*dravya*) of utility, because of its corporeality, just like clay.
For it has been said:
"Indeed, that which is material does not become immaterial, nor does that which is immaterial attain materiality; the immaterial does not become material, nor does the material become immaterial."
The reading "substance does not perish from its own nature throughout the three times" is also possible here; for comparison: "the formless does not become form, nor does the formed become formless."
— Śāstravārtāsamuccaya 3.41:
That which is formless does not become possessed of form, nor does that which is possessed of form attain the state of being formless.
"Substance does not deviate from its own nature even throughout the three periods of time"—
Sanmativṛtti 1.53, p. 456.
Substance does not perish even across the three periods of time, nor does it deviate from its own nature.

Now, because their essential natures are mutually interpenetrating—just as in the case of the substance of the soul which consists of the body, the instruments, the senses, and cognition—is the material sense-organ (dravyendriya) the substance of formless cognition?
Indeed, the material sense-organ is the substance of formless cognition.
Because of the production of the body and so forth, the substance of the body and so on belongs to the self of another existence; and as for the pot, [it belongs] to the space within the pot.
Here he says: "But surely, because of mutual interpenetration," and so on, up to "of the space within the pot.

It is incorrect to say that [the space] does not abandon its own nature nor acquire the form of another, because—like milk and water—it consists of the mutual interpenetration of itself and the other.
The demonstration of their mutually interpenetrating nature begins with "in manifestation" (*nirvṛtti*) and continues up to "like a substance" (*dravyavat*).

The suffix *-vat* is applied to each term, as in "like the manifesting and auxiliary sense organs" (*nirvṛtty-upakaraṇendriya-jñānavat*) and "like the substance of the body and the self" (*tanv-ātmadravyavat*).

Substance (*dravya*) is the cause; the material form (*mūrta*) is the cause of the immaterial (*amūrta*) cognition (*jñāna*). There are two kinds of substantial sense organs (*dravyendriya*): the manifesting (*nirvṛtti*) and the auxiliary (*upakaraṇa*). Manifestation (*nirvṛtti*) is the production of the physical substance, such as the eyelids, the black pupil (*kṛṣṇasāra*), and so forth. That which assists the manifested organ is called the auxiliary (*upakaraṇa*); these include the regions in the middle of the eye shaped like a lentil (*masūraka*), as well as light, collyrium, and other such aids.
Both of these are seen as the substance (*dravya*) of knowledge;

its explanation is as follows: "The material sense-organ (*dravyendriya*) is corporeal (*mūrta*), the substance of incorporeal (*amūrta*) knowledge, just like the body-self. The explanation of this is: because of the instrument consisting of the body and so forth, there arises for the self in another existence the *nāmakarma* (name-karma) pertaining to the body, limbs, and minor limbs, which is the effect of the threefold yoga of body and so forth. Because of that [karma] as an instrument, the body and so forth become the substance—that is, the cause—for the self in another existence, that is, in a future birth.

And [the relation] of the jar to the space within the jar is such that the jar, being corporeal, possesses the nature of a receptacle for the space which is inferred through its own occupation; for this reason,
the reading "because of its own nature" (*svarūpatvāt*) found here appears to be the correct one.
The substance of knowledge is the material sense organ (dravyendriya), while the eyes and so forth are the auxiliary causes (upakaraṇas).
And what are the auxiliary factors?
The reading contained within this [passage] does not exist in the middle of manuscript Ya; however, it has been included here:

"That object which is a substance (*dravya*) is independent, yet it is manifested in various ways through its specific qualities (*viśeṣa*); whereas knowledge and the self (*ātman*) are themselves nothing but specific qualities."

In that regard, if sensory-cognition (*mati*), scriptural-cognition (*śruta*), clairvoyance (*avadhi*), and mind-reading-cognition (*manaḥparyāya*) were [the forms of] knowledge possessed of sense organs, then because they are produced by the senses and are therefore not true knowledge, *kevala* (perfect) cognition alone would be the only knowledge.

Furthermore, since the self is an independent agent only when it is bodiless, action performed by a perfected one (*siddha*) possessing *kevala*—who is bodiless—would have to be sought; there would be no action performed even by one who possesses hands and other limbs and is subject to passion, for such a one is held to be in the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsārin*).
because of their difference from the self;

likewise, since space and the jar consist respectively of non-obstruction and obstruction, how could there be "jar-space" or "space-jar"? Thus, how can there be such a nature of mutual interpenetration?
However, because of the conformity to another form, through the relinquishing of the self-nature of both the conscious and the unconscious, there occurs the universal becoming of the substance.
To this it is said: "Then this [consequence] follows," and so on, up to "it becomes a particular.

Whether the meaning be the substance, the universal, or the particular—whether it be the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) or the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*)—let it be "becoming" or "existence" (*bhāva*); let it be whatever it may be. In every respect, that which is independent is manifested in such and such a way by a specific cognition; whether it be a substance, a sense organ, or the like, all of these are entirely knowledge, and the Self is the particular; it is that [Self] which brings [the object] into being.
Although for you the universal (*sāmānya*) is an existent (*bhāva*), it is nonetheless subordinate, while the particular (*viśeṣa*) is primary; this is what has been stated.

In that regard, the undesirable consequence brought against the opponent beginning with "if" (*yadi*)—up to the point where "there would be only one cognition"—is already explained by the relationship of cause and effect (*hetu-hetumadbhāva*). [Specifically:

the cognitions consisting of sensory perception (*mati*), scripture (*śruta*), clairvoyance (*avadhi*), and mental perception (*manaḥparyāya*), along with their associated sense organs, would be non-cognitions (*ajñāna*) because they are produced by the senses; thus, only isolated cognition (*kevalajñāna*) would be the single true cognition.
Or is it so?
Is it [present] in its entirety, like the material sense organ (*dravyendriya*) and so forth? Furthermore: "the self of the self," and so on.
The self alone is independent because it is conscious, not the body; and that which is independent is the agent.

Consequently, an action performed by one who is bodiless, pure, and a perfected liberated soul (siddhakevalin) would have to be sought after [as its fruit], yet that is extremely difficult to find and undesirable as it would entail the consequence of liberation while still in saṃsāra.

Nor can an action performed by one possessing hands and so forth and characterized by passion be accepted even if it is desired, since that very person is held to be a transmigrating being (saṃsārin). Thus, as before, the establishment [of the relationship] through the logic of cause and effect proceeds until the conclusion that [action] is distinct from the self.
Thus, the first two examples cited by the opponent are shown to be inconclusive;

the third is likewise so, because of the nature of space and the jar as respectively non-obstructive and obstructive. For if space, being non-obstructive in nature, were to become a jar which is obstructive in nature, or if the jar, being obstructive in nature, were to become space which is non-obstructive in nature, then it would follow that "space-in-the-jar" (ghaṭākāśa) could exist; however, that is not the case according to your own position.

Space alone is formless (*amūrta*), whereas a jar, being its opposite, is indeed formed (*mūrta*). How, then, can the "space within a jar" (*ghaṭākāśa*) serve as an example? For space cannot attain the nature of the jar, nor can the jar attain the nature of space; or rather, how can "the jar-space" or something with contrary qualities serve as an example? [The answer is: because it is not of the nature of being obstructed, space consists of both obstruction and non-obstruction. Here, "obstruction" (*āvṛti*) means covering (*āvaraṇa*), and "non-obstruction" (*anāvṛti*) means the absence of covering (*anāvaraṇa*). This is the meaning.
By way of [the word] *vṛttyā*,
it should be understood that the same applies hereafter;
[is it] because of not attaining the nature of space?

Having stated the impossibility of using "space within a jar" as an illustration, he now states the impossibility of using "the jar of space" as an illustration: "Space is not the self," and so forth; "in this manner," and so forth. Since the substance (*dravya*) is understood to exist in this way, the example functions as a proof of the opposite; how then can there be that mutual interpenetration (*anyonyānugama-rūpatā*) which you have asserted? For, according to the logic I have stated and according to your own doctrine, the substance, as the cause, never abandons its essential nature (*ātma-rūpa*). Thus has the undesirable consequence for the opponent been established.

For this very reason, in order to demonstrate that his own specific view holds the primary position while the general theory of existence is subordinate, he says: "But because of the conformity with another form," and so forth.
The word "but" (tu) distinguishes his own established position from the views of others.

Because both the conscious and the unconscious abandon their own essential nature (*ātmabhāva*), as you have stated, the general existence of a substance becomes merely subordinate; thus, it exists only as a subordinate unity and not as a particular, because it cannot be sublated by anything through the absence of a distinct object or through its own becoming and non-becoming.

And just as a particular is independent of the universal, so too, in its own object—such as the occurrence of a single tree—it must exist with that same identical gender, number, and so forth, even while being independent of other particulars such as the dual number.

If [you ask]: "If it is one *nakṣatra*, how can there be two *punarvasū*? Or if there are two *punarvasū*, how can there be one *nakṣatra*? For oneness and duality are contradictory. All such [objections] are to be refuted according to their respective objects, just as in the case of a jar and a cloth.

If it is argued that its status as such is due solely to cognition (*pratīti*), we say no; for the use of singular and other number-terminations is well-established based on the very cognition of each individual part in relation to unity and so forth.

However, this [position of yours] contradicts experience because there is a discrepancy between the expression, the object expressed, and the cognition—like the case of a lifelong celibate being a father.
Therefore, since there is no other entity [than existence], and because existence itself exists, the lack of distinction from anything else is not sublated.

As you previously stated—that a tree becomes only one, having subordinated the commonality of "tree-ness" and not even two or more, because a name is subject to its particularities—and so forth; therefore, this undesirable consequence follows: the non-existence of particulars.
Due to that non-existence, the non-existence of the universal results, which contradicts both what is perceived and what is accepted.
The reading "the non-existence of the substantial cause is always the non-alteration of its own nature" might also exist here,
because of what you have stated.
In this regard, a certain reading appears to be fragmentary:

"The subordinate element (*upasarjana*) is indeed one and the same; it is not a particular (*viśeṣa*), because it cannot be sublated by anything through either the absence of another meaning or its own existence and non-existence. And just as a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*) exists independently of the universal (*sāmānya*), so too, in the case of the existence of a single tree and so forth within its own domain, it must exist with an identical gender and number, precisely without depending on other particulars such as the dual number."

If [the constellation] Punarvasu is one, how can there be two [stars]? Or, if there are two Punarvasus, how can it be a single constellation? This is because of the contradiction between oneness and twoness, and so forth. All such [objections] must be refuted according to their respective domains, just as in the case of a jar or a cloth—the comparison is at p. 568, l. 22.

If it is argued that the purpose [of the word] is simply to conform to cognition (*pratīti*), we say no; for the use of singular and other number-terminations is well-established precisely through the cognition of each individual part (*pratyavayava*) with reference to oneness and so forth.

However, this [position] contradicts common experience because there is a discrepancy between the designation, the designated object, and the cognition [of them], like the case of a celibate student being a father.
This is comparable [to other arguments], because it cannot be sublated by anything through the presence or absence of another object—*Nayacakravṛtti*, p.
It becomes exactly as it was made;
furthermore, as for how it is distinguished, and so forth.

And just as a particular [quality] exists independently of its general opposite, being indeed distinct from it, so too in its own domain—such as in the case of the existence of a single tree and so forth—it ought to exist with that very same gender, number, and so on, independent of other particulars such as the dual number;

yet according to your view, that particular does not exist in that way, because we observe differences in gender, number, and so on in words standing in apposition to "nakṣatra" (star), "punarvasu," and the like.

He explains that: "If one," and so forth—the two means of proof [presented] result in the establishment of the undesired, because of the contradiction between oneness and duality; thus, everything such as "because of the contradiction between one and two" should be refuted according to its respective domain. By way of this extension (*atideśa*), the means of proof for establishing the undesired should also be seen to apply to gender, time, and so on—for example: "If Punarvasū are two males, they are not a neuter constellation, because they are male, like a tree;
or, if it is a constellation, it is not two males, because it is neuter, like a water-jar (*kuṇḍa*)," and so forth.

Likewise, [the argument] beginning with "Tārā is a woman" and so forth should be applied; like a jar or a cloth, there is no mutual transformation of essential nature among particulars, because of the absence of a universal (sāmānya),
and this is observed in the case of constellations such as Nakṣatra and Punarvasu.
Therefore, it is incorrect to say that "the meaning of a word is the particular alone, independent of the universal, because that is what is intended to be expressed.

Accordingly, one should apply the following reasoning: if Tārā is a female and not a lunar mansion (nakṣatra), because she is a female like Gaṅgā; or else, if she is a lunar mansion and not a female, because she is neuter like a water-jar (kuṇḍa).

"If it be thought that the objectivity [of the term] is simply for the sake of cognition— [that is,] because it is commonly understood in the world, it is well known among people, down to the cowherds, that the meaning of *punarvasu* is indeed the meaning of the asterism (*nakṣatra*), and the meaning of the asterism is indeed the meaning of *punarvasu*" (see page 568, line 3).

"Therefore, because the universal is itself a particular, there is no fault; otherwise, it would be entirely purposeless. To this it is replied: "No, for we too speak solely on the basis of worldly convention, such as: 'The dual and singular endings are used for two and one [respectively], and the plural ending is used for many' (Pāṇini 1.4.22)."

Thus, since it is well known that words such as the singular are employed with respect to things intended to be expressed—whether part by part—with reference to their oneness and so forth, if a word ending in the singular suffix is to denote its object, it must be denoted by a single [entity], not by two or more;
and if it consists of two or more, it cannot be expressed by a word in the singular, as has already been stated.

However, this grammatical analysis—which consists of the division of words into bases (*prakṛti*), suffixes (*pratyaya*), and so forth—is indeed distinct from both the denotation (*abhidheya*) and the cognition (*pratyaya*). For, when the meanings of the bases and so forth are not established, the defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) themselves cannot be established; how then could there be an understanding of the reality of that which is to be defined (*lakṣya*) produced by such [analysis], or a systematic arrangement of words? This is because its object is a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) that has not been clearly discerned, just like the confused cognition of a post or a person whose specific characteristics have not been clearly discerned.

Having understood that "the tree stands," one might then think, "Come back; I think you will go by chariot. Even from such a contrary [statement], there is likewise a failure to characterize the *prakṛti* and so forth through such understanding, and the non-understanding of what is actually understood because of acting according to whim. This contradicts common experience (*pratīti*) despite the correspondence [of the words]. Furthermore, the word *punarvasū* has two meanings because it ends in the dual number; thus, the cognition [of its meaning] contradicts the cognition whose object is the constellation [it denotes], and this [contradiction] is [pointed out] by him.

What is it like? It is like the state of being a father of one who is a celibate student from childhood (*kumārabrahmacārin*). If he is a celibate student from childhood, how can he be a father? Or if he is a father, how can he be a celibate student from childhood? It is just so in this case.

For grammar (*lakṣaṇa*) is indeed the formal explanation of words through the division of base (*prakṛti*), suffix (*pratyaya*), and so forth; yet, since the grammatical rules (*lakṣaṇa*) are not established when the meanings of the base and so forth are not fixed, how can there be an understanding of the reality of the object to be defined (*lakṣya*) produced by them, or a fixed status of the word? This is because their objects are particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) that have not been clearly distinguished, just like the confused perception of a post or a person whose specific characteristics have not been clearly distinguished.

Having understood that "that tree stands," one might then think, "Come, I believe you will go by chariot. Even from such a contrary [thought], through a similar understanding, there occurs the non-characterization of what is characterized by its nature (*prakṛti*) and so forth, and the non-understanding of understanding itself, because of proceeding by chance (*yadṛcchā*). See page 571, line 17. He elucidates this with the words: "For that which is called a characteristic... and so on.
The definition of words consists in the grammatical analysis of their stems, suffixes, and so forth, on the grounds that "it is by this that I establish the words which are to be defined.
However, there is no fixed determination of those divisions into stems and suffixes, because the meanings of the stems and so forth are not as they are represented.

And when there is such a lack of determination regarding the meanings of stems and suffixes pertaining to words, there follows a consequent lack of determination regarding the definitions that depend upon them.

Since the definition [of the object] is not established, how can there be an understanding of the reality of the "definable" produced by that [definition], nor an understanding of the reality of the word, nor the establishment of the word?
Why do these two not exist? Because their objects consist of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) that have not been distinguished and cultivated.

The illustration begins with "unseparatedly conceived," and so forth. Just as when a post and a person, though actually distinct, are conceived as non-distinct by virtue of their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), the cognition and determination regarding the post as being a person are both erroneous cognition and determination; why? Because their object is one whose specific characteristic has been conceived as non-distinct. Likewise are the cognition and determination regarding words and their referents.

Furthermore, due to the non-comprehension of the indicated object (*lakṣya*) and the lack of systematic determination, there is a discrepancy between the two cognitions regarding the subject matter of the signifier and the signified; thus, just like the cognition that "the father is a celibate student" (*kumārabrahmacārī pitā*), there is a contradiction regarding the singularity, duality, and so forth of the *nakṣatra* Punarvasu and others—this is the connection [of the argument].

From what source, then, could there be comprehension of that which is produced by it, namely the indicated object, the comprehension of the true nature of the word, and the systematic determination of the word? [The same applies to] from what source could there be comprehension of that which is produced by it, namely the indicated object, the comprehension of the true nature of the word, and the systematic determination of the word? (Bhāṣya and Yāska).
"How could there be the realization of the reality characterized by that which is produced [by words], and the systematic application of words?"— thus might the reading here also be;
"without case-endings" (avibhaktau) is found in the Prajñāpāramitā, while "distinct" (viviktau) is not present in the middle of the Santānāntara-siddhi.

Thus, first, the contradiction regarding the understanding of the base and the suffix in relation to the object "number" has been stated. Hereafter, that which pertains to the object "person" (puruṣa) is discussed, as follows: "That tree stood," and so on, up to the state of non-understanding.

In the case of "saḥ" (he), when the word *āste* (he sits) is used as a subordinate supplement (*śeṣopapada*), one first understands it for oneself through the correspondence between the base and the suffix regarding the person (*puruṣa*) of the action; yet, by subsequently using the contrary understanding "ehi manye" (come, I think [you go]), the characteristics of the base and so forth are rendered non-characteristics, and the actual understanding is rendered non-understanding. It is for this reason—namely, by way of the instability resulting from the failure to understand the true nature of the object of definition—that [the expression is invalid]. Why? Because it proceeds by chance (*yadṛcchāpravṛttitvāt*), and because there is a contradiction with the action under discussion in the phrase "ehi manye," it is incorrect, non-expressive, and ungrammatical (*asādhu*), just like the usage "tvaṃ yāmi, ahaṃ yāsi" (you go, I go).
Alternatively, because it would contradict the intended suffix, like the usage "Devadatta becomes" (*devadatto bhūyate*);
and because it functions with a grammatical non-co-referentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) that contradicts the accepted human purpose, like the usage "you cook" (*tvaṃ pacati*).

In this case, the stem (*prakṛti*) should be employed as subordinate to the suffix (*pratyaya*), since at the time of actual usage, a mere stem or a mere suffix is impossible, and such [isolated] forms are meaningless, like the cry of a crow.

However, for the sake of instruction, the connection is as follows: "Because the suffix depends on the sequence of the preceding and following [elements], like a father toward a religious student (*brahmacārin*).

Here is the formal argument (*prayoga*): starting from *ehi manye* and so forth, up to the point where it is "untrue, non-expressive, and ungrammatical"—this constitutes the three propositions (*pratijñā*).

The verb root *man* (to think) is the action under discussion; its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is contradicted by the suffix known as the first person (*uttamapuruṣa*), because of the contradiction with the second person (*madhyamapuruṣa*) employed by the word *ehi*. This is the meaning of the reason (*hetu*).

The phrase "just as in the usage 'you go' (*tvaṃ yāsi*) and 'I go' (*ahaṃ yāmi*)" is an illustration of that meaning; it is like an incorrect [expression] that fails to convey the intended sense due to contradiction, because the specific meanings of the middle and first persons (*madhyama* and *uttama*) differ according to the sense of the verb root (*yā-*) while following the sense of the suffix (*hetu*). This is the second reason, namely, "due to the contradiction with the expected suffix," with the example being "just as in *devadatto bhūyate*" ("Devadatta becomes").

The term *devadatta*, specified in the nominative case as the agent (*kartṛ*), cannot enter into grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *bhūyate*, which denotes the mere meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛtyarthamātra*) and functions as an abstract noun (*bhāvasādhana*); however, it could do so with *bhavati*. Likewise, one must supply [the following examples] to demonstrate the lack of correctness (*asādhutva*) due to the non-correspondence of the intended sense: the second person introduced by the word *ehi* ("come") being construed with *manye* ("I think"), which ends in the first person; this serves to clarify the discrepancy between the intended suffixes. He states the reason for this: "because it functions with a difference of grammatical coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) regarding the accepted person-meaning.
An illustration of that is: *tvaṃ pacati* ("you cook").

In the case of "tvam" (you) being used as a proximate word (*upapada*) with the verb "pacati" (he cooks), the use of the third person (*prathamapuruṣa*), which is the domain of the remaining proximate words, is inconsistent; likewise, in the example "ehi manye yāsyasi" (Come, I think you will go),
see page 571,
line 18, where it is stated that the first person is used when there is a remainder (*śeṣe*).

The term "remainder" (*śeṣa*) refers to that which is other than the objects of the middle and highest persons; where the pronouns *yuṣmad* and *asmad* do not occur as coreferential (*samānādhikaraṇa*) words, there the first person occurs in the remainder— e.g., *pacati*.
"pacataḥ pacanti"— Pāṇini, Kāśikā.

When a remainder [i.e., a word other than the one being defined] is present as a subordinate element (*upapada*), the nominative case is prescribed; a word uttered in proximity is a *upapada*— Pāṇini-Mahābhāṣya 2.3.46.
And when *prahāsa* (mockery) is intended, and when a word meaning "to think" (*manya*) is the upapada, the suffix *uttama* (the first person) is used and the verb is treated as singular.

In the sense of "jesting" (*prahāsa*), when jesting is implied, the second person (*madhyamapuruṣa*) is used for the verbal root and the first person (*uttama*) for the verb *man* (to think), and that [first person] becomes singular. For example:
*ehi manye odanaṃ bhokṣyase* ("Come, I think you will eat rice"), [the meaning being] "you certainly will not eat it; it has already been eaten by the guests."

"Come, I think you will go by chariot; indeed, you will not go. When [the speaker] has reached the middle or the highest [degree of certainty], the middle or the highest [form of the verb] is prescribed. Is this for the sake of ridicule? "Come, you think you will eat rice."
"You think well, you think rightly"—according to the *Pāṇinīya-kāśikā*, the phrase "ehi manye" means:
"Come, I think you will go by chariot; you think, 'I shall go by chariot. This is the meaning.
Because it proceeds from mere whim?
See page 571, line 18:

since there is a discrepancy with the action under discussion in the phrase "ehi manye" (come, I think), it is like the usage "you go" and "I go"; thus, it is untrue, non-communicative, and ungrammatical.
Alternatively, because it would contradict the intended suffix, like the usage "Devadatta becomes" (*devadatto bhūyate*);
and because it would function with a grammatical non-co-referentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) regarding the accepted human goal, like the usage "you cook" (*tvaṃ pacati*).

In this case, the stem (*prakṛti*) should be employed as subordinate to the suffix (*pratyaya*), because at the time of actual usage, the stem and suffix cannot exist in isolation, and thus [a solitary stem] would be meaningless, like the cry of a crow.
For the sake of instruction, let it be seen through variegated patterns and dots; see page 571, line 18.
[Is it] by means of silver?

The intention appears to be that there is a distinction between the middle and the highest [persons] regarding the two meanings of the verbal root— that which is beneficial and that which is harmful— among those two meanings, namely, the beneficial and the harmful.
What is the proof for the non-identity of two objects that have different meanings? [The proof is] the fitness of being a signifier and the fitness of being a signified,
which are common to both.
See page 571, line 13.

Here, whether the meaning to be conveyed extends to the limit of a sentence (*vākya*) or to the limit of a word (*pada*), a sentence or a word conveys its sense only in dependence upon the meaning of a correlative term (*pratiyogi-śabda*), because they are never used in isolation.
First, regarding the limit of a word, this is the rule: "A stem (*prakṛti*) must be employed followed by a suffix (*pratyaya*)," and "A suffix must follow after a stem" (Pāṇini-Mahābhāṣya 3.1.92).

Since this has been established, at the time of formal application (*prayoga*), it is impossible for the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*) to exist in isolation; and this impossibility is due to their being devoid of meaning (*anarthaka*) when so isolated. For instance, like the "crow-sitting" (a meaningless phrase), just as there is no denotable referent for expressions such as "crow-sitting," likewise there is no referent for *bhū*, *laṭ*, *tip*, *śap*, and so forth, when they are isolated from one another, even in the case of the present tense marker *laṭ*.
ti, tas, jhi; si, thas, tha; mi, vas, mas; ta, ātām, jha; thās, āthām, dhvam; iṭ, vahi, mahiṅ.
The affix *śap* occurs after a verbal root when it ends in a consonant and forms the agentive (*kartṛ*) case.
1.68 – pāda commentary.
See footnote 1 on page 58.

Why, then, is it stated that *bhū* in the sense of "existence" (*sattā*) [is used] with the agentive suffixes (*kartari kṛt*), according to Pāṇini 3.4.69, and with the personal endings (*laḥ*) in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*), according to Pāṇini 3.4.69?

If it is argued that [the separate mention] of "67" and "69" and so forth is for the sake of the meanings of the base (prakṛti) and the suffix (pratyaya), it is replied: however, for the purpose of instruction, the base and suffix meanings are shown by dividing them, just as one might separately study the arrangement of various decorative patterns and dots, thinking, "I shall cause the students to grasp [the material]."

Just as a master painter, intending to have a single decorative panel (*bhakti*) made of wood or similar material, first has his pupils apply the placement of dots (*bindu-vinyāsa*) and afterwards joins them together, so that it becomes a beautiful and pleasing-to-the-eye composition—consisting of the forms of flowers, creepers, houses, men, women, elephants, and so forth—and fit for practical use; even so, the meanings of bases (*prakṛti*) and suffixes (*pratyaya*) are demonstrated separately, because they serve as a means for understanding the meaning of the inseparably established whole (*apṛthaksiddha-samudāya*). See page 126, line 11, note 7:
*°pratyayārtho pra*.
The statement "one should show" (darśayet) is a separate recitation, just like the placement [of phonemes].
And having done so, it was said: "The base and the suffix express the meaning of the suffix together" (Pāṇini-Mahābhāṣya 3.1.67).
And for this very reason, the suffix should be employed after the base, and the base before the suffix; Pāṇini’s Mahābhāṣya 3.1.2.

And for this very reason, because the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*) is not lost, the use of the first-person singular suffix in the word "manye"— which abandons the topical grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)— constitutes a statement that does not correspond to the actual state of affairs (*ayathārthābhidhāna*).
Even if the person who is the object of cognition is unreal, this same process of contemplation (bhāvanā) applies;
thus, there is unreality regarding these three objects,
and this constitutes unreality in terms of substance (dravyataḥ).
If it is argued that this [statement] is merely a joke and not true, then there would be a great deal of non-characterization of the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) by the characterized (*lakṣya*).
And he provides an indicator (*jñāpaka*) showing that it was stated precisely with this understanding:
"The base and the suffix express the meaning of the suffix together. Thus, the meaning of the suffix is intended as primary, while the meaning of the base is intended as subordinate.

"And for this very reason," as it is stated in the Bhāṣya: "The suffix should be employed subsequent to the base, and the base should be [employed] subsequent to the suffix. Here, "pratyayaparā" means that base for which the suffix is the subsequent [element], i.e., the particularity (*viśeṣa*) and the primary factor (*pradhāna*). Thus, the word *para* is explained as having the sense of "primary" (*pradhāna*). And so it is in the Bhāṣya: "the base... (*prakṛtiya*)...

And thus, by this reasoning, the base (*prakṛti*) does not deviate from the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*), because it is directed toward that [meaning]; and for this very reason, because it does not deviate from the meaning of the suffix, he concludes after having reasoned through the example of the root *man* and so forth, up to the point of "denoting what is not as it is" (*ayathārthābhidhāna*).

For, by abandoning the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) introduced by the use of the word *ehi*, there is a lack of correspondence to the meaning of the first-person singular suffix (*uttamaikavacanapratyaya*) which shares the same coreferential basis as "I," because its operation involves a lack of coreferentiality with the person-meaning (*puruṣārtha*), just like the usage "you cook" (*tvaṃ pacasi*). Thus, it has been well said.
Thus, first of all, the non-correspondence to reality of the *prakṛti* has been stated by way of the non-correspondence to reality of the *pratyaya*, because it is inseparable [from it];
see page 570, line 3.
Even regarding the non-correspondence to reality of both the *pratyaya* and the *puruṣa*, this same single argument applies.

Because the suffix is inseparable from its inherent nature by virtue of being a suffix, even from a contrary expression such as "Come, I think you will go by chariot," there occurs—just as in the previous case—the characterization of what is characterized by a suffix and so forth as uncharacterized, and the non-comprehension of what is comprehension, because it proceeds by chance; this continues until this limit, where [the suffix] is applied according to the person who possesses the corresponding cognition.

This is the conclusion: that there is a lack of correspondence with reality (*ayathārthatva*) regarding these three objects, because the word *iti* serves as a conclusion. It should also be understood through the eye of the intellect that by this cultivation (*bhāvanā*), that which is non-conducive to knowledge (*agamaka*) becomes indeed "unwholesome" (*asādhu*). And this is a lack of correspondence with reality in terms of substance (*dravyataḥ*), because this lack of correspondence arises from the reversal of the substances of "I" and "you," expressed as "I am not you."

And just as this is the case, so too is the distinct linguistic usage regarding specific qualifiers such as "pot" or "cloth" refuted, just like the employment of words with reversed genders and so forth caused by the suffixes *ku* and *tuka* in expressions such as "you cook" (*tvaṃ pacasi*).
The reading "this very same [is] the productive operation" (*bhāvanā*) may also be possible here;
see page 569, line 5.
Is it by means of the formless? This is the question. The answer is:
No.
If it is argued that this is merely a joke and therefore unreal, since it was spoken by you as something contrary to reality;

It might be thought: "Come, I think you will go by chariot; indeed, you will not go, for your father has gone"—this [statement] is certainly untrue because it is the object of a joke. For this very reason, the grammatical rule was stated: "And in the case of a joke, when *manye* is the accompanying word, the verb *man* takes the first person and is treated as singular" (Pāṇini 1.4.106).

106. Thus, examples for the dual and plural cases have also been cited: *yāsyathaḥ* (you two will go), *yāsyatha* (you all will go); *ehi manye odanaṃ bhokṣyase* (come, I think you will eat rice); *bhuktaḥ so'tithibhiḥ* (it has been eaten by the guests);
*etam eta vā manye odanaṃ bhokṣyethe bhokṣyadhve* (come here, I think you two [or you all] will eat this rice).
— Pāṇini Siddhāntakaumudī 7.3.101
The designation of names is a non-apprehension of apprehension because it is unreal, since it functions as the opposite of the object to be communicated, like a humorous utterance;
yet there is no notion of unreality regarding them,
just as there is no notion of unreality regarding the action whose locus is the mountain.
The locus is the substratum (adhikaraṇa),
because otherwise there would be no substratum for anything else.
"Past" and "future" are contradictory meanings;
likewise, the asterism Śatabhiṣaj, the village Godau, the two stars Punarvasū, and the mango grove—regarding these, it is said:
"In that case, there would be many [such instances]," and so forth.
In that case, there are many rules [such as] Pāṇini 3.4.1, *dhātusambandhe pratyayāḥ* ("suffixes [are introduced] when there is a connection with a verbal root"),
and Pāṇini 3.1.85, *vyatyayo bahulam* ("there is extensive transposition [of suffixes]").

1.85 Thus, the non-characterization of such things [as the subject], and the non-characterization of their objects—such as "his son will be a performer of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice"—and the non-apprehension of apprehension, all result from the unreality of everything. That unreality arises because it functions by way of a reversal of the object to be communicated, like a humorous statement; this has already been explained.

Furthermore, there is no notion of unreality regarding those characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and the characterized (*lakṣya*); moreover, unlike the case of an action having a mountain as its locus— wherein one says "he dwells on this mountain" (*parvate vasati*) to express the sense of a locus— the verbal expressions "he dwells upon the mountain" (*parvatam adhivasati*) or "he occupies the mountain" (*adhyāste*) would be inappropriate if [the mountain] were not treated as the object (*karman*).

Here is the formal argument (*prayoga*): "He dwells upon the mountain" and so forth is false, because it functions with a locus distinct from its own grammatical factors (*kāraka*), just like the case of "Devadatta becomes.
The meaning of this *bhāvanā*—from "the substratum is the locus (*adhikaraṇa*)" up to "or because another thing lacks a substratum"—is already explained in the text;
and this has been stated as the lack of correspondence to reality regarding the object that is the field (*kṣetra*).

Likewise, there is a proof that is incorrect regarding time and its objects—such as [the statements] "it was" and "it will be"—because they possess contradictory meanings. Therefore, the answer begins with "Śatabhiṣaj," and so forth. In such cases as "Are both gods and humans two *rāśis*? and so on, there is a lack of correspondence to reality (*ayathārthatā*) in terms of existence (*bhāva*), because the discourse contradicts the objects of substance (*dravya*), space (*kṣetra*), time (*kāla*), and existence (*bhāva*), and because it serves to negate the meaning of what was previously stated, like the prattle of a madman. [Objection: But since Puṣya is a specific deity, the two objects—the constellation and the star—are general in nature, just as the clay is a general object relative to a specific jar.

For it has been said: "He who, being skilled in the distinctions [of words], employs them correctly in accordance with established usage, attains infinite victory in the hereafter; but the knower of the application of speech incurs fault through corrupt words" (Pāṇini-Mahābhāṣya 1.1.1).

1.1 Therefore, since the application of words is preceded by the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*), words—by virtue of their adoption of specific objects—may be either indicative or non-indicative, as in the case of *gāvī*, *goṇī*, *gotā*, *gopālikā*, and so forth.

If this is so, then by what intention is the plural number used in the word *āpaḥ* even when referring to a single drop? Furthermore, in cases such as "the state of being one" (*ekabhāva*) or "as far as the meaning is conveyed" (*yāvad-artha-pratipādana*), there is a lack of correspondence with reality (*ayathārthatā*) in terms of the actual state of things (*bhāvataḥ*). Thus, the purpose [of the discussion] is exhausted.
And thus, there is neither denotative capacity in the word nor denotedness in the object, because they do not correspond to reality, just like the previously mentioned words and objects;
for it has been stated in the *Tattvārthabhāṣya* (1.35) that "a word is a designation that corresponds to reality."

Having summarized all of that, he states the proof: "Because it functions in contradiction with the objects of substance, place, time, and state" is the reason (*hetu*) whose meaning has already been explained;

"because it serves to refute one's own stated position" is the reason for summarizing the established point; or, "like the prattle of a madman" is the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) intended to demonstrate a separate lack of correspondence with reality (*ayāthārthya*).
And since this proof has its meaning already established through the preceding elaboration, it is not further explained here;
[the rule] "affixes [occur] when there is a connection between verbal roots" (Pāṇini 3.4.1).
Wherever suffixes have been prescribed in connection with the meanings of verbal roots (dhātvartha), they may also occur at times other than those specified.
Because the action expressed by a verbal suffix (tiṅanta) is primary, the suffixes expressing subordinate actions must conform to it; thus, in the example "vasan dadarśa" ("while dwelling, he saw"),
the present tense (*laṭ*) is used to denote the past.
The meaning is that the act of seeing has as its agent one who has performed the Soma sacrifice;
"the son of one who has sacrificed with Soma shall be" means the coming into existence having as its agent that son who is about to sacrifice with Soma.
— See the Siddhāntakaumudī, page 154, line 26, and the Āśrityamati-bhāṣya.
The object of the roots √adhi-śī, √adhi-sthā, and √ās is called *amṛtyamati* (the locus of rest) according to Pāṇini 1.4.46.
4.46 When the designation of locus (adhikaraṇa-saṃjñā) would otherwise apply by the preceding rule, the designation of object (karma-saṃjñā) is prescribed.
The substratum (*ādhāra*) of those verbs preceded by *adhi*—namely *śīṅ*, *sthā*, and *ās*—is designated as the object (*karman*). For example:
*grāmamadhiśete* (he lies down upon the village), *grāmamadhitiṣṭhati* (he stands upon the village).
The verb *vas* (to dwell) takes the locative case when preceded by the prefixes *upa*, *anu*, *adhi*, and *āṅ*. For example: *parvatam adhyāste* (he dwells upon the mountain).
When the verb *vasati* (to dwell) is preceded by *upa*, *anu*, *adhi*, or *ā*, that which serves as its locus (*ādhāra*) is designated as the *karman* (object) kāraka; for example:
*grāmam upavasati* (he dwells near the village), *senā parvatam upavasati* (the army dwells upon the mountain).
He dwells near the village;
he dwells in the village;
he inhabits the village.
—Pāṇini’s Kāśikā:
The locus is the *adhikaraṇa* (locus).
4.45 That in which actions are supported is called the locus (ādhāra).

The *kāraka* which serves as the substratum (*ādhāra*) for the action of supporting with respect to the agent and the object—which are themselves the substrata of the primary action—is designated as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). For example: "He sits on a mat" (*kaṭe āste*), "He lies on a mat" (*kaṭe śete*).
"He cooks in a pot" (sthālyāṃ pacati). According to the Pāṇinian Kāśikā, a word (śabda) is so called because it curses (śapati), signifies (artha), calls (āhvayati), or makes known (pratyāyayati).

A word that, when uttered by a person who has established its conventional connection, produces a cognition regarding its own denotatum is called a "word" (śabda); and this [definition] is intended to exclude any deviation regarding gender, number, grammatical means (sādhana), and so forth.
Gender consists of femininity, masculinity, and neuter;
number consists of singularity, duality, and plurality.

Since it is not logical for there to be deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of "ourself" (*asmadādi*) and similar [words] used as proof (*sādhana*), this method is intended to exclude such deviation;
for example, regarding the deviation of gender (*liṅga-vyabhicāra*), there is the designation of the masculine gender for a feminine word, as in "the star Svāti" (*tārakā svātiriti*).
The designation of the feminine for a masculine gender is seen in "knowledge" (*vidyā*) for [the word] *avagama*;
the designation of the neuter for the feminine is seen in "lute" (*vīṇā*) for *ātodya*;
and the designation of the feminine for the neuter is seen in "weapon" (*śakti*) for *āyudha*.
The designation of a neuter term for a masculine gender, as in *paṭo* (cloth) or *vastram* (garment);
the designation of a masculine term for a neuter gender, as in *dravyaṃ* (substance) or *paraśuḥ* (axe);
and the deviation regarding number—such as using the dual for the singular, as in *nakṣatraṃ* (constellation) or *punarvasū* (the Punarvasu stars).
In the case of unity there is plurality, as in "the constellation Śatabhiṣaj"; in the case of duality there is unity, as in "the village Godau";
and in the case of duality there is plurality, as in "the two Punarvasus are five stars."
The deviation of the means of proof (*sādhanavyabhicāra*) consists in [the following cases]: unity within plurality, as in "mangoes" or "a forest";
duality within plurality, as in "gods and humans" or "two heaps";
and [the use of the optative] in the sense of prohibition, as in "Come, I think you will go by chariot," "You certainly will not go," or "Your father has already gone."
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), the deviation regarding time and so forth is included.
The deviation regarding time is as follows: "The son of this All-Seeing One was born," and "the future task had already been accomplished.
The deviation regarding verbal suffixes (upagraha) is as follows: [the same action is expressed by] *saṃtiṣṭhate*, *pratiṣṭhate*, *viramati*, and *uparamati*.
Why are such fallacies as these improper? Because there is no connection between one thing and another thing;
for if there were, then let a jar become a cloth, or a cloth a palace! Thus [the argument fails].

Therefore, it is logical that the designation [of the categories] should be according to their characteristics, according to their number, and according to their means of proof, and so forth; thus it is stated in the *Tattvārtharājavārtika* (1.33).

In such statements as "both gods and humans are two groups," there is a lack of correspondence with reality (*ayathārthatā*) in terms of its underlying state (*bhāva*), because it functions in contradiction to the objects of substance, place, time, and state, and because it serves to negate the meaning of what was previously stated, like the prattle of a madman. Now, [the opponent might argue]: since Puṣya is a specific type of deity, the terms referring to it denote the general category of constellations and stars, just as the term "clay" denotes the general category when referring to a specific jar.
For it has been said:

"But he who employs words skillfully according to their specific distinctions, as they are used in correct linguistic practice, attains infinite victory in the hereafter; yet one who knows the application of speech is defiled by corrupt words. (Pāṇini-Mahābhāṣya 1.1.1) Therefore, because the employment of words is preceded by the intention to speak, words—such as *gāvī*, *goṇī*, *gotā*, and *gopālikā*—are both indicative and non-indicative depending on the adoption of a specific context.

If this is so, then with what intention is the plural number used in "āpaḥ" even when referring to a single drop; [is it] for the sake of expressing the non-correspondence to reality (*ayathārthatva*)? Or is it for the sake of expressing the correspondence to reality (*yathārthatva*)?
And in the Tattvārthabhāṣya, there is no [reading] "yathārthyam" (Bhāṣya); rather,
it is "yathārtham" (Yaśovijaya).

Now, the prima facie argument beginning with "nanu puṣyasya" and so forth is intended to resolve the objection by relying on the principle that words are employed for the sake of a specific intention (*vivakṣāviśeṣa*). As long as there are both indicators (*gamaka*) and non-indicators (*agamaka*), [the following applies]: *puṣya* is a male deity who is a particular; the two terms referring to him have that same referent (*tadartha*), meaning they refer to the general category of the asterism or star, just as the general term "clay" refers to a particular jar. Therefore, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is established. And regarding this, he states the proof: "For it has been said," and so forth, as stated by the author of the Bhāṣya.
As for the verse beginning with "yastu prayuṅkte":

When a specific distinction is intended to be expressed as the primary element, one who is skilled employs words that have become subordinate qualities, because the employment of words is for the sake of conveying meaning. Demonstrating this, he says: "Because the application of words is preceded by the intention to speak (*vivakṣā*). In the context of correct linguistic usage, whichever word, at the time of usage, is intended to be the specific signifier of whichever specific intended object, that very word is employed there and not another, nor elsewhere—whether in a secondary (*gauṇa*) or primary (*mukhya*) sense—since all words possess the capacity to convey their own denoted objects.

Who else attains infinite victory in the hereafter? Only he who knows the application of speech (*vāgyoga*) and understands the relationship between words and their meanings as specified above; whereas one who does not know the application of speech and is ignorant of the specific usage of words is corrupted by corrupt forms (*apaśabda*).

Therefore, because the application of words is preceded by the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*), the correctness (*sādhutā*) or incorrectness (*asādhutā*) of words is determined by their adoption of a specific object. Even for words like *gavī* and so forth, which are considered incorrect, there is correctness because they refer to a specific [intended] object; likewise, even for words like *gavyā* and so forth, which are considered correct, there is incorrectness.
He demonstrates this: "The cultivation of meaning through the derivation of words [is seen in cases such as] *gāvī*, *goṇī*, etc., when joined with the sense of 'cow'.
It is likely that the reading *hārayukte* is appropriate here.
See page 128,
line 21: *grahaṇe ya* [and] *gāvy-ādi*.
See footnote 57, lines 22–26:
"gavādīnām... [the meaning is already understood] from the word *ādi*."
Regarding this, the Teacher says: "If that is so, then... and so forth, up to "...gravel.
This reasoning also fails due to deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
Desiring to demonstrate such deviation through examples, he asks—as if not knowing—the very same thing: "With what intention regarding a specific distinction?"
If it is argued that the plural form "āpaḥ" (waters) is observed even when referring to a single drop— wherein there is no relation of genus and individual—

and likewise "dārāḥ" (wives) or "gṛhāḥ" (houses) is used for a single woman, and "sikatāḥ" (sands) for a single grain of sugar, because [these terms] always denote many constituent parts; then, for the very same reason, the plural would necessarily apply even to a single jar, just as "āpaḥ" does to a drop and so forth.

Or rather, the word *ap* (water) might take the singular number like the word *ghaṭa* (pot), provided that one desires the correctness of its usage regarding a particular instance by setting aside its nature as a single essence (*ekātmaka*). Why, then, on that very same principle, is the word *ap* not used in the singular when referring to a drop of water? Since it refers to a particular instance, like the word *go* (cow) and others, it ought to be used only in the singular, because it is apprehended as "one," just as in the case of a cloth [which is perceived as one] despite being composed of threads.

Likewise, regarding *taṭaḥ*, *taṭī*, and *taṭam*, based on what distinction is the difference in gender established, or what commonality is extended [to them]? Is it not the case that the difference in gender has as its object the distinctions of stability (*sthiti*), production (*prasava*), and contraction (*saṃstyāna*), whereas there is no such distinction of objects for *taṭaḥ*, *taṭī*, and *taṭam*, because their essential nature (*svarūpa*) is undifferentiated, like the self-nature of a jar (*ghaṭa*)? [If so,] the question remains: by what intention is the plural number employed?

And regarding a single minute particle of sand, one says "sikatāḥ" (sands); because the word *kiṃ* has the sense of censure, with what intention [could one say this]? With the intention that it is contrary to the meaning?

If it is argued that it is so because [the term] always refers to many parts—[that is,] if it be thought: "Even in a drop there are many parts such as atoms (*paramāṇu*) and dyads (*dvyaṇuka*); with reference to those, the plural form 'āpaḥ' (waters) is used."
To this it is replied: "Even in a single jar," and so forth.

For this very reason—namely, from the reason you stated, "because of residing in many parts"—it follows that even for a single jar, the plural number would apply eternally. By means of this undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭāpādana*), such as "water" in the case of drops and the like, the opponent's reason is shown to be fallacious (*vyabhicāra*).
Furthermore, from the word "water" (*ap*) alone, the singular number would also result, because—even though it is eternal—it resides in many parts, just like a jar; and this is undesirable.

If it is argued that [the plural] "wives" (*dārāḥ*) applies to a single woman, and "sands" (*sikatāḥ*) to a single grain of sand, because they always reside in many parts [of a whole], then for the same reason, the plural would necessarily apply even to a single jar (*ghaṭa*). Consequently, just as with "water" (*āpaḥ*) or "in waters" (*apsu*) regarding drops and so forth, there would have to be a singular form for the jar as well.
The reading *bindāvavicāryaḥ* (or even *bindāviva apaḥ*) may also be possible here.

If one desires the grammatical correctness of a usage referring to a specific instance by means of excluding the [general] nature of being "excessively one" (*atiśayyaikātmya*), then for what reason— by that very same logic— is the word *apaḥ* not used in the singular (*bindau*) when it refers to a specific instance, just like the word *go* and others?

It would have to be in the singular number alone, because it is apprehended as "one," like the case of a thread and a cloth; likewise, with respect to *taṭas*, *taṭī*, and *taṭam*, based on what specific distinction is the difference in gender established, or what commonality is extended [to all]?
Is it not the case that the difference in gender has as its object the distinctions of maintenance (*sthiti*), production (*prasava*), and dissolution (*saṃstyāna*)?
There is no distinction between the objects *taṭa*, *taṭī*, and *taṭā*, because they possess an undifferentiated essential nature (*abhinnasvarūpatva*), just like a jar and its own self;
the reading *bindāvavicāryabhāḥ* (or *bindāviva apah*) may also be possible here.

Regarding the passage beginning with "consisting of a single superior essence" (*atiśayyaikātmaka*): you have accepted that our stated position—that there is only one superior essence such that whatever exists is [included therein]—is correct because, by refuting that [position], your application of a term to a specific object is as valid as the word *gāvī* (a dialectal variant of *go*). To this, we point out the following undesirable consequence for you: why is the word *ap* ("water"), when referring to a single drop, not used in the singular number? For it too would be a term denoting a specific object, just like the word *go*. Therefore, this logical principle [of yours] is itself inconsistent.

Furthermore, that word "water" (*ap*) would have to be in the singular number alone, because even though it consists of many parts, it is apprehended as "one," just like a cloth made of threads; since this point has already been explained, it is not further analyzed here.
[Question: Why is it said "whatever it may be" (*yat sa kiñcit*)?
[Answer: Because [the opponent] says "that which is it" (*yaḥ sa kiñcit*).
By this very [argument], first of all, this investigation regarding the object of number does not hold;
nor does the logic concerning the correctness of specific grammatical usage regarding the object of gender hold.

Just as a difference in number is untenable when there is identity of meaning, so too is a difference in gender untenable; therefore, he says: "In the same way, in cases such as *taṭaḥ* (masculine) and *taṭī* (feminine), what specific distinction (*viśeṣa*) is being taken here upon which the difference in gender depends? Or what commonality (*sāmānya*) is being extended [to the other genders] for the sake of conveying that specific distinction? The meaning is that none of these is possible here."

He says: But surely, the distinction of gender has as its object the specificities of maintenance (*sthiti*), production (*prasava*), and dissolution (*saṃstyāna*). Or rather, if that [distinction] arises from a difference in the objective domain (*gocara*), then even that does not exist; for the bank (*taṭaḥ*) is not the domain of production, because it consists of dissolution, like the feminine *taṭī*;
nor is the bank (*taṭī*) the domain of dissolution, because it consists of production, like the masculine *taṭaḥ*.
The shore is not the domain of that which is neither, because it consists of both cessation and production, like a woman and a man;
or alternatively...
Just like a riverbank [in the absence of water],

so too there is an absence of gender (liṅga) for these [entities]; consequently, they are non-existent as well, because they lack gender while being neither verbs nor indeclinables, like a sky-flower.

Now, it might be argued: "But surely, by the passage beginning with 'because its nature is contraction' (*saṃstyānātmakatvāt*), the threefold gender has already been established: 'A woman (*strī*) is [derived] from the root *styai* with the suffix *ḍraṭ* in the sense of contraction; a man (*pumān*) is [derived] from the root *sū* with the suffix *sap* in the sense of procreation;
and that which is the interval between these two, in the absence of both, is the neuter (*napuṃsaka*)" (Pāṇini-Mahābhāṣya 4.1.3).

1.3 Stability is neuter, contraction is feminine, and procreation is masculine; these meanings are possible in all embodied things. The distinction of gender is based on whatever specific quality one intends to express here. However, in the case of *taṭa*, *taṭī*, and *taṭa*, there is no such distinction in the object, because the referent is one and the same. That very distinction does not exist, which would serve as the basis for a difference in gender; it is absent because their essential nature (*svarūpa*) is non-different, like the pot and the pot's own self. Just as the pot is itself the pot's own self, so too is the bank (*taṭa*) itself the bank-feminine (*taṭī*) and the bank-neuter (*taṭa*); because their essential nature is non-different, there is no distinction.

[The opponent] says: "Because of the occurrence of specific objects of perception—such as a 'taṭī' having the configuration of a wall and so forth, a 'taṭa' having the configuration of a ridge or a slope, and a 'taṭa' having the configuration of a wall—the occurrence of a specific mark (liṅga) follows from the occurrence of a specific object.

To this it is replied: Even in the case of the occurrence of specific objects of perception, that specific distinction does not exist, because a 'taṭa' is not an object of procreation (*prasava*), since its nature is contraction (*saṃstyāna*). That the nature of that object is contraction is established, for you yourself have accepted the three-natured character (*tryātmakatva*) [of all things], just as in the case of a woman; just as there is an absence of procreation in one who possesses breasts and hair.

In this way, the remaining proofs have already been explained, up to the point "like a woman and a man"; thus, by the force of the examples of external women and so forth, the negation of the [object's] objective domain has been established. Now, for that very same purpose, it is established with reference to its threefold nature—beginning with "Alternatively" and so forth—the proofs having already been explained, up to the point "like a riverbank."

Thus, the application (*upanaya*) is that the very absence of gender (*liṅga*) [serves as the reason] for the absence of properties such as birth (*prasava*) in words like *taṭa*, because of the absence of a specific object-domain. It is not merely the absence of gender that is the fault; what then? From this, their non-existence (*asattva*) follows by uprooting the very foundation: because, while being neither an action nor an indeclinable (*avyaya*), they lack gender, like a sky-flower. Let it not be suspected that there is an attribution of existence (*sattva*)—as there is in the case of the referents of verbs such as *pacati* or of indeclinables such as *svarādi*—therefore the qualification "neither an action nor an indeclinable" is employed. Now, it might be argued... and so forth.

Another might offer this rebuttal: "But surely, by this elaborate explanation refuting the gender-indicators (*liṅga*) of the objective domain—beginning with the argument 'because it consists of contraction' (*saṃstyānātmakatvāt*) and so forth—you yourself have established the three genders by adopting their respective grounds for establishing gender;

thus, it is not the case that 'the riverbank (*taṭī*) is feminine because it consists of contraction,' nor that 'the bank (*taṭaḥ*) is masculine because it consists of production, like a man (*puruṣavat*),' and so on, since there is no ground for establishing gender."

If the procreative faculty and the other [faculties] were present together in a single object, that person would not exist at all; because of being female, like Devadatta and others, he would not be a woman;
because of being male, they [the two faculties] would not exist; and because of being neuter, like any other [such case].

If it is argued that the three-genderedness (*triliṅgatva*) of the words *parvata* (mountain), *nadī* (river), and *bhavana* (house) pertains to specific objects, we say no; for [words like] *bāhu* (arm) and others, which are distinct from masculine and so on, possess only a single gender, and because no such distinction is observed in the case of *ardharca* and other such words, this argument remains unrefuted. If it is further argued that the three-genderedness of a single entity is observed—as in the case of *bhūti*, *bhavana*, and *bhāva*—we reply: if we were to accept it because it is observed in common usage, then why should we not accept it in the case of *taṭa* (bank) simply because it is observed there as well? That [argument] is poorly conceived.

Furthermore, this is what must be proven: "This [Prakṛti] is also a single entity, whether it be a *bhāva* (positive being) or not, because its nature is procreation (*prasavātmakatvāt*), like the *puruṣa*. Thus you have stated that the various masculine forms [of the word *prakṛti*] are due to its nature being procreative, like the *puruṣa*. By the inclusion of the term "etcetera" (*ādi*), you imply that the three genders of the three [terms] are caused by their respective natures of contraction (*saṃstyāna*) and neither [procreation nor contraction].
But this is not so, because there is no established cause for determining gender.

But has it not already been established immediately prior that those very factors—procreation and so forth—are not the causes for establishing gender? Therefore, this [objection] is of no consequence.

Furthermore, even granting that procreation and the rest exist in proximity within a single entity, that entity would simply not be a male, because it would possess femininity, like Devadatta and others; for you have admitted its femininity due to its having all three genders.

Likewise, it would not be a female because it possesses masculinity; nor would both be female and male because it possesses neuter-ness. In this regard, the other [gender] serves as the counter-example.

Or rather, even that [distinction] does not exist when there is the occurrence of a specific objective domain (*gocara-viśeṣa*); for *taṭaḥ* (the bank) is not the objective domain of procreation (*prasava*), because its nature is contraction (*saṃstyāna*), just as *taṭī* (the female bank) is not the objective domain of contraction, because its nature is procreation, like a man;
nor is *taṭam* the objective domain of non-duality (*anubhayatva*), because it consists of both contraction and procreation, like a woman and a man.
Or else... like a riverbank.
Thus, there is simply an absence of gender (liṅga) for them,

and consequently they are non-existent as well, because they lack gender while being neither verbs nor indeclinables, like a sky-flower; the basis for this should be inferred here according to the circumstances.
Now, it might be argued: "But surely, by the passage beginning with 'because its nature is contraction' (*saṃstyānātmakatvāt*), the possession of the three genders has already been established;

for [the word] *strī* (female) is derived from the root *styai* with the suffix *ḍraṭ* in the sense of contraction, while *pumān* (male) is derived from the root *sū* with the suffix *sap* in the sense of procreation. Regarding that procreation:
*pra*.

Furthermore, having observed what in the world is it determined that "this is a woman," "this is a man," or "this is a neuter"? What, then, is that characteristic mark (*liṅga*)? A woman is one who possesses breasts and [facial] hair; a man is traditionally defined as one who is hairy;
and in the absence of both of these, there is a neuter.
And having seen all the lingas on the bank, who will be able to determine [which one is the true one]?
Therefore, it is not possible for grammarians to rely upon worldly gender; rather,
some established doctrine of their own must necessarily be adopted.
What is this "own conclusion" (*svakṛtānta*)? ...

"In the sense of contraction, from the root *styai* comes the suffix *ḍraṭ*, [forming] *strī*; in the sense of procreation, from the root *sū* comes *sap*, [forming] *pumān*" — Pāṇini-Mahābhāṣya 4.1.87.
1.3 By the word "saṃstyāna" (congealing), he demonstrates that it functions as a term denoting an abstract state (*bhāvasādhana*).
Regarding the word *sūteḥ*: the meaning is that the suffix *sap* occurs after this root *sū*, the letter *s* of which becomes *p*;
furthermore, the *masun* suffix is derived from the *uṇādi* class, and its vowel is shortened by virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*).
... *saṃstyāna* means concealment (*tirobhāva*).
"Activity is manifestation;
stability is the state of equilibrium"—
this is from the *Pātañjala-mahābhāṣya-pradīpa*.
"That which is the interval between both, in the absence of that, is the neuter" (Pāṇini-Mahābhāṣya 4.1.3).
Furthermore, "atha ca" and so forth [refer to] the verb "pacati" and so on; "svarādi" refers to the indeclinables (avyaya).
Now it is said:
"The one whose eyes are three fathoms long," because of his nature as a condensation of substance (*dravya-saṃstyānātmakatva*), etc.;
even the reading in the Bhāṣya, "because of his nature as a condensation, etc.," appears correct.
See page 575,
line 1: "The gender [of the word] *taṭaḥ* is masculine according to the *Vyavahārabhāṣya*, because it possesses the nature of procreation, like a man," and so forth.
No, because there is no cause for establishing a fixed gender;
for if procreation and so forth were present in a single object, that [object] would not be a male at all, because it would possess femininity, like Devadatta and others;
nor would it be a female, because it would possess masculinity.

If it is argued that those two [words] do not [possess all three genders] because they are neuter, and that—unlike others—the possession of all three genders regarding mountains, rivers, and houses is restricted to specific objects, we say no. This is because words such as *bāhu* (arm), which are distinct from masculine and so on, possess only a single gender; furthermore, since no such distinction is observed among words like *ardharca* (half-verse) and the rest, the objection remains unrefuted.
[Objection: But is it not seen that a single entity possesses all three genders, as in the case of *bhūti*, *bhavana*, and *bhāva*?

No; if we accept [the existence of the Self] because it is seen in the world, then why do we not accept [the existence of] the riverbank simply because it is also seen? Furthermore, this very point to be proven—that "this too is a single object" or "an entity," and so forth, such as "distinct from the person"—is itself poorly perceived.

The intention here is as follows: the limbs such as the arms and the tongue existing in the bodies of males, females, and neuter beings are observed to possess a single gender (liṅga), even though they refer to objects distinct from [the gender of] the male and so forth. Indeed, there is no difference in gender regarding the arm, even though it refers to an object distinct from the male and so forth. Thus, referring to a specific object is not the cause for a difference in gender. Furthermore, in the case of words such as *ardharca*, a difference in gender is observed despite the absence of reference to a specific object. Therefore, the previously stated objection—that "if the meaning is one, a difference in gender is untenable" (p. 574, l. 23)—remains entirely unrefuted.
See page 575, lines 2 and 3. Likewise, is it "tathātaḥ puṃliṅgam" in the Prākrit? Or is it "tathāttha puṃliṅgam"?
[Is it] because of the inclusion of the phrase "and so forth" (*ityādi*)?
[If so,] Devadatta would be a male here; he appears as a counter-example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).

The meaning is that just as Devadatta is indeed a male, so too the riverbank (taṭaḥ) is not exclusively a male; rather, femininity is distinct from masculinity, just as other things are. (Śābarabhāṣya 1.3.30)
Regarding the reading *itaratvena dṛṣṭānto'tra*, this is correctly understood here as meaning "by way of otherness," that is, by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyeṇa*).
"Is it like other cases? One might think: "The mountain is masculine; therefore, its bank (taṭa) is also [masculine]."

The word *nadī* (river) is feminine; its corresponding bank (*taṭī*) is also feminine, while its corresponding bank (*taṭam*) is neuter. Therefore, the possession of all three genders (*triliṅgatva*) pertains specifically to that particular object.

And this is not so, because in a single body there is a fixed gender for arms and other parts distinct from the person—for instance, "the arm is masculine," "the tongue is feminine," and "the eye is neuter. Therefore, this [argument] is also not sufficient. Furthermore, because no distinction is observed in cases such as *ardharca* and others, and since there is no exception, the word "not" carries over; for in examples such as *ardharcaḥ*, *ardharcaṃ*, *gomayaḥ*, and *gomayam*, there is an absence of the feminine gender, and thus the state of having three genders does not apply to a single object.
The term *ardharcaḥ* (a half-verse) is derived from *ṛcaḥ* (of a verse); it is used in the masculine as well as in the plural.
4.31 Words such as *ardharca* are used in both the masculine and neuter genders.
Each half-verse was a ball of cow dung.

Regarding "gomayam"—the *Kāśikā* says: "But surely the three genders are observed for a single word—'bhūtiḥ', 'bhavanam', and 'bhāvaḥ'; therefore, there is no deviation [from the rule]. To this it is replied: "No," starting with "yadi vayam" and so forth. If we were to accept [the gender] merely because usage is observed in the world, then like those such as yourself who rely on the understanding of others, why do we not accept it simply because it is observed in the sense of a riverbank (*taṭa*)? What is the use of dispute? Therefore, that very [usage] is poorly observed; the meaning is that what is well-known is actually a false reputation.

Furthermore, regarding the passage beginning with "api cedam" (and also this): even these three meanings—*bhūti* (coming into being), *bhavana* (the process of becoming), and *bhāva* (existence)—are distinct according to the view of the *Yathārthābhidhāna-śabda-naya*. Therefore, this must be established: that this single meaning is not manifold. Moreover, in the investigation of the logic regarding the three genders of a single [word], the presentation of various terms such as *bhūti* and so forth is highly competitive; and since the word *bhāva* falls within the scope of the *paryāya-naya*, here the agent alone is the single *bhāva*. Consequently, because there is no existence of multiple becomings, there is no plurality of meanings either. As for what was said regarding the extension of the meaning of "constellation" (*nakṣatra*) and "star" (*tārā*)...
...this Devadatta; the tree is the referent (artha),
and by virtue of the commonality [of being a tree], there is an extension (atideśa) of the term "Puṣya" [to the tree], just as [there is an extension] of the word "this" to Devadatta.

In this regard, the extension [of a term] is appropriate when there is a logical connection; for instance, the extension applies to Devadatta because he is the object of the notion "this," but it does not apply to the constellation Puṣya, as it is not its object.

Alternatively, a tree might be extended by means of its purpose because it is the object of that purpose, but Puṣya is not something to be extended by means of a constellation and so forth, because it is not its own object, just like the case of a post and a person.

If this were extended even to that which is not its proper domain, then the application of the extension [of properties] such as "constellation" (nakṣatra) would also be appropriate for things like a jar, because they are not its proper domain; this is to be proven just like the case of Puṣya.
