Existence is an action, not an agent denoted by words such as "becoming" (bhūti);
and that [existence as an agent] does not exist for the Śabdanaya, because the meaning of the verbal root has become subordinate.
Since the existence of the agent alone is established according to my view, even the cognitions of others [are accounted for].

Furthermore, when examining the logic of the three genders of a single entity, the introduction of various words such as *bhūti* and so forth is highly contentious; and because the word "being" (*bhāva*) falls within the scope of the mode of synonymy (*paryāya-naya*), here the agent alone is the single being. Therefore, due to the non-existence of multiple beings, there is no plurality of meaning either.
As for what was also said regarding the extension of the meaning of constellations and stars...
this Devadatta is the referent, and the tree becomes the referent.

The extension (*atideśa*) of Puṣya by means of the general category "constellation" is not tenable; for example, just as this [designation] is applied to Devadatta here because Devadatta is the object of that [term], such an extension is appropriate, but the extension of Puṣya by means of "constellation" is not, because Puṣya is not the object of that term.
Alternatively, a tree might be extended [to another thing] by means of its meaning, because it is the object of that [meaning].
The asterism Puṣya is not subject to the extension [of properties] belonging to the asterisms and so forth, because it does not have that as its object, like a post or a person;

for if it were extended even by something that does not have that as its object, then the application of the extension of the asterisms and so forth would also be appropriate for a jar and other such things, because they do not have that as their object, just like Puṣya (see page 573,
line 3).

An extension (*atideśa*) of "tree" is appropriate for Devadatta either by means of this [word] or by means of its referent (*artha*), but not by means of the asterism Puṣya, because that is not its domain; such might also be the reading here—see *bhūyādi* (Ya), fol.
557, line 5.
Furthermore, regarding the passage beginning with "api ca" and so forth:

when examining the logical consistency of the single meaning of the word *taṭa* having three genders, the presentation of various words such as *bhūti* and others, which possess various genders, is highly inconsistent; thus, that presentation is not tenable. This is because the universal (*sāmānya*), known as *bhūti*, *bhavana*, and *bhāva*, is unitary in its substantial sense (*dravyārthatva*); therefore, the example would pertain to that [universal], not to the scope of the modal standpoint (*paryāyanaya*). Since the word *bhāva* pertains to the scope of the modal standpoint, here the agent is indeed one alone. Thus, the entity (*bhāva*) is specifically one, such as a jar and so forth; it is not the case that the agent is a single particular (*viśeṣa*) in the form of *bhūti* and so on.

Therefore, because there is no existence as a single entity, there is likewise no unity of meaning; for while the existence as a universal (*sāmānya*) is subordinate, the existence as a particular (*viśeṣa*) consists of a single form qualified by prosperity (*bhūti*) and so forth. Thus, in this system, there is no unity of meaning here; consequently, the unity among prosperity and the rest produced by the substantial entity (*dravya*) is unproven for me—this is the sense. Therefore, it is not an example, and furthermore, because it pertains to the three [types of] objects (*tiviṣayatva*).
According to the method [of the Dravyārthika],
the example is "therefore" (tasmāt); according to the Bhāṣya, the example is "therefore" (tasmāt).

Furthermore, as for what you said regarding the extension of the meaning of the constellations and stars (*nakṣatra-tārā-artha-atideśa*), and so forth—that is merely a repetition of what has already been stated.
The illustration of the extension of a general meaning to convey a specific meaning is "this is Devadatta"; and "the tree becomes the object" is the second [example].
The remainder, up to the point concerning Devadatta, is self-evident; this constitutes the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).

The rejoinder (*uttarapakṣa*) here provides a logical argument by demonstrating dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) through the example "this belongs to Devadatta" and so forth, for the purpose of making clear the absence of extension (*atideśābhāva*). Up to the point of the phrase "because it does not have that as its object," he shows the dissimilarity of the first example with respect to its meaning;
then, with the phrase "or by means of an object," he demonstrates the dissimilarity of the second example:

a tree, being perceptible, would be extended [to another] by means of a real object that is a specific property (*dharma*), which is perceptible, and not by means of something that exists only as a universal (*sāmānya*) or as something like a sky-flower (*khapuṣpa*).

Because the stars and so forth do not have that [the individual] as their object, whereas the individual mass—the referent "Devadatta"—which is demonstrable by perception, does have that as its object; and because a tree has the external object as its object, there is a difference in nature (*vaidharmya*).

Therefore, it is not a valid example; the star Puṣya cannot be extended [to Devadatta] through the analogy of the stars, because it does not have itself as its object, just as a post is not [extended to] a person, or a person to a post.

If this were extended even to that which does not belong to its domain, then even in the case of a jar and so forth, the metaphorical application (*atideśavṛtti*) such as "the jar is a star" or "the jar is a constellation" would be appropriate; thus there would be the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) [of metaphor] because they do not belong to that domain, just like the word *puṣya*. [This is refuted] by the passage beginning with "because of the distinction...
and so on.
Of the exposition, [is it] not? Therefore, is it not? Therefore, is it not that?
Just as the constellations and stars [are impermanent],
is it not likewise with the person?
...the word *goṇī* is truly used for a cow and so forth, but not in contradiction with the specific qualities inherent therein...
This procedure for refuting [the charge of] inconsistency should be applied in its entirety even to the inconsistencies regarding the base form (*prakṛti*) and so forth.

Now, one might object: since it is impossible for a speaker to express a thing without the specific qualities inherent in that thing to be expressed, the employment of qualifiers is necessarily implied; and these qualifiers are precisely the distinctions of number, gender, and so on.
No, for an explanation is possible through distinctions such as action (*kriyā*) and etymology (*vyutpatti*).
For it has been said: "Explanations are given by means of the distinction between action and its factors (*kāraka*), by synonyms (*paryāya*), or by another sentence.

Thus, from the passage beginning with "But the person also... up to the point where the non-establishment of [the word's] having itself as its object is raised, [it is shown that words like] "cow" and so on are used figuratively (*gauṇa*).

The answer to that is as follows: "It is true that it is said," and so forth. For a word expresses a specific object of denotation (*vācyaviśeṣa*) in a manner that is consistent; by virtue of its grasping that [object], that specific meaning is called "true. However, it is not expressed through contradiction with the particularities inherent in that object, such as the contradictions between feminine, masculine, and neuter genders, or between singular, dual, and plural numbers when they refer to a single entity. Thus, the text—which demonstrates consistency and inconsistency—functions until the exclusion of inconsistency is achieved; this is the understood meaning. In this way, an extensive discussion of objections and their refutations has been stated, occasioned by the inquiry into the causes for inconsistencies regarding gender and number.

This entire detailed exposition of objections and refutations should also be applied to the contradictions regarding *prakṛti* (roots) and so forth, because the mode of discussion is the same; for the difference consists merely in the pronunciation of specific syllables such as roots and suffixes. From the initial objection beginning with "this is indeed false" (*prahāsa*) up to this point, it should be understood as a construction of the preceding and following positions (*pūrvapakṣa* and *uttarapakṣa*), omitting the specific distinctions of gender and so on, according to the sequence. See page 571, line 6, under the heading "The Method of Grasping Qualities."
"Now, as for the passage beginning with 'nanvevam' (but surely thus, etc.):

surely, when a narrator is engaged in the act of narration, since it is impossible to narrate that [subject] without the specificities inherent in the object to be narrated, the employment of qualifiers is necessary (*nāntarīyaka*). And those qualifiers are precisely the distinctions of number, gender, and so forth; otherwise, there would be no instruction regarding the meaning, because the use of words is for the purpose of conveying meaning. Just as there is necessity (*nāntarīyakatva*) for that which is dependent on the meaning, so too is there necessity for the distinctions of gender and so forth.
This is not so, because the explanation [of a word] is possible through various means such as the derivation (*vyutpatti*) of the action and so forth.
He demonstrates this with the words "For it has been said," etc., [stating] that by means of the indicator, there is a distinction between action and its factors (*kriyā-kāraka*).
Here, the reading "just as [the word] 'this' is inseparable from its meaning" (*asyārthānāntarīyakatvavat*) appears correct;
[the manuscript reads] *dānānta* (pra).

Substantiality, functioning as a substratum, being established in itself, being established by another, being expressed, being unexpressed, being remote, the two voids, and being subject to decay— these eight are to be known as the distinctions of action (*kriyābheda*).
The distinctions of the *kārakas*, such as the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth—whether six or eight—are the same when accompanied by time and means;

these are expressed through synonyms such as *ghaṭa*, *kuṭa*, and *kumbha*, or through other sentences, according to the rule: "A substitute is like the original, except in the case of an operation concerning an *al* (phoneme)" (Pāṇini 1.1.56).

56. Thus, because the original element (*sthānin*) and its substitute (*ādeśa*) are distinct, there is an extension of properties as if they were identical (*sthānivad-atideśa*). As it is said in the *Pāṇinīya-mahābhāṣya*: "One should behave toward the teacher's son as one would toward the teacher himself, except for eating his leftovers and clasping his feet."
1.1.56 and so forth.
According to the classification of actions, the root *div* (DhP 1107) is used in the senses of play, desire for victory, commerce, brilliance, praise, joy, intoxication, sleep, beauty, and motion.
Likewise, this tree also flourishes here through the distinction between action (*kriyā*) and its factors (*kāraka*).
...the introduction to the sky-flower...
...the application of the topical section concerning the definition of differentiation...

...What is the explanation, or how is there an inconsistency, even when the gender and other properties are identical? Even by accepting that a single word has multiple meanings, the comprehension of the meaning occurs through interpretation despite the identity of gender and so forth;
as it has been said: "A wise man should understand the word *go* in ten senses: speech, direction, earth, ray, cow, speech, direction, earth, ray, thunderbolt, arrow, cattle, eye, heaven, and water."
...or by means of vision;
for this very reason, one should apply effort to the study of grammar.
For it has been said—... [text missing] ... —[end quote].
Words alone are the basis for the reality of the functioning of meanings;
there is no comprehension of the true nature of words apart from grammar. (Vākyapadīya 1)

Alternatively, the Teacher himself has already explained [the roots] such as *div* (to play) through the differentiation of actions, up to the point where it was said "that tree," the meaning of which is understood.

Having thus demonstrated the established explanation here as well, he applies the present topic [starting] with "it flourishes" (*puṣyati*) and so on, up to "sky-flower" (*khapuṣpa*), the explanation of which is understood.

Or, there is another explanation—beginning with "introduction" (*upoddhāta*) and so on, up to "of the definition of difference"—[wherein] the question "what is the inconsistency here, or how [could there be one], even though the gender and other [linguistic markers] are not different? will be connected [to the following].

Alternatively, there is this other method of explanation: namely, [the discussion] beginning with "the locus, the connection, and the meaning of the word," and so on, up to "what or how is the impossibility even when the mark (*liṅga*) and so forth are non-different?
However, its detailed explanation, along with examples, should be understood from the *Tattvārthasaṅgraha* and other such works.
[In the case of] the statement "a jar" (*ghaṭa*), [it is as follows].
Regarding the statement "as if the original" (*sthānivad*):

for what purpose is this stated? Because the original (*sthānin*) and the substitute (*ādeśa*) are distinct, the designation "as if the original" applies to the substitute, just as in the case of "the teacher's son is like the teacher," where the original is one thing and the substitute is another.
Because of the distinctness between the original element (*sthānin*) and its substitute (*ādeśa*), for this reason, the operation applicable to the original does not apply to the substitute.

What is the fault in that? [The rule] *āṅo yamahanaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.28), which prescribes the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), would apply only to the root *han*, and not to *vadh*; yet it is desired that it should apply to *vadh* as well.
Since this cannot be established without an effort, therefore there must be an extension of the status of the original to the substitute (*sthānivadanudeśa*).
It is for this purpose that it is said, "As toward the teacher, so toward the teacher’s son. Just as—

namely, "one should behave toward the teacher’s son as toward the teacher"— whatever duty pertains to the teacher is extended (*atidiśyate*) to the teacher’s son, so too here, the operation (*kārya*) pertaining to the original element (*sthānin*) is extended to the substitute (*ādeśa*).
[this] extends the specific duties of the resident [pupil] to the substitute, just as in the case of "one should behave toward the teacher's son as toward the teacher.
For example: "One should behave toward this teacher's son as toward the teacher, except for eating the leftovers and clasping the feet."
And even if the teacher’s son is also a teacher, that [initiation] must still be performed— Pāñcārthabhāṣya 1.1.1.
By way of a distinction in action, [the root] *div* is used in the senses of play, desire for victory, commerce, brilliance, praise, joy, intoxication, sleep, beauty, and motion (Dhātupāṭha 1107).
... That tree.
Here too, it flourishes through the distinction between action and its factors;
[this is] the introduction regarding the sky-flower.
Regarding the analysis of the application of grammatical gender (*adhikaraṇayoga*) characterized by distinction:

(VP 1.1)
Thus this verse is seen;

in its commentary, Bhartṛhari, having stated "and so it has been said," [writes]: "The true nature of the cause of the relationship between word and meaning, even when there is no difference in what is expressed, [distinguishes] between correct and incorrect words."
The verse "He who does not know grammar does not know the refined [words] inferred from correct usage" has been cited; however,

Vākyapadīya 1.13: The reality of the operation of meaning is the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*), and not existence or non-existence by way of the intrinsic nature of the object;
for intention is based on words that are [semantically] appropriate.
For the speaker employs the appropriate word for each respective object among those meanings brought into proximity by the intention to speak;
just as one desiring to perceive applies the very sense-organ suitable for each specific object toward perception.
Alternatively, what is the reality of the engagement with objects? It is the form of the object, consisting of the cognition itself, which is projected onto external things,
and that [projection] is based on words.

The realization of the reality of words consists in the reality of the word itself, which is its complete and unimpaired nature as a refined (sādhū) form. For that [correct form] is indeed unimpaired for him, whereas others, employing them with the desire to use that very form, may employ them in an incomplete manner as corrupt forms (apabhraṃśa).
Thus it is stated in the *Svavṛtti* on the *Vākyapadīya* composed by Bhartṛhari.

The engagement with meaning is linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*). Its "principles" (*tattva*) are either "meaning and engagement" (as a copulative compound), or "meaning" is the substance (*dravya*) and "engagement" is the action (*kriyā*), [the principles being] the reality of those two. Language is their basis; the "realization of the principles" is the realization of grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*).
"Based on a suitable word" means that the word is suitable, being capable of conveying the intended meaning of that [object].
The phrase "having cognition as its essence" refers to the nature of consciousness itself.

The expression "projected onto external objects" means that consciousness alone is presented in the form of the denotable object; it is said to be "cast upon" them because it is apprehended as if external, but it does not mean that an external entity actually exists.

While it was stated previously that when an external object exists, the speaker’s intention based upon it constitutes the true nature [of the word], the distinction now is that it is cognition alone [that constitutes it].
Thus, in the commentary composed by Vṛṣabhadeva:
"The comprehension of the true nature of words does not exist apart from grammar" (Vākyapadīya 1.13).

he demonstrates this— just as it was said— the verse beginning with "Speech, direction, earth, ray," and so forth, has been explained by the Teacher himself in the passage ending with "or by vision."
Thus, the pervasiveness of the commentary over the entire range of subjects to be explained has been demonstrated.
For this very reason, it is said:

Having attained the state of *abhijalpa*, which is the nature of superimposition (*adhyāsa*), the word itself, characterized by its own form, becomes the denotable object of the word.
He states the nature of *abhijalpa*: "When, through the connection 'this is that,' the form [of the object] is made one [with the word]."
The *Vākyapadīya* (2.129) states: "That [connection] of a word with its object is called *abhijalpa*.

This relationship of identification, expressed as "this is that," is termed *adhyāsa* (superimposition). By means of this, the true nature of the object is veiled, and it is presented as if unified with the word; at that time, the word is called *abhijalpa*. Due to the force of this superimposition, although word and object possess a single identity, the objective aspect alone is predominant by virtue of its utility.

To show that in worldly usage it is specifically the aspect of the meaning that is predominant, he says: "In the world, the word proceeds having attained the form of the meaning.
Having attained the form of the meaning—that is, having reached a state of virtual identity with the meaning—the word proceeds, as in "This is a cow" (*ayaṃ gauḥ*), and so forth.
In that regard, it is the object alone that is determined as primary by virtue of its externality;

however, in the treatise (*śāstra*), the dual nature of the word is also observed through its differentiation. Thus he says: "But in the treatise, the dual nature [of the word] is distinguished according to the speaker's intention" (*Vākyapadīya* 2).

For in the treatise (*śāstra*), an instruction is sometimes primarily concerned with the word-form (*svarūpa*) and sometimes primarily concerned with the meaning (*artha*); thus, the dual nature of the word is observed.
As stated in the *Vākyapadīya-vṛtti* composed by Puṇyarāja:
"Others, however, say that the word itself, having attained the state of being expressed (*abhijalpatva*), is the word-meaning."

The two verses beginning with "It has been said" (*uktaṃ hi*) demonstrate that grammar is for the purpose of praising it:

the word *go* is one while having many meanings [such as speech, earth, etc.], and the words *ghaṭa*, *kuṭa*, and *kumbha* are many while applied to a single object characterized by a broad base and so forth. Thus, grammar is the illuminator of such objects to be illuminated, just as the sun is for all things to be illuminated, whether stationary or moving.

Likewise, without grammar, there can be no knowledge of the subtle meaning to be expressed nor of the expressive word itself; for instance, regarding a word whose function is verbal action—such as *hasati* (he laughs) or *jalpati* (he prattles)—knowledge concerning that is not possible [without grammar].
And one who knows grammar understands all of this, as well as the reality of the application of meanings, and so forth.

Meanings (*arthāḥ*) are the things to be expressed; activities (*pravṛttayaḥ*) are actions that are either causes of benefit or causes of harm for persons. The true natures (*tattvāni*)—that is, their own non-erroneous forms—of both these categories are known through words alone.
However, the true nature of words themselves is not known except through grammar (*vyākaraṇa*).

Alternatively, the true natures of the meanings and activities—the infinite transformations of the essence of each individual thing according to its own nature—are known through words, while the words themselves are known through grammar.

Alternatively, "objects" (arthāḥ) refers to dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa; their "activities" (pravṛttayaḥ) are the means toward them; and their "realities" (tattvāni) are the respective relationships between the goal and its means.

In such specific explanations, words are the causes for the correct knowledge regarding those objects, whereas grammar is the cause for the correct knowledge of words themselves—meaning that they are their own unerring forms.
As for what was said, beginning with "yadapyucyeta" and so forth:

it is illogical that there should be a single substratum (*aikādhikaraṇya*) for the mutually contradictory individual entities of female, male, and neuter, which have the stars of the Puṣya constellation as their referents; for if those two were not distinct in essence, then, given the non-deviation of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), only one particular form would prevail as primary in any given instance.
In common worldly usage, speech proceeds having assumed the form of meaning;
however, in the treatise, it possesses both forms, distinguished according to the speaker's intention— Vākyapadīya 2.1.1.

According to the view of Bhartṛhari and others, the "inner discourse" (*abhijalpa*) is the nature of the word (*śabdātmā*), characterized by consciousness (*vijñānalakṣaṇa*), which, having grasped an object through perception and imagination, has its own power subordinated therein; it fluctuates within the intellect and serves as the cause for the operation of another [subsequent] audition.
However, the view of Vasurāta, the teacher of Bhartṛhari, is that this [word] arranges the object—which conforms to its own form—within itself through internal differentiation.

"Why do you suddenly cause this weariness of speech by stating such things as, 'The cognition regarding [the asterism] Punarvasu and so forth is also untenable because of the contradiction with the number [of stars], etc.'? For the meaning of a word (*śabdārtha*) is indeed conceptual proliferation (*abhijalpa*). The particle *hi* is used in the sense of 'because'; since the meaning of a word is conceptual proliferation, there is no purpose in the weariness of investigating gender and so forth, because its object is non-existent, like the weariness of investigating an object such as a sky-flower. It might be asked: 'What is this conceptual proliferation? To this it is replied: It is precisely the word itself; that conceptual proliferation is nothing other than the word."

"In the world, speech proceeds having assumed the form of an object; in the treatise (śāstra), however, it possesses both forms, distinguished according to the speaker's intention. (Vākyapadīya 2.129–131) According to the view of Bhartṛhari and others: having grasped an object through perception or imagination, the inner essence of speech—characterized by cognition, whose own power is latent therein, and which fluctuates within the intellect—is called *abhijalpa*. It is the cause for the subsequent application of audible speech (*śruti*).

However, the view of Vasurāta, the teacher of Bhartṛhari, is as follows: he establishes the meaning in accordance with its own nature through internal differentiation. Furthermore, even this verbal expression (*abhijalpa*) exists only within the intellect;

for instance, since a distinction between external word and object is established by the fact that they are perceived by different sense organs and so forth, their unification is ultimately untenable. Therefore, it is logical that the unification of word and object occurs only when they reside within the intellect, because they are contained within a single cognition.

For instance: the nature of the word (*śabdātmā*), which has assumed the form of the object of denotation (*abhidheya*) while its own verbal essence remains concealed, revolves within the intellect (*buddhi*). As it internalizes the object—which follows its own form—without distinction, it is called "internal discourse" (*abhijalpa*). And this [discourse] is rightly understood as a form residing solely within the intellect, not as something external, because the two possess absolutely distinct natures from one another. —*Sanmativṛtti* 1.1.24.

In this way, word and object possess a non-distinct nature, like milk and water.

Since these two are non-distinct in essence, and since they possess an inseparable mutual relationship (*avinābhāvitva*) that is never-failing, nevertheless, by the force of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), one form or the other—either the form of the word or the form of the meaning—remains predominant. "Let it be seen (pṛṣṭha 397–1):

'Whether due to incapacity or due to omnipotence, [power] is fashioned by words alone. Now, power does not exist separately among objects; rather, it is dependent upon words. Thus, just as they are enjoined by words, so too are they understood. Therefore, the word-meaning is established solely through its own majesty. To demonstrate this eighth position, he says: "Whether due to incapacity or due to omnipotence, [power] is fashioned by words alone."

"Either the conceptualization of action and so forth is restricted to a single object" (Vākyapadīya 2.132), or "the object is established as possessing all powers, and it is by means of a word that its specific power is denoted"— this ninth alternative is shown here by the statement: "or [the word denotes] that which possesses all powers."

The meaning [of a word] is sometimes expressed as having the nature of an action (kriyā) and sometimes as having the nature of an accomplished entity (siddha); thus, the fixed nature of being an action and so forth is presented as the meaning of the word. This is stated in Puṇyarāja’s commentary on the *Vākyapadīya*, regarding "the conceptualization of a single object as necessarily an action and so forth" (*vākyapa°* 2.132).
In this case, a single objective entity is expressed at one time and in one state simultaneously or successively by means of contradictory properties;
for example: "He cooks rice" (*odanaṃ pacati*), "He brings about the cooking of the rice" (*pākam odanasya nirvartayati*), or "He effects the completion of the cooking" (*nirvṛttiṃ pākasya karoti*).

In that regard, if [the rice] has the status of an object (*karmatva*), how can it have the status of a residual factor (*śeṣarūpatva*)? And if it has the status of a residual factor, how can the cooking have the status of a residual factor?
Therefore, either non-existent capacities are superimposed upon this object by the word through the force of the speaker’s intention,
or the word reveals those capacities which are restricted despite the object being endowed with all possible capacities;
in that case, under the view that [capacities] are non-existent, the capacity residing in the thing itself is not the operative factor.
Indeed, there is no purpose whatsoever for that [mental verbalization] in the proximity or non-proximity of the object and the referent;
for the intention to speak is based on words that are capable [of evoking it].

To demonstrate the independence of mental verbalization (*abhijalpa*) from the external object—even when such an object exists—in the mind of the hearer, he says: "Because of incapacity, or because of being all-powerful," and so forth.

These actions—such as going, staying, speaking, and thinking—which are expressed by verbal roots and are considered to possess external objective power: whether that external object which possesses them exists, or whether it is merely a lack of power, in either case—whether one holds the position of the possessor of power (*śaktimat*) or the position of the absence of power (*aśakti*)—these powers of action and so forth are strictly restricted: speaking and such belong only to humans and the like, while crawling, flying, and so forth belong only to snakes, birds, and the like. Indeed, all these various [powers] are attributed to some single object solely by means of words; the meaning is that they are brought forth by the power of words (*śabda-śakti*).
He elucidates this very point with a commentary: "In this world, a single objective entity," and so forth.

In reality, a single *odana* (boiled rice) is spoken of simultaneously by many speakers, or by one speaker through successive turns, at a single time such as a *muhūrta*, while in a state of being cooked, by means of contradictory attributes (*viruddhair dharmaiḥ*). He illustrates this with the example: "*odanam*" refers to the object (*karman*) upon which the action is mounted by an agent such as Devadatta; "*pākam odanasya*" indicates a mere relation (*sambandhamātram*) through the genitive case, namely the status of being the object of the cooking; and "*nirvṛttim pākasya*" indicates the connection to the cooking itself.

It would be stated [as follows]: there, by means of the passage beginning with "yadi" (if) and ending with "pākasya" (of cooking), he demonstrates that in the case of an external object, because of the absence of a connection with contradictory properties (*viruddhadharma*), it is not possible for [multiple states] to exist simultaneously at one and the same time. Thus.

Nor is it [the case] in sequential application, because the entity is one— the state of being cooked belonging to that which is inherent in the cooking, namely the substance called *odana*, as well as time—

and for this reason, etc., he shows in the first alternative, by means of the phrase "or non-existent," etc., that the capacity belongs to the word alone, up to the point where it says "are superimposed. Furthermore,

in the second alternative, beginning with "or when there is a connection with all capacities," etc., he likewise shows that the capacity belongs to the word alone, up to the point where it says "it manifests."

In that case, regarding the position of incapacity (*aśaktipakṣa*), since it is admitted that the capacity inherent in the object simply does not exist, it cannot serve as a basis for the employment of words; for, like a sky-flower, it is non-existent, and thus the contemplation beginning with "not of that" and so forth has already been explained up to the point where there is no purpose whatsoever. Indeed, one superimposes this or that capacity only when there is a purpose. However, in the position of universal capacity (*sarvaśaktipakṣa*), words are employed as restricted to their own respective objects by taking up those various capacities which are established and non-confused.

This too is a result that establishes our intended meaning:
for the speaker's intention, which is based on appropriate words, superimposes various capacities upon the intellect of the listener.

In this regard, first of all, the *vastu* (the objective entity) is established as something other than the word by your very statement; for there is a distinction between the word—which consists of the relationship [between signifier and signified]—and its object. That *vastu* is the substratum of all this: it is that upon which the word is employed, that which is intended to be expressed, and that upon which capacity (*śakti*) is superimposed.
It is the fit and corresponding word.

for in accordance with the form of the object, that word is fit to be its designator.

To this we reply: this too is a result of establishing our own position; it establishes precisely that "particulars alone exist, with the universal as a subordinate factor. This will be the fruit of your statement.

Desiring to bring that about, you repeat the passage beginning with "the word is capable" and so forth, up to "it superimposes. In the context of the position regarding incapacity, the final part is the conclusion showing the capacity of the word; because the remainder of the text has that as its fruit, [the author says] "first, the object," and so on.

By this very statement of yours, an entity other than the word—whether called "power" (*śakti*) or the "possessor of power" (*śaktimat*)—is established. If it is asked what kind of entity that is, he shows it: "consisting of the relation between 'that' and 'this'," and so forth. From this very expression, "due to the relation of 'this is that' (*so'yam*)," the entity denoted by the word "that" is distinct from the word denoted by the word "this," or rather, from the object; or conversely, the object denoted by the word "this" is distinct from the word denoted by the word "that," because of the difference between the locus and the located. This is the case for both the word and the object, which consist of the relation between "that" and "this."

The meaning is this: that object upon which a word is employed, that toward which the speaker intends to produce a cognition, and that upon which a capacity (śakti) is superimposed—that entity is the substratum for this entire collection of factors known as the word, the capacity, the cognition, and the intention to speak. This is because the establishment of things to be supported depends upon the existence of their substratum.

Furthermore, the external object is established through a "suitable" word; a "suitable" word is one that is concordant [with its referent]. A specific word is employed only in accordance with a specific object—for instance, the word "jar" is used for an object characterized by a broad base and so forth.

Therefore, the word comes into being after the object called "pot" has been established; since the prefix *anu* has the meaning of "after," the connection of the word with the object after the object has been established is appropriate (*anurūpa*). As in the expression "according to the form of the object" (*yathārtharūpādi*), and so forth; or else, it means "conformable" (*anurūpa*) or "suitable. The prefix *anu* signifies "according to" (*yathā*); thus, "according to form" (*yathārūpam*) means whatever form [it may be], "according to form" (*anurūpam*) means in such a way as it is fit to be joined. This is the meaning.

And how is this appropriate? To this he says: "For in that way," and so forth. For in that manner, this word is "fit" (*yogya*), meaning it is capable of being joined; because we observe its usage with the thought, "I shall cause that object to be understood," it is endowed with the capacity to denote that object. This means that what is not a denoter of an object is neither suitable nor fit—this is what has been stated by you yourself, since the intention to speak is based on the object, for the word *hi* has the sense of a reason. Otherwise, it would be impossible for speech to function apart from the communication of an object.
For a word is not intended to be spoken without its relationship as signifier and signified being grasped;
nor can a word, merely by the speaker’s intention, instill various powers within the hearer’s intellect.
Thus, by this very statement of yours, you have indeed admitted that the powers are characterized by their specific distinctions.
And according to our own view, there is no other entity possessing power apart from the operation of the specific nature [of things];
the particulars themselves are the powers, true in their own objects, and it is the speaker's intention alone that manifests them in their respective instances.
The intention to speak (*vivakṣā*) alone superimposes that respective capacity first upon itself and subsequently, prior to the actual usage, upon the cognition of the listener;
the capacity superimposed by the intention to speak exists in the object independently of the word, for otherwise activity would be impossible.

Indeed, as for the phrase "for the word," etc.: a word is intended to be spoken only when its relationship as signifier and signified has been observed; for a word whose status as signifier and signified has not been grasped [cannot function].

Since the intention to speak (*vivakṣā*) is impossible without an object, it is not by mere intention alone, and so forth. The word "and" (*ca*) is employed here to indicate that when a word is applied to an appropriate intended object, it is able to instill its respective capacity (*śakti*) in the intellect of the listener, but not otherwise. This is because the capacity belongs to the word, the object, and the word-object relation; for it is from this capacity that the word is able to speak (*śaknoti vaktum*) and the object can be spoken (*śakyate vaktum*). (See *Prāyasādhana*, p. 580, l. 3).
And is it non-existence,
or [is it] existence?

*Yogyānupravṛtti-prayoga*: a linguistic usage that conforms to fitness and follows from application, intended for the communication of meaning.

Because activity would be impossible;
for a word is not intended to be spoken without its relationship as signifier and signified being grasped,
nor can a word, by mere intention to speak, instill its various powers within the listener's intellect.

powers are simply the specificities themselves, which are real in their own right.
And among those [powers], it is precisely the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*) that manifests them;

it is the intention itself that superimposes this or that power—first upon itself, and subsequently, through the act of utterance, upon the cognition of the listener. Thus, the power superimposed by the intention exists in the object independently of the word.
Does that which is intended to arise occur without [the cause], or does it occur by virtue of the intention?

the nature of sound, the nature of meaning, the nature of both sound and meaning, and the nature of both meaning and sound.

Furthermore, from your own statement beginning with "just as in our view," you imply that non-existent powers are superimposed upon this object; therefore, by raising this conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), we too declare the impossibility of anything other than the possessor of power (*śaktimat*).

Apart from that which is the manifestation of the specific nature (*svarūpa*) of the particulars (*viśeṣa*), there is no other thing called "power" (*śakti*). However, if you say, "Let it be said that the particulars themselves, by their very particularity, are the powers we intend," then let it be so; who can prevent it? And these powers exist as true in their own right, existing in their own form as powers in the form of particulars—meaning they exist precisely as particulars whose forms are distinguished from other powers through states such as feminine, masculine, and neuter.

And for those powers (*śakti*), it is the speaker’s intention alone (*vivakṣā*) that manifests them within their respective objects of activity, such as femininity and so forth; by means of that intention, they are manifested—that is, made manifest—through the actual employment of words. For it is that very intention which manifests the existing distinctions, such as *taṭas*, *taṭī*, and *taṭam*; this is the meaning.

What is the intention (*vivakṣā*)? It is the desire to speak. That very [desire] superimposes upon itself—that is, upon the speaker—prior to the utterance, those respective capacities residing in the object that are established independently of the word; subsequently, through the act of usage, it superimposes them upon the cognition of the listener. It does not [superimpose] what is non-existent, because the person exerts effort toward the object for the sake of grasping the speaker’s intention, establishing a cognition of no other [object], such as: "This man is intended by him to be spoken of," "This woman [is intended]," "and not others," and so forth. (See page 582, line 6 et seq., where non-existents are discussed).
There is no establishment of non-existent destinies by means of this [method].

The formal argument here is as follows: The thesis is that the meaning is indeed the power superimposed upon the intention to speak independently of the word, because it is that which is to be communicated (*pratyāyyatvāt*). That the meaning termed "power" (*śakti*) is established as that which is to be communicated is proven by the fact that the speaker, as the communicator, produces a cognition in the listener; for whatever is to be communicated is independent of the word because it is that which is to be communicated, like the parts of a conceptual designation (*abhijalpa*), and because this very power is the seed of the intention to speak due to its being the motivator (*prayojakatvāt*).

Even on the view that [all things] possess all capacities (*sarvaśakti*), you are merely stating our own position; for the employment of words is for the sake of a purpose, and words are employed restricted to their own respective objects by taking up those specific capacities which are established and non-overlapping, since otherwise there would be the contingency of confusion in grammatical gender, number, coreferentiality, and action.
In ultimate reality, however, this is indeed the doctrine of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara-vāda*), because each single substance possesses infinite modes (*paryāya*).
As for the claim that an object, when apprehended, is endowed with contradictory properties, this is not entirely correct, for it is established precisely through mutual dependence (*pratyapekṣā*).

It is like that which possesses the meaning of its constituent parts through verbal expression (*abhijalpa*). For example, regarding the word *abhijalpa* employed by you, its denoted object is a composite whole: "speech directed toward" (*ābhimukhyena jalpaḥ*) is *abhijalpa*. This identity consisting of the relationship between the word and its object has been established by you; and that [identity] is to be conveyed by the meanings of the two constituent parts—the meaning of the prefix *abhi-* and the meaning of the root *jalpa*—because the comprehension of the composite meaning of "speech directed toward" (*abhijalpa*) is preceded by the comprehension of the meanings of the constituent parts.

Lest your [proposed] intention (*vivakṣā*) and application (*prayoga*) be rendered purposeless, you must admit them as being distinct from a sky-flower and independent of words, because they are what is to be communicated by you; likewise, the object called "capacity" (*śakti*). Otherwise, the term "interpenetrated discourse" (*abhijalpa*) would be meaningless.
Furthermore: "And because this [intention] is the motivator," and so forth.

As for what you said regarding the position of incapacity—that the capacity inherent in the object is not a causal factor, since proximity or non-proximity of that capacity to the object serves no purpose whatsoever—this collection of arguments turns out to be the very opposite of your intent; for it is precisely capacity that constitutes the seed of your intended meaning and is its causal factor.
Thus, the position of incapacity does not exist even according to your own words, as it is established by our own doctrine;
let this be seen on page 394.2.

Because it is that which is to be made known, like the parts of an object denoted by a conventional term (*abhijalpa*); and because this very power (*śakti*) is the seed of the intention to speak (*vivakṣā*), for even in the view that all powers [inhere in everything], you are merely stating our own position. Since the employment of words is for the sake of meaning, words are employed as restricted to their own respective objects by taking up those various powers which are established and non-confused; otherwise, there would result a confusion in the grammatical gender, number, and coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) regarding the action.
However, in the ultimate sense, this is indeed the doctrine of the Supreme Lord of Speech (*vādaparameśvara*), because each single substance possesses infinite modes (*paryāya*).

As for the claim that [an object] is endowed with contradictory properties when its objective aspect is grasped, this is not entirely correct; let the meanings of the constituent parts be examined as they appear on page 582, line 7.

Even in the view that all [powers] are present [in every word], you are merely stating our own position; why? Because the employment of words is for the sake of a specific meaning, as expressed by the phrase "established" (*vyavasthitām*) and so forth. For instance—having taken up only those specific powers, such as feminine, masculine, or neuter, which are established, not brought about by another word, unmixed, not denotable by any other word, intended through the exclusion of other powers, and distinct—words, restricted to their own respective objects, are employed, being fixed upon a single power characterized by non-different gender, number, and so on.

What is the reason? Because in a grammatical construction (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) involving different genders and so forth, there would arise a confusion of usage; as was stated previously: "The use of stars such as Tārā, Puṣya, and Nakṣatra—which are feminine, masculine, and neuter—interchangeably is ungrammatical (*apaśabda*).
And this position of universal power is, in ultimate reality, nothing other than the doctrine of the Supreme Lord (*vādaparameśvaravāda*).
Why? Because each substance possesses infinite modes (*paryāya*), our view alone is correct. For I am in conflict only with you, not with that Supreme Lord of Discourse;

what contradiction could there be with him? His doctrine is as follows: each individual substance has infinite modes. Transformations (*pariṇāma*)—whether dependent or independent—are called "modes" (*paryāya*) and "potencies" (*śakti*). Furthermore, because substances possess mutually interpenetrating potencies, they are all-potent, as it has been said:

If it were due to another capacity,
then [the entities] would be dependent;
and for things that are mutually interconnected, it is illogical to say "this" or "that."
And [the reading] *anyonyābhāva* is not appropriate according to the manuscript (*pra*).
Just as there are as many specific states of differentiation between milk and water as there are... [Sūtra 1.47] ...[text fragment] ...bhāva.

As for the passage beginning with "the grasping of the object" (*viṣayodgrāha*), which concerns the subject matter of the verse *Vākyapadīya* 2.132— "because of incapacity or because of all-capacity"— stating that "conceptual constructions such as action (*kriyā*) are produced by words," this [verse] is cited as an illustration of this point: that which is said to be "endowed with contradictory properties" refers to its own meaning (*svārtha*), because everything here possesses a single, non-contradictory meaning.

Is it not the case that all meanings are indeed non-contradictory? That which is the object (*karman*) in "he cooks rice" (*odanaṃ pacati*) is expressed by the genitive case as "the cooking of the rice" (*pāka odanasya*).

Furthermore, the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) in *pacati* expresses the agent (*kartṛ*), while the noun-forming suffix (*kṛt*) in the word *pāka* expresses the action (*bhāva*). Since the agent possesses the quality of being a substance whose action is denoted by a *kṛt*-suffix, and because the agent is yet to be accomplished (*sādhya*), when the rice is already perceived but there is doubt regarding the action directed toward it—such as in the question "What is he doing?"—then because the rice itself cannot be further explained, the very act of cooking is prescribed for it, as in "He cooks."

In the explanation of that very same *apūrva* as "pacati" (he cooks), [the agent] is designated as the object (*karman*) because it is expressed by the verb "pac" in the phrase "pākaṃ karoti" (he performs cooking).
As previously stated, [the agent] explains the meaning of the agentive suffix (*kartṛ-pratyaya*) as "he brings about the accomplishment of the cooking" (*pākasya nirvṛttiṃ karoti*);
thus, even the pot and other such implements function within the act of cooking.

"...thus" (*itye*)—the very same passage beginning with these words is to be recited again: "In this case, there is but a single objective reality," and so forth, up to "and the state of being the residual form of the cooking. Having illustrated this and then developed the argument starting from "Therefore, the powers are either non-existent," etc., it was stated in the conclusion: "Therefore, in both positions... and so forth, up to "...is possible.

Having thus recited [the opponent's position], the Teacher states the reply: "This is not entirely correct, as its own intended meaning has not been properly considered. Why? Because all this cited meaning possesses a single, non-contradictory sense."
He explains that: "Indeed, all [this is so]," and so forth.

That very object of the action of cooking (*paciviṣaya*) called *odana* (rice), which one cooks, is expressed by this genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) as "the cooking of the rice" (*pāka odanasya*). According to Pāṇini 2.3.1–2, the accusative is used for an unexpressed object;

however, in another instance, Pāṇini 2.3.65 prescribes the genitive for both the agent and the object when a *kṛt* suffix is present. Thus, in one case [the accusative] and in the other [the genitive], the same thing is expressed.
Thus, by the genitive case [in *pākasya*], that very same object (*karman*) is expressed;

and by the word *pāka*, the state (*bhāva*), which is the meaning of the root *pac*, is expressed through the suffix *ghañ*. By the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) in *pacati*, the agent (*kartṛ*) is expressed. It is shown and described that this very [agent] brings about the cooking (*pāka*); it is not [the agent] that is expressed by the verbal suffix.

What is the reason? Because it possesses the nature of a substance (dravya) through the state (bhāva) expressed by a *kṛt*-suffix; for it is said: "A state expressed by a *kṛt*-suffix becomes like a substance" (*Pāṇini-Mahābhāṣya* 3.1.67).

Thus, in the expression "he performs cooking" (*pākaṃ karoti*), the accusative case is used for the object as if it were a substance; and the term "nirvartayati" (he brings about) has the same meaning as "karoti" (he does/performs).

Why? Because the agent is that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Cooking is the softening (*viklitti*) of rice grains; the agent whose object is that [softening] is what is to be accomplished. Devadatta brings about the accomplishment of the softening; he moistens, he cooks, he effects the cooking—since these have the same meaning, the sense is that Devadatta is accomplished by virtue of being engaged in the act of cooking.

And when the boiled rice (*odana*) is already known, if there arises a doubt regarding the actions such as eating or cooking that have it as their object—namely, the question "What does he do?"—since the well-known rice being restated is not in need of explanation, the word "cooks" (*pacati*) serves to enjoin this very act of cooking as distinct from eating and so forth. When that very act of cooking, which was previously unknown, is explained in response to the question "What does he do? by saying "He performs cooking" (*pākaṃ karoti*), its status as an object (*karmatva*) is expressed; thus, since the object is not otherwise expressed (*anabhihite karmaṇi*), the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) applies, because it possesses the nature of a substance (*dravya*) whose state (*bhāva*) has been expressed by a *kṛt* suffix.

He explains the meaning of the agentive suffix (*kartṛpratyaya*) by stating, "he brings about the accomplishment of the cooking" (*pākasya nirvṛttiṃ karoti*). By saying "he does," he distinguishes Devadatta’s specific activity from the activities of the pot and other implements. Through such statements as "the pot and so forth also function toward the cooking because they bring it about, support it, and so on, and because [Devadatta] is their instigator (*tatprayojakatvāt*) within the context," he demonstrates both the general status of being a factor of action (*kārakatva*) and the fact that Devadatta’s specific agency consists in the absence of instigating other distinct factors of action. In this way, through various explanatory applications, one and the same meaning is explained, just as in the rule *vṛddhir ādaic* (Pāṇini 1.1.1).

This is the meaning: the term "vṛddhi" is a technical designation (*saṃjñā*) for the phonemes *ā*, *ai*, and *au*, as well as for the vowel *ā*—just like the explanatory rule [Pāṇini 1.1.72] which depends on what is already understood. Is this for the purpose of grasping the scope (*viṣayodgrāha*)?
Or for its own sake (*svārtha*), since all of this has a single, non-contradictory meaning?

Is it not the case that all meanings are non-contradictory? That which is the object (*karman*) in "he cooks rice" (*odanaṃ pacati*) is expressed by the genitive case as "the cooking of the rice" (*pāka odanasya*).

Furthermore, the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) in *pacati* expresses the agent (*kartṛ*), while the noun-forming suffix (*kṛt*) in the word *pāka* expresses the action (*bhāva*). In explaining that very same unprecedented *apūrva* [of the root], since it is answered by the verb *pac-* as "he performs cooking" (*pākaṃ karoti*), [the object] possesses the status of an object (*karmatva*).
As previously stated, in the sense of performing the accomplishment of the cooking, he explains the meaning of the agent-terminations (*kartṛ-pratyaya*):
"The pot and so forth also function in the act of cooking (*pacane vartate*)."...

Regarding the passage beginning with *ecośca*, etc., compare it with the following: "From those [vowels] as well, *e* and *o* are substituted when followed by an open vowel (*vivṛta*), and from those two, *ai* and *au* are likewise substituted.
