By means of various other applications such as *vam* and so forth, a single meaning is explained.

Thus, in all cases, the action (*pāka*) is established precisely in its state as the object-to-be-accomplished (*sādhya-rūpatā*), and it requires a means of accomplishment (*sādhana*). At that very time, its status as an object (*karmatva*) and its status as a residual factor (*śeṣa-rūpatva*) are not contradictory, because it exists for the sake of that [action], and because a residual factor is intended to be expressed as non-an agent (*akāraka*). Therefore, the conceptualization of [the action] as an object and so forth is not contradictory.
Therefore, your statement has been examined incorrectly in this way;
since the word is not the primary factor, how could it possess the power of conceptualization? Consequently, the verse should be read as follows:
"Whether by its own power or by all powers, [conceptualization] is constructed solely through its own object."

The fixed conceptualization of action and so forth regarding a single object, as well as the claim that the meaning of a word is "discursive speech" (*abhijalpa*), has been stated merely out of partiality; for there is no actual movement toward discursive speech [in the object],

and it is only when that [object] has attained the state of being discursive speech that it would become the denotable referent, through the identification of the word with its object by means of the connection "this is that."
And that is not so, because the word itself is the object;
for there is no object whatsoever that exists separately from the word,
and so forth.

In this manner of explanation, in all cases, the *pāka* (the act of cooking) remains established solely in its state as that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*), and thus it requires a means of accomplishment (*sādhana*). At that very time, it assumes the status of both the object (*karman*) and the subordinate element (*śeṣa*). Therefore, this is logical and non-contradictory; for, by virtue of being for the sake of that [accomplishment], that same object in its state of being to be accomplished is said to have attained the form of the object and the form of the subordinate, with its fulfillment dependent upon the means.

Why? Because the "remainder" (*śeṣa*) is intended as that which is not a factor of action (*akāraka*). For the "remainder" is defined as the non-intentional expression of those very factors of action that do exist; therefore, the conceptualization of action and so forth is not produced by the word, but pertains solely to the capacity of the object itself.
Thus, because there is no conclusion corresponding to the initial statement (*udgrāha*), your speech—which fails to properly consider its own meaning—is concluded as being "thus" (*evam*).
Consequently, since the word is subordinate and merely follows the established object, how could it possess the power of conceptualization? The meaning is that it does not.
Therefore, according to the aforementioned reasoning, the verse should be read as follows: "Whether from power (*śakti*) or from all-powerful [Śiva]," and so forth.

The specific particulars (*viśeṣāḥ*) are indeed powers (*śaktayaḥ*) in which the universal has become subordinate; for the employment of words is for the sake of those [particulars], since they are what is intended to be expressed. And our view is that "a word denotes its object exactly as it is" (Tattvārthabhāṣya 1.35); this is seen from the perspective of the principle of dual restriction (*ubhayaniyamanaya*).

Or, according to the view of the Supreme Lord (Vādaparameśvara) as stated [in the verse], "or of the all-powerful one," the conceptualization of action, object, accessory, agent, and so forth—belonging to a single reality that possesses non-contradictory specific powers or consists of multiple powers—is constructed by the object itself; it is not fixed or established by the subordinate word. (See *Aruddhakriyādi*, p. 573, l. 11, n. 2).
Let it be seen that on page 585, line 5,
according to the view of the Lord of Debate (Vādaparameśvara),
there would also be a syntactic connection here [in the phrase] "of one and the same object," as previously stated.

Furthermore, as for what you have postulated—that the meaning of a word is "verbal discourse" (*abhijalpa*)—this too has been stated merely out of your own partiality and simply to satisfy your own view, not through logical reasoning. Why? Because there is no such thing as the movement of verbal discourse; it will be explained that the movement of the word is itself the movement of the object.

And that sound, having attained the state of *abhijalpa* (internal verbalization), would reach the status of being denotable; it would express, or could be conceived as expressing, itself alone as having assumed the form of the object. By what reasoning? To this he says: "Because of the connection 'this is that,' through the unification of the word with the object. Precisely from your own statement, it follows that it is not the case that "having attained the state of *abhijalpa*, it reaches denotability. Why? Because the word itself is the object, and it is not that [other] thing.

He demonstrates the impossibility [of such a relation] with the words "for no one," and so forth, up to "by means of a relation. According to your view, that object with which a word might be identified cannot exist by means of a relation; for it has been established that because that particular (viśeṣa) is subordinate to the existence of the substance (dravyabhavana), it lacks primacy.

Even when an external object is being denoted by a name, that particular attribute by which it is characterized is subordinate to that name; for the employment of words is for the sake of conveying meaning, and [the word] functions under the influence of that [meaning], like a servant.
Furthermore, a name is subject to distinctions such as number and so forth, because it is a word corresponding to its object.

In the case of the word "tree" (*vṛkṣa*), although the fivefold nature of the word is its primary meaning, that which is unified [with it] is subordinate. Thus, if the object were established separately from the word, one might effect a unification of these two; however, that does not exist according to your own view, because for you there is no object [distinct from the word].
Furthermore, because a relation resides in two things, there is the establishment of distinct meanings; otherwise, there would be no relation.

Therefore, whichever specific quality is present, that very meaning possesses primacy. Since a noun is subordinate to the becoming of a substance (*dravyabhāva*), it is subordinate to the becoming of the substance. Because of that state—namely, its subordination to the becoming of the substance—the characteristic of formlessness belonging to this absolutely unprecedented embodied entity is a specific quality (*viśeṣa*) of the formless, while the characteristic of embodiment belongs to the formless.
Consequently, it is established that this specific quality possesses primacy.

This being the case, since the predominance of the particular is established, the predominance of the particular has thus been explained in that which is called "internal" (āntara), even though it is not fit for formal application— by means of the aesthetic essence (*rasa*) alone, indeed by means of the aesthetic essence alone.
Let it be seen on page 591, line 3:
*sambhāvyeta bhayor upapattyābhā* (in Bhāṣya) vs.
*sambhāvyeteto bhayor upapattyā* (in Yaśomitra).
According to your view, the word would be unified with that [external object] by means of a relation;
however, since that particular (viśeṣa) is subordinate to the substance and its becoming, it has been established that its primacy [belongs to the substance].

This remains true even when a name is employed externally: whatever particular it possesses is subordinate to that name, because the employment of a word is for the sake of conveying meaning, and because [the word's] activity proceeds under the control of that [meaning], like a servant.
And a name is subject to distinctions such as speech and so forth, because it is a word corresponding to its object;
thus, in the case of the word "tree," although the pentad [of sense-bases] is present, [it is designated by that name]. *Abhidharmapradīpa*.
In this passage, it appears that a great portion of the text has been lost in all the manuscripts;
we have therefore supplied it in this manner through conjecture, based on the respective context.
Because of the absence of those [names],
[it is] not suitable for the application of names [that are] unsuitable for application;
[it is] suitable for the application of names [that are] suitable for application.

Even when it is designated by the name of that which is being applied to it externally, whatever specific quality it possesses—that specific quality becomes its subordinate; that external [object] is subordinate to that very specific quality. This is because the employment of words is for the sake of conveying meaning, and a word is employed as dependent upon the object. He states this very point as the reason: "because it functions under its control. The example is "like a servant."

For a servant acts under the control of his master and is dependent upon him; he is subordinate. Likewise, the word is subordinate while the meaning is primary. The word functions under the influence of that [meaning] toward which it is employed; the specific meaning alone is primary. He demonstrates this: "The name (nāman) is subject to the distinctions of number and so forth. Number (*vacana*) refers to count; by the inclusion of "and so forth" (*ādi*), gender, tense, case-role (*kāraka*), person (*puruṣa*), and voice (*upagraha*) are understood as the distinctions. The name is subject to these.
He states the reason established in his own system for the definition of a word (*śabda*) as "because it is a word that accords with its object" (*yathārtha-śabdatvāt*).

Whatever object a word denotes according to its actual state—just as it denotes [the distinctions of] gender, number, tense, case-role (*kāraka*), person (*puruṣa*), and voice (*upagraha*)—so it is said by the teacher Siddhasena: "For where the object does not deviate from the speech, there is no deviation of the denotation."

Likewise, although commentators [hold that] the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is [the general form], nevertheless, because the application of words is preceded by the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*), the grammatical number (*vacana*) is prescribed as expressing precisely that number intended. Thus, because there is oneness (*ekatva*) in the tree, the singular (*ekavacana*) is used; "singular" is defined as the expression of one. By this, the meaning is established.

And so, in common usage when the word *vṛkṣa* (tree) is employed, it is understood that the universal (*sāmānya*) is subordinate (*upasarjana*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*) is primary (*pradhāna*), because through the comprehension of a single object, the exclusion of two or more is achieved.
Otherwise, there would be either a universal application, a lack of application, or doubt;
[for example,] the nominal stem occurs in relation to a tree.

Now, since particulars (viśeṣas) also lack independence and are unstable, it is indeed observed that the predominance belongs to the occurrence of the general (sāmānya), as seen in the case of speech and so forth; therefore, one departs from the particular, just as the singular number [is used] for the sake of the dual, or as the constellation Punarvasū [is treated as a single entity].
[In this context,] the cause is the action (karman).

In all cases, it is established in this very way: a word that denotes something endowed with actual existence (*bhāva*) is so called because it does not effect the desired [meaning] when there is a difference between name (*nāman*), representation (*sthāpanā*), and substance (*dravya*).
The illustration for the purpose of making this meaning known is "tree" (*vṛkṣa*), and so forth, along with its conceptualization (*sabhāvana*).

The meaning of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) consists of five factors: its own referent (*svārtha*), gender (*liṅga*), substance (*dravya*), number (*saṅkhyā*), and the case-role (*kāraka*) such as object (*karman*) and so forth; or it may consist of four or three factors, ending with number and substance. Likewise, although a fivefold meaning is possible for every verb (*ākhyāta*) as well—since there is no difference in their being "names" (*nāman*) according to the etymological derivation that they "bend" (*namayati*) or "convey" (*gamayati*) the meaning—nevertheless, because the application of a word is preceded by the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*), the word abandons the assumption of the totality [of meanings] and expresses only that single specific [meaning] which the speaker wishes to communicate.
When the singular, dual, and plural numbers are applicable, only that number which expresses the intended count is prescribed—namely, one of the three—and not the others.

Furthermore, the singular number [in the word *vṛkṣa*] is determined by the singularity of the individual tree, not by the universal (*sāmānya*) residing in all trees, because that [universal] serves no purpose.
The same applies to the dual and plural numbers as well.

Regarding the term *ekavacanam* (singular), because two types of compounds are possible, there arises a doubt; therefore, he determines it: "Is *ekavacanam* the expression of one (*ekasya vacanam*), or is it that which is both one and its expression (*ekaṃ ca tad vacanaṃ ca*)? It is said that the expression of one is *ekavacanam*; this is the meaning [of the compound]. By deriving the word thus—with the genitive case in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi ṣaṣṭhī*)—and so forth, and having established it in this way, it is understood in common usage that when the word *vṛkṣa* is employed, the general property (*sāmānya*) is subordinate (*upasarjana*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*) is primary (*pradhāna*).
Why? Because from the cognition of a single object there follows the exclusion of two or more;

otherwise, due to the predominance of the universal (*sāmānya*), there would be either a cognition of everything, no cognition at all, or doubt. However, the cognition of the particular (*viśeṣa*) is logical because the name (*nāman*) is subordinate to it;
the cultivation of that [particular] has already been explained—starting from "the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) refers to a tree" and so on, up to "it exists."
One should know that the Śabdanaya consists of words according to their actual meaning (*yathārthaśabda*), characterized by qualifying terms (*viśeṣitapada*). (Tattvārthabhāṣya 1.35)

He states the nature of sound: "One should know the word according to its actual meaning. By this, however, it is indicated that [the word] is indeed *evambhūta* (corresponding to the reality it denotes), because of its total purity.

Since he accepts this—that when an object is engaged in purposeful activity (*ceṣṭā*), then the designation "jar" (*ghaṭa*) is to be applied there and no other—why then are the *sāmprata* and *samabhirūḍha* not repeated? It is said in reply: those two are indeed also implied, since he says: "But the word 'qualified' (*viśeṣita*) refers to the *śabda-naya*."

The term "qualified word" (*viśeṣitapada*) refers to qualified cognition (*viśeṣitajñāna*). For the cognitions of the *sāmprata* and *samabhirūḍha* [nayas] are of a different kind: in the case of the *sāmprata*, there is the comprehension of an object from a word previously established for it among the [fourfold] categories such as name (*nāman*); whereas in the case of the *samabhirūḍha*, the meaning expressed by one word does not become the denotable referent (*abhidheya*) of another word. Such is the specific understanding of the *samabhirūḍha*.
—Thus, in the commentary on the *Tattvārthasūtra* composed by Siddhasena Gaṇi, [at] 1.35, page 128: "the specific inclusion of the grammatical factors (*kāraka*). (pra.)
Is it non-designation (anabhidhāna) according to Bhāṣya,
non-designation according to Yaśomitra,
or [simply] non-designation?
The *śabdanaya* is the standpoint of words alone;
by rejecting distinctions among things based on their objects, it considers distinctions among objects to be produced solely by words...
it accepts only that entity which is manifested by words possessing identical gender and other such attributes, and nothing else.

For a man is not a woman; if it were so intended, there would be a loss of the meaning of the word, since a word is used for the sake of denoting difference. Thus, from the perspective of gender (*liṅga*), we have "the star Svāti" and "the constellation"; from the perspective of number (*vacana*), we have "the neem, mango, and kadamba trees" as "the forest"; and from the perspective of person (*puruṣa*), we have "he cooks," "you cook," "I cook," "we two cook," and "we all cook. All such [distinctions] are unreal (*avastu*) because they involve a mutual contradiction of specific qualities.

Furthermore, on account of mutual contradiction, such things as these must be understood as non-entities (*avastu*); for example, "the cold fire" is a non-entity because its attributes are contradictory.

Likewise, "the bank is *taṭas*, *taṭī*, and *taṭam*" is a non-entity. Just as "red-blue" [is a contradiction], the wise accept that whatever is a real entity (*vastu*) possesses non-contradictory attributes, as in the case of "pot," "jar," and "vessel."
And so it is said: "For where the object does not deviate from the word, that is indeed expression.
Thus, this word possesses identical gender, number, person, and voice—so it is stated in the commentary (*vṛtti*) on the *Tattvārtha-sūtra* composed by Siddhasena Gaṇi (1).

See page 572, note 6. Although the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) [is singular], nevertheless, because the application of words is preceded by the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*), the grammatical number (*vacana*) is prescribed as expressing precisely the number intended.

And because the tree is a single entity, there is the singular number; "the expression of one" is called the singular number. By this, the meaning is established, and thus in common worldly usage, when the word *vṛkṣa* (tree) is employed, it is understood that the universal (*sāmānya*) is subordinate (*upasarjana*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*) is primary (*pradhāna*). This is because the understanding of a single object results in the exclusion of two or more; otherwise, there would be either a comprehension of everything, a lack of comprehension, or doubt.
The nominal stem (*prātipadika*) occurs in the word "tree" (*vṛkṣa*).
But surely, since even particulars lack self-dependence and do not persist, the predominance belongs precisely to the becoming of the universal.
For indeed, speech and so forth are observed to deviate from that specific [rule]; just as the singular number may have the sense of the dual, as in "the *nakṣatra* Punarvasū," and likewise,
the cause (*hetu*) and the action (*karman*) function in exactly this same way everywhere.
See page 596, line 8.
This is also cited in Koṭṭārya’s commentary on the *Viśeṣāvaśyakabhāṣya*:

the intention is that because those things expressed by name (*nāma*), expressed by representation (*sthāpanā*), expressed by substance (*dravya*), or expressed by different genders (*liṅga*) and so forth do not bring about the intended object, the Śabdanaya accepts only that which is endowed with actual existence (*bhāva*).
See page 56, line 13:
"That which has meaning, is not a verbal root (dhātu), and is not an affix (pratyaya) is a nominal stem (prātipadika).
2.45. With the exception of a stem (dhātu), an affix (pratyaya), and that which ends in an affix, a meaningful verbal form shall be designated as a nominal stem (prātipadika).
— Pāṇinian Siddhāntakaumudī, Fourth Trika, see page 568, line 11.
Here he says: "But surely, even of the particulars," and so forth.

For those particulars are also entirely dependent; therefore, because they lack self-autonomy and because there would be an infinite regress, the predominance of the universalization (*sāmānyabhavana*) alone [is established].

Indeed, a singular number like that of the word *vṛkṣa* (tree) is not observed everywhere. If it were so, there might be a predominance of the particular; therefore, since particulars are subject to deviation, the predominance of the universal alone is logical.

Do not think that there is an invariable concomitance due to the predominance of specific distinctions (*viśeṣa*); for indeed, speech and other such things are seen to deviate from those specific distinctions. In the world, one observes the transgression of their own established state by specific distinctions—such as number, gender, tense, grammatical case, person, and voice—as well as their departure from the specific distinction that is their own coreferential substratum.

Examples of this are: the singular number used in the sense of the dual, as in "the *nakṣatra* Punarvasū," and so forth, with meanings that are straightforward, up until the cause is [treated as] the object (*karman*).

It is exactly the same everywhere as in the final example cited, where there is deviation from a non-distinct mark (*liṅga*). This applies to the preceding cases as well, such as speech and so forth; therefore, because there is no stability in the particular (*viśeṣa*), a particular cannot truly be a particular.
Consequently, it would not exist at all, because it is undifferentiated, unstable, and lacks autonomy, like a sky-flower.

Furthermore, the universal (*sāmānya*) also does not exist, because there is no agent to bring it about, because it lacks autonomy, because it exists in isolation, and because it is like one who is liberated—since it cannot be sublated by anything through its arising or non-arising in the absence of any other object.

Now, if that object also exists as distinct from the word, then it is not the word itself that has become the "expressed" (vācya) through the process of coalescence (abhijalpa); rather, the object is what is expressed.

This is because, just like the word, the object is established as separate [from the cognition] since it is unified with the word by means of their relation; for both are equal in being unified, like milk and water.
Furthermore, as stated previously, because it is the object of comprehension, the object is indeed the object itself, just like the parts of the object within the coalesced expression.
In the case of the deviation of a particular, there is the conceptualization of that [particular];
therefore, because particulars do not have a stable existence, a particular cannot truly be a particular, since its form is permeated by generality and its nature as a particular lacks stability.

What follows from this? Consequently, it would not exist at all; it would not even experience coming into being, because it is non-distinct from what was just mentioned. Its non-distinction is due to its lack of stability, just as was explained; and its lack of stability is due to its inability to abide in itself and its lack of self-mastery, exactly as was explained.
"Like a sky-flower" is the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) applied everywhere;
alternatively, even though there is no distinction [between them], all three reasons (*hetu*) have the sky-flower as their illustrative example.
Therefore, and so forth...

And consequently, because there would be no distinction, even the universal (*sāmānya*) would not exist; why? Because of the absence of an instigator (*pravartaka*). For the universal, which is the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛti*), such as "becoming" (*bhavana*) and so forth, and which consists of action (*kriyātman*), its instigator would have to be the agent (*kartṛ*), which is the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*); that [agent] is the particular (*viśeṣa*). In the absence of that, the universal does not proceed.

If it is asked why the particular (*viśeṣa*) does not cause [the universal] to function, while the universal (*sāmānya*) does, [the answer is: because of its independence. For the particular is independent; it is not dependent on anything else. Why? Because it functions in isolation (*viviktavṛttitvāt*). How so? Like liberated beings (*mukta*). Just as liberated souls, being free from subjection to karma, function in isolation—they do not cause anything to function, nor are they caused to function by anything, but rather they exist by themselves—therefore, these are the examples based on the commonality of non-causality. Likewise, the particular is non-causal.
Or rather, it is simply non-existent, for due to the absence of a causal agent, it is not existent like the universal, which is like a sky-flower.

He explains that: because it is not sublated by anything through the presence or absence of other objects, and because there is no other object due to its particularity (viśeṣa). [Note: The text contains scribal fragments such as "vacana" and "pra°" which appear to be marginalia or citations.]
Because of this non-abiding of the particularity (*viśeṣa*), the particularity cannot truly be a particularity;
therefore, it would not exist at all, because it is undifferentiated, non-abiding, and lacks self-mastery, like a flower in the sky.

Consequently, even the universal (*sāmānya*) does not exist at all, because there is no agent that causes it to function, because it is independent, and because it exists in isolation like a liberated being; furthermore, it cannot be sublated by anything, since its existence or non-existence is not determined by the presence or absence of another object. Now, if that object also exists as distinct from the word, then the word itself is not the denotatum (*vācya*)—even when it has attained the state of "blending" (*abhijalpa*)—for that [object] is established separately from the word, since they are unified through a relation, just like milk and water; for when both are unified, they are equal.

Moreover, as previously stated, because it is that which is to be made known (*pratyāyyatva*), the object (*artha*)—just like the parts of the verbal expression (*abhijalpa*)—is indeed the object itself;
from the cultivation of that [object], there is a distinction [in the object].
[This concerns] the establishment of the linguistic entity (*vacanavasthāna*).
Because of its non-existence, would it not exist as a reality?
See page 568, line 1.

Lest this fault arise in the absence of an object, suppose that object does indeed exist as something distinct from the word, such that its manifold nature is rendered one [by the word]. What follows from this? It turns out that it is not the word itself—whether as the word-meaning or as having attained the state of *abhijalpa*—that is the denotable object; rather, it follows that there must be a specific power (*śakti*) distinct from the word, or else the object, possessing all powers, must be something other [than the word].

Therefore, what you have stated is also illogical—namely, that "they call that [cognition] the verbal expression of the word, and that word is the meaning"—because, just as the word is, so too is the object established as distinct, since they are unified through their relationship. Why is this so? Because both are equal in being unified, like milk and water; this is the demonstration of the concomitance between the property to be proven and the probans.

Furthermore, in the passage beginning with "api ca," it was already stated previously that [the word] has the object as its referent because it is what is to be made known (*pratyāyyatva*), just like the components of a verbal designation (*abhijalpa*). Therefore, the reminder of that meaning is redundant. See page 580, line 4; see page 585, line 1. The restriction is that the object is precisely as far as its meaning extends.
See page 590,
line 12: "And when this is so, then our own position alone is accepted, because of the reality of the object."
That which is this sound is not that [object]; it is indeed something other than that.
The sound has such an object as its domain; the object is not the domain of the sound.
By that sound, the object is sought (*aryate*), and therefore it is called "the object" (*artha*); it is understood.
The movement of the word is nothing other than the movement of the meaning;

and this being so, it is the speaker’s intention—conditioned by the appropriate word—that superimposes its respective power upon the intellect of the listener. Thus, the passage you cited is consistent with this view: "Only an appropriate word, not an inappropriate one, is employed—whether intentionally, as in 'let there be play,' or unintentionally, like the cawing of a crow—because it is impossible to unify [the word and the meaning] when there is a discrepancy between them."
The word *hi* also has the sense of a reason (*hetvarthe*), [meaning] "because" the capacity for yoga... or by way of a limit (*maryādayā*).

Furthermore, as for the two verses beginning with "If those two were not of a non-distinct nature," etc., even that results in our own position alone: their non-distinct nature arises from conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) through metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), like the expression "going on the road. And when, according to the sequence stated in the verse "And when thus," there is separate establishment and predominance of the object, then our position—that words denote objects according to reality—is precisely what has been accepted, because the object is the reality.

He explains that: "That which is this word is not the object; for it has been stated that 'the word is not the object, the object itself is the object. Therefore, distinct from this object which is directly indicated, that [word] is indeed something else, being indirectly indicated.
Thus, the word has precisely such an object as its domain—that is, the object as its domain; the object does not have the word as its domain, nor is it subordinate. This is the meaning.

The meaning (*artha*) is so called because it is understood (*aryate*) by that word. What is meant by this? It is said: "it is understood" (*gamyate*). The root *ṛ* (in the sense of "going," *pāṇini-dhātu-pāṭha*) has as its meaning the object of the word; since the possessor of the object (*viṣayin*) is dependent upon the object (*viṣaya*), the understanding of the meaning is itself the understanding of the word, not something separate or independent for the word itself. Thus has been explained the predominance of the meaning and its distinctness [from the word]. [The roots] *ṛ* and *sṛ* (both in the sense of "going," *pāṇini-dhātu-pāṭha* 1098 and 1498) [are used here].
The root *ṛ* (pāṇini-dhātupāṭha 936) means "to go" or "to reach";
see page 587, line 24.

And thus, by saying "having done so," etc., we shall demonstrate the excellence of our qualities in our own system; as for the passage you cited beginning with "the word 'worthy'" and ending with "superimposes," that text is consistent with this philosophical view.

He explains this: only a suitable word—such as the word "jar" for an object characterized by a broad base and so forth—is appropriate, not an unsuitable one such as the word "cloth" or any other which might be employed arbitrarily, like the cawing of a crow, either intentionally or without prior reflection. Why? Because of the lack of correspondence with the object (*arthavisaṃvādāt*). This lack of correspondence with the object means there is no relationship between the signified and the signifier; and that [relationship], because it cannot be unified, cannot be established.

The word *hi* [in the phrase] "also, moreover," and so forth, is used here in the sense of a reason (*hetvartha*) in the passage "for [it is] based on the word 'yogya'"; since [it begins with] "because of the capacity for yoga" and so on, its explanation is already understood up to the point "or by way of limitation"— see page 582, line 9,
as stated by you.

Regarding the passage beginning with "yadapi ca" and ending with "so'yamityabhisambandhāt," it was stated that the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) being the object of verbal expression (*abhijalpa*) supports our own position.

Furthermore, that which was stated subsequently for the purpose of demonstrating the pervasion of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and for the purpose of establishing the conventional usage of words and meanings as they exist in the world—that too results in our own position that the meaning [of a word] is distinct from the word itself. What is the fruit of this? It is these two verses beginning with *vākyapadīye* regarding their non-distinct nature. We determine here: their non-distinct nature arises from convention (*rūḍhi*), that is, from worldly cognition; and because of the metaphorical application (*upacāra*) of that [non-distinctness] to what is not that, there is the metaphorical attribution of non-difference to things that are distinct.

What is it like? It is like the act of going on a path. Just as when one says, "The path goes to Pāṭaliputra," the path—which is actually devoid of motion—is said to go because of the metaphorical attribution (upacāra) of non-difference from the person’s movement; because that [movement] is invariably concomitant with it, and because the two have a dual sense, it is so expressed. Likewise, because word and meaning are inseparable and invariably concomitant, and because of the metaphorical attribution of non-difference based on worldly convention, they possess a non-distinct nature, even though they are indeed distinct entities. Furthermore, [the word exists] through the existence of the other, like a good friend.

Thus, in common worldly usage, a word functions having assumed the form of an object; however, in the science of grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), it functions having assumed the form of a word. Just as there is a distinction between the activity directed toward the comprehension of a word and the activity directed toward an object—wherein the object "cow" has a distinct form consisting of the dewlap and so forth, while the word, being for the sake of that object, consists merely of the sequence of phonemes such as *ga* and the like, which are nothing more than sounds perceived by the ear—for that [sequence] can never become the object, nor can it be conceived as such, because it is unstable, disordered, and non-restrictive.
The external object, however, is established as distinct and determinate;
therefore, a word does not exist having attained the form of the object.

Even if it were so attained, it would be through its own relation—since a relation resides in two things, the identity of word and object would follow from that relation—and not otherwise, as has been stated.
The fact that the knowledge of what is correct and incorrect has the purpose of regulating merit (*dharma-niyama*) also indicates the separate establishment of the object;

because of the predominance of one and the subordination of the other, since the word is subordinate and the object is predominant, there is indeed a dual nature [of the word]. How so? Like a good friend. Just as between two affectionate friends who are separately established yet engaged in a single task, there is a rule of mutual predominance and subordination, so it is with word and object. And that is established from your own statement alone, as you have said: "Only in some cases... (p. 580, l. 3).

thus, in common worldly usage, speech proceeds having attained the form of meaning, whereas in the science of grammar, it proceeds having attained the form of the word itself. Furthermore, the form of the object, such as a cow with its dewlap and so forth, is distinct [from the word]; for since the word exists for the sake of that object, the sequence of phonemes such as *ga* and so on is merely an auditory sound.

whereas the external object is stable, non-intermingled, and restrictive.

even if it were attained, it would be so only through its own relationship, because a relationship resides in two things and thus implies the unification of the word and the object, and not otherwise.

Otherwise, there would indeed be futility;

The distinction lies in the fact that its activity proceeds for the sake of apprehending the word, just as in the case of the verb *bhavati*. The intended meaning is that the nature of the cow consists of its dewlap and so forth as distinct from those objects, whereas the nature of the word "cow" consists of the sequence of phonemes beginning with *ga*; this [distinction] is merely conceptual, being purely imagined.

The external object, however, remains established; for even amidst a confusion of hundreds of words differentiated by place, time, and so forth, the word "jar" is applied to its own denotation—such as that which has a curved neck—and is thus non-confused and restricted. This is because it must necessarily be expressed in order to convey [the object], such that by that very word, that very thing is understood, and a cognition arises specifically regarding that object.

Therefore, due to its being established, non-confused, and restricted, the external object is distinct from the word, owing to the difference in their forms, and distinct from other words or those that are merely conceptualized.
Consequently, the word does not exist as having attained the form of the object.

Even granting that the realization of their non-distinct nature arises from conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), because this realization is invariable for these two, once it is established, the relationship between the signifier and the signified—being a relation that resides in both parties—must consist of a unification of word and object; as has been stated, the specific relationship between the word "jar" and its object cannot exist without their being distinct [yet unified], since unification is otherwise impossible. Therefore, he says: "Not otherwise, as previously stated.
Furthermore, in the *Vākyapadīya* (2.1), it is said that in the treatise (*śāstra*), however, both forms are distinguished according to the speaker’s intention.

And in this very way, [the statement] beginning with "through perception and conceptualization" (darśanotprekṣābhyām) is consistent with the establishment of external objects from words; otherwise, what would be perception? What would be conceptualization?... Furthermore, the claim that "from what [source] is conventional discourse (abhijalpa) to be abandoned, as it is the cause for the engagement with other scriptures?"—this too is not tenable in the case of conventional discourse as imagined by you.

If sound were not set in motion by word and meaning—which, being non-agents, function as instrument and object—then because it possesses a conscious nature, the soul would be an independent agent; thus, this [position] follows our own view. Furthermore, the sequence found in Patañjali’s *Mahābhāṣya*—"one who is skilled applies [words] to their specific distinctions"—and so forth, does not otherwise hold true for the correctness (*sādhutva*) of the word "cow" (*go*) when applied to that which possesses a dewlap and so on, nor for its incorrectness (*asādhutva*) in cases like "gaṇī" due to conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), nor for the correctness of "gaṇī" in the sense of "covering" when a specific meaning is intended to be expressed, provided that the word, its referent, and the relationship between them are established as distinct entities.

Furthermore, regarding the purpose of that knowledge of correct and incorrect forms, it has been stated [in the *Pāṇini-vārttika*] that "the restriction of merit (*dharma-niyama*) [is the purpose] once the relationship between word and meaning is established. This too indicates the separate establishment of the meaning;

for words are employed by people toward an object to be denoted either for the sake of a specific purpose or [simply] because the object exists. In that case, since the object is established separately from the word, the restriction on the use of the correct word—which has that object as its domain—is prescribed by the treatise for the sake of merit (*dharma*), just like the rules concerning what is fit to be eaten and what is not.
Therefore, the meaning is not a mere mental verbalization (*abhijalpa*).

...If, then, the world is the authority regarding these words, what is accomplished by the treatise? When the use of words is prompted by worldly purpose, the treatise establishes a restriction for the sake of *dharma*.
What is this "restriction for the sake of *dharma*"? It is a restriction (*niyama*) for the sake of *dharma*; hence, it is called a "restriction for the sake of *dharma*" (*dharmaniyama*).
Or, *dharmaniyama* is a restriction for the sake of *dharma*;
or, *dharmaniyama* is a restriction whose purpose is *dharma*. — Pāṇini-Mahābhāṣya 1.1.43.
1.1 The rule concerning what may and may not be eaten. Primary [section].
Regarding the rule concerning what is fit to be eaten and what is not:
in the world, it is said that the domestic cock is unfit to be eaten and the domestic pig is unfit to be eaten;
furthermore, that which is called "fit to be eaten" (bhakṣya) is taken up for the purpose of counteracting hunger.
It is possible for one to satisfy hunger even with dog meat and the like;
yet, a restriction is established therein: "This is edible, this is inedible.

...so too here, although the comprehension of meaning is the same whether by means of a correct word (*śabda*) or an incorrect word (*apaśabda*), a restriction regarding *dharma* is established: that the meaning must be expressed only by a correct word and not by an incorrect word.
When this is observed, it becomes a cause for spiritual prosperity (*abhyudaya*).

In the same way, regarding the passage beginning with "cetyādi," there is also a detailed exposition (*varṇakadaṇḍaka*) of the very meaning expressed in these three verses, starting with "by means of perception (*darśana*) and conceptualization (*utprekṣā*)," and so forth. Views such as [the world] being composed of *pradhāna*, *puruṣa*, *īśvara*, and so on, are consistent with the establishment of external objects from words; however, when the external object—such as a jar—is a non-differentiated reality, the conceptualizations of persons regarding its existence as permanent, impermanent, and so on, occur only through a restrictive rule (*niyamena*), and not otherwise.

Otherwise, as indicated by the phrase "it would be different," if there were no fixed external object due to the identity of the mental designation (*abhijalpa*) and the object, views such as that of *pradhāna* would be impossible.
In that case, what view could there be? The meaning is that none exists.

"What kind of imagination? and so forth; according to that text, he demonstrates the impossibility [of such imagination] along with its logical justification, up to the point: "Why should verbal designation (*abhijalpa*) be abandoned? This inclusive statement has already been explained.
The summary meaning is: [imagination] is not possible in the absence of an object, whereas it is appropriate when an object exists (pṛ.

The intention here is that the conceptualization by persons of an external object such as a jar—which is a single, undivided entity—as being permanent, impermanent, and so forth, is possible; however, this is not possible in the absence of an external object. If there is dissatisfaction with this, one should instead read the text as "vastuni bhinne" (in a divided entity), though this reading does not appear in the Tubhā manuscript.

Regarding the meaning "from what [source] is discursive proliferation (*abhijalpa*) to be abandoned, since it is accessible through causes," the reading exactly as heard is correct; otherwise, however, the readings "from what [source] is discursive proliferation not to be abandoned" or "from what [source] is discursive proliferation the denotable object" might be possible here—
see page 581, line 25.

Furthermore, the reason for the occurrence of another Vedic text (*śrutyantara*) is also not tenable according to your imagined discourse, whereas it is indeed tenable according to our position. For example: "another Vedic text" means a Vedic text distinct from [the first]; it would be a sound (*dhvani*) that has emerged as something separate from the internalized discourse (*abhijalpa*), and it would conform to linguistic usage. However, that [sound] could not be set in motion by the word and its meaning as you conceive them—since they are non-agents, insentient, and [merely] instruments and objects; rather, it must be the cause for the occurrence of another Vedic text.

When the word and its meaning have become one and exist within [the cognition], what other "hearing" (*śruti*) could there be that might be called a "subsequent hearing"? And by what distinction is it said to be the cause for the operation of that [subsequent hearing]? There is indeed a distinction, as follows: because the effect—the production of a sound consisting of articulated noise—is observed for the purpose of conveying the object "jar," the jar-word, which is the corresponding cause, is inferred; the object is not so inferred, because it is of a different nature.
Therefore, it is the hearing that initiates another hearing, because it is a hearing, and neither the object nor the self [can do so].
Now, since that other scripture is also a *śruti*, the word is set in motion toward its object just as in the previous *śruti*; for in the absence of an object, usage would be purposeless.

The word "abhijalpate" (speaks toward) means it speaks toward the object; the object "abhijalpati" (speaks back to) that word; thus, "abhijalpa" is said to be precisely that which has the object as its domain.
In this way, the view of Bhartṛhari and others is indeed untenable.

Since sound and meaning function respectively as instrument and object, and since the self is conscious by nature, it is independent; being independent, it is the agent, and as such, it must be the cause of the activity of the other Vedic revelation, as it has been said:
"The self, through the intellect, accomplishes its objects" (Pāṇinīya Śikṣā).

This and other such statements constitute an improper analysis by speaking of "another scripture" (*śrutyantaram*). For when word and meaning exist internally as one, what other scripture could there be that would be called "another scripture"? Therefore, in the absence of any distinction, how can the undifferentiated essence of the Word (*śabdātmā*) be spoken of as differentiated by those who are not deluded? And by what specific distinction—apart from the absence of another scripture—is it said to be the cause for its manifestation? Since another scripture is impossible without the specific agency (*kartṛtva-viśeṣa*) produced by consciousness and sovereignty, what could possibly be the cause for its manifestation?

Having become manifold, having become differentiated and distinct,
it would proceed; [thus] it ought to be the cause of the manifestation of another scripture.

When the word and its meaning have become one and exist within [the cognition], what other "hearing" (*śruti*) could there be that might be called a "different hearing"? And by what distinction is it said to be the cause for the application [of the word]?
There is indeed a distinction;

namely, because the effect—the production of a sound consisting of articulated phonemes—is observed for the purpose of conveying the object "jar," an antecedent cause corresponding to that [effect] is inferred as the word "jar," but not the object itself, because the object is of a different nature.
Therefore, one scripture is the motivator of another scripture because it is a scripture; it is neither the object nor the self [of that other].

But surely, since that other scripture is also a scripture, its word must be motivated by an object, just like the previous scripture, for in the absence of an object, its employment would be purposeless.
A word "chatters" (*jalpati*) toward an object; the object "chatters back" at it, and thus the chattering directed toward that very object is called "abhijalpa."
Thus, for the time being, the view of Bhartṛhari and others is untenable;
[it is] the cause of comprehension,
[as stated in] Prajñālaṅkāra, page 565, line 14.
"Because it has become so, and because in the absence of another scriptural authority its application [occurs]," this appears most excellent;
here he says: "There is a distinction."
For example: "In order to convey the object 'jar,' and so forth.

Because effects conform to their causes, and because we observe the effect consisting in the production of sound in the form of phonemes (*dhvani*), that which is internal to it—its corresponding cause—is inferred, just as a rice seed is inferred from the sight of a rice sprout. It is not the object characterized by a long neck and so forth [that is inferred], because it is dissimilar to that [sound]. Furthermore, for the auditory perception (*śruti*), the appropriate material cause (*upādāna*) is necessarily sound itself, not an object such as a jar, because of the dissimilarity between them.
Therefore, it is not the case that one scripture is the motivator of another scripture, nor is it the object, nor even the self; this is the distinction.
To this, it is replied: "But for that other scripture as well," and so forth.

This inference too is sublated by a counter-reasoning (*pratitarka*): that scripture which motivates an object such as a pot already present within consciousness is [itself] a scripture, because it possesses the nature of being a scripture.
But was it not previously stated: "A word is employed for the purpose of conveying a meaning, not without purpose like the cawing of a crow; let it rather be a mere plaything," and so forth?
Therefore, because it is a *śruti* (scriptural utterance), a word is set in motion toward a meaning just like a previous *śruti*; for in the absence of a meaning, its employment would be purposeless.
Thus, [the claim that it is] meaningless is refuted.
And so forth; see page 591, line 6.

The etymological meaning of *abhijalpa* also fits [this interpretation] and not otherwise. According to the roots *japa* and *jalpa* (Dhātupāṭha 397, 398), which mean "in distinct speech," a word (*śabda*) speaks toward an object; the object employs that [word], and thus the object "speaks toward" (*abhijalpayati*). That which has this as its object is called *abhijalpa*. If one speaks toward an object situated directly before one, then *jalpa* is the word; since that object is its domain, the word whose domain is that [object] is *abhijalpa*. What is meant by this is: in the conceptualization of word and object, it would be more logical for the word to have the object as its domain; the conceptualization of the word as *abhijalpa*—where the word is produced by the object—would be more logical than in your own proposed view where the word is merely impelled [by the speaker].

Thus, the view of Bhartṛhari and others is first of all untenable. As for Vasurāta’s statement that Bhartṛhari’s teacher arranges the meaning inherent in the word-form itself through internal differentiation— by which both word and meaning are accepted—

that [teacher] is nonetheless unable, by means of that theory of words (*śabdanaya*), to avoid such defects as the absence of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between different genders and so forth.

But surely, by saying "according to the internal division of the object which follows the word," you have stated that the word is dependent on the object (arthatantra), not that the object is dependent on the word (śabdatantra).
Therefore, because the application of the word is dependent on the object, those same defects [previously mentioned] remain as they were. (p.

Just as color-form (*rūpa*) and other such qualities, being individual entities, do not depend on another synonym because they are specific particulars (*viśeṣa*), so too [the terms] *puṣya*, *tārā*, *nakṣatra*, and so forth—possessing masculine gender and the like—are mutually exclusive due to the nature of specific particulars; how, then, could there be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)? As for what Vasurāta, the teacher of Bhartṛhari, stated—that [the word] "follows its own form" (*svarūpānugata*) and so on—he admitted both the word and the object, since a relation must reside in two relata.

Compared to the utterly blind perception of the former, this perception of one afflicted by cataracts (*taimirika*) is closer to the vision of reality; it has not yet departed far from it. However, even that [perception] is discarded by [the vision of reality], for its nature consists of verbal conceptualization (*abhijalpa*).
Furthermore, "but not by him" and so forth.

Even in this view, just as the meanings of the words "puṣya" and "artha" are internally contained without distinction despite the differences in their respective gender, number, and case-role (*kāraka*), so too will that [proponent] incorporate other genders and so forth belonging to other word-meanings, even though they differ from the desired gender and so on. Thus, by the *śabdanaya*, which asserts that the particular is primary while the universal is subordinate, he is simply unable to avoid the faults such as the lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
Why is this so? Indeed, because [the object] conforms to the words, and so forth.

An object follows its own essential nature (*svarūpa*); by stating that "one [perceives] that object through internal differentiation," it is declared that the word is dependent upon the object (*arthatantra*), not that the object is dependent upon the word (*śabdatantra*). If the word, following the object, were arranged through internal differentiation, then because the word would be impelled [by the object], the object would be excluded from the determination of the word. However, the opposite is the case: by excluding the determination of the word, one takes recourse in the primacy of the object.

Therefore, because the application of words is dependent upon the object—that is, because the word's function is primarily directed toward the object—the object is indeed the motivator of the word. Consequently, those defects [previously mentioned] remain in that state; however, they would be avoided if one were to determine that the word itself is primary.

Thus, according to the theory that the particular (viśeṣa) is primary, there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between particulars such as Puṣya, Tārā, and Nakṣatra when they are independent of other objects. Therefore, the particular alone remains established.

Is it "of the proponent of a different object" (vādinārthāntara°), as in the Bhāṣya,
or "by the proponent of a different object" (vādinārthāntara°), as in the Yaśomitra commentary? Or perhaps "of the proponent of a different object" (vādino'rthāntara°)?

This [explanation] has first been provided regarding the conceptualization of the various synonyms for an entity (*vastu*) that transcend the range of words; now, by means of this, an extension (*atideśa*) is made to the various synonyms for phonemes (*vyañjana*). The phrase "and just as," etc., constitutes the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*): even those things such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth, which are intended to be produced simultaneously, consist in the production of each one individually and do not depend on another synonym, because they are specific particulars (*viśeṣa*).

Terms such as *puṣya*, *tārā*, and *nakṣatra*—which possess masculine gender and so forth—are mutually contradictory because their specific attributes (*viśeṣa*) are opposed; this is the illustrative example (*dārṣṭāntika*). Since there is only one single "becoming" (*bhavana*) and no second, how can there be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)? How could that which is *puṣya* and masculine become feminine, i.e., *tārā*, or neuter, i.e., *nakṣatra*? In this way, the distinctions of number, time, case-role (*kāraka*), person (*puruṣa*), voice (*upagraha*), and so forth, are not mutually dependent, because there is only a single becoming of the specific attribute (*viśeṣa-bhavana*). Thus should it be contemplated: "becoming, becoming" (*bhavanaṃ bhavanaṃ*).
And this is the view of the Śabdanaya: "Word is the designation of an object according to its reality" (Tattvārthabhāṣya 1.35).

Likewise, because it does not effect the desired [designation] for objects distinct from name, representation, and substance—such as gender and so forth—a word denotes that which is endowed with actual existence (*bhāva*).

However, in order to demonstrate that the *sthāpanā* (representation) included within the scope of the Vyavahāranaya does not effect the desired [designation], the nature of the *sthāpanā* and *dravya* (substance) meanings is first explained.
That in which one abides is the "place" (sthāna).
By what is one made to abide? Since no specific [place] is mentioned, it would follow that [the soul] goes everywhere;
so where does one abide? One abides in the form (ākāra).
The suffix *ākāra* denotes either a limit (*maryādā*) or an inclusive range (*abhividhi*);
in this case, it is *abhividhi*.
The phrase "and thus it is so" (*evañcaitaditi*) and so forth constitutes the application (*upanaya*) of the stated meaning.

In this regard, the view of the Śabdanaya (the perspective of words) is as follows: it is only logical that a word denotes its object exactly as it is; and the definition of a word is that which denotes its object exactly as it is (Tattvārthabhāṣya 1.35).

Likewise, another definition is that "a word denotes the actual state (*bhāva*) because it does not perform the intended function regarding those things expressed by different genders and so forth in terms of name (*nāman*), representation (*sthāpanā*), and substance (*dravya*).

In this regard, by means of its specific divisions, the object denoted as substance (*dravya*) and substantial-object (*dravyārtha*)—which was previously stated and accepted in the earlier systems—is excluded by this [definition] as being within the scope of the *naigama* and other [lower] viewpoints. Furthermore, that which is within the scope of the *vyavahāra* [viewpoint] and is denoted as name (*nāman*) and substantial-object (*dravyārtha*)—which is also accepted [by the *śabda-naya*]—is now excluded by this [definition], because it does not perform the intended function.

The Śabdanaya proceeds by considering that which is expressed through different genders and so forth—namely, the object-sphere (*gocara*) of the *ṛjusūtra* and its synonyms (*arthaparyāya*)—to be improper, thinking, for instance, that "speech and so forth must be correct. Furthermore, the manner in which his view regarding the word (*śabda*) is established has been demonstrated through reasoning in another way;
and thus the teacher Siddhasena also says: (p. 573).

vācanādi pra॰.
Is it thus by another way? Is it of such a kind?
And so, the Master says:
"Name, representation, and substance—this is the fourfold application (nikṣepa) for one who maintains the substantial standpoint (dravyārthika)."
"Existence (bhāva), however, is the exposition of the standpoint of modes; this is the ultimate truth. — *Sanmati-tarka-prakaraṇa* 1.6.

Now, desiring to differentiate the general category of "representation" (*sthāpanā*)—which has not yet been distinguished from the "substantial object" (*dravyārtha*)—the author establishes a connection: for the purpose of demonstrating that what is expressed by representation, when it falls within the scope of the conventional standpoint (*vyavahāra-naya*), does not perform its intended function. This will be demonstrated as follows: representation belonging to the conventional standpoint does not effect its desired referent; however, since this cannot be demonstrated unless the nature of representation and the substantial object is understood, the nature of representation and the substantial object is first explained.

In that context, the action of causing one who is standing— the agent of the action of staying— to stand, which is inherent in the instigator and expressed by the causative suffix (*ṇic*), is the action of "establishing" (*sthāpanā*), according to the rule *ṇyāsa-śrantho yuc* (Pāṇini 3.3.107).

Desiring to speak of that [topic], he first explains the term *sthāna* (place/abode): "That in which one stands is a *sthāna*. First, regarding the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) among the categories of being (*bhāva*), instrument (*karaṇa*), substratum (*adhikaraṇa*), and object (*karman*), he says:

because of its connection with the meaning to be explained, *sthāna* is "being" (*bhāva*), which is action (*kriyā*). It is "stood" (*sthīyate*) by the agent who stands; therefore, for the sake of determining that, he asks: "By what is it stood?
The reply to that is: "Because no specific [agent] is mentioned, it is all-pervasive (*sarvagati*)."

The word *iti* has the sense of a reason (*hetu*); because [it is said] "the abode of one who possesses consciousness, such as Devadatta, or of that which is without consciousness, such as a jar," and since the specific subject has not been stated, [the author] asks—in order to determine the general locus by means of whatever [subject] it may be, namely, "in what is one to abide?"—as it is said:
"one abides in the *ākāra*."

The prefix *ā* is used in the senses of limit (*maryādā*) and inclusion (*abhividhi*). It functions either as a limit or through inclusion, which is to say, pervasion. Since the roots *bhū* (to be) and *kṛ* (to do) pervade the meanings of all verbal roots, "inclusion" refers here to the completion of the form under discussion. Thus, it means "making [it] so" (*ākaraṇa*). The "place" (*sthāna*) therein is by way of a limit;
or, the limit is the distinctness of this place from other forms. Its purpose is its establishment (*sthāpanā*).

Standing slightly with one-pointed concentration is "standing" (*sthāna*); standing by oneself through non-existence (*asadbhāva*) while being established everywhere as a qualified object is "standing. This is like being employed for a single, indeterminate action, or like a pillar [supporting] Indra despite not being of his nature due to non-existence. Likewise, it applies to the senses and so forth;

therefore, the meaning is that when various substances such as children arise with distinctions of name and state, there is the manifestation of the undifferentiated form of Devadatta, which is the instrument of appearance.

Therein, he explains *abhividhi* (inclusive limit): *abhividhi* is completion (*parisamāpana*) or pervasion (*abhivyāpti*). Of what? Of the form, nature, or essential being (*vastvātman*) under discussion. By that *abhividhi*, which is the completion of the form under discussion, there is the act of making (*ākaraṇa*) or becoming (*ābhavana*); in that [act], "standing" (*sthāna*) or "limit" (*maryādā*) are used as synonyms. Thus he connects the terms.

What is the limit (*maryādā*)? It means the distinctness from other forms, the exclusion of other forms, which is a restriction. For there is nothing whatsoever that is formless; everything exists and persists by assuming a form. "Persistence" (*sthāna*) refers to form, [denoted] by both the locative (*abhividhi*) and the ablative (*maryādā*). The causative suffix (*ṇic*) is prescribed for the causal agent (*hetu-kartṛ*) who is the independent sustainer inherent in this persistence. The state of that [suffix] is "action" (*kriyā*), the application of excellence, the purpose, the causality, the status of being a causal agent, and "establishment" (*sthāpanā*).
What is being said? When one who stands in a slightly scattered form establishes himself with one-pointedness, that is the "establishment of one-pointedness.

He explains this: "While standing by himself through non-existence everywhere"—that is, while he himself stands by way of non-existence in the form of incomplete intended shapes such as dice, cowries, and so forth; yet, when that [form] is specifically established, it remains having pervaded its own particular form as a completed state, or it is restricted by a boundary through the exclusion of other forms, such as "This is Indra" or "This is Skanda."

What is this like? To this he says: "Like being employed for an action whose specific performance is not yet determined. For example, when there is no determination of a specific action such as cooking (*pac*), reading (*paṭh*), or going (*gam*), an independent agent whose action is undetermined is directed by a causal agent with the command, "Cook, cook! He establishes him in "cooking" alone, excluding other actions; he restricts him to that very state in the form of cooking. This is *sthāpanā-niyama* (the restriction of establishment). Likewise, in every case, *niyama* consists in the establishment of existence within a particular form—either through the completion of the intended form, by its distinction from other forms, or by a boundary. Such is the meaning of *sthāna* (establishment).
Having explained that, the word "establishment" (sthāpana) has been explained through its etymological derivation (vyutpatti).

If it is argued that, in that case, because there is no one to establish the state of non-existence, the definition lacks pervasiveness (*vyāpti*), we say: "No. It is stated thus because establishing existence is easier to demonstrate, and so it was demonstrated first; the demonstration for the other [non-existence] is exactly the same. Therefore, he says: "Or by means of non-existence, even in that which has not yet attained its own form, like the pillar and Indra. For that very object, undergoing transformation into manifest and unmanifest forms, remains in various ways and is established as the intended particular (*viśeṣya*). Just as a pillar, even in its unrefined state where its constituent parts are less manifest, when being distinguished, is established as "Indra" as it approaches a painted state where its parts are manifest; therefore, that [non-existence] is also restricted to its proper place. Thus, the definition is indeed pervasive.
By this, he extends the explanation to the state that is even more unmanifest, stating "likewise in the senses and so forth," the meaning of which has already been explained.

As in the case of Sthūṇa [and] Vaprakāra, [and] Viśākha; therefore, the conclusion of the stated proof beginning with "just as a child," etc., together with its illustration including the possibility, extends up to Devadatta.

The substances that are the causes of childhood, such as the *pīṭhaka* (the body of a child), and those of youth and so forth, are distinct; thus, a difference in substance (*dravyabheda*) is established. Likewise, although Devadatta is one—possessing the essential nature of those forms such as being a cook, a cutter, or a teacher—and remains the same despite all these differences, there arises a distinction based on various media such as paintings, clay models, or puppets. Because he remains present for the sake of each particular location, and because his action attains the reality of that state, the "deposit" (*nikṣepa*) by way of representation is the "representational deposit" (*sthāpanā-nikṣepa*). Through representation, one deposits an object by means of both its actual existence and its non-existence.
Just as from a person arises the act of naming, and from the act of naming arises the designation "Devadatta" and so forth, so too [is it] with the painter and others...

Thus, there is a distinction of names; and because action consists of energy (*vīrya*) characterized by the subsidence-cum-destruction (*kṣayopaśama*) of karma, a distinction of states (*bhāva*) is also established. By the word "various" (*vividha*), distinctions such as these are included.

Since this distinction between substance, name, and state is thus established, one should reflect that Devadatta—whose essence is that very form—is a single entity despite all his differences, and is neither different nor non-different from others, because there is no difference in the ultimate reality of his form. Having reflected on this, he says, using that as an illustration, so that it may be understood to apply to the subject at hand, such as paintings and the like: "In the same way, although distinctions such as painting, modeling, and sculpture are possible, that 'installation' (sthāpanā) exists for each respective location according to its specific purpose."

What is the reason? Because that action attains the state of being that very thing—just as the work of a painter attains the state of being Indra, or as the actions of substances such as seats and so forth, and of names such as "cooker" and so forth, which differentiate states, attain the form of Devadatta. Thus, there is pervasiveness of the doctrine of representation (sthāpanā).
However, the proponent of *syādvāda*, desiring a reality whose essence consists of the distinctions of existence, non-existence, substance, name, state, and so forth, speaks thus;
whereas for those who maintain the absolute view of representation and substance, nothing exists apart from the [subjective] form, and therefore these distinctions are merely illusions.
