That is to say, a thing whose essence is not yet that [particular state] brings about for itself—by means of itself—the state of being that [state], which consists of its specific form; this is what is meant by "itself by itself.
How is this so? Just as *nāma-karma* from a person: although it is essentially formless (*amūrta*) prior to its manifestation, it transforms and becomes embodied (*mūrta*) in the form of karma.

And thus, from the act of naming (*nāmakarman*), there arises the state of being "Devadatta" and so forth; from that appropriated action, there occurs the attainment of the status of a hell-being, an animal, or a human named Devadatta—this is the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*). The subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*) is expressed as "and likewise the painter and so forth. Its explanation is as follows: therein, because that which is not yet such is brought to a state of being such, there is a unity between the painting and the like and Devadatta. Just as it was explained that through the mutual attainment of each other's nature by the soul (*jīva*) and the action (*karman*), there is an attainment of oneness between those two which were considered distinct, so too is there the attainment of the state of Devadatta by the pigments and so forth belonging to the painting. This is the meaning.

Alternatively, we may even accept a distinction between the soul (*jīva*) and its karma; yet the single entity called the "soul" undergoes transformations into various states such as being a *pāriṇāmika* (essential) soul, being destined for liberation (*bhavya*), or being undestined (*abhavya*), as well as *kṣāyopaśamika* (subsidential-cum-destructive) and *audayika* (emergent) states, and takes on forms such as one-, two-, three-, or four-sensed beings, animals, hell-beings, and so forth—all of which are like Devadatta himself due to the identity of the soul and its karma. This is the illustrative example.
The application to the subject is that even in a painting, there is no difference in the form of Devadatta characterized by his great whiteness and other traits.
He demonstrates this: "And just as the nature of being a soul and so forth is the prior form," and so on; the meaning of this verse is already explained.

Alternatively, there is indeed no difference between the soul (*jīva*) and the karmic matter (*karmapudgala*), because, due to the absence of distinct modifications such as the *kṣāyopaśamika* (subsidence-cum-destruction) or *audayika* (arising from karma), there is only one transformative (*pāriṇāmika*) state. Therefore, even for those two [the soul and matter], there is no [separation] therein, just as with the self, because that which is not of such a nature is brought to a state of being so; their unity is like that of Devadatta and his various actions, and just as the nature of being a soul (*jīvatva*) and so forth is its prior form...
And just as the state of being alive [is established] prior to that...
because of the identity of the reality of the form,

if a painting or the like, when established by means of ritual installation (*sthāpanā*) with reference to Devadatta, attains the very nature of Devadatta, then why does Devadatta likewise not attain the nature of the painting or the like?

Likewise, in the case of the statement "the dice and so forth attain the status of Indra, but Indra does not attain the state of dice," what is the specific reason [for this distinction]? Surely even that [status of Indra] does not transcend the nature of a "nominal designation" (*sthāpanā-nikṣepa*), because it is established by karma belonging to the lineage named Indra;
therefore, this is indeed logical and not illogical.
Alternatively, the "nominal designation" (*sthāpanā*) is itself the "designation" (*nikṣepa*); thus it is a "nominal-designation" (*sthāpanā-nikṣepa*).

Establishment (sthāpanā) is the form (ākāra) which has the nature of a substance (vastu); it is deposited within its own self, such as a jar and so forth by potters and others, or the Self by those seeking liberation.

Likewise, even Indra is not distinct from the "Indra" [status] because there is no difference in their underlying nature (*dharma*). To this he says: Just as the state of being a soul (*jīvatva*)—which is preceded by the soul itself—is constantly established through its transformative consciousness (*caitanya*) that is oriented toward all modifications, remaining in an unmanifest form while maintaining the status of non-existence (*asadbhāvasthāpana*), so too are the transformative states of color and so forth belonging to *pudgala*s established through the maintenance of the status of non-existence, such as the collection of colors like great white, vermilion, and so on. Therefore, there is identity between the two. Why? Because of the unity of the reality of their forms; because they are non-different insofar as they are fashioned by the intellect (*buddhi*); because they consist of those very transformations; and because there is no difference due to the fixedness of their respective positions in each case.
Those who desire to know this in detail should consult such works as the *Anuyogadvāra-sūtra*. See the section on "that which consists of what is not that" (*atatadbhūtātmaka*), page 599, line 20.
The very non-arising of the action of [the agent] is the non-existence of those things considered to be different or non-different.
The subsidential (aupaśamika), the destructive (kṣāyika), the mixed (miśra), as well as the emergent (audayika) and the transformational (pāriṇāmika) states are the intrinsic nature of the soul.
And [the qualities] such as being a living being (jīva), being capable of liberation (bhavya), and being incapable of liberation (abhavya) [are established by their own nature]. —
Tattvārthasūtra 2.7.
Those seeking a detailed exposition should consult these commentaries.
The reading enclosed within these brackets is not present in manuscript Ya;
therein, because that which is not of such a nature is brought to suchness by means of the self, there is its identity with Devadatta, as in the case of a painting and so forth.
And just as the state of being alive and so forth is its prior form...
and just as the state of being alive is prior to that...

...because of the identity of the reality of their forms, if by means of ritual installation (*sthāpanā*) a painting or similar object being installed becomes the very nature of Devadatta with reference to Devadatta, then why does Devadatta not likewise become the nature of the painting or similar object?
Similarly, why does Indra become the nature of the dice and so forth, but the dice and so forth do not become Indra? What is the specific reason for this distinction?

Now, one might object: since this [name] also does not transcend the nature of a "nominal designation" (*sthāpanā-nikṣepa*), because it is established by karma consisting of the lineage (*gotra*) of the name "Indra," therefore this is indeed appropriate; it is not inappropriate.
Alternatively, the "nominal designation" (*nikṣepa*) of the "nominal designation" (*sthāpanā*) is the "nominal designation of nominal designation" (*sthāpanā-nikṣepa*).

Establishment (*sthāpanā*) is the form (*ākāra*) consisting of the substance (*vastu*); for example, a jar or similar object is placed by potters and others within its own self, and likewise the Self is [placed] by those seeking liberation, as is Indra by the worshippers of Indra. (Praśastapāda-bhāṣya)
Mahāśvetā asks:
"In that case, [there would be] a restriction of place," etc.
Here he raises an objection: "If by means of establishment," and so forth.

The intention is as follows: If the nature of the object to be established (sthāpya)—such as Devadatta, who is distinct from the thing being established (sthāpya-vastu) and its form—is attributed to the painting or other medium that serves as the basis of establishment, then why is it that the nature of the painting or other medium, which is itself the object being established, is not likewise attributed to the intended object such as Devadatta? For in both cases, the reason for the attribution of a distinct nature to the object is equally the act of establishing (sthāpanā) by virtue of the establisher. Similarly, what is the specific reason why the die or other object attains the state of Indra, but Indra does not attain the state of the die? This is the objection regarding the establishment of existence and non-existence.
To this it is replied: "Now, as for the passage beginning with 'nanv asāv api' and so forth, up to 'na na yujyate'—this is not undesirable; indeed, this is accepted, and therefore there is no fault.
Just as a painted image or a clay figure established for the sake of Indra becomes Indra, so too Indra becomes the dice and other such objects."

Moreover, because he is established by the name-gotra-karma called "Indra," he does not transcend the nature of being a *sthāpanā-nikṣepa* (representational designation). This is because it has been demonstrated in the text beginning with, "From the person comes the name-karma; from the name-karma comes the state of Devadatta and so forth.

Therefore, while existing as a *sthāpanā-nikṣepa*, the soul and the karma do not transcend the variety of transformations such as the curvature of the yoga, the manifoldness of manifest forms, and the similarity to the examples of painted clay figures and the like that have been mentioned.
Thus, this is indeed logical; it is not illogical, for a double negation results in the affirmation of the original state (*prakṛti*).

Thus, first of all, by the compound "sthāpanayā nikṣepaḥ" (deposition by means of representation), the pervasiveness of the *arthanaya* regarding the substance of representation and deposition is shown in the third compound; see page 598,
line 4 of the *Pra* [commentary].
Alternatively, beginning with the words "athavā" (or), he says [the following] to demonstrate that it is also a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*):
"The deposit (*nikṣepa*) of the installation (*sthāpanā*). Having formed the genitive case in the sense of the object (*karma*), [he asks] what is the object? The object is the installation itself.
What is this "establishment" (sthāpanā)? It is the form (ākāra). What is this form? It is the very nature of the object itself; where is it deposited? In its own self.
"Who? "The jar and so forth.

"By whom? "By the potter and so forth"—thus the meaning of the genitive compound has been explained. However, for the purpose of demonstrating pervasiveness in the present context, he says: "The Self is deposited by those seeking liberation within their own self"—this is understood. If one asks, "Of what kind [is it]?"—it is established unmixed with karma, being placed in its own form while previously undifferentiated, now as something differentiated. Likewise, Indra is directly shown to those men who do not perceive the distinction between the senses (*indriya*) and the Lord (*indra*); because Indra is never inseparable from his own form, unlike a jar which is inseparable from its wide belly (*vikukṣi*).
Alternatively, "deposition in the figurative sense" (sthāpanā-nikṣepa) refers to a deposition within the figurative sense;
it is not deposited in the name,
because even the name is dependent upon that very [figurative sense] along with its object.

All forms of words arising from vocal organs and articulations, as well as the forms of meanings cognized through them, are merely the manifestation of *sthāpanā* (representation) and *vipariṇāma* (transformation).

This is because in the absence of those [forms], there is an absence of both word and meaning; and since they are not apprehended when their forms are not apprehended, even substance (*dravya*) is indeed a *sthāpanā-nikṣepa*, owing to the fact that substance consists of form.

Just as the substance of the *śrīparṇī* tree possesses internal forms, so too the world—consisting of the nature of placement (*sthāpanā*) and deposition (*nikṣepa*), characterized by the distinction between the undifferentiated and the differentiated—is perceived through this all-pervasive characteristic. Why is that Indra directly shown to men who do not know the distinction between Indra and non-Indra? Because, as stated in the passage beginning with "not in that form" (*na tadākāra*), since Indra does not exist apart from the forms of the eyes, words, colors, and so forth, Indra is said to be the reality (*tattva*) of those very forms.

Like what? Like a jar, which is inseparable from its having a concave belly and so forth; just as a jar does not exist apart from the form of having a concave belly and so on, but exists as being of that very nature, so too Indra does not exist apart from his own form, but exists as being of that very nature.
[Question: Is it by means of a potter and so forth?
Is it the mixed karma (*karmamiśra*) that is introduced as being of a uniform nature?

The distinction between the two [types of] sense organs (*indriya*) is directly demonstrated for those men who do not understand it; because Indra is never found apart from that form, unlike a jar which is not inseparable from its belly.

Alternatively, "the placement-deposit" (*sthāpanā-nikṣepa*) refers to a deposit within the category of "representation" (*sthāpanā*); it is not deposited under the name (*nāman*), but is deposited specifically within representation.
Since even the name is dependent upon its corresponding object,

the forms of words produced by the places and organs of articulation, as well as the forms of objects understood through them, are all merely the manifestation of mental construction (*sthāpanā-vipariṇāma*).
This is because in the absence of that [object], both word and meaning would not exist, and if their forms are not apprehended, they themselves cannot be apprehended.
Substance (*dravya*) is also indeed a deposit of representation (*sthāpanā-nikṣepa*), because substance consists of form (*ākāra*);
just as the wood of the *śrīparṇī* tree is a substance containing an internal form, which is the undifferentiated locus for each of those specific forms.
Or else, it is a locative compound (*saptamī-samāsa*), such as "in the establishment" (*sthāpanāyām*), and so forth.

In the term *sthāpanā-nikṣepa*, the compound should be understood as "the deposit (*nikṣepa*) in the installation (*sthāpanā*)," which conveys the sense of the particle *eva* (only/indeed). He explains this: it is not deposited in the name (*nāman*) nor in the word (*śabda*); what then? It is deposited in the installation (*sthāpanā*) alone.
If one asks why, he says: because even the name is dependent upon that [object] along with its meaning; both the word and the meaning are dependent solely upon the form (*ākāra*).

He meditates upon that [as follows]: "The places of articulation (*sthāna*), the organs of production (*karaṇa*)," and so forth. The phonemes beginning with *a* arise from specific locations such as the throat; when uttered in succession and without interval, they take on particular forms such as nominal endings (*sup*) and verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*). Furthermore, the forms of the objects denoted by nouns and verbs—namely, substances (*dravya*) and actions (*kriyā*)—are all merely the manifestation of the establishment and transformation of the reality of internalized forms. Why is this? Because of the phrase "in the absence of that," and so forth: because both word and meaning would be non-existent in the absence of form, and because both would not be apprehended if their form were not grasped.
This is the sense of the particle *eva*.
There are eight places for the articulation of sounds: the chest, the throat, the head, as well as the root of the tongue, the teeth, the nose, the lips, and the palate. (13)
...it should be known that the closed [articulation] has one measure (mātrā), while the open [articulation] has two measures;
all voiced [consonants] are closed, and the unvoiced are traditionally held to be open.
The articulation of the vowels and the sibilants is traditionally taught as being wide-open (*vivṛta*).—
*Pāṇinīya Śikṣā*:
"This sound which..."
"...it unfolds, assisted by [the organs of] place, articulation, and so forth"— Vākyapadīya, with its own commentary, 1.1."
The reading "dināsthāya sthānakaraṇajanmānaḥ" also appears appropriate here.
To be approached with joy,
to be approached by persons, to be approached by those who possess consciousness, O Prajñā.

Thus, it has been stated that the designation of name (*nāmanikṣepa*) is included within the designation of representation (*sthāpanānikṣepa*). We now state that the designation of substance (*dravyanikṣepa*) is also included within representation; as follows: "Substance also," and so forth. The designation of substance is indeed the designation of representation because a substance consists of form (*ākāramayatva*); for example, the *śrīparṇī* wood is a substance whose cause contains an internal form, and since it is merely the assumption of that specific form—the manifestation of its unmanifested general nature—it is representation alone, even though it is a substance. In this way, both the designations of name and substance are simply the designation of representation.
Non-distraction is likewise; existence (*bhāva*) is also simply establishment (*sthāpanā*).

The distinction between action, application, form, color such as blue, and substances such as a *śivaka* is merely a state of being (*bhāva*), which is nothing other than a configuration (*ākāra*). Even when establishing the existence of the senses and so forth, because one excludes other forms while not producing another form, there occurs a mental superimposition (*adhyāropa*) of names and concepts upon the intended configuration. This is like the "pillar-king" (*sthūṇendra*) used for establishing the substantial reality (*dravyārtha*) of an action;
it is precisely through this determination of the true nature that there exist in the world practices such as [observing] signs, conduct, and bowing to images of deities.
Here too, the ultimate reality is precisely the specific form;
for instance, even the existence [of a thing] occurs when there is the action of placing or removing that single house, and so forth.

The "deposit as development" (*bhāvanikṣepa*) is indeed just "establishment" (*sthāpanā*), both from the perspective of scripture (*āgama*) and from the perspective of non-scripture (*no-āgama*). From the perspective of scripture, it is one who knows that particular *prābhṛta* [text] and is currently engaged in its study; thus, the "engaged" state (*upayukta-bhāva*) is a transformative (*pāriṇāmika*) state, and the active state of the soul (*iṣṭā-jīva*) is a state born from the subsidence-cum-destruction (*kṣayopaśama*) of the energy-obscuring karma (*vīryāntarāya*). Regarding matter (*pudgala*), however, there are distinctions such as the simultaneous transformative state consisting of color and so forth, or the specific qualities like blue and so forth, or the non-simultaneous states like the *śivaka* (a small clay model) and so forth. Such are the various types of this "state" (*bhāva*), which takes the form of action, engagement, color, blue, the *śivaka*, and so on.
This very state is simply an "aspect" (*ākāra*), because it is precisely the manifestation (*ābhavana*) according to the method previously described.
Furthermore, there may also be the reading "anāgamataśca" (and not from scripture) here, rather than "nāgamaśca" (and scripture) or "bhā" (or).

Existence (bhāva) should be understood as being of two kinds, as previously [stated], through the distinction between that which is based on scripture (āgama) and that which is not based on scripture (no-āgama).
An *ātman* permeated by the utilization (*upayoga*) of the objects of those [scriptural] categories (*prābhṛta*) is "based on scripture" (*āgama*).

An *ātman* permeated by the utilization of the objects of the categories such as the living beings (*jīva*) and so forth is called a "living being based on existence" (*bhāvajīva*) and "right vision based on existence" (*bhāvasamyagdarśana*).
— Tattvārtharājavārttika 1.5, etc.,
simultaneous [cognition]... [pramāṇa]

Thus, the three types of *nikṣepa* [are included] within *sthāpanā-nikṣepa* alone, because, in brief, they do not transcend the essential nature of *sthāpanā*, which consists in setting aside one form to produce another form; and since they are supported by this definition, [the author], desiring to establish that even non-existent *sthāpanā*—which possesses an unmanifest form—is indeed *sthāpanā*, says "akṣādyasadbhāva... and so forth, in order to dispel the doubt of others: "In this case too, if one were to set aside another form but not produce another form, there would be no 'avarodha'—that is, no comprehension—of another form such as Indra, which is to be conveyed through the *nikṣepa* of the die; yet, such comprehension does indeed occur."

Therefore, there is no contradiction in the mental superimposition (buddhy-ādhyāropa) of the name "Indra" upon that which exists in the intended form; this refers to the action of casting the die and establishing it. How is this so? It is like a pillar established as Indra for the sake of the substance (dravyārtha). Just as a pillar, by excluding other forms and not producing other forms, serves the purpose of the substance-established Indra, so too is the die and the rest;

because the nature of establishment (sthāpanā) consists of its form, the intention appears to be that one does not deviate from the nature of establishment, which consists in the exclusion of other forms and the production of another form.
One who desires to take up [the practice] beginning with the syllable *kāra* should not act [otherwise].
Let it be seen on page 602, line 14:
"°avabodhaḥ" appears correctly as "bhavitum" in the manuscript (pra).
See page 602,
line 20; [the reading] "rūpāntarakaraṇāt" in manuscript Bhāṣya and "rūpāntakaraṇāt" in manuscript Ya.
See page 601, lines 12 and 14.

It is precisely from the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of this reality that there occurs in the world the practice of [observing] signs, conduct, and the salutation of images of deities; this is not to be established through logical reasoning (*upapatti*), for everything is merely a conventional establishment (*sthāpanā*), as it is well-established in the world.

For instance—the assumption of sectarian marks by heretics is observed to be based on specific forms well-known according to their respective scriptures; likewise, the observances associated with them, the installation of images of deities such as Arhat, Rudra, Indra, and Buddha, and the worship of those [images] with prostrations, recitations, hymns, offerings, garlands, and so forth, are seen to be grounded in particular forms. Since there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) more authoritative than what is perceived, thus is stated the view of the *sthāpanā-dravyārtha-naya*.
Thus ends [the section]. Here too, etc.
The response to this view is as follows:
even the "form" (ākāra) is twofold—the general form and the particular form.
Among these, the particular form alone is the ultimate reality (paramārtha), not the general form.

In the act of establishing or depositing that ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) as a single entity, the substance-aspect in its general form (*sāmānyākāra-dravyārtha*) is subordinate because it serves the purpose of the primary existence of the ultimate reality. Just as the fingers of the hand are subordinate to the substance-aspect in its general form, yet from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārthataḥ*), they are not [the hand] in their own right because their nature is non-conceptualizable; how then could there be a "representation" (*sthāpanā*) of them as substances? From the perspective of space (*kṣetra*), since there is no object apart from the specific modifications (*viśeṣa*) occurring simultaneously, there is no representation.

Since there is no object apart from its specific distinctions even within the temporal sequence of states such as "child" and so forth—which do not arise simultaneously—how could a figurative designation (*sthāpanā*) be made, or for what? Furthermore, because figurative designation of non-existence pertains to the substantial aspect (*dravyārtha*), while figurative designation of existence pertains to the modal aspect (*paryāyārtha*), when the substantial aspect is primary, there is the exclusion of the other.

As for that which was called "superimposition by name and cognition," that too is the domain of the substantial and modal aspects; and that is nothing other than the manifestation of specific distinctions (*viśeṣabhavana*).

The substance-substance-meaning (dravya-dravyārtha), however, has been explained and refuted in the analysis of the [seven] modalities (bhaṅgas) beginning with the affirmative (vidhi). But here, the word denotes that which is associated with actual existence (bhāva), because the name, representation, and substance are not accepted as the primary meaning; thus it is established.
...simultaneously, however,
in the case of each particular reality among the distinctions such as skin, joints, color, lines, limbs, atoms, and forms, the other [elements] are subordinate to that specific reality.

From the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), however, there exists an indistinguishable essence (*tattva*) that is absolutely distinct [from its parts]; those hands and so forth do not exist by way of their own nature (*svarūpa*). How, then, could there be an establishment (*sthāpanā*) of them as substantial entities (*dravyataḥ*)? Likewise, from the perspective of space (*kṣetra*), since there is no object apart from the specific modifications (*viśeṣa*) occurring simultaneously, there is no establishment; for an "appearance" (*ākāra*)—which is the manifestation (*ābhavana*)—cannot exist in an object that is either the effect (*ākārya*) or the agent (*ākartṛ*), because establishment itself consists of such an appearance.

Even from the perspective of time, among successive states such as childhood and so forth that do not occur simultaneously, the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is the arising of each individual particularity. He explains this: "childhood and so forth occurring non-simultaneously," and so on, up to "how could a representation be made, or of what?"—the meaning here is already understood.
In this context as well, the substance-aspect (*dravyārtha*) consisting of the general form is subordinate.

From the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), however, because the true nature (*tattva*) is non-conceptualizable, hands and other limbs do not exist by way of their own intrinsic form (*svarūpa*);
how then could there be an installation (*sthāpanā*) of them as substantial entities (*dravyataḥ*)?

As for spatial location (*kṣetrataḥ*), since there is no objective referent apart from the specific distinctions among successive states (*paryāya*) that arise simultaneously, there is no such thing as an installation.

Since there is no object apart from its specific distinctions even within the temporal successions of states such as "child" and so forth—which do not exist simultaneously—how could a figurative designation (*sthāpanā*) be made, or for what? Furthermore, because figurative designation of non-existence pertains to the substantial aspect (*dravyārtha*), while figurative designation of existence pertains to the modal aspect (*paryāyārtha*), when the substantial aspect is primary, there is the exclusion of the other.

Even that which was called the superimposition (*adhyāropa*) of name and cognition is the domain of the substantial and modal aspects; and that too is simply the coming-into-being of specific distinctions.

The substance-as-substance (dravya-dravyārtha), however, has been explained and refuted in the analysis of the [seven] modes beginning with injunction (vidhi-bhaṅga). But here, the word denotes that which is associated with existence (bhāva), because the terms name (nāman), representation (sthāpanā), and substance (dravya) are not intended [here]. Thus it is established.
[the] reality simultaneously. *Arthaprakāśa*. *Prakaraṇa*.
Then, in the final particularity,
there is the manifestation of a single particularity within the substance desired by the child and others.

Regarding the phrase "in the case of the ignorant and others, there is one single specific state" (*bālādiṣvekameva viśeṣabhavanam*), this reading might also occur here. Furthermore, since the establishment of existence (*sadbhāvasthāpanā*) pertains to the mode of manifestation (*paryāyārtha*), whereas the establishment of non-existence (*asadbhāvasthāpanā*) pertains solely to the substantial aspect (*dravyārthamātra*), by defining those two [establishments], you have thus refuted the reliance on the primacy of the mode of manifestation (*paryāyārthaprādhānya*). Alternatively, when the primacy of the substantial aspect (*dravyārthaprādhānya*) is maintained, the modes of manifestation are refuted by the passage beginning with "the non-existence of the senses, etc. (*akṣādyasadbhāva*); he demonstrates this in the passage beginning with "of the establishment of non-existence" (*asadbhāvasthāpanāyāśca*) up until the refutation of the other.
Those two bhā...
those two ya...
page 601, line 3.

Furthermore, that which was described as the superimposition of name and cognition—such as "the occurrence of the intended form" and so forth—is also the domain of two other standpoints (*nayas*): the name-substance standpoint (*nāmadravyārtha*) and the mode standpoint (*paryāyārtha*).

Among these, the superimposition of name has the name-substance standpoint as its object, while the superimposition of cognition has the mode standpoint as its object—as in the scriptural statement: "One who knows [it] through scripture and is attentive possesses the substance-equanimity (*bhāvasāmāyika*). And that [cognition] is indeed the manifestation of a particular state.

Regarding the passage beginning with "dravyadravyārthas tu," etc.: since the "substance-of-substance" (dravyadravyārtha) has already been explained and refuted among the previously discussed modes (vidhi-ādi-bhaṅgas), it need not be stated again. See page 601, line 16.
What is the nature of *bhāvasāmāyika*? It is of two kinds, namely: from the perspective of scripture (*āgama*) and from the perspective of what is not scripture (*noāgama*).
What is *bhāvasāmāyika* from the perspective of scripture? "The knower who is attentive" (Anuyogadvārasūtra 150).

From "vibuddhyādi" [in the previous section] onwards, however, [the text begins with] "bhāva" and so forth; and in this verbal perspective (*śabdanaya*), which is characterized by the breaking of both [types of] restriction, there exists only the particular (*viśeṣa*). Thus, through the explanation of the meaning of words, it has already been demonstrated that [this perspective] does not intend to express a substance as a substance (*dravyadravyārtha*)—namely, what is expressed by name, representation, or substance (*nāma-sthāpanā-dravyārtha*). Therefore, he introduces the nature of the perspective [with the words]: "It stands thus," and so on, up to "simultaneous reality" (*yugapattattva*).

As for those who think that [the word] denotes either the universal (*jāti*) alone or its connection (*yoga*), because of the facility of the relationship and the absence of deviation—that is incorrect. For it would not be heard as non-distinct from words denoting particulars (*bhedārtha*) whether it denotes the connection or the universal; for instance, there would be no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with words such as "substance" (*dravya*) which denote particulars—as in "existent substance," "existent quality," or "existent action"—yet this is observed.
For neither existence (*sattā*) nor conjunction (*yoga*) is a substance (*dravya*) or a quality (*guṇa*); what then? It is [the substratum] of the substance or the quality.
And it has been said:
[this reading is not present within the text of PSV2].

The reading contained within this [passage] is not present in the middle of the PSV₂; for there is no established grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) between two words denoting substance (dravya), due to the rule governing the distinction between the case endings of those denoting quality (guṇa) and the possessor of quality (guṇin).
Vākyapadīya 3.14.8

In this context, even a relation is expressed as being a property of the relata; likewise, having been made into an entity (bhāva), it is said that even an entity is joined with another by means of a relation.
Thus, a relation is [defined] by relating.
Like passion (*rāga*) and so forth, it is connected with something else;

therefore, since a relation is denotable by means of the property of the relata, there is no word that expresses the relation by its own property. Thus, its being denotable by a genus-word (*jātiśabda*) is not tenable.
(In the middle of this [section], there is a different restatement.)

As for those who say that by virtue of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with specific words, the ease of the relationship, and non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*), it is merely the possessor of the universal (*jātimat*) that is intended—regarding that [position]: "The possessor of the universal is not [the referent] because it is not independent; because of metaphorical usage; because it is impossible;
because the possessor of the universal is not independent; because of difference; and because the universal would then not be a universal."

It should be noted that in the *Nayacakra*, a refutation is seen of the verse from another work by Diṅnāga which states: "Even when there is an implication of the meaning (*arthākṣepa*), [the word] is not non-conclusive; therefore, the word effects the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*). For [the word] does not possess independence with respect to that [exclusion].

Nevertheless, the word "existent" (sat) denotes a substance that has as its adjuncts only the genus (*jāti*) and the essential nature (*svarūpa*), but not directly; thus, because it does not imply specific differences such as "pot" and so forth residing within that [substance], there would be an absence of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) when those differences are not [identical] with it.
For there is no coreferentiality in the absence of pervasion (*vyāpti*);

just as the word "white," by denoting a substance qualified by its own expressed quality alone, does not imply sweetness and other qualities even though they exist in the substance—and therefore, in that case, there is a lack of identity with its differences—so too here, the same consequence would follow.
Furthermore, by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*),

the word "existent" (*sat*)— which in its primary sense (*bhūtārtha*) denotes either the essential nature (*svarūpa*) or the universal (*jāti*)— is applied figuratively to that which possesses it (*tadvati*).
For that which is metaphorically applied to something does not denote that object in its actual sense,
because even a similarity of form is impossible;
and in the case of [the word] "possessing that" (*tadvat*), a similarity of quality is possible neither through the transfer of the cognition nor through the assistance of the quality.
If it is asked, "How is it not by the transfer of conditions? [the answer is] in the *Upacāra*—that is, the *Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā*, page 310:
"For when there is no pervasion (*vyāpti*), etc."
Pervasion (vyāpti) is implication (ākṣepa).

For example, by the word "color" (rūpa), there is no implication of "sweetness" and so forth, because they are not its sub-classifications; therefore, grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with those words does not occur, as in "color is sour. However, such coreferentiality does occur when pervasion exists, as in "color is blue."

—Viśālā, p. 243. For comparison: furthermore, as for the other fault stated regarding this very position—that even the word "existent" (sat), when it denotes its own form or a universal (jāti) through its primary meaning, would be figurative (gauṇa) when applied by metaphorical transfer (upacāra) to that which possesses it—this too is the same [in our case].
—Mīmāṃsā-śloka-vārttika, Śarkarikā, p. 61:
"Because the nature of the cognition is distinct, it is like the metaphorical application of the term 'king' to a servant.
Just as when a servant is designated by the word 'master' in the sense that 'this servant is the master,' there is no identical cognition regarding both the king and the servant."
Furthermore, there is metaphorical application (*upacāra*) of a genus-term (*jātiśabda*) to that which possesses it,
as in the case of "he who is a master is a servant," where [the term applies] to both the king and the servant;
and because it is not denoted sequentially, it is like the whiteness found in a *kunda* flower or a pearl oyster.
Where there is a common cognition, there expression is observed to occur sequentially, as in the case of "the whiteness of the *kunda*, the *kumuda*, and the conch.
Since the word is applied simultaneously to both the genus (*jāti*) and the possessor of the genus (*tadvat*), there is no similarity resulting from the transference of the cognition;
for if there were identity due to the influence of the quality, there would be a sense of excellence [of the quality] even without the intellect [to perceive it]. (5)
On this point, the Bhikṣu said: "Something existing in some place may exist by way of providing an assistance, just as lac exists in a crystal by way of providing the assistance of coloring it.
If a universal (jāti) exists in a substance, then it must provide such assistance to it as coloring and so forth;
consequently, there ought to be a cognition of that substance alone as assisted by it, even without a cognition of the universal."
For when a crystal colored by lac is perceived, that perception does not depend on anything else;
and this is not the case here. Therefore, there is no occurrence [of a quality] in a substance based on mutual assistance—as it has been said:
"The excellence [of a substance] in a substance would arise from the assistance of its qualities, even without [the mediation of] cognition."
— thus [it is stated] in the *Śarkarikā* commentary on the *Mīmāṃsā-śloka-vārttika*, p. 65–66:

"If, like a crystal, that which possesses qualities (the substance) were to become identical in nature with the qualities due to the assistance of those qualities, then, in that case, there would arise in the substance a cognition of excellence independent of the cognition of the excellence of the qualities."

For the existence of the cognition of redness in a crystal does not depend upon the cognition of the substrate (the red object), because in the case of those that are not stainless, there is an absence of the cognition of difference;
furthermore—[as stated in] the *Vimale* commentary: "in the case of those that are not stainless."
It would follow that false cognition (mithyājñāna) would prevail everywhere because of the nature of association;
for every verbal cognition is determined through the form of association with objects, and therefore, like the cognition of a crystal [as colored], it would be unreal.
Furthermore—

Like a crystal, all cognition would be non-correspondent with its object (ayathārtha). Furthermore, if there were a multiplicity of universals (sāmānya) and so forth, and they were perceived simultaneously by multiple perceivers, then the mutual assistance [of the causes] would be contradicted; thus, the perception of a variegated color (mecaka) would occur for everyone.
[Otherwise] there would be the perception of everything as black.

Furthermore, if there were a multiplicity of universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth, a simultaneous benefit [to the perceiver] would be contradictory when there are many perceivers of a quality-possessor such as white and so on—for example, "the jar is earthen, a substance, existent, white, sweet, fragrant," and so forth; in that case, the benefit conferred by the qualities would be contradictory.
For it is not possible for that substance to exist at that time in the form of a single quality, because [the substance] is undifferentiated;
nor is it possible for it to experience the form of a quality in only one part, since the entire form of the jar or other object is perceived by everyone as being variegated (*mecaka*).

Furthermore, if the assistance [of the universal] were produced for the entire object simultaneously by all [particulars] such as "pot-ness" and so forth, then, because there would be no apprehension of the form of each individual pot and so on, there would result a variegated perception due to the simultaneous occurrence of all forms— [as stated in] PSV1,

Because of the cognition of all forms; VT. cf.—The individual, the configuration, and the genus are the referents of a word (padārtha).
some [maintain] that the individual, the form, and the genus are not the referents of a word.
Why? Because no alternative is possible.

This very term "existent" (sat) is considered by virtue of its pervasiveness; furthermore, by this word "existent," is it the universal (jāti) that is denoted, or the individual (piṇḍa), or the relation (sambandha), or the entity possessing the universal (jātimat)?
In this regard, the universal (*jāti*) is not what is denoted first, because [the word "existent"] has the same case-ending as words denoting particulars;

for if this word "existent" were a denoter of a universal, it could not achieve grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "substance," which denotes a particular—as in the expression "existent substance.
Indeed, we do not observe coreferentiality between words that denote distinct objects.
For grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is not observed in the case of "cow and horse" (*gavāśvam*).

Now, if it is argued that because existence (*sattā*) resides in substances and so forth, it alone possesses coreferentiality with words such as "substance," even so, existence is a quality (*guṇa*) due to its dependence on another; and coreferentiality between two words denoting a quality and a qualified object is not observed, as in the case of "the whiteness of a conch shell.
By this, the relation (*sambandha*) is also explained.
It is not logical that the word *sat* should be the designator of individual objects (*piṇḍa*), because individual objects are infinite;
for it is impossible to declare the relationship of a single word with the manifold expansion of multiple substances and qualities.

Furthermore, when the relationship between a word and its meaning has not been declared, the comprehension of the meaning from the word is not tenable, as one would only perceive the word's own form (*svarūpa*). Moreover, there is the fault of deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
Furthermore, upon hearing the word "sat" (being), the intellect, oscillating among substance, quality, and action, comes to rest;
yet it is not logical to say that the term from which the intellect does not waver is the designator [of those categories].
Therefore, the word "sat" is not the designator of the particularities (bhedas).
Why is it that the word *sat* does not denote merely the genus (*jāti*)? Because it is not independent;

for the specific instances such as jars and so forth are not understood from the word *sat* alone. Thus, since it does not imply the specific instances like jars and so forth, there is an absence of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

Alternatively, regarding the phrase "because of lack of independence": the word *sat* primarily denotes existence (*sattā*). While denoting that [existence], it is applied metaphorically to that which possesses it.

And when a word, while denoting one thing, is applied metaphorically to another, it is not the direct designator of that [other thing], just like the word "bed" [is not the designator of the people on the bed].
And it has been said in this regard:
what was said? That because those who possess the qualities (tadvat) are infinite, it is not logical for them to be denoted by the word "existent" (sat).
Furthermore, there is no transfer of cognition [from the quality to the possessor] based on similarity of quality, as is the case with the word "master" applied to a servant.

It is not [the case that the word denotes the object] through the coloring by a quality, as in the case of "the blue crystal," because there is an absence of sequential operation and because it is impossible for them to occur simultaneously; furthermore, it would entail the undesirable consequence of the arising of an incorrect cognition.

Therefore, it is not tenable to claim that [the word], while denoting merely that which possesses a genus (*jātiman*), will also denote the uncommon qualifier and the qualified, for this would result in the undesirable consequence of there being no cognition [of these] elsewhere.

"And there is no other way [to explain it]; therefore, a word functions by excluding other meanings. For a word is said to denote its own meaning while performing the exclusion of other word-meanings"—*Nyāyavārttika* 2.2.66.
"The word is the designator because it is stated for the purpose of restriction, like that which possesses a universal; thus [it is] the possessor of exclusion (apoha)."

A genus-word (*jātiśabda*) does not denote particulars (*bheda*), because it is stated that its meaning is restricted to a specific [genus]; furthermore, there would be deviation (*vyabhicāra*) and infinity (*ānantya*).

Moreover, whatever faults exist in the view that a word denotes the possessor of a genus (*jātimat*), those same faults apply to the theory of the denotation of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*). This is the thesis (*pratijñā*).
*This page consists merely of footnotes.*

This page consists merely of footnotes. How so? It is said that "a word effects the exclusion of others" (anyāpohakṛcchrutiḥ), for a word, while effecting the exclusion of the referents of other words within its own meaning, is what is called "denoting."

Furthermore, two types of objects (*artha*) have been mentioned: the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). Since a third type of object is impossible, the "own-object" (*svārtha*) must first be determined. What is the own-object? The own-object is the particular characteristic, which is unique and the domain of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*);
that [own-object], being the domain of direct perception, is not possible here as the object of conceptual cognition (*savikalpa*).
Nor is there any other self-referential meaning (svārtha) than that;
the exclusion of the meanings of other words (śabdāntarārthāpoha) is not the self-referential meaning,
and there is no third thing whatsoever distinct from those two.
"Let alone its own meaning;
even in the implication of an object, there is uncertainty; therefore, a word effects the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*).

This is seen in the twelfth verse of the fifth chapter, the *Apohapariccheda*, of the *Pramāṇasamuccaya*. However, since this is not found in Dignāga’s own commentary on that work—specifically in the explanation beginning with "for [the word] excludes the meaning of other words" (*śabdāntarārthāpohaṃ hi*)—it appears that this was extracted here from another work by Dignāga.
Let it be seen (pṛṣṭha 416–1):
"And thus, because the denotation of a universal, a relation, and that which possesses a universal is impossible, the word effects the exclusion of others;
the two means of valid cognition have been stated."

Some consider verbal testimony (*śābda*) to be a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); regarding this, the *Pramāṇasamuccayavṛtti* (PSV) states: "Verbal testimony is not a separate means of valid cognition from inference;
for it expresses its own object through the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), just like [the reason] 'being produced' (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth."

5.1 A word, when employed with respect to a particular object, illuminates that [object] by means of exclusion of other referents (*arthāntara-vyavaccheda*), because it is connected to a specific part of that object through an inseparable relationship (*avinābhāvitva*), just like the property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth; therefore, it does not differ from inference (*anumāna*).

Since it is not logically possible for a genus-term (*jātiśabda*) to denote, in any way whatsoever, either a particular, a universal, a relation, or that which possesses a genus, therefore the word effects the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*). (Pramāṇasamuccaya 5)

Therefore, that which was stated [by Dignāga] in the fifth chapter on Apoha in the *Pramāṇasamuccayavṛtti*, namely: "Thus, it stands as it was said: 'Like [the property of] being produced and so forth, it expresses its own object by means of the exclusion of others'" (p. 160), is indeed established. This is what was stated by Dignāga.
"How?"— this is the question regarding the logical justification.

Since faults are seen in the positions that hold that words denote [objects] possessing particularity (*bheda*) or genus (*jāti*), it follows by implication that "the word effects the exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha-kṛcchrutiḥ*); thus the proponent of Apoha describes *anyāpoha*. For it has been stated by the proponent of Apoha: "A word is said to 'denote' when, while effecting the exclusion of other objects within its own referent, it expresses that [referent]. Furthermore, the two types of objects have been described as the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*); since there is no object of cognition (*prameya*) other than these, and because a third object distinct from them is impossible, one must first determine the word's own referent (*svārtha*). This is because the word *tāvat* implies a sequence, as another object will also be determined later. If one were to state merely the exclusion of the objects of other words, the fault would be the consequence of non-existence (*asattva*). Therefore, being dissatisfied with that much alone, he says: "while effecting its own referent. What is this "own referent"? It is said: the own referent is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). "Own" (*sva*) means other than "other" (*anya*); "not other" (*ananya*) means that very thing itself. This is because the respective objects of the two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are determined; thus, that which is the object of perception (*pratyakṣa*) is the "own referent."

Regarding the passage beginning with "sa iha" (it is here), in this sense of the word "here"— that is, in the sense of conceptual construction (*savikalpa*), in the general form of conceptualization consisting of superimposition and negation— that specific object (*svārtha*) which is the domain of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the inexpressible particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) [as stated in] *Pramāṇasamuccaya* 1.5, 2, is not possible.

Because it has been stated thus, [the opponent] might think: "There is a self-referent (svārtha) distinct from the object of perception. If this is the claim, it is not so; for that self-referent is not other than the object of perception, nor is it the referent of another word, and so forth.

The exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) is not its own object (*svārtha*), and there is no third [category] distinct from those two, because it is determined that the objects of definition (*lakṣya*) are only two; and since it is determined that the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are only two, there is therefore no third object either—how then could there be its own object? To this he says: "Let the own object be set aside for now," meaning it is not to be considered because of its non-existence (see pp. 547–548).

Comparison: The nature of a word is such that it is unrestrained in negating the meaning of other words; thus, it expresses its own object as a universal, which is to be expressed like a sky-flower. (111)
Thus, in the *Āptamīmāṃsā* composed by Samantabhadra,
as well as in the *Pramāṇasamuccayavṛtti* and other works, one should consult what was stated by Diṅnāga; see footnote 1 on page 10, line 1.
Is the fault the non-attainment of existence?
No, the fault is the non-attainment of existence because of dissatisfaction with others.
For the satisfaction of others, please see page 104, line 13 of the notes;
in the first chapter of the *Pramāṇasamuccaya*, the following verse is seen: "The form that is self-cognizable and inexpressible is the object-domain of the sense-faculties."

The reading "the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is inexpressible; form (*rūpa*) is the domain of the sense faculties" is cited here from the eighth chapter (*ara*), page 437–2, of the *Nayacakravṛtti* with a variant reading. Therefore, it appears that this verse was extracted here from another work of Dignāga. However, in the second verse of the second chapter of the *Pramāṇasamuccaya*, the reading appears as: "The particular characteristic is inexpressible; because of the difference in the apprehended object, it is otherwise than that," and so forth.

And having established this, when the investigation into what is denoted by words is underway, you stated that [words] denote the universal (*jāti*), the relation, or the possessor of the universal; however, since these are not objects of perception as their own referents,
even the object of inference cannot be its own referent, because its nature consists in the exclusion of others (*apoha*),
as in "fire is not non-fire."

...Or, if a distinction [between the word’s own meaning and the exclusion] were admitted, there would be a lack of self-referentiality (*asvārthatva*), because the meaning of exclusion (*apohārtha*) is different from it, and because it would result in the communication of something other than the intended object and thus have a different meaning. Furthermore, even if the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) is not perceived in some instances, the own-meaning (*svārtha*) must be understood from this very word; that in which another is excluded is the own-meaning.

That too is not correct. Since, in the case of its own referent (*svārtha*), no locus or located is perceived, and because [exclusion] is inseparable from a positive injunction of essential nature (*svarūpa-vidhi*), in what "own referent" would exclusion (*apoha*) take place? Furthermore, since the word for "other" and the referent of another word lack a stable form, what indeed is this "other," and from what would the exclusion be performed? Because [such an other] is impossible, you have stated that "the word effects the exclusion of others" (*anyāpohakṛcchrutiḥ*); thus, since the position of difference is held to be no different from the position of possessing a universal (*jātimatpakṣa*), you have spoken having determined the word and its referent, and not as being the own referent that is the object of perception (*pratyakṣaviṣaya-svārthatva*). Your very statement is the proof, as you yourself said: "not as being the own referent that is the object of perception."
Even the object of inference is not its own referent (*svārtha*), because its nature consists in the exclusion of other meanings (*apoha*); for example, "fire is not non-fire..."

Alternatively, if a distinction is admitted, the word would lack its own meaning (*asvārthatva*), because [the exclusion] would be different from the excluded object (*apohārtha*), since it would consist in making another understood and thus have a different referent. If it is argued that even where it is not perceived, the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) must be understood from this very word as its own meaning—that which is the locus from which another is excluded being the "own meaning"—that too is not correct. For in the case of "in its own meaning," no relationship of container and contained (*ādhārādheya*) is observed, as it is inseparable from the affirmation of its own nature (*svarūpavidhi*). In what "own meaning" then would it be excluded? Since the form of both the other word and the meaning of the other word is not established, who is this "other" from whom or from which the exclusion would be performed?
Or [it is] the exclusion of others (anyāpoha), because it is accepted as not being distinct from my own perception (pratyakṣa). (Bhāṣya) *Nyāyāpoha* (Pra.

*matpratyakṣāviśiṣṭatveṣṭeḥ* (Bhā.).

It might be thought: "The object of inference is for one's own sake (svārtha)," yet even that which is the object of inference is not the svārtha of this word, because its nature consists of the meaning of *apoha*.

He demonstrates this with the words "fire is not non-fire," and so forth; for even that meaning of *apoha* is something to be expressed (*ākhyeya*), and it cannot be specified as "this is the svārtha" in such a manner.

It might be thought: "The object for oneself (*svārtha*) is the locus and so forth, qualified by the possession of fire, which is distinct from and related to that [exclusion]. If this is so, then in the case of positing such a distinction, it would not be an object for oneself, because it is other than the object consisting of exclusion (*apoha*), and you yourself maintain that the object of inference is exclusively the object consisting of exclusion. Furthermore, because it is for the purpose of communicating to another and because its object is distinct, the "object for oneself" (*svārtha*)—which is the domain of inference—is, when communicated to oneself, a real entity (*vastu-rūpa*) such as a logical mark (*liṅga*), whereas when communicated to another, it is the form of cognition (*jñāna-rūpa*) denoted by words, since the employment of words has cognition as its object. Thus, it is incorrect to claim this "object for oneself" has two forms.
Thus, according to your own view, the object for one's own sake (svārtha) of a word is established as neither the object of perception nor the object of inference; rather,
it is the form of the thing itself (svarūpa).

In this context, the reading *ātmane* also appears correct; with the intention that "this is for oneself" (*svārtha*) and "this is for another" (*parārtha*), the reading *ātmane* may also be intended here.
[The variants] *jñānāt nānārthatvāya* (Ya) and *jñānāt nānānārthatvā* (Bhā) [are noted].
In this context, there might also be a reading such as "because it has the purpose of instilling knowledge.

Now, if it is argued that the investigation into whether [the object] is within the scope of perception or inference is irrelevant to the investigation into the meaning of words starting with "atha kvacid," that is not so; for it has already been demonstrated that a third alternative is impossible, and so forth.

Nevertheless, out of deference to you, even though exclusion (apoha) of others is not perceived in the objects of perception and inference, the own-meaning (svārtha) must be understood from this very word as "exclusion of another" (anyāpoha), and not as the exclusion of its own meaning; nor is the exclusion of another within its own meaning without a substratum, because of the aforementioned fault.

Therefore, that in which another is excluded is the own-meaning. Thus, when "jar" is said, it is not the case that "it is not a non-jar such as a cloth"; since the exclusion of cloth and so forth occurs in the jar, the jar is the own-meaning. Consequently, it is held that the own-meaning is determined as being precisely the object of the word.

Nevertheless, even that [exclusion] does not have its own meaning as its object, because neither the locus nor the located is perceived. That very thing intended as the locus and the word intended as the located are not seen, because they are inseparable from the positive prescription of their own nature. That which is said to perform the exclusion (*apoha*) of another word's meaning is that very object as the locus, yet it is not positively prescribed; nor is the word as the located [positively prescribed].

Therefore, since those two are not perceived, one must connect [the question]: "In what respect is its own object excluded? If it is not positively enjoined—that is, if there is no positive statement of another object as spoken of in the Sūtra, as spoken of in the Bhāṣya, or as the meaning of another word—then surely that very thing which is not other than the injunction is directly perceived. Otherwise, if it were merely established as a negation of "not being other" (i.e., "other"), then because both [terms] would lack a stable basis for their own objects due to residing solely in exclusion, there would be no apprehension of them; how then could there be "another," or "who is other"? Furthermore, there is the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*), such that "this is other than that" and "that is other than this. Therefore, it is "other" in relation to "another."

Now, by following the statement defining the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), it is the object itself as possessing exclusion that is apprehended, not mere exclusion, nor something neither existent nor non-existent.

For the word "hi" has the sense of "because"; because the word "tree," while effecting the exclusion of the word "non-tree" within its own referent, causes the understanding of its own referent characterized as a tree. Thus, the meaning of a word is a real entity (*vastu*) qualified by exclusion—such as substance (*dravya*) and so forth—which is existent, and not mere exclusion, which would entail a lack of self-abiding (*svarūpānavasthāna*) due to the failure of the positive referent being established.

However, since that [positive entity] remains as the object to be enjoined (*vidheya*), it would be appropriate to say that "another word" is a different word and has a different meaning; therefore, he says: "Because another word and the meaning of another word lack a fixed nature (*asthitarūpatva*), what indeed is this 'other' for whom or from which an exclusion (*apoha*) could be made, being devoid of a positive determination of its own nature (*svarūpavidhi*)? The meaning is that such a thing is not possible. (Satyākṣara-prakaraṇa, Saṃbandhaprakaraṇa)

The reading "anyārthasyābhāvaḥ" in this commentary (bhāṣya) is indeed correct; for the intention is that the nature of the "other-meaning" mentioned in the sūtra composed by Diṅnāga— "the word effects the exclusion of other meanings"— as well as the "meaning of another word" mentioned in the commentary (bhāṣya)— "for [it] excludes the meaning of other words," and so forth, does not have a stable existence.

If it is argued that [the object] is not non-different from the cognition for the sake of its own nature, then surely that very [object] is perceived as non-different from the positive affirmation (*vidhi*).

Otherwise, if it were "not different" merely by way of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), there would be no apprehension of those two—the cognition and the object—since their own natures would remain unestablished; for how could one be "different" from another? Furthermore, there is the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*), namely: "this is different from that," and "that is different from this. Therefore, it is different from that. From that, it is this.

Now, following the statement defining the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), it is the object itself (*svārtha*) as possessing exclusion that is apprehended, not mere exclusion, nor [an object] that is neither existent nor non-existent.

The word *hi* has the sense of "because" (*yasmāt*); because the word "tree," while effecting the exclusion of the word "non-tree" within its own referent, causes the understanding of its own referent characterized as a tree. Thus, the meaning of a word is a real entity (*vastu*) qualified by exclusion—such as a substance (*dravya*) and so forth—which is existent, and not mere exclusion alone.

If you argue that "that which is non-other does not exist," and you think: "Just as one's own referent (*svārtha*) is cognized through the exclusion of the other because it is not other, so too the 'other' is cognized through the exclusion of that [non-other] because it is not non-other," we reply: "Is it not indeed [the case that] this very [referent] is the positive injunction (*vidhi*), etc.? For when the non-other is characterized by its own enjoined nature, the cognition of the "other" arises from what is distinct from the vital breath (*prāṇa*); thus, that very own referent is the enjoined non-other. Since there would be no cognition of "non-other" if that were not apprehended, it follows that the non-other is the own referent of the positive injunction.

Otherwise, as in the passage beginning with "another is not" and ending with "due to the absence of apprehension": just as when it is said that "a cloth is other than a jar," it does not exist [as such], so too when it is said that "a jar is other than a cloth," that too does not exist at all, because both are established merely through mutual exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*). Consequently, since their own referents are not established, there is no apprehension of "this is its own" or "this is other than that.
Therefore, from what could anything be other? From what could there be the exclusion (*apoha*) of what? Thus, the meaning of the word *apoha* is non-existent.

Furthermore, if it is asked how there is the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*), it is said: "It is other than that" and "that is other than this"—in the sense of a logical reason—because that which is established by the power of the other is other by the power of that [other]; and it has been stated that things dependent upon one another cannot be logically established.

Thus, when examining the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) according to the mere meaning of the word "exclusion" as used in common worldly parlance, its own referent is not established; it does not exist [as a distinct entity]. It exists only through mutual dependence.
When there is the grasping of that which is characterized by its own nature through a reciprocal process,
it becomes [the object] for the sake of the intellect.
Thus, "iti" has the sense of a reason;

[The author] now states the examination [of the opponent's view] in accordance with the statement defining "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*), beginning with "Now, as for 'exclusion of others'... and ending with "...neither existent nor non-existent. He says: "Therefore, the word that performs the exclusion of others is a 'bad word' (*kuśruti*). Its explanation is as follows: "For it is said that a word (*śruti*) denotes its own object by performing the exclusion of the objects of other words. Following that [definition], that which possesses exclusion within its own object is what is grasped, not mere exclusion alone; this is because the particle *hi* has the sense of providing a reason.

He demonstrates this—the word "hi" has the sense of "because," and he explains that through a worldly example: "Because the word 'tree'... and so on, up to "...it causes [the object] to be understood.

Thus, the meaning expressed by a word is an entity qualified by exclusion (*nivṛtti*). What is this? It is substance and so forth—being a substance, earth, clay, potness, and so on—not the exclusion itself. Just as sound, being produced, is inferred as being qualified by impermanence, so too a word illuminates its own denoted object as qualified by the exclusion of other things, because it is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Here too, only a positive injunction (*vidhi*) is accepted, because [the word] has as its purpose its own meaning which is not excluded, just like the sentence "Devadatta! Bring the white cow," which enjoins the bringing of a cow. You yourself have stated that there is an enjoining of one's own meaning distinct from exclusion; for you say that "the auditory organ (*śruti*), while effecting the exclusion of the meanings of other words within its own meaning, denotes [it]. The word *hi* is used in the sense of "because" (*yasmāt*); because, according to your own statement, the word "tree" (*vṛkṣa*), while effecting the exclusion of non-trees within its own meaning, causes the understanding of its own meaning, namely the tree-characteristic (*vṛkṣalakṣaṇa*). Thus, by your very words, the enjoining of one's own meaning is demonstrated.

Even by the passage beginning with "The word-meaning is an entity qualified by exclusion (nivṛtti), such as substance and so forth, which exists," it is demonstrated that there is indeed a positive prescription (vidhāna) of its own meaning;

otherwise, if there were everywhere merely an exclusion (vyāvṛtti) and no such thing as a "own-meaning" at all, the statement "the scripture effects [its function] regarding its own meaning" would be meaningless.
The example given is that "mere [exclusion]" is like a sky-flower.

Alternatively, considering that the very relationship between the means of inference (*anumāna*) and the object of inference (*anumeya*) is the relationship between the signifier (*vācaka*) and the signified (*vācya*), [the author] provides an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) along with its own explanation starting from "just as in the case of 'being produced' (*kṛtakatva*)," and concludes with the application to the subject (*dārṣṭāntika*) starting from "so too is the word," providing its own explanation. He states "because it is a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇatvāt*) as the logical reason (*hetu*), which is common to both; the rest is self-evident, since the essential point is that both are equal in their capacity to convey an object qualified by the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*). This is the summary of the meaning.
As he will state by way of illustration: "Verbal cognition is not a means of knowledge distinct from inference" (Pramāṇasamuccaya 5.1);

Here too, only affirmation (*vidhi*) is accepted, because [the word] has as its purpose an object that is not excluded [from its own referent], just like the sentence "Devadatta, bring the white cow," which enjoins the bringing of a cow.

Indeed, you yourself have stated that there is a positive prescription (*vidhāna*) of its own referent (*svārtha*) distinct from exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*). For it is said that "a word denotes (*abhidhatte*) by effecting the exclusion of the referents of other words within its own referent. Here, the particle *hi* signifies "because" (*yasmāt*); because, according to your own statement, the word "tree" (*vṛkṣa*), while effecting the cessation of non-trees within its own referent, causes the understanding of its own referent characterized as a tree—thus, even by the passage beginning with "the object qualified by exclusion is the word-meaning, [namely] substance (*dravya*) and so forth, which exists," it is precisely the positive prescription of its own referent that has been demonstrated.

Otherwise, there would be nothing but exclusion everywhere, and since there would be no such thing as a "positive object" (*svārtha*), the statement that "scripture produces a positive object" would be meaningless. The meaning is that when [the word] is accompanied by an explanation of its own nature, it is that very nature [which is produced]. (Cātayo॰bhā॰)
And why is this so? Verbal cognition is not a separate means of valid knowledge from inference;
for it expresses its own object through the exclusion of others (anyāpoha), just like [the property of] being produced and so forth.

Even by you speaking thus, a positive meaning (svārtha) distinct from exclusion (apoha) has been stated; therefore, why is affirmation alone accepted? Because its purpose is an object whose own meaning is not excluded (*avyāvṛttasvārthārthatvāt*). This phrase "its purpose is an object whose own meaning is not excluded" means that the sentence beginning with "an object possessing exclusion is apprehended as its own meaning" is intended.

It has been observed that a sentence which possesses its own meaning as something excluded from others is seen to accept a positive injunction (*vidhi*), just as the sentence "Devadatta, bring the white cow" is an injunction for the bringing of a cow whose purpose consists in the act of bringing a white cow performed by Devadatta, which is distinguished from [the bringing of] non-cows and so forth. Likewise, you yourself have stated that the sentence "a jar is not a cloth" is a sentence whose own meaning is characterized by the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*). As you said: "Of that which is distinct from the exclusion," and so forth—this is a restatement of the opponent's argument.

Furthermore, regarding its explanation, starting with the phrase "the word *hi* [is used] in the sense of 'because' (*yasmāt*)," and so forth, you yourself have clarified the establishment of your own position by demonstrating—up to the point of providing an example for the cultivation of the meaning of the reason (*hetvartha*), namely the word "tree" (*vṛkṣa*) along with its commentary, its list of terms (*daṇḍaka*), and the restatement of the previous and subsequent positions along with their commentaries; see page 611, line 4:

If you do not accept this, there is a fault: just as when the word "tree" is employed, the exclusion of other word-referents that are non-trees—such as cloth and so forth—is also entailed; consequently, in every case there would be mere exclusion, and no such thing as a "positive referent" (svārtha) would exist. for even among things that do not arise simultaneously, [the jar] exists as "being" through the arising and non-arising of the preceding and succeeding stages, such as the lump of clay (*piṇḍa*) and the pot-sherd (*śivaka*), because it could not otherwise be accounted for (anyathānupapattiḥ).

To this, he says: This might be so if some positive meaning of its own were understood through the exclusion of non-trees; what, then, is it? Since even that existence of the tree—namely, "being a tree" [means] "not being non-existent"—has as its sole purpose the non-existence of non-trees, we accept that the meaning of a word is indeed the exclusion of others (anyāpoha).

To this we reply: Even as for what you have stated—that when one says "that which is existent does not become non-existent," the word "existent" excludes the meaning of the word "non-existent," and therefore, when "existent" is said, the sense that "it does not become non-existent" is understood, and thus it is merely an *anyāpoha* (exclusion of others)—this too is extremely flimsy; the meaning is that it falls apart like a poorly bound load of wood.
Why? Because existence is invariably concomitant with non-existence at every single moment.

In this regard, it is indeed observed that the coming-into-being of a jar occurs simultaneously with the non-existence of a cloth and so forth, and the coming-into-being of color occurs simultaneously with the non-existence of taste and so forth. That which is the existence of the jar is the non-existence of the cloth; that which is the non-existence of taste is the existence of color.
Therefore, what exists does not become non-existent, yet what is non-existent necessarily comes into being.

Otherwise, if that [non-existent] were to come into being, the jar would not exist; for if the existent cloth were to come into being within the jar, the jar itself would not exist, because there would be no space for the jar due to its being occupied by the existence of the cloth.

What is it like? It is like your own view; for in your view as well, it is held that the word, while effecting the exclusion (*apoha*) of the meanings of other words within its own referent, expresses that reality which consists of mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*).

Furthermore, it has been stated [in the previous section], beginning with the discussion on the cultivation of existence and non-existence in the immediately preceding system, that this has been explained in many ways.
Therefore, it is not logical to say that "the existent does not become non-existent."
The same should be applied to color, taste, and so forth, which arise simultaneously;
thus far it has been explained regarding those that arise simultaneously.
Regarding those that do not arise simultaneously, it is said: "having arisen non-simultaneously," and so on.
If the lump (*piṇḍa*) were not to exist, or if the husk, the stalk, the granary, and so forth were not to exist, then the seedling (*śivaka*) would come into being;

thus, even in the case of the husk and so on, the existence of the present moment occurs through the absence of the preceding and succeeding states. It is not [the case] that it exists within the state of existence itself;

rather, this should be applied likewise to the states of the potsherd, the fragment, the gravel, and so on, as well as to the child, the youth, the adult, the middle-aged, and the old man. Just as it has been demonstrated in many ways previously, that which was non-existent comes into being.

That too is not correct, because it is a restatement of what is already known, because it accepts what is existent, and because it attributes existence to what is non-existent;

furthermore, in this way there would be no comprehension of the specific meaning of its own object, since its power is exhausted by the rejection of the opposing position. The meaning is that the "proposition" (*pratijñā*), which is the statement of the probandum, is not as it is intended by you according to the facts—it is false.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) here is as follows: [The term "existent"] would not exclude [the non-existent] in this way, because according to your stated method, that which is both existent and non-existent does not exist due to contradiction; whereas according to our view, that which is both existent and non-existent exists due to the absence of contradiction. Since the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) is established in both ways—by way of contradiction and by way of non-contradiction—it is like the case where "existent" is indeed non-existent because it does not exclude it, despite the presence of contradiction, yet due to the absence of contradiction. Likewise, in the case of "a tree is a *śiṃśapā*," it would not exclude non-trees, non-*śiṃśapās*, and so forth; thus, there is an absence of exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*).
