nor can it be excluded, because of the contradiction or non-contradiction [involved].

Furthermore, the claim that there is a restriction on the manifestation of all diverse entities—whether occurring simultaneously or non-simultaneously—by means of the exclusion of non-existent things such as a jar, is also not tenable. This is because it would merely be a restatement of a manifestation already known; because it would involve the acceptance of existence [only] through the negation of non-existence; and because in this way, there would be no comprehension of the specific nature of the object itself, as its power would be exhausted by the mere casting aside of the opposing position. A proposition (*pratijñā*) is the statement of what is to be proven.
By the very words of Diṅnāga, Diṅnāga’s own position is here refuted;
for Diṅnāga stated to Akṣapāda regarding the definition "the statement of the probandum" (*sādhyanirdeśa*): "If [the probandum] is not established, then the purpose is already achieved;
consequently, the doctrine of unestablished examples and reasons would follow as a logical consequence."

Regarding "cāyuga," it is possible that the reading here might also be "pra-sanneva na tv asan bhavati" (it becomes existent indeed, not non-existent), or "sanneva na tv asad bhavati" (existent indeed, not becoming non-existent), or even "sanneva tad bhavati" (that becomes existent indeed).

To this it is replied: That too is not the case, because it is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of what is already known. For one who speaks thus, since the form and other qualities of a jar and so forth do not exist, they are unestablished; consequently, statements such as "the jar or its form and so forth exists or does not exist," "it is excluded or not excluded," or "it is its own referent or not its own referent" are illogical as restatements. This is because a restatement must have as its object a thing already established and known. Furthermore, by you, as one who makes such a restatement, it has been admitted that the jar and its form and so forth are existent (*sat*). Therefore, from the admission of their existence, the existence of the non-existent (*asat-sattva*) follows all the more clearly. Consequently, due to this existence of the non-existent, the failure to escape the aforementioned fault remains exactly as it was. (Note: *asattvamā* in the manuscript *ya* is corrected to *asat-sattvamā*.)

Furthermore, if one accepts the non-existence of jars and the like as distinct from form and so forth—expressed as "it is not thus"—and if one accepts the non-existence of a continuum of form and so forth as distinct from an indescribable, ultimately ceased, momentary continuum, then the statement that "the particularity of the jar and so forth is its own object" would be untenable; for there would be no comprehension of the particularity of the object itself in the form "this is a jar," since one would have accepted the comprehension of the meaning "it is not a non-jar."

Why? Because its power has been exhausted by the rejection of its opposite. [The phrase] "it does not exist" means that the power of this word "jar" (*ghaṭa*) has been exhausted by the rejection of its opposite. And where a word has its power exhausted by the rejection of its opposite, there is no comprehension of the specific meaning intended by it, just as there is no comprehension of the specific thing to be proven (*sādhya*) in the sentence from the *Nyāyasūtra* (1.1.33): "The statement of the thing to be proven is the proposition (*pratijñā*). This is because the definition of a "proposition" excludes the opposite.
Since conventional objects such as jars do not exist, there is likewise no comprehension of the object that is the universal, because it is accepted as being non-existent;
moreover, for you, the specific object is indeed inexpressible.
However, according to our view, whenever [the universal is apprehended], it must necessarily be by means of this very object, as has been stated.
And thus, the exclusion of others (anyāpoha) should be disregarded; for surely, even here, there is an exclusion of spatial and temporal distinctions from one another,
and for that very reason, it must be disregarded.

— In the *Āptamīmāṃsā*, according to our own view, whenever [the term "existent" is used], it must necessarily refer to this very object; and as has been stated, the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) should therefore be disregarded.
But surely, even here, the exclusion (apoha) of differences in place and time from one another must be disregarded for that very reason; or let it be so.
Likewise, *ghaṭoya* [is] *tathā*; *ṭo bhā* [is] *aghaṭa* *ya*.

[Objection]: It might be thought that, just as there is a cognition of the general property of the "probandum" (*sādhyasāmānya*), there should likewise be a cognition of the general property of the "jar" (*ghaṭasāmānya*). [Response]:

That is not so. Since all conventional objects such as jars are non-existent, you yourself have admitted that there is no cognition at all because the object of the general property is also non-existent. For this very reason, we have specified [the term] with the word *eva* (only) in reference to the immediately preceding non-existent entity, because even according to the view of this system—which maintains that the referent of the word "real" is real only when its limiting conditions (*upādhi*) are unreal—the object of the general property is inexpressible; thus, the word has no intrinsic referent of its own.

For this reason as well, it does not exist; because for you, the specific object is indeed inexpressible, as it has been said: "The denotative relationship is not admitted for a specific object or word, because that was not previously perceived; rather, the universal will be taught."

Since the universal does not exist and the particular is inexpressible, what other "own-object" could there be? According to your own view, there is none; for by your very position, there is no comprehension [of an object]. It is also possible that the reading here is *viśeṣita* (qualified).

Thus, since this *śabdanaya* accepts the universal (*sāmānya*), the commentators must have intended to specify [the object] with the words "by you yourself" in order to avoid the charge of inconsistency; for they do not accept the relationship of signifier and signified (*vācyavācaka*) for a specific instance of an object or word, because such a specific instance has never been perceived before, whereas the universal will indeed be taught. So it is said.

According to our view, however, the denotable object must necessarily be [grasped] through affirmation alone; for this sentence must at all times have this very thing as its object. If the purpose is served by a meaning that is the denotation of a word, then even after traveling a very long way along the path of inquiry, since at some point or other only a particular (viśeṣa) possesses the nature of a real entity and no other object exists, it must have this particularity alone as its object, and not anything else—just as has been stated.

Now, [the opponent argues] that from the passage beginning with "Is it not the case that [an entity] exists precisely through the simultaneous non-existence of things such as cloth? up to "it exists by means of both existence and non-existence, for otherwise it would be untenable," and further from "if it were neither existent nor non-existent" up to the limit of the text ending with "like the failure to reach a specific probandum," the state of non-existence has already been established. Consequently, the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) should be disregarded; since an entity is of the very nature of excluding what is other, there is no exclusion of another, and thus the exclusion of others is to be disregarded.
See page 613, line 1;
see page 615, line 1.
He says: "But surely here too, there is an exclusion (apoha) of the distinctions of place and time from one another."

Spatially, a cloth is not a jar, and a jar is also not a cloth; thus, mutual exclusion (*anyonyāpoha*) is established. Likewise, color is not taste, and taste is also not color; and temporally, the preceding moment does not possess the object that will exist in the succeeding moment, nor does the succeeding moment become the preceding one. Thus, it is precisely the establishment of mutual exclusion.

To this it is replied: for this very reason, exclusion (*apoha*) is to be disregarded. Since it has been demonstrated in many ways that mutual relation (*parasparatā*) is indeed of the nature of affirmation (*vidhi*), and since existence belongs only to affirmation as its specific object—there being no referent of a word other than that—and since mutual relation has a specific object and exclusion is itself of the nature of differentiation, it is well said that "exclusion is [merely] within affirmation. Nevertheless, it is observed that the cognition of one's own object occurs precisely as endowed with all its particularities.
Nor is it [the case] for what was previously seen, because the purpose of the listener is the knowledge of the unknown;
and thus,
the relationship of signifier and signified is intended for the specific word and its meaning.

If that [object] has not been previously perceived, then because it is subordinate through its generality (*sāmānya*) and lacks differentiation from that [generality], there would be an absence of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Furthermore, if the entity denoted by the words "existent" and "non-existent" were indistinguishable, it would not be directly stated [as existent]. Even granting your position according to your own logic, we maintain that what is expressed is indeed a positive form (*vidhi-rūpa*) as desired by us—namely, the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*). Or, even if there were exclusion (*apoha*) in that case, it is observed that the word conveys its own object precisely as endowed with all its specific qualities (*viśeṣa*), because an exclusion is impossible without a positive determination of its own nature, and because only the specific qualities truly exist; thus, it is in the form of a positive affirmation, just like the meaning already grasped.
Regarding that which has not come into being through its own-nature injunction (*svarūpavidhi*), see page 610,
line 6 of the *Bhāṣya*.
Regarding the reading *°dityudyudgrāhi* in *pra°*, it is possible that the reading should be *°dityādyudgrāhi*.

Furthermore, as for what was stated—that the denotation by a word is of the universal (*sāmānya*) and not of the particular (*viśeṣa*), because the particular has not been previously perceived, just as fire is inferred from smoke by means of a previously perceived universal—this is not so. For there is no such thing as "previously perceived" [in this context], since in the world a word is not employed for the sake of making known what has already been established, which would be as futile as illuminating what is already illuminated.

Furthermore, because of momentariness, where is that previously perceived object which has long since perished? Or how can it be expressed by a word? But was it not said [that it is expressed] "by way of the universal of what was previously perceived"? This was indeed said, but it was wrongly said; for the universal—whether called "conventional" (*saṃvṛti*) or "exclusion" (*apoha*)—is non-existent.

Therefore, there is no cognition of what was previously perceived by means of a word; hence he says: "And not of what was previously perceived. For that [object] is not already perceived, nor is its purpose [already known] through what was previously perceived. What is the reason? Because the purpose of the listener is the knowledge of the unknown; for the listener is one who desires the knowledge of an object not yet known, and it is for the sake of instilling that knowledge in him that the word is employed by the speaker, not for the sake of making known what has already been seen, because words are not used for things whose meaning has already been stated. (Note: Correcting *uktārthānāmaprayogāt* based on the context). The purpose of the listener is the knowledge of the object not yet known. (Variant readings noted: *uktārthajñānenārthī*, *uktārthajñānenārthāṃ*).

And thus, regarding the verse beginning with "arthaśabdaviśeṣasya" and so forth: having established this, since the specific meaning is what exists because its meaning was previously unknown, we recite it as follows: "The relationship of signifier and signified is held to belong to the specific word-meaning;
for that [specificity] was not perceived before, due to the generality which is subordinate."

Thus, according to the respective order, we maintain that a specific object is the denoted meaning and a specific word alone is the denoter, because these two [the particular] alone exist, whereas the general object and the general word do not.
Since that particular was previously unperceived, it is precisely that which is made known; and by what means? It is said: through the general [word] acting as a subordinate factor (*upasarjana*).
The reading "because it has the purpose of making known what was not already known" (*ajñātajñānārthatvāt*) appears correct;

for it is accepted that the relationship of signifier and signified belongs to the specific word and its meaning, since [the specific meaning] was previously unperceived, except as a subordinate element through the general [form].
It should be noted that although the reading here on page 460–2 is "dṛṣṭatve," the reading "dṛṣṭatvāt" is indicated in the Navamāra.

"If there were no differentiation from that, there would be an absence of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). To explain what is meant by "if there were no differentiation from that," he says: "It is non-existent, it is not non-existent," and so forth. When "existent" (*sat*) is stated, "non-existent" (*asat*) is excluded; thus, "it is not non-existent" means it is non-non-existent (*asad-asat*). That very thing denoted by the word "non-non-existent" is the universal (*sāmānya*) consisting in the exclusion of the non-existent (*asad-vyāvṛtti*). Pots and other such things which possess existence are not its particulars (*viśeṣa*) or differentiations (*bheda*). Since they are not explicitly stated to be non-distinct from the entity denoted by the word "non-non-existent," the phrase "there is an absence of coreferentiality for the existent" applies.

How is it that [the word] does not directly express "existent" (*sat*)? Because even when [the word] functions directly through the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), it does not imply the distinctions such as permanence (*nityatva*) inherent in that [existent]; how much less, then, will it imply the specific entities such as pots (*ghaṭa*) and so forth, which are separated from it by the exclusion of others? To clarify this meaning, since the word "exists" (*bhavati*) must necessarily be employed in the sense that "existent is not non-existent," the primary meaning of "it exists" (*bhavati*) must be accepted as unimpeded;
otherwise, there would be a confusion of the meaning of "existing" (*bhavati*) with its various particulars.
Your error lies precisely in the attainment of a single entity that is both non-existent and isolated; how then could there be the exclusion of anything else?

Since there is no distinction, in the attainment of a single undifferentiated entity, your effort toward "exclusion of others" (anyāpoha) is utterly futile. Here, [the author] refutes Dignāga’s intention, which holds that even by excluding the nature of a cloth from a jar, properties such as permanence—which are characteristics of a universal (jāti)—are nonetheless subsumed within that exclusion.
For it was said by Diṅnāga: "The establishment of the properties of a genus. (5.36)

Furthermore, the properties of the universal (*jāti*), characterized by oneness, permanence, and complete presence in each individual, reside in this very [universal], because it is non-different [from its instances], because its substratum is not destroyed, and because it is fully present in its entire referent.
Thus, due to the absence of such faults and the excellence of its qualities, a word denotes entities as qualified precisely by the exclusion of other objects— *Pramāṇasamuccayavṛtti* 5.

For comparison: here, the Bhikṣu has extended [the critique] by showing that the position of Apoha is equivalent to the position of Jāti (Universal), as he says: "The establishment of the properties of a Universal"—meaning that the properties of a Universal, characterized by unity, eternity, and complete presence in each individual, reside in this very [Apoha] alone.

These properties of real entities, when extended to non-entities, indicate that they are like a cloth made without a warp; thus he says: "Moreover, for one who attributes oneness, permanence, and individual inherence to apohas—which are devoid of any defining characteristic—it is a cloth made without a warp.
Thus—[as stated in] the *Śarkarikā* commentary on the *Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika*, p.
74—one who wishes to contemplate this asks: "Why does he not state directly that it is 'existent' (*sat*)?"

The purpose of this [verse] is to provide an exposition and to demonstrate that the [opponent's] position regarding "possessors of a universal" (jātimat) suffers from the same fault. This begins with the words "Since even when there is exclusion of others... and continues until "...it will imply the particulars such as jars contained therein. The summary of the point is as follows: Just as in the case of a possessor of a universal, even when there is an exclusion of others, a word that operates directly upon the mere exclusion of the non-existent does not imply the particulars—such as eternality and so forth—contained within the general property of "exclusion of others," because its capacity is exhausted by that very exclusion. How much less, then, can there be any possibility that it will imply the particulars such as jars contained within the "excluder" (apohavat)—that portion of the denotable object which is delimited by the status of being existent (sat) through the exclusion of the non-existent (asat), namely, "existent is not non-existent"? This is the essential meaning.
He will state an illustrative example that fully accounts for this meaning;

by explaining precisely the intended sense of the word "existent" (*sat*), he first addresses the proponent of *anyāpoha* (the exclusion of others), saying: "For the sake of this meaning," and so forth, up to "how indeed could there be the exclusion of others? To clarify this meaning of the exclusion of others, the statement "the existent is not non-existent" must necessarily be employed, because [the meaning] is not manifested by the mere word "existent."

And in that case, the word *bhavati* must necessarily be employed; for when used with the word *sat*, the negative particle (*nañ*) has no meaning in the absence of a verb, whereas it becomes effective when accompanied by the word *bhavati*. As it has been said: "Even where another verb is not heard, there too the verb *as-* (in the form *asti*), referring to the present tense (*bhavantīparah*), is understood to exist in the first person, even if it is not explicitly uttered" (Patañjali’s Mahābhāṣya on Pāṇini 2.3.1).

Thus, the meaning "it exists" (bhavati) from that [root] is the primary one to be accepted. What is this? It is the very meaning of existence (*sadartha*), and it should be understood as unimpeded and non-exclusive in every state of being.

If existence (*sattva*) residing in a distinct jar were not to reside in cloth and other things, then [existence] would be non-existent [in them]; and thus there would be a confusion of the meaning of "becoming" (*bhavati*). Fearing this fault, and for the sake of avoiding such confusion, there is no implication of distinction. If the attainment of existence—which disregards the distinctions of substances such as jars that are about to be reached—were to depend on [the exclusion of] cloth and so forth, it could not be obtained even by one's desires. Your ruin lies precisely in the attainment of an existence that is distinguished from non-existence; how then can there be an exclusion (*apoha*) of anything else? This, however, is merely a quality of the attribute (*guṇadharma*), which [excludes] others by its own nature...

...there would thus be an absence of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). [Objection: Coreferentiality will still occur even with respect to things that are not implied and not pervaded, by virtue of the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*);

for coreferentiality does not exist in the absence of pervasion. Since the word "color" (*rūpa*) does not imply sweet and other such qualities, and since it does not pervade them, coreferentiality with words denoting those qualities does not occur; however, when there is pervasion, it does occur, as in "the color is sour" or "the color is blue."

If this were the case, there would be an absence of expressive power; since "exclusion of others" (anyāpoha) is even further removed, the word "existent" (sat) could neither denote its own object nor perform an exclusion of others. Consequently, there would be no comprehension of the word-meaning at all—see page 619, line 3.
Therefore, let the exclusion of the non-existent (asat-apoha) be examined; see page 261, line 5.
[The meaning is: that very [thing]... [the original manuscript reads] "pra... [incomplete].
In the case of existence, it must be accepted;
in the case of non-existence, it must not be accepted.
See page 618, line 7.
The reading here might also be "bhāve sanneva iṣṭavyaḥ" (in the case of existence, it must be accepted as existing),
[which is] not dependent on its non-existence.
But this quality-attribute itself [indicates] others by its own nature...

in this way there would indeed be an absence of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya); however, even with [entities] that are not implied or not pervaded, coreferentiality will occur by virtue of the speaker's intention.

For when there is no pervasion (*vyāpti*), there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*); because the word "color" (*rūpa*) does not imply sweet and other such qualities, and thus does not pervade them, coreferentiality with those words does not occur. However, it does occur when there is pervasion, as in "color is sour" or "color is blue. This [word "color"], however, is merely a property of the quality (*guṇadharma*), for it is incapable by itself of implying other specific instances (*bheda*), just like the word "blue" and so forth.

Therefore, since the distinctions such as "jar" and so forth are not implied [by the word *sat*], there would be an absence of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) when those distinctions are not its own; this, however, is merely a property of the quality (*guṇadharma*), because it denotes existence (*sattva*) and substance (*dravya*) by excluding others through its own nature, just like the color "blue" and so on.

Consequently, since the distinctions such as "jar" are not implied, there would be an absence of coreferentiality when they are not its own distinctions—this is perhaps the intended meaning here. (Compare p. 607, l. 26)

Comparison—Having thus stated that the fault is equal whether one asserts the denotation of mere exclusion (*apoha*) alone, [the author], wishing to demonstrate that what was stated by the Bhikṣu—that there is an absence of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and so forth because the possessor of the universal (*tadvat*) is not independent even when asserting the denotation of the universal—is equally applicable when asserting the denotation of that which possesses exclusion (*apohavat*), first adopts his own position: "Now, if it is asserted that the object possessing the exclusion of others is the denotable meaning.

Here the Bhikṣu says: "A word for a universal, such as 'existent' (*sat*), while denoting the substance qualified by that [universal], implies only the specific form of a jar or the like residing within that [substance]."

For that [word "existent"] is dependent, as it functions with respect to a substance by taking "existence" (sattā) as its basis; it does not independently denote a substance qualified by all its qualifiers.
Consequently, since a jar or other such objects are not implied by that word "existent," there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between it and a word denoting those objects.
Indeed, when a substance is expressed as qualified by one attribute, coreferentiality with another attribute does not occur.

Just as the word "sweet," denoting a lump of sugar characterized by the attribute of sweetness, does not imply other qualities such as whiteness and therefore lacks grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with it—as in the expression "this sweet [thing] is white"—so too must it be with this [expression] "the pot is existent.
He says that all of this is the same even in this [present] position: "In that case as well, because of its dependence on another, pervasion (vyāpti) is difficult for a word to achieve" (1.20).

Thus, even in that case, the word "existent" (*sat*), while conveying a substance qualified by the exclusion of the non-existent (*asadapoha*), functions dependently; its intention is that it is not capable of implying another property residing within that substance, such as the exclusion of jars and so forth.

And for this very reason, in the same way, when words such as "sweet" are applied to a substance like a piece of sugar-candy, they function solely to exclude what is not sweet or not white; since there is no possibility of a mutual pervasion between whiteness and sweetness, there is no implication [of one by the other].
And for this reason, the qualification "sweet" or "white" does not apply at all;

for even by the word "existent," which denotes a substance qualified merely by the exclusion of the non-existent (*asat*), it is impossible to imply further exclusions such as its being other than a jar or the like. Therefore, how can there be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) here in the expression "the existent jar"? — *Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika-śarkarikā*, p. 60.
[See] *Tulanā*, p. 607, l. 27:

Now, if it is argued that there should be no confusion regarding the meaning of "being" (*bhavati*) due to the non-existence of cloth and so forth, and that therefore the meaning of "being" alone is intended in all cases, then—since there would be no differentiation [of objects] and a single undifferentiated existence would result—the effort you have made toward the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) would be rendered utterly futile.

What is the reason? Even because of the existence of a jar within the state of a cloth: if it is said that "the jar exists," then the cloth and so forth would also exist; and if everything were thus pervaded by existence alone, then regarding the statement "it is neither existent nor non-existent," what could be the object of the exclusion (*anyāpoha*)? For there is an absolute absence of any object named "non-existent. Enough of this excessive harping; let us return to the subject at hand.
[Sambhede... *vivi*... *pra*... *ntatve*... *va*... *ya*]
"But this [quality] is indeed a property of quality (*guṇadharma*)," and so forth;

the qualification is "quality," and this is its property. From "by itself, other than [the substance]" up to "the absence of grammatical coreferentiality" (*sāmānādhikaraṇyābhāva*), the meaning has already been explained.
The word *sat* is a quality (*guṇa*) because it is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), like "blue" and so forth; this is the summary meaning.

A qualifier is that which assists (*anugrāhaka*), while the qualified (*viśeṣya*) is that which is assisted (*anugrāhya*); the former is subordinate (*guṇa*), the latter is primary (*pradhāna*). Qualifier, qualified, subordinate, primary.

Like the "blue-lotus" [compound], the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) is the primary object of apprehension (*pradhāna-grāhya*). *Note: The variants indicate that in manuscript *ya*, the term *pradhāna* is repeated.*

The following objection was raised in the *Ṭīkā*: "Even if [the terms] are not implied and not coextensive (*avyāpta*), grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) will still occur by virtue of the speaker's intention, such that 'this is the qualificand' and 'this is the qualifier.

To this, the opponent himself provides the answer in the *Bhāṣya*: "For it is not the case when there is no pervasion (*vyāpti*)," and so forth, up to: "By means of similarity and difference, as far as the form [is concerned], the form is sour; the form is blue."
The reasons are "because it is not projected" and "because it is not pervasive. [Regarding the statement] "the color is yellow" or "the color is blue": "the color is blue" is from the Bhāṣya.
There is no implication [of other qualities] because the distinction or non-distinction is already established by what has been heard;
for example, just as the word "white" does not imply sweetness and so forth,

here too, the qualities of the exclusion (*apoha*) are spoken of as "qualities" with respect to their being auxiliary, while the exclusions, qualities, and substances are spoken of as "substances" with respect to their being the primary objects to be assisted.

For the word "white" (śukla), while denoting a substance qualified by its own expressed quality alone, does not imply [the presence of] sweetness and so forth, even though they exist in that substance; consequently, there is no non-difference from those [other qualities]. Likewise here as well, the word "existent" (sat), having first denoted a mere portion delimited by non-existence—since it was previously non-existent—and then denoting a substance that possesses existence, does not imply that specific [substance] or its particulars, such that [those things] would be characterized merely by existence. Thus, there is a non-difference between the referent of the word "existent" and substances and so forth, or jars and so forth. (Tulanā, p. 607, l. 27)

He says this for the sake of explaining the cultivation of the white example that is about to be mentioned: "Because there is non-difference from the qualities residing in what is heard, there is no implication;

the quality heard is the qualifier, such as 'white' or 'existent. The differences residing in that [quality] are 'whiter' and so forth, or [the categories] substance and so on. Their non-difference resides in that which possesses them (the qualified). Whether in the view of positive inclusion (*anuvṛtti*) or the view of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), because [the universal] is merely subordinate to the nature of the genus (*jāti*), or because it is subordinate as a quality, or because it is subordinate as the mere exclusion of others, there is no implication. Of what? Therefore, there is no implication of anything other than the genus, or of the exclusion of others, or of that which possesses them."
The example begins with "Just as" (*yathā*) and so forth; it is an illustration for the purpose of cultivating the meaning already set forth, establishing parity between the two positions.

In your position (*satvatpakṣe*), the nature of the word is indeed a quality (*guṇa*); genus (*jāti*) and quality are [both] qualities, while substance (*dravya*) is simply substance. The meaning is that a quality is auxiliary (*upakārī*) and substance is primary (*pradhāna*), depending on the speaker's intention (*vivakṣāvaśāt*) regarding the object to be communicated.

In the theory of *apoha*, the nature of the word (*śabdasvarūpa*) is merely a quality (*guṇa*); and since both *apoha* and quality are qualities, while substance (*dravya*) is indeed substance—thus, in both these positions, because the fault is equally incurred through the sequence of distinguishing between qualifier and qualified, the passage proclaiming the absence of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), up to the words "as much as existence itself" (*yāvat sattvamātravat*), has for the most part already been explained. However, the specific point is now being clarified: here, the nature, the universal (*jāti*), and the quality are spoken of as "quality," whereas the universal, the quality, and the substance are spoken of as "substance"—this is not stated [here] because it was already stated by the opponent.

In this context, from the passage beginning with "svarūpāpoha" up to "anugrāhyatvāpekṣayā," that [explanation] should also be understood, as it expresses the same meaning. The contemplation of this point—beginning with "for the word 'white'... and continuing up to "...therefore, its non-difference from that is its non-difference from white"—is already explained by way of illustration through the presentation of the faults in the theory of denotation (*abhidhānapakṣa*).

In the same way here as well, the very same sequence applies—beginning with "the word *sat* does not previously exist" and so forth—as an illustration, up until the point where it denotes the substance (*dravya*) as being existent (*sattva*), according to this method. From this point onward, whether by means of water and so forth as a distinction of substance (*dravya-bheda*), or by means of qualities such as color and form as a distinction of quality (*guṇa-bheda*), or by means of actions such as going and so forth as a distinction of action (*karma-bheda*), the phrase "as being existent" (*sattvāt*) does not imply at all that particularity (*viśeṣa*), whether it be a single thing possessing exclusion (*apoha*), or any one among the distinctions of substance and so forth, or those various particularities, or indeed all the distinctions. This is how the text continues.

Regarding the phrase "like that which possesses [the universal] existence" (*sattvavat*): let alone whether it refers to one among the particulars or all of them; rather, a single intended object such as a jar, being devoid of qualities and so forth, does not imply that very substance, nor does it imply anything remote from it, such as another substance or the like, nor does it imply those particulars or their specific attributes. Since there is no differentiation even regarding particulars that are remote, it is "like mere existence" (*sattvamātravat*). Just as [an object] is excluded from existence because there is no implication in the case of the position of "mere existence," so too it is in your desired position of "exclusion of others" (*anyāpohavat*).

Thus, the conclusion follows according to the intended meaning: that substances (*dravya*) and so forth, or jars and so forth, are non-different from the referent denoted by the word "existent" (*sat*);
because they are non-different from that, [existence] is independent and consists of mere existence (*sattvamātra*).
See page 619,
line 25; since the meaning is the same, the reading "tatsamāno'rthokteḥ" (rather than "tatsamānorthokteḥ") might also be found here.
Does that which proceeds here [in this context] as "thus" (tadvat) mean "like that" (tadvat)?
Let it remain so.
In the same way,
even though the object is qualified,
it is not qualified by the qualifiers.

The reading "yathā tv anirākriyate, yathā sattvān nirākriyate" appears to be intended here; that is, because it exists, it is "existent" (*sattvāt*). The underlying intention seems to be that just as it is not refuted by you when [the object] is taken as mere existence (*sattvamātra*), so too it is not refuted in the position that it possesses the exclusion of others (*anyāpohavat*).

In this context, since there is no objection [to the reading], the reading might also be "tathā"; furthermore, in manuscript *ya*, it is stated that they are expressed as having the nature of genus and quality (*jātiguṇaguṇatvena*),
whereas in manuscript *bhā*, it is stated that they are expressed as having the nature of genus and quality (*jātiguṇatvena*).

For the word *sat* denotes merely that portion of the substratum (*dharmin*) which is excluded from non-existence, because it expresses a substance qualified by the genus of the nature of existence, just like the word "white.
And the word "substance" (*dravya*) denotes merely the exclusion of non-substance, not its specific qualities.

Thus, since these two have as their object only a delimited portion, possess no [intrinsic] difference, and lack a common objective referent, how could they have the same meaning? Therefore, even though they are of the form of the non-existent and the existent, there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), because they do not exclude each other and are not mutually implied.

Here too, because the word *sat* denotes a substance qualified merely by the exclusion of the non-existent (*asad-vyāvṛtti*), it does not imply [the specific categories of] substance and so forth; and consequently, there is no identity with them.
But surely, co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is observed there—as in "the white sugar-cube," "and that is sweet," or "the word *sat* is whiter"—such is the consideration of the cause.

The word "existent" (*sat*) denotes a mere portion of the substratum (*dharmin*) as delimited by its non-existence, according to the principle that "the existent does not become non-existent"; it does not denote anything else [such as exclusion (*apoha*), eternality, and so forth]. Do not think that this is impossible—just as [the word] denotes a portion [of the object]. Therefore, he says: "Because it denotes a substance (*dravya*) qualified by the genus (*jāti*) of its own existent nature. This reason has already been explained; however, it is stated in general terms as "like that" (*tadvat*) in order to establish both alternatives in accordance with the example.

Regarding the phrase "like the word 'white'": just as the word "white," while denoting the substratum (dharmyaṃśa) as the mere exclusion of non-white, does not denote any other part [of that substratum], so too the word "existent" (sat), having expressed the mere exclusion of the non-existent, expresses nothing else. Therefore, this reason is intended for the purpose of explaining the proposition "it is not thus" (*naivaṃ na bhavati*), in accordance with the example; however, it is not [intended] according to the Bhāṣya.

It appears most fitting that this reason (*hetu*) is for the sake of explanation alone, while the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is merely illustrative; thus, when he says "it expresses a substance as subordinate," the word "substance" (*dravya*) denotes only the exclusion of non-substance (*adravyāpoha*) by that very same logic, and not its specific [quality], nor a specific substance.

If it is asked, "What follows from this?"—it is as follows: because those two words, *sat* (being) and *dravya* (substance), have as their object only a delimited portion [of reality], they possess non-difference; because they possess non-difference, they lack an objective referent (*nirviṣayatva*); and because they lack an objective referent, how could there be a single meaning for the words *sat* and *dravya*? Therefore, even though the form of "non-being" consists in the exclusion of non-being (*asad-vyāvṛtti*), the distinctions such as "substance" do not belong to "Being" (*sat*), nor do "pot" and so on belong to "substance," nor do the words "substance" and so on belong to the word "Being. Consequently, because they do not denote these distinctions and because they are not implied [by one another], there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*asāmānādhikaraṇya*).

This passage—beginning with "atrāpi sacchabdena" and so forth—is intended to demonstrate that the fault [of the opponent's position] is identical to that of the position they themselves have refuted, in order to show that it does not entail the non-distinction from that [exclusion]. Even in the theory of *anyāpoha* (the exclusion of others), this remains the same up to the point of "tadabhedatvam," provided one does not reverse the literal meaning of the words.

Observe that the co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) which is both observed and accepted would not be established in this manner if one were to denote either "that which possesses existence" (*apohavat*) or "existence itself" (*satva*). See page 607, line 26.

Because it is an indirect expression, whereas in your own direct expression, the specific entity characterized by qualities and modes (*guṇa-paryāya-lakṣaṇa*) is denoted as "existent" precisely because it is becoming (*bhavat*) in its primary sense; thus, the entity is not a dependent qualification.

And that [entity] is either subordinate to existence and non-existence, or subordinate to the universal (*jāti*), as they have said: "Words denoting particularity are not in grammatical apposition with the word 'existent' (sat); there is no fault in this, because when that [existence] is expressed, [the particularity] remains. What then? This very observed grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—which occurs when a word functions as a quality term by means of its qualifier, with the word’s own form or its universal being subordinate, and the denotable object being either that which possesses [the quality] or that which possesses exclusion (*apoha*)—does not obtain [for you]. Thus, a fault is stated against the opponent;
for how could a quality be "existent" while being a non-existent quality?
He brings forward the point that both [positions] suffer from equal defects: "And just as in these cases such as 'possessing a genus' (*jātimat*) and so forth—

just as in the opponent's position, when using the word 'existent' (*sat*), there are the defects of not implying jars and the like, of not being a differentiation of that [genus], and of lacking grammatical coreferentiality (*asāmānādhikaraṇya*), with examples such as the non-implication of 'white' or 'sweet'— so too in the position of *anyāpoha*, even for the word 'existent,' there are examples such as the non-implication of jars and the like by the word 'existent' which possesses a genus."
In both cases, the reason is the same— namely, "because it is not a direct statement.
The reading might also possibly be "not because of [the fault of] an implication (ākṣepa)," "like the example," "like the position possessing a genus (jāti)," or "like the word 'existent' (sat)."

And all this collection of faults does not exist in the position that there is a direct statement of a specific real object which ascends the ladder of the universal of unreal adjuncts; furthermore, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is established [in that view]. Just as in the case of "the blueness of form," there occurs the cognition of a specific blue object—which is already existent—either by way of the accompaniment of the unreal adjunct consisting of the universal genus "form" (*rūpa-jāti-sāmānya*), or by way of the exclusion of the unreal adjuncts consisting of "non-form" and "non-blue"; so too here, the particular entity characterized by our accepted qualities and modes (*guṇa-paryāya*) is designated directly and primarily in its principal sense as the "existent" (*bhavat*) itself. For since the particular (*viśeṣa*) alone is characterized by qualities (*guṇa*) and modes (*paryāya*), it is not something distinct from the finger like a fist, nor distinct from the cranes and so forth like a row; and thus the substance (*dravya*) and other categories are also that very same thing. For this reason, the entity (*vastu*) as qualified by something non-independent does not exist. In the expression "the beds cry out" (*mañcāḥ krośanti*), since the connection with the action is possible only for a living being situated upon the bed—the locus (*ādhāra*)—it is determined that the word *mañca*, although denoting the locus, denotes that which is contained within it (*ādheya*) by way of non-difference from the form of the locus. For there are two ways in which metaphorical designation occurs: either through similarity (*sārūpya*), as when the cognition "this is that very person" is transferred to one of a pair of twins, or as when the cognition "king" is applied to a king's servant, such as a minister.
Or rather, due to the influence of qualities, there arises the cognition of redness and so forth in a crystal, as if from the coloring of a proximate object.

In this regard, first of all, a metaphorical application based on the transfer of a cognition (*pratyayasaṅkrānti*) due to similarity is not possible; for where there is no similarity, there can be no transfer of cognition, since the master and the servant are distinct. If that very same cognition were transferred, it would be non-different from the master and present in the servant as well, like a pearl necklace permitted by the master; but such is not the case. Furthermore, because [the cognition] does not grasp the excellence of the qualifier—as in the case of a crystal—the consequence would follow that the cognition would apply to the qualified object even without grasping the excellence of the qualifier. This results in the arising of a cognition that does not correspond to reality (*ayathārthajñāna*), and because [such a cognition] cannot occur simultaneously with the operation of its own word-meaning (*svaśabdārthapravṛtti*).

Only the particular (*viśeṣa*) exists as a real entity from the perspective of ultimate truth; the universal (*sāmānya*), which is the referent of the substance (*dravya*), does not exist because it lacks reality.
Therefore, only the particular is independent, with the imagined universal serving as its subordinate attribute, just like the word "bed" [refers to the bedstead].
Furthermore, according to your own view, the word is not expressive of the possessor of the quality (*tadvat*) because of the difference between them.

For [the two] are indeed distinct and possess exclusions; what then? Just as "the minister is like the king," there is a metaphorical attribution of non-difference to things that are actually distinct.
Therefore, there is no transfer of the cognition, nor is there similarity between the exclusion (*apoha*) and that which possesses the exclusion;
thus, there can be no metaphorical usage because the necessary basis for it is absent.

Furthermore, because there is no successive occurrence [of the cognition], a word uttered once cannot, due to its momentariness, first operate upon the exclusion of the non-existent (apoha) and then subsequently operate upon the possessor of that exclusion, like the cognition of a king and his servant.
Therefore, since the transfer of the cognition and the similarity [required for it] are impossible, there can be no metaphorical designation (upacāra).
It might be argued: "Because of the assistance provided by the quality (guṇa)."

Nor can it be due to the assistance of the quality (*guṇa*), because otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of a cognition arising with respect to the qualified object (*viśeṣya*) even without apprehending the excellence of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). Just as a cognition of redness and so forth arises in a crystal even without apprehending the excellence of the substrate (*upadhāna*), so too a cognition of the qualified object would arise without apprehending the excellence of the qualifier; however, this is not the case.

Furthermore, because it would result in the production of a non-correspondent cognition (*ayathārthajñāna*): just as the cognition of redness in a crystal is a false cognition (*mithyāpratyaya*), so too the cognition that conforms to the form of the qualifier would be a false cognition regarding the qualified object.

Furthermore, because [multiple qualities] cannot exist simultaneously: when there are many perceivers of a quality such as white, for instance—as in the case of a jar being characterized by such particulars as "it is earthen," "it is a substance," "it is white," "it is sweet," and "it is fragrant"—then the assistance provided by the qualities becomes contradictory.
For it is not possible for the substance to exist at that time in the form of a single quality, since it is not distinct from its manifold nature;
nor can it experience the form of the qualities in only one part, since the jar and so forth are perceived in their entirety.

Furthermore, if the assistance [of the substance] were produced all at once for its entirety by all [its qualities], such as "jar-ness" and so forth, then because each individual perceiver would lack the apprehension of the form of the jar and so on, there would result a variegated perception (*mecakadarśana*) through the confusion of all qualities, since all forms would simultaneously arise, just as in the case of a crystal. But this does not happen; therefore, the metaphorical designation based on the transfer of cognition due to identity with that [quality]—as in the case of a jaundiced person (*yamala*) and so forth—is untenable. Nor is it [untenable] because of the assistance of the quality, as in the case of a crystal; thus, your [position] is not [correct].

It would follow that [the cognition] would be like a string of pearls (muktāvalīya) from the letter *ya*, because— like a crystal— it would result in a cognition of the qualified object (*viśeṣya*) without grasping the excellence of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), which entails the arising of an incorrect cognition, and because [such a sequence] is impossible simultaneously.
The occurrence of the meaning of its own word...
