Furthermore, having raised the objection that the monk [Dignāga] might intend the "mere possessor of the universal" (*jātimanmātra*) to be the denotable object, he considered the alternatives: "Now, what is this 'possession of the universal'? Is it the relation between the universal and its possessor, or is it a form of generality (*sāmānya*")?

Having thus formulated these alternatives, one should apply the previously mentioned defects regarding the expression of the relation between the universal and its possessor; so it was said: "In the same way, the question of whether the relation or existence resides in the 'mere possessor of that' has been examined."
—*Śarkarikā*, p. 62; *Nyāyaratna*, p. 601:
For "possessing that" (*tadvattvam*) is merely that [state], as indicated by the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*).

And that [denotation] would have to be either a relation or a quality, as it has been stated: "In compounds, primary derivatives (*kṛt*), and secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), there is the denotation of a relation by means of an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*); except in cases of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), non-differentiation of form, or an invariable relation. Even in those cases, it has been said that [the word] is not a designator [of the relation], because the word for the relation is not heard separately from the words for the connection (*yoga*) or the genus (*jāti*), which are the meanings of the distinct [constituent] elements.
Would it be a relation or a quality?
For comparison: furthermore, regarding the term "possessing exclusion" (*apohavat*), this abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) ending in *matup* is also traditionally taught to denote a relation.

As it has been said: "In compounds, primary derivatives (kṛt), and secondary derivatives (taddhita), there is the denotation of a relation by means of an abstract suffix (bhāvapratyaya), except in cases of conventional usage (rūḍhi) or where the relation is invariable.
And it has been stated that a relation cannot be the denoted meaning—*Śarkarikā*, p. 63.
*Nyāyaratna*, p. 601, p. 607, l.
"If the object possessing that [universal] is a jar or the like, it does not exist in cloth or the like; how then can it be the universal?"

Furthermore, regarding what was stated by the Bhikṣu in this position— that when it is accepted that the individual cow Śābaleya, as qualified by the universal "cowness" (gotva), is the denotation of the word "cow," then since that [individual] does not exist in the case of Bāhuleya, the application of the word "cow" would not occur there— it has been replied: "If the object possessing that [universal], such as a jar, does not exist in the case of a cloth and so forth, how can the universal itself be the object?"
That too is the same—
the monk [Śarkarikā] said on page 63: "If that object possessing [the universal], such as a jar and so forth, does not exist in cloth and so forth..."
"If that object is a universal, how can it be so? Therefore, it is inexpressible"— Nyāyaratna 601.
For a universal has multiple occurrences;

and if that which possesses the universal is a pot or the like, how is it logical for it to be their universal when it does not occur in cloths and other such things? If it is argued, "But it is designated as 'possessing a universal'—why then is the state of being a universal superimposed upon it? [the answer is: because it is asserted that the word *sat* (existent) denotes a universal, and since existence (*sattā*) and so forth do not exist within existence itself and the like, it is not called "possessing that" (*tadvat*).
Therefore, one must necessarily admit a commonality of meaning with respect to the object;
yet that [commonality] does not exist in the object itself.
Consequently, in this case, it is only the word that is identical.

A thing such as a jar is similar [to existence] because it is denotable by the word "existent" (sat), but not because it possesses some [other] entity possessing that [existence]. Furthermore, the connection with existence has already been refuted previously;
nor is that [connection] considered to be without a cause.
Furthermore, it is never observed that a word remains non-different when its objects are different and there is no [common] cause;
therefore, why would this not be logical? Consequently, there would be an absence of the relationship between qualifier and qualified.

If it should be argued: "In the case of the quality 'existence' (sat), which resides in substances that are not distinct from one another, the relationship of qualifier and qualified will occur when there is a doubt regarding jars and so forth caused by the word 'existent'—just as in the case of 'bluer' and so on"—[we reply: if [this were so], then it would be like the case of blackness and so on in a single object.
And that [universal] does not exist;
for the word "blue" is not applicable to things such as "bluer" and so on if it were restricted to its own referent and excluded from others.
Furthermore, it has been stated that neither the property of blueness nor the relation [between the universal and the individual] is the meaning of the word.
Furthermore, even if this [existence] were accepted as a genus (*jāti*), it would not be so because it lacks the nature of a genus;

for even if one accepts a universal of blueness (*nīlasāmānya*) in things such as "bluer" and so on—just as the quality of blue is divided into three kinds—there exists no genus "existence" (*sajjāti*) that possesses universals such as "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*). This is because, since such a genus does not exist, one could not conceive of its occurrence in a substance by way of particular instances, such as a pot, without first assuming those particulars.
Therefore, this [position] also is not to be imagined.
It is not tenable that a universal is superimposed there, nor is it said that [the word] functions with respect to it.
A universal must necessarily be admitted,
because the object of a word is exclusively common [to many].
In this regard, the word alone is identical [in both versions].
This is what must be noted here: this portion of a *kārikā* is seen in the middle of *Phṣ₁*, but it is not seen in the middle of *Phṣ₂*;
therefore, it is impossible to determine whether this is actually a portion of a *kārikā* or a portion of the *vṛtti*.
"It is not intended to be signless" (*nānimittaḥ sa ceṣyate*); or perhaps the reading here should be "and that is not intended to be without signs" (*nirnimittaṃ ca tanneṣṭam*).
Furthermore, the reading "a real quality residing in no other substance" (*ananyadravyavartī sadguṇaḥ*) is also to be considered;
[see] Śarkarikā, p. 64.

Comparison—As it has been said: "Let there be no application [of the word] to another object; yet, just as in the case of 'black' and so forth, there may be a state of being qualified by excellence and the like in a single [object].
Having raised this objection, it was refuted: "Not so, because a universal (jāti) cannot be a non-universal."
—Nyāyaratna, pp. 601–602.
There might also be a reading: "of that which exists in a substance.

If it is argued: "In this case, even for objects such as jars, which are not directly denoted by words but are implied by the meaning, there will necessarily be a relation of qualifier and qualified (viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣyabhāva), because the object possessing that [universal] must be connected with some [universal] such as 'jar-ness' (ghaṭatva)," [we reply]: even in the case of implication by the meaning, there is an inconclusiveness (anaikāntika).

For "implication by meaning" (*arthākṣepa*) occurs where a certainty arises through the force of the meaning, as in the case of "he does not eat during the day," which implies the certainty of eating at night. However, in this case, when "existent" (*sat*) is uttered, there is no such implication because uncertainty remains regarding jars and other things; thus, it is a doubt. Therefore, there is no implication by meaning, and consequently, it is not logical for a genus-word (*jātiśabda*) to denote, in any way whatsoever, either the particular, the universal, their relation, or that which possesses the genus. Thus, the word functions through the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*).
Therefore, it is established that [a word] expresses its own meaning through the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), just like [the property of] being produced (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth;
and as it has been said in the *Śarkarikā*: [p. 607, l. 8].
pṛṣṭha 64,
Nyāyaratna pṛṣṭha 602: "Implication by the object" (arthākṣepa) is the name [of the section] in PSV1.
Devadatta does not [speak] by day;
since it is established that [the word "born"] is a word denoting a genus (jātiśabda),
that very point remains [unchallenged].

Although that which is to be expressed has many aspects, it is not understood in its entirety from a word; rather, by virtue of its own specific relationship, it functions to effect the exclusion [of other meanings].
(Nayacakravṛtti, p. 427–2)
"In accordance with its own relationship—[as stated in] *Śarkarikā*, p.

46—the word, though possessing manifold properties (*anekadharma*), does not deviate from that [property] by which it causes the object to be understood; it [causes understanding] by that alone, and not by means of the qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth of the word. These are the summary verses (*saṅgrahaśloka*) of PSV1.

If the meaning of a word is the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), how can there be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) in words such as "blue lotus"?
If it is asked, "How could they not exist?"—if it is argued that this is because the objects excluded by words denoting universals and particulars are distinct, then this fault does not apply;
for those [words] also—
And how could there be [the cognition of] non-existence?
Because the objects to be excluded are distinct, [words] have distinct referents; they are dull [instruments] for the comprehension of the distinctions within their own respective objects.
(Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā, p. 307)
In the *Sanmatitarka-vṛtti*: "Because they have a single, non-different effect in one [referent],

words such as 'blue lotus'— though their excluded objects (*apohya*) are distinct— are used together in a single location as co-referential (*samānādhikaraṇa*), like [the expressions] 'a post' or 'a crow's nest,' for the purpose of manifesting a specific individual within their own referent and for the sake of excluding their own respective exclusions."
For instance: taken individually, they are causes of doubt regarding their own specific objects;
however, because the object manifested by them together with other words is impossible [if taken alone], they function as qualifier and qualified through their collective assembly (samudaya).

If it is asked: "How can that which is a single substratum be neither blue nor lotus, yet be called 'blue-lotus' (nīlotpala) as being both blue and a lotus?"—if one asks this because [the object] is neither blue alone nor a lotus alone, it is replied: It is not merely that...
[PSV1]
For that is neither merely blue nor merely a lotus;
[as stated in] *Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā*, page 308, and *Sanmatitarka-vṛtti*.
Because they denote a composite [meaning],
those two [words] are understood as combined by the words "blue" and "lotus," not individually; for their individual [meanings] are as meaningless as phonemes— for example,
just as the word-elements "nī-" and "-la" are indeed present in the denotation of "blue," yet are themselves meaningless, so it is here as well.
— PSV1 C. edition d.
Edition, pages 67B–69A, N.
ed. pṛ॰ 75 B–77 A PSV2.
N. ed. pp. 159 A–160 B
P. ed. pp. 157 B–159 B

That [meaning] is expressed by the two words "nīla" and "utpala" when combined, not by them individually; however, according to PSV₁ and VT, there is also a reading suggesting that taken alone, they are meaningless, just like a mere phoneme (*varṇa*).

The extensive and stainless commentary (*Viśālāmalavatī*) on this *Pramāṇasamuccaya* with its commentary, composed by Jinendrabuddhi, is presented here after being translated back into Sanskrit from its Tibetan version—

beginning with the words "In the case of the particulars" (*bhedeṣu*), etc., he extends the fault stated regarding the position that [the universal] possesses those [particulars] to other positions by means of the second half-verse; herein he states the logical justification.

The form of the universal (*jāti*) is not applicable to the particulars (*bheda*); rather, it resides in the universal as the very nature of the word. Just like the nature of the word itself, the form of the universal exists in the relation as the form of the related entity;
for an object that exists [as such] cannot itself be made the object of verbal expression. Therefore, it was stated [in the *Vākyapadīya*] that "it must necessarily [be expressed].

If it is asked: "What is the distinction between the view that [the word denotes] the possessor of the universal (*tadvatpakṣa*) and the view that it denotes the particular (*bhedapakṣa*)?"—in the *tadvatpakṣa*, the denotation is by the word "existent" (*sat*) through the form of the existent universal (*sajjātirūpeṇa*); whereas in the *bhedapakṣa*, it is through the form of substance (*dravya*) and so forth.
For in this way, they would be denoted by way of their differentiated forms; this is the distinction.

Even in that case, since there is a metaphorical application (*upacāra*) to the differences such as "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) which are themselves direct [differences], the same fault must be stated as before: namely, the occurrence of metaphorical application directly [to the universal], the failure to denote [the object] through a sequence, and the contradiction regarding the assistance provided by the qualities—since these are possible, there can be no excellence in the denotation of the genus (*jāti*) without the intervention of the intellect (*dhī*). This is because [the aforementioned faults] are impossible [only if the intellect intervenes].
Even when the relationship is explicitly stated, for this very reason, the word "possibility" (sambhava) is employed.

[Objection: Was it not previously stated that the relation (*sambandha*) is not denotable? How, then, is its denotation now resorted to in the form of "being" (*sat*), and how is the metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*) of the relation accepted here? For previously, because it was of the nature of a non-entity (*asattvabhūta*), the impossibility of the metaphorical identification of the word with the meaning of the verb was stated, resulting in its non-denotability; the relation, too, is indeed a non-entity. Therefore, how can it possess existence (*sattva*), or how can there be a metaphorical identification with the word "existent" (*sat*)? And in the absence of such metaphorical identification, from where would the aforementioned fault follow? If it is argued that it is expressed through the metaphorical identification with "existence" (*sattā*), then why is the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the words "existent" (*sat*) and "relation" (*yoga*) untenable? [Response: This is not a fault, for this objection was raised while assuming the denotation of the relation itself.

And even if the relation itself were denoted, it would still not escape the defects of the "possessor-of-that" (tadvat) position, because its capacity is equal to that of the possessor of a genus; this was stated for the purpose of demonstrating that.
With the words "tadvāṃśca" and so forth, he refutes that this is indeed a separate position;
and with the words "nanu coktam" and so forth, he demonstrates that it is a distinct position.

In this case, the particulars (*bheda*) are not denoted in their form as distinct entities; rather, that very nature of theirs which is devoid of differentiation—superimposed as "Being" (*sattva*) and untouched by the form of particularity—is what is denoted.
Thus, [the opponent] considers this to be a different position from the view of particulars.

With the words "If it were so," etc., [the author] refutes its status as a separate position because it is actually included within the two positions concerning the connection with the universal (*jāti*).

If it is asked, "How then does that which possesses it (tadvanmātra) become existence (sattā) or a relation (sambandha)? it is replied: regarding the phrase "that which possesses it alone" (*tadvanmātraṃ hi*), etc., by the word "alone" (*mātra*) the exclusion of particulars is intended, and thus it is stated that the meaning of the word is the universal (*sāmānya*) whose nature is to pervade all things.

And since that [universal] is expressed by an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) as the ground for the application [of the word], nothing other than existence or a relation is perceived; for the abstract suffix is prescribed precisely for those two.

To demonstrate this through authoritative scripture (āgama), he says: "In compounds, primary derivatives (kṛt), and secondary derivatives (taddhita)," and so forth. Regarding the fact that relation (*sambandha*) is the expressed meaning, there is the following scriptural authority:

in these instances such as compounds, namely *rājapuruṣatvam* (the state of being a king’s man), *pācakatvam* (the state of being a cook), and *aupagavatvam* (the state of being Upagu’s descendant), the relations of owner and owned, action and agent, and cause and effect are expressed respectively in these compounds and the like.
Therefore, here too, because the word *sat* ends in a primary suffix (*kṛt*), it must be expressive of a relation.
Others offer this as an exception (*apavāda*) to it— starting with "elsewhere" (*anyatra*) and so on—
stating that this traditional authority (*āgama*) applies when [the word] denotes a quality (*guṇavācitve*), but not when it is used in its conventional sense (*rūḍhe*).
...here only the genus (jāti) is denoted, not the relation, because of the secondary derivative suffix (taddhita) which possesses an undifferentiated form;
and here it is the quality (guṇa) itself that is expressed.
Because of the non-deviating relationship...
here it is that very existence (*sattva*) which is denoted, not the relationship;
by the statement "the object possessing that [existence], such as a jar," the reason for its not occurring in multiple locations is revealed.
If that object were a universal (*sāmānya*), how could it be so?

That which does not subsist in multiple locations is not a universal, just like a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); and that [which you claim to be the result of valid cognition] is likewise [not subsisting in multiple locations]. Thus, there is an absence of the pervader (*vyāpakābhāva*).
For a universal indeed subsists in multiple locations; this is the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
With the words "And that" (*taccetyādi*), he explains the meaning of the reason itself;
with the words "How? (*kathamityādibhiḥ*), he explains the meaning of the thesis (*pratijñā*);

and with the words "But surely" (*nanu caityādinā*), he states that [the argument] proves what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), because that which possesses [the quality] is not intended [by us] as having the nature of a universal (*sāmānya*).
Revealing that such [an interpretation] is undesirable, he says "For what purpose? and so forth, and "Since...
and so forth. This is the rebuttal of the charge of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*).

He considers it thus: the word *sat* is accepted as denoting a universal (*sāmānya*) because of the facility of its connection [with particulars], because of the statement regarding its non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*), and because of the admission of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with words denoting particulars; for without the relation of universal and particular, grammatical coreferentiality would not be possible.
To explain: the cognition proceeding from a general term (sāmānya-śabda) without distinction is established upon a specific object by being excluded from other differences through specific terms;

this would not be possible in the absence of a universal (sāmānya). Furthermore, regarding the acceptance here that "it possesses that" (tadvān), there are two alternatives: does the possession belong to the universal such as "existence" (sattā), or is it the commonality of the possessor, such as a jar?
In this regard, he demonstrates that the first [alternative] is impossible— starting with "and in existence, etc.
Since there is no further genus within existences and so forth, because genera themselves lack the nature of being genera,
he demonstrates that the second alternative must necessarily be accepted— starting with "therefore," etc.

Since "in the object" (*arthe*) is the topic under discussion, might this [cognition] pertain to something possessing that [quality], such as a jar? If it is argued, "But surely it pertains to that very thing," it is said in response: "And that... and so forth.
If it is asked, "Why does it not exist? [the answer is] "Because... and so forth.
By means of the word "only" (*kevala*), he refutes the [objection that] the denotatum (*abhidheya*) is identical [in all cases].

The meaning is: the word alone is the denoter (*abhidhāyaka*) of these [words], and it is identical; there is no denotatum whatsoever that is thus [identical]. By the phrase "not by anything possessing that," he means that the similarity of these [words] is based solely on the similarity of their denotation, and not on any denotatum in the form of a thing (*vastu*) possessing that [quality].
If it is argued: "Surely existence (*sattā*) is denoted as possessing that [universal] by means of the word's own form, and the relation is [denoted] by means of the form of existence;

therefore, there will be a similarity between existence or the relation and the possessor of that [universal], which is the denotable object," we reply: The statement "And the connection with existence," etc., has already been refuted previously by the passage beginning, "For the fault is the same in those cases too—whether in the difference, in the genus, or in its connection" (p. 630, l. 2)—regarding the denotation of the genus and its connection as being the possessors of that [genus].

If it is argued that if the word "sound" (śabda) is common to jars and other such things, then that very word, by virtue of being sound-ness (śabdatva), would be their universal (sāmānya), it is said in reply: "Not without a cause," and so forth...
[etc.]
For a word that possesses a cause (nimitta), its application cannot occur where that cause is absent—just as the word "staff" cannot apply to a person who lacks a staff.
Likewise, for a genus-word (*jāti-śabda*) which possesses a cause, there is an absence of that cause [in the case of jars and the like]; thus, the non-perception of the cause has been stated.

Regarding the passage beginning with "tataśca" and so forth: if the universal (*sāmānya*) were the denoted object, then the word "jar" would be stated for the purpose of qualifying it, and thus there would be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
In the absence of the denotation of a universal, what could be the qualifier of what? Consequently, there would be a loss of your own accepted position.
Furthermore, the phrase "even if" indicates that even in the absence of the relation between universal and particular, the status of qualifier and qualified can be understood through another mode.

"Does not exist in another substance" means that it exists in no other substance; "the substance such as a jar possesses the quality of existence" (sadguṇa) means that it possesses the quality of being (sattā); by stating that "existence is its quality," the inequality [of the universal] with respect to this [substance] is expressed.

Thus, even though there is no identity [between existence and the pot], when the word "existent" (sat) gives rise to the apprehension of a pot or similar objects, the relationship of qualifier and qualified will occur, just as in the case of "bluer" and so forth.

A substance possessing the quality of blue does not reside in another substance that is bluer or otherwise devoid of that quality; thus, it is not a universal (*asāmānya*). Nevertheless, when one says "blue," a doubt regarding its specific distinctions arises as to whether that which is called "blue" is "bluer" or "bluest"; therefore, it is indeed qualified by words denoting these differences, such as "bluer" or "bluest. Similarly, when one says "existent" (*sat*), a doubt arises as to whether this existent is a jar or a cloth; consequently, it is qualified by those terms as "a jar" or "a cloth. This is just as in the case of blackness and so forth with respect to a single object.
If it is asked, "Since this [object] does not exist, how can that be? it is said: "For the word 'blue'... and so forth;
for the word 'blue' denotes a substance possessing the quality of blueness.
Furthermore, that [universal] does not reside in other substances such as a deeper blue;
nor does its relation to that which resides as blueness constitute the meaning of the word.
Therefore, in this case as well, it is considered to be without a basis (animitta), as stated at page 631, line 19; thus, it is the same, and so the example being compared is likewise unestablished.
Regarding the phrase "even in the case of the means" (*abhyupāye’pi*): although the example is established, nevertheless, there is no equality with that [example] in the case of *sattā* (Being).
He demonstrates this: "This is not so because of the non-genusness of the genus" (*naitajjāterajātitaḥ*).

This means that the genus "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) and so forth does not exist within this genus *sattā*; thus, it is a "non-genus" (*ajāti*), a "genus of Being" (*sajjāti*), or "possessing non-genusness. Consequently, specific sub-genuses such as "pot-ness" do not exist within *sattā*, just as the specific degrees of blueness such as "bluer" do not exist within the quality of blue. For [if they did], those sub-specifications would have to subsist in the substance by taking up those [sub-genuses].
Therefore, it is not reasonable to suspect that specific objects such as jars and the like are denoted by the word "existent."
The quality of blue, however, has many subdivisions;

even when residing in a single substance, it exists by taking on its own specific variations as far as possible. Thus, he shows that the apprehension of degrees such as "bluer" and so forth is appropriate from the word *nīla* which denotes that [quality].
With the words "But if this were so," he states the possibility of apprehending specific variations through another method.
"...the object possessing that [quality] necessarily exists," and so forth.
For an object possessing a genus (*jātimān*) is indeed conveyed by the word,
and that [object] is necessarily connected with some universal such as "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) through the force of the injunction (*niyoga*).
Consequently, when that [universal] implies its own particulars, the specific instance such as a pot is implied.
Refuting this alternative as well, he says: "Even in the case of implication (*arthākṣepa*), there is no certainty.
By the words beginning with "for implication of meaning" (*arthākṣepo hi*), he states the nature of implication;
then, in order to demonstrate its absence here, he provides the example of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-nidarśana*): "as when one says, 'He does not eat during the day.'"
With the words "But here," and so forth, he demonstrates the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) in the formulation by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyaprayoga*):
"The absence of an implication is the fruit of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
where there is an implication of a fact, there is certainty, as in the case 'he does not eat during the day,' which implies eating at night."
Furthermore, when the term "existent" (sat) is applied to things such as jars, there is no certainty; rather, there is doubt.
Thus, there is a contradiction in its own nature.
by means of the concluding summary [of the refutation] of the aforementioned designations of universals (*jāti*) and so forth, beginning with the words "Therefore," he demonstrates his own position.
he says this; by demonstrating the portion [of the meaning] that is understood through implication, he causes one to grasp that the word-meaning is indeed the exclusion of others (anyāpoha).

"Bahudhā" (in many ways) means that although there is a multiplicity of kinds through specific distinctions such as *śiṃśapā* trees and so forth, or through specific states such as being in flower or bearing fruit;
"abhidheya" (the denotable object) refers to the object such as the *śiṃśapā* tree itself—
and even though that very object has a multiplicity of kinds, there is no complete comprehension [of it] from the word.

"Because it conforms to its own relationship": its own relationship consists in invariable concomitance (*avinābhāvitva*), which is characterized by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
And that [relationship] is with respect to their generalities (*sāmānya*), not with respect to particulars (*viśeṣa*).
Therefore, whatever kind of relationship [exists], a similar kind of indicative capacity (*pratyāyakatva*) is likewise appropriate.

This is what is meant: its connection is with respect to the universal (*sāmānya*), and the universal consists precisely in exclusion (*vyavaccheda*), as previously stated, because no other [function] is possible;
therefore, it causes comprehension by effecting exclusion itself.
If it is asked, "By which aspect does it cause comprehension?", it is said: "The word also possesses manifold properties," and so forth.

"By means of its own specific and general properties, which consist of multiple properties, it does not deviate from the object"—this means that by means of that general property, such as "treeness," which it does not err in indicating, it indicates by that very [property]; the sense is that this alone is the indicative property.
By the word "alone" (eva), he shows what is excluded: namely, [it is not indicated] by means of the word's qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), properties such as being audible and being knowable by cognition are included.
These [properties] lack the capacity to convey meaning because they are non-deviant;
for instance, they are observed even in relation to taste and so forth, which are devoid of the referent "tree," whereas the universal "tree-ness" (*vṛkṣaśabdatva*) and the like are not.
"If it were merely the exclusion of others," and so forth;
"how [could that be]," and so forth.
If it is asked, "How could this not be so? and so forth...
Because [the word] "different" and so forth—this reason demonstrates a difference in meaning based on the difference in the objects to be excluded (*apohya*) due to their co-occurrence:

those words whose referents are different are neither coreferential (*samānādhikaraṇa*) nor related as qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhūta*), like the words "pot" and "cloth"; and since words such as "blue lotus" are likewise [different in referent], there is a contradiction with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddha*).
"Those too," and so forth.

Although these words have different referents due to the difference in what is excluded (*apohya*), nevertheless there is a distinction: [the words] are dull (*jaḍa*) regarding the comprehension of the difference within their own referent; "each individually" is the ellipsis.
Their own referent (*svārtha*) is the universal (*sāmānya*); for the word "lotus" (*utpala*), it is simply "lotus. Its particulars (*tadbheda*) are the red lotus and so forth.
The word "blue" also denotes merely "blue," while its particulars—such as bees and so forth—are insentient causes of doubt regarding that [blue].

By this, it is stated that each [particular] is a cause of doubt regarding its own specific meaning, whereas when combined, they are the cause of certain determination; this is the distinction [between the two].

Since, in this way, words such as "blue" and "lotus" are each individually causes of doubt regarding the specific meaning of the other, yet together they are the cause of certain determination, it is therefore logical that in a single object there is a non-differentiated functional unity (*abhinnakāryatva*) characterized by the manifestation of a qualified meaning, such as "blue lotus.

Consequently, because there is a non-differentiated functional unity in one [object], there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*); and from that, the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) is established.
even though there is a difference in the objects to be excluded (apohya)"— this also, as before, demonstrates a difference in meaning based on the difference in the objects to be excluded.

"For the sake of manifesting a specific [instance] of its own referent" means that the specific referent of words such as "lotus" or "blue" is the lotus or the blue [color]; "for the sake of manifesting that" indicates by this that they have an identical function (*abhinnakāryatva*), like the term "post" (*sthāṇu*) and the phrase "that which has a crow perched on top. "For the sake of excluding their own [respective] exclusions" means for the sake of excluding the universal "blue" and the universal "lotus" [respectively], so that they may be combined in a single [referent].
...for instance— each of those is a cause of doubt regarding its own specific object.
It is stated that words, when combined with presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*), serve as the cause for certain determination;

because words such as "blue lotus" are individually causes of doubt regarding their specific referents, yet only when combined are they causes of certain determination, therefore, when combined, they manifest a single specific object of their own meaning and function as grammatical coreferents (*samānādhikaraṇa*),
since the meaning to be revealed by them cannot possibly exist apart from the other words with which they are combined, and so forth.
The specific object manifested by the word *utpala* when accompanied by another word such as *nīla* does not exist at all in the word *utpala* alone;

likewise, that which is manifested by the word *nīla* when accompanied by the word *utpala* does not exist in the word *nīla* alone. Thus, because they function toward a specific object through the proximity of another word, there exists between them a mutual relationship of qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and qualified (*viśeṣya*).

...But surely, that which has a single substratum is [expressed as] "that which is blue and that which is a lotus" at the time of analysis (*vigraha*); therefore, he asks [this] because [the opponent] has stated that the qualified object is revealed only by a word accompanied by another word. Here, he states a contradiction of the [opponent's] own admission:
"For it is not 'merely blue,'" whereby, by negating the state of being merely blue, he negates the fact that it is denotable by the word "blue" alone.
Thus, it is not merely the case that [the object] is "lotus"; for there is the mere denotability by the word "lotus" alone.
To explain: that which is expressed by the word "blue" alone and by the word "lotus" alone is known as "mere blue" and "mere lotus.
But why is it not expressed by the two words "blue" and "lotus" taken separately? It is said in response: because it is the denotation of the aggregate (samudāya).

Since that object is expressed only by the words "blue" and "lotus" when they are combined, and not by them individually—otherwise, if its meaning were already expressed by one of them, their simultaneous usage would be untenable, like synonymous terms—it is shown that there is no contradiction with one's own tenets, because it is accepted that even at the time of the analytical compound (*vigraha*), that object is expressed by the words "blue" and "lotus" together. If it is asked, "What is cognized by the two words alone? [the answer is: nothing at all; for, like individual phonemes, that [usage] is devoid of meaning.
But how, if the parts are devoid of meaning, can their collection possess meaning? To this it is replied: "Just as," and so forth—[the word] *viśālāmalavatī*.
ed. pp. 248A–258A, P. ed.
As for the arising of blue, as it occurs... [P. ed. pṛṣṭha 280 A–291 B.
By means of the application of dissimilarity (vaidharmyopayogena).

The intended meaning appears to be as follows: since an object does not exist elsewhere because of the presence or absence of the manifestation of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), it is distinct [from that other]; and because of this distinctness, if it were not excluded from that [other], the same fault would ensue.
