For [the word] is a mere sound...
because of the absence of its cause, like [the words] "umbrella" and "staff."
Regarding the exclusion of universals based on differences:

when there are many speakers concerning a single object, using such qualifiers as "it is a jar," "earthen," "a substance," "existent," or "white," is that object then denoted in its entirety by the form of "jar," or only in part? It cannot be in its entirety, because it would follow that it would be impossible for another speaker to denote it as being "earthen."

There is an absence of any mutual generalization or specification, because the word expresses the nature of the entire denotable object; for only the word "pot" is common, but the object and the word proceed by taking up different causes (nimitta). Therefore, in the view that [the word] possesses exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) among the distinct things possessing that exclusion, because the cause for it does not exist in a single locus, like [the expressions] "umbrella-bearer" and "staff-bearer"—this is the intention here.

The phrase "merely a word" (*śabdamātram*) and so forth is a statement of the fault in your own position, which applies equally to you as well, because of the absence of a cause for that [denotation], just like the case of the "umbrella-bearer" (*chatrin*) and the "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍin*).

Just as the umbrella-bearer is designated by the umbrella as the cause and the staff-bearer by the staff as the cause—being non-co-referential (*asamānādhikaraṇa*) with one another due to having distinct causes—so it is also in the case of the view that the word "existent" (*sat-śabda*) refers to that which possesses exclusion (*vyāvṛtti-mat*).

"Because of the difference between exclusions (vyāvṛtti) and universals (sāmānya)," and so forth. Just as in the refutation of the position of affirmation (vidhipakṣa), here too, the universal of the exclusion of non-existence (*asadvyāvṛttisāmānya*) is distinct from the universal of the exclusion of a non-pot (*aghaṭanivṛttisāmānya*), which possesses the exclusion; therefore, [the reason] is "because of the difference between the universal of existence and the universal of pot-ness qualified by a distinct exclusion," namely, "the pot exists."

From this point forward, everything is to be understood as being identical to the refutation of the position of the [Vaiśeṣika] Proponents of Categories (*vidhipakṣa*); thus, this very commentary is now written: Regarding a single object, such as a jar, when there are various speakers—some saying "jar," some "earth," and so on, up to "existent"—among these diverse attributes such as "jarness" (*ghaṭatva*), "earthness" (*pṛthivītva*), "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*), and "existence" (*sattva*), when that object is designated as a "jar," is that object denoted in its entirety as the form of a jar, or only in part? It cannot be in its entirety, because at that very same time, it would follow that it is impossible for another speaker to designate it as "earth" and so forth. Indeed, having grasped a universal (*sāmānya*) defined by the exclusion of non-jars (*aghaṭavyāvṛtti*), it is not logical to employ a word intended to convey a nature other than that [of a jar]. If that object, by the influence of the other speaker, were to remain in its entirety in the form of a jar, then the existence of any other form within that single, entire entity would be impossible.

Because there is a cognition of a universal form that occurs in many instances, the application [of the word] "existent jar" is appropriate— simultaneously with its possessor and through its similarity to it— due to the difference in the speaker's intention; this holds as long as one does not depend on a word that excludes everything else.
Alternatively,
the reading here might also be "bhedād vā vyāvṛttiḥ" (or exclusion due to difference), and [the phrase] "vaktṛṣu vaktṛṣu" (among speakers, among speakers) would also occur in the Bhāṣya.
In the speakers [it is] because of being of that nature; in the manuscripts Ya and Bha, it is because of not being of that nature.
The proof for this is as follows: the thesis is that there is an absence of any other qualifier or general property (*sāmānyaviśeṣaṇa*).

This is because [the word] expresses the nature of the entire denotable object through its own formative application. Wherever the nature of the entire denotable object is expressed by a word through its own formative application, there no other [qualifier] exists, such as "earthen-ness" (*pārthivatva*) and so forth.
Now, if one were to claim that it [the particular] is grasped as a part of that [the universal], that is incorrect because it is not perceived;

for it is impossible to express a part of a possessor of a property by means of words denoting the exclusion-universal (*vyāvṛtti-sāmānya*), since those words have as their object a universal that is not that [particular], just as when one says "the teacher is my maternal uncle."

Now, it might be argued: even though there is no observed use of words denoting specific differences such as "jar" when there is a suspicion of multiple referents for that which possesses a genus excluded from the non-existent—as in your example to another person where you say "the jar is earthen," and the fault is accepted by the opponent that if every object were qualified by "jar-ness," there would be no room for "earthen-ness" and thus it would be illogical—likewise, if every object were said to be qualified by the exclusion of "non-jar-ness," then it could not be qualified by the exclusion of "non-earthen-ness";
thus, [the objection] is the same as in the case of "earthen-ness" and so forth.
Now, if one were to take a single part of this [object], that is incorrect because it is not perceived;

for it is not possible to express a single part of that which possesses [the property] by means of words denoting the exclusion-universal (*vyāvṛtti-sāmānya*), since those have as their object a universal characterized by the absence of what is other than that. Just as in the *Mahābhāṣya* (Pāṇini-Mahābhāṣya 3.1.87) it is stated: "The teacher is the maternal uncle"—wherein a single entity appears in multiple forms due to the difference in its relations.

He explains the illustrative example that was presented: "Just as a single person is designated as both 'teacher' and 'maternal uncle' due to a difference in relationship, so too is that which is the essence of the object [the same] in the states of being a rule and being cooked."
Vākyapadīya 3.8.63: This has been stated in the Bhāṣya—having gone from his teacher’s son to the daughter of his maternal uncle, he says: "May you pay homage to my teacher."
Having gone there, he pays homage to his maternal uncle;
likewise, the nephew goes to the teacher's pupil and says, "May you pay homage to my maternal uncle," and that [pupil],
having gone, pays homage to the teacher.

And in this regard, just as a single person may be a teacher with respect to one person and an uncle with respect to another, so too is that category [of action]—the root *pac*—a particular with respect to the state (*bhāva*) even though it possesses a universal nature with respect to its own internal distinctions; yet the state (*bhāva*) is indeed a universal with respect to the root *pac*. Thus it is stated in Helārāja’s commentary on the *Vākyapadīya*, section 3.

8.63 Now, it might be argued: when there is a suspicion regarding many objects concerning that which possesses a genus (jāti) excluded from the non-existent, [the word] denoting the exclusion of jars and so forth—
Comparison—As for what was doubted by the monk: "Let there be no relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*) between two distinct entities;

rather, when that very entity is denoted as qualified by existence (*sattā*) and so forth, the linguistic usage of qualifiers and the like will occur upon a desire for further particulars belonging to it, just as when the word 'blue' denotes the quality of blueness, a qualifier such as 'more blue' (*nīlatara*) or 'most blue' (*nīlatama*) occurs in view of further distinctions belonging to it."

As it has been said: "If [it were so], then in one case, like blackness and so forth" (p. 630). Having raised this objection, it was refuted as follows: "In that case, it is logical that the quality 'blue,' being differentiated by distinctions such as intensity or non-intensity, is qualified by suffixes such as *-tara*.

However, the universal *sattā* (existence), being devoid of universals such as 'pot-ness' and the like, while establishing an object qualified by its own self, does not at all require [subordinate] universals such as 'pot-ness'; therefore, there is no expression of a qualifier in that case."
As it has been said: "This is not [the case] because the universal is not a non-universal" (p. 630).
This point is likewise equal for you as well; for in your view, when there is the exclusion of the non-existent (*asat-apoha*), there can be no exclusion of the non-pot (*aghaṭāpoha*).

Therefore, since the exclusion of the non-existent (asadapoha)—which is the exclusion of the non-pot (aghaṭāpoha) and does not exist within itself—is incapable of being projected [onto it], it is not qualified by those exclusions of the non-pot; just as the exclusion of the non-blue (anīlāpoha) is qualified by its own internal exclusions of non-intensity (aprakarṣāpoha).
He states all of this as follows: "Because it does not exist within itself, there is no indication of specific exclusions;
therefore, it cannot be qualified by them, unlike 'blue' which is [qualified] by intensity."

Furthermore, having raised the objection that "the linguistic usage of qualifiers and so forth will occur by means of jars and the like, which are not directly denoted by words but are implied by their existence-class (*sajjāti*)," the Bhikṣu refuted this, stating: "The implication of the jar is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because its transfer is possible even in the case of a cloth."
As it has been said: "Even in the case of implication by meaning (*arthākṣepa*), there is no certainty" (p.
630, l. 7). This [objection] is likewise equal;

for the exclusion of the non-existent (*asadapoha*) is not non-conclusive (*anaikāntika*) in its capacity to imply the exclusion of non-pots [which are] like fire [implied] by smoke. Thus he says: "There is no implication of meaning at all, because of doubt, just as in the case of the sign (*liṅga*) and the signified (*liṅgin*)."
Thus—Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, Śarkarikā, p. 64; compare p. 608, l. 14.

Now, as for the view that one [perceiver] grasps a portion of this [object] as "pot" by means of the exclusion of non-pots (*aghaṭa-nivṛtti*), while another grasps the portion as "earthen" (*pārthiva*) by means of the exclusion of non-earthly things (*apārthiva-nivṛtti*): that is incorrect, because such is not perceived. For a perception of a specific portion is never observed when something is being described by means of other [exclusion-based] causes, as in the case of "the teacher is the maternal uncle. Likewise, it is impossible to express a portion of a possessor of a property (*tadvat*) by means of words denoting exclusions or universals.
Why? Because [such words] have as their object a universal that is not that [specific portion].

The non-existence of that which is other than and excluded from this [object] exists in this [object]; thus, in a universal such as "the jar exists," that [universal] is the object of this word. Therefore, it has as its object a universal characterized by the non-existence of what is other than itself (*atadasattvatsāmānya*). Wherever a word has as its object a universal characterized by the non-existence of what is other than itself, it is impossible to state only a part of it.
Why? Just as when one says "the teacher is my maternal uncle" (*ācāryo mātulaḥ*), one does not state a part of the various grounds already mentioned.
Now, there might be the following objection regarding the position of another (*paramata-āśaṅkā*): [text continues].

Just as the view of the proponents of positive injunction (*vidhivādin*) is suspected, so too is the view of the proponents of exclusion (*apohavādin*); for the passage beginning with "possessing a genus that is the exclusion of the non-existent" and ending with "or even 'the bluest'" is equal in meaning [to the former], as its commentary explains:

there will be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with words because it possesses those general qualities, since the word expressing that [exclusion] also has as its object the exclusion of those [other things].

Wherever that quality of being a general property (sāmānyaguṇatva) exists, there co-referentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) is observed. For example, in the case of the quality blue residing in a substance that is not other [than itself], because the generality of the exclusion of non-blue (anīlanivṛtti-sāmānya) resides in substances such as "bluer" and so on, there is co-referentiality with them, as in "bluer" or "bluest.

This is not so, however, because the relationship of general property and particular (sāmānyaviśeṣabhāva) must be examined, since the referent of those words [“bluer,” etc. does not exist [as a distinct entity].
Furthermore, the word "blue" also does not denote a substance by way of blueness; what then? It denotes the absence of what is non-blue.

And in that case, there is no possibility whatsoever for distinctions such as blue and so forth, because it would be the existence of the absence of non-blue. If you say this, then the meaning of a positive term must be as follows: even so, there is no grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) because the universal and the particular are unreal.

Although, like that [universal], existence (*sattā*) does not reside in cloth and so forth in the same way it resides in a jar and so forth, nevertheless, existence resides in a single substratum through the exclusion of what is other than itself (*atad-vyāvṛtti*); therefore, there is a suspicion of multiple referents. When that suspicion exists, the proposition is that there will be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with those words denoting the various particulars—such as "jar" and so on—in which that existence resides;

the reason (*hetu*) for this is "because it is a common quality" (*tatsāmānyaguṇatvāt*). Those many referents for which it is a common quality are "those having it as a common quality" (*tatsāmānyaguṇāḥ*); because of that state, it is "because it is a common quality."

Because the word expressing that [existence] also has as its object that which is excluded by it; all objects, that is, all referents, are excluded by that existence. Those objects belong to this word; thus, it has "that-excluded-as-its-object.
Because of that state—namely, because of having that-excluded-as-its-object—the application (*upanaya*) beginning with "wherever... and so forth should be performed.

The illustration: "For example, that which resides in no other substance," and so forth. For a quality such as blue, which is distinct from non-blue, resides in no other substance; it resides only in the substance that possesses the blue quality. Even though it does not reside in [substances] such as bluer (*nīlatara*) and so on, because the universal of the exclusion of non-blue (*anīlanivṛtti-sāmānya*)—which is the universal of the blue quality—resides in substances such as the bluer, there is coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with them, just as one says, "the cloth is bluer" or "bluest."

Regarding this refutation which includes an example and a conclusion, we say here: that is not so; for the relationship of generality and particularity—characterized by the exclusion of non-blue-ness, non-blue qualities, and non-blue substances, such as the case of blue-ness, the quality blue, and the substance blue—is to be considered, because the referent of the word "that" (tad) does not exist [in the opponent's view]. Furthermore, since there is no referent for the word denoting the universal "blue-ness" characterized by the exclusion of non-blue, nor for the word denoting the "quality blue," and since there is no instance of a genus, quality, or substance other than blue to serve as an example, the relationship of generality and particularity must likewise be considered in this case as well.

The cause for that cultivation is as follows: "And because even the word 'blue'... and so forth. For that word 'blue' does not denote a substance as being blue such that it would be a universal (*sāmānya*) of the various distinctions of degrees such as more blue or most blue; what then? It denotes the absence of what is non-blue—the negation of the universal of non-blueness or of the quality of non-blueness. And since no distinction among blue, bluer, or bluest can possibly exist within that absence, there is no relationship of universal and particular (*sāmānyaviśeṣabhāva*) because it merely expresses an absence.

There will be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with words because it possesses that common quality (*sāmānyaguṇatva*); for the word expressing it also has as its object the exclusion of that [quality]. Wherever there is possession of that common quality, there coreferentiality is observed, as for example, in the case of the quality blue residing in a substance that is not other [than itself], the universal of the exclusion of non-blue (*anīlanivṛtti-sāmānya*) possesses coreferentiality with [words] such as "bluer" (*nīlatara*) and "bluest" (*nīlatama*), because it resides in substances that are bluer and so forth.
Or rather, [this is not the case], because the relationship of universal and particular (*sāmānyaviśeṣabhāva*) must be examined, since those words do not have that [universal] as their referent.
And since even the word "blue" does not denote a substance as being blue—what then? It denotes the absence of what is non-blue;

and in that [absence], there is no possibility of any distinctions such as "blue" and so forth, because it is of the nature of the absence of non-blue. If you say this is not so, then in that case, the meaning of a word must be a positive entity (vidhi).

Since, even though [the object] exists in this way, there is no grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) because the universal and the particular are unreal—this is the comparison—[as stated in] the *Tulanā*, p. 474, line 1; [and] regarding the word "object" (*artha*), see the *Pra*. [text].
In the comparison on page 630, line 1 of Pañjikā 28, "nīlaguṇe" is a word ending in the locative case.

Is it "the quality of blue belonging to the object" (lakṣyābhy-anīlaguṇa), or "the quality of blue belonging to the two objects" (lakṣyābhyāṃ nīlaguṇa), or "the quality of blue belonging to the object" (lakṣyasya nīlaguṇa)?

If it be thought that [the object] is not [blue] because it is the existence of the absence of non-blue—meaning that the absence of the universal and quality of non-blueness is precisely the presence of the substance possessing the quality of blue, and that this is the commonality (*sāmānya*) of the various particulars such as blue—if you think thus, it is said in response: in that case, there is indeed a positive referent for words; for that very thing is the affirmation (*vidhi*) of the substance which is the locus of the universal and quality of blueness.

If it is asked, "Let it be so; what is the fault?", we reply: Because, according to the logic you have stated, even for that which exists (*sat*), there can be no co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) since it lacks the nature of a universal-particular (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*). For instance, in the case of the quality blue (*nīlaguṇa*) residing in a substance that is not distinct [from its locus], there is an absence of the distinction between excellence such as blue, bluer, and bluest; therefore, it lacks the status of being a universal-particular.

Consequently, because they have as their object that which lacks the nature of a universal-particular, we maintain—having accepted your own definition of "blue"—that universals lack the status of being universals-particulars, on the grounds that they exclude non-existent things like jars and the like, due to the non-existence of a genus within a genus (*jāterajātitaḥ*).

For there is no universal such as "pot-ness" (ghaṭatva) within a universal that is non-existent in nature—the cause of verbal designation and cognition—such as the absence of a non-pot (aghaṭābhāva), in the same way that there is a distinction of degrees of blueness in a substance possessing the quality of blue; because [the former] is non-existent, it cannot serve as a basis for employing [terms like] "non-pot," "absence," or "pot-ness. Furthermore, an object that does not exist in itself cannot be superimposed upon a qualified entity by means of a qualifier, just as its own essential nature [cannot be superimposed].
Therefore...
...there would be grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya),
but "existent" will not qualify "the jar" and so forth, because the nature [of existence] does not exist [in them], just as "sweet" does not qualify "blue."

In that case, jars and the like must be implied by the meaning [of the word "existent"]. However, because there is an absence of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—just as in the case of "any one of jar-ness" and so on versus "bluer" and so on, which possess the exclusion of the non-existent—the example is unestablished. Whether in the view that the exclusion of the non-existent constitutes the difference within the word "existent," or in the view that it is a positive affirmation, there is no coreferentiality.

Even if we accept the positive affirmation, we maintain that there is an absence of the relationship between universal and particular among those things that possess the exclusion of non-existent jars and the like, because a genus (*jāti*) lacks the status of being a genus itself.

For there is no universal such as "pot-ness" (ghaṭatva) within a universal that is non-existent by nature—the cause of verbal designation and cognition—such as the absence of a non-pot (aghaṭābhāva), in the same way that there is a distinction of excellence in blueness within a substance possessing the quality of blue; because [the latter] proceeds by taking up non-existence, the absence of a non-pot, pot-ness, and so forth. Furthermore, an object that is not present in its own right cannot be superimposed upon a qualified entity by means of a qualifier, just like its own intrinsic nature (svarūpa).
Therefore...
...there would be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*);
[but] "existent" will not qualify "pot" and so forth, because the latter do not possess that nature [of existence], just as "sweet" does not qualify "blue."

Therefore, since there is no exclusion of the non-pot (*aghaṭāpoha*) within the exclusion of the non-existent (*asadapoha*), the exclusion of the non-existent is not capable of implying the exclusion of the non-pot which does not exist within its own nature. Thus, the word "existent" (*sat*) lacks grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with words such as "pot," for coreferentiality would only occur in the case of a relationship between a qualifier and a qualified. [Objection: In that case, pots and so forth must be implied by the meaning; for one who possesses the exclusion of the non-existent must possess one or another property such as "pot-ness. [Response: The word "existent" [does not imply them]. [End of fragment].

Furthermore, even if one were to admit that the word "existent" (*sat*) does not denote something possessing exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), but rather denotes an existent that is excluded from the non-existent (*asat*), we still maintain that there is an absence of the status of universal and particular (*sāmānya-viśeṣatva*) among those things excluded from non-existent jars and so forth.

Why? Because of the "non-genus-ness" (*ajātitva*) of the genus (*jāti*). This is because the analysis of the term *ajāti*—as in "that in which no genus exists"—demonstrates that universals do not serve as the substratum for further universals.

The passage beginning with "for [it] is not the cause of the designation and cognition" and ending with "would proceed" demonstrates the dissimilarity between the example and the case in question: existence (*sattā*) is the cause of the designations and cognitions of "existent," and it consists of the absence of non-existence; however, within that [existence], there is no universal of "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*), which consists of the absence of non-pot. This shows the impossibility [of the opponent's position] regarding other things, because [the universal] would have to proceed by taking up the absence of non-pot and pot-ness and so forth from an entity that is [simultaneously] existent and non-existent—just as there is a distinction of the excellence of blue in a substance possessing the quality blue. Thus, he shows the impossibility of [the universal] applying to others.

To begin with, for the proponents of apoha, those substances—such as the designations "pot" and so forth—are not the causes [of the exclusion], just as they are not for us, the proponents of the affirmation of real particulars qualified by unreal adjuncts.
Those causes, such as the non-existence of non-pots and the like, do not exist within the non-existence of the non-existent;
therefore, it is established that [the universal] is a genus (*jāti*) and not a non-genus (*ajāti*).
How can a jar be established by means of a real word through a real word? It does not exist.
Is it the state of being a non-different substratum for others? Or is it the state of being a substratum for the measures of others? Or is it the state of being a non-different substratum for others?

What follows from this? Consequently, an object that does not exist within itself cannot be superimposed—by means of qualifiers such as "existence" (*sattā*) or "blueness" (*nīlatva*)—upon a substrate entity such as a jar or a blue lotus.

Why? "Like its own nature" (*svarūpavat*); this is a dissimilar example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), meaning that while a word superimposes its own nature upon the substrate, it does not do so in this case.

Therefore, the summary of the subject at hand, beginning with "therefore" (*tasmāt*) and continuing until "there would be grammatical coreferentiality" (*sāmānādhikaraṇyaṃ syāt*), has already been explained.

And the formal argument (*prayoga*) here is as follows: "The jar and so forth will not qualify [the universal], because they do not possess that nature; and their lack of that nature is established because it has been demonstrated.
The example 'sweetness like blue' has its meaning explained; the qualification is to be superimposed."
The specific superimposition (viśeṣādhyāropa) has already been explained; [the phrase] "then [they are] implied by the meaning" (arthākṣiptās tarhi) and so forth [refers to this].

If jars and the like are not implied [by the term "existent"] because they are not non-different from it, since they lack the commonality of being named by that general term, then they must nonetheless be implied by the force of the meaning. Why? Because they are invariably connected with some specific universal such as "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) which possesses the exclusion of the non-existent (*asad-vyāvṛtti*). For an entity possessing the exclusion of the non-existent is necessarily connected with at least one of the specific universals such as jar-ness; if it were non-existent, it would not exist, and it must therefore be existent, and what is existent is necessarily one or another of the universals such as jar-ness—so the opponent might think. [But this is not so,] for if it were non-existent... [the argument fails].
Because it is invariably connected with non-existence (*asattva*) and with general and particular properties (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*),
this [objection] does not hold; even if there is an implication of the object (*arthākṣepa*), there is no inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*).

If it is argued that the implication of a specific [property] is tenable because [the reason] possesses the exclusion of the non-existent (*asadvyāvṛtti*), then there would be the implication of "substanceness" (*dravyatva*) alone, since the various distinctions such as "pot" and so forth are deviant; but even that is not the case, because of the deviation [of substanceness] from qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth.

The following intention appears here: even in the case of implication (*arthākṣepa*), there is no necessity; for from the word "existent" (*sat*), there is the possibility of implying not only a jar but also a cloth, by way of an object possessing the exclusion of the non-existent (*asadvyāvṛtti*).

Thus, in the expression "the existent jar," because there is no necessity of implying the jar, the word "existent" does not stand in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "jar.

Now, suppose it is argued that while there may be no implication of jars and the like due to deviation (*vyabhicāra*), there will be an implication of "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) alone, since that is never deviant from an object possessing the exclusion of the non-existent.

That too is incorrect, because the word "existent" (sat) can apply to qualities and so forth as well— due to their deviation [from substance]— and thus there is no necessary implication of "substance-ness" alone;
and this much...
nor is there any possibility.
Therefore, the word does not effect exclusion (*apoha*).

At most, this much could be the case here: either the particulars possess the exclusion of others, or there is the exclusion of others, or there is a connection with the exclusion of others, or there is the locus of the exclusion of others for itself—this is the intended sense here; compare p. 628, l. 1.
"Is it not the case that if there were otherness (*anyatva*), there would be no exclusion of synonyms for universals and particulars?
And even if there were otherness, there would still be no exclusion of synonyms for universals and particulars? Thus it was stated by Diṅnāga in the *Pramāṇasamuccaya* and elsewhere.

Therein, since the non-exclusion of terms denoting universals, particulars, and synonyms is in fact due to positive affirmation (*vidhi*) alone, the intention is that the status of the word-meaning as positive affirmation is established; with this aim, he introduces the method of the restriction of both (*ubhayaniyamanaya*).

Comparison—In this context, the monk, while demonstrating the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the expression "the tree is a *śiṃśapā*," stated that synonyms such as "tree" and "taru" are not mutually excluded (*anapohyatva*), because there is no contradiction between general terms, particular terms, and synonyms even though they are distinct.
He says that this reason for non-exclusion is not at all understood: "And the non-exclusion of the universal and so forth is not possible without contradiction."
To the question "Why is this not possible?", he says: "For there can be no such thing as contradiction or non-contradiction among the essential natures of words themselves.
— *Mīmāṃsā-śloka-vārttika*, *Śarkarikā* commentary, pp. 69–70.

Here it is said: "This is not so; even in the case of implication (*arthākṣepa*), there is no lack of ambiguity. The meaning of this [passage], along with its commentary and sub-commentary, has already been explained. If it is argued that the implication of a specific [entity] is appropriate for something possessing the exclusion of the non-existent (*asadvyāvṛtti*), then, because of the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) among the specific differences such as 'pot' and so forth, there will instead be an implication of 'substanceness' (*dravyatva*) alone. By the use of the word 'mere' (*mātra*), only the generality of substanceness (*dravyatvasāmānya*) is grasped through the qualifier 'existent' (*sat*)."
To this it is replied: that too is not so, because of the deviation regarding qualities and so forth;

since qualities and actions also possess existence (*sadbhāva*), there would indeed be doubt as to whether a substance, a quality, or an action might be "existent" by virtue of its exclusion from the non-existent (*asad-vyāvṛtti*).
This is because the distinctions such as pots and the like do not deviate [from this].
If the non-deviation of the distinctions such as the jar and so forth is to be seen [as stated] on page 627, line 7,
this concludes the summary beginning with "only this much" (etāvat).
Just as there was a summary of the refutation of those who maintain that [the word] has a positive injunction as its primary meaning, so too is there a summary regarding mere exclusion (anyāpoha);
for these alternatives are impossible due to their being fraught with defects, and therefore the word does not effect exclusion— let this be seen on page 628, line 1.
Therefore, due to the bondage of defects,
there is the exclusion (apoha) of the primary [meaning], the exclusion of the secondary [meaning], and the exclusion of the universal.

Regarding what was stated by Diṅnāga—that even when there is an implication of a meaning (*arthākṣepa*), there is no certainty, and therefore "the word effects the exclusion of others" (*anyāpohakṛcchruti*)—the venerable teacher Mallavādin has here provided a rebuttal, stating that "therefore, the word does not effect exclusion."

Do not think that the faults belonging to the proponents of positive injunction (*vidhi*) and the proponents of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) apply equally to the proponent of a theory in which the universal is subordinate and the particular is primary; nor should you think that, because its definition is over-extensive (*atiprasakta*) like the definition of the exclusionist, a refutation (*apavāda*) must also be undertaken against this definition. To this he says: "Is it not the case that [the universal] is expressed by the words 'universal,' 'particular,' and 'synonym' when there is difference? Because there is no contradiction"—this is the completion of the sentence.

"What? is used as an interrogative. What do you think? [Is it that] in the case of difference (*anyatva*), the word "tree" does not exclude the referents of the synonymous terms "universal," "particular," and "synonym," because there is no contradiction with words such as "earth," "śiṃśapā," and "tree," whereas it does exclude "cloth" and so forth because of contradiction? Since, for you as well as for me, the consequence of exclusion (*apoha*) and non-exclusion is equal due to the difference between what is contradictory and what is not contradictory, the definition—"for a word, while effecting the exclusion of the referents of other words, expresses its own referent"—must be undertaken out of fear of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). [The answer is: "Affirmation" (*vidhi*).
Is this not itself the inference for the denotative capacity of a word according to the *vidhi* [view], namely:

"Even when there is difference [of the individual], there is no non-denotation of the universal, the particular, or the synonym, because there is no contradiction"? For what reason, then, is the *vidhi* not undertaken?

For, according to the established rule, a word denoting a particular as having the universal as its subordinate element conveys those [particulars] as well, because there is no contradiction due to their being constituent parts of it. However, you have abandoned the theory of *anyāpoha* (exclusion of others), which expresses synonyms for difference, because it is incapable of providing a coherent explanation.
A word, while performing the exclusion (*apoha*) of the referents of other words with respect to its own referent, would have that as its meaning;
however, because it does not abandon the referents of other words such as "universal" (*sāmānya*), this very thing— which you do not accept— is indeed the supreme affirmation (*vidhi*),
for affirmation (*vidhi*) is the act of establishing (*vidhāna*).
He will state the reason as "because their meaning has become unified with the injunction.

But is this not itself an inference for the denotative capacity of a word through its injunction—that even when universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth are distinct, there is a comprehension [of them] as being conducive to particulars, and that the aggregate of bases (*prakṛti*), suffixes (*pratyaya*), and so on, likewise denotes a different meaning; this we shall explain by means of reasoning.
See page 638, line 7;
page 673, line 25.

"What do you think? Must I also, like you, begin [this argument] out of fear of an over-extension—that even if there is difference, a word does not denote a universal, a particular, or a synonym? This is the connection. [Objection: But surely this very thing is the inference of the denotative capacity of a word by means of a positive affirmation (vidhi).
Even though there is a difference [between the two],
that which was stated by Dignāga in his *Pramāṇasamuccayavṛtti* is here presented after being translated back into Sanskrit from the Tibetan version;
this should be understood here as appropriate.
In that regard, even though there is difference, the word does not exclude the denotations of the general term, the particular term, and the synonym.
(25) If it is asked why the word does not exclude the referents of the general, particular, and synonymous terms even when their difference is equal, it is because there is no contradiction.
First, the object to be excluded (*apohya*) by synonymous terms is the same, because they are not used simultaneously; furthermore, it is not logical to reject their own specific meanings,
since even a general term excludes other objects within its own sub-classes, and a particular term does not fail to do so, as it possesses that capacity.
Just as a *śiṃśapā* tree is not a *palāśa* or other such trees, so too a jar (*ghaṭa*) and the like are not [the same].
By this, it has also been stated that there is no rejection of the general term or its referent.

Thus, how could a general term (*sāmānya-śabda*), while establishing its own meaning within its intended domain, not be disregarded by a particular term (*bheda-śabda*) or a term expressing a particularity-and-difference (*bhedābheda-śabda*)? Therefore, because there is no contradiction, the exclusion (*apoha*) of the referents of general terms and the like is not tenable.

And likewise, a collection denotes a different object; thus, when two words—one denoting a universal and one denoting a particular—are applied to their own respective universals, it is established, as previously stated, that they denote a different object qualified by those [universals], whether that object consists of two or many things. And he says:
Regarding the term "synonym" (*paryāyaśabda*): First, a synonym has a common object of exclusion (*tulyāpohya*). Furthermore, it is not logical for it to exclude its own meaning.
The reading "it is also admitted" (anumanyate) might also occur here;
[is it that] what has not been grasped does not exist? [Or is it that] it is not tolerated?
The rejection of the meaning of the term "universal-universal" has already been answered;
[what does it mean to] "establish" or "cause to function"?
It should also be noted that "it is not required" appears as "it is seen" in the middle of the *Pramāṇasamuccayavṛtti* (PSV1).
Because it requires only that [particular], the particular is not abandoned by its own universal (*tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā*, p.
Sanmativṛtti, Tattvārthasiddhivṛtti, p. 412;
Śarkarikā, p. 72.
"It is not apprehended because doubt arises; and when there is equality, those two have the same referent.
Even though the universal is manifold, it is apprehended through a non-deviant particularity;
thus, the relationship of qualifier and qualified between those two is not equal. These are the summary verses (saṃgrahaśloka) of the *Pramāṇasamuccayavṛtti* (PSV1).
If it is asked what the reason is here by which the word "tree" excludes the referent of another particular (bheda), [the answer is:
"A particular, however, excludes the referent of another particular because of their mutual opposition.

On this point, the monk, demonstrating that there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between "palāśa" and "śiṃśapā," stated: "A particular, however, excludes the referent of another particular because of their mutual opposition."

For particular words such as *palāśa* and *śiṃśapā*, like princes contending for a kingdom, exist in mutual opposition while each excludes others and establishes its own domain within the single universal of "treeness" (*vṛkṣatva*).
Therefore, the meaning is: how can one [particular] that functions through the exclusion of one [other] attain grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with that [universal]?
— *Śarkarikā*, p. 69.
*Nayacakra-vṛtti*, p. 613, l. 6; p. 613, l. 27: For words whose meanings are particular are mutually contradictory because they exclude the meaning of the universal, like a prince;

therefore, they do not tolerate each other’s meaning. Just as when the word "śiṃśapā" is used together with the word "tree" in the phrase "this is a tree, a śiṃśapā," the word "śiṃśapā" excludes the quality of being a tree from the dhava and other trees, and establishes it within its own specific domain.
The same applies elsewhere as well.
Thus, first of all, it is logical that the word "difference" excludes the referent of another word for difference because it takes away [the application of] the same substance;
and from that, what follows?
How does [the cognition] exclude "treeness" and establish it? (as in PSV2 and PSV1)
In the *PSV* (Pramāṇasamuccayavṛtti), regarding the term "differentiation" (*bheda*),
there may also be a reading here: "...by means of the word 'differentiation,' the exclusion of the referent of a word (*śabdārthāpoha*) is appropriate."
Is it logical to exclude [it] while [the object] is being excluded?

If it is asked: "Then why does one exclude an unrelated object such as a jar for the sake of another universal-particular (*sāmānyāntarabheda*)?", [the answer is: because the objects that are other universal-particulars are contradictory to their own universal. || 28 ||
However, because the term "tree" excludes [the category of] "earthen-ness" and so forth belonging to jars and other objects, there is a contradiction;
therefore, the exclusion of those [other categories] by it is accepted as being like [the case of] a friend or an enemy.
It is understood that, by implication, they are excluded by it.

By this, it should be understood that through a connection of the connected (sambaddhasambandha)—like a friend’s friend’s enemy, or like a friend’s enemy’s friend—the exclusion (apoha) and the indifference (upekṣā) toward qualities and so forth, as well as their subdivisions, which are distinct from the general [exclusion], are established.
—PSV1 C. ed.
D.
ed. folios 72B–73A, N.
Edited pages 80B–81B, PSV2, Manuscript N.
ed. pṛ॰ 164 B–165 A, P. ed.
From the sense [of the context], that [is understood] from the *PSV* (Pramāṇasamuccayavṛtti);
there might also be a reading: "therefore it is excluded" (*tenāpohyate*), meaning "it is understood."

The qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth, which are subdivisions of other universals (*sāmānyāntara*), and their further subdivisions such as color (*rūpa*) and so on, should be understood as being excluded or disregarded due to a connection with what is connected (*sambaddhasambandha*), like a friend’s friend’s enemy or a friend’s enemy’s friend. There may also be a reading here: "they are to be known as excluded and disregarded. The extensive commentary *Viśālāmalavatī* by Jinendrabuddhi on this is presented here, translated from the Tibetan version: It was previously stated [in verse 607]: "Just like 'being produced' (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth, it expresses its own object through the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*). Now, he states an exception (*apavāda*) to that with the words "even though there is otherness" (*anyatve’pi*) and so forth.

That which is the ultimate exclusion (*parihāra*), namely *anyāpoha* (the exclusion of others), occurs by way of excluding the objects denoted by words that are synonyms for both "universal" (*sāmānya*) and "particular" (*viśeṣa*).

He states the reason for the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*)—namely, "even though otherness (*anyatva*) is equal"—because a negation (*pratiṣedha*) must be preceded by such a consequence; and since otherness is the cause for [distinguishing] the exclusion (*apoha*), its absence serves as the logical reason (*hetu*) for the lack of exclusion.
Those things which are not contradictory do not exclude or negate one another, just as color and other qualities do not negate one another within a substance.

Having thus stated the non-contradiction of the three [categories] simultaneously, he now says "of the word denoting a mode" (*paryāyaśabdasya*) and so forth, in order to demonstrate each one individually;
by stating that "the object to be excluded (*apohya*) is the same," he expresses their identity of referent (*ekārthatva*).
"Because they are not used simultaneously" is the proof for their having a single meaning;
because the two have been made to convey a single meaning, there is no simultaneous usage of both.
Where there is non-usage of both despite their capacity [to express], those two have a single meaning, as in the case of two qualifiers.
Those which have a single referent are non-contradictory, just as color and other qualities reside in a substance, or as friends [do].
Since synonymous words also have a single referent, there is a contradiction with the pervader (*vyāpakavirodha*).
Those which are non-contradictory are not mutually negated, just as those very examples [show]; since synonymous words are also non-contradictory, there is likewise a contradiction with the pervader.
Furthermore, it is not logical to reject one's own meaning; thus, he states another reason for the non-exclusion [of synonyms]:

whatever is the specific meaning of something is not excluded by it, just as an object is not excluded by its own cognition; likewise, even a synonymous term is the specific meaning of another synonymous term, and so too with a general term, and so forth.

The particularities (viśeṣāḥ) or sub-divisions (svabhedāḥ) of the universal (sāmānya) "tree-ness" (vṛkṣatva)—which belongs to the general term "tree"—are the *śiṃśapā* and so forth. Regarding these, the exclusion (*apoha*) of other objects such as a jar by means of the word "tree," or by the specific word "śiṃśapā," is indeed admitted because of the speaker's intention; for the exclusion of jars and the like is intended by the word "śiṃśapā.
To demonstrate that very intention, he says: "Just as... and so forth.

By this exclusion of jars and so forth, he demonstrates that because they share a single referent due to being sought after [as trees], the word expressing difference is not contradictory to the general term;

for just as the meaning of the word "śiṃśapā" does not consist of the form of a *palāśa* tree and thus *palāśa* and others are its objects of exclusion (*pratikṣepya*), so too it does not consist of the form of a jar and thus jars and others are also excluded, and these are excluded by the word "tree."

By the words "by this" and so forth: that which is the generality (*sāmānya*) of the generality of its own [specific] generality—namely, *pārthivatva* (earthiness)—is expressed by the word "earthy" (*pārthiva*), which is thus a word for a "generality-of-generalities. By that [word], whatever is excluded, such as the watery element (*āpya*) and so on, is also admitted by the word "śiṃśapā," because of the speaker's intention (*arthitva*).
Just as a śiṃśapā is not a palāśa or other [trees], likewise the watery nature and so forth do not exist [in it].
...In this way, regarding the term "general" (*sāmānya*) and so forth:

just as a particular term does not reject the meaning of a general term because there is no contradiction, so too a general term such as "existent" (*sat*), while establishing its own referent—existence (*sattā*) and so forth—within the intended object, does so by being non-restricted to specific particulars; thus, while establishing [the referent], it locates it within substance (*dravya*) and so forth, which are distinguished from qualities (*guṇa*) and the like.

...Why is it not disregarded by a word for a particular (*bhedaśabda*), such as "substance" (*dravya*) and so forth, or by a word for both particular and universal (*bhedābhedaśabda*), such as "earthen," "tree," or "śiṃśapā"? It is indeed disregarded, because [the general term] remains within its own domain due to the [speaker's] intention; otherwise, its own meaning would be untenable as it would lack a domain. By this, he demonstrates that the word for a particular assists the word for a universal by accomplishing the intended object, and therefore the word for a universal is not contradictory with it.

The passage beginning with "the aggregate" (*samūha*) and so forth demonstrates the excellence of its qualities because there is no contradiction and thus no mutual rejection; alternatively, it states another reason for their not rejecting one another:
for when they do not reject each other's referents, it is logically possible for them to express a meaning qualified by their own respective referents, and not otherwise.
"...and thus" means precisely the non-rejection of their mutual meanings; "of the two" refers, for example, to the base and the suffix in the word *vṛkṣam*...
...in the same way, [there is a relationship] between the two words "blue" and "lotus" in the expression "blue lotus"...

Regarding the phrase "of many": just as in the case of "the handsome king’s man arrives," where all the words and phrases of a sentence, though functioning toward a common general sense, must be applied without exclusion as denoters of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), the fact that they denote other meanings has already been established. Thus he says, "as previously stated. For it was shown by the passage beginning at p.

630, l. 22—"for that is not merely blue, nor is it merely a lotus"—that because each individual word in the pair *nīla* and *utpala* is seen to be devoid of meaning [in isolation], the aggregate (*samūha*) denotes a distinct meaning.

He says "and so on," referring to the fact that there is no contradiction between a general term and its particular terms; with regard to the non-abandonment and non-apprehension of particulars by the general term, he states the verse beginning with "tanmātrākāṅkṣaṇāt" (because of the requirement for that alone), which means "because of the requirement for its own particulars alone.
"Requirement" (*ākāṅkṣā*) refers to the desire for the elimination of doubt regarding them.
The word *mātra* is for the purpose of excluding the expectation of other distinctions;
for instance, from the word "tree," an expectation arises only regarding objects such as the *palāśa* tree and the like, not regarding objects such as a jar and the like.
...therefore it is not abandoned...
If it is argued that [the self] is indeed apprehended because it is not abandoned, it is replied: "It is not apprehended," and so forth;
the meaning is that it is neither apprehended nor established.

Those things which are causes of doubt regarding certain objects have not been established by that [word], just as in the case of that very same [example]: even a general term (*sāmānya-śabda*) is a cause of doubt regarding its own particulars. This constitutes a contradiction of the reason (*kāraṇa-virodha*).

Furthermore, when there is equality, there is identity of meaning (*ekārthatā*) between the two; this means that where both are neither excluded nor taken up by the general and particular terms, there is identity of meaning—that is, co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). For example, if the particulars are not rejected or abandoned by the general term, one might ask: "Is it the same with the particular term regarding the general? Anticipating this objection, he says: "Even though it is manifold," and so forth.

Although the universal is manifold, the meaning is that it is nevertheless conveyed— that is, expressed— by the word "particular" (*bheda*), because it is impossible to express something without employing a term distinct from what is being expressed.

...by the term "non-deviating" (*avyabhicārin*); because the particular (*viśeṣa*) does not deviate from the universal (*sāmānya*), since in the absence of the universal there is an absence of the particular, it is therefore included by that [term]. Are their relations as qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya*) not desired to be equal? There is indeed a relation of qualifier and qualified because [the word] "tree" requires the exclusion of deviation from [other trees such as] the *śiṃśapā* and so forth; however, the *śiṃśapā* does not require non-deviation from the universal "tree," and thus there is no [such requirement].
But for two qualifiers that do deviate, the relation of qualifier and qualified is equal, just as in the case of "blue lotus."
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "what then here," and so forth:
because two universals are distinct in relation to their own respective universals, they are not mentioned separately [as if they were identical].
A particular is for the sake of another particular; thus, the particularity of "treeness" consists in the *śiṃśapā* and so forth, since these are mutually distinguished from one another.

In this context, it should be understood that because the object (*viṣaya*) indicates the subject (*viṣayin*), "word" (*śabda*) is both a difference (*bheda*) and another kind of difference (*bhedāntara*);
the meaning is that the word "difference" signifies the referent of the word "another kind of difference.
The reason for this is "because of opposition" (*virodhitvāt*).
"Because they seize the common property" is the reason for their enmity;
"like the sons of a king" is the illustration.

When the father of the princes has died, the kingdom is the common property; because it has been seized by them with all their might, they are enemies, and consequently, they do not tolerate one another's interests.
Those which subvert the meaning of a universal are mutually contradictory, like the sons of a king; and since general terms are also like that, this is their essential nature (*svabhāva*).

Those which are contradictory do not tolerate each other’s meaning, just as in that same example; and since particular terms are also like that, this is a contradiction of the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddha*).
By the word "like," he demonstrates the quality of subverting the meaning of a universal.
"Because it takes away a single substance" is a restatement of the very fact that it takes away the general meaning...

Therefore, the exclusion (*apoha*) of jars and so forth, which is being effected by that word "tree," is implicitly accepted by the word "śiṃśapā," like a friend or an enemy; for in effect, it belongs to that [word]. The word "śiṃśapā" has no direct operation upon that [exclusion], yet by means of that word "śiṃśapā," it is understood as being excluded from jars and so forth; this is because, through that understanding, it is in fact excluded from them.

If it is asked how this is so, it is said: "Like the friend-of-a-friend's-enemy," and so forth.

Here, the repetition of the word *mitra* (friend) as *mitramitra* should be understood as not intending to establish a friend through a series of intermediaries; otherwise, since a friend is already perceived by means of the single [term] *mitra*, the qualities and actions being excluded there by the word *śiṃśapā* (a type of tree) and the word *dravya* (substance) would be accepted as being like the "friend-of-a-friend's-enemy."

The specific qualities such as color and so forth, as well as the specific actions such as upward throwing and so forth, are disregarded when being excluded by the word "śiṃśapā" through the word "substance"— just like a friend's enemy's friend— just as in the case of [the words] *viśālā* and *amalavatī*. For a synonymous word such as *ghaṭa*, *kuṭa*, and so on, the meaning is precisely that which is to be predicated (*vidheya*). Why? Because it is observed; because it is observed to be something to be predicated. For that alone is to be predicated: either the act of joining (*ghaṭana*) or the act of bending (*kuṭana*), or both.

What is it like? It is like "having two mothers" (*dvimātṛvat*). For example, in a designation where the substantive is primary through the medium of its qualifiers—such as *rādhakamātā*, *pūrṇakamātā*, or *rādhakapūrṇakamātā*—that very same [person] is qualified by either one or both [of the two]. This is because there is a cognition of the substantive which has assumed the nature of the qualifier; the meaning is that there is a comprehension of a form qualified by the related [qualifiers]. Thus, even when not used simultaneously—that is, even though the causes differ—the very same distinction characterized by those causes is cognized, since the referent is one and the same despite the difference in the causes.

It might be thought: "Since there is a difference in the causes (nimitta), why does the exclusion of other causes not occur? This is not so; for a positive injunction (vidhi) that has naturally arrived at its own object cannot be rejected, because it follows its own inherent meaning. Even by means of another cause, it is precisely that specific object which is intended. For this very reason, even by a general term, that same specific object is perceived through a direct and immediate application of the injunction. In every way, by an injunction of immediate application, its own particulars are implied, as they are understood through the relationship of subordinate and principal (aṅga-aṅgin) based on their ultimate reality as being of that nature.

When the meaning of a positive injunction (*vidhi*) is understood as being free from any further requirement for the operation of negation (*pratiṣedha*), the cognition of exclusion (*apoha*) arises merely as a subordinate element; thus, the positive injunction is primary and exclusion is secondary. Just as in the case of the word "tree," which conveys a *śiṃśapā* and so forth, there is no introduction of "non-pot" or "pot" once [the tree] is cognized—since that very object has arrived with its own inherent flavor and is intended to be communicated—why should it be rejected? Indeed, the rejection of one's own referent is not logical.

What is the reason? Because even after going far away, without that [specific form], there is no cognition of it; for when "pot" is said, by means of two negations—namely, "it is not a non-pot"—even though other objects are excluded, the pot itself must necessarily be understood. And since that [pot] is indeed a *kuṭa* (a specific type of jar), and because "pot-ness" does not exist without "kuṭa-ness," the *kuṭa*-ness—which is invariably concomitant—is also cognized through its own essence (*rasa*). Thus, the affirmative meaning (*vidhi*) arrived at without effort is the very synonym (*paryāya*) of the word's meaning; this is entirely uncontradicted. (Yaśomitra: *avihitameva*; Bhāṣya:
*avihitameva*).

For this very reason, even by means of a general term (*sāmānya-śabda*), that same specific object is directly perceived through an injunction (*vidhi*) whose operation is immediate and unmediated. Since all its own particulars (*svabheda*) are entirely included by an injunction whose operation is immediate and unmediated, they are understood as being of the nature of that [general] form; thus, through the realization of the relationship between the subordinate and the principal (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*), the function of negation (*pratiṣedha-vyāpāra*) becomes independent of expectation. Consequently, in the comprehension of the meaning of the injunction, because the cognition of exclusion (*apoha-buddhi*) arises as a subordinate element, the injunction is primary and exclusion is secondary. This is just as, in the case of the word "tree" which includes *śiṃśapā* and other species, there is no introduction of "non-pot" or "pot" [as a subordinate].

In our position, however, according to the theory of affirmation (*vidhivāda*), because this word "tree" implies its own object—which consists of the distinctions such as *śiṃśapā*—as being non-different from itself, while [simultaneously] implying the object "tree" as being different from jars and so forth, it therefore attains grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with it, as in "the tree is a *śiṃśapā*. This is due to the unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) within the single act of affirming that [specific] existence. But in the absence of the affirmation of that [specific] existence, such [coreferentiality] would not be logical.

The existence that has the same locus as that [difference] is its "existence-existence" (*tadbhavanabhavana*); the rule (*vidhi*) regarding that existence-existence is its acquisition of self-nature (*ātmalābha*), its persistence, and its mode of being (*ācāra*). Without that—meaning in the absence of it, or in its separation—it is not possible; it does not attain coherence. This is because for that which is devoid of the rule of existence, there is no implication of difference (*bhedākṣepa*). For that which does not exist has neither differences nor the capacity to imply them, by virtue of which there could be co-locus (*samānādhikaraṇatā*).

The proof for this is as follows: Your intended object, "the tree is a *śiṃśapā*," would be something devoid of the process of becoming (*bhavana*) and incapable of implying a distinction [between the two], yet it would possess co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). This is because it is non-existent (*abhavattva*), like the son of a barren woman.

Furthermore, that which you accept as denoted by the two words "tree" and "*śiṃśapā*"—which lacks the implication of a distinction and the admission of co-referentiality—is untenable because it is non-existent, like the son of a barren woman.
