that which has become the process of arising is the state of being beyond the nature of manifestation.
See page 647, line 6 and page 644, line 2; the "assent" (anumati) indicated there is intended here.

Why does this [tree] possess the nature of being a particular (bheda)? How then is it also non-different (abheda)? If even this were not a particular, then it would not be a tree, because it would lack the particularity of being a *śiṃśapā* and so forth, like a jar.
That [pot] likewise does not exist as such, because it lacks the distinctions of a neck and so forth, just like a tree;
and so on, up to: it does not exist even as atoms, because it lacks the distinctions of form and so forth, just like consciousness.
And thus, all this results in being empty.

Who negates what, by what means, or from what cause? (Page 644, Line 14) Now, if somehow a tree does indeed exist, then, because it is expressed through its own meaning and so forth, that very thing becomes the object of affirmation (*vidhi*). It is the referent (*artha*).
And exclusion (apoha), being subordinate to that [positive entity], is unreal due to its non-existence;
the word-meaning, which is real, has an unreal adjunct, and it is the prescription of a particular object.
See page 646, line 19.

The other [opponent] says: "From what does this difference (bheda) derive its nature as a difference? How can there be the nature of being a difference for things like the *śiṃśapā* tree, which are intended to be differences from 'tree'? Since the universal 'tree,' characterized by persistence (*anuvṛtti*), is unestablished insofar as it consists in the absence of non-trees, of what would the *śiṃśapā* and so forth be the difference? Therefore, from what could the *śiṃśapā* and so forth have the nature of being a difference? The meaning is that they do not exist at all."

How, then, can that [tree] also be non-different? A *śiṃśapā* and so forth does not become a tree if it is non-different—that is, if it is not excluded from another, being a non-exclusion (*anapoha*), and thus not excluded from the absence of both *śiṃśapā* and tree; in that case, it would not even be a tree. How then could there be a distinction such that "the *śiṃśapā* and so forth is a tree"?
To this it is replied: "If even that... and so forth, which is a proof for establishing an undesirable consequence.
If even that *śiṃśapā* and so forth is not a distinction, then it does not become a tree; thus, by this very statement, the non-treeness and the non-substantiality of the tree itself are asserted.
The reason is: "Because it possesses the distinction of being a non-existent *śiṃśapā* tree, like a jar"—this is the example;

and that [jar] is also exactly like this, and so forth. However, if it is maintained that even that jar is not a jar because it possesses the distinction of being a non-existent neck and so on, then its non-jar-ness follows from its possessing the distinction of being a non-existent neck and so on, just like a tree.

In this way, the neck and so forth do not exist because they lack the nature of [independent] skulls and so on, and so on, up until: the atom does not exist because it lacks the distinction of being composed of unreal form and so on; form and so on are also non-form and so on, like consciousness, because they lack the distinction of moments of unreal form and so on;
or rather, in all cases generally, these objects do not exist at all because they are devoid of their own specific distinctions, like a flower in the sky.
These objects become momentary in nature.
Therefore, objects [do not exist], and so forth;
this concludes the demonstration of the aforementioned fault.
Thus, by this method, all this—whether perceived, inferable, or expressible, such as the visible world and so on—is reduced to emptiness according to your own doctrine.

Who excludes what, by what means, or from what? Since everything is empty, who, what, and so forth—given the absence of the agent, the object, the instrument, and the source such as sound and the rest—there is simply no exclusion. This is the meaning. Thus, the aforementioned faults do not apply. (Yaśomitra’s commentary).
"Because emptiness is empty of emptiness," and so forth, for the sake of [explaining] the object and the instrument of action.
Now, [regarding the passage] beginning with "In some way or other" (*atha kathañcit*):

lest there be the fault of universal emptiness (*sarvaśūnyatva*), someone—having abandoned the conceptualization of exclusion (*apoha*) as being a one-sided negation whose sole object is the absence of existence—maintains that, in some manner, even while a tree exists, it is not a non-tree, and even while a *śiṃśapā* exists, it is so intended, for fear of the fault of the meaning of words being empty. To this we reply: because of the statement that "the word, by its own power (*svārtha*), when uttered, expresses its own object," and so forth, that very positive injunction (*vidhi*) has become the object.

Now, according to the method under discussion, he applies this to the meaning of words: "And exclusion (apoha) is secondary to that [positive entity], and because it is non-existent, it is unreal. Exclusion is secondary to the positive entity which is the specific object; and because it is non-existent, it is unreal. Just as was stated previously at length, the word-meaning is real despite having an unreal adjunct; and that [word-meaning] enjoins only the specific [entity] and does not exclude—it is this that is the injunction of the word-meaning.
[The text reads: *kāntyapoha* (pra. and *vṛkṣo vṛkṣobhā* (bhā.).
It is not a *śiṃśapā*, it is not a *śiṃśapā*; [this is] precisely the destruction of speech. (Bhāṣya, p. 609)
The meaning of the word *saṃvṛta* (conventional) is precisely that which is a portion of speech (*vacanāṃśa*). (Yaśomitra; Bhāṣya)
This reading in the Bhāṣya is indeed correct;
such is the meaning of the word "iti" according to the Ya [commentary],
and such is the meaning of the word "iti" according to the Bhāṣya.

By this, the fact that the word for a universal has a particular as its meaning is also stated. A particular-word denotes its own object by establishing itself as that [universal], while abandoning the consequence of non-difference and non-existence; it does so by embracing the *śiṃśapā* and so forth without abandoning the continuity and exclusion [of the universal]. It thus becomes the seed for the non-existence of the "non-śiṃśapā" as subordinate to that [universal]. If, however, that [particular-word] were also solely intent upon exclusion (*apoha*), then the word "śiṃśapā" would not establish the object "tree," because it is excluded from it; nor would it be accepted through presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*) as being non-contradictory with the included object, just like the non-existence of the "non-śiṃśapā."
See page 644, line 1.
By this, the fact that the meaning of a general term (*sāmānya-śabda*) is itself a particular (*viśeṣatā*) has also been stated.

Just as, despite their difference, because the particular is predominant, the meanings of words for generalities, particulars, and synonyms are not excluded—either because they are subordinate to it or because they are of its nature—likewise, a particular word denotes its own object, whether it be a particular meaning other than the intended meaning of the [general] word, or a generality that is the meaning of a particular word.

How so? By effecting an identification of the self with the universal through its true nature (*tattvena*), and by causing the self to act as an auxiliary in its subordinate state, what does it accomplish? It accomplishes its own purpose; this is how it continues.

It does not abandon the non-difference [of the particular] and the risk of falling into non-existence; nor does it, having abandoned the universals of "tree," "earthen," "clay," "substance," and "existence," establish the particular as being absolutely distinct from them, because such an object is impossible, since the particular is established by means of having the universal as its subordinate and because it acquires its own nature through that subordination. Nor does it state that "it is not a non-tree, a non-śiṃśapā, etc.," which would result in the fallacy of non-existence devoid of the cognition of its own meaning, for if there were no denotable object, the linguistic usage of words would necessarily come to an end.

If it is asked, "What is this particular term (*viśeṣa-śabda*), or what is its meaning?", it is said: [it is] "śiṃśapā" and so forth. By the inclusion of that [particular], there is the inclusion of the universal (*sāmānya*) such as "tree," which persists (*anuvṛtti*) among existing things like trees; and by the inclusion of the exclusion (*apoha*) consisting in the removal of non-existence—namely, the exclusion of non-trees and so forth—there is the inclusion of the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*). Why does it not abandon those two? If it is asked why it does not abandon them, it is said: because, while expressing its own referent (*svārtha*), it proceeds toward the state of being the seed for the non-existence of the *śiṃśapā* (which is subordinate to it)—the sense being that it goes or moves [toward it]. For the word *śiṃśapā*, its own referent—the object *śiṃśapā*—is the seed of both that persistence and that exclusion: namely, the subordination of the universal of persistence to its own referent, and the universal of exclusion characterized by the non-existence of non-*śiṃśapās* such as jars and the like therein. Otherwise, if it did not convey anything, what would it exclude?

In the *Pramāṇasamuccayavṛtti*, at the point of demonstrating that a general term is not contradictory with a particular term, the expression "the word for difference and non-difference" (*bhedābheda-śabda*) is also employed;
see page 638, line 10.
Therefore, the reading here might also be "of the meaning of the words 'particular' and 'particularity'" (*viśeṣaviśeṣa-śabdārthasya*).
Comparison— on page 643,
line 1, it was stated immediately prior that "it denotes its own meaning," and it will be stated again on page 644,
line 16; therefore, the reading "svārtham abhidhatte" (denotes its own meaning) is likely intended here.
Because of being [the cause of] the attainment of sentient beings;
by those possessing distinctions,
it is distinguished.
The manifest is the non-manifest of existence; the non-manifest is the non-manifest of both existence and non-existence.
In this case, "of the one ending in -da" (*sadaṃśasya*) appears correctly; likewise, in what follows,
[the reading] "ending in -da" (*sadaṃta*) is correct.

The passage beginning with "yadi tu so 'pi" (if, however, even that... is a slightly modified version of the previous text; it constitutes the application (*upanaya*) up to the point where the injunction for the specific meaning is stated.

In this regard, the distinction is stated: in the case of "the tree is a *śiṃśapā*," the word "*śiṃśapā*" would not establish the meaning of "tree" as having attained the nature of a specific *śiṃśapā*, because [the former] is excluded [from the latter], as understood previously; or else, one might not accept it through presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*), thinking that when it is said "it is not a non-tree," the sense "it is a tree" is already implied by the fact. Let this [implied] meaning not be [the primary meaning]; yet it is desired. Why? Because there is no contradiction with the expressed meaning (*upāttārthāvirodhāt*). Here, the word "iti" has the sense of a reason (i.e., "because").
The [inference] "it was not a śiṃśapā" and so forth is equivalent to "it was not a tree" and so forth; because of its reversal from the general [concept],
due to its being a non-existence and its being a non-tree...
Regarding the rule for specific meanings:

as for the statement that, because there is no contradiction, there is no exclusion (*apoha*) of the referents of words such as "universal" even when there is difference, that non-contradiction is established in this very way, because [the universal] has become one in meaning with the rule of existence (*bhavanavidhi*); and likewise, the aggregate denotes a different object.

And thus, when general and particular words function within their own respective general meanings, they denote objects qualified by those [particulars]; the denotation of the meaning of a sentence as a collection of two or more [words] is to be understood through the process of reaching a particular object that is invariably concomitant with them. This is based on reasons such as "because of non-existence" (*abhavatvāt*) or "because of not being a tree" (*avṛkṣatvāt*). Furthermore, the establishment of the reason follows from the acceptance of mere non-existence; in its opposite case, one falls into our own position. The contemplation of the remaining text is similar to the contemplation of the preceding text.

Thus, first of all, it has been stated that just as the referents of words for generalities, particulars, and synonyms possess *apoha*, so too does the referent of a word for a generality-of-generalities possess *apoha*; furthermore, it has been stated that the referent of a word for a generality—which expresses its particulars while remaining internal [to itself]—is a positive injunction (*vidhi*), because the referent of a word is indeed a positive injunction. As for the reason you have provided, beginning with "because there is no contradiction," namely that even though the referents of words such as "generality" are distinct from *apoha*, there is no contradiction between them—that contradiction is established in this very same way, because they have become one in meaning through the positive injunction of existence (*bhavanavidhi*).

Whatever object there may be, whether termed a universal (sāmānya) or a particular (viśeṣa), all that is merely becoming (bhavana); it has become one through the attainment of mutual identity. That alone is the meaning of a word; because it is invariably concomitant with the assistance of the intended object and because it is being positively enjoined (vidhīyamāna), it is logically consistent as a unified whole. This is not the case, however, in the theory of exclusion of others (anyāpoha). Since there is no distinction in their "otherness" and they are equal in being non-existent (abhāva), what contradiction or non-contradiction could there be? Thus, the reading "because of its engagement with exclusion" (vyāvṛttivyāpṛtatvāt) appears correct here; see page 644, line 1 and page 644, line 2.
because of being non-existent, because of being non-tree...

The injunction regarding a specific object—such as a non-śiṃśapā tree, a jar, or the like—is exhausted solely in establishing the absence of that [specific object]. Consequently, it has no further operation toward enjoining the object of a "tree" in its essence as a śiṃśapā. Therefore, it attains grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with that [term for "tree"], because it has become a single unified meaning with the injunction of that [tree's] existence.
However, it is not tenable for that [particular] to be devoid of the rule of existence, because there would be an absence of the rule of generality.

A generality that does not establish existence and is devoid of the rule of existence cannot be a co-referential entity as you intend; for, being non-existent and lacking the nature of a tree, it would be like the son of a barren woman.

How, then, could this generality possess the status of a generality? If it were thus a non-generality, how could it be a *śiṃśapā* (a specific type of tree)? It would not be a *śiṃśapā*, because it lacks the nature of a tree and so forth, just like a jar.
That [exclusion] likewise continues in this very manner until it reaches the atom (*paramāṇu*), because it lacks any real commonality (*abhūtasāmānyatva*), like a flower in the sky (*khapuṣpa*).

And if everything is thus empty, who excludes what, by what means, or from what? Now, if somehow a *śiṃśapā* tree does exist, then, because of the application of its own meaning and so forth, that very thing becomes the object of affirmation (*vidhi*); and exclusion (*apoha*), being subordinate to it, is unreal due to its lack of existence.
The referent of a word is real despite having unreal adjuncts,
and that is the prescription for a specific meaning;
some such root-cause is conceivable here.

As for the claim that, despite their being distinct due to the absence of contradiction, there is no exclusion (apoha) of the referents of words such as "universal" (sāmānya), that very lack of contradiction is established in this same way because [the universal] has become one in meaning with the positive injunction (vidhi) of its existence;
see page 638, line 6.
And likewise, a collection (samūha) expresses a different object.

And thus, when the general and particular terms function within their own respective general meanings, they denote an object qualified by that [particular]; or rather, a collection of two or more [terms] denotes the meaning of a sentence. (Compare—p. 644, l. 8; compare—p. 643, l. 11).
See the internal distinction, page 640, line 4; compare— page 647, line 20.
Comparison, generality, and the exclusion of others (apoha) cannot be conceived without contradiction;
for there can be no state of being both contradictory and non-contradictory in the essential natures of words themselves.
Thus, in the *Mīmāṃsā-śloka-vārttika*, in the discussion on Apoha (*apohavāda*), it says:

"And likewise, a collection [of words] denotes another object. Its commentary begins with "And thus," and so forth; and having established this, because the meaning of a word is primarily positive (*vidhi-pradhāna*), it proceeds from "of the words for universals and particulars" up to "the denotation of the sentence-meaning" (*vākyārtha-vācakatva*).

When the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*), without abandoning their general state of being (*bhavana-sāmānya*), come to denote the specific agential referent through their combination, this occurs as in the case of *nīlotpalam*. Here, the two words denoting the general state of being of the resultant referent of the compound (*vṛtti-padārtha-bhavana-sāmānya*) possess the status of expressing the meaning of the compound through the relationship characterized by the qualifier-qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya*) relation. The same should be understood for compounds such as *rājapuruṣa*, where the king and so forth function as qualifiers through their specific connection.

Regarding the phrase "of a collection of two or more": [this refers to] the fact that collections of two, three, four, five, or more words—such as "Devadatta stands," "Devadatta stands in the house," or "O Devadatta! Bring the white cow"—express the meaning of a sentence. This statement by Dignāga, cited in the *Anyāpohavāda*, shows that it is only consistent with the view that the primary referent of a word is a positive injunction (*vidhi*), because all words have as their purpose an injunction assisted by a general property (*sāmānya*) that does not contradict the specific meaning conveyed.
See page 638, line 11.
The meaning of the term *vartipadārtha* is "the meaning of the constituent members [of a compound]"; that is to say, it means "compound" (*samāsa*). (Page 647, line 12)
And this [cognition],
as previously stated, does not at all imply the various distinctions of real entities; why then do you wander about in vain?
By this, the co-referentiality with negation (pratiṣedha-sāmānādhikaraṇya) is to be understood as refuted;
and it has been said:
"Because it requires only that [particular], the particular (bheda) is not abandoned by its own universal (svasāmānya)."
See page 638, line 13:
the author refutes [the opponent's view] by slightly modifying a statement of Diṅnāga himself:
"Because they are apprehended together and because they are identical in essence, those two have the same meaning."
And a manifold universal is apprehended by means of a non-deviating particular;
therefore, the two possess a variegated qualification, for even a manifold universal is [apprehended] by means of a non-deviating particular.
The author refutes what was stated by Dignāga on page 638, line 15— that for those two [the word and its meaning], there is no equal relationship of qualifier and qualified—
by means of this verse beginning with "And this... and so forth.

As for what you have said—that because the word "existent" (sat) does not imply specific differences such as a jar, and because it denotes only the substance with the universal's own form as a subordinate factor, it lacks grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with those specific differences like jars due to its dependence and its non-identity with them—then just as this is a fault for others, so too is it a fault for you: since [the word] depends on denoting the mere negation of the non-existent, it certainly does not imply specific existents such as jars. When the possibility of this same fault is equal, why do you wander about in vain? See *Citsukhī*, p.

Because it is not implied [by the word "existent"], by this [statement] beginning with "by this," etc., the co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the expression "the pot exists" (*san ghaṭaḥ*) is refuted; it should be understood that this negates the co-referentiality of the negation, since the cultivation of that [existence] depends on another. This is stated by the expression that does not imply the word "existent. It should be known that the co-referentiality of the negation is thus precluded.
And it is said: this is a summary verse (kārikā) that condenses the meaning already explained.

"Because it requires only that much," and so forth. A universal (*sāmānya*) requires only its own specific instance (*svabheda*). Therefore, because it requires only that much, the particular *śiṃśapā* is not abandoned by the universal "tree," even though there is difference (*anyatva*). Why, then, is it indeed grasped? Because of its essential identity (*tattva*) through that connection; for when the universal is bound together with the particular, due to that essential identity—namely, the attainment of oneness—and because of its inclination toward the particular, there is a single purpose (*ekārthatā*) despite the difference, since they have a single effect. This co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) exists when the universal and the particular do not abandon one another, because their own nature is attained only through this mutual non-abandonment; whereas if either were abandoned, its own form would not be realized.

For it is not the case that there is no *śiṃśapā* without a tree, nor a tree without a *śiṃśapā*. Regarding what was stated here—"Because doubt arises, they are not [mutually] inclusive; and when they are equal, they have the same referent" (*Praśastapādabhāṣya-samuccaya* 5.26)—from where does the doubt arise? Or from where do their equality and identity of referent come? First of all, as for the doubt, since only the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) is expressed, there is no doubt because the particulars are not included by the general term; if the particulars were included, there would be doubt.

Furthermore, there is no identity because [the universal] is not grasped; how then could there be grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇya*)? If it is argued that "there would be no doubt because it is grasped, as in the case of a tree," we say no, because it has already been stated: "Because [the universal] is a general term, a subordinate element, and serves the purpose of specifying a rule, certainty is observed when there is a restriction. Thus, the reading *nāstīty anyacca* is possible here, or alternatively, the reading *nojjhito 'nyatve 'pi*—meaning "not abandoned" or "not relinquished"—is also conceivable.
Because it would follow that there is no reality due to the absence of that connection, the qualification [is applied]; otherwise, there is no tree without the *śiṃśapā*.
See page 638, line 14;
the meaning is "the object of those" (teṣām arthaḥ).
In the manuscripts *tebhā* and *ya*, it appears as "the object of them" (*teṣām arthaḥ*).
"Even for you, there would be doubt" (saṃśayaḥ syāt tvam api bhāṣye);
see also "even for you, regarding doubt" (saṃśayasya tu tvam api ca) on page 616, line 4.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "and manifold," etc.:

here, when the meaning of a word is primarily governed by affirmation (*vidhi*), as in the expressions "tree" or "śiṃśapā," everything— both the manifold and the universal, such as earth, substance, existence, and so forth, as well as the categories known as name, representation, substance, and mode— is included by means of the non-deviating particular (*bheda*), because it has become a single referent with the affirmation of the *śiṃśapā* and other particulars.
Therefore, between those two—the particular term *śiṃśapā* and the general term *vṛkṣa*—there exists the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyatā*).

Since the general term, such as "tree," denotes multiple things and is grasped without deviation from its particulars, it serves as the qualifier; consequently, for the purpose of eliminating doubt, the term *vṛkṣa* functions as the qualifier and the term *śiṃśapā* functions as the qualified.
...it is thus: "And difference, whose power is bound to its own object, excludes other differences."

Because of the hearing of injunctions regarding general meanings and specific meanings, as well as rules and restrictions, depending on the speaker's intention, sometimes a *śiṃśapā* is qualified by "tree" (*vṛkṣeṇa śiṃśapā*), and sometimes a "tree" is qualified by *śiṃśapā* (*śiṃśapayā vṛkṣaḥ*). Since we observe this lack of restriction—as in the cases "the *śiṃśapā* is a tree" (*śiṃśapā vṛkṣaḥ*) and "the tree is a *śiṃśapā*" (*vṛkṣaḥ śiṃśapā*)—he shows the cause of that lack of restriction with the words "name and so forth are manifold," etc.: namely, the name-śiṃśapā (*nāma-śiṃśapā*), the installation-śiṃśapā (*sthāpanā-śiṃśapā*), the substance-śiṃśapā (*dravya-śiṃśapā*), and the mode-śiṃśapā (*bhāva-śiṃśapā*).
When the name "Śiṃśapā" is applied to a girl, that girl is a "named Śiṃśapā";

and this is a universal (*sāmānya*) because, according to the previously stated rule, everything is a name. Alternatively, the Śiṃśapā tree itself is a universal in relation to its names and so forth.
And this [universal] is expressed through its distinction from the tree, which is non-deviant [from it], because they have become a single referent through the application of the suffix (*vidhi*).
From that, a doubt might arise: "Is it a non-tree that is a *śiṃśapā*? Or is it a girl named *śiṃśapā*?

To exclude those [possibilities], one says, "Bring a tree-śiṃśapā, which consists of the state (*bhāva*) of arising. Thus, the tree indeed functions as the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), and the *śiṃśapā* functions as the qualified (*viśeṣya*). This is not a matter of fixed rule; however, it is not as you claim—that the relationship of qualifier and qualified between those two is equal (Prasamuccaya 5.27)—for their equality is observed only through a restrictive rule.
In this way, it should be understood up to the point where "existent" (sat) is the qualificand,
and the manifold universals such as "name" (nāman) and so forth are presented through their non-deviating distinctions.
Therefore, for the purpose of eliminating doubt, the tree indeed functions as the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the *śiṃśapā* functions as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*).
[this is] true.
In this way—
differentiation, whose power is bound to its own specific object, excludes other differentiation,
because of the scriptural injunctions regarding general meanings, particular meanings, prescriptions, and prohibitions.
The tree is a *śiṃśapā* [because it] will be [a *śiṃśapā*], according to Bhā[ṣya]; it will be [so], according to Ya[śomitra].
See page 638, line 16.
Furthermore, as for what you have stated: "A particular excludes another particular because of their mutual opposition;
particulars belonging to one general category exclude those belonging to other general categories because they are opposed to their own general category."
As stated in *Prakaraṇasamuccaya* 5.28:

"In that case as well, it does not exclude [the other] because of opposition, since there is no opposition; rather, through the relationship of part and whole (*aṅga-aṅgibhāva*), it attains the state of universal and particular according to the aforementioned logic. Why, then, does everything dependent on name and so forth exclude [the other]? It is said: Because a particular, whose power is bound to its own object, excludes another particular.
"Because of the hearing of injunctions regarding general meanings and specific meanings, and regarding prescriptions and restrictions"—
thus,

the capacity of this word *śiṃśapā* is fixed upon its own referent; although it is assisted by the generality of "tree," its capacity is fixed upon the *śiṃśapā* alone, because that alone is intended to be expressed, and because it is not perceived to function as an assistant in conveying the meaning of another word.

Therefore, because its capacity is restricted to its own specific object, the word *śiṃśapā* excludes *khadira* and other trees. What is the reason? It is because of the hearing of a restrictive rule regarding both the general meaning and the specific meaning. This specific term, which is desired as a restrictive rule for the particulars denoted by the general term—wherein the general meaning serves as a subordinate qualifier—is intended for the communication of the desired *śiṃśapā*, since that [general term] is the means to it. As we have previously explained at length, this [specific term] possesses a predicate meaning that is joined with the subordinate and primary qualities of both the general meaning and the specific meaning.

Therefore, for that reason—because in the Vedic injunctions concerning both general and specific meanings, other distinctions are not intended to be expressed due to a lack of purpose and because their capacity is restricted to their own respective objects—the particular, such as the *śiṃśapā* tree, excludes another particular, such as the *khadira* tree; it does not do so, however, out of mutual opposition. Since the general and the particular are invariably concomitant (*avinābhāvitva*), how could a particular like the *śiṃśapā* be opposed by another particular like the *khadira*, which is itself of the very nature of being invariably concomitant with the general? Thus, a particular excludes the object of another particular only on account of opposition.
Objects that are sub-divisions of a higher generality are contradictory to their own [specific] generalities. (Pramāṇasamuccaya 5.28, p.
18) And a particular, whose power is bound to its own object, excludes another particular.
Because of the scriptural hearing of injunctions regarding general meanings and specific meanings, as well as options and restrictions. (Tattvāloka, Tattvaprakāśa, Tattvayukti)

Because it is intended [to be so], the phrase "other words" (śabdāntara) appears beautiful; [it is] because the meaning is not realized through the [intended] sense, and because of the distinction between the meanings of the suffixes, there is no restriction.
Is it *niyama* because of the various purposes of the meaning (*artha*), or is it *niyama* because of the prescription of the meaning? [The answer is:
It is the general state of being a subordinate element (*upasarjanī-sāmānya*).
[The example of] *śiṃśapā* and so forth—

by this, everything such as [the verse] "particulars of other universals are contrary to their own universal" (Samuccaya 5.28) has its meaning refuted; therefore, enough with this excessive digression.
See page 638, line 24.

As for what was asked: "How, moreover, is there no recurrence of the previous fault when a word denotes its own meaning through the exclusion of other meanings (anyāpoha), or how is it that it denotes its own meaning by excluding other meanings?"—on this point, it cannot be determined from which of Dignāga’s works, along with a commentary composed by someone, all these views of the proponent of Apoha were extracted here by Mallavādin Kṣamāśramaṇa; see page 606, note 7.

However, as it was stated by Dignāga in the *Apohapariccheda* of the *Pramāṇasamuccaya*, I shall present it here after translating it from the Tibetan version into Sanskrit. Throughout, this text of the *Pramāṇasamuccaya* should be connected appropriately with the preceding and following arguments:
"But how is it that when a word denotes its own object through the exclusion of other objects (*anyāpoha*), the aforementioned faults do not arise?
Because [the word] is not observed to apply to the objects of other words, yet it is observed to apply even to a portion of its own object."
*Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā*, p. 307;
*Sanmativṛtti*, p. 196:
"The scripture possesses ease of connection and there is no deviation [from the truth]. (34)
For positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) are the gateway for a word to denote its meaning;
these consist in its occurrence and non-occurrence respectively with respect to similar and dissimilar instances.
Among these, it is not necessary to state that the word occurs in every single instance of the similar class, because in some cases, due to the infinity of the object, such a statement is impossible.

However, even though the dissimilar class (*atulya*) is infinite, it is possible to declare its non-occurrence there merely by not observing [the term] in it; for this very reason, the inference that excludes [the object] from what is other than its own correlates—because it is not observed elsewhere—is called "denotation of its own referent" (*svārthābhidhāna*).

But if the inference were by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), then regarding a word such as "tree," no doubt could arise concerning a single object as to whether it is a *śiṃśapā* or something else.
In that case, there would also have to be doubt regarding the appearance of "earthiness," "substance-ness," and so forth,
because the word "tree" is not observed in things that are not earthy and the like; therefore, he states the inference solely by way of negative concomitance (vyatireka), and says:

"Tree-ness," "earthen," "substance," "existent," and "knowable"— if the word were applied by way of the ascending order (anuloma), it would result in the apprehension of an object possessing all these attributes;

therefore, just as there is a determination of four, three, two, or one [attribute] from the words "tree," "earthen," "substance," "existent," and "knowable" respectively in the ascending order, so too should there be determination through the descending order (prātilomya)."
And yet it is not observed to be so;

for from the word "knowable" (jñeya), there arises doubt regarding the four [categories] beginning with existence (sattā); from the word "existent" (sat), regarding the three beginning with substance (dravya); from the word "substance" (dravya), regarding the two, namely earthiness and treeness; and from the word "earthy" (pārthiva), regarding the one, namely treeness. Therefore, words do not function by way of affirmation (vidhi).

As it has been said: "The [concepts of] 'treeness,' 'earthen substance,' 'existent,' and 'knowable' are, in reverse order, the causes for doubt regarding four, three, two, or one [property]; otherwise, they serve as the cause for certainty. — *Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika-śarkarikā*, p. 72.

"Regarding the doubt of four, three, two, or one [alternatives], the cause [of certainty] is the [correct] determination; otherwise, it is not. This is an intermediate verse. Furthermore, apart from the medium of a relation (*sambandha*), a word or a logical mark (*liṅga*) possesses no power to manifest its own object, because even though that object possesses many properties, it is impossible to comprehend it in every respect.
Furthermore, there is no deviation regarding its own referent because it does not denote a particular distinction;
thus, for the time being, the aforementioned fault is absent.
— PSV1 C.
Ed. p. 74, N.
ed.
Page 83, A, PSV2, N. edition.
