page 165.

The extensive and stainless commentary (*Viśālāmalavatī*) on this *Pramāṇasamuccaya* with its sub-commentary, composed by Jinendrabuddhi, is also presented here after being translated from the Tibetan version into Sanskrit: "But how [is it so]?

In the position that 'the word denotes its own meaning through the exclusion of other objects' (*arthāntaravyavacchedena*), how is it that the faults previously stated regarding the four positions do not occur? Thus he asks."
Regarding the phrase "due to non-perception in the meaning of another word," the mention of "the meaning of another word" is an indication of the *vipakṣa* (heterologous instance);
the meaning is "because of its non-perception in the *vipakṣa*.
In the expression "because it is perceived even in a portion of its own meaning," "its own" (*sva*) and "meaning" (*artha*) constitute "its own meaning" (*svārtha*).

If it is asked, "What, then, is this [term]?"—it is a collection of persons possessing the desire to speak (*vivakṣā*). A part or member (*aṃśa*) of that collection is a person possessing the desire to speak; thus, "possessing the desire to speak" is a synonym for a "member."

This is what is meant: although the aforementioned parts of its own meaning are infinite, nevertheless, because it is seen even in a single instance, the word "even" (api) indicates that it is also seen in many instances; for the statement regarding "parts" (aṃśa) is not intended as a member of the proof for pervasion over the similar class (sapakṣavyāpti).
Even though it is not all-pervasive,
the ease of connection with the Veda is indicative, because of the reason already stated;
nor is there any deviation, since [the mark] is absent when its own object is absent.
The passage beginning with "For positive and negative concomitance... elucidates this very point:
the door is the means, because a word functions as a logical mark (*liṅga*), and that [mark] brings about cognition by virtue of its connection characterized by positive and negative concomitance;
and "those two" refers to the description consisting of positive and negative concomitance.

The definition of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is this: the presence of the logical mark (*liṅga*) only in what is similar to that [the probandum], and its absolute absence in what is not similar to that.
In this regard, because it is not necessarily the case that [the mark] exists "in all" similar instances, its presence in every member of the class of similar things need not be stated.
If one asks why, it is said: "In some cases," and so forth.
For it is not possible for a word such as "tree" to be observed in every instance of a tree, because those [individual trees] are infinite;
however, in the case of arbitrary (yadṛcchā) words, observation is possible everywhere, because their referent is a single entity.
Therefore, it was stated [in the sūtra], "in some cases."
Thus, there may be ease in stating the positive concomitance (*anvaya*).
This might be argued: "Because those things that are not similar [to the subject] are infinite, it is impossible to state the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) in all cases.

To this he says: "But even though there is infinity regarding the dissimilar" (*atulye tu satyapyānantye*). Even though there is an infinity of those cases where the word and its referent are absent, the negative concomitance—characterized by the absence of the word when its own referent is absent—can be demonstrated; for non-perception is merely the absence [of perception].

When the causal relationship between word and object is established, the non-perception [of the word] is understood simply by the fact that in the absence of the object as cause, its effect— the word— will be absent; in that case, the observation of the locus (*āśraya*) is useless, because the certainty of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is achieved even without it, for indeed,
when the cause is absent, the effect cannot possibly exist.

Therefore, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is also easy to state; for this very reason—because perception is impossible everywhere in that which is similar to the subject, whereas non-perception is possible in that which is not similar to it—one infers its exclusion from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), which is other than its own related similar instances. Where there is non-perception in the absence of the object itself, there is the inference of those exclusions; this inferential cognition is called the "statement of the object for oneself" (*svārthābhidhāna*).

By this [statement], although both positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) are limbs of inference, he shows that because of the predominance of the negative concomitance, it is precisely through that means that [the reason] functions as a prover.
In the phrase "but by way of positive concomitance," the word "but" (*tu*) has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*).

If it is maintained that denotation occurs solely by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), then, since the word "tree" (along with its meaning) would be present in *śiṃśapā* and other instances, there could be no doubt regarding a single object arising from the mere word "tree," but rather there would be certainty.

If, on the other hand, it is argued that doubt arises because [the word] is observed in many instances, then in that case, there should likewise be doubt regarding the appearance of "earthiness," "substantiality," and so forth, because these too are observed in many instances;
yet, in fact, certainty is observed.

Since it demonstrates that even when [the reason] occurs in many instances, it does not exist in the absence of that [probandum], and not anything else, therefore this inference proceeds solely by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*);
showing this very point, he says: "Because," and so forth.
To demonstrate that [the word] is a means of cognition solely by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), he states an intermediate verse:
the word "knowable" (*jñeya*) is a cause of doubt regarding four things—existence, substance, earthenness, and being a tree—because it is observed even in the absence of those;
the same should be stated for the subsequent [words] as well.

The word *sat* [functions as] a cause for certainty in three respects: substance (*dravya*), earthenness (*pārthivatva*), and treeness (*vṛkṣatva*). The word *dravya* [functions as a cause for certainty] in two respects: earthenness and treeness. The word *pārthiva* [functions as a cause for certainty] in one respect: treeness. "Otherwise" means that it functions as a cause for certainty in a manner contrary [to the previous]. "In the other way" means that, by way of positive concomitance (*ānulomyena*), the word *vṛkṣa* is the cause for certainty regarding the four: earthen, substance, existent (*sat*), and cognizable (*jñeya*).
For instance—it is observed even in those [substances], and it is not observed in their absence;
the same should be stated for the subsequent categories as well.

Thus, the word "earthen" (*pārthiva*) and others should be understood as the causes of certainty regarding [the category of] substance (*dravyatva*) and so forth, through the successive elimination of each [lower category].

Furthermore, if one were to lead [the understanding] according to the rule as seen [in the examples], such that there would be a determination of four, three, two, or one meaning respectively, then it would occur in reverse order; for words such as "knowable" (*jñeya*) are seen to apply to [qualities like] existence (*sattva*) and so forth.
Since doubt arises because they are seen even in the absence of those [qualities], their capacity to convey meaning occurs solely by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
Thus, [the text says] "setting aside the door of connection," and so on.
The relationship of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) is precisely that door—
the instrumental cause— of inference; abandoning that, a word lacks the power to reveal its own object, just like a logical mark (*liṅga*).
The word *iva* is used in the sense of comparison (*aupamye*).

Just as a logical mark (*liṅga*), which consists of an object, makes its own meaning understood through the door of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva-sambandha*) by means of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) alone, so too does the word; it is for the purpose of making this known that the phrase "just like the logical mark" is employed.

Regarding the phrase "even though it possesses manifold properties": although the referent such as a "tree" possesses manifold properties—either through distinctions such as *śiṃśapā* and so forth, or through distinctions such as being in flower or bearing fruit—it is impossible to comprehend it in every single respect. Thus [the word conveys its meaning through exclusion].

If [the object] were understood in every respect through such qualities as being in flower or bearing fruit, then it would be understood by way of injunction alone even without the aforementioned relationship;
however, that is not possible, because there is deviation regarding specific instances such as being in flower,
for an injunction is indeed a cognition based on what has been perceived.

Therefore, there is no comprehension [of the object] through the positive injunction (*vidhi*), but rather through the exclusion of other objects (*arthāntaravyatireka*) because the particular differences are not denoted. Since those [particulars] exist even in the state of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*); however, this is not the case when the universal (*sāmānya*) is the denotable object, because that [universal] is undifferentiated, and in its absence, the word itself would not exist.
— *Viśālāmalavatī*, D. edition.
ed. pp. 275A–277A, P. ed.

By this, all [arguments] such as "the objects that are sub-classes of another universal are contradictory to their own universal" and so forth, have been refuted by the logic already stated—namely, through the fact that the meaning [of the term] is unified with the positive existence (*vidhi*) of the particular universal (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*). Your statement and others like it have thus been answered—that is, their meaning has been negated.

Enough of this excessive digression; let the investigation remain within the context of refuting the theory that the word-meaning is the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), for the point at hand must now be addressed.
The self-nature [of the word] has been refuted;
as for what was stated beginning with "another exclusion" (*anyo'poha*), and so forth.

Furthermore, the objection beginning with "How then [could a word apply] to another object? is raised by restating his own position in order to demonstrate the faultlessness of his own view, having first grasped the opponent's intention—up until the point where it says "there is no recurrence of the previous faults"—asking: "How could the faults pertaining to the positions of difference (*bheda*), genus (*jāti*), their relation (*tatsambandha*), and the possessor of that genus (*tadvat*) not also apply to you, such as infinity (*ānantya*), deviation (*vyabhicāra*), and so forth?"

[The opponent] asks: "But surely, by merely pointing out the faults in the opposing position—that a word [denotes its object] through the exclusion of other objects (arthāntarāpoha)—one's own position is not established; how then is the establishment of one's position (pakṣasiddhi) through the denotation of its own object by means of the exclusion of other objects? And how is it that the previously mentioned fault does not apply when there is denotation of its own object through the exclusion of other objects? That, however, is the [meaning of the] word... [fragmentary].
In that regard,
since a word is not observed [to apply] to the referent of another word, yet it is observed even in a portion of its own referent,
positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) constitute the gateway for a word’s denotation of meaning.
And those two— presence and absence in the similar and dissimilar cases—
are such that, regarding the similar case, presence need not necessarily be stated as applying everywhere,
because in some instances it is impossible to state it due to the infinity of the object.
However, even though the dissimilar class (*atulya*) is infinite, it is possible to declare its non-occurrence based on mere non-perception;
for this very reason, because it is not perceived elsewhere than among its own related instances, there is an inference of its exclusion (*tadvyavaccheda*).
And by proceeding in this manner, the inference of "substancehood" (*dravyatva*) and so forth from the word "tree" becomes logically established.

Furthermore, in an inference by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), since there is a positive presence of the word "tree" in *śiṃśapā* and other such instances, it would follow that an inference could be made even by means of the word alone.

If, on the other hand, because it is observed in many instances, doubt were to arise, then in the case of the object "tree," there would be doubt regarding its being earthy, a substance, or an existent;
yet, in fact, certainty is observed.

For instance, you have stated here that the words "tree," "earthly," "substance," and "existent" [function] because a word is not seen to apply to the referent of another word, yet it is seen to apply even to a part of its own referent; the completion of the sentence is that "the establishment of the denotation of a referent occurs through the exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*).
For the relationship between the signifier and the signified is indeed the relationship between the means of inference (*anumāna*) and the object of inference (*anumeya*).

In this regard, just as the cognition of fire arises through the exclusion of non-fire by virtue of seeing smoke in one place and not seeing it where there is no fire, so too positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) are the means for the denotation of meaning by a word.
These two consist in the occurrence and non-occurrence [of the word] with respect to similar and dissimilar instances.

Among these, its occurrence across all similar instances need not necessarily be stated, because in some cases, due to the infinity of the referent, such a statement is impossible. For instance, it is not possible to observe the word "tree" in every single tree; nor is it possible to observe every inferential mark (*liṅga*) in every locus of inference (*liṅgin*), as is the case with fire and smoke.

And although there may be some possibility [of such a term] in cases like "Ḍittha" and the like, nevertheless, inference does not occur by way of that [term], because it is not perceived in its entirety.
For the object designated as "Ḍittha" is a collection of qualities; yet, all qualities such as being one-eyed or having a withered arm are not understood from the word "Ḍittha.
Thus, there is an absence of inference by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*).

In this regard, it should be noted that a portion of a certain treatise on *apoha* composed by Diṅnāga has been presented here almost verbatim, along with a commentary (*ṭīkā*) composed by someone else, by Siṃhasūri Kṣamāśramaṇa, the author of the *Nayacakravṛtti*. It is not possible to discern precisely how much belongs to Diṅnāga and how much to the author of that commentary; furthermore, it cannot be properly determined how much was incorporated here by Mallavādin Kṣamāśramaṇa in its original form.

However, we have presented here in this commentary in bold type whatever was stated by Diṅnāga as far as it appears to us; how it actually occurs in the *Pramāṇasamuccaya* has been previously demonstrated by us at page 650, note 2,
and that should be followed accordingly throughout both the prima facie and the final positions on pages 432–1 and 472–1.
Page 432—1, 433—2; compare page 459—2;
page 432—1; compare—page 461—2.
This might be so—but there is also the impossibility of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).

To this he says: "But even though [the number of dissimilar instances] is infinite and unequal, it is possible to state the non-occurrence [of the reason] in those where [the probandum] is not seen, merely by virtue of its not being observed; for it is a mere non-observation, since non-observation is simply the absence of observation."

"And for this very reason" means that because perception is impossible in all cases, and even when perception does occur, there is in every instance an absence of inference; therefore, [the term] "from its own correlates" (*svasambandhibhyaḥ*) refers here to that which has been perceived as a correlate, and not by way of a relationship of inseparable connection (*avinābhāvitva*), because it is not observed elsewhere—since it is not observed in the absence of the object denoted. Otherwise, one would have to say that the word "tree" is observed even in the absence of earth, substance, and so forth, in that particular entity. Thus, "inference through exclusion" (*tadvyavacchedānumāna*) means that where non-perception was stated—in the case of a non-tree where a tree is absent—from that follows the inference of exclusion: "it is not a non-tree."
And by doing so, the inference of substance-ness and other properties from the word "tree" becomes logically established. (Compare—page 459; compare—page 460).
The reading "the description of the non-occurrence in the case of non-perception" appears correct;
compare page 466—2;
see also page 466—2.
The reading "adarśanam" (non-perception) is also possible here, as in the comparison with Aṣṭaprakaraṇa, page 466, line 2.

Folio 466–2: Regarding the inference by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), this fault arises— since there is a positive concomitance of the word "tree" together with its referent and so forth in [instances such as] the *śiṃśapā* tree, it follows that an inference would also occur based on the word alone.

Now, since [the word] is observed even in many cases such as the *palāśa* tree and others, doubt certainly arises. This being so, in the meaning of "tree," there exist the properties of being earthen (*pārthivatva*), being a substance (*dravyatva*), and existence (*sattā*); because the word "tree" applies equally to these, doubt would occur. However, certainty arises through positive concomitance (*ānulomya*) by means of the causes for determining three, two, or one object respectively.
Thus, the denotation of another object by the exclusion of other objects is established;
and indeed, apart from the medium of a relation (*sambandha*), a word or a logical mark (*liṅga*) possesses no power to manifest its own referent.
And it has been said: "Although the object of expression has many aspects, there is no comprehension of it in its entirety from a word;
rather, by virtue of its own specific relation, that word performs the function of excluding other things. Even though a word possesses manifold properties, it does not transcend its object."
It causes cognition by that [form] alone, and not by means of the word’s qualities and so forth;

furthermore, there is an absence of the aforementioned defects because the connection with the *śruti* is easy to establish and there is no deviation, since it does not denote particularities (*bheda*).
This [position] is incorrect.

Since even positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) are not possible here—because the object of "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*) is devoid of substance and its own referent is not observed even in part—let alone their connection with words; let alone their non-deviation; for [the object] is not perceived from the word.

The word "tree" (vṛkṣa), while having as its primary meaning the exclusion of non-trees, also functions toward its own referent through the exclusion of non-earthly substances; for instance, the words "tree," "earthly," "substance," and "existent" are, in their ascending order, the causes for determining three, two, and one object respectively.
Thus, it is established that the denotation of one object occurs through the exclusion of other objects.
Furthermore, he demonstrates that this is not possible for a word except by way of a relation, just as it was previously stated that difference and so forth are not directly denoted.
See the entry for *anugata* accompanied by the word-meanings and so forth on pages 468–1 and 469–1.
On pages 468–1, 2:

"By way of positive concomitance (ānulomya), they are the causes for the ascertainment of three, two, or one object; thus, the designation of another object through the exclusion of other objects is established."
Nor does a word or a logical mark possess the power to manifest its own object apart from the medium of a relationship;

and it has been said: "Even though the denotable object is manifold, there is no comprehension of it in every respect from the word; rather, it effects the exclusion [of others] in accordance with its own relationship."

Even though a word possesses many properties (*dharma*), it causes its object to be understood by means of that [property] alone through which it does not deviate from the object; it does not do so by means of the word’s qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth.

Furthermore, there is no absence of the previously mentioned defects, because the connection is easily established for the heard word, and there is no deviation since it does not denote [other] particulars (*bheda*).

"Even though the object to be expressed has many aspects, it is not understood in its entirety from a word; however, by virtue of its own specific relation, that word performs the function of excluding [other meanings]. (See page 630, lines 11–14).

It is incorrect to say that even though a word possesses many properties, it causes the object to be understood by means of that [specific property] alone, and not by means of the word's qualities and so forth.
For, in this case, even positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) are not possible,
because the object of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) is devoid of essence and its own referent is not observed even in part;
see page 432–1.
Let your connection with words be set aside; let your non-deviation be set aside;
[the object] is established by its very occurrence.
(Compare page 468–2).
Nevertheless, the reading "vṛkṣa pra" followed by "tathā vṛkṣa" also appears correct here; compare— page 468–2, 469–1.
He states "and so it is said," and demonstrates this very point with two verses as well, following the sequence of the words on page 663, line 9.

Regarding the phrase "even though the denotable object is manifold," the distinctions intended here are those such as *śiṃśapā* and so forth, not [the categories] such as substance (*dravya*) and the rest. For instance, while doubt is observed regarding the specific varieties of trees, there is in fact certainty regarding substance and the rest;

this is because [the word] conforms to its own relation. Since this [word], when perceived among things of that same class, is seen to be expressive only by means of the exclusion of other objects—and even more so when it is not perceived elsewhere—it therefore denotes the object as qualified by that [exclusion] in accordance with its relation.

Even though the word "tree" possesses many properties, it does not denote the object "tree" by means of its general properties such as being a quality of space (*khaguṇatva*) and so forth; for these [general properties] are observed even in the absence of the object "tree," as in the case of taste and other qualities, whereas the word "tree" is never observed elsewhere. Therefore, it is logical that the cognition [of the tree] occurs through the word "tree" alone. Thus, the proof for the establishment of our own position and the absence of the previously mentioned defects have been stated; because the relationship is easy to establish upon hearing [the word], and because—despite the multiplicity [of properties]—there is application (*vṛtti*) to the similar and non-application (*avṛtti*) to the dissimilar, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) either, since it does not denote individual particulars (*bheda*).
Thus, the objections raised regarding the statement of differentiation have been refuted; let the position of the proponents of *anyāpoha* (exclusion of others) be examined (pp.
630, l. 10–15). For comparison, see pp. 440–2.
By means of common properties such as being a single quality (*ekaguṇa*), etc.;
"space" (*kha*) refers to *ākāśa* (ether), meaning by means of the qualities of space, i.e., the qualities of *ākāśa*, etc.— this is the meaning according to the Kṣārthībhāṣya.
See the discussion regarding the non-occurrence of [the object] for one seeking [it], on page 431–2.
Even in that [other] position, there are faults.

The Teacher, wishing to state a refutation of this as well, first addresses the very seed of the opponent’s defense—that which is called "the ease of connection with the Veda"—in order to refute it, saying: "This is incorrect, because... and so forth, up to "...it is not possible.

This means that since even positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) are not possible here, let alone those two—which are intended to be the causes for denoting an object through their occurrence in similar instances and non-occurrence in dissimilar instances—how could they possibly apply?
Therefore, the proposition that the ease of connection [between word and meaning] is untenable;
to demonstrate this, he states the verse beginning with "Because the object of exclusion (apoha) lacks reality," and so forth.

Since the object of exclusion does not exist, there is no connection [between word and meaning]; because not even a trace of its own referent is perceived, there is not even a seed for doubt, so how could there be any suspicion of deviation? Such is the presentation.
First, positive concomitance (anvaya) is established; first, negative concomitance (vyatireka) is established.
See the *Svārthasaṃgraha* for the cause of [this] establishment; cf. page 655, line 11.

Regarding the reading *vyabhicārāśaṅkā* (or, according to another reading in the Bhāṣya, *vyabhicārāvyabhicārāśaṅkā*), what is the meaning? Does it mean "is that [object] the same or not the same? If it means "it is the same," then, since the object produced by the cognition of that word is understood through a positive injunction (*vidhi*) without exclusion (*avyāvṛtti*) regarding the other referent, what is accomplished by exclusion (*apoha*), given that the comprehension of the object has already occurred?

For then, by implication (*arthāpatti*), the reality of both [the positive entity] and its other would be established intrinsically; therefore, there might also arise in these two the cognition of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), because the referent of a true word has a real nature despite having unreal adjuncts (*upādhi*). Furthermore, if it were not otherwise, the determination of the question would likewise remain unsettled.

Furthermore, since otherness (*anyatva*) pertains to both [the thing and its opposite], if that is not apprehended, what is this "other," or from what is it said that something is "not other"? Therefore, regarding what was stated in the position of the objection—that one’s own object is denoted by the exclusion of another object (*arthāntarāpoha*)—we must first investigate what is called "another object" (*arthāntara*), namely, that which is "other. Is that other object denoted as a positive entity (*vidhi*) under the name of "other," or is it denoted through the exclusion (*apoha*) of "it is not other"? Thus, there would be two possible alternatives.

In this regard, if it is first held that "it is other" means that very thing becomes what is called "other," then the cognition produced by the word "that" has as its own object—that which is to be expressed—the very thing called "other" as its referent.

Consequently, since that "other" thing is understood through a positive injunction (*vidhi*) without exclusion (*avyāvṛtti*), what is accomplished by exclusion (*apoha*)? The meaning is that there is no purpose for exclusion.

Why? Because the comprehension of the meaning has already occurred; for the employment of a word is for the sake of comprehending its meaning. And the conceptualization of the exclusion of others (anyāpoha) is intended for the purpose of fully understanding the nature of that denotation; once that meaning has been comprehended, such [conceptualization] is useless. (p.
...would arise... it arises; cf. p. 658.

Is the own-meaning (svārtha) the denotable object (abhidheya), or is the own-meaning the thing to be enjoined (vidheya)? Moreover, there may be a purpose through the exclusion of others (anyāpoha); it would be thus, and not otherwise.

For example—at that time, during the occurrence of one cognition by means of a rule, if another [cognition] exists, then that [first one] does not exist; or if that [first one] exists, the other does not exist. Thus, it follows by implication that the reality (*tattva*) belongs to both of those two others, and that is established through itself (*svataḥ*).
Therefore, there may indeed arise in these two others the cognition of the exclusion of the other (*anyāpoha*).

And that [qualification] cannot be a subordinate rule (upasarjana-vidhi). Why? Because the meaning of the word "real" (satya) consists in reality despite the presence of unreal adjuncts (asatyopādhi).
Thus, the cognition of another [object] is itself the positive injunction (vidhi), not the exclusion (vyāvṛtti).
(Tulanā, p. 658)

If it is argued that "it is not other" so that this fault may not arise, then for that very object called "other," its nature must be simply the exclusion of others, namely, "it is not other. What follows from that? Even from that, the question remains unsettled: when you say "it is not other," is that which is being described actually that very thing, or is it "not other"? You must be asked this: if you were to say "it is that very thing," then, as before, the meaning would be a positive affirmation (*vidhi*).

Now, if that which is said to be "not other" is itself another, then it must be asked what that "other" is; and from that [second] one, yet another must be asked. Why is there this infinite regress of questions? Because this same objection applies equally in every case, as previously stated. Furthermore, because "otherness" has two objects: when one is called "other" in relation to another, and that [second] one is also [called "other"] in relation to this [first], then only when both of them are established by their own nature does "otherness," which resides in both, become established.

Therefore, since that "otherness" has both [the things] as its object, if those two are not apprehended, what is this "other"? If those two, which are designated as "other," are not apprehended in a positive form, what indeed is this so-called "other" such that through its exclusion there would be an "exclusion of the other"? Or from what is it said that "it is not other," whereby the otherness of this "other" might be established? The intention is that since otherness is a property residing in two things—namely, "that which is other than what is other"—this otherness must be determined; otherwise, it cannot be determined. (Compare page 659).
In this way, however, no such object can exist, because it follows that both [self-nature and other-nature] would be non-existent; not even a fraction of its own nature is perceived.

When it is said that "it is not other," since both are non-existent, the exclusion of otherness lacks ultimate reality; and because it is not produced as something other than itself, like the son of a barren woman, it is simply not an object of experience.
And that would be the basis for the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*).

Now, it might be argued: "Even if 'other' does not become 'not-other,' and if being 'other' means it does not become 'not-other,' then since this is merely a restatement of 'other' itself, what is this so-called 'not-other' other than something equal to 'otherness' and 'non-otherness'? Furthermore, if the referent of the word 'other' were distinct from the referent of the word 'not-other,' then the meaning of the exclusion (*apoha*) would be: 'being other does not become not-other,' because [the term] does not apply to an 'other' that is dissimilar."

"Thus, however," and so forth: according to the principle stated in this manner, no such object will ever exist, nor has anything of that kind ever existed; for since one thing does not become another, and that [other] does not become that [first], there follows the consequence of non-existence from both sides. Thus, not even a fraction or a scent of its own objective reality is perceived at all. (Tulanā, p. 658)

The reading *so 'pi na bhavati* (even that does not exist) is also appropriate here; the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) of this meaning is as follows: when it is said "it is not another," what has actually occurred? It is simply the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of "another" by means of the phrase "it is not [another]," and there is not even a trace of any positive injunction (*vidhi*). Therefore, because of this exclusion of another, non-existence (*abhavana*) alone is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Since that is the ultimate reality, there is an absence of otherness from the Self (*ātman*).

Consequently, because its otherness is unreal, it is simply not an object of cognition, like the son of a barren woman; for a non-entity such as the son of a barren woman cannot possibly be the referent of a word.
And that non-existence would become the basis for your "exclusion of others" (anyāpoha);
consequently, there would be no comprehension of the word-meaning at all, because it would be based on absolute non-existence, just like the non-comprehension of the son of a barren woman.

Thus, first of all, if the two conceptual constructions—"it is this" and "it is not another"—result in a doctrine of positive affirmation (vidhi), then the two faults mentioned—namely, the futility of exclusion (anyāpoha)—would follow.
comparison, p. 658.

Now, in order to avoid those two faults, it might be argued: "The other is neither non-other, nor is 'the other' simply that very thing, nor is it not the other. What then? It is not non-other than what is other than it. Because the meaning of the word *anyāpoha* (exclusion of the other) pervades [all things], it conveys [its object] solely through exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*). Therefore, there is no consequence of affirmation (*vidhi*), nor is it a mere negation (*abhāvamātra*)."

To this it is replied: If "the other" is not non-other, then because one is merely reiterating the other, and so forth, up to the point where it is said that [the term] does not apply to an unequal other—what is the meaning of this counter-argument? It means that this which is "other," being indeed other, is called "other"; yet that very same thing, being non-other, exists by itself without depending on anything else. What follows from this? Therefore, that which is called "non-other" is in fact the other; that very thing designated as "other," while being other, is said to be "non-other."
Therefore, since that very otherness is also expressed by the word "non-other," what is this "other" that is called "non-other" in relation to something else? The meaning is that there is none.

He analyzes whether there might be dependence on another: "The referent of a word (*śabdārtha*) is dissimilar to both difference-from-another and non-difference-from-that. Here, *anyānya* means different from another; the state of being so is *anyānyatva*. Therefore, [the referent] is dissimilar to that which is non-different from what is different. What, then, is this referent of a word that is dissimilar to both difference-from-another and non-difference-from-that? For example, when one says "a jar" by way of contrast (*vaidharmyeṇa*), that which is dissimilar to the jar’s difference-from-another and its non-difference-from-that—being itself different from the jar—is called "different. Indeed, the jar’s difference from a cloth is dissimilar to its difference from this other [jar].

For the difference of a jar from a cloth is not like the difference [of a cloth] from something other than it; nor is the difference of a cloth from a jar like the difference of the jar itself [from that same jar]. Even though there is an equality in the aforementioned mutual duality, for that very reason, the reality is non-difference from the Self; for the non-difference of a jar from that very jar is not like the non-difference of a cloth [from it].
But surely, in this way, that [non-other] also, being other than another, while being other, becomes non-other;

thus, by negating the reality of non-otherness (*tadananyatva*), the very exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) becomes the exclusion of that [non-other]. Consequently, there arises a contradiction with one’s own words and with the entirety of the proposed position.

It is observed that cloth and the like are excluded by the word "pot," but here there is no such distinct "non-other" denoted by the word "non-other" from which this "other"—being distinct from another—could have a non-occurrence (exclusion), as in the case of cloth. This is because otherness is mutually dependent, and such [a basis for dependence] does not exist in this manner.
Furthermore, [the author] demonstrates the logical principle regarding the meaning of the word "other" in the passage beginning with "and of the meaning of another word," and so forth:

when the meaning of a non-other word is distinct from the meaning of an other word, and conversely, the meaning of an other word is distinct from that [non-other], then, when one says "other," it follows that it is not non-other; thus, the meaning of exclusion (*apoha*) would be distinct from the positive injunction (*vidhi*).
What is the reason? Because [the term] does not apply to what is not similar to the other, just as [the term "pot"] does not apply to a cloth.
But it does not exist [as such], because one thing is not non-different from another;
therefore, the meaning of exclusion (*apoha*) would be merely the exclusion of its own referent. Now, it might be argued: [Prakaraṇa...]
Compare page 659;
or "only that much," compare— page 659.
...of otherness itself...?
Thus, according to the manuscript (pratau), "sabhā... is not present; because of that, it is equal to the beginning.
Because of mutual difference;
because of mutual difference? Because of [that] it is equal.
That which is different from that because of its dissimilarity to it is called "other" by virtue of being other than the self (ātman) while existing as something else.
For the otherness of a jar from a cloth is indeed incomparable with its otherness from something else;
for the otherness of a jar is not like the otherness of a cloth from something other than it, nor is the otherness of a cloth from a jar like the otherness of a jar [from itself].
Even if there were equality in the aforementioned dual-location [of otherness], for that very reason, the reality is its non-otherness from itself.

For indeed, there is no non-difference of a jar from that very same jar, as there is no non-difference of a cloth [from the jar]; yet, if it were the case that even that [cloth] is distinct from another and, being distinct, becomes non-distinct, then by negating that non-distinction—which is its true nature—the "exclusion of others" (anyāpoha) would itself become an "exclusion of that" (tadapoha). Thus, there arises a contradiction with one's own words and with every other position.
The reading "not different from another" (anyasyānanya) might also occur here; [the text] reads: "not different from another, not different from what is not another."
This [reading] is not [found] in the Bhāṣya;
comparison— page 657, line 14.

The opponent says: "This might be so if one thing, being established as distinct from another, were called 'other' due to its otherness in relation to that other; however, that which is non-other is itself the other.
What then? It is called 'other' precisely because of its otherness in relation to itself."
Desiring to explain that, he says: "He who is this... and so forth, up to "...non-difference from the jar, like [the non-difference] of cloth [from the jar].

That which is this [entity], being different from that other [entity] by virtue of its own nature—which is not that [other], which is not of the nature of that, and which is unequal to it—is itself "different" precisely because it is different from another; being different from another by way of its own distinctness, it is called "different."

The illustration: For the otherness of a jar from a cloth is indeed unequal to its otherness from something else; by the passage beginning with "for [the otherness] of the jar," he shows the non-confusion of the jar's otherness with the cloth's otherness, up to the point that its otherness is like the otherness of the other [entities]; and by the passage beginning with "or of the cloth," he shows the non-confusion of the cloth's otherness with the jar's otherness, up to the point that it is like the otherness of the jar. This example, whose meaning has been explained, should be observed (p. 659).

Is the self [identical] to this very thing because it is non-different from it— just as a cloth is non-different from a jar— or is the self [different] from this very thing because it is different from it?
Because it is different from the self,
it is other than the cloth and so forth; therefore, due to its non-existence as a cloth, it does not exist.
By means of the non-bending of the cloth,
whatever other [thing] there may be,
by that other [thing].
The reading *paṭāditarā* might also occur here; the portion of the text within these brackets, beginning with *°ṭānyatvā* and ending with *°kṣatā*, is not present in the Bhāratīya manuscript.
This is the application of the meaning: "even though there is equality in the aforementioned state of being located in two," and so forth.

The "otherness" (*anyatā*) spoken of by you consists in mutual dependence because those two [entities] reside in each other; yet, even though that mutual dependence and otherness are equal, the reality (*tattva*) is non-otherness (*ananyatva*) of the self from that very [entity], arising from itself alone. That very jar is non-other than the remainder; this section on the demonstration of non-confusion is similar to the preceding section on the conceptualization of otherness. Therefore, since it is established that otherness also arises from itself and non-otherness likewise, there is the exclusion of the other (*anyāpoha*).
In this regard, your faults are stated as follows: "But if it were so," and so forth, up to "the consequence of contradicting all positions, such as your own words.
Here, the word "but" (*nanu*) serves to grant a concession to the opponent.

Now, even in this case, that which is other—being distinct from another due to its own inherent distinctness from an object designated as "other"—is indeed other; yet, while being other, it becomes non-other, becoming that very same thing.

Thus, for that other which is established within its own self, its non-distinctness is not what is called "exclusion of other" (*anyāpoha*), nor is it the case that it is not "non-exclusion of non-other. This is because, when there is an exclusion of its own referent through the exclusion of a different referent (*arthāntarāpoha*), the operation upon the referent results in an exclusion qualified by the other.

Just as "exclusion" (*apoha*) does not become "non-exclusion" (*anapoha*), so too, when one excludes "selfhood" (*ātmatva*)—which is the reality of the exclusion of other qualifiers—the "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*) becomes that very exclusion; it is indeed its own exclusion (*svāpoha*), and not the "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*) as you intend, namely, the "exclusion of another" (*parāpoha*). Thus, there is a contradiction with one's own words because of the statement "exclusion of others," and there is a contradiction with one's own tenets because of such an admission.
There is contradiction with the world (*lokavirodha*) because it is observed thus in the world that there is cognition of one's own object;
likewise, there is contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣavirodha*) because of such direct observation,
and contradiction with inference (*anumānavirodha*) because of such inference.
Thus, all the faults of the thesis (pakṣadoṣa) are incurred, as is the consequence of falling into the position of an affirmative assertion (vidhivādāpatti);
in this way, the refutation has first been stated according to the characteristics of the entity (vastu).
See page 659.

Furthermore, the claim that "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*) does not mean "non-exclusion of non-others" is not a valid resolution. For when it is said that "exclusion of others" does not mean the exclusion of the absence of non-others—since, through the exclusion of other objects, there is an exclusion of its own object by way of its function, such that the exclusion is qualified by another—just as in the case of "exclusion" (*apoha*), it is not "non-exclusion," so too [is it] the exclusion of the qualifier "other."

It might be thought: "I shall avoid [this objection] merely by following the shadow of the meaning of the word 'exclusion of others' (*anyāpoha*)," as follows: "Exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*) does not mean "non-exclusion of others" (*ananyāpoha*). The meaning is that the exclusion qualified by the attribute "other" has as its counter-positive the exclusion qualified by the attribute "not other," and that [counter-positive] does not exist; and that [which does not exist] is "other" in relation to itself.
Therefore, let it be seen that even here, it is indeed the exclusion of others (anyāpoha); see page 660, line 13,
and also [the section on] non-otherness (ananyatva).

To this it is replied: Why is even this not a valid rebuttal? Because the term "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*) does not mean the exclusion of the non-existence of what is not other. For if one's own object were excluded by the exclusion of another object, then in the sense of its function, it would be an "exclusion qualified by another. What, then, is being said? The non-existence of the non-other is "other," or the non-existence of the other is "non-other"—that is, the opposite.
In the same way, the non-exclusion (*anapoha*) of exclusion (*apoha*) is its opposite, and the exclusion of non-exclusion is [the definition of] exclusion;

he demonstrates this principle by means of an illustration—just as "exclusion" does not mean "non-exclusion"—and so forth, which serves as the application to the case at hand (*dārṣṭāntika*) for the purpose of showing the exclusion of other qualifiers.

What is meant? Just as when "exclusion" (*apoha*) is stated, because of the application of a double negation to the word-meaning—namely, that "non-exclusion does not exist"—the meaning becomes exclusion itself; likewise, for the purpose of demonstrating exclusion qualified by another qualifier, when "exclusion of the other" (*anyāpoha*) is stated, "non-other" (*ananya*) is the absence of the other. That [absence] is its object, thus the word "other" has the non-other (i.e., the absence of the other) as its object. When that state of the word "other" having the non-other as its object exists, the meaning of "exclusion of the other" (*anyāpoha*) results in the non-exclusion of the non-other (*ananyāpoha*), because of the exclusion of that [other]; thus, the meaning "exclusion does not exist" is established.

If there is no exclusion (*apoha*) of that non-otherness (*ananyabhāva*) which is itself non-other, then there is likewise no exclusion of the other (*anyāpoha*), because the exclusion of the other is its opposite. Just as there is an exclusion of the opposite of the qualified object (*viśeṣya*), so too here, in your own sense of the word "other" (in the phrase "this is not other than that"), there is no exclusion of the other; thus, there is no exclusion of the non-existence of non-otherness. The non-existence of one's own non-otherness is the "other," and the non-existence of that [other] is the "non-other. Since there is no exclusion of that, there is simply no exclusion of the other; for the exclusion of the non-other is indeed its own exclusion—such is the meaning of the non-existence of non-otherness.
And that fault, which you find undesirable, would still follow even according to the theory of following the word;
however, it might be thought that there is no fault because of the restriction: "exclusion belongs only to another, not to what is not other."

And that is not so, because even in that case, when one investigates: "What is other? What is non-other? What is exclusion (*apoha*)? What is non-exclusion (*anapoha*)?"—since there is no determination as stated before, it follows the logic of affirmation (*vidhi*), such that "only the other exists, not the non-other," and "only the exclusion of the non-other exists, not its non-exclusion. Thus, through the determination and non-determination of its own exclusion and non-exclusion, and in the investigation of the other and the non-other via affirmation and negation, it is shown for the sake of illustration that when it is said "exclusion of the other" (*anyāpoha*), if the word "other" has the meaning of the absence of the other, then the "exclusion of the other" (*anyāpoha*) does not become the exclusion of the absence of the non-other (*ananyābhāva*).

If it is argued that "non-exclusion of others" (ananyāpoha) is merely its own exclusion (svāpoha), then even in this approach, no such object would exist at all; thus, not even a fraction of its own referent is perceived.

When it is said that "it is not non-other," since both [terms] are absent, there is no occurrence of the exclusion of the non-other; because its non-occurrence is the ultimate reality and its non-otherness is unreal, it is simply a non-object, like the son of a barren woman.
Furthermore, that [exclusion] would be the basis for the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*).

For those who maintain that a word denotes its own object through the exclusion of other objects (*arthāntara*), is that "other object" something existent (*bhavat*) that is excluded, or is it non-existent (*abhavat*)? If, first of all, the other object is existent, then since the object of the cognition produced by that word is established as being characterized solely by a positive operation (*vidhi*)—due to the absence of exclusion (*avyāvṛtti*)—and since a more extensive range of objects consisting of a heavier comprehension has already been understood through the theory of affirmation (*vidhivāda*), what further purpose is served by exclusion? For the comprehension of the object has already been accomplished.

For in that case, because a positive injunction would follow by implication (*arthāpatti*), there would be a total loss of foundation through the exclusion of everything else (*anyāpoha*); thus, this too is not a means of escape.

This is established: there can be no exclusion (*apoha*) of that which has no other [corresponding] entity, since if one were to express its own object through the exclusion of other objects, [it would be impossible]. (See p.
In the case of the exclusion of its own meaning,
there is a negation by means of a suffix;
in the case of the exclusion of the base meaning, there is a negation by means of the root itself.

In the case of negation, [it occurs] by way of the original form (*prakṛtyā*). Is it that exclusion (*apoha*) arises through the non-existence of other various things? Or is it that this [exclusion] exists?
Regarding "ananyāpoha" and "anyāpoha," the reading "anyasyānapoha" should also be considered here;
[this concerns] the *vṛtti* of [Yaśomitra].
He becomes non-different; for what other [self] could there be that is not to be excluded?

When "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*) is stated for the sake of illustration, if the word "other" has the meaning of the non-existence of others, then in the expression "exclusion of others," there would be no exclusion of the non-existence of non-others; rather, "non-exclusion of non-others" would simply be its own exclusion. Even though this is the case, no such object whatsoever would exist, and thus not even a fraction of its own referent would be perceived.

If it is said that "it is not non-different," then because both [the entity and its negation] are absent, there is no exclusion of non-difference; since non-existence is the ultimate reality, it would be non-existent as non-different, and like the son of a barren woman, it would simply be a non-entity, serving as no basis for the exclusion of others (anyāpoha).

Furthermore, regarding those other objects through the exclusion (*apoha*) of which one’s own object is denoted: is that other object something existent (*bhavat*) that is excluded, or is it non-existent (*abhavat*)? If, first of all, the other object is existent, then since the object of the cognition produced by that word is established as being characterized solely by a positive function (*vidhi-vṛtti*)—consisting of a more extensive comprehension directed toward a greater number of objects—what further purpose is served by exclusion once the theory of affirmation (*vidhivāda*) has been understood? For the comprehension of the object has already occurred;
for at that time, [the exclusion] would be [known] through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).
(Page 657, Line 2)

The intention appears to be that if [the term] "bhavati" were used as a designation for existence (*bhava*), then [the suffix] *ta* would apply; however, it would not [apply], because of the consequence of the aforementioned fault.

The reading "svārthābhidhānaṃ te syāt" (your [word] would have its own meaning) should also be considered here; likewise, even in this context, and so forth—even when the logic regarding the word and its referent has been thus established—he concludes by undermining the value of *apoha* with the words "na sa kaścit" (it is not any such thing), and so on. Just as there was a refutation of the alternative of "otherness," he provides a refutation of the alternative of "non-otherness" through inversion: because it is non-existent and non-different from itself, like the son of a barren woman, it is simply not an object at all; and yet, that [non-object] would be the basis for *anyāpoha*—this has already been explained.

Regarding the passage beginning with "And as for those other objects" (pṛ. 655, 659, 660), which states that "in the denotation of its own object by means of the exclusion of other objects," here "other objects" (*arthāntarāṇi*) refers to things different from the [intended] object; among those other objects, that which is an "other object" is an object distinct from the [intended] object. What is that? As before, there are two alternatives.
The question is: is it something other than existence that is excluded, or is it non-existence?

Regarding the first alternative, beginning with the words "yadi tāvat" (if, first of all), this is the refutation: if it is claimed that the very object [denoted by the word] remains as a distinct entity (*arthāntara*) and thus "becomes that," and if that which is the object of the cognition produced by that word is intended [to be the referent], then because that object is already established, the resulting comprehension would be more cumbersome than our own desired view—which maintains that the function of a word is solely affirmative (*vidhi*) and directed toward a single object—since our view involves the comprehension of many objects through a single term. Furthermore, that theory of affirmation (*vidhivāda*) itself has many objects and consists of a more weighty comprehension; once that theory of affirmation, which possesses a vast range of objects and consists of a more significant comprehension, is understood, what further purpose is served by exclusion (*apoha*)? For the affirmative comprehension of "that very thing" regarding all objects has already occurred prior [to the application of exclusion].

For you yourself have become a proponent of verbal injunctions whose scope consists of a vast multitude of objects, and a proponent of words with infinite meanings; therefore, what is achieved by the postulation of *apoha*? For then, by means of *arthāpatti* (presumption), both the intended meaning (*svārtha*) and those other meanings (*arthāntara*)—this entire duality—is established by its own nature through positive affirmation (*vidhi*) alone.

Furthermore, regarding what is stated here—"the jar exists"—there arises both the general cognition of inclusion (*anugama-sāmānya-jñāna*) that "it is existent," and the general cognition of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti-sāmānya-jñāna*) that "it is not a non-existent jar. If both of these occur through presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*), let them be; like the sweetness of molasses, their own essential natures are rendered subordinate. For who can establish the reality of things and other objects by themselves? Thus, whether the general cognition of inclusion and the general cognition of exclusion occur or not—since the meaning of the word "existent" is a reality qualified by the unreal—if there is no further object [beyond this], then the question would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
