Consequently, it is strictly a doubtful reason (*saṃdigdha-hetu*).

In reality, it is merely included within the subject (*pakṣa*) itself as possessing that specific nature; thus, it lacks one of the necessary conditions of a valid reason, namely, that it must reside in any positive instance (*sapakṣa*).
*Nyāyamukha*, pp. 32–33:

Having summarized that, it is asserted as follows: "Whether that word 'tree' has that tree as its object or something other than it, the relationship between the word 'non-tree' and the object 'non-tree' is for the sake of understanding the word 'tree' and its object. This is the position: that a relationship cannot be established between that word and its object by means of what is well-known in the world, nor according to your own intention. The proof is already explained: because [the word] has never been perceived together with that [object], just like audibility and permanence/impermanence.
He shows that you yourself have stated this principle: that neither a word nor a logical mark has the power to reveal its own object except by means of a relationship;

and yet, as previously stated, that relationship does not exist, for the difficulty of establishing a relationship has already been explained. Furthermore, it is impossible [to establish it] even through usage (*prayoga*).
It is generally impossible [to establish this],
as stated on page 653, line 14 and page 650, line 25;
therefore, etc.

Precisely because of this difficulty regarding the relationship [between word and object], as for what you stated—that the collection of faults, such as deviation (*vyabhicāra*), exists in the position that the particular (*bheda*) is denoted, those faults do not exist in the position of Apoha; for there is no fault of deviation, since the particular is not denoted.

That too is not the case; it is not that there is no deviation (*vyabhicāritā*), for it has already been stated that the difficulty of establishing a relationship certainly exists—it is not as if there is no such thing as the fault of deviation. Furthermore, regarding this point, we do not understand with what intention you first state that "positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatirekau*) are the gateway for a word’s denotation of meaning," and then subsequently reject positive concomitance (*anvaya*). For when you examine the subject of positive concomitance in a single instance—such as "tree" [meaning] "it is not a non-tree"—by way of excluding the non-tree (*avṛkṣavyudāsena*), surely in this way...

...where could this positive concomitance (anvaya) exist? Since it is impossible to perceive all things that are trees, [the word] does not apply to even its own specific referent alone—just as a mark (liṅga) cannot exist in a single part of the object to be marked (liṅgin)—because when there is an infinity of distinctions such as the roots of individual perceptible trees, a relationship [between word and meaning] is impossible and comprehension would be absent.
Furthermore, the word "tree" would be incapable of either inferring or denoting its own referent as excluded from non-trees; this is the thesis.

The reason is "because of being an uncommon property" (*asādhāraṇadharmatvāt*). Being an uncommon property consists in its not being observed in either the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) or the dissimilar instances (*asapakṣa*). He explains this: "For that which is an uncommon property of the subject," and so forth, up to "because of its exclusive exclusion. The meaning of this has already been understood through that explanation. The passage beginning from "the fallacy [of inconclusiveness]" (*abhicāra*) and ending with "the difficulty of establishing a connection" (*sambandhadauṣkaryasya*), which is contained within these marks, does not exist in manuscript *ya*.

*Sadāpibhaṭṭa*: Furthermore, regarding this point, we do not understand with what intention you first state that positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) are the means by which a word denotes its object, and then subsequently reject positive concomitance. For, while you examine the subject of positive concomitance in a single instance—namely, that "tree" [denotes] "not non-tree"—by way of excluding the non-tree (*avṛkṣa-vyudāsa*), is it not thus...?

...where could this positive concomitance (*anvaya*) exist? Since it is impossible to perceive all trees as its referents, it does not apply to even a single portion of its own meaning—just like a mark (*liṅga*) that exists only in a portion of the thing to be marked (*liṅgin*). This is because, given the infinite variety of perceptible features such as the roots of individual trees, it would be impossible to establish a relationship, and thus no comprehension [of the universal] could occur.
Even for its own referent as excluded from non-trees, the word "tree" would be incapable of either inference or denotation, because it would be common to external [objects].
Furthermore: "And this also here," and so forth.

Since positive concomitance (*anvaya*) has already been uprooted, we do not understand with what intention you state that positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) are the means by which a word denotes its meaning, and then subsequently reject positive concomitance again.
Is this due to ignorance, an attempt to disparage our intellect, or a lack of fear regarding this world, the next world, or infamy?

If you ask, "What is this rejection of positive concomitance? it is said: It is that which you examine in a single instance concerning positive concomitance—namely, [the understanding of] "tree" through the exclusion of non-trees (*avṛkṣa*), such that [one thinks] "it is not a non-tree."
Folio 652, line 2: For comparison, see folio 459–2.

If it is asked, "How, moreover, is positive concomitance (*anvaya*) refuted by this? we reply: the underlying intention of the passage beginning with "Is it not so... and ending with "...where is that positive concomitance? has already been explained.
Regarding this, he states the reason: because it is impossible to perceive the meaning of all trees; and because of the infinity of their differences, impossibility has been stated.

Furthermore, it has been stated that there is no concomitance (anvaya) pervading the locus of its own referent, and since [the word] is merely a collection of qualities, you yourself have stated that perception does not exist in the constituent parts which are themselves subordinate qualities.

Therefore, just as inference is untenable due to the absence of inference and the object of inference when there is an absence of concomitance, so too the relationship between the designator and the designated is untenable.

Regarding the phrase *kvāsābaṃdhaya* (in the Bhāṣya) or *kvāsāsaṃbaṃdhaya* (in the Yāyāvara), it might be thought: "Since we observe that a name applies to a portion of the object to be named, just as a mark applies to a portion of the marked object, there exists both a connection (*anvaya*) and a naming (*abhidhāna*)."

To this it is replied: even granting that [the objection holds], [it is as follows]: just as smoke (*dhūma*), which exists in one part (*ekadeśa*) of fire—the *liṅgin*—namely in a single fire, serves as the indicator (*gamaka*) of that fire, so too [the word] does not exist in only a portion of its own referent (*svārthāṃśa*). Therefore, the comprehension of the denotable object from the word cannot occur.

As for the phrase "direct perception of the tree" (*pratyakṣavṛkṣa*) and so forth: at the time of establishing the relationship [between name and object], there is no such establishment of a designation for a tree possessing roots and so on, even though it is being directly perceived as "this is a tree."

Just as there is a lack of comprehension when it is impossible to establish a relationship between a genus-term and its infinite particular instances—such as *śiṃśapā* and so on—due to the infinity of those particulars, so too, even regarding a single part designated as its own referent (the individual), there is an impossibility of establishing a relationship because of the infinity of distinctions such as roots, hollows, shortness, length, thinness, and breadth, since these are not observed in every case. How much more so, then, for words like "heaven" (*svarga*), whose referents are entirely beyond perception? For, if that were not the case, the word "tree" would have to denote an infinite number of particulars such as *dhava* and *khadira*, because its own referent-part would be unobserved. [This is based on the principle of] "denoting what is possible. (Praśastapāda-bhāṣya).
Even when [the meaning] is possible, there is no designation;
in the mere non-existence of its own referent,
it is like the state of being a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*).
The reading "even in one part" (*ekadeśe 'pi*) might also occur as "even in one [instance] of itself" (*ekasminn api*).

Here, the means for establishing an undesirable consequence is as follows: the word "tree" would not be capable—meaning it would not be able—for either inference or denotation of its own referent even when that referent is excluded from non-trees. This is the meaning.

Because it exists in only one part of that [subject]: this property (dharma) has the habit of existing in one part of its own object—the subject (dharmin), the thesis (pakṣa), the inferable (anumeya), or the thing to be expressed—or it is that whose existence therein is sound. What is meant by "existing in one part of that"? Because it is a non-pervasive property of the subject; because it exists in only one part of that, i.e., because it is a non-pervasive property of the subject, like sleep which is intended as a proof for consciousness as distinguished from insentient matter, and thus does not pervade the entire subject.
If,
however,
one were to accept that [the self] exists in an unseen location independently of the example of sleep, then it would follow that its activity occurs even in what is dissimilar [to the body].

Or rather, precisely because of that infinity, there is no fault even if words for universals (*jāti*) and particulars (*bheda*) have not had their relations [with objects] established; the meaning is that, with respect to those objects, there is no observed occurrence of all [words] as inferable [entities].

It is like the argument for establishing consciousness in plants by means of sleep, as in the proposition "plants are conscious" with the reason "because of sleep. Although this reason exists in one part of the subject—plants—such as in the *śirīṣa* tree, it does not exist in others such as the *tāla* palm; thus, due to its lack of pervasion (*avyāpitva*), it is incapable of proving consciousness. Similarly, the word "tree," which functions to exclude non-trees while functioning only within a portion of the tree's own referent, is incapable of either inferring or denoting [consciousness].
This, however, is an undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭāpādana*) resulting from the admission that the word functions only within a portion of its own referent.
It has already been stated that there is no functioning [of inference] at all, and we shall further explain the absence of its own object (*svārtha*) even in the case of inference.

This reading—contained within these brackets—is duplicated in the manuscripts because it occurs in only one part of them; for [inference] lacks the property of being a characteristic of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) in an all-pervasive sense, just as in the case of deep sleep, which serves to establish consciousness as excluded from non-vegetative matter.
Not pervading all positions...
Comparison: Now, there is also another type of unestablished reason (*asiddha*), and that is twofold:
the unestablished because it is a part of the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñārthaikadeśāsiddha*), such as "Sound is impermanent because it is impermanent."
And [the fallacy] called "unestablished due to non-pervasion" (*avyāpakāsiddha*): as in the case of "trees are sentient because they sleep" (from the *Nyāyapraveśaka-vṛtti*, p. 23).

The analysis of the compound is: "being a part of the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñārtha*), it is unestablished. The meaning is that because the meaning of the proposition is unestablished, the reason (*hetu*), being a part of that [proposition], is also unestablished.
Regarding the term "unestablished due to non-pervasion" (*avyāpakāsiddha*): here, that which does not constitute a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) is precisely what is called "unestablished.

Since it is this unestablished [reason] that is being investigated here, one must supply the word "of the subject" (*pakṣasya*) and then compose the compound accordingly: being non-pervasive with respect to the subject in its form as the locus (*dharmirūpa*), it is "unestablished due to non-pervasion" (*avyāpakāsiddha*).

In this case, among the trees taken as the subject (*pakṣa*), sleep characterized by the closing of leaves is not established even in one part [of the subject], for not all [trees] undergo closing at night; since this is not observed in the case of the *nyagrodha* and others, it occurs only in some—*Nyāyapraveśaka-vṛtti-pañjikā*, p.

If it were admitted that [the word] exists in a location not perceived independently of the example of sleep, then there would be the undesirable consequence of its application even to dissimilar things;

or rather, because of that very infinity, there is no fault even if the word denotes a distinction within the genus (*jāti*) for which the relationship has not been established, since its objective aspect is unperceived—
just as in the case of consciousness (*cetana*).
Comparison—page 428, line 18:
It is not so.

It might be thought: "Would this be an inference like 'being produced immediately after an effort' (prayatnānantarīyakatva), which does not pervade all impermanent things that are to be proven (sādhyāśeṣānityatva)? Or would it be a fallacious inference (anumānābhāsa), like 'sleep,' which does not pervade trees (vanaspati)? Such is the doubt.

And this is not so; [the objection that] "it does not pervade the entire class," and so forth, is answered as follows: for while the property of "being produced immediately after effort" does not pervade the similar class (*sapakṣa*), "sleep" does not even pervade the subject (*pakṣa*) itself.

For the word "tree," according to our view, excludes everything that is not a tree and establishes the referent "tree"—whether it be a non-tree such as a human being, a conventional tree such as a painting, or anything else—without failing to pervade the similar class (*sapakṣa*) which is similar by virtue of the general property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*). Nor is there any fault here in the inference, because it functions within its own domain; thus, the example "consciousness in plants, like sleep" was cited precisely because the reason is a *pakṣadharma* that is not over-pervasive.

Therefore, it was rightly stated that the word "tree" cannot serve for inference; for what connection could there be [between the word and the property], since it would result in the inference of being produced immediately after effort—which is non-eternal and does not pervade all trees? These [objections] are not valid.
A tree for the installation of humans and so forth is a "human-installation-tree"; [this applies to] a human-installation-tree, a painting and so forth, and our own [tradition];
a human-installation-tree, three, or a painting and so forth, or our own [tradition], or indeed the method.
This reading from the Ya manuscript (p. 664, l. 7) must also be examined.

It might be argued: "Disregarding the aforementioned example of the wild beast (*svāpa*), the word 'tree' (*vṛkṣa*) also causes one to understand those things other than its own referent where it has not been observed [to apply], because it possesses a power observed in part, due to its similarity with the inference of its own observed referent."

This is incorrect, because it would entail the [absurd] consequence of the word functioning with respect to what is to be excluded (*apohya*). Therefore, he says: "But if one accepts that [the word] exists in a location not perceived, independent of the example of sleep, then there is the consequence of its functioning even with respect to what is dissimilar; that is, the word 'tree' would function with respect to a non-tree such as a jar, because it exists in an unperceived location, just like its functioning with respect to its own referential part—the *palāśa* tree which possesses roots and so forth—or like the absence of functioning [with respect to the exclusion]. The meaning is: therefore, even if there is no denotation of a distinction between the universal (*jāti*) and the word due to their lack of a conventional relation—because of infinity [of individuals]—there is no fault, since [the word] is unperceived with respect to that [excluded] object, i.e., because it is unperceived with respect to its own referential part, just like the exclusion (*apoha*) itself.

Thus, from where would there be positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), or from where the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), or from where the three-fold characteristic (*trailakṣaṇya*), or from where the nature of inference (*anumānatva*) for a word? If a word, like a logical mark (*liṅga*), possesses the three characteristics and makes its own object known through the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), then the word "tree" would apply to things excluded from non-trees; because it would be an inference, like a pot or other objects employed to demonstrate positive concomitance.

However, it would not apply to actual trees, because trees constitute the subject (*pakṣa*)—since the meaning of the word "sapakṣa" (similar instance) is that which is excluded from the meaning of the word [in question]—just as [the word] does not apply to eternal things in the case of "produced.
Therefore, the word has no application to what is similar to that [subject].

"Just as [the word] has its own object (*svārtha*) in the case of exclusion (*apoha*": for instance, in the case of "it is not a non-tree," the exclusion of non-trees (*avṛkṣāpoha*) has as its own object the infinite [tree] possessing roots and so forth, distinguished by hollows and the like; and since it is observed that there is no fault even when denoting that, in the same way, for the proponent of difference (*bhedavādin*) as well, there would be an absence of fault despite the infinity of differences, even if no relation has been established."

Or rather, even regarding the very object of your own position, there would be the same fault; thus, how could there be positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) through the presence and absence [of the reason] in similar and dissimilar instances? How could the subject (*pakṣa*), which is the denotable object of the word, possess the property of being a mark (*liṅgatva*), as a mark possesses the property of having a marked object (*liṅgitva*)? How could there be the three characteristics (*trailakṣaṇya*)? How could there be the nature of inference (*anumānatva*)? And thus, since there is a lack of similarity (*sādharmya*) due to the contradiction between the subject, the non-subject, and the similar instance pertaining to the word and the mark, how could the word have the nature of inference? Thus, [this] should not be overlooked... [text fragment].
Is it because of their infinity,
or because of the infinity [of objects]?
Likewise, because [the universal] is seen in a portion of the object.

Because [the word] possesses its own object through exclusion (apoha), how can there be positive concomitance (anvaya) and negative concomitance (vyatireka)? How can there be the property of being a characteristic of the subject (pakṣadharmatva)? How can there be the three-fold definition (trailakṣaṇya)? How can there be the nature of inference (anumānatva) for the word?

If the word, like a logical mark (liṅga), possesses the three-fold definition and makes its own object known through the exclusion of others (anyāpoha), then the word "tree" would have application toward things excluded from non-trees, because it is an inference, just like a pot or other objects employed to demonstrate positive concomitance.

But there would be no occurrence [of the reason] in trees, because trees constitute the subject (pakṣa), and because the meaning of the term "similar instance" (sapakṣa) excludes that which is the meaning of the subject; thus, as in the case of "producedness" with respect to eternal things,
the word does not occur in what is similar to that, and this constitutes two faults.
In this regard, the following should be noted:
in the Ya manuscript, at the phrase *śabdaliṅgagatapakṣāpakṣa*, the page number 230 ends;

however, on the subsequent page (which should be 231), the number 234 was written by mistake. On what should have been 231, the number 232 was written; on 232, the number 233; and on 233, the number 234 was written.
Although incorrect folio numbers were written in the manuscript Ya due to negligence, the correct numbers were also provided in the left-hand corner of those very pages;
likewise, the reading in the manuscript Pā follows the correct numbering.

However, because other scribes who copied their manuscripts based on the manuscript Ya did not recognize this, they wrote their own copies according to the incorrect numbers, resulting in a significant displacement of the text—for instance, the folio numbered 234 was written immediately after folio 230. Thus, a great deal of textual confusion has arisen in those [copies].
Therefore, beginning from "atassu ॰miṣyete" and ending with "atraśabdavācyasyāgniviśiṣṭasya dhū॰," the passage to be cited here has appeared unexpectedly;
hence, it is entirely incoherent.

However, we have presented the reading exactly as it appears in the Bhāratīya (Bhā) and Pāñjābī (Pā) manuscripts, and as it was written on the pages marked with clean numbers in the Jaina (Ya) manuscript; therefore, that alone is to be accepted.
In the contradiction between the thesis and the counter-thesis.

The explanation of that is as follows: "If [the word] is like the logical mark (*liṅga*)," and so forth. If you think that the word, like the logical mark of "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) and so on, possesses the three characteristics and makes its own object known through the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), then there would be a presence of the word "tree" in the dissimilar instances (*asapakṣa*)—that which is not excluded from non-trees—other than its own denoted portion called the "own object. This is because, being an inference, it would have a presence in what is excluded from the denotation of the word "tree" (which is the subject-property, *pakṣadharma*), just as there is a presence in a jar which is the locus of producedness and impermanence, like a jar used for the purpose of demonstrating positive concomitance (*anvaya*). This has already been explained.

But there would be no application [of the word] to trees. Why? Because trees constitute the subject (*pakṣa*). The objects denoted by the word "tree" are the substrata (*dharmin*) of the property (*dharma*) designated by the word "tree," which are distinguished from the similar instances (*sapakṣa*); it is only in those that there would be no application. Precisely because it is an inference, "treeness" is merely the exclusion from non-trees according to your own view, and not in any other object even if it is similar by virtue of the generality of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*). Therefore, according to your own position, the word "tree" has no application to those other objects distinct from the tree—the subject—which are considered equal to it; for that which is intended as the property of the subject does not apply to them.
Why? Because its meaning is delimited by the referent of the term "sapakṣa" (similar instance).
How so? Just as [the property of] being produced [is absent] in eternal things;

therefore, by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), because there is an absence of a similar instance (*sapakṣa*), the word has no occurrence in what is similar to that. What then? Its occurrence is in that very [dissimilar instance] itself.

Therefore, because it lacks the three characteristics [of a logical reason], verbal testimony is not inference. [In the case of the word "tree,"] the word is not excluded from non-trees; [in the case of the word "arrow,"] the word is not excluded from those things that have not been pierced.
Therefore, since there is no interruption,
the meaning is already established by the example of the jar and so forth;
"by the jar and so forth" means the meaning is already established.
In those very [entities] delimited by their respective objects,
there is the manifestation of the mental state (*mati*).
The subject is established by your own intention; its property is delimited by the meaning of the similar class (sapakṣa),
because it is the beginning of that [inference].

If it is argued that there is no occurrence of the fault pertaining to presence in the dissimilar instance (*asapakṣa*) precisely because of the restriction of the fixed determination of the exclusion of the reason (*hetvapavāda*), [we reply: no, because such a determination does not exist when the distinction between the subject (*pakṣa*), the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), and the dissimilar instance (*asapakṣa*) is not established; and if that [distinction] is unestablished, [the reason] remains unestablished. Furthermore, if one does not accept this consequence, there would be a contradiction with the theory of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*): since even that which is delimited by the similar instance would itself be a similar instance, the [reason], whose capacity is exhausted by including the similar instance, would be unable to convey the distinction between the subject and the dissimilar instance, just like the statement of the probandum (*sādhya*).
Furthermore, according to your own position, if the term were to apply only to that [tree], the fallacy of applying to the dissimilar instance (*asapakṣa*) would follow;

for the dissimilar instance (*asapakṣa*) must be either something other than the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) or the absence of a similar instance. Now, a similar instance (*sapakṣa*) is an object that is similar by virtue of possessing the general property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), while a non-similar instance (*apakṣa*) is either something other than the subject (*pakṣa*) or the absence of the subject.

In this case, since the word "tree" applies only to the object that is a tree, even though it possesses that property, it would be contradictory, or else it would be an uncommon inconclusive (*asādhāraṇānaikāntika*) reason.

"Sapakṣa" (the similar instance) is that which is other than the sapakṣa; "that which is other than the pakṣa" [is] the absence of the pakṣa, which is precisely the apakṣa—this may also be the reading. Furthermore, the reading "that which is other than the pakṣa, the absence of the pakṣa, is the apakṣa; the pakṣa itself is the asapakṣa" should also be considered here.

If it be thought— as expressed in the passage beginning with "the denial of the reason" (*hetvapavāda*) and ending with "no"— that according to the definition [in the *Pramāṇasamuccaya*], "The reason is contrary to this [thesis] when it is contradictory; otherwise, it is uncertain" (PS 3.22), the denial of the three-fold reason constitutes a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*), such as the contradictory, the unshared (*asādhāraṇa*), the shared (*sādhāraṇa*), or the unestablished (*asiddha*), then by virtue of this restriction, the word "tree" (*vṛkṣa*) would be free from the defect of occurring in the dissimilar instance (*asapakṣa*).

And this is not the case, because there is no establishment of that [the reason] when the distinction between the subject (*pakṣa*), the similar class (*sapakṣa*), and the dissimilar class (*asapakṣa*) has not been established. The establishment of the distinction between a valid reason (*hetu*) and a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) would only be possible once the distinction between the subject, the similar class, and the dissimilar class is established; if that is unestablished, it remains unestablished. This is because the rule for distinguishing between a valid reason and its fallacies depends upon the establishment of the subject and so forth, and it has already been stated that the subject itself is unestablished, since it does not exist ultimately from either perspective.

The similar instance (*sapakṣa*), however, would not exist according to the immediate logic [of your position], while the dissimilar instance (*asapakṣa*) would be that very same subject (*pakṣa*) because you accept your own thesis; this is because there would be a mere absence of a similar instance. Otherwise, it would not exist at all, precisely as previously stated.
Therefore, due to the restriction of the reason (*hetu*) and so forth, the occurrence of the fault regarding the presence [of the reason] in the dissimilar instance remains exactly as it was.
"But if there is no admission of the fault of the [logical] consequence," and so forth:

if you do not admit this fault of the consequence, then the fault is the "alteration of the exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*) as it pertains to its occurrence in non-concordant instances (*asapakṣa*). In that case, even the "exclusion of others" would result in the exclusion of its own referent (*svārthāpoha*) because of the absence of "others" and the consequent absence of their exclusion. Why? Because even that which is delimited by the concordant instances (*sapakṣa*) is itself a concordant instance; and that which is other than the concordant instance—whether it be the subject (*pakṣa*) or the non-concordant instance (*asapakṣa*) delimited from it—is precisely that same concordant instance. Therefore, it is other than the subject.
The very thesis (pakṣa) is other than the thesis because it is other than the similar instance (sapakṣa);
therefore, the exclusion of what is other than that results in the exclusion of the thesis, which amounts to the exclusion of its own meaning (svārthāpoha).
See Tippaṇī p. 74, l. 4 – p. 75, l. 1.
*°dvṛtti* (Ya);
*hetuhetutvābhāsa* (Ya);
*hetvābhāsa* (Bhā).
Page 655,
line 2: Is it "there is no logic" (°nyāyo nāsti) or "it does not exist by way of logic" (°nyāyena nāsti)?
Not accepted as being of the same class (*asapakṣa*); accepted as being of the same class (*sapakṣa*); other than the same class (*sapakṣa*).

Furthermore, its capacity is exhausted by the exclusion of the similar instances (*sapakṣa*). When it is said that "the dissimilar instance (*asapakṣa*) is other than the similar instance," its purpose is fulfilled merely by the exclusion of the similar instance; thus, it is not capable of conveying the distinction between the subject (*pakṣa*) and the dissimilar instance, such as: "This is indeed the subject, not the dissimilar instance.

What is it like? It is like the statement of the probandum (*sādhyanirdeśa*). As it is said: "The statement of the probandum is the proposition" (Nyāyasūtra 1.1.33).

1.33 Thus, according to the definition of the "pakṣa" (the subject) as held by Akṣapāda, once the [logical] accomplishment has ceased, the argument—having fulfilled its purpose—is no longer capable of making known the specific subject (*sādhyaviśeṣa*) as distinct from the unestablished reason (*asiddhahetu*) and example (*dṛṣṭānta*), because its power is exhausted by the exclusion of the counter-example (*vipakṣa*). If it is argued that the word "tree" applies to what is similar [to the subject] precisely because its property-status (*pakṣadharmatva*) is restricted to that object, then sound (*śabda*) would not be an inference; for it would reside in the subject alone, thus possessing only one characteristic (the absence of the second), like an uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*) reason. Or, because it lacks both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it would be contradictory (*viruddha*) due to having only one characteristic. Furthermore, since the meaning of the word "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*) consists solely in its being restricted to that object, exclusion (*vyatireka*) would be impossible in relation to its own referent, and thus it would be utterly useless, as even the mere subject lacks the defining characteristics, just like an unintelligible utterance.

For the object designated as a "tree" is indeed a collection of qualities; thus, since the roots, hollows, and so forth of a tree are infinite, there can be no denotability [of the word "tree"] with respect to them, because the collection is merely conventional and does not convey those specific particulars.
Therefore, as stated previously, inference by means of that [collection] is impossible;
consequently, even the property of having a single definition does not exist, so how could there be any *anyāpoha* (exclusion of others)?

Therefore, the word "tree" (vṛkṣa) is indeed purposeless, because it does not characterize even a single part [of the object], just like an indistinct sound; just as the meaning of a word used by barbarians is purposeless because it signifies only exclusion and does not characterize even its own primary meaning—as in the case of words like *histamis*—so too would the word "tree" be. Therefore, he recalls that very position previously stated—that inference is impossible by way of that [universal], because the so-called universal or aggregate, being a conventional reality (*saṃvṛtisat*), lacks existence, and because particulars such as straightness, curvature, cavities, hollows, and so forth, are inexpressible.

The passage beginning with "Since there is no [individual] tree-entity as a subject (pakṣa), the word 'tree' lacks the property of being a predicate of that subject" is the section explaining that [point]. How so? This is explained from the words "How so? up to "like the word 'army,'" the meaning of which has already been established.
The reason is: "because it has as its referent a conventional designation for a collection of qualities."

If it is argued that the word "tree" (*vṛkṣa*) functions solely as a collective referent (*samudāyārtha*), we say no. This is because [the tree] would then share the same status as its parts, such as the roots and so forth, which are already accepted [as the referents]; consequently, since the meaning of "tree" would not be distinct from them, statements regarding its occurrence in similar instances and non-occurrence in dissimilar instances would be utterly redundant.

Furthermore, because the collective is merely conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*), it would be as devoid of objective reality as the individual tree; thus, even [collectives] such as "army" (*senā*) and "forest" (*vana*) would likewise be devoid of any real referent.

Furthermore, even when examples such as "Ḍittha" are cited for the purpose of establishing the reality of form (*rūpa*) and so forth, since there is no positive concomitance (*anvaya*) due to the mutual exclusion of form and the other [senses], there is likewise an absence of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). Consequently, nothing whatsoever is real, because [the object] has a nature that is excluded from both similar and dissimilar classes, because it is absolutely unprecedented, and because its specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is inexpressible.
Therefore, the operation of a word occurs only upon a dissimilar instance;
indeed, there is no operation of a word upon an [ultimately real] object. In the treatises, ignorance itself is described through various analytical distinctions (*prakriyābheda*).
"But non-occurrence, being free from conceptual construction, manifests by itself as knowledge" (Vākyapadīya 2.235).
Thus, because it occurs only in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), a word— like a logical mark (*liṅga*)— is not inference, nor is it even a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

If it should be thought that a word functions solely by virtue of its collective meaning—that is, if the view were held: "The word 'tree' possesses meaning through a collective object; and since the collection of roots and so forth is called a 'tree,' there is no fault because it possesses a collective meaning"—this is not so. [This is shown by the passage beginning with] "because they are accepted," and so on. Since the accepted roots and so forth are considered one through their identity with that [collective], they constitute the "similar instance" (*sapakṣa*). Being other than the similar instance constitutes the "subject" (*pakṣa*). Therefore, the meaning of the word "tree" is different from the similar instance; because it is not identical to it, any statement regarding its occurrence in what is similar or its non-occurrence in what is dissimilar is indeed redundant.
Furthermore, because the aggregate is a conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*), it is likewise devoid of reality—just like a tree—therefore even things such as an army or a forest are indeed unreal.

The application [of the term "tree"] in the statement "a non-tree is not a tree" is entirely dissimilar even to the mere existence of the essential nature of the roots and so forth, because this [term] has as its referent the conventional reality of the aggregate of distinct factors such as form (*rūpa*) and the rest. Since this [aggregate] exists, [the individual parts do not].

If it is argued that the word "tree" functions solely as a collective referent (*samudāyārtha*), we say no; for since the roots and other parts have been accepted as its homologous instances (*sapakṣa*), the meaning of "tree" would not be distinct from them. Consequently, statements regarding whether it applies to what is similar or dissimilar, or whether it does or does not apply, would be entirely redundant.

Furthermore, because the collective is merely conventional reality (*saṃvṛtisatya*)—just like the individual tree—it would follow that even [collectives] such as an army (*senā*) or a forest (*vana*) would likewise be devoid of referential meaning.

Furthermore, even when examples such as "Dittha" are cited for the purpose of establishing the reality of form (*rūpa*) and so forth, since there is no positive concomitance (*anvaya*) due to the mutual exclusion of form and the rest, there is likewise an absence of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). Consequently, nothing at all is real, because [the object] has a nature excluded from both similar and dissimilar classes, because it is absolutely unprecedented, and because its specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is inexpressible.
Therefore, the operation of a word occurs only upon that which is dissimilar [to the exclusion], or rather, there is no operation of the word upon the object at all.

If it is argued that [the word] would possess meaning because of the existence of form (*rūpa*) and so forth—due to the non-concealment of its referent—that too is not the case. For even when you employ examples such as *Ḍittha* in order to establish the reality of form and so forth, since you yourself state that there is no positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with a collection of qualities such as "one-eyed" or "lame," and since you thus exert yourself in the effort of "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*), there is an absence of positive concomitance through the mutual exclusion of form and so forth. Consequently, because there is an absence of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), and because the ultimate reality is non-becoming in the sense of "it does not exist, it does not exist," nothing at all is real.

He states the reason for this: "Because its nature is excluded from both what is similar and what is dissimilar. For it has been said: "The inexpressible specific characteristic, the form, is the domain of the senses" (Pramāṇasamuccaya 1.11). Therefore, since the subject (*pakṣa*) is incomparable, the function of the word occurs only therein through exclusion from both similar and dissimilar instances.

Either there is no application [of the word] at all to the object, or else you have already accepted the lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) of the word; for this very reason, the proof follows your own view—the verse beginning with "In the treatises, through various analytical procedures" (*śāstreṣu prakriyābhedaiḥ*) has its meaning already explained.

Regarding the phrase "of its own object" (*svārthasya*), there is the absence of even the mere property-possessor (*pakṣadharma-mātra*), as in the case of non-determination (*anadhyavasāya*), as in the cognition of a barbarian's word, or as in the case of error (*viparyaya*), i.e., like contradictory cognition (*viruddhajñāna*).

He explains that: even in this inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*)—“there is fire here because of smoke”—the object called “smoke” is indeed a collection of qualities (*guṇasamudāya*). Just as a tree lacks denotability (*vācyatvābhāva*) due to the infinity of its parts such as roots and hollows, so too there is an absence of "smokeness" (*dhūmatvābhāva*) due to the infinity of its properties such as density and curvature. Because the relationship [of concomitance] is not known and because the collection is merely conventional (*saṃvṛtimātra*), the meaning is not apprehended through it; therefore, by way of that, there is no inference. Thus, the mark (*liṅga*) is not a definition even for inference for oneself alone. Consequently, the state of having only one characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇatā*) does not exist at all; in this way, it is stated that there is no definition for inference for oneself alone.

If [the word] were characterized solely by its own meaning (*svārtha*), how could there be the cognition of both [affirmation and exclusion], given that [the object] is not apprehended as "this is smoke, not non-smoke" because it would be something else? In the absence of such a dual comprehension, how could there be the exclusion of the other (*anyāpoha*) based on the absence of the other? Furthermore, how could there be the cognitions "it is fire, not non-fire" and "it is smoke, not non-smoke"? This [position] does not hold even from afar; it is utterly untenable due to its futility. Thus ends the *Vaiśeṣika-prakaraṇa-bhāṣya*.

What is meant? However, since the similar instance itself does not exist, there is no expectation for negative concomitance.
Therefore, both positive and negative concomitance are absent.

Therefore, this was stated merely without considering what precedes or follows it;
verbal cognition is not a separate means of valid knowledge from inference, nor is it non-distinct from inference.

If verbal cognition were not a separate means of valid knowledge from inference, then even properties such as "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) would destroy their own object by excluding themselves. For it is thus: that [verbal cognition] expresses its own object through the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), just like "being produced" and so forth. Consequently, the faults resulting from the function of excluding others would not belong to the word alone; rather, they would apply to inference as well, since it too is connected with the occurrence of that same web of faults.

If one asks, "What is that [rule]? it is said: that which you stated as "likewise the limb" (*tathāṅgam*), and so forth.

The mark (*liṅga*), such as smoke or being produced (*kṛtakatva*), does not exist by overstepping the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*)—the object characterized by fire, impermanence, and so forth, such as a location or a word—in the form by which it exists, nor in the form by which it does not overstep it. How does it not overstep it? "Smoke" is not non-smoke; "produced" is not unproduced. Thus, by its nature of excluding what is non-smoke and unproduced, it does not overstep [its object]. And by that very form, consisting of exclusion from others, it makes [the object] known. Although it possesses many properties such as existence (*sattva*) and substantiality (*dravyatva*), it does not make [the object] known through these general properties like existence because they are inconclusive (*vyabhicāra*). This, then, is the rule regarding the indicator.

The restriction regarding the object of inference (*gamyaniyama*) is as follows: the general properties (*sāmānyadharma*) such as existence (*sattva*), substantiality (*dravyatva*), and so forth, which are concomitants (*anubandhin*) of the probandum, are indeed inferred by means of the probans (*liṅga*). However, those specific features (*viśeṣa*) which are also concomitants of the probandum are not inferred, because they are subject to deviation (*vyabhicārin*).

However, meanings connected with a logical mark (liṅga) do not make known the possessor of that mark (liṅgin), because of the possibility of deviation; rather, it is the specific instances (viśeṣa), when they are perceived, that are the communicators [of the universal]. (Pramāṇasamuccaya 1.16ab)

As for what was said—that the mark (*liṅga*) is not present everywhere in that which possesses the mark (*liṅgin*), as in "there is fire here because of smoke"—this too is a statement made through lack of foresight. If that [fire] were indeed the possessor of the mark, how could it not have a mark? Or, if there is no mark, how can it possess one? Furthermore, in the example of fire and smoke, since the statement "there is fire here" indicates that the locus is to be proven as possessing fire, the state of possessing smoke exists as a mark throughout the entire area that possesses fire.

Because the logical mark (*liṅga*) is inseparable from them, specific qualities such as being produced by cow-dung (*gauḥ*) or being produced by dried cow-dung (*kārīṣa*) are not inferred; for that very mark is deviant with respect to those particulars, since it has never been observed in conjunction with them.
Thus, it is the universal (*sāmānya*) of the mark, as excluded from others, that is the indicator, and not a universal such as "existence" (*sattva*), which is not so excluded from anything else.

Thus, it is like a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*); how is it not like a characteristic?

As for what was said—that a mark (liṅga) does not exist everywhere in that which possesses the mark (liṅgin), as in "there is fire here because of smoke"—this too is the speech of one who has failed to consider the matter. If it is indeed the possessor of the mark itself, how is it that it lacks a mark? Or, if there is no mark, how can that which possesses it be perceived? (See page 652, line 13; page 662, line 1).

And in the example of fire and smoke, because of the indication "there is fire here," the location is established as possessing fire; thus, the mark (liṅga) of possessing smoke exists everywhere in that place which possesses fire.
Furthermore, regarding the mark being invariably concomitant with fire, there is this specific point expressed in the verse beginning: "But the objects connected to the mark... and so forth.

The general properties (*sāmānyadharma*) such as existence (*sattva*) and so forth, previously cited, do not lead to the cognition of the probandum (*liṅgin*) smoke, because of the reasons already stated. However, certain particularities (*viśeṣa*), such as whiteness, abundance, and so forth, which are known to be invariably concomitant (*avinābhāvin*) with the probandum, are the means of proof; this is the meaning of the verse.

Furthermore, how is this "without characteristics" as before? To this he says: the three verses beginning with "What limb... are presented by way of a *kṣepaprastāra* (an array of negations). [The point is that] for the entire collection of meanings you have stated, there is no correspondence with what was previously said; because of the ultimate reality of non-becoming (*abhavana-paramārthatva*), there is simply no fixed rule of the signified and the signifier due to its non-existence, like a sky-flower. This is understood from the *kṣepapraśnāre* (or *prepapraśnāre*) in the *Bhāṣya*, and the *prepaprastāre* in the *Ya*.

Furthermore, regarding the restatement of the opponent's position beginning with "And what more... up to "...because smoke [is seen]," which was stated while supporting the capacity of a sign to indicate its object even when it is perceived in only one part—namely, that "the sign does not necessarily exist in every case where the signified is present"—this too is due to a lack of circumspection in speech; the intention is that it is not a display of skill in debate.
He explains this: "If it were only the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*)," and so forth.

That which possesses a mark (*liṅga*) is a *liṅgin*. If all that is a *liṅgin*—namely, the things called fire, such as ash, embers, iron balls, and the heat of cooking—how could they not have a mark? For in the absence of a mark, the very status of being a *liṅgin* would be non-existent. The intention is that the existence of the mark follows precisely from the acceptance of the status of being a *liṅgin*, which is expressed by the suffix denoting possession (*matvarthīya*).

Now, if the mark (liṅga) does not exist, how can there be one who possesses it? "One who possesses the mark" (liṅgavān) means "one for whom the mark exists" (liṅgam asya asti); that object [the possessor] ought not to be denoted by a suffix expressing possession (matvarthīya), because the mark—which is the cause for such a designation—is absent. Thus, your statement contradicts your own words.

Is it not the skill in the speech of the proponent?
[It is] the indication of the sign (liṅga) by means of the indication of the probandum (liṅgin). The indication of the probandum is the sign. Ya.
And in the example of fire and smoke, etc.

First, this must be asked: regarding the statement "there is fire here because of smoke," when the base noun *idam* (this), which has a perceptible object as its referent, is indicated in the locative case as *atra* (here), there is a connection with the specific location where the smoke is perceived. This is because, just as in the phrase "there is fire here because of smoke," the location possessing smoke is indicated through perception, while the fire is an object of inquiry since it is imperceptible; and because smoke cannot exist in glowing iron balls or embers where fire is present. If you argue thus, we say no. For the existence of fire is already established; therefore, that [location] cannot be a mark (*liṅga*) for the fire, as it is not itself marked by it (*tad-aliṅgita*), just like any other object that is not the subject of perception.

If that [the locus] is not established, then because the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and so forth would lack a foundation, the term "here" (*atra*)—which denotes the locus—would itself be the probandum (*liṅgin*). Furthermore, if one intends to express the distinction between fire and smoke, then both would be the probandum. Otherwise, the mention of "here" would be meaningless. Therefore, when a location possessing fire as established by universal consensus is the probandum, the possession of smoke exists as the probans (*liṅga*) everywhere;

yet, the state of being a probandum does not apply to every location possessing fire, because in that case there would be an absence of an example (*dṛṣṭānta*), leading to fallacies such as the "uniqueness" (*asādhāraṇatā*) of the reason.
Therefore, the conclusion is that the mark (liṅga) exists everywhere in the possessor of the mark (liṅgin).

If it is argued that this is not the case because smoke is impossible in fire such as that of a red-hot iron ball or glowing coals, we say no; for the existence of fire is established, and since the mark has that [fire] as its object, it is not a non-mark with respect to it, nor is it a non-indicator of it, just like an object that is not within the range of perception.

If it is argued that, since that [fire] is unestablished, the indicator (*liṅga*)— which is what is denoted by "here"— would lack its basis in the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and so forth; and furthermore, if one intends to express the distinction between fire and smoke, smoke would be impossible in the case of fire such as glowing iron balls or embers.

It might be thought: "The probans (liṅga) does not exist everywhere in the locus of the probandum (liṅgin), because smoke is not perceived at all through direct perception in iron-fire, molasses-fire, and charcoal-fire, even though they are burning and glowing.
But this is not so, because the existence of fire is established [by other means].

For in the proposition "there is fire here," it is not the universal of fire (*agni-sāmānya*) that is being proven, because the existence of fire is already known in the world through direct perception. Rather, what is intended to be proven is the fire as qualified by a specific location ("here"), which is not currently perceived, on the strength of smoke that has been directly observed. This is because smoke is seen in some form even in fires covered by iron balls, embers, or ashes; yet, since it is invariably concomitant (*avinābhāva*) with fire, it serves as a mark (*liṅga*) for that [fire]. The meaning is that the smoke which is the mark regarding iron balls, embers, and so forth, is not a [valid] mark (*aliṅgatvāt*), because it is non-existent [in those cases], because it is not intended [to prove the specific fire], and because it is not perceived [as such].

Because they lack a mark (*liṅga*), like the objects of perception; for those fires in the iron balls, coals, and so forth are not possessors of a mark (*liṅgin*) due to the absence of a mark in them at that state, and because they are already intensely known in that place.
Furthermore, an object possessing a mark (*liṅgin*) is marked by the power of seeing the mark;
however, those [fires] are not marked because no mark is seen, and because their establishment is independent of a mark, just as it is at the time of direct perception.

Therefore, because smoke is not a mark for them— just as it is not a mark for perception— wherever smoke is a mark, it is a mark only because it is already established in that place which possesses the mark (the *liṅgin*); since it is not established there [as fire], in that place it is merely the marked object (*liṅgin*) by virtue of being fire,
as in the case of a sugar-cane house.

And there might also be the reading "even though smoke exists in the kitchen" (guṇḍāgārāya ca satsu api dhūmasya); furthermore, the word "well-known" (pratīta) would appear here in the manuscript (pra).

If the general property of fire were to be proven independently of its specific location, there would be no similar instances (sapakṣa), resulting in the fallacy of being "uncommon" (asādhāraṇa), and the statement "here" would be redundant. To prevent this, [the author] states that because the very thing denoted by the word "here"—which is qualified by fire—is itself the probandum as qualified by smoke, and is also the means of proof, it possesses both the nature of the signified (liṅgitva) and the nature of the sign (liṅgatva). Therefore, he says: "Because the thing denoted by 'here' is the signified, and because there is the state of being the property to be proven and the proving property when one intends to distinguish between the possession of fire and the possession of smoke."

For that very same location is what is to be proven as possessing fire, since the fire is not perceived; and because the probans exists where the property to be proven exists, the impossibility of the mark being present in the locus of the marked does not occur, because those two are invariably related to one another through the relationship of primary and subordinate with respect to that very [locus] when there is the desire to determine a location as possessing fire.
...and there is the cognition of that which possesses the connection; and if that place...
obtains the status of being its mark (liṅga), because those two are properties of a single entity.
Smoke that does not exist [in the subject] cannot attain the status of a logical mark (*liṅga*), because it would lack the property of being a characteristic of the subject (*apakṣadharmatva*).

Just as sleep [is used to prove] the sentience of trees, smoke would be a cause for doubt, because the probans (*sādhana*) would not pervade the subject (*pakṣa*), and because it would be the cause for the non-establishment of the cognition consisting in the presence or absence of the property that serves as the basis for the apprehension of that [subject]. This is like the cognition of the presence or absence of a post or a person.
[If one argues] that the proof is by means of "possessing smoke" (*dhūmavattva*) because it is the state of having perceptible smoke—[we reply: no.

Therefore, because the properties of the locus to be proven (*sādhya*) and the means of proof (*sādhana*) exist in a specific location, the impossibility of the sign (*liṅga*), which is the means of proof, occurring where the object to be proven (*liṅgin*) exists, does not obtain; rather, its occurrence certainly obtains.

Why? Because those two are mutually restricted to that very place by way of the relationship of primary and subordinate. Fire is primary in the production of smoke, since smoke is a transformation of fire and is produced by it;
smoke is subordinate in the production of fire, since it lacks the nature of being a transformation of fire and is not produced by it.

Smoke is the primary factor in the cognition of fire because it is its mark (*liṅga*); since fire cannot be established without it, and because they are inseparable (*avinābhāva*), fire is subordinate in the cognition of smoke because it is not perceptible at that time and place, as it has been stated that otherwise [fire] would indeed exist. Thus, these two properties called "fire" and "smoke," which occur through a necessary relationship of mutual primacy and subordination, function as the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) when one wishes to express the differentiation of a single location.

Because the property to be proven (sādhyadharma) exists, the non-occurrence of the mark (liṅga) in the locus of the marked (liṅgin) is not possible; for those two are mutually restricted to one another through the relationship of primary and subordinate precisely therein, when there is the desire to determine a location as possessing fire...

[obtains] the status of being its mark (liṅga), because those two are properties of a single entity.
Smoke that does not exist [in the subject] cannot attain the status of a logical mark (*liṅga*), because it would lack the property of being a characteristic of the subject (*apakṣadharmatva*).

Just as sleep [is used to prove] the sentience of trees, smoke would be a cause for doubt, because the probans (*sādhana-dharma*) does not pervade the subject; and because it is the cause for the non-establishment of a cognition consisting in the presence or absence of the properties that serve as the basis for the apprehension of that [subject], just like the cognition of the presence or absence of a post or a person.

The explanation of that [passage] is as follows: by the words "in the desire to delimit a location possessing fire," and so forth, it first shows the predominance of the mark (*liṅga*), smoke, as the means of cognition (*gamaka*), and the subordinate status (*guṇabhāva*) of the marked (*liṅgin*), fire, which is the object of cognition (*gamya*), up until the point of "the cognition of that which possesses its connection. Thereafter, by the words "if, moreover, of that location," and so forth, it explains—up until the point where "it acquires the state of being a mark"—that fire is predominant and smoke is subordinate once [the location] has been established, and that [smoke] takes on the form of being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), positive concomitance with similar instances (*sapakṣānugati*), and exclusion from dissimilar instances (*vipakṣavyāvṛtti*). Having thus explained this, it indicates through the preceding [text] that smoke is that which is to be proven (*sādhya*) by fire.

Having explained above that [the inference] is to be accomplished in a specific location distinguished by fire, he now explains how smoke possesses the capacity to signify through its three characteristics (*trailakṣaṇya*) when there is the perception of smoke produced by the power of that [fire], stating:

"because those two are properties of a single entity. This is what is meant: the relationship of probandum and probans exists only between a possible mark (*liṅga*) and the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*), primarily due to positive concomitance (*anvaya*), not primarily due to exclusion (*apoha*). If you do not accept this, then the proof for an undesired consequence follows: smoke does not attain the status of a mark if it is impossible [to exist in the subject], because it would then lack the property of being a characteristic of the subject (*apakṣadharmatva*).

Precisely because of your own position, it is established that [the reason] lacks the property of being a feature of the subject (*apakṣadharman*), since there is no possibility of any possessor of a mark (*liṅgin*).

Wherever there is the absence of the property of being a feature of the subject, there is an absence of being a mark for that [subject], just as smoke and so forth are not marks for fire in a place where there is no fire, or as smoke and so forth are not marks for fire at a time when there is no smoke.
Furthermore, what else? That which was previously explained regarding the word is now stated regarding the mark as well: "As in the case of sleep, etc., with respect to the sentience of trees."

In this proof—"This place possesses fire because it possesses smoke"—according to your own view, smoke would be a cause for doubt, because it is a probans-property (*sādhanadharma*) that does not pervade the subject (*pakṣa*). To explain that: the phrase "the production of its cognition" (*tatpratipattyādhāna*) and so forth refers to the "staff-like" reason (*daṇḍakahetu*). Its cognition is "its cognition" (*tatpratipatti*); the production thereof is "the production of its cognition" (*tatpratipattyādhāna*); the property that is the locus of that production is "the property that is the locus of the production of its cognition" (*tatpratipattyādhānādhāradharma*); and that which has the state of being such a property as its essence is "that which consists in the state of being a property that is the locus of the production of its cognition" (*tatpratipattyādhānādhāradharmabhāvātmaka*). Such is the conceptual cognition (*pratyaya*) as we have explained it.

If that probans (*pratyaya*) were not established, then according to your own view, that smoke would fail to be a valid reason because it would lack the property of being present in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), since it would be absent from every instance of the inferable object (*liṅgin*). This is because its occurrence would be restricted to a non-fixed set of inferable objects.
How so? It is like the cognition of the presence or absence of a post or a person.

For example, the property of being bound by a cloth is absent in a post but present in a person; yet, when one infers that smoke is not seen elsewhere—in iron balls, glowing coals, fire, and so on—it is not a fault, because the status of smoke as a probans is explained precisely by its non-perception there.
But if the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*) were not perceived, there would indeed be a fault.

And thus, by this very logic, that reading which is the opposite—namely, the distinction between the illuminated and the illuminator—is also incorrect. For although a relation resides in both [relata], its occurrence in the case of the mark and the possessor of the mark is like that of the container and the contained, and not like that of conjoined things.

Because it is the cause for the non-establishment of a cognition consisting of the relationship between a substratum and the act of establishing—such as the cognition "this is a post"—it creates doubt regarding two objects, since it is absent in both at once; one might wonder, "Is this a post? Or is it a person? Thus, the presence of bird-nesting and so forth in a post, while their absence in a person, produces a doubt concerning both objects.

Where [the feature] is observed, it is indeed a cause of certainty—for instance, bird-nesting occurs in a post and the binding of a garment occurs in a person; because it occurs there, this [feature] would likewise be a cause of doubt in the case of "there is fire here because of smoke," due to the lack of necessity in its occurrence within the probandum (*sādhya*).
In the *Bhāṣya*: "due to the investigation of my location"; in the *Yaśomitra*: "due to the investigation of my insertion";

Its mode of existence is like that of the container and the contained, and not like that of things in conjunction;

And thus it has been said: "Although the relation resides in both the co-existent probans and the probandum, its occurrence is like that of the container and the contained, and not like that of conjoined entities" (Hetubinduṭīkā, p. 19).

Anticipating the objection—“Since a relation resides in two things, how could there not be a single uniform form for the pervasion (*vyāpti*) in both?”—the author provides a rebuttal by means of the phrase “even though” (*yadyapi*), while accepting the relation as something real that resides in two things. He states which two [things] these are: “of the *aṅga* and the *liṅgin*. Here, the word *aṅga* is understood as referring to knowledge; thus, because one is known (*aṅgyate*), indicated (*liṅgyate*), or cognized (*pratīyate*) by means of it, the *aṅga* is the *liṅga* (the sign). Therefore, the meaning is “of the sign (*liṅga*) and the signified (*liṅgin*).”

What is its nature? He says: "Together" (saha), because those two alone are presented as occurring simultaneously; and precisely because their existence in two [distinct] locations is admitted, the admission of their coexistence also follows, even though this is explicitly stated by the proximity of the word "even" (api), it should nevertheless be understood from the sense of the passage.

The "functioning" (*vṛtti*) or occurrence of that relationship—meaning, of those two, the indicator (*liṅga*) and the indicated (*liṅgin*)—is such that one might ask, "Of what two things is it like? To this he says: "Like that of the locus and the located. Because the suffix *-vati* here follows a word ending in the locative case (*saptamī*), it means:
just as the relationship characterized by the state of locus and located, though residing in both, does not exist in both with a single uniform mode of functioning.

Just as even when there is a single relation, the substratum does not possess the property of being the superstratum, nor does the superstratum possess the property of being the substratum, so too is the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between the mark (*liṅga*) and the marked (*liṅgin*): it exists in one way in the case of "smokeness" (*dhūmatva*) and so forth, and in another way in the case of "fireness" (*vahnitva*) and so forth.
For this very reason, only "smokeness" and the like are the indicators by virtue of being the pervaded (*vyāpya*), and not "knowability" (*prameyatva*) and the like;

only "fireness" and the like are the indicated by virtue of being the pervader (*vyāpaka*), and not "being produced from grass" (*tārṇatva*) and the like; nor is smoke the indicated and fire the indicator.

In the manner described, when there is a reversal—that is, a contrariety—of the restriction (niyama) or determination; and since this reversal consists in [the former] being a qualification by the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*) in one case, and [the latter] being an exclusion of connection with anything else (*anyayogavyavaccheda*) in the other; when such a reversal occurs, the meaning is that the inseparable relation between the mark (*liṅga*) and the bearer of the mark (*liṅgin*) is pervasion (*vyāpti*).

For although "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) pervades the objects that are impermanent (*anitya*), its capacity to convey [the conclusion] is through the negation of permanence (*nityatva*); likewise, although "impermanence" (*anityatva*) pervades the objects that are produced, its capacity to convey [the conclusion] is through the negation of being unproduced (*akṛtakatva*). Therefore, since "producedness" pervades the objects that are impermanent, there is no room for it to be unproduced; thus, by the negation of being unproduced, "producedness" would be understood as impermanent, and not as a means of conveying [the conclusion].

Regarding the statement beginning with "In the case of being a horn," etc., there are two verses for the purpose of cultivation (*bhāvanā*) as an illustration of this meaning: "Because of being produced, [there is] perishability," and so forth, and "Because of being a horn," and so forth.
By the preceding verse, perishability is pervaded by being produced; it is not the means of proof (*sādhana*), because it is not intended to be expressed.

Because the non-existence of permanence is not demonstrated as impermanence in the case of a produced object—namely, that "whatever is impermanent is produced"—what then? Rather, because it is intended to demonstrate the pervasion of the unproduced by the absence of permanence, impermanence is demonstrated in the case of the produced object—namely, "whatever is produced is also impermanent. This is done for the purpose of clarifying that second meaning, by providing an illustration of the deviation or non-deviation of the two types of pervasion, namely those intended and unintended.

"The [inference] 'it is a cow because it has horns' deviates [from the rule], whereas 'it has horns because it is a cow' does not deviate; therefore, it does not cause comprehension [in the former case] but does cause comprehension [in the latter]. Precisely because of the observation of that state (tadbhāva), the occurrence of the properties of the probandum and the probans is like that of conjoined things, and not like that of container and contained; for it is not merely by the observation of that state that smoke makes fire known, but rather, by the very fact that when something exists, another necessarily exists, it is through the observation of that state alone that smoke indicates fire.

If the meaning of the word were the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of the absence of that [the probans], then the absence of smoke—such as a cloth, a jar, or the son of a barren woman—would be the [meaning]; likewise, the absence of non-fire—such as wind, water, or a sky-flower—would be unrelated to that [the probandum].
This is because such a word would not have the intended meaning for the purpose of establishing a positive concomitance of that nature.

However, because one observes the existence of that [probans] in the probandum, and because one observes such a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) between the property to be proven and the proving property, their subsistence is held to be like that of two conjoined things (*saṃyogin*), and not unequal like that of a container and its contents. For both [properties], since they reside in the same substratum (*liṅgin*), possess the nature of a single entity, and are inseparable through the relationship of mutual cognition as primary and subordinate—just like "producedness" and "impermanence"—we state here: the verse beginning with "because one observes the existence of that" has a meaning contrary [to what you suggest]; it is "like conjoined things," not "like container and contents."

Regarding the passage beginning with "the perception of that state" (*tadbhāvadarśanaṃ yat tad*): that very fire becomes smoke; by means of that very fire, it exists as smoke when connected to the fuel and other factors in that specific location. It does not exist as smoke through anything else, such as non-fire or water. That fire does not fail to be smoke—it certainly is smoke. Precisely because one perceives the non-existence of the cause for the cessation of its own nature, smoke, while being smoke, leads to the cognition of fire. It is not the case that, according to your view, it is "not non-smoke" merely by the exclusion of where it has not been seen, from which it follows that it is "not non-fire. This is because we observe the fault [of over-extension] if one fails to grasp that state.

If it is asked, "What is the fault?", it is replied: If the meaning of the word [denoting] the positive concomitance of that absence were to be conceived as the opposite of the meaning of a word denoting the positive concomitance of its presence—then, in the inference "There is fire here because there is smoke," if one were to accept merely the exclusion of fire from the counter-examples (vipakṣa) of smoke, an undesirable consequence would follow: the absence of non-smoke might be a cloth, a jar, or even the son of a barren woman. And this is undesirable; this is the fault regarding the logical mark (liṅga). Similarly, regarding the possessor of the mark (liṅgin), the absence of non-fire might be wind, water, or a sky-flower, which would be incoherent; and this too is undesirable.

What is the reason? Because in that case, the purpose of establishing a non-existent positive concomitance (anvaya) would lack suchness (tathārthatva). Where there is smoke, there is fire: this purpose of establishing a concomitance is "such-like" (tathārtha), meaning it is true, because of the existence of that [concomitance], namely, the existence of fire and smoke connected to that location. Otherwise, since the purpose of establishing a non-existent positive concomitance—which you desire—is not such-like (atathārthatva), there follows the attainment of the undesirable consequence just mentioned.

Therefore, precisely because we accept the observation of that state [of concomitance] between the property to be proven and the proving property—namely, fire and smoke—the occurrence of both is held to be characterized by that same state, just as it is for one [of two] conjoined fingers. This is due to the cause of observing such a positive concomitance (*anvaya*); it is not unequal like the relationship of container and contained, wherein the container is simply a container and the contained is simply the contained, and not otherwise.

Why? Because both [reason and probandum] reside in the same substratum (*liṅgin*), such as a location or fuel; because they are invariably concomitant (*avinābhāva*) through the relationship of mutual cognition and the relationship of container and contained (*ādhārādheya-bhāva*), as well as the relationship of primary and subordinate; and because, as previously explained, they stand in the relationship of producer and what is produced (*nirvartaka-gamya-bhāva*) and thus share the nature of a single entity, just like "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) and "impermanence" (*anityatva*). For just as a single entity—characterized by prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and non-existence after destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*)—which, having not existed, comes into being, and having existed, ceases to be, receives the designations of "produced" and "impermanent," and thereby acquires the names of "probandum" (*sādhya*) and "probans" (*sādhana*); so too here, fire and smoke are one and the same. Thus, for the purpose of demonstrating the coexistence of the properties of the probandum and the probans in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya-vṛtti*), the example of similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) is stated, with the intention of showing their connection as perceived.

Since a well-known property (*dharma*) is the means of proof (*sādhana*) and an unknown one is the object to be proven (*sādhya*), how can there be any suspicion of the fault of confusing the mark (*liṅga*) with the bearer of the mark (*liṅgin*)? For it is the single substratum (*dharmin*) alone that possesses both the state of being the mark and the state of being the bearer of the mark; smoke is not the mark, nor is fire the bearer of the mark. Furthermore, this attempt by the proponent of the relation (*sambandhavādin*) to establish an identity of form between the mark and the bearer of the mark is unjustified. What rule is there that a related entity must necessarily take on the form of its second correlate?
For a thing such as a location or fuel does not receive the designation of "probandum" or "probans" from Caitra;

Since a well-known property (*dharma*) is the means of proof (*sādhana*) and an unknown one is the object of proof (*sādhya*), how can there be any suspicion of the fault of confusing the mark (*liṅga*) with the bearer of the mark (*liṅgin*)? And this very principle stated by us is supported by the application of the example based on similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), which is well-known both in common worldly usage and in the treatises on logic (*nyāya-śāstra*).

For instance: "Where there is smoke, there is fire," or "Whatever is produced is impermanent. These are called examples based on similarity by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya-vṛtti*), for the purpose of demonstrating the coexistence of the property to be proven (*sādhya*) and the proving property (*sādhana*)—namely, fire and smoke, or being produced and impermanence—within the similar class (*sapakṣa*), whether in another location or in another object such as a jar.

Why? Because of the intention to express the logical reason (*hetu*) as being related to perception in that manner; the meaning is that what is well-known is intended to be the property of the means of proof (*sādhanadharma*), while what is not well-known is intended to be the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*).
Thus it is: *evameva bhā° nāsamanvaya° ya*.
