Regarding that which you further suspect here on the grounds of similarity—that it would follow that the mark (*liṅga*) possesses the nature of the marked (*liṅgin*), or that the marked possesses the nature of the mark—this suspicion is simply untenable. Since a well-known property (*dharma*) is the means of proof (*sādhana*) and an unknown one is the object to be proven (*sādhya*), how could there be any suspicion of the fault of confusing the mark and the marked? The meaning is that the suspicion of this specific fault in the mark is indeed impossible.

Since it is the single substratum (dharmin) itself—such as a location—that functions as both the sign (liṅga) and the signified (liṅgin), or because the signified is not a part of the sign, it follows that the substratum alone is both the sign and the signified. Consequently, fire is not the signified and smoke is not the sign; likewise, producedness and impermanence [are not related as sign and signified]. Therefore, because smoke is not a sign and fire is not the signified—and because fire is not the signified and smoke is not the sign—the two, sign and signified, would not be confused, provided that one intends to express their relationship with something other than the perceptible object.

Therefore, since one and the same [entity] functions as both the means of proof (*sādhana*) and the object to be proven (*sādhya*)—by way of the well-known property as the mark (*liṅga*) and by way of the unknown property-bearer (*dharmin*) as the marked (*liṅgin*)—the relationship between the mark and the marked is indeed established.

Furthermore, regarding this [objection] of the proponent of the relation (*sambandha*) beginning with "perceptible" (*pratyakṣa*), namely that it is illogical for the sign (*liṅga*) and the signified (*liṅgin*) to be reduced to a single form: what is this restrictive rule—that a related thing must necessarily exist in the form of its second correlate? There is no such rule, because we observe the distinction between perceptibility and imperceptibility in the case of smoke, fire, and so forth.

He demonstrates this with the words "for [in the case of] Caitra’s horse," etc.: among the seven kinds of relations, such as that between owner and owned, there is no fixed rule regarding the perceptibility or imperceptibility of the related entities, such as Caitra and his horse—namely, that if one is perceptible, the second must also necessarily be perceptible; or if one related entity, such as a horse, is perceptible, its counterpart must likewise be perceptible. This applies similarly to the relations of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), the proven and the prover (*sādhyasādhakatva*), and so forth.

If it is by way of ownership (*svatva*) and so forth, then because the property is connected to its owner and because the property is dependent upon the owner, memory at a later time would be purposeless.
If, however, it is otherwise, that has not been stated.
If it is argued that [the process] is the same regarding the apprehension of the *liṅga* (the mark), we say no; because it is not apprehended as being related [to the probandum].

First, the *liṅga* residing in the object of inference is apprehended as smoke and so forth; subsequently, its inseparable connection (*avinābhāvitva*) with fire and so forth is remembered, due to relations such as owner and owned. Therefore, what was stated—that "inference is the establishment of the remainder from one [part]"—is incorrect.

Why? Because it is observed that even for one who is unlearned, a certain cognition arises from the perception of mere invariable concomitance (*avinābhāvitva*) despite being ignorant of the specific relations of ownership and so forth;
furthermore, an ungrasped relation cannot be the cause of inference, since it functions as a means of knowledge (*jñāpaka*) by virtue of being a cause of cognition.
Furthermore, the non-deviation of the relationship between owner and owned and so forth is not necessarily universal;
therefore, inference does not arise from such a connection.
It is not logical for an inference to depend on the non-deviation of a relationship already perceived, as that would result in the relationship itself being the manifestor [of the knowledge].

In this case, there would also be the undesirable consequence of inferring smoke from fire, because the relation is no different; for the relation between fire and smoke as cause and effect is indeed indistinguishable.
However, for one who maintains that the relation intended is "inseparable concomitance" (*avinābhāvitva*), this fault does not apply.
Thus it is stated in the second chapter, on inference for oneself, in the *Pramāṇasamuccayavṛtti* (PSV1 C).

Is the apprehension of that which belongs to an owner to be grasped in the form of ownership (*svatva*) and so forth, or rather in some other form? If it were grasped in the form of ownership as "this is one's own" (*svam*), then, because the "own" is related to an owner, ownership would be untenable in the absence of an owner; since it depends upon the ascertainment of an owner, the owner must be cognized even prior to the observation of the inferential mark (*liṅga*). Otherwise, the apprehension "this is his own" would not be possible. Consequently, the subsequent recollection of the relationship would be purposeless, because the owner would have already been established, leaving no room for a "remainder" (*śeṣa*).

Since it is accepted that [the cognition] is established by the remainder as being inferential, if apprehension is instead desired through another manner—that is, in a different way—then because that has not been stated, the definition is incomplete. This applies equally to the apprehension of the mark (*liṅga*). For if the mark is apprehended by way of its inseparable connection (*avinābhāvitva*), then since that inseparable connection itself depends upon another counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), the object to be proven (*sādhya*) would have to be understood even prior to the apprehension of the mark.
And likewise, if the probandum is established as the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), the recollection of the relation is rendered purposeless;
if it is otherwise, that has not been stated—this is equal [to our position].
No, for [the text says] "of that," and so forth.
"Located in the object of inference" means that only the mere presence of smoke and so forth in the locus (*dharmin*) is apprehended, not its state of being related [to the probandum].
To the question "When, then, is that [relation] apprehended?", he says: "Subsequently," and so forth.

The meaning of "because of its comprehension by one who is unlearned" is that even one who is ignorant of the relationship between property and owner, and so forth, still attains the understanding of the remainder.

For in the case of the relationship of cause and effect, just as the relationship of cause and effect has been analyzed in the treatise, it is precisely that state of being unperceived which is intended here, and not [non-existence] in every respect; this is how it should be understood.

For in the treatise (*śāstra*), the relationship of cause and effect is established through transformation (*pariṇāma*) of a single entity itself, without its abandoning its own nature (*svarūpa*). Those who do not understand this relationship of cause and effect, however, understand it otherwise; they determine the inferable object solely from the perception of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāvitva*). Thus, the relationship of cause and effect as seen in the treatise is indeed untenable [for them].
Because if cause and effect were identical, there could not even be the distinction that "this is the effect" and "this is the cause.
Now, if there is some such excellence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvātiśaya*) belonging to those two, then the consequence of their being distinct follows;
for even in the case of [the categories] such as existence (*sattva*), it is precisely a difference in intrinsic nature that is the cause for the occurrence of different modes.

If it is argued that even though the relation of cause and effect exists, there is no difference between them because they are one due to the non-difference of the genus "the three qualities" (*traiguṇya*), we say: no. For the "three qualities" are not perceived as distinct from the cause and the effect.
Furthermore, transformation—whether successive or simultaneous—is impossible for that which is eternal.
Therefore, how could there be a distinction between cause and effect, as in the case of [your] cause? Enough of this digression.
It might be argued: "That [subject] is indeed the cause of its inference even when unperceived. To this he says: "No," and so forth, which is easy to understand.

Regarding the phrase "not necessarily," etc.: if it is asked, "Is not the establishment of one's own nature dependent solely upon ownership? Whence, then, could there be a deviation from that?"—the intention here is as follows: does the mark (*liṅga*), perceived as belonging to oneself at the very time of inference, establish the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*)? Or rather, was it determined as such at the time of grasping the relationship, yet is now perceived otherwise at the time of inference?

If, at the time of inference, that which is ascertained as "this is his own" is intended to be the indicator (*gamaka*), then the fault already mentioned applies—namely, that "ownership (*svatva*) [depends] on its relation to an owner" (p. 683, l. 31), and so forth. Therefore, the second view must be accepted; however, in that case, there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*), because a state of mutual exclusion (*vyatireka-bhāva*) between property and owner is possible [in some cases]. Thus, one cannot infer in this way: "Since this was previously grasped by the self as being his own, therefore wherever this exists, there his owner must necessarily exist."

Since perception is possible even when a king lacks wealth and so forth, or when a mere umbrella lacks its presiding owner, one should likewise assume such deviation (*vyabhicāra*) elsewhere as well, according to the circumstances.

This might be argued: "Not every relationship, such as that of owner and owned, is indicative; rather, what is it? It is where there is no deviation. To this he says: "Not for one who has perceived the relationship," and so forth.

If, even when the aforementioned relationship has been grasped, one must further depend upon whether the logical mark (liṅga) is deviant or non-deviant, then it would follow that invariable concomitance (avinābhāvitva) alone is the cause of inference, and not relationships such as ownership and owned.

If it is argued that inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) is the cause of inference, and that this occurs when the aforementioned relationship exists—therefore, [the indicator] is designated [as such]—that is incorrect. For even when that [relationship] exists, [the indicator] may be absent, since the relationship itself is undifferentiated. Since the relationship between cause and effect (*nimitta-naimittika*) resides in both members, just as it exists in one, so too does it exist in the second; thus, the capacity to indicate (*gamaka-bhāva*) would apply to both. — *Vādanyāya-ṭīkā* (VT), p. [X].
The reading "bhavitavyameva" or "bhavitavyamiti" is correctly understood [as the intended text].

For this very reason, it is improper to speak in such a manner as you do—speaking so confidently, without regard for the investigation of merits and defects, and without hesitation, asking "which [of these] is incorrect? If you ask why, we shall demonstrate that: for just as [it was said] "even though there is a duality" and so forth, up to "so here it is not," it is not like the case of two conjoined things, but rather like the relationship between a container and its contents; thus [we say] confidently.
*viśrabdha* (Y).
"That is not tenable"—to this we say it is not tenable;

for example: "Is it not the case that here, just as in that [other] instance, the relationship between the sign and the signified (liṅga-liṅgin)—such as smoke and fire—is like that between a container and its contents? The position is that the conjunction of one [the visible smoke] is not the same as the conjunction of the second [the invisible fire]; the reason (*hetu*) being 'because they are conjoined'."

The example is "like the conjunction of a post and so forth. For just as there is a conjunction between a post and a hawk—where the post is without action and the hawk is with action—and this conjunction is unequal due to their being respectively without and with action; likewise, among the conjuncts such as two wrestlers, two fingers, or space, and also among Caitra, a horse, and so on, even when characterized by being extremely dear, a vehicle, and so forth, the distinction lies solely in their being perceptible or imperceptible.
Thus, the intended meaning of the phrase "like a jar" is that it is like something perceptible.

The reading "of those connected by conjunction" (*saṃyogisaṃyoginām*) may also occur here, as in the phrase "where it has been stated regarding the grass," and so forth. Having thus interrogated the proponent of relation (*sambandhavādin*) by means of the exclusion of others (*anyāpohika*), the collection of faults that was stated is as follows: "Because of being connected to an owner, and because the thing itself depends upon its owner, memory at a later time would be purposeless."
Otherwise, it was not stated [by him],
as in *Prajñāpāramitopadeśa* (Commentary on the *Prajñāpāramitāsūtra*) 2.37.
To this we reply: nothing has been left unsaid here.

[The relationship is known] from perception regarding its correlates, and likewise from inference. If one correlate—whether as owner or owned—is perceived through the relation of ownership, then because the second correlate (either the owner or the owned) is already reached along with that first one, and because a relationship is mutually dependent, the recollection (*smṛti*) would be useless for establishing the remaining part of the relationship.
Yet, it is observed that the establishment of the remaining part occurs by the power of recollection.
Therefore, it is incorrect to say that ownership and so forth are objects of direct perception.

Now, if you think otherwise—that is, if you think that in order to avoid this fault, there must be some single perceptible relation other than those such as owner and owned, and that from the recollection of that relation inference occurs—this is not so, because that alternative has not been stated. Since it is stated [in the Sūtra] that "the relation is by way of owner and owned, etc.," it follows that some object becomes perceptible to a certain sense-faculty through the relation of owner and owned, or through the relation of material cause and modification, or the relation of cause and effect, or the relation of occasion and occasioned, or the relation of part and whole, or the relation of companion, or the relation of victim and slayer; for no relation distinct from these is mentioned, while these alone are mentioned.
Let that which was stated [by the opponent] be questioned: since it is defective,
and because the self is connected with its master, and because the self is dependent upon its master, memory at a later time would be purposeless.
Otherwise, that was not stated [in the *Prasannapadā* on the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, chapter 2,
verse 37].
To this we reply: nothing has been left unsaid here;
for that [object] is established precisely through perception related to it, and likewise through inference based on perception.
See the discussion regarding indifference on page 685, line 26;
[it is] incorrect.
Then,
from that [state], there is the binding of the stalk;
that is the connection with the Yajus.
Therefore, the reading "tataḥ sambandhaḥ" or "tatsambandhaḥ" is indeed correct here; this has been stated in the Vārṣagaṇatantrabhāṣya— see page 685, line 3, 20, note 1, and page 240, line 12.

Regarding this collection of faults stated by the opponent, we state the rebuttal: the intention is that nothing has been left unsaid here; rather, everything that was to be said has been stated in its entirety, because it leads to liberation (tāraṇāt).

But when the relationship between two related things has been perceived, why should the memory—which follows that previously perceived relationship—be useless at a time subsequent to the direct perception of one of the two, as in the case of smoke which depends upon fire? And it is with this in mind that it was said: "A certain object becomes perceptible to a certain sense organ."

Therefore, based on the object of sensory perception at present, one first apprehends the existence of an undifferentiated object through a cognition that has previously established a connection with the aggregate [of its parts], just as one previously perceives the existence of fire upon seeing smoke after having observed the connection between smoke and fire.
As for what he replies—that this is the same as the apprehension of a logical mark (*liṅga*)—that is exactly so. (Praśastapādabhāṣya-vṛtti 2.37)

I too say this: since the mark (*liṅga*) is related to that which possesses the mark (*liṅgin*), its status as a mark is dependent upon the possessor of the mark. Therefore, if the mark is apprehended, the possessor of the mark is apprehended along with it;
or else, it is not as you have stated.

For inference proceeds from a relationship characterized by the aforementioned distinctions, and because of the statement that "it [inference] arises from the perception of one thing which is related to that [other]," inference is introduced in that very manner.
He explains that [passage], beginning with "But of two related things... and continuing up to "...like smoke which depends upon fire."

Just as smoke, being perceived as a single entity, yet distinguished by specific qualities such as being thick, circular, rising upwards, and pale—which are invariably concomitant with fire—indicates fire in a nearby location because these specific qualities are invariably concomitant [with it]; and just as the horse’s specific qualities, such as its ornaments, grooming, and fondness for [certain things], which are invariably concomitant with Caitra, indicate Caitra precisely through that relationship; likewise, Caitra’s specific qualities, such as his rider, his nourisher, and his devotion to those virtues, which are invariably concomitant with the horse, certainly indicate the horse. Therefore, once the relationship has been apprehended, at a subsequent time when one of the two (the horse or Caitra) is perceived, the memory that follows from the previously apprehended relationship—namely, "wherever this one is perceived, there the other is also"—how could it possibly be useless? It is by no means useless; this is the meaning.
What is it like? It is like smoke that depends upon fire.

Just as smoke, which acquires its own existence produced by fire, when endowed with the aforementioned specific qualities, is sufficient for the inference of an unperceived related entity (*sambandhin*) through the recollection of its connection to fire; or alternatively, fire itself, being perceived, [is sufficient] because of its being a transformation of that [smoke], and because of its connection to future or past space and time, since one of the two related entities is directly perceived. Or, according to the reading "inference is the establishment of the remainder from one perceived related entity through the connection," there is the mention of a co-referential (*samānādhikaraṇa*) perceived related entity.
(Datta-pra.)

Since the relationship between two related things is perceived through their connection, why should the memory that follows from having previously perceived that relationship—which occurs after one of the two has become perceptible—be useless, as in the case of smoke which depends upon fire?
And it is with this in mind that it was said: "A certain object becomes perceptible to a certain sense organ."

Therefore, it is understood that this has been stated in the *Vārṣagaṇatantrabhāṣya*— see page 240, line 12; tippanī page 78, line 19— that by means of sensory perception, one first perceives the existence of an undifferentiated object for which a connection has previously been established with its aggregate, just as one perceives the existence of fire upon seeing smoke after having previously observed the connection between smoke and fire.
"Comparison is an object that becomes perceptible to some sense organ," according to the statement in the *Bhāṣya* (D.
edition, p. viśālā).
As for what he replies— namely, "If it is argued that [the process] is the same regarding the apprehension of the mark" (Praśastapādabhāṣya, Samuddeśa on Inference, verse 37)— that is indeed so.

I also say this: since the mark (liṅga) is related to that which possesses the mark (liṅgin), its status as a mark is dependent solely upon the liṅgin. Therefore, if the mark is apprehended, the liṅgin is apprehended along with it;
otherwise, what has been said [by you] is not the case.
See page 683, note 2.
See page 240, line 11:
*°vartalodvapāṇḍu* (Bhāṣya) / *°vartaloccapāṇḍu* (Yaśomitra).
Regarding "saṃbandhinītara," there may also be the reading "asambandhinītara" here; [regarding] "mānāvālāmagni," there may also be the reading "pra."
See the connection with the name; one proof, see page 240, line 11.

And having established this, he states that the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on this very definition—beginning with "some object is perceptible by some sense organ," etc.—is the indicator (*jñāpaka*). [The commentary uses] an interrogative pronoun expressing a general sense, up to "one understands the existence of fire.

There are two readings: *avaśiṣṭasya aviśiṣṭasya* (of the remaining and of the non-specific), or *avaśiṣṭasya viśiṣṭasya* (of the remaining and of the specific). Here, *avaśiṣṭasya* means of that which is not perceived; *aviśiṣṭasya* means of that which is equal to the time of perception, or of that which exists in the same location.
The remainder of the text has its meaning already explained;
"of the undistinguished, the undistinguished" (aviśiṣṭasyāviśiṣṭasya) according to Bhāṣya,
and "the undistinguished of the undistinguished" (aviśiṣṭasyāviśiṣṭaḥ) according to Yājñavalkya.

Regarding the phrase "aviśiṣṭasya... tulyasyātaddeśasya yattu tena" and so forth: it refers to that which is undistinguished [from others], equal, and located in a place other than that [specific locus].

Since ownership depends upon the owner because of the relationship with the owner, it follows that the subsequent recollection (of the relationship) would be purposeless; to this, [the author] replies by anticipating the opponent's view—that which excludes other possibilities (*anyāpohika*)—stating: "If it be argued that [the case] is the same regarding the apprehension of the mark (*liṅga*)," the thought might be: "The futility of recollection arises because the relationship between property and owner and so forth is directly perceived"; however, that same collection of faults applies equally here because there is no difference in the relationship between the mark and the bearer of the mark (*liṅgin*). That is indeed so; if this fault were to apply to the state of being property and owner, it would certainly apply to the mark as well, because the mark and the bearer of the mark are mutually dependent.

Now, if it is not accepted there [in the case of the self], then let it not be accepted even in the case of owner and owned and so forth; thus it is well said: "I too say this—why? Because that which is called the 'inferential mark' (liṅga) is not grasped as having a relationship [to the subject]. First, the inferential mark residing in the object of inference is grasped as smoke and so forth, and afterwards its invariable concomitance with fire and so forth is remembered" (Pramāṇasamuccayavṛtti 2.37).

In this case as well, the principle is the same: first one perceives one's own [property] residing in the object of inference (*anumeya*), and subsequently one remembers Caitra—who resides therein—as being invariably concomitant (*avinābhāvī*), but not as being connected to that specific location. This is just like fire and smoke situated in a particular place and so forth.

As for what was stated—that "inference is the establishment of the remainder (*śeṣasiddhi*) through relations such as owner and owned"—this is incorrect; why? Because even one who is unlearned (*avyutpanna*) can grasp that [relation].

It is argued that even for those ignorant of specific relations such as that between owner and owned, there is a certain determination [of the object] based on the perception of mere inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāvitva*); furthermore, an ungrasped relation cannot be the cause of inference, because it is a cognizer (*jñāpaka*) by virtue of being a cause of cognition (Pramāṇasamuccayavṛtti 2.37).

This is incorrect, because inseparable concomitance is a relation consisting of co-occurrence (*sahacaribhāva*); therefore, any certainty derived from that also belongs only to those who are conversant with the meanings of "owner" and so forth, since co-occurrence is preceded by such [specific relations].

The passage beginning with "sambādhitvā liṅgasya" and so forth, which demonstrates their equivalence, has already been explained up to the point where it says "the possessor of the mark (liṅgin) is grasped. Now, as for the statement "otherwise, that was not said": just as you challenge [us] by saying that if there is no grasping [of things] as master and so forth, then there is a grasping otherwise, and thus "that was not said," so too do we challenge you—if you think that the grasping of the mark (liṅga) is one way and the grasping of the self, the master, and so forth is another way, then "that was not said. This is the comparison (pṛ. 684, l. 1).
Because it is equal in its state of being grasped,
he speaks here and there.
As for what is said— "No, because it is not apprehended as a relatum;

first, the mark residing in the object of inference is apprehended as smoke and so forth, and subsequently its invariable concomitance with fire and so forth is remembered" (Pramāṇasamuccayavṛtti 2.37)— [that is incorrect].

This is the same here as well: first, one's own [liṅga] residing in the object of inference (anumeya) is perceived; subsequently, Caitra—who resides therein—is remembered as being invariably concomitant (*avinābhāvī*), but not as being connected to that specific place. This should be seen as being like fire and smoke situated in a particular location, etc. (see p. 683, note 2).

As for what was stated—that "inference is the establishment of the remainder (*śeṣasiddhi*) through relations such as owner and owned"—this is incorrect. Why? Because even one who is unlearned (avyutpanna) attains that [knowledge].

A certainty [of the relationship] is observed even by those ignorant of specific relations such as that between owner and owned, because it is apprehended merely through invariable concomitance (*avinābhāvitva*). Furthermore, an unapprehended relation is not the cause of inference, because as a cause of cognition, it functions as a signifier (*jñāpaka*); see *Pramāṇasamuccayavṛtti* 2.37, p.
683, note 2.

This is incorrect, because inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāvitva*) is a relationship of coexistence (*sahacaribhāva*); therefore, even the certainty derived from that occurs only for those who have mastered the meanings of terms such as "owner" (*svāmin*), since coexistence begins with such [relationships]. [Tulanā—page 684, line 1] Regarding what you say—"Do not think that it is the same in the apprehension of the mark (*liṅga*); for there is a distinction in the case of the mark"—no, because it is not apprehended as being a related entity (*sambandhin*).

For a logical mark (*liṅga*) is not apprehended merely by its state of being related; what then? First, it is apprehended as smoke and so forth, residing in the place where the object of inference is located; subsequently, its invariable concomitance (*avinābhāvitva*) with fire and so forth is remembered. By the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), it is shown that first there is the apprehension of sound as being produced and so on, and subsequently its invariable concomitance with impermanence is remembered; thus it pervades all cases. To this it is replied: "That is equal here as well," and so forth—the cultivation of that equality begins with "residing in the object of inference" and extends up to "not related to that place," the meaning of which has already been explained.

The example is "like smoke situated in a place such as a region [which indicates] fire. Just as smoke, which has not yet become fire, is first perceived while situated in a place such as a region—being perceptible because it is distinct from the imperceptible fire—and subsequently one remembers, "Fire is here," so too a horse, which is distinct from Caitra, is perceived while situated in a village or similar location; thereafter, one remembers that Caitra, who is present there, is invariably concomitant with it, just like the remembrance of fire connected with smoke in the thought "Fire is here. Thus, the grasping is equal, and the state [of the object] is equal.

Regarding what was stated in the section on perception (*pratyakṣa*), beginning with "As for that which has been said," etc., he pointed out a flaw in the definition: "Inference is the establishment of the remainder through a connection based on relations such as owner and owned. To this, we say: this is incorrect.

Why? Because it is said, "because that [inference] is understood by one who is unlearned," and so forth; this restatement of his [the opponent's] view continues up to the point where it says, "because it is a means of cognition. Even those ignorant of relations such as owner and owned are seen to ascertain fire from smoke due to the relation of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*). And let it not be argued that this is not a certain cognition because the relation has not been grasped; for a probans (*hetu*), such as a logical mark (*liṅga*), functions as a cause of knowledge only when its own nature has been grasped, unlike a productive seed or similar causes.
*Note: The text contains scribal variants: *saṃbaṃdhātvānni॰bhā॰* (variant) and *॰jāditibhā॰* (variant).*
This is incorrect;

why? Because inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāvitva*) is a relationship of coexistence (*sahacaribhāva*). "Not existing without" (*na vinā bhavati*), "existing together" (*saha bhavati*), and "moving together" (*saha carati*) have one and the same meaning.

Therefore, the certainty that arises from this relationship of coexistence occurs only for those who are proficient in the meanings of terms such as "ownership" (*svāmin*), and not for those who are unproficient.

Why? Because of its being the first among those [relations], namely, because it is the primary relation such as that between owner and owned; for, since the seven types of relations have as their objects meanings distinct from what is understood through inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), inference is observed even without the relation of coexistence (*sahacaribhāva*) in one whose intellect is already proficient in relations such as that between owner and owned.

For example: the crow’s nest, the time of its laying eggs, the building of the nest by the crow, the hatching of the eggs, their growth, their nourishment, the crowlings of the fledglings, and the fledglings’ following after the female crow—none of these are causes for the cognition that they are cuckoos, even though they possess a pervasive and inseparable nature. Rather, because the relationship of owner and owned is not immediately perceived, the realization occurs later through that relationship: "This is a cuckoo fledgling, because it is endowed with its specific song, like other cuckoos."

Thus, relations such as that between property and owner are indicators, because they are perceived in that manner at the time of the object to be inferred; for they are of the same nature as well-known logical marks (*liṅga*).

Furthermore, that concomitance (*sahacaribhāva*), which is inseparable presence (*avinābhāva*), is the cause of inference only when it is being apprehended, since a means of cognition (*jñāpaka*) functions as the cause for the arising of knowledge regarding what is already known.

Therefore, the knowledge of the relationship of inseparable concomitance (avinābhāva), which includes [relationships such as] that of owner and owned, belongs only to those who are proficient [in logic], not to those who are unproficient;
see *Sahacārin*, p. 696, l. 16.
The meaning is "he moves," because it is connected with the state of being accompanied,
due to its relation to the master and so forth, as the state of being accompanied [is established].

However, inference is observed to have as its object a meaning distinct from that which is accessible through invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), even in the absence of coexistence (*sahacaribhāva*), provided there is an understanding of relationships such as owner and owned;

for example: the crow’s dwelling, its acceptance [of the nest], the time of its laying, its building of the nest, the hatching of eggs, their growth, nourishment, its accompanying the fledglings, and its following behind the female crow—these are not the causes for the cognition of "cuckoo-ness," because even though these possess the nature of being pervasive and invariably concomitant, one recognizes the relationship of owner and owned from afar.
Subsequently, the cognition of that [relationship] occurs through the connection between property and owner: "This is a cuckoo chick, because it is endowed with its specific cry, like other cuckoos.

Thus, connections such as those between property and owner are inferential indicators (*anumāpaka*), because they are perceived in that manner at the time of the individual instance to be inferred (*anumeya-vyakti*), just like a well-known logical mark (*liṅga*). This is the cause of inference.
It is known that [inference] arises from knowledge;

or rather, even without the relation of inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāvitva*), it is considered an inference because of the established relationship of owner and owned, and so forth. To this he says: "But by virtue of having as its object a meaning distinct from what is cognized through inseparable concomitance," and so on, up to "like another cuckoo. This is the conclusion by means of the proof.
That which is the pervader (*vyāpaka*) of this meaning is the very part to be grasped (*grāhya*), while the pervaded (*vyāpya*) is the indicator (*sūcaka*).
The possessor of manifold dharmas is not other than the dharma of the grasped and the grasper.

Thus, by way of the reversal of these characteristics, inference is observed even in the absence of concomitance (*sahacaribhāva*), provided there is an understanding of relationships such as owner and owned; for example, in the compound series beginning with "the birthplace of the crow" (*kākabhavana*), which demonstrates concomitance through both pervasion (*vyāpaka*) and being pervaded (*vyāpya*). Even when there is the state of being endowed with the nature of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), these factors—the birth from the crow, its pervasive presence, the time of its acceptance, the laying of the nest, the hatching of the egg, its growth, its nourishment by the male and female crows out of affection, its wandering with a second crow chick, and its following behind the female crow—are all preceding states that are pervasive and to be proven (*sādhya*), while the succeeding ones are pervaded and intended as the means of proof (*sādhaka*). Nevertheless, although these other properties exist in a relationship of invariable concomitance, they are not the causes for the cognition of it being a *kokila* (cuckoo).

Why is this so? Because of the immediate recognition of the relationship between owner and owned: as long as one does not perceive the connection between owner and owned, there is no cognition of "cuckoo-ness"; subsequently, that cognition arises through the relation of owner and owned. Thereafter, people in the world—both those who perceive and those who speak—set aside those various properties considered to be invariably concomitant (whether pervaders or pervaded) and infer, "This is a cuckoo chick, not a crow chick," because it is endowed with its specific nature and possesses a voice characterized by a particular sweetness, just like other cuckoos.

By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (ādi), it is meant that just like the relationship between owner and owned, other relationships such as that between material cause and modification (prakṛti-vikāra) are also causes for inference only for those who are linguistically proficient (*vyutpanna*).
That which is the pervader (*vyāpaka*), such as ownership (*svāmitva*) and so forth, is the part to be grasped; however, the pervaded (*vyāpya*) is the indicator (*sūcaka*).
Is it not the case that for those possessing manifold dharmas, there is no other [entity] apart from the dharmas of the grasped and the grasper,
which pervades the birth of the crow?
Or rather, do they pervade the birth of the crow?
The distinction between the production and the wool [is] the manifestation;
the cognitions [are] the objects.
Page 687, line 1.

Therefore, the means of proof (*sādhana*) for the collective sense is stated here: why are these relations, such as owner and owned, inferential in this manner according to the logic already explained? Because they are perceived in that same way at the time of the manifestation of the object to be inferred (*anumeya*), since the object to be inferred—such as fire, the cuckoo, or impermanence—is perceived by that very same mode of owner and owned at the time of its manifestation.

What is it like? It is like a well-known inferential mark (*liṅga*). A well-known inferential mark, such as smoke and the like, in its respective manner, leads to the inference of its related object, such as fire and the like, precisely because of the relationship between them—such as that of property and owner—and just as a cuckoo chick [is recognized] by its cry which imitates those of its own kind. As for what was also said: "And it is not necessarily the case that there is an invariable concomitance (*avyabhicāra*) of property, owner, and so forth everywhere; therefore, inference does not arise from such a relationship. [This is refuted by the following: Even in the case of a property and its owner, there is indeed an invariable concomitance, because they are related through the relationship of being the basis (*āśraya*) and that which is based upon it (*āśrita*), or through the relationship of cause and effect. For example, Devadatta is the owner of his house because he is its maker, and the house is his property because it is the result of his action. Furthermore, since the relationship between the cuckoo chick and its species is established through the relationship of cause and effect, the inference of the species from the chick is valid. Therefore, the aforementioned objection—that inference does not occur due to the lack of invariable concomitance—is not tenable. Thus, the inference of the self (*ātman*) from the body and other such things is established. Consequently, the claim that the self is non-existent because it is not perceived is also rejected. This concludes the section on the refutation of the non-existence of the self. Now follows the section on the refutation of the view that the self is eternal. To begin with, the following objection is raised: "The self is eternal, because it is imperceptible, like space (*ākāśa*). This is not correct, because the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). For instance, the universal (*sāmānya*) is imperceptible yet is not eternal. Therefore, the argument is fallacious. Furthermore, if the self were eternal, it would follow that it is inactive, because it is devoid of the qualities of motion (*karma-guṇa*). Alternatively, if it were active, it would follow that it is non-eternal, because it possesses the quality of motion. Moreover, if the self were eternal, it would follow that it is not an agent, because it is devoid of the quality of motion. Or, if it were an agent, it would follow that it is non-eternal, because it possesses the quality of motion. Therefore, the self is not eternal. This concludes the section on the refutation of the eternity of the self. Now follows the section on the refutation of the view that the self is a single entity. To begin with, the following objection is raised: "The self is one, because it is all-pervading, like space. This is not correct, because the reason is inconclusive. For instance, universals such as "existence" (*sat-tva*) are all-pervading yet are not unitary. Therefore, the argument is fallacious. Furthermore, if the self were one, it would follow that it is not an enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*), because it is devoid of pleasure and pain. Or, if it were an enjoyer, it would follow that it is manifold, because it possesses pleasure and pain. Moreover, if the self were one, it would follow that it is not an agent, because it is devoid of pleasure and pain. Or, if it were an agent, it would follow that it is manifold, because it possesses pleasure and pain. Therefore, the self is not one. This concludes the section on the refutation of the unity of the self. Now follows the section on the refutation of the view that the self is of the nature of consciousness (*caitanya-rūpa*). To begin with, the following objection is raised: "The self is of the nature of consciousness, because it is conscious, like the individual soul (*puruṣa*). This is not correct, because the reason is inconclusive. For instance, pleasure and the like are conscious yet are not of the nature of consciousness. Therefore, the argument is fallacious. Furthermore, if the self were of the nature of consciousness, it would follow that it is not an agent, because it is devoid of the qualities of motion. Or, if it were an agent, it would follow that it is not of the nature of consciousness, because it possesses the quality of motion. Moreover, if the self were of the nature of consciousness, it would follow that it is not an enjoyer, because it is devoid of the qualities of motion. Or, if it were an enjoyer, it would follow that it is not of the nature of consciousness, because it possesses the quality of motion. Therefore, the self is not of the nature of consciousness. This concludes the section on the refutation of the view that the self is of the nature of consciousness. Now follows the section on the refutation of the view that the self is momentary (*kṣaṇika*). To begin with, the following objection is raised: "The self is momentary, because it is a thing (*vastu*), like a lamp-flame. This is not correct, because the reason is inconclusive. For instance, space is a thing yet is not momentary. Therefore, the argument is fallacious. Furthermore, if the self were momentary, it would follow that it is not an agent, because it does not persist. Or, if it were an agent, it would follow that it is not momentary, because it persists. Moreover, if the self were momentary, it would follow that it is not an enjoyer, because it does not persist. Or, if it were an enjoyer, it would follow that it is not momentary, because it persists. Therefore, the self is not momentary. This concludes the section on the refutation of the view that the self is momentary. Now follows the section on the refutation of the view that the self is of the nature of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha-rūpa*). To begin with, the following objection is raised: "The self is of the nature of the five aggregates, because it is the locus of the aggregates, like a jar. This is not correct, because the reason is inconclusive. For instance, the universal "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) is the locus of substances yet is not of the nature of the five aggregates. Therefore, the argument is fallacious. Furthermore, if the self were of the nature of the five aggregates, it would follow that it is non-eternal, because the five aggregates are non-eternal. Or, if it were eternal, it would follow that it is not of the nature of the five aggregates, because the five aggregates are non-eternal. Moreover, if the self were of the nature of the five aggregates, it would follow that it is not a single entity, because the five aggregates are manifold. Or, if it were a single entity, it would follow that it is not of the nature of the five aggregates, because the five aggregates are manifold. Therefore, the self is not of the nature of the five aggregates. This concludes the section on the refutation of the view that the self is of the nature of the five aggregates. Now follows the section on the refutation of the view that the self is of the nature of the six elements (*ṣaḍ-dhātu-rūpa*). To begin with, the following objection is raised: "The self is of the nature of the six elements, because it is the substratum of the elements, like the earth. This is not correct, because the reason is inconclusive. For instance, the universal "earth-ness" (*pṛthivītva*) is the substratum of earth yet is not of the nature of the six elements. Therefore, the argument is fallacious. Furthermore, if the self were of the nature of the six elements, it would follow that it is non-eternal, because the six elements are non-eternal. Or, if it were eternal, it would follow that it is not of the nature of the six elements, because the six elements are non-eternal. Moreover, if the self were of the nature of the six elements, it would follow that it is not a single entity, because the six elements are manifold. Or, if it were a single entity, it would follow that it is not of the nature of the six elements, because the six elements are manifold. Therefore, the self is not of the nature of the six elements. This concludes the section on the refutation of the view that the self is of the nature of the six elements. Now follows the section on the refutation of the view that the self is of the nature of the eighteen bases (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu-rūpa*). To begin with, the following objection is raised: "The self is of the nature of the eighteen bases, because it is the substratum of the bases, like the eye. This is not correct, because the reason is inconclusive. For instance, the universal "eye-ness" (*cakṣustva*) is the substratum of the eye yet is not of the nature of the eighteen bases. Therefore, the argument is fallacious. Furthermore, if the self were of the nature of the eighteen bases, it would follow that it is non-eternal, because the eighteen bases are non-eternal. Or, if it

"It is not logical for one who has already apprehended the relationship to have an inference that further depends on non-deviation, because that [non-deviation] would then result in being merely a manifestor" (*Pramāṇasamuccayavṛtti* 2.37).
This too is not correct, because by the expression "establishment of the remainder" (*śeṣasiddhi*), the operation of a rule regarding non-deviating [reasons] is already included;
for this [text] prescribes the inference of the relationship by way of excluding all fallacious appearances.

The subject (*pakṣa*), defined as the aggregate of the property and the property-bearer, which is to be inferred through a connection other than perception and whose object is not contradicted by perception and so forth, is understood by this statement regarding the "establishment of the remainder" (*śeṣasiddhi*) as being entirely free from defects.

From one [probans]—whether it be a perceived connection or something well-known like perception—there arises, through its relation to the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), the establishment of the remainder by means of the remainder; thus, by the very mention of the "establishment of the remainder," the contradictory (*viruddha*) and the over-exclusive (*asādhāraṇa*) reasons are excluded.

Furthermore, the inclusion of the word "establishment" (*siddhi*) is intended to ensure that there be no non-establishment (*asiddhi*), as would occur in the case of a common inconclusive (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*) reason.
Non-establishment [of the reason] consists in its having a deviant property (*vyabhicāridharmatā*), such as, for example, the alteration of Caitra despite there being no gift from his owner.
...the comparison is like that for an exceedingly beloved son— page 683,
note 2; furthermore, the statement beginning with "as for what was said," etc., is a refutation of the faults asserted by the proponent of relation (*sambandhavādin*).

Regarding the passage beginning with "And not necessarily," etc., what is being stated is this: inference does not arise from a relationship such as that between owner and owned, because it requires a specific qualification (*viśeṣa*) for the sake of non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*). Even when the owned object (the horse) or the owner (Caitra) is perceived, there is still a requirement for their absolute non-separation while living independently; these alone are required because they are non-deviant, and thus they would be the true inferential indicators (*anumāpaka*). The relationship of owner and owned is deviant, because even when it exists, inference does not occur.

Having thus restated [the objection], the Teacher replies: "This too is not [correct], because by the expression 'establishment of the remainder' (śeṣasiddhi), the occurrence of a non-deviant positive concomitance (vidhivṛtti) is already included. In this definition of inference for oneself—'Inference is the establishment of the remainder from one [thing] that is perceived through a relation'—by the expression 'establishment of the remainder,' the occurrence of a non-deviant positive concomitance is indeed included; therefore, this is not a fault. [The text fragment] "...is the means of knowledge... ends with the separation... [is corrupt].

If it is asked how this practice (*cāravidhi*) is to be cultivated, it is said: for all fallacies of the thesis (*pakṣa*), the reason (*hetu*), and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*)— beginning with the phrase "by the exclusion of all appearances" (*sarvābhāsavyudāsena*) and so forth— are sublated by that very method of inferring the relationship (*sambandhānumānavidhāna*).

The "remainder" (*śeṣa*) refers to that which is other than perception and the rest; it is a related entity (*sambandhin*) such as a location and so forth, being qualified by [the probans] "possessing sweetness" (*svādimat*) and the like. This related entity is the object of inference (*anumeya*). It is connected with the various types of fallacious inferences (*anumānābhāsa*) through contradictions with perception and so forth. The "thesis" (*pakṣa*), known as the aggregate of the property (*dharma*) and the property-bearer (*dharmin*), whose meaning is not contradicted [by valid means of knowledge], is what will be described later as "the statement of the probandum" (*sādhyābhidhāna*) in the context of the formulation of the members (*avayava*) of inference-for-others (*parārthānumāna*) called *vīta*. By this statement regarding the establishment of the remainder (*śeṣasiddhi*), that very thesis—being free from defects—is here grasped.

In accordance with the specific application, because of the connection through various relations—such as that of owner and owned, cause and effect, and so forth—with what is perceived (*pratyakṣa*), that is, with what is established through the perception of *dharma* (the property); therein, that which is perceived is the "property of the subject" (*pakṣadharma*), while the remainder is the object to be inferred (*anumeya*).

If it is argued that [the reason] is non-pervasive because being a product (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth is not perceived, to this he says: "Or like perception" (*pratyakṣavat*). Like perception, it is well-known (*prasiddha*); therefore, because it is well-known, the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) which is related—namely, the horse as its own—is established through the remainder (*śeṣa*) by means of the relation of that property of the subject, which was previously perceived and is now being recollected. Precisely from the statement of the "establishment of the remainder," there is the exclusion of contradictory and uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*) properties. Since wherever there is the horse as owner, there is Devadatta as the master, it is connected with a relation of absolute non-separation; thus, it exists in the similar class (*sapakṣa*). How could it exist only in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*)? Because the establishment is achieved merely by one relation, such as perception, for the sake of the remainder or in the remainder, the word "establishment" (*siddhi*) is used to ensure that it is indeed an establishment and not a non-establishment, so that it does not become a non-establishment like the common inconclusive (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*) reason, such as "eternal because knowable" (*prameyatvāt*).

What, then, is non-establishment (*asiddhi*)? It is the state of having a deviant property (*vyabhicāridharmatā*), such as: "the absence of a transfer by the owner," and so forth, up to "like the death of a very beloved son," which refers to the transformation/death of Caitra.
The remainder has its meaning already explained. anumevaunumā bhā;
anumevānumā ya.
In that very context, it says "the body" (*kāya*).
Alternatively, some say as follows: the word "perception" (*pratyakṣa*) in the phrase "from one perception" is an indicator of what is well-known;

thus, the meaning is "from what is well-known through perception. Consequently, even for another cognition whose object is a mark (*liṅga*), the designation "perception" occurs because it is the effect of perception.
— Viśālāmalavatī, P. ed., folios 135b–136a.
Thus, even by means of excluding specific instances of deviation, that very related entity (*sambandhin*) is the indicator (*gamaka*) of another related entity;
those specific features (*viśeṣa*) are not the indicators, because they serve only to support that [relation].

For smoke does not possess the quality of being a manifestor of fire merely by the exclusion of its association with a whirlwind; for indeed, jars, cloths, and so forth are likewise excluded from being whirlwinds. Smoke is not a cognizer of fire in that same way as a jar or a cloth is not, nor can the absence of a whirlwind be the manifestor of fire.
Rather, it is precisely the state of being smoke—existing only when the state of being a non-smoke (such as a jar or cloth) is absent—that serves as the manifestor of the state of being fire.

Likewise, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is stated for the purpose of demonstrating that the property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*), whose connection with impermanence has been perceived, does not deviate from impermanence;
for if inference were not dependent on the non-deviation of that which has had its connection perceived, there would be no statement of negative concomitance,
nor would it result in the manifestation of that very [connection].

And thus, it is logical that there is an inference based on the non-deviation of "producedness" (kṛtakatva), whose connection with impermanence has been perceived; for it is precisely this—such as smoke or a horse—that, by excluding specific instances of deviation, becomes the indicator (*gamaka*) of another related entity, namely the second related object which is perceptible and inferable, because it possesses the status of being related to that other related entity.

Those specific features (viśeṣas) are neither to be excluded nor to be enjoined as indicators [of fire], because they serve only to support that [essential nature]. For instance, the manifestation of smoke is not due to the exclusion of the possibility of a whirlwind (vātyā), such that one might say, "A whirlwind is not smoke; this is not a whirlwind, therefore it is smoke. Once the whirlwind has been ruled out, smoke does not become an indicator of fire merely by the exclusion of that which is not seen there. This is because there are many things other than whirlwinds, such as pots and cloths; smoke is not a non-indicator of fire simply because of those. Nor can a "non-whirlwind" be an indicator of fire, provided that the pot, cloth, and so forth are not themselves smoke. What then? It is precisely the state of being smoke (*dhūmatā*)—existing as related to the state of being fire (*vahnitā*)—that manifests its correlate through its own relation to it.

Therefore, because of the statement regarding the establishment of the remainder (*śeṣasiddhi*), inference based on the relation— whose suspicion of deviation has been removed by the two qualifiers "perceptible" (*pratyakṣa*) and "identical" (*eka*)— is itself [the means of knowledge] that excludes all fallacious appearances;
it establishes the non-manifestation of fire when smoke is not manifest.
...that [is] the name of Agni;
indeed, it is like a great wind, indeed, it is like a great wind. (Bhāṣya)
The positive form of "smokiness" alone is the indicator, not the absence of "non-smokiness.
For even if a pot or a cloth lacks the non-smokiness found in a whirlwind and the like, they are not seen to indicate fire;
therefore, the intention is that smokiness alone is the indicator.

If this intention is not acceptable, then one should instead adopt the reading: "Or else, 'it does not blow' [is] the manifestor (*vyañjaka*), which ought to be the indicator (*gamaka*) of fire, even though jars, cloths, and so forth lack the state of being smoke. [Variant readings:
*°nyāṃ vyañjaketi* in Bhāṣya;
*°nyāṃ vyañjakateti* in Yaśomitra.]

Furthermore, you yourself accept this: that only a well-known related thing can be the indicator of an unknown related thing, and that the exclusion of specific deviant instances is stated for the purpose of determining the essential nature of non-deviation. Therefore, in order to demonstrate that, he says: "In the same way, of the state of being produced," and so forth.

"Sound is impermanent because it is produced; whatever is produced is impermanent"—having thus demonstrated this by means of a positive rule (*vidhi*) regarding the relationship [between the reason and the probandum], the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is stated as "whatever is not impermanent is not produced," for the purpose of demonstrating that the state of being produced does not deviate from impermanence. If inference were not required for the sake of the non-deviation of a relationship already perceived, then the statement of the negative concomitance would not serve to support the presence of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and its necessary connection with the probandum (*sādhyānugati*); yet such a function is observed, nor does it result in the negative concomitance itself becoming merely a manifestor (*abhivyañjaka*) of that [relationship].

And thus, acting in this manner according to our own logic, it is correct that there is an inference based on the expectation of non-deviation (avyabhicāra) regarding the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*), whose connection with impermanence has been perceived; but it is not so according to your view. Why? Because of the manifestation of its very power as a manifestor (*abhivyañjakatvavyakteḥ*). That aforementioned non-deviation manifests the manifesting power of that very property residing in the subject (*pakṣadharma*); it does not itself move out of compassion [to provide the inference]. It is the same here as well, because of the manifestation of its manifesting power.

Likewise here as well, the example of Caitra’s horse is for the purpose of illustrating the relationship between owner and owned; it applies to cases such as fire and smoke, or impermanence and being produced, because that [relationship] exists there just as it did previously.
But if this is so, is this not merely a description of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*)?

It is exactly so; for, because the distinction between the locus and the located, as well as the conjoined, has been excluded from what you have stated due to the non-difference of their occurrence (*vṛtti*), whereas that which we have set forth is prior, the nature of inference—which you claim to know—is actually known by me.
As you have said, this is merely an exposition of a single part of the relationship of inference, because it does not exceed its meaning, just like the commentary on the rule *vṛddhir ādaic*.

And thus, one applies the similarity [of the subject] to that which is non-existent in terms of its substantial reality (*dravyārtha*), as in the case of "Caitra’s horse" and so forth. Furthermore, the example of Caitra’s horse mentioned here in the *Anumānalakṣaṇabhāṣya* is for the purpose of illustrating the relationship between owner and owned; for the same logic applies to cases such as fire and smoke, or impermanence and being produced. In this context, the phrase "that is here" refers to the property (*dharma*)—such as fire, Caitra, or impermanence—which is not directly perceived. "Here" refers to the location where the probandum is understood from the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), such as smoke, a horse, or being produced, which are directly perceived. Thus, the object to be proven (*sādhyārtha*) is the subject (*pakṣa*).

In the same way, the reason is "because of existence in that which possesses it" (*tadvatsattvāt*). That [reason] is "possessing it" (*tadvān*) because the relationship—such as fire, Caitra, or the word [itself]—exists in this [subject], namely smoke, the horse, or the property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*), and so forth. Since that very property exists, it is "because of existence in that which possesses it. Wherever there is existence in that which possesses it, there that [property] exists, as before; just as in the previous case, smoke and so forth belong exclusively to their owner due to their connection with fire and so forth, so it is here as well. The example of Caitra and the horse is for the purpose of illustrating such cases; thus, the indicator (*gamaka*) is non-deviant (*avyabhicārin*).
Would there not be a request for [the cause] itself? Does it manifest by itself?
Because of the manifestation of its nature as a manifester.

Likewise here as well, the example of Caitra’s horse is for the purpose of illustrating the relationship between owner and owned; it applies here to cases such as fire and smoke, or impermanence and being produced, because that [relationship] exists there just as it does in the previous case.
But if this is so, is this not merely a description of inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*)?

It is exactly so; because your statement has been refuted due to the non-difference of its occurrence—like the relationship between a substratum and that which is contained therein—and because what was stated by us is prior, you did not understand the true nature of inference which I have understood.

As you have said, this is merely an exposition of a single part of the inference of a relation, since it does not possess a meaning distinct from that [relation], just like the commentary on the rule "vṛddhir ādaic" [Pāṇini 1.1.1].
And thus, where [the text] reads *dravyārthāsatya*, it should read *pratyakṣo*; and where it reads *ityatra pratyakṣo*, it should read *ityatrāpratyakṣo*.
And that [inference] is preceded by the perception of smoke and so forth in this case.

Regarding this, here [the opponent] says: "But surely, this is merely a description of inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*). Indeed, such a relationship of inseparable concomitance is precisely what I desire, because inference consists in the requirement for non-deviation."

To this it is replied: We too say—this is exactly so. Why is there inference from the relationship of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) through conceptual distinctions such as "self" and "possessor"? Because there is no difference in the mode of subsistence (*vṛtti*), being like that of the locus and the located, and like that of things joined by conjunction; for there is no difference between the mode of subsistence as locus and located, and the mode of subsistence as things joined by conjunction. As for what you said—"its mode of subsistence is like that of the locus and located, but not like that of things joined by conjunction"—that has already been refuted.

Furthermore, because [the system] was taught by us earlier—since the *tantra* of Kapila predates Dignāga, Vasubandhu, and others, as well as the Buddha—and because it follows the doctrine of a specific school of the Ārhata, its inference is merely dependent upon our own view; yet you did not realize this, thinking, "I have understood the nature of inference," whereas it is actually my own view that has been brought forth.
(pra-bhāvopavarṇana)

The explanation of that [is as follows]: the position is that this [work] consisting of "yathā tvam" and so forth is merely a commentary (*bhāṣyamātra*). This definition, which constitutes a single part of the inference of relationship (*sambandhānumāna*), is merely a commentary whose fruit is your own effort, because its meaning does not exceed that [inference]. Whatever is an explanation whose meaning does not exceed something else is merely a commentary on a single part of that [thing], just as [the rule] "this is the technical name *vṛddhi*; it consists of the vowels *ā*, *ai*, and *au*" (Pāṇini 1.1.1), followed by "the section on technical names (*saṃjñādhikāra*) is for the purpose of making the technical names understood," and so forth.

The intention is that this exposition of yours regarding the relationship of inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) is merely a commentary on a portion of the theory of inference based on relationship known to us; furthermore, even all of that is not fully understood.
Moreover, the intention is that even the Sāṃkhya system is indeed our own invention, as it is but a partial aspect of the conceptualization of the substantial entity (*dravyārtha*).

Therefore, he says: "And thus, you have granted the explanation that while the substance-aspect (*dravyārtha*) is unreal, the adjunct (*upādhi*) is real; for by stating that 'the meaning of a word is a particular qualified by a universal,' you have also granted the substance-aspect. Indeed, there is no fault whatsoever in the sign (liṅga) being the possessor of the sign (liṅgin), or in the possessor of the sign being the sign, because of the difference in intention (*vivakṣā*). This is because, according to the respective intentions, they function as the signified (*gamya*) and the signifier (*gamaka*) in the relationship of property (*sva*) and owner (*svāmin*), and so forth. At times, either the property or the owner may be intended as the signified or the signifier; thus, whichever one is intended is seen to possess the status of the signified or the signifier according to that intention. For example, consider the illustration of Devadatta and others: at a certain time, Devadatta is joined with Yajñadatta through a particular action, or Yajñadatta is joined with Devadatta. Due to the force of intention, the status of being the sign and the possessor of the sign belongs to these two alternately. Or, because the conjunction arises from the actions of both simultaneously, it occurs at once. It is the same in the case of property, owner, and so forth.
