See the Ājapeya-prakaraṇa; for its cause, see page 695, line 15.

To this, he says: No; because [the relation of] being conjoined (*saṃyogitva*) is of a single nature, etc., it is not intended to lead to an undesirable consequence by thinking that smoke is not conjoined with fire either before or after it, nor that smoke belongs to fire alone. What then? Since smoke exists at that very time—the very time of perceiving the fire—this undesirable consequence, namely the contingency of a confusion (*vyatikara*), certainly follows.
(Note: *svarūpatvāt* is the reading in manuscript *ya*).

Regarding this [objection] that "this is not so," it is replied: No, because it is impossible. It does not follow that smoke is the mark (*liṅga*) of fire simply because there is no difference in their relationship; rather, smoke is not the probandum (*sādhya*), but the means of proof (*sādhana*), because it is perceptible (*pratyakṣa*); whereas fire is the probandum because it is imperceptible and thus inferable, and therefore it is not the means of proof.
If smoke were also the probandum, then perception would be an invalid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*); and if perception were invalid, inference would be rootless (*nirbījā*).

Furthermore, the imitation of others using the corrupt term "anumiti" would constitute a fault; moreover, because the inference [of fire] would possess a single form through conjunction, there is the undesirable consequence (aniṣṭāpādana) that smoke could be inferred even from fire. This proof of yours, which establishes an unintended point, is intended to demonstrate that very proof—namely, the undesirable consequence beginning with "saṃyogitva," the meaning of which has already been explained.
Because of this, [it follows that] truth is a specific type of bondage.

Regarding what was stated by you—beginning with "Furthermore, this... and so forth—in order to demonstrate the absence of faults in our own position, namely the passage beginning with "That which has an inseparable connection (*avinābhāvitva*) with the foremost [elements]... and so on: [this is not a fault].

Having spoken thus, that which is further stated by the one who is confused regarding the direction of the *nyāya*— namely, that there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of inferring smoke even from fire— that is [refuted].

Having stated here that [the object] is to be established by location, it must be explained as follows regarding the operation of determining the reality of the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*) and the mark (*liṅga*): there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of inferring fire from smoke, even though [fire] possesses smoke;
for in both cases, the meaning of the possessive suffix (*matup*) occurs in exactly the same way as in the desired instance.
In the case of smoke as an object, this very [objection] would apply;
however, here there is not even a scent of a fault,

for it is logical that "possessing smoke" (*dhūmavattva*) is the probans (*liṅga*), while the state of being the probandum (*liṅgitva*) belongs to the location itself as qualified by "possessing fire," when that location is intended to be expressed.
For it is not logical for "possessing fire" (*agnimattva*) to function as a logical mark (*liṅga*), because it is itself that which is to be proven (*sādhya*);

for this very reason, I state that it is precisely that [the smoke] which is the primary factor— otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of inferring smoke from fire, until such time as this fault is removed.

We, however, say here that by stating "the conceit of qualities and defects" (*guṇadoṣābhimāna*) and so forth—having first described the location and other factors as being inferable like the properties of the probandum and the probans—and then again mentioning the defects of that very same [location], you yourself have demonstrated through the passage beginning with "not recognized as related to fire and so forth" (*apratyabhijñātam agnyādisambandhi*) that this is precisely your own position. By the words "of that very location" (*tasyaiva deśasya*), he shows that it is the location itself which possesses the status of the mark (*liṅgatva*) and the marked (*liṅgitva*), and not the two properties of fire and smoke; thus, by the words "again" (*punaḥ*) and so forth, he causes you to recognize that this is indeed your own view regarding the subject (*liṅgin*). As for the phrase "related to fire and so forth" (*agnyādisambandhī*):...

Having spoken thus, the one who bears the marks (the logician) says again: "This objection—that there would be the undesirable consequence of inferring smoke even from fire—is [merely] the talk of one who is confused about the direction of the system."

Having stated here that [the object] is to be established by location, this must be said regarding the operation of the determination of the reality of the possessor of the mark (liṅgin) and the mark (liṅga): there would be the undesirable consequence of inferring fire from smoke, even though [fire] possesses smoke;
for in both cases, the possessive suffix (*matup*) functions in exactly the same way as intended.
In the case of smoke as the object, this very point would apply; however, here, moreover, there is not even a scent of error,

for it is logical that "possessing smoke" (*dhūmavattva*) is the mark (*liṅga*), while the state of being the bearer of the mark (*liṅgitva*) belongs to the location itself as qualified by "possessing fire," when that location is intended to be expressed.
For it is not logical for "fire-possessiveness" (agnimattva) to function as a logical mark (liṅga), because it is itself that which is to be proven (sādhya).
For this very reason, I have stated that it is precisely that [the fire] which is primary; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of inferring smoke from fire.
See page 683, note 2.
Indeed, the reading here might even be: "For it is logical that only the location qualified by the possession of smoke is the inferential mark (liṅga).

Having stated this, when it is further argued—"This leads to the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that smoke could be inferred from fire as well"—that is said by one who is confused regarding the direction of the Nyāya system.

If you ask how those who are not deluded speak, we reply that we shall instruct you: namely, having stated here that [the proof] is to be accomplished by means of a locus (*deśa*), one must speak as follows regarding the operation of establishing the reality of the sign (*liṅga*) and the bearer of the sign (*liṅgin*): "By you, following this systematic logic (*nyāyavyavasthā*), it must be said that there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of inferring fire even from smoke," and so forth—this is the instructional text up until the point where it states, "because in both cases the possessive suffix (*matup*) functions in such and such a way according to what is accepted. This is the statement of its cause.

In the case of smoke as the object, this very same [fault] would apply: either smoke alone, independent of a specific location, would be the inferential mark (*anumāpaka*), or fire alone would be the object of inference (*anumeya*). Consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the inference of smoke from fire would be just like the inference of fire from smoke, because there is no distinction between the two things joined in conjunction (*saṃyogin*).
Now, if you argue that there is not even a scent of this fault because the location itself serves as both the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*), then listen to our instruction.
The reading *liṅgiliṅgitatattva* might also occur here; in that case,
the suffix *-matup-* would be absent.
Having reflected upon that, what is the statement of its cause? What is the statement of its cause?
The reading "etadevaṃ syāt" might also exist here; the reading "ityapi bhavet" might also exist;
and furthermore, the reading "atha punardeśasya sādhyasādhanatvaṃ nāsti doṣagandho'pīti" might also be possible.
He explains this: "For [the reason] 'because of possessing smoke,' etc.

It is logical that the locus (*deśa*) itself, as qualified by the property (*dharma*) of possessing smoke, is the sign (*liṅga*), because it is that which, being established through the possession of smoke, acts as the means of proof. Likewise, when that same locus is intended as the probandum (*liṅgin*), it is logical that the locus itself, as qualified by the state of possessing fire, is the probandum."

However, it is not logical for the location to function as a *liṅga* (inferential mark) with respect to fire. Why? Because it is not proper for "fire-possessingness" (*agnimattva*) to be the *liṅga*, since it is the thing to be proven (*sādhya*); it is the thing to be proven because it is the possessor of the *liṅga* (*liṅgin*); and it is the possessor of the *liṅga* because it is unestablished (*asiddha*).

According to our view, however, it is possible to conceive of even the *liṅga*-status as belonging to the location itself as qualified by fire-possessingness. Furthermore, when fire is perceptible but smoke is imperceptible, [the inference would fail];

for this very reason, I have stated that the location itself is the primary factor—not the inference of smoke from fire. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of inferring smoke from fire.
For the sake of explaining the state of being a sign (*liṅgatva*),
the state of being the signified (*liṅgitva*) is also [explained].
But in that case, setting aside the location, fire itself would be the possessor of the mark (liṅgin), because it is the object of inference;
yet it cannot be the possessor of the mark, because it is already established in the world and is therefore not an object of inference.
Thus it has been said:

The subject (dharmin) is not to be proven by means of the subject, nor is the property (dharma) [proven] by that [subject]; yet the property is to be proven by means of that property, and likewise the subject is to be proven because it is the subject that is being proven. (Pramāṇasamuccaya 3.13) If it is argued that this is stated merely as a figurative designation (upacāra), we reply: here the true nature (tattva) is being sought; a figurative designation is for friends...
likewise, because the subject (*dharmin*) is that which is to be proven (*sādhya*).

In this way, however, the location possessing fire possesses the status of being the *liṅgin* (the possessor of the mark), because it is not distinct from the mark that establishes the presence of smoke, just like the nature of smoke itself.
To this, he says: "But in that case, setting aside and disregarding the location, it would be appropriate for fire alone to be the *liṅgin*.
Why? Because it is the object of inference (*anumeya*)."

To this it is replied: Fire cannot be the possessor of the mark (liṅgin) here; why? Because it is already established in the world, and therefore it is not something to be inferred. Furthermore, your own statement—namely, that according to our view, it is the subject (dharmin) as qualified by the property (dharma) that is the probandum (sādhya), and [the same] is the means of proof (sādhana)—is itself the evidence for this, not the verse beginning with "The subject is not [established] by the subject," and so forth.

A subject (dharmin) is not to be proven by means of a subject, as fire is [not proven] by smoke; because fire is already established, smoke lacks the status of being its property (*taddharmatva*), and thus it follows that "the property is not [proven] by the subject. For example, the hot touch is [not proven] by fire, because it is already established and because it lacks the status of being its property. Therefore, the subject itself is also not to be proven by that aforementioned property—this being indicated here through a change in grammatical case—as in: "Primal Matter (*pradhāna*) exists, because a commonality is observed among diverse things. This is because the property cannot be established unless the subject itself is established.

[Objection: By the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), it must be the property (*dharma*) that is to be proven by means of another property; however, even between two properties, their mutual status as properties is not established in the absence of a subject (*dharmin*). Therefore, the relationship of "probandum" (*sādhya*) and "probans" (*sādhana*) is untenable.

[Reply: This is not so. It is because the subject is the probandum in that same manner. That is to say, in that way, because a real entity (*vastu*) which is a subject possessing multiple properties is the probandum when it is qualified by the property one wishes to prove (*sisādhayiṣita-dharma*), and it is the probans when it is qualified by a property already established (*siddha-dharma*).

And thus he said: "In this context, the distinction between the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmī*) is made with respect to their being the object of proof (*sādhya*), and not by way of quality and possessor of quality (*guṇa-guṇitva*); therefore, there is no fault.
Thus [ends] the preceding section on properties (*dharmāḥ*).
Are the properties [the subject],
because they possess that nature?
Or is it the substratum [that possesses them]?
Is it a change of case-ending (*vibhaktivipariṇāma*)?
Surely a property (*dharma*) is to be proven by means of a property; for even between two properties, there is [a relationship].

The existence (*bhāva*) of both property (*dharma*) and substratum (*dharmin*); [that is,] the existence of a real entity (*vastu*) which possesses manifold properties (*anekadharman*), and the non-existence (*abhāva*) of a real entity which possesses manifold properties.

There might also be a reading here as "anekadharmakasya vastunaḥ" (of an entity possessing manifold properties). If it is argued that this is stated merely by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), [we reply: because of its being established... [as in the manuscripts *siddha* and *ya*.]

It might be thought: "True; although from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*) the relationship of sign (*liṅga*) and signified (*liṅgin*) belongs to a single entity qualified by the properties of the proven (*siddha*) and the to-be-proven (*sādhya*), nevertheless, due to a distinction of properties produced through metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), that which is non-distinct is spoken of as if it were distinct.

This is incorrect, because here the true nature (*tattva*) is being investigated—starting from "a metaphor is [used] toward friends" up to "because the property-possessor (*dharmin*) is both the probandum (*sādhya*) and the locus (*dharmin*)," the meaning of which has already been explained along with its commentary.

Therefore, it is established that the status of being the sign and the status of being the signified belong only to the location (*deśa*) as qualified by both the possession of fire (*agnimattva*) and the possession of smoke (*dhūmavattva*).
Having set that aside, we shall now establish for you that which was proposed but not yet proven: that the place possessing fire is a logical mark (*liṅga*).
This is as follows: the thesis is "the place possessing fire is thus a logical mark," and the reason is "because it is not distinct from the logical mark that establishes the presence of smoke."

The illustration is as follows: just like the nature of possessing smoke itself. Just as the nature of possessing smoke is the mark (*liṅga*) of a location because it is non-different from it, so too the nature of possessing fire is the mark of the location because it is non-different from it; and this non-difference has already been established.
Thus, the nature of possessing fire is not a mark because of its variability (*vyabhicāritva*), like "knowability" (*prameyatva*);
rather, its status as a mark is fixed by its being the very reality of smoke, which serves as the basis for inference.
Since the nature of smoke is established precisely by its inseparable connection (*avinābhāvitva*) with fire through the demonstration of its non-deviation, one might then ask:
what should be understood here? Just as there is the cognition of fire from the mark of smoke, would there also be the cognition of smoke from fire?

Now, what is the object of this deliberation? It is entirely appropriate that, according to the principle shown regarding the state of being the probandum (*sādhya*), either the mark or the marked may possess the character of being the mark (*liṅgatva*) or the marked (*liṅgitva*).

If, however, smoke-possessingness were to become a logical mark (*liṅga*), it would lack the status of a mark precisely because it deviates from fire-possessingness— just as "knowability" (*prameyatva*) does—
since one cannot infer smoke in every instance of fire due to the absence of positive concomitance (*anugama*). Furthermore,
even if the location were the probandum, there would be the fault of contradicting the principle of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).

Here he says: "The state of possessing fire (*agnimattva*) cannot be a logical mark (*liṅga*) because it is fallible; for the state of possessing fire deviates [from smoke], since it is observed in other places and at other times—such as in iron balls, glowing coals, and so forth—even in the absence of the state of possessing smoke. Why is this? It is like 'knowability' (*prameyatva*). For instance, when it is said, 'Sound is eternal, because it is knowable, like space,' knowability is observed in jars and the like which are non-eternal even without eternity; likewise, the state of possessing fire is observed without the state of possessing smoke. Thus, because it is fallible, it does not prove identity."
As for the state of possessing smoke, however, it is because it has never been observed without the state of possessing fire; thus,
it has never been observed without fire.

Regarding the claim that [the mark] is perceived without [the object], we say: no. For smoke possesses the status of a logical mark (*liṅgatva*) precisely by virtue of its being a real entity (*vastutva*), which is to say, by its very acquisition of selfhood (*ātmalābha*) as an inference that is inseparably connected with fire; this occurs through forms such as its whiteness, abundance, and unbroken root, which determine its nature as smoke. In that case, there is no possibility at all for the fault of being the "possessor of the mark" (*liṅgitva*) to arise, because it is established by its very nature as a logical mark, being [already] directly perceived (*pratyakṣatva*).

Likewise, even when fire is perceptible, smoke functions as the mark (*liṅga*) of that which possesses the mark (*liṅgin*) by way of establishing its non-deviation (*avyabhicāritva*), and so forth. However, if the state of possessing fire were to deviate from smoke—just as the state of being an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*) might deviate—then the very nature of smoke (*dhūmatva*) would be called into question, because it would lack a fixed basis due to its possible identity with vapor, mist, and the like.

Therefore, smoke would be a reason that is "doubtfully unestablished" (*sandigdhāsiddha*); how then could it possess the status of a logical mark (*liṅgatva*)? However, because its nature as smoke is established through its being firmly rooted in the state of being inseparable from fire, it possesses the status of a logical mark by virtue of its presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*). Likewise, fire also possesses the status of a logical mark for the establishment of smoke; [this is] the status of smoke as a logical mark, as inferred in the *Bhāṣya*.

Or rather, even for you, there would be no effort [to establish the distinction]. The other says: "In that case, what should be understood here? Just as fire is understood from the mark of smoke, there should also be an understanding of smoke from fire, because in reality there is no difference between being a mark and being the possessor of a mark."
The intention is that a distinction is indeed observed in the case of actual practice (*pratipatti*).
Here, the Teacher (*ācārya*), wishing to show that there is no such distinction even in this case, says in order to have that very point recited: "Now, what is the object of this deliberation?

The other replies: "Of the reason (*hetu*) whose nature as being to be proven (*sādhya*) in a particular place has been shown by the stated logic. This logic has been shown: namely, that the place itself is to be proven as possessing fire (*agnimattva*), while the means of proof (*sādhana*) is its possessing smoke (*dhūmavattva*).

Therefore, it is entirely logical that either the mark (liṅga) or the possessor of the mark (liṅgin) may possess the status of being a mark or the status of being the possessor of the mark; this is not contradictory.

However, regarding the consequence that [fire] would possess the status of being the possessor of the mark in the form of "possessing smoke" and so forth—even though there is no difference in the fact of being conjoined, it is observed in experience that only the state of being conjoined with smoke is the indicator of fire, as expressed by the rule: "Wherever there is smoke, there is fire."

If "possessing smoke" were the probans (*liṅgin*), it would lack the status of a probans (*liṅga*) precisely because it would deviate from "possessing fire," just as the property of being knowable (*prameyatva*) does.

Therefore, the nature of fire is one thing, and the nature of smoke is another; for it is not the case that "wherever there is fire, there is smoke"—an inference such as this is suspect because of a lack of positive concomitance (*anugama*), since smoke is absent in many instances of fire.

To avoid this fault, it is maintained that [the subject] must be unestablished by way of its location (*deśāsādhyatā*). However, even in that case of being unestablished by way of location, there is the fault of contradicting the principle of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), because fire is already established in the inference "fire from smoke. Consequently, the definition [of a thesis] as stated in the *Nyāyamukha*—"that which is intended as the subject (*pakṣa*) by way of being the thing to be proven"—does not apply; furthermore, it would be as useless as illuminating what has already been illuminated.
[Note: The phrase *dhūmatvaliṅgitvā* does not appear in the Vāya manuscript.]
Is inference impossible? Is it a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) according to logic? See footnote 128, line 3.
For just as in the case of proving fire, even in the case of proving smoke, inference is not possible due to deviation (*vyabhicāra*), since smoke is observed even without fire;

however, it is conceivable that from the sight of smoke one might think "there is fire here," or from the sight of fire one might think "there is smoke here. This is like [inferring] a kitchen from fire, whereas where smoke is impossible, there fire is also impossible, as in the case of water within [the earth].
The meaning of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is [established] by way of its possibility; likewise, the cognition [of it] is also [established] as in other cases—
or rather, let it be sufficient [to say this].
Regarding the proposition "there is fire here," one cannot determine that "only fire is here," because earth, fuel, and so forth are also present there;
nor can one determine that "fire is here alone," because that would contradict what is established by perception and other means of valid cognition;
nor can one determine that "fire certainly exists here," because fire and smoke are not always present there.

Therefore, the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*) is that "fire exists in the intended place and time," because there is no determination of the rule [of concomitance] through non-observation [of deviation], just like the proposition: "This *karavīra* flower is red. To this we reply: "Just as in the case of the means of proving fire," and so forth. The passage concerning the production of the relationship between the signified and the signifier (*gamyagamakabhāva*) without distinction between fire and smoke has already been explained. For smoke is seen even without fire in a room where the fire has been removed, or when produced by the friction of fire-sticks (*araṇi*) where no fire was previously present; therefore, the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is equal in both cases.
The reading *na ca deva* found within these brackets does not exist in the Bhā manuscript.

Or, in the case of a request for something that has already occurred, such as "Is there fire here?"—how, then, can inference be possible? It is indeed possible to conceive, upon seeing smoke, that "there is fire here," or upon seeing fire, that "there is smoke here. Furthermore, in a location known through another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), smoke arises from fire alone; or conversely, from smoke characterized by its firmly rooted nature and so forth, fire is inferred.

In this regard, the example is: "like a kitchen [where fire is known]. This refers to a kitchen where a cook, commanded to act with great haste, holds fire in his hand; in such a kitchen, the presence of smoke is possible.

By way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), where there is an impossibility of smoke, there is also an impossibility of fire, as in the case of the interior of water; thus, the meaning of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*)—"smoke does not occur elsewhere than in fire"—is established through the sense of possibility, as in "like the other" (*itaravat*), meaning "like smoke. Just as smoke is possible in fire—occurring there at some time and in some place—so too fire is possible in smoke; thus the meaning of the positive concomitance is indeed feasible, and the cognition is likewise.

Alternatively, let it be as it is; enough of this play. Although we have already explained this both in terms of the actual state of affairs and through formal understanding, you still do not accept it. Why is there no distinction between the mark (*liṅga*) and that which possesses the mark (*liṅgin*)? Even if you do not accept it, nevertheless, we shall explain the answer to this by means of defining the members (*avayava*) [of the syllogism]. [Text fragment]: ...from smoke... [text fragment] ...the nature of being a reason... [text fragment]...ya...
Having bowed down... [comparison]—page 691, line 5:
˚sambhavonnarjala˚ Bhā. (variant).
In the *Ya* manuscript it reads "nirjala" (waterless),
whereas in the *Bhā* manuscript it reads "athavā liruvat" (or like the sound of bees),
and in the *Ya* manuscript it reads "athavālisaruvat" (or like the sound of bees).
Regarding the proposition "fire is here," and so forth:

it cannot be determined that "fire alone is here," because earth, fuel, and so on are present there; for in their absence, fire itself would be difficult to find, or else, due to the non-existence of the location itself, both fire and smoke—which depend upon it—would necessarily be absent.

Nor can it be determined that "fire exists here alone," because if one were to accept that fires other than those in that specific location are not fire, this would contradict what is established by perception and other means of valid cognition (*pratyakṣādi*), resulting in a flaw in the thesis (*pratijñādoṣa*). Furthermore, since there is no absence of fire in locations other than that specific place, it is impossible to state the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) that "wherever there is fire, there is smoke. Therefore, that [position] is refuted.
Nor can it be determined that "fire definitely exists here" by means of the linguistic usage of the verb "to be" (*bhavati*), for it is not the case that it does not exist even at some time.

What is the reason? Because fire and smoke are always absent there—in that place—the occasional exclusion of fire is purposeless, since both fire and smoke are constantly absent; and because of their absence, there is no possibility of their occurrence.
Is it by the non-usage of the application (*prayoga*)?
Or by the supplying of the application (*adhyāhāra*)? It does not even exist in this way.
The word "dāsa" (servant) is redundant [according to Bhāradvāja].
Therefore, the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*) is: "In the intended place, at that very time, fire exists.

Why? Because the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), namely smoke, exists as something invariably concomitant (*anubaddharūpa*) with fire; this is for the purpose of making known its coexistence with fire and its being caused by fire.

In some cases there is a relationship of concomitance (*sahacaribhāva*), and in others a relationship of cause and effect (*nimittanaimittikabhāva*); however, in this context, the probans (*liṅga*) consists of only two members,
among which the concomitant is that which is inseparably connected (*avinābhāvī*).
Fire and smoke are concomitants;
because a concomitant exists in this, it is called "concomitant" (*sahacarī*).
In this case, fire certainly exists in smoke, yet it does not exist [invariably], nor is it the case that it never exists anywhere at all.

For when that [coexistence] exists, fire indeed exists, and it is not non-existent like wind and so forth; nor is it non-existent even though not co-present with smoke, as fire is not co-present with smoke; nor does it fail to exist in the similar class (sapakṣa), as a produced thing is not found in the eternal.
Thus, by the exclusion of the unestablished (asiddha), the contradictory (viruddha), and the inconclusive (anaikāntika), inference based on the state of coexistence is established.

[Objection: But for what purpose is the relationship between the sign (*nimitta*) and the signified (*naimittika*) thus assumed? [Reply: No, because—unlike fire—there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*), and because the restriction is not established through the rule of linguistic derivation (*avyutpatti-vidhi*). This is because it is stated by the rule itself through a restriction that has not been previously derived; just as for a person who has not distinguished between the qualifiers "red" and "white," the statement "this *karavīra* flower is red" is made for the sake of defining it, without requiring a restrictive determination such as "it is red only" or "it is white only. Likewise, the smoke, which is a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), exists as something invariably connected (*anubaddharūpa*) with fire, for the purpose of making known its concomitance with fire and its being caused by fire.
In some cases there is a relationship of coexistence (sahacaribhāva), and in others a relationship between cause and effect (nimittanaimittikabhāva);
however, in this instance, the mark (liṅga) consists of only two members,
among which the coexistent is that which is invariably concomitant (avinābhāvī).
Fire and smoke are companions;
because a companion exists in this [smoke], it is called "sahacarī" (having a companion).
In this smoke, fire certainly exists, yet it does not exist [invariably]; nor is it the case that it does not exist at all in some instances.

For when that [sahacara-bhāva] exists, fire indeed exists; it is not non-existent like wind and so forth, nor is it the case that it does not exist even as something not co-present with smoke, like fire that is not co-present with smoke; nor is it the case that it does not exist at all in the similar class (sapakṣa), like the "produced" in the "eternal.
Thus, by the exclusion of the unestablished (asiddha), the contradictory (viruddha), and the inconclusive (anaikāntika), inference based on concomitance (sahacara-bhāva) is established. [Objection:

And why is it that smoke, as a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), exists as something invariably concomitant (*anubaddharūpa*) with fire? It is for the purpose of demonstrating its coexistence with fire and its being caused by fire. This is explained here [by the passage] beginning with "In some cases... and so forth: there is a state of coexistence between color and touch; there is a state of cause and effect, such that a staff or the like is the cause and a jar is the effect. These two—the states of coexistence and of cause and effect—are the two components. For that [invariable concomitance] indeed consists of those two; however, in this case, the logical mark (*liṅga*) has exactly two components.

Regarding the passage beginning with "there, the inseparable" (*avinābhāvī*), we shall first examine the state of concomitance (*sahacaribhāva*); that [concomitance] is indeed inseparability itself, and the following explanation is for the purpose of defining it. In the phrase "sahacara" and so forth, the suffix *-in* (in *sahacarī*) is used in the sense of the locative case (*saptamyarthe*), meaning "that in which a companion exists. For example, fire is the companion of smoke. This term has a threefold meaning: 1. "In this [smoke], fire certainly exists"—this is the determination of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*). 2. "It does not fail to exist"—this is to exclude the possibility of being a contradictory (*viruddha*), an uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*), or an inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) reason, by ensuring it is not absent from the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and exists only in the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*). 3. "From fire alone does this [smoke] arise"—this establishes the necessary connection. Thus, the doubt regarding these fallacies may be avoided.

And lest there arise the suspicion that [the reason] might be a "common inconclusive" (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*)—on the grounds that smoke is not found anywhere even in the absence [of fire]—he explains it thus: "for when that [fire] is present," etc. These examples are intended to exclude the view held by opponents that smoke possesses the status of being a mark (*liṅga*) for fire as its marked (*liṅgin*). By stating "when [fire] is present, it is indeed found, and it is not the case that it is not found, like a whirlwind (*vātyā*) and so forth," he excludes the charge of being "unestablished" (*asiddha*). Furthermore, by stating "nor is it the case that it is not found at all, like fire which is not accompanied by smoke," he excludes the suspicion of being a "common inconclusive" reason.

Alternatively, since it does not exist even in that which coexists with the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), such as "the eternal is not like the produced," the conclusion stated as "thus, [the reason] is unestablished" (*asiddha*) and so forth— by way of eliminating the suspicion of being contradictory (*viruddha*), uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*), or inconclusive (*anaikāntika*)—
has already been explained. (The portion regarding the absence of activity in the *bhāṣya* is thus concluded.)

This is not so, because smoke is just as subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*) as fire is; for just as fire deviates from smoke—since it is absent in things such as non-fire—so too does smoke deviate from fire, as in a smokeless dwelling-house or through the churning of fire-sticks. since smoke—which has a pale upper portion, a broad lap, and roots bound in one place—rises again and again, it cannot exist without fire; therefore, the relationship between cause and effect (nimitta-naimittika-bhāva) must be accepted.

Furthermore, their state of being concomitants must be accepted as being like that of a crane and its banner; for even when there is a relationship between cause and effect, smoke is seen to deviate from fire.

However, once the possibility of the cause and the concomitant is established, there is no room for deviation, because smoke moving to another location is caused by fire present at that time. Thus, it is only specific smoke that serves as the indicator of fire, since the qualification [of smoke] is purposeful.
Just as that [smoke] makes known the possession of fire, so too does it make known the state of having fire as its proximate cause.

And since the fire is thus apprehended, no other means of valid cognition, such as perception, need be required. By the mention of "being produced" (*kṛtakatvena*), there is the apprehension of smoke characterized in such a way that, in that very place and at that very time, the fire has not failed to arise, nor has it passed away, nor has it been removed; this is for the purpose of making manifest this meaning.

Even though there is a state of coexistence (*sahacaribhāva*), a relationship of cause and effect (*nimittanaimittikabhāva*) must be accepted, because smoke itself would simply not exist without that fire which serves as its cause.
Then, demonstrating the signs for the purpose of ascertaining that [state], he says: "pāṇḍūrdhagati," and so forth.
The qualification "pāṇḍu" (pale-white) is for the purpose of excluding vapor, mist, and the like;
by means of its upward movement and its density, "dhūmikā" (smoky haze) is excluded.

By the mention of "held in the lap" (*utsaṅgin*), the state of being spread upwards like the shape of a shallow bowl (*śarāva*) is indicated; by the mention of being spread across the sides, the exclusion of mist and the like is established;

by the mention of having roots bound in one place, the exclusion of non-existent or removed fire, wind, and so forth is established; and because they involve whirling in many directions, the exclusion of smoke that repeatedly rises from a smoke-house with its fire removed or from the friction of kindling-sticks (*araṇi*) is established.

Therefore, because a deviation [of cause and effect] is observed between fire and smoke—just as it is between water and a crane, which are co-occurring—the relationship of cause and effect (*nimitta-naimittika-bhāva*) is also accepted.

Yet, demonstrating that even this relationship of cause and effect certainly deviates in the absence of a relationship of co-occurrence (*sahacari-bhāva*), he says: "Like a crane and a banner," and so forth, up to "because a deviation of fire from smoke is observed. The underlying intention is already explained: since the presence of the effect (*naimittika*) is observed even in the absence of the cause (*nimitta*), as in the case of a palace built by an architect, the same applies to smoke.

Since smoke—which has a pale upper portion, a broad belly, a base fixed in one place, and which repeatedly rises—cannot exist without fire, a relationship of cause and effect (*nimitta-naimittika-bhāva*) must be admitted;

and just as in the case of a crane or a banner, a relationship of concomitance (*sahacari-bhāva*) must also be admitted. Even though the relationship of cause and effect exists, because fire is observed to deviate from smoke [in cases like lightning], there is no possibility of deviation when both the relationship of concomitance and the causal relationship are established.

Since smoke that does not move to another location is caused by fire present at that very time, it is only specific smoke that serves as the indicator (*gamaka*) for fire; for the qualifying attribute must have a purpose.
Just as that [smoke] indicates the possession of fire, so too does it indicate its being caused by fire present at that time.

And thus, since the fire has already been apprehended, no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such as perception, need be relied upon—just as in the case of [inferring impermanence] through the property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*).
Neither brought from the past nor extending into the future,
the pale ones have departed.

To avoid the faults inherent in both [theories] and to demonstrate the merits of the two-membered [syllogism], he says: "When the occurrence of the cause for concomitance... and so on, up to "...because the qualifier has a purpose."
When there is the perfection of both qualifications, no possibility of deviation can arise.

How is that so? He demonstrates this with the passage beginning "not moving to another place," and so forth: because smoke has as its cause fire present at that time, it possesses the capacity to indicate the co-existent fire only when it is purified of the stain of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) by those aforementioned qualifications. Otherwise, since smoke would deviate from fire just as fire deviates from smoke, the purposefulness of inference would depend solely on the power of the qualifications; for if the qualifications were not employed, the mere state of having fire (*agnimattva*) would not be indicated. Since there is co-existence in both directions, whether in terms of cause and effect or otherwise, therefore, just as it indicates the state of having fire, it also indicates the state of having fire present as its cause. Just as the state of possessing smoke does not exist without the state of having fire, so too it does not exist without that [fire] being its cause; thus, like the state of having fire, it indicates the state of being caused by it, because there is no deviation in either case.

That very fire is the cause (*nimitta*) and the concomitant (*sahacara*) of the smoke; for there is no other cause for that smoke, and so forth, up to "would be produced," and so forth. Indeed, for that smoke, there can be no cause other than fire—such as stones, water, or jars located in another place resulting from the transformation of the site—nor can there be a concomitant, because that would entail the absurd consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the entire three worlds being marked by [the smoke], since it would follow that [the smoke] is produced by a different transformation (*pariṇāmāntara*) while being distinct from the transforming and the non-transforming, and thus would itself be the means of accomplishing that other transformation. In this way, for the sake of contemplating the relationship of cause and effect (*hetu-hetumadbhāva*) in this very instance, he says: "previously perceived," and so forth. Just as previously, at the time of perception, the smoke was connected with fire and the fire with the smoke, so too at the time of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), through the recollection of that connection, there is the manifestation of the other—the probandum (*sādhya*)—by means of one of the two intended reasons, such that "wherever there is fire, there is smoke" and "wherever there is smoke, there is fire. For example: "Those too," and so forth; the proposition (*pratijñā*) is that even those things such as clouds and rainbows are indeed produced immediately after an effort established by proof; the reason (*hetu*) is the compound series beginning with "perceived by the world" and ending with "because their occurrence is established";
and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is walls and the like.

The explanation of that [sūtra], as well as the purposes of the qualifiers such as "perceptible by the world" (*lokapratyakṣa*), are stated in summary: first, the sentience of lightning and so forth is established. Wind and the others are the bodies of living beings (*jīva-śarīra*), because they possess touch and other qualities while not being atomic (*anaṇu*) and so on, like a cow. To avoid the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*)—since even a dead cow lacks the state of being a living being—the qualifier "even though it is a body of a living being" is used, followed by the series of qualifiers up to "because it acts spontaneously," just like a carpenter (*sthapati*). This is like the sentience of a carpenter.

Once the consciousness of wind and so forth is established, [the text] shows that lightning, clouds, thunder, and the like arise from the effort of conscious wind, by means of the passage beginning with "the activity is ordained by a conscious being. Regarding the passage beginning with "the movement of the sun," although the activity is like that of a container and its contents—wherein the signifier (*liṅgin*) exists only in the sign (*liṅga*), and conversely, the sign exists only in the signifier—the relationship between the sign and the signifier remains even when this rule is inverted. Since the signifier exists only in the sign, it is logical that smoke, like fire, is an indicator of properties such as substantiality (*dravyatva*) and the like, but not of properties such as sharpness (*taikṣṇya*).

And since the mark (liṅga) exists only in that which possesses the mark (liṅgin) and not elsewhere, it is logical that smoke indicates [its locus] by means of its whiteness and so forth, just as by its nature as smoke, and not by means of its substantiality (dravyatva) and so forth; for in this way, through the reversal of restriction, the relationship between the mark and the possessor of the mark is established. Regarding the relationship you consider to be like that between the container and the contained—namely, the verse beginning "the possessor of the mark (liṅgin) exists in the mark (liṅga)" and so forth—the commentary on it is as follows: because the possessor of the mark, fire, necessarily exists in the mark, smoke, and does not fail to exist, therefore [the former relation] is logical; this demonstrates the purpose of the restrictive determination (*avadhāraṇa*).

Furthermore, the passage beginning with "because [the mark] exists in the possessor of the mark alone," extending up to "by means of substanceness and so forth," demonstrates the opposite restrictive determination, the meaning of which has already been explained.

The prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: it is observed that it is the universal (*sāmānya*) that is to be cognized in the inferential subject (*liṅgin*), not the particulars (*viśeṣa*); and it is the particulars of the mark (*liṅga*)—and not the universal—that possess the capacity to make [the object] known. All this occurs because of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), due to the relationship of subsistence like that between a container and its contents (*ādhārādheya-vat*). [This was stated] by us, excluding [the view of] Bhā[radvāja], in the *Pra[karaṇa]*.
The answer to this [charge of] non-indicative capacity is as follows: "This too," and so forth.

This occurrence, like that of the container and the contained, indicates that [object] where it has been observed by virtue of the rule of observing its existence; it does not indicate it by the power of exclusion through the negation of what has not been observed.

Here too, the passage beginning with "for not" (*na hi*) and ending with "not" (*na*) means: the paleness on a woman’s cheek does not indicate fire, because that paleness is not smoke that has arisen from fire; however, paleness that *is* smoke does indicate fire, because it is smoke that has arisen from fire, and because only a positive presence (*vidhi*) can indicate another positive presence by virtue of being that very presence.
Regarding this, the response is the passage beginning with "of these too" (*eṣām api*) and so forth.
Here, the reading might also be "this too is the response" (*iyam apīti*).
In this context, something appears to be either incorrect or incomplete;
for there is no such cultivation [of thought] as "the paleness of a woman’s cheek is not...
and so forth.
If the reading is thus, then it coheres correctly:
"the positive [inference] alone, by virtue of being a property of smoke... etc.

Regarding the passage beginning with "yathā cedam" and so forth: just as specific qualities such as paleness (*pāṇḍutva*) are indicative of fire because they constitute smoke, so too is the generality (*sāmānya*) of substantiality (*dravyatva*) and the like indicative of fire because it constitutes smoke. This is the intended meaning up to the point "just like paleness.

Thus, the capacity to indicate is equal for both the general and specific properties that constitute smoke; there is no difference in the rule that only a positive affirmation (*vidhi*) is what is to be known.
For instance: there is the cognition of the generality of "substance-ness" (*dravyatva-sāmānya*) even in fire, because it is a primary element (*bhūta*);
yet there is no cognition of its being a substance distinct from water and so forth, because it is not of that nature.

As for the statement, "smoke [is] lightness, etc.," inference is indeed the arising of a cognition through the continuous observation of the presence of specific qualities such as luminosity and sharpness.
When smoke-possessingness is understood as being invariably concomitant with fire-possessingness, inference occurs due to that non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*);

however, when there is deviation, it is a fallacy of inference (*anumānābhāsa*). For example, just as [the presence of] trees, bushes, and so forth deviates from the sharpness of fire, so too inference is that which is invariably concomitant with the cognition resulting from such observation.

not relying on the exclusivity of either of those two positions—that [object] is or is not [the object of knowledge]—cognition whose object is not determined is non-ascertainment (*anadhyavasāya*) and error (*viparyaya*); these are fallacious forms of inference (*anumānābhāsa*).

However, there would be the consequence of inference being invalid regarding exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), because it is like non-apprehension due to absolute ignorance, or like error because the cognition does not conform to the operation of the object to be grasped. Furthermore, even the apprehension [of a thing] occurs only through the rule of perceiving its presence, since there is deviation—because it is seen both in that way and otherwise, such as in the form of brilliance, sharpness, and so on, and as being devoid of them. It is not the case that there is no apprehension simply because of deviation from something absolutely non-existent, like coldness, which is unconnected; rather, it is precisely because of deviation from what is connected that there is only affirmation (*vidhi*).
Likewise, in the commentary (*pra*), there might also be the reading "and likewise from fire" (*tathā cāgner api*) here (p. 681, l.
For the arising of cognition through the continuous connection with the observation of that state is inference;
since the possession of smoke is invariably connected with the possession of fire, inference occurs when there is the apprehension of such necessity, because of its non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*).
However, due to deviation, there is a fallacy of inference (*anumānābhāsa*), as for example, [inferring] the heat of a flame from trees, bushes, and so forth, where there is deviation.
Inference, too, is likewise bound to such a perception and cognition...

Without relying on the exclusivity inherent in either of the two positions—that [the object] is that or not that—there arise non-determination (*anadhyavasāya*), where the object is not ascertained, and error (*viparyaya*); these are fallacious forms of inference (*anumānābhāsa*).

Furthermore, because of the exclusion [of other possibilities], there would follow the invalidity of inference, just as there is non-determination due to absolute ignorance, or just as there is error due to a cognition that does not conform to the operation of the apprehended object.
In perception, however, there is only affirmation (*vidhi*).

Furthermore, since the definition of inference is established precisely through the rule of observation (*darśanavidhi*), that alone should be accepted; therefore, he says: "Inference is the arising of cognition through the constant connection with the observation of the existence of that [object]"—this is the definition of inference.

He explains this with the words "the state of possessing smoke," and so forth: when the state of possessing smoke is grasped as being invariably concomitant (*aikāntika*) with the state of possessing fire in a particular location—that is, when there is the certain apprehension that "there is fire here because of smoke"—then inference occurs. For that fire is grasped with absolute certainty due to its non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*).

However, that which is fallacious due to deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is a pseudo-inference (*anumānābhāsa*). For example, as in the case of [inferring] the sharpness of fire from [the presence of] trees, shrubs, and so forth; for instance, when one says, "There is a tree or a shrub here, because there is smoke," it becomes a pseudo-inference. Since this is observed even in the absence of a tree or the like, it is deviant; and because its conclusion is based solely on the force of such observation, inference itself is likewise bound to the cognition of such observation. This meaning has already been explained. In the same way, there is the pseudo-inference of doubt (*sandeha*), as well as the pseudo-inferences of non-determination (*anadhyavasāya*) and error (*viparyaya*), such as in the passage beginning with "that side or not that side" (*tadatatpakṣa*), and so forth.

The "that" and "not-that" sides are the two positions (*pakṣau*). Not relying on the absolute certainty regarding those two—whether it be "it is truly so" or "it is not truly so"—but rather having a cognition that is indeterminate and non-doubtful in form such as "fire is only here" or "fire is indeed here," yet which does not ascertain the object, is *anadhyavasāya* (non-ascertainment). Furthermore, error (*viparyaya*) is the cognition of what is real in what is unreal, or the cognition of what is unreal in what is real, such as the cognition of a person in a post.
These two [non-ascertainment and error] are also fallacies of inference (*anumānābhāsa*).

Inference is understood as being connected with such a perception and cognition through the uninterrupted transformation of that [perception], just like direct perception; likewise, even the fallacy of inference possesses the same characteristic.
The meaning is already explained; likewise, the fallacies of inference based on doubt are also [explained].
"It is precisely that" refers to the unmanifested.
How can one know that very [non-existence] as such?

Since, according to your view, there is an exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) based on such a perception, there follows the consequence that inference is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇya*). This is because, whether one says "it does not exist" or "it does not exist," non-existence is ultimately nothing but non-occurrence; or else, it is a different object (*arthāntara*), since it is absolutely unperceived—such as "fire does not exist," "water is not fire," "that is not a jar," or "it is a sky-flower. Thus, by the logic previously stated, there follows the consequence that it is merely ignorance (*ajñāna*), and therefore lacks validity.

Why? Because, like non-determination (*anadhyavasāya*), it lacks validity due to absolute ignorance; likewise, for the purpose of establishing its lack of validity like that of error (*viparyaya*), he says: "Or because the cognition does not conform to the mode of the object, like error."

The occurrence of the object of apprehension, fire, in its positive form is "fire-being"; that cognition which does not conform to it is "not conforming to the occurrence of the object of apprehension. Because such a cognition does not conform to the occurrence of the object of apprehension, there is invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) of the exclusion-inference (*vyāvṛtty-anumāna*), just like the notion of a post with respect to a person. The undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭāpādana*) based on the force of the previously stated reasoning is thus understood.

Therefore, inference and pseudo-inference (*tadābhāsa*) are just like what is perceived, because they are bound to the cognition of things as they are perceived; [otherwise] there would be no difference from what is not perceived. *Note: The final portion of the sentence appears to be a fragmentary commentary or marginal note regarding the distinction between what is perceived and what is not.*
"Only that [is the case]," according to the *Prabhā* and *Yaśas* commentaries;
"like a [specific] place," according to the *Pra*.
Is it by perception that inference is [established]?

And thus, that which is indeed alleged as a refutation— namely, that this [inference] characterized by the inference of a relation consists of "this is the effect of that" or "this is the cause of that" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 9)— is also not a refutation.

And the refutation of such [positions] has already been stated, because inference—due to its nature as a cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of the activity of the stated rule—does not [establish] the probandum (*liṅgin*) without the logical mark (*liṅga*). ... ... ...
Furthermore, the second quarter [of the verse] here might also be "liṅga evetarat punaḥ" (the other [property] is only in the mark);
for if there were a restriction [of the property] to the possessor of the mark (liṅgin), why is sharpness not accepted [as being present there]?
See page 702, line 9–10.

As it has been said: the probans (liṅga) necessarily exists in the locus of the probandum (liṅgin), but the probandum does not necessarily exist in the locus of the probans; for even when the probandum exists, the probans may be absent, as in the case of fire and iron. Thus, smoke existing in a location that is the locus of the probandum constitutes the property of the subject (pakṣadharma).

Or as he says: "The mark (liṅga) exists only in that which possesses the mark (liṅgin), not in that which does not possess the mark. That too is not tenable; for if its existence were restricted [to that alone], then it would be a mark only with respect to that fire.

And thus, by means of this extended application (*atideśa*), the definition of the inference of relation—beginning with "from one [term] of the relation" and so forth, and "this is the effect or the cause of that" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 9)—is connected.

1.18 And thus, the following objections are indeed applicable: since the relationship [between the sign and the signified] is indistinguishable, there would be the cognition of qualities such as brilliance and sharpness just as there is of fire-substance from smoke; there would be the cognition of generalities such as substantiality and existence just as there is of specific qualities like the paleness of smoke; or fire would be the signifier just as smoke is, or smoke would be the signified just as fire is—these faults follow because inference is stated as having a positive function (*vidhivṛtti*) based on what is perceived, according to the accepted principle that "just as it has been perceived, so does it produce doubt, non-determination, error, or certainty."
This too is not a refutation, because inference functions according to the method already described;
this refutation was established in detail by Dignāga in the second chapter of the *Pramāṇasamuccayavṛtti* during the examination of the Vaiśeṣika doctrine (p. 240, l. 11).

Those seeking further detail should consult the examination of Vaiśeṣika inference extracted from the *Pramāṇasamuccaya* along with its commentary (*vṛtti*) and sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*), found on pages 184–196 in the seventh appendix of our edited edition of the *Vaiśeṣikasūtra*, published in the Gaekwad’s Oriental Series, Baroda. (Note: The source text contains a scribal error; it should read *dṛṣṭaviṣayavivṛtteḥ*.)

Furthermore, regarding the meaning of the verse "the possessor of the mark (liṅgin) exists only where the mark (liṅga) is," which was stated as inference by reversing the restriction [of the original], the Teacher says the following to refute it—the verse beginning with "without the mark, there is no possessor of the mark," and so forth.

This includes the presentation of the opponent's view starting from "it is not as he says" up to "like fire," which provides an example for the reversal of the rule. Here is the response: smoke, while existing in the place that is the possessor of the mark—namely, the locus possessing fire—is indeed a property of the subject (pakṣadharma); it is not [a property] while not existing, because [if it were non-existent], it would be unestablished (asiddha) and thus not a valid mark (aliṅga).

Since only that which has its property-in-the-subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) ascertained through qualifiers such as "having its root firmly established" can function as a logical mark (*liṅga*), it indeed becomes a mark for the object-to-be-marked (*liṅgin*). However, by excluding [the case of] a whirlwind and so forth, that smoke does not become a mark for qualities residing in the fire, such as its sharpness; for while that [sharpness] is not perceived in the fire, it is not perceived in the smoke, nor does it exist in the smoke through a positive concomitance (*vidhivṛtti*) with sharpness and the like (p.
The realization of the meaning of reality, the realization of the meaning of reality, the root of non-binding, primordial.
The mark [of fire] such as sharpness and so forth does not exist;

it does not exist because that fire is seen in the smoke, whereas sharpness and so forth are not seen [there], and because [the relationship] occurs through positive concomitance (*vidhivṛtti*) with those [qualities like sharpness]. This reading might also occur here, as in the passage beginning with "vāha" and so forth.

The determination of this restriction, "only in that which possesses the mark" (liṅgin), is as follows: when there is smoke, it does not exist in that which lacks the mark, such as water and so forth;

yet even that [objection] is not tenable. Why? Because of the phrase "by necessity" and so on. When that smoke exists—its presence being delimited by specific characteristics such as having a fixed root—it functions as a mark only for that very fire, and not for anything else, such as non-fire.

What is the reason? Because in the expression "fire is here," the word "here" (atra) denotes a locus and thus possesses meaning; since the state of being the possessor of the mark (liṅgitva) belongs only to the fire connected with that specific place denoted by the word "here," otherwise the fault of the absence of inference would have been stated.
Therefore, it is established that only that [specific property] is the mark (liṅga) of that [object].

As for the fact that the substantiality (dravyatva) and other properties residing in smoke do not indicate fire, that is due to the very rule of our accepted observation, because they deviate from it in that manner. (p.
Because it is characterized by being that which expresses [the object] exactly as it is,
and because it is that which is expressed [by the word].
If there is a necessary connection between the mark (*liṅga*) and that which possesses the mark (*liṅgin*), why is its sharpness (*taikṣṇya*) not also accepted? (Praśastapādabhāṣya, p. 676, l. 6).

If it is argued that [the fire] is not perceived, that is not so; for smoke, having abundant green grass as its fuel, makes known the fire by means of specific qualities such as its slight or intense nature, its abundance, and so forth.
...smoke makes known specific qualities such as great heat; smoke located in the courtyard of one's hand or house makes known the fire that is present there.
Thus, the existence of the signified (liṅgin) resides in the sign (liṅga) itself.
Now, it might be argued: "The specific qualities are not what are cognized [by the sign], because that very [sign] is deviant" (Pramāṇasamuccaya 2).
No; because of the mention of sharpness and so forth,
it has already been stated there as well that this [sharpness] belongs to that [iron] precisely because of the rule for perceiving its existence.
See page 675, line 2:

Nor is there a rule that the mark (liṅga) must reside only in the bearer of the mark (liṅgin), as in the case of a bedchamber; for it can be said that fire exists in smoke by way of a necessary rule (niyama), because [smoke] cannot exist without being ignited by fire.

But as for what you say—that "the possessor of the mark (liṅgin) exists in the mark (liṅga)"—if there were such a rule regarding the mark, then this collection of faults would follow: why is sharpness not accepted [as being present in the smoke]? Since the specific causes for determining [smoke] are invariably accompanied by specific qualities such as intense or faint luminosity, just as fire is inferred from smoke, why is it not accepted that the specific fire is also inferred from those same specific causes for determining smoke, which are accompanied by those specific qualities?
(Page 679, Line 4:
...of the specific causes for making known...)

It might be thought: "If [the opponent] says 'there is no perception,' we reply that it is not so, for perception does exist. This is as follows: in a place such as one abounding in green grass, where there are no men who are milkers and the cows are left unattended, in a cow-pen strewn with green grass and newly constructed, a fire is made with green grass as fuel to ward off mosquitoes; in that case, the specific smoke mentioned in the *Daṇḍaka*—characterized by its smallness due to being made of grass and so forth—makes known the fire. Likewise, through the increase of heat indicated by terms such as "intense" (*bahala*) and so on, a specific [inference] arises.

Potters are artisans who work with clay; since the heat located in their courtyard causes the fire to become manifest, we observe that even particular instances possess the nature of a mark (*liṅgin*). Thus, smoke alone is the mark (*liṅga*) for the existence of the fire, which is the marked (*liṅgin*).
Therefore, there is no reversal of the relationship between mark and marked, nor is it the case that the particularity is not apprehended; thus, the cognition is not devoid of [the object].
In that very place, there might also be the reading "taddaṇḍyalpatāpādi"; compare page 673, line 5.

Now, it might be argued as follows: "The fault has already been stated by me regarding the qualified object; however, its specific qualities are not perceived. Which ones? Those which belong to that very [object] which is subject to deviation.

This too is not correct, because of the mention of "sharpness" and so forth. For, while explaining the meaning of the verse, you stated that "brilliance, sharpness, and other such qualities are not perceived," and furthermore, you have demonstrated that sharpness and the rest are indeed perceivable realities.

Is it that there is no such fault because of the specificities? Or is it that there is indeed such a fault because of the specificities?
See page 606, note 7:
in the *Pramāṇasamuccayavṛtti*, [it is stated] that "there is no comprehension in every respect of an object possessing multiple properties from a logical mark (*liṅga*)."
It should be understood that this sentence is seen in the commentary on the half-verse beginning with "iti" (2.12).
The reading "gamyatattvadarśitatvāt" is possible, and even "gamyatvasya darśitatvāt" might be considered as an alternative;

furthermore, I have already stated there that this is due to the very rule for observing their existence (*tadbhāva*). Moreover, it has been declared that the relationship of indicator and indicated (*gamya-gamaka*) between particulars occurs through the power of observation alone—by way of affirmation (*vidhirūpeṇa*)—when the properties to be proven and the means of proof are observed as being present by virtue of that existence, just like [the relation] of conjunction, and not by way of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*).

Therefore, it is incorrect to say that "the possessor of the mark (liṅgin) exists only in the mark (liṅga)," and the verse beginning with "without the mark, there is no possessor of the mark" is well-stated (pṛṣṭha 681,
line 2).
Regarding what was stated [on] page 679,
line 4 and page 701,

line 3— that "the mark (liṅga) exists only where the bearer of the mark (liṅgin) exists"— that too is not a restrictive rule that the mark exists only where the bearer of the mark exists, as in the case of a bedchamber. And having established this, the formal argument (*prayoga*) here is as follows: the mark (*liṅga*), namely smoke, possesses the capacity to indicate the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*), namely fire, precisely because of its pervasion (*vyāpitva*), and this occurs through a positive function (*vidhivṛtti*) alone; this is the meaning.
"Like producedness and impermanence" is the example (*dṛṣṭānta*); just as producedness, by pervading impermanence, makes it known, so too does smoke [make fire known].
In this way, it should also be understood that the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*) is indeed the mark (*liṅga*).
Thus, [the objection] beginning with "like your own view" and so forth is refuted;

for according to our view, it has been stated that the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) are one and the same. Since they mutually pervade one another, the relationship of the signified (*gamya*) and the signifier (*gamaka*) exists in both cases by way of positive affirmation (*vidhi-rūpeṇa*) alone, not through exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*). What is surprising about this? Even according to your own view, having made a distinction such that the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), fire, is the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*) and the property serving as the means of proof (*sādhanadharma*), smoke, is the mark (*liṅga*), we say: "Just as the mark is also pervasive," and so forth, as in the verse.

What is meant by this? It is said that even though, like produced and impermanent things, there is a mutual pervasion through the mode of subsistence as conjoined entities, smoke alone is the indicator (*gamaka*) of fire, and not fire of smoke. This is just as "horned" [is indicated] from "cowness" (*gotva*); thus cowness is the indicator of hornedness, but hornedness is not [the indicator] of a cow, because it deviates (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of elephants, bulls, buffaloes, boars, and so forth.
Here too, according to our view, there is a fixed rule regarding the indicated and the indicator; such is this verse: "Just as the mark (*liṅga*) is also pervasive... [and so on].

Having stated that positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) are the gateway to inference of objects, you have established the impossibility of positive concomitance by pointing out that in an object called "Dittha," which is a collection of qualities, there is no mention of the positive concomitance of constituent parts such as being one-eyed or lame. Then, having raised the doubt that just as positive concomitance is impossible, so too is negative concomitance impossible, you said: "This might be the case; negative concomitance is also impossible. That which you have said is indeed correct, because, as in our [view of] conjunction, positive and negative concomitance do not exist without an affirmative mode of operation (*vidhi-vṛtti*).

First, let us consider the definition of those two: positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) are indeed of the nature of cognition. Positive concomitance is the cognition of a uniform persistence in similar instances; negative concomitance is the opposite of that. Why are the occurrence and non-occurrence in similar and dissimilar cases—not as properties of the object itself—as you have stated? Because, according to this perspective within the *syādvāda*, the object possesses a manifold nature due to its specific qualities;
thus, the absence of positive concomitance in that regard has already been asserted both by you and by us, just like your own position.

This which you have said is correct; [it is] what was stated by us, O Prajñā.
The absence of such exclusion (vyatireka) between those two is now stated: "And there is no possibility," and so forth;
that is, the word "tree" lacks the capacity to exclude all non-trees.

Why? Because of infinity; for, just as in the logic of explaining such passages as Praśastapāda’s *Padārthadharmasaṃgraha* (vṛtti 5.2) regarding the infinity of particulars (*bhedānām ānantye*), one should observe the same principle here: since objects such as jars, cloths, and so forth—which are non-trees—are infinite, there can be no process of exclusion (*vyatirecana*).

The example is "like the concomitance (anvaya) of all trees. Just as all tree-objects are inexpressible because they are infinite, because it is impossible to establish a relation [with them], and because there is no concomitance, so too there is a lack of exclusion (avyatireka) because there is an infinity of further things to be excluded, such as pots, cloths, and so forth. Likewise, one must state that smoke lacks the capacity to exclude all non-fire things, such as water and the like, because of the infinity of all trees, just as in the case of concomitance; for one would have to perceive all trees [to establish such an exclusion]. for, as stated on page 652, line 3, if the logical mark (liṅga) did not manifest [the object] by way of a positive injunction (vidhi-rūpeṇa), like that which has been seen.

there would either be no comprehension at all, or there would be comprehension in every respect.

*Liṅga*, *apadeśa*, *kāraṇa*, and *nimitta* are synonymous terms.

The universal (*sāmānya*) is the mark (*liṅga*), its unity having been brought about by the non-intention of [its] differentiation; it makes known the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*) whose unity has been similarly conceived through that very state of being. Thus, there is no fault in the mark being the means of cognition and the possessor of the mark being the object of cognition. For comparison: "Cause (*hetu*), indicator (*apadeśa*), mark (*liṅga*), motive (*nimitta*), means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and reason (*kāraṇa*) are synonymous"—Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 9.1.16.
Here, the refutation stated by you is anticipated— the passage beginning with "As for what is said," etc.,

shows the absence of defects in the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and the excellence in the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), starting with "Even though there is an inequality despite the infinity," and so forth.

The resolution is that there is no fault, because the word or the logical mark (liṅga) excludes [the object] by means of the mere absence of anything other than it in a general sense, without touching upon its specific varieties; thus, that which is to be excluded is [defined]. *Vyatirecanīyaṃ pra*. [End of fragment].
In that case, must one not state, in general, the mere absence [of the reason] elsewhere in the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)? [The text reads: *aspṛtābhāva* / *aspṛtā ya*.

To this we reply: No. Regarding the phrase "as in the case of what is seen" (*dṛṣṭavat*) and so forth, if the mark (*liṅga*) did not manifest the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*) in a positive manner (*vidhirūpeṇa*) like that which is seen, then—since the possessor of the mark would not be perceived anywhere—that mark would not even be a mark; or else, there would be no comprehension whatsoever of any object at all. This is the summary meaning. The explanation of this is as follows: "mark," "indication," "cause," "instrumental cause," and so forth, are synonyms.

Sound is for the sake of another (*parārtha*), while smoke and the like are for one's own sake (*svārtha*). Since the relationship between the signifier and the signified (*vācyavācaka-sambandha*) is not different from the relationship between the means of inference and the object of inference (*anumānānumeya-sambandha*), both types of inference are included as one. In that regard, because only the particular (*viśeṣa*) is the signified and the object of inference, and because the universal (*sāmānya*) is non-existent—since you have stated that the meaning of a word is a "truth" qualified by the "unreal"—we maintain that the signifier-signified relationship belongs only to the particular aspect of the word and its referent, since the universal is non-existent and only the particular exists. For a non-entity cannot be signified, just like a sky-flower.

Since that universal does not exist at all, it was not previously perceived; rather, it is only the particular that has been perceived. Because the [particular] is denoted by means of a superimposed, unreal universal as a subordinate element, the word also functions as a signifier in exactly that same way.
Thus, even in inference, there is a positive formulation (*vidhi*) by means of employing the universal as a subordinate factor, as in the case of smoke and so forth.

How does a mark (*liṅga*), such as smoke or a word, become a means of cognition (*gamaka*) on account of reality (*tattvāt*)? It is said: because the distinctions are not intended to be expressed, the universal (*sāmānya*) is one; thus, their unity is established. That mark (*liṅga*) is the universal whose unity has been brought about by the non-intentionality of distinctions. The property (*dharma*) consisting of smoke, sound, and so forth, has attained that state [of being the universal]. If it were held that the tree—which possesses distinct parts such as branches—does not manifest in that way [as a single entity] through that kind of manifested unity (i.e., the unity manifested in the form of the sound or smoke), but rather [manifests] through the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), then it would not be a manifester at all, because nothing would be perceived; for no object to be excluded (*apohya*) is perceived in every individual substance.
For it is neither that [entity] nor something other than it, because it is not perceived, like the son of a barren woman.
Nor can that which is unequal to it, lacks its name, and lacks its form—being thus unperceived—be apprehended;
and if that is not apprehended, of what could there be an exclusion (*apoha*), or how could it occur? If you argue that it would be like "not being a father," [we reply: no.

Just as one who is not the father [is still called] "father" by mere conceptual exclusion (*vyāvṛtti-buddhi*), and just as fire—possessing distinct actions such as burning and so forth—and the possessor of marks (*liṅgin*) are [designated] by their own nature; because of the non-difference between the denotable (*vācya*) and the possessor of marks (*liṅgin*), according to the previously stated logic, they are the denoters of themselves and the inferables of themselves. Precisely through the perception of that state (*tadbhāva*), the general (*sāmānya*) serves to convey the particular (*viśeṣa*), like the vehicle of a palanquin-bearer serving as the vehicle of a lord. It is by that very state [of being smoke] that it is indicative: because smoke is indeed fire, since it is fire characterized as having a fixed base and so forth; and because smoke itself is fire, since the *pudgala* atoms of smoke—in states such as being kindled by forest fuel at the beginning, middle, and end, or as embers and so forth—are fire.

By the logic thus stated, there is no fault in the fact that the *liṅga* (the sign) is the means of cognition and the *liṅgin* (the possessor of the sign) is the object of cognition; he recalls the aforementioned logic: "Because of that, the *liṅga*... [and so on]. From that, the *liṅga*... that *liṅga*... likewise the *liṅga*...
