If, however, it is not accepted that [the word] manifests [the object] in that way, but rather by means of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), then it would not be a manifestor at all, because nothing would be seen; for since the thing to be excluded is not perceived in relation to every individual substance—whether it be that very thing or something other than it—it is like the son of a barren woman, as it has never been seen.
Furthermore, it is impossible to comprehend something that is not equal to it, does not have its name, and does not have its form, if it has not been perceived in such a manner.
And if that [object] is not apprehended, how or for whom could there be exclusion (*apoha*)?
If it is argued that it would be like "non-fatherhood"—just as anyone other than a father is called a "non-father" merely by virtue of the cognition of exclusion—[we reply: no.

[Regarding the reading] "possessing distinct properties" (*bhinnadharmavat*):
if it were not so, then the following would be a fault in the opponent's position (*paramata*).

It must simply be unperceived.

And since the exclusion [of an object] from cognition is intended, for this [exclusion]—namely, "this exists" and "this does not exist"—positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) cannot belong to cognition unless the object has been perceived; cognition would only follow after objects have been perceived and would exclude itself only from those very [perceived] objects, as in "This is Devadatta, not Yajñadatta," and so forth. An object that is absolutely unperceived, such as a sky-flower or the son of a barren woman, is not what is intended here as the perceived [object], nor does a word or smoke appear here as something perceived by that very [cognition].
Is it not so?
Having turned away from trees, O Agni,
[seek] other objects that are non-trees.
To demonstrate this point, he says: "For that [object] is neither a tree nor fire, nor is it something else such as a jar, because it is not perceived, like the son of a barren woman.
Or rather, when it is indeed perceived, it is either that [very thing] or something else;

and since it is not dissimilar to what is perceived, it does not have a non-corresponding word (*atacchabda*). That is to say, it is not the word 'tree' or the word 'fire' applied to it; thus, this is a case of having a non-corresponding word, such as 'non-tree,' 'non-fire,' and so forth."

Likewise, its form is not form, for its form is not that [other] form. Why? And since there is no grasping and the other is absent, of what could there be an exclusion (*apoha*), or how could it occur? If it is argued that [the universal] would be like "non-fatherhood" (*apitṛtva*), this suspicion might indeed arise. The explanation beginning with "just as" (*yathā*) and so forth is its clarification: just as all persons other than a father possess the nature of non-dependence on difference (*anāśritabheda*), even without that [specific] connection, they are perceived as being entirely without parts (*niravayava*) through the mere cognition of exclusion from what is other than the father, regardless of their own internal differences; likewise, all things other than fire and trees—namely, non-trees and non-flames—would also be perceived as partless through the mere cognition of exclusion. What is the fault? It would not be so, because nothing [of that kind] is observed.

It is logical that, after perceiving a visible father and subsequently grasping his distinct identity, one might establish the non-fatherhood of another by excluding the father; however, this cannot apply when the father himself is not seen, for he is the father... [in that case].
...the arising from conditions;
for indeed, it is as you have asserted: that there is occurrence with respect to what is similar, and non-occurrence with respect to what is dissimilar.

In that regard, it need not necessarily be stated that [the application] occurs everywhere; for in some cases, because the object is infinite, its expression is impossible. Indeed, it is not possible for the word "tree" to be observed in all trees, nor is it possible for every gender-mark to be present in every gendered object, as in the case of fire and smoke. Even though in some instances—such as with the name *Ḍittha*—there may be such a possibility, nevertheless, it is impossible to observe the entire collection of qualities, such as being one-eyed or having a crooked nose. Furthermore, even if such observation were possible, inference would be entirely impossible; thus, because everything is unobserved, [this applies] to one who is like a father...
...or there would be no comprehension of that exclusion (apoha).

For if both the meaning for oneself and the meaning for another were grasped together through a positive injunction (vidhi), then one could understand it thus: "This is a tree; this is not [a tree]. This would not be possible, however, when the meanings of the words "tree" and "non-tree" are entirely unknown.

They are perceived; thus, as in the example, other things than fire and tree—namely non-trees and non-fires—are also perceived as partless through the mere cognition of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti-buddhi*), even though they consist of infinite distinctions. What is the fault? It would be perceived as partless. Likewise, all things other than fire and tree—namely non-trees and non-fires—would be perceived as partless through the mere cognition of exclusion. What is the fault? [One might object that] it would not be so, because everything is not seen.

It is logical that, after perceiving a man who is both a father and a non-father, one might establish the "non-fatherhood" of another by way of excluding the father; however, this cannot be so when the father himself is not perceived at all, for he [is the father]... [in the case of the father being seen].
...the arising from conditions; however,
this which you accept— namely, that there is activity toward what is similar and non-activity toward what is dissimilar— is not so.

In that regard, it need not necessarily be stated that [the relationship] applies everywhere; for in some cases, where there is an infinity of objects, its expression is impossible. Indeed, it is not possible to observe the word "tree" in all trees, nor is it possible to observe every gender-sign in every gendered object, as is the case with fire and smoke and so forth. Even though in some instances—such as with the name "Ḍittha"—there may be such a possibility, nevertheless, it is impossible to observe the mere collection of qualities, such as being one-eyed or having a crooked nose, in every instance. Furthermore, even if such observation were possible, inference would be entirely impossible because [the subject] is not seen in its entirety, as is the case with one who resembles his father.

"For if both its own meaning and the meaning of another were grasped by a rule in combination, then one could understand it thus: 'This is a tree,' and 'This is not [a tree],' provided that the meanings of the words 'tree' and 'non-tree' are not entirely unknown."
If there is curiosity regarding the fault here, we shall explain it: [the cognition] would not arise because of the non-perception of everything.

It is logical that one’s father should be seen by us in his true form as the Creator, according to the principle from the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa (2.7) stating, "You are born from limb after limb. Having bestowed his own life-breaths—his son who is the aggregate of all virtues—one should, through exclusion (*paryudāsa*), distinguish him from other kinsmen such as brothers who possess contrary notions due to superimposition (*adhyāsa*). After clearly identifying the father with the thought, "This is Father Devadatta; these are not Vasurāta and the others," one should establish the status of the other person as a stranger and not a father. This is the established rule.

Furthermore, it is logical that [the perception of] the collection of qualities occurs upon seeing you, and not upon the non-perception of the father alone; this is what follows. Since it is impossible to grasp the father alone, or in the absence of the father, there is no statement regarding the grasping of the mere object consisting of the collection of qualities—this being expressed by the passage beginning with "For he [sees] the father," which describes the rule of perception for the father, and through the phrase "from the perception of the father" up to "the production of the cognition," it explains the distinction of those others who are not fathers.
This is the description of the illustrative example.

Now, regarding the inconsistency of the Dārṣṭāntikas, the text beginning with "But as for this... and so forth—referring to the thesis that "the occurrence [of a term] is in what is similar, and its non-occurrence is in what is dissimilar," as you have asserted—proceeds until the point where it is stated that "in every way inference is impossible. While explaining this passage, [the author] has already refuted the opponent's position through the very logic you yourself have stated. Furthermore, the demonstration of the disparity between the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the subject (*dārṣṭāntika*)—beginning with "because everything is not seen by one who is like a father" and so forth—is already understood, up to the point where it concludes: "or else there is no comprehension of that exclusion (*apoha*)."
The summary of the point is that, according to your own view, since no self-interest or interest of another is ever perceived, there can be no cognition of fatherhood at all.

Alternatively, we state the fault by means of another method, beginning with "because everything is not perceived": if [the word] were indeed for its own referent (*svārtha*), and so forth—when "tree" (*vṛkṣa*) is uttered, according to the logic stated by us, the particular (*viśeṣa*) qualified by the universal (*sāmānya*), such as the *śiṃśapā* and others, would be denoted in its entirety; and the non-tree (*avṛkṣa*) along with its subdivisions, such as the jar and the cloth, being excluded (*apoḍha*) from that, would be subsumed as "this other [thing] is different from this tree. Thus, because the word "non-tree" (*avṛkṣa*) is different from the word "tree," it would be a non-tree; likewise its referent. For fire, [the term] "non-fire" (*anagni*) would be different from "fire" (*vahni*) and so on;

In that regard, concerning the meanings of general terms, there are two possible modes of operation for the word *sat* (existent) in the statement "it is not non-existent": either the word *sat* does not admit of another referent (*arthāntara*), or it does admit of another referent.

To illustrate this point, he provides an example: from the word "tree" (*vṛkṣa*), the word "foot" (*aṃhri*) is non-tree because it is different; likewise, its referent [is non-tree]. "Indeed, nowhere," and so forth: indeed, for you, there can be no determination of the occurrence of a term based on mere observation, nor is there any fixed rule. Why? Because of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). In this regard, first, an example concerning the meanings of general terms is given: "existent" (*sat*) does not become "non-existent" (*asat*). For here, two possible modes of operation are considered: would the word *sat* have its operation restricted to a single object while excluding other objects, or would it have its operation extended to include other objects? Regarding the first case, if one asks what kind of word that is which operates solely upon a generality from which differences have been excluded—that is, a word whose operation does not admit other objects—the author says, for the purpose of defining it: "Apoha alone, having the sense of exclusion, is said to be without a basis."

The illustration of this is as follows: when "existent" (*sat*) is stated, because of the use of two negatives—namely, that "it does not become non-existent" (*asad na bhavati*)—the result is the attainment of the original state (*prakṛtyāpatti*), and thus it is understood that "it indeed comes into being," which is the meaning of an injunction (*vidhyartha*). What follows from that? Since an undertaking is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*) once something is already established, by means of these two negations—"it does not become non-existent"—that which was enjoined, namely existence itself (*sattva*), is restricted.

If one asks how that is so, it is said: [The meaning is] that neither that which does not exist, such as a sky-flower, nor that which does not exist in the manner of a jar or a cloth—of both these types of non-existent entities—there is no relation here to this tree; this is what is stated.

And since this negation is a *paryudāsa* (exclusion) primarily characterized by an affirmation, there follows the abandonment of the word "non-existent" (*asat*) having as its referent the exclusion of the non-existent in the form of a *paryudāsa*. Consequently, because it would consist merely of a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation), there is the abandonment of the accepted definition of the exclusion of other objects (*anyāpoha*) as the expression of its own meaning through the absence of others.

Now, if it is maintained that *apoha* functions upon a distinct entity (*arthāntara*) precisely because of these aforementioned defects, then this [position] falls apart: "That which is existent does not become non-existent.
For every thing, such as a jar, is itself existent while also being non-existent, due to mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*) and the like;
for even that which is non-existent must be [conceived] as some existent, because it subsists in each individual instance. Just as "a jar" is not a non-jar, and "a tree" is not a non-tree.

The term *vidhi* (affirmation) and the word *asat* (non-existent) would have that [affirmation] as their meaning; and thus, by the logic already stated, the meaning of the word *asat*—which consists of an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) primarily characterized by affirmation—would be abandoned. That very tree would become existent (*sat*), because there is an absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of an "asat" other than the "sat. Consequently, the "asat" would be a mere non-implicative negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), meaning simply that what was possible has been negated. Therefore, since its meaning would be a mere non-implicative negation, the acceptance of the principle that "the word is an exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) because there is no 'other' such that one could say 'this is different from that'" would be abandoned; this would constitute a fault.

Furthermore, because the word, while effecting the exclusion of other objects (*arthāntarāpoha*) within its own referent, expresses that very [referent], the definition—"the expression of its own referent by means of the exclusion of other objects"—would be abandoned. This too is another fault of abandoning one's own accepted position (*abhyupagamatyāgadoṣa*). Thus, insofar as the operation [of a word] upon other objects is not admitted, since "existent" is not non-existent, the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) is not tenable regarding the meaning of a general term (*sāmānyaśabda*); rather, only a positive injunction (*vidhi*) is tenable. Why? Because everything, including jars and the like, exists in its own right (*pratisva*). The formal argument here is as follows: the thesis is that even by means of that which is non-existent, something existent must come into being; the meaning is that whatever comes into being and in whatever manner it comes into being, it must do so by means of both these two kinds of non-existence.

Why? Because it exists individually (*pratyekavṛttitvāt*), that is, because it exists in its own form for each [individual]; or else, because it exists (*sattvāt*). Whatever exists and exists individually is an entity seen to exist in some manner even though it is non-existent; just as a cloth, which is other than a jar, is seen to exist as a cloth even while being non-existent as a jar, so too this [non-existence] becomes existent while being non-existent. Likewise, because it exists individually, even that which is non-existent becomes existent when the distinction of objects is not admitted.

Moreover, this has been accepted by you as well, though it was forgotten; now I shall remind you of it: just as "a jar" is not a non-jar, and "a tree" is not a non-tree—since you maintain that the meaning of a word consists in the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*)—this is what is called the general meaning of the word "existent" (*sat*).
Alternatively, [the reading] "because of existence" (*sattvāt*) does not appear in the Bhāṣya manuscript.
Just as in the case of "existence" (*bhāva*), so too when the distinction between objects is not accepted—

even regarding the referents of general terms such as "substance" (*dravya*) and so forth— if no separate object is admitted, then by that same logic, one must abandon the position previously asserted, just as was explained.
Regarding the exclusion of other referents (*arthāntarāpoha*), this should be applied accordingly according to its own specific logic.
Is it not the case that this is established just like the word "existent" (*sat*) when it is being uttered?

To this we reply: If the word "existent" were also the word "non-existent," then only on that basis would examples such as the word "jar" find their scope; otherwise, what scope would there be for them? For it is precisely the word "existent" that becomes the word "non-existent"; otherwise, if the non-existence of a cloth and so forth did not belong to an existent jar, of which existent thing would the word be a designation, such that it could be called the word "existent"?
Thus, in this sense, the word "existent" (sat) does not become the word "non-existent" (asat);

even regarding the referents of general terms such as "substance" (dravya) and so forth, that [existence] is twofold, because it functions with respect to objects that are either accepted or not accepted.

In that regard, concerning the phrase "when no other meaning is admitted" and so forth, the same logic as previously stated applies: since it is established that [the term *adravya*] is not a non-substance (*adravya*) because of its connection with two negatives (*nañ*), and thus it is indeed a substance (*dravya*), the restatement is for the purpose of restriction. The passage beginning with "that which does not exist" and "by means of which it does not exist," etc., serves to introduce faults such as the abandonment of the meaning of the word *adravya*—which consists of an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) primarily intended as a positive injunction—on the grounds that it would otherwise have the meaning of a mere non-prescriptive negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*). This extension of the argument is self-evident up to the point where there is an abandonment of the accepted position, as if it were already manifest.

In the second alternative as well, he extends that same logic to the case of "the exclusion of other objects" (*arthāntarāpoha*) and so forth: by virtue of its own specific principle, and because each substance is a substance in itself, no substance is not a substance; this is to be applied accordingly, starting from "due to mutual non-existence" (*itaretarābhāva*) and so on. Likewise, the reading here might also be "that which is not accepted [as such] becomes accepted," and so forth.

Here he says: "But surely this is established like the word *sat* (existent) when it is being spoken; for one who considers the established word *sat* to be free from the nature of non-existence (*asat*) raises this objection: 'Since the word *sat* is so called because it denotes or invokes that which exists, then just as the word *sat* itself—and not the word *asat*, nor that which has the sense of non-existence—is the designator of the existent object, so too the real entity [the existent] must be such.
Thus, even particular words such as 'jar' and their respective objects would be of that same nature, and words such as 'cloth' and their objects could not possibly exist [in that way]."
Therefore, it is incorrect to say that "what exists becomes non-existent"; the word "existent" (sat) refers only to that which is denoted by the term "existent."

Regarding this, we say: if we do not accept that "the word 'existent' (sat) is also the word 'non-existent' (asat)," and so forth— namely, that "the word 'existent' is not the word 'non-existent'"— then an example would be impossible, because the status of being an example is established only through the very fact of the word 'existent' being the word 'non-existent'.

For if the word "existent" (sat) also becomes the word "non-existent" (asat), only then does the example of the word "jar" and so forth find its place both in common worldly usage and in the theory of the exclusion of others (anyāpoha); otherwise, what occasion would there be for this example of the jar and so forth?

He explains this: indeed, the very word "existent" (sat) becomes the word "non-existent" (asat); for when denoting an existent thing such as a jar, it becomes the word "non-existent" precisely because it does not denote a cloth or other things. Otherwise, if the non-existence of a cloth were absent in an existent jar, there would be an absence of existence [in that jar]; and due to the absence of existence, as well as defects such as confusion (*saṅkara*), if there were non-existence, of which existent thing would there be a denotation by a word, such that the word "existent" could have its distinct referent admitted? Therefore, it is incorrect to say that the existent entity does not become non-existent, just as the word "existent" [does not become the word "non-existent"].

Thus, since the word "existent" (sat) refers to that which exists in meaning, it is incorrect to say that the word "existent" does not become the word "non-existent" by way of its referent; for it certainly does [become so]. Furthermore, this is due to the fault of [the opponent's] position regarding existence (*sattva*).
From [the acceptance of] existence, sound would arise;
from the acceptance of sound, [it would follow that] even for one who has no distinction [between them], [sound would arise].
The reading "viśeṣa" in the Bhāṣya is incorrect;
for even from the perspective of the word itself, there exists another word entirely, namely "sat."
The word *sat* is indeed distinct from the verbal root *sad*;
the same should be understood regarding words such as *dravya* (substance) and others.
However, in the case of specific terms, although one might say "a jar is not a non-jar," even here it is not that "it is not a non-jar."

For example, jars that are unbaked, cracked, or otherwise defective are indeed non-jars because they lack functional activity; or, if one were to call something a jar only by the act of making it so, then in the absence of that act, it would certainly be a non-jar.

Even that which is not a jar becomes a jar; for the weaver, the cow, the horse, and so forth, as well as raw clay, holes, and the like, "function" (ghaṭate) or "cause to function" (ghaṭayati), because they are devoid of motion—
namely, the raw clay, the holes, and so forth, due to their lack of activity.
Or rather, the root should be considered thus:
the non-difference of the word "go" when it refers to speech and so forth is established by its being well-known through direct perception;

furthermore, even from the perspective of the word's etymology, the word *sat* is indeed different [from the word *go*], because the form *sat* is derived from the verbal root *as* with the suffix *śatṛ*. Thus, that which is the word *sat* is entirely distinct.

The word *sat* derived from the verbal root *sad-* with the suffix *kvip* is indeed something else entirely; it is not at all the word *sat* whose original form (*prakṛti*) is *sad-*. Since it is the word *sat* whose original form is *as-*, therefore, even from the perspective of its linguistic form, the word *sat* is indeed the word *asat*; it is not the case that it is not [the word *asat*]. (Praśastapādabhāṣya)
Is the nature of that which is non-existent "existent," or is the nature of that which is existent "non-existent"?
The word "sacchabda" (true word) is not [applicable] here;

Just as the existence and non-existence of the word *sat* are determined by its grammatical derivation and its various forms, so too should they be understood for the word *dravya*.
Thus, *dravya* is either "a modification of a tree" (*dru-vikāra*) or "a part of a tree" (*dru-avayava*), according to Pāṇini 5.3.104: *dravyaṃ ca bhavye*.

"Being" (*bhavati*) thus [it is] "existent" (*bhavya*); "flowing" (*dravati*) or "being flowed toward" (*drūyate*) thus [it is] "substance" (*dravya*). Because qualities flow [into it], substance is the confluence of qualities (*guṇasandrāva*). By such etymologies, and with respect to its own subdivisions such as earth and so forth, the word "substance" (*dravya*) and the word "existent" (*sat*) apply to terms like "substance" and so on—by the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), this is intended as an extension of the rule to general terms such as "earth" and "water" when they refer to their own subdivisions; the same should be understood regarding the meaning [of these terms].

Thus, first of all, since everything is unobservable within the referents of the terms "great generality" (*mahāsāmānya*) and "lower generality" (*aparasāmānya*), the theory of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) is untenable.

Regarding the phrase "in the case of the meanings of particular words," etc., the word *tu* (but/however) demonstrates the absence of an alternative regarding the acceptance or non-acceptance of difference between the meaning of a general word and the meanings of particular words.
Even in the case of [the statement] "a jar is not a non-jar," it is not that "it is not [the case that] it is not a non-jar"; rather, it is a non-jar.

For example, regarding the phrase "an unbaked jar, a cracked jar, etc.": an unbaked jar is not a [functional] jar; by the inclusion of the word "etc.," jars such as those made of painted clay and so forth are likewise merely jars that are non-jars, because they lack the capacity for joining (ghaṭana) and are devoid of activity.
Alternatively, a jar might be defined as that which performs the act of joining (*ghaṭayan*) when there is an agent who employs it; since that is absent, it is indeed a non-jar.

Furthermore: even that which is not a jar becomes a jar because it possesses purposeful activity; it is independent and is the agent [of action]. Likewise, regarding the passage beginning with "perception" (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth, the claim that "a cow is not a non-cow" is also not tenable; for it is demonstrated therein that a cow becomes a non-cow, and a non-cow also becomes a cow.
For in that regard, there are two ways in which words function: either a single word has multiple meanings, or multiple words have a single meaning.
In this regard, that which is a single [entity] having multiple meanings is now considered.

First, regarding the word "cow" (*go*), its oneness while it subsists in speech and so forth is established by direct perception; because its specific [referents] cannot be determined, it is impossible to establish a connection [with them individually].
Therefore, the word "cow" has a single nature.

And in that case of a single essence, distinct powers for the communication of various meanings must be postulated, because— as in the case of one man being a father, a son, and so forth— the function varies according to each relationship; or else, if it were differentiated by specific qualities such as "speaking" (*gadana*) and so on, then like one individual cow among many, it would simply be "cow," and thus the statement "a cow is not a non-cow" would also be untenable, because there is a distinction between the "cow" as speech (*vāk*), etc., and because the word "cow" is observed to apply simultaneously to speech, the quarters, the earth, rays, and so forth.

Therefore, the non-difference [of the word] from what is established by perception is proven, and that is not to be doubted—namely, whether the word "cow" is different or non-different [from its referent]. Thus, the notion that there might be a difference would be improper. It might be thought that the word "cow" is different because it leads to a different object, yet due to similarity, it appears as if it were the very same; but this is not so, because its specific nature as a word cannot be determined. Since its specific form—such as "this is acute," "this is grave," "this is circumflex," "it resides in speech," or "it resides in a direction"—cannot be determined, there is no difference; furthermore, perception is more powerful than inference.

What follows from that? It follows that a connection [between the word and its object] is impossible. For it is impossible to establish a connection between non-existent things—whose own forms cannot be determined and which are not perceived separately—with various objects.

Furthermore, it is illogical for words whose connections have not been established to convey meaning, as this would lead to the absurd consequence that one could understand the meaning even upon hearing a word used by a barbarian (mleccha).
Therefore, the word "cow" (go) must possess a single, unitary essence.

And since that word is a single essence, its various capacities for conveying this or that specific meaning must be postulated as manifested by the various related entities due to a difference in their powers; how so? Like the case of a single person’s fatherhood, sonship, and so forth. Just as a single person receives designations such as "father," "son," "maternal uncle," or "nephew" depending on the difference in the various related entities possessing those multiple powers, so too does the word "cow" [function] with respect to speech and other objects.

Why? Because the counter-correlate (*pratisambandha*) functions differently. That very [word] functions in various ways toward each respective relation (*sambandha*), which is the counter-correlate; it is the distinctness produced by the relations that functions differently and differently.

Therefore, because the word "cow" (*gośabda*) is a single entity, yet denotes objects distinct from speech and so forth, the cow itself becomes speech and so forth, and even what is not a cow becomes a cow, since its specific nature cannot be determined due to the impossibility of establishing those relations.
Therefore, the word "cow" (go) must have a single essence;

and since that essence is one, the capacities to convey various respective meanings must be postulated based on a difference in power (*śakti*), just as in the case of a single man who is both a father and a son, whose status varies according to each relationship.

Alternatively, even if it were distinct [in each instance] as determined by specific qualities such as "lowing" (*gadanādi*), it would still be simply "cow," like one cow among many others. Thus, the claim that "it is not non-cow" (*agaurna bhavati*) is also untenable, because there is a distinction between the cows of speech (*vāk*) and so forth.

Or perhaps it is thought: "The word *go* differs due to a difference in its causes (*nimitta*), and those causes are [actions such as] bellowing (*gadana*), roaring (*garjana*), going (*gamana*), swallowing (*giraṇa*), and so forth; because it belongs to the class of words beginning with *pṛṣodara*, the formation of the form is established as being distinct [in each case]."

Even if one were to concede, contrary to the aforementioned reasoning, that this [cognition] is not logically tenable, it would still be a cow itself—distinct only as determined by specific qualities such as bellowing and so forth—just like any other cow. For instance, although the word "cow" (go) applies to a single object possessing a dewlap and other features on the basis of the common property of "going," it remains a cow even when applied to various other cows such as Khaṇḍa, Muṇḍa, Śābaleya, Bāhuleya, and Saurabheya.

The word "iti" has the sense of a reason (*hetvarthe*); because the general term "cow" (*gośabda*) depends upon specific instances such as Khaṇḍa and others, therefore—as in the previous case—under this view as well, it is not the case that "a cow is not a non-cow. Why? Because of the distinction (*vyatireka*) among cows such as Vāk (Speech) and others. For example, when "cow" is said, the nature of being a cow (*gotva*) is not excluded from Vāk and the others, just as the word "cow" [is not excluded] from them; but when "Vāk" is said, Vāk is distinguished from direction (*dik*) and so forth, such that Vāk is not the direction. Therefore, a cow is also a non-cow. The illustrative example is thus explained. *garāṇā* (variant: *pra*).

When it is said "speech" (*vāk*),
because water has one hundred and one names, even non-poisonous water becomes poison, and so forth;
likewise, a *pīlu* tree, by virtue of being a tree, may become a non-*pīlu*, like a *dhava* tree or others, or it may be a *pīlu* like an elephant.
Therefore, [the word] *pīlu* is both a *pīlu* and a non-*pīlu*, and it is both a *pīlu* and a non-*pīlu*; likewise for *hari*, *rāma*, *arjuna*, and so forth.
Thus, if a single word has multiple meanings, there can be no exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*).

Even when there is a single meaning for many words, it is as follows: because water has one hundred and one names, such as "salila," "udaka," "amṛta," "jīvana," and "viṣa," one hundred and one names for water are recited in the *Nirukta*. Therefore, poison (*viṣa*) becomes non-poison (*aviṣa*); even that which is not poison becomes poison. Water that is not drinkable—such as the venom of a knot-snake (*granthisarpa*) and the like—is not of a nature to kill, but is of a nature to sustain life.
Even water and such things, though life-sustaining, become life-destroying through improper application; this is the method of interpretation.
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), one should understand examples such as "clarified butter is not clarified butter," and likewise:
"The *pīlu* tree is not a tree because it is a *pīlu*, like a *dhava* tree and others," or "the *pīlu* is like an elephant."
Even an elephant is "not-pīlu" because it is an elephant, just like a human;
likewise, by way of reversal, a pīlu tree is "not-an-elephant" because it is not an elephant, and an elephant is "not-a-pīlu" because it is not a tree.
He concludes with the words "therefore."
"Pīlu, apīlu, and pīlu; likewise apīlu, apīlu, and even pīlu"—
in this way, he demonstrates the pervasiveness of this principle through a multiplicity of examples,
such as Śakra, Siṃha, Vāsudeva, Maṇḍūka, Vānara, and Haya, since the word "hari" is observed [to apply] to both what is not Hari and that which is Hari.
