kṣīra, puṣkara, meghapuṣpa, kamala, āpas, pathas, pāthas, kīlāla, bhuvana, vana, ghanarasa, yādas, nivāsa, and amṛta are synonyms for water.
Kulīnasa, Kabandha, Prāṇada, and Sarvatomukha—
Abhidhānacintāmaṇi.
And here is the remainder: water, the divine, irā, āsevyam, kṛpīṭam, ghee, a sprout,
poison, piṣpala, pātāla, water, kambala,
the purifier, that which has six tastes, dried meat, tusita, and milk.
Sedimentary water is *kiṭṭima*; that which has diarrhea-like impurities is *sālūka*; that which smells of mud is *paṅkagandhika*; turbid water is *andha*; and very clear water is *kācima*.
— *Abhidhānacintāmaṇi-svopajñavṛtti* 4.
Even poison [is not poison]; even poison [is not poison]. (Bhāṣya)
Death, [the world] beyond,
wealth and so forth, trees, various types of elephants, stalks, flowers, and shrubs.
— Amarakośa 3.3.193
The meaning is "because of having hands";
[the word] *pīlu* is also [found as] *pra°* and *lupīlur api ya*.
Thus, in the *Vyāpibhāṣya* it says "vyāpi," whereas in the *Yājñavalkyasmṛti* it does not show [it] due to its abundance.

The word *hari* refers to Yama, Anila, Indra, Candra, Arka, Viṣṇu, Siṃha, Aṃśu, and Vājī; it also denotes a parrot, a snake, a monkey, and a frog. In the sense of "tawny," it is used for three genders.
In the *Bala* [Khaṇḍa], Rāma is described as blue, beautiful, and white in three [verses].
— Amarakośa 3.3.140
*Rāma* may denote a particular animal, Paraśurāma (the son of Jamadagni), Balarāma (the wielder of the plow), and Rāmacandra; it is also used as an adjective meaning white, bright, or beautiful.
— Viśvaprakāśa.
*Arjuna* refers to Kakubha, Pārtha, and the peacock of Kārtavīrya;
it may also mean "the only son of a mother" or, like other words, "white.
In the neuter gender, it denotes grass; *arjunī* refers to a disease of the eyes or a cow.
In the Uṣā, the Bāhudā river, and even in the Kuṭṭanī,
the earth itself—

thus, a single word such as "cow" (*go*), whose reality is known through scripture alone, possesses the power to indicate multiple meanings, just as the light of the sun performs the act of illuminating.
...like that which performs multiple functions, [the mind] operates toward each respective object...
association, dissociation, coexistence, opposition, and visibility; see page 127, lines 11–14.

Ṭippaṇī 56, Note 1: Meaning, context, indicative mark, proximity of another word, capability, propriety, place, time, gender, and accents and so forth [are the factors that determine the specific meaning].
"In the exclusion of the object by a word, they are the causes for the recollection of the specific. (Vākyapadīya 2.317;

318). Now, it might be argued: since [the particular] is not perceived in any way, and its own object being non-existent, there is merely the cessation of the absence of the universal, because of the non-contact with the distinctions of non-existence. (Compare page 705).

Now, if [the word] were merely the absence of the absence of its own referent, what would be the meaning of the word? In the case of "It is a tree, not a non-tree," since the non-trees and non-fires—the objects to be excluded by that word and by the mark (liṅga) of smoke—are not touched upon as distinct entities, and since the purpose there is a simple negation, only that [negation] itself would be understood;
no other object-entity such as a jar would be obtained through the exclusion of "tree."
"Thus, by mere hearing," and so forth:

by this stated principle, a single word such as "cow" (*go*), whose reality is known through mere hearing and which has not yet attained its internal divisions, possesses the capacity to indicate multiple meanings.
How is this so? The phrase beginning with "like a single sun" and ending with "possessing the power of action" summarizes the previously explained meaning; the sense is already understood.
It might be thought: "If one [word] performs multiple functions, there would be no apprehension of distinction, resulting in the undesirable consequence of non-discrimination.

This is not so. The two verses—beginning with *pratyarthavṛtti* and ending with *viśeṣasmṛtihetavaḥ*—have their meanings illustrated by the examples of *sakara-bhā* and so forth, respectively. They explain the delimitation of a single meaning based on different causes;
and by the inclusion of the word *ādi* ("etcetera"), they account for the delimitation of meanings produced by figurative (*gauṇa*) and primary (*mukhya*) senses, praise, censure, and so forth.
In the expression "Let the cow with a young calf be brought," the cow is understood as being qualified by its association with the calf;
other examples of this kind are to be understood from the commentary on page 56, note 1. Now, it might be argued, etc.

Now, another might say: "But has it not already been stated that for a mere collection of qualities, such as being one-eyed or lame, perception is impossible; and even if perception were possible, inference would be entirely impossible because [the object] has never been perceived in any way? Since this has been resolved from the very root, what further deliberation is there now as to whether perception might occur or not? For when the existence of its own specific object is established, the cessation of the mere absence of the universal form occurs without contact with the distinctions of non-existence—just as it is said, 'it is a tree, thus it is not a non-tree,' or 'it is fire, thus it is not a non-fire'—without contact with the distinctions of the non-trees or non-fires; nor indeed do distinctions of non-existence exist."
Therefore, exclusion (*apoha*) is the indicator even without the perception of the distinction between all non-existences; thus it is said [in the *Pra*]. (Compare: p. 652, l.
pṛ॰ 662 paṃ॰ 2; pṛ॰ 709 paṃ॰ 9: *syāt* is not present in the Ya manuscript. For comparison, see pṛ॰ 717 paṃ॰ 27.
There may also be the reading "of non-existence" (*vābhāvasya*) or "of the non-existence of [something]" (*prābhāvasya*);
[this is] by means of the observation of the beginning (*pra°*).

To this it is replied: Now, if you maintain that [the word-meaning] is merely the absence of the absence of its own referent, then what is the actual meaning of the word? Desiring to demonstrate that even here [in the case of "tree"] there is only the absence of an exclusion (apoha), he asks "tree," and so forth. The intended sense is as follows: in the inference for the sake of another (*parārthānumāna*), the word "tree" is like smoke as a logical mark (*liṅga*) with respect to its own referent; by these two, other exclusions—namely non-trees and non-fires in the form of distinct entities such as jars—are not touched. In that context, if the meaning were merely the negation of a possibility, namely "non-tree" in the sense of "it is not a tree," then only that much would be understood; however, that is not what is understood. This is the intended point.

In the statement "that which is other than a tree is a non-tree," no distinct entity such as a jar or the like is obtained through the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of the tree, because such another thing does not exist and is not intended to be expressed. Therefore, it is the tree itself that must be explained and intended; for how could the tree, being itself uncomprehended, be able to qualify a negation by saying, "the non-tree is my absence"? Since its own existence is only attained through the presence of the tree, it follows that "tree" means "it is not a non-tree"—that is to say, that which is the negation of a negation is the tree.

Consequently, since [the negation of non-existence] for things such as jars and cloths is merely the cessation of non-existence, it follows that they possess the status of being the referents of the word "tree. From what, then, could their *apoha* (exclusion) arise? Alternatively, there would be a total comprehension [of all things], such that through either verbal testimony or inference, one would have no further expectation regarding any other view; thus, specific statements and cognitions such as "tree" or "fire" would become meaningless, because the mere absence of non-existence is a single unity, and because there would be no objective basis for linguistic usage, inference, or discourse concerning distinctions—since such distinctions would not exist, just like a sky-flower.
To this it may be replied: nor indeed [is there] the entirety...

What then? Because it is related to itself; how could that [entity], being itself unapprehended, be able to qualify a non-existence—as in "non-tree" (meaning the absence of a tree) or "my absence"? It would be like a barren woman’s son qualifying a sky-flower. Why? Because that non-existence derives its very existence from a positive entity; being itself non-existent, how could it be a qualifier of what is non-existent? Furthermore, since in both cases—positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—it is accepted that things such as jars, which consist of differentiated forms, do not touch upon either the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) or the dissimilar instance (*asapakṣa*), nothing can be qualified by anything.
This word ends in the dual number.
And the *arthasūtra* for the two suffixes [matup and vatup]— is it a *prasajya-pratiṣedha*? Only the word "tree" (*vṛkṣa*) is to be explained.

How could that [non-existence], being itself unperceived, be able to qualify another non-existence, such as "my non-existence is not a tree"? For its own self-acquisition is obtained through the existence [of something else];
therefore, what is stated would be: "A non-tree is not [a non-tree]," meaning that which is the negation of non-existence is a tree.

Consequently, since trees are merely the cessation of the non-existence of jars, cloths, and so forth, they would attain the status of being the referents of the word "tree. How, then, could there be any *apoha* (exclusion) for them?

Alternatively, if the cognition were of every kind [simultaneously], then once there was no further desire for any other view, words or inference would become useless as specific verbal expressions and cognitions—such as "tree" or "fire"—because non-existence is merely a single absence; consequently, linguistic usage based on inference regarding distinctions would have no object, since it would have as its object a distinction that has not come into being, like a sky-flower. (Page 707, line 12; Page 719, line 19)
To this it may be replied: nor indeed [is there] the entirety...
What then? It is the non-tree entity related to itself [which is excluded], because it does not touch the state of being a tree.

Regarding the passage beginning with *tataśca* and so forth: from the reasoning stated here, this meaning of the word is established. When it is said, "A tree is not a non-tree," what is being said—or rather, what is implied—is that which begins with "the absence of absence" (*abhāvasya abhāvaḥ*). It would thus be stated that the tree is the absence of absence; there is nothing other than the cessation of absence. Consequently, since jars, cloths, and so forth consist merely in the cessation of their own absences, they would possess the status of being trees and the status of being the referents of the word "tree," just like a tree itself. How then could there be any exclusion (*apoha*) for them? For an exclusion of them would only occur upon contact with that [tree], such as when one says, "This is not a tree."
Thus, there would be an absence of apoha, and this is undesirable; this is what is being considered. (Variant readings: *sabhāvyeta* / *sabhāvya*).
Would there be "treeness" [in them]? Is it that "the tree does not exist in those hands," or is it that "the tree does not exist in the hand"? (Compare page 718, line 24).

Furthermore, in every way, if there were movement [of the term], then a tree or fire would be merely the absence of non-existence (*abhāvābhāvamātra*); it would not be perceived as being in contact with the distinctions between similar and dissimilar instances (*sapakṣāsapakṣabheda*). Consequently, there would be no desire for any further observation. And that being the case, from the word "tree" or from the inference from smoke, because of the mere absence of non-existence—namely, the state of being a tree or fire—which does not touch upon the unseen distinctions you have mentioned, the specific verbal cognition and expression "the tree is fire" would be rendered purposeless.
Why? Because there is unity in the mere absence of non-existence; this is the general reason for both inference for oneself and inference for others. "Like a sky-flower" is the example.

Alternatively, the reason is qualified: because [inference] lacks an objective basis for linguistic usage and inferential discourse regarding distinctions, since its object is a distinction that has not [ultimately] come into being.
That same example applies everywhere as a general case, because it is stated at the conclusion.

This is another type of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), namely: the conceptual construction that "there would be no understanding at all," because [the meaning] is obtained through phonetic conjunction; or that "there would be non-understanding" upon the utterance of the word "tree. Why [would there be] no understanding at all? Because of the absence of anything to be understood.
And there is an absence of an object to be traversed because words and inferences function solely with respect to the absence of an absence; thus, it might be argued [as follows],
etc.

Regarding the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) characterized by the absence of its own internal distinctions, the faults of infinity, impossibility, lack of connection, and the inability to denote were stated;

regarding the mere absence of the absence of a universal (*sāmānya*), the faults of the identity of all things, futility, and the non-existence of apoha were stated. Since neither of those two positions is accepted, the rebuttal is as follows: "Nor [is it] 'without remainder'... and so forth.

What then? [The author] resorts to an alternative position, considering it to be faultless: there is no fault because the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) functions through the perception of the general properties and their inseparable particulars belonging to either the tree or the fire with which [the term] is related, and through the non-perception of those things distinct from them. For this very reason, this is an inference of exclusion (*tadvyavacchedānumāna*) based on the non-perception [of the term] elsewhere than in its own correlates;
that in which it is observed is intended here as the correlate, but not by way of a relation of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāvitva*).

"Because it is not observed elsewhere" means because it is not observed in the absence of the object to be inferred (*anumeya*). For otherwise, one would have to say that the word "tree" and smoke are observed even in the absence of earth-substance and so forth in that object;

[but] the inference by exclusion (*vyavacchedānumāna*) occurs precisely where non-observation has been stated—namely, in the absence of a tree, i.e., in a non-tree, or in the absence of fire, i.e., in a non-fire. From that, there is the inference by exclusion: "it is not a non-tree," or "it is not a non-fire.
And by doing so, the inference of substanceness (*dravyatva*) and so forth from the word "tree" and from smoke becomes logically established.

Otherwise, however, because substances and so forth would also be distinct [from the subject], there would be the defects of the inference—namely, that its occurrence is not a property of the subject (*apakṣadharmatva*), that it is inconclusive (*anaikāntikatva*), that it is contradictory (*viruddhatva*), and that it is a non-inference (*anumānābhāva*).
Furthermore, upon abandoning the substance and so forth, its own object, which is invariably concomitant with it, would be impossible.
Therefore, the establishment of inference occurs through the non-perception [of the mark] in the absence of its own related [subject].

In that case, if the qualifiers such as "existence" (sattā) and so forth are the tree, or if the tree is those [qualifiers], then the referent of this word "tree" consists of a single being; for, like its own self, it is non-different from them. Consequently, the general properties (sāmānyadharma) such as substancehood (dravyatva) and the existence of the tree, which are inherent in it, as well as the particularities (bheda) such as the *śiṃśapā* tree and so forth, which are bound to it—since the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) functions through perception and contact with these [inherents] and through non-perception and non-contact with jars and the like, which are distinct from them, as well as with water and the like—the faults pertaining to both positions do not arise.
The relationship between the possible and the impossible (saṃbhava-asambhava-sambandha), Prabhāvakacaritra, p. 716, l.
On page 717, line 20,
and on page 717, line 17:

there is no fault, because the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) functions through the perception of general properties (*sāmānyadharma*) and their inseparable particulars (*tadanubandhibheda*), and through the non-perception of those things distinct from them.
For this very reason, this is an inference through the exclusion of others (*tadvyavacchedānumāna*) because it is not observed elsewhere than among its own correlates;

that in which it is observed is intended here as a correlate, but not by virtue of a relationship of inseparable connection (*avinābhāvitva*), since it is not observed in the absence of the object to be inferred. Otherwise, one would have to say that the word "tree" and smoke are observed even in the absence of earth-substance and the like in that object.

Inference by exclusion (*tadvyavacchedānumāna*) is that which was stated regarding non-perception: namely, in the case of the absence of a tree, [one infers] "it is not a non-tree," or in the case of the absence of fire, "it is not a non-fire. From this, inference by exclusion occurs—[concluding] "it is not a non-tree" or "it is not a non-fire. By establishing it in this way, the inference of substantiality (*dravyatva*) and so forth from the word "tree" and from smoke becomes logically tenable.

Otherwise, however, since substances and the like would also be distinct [from the subject], there would be the defects of the inference being equally [invalid] due to the fallacies of non-residence in the subject (*apakṣadharmatva*), inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*), contradictoriness (*viruddhatva*), and the non-existence of the inference itself.
If the substance were abandoned, its own object, which is invariably concomitant with it, would be impossible;
therefore, inference is established because [the sign] is not observed in the absence of that which is related to itself—this is the comparison, p. 652, l. 22.

The reading *svasambandhyabhāvādarśanāt* might also occur here, following the Bhāṣya manuscript; alternatively, *sambandhyabhāvādarśanāt* might also occur. If that is so, then if the qualifiers such as "existence" (*sattā*) and so forth are the tree, or if the tree is those [qualifiers], then the object consisting of this single being is, for this word "tree," non-different from its own self, just like its own nature; therefore, [it is not different] from substance and so forth, and from the tree.

For this very reason, the author states the passage from the Bhāṣya beginning with "ata eva cedam" and so forth, in order to demonstrate the adoption of this particular position. The commentary on this, found in the Ṭīkā, begins with "yatra dṛṣṭaḥ" and so forth, up to "na bhavatīti avṛkṣo 'nagnir vā," the meaning of which has already been explained.

And having established this, [the text continues] from "evam ca kṛtvā" up to "upapannaṃ bhavati": the inference of the concomitants—such as being a substance of earth (pṛthivī-dravyatva) and so forth—which are invariably connected with many [properties], is logical through the perception and touch of the tree and the smoke, [in the form]: "Because it is a tree, it is earth, a substance, and existent; and because it is smoke, it is like a tree and like fire.

However, [the text says] "otherwise," etc.: if there were absolute exclusion (atyantavyatireka) and thus an absence of relatedness, then because the concomitants such as substance and so forth would be entirely different, there would be the faults of the inference's non-existence, namely: being a non-property of the subject (apakṣadharmatva), being inconclusive (anaikāntikatva), and being contradictory (viruddhatva), due to its occurrence only in the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa).
Furthermore, there is the fault that when the substance and other concomitants are abandoned, the tree—which is inseparable from them—cannot possibly exist as its own referent;
consequently, the relationship between the signified object and the signifying word becomes untenable.

Therefore, the conclusion is stated: "Because of the absence of its own related [factors]," and so forth. Since the related entity is observed to exist when the other related factor exists, and since it is not observed to exist when the related factor is absent, the intended inference is established.
Page 652, line 4; page 652, line 18, etc. (Ya).
pṛ॰ 652 paṃ॰ 22: *vṛkṣavādāt* (Bhāṣya); *vṛkṣatvāt* (Yaśomitra)
Because of this [absence], it is not [the case that]...; therefore, this reading *sambandhy-abhāva* also appears correct, as it is seen in the commentary [to state]: "of another related object."
To this, the following reply is stated: "If that is so," and so forth.

If [the qualities] such as existence (*sattā*), substance (*dravya*), earth (*pṛthivī*), and so on—which are qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*)—are non-different from the tree, then they exist as the tree; the meaning is that they are simply the tree itself. Alternatively, the tree becomes those [qualities], and by that, they are qualified. Because of their identity in a single existence (*ekabhavanātman*), like Devadatta’s hand and so forth, this consequence follows. Regarding that single existence, it is said that the application [of the word] is "perception in that which possesses branches and so on. The meaning of this is that the object consisting of that single existence is the referent of this application of the word "tree."

What is it like? It is like its own self; that is to say, it is like the existence (*sattā*), substantiality (*dravyatva*), and so forth, of a tree, or like the existence, substantiality, and so forth, which constitute the very self of the tree, or like the nature of a single becoming (*ekabhavana*). Why? Because, according to the reasoning already stated, it is non-different from them, since the tree is not other than those [attributes], or because they are not other than it; this means that one observes the state of the substance and so forth as being the tree, and observes the state of the tree as being the substance and so forth. Since you do not admit the observation of the absence of substance and so forth when there is the observation of their presence, you have clearly accepted this *vidhi* (affirmative) doctrine by virtue of your acceptance of "becoming" (*bhavana*) as the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
Whatever exists does so only from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*);
by way of contrast (*vaidharmyeṇa*), it is like a flower in the sky.

Even that which is excluded is excluded from existence itself, in the ultimate sense, because it is an exclusion from existence—just like the exclusion of Devadatta and others, and not like the exclusion of a sky-flower.

Thus, when the nature of existence and non-existence is examined, the object remains established; and whether it be "that" or "other," if one adopts the theory of the exclusion of others (anyāpoha), the result would be either a total negation or a positive universal concomitance (anugama).

Alternatively, because it demonstrates the conceptual construction of an exclusive interpretation that fails to carry through [the argument], the scope of all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) is non-absolutism (*anekānta*); that very [non-absolutism] would thus result [from this].
Even a positive conceptual construction (*vidhi-vikalpa*) [is non-absolutist], because it apprehends an object consisting of existence and so forth;
why? Because it does not admit the observation of the absence of substance (*dravya*) and the other categories.

Since the perception of a tree is not admitted when the substance of earth is absent, nor is the perception of the existence of earth and so forth admitted when the tree is absent—because that [perception] would have the nature of the tree as its object—it follows that, by admitting that the single entity is the essence [of all], this is a very clear *vidhi-vāda* (affirmative theory) accepted by you. Even in the previous positions, the *vidhi-vāda* was evident, but in this one, it is extremely clear.

Why? Because of the acceptance that existence (*bhavana*) is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). For it is accepted that the referent of the word "tree" is, in ultimate reality, the nature of the single existence (*ekabhavana*) consisting of the existent substance, earth, clay, and so forth.

By stating "whatever comes into being," etc., he demonstrates that it is indeed existence; and by the contrast with a sky-flower, he demonstrates that even that which is intended as the excluded object (the non-existent) is, in ultimate reality, existence.

The reason is "from that which exists" (*bhavata eva vyāvṛtteḥ*). Since the genitive case-ending arises in the sense of the agent, it means "that which exists itself is excluded," just as Devadatta is excluded when he has struck against a mountain. Alternatively, the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is used according to the definition of the *apādāna* (ablative), meaning "from that which exists. Just as Devadatta is excluded from a mountain or the like—which is something that exists—it is not [excluded] like a sky-flower; thus, the doctrine of affirmation (*vidhivāda*) alone is made clear. Does this not result in the conclusion that "it is not non-self"? This is the meaning of this passage. *Bhāṣya*: The meaning of this is as follows.

Because you accept the perception of existence and do not admit the perception of the non-existence of substance and so forth, this doctrine of affirmation (*vidhi*) has been very clearly accepted by you; for you accept that the ultimate reality is becoming (*bhavana*),
such that whatever exists does so precisely through the ultimate reality of becoming.

If the reading were: "By way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyeṇa*), even that which is excluded, like a sky-flower—even that is [excluded] only because it exists in its ultimate sense of being, just like the exclusion of Devadatta and others, and not like a sky-flower or the like, such that 'whatever it may be' [is excluded]," then the root principle should be understood as: "Whatever exists, that exists only in its ultimate sense of being."

Thus, when determining the nature of existence and non-existence, the object remains as it is; yet, if one adopts the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), there would be a movement in every respect toward either the universal concomitance (*anugama*)— which is indeed affirmation—

or, by demonstrating the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) of an exclusive interpretation that fails to carry through, there would be a movement toward non-absolutism (*anekānta*) in all respects, and that alone would be the case.
Even the conceptual construction of a positive injunction (vidhi-vikalpa), because it grasps an object consisting of existence and so forth,
does not exclude [the exclusion of others] (apoha). *Abhyabhāṣa* (variant reading).
...due to the exclusion of [the state of being] an object,
whatever [is established], that is the primary [reality].

In this context, even the reading "yaḥ kaścit" (whoever) might occur; what follows from that? From that comes this: in the determination that "thus, being, it becomes," etc., the established meaning of this [word] is simply that it becomes in such a way—that is, it is both that and other. This is the adoption of *anyāpoha* (the exclusion of others). And when that exists, there may be a movement in every respect; he concludes that this is indeed the positive concomitance (*anugama*) or affirmation (*vidhi*).
The passage from page 707, line 12, to page 717, line 18 does not exist in the Bhāṣya manuscript;

alternatively, it begins with "anirvāhaka" and so forth: "However, those various conceptual alternatives that have been imagined regarding the theory of affirmation (vidhivāda) and the theory of exclusion of others (anyāpohavāda), being of an absolute nature, all fail to hold together and must therefore be disregarded."

By demonstrating that, the word "in every way" (*sarvathā*) becomes delightful through its thorough refinement; this is the summarized meaning (*piṇḍārtha*) of all prior investigation, intended to explain what that summarized meaning is.

If one asks, "What is that summarized meaning?", it is said: the word *vā* (or) has the sense of an alternative (*vikalpa*). The "course of alternatives" (*vikalpānāṃ gatiḥ*) means the knowledge, the certainty, and the final consummation of those very alternatives—namely, the certainty such as "in every way, a jar is a jar, yet it is also not a jar," and so forth.

What is that goal? It is non-absolutism (*anekānta*). That very [non-absolutism] would thus come to be; that same non-absolutism, capable of withstanding friction, would remain thus at the conclusion of inquiry, because it is the fruit of the complete purification of all logic. All conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), in brief, consist of affirmation (*vidhi*) and negation (*pratiṣedha*); he shows that both of these are grasped in this manner: "Even the conceptual construction of affirmation [is so], because it grasps an object consisting of existence and so forth"—this refers to affirmation; "even the conceptual construction of exclusion (*apoha*) [is so], because its purpose is the negation of others related to itself"—this refers to negation.
These two follow directly from your own words.
Therefore, the movement of all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) consists of *syādvāda*;

and that [syādvāda] consists of two one-sentence cognitions whose nature is the abandonment of absolutism regarding substance-aspect (*dravyārtha*) and mode-aspect (*paryāyārtha*). By means of the division of their respective objects, having subsumed the referent of the word, even the conceptual construction—because its purpose is the negation of others related to itself—is [established] from the perspective of substance-aspect...
...it would be "non-exclusion" (anapoha), and so forth;
yet there is no contradiction with that [position] for anyone, because [the Buddha] is the object of veneration and the refuge for all.
Consequently, this too has been poorly studied by the proponent of *anyāpoha*: "If the logical mark (*liṅga*) were to manifest [its object] as a positive form (*vidhirūpa*) like what is perceived,
there would either be no comprehension at all, or there would be comprehension in every respect" (Pramāṇasamuccaya 3).

14. As for what was stated—that this fault applies to inference by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*): because the word "tree" (*vṛkṣa*), together with its referent and so forth, is found to follow even in the case of *śiṃśapā* trees and others, therefore the word "tree" would also denote the *śiṃśapā* alone.

Now, if a doubt were to arise because [the term] is seen to apply to many things such as the *palāśa* tree and others, then—given that the properties of existence (*sattva*), substantiality (*dravyatva*), and earth-ness (*pārthivatva*) exist in the sense of "tree" and the word "tree" is common to them all—there would indeed be doubt. However, certainty is observed; for just as there is the expression of the object through the exclusion of non-trees (*avṛkṣa-nivṛtti*), the expression of "tree" occurs through the exclusion of what is not earth, what is not a substance, and what does not exist.

Just as the word "tree" (vṛkṣa), while having the exclusion of non-trees as its primary meaning, also functions toward its own referent through the exclusion of non-earthen things, so too the words "tree," "earthen," "substance" (dravya), and "existent" (sat) are, in their direct order, causes for determining three, two, and one referents respectively; in their reverse order, they are causes for doubt.

This is shown according to their respective numbers. The passage beginning with "from the perspective of substance" (*dravyārthataḥ*) has already been explained along with its examples, up to the point where it says "it may be that there is no exclusion" (*syādanapohaḥ*).

By the inclusion of the term "etc. (*ādi*), the intention is that whatever other matter has been proposed by others—such as the cause-and-effect relationship between the all-pervasive and the non-all-pervasive—is likewise merely an example of this [principle].

The passage beginning with "na ca tena" and ending with "sarveṣām api" serves as a demonstration of the status of Syādvāda as the supreme lord of all doctrines; its meaning has already been explained in the section on the refutation of the extremist views (ekāntavāda).
The reading "for the purpose of making known" (*-dākhyāpanārthaḥ*) might also be possible here; furthermore,
even a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) has the purpose of negating other things related to itself.
From the perspective of substantial reality (*dravyārtha*),
there may be non-exclusion (*anapoha*), and so forth.
Furthermore, there is no contradiction with anyone regarding that [Buddha], because he is to be venerated and is the refuge for all;
see page 436, lines 3, 18–21.
Therefore, this too has been poorly studied by the proponent of *anyāpoha* (exclusion of others):—
"If the logical mark were to manifest [the object] through a positive form, as in the case of direct perception,
there would either be no comprehension at all, or there would be comprehension in every respect. (Pramāṇasamuccaya 3.14)

As for what was stated—that this fault applies to inference by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*): because the term "tree" (*vṛkṣa*) occurs along with its referent and so forth even in the case of *śiṃśapā* trees and others, therefore the word "tree" might denote the *śiṃśapā* alone;

yet, since it is also seen in many other cases such as the *palāśa* tree, doubt arises. If this were so, then since existence (*sattva*), substantiality (*dravyatva*), and earth-ness (*pārthivatva*) exist in the referent "tree," doubt would arise due to the word "tree" being common to them all; however, certainty is observed, because the word "tree" denotes the object through the exclusion of non-trees, just as it denotes the object through the exclusion of non-earth, non-substance, and non-existence.

For just as the word "tree" (vṛkṣa), while having the exclusion of non-trees (avṛkṣa-nivṛtti) as its single primary meaning, also functions toward its own referent through the exclusion of non-earthen things (apārthiva-vyāvṛtti), so too the words "tree," "earthen," "substance" (dravya), and "existent" (sat)—when taken in their direct order—are the causes for the determination of three, two, and one meanings respectively; when taken in reverse order, they are the causes of doubt. This is the comparison. (Page 652, Line 23). If this is the case, the following might also serve as the root [of the argument]: why does the determination [of a specific meaning] arise regarding existence, substantiality, earthenness, and so forth, within the referent of "tree"?
See page 721, line 14;

for just as the words "tree," "earthen," "substance," and "existent" are, in their direct order, causes for the ascertainment of three, two, and one object respectively, so too, in their reverse order, they would be causes for doubt—this reading might also be applicable here.

Therefore, he refutes this verse by means of an extended application (*atideśa*) according to the meaning already stated, showing that even this [position] of the proponent of "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*) is poorly studied; for since the mere exclusion of others has already been refuted and the comprehension of word-meanings through the power of perception alone has already been explained, any further refutation of the doctrine of absolute affirmation (*ekānta-vidhi-vāda*) at the end would be as futile as illuminating what is already illuminated, especially since it concludes with the *syādvāda*. Thus, wishing to refute the collection of faults raised by the opponent against the proponent of affirmation (*vidhivādin*), he sets forth the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).

Since the word "tree" is observed even in the case of *śiṃśapā* trees through the context of the meaning—such as "the tree is being made into a bed"—and through the proximity of other words, it would follow that the word "tree" alone could denote all *śiṃśapā* trees in every respect. However, this is undesirable, because the isolated word does not convey [the specific meaning];
see page 652, line 23; page 127, lines 11–14; and note 1 on page 56.
"...by means of [the words] *adhyādi* and *śiṃśapādi*, [there is] also [the cognition] regarding *śiṃśapā* and so on.

Here, it appears that the reading "*adibhiḥ śiṃśapādibhiḥ śiṃśapā*" has been doubled. Now, with the words "in many," etc., he who maintains the theory of *anyāpoha* (exclusion of others) anticipates the position of the opponent.

Anticipating the objection that "this word 'tree' (vṛkṣa) is observed even in many things such as the *palāśa* tree and others; therefore, which among these is intended?"—thus giving rise to doubt due to its commonality—the proponent of *anyāpoha* (exclusion of others) would state the fault in that case as well, beginning with "If this were so," and so forth. [The opponent asks: "In the referent of the word 'tree,' existence (*sattva*), substantiality (*dravyatva*), and earth-ness (*pārthivatva*) are observed; since a determination is seen among these, this [argument] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

By what logic is this so? [The proponent replies: "By the force of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), because the word 'tree' denotes its object through the exclusion of non-trees, just as it denotes its object through the exclusion of non-earth, non-substance, and non-existence."

And the description of the accumulation of qualities according to this principle—namely, "just as in the case of a tree," etc.—is already explained up to the point where it says "the causes of doubt" (saṃśayahetavaḥ). (Comparison—p. 652, l. 24; Comparison—p. 652, l. 24)
"Certainty is not [derived from] views"—this is the comparison (tulanā), page 653, line 12.
Here we say: your pride regarding virtues and faults arises from attachment to your own position.

Furthermore, this is an advantage in inference by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*): because the word "tree" is observed in instances such as the *śiṃśapā* tree together with [the properties of] substance, etc., through the force of what has been perceived, certainty arises; otherwise, there would be doubt alone, since inference proceeds according to what has been observed.

And just as the state of being a tree is understood from the word "tree" as being inseparable from the existence of the object "tree," so too are earthiness, substantiality, and existence understood, for the existence of a tree is never observed without them.

By their affirmative nature and by the very capacity for perception, the words *vṛkṣa* (tree), *pārthiva* (earthen), *dravya* (substance), and *sat* (existent) are, in direct order (*ānulomyena*), causes for the determination of three, two, and one objects respectively; in reverse order (*prātilomyena*), they are causes of doubt. Let it be understood thus.

Even in a case where a *śiṃśapā* tree is perceived as indeterminate, there is non-apprehension due to the non-perception of its specific qualities, and apprehension due to the perception of its specific qualities,
just as in the case of an undifferentiated part.
...likewise, from the word "tree"...
...there is doubt;
however, we say here that this [notion] of "merit" and "defect" arises from attachment to one's own position—this is the explanation.

Furthermore, in the case of inference by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), such as "this is a merit," certainty occurs because [the mark] has been observed in *śiṃśapā* trees and the like together with the object, the context, specific qualifiers, and so forth, due to its very power of being perceived; for without those, it has not been observed, and thus there is doubt from the mere [mark] alone. What is the reason? Because inference proceeds according to what has been observed.

The object and so forth are indeed particulars, just like a *śiṃśapā* tree; for it is precisely because one does not perceive a particular that doubt arises regarding even a *palāśa* tree due to its belonging to the common genus "tree. However, certainty occurs with respect to that which is accompanied by a particular, because that which is devoid of a particular has never been perceived.

As for what is also said—"Why does certainty arise regarding [properties] such as existence (*sattva*), substantiality (*dravyatva*), and earthiness (*pārthivatva*)?"—in that case too, it is solely by the force of perception (*dṛṣṭabala*). And this is exactly how it is with the meaning of "tree" and so forth, up to the point where it is said "because the coming-into-being of the tree itself is not observed. What is meant is this: just as a tree does not come into being without its own objective coming-into-being (*svārthabhavana*), and thus the coming-into-being of that [tree] is understood from the word "tree," so too, because "treeness" does not come into being without earthiness, substantiality, and existence, earthiness, substantiality, and existence are understood just like the understanding of the coming-into-being of treeness, since that [treeness] is not observed at all without them.

Furthermore, as for the claim that from the word "tree" (*vṛkṣa*) there is the comprehension of three objects—earth-substance (*pārthiva-dravya*), existence (*sattva*), and tree; from the word "earthly" (*pārthiva*) the comprehension of two objects—substance and existence; and from the word "substance" (*dravya*) the comprehension of existence—and that, whether in reverse order starting from "existence" (*sat*) or in forward order through the subsequent terms, doubt arises from each preceding term—that too has already been explained by the demonstration that the words "tree," "earthly," "substance," and "existent" function in forward order, etc., up to the point where they are causes of doubt. This is because perception itself is the cause of both certainty and doubt, and it is by means of this [perception] that [the process occurs].
The passage contained within this is not present in the manuscript Ya because it has been lost;
"artha-ādi" refers to the meaning, context, indicative mark, and so forth.

The concluding summary of what has been stated, beginning with "Thus it should be understood," [is as follows]: from the word *vṛkṣa* (tree), when accompanied by context and other factors, there arises [the cognition] of the reality of the *śiṃśapā*-tree-ness, which is distinct from objects such as the *dhava* tree, just as from the word *śiṃśapā* there arises [the cognition] of that which consists of a particular, due to the perception of a particular.
Here, a certain reading appears to be truncated.
Regarding the statement "from the reality of the tree [arises] the cognition of the śiṃśapā," etc., which is not necessarily restricted:

this lack of restriction—namely, that upon the utterance of the word "tree" there is sometimes the cognition of a *śiṃśapā* and sometimes the non-cognition of it—is due to the non-perception of the particularity; through the perception of the particularity, there is cognition.

In this regard, the illustration is as follows: just as the previously described perception concerning smoke—beginning with "the undifferentiated part" (*avibhātaikadeśa*) and so forth—leads to doubt, whereas a specific [perception] leads to certainty, such is the analogy for the subject at hand; namely, that from the word "tree" and so forth, up until the point of doubt. But by what logic is this so? He explains that: it is according to the same logic as the observation of its existence (*tadbhāvadarśananyāyavat*). Just as was previously described—that the very place, consisting of fire and smoke, being perceived through its own presence (*tadbhāvena*), establishes itself by itself through its own nature, and so forth—the same applies here as well.
"Without doubt," and so forth;
the description [of this] is as previously stated;
it is distinguished by the *prāya*.
In the case of "deśa," "vāk," "agni," and so forth,

as well as in the case of "tree-ness" (*vṛkṣatva*)— which is observed in a positive concomitance (*anulomya*) with the three [higher genera] such as "earth-ness" (*pṛthivītva*), with "earth" (*pṛthivī*) through "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) and "existence-ness" (*sattva*), and with "substance" (*dravya*) through "existence-ness" (*sattva*), and is not so observed in a negative concomitance (*prātilomya*)— there arise certainty (*nirṇaya*) and doubt (*saṃśaya*).

Now, one might think: these two [alternatives] are not tenable; for from the observation [of commonality], there would be either no distinction between the two sides or a certainty [on one side]. In my view, however, they are tenable because of their inequality, since activity and non-activity in the absence of one's own specific referent are the causes of doubt. For instance, words such as "tree" are causes of doubt, because even in the absence of their own specific referent (the tree), they apply to things like the *palāśa* tree. On the other hand, words such as "śiṃśapā" do not apply to the *palāśa* even in the absence of their own specific referent. Thus, there is a difference.

The causes of certainty, however, pervade the parts of the tree and the objects associated with them; for they do not function in the absence of their own object, because perception itself constitutes both the general rule (*utsarga*) and its exception (*apavāda*), as the entity [in question] is not uniform—just like the perception of the common property of height in a post or a person, or the specific details of a bird’s roosting or a cloth being tied.
But was it not said: "Because it is not observed in non-trees and so forth, the inference that excludes them is the expression of its own object" (*Pramāṇasamuccayavṛtti* 5)?
34. This being so, where is that vision? Let it be seen on page 650, line 20.

The phrase "in this way, of the nature of being a tree," and so forth, is the conclusion of the present topic. Although the nature of being a tree (*vṛkṣatva*) occurs equally in specific instances such as the *śiṃśapā* tree and in general categories such as earth (*pṛthivī*), because it occurs together with its own specific object, it is understood through the three [categories] of earth, substance (*dravya*), and existence (*sattva*) in a forward order (*ānulomyena*). Specifically, it is understood as "earth" by means of earth, substance, and existence; as "substance" by means of substance and existence; and as "existence" by means of existence alone, since it is observed in that way in the forward order. However, doubt regarding subsequent categories such as existence arises from the lack of observation in the reverse order (*prātilomyena*). Thus, the meaning is established up to the point of certainty and doubt.
The summary of the subject at hand has already been explained; thus, there is a connection with what is to be said next:
*vṛttaṃ vṛttaṃ bhā॰ vṛttaṃ vṛttaṃ ya*.
If [it is argued that] there is only one *pra* in *satve*, or only one *sattve*?
Then, with the words "if he should think," etc., [the author] raises the objection representing the opponent's view.

Therefore, these two—certainty and doubt—are not tenable, because the perception of a tree occurs in both cases without distinction between a *dhava* and a *śiṃśapā*; thus, there would have to be either certainty or [the absence of] certainty.

In my view, however, since the term functions in the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) while its own referent (*svārtha*) is absent, doubt is appropriate when it does not function [toward that referent], and certainty is appropriate when it does function; why? Because the functioning and non-functioning toward the absence of one's own referent are unequal; for those two—the functioning and non-functioning toward the absence of the own-referent—are respectively the causes of doubt and certainty.

He explains this: words such as "tree" (vṛkṣa) are causes of doubt because they apply to things like the *palāśa* tree even in the absence of their own specific referent, the *śiṃśapā*. Likewise, words such as "existent" (*sat*) are causes of doubt because they apply to qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth even in the absence of their own specific referents, such as substance (*dravya*). On the other hand, words that are causes of certainty—such as those denoting the parts of a tree like branches (*śākhā*) which pervade them, or properties like being made of earth (*pārthiva*), being earthen (*mṛd*), or being a substance (*dravyatva*)—do not apply in the absence of their own referents; therefore, by the power of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), they are causes of certainty.

And this is not so, because perception itself consists of both generalization (*utsarga*) and exception (*apavāda*). For why is it that the perception of "tree-existence" alone, when applied generally to *palāśa*, *śiṃśapā*, and other trees, leads to doubt, whereas the perception restricted to "śiṃśapā-existence," being an exception, leads to certainty? It is because the entities are unequal; for the specific entities called *śiṃśapā* and *palāśa* are mutually unequal. This is because the general tree-existence is subordinate to the universal [of "tree"] due to its dependence on them, according to the principle already stated.

What is it like? It is like the example beginning with "a post or a person," up to "like seeing. Just as verticality, which is a common property (*sāmānya*), is a cause for doubt—[thinking] "it might be a post" or "it might be a person"—whereas the presence of a bird's nest is a cause for certainty that "it is indeed a post" because of its specific nature, or the binding of a garment is [a cause for certainty] that "it is indeed a person"; in exactly the same way, even among trees such as the *śiṃśapā*, [the common property of] verticality is [perceived] from seeing alone. (Page 614, Line 4; Bhāṣya)
Here he says: "But has it not been stated," and so forth.

For the absence of a tree and the like is indeed "non-tree" (*avṛkṣādi*); non-perception occurs precisely therein. Therefore, that which is being excluded—namely, that it is not a non-tree—is itself the expression of its own meaning.
This being the case, where is that perception which you desire? For, in this way, the establishment of perception itself proceeds from non-perception.

If perception (*darśana*) were not admitted, then in the case of "a tree," only the absence of a non-tree would have been stated; consequently, this very non-perception [of a non-tree] would mean the absence of the non-tree itself. But how could there be that non-perception of a non-tree? For such non-perception is pervaded by the perception of the tree itself. Therefore, it is perception alone that is thus established.

If it is argued that "non-perception" refers to not seeing [the object] as something other than its father or a tree— that is, as a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)— we say no; for, as previously stated,
it is that which establishes the definitive arrangement [of the relationship].
For while the tree stands, if there were the perception "it is not a tree," when would that [perception] ever occur for you?
...And that [universal] is certainly not accepted [as the word-meaning].

However, if the emphasis were on a positive injunction (*vidhi*), then the subsequent becoming of "earthness" and so forth would have to be brought about by the injunction for the cognition of the becoming of a "tree"; yet, because the entity is not uniform due to general rules and exceptions (*utsarga-apavāda*) regarding the perception of its essence, doubt and certainty would fail to be established. But such perception does not exist;

for we, considering the defects of infinity, deviation (*vyabhicāra*), and so forth in the position of perception, postulate that the meaning of words such as "tree" is the absence of non-trees and the like, in order to establish non-perception. This is because perception itself is absent, because it is untouched by those defects, and because mere non-perception is undifferentiated.
The reading "vyavacchedānumānam" (inference by exclusion) appears correct here; compare page 650, line 20:
"tatobhāḥ nanvadarśanād darśanasyaiva siddhirevam" (But is it not the case that from non-perception, the perception itself is established in this way?).

If perception (*darśana*) were not admitted, then in the case of "tree," only the absence of non-trees would have been stated; consequently, this very non-perception [of non-trees] would mean that non-trees themselves are absent there. How then could there be non-perception of non-trees, since such non-perception is pervaded by the perception of the tree itself? Therefore, it is perception alone that is thus established.
If it is argued that "non-perception" refers to not seeing [the object] as one would not see a father or a tree, [we reply: no, for— as already stated— it is that which establishes the distinction.
For while the tree stands, if there were the perception "it is not a tree," when would that [perception] occur for you?
...and that is indeed not accepted;

however, if the injunction (*vidhi*) is primary, then the subsequent becoming of earthness and so forth— which is to be brought about by the injunction for the cognition of the becoming of a tree— is [the object], whereas in the view that it is identical with that [tree], there is no observation of a distinct alternative (*apakṣa*).

To this it is replied: "Now, as for the argument beginning with 'because of non-perception' (*adarśanāt*), surely the establishment of perception itself follows from the non-perception of non-perception. He explains this: if perception—meaning positive concomitance (*anvaya*) or affirmation (*vidhi*)—is not admitted, then in the case of the word "tree," only the absence of a non-tree would be expressed, and there would be no such thing as a "tree" at all.

What follows from this? From this, it follows that non-perception itself is "non-tree," meaning it is simply the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). Consequently, as previously stated regarding things like "sky-flowers" and so forth, nothing at all would have been said; for if "tree" were merely the absence of "non-tree," then since everything would be a mere absence, the absence of the "non-tree" itself would have become the tree. How, then, could there be the non-perception of the "non-tree"? This is because the non-perception of the "non-tree" is pervaded by the very perception of the tree. Furthermore, the establishment of the non-perception of the "non-tree" occurs solely through the power of perceiving the tree; and from the perception of the tree, the establishment arises that "this is a tree" and "this pot and so forth are non-trees"—not when [the tree] is unperceived.
Therefore, it is only through perception (*darśana*) that this is established, not through non-perception (*adarśana*).
As for the objection beginning with "But [it is] beginningless," etc.,
see the comparison on page 716.

If it is argued that "not seeing non-trees" is the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), just as [one says] "not seeing one's father": *staddarśa* (pra), *vṛkṣāvṛkṣadarśa* (ya), *apitṛvadavṛkṣādarśanaṃ vyatireka iti cet*.

It might be thought: "Every father other than [a specific] father is [excluded]," and so forth, as previously stated; this, however, is not the case. As stated before, there would be a perception here too of that which is similar to a father. If there were no such perception, then—as previously explained—the logical inconsistency remains. For it is by the force of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) that the determination is established: "This is a tree; this other thing, such as a jar, is not a tree. Only when something is perceived through affirmation (*vidhi*) could there be a non-perception characterized by the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*); it cannot be otherwise.

This treatise is intended to demonstrate this point—beginning with "establishing a rule" (*vyavasthākārī*) and continuing up to "for when the tree is the object to be enjoined, if the perception were [defined] as 'not a tree,' this would follow; but since the perception is connected through a positive injunction (*vidhi*), this is established"—this text shows that. However, regarding the position of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), there is the consequence of an undesirable result: "But when will that be for you? and so on, up to "and that is certainly not accepted by you. By changing the case endings, it follows that if there is exclusion from jars and the like, the tree and so forth are established; and if the tree and so forth are established, the exclusion from jars and the like is established—thus there would be a mutual infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Lest that [undesirable consequence] occur, one must seek an establishing perception (*darśana*) by means of a positive injunction (*vidhi*), [which functions] as the excluded and the excluder between "tree" and so forth as existent, and "non-tree" and so forth as non-existent;
[as stated on] page 708, line 6 and page 709,
line 3.
"paṭādivyāvṛttisiddhi" (Bhāṣya) / "paṭādivyāvṛttyasiddhi" (Yaśomitra).
It is a universal (sāmānya), because it is the state of both the excluded and the non-excluded,
or of that which is excluded and that which is not excluded.

But how is it that there is no such fault when affirmation (*vidhi*) is predominant? It is said: When affirmation is predominant, [the argument] from "earthness" and so forth as the subsequent [reason], up to "like its own self," shows that trees, earth, substances, and existents—such as trees, *śiṃśapā* trees, crooked ones, flowering ones, roots, trunks, branches, and so on—are observed through affirmation as both prior and subsequent entities. Furthermore, the existence of earth is necessarily brought about by the rule of the cognition of the existence of trees, because it consists of trees, because it is of the nature of a tree, and because it is non-different from it, just like the very self of a tree.

Likewise, the prior existence of a tree and so forth is to be established by the cognition of the subsequent existence of a *śiṃśapā* and so forth, because it has that as its essence and is not other than it, just like the roots and so forth of a tree. However, when exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) is primary, if "earthen-ness" and so forth are not established through perception, then a tree would not be a tree at all, because it is not established as earthen, just like water;
likewise, being earthen would not exist at all because it is not established as a substance (*dravya*), just like a quality (*guṇa*).

In this way, a substance would not be a substance because it is unestablished as existence, like a sky-flower; likewise, even that which exists is not truly existent because it is unestablished as a substance and so forth, since it is non-different from that [existence], like the very nature of a tree. Furthermore, the fact that earthiness and the other qualities possess the nature of the tree was established previously, as was the case for the subsequent states such as the roots and so on; therefore, when their identity as a single essence is established, the proof becomes most effective.

Likewise, the becoming of the earth is itself the becoming of the substance (*dravya*), and the becoming of the substance is itself the becoming of existence (*sat*). Thus, the proof beginning with "prior to the tree, etc. establishes that [the prior state] possesses the properties of the subsequent becoming by way of its opposite; for it does not exceed that [substance], as it is not other than it. The example is "the root of the tree, etc.": the tree is that which is established by the rule of cognition regarding the subsequent becoming of the *śiṃśapā* and so forth, because it has that as its nature. Just as the tree is seen to exist precisely as a tree through the properties of roots, trunk, leaves, and so on, so too the tree exists precisely as a tree through the nature of the *śiṃśapā* and so forth.

Thus, inference based on what is perceived as a positive form (vidhi-rūpa) is appropriate when the positive aspect is predominant; and its verbal expression is likewise appropriate because it is non-different from that [positive reality], just as a tree is non-different from its own nature.

Similarly, the prior existence of a tree and so forth is to be established by the cognition of the positive form of the subsequent existence of a *śiṃśapā* tree and so forth, because it is of that same essence and non-different from it, just like the roots and other parts of the tree.

But if exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) were predominant, then just as in the case of [the previous] perception, since earthiness and so forth would not be established, a tree would simply not be a tree because it is not established as having earthiness, like water;
likewise, being earthly would not exist at all because it is not established as having substantiality (*dravyatva*), like a quality (*guṇa*);
and similarly, a substance would not be a substance because it is not established as having existence (*sattva*), like a sky-flower.
Likewise, even that which exists is not [ultimately] existent, because it is not established as a substance (*dravya*) and so forth; [this is] because of the non-existence of entities (*bhāva*).
Here, there might also be the reading "the roots and so forth of existence" (*bhāvanām mūlādīni*).
However, in your view where exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) is primary, there is a fault as follows:

just like [the case of] "seen," if earthiness and so forth are not established, then for one who does not accept that the becoming of a tree is simply the becoming of a single essence consisting of an earthly substance, according to our view, the tree would not be a tree at all, because it is not established as being earthy, just like water; for just as water, not being established as earthy, is not a tree, so too the tree would not be a tree.

If it is argued that "the earthy substance would not be earthy because its status as a substance is unestablished; just as a quality is not earthy because its status as a substance is unestablished, so too the earthy would be non-earthy.

Likewise, a substance would not be a substance because its existence is unestablished, like a sky-flower"—thus making the [alleged] non-establishment of the existence of the earthy substance itself unestablished—[we reply: no, because when exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) is primary, there is a difference [in meaning]; for even the differences associated with their own referents are excluded, since the word-meaning consists in the absence of the absence of its own referent.

If it is argued that this is the fault of contradicting common consensus (*prasiddhi-virodha*), [we reply: the fault belongs to you alone because you admit the primacy of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti-prādhānya*), not to me.
Thus, even though it exists, it is "not existent," because it is unestablished as a substance (*dravya*) and so forth, like a sky-flower; this remains the case.

In this way, each preceding [state] would not possess its own nature, because it has not become [the state of] the subsequent form, just like fire; thus, the undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭāpādana*) is established as explained.
In this context, the reading might also be *anuvartibhedā*;
[the text] reads *śabdārthatvābhāvāt*.

As for what was also stated: "By means of the qualities, odor, fragrance, and its specific varieties, there is a successive exclusion of non-substance and so forth, through an increase of one [term] at a time, as in the case of the *utpala* and other [lotuses]," (*Pramāṇasamuccaya* 2).

14. Thus, when exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) is predominant, the exclusion of non-substances (*adravya*) and so forth by means of "possessing qualities" (*guṇavattva*) and the rest is appropriately joined with the increase of one [successive term] (pṛ.
727, l. 12). That too connects with this [term] by means of the word *tadapi*;
[the sequence is] by means of "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*), "odor" (*gandha*), "fragrance" (*saurabhya*), and its specific varieties, respectively.

That which was stated by Diṅnāga in the second chapter, on inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*), of the *Pramāṇasamuccaya* along with its commentary (*vṛtti*), is here presented after being translated from the Tibetan version into Sanskrit:
"An object possessing manifold properties is not understood in its entirety through a logical mark (*liṅga*).
Rather, it is only the exclusion of what is concomitant (*anubandhin*) that is cognized from another [mark]. (2.12½)
Whatever specific qualities fire possesses, such as its brilliance and sharpness, although they exist, they are not inferred by smoke because of their deviation [from it].

However, those concomitant properties—such as its being a substance (*dravyatva*) or a quality (*guṇatva*), and so forth—in the absence of which fire does not exist, are indeed cognized through their exclusion from non-substances and the like. Just as the mere exclusion of fire from what is not fire is cognized in accordance with its own connection, so too is it the case: this [fire] is never seen in what is not fire, yet it is seen elsewhere, sequentially through its being a quality, its having the smell of fragrance, and its specific varieties.

The exclusion of non-substances and so forth occurs through the successive addition of one [attribute] at a time, as in the case of "lotus" and so on. (2.13½) In that regard, by its nature as a quality (*guṇatva*), it excludes what is not a substance; by its nature as odor (*gandhatva*), it excludes what is not earthy and what is not a substance; and by its specific nature as fragrance (*saurabhya*), it excludes what is not fragrant and what is not a lotus.
Otherwise, [the distinction would not be established].
If the logical mark (*liṅga*) were to manifest [its object] in a positive form (*vidhirūpeṇa*) like that which is perceived,
there would either be no comprehension at all, or there would be comprehension everywhere.
In the *Viśālāmalavatī*, the reading "it would not exist because it is not seen everywhere" (*sarvatrādarśanān na syāt*) appears to be the one adopted.
And if smoke, having been observed in fire in a certain way, were to manifest it at a later time exactly as it was seen, it would never manifest it otherwise;
for just as it has never been observed anywhere in what is not fire, so too it has never been observed in every instance of fire.
Furthermore, if it manifests it exactly as it was seen, then specific qualities such as brilliance and intensity would also be perceived.

Since it is manifested by the negation of non-fire precisely in its general form, therefore it is understood that even through affirmation, only that same form of it is seen, and not its specific form.

Even if there were a generality, it would not be perceived as distinct from its substrates due to the non-perception of those substrates; or rather, the distinction [of particulars] is not seen because they are perceived together in one place. (2.15½)
First of all, "fire-ness" (agnitva) is not a generality (sāmānya) distinct from fire;
even if it were existent, its perception would be impossible because none of its substrata are perceived.
It is observed that for things such as "duality" and so forth, which are common to many, there is no apprehension when their substrata are not apprehended.
For some proponent of similarity, that [similarity] does not belong even to the object of perception.
Now, if the universal were grasped in its entirety even when only one of its substrata is perceived, then it would be manifold like its substrata;
and just as an object of inference is understood through a certain part [of its evidence].
The meaning is that, for that long, there is no possibility of another [mark] in the fire;
likewise, the "limb" (aṅga) is that form by which it does not deviate from the possessor of the mark (liṅgin).
By that very [aspect], even a property with multiple attributes causes [the object] to be known, but not by others.

(2.16½) Even smoke causes [fire] to be known only by that aspect through which it does not deviate from fire, such as its being smoke or its being pale; not by [its being] a substance (*dravyatva*) and so forth, because of deviation.
And it has been said: "Those [attributes] also are understood by means of the mark (*liṅga*) which are invariably concomitant (*anubandhin*) with the bearer of the mark (*liṅgin*)."
But the specific qualities of that very same deviant [reason] are not apprehended.

However, meanings connected with a mark (liṅga) do not lead to the comprehension of the bearer of the mark (liṅgin) due to deviation; rather, it is the specific particulars (viśeṣa), once perceived, that are the conveyors [of the meaning].
These are the two intermediate verses (antaraśloka), [numbered] 18 1/2
