Those specific features which are invariably concomitant with the possessor of the mark (liṅgin) are also understood through the mark; however, those very [features] that are deviant are not understood.
But the objects that are invariably concomitant with the mark cause the understanding of the possessor of the mark, not [the understanding of] the mark itself.

"Because of deviation, however, the particulars (viśeṣas), when perceived, are the conveyors [of the meaning]. (2.18½) These two intermediate verses were composed by Jinendrabuddhi; his extensive commentary, *Viśālāmalavatī*, is also presented here after being translated from its Tibetan version back into Sanskrit: "The exclusion of the concomitant (*anubandhin*)": by means of that part which is concomitant—that is, related—by which fire is cognized, the exclusion or differentiation (*vyāvṛtti*) of that [part], such as substantiality (*dravyatva*), from the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) or from anything else, is what is cognized.
If it is asked, "What then are these concomitant particulars? [the answer is: "In the absence of which fire does not exist," and so forth.

Now, since smoke is that which makes [fire] manifest, one ought rather to say, "In the absence of which smoke does not exist. If it is asked why it is stated in this way, there is no fault, for this very same meaning is expressed by means of this formulation.
To explain: in the absence of that in the absence of which fire does not exist, smoke also certainly does not exist.
Alternatively, the phrase "those which are concomitants" should be construed as "concomitants of smoke alone.
To demonstrate precisely those which are concomitants of smoke alone, he says: "In the absence of which," and so forth;
those in whose absence fire does not occur are indeed the concomitants of smoke.

Regarding the point that the exclusion [of a thing] from others is understood through its concomitants, he provides an example: "Just as [the cognition] of fire [is understood] as the mere exclusion from non-fire," and so forth.
To the question, "From what is this mere exclusion understood, and not a specific property? he says: "Because of conformity with its own relation," and so forth.
This is a productive cause (*kāraka-hetu*), not an indicative mark (*liṅga*).
To explain: by the phrase "this [is smoke]," he expresses its conformity with that [fire];

by the phrase "not seen anywhere in what is not fire," he indicates the predominance of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) through its non-observation in all dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*); and by the word "ca" in the phrase "and seen elsewhere," he indicates the non-predominance of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), as this suggests that there is also non-observation in some cases.

Thus, since positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is merely figurative while exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) is the primary relation—and that [exclusion] is possible only through a universal (*sāmānya*) and not through a particular (*viśeṣa*)—therefore, in accordance with that [nature], it is by way of exclusion that one understands here: "This is fire alone; it is not non-fire. Thus, only the mere exclusion from non-fire is cognized, not a particularity.

And just as the relation exists by way of "fire-ness" (*agnitva*), so too it exists by way of "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*), "quality-ness" (*guṇitva*), and so forth; therefore, their exclusion from non-substance-ness and the like is also what is cognized.

He states another reason for the fact that a logical mark (*hetu*) is a means of cognition only by way of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*): "By means of quality-ness (*guṇatva*), odor (*gandha*), fragrance (*saurabhya*), and its specific qualities," and so forth.
The phrase "by the increase of one" means "by the increase of each one individually.

By means of "quality-ness," there is the exclusion of non-substances (*adravya*); thus, the exclusion of non-substances from things such as blue lotuses (*utpala*) is established by the statement, "This is a substance because it possesses quality-ness."
For instance—that [increase] is not observed anywhere in a non-substance (adravya), but is observed in a substance (dravya).

Here, in the first [definition], there is the exclusion of the non-substance; it is stated as "from the non-substance by virtue of being a quality" (guṇatvena adravyāt) for the purpose of demonstrating that which, in relation to which the exclusion is made through the single increase of odor (gandha), so that there is no increase in one [of the other qualities].
For this very reason, even *guṇatva* (the state of being a quality) possesses a contributory role (*aṅgabhāva*) toward the exclusion [of substances] by means of "one increase" (*ekavṛddhi*).
If, by that [term], the exclusion of non-substances (*adravya*) is enjoined, then the exclusion is effected by "one increase" through *gandha* (odor); it is not otherwise.
And thus, in the verse, there is no contradiction in the word *guṇatva* having the suffix of a copulative compound (*dvandva*), because its capacity is equal to that of the other word.

"By means of being odor (*gandhatva*), [it is distinguished] from what is non-earthen and from what is not a substance; thus, 'this is an earthen substance because it is odor' effects an exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) from what is non-earthen and from what is not a substance.

By means of being fragrant (*saurabhya*), [it is distinguished] from that which is common to the non-fragrant; thus, by means of being fragrant, an exclusion is effected from the two preceding [categories] and from that which is common to the non-fragrant.
The universal (*sāmānya*) common to fragrance—that is, the specific odor—is 'common to fragrance'; that which is not common to fragrance is what was stated [in the previous clause]."
The meaning is "the absence of odor";
[it refers to] a specific fragrance, a particular kind of odor found in things such as the blue lotus (*utpala*).

In this way, the exclusion of non-substances and so forth—being performed by means of categories such as "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*) and the like—is observed to occur in the case of the blue lotus and other such things through an incremental increase of one [property] at a time.
How so? If the logical reason (*hetu*) is a means of cognition by way of its exclusion from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), otherwise it would not be tenable;
for if it were through a positive affirmation (*vidhi*) as in the case of what is perceived, there would be an identical cognition for all observers everywhere, since they would be indistinguishable.
Therefore, it must be admitted that the logical reason is a means of cognition solely by way of exclusion.
To those who do not accept this, he says: "Like what is seen" (*dṛṣṭavat*), and so forth.
"Like what is seen" means equal to what has been seen;
the meaning is that it should manifest in the same way as the mark (*liṅga*) was previously perceived at the time of establishing the relationship.

It should be understood that [the cognition] would not be an illumination [of the object] because it is not observed everywhere in the form of a positive affirmation (*vidhirūpa*)—such as "fire exists here"—nor in the form of a negative exclusion (*vyatireka*), such as "only fire is here, not non-fire. This is because the term "it would illuminate" (*prakāśayet*) is the subject under discussion. Furthermore, if the proponent of the positive formulation (*vidhivādin*) were to accept the argument starting with "just as smoke is seen in fire," namely, that "because smoke is seen only in fire and not in non-fire, therefore it causes cognition," then in that case, it would illuminate the object solely by way of negation (*pratiṣedhadvāreṇa*).
Therefore, he must accept this: that because [the capacity] is seen only in fire and not in what is not fire, it causes that [fire] to be understood.
Consequently, it would not illuminate at all, because it is not seen in every instance of fire; for it is impossible to perceive it in every fire that differs in location, state, and so forth.
With the words "yadi ca" (and if), he states another fault:
when smoke is seen in fire, it is seen as necessarily conjoined with one or another of its specific qualities such as luminosity;
consequently, those [qualities] too would be manifested.
And thus, mere perception is not the cause for the cognition of the object to be inferred, because even when that [perception] exists, the [cognition] may be absent.

Now, it might be argued: "Even by the proponent of negation, perception is indeed accepted; for instance, smoke is the mark of fire because it is invariably concomitant as an effect, and the relation of cause and effect is established through both perception and non-perception taken together, not from non-perception alone. To this, it is said: "Because," and so forth.

This demonstrates the following: since fire is manifested by smoke only in its general form (*sāmānyarūpa*) and not in its specific forms such as its brilliance (*dīpti*), therefore, for the sake of establishing the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), even through positive affirmation (*vidhi*), it is that very same general form of it which is seen; thus, because the designation of cause and effect is established, it is perceived as the cause, and not in its specific form—this is the intended meaning.
The perception of specific qualities such as brilliance is not the cause for establishing the designation of cause and effect, because smoke is seen even in the absence of those [specific qualities].

It might be argued as follows: "The universal is a single entity that exists in the individuals either as distinct from them or non-distinct from them; and since it is fully present in its entirety within each individual, its perception is logically possible in one particular fire-individual alone. Consequently, because it is not perceived elsewhere, its manifestation [in other instances] would not occur. This is not tenable, and it is said in response: "Even though the universal... and so forth.
By the phrase "even though," he shows that although that [universal] does not exist at all, the fault is nevertheless stated by way of concession;
this is indicated by the words "first of all, fire-ness does not exist," and so forth.
For if the universal were something other than the individuals, it would appear in cognition; yet there is no such appearance.
...Even if it were non-different [from the individual], that universal would still not exist as such, just like the individual;
nevertheless, accepting that for the sake of argument, he says "even if that exists," etc., in order to prove the impossibility of perceiving it.

That which is common to many and whose entire substratum has not been apprehended cannot be perceived, just as duality and so forth cannot be perceived when their entire substratum is unapprehended; since "fire-ness" (agnitva) is likewise [unperceivable], there is a contradiction with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddha*).
As for similarity (*sādṛśya*), it is not [unperceivable] because it is non-different from its substratum; however, it is presented here as if distinct [from the object].
In this case as well, the same formal argument (*prayoga*) must be stated.

Now, even if there is a single apprehension, if the whole is apprehended [in each part], then, because it would be fully present in its entirety within each individual part, it would possess plurality like a quality (*guṇa*).
And because of this plurality, it would not be a universal (*sāmānya*) at all, just like its substrata (*āśraya*), since a universal is intended to be unitary.
"Thus," and so forth...
"the limb is called the sign."
"Does not deviate" means that it does not fail [to be concomitant];
"even though possessing many properties" refers to general and specific properties such as "smokiness," "whiteness," and so forth.
not by means of substantiality and so forth.

...those [properties] such as substantiality (*dravyatva*) and so forth, which are the concomitants (*anubandhin*), are also understood through the inferential mark (*liṅga*) for the sake of easily establishing the very meaning already stated by means of two summary verses (*saṃgrahaśloka*).
...but the meanings connected with the *liṅga* (the inferential mark) are "unqualified," meaning they are general properties such as substantiality (*dravyatva*) and so forth;
whereas "particulars" (*viśeṣa*) are [specific properties] such as "smokeness" (*dhūmatva*) and so forth.

And these are called "particulars" (viśeṣa) with respect to universals such as substance-ness (dravyatva), which are not distinct [from them], but not with respect to their own unique, specific forms (asādhāraṇarūpa).
— VT.

The exclusion of non-substances and so forth occurs through the addition of one [term], as in the case of "lotus" and so on; because of the conformity with what is observed. (Pramāṇasamuccaya 2.14) ... ... ...
Certainty arises only from the persistence of what is perceived, not from the exclusion of the unperceived; likewise, doubt arises from the reverse.

For, while their difference is equal, there is certainty regarding the quality of whiteness, but not regarding substance or action; and the exclusion (*apoha*) of those two does not apply to existence (*sattva*) or the quality [of color].

If it is argued that in those cases there is no difference because one perceives an inherent connection (*anubandha*), then white would also be blue and so forth, since it is non-different from form (*rūpa*), just like the essential nature of the quality of white.

In this very way, form, as well as taste and the other [qualities], would be non-different from the quality itself, because they are not distinct from it, just like the essential nature of the quality.
Even a dyad and so forth would be a dyad, upward motion and so forth, and color and so forth, because they are dependent [on their causes]; thus,
there would be no doubt, due to the identity with whiteness.
But if exclusion were predominant— if establishment were [possible] as in the case of what is seen, based on the quality of the property of whiteness—
then, just as in the forward order, there would also be the comprehension of two, three, or one object in the reverse order.
(Pramāṇasamuccaya 3)

44. Thus, regarding the verse beginning with "dṛṣṭānuvṛtteḥ" (because of the conformity to what is seen), etc.: just as there is a movement toward two, three, or one object in the direct order (*ānulomya*), so too in the reverse order (*prātilomya*) there is no such movement toward two, three, or one object; this is because it is observed to be so and not otherwise.

Its explanation is as follows: certainty arises from the very conformity to what is seen, and not from the exclusion of what is unseen; nor does doubt arise from the non-conformity to the unseen, whether in the direct order or in the reverse order.

Why? Because, although otherness (*anyatva*) is equal in those cases, there is certainty regarding the quality (*guṇa*) of whiteness (*śuklatva*), but not regarding substance (*dravya*) or action (*karman*). Furthermore, there is no exclusion (*apoha*) of those two from existence (*sattva*) and quality; nor is there certainty [regarding them] because of the identity (*aikātmya*) of whiteness, color-form (*rūpa*), and so forth. And precisely because of perception, there is doubt regarding the quality, the color-form, and the whiteness, based on qualities and color-forms that are supported by things possessing both unitary and manifold natures. Thus, if there were establishment [of the object] as seen, it would follow from that which is supported by the quality of the color-form of whiteness.

If it were perceived exactly as it is seen, rather than by way of exclusion (*vyavaccheda*), then just as there is a sequential perception of the three—colorness (*rūpatva*), qualityness (*guṇatva*), and subsistence (*āśritatva*)—whereby from qualityness there is the perception of the two, colorness and subsistence, and from qualityness alone there is the perception of the one, subsistence; so too, in reverse order, from subsistence there would be the perception of the three—qualityness, colorness, and whiteness (*śauklya*)—from qualityness the perception of the two, colorness and whiteness, and from colorness the perception of whiteness alone.
For it is not the case that subsistence and the other properties are not observed in qualityness and the rest.

Now, just as "being dependent" (āśritatva) is observed in the case of [the universal] qualityness (guṇatva) and so forth, it is likewise observed in the case of action (karman) and so forth; thus a doubt arises. Furthermore, since whiteness (śauklya) is also observed in things that depend on the quality of color (rūpa), there would be doubt because it is common to both.
However, there is no fault if the cognition occurs by way of exclusion (vyāvṛtti);

for just as whiteness is a reason for [the presence of] colorness (rūpatva) because it is absent when colorness is absent, so too are qualityness and being dependent [reasons], since they are absent when those two are absent.

However, since dependence is observed even in the absence of being a quality (*guṇatva*) and so forth, there is no certainty regarding [the subject] being a quality and so on—*Viśālāmalavatī Pramāṇasamuccayaṭīkā*, VT.
As it is said [in the *Pratyabhijñāsamuccaya* 3.44]: "Just as in the forward order, so too in the reverse order, there occurs the comprehension of two, three, or one object. (ed. p. 203 B–204 A)

Although the reading *dvitryekārthagati* is observed here [in the Pramāṇaviniścaya], nevertheless, the reading *tridvyekārthagati* is recognized in the *Pramāṇasamuccaya*; and considering that this [latter] is both more correct and consistent with the meaning, it appears that the reading *tridvyekārthagati* should be adopted here. [This note is not present in the Bhāṣya manuscript.]

Although the reading *dvitryekārthagati* is observed here [in the *Pramāṇaviniścaya*], nevertheless, the reading *tridvyekārthagati* is recognized in the *Pramāṇasamuccaya*; since that [latter] is both more correct and consistent in meaning, it appears that the reading *tridvyekārthagati* should be preferred here.

Although the reading *dvitryekārthagati* is observed here, nevertheless, in the *Pramāṇasamuccaya*, the reading *tridvyekārthagati* is recognized; considering that this latter is both more correct and coherent in meaning, it appears that the reading *tridvyekārthagati* should be adopted here.

If it should be argued: "There is no difference [between them] because their inherent nature (*anubandhitattva*) is seen there"—just as earthiness, substantiality, and existence are not different from a tree, so too whiteness and other qualities, which are dependent on color, are inherent [to it].

Therefore, regarding the certainty [of exclusion] there and the fact that it is not an exclusion (*apoha*), as for those others which are formless, non-qualities, and non-substantial—just like their lack of being earthen and so forth—their exclusion from "tree" would follow.
To this we reply: "In that case, [the word] 'white'... and so forth.

Blue, red, yellow, and so forth would also be white, because they are not different from color (rūpa), just like the essential nature of the quality of whiteness; and in this very same way, other undesirable consequences (aniṣṭāpādana) have already been explained, up to the point that even the dyad (dvyaṇuka) [would be white]. If the dyad, which is an effect-substance (kāryadravya) residing [in its causes], were indeed different from the atoms, then it would be unequal to whiteness and the like.
Color and the other [sensory qualities] are not distinct from whiteness and the like, for that would lead to an undesirable consequence:

if whiteness were not [identical with] color and so forth, it would not be whiteness at all, because it would lack the nature of color and so forth, just like upward motion (*utkṣepaṇa*) and the like.
Therefore, since it is non-different from them, there can be no exclusion (*apoha*) of color and the rest from it.
Furthermore, regarding other qualities such as "dependence" (āśrita) and so forth, there arises doubt through both exclusion (apoha) and non-exclusion (anapoha).
Why is this so? This is established precisely by the observation of positive concomitance (anvaya) as we have asserted.
Thus, for the time being, the faults of infinite regress (ānantya) and lack of universal application (avyāpti) exist even in the theory of the exclusion of others (anyāpoha).

Moreover, there would be the existence of even that which is immediate, because [otherwise] upward motion and so forth, as well as color and so forth, would [not exist]; for this reason—namely, because they are dependent—there would be no doubt regarding actions and qualities along with their subdivisions, since [action] is non-different from [the substance] like a continuous connection. Why, then, is the demonstration of the means [to liberation] presented through the sequence of all qualities and so forth? Because, according to your own view, there is identity with whiteness (*śauklya*).
If it is argued that the effect is indeed different from the substance, then it would follow that whiteness and so forth are not distinct from color-form and so forth, which is undesirable.
If whiteness were devoid of color and so forth, it would not be whiteness at all, precisely because it lacks color and so forth, just like upward motion (*utkṣepaṇa*) and other such qualities.

Therefore, since it is non-different from those [qualities], there is no exclusion (*apoha*) of color and the rest. As for other qualities such as inherence (*āśrita*) and so on, there remains doubt regarding them through both exclusion and non-exclusion.
Now, why is this so? This is established precisely by the observation of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) as we have asserted.
Thus, first of all, even in the theory of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), the faults of infinite regress and non-exclusiveness (*vyabhicāra*) remain present;
furthermore, there is the presence of what follows immediately thereafter, because:

How is there also the non-existence of that which is immediately following? Because, since the negation of others [is established] through pervasion, there is non-difference from those things whose meanings are distinct from it;
and because of its direct occurrence and its lack of difference, the determination of the properties of the universal (jāti) is established.

For the function of a general term (*sāmānyaśabda*)—which consists in the exclusion of other referents—is performed without rejecting its own particulars; thus, its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with a word denoting a particular is established.
It is here that [the author] begins to refute the position of Diṅnāga, starting with these words.
See page 728, note 9.
Here he says: "In that case, then, the difference [of whiteness and so forth] from [the cloth] is indeed unequal;
if this is so, then there is no non-difference—what then? There is indeed difference."

Showing that this undesirable consequence must not occur, he says: "Color-form and so forth are not other than whiteness and so forth. Why? Because they are invariably concomitant with them, just as being earthen is [invariably concomitant] with trees and the like. What is the reason? Because it would lead to an undesirable consequence.

If it is asked, "What is that undesirable consequence? [the answer is: if whiteness were not color-form and so forth, it would not be whiteness at all, because it would lack the nature of color-form and so forth, just like upward motion (*utkṣepaṇa*) and the like.
Therefore, because it is non-different from that [the universal], there is no exclusion (*apoha*) of color and so forth by means of whiteness; that is, there is no exclusion of color and the like.
However, as for those other [properties] distinct from that, there is doubt regarding their exclusion or non-exclusion.

Which ones are they? They are stated: "Qualities and so forth, such as being dependent. For example: "This is a quality because it is dependent"; thus, by necessity, a quality is only dependent, and there is no such thing as a non-dependent quality.
However, there is no fixed rule that a quality (guṇa), an action (karma), a generality (sāmānya), a particularity (viśeṣa), or inherence (samavāya) must necessarily be dependent;

therefore, because those [categories] such as quality and so forth are distinct from it by virtue of being dependent upon it, there would arise a doubt as to whether they are exclusion (apoha) or non-exclusion (anapoha)—
such is the case.
Trees and so forth are composed of earth;
furthermore,
those [beings] are dependent upon them.

The Teacher says: Now, why is this so? You must state the specific reason why you have concluded that there is certainty regarding color and other qualities—as in the case of whiteness and so forth—due to their being dependent [on a substance], whereas there is doubt regarding qualities and so forth; for one who maintains the primacy of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), it is impossible to perceive a real entity through affirmation (*vidhi*) alone. This is established precisely by the perception of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of the entity as we conceive it, because in its absence, neither the necessity nor the lack of necessity of that [perception] can be established. *Note on variants:* *ya* reads *°didrūpā*;
*bhā* reads *°ididrūpā*.

This concludes the summary: first, regarding the position of difference (*bheda-pakṣa*), the faults of infinite regress and non-expressiveness mentioned to the opponent have not been avoided even by [the argument] beginning with *adṛṣṭer anya-śabdārthe* (Pramāṇasamuccaya 5.34); therefore, it has been shown that [the exclusion of others] exists even in the case of the qualified exclusion of others (*saviśeṣa-anyāpoha-pakṣa*).
The reading "non-mention due to infinity" (ānantyād-anukti) might also exist here; see page 650, note 2.
Furthermore, there is the state of what follows immediately.

As for what was also stated regarding the two positions concerning the denotation of the connection with the genus (*jāti*) of that which is immediately preceding: because there is no negation of the non-existent, there is a differentiation of the specific meaning of the general term;
for the function of a general term, which is the exclusion of other referents, occurs without rejecting its own internal particulars. (*Pramāṇasamuccayavṛtti* 5).
36. Thus, it was stated merely by way of speech;

for that [statement] serves only to exclude its own internal distinctions. Since the negation of the non-existent is itself non-existent, and since distinctions are neither existent nor non-existent in relation to one another, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "distinction" is untenable.

Furthermore, because a relationship is impossible for a non-entity with respect to distinctions, to whom would those distinctions belong? Therefore, the fault of the scriptural statement being non-distinct [from the Brahman] certainly remains.

For the relation of a word [to its object] by means of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) is indeed easy to establish. A word is not the denoter of a mere universal (*jāti*) nor of its connection [with that universal], because it is heard as non-distinct from words whose objects are particulars.

For instance, there would be no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with particularizing words such as "substance" and so on—as in the cases "existent substance," "existent quality," or "existent action"—yet this is observed.
Indeed, neither existence (*sattā*) nor its connection is itself a substance or a quality; rather, what is it? It belongs to the substance or the quality.

For in the same way, there is no occurrence of the collection of faults consisting in the consequence of the absence of co-referentiality for the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*). As it is said: "The exclusion of others, because of its pervasion, is non-different from the objects that are distinct from it" (Pramāṇasamuccaya 5.36).

"It is 'sat' (being); non-being does not exist"—this negation of non-being (*asat-nivṛtti*) pervades all distinctions among substances, qualities, actions, jars, forms, and upward movements. Because this negation of non-being pervades all such distinctions, and because [the word "sat"] has an identical referent with them, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is established;
however, this is not so, because since it is a non-existence consisting of the negation of non-being, it is distinct from the specific objects [it negates].

The explanation of that is as follows: "For a general term," and so forth. For the function—the activity—of a general term such as "existent" (sat), which consists in the exclusion of other objects (*arthāntara-vyudāsa*) by way of [the cognition] "it is not non-existent," has been determined by you in this manner, namely, "without the rejection of its own particulars. This was stated by mere words, having forgotten what was previously said; thus, the opponent's position is restated here.
To this, we reply: "It is precisely by the rejection of its own particulars."

Why? Because that word "existent" (sat) has the purpose of a restrictive rule (*sanniyama*): since there is a double negation in the phrase "it does not become non-existent," it results in the recovery of the original state; thus, because the negation of the non-existent is restricted by existence, it lacks the nature of a mere absence.

What follows from this? From this, because individual things (*bhedas*) possess both existence and non-existence in relation to one another—non-existence due to their being mutual absences (*itaretarābhāva*), and existence due to the restrictive rule of existence—it follows that their own particular differences are indeed rejected; for even though they are existent, they do not exist as such. This is the conclusion reached.

Furthermore, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with that which possesses difference—such as substance and quality, or jars and cloths—is untenable, because [the term "non-existence"] functions to establish only the negation of existence. Moreover, coreferentiality in terms of a single case-ending (*ekavibhaktitva*) with non-existence is also untenable; for instance, in expressions such as "existent substance" (*sad-dravyam*), "existent quality" (*sad-guṇaḥ*), or "existent jar" (*san ghaṭaḥ*).

It is not merely the coreferentiality of the case-endings that is untenable; rather, coreferentiality of the word itself is untenable even when there is a difference in case-endings, as in "of the existent substance" (*sato dravyasya*) or "of the existent quality" (*sato guṇasya*), and so forth.

Since it is untenable for even a relation to exist as distinct from categories such as substance (*dravya*) and so forth, to what would those distinctions belong? For the word "existent" (*sat*) merely adopts the exclusion of non-existence (*asattva*) without implying any identity [with other categories]. Therefore, the fault of not being heard separately certainly remains. See page 650, lines 11–26. What was stated by Diṅnāga in the fifth chapter, the *Apoha-pariccheda*, of the *Pramāṇasamuccaya* along with its commentary (*vṛtti*), is here presented after having been translated from the Tibetan version into Sanskrit: [The Tibetan text follows... ...Therefore, the fault of not being heard separately certainly remains. See page 650, lines 11–26. What was stated by Diṅnāga in the fifth chapter, the *Apoha-pariccheda*, of the *Pramāṇasamuccaya* along with its commentary (*vṛtti*), is here presented after having been translated from the Tibetan version into Sanskrit.
Because the exclusion of others is pervaded [by the universal], it is non-different from those things that possess its particular forms;
and because it exists directly [in each individual] and is non-different [from them], the properties of the genus are established.
(5.36) There is also the absence of even what is immediately adjacent.
How so? Because the exclusion of others through pervasion is non-different from the objects that are its own particulars.

For the function of a general term (*sāmānyaśabda*) is the exclusion of other referents; since this occurs without rejecting its own particulars, its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with particularizing terms is established. Therefore, there is no fault of separate verbal expression regarding the objects that are its own particulars.

When an object is denotable by both words, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with respect to that other object; for thus there is no deviation from its own referent, since the individual term does not occur elsewhere [than in its own primary sense],
and thus the latter fault is also absent.
How so? Because there is no difference from the direct function (*sākṣād-vṛtti*), the word does not operate upon its own particulars by taking up a different object;
therefore, neither the fault of not implying its own particulars through dependence (*pāratantryeṇa*) nor the fault of being figurative (*bhākta*) exist.

Nor do the defects of non-denotation and non-universality arise from the instability of distinctions and lack of pervasiveness, because the mere exclusion of other objects (*arthāntarāpoha*) is undifferentiated and non-substantial.
For that very reason, one need not pursue a connection with further generalities or particularities, since it consists directly in the negation of other objects.
Thus, in the absence of the aforementioned defects, the exclusion of other objects alone is the correct meaning of a word.
And for this reason, the establishment of the properties of a universal occurs precisely here;

and the properties of a universal—characterized by oneness, permanence, and complete presence in each individual—are established in this very context because of non-difference, the non-annihilation of the substratum, and the cognition of the entire object.
Thus, due to the absence of defects and the excellence of its qualities, a word expresses entities as qualified by the exclusion of other things.

Therefore, why is there no occurrence [of this] elsewhere in isolation from things that possess distinct meanings? Why? Because it possesses the properties of a genus (*jāti*).

The extensive and stainless commentary (*Viśālāmalavatī*) composed by Jinendrabuddhi on this [text] is also presented here, having been translated back into Sanskrit from its Tibetan version: "Of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) which is the exclusion of others (*anyaniṣedha*).

The meaning is: pervasion is the non-rejection of one's own particulars (*svabheda*); "exclusion of others" refers to the universal (*sāmānya*) as previously described; the sense is that because that pervasion is pervasive (*vyāpaka*) within its own particulars.
The genitive case in the phrase "of the exclusion of others" (*anyaniṣedhasya*) is the agentive genitive (*kartari ṣaṣṭhī*), characterized by its connection with a verbal noun (*kṛd-yoga*).

The phrase "non-difference from the objects that are its particulars" means that there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between words such as "existent" (*sat*) and words such as "substance" (*dravya*), which denote objects distinguished by the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*).

As for the statement beginning with "for of the general term," if one asks what kind of operation is perceived in a general term, it is the exclusion of other objects; and this [exclusion] occurs without the rejection of its own referent.

By this he states its pervasiveness: just as when a genus is denoted there is the exclusion of other genera, so too when the exclusion of other objects (arthāntarāpoha) is denoted, there is no exclusion of specific properties such as substantiality (dravyatva).

The word *hi* has the sense of "because," and the word *iti* has the sense of "therefore"; since it is thus, therefore the coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the word *sat* with words such as *dravya*, which denote distinct entities, is logically established.

Therefore, a single entity, being manifested through both existence (*sattva*) and substantiality (*dravyatva*), is denoted by the two words "existent" (*sat*) and "substance" (*dravya*). For indeed, there is no deviation from its own referent; for the collective meaning is specific, and if the individual word were to denote that [collective], then even in the absence of that [collective], the cognition of it would not arise because the word still functions [independently].
Since the collective is denoted by a different word altogether, there is thus no deviation.
Regarding the phrase "of the latter as well," this refers to its direct application [to the rule] "not because that which possesses it is dependent."

In this context, he demonstrates that a word operates upon an entity consisting of the exclusion of the non-existent (*asadapoha*), without depending on other qualities such as existence (*sattā*)—by means of the passage beginning with "taking up another object" and ending with "therefore, by way of dependence. That other object upon which the word operates in relation to the substance is the exclusion of other objects (*arthāntarāpoha*); it is not some distinct category like a universal (*jāti*) or the like. Consequently, since there is no mediation, how could there be dependence? For that very entity, as excluded from "non-existent" and so forth, is denoted directly; therefore, its differentiation [from other things] is not rejected therein, because of its identity [with the exclusion].
For this very reason, there is no fault of figurative usage (*bhāktadoṣa*);
for a word that functions primarily in one sense is not metaphorically applied (*upacaryate*) to substances and so forth, nor is it the case that... [and so on].

There is an infinity (*ānantya*) and instability (*anavasthāna*) of particularities (*bhedānām*). Therefore, there is no fault of non-denotation (*anabhidhānadoṣa*). Furthermore, that which possesses those [particulars] is said to be the particular itself, and that has already been refuted; this is what is stated by the phrase "by this [it is] stated."

He asks why the fault of being a non-universal (*asāmānya-doṣa*), which was stated in the passage beginning "the object possessing that [exclusion], such as a jar," does not exist because of its pervasiveness; he replies: "Because the mere exclusion of other objects (*arthāntarāpoha*) is undifferentiated. By this, the word "non-difference" (*abhedāt*) is explained.
For if there were actual differentiation, there would be the fault of infinity (*ānantya-doṣa*) and the fault of being a non-universal, since one thing does not reside in another.

But the mere exclusion of other objects (*arthāntarāpoha*) is undifferentiated; therefore, how could there be any room for this fault? If it is asked: "But surely, that form of cognition which is established as the universal (*sāmānya*)—since it is non-different from cognition and does not subsist elsewhere—how can it be a universal? It is replied: because it is not a substance (*adravyatvāt*), etc. Even though it is a form of cognition, it is a universal precisely because it is not fully established as a universal [in the sense of being a real entity]; thus, it is indeed a universal that exists as a non-substance (*adravyasat*), and this is not at all undesirable.
"...from that very [source]" means because it functions directly.
In that case, because existence (*sattā*) is denoted as a qualifier, there is an intervention of the thing's own nature (*vastusvarūpa*);

for potness (*ghaṭatva*) and so forth are related to that [nature], not directly related to existence, since one genus does not exist within another genus. Therefore, by way of that [existence], it is not the cause for the expectation of multiple referents.

In this case, however, the word functions in its own primary sense (*svārthe*) by means of a direct negation of non-existence; therefore, its capacity to require a specific qualification is established, because it directly negates other objects even in the absence of a connection with another [actual] universal. Thus, the denotation of its own primary sense—which serves as the means for negating other objects—is so described, meaning "by virtue of the direct denotation of its own primary sense. By this, the meaning of the phrase "precisely from that" is demonstrated. And here, what is intended is the negation of a connection with another real universal (*vastusat-jātyantara*), not even a connection with a figurative (*upacarita*) universal.
They remain established right here...
[etc.]
...the conceptualization [of the whole] as being eternal is also tenable; however, because the cognition of the entire object occurs, [the universal] is fully present in each individual instance.
"...because of the excellence of qualities," for it is precisely here that the establishment of the laws of caste is logical—

14: Because it is not the absence of the negation of non-existence, there is a distinction from the specific object.

For that operation of a general term which consists in the exclusion of other referents has been stated merely in words [in the *Pramāṇasamuccayavṛtti* 5.36] as "without rejecting its own particulars";

however, it is actually by means of the rejection of its own particulars. Because that [exclusion] has the purpose of restriction (*sanniyama*), and because the negation of the non-existent is a non-entity, and because particulars are both existent and non-existent in relation to one another, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with a word denoting a particular is untenable.

Since it is impossible for even a relation to exist without distinctions, to what would those distinctions belong? Therefore, the fault of being heard as non-distinct certainly remains; for the relation of a word with the exclusion of others (anyāpoha) is indeed easy to establish. A word is not the designator of a mere universal (jāti) nor of its connection [with particulars], because it is heard as non-distinct from words whose meanings are particulars. For instance, there would be no grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with particular-meaning words such as "substance" and so on—as in the cases "existent substance," "existent quality," and "existent action"—yet that [coreferentiality] is observed.
For neither existence nor conjunction is a substance or a quality; what then? It belongs to a substance or a quality.
For in that very same way, there is no comparison with the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*)—page 607, line 16.
The absence of the basis for concentration (samādhikaraṇābhāva) should be seen on page 728, note 9;
it appears clearly that the quality is existent.
Comparison—page 607, line 17;
comparison—page 607, line 18. Of which root are these the divisions? (bhā.)

The commentary (*ṭīkā*) which explains the divisions of that very *dhātu* belongs to it alone— beginning with "for [it is] easy" (*sukaro hi*), etc., which has its meaning understood as an illustration up to "of a substance or a quality" (*dravyasya guṇasya vā*);

likewise, beginning with "for in that same way" (*tathaiva hi*), it is precisely the demonstration of your own position as the subject of the illustration, up to the point where "co-referentiality would not exist" (*sāmānādhikaraṇyaṃ na syāt*).

Just as existence (*sattā*) is neither a substance (*dravya*) nor a quality (*guṇa*), and so forth, likewise, for you, the negation of both the existent and the non-existent is not the absence of negation; rather, since you do not admit that the existent—which is the object to be enjoined by the double negation and which possesses internal differentiation—is either a substance or a quality, what then? It is the designator of the state (*bhāva*) of a substance or a quality, because it is heard as non-different from words denoting differentiation. For instance, there would be no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with words denoting substances and so forth that signify differentiation, such as "the existent is a substance," "the existent is a quality," or "the existent is an action."

Just as existence (*sattā*) is neither a substance (*dravya*) nor a quality (*guṇa*), but rather belongs to a substance or a quality; likewise, the absence of the negation of existence and non-existence is neither a substance nor a quality, but rather the presence or absence of a substance or a quality. And it has been said: "Due to the rule regarding the difference in case endings between words denoting a quality and the possessor of that quality, the co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of two words for substances is established."

Regarding what was stated in *Vākyapadīya* 3.14.8 for the purpose of demonstrating the specific reason why the theory of exclusion (*apoha*) is superior to the two theories of denoting existence (*sattā*) or relation: "In that case, because existence and relation are qualities (*guṇa*) and the entity is the possessor of qualities (*guṇin*), there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*); the meaning is 'merely existent and non-existent'. This interpretation follows your own view; thus he says "and so forth," providing further evidence with the verse beginning: "The distinction of case-endings [is due to] necessity... and so on.
In that case, is it not easy to understand that non-existence is indeed the absence of existence, meaning it is merely the non-existent?
[No,] because the term is not heard as separate from words denoting specific distinctions.

For instance, there would be no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with words such as "substance" (*dravya*), which denote distinct objects, as in "existent substance," "existent quality" (*guṇa*), or "existent action" (*karman*). Indeed, existence (*sattā*) is not itself a substance or a quality; rather, it belongs to a substance or a quality. Similarly, the non-existence of being and non-being (*sadasad-abhāva*) is not itself a substance or a quality; rather, it is the presence or absence of a substance or a quality.
And it has been said:
"There is a difference in case endings due to the restriction between that which expresses a quality and that which expresses the possessor of the quality.
Regarding this, it should be noted that in the *Nayacakravṛtti*, only the pratīka "vibhaktibhedo niyamād" and so forth is found.

In the *Nyāyavārttika* (2.2.66), in the context of refuting the view of Diṅnāga, it is stated: "The difference in case endings [is established] by rule for those [words] that denote a quality and a substance."

The verse, "The co-referentiality of the words 'existent' (sat) and 'substance' (dravya) is unestablished," was presented by Uddyotakara as a prima facie objection; therefore, it is probable that this [verse] belongs to Dignāga, or perhaps to Bhartṛhari in his *Vākyapadīya* 3.1.68.
14.8 However, due to the difference in case endings between words denoting a quality and its possessor,
the well-known grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) of two substance-words [is established] by necessity.
Thus, a *kārikā* is seen;
this has been demonstrated by us in detail at page 731, note 3.
Therefore, it is not possible here to determine what kind of *kārikā* was intended by the venerable Mallavādi Kṣamāśramaṇa.

Nevertheless, Bhartṛhari’s verse has been cited by Diṅnāga as well at *Pramāṇasamuccaya* p. 607, l. 19, in this very context; therefore, wise readers should understand that we too have presented that same verse here out of consideration.
[The verse reads: "The establishment of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) belongs to two words denoting substances" (*Vākyapadīya* 3.14.8).

As for what was stated in order to demonstrate the specific reason why the theory of exclusion (*apoha*) is superior to the two theories of denoting existence (*sattā*) or relation: "For in that case, because existence and relation are qualities (*guṇa*) and the entity is the possessor of qualities (*guṇin*), there is coreferentiality... [the text continues].
Or rather, as [the author] says in the *Tulanā* (p. 607, l.
18): "There is a difference in case endings due to the rule governing those words that denote a quality and its possessor."
The establishment of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) occurs between two words denoting substances (dravya). Vākyapadīya 3.14.

8. In the expression "the whiteness of the cloth" (*paṭasya śuklaḥ*), where words denoting a substance and a quality are employed, there is a verbal predominance and subordination (*guṇapradhānabhāva*). For instance: here, the subordinate term denotes its own meaning as it has been transformed into something that assists the principal; thus, it takes the genitive case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) which is the case-ending of a quality.

The principal term, however, being established in itself and not assisting another, is joined with the nominative case-ending (*prathamā*). Thus, a fixed distinction of case-endings occurs in the domain of different substrates (*vyadhikaraṇa*).

In cases such as "the hero is a man" (*vīraḥ puruṣaḥ*), where there is a relation of grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*), both words are substance-words (*dravyaśabda*) that express their own meanings established in themselves;

thus, in that case, only the nominative case is used, while the relationship of primary and secondary status (*guṇapradhānabhāva*) is said to be based on semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*). As stated in the *Vākyapadīya* (3): "The qualificand is that which is not yet determined."

14.7 Even though such is the case regarding the relationship of subordinate and principal, there is a distinction between grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and non-coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) based on whether [the meaning] is verbal or non-verbal; thus, there is a difference between the two types of compounds: the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) and the coreferential compound (*sāmānādhikaraṇasamāsa*).

Thus, in the *Vṛttisamuddeśa* of the *Vākyapadīya-ṭīkā* composed by Helārāja, as for the argument that "this [is not so] because it has the same case-ending as words denoting distinct objects," that is incorrect, due to a failure to understand the identical meaning [intended].

We do not say that there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "Being" (*sattā*); rather, substances, qualities, and actions are denoted by the word "existent" (*sat*), which expresses the primary substratum of Being.

Even by means of words denoting qualities or actions, when they have entered into a relationship of mutual qualifier and qualified, those very same [entities] are thus appropriately expressed in grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), because both the word "existent" (*sat*) and the word "substance" (*dravya*) share a single referent. However, when this word "existence" (*sattā*) denotes the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) as a subordinate element while existence itself is the primary focus, then there is no grammatical coordination; rather, the expression becomes "the existence of the substance" (*dravyasya sattā*).
Therefore, the impossibility of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is not a fault; rather,

due to the difference in case endings, there is no establishment of coreferentiality between the words "existent" (*sat*) and "substance" (*dravya*), which denote a quality and a qualificand respectively according to the rule.
Thus, by this [statement], that [objection] has been refuted—
[as found in] the Nyāyavārttika, a manuscript located at Jesalamera,
folio 2.2.

The refutation of Diṅnāga’s doctrine is the subject under consideration here; therefore, it is probable that this verse belongs to Diṅnāga himself from some other work of his. As for the verse by Bhartṛhari which was cited by Diṅnāga, that is to be found at page 607, line 19.

As for the objection that in the two positions of denoting "existence" (*sattā*) or its relation, there is the fault of non-distinctness in verbal expression, whereas this fault does not exist in the position of exclusion (*apoha*) because of the presence of a specific reason—this specific reason is set forth in the passage beginning with "For in that case," and so on. In the two positions of denoting existence or its relation, it is logical that existence (*sattā*) is a quality (*guṇa*) and non-existence (*abhāva*) is a universal (*jāti*). But here, the meaning of the word is the substance (*dravya*) in which the exclusion of other objects (*arthāntarāpoha*) is performed, and not mere exclusion alone.
And that [existence] is pervaded by the word "existent" (*sat*) because it is not abandoned, yet it is not expressed directly.

For example, the word "existent" denotes a substance (*dravya*) with the exclusion of the non-existent (*asat*) as its subordinate element, but not directly, because doubt would otherwise arise. Therefore, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the word "existent" with specific terms such as "substance," "quality," and "action" is appropriate for the meaning of the sentence—as in "existent substance," "existent quality," "existent action. For thus, when accompanied by a specific term, there is no deviation from its own primary referent.

Since the meaning of the whole is distinct from the meanings of its constituent parts, and those two [words] together denote that [whole], it is not the case that the word *sat* expresses the object "substance" (*dravya*), nor does the word *dravya* express the object "existent" (*sat*). How then can it be said that "whatever is existent is a substance" and "whatever is a substance is existent"? This is stated because the single composite meaning denoted by the two words—being assisted by the exclusion of both individual word-meanings—is treated as one; it is not because the meaning of "existent" is expressed by the word "substance. Since they are related as qualifier and qualified, it is logical that there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between them. Thus, that entity is a "possessor of qualities" (*guṇin*). Therefore, the absence of coreferentiality is appropriate.

In this context, however, "exclusion of other objects" (*arthāntarāpoha*)—in the sense that "the existent is not non-existent"—does not denote the mere absence of existence. What then? It is the very entity (*vastu*) qualified by the exclusion of other objects that is called "existent. That entity upon which this exclusion is performed is the substance (*dravya*), which is the meaning of the word; it is not mere exclusion. Furthermore, that object qualified by exclusion—such as substance and so forth—is pervaded by the word "existent" because it is not abandoned [by the word], yet it is not directly denoted [by the word]; for it is not logical [for the word] to denote a negation (*abhāva*). In this case, however, the substance upon which the exclusion of other objects is performed is the meaning of the word, not mere exclusion.

In this context, there is no purpose served by investigating whether [the object] is a distinct entity or not a distinct entity, since it is not a factor in either assisting or obstructing the subject matter at hand. Rather, what is relevant here to the subject matter is as follows: for one who knows the relationship between word and meaning, from the use of a word there arises a cognition through the distinction between affirmation and negation—namely, "this exists" and "this does not exist"—regarding an object that resides in the intellect, is characterized by the knowledge produced by the use of the word, and is determined by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), such that it comes under its control in accordance with that object. Or, [this applies] according to the view that the meaning of a word is a particular qualified by a universal (*sāmānyopasarjana-viśeṣa*).

Furthermore, since the qualifiers are subordinated in both positions (*pakṣa*), there is an equal lack of expression due to the non-implication of particulars (*bheda*) and a lack of independence; such is the purpose of this effort of investigation. He demonstrates this by means of an example, starting with "just as the nature of the universal" (*yathā jātisvarūpa*) and so forth, up to "non-implication" (*anākṣepa*) according to the view of the proponent of the position (*pakṣavādin*); and by means of the application to the subject (*dārṣṭāntika*), starting with "in that way, however it may be" (*tathā yathākathaṃcit*) and so forth, up to "because of being the cause of a lack of independence" (*asvātantryahetutvāt*). It is well said: "Even for the latter fault, its existence is indeed characterized by excellence" (*sātiśayasya bhāva eva*). Where [the text] says *pra*.

Regarding what was stated on page 733, line 4 of the *Prakaraṇa*: "Even though it has been said that the exclusion of other objects (arthāntarāpoha) is the negation of a non-existent jar, such that 'the jar is existent,' therefore there is no fault regarding universals (sāmānya) in the theory of apoha—even that was spoken by you while forgetting your own previously stated position. Since the exclusion of other objects (*arthāntarāpoha*) is not a distinct absence (*abhāvāntara*), an object that possesses exclusion (*apohavān arthaḥ*) cannot be the denotation of a word. Therefore, if it is your position that exclusion is not the qualifier and that object is not "possessing exclusion," then this is stated in order to demonstrate a contradiction [in your view]. We have raised the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) beginning with "How is this... and so forth, up until the point where it was indicated by the aphorism (*sūtra*)—"because the existent object is denoted by the word 'substance' (*dravyaśabda*)"—up to the phrase "not mere exclusion" (*nāpohamātram*), the meaning of which has already been explained.

If it is asked what is meant by this, it is replied: whether it be a substance (*dravya*) or a non-substance (*adravya*), the exclusion of other objects (*arthāntarāpoha*) is indeed expressed as the meaning of a word, because that object is intended to be conveyed as the word’s own referent. This is stated because we observe the arising of cognitions of distinct objects characterized by positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative exclusion (*vyatireka*) residing in the intellect.

Indeed, one cannot postulate another word-meaning by denying the determination of the cognition produced by the use of words in common worldly practice; for even if one goes to the furthest extreme, arguments must ultimately rest upon actual comprehension. Therefore, this [denial] is not a means of escape.
Therefore, the final fault has also not been avoided.
