And here, the aggregate (*saṃghāta*) is the meaning of the word, whether in the sense of production or manifestation.

If words, whose simultaneity is not established, are determined by a well-known effect or simply by worldly convention—since human reasoning is unstable—then this is merely tradition (*āgama*); for a sentence is a collection of words with an unrestricted sequence.
(Page 448, Note 2)

According to the doctrine under discussion, the meaning of the word (*śabdārtha*) is now established: here, in the context of injunction (*vidhi*), restriction (*niyama*), and further restriction (*niyamaniyama*), the aggregate (*saṅghāta*) of phonemes, words, sentences, and so forth constitutes the meaning of the word, whether in terms of its production (*utpatti*) or its manifestation (*abhivyakti*).

Thus, whether phonemes and the like are produced or manifested, the aggregate such as the sentence remains uncontradicted in both the view of it being an effect (*kārya*) and the view of its being eternal (*nitya*); therefore, the sentence and so forth are the word.

It might be thought: "Since phonemes and the like perish as soon as they arise, how can there be a combination (*saṅghāta*) in the absence of simultaneity? To this it is replied: If words, which do not attain simultaneity, are established in the world by their well-known effect, what is that effect? It is the communication of meaning. For example—whether phonemes and the like have disappeared, undergone a transformation, or perished—they deposit a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) in the intellect and thereby become the cause for the arising of the cognition of the denoted object. This is inferred because, in the absence of those [phonemes], that [cognition] does not occur, and because the cognition follows immediately upon their employment.

Or rather, the determination [of the word] is based solely on worldly convention (*lokaprasiddhi*). For it is observed in the world that since those individual sounds—such as phonemes (*varṇa*) and words (*pada*)—lack the capacity to convey meaning, the power (*śakti*) to convey meaning is established as belonging to their aggregate (*samudāya*). Now, some say that this aggregate is distinct from its constituents—the phonemes and so forth—because a different effect, impossible for those constituents, is observed. Others, however, say that because the conveying of meaning would otherwise be causeless, the aggregate cannot be something distinct from them; for it is impossible for it to exist either distributively in each of them individually or collectively in all of them together.

Some maintain that it is the collection (*samudāya*)—in which all remaining parts have been withdrawn—that expresses the meaning upon the final phoneme, depending on the impressions (*saṃskāra*) deposited by the cognition of the preceding phonemes, due to the maturation of the cognitions produced by the preceding phonemes. Others, however, argue: "Like sand and water, how could there be a manifestation of the signification if [the word] does not exist in other locations [of the phonemes]? Rather, like sesame oil, the collection of the maturation of mental impressions (*buddhi-saṃskāra*), which exists pervasively even though its constituent parts are held to be latent and have attained subtlety, is the manifestor of the cognition."

Furthermore, these are merely other points of inquiry, such as whether that word, which consists of a collection [of phonemes], is a single undivided signifier of meaning because a single cognition is observed, or whether it is indeed manifold because the knowledge of the meaning is produced by the force of the mental impressions (saṃskāra) deposited by each individual phoneme.

Since this is the domain of dry logic (*śuṣka-tarka*) produced by human intellect, what is the use of these [arguments]? Whether [the word] is distinct [from its parts] or non-distinct—if it were non-distinct, in the final analysis, would the whole (*samudāya*) be the communicator of meaning when all remaining parts are combined, or would it be the individual parts themselves? Let it be whatever it may be; for the purpose of conveying a meaning, which is the fruit, it is sufficient that "the word is the whole.
What is the reason? Because the reasoning of men is unstable, as it has been said: "Even an object inferred with great effort... (*Vākyapadīya* 1.34), and likewise:
"...like a blind man using the touch of his hand... (*Vākyapadīya* 1).

42. If this is so, what then should be understood? This is merely traditional scripture (*āgama*); for it has been stated that a sentence is a collection of words: "In the context of the doctrine of logical reasoning (*hetuvāda*), one is a logician (*hetuka*), and in the context of traditional scripture (*āgama*), one is a scripturalist (*āgamika*)."
Thus, one who explains according to the doctrine is a follower of the established tenets (*siddhānta*), while the other is a transgressor of the tenets;
this [latter] consists of a collection of words with an indefinite sequence. (3.45) Thus ends the section on Right Belief. 3.45. And that [collection of words] has an unrestricted order.

Successive existence is *ānupūrvya*. That for which this [succession] is not fixed is "one whose succession is indefinite" (*aniyatānupūrvya*). And this is a *paryavāstika* because it is a part of the word [paryava];
*pari* has the sense of "all around," and *ava* has the sense of "going"; thus, "going all around" is *paryava*.
What is it that flows away on all sides? It is difference (bheda), which is subordinate to the entity (bhāva).
He who holds the view that "this exists" is a Paryavāstika.
Its concluding statement is also: "The twelve-fold collection of the Gaṇipiṭaka, with respect to a single person, has a beginning and an end" (Nandīsūtra 42), and so forth.
Thus ends the eighth spoke, the rule of injunction and restriction, and the second path is completed.

A collection of words (*padasamūha*), such as "Devadatta, bring the cow" at one time, and at another "Devadatta, bring the white cow," or "Devadatta, [bring] a young, auspicious buffalo," or "Bring a vessel," "Bring a golden vessel," and so forth; or a mere treatise belonging to any one of the systems such as Grammar, Sāṅkhya, Vaiśeṣika, or Buddhism; or the Āgama of the Arhat, which consists of a collection of all scriptures—this is a sentence (*vākya*). The meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*) is also said to be the object denoted by it, which is the meaning of the word (*śabdārtha*).
The reading "śabdārtho 'bhidhīyate" appears correct; [the variants] "māvayor abhidheya" (Bhāṣya) and "māvayor abhidheya" (Yaśomitra) are not so.
Having withdrawn all faulty parts, [he is] one whose remaining parts are gathered together.
(Bhāṣya) / Having withdrawn all remaining parts, [he is] one whose remaining parts are gathered together. (Yaśomitra)
It should be understood that even the reading [of the commentary] is excellent;
for an object, though inferred with effort by skilled inferents, is demonstrated in quite another way by others who are more proficient.
Thus, let the complete verse be seen on page 36, line 4:
"In the position of the proponents of logic (*hetuvāda*), there is the logical (*hetuka*) and the scriptural (*āgamika*)."
One who examines the reason (*hetu*) from the perspective of the opponent (*vādyapakṣa*) is an expounder of his own doctrine (*sasamayaprajñāpaka*);
the other is a violator of the established tenet (*siddhāntavirādhaka*). Thus [ends] the third [section] on right conviction (*samyaktva*). 3 | 45.
He said:
"Even though it is undivided in its entirety, it is like a blind man running on a rugged path by means of the touch of his hand."
"For one who relies primarily on inference, a downfall is not difficult to encounter"—
this is the complete verse;
and because this is only a portion of the [original] word, it is a *paryavāstika* (an elliptical expression).
*Pari* has the sense of "on all sides" (*samantāt*); *ava* has the sense of "going" (*gati*). *Paryava* means "running on all sides," as in "he runs all around."
Who is he? He is one whose conviction is that "that distinction, which has existence as its subordinate element, exists"; he is a *paryavāstika*.
The reading "he protects on all sides" (*samantād avati*) would be correct.
A comparison [is found] on page 7, line 11.
Its concluding statement is also: "The twelve-fold collection of the scriptures (gaṇipiṭaka) is, with respect to a single person, having a beginning and an end" (Nandīsūtra 42);
see also page 3, line 7, and footnote page 5, line 23.
Thus ends the eighth chapter on the regulation of rules and observances, and the second path, concerning the meaning of sentences, is completed.

Furthermore, in which category is this method (naya) included—is it within the substantial standpoint (*dravyārtha*) or the modal standpoint (*paryāyārtha*)? It is said: because it is a part of the verbal [standpoint], this is a modal standpoint (*paryavāstika*). According to the root definition, it is a division of the straightforward statement (*ṛjusūtra-vacana*); its various linguistic formulations are subtle distinctions of the word.
In the *Sammatīya* [treatise], even though seven hundred *nayas* are traditionally taught, the meaning is that the *paryāyāstika* (modalist) variety is a sub-division of the *śabdanaya*.
According to the root classification, the *paryavanaya* is the differentiation of the statements of the *ṛjusūtra*.
The blinking of the eyes;
*suyaya*.
But for him, the various grammatical forms of words have subtle distinctions. (Sammatitarka 1.5;
"tassa u ya" is used in the sense of "and so on").

Regarding this meaning: what is the etymological sense (*śabdārtha*) of the term *paryavāstika*? It is said: the prefix *pari-* has the sense of "all around," and the verbal root *ava-* has the sense of "motion. Thus, *paryava* means moving all around or going completely around.

He explains this: having thus stated the literal meaning of the word—that it "flows" (dravati) everywhere—he shows the actual meaning: what is this? It is "difference" (*bheda*) with "existence" (*bhāva*) as its subordinate element. That difference which exists, such as a jar or the like, is a "mode" (*paryāya*) whose subordinate element is the action of coming-into-being (*bhavana-kriyā*). The meaning of the term *paryavāstika*—which ends in a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita-pratyaya*)—is to be understood as qualified by the meaning of its base (*prakṛti*), namely, the view of that *naya* which holds that "it exists."
In this sense, [it is] "non-destruction" (avayava);
the meaning is "descent" (ava-bhā).
Thus he explains it.
The reading "samantād avati" would be correct.

Are these [explanations] merely stated according to one's own imagination, or is there some scriptural basis for this as well? It is said that there is; for instance, he cites as a witness an Ārsa text consistent with this doctrine, namely the concluding statement of this [work]: "The twelve-fold collection of the Gaṇipiṭaka is based on a single person," and so forth.

Although this scripture has always remained established through a lineage of many persons, nevertheless, for the sake of certain determination, it rests upon each individual person, because the meaning of the verb (*bhavati*)—which is the primary reality—is subordinate to the general action and directed toward the particular.
Furthermore, that twelve-fold *Gaṇipiṭaka* is therefore both with beginning and with end, and its meaning is that it is strictly momentary.

By the inclusion of the phrase "and so forth," one should also understand that other expositions—such as those concerning the nature, duration, intensity, and extent of karmic bondage (*prakṛti-sthiti-anubhāva-pradeśa-bandha*), as well as the exposition of the mental dispositions (*adhyavasāya*) resulting from the transformation of false view (*mithyā-darśana*) and the like—all have only a single moment as their object.
By the lineage of Siṅghabhūti Megha... the donation is established.
Whether it be immediately,
or at another time,
or even at some other time.
Due to the presence of passions (kaṣāya), the soul (jīva) takes up matter (pudgala) suitable for karma;
that is bondage (bandha).
Its types are nature (prakṛti), duration (sthiti), intensity (anubhāva), and extension (pradeśa).
—*Tattvārthasūtra* 8.2–4.

Thus, at the conclusion [of these sūtras], this eighth chapter, which demonstrates the application of injunction (*vidhi*) and restriction (*niyama*) through their relationship as subordinate and primary, is completed. And the second path, which presents the distinctions between the two types of alternatives, is finished.
This is the demonstration of the restriction (*niyama*) alone;
the second [verse] concerns the alternative of both (*ubhaya-vikalpa*).
Oṃ Arhaṃ.
Salutations to the True Gurus. Now begins the ninth chapter on Observances (niyama).

If existence is primarily characterized by duality, how can it be such? Being devoid of an existent subject, it is incapable of even attaining its own nature; due to its lack of independence, it is non-existent, like a flower in the sky.
In the absence of that [distinguishing property], there would be only scattered differences;

consequently, since there would be no object to be distinguished (*bhettavya*), even the differences themselves could not exist. Thus, there is a contradiction regarding the essential nature of the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*):
the non-existence of differences such as those of a jar and so forth, because there is no object to be distinguished, like the flowers of the *udumbara* tree in the sky.

Furthermore, because [the earth] is utterly indefinable, there are contradictions with one's own words, with accepted tenets, with inference, and with perception regarding the statement "the earth becomes a jar. If, in this case, only the particular (*viśeṣa*) exists, then in the absence of the universal (*sāmānya*), the particular cannot exist either;
and if the particular does not exist, how can the universal possess the capacity to assist the non-existent primary cause (*asat-pradhāna*)?

While abiding in the section on the single reality consisting of the function that sublates all injunctions and restrictions (*vidhi-niyama-sarvabhaṅga-vṛtti-ātmaka-eka-tattva*), one who remains dissatisfied even with the observation of the sublation of both injunctions and restrictions gives rise to the subsequent *naya*, which consists of the sublation of restrictions (*niyamabhaṅga*).

Since it is appropriate to demonstrate one's own position once that [subsequent view] has been refuted, he says—in order to refute it—the passage beginning with "If an entity were primarily characterized by difference" and ending with "the contradiction between the nature of the property and the property-bearer."

It has been stated that where difference (*bheda*) is primary, its persistence (*anvaya*) is secondary; regarding that, we must ascertain the nature of such a state—how is it so? That intended persisting state (*anvaya-bhāva*), being distinct from the action of difference (*bheda-kriyā*), is incapable of even attaining its own essential form without a subject (*kartṛ*) who brings it about.
Why? Because, being dependent, it is not an agent; not being an agent, it does not exist, like a sky-flower.
In the absence of that persisting state, differences alone would remain scattered, devoid of any object to be differentiated.
Furthermore, because there is an absence of any lineage (*anvaya*) that could be differentiated, even distinctions (*bheda*) cannot exist.

For a distinction is that which is being differentiated; how can it be differentiated? Because it is indivisible, like a sky-flower. Thus, due to the absence of distinctions, there is an absence of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of both the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*). Consequently, the statement that "the meaning of a word consists primarily of distinction, with the underlying continuity (*anvaya*) as subordinate" has become one whose very nature of property and substratum is refuted. Having concluded this, he states the proof: "The absence of distinctions such as 'pot' and so forth, because of the absence of anything to be differentiated, like a sky-udumbara flower."

There is an absence of both the divider and the object to be divided; for example, a sky-flower is neither the divider nor the object to be divided in relation to an udumbara flower, nor is an udumbara flower such in relation to a sky-flower—this is the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*). Likewise, the point illustrated (*dārṣṭāntika*) concerns the subordinate and the principal, as well as the universal and the particular. Consequently, in the event that [the entity] results in emptiness due to being utterly indefinable (*nirupākhya*), contradictions with one's own words, accepted tenets, inference, and perception would ensue; and these are undesirable.
Regarding the [reading] ˚katatvādhi˚bhā˚ ˚katvādhi˚ ya˚,
see page 737, line 2.
Is it for the sake of certainty? Is it by means of uncertainty? Is it something indeterminate? Is it indefinable? Or is it existent?

Furthermore, regarding the statement "the earth becomes a jar," that which must be determined is this: does the earth become [something] but not a jar; or does the jar become [something] but not the earth; or do both become [something]; or do neither become [anything]?

In that regard, as for the argument beginning with "if it were only the particular," since it was just stated that in the absence of the subordinate universal, the particular does not exist either, and since the particular (the jar) is non-existent, how could the universal—which is itself non-existent—exist? Furthermore, if the continuity of earth and so forth arises from activity, then the universal cannot be subordinate;

yet, if both are absent, if that difference were indeed a non-entity, then by virtue of that very difference, there would be no further manifestation, because it is a non-entity like a sky-flower, for a non-entity never becomes an entity.

Now, if it were already an existent (*bhāva*), then because it would not be distinct from existence and would already have come into being, it could not come into being again in either case—just like a pot that has already been produced, or like space. For that which has already come into being does not come into being [again], as that would result in its becoming non-existent. If that which has already come into being were to arise once more, it would then be non-existent, because it would be something currently arising, like a pot that has not yet been born.

If it is argued that the persistence (*anvaya*) within the particulars (*bheda*) is merely figurative (*aupacārika*), then surely the persisting substance (*anvayadravya*) abides in its own self alone; consequently, since the particulars such as jars are merely states (*avasthāmātra*) of that [substance], it follows that the particulars such as jars are themselves merely figurative.

This is just as when it is said, "the finger becomes curved," the curvature is merely a state of difference belonging to the finger. Is this not the primary assistance? Thus begins the passage starting with "atha" and so forth.

Now, lest there be the fault of the non-existence of both the universal and the particular due to their being subordinate to earth and so forth, [it is argued that] earth and the like possess the nature of a concomitant (anvayitva) because they exist as the basis for activity; consequently, the universal does not have subordination, because it pervades its own essence, because it is a positive entity (bhāvatva), and because it functions, just like a particular. Even in this way, subordination is excluded.
(Note: *viśeṣaṇove nāstye* is a fragmentary reading from page 738, line 4 of manuscript *Eya*.)
[Regarding] the [section] called "Ascertainment":
Now, if earth and so forth were the correlates (*anvayin*) of activity, then the generality would not be subordinate;

but since both [of these conditions] are absent, if that difference were indeed a non-entity (*abhāva*), then there could be no further differentiation by means of that very difference, because it is a non-entity, like a sky-flower.

For non-existence does not become existence; nor does existence itself [become non-existence]. Therefore, because it is not distinct from existence and because it has already come into being, in either case there would be no further becoming—just as with a jar or the like that has already come into being, or like space and the like.
For that which has already come into being does not become [existent] again, as that would entail its falling into non-existence.
If that which has already come into being were to exist [again], then it would be non-existent, because it is in the process of arising, like an unproduced jar or similar object.
Furthermore, there would be the fundamental point here that by means of the very distinction through which something exists, it would not exist by that same distinction.

If it is argued that the continuity of existence (*bhavanānvaya*) among the distinctions is merely figurative (*aupacārika*), then surely the substance of continuity (*anvayadravya*) abides only in itself; consequently, since the distinctions such as the jar are merely its states, it follows that the distinctions such as the jar are themselves figurative.
Just as when it is said, "the finger is curved," the curvature is merely the state of the finger's differentiation (*bhedāvasthāmātra*), because [the finger] is not pervasive (*avyāpitvāt*).

Regarding the phrase "in both": if that which exists in both—the universal (*sāmānya*) in earth and the particular (*bheda*) in a jar—is non-existent; and if there is no positive concomitance (*anvaya*) in the entity (*bhāva*) nor in the particular (*viśeṣa*) which is the substratum (*bhavitṛ*); then if that differentiation is indeed a non-entity (*abhāva*), such that by means of that differentiation one becomes differentiated—that very differentiation would not exist, because it is a non-entity. It is a non-entity because its nature consists in the absence of the action of becoming (*abhavanakriyātmakatvāt*), like a flower in the sky.

For it is shown through the meaning of the example that "non-existence does not become existence. Now, if [the difference] were indeed existence, so that this fault might not occur, then that difference would be accepted as having the very nature of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and being existence itself. Consequently, because it is not distinct from existence, because its essence is existence, because its essence is positive concomitance, and because it is already existent, it could not arise again—whether as the primary or the subordinate factor—through the two states of "earth" and "pot-ness," since it is already existent, like a pot that has already come into being; and because it would be redundant, like space and so forth. He demonstrates this by saying: "for that which is already existent does not come into being."
Why? Because it would result in non-existence (*asattva*).

If that which has already come into being were to become [something else], or if that which has already arisen were to arise again, then it would be non-existent, because it is currently in the process of arising, like an unproduced jar or similar objects; thus, there is the consequence of non-existence. And since that is undesirable, neither a positive entity (*bhāva*) nor a negative non-entity (*abhāva*) exists. Furthermore, the distinction between "earth" and "jar" is also experienced as both.
Difference is experienced as a positive entity (bhāva),
not as an absence (abhāva).

Regarding "na bhāvaḥ," the following should be noted here: due to a scribe's error, it is possible that there is a double occurrence (dvirbhāva) such as "na bhāvo bhavati na bhāvo bhavaḥ. However, if that were accepted, it would lead to an undesirable consequence; thus, the reading "na bhāvo bhavaty ubhayaṃ pṛthivī ghaṭaśca" might also be possible here, [as applied] to the various particulars (bhedeṣu), and so forth.

It might be thought: "Since the particularities such as jars and so forth exist separately in ultimate reality, that continuity of being (*bhavanānvaya*) which occurs in the form 'it is, it is' is merely figurative. To this, it is said: "But surely, [regarding] continuity," and so on. Indeed, you yourself have stated that earth and the other elements abide in their own substance, within their own selves; therefore, those particularities such as jars are merely states of the continuity of the substances earth and so forth, and thus the particularities such as jars are themselves figurative. It follows that the universal alone—earth and so forth—is the true reality.

What is this like? To this he says: just as curvature belongs to the finger and not to the finger itself—for curvature does not become the finger because it is unproduced, like a sky-flower, and because it is distinct, like color—therefore, by the logic already stated, the three worlds, though conceived as distinct, are indeed non-distinct, since distinctions are dependent upon substance.
Because it occurs through successive stages, the process of becoming is in every respect untenable.
Upon examining its specific nature, if becoming were to exist separately by its own power,
then— since prior becoming would be non-independent and not occurring separately— it would follow that the jar is non-existent due to being rootless, like a flower in the sky.
Nor is that [curvature] the entity itself, because that would entail the abandonment of the position that the particular (*viśeṣa*) is primary;

nor is it the state of being of this [entity], and thus, due to the lack of distinction from non-existence, [it follows that it is unreal], and so forth. For example, when it is said "the finger is curved," the curvature is a state of the finger; it is merely a particular state of the finger as a universal (*sāmānya*), and thus curvature is figurative (*aupacārika*).
It does not belong to the finger, because the finger does not become curvature, since curvature is a state and the finger is the substratum.
It is the finger itself that becomes curved; curvature does not become the finger.
Why, then, does curvature not become the finger? It is said: because it is unproduced, like a flower in the sky.
Thus, first, the state of being merely substance (*dravyamātratva*) has been explained regarding those modes (*paryāya*) that are intended to be non-simultaneous and distinct in time.

Furthermore, because there is a state of differentiation even among the desired successions (paryāyas) that exist simultaneously yet differ in location, [the object] is merely a state of that [consciousness], just like color (rūpa).

For example, just as a jar itself is designated by different names such as "color," "taste," or "smell" due to its being qualified by the designations of perception through the eyes and so forth, or as a finger [is designated differently]; because in those cases, the differentiation belongs to consciousness alone while the substance—the jar—remains undifferentiated, so too are the specific instances of the general categories such as earth, the jars and so forth, and stones, sand, and so forth, [mere manifestations] of consciousness alone.
Thus, [it is said]: "But surely, by you... and so on.

Regarding the passage beginning with *nacvayā* (Bhāṣya): here, this should be noted. If one accepts that the pratīka *nanu tvayetyādi* is the correct reading, then it follows that by saying "surely those very states are the distinctions such as the jar," it is stated that the distinctions such as the jar are merely metaphorical (*aupacārika*). Thus, the root text here should be understood as *svātmano 'vabhāsaḥ*.
By its own self alone; [it is] merely the state of being a constituent part of the substance by its own self alone.
In this context, the reading "merely a state of the substance" (*dravyasyāvasthāmātram*) is also possible;

for "becoming" (*bhavati*) refers to the figurative nature of curvature, not to the finger itself. Indeed, curvature does not become the finger, because it has not yet arisen, like a flower in the sky.
And because difference is a quality like color,

according to the logic already stated, the three worlds— though conceived as distinct— are indeed non-different, since differences are dependent upon substance and the occurrence of modifications (paryāya) [is impossible otherwise]; thus, the process of existence cannot be established in any way whatsoever [if this were not the case].
In the investigation of the specific nature [of an entity], existence (bhavana) exists separately by its own power;
if that prior existence were not independent and did not exist separately, then, being rootless, the jar would be non-existent like a sky-flower,
nor would it be an entity in its own right, because that would entail the abandonment of the position that the particular is primary.
Nor does its existence [as a separate entity] occur; and consequently, because there is no distinction in its non-existence,
the reading here might even be "the finger becomes curved"— see Pañjikā 10,
section on the state of difference (bhedāvasthā).
The reading *tadavasthā* might also be possible here; see Pañjikā 12.
*Bhavatīti bhāvaḥ* is stated by you [in the] Prakaraṇa.
See page 739, line 23 of volume 8.

Furthermore, according to the aforementioned reasoning and so forth, within the past *dravyārthika* (substantial) viewpoints such as those of the Sāṃkhya and others, the three worlds—though conceived as distinct—are in fact non-different from the single, all-pervading, eternal causal substance alone, just as waves and the like are not different from a still lake; for it has been established in the doctrines of the *puruṣa* and others that distinctions, such as various states and designations, are dependent upon substance (*dravya*), and that substance itself does not depend upon its modifications (*paryāya*).

"Because of the occurrence of modes," and so forth; thus, in every respect, the process of becoming is untenable, because in this way, according to the perspective of the substance-view (dravyanaya) of the past,
there is no occurrence of modes,
and so on.

Now, as for the statement "in every way indeed non-existent, having the nature of a particular," and so forth—even that particular, when its own nature is examined, cannot be found apart from the power of continuity (*anvaya*). For example: that which fills and protects the nature of its own effects, such as its states and so forth, is the cause; this becoming, which is continuity, exists by its own majesty even as something distinct, apart from differentiation (*bheda*), in the many ways described in the past systems.

If, as you desire, the prior existence were independent and distinct from the manifestation (*bhavana*), then what follows? From that [consequence], starting with "because it would be rootless" and so forth: because it would be rootless, the jar would be non-existent, like a sky-flower—this might be your thought: "What is the use of existence as the root of the jar? Why does it not exist by itself? But this is not the case; the jar is not an entity by itself. Why? Because it would entail the abandonment of the position in which the particular (*viśeṣa*) is primary.

If the particular (*viśeṣa*) itself were the existent (*bhāva*), then the pot alone would be the particular; that very thing would be the existent, the "coming-to-be" (*bhavana*), and it would exist as a pervasive (*anvaya*) existent. Therefore, because of being such an existent, would not even the pot have "mere existence" (*bhāvamātra*) as its universal (*sāmānya*) referent? [In that case], like a sky-flower, there would be no distinction, leading to contradictions such as the impossibility of the aforementioned distinctions of manifestation (*āvirbhāva*) and so forth.
[Objection: But surely the particular is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
[Response: Even though it is seen, its non-existence is observed because it does not exist in that manner [as a real entity], just as in the case of a mirage or a city of Gandharvas.

For it is observed that mirages and cities of the Gandharvas, despite being perceived by the senses, are non-existent because they lack specific qualities such as coldness; likewise, even if a particular object is perceived, it may be non-existent. Now, it might be argued: "In the water of a mirage and in a city of the Gandharvas, there is no specific quality such as coldness or the categories of soul and non-soul; thus, due to the absence of specific qualities, there would be non-existence. However, it is not necessary that a thing must possess further specific qualities for it to exist, such that the absence of those qualities would lead one to infer its non-existence. If there were indeed further specific qualities within a specific quality, then that very specific quality would become a non-specific universal (aviśeṣa), precisely because it possesses specific qualities, just like the universals of 'existent substance' (sat-dravya) or 'earth' (pṛthivī)."
Moreover, we too say this very thing: that there would be only positive concomitance (anvaya),
yet that does not exist, just like a sky-flower, nor even the collection of particular things such as jars and the like.
Because that [particular] is predominant and because existence conforms to the particular, there is a loss of the thesis which holds the particular as primary with the universal as subordinate;
thus, upon examination, it is first of all untenable to say "the jar is existence."
It would follow that [the universal] is obtained;
for it is obtained as something existing separately, just as you have asserted.
Regarding the occurrence of distinctness: just as it is desired by you that [qualities] such as number and so forth are rootless,
they do not exist by themselves.
The reading *sāmānyam arthabhāgaḥ* (the universal is the objective portion) may also occur here; furthermore, there might also be the reading *sāmānyam artho yaḥ sāmānyam evam*.

If it is argued that there is no distinction [between the cause and effect] just as in the case of a sky-flower, then—as previously stated—there would be contradictions such as the impossibility of distinctions like manifestation (*āvirbhāva*) and so forth.
But surely, a distinction is perceived through direct perception itself.
Even though something is seen, its non-existence is observed because it does not persist in that way, just as in the cases of a mirage and a city of Gandharvas.

For it is observed that even though a mirage and a city of the Gandharvas are perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), they are non-existent because specific qualities such as coldness and so forth are absent; likewise, there may be non-existence even when a particular is perceived. Now, if it should be argued: "In the water of a mirage and in a city of the Gandharvas, specific qualities such as coldness or the categories of soul (*jīva*) and non-soul (*ajīva*) do not exist; thus, due to the absence of specific qualities, there might be non-existence. However, a particular does not necessarily have to be constituted by further particulars, such that one would postulate non-existence based on the absence of such particulars. If there were particulars within a particular, it would be nothing other than a non-particular (*aviśeṣa*), because it would possess particulars, just like the generalities (*sāmānya*) of existent substance (*sad-dravya*) such as earth and the rest."

Moreover, we too say this very thing: that there should be positive concomitance (*anvaya*), yet that does not exist, being like a flower in the sky; therefore, [your objection] is incorrect. *Pra.* [1.23]

In the water of a mirage, there is non-existence because of the absence of specific qualities such as coldness, softness, and liquidity; and in a city of the Gandharvas, there is non-existence because of the absence of the specific properties of living and non-living beings that appear therein. However, it is not necessarily the case that in a particular entity such as a jar, there must be specific earth-derivatives like stones, sand, and so forth, on account of which the non-existence of particulars would be postulated. If there were particulars within a particular, it would be a non-particular (a universal) alone; it would be a universal, a commonality, because a particular, by virtue of possessing particulars, would be like the universal "existent" (sat), "substance" (dravya), "earth" (pṛthivī), and so forth.

Regarding the existence of substance and earth, the Teacher says: "Moreover, we too say this very thing—that if there were only positive concomitance (*anvaya*) without distinction, there would be only a universal (*sāmānya*);

But does a mirage, although lacking the specific quality of water, not possess distinctions such as coldness and so forth? Precisely because of its existence and non-existence, just as that [mirage] is, so too the specific qualities such as a jar do not exist due to the presence or absence of a common substrate (*anvaya*).

If the particular (*viśeṣa*) alone were primary, then even a jar and the like would be non-existent—like a mirage and so forth—because they would not be connected to the state of being water; and due to being indefinable (*nirupākhya*), it could not be designated as "this is that."
Consequently, nothing at all would exist, because it would lack support through a commonality such as "earth" and so forth, like a sky-flower.

Likewise, why is earth not manifested by water and other elements that are distinct from it? Or, due to absolute dissimilarity, why might there not be some entirely inexpressible object, since it would be devoid of any underlying continuity (*anvaya*)? For this very reason, because of the absence of continuity known as the stream of connection between the soul and karma, there would be no possibility of saṃsāra, liberation, and so on. If there were continuity without a particularity called "form" (*ākṛti*) consisting in such becoming, then the particularity itself would be without a universal; and that does not exist, like a sky-flower.

Nor is the universal alone devoid of particularity; what then? It is because when a specific form is produced, there is the production of jars and the like, since the manifestation of the universal existence consists in its assuming a particular nature. Likewise, because forms, tastes, smells, and other such particulars abide within the jar, and because the substance comes into being in various ways through the production of these manifested particulars (pṛ. 172, l.

Consequently, nothing would exist because it would not be supported by a commonality such as earth and so forth, like a sky-flower.

For this very reason, because there is an absence of continuity known as the stream of connection between the soul and karma, there would be no transmigration, liberation, or anything else.

If the particular were independent of the universal, then why would earth and so forth not be manifested by water, fire, wind, space, and so on, in the same way that they are manifested by a specific mode of existence such as "pot" or "cloth"? Or, because it is utterly different from earth due to its distinctness from the substance of earth, why might there not be some entity that is entirely devoid of continuity, indefinable, inexpressible, and unknowable, existing as something distinct from the entire collection of substances? [This would be the case] because it lacks any underlying continuity (*anvaya*). Furthermore, the construction "distinct from earth" (*pṛthivīvibhinnena*) could also be applied [to the other elements]. (Note: *manyasthā* appears to be a scribal error for *anyasya*.)
The reading *anyasmāt* (from another) is likely correct here;
for this very reason, and so forth:

because there is no existence for that which is devoid of continuity (*anvaya*) and lacks any defining characteristic (*nirupākhya*), there follows the impossibility of meritorious and non-meritorious karma—the engagement with specific objects of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*) such as the specific states of rebirth like hell, characterized by the fruits of pleasure and pain—due to the absence of continuity known as the stream of connection between the soul, karma, and causal conditions such as false vision (*mithyādarśana*). Because of that impossibility, the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) is impossible, and consequently, the specific transformations of right vision (*samyagdarśana*) and so forth, which are its antidotes, are impossible. This results from the lack of a fixed, directed engagement [of the soul].

And since such an indeterminate application [of the term] occurs, one must maintain that in the expression "the earth is a jar" (*pṛthivī ghaṭaḥ*), the predominance belongs precisely to the positive concomitance (*anvaya*); for in common usage, the particular (*viśeṣa*) follows the general (*pṛthivī*), as it is the predominant factor that is followed, not the subordinate.
If it is argued that this is not so because, as previously stated, the particular always follows [the general], we reply: no, because in this case there is an absence of such a particular.
Therefore, having abandoned these two extremist positions—that there is only the universal or only the particular—one must understand the ineffable reality (*avacanīya-vastu*).

It is not non-existence, nor is it a subordinate [element] to that; it is not existence alone, nor is it without distinction, nor is it with distinction as subordinate; it is not the particular alone, nor is it with both as subordinate, nor is it with both as primary.
The ineffable reality is that which consists of the cause and effect of existence and distinction, being both unitary and manifold, and having both as primary and subordinate.

Furthermore, liberation as something to be attained would be impossible; consequently, human effort such as the study of scriptures would be untenable, because activity would not be directed toward a specific end. Now, if one were to maintain that activity is directed toward a specific end so that these faults do not arise, then—given that such directed activity exists regarding the connection between the soul and karma, as well as saṃsāra, liberation, and so forth—one must accept that the primary relation is one of grammatical coreference (anvaya), as in "the soul is a hell-being," "the soul is in saṃsāra," or "the soul is liberated. In this case, the particularity (viśeṣa)—such as being a jar or being a hell-being—is what conforms to the universal (jīvatva). Thus, "jar" conforms to "earth," and "hell-being-ness" conforms to "soul-ness."

Why? Because in the world, it is the primary factor (*pradhāna*) that is followed, not the subordinate quality (*guṇa*); whereas the subordinate quality follows, the primary factor does not, as in the case of a "blue lotus" (*nīlotpala*). [Otherwise] there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasanga*) of non-exclusion, because [the relationship] would function without such fixed regularity.

And since such an indeterminate application [of the term] is possible, one must maintain that in the expression "the earth is a jar" (*pṛthivī ghaṭaḥ*), the predominance belongs solely to the positive concomitant (*anvaya*); for in common usage, it is the particular (*viśeṣa*) that follows the general (*sāmānya*), as the principal is followed, not the subordinate.

If it is argued that this is not so because, as stated, there is always a following of the particular due to the absence of a [corresponding] general, we reply: it is just like that, because there is no such particularity here.

Therefore, having abandoned these two extremist positions—that there is only the universal or only the particular—one must understand the ineffable reality (*avacanīya-vastu*). It is not non-existence, nor is it that [non-existence] as a subordinate factor; it is not existence alone, nor is it without distinction, nor is it with distinction as a subordinate factor, nor is it the particular alone. It is not a reality where both are subordinate, nor where both are primary; rather, the ineffable reality consists of the cause and effect of existence and distinction, being both primary and subordinate in various ways.

A thing that is an inexpressible reality (*avaktavya-tattva*) comes to be when it is conceptualized through such alternatives as existence and distinction, cause and effect, unity and plurality, primary and subordinate, and so forth.

Nor is it a non-entity devoid of continuity; nor is it a thing that is subordinate to that [non-existence], or subordinate to existence, with the particular as its primary element—this is what is intended by the connection. It is not existence alone from which the particular has been excluded; likewise, it is not without distinction, i.e., devoid of particularity; nor is it a universal as the primary element with the particular as subordinate—nor is it the particular alone with the universal utterly disregarded. Nor is it a thing where both are subordinate, such that both the universal and the particular have their independence utterly discarded; nor is it one where both are primary, such that the universal and the particular are entirely independent and of equal status. This is because all these conceptual alternatives are seen to entail the fault of resulting in non-existence.

If there were identity [between fire and fuel], then, like a burnt-out fuel, fire would not proceed because it would be devoid of fuel; and since that which lacks fuel does not proceed, fire would simply be non-existent and would not proceed due to its oneness, like burnt-out fuel. If it is argued that just as fuel proceeds even when devoid of fire—meaning it exists without fire having yet arisen—so too fire will proceed even when devoid of fuel, being in a subtle state, then who says that "the fuel is devoid of fire"?

In that regard, one must consider whether fire and fuel are identical, distinct, both, neither, or whether one is primary and the other subordinate; having thus raised these alternatives, the meaning of the example—which will be explained—is that they are in every respect inexpressible (*avaktavyatā*), because none of those conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) are tenable.

How so? As for the statement "how there is no oneness," etc., that oneness would have to exist either of fire together with fuel, or of fuel together with fire. Since the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used for a subordinate element associated with "together" (*saha*), it would follow that either the fuel alone is the fire, or the fire alone is the fuel.
First of all, the identity of fire with its fuel is not tenable. Because of that identity with it, and because of the predominance of that [fuel], a fault will be stated: namely, non-existence.

If there were identity between fire and fuel, then, like a fire whose fuel has been consumed, the fire—being devoid of fuel—would not proceed; just as a fire whose fuel is consumed does not proceed, so too would this [fire] not proceed.

Because there is no activity for that which lacks fuel, fire would simply be non-existent; for it is stated that "the roots *asti*, *bhavati*, *vidyati*, *padyati*, and *vartate*, with *sannipāta* as the sixth, have the sense of existence (*sattā*)," and since activity has the sense of existence, non-activity is a synonym for non-existence. Having concluded this, he states the proof: [Fire] would not proceed, because of its oneness, like a fire whose fuel is burnt.

Just as a fire whose fuel is burnt does not proceed because it is one with the fuel—since it does not exist apart from the fuel—and thus, due to its oneness and lack of activity, it is non-existent, so too is fire.
