He explains that: because the state of being fuel (*indhana*) is dependent upon that [fire], fire is the illuminator; since it serves the purposes of illuminating, burning, and reducing to ash, the fuel is only "kindled" (*idhyate*), "burned" (*dahyate*), or "illuminated" (*dīpyate*) when it has undergone that very transformation. For those who maintain the doctrine of identity, there is no distinction between the states of fire-ness and fuel-ness when they have not undergone that transformation, because the state of being fuel belongs only to that which has transformed into fire-ness. Thus, that which is not being burned is non-fuel, for only those things that are active agents (*kāraka*) possess the status of being agents.

And the attainment of a specific state from a subtle state would occur once it is established that there is no difference between the universal and the particular, the effect and the cause, and the subordinate and the predominant qualities.

To this, it might be argued: "If it is said that fire is one with its fuel—even though non-existence might be suspected because fire does not function [as distinct] due to its oneness with the fuel—nevertheless, there is no fault because of oneness with the fuel as in the case of the 'original' (ādi), since this is observed; and coexistence resides in both."

Now, how does activity proceed in the case of difference? Why is fuel not fire? Because of the oneness of the burner; [is it] because of having an end? Because it exists at the end, and because of the contradiction with the traditional rule (smṛti) "the root *indh* [means] to kindle" (Pāṇini Dhātupāṭha 1449), that which is not being kindled lacks the nature of fuel. Therefore, he says: "That which is not being burned is without fuel, provided it is not being kindled. What is the reason? Because of the agency belonging to the factors of action (*kāraka*) themselves. Only in the state where the powers of agent, object, and so forth are infused is there the agency of agent, object, and so forth for the factors of action, through the acquisition of their own unmixed natures; otherwise it would not be so, as it would entail the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that everything would be clay, a jar, and so on.
See page 487–1;
as in the *Pra*,
therefore there is no [single] entity (*ekārtha*).
Let it be seen on page 487— 1.
*katābhā* (in the editions of Bhāṣya and Ya), it is accepted by Ya.

Since the state of being fuel (*indhanatva*) does not transform into that [state of being fire], fuel remains non-fuel when it is not being burned, precisely because it has transformed into the state of being fire; for it is only through the transformation of the causal factors (*kāraka*) themselves that they possess the status of being causal factors.

And the attainment of a specific state from a subtle state would occur once it is established that there is no difference between the universal and the particular, the effect and the cause, and the subordinate and the predominant qualities.

To this, it might be argued: "If it is said that fire is one with its fuel—even though non-existence might be suspected because fire does not function [as distinct] due to its oneness with the fuel—nevertheless, there is no fault because of oneness with the fuel, just as in the case of the 'primordial' (ādi), since such a state is observed; moreover, coexistence resides in both."

Now, how does activity proceed in the case of difference? Why is fuel not fire? Because of the identity of the burner; [is it] like the end? At the end, because of the presence of non-existence. Presence. (bhā. [End.]
See page 482–2.

Regarding what was also stated—that fire in its subtle state is devoid of fuel—that too is not tenable; in order to demonstrate this, he says: "And by virtue of being in a subtle state," and so forth.

That which you describe as the attainment of a specific state of flame by fire—which exists in a general state of blazing—not distinct from its fuel, specifically the flame that has merged with the subtle, supersensory blackness of the fuel; likewise, the attainment of a state of quality (*guṇa*) by that which exists in the state of a qualified entity (*guṇin*), or the attainment of a causal state by that which exists in the state of an effect—this would be possible only if the non-difference between the universal and the particular, the effect and the cause, and the quality and the primary substance were established, and thus it would be appropriate to speak in such a way. However, even that non-difference of these [entities] is indeed questionable, because the difference between the states of the universal/particular and so forth remains unestablished.
If difference is established, how can the identity of fire and fuel be asserted? See page 744, line 5;
and [the term] "sāmānya" [is used].
°manya ? ? ? comparison—page 487—2 °sthayo bhedā° ya.
Now, it might be argued as follows: "I am not saying that fire is one with the fuel; rather, I say that the fuel is one with the fire.

To explain this: although [it is said] "of the fire," etc., it is true that if there were identity between fire and fuel, then due to that established identity, there would be a lack of activity—as in the case of wood that has already been burned. And since there is no activity for that which lacks fuel, the fault of non-existence is possible. Even so, when the possibility of the fault of non-existence exists despite their being identical, there is a logical principle regarding the absence of such a fault.
For example—like the initial [case]—because of the identity of fuel and fire, there will be no fault because the fuel is one with the fire.

Why? Because it is observed; for it is observed that in fuel where fire has not yet arisen, there is subsequently the manifestation of fire which was previously unmanifested, through the friction of the upper and lower kindling sticks.

Furthermore, because "coexistence" (sahabhāva) resides in two things, and since the word "iti" here has the sense of a reason, just as fuel exists together with fire, so too fire exists together with fuel; therefore, just as fire exists prior to its manifestation, fuel must likewise exist within the fire. Otherwise, coexistence would be impossible. (Page 744, Line 2). [Variant reading: *indhyanena*].
By means of the *nādha* [vowel], the *ya* [consonant],
and the *satva* [suffix],
likewise in the state of oneness (*ekatva*), it is manifested.
Is it the state of simultaneous existence with the primary [cause], or the state of non-simultaneous existence with the primary [cause]? See pages 484–2, 485–1, and 492–1.
Thus, thus; [this is] the word *iti*; because of the non-arising of the person (*nara*).

To this we reply: you yourself must be asked this—how can there be activity toward a distinction? If fire and fuel were one, what distinction would there be, or how could fire attain the state of being fuel, since it is identical with the fuel? Furthermore, because of the aforementioned dilemma, their oneness is contradicted.
If they were one, from where would this distinction arise—that "this" does not burn while "that" does?
Furthermore, because the action of churning, as well as its substratum, instrument, and so forth, would be untenable;

even if some kind of unity were somehow established, one still could not say "one is one," because of that very [logical] unity. Just as with the many parts such as the hands of a single Devadatta, one cannot say that the hand itself is "only one," because of the multiplicity of the fingers and other members.
A finger consists of many joints; a joint consists of many segments; and a segment consists of many atoms.
Because an atom consists of multiple components such as form and so forth;
because form and so forth are different at every moment;
and because even that which is unitary at each moment is ultimately manifold.

By what reason do you state that "co-existence (sahabhāva) resides in two [entities]"? Here, the proof for establishing an undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭāpādana*) is as follows: Why is it not fuel (*indhana*)?
Because, by accepting the mutual assumption of a single nature, fuel and fire would each become the other—just as in the forest state and the flaming state.

That is to say, in that case, fuel would be fire itself, because of the identity of the burner; it would be like the end, like the time of destruction, like the time of mere fire, or like the states of flame, embers, and so forth.

Or else, by the reverse of that, fire in its state as a flame and so forth would incur the status of fuel; because it is identical with the fuel, it would be as it was before, like the state of the forest [before the fire]. And this is undesirable for you. See page 488, line 2; see page 487, line 2.
Fire would incur the state of being fuel because of its identity with the fuel; as before, there is a contradiction of oneness due to the dilemma,
and if there were oneness, from what source would this distinction arise— that "this does not consume" while "that does consume"?
Furthermore, because the action of churning, as well as its locus, instrument, and so forth, would be untenable;
even if some kind of unity were somehow possible, one still could not say "one and only one," because of that very unity— just as in the case of the multiplicity of Devadatta’s hands and other limbs,
one cannot say that "the hand is also only one," because of the multiplicity of the fingers and so on.
Even a finger [is not a single entity] because it consists of many joints;
even a joint because it consists of many segments; and even a segment because it consists of many atoms.
As long as the atom consists of multiple components such as form and so forth,
and since form and so forth are distinct at every moment,
even that which is unitary at each moment is ultimately manifold.
See page 755, line 4:
"...from [the state of] having abandoned fuel... (vyatyaktendhana-). Bhāṣya.
Is it from [the state] where the fuel is manifest, or from [the state] where the fuel is both manifest and unmanifest?
In this regard, the accumulation of one [element] through burning,
and by means of the burning of one, [is established]. *Bhāṣya*.
Furthermore, there is another point: there is a contradiction of oneness due to conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

If one accepts the conceptual constructions that "fire is one with the fuel" and "fuel is one with the fire," the thesis of oneness is abandoned; for these two conceptual constructions are only tenable if there is difference, since they are untenable if there is oneness.

Therefore, demonstrating this, he says: "If there were oneness, whence would this distinction come—that 'this does not tolerate that' and 'this tolerates that'? This demonstration of the impossibility of conceptual differentiation has already been explained as being like [the argument] of those who maintain non-duality based solely on a single cause, such as the Puruṣa.

Furthermore, because of the impossibility of the action of rubbing, its substratum, its instrument, and so forth, if there were oneness, there would be a contradiction of that oneness; this is what follows. In the act of rubbing, the lower fire-stick is the substratum, the upper fire-stick is the instrument, and thus [the resulting fire] is the object—this entire variety of the operation of the *kārakas* (factors of action) well-known in the world would be untenable, because of the oneness of fire and fuel, just as there is no such thing as rubbing the sky.
Yet, this conventional usage of the distinction between the operations of the *kārakas* is observed; therefore, oneness is incorrect. See page 756, line 1.
With body (sadehaṃ),
with doubt (saṃdehaṃ);
see page 756, line 1.
Therefore, that is incorrect.
Furthermore,

even if one were to somehow accept the identity of fire and fuel by following your own position— meaning by some other line of reasoning from the perspective of the *dravyārthika* (substantialist) school— it remains untenable.
Nevertheless, that which is intended as "one" should not be called "one," meaning it should not be called "the one itself.

Why? Because of its unity (*ekatva*). Where there is unity, it is observed that "the one itself" is inexpressible, just as in the case of the multiplicity of Devadatta’s hands and other limbs. Just as Devadatta—who is intended to be "one"—cannot be said to be "only one" because of the plurality of his parts such as hands and feet, so too will it be stated regarding fire and fuel in the application of the example (*dārṣṭāntika*).
It cannot be said that the hand is also one, because of the multiplicity of its fingers and so forth; because of the plurality of fingers, forearms, inner and outer surfaces, and so on;

and because even a finger consists of multiple joints and parts. Now, if you accept the distinctness of fire and fuel in order to avoid these faults, then this consequence follows: its form must be described as separate from the fuel, just as the form of other things such as jars is described as separate from cloth and the like.

It is impossible to provide a definitive description of form (*rūpa*), for one thing cannot be established as distinct from another. Just as fire cannot be pointed out separately from its fuel—due to the instability of the reality of universals, particulars, identity, and difference, like the conventional designations of pots and cloths—if it were not so defined, fire would become non-existent. The same applies to a "joint" (*parvan*): because a joint consists of many parts such as bark and so forth, and a "trunk" (*skandha*) consists of many atoms (*paramāṇu*), one cannot say that "it is only one. This continues until the atom itself. Since material substance (*mūrtadravya*) is the ultimate limit, should one say that the atom is one? No, it is said, because the atom possesses multiplicity through its qualities such as form; since it consists of form, taste, smell, and touch, it is manifold by nature.

Should it be said that form (*rūpa*), taste (*rasa*), smell (*gandha*), or touch (*sparśa*) is one? No, it is said, because form and the others are different at every moment. Since form also arises and perishes as something distinct at each and every moment, it is multiple due to its difference; therefore, it cannot be called "one. The same would have to be said for taste, smell, and touch. This might be thought: since the forms of fingers, joints, skin, and so forth, which differ in location, are multiple, they could not be called "one"; however, why is a single, unique object such as form—which is momentary and distinct in time—not called "one"?

To this it is replied: Even that which is "unitary per moment" (*pratikṣaṇaika*) is ultimately manifold. For "unitary per moment" means unitary in each and every moment; since the prefix *prati* functions as a *karmapravacanīya* with the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*), it signifies "occurring in relation to each moment. That [momentary entity] too is manifold, having a form that is mutually non-intermingled, because it is never connected with anything at any time, and thus it is dissimilar and unique (*asādhāraṇa*). And what is dissimilar is manifold; for if there were similarity, there would be unity. Therefore, due to its lack of connection and its dissimilarity, even though it is manifold, it is simply inexpressible. For an object that is connected might be expressed by way of a universal as "this is that," or "this is such-and-such."
But since that universal does not exist, it is indeed inexpressible;
thus, first, the inexpressibility of fire and fuel in terms of identity has been stated (cf. Tattvasaṅgrahapañjikā, p. 756, l. 3).
...the scripture says "that body"... the scripture says "that body"... the scripture says "that body".
If,
moreover,

in order that these faults may not occur, one accepts the distinctness of fire and fuel, then this consequence follows: its form must be described as separate from the fuel, just as the form of other things, such as a jar, is described as separate from a cloth and so forth.

It is impossible to provide a definition of form (*rūpa*), for one thing cannot be defined by another; fire and its fuel cannot be pointed out as distinct, just as in the case of the conventional designations of pots and cloths, whose reality is unsettled due to the non-establishment of their identity or difference as generalities or particulars. If [fire] were not thus determined, it would follow that fire does not exist, because of the absence of the distinction between [fuel] and its form (*mūrti*).
p.
Now, [the phrase] "lest they should not exist," and so forth.

Explaining the reason for abandoning this position and adopting another, he causes you to accept an alternative view: "If you, thinking that the position of the distinctness of fire and fuel is faultless, should accept it, do not think that it too is faultless. By the phrase "by that [acceptance]," etc., it follows from that acceptance of the distinctness of fire and fuel that the following consequence ensues: the form of that fire, as something separate from the fuel, must be described, just as the hollow space of a jar is distinct from the jar itself.
For if form were shown to be distinct [from fire], then otherness would be established and it would be possible to apprehend that "this is other than that.
How so? Just as in the case of others, and so forth; for example, jars and the like are other than fires and fuel, and fires and fuel are other than cloths and the like.
But you are not able to demonstrate a reality of fire that is distinct from its fuel.

Because one thing is not common to another; for the word "hi" (indeed) has the sense of "yasmāt" (since), since a jar or the like does not possess a nature common to cloth or the like—such as [the nature] of threads and so forth—it is possible to designate it by means of its essence as something distinct from them. However, it is not possible to state that the essence of fire, which is distinct from fuel, is uncommon [to it] in such a way, like the carrying of water and so forth belonging to a jar, which is distinct from cloth and the like. (Page 756, Line 5) [This is] thinking and accepting... [Ya].
That too is a fault; that too is a fault.
(See page 756, line 6; page 495–1).
Is it not possible for others to arise from this— such as fire, fuel, and so forth, or cloth and so forth— but not by you?

If it is thought that the thread [is distinct] from the cloth submerged therein— how then have you now designated form with the specific multiplicity of "the cloth is other than the jar" and with the unity produced by the universal as "the earth is the jar"? Likewise, in the case of fire and fuel as well, it is certainly possible [to designate them] as the "burner" and the "burnt," and so forth, as will be explained.
Because it would lack fuel and, consequently, lack form, like a flower in the sky.

Now, if it were argued: "How is it that this flame in its location lacks fuel? If fire were without fuel, then even when all its fuel has been completely consumed, it would still persist because it is fire, just like the flame."
Now, it might be argued: "Even if fire has no otherness from the fuel, nevertheless, the fuel does have otherness from the fire because this is observed;
for fuel is indeed seen even when separated from fire, as in the expressions 'he brings fuel' or 'he brings wood'; thus, this is merely a figurative usage (upacāra) with respect to that [fuel]."
If it were other than that, it would not exist at all.

"For this very reason, however, the state of being fuel is established"—to this it is replied: "For me, who maintains that nothing can be said [of ultimate reality], there is no entity whatsoever established through identity or difference, such as universals (sāmānya) or particulars (viśeṣa). What then? Following your own position for the sake of exposition, it is illustrated by way of conventional truth (saṃvṛti) as being like earth, a jar, and a cloth, in terms of their identity with or difference from universals and particulars; but not according to my own view. According to my view, they are simply entities whose true nature is not fixed. Demonstrating this, he provides an example: 'The universal and the particular,' etc. These two, the jar and the cloth, are those whose true nature is not fixed in terms of identity or difference between universal and particular—these are the 'jar and cloth whose true nature is not fixed in identity or difference from universal and particular. Their 'conventional' (saṃvṛti) means a figurative designation (upacāra); the illustration is made by accepting the conceptual construction of the opponent. 'Like that convention' (saṃvṛtivat) means: just as a jar and a cloth, though accepted [by convention], are designated as having unique forms, fire and fuel are not so [designated]."

Therefore, fire would be indefinable; and being indefinable, it would follow that it is non-existent. Why? Because, while lacking fuel, it is formless, like a sky-flower; the meaning is that its own nature is not established as distinct from the nature of its material cause (*upādāna*). This same proof applies to jars, cloths, and so forth: "Being non-existent, a jar is formless and thus non-existent like a sky-flower," or "Being non-existent, a cloth is formless and thus non-existent like a sky-flower," and so on, to be applied accordingly—because, while lacking fuel, it is formless, like a sky-flower.

Now, it might be argued: "How is it that this flame in its location is without fuel? If fire were without fuel, then even when its fuel has been entirely consumed, it would remain forever, because it is fire, just like a flame. Or it might be argued: "Even though fire is not distinct from its fuel, nevertheless the fuel is distinct from the fire, because this is observed to be the case."

For it is observed that fuel is indeed sometimes separated from fire; yet, when one says "he brings fuel" or "he brings wood," this is merely a figurative expression (upacāra) regarding that very object.
If it were something other [than the fire], such a usage would not occur at all.
For this very reason, however, fuelhood is established [as being] due to the oneness of the fire; page 757, line 1.
Now, it might be argued: "If you say that there is a form of fire distinct from the fuel, just as a flame exists in the space of the sky,
therefore I have explained to you the form of fire as distinct from the fuel."
Therefore, since its lack of form is not established, it is not non-existent;

to this we reply: Whence could that [flame] be without fuel? That which is the form of the flame of fire in the region of space is also indeed accompanied by fuel, because the flame is supported by the presence in the region of space of material atoms (*pudgala*) of fuel that have been transformed into the state of fire; thus, the flame is not without fuel, because it is fire, like charcoal and other forms of fire.
Since even lightning has water as its fuel, there is no inconclusiveness [in the argument];
therefore, fire does not exist as something separate from the fuel;
as long as there is fuel, so long is there fire, and when the fuel is exhausted, it is said that the fire is extinguished.
Therefore, fire cannot be said to exist apart from fuel.

To state the fault for one who does not accept this: if there were fire without fuel, then even after the fuel has been completely consumed and it is in a state such as embers and so forth, it would continue to exist because it is fire, just like a flame;
and this is undesirable.
Thus, first of all, just as with the previously mentioned identity, one must not assert that fire is different from the fuel; [this is because] its difference is not established. (p.
757, l. 3; 495–1; *°tvasiddhe* in the manuscript).

Whether it be "where there is flame" (yatrajvālā) or "that which has flame" (yatrajvālā), or "that which is flame" (yatrajvālā)— if another alternative such as this were to be stated, it is to be understood as before.

The fuel is distinct from the fire, because it is observed as such; for in the world it is observed that one says, "he brings the fuel" or "he brings the wood. Indeed, there is no means of knowledge more authoritative than what is observed. As for the scriptural passage beginning with "if [it were] of the fire," etc., up to "he brings," the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) has already been explained.

Here is the reply: this is a metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) applied precisely to that object [the fuel], during the time of its transformation into the state of fire; for a figurative usage must have a primary basis.
According to the root *dīp* (Pāṇini Dhātupāṭha 1449) in the sense of "shining," fire itself, whose nature is luminosity, is the fuel;
and because it exists within that [fuel] as previously stated, there is no difference between them, just as in the case of its own self.
Thus, even when the conventional term "wood" is used, there is a contradiction in asserting a difference between fire and wood.
When this is so, then there is nothing other than that;
for surely, at the very moment wood is seen to be without fire, at that same moment its "otherness" is established.
If, on the other hand, there is the occurrence of non-difference, then "otherness" cannot obtain.

The status of being fuel (*indhana*) in wood that has not yet been transformed into fire occurs only metaphorically, with reference to its primary [fuel] nature which has already achieved its true purpose.

If it were other than that—that is, if there were a difference between fire and fuel—then that metaphorical usage would not occur at all, because of the absence of primary fuel; for just as there is no metaphorical usage when there is an absence of common properties such as sharpness or bluntness in relation to a donkey’s horn, so too there can be no metaphorical usage in the absence of such a basis. (Page 757, Line 3)
It burns, according to the Bhāṣya; it causes burning, according to the Yāska commentary, because figurative usage is rooted in the primary sense.
According to the *Pāṇini Dhātupāṭha* (1449), "ñiindhī" means "to shine"; thus, fire, whose very nature is luminosity, is itself the fuel.
Furthermore, because it subsists within that [fuel] as previously stated, there is no difference between them, just as in the case of its own self.
Even when employing the conventional term "wood," there is a contradiction in asserting a difference between fire and wood.
When this is so, there is indeed nothing other than that;
for when wood is seen to be without fire, at that very moment there is otherness.
Thus, if there is otherness, the occurrence of non-difference is not possible.
The reading *bhāvavat* appears appropriate here;
for this very reason, the passage beginning with *tu* [is explained as follows]:

precisely because it is primarily fuel consisting of wood transformed by fire, its status as fuel is established even when not so transformed, through figurative usage (*upacāra*). Why? Because a secondary [usage] has the primary as its root. For only when a primary lion exists can a young boy be called a "lion" due to his similarity to it—such as in bravery or ferocity—not in the absence of a primary lion.

Or, as in the case of a painter and others: the designation "painter" is obtained through the state of transformation resulting from the activity of painting and so forth; it does not exist when that transformation of activity is absent. He states a traditional teaching (*smṛti*) as a proof for this, which corresponds to [the fact] that fuel-ness exists only when there is a transformation into fire: *indhī* (root Pāṇini Dhātupāṭha 1449) means "to shine. Now, the learned grammarians, who know the relationship between word and meaning, remember that fire is "illumination" (*dīpana*). Since fire is indeed of the nature of illumination, and since the root *indh* has the sense of "shining," it is established that the metaphorical usage [of the term "fuel"] is valid.
Furthermore, because it is easy [to establish] and because it resides in that [substratum] as previously stated, it is not something other [than it], just like its own self.

Just as identity (*ekatva*) was refuted by the reasoning stated in the text—beginning with "If fire were identical with the fuel, then, like the burnt fuel, because there would be no activity of the one, it would result in non-existence," and so on, up to "because of being together, not being together, and residing in two"—so too should the text be applied to difference (*anyatva*) through the same line of reasoning regarding the understanding of the identical point: "In the case of difference, because there would be no activity of the other, like the burnt fuel, it would result in non-existence," and so forth; for even in the case of difference, the consequence of non-existence is the same.

"There is no otherness [of fuel] from its own self. Just as fire's own self is not other than fire, so too is that fuel; because it exists therein (*tadvṛttitvāt*). "Existing therein" (*tadvṛtti*) means either "that which exists in it," or "that very existence is its existence," or "fire is that whose existence is precisely existing therein. Blazing itself is the existence of being fuel; because its existence consists in the form of blazing, fuel is indeed fire, just like the nature of fire. For that which is not being burned is not fuel at all, since it has already been explained that the status of being an agent belongs only to agents, and so forth. Thus, in the example of fuel, the contradiction regarding the otherness of fire has been stated.
Its occurrence is like its own self;
[see] page 744, line 2;
page 745, line 5.
The ascent of praise,
its state of activity,
and its radiant manifestation.

On page 745, line 1, regarding the example of wood as well: "In the linguistic usage of the word 'wood,' etc."—even in the conventional usage of the term *kāṣṭha*, the distinctness (*anyatva*) between fire and wood is contradicted. For instance: "When this [fire]... and so forth; there is no fire that is other than its own fuel (*svendhana*).

Even the lightning-fire does not exist as something separate from its fuel, which is water; here there is a doubt: "But surely, when wood is seen without fire, since it is seen in the absence of that fire, its distinctness is established. To this we reply: Now, the state of non-distinction is indeed observed. This state of non-distinction is seen in the case of burning wood, which is the fuel; why then is the wood not the fire? Or why is the fire not the wood? Is it because of their distinctness, as before or as after? If it is wood, how can it be without fire? [The root] *kāś* (meaning 'to shine') [is found in Pāṇini’s Dhātupāṭha 647 and 1162]; thus all contradictions are resolved.
Even in the case of wood (*dāru*), [the property of being fuel] is already established in the senses of "cleansing" (*śodhana*) and "cutting" (*avakhaṇḍana*);

since it is impossible for it to have the senses of "giving" (*dāna*) and "protecting" (*rakṣaṇa*), wood in those senses is not an example. Furthermore, co-existence or non-co-existence [of fuel and fire] would be possible only if their difference were established, as in the case of space (*ākāśa*), which lacks fuel. This is because [co-existence or non-co-existence] resides in two distinct entities.
But that [reason] is not established;
furthermore, that occurrence of non-difference does not obtain if there is otherness (*anyatva*), just as the state of being fuel for a non-burning sky is unattainable.

Why? Because, by means of attributing each other's natures, there is the production of an undesired consequence (*aniṣṭāpādana*), as before or as after, according to the respective order; thus, the two proofs based on "because it is other than that" have already been explained.
pṛ॰ 758 paṃ॰ 2:
"The non-existence of fire is seen" (in the manuscript *pra*);
"the metaphorical designation being established" (*ya*).

The reading *tena vinā* (without that) is also excellent; why [is it said] "fire is not wood, nor is wood fire," as before or after, because they are different? If it is wood, how is it not fire? [The root] *kāśṛ* in the sense of "shining" (*pāṇini-dhātu-pāṭha* 647, 1162) [explains this]; thus, all contradictions are resolved. Furthermore, even in the case of wood, [the meanings of] "purifying" and "not breaking" are already established.

Because [the concepts of] giving and protecting are impossible, a wooden post intended for those purposes is not an example; like space, it is not fuel because it does not exist either together with or apart from [the fire], for coexistence or non-coexistence would only be established if a difference were proven,
yet that difference is not established.
Why?

[The opponent asks: "Furthermore, if it is wood, how can it be non-fire? Because it shines—shining means burning and glowing—it is precisely fire due to that shining; otherwise it would not be so. Therefore, the statement "that wood is non-fire" is a contradiction of one's own words.

Likewise, the statement "fuel is not fire" is also a contradiction of one's own words (*svavacanavirodha*). This is because wood is necessarily fire, and fire is necessarily wood; thus, fuel and fire are identical, which results in a contradiction of one's own words. To demonstrate this, he cites a traditional authority (*smṛti*) that supports that meaning as proof: from the root *kāś* (meaning "to shine") [Dhātupāṭha 647, 1162], the form *kāṣṭha* is established by adding the *kthan* suffix in the sense of the agent according to the *uṇādi* rules. For this reason, all contradictions arise;
furthermore, because it is observed as such, there is a contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣavirodha*).
Because it is well-established in the world, there is contradiction with common usage; because it is thus inferred, there is contradiction with inference;
and because it is so accepted, there is contradiction with one's own tenet.
How is it "without fire"?
[It is] when fuel is fire,
or when fuel and fire are identical.

Since the form *dāru* is established as the derivative of any one of these four roots— *dāñ* (to give) Pāṇini Dhātupāṭha 1091, *deṅ* (to protect) Pāṇini Dhātupāṭha 962, *do* (to cut) Pāṇini Dhātupāṭha 1148, or *daip* (to purify) Pāṇini Dhātupāṭha 924—
what person indeed would not be able to say so?

First, [the examples] for the meanings of "purifying" and "breaking" are indeed established; since the root *dah* (Pāṇini-Dhātupāṭha 991) has the meaning "to reduce to ashes," it shares the same sense [as the others]. Nevertheless, because the meanings "giving" (*dāna*) and "protecting" (*rakṣaṇa*) are impossible [in that context], wood (*dāru*) used in those senses is not an example; it is not intended to be cited as an example.

Why? Because, like space (*ākāśa*), it lacks fuel (*indhana*), and since the meaning of "shining" (*dīpti*) is impossible, the word "wood" (*dāru*) is not intended [there]; thus there is no fault here, just as [space] was not intended [as an example] previously. Both "co-existence" and "non-co-existence" are mutually dependent; therefore, whether fire exists with wood or wood exists with fire, or if they are distinct, in every case there occurs this [relation] between these two which are invariably concomitant. Yet, it is impossible to say that one of these two is different from the other; therefore, that is not something else.
4) This is so.
But that is not so.

Even if there were some kind of difference, one could not say "the other is simply other," because of its being "other," like Devadatta who is other than [but not distinct from] his hands and so forth, or like an atom which is neither other nor non-other than the preceding moment of form and so on.
In that case, for you, it would be a non-entity, because of the exclusion of both "fire-ness" and "non-fire-ness," like a sky-flower.

Now, one might object: since their characteristics are established as distinct, it should not even be said that they are "neither," provided there were no fixed rule regarding the nature of the combustible and the combustor; for otherwise, even fire [would be indeterminate].
To this, [the author replies] with "in some way" (*kathañcit*) and so forth.

As before, having accepted [the premise], one must not say according to your own view that "one thing is simply different from another," because they are indeed different—just as Devadatta is both different and non-different from his hands and so forth. Even though there is a difference between the hand, the finger, the joint, the skin, the aggregate (*skandha*), the atom (*paramāṇu*), form, taste, and momentariness, Devadatta alone is perceived in such and such ways; he is one and the same, like a jar which consists of form and other qualities qualified by designations such as "eye" and so on, or like Devadatta who consists of designations such as "fatherhood" qualified by dependence on another related person. Otherwise, if that unity were absent, since there would be no distinction [between them], it would be impossible to say that "those very things are different and others," because they consist of the essence of Devadatta and the essence of the jar and so forth. Therefore, this treatise demonstrates the means for establishing that: up to the point where, like atoms, there is neither difference nor non-difference from subsequent moments of form and so on. This is the illustrative example for the intended meaning, and in this way it should be contemplated in other cases as well, such as the jar.

Here he says: "In that case, non-existence... and so forth. If fire and fuel do not exist [as such], why? Because of the exclusion of being fire or non-fire; since fire and non-fire are excluded, then in the case of identity, fire itself would be the fuel, and in the case of difference, it would be non-fire. Likewise, because of the exclusion of being fuel or non-fuel, this also serves as a reason, since it has the same meaning as that [previous argument]. Like a sky-flower: just as a sky-flower is neither fire nor non-fire because it is excluded from both identity and difference, and thus is non-existent, so too fire and fuel would not exist. The meaning is that neither of the two exists.

regarding this, we say: "But [the statement] beginning with 'distinct' (*bhinna*)," etc.—even this "neither-nor" (*anubhayatva*) is not expressible. Why? Because its characteristic is the definition of a distinct establishment (*vyavasthāna*).

[The fuel] is distinct, separate, and unmixed; its established nature (*vyavasthāna*) is characterized solely by combustibility and so forth, while this fire is characterized solely by heat, burning power, and so forth. This very established nature is the mark (*cihna*) and characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of both. Because of that state—namely, because they possess the characteristic of distinct establishment—they do not have the nature of being neither [fuel nor fire], just like a conventionally existent jar or cloth.
Therefore, due to the existence of these characteristics, it is also simply inexpressible to say that "it does not exist. (p. 759, l. 4)

Regarding the *saṅghaṭa* [treatise], it might be thought: "The definition characterized by the burned and the burner and so forth is unestablished, because the substratum (*dharmī*) possessing those characteristics is unestablished.

But this is not so; for the existence of both the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmī*) is established. To prove that, he says: "If [there were] the state of being the burned and the burner," and so forth.

If wood were exclusively the object to be burned and fire alone the burner, there would be no fixed rule of definition for the two; consequently, fire itself would be burned like wood, or cooked like rice, because its characteristic as the "burner" or "cooker" would not be fixed, and it would thus be something to be cooked. Furthermore, it would then have to be consumed separately, just like the rice. This is undesirable;
therefore, the characteristics of fire, such as being the burner and the cooker, are established.

Likewise, if fuel also did not possess distinct characteristics established as being combustible, cookable, and so forth, then it would burn separately even without fire; wood, grass, and the like would burn, and rice and such would cook, just as wood does. Furthermore, it would be eaten separately, and likewise, fuel would also burn and cook rice and so forth independently, just as fire does. Thus, since both are observed to exist as distinct entities established in their own respective states, they cannot be described as neither [identical nor different].

If, however, one does not accept "duality" as functioning through a distinct arrangement [of parts], then duality would have to be either a single entity consisting of all things or an absolute non-existence;
for if it were argued that duality arises from the negation of non-duality, we say no, because otherness is inexpressible.
If it were argued that the negation of otherness is oneness, we say no, because that too is inexpressible.
Furthermore, by the negation of identity, difference, both, and neither, the relationship of primary and subordinate is also necessarily negated.
Therefore, since [the agent] is in every respect inexpressible—just as fire is not "fire-ness"—cooking would occur even without the act of burning; however, it does not so occur.
He concludes this: "Thus, even the state of being neither is indeed inexpressible.

It might burn like wood, it might cook like rice, and it might be enjoyed separately; likewise, fuel too would burn separately, and [the fire] would cook rice and so forth like the fire itself. Thus, "bothness" (*ubhayatā*) is indeed inexpressible. If both were to exist as functioning within distinct determinations (*bhinna-vyavasthāna-vṛtta*), then bothness would be possible; however, if one does not admit bothness as functioning within distinct determinations, then bothness would result in either a single entity consisting of all things or an absolute non-existence.
If it is argued that "duality [of the two] follows from the negation of both," we say no, because otherness is itself inexpressible.
If it is argued that "the negation of otherness constitutes oneness," we say no, because that too is inexpressible.
Furthermore, by the negation of oneness, otherness, both, and neither, the relationship of primary and secondary is also effectively negated.
Therefore, it appears clearly that it is correct to maintain that both [the self and the non-self] are in every respect simply inexpressible; let this be observed (p. 759, l. 6).

Now, if this is not accepted, then, in the absence of the acceptance of "bothness" as existing in a distinct state or arrangement, what kind of "both" would result? For example: "the one consisting of all things," and so forth. This "both" would have to be either (1) a single entity that is the essence of all, eternal, omnipresent, without arising or decay—being one of the categories such as time (*kāla*), necessity (*niyati*), inherent nature (*svabhāva*), primordial matter (*pradhāna*), or the self (*puruṣa*)—or (2) a non-entity that is unreal, false, indefinable, and utterly non-existent, like a sky-flower. Since there is no other alternative when neither identity, difference, nor bothness exists, such a "both" cannot exist, because these positions have already been refuted.

If it should be thought that the negation of otherness implies oneness— that is, if one thinks that when otherness is negated, oneness itself is established—
this is not so, because that too is inexpressible; for I have already stated at the very outset that oneness, being non-existent, is precisely inexpressible.
In this way, identity, difference, bothness, and neitherness have been refuted.

One might raise the objection: "Even if identity and so forth do not exist between the universal and the particular, or between fire and fuel, let there still be something to be said for their operation through the relationship of one being primary and the other subordinate.

This is incorrect; because that [relationship] is untenable for the same reason that identity and so forth are untenable. Pointing this out by extension, he says: "By the refutation of identity, difference, bothness, and neitherness, the relationship of primary and subordinate is also necessarily refuted."

Since it has been established that because these two—generality and particularity—do not function, fire and fuel are indeed non-existent under the alternatives of identity or difference, then, given their non-existence, what primary-subordinate relationship (*pradhānopasarjanatā*) could there be between them? It is like that of a sky-flower and the son of a barren woman. For such a relationship is observed only between two existing entities, such as a master and a servant. Furthermore, this primary-subordinate relationship is only tenable under the alternative of difference, and that [alternative] has been refuted.

And regarding the operation of fire and fuel, this is the extent of the analysis: if, in this way, there were identity between the particular and the entity such that they were not distinct, then, because the non-self entity would not operate—just like a donkey's horn—it would be a mere non-existence and not an operation, due to its being non-self, like a donkey's horn.

If it is argued that just as a particular (viśeṣa)—whether a single quality such as color or taste, or an object such as a jar or a cloth—proceeds even while devoid of a general being (bhāva), so too shall a single entity in its subtle state proceed; we ask: who says that a particular is devoid of being? A "particular" is so called because it is a particularization of that which exists (sat); and since it depends upon that [being], it is particularized by the relation "it is particularized by that," "it is particularized for that," or "it is particularized with that. Therefore, that which is not particularized or does not particularize cannot be a particular, because only those things that function as causal factors (kārakas) possess the status of being causal factors.

What assurance is there that a particular [viśeṣa] proceeds as a single entity, like a pot or a cloth which exist only conventionally (*saṃvṛtisat*)? It might be argued that it is oneness, plurality, both, or neither; or that fire is subordinate and fuel is primary, or fuel is subordinate and fire is primary—but in every way this is not tenable. Therefore, since it is in every respect inexpressible (*avaktavya*), this description of an analogy has been made:

if the particular were one with the entity (*bhāva*), it would not be different from it; consequently, since an entity devoid of self-nature (*anātman*) does not function—like the horn of a donkey—it would simply be non-existent.
There is no manifestation [of a particular], because it lacks substantial existence (*anātmatvāt*), like the horn of a donkey.

If it is argued: "Just as a single particular (*viśeṣa*)—such as color, taste, or the like, or a jar, a cloth, or the like—manifests even while being devoid of a [further] entity (*bhāva*), so too a single entity in its subtle state will manifest," we ask: who says that a particular is devoid of an entity? A particular is called a "particular" precisely because it is a particularization of that which exists; and it is particularized through dependence upon that [entity], according to such expressions as "it is particularized by that," "it is [particularized] from that," or "it is [particularized] for that. Therefore, that which is neither being particularized nor particularizing another does not constitute a particular, because only those things that function as causal factors (*kāraka*) possess the status of being causal factors.

Or rather, what assurance is there that the distinction [of the two] occurs one by one, like a pot or a cloth which exist as conventional realities (*saṃvṛtisat*)? [This is because] both [the pot and the cloth] are dependent on both [their parts].

The subsequent passage beginning with "evam" (thus) and so forth is intended to describe the subject under discussion—the illustration of the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*), etc. Regarding the universal and the particular, it is as follows: if the particular, such as a jar (*ghaṭa*), were identical with the entity (*bhāva*) through its concomitance (*anvaya*) with earth and so forth, what would this imply? It would mean that the universal itself becomes one and devoid of particulars; therefore, to demonstrate this, he says: "not other than... (*nānyatā*).

What follows from this? Consequently, there is no selfhood (anātmatva) for the non-self entity—such as stones, sand, clay, clods of earth, diamonds, and so forth—which lacks the specific nature of objects like pots; nor is there selfhood for the general category of earth and the rest. And because it is non-self, there is no activity, just as in the case of a donkey’s horn. Due to the absence of activity, it would be a mere non-entity, just like a donkey’s horn.
He demonstrates this through proof: "There is no activity," which has already been explained (p. 760, l.
[The opponent asks: "Is this not so?

[The author replies: Indeed, the objection beginning with "just as fuel... and the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) beginning with "even though the particular (*viśeṣa*) is one... are valid; however, having cited as an example that which is established for the proponent of particulars (*viśeṣavādin*)—namely, the simultaneous occurrence of successive states (*paryāya*) such as color-form (*rūpa*) and so on—the proponent of existence (*bhāvavādin*) might say: "Just as those [successive states] proceed in your view, in my view a single entity (*bhāva*) in its subtle state will proceed."

Here, the proponent of the "inexpressible" (avaktavyavādī) offers a reply according to his own view: "Who indeed says... and so forth. By demonstrating the impossibility of the occurrence of particulars without a universal, he describes the non-establishment of the example, on the grounds that only what exists can be a particular; it is only that which exists that becomes a particular, and only the universal itself—not a non-existent thing like a sky-flower—that does so. Furthermore, because of its dependence upon that [universal], form, when being distinguished from taste, becomes a particular only in relation to the related taste; likewise, taste [is a particular] in relation to form, and a jar and a cloth in relation to each other, but not in relation to an absolutely non-existent sky-flower.
He demonstrates this through the analysis of the grammatical factors (*kāraka*): "it is distinguished by that," "from that," or "by that," and so forth.
When three factors have been shown, the inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*) indicates that other possible factors should also be inferred.

Regarding the phrase "if not distinguished" (*aviśiṣyamāṇe*), such as "the suffix *ṇa*," etc., [this would apply] if even the attainment of a subtle state were established despite the difference between parts and the whole, or between universals and particulars, or between cause and effect.
And thus, that [theory] is untenable, because it is admitted that [the states] would result in non-existence,
since the two states— the subtle and the gross— consist of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and posterior non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*).

If, on the other hand, the entity itself were indeed non-existence, then the production of form and so forth characterized by the eyes and other senses, as well as space and so forth, would be non-existent.

A particular (*viśeṣa*) devoid of actual activity would not even deserve the designation "particular," for it becomes a particular only by distinguishing one thing from another; this is because the status of being a "factor" (*kāraka*)—such as the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth—belongs to factors precisely through their engagement in an operation. For in the absence of engagement in the act of qualifying, there would be no distinction at all.
Therefore, this remains established: the universal itself is the particular, or rather, [the particular] exists only in dependence upon the universal.

Even the attainment of a subtle state could only occur if a distinction between parts and wholes, universals and particulars, and causes and effects were established; however, that is untenable, because you admit that these two states— the subtle and the gross— consist of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and non-existence after destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), which would result in their being mere absences.

Now, if non-existence itself were the nature of an entity, then the arising of things characterized as the eye and so forth, as well as forms and so forth, and of space and so forth, would be non-existent; thus,
in accordance with your own position, [this is established] by way of conventional truth.

As for the state of subtlety and so forth, whatever direction you might infer by some other method—that a thing remains in a subtle state devoid of particularity—that too could only be possible if the distinction between the parts and the whole, and between the particulars and the universal, were established as being caused by the effect; it cannot be otherwise.

For the state of *pradhāna* is the subtle equilibrium of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*; it exists only in relation to the gross states of objects such as the *mahat* and so forth. Indeed, these very *guṇas* are both subtle and gross; and these two states are mutually dependent, just as the coiling, the winding gait, and the coiled state of a snake do not exist apart from the snake, nor does the snake exist apart from those particularities. Thus, by your very mention of the subtle state, you have effectively admitted this: that an entity which undergoes subtlety is nothing other than the specific states of childhood, youth, middle age, old age, and so forth, since it cannot exist independently of them.

And thus, that [existence] is untenable; for this being the case, it is impossible for an entity called "succession" (anvaya) to possess the nature of an entity, because you admit that it results in the state of non-existence. Why? Because the two states—the subtle and the gross—consist of prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) and posterior non-existence (pradhvaṃsābhāva). Just as a jar, having not existed previously, comes into being, and having existed, ceases to be, is thus non-existent both before and after due to its nature as non-existence; likewise, the non-subtle becomes subtle and then ceases to be, and the gross does the same. Consequently, you have fallen into the position of a proponent of non-existence (abhāvavāda), and there is a loss of your own accepted doctrine (abhyupagama-hāni).

Now, lest there be an abandonment of your own position, you might instead accept that an entity is indeed non-existent; and in that case, [the consequence follows] regarding the definition of the eye and so forth.

If the non-existence of the universal (*sāmānya*) is accepted, then from that non-existent universal, the arising of particulars—such as form (*rūpa*) characterized by the eye and so forth, and space (*ākāśa*) and the rest known as states (*avasthā*)—would be seedless and thus non-existent. This would entail the absence of all worldly and scriptural conventions, such as "form has the eye as its characteristic" (the inclusion of "and so forth" refers to the ear, skin, tongue, and nose being the characteristics of sound, touch, taste, and smell; and form and the rest being the characterized objects), and the fact that the elements such as space have sound and the rest as their nature. Therefore, one must not even accept the non-existence of an entity (*bhāva*). — *Gacchami bhā* [End of citation].

Or, it might be said: there is identity between the particular and its existence (bhāva).

If the entity (*bhāva*) pervades the particulars (*viśeṣa*), but the particular does not pervade the entity, then there is no identity between the entity and the particular; however, the particular does have identity with the entity, because its existence as a particular is subsumed within the apprehension of the entity. Now, if it functions as distinct [from the entity], how is this so? Why does it not become non-distinct in form, being identical to the entity? Or rather, why is the entity not of the nature of a particular due to its being qualified, since they are one, like the particular? To this, it might be said, etc.

Regarding the prior [argument] concerning the identity of fire and fuel—just as an opponent, perceiving no fault in the identity of fuel with fire while seeing a fault in the identity of fire with fuel, offers a rebuttal, so too here, one who perceives no fault in the identity of the particular (*viśeṣa*) with the entity (*bhāva*) while seeing a fault in the identity of the entity with the particular, states the rebuttal as follows: "If the entity, such as 'earth-ness' (*pṛthivītva*), which is the universal (*sāmānya*), pervades the particulars such as pots, cloths, stones, and sand, but the particular—such as the stone or the pot—does not pervade the entity 'earth-ness' because it exists only in a single part."

Therefore, there is no identity between earth and a particular (viśeṣa), whether that particular be a jar or a cloth; however, for the jar, there is identity with its particularity through its existence as a commonality such as earth. Why? Because a particular has its function included within the apprehension of existence (bhāva); since it is grasped by that apprehension of the commonality which is existence, its function—its operation or its being—is included therein. This is because the particular has assumed the nature of the essence of existence; it is for this reason that a particular is a particular, and not otherwise.

Therefore, since a particular (*viśeṣa*) has its function included within the apprehension of an entity (*bhāva*), let there be identity between the particular and the universal, because its nature is not distinct from the entity; what fault is there?

This much is asked by the proponent of the identity of universal and particular, because the same objection remains unrefuted: "But how can there be a distinct function? In this regard, it is observed as before that in the world, the function of these two is seen to be distinct.

For example: "earth" is the undifferentiated state of a being (bhāva) common to jars, cloths, and so forth; whereas "the jar is not the cloth" is the differentiated state (viśeṣa) of the jar, the cloth, and so on. And these two modes (vṛtti) are mutually distinct. How can they arise if there is identity, given that their mutual non-attainment of each other's form constitutes their diversity? He demonstrates this by way of an undesirable consequence (aniṣṭāpādana): Why does that which is a common entity not become exclusively of an undifferentiated form? This jar, or a specific quality such as color, although excluded from cloth and so forth, or from taste and so forth, is nonetheless not excluded from "clay is indeed clay"—being a common entity, existing as it exists, being as it is, or simply "earth is earth"—why does it not become indistinct like the universal being (bhāva)? [This is asked] because the undesirable consequence of the lack of distinction follows from the double negation. He supports the observed particularity: why does the universal being (bhāva), due to its being qualified, not become of a specific form? It continues: because of that identity with the particular, why does it not become precisely the specific qualities of color, taste, and so forth, having abandoned its form as clay, as becoming, and as earth? In both cases, "because of that identity" is the reason.
Examples for these two distinct natures have been seen;
and this mode of differentiation through the persistence and exclusion of the universal and the particular has been observed.

Furthermore, there is a means for establishing an undesirable consequence: an entity (*bhāva*) would be nothing but a particular, because of their identity, just like the nature of that particular itself; or a particular would be nothing but an entity, because of their identity, just like the nature of that entity itself; a jar would be nothing but clay, because of their identity, just like the nature of that clay itself; or clay would be nothing but a jar, because of their identity, just like the nature of that jar itself.

Furthermore, due to conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), there is a contradiction regarding oneness.

From what source does this distinction arise—that "this is with it" and "this is not with it"—given that the state of being together or not together resides in two [distinct things], and because it is untenable for there to be qualifiers, actions, substrata, instruments, and so forth?
Even if oneness were somehow established, one still could not say "one is only one," and so forth, as previously explained up to the point regarding atoms (*paramāṇu*).
Now, lest these faults should arise, one might posit the distinctness of the entity and its particularity.

In that case, if the distinctness of the entity from its particularity is admitted, then this consequence follows: its form must be declared as separate from its particularity, just as the form of other things, such as a jar, is declared to be separate from a cloth.
However, it is impossible to declare such a form, for one thing cannot be [separate] from another.
Furthermore: "And because of the conceptual alternatives (vikalpa), there is a contradiction regarding oneness.

If there were oneness, from what would this distinction arise—namely, that 'this does not coexist with this,' while 'this does coexist with this'? The entity is one with the distinction, but the distinction is not one with the entity; the distinction is one with the entity, but the entity is not one with the distinction. These two alternatives are not compatible with oneness, because of the absence of a cause for distinction. They are compatible only with difference, because the state of coexistence and non-coexistence resides in two distinct things."

For this reason as well, the oneness of the particular (*viśeṣa*) with the being (*bhāva*) is not tenable, because the functions of qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*), the locus (*ādhāra*), the instrument (*karaṇa*), and so forth, are untenable. The act of qualifying (*viśeṣaṇa-kriyā*) inheres either in the agent (*kartṛ*) who qualifies, or in the object (*karman*) which is qualified, such as the earth or a jar. These two serve as its loci according to the speaker's intention. That cloth or other entity by which it is distinguished is the instrument (*karaṇa*). Or, the particularity of the being itself from which the jar is distinguished—such that "this is a jar and not a cloth"—is the source (*apādāna*). That for whom it is distinguished and communicated, namely the listener, is the recipient (*sampradāna*). Since these grammatical factors (*kārakas*) and the action expressed by the verbal root *vi-śiṣ* (to distinguish) are based on distinct meanings, their occurrence would be untenable if there were oneness.
Furthermore, this observed linguistic usage regarding agents is based on difference;
therefore, because it is observed, unity is untenable. (p. 746, l. 2)

Even granting their identity, we say it is not at all logical. Thus, with the words "But even somehow... and so forth, he refers back to the previous section on the refutation of identity to establish that [the substance] is inexpressible; this extends up to the point "like an atom," which concludes the demonstration of inexpressibility by means of a specific reason and example. Since the logic is identical, the meaning has already been explained.
In this way, the faults regarding the identity of the universal and the particular have been stated.
Even [granting] oneness, it is not tenable. (Bhāṣya, Yaśomitra, p.

If the opponent, fearing these defects, should adopt another position which he considers faultless—thinking, "Let these defects not arise"—what is that other position? It is the distinctness (*anyatva*) of the entity (*bhāva*) and its particularity (*viśeṣa*).
In that case as well, as with their identity, there are two possibilities: either the entity's distinctness from the particularity, or the particularity's distinctness from the entity.

In that regard, first of all, if it is accepted that the entity (*bhāva*) is distinct from its particularity (*viśeṣa*), then this collection of faults follows—namely, "Therefore, then," and so forth, up to "like a conventional jar and cloth. This is understood in the same way as before.
Here, because the general and the particular are under discussion, it is specified that [the entity] is separate from its particularity;
the rest is to be understood in the same manner, starting with "it is impossible to provide a designation such as 'form' (*rūpa*)," and so on.

The proof by way of summary: If it were not defined, it would follow that it is non-existent, because in the absence of specific distinction it would lack form, like a sky-flower. The absence of specific distinction in an entity arises from its absolute difference from its particularities; for example, earth possesses common characteristics throughout its various states, such as stone, sand, and so forth, just as a pot or a cloth exists through the conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*) of a principle that is neither established as identical to nor different from its general and particular aspects. If it were not defined, it would follow that it is non-existent, because in the absence of specific distinction it would lack form, like a sky-flower.
Now, it might be argued: "Form is distinct from the entity, since it follows upon the exclusion [of others] based on specific distinction."

Furthermore, from what would it be non-distinct? If an entity were devoid of distinction, then even in the absence of all distinctions, it would have the nature of occurring [as a positive presence] in things like a sky-flower, because it is an entity, just like a jar and so forth.
Even though there is no difference of the universal from the particular, nevertheless there is a difference of the particular from the universal, because it is observed;
for a particular is indeed observed to be inseparable from the entity, as in the case of "a distinct jar."
This metaphorical attribution of difference pertains only to an existent entity (*bhāva*);
if it were otherwise, it would not exist at all because it would be a non-entity (*abhāva*), like a sky-flower.
For this very reason, its establishment [is possible], since a metaphorical usage must have a primary basis that is a distinct co-referential term.

Furthermore, because it does not abide by the aforementioned mode of operation, for one who does not accept its identity [with the entity], there is absolute non-distinction; and since there is non-distinction, the entity is devoid of form, because its form cannot be defined apart from that [non-distinction].

Therefore, non-existence results, because if it were different from the thing, its distinct form would necessarily follow, and if it were impossible to describe it, it would be non-existent. This is the inevitable conclusion.

To this we reply: Whence is that non-differentiation? For this form characterized by the continuity of "earth-ness" (pṛthivītva) in jars, stones, and so forth, does not exist at all without a particularity (viśeṣa). Thus, the impossibility of designating a distinct form remains as it was.

Even granting, for the sake of following your position, that existence is devoid of specific qualities, we shall state the fault for you who maintain absolute difference: if existence were devoid of specific qualities, then even in the absence of all specific qualities whatsoever, it would—due to its being existence—possess a nature of occurring in things such as a sky-flower, just as it does in things such as a jar;

To this it is replied: this metaphorical attribution of difference (*bhedopacāra*) pertains solely to the entity (*bhāva*).

It refers to that very entity called "jar," which is experienced as being qualified by the specific action of breaking, and which is permeated by the process of becoming—beginning from the undifferentiated lump of clay, the shaped pot-fragment (*śivaka*), and so forth—and which acquires its own nature through the aggregation of parts in a sequence of states such as produced, new, middle-aged, old, and finally disintegration; this [breaking] is merely a particular state within that sequence of potsherds.

Therefore, because it consists of the transformation of objects through the aggregation and disintegration of imperishable atoms and so forth, as well as of the person (*pudgala*), the metaphorical designation "arisen" or "destroyed" is possible only for an entity (*bhāva*) and not for a non-entity (*abhāva*) such as a sky-flower.

If you should think that this is a metaphorical designation of non-difference from the entity, then if it were other than the entity, it would not exist at all—just like a sky-flower—or else one could not metaphorically designate a jar as "distinct" or "arisen," because, being a non-entity, it would lack specific characteristics, just like a sky-flower.

Because it exists as the very self of the one who maintains it, there is no otherness from it, just as there is none from one's own self.

But the ultimate particular (*antyaviśeṣa*) is not at all distinct from existence (*bhāva*), because it is a particular, like a jar; and since this [particular] is perceived as non-different from existence, it never becomes non-existent, like a sky-flower. Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that whenever there is a universal (*sāmānya*) without particularity, there is necessarily otherness (*anyatva*)? No, because there is no such distinction.

Furthermore, for this very reason its establishment occurs:

this must necessarily be so—this metaphorical designation of difference applies only to existent entities (bhāva); the establishment of difference arises from the metaphorical designation of difference, or rather, the establishment of the metaphorical designation of difference arises from the entity itself.

What is the reason? Because the primary [usage] is the root of the secondary (*gauṇa*). The metaphorical application of "difference" (*bheda*) as being in grammatical apposition with "pot" in the expression "the pot is different" is secondary; it depends upon a specific state—such as new, young, middle-aged, or old—which accompanies and is concomitant with the primary difference, just as one refers to a snake by its specific states such as the expansion of its hood, its winding gait, or its coiled, extended, and long body. Thus, even when [the object] has perished, the metaphorical usage "it is different" is employed, since the secondary is rooted in the primary.

Alternatively, even when the entity (*bhāva*) remains entirely undivided, difference (*bheda*) is metaphorically attributed to it during states such as that of the potsherds; for the entity—being merely caused by factors such as the person (*puruṣa*) or time—is devoid of arising and destruction, like the water of a still lake.

Furthermore, "difference" (*viśeṣa*) is so called because it differentiates (*viśiṣyate*); since it is a differentiation of the existent (*sat*), and because it depends upon that [existent], it is said that "it is differentiated by that," or "it is differentiated from that," and so forth. By stating that what does not differentiate, or that which is not being differentiated, is not truly a "differentiation"—for only the causal factors possess the status of being causal factors (p. 753)—the author extends this principle to what was previously stated.

Furthermore, [the phrase] "and because it resides in that" and "from what was stated before" carry over. Because existence (*bhāva*) resides in the particulars (*viśeṣa*), it is not other than the particulars, just as it is not other than its own self. Likewise, because the particular resides in existence, the particular is not other than existence, just as existence is not other than itself. And this fact of their residing in one another has been well-demonstrated by the previously mentioned reasoning; for even though they have the nature of persisting through existents such as jars and cloths, they cannot be designated as having separate forms (see page 753, line 5;
