Regarding the absence of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), he says: "But surely, when the universal is without distinction, at that very moment there is otherness (*anyatva*). Surely a positive entity (*bhāva*) characterized by persistence (*anuvṛtti*), from which all particularities such as pots and cloths have been excluded, does not exclude itself from anything anywhere; therefore, it is established that it is 'other' than a particular characterized by mutual exclusion. This is not so, because of the lack of distinction. As has been stated previously in many ways, an entity from which all particularities are excluded lacks the acquisition of its own nature and is thus non-existent (*abhāva*); and since it is without distinction, being non-existent like a sky-flower, how could there be otherness?

Furthermore, even if an entity (*bhāva*) exists together with its particularity (*viśeṣa*), yet the particularity does not exist [as a separate thing] with the entity, and the particularity exists with the entity, yet the entity does not [exist as a separate thing] with it—even if these two were somehow different, one should not say that "the different is indeed different," because they are different, like Devadatta who is different from his hands and so forth, or like an atom which is neither different nor non-different from subsequent moments of form (*rūpa*) and so on.
In that case, those two would be absolutely non-existent, due to the absence of both particularity and the state of being a particularity, like a sky-flower.
But surely, because their definition consists in being established as distinct, even the state of being "neither" is inexpressible.

For if there were no fixed rule characterized by inclusion and exclusion, then even a particular such as form would function as a universal, just like existence; and existence itself, being of the nature of inclusion, would be excluded, just like a sky-flower. Therefore, let there be a state of duality characterized by distinct establishment.

The claim that "they are not simultaneous with one another" refers to a distinction in their modes of existence (*vṛtti*), but that is unestablished; for the difference between those two is itself unestablished.

Indeed, if their difference were established, then their simultaneous or non-simultaneous existence might occur, since such states reside in two distinct things; however, that [difference] is not established.
Therefore, the conceptualization of their simultaneous or non-simultaneous existence—and their mutual difference—is untenable.

Furthermore, even if there were some kind of difference, one could not say that "the other is simply other," because it is a difference, like Devadatta who is both different and non-different from his hands and so forth, or like atoms which are both different and non-different from subsequent moments of form and so on.
In that case, those two would be absolutely non-existent, due to the absence of both specific and general characteristics, like a sky-flower.
But surely, since their definition consists in being established as distinct, their state of being neither [different nor non-different] is also inexpressible.
For if there were no fixed rule characterized by inclusion and exclusion, then even a particular such as form would function as a universal, just like existence;
and existence too, being of the nature of inclusion, would be excluded, like a sky-flower.
Therefore, let there be "duality," which is characterized by a distinct establishment of both.

Even granting [the opponent's position], we say: "Nevertheless, in some way... and so on, up to "...like an atom. This same passage, which serves as a means of explanation, has already been explained; it is intended to negate otherness. Having proposed the thesis that "one thing is not to be called 'other than another,'" the meaning is established by demonstrating the method of explanation through the reason of "otherness," from "like Devadatta, who is neither other nor non-other than his hands, etc.," up to "like an atom, which is neither other nor non-other than its preceding moment of color-form (rūpa), etc. (p.
From the hand, another [is produced]; from the hand, another [is produced]. Bhāṣya, page 751, line 1.

In the Bhāṣya, after [the options] such as "other than one another" and "neither one nor other" have been refuted, the opponent says: "In that case, those two are absolutely non-existent, because they lack both specific and general characteristics, like a sky-flower."

The non-distinction between an entity (*bhāva*) and its particularity (*viśeṣa*) is identity; distinction is otherness. Since both of these are negated, there is an absence of both distinction and non-distinction. That which lacks both distinction and non-distinction is non-existent, just like a sky-flower (as stated on page 751, line 3). [Text correction: *bhāvaviśeṣayor aviśeṣa*].

To this it is replied: Now, as for the argument beginning with "distinct," etc.—is it not the case that being neither [of the two] is non-existence? That too is inexpressible. Why? Because its characteristic is the establishment of difference. Just as in the case of fire and fuel, since their characteristics—the burner and the burnable, and so forth—are established as distinct, it is said that there is no state of being neither; likewise here, since the persistence and exclusion of the entity and its particularity are established as distinct characteristics, the state of being neither is also inexpressible. This is to be understood as before. To establish that point, he says: "If indeed persistence," and so forth.

However, there is a distinction regarding the example of the undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭāpādana*): "From that, even color and so forth... and so on. Color would be a particular (*viśeṣa*), yet taste would also proceed as something entirely separate because it lacks the nature of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) by its own form, just like a positive entity (*bhāva*).

Furthermore, a positive entity, being of the nature of persistence (*anuvṛtti*), would exclude itself from color and so forth as something entirely separate because it lacks the nature of persistence, like a sky-flower.

If the persistence and exclusion of the universal and the particular were not established as distinct, then this undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) would apply to the case at hand. However, since an entity (*bhāva*) is observed to persist through forms, tastes, and so forth, while the particular is observed to exclude itself from other forms, tastes, and so forth, therefore there is no such thing as "neither-nor" (*anubhayatva*);
rather, let there be "both-ness" (*ubhayatva*), characterized by distinct establishment—that is to say, "otherness" (*anyatva*).
To state the fault in not accepting this, it is said: "distinct establishment," and so on, up to "there would be both-ness."

If one does not admit that "bothness" (*ubhayatva*) consists in the occurrence of the characteristics of distinct establishment within a single entity that is essentially everything, then "bothness" would have to be either the single entity that is essentially everything or its absolute non-existence.
If it is argued that "bothness" is the negation of "neither-ness," we say no; for [the concept of] otherness is inexpressible.
If it is argued that the negation of otherness is oneness, we say no; for that too is inexpressible.
Furthermore, by the negation of identity, difference, bothness, and neitherness, the relationship of primary and subordinate is also necessarily negated;
therefore, in every respect, there is indeed inexpressibility regarding substance, quality, cause, effect, and so forth, exactly as in this case.

Therefore, stating otherwise results in a contradiction with the actual state of things (*vastu-viṣamvāda*), because one would be determining that which is other as non-other, the one as many, and both as neither; this is like the erroneous determination of a pot as a cloth or vice versa.

Furthermore, he maintains that this very restriction (*niyama*) is itself the reality (*vastu*). For if the existence of a thing were restricted exclusively to its being either identical with or different from its general and particular aspects, then duality could only result from the certain restriction of an excess [of one over the other], or else it would be an absolute non-existence, like a sky-flower, since there is no other possible alternative.
And that is undesirable: either the state of being both would consist in a single entity possessing the nature of all things, or it would consist in the absolute non-existence of both.

However, if one does not accept a state of being both characterized by distinct definitions and modes of existence, then the state of being both would result in nothing other than a single entity possessing the nature of all things, or else it would be nothing other than absolute non-existence.
If it is argued that "bothness" follows from the negation of "neither," we say no, because "otherness" is itself inexpressible.
If it is argued that the negation of "otherness" implies "oneness," we say no, because that too is inexpressible.
Furthermore, by the negation of oneness, otherness, bothness, and neitherness, the relationship of primary and subordinate is also necessarily negated.
Therefore, in every respect, there is indeed inexpressibility even regarding substance, quality, cause, effect, and so forth; for it is exactly thus.

To speak otherwise than this results in a contradiction of reality (*vastu-visaṃvāda*), because one would be determining that which is other as non-other, the one as many, and both as neither. This is like the erroneous determination of a jar as a cloth, or vice versa.

And this restriction (*niyama*) intends that the restriction itself is the real entity (*vastu*), because it restricts with certainty and necessity the occurrence of the absolute identity or difference between the universal and the particular;
[this is] the word ending in the locative case (pṛ॰ 752, l. 3).

The passage beginning with "Because of the negation of being neither" (*anubhayatvapratiṣedhāt*) and so forth is to be understood as identical to the preceding text, up to the point where it concludes that [the self] is indeed inexpressible in every respect (*sarvathaivāvaktavyataiva*). This has already been explained by the application of the specific nature of the subject under discussion (*dārṣṭāntika-bhāva-viśeṣa*), just like the application of the example of fire and fuel (pp. 752, l. 5 ff.).

Having thus established the inexpressibility of both the general and the particular, he extends [this principle] to substance, quality, cause, effect, and so forth, stating: "It is exactly the same in the case of substance, quality, cause, effect, and so on.

For, beginning with the statement, "In this way, becoming occurs, as in the case of fire and fuel," that very same passage concerning the illustration continues until the conclusion: "in every respect, there is indeed only inexpressibility."

If, regarding that [substance], there is oneness of the quality with the substance and not otherness, and so forth—by means of the negation of mutual oneness, otherness, both, neither, primacy, and subordination between substance and quality—then the conclusion is that it is in every way inexpressible; as far as this extends, the entire text is to be applied accordingly.
Furthermore, the same application of the text applies to cause and effect as well.

By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (ādi), it is established that the same detailed investigation applies to the conceptual constructions of the all-pervading and non-all-pervading, the eternal and non-eternal, the state and the possessor of the state, the object of enjoyment and the enjoyer, and so forth; thus, it remains an inexpressible reality— this is the illustrative example [found] on page 744, line 1.
Therefore, the proposition (*pratijñā*) is that "there is a discrepancy with the actual object (*vastuvisaṃvāda*) when stated otherwise";
the reason (*hetu*) is "because [it is said] 'by treating one thing as non-different from another,' and so on, up to 'due to restriction' (*avadhāraṇāt*)."
The illustration is "like the determination of the reversal between a jar and a cloth.

Just as there is a contradiction when a cloth is determined to be in a jar, or a jar is determined to be in a cloth, so too should [the cases of] "otherness" and "non-otherness," and so forth, be applied. An entity, when determined through its identity, difference, both, neither, or through the predominance or subordination of either one, contradicts itself in relation to others; thus has the entity been explained.
[Otherwise stated in the *Prakaraṇa*].
The explanation of the object (*vastu*) as the functioning (*vṛtti*) of the pot (*ghaṭa*).

The nature of the method (*naya*) is stated: this rule [is explained] in the section concerning the demonstration of the correctness of the collection of all injunctions (*vidhi*), restrictive rules (*niyama*), and negations (*bhaṅga*). Here, moreover, the meaning of a word is "discourse" (*abhijalpa*);

for it has been said: "When a word, having attained the state of discourse, reaches the status of being denotable through the relation 'this is that' (*so’yam*), its form becomes unified with the object, which is of an unestablished form [prior to that]."
The internal verbalization (*abhijalpa*) of a word with its object is called "speech" (*vāk*); the remainder is to be inferred. (Vākyapadīya 2.128–129)

Because the form of the word and the object are unified as "this is that," it is stated that their difference is inexpressible; and because the oneness with the object resides in both, due to this unification, it is stated that their identity is inexpressible.
In the inquiry into the true nature [of things], this method maintains that the very restriction [itself] is the reality.

He connects the literal meaning of the word *niyama* as previously described with the actual subject matter, demonstrating the impossibility of past conceptual constructs—namely, the absolute identity or difference of the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*), and their respective modes of existence. The term *niyama* is derived from the root *yam* preceded by the prefix *ni*, with the suffix *ghañ* and a *prādi* compound; thus, it means "ascertained restraint" (*niścito yamaḥ*), "fixed restraint" (*niyataḥ*), or "excessive restraint" (*adhikaḥ*). Why? Because, according to the method already stated, when the universal and the particular are in a state of absolute identity, absolute difference, duality, bothness, or the predominance/subordination of one over the other, they lack an ascertained, fixed, or excessive [restraint] due to their uncontrolled mode of existence (*ayatasvavṛttitvāt*). However, in the case of the "inexpressible" (*avaktavya*), because there is an ascertained, fixed, and excessive [restraint] due to its controlled mode of existence (*yatasvavṛttitvāt*), this branch of analysis is designated as the "Restraint of Reality" (*yathārthaniyama*).
And here, the object of speech (*śabdārtha*) is the mental discourse (*abhijalpa*);
for it has been said: "Or rather, when a word has attained the state of being a mental discourse, it becomes the denotable object;
through the connection [of the cognition] 'this is that,' its form becomes identified with the form of the object."
The internal discourse of a word with its meaning is called *abhijalpa*;
the remainder of the verse is to be inferred... [Vākya-paṭala 2.128–129].
Or even a word, having attained the state of being associated with mental discourse,
becomes the denotable object through the relation "this is that"; when the form [of the object] is unified with the accepted form [of the word].
The internal verbalization (*abhijalpa*) of a word with its object is called "discourse" (*jalpa*);
because of the unification [of the two] through the thought "this is that," it is stated that the identity of the form of the word with the object is "inexpressible.
By the phrase "with the object," it is stated that their unity is "inexpressible" because the act of unification resides in both.

Having thus explained the nature of the rule both according to the actual fact (*vastu*) and according to the literal meaning of the words (*akṣarārtha*), he states the meaning of the term itself: "In this state of such being, *abhijalpa* is the meaning of the word. He does not explain this again, as this *abhijalpa* was already mentioned incidentally in the context of rejecting [theories of] entities such as the individual (*vyakti*). However, to indicate that [point], he says "For it is said," etc., providing the relevant passage by means of the two-and-a-half verses beginning with "Or the word has attained the state of *abhijalpa*," which serve as the defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of that [term].
The remainder is to be inferred, etc.; this has already been explained previously in the Abhibhāṣya and the Ubbhaya.
See the *tallakṣaṇakārikā*s, Bhāṣya, p. 580, note 1.

If it is asked, "How, then, is 'inexpressibility' (avaktavyatā) stated by that passage? he says the following to demonstrate it: Because of the unification [of word and object] through the thought "this is that," when it is said, "by virtue of the relationship of non-difference as 'this is that,' they are unified," it is thereby stated that their difference is inexpressible (*anyatvam avaktavyam*).

By the phrase "with the object" (*arthena*), the unification with an object distinct from the word is meant; since unification resides in both, the manifold is made one. By the statement "the form of the word is unified with the object," it is thereby stated that their identity (*ekatvam*) is inexpressible.

By these very same arguments, it should be understood that bothness, neitherness, and the states of being primary or subordinate are also inexpressible; thus has the meaning of words been explained— this is the meaning of the term *padārtha*.

A sentence (*vākya*) is a collection (*saṅghāta*), such as "Devadatta, bring the white cow. Because [the words] function individually and because they reside in a single meaning characterized by generality, particularity, unity, difference, and multiplicity—it being thus, and speaking merely by way of illustration—that a word expresses its object through proximity to that object, one might ask:
"What then is the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*)? He replies: "The sentence-meaning is known precisely when the sentence is known," for a sentence is a collection.
A word (*pada*) is a collection of phonemes (*varṇa*); since even a single syllable is a collection of vowel and consonant, a sentence (*vākya*) is a collection of words.

If it is asked why, it is said: because in the sentence "Devadatta, bring the cow, white," there is a state of being manifold objects due to the unity and difference of the general and particular meanings residing in each [word]. Since words such as "Devadatta" and so forth, while residing individually in the general meaning of word-objects (*padārtha-sāmānya*), reside in a specific relational meaning (*viśiṣṭa-saṃsarga*), that is the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*). As it has been stated: "The sentence-meaning is the abiding of words, which reside in the general, in a particular. And because the manifold nature of the object consisting of both unity and difference, as well as neither-unity-nor-difference, between those two—the general and the particular—is held to be inexpressible (*avacanīya*), a word situated in manifold objects cannot be determined in a single form; therefore, its meaning is inexpressible.

Now, in order to demonstrate the position of the "composite" (saṃghāta) by resorting to the theory of "connection after utterance" (abhihitānvaya), he says: "The meaning, however much it may be expressed by a word in isolation, that much alone they say is denoted by the word when situated in a sentence.
But that other surplus [meaning] which arises when there is a connection [between the words], [is not denoted by the word]."
They say that this very meaning of the sentence, which rests upon many words, is [the object]; [Vākyapadīya 2.41–42], [and] by the word "kevalena" (by the solitary).
Whatever single word expresses a certain meaning, that very same meaning it conveys even when situated within a sentence;
therefore, when there is an addition resulting from the mutual connection of the word-meanings within the aggregate of words, that relation (*saṃsarga*) is the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*).
And it has been said: "That which is the addition here is the sentence-meaning" (Pāṇini-Mahābhāṣya 2).
3.46 By the phrase "relying on multiple words," it is shown that a sentence is a collection [of words].

To demonstrate the two positions—that this sentence-meaning is fully present in each individual [word] like a genus (*jāti*), or, according to some, is fully present in the collection [of words] like a number (*saṃkhyā*)—he says: "But that [sentence-meaning], although residing in many words, is completed in each individual part like a genus;
it is also conceived by others as being in the collection like a number" (Vākyapadīya 2).

"43"—thus, in the *Vākyapadīya-vṛtti* composed by Vṛṣabhadeva, [in the section on] "the multiplicity of both [general and particular]... And having established this, it has also been said: "The general meaning, once vanished, does not give rise to the particular."
As for the objection, "How can there be the abandonment of that which is appropriated? Where could its cessation abide?

(Vākyapadīya 2.15), that too has already been refuted by the fact that a thing is determined as being inexpressible in every respect once it has been investigated; thus, it is said that a word expresses [its object] merely by indicating its direction, through its proximity to the object, and by causing the cognition [of that object].
When the general object has disappeared, no particular arises;
[therefore] the general object is the general object. (Yaśomitra / Bhāṣya)

For how could there be the abandonment of what has already been taken up? Once it has ceased, where could it abide?

In that case, a word by which a qualified object has not been apprehended at the very moment of its manifestation—that word, having its general meaning disappeared, is no longer capable of remaining fixed upon the particular;
nor is it possible for the intention to express both the general and the particular simultaneously.
For when there is a desire to express a particular [meaning], the exclusion of everything from the universal is understood without restriction;

in that case, since the relation between word and meaning is eternal, how could there be an abandonment of what has been taken up? Furthermore, when the essential natures of objects are being investigated through reasoning, if the word lacks connection with the act of denotation, it ceases to function and its nature remains undetermined. Thus, due to the absence of the object upon which the word was initially directed, where could the word—now having no referent—be established?
This is stated in the *Svavṛtti* on the *Vākyapadīya* composed by Bhartṛhari.

Furthermore, as for what is stated by the Mīmāṃsakas—that a mere collection of words, through the force of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), compatibility (*yogyatā*), and proximity (*sannidhāna*), becomes mutually connected as a sentence (*vākya*), and that the relational connection (*saṃsarga*) is the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*)—he speaks in order to refute that: "The general meaning... [in the passage] "O Devadatta, drive the white cow with a stick" (Pāṇini-Mahābhāṣya 1.1).
Thus, sentences are merely words such as "Devadatta" and so forth.

In that regard, if the word "Devadatta" first functions as a mere universal (*sāmānya*), then because speech occurs sequentially, that word would have ceased to exist at the time of the word "cow" (*go*) and others due to its disappearance; how then could there be a cognition of its meaning at the time of hearing the other words? Furthermore, precisely because of its non-existence, it cannot abide in a specific state (*viśeṣa*) upon the proximity of other words. Even granting that a word exists through being remembered when other words are in proximity, it is not logical for it to abide in a specific state; thus he says: "of that which has been grasped... (*upāttasya*).

Why is the abandonment of the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*)—an object common to all things that was previously adopted as the denotable meaning—justified now upon the proximity of another word? For this would entail the non-eternality of the relationship between word and meaning. Furthermore, such a position is not accepted by the Mīmāṃsaka; nevertheless, it is stated even while assuming it: "Withdrawn" means that when another word is proximate, this word has withdrawn from its own meaning. Where, then, could it abide now? Since it lacks the status of a denoter with respect to a meaning cognizable through another word, how can its continued existence be justified?

And in this very way, it is appropriate that [the word] expresses a mode (*bhāva*)-endowment; for when it says "it is inexpressible," it speaks merely of a mode (*paryāya*), because it belongs to the domain of the *śabda-naya*. This is a proponent of modes (*paryavāstika*), because it expresses a distinct meaning of the verbal root *bhū*, such that it "modes" (*paryavati*) or comes into being.

In the same way, as for that definition of the *śabdanaya* stated by the author of the *Lakṣaṇa*: "The *śabda* [is so called] because it expresses that which is intended among the denotations of name (*nāma*), representation (*sthāpanā*), and substance (*dravya*); it is that which expresses what is joined with the mode (*bhāva*)," where *bhāva* means a modification (*paryāya*), a restriction (*niyama*), or a quality (*guṇa*), and thus it expresses an object joined with those—this view of the *śabdanaya* is also consistent in this regard, insofar as it concludes that something is "inexpressible" (*avaktavya*), because an entity consisting of a manifold nature of unity and difference between the universal and the particular cannot be expressed by words.

This [view] belongs to the *paryāyāstika* because it teaches the *śabdanaya*. For it is stated in the *Sanmati-tarka*: "The various alternatives of words (*saddavikappa*), such as *sāha* and *pasāha*, which possess subtle distinctions, are included within the *śabdanaya*" (1.5). If one asks: "What is the reason that when [a word] expresses something endowed with a state (*bhāva*), there is a grasping of the synonym (*paryāya*) and not a grasping of the universal (*sāmānya*)? And why is it so when the word for 'state' (*bhāva-śabda*) expresses the universal? It is said in reply: Because the root *bhū* expresses the meanings of various distinct roots; all roots beginning with *bhū* have the sense of "being" (*bhvartha*). Regarding the term *bhūvādayaḥ*, by applying the *auṇādika* suffix *iñ* to the root *vad*, we derive *bhūvādayaḥ*, meaning "all the roots beginning with *bhū*."

Therefore, *bhū* does not have only the meaning of "existence" (*sattā*), because both *bhū* and *kṛ* express the meanings of all verbal roots (*sarvadhātvartha*). [The term] *bhāva* means "it comes to rest" (*paryavati bhavati*). And "coming to rest" (*paryavaṇam*) is "entering" (*praveśanam*). This is because the root *ava* is listed [in Pāṇini’s Dhātupāṭha] as having the following meanings: protection, motion, beauty, affection, satisfaction, understanding, entering, hearing, ownership, requesting, action, desire, radiance, attainment, embracing, injury, burning, state, and increase (Pāṇini, Dhātupāṭha 60). Thus, *bhāva* is *paryava*, which is "entering.
In the compound *paryava*, the prefix *pari-* has the sense of "all around," and the word *ava-* has the sense of "entering."

He demonstrates that [meaning] in reality: "That object which enters into identity, difference, both, and neither from all sides is the *paryava* (the ultimate limit). Therein, having first stated the permutation of restriction, he next declares that because the meaning of words is "discourse" (*abhijalpa*), and because a real entity cannot be directly expressed due to its state of being difficult to determine through various conflicting assertions such as identity or difference regarding its general and particular aspects, there is "inexpressibility" (*avaktavyatā*). Since this was stated within the framework of the restrictive *naya* (*niyamanaya*), one who remains unsatisfied even here, taking his stand on the permutation of the restriction-affirmation (*niyamavidhibhaṅga*), says: "Such a restriction is not tenable, because of faults such as self-contradiction in one's own words, and because of the lack of fixedness when multiple states occur; for this statement of yours has become nothing more than a common worldly proverb."
That is to say: this very same thing is being asserted by you, and that very same thing is being denied; the meaning is that you both affirm and refute it.

The ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is understood by those who possess meditative concentration and are free from delusion: that each individual particular is distinct from every other. What is it like? It is like the particular unity of a jar consisting of color, taste, and so forth. Just as properties such as color, taste, smell, touch, number, and shape—though distinct and perceivable by different sense organs—are collectively called "one jar," so too, through delusion, there is a notion of unity in the collection even though it does not exist; yet, these particulars themselves remain distinct: color is not taste, and taste is not color. In the same way, there is no otherness—whether through distinction or non-distinction—by virtue of which neither-ness could be excluded, nor is there unity; likewise, there is no neither-ness by virtue of which unity, otherness, or both could be excluded, or by grasping whose denotability the "inexpressible" (avācya) could be excluded. (Gaṇakārikā-bhāṣya)
The reading "ekatva...vadhā" contained within this [passage] does not exist in the Bhāratīya manuscript,
folio 756, line 6.
[Regarding] the *anyatva-viśeṣya* on page 768,
line 23, you might say: "But surely there is no fault, because [the objection] is refuted from both sides."

Having negated oneness, otherness is likewise negated; and having negated bothness and neitherness, it is precisely "inexpressibility" that is established. Regarding this, you must be asked: what, then, is the object of this inexpressibility? If it is simply the negation of both, what is that entity which is inexpressible? Must it be determined whether it is an existent, a particular, or both? For, given that it is an entity, it cannot transcend these three alternatives. Among these, it cannot be an existent, nor a particular, nor both, because of the persistence of the negative particle (*na*).
The oneness, otherness, bothness, and neitherness of an entity may exist either through differentiation or non-differentiation.
Non-differentiated oneness is as follows: "All this is indeed the Self alone" (Śukla Yajurveda Saṃhitā 31.2), and so forth.

If there were a distinction from a second, then by virtue of not being in contact with that second, it would be "one"; as in the examples: "A pride of lions has never existed on earth, nor is there a pride of venomous serpents;
those wise ones wander alone," and "For the spirited, there is no need for assistance"—for here the word "alone" (eka) signifies the absence of companions.
In what state?
On earth, a pride of lions has never existed before, nor does a pride of venomous serpents exist.
"These wise ones wander alone; for those possessed of splendor, there is no need for assistance.
These heroes wander alone"—thus it is stated in the *Tattvārtharājavārtika* (1.5).

First of all, there is no oneness of an entity—whether of its particularity (*viśeṣa*) or of both—by way of non-distinction (*apravibhāga*), because you yourself have refuted that which is devoid of a second, since it is impossible to describe a form [in such a state].

Nor is there oneness by way of distinction (*pravibhāga*), precisely because this has been refuted through such arguments as: "because co-existence and non-co-existence reside in two [distinct] things."

Thus, it has been stated that there is no unity of either the particular (*viśeṣa*) or both [the universal and the particular]; and if unity were established, then by its power otherness (*anyatva*) would be excluded. One might conceive of grasping unity and, through that means—that is, by that method—exclude otherness; however, that unity does not exist, and due to its absence, there is no negation of otherness (p. 756, l. 2).
And how can oneness be conceived? For the word "one" has as its meaning a number that is independent of anything else, because it signifies an indivisible unity;
yet that is not tenable, since the conceptual alternatives of identity, difference, both, and neither are mutually dependent.
Now, although the word "one" (eka) signifies "without a companion," nevertheless, because it does not exclude [the possibility of] being accompanied by two or more, oneness is not established.
However, in the sense of "other," there is directly otherness itself, which has a specific object;
likewise, non-otherness is either inexpressible due to the implication of its opposite, or else it lacks a referent. Otherwise, [it would be untenable].
Thus, another might think: "Difference is established, and by its power, identity, duality, and so forth, are negated.

But that difference is not established; for in the same way, whether through distinction or non-distinction, difference—whether as conceived in the case of a jar and a cloth, or as in the case of the soul and the body—is impossible, since you yourself have already negated it. It is by the power of such [established] difference that non-duality or identity would be excluded through the gateway of difference.
By exclusion (vyāvṛtti), O Bhagavatī;
by exclusion, O Jina.

Likewise, "neither-nor-ness" (anubhayatva) does not exist either, because it has been stated that there is a fixed distinction in the characteristics of identity and difference by virtue of which identity, difference, and both would be excluded; or else, having grasped what is expressible, one must state whether this [object] is seen to be identical, different, or both, whereas this [object] is inexpressible because it is not like those. Similarly, "neither-nor-ness" is expressible in that same way, yet those [three] are not expressible; thus, the inexpressible might be excluded by the force of the expressible. This is because the exclusion of one thing presupposes the establishment of another, and because the comprehension of the meaning occurs through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka). (Tattvasaṅgrahapañjikā)
Or rather, how is that [state] brought about—namely, how is it that the previous state is established as one thing and the subsequent state as another? Thus he asks.

It is said: For the word "one" (*eka*) signifies a number that is independent of anything else, because its meaning is the indivisible unity of the word itself; the particle "hi" has the sense of "because. Because the word "one," while denoting a number, expresses a number independent of others by emphasizing the thing numbered—meaning for the purpose of excluding other numbers, as in common usage: "This is one, not two, three, or more"—therefore, when "one" is said, it implies that "there is no other. Yet that [exclusive] meaning does not hold, for it is not independent; this is because, according to the method previously stated, the conceptual alternatives of oneness, otherness, bothness, and neitherness are mutually dependent.
The differentiation of the *tha* [phoneme] is one; the non-differentiation of the meaning is one; the number of the *bhā* [phoneme] is not reached by the *bhā*.
In the context of enumeration, the word "one" (eka) refers to a single entity; however, here it signifies being without a companion.

Now, [the opponent might argue]: "Let this fault—caused by the word 'one' having as its meaning a number that is independent of anything else—not arise; therefore, let the word 'one' be conceived as denoting that which has no companion (*asahāya*). Consequently, oneness exists; and because oneness exists, otherness and so forth also exist; thus, the existence of the object that is 'inexpressible' (*avaktavya*) is established. To this we reply: "Even so," and so forth. *Saha* means a companion (*sahāya*). A "companion" (*sahāya*) is one who goes together (*sahagati*), for going together occurs between two or many. Since "going together" is not distinct from the meaning of "two" and so forth, oneness does not exist; thus, the state of being an "inexpressible" object remains as before. Furthermore, only otherness would be established, and thus there is once again only otherness.

Thus, it has been stated that the single word "one" (eka) denotes "otherness" (anyatva) by way of implication (*arthāpatti*). Similarly, [the compound] *atīta* and so forth... [as in the *Yuktiṣaṣṭikāvṛtti*].
By the meaning of "and so forth," there is the exclusion [of others]; the word "only" (eva) expresses precisely that exclusion.

Furthermore, one is "other" than that, and that [second] one is also "other" than the former; thus, the word *eka* (one) denotes the sense of "other. Now, when it refers to the sense of "other," the very state of being other (*anyatva*) is directly the object of distinction. Consequently, the negation of such "otherness" is an extremely clear contradiction of one's own statement—this has already been explained. Moreover, in this way, even non-otherness (*ananyatva*) is established:

just as the word *eka* functions in the sense of "other" according to the logic we have stated, by that same method, non-otherness is also proven, because there can be no "otherness" without "non-otherness."

To this he says: "Because of the rejection of the counter-position" (*pratipakṣākṣepāt*). [The question is: Are the negations of oneness and so forth [applicable] even in the case of fear and the like? How is it "inexpressible"? They do not exclude the "inexpressible" itself because the things to be negated lack such a nature and are thus rootless; rather, they serve the purpose of excluding the one-sided views (*ekānta*) such as oneness that reside within the opponent's intention.

Now, if those [attributes] such as oneness and so forth, being existent, are negated, then the state of being "inexpressible" (*avaktavya*) therein would be devoid of an object. Alternatively, if they are non-existent, how could they have been apprehended by the opponent? For you do not negate their absolute existence nor establish their non-absolute existence, as is the case in the doctrine of the Supreme Lord of Disputation (*vādaparameśvara*). This point has already been explained: just as oneness and otherness are mutually contradictory, so too are bothness and neitherness.

Thus, first of all, it has been stated [on page 766, line 6] that oneness— being established by the power of its proven counter-position— is what is excluded, and not anything else; otherwise, there would be the consequence of the "ineffable" (avaktavya) being devoid of an object,
as is the case with both [existence and non-existence] and so forth.

What is the purpose of these negations of oneness and so forth? How is [the self] inexpressible? They do not negate the inexpressibility itself because it would be groundless if those things to be negated—oneness and so forth—did not exist; rather, their purpose is to exclude the one-sided views (ekānta) such as oneness that reside within the intentions of others. If, however, those existing attributes such as oneness were being negated, then in that case, the inexpressibility would be rendered devoid of an object.

But if they do not exist, how were they apprehended by another? For it is not the case that their absolute existence is being negated and their non-absolute existence established by you, as in the doctrine of the Lord of Disputation (*vādaparameśvara*);
[rather,] direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is what is being negated.

By the phrase "not otherwise" (nānyathā), he extends the principle by stating that the remainder is thereby expressed: "In the same way, this logic should be applied to otherness, bothness, and so forth"—
by the inclusion of "and so forth" (ādi), it is meant that this same reasoning should be introduced regarding non-bothness as well.

Having begun by stating that there is no "otherness" or "bothness" of an entity, a particular, or both—whether through differentiation or non-differentiation—and having established that in the absence of otherness there is an absence of oneness, and in the absence of bothness there is an absence of oneness and otherness, [the author] concludes:
"Thus, the negations of oneness and so forth... [they] exclude... and so on, up to "...they turn away. *Note: The ellipses indicate the reconstructed portions of the text based on the context.*
What is the purpose of the negations of oneness and so forth according to the method thus stated? What are those negations? The meaning is that they do not exist;
since there is an absence of such negations, how could it be "inexpressible"? This means it would be without logical justification and without an object [of negation].

However, those negations of oneness and so forth—being themselves rootless because the things to be negated are not as they are claimed and thus lack the status of being negatable—exclude the very notion of "inexpressibility" precisely because they are rootless.

Regarding the statement "rootless because they are rootless," [the opponent] here objects: No, for the negations are not rootless because their purpose is to exclude the one-sided views such as unity that reside in the opponent's intention; nor is it inexpressible due to being devoid of an object, because its purpose is precisely the negation of unity and so forth.

For these [statements] are intended for the purpose of excluding the absolute positions—such as oneness and so forth—which are the objects of negation and reside within the intentions of others; therefore, there is no fault.
Because they have the purpose of turning [others away], they are not baseless. (Bhāṣya: because they have the purpose of turning [others away], they are not baseless. (Yaśomitra)

Regarding those [objections] concerning the opponent’s intention regarding oneness (*ekatva*) and so forth, it is said here: "Now, as for those [qualities] such as oneness," and so on, up to "how were they apprehended by the opponent?

If, first of all, oneness and the rest are negated while being apprehended by the opponent exactly as they exist, then the aforementioned lack of a referent (*nirviṣayatā*) for the "inexpressibility" (*avaktavyatva*) applies there.

Now, since they do not exist at all due to being utterly non-existent—like a flower in the sky—how can they be apprehended? It might be thought: "Even in the doctrine of *syādvāda*, when asked whether the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*) are identical, different, both, neither, or inexpressible, the denials are made: 'Neither identity, nor difference, nor both, nor inexpressibility; what then? It may be identity, it may be difference, it may be both, it may be neither, it may be inexpressible,' and so forth. But this is incorrect because of their dissimilarity. To demonstrate this, he says: "For these do not belong to you," and so on.

For the *syādvāda* (the doctrine of manifoldness) reigns over all doctrines because it is capable of both refuting and favoring them; and while properties such as oneness and so forth may exist within it, they are conceived as the opposite of the word "inexpressible" (*avaktavya*), due to its connection with the negative particle (*nañ*), just like the term "non-Brahmin" (*abrāhmaṇa*).

Furthermore, you yourself have admitted that the object to be expressed must be stated according to its proximity to the directions [of space], yet that very object is negated by the negative particle as being "inexpressible."

If it is argued that the employment of two negatives is implied by that meaning—since a negation of a negation returns one to the original state—and thus leads back to the primary subject, just as in the case of "non-non-Brahmin," and that verbal usage exists merely as a conventional designation (*saṃvṛti*); then, in that case, "inexpressibility" (*avaktavyatva*) is not ultimate, because its meaning consists of a collection of words belonging to conventional truth. Just like the stories of a frog wearing a crown of matted hair, a barren woman’s son adorned with artificial locks, or a garland of sky-flowers, there is an absence of any established distinction between property (*dharma*) and substratum (*dharmin*). Since such a position cannot serve as a proof, the inexpressibility of a real entity (*vastu*) can only be conceived in this manner, and not otherwise.

In this way, by negating the grasping at extremes (*ekāntagrāha*), they are both refuted and favored through the demonstration of non-absolutism (*anekānta*). It is not so for you who maintain the doctrine of the "inexpressible" (*avaktavyavādin*); for you, the absolute existence of those [qualities] such as oneness and so forth is not merely set aside, but rather their non-absolute existence is being established.
Therefore, because it negates what is non-existent, this example—“like the doctrine of the Supreme Lord of Speech” (*vādaparameśvaravāda*)—is inconsistent.

For in that case, since entities possess opposites, it is precisely those things which are existent that are said to be "inexpressible" in an absolute sense, while being expressible in a non-absolute form, such as: "it may be unity, it may be plurality," and so forth. Thus he says:
"You speak of manifoldness," and so forth.
However, an opposite [meaning] to the word "inexpressible" (avaktavya) is conceivable because it is joined with the negative particle (nañ), just as in the case of "non-Brahmin" (abrāhmaṇa).

Moreover, you yourself have accepted that an object must be expressed through proximity to a direction; yet that very object is precisely what is to be left unexpressed, as it is negated by the negative particle (*nañ*).

Therefore, the employment of two negatives—which follows logically from this fact—indicates the original positive state because it constitutes a negation of a negation, just as in the case of "non-non-Brahmin" (*anabrāhmaṇa*).

If it is argued that verbal usage exists only conventionally (*saṃvṛti*), then "inexpressibility" (*avaktavyatva*) is not the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), because it is merely the collective meaning of a set of conventional terms. Like the stories of a frog’s load of matted hair, a barren woman’s son adorned with artificial locks, or a garland of sky-flowers, there is no established distinction between property (*dharma*) and substratum (*dharmin*); thus, since it cannot function as a formal argument (such as a thesis), the inexpressibility of a thing is merely a conceptual possibility and nothing more. Otherwise, these [positions] would have their opposites; therefore, they are not truly expressible.
"For if one were to speak with absolute [denial], the charge of false speech would follow.

Regarding this, the system of restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhinaya*) states the proof: "However, an opposite [meaning] is possible for the word 'inexpressible' (*avaktavya*), because it is joined with the negative particle (*nañ*), just like the word 'non-Brahmin' (*abrāhmaṇa*); thus, the position is that the word 'inexpressible' and its referent possess a possible opposite."

The reason "because it is joined with the negative particle" (*nañ-yuktatvāt*) should be applied both to the word and to the meaning; likewise, the example is "like a non-Brahmin" (*abrāhmaṇavat*). Just as a "non-Brahmin" is one who is not a Brahmin or someone other than a Brahmin—and thus exists only when the counter-correlate, the Brahmin, exists—so too, when a counter-correlative entity is to be expressed, there must be either a word or a meaning that is "not to be expressed.
This passage is not present in the Bhāṣya manuscript;
furthermore, [it continues] with "And by you also," and so forth.

The state of being expressible or inexpressible regarding an object is not established merely by our own assertion; rather, even you, who maintain that the meaning of a word is a conceptual construction (*abhijalpa*), have accepted that an object must be expressed through its proximity to spatial directions. In this matter, there is agreement between our views. Furthermore, according to your own position, that very object which is said to be expressed by a conceptual construction is itself inexpressible; thus, it is precisely that which is expressible which is negated by the negative particle (*nañ*).

Therefore, this double application of the negative particle (*nañ*) is obtained by implication: "inexpressible" means "not inexpressible. And that double application of *nañ*, being a negation of a negation, leads back to the original state (*prakṛti*), just as in the case of "non-non-Brahmin" (*anabrāhmaṇa*).

Alternatively, just as someone in the world might say, "He is not inexpressible" or "He is not a non-Brahmin," so too, through this double application of *nañ* to the term "inexpressible," because it is a negation of a negation, it leads back to the original state.
This is the summary meaning: having pointed out the contradiction between one's own words and one's own accepted position, he states the proof for [the object] being expressible.
pṛ॰ 762 paṃ॰ 3, pṛ॰ 765 paṃ॰ 12: *bādhayo* (Ya), *bādhayo* (Bhā)
Is it indeed inexpressible? Because it is a negation, [it is] beyond [the scope of] speech.

If it should be thought that "the conventional usage of speech arises from mental construction (saṃvṛti) alone"—that is, that sound does not express any object at all, as it has been said: "Words have conceptual construction as their source; conceptual constructions have words as their source."
There is no absolute connection between them; words do not even touch upon objects.

Now, regarding that inexpressible [reality] of which these attributes—such as generality, particularity, identity, difference, and so forth—are predicated: is it non-different from those attributes, or is it different? Because that inexpressible reality is established precisely through the restriction of its own constituent parts, whatever object is conceptualized by whichever conceptualization, [it remains inexpressible].

"This very nature is merely imagined; it does not exist at all," as stated in the *Triṃśikā-vijñapti* and other texts—what is the meaning of these words? Or what is the point of the thought: "What I have said is true, but what you have said is not"? Therefore, because they fall within the sphere of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and worldly discourse (*vyavahāra*), everything is without fault.
Words have conceptual construction as their source, and conceptual constructions have words as their source;
their connection is absolute, yet words do not even touch the objects [they denote]. (Page 547, Line 7, Note 5)

Now, regarding that which is inexpressible (*avaktavya*), of which these—generality, particularity, identity, difference, and so forth—are the attributes: is it non-different from them, or is it different? Because its determination arises precisely through the restriction of its own constituent parts (*svāvayava-tathā-niyama*), [the author], demonstrating the infinity of things to be conceptualized by means of various conceptualizations—distinguishing between internal and external objects of conceptualization—says: "by whichever conceptualization whatever object is conceptualized... and so on.

Whatever entity is conceptualized—whether internal or external, even including the qualities of a Buddha (buddhadharma)—that is merely an imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). Regarding this, he states the reason: "it does not exist.

Because that entity which is the object of conceptualization does not exist due to the absence of its own-being (*sattā*), therefore that entity is indeed of an imagined nature, and not a nature established by causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).

For instance: it is observed that with respect to a single entity and its absence, there occurs the activity of numerous mutually contradictory conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*). Yet, it is not logical for a single entity or its absence to possess multiple mutually contradictory intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*).
Therefore, all this is merely conceptual construction, because the object thereof has a purely imagined nature.
And it is said in the Sūtra: "Furthermore, Subhūti, phenomena do not exist in the way that foolish ordinary people are attached to them."
— Thus, in the commentary composed by Sthiramati on the *Triṃśikāvijñaptikārikā* written by Vasubandhu, [it is stated]:
"This imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) does not exist at all. *Triṃśikāvijñapti*, verse 20; *Satya*, verse 1.

To this we reply: If it is not ultimately real (*aparamārtha*), then why is it "inexpressible" (*avaktavyatva*)? Because its meaning consists in a collection of words belonging to conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*). That collection of words which you have designated as "sentence"—both the sound and its referent—is not ultimately real because its meaning is merely conventional. The example is: "the hair of a frog," and so forth.

A "frog-hair-tuft-made-hair-ornament-barren-son" refers to one who has fashioned a hair-ornament from a mass of frog-hairs for a barren son; for such a person, a garland for the head was made from a wreath of sky-flowers, and its description—such as "fragrant, five-colored, consisting of well-formed celestial flowers," and so forth—is not the ultimate truth because it is a collection of words based on conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*). Likewise, all this [the world] is also thus. There is no state of being "inexpressible.
Why is it inexpressible?
(Page 762, Line 1)
"This entire description of the doctrine would be as baseless as the account of a woman whose hair-ornament is a mass of frog-hair, or of a son of a barren woman wearing a garland of sky-flowers"—
thus it is stated in the *Siddhasenīya-vṛtti* on the *Tattvārtha-sūtra*, page 319, line 5.

Furthermore, [the argument] beginning with "property and property-bearer" (dharmadharmin) is understood as follows: the entity is thus "inexpressible" (avaktavya), because there is no means of proof for its demonstration;
there is no means of proof for its demonstration because there is no established distinction between property and property-bearer; and that absence [of distinction] is due to its inexpressibility.

For the property and the property-bearer, established separately and then combined again, would constitute the thesis (*pakṣa*), just as the thesis is "the property-bearer qualified by the property to be proven," such as "sound is impermanent.
Then, another property of that property-bearer, such as its being produced (*kṛtakatva*), would indeed be established as the logical reason (*hetu*).

And those two properties—the property to be proven (*sādhya*) and the proving property (*sādhana*)—are demonstrated together in another locus (*dharmin*), as in: "Whatever is produced is seen to be impermanent, like a jar"; this is the *dṛṣṭānta*. However, this means of proof (*sādhana*), which consists in the formal establishment of the distinction between property and locus, is not tenable, because the formal establishment of the distinction between property and locus has been refuted. Furthermore, the refutation of property and locus occurs by way of refuting [the categories of] "inexpressibility," "particularity of being" (*bhāva-viśeṣa*), "identity," "difference," and so forth; for it was just stated that such a thing lacks any objective referent (*nirviṣayatva*).

Therefore, because it lacks the nature of a synthesis consisting of both property (*dharma*) and property-bearer (*dharmin*), the thesis (*pakṣa*) and so forth are non-proofs, like a donkey’s horn—which is hard because its back is cracked. This is because, if there were no distinctness from the particular (*viśeṣa*) due to the non-separation of the oneness produced by the universal (*sāmānya*) and the otherness produced by the duality, then there would be a contradiction with the meaning of "inexpressible" (*avaktavya*); for inexpressibility is a rule [only] when there is such correspondence with the object. Likewise, since it is not distinct from the particular, there is no acceptance of otherness through separation from it. Is it not, then, merely the particular itself that is thus [the case]?

Just as space, though divided, is one—like a single sound (sphoṭa)—so too, because [your] "proposition" and so forth do not constitute a proof, the state of being inexpressible (*avaktavyatva*) of the entity postulated by you is to be considered possible, and not otherwise; this is the refutation [beginning with] "the subject (*dharmin*), the property (*dharma*)," etc. (Pramāṇasamuccaya).
Ah! It is thus understood that the object is inexpressible (p. 768, l. 4).

If, because of the non-penetration by the specificities of oneness produced by the universal and otherness produced by both, there is non-separateness from the specificities of oneness produced by the universal and otherness produced by both—since inexpressibility is a rule due to the correspondence with the inexpressible object—then, because it is not separate from the specificities in such and such a way, and because it does not tolerate otherness due to its separation from them, is it not simply the specificities alone?
Just as that which is divided is also said to be one, so too is the state of being expressed.

Even having accepted the position that [the whole] is inexpressible, we state a fault: you must be questioned as follows—"Now, regarding that which consists of the inexpressible, such as 'belonging to whom' and so forth;

concerning those parts of the whole (*deśin*)—namely, the universals, particulars, identity, difference, and so on—by means of which it is held to be inexpressible—is that [whole] non-different from the particular part (*viśeṣāvayava*), and so forth? For this proponent of particularity (*viśeṣavādī*), who follows the method of restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhinaya*), raises an objection by taking up that very particular intended by himself, [asking] "from the particular part... and so on.

It might be thought: "By the very refutation of the identity of the universal and the particular, etc., the entity as an indescribable distinct category has been determined and established with a fixed and certain superior status; therefore, how can there arise a question such as 'Is it non-different from that?'? To this, it is said: Since the indescribable [entity] is established precisely because it is determined as having its own parts and constituents, the question arises—'Is it non-different from those or different?'—and because it possesses those parts, the possibility of doubts regarding its being a universal, a particular, their identity, and so forth, occurs just as in the case of [ordinary objects]. Demonstrating the validity of this, he anticipates the opponent's view with the words: "For example, if the universal... and so on.
For the Sāṅkhya and others, only the universal is the single reality; for the Buddhist, only the particular;
for the Vaiśeṣika, both; and according to the ultimate view, it is something other than these.

In that regard, concerning the doctrine of the inexpressible (*avaktavya*): if that unity produced by the universal (*sāmānya*) were to be occupied by the particular (*viśeṣa*), such that the particular, by presenting its own nature to the entity, would exclude the distinction produced by the universal's unity rather than the universal itself—thereby resulting in non-distinction—and if, moreover, the otherness produced by both [unity and difference] were neither the universal nor the particular, then only if those two, unity and otherness, were also non-different from the particular would the meaning of "inexpressible" be consistent; not otherwise. For if those particulars such as unity were independent, the state of being inexpressible would cease. Indeed, since particulars are dependent upon the entity, the meaning of the inexpressible, when thus regulated, becomes consistent. Therefore, he says: "Because inexpressibility is a regulation. And because that regulation, through various modes, results in the exclusion of one nature and the attainment of another nature for the universal, particular, unity, otherness, duality, and so forth, it is a regulation of that which is being qualified. Thus, inexpressibility is indeed a particular; therefore, the inexpressible entity is non-different from the particular.

If, however, [the substance] were distinct from the particularities, then because of that distinction, there would be a difference between the particularities and the entity, as well as among oneness and so forth; yet such difference is not tolerated by the entity, because it would lead to the fallacy of absolute [duality], resulting in the loss of its "inexpressibility" (avaktavyatva), which you yourself accept. Therefore, he says: "because of the inability to tolerate difference due to that distinction."
Thus, the proof of the non-distinction from particularities regarding an inexpressible entity [is established],
as stated on page 761, line 10;
likewise, "it exists" [is said] of that, according to the Bhāṣya.
Having demonstrated that, is there a difference from the perspective of another system, or is it different from one another within the perspective of another system?

Likewise, because the entity (*bhāva*) is pervaded by its modes (*bhāva-upādhi*), there is a non-separation from both unity produced by the particular (*viśeṣa*) and difference produced by both; since this accords with the meaning of the "inexpressible" (*avaktavya*), inexpressibility is established as a rule. Thus, because it is not separate from the particular in each respective way, and because it tolerates difference due to its separation from that [particular], one should read: even in the position of the proponent of the entity (*bhāvavādin*), the logical consistency of non-separation is to be applied in exactly the same manner.
Accordingly, because the particular is non-separate from its own nature (*svarūpa*), it is accepted as being nothing other than the particular itself.

That entity (*bhāva*) by whose existence identity, difference, and so forth are investigated, and because of which that entity is declared "inexpressible" (*avaktavya*) by those who advocate for identity or difference—this particularity (*viśeṣa*) is also each one [of them] non-distinct (*avyatireka*), for its single characteristic is non-distinction.
And since it is not distinct from the particularities, it is like their own self; furthermore, it is called "existence" (*bhāva*) because the root *bhū* has the sense of being (*sattā*).
And therefore, since that [entity] is nothing but a particular (*viśeṣa*) due to its oneness, how could it be inexpressible?
For a particular is not inexpressible, because it is not distinct from itself, just like its own nature.

And likewise, because the determined object is pervaded by the inexpressible universal and particular, [the passage] beginning with "in the state of non-distinctness from the particularity of existence consisting in oneness and otherness" and continuing through that same text up to "due to the non-tolerance of oneness"—this application of non-distinctness is established in the position of both disputants in exactly the same way;
thus, the reading "viśeṣaḥ bhāvākrānteḥ" (particularity due to being pervaded by existence) would also be possible here.
[Note: *krāntervi* and *bhā* appear as variants in the manuscript.]
Because it is a specific [instance] of that which has transcended [the world],
it should be applied in exactly that same way.

A particular (*viśeṣa*) is accepted as being nothing other than the thing itself (*svarūpa*), since it is not distinct from it; it is that with respect to whose existence identity, difference, and so forth are investigated, and because of which the entity is said by those who maintain [theories of] identity or difference to be "inexpressible. This particular, too, is unitary, for non-distinction is the defining characteristic of unity.
And since that [entity] is not distinct from its particularity, it is like its own self; furthermore, because "bhāva" means existence (sattā) in the sense of "it comes into being" (*bhavati*),
it follows that it is merely the particularity itself due to their identity— so how could there be any indeterminacy regarding it?

For a particular (viśeṣa) cannot be inexpressible, because it is not distinct from [the thing itself], just like its own nature; and thus, since the object has been determined, it is indeed expressible.
In this way, because of the agreement with the position of those who maintain that [the whole] is inexpressible, the entity is not distinct from its particulars.

What follows from this? If it is thus not distinct from the particular (*viśeṣa*), then this consequence arises: surely, it is the particular alone that fulfills the desire of this restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*). He demonstrates this with the words "just as even though distinct," and so forth. Just as, because particulars possess mutually distinct and unique forms, even though a single particular such as color (*rūpa*) is distinct [from others], it is nonetheless a particular because it is not distinct from its own nature, which consists of color and so on; this description of the example is accepted because it will be explained later, and you yourself have admitted it—thus he infers.

It might be thought: "How have I accepted that? To demonstrate this, he says: "By whose existence," and so forth. That particularity (*viśeṣa*) which you have accepted in your investigation—asking whether it is identical to or different from existence (*bhāva*)—and that particularity by virtue of which existence is said to be inexpressible in terms of identity, difference, and so on, why is each such particularity [considered] one? For non-distinction (*avyatireka*) is the defining characteristic of the one; for that which is not distinguished from anything is called "one," as in: "All this is indeed the Person" (Śukla Yajurveda Saṃhitā).

31.2 And that particular state (*viśeṣabhāva*) is a real entity (*vastu*), because it is not distinct from the "inexpressible" (*avaktavya*); the reason is established by the method stated above, as in the case of its own self. The connection is as follows: just as the particularity of a particular is indeed a particular and is thus not distinct from the particular, so too is that which is called "inexpressible."
Wherein and how is this one [quality] alone present even in the specific instance? Ya:
This one alone is present in the specific instance. Bhā: [The same].

Is "existence" (*bhāva*) a particular? Lest there be the notion that the word *bhāva* is synonymous with the previously mentioned "universal," he says "existence is a real entity" (*vastu*) in order to prevent confusion, thereby demonstrating that *bhāva* is a synonym for *vastu*. He explains: "It is called existence (*bhāva*) because it exists (*bhavati*)," since its meaning is "being. Consequently, [the statement] "it is merely a particular" serves to dispel the suspicion of it being a universal; and the phrase "and it is a synonym for real entity" is the meaning of the application (*upanaya*). Although the restriction is already established by the use of the word "merely" (*mātra*), the use of the particle "only" (*eva*) is for the sake of clarification and to emphasize the intended point.

This has been established: that there is only one particular (*viśeṣa*), and that this is the "inexpressible universal" (*avaktavyasāmānya*). Now, since that [particular] exists as a unity, how can there be inexpressibility? Because of the absence of a second [entity], with what could there be an inexpressibility of identity or difference for that entity which is merely a particular? This is the contemplation of that point: "Indeed, the particular... and so forth. A particular is not inexpressible, because it is not distinct from itself, just like its own nature; thus the proof is already explained for the purpose of summarizing the stated meaning.
In this way, the particular has been determined. Because it is determined, it must necessarily be expressible; for only that which is undetermined would be inexpressible.
Because it would follow that [the object] is subject to arbitrary conventional usage due to the statement that its own nature is [inexpressible],

it must therefore be stated that the particular (*viśeṣa*) itself is the meaning of the universal (*sāmānya*) which is inexpressible; for it is not distinct from the particular, just like its own nature.

Now, if you still maintain that the "inexpressible universal" (*avacanīya-sāmānya*) is indeed inexpressible, then in that case, the "particular" (*viśeṣa*) must also be inexpressible as "particular," because it is not distinct from the particular, just like the inexpressible universal.

If that [particular] were also inexpressible, and the entity (*vastu*) itself were inexpressible, then since those two would be mutually inexpressible, it would follow that the universal is expressible even though it is inexpressible on both counts; the same would apply to the particular.
Furthermore, if the entity were distinct from the particular, it would be so because of its inexpressibility.
Now, if it is thus a positive entity (*bhāva*), it must be expressible; if it is a non-entity (*abhāva*), it too must be expressible.

Furthermore, as you have stated, it would likewise be a non-substantiality (*avastutā*) because it is non-existent and inexpressible. And just as the substance is distinct from its particularities (*viśeṣa*), so too the particularity is indeed distinct from the substance. In this way, the non-existence of these two is identical.
And so on:

even though you have thus determined a specific [attribute], out of attachment to your own position you consider it to be simply inexpressible; and thus, from "and so, having determined... up to "the consequence," this linguistic practice (*vyavahāra*) which you perform is unintentional and arbitrary, because you speak of a determined object as being inexpressible—just like the linguistic practice of saying "fire is cold" regarding fire that has been determined by its quality of heat.
[This is] because it is not determined as being hot...

Therefore, since the meaning of the "inexpressible universal" has been determined to be precisely the particular (*viśeṣa*), it must be stated that it is indeed the particular, not inexpressible; for it is not distinct from the particular, just like its own self.

Now, if—out of attachment to your own position—you maintain that even though it is not distinct from the particular, the inexpressible universal is nonetheless inexpressible, then in that case, the particular itself would be inexpressible as "the particular," because it is not distinct from the particular, just like the inexpressible universal.
It might be thought: "The inexpressibility of the particular (*viśeṣa*) is indeed established.

But this is not so, because you have already established its inexpressibility by means of a negation, having accepted that the particular is expressible as "one" and so forth; [this is what is meant by] the passage beginning with "not so," etc.

If that very particular is inexpressible, and if the generality—which is the "inexpressible" as a category—is also inexpressible, then the particular cannot be expressed by means of the inexpressible generality, nor can the generality be expressed by means of the particular. Since both of these are inexpressible, they are mutually inexpressible. What follows from this? Consequently, because the double negation (of "inexpressible") results in its natural state [of being expressible], it follows that the generality must be expressible; likewise for the particular. Thus, both would indeed be expressible.

Thus, first of all, it has been stated that because [the substance] is not distinct from its particularities, it is both inexpressible and indeed expressible. Now, [it is considered] as being distinct from the particularities, and so forth.
Now, lest these faults should arise, one might desire that the entity be distinct from the particular due to its specific nature.

To this as well, at the commencement of the objection raised by the previous question, he states the reason for its distinction from the particular: "because it is inexpressible. Since the object, characterized by different attributes, is inexpressible through expressible particulars such as the identity of the universal and the particular, it follows that because of this very inexpressibility, the entity is distinct and separate from the particular which possesses its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). This same logical proof—which was previously applied to the cases of identity and difference between the entity and both [the universal and the particular]—is to be joined here as well to demonstrate its distinction from the particular in this position.
That entity which is intended as the object of cognition is non-existent, because it lacks specific characteristics, like a flower in the sky.
The particular (*viśeṣa*) is also non-existent because it is distinct from the real entity (*vastu*), like a sky-flower.

Thus, the elaborate proliferation of conceptual alternatives—such as the identity or difference between the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular—is merely a fruit of exhaustion, like rubbing one's belly against the sky, because it is not in accordance with reality.

Furthermore, even if one posits that the particular is both distinct and non-distinct from the "inexpressible" (*avaktavya*), nevertheless, since the term "particular" occurs twice, this results in a position where the particular is primary and the inexpressible is subordinate.
Furthermore, its nature must be examined: upon the negation of oneness, is there otherness?

Upon the negation of otherness, since it is distinct from both [oneness and otherness], there are indeed two possible courses: either absolute existence or non-existence; there is no third alternative.

If it were existence, it would simply have to be called "existent"; if it were non-existence, it would likewise have to be called "non-existent. Thus, the removal of the "inexpressible" (avaktavya) results in this fault according to our own logic.

There may also be the reading "absolute existence or non-existence" (*atyantabhāvo 'bhāvo vā*). Furthermore, as you have stated, there would likewise be a lack of substantiality (*avastutā*); by that method, according to the principle of being distinct from the qualified object (*viśeṣya*) as you yourself have asserted, that entity called "inexpressible" (*avaktavya*) would be a non-entity. Why? Because its inexpressibility is unreal (*abhūta*). For inexpressibility was asserted by way of the non-distinction between existence and unity; if it were distinct from those, its inexpressibility would be unreal. And because its inexpressibility is unreal, it is a non-entity, like a sky-flower.

Even in the case of existence (*bhāva*), since it must be stated that "it exists," there is the state of being unutterable as non-existent; therefore, according to your own view, because even in the case of existence it is unutterable as non-existent, it is a non-entity (*avastu*), like *pradhāna* and so forth. Thus it should be. (Note: *syāt* appears twice in the manuscript variants.)
Furthermore, as expressed in the passage beginning with "and just as," etc.:

just as that entity called "inexpressible" is held to be distinct from its particularity (*viśeṣa*), so too the particularity must be distinct from the entity called "inexpressible," because distinction resides in both relata. And this being the case, it follows that both of these—the entity and the particularity—are non-existent.
The object desired by you is non-existent, because it lacks specific distinction and is distinct from specific distinction, like a sky-flower.
Specific distinction is also non-existent, because it is distinct from the object, like a sky-flower.

If this were not so, then the sky-flower would exist, because it is distinct from specific distinction, like the object; or the sky-flower would be existent, because it is distinct from the object, like specific distinction.
It must be stated that the nature of the thing (*vastu-bhāva*) is likewise [inexpressible], and so forth.

Thus, the proliferation of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa-prapañca*)—such as whether that thing is non-existent, or whether generality (*sāmānya*) and particularity (*viśeṣa*) are identical, different, or inexpressible—is like chewing the cud on the air; its fruit is merely exhaustion, because it is not in accordance with reality (*ayathārtha*). Just as the investigation into the fragrance of a sky-flower and so forth is unreal, the unreality of this investigation is established by the method already described.

Thus, even in the case of the position of exclusion (vyatireka-pakṣa), there is an absence of "inexpressibility" (avaktavyatva); furthermore, the reading "itself is inexpressibility" (tad evāvaktavyatvam) is also to be considered; [this refers to] the investigation of this investigation. (pra.)

Now, it might be thought: "Just as [a thing] is inexpressible in terms of its identity with or difference from its generalities and particulars (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*), I accept that the entity is inexpressible in terms of both its difference and non-difference [from its particulars]. Therefore, the labor of investigation is useless; for since this entity is inexpressible even in terms of its difference and non-difference from the particular, that entity in which the particular, its difference, and its non-difference are all inexpressible is 'an entity whose particular, difference, and non-difference are inexpressible'—this is my position."

The passage beginning with "marked by this sign" (etaccihnāṅkitaḥ) and ending with "because of the difference" (vyatirekatvāt), up to "the particularity" (viśeṣa), does not exist in manuscript Ya. There, the reading should perhaps also be "along with the inexpressible" (sahāvaktavyasya). Is there oneness? If both of those are negated, is there non-duality of both? And if non-duality of both is negated, is there duality of both? One must resort to a form that is the opposite of what is being negated; otherwise, if it is not resorted to, what [is there]? If it is resorted to, then because it takes the form of the opposite of what is being negated, one incurs the faults such as non-difference found in the doctrines of the Sāṃkhyas and others.
