Now, if this is not accepted, then in the absence of recourse to the nature of the counter-position, all conceptual constructions would [collapse into] one;

to this it is replied: even so, because the function [of the word] pertains to two distinct specific parts, there remains the position that the specific aspect is primary while the inexpressible is subordinate.

Because the particular (*viśeṣa*)—such as existence, particularity, unity, and so forth—obtains its function through the aspects of the properties of being inexpressible (*avaktavya*), such as being distinct from or non-distinct from existence, particularity, unity, and so on; and because the particular itself is qualified by inexpressibility due to obtaining its function through the aspects of the properties of being distinct, non-distinct, and inexpressible, it would follow that the primary [element] is the particular and the secondary (*upasarjana*) is the inexpressible, just as in the case of Devadatta who is qualified by the two attributes "fair-complexioned" and "tusked. Consequently, this position—in which the particular is primary and the inexpressible is secondary—would arise unexpectedly, and it is undesirable. (Note: *pra* refers to the manuscript reading *°śāvṛtti*).

Furthermore, its nature must also be defined. If you ask how it is to be defined, it is said: "Is it oneness? and so forth. It must necessarily be defined by one of two logical principles (*nyāya*), as follows: if oneness is negated, otherness (*anyatva*) results; if otherness is negated, oneness results; if both are negated, neither-ness (*anubhayatva*) results; and if neither-ness is negated, both-ness (*ubhayatva*) results. Therefore, a form that is the opposite of what is being negated must be resorted to, and that is resorted to by you for that [entity] which has particularity as its primary aspect, with the inexpressible as its subordinate aspect, and which functions through a twofold particular aspect.

Now, we ask: "What is it that is not accepted? [The answer is: "Because one cannot escape these two alternatives. Why is that? You yourself must determine this; for in both cases, there is a fault, as [the object] is not other than the two [means of knowledge].
In the negation of oneness,
[is it] the negation of oneness? Why is it that you yourself [assert] manifoldness?
"Is it by you alone? Is this by you alone?

In that regard, if first of all the nature of being the counter-position to what is being negated is relied upon, then, by way of synonymy, the faults such as non-difference found in the doctrines of the Sāṅkhyas and others would be incurred; for when the difference of specific qualities is negated, the Sāṅkhya doctrine of identity would thereby be accepted.

If the unity of the parts is denied, then the acceptance of "otherness" as favored by the Vaiśeṣikas follows; and by the inclusion of the word "etcetera," the acceptance of theories such as those regarding the Person (Puruṣa) or Time as causes, as well as the acceptance of the theory of the collection of all effects, follows. In that regard, whatever faults were stated by you yourself as a proponent of the "inexpressible" (anirvacanīya), all of them without exception fall upon you, just as it is accepted [by us] that the unity of the parts exists.
It may be that there is multiplicity;
where [that] exists, here there is seen a great transposition of readings among the manuscripts.
The text located on pages 776–779 within these brackets appears after the passage marked by these same brackets on page 781, line 11;
nevertheless, having carefully considered the connection between what precedes and follows, we have extracted it from that place and inserted it here.

Now, if [the opponent] does not resort to the form of the counter-position (*pratipakṣa*) to the object of negation (*pratiṣedhya*)—thinking, "Let these faults not arise"—then, by not resorting to the form of the counter-position, [the consequence follows] from the passage beginning with "of all conceptual constructions" up to "whence has this inexpressibility come? For, if one were to negate a particular conceptual construction while not resorting to the form of the counter-position to the object of negation, and having achieved one's purpose by that much, one were to proceed to negate other conceptual constructions as well; then, by this very sequence, once each one has been negated and all conceptual constructions such as "particularity," "oneness," and so forth have been negated, it would become absolutely non-existent, not a real entity. And if that were so, whence could this inexpressibility come? Indeed, it is through the negation of one conceptual construction while accepting another that the arrival of inexpressibility occurs by way of refuting that [first] extreme. For there can be no inexpressibility for things like a sky-flower, which transcend all conceptual constructions.
In the case of *rūpāśrayaṇa*,
[the reading] *pratipakṣarūpa* is found in Bhā and Ya.
If there were no conceptual construction (*vikalpa*),
would that object not be a non-entity? Or would that object be an entity?

If, upon the cessation of [the categories] beginning with "you" (*tvam*), the entity were absolutely non-existent, from where would its "inexpressibility" (*avaktavyatā*) have come? Since you have taken refuge in Syādvāda—the Supreme Lord of doctrines—by accepting it without definitive restriction, there is nevertheless a contradiction with your own tenet.

If you argue that because of the fault in accepting an absolute [position], and because of the contradiction with your tenet in accepting Syādvāda, that entity is indeed non-existent, this too is unsatisfactory; for the negation of a specific door [of predication] is untenable. Therefore, even that [argument] is incorrect, because [the entity] is inexpressible due to its specific nature as being neither identical nor different and so forth.
Now, if it is merely a matter of communication, then surely, since both characteristics are applicable, it is indeed "inexpressible" (*avaktavya*).

If that is so, then surely even "communication" itself is inexpressible, because of its absolute non-existence, like a sky-flower; for a specific statement is inexpressible as being a particular, a non-particular, unity, and so forth, and because the communicated object and the communicator are also inexpressible as being identical, different, both, or neither.

It might be thought: "That entity is accepted as being of every aspect—even though it is one, even though it is other, even though it is inexpressible, and so forth—provided its specific qualities such as oneness and the rest are not determined. If this is so, then what follows? Because of accepting [the entity] through non-determination, and because of accepting all conceptual alternatives such as oneness and the rest by way of assent without any fixed determination, one must admit that the substance is a single entity possessing infinite modes (*paryāya*). Thus: it may be one, it may be many, it may be both, it may be neither, and it may be inexpressible.

Even so, you have taken refuge in Syādvāda, the Supreme Lord of all doctrines; thus, nothing further remains to be said. Nevertheless, your taking refuge in the Supreme Lord of doctrines obstructs the desire for victory in debate on the part of an intelligent person because it contradicts your own formal admission, as it was previously stated that [the position] is "contradictory even with that" and so forth, beginning with "if it were absolute" (*athaikānta*).

Now, if it is thought: "If one accepts an absolute position that is the opposite of what is to be negated, those very faults mentioned by me arise; if one accepts the doctrine of manifoldness (syādvāda), there is a contradiction with one's own [prior] acceptance. Therefore, in order to distance oneself from the faults inherent in absolute doctrines, if you were to say that this object is simply non-existent—without accepting the existence of the opposite of the negated in turn [i.e., without the relativism of syādvāda]"—then this is what you would be saying.

This too is unseemly, because the negation of specific doors [of predication] would be untenable; for that reason, even [the claim] "it is improper in this case as well" and so forth is incorrect. If that entity were absolutely non-existent, then—like a sky-flower—because of its absolute non-existence, it would be improper to say that the identity or difference between the entity and its specific qualities is "inexpressible. This is because, in the absence of specific attributes (*viśeṣadharma*), there can be no status as a qualificand (*viśeṣyatva*), just like a sky-flower.
Thus, it is improper to maintain the inexpressibility of the entity and its specific qualities through identity or difference taken individually, given their non-existence.

It is also untenable as being both, because the characteristic of being both exists by virtue of having a real locus, since identity and difference are existent; and since you yourself have already established the intention that, by way of those two, even the absolute non-existence of being neither is proven to be "inexpressible," this [objection] should have been stated immediately [at that point]. If it were said now—[this is the beginning of the Pratyākhyāna section].
Because of its being distinguished... [fragmentary text] ...of the one who has attained [the goal].
Or it might be argued: "This is merely an exposition, a means for the sake of instructing the ignorant;
by abiding on a path that is not the ultimate reality, one subsequently attains the truth."
Vākyapadīya 2.240: Now, it might be argued that there is no fault because this entire [work] is a statement intended to convey a meaning that is inexpressible.

But if it is inexpressible, how can there be a conveying of it? And if there is a conveying of it, how can it be inexpressible? If it is further argued that even the term "inexpressible" is itself inexpressible—because it is a real entity (vastu), just like its referent—then...
Is that [inexpressibility] somehow inexpressible, or in every respect? If it were inexpressible in every respect, there would be contradictions with perception and other means of knowledge;

therefore, [the categories of] difference, identity, and so forth—which are actually non-existent—are postulated for the sake of demonstration. This method of demonstration is like pointing out directions when giving instructions on the path to a village, or like the arrangement of dots and patterns in a painting.

In this regard, [one might object that] there is indeed the occurrence of the characteristic of both [identity and difference]. For, in the absence of the negandum and its counter-positive, the existence of identity and difference would entail the characteristic of both, established by the logical necessity (arthāpatti) of their mutual negation; and this is undesirable.
Therefore, in that case, regarding the inexpressible entity, those two—identity and difference—are simply inexpressible in their own nature.
Thus, [the teaching of] means is for the purpose of instructing and leading the immature.
The skillful means (*upāya*) for those in training are the consoling devices for the foolish;
standing upon the path of unreality, one thereby strives for reality.
Therefore, the skillful means—the scriptures—for those who desire to know but lack understanding, should be understood as nothing other than consolations intended to carry them across.

Because, as stated in the *Vākyapadīya-ṭīkā* composed by Puṇyarāja: "Since, by remaining there upon an object that is unreal in form and consists merely of the grammatical system (*śāstra-prakriyā*), one casts off ignorance (*avidyā*) and strives for—that is to say, attains—the true Brahman which is the very nature of knowledge (*vidyā-svarūpa*).
[This is] for the purpose of [removing] the misconception (*ālāpanāya*).

"Abiding on the path of non-reality, one subsequently attains reality. (Vākyapadīya 2.240) Now it might be argued: "There is no fault here because this entire statement serves to communicate an inexpressible object.
But if it is inexpressible, how can there be communication? And if there is communication, how can it be inexpressible?
Now, it might be argued: "This [statement] 'it is not to be spoken' is itself indeed not to be spoken, because it is a real entity (*vastu*), like that object.
Is that [object] inexpressible in some way or in every way? If it were inexpressible in every way, there would be contradictions with perception and other means of knowledge.
(Padeśibhā)

Regarding the [objection] concerning the characteristic of the three nights and the reality [of the teaching], we say here: if that is so, then surely even "the demonstration" is something that cannot be spoken of; for that demonstration of oneness and so forth—which is unreal, imagined, and intended as a means—that demonstration is "unspeakable" because of its absolute non-existence, like a sky-flower.

And you speak of "establishment" (*pratipādana*); for in the world, establishment is observed to be a specific statement, such as "he who is fair-skinned is Devadatta. By contrast with that, since it [the universal] is non-existent, establishment as a specific statement is not tenable. (The reading *mataṃ pratipā°* is found in the Bhāṣya.)

Furthermore, because a specific statement cannot be expressed as being specific, non-specific, identical, different, both, neither, or inexpressible—given such alternatives as "is the statement itself specific, non-specific, one, other, both, neither, or inexpressible?"—it is therefore inexpressible. Consequently, since even a specific statement is not something that can be spoken, the act of "explaining" is itself inexpressible. Moreover, regarding the word that is explained and the speaker who explains, their identity, difference, bothness, neitherness, and so forth are also inexpressible; for this reason as well, "explaining" is inexpressible.
And since it is inexpressible, its existence must necessarily be asserted, just as that which is to be spoken [is asserted]. To this, it might be replied:

"There is no distinction between the expresser and the expressed regarding that which is inexpressible; nor do any qualifiers differ from the general object to be expressed. Rather, there is no fault because this entire collection of sentences—consisting of both qualifiers and the qualified—is a single unit that, in the manner described, expresses the meaning of the inexpressible."
Now, it is said [in the verse beginning with] "athocyate" and so forth;
by someone [it is stated that] it is a qualifier of everything.

To this we reply: Surely, the objection beginning with "if it is inexpressible" and so forth, which results in a contradiction by returning to what has already been addressed, is redundant. Now, if you were to say: "Even this [statement] 'it is inexpressible' is itself inexpressible; oh, how I am a proponent of the inexpressible! For I accept whatever is inexpressible. However, even this entire verbal discourse involving all modes of operation—which is devoid of the distinction between the object to be communicated and the communicator—is not actually uttered at all, because it possesses substantial reality (vastutva), just like its referent. [This is our response.]

Now, let this be considered for the sake of your ultimate certainty: regarding that which is called "perception," when it is being spoken of or heard, if it is said to be ineffable, there are two possible courses. One must inquire: "Is it ineffable in some way, or in every way? Having thus raised the objection, the refutation follows: [If it were] "in every way," such a non-entity would be entirely formless, or else it would contradict everything by this very fact, like a sky-flower; whereas the other case [if it were not ineffable] would be like the form and so forth of perception. Therefore, an entity is neither ineffable, nor is it expressible without deliberation, because that would entail the fallacy of extremist views (ekāntavāda), and because the aforementioned defects apply therein.
There is no distinction, because it is a composite whole, like a chariot and so forth;
nor is it an entity, since that has been refuted by you yourself.

Whence, then, this "inexpressibility" of oneness and so forth? [The phrase] "whether in one way" and so forth means: whether in some manner or in every way. If it is by some particular mode, or if it is in every way—this is the meaning.

In this regard, if [the subject] is in some way inexpressible—just as you yourself have repeatedly stated through any one of the alternatives such as identity or difference between the universal and the particular—then because you have established its inexpressibility, there is a contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣa-virodha*) since it is being heard directly as expressible in various ways: as identical, different, both, neither, or by way of the subordinate and the primary; there is a contradiction with one's own words (*svavacana-virodha*) because of what you yourself have said;
and there is a contradiction with one's own commitment (*abhyupagama-virodha*) because of what you yourself have accepted.
There is contradiction with inference because of such inferences as those characterized by the distinction of different established definitions, and so forth, in the manner already stated.
There is contradiction with the world and with scripture because the distinction between the signified and the signifier is well-known in both the world and the treatises.
Thus, insofar as [the object] is inexpressible in some respect, there are contradictions with one's own words and so forth.

If [the self] were in every respect inexpressible, then the same contradictions with perception and other means of valid cognition would indeed persist; for by stating that "it is in every respect inexpressible," one opens the door to the occurrence of all remaining faults. Let it be so! Let it be so! (riṃtyatāṃ bhā॰ riṃtyāṃtāṃ ya॰)

This non-entity, such as "this sound is being heard" or "thus," is in every respect devoid of form, and because it is contradictory to all this [perceptual experience], it is like a sky-flower; whereas the other [entity] is like perceptible form and so forth.

Therefore, it is neither an inexpressible entity nor is it expressible without investigation, because that would entail the fallacy of extremist views (ekāntavāda) and because the aforementioned defects would apply there;
furthermore, there is no distinct individuality, because it is a composite whole, like a chariot and so forth.
It is not an existent entity, because it has been refuted by you yourself; how then can there be the inexpressibility of oneness and so forth?
[This is] because of the status of being either one or the other.
See the world's own words, etc., page 776, note 7.

The word "iti" in the phrase "ity evaṃvidham avastu" (thus, such a thing is non-existent) serves to conclude the reason; for this reason, that which you have conceptualized as a "thing" called "inexpressible" is, in fact, no thing at all.

Why? Because it is formless in every respect (*sarvathāpy-arūpatvāt*). "In every respect" means in all possible ways: whether it is expressible or inexpressible through conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) such as the identity or difference between the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṇa*); or whether it is expressible or inexpressible through conceptual constructions such as non-distinction or distinction; or whether it is expressible or inexpressible through conceptual constructions such as the relationship between the signified and the signifier (*pratipādya-pratipādaka*) regarding the terms "universal" and "particular"—according to the aforementioned method, when examined in every way, no form (*rūpa*) remains established. Therefore, because it is formless in every respect, it is a non-entity (*avastu*), like a sky-flower (*khapuṣpa*).
[The reading *apakvat-khapuṣpa* is found in manuscript Bhā.]

Furthermore, because it contradicts all this, it follows that it is a non-entity (*avastu*). By the very method already stated, it is indeed contradicted by all these means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such as one's own words; therefore, for this reason too, it is a non-entity just like a sky-flower—this is the example based on similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).

The meaning is that "the other [is like] perception, form, and so forth" is an example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*). Whatever possesses form is not contradicted by anything at all, just as perception—which is self-cognized—is [accepted] by every proponent [of philosophical systems], such as cognition, pleasure, and so forth, being like form and the rest. This is said with respect to everyone except for the proponents of Consciousness-Only (*vijñānavādin*) and the proponents of Emptiness (*śūnyavādin*). Therefore, the conclusion is that the entity is not "inexpressible" (*avaktavya*). Thus, the conclusion is that it is not inexpressible. *Note: The text provided contains several scribal errors (e.g., *tasmāṃtāvaktavyaṃ pra॰ ॰hārastāpiya॰*), which have been corrected for the sake of clarity in the translation.*

Nor can it be said that [the object] is "inexpressible" when devoid of discursive thought (*nirvicāra*), because that would entail the fallacy of an extremist position (*ekāntavāda*) and because the aforementioned defects apply there as well. By negating the previously apprehended conceptualizations—that it is not a substance, not a cause, and not a universal—it is shown that their unity is not established, just as you yourself, as a proponent of inexpressibility, have refuted it (see page 760, line 5;
page 753, line 1). [The text reads: *pratiṣedho nānaikatvam* (negation, not non-unity).
The reading here might also be "by the negation [of oneness], there is multiplicity" (*pratiṣedhena anekatvam*) or "in the negation [of oneness], there is not non-oneness" (*pratiṣedhe nānaikatvam*).
It might be thought: "In that case, let the particular things such as a jar be real entities;

but even those are not real entities, just like a chariot and so forth. What then is a real entity? Only the constituent parts, such as color-form (*rūpa*) and the rest, are real entities; for it is they alone that exist. That which is produced by them is the "being" (*bhāva*).
It cannot be called a "universal" (sāmānya), because it lacks form and other qualities, like a sky-flower.
For what indeed is the absence (vinābhāva) of earth and the rest? What is earth without stone and so forth? ... [and so on].
...are atoms distinct from form and the other [sensory objects]? These are merely words;
there is no such thing as a "self" (ātman) other than these, because it lacks form and the rest, like a flower in the sky.

Just as the designation "chariot" applies to a collection of parts such as wheels, axles, and so forth, and the designation "army" applies to a collection of parts such as elephants and so forth; and just as this aggregate, when analyzed, resides in its parts, or further still, resides only in [the elements] such as form (*rūpa*) and so on—since form and the rest are particulars because they are aggregates, like chariots and the like, there is no entity called a "universal" that serves as the opposite of the particular—even if such a universal were implied by the very necessity of negating those particulars, it has already been refuted by you yourself.

Whence does this indeterminacy of oneness and so forth arise? Since the existence (*bhāva*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*) themselves are not established, how much less can there be an indeterminacy to be understood through the properties of oneness, otherness, and so forth residing within them?

What, then, is that entity (*vastu*)? It is simply the constituents such as form (*rūpa*) and the rest; for it is they alone who exist, and that which is constituted by them is the existence (*bhāva*).
It is not something called a "universal" (*sāmānya*), because it lacks form and other such qualities, like a sky-flower;
for what indeed is the absence (*vinābhāva*) of earth and the rest? What is earth without stone and so forth?... [and so on].
...Are atoms distinct from form and the other [sensory qualities]? These are merely words;
there is no such thing as a "self" (ātman) that is anything other than these, because it lacks form and the rest, like a flower in the sky.

Just as the designation "chariot" applies to a collection of parts such as wheels, axles, and so forth, and the designation "army" applies to a collection of parts such as elephants and so forth; when that aggregate is analyzed, it subsists in its parts, or further still, it subsists only in form and the other [sensory bases]. Form and the others [are likewise empty], as are their opposites and even the analysis of those opposites.

If it is asked, "What then is the real entity (vastu)? it is said: It is precisely the constituent members (samudāyin)—form and so forth—which, although the aggregate (samudāya) does not exist in the ultimate sense, do exist as conventional realities;
for it is these alone that exist, and one must conclude that there is no such thing as an "aggregate" apart from them.

That which is produced by them is *bhāva* (an entity). The word *bhāva* is derived from the root *bhū* in the sense of "becoming" (*bhavana*), "coming into existence" (*bhūti*). For those [factors] are, through the conventional usage of words and meanings, the agents of that action of becoming. That aggregate, cause, substance, and so forth, which is postulated by others, is not *bhāva*. There exists no such thing as a "universal" (*sāmānya*) called *bhāva*.

Why? Because it lacks color-form (*rūpa*) and other qualities. All color-forms and the rest are stated to be the causes; the meaning is that [the universal] does not consist of any one of those [qualities], such as color-form.
Of what sort is it? Like a sky-flower.

Having thus demonstrated the non-existence of the universal (sāmānya) through the means of proof (*sādhana*), he shows it in reality: "For what [entity] exists apart from earth and so forth? and so on.
What is that entity distinct from the collection consisting merely of earth, water, fire, air, ether, self, time, direction, and the rest? The meaning is that there is nothing apart from those.
In this way, the statement "what is earth without stone and so forth," and so on, up to "what are atoms without color-form and so forth," has already been explained.

These are merely designations (*abhivacana-mātra*); they are words used in the sense of being directed toward something, meaning for the purpose of apprehending color-form and the rest. "Color-form and the rest" (*rūpādayaḥ*) refers either to color-form, taste, odor, touch, and sound, or to color-form, sensation, consciousness, and mental formations. Whatever else exists apart from those, such as earth and so forth, is merely a designation for them. Therefore, he says: "And the self (*ātman*) is not some other thing at all, because it lacks color-form and the rest, like a flower in the sky."
The state of that [is] the non-existence without earth, water, and so forth; [it is] without earth, water, and so forth.
To demonstrate that [the person] is merely a collection of form and so forth, he provides an illustration: "Just as in the case of the wheel, the axle," and so on;
that is, the designation "chariot" applies to a collection of parts such as wheels, and the designation "army" applies to a collection of parts such as elephants.

Just as a composite whole, when analyzed, resides in its parts; and those parts, when further analyzed, reside in their own constituent portions—progressively further and further until, having been divided down to the level of atoms, it resides only in [the elements of] form and so forth—even when one carefully observes each individual part, dividing it down to the limit of an atom, the chariot is not seen. Likewise, an army, a forest, a person, or any other object is not seen apart from its parts; rather, it is that collection which appears. Thus, it is only form and the other [elements], when combined, that manifest in such a way—as in the case of the wheel, the spokes, and the axle.
In the case of *cakeṣātkeṣākṣe*, whether it be *bhā* or *vāthaubhā*, there is attainment (*āpti*) in *ya*.
Just as earth, space, and so forth appear when combined,

if that Self were likewise present within its constituent parts, then— being by nature an object of perception— it would be perceived like color and other qualities, provided there were no absence of the causes for its apprehension, because it is a real entity.
If the aggregate were distinct from form and the other [sensory objects], it would be like a sky-flower, because it lacks form—just as [the aggregate] is distinct from form and the others.

Alternatively, if there is no difference [between the aggregate and its parts], how is it that functions such as carrying a burden, which are impossible for form and the others individually, are observed in things like a chariot? That [function] is observed in those very forms and so forth;
indeed, this is established without dispute between us both—even without an assistant distinct from the bearers of the palanquin.

If that [chariot] were "in its parts," etc., it would possess a self—that is, it would be *sātmaka* (endowed with a self)—if the chariot or something else were distinct from the self consisting of form (*rūpa*) and so forth. In that case, being of the nature of an object of perception, it would be perceived—just like form and the rest—provided there is an absence of causes for non-perception, such as extreme distance, excessive proximity, or overpowering; for it is a real entity (*vastu*). Yet, it is not so perceived. Therefore, the composite whole, such as the chariot, does not exist.
But it is not perceived?
[It is] like the beginning of non-existence, etc. (pra°).

If, however, it were something other [than its parts], an undesirable consequence would follow: if a collection (*samudāya*) exists as distinct from form and the rest, then, being of a nature other than those [parts] and being unperceived, it would be like a sky-flower—because it lacks form and because its essence is not form and so forth, just like form and the rest themselves. For when a collection that is not of the nature of those [parts] arises, form and the rest do not function as its causes, just as they do not for a sky-flower. In this regard, what is the specific reason why form and the rest are the causes of a collection such as a jar, but not of a collection such as a sky-flower; or why form and the rest alone are the causes of a collection such as a jar, and not of a sky-flower?

[Is it] in the collection? Or, if there is no difference in meaning [between the collection and its parts], and so forth, up to: "How could this be? It might be thought: if the collection of a chariot and so forth were not different in meaning from form and the other [sensory qualities], then the function of carrying a load and so forth—which is not observed in form and the others—is seen in the world as occurring in the chariot and such; how could that be? Because effects are to be accomplished by specific causes, just like the case of threads and cloth.

Here is the formal argument (*prayoga*): Form and the other [sensory objects] are connected with auxiliary causes distinct from themselves, because their effects are seen to be impossible [without them], just like the eye and so forth. For example, just as the eye-organ—which is distinct from the black pupil (*kṛṣṇasāra*) and other parts—is inferred to be the cause of perception when it is conjoined with its auxiliary, the eye, upon seeing an effect such as the cognition of form which is impossible for the eye alone; likewise, because an effect such as carrying a load is seen to be impossible for form and the rest [alone], the fact that they are distinct from the collection [of parts] such as the chariot is to be inferred. [The phrase] "it occurs in the chariot, etc. [is part of the original].

To this it is replied: Where, then, has that been observed? That effect, such as carrying a burden and so forth, is observed in those very things—form and the rest; therefore, the qualification "impossible for itself" is unestablished (*asiddha*).

Even granting its establishment, the observation of an effect is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). He demonstrates this with the words "Now, without dispute," etc.: even without an assistant distinct from the four bearers of the palanquin, the act of carrying the palanquin is observed by us both without dispute; therefore, that [reason] is inconclusive.

[The commentary] says: "The assistance... and so forth, up to "...like a fire-brand wheel. This states the logical principle (*nyāya*) for the purpose of negating the [existence of a] composite whole (*samudāya*), in order to demonstrate that actions such as carrying a load are possible only in the constituents (*samudāyin*) and impossible in the composite whole.

In that manner, color-form (*rūpa*) and the other [sensory qualities] abide within their own respective functions without ever overstepping the individual occurrence of each entity. It is precisely by virtue of this established non-abandonment of their own functions that they initiate actions such as carrying a burden, for it is these alone that constitute the "entity" (*vastu*). Otherwise, if the nature of the entity were otherwise, one would observe the effect of carrying a palanquin (*śibikā*) being performed by color-form and the rest alone, situated in distinct locations without any intervening space.

In this way, form and the other [sensory objects] abide in their own respective modes of existence without overstepping the mode of existence of each individual thing, precisely because those [individuals] alone possess the nature of real entities (*vastu*). Otherwise, since the object designated as a "collection" would be a mere conceptual construction, it would lack a single, stable intrinsic nature, like a fire-brand wheel (*alātacakra*).

[Objection: But surely, even in the case of a jar and so forth, there exists a state of being (*sattva*) despite its having a single, stable form. [Reply: No, because it is a collection and is therefore something to be proven (*sādhyatva*).

[Objection: If it is argued that there is a state of being even when there is a single, stable form residing in the forms and so forth, [Reply: No, because that too is to be proven as a collection of the general property of form (*rūpasāmānya*).
Each individual manifestation of form and so forth exists as nothing but difference;
it is only this [difference] that is the true reality,
while the expression "collection" is merely a conventional designation for it.
A chariot, being contrary to reality through verbal conceptualization, exists as a conventional truth (saṃvṛti) as a mere referent of words, like the continuous succession of saṃsāra;
but in the ultimate sense (paramārtha), because it does not exist either after or before [its parts], the chariot does not exist in its constituent parts.

Because they are real entities, the object designated as a "collection" (samudāya) is otherwise merely a conceptual construction (parikalpanāmātra), lacking a single, stable intrinsic nature (*svatattva*), like a firebrand-circle (*alātacakra*). Just as the appearance of a firebrand as a circle when it is whirled is a mere delusive construction due to its lack of gaps, so too the appearance of form and other [sensory objects] as being gapless—like atoms and the like—is a mere delusive construction. How much more so, then, for collections of parts such as pots, cloths, cities, and the earth, which possess gaps, greater gaps, and greatest gaps? For these collections do not possess a single, stable intrinsic nature that is distinct from one another in the way that form and the other [sensory objects] are. Therefore, like a firebrand-circle, they are non-existent, because they are merely designated by the ultimate reality of form and the rest.
Therefore, what kind of action, such as carrying a load, can there be for a non-existent collection? Thus,
Praśastamati states the following regarding the action of carrying a load.
The carrying of a palanquin, which is observed to be the effect of the entities such as form (rūpa) and so forth,

occurs in such a way that form and the others remain established in their own respective functions without overstepping the function of each individual entity, because they alone possess the nature of being real entities; otherwise, since the object designated as a "collection" would be a mere conceptual construction, it would lack a single, stable intrinsic nature, like a fire-brand wheel (alātacakra).

[Objection: But surely, even though a jar and the like possess a single, stable form, they do exist [as real entities]. [Response: No, because they are merely aggregates and thus constitute the very probandum [of your argument].

[Objection: Even though color, taste, and so forth possess a single, stable form, they do exist [as real entities]. [Response: No, because they are established as aggregates of the universal "color" and so on;
for the individual manifestation of color and the rest, while residing in each [particular], is itself of a differentiated nature, not a single, stable form.
This reality is true only as these [atoms] alone;

however, its designation as a "collection" is a mere verbal expression. A "chariot," for instance, is contrary to the actual thing due to verbal conceptualization; it exists only as a conventional truth (saṃvṛti), being nothing more than the referent of a word, like the continuous flow of saṃsāra.

But from the perspective of ultimate truth, because it does not exist either subsequently or previously, there is no chariot in its parts by virtue of its own independence; for [the chariot] lacks the state of being a single independent entity.

One [opponent], Svatantra, says: "But [in the case] of a jar and so forth"—that is to say, up to the point where it is argued that "the existence of its own-ness" constitutes an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*). To this it is replied: No, because it is a composite whole (*samudāyatva*). There is no inconclusiveness in this reason (*hetu*), because the jar, being a composite whole like a cart and so forth, is itself the probandum (*sādhya*); thus, the existence of the jar is merely a semblance of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikābhāsa*). This is the meaning.

If it is argued that "existence" (*sattva*) consists in having a single form established across various forms such as color and so forth, and if it is further argued that this is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because we observe a commonality of form (*rūpasāmānya*) among white, blue, and other colors which is neither fixed nor of a single form, we reply: no. This is because [the reason] is to be proven by the collection (*samudāya*) of the commonalities of form; for a "commonality-form" distinct from the specific forms such as white—which is what is called a "collection"—is not established as existing, and thus, being a non-entity, it does not exist in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*). Therefore, there is no inconclusiveness regarding whether existence is non-fixed or whether it is a fixed single form.

Now he defines the true nature of reality: Each individual manifestation of form and so forth is exclusively of the nature of difference (*bheda*) and not a universal (*sāmānya*). That [manifestation] is of a fixed, single form, and its nature is mutually distinct; this alone is the truly real entity. However, terms such as "pot," "cloth," or "chariot" are merely verbal designations for that entity—collective expressions used for the purpose of directed cognition. When such a thing is called a "chariot" and so on, that chariot is conceptually constructed by words, contrary to the actual reality, and is merely conventional (*saṃvṛti*), being nothing more than the word's referent because the word’s object consists solely of conceptual construction.

What is it like? It is like the continuity of saṃsāra; just as the cause for the continuity of saṃsāra might be stated as "my mother," "my father," "my brother," "my wife," or "my son"—which would be a real effect—so too [is it] by means of form and so forth.
That which is called "existence" (sattva) must be something entirely different from its effect, because they possess unequal conceptual natures, like form and a sky-flower.

In this case, there would be only two possible alternatives regarding both the causes, such as sound and so forth, and the effects, such as space and so forth: either both possess existence, or only the existence of the effect-space possesses existence. This is because the other two alternatives are contradicted by what has already been accepted, and thus no further debate can occur.

Thus, if first of all— starting with "u" and so forth— the conventional usage [of a collection] occurs toward even those things that do not provide assistance due to a notion of assistance arising from the force of the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of affection, then likewise the collection is produced spontaneously through the latent impression of unreal conventional usage; herein there is no ultimate reality (*paramārtha*),
and that is the nature of the property (*dharmatā*) which is the cause of bondage.
Just as it might be said that the effect exists [prior to its production], for example, by means of form and so forth...
[omission]...
That which is called "existence" (sattā) is indeed different from its effect, because they possess unequal conceptual possibilities (*vikalpa*), like form (*rūpa*) and a sky-flower (*khapuṣpa*).

In this case, there would be two possible alternatives regarding both the causes, such as sound (*śabda*), and the effects, such as space (*ākāśa*): either both possess existence, or only the existence of the effect-space possesses existence. Since the other two positions are contradicted by what has already been accepted, there can be no debate [regarding them]. Therefore, if first—

What, then, is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*)? From the perspective of ultimate reality, because it does not exist either after or before [its parts], the chariot has no self (*ātman*) in its constituent parts prior to the conjunction of the wheels, axle, and so forth; nor does it exist afterward when the wheels and other parts have been disjoined. Likewise, even in the state of conjunction, the chariot does not exist within the parts because they lack their own self-nature. Thus, as it was said previously regarding existence, and so on.

By this very logic, it is stated that the claim—that some effects such as jars or cloths are produced by a person with prior intelligence, while other effects arise spontaneously from their own causes—is false. To demonstrate how that effect actually arises from its cause, according to the view held by others and how that is logically consistent, he says: "The effect pre-exists [in the cause] (satkārya) as they describe it—namely, by means of form and so forth. Here, the subtle elements (tanmātras) of sound and the rest are included under the mention of "form and so forth," because they are distinct only through verbal convention due to the requirements of the system's methodology.

This process regarding the fact that the elements, such as space and the rest, are effects—due to their being arranged with a successive increase of one quality each, such as sound and so forth—is not explained here again, as it has already been explained in another section [of this work].
There may also be a reading here as "sata eva" (from the existent alone); see for comparison page 168, line 8.
...would arise;
thereafter again, ...

The proof: That which is called "existent" (sat) must have an effect that is indeed other than it, having a nature distinct from the existent; that is to say, it does not possess the nature of the existent. Why? Because its conceptualization (vikalpa) is not identical to that [of the existent]. Whatever has a conceptualization not identical to another is indeed other than it, having a different nature, and does not possess that as its essence. Like what? Like form and so forth versus a sky-flower. Just as forms and the like are existent while a sky-flower is non-existent, and thus the latter does not have a conceptualization identical to the former, so too the effect—such as space—is not of a conceptualization identical to the causes, such as existent forms and the like. Therefore, like a sky-flower, the effect has a nature other than that of the existent.
See page 430,
line 1; the passage contained within this is not present in the Ya manuscript, and therefore it is equal to [the reading of] Ya.

Desiring to begin the explanation of this proof in order to dispel the doubt that its property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) is unestablished, he himself asks, employing the words of another for the sake of exposition: "How is there no alternative possibility? He then sets forth those two alternatives among the four possible permutations (*bhaṅga*), which are applicable here: "In this case, of sound and so forth," etc.;
[that is,] sounds and the like are causes, while ether and the like are effects; the existence of both of these is one alternative.

The second [position]: Effects such as space and so forth simply exist; therefore, there is neither the alternative of the cause being real while the effect is unreal, nor the alternative of both being unreal.

Why? Because these two contradict the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) which has been accepted [by us], and since they fall within our own position, these two alone are applicable, as there is no other [contradictory] doctrine.
Desirous of attaining [it], whatever conceptual constructions might arise...
If one accepts [the existence of] non-existence (*asatkārya*) for both [cause and effect],

then because there is no distinction in their beingness (*sattva*), and since there is no distinction between causes such as sound and so forth and effects such as space and so forth, just as sounds and the rest arise possessing their own essential nature (*svarūpatattva*), so too would space and the rest arise possessing that same essential nature, because there is no distinction in their beingness, just like form (*rūpa*) and the other [sensory objects].
Therefore, because it is not a non-concordant conceptualization, the effect has a nature other than that of the existent;

yet, just as there is no manifestation of earth and so forth [apart from] the manifestation of form and so forth, it is certain that the effect is indeed existent. Consequently, only the effect is existent, whereas form and so forth are non-existent, because they possess characteristics distinct from the existent, like a sky-flower, since they have never existed as the reality of their own essential nature apart from the existent effect.

In that regard: if, first of all, the first alternative—that both [cause and effect] exist—is accepted, then because existence is not distinct, there would be no distinction between causes such as sound and their effects such as space. And since there is no distinction, just as the very principles of their own nature—the principles of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell—arise or are manifested as sound and so forth, so too space and the others should arise with those very same natures, and not with a nature either less or more;

why? Because existence is not distinct. Let it not be that, like form and the other [sensory objects], there is an arising of successive principles one after the other, such as sound, touch, and so on; yet that [successive arising] is indeed accepted.

Therefore, its dissimilarity to conceptual construction is established; consequently, the meaning is that an effect which has a nature other than that [of the cause], such as space and so forth, is non-existent—its own essential form being absent.
(Variant readings: *svāsvarūpa-bhāva*, *raṃtonādhika*)
And those [properties] are desired to be produced here and there.

Now, for fear of this same logical consequence, if it is maintained that the manifestation of earth and so forth is not subject to the inequality of increase or decrease in the nature of one or more forms, etc., but rather is like the manifestation of a distinct intrinsic nature free from such variations—because of this difference in character, the conceptualization of them as unequal is not tenable—then it is certain that the effect must be existent. Therefore, let the effect itself be what exists, and not form and so forth; for because of the difference in their manifestation as having or lacking their own and other natures, form and so forth would be non-existent, since they are distinct from existence, just like a sky-flower, due to being distinct from existence.

He demonstrates that the reason is characterized by being different from existence: "Because form and the rest, being existent, are real in their own essential nature, they are different from an effect which manifests the essential nature of another; therefore, the effect is perceived," [as stated in] the *Pratyabhijñāhṛdaya*, [referring to the fact that] it possesses its own and other natures.
[Regarding the phrase] "pararūpā... bhā... and so forth:

even if there is a distinction in the manifestation of the intrinsic nature (*svatattva*) of form and other [sensory objects], if it is maintained that form and the rest are existent and consist of the manifestation of their own intrinsic nature, then—due to that distinction from them—the effect would follow as being non-existent, because it consists of the manifestation of what is not its own intrinsic nature; for the production of the nature of another form and so forth, which is one degree higher, is the manifestation of what is not its own intrinsic nature.

And of what, then, is this distinction from existence? To this he says: "like a circle of fire. Just as a firebrand, when whirled around, produces the appearance of a wheel by abandoning its own true nature as a mere spark, yet that [wheel] is non-existent; so too is the effect.

Now, if it is maintained that the effect must indeed exist [prior to its production] so that no fault may arise, then, since it exists, the effect would manifest by itself alone. Just as form manifests without assuming the nature of taste, and likewise taste manifests without the nature of form, and similarly touch, sound, and smell manifest without the nature of one another, yet each appears in its own specific form; so too the effects such as space (ākāśa) and the rest would have to appear in their own essential form. However, it is held that they appear through the predominance of one or another [quality] via the other forms; therefore, because of their existence, you have arrived at an undesirable consequence: that they must manifest identically, just like color-form and the other [sensory objects].
Thus, because of this difference in the manner of manifestation, the effect is established as having a distinct conceptualization from its causes, such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth.

For one who does not accept this [distinction], there follows a circular argument (*cakraka*) culminating in the undesirable consequence that there would be no difference in the manifestation of the effect. Within that very context of the reductio, the argument "because of existence, like form and so forth" is raised; and then, precisely "because of existence, like form and so forth," this [point] follows.
The nature of non-existence; the nature of non-existence;
wandering; primordial.
In the manifestation of the task,
there is the completion of the tasks to be performed.
The analysis of the "wheel" (*cakraka*) should be consulted in another manner on page 170 et seq.,
because of its distinct nature.

Now, even if it is accepted that form and so forth are existent and consist in the manifestation of their own essence, then by virtue of being distinct from that [existence], the effect is non-existent, because it consists in the manifestation of what is not its own essence, like a fire-brand wheel (*alātacakra*).
Now, if it is maintained that the effect already exists [in the cause], then, because of its existence, it would manifest by itself; because of its existence, like form and so forth—
because of its existence, like form and so forth.
...because of the non-existence [of the effect] in the cause, as in the case of form and so forth;
because the effects such as earth do not exist [in the cause], due to their being dissimilar to what exists and because they do not arise from its own nature...
...like [the elements] earth and so forth;
therefore, because it is a distinct conceptualization, the effect must have a nature other than that of the existent.
However, because they do not manifest [in this way], earth and the other elements are not perceptible individuals, since they are not objects for specific senses such as the eye, like a sky-flower.

Whatever is directly perceived, such as form and so forth, exists as that very thing because it manifests by its own nature and because there is no contradiction in its being perceptible like other things;
thus, having abandoned the existence of both [cause and effect] and accepted the existence of only one, the effect alone is real, thereby avoiding the admission of the non-existence of the effect.

In this context, the particle *eva* (only) is used in proximity to "effect" (*kārya*). Thus, there is a restriction regarding the meaning of the word "existent" (*sat*) and its opposite: existence (*sattva*) is restricted to the effect alone. Now, for one who—out of fear that the effect might be non-existent—desires the manifestation of form and so forth to be equivalent to the manifestation of earth and so forth, he must likewise raise the issue of the non-existence of the effect such as earth, because it is distinct from the existent (*sad-vailakṣaṇya*) and because its production would not be from its own nature (*asvarūpotpatti*). This results in a circular argument (*cakraka*) ending in that very point. By reversing that [logic], it should be understood to extend as far as the case of earth and so forth. Therefore, the concluding sense is that because the conceptualization is dissimilar, the effect possesses a nature entirely other than the existent.
Furthermore, "In this way," and so forth.

Regarding objects such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth, there is a specific apprehension by the eyes and other senses—namely, that "only form is apprehended by the eye," "only taste by the tongue," and so on. This apprehension is manifestation (*vyakti*), which would not occur [if earth and the other elements were manifest], because they would not be objects of the eyes and other senses. For it is only form and the other [sensory qualities] that are specifically restricted as the respective objects of the eyes and so forth; however, earth and the other [elements] do not possess a distinct intrinsic nature (*svatattva*) consisting of form and the rest, and thus they are non-manifest. Therefore, because they are non-manifest, earth and the others are not perceptible manifestations, since they are not the specific objects of the eyes and other senses, like a flower in the sky.

By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (ādi), it is also indicated that [the object] is not the domain of inference and so forth; thus, the non-substantiality of the aggregate of form and so on has been stated.
When the intention is to say that [the sense organ] grasps only taste, then the literal reading is also correct;
however, as for the phrase "but only form and so on," etc., [it refers to the following].

By the general statement "whatever [is perceived]," a specific instance is made the subject (*pakṣa*): "Form alone is perceptible, because it manifests by itself, like other things. From this general statement, "like taste" serves as the specific example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

In the same way, for the remaining [objects] such as taste and so forth, their perceptibility as specific instances is not contradictory, since it is to be established by examples other than themselves.
There is no contradiction with [the definitions of] inference and the like, because inference is preceded by perception.
Therefore, since there is no contradiction with its being directly perceived and so forth, it is established that the entity is precisely that—namely, form and the rest.

Now, having abandoned the position that both [cause and effect] exist because of the fear of the aforementioned defects—namely, that one [of the two] exists as the cause, such as form (*rūpa*), etc., while the other exists as the effect, such as space (*ākāśa*), etc.—if you, in opposition to me who am a proponent of the existence of the effect (*kāryasadvādin*), should abandon the position of the existence of the cause and instead resort solely to the position of the existence of the effect so as not to end the debate by accepting the non-existence of the effect, then your position would be definitively established as "the effect alone is existent."
Regarding that view, what proponent indeed maintains that only the effect is real and not the cause, such that nothing else is real?
Consequently, form and so forth would not be real;
and if form and so forth were unreal while the effect were real, a contradictory designation would be made—calling the real "unreal" and the unreal "real."
The existence of the effect in things such as a donkey’s horn is a mere name, like the word "existent" itself;

for by abandoning the absolute negation of the effect's non-existence, there arise contradictions with one's own assertions and so forth, similar to the contradiction of one's own position. If it is an effect, how can it be existent? If it is existent, how can it be an effect? According to the logic that the effect exists in the cause, this is simply the doctrine of the existence of both [cause and effect], and the faults already mentioned apply there. Furthermore, if the particle *eva* ("only") is attached to "existent" (*sat*), then because the existence is not determined, the same previous fault remains.

"If, in his system, form and the like do not exist, would there not be only space and the like? To this it is replied: This position might belong to that very Sāṅkhya who maintains the doctrine of the existence of both [cause and effect], because of his established tenet that the effect exists within the cause. Since the effect is inseparable from the cause, when the effect is accepted, the cause is necessarily accepted as well; however, it is not restricted whether the cause is non-existent or existent. If it were so, let it be—what could prevent it? But the effect is restricted by its existence.

And even there, there are two possible positions: either that "only the effect is existent" (*kāryameva sat*) or that "the existent is only the effect" (*sadeva kāryam*). Regarding the former, "only the effect is existent," the particle *eva* is placed immediately after the word "effect" (*kārya*), because the restriction applies to what follows the particle. Thus, when it is restricted as "the effect is indeed existent" (*kāryaṃ sadeva*), since the existence of the effect is thus restricted, but existence itself is not restricted to the effect, it would follow that existence also exists in the cause. Consequently, the position previously examined—where both [cause and effect] are existent—would result, rendering the restrictive particle (*eva*) useless; and that is undesirable. Therefore, for the effort regarding the particle *eva* to be fruitful, the restriction must apply elsewhere than to the referent of the word "effect"—namely, to the referent of the word "existent" (*sat*), which is its correlative: "The effect is indeed existent" (*kāryameva sat*).
He shows this: "Sattva (being) is restricted to that which is an effect; nothing else is existent.
What follows from this? It follows that for you, form and so forth are not existent.

Since that form and so forth, which are perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), are non-existent, while the effect—which is non-existent and not perceived through direct perception and the like—is existent, you are inventing a contrary designation through your own whim: calling the existent "non-existent" and the non-existent "existent," like the names "Agni" and "Maṅgala," or like [calling] the west "not-west."

Furthermore, even that existence of an effect [imputed] to things such as a donkey's horn is merely a name, like the word "existent," and not an actual object; this is the comparison (see p. 432, l. 1; p. 164, l. 2). Regarding the non-existence of the effect (kāryāsattva): *ya*.
The absence of the skin;
the skin;
the state of being a support.
Just as [the practitioner] remains amidst the fear of beings and so forth, in that very same way, he remains amidst the state of being [of those beings]. Ya. Bhā.
Ya.
Nothing else exists;
therefore, form and so forth do not exist.
Since form and so forth are non-existent, if the effect were to exist, a contrary designation would be made: calling what exists "non-existent" and what does not exist "existent."

The existence of the effect (*kāryasattva*) in things such as a donkey’s horn is a mere name, like the word "existent" itself; for by abandoning the absolute negation of the non-existence of the effect, there arises a contradiction with one's own tenets, as well as contradictions with one's own words and so forth. If it is an effect, how can it be existent? If it is existent, how can it be an effect? Furthermore, according to the principle that the effect exists within the cause, this is simply the doctrine of the existence of both [cause and effect], and the faults already mentioned apply there as well. Moreover, if the term "existent" (*sat*) is used without the restrictive particle *eva* (i.e., as "it is existent"), then because the existence is not definitively determined, the same previous fault remains.
The phrase "sadeva" does not appear in manuscript *ya*;
see page 164, line 3.
[The objection is: "There is no necessity regarding its counter-correlate, because the effect exists as something already existent (*sadeva*). (Pra.)
Comparison, page 164, line 3: *kiṃmatataśca* (Bhāṣya);
*kimattataśca* (Yaśomitra).
Furthermore, there might also be a reading here as "like that which has the name 'existent'.

Moreover, because of the abandonment of the absolute negation of the non-existence of the effect, there is the abandonment of the accepted position that "the effect is absolutely existent. For you do not admit that the effect is non-existent in any way whatsoever; thus, like a contradiction with one's own tenets, there are contradictions with one's own words and so forth.
If the effect is [already] existent, how can it be produced? For it is by being produced that something is called an "effect" (*kārya*).
Furthermore, [the claim] that "the effect must be existent" involves a contradiction with one's own words;
it contradicts common worldly experience because people observe efforts made to achieve the production of an effect while assuming its non-existence in the world;
and it contradicts inference because we see the payment of wages to potters and others for the purpose of producing jars.

Because it is seen to be so, there is a contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣavirodha*). [End of] commentary (*vṛtti*). [End of] treatise (*pra*). [End of] increase (*ṛddhi*). [End of] application (*prayoga*). [End of] chapter (*ya*).

Furthermore, according to the principle that the effect exists within the cause, this is precisely the doctrine of the existence of both [cause and effect]. Since the effect is inseparable from the cause, the existence of the cause follows from the existence of the effect; thus, by the very logic previously stated, the doctrine of the existence of both is inevitable. And regarding that, it has been said: "Just as the earth and so forth, so too is the Self like a heap and like a caravan..."

[One might object: "Is it not the case that he does not exist simply because of the use of the word 'pure' (śuddha), since he is non-different precisely because he is denotable by other words as well? For example: 'possessing men, chariots, horses, and elephants'..."
because [the notions of] "man" and so forth function separately, there might be non-existence in that case, but not in the self (ātman).

This also is not the case, because even though it does not occur as something other [than its parts], the whole is not a different entity from its constituent members; for example, just as [a mountain] is not different from its peaks and so forth...

Having begun with the passage, "Because the defects [of the argument] consist in the lack of equivalent alternatives, the effect must indeed be something other than the existent," and so forth, regarding the two circles [of reasoning], they remain exactly as stated;
thus, first, these are the defects in the restriction that the effect alone is the existent, while the cause is... [non-existent].
But the principles [are as follows]: Bhāṣya, p. 783, l. 2; Yaśomitra, p.
And just as with earth and the other elements, so too the self is like a heap and like a caravan... [and so forth].
But surely, by the very use of the word "pure" (*śuddha*),
it is not [merely] that; for it is non-different precisely because it is denotable by other words as well, just as, for example, [the terms] "heap" (*rāśi*) or "caravan" (*sārtha*).
possessing men, chariots, horses, and elephants...
There might be non-existence [of the whole] because it occurs separately from the man and so forth; however, this is not the case with the self (ātman).

Nor is this even possible, because the aggregate is not a different entity from its constituent parts, since it does not occur apart from them—just as, for example, [it is said]: "And just as from the peaks and so forth..."

...Now, lest these faults should arise, it is determined that "only the existent" (sadeva) is the effect; for the restriction applies to what is other than where the particle *eva* is placed. Thus, the effect is restricted by existence (*sattva*), while existence itself is not restricted, since one admits the existence of the cause as well, and because there is no restriction to [the effect] being existent alone, the very same previous fault remains—the fault of the doctrine that both [cause and effect] are existent. This is what is refuted.

As with earth and so forth, so too is the self (*ātman*). Just as earth, pots, and the like do not exist as something other than form (*rūpa*) and the rest, likewise there is no self other than the aggregates (*skandha*) of form, feeling (*vedanā*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and mental formations (*saṃskāra*). What then? It is designated (*prajñapyate*) through conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*) upon their collection or within their continuum. Examples such as "like a heap" or "like a caravan" are intended to demonstrate the non-existence of a collection and to demonstrate that the only real entities are form and the rest.

The abundance of examples is for the purpose of generating cultivation in the mind and for the purpose of strengthening the understanding of that meaning; [this refers to] the formations of consciousness and perception (*vijñānasaṃjñāsaṃskāra*).
"This verse" will be explained on page 530 of the twelfth chapter.

Here [the opponent] says: "But surely, because that existing Self is expressed by the word 'pure' (*śuddha*) through another word, it must be different from those [qualities], just like color and so forth. To this we reply:
No; for precisely because it is expressible by another word, it is not different. For example: [the expression] "possessing men, chariots, horses, and elephants," and so forth.
Do not think thus; this is for the sake of the destruction of the chariot.

In the twelfth chapter [of the *Nyāyaratnākara*], on page 531, this verse is cited for the purpose of demonstrating the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) of the argument based on being expressible by other words, and for the purpose of establishing its dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). He states again: "Because it functions as something distinct from men and so forth, there would be non-existence (*asattva*) in that case, but not in the case of the Self (*ātman*). Since one observes the functioning of men, horses, and so on as a distinct aggregate, and since such functioning is not observed elsewhere than in that aggregate—such as in an army—there might be non-existence in the case of the army; but let there be no such non-existence in the case of the Self, because it is not separate from name and form (*nāmarūpa*), and because it is of the very nature of that [aggregate]."
To this it is replied: even this is no answer, because the aggregate is not a different entity from its constituent members, despite the fact that [the term] applies to nothing other than them;
for example—as in the passage beginning "just as [a mountain] from its peaks," and so forth—this is not [the case].

If it is argued that even there [in the case of a mountain], [the whole] would not exist because of the division into parts such as the peaks, we say no; for even when there is a division of the intellect, there is non-difference, just as in the case of a beverage (*pānaka*). For example: [the powder of black pepper...]
...a beverage [prepared] from ingredients mixed according to the proper method...
Happy, suffering...
[and so forth]
Just as sweetness [is inherent in sugar],
so too is it with the person.
Furthermore,

due to indifference toward the principles (tattvas) and because of the latent tendencies of unwholesome formative forces (saṃskāra) consisting of the conceit of "I" (ahaṃmāna), the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) proceeds with the thought, "The self exists."

If it is argued that, therefore, there is no person (puruṣa) distinct from the five aggregates (pañcaskandha), because even in that case [the mountain] would not exist apart from its divisions such as peaks; if it is further thought: "Peaks and so forth, when divided by the intellect, are perceived separately, and thus the mountain is separate [from them]; but the self (ātman) is not separate from form and the other aggregates in that way"—that too is not correct, because even when divided by the intellect, it is non-different [from its parts], like a beverage (pānaka).

For example—the description of the illustration beginning with "the powder of mirage" and ending with "beverage"—and the description of the illustrated subject (dārṣṭāntika) is as follows: because of the commonality of the non-existence of a self distinct from the associated factors such as consciousness, [it is said] "happy," "suffering," and so forth; the analysis of the qualities of the substances that are components of the beverage, beginning with "sweetness" and so forth, is not sufficient to establish a separate entity—this is the illustration. The illustrated subject is likewise "the person" and so forth.

Just as the accomplishment of purposes such as the severing of craving occurs even in the absence of any object beyond those [five aggregates], so too the accomplishment of the purpose of conventional worldly transactions—such as the connection between karma and its fruit—occurs within the five aggregates of form and so forth alone; therefore, the conceptualization of a self distinct from them is useless. Thus, the separate peak [of this argument] is established. (Pṛthagucchikharī-prakaraṇa, Chapter on Refuting [the Self]).
The comparison for *ratadrūpā* (Ya) is to be found at page 531, line 1, in the twelfth chapter; *kṣodre* (Bhā).
If *kṣaudra* is intended to mean honey, then the reading *°kṣaudre* is correct; compare [this] with page 531–2 in the twelfth chapter.
Compare page 530 on the twelfth day—1;
compare page 531 on the twelfth day—2.
Why, then, does the grasping at a self (ātmagrāha) arise? To this it is replied: "Because of indifference toward non-realities," and so forth.

Because the mind is indifferent toward the investigation of reality (*tattva-vicāra*), because it has become a state of erroneous cognition through the conceptualization of a self contrary to the reality of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha-tattva*), and because of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of unwholesome formative forces (*akuśala-saṃskāra*)—specifically the pride of "I" (*ahaṃmāna*) included within the seven types of pride such as conceit (*māna*) and overweening pride (*atimāna*)—as well as from the ripening of the impressions (*vāsanā*) deposited by the unwholesome factor called the pride of "I," the ego-grasping (*ahaṅkāra*) that "the self exists" proceeds. Therefore, [the notion arises] that there is no person (*puruṣa*) distinct from the five aggregates.
Thus, in the *Bhāṣya* passage beginning with "even regarding reality" (*tattve 'pi*)... [is this not so]?
What is the fetter of pride (*māna-saṃyojana*)?

It consists of the seven types of pride: pride (*māna*), excessive pride (*atimāna*), pride beyond pride (*mānātimāna*), the pride of "I am" (*asmimāna*), overweening pride (*abhimāna*), the pride of inferiority (*ūnamāna*), and false pride (*mithyāmāna*).
What is pride? It is that inflation of the mind which thinks, "I am superior to one who is inferior," or "I am equal to one who is my equal."
What is overweening pride (*atimāna*)? It is the inflation of the mind thinking, "I am superior to my equals," or "I am equal to those who are superior.
What is pride beyond pride (*mānātimāna*)? It is the inflation of the mind thinking, "I am superior to those who are superior.

What is the pride of "I am" (*asmimāna*)? It is the inflation of the mind arising from the attachment to a self and what belongs to a self within the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*).
What is overweening pride (*abhimāna*)? It is that inflation of the mind which thinks, "I have attained it," regarding a superior, distinguished realization that has not yet been attained.
What is inferiority pride (*ūnamāna*)? It is that inflation of the mind which thinks, "I am only slightly inferior," in relation to one who is vastly superior.
What is false pride (*mithyāmāna*)? It is that inflation of the mind which thinks, "I possess virtues," when one actually lacks virtues.
One who is bound by the fetter of pride does not perceive "self" and "what belongs to self.
Due to this non-perception, there arises the grasping of self and what belongs to self, which is the manifestation of unwholesome states and the non-manifestation of wholesome states;
thereby, when suffering is produced in the future, one becomes conjoined with suffering.
Thus, in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* composed by Asaṅga, within the investigation of the fetter of pride among the nine fetters, page 45 (*Viśvabhārati Studies* 12):
"Indeed, all that is called pride proceeds based upon the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*);
furthermore, it is characterized by the inflation of the mind."

For instance—having superimposed the notion of "self" and "what belongs to self" upon the aggregates (*skandhas*), one elevates the self through various specific attributes, thinking "I am this" and "this is mine," and considers oneself superior to others.
Its function is to provide a basis for the arising of disrespect and suffering.

Disrespect (*agaurava*) is rigidity toward persons who are venerable or possessed of qualities, characterized by a lack of deference in body and speech. Furthermore, the arising of suffering here refers to the arising of renewed existence (*punarbhava*).

Furthermore, although there is no difference in the essential nature of the inflation of the mind (*cittonnati*), it is divided into seven types based on the difference in the causes of that inflation— namely, pride (*māna*), excessive pride (*atimāna*), and so forth.
thus, in the *Triṃśikāvijñaptibhāṣya* composed by Sthiramati, page 28;
thereafter, from the Pañcaskandhaka.

And this [naya] would involve a transition from one aggregate-entity such as a jar to another entity, because it is free from the determination of the reality of form and so forth; and that [transition] serves to establish the non-substantiality of both. Thus, according to the understanding [of this naya], the *samabhirūḍha* is characterized by the following: "In the *samabhirūḍha* doctrine, there is a transition between entities (*vatthūṇaṃ saṃkamaṇaṃ*), even if they number in the hundreds, yet they become non-entities (*avatthū*) [in that sense].
Thus, in that regard, this is his very subdivision known as *guṇasamabhirūḍha*.
And this is a restrictive rule (niyamavidhi);

furthermore, it is not connected even with the three states of arising, destruction, and persistence, because there is an absence of transition into the triad of arising and so forth. "The transition between those two entities occurs; in the Samabhirūḍha [naya], it is non-entities" (āva. ni. 757).

Thus, the vision of this system has been demonstrated according to its actual nature; now, in order to determine what kind of classification of systems this is, he says: "And this [is the view] of the reality of form and so forth," and so on.

This method maintains that the object consists of nothing but form (*rūpa*) and so forth, and that this object does not transition into another object called a "collection" (*samudāya*). Therefore, because the transition into another object such as a collection like a jar would entail the fault of being non-correspondent to reality, one should abandon the course of establishing the nature of objects. Consequently, by being freed from the course of establishing the nature of objects, there would be a transition into another object such as a collection like a jar; and that [transition] would result in both being rendered non-entities. Both the forms and their collection would become non-entities: the forms would be non-entities because they do not abide in their own nature due to assuming the form of a collection; and the collection would be a non-entity because its own nature is not established, just like the nature of the forms themselves. Thus, this transition into another object would result in the non-existence of both. Thinking thus, the *samabhirūḍha* [naya], through a unifying orientation, holds that the single object is indeed just the form and so forth. Whatever designations (*saṃjñā*) there may be for it, the *samabhirūḍha* applies each of them. This very definition applies even to the hundredfold [nayas]; as stated in the *Āvaśyaka-niryukti* (verse 759): "Each one is sevenfold. Thus, this definition pervades the hundredfold [nayas] along with their subdivisions, according to the *evambhūta* [naya].
He states the definition of the *niryukti* as that which bears witness to it and is in agreement with it:
"And thus" (evaṃ ca), [as found in] the Yaśas commentary and the Bhāṣya.
Thus, from this [text],
the reality of form and so forth, such as the posterior [object], is established.
The collection of aggregates is a posterior entity;
its establishment as a collection occurs by way of its own nature.
