Its state of abiding in its own nature is the cultivation of existence;
see page 550, note 1.
"In the *samabhirūḍha* doctrine, the transfer of a thing becomes non-existent" (*āvaśyaka-niryukti* 757).

Now he explains the *samabhirūḍha*: "In the *samabhirūḍha* doctrine, the transfer of a thing becomes non-existent. When the doctrine is being examined—what doctrine? He says: in the *samabhirūḍha*. That which "ascends" (*abhirohati*) by way of unification (*sam-ekībhāvena*) to the etymological ground (*vyutpatti-nimitta*) in the application of a word is the *samabhirūḍha*. The "transfer" (*saṃkramaṇa*) of a thing (*vastu*)—such as that called a "jar"—is its movement elsewhere, such as to that called a "pot" (*kuṭa*). Why is this? It "becomes non-existent" (*avatthu*), meaning it is unreal (*asad*), when the doctrine is considered. Which doctrine? He says: in the *samabhirūḍha*. Thus, when one considers the specific etymological derivation of a term, the application of a word like "jar" to an object that has a different etymological derivation—such as "pot"—is considered invalid. Therefore, in the *samabhirūḍha* doctrine, the transfer of a thing from its own etymological basis to another is regarded as non-existent.

For this [proponent] maintains that even synonymous terms possess distinct meanings; for example, it is called a *ghaṭa* because of its "striking" (*ghaṭana*), and a *kuṭa* because of its "bending" (*kuṭana*).

An entity—whether a substance (*dravya*) or a mode (*paryāya*) denoted by one word—does not undergo a transformation into the form of the word or the object denoted by another word. Indeed, the referent denoted by the word "cloth" never at any time assumes the nature of the entity denoted by the word "pot," because such a thing is never perceived; otherwise, there would be a confusion of entities (*vastusaṃkara*).

And this being the case, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the total cessation of worldly conventions— such as engagement with and withdrawal from specifically determined objects— which are well-established for all people;
thus it is stated in the *Āvaśyaka-niryukti-vṛtti* composed by Sūri Malayagiri, on pages 376–377,
beginning with "tatrāyam" and so forth.

In this regard, the definition is: "The transition from one state [of meaning] to another occurs when it is groundless according to the *samabhirūḍha* perspective" (Āvaśyaka-niryukti 757). When that hundred-fold division—within the *Sapta-naya-śata-ara-naya-cakra*—is divided a hundred times according to the *samabhirūḍha*, and one asks, "Which of these is this *samabhirūḍha*?"—upon such inquiry, it is found that this is the one called *guṇa-samabhirūḍha*, which is distinct from the *paryāya-samabhirūḍha* and is itself a subdivision thereof, as will be explained hereafter.

And this is a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*). Furthermore, these are the subdivisions of this very "equally ascended quality" (*guṇasamabhirūḍha*): (1) the injunction (*vidhi*), and (2) the injunction of injunction (*vidhividhi*). Now, form and so forth are both non-existent and existent; because they transition into another entity, both [non-existence and existence] are indeed sublated. Moreover, since even persistence (*sthiti*) is essentially a process of becoming (*bhāvanātmikā*), it truly "comes to be" (*bhavati*). Therefore, because of its pervasion by the act of becoming, becoming transitions everywhere into another entity; thus, even persistence is not merely a state of being.

Now, if it is argued that because "it becomes" in such and such a way, there is the pervasion (*abhivyāpti*) of that very single entity alone—that is not so; for since becoming "in such a way" occurs with respect to every object, does it not follow that there is indeed a pervasion even by non-becoming? Thus, because of the transition between existence and non-existence, [the object] is a non-entity.

Therefore, when there is the nature of mere form and so forth, independent of persistence, origination, and cessation, everything is established. However, according to the view of the *mūḍha-samabhirūḍha* [type of logician], there is indeed the connection of origination and destruction in form and the other [qualities].

[The twelvefold division is as follows: (1) injunction of both (*vidhyubhaya*), (2) injunction-restriction (*vidhiniyama*), (3) both (*ubhaya*), (4) injunction of both (*ubhayavidhi*), (5) both of both (*ubhayobhaya*), (6) restriction of both (*ubhayaniyama*), (7) restriction (*niyama*), (8) injunction of restriction (*niyamavidhi*), (9) both of restriction (*niyamobhaya*), and (10) restriction of restriction (*niyamaniyama*). This is the variety named "injunction of restriction" (*niyamavidhi*) within the hundred-fold division of the *samabhirūḍha* [naya], which itself is divided into twelve types; for its specific location, please refer to [the relevant section]. 511–2.
The non-existent is form and so forth, and the existent is that which has come into being; since there is a transition from one thing to another between these two, are not both undermined?

Furthermore, even "stability" (sthiti), being of the nature of becoming (bhāvanā), truly becomes as it "becomes" (bhavati); thus, because of the pervasion by becoming, becoming transitions into every other entity, and therefore stability is not a reality either. If, on the other hand, it is argued that in such and such a way only the state of being (bhāva) itself comes into existence, and thus there is the pervasive extension of that single [state] alone—that is not so, because such becoming occurs in relation to every individual object. But surely, there is likewise a pervasion even by non-becoming (abhavana); thus, due to the transition between existence and non-existence, there is a lack of substantiality (avastutā).

Therefore, when there is the nature of mere form and so forth, independent of persistence, origination, and cessation, everything is established. However, according to the view of the *mūḍhasamabhirūḍha* [the deluded conventionalist], there is indeed the connection with origination and destruction for forms and so forth.

Furthermore, just as this [view] does not accept the transition of forms and so forth into another object such as a jar, likewise this *naya* (perspective) is not connected even with origination, cessation, and persistence, because there is an absence of transition even among the triad of arising and the rest.

If there were a transition into another entity such as arising and so forth, how could this [naya] possess the quality of being *samabhirūḍha*? How so? This is shown: since arising and passing away consist respectively of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and non-existence through destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), arising is prior non-existence and destruction is non-existence through destruction; both of these are non-existent (*abhūta*), whereas form and the like are existent (*bhūta*). If there were a transition from one entity to the other between that which is existent and that which is non-existent, then both would be contradicted: if it is existent, how can it be non-existent? And if it is non-existent, how can it be an existent entity such as form? Thus, there is no transition. (Variant reading: *saṃkrāntībhāḥ*)
Does he not desire the transitions (*saṃkrānti*)?
The usage of the verb *pat* preceded by the prefix *ut-* is seen at the beginning of the eleventh day as well.

Comparison: In the *Tattvārtha-siddhasenīya-vṛtti*, page 389, line 6, [it is argued]: "If it is claimed that stability (*sthiti*), being independent of origination and destruction, is not contradicted because it is a 'become-ness' (*bhūtatva*)—just as in the case of form (*rūpa*) and so on—it is said in reply: True, it is 'become'; yet stability (*sthiti*) is also of the nature of becoming (*bhavanātmikā*), for it truly becomes in the sense that 'it is becoming. Therefore, due to the pervasion by becoming, everything becomes in every way—a pot, a form, a taste, and so forth. Since this process of becoming extends everywhere to other entities, stability itself does not possess the status of a real entity (*vastutva*)."
The comparison of this [process], beginning with form and so forth, occurs precisely here; it should be examined in the eleventh and twelfth movements (*cāra*).
Regarding the analysis of existence (*bhāvanavyutpatti*):
now, as for the phrase "in such and such a way" and so forth—

if you think that in each respective manner, such as through the form or taste of a jar, it is indeed existence itself that comes into being, and thus there is only the manifestation of that single [existence] and no transition into another entity— [then we reply:]...

That is not so. Why? Because such a state of being occurs for every individual thing; for form [is perceived] through the nature of taste and so forth, taste through the nature of form and so forth, and even smell through the natures of the remaining [qualities], as all things and non-things are mutually excluded from one another. Now, if it is argued that pervasion indeed exists even through non-being—such that being passes over into non-being, or non-being into being—this would be a great transmigration. For that very reason, there is the unreality (avastutā) of that [transmigration]. In that case, [the object] is a non-entity.
Because it is obstructed by its daily [impurity].
The state of being is non-being;
"non-being" is the state of being and non-being (according to Ya);
"non-being" is the state of being (according to Bhā).
Is non-existence existence?
A great [error]?
Of the great?
From the cause [it arises],
from the cause [it arises];
indeed, such is the fixed rule.

If [the universal] were a real entity (*vastu*), then because it does not exist in that manner, the universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth, as well as the collection (*samudaya*), would have to be abandoned; only the particulars (*viśeṣa*) would be acceptable. Therefore, [the universal] is even more non-existent. Its prescription (*vidhi*) is stated by way of its differentiation (*vikṣepa*). This is the rule (*niyama*) of the prescription; by means of the rejection of the immediately preceding method (*naya*), or by means of the activity of the exception (*apavāda*) regarding "self" and "belonging to self" through the established general rule (*utsarga-vidhi*) of investigation, the meaning of the word is the "mode" (*paryava*), which is manifoldness (*anekatā*) as a quality (*guṇa*). Whether it be *paryāya* or *paryava*, the cognition that "this alone exists" is the *paryavāstika*.
The meaning of the sentence consists of distinct words;

therefore, form and the other [sensory objects] are independent of persistence, origination, and cessation. This [world] has the nature of those [objects] alone—that is, it is the reality of those alone. That state is the state of having the nature of those alone. And in that state of having the nature of mere form and so forth, which is independent of persistence, origination, and cessation, everything is established; everything is proven, and there is no fault here whatsoever.

According to the view of another [type of] *mūḍha-samabhirūḍha* included within the hundredfold divisions of *samabhirūḍha*, there is indeed the conjunction of origination and destruction in form and the other qualities; yet, what is the use of that which is even slightly deluded (*āmūḍha*)? He does not accept this because of its state of being deluded (*āmūḍhatva*).

Thus, this rule and injunction regarding the *guṇa-samabhirūḍha* has been stated. Here, for the purpose of cultivating an understanding of that very injunction and rule which immediately follows—characterized by the "inexpressible" (*avaktavya*)—he says: "For in this way the rule comes to be," and so forth.

How so? If [the object] were a real entity (*vastu*), then because it does not exist in that manner, universals (*sāmānya*) and the like, as well as collections (*samudaya*), would have to be rejected; rather, only particulars (*viśeṣa*) such as color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth, which are differentiated by location, would be accepted because they fall within the scope of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). To say more than that is incorrect. When there is a distraction regarding that which is unreal (*asat*), a positive injunction (*vidhi*) is stated: "If it were a real entity, then this restriction (*niyama*) would be appropriate for it. Thus, this restriction is established and enjoined by way of an exception (*apavāda*) against one's own and others' views concerning the operation of the positive injunction established by the prior investigation—which rejected the immediately preceding principle (*naya*)—and by way of the operation of both the positive injunction and the exception regarding the immediately following [views]. In this way, the *naya* has been explained as the act of establishing a restriction through the exception of one's own and others' views concerning the operation of the positive injunction established by that investigation.
Is it by way of censure? It is investigated; [it is] past, beyond investigation. (vidhīyate bhāṣye atītavicāre prāpte)

The meaning of the word *paryava* is "complete comprehension" (*parigamana*). This consists of multiplicity (*anekatā*), which is a "quality" (*guṇa*). [The root] *gaṇ* means "to count" (*saṅkhyāna*); thus, form and the other [sensory objects] are "qualities" (*guṇa*) because they are correctly enumerated (*samyak-khyāna*) as being mutually distinct. Furthermore, that quality is a "mode" (*paryāya*) because it proceeds everywhere (*parito gamanāt*), or it is a *paryava* for the same reasons as previously explained.
The explanation that "that very [root] exists" (*sa evāsti*) and so forth has already been covered.

In the *Pāṇinīya-dhātupāṭha*, the roots *gaṇ* (numbering) at 321, *saṃketa* (signaling) at 359, *grāma* (village), *kuṇa*, and *guṇa* (all meaning "addressing" or "invoking") at 360–362 are seen in the *curādi* class as distinct words;

yet the meaning of the sentence is formed by their respective individual meanings. In the case of "Devadatta, bring the white cow," the words "Devadatta" and so forth are themselves the sentence, and the meaning of those very words is the explained meaning, because the aforementioned kind of aggregate lacks substantial reality.
See page 448, note 2:
what is the meaning of the commentary? Is it the meaning of the individual word (*padārtha*) or the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*)?

The basis for this and the source from which it emerged is as follows: "O Blessed One, how many kinds of substantial atoms (bhāvaparamāṇu) are taught? O Goyama, four kinds: namely, those possessing color, those possessing taste, those possessing smell, and those possessing touch" (Bhagavatī Sūtra 20.5.670).
In the instruction beginning with "they possess color" (*varṇavantaḥ*), those very same colors and so forth possess one another; since the suffix *matup* here denotes association,
this is the tenth alternative, the restrictive method (*niyamavidhinaya*).

The scriptural basis for this system is stated, from which it originates, as follows: In response to the question, "Venerable sir, how many kinds of substantial atoms (bhāva-paramāṇu) are taught? the explanation is given: "Gautama, they are of four kinds, namely: possessing color, possessing taste, possessing smell, and possessing touch."

Regarding the passage beginning with "possessing color" (*varṇavanta*), if it is asked: "When only color and so forth are questioned in terms of their existence (*bhāva*), what other things possessing those [qualities] have been explained?", it is said in reply: none at all; rather, it is those very same things—color and so forth—that possess one another. Taste, smell, and touch possess color; color possesses them. With the exception of taste, they possess taste; with the exception of smell, they possess smell; with the exception of touch, they possess touch. These are indicated by the suffix *matup*, because here *matup* signifies association (*saṃsaṅga*); thus, color and the others are indeed mutually associated. (Compare page 518–2, *pannatteya*).
[Question: "And of four kinds...

[How many kinds, O Venerable One, are atoms (paramāṇu) taught? [Answer: "Gautama! Four kinds of atoms are taught; namely: substance-atom (dravya-paramāṇu), space-atom (kṣetra-paramāṇu), time-atom (kāla-paramāṇu), and mode-atom (bhāva-paramāṇu). [Question: 'O Venerable One, how many kinds of substance-atoms are taught? [Answer: 'Gautama! Four kinds of substance-atoms are taught; namely: indivisible (acchedya), inseparable (abhedya), unburnable (adahya), and ungraspable (ageyya)."

“Blessed One, how many kinds of field-atoms (khetta-paramāṇu) are there? “Gautama, they are of four kinds, namely: without parts (anaddha), without middle (amajjha), without spatial location (apadesa), and indivisible (avibhāima). [Question: “Blessed One, how many kinds of time-atoms (kāla-paramāṇu) are there? “Gautama, they are of four kinds, namely: without color (avanna), without smell (agaṃdha), without taste (arasa), and without touch (aphāsa).

[Question: “Blessed One, how many kinds of state-atoms (bhāva-paramāṇu) are there? “Gautama, they are of four kinds, namely: possessing color (vannamaṃta), possessing smell (gaṃdhamaṃta), possessing taste (rasamaṃta), and possessing touch (phāsamaṃta).”
"So be it, venerable sir," [he said], and he remained there, up until [the end of] the Bhagavatī Sūtra, chapter 20,
section 5.
670. Because this discussion begins with the atom (*paramāṇu*) and so forth, he says "ka" and so on.

In that context, a substance-atom (*dravyaparamāṇu*) is a single atom in the form of a substance; this is because color and other qualities are not intended to be expressed, while the nature of substance alone is intended to be expressed.
Likewise, a space-atom (*kṣetraparamāṇu*) is a point of space (*ākāśapradeśa*).
The time-atom (*kālaparamāṇu*) is a *samaya*;

the substance-atom (*bhāvaparamāṇu*) is the atom itself, because one intends to emphasize its states such as color and so forth, or because it possesses the shortest possible duration of time and other qualities.
As for "fourfold" (*cauvviha*): even a single substance-atom is fourfold in nature according to one's intention.
"Acchejja" means that which is to be cut (*chedya*) by means of a weapon or the like, such as a creeper; because that is negated, it is "uncuttable" (*acchedya*).
"Abhejja" means that which is to be pierced (*bhedya*) by means of a needle or the like, such as leather; because that is negated, it is "unpiercable" (*abhedya*).
"Aḍajjha" means that which is not to be burned (*adāhya*) by fire, due to its subtlety.
For this very reason, it is "ungraspable" (*aggrāhya*) by the hand and so forth because of the absence of an even number of parts;
it is "without middle" (*amajjha*) because of the absence of an odd number of parts.

"In the commentary on the *Bhagavatīsūtra* composed by Abhayadevasūri, [it is stated]: 'It is called *niraṃśa* (partless) because of the absence of parts; it is called *avibhāgima* (indivisible) because it is produced without division, meaning it is of a single form, or rather, it is impossible to divide.'"
In this way, [the suffix] *pra* is used in the sense of abstract state (*bhāva*); what is its meaning? It means "possessing that," namely, possessing taste, smell, and touch.
The suffix *matup* [is applied] after a word ending in the sixth case (*praṣṭhī*) in the senses of abundance, censure, praise, constant connection, and excellence;
it signifies "that belongs to him" or "it exists in this."

If it is argued that suffixes such as *matup* and others apply to "mere existence" (*sanmātra*), there is the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). If suffixes such as *matup* applied to mere existence, it would follow here as well: "this man has rice" (*vrīhir asya*) or "this man has barley" (*yavo 'sya*).
Therefore, the mention of "abundance" (*bhūman*) and so forth must be made. What, then, are "abundance" and the rest? They are: abundance, censure, praise, constant connection, and excellence.
When there is a desire to express a relationship, suffixes such as *matup* and others are employed:
*gomān* ("possessing cows") and *yavamān* ("possessing barley") in the sense of abundance;
*kakudāvartī* ("having a hump and a curl") and *saṃkhādakī* ("one who eats together") in the sense of censure.
The word *daśana* is used for a horse in the sense of praise (*praśaṃsā*), as in "one possessing teeth" (*rūpavān*, *varṇavān*);
it is used in the sense of constant connection (*nityayoga*), as in "milk-bearing trees" (*kṣīriṇo vṛkṣāḥ*) or "thorny trees" (*kaṇṭakino vṛkṣāḥ*).
In the sense of excellence, [the suffix] is used as in *udariṇī* ("having a prominent belly");
in the sense of association, as in *daṇḍī* ("carrying a staff") and *chatrī* ("carrying an umbrella").
Therefore, in that case, the mention of "ground" (*bhūmi*) and so forth must be made.
Why should it not be formed? [Because] it has been stated that "this is rice" (*vrīhir asya*) or "this is barley" (*yavo 'sya*). What was stated? That there is no denotation (*anabhidhānāt*).
Furthermore, the particle *iti* is indeed employed; therefore, if there is such an intention to express (*vivakṣā*).

And it is only when abundance and so forth are intended that one says "possessing cows" (gomān) or "possessing barley" (yavamān); it is only the existence of those possessing abundance and so forth that is expressed. For there is no one who lacks barley—such as a *saṃkhādakī* or a *kakudāvartī*—nor is it only the existence of one associated with censure that is expressed, for there is no one who is not a *saṃkhādakī*.
The existence of one who possesses beauty or color is spoken of only as being connected with praise; for there is no one who lacks form.
The existence of "milk-bearing trees" or "thorn-bearing trees" is spoken of only as being eternally connected [to those qualities]; for there is no tree that does not have milk [or thorns].
The existence of "a pregnant maiden" is spoken of only as being connected with excellence; for there is no one who lacks a belly.

The one with a staff (*daṇḍin*) and the one with an umbrella (*chatrin*): existence (*sattā*) is predicated only of that which is associated with a connection [to an attribute]. Indeed, there is no one who lacks a staff;

however, existence is predicated only of as many cows as suffice for carrying, milking, and breeding. For some, these purposes are served by four cows, while for others they are not served even by a hundred.

Since the seer perceives existence in the mere being (*sanmātra*), the seer further indicates the possessive suffix *matup* in reference to the mere being: "He sprinkles the sacrificial post with water containing barley."

"—Thus, in the *Pātañjala-Mahābhāṣya*, in the section on *saṃsaṅga* (the discussion on *vivaśtivivakṣā*), it is stated: 'In the case of the desire to express [the sense of] possession (*vivaśtivivakṣāyām*), the suffixes such as *matup* and others occur. (*Pā. Ma. Bhā.* 5.2.94; Kaiyaṭa)."
For example: *gomān* (possessing cows) and *yavamān* (possessing barley) denote abundance;

*kakudāvartī* (having a hump and a curl) denotes censure; *vyādāya hāsī* (laughing with mouth wide open) denotes praise; and *rūpavān* (possessing beauty) and *śīlavān* (possessing virtue) denote commendation.

In the sense of constant connection (*nityayoga*): "milk-bearing trees" (*kṣīriṇo vṛkṣāḥ*), "thorn-bearing trees" (*kaṇṭakino vṛkṣāḥ*). In the sense of excellence (*atiśāyana*): "very angry" (*krodhī*), "very proud" (*mānī*). In the sense of accompaniment (*saṃsarga*): "carrying a staff" (*daṇḍī*), "carrying an umbrella" (*chatrī*).

In the statement "one sprinkles with barley-grains" (*yavamadbhiḥ prokṣati*), where there is a mere existence [of the quality], the suffix *matup* occurs in the indication "they possess color" (*varṇavantaḥ*) and so forth; this would apply in this system of conjunction (*saṃsaṅga*), yet in the Syādvāda system, it depends upon the substantial atom (*dravyaparamāṇu*), as for example:

*bhūmi* means "possessing land"; *gomān* and *yavamān* mean "possessing cattle" and "possessing barley" respectively; *bhūmān* means "possessing much land"; *gomān* and *ya[vamān]* mean "possessing cattle" and "possessing barley" [in the sense of] excellence.
Prekṣā-prakaraṇa: Commentary on my cognition; Yaśasvī’s commentary on my cognition; Bhāṣya.
There is no substance devoid of modes, nor are there modes devoid of substance;

there is no arising [devoid of decay and permanence], and a reality shown by either one-sided perspective (naya) independently of the other does not exist due to the absence of valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa). Thus he says: "There is no substance devoid of modes, nor are there modes devoid of substance."
Indeed, arising, persistence, and dissolution— this is the characteristic of substance.
Substance does not exist apart from its modes, because clay is perceived as a commonality persisting through the lump of clay, the bowl, the jar, the granary, and so forth;

nor do modes exist devoid of substance, because the particularities such as the lump of clay, the bowl, the jar, and the granary are understood as being permeated by a single, continuous form of the commonality of clay.

Therefore, the entity favored by the substantialist (dravyārthika) is necessarily pervaded by modes and is not separate from them; likewise, that which is favored by the modalist (paryāyārthika) is also connected with the substantial aspect and is not devoid of it, for the two, being mutually distinct, are never perceived at any time.

Furthermore, he asks: "What kind of substance (dravya) exists? He replies: Origination, persistence, and destruction—possessing the natures as previously described, existing in mutual inseparability—are, indeed (*handi*), the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of substance; that is, they are the attributes that establish the existence of substance. Let this be observed: since the cognition of a single underlying continuity (*anvaya*), consisting of the relinquishment and acquisition of preceding and succeeding modes (*paryāya*), establishes the existence of such a substance, one must accept that a real entity (*vastu*) is characterized by origination, decay, and permanence.
And these three are mutually interpenetrated, for in the absence of any one of them, the others would also be absent; thus it is said in the *Sanmativṛtti* composed by Abhayadevasūri, page 410:
"Indeed, arising, persistence, and destruction—this is the characteristic of a substance. (*Sammati-tarka-prakaraṇa* 1.12).

Thus, according to the Jina’s doctrine, this is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). However, because it explains through individual perspectives (*naya*), only existence (*bhāva*) is grasped by this [statement].
Thus ends the tenth alternative (*bhaṅga*), the restrictive method of perspective (*niyamavidhinaya*).
Oṃ Arhaṃ.
Salutations to the True Gurus.
Now begins the eleventh chapter, "The Refutation of Both [Origination and Non-origination].

Having established that whatever is impossible even to hear—namely, the manifestation of form and so forth—is itself the nature of existence (*bhāva*), there follows this statement which negates the transition of entities: "There is no origination of existence, because of the non-existence of origination."

For they must necessarily exist in some manner, either as a positive entity (bhāva) or as a negative non-entity (abhāva). Among these, that existence which consists in absolute being has been excluded; therefore, their existence remains unexcluded only through arising and perishing. If that were excluded, they would indeed be non-entities. Yet, you yourself have stated that whatever is produced by them is itself an entity.
[Objection: But surely they exist precisely by way of being unproduced.

[Response: In that case, they do not exist at all, because they are characterized by non-production and non-destruction, like a sky-flower; this is by way of a dissimilar instance (vaidharmya), such as the earth, a clod of clay, a stūpa, and so forth. Since there is no time [for them], they lack temporal status, because no production and so forth are admitted, and thus they are timeless.

Since knowledge of the *nayacakra* (the wheel of viewpoints) is preceded by a thorough understanding of the nature of each individual viewpoint (*naya*), and since there is dissatisfaction with the presentation of the preceding viewpoint when one encounters the subsequent one, that very [dissatisfaction] constitutes the connection [between them]. Because the refutation of the former and the method of one’s own system are stated together in this "rule for both viewpoints" (*niyamo bhayanaye*), he says: "This is impossible," and so forth.

This is impossible even to hear, let alone to speak, because it contradicts one’s own words and so forth. What is impossible? That which begins with "yad yat tad" (whatever that may be); "yad" means "because. The statement "yad tat" is connected as follows: having established one's own position that the very becoming of form and so forth is "existence" (*bhāva*), [the opponent] denies the transition of entities, claiming there is no arising. Both [positions] are in this... [text fragment]. Page 66, line 9; page 789.
But how is this impossible? To this he says: "Necessarily," and so forth.

For those [objects], such as form and the rest, must necessarily exist in some manner, either in the form of an entity or in the form of a non-entity; for this very reason, according to your own statement, because the word "hi" (for) has the sense of providing a reason for the statement.

To determine that, he says: "In that regard," and so forth. Among these *paryāyāstika* systems, which follow the *dravyārthika* perspective, that existence (*bhavana*) which consists in the absolute non-existence of those two—existence and non-existence—is excluded. Therefore, because existence is excluded and there is no existence in the form of a positive entity (*bhāva*), by process of elimination, the existence of these [qualities] such as color and so forth is determined to be exclusively through arising and destruction (*utpāda-vināśa*).

What is the reason? Because if their non-existence (*abhāvatā*) were excluded—that is, if the existence of those [entities] such as form (*rūpa*) were excluded even in the form of arising and perishing—they would become non-existent like a sky-flower. For that [sky-flower] is absolutely non-existent because it does not exist in any form whatsoever; lest that be the case, you yourself must accept that existence takes the form of arising and perishing. This is shown: "Indeed, that which is produced by them is itself existence," as you yourself have stated, since you admit the existence of birth and destruction. And regarding their destruction... [text fragment].

"By you, [it was said that] existence is produced by them; [this is] not so. The other says: "Indeed, it is incorrect [to say they produce it], because I have stated that they exist precisely as unproduced."

To this it is replied: In that case, they do not exist, because they are neither produced nor destroyed, like a flower in the sky; by way of contrast, like the earth, a clod of clay, a stūpa, and so forth. For production and destruction are indeed the seeds of the existence of entities, just as color-form (*rūpa*) and other qualities are the seeds for the existence of threads and the like. This is because in the absence of those [seeds], there is an absence of that [existence], and in the presence of those, there is the presence of that. Otherwise, due to being unproduced and undestroyed, being non-distinct [from non-existence], and being rootless, an entity would not exist, like the son of a barren woman. Furthermore, impermanence itself is the very nature of an entity, free from its opposite.
Let it be understood that these [entities] are momentary (*kṣaṇika*).

For whatever entity has arisen, if it is destined to perish, what obstacle to its destruction could there be? Indeed, once an entity has arisen, because its very nature consists in becoming the form of destruction, it does not exist thereafter; for, being "without time" (*akāla*), it lacks duration. These two are the examples of similarity and dissimilarity: it is "without time" because it has no time. Since it is without time, and because it is without time, there might be a suspicion that it possesses existence just as time does; lest this be so, it is specified: "because it is without time, while being without time."

Because, as you have stated, origination (*utpāda*) and so forth are not admitted, there is a lack of temporal existence; by the inclusion of the term "and so forth" (*ādi*), the non-admission of destruction (*vināśa*) is also implied.
This passage is absent from manuscript *Ya*.

For indeed, origination and destruction alone are the seeds of the becoming of entities, just as color-form (*rūpa*) and other qualities are the seeds for the becoming of threads and the like; because in the absence of those [seeds] there is an absence of that [becoming], and in the presence of those [seeds] there is the presence of that [becoming].
Otherwise, because they are subject to non-arising and non-destruction, because they lack synonyms, and because they are rootless, they would not be real entities, like the son of a barren woman.
Furthermore, impermanence exists as something distinct from its opposite;
therefore, let it be understood that those things are momentary.

For if an entity that has arisen is itself subject to destruction, what obstacle to its destruction could there be? For if an entity, having arisen, [remains] as an entity... [then its arising would be... its existence.
Why [is it] "arising from you"? Because of the words "arising" and so forth;
for arising and destruction alone are the seeds of the existence of entities such as form and the rest.
The word *hi* has the sense of a reason (*hetvartha*). The existence of a thing characterized by the properties of arising and perishing [is established] because it is the seed of that [existence].

What is it like? It is like color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth being the seed for the existence of threads, cloth, and so on; for in the absence of those [threads], they [cloth, etc. do not exist, and in the presence of those [threads], they exist. Indeed, the collection of color-form and so forth constitutes the threads, cloth, and so on; in their absence, these do not exist because they have those as their seed, and only when those are present do they come to be. In the same way, a thing (*vastu*) also, because it is the seed of arising and perishing, possesses the nature of existing as such. [The portion of the text from *bhavana* up to *evam ca* is missing in the Bhāratīya manuscript.]
That which possesses its existence is that which exists as such.

Regarding the refutation of [the opponent's] position: if this is not accepted, there is a fault—as indicated by the passage beginning with "otherwise" (*itarathā hi*) and ending with "like the son of a barren woman" (*vandhyāputravat*).

This is explained through a sequence of cause and effect: because it is without production or destruction, it is non-sequential (*aparyāya*); because it is non-sequential, it is rootless (*nirmūla*); and because it is rootless, it would not exist. Thus, the meaning is established.
Or rather, each of these reasons individually establishes that an entity must be impermanent by virtue of having the nature of arising and perishing; thus [ends] the section on arising and perishing.

Nor do we satisfy ourselves with a mere general impermanence—such as that inferred from the observation of the arising and destruction of earth, water, form, and so forth, which endure for a period of time and are connected with the touch of permanence as the opposite of impermanent things; for even endurance over a period of time is itself the opposite of impermanence. What then? Impermanence belongs to an entity precisely as something free from such opposites.

It should be understood that those [entities], such as form and so forth, are momentary (*kṣaṇika*). "Momentary" means that which possesses a moment (*kṣaṇa*); a moment is the most subtle unit of time. It should be determined that this [moment] alone belongs to it, and that it does not persist through a second or any subsequent interval of time—this is the certainty regarding the related entity.
Comparison—page 529—1.
That very time is its state of stillness (sthitibhāva).
He alone possesses "black eyes" (kālākṣa) who is "ever-abiding"—
this is also the principle here: for what obstacle to destruction could there be for that entity which, having arisen, has perished?

The explanation of that [passage] beginning with "If indeed... is as follows: Arising and destruction have just been established. If that entity, having arisen, possesses the nature of destruction, then what could be an obstacle or impediment to its destruction—that is, to that which has the nature of destruction—by virtue of which it might persist for even the briefest duration of time? If there is no such impediment, it will certainly not perish; otherwise, if this is not accepted, then it will never perish at all, remaining as it was before.
There is an objection: [what is] the absence of a cause of destruction?

What is the cause of destruction for what? For example, the striking by a stone or similar object is the cause of destruction for a jar; contact with fire is the cause of destruction for the color and other qualities of earth as well as for water.
As for the property of being a cause of destruction, it is to be established either by you or by me alone.
In that case, a specific reason must be stated;
for if such a reason exists, then because there is no subsequent apprehension when a jar or similar object has perished, that [reason] would be the cause of its destruction.
This applies equally to self-destruction, since there is likewise no apprehension due to its non-arising.

For, by the very indication of their respective enumeration, the clay, the jar, the form (*rūpa*), and so forth, when arising in the form of a jar, receive the designation "jar. Yet, once they have perished, since [existence] is a property (*dharma*) of arising itself, what obstacle could there be to the obstruction of destruction such that it might persist for even the shortest duration of time? [Otherwise], it would not experience destruction immediately upon arising; for, given its immediate non-existence, it would possess that very nature, just like the moment of destruction.
(Compare: p. 529–1;
compare: p. 528–2)
"If it has perished, what obstacle to its destruction is there? And if it has not [perished], it will certainly not perish"—
this portion is also cited in the *Siddhasenīya-vṛtti* on the *Tattvārtha-sūtra*, page 329, as noted in the *Prabhāvitau*.
If its nature is existence, what obstacle could there be to its destruction that would cause it to persist even for the shortest moment? If there is no such obstacle, it will certainly not perish.
Furthermore, if it is not accepted in this way, then that [entity] would never perish, as before;
yet there is an obstacle—the non-presence of the cause of destruction.

What is the cause of destruction for what? For example, the striking against a stone or similar object is the cause of destruction for a jar, while contact with fire is the cause of destruction for the color and other qualities of earth and for water.
Regarding the point that "the state of being a cause of destruction belongs to you" and "it belongs to me myself," you must state the specific reason for that distinction;
for if such a reason exists, then that [specific cause] would be the cause of the destruction of a jar or similar object, since [destruction] is not perceived subsequently [without it].
Even though their destruction is identical, there is likewise no perception [of them] due to non-arising; for,

as indicated by the respective enumeration, the color and other qualities of the earthen jar itself, when arising in the form of a jar, receive the designation "jar," whereas once they have perished, they are nothing but ashes due to that very cessation of arising.
"Distinct in two ways" (dviśiṣṭa):

if it were not so, it would never perish. The commentary on this, up to the words "as before," establishes a proof for an undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭāpādana*) against one who does not accept this; thus the meaning is already explained.
One who maintains that impermanent things endure for a period of time says: "There is an obstacle to destruction."

Who is this [person]? Desiring to explain by means of that very [example] the absence of a cause for destruction, he asks: "What is the cause of destruction for what, such that through its presence or absence there occur destruction or non-destruction?

He would reply: "For example, in the case of a jar," and so forth; the impact of a stone, a mallet, or the like is the cause of the jar's destruction; the conjunction with fire is the cause of the destruction of the color and other qualities of earthy things as well as of water; when that [cause] is present, there is destruction, and when it is absent, there is persistence.
Comparison, page 529–1; in our manuscript,
"pra" [is read as] "vināśa" in the edition of Yaśas.
"There is conjunction" [is the claim].
To this it is replied: "The state of being a cause of destruction is yet to be proven.

How is it to be proven? You say that the destruction of a jar occurs through the impact of a stone and so forth, while the destruction of the color and other qualities of earth, as well as water, occurs through contact with fire; whereas I maintain that it occurs by itself. Between us two, whose word is the truth? Therefore, because it is unestablished for one or the other, how can it be determined that this is indeed a valid reason? A specific reason must be stated.
Comparison, page 529—1.

˚smadyabhi˚ Yaśomitra.

Regarding the phrase "by itself," another [opponent] says that there is a specific cause for destruction; for when that [cause] exists, there is no subsequent perception, whereas when it is absent, there is perception, and when it is present, there is no perception— thus, in the case of the destruction of a jar or similar objects, it is determined that this very thing is the cause.

To this it is replied: This is not a proving argument, because even on our own position, where there is self-destruction, the non-perception of those [atoms] when they are non-existent is exactly the same.

Why? Because there is no perception due to their not being produced in that manner; there is perception prior to impact and so forth because they are produced in that manner, and there is non-perception afterwards because they are not produced in that manner when those [impacts] are present.

In what way does such-and-such a state come about, and what is the cultivation [of it]? To this he says: because of the instruction according to their respective order, the form and other qualities of an earthen jar—since earth is the cause of their destruction—are suppressed there by the impact of stones and other such things, which brings about the production of other forms and qualities.
Other [factors], such as color and so forth, do not arise in that same manner;
therefore, at that time, there is no apprehension of it as a jar,
because it has not been destroyed by that impact.
Likewise, even the earthy elements such as color and so forth do not arise in that manner due to the efficacy of contact with fire;
similarly, for water as well, contact with fire is the cause for the cessation of further production in its continuum,
while the destruction of those already produced occurs spontaneously.
A jar or similar object perishes by itself because it has been produced, like the flame of a lamp;
for instance, it is held that the very birth of entities is the cause of their destruction—so how could that which has been born and is not yet destroyed perish later? By what [cause] would it do so?

There are five colors, six tastes, and two smells; there are eight touches; and in the remaining elements—water, fire, and air—these qualities are progressively fewer. This means that whichever number applies to whichever element, it is according to their respective order and as far as possible.

It is precisely the [elements] such as visible form (*rūpa*) that, arising in the shape of a jar, receive the designation "jar" due to a specific configuration of the aggregate. Furthermore, these [elements] perish by themselves, because arising itself is the cause of their destruction. In that regard, when struck by a stone or similar object, the production of other visible forms and so forth occurring within the continuum is obstructed. Consequently, due to the condition of the impact, other visible forms and so forth do not arise again in that manner; thus, because the continuum has ceased, at that time—during the moment of impact—the visible forms and so forth are no longer perceived as a jar. Therefore, by that impact, the jar is not destroyed.

The same applies to earth as well, and so forth; regarding those [elements] such as form (*rūpa*) and the rest, the process of cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is identical. Here, the capacity of the connection with fire acts as a cause for the cessation of other forms and qualities that are about to arise in that continuum, but it is not the destroyer of those that have already arisen.

Likewise, in the case of water, the connection with fire is the cause for the cessation of the further arising of such [qualities] in its continuum; the destruction of those already arisen occurs spontaneously.

However, because the final waters possess an extremely dense continuity and lack the capacity to produce a further continuum, there is a total destruction [of that specific series], since no other waters arise to replace them.

Thus, the destruction of things that have arisen occurs by themselves alone, because they are not destroyed by anything else; this is according to the sequence [of the text]. (Compare with page 530–1).
Regarding the comparison on page 529:
because it is the cause of destruction,
there, through the impact of stones and the like, the production of other qualities such as color-form (*rūpa*) is obstructed.
Other [factors], such as color and so forth, do not arise in that same manner;
therefore, at that time, there is no apprehension of it as a pot,
because it has not been destroyed by that impact.
Likewise, even the earthy elements such as color and so forth do not arise in that manner due to the power of contact with fire;
similarly, for water as well, contact with fire is the cause for the cessation of its further production in that continuum,
while the destruction of those already produced occurs spontaneously.
A jar or similar object perishes by itself because it has been produced, like the flame of a lamp; for instance,
it is held that the very birth of entities is the cause of their destruction.
That which has arisen and is not yet destroyed might later perish; by what means could that be?
In this regard, [the verse says]:
"When there is arising, it ceases. *Abhidharmapradīpa* (Abhi-pra).
Therefore, a pot is [an example],
because it is earthen; likewise,
its production is [an example] because it is produced.
Likewise, even an atom,
and likewise a part,
[is] at the end the cause for the cessation of the further arising of that; thus [it is said].
But for the final waters, because they are not thought of, there is no *bhā*;
because they are thought of, there is *bhā*.
Thus it is for the others as well.

Here he asks: How is this to be understood—that when causes of destruction such as being struck are observed, jars and the like perish by themselves and are not destroyed by that cause? One must be convinced of their self-perishing through an oath; see page 62, line 12 of the commentary. This is now demonstrated by inference: "A jar and the like perish by themselves, because they have come into existence, like the flame of a lamp. This is the inference.
This scripture (*āgama*) also serves as a witness, corroborating that very meaning, as follows: "For birth alone... and so forth.

Likewise: "Therefore, in that case, because form and the rest perish at every moment, they lack reality (*asattva*) due to their being unreal in their true nature, just like a collection (*samudāya*).

For just as a collection lacks reality because there is no occurrence of it as a non-differentiation of space (*deśa*), so too form and the rest lack reality because there is no occurrence of them as a non-differentiation of time; the meaning is that form and the rest do not persist through a non-differentiation of the time characterized by their own form.
If that form were such that it remained as form in the same way throughout, then it might be called "form" at the second moment and subsequent moments on the grounds that "this is that";
however, this [subsequent state] has fallen into a succession of absences and is therefore non-existent, like a collection (*samudāya*).
Just as a collection is non-existent in its own right apart from the form and other constituents, so too is form [non-existent], because its referent does not persist as a distinct reality.
When a clod of earth is thrown upward, there is a cause for its rising,
but there is no cause for its falling other than the cause of its being thrown upward;
therefore, it is established that for forms and the like, destruction consists simply in their arising at every moment.
"For it is birth itself that is accepted as the cause for the destruction of entities;
and how could that which has been born and not yet destroyed be destroyed later by anything?
(Sūtrakṛtāṅga-vṛtti composed by Ācārya Śīlāṅka, p. 24).

Therefore, since form and the other aggregates are thus subject to destruction at every moment, they lack reality because their nature is not as it appears; they are non-existent in the same way that a collection [is non-existent].

For just as a collection lacks existence because there is no occurrence of an undifferentiated location in such a manner, so too form and the rest lack existence because there is no occurrence of an undifferentiated time in such a manner—that is to say, because form and the rest do not persist through time.
If that form were truly form, and form were truly form, then it would remain that form in the second moment and subsequent moments; only if it remained so could it be called "form" on that basis.
But this [entity], having fallen into a succession of absences, is non-existent like a collection;

just as a collection is non-existent in its own right while being merely the [aggregation of] form and so forth, so too is form [non-existent], because its object does not abide as a separate reality. As it is said:
"When a clod of earth is thrown down, there is a cause for its production."
And regarding the *leḍa* (clod of earth), there is a comparison on pages 529–2,
for it has been said: "Just as when a clod of earth is thrown, there is a cause for its being thrown."

"There is no cause for falling other than the cause of lifting"—just as here, even though there is throwing down, there is also lifting; so too, we describe birth alone as the cause of destruction and nothing else. Thus, there is no lack of a cause for destruction, because it has birth as its cause. And since its emergence itself is the cause of destruction, this verse also is well-established: "Thus these conditioned phenomena arise with a cause."
"That which things arise from is indeed their very being"—thus [it is stated] in Candrakīrti’s *Madhyamakavṛtti*, pp.
222–223: "In falling, there is no cause other than the cause of its upward projection."

In the reading *pra*, there is no *anyākhyukkhakāya*. What follows from that? From that, since there is such momentary perishability (*pratikṣaṇanaśvaratā*) therein, there is the state of being unreal for form (*rūpa*) and the other [sensory objects]. Because their reality is unreal, the object—namely form and the rest—is non-existent in the same way as a composite whole (*samudāya*), because it does not exist in that manner through the nature of occurring without spatial differentiation. That unreality of the object is so called because momentary perishability has been stated [to be its defining characteristic].
And therefore, due to its lack of reality as it appears, it is non-existent; how so? Like a collection (*samudāya*).

This is explained as follows: Just as form and the other [sensory objects], though existing as form and so forth, do not exist as a collection such as a "jar" because they are not distinct in location, so too, because there is an absence of the occurrence of such non-distinct locations, the collection—which exists only conventionally (*saṃvṛtisat*)—is ultimately non-existent.

Likewise, even though form and so forth exist as the ultimate reality of form and so forth, the ultimate reality of form and so forth exists indeed in a single moment; however, it does not wait for another moment because of temporal difference—just as the form of the subsequent moment is entirely different from the form of the preceding moment—and the same applies to taste and the rest. Therefore, due to the absence of existence without temporal difference, they do not exist like a collection which lacks existence without spatial difference. To clarify this, he says: "the meaning is that [they do not exist] because of the non-difference of the time-forms of form and so forth."

Because it does not persist into a subsequent time, its form cannot be described as "this is that very same thing," since it is absolutely different [from itself at a later time], just like taste and other qualities.

To establish its difference [from the previous moment] by means of an *āvīta* (negative) inference, he says: "Having constructed it through conceptualization, it might be thus, if it were so"—for example: if that form (*rūpa*) were, at some time in the second moment and so forth, exactly as it was in its own nature—that is, if it were a form consisting of form alone, distinct from taste and the rest, and existed in that very essence as form; if it were so, then, having established it as "that," it would be called "form. But it does not exist, because it perishes every moment. What then? This restriction is established as a specific negation through non-existence. Is it then merely non-existence? No; rather, the meaning of "non-existence" is...

That which is its non-existence at every moment—that very existence [of it] consists in a mode of being that is the opposite of absolute non-existence; how then could it be considered a lack of purpose?
It would not fail to exist moment by moment, because it is not absolutely non-existent, like a sky-flower.
[Objection: But surely, like the doctrine of eternalism (*nityavāda*), this designation of "existence" is only applicable if there is actual being.

Otherwise, how could there be any designation for this [entity] which lacks the characteristic of being? Or, if its object were non-existence (*abhāva*), then another object—denotable by the word "this" (*asya*)—would have to be connected [to it], because non-existence requires a substratum; otherwise, antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and destructive non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) would be without a substratum.

For indeed, that form which exists as part of a continuous succession cannot exist in that very same moment; nor can it exist again in another moment, for having existed, it does not exist again, and thus, being permeated by a succession of non-existences, it is non-existent like a mere collection,
since it is perceived differently according to the distinction of place.
See the correction on page 314,
note 2: *pratipakṣanaśva* for *pratipakṣena*.
Tulanā 516–2:
Thus, the restriction is restricted by non-existence as a specific qualification. Is that then merely non-existence? No;

for the meaning of "non-existence" is that which is the non-becoming at every moment, and its becoming is likewise a mode of existence contrary to absolute non-existence. How, then, could it be considered a lack of purpose?
It would not exist moment by moment, because it would be an absolute non-existence, like a sky-flower.
Now, surely that designation of "becoming" (bhavana) is applicable only if there is existence, as in the case of the doctrine of permanence;
otherwise, how could there be any description of this thing which lacks the characteristic of becoming?

Or, the meaning is that "this" [the object] has non-existence (abhāva) as its property; thus, another entity denotable by the word "this" is connected [to non-existence], because it serves as the substratum (āśraya) for non-existence. Otherwise, prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) and destructive non-existence (pradhvaṃsābhāva) would be without a substratum. Indeed, one cannot exist without depending on an existent entity.

Having concluded the explanation for the sake of clarification, he states the proof: "Just as the aggregate, though itself non-existent in its own nature, [is perceived] in relation to color-form and so forth"—this is the example. "In the same way, color-form also"—this is the statement of the thesis (sādhyanirdeśa), because the phrase "itself non-existent" continues to apply.

The reason is "because its objects do not abide as distinct entities. Since it functions moment by moment, its objects do not abide as distinct entities; therefore, form is non-existent in its own nature, being non-existent as the intrinsic nature of form.
Is "form-form" non-existent?
Is form non-existent in its own nature? Or is "form-form" non-existent in its own nature?
In this way, the restriction is established by means of non-existence; the specific [characteristics] such as form and so forth are thus determined.

Now, since there is no specific distinction [between them], is it not simply a restriction? Is it indeed non-existence (*abhāva*) itself? No, it is said; rather, it is the "object of non-existence" (*abhāvārtha*), meaning that which is both non-existence and an object, or existence (*bhāva*).

How so? That which is the non-existence of that entity such as form (rūpa) at every moment—that very existence of it, occurring moment by moment, being an occurrence contrary to absolute non-existence (atyantābhāva) such as a sky-flower, how could it be non-substantiality or lack of reality? What would happen then? It would be this: it would not exist; it would not exist moment by moment, because of its being an absolute non-existence, like a sky-flower. And this is undesirable, because of the specific admission that "it does not exist, it does not exist" at every moment. Therefore, that non-existence is an existent thing and a real entity, because its occurrence is contrary to the absolute non-existence of things like sky-flowers.
This is that; that is this.
The absolute non-existence of a sky-flower.

Now, [the passage beginning with] "nanu saityādi" (But is it not so... shows that this [entity] is permeated by the process of becoming (*bhavana*). In the doctrine of absolute difference at every moment, just as in the doctrine of permanence (*nityavāda*), so too here—just as in the Sāṅkhya and other doctrines of permanence where "form is indeed form, form is indeed one," so here also "that very form is indeed form," and so forth—the designation of "becoming" (*bhavana*) is applicable only if there is existence (*sattva*). Otherwise, how could there be for this [entity], which is absolutely distinct and devoid of any absolute continuity, the designation "it becomes" (*bhavati*)? For how could there be even a mention (*upākhyā*) of something that is not characterized by the characteristic of "becoming"? Far from being possible, the designation "it exists" (*bhāva*) is simply not tenable.
The passage ending with *etadantargataḥ* is not present in the Bhāṣya manuscript;
the passage from *°vikṣaṇādeya°* to *etadantargataḥ* is not present in the Ya manuscript.

Of one who is entirely devoid of passion (*sattva*), or of one who is entirely devoid of being (*sattva*)? Of one who is devoid of characteristics (*lakṣa*)? Or of one who is devoid of existence (*bhāva*)?

Alternatively, it may be a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has non-existence as its object" (*abhāvo vārtho'sya*). Or, in the analysis "non-existence is its object," another object denoted by the word "its" (*asya*) is connected with that which is non-existent, because a *bahuvrīhi* refers to something external [to its constituent members].

Why? Because non-existence requires a substratum; thus, only an existent entity (*bhāva*) is capable of being the locus for prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and non-existence after destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*). Alternatively, the negative particle (*nañ*) used as an adjunct to denote that [non-existence] is not possible without an existent entity.

Now, it may be argued that an object consisting of form and so forth, even while momentariness exists, cannot come into being without non-existence, nor can non-existence come into being, because it has the negative particle (*nañ*) as its prefix, like "non-Brahmin" (*abrāhmaṇa*). [Objection: If this is so, how is there confidence when an object such as a son or a jar has arisen, and how is there lack of confidence when it has perished? [Reply: Indeed, this worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) has no objective basis at all, because it is impossible for it to exist in a thing that is momentary, as has been stated.
In this very way, the cultivation of detachment is possible, and this undertaking is for that purpose;
however, conventional discourse concerns the continuum,
wherein arising occurs through the arising of the great [elements] and destruction occurs through their destruction— [processes that are] subtle and to be inferred.

"Great arising" and "subtle arising"—destruction is likewise [distinguished as] great or subtle. Regarding the arising and destruction of the continuum (*santāna*), "greatness" refers to its manifestation;
in great arising there is confidence, while in destruction there is lack of confidence.

For the state of being inferable must indeed have the other two [past and future] as its substratum, just as the investigation into the existence or non-existence of form and so forth has a single momentary cognition as its substratum.

Otherwise, antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and destructive non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) would be without a substratum; yet these two are accepted, for antecedent non-existence and destructive non-existence cannot possibly exist without depending upon a positive entity (*bhāva*), since they are specific types of non-existence and thus differ from absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*).

And that substratum is indeed the referent of those two [negations], because they are described as being non-existent prior to their state of arising, existent at the time of arising, and subsequently non-existent;

thus, they can only be the antecedent negation (*prāgabhāva*) and the negation of destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*). Alternatively, even if the word "negation" itself is taken as the referent, it cannot function without an underlying entity (*bhāva*).

[Objection: But surely an object, such as form and so forth, even while possessing momentariness, cannot exist without non-existence, nor can non-existence come into being, because it has the negative particle (*nañ*) as its prefix, like "non-Brahmin" (*abrāhmaṇa*). [Reply: If this is so, how is there confidence when an object such as a son or a jar has arisen, and how is there lack of confidence when it has perished? [Objection: Surely this worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) has no objective basis at all, since it is impossible for a thing that is momentary. [Reply: As has been stated...
In this very way, the cultivation of detachment is possible, and this undertaking is for that purpose;
however, conventional usage is merely a matter of the continuum,
wherein arising occurs through the arising of the great [elements] and destruction through their destruction, both of which are subtle and to be inferred.
"Great arising" and "subtle arising"—destruction is likewise [divided into] great and subtle.
Regarding the arising and destruction of the continuum (*santāna*), "greatness" refers to its gross manifestation, while "subtlety" refers to its subtle operation.
In the case of great arising, there is confidence; in the case of destruction, there is no confidence.
In the other two cases, there is indeed inferability; thus, in these two [cases], [it is so]. Bhāṣya.
Yaśas. These two.

Furthermore, since a negation (*nañ*) following a term or its derivative signifies that very object, non-existence (*abhāva*) cannot prevail without existence (*bhāva*); thus, the employment of a negation with an existent term is established as having a real referent because it expresses a prohibition, and does not concern an unreal object.

[Objection: But surely the object is an existent thing such as form (*rūpa*), and even though momentariness exists, an object such as form is an existent and does not fail to prevail; indeed, it is quite capable of existing.

Furthermore, non-existence (*abhāva*) cannot function as a [real] entity, because it has the negative particle (*nañ*) as its prefix, just like "non-Brahmin" (*abrāhmaṇa*). Just as the designation "non-Brahmin" refers to someone other than a Brahmin, so too the designation "non-existence" would logically refer to something other than the existence of form and so forth; this is possible only if momentariness (*kṣaṇikatā*) truly exists. Thus, since existence itself is permeated by non-existence in the sense that "it does not exist," the objectivity of what is unreal—namely, non-existence—follows from the existence of form and so forth.
(Note: *ratho pra* and *°nucitvobhā* appear to be scribal corruptions or fragments.)
Someone who is unaccustomed [to this] says: "But if this is so," and so forth.

If, due to momentariness, there is non-existence, how could there be this confidence—such as "it has happened"—regarding an object like a son or a jar that has arisen, [thinking], "I must do this by me, I must do that"? And how could there be the lack of confidence regarding those things that are burnt, dead, or destroyed, [thinking], "the task is finished"? This worldly transaction would not be possible, because [momentary things] lack an objective domain.
Alternatively, if this conventional discourse has an object, confidence is appropriate when sons and so forth are non-momentary, whereas there is no confidence if they were to perish at another time.

To this it is replied: Surely this conventional discourse has no object at all, because it is impossible for it to apply to a momentary entity, as previously stated. Just as the aggregate of form and so forth does not exist due to the absence of its occurrence as an undifferentiated spatial location, so too it does not exist due to the absence of its occurrence as an undifferentiated temporal duration; thus, by the aforementioned logic, since form and the rest are non-existent, how could there be any scope for the conventional discourse of confidence or lack of confidence? In this very way, the cultivation of detachment is consistent with the hostility toward passion and other defilements that cause *saṃsāra*, arising from a sense of indifference toward the body, kinsmen, wealth, and so forth, due to a lack of confidence in anything whatsoever; and it is for this purpose that this undertaking is begun—thus, there is an accumulation of merit even within the state of momentariness.
It would not occur;
see page 798, line 3:
"consolation and consolation" (āśvāsanāśvāsa). Original.
In that case, the two [origination and destruction] do not exist at all as subtle, because they lack a cause, like a flower in the sky.
[Objection: It is unestablished that subtle origination and destruction lack a cause, because they are mutual causes;
birth is the cause of destruction, and destruction is the cause of birth, since the two exist simultaneously. For:

Just as the destruction and arising [of the two ends] of a scale occur simultaneously, like the rising and falling of its two pans, so too is the establishment of the continuum (saṃtāna). Otherwise, there would be neither cause nor action;
for all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are momentary—how can there be action for those that do not endure?

What is the nature of those for whom this [existence] exists? That very activity is itself called the agent, and that which was stated regarding its being outside the scope of conventional discourse does not hold; for it is joined with conventional discourse by way of the relative truth (*saṃvṛti*), since conventional discourse has the continuum (*saṃtāna*) as its object.

In order to determine the scope of that [consciousness], he conceptualizes arising and destruction as follows: "subtle arising through gross arising, and subtle destruction through gross destruction. Because each of these two is twofold, there is a fourfold division; he demonstrates this by stating, "gross arising and subtle arising," and by extending the same principle to destruction with the phrase, "destruction is also thus," thereby showing their distinction. The subtlety of arising and destruction within the continuum of the gross is due to the operation of those two; for one observes the operation of those two—gross arising and destruction—just as one does in the case of hunger and satiety.

In that regard, when there is the production of something large—such as a son or a jar within a continuum—there is confidence; upon its destruction, there is lack of confidence. As for the other two, namely subtle production and destruction, they are to be inferred like the cessation of the error [of movement] inferred from inhalation and exhalation; thus, "large production" and "destruction" are established. (Pratītyasamutpādahṛdayavyākhyā)

The other says: "In that case, the subtle [states] do not exist at all because they lack a cause, like a sky-flower; therefore, those two—destruction and origination—which exist within the continuum, must have causes. Origination is like that of a jar on a potter's wheel, and destruction is like that of a jar struck [by a hammer].
To this, it is replied: "The lack of a cause for subtle origination and destruction is unproven, because they are mutually causal."

He explains this: "Birth is the cause of destruction, and destruction follows from birth; because these two occur simultaneously, what is the illustration? To this he says: "Because destruction and production are simultaneous, just like the depression and elevation of the ends of a balance scale. Just as one end of a balance scale sinks while the other rises at the very same moment, so too do the production of one form and the destruction of another form occur.

In this very way, the establishment of a continuum (*saṃtāna*) occurs through the uninterrupted succession of simultaneous arising and perishing, because it exists continuously and without interruption due to the lack of gap between forms; otherwise, according to the aforementioned reasoning, there would be no cause, since in the case of arising and perishing being non-abiding in every respect, there would be no action due to the absence of an agent or an actor. (Note: *mṛṇoti* in Bhāṣya;
*sṛṇoti* in Ya.)

To provide a corroborating proof for this meaning—that existence is subject to destruction—he states the verse: "All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are momentary. Because their arising has a cause, conditioned phenomena are born from conditions (*pratyaya*).

For those things that exist for only a single moment and do not persist into a second moment, how could there be action (*kriyā*)? What, then, is the action accepted in the world when one says, "A jar is being made," or "The potter performs the act of making a mat," and so forth? To this it is replied: For those [things] whose very arising (*bhūti*) is their birth (*janman*), that [arising] itself is the action, and that same [arising] is the agent (*kāraka*). It is said that arising itself is the cause of destruction, because it brings about its own cessation by itself. This is merely for the purpose of making it known. (Jñānaprasthāna, Chapter on the Second Moment).
For those who are thus established,
there might also be the reading here: "What is the restrainer (vāraka), or what is the agent (kāraka)?"
"It brings about" means that birth is of such a nature;
for one thing after another, such as form and so forth, is seen arising through direct perception itself, just as it is seen when water is flowing.
Now, if it were like a continuum, then even amidst subtle arising and destruction, the entity—form and so forth—would still be visible.
Or rather, the continuum would not be perceived as persisting during the interval between its own arising and destruction, like subtle arising and destruction;
for indeed, there is nothing that is impossible when it is actually observed.
To explain:
If [something] has arisen in a single moment,
its destruction at the end is observed; therefore, its destruction at the beginning is inferred, just as in the case of a lamp-flame.

Alternatively, this matter is not to be established by reasoning because it is directly perceived; for it is seen through direct perception itself that form and the other [sensory objects], as they arise, are indeed distinct from one another. For example: "It flows as if in water. Just as in the case of rivers and the like, the flowing water comes as something new and distinct at every moment, while what has passed away is simply gone; yet, due to the uninterrupted flow of the stream, a false cognition arises in the mind of a dull-witted person that "it is the very same [water]. In the same way, regarding all forms and the rest, there is a similar flow of water.
Regarding this, [the author] says in the *Bhāṣya*: "Now, like a continuum," and so forth.

Just as a continuum (*santāna*) is observed to persist between its own arising and destruction, so too should an entity such as form (*rūpa*) be observed to persist between its own subtle arising and destruction; for these subtle arising and destruction would be the causes for their own designations while being perceived within their own interval, because they are instances of arising and destruction, like the arising and destruction of a continuum. Alternatively, the arising and destruction occurring in a continuum would be the causes for their own designations while not being perceived within their own interval, because they are instances of arising and destruction, like subtle arising and destruction.
Regarding the phrase *labhyavyapa* / *ālambavyapa* in the Bhāṣya, it is said here: "Indeed, there is nothing that is untenable when it is directly perceived."

For it has been said: due to dullness of intellect, the appearance of a non-existent continuum as persisting like the flow of a stream is not to be challenged simply because it is seen through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Indeed, it is not appropriate to maintain a position contrary to direct perception by disregarding that which is the foremost of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), since direct perception cannot be sublated by any other means of valid cognition.

To provide further supporting evidence for this point, he states the explanatory verse beginning with "tathāhi" (for instance): "If [an entity] were born in a single moment... This means that if origination itself were not the cause of destruction, then—just as it persists through a second moment and so forth—it would persist eternally due to the absence of any cause for its destruction; however, this is not the case.

Therefore, it is established that origination itself is the cause of the self's destruction, and its destruction is the cause for the subsequent origination. Thus, it is logically proven by observation that external entities such as form (*rūpa*) and the like are momentary.
That which is established in the seen;
page 802, line 10;
*śroto* (stream); manuscript reading.
[From the *Saṃvādādyupadeśa*:

Therefore, by these two very [processes] of great arising and destruction produced within the continuum (*saṃtāna*), subtle arising and destruction are to be inferred at every moment. For example: because decay is observed at the end, decay at the beginning is inferred, as in the case of a lamp-flame. Just as a lamp-flame, having begun to decay from the moment of its production, is completely extinguished even in a windless place at the end; and it has been stated that if it were to persist for another moment, it would never be extinguished, yet it is indeed extinguished entirely.
Therefore, starting from the very beginning, it is inferred that [the jar] has ceased, or rather, it is perceived as such;

likewise, even a jar or similar object [is seen to cease] from its birth. And this method (naya) accepts that "it becomes something else at every moment"; thus, it desires both [the permanence and the change] as a rule.

Furthermore, regarding the fourfold classification of categories (nikṣepa), it adopts the category of existence (bhāva-nikṣepa)—that is, functional utility (upayoga)—from the perspective of non-scriptural tradition (anāgamataḥ), because for this *evaṃbhūta* method, functional utility constitutes a single part of its definition.
This is the distinction between the modes (*paryāya*) and the root-standpoints (*mūla-naya*).
It is called *paryāya* because it extends (*ayate*) everywhere through its various modes; that which has "existence" (*asti*) as its object through these modes is the *Paryāyāstika*.
Indra exists only at the time of experiencing Indra-hood or at the time of employing that [name], whereas at other times he is not Indra, because being that [state] constitutes his very nature.

Furthermore, in this context, since a thing passes away moment by moment, the object present in the intellect is the meaning of the word; thus it begins to perish and is seen to reach its end in destruction.
Likewise, it has been stated that cognition (*buddhi*) is also momentary; thus, the object is momentary, having ceased.

Furthermore, this *naya* maintains that "it becomes something else at every moment"; thus, it accepts both [the persistence and the change] as a rule. Within the fourfold classification (*nikṣepa*), it adopts the conceptualization of the substantial (*bhāva*) *nikṣepa*—namely, *upayoga*—from the perspective of the *anāgamata* [naya], because for the *evambhūta-naya*, *upayoga* constitutes its very essence.
This is the distinction between the modes (*paryāya*) and the root-standpoints (*mūla-naya*).
It is called *paryāya* because it extends everywhere through its various modes;
that which has "existence" (*asti*) as its object is the *paryāyāstika*.
Indra exists only at the time of experiencing Indra-hood or at the time of employing it; at other times, he is not Indra, because that state itself constitutes his being so.
