In this context, since a real entity passes away moment by moment, the object present in the intellect is the meaning of the word; this is now applied according to the perspective of the *naya*—beginning with "And this," and so forth.

And this *nayavāda* (perspectival approach) maintains that [an entity] exists only by becoming different at every moment; therefore, it seeks both "determination" (*niyata*)—meaning it performs and regulates—and "restriction" (*niyama*). Furthermore, regarding the fourfold deposition (*nikṣepa*), it accepts the following: from the perspective of non-scriptural (*anāgama*) conceptualization, it accepts the "substantial" (*bhāva*) deposition as actual existence (*bhāva*), the "functional" (*upayoga*) deposition as the state arising from the subsidence-cum-destruction of karma (*kṣāyopaśamika-bhāva*), and the "modal" (*pāriṇāmika*) deposition as existence manifested through function (*upayoga-sādbhūta*) characterized by consciousness (*vijñāna*), as well as external objects such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth.

This is because the *evambhūta-naya* (the "such-as-it-is" approach) is but a single part of the functional (*upayoga*) approach, and thus it is distinguished from the scriptural (*āgama*) and non-functional (*anupayoga*) *evambhūta* approaches.
"Thus, it distinguishes between the expression, the meaning, and both of them" (Āvaśyaka-niryukti 758); because this is a general definition,
it is a division of the root *paryāya* [naya], since *paryāya* is derived from the sense of "to go around" (*pari-ayate*) or "to proceed through successive states" (*paryayata*).
He who holds that "this object exists as being identical with its utility" is a *paryāyāstika*; this is the *naya*. (Yaśastilaka 2.103) [Variant: *upayogasādrūpaṃ*].
The arrival of that which is wonderful;
that arrival which is through non-application, and that arrival which is through application.
Comparison: Page 24, line 6804, line 13; 518–2.
"The *evaṃbhūta* [naya] distinguishes between the word (*vaṃjana*), the meaning (*attha*), and both of them. Āvaśyaka-niryukti 758.
Now he states the *evaṃbhūta*: "The *evaṃbhūta* distinguishes between the word, the meaning, and both of them."

That by which something is manifested (*vyajyate*) or that which manifests (*vyanakti*) is the "manifestor" (*vyañjana*), namely the word; the object (*artha*), however, is its domain. Both of these—the word and the object—constitute the definition of the "word-and-meaning" (*śabdārtha*). A perspective (*naya*) of this kind qualifies [the object]; the point here is this: it qualifies the word by means of the meaning, and the meaning by means of the word.

And so the author of the Bhāṣya said: "The indicator (vyañjana) [specifies] the object by means of the meaning, and the object [specifies] the indicator by means of the indicator; just as the word 'pot' is specified by its activity, so too is that [activity] specified by that very [word]. (Viśeṣāvaśyaka-bhāṣya 2252). A brief explanation of this verse is as follows: the indicator, which is the word, specifies the object; the meaning is that it establishes [the word] in a state of necessity through the power of the object. The sense is that, in reality, it is only that word 'pot' which establishes a specific object endowed with activity.

Or, for example, the activity well-known as being denoted by the word "jar" (ghaṭa) should be understood as consisting of actions such as carrying water, performed by a jar placed upon the head of a woman or another person—based on the power of reflecting upon the etymological meaning that "it is a jar because it is joined together" (ghaṭanāt)—and not as consisting of the action of supporting its own location.

Thus, both [the word and the object] qualify one another—the word by means of the object, and the object by means of the word. Regarding this very point, he provides an example: "Just as the word 'jar' (*ghaṭa-śabda*), etc. Just as one restricts the word "jar" by means of the object characterized by action—that which truly is the word "jar" is that which conveys the object characterized by action—likewise, one also restricts that object by means of that very word; for instance, by the force of the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) that "it is a jar because it joins together" (*ghaṭanāt ghaṭaḥ*), the action consisting of the fetching of water by a jar mounted on the head of a woman or the like is to be understood as being denoted by the word "jar."

The etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) of the term *evambhūta* is as follows: the word *evaṃ* (thus) denotes a mode (*prakāra*). That which has become (*bhūta*) or attained that mode, exactly as it was etymologically derived, is an *evambhūta* word. By metaphorical extension (*upacāra*), the *naya* (perspective) whose primary concern is the substantiation of such [words] is also called *evambhūta*. The substantiation of the term *evambhūta* has already been demonstrated: when a word is etymologically derived for a particular meaning, that meaning is the "etymological occasion" (*vyutpattinimitta*). Only when that object exists in its own essential form (*svarūpataḥ*) does one intend for that word to apply to it, and not at other times. For example, a jar (*ghaṭa*) mounted on the head of a woman or another person, possessing a specific activity (*viśiṣṭaceṣṭā*) at the time of fetching water and so forth, is denoted by the word "jar," but nothing else is, because the latter lacks the occasion for the application of the word "jar," just like a cloth (*paṭa*) or similar objects. Likewise, in reality, only that which expresses an object possessing such activity should be regarded as the word "jar," and not anything else, because everything else is devoid of the object that constitutes its own denotation.
Thus, this verse [numbered] 2185 in the *Viśeṣāvaśyakabhāṣya* is the root text for the section on "Paryaya" in the *Āvaśyakaniryuktivṛtti* composed by Malayagiri, pages 377–378.
Or rather,
that object which is the domain of the intellect and is based upon an external thing, [is the referent].
Some maintain that the meaning of a word is known as an external object (VP 2.133). Furthermore, the meaning of a sentence is the sequence occurring within a continuum;
an example of this is "Indra," and so forth.

Indra is both non-Indra and Indra; according to the root *idi* (meaning "supreme sovereignty") in Pāṇini’s Dhātupāṭha (63), he is Indra only at the very moment of experiencing supreme sovereignty, and at other times he is non-Indra.
Or rather, he is the Indra of cognition (*upayoga*) only during the time of that cognitive application; immediately after that moment he is non-Indra due to its cessation.
There is no possibility for [the status of] Purandara and so forth, because both the cognition and its object are momentary.

Likewise, why was he Purandara at the time of the destruction of the city or during its utilization, but not Purandara at other times? Because that very state (bhāva) itself constitutes that [condition]; it is that same state which, having become functional, manifests as any one of the various modalities such as Purandara, and only at that specific moment and not at others—this is the intended meaning.

What is the meaning of a word here? To this it is said: Here, because an entity passes away at every moment, that object which resides in the intellect is the meaning of the word. Although an entirely different entity arises and passes away at every single moment, it persists in the intellect; and that momentary object residing in the intellect is what is meant by "form," "taste," "smell," and so forth. He cites another corroborating scripture as proof, since the various *nayavāda*s originate from the Jaina scriptures: "Or rather, that object which is the domain of the intellect," and so on. This is not further explained here, as its meaning follows from what has already been discussed.
The phrase "is accepted by some" means that this is the opinion of one who employs such a lack of scriptural authority;

or rather, it states the tenth position—that the object of a word is only that which is mounted upon the intellect and not something external—by saying: "Or, the object which is the domain of the intellect and is based on an external thing, when known as that external thing, is accepted by some as the meaning of a word."

Regarding the conceptual [object] that has ascended into the intellect (*buddhyupārūḍha*)—that which has ascended into the intellect and is based upon an external object; that is to say, it is such that its basis is the external object by way of generating a conceptual construction—and this conceptual object, through the power of delusion, is superimposed as having an external form, even though it is not external, being conceived in a single form as the perceived and the conceptualized. Thinking "I understand the very object thus superimposed from the word," it is accepted as the meaning of the word (*śabdārtha*), being caused by the word.

Thus, in the commentary on the *Vākyapadīya* composed by Puṇyarāja, [the phrase] "having the intellect as its object" (*buddhiviṣaya*) means existing within the intellect—that is, residing in the intellect. "Based on an external object" (*bāhyavastunibandhana*) means that which has an external object—whether existent or non-existent—as its basis; it is that which proceeds to demonstrate its own nature, which stands in the place of a written sign (*akṣaracihna*). That which is thus based on an external object is called "based on an external object."

The phrase "known as an external object" means that [the form] manifested as the nature of cognition is determined (adhyavasita) as being external. For instance, as long as the nature of cognition is not superimposed upon objects and is grasped merely as the nature of cognition through the contemplation of its true reality (*tattvabhāvanā*), its status as the meaning of a word is not apprehended; this is because there is an absence of connection with specific actions in that state. Indeed, actions such as "bring the cow" or "eat the curd" are not possible in such a nature of cognition, and it is an object capable of being connected with action that is denoted by words.

Therefore, according to the *Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā* (p. 285), the essential meaning of this verse is as follows: when [the object] is apprehended as having the form of cognition (*buddhi*), it is not the referent of the word; however, when it is projected onto an external object, the cognizer, being mistaken regarding its externality, considers it to possess the capacity to accomplish an action, and thus it becomes the referent of the word.

What, then, is the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*)? It is said: the meaning of a sentence is the sequence occurring within a continuum (*santāna*). That is, the sequence of arising and ceasing that exists within the continuum of consciousness and the continuum of external objects such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth, is the meaning of the sentence. [Question: Is it not the sequence of the successive utterance of the sounds of sentences, phonemes, words, and so on—their respective order of birth and cessation—that is the sequence? [Response: Thus [it is asked] by the opponent.

The connection [of this topic] is that from which its emergence proceeds, as follows: "O Venerable One! Is this Jewel-Luminosity Earth eternal or non-eternal? O Gautama! It is eternal in terms of substantiality (*dravyārthatayā*), but it is non-eternal in terms of color-modes (*varṇaparyāyaiḥ*), odor-modes (*gandhaparyāyaiḥ*), taste-modes (*rasaparyāyaiḥ*), touch-modes (*sparśaparyāyaiḥ*), and shape-modes (*saṃsthānaparyāyaiḥ*). (Jīvājīvābhigama Sūtra 3.1.78)
Thus ends the eleventh section, the "Destruction of Both [Views] regarding the Restriction.
Do not think that this is merely being stated according to one’s own imagination;

for the Jaina scripture also teaches thus. To show this, he says: "The basis from which its emergence occurs is as follows"—the passage beginning with "Imā ṇaṃ bhaṃte" has its meaning already explained, because it provides a description of the *paryāyas* (modes) as being non-eternal.
See the introduction, pages 450–451;
[the term] *aśāśvatena* is in the Jaina manuscript.
Thus ends and is completed the eleventh chapter, "The Refutation of Both [Views] regarding Restriction," in the *Nayacakra-ṭīkā*. Ya.
Oṃ Arhaṃ.
Salutations to the True Gurus. Now begins the twelfth chapter, "The Non-Restriction of Observances.
If [the object] were thus [non-existent] at the end due to destruction, then an admission of its established existence as a real entity would have been made.

In that case, it [the world] must be established as having a limit, because it does not transcend the constraints imposed by the establishment of the nature of things; for, like objects such as jars, it is established, and being established, it is also produced. Thus, those [objects] are dependent on previously existing entities, because they are actions, and therefore they have an end.

The subsequent system arises because of dissatisfaction with the views of the preceding system; it is undertaken because, through increasingly subtle analysis, one perceives defects in the former while maintaining the conceit that one's own position is more sound. Therefore, he says: "If, at the end, due to destruction... If you infer from the observation of destruction at the end that the very nature of an entity is such that it must perish even at the beginning, then what follows? From that, you have effectively accepted the established status of an entity, as in the case of an actual thing (*vastuvat*). Just as there is a well-known fact in the world regarding established things like jars and so forth—that they undergo destruction—so too have you accepted this. This is because both destruction and origination necessarily pertain to entities that are already established.

Otherwise, just as in the case of a donkey's horn, there would be an absence of both destruction and arising due to the absence of persistence, because there is no reconnection [of the entity]; for your own position is that "the becoming of what already exists is indeed persistence," as you have accepted through your own inclination.
Acceptance of what is well-known.

Therefore, because of this reason—that one does not transgress the rule established by the proof of the determination of real entities (*vastu*)—the determined entity is proven by you alone through the connection of arising and destruction; it remains fixed and necessarily participates in the designation of arising and destruction. It does not transgress this rule, which is established by its distinction from things like "sky-flowers. Thus, understand that it is "decidedly situated" (*niścayena sthitam*), "established" (*niṣṭhitam*), and "determined" (*vyavasthitam*) solely on the basis of your own statement. For this reason, he says: "In that case, it is established (*niṣṭhitam*), because it has an end, like an object such as a jar. This is the illustration: just as a jar certainly exists at the end of states such as the lump of clay, being indeed established because it has an end, so too is it [established] even in states such as the clay-clod.
Because it has reached completion, that object is "done" (*kṛtam*), just like an object such as a jar;

and because it is produced (*kṛtakatvāt*), it is also "begun" (*ārabdham*), just like an object such as a jar. Having thus established the states of beginning, action, and completion through the relationship of cause and effect, he summarizes them as being one and the same, saying "In this way, those... and so forth. The states of beginning, action, and completion are dependent upon a previously existing entity, because they are actions, and because they are "terminating" (*antavat*)—that is, like the end, as at the end. Just as at the end, at the time of cessation, the action of becoming, birth, or the acquisition of self-existence is dependent upon a previously existing entity, so too are the actions of beginning and the rest.
"It exists"— this restriction is not exceeded by Bhāti, nor is it exceeded by Ya; these are the Savitṛs of Pra.
Having summarized [it] in one place,
Bhāṣya says;
having summarized [it] in one place, Yaśomitra says?
Because of the state of having action; because of possessing action? [The reading] "pūrvanivṛtta" is in the manuscript (bhā).
Whence can there be action? Because of momentariness. For it has been said:
"All conditioned phenomena are momentary; how can there be action for those that do not endure?
That which is their very arising is itself the action, and that very thing is called the agent."
Let alone the acceptance of action and so forth;
the refutation of the doctrine of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅgavāda*) can be established simply by examining the true meaning of the word "momentary.

For the meaning of the word "momentary" is not tenable without a moment itself, nor with its possessor—the object that is its master. Therefore, the object must be a substantial entity (*dravyārtha*) that exists as the master of that moment and abides together with it.
No, for its status as the master [of the moment] is established only with respect to the successive states (paryāya), since the moment is twofold:
the moment of arising and the moment of destruction;
and the expression "immediately after" (tadanantaram) is intended to exclude any intermediate state of duration.

Regarding this [objection] concerning origination, the other says: "How can there be activity? Because of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*). Even at the end, activity is not admitted by me because of momentariness and because of being non-existent (*abhāvatva*) according to the method previously stated; how much less so in states such as the commencement of action, since a persisting entity is not admitted? For it has been said," and so forth—the proof consisting of the verse beginning with "All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are momentary" and so on—has its meaning already explained previously, and thus it is not explained again.
Regarding the state of non-abiding, it is said here: "Let that be for now," and so forth.

Let aside for now any other means—such as the acceptance of activities like destruction and origination as taught by the Dravyārthika-naya, or whatever else serves as a cause for establishing the stability of entities, or is capable of proving the absence of momentary flux (kṣaṇabhaṅga). Rather, the refutation of the doctrine of momentary flux can be accomplished simply by examining the true meaning of the word "momentary" (kṣaṇika). Why? Because the word "momentary" ends in the suffix *ṭhan*, which denotes a relationship between a thing and its owner characterized by possession (*astyastimad-sambandha*); therefore, in the absence of a stable referent, it would follow that the word has no denotable object at all.

He demonstrates this with the words "for [the word] 'momentary' (*kṣaṇika*)," and so forth. That which possesses a moment (*kṣaṇa*) is "momentary," just as that which possesses a staff (*daṇḍa*) is "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍika*). And just as the word "staff-bearer" would indeed be devoid of meaning without the staff—the object related to it—and without its owner, Caitra; in the same way, the word "momentary" is also devoid of meaning without the moment and without the object possessing it, which serves as its owner.

Lest that [moment] be rendered meaningless, there must be for that moment a master—denoted by a suffix such as *-mat* (possessing)—just as a staff belongs to Caitra; that object characterized as substantial (*dravyārtha*), which has the nature of persisting together with its modifications (*paryāya*) of arising and perishing as expounded in the Jaina scriptures, ought to exist like a substance (*dravya*) that persists while accompanied by those modifications. Otherwise, the etymological meaning of the word "momentary" (*kṣaṇika*)—namely, "that which possesses a moment" (*kṣaṇo 'syāsti*)—would not be logically consistent; however, it is consistent if the term refers to a persisting substance (*avasthātṛ-dravya*).
[Note: *darśanaṃsyokta-bhā-vāci-ut-pratya-pra-*.]
"From this [root], the suffixes -ini and -ittha [are applied]" (Pāṇini 5.2.115).

Comparison: As for this possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*) in the term "momentary" (*kṣaṇika*), how is it possible? If, according to the etymological rule, "destruction" (*kṣaya*) is the "moment" (*kṣaṇa*), and [the object] is called "momentary" because it possesses that moment—that is, because it has destruction—then that is not logical due to the difference in time. For when there is destruction, the thing possessing destruction does not exist; the possessive suffix is never seen to apply to two things existing at different times. Alternatively, if the entity itself, as qualified by immediate destruction, is called "momentary," even so, since that very thing cannot be identical to itself [in the subsequent moment], the possessive suffix is still not logical.
Nyāyavārttika 3.2.14

Regarding the state of being the substratum (*āśrayatva*) [of existence], it is appropriate here; to this, he says: No, for the status of ownership (*svāmitva*) is established only with respect to a mode (*paryāya*). Since one mode is the owner of its own other modes, the relationship between the possessor (*astimat*) and the possessed (*asti*) is logically consistent, and the suffix [denoting possession] has that as its referent.
He explains this with the words "for the moment is twofold," and so forth. The twofold nature consists of the moment of origination and the moment of destruction immediately following it;

this is the clarification of that [statement]. The expression "immediately following" (anantara) means that there is no interval between moments; that very [moment of destruction] is the subsequent state (paryāya) of that [preceding] state.
Even so, such a designation is not tenable, because the absence of one thing would likewise entail the absence of the other.
When a staff exists, Caitra also exists; in that case, it would be logical for him to possess it by virtue of that [staff].

But here, when the moment of origination occurs, the moment of destruction does not, and when the moment of destruction occurs, the moment of origination does not. Thus, it is not reasonable to designate the former by means of the latter.

Furthermore, as for the example that was stated, that too would apply to the two ends of a scale existing simultaneously; however, there can be no simultaneity between a moment that exists and one that does not exist, just like a jar and a sky-flower.
And because both [the perishing and the arising] would exist as neither too high nor too low, there would be simultaneity;
therefore, there is a lack of correspondence between the example and the thing exemplified.
If [the perishing] exists while perishing, it would coexist with that which is arising; if it does not exist, the lack of correspondence remains exactly as it was.

This is for the purpose of excluding [the notion of] abiding and for the purpose of demonstrating the fact that there is nothing whatsoever in the interval; its indicator has been stated previously— namely,
that the moment of destruction immediately following the moment of existence is itself the "existence" (asti) of that mode (paryāya), being a mode of that very mode.
Even so, this designation—that "the absence of one is [the presence] of the other"—is not logical, because the other is likewise non-existent.
When a staff exists, Caitra also exists; in that case, it would be reasonable for him to possess it.

But here, when the moment of origination occurs, the moment of destruction does not; and when the moment of destruction occurs, the moment of origination does not. Therefore, it is not logical to designate the former by means of the latter.

Furthermore, even the illustration that was stated would be applicable only if two ends of a scale existed simultaneously; however, there can be no simultaneity between two moments—one existing and one non-existing—just as there is none between a jar and a sky-flower.
Moreover, since "not high" and "high" exist [simultaneously], their simultaneity would follow [as a consequence].
Therefore, there is a lack of correspondence between the example and the subject of the illustration.

If [destruction] exists while [the entity] is perishing, there would be coexistence with that which is arising; if it does not exist, then let this same inconsistency be observed (see page 801, line 4):
"Destruction and arising are simultaneous, just like the lowering and raising of the two ends of a balance scale."

Thus, regarding two uninterrupted moments, that moment of destruction which immediately follows the moment of origination—when analyzed by the intellect through the delimitation of time up to the limit of the shortest duration—is that very thing which does not admit further division; this is the "moment" (paryāya) of that [substance] in its modal aspect (paryāya). Therefore, the word "momentary" (kṣaṇika) is meaningful because a moment depends upon another moment. Consequently, there is no fault in accepting the substantial aspect (dravyārtha), as it seeks an enduring object.
To this, it is replied: even so, the designation "momentary" in the sense that "it has a moment" is not logical, even when considering it in relation to another mode.

Why? Because in the absence of one, the other likewise does not exist; just as in the absence of a staff, Caitra is no longer called "staff-bearer" due to his own non-existence as such, so too, because at the time of the moment of destruction the moment of origination is absolutely non-existent, and vice versa, the moment of destruction does not possess the moment of origination, nor does the moment of origination possess the moment of destruction—just like Caitra’s non-existence when he is characterized by a donkey's horn.

When a staff exists and Caitra also exists, then Caitra’s possession of that staff—his being "staff-possessed" (*daṇḍavattā*) or "staff-bearer-ness" (*daṇḍikatā*)—is consistent with logical principle (*nyāyādanapetā*). This is an illustration by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyeṇa nidarśanam*). However, here, by the passage beginning with "when at the moment of origination," he demonstrates the lack of similarity (*asādharmya*) between the moments of origination and destruction, up until the point where it is stated that "designation based on the prior [state] is not tenable. The phrase *dyāpādapetā* [is] explained.
See page 813, line 4.

Furthermore, as for the illustration of the relationship between cause and effect stated thus: "Just as the destruction and arising [of the two ends of a scale] are simultaneous, like the descent and ascent of the two ends of a balance," that too would be appropriate only if the two ends of the scale were distinct entities existing simultaneously; however, there can be no simultaneity between a moment that exists and one that does not exist, any more than there is between a jar and a sky-flower. Likewise, if there were simultaneity between the descent and the ascent, it would imply their actual existence; therefore, the analogy and the subject of the analogy are inconsistent.
It might be argued: "There is no fault, because there is consistency when the destruction and the arising are simultaneous."
This is also incorrect: if [the entity] is existent while perishing, there would be co-existence with that which is arising; if it is non-existent, that same inconsistency remains.

Therefore, it is illogical to designate the former by means of the latter, saying "it has a moment (kṣaṇa), thus it is momentary (kṣaṇika)," for destruction and arising are simultaneous, just like the simultaneous lowering and raising of the two ends of a scale.
"na" is found in the Carya manuscript; "na" is found in the Bhāṣya manuscript regarding the two states of "not-arisen" (anutpanna) and "arisen" (utpanna).
This objection would be improper: that since one of the two remains, the designation is established.
Or, if there were some enduring entity for both, then [what would happen] if [something] were produced in a single moment?

thus, because there is no connection between two moments, the meaning of the word "momentary" does not exist if the word "immediately following" (anantara) is intended to exclude any intermediate state.
If it is produced in a single moment...
[then] its very acquisition of self-nature is immediately followed by destruction.
"Immediate destruction" (*anantara-vināśa*) means destruction that follows immediately; that which possesses this is "momentary" (*kṣaṇika*), and thus the word "momentary" is meaningful.

For there is no arising distinct from the destruction of form and the other aggregates; that which is arising is itself destruction. That which possesses this [arising/destruction] is "momentary," just as a sprout is said to possess arising.
And that sprout is not something other than its arising, because a sprout distinct from its arising is impossible;
likewise, that which is the arising is itself the destruction, and there is no moment of arising distinct from destruction.

This might be the objection: "Since one or the other of those two moments—precedent or subsequent—persists, the designation [of 'one'] is established. To this we reply: suppose there were some persisting entity for both moments; whether it be the latter or the former, let it be as you wish, and let it indeed persist. Even if that is accepted, the fault remains—the very fault expressed in your verse beginning with "tato yadyekasmin," namely, that because there is no cause for destruction, it would endure for infinite time.

Thus, since there is no connection between two moments, the meaning of the word "momentary" (*kṣaṇika*) would be non-existent; [this is the case] provided that the term "immediate" (*anantara*) is established as a designation for the purpose of excluding any intermediate state— this is the position of the opponent, as it occurs in each recitation of the *Abhidharmabhāṣya*.
See page 802, line 5:

"Now, as for 'the acquisition of self' (*ātmalābha*), etc."—if one thinks, "Let this fault not occur," [and thus proposes] "the moment of destruction immediately following production" (*utpattyanantaravināśakṣaṇaḥ*), then the word "immediately following" (*anantara*) refers to the very moment of production; that same moment of production is "immediately destroyed," because it is a coordinate compound (*samānādhikaraṇasamāsa*).
He demonstrates this with the passage beginning "immediate destruction" (*anantaraśca vināśaśca*) and so forth:

since the property of destruction belongs to that very acquisition of self-nature (*ātmalābha*), and because the [destruction] exists in relation to its correlate, the word "momentary" (*kṣaṇika*) is meaningful.
This is its explanation: "For there is no destruction of form and so forth," and so on, up to "it is momentary."

If it is asked, "Where is the status of this as a suffix expressing a relation observed? it is demonstrated: Just as it is said that "the sprout possesses arising," there is no arising distinct from the sprout here, nor is there a possessive suffix-meaning (*matup-artha*) distinct from the arising for that which is called "the sprout possessing arising. And yet, this designation is observed; therefore, showing that [the possessor] is not other than that [possession], he says: "And that sprout is not a different entity from arising. Why? Because a sprout distinct from arising is impossible.
(Compare *Tattvasaṃgraha*, p. 142, l. 20).
See page 810, line 12; page 810, line 21; page 811, line 24;
and page 808, line 11.
Where [is] the proof?
Manu,
showing the sequence, said:
"One who is afflicted by the calamity of [losing] his wife..."

To this we reply: your restatement of their doctrine, beginning with "Thus, those which are arising... and so on, up to "...because nothing other than arising is possible," is undesirable for you yourself. Why? Because by you—who are engaged in explaining the identification of the meaning of the word "momentary" (kṣaṇika)—that very [doctrine] has been destroyed.
How so? Because nothing other than arising is possible;
yet that [arising] is not the moment of anything, nor is that which is the moment [the arising].
Therefore, that momentariness does not exist at all;

consequently, this interpretation is untenable because it contradicts the subject at hand. Furthermore, even here, the designation using the word "destruction" (*vināśa*) ending in the suffix *-ini* is improper, as its meaning is impossible in this context.

Therefore, the conceptualization based on that [notion of] duration is untenable, whether it be a *bahuvrīhi* compound or otherwise; for, while accepting the linguistic convention of difference and thereby undertaking an investigation into the meaning of words, there is no connection [between cause and effect] because of the duality of moments in the immediately preceding moment of destruction—
since destruction, which is the opposite of arising, finds no opportunity at that time, the very meaning of "momentary" would be non-existent.
In the absence of one, the other likewise does not exist; thus, there is an absence of designation.

Furthermore, since arising and destruction reside in a single object, their meanings are mutually exclusive, and therefore they lack reality. He demonstrates this by saying, "And that [object] is not for a moment," meaning that the object is not such that it can be called "momentary" on account of that moment—just as Caitra is called "possessing a staff" because of his staff—since you yourself have stated that no object exists apart from the moment of its arising.

Furthermore, that which is called a "moment" (kṣaṇa) does not exist as such; nor is there any moment that possesses a "property-ownership" (svatva)—which stands in the place of the staff that serves as the cause for the designation "Caitra is staff-bearer"—by virtue of which connection one could say "this has a moment," and thus be called "momentary" (kṣaṇika). Since it is other than that [designation], the meaning of the word here is simply that this "momentariness" does not exist at all.

Therefore, because it contradicts what is under discussion and contradicts the meaning of the word, this interpretation—that "the very acquisition of its own nature is immediately followed by destruction"—is untenable.
Since nothing other than arising is possible,
that which is the moment does not exist, nor does that which is the moment;
therefore, that momentariness simply does not exist.
Therefore, because it contradicts the subject at hand, this interpretation is incorrect.

Furthermore, even here, the designation of the word *vināśa* (destruction) as ending in the suffix *-in* is improper, because its meaning is impossible [in that context]. Consequently, the assumption based on the inclusion of the suffix *-in*—or alternatively, the *bahuvrīhi* compound—is incorrect, since it accepts the investigation of word-meanings while presupposing the conventional usage of difference (*bhedavyavahāra*).
In the moment immediately following destruction, because there are two distinct moments, there is no connection;
for since destruction, which is the opposite of arising, finds no occasion, at that time the very meaning of "momentary" would be non-existent.
Since one does not exist in the absence of the other, the latter likewise does not exist, and thus there is an absence of designation.

Furthermore, since arising and destruction fall upon the same object and their meanings are mutually exclusive, they lack reality; [is the possessor of that, O Prince, momentary? (Kumāra-tadvān kṣaṇikaḥ?
— Bhāṣya-prakaraṇa.
From here until the end of this marker, the passage ending with "iti" (on folio 812, line 27) is not found in manuscript Ya;
see folio 809 and folio 811.
Furthermore, there is another point: "Moreover, even here... and so forth.

In order to equate the meaning of the word "momentary" (*kṣaṇika*), the designation of the word "destruction" (*vināśa*) ending in the suffix *-in*—as in the phrase "that which perishes immediately after" (*anantaravināśī*)—is also improper, because its meaning is likewise impossible. Not only is the word "momentary" itself [improper] according to the logic already stated, but the conceptualization involving the suffix *-in* is also improper; furthermore, it is improper whether one takes it as a *bahuvrīhi* compound or otherwise. Even if it were simply stated as "that which has destruction immediately after" (*anantaro vināśo 'syeti anantaravināśaḥ*), it remains improper due to the aforementioned logic, because a *bahuvrīhi* refers to a distinct object (as in the case of "one who has variegated cows") and its meaning is thus unattainable here.

It might be thought: "There is no fault, because we observe suffixes such as *matup* in cases where the meaning is non-different—as in 'Devadatta possesses a self' (*ātmavān*) or 'the sprout possesses arising' (*utpādavān*)—and because we observe Bahuvrīhi compounds with multiple words where the meaning is non-different, such as 'a word consisting of a single syllable' (*ekākṣaram padam*).

This, however, is incorrect; for while one may accept the investigation of word-meanings by relying upon conventional usage of difference, this contradicts the actual nature of the thing (*vastu*), which is [in reality] immediate to the action of proximity (*samīpakriyārthasamanantara*).
Furthermore, on page 809, line 24, regarding the state of being human and so forth:

there is a lack of connection due to the duality of moments in the moment immediately following destruction. For one who asserts that "the very acquisition of self-nature is what is destroyed immediately thereafter," it follows that arising and destruction are one and the same thing, which results in a single entity functioning in two ways; moreover, this constitutes a lack of connection because of the mutual contradiction between those two—arising and destruction—and because it does not escape the previously mentioned faults.

Regarding the passage beginning with "in the sense of arising" (*utpādārthena*), since "attainment of self-nature" (*ātmalābha*) is a synonym for "arising," there is no room for destruction (*vināśa*), which is its opposite; therefore, at that time, the meaning of "momentariness" would be non-existence itself. This is untenable because it would result in an interpretation of the subsequent statement as having the purpose of excluding an intermediate interval, thereby incurring the previously mentioned faults. He demonstrates this with the words "the absence of the other" (*itarābhāva*), etc., which has already been explained, up to "the absence of designation" (*vyapadeśābhāva*) on page 809, line 6.
...clay... Bhāṣya; ...the reversal of arising... Bhāṣya; ...ending with the statement... Bhāṣya.
The commentary (*vyākhyā*) [states] that it is like the state of being a celibate student (*brahmacārin*) and the state of being a father (*pitṛtva*). (Compare page 808, line 2).
Consequently, if that [quality] were unreal, it would follow that the substance itself is real;
and since [the quality] is not distinct from its arising, the possessive suffix (*matup*) would be entirely absent everywhere, even in the case of "form" (*rūpa*) and so forth.

Nor is its usage observed when it does not possess that nature [of being present], for the usage "he was a staff-bearer" (*daṇḍī āsīt*) and "he will be a staff-bearer" (*daṇḍī bhavitā*) occurs precisely by way of grasping the coexistence of the staff and the bearer in relation to past and future time.
Therefore, the notion that "destruction is indeed the very acquisition of self-nature" is an untenable conception.

Furthermore, regarding the proof beginning with "and of arising and destruction," and so forth, up to the demonstration of the fault of contradiction with one's own words (svavacanavirodha), it is as follows: arising and destruction both apply to a single object and have the nature of non-existence, because their meanings are mutually exclusive, like the state of being a celibate student (kumārabrahmacārin) and the state of being a father. For example, if someone were to say, "My father is a celibate student," therein the state of being a celibate student is negated by the state of being a father, and the state of being a father is negated by the state of being a celibate student; therefore, these two properties—birth and decay—are likewise contradictory when occurring in a single moment, and thus they are unreal in meaning.
Is it *asadarthau* due to a scribal error?
Or is it *sadarthau* as found in the Bhāṣya?

What follows from that? From that, if that unreality were real, it would necessarily follow that the substance is real; for if production and destruction do not exist in an entity, yet that entity is admitted to be existent, then by the very fact of the matter, it follows that it must be permanent—and that is undesirable to you.

Furthermore, because production is not distinct from [the entity], it follows as a logical conclusion that the possessive suffix *matup* is entirely absent everywhere, even in the case of "form" (*rūpa*) and so forth.

As you have stated—that the very acquisition of self-nature (*ātmalābha*) is destruction, and that the possessive suffix (*matup*) has that same meaning—since, like arising (*utpāda*), there is no possible referent distinct from sprout-ness (*aṅkuratva*) or arising itself, everything is merely arising. In that case, what other entity could there be, apart from arising, by virtue of which a sprout or the like would be designated as "possessing arising" (*utpādavat*) through that arising? Since nothing distinct from it is possible, because form (*rūpa*) and so forth are also merely arising, there would be no sense at all in saying "form possesses arising," or "taste, smell, sound, or touch possesses arising. In the absence of such an entity, the designation "possessing arising"—ending in the possessive suffix *matup*—would be meaningless.

It might be thought that even in the case of a non-existent entity (*abhāva*), the suffix *matup* occurs after a word denoting that [entity], and thus your reasons for refutation—being fallacious because they deviate from the rule—are invalid; for example: "He was possessed of a staff" (*daṇḍī āsīt*) or "He will be possessed of a staff" (*daṇḍī bhavitā*), and so forth.
To this it is replied: "Nor [is it the case] that even when not co-existent with it... and so forth.

One should not think thus—that the designation ending in the suffix *matup*, which expresses the sense of "possessor," applies to the possessor and the possessed when they are not co-existent. What then? It is precisely by grasping the co-existence of the staff and the staff-bearer with reference to past and future times that one employs such expressions as "he was a staff-bearer" (*āsīd daṇḍī*) and "he will be a staff-bearer" (*bhavitā daṇḍī*), according to the rule: "Suffixes [are applied] in connection with verbal roots" (Pāṇini 3.4.1).
Thus, because [the opponent's position] possesses the characteristics [of a valid argument], its formal application (*prayoga*) is correct;
therefore, since it remains in that state, it is not a refutation [of our position]. Is it not the case that [your objection] falls into the category of having an unreal meaning (*asadartha*)?
The commentary on the *matup* suffix section: "Suffixes [are employed] when there is a connection with a verbal root" (Pāṇini 3.4.1).
4.1. In the connection of verbal root meanings, suffixes have been prescribed for [specific] tenses; they should also occur in other cases besides those.

Because the action expressed by the verbal suffix (tiṅanta) is primary, the suffixes attached to words expressing subordinate actions conform to it; thus, in "vasan dadarśa," the present tense suffix (laṭ) is used to denote the past.
The meaning [of the example] is that the act of seeing has as its agent one who performed a residence in the past;
"the son of a Soma-sacrificer will be" means that the act of becoming has as its agent the son who is about to sacrifice with Soma— thus it is stated in the *Pāṇinīya Siddhāntakaumudī*.

The "connection between verbal roots" (*dhātusambandha*) refers to the relationship between two roots; here, by a figurative usage, the meaning of the root is expressed by the word "root" itself. In this context, this sūtra is intended to authorize the grammatical correctness of suffixes prescribed for one time-period when they are used in connection with another time-period.
Thus, Kaiyaṭa concludes in his *Pradīpa*: "Therefore, that which is stated [in the objection], beginning with 'it follows,' etc., is a redundant conclusion;
because it is subject to the aforementioned defects, the conceptualization that 'destruction is itself the acquisition of self' is untenable."
The meaning derived from such passages may be seen on page 809, line 6; page 810, line 12; and page 811, line 14.

Nevertheless, even if one overlooks these faults, if that which is arising—such as a sprout—is not a different entity from its arising, then a jar or the like would also arise [from that same arising], and the sprout too [would arise in the same way].

Therefore, because they are nothing more than arising (*utpāda*), pots and so forth are indeed sprouts and so forth, since they are not different in essence from the nature of the sprout, just like the self-nature of the sprout;
and just as that [sprout] is thus, so too are the pot and the rest.
Consequently, there is the identity of all things with everything, because they are not different in essence from arising.
Consequently, there would follow the consequence that all things in the world are identical with their substance; from that, it follows that the fundamental substance is the causal substance as well,
such that the cause is indeed the effect, because it possesses the very form attained [by the effect], just as the sprout produced through origination is not different from the origination itself.
[Objection: Is it not the case that the nature of the cause is attained precisely through the effect? [Reply: No, because [the following] has the same purpose as the preceding inquiry.

Furthermore, the phrase "even so" (*athāpi*) and so forth refers to the statement of faults—such as contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣavirodha*) and others—having disregarded or set aside these aforementioned faults.

For example: if that which is arising, such as a sprout, is not a different entity from its production, he recalls what has already been stated in order to refute it. What follows? From that [production], a sprout arises just as a jar or other things do; therefore, because they are merely productions, there is no difference between jars and so forth and sprouts and so forth. It follows that jars and the like are the sprout itself. Why? Because they are not different entities from the nature of the sprout, just like the sprout's own self. Furthermore, since jars and the like are perceived as distinct from the sprout through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), there is a contradiction with direct perception.
And because they are established as such in the world, there is a contradiction with worldly consensus (*loka-virodha*).

There is a contradiction with inference due to the distinction between cause and effect, and likewise a contradiction with one's own tenets because of the acceptance of linguistic usage regarding words and their referents.

For example, that very [sprout] is the jar and so forth; just as the sprout itself is the jar and so forth because they are not different from the production of the sprout’s own nature, like the sprout’s own self, so too the jar and so forth are the sprout because they are not different from the production of the jar’s own nature, like the jar’s own self.

"From that [it follows] 'the state of being the self of all' means that everything has everything as its essence: the pot is the cloth, the cloth is the sprout; the sprout is the pot, the chariot, the man, and even the buffalo; the buffalo is the man, the buffalo is the ram, the horse, and even the elephant, and so forth. This state of everything being the essence of everything exists because there is no difference from the production [of all things], just as [there is no difference] between the single cause such as the Puruṣa and the conscious nature of the Puruṣa.
(Variant readings: *atyābhā* / *tpādanārthā*)

The reading *sārvātmya* might also occur here, as in "O Sarvātman, even a jar [is you]"; and from that, there would follow the consequence that all the substances of the entire world are [identical], resulting in the conclusion that everything is indeed one and there is no such thing as a particular (*viśeṣa*).

And this is undesirable for you who maintain that things are merely absolute particulars characterized by momentariness. Furthermore, not only does the consequence of the substantiality of the entire world follow, but from that, the consequence of the substantiality of the root and the substantiality of the cause also follows. How so? He explains: the position that "whatever is the cause, that very thing is also the effect" is intended to demonstrate an undesired consequence.

The reason is "because it has acquired the form [of the cause]. For that reason, this effect has acquired the form of its cause; just as a cloth acquires the form of the threads [which are its causes]. Since the form of the effect is acquired from the form of the cause, the effect is indeed the cause. Like what? Like the non-difference of the production of a sprout from the production [itself] as conceived by you. Just as a sprout, having acquired its own form through production, is nothing other than that [production] and is therefore production itself, so too an effect such as a cloth, having acquired its form from the form of causes such as threads, is indeed the cause. Thus, the thesis [of the opponent] is also undesirable.

He says: "But surely it is by the effect alone that the nature of the cause is attained; it is by the cloth alone that the threads attain the form of the cloth. Therefore, the reason is unestablished for one of the two parties, because the opposite is admitted; or else the example is devoid of the property to be proven.

This is not so, because [the cause and effect] are equal in substance. Indeed, according to the doctrine of the reality of what has been stated, that which is becoming is indeed becoming; therefore, by that very substance which is the cause, the form of the effect is attained.

Otherwise, even the form of a sky-flower would be attained, and [an entity] would arise even without a seed, because that [seed] would not exist as something distinct from its own arising, just like a sprout.
As for the objection that "the designation of the former by the latter is not logical," the answer is stated: "No, because of the designation of a future property.
This is said with reference to a future moment; [one is called] "momentary" (kṣaṇika) because "this has a moment" (kṣaṇo 'syāsti), just as one is called "subject to death" (maraṇadharmin).

And this designation—that the destruction of that very entity belongs to the preceding one—is indeed logical; for I have already stated that the connection with the subsequent moment is acquired at the very first [moment], immediately after its own acquisition of self-nature. Therefore, by eliding the word "immediately" (*anantaram*), the suffix *ṭhan* is produced because it serves the purpose of inquiry. We say: "The effect, such as cloth, is made one's own by the cause, such as threads"; you might say: "The causes, such as threads, are made one's own by the effect, such as cloth. Of which of our two statements should the determination of the specific distinction be made?
See page 810, note 3.
Now, it might be argued that it exists only as that which has been stated, and therefore this effect-form is attained by means of that very substance which is the cause;

otherwise, even the form of a sky-flower would be attained, and even that which is without a seed would arise simply from arising, because it would not have existed as something distinct from its arising, like a sprout.
To this, the following answer is given to the objection that the designation of the former by the latter is not logical: "No, because of the designation based on future properties."

With reference to the future moment, it is said that "it possesses a moment" (kṣaṇika), just as one is called "subject to death" (maraṇadharmin). It is entirely logical to designate the passing away of that very same entity as belonging to its prior state. Furthermore, the connection with the future moment was already established by me at the very outset, since it was stated [in the sūtra] "immediately after the acquisition of its own nature" (ātmalābhānantaram);
therefore, by eliding the word "anantaram," the suffix *ṭhan* is produced.
We shall also state the specific reason for this here: "Is it not as was said regarding the nature of things," and so on, up to "is obtained by having been obtained.

Indeed, I have previously stated that, just like the doctrine of the Ārhats, a thing must possess duration even while undergoing origination and destruction, because it exists; and that which exists only comes into being, not that which does not exist. Furthermore, that which exists is the cause, the substance itself, which appropriates and attains both origination and destruction as its effects.

Therefore, by that very substance which serves as the cause, the production of effects is attained; thus, a non-existent effect cannot attain any purpose because it lacks existence, like a sky-flower. If this is not accepted, then conversely, even the nature of a sky-flower would indeed be attained; even without a seed, it would exist simply through production, for you have admitted that production is seedless. And since that seedless production is held to appropriate causes for itself, then by that production, even things such as a sky-flower or the son of a barren woman would be appropriated.

What is the reason? Because that [entity], such as a sky-flower and so forth, does not exist as something distinct from its arising. Whatever does not exist as something distinct from its arising is seen to be attained and assimilated by it, just as a sprout is [attained] by its arising; and this is undesirable, for either the sprout or the arising would not attain [the other], because they do not exist as distinct entities, like a sky-flower or the son of a barren woman.

Regarding the objection we have stated— namely, that "without a subsequent destruction, it is not appropriate to designate the prior non-existent thing as 'non-existent' either at that time or now by means of that destruction"— the answer you offer as an alternative refutation is: "Because there is designation based on a future property (*bhāvidharmavyapadeśāt*)."

The explanation of that is as follows: with reference to a future moment, it is said that "that which possesses a moment is momentary" (*kṣaṇika*). Even by means of a future [moment] that does not coexist [with the present], the state of possessing it occurs;

how so? Like one subject to death (*maraṇadharmivat*). Just as a living being, such as a human, is designated as "possessing that" by virtue of the future property of death, so too the first moment is designated as "momentary" by the second moment, even though they do not coexist and the latter is future. Thus, this designation is free from fault.
(Page 808, Line 2)

When destruction occurs, it is indeed logical to designate that very entity as "perishing," provided that this perishing is its own property even if it occurs at a later time through the nature of death. Why, then, is the entity not called "momentary" (kṣaṇika) in its very first moment by means of its own destruction which follows immediately upon its acquisition of selfhood? [The term] "momentary" refers to the connection with future moments; it is used to indicate that the activity of what has arisen is devoid of duration, just as one says, "he sits for a moment" or "the dwelling is momentary."

This too is appropriately slender: that while the entity called the self remains— being distinct from non-existence and distinct from other existing things— the designation "subject to death" is applied to it,

just as the impermanence of a jar and the like, which remain while possessing the properties of being produced and impermanence, is designated by the property of "being produced," so too is the designation "death of the person" applied to the persisting individual.

"Like the designation of impermanent subjects such as a jar, there is the designation of a subject characterized by death," and so forth—do not think thus, [supposing] that another reason has now been introduced by one who was previously obstructed. What then? It is because it was stated as a qualification that "the connection with future moments was already grasped by me immediately after its own acquisition" (see page 815, line 21; page 817, line 23).
If it is argued that because an entity is momentary, its existence after arising is empty of functional activity— just as one says "he dwells for a moment" or "the dwelling is momentary"—
this too is utterly insignificant.

It is logical that, while the entity called the "self" remains present— characterized as distinct from non-existence and distinct from other existing things— the designation "subject to death" is applied to it;

just as the impermanence of a jar or similar object, which persists while connected to the properties of being produced and impermanence, is designated by the term "produced," so too is there the designation of the death of a persisting person,
and the designation of the subject to death is like the designation of the impermanent jar or similar object.

Immediately after this, by eliding the word *anantara* and analyzing the compound as "that which has an immediate moment" (*anantarakṣaṇo 'syāsti*), one elides the word *anantara* and applies the suffix *ṭhan*, resulting in the form *kṣaṇika*. This is according to Pāṇini 5.3.83: *ṭhājādāvūrdhvaṃ dvitīyādacaḥ*, which states that when a suffix beginning with *ṭha* or a vowel follows, [the portion] from the second vowel onwards is dropped. For example, *devadatta* becomes *devika* or *devila*.

But for what purpose is it stated thus? We reply: it is for the purpose of making known the state of that [entity] having arisen as being devoid of activity; that is, to make known that what has arisen is devoid of action and devoid of stability.

In the examples for these, respectively: "just as one who is momentary remains inactive" means that he is without action; "a momentary dwelling" means a house devoid of a person or the like who is staying there. [Note on the suffix: *ṭha* is the suffix.
Pāṇini Sūtra 5.3.83: *pratyaya* [is applied] after the second vowel, following the suffixes *ya*, *ṅ*, and *ṭha*.

In this section, when the suffix *yaṣṭha* or a suffix beginning with *a-jādi* follows, everything after the second syllable of the base (*prakṛti*) is elided. Thus, an anukampita (one who is pitied) Devadatta becomes *devikaḥ*, *deviyaḥ*, *devilaḥ*, or *devadattakaḥ*; likewise, an anukampita Vāyudatta becomes *vāyudattakaḥ*.

The mention of *ṭha* is for the purpose of prescribing *ka* when it follows a second [suffix] ending in *u*, as in *vāyukaḥ* and *pitṛkaḥ*. It should be stated that there is optionally the elision (*lopa*) of what follows the fourth vowel; thus, one who is treated with compassion, such as *Bṛhaspatidatta*, becomes *bṛhaspatikaḥ*.
It should be stated that after [the suffix] *ka*, when followed by a vowel other than *a* or *ā*, the elision (*lopa*) is optional: *devadattakaḥ* or *devakaḥ*.
There is also the elision of the preceding member (*pūrvapada*): *dattikaḥ*, *dattiyaḥ*, *dattilaḥ*, or *dattakaḥ*.
It should be stated that even without a suffix, the elision of either the preceding or the following member may optionally occur: *devadattaḥ*, *dattaḥ*, or *devaḥ*.

From *satyabhāmā*, *bhāmā*, and *satyā*, [the suffix] *ila* is applied after a word ending in *u*; from *bhānudatta* and *bhānu*, [the suffix] *la* is applied; from *savitṛ* as well, [the suffix] *iya* is applied after a word ending in *ṛ*, resulting in *savitriya*;
and after a fourth [vowel], when followed by a consonant-initial suffix, there is elision of the preceding member.
"In the absence of a suffix, [the suffix] *t* is desired after that very [word]; and after a word ending in *u*, *i* is substituted for *la*.
— thus in Pāṇini’s *Siddhāntakaumudī*.

To this it is replied: even this [argument] is quite feeble. It is reasonable that birth and death belong to that which is characterized by mortality and so forth, according to the substantial sense (*dravyārtha-naya*); for it is precisely an enduring entity—experiencing the sequence of states such as childhood and the rest, possessing activity, distinct from non-existence, and distinct from other entities—that is called the "self" (*ātman*). By showing the dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) with the example [of a lamp], he demonstrates that the reason (*hetu*) is contradictory (*viruddha*), because it proves the opposite [of what was intended].

Thus, that which is already established is born, and that which is born dies; birth and death are inseparable from stability, and birth is inseparable from death, because this is so observed in the world.

And as for the illustration (*udṛṣṭānta*): "because of being produced" (*kṛtakatva*), "impermanence" (*anityatva*), and so forth. A jar or the like, in which the property of being produced and the property of impermanence are indeed established, is stated as the illustration in the proposition that sound is impermanent: "Whatever is produced is seen to be impermanent, such as a jar, etc. It is not unestablished, nor is it absolutely non-existent, nor is it something other than that [subject] unrelated to its properties, such as space (*ākāśa*). Just as the impermanence of the established jar and so forth is designated by means of its being produced, so too is the designation of the death of an established person made by means of birth, because of their invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*). Having thus established that the illustration serves as a proof for one's own position, he concludes with the application to the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*): "Just as there is the designation of the impermanent subject, such as a jar, there is likewise the designation of the subject characterized by death."
The reading "kṛtamevāyuktaṃ ya" might also exist here; furthermore,
the passage contained within these marks, beginning from "na sthitasya" and ending with "sthitasyaivārtha," does not exist in manuscript *ya*.
Furthermore, the reading here might also be "vā sthitaḥ" or simply "sthitaḥ"; [the text] reads "vaddharmā pra° sādhakatā° ya°".

O Śiva-prakāśa, the self (*ātman*), which undergoes the transformation of birth and death while being existent, is born and dies; for [birth and death] would be impossible if it were non-existent, since action cannot occur in the absence of a substrate. Thus, the learned recite: "The root *mṛ* (Pāṇini Dhātupāṭha 1404) means 'to abandon the vital breaths' (*prāṇatyāga*). The established soul (*jīva*) abandons and acquires the vital breaths; since it is already present there, what is the need for a [new] conjunction?
As for what was said—that the designation "the destruction of that very state" is indeed logical—that too is of no consequence.
Regarding the phrase "the producer of life" (*āyuṣkajananā*) and so forth:

the birth and death of a living being (*jīva*) are determined by the karma of lifespan (*āyuḥkarman*). It is not through that which is non-existent, such as a sky-flower; nor through something other [than the self], such as atoms or space not appropriated by a self.
As it has been said: "By the power of lifespan, the living being is born and lives when there is the rising (*udaya*) of lifespan."
Whether death occurs at the end of a partial lifespan (*aṇṇāyu*) or through the exhaustion of the entire lifespan (*savvāyu*),

because both of those two— birth and death— are present when that life-force karma (*āyu-karma*) exists, the self (*ātman*) itself, having been transformed by the activated life-force karma, is born while already existing and dies for the same reason, namely, because its life-force karma has been exhausted;

for action is not possible in the absence [of a substrate], nor is the action of birth, death, and so forth possible in what is absolutely non-existent, such as a sky-flower, nor in something else entirely different from it, such as space, which is devoid of that transformation.
And thus he states the evidence that those who are experts recite [this]:

"Who, then, are the experts? They are the grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇas*), who are experts in grammar—characterized by the thorough knowledge of the nature of words based on the reality of their application to meaning—as it has been said:
A living being is born and lives by virtue of its lifespan;
it is born and lives through the rising of the life-span karma (*āyuṣka*),
whereas it dies either upon the rising of another [life-span] or when all its lifespan is exhausted.
Is it that the self is born when half of its lifespan has passed, or does it die when the entire lifespan is exhausted, [only] while existing, indeed while existing?
Is it *papatti*? Or *papattiḥ*? [It is] by means of the action beginning with *pra*.
"Words alone are the basis for the reality of the manifestation of meanings; see page 579, note 2.
'The comprehension of the reality of words does not exist apart from grammar' (Vākyapadīya 1.13)."

Therefore, because they have set out to establish the true nature of reality through their activity aimed at determining that very reality, the Grammarians recite [the root]: *mṛṅ* (Pāṇini’s Dhātupāṭha 1.4), meaning "to die. A living being (*jīva*) who has attained stability dies—that is, he abandons the vital breaths characterized by the senses, life-span, strength, and respiration—and he takes them up again when he is born.

In that regard, because it has become that [state], and because its own nature has become one with the life-force (*āyuṣkarma*)—which consists of birth and death characterized by the acquisition and abandonment of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) in such a manner—what is the use of reintegration? What purpose is served by an imagined reintegration? The meaning is that there is none.

The ten kinds of vital breaths are: the five sense organs, life-force, the powers of mind, speech, and body, and respiration; the acquisition of these is birth, and the abandonment of those once acquired is death—this is the intended sense.
In the syllable *kā*, [it is] non-abiding; it arises from the characteristic of selflessness.
*Bhā* [arises] from the characteristic of selflessness.
*Ya* [arises] from the characteristic of selflessness.
By this means of proof [establishing] the connection,
page 813, line 22; 28.
Furthermore— regarding what was stated previously,

namely that because that very entity is subject to passing away, its moment exists through destruction, and thus it is designated as "momentary" (kṣaṇika) in accordance with logic— that too is of no consequence, for there is no point in it since it is illogical.

He demonstrates this with the words: "Even for those that are arising and perishing," and so forth. As long as these two entities—the producer and the perisher—are themselves in the process of arising and perishing, there is an absence of relation between them, just as there is none between a sky-flower and [another] sky-flower, because they have not yet come into being. How much more so, then, in the case of arising and perishing themselves, which, being non-existent and unreal, are incapable of any activity? Furthermore, even here, the sense of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhy-artha*) is untenable due to the lack of relation and the absence of coexistence. Now, one might argue that even in the absence of coexistence, the genitive can refer to a transformation (*vikāra*), as for example: "flour from barley grains" (*dhānānāṃ saktavaḥ*) or "cooked rice from rice grains" (*taṇḍulānām odanaḥ*).

This too is not [correct], because substance and mode coexist; just as in the case of "the destruction of the jar," it refers to the substance of clay itself, so here too the genitive case in "the destruction (vyaya) of the entity (bhāva)" is justified by the relationship between two coexistent things. Otherwise, if production and destruction were devoid of substance and seedless, the entity would be inexpressible.

Moreover, even these two do not exist according to your own position; because of the statement that "the sprout is indeed its arising," and since those two have not yet come into being, they possess non-existence like a sky-flower, and thus there is an absence of a relationship between them.

Therefore, it is improper to say that "they perish at the very moment of arising. How much more so, then, for the subsequent points? Since the objects that arise and perish do not exist, what talk can there be of a relationship between their arising and perishing, which are themselves dependent upon those objects? Why? Because those two [arising and perishing] are non-existent entities (*asattvabhūta*). They are non-existent entities because they are not real things (*avastutva*). Arising and perishing are "non-things" (*avastu*) because they are not real things in which those two [arising and perishing] reside; since they are non-things, they lack the possibility of occurrence, just like a flower in the sky. And for two things whose occurrence is impossible, there is simply no relationship. This is the sense.
Page 817, line 23; Page 813, line 26:

There is no relation between "not-yet-arisen" (*ananāta*) and "not-yet-perished" (*pra-anāta*), because even though they are in the process of arising and perishing, they lack existence, like a sky-flower; how much more so, then, between arising and perishing themselves, which—being non-existent and non-substantial—are incapable of any activity? Furthermore, in this case as well, the meaning of the genitive case is untenable, due to the absence of a relation and the lack of coexistence.

[Objection: "But even if they do not coexist, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) refers to a modification (*vikāra*), as for example: 'flour of grains' (*dhānānāṃ saktavaḥ*) or 'cooked rice of rice-grains' (*taṇḍulānām odanaḥ*).

[Reply: This is also not so, because substance and its modifications coexist; just as in the expression "the destruction of the jar" (*ghaṭasya vināśaḥ*), it is the very substance of clay that is meant.
Therefore, since the relationship exists only between two coexisting things, the genitive case is appropriate here as well: "the decay of the state" (*bhāvasya vyayaḥ*).
Otherwise, since arising and destruction would be devoid of substance and thus seedless, the entity itself could not be spoken of as "destroyed.
Furthermore: "Moreover, in this case also," and so forth.

Just as there is an absence of the suffix *ṭhan* [in the word *kṣaṇika*] because of the lack of a relationship between "existence" (*asti*) and "that which possesses existence" (*astimat*)—since arising and destruction do not coexist—likewise, the genitive case in the expression "the destruction (*vyaya*) of that very entity (*tasyaiva bhāvasya*)" is also untenable due to the lack of a relationship; for case endings are characterized by their denoting relationships, since the rule for the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is prescribed when there is a "remainder" (*śeṣa*), that is, a relationship other than the primary nominal meaning (*prātipadikārtha*), provided that the specific grammatical functions (*kāraka*) are not intended to be expressed. And the absence of a relationship follows from the fact that they do not coexist. The opponent says: "But even if they do not coexist, the genitive can have 'modification' (*vikāra*) as its object, being characterized by modification."

Furthermore, modification (*vikāra*) is the suppression of the original nature (*prakṛti*), as for example: flour from grains, or cooked rice from rice-grains. For in this case, the original nature does not exist in the state of modification; yet, the genitive case is heard in relation to the original nature, as in "of the grains" (*dhānānām*) and "of the rice-grains" (*taṇḍulānām*).

To this we reply: even this is not so. Why? Because substance (*dravya*) and mode (*paryāya*) coexist. Substance is the original nature, such as the grain or the rice-grain, which exists together with its specific mode—that is, its modification. This is because the very original nature of the grain or rice-grain undergoes the transformation into modifications such as flour or cooked rice, and thus establishes itself in various ways accordingly.

What is it like? It is like the destruction of a jar. Just as the very substance of clay—which possesses sequential attributes such as the state of a lump or a small pot, as well as simultaneous attributes such as color and form—exists in the form of shards; and just as that which is essentially clay exists through a change in the configuration of its constituent parts, which are themselves transformations of a collection of atoms and so forth, this is called the "destruction of the jar. Therefore, for all entities, there is only manifestation and disappearance within a process that does not abandon their own inherent nature (*svajāti*).

Therefore, since the relationship exists only between two co-existent things, the genitive case is justified here as well in the expression "the destruction (vyaya) of the state (bhāva)," meaning that the state perishes. It is said that while it exists, it persists; it perishes or arises. Thus, arising and perishing occur without abandoning the substantial aspect (dravyārtha). Otherwise, if arising and destruction were devoid of substance and lacked a seed, they would be impossible to describe, being as inconceivable as a crooked thing that cannot be described. That which is intended to be a real entity would not even exist as a state (bhāva); how then could arising or destruction be its property, given the absence of the substantial aspect, like a flower in the sky? [This is stated] from the perspective of modification (paryāya).

For that which "comes into being" exists as a substantial entity; for example, when a mound (*śivaka*) takes on the form of a stupa through its arising, it is called a stupa. And that [mound], while arising as a stupa, passes away.
For a "being" (*bhāva*) is so called because of its coming into being (*bhavana*).

However, in this way, it is not truly a "being," because it did not exist previously, because it does not exist afterwards, and because it does not exist both before and after—just like the son of a barren woman.
However, according to your own assertion, since [the entity] does not exist prior to, after, or even in the middle, it is as follows: for you say, "the destruction of that very entity.

In this case, would the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) characterizing the agent (*kartṛ-lakṣaṇā*) or the object (*karma-lakṣaṇā*) be intended? If it characterizes the agent, then that very entity itself undergoes destruction; thus, there would be no arising at all.

If [origination] were characterized by action (*karma-lakṣaṇa*), then by what could origination—which has destruction as its agent—be prevented? Therefore, that very origination does not exist; thus there is non-existence even in the middle.

To demonstrate the possibility of origination and destruction for the proponent of substantiality (*dravyārthavādin*) through its contrast with that [view], he says: "For earth, while coming into being as a substance (*dravyārthena*), truly comes into being; while coming into being, it exists without abandoning its own nature (*svarūpa*). It originates, just as, for example, the state of a *stūpaka* from the [clay] lump (*śivaka*) due to origination—this is the illustration."

And that very same clay, while coming into being, passes away; this is the illustration: as it arises in the form of a stūpa, it passes away from the state of being a *śivaka* (a small lump). For "existence" (*bhāva*) is derived from "coming into being" (*bhavana*). Regarding the phrase "the passing away (*vyaya*) of existence," the word "existence" (*bhāva*) used here is applicable only in the sense of a substance (*dravya*) as we have described, for it is the passing away of such an object that is spoken of, and not otherwise. As for that which does not exist, such as a sky-flower and the like, which is not a substance, it neither arises nor passes away.
(The reading "it arises" is also possible here.)
If [it is argued that] the object [exists],
then by the reasoning thus stated— namely, "in this way" and so forth— that entity (bhāva) spoken of by you does not exist as an entity at all.
Why? Because of non-existence prior [to arising]; the meaning is that there is an absence of becoming.
Likewise, because of non-existence posterior [to cessation]; the sense is that "that very thing does not exist.
Thus, these two are each a reason individually, and they are also combined together, as follows: because of non-existence both prior and posterior.
For all three reasons, there is but a single example: like the son of a barren woman.
Furthermore, according to your own view, these reasons are established, since you admit that existence belongs only to the moment of arising;
therefore, it is well said that "it is not an entity at all."

The meaning is: because of non-existence previously, because of non-existence later, and because of the absence of becoming (*bhavana*). There may also be a reading here as "that is not existence at all.
One might harbor the hope that it could be an existence in the present moment;

however, even that hope should not be entertained, because it is non-existent in every state. Therefore he says: "But just as you have asserted, because of its non-existence before, after, and in the middle, it is simply not existence"—this is how the passage continues.
Previously, it was stated according to our own view that [the entity] lacks existence prior to and after [its production] because it is not a substance;

now, however, since its non-existence even in the present moment has been established in your own system, its lack of existence prior to and after [production] is already proven. To establish this, he says, based on your own words as follows: "For you indeed say, 'And this is the destruction (vyaya) of that very entity,'" by means of this statement intended to establish the conventional usage of the designation.

And regarding this [genitive] "of the entity" (*bhāvasya*), would it be a genitive characterized by the agent (*kartṛ*) or characterized by the object (*karman*)? If it were characterized by the agent, then that very entity which is arising (*utpāda*) would pass away—that is, it would perish and cease to exist; it would be said that by that very [entity] it is lost, it no longer exists, and it perishes.
