What is it that ceases to exist? It is arising itself. If, on the other hand, it were characterized by the object, then by what could arising—which has destruction as its agent—be turned back? Thus, the entity is indeed untenable.
Furthermore, in the case of "rice-gruel from rice grains," the rice grains would undergo a different modification while abiding as a substance during their own time.

In your view, however, since even that [entity] cannot undergo another modification while abiding as a substance in its own time, how can it be said that "this entity, being then non-present, passes away"? If it passes away at the very moment it is present, then it does not arise at all; nor is it the case that it is not present and then arises, or that it exists and becomes present, for then it does not pass away, because arising and passing away are mutually contradictory. How, then, can there be your statement that "that very same entity passes away"?

Furthermore, its subsequent moment of destruction cannot exist either, because it depends upon that [prior moment] to be called "momentary," yet it has not arisen—just like a sky-flower or like space.

If, in the absence of these two, an entity is asserted to be existent, then, given the existence of substance as maintained by the Ārhats, that very thing does not arise in every moment; thus there would be non-existence even in the middle.

Consequently, because of the statement that "there is the passing away (vyaya) of an entity due to its non-existence before, after, and in the middle," the word "momentary" would be devoid of meaning.
Why are these two not established? (Praśastapādabhāṣya, p. 813, l.
By that very [cause] it is maintained, and by that very [cause] it is produced.
Who is the agent of destruction? By what could production be averted? This reading might also be found here.
Moreover, in the case of "rice-grains [becoming] boiled rice," the grains would undergo a transformation while abiding as substances during their own time;

however, in your view, since even that [transformation] is impossible because it would involve a further transformation of a substance abiding during its own time, that entity is simply non-existent at that time. How then can it be said that "it passes away"? If it passes away only when it is present, then it does not arise at all; for what is not present does not exist.

If it arises and exists as present, then it does not perish, because arising and perishing are mutually contradictory; how indeed could there be a statement of its true nature such that "the very same entity perishes"? Furthermore, its subsequent moment of destruction cannot exist at all, since it would depend upon that [prior moment] to be called "momentary"; for, being unarisen, it is like a sky-flower or like space. But if, in the absence of these two [arising and perishing], the entity is held to be existent, then, in the case of the substantial reality (dravyārtha-sadbhāva) favored by the Ārhats, in every single moment—

Furthermore, in the expression "rice from grains" (*taṇḍulānām odanaḥ*), at the time when the modification (*vikāra*)—the cooked rice—attains its own existence, the grains persist as the substantial entity (*dravyārthatas*). Because they remain together with the rice, the state of being rice, which is a further modification, would occur or be reached by the grains within that substance; such a course of events would indeed be possible.

In your view, however, since even that [destruction] cannot occur as a further modification residing in a substance that persists through its own time, and because it is of a different nature [from existence], that entity—being non-existent at that time—is indeed absent. How then can it be said that "the production you desire, though non-existent, perishes"? By what logic can it be asserted that something which is as absent as a sky-flower "perishes"? If it be thought that "it is said to perish when it is present," has this not already been addressed?

To this it is replied: that very deliberation remains—namely, that "this is improper. For if, when it is present, it simultaneously passes away, then it does not arise at all; it is not present, it does not exist—this is the meaning.
Or, if it arises, exists, and is present, then it does not pass away.

Why? Because of the contradiction between arising and passing away. "Contradiction" (*vipratiṣedha*) means a mutually exclusive negation; arising is contradicted by passing away, and passing away is contradicted by arising. Therefore, because they are contradictory and mutually preclusive due to this contradiction, how could there even be a statement of their true nature, such as "the passing away of that very entity"? It is not possible even from afar, because of the non-existence of the entity [if it has passed away].
(Page 820, Line 11). Thus ends that statement in the Bhāṣya.

Thus, for now, it is improper to say that the moment of arising is itself the moment of destruction, because they are contradictory. Not only is this [position] untenable, but what else? In this way, its subsequent moment of destruction also cannot exist; for it is on account of that [subsequent moment] being dependent upon it that it could be called "momentary" (kṣaṇika), since it possesses such a moment. The meaning is that it is untenable precisely because of the absence of that [subsequent moment].
Why? Because it has not arisen, like a flower in the sky—the sense of which has already been explained—or, against the Sautrāntika, like space.

Thus, first of all, arising and destruction are not tenable either in a single moment or in a subsequent moment, from which [the property] denoted by the word "momentary" (kṣaṇika) could [arise]. It is said: "First of all... [as above].

And likewise, if even in the absence of duality—that is, in the absence of the moments of arising and destruction—if a thing is held to be truly existent, then this consequence follows: because of the existence of the method of modalities (*paryāyanaya*) and the acceptance of arising and destruction, all entities are momentary; thus, the meaningfulness of the term "momentary" is established. And in this very way, the verse beginning with *jātireva hi* should be read as follows: "For it is precisely the birth of entities that is accepted as the cause of their non-destruction.
That which has been born and has not yet perished, how could it perish later?"
The substantial entity (*dravyārtha-ātman*) of the pot exists, arises, and does not perish;
for it is not non-existent, because it possesses the nature of neither arising nor perishing, like the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*).

However, if its nature consisted solely of arising and perishing, then in the absence of a seed (a substratum), the non-existence of those two [arising and perishing] would follow. Rather, as has been explained, that which is already established arises and perishes.

since the Arhat accepts that while the substance (dravyārtha) exists as it abides, there is the acceptance of arising and destruction due to the existence of the mode-aspect (paryāyanaya) in every moment, it is logically consistent that all entities are momentary (*kṣaṇika*), which makes the meaning of the word "momentary" applicable; it would not be so otherwise.

Because of the existence of the method of figurative interpretation (*paryāyanaya*) and because of the acceptance of arising and destruction, it is indeed established that all entities are momentary; thus, the meaning of the word "momentary" is justified.
In this very way, the verse beginning with "jātireva hi" should be read as follows: "For it is held that the very birth of entities is the cause of their non-destruction;
and how could that which has been born and is not yet destroyed be destroyed later?"
The substantial entity (*dravyārtha*) of a jar is neither stationary nor does it perish;
for it is not the case that it is non-stationary, because its nature consists of non-arising and non-destruction, like the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*).
Indeed, arising itself is held to be the cause for the non-destruction of entities.
That which has been born and is not yet destroyed would have to perish later; by what [cause] could this be?

For if their nature consists merely of arising and perishing, then, being without a seed, the non-existence of those two follows. Rather, like that which has already come into being, it arises and perishes while remaining established.
...let it be seen on page 824, line 15.

And in exactly the manner thus explained, the verse beginning with "jātireva hi" should be read as follows: "For it is *jāti* alone that is held to be the cause for the non-destruction of entities"—the latter half of the verse is precisely that.

However, regarding your statement "because there is no destruction of entities" (*bhāvānām-anāśe*), the letter *m* arising from the *saṃhitā* reading has been corrupted by someone who did not understand it—either due to a faulty transcription or through erroneous instruction by another. For it has been established that, according to the method explained, an object arises only as something already existing, not as something non-existent; therefore, existence itself is the cause of stability. Since what is born is precisely what is stable, it is not destroyed. For that which is indestructible at the very moment of its birth and consists of continuous persistence, what subsequent cause for destruction could there be? Thus, there is never any destruction.
Page 797, Line 7:

Do not think that this is a reckless assertion—that [the substance] remains as it is while being born, and having been born, does not perish. To that end, it is proposed: "The self-nature of the substance of the jar remains, is born, and does not perish.

Since it is impossible to demonstrate these simultaneously, they are demonstrated sequentially. First, regarding its state of remaining, it is proposed that "it is not, for the time being, non-remaining"; for when the state of non-remaining is negated, the state of remaining is established.

Why? Because its nature is non-arising and non-destruction. That which is neither of the nature of arising nor of the nature of destruction is not unstable; it is indeed stable, like the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*). For example: analytical cessation (*pratisaṅkhyānirodha*), non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṅkhyānirodha*), and space (*ākāśa*). These three exist because they are cognizable by the intellect, unlike [non-existent things]; and because they are not produced by conditions, these three are unconditioned. Furthermore, because they are denoted by the word "existence" (*sat*), they are existent yet not unstable. Let it be seen that a jar is likewise so (p. 820, l. 25).
See page 104, line 5–7, note 1; see page 49, line 26;
see page 104, line 5, "ghaṭāpi" (also the pot), Prajñā.
And what about [the case of] a jar and so forth?

Furthermore, according to your own view, if [existence] consists merely of arising and perishing, then since these two—arising and perishing—are without a seed and devoid of a persisting object, it follows that those two (arising and perishing) themselves would be non-existent.

As for the statement, "and this very destruction belongs to that entity," that too is nothing at all. Thus, the verse "all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are momentary" should be read as follows: "All entities are non-momentary; how can there be activity in things that are momentary?"
For those [entities] whose very existence (*bhūti*) is action (*kriyā*), that same [existence] is called the causal factor (*kāraka*);
all such entities (*bhāva*) are non-momentary (*akṣaṇika*) by virtue of their duration and action.
Thus, by virtue of their persistence and activity, these [entities] are non-momentary;
for if they were momentary, then their arising and destruction would not occur at all, because they would be devoid of activity and persistence, like a sky-flower.

If entities were non-momentary, then since no activity distinct from arising and destruction is possible—and because [activity] is distinct from them—they would indeed be non-existent, like a sky-flower.

Furthermore, the claim that this momentariness has become devoid of activity is not at all correct; for it is accepted that "the very arising (*bhūti*) of things is itself their action. Indeed, the state of being devoid of activity belongs only to the arising of a substance-entity (*dravyārtha-vastu*), as established by the preceding discussion starting from "by way of word and meaning" up to "because of contradiction. Thus, he extends [the argument] by saying "as it was explained, so it is here," [concluding that] what is already established arises and perishes, and so forth.
As stated on page 815, line 11, and page 818, line 4, the verse "All conditioned phenomena are momentary" should also be read as follows:
"All entities are non-momentary; how could there be activity for those that are momentary?"
For those things whose very existence is action, that same [existence] is called the agent;
all such entities, being things, are non-momentary by virtue of their existence and their activity.
Thus, by virtue of their activity and duration, they are non-momentary;
for if they were momentary, then their arising and destruction would not occur at all, because they would be devoid of the operation of duration, like a sky-flower.

If entities are non-momentary, then since no activity distinct from arising and destruction is possible—and because [activity] would be distinct from those two—they would indeed be non-existent, like a sky-flower.

Furthermore, the claim that this momentariness has become devoid of activity is not at all correct, because of the accepted principle that "for those things, their very arising is itself their action. For the state of being devoid of activity belongs only to the arising of a thing that exists as a substantial entity.
Even the verse beginning with "All conditioned phenomena are momentary," and so forth, should be read in this way: "For this reason," since the word *iti* here carries the sense of a cause (*hetu*).

For example: "All entities are non-momentary; how can there be activity in momentary things? The second half of the verse, however, is as in your reading; this stanza is intended to demonstrate that what has arisen does not perish. Its commentary is as follows: "Entities" (*bhāvāḥ*) and "things" (*vastūni*) are synonyms. All of them are non-momentary because they possess duration and activity—namely, the activities of arising and perishing—which consist of the continuous process of becoming. Thus, the explanation concludes that they are non-momentary by virtue of their duration and activity. This is precisely the interpretation of the summarized meaning.

If, according to your view, things were momentary, then their arising and destruction would not occur at all, because they would be devoid of the persistence of activity, like a sky-flower; this proof, which establishes an undesirable consequence, has already been explained.
Therefore, since arising and destruction are established only for that which persists, entities are non-momentary. (Page 801, Line 6)
Having been addressed thus, [the opponent] says at this point: "If they are non-momentary," and so forth.

If an entity is stable, then it is non-momentary; for such an entity, there can be neither arising nor destruction. Furthermore, no other activity whatsoever is possible apart from arising and destruction. Since that [other activity] is impossible, [the entity] is "distinct from those"—that is, distinct from arising and destruction. Because it is distinct from arising and destruction, and because it is therefore neither arisen nor destroyed, it is indeed not stable according to the method you have stated, like a sky-flower. For things that are not stable, how could there be action? Thus it has been said.

Furthermore, it is established that this [momentary nature] has become a mere state of being devoid of activity, a momentariness that is itself free from operation; thus it remains unshaken. (Pra.vā.bhā. p.
Regarding the statement "only conventionally" (saṃvṛttyaiva) found in the Yaśomitra and Bhāṣya commentaries, it is replied here:

this too is not so. For we have already established previously that for those things whose very arising is their activity, they are both "existent" and "arisen," and yet they do not perish; thus, the state of being devoid of activity is precisely the state of being endowed with activity, for such is the nature of a substance as a real entity.

Why? Precisely because of *bhūti* (coming-to-be). For an entity would exist in this way only if it exists as something that truly comes to be; however, that further coming-to-be which you propose is accepted as being seedless and unstable. Furthermore, for those entities whose nature is *bhūti*, that very [process] is their activity—not non-existence (*abhūti*), nor the absolute destruction of what has arisen, nor arising and destruction [of something already existing], since these belong only to that which remains in the states of manifestation (*āvirbhāva*) and concealment (*tirobhāva*). Therefore, entities are neither devoid of activity and momentary, nor are they momentary in the sense of remaining [static] for a moment.

And that very *bhūti* (coming-into-being) is the causal agent (*kāraka*), because its nature consists in the substance (*dravya*) as the locus of what is to be brought about (*bhavya*) and the process of becoming (*bhavana*). Thus, even such expressions as "it perished suddenly" or "it was destroyed" refer to the production (*utpāda*) of an existing entity itself, while destruction (*vināśa*) is simply its specific non-perception.

In this regard, who is the destroyer? What is the destruction for which an obstacle is considered? Who will be destroyed? There is no such thing as destruction; how then can there be a cause for it, such that it is said: "The state of being a cause of destruction is something to be established"? Furthermore, we read as follows: "What obstacle could there be to the coming-to-be of that which is destined to exist? If there were none, it would not come to be in that way.
Whether it be an obstacle or destruction itself, what is the cause of destruction for whom?"
One must determine that existence itself is indeed existence, being free from the contact with its opposite.

For just as an entity that has arisen does not constitute "birth" [in the sense of a new coming-into-being], he demonstrates this: "And even this is accepted," and so forth. That very manifestation (*bhūti*) of those entities which was previously accepted by me is itself the operation; thus, non-existence is not a prior absence (*abhūti*), nor is it the production of what was previously non-existent, nor is it the absolute destruction of what has arisen, which is non-existence through destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*). What, then, are birth and destruction? They are merely the manifestation and disappearance of that which is already established. This has been explained at length.
Therefore, because they are endowed with such activity, entities are neither devoid of operation nor are they momentary in the sense of remaining for a duration;
for it is also accepted that the very arising of those entities constitutes their operation, not their non-arising or the absolute destruction of what has already arisen.
Arising and destruction are merely the manifestation and concealment of that which already exists;
therefore, entities are neither inactive momentary things nor non-existent momentary things.
Furthermore, that very coming-into-being (*bhūti*) is the agent, because it constitutes the substance (*dravya*) in its capacity as the object of becoming (*bhavya-bhavana*).

And thus, even that which is suddenly distressed—if it were to perish, and so forth—then production (*utpāda*) is simply the arising of an object already established, and destruction (*vināśa*) is its specific non-perception.

In that case, who is the one that perishes? What is the destruction for which an obstacle is considered? Who will be destroyed? Destruction itself does not exist; how then can there be a cause for it, such that it is said: "the state of being a cause of destruction is to be proven"?
Moreover, we recite it as follows:
"What obstacle could there be to the coming-to-be of that which is destined to exist? For if there were none, it would not come to be in that way.
What is an obstacle, and what is destruction? Who is the cause of whose destruction?"
One must determine that existence itself is indeed existence, being entirely free from contact with its counter-factors;
for just as an entity has arisen, it remains exactly as it is.

For this very reason, that same manifestation (*bhūti*) is the causal factor (*kāraka*); it is the causal factor because it consists of the appearance and disappearance of that which already exists. Why? Because its nature is the substance (*dravya*) that undergoes becoming (*bhavya*). "Becoming" (*bhavya*) is derived from the agentive sense as "that which becomes," while "becoming-ness" (*bhavana*) is derived from the impersonal sense as "that by which it is brought into being. Since the self is attained through both the agentive and impersonal means of accomplishment—just as a finger possesses both curvature and straightness—the self is simultaneously the goal and the instrument. Thus, even that [which is considered to perish] is merely exhausted; for if production and destruction consist solely in the appearance and disappearance of an existing entity, then if it is said to have perished, [it has not truly ceased to exist].

Regarding this verse and others: "Sudden distress" refers to the production of an object that was already established. "Destruction" (*vināśa*) is its specific non-perception; otherwise, it would be perception as before, which is non-perception. In that case, who is the destroyer? According to your view, nothing can be destroyed because its nature is ultimately imperceptible. What is destruction? It is a non-existence consisting of annihilation (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*). Of what thing, characterized in such a way, is an obstacle considered? Who will perish? The meaning is that no entity whatsoever will perish.

Why? Because precisely due to the non-existence of destruction, all this is like the ravings of a madman and cannot withstand critical inquiry; therefore he says: "Destruction itself does not exist—how could there be a cause for it, such that it is said [in verse 795, line 5] that 'the state of being a cause of destruction' is something to be proven? (myadana, pra).

Furthermore, we read it in this way; however, your reading has a corrupted tradition (*bhraṣṭāmnāya*), whereas mine is uncorrupted. Listen: it is as follows—the verse beginning with "bhavitum" and so forth.

The explanation of this is as follows: "Free from contact with its opposite," and so forth. Because of the permanence of the substantial entity (*dravyārtha*), it must be determined that "existence itself is existence"; the opposite, which is momentary, is not [existence]. If that [opposite], consisting of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and non-existence through destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), were to exist, then if he (the entity) were likewise to exist, what obstacle would there be to his being? For if the entity has already come into being, what obstacle could there be to its being even at a later time? Indeed, that existing entity must always be in the state of being;
if it were not, it simply would not exist in that manner.

Now, if it is not accepted in this way, then because its nature is non-existence (*abhavana-dharmatva*), it would never exist even now, nor would it ever exist at any time. Furthermore, there would be an obstacle to its existence—either self-destruction or the proximity of a cause of destruction.

But what is the cause of destruction for what? For example, the striking of stones and the like is the cause of destruction for jars and such, while contact with fire is the cause of destruction for the color and other qualities of earth, as well as for water.

Or, if birth itself is the destruction—that is, if destruction is your thesis—then it would dissolve by its own nature; how then can this be determined? One must determine that, having come into contact with the opposite side, "it indeed comes to be."

How is this to be determined? It is said: Just as an entity that has arisen is [already] becoming, having been, and existing—if it exists in that manner, what obstacle could there be to its continuing to exist? The intended meaning is that there is no obstacle at all. He explains this further: If an entity has already come into being, what obstacle could there be to its existing even at a later time? For it must always exist—in the past, in the future, and at that very moment; in all three times, that existing entity must exist, and it can never not exist. (Tulanā, p. 795, l. 20)
Because it is of the nature of that which is touched,

because of that, there is duality.

If it is to come into being again in that same way, what obstacle could there be to its coming into being? For if it has already become [existent], what obstacle would there be to its coming into being at a later time as well? Indeed, it must always exist by virtue of that nature of being;
if it were not so, it would simply not exist.
Furthermore, if this is not accepted, then because it possesses the property of non-existence, it would not exist even now, nor would it ever exist in that manner.
There is an obstacle to existence—either self-destruction or the presence of a cause for destruction.

What is the cause of destruction for what? For example, the striking by a stone and so forth is the cause of destruction for things such as a jar, while contact with fire is the cause of destruction for the color and other qualities of earth and for water;
or else, birth itself is destruction.
In the case of the nature of destruction being the probandum, those two [the cause and the effect] dissolve by themselves; thus, the nature of destruction is established as the probandum.
Is the reality of destruction [already] established? Or is it to be established by the reality of destruction? Is the reality of destruction to be established by you?
Therefore, how is this determined?
For it is determined that if [an entity] does not exist [in the past], it could not possibly exist [now] in that same way.

This is the explanation: "But if," and so forth. Now, if it is not accepted that because it is currently a "becomer" (bhavitṛ), it must necessarily exist in all three times, then it would follow that it is of a non-existent nature (abhavanadharman). Consequently, due to being of a non-existent nature, it would not exist even now; since it is not observed to be a "becomer" at this moment, it would never exist at any time, resulting in its status as being like a sky-flower by virtue of its present non-existence.
And this is undesirable; [as stated in] the *Tulanā*, p. 796, l. 2: "...ityādipannamya... [etc.]

Prior existence, simultaneous existence, and momentary existence [are untenable],
because there is no subsequent apprehension when that [moment] has occurred.

This is non-indicative: for even when a thing perishes spontaneously, since its occurrence follows a fixed sequence even though it is uncreated, that which was previously seen is not perceived in that same way, but is perceived otherwise; therefore, how can their non-perception in that manner be called "destruction"? For, according to the sequential designation, the forms of clay and so forth receive the name "small lump" (*śivaka*); yet they are not destroyed by their own nature, but rather, having dissolved through the very production of those respective intrinsic natures, they arise as a "clod" (*piṇḍa*) and are called a "stūpaka," or, by the force of the condition of impact, they become potsherds (*kapāla*).
Therefore, the non-perception of the jar and so forth at that time does not result from its own absence or from its destruction;

rather, in order to exclude the fallacy of "unestablished for either party" (*anyatarāsiddhi*), they state: "Because it is not perceived afterwards when that [cause] exists. This should be understood as being consistent with the explanation of the previous method.

To this, the reply for both [positions] is as follows: This is not a proving argument, because even in the case of a thing’s own destruction, the "own-destruction" of a thing is said to be its dissolution, which consists of its manifestation and disappearance. And that, being a thing, is uncreated (*akṛtaka*) just like what was stated before. In that uncreated thing, whose activity is obtained through a fixed sequence—where "fixed sequence" means a restriction by sequence—the thing whose activity is obtained by such a fixed sequence is uncreated. A strictly determined activity is indeed obtained through the sequence of the lump of clay, the shaped piece, the bowl, and so forth; from the lump comes the shaped piece, from the shaped piece the mound, and so on, occurring spontaneously. Even the other causal factors, such as the agent, are necessarily produced in sequence, appearing in the form of the clay-lump, the wheel, the string, the water, the potter, and so forth.

And in that entity whose mode of existence is governed by a fixed sequence of stages, the absence of pot-ness previously observed manifests as shards; and while it is disappearing as pot-ness, it is not perceived as such due to causes such as the impact of a stone, but is perceived as shards. Therefore, according to our view, the non-perception of the concealed pot and its earthy form, etc., as well as water, is established. Non-perception in this sense is simply their non-apprehension in that specific form, which constitutes their destruction and their particular invisibility, or rather, it is perception in another form. [This refers to] "this" and "that," the "small stone" (*śivaka*), and so forth.
It is grasped by them;
for them,
that which has become the higher has become the lower.
The question concerns its cultivation (*bhāvanā*): "How is this done?

The explanation follows: "Because they are indicated according to their respective numbers," and so forth. The term *mṛd* (clay) is expressed with the number one because of the unity of the manifestation of the substance-aspect (*dravyārtha*). The terms *rūpa* (form), etc., are expressed with the number of plurality because of the differentiation of the manifestations of the aspect-aspect (*paryāyārtha*) consisting of appearance and disappearance. Both of these receive the designation "brick" (*śivaka*) while remaining undestroyed in their own essential form.

If it is asked, "Why are they not destroyed by their own nature? [the answer is: because they arise through that very nature which constitutes their respective individual essences (*svabhāva*), depending on themselves and others—such as the striking of a lump or a stone—they are "dissolved" or "concealed" in their state as a lump; yet, by the power of the agent's cognition, they arise in the form of a stūpa, and thus clay-forms and the like are called "stūpas. Or, by the power of the causal condition of striking, they are called "potsherds. For the Omniscient One knows whatever substance transforms into whatever state through either conscious effort (*prayoga*) or spontaneous disintegration (*visrasā*); the Jina knows it exactly as it is. There is no cognition of a thing apart from its specific modifications (*aparyaya*).
Because of the statement in the *Āva* and *Ni* (794), he perceives and withdraws [the object] in such and such a manner;

therefore, at that time, there is no apprehension of Śiva, Kāla, and so forth, neither because of their own non-existence nor because of destruction— this subsequent statement serves to clarify both points.

Even the earthy qualities such as color and so forth, through the power of contact with fire, disappear from their previous form and arise again in another way.

Similarly, because water is manifested in a very slight degree by fire, the final particles of water lack the capacity for manifestation; thus, there is non-perception. This is not due to their destruction.
Do not, therefore, give way to despondency.
All other assertions of substantialists (vastuvādins) likewise fall into the state of being Ārhatas, just like your own assertion;
this applies even to those who say: "Like a heap, like a caravan... [and so forth].
this is precisely the *syādvāda*, because its meaning is non-absolutism (*anekānta*),
through the conceptualization of the identity and difference of distinct capacities.

A distinct capacity for conquering a powerful enemy, which does not exist individually in each person such as a soldier but is seen in the army as a whole—even though kings possess it individually—is explained here in the same manner as in that [previous] text. However, the distinction is that [the soldiers] arise again in a different form once their previous form has disappeared; this is according to the interpretation of the meaning, and the specific capacity arises from the connection with fire.

The same applies to water and so forth; however, the distinction is as follows: because the manifestation of water is extremely slight, its existence as a distinct entity depends on whether it relies on other factors or not, and thus the manifestation of water is exceedingly subtle due to the power of its connection with fire. Consequently, because the final particles of water are extremely subtle, they lack the capacity for manifestation; they cannot be clearly perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), but they are inferred to exist even when concealed. In this manner, there is non-perception [of them], and not because they are destroyed by that conjunction with fire.

Therefore, we have rightly stated: "The doctrine of momentary entities supports the Jaina theory of substantiality (*dravyārthavāda*) when it requires the perspective of modal aspects (*paryāyārtha*).

And by this very [reasoning],
a subtle imperishable [entity] is inferred.

the Arhat has spoken. Bhāṣya.
"Page 819, line 10:

'Do not feel despondency,' etc.—do not feel regret that the status of an Ārhata has fallen upon me, the proponent of momentariness, even though I do not desire it. What then? All other assertions of the proponents of real entities (vastuvādins), from the affirmative mode (vidhi) up to the modes ending in negation (bhaṅga), are equal to your own assertion; they too fall into the very state of being Ārhata, because the assertion of a real entity necessarily results in non-absolutism (anekāntatva). And this contradiction with their own prior tenets is a calamity for them. Since the calamity of others provides consolation, take heart by observing their calamity and cultivate fortitude."
And [there is] non-return through intense grasping,
for the sake of non-opposition.

First, we shall cultivate the vision of the principle of what has just passed: namely, the verse beginning with "Those who say it is like a heap," and so forth. This verse pertains precisely to *syādvāda* (the doctrine of conditional predication), because its meaning is non-absolutist (*anekānta*).

He states the explanatory verse for that: "Because of identity with another power," and so forth. Since [the principle] will be cultivated in all illustrative examples—such as an army, a heap, a caravan, and the rest—once it has been cultivated in the case of an army, this is for the sake of brevity.

A distinct capacity, such as the victory over a powerful enemy, is observed in an army composed of the four divisions—infantry and the rest—which does not exist in each individual person and so forth. Since those very same components, such as the men and others, are individually designated as the "army" by way of the nature of the army, one thereby accepts both their identity and their difference; thus, the application of the substantial view (dravyārtha) and the modal view (paryāyārtha) is established.

Furthermore, even while sharing identity with the general category of "men" and so on, the army is something other than them because its nature is defined by a different form, just as color and taste are distinct entities from the object they qualify, or as it possesses men, chariots, horses, and elephants.
likewise, a mountain (śikharin) is neither different nor non-different from its peaks and so forth.
Just as a beverage is both different from and not different from its constituents such as pepper and sugar,
so too the self is both different from and not different from pleasure and the like;
and the same applies to sweetness, sourness, and so forth.

In the same way, when pungency and other qualities have been processed within a composite mixture, the substance of the drink— though possessing its own essential nature— is, because it has been processed in that manner, like a sweet taste;
for it is not as [it appears].

For it is precisely those very limbs of men and so forth that constitute the "army"; thus, when the proponent—by means of that very [identification]—causes the two entities designated as "men" and the "army," which are respectively the constituent parts (*aṅga*) and the whole (*aṅgin*), to be accepted as being either identical or different, then by virtue of that acceptance, the adherence to both the substantial view (*dravyārtha*) and the modal view (*paryāyārtha*) constitutes an adherence to the non-absolutism (*anekānta*) consisting of both standpoints (*naya*).
So they say.

"Your army is that very nature; however, the reading 'the nature of the army' (*senātmatā*) might also occur here.

For indeed, those very same parts, such as men and so forth, individually constitute the army; thus, by accepting both their identity and their difference through that very [perspective], the adoption of the substantial standpoint (*dravyārtha*) and the modal standpoint (*paryāyārtha*) is accomplished."

And even though there is identity with the generality of men and so forth, because it possesses a nature defined by a different form, the army is also distinct from them— just as color and taste are distinct objects— and just as [the army] consists of men, chariots, horses, and elephants.
...so too a mountain is both different from and non-different from its peaks and so forth;
likewise, a beverage is both different from and non-different from the pepper, sugar, and other ingredients that compose it.
Likewise, the self (ātman) is both different from and non-different from pleasure and so forth;

similarly, sweetness, sourness, and the rest are established in that same way. Furthermore, when pungency and other qualities are combined in prepared elixirs (pānaka), the substance itself is established as having its own essential nature, just like the sweet taste.
For it is not like that...

He states the proof for its consisting of both methods [the general and the particular] in the passage beginning with "even though there is identity with the universals such as 'man'" and ending with "just like the difference between color and taste."

For just as form (*rūpa*), although it exists through its commonality of being an entity (*bhāva-sāmānya*), is a different object from taste (*rasa*), and taste is also a different object from form because its nature is defined as distinct from form—and the same applies to smell and so forth, and smell and so forth are likewise distinct from those two—so too, that form is a different power (*śakti-antara*) from those two; and when they function together, form and taste are distinct from each other. In this way, although humans and the like constitute an "army" (*senā*) through their identity with that generality, the army is both distinct from them—as indicated by the word "also" (*api*)—and yet not distinct from them, because it is merely their aggregate and identical in essence to them.

Therefore, this principle applies even earlier, as in the verse beginning "man, chariot, horse," and so forth: [the mountain] is other than its various powers because it is not identical with them, yet it is not other than them because of that identity.

Likewise, in the case of the peaks and so forth—the mountain is other than the peak, the ridge, and so on, because it does not exist in each of those individually; yet it is not other than them, because it exists precisely in those when they are combined. Thus, the peaked one is other than those [parts].

Likewise, regarding "black pepper" (*marica*) and so forth, because of the statement "in those mixed according to the proper method," the drink is distinct from black pepper and the other ingredients; yet, because it possesses the six tastes, it is not non-distinct from them. Furthermore, it is distinct from the individual components due to the presence or absence of a different capacity—such as the provocation or pacification of diseases like wind (*vāta*)—and it exists within the aggregate as a whole.

Likewise, the self (ātman) is also non-different from pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and so forth, because it consists of these successive states (paryāya) that arise in sequence, since those [qualities] such as pleasure are merely modifications (pariṇāma) of the self and are not distinct from it. On the other hand, it is different [from them], because each of them is distinguished by being either contradictory or non-contradictory, because the self is fully accounted for by that many [states], and because the conceptualization of difference or non-difference arises from the presence of distinct capacities or from their identity with that [self].

Likewise, there are sweetness, sourness, and so forth; those things which possess these qualities, such as sweetness and the rest, are "possessors thereof" (*tadvantah*). From those possessors, pungency and other qualities are established. When these are combined, they constitute the substance of the *pānaka* (a medicinal drink). Here, the proposition (*pratijñā*) is that it possesses its own nature (*svatattva*); by the word "also" (*api*), it is implied that it also possesses the nature of others (*paratattva*), because it is established in that manner, like the sweet taste. Just as taste exists even when earth and the other elements are not admitted [as separate entities], in the same way, the substance of the *puruṣa* and the aggregates (*skandhas*) may be formless yet be form, ...because their essence is consciousness (*vijñāna*);
thus, all five are likewise.

Since the self is also those very [aggregates], both self and non-self are therefore those very [aggregates]; thus, those who say that the self is merely the aggregates are ignorant in the doctrine of difference (bhedavāda).

...and because of your indifference toward the principles (tattvas) and your false attachment [to them], you do not perceive the Self as it is described by the Advaita— that which consists of knowledge, bliss, and so forth, and is neither different nor non-different [from Brahman].

Therefore, because [a substance] is not perceived apart from its connection with other concomitant factors consisting of both the universal and the particular—such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth—it follows that it is neither its own essence (*svatattva*) nor another's essence (*paratattva*); likewise, even a beverage (*pānaka*) is not like that, and so on. Thus, the explanation of the examples, beginning with "form" (*rūpa*), has its meaning already established.
That bliss is mutual,
pervading all beings.
