Because of the sixfold nature of existence (satva), and because of the sixfold nature of non-existence (asatva), [it is] not other than the elements such as wind and so forth.
In the same way, the substance of the person—the aggregates—though formless, may also be form... because their very nature is consciousness;
thus it is for all five.

Since the self is also those very [aggregates], both self and non-self are therefore those very same things; thus, those who say that the self is merely the aggregates are unwise in their doctrine of difference.
Furthermore,

due to indifference toward the principles (*tattva*) and because of your false attachment to them, you do not perceive the Self as it is defined by the non-dual doctrine (*advaita*), which is neither distinct from nor identical to knowledge, bliss, and so forth.

Therefore, since the substance of the person (*puruṣadravya*) consists precisely of the nature of both the universal and the particular, and so forth, why is the mode of "self" not subsumed within the mere aggregates (*skandhamātra*),
such that it would not be included? For the aggregates themselves are the subject of this proposition.

The explanation is that even that which is formless (arūpa) may be called "form" (rūpa), and so forth. That which is called form—consisting of the objects such as visible matter and the sense-faculties such as the eye, as well as non-informative matter (avijñapti)—is "formed" because it is appropriated by consciousness as its own nature; therefore, although it is formless, it is [called] form precisely because its essence is consciousness. He extends this principle to the other five aggregates as well. This is because feeling and the rest are invariably connected with the characteristics of having the nature of form and so forth, as well as the distinctions of being gross or subtle; for it is accepted that they exist in a state of mutual inseparability, as it has been said: "Just as two bundles of reeds stand leaning one against the other."
Thus, name and form exist as mutually dependent; likewise,

the self (ātman) is also of the nature of consciousness, for those very aggregates (skandhas) such as form and the rest constitute both the self and the non-self through their respective states of being either distinct powers or identical with that [consciousness].

Therefore, because they do not deviate from the position established by the Master [Vasubandhu], it is incorrect that even they recite with absolute certainty [the definition] "like a heap" and so forth;
for form consists of the five sense-faculties, the five objects, and non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) alone.
Thus, in the Abhidharmakośa, Chapter 1,
Verse 9: the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) is threefold— the five faculties beginning with the eye, the five objects beginning with visible form, and non-informative matter (avijñapti).
That formless form also exists;
just as two bundles of reeds stand leaning against one another,
so too do name and form exist leaning against one another.

Therefore, those who claim that the self—which is neither distinct from nor non-distinct from the aggregates—is merely the aggregates themselves, are indeed lacking in wisdom; this is the summary [of the argument]. (Page 787, line 2; Page 824, line 24)

For this reason as well, their doctrine of duality is a sign of their lack of wisdom, and so forth. Just as in the *Atītanaya* (the "Past Doctrine"), the reality was accepted as being merely an aggregate of form and the other [sensory qualities], whereby that proponent of particulars was refuted because he admitted that the aggregate is the universal (*sāmānya*) of the particular qualities such as form; likewise here too, you must be refuted by the followers of Siddhārtha—who accept both [the universal and the particular]—on the grounds that the aggregate of the five aggregates is itself merely a universal. Therefore, do not grasp at a "real entity" (*vastu*).
Furthermore: "And because of indifference," and so forth.

Due to a lack of respect for the thorough knowledge of reality, due to false attachment, and due to the self-conceit of thinking "I am a seer of reality," you do not perceive yourself as "I am happy, I am suffering, I am attached, or I am hateful"—a state brought about by your own grasping, which is described in the *Advaita* (non-dual) doctrine as being neither different nor non-different from the essence of knowledge and happiness.

Therefore, because you do not transcend that identity [with the self], even one who asserts that there is merely an aggregate of form and so forth falls into the position of a follower of the *Siddhārtha* school, since they are asserting a real entity (*vastu*).
This applies likewise to the remaining doctrines.
Enough with this digressive discourse; desist from mere talk and grasp the reality thus: all this is devoid of intrinsic nature, like the experience of one who is asleep or insane.

Because consciousness follows the conceptualization of forms as "this" or "not this," it is logically correct to conceive that, in the ultimate sense, this [consciousness] is empty—devoid of those respective forms—and is indeed emptiness itself, like an empty house, being devoid of the conceptualization of an enterer, a dweller, or an exit, as well as arising and so forth.
Furthermore, that intrinsic nature (svabhāva) does not arise from itself, nor from another, nor from both, nor without a cause.

Now, how is it that even for one who asserts a mere collection of form and so forth, the consequence of being a follower of the Sāṃmitīyas follows, because of being a proponent of real entities (*vastuvādin*), since they do not transcend the nature of possessing general and particular characteristics which are preceded by the apprehension of internal capacities belonging to self, other, or both? Thus it was rightly said.
"From the wise one," etc.; "the meaning of 'grah' is to seize," etc.
If the intended meaning is "due to a lack of regard for the thorough knowledge of reality," then the reading *tattvaparijñānādarāt* is also correct.

[Regarding the phrase] *jñānamukhyādyanyānanyātma* (Bhāṣya) or *jñānamukhyādyanyātma* (Yaśaḥ), there might also be the reading: "The non-dual nature of that which consists of pleasure and so forth, as well as what is other than them, has been described in the *Advaitavāda*; you perceive yourself as 'I am happy,' 'I am miserable,' 'I am attached,' or 'I am hateful.'"

Because they do not transgress [the principle of] "you" (tvānatikramāt), even those who maintain that there is merely an aggregate of form and so forth would fall into being followers of the Saiddhāntikas, since they are proponents of real entities (vastuvāditvāt);
this applies likewise to the remaining doctrines.
Thus, enough of this digressive discussion.
Desist from this discourse on things;

rather, let it be understood thus: all this is without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), like one who is asleep or insane, because consciousness follows the conceptual construction of various forms—both those [forms] and their opposites. Therefore, it is logical to conceive that, in the ultimate sense, this is empty, being devoid of those respective forms, like an empty house, lacking the conceptualization of an enterer, a dweller, or an exit, as well as arising and so forth.
And that intrinsic nature does not arise from itself, nor from another, nor from both, nor without a cause;
how then [could it exist] from self, other, or both? (p.
The same applies to the remaining doctrines; this is an extension [of the principle].
Thus, even in the remaining doctrines such as those concerning the Person (Puruṣa) and so forth, the Syādvāda necessarily follows by force, having been applied in each case in that very manner.

Enough with this digressive discussion—how much more could be said? Desist from the doctrine of absolute entities, for there is no connection between the pursuit of absolute certainty and the acceptance of the doctrine of reality.
Thus it is said;
enough with these afflictions.

Desist from this praise; setting aside what was previously stated, how then should it be understood? It should be grasped thus: all this is devoid of intrinsic nature, like one who is asleep or insane.

Just as for one who is asleep, the vision of a herd of elephants and so forth—even though there is no physical space [for them]—has objects that lack intrinsic nature and are empty of that or any other nature, so it is for one who is awake; or just as for one who is intoxicated and agitated by liquor and the like, the heretics (pākhaṇḍins) who are attached, hostile, or deluded are indeed equivalent to those who are asleep or intoxicated.

Because consciousness follows the conceptualization of forms that are both "that" and "not-that," its forms are constructed by consciousness through the nature of being "that" or "not-that," like the objects of consciousness in states such as sleep or intoxication—appearing as "something or other. However, in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), no form exists at all because of the non-existence [of such objects]. Even though this [consciousness] is perceived by the intellect through various forms, it is empty of those forms due to the fluctuation of the subjective form (*grāhakākāra*) and the delusion regarding the objective form (*grāhyākāra*). Therefore, it is logical to conceive that there is no subject, but rather only emptiness. How so? Like an empty house, which is devoid of the conceptualization of an enterer, a dweller, or a leaver; just as in an empty house there is no enterer, no dweller, and no leaver related to arising, staying, or perishing, so too this [reality] accepted as knowledge and the object of cognition is devoid of arising, staying, and destruction. This is the summary statement.
In the syllable *va*, there is the elephant-faced one;
in *ma*, the primordial one; in *ya*, the one beginning with the well-intoxicated.
Comparison—page 553—[is there] because of the absence of "1"?
[It is] an error; therefore, [it is] from Ya.
Comparison— page 553—
1. *sthātā* (Ya), *nirgantā* (Ya),
*sambandhāya* (Ya).
And when that intrinsic nature is examined, it must arise either from a cause or without a cause;
if from a cause, it would have to arise from itself, from another, or from both.

Yet that intrinsic nature does not arise from itself, nor from another, nor from both, nor without a cause. Herein lies the question of logical proof: how, then, can there be an entity? [The answer follows] from the non-establishment, the illogicality, the non-arising, and the observation or non-observation of causal conditions.

Is there an absence of self, other, and both? We reply: From these reasons—namely, non-establishment, illogicality, non-arising, and the observation and non-observation of the causal complex—what intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) could there be in non-establishment and illogicality? If there were arising, there might be an entity that is either self or other; but if there is no arising, how could such an entity exist? First, regarding non-establishment: length does not reside in the long itself, because length is dependent upon something else.
For if this [quality of length] belonged solely to its own object, then the shortness of the ring finger would not exist, since it would not depend on anything else.
And if that [middle finger] were not short, there would be an absence of medium and long lengths;

and because of that, there would be an absence of shortness in the ring finger. Since these two are mutually dependent, when will the middle finger ever be established as long—only when the ring finger becomes short? And when will the ring finger become short—only when the middle finger is established as long? Thus, due to this mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*), neither is established.
Length does not exist even in what is short, because it is the opposite of that;

or, if there were length in that which is long, then since length would be absent [in the short], length would not be its own nature (svo bhāvaḥ) even when perceived within the causal complex (sāmagrī).
Furthermore, when it is not perceived, it certainly has no intrinsic nature (svabhāva); thus will be the conclusion.

This prima facie argument for the doctrine of emptiness (*śūnyavāda*), presented in the *Viśeṣāvaśyakabhāṣya* with its commentary, should be followed here as appropriate at various points during the investigation of the doctrine of emptiness: "The Blessed One, clarifying the reasoning that has entered the minds of the discerning, said: 'Just as, O wise one, the establishment of entities is not from themselves, nor from another, nor from both, nor even from no cause; just as [the relationship] between long and short... (1692)

O Manifest One! This is your intention: namely, that the establishment of entities (*bhāva*) cannot possibly occur either from themselves, nor from another, nor from both, nor even from anything else. Why? He says: "Because of dependence" (*apekṣātaḥ*), meaning because the relationship of cause and effect and so forth is relative. This is due to the designations of "short" and "long";
for instance, whatever collection of entities exists, all of it must be either an effect or a cause.

In this regard, since the effect is produced by the cause, its designation as an "effect" depends entirely upon the cause; there is no such thing as the "effect-ness" of the effect that is established independently.
Likewise, since the cause produces the effect, its designation as a "cause" depends entirely upon the effect; there is no such thing as the "causality" of the cause that is established independently.
Thus, the state of being an effect and so forth is not established by way of its own nature.
And that which is not established by itself cannot be established even by another, just as the horn of a donkey;
therefore, the existence of an effect and so forth is not established through itself, nor through another, nor through both self and other— if this is your position.
That is incorrect, because its establishment does not occur from either one individually, nor is it possible for it to occur in their collection;
for oil, which does not exist in each individual grain of sand, does not appear in their collection.
Furthermore, in the position that it is established from both, the fallacy of mutual dependence (itaretarāśraya) ensues.
For as long as the effect is not established, the cause is not established; and as long as the cause is not established, the effect does not attain establishment.
Therefore, there is the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).
Consequently, the existence of both cause and effect cannot be established in either case.
Nor from another; that is to say, not from both [self and other]. This is because, since no entity exists apart from self, other, or both, it would follow that it is causeless.

In this way, regarding the example of the characteristics of "short" and "long," one should contemplate the logical concomitance (*anvaya*) of the reason "due to dependence" with the probandum characterized by the non-establishment of shortness and length.

For instance: the length of the index finger is perceived in dependence upon the thumb, while its shortness is perceived in dependence upon the middle finger. However, in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), this finger is neither inherently short nor inherently long.

Thus, in this way, there is no establishment of shortness and length *per se*; therefore, the absence of their establishment from another, from both, or from neither should be contemplated as previously explained. As it has been said:
"In this case, length does not exist in that which is long, nor in that which is short, nor in both."
Therefore, because of its emptiness, how could it be designated as "existent"?
(1) Depending on the short, the long is established; depending on the long, the short is also established.
Nothing exists as established in itself; they speak thus only by the force of conventional usage. (2)
Furthermore, from what [source] does the emptiness of the entire world arise? To this he says:
Because of the faults such as the non-existence of the pot, its multiplicity, or its oneness.
"All entities are either inexpressible or entirely void.

(1693) Now, is there identity or difference between existence (*astitva*) and the jar? If there is identity, then the consequence of universal oneness follows: since whatever exists is that very jar, because the jar enters into existence, it would follow that everything is a jar; nor would other objects such as cloth be distinct from the jar, and thus, due to its non-difference from all that exists, the jar would consist of the nature of everything.

Alternatively, if one holds that "whatever is a pot, that alone exists," then existence is restricted solely to the pot. Since there would be no existence elsewhere, it follows that everything other than the pot would be non-existent; consequently, the pot would be the only thing, or else even it would not exist at all. For a pot is defined by its exclusion of what is not a pot (*aghaṭa-vyāvṛtti*); when its opposite, the non-pot, does not exist, then in relation to what could this pot exist? Thus, there is universal emptiness (*sarva-śūnyatva*). Now, for the second alternative: if the pot and existence are distinct, then the pot is non-existent because it lacks existence, like the horn of a donkey.

Furthermore, existence (*sattva*) is said to be the state of being existent (*sat*). If that [existence] were different from the pots and so forth which serve as its own substrata (*ādhāra*), then it would simply be non-existent, because it is logically impossible for that which is supported (*ādheya*) to exist apart from its substratum.

Thus, by means of the alternatives of identity and difference with respect to existence, according to the reasoning already stated, all things such as pots would entail defects such as the oneness of all things; consequently, all entities would either be inexpressible, or entirely void, or else there would be a total absence of them altogether—this is the meaning.
Furthermore, that which does not arise is indisputably non-existent, like the horn of a donkey; thus, discussion of it has ceased.

As for that which is accepted in the world as having origination, its arising is also untenable when analyzed through the logical alternatives of whether it arises from what is already born or what is unborn. Therefore, emptiness alone is logical.
He says this very thing:
Since that which is being born is not born from the born, the unborn, or both,
because of the faults of infinite regress and non-existence, therefore there is emptiness.
First of all, that which has not yet arisen does not arise, precisely because it has not arisen, like a finished jar.

Now, if even that which has already arisen were to arise, there would be an infinite regress, due to the consequence of arising again and again, since there is no distinction in its state of having already arisen.

Now, if that which is unborn is born, the author provides the following answer: because the aphorism is indicative [of a flaw], then even a non-entity characterized as a donkey’s horn should be born, since there is no difference in its being unborn.

Furthermore, if that which has both the nature of the born and the unborn is born, that too is incorrect. Why? He says: "Because of the faults of both," meaning that the faults stated for each of the two positions would result [here].
Moreover, does this duality characterized by the born and the unborn exist or not?
If it exists, then it is already born; thus it is not "both," and the fault in that case has already been stated.

Or, if it does not exist, even so it is not "both," but rather it is simply unborn; and the refutation for that case has also already been set forth. Nor is that which is currently being born born, because it does not escape the two aforementioned alternatives. To explain: is that which is being born existent or not? If it exists, then it is already born.
If it does not exist, then it is simply unarisen;
and in both these positions, the fault has already been stated.
As it was said: "That which has already moved is not being traversed, nor is that which has not yet moved being traversed."
"That which is presently being traversed is not being traversed, as it is free from both what has been traversed and what has not yet been traversed," and so forth.
Since this is so, therefore, because of the consequence of faults such as infinite regress and because the arising of entities is impossible, it is logical that the world is indeed empty.
(Verse 1694) That which has already been traversed is not being traversed, nor is that which has not yet been traversed being traversed.
That which is free from having gone and not yet gone—the present process of going—is not being gone over.

Furthermore, because the arising of an entity is impossible through any other mode, he says for the purpose of establishing emptiness: "Since the effect does not exist within the causes, the conditions, their assemblage, or their individual states..."
The effect is seen as consisting of the totality [of causes]; yet, when there is an absence of all [causes], there is no totality.

(1695) The "causes" (*hetavaḥ*) are the material causes (*upādāna-kāraṇa*), while the "conditions" (*pratyayāḥ*) are the instrumental causes (*nimitta-kāraṇa*). The meaning is this: that effect which is not seen in the various separate states (*viṣvag-bhāveṣu*) of those causes and conditions—that is, in their individual existences—is nevertheless seen as consisting of the totality when they are in a state of complete assembly. And this being so, the logical conclusion is that the total non-existence of the effect [in its parts] is established; such is the remainder of the sense.

And if all [factors] are absent, there is no causal totality (*sāmagrī*); the meaning is that the existence of a causal totality is not attained. Therefore, the implication is that everything is empty (*sarvaśūnyatā*). This is the core point here: do causes (*hetu*) and conditions (*pratyaya*) produce the object they generate individually or collectively? First, it is not individually, because such is not observed.
Consequently, since the effect is absent in each individual constituent, it would likewise be absent in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) itself—just as there is no oil in a grain of sand.

And thus, if the production of every effect were impossible, the existence of the causal complex could not be established, because a causal complex that has not produced an effect is itself untenable.
Therefore, the entire world would result in total emptiness.
And it has been said: "Because they are not perceived when separated from the collection of causes and conditions,
all those entities are indeed inexpressible by way of their own-being."
Since whatever designations exist in the world are seen only in relation to a causal complex, therefore entities do not exist; when an entity exists, the complex does not exist.
The explanation of this passage and so forth is as follows: the phrase "because [the effect] is not seen in separate entities" is the ellipsis to be supplied.

Therefore, all those entities such as pots and the like are by their own nature—that is, by their very essence—inexpressible. This is because an effect is not produced in each individual separate state; and since the designation "pot" and so forth does not apply in the absence of production, and because it is impossible to express something that lacks a designation.

Furthermore, why does conceptual designation (*saṃjñā*) not function when things exist separately? To this he says: "In the world, as long as... and so forth. In the world, as long as there is the functioning of conceptual designations such as "this is a jar," so long is the complete effect seen only when the causal totality (*sāmagrī*) is complete; for if they were separate, the causal totality would be absent, and thus entities (*bhāva*) would not exist at all, like oil in sand. And if entities do not exist, how could there be the existence of a causal totality? (Verse 1695) This is because [the effect] is not observed in the separate parts of the causal conditions and their totality.
Therefore, all those entities are indeed inexpressible by their very nature.
Since in the world whatever designation exists is seen only in dependence upon a causal complex, therefore entities do not exist; when an entity exists, the complex does not exist. 1–2.

He speaks again in another way for the sake of establishing emptiness: "Because of the non-perception of other parts, because of the subtlety of all parts, because of the non-apprehension of both, and because of the non-apprehension of everything, it is empty. (1696)
In this regard, whatever is perceived here is indeed non-existent, because it is not apprehended, like the horn of a donkey; thus, talk of such things has ceased.

Furthermore, even for visible objects such as pillars, jars, or walls, there is indeed non-existence at both the far and middle parts, because those two are not perceived due to being obscured by the near part. Moreover, since the near part itself possesses constituent parts, it must have another near part, and that too another, and yet another; thus it continues until the most distant part reaches a state of extreme subtlety, consisting of nothing more than a layer of atoms (*paramāṇu*). This is because the preceding near parts are not perceived, as each is obscured by the one following it.

Furthermore, according to the logic already stated, because neither of the two parts—the part that is "other" nor the part that is "all-enemy" (the internal)—is perceived, there is no perception of any category of entity whatsoever; thus, the world is empty.
And it has been said: "As far as there is anything visible, so far there is an 'other' part, and that is not seen;
therefore, all entities are indeed inexpressible by their very nature."

Thus, by the reasoning already stated, it follows that everything beginning with the gross elements (*bhūta*) would be non-existent; yet, the existence of the gross elements and so forth is also heard in the Śruti. This constitutes the doubt, which forms the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).
"As long as there is an object of perception, so long is there a part [of it]; yet that [object] is not perceived.
Therefore, all things are indeed inexpressible by their very nature. (1)
—Thus, in the *Viśeṣāvaśyakabhāṣya-ṭīkā* composed by Maladhārī Hemacandrasūri, folios 722–725;
compare with folio 553:
"What is the state [of proof]? It is [established] through non-establishment, lack of logical consistency, non-arising, the observation of causal conditions, and non-observation."
First of all, length cannot exist in that which is not long, because length is dependent upon something else.

For if this [notion of length] were restricted solely to its own object, then the ring finger would not possess shortness, since it would not depend on anything else; and in the absence of shortness for that [ring finger], there would be an absence of medium length and so forth.
And therefore, there is no absence of shortness in the ring finger (*anāmikā*), because those two are mutually dependent:

when would the middle finger (*madhyamā*) be established as long, if the ring finger were short? And when would the ring finger be short, if the middle finger were to be established as long? Due to this circularity (*itaretarāśrayatva*), there is no proof;
for even in the case of the short, there is no length, because they are opposites.
Or rather, because length is absent within length itself, length is a comparison— [page 544]— furthermore,
it is a distinction of intrinsic nature.
Since these reasons are to be established in sequence, he says: "First, because of non-establishment," and so forth.
The middle finger is long, the ring finger is short; that which is the nature of length—the lengthiness—of the long middle finger does not first exist within itself, [the long finger].

Why? Because that length of the middle finger (*madhyamā*) is dependent upon another; for that length of hers is dependent upon the shortness of the ring finger (*anāmikā*). Indeed, it is only in relation to that short ring finger that the middle finger is called "long. How could that which is unestablished in itself—like a donkey's horn—be established through something else? (Compare: p. 553, l. 1; compare: p. 831, l. 16; p. 833, l. 3).
It might be thought: "This [length] is indeed dependent on itself.

That is not so, because it would follow that the ring finger (anāmikā) would lack its shortness. For if this [length] were restricted solely to its own object—that is, if the length of the middle finger (madhyamā) were dependent solely on itself—then the shortness of the ring finger would not exist, since it would not depend on anything else; it too would have to be long. Just as the middle finger is considered long independently of the ring finger, so too the ring finger should be considered long by itself, independently of the middle finger, just like the middle finger. But this is not the case, because its shortness is desired. (Tulanā, p. 833, l. 22)
Just as with the self (*ātman*) and so forth:

if it is maintained that the ring finger (*anāmikā*) is indeed short, then in its state of being short, there would be an absence of "medium" and "long" [dimensions]. Since the ring finger lacks shortness in relation to itself, there could be no length in the middle finger (*madhyamā*); for it is only in dependence upon that very ring finger—which is designated as "short"—that the [middle finger] is designated as "long. If that ring finger is not short, in relation to what else could the middle finger be long? Thus, there is an absence of length in that [middle finger].
And because that middle [finger] lacks length, there is an absence of shortness in the ring finger, which is the opposite of length; for these two are mutually dependent.
He contemplates this: "When will it be middle-sized? and so on, up to "when will it be established. This contemplation of mutual dependence has already been explained.

Due to this mutual dependence, there is no establishment; thus, because of the aforementioned mutual dependence, the conceptualization of shortness and length falls apart, like two boats tied together and struck by winds upon the water.

Thus, for one who desires that length exists as a property of the long, a consequence has been established through the undesirable result (prasaṅga) that both [length and the possessor of length] are non-existent.
[Note on *varddhābustha*]—Compare page 34, line 9.

It might be argued: "In that case, length would exist even in what is short; for according to the method you have stated, since length is dependent upon shortness, the length of the middle finger ought to exist in dependence upon the shortness of the ring finger. Therefore, length is established, and likewise shortness is established because it is dependent upon the other."

To this it is replied: Even when there is shortness, there is no length, because of their mutual opposition; since length is contradicted by shortness, the short [atom] itself has become [the state of being], for that [shortness] consists in the absence of length. How, then, could another length arise? Furthermore, due to the absence of shortness, there is no length.

Nevertheless, if one were to again admit the existence of both length and shortness, there would be no length because of the absence of length which is the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) to shortness.
Nor is there [length] in both, according to the logic already stated, or because of the mutual opposition between self and other.

This mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*) must also be examined: does the long [vowel] arise when shortness is present, or when length itself is present? If the quality of length, while residing in the short, attains its manifestation in both, then how can length residing in the short establish the identity of the short and produce the cognition of it? For shortness and length are mutually contradictory—like darkness and light, or life and death—and thus cannot coexist in one place. Alternatively, if that [short vowel] possesses length, then because of the absence of length [in the short], upon accepting that the short has length, it follows that length, having departed from the long and settled in the short, has itself become short; therefore, there is an absence of length [in the short].
Why? Because that shortness consists in the absence of length;
for in the world, that which is not long is called "short.

Therefore, since it consists in the absence of length, from where could another length have come? Furthermore, due to the absence of shortness, there is no length; because length exists in the short, and since that which is occupied by length finds no room [in its absence], where could length reside when shortness itself is absent? For this reason also, there is an absence of length.
Comparison—page 834, line 17:

By means of length, the short [vowel] becomes [the long]; since that [short vowel] consists of the absence of length, from where could another length have come? And because of the absence of shortness, there is no length.
Nevertheless, if one further accepts the existence of both length and shortness, then because there is no length—which is the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*)—of shortness, length does not exist;
nor do both exist, according to the logic already stated, or because of the mutual opposition between self and other.

This reciprocal conjunction (*itaretarayoga*) must also be examined: when shortness exists, does length become long, or does it exist only when length itself exists? If length existing in shortness attains its manifestation in both, then length existing in shortness would constitute the very nature of the short and its cognition.
This passage is not present in manuscript Ya; nevertheless, it is stated in Ya as "punar" and so forth.

Furthermore, even if one accepts the existence of both length and shortness, length is not established because of the absence of its counter-correlative, shortness; for it is impossible for something to reside in itself or in another.
It might be argued: "It exists in both, because both depend on each other; shortness is established in relation to length, and length is established in relation to shortness."

And this [longness] does not exist in the pair [of long and short]. Why? Because of the logic already stated. Just as, having begun with "lengthiness does not reside in the long because it would be dependent on another," and continuing up to the point where it was said that "it is unestablished due to mutual dependence," lengthiness is not established; likewise, it is not established in the short either, according to the logic just stated. How can there be establishment in both when it is unestablished in either one of the two? Or, because they are opposites of each other—just as lengthiness exists in both the long and the short, so too shortness exists in both the long and the short—therefore, the presence of both in both is contradictory. It has been stated that their coexistence is untenable precisely because of their mutual opposition.

Therefore, neither length nor shortness is established from itself, nor from another, nor from both; this is because the same will be applied by analogy to shortness as well. [Is it] "mutually dependent"?
And this is the second [point].
Page 834, line 22; page 830, lines 1–5;
page 833, line 2.

Furthermore, this [property of] lengthness functions in both cases; however, that is a mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*), which must also be examined: does "length" become long when it exists elsewhere than its own substrate—the short vowel—or does "lengthness" exist only in its own substrate, which is already long? This must be determined.

What follows from this? If [the first alternative is maintained], namely, that "if" (yadi) and so forth—that is, if it is accepted as the first alternative that length residing in the short obtains existence in both [entities] through mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*), then what of it? Consequently, length residing in the short, without producing lengthiness in the short, would neither produce the nature of length nor the cognition of length in the long, because it resides elsewhere, just like the cognition of length in the short.

When length is already present, it becomes long; therefore, it is only in that which is already long that it produces length and establishes its causal condition (*tatpratyaya*). However, there is no purpose served by a short [vowel] or by its causal condition.

Now, if it does not produce length therein, nor establish its causal condition, then how could it produce length in a short vowel? For it would be operating elsewhere, like the causal condition for length applied to a short vowel.
Or, if it were said: "In a short vowel, it certainly does not produce length, nor does it establish its causal condition."

This also is not [the case], because in the world it is observed that shortness and length are established through mutual dependence, and their cognition is likewise— as for example, in the case of a mustard seed...

It neither produces nor instills that cognition; for how could that which does not produce the state of being its own substrate nor the cognition based upon it, [and thus] does not produce the "longness" in a short vowel—which lacks that as its substrate—nor the cognition "it is long," do so? It would neither produce nor instill that cognition, because it subsists elsewhere. Whatever subsists elsewhere than something else does not produce the state of being that thing for it, nor does it instill the cognition thereof, just like the cognition of "longness" in a short vowel. Just as "longness" does not produce or instill the cognition of "longness" in a short vowel, so too "longness" would neither produce nor instill the cognition of "longness" in what is already long.
Comparison: pṛ॰ 833 paṃ॰ 2 bhavatyataḥ svā॰ ya॰; dītve bhavatibhā॰.

The passage beginning with "etadantargato na" and ending with "dīrghatām" is not present in manuscript *ya*. Furthermore, one who does not perform [the action] would not produce the state of length (*dīrghatā*) nor the cognition (*buddhi*) of that [length], because [the action] occurs elsewhere; for example, like the cognitions of shortness and length. When length itself exists in the long [object], it becomes long; therefore, it is the long [object] itself that produces the state of length and instills its cognition. However, there is no purpose served by the short [object] or its cognition.

Now, if it does not produce length therein, nor establishes the cognition thereof, then how could it produce length in what is short? For it would be functioning elsewhere; it would be like the cognition of "short" and "long" [occurring with respect to different things]. If it were argued: "It does not produce length in the short, nor does it establish the cognition thereof"—this too is not correct, because in the world it is observed that the establishment of "short" and "long" occurs through mutual dependence, as does their respective cognitions.
Namely: siddhārthaka...
[and] long, very long, [having] confidence in the condition.

Now, lest this fault should arise, if it is maintained that "length" itself exists as length, we reply: if it is held that "length existing in length alone," and so forth, then this follows: "Length, existing in length alone, produces lengthiness and establishes its own cognition therein. This is indeed accepted; however, there is no need for a short vowel—other than long—to be postulated for the sake of mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*), nor is there any need for its cognition, since that is established by the power of its own substrate alone.
Thus, "length does not produce lengthiness."
It does not produce length;

moreover, this is a fault arising from the context of mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*). Now, regarding the passage beginning with "therein" (*tatra*) and so forth: if you think that even though there is mutual conjunction, [the rule] "therein" (*tatra*) does not produce length nor bestow the designation of "long" (*dīrgha*) for the sake of avoiding the fault of the redundancy of the short-short designation, then another set of faults follows: it would follow that even in the case of a short vowel, it would not produce length nor would it bestow the designation of "long."

The demonstration of this meaning is as follows: the passage beginning with "How [could it arise] in the short," etc., has its meaning already explained as before, up to the proof that it is like the cognition of short and long; thus, the word "short" (hrasva) will produce [the cognition], according to the manuscript *pra*.
Might there also be the reading "mādadhāti" here?
[This refers to] the previous argument,
Pañjikā 1.20.

Now, if it were said by you for the sake of avoiding this fault: "It does not produce length in what is short, and thus it does not even establish the cognition of length"—this too is untenable, because in the world it is observed that the establishment of shortness and length is mutually dependent, as is their cognition; for it is seen that even a single entity, when viewed in relation to another object, possesses both shortness and length.
(Note: *apekṣyasi* is the reading in manuscript *bhā.*)

For example— starting from *siddhārthaka* and so forth, as mentioned in the *Daṇḍaka* [section], among the things seen to be short or long in mutual dependence, beginning with *siddhārthaka* and ending with Meru— if one accepts that there is no production of length in what is short and that the cognition of "long" is not applied to it, then there would be an absolute absence of length; just as there is no length,
the cognition of it would likewise not exist.
...just like the cognition of "shortness" itself,
even in the case of shortness,

both sides [of the argument] are not freed from the faults already stated for each individually; for even when there is a mutual dependence between two things that are individually unestablished, there is still non-establishment and contradiction.
If even a sky-flower could exist without a cause,
then even for things such as a jar, there would be no establishment of its own nature at all;
for the "jar-ness" of a jar does not belong to it by its own nature, since that jar-ness is dependent on something else.
For if this [notion of "non-pot"] were restricted solely to its own object, then it would not be "non-pot" even when facing a pot;
yet it is indeed "mutually other.
And if that [specific non-pot] is a non-pot, then all other pots are likewise non-pots, which results in the total absence of pots.
In the absence of that [longness], the non-existence of the "non-pot" follows as a consequence, because the state of being a non-pot is dependent upon the pot;
here, the proof for establishing an undesirable conclusion is already explained by the passage beginning with "it is not long at all," and so on, up to "just like shortness."
Likewise, its cognition also does not exist; this has already been explained up to the point that, just as with the cognition of shortness,
there is no such thing as "long," nor indeed is there anything like "shortness."
The cognition of that [longness] also does not [arise],
just like the cognition of shortness;
likewise, this applies to shortness as well.

However, the position that [the cause] belongs to both categories is not freed from the faults already stated for each individual case; for even when there is a dependence between two things that are individually unestablished (*asiddha*), they remain unestablished and involve contradiction.
If it were so that even a sky-flower could exist without a cause, then even jars and other such things would lack any established nature at all.
Pot-ness does not reside in the pot because pot-ness is dependent on something else;
for if this [pot-ness] were restricted solely to its own object, then the pot would never be a non-pot,
yet it is indeed both.
And if that [specific jar] is non-jar, then other jars would also be non-jars; thus, there would be an absence of jars.
In the absence of jars, there would be an absence of non-jars, because the state of being a non-jar depends upon the jar—this follows from the mere fact of its being proposed.
The extension (*atideśa*) applies thus even to shortness (*hrasvatva*):

if one begins with "if there is shortness in the short," and substitutes the word "short" for the word "long," that same text should be recited up to this limit. However, the position of mutual dependence—namely, that the short is both long and short, and the long is both long and short—is also not liberated from the faults stated for each individual case; for even when there is a mutual dependence between two things that are individually unestablished, that dependence itself lacks an independent foundation.
Furthermore, because of contradiction— since it has been stated that there is no occurrence due to the opposition between shortness and length—
it is thus established that neither shortness nor length is established through itself, through another, or through both; therefore,
the extension [of the rule] regarding "shortness" applies.
See page 831, line 21; page 835, line 13. Compare page 830, line 1.
Compare page 835, line 7.
It might be thought: "It is established without a cause.
To this it is replied: If even a sky-flower were to exist without a cause, then length would not be established without a cause; because of its lack of a cause, [length] would be like a sky-flower.
If it were established, then a sky-flower would also be established, because of its lack of a cause, just like length.
Comparison—page 835, line 8:
It might be thought that this principle applies to relative terms such as "short" and "long," but not to things like jars;
however, one should not think thus, because in this way, even jars and the like do not possess an established intrinsic nature (svarūpa).

He explains this: "In a jar, there is no 'jar-ness' because jar-ness is dependent on something else," and so forth. The same logic that applies to the negation of length applies here as well; by substituting "jar" for "long" and "non-jars"—such as cloth or another jar—for "short," one observes that even a jar is a non-jar, because one jar lacks the jar-ness of another jar, and because they differ from one another due to distinctions of place, time, form, and so on.
Therefore, jar-ness is dependent on another jar and dependent on cloth and other things.
If this [cognition] were indeed restricted to its own object, then a jar would not even be a non-jar.
But how, then, can it also be a non-pot? To this he says: "It exists as mutual [negation].

And when that very pot is a non-pot, just as that one is a non-pot, so too all other pots are indeed non-pots; thus, the absence of the pot—such as cloths and the like—is established as being simply non-pots.

In the absence of that jar, there is an absence of the non-jar. Why? Because the state of being a non-jar is dependent upon the jar; thus, that [non-jar] also does not exist as a non-jar. Therefore, the "non-jar" is either a jar other than that one or a cloth. When will this jarhood—which constitutes the essence of each individual instance—be established as a jar, such that this jar becomes a non-jar? And when will the non-jar be established, such that it becomes a jar? Since they are mutually dependent, neither is established.

If it is argued that, in that case, "pot-ness" (ghaṭatva) resides only in a pot whose directions have been shown, because it is observed as such, [we reply: even in a non-pot there is no pot-ness, precisely because of direct perception; for pot-ness is absent in what is not a pot, due to their being contraries, just like shortness and length. Or, if a non-pot were to possess pot-ness, then that very non-pot would have become a pot; what indeed is a pot other than a non-pot? For "non-pot-ness" consists in the absence of pot-ness.
Nor does it reside in both, just as pot-ness does not reside in a pot because pot-ness is dependent [on another], so too it does not reside in a non-pot.

Since it is unestablished in either one of the two, how could it exist in both? This is because of its opposition to both self and other. Furthermore, this mutual conjunction must be examined: when the property of being a jar (*ghaṭatva*) exists in what is not a jar (*aghaṭa*), does it thereby become a jar, or does it exist only in that which is already a jar? If the property of being a jar existing in what is not a jar were to acquire existence in both, then—since it exists elsewhere—that property of being a jar existing in what is not a jar would not produce the nature of a jar nor the cognition thereof in the jar, just as the cognition of "not being a jar" applies to a cloth. This is because it is functioning elsewhere.

While the jar itself exists, the nature of being a jar (*ghaṭatva*) comes into being; therefore, the jar itself effects its own jar-nature and instills the corresponding cognition. However, there is no purpose for that which is not a jar nor for the cognition thereof.
Now, it does not effect its jar-nature therein because of the very essence of jar-nature; for jar-nature and non-jar-nature exist in mutual dependence.
He demonstrates this: "When will the jar be established as an individual entity, with a distinct and manifest nature excluded from other jars?"

The passage beginning with "When this [is called] a jar," etc., is to be understood as before; just as in the case of long and short, so too for the jar and non-jar, there is non-establishment due to mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*).
Thus, first of all, jar-ness does not exist in the jar. (Page 830, Line 1)
"Let there be no jar," and so forth;
compare page 830, line 2.
The non-existence of a jar is the state of being a non-jar; the state of being a non-jar is the existence of a jar.

Therefore, when will the jar be established as having the nature of each individual instance? When that which is a non-jar becomes a jar. And when will the non-jar be established? When that which is a jar becomes a non-jar. Thus, because of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*), there is no establishment [of either].

If it is argued: "In that case, according to the direction shown, the non-jar itself possesses jar-ness, because it is perceived as such," [we reply: even in the non-jar there is no jar-ness, because by direct perception (*pratyakṣataḥ*) jar-ness is absent in the non-jar, and because of their opposition (*pratidvandvitva*), like shortness and length.

If a non-pot were to possess potness, then that very non-pot would have become a pot; for what indeed is a "pot" other than a non-pot? Since non-potness consists in the absence of potness, [potness] does not exist in both. Just as potness does not reside in a pot because potness is dependent upon something else, likewise it does not reside in a non-pot either, because it is unestablished in either one of the two. How then could it reside in both? For they are opposites, even in relation to self and other.

This mutual conjunction (itaretarayoga) must also be examined: does the pot come to be when "pot-ness" resides in what is not a pot, or only when it resides in that which is already a pot? If the pot-ness residing in what is not a pot were to acquire its existence in both, then that pot-ness—while residing in the non-pot and failing to produce the nature of a pot or the cognition thereof in the non-pot—would likewise fail to produce the nature of a pot or the cognition thereof in the pot, because it is residing elsewhere, just like the pot-ness in a cloth or the cognition thereof.

While the jar itself exists, it becomes a jar by virtue of its "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatva*); therefore, the jar itself effects its own state as a jar and instills the corresponding cognition. However, there is no purpose served by that which is not a jar or by the cognition thereof.
Now, [if one argues] that it does not effect its state as a jar therein... (p. 830, l. 3).

[The opponent] might think: "In that case, as in the example of the 'non-pot' shown in the indicated direction, and according to the method explained now, you must admit that 'pot-ness' actually resides in what is a non-pot, because it is observed to be so. To this we reply: even in a non-pot, there is no pot-ness. This is evident from perception itself, since pot-ness is absent in things like cloth which are non-pots; moreover, due to their opposition, how could pot-ness exist in its contradictory, the non-pot? For two contradictories cannot coexist, as illustrated by the example of shortness and length.

Or, if non-potness were to become potness, [we must ask: if potness resides in what is not a pot, then that very non-pot has become a pot. Therefore, what indeed is a "pot" other than a non-pot? Thus, there is an absence of a pot. Why? Because non-potness consists in the absence of potness; this should be understood here as well, just like the previous discussion on long and short [in relation to each other], from page 830, line 24 to page 831, line 7.
One might think, as in the case of the short vowel, that [the rule] applies "in both cases";

but that is not so for the two [categories], because— just as with the short and long vowels— the individual establishment of "pot" and "non-pot" has already been demonstrated in such examples as "a pot," and the same logic applies here as well, up to the two supreme [energies].

"This too," and so forth. This is the same reasoning; however, the initial formulation is "pot-ness in what is not a pot" because it is easier to demonstrate that no cognition of the non-making of a pot can be applied to what is not a pot. The rest is as before. Furthermore, the pointing out of the contradiction with one's own words [is as follows]: "How is it that you say 'it is a pot' and yet maintain that it is a pot? The rest should be understood in the same way, up to the comparison with the cognition of a cloth, due to the distinction between the objects "pot" and "non-pot"; the same method of analysis applies. (Compare pṛ॰ 831, paṃ॰ 22).
Furthermore, it does not possess that qualification of the object [of the word "jar"];

therefore, how could it produce the cognition of "jarness" or the cognition [of a jar] with respect to what is not a jar? For, because it occurs elsewhere, it would be like the cognition of a cloth or a non-jar [produced by the word "jar"].
Now, it might be argued that [the cause] does not produce potness in what is not a pot, nor does it instill the corresponding cognition;
but this too is not correct, because in the world it is observed that the non-pot and the pot are established in mutual dependence, and so too is the cognition thereof—
for example, as in the case of the *siddhārthaka* [mustard seed]...
...just as a pot is not [itself] a non-pot.
Even that cognition [of it] does not [arise],
just like the cognition of a cloth.

Thus, even though there is no "non-pot-ness" in what is not a pot, having begun with the statement "there is no non-pot-ness in the non-pot," one should follow the same reasoning as for "pot-ness," substituting the word "non-pot" in place of the word "pot," up to that limit;
however, the position that [the two] belong to both [categories] is untenable due to the occurrence of both faults and because of contradiction.
If [an entity] were established without a cause, then even a sky-flower and the like would exist;
thus, since this applies to all objects, there would be no establishment at all.

Now, if it is argued that a jar is established by itself even without mutual conjunction, then if a single jar exists, the logical connection between its existence, oneness, and jar-ness is impossible—whether they are identical or distinct.

When one says, "Today there is one jar," the oneness of these three [existence, jar-ness, and the jar] implies that wherever there is oneness, there must also be existence by means of its own undivided essential nature (*svatattva*).

This principle applies even to the state of being a non-jar; thus, the author himself indicates this extension (*atideśa*) through the passage beginning with "not in a non-jar is there non-jar-ness," and so forth, up to the word "likewise" (*tadvat*), because the underlying logic has already been established. One should follow this reasoning as far as the case of jar-ness extends.

The position that [the self] is both [agent and enjoyer] is subject to the faults of both [positions], and thus its explanation—consisting of similar preceding and subsequent arguments—is already covered by the preceding section. Furthermore, the phrase "and because of contradiction" (*vipratiṣedhācca*) is to be understood in exactly the same way. (Page 833, line 2)
It might be thought: "Even if [the probandum] is not established by way of a cause that functions for itself, for another, or for both, it is nonetheless established without a cause.

But that is not so, because there is no establishment without a cause, as in the case of a sky-flower. If it were established even there without a cause, then a sky-flower and the like would also exist; thus, one should understand the undesirable consequence (aniṣṭāpādana) as before.
Even so?
The commentary on *sidhyata* (p. 833, l.

3) states: "In the same way, with respect to all objects"—this is an extension (*atideśa*) [of the argument], meaning that by the non-establishment of the jar, there follows the non-establishment of all intended objects, such as cloth, chariots, mats, and so forth, which are asserted to be established independently [of one another].
Thus, "it is indeed unestablished" is the conclusion that the reason, as proposed in the thesis, is proven to be unestablished.

The establishment of the reason (*hetu*) through the argument just mentioned is now stated; first, in order to demonstrate its connection, he says: "Now, even without mutual conjunction—that is, even without the reciprocal union of things—there exists a seed for the establishment of a jar in relation to one another. Why? If you think that 'the jar is established by itself, of its own accord,' we reply to this: 'If there is a jar,' and so forth. Because it is said 'it exists,' the jar is existent (*san*); and because it is expressed in the singular, it is a single substance (*dravya*). Therefore, in the investigation of whether there is a logical justification (*yukti*) or not for the existence, singularity, and jar-ness of that jar, the logical justification is their inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*). But that [concomitance] is not possible if those three are either identical or different."

How so? If it is accepted that there is unity among the three entities expressed by the words "it exists," "one," and "jar"—namely, "that which exists, is one, and is a jar"—then that unity must reside where [the other two] are; for they are not distinct from one another.

Wherever something is non-distinct from another, its own essential nature (svatattva) therein is exclusively undivided (*niṣkala*), just as the jar is the undivided essential nature of the jar itself.
And all existing things possess the essential nature of existence.

Likewise, having formulated the proof as before starting with "where there is existence," etc., the application (*upanaya*) is by way of that identity: "And all entities, such as cloth and so forth, which are not other than existence and unity through their own essential nature of unity in every single thing—
whatever exists is entirely a jar because it is non-different from the jar."

The single jar is existence (*astitva*) non-different from that [existence], and the existing jar is oneness (*ekatva*) non-different from that; thus, since it is not distinct from the existing jar, the jar itself is the establishment of everything. Likewise, wherever there is jar-ness (*ghaṭatva*), there must also be existence and oneness by way of their own indivisible essence (*niṣkala-svatattva*), because they are not different entities. Wherever something is not a different entity from another, there its own essence is necessarily indivisible, just as in the case of the jar and the jar’s own essence.

Therefore, the demonstration of that fault is as follows: if there were non-difference from the jar, then existence (*astitva*) and oneness (*ekatva*) would each be a single jar and so forth, such that everything would be [merely] a jar; we maintain that wherever there is oneness, there existence must also be partless, without remainder, and exist by its own very nature.
Why? Because of non-distinctness (*anarthāntaratva*).

This is the demonstration of the logical reason (*hetu*) through its positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with the probandum (*sādhya*), beginning with "wherever there is [oneness], of which... and so on.
In this context, "tatra tasya" and so forth constitute the application (*upanaya*). The meaning of the thesis (*sādhya*) is that one's own essential nature (*svatattva*) is indeed partless.

The example (*udāharaṇa*) is: "like the essential nature of a jar," meaning just as the essential nature of a jar exists in its entirety within the jar because it is not distinct from it, so too the essential nature of existence exists in its entirety within oneness. Consequently, since the essential nature of existence is all things, it follows that all things would be jars; for whatever exists is a jar because it is not separate from the jar—this conclusion will be stated later.
If there is one [in the] interval between the *nā* and *pa*, [then]...? For comparison— page 555–1.
Comparison—page 836, line 15; page 555–1:
It must be so, because there is no difference in meaning (*anarthāntaratva*).

Wherever something has no difference in meaning from another, there its own essential nature (*svatattva*) is indeed partless (*niṣkala*), just as the essential nature of a jar [is partless] in relation to the jar itself.
The own-nature of existence (*astitva-svatattva*) belongs to all things;

having established the proof as before with the words "wherein there is existence," and so forth, the application (*upanaya*) is by way of their identity: the own-nature of unity (*ekatva-svatattva*) resides in every single thing, and all entities such as cloth and the like are non-different from existence and unity.
Whatever exists is entirely the jar because it is not distinct from the jar;

and since the jar is one, existence is not other than that [oneness]. Furthermore, since the jar is existent, oneness is not other than that [existence]. Thus, because existence is not distinct from the jar, the establishment of everything is the jar alone.
Likewise, wherever there is "jar-ness," there too existence and oneness must exist as nothing but the partless intrinsic nature [of the jar], because they are not different entities.
Wherever something is not distinct from another, there its own essential nature (svatattva) is indeed partless, as in the case of a jar and the essential nature of a jar;
therefore, when there is non-difference from the jar, existence and oneness are both one and the same, such that every jar and so forth is a single entity. (Pañcadaśī 6.24)

Likewise, having performed the proof as before—beginning with "wherever there is existence," etc.—by means of this extension (*atideśa*), it follows that wherever there is existence, there must also be oneness (*ekatva*) by way of its own essence (*svatattva*) as something partless (*niṣkala*). This is because there is no difference in meaning (*anarthāntaratva*); for wherever something has no difference in meaning from another, there its own essence is necessarily partless, just as the own-essence of a jar is partless in relation to the jar itself. The distinction here, however, lies in the application (*upanaya*) by way of oneness, as follows: and the own-essence of oneness exists in every single thing, because each and every one of all things is individually one.
In both proofs, since all entities such as cloth and so forth are not other than existence (*astitva*) and unity (*ekatva*), the consequence of non-difference is equal.

In the former case, "the jar is one, and existence is non-other than that"; in the second, "the jar exists, and unity is non-other than that. In the first proof, the jar would result in being everything; in the second, everything would result in being a jar.

Alternatively, there is a second alternative explanation of the proof regarding "oneness as non-different from that": the jar is non-different from that [Being], and what is that? To this question, the answer is: "It is not distinct from the existent jar"; thus, the jar itself is the establishment of all things.

However, in the previous case, to the question "And what is that?", the answer was "all entities. This is the distinction: by this [second explanation], it is established that within the jar, all entities are non-distinct from oneness. This is the meaning.

Thus, by establishing non-difference through existence and oneness, there arise the faults that the jar would be everything and that all things would be established within the jar. (Compare: p. 555–1; compare: p.
The passage beginning with "marked by this sign... [he] falls into" and ending with "not other than" is not present in manuscript *ya*.

Furthermore—likewise, regarding the passage beginning with "wherein there is jar-ness," etc.: now, the bringing about of existence (*astitva*) and oneness (*ekatva*) within jar-ness is itself the proof (*sādhana*), along with the illustration (*sabhāvana*) and the conclusion (*upasaṃhāra*). Therefore, since existence and oneness are non-different from the jar, each single jar and so forth is "jar, jar, jar" through differentiation; and thus, there would be contradictions with perception and other means of knowledge.

These [logical consequences] should be applied to the establishment and refutation of the production, persistence, and destruction of manifest and unmanifest substances, qualities, and actions; if these are not accepted, then it must be understood that "the pot does not exist," and thus all entities [would likewise be non-existent].
Where there is the non-existence of a jar, there is the non-existence of all entities; for [the jar] is not distinct from [the nature of] things.

Or, if it were a distinct entity, then because it would be devoid of the generality of existence and devoid of the particularity of oneness, the jar would simply be non-existent like a sky-flower. Likewise, a chariot, a cloth, and so forth—water, fire, wind, earth, and all else—is each and every one of them identical with the nature of everything.

Therefore, he says: "Every jar is [identical] with each [other]," which means that everything is of the nature of everything. If it is asked, "Let it be so; what is the fault?", the faults are stated as follows: thus, there would be contradictions with perception and other means of knowledge.

Since jars and the like are perceived as not being of the nature of everything, there is a contradiction with perception (*pratyakṣavirodha*). Because inference and the other means of knowledge are preceded by perception, contradictions with inference and the rest (*anumānādivirodha*) are likewise to be applied.

"The manifest, the unmanifest," and so forth;
and these [arguments] contradict perception and other means of knowledge regarding the states of being manifest and so on.

Manifest sound and so forth, earth and so forth, cows and so forth, and jars and so forth—each one exists as a single "existent" (*asti*). Regarding these three—the word "existent," the word "one," and the objects themselves—there must be either identity or difference, according to the logic previously introduced. Thus, having established that existence (*astitva*) is the very nature of oneness and that this is the very nature of sound, and so on, up to the point where everything is the self-nature of everything; if that were accepted, there would be contradictions with perception and other means of valid cognition.

In the case of the unmanifest (*avyakta*), there exist [contradictions] among each of the three unmanifests—sattva, rajas, and tamas—and so forth; likewise, [contradictions] among single instances of sattva, and so forth; among single instances of rajas, and so forth; and among single instances of tamas, and so forth. This same principle should be applied to earth and the other elements individually, as well as to cows and the like. It applies similarly to substance, quality, and action; to origination, persistence, and destruction; to the means of proof (*sādhana*) and its subdivisions such as the thesis (*pratijñā*) and so on; and to the refutation (*dūṣaṇa*) and its subdivisions, such as contradiction with one's own words, unestablished reasons (*asiddhi*), and deficiency in the property to be proven (*sādhyadharmavaikalya*). By the logic already stated, contradictions with perception and other means of knowledge are to be attributed [to these], because this logic is all-pervasive (*vyāpin*).

If these [reasons] are not accepted, then it must be understood that "the jar does not exist. Alternatively, if you do not accept these faults such as contradiction with perception (*pratyakṣavirodha*), then you should understand that "the jar does not exist"—this is the demonstration of the emptiness of your own position. Just as you do not desire [the existence of] a jar in that manner, so too all entities exist; this is the extended application (*atideśa*).

Just as the non-existence of a jar has been established through reasoning—since the three types of jars are not different from the single jar—in the same way, the non-existence of all entities, such as cloth, chariots, and so forth, must be established.

Therefore, demonstrating the method for applying this according to the previously stated logic, he says: "Where there is the non-existence (non-occurrence) of a jar, why is there the non-existence of all entities? Because they are not different from the jar; it has already been established that all entities are not different from the jar. Where? In the case where existence and oneness are not different [from the jar]. Since the existence and oneness of cloth and other things are also not different from the existence and oneness of the jar, they are not different from the jar. And thus, because all entities are not different from the jar, when the jar is absent, they too are necessarily absent. Therefore, there is a logical flaw in the claim that multiple jars are not different from one another.
Regarding the non-existence of the jar, it might be argued: "It is a distinct entity.

Even if existence and oneness were distinct entities from the jar—wherein existence is the universal (*sāmānya*) and oneness is the particular (*viśeṣa*) of the jar—then those two, the universal and the particular, would not exist [in the jar]. Consequently, due to being devoid of both universal and particular, the jar would simply be non-existent, like a flower in the sky.

Now, even though entities such as pots and cloths possess non-difference in terms of existence and unity, they indeed have mutually contradictory natures, since the Pradhāna and other principles operate for the sake of differentiation.

Therefore, if this is accepted, just as a pot becomes the opposite of a cloth—which is of the nature of existence, of a single nature, and of a nature not different from that [existence]—so too the pot would necessarily become the opposite of its own essential nature as a pot, because it would be the opposite of existence and unity, like the nature of a cloth which is the opposite of a pot.
Thus, once again, the pot does not exist;
likewise, all entities do not exist either, because they possess a nature contrary to being non-different from cloth, to oneness, and to existence—just like a flower in the sky.
Consequently, there is the consequence that all things are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).

Now, it might be argued: "The mutual opposition between cloth and other objects is established because they are non-omnipresent and thus non-pervasive; however, this is not the case for existence (*astitva*) and unity (*ekatva*), since these are omnipresent and thus pervasive.
If these two were one, why would it be that they are omnipresent while the jar is not?
[To this we reply: Indeed, in this way, all things must possess a single form, because they are not different from one another, just like the essential nature (*tattva*) of each individual object.
To this, he says: "Now," and so forth.
Entities such as pots and cloths possess mutually contradictory natures, even though there is no difference in their existence or unity.

For what purpose, or for what reason? It is said: for the sake of differentiation (*bheda*). Since the activity of *pradhāna* and the rest is directed toward the goal of the person (*puruṣārtha*), and since *pradhāna*—which has synonyms such as *prakṛti* and *bahudhānaka*—operates for the sake of the person with two objectives in view—the initial one being the enjoyment of the person consisting in the perception of sound and so forth, and the final one being the perception of the distinction between the *guṇas* and the *puruṣa*—it cannot accomplish the goal of the person without the differentiation into sound and so forth, earth and so forth, cows and so forth, and jars and so forth. Therefore, because the activity of *pradhāna* and the rest is for the sake of differentiation, jars, cloths, and other such things possess mutually distinct natures.
Therefore, the fault of the self belonging to all selves does not apply here, as in the case of "there is one pot."

Therefore, the jar is now accepted as being the opposite of the cloth, which is characterized by existence; yet once this is accepted, the following fault arises: just as the jar has become the opposite of the cloth—which is characterized by existence, unity, and non-difference from it—such opposition would occur in this way and not otherwise. Consequently, the jar would likewise become the opposite even of its own nature as a jar, because it would possess the characteristics of being the opposite of existence, unity, and non-difference from them, just like the cloth which is the opposite of the jar. Thus, due to its very nature as a jar being absent, the jar does not exist at all.

The meaning of differentiation (bhedārtha) is the goal of the person (puruṣārtha); [this is] the primary [reading]; the goal of the person is the primary [reading]; the person and the non-person are the primary [reading]; [this is] the commentary (ya).
The reading might also be "sārvātmyadoṣaḥ" or "sarvātmatādoṣaḥ," but here it remains without fault;
for by the extension [of the principle] that "all things are likewise," each individual entity, such as a mat or a chariot, would become a non-entity.

Why? Because it possesses a nature contrary to the existence of oneness and non-difference from the cloth; therefore, its conclusion is that it is just like a sky-flower, and thus it results in the state of being an entity devoid of intrinsic nature—this meaning is already understood.

Now, it might be argued: "The mutual opposition of things such as cloth and so forth is established because they are not all-pervasive and lack universal extension; however, there is no opposition between existence (*astitva*) and unity (*ekatva*).
