Jars and the like, however, may be mutually opposed because their natures are excluded [from one another];
therefore, there is no consequence of being devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*), owing to the universal extension of existence and unity."
In this context, [the word] "asti" (exists) [is used];
from what [source], O Bhagavan, would things such as jars and so forth be conceptualized?
To this we reply: regarding this unity, how is it that [the text says] "these two," and so forth?

When the unity of the jar is accepted based on those two—existence and unity—whence does this distinction arise: that existence and unity alone are omnipresent, while the jar is not; or that the jar alone is non-omnipresent, while existence and unity are not? If this is not accepted, and instead their being distinct entities is accepted, then it follows that there must be a plurality of jars: the jar exists as a distinct entity, the jar is one, and the jar is also a jar—thus there would be three jars.

Now, if the pot itself is desired to be the single [entity] "pot," then it follows that the pot does not exist; for its existence would be something other than itself, like a sky-flower. Furthermore, because it is not "one" and because it abandons the existence of oneness, it follows that there is no pot even in the parts of the pot such as color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth. Since it abandons beingness (*bhūti*), it is not merely beingness; therefore, the pot is non-existent.

Now, if a rebuttal were to be stated: "There is much that exists and much that does not exist; in some cases there is only existence or only non-existence. Therefore, in order to specify the existence of one particular jar or one particular cloth and so forth, one says 'the jar exists,' and likewise, even a single [entity] is indeed many, because of its plurality. To this, the proof is as follows: the thesis (*pakṣa*) is that all things—the existence, the oneness, and the jars—must also be of a single form;
the reason (*hetu*) is "because they are not different" (*ananyatvāt*).

The analogy is "like the reality of each individual object" (*prativastutattvavat*). Just as the essential nature (*ātmasvarūpa*) of each individual object—such as a jar and so forth—is seen to be of a single form because it is non-different from that [universal] object, and its specific nature as "form-ness" (*rūpatva*) does not consist of taste and so on, and thus remains undifferentiated; likewise, this applies even to multiple jars. Therefore, there is no distinction between being omnipresent and non-omnipresent, and thus their lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) remains as it was. (Tattvapradīpikā)

Now, if this [existence] is not accepted, and instead a different entity (arthāntara) is accepted, then it follows that there must be a plurality of jars—since the jar exists as a distinct [entity], and yet it is "one jar," and it is also "a jar," there would thus be three jars.

Alternatively, if the jar itself is accepted as the single jar, then it is established that "the jar does not exist," because existence is a different entity from it, like a sky-flower; and since it is "not one" due to the abandonment of both oneness and existence, it follows that even in the parts of the jar such as color and so forth, there is no jar, because its substantiality (bhūti) has been abandoned, and thus it is not merely substantiality.
Consequently, the pot would be non-existent;

yet, if a rebuttal were offered—that much exists and much does not exist, and that in some cases there is only existence or only non-existence—therefore, the statement "the pot exists" is made for the purpose of specifying the existence of this particular pot as distinct from other pots, cloths, and so forth;
likewise, even a single entity is indeed manifold.

Now, if it is not accepted that there is an absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*) and non-difference, but rather that for multiple jars there exists only a difference in entity (*arthāntaratva*), then we say that a plurality of jars would follow. This is because the jar exists as distinct [from existence], and thus "even a single jar" exists as distinct; likewise, since "the jar is also a jar," there would be three jars. And this is undesirable. Alternatively, if this fault is to be avoided, and it is maintained that only the jar itself is the "one jar," and not that the jar is [identical to] existence and oneness, then it follows that the jar does not exist at all. Thus, the point is established.

Why? Because it would be a separate entity from existence (*astitva*), like a sky-flower; thus, the established conclusion is that "it is not one. Furthermore, by abandoning both oneness and existence, it follows that even in the case of form (*rūpa*) and other qualities—which are parts of a jar—the jar would not exist, because oneness has been abandoned. And since form and the others are each individual units, if they do not exist as form and so forth [within themselves], then the claim that "the jar is the collection of form and the other qualities" is merely conventional (*saṃvṛti*) and is thereby refuted.

Likewise, in the doctrine of momentariness (*kṣaṇikavāda*), existence is accepted as belonging to that which lasts for a single moment, according to the principle that "the very arising of things is their activity. Consequently, by abandoning the existence of arising, it follows that there is not merely arising;
and both of these [conclusions] are undesirable.

What follows from this? From this, it follows that the pot is non-existent (*anastitva*). That which lacks existence is "non-existent"; thus, that which is called a "pot" is non-existent. Furthermore, this implies the acceptance of the position to be stated later: that all this is mere consciousness (*vijñānamātra*) and devoid of external objects.

Therefore, "one" is used as a qualifier for "two" and the rest. In such a case, when one says "there is one jar," the term "one" qualifies the jar, while "two" and the rest qualify the triad consisting of that [jar] and the others. Thus, "one" is used as a qualifier for "two" and the rest.

In that regard, if there were no difference between the three [aspects]—namely, "there," "is," and "one jar"—it would follow that everything is one; or if they were different, it would follow that there is a multiplicity of jars. Why? Because this is not a statement that provides a resolution, as it is not established by any philosophical system (*samaya*); for existence (*astitva*) has no other form, so if there is non-difference, everything becomes one, whereas in the case of difference, there is a multiplicity of jars.
Furthermore, even so, non-existence (*nāstitva*) alone would result, like a sky-flower.

Furthermore, since their mutual non-existence is admitted, how can there be existence for them? Even if they were not different [from one another], their non-existence has already been stated. If they were not different, there would be the undesirable consequence of everything being one; or, if they were different, even though it is "one pot," it would also be "pot," leading to the undesirable consequence of a plurality of pots. The existence (*astitva*) of a jar is indeed distinct from the existence of a cloth and other objects, because each acquires its own unique essence (*asādhāraṇātmalābha*) through distinctions such as place, time, form, and cause. This too is not [the case], because it is equal to the aforementioned existence (*sattva*). Likewise, even as for oneness:

Now, if it is not accepted that all entities such as jars possess the nature of being a jar (*ghaṭatva*), yet their non-distinctness from existence (*anarthāntaratva*) is not abandoned, then even a jar would not be a jar, because there is no cause for its specific mode of being (*bhavanaviśeṣa*), just like a cloth.

This [objection] is also not valid, because it is equal to the [already] stated existence (*sattva*). This too is equal to the existence of a jar intended to be distinct from the cloth and so forth mentioned immediately before; therefore, the meaning is that because it is equal to the stated existence, it is indeed non-existent.

Whether the reason "because of having different modes" (*bhinnaprakāratvāt*) or the formulation "because of not having different modes" (*abhinnaprakāratvāt*) is used, they are equivalent in their capacity to prove the pervasion by existence (*astitva*). Thus, in both ways, because of the stated equality of existence, the connection is that "the jar does not have an existence distinct from what you intend.

It has been stated that if there were a plurality of forms, there would be either existence, non-existence, or both existence and non-existence.

Now, regarding the passage beginning with "athaivam" (now, even so):

if it is not accepted that all entities such as pots possess the nature of being a pot (*ghaṭatva*)—even though this has been established by logic—and yet, on the strength of common consensus and other factors, one does not abandon the view that [the pot] is not a different entity [from its existence], then let the pot itself not be a pot, because there is no cause for any distinction in its coming-into-being (*bhavana*). Or, if this is not admitted, then since there is no difference in their existence or unity, the pot must be desired to be nothing but a pot; in that case, the pot would be a non-pot, for that very same reason, just like [the nature of] a pot.
Surely this same reversal of the designation of consciousness and its object should also be applied to form and the other [sensory objects],
or else there would be the consequence of their being manifold;
therefore, jars and the like do not exist.
But surely, if non-existence were thus established, it would contradict the satisfaction, pleasure, and so forth that are established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Is it not the case that even in all philosophical systems, one strives for liberation while regarding those very things—though established by direct perception—as not being [ultimately real]? Therefore, the emptiness (*śūnyatā*) of jars and other such objects is untenable.

Likewise, even from the perspective of non-arising, there is emptiness of the entity; for if existence and oneness were not distinct from the object, there would be no difference whatsoever between the arising of a jar and the arising of a cloth or other things, nor would there be a cause for such [distinction]. Therefore, due to the absence of a cause for any distinction in their arising, just like a cloth, even a jar would not be a jar; thus, the jar lacks the nature of being a jar.

If this is not accepted, then since existence (*astitva*) and oneness (*ekatva*) are equal, exist everywhere, and are present in all things, it would follow that a jar is necessarily a jar alone and not a non-jar that is a jar. Why? Because there is no distinction between existence and oneness. In that case, a non-jar would likewise be a jar. For that very reason, even though it is a non-jar, it would be a jar, just like a jar. Alternatively, if this is not accepted, then since there is no distinction between existence and oneness, a jar would have to be desired as a jar alone; in that case, a non-jar would likewise be a jar, for that same reason, just like a jar.
Surely this same reversal of designation and cognition regarding their objects should also be applied to form and the other [sensory domains],
or else there would be the consequence of their being manifold;
therefore, jars and so forth do not exist.
But if non-existence were thus [the case], would it not contradict the satisfaction, pleasure, and so forth established by direct perception?
Indeed, since that [pleasure] is established by direct perception even in all philosophical systems, one strives for liberation while not regarding it as such;
therefore, the emptiness of jars and other things is untenable.
Likewise, emptiness arises even from the non-arising of a thing; for example, the absence of a cloth [is established] through the absence of a jar.
Likewise, there might even be a reading here such as "the cloth itself is the jar.
By thus granting that very point—namely, "is this not so? and so forth—one incurs an undesirable consequence regarding form (*rūpa*) and the rest:

just as the reversal of jars and other things into being cloths and so on occurs precisely when their existence and unity are present, so too, although it is established in the world that "form is indeed form and not taste," that form would no longer exist; and just as taste would not be taste, it might instead be form. Thus, one must also apply the reversal of the cognition and designation pertaining to those objects.

Likewise, there would be the consequence of a plurality [of pots]; these faults in the position that existence, oneness, and potness are one and the same must not occur. Thus, if one accepts the position of their difference, there would be the aforementioned consequence of a plurality of pots.
Therefore, pots and the like do not exist.

[The opponent] says: "But if [the object] were thus non-existent, it would contradict the satisfaction, pleasure, and so forth established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). For those afflicted by the sensations of fatigue, disease, fear, and the like, pleasure is seen through direct perception upon the alleviation of those [sensations] through their remedy; and for those afflicted by hunger and thirst, satisfaction is likewise seen through direct perception. Therefore, this conceptualization is untenable because it contradicts direct perception."
Page 867, Line 14:

To this it is replied—[the objection] beginning with "But all that [is established by] our own tenet," etc., is incorrect because emptiness does not apply to jars and the like. This is because, by refusing to accept as valid means of knowledge the erroneous cognitions of perception and so forth belonging to the unlearned and the impure masses of people, one would lack confidence in the satisfaction and pleasure produced by objects such as form; and since those [objects] are not truly real, one would be like one who lacks confidence in the water of a mirage. Consequently, it is established in all the treatises aimed at liberation that one must strive for liberation alone. Thus, [the claim regarding] the emptiness of jars and the like is illogical.
Page 867, line 11: ...because of non-arising, and so forth. (Sanskrit: *tathānutpādād ityādi*)

For the proponent of real entities (*vastuvādin*), emptiness follows from non-arising just as it does from irrationality; for if arising and destruction do not exist, then because things are neither arisen nor destroyed, they would be like a sky-flower—this being the emptiness that will be concluded [later].
Since there is no arising of what is already born or what is unborn at the beginning and end, [the entity] is non-existent.

In this context, "beginning" (*ādi*) means arising (*utpatti*), and "end" (*anta*) means destruction (*kṣaya*). Do these two, the beginning and the end, exist through knowledge (*vidyā*) or not? If they do not exist, then because those two are non-existent, all entities would have neither beginning nor end, and thus their state would be one of mere persistence (*sthiti*).
Furthermore, that [position] contradicts perception and other means of valid cognition;
because it is a non-entity (*avastu*)— the opposite of an established entity— like a sky-flower,
it results in the subversion of all established tenets by virtue of its acceptance of non-arising (*anutpāda*).

Now, it might be argued: "For the Sāṅkhyas alone, there is no contradiction because they maintain the doctrine that the effect pre-exists in the cause (satkāryavāda). But this is not the case; for since they admit that the primordial matter (pradhāna) and other principles are eternally established, they must also admit their origination. Since there can be no activity without origination, and no establishment without activity, those principles must indeed be originated, because they are established, like a jar.
Because they have been initiated and are produced, things such as pots are indeed subject to an end.
However, that which does not possess these characteristics is non-existent, like the primary matter (*pradhāna*) and so forth, or like a flower in the sky;

and there are also two conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*). Which of these two do you accept? If you maintain that they do not exist, then, given their non-existence, all entities would be without beginning or end; consequently, for things such as pots, there would be permanence—that is, mere persistence—and such persistence contradicts perception and other means of knowledge, since we observe their arising and destruction.

Furthermore, since inference and the other means of knowledge are preceded by perception, [this view] would also contradict inference and the rest. Moreover, because it is the opposite of an existing entity (*vastu*), it follows that it is a non-entity (*avastu*); since it is the opposite of an existing entity, it results in being a non-entity, like a flower in the sky. Furthermore, if one accepts the position that "all entities are indeed unproduced," there is a contradiction with all established doctrines. For instance, in the Vaiśeṣika system, having accepted production, it is stated in the *Vaiśeṣika Sūtra*: "Substances originate another substance; qualities originate another quality" (VS 1.1.8).

1.8–9: Because of the absence of action, qualities, and designation, [the effect] is non-existent prior [to its production], according to the Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 9.1 and other passages explaining the production of an effect that was previously non-existent.
Śūnyavāda, Bhāṣya; compare page 867, line 22; page 846, line 21.

Should the beginning and the end be known or not? If they do not exist, then because those two are non-existent, all entities would be without beginning or end; consequently, there would be only "staying" (static existence), and that would contradict perception and other means of knowledge.
Furthermore, because it would be a persisting entity, it would be the opposite of a non-entity, like a sky-flower.
Furthermore, by accepting non-arising (*anutpāda*), there would be a contradiction with all established tenets.

If it should be argued that there is no contradiction for the Sāṅkhyas alone because they maintain the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*), this is not the case; for they accept that the *pradhāna* and other principles are eternally established, yet they also accept origination (*ārambha*). Since there is no action (*kriyā*) without origination, and no establishment (*niṣṭhā*) without action, [the two positions are contradictory].
Therefore, those [entities] have indeed been commenced, because they are completed, like a jar;
and because they have been commenced and are produced, they are also subject to termination.
However, that which does not behave in this way is non-existent, such as primordial matter (*pradhāna*) and so forth, like a sky-flower.
Thus, by means of the name "cebhā," the primordial state (pra-sthiti) is established as such.

Here he says: "It was stated by you that there is a contradiction of all established doctrines (*sarvasiddhānta*) through the acceptance of non-arising (*anutpāda*); that is incorrect. Let alone the doctrines of the *puruṣa* and so forth—for the Sāṅkhyas alone, because they maintain the theory that the effect pre-exists in the cause (*satkāryavāda*), there is no contradiction.
To this we reply: first, let us restate your position—namely, "Now it might be said: 'For the Sāṅkhyas alone... and so forth; the response to that is:
"There is no lack of contradiction" and so forth. There is indeed a contradiction, not a lack thereof, because a double negation results in the affirmation of the original state (*prakṛti*).

How is it that [the Sāṃkhya] does not accept the theory of the non-existence of the effect (asatkāryavāda)? It is said: because they accept that the primary cause (pradhāna) and so forth are eternally established; for they accept that everything—whether manifest or unmanifest, known as the Great One (mahat), the I-principle (ahaṃkāra), and the rest—is eternally and already established. Thus, "origination" (ārambha) is effectively accepted; since there can be no action without origination, and no establishment without action.

Having thus concluded that [section], he states the proof: "Therefore, those [principles]," and so forth. Those [principles], such as *pradhāna* and the rest, have indeed been commenced, because they are completed, like a jar. Since the commencement of the action of completing a jar is well-known in the world, the example is established; therefore, the application (*upanaya*) of *pradhāna* and the others is established.

Because they are thus commenced, their being produced (*kṛtakatva*) is established; likewise, because they are produced, they also possess an end. Therefore, *pradhāna* and the others have both a beginning and an end.

As for the statement "that which is not thus," etc., this is either a dissimilar example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) or another means of proof (*sādhana*). The implication is that if things lack a beginning and an end, they must be non-existent like a sky-flower; by the inclusion of the word "etc.," the same argument applies to the *puruṣa* (the primal spirit) and others as well.

Now, if even this is not accepted, then [the consequence is] that because it exists eternally, being unoriginated (*anārabdha*), and being uncreated (*akṛtaka*), it would be unestablished and non-existent like space (*ākāśa*). [Objection:
But surely space is established and perfected because it is denoted by a pure term, and it is indeed existent, just like the cognition of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa-jñāna*).

Whence does its status as a pure word-form (*śuddhapadatā*) arise? The prefix *āṅ* has the sense of "slight" (*īṣadartha*). The root *kāśṛ*, meaning "to shine," is listed in the Dhātupāṭha as number 647. That which "shines" (*ākāśate*), appearing like a mirage, is called *ākāśa*.
And if there were a cognition of pure objects such as ether and the like, then we would not accept that "all this is indeed consciousness-only" (*vijñānamātra*);
for according to us, even pure objects such as ether are themselves nothing but consciousness-only,
by which [reasoning] all words have only non-existent referents.

Now, lest there be the undesirable consequence of [the world] being mere consciousness (*vijñānamātratā*), [one might argue that] the *pradhāna* and so forth are the "beginning" (*ādi*). Even though the point has already been established by this very proof—that this [world] is merely that cause—it is nonetheless presented as a proof for establishing an undesired consequence (*aniṣṭāpādana*) by means of the example of space (*ākāśa*), in order to refute other possible arguments. If, however, even this is not accepted, [the author] says: "But if it is not admitted from the beginning... and so on, up to "...like space.
He then states: "Is it not the case that space... and so forth; this inference is intended to demonstrate that the non-existence of space is not established.
"Because it is denotable by a simple word (*śuddhapada*), that which is accomplished and established is indeed existent, like valid knowledge (*pramāṇajñāna*).

To this, it is replied: "From what does its status as a simple word follow? This points out the non-establishment of the reason (*hetvasiddhi*). He demonstrates that it is actually a compound word (*samāsapada*): *āṅ* is a prefix (*upasarga*) meaning "slight," and *kāsṛśṛ* is a verbal root (*dhātu*) meaning "to shine. That which shines forth (*ākāśate*) is "space" (*ākāśa*). [This is according to] Pāṇini 2.2.18: *kugatiprādayaḥ*.

18. Since this is a compound, what is its meaning? To demonstrate that, he says: "It appears like a mirage, [and thus it is] space. Just as a mirage, though non-existent in the sense of being water, appears as such, so too space, though non-existent, is grasped by consciousness as if it were existent, because consciousness itself arises in various such ways (pṛ. 846, l. 19).
"Unmanifested and unestablished... [from] *pra*... [the root] *prakāsṛ* in the sense of contemptuous sound—*Pāṇini’s Dhātupāṭha* 6.23.
It might be thought: "There is no lack of proof (*asiddhi*), because it is denotable by pure terms such as 'space' (*kha*), 'ether' (*viyat*), and 'void' (*vyoman*)."

And this is incorrect; for if [it were the case that] "space and so forth are pure entities," etc.—if we were to admit even a word-referent (*śabdārtha*) denoted by a pure word, then we would neither accept nor say that "all this is indeed consciousness-only" (*vijñānamātra*). For it is established for us that even for words such as *viyat*, *gagana*, *kha*, *ambara*, *vyoman*, *māyā*, *śūnya*, *ghaṭa*, and *paṭa*, there is no referent at all distinct from consciousness; and we shall strive to demonstrate that. (Not established—Prakaraṇa).

*khāpara* (Bhā);
"by this," and so forth.

By this denial of external objects that are pure [in themselves], such as space and so forth, there would be no denoted meaning whatsoever for any word—whether it be a proper name (*yādṛcchika*) according to the theory of derivation (*vyutpatti*) favored by the etymologists (*nairukta*), or a name like *Ḍittha* according to the theory of non-derivation (*avyutpatti*), whether accompanied by negations such as *nañ* or used alone. This is because they would serve merely as causes for instilling a cognition; thus, all words would have only non-existent things as their referents.
[The opponent says: "Let it not be so," and so forth.

It might be thought: "Since [the jar] is already established and so forth, there is the consequence that it is mere consciousness (*vijñānamātratā*); let this not be the case, therefore the 'origin' (*ādi*) is sought otherwise. What is this "origin"? It is the primal cause (*pradhānādi*), namely *pradhāna*, *puruṣa*, *kāla*, *svabhāva*, and so on; and that alone is the cause. And this effect, the jar, consists of that alone, because it was previously established through the summary [of the argument]. Therefore, the existence of the elements (*bhūta*) themselves is the origin, along with that summary. Is that [origin] eternal or non-eternal? If it is eternal, then, because it is uncreated, unproduced, and not yet established, it is non-existent, like a sky-flower.

Now, because there is a fault in the permanence of the beginning, it must be accepted as eternally established; therefore, as before, existence is untenable. If the end were permanent, there would be non-existence.

Alternatively, seeing the fault in permanence, if the beginning is held to be impermanent, is that [beginning] born or unborn? If it is born, then it cannot have an origination, because it has already been born, like a finished jar.
Now, if it is unarisen, even so there is non-arising because of its state of being unarisen, like a sky-flower;
because it is unproduced, it is non-existent.
If it were both arisen and unarisen, it would be impossible due to contradiction and because it would possess the defects of both.

The effect, such as cloth and so forth—why? Because it is contained within the prior reabsorption (*pūrvapratyupasaṃhāra*). Even prior to the effect, the modifications (*vikāra*) were already contained within that very state of being merely one of the causes, such as *pradhāna* or others; likewise, at a later time, they remain latent within that same [cause]. Therefore, the existence (*sattva*) and eternality of existing things, such as jars and so forth, consist in their [pre-existence] as a beginning, and not in their being newly produced (*ārambha*), etc.—this is the meaning of the connection according to the *Nirukta-bhāṣya*.
Someone [perceives] another triad for the sake of the ten objects; such are the objects in the Bhāṣya.

The effect [is not established], because it was previously withdrawn and subsumed; therefore, the existence of the elements themselves is the beginning, and that which includes this withdrawal—is it eternal or non-eternal? If it were eternal, then, being uncreated, unoriginated, and unestablished, it would be non-existent like a sky-flower.

Now, because there is a fault in the case of eternal permanence, it is therefore accepted that [the entity] is eternally established; however, as before, the existence [of such an entity] is untenable.
If, on the other hand, there is eternal non-existence, then it is simply non-existent.

Furthermore, seeing the fault in permanence, if it is accepted that the beginning is impermanent, is that [beginning] born or unborn? If it is born, then it cannot have an origination, because it has already been born, like a finished pot.
Furthermore, if it is unborn, it is likewise non-arisen because of its state of being unborn, like a sky-flower;
because it is unarisen, it is non-existent.
If it were both born and unborn, there would be a contradiction and an impossibility due to possessing the defects of both.
Regarding the phrase "from the egg, etc.," you are asked:

"That which begins with the dissolution," and so forth—that primordial cause known as Pradhāna and the rest—is it eternal along with its dissolution, or rather, is it non-eternal? This must be determined.

In that case, if it were eternal, it would not have a beginning at all, because it is uncreated and unproduced. What follows from that? Consequently, it would be unestablished; and because it is unestablished, it is non-existent, like a sky-flower. (Page 869, Line 4)
The passage beginning with "evañcihnāṅkitaḥ" and ending with "nityatve" does not exist in the Bhāṣya manuscript.
Now, regarding the phrase "athādinityatāyām" and so forth:

for fear of this defect, if [the entity] is held to be eternally established and existing at equal times both before and after, then the previously mentioned defect remains—the defect that because it exists eternally, is unoriginated, and is uncreated, it is like a sky-flower or like space, and so on. He extends that very [argument] as far as the point that [the object] has the nature of mere consciousness; as before, the existence [of such an object] is untenable.
Thus, non-existence has been stated regarding permanence of origination or permanence of duration;
whereas permanence of end is the permanence of destruction, and in that case of permanence of end, there is indeed non-existence.
Such, then, is the fault in the permanence of the beginning.
As before, [the text] from page 870, line 3 to page 844, line 1 is missing in the manuscript (asaṃyata).

Now, regarding the passage beginning with "athanityatvetyādi": having seen the fault in the eternality of the "beginning" (ādi), and in order to avoid that, if it is maintained that "the beginning is non-eternal," there are three possible alternatives: [is it] born, unborn, or both born and unborn? By the very act of posing these two alternative questions—"Is it born? or "Is it unborn?"—the third alternative, consisting of their conjunction, is established.

If [it is argued that] through the first two alternatives beginning with "if it is born," there is an absence of production, then, because it has not been produced, it is non-existent; this point is already understood.
The third alternative—that it is both produced and unproduced—is impossible due to its internal contradiction;

furthermore, because it possesses the defects of both positions, the view that it is both produced and unproduced must be abandoned, as it is fraught with the faults inherent in both being produced and being unproduced.
Thus are the defects regarding arising.

And because of the bondage of defects,
even at the point of completion, those same conceptual constructions persist.
If that which is already completed does not come to completion, because it is already completed, like a finished jar;
and that which is not yet completed also does not come to completion, because it is uncompleted, non-existent, and lacks agency, like a sky-flower;
nor does both [the completed and the uncompleted] do so, as has been explained.

Furthermore, regarding that which has already perished, does it perish while already destroyed, while not yet destroyed, or while both destroyed and not destroyed? If that which has already perished were to perish, it would not perish, because it is already destroyed, like a destroyed jar;

nor would that which is not yet destroyed perish, like an intact jar, because it is a state of being that has not yet become subject to destruction, like an intact jar or like space; nor can it be both, as explained above.
In this way, because it is unarisen, non-abiding, and non-perished, the entity would be a mere non-existence, like a flower in the sky.

If it should be argued: "What is the point of investigating these two—the beginning and the end—which are not the true nature of the entity? [We reply: The entity itself is what must be investigated, for these two are the prior and subsequent moments relative to the entity’s acquisition of its own-being (*ātmalābha*).
Even in the absence of that [cause], the entity ought indeed to exist;

and likewise in the case of its culmination (*niṣṭhā*)—and so forth—is it one that has already culminated (*niṣṭhita*) that culminates, or one that has not yet culminated (*aniṣṭhita*), or one that is both culminated and unculminated? These are the very same alternatives [as before]. In those three cases as well, the faults have been established by the same logic as was stated regarding production, up until the point where "neither" is said to be the case.

Being unestablished and non-existent, it is a non-agent due to its non-existence; and because it is a non-agent, like a sky-flower, it does not come to rest—this is the distinction. The remainder has been explained [in the previous section]; the distinction has been explained [in the previous section]. (Page 869) The distinction has been explained [in the Bhāṣya].
The meaning of "viśeṣaṃ gatārtham" is already understood; there may also be the reading "śeṣaṃ gatārtham" here,
as well as "ante'pi" and so forth.

Regarding destruction as well: does that which has already perished perish, or that which has not yet perished, or that which is both perished and not perished? Beginning with the proposition, "If it is maintained that what has already perished perishes," and proceeding through all three alternatives up to the point where it is said, "neither is the case, as previously stated"—this is the explanation of the phrase "it is not [the case] that what has not perished [perishes], like an intact jar": because its state of being in the process of perishing has not come to be (*abhūtavinaśyadbhāvatvāt*). That whose state of perishing (*vinaśyadbhāva*) has not come to be (*abhūta*), i.e., has not arisen, is "one whose state of perishing has not come to be" (*abhūtavinaśyadbhāva*); therefore, because its state of perishing has not come to be, it is like an intact jar.

Or, "like space" is another example for this very reason—that it is a non-existent entity perishing—after demonstrating its concomitance (*anugama*). A reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) should then be formulated, starting from "because it is denotable by pure words" and so forth, up to "because it is mere consciousness," and so on. As stated previously, neither [the existent nor the non-existent] perishes, because it is impossible for something to be both destroyed and not destroyed simultaneously; this impossibility arises from contradiction and from the faults inherent in both positions, according to the logic already explained.
Thus, arising, persistence, and destruction are not established. Since these are not established, the entity would be a mere non-existence—unborn, non-persistent, and non-perishing—like a sky-flower.
What is the meaning of "something destroyed" (*kiṃcinnaṣṭa*)? It means "like a pot that has not been made" (*akṛtaghaṭavat*). What is the point (*kaḥ arthaḥ*)? [It is] "non-existence" (*abhāvaḥ*).
What is the point? [It is] "perception" (*pratyakṣam*).
Now, it might be argued: "What is the use to us? and so forth.
This could be the thought: "What is the purpose of investigating these two—the beginning and the end—which are not the true nature of the entity? It is the entity itself that must be investigated;

for these two, the beginning and the end, are respectively the times prior to and subsequent to the acquisition of the entity's own-being. The time prior to the acquisition of the entity's own-being is called the 'beginning,' and the subsequent time is the 'end.'"

Even in the absence of those two [the prior and posterior limits], the entity must indeed exist between them; therefore, since the entity exists, is that which is "between" (madhya)—whether it be the interval itself or the intermediate moment—something produced or unproduced? If it is produced, then there is no arising for it because it has already been produced, like a pot that has already been finished; and so on, according to that same text, because the fault is equal, the prior and posterior times also do not exist, since they are respectively destroyed and unproduced. Because they depend upon those [two], the entity between them does not exist, like a flame when the fuel is burnt.
It is non-existent because it lacks existence in the prior and subsequent times, like a sky-flower.

If it should be argued: "The effect is indeed non-existent at the beginning, middle, and end because of its merging into the ultimate reality (*tattva*); yet, prior to that merging, it exists at the beginning and middle because of the activity directed toward it, and after that merging, it exists because there is no further activity directed toward it."
This is untrue, because it does not transcend non-existence;
that [object] would be simply non-existent, since it is non-existent in the beginning, middle, and end, like a sky-flower. To this we reply: "Is there a middle in that middle? and so forth.

Regarding that entity which you consider to exist between those two times—the prior and the posterior—or that intermediate moment between the prior and posterior times which is being examined: would both of these be an entity that has arisen or one that has not arisen? If it has arisen, then there is no production for it, because it has already arisen, like a finished jar; thus, the same passage introducing the faults should be applied to these three alternatives, as the fault is identical. (Bhāṣya, p. 845, l. 20)
The term *nivṛtta* should be applied to all three [versions]: *nivṛtta-bhā*, *nivṛtta-ya*, and *yojyo-ya*.

Furthermore, those two times—the prior and the posterior—do not exist even according to your own view, because [respectively] they are destroyed and unarisen; in the absence of those two times, due to their dependence upon them, the entity existing between them cannot exist.

What is it like? It is like a flame from burnt fuel. Just as a flame dependent on fuel exists only in relation to that fuel—and though it may be conceived [as existing], it does not exist once that fuel has been completely consumed because it depends upon it—so too, a thing intended as "middle" in dependence upon prior and subsequent time does not exist in their absence because it depends upon them. Alternatively, how could the existence of something that does not exist at the prior and subsequent times be conceivable in the interval? The intention is that it is not conceivable.
"It becomes non-existent," and so forth; here the proof is: "That is non-existent, because it lacks existence in the prior and subsequent times, like a sky-flower.
[End of] *Asadgraha*.
Now, if it should be argued, and so forth...

Why is it that the effect—such as a substance or its qualities—is non-existent at the beginning (the commencement), in the middle (the time of the activity), and at the end (immediately upon the completion of the activity), because it is not yet subsumed under its true nature such as "substance-ness"? Because one exerts effort toward it at the beginning and in the middle; for such desire for it would not be possible if it already existed after it has been subsumed under its true nature. Why? Because there is no further exertion toward it once the activity has ceased; for one who desires something does not fail to act toward it when that thing is non-existent.
And at the end of the time, O [Bhagavān], at the end of the time, O [Bhagavān],
[the nature of] substances and so forth... Bhāṣya.
To this we reply: This is untrue, because it does not transcend non-existence;
it would remain non-existent even then, since it has never come into being at its beginning, middle, or end, like a flower in the sky.
Thus, for this reason, all entities are empty due to their non-arising.
Because there is no non-occurrence at the ends of meditations,
even from the observation of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*).
In this context, whatever designations there may be—such as "pot," "cloth," or "form"—each is merely a causal complex (*sāmagrī*).
What is this causal complex? It is the activity of entities toward another entity, such as the activity of threads toward a cloth.
And in that [activity], each individual [factor] among those engaged in it is not a composite whole (*avayavin*); and if they are non-existent individually, they are also non-existent when combined.

The causal totality (*sāmagrī*) does not exist either in the individual causes and conditions, nor in their distinct individual natures, because it is perceived only when they are present together, like a jar and a cloth. Furthermore, how can that which does not exist in its own nature within those [causes] exist even in the totality? For water, which is not seen in grains of sand, is certainly not seen in a jar either.

For this reason as well, there is no real entity (*vastu*): because even when a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is observed, things such as jars and cloths are seen within that complex, but not each in its own individual form (*svarūpa*). And how can that which does not exist in its own form have existence even within a causal complex? It would be like [the existence of] water in sand. This will be the meaning of the application (*upanaya*);
its cultivation is expressed as: "Whatever exists in this world," and so forth.

The designation "jar" refers to the collection of potsherds; "cloth" refers to the collection of threads; "form" (rūpa) refers to the continuum of moments arising and perishing within that [collection]; and by the word "or," whatever else there may be—such as taste and so forth, or a fist, a row, and so on—it is merely a gathering of parts differentiated by space and time, that is, a mere collection (*sāmagrī*).
What, then, is this collection? It is said: it is the operation of entities toward another entity.

The demonstration of that [is as follows]: just as there is an operation of threads toward a cloth, the very parts that function as the constituents of a whole (*avayavin*), existing in such and such a state, are called the "causal complex" (*sāmagrī*). This is because in the absence of a part, the whole is absent; and regarding that [complex], and so forth—it being such a causal complex, not even a single constituent part, such as a thread, among those functioning therein can be a whole, due to the lack of its capacity. And since there is non-existence in each individual [part], there would be non-existence even when they are combined; thus, the whole would be entirely non-existent. Therefore, up to this point... [text fragment]... *pra* (fragmentary).

Thinking "it is like a vehicle," he contemplates that [vehicle] as being deficient in its constituent parts— beginning with the words "not yet," and so forth.

Because it cannot exist in the causes, the conditions, or their individual states, the cloth does not exist in its causes—the threads—nor does it exist in the conditions, which are the instrumental causes such as the shuttle, the loom, and the pins; therefore, the meaning is that the composite whole does not exist in the collection [of its parts].

Nor is it perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) in its own nature or in its distinctness from its parts. For by the very means of direct perception, the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) designated as "cloth" is not apprehended separately from the nature of the threads or the nature of the shuttle and other tools; furthermore, it is inferred that it does not exist, because activity toward that object occurs only when those [causes] are present. Indeed, when the causes and conditions—the threads, the shuttle, and so forth—are present, one who seeks cloth exerts effort for its sake while thinking, "the cloth does not exist. Therefore, it does not exist. How so? Like a jar or a cloth. Just as when a jar is present, one seeking cloth thinks "the cloth does not exist" and exerts effort for the sake of cloth, or when a cloth is present, one seeking a jar exerts effort for the sake of a jar.

And the application (*upanaya*)— "that which does not exist in those [things]"— has its meaning already explained; it continues up to "for it is not seen even in a jar," [meaning] that which does not exist in those things [is not seen] in their own nature or in their separateness.

the reading "etadartham" found within this [passage] does not exist in manuscript Ya.
Page 848, line 8:
Even if there were a separate existence [of the effect] apart from the collection of causes and conditions, my statement would still hold;
for indeed, the emptiness of all things is established because they lack intrinsic nature (asvabhāvatva).

If my words do not exist in the causes—whether in the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), the associated (*samprayukta*) or dissociated (*viprayukta*) factors, or in the conditions (*pratyaya*); if they do not exist in the efforts of the chest, throat, lips, tongue, teeth, palate, nose, head, and so forth; nor do they exist in the totality of both; nor do they exist separately, apart from the totality of causes and conditions—then they are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). Because they are devoid of intrinsic nature, they are empty.
Thus, is emptiness not established by the very lack of intrinsic nature of these words of mine?

And just as this statement of mine is empty because it lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*), so too all things (*sarvabhāva*) are empty because they lack intrinsic nature—thus [ends] the *Vigrahavyāvartanī* composed by Nāgārjuna, together with his own commentary (*svopajñavṛtti*). Chapter Four. Section Bha.
Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that a jar, though not seen in each individual grain of sand, is seen when the causal totality (*sāmagrī*) is present?
No; because the causal totalities are equivalent, we would not have said that the jar is absent even from the totality if it had been seen by us [in the grains].
But surely this very point is being established: that the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) exists.
If it is argued that the parts therefore exist, we say no; for it has already been stated that the whole (*avayavin*) does not exist apart from its qualities such as color (*rūpa*).

Rather, color and the other qualities have their essence in consciousness (*vijñāna*) as determined by the acts of coloring and so forth. Their distinctness and their causality are consistent with the occurrence of cognition, because they lack any intrinsic nature apart from cognition.

"In the absence of causes and so forth, all entities do not exist because of the absence of their causal complex (*sāmagrī*), and because of the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*) as they are not observed to be so.

To this, the opponent says: "But surely, a jar—which is not seen in each individual grain of sand—is seen in the causal complex; thus, one might raise the objection that [your argument] suffers from the fallacy of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), since the nature of being a jar is seen in the causal complex despite not being seen in each individual grain of sand."

To this we reply: No, because the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is identical. It is not an inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika*), for what is non-existent in each individual part is likewise non-existent in the aggregate. Since even the jar, which is intended as a counter-example (*vipakṣa*), is equal by virtue of being produced by that same causal complex, it is in fact a subject (*pakṣa*) itself because it is also an object to be proven. Furthermore, since that transformation into a jar is itself an aggregate, the counter-example is unestablished; therefore, this objection regarding inconclusiveness is a fallacious rejoinder (*jātyuttara*).

The explanation of that is as follows: if we had ourselves seen [the whole], we would not have said, "there is no such thing as a causal complex" (*sāmagrī*). That very point under discussion is being recalled. Indeed, it is precisely this that is being proved—that the causal complex exists or does not exist—since that alone is what is being introduced. Therefore, the objection regarding its inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) based on the notion of its opposite is merely a matter of words, like seeing a jar in sand when it was not previously perceived in each individual grain.
