If it is argued that "the non-existence of magnitude is being established here," and that "therefore parts must exist," then this might be the thought: "The threads are the parts of the cloth."

That is not so; why? Because it has already been stated that the whole (*avayavin*) does not exist apart from its parts, such as form and the rest—for example, threads do not exist in their fibers, fibers in their filaments, filaments in eyelashes, and eyelashes in their own constituent parts, and so on, until the division reaches the level of atoms.
If you argue that the atom itself is the whole because it is partless and indivisible, even that is merely a whole, being distinguished by the differences of color, taste, smell, and touch.

If it is argued that, in that case, only the parts such as form (*rūpa*) exist and not the whole (*avayavin*), even those parts do not acquire the nature of form and so forth by themselves. This is because form and the rest have consciousness as their essence, as defined by the cognition of "form-ness" and so on; for form and the rest are defined only through cognitions such as "it is formed (*rūpyate*)," hence it is form (*rūpa*), or "it is tasted (*rasyate*)," hence it is taste (*rasa*). Their essential nature is thus conceptualized along with consciousness. In that regard, the mutual distinctness and causality of form and the rest are established only when the intellect (*buddhi*) functions, and not by their own nature alone when that intellect does not function.

Therefore, it is not possible for you to establish existence external to that [consciousness], because if there were a causal distinctness, there would be no intrinsic nature apart from cognition; [the phrase] "like the eyelashes, etc. does not exist in the manuscript.

Having withdrawn that [objection], he says: "Because of the absence of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) due to the absence of causes and so forth; in the absence of causes, conditions, and the distinctness of intrinsic natures (*svarūpa*), what causal complex could there be for form and the other [sensory objects]? In the absence of a causal complex, what is substantiality (*dravyatā*)? Thus, there is an absence of substance (*dravya*); and since substance is absent, the non-existence of everything is established.
Therefore, it is incorrect to say that 'the whole (*avayavin*) exists as a causal complex,' or that 'only the parts (*avayava*) exist.'"
The absence of [the] primary [element]; the absence of substance; [the term] "muktāvayavīya" does not exist in the Ya manuscript.
In every respect, though things are perceived through direct perception, they nevertheless do not exist because that perception is impossible; and that perception itself does not exist at all,
for as far as there is the visible part, so far is there the back side.
Only the near part is seen, not the middle or far parts;
therefore, there is simply no perception of the object as a whole, for the object is not merely its near part.
Now, if it is thought: "The near part will indeed be apprehended through direct perception (pratyakṣa) by necessity, and likewise the middle and far parts will also be apprehended."
No, because even there, the three parts are equal;

furthermore, due to the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*): the existence of the whole (*avayavin*) is established because its parts exist as its parts and because they serve as its cause; and since those parts exist, the whole is established because it possesses those parts and is their effect. This is a case of mutual dependence, and things that depend on each other cannot be established—just as a boat tied to another boat does not serve as a support for either. Thus, even from the observation of a causal complex (*sāmagrī*), all entities do not exist.
And these [are] the basis for the proclamation of the supreme.

They are postulated [as being non-existent] because they are not perceived in that manner, and from their non-perception, they do not exist in that very way. (Pra*tulanā—p. 34, l. 9). And furthermore, they do not exist because they are not perceived; even from non-perception, they do not exist by that same mode.
In this regard, there is the following suspicion concerning the supreme [view]: "In every way they are illogical," and so forth.

Even if those objects for which there are no logical grounds—being "illogical"—are not apprehended through reasoning, yet they are apprehended and seen through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and being seen, they cannot be refuted; therefore, since their existence is grasped by perception, these existing objects must be postulated—if they were thus postulated, even so they do not exist, because that perception itself is impossible.
This is the explanation thereof: furthermore, that perception does not exist at all.

How is it that there is no perception? It is said: "Insofar as... and so forth. As long as there is an object of sight, so long is there a far side (*parabhāga*). For of an object conceived as visible, only the far side is seen; the near and middle sides are not seen. Yet the object must necessarily possess those [other] parts—the near, the middle, and the far. In this regard, if the perception of the far side is accepted as being direct perception (*pratyakṣatva*), why is its non-perception due to the non-seeing of the near and middle sides not also accepted? Therefore, there is simply no perception of the object; for one should not conceive that the object consists merely of its far side.

Now, as for the passage beginning with "atha matam" (if it is thought): this might be your view—that first, the near portion will certainly be grasped through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); likewise, the middle and far portions will also be grasped through inference (*anumāna*) and subsequently through direct perception; therefore, it is not merely non-perception, but rather [it is] perception.
Comparison—[as stated] in Pañjikā 14:

Here we reply: No, because even there, the state of having three parts is equal. Even in the case of the part nearest [the observer], which is intended to be visible, three parts indeed exist: those called "near," "middle," and "far," since it possesses constituent parts (*sāvayavatva*). For that which is divisible, possessing constituent parts, necessarily remains established as threefold. Therefore, in this case as well, the non-perception of the "far" and "middle" parts is due to the equality of having three parts, just like the non-perception of an entire object. Thus, for that which has constituent parts, perception is impossible because of its state of having three parts.
The phrase *vastudabhāgasyādarśanya* does not exist in the Bhā manuscript; it is seen in the Bhā manuscript [only as a marginal correction].

Now, if it is thought that partless atoms will be seen, then let them be perceived; for while they themselves are not being seen, what talk can there be of seeing something that possesses parts? Or, if the collection of atoms—which possesses those parts—is not being perceived, how can its constituent part, the partless atom, be seen? And when the atom itself is not perceived, from where will that which possesses parts be grasped? Or, while that which possesses parts is not being grasped, how will its constituent parts—the partless atoms—be grasped?
This conventional usage, however, is merely projected by consciousness.

Consciousness, even in the absence of an external object, appears as if it were an external object while revolving in various ways within itself, because it is consciousness, just like a dream-consciousness.
If it is argued that in those cases too, the object perceived during the waking state is the cause, then in each instance, consciousness alone is the cause;
or, if there exists some non-conscious object, let it be shown.
In a dream, however, it is consciousness alone that constitutes the object, though it is devoid of external reality;
or perhaps it is thought that one will perceive [the object] as partless.

If you think that "only that partless portion which is on the side facing the object is perceived," then this is undesirable for you: atoms would then have to be perceived. For it is not accepted that atoms, being beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), are visible to anyone. Since those partless atoms are not seen, what talk can there be of something appearing as having parts when no other parts are seen? Or, like oil in sand, if there is no perception of each individually, there is likewise no perception of their aggregate. Furthermore, if the collection of atoms as a whole is not perceived because its central and intermediate parts are unperceived, then what talk can there be of perceiving a partless atom as a constituent part of that? Thus, by following this line of reasoning, there is no perception [of atoms].

The explanation of these two points is as follows: "And when [they conceive] an atom," and so forth, up to "they will grasp," has already been explained; this is because the word "why" (*kutaḥ*) recurs, and because the portion of the view is present.

If it is asked, "In that case, how can the conventional operation of the seen and the seeing be possible when the seen does not exist?", it is said in reply: This conventional operation is indeed produced by consciousness alone;

and consciousness, even in the absence of an external object, manifests internally as if it were an external object, appearing in various forms because it is a reality and because it is consciousness.

What is it like? It is like a dream (*svapnavat*). "Like a dream" means as in a dream; just as one who is asleep perceives the forms of elephant herds, mountains, and so forth—which are impossible even within a confined space—despite the absence of any external objects such as elephant herds, so too do the cognitions of waking states, such as those of healthy forms and the like, consist merely of internal transformations of consciousness appearing as external objects. There is no object whatsoever distinct from that [consciousness], as it has been said: "It is possible... (*saṃbhavīti cet*) and so forth.
And [the term] *satya* [is used] in the *Yogācārabhūmi*,
*Satyavibhaṅga*, and likewise in the *Tathatā-vibhaṅga*.
Likewise, within [the body]:
heaven, earth, wind, space, oceans, rivers, and the directions;
see page 105, line 22, and tippanī page 50, line 4.

"Parts of the reality of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa-tattva) exist externally. (Vākyapadīya 3.7.41). If it is argued that even in that case, the object perceived during the waking state is the cause [of the dream], we reply: for even in a dream, consciousness arises only in the form of pleasure, pain, color, taste, and so forth—constructed from what was seen, heard, or experienced—but never in the form of something absolutely unperceived, such as a sky-flower. Therefore, if you think that the external object alone is the cause, we say this: in each of those instances, consciousness itself is the cause; and here, "consciousness" is the meaning of the word.
And that is merely a mental construction;
the meaning of the sentence is the synthesis performed by the intellect,
and this conceptualization is a part of such a [synthetic] whole.

Paryavāstika is a cognition that possesses a comprehensive understanding; because of the lack of intrinsic nature (*naiḥsvābhāvya*), it is an understanding that encompasses everything, being merely an understanding.
This is the *paryavāstika* perspective (*naya*), according to which even an existent is simply an existent.
Only an object that is actually brought forth by cognition itself can be understood as an "object," and not otherwise.

For even if an object were to arise as inseparable from cognition, since it lacks its own intrinsic nature (svarūpa) and is thus unperceived, how could it possibly be the cause of a dream? Therefore, he says: "Or, if there is some object that exists independently of cognition, let it be shown. The intention is that an object imagined by your cognition cannot be demonstrated [as existing independently].

Furthermore, it is possible for me [to maintain] that consciousness itself is the object, even without an external object; for example, it is shown that in a dream, consciousness itself is the object despite being devoid of an external referent.
Therefore, it is a logical hypothesis that in both the dreaming and waking states, consciousness alone is the object, as it is non-deviant.
And in that regard, Vijñāna-bhāṣya...
And here, in the phrase "the cause of wakefulness," the word-meaning is *vijñāna* (consciousness),
and that is merely conceptual construction (*kalpanāmātra*).
The meaning of the sentence is the synthesis by the intellect, and this is indeed a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

It is a "partial aspect" (*ekadeśa*) of such [an object], a comprehensive understanding (*parisamantādavagama*); because of its lack of intrinsic nature (*naiḥsvābhāvya*), it is a comprehensive understanding that is merely an act of understanding.
The view that "it possesses this" is the Paryavastika-naya;
it holds that even a state (bhāva) is indeed a state,
and nothing but a functional activity (upayoga).

Regarding that which is inseparable from consciousness: if it were devoid of consciousness, what would be the meaning of the word in this system? To this we reply: here, consciousness is the meaning of the word; for it is consciousness itself—aroused by consciousness—that is intended as the expressive word. Even external denotables such as form, taste, pot, cloth, and so forth, which are indicated by it, are indeed consciousness itself, as it has been said: "O Son of the Victor, all this which belongs to the three realms is nothing but representation-only," and so on.
That which is of the nature of internal cognition appears as if it were external;
that is the object, because it is of the nature of cognition and because it serves as its condition. (Ālambanaparīkṣā)

If it is argued that, in this case, there would be no distinction between valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and what appears to be valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāsa*), we accept this; for that consciousness is indeed conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), mere conceptualization alone. Since its location, time, form, cause, and effect are indeterminate, even the consciousness claimed to belong to the waking state lacks validity, just like the consciousness of one who is asleep or suffering from ophthalmia.
This is the meaning of the term:
it is indeed the very nature of the suffixes beginning with *ṭa* and ending with *ya*.
In the Mahāyāna, the threefold world is established as representation-only (vijñaptimātra), based on the sūtra which says:
"O Sons of the Conqueror, the threefold world is mind-only (cittamātra). (Ṭīkā, p. 50, l. 12)
Mind (*citta*), intellect (*manas*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), and representation (*vijñapti*) are synonyms.
Here, "mind" is intended as being accompanied by its associated mental factors (*sasaṃprayoga*);
the word "only" (*mātra*) is for the purpose of negating external objects.
Thus, in the *Vṛtti* composed by Vasubandhu on his own *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*:
"That which is internal in the nature of cognition appears as if external;
that is the object, because it has the nature of cognition and because it serves as its condition. (*Ālambanaparīkṣā*, verse 6).

The reading here might also be "consciousness is merely conceptual construction" (vijñānaṃ kalpanāmātrameva); [the variants] "jāgradavasthabhi" (in the waking state) and "jāgratsvasthabhi" (in the waking, healthy state) appear in the manuscripts Y and Bhā.
The reading *°jjāgratsvasthābhi°* also appears correct; see page 851, line 20.

What, then, is the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*)? It is said: the meaning of the sentence is the synthesis (*anusaṃhṛti*) by the intellect. For the sentence and its meaning consist in the cognition that connects individual cognitions through the synthesis of the cognitions of the objects appearing in temporal sequence—this is stated in footnote 2 on page 448.
And this conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is a single part of such [a totality];
this method (*naya*) is a single part of such [a totality] divided a hundredfold.

And since that which is thus constituted is distinguished by its aspects (*paryavāstika*), the literal meaning must be understood as "pertaining to the aspects" (*paryavāstika*). Therefore, he says: *pari* is a prefix meaning "on all sides" (*samantāt*); *ava* is a verbal root meaning "understanding" (*avagama*). As it is said: "The root *ava* [is used] in the senses of protecting, going, shining, delighting, satisfying, understanding, entering, hearing, ownership, requesting, action, desire, shining, obtaining, embracing, harming, burning, state of being, and increase" (Pāṇini Dhātupāṭha 1.60). Since "understanding" (*avagama*) is intended here, and because of the absence of intrinsic nature (*naiḥsvābhāvya*), there is an understanding on all sides (*parito'vagamaḥ*) of the external object under investigation. Furthermore, this word "substance" (*dravya*) refers to consciousness (*vijñāna*). This term *dru* has six meanings; its modification (*vikāra*) is "substance" (*dravya*). It has been explained previously in various ways according to the perspective, such as "that which has come from the Tathāgata" (*tathāgati*).

What is its connection? What are the categories of existence (*bhāvaskandha*)? The categories of existence are declared to be twofold, namely: from scripture (*āgama*) and from reasoning (*vyatirikta*). [The latter] means mere cognition (*vijñānamātra*), in the sense that there is only an understanding of the absence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) due to the exclusion of all logical constructs.

That which possesses this [understanding] is "one who has the intellect" (*mati*); that which possesses such an intellect is a "perspective" (*naya*). The perspective is sixfold, even when past, as it consists of the intellect regarding "it is," "it is not," and "it is designated" (*diṣṭa*). (Pāṇini 4.4.60).

60. Thus, considering that the form is established by the addition of the suffix *ṭhak* and that only *paryava* exists, this is the *paryavāstika* method; see page 763, lines 12–14, and tip-page 94, line 18.

And this word *dravya* (substance) applies to all six [categories], for it is derived from the root *dru* meaning "to go"; thus, its modification (*vikāra*) is *dravya*. This has been explained previously according to the various perspectives as a basis for understanding the Tathāgata. What, then, is the category of existence (*bhāva-skandha*)? The category of existence is declared to be twofold, namely: through scripture (*āgamataḥ*) and through non-scriptural [inference] (*no-āgamataḥ*).
It appears that by the word *asya*, the portion *asya* found in the expression *so 'syāsti* ("he has this") is being referred to; thus, is it a past [usage] based on a completed state?
(Page 446, Note 5)

And since that entity—the object, the word, or what is intended as denoted by another—is in fact nothing but the reality characterized by consciousness (*vijñāna*), he says: "An entity is indeed an entity. One should not take it to mean that an entity is simply something that "exists," such as a jar, a cloth, or the categories of substance, quality, and action; rather, an entity is precisely *upayoga* (active engagement), and an entity is not substance and so forth.

Furthermore, that entity is either *kṣāyika* (resulting from total destruction of karma), *kṣāyopaśamika* (resulting from partial destruction and subsidence), *aupaśamika* (resulting from subsidence), or *pāriṇāmika* (inherent transformation). And that is precisely *upayoga*, whether with form (*sākāra*) or without form (*anākāra*), being devoid of conceptual constructions such as valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or fallacious cognition (*pramāṇābhāsa*).
Therefore, this is a specific variety of the *paryavāstika-naya*, namely the *evambhūta* [naya], which grasps only the aspect of the transformation (*paryāya*) of absolutely pure consciousness; thus,
the reading here might also be "that which is intended as other than the word" (*śabdānyavācyābhimata*) or "that which is intended as external to the word" (*śabdānyabāhyābhimata*).

Just as in the first six alternatives among the *dravyāstika* [schools], such as the *vidhi* (affirmation) and others, the word *paryava* was explained as having that [substance] as its meaning due to the predominance of substance (*dravya*), so too here, in the subsequent alternatives such as "both-and-both" (*ubhayobhaya*) and others, the word *dravya* should be understood as having that [state/part] as its meaning due to the predominance of state (*paryava*). Therefore, he says: "And this word *dravya* [is used] even in all six," etc. [The root] *du* means "going" (*gati*); according to Pāṇini’s Dhātupāṭha (944–945), the root *du* signifies motion. By adding the suffix *yat* to the word *du* in the sense of a modification of that motion, the form *dravya* is produced.

Substance itself is the object; thus, "substance-object" (*dravyārtha*). Furthermore, that [substance] has been previously explained in various ways through such conceptual distinctions as past, both [past and present], and so forth. Whatever the perspective (*darśana*) may be, according to that perspective, each of those six perspectives is indeed the "mode-object" (*paryāyārtha*) by virtue of its own respective perspective. This is because, through such understanding (*tathāgati*), one proceeds completely (*parito gamanāt*) in each respective way. (Note: *pra* appears to be a scribal error for *api*).
Tipṛ 115, line 11;
Tipṛ 16, line 30; Tipṛ 52, line 32:
"This was not overlooked" (nākṣimetat bhā).
Is this not acceptable?

Is this merely an exposition of one's own personal opinion, or is there also a scriptural (ārṣa) basis for this view? To this it is replied: There is indeed a scriptural basis for it. [The text begins] with the question, "What is that aggregate of existence (bhāvaskandha)?", and continues until: "It is from the perspective of non-scriptural knowledge (noāgama); and what is that aggregate of existence from the perspective of scriptural knowledge (āgama)? From the perspective of scriptural knowledge, the aggregate of existence is one who possesses knowledge and is attentive."
Thus, from the perspective of scripture (*āgama*), the categories of existence (*bhāvaskandha*) are as stated in *Anuyogadvārasūtra* 54–55 and so forth.

This is the restriction even of the doctrine of momentariness (*kṣaṇikavāda*): namely, that "even that object is nothing but consciousness. This is the twelfth limb (*bhaṅga*) of the *Dvādaśāra-naya-cakra*, called the "refutation of the restriction of restrictions" (*niyamaniyamabhaṅga*).

"Thus, from the perspective of scripture (āgama), it is the 'substance-aggregate' (bhāva-skandha)"; this concludes the grammatical exposition. Since the substance-aggregate of scripture, characterized by its application (upayoga), is nothing other than the very nature of consciousness (vijñāna), and because of the inclusion of the word "etcetera," whatever else there may be—such as the Śruta-Āvaśyaka, the Sāmāyika, or anything else to be understood through the sequence of the nominal and other types of figurative designation (nikṣepa)—all that, from the perspective of scripture, is indeed application, meaning it is knowledge itself.

Now, for the purpose of defining the substance-aggregate, he says: "What is the substance-aggregate? The substance-aggregate is declared to be of two kinds, namely: from the perspective of scripture (āgama) and from the perspective of non-scripture (no-āgama)."
To this, the reply is: "The category of existence (bhāvakhaṇḍa) is of two kinds," and so forth.
It is a category (skandha) that is itself existence (bhāva), hence "existence-category" (bhāvakhaṇḍa); or, a category based upon existence is an "existence-category.
And that is designated as being of two kinds, namely: from scripture (āgama) and not from scripture (no-āgama).

What, then, is the category of substance from the perspective of scripture (*āgama*)? The category of substance from the perspective of scripture is one who knows [it] and is attentive (*upayukta*) to it. That is the category of substance from the perspective of scripture.

In this context, one who knows the meaning of the category of substance from the perspective of scripture and is attentive to it is the "substance of existence" (*bhāvaskandha*), because there is no difference between that [knowledge] and its application (*upayoga*).

Thus ends [the section on] the aggregate of dispositions from the perspective of non-scriptural authority (*no-āgama*) in the commentary on the *Anuyogadvāra-sūtra* composed by the master Maladhāri Hemacandra Sūri.

Now, what is the aggregate of dispositions from the perspective of scriptural authority (*āgama*)? The aggregate of dispositions from the perspective of scriptural authority is one who possesses knowledge and is attentive (*upayukta*).
Thus, from the perspective of scripture (*āgama*), the categories of existence (*bhāvaskandha*) are as stated in *Anuyogadvārasūtra* 54–55 and so forth.

This is the rule even for the doctrine of momentariness (*kṣaṇikavāda*): namely, that "even that object is nothing but consciousness. This is the twelfth limb (*bhaṅga*) of the *Dvādaśāranayacakra*, named the "Refutation of the Rule of Rules" (*niyamaniyamabhaṅga*).

[The term] *tvādigra* [refers to] this rule (*niyama*) even of the doctrine of momentariness (*kṣaṇikavāda*), namely the view that "only a momentary entity exists. This too is a rule: that momentary entity is consciousness alone; there is no external form (*rūpa*) or the like distinct from it. What then? It is merely the manifestation of the transformation of internal consciousness. Thus ends the twelfth limb (*bhaṅga*), named "the breaking of the rule of rules" (*niyamaniyamabhaṅga*), as counted from the beginning starting with the "breaking of the injunction" (*vidhibhaṅga*), in the commentary on the *Dvādaśāranayacakra* composed by the venerable Mallavādin, written by the venerable Siṃhasūri Gaṇi.
Oṃ Arhaṃ,
salutations to the True Gurus. Now begins the section on the twelve spokes within the twelve [spokes].

This too is as unreasonable as before due to its absolutism, because the possible alternatives are untenable: if you say that both cognition and speech are thus devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*),

then, lest this fault arise, if you instead accept that cognition and speech possess intrinsic nature (*sasvabhāva*), there is a contradiction with your own tenet that "everything is devoid of intrinsic nature."

Furthermore, if speech itself possessed intrinsic nature, then it would contradict your own statement that "everything is devoid of intrinsic nature"; this would constitute the fault of self-contradiction.

In this section concerning right vision (*samyagdarśana*), which consists of the total negation of all [extreme] positions such as "existence" and so forth, he says the following in order to demonstrate that each individual position results in wrong vision (*mithyādarśana*): "This view as well—as that everything is devoid of intrinsic nature—is improper for the same reasons as before, because it is based on absolutism (*ekānta*). For instance, [absolutist] views such as 'only momentary,' 'only a collection of form and so forth,' 'only inexpressible,' or 'only identity, difference, both, or neither' are improper due to their absolutism. Alternatively, it has been stated that the Jaina perspective is the supreme one because it is established upon non-absolutism (*anekānta*); likewise, this view that 'everything is devoid of intrinsic nature' is also [subject to the same critique]."

Why? Because the possible alternatives are untenable. Even in this view, whatever alternatives are possible—in brief, whether consciousness and speech are devoid of intrinsic nature (*naiḥsvābhāvya*) or possess intrinsic nature (*svābhāvya*)—the distinctions between these two that will be stated hereafter are in no way tenable. Since those are untenable, this view is also irrational;

therefore, the conclusion will be that the nature of reality as conceived by the Jains, characterized by non-absolutism (*anekānta*), is superior. [The phrase] "only this must be said" refers to the identity or difference of the universal and the particular.

It is precisely this [collection] that is the general; because of its distinctness from the particular (*viśeṣa*), the reading "it is precisely this that must be expressed" or "it is precisely this that must not be expressed" is also possible here.
Because of its distinctness from the particular... *ya*.

For example: when you say "thus everything is without intrinsic nature" (*niḥsvabhāva*) by means of the logical arguments such as the non-establishment of the past, then at every repetition of the word "your," because of the first *evaṃ* and the second *evaṃ*, even consciousness (*vijñāna*) and speech (*vacas*)—which are spoken by you—are included within "everything" without exception; since you have stated that "everything is without intrinsic nature," this statement that "consciousness and speech are without intrinsic nature" overextends beyond the reality of consciousness itself. Furthermore, that [statement] is undesirable, as it would entail the consequence that consciousness and speech could not be communicated.

For when consciousness (*vijñāna*) is non-existent, then all this is without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). Since you yourself have not ascertained this, yet desire to make it known to us, your statements establishing the thesis and so forth are themselves non-existent. Therefore, it is illogical for you to communicate with another, because consciousness and speech lack the status of an ascertained thesis and so on, being like the delirious ravings of a madman. Thus, the conceptualization of "lack of intrinsic nature" excludes the lack of intrinsic nature in all things from both knowledge and speech; this is the fault [of your position], which is undesirable to you.

Now, if—out of fear of this fault expressed by "lest it be so" and the rest—you were to accept that both your cognition and your words possess intrinsic nature (*sasvabhāva*), there would be a contradiction with your own thesis that "everything is devoid of intrinsic nature" (*niḥsvabhāva*). By what means? By the acceptance of the intrinsic nature of cognition and speech; thus, there is a contradiction with your own tenet (*abhyupagama-virodha*). Furthermore, in this way, even a jar and the like must exist, because they function within conventional discourse (*vyavahāra-vṛtta*), just like those words;
for if they were empty of that [intrinsic nature], there would be contradictions with perception and other means of valid cognition.

However, if there were total absence of intrinsic nature (*naiḥsvābhāvya*), contradictions with perception and other means of valid cognition would be quite evident; furthermore, the absence of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and so forth within the position of universal emptiness cannot be established.
Moreover, because consciousness is admitted, all this is indeed consciousness alone, since everything that exists has the characteristic of consciousness.
And that person alone is the knower; if this [universe] were identical with him,
as was stated previously, there would be a flaw in the proposition.

Not only is there a contradiction with one's own tenets (*abhyupagama-virodha*) regarding the object of knowledge, but there is also the fault of contradiction with one's own words (*svavacana-virodha*). This is because, at the conclusion of the definition of the thesis (*pakṣa*) and so forth, you stated previously that "if [the word] possesses intrinsic nature (*sasvabhāvatva*), then not everything is without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*)," since you now accept that it does possess intrinsic nature; for the word *iti* has the sense of a reason (*hetu*). Thus, for you who follow the path of the worldly conventions of proof, refutation, the object to be established, and the means of establishment, there are also contradictions with inference (*anumāna*), scripture (*āgama*), and common experience (*loka*). Therefore, he says: "And if [it is] accepted... (*ce'bhyupa°*).
And in this way, even a jar or the like exists, because it functions within conventional discourse, just like that statement [of yours].
However, if it were empty of that [existence], there would be contradictions with perception and other means of knowledge;
indeed, if everything were devoid of intrinsic nature, contradictions with perception and the rest would be perfectly evident.
Furthermore, the absence of the properties of the subject (pakṣadharma) and so forth, which follows from the doctrine of universal emptiness, cannot be established as the probandum (*sādhya*).
Moreover, because consciousness is admitted, all this is indeed nothing but consciousness alone, since everything that exists has the characteristic of consciousness;
and that [consciousness] is precisely the knowing person (*puruṣa*).
And this, as previously stated, consists of that very [nature]: "The definition would be... (Bhāṣya).
Is this the characteristic of yours? Or is it the characteristic of yours?
Because of its being the cause...
Because there is also contradiction with worldly convention, he says: "Even [contradiction] with worldly convention" (bhāṣya);
because there is also contradiction with inference and worldly convention, he says: "Even [contradiction] with inference and worldly convention" (yā).

And thus, even a jar or the like is asserted to be "existent" for you, because it is unestablished [for you]; the word "thus" (evaṃ) serves as a reminder that, although [existence] is well-known to all the world, it consists in the aforementioned nature of being (*sasvabhāvatva*) in the case of consciousness and speech.

If it is asked, "Why is the pot and so forth existent? it is said: because they function within the sphere of conventional discourse (*vyavahāra*), like that very statement [you have made]. Just as the cognitions and words regarding things such as sky-flowers—which are caused by conceptual constructions such as non-establishment, illogicality, non-arising, the observation of causal complexes, the positions of observation and non-observation, dependence on other factors, both, contradiction, and so forth—are endowed with intrinsic nature (*sasvabhāvatva*), so too the pots and other things that function within conventional discourse must possess intrinsic nature.

However, if that [all] were empty, there would be contradictions with perception and so forth. For you—who do not accept the existence of intrinsic nature—there would be contradictions with perception and so forth regarding the emptiness of each respective statement, the auditory perception, the division of the members of the syllogism such as the thesis (*pakṣa*), and the cognition of those [members] together with the objects to be established, such as a pot; these are all directly experienced by both yourself and me. Furthermore, for one who does accept [intrinsic nature], the contradictions with one's own assertions and words have already been stated.

By the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), contradictions with inference and scripture are also implied, because [the doctrine of emptiness] contradicts the scriptures proclaimed by the Arhats, Buddha, Kapila, Kaṇāda, Brahmā, and others.

However, you have forcibly embraced a contradiction with the world, for you proceed by disregarding all common worldly consensus that jars and other external objects as well as cognitions and words do exist, asserting instead that "all things are empty.

Thus, there are all the faults such as the contradiction between your own assertions and the emptiness of both cognition and words; moreover, if everything were devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), all contradictions with perception and other means of valid cognition would be manifest, since both cognition and words are included within "everything," just as has been applied according to that same method. In this way, the faults of the thesis have been stated in general.
"Like your statement? (p. 828, l. 1; p. 830, l.

1). The additional reading "the conceptual construction of fear, contradiction, and so forth" found here in manuscript *Ya* has entered this text due to the scribe’s oversight from the preceding line.
The state of being a cause for that emptiness is to be inferred;
page 855, line 5.
[The portion beginning with] *prayatnaṃ* and ending there is not present in manuscript *Ya*;

however, for the sake of indicating the direction of the error, he says by that very same method: "Furthermore, the absence of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and so forth, which belongs to the doctrine of universal emptiness, cannot be the probandum (*sādhya*). Since the thesis itself is unestablished due to [the faults of] non-establishment (*asiddhi*) and so on, the reasons such as 'being dependent on another' (*parāyatta*) and the like are certainly not established by this aforementioned method; therefore, we do not dwell upon this here, as it is obvious."

Moreover, from the statement "because of the admission of consciousness" up to "because that which exists has the characteristic of consciousness," you yourself have established the lack of intrinsic nature (*naiḥsvābhāvya*) of external objects through reasons such as their non-establishment; having thus demonstrated that all this is merely consciousness alone—like a lion in a dream, or like the perception of a lion by a man while awake—it is said: "The Person alone is all this, whatever has been and whatever will be, and he is the lord of immortality, who by food surpasses [all]."
In the Rigveda (10.8.90),
is it not the case that by the word "vijñāna" mere imagination is expressed, and not the functional efficacy of consciousness?

As it was said: "In the absence of that, this also does not exist," by those who cite dreams as an example— this too is incorrect, because by citing a dream as distinct from the waking state, the doctrine of consciousness-only (*vijñānamātratva*) is itself refuted.

If it is merely that [mental representation], is it a dream or not a dream? A distinction between dreaming and waking cannot be established, because both are equal in their lack of objective existence.

Even the cognition of fear, joy, pleasure, pain, and so forth arising from the birth of a son and other such events is included here; since everything exists solely as having the nature of consciousness (*vijñāna*), and since that [consciousness] is all-encompassing, all this is merely consciousness (*vijñānamātra*). And that is indeed the knowing Person (*puruṣa*). This world—even that which is considered past or future—is nothing but the present itself. Just like the states of a calm lake’s water, its waves, bubbles, and so on, it exists as a single undivided reality, distinguished only by the four states known as deep sleep, dreaming, waking, and the fourth (*turīya*). Thus, it is accepted that "it truly exists."

As it was stated previously in the *Vidhividhinayārambhaṅga*—beginning with "The Person alone is all this," and so forth—the *Puruṣasūkta* was explained therein; therefore, it is not explained again here. Whatever exists... [is that].
Of all that exists, as far as all that exists—
this whole world is indeed the Person (puruṣa), whatever has been and whatever is yet to be.

"And he is the lord of immortality, that which grows by means of food" (Ṛgveda 10.8.90). Now, it might be argued that by the word "knowledge" (*vijñāna*) mere imagination is expressed, and not the actual efficacy of knowledge;
as it has been said: "In the absence of that [efficacy], even that [knowledge] is non-existent."
...This too is incorrect, because by citing the dream as distinct from the waking state, one actually excludes the [thesis of] "consciousness-only" (vijñānamātratva).
If it were merely that, would the dream be a dream or not a dream? A qualification of the dream as distinct from waking is not tenable, since both are equal in their lack of substantiality.
All is indeed consciousness;
if all is consciousness, [then] deep sleep... [this phrase is not present in the Ya manuscript].
...mastevā... (Pra., p.
2). Here it is said: "But surely, by the word 'consciousness' (*vijñāna*), mere imagination is expressed, not the fact that consciousness possesses an object."

By citing the example of "the fear arising from seeing a lion in a dream," it has been established that [the object] is a mere mental construction; thus, there is an absence of the apprehended (grāhya), and in the absence of the apprehended, there is an absence of the apprehender (grāhaka).
As it has been stated: "In the absence of that, this too is non-existent"—this very point was reiterated by those who cited the dream as an illustration.
To this, it is replied: even this is incorrect, because by citing a dream as distinct from the waking state, the doctrine of "consciousness-only" (vijñānamātratva) is itself refuted.

Furthermore, because all entities possess their opposites—just as there is the distinction between a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and a fallacious appearance of such a means (*pramāṇābhāsa*)—the acceptance of a distinction between the thesis (*sādhya*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is necessarily entailed.

For instance, [if one asks] "If that alone [is the case]," and so forth: if consciousness itself is the dream and not the non-dream, then within that dream, the sight of a lion is indeed unreal and serves as a cause for fear; yet for one who has awakened, the cessation of fear occurs despite the unreality of the dream-lion. Conversely, the sight of a lion while awake is truly real and is a direct cause of death, whereas the sight of a son while awake is a cause of joy; and in the dream, this [joy] is independent of that [waking state], since upon awakening, the joy ceases.

Having understood that those two are distinct, the illustration of dream as being distinct from waking consciousness is appropriate; however, in your position, that qualification of dream as being different from waking does not hold. Why? Because both are equally non-existent, like a sky-flower or the son of a barren woman. This is well said when the intention is to maintain that waking cognition is of the nature of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) while dream cognition is of the nature of a semblance of valid knowledge (*pramāṇābhāsa*). Thus, "because of existence" (*sattvāt*) is correct.

Demonstrating that if all emptiness (*sarvaśūnyatā*) were accepted, it would follow that conventional distinctions such as "dream" and "non-dream" would cease to exist, [the author] says: "In the absence of everything, how can there be 'this is a dream' or 'this is not a dream,' or 'this is true' or 'this is false'? (Viśeṣāvaśyakabhāṣya 1705). The meaning is: if the non-existence of everything—that is, universal emptiness—is admitted, then from where [would such distinctions arise]? By what would this distinction be produced? Thus it is stated in the *Viśuddhasyabhāṣya-ṭīkā* on the *Viśeṣāvaśyakabhāṣya*, composed by Maladhāri Hemacandrasūri.
Having purified [it], as on page 858, line 5; in the *Viśuddha* [recension].
If it is argued that [the statement] "both are non-existent" is understood with respect to the object to be established, we say no; for both are equal in their non-existence,
and the expression is appropriate because, like the sight of a lion in a dream, it serves to exclude the "sky-flower."
But surely, existence as the object of consciousness remains established;
and non-existence, being undifferentiated, simply does not exist— that is, it is indeed existence itself in that manner.

Now, it might be argued: "Who establishes even the existence of consciousness (*vijñāna*), since it is merely a conceptual construction? For consciousness arises from consciousness; in the absence of an object of cognition (*vijñeya*), how could that [consciousness] exist? Just as in a dream there is an absence of the object of cognition which is its cause, so it is even when one has awakened.

Even if this were so, by your admission of the distinctions between consciousness and the object of cognition, and between non-consciousness and the non-object of cognition, you have in fact accepted the doctrine of existence (*sadvāda*) here.

If it should be thought: "It is in consideration of the understanding of the person to be instructed"—that is, even though the waking consciousness and the dream consciousness (the two examples) are equal in their lack of objective reality, nevertheless, for the sake of following the recipient's own view, it is easier to demonstrate that the waking state lacks objective reality by means of the dream itself, which you yourself accept as lacking objective reality;
for this is a skillful means of instruction that conforms to the intellect of the person being taught, even while establishing their equality in terms of non-existence.
Comparison, page 857, line 17:
°garaṇasva° Ya; jāgaraṇobhā° Ya.

And this [argument] is not [valid], because both are equal in their non-existence. Furthermore, the qualification of cognition by "non-cognition," or the qualification of the speaker and so forth by [the distinction from] the person to be informed, is likewise untenable because they are all equal in their non-existence. Moreover, even the example of a dream is consistent with the statement, "like seeing a lion in a dream," which excludes the sky-flower; for [in that case], it is said that the lion is not a sky-flower.
And in the explanation of the analogy of the dream, the qualification "groundless fear, joy, and so forth" cannot exist without "not groundless fear, joy,
and so forth," just as a pot [cannot exist] without its own nature.
In the example,
[the word] "nanu" implies that it must indeed exist without [the other].

Furthermore, the existence of the objects of consciousness is indeed established; by asserting "consciousness-only," you have already admitted the existence of consciousness. Consequently, the claim that "everything is without intrinsic nature" is false, because existence [of consciousness] persists.

Furthermore, non-existence that is devoid of differentiation does not exist at all; for it is only possible to say "it does not exist" by qualifying some existing entity, as one might say, "the flower of the sky-flower exists, but the flower of the *aśoka* does not. Therefore, emptiness is not established for everything without qualification. That which is called "everything" is indeed existence itself in such a manner. Thus, even the non-existence of things like the lion in a dream-cognition establishes the existence of something else; this is the specific point.

Now, it may be argued: "Who establishes even the existence of consciousness (*vijñāna*), since it is a mere conceptual construction? Precisely because of the reasons such as non-establishment [of its object], consciousness does not exist either, just like a dream. For consciousness would be that which cognizes; however, that act of cognition or the agency of consciousness does not exist in a dream due to the absence of an object to be known (*vijñeya*).

Demonstrating this, he says: "For [if] consciousness arises from consciousness, in the absence of that which is to be known (*vijñeya*), how could it exist? The nature of consciousness would consist in its being 'that which cognizes'; if that object of cognition—the *karman*—is absent, how could it [exist]? It does not exist for any reason whatsoever, because in a dream the object of cognition, which is the cause of that [consciousness], is absent; and it is exactly the same even upon waking. Thus, since even waking consciousness lacks the nature of consciousness in the absence of an object of cognition—just like dream-consciousness—what hope is there for the existence of consciousness?
Thus ends the section on the non-existence of consciousness.
Regarding the statement that consciousness is not [produced] from that cause of consciousness, it is said here: "Even so," and so forth.

You yourself have distinguished waking consciousness from dream-consciousness by stating that "consciousness cognizes," whereas dream is "non-cognition"; likewise, you have distinguished the dream object as "uncognizable" relative to waking consciousness. In the same way, regarding expressions such as "the absence of consciousness" (*vijñānābhāva*), what is the function of the negative particle (*nañ*)? Does it mean that [the object] does not exist with specific qualifications such as "prior" and so forth, or does it mean it does not exist at all without such qualifications? If it means it does not exist with specific qualifications, then—due to the lack of capacity for priority, posteriority, mutual relation, or conjunction—it would follow that the existence of a jar is established as something that has never arisen and has never perished, even while being connected to those very capacities.

Now, it might be argued: "The consequence of [the existence of] a produced entity and so forth does not arise; rather, like the son of a barren woman and the like, it is said to be absolutely non-existent because it lacks any qualification.
But how, then, is the son of a barren woman not [absolutely non-existent]? If there were an absolute negation (atyantābhāva) regarding him as its object, the son of a barren woman would not exist;
however, he exists by virtue of being an existent thing in himself.

For example—that substance which exists as both sentient and insentient; the object such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth, which is the waking-state domain arising from the manifestation of consciousness; and the dream-state object, which is the unknowable arising from the knowable waking-state domain—these are accepted by you as distinct entities, both existent and non-existent, by virtue of being objects of cognition and verbal expression. Thus, the doctrine of existence (*sadvāda*) alone is accepted here by you.

Otherwise, if there were no distinction between the qualifiers of cognition and verbal expression—such as the knowable and the unknowable, or the cognized and the uncognized—then, due to the lack of any distinction in their non-existence, silence would have to be your recourse.

Likewise, what is the status of the negative particle (*nañ*) in cases such as "the existence of consciousness" (*vijñānabhāva*)? Does it denote non-existence through specific qualifications such as "prior" and so forth, or is it simply non-existence without such qualifications? If it were non-existence with qualifications, then—due to the mutual incapacity and lack of connection between "prior," "subsequent," and so on—it would follow that there is indeed the existence of a jar that is produced, not destroyed, and connected to those [qualifications].

If it is argued: "There is no such consequence of [existence as] being produced and so forth; rather, like the son of a barren woman, it is said to be absolutely non-existent because it lacks any qualification."

Now, how then is it that the son of a barren woman does not exist? If there were an absolute non-existence regarding him as an object, the son of a barren woman would not be possible; however, he exists by virtue of being a self-existent entity, just as that substance which exists is either conscious or unconscious.
Furthermore, regarding the passage beginning with "likewise, consciousness" (*tathā vijñāna*) and so forth:

if even consciousness does not become consciousness, and an entity does not become an entity, what is the status of the negative particle (*nañ*) in such cases? You must deliberate and explain this: is the non-existence of consciousness and the rest here determined as being qualified by distinctions such as "prior," etc., or is it without any such qualification? Having ascertained this, speak.

In this regard, if it is said that "the qualified object does not exist," then, following the sequence [of examples] from prior non-existence, posterior non-existence, mutual non-existence, incapacity, and non-conjunction—just as a jar does not exist prior to its state as clay and so forth, nor later when it has become shards, nor through mutual relation when it is a cloth, nor in its incapacity when its bottom is perforated, nor in its non-conjunction when it is not in the house—the negative particle (*nañ*) qualifies [the verb] accordingly: in the case of prior non-existence, it qualifies it as "it exists having been produced" (*nirvṛtto'sti*); in the case of posterior non-existence, "it exists having been destroyed" (*adhvasto'sti*); in the case of mutual non-existence, "it exists as that"; in the case of the absence of incapacity, "it exists as capable" (*samartho'sti*); and in the case of the absence of conjunction with the house, "it exists in conjunction with the outside" (*bahiḥsaṃyogo'sti*).

Therefore, it is precisely the existence of the jar that the negative particle (*nañ*) qualifies; [the meaning is] "consciousness does not become non-consciousness" or "being does not become non-being. Furthermore, the reading *viśeṣo nāsti* (there is no distinction) is also possible here.
...from the non-attachment to objects of sense;
Now it is said: "Not at all," and so forth.

Now, if you think: "Lest there be such an undesirable consequence as the existence of a completed entity and so forth, [the word] 'non-existent' (*nāsti*) is used without qualification through synonyms such as 'it does not come into being' (*na bhavati*), etc.; because of reasons such as its non-establishment (*asiddhi*), like the son of a barren woman, it is said to be absolutely non-existent (*atyanta-nāsti*) due to its lack of distinction"—if you hold this view, we reply to this as well: "Then how again... and so on. Even the non-existence of the son of a barren woman, which is intended to be an absolute non-entity (*atyantābhāva*), is itself unestablished (*asiddha*). Therefore, because of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the negative particle (*nañ*) that expresses the negation of specific qualifications—such as being produced, having perished, possessing its capacity, or being related to a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—we consider that it indeed exists.
Bhūdevaśāstrī, page 872,
line 17: "If that object," and so forth.

If the son of a barren woman were an absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), he could not exist within the natures of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and so forth, which possess cessation and other such properties; yet he does exist as something that is itself a being. Therefore, he is not an absolute non-existence. What then? His cessation and other states certainly do occur in relation to things that possess the capacity to be (*bhavitṛtva*). For example: "That which is coming into being is possible," and substance is twofold—sentient and insentient—and that [substance] is also twofold.
In that regard, for a conscious being, there is the state of having experienced existences without beginning or end, due to the transformation of the cycles of karma; unlike other substances,
[the continuum] is not barren with respect to subsequent existences.

...because it consists of a continuous series (*prabandha*), even though it is not barren, it is not distinct from that state; likewise, for the insentient as well, because it is not distinct from that state, and because of its transformation through beginningless and endless revolutions, the state of being the son of a barren woman is not contradictory, since—just like the commencement of a body—it does not exist without mutual interpenetration.

Regarding the passage beginning with "therein, of the sentient one" (*tatra cetanasya*), this conscious self-substance (*ātma-dravya*) is capable of existing throughout beginningless and endless births. Why? Because of the transformation of the cycle of karma (*karma-parivarta*). The transformations of the beginningless and endless continuum of karmic bondage consist of births as animals, humans, hell-beings, and gods. These are indeed beginningless and endless by nature, changing from state to state without abandoning their own essential character (*svajāti*). Just like other substances, such as the substance of matter (*pudgala-dravya*), which possesses the characteristics of form, taste, smell, and touch, and experiences various transformations—such as earth, water, fire, air, plants, mobile beings, bodies, cold, heat, darkness, shadow, sunlight, and radiance—without ever abandoning its non-conscious nature; so too does the conscious self experience the transformations of the cycle of karma. For instance, when a woman who was previously barren falls away from her state of being a human woman and is born again in another life as a human woman, she may become possessed of sons. Since there is no difference in terms of the substantial reality (*dravyārtha*), that very same barren woman is born as one who has sons. Here, he demonstrates the meaning of "the son of a barren woman" through a formal sequence (*daṇḍaka*): starting from "barren in the immediately preceding birth," and so on, up to "because of having the nature of a continuous series," even though she is no longer barren. Why? Because she is not distinct from that state of being. Therefore, the conscious self together with its karma is not distinct from its previous state. Similarly, just as in the case of the previous state of being barren, when the modification (*paryāya*) of having sons arises, it is like the example of a child, a youth, and so forth—a worldly illustration. Just as it remains the very same person despite the modifications of being a child, a youth, or an adult, so too is the living being (*jīva*) one and the same in both the states of being barren and having sons.

Thus, first of all, because the conscious [self] has been cultivated throughout beginningless and endless existence and is not distinct from that [existence], the existence of the son of a barren woman was stated in reality; [this is] because of the non-existence of its object.
*Viśvabhāṣā*.
The reading "in these non-entities" (*adiṣvabhāveṣu*) here is also to be considered;
[on page 872,
line 17] "nor for him is there cessation and so forth" (*na nirvṛttyādi*).

And therein, regarding the objects of existence, there is for the conscious being a state of being conditioned by beginningless and endless existences, because of the transformation and alteration of karma, unlike other substances.
The intermediate existence (*anantarabhava*) is not barren...
because it consists of a continuous series; and even though it is not barren, it does not exceed that state [of being a continuum], just like [the states of] a child or a youth.

Since even that which is insentient is not distinct from its state [of being], and because there is no alteration in its beginningless and endless revolution, its status as the son of a barren woman is not contradictory; for, in the absence of mutual interpenetration, it would not exist, just like the commencement of a body,
or like the states of existence in the realms of animals and hell-beings.
Existence (*bhava*) is the state of being otherwise for a person (*pudgala*), as if it were a substantial entity (*dravyavat*).

We state that even for the insentient, there is existence due to the distinction between substance and mode.

For example: when the *pudgala* particles residing in the body of a barren woman—which have been cast off as hair, nails, teeth, urine, feces, sweat, lymph, blood, flesh, and so forth—are transformed into the state of earth or rice and the like, or are ingested by a non-barren woman or man and assimilated into the form of blood, semen, and so on, and subsequently arise as a son, the existence of the "barren woman's son" (*vandhyāputra*) is not contradictory. This is because he is not distinct from those states [of matter], and because of the principle of the transformation through beginningless and endless cycles of rebirth (*viparivarta*). Thus, by such reasoning, the status of being a "barren woman's son" is not a contradiction.

He establishes this: because that [the son] does not exist without mutual interpenetration; for whatever does not exist without mutual interpenetration is either that very thing itself or belongs to that very thing, like the commencement of a body. Just as a body, due to its transformation through the transitions occurring in beginningless and endless states of existence belonging to those *pudgala*s, cannot exist without mutual interpenetration, so too those very substances of *jīva* and *pudgala* are such that the *pudgala*s of a barren woman are the *pudgala*s of her son; thus, the state of being a barren woman's son is not contradictory.
Therefore, the barren woman's son exists.

In the case of the birth of a child from a barren woman or a man, [the reading] "bandhyāyāḥ" (of a barren woman) or "puṃsā" (by a man) in the Bhāṣya contradicts the reading "vadhyāyāḥ" (of a woman to be killed) or "puṃsā" (by a man) in the Ya[panīya] tradition.

Therefore, it must be understood that all this is non-empty (*aśūnya*) by its very nature, like a house that is not empty. Everything—whether one or manifold in essence—is accompanied by the conceptualization of an enterer, a dweller, and an exit-er, as well as by arising, abiding, and destruction. It exists indeed, both by itself and from another, or from both, manifesting through worldly convention in imagined and non-imagined forms, whether that or not that. Now, how does the existence of self, other, and both occur? It occurs through establishment, conjunction, non-arising, the totality of conditions (*sāmagrī*), vision, and constant manifestation. First, "establishment" (*saṃsiddhi*) is existence through the unification of the distinctions of those natures.
Length indeed exists in that which is long, because it is not dependent on anything else;
for if this [notion of length] were not restricted to its own object, then the middle finger would be longer than the little finger even when compared to the length of the Śakra-staff,
and the same would apply to shortness as well.
Therefore, "all this," and so forth.

In the doctrine of universal emptiness (*sarvaśūnyavāda*), because proof and refutation are impossible, there is an absence of the conventional discourse between the one who explains and the one who is explained. Furthermore, even the position of "consciousness-only" (*vijñānamātra*) would entail the admission that everything is merely a single omniscient person. Moreover, since all things are of the nature of everything, examples such as dreams or the son of a barren woman are unestablished. Therefore, it must be understood that this entire world is non-empty (*aśūnya*). "Accomplishment" (*saṃsiddhi*)—the word *sam* here meaning "unification"—refers to the fact that all entities conceived as distinct are established by being included within a universal and becoming unified with one another; thus he says: "Accomplishment is the existence [of things] through the unification of their distinct natures. Accomplishment, co-existence, simultaneous origination, and simultaneous occurrence are synonymous. He illustrates this: length exists in a long object precisely because it is independent of anything else, meaning it is self-dependent; for that length belongs solely to the ring finger itself.

If, according to your view, this length of the ring finger (*anāmikā*) were dependent on the shortness of the little finger (*kaniṣṭhikā*) while having its own [shortness] as its object, then even when the middle finger is long, the ring finger would not be longer than the little finger. For, having seen the middle finger as long, it would become short through the transformation of its own inherent shortness and could never again be long; for even with respect to another object, it lacks the quality of length within itself, like a sky-flower, because its shortness is dependent upon the middle finger. Yet, it does indeed become long, due to the transformation of its own inherent length which is dependent upon the little finger.

Therefore, the length of the ring finger is dependent upon itself; likewise, the middle finger does not possess length in relation to Indra’s staff, because it is transformed into a shortness relative to that staff based on its own inherent shortness. Nor is its own length dependent upon the ring finger, because it does not transcend its own inherent manifold forms—just as a single person can be both father and son. Thus, through such regulated functioning, there is no contradiction between shortness and length;
in this way, there is no mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*), nor circular dependence (*itaretarāśraya*), nor lack of proof (*asiddhi*).

Even in what is short there is length, and even in what is long there is shortness, because there is no mutual obstruction; just as in the case of one's own desired nature of being short or long, so too, due to transformation (*pariṇāma*), the investigation into their mutual conjunction does not arise [as a contradiction], for it is said that "it would be long," yet it indeed comes to be so.

Therefore, the length of the ring finger (*anāmikā*) and the middle finger (*madhyamā*), which is intended in relation to the little finger (*kaniṣṭhikā*), is indeed dependent upon itself; for even when shortness is established in relation to something longer, length remains inherently established in relation to something shorter.
By this same logic—that shortness is also [dependent on itself]—he extends the argument to show that the shortness of the little finger is likewise dependent upon itself.

For if this were a matter of absolute [intrinsic] objects, then the little finger would not be long even in relation to the length of the ring finger, due to its own joints and constituent parts; nor would the ring finger be long in relation to the middle finger.
