likewise, all phenomena exist even because of their non-arising.

For if that entity were to arise or perish, then—just as there is non-existence prior to it and non-existence after it—it would also lack existence in the interim due to its inherent nature of non-existence, and thus it could not be of a single uniform nature, or it would be the emptiness you assert.

"Do not think that the reason is unestablished"; therefore, he says: "For there is no otherness of the jar from those two—existence and oneness. Since that very single jar is [identical to] the jar which possesses all distinctions, there is no otherness of existence and oneness from it; the word "for" (hi) continues [from the previous sentence]. Because the jar possesses all its own internal distinctions, such as cloth, mat, and so forth, just as it possesses its own [qualities] like height and so forth, there is no plurality in existence and oneness;
is there not the non-otherness of the jar from all [these]?

What follows from this? From that, once it is established—by the logic already stated—that [the jar] is non-different from its existence and unity, then all entities, such as cloth and the like, are also non-different from that [Being], because they are not distinct objects from its existence and unity, just like the jar; for this has been said.

Therefore, he says: "Cloth and the others also have the nature of the jar, because they are not distinct from it, since they are not distinct from the existence and unity of the jar, just like the jar's own self. This concludes the previously discussed matter (p. 841, l. 5).
"All entities, such as jars and the like"—here [the opponent] says: "But if there were oneness, then the satisfaction, pleasure, and so forth established by direct perception would be contradicted.

Thus, for you who assert that "everything is one and everything is of the nature of all," what is seen through direct perception—namely, that hunger is distinct from satisfaction which follows immediately after eating and is opposed to hunger, and that pleasure which arises immediately thereafter is opposed to pain, and so forth—is contradicted. For it is not proper to maintain a thesis that contradicts direct perception.
To this we reply: But surely, even in all established philosophical systems, one strives for liberation by considering that which is established through direct perception to be otherwise?

Now, one might argue that since sensual pleasures are not truly so, being merely a remedy for suffering, intermingled with suffering, abounding in suffering, and non-ultimate, they are indeed suffering; and since even satisfaction is a cause for generating greed and longing, it is itself a form of dissatisfaction. Thinking thus, one may ask: "How can we attain the bliss of liberation—which is free from affliction, independent of others, absolute, exclusive, the opposite of sensual pleasure, and beyond dualities? To this, it must be accepted that all things exist even for one who is conjoined [with the world], because the authority of the scriptures establishes this through practices renowned in all philosophical systems; therefore, you should not harbor further doubt.
He exerts himself for the sake of liberation. (Praśastapādabhāṣya, p.
Furthermore, because they do not arise from that which is mixed with the non-existent, all phenomena exist.

Regarding the passage beginning with "yadi hi": if indeed that entity were to arise, and because of having arisen it would necessarily perish, then it would either arise or perish. What follows from that? From that, there would be non-existence prior to its arising and non-existence after its destruction; likewise, in the middle as well, because its nature is non-existence, it could not be of a single uniform form. Or else, it would have to possess differentiation, or else [it would be] the voidness you desire; however, no entity has a beginning or an end, because that would entail the abandonment of its status as a real entity (*vastu*). Just as in the case of a jar made of clay—such as a *śivaka* (the initial lump) and the shards—it is directly perceived to be without beginning or end.
Therefore, that single entity, remaining as it is, is without division, since division is impossible;
for division could only be conceived through arising and perishing,
yet [the entity] was not previously completed, because completion occurs through action following its commencement.
If it were already completed, then because it is completed, it would not be commenced, like a finished jar;
this is a contradiction.

If it were uncompleted, then because it is uncompleted—and thus non-existent—it would not be commenced, like a flower in the sky; otherwise, it would be like a jar [which is commenced while being made].

Why not begin with a sky-flower or a non-substance (*adravya*)? It might be so; for by the word "or" (*vā*), the possibility of the occurrence of that which you imagine—namely, the existence of arising and destruction—might be entertained.

But what then? There is no beginning, i.e., arising, nor end, i.e., destruction, of any real entity (*vastu*). Why? Because it does not abandon its status as a real entity (*vastutva*); for a real entity does not relinquish its own nature, which is its very status as a real entity.

What is it like? It is like the clay of a jar and its stages such as the *śivaka*, *stūpaka*, *chatraka*, *kuśūla*, and the jar. For just as a jar—despite the perceived differences in its states such as the *śivaka*, *stūpaka*, *chatraka*, *kuśūla*, and the jar—is nothing but clay because of its non-difference from the nature of clay (*mṛttva*); and even in the fragments, gravel, dust, shards, and atoms, it remains nothing but clay because of the persistence of the reality of clay (*mṛttattva*), being devoid of beginning or end; so too, other things such as consciousness (*vijñāna*) do not undergo origination because they do not abandon their status as real entities (*vastutva*). Since that [origination] is absent, there is an absence of destruction (*vināśa*).

Furthermore, because it is directly perceived as being without beginning or end—even amidst the transformations of clay, pots, shards, and so forth—there is no arising or destruction of the reality of form and other qualities; thus, the embodied is without beginning or end. And like the embodied, the unembodied is also without beginning or end due to the absence of arising and destruction, since it does not abandon its status as a real entity.
Therefore, the real entity exists eternally. (Page 842, Line 25)
[The nature of] existence is [the nature of] non-existence (pṛ.

842, l. 18). However, no entity whatsoever has a beginning or an end, because it does not abandon its status as an entity—just as a jar, clay, and so forth [are related to] shards and so forth; for it is directly perceived as being without beginning or end.
Therefore, this single entity, remaining as it is, is without differentiation, because differentiation is impossible;
for differentiation could only be conceived through arising and perishing.
But [it was argued] that it was not completed previously, and that completion occurs through action after its commencement.
If it were already completed, then because it is completed, it would not be undertaken, like a finished jar;
this is a contradiction.
If it were not yet completed, then because it is not completed—and thus non-existent—it would not be undertaken, like a sky-flower; otherwise, it would be like a [clay] jar.
Why not begin with a sky-flower or other non-substantial entities? He concludes [the argument] regarding the jar and so forth:
"Therefore, this single reality, as it exists in such a state, is without division," because division is impossible and because there is an absence of any cause for the occurrence of division.

He demonstrates this by way of contrast (*vaidharmyeṇa*): for difference might be conceived through origination and destruction; however, because [the world] is beginningless and endless according to the method already stated, that [difference] is not possible—it does not exist.
Here he says: "But surely it is not established," and so forth.

But has it not been stated that substances originate another substance? Substances such as the atoms of earth, whether two or many, originating from themselves within their own selves, depend upon mutual conjunction to originate another effect-substance.
And qualities, inhering in those four kinds of originating substances, necessarily originate other qualities—within themselves or in another—from the effect-substance originated by them.
Action, however, originates conjunction, disjunction, and impression in another, within another.

By such introductory statements as these, it was previously stated that [an action] is uncompleted; subsequently, there is action because of the commencement, and completion arises from action. Thus, it is uncompleted.
In that regard, if it were already completed, it would not be commenced because it is already completed, like a finished jar (pṛ. 843, l.
p. 843, l. 13: This is to be understood here—substances originate another substance, and qualities [originate] another quality; Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.2.
The two Vaiśeṣika sūtras numbered 8 and 9, accompanied by a certain ancient commentary, appear to have been excerpted here; for comparison, see page 437, lines 10–13.
Here we say: "This is contradictory," and so forth.
He demonstrates the contradiction with the words "if it is not yet established," and so forth:

because it is not yet established, it is non-existent like a sky-flower; because it is non-existent, like that [sky-flower], it is neither being commenced nor does another [cause] commence it, as in the case of a jar—this is a dissimilar example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*). However, all this is merely a manifestation of the power of its own form, due to the identity of existence (*bhāva-aikya*).
Therefore, an object is not unestablished, because it has begun its process of being undertaken, like a carrying-net (*śikyaka*) and so forth.

If, even so, the persistence of the object is not admitted, then those distinct substances (*dravyāntara*) have not been undertaken, because they are unestablished, like a flower in the sky (*khapuṣpa*).
Or, if it should be argued: "The beginning itself is seen as the cause of differentiation through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)."

Is it eternal or non-eternal? If it were eternal, there would be eternity for all things, because it is their primordial nature and because of its own eternity. Furthermore, regarding the produced and the already established: just as a jar, being already established in the form of clay and so forth, is then commenced in the manifestation of another form—namely, with its broad base, upward neck, and so on—it should not be commenced in that same way [as if it were non-existent]. Why then is that manifestation not commenced from something like a sky-flower or a non-substance? Thus, since there is no commencement from anything other than what is already established—which possesses distinctions such as substance, quality, and action—the production or manifestation [of an effect] is simply the commencement [of what was already present].
Because of its embodied nature (mūrtatva),
all this is merely an evolution of the power of that form, due to the unity of being.
Therefore, an object is not uncompleted, because it has begun its process of being undertaken, like a carrying-net (*śikyaka*) and so forth.
Now, if even in this way the persistence of an object is not admitted, then those other substances have not been undertaken, because they are uncompleted, like a flower in the sky (*khapuṣpa*).
Or, if it should be argued: "The beginning itself is seen as the cause of difference through direct perception."

Is it eternal or non-eternal? If it were eternal, there would be eternity for all things, because [the world] has that as its primordial nature and because of its own eternity; thus, the distinction between the "being made" and the "completed" would be destroyed in form.
Is it that which is destroyed by way of its form, or that which is manifested by way of its form?
This is what is meant in brief: all this is merely the manifestation of the power of that [Supreme] Form.

What is the reason? Because of the identity of existence (*bhāvaikyāt*); for it is due to the manifestation of a single entity such as *puruṣa*, which is merely the cause, that there is a distinction consisting solely in the state of being an effect.
Since that [distinction] is merely [the manifestation], it is because of the identity of existence (*bhāvyaikyāt*).
Because of the identity of that which is to be cultivated,
he summarizes it by saying: "Therefore, it is not unestablished," and so forth.

An entity is indeed already established (*niṣṭhita*), not unestablished. Why? Because it is both uncommenced and commenced: it is uncommenced in the sense of being the manifestation of the effect, and it is commenced in the sense of existing as a potentiality latent within the cause. That which is both uncommenced and commenced is indeed established, not unestablished. Like what? Like a loop (*śikyaka*) and so forth. Just as a thread, though not yet commenced as a loop, is established because of its capacity [to become one], so too is every other entity. This should be contemplated through examples such as the thread of a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*). *anārabdhakarmābhi° bhāṣya; anārabdhakarmābhi° yaśas*
Is it begun solely by causes? And that which is not begun by causes,
as it is.
"Just as [in the previous case], so too here," and so forth.

Even though such a persistence of the entity has been established through reasoning, if it is not accepted by you, then this undesirable consequence follows: those other substances which are intended to be "begun" are actually unoriginated, because they are not completed, and thus they are absolutely non-existent like a sky-flower; this is the intended meaning.
Page 843, line 21:

Now, it might be argued, etc. "Arising" (ādi) refers to origination; this is indeed perceived directly in the case of a jar and other such things. And that [origination] is the cause of the difference of a thing, such as a jar; for if it were unarisen and undestroyed, it would be non-different.

Here you are questioned: "What is that," and so forth. That which is the beginning (*ādi*), the commencement—that which is intended as perception—is it eternal or non-eternal? This must be determined. And what follows from this? If it were eternal, there would be the eternity of all things; all entities, such as jars and the like, would without distinction be nothing but eternal, because they would possess the nature of the beginning and because that beginning is eternal.
And this is undesirable for one who speaks [thus].
Furthermore,
because of the non-existence of both the being-produced and the completed [states], there is likewise an absence of distinctness in what is produced.

Because the beginning (*ādi*) is eternal and because the beginning alone possesses substantiality (*vastutva*), the term "beginning" applies only to the initial state (*ārambha*); it does not apply to the two states of being in the process of action (*kriyamāṇa*) and having reached completion (*niṣṭha*). Furthermore, since those two states—being in the process of action and having reached completion—are absent [in the case of the eternal beginning], there is likewise an absence of any distinction (*bheda*) of that which is to be produced (*janayitavya*) in the form of a jar or the like.
Consequently, our preferred position—that things abide as they are—is victorious, for there is no such production of distinctions from an existing entity.

Furthermore, by making the initial perception the sole authority, there is an abandonment of both the perception of the action and the perception of its completion. Since deviation has been observed in those two, how can one perception—among the others—be made authoritative? Thus, that [authority] is lost once again. Moreover, if you accept "permanence through cessation" (nirvṛtti-nityatva) because of the defects in "eternal permanence" (ādi-nityatā), then in this case of permanence through cessation, there is no universal unity, because things possess distinct and differentiated natures.
But even so, since there is neither commencement nor action, there is indeed an absence of distinction.

Now, if the beginning is admitted to be impermanent, is that [beginning] born or unborn? If it is born, then its very production is impossible because it is unborn, like a finished jar; thus, as stated previously, this is not tenable. Furthermore, what was stated regarding the end is also not tenable because it does not escape the faults already mentioned by you; as before, there is an absence of production at the end as well. Thus, due to this non-production, the identity of all distinctions is established.
Furthermore, regarding the passage beginning with "ādipratyakṣa" and so forth:

since the cause of difference is seen through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) itself, the specific object (*viśeṣya*) is qualified by making direct perception the authority for the *ādi* (beginning) alone, and not for that which resides in action; moreover, even those two [the *ādi* and the action] have been abandoned, and that is improper because it contradicts direct perception.

Regarding the passage beginning with "tayośca" and so forth: if those two types of perception—those consisting of action and those consisting of completion—are rendered invalid, then even direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) becomes invalid; thus, a deviation from the rule is observed. Because of that observation, since the initial perception (*ādi-pratyakṣa*) would likewise be invalid, there would be a further abandonment of the initial perception. Consequently, you yourself have entirely invalidated direct perception.
Such, then, is the fault regarding the eternality of the *ādi* [sound], as found on page 869, line 4, and page 870, line 27.
Even for perception, [the status of] valid cognition... now, regarding eternality and so forth.

Out of fear of this defect, you abandon the position of primordial eternity (*ādinityatva*) and instead accept the eternity of manifestation (*nirvṛttanityatva*), [claiming] that there is no fault because "there is no otherness. For in this way, you have stated that all things are one within the eternity of manifestation; yet that is not so, because they possess distinct and separate natures (pṛthak-vibhinna-svarūpatvāt). (Page 845, Line 3, Bhāṣya)
Regarding the point that "the state of being distinct [from consciousness]... we say this: [The opponent asks], "But even so," and so forth.

If the object is eternally established, then since it is admitted that there is neither commencement (*ārambha*) nor action (*kriyā*), how could difference, commencement, or action be obtained? Thus, the very absence of difference—which is our desired position—is what follows.
Thus, first of all, there is a fault in [the doctrine of] primordial eternity; for you, there would be no commencement of entities,
etc.

If you accept the beginninglessness of things out of fear of these defects, then you are to be questioned as follows: "Is that beginning born or unborn? and so forth. Just like your own questioning, there are defects in all three alternatives that correspond to the defects you have stated; thus he shows the direction of the argument: "If it were born, its very non-arising would follow because it is unborn, like a finished jar," and so on. Having stated the first alternative, he extends the same logic to the rest of the text: "This is not tenable in the same way as what you said. Thus, the very same defects you mentioned apply to the alternatives of the unborn being born or the unborn not being born; therefore, there is an absence of arising.
...due to [the statement] beginning with "for the sake of the fault of the fault... (°dovaddoṣāya°) and so forth; iti ya.

And regarding the passage beginning with "Even at the end," etc.: even at the end there is an absence of production, because one cannot escape the faults you have stated regarding the alternatives of [the cause being] destroyed, undestroyed, both destroyed and undestroyed, or neither. Furthermore, if it should be argued that "at the end, difference itself is seen as the cause of perception"—in response to this prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa), is that [cause] eternal? From the observation of the causal complex (sāmagrī) as well, the existence of all things is established;
and thus, that very same single [entity], which is the essence of all, is the causal complex.
It is the occurrence of one state of being toward another state of being for all phenomena without exception.
Just as from the causal complex of earth and so forth, there arise cotton, its color and other qualities, atoms, particles, threads, cloth, and so on—
and because of the correspondence with these, the designation "pot," "cloth," and so forth is seen to apply to the world of sentient and insentient things—
so too, if everything were to function everywhere due to the totality of causal complexes, then just as there is oil in sesame seeds, there would also be oil in sand.

The same objection applies regarding [the claim that the Self is] eternal and so forth; however, the specific distinction here is that by making the perception of the end (*anta-pratyakṣa*) the authoritative means of knowledge, there is an abandonment of the two perceptions—the initial one and the one being performed. Furthermore, since deviation has been observed in those two, how can one perception among them be made authoritative? Thus, it must be stated that there is yet another loss of that [authority]; this is the result of the extended application (*atideśa*). In this way, because of non-origination, the identity of all distinctions is established (p. 846, l.
The existence of all things is established even through the observation of causal complexes (*sāmagrī*);
thus, that very same single [entity] is the totality of all natures, for a causal complex is the occurrence of one entity toward another entity among all remaining entities.
Just as from the causal complex of earth and so forth, there arise cotton, its color and other qualities, atoms, particles, threads, cloth, and so on—
and because of the correspondence with these, the designation "pot," "cloth," and so forth is seen to apply to the world of sentient and insentient things—
so too, if everything were to function everywhere due to the totality of causal complexes, then just as there is oil in sesame seeds, there would also be oil in sand.

Furthermore, the proof of the existence of all things (*sarvāstitva*) follows from the observation of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*). Even though the causal complex consists of various factors—such as the person (*puruṣa*), necessity (*niyati*), time (*kāla*), inherent nature (*svabhāva*), or the entity itself—it is observed precisely within this complex of distinct states and so forth.

Thus, because there is no arising or destruction apart from that manner [of the complex], the causal complex itself accomplishes the meaning of that single reality which is the essence of all—be it self, other, or both—since it consists of its own constituent parts;
and that causal complex is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

If it is asked, "What is the characteristic of *sāmagrī*? it is said: *Sāmagrī* is the occurrence of each distinct entity with respect to every other entity; that which is the occurrence of each individual distinction within an entity that consists of nothing but the differentiation of a single, undivided essence is called *sāmagrī*.

He demonstrates this with the words "just as by the causal complex of earth, etc. and so forth: cotton consists of the entire collection of earth, water, fire, air, space, self, and so on; its color and other qualities [belong to that]; the atom (*aṇu*) is the collection of those; the fibers (*pakṣman*) are the collections of atoms; the threads (*tantu*) are the collections of those; and the cloth (*paṭa*) is the collection of those. With respect to each such object, the causal complex—consisting of earth, water, fire, air, space, their colors and other qualities, and the collection beginning with the cloth—is thus perceived because a single entity, which consists of multiple potencies, depends upon both manifest and unmanifest potencies, and because everything has everything as its nature.
(Page 848, Line 1)
One's own state?
[It is] the cessation toward each subsequent state of all phenomena.
The entity that functions toward each subsequent entity,
such as earth and so forth, is primordial matter (prakṛti).
Is it precisely the collection [of atoms]?
Page 871, line 10.
"By this correspondence," and so forth.

By this, it is seen that form and the rest, as well as earth and the rest, are consistent in their nature because they are manifestations of a single reality that is the totality of all things; likewise, jars, cloths, and so on, are seen as mutual totalities. From this, the world—both sentient and insentient—is designated and proceeds. As was previously explained in the analysis of the *vidhi* (positive) method, therefore, even by means of reasons such as "establishment" (*saṃsiddhi*) and the like, it is proven that this [world] is merely the unfolding of a single reality consisting of both the sentient and the insentient.
In this [text], page 848, line 1: "the world is conscious" (cetanaṃ jagat). Ya.
Page 175.
Here it is said: "If [it were] the non-remainder of the causal complex," and so forth.

If the entirety of its own specific causal complex alone were the cause for the presence of everything everywhere—just as oil exists in sesame seeds, so too would oil exist in sand—then, just as there is an absence [of oil] in sand, there would likewise be an absolute absence [of oil] even in sesame seeds; however, this is not the case.

Therefore, it is not the case that the mere collection of causes [is sufficient] for the destruction of everything. As for the point that has been raised: "Just as oil is not perceived even though it exists unmanifestly in sesame seeds, so too oil is not perceived even though it is unmanifest in sand; this is because sand is transformed in such a way that, in the absence of sand, there is an absence of sesame, roots, and so forth."
In the same way, [it is] with respect to substances such as water...
because one always perceives the existence of another within oneself in that same way.

If it were thought that those [entities], being composed of the unity of all selves through causes such as perfect accomplishment (*saṃsiddhi*), are absolutely real, yet are considered non-existent because they are not perceived—
that too is not the case, for there is no such non-perception, since they consist of a single becoming just as if they were manifested;
therefore, that very [reality] is transcendent...
As it has been said:
"It moves, and it moves not; it is far, and it is near;
it is within all this, and it is outside of all this. (Śukla Yajurveda Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā 40.5)
To this it is replied: "Now, as for [the objection] beginning with 'yathā'..."

Who indeed says that there is no oil in sand, while it exists only in sesame seeds? However, just as even in sesame seeds, the oil—though unmanifest—is not perceived without the means for its manifestation, such as pressing with a machine and so forth, nor in the acts of chewing and the like; and just as it is not tasted like milk in sesame seeds that have been processed, nor in their states as roots, sprouts, and so on; likewise, oil is not perceived in sand because it is unmanifest there. For when a sesame seed is sown in a sandy region, through the production of sprouts, roots, leaves, and so forth, the sand itself undergoes such a transformation that oil exists in the sand, since in the absence of the sand, the root and other parts of the sesame plant would not exist. Just as oil exists in the sand, so too does oil exist in the substances mentioned in the *Samāsa-daṇḍaka*, such as water and others, according to the principle that "as long as a substance exists, another [quality] exists within it. This is the same for all things, because everything exists everywhere, both in manifest and unmanifest forms, even for a living substance (*jīva-dravya*) produced in the form of a sesame seed, which possesses oiliness. Thus, this principle is equal [for all].
...stained by the teeth...?
Because it is always perceived as "not being a non-x," there is indeed perception at all times, even though no other part of the entity is perceived.

Why? Because all things are established as a single reality whose nature is everything (*sarvātmaka*) through causes such as perfect accomplishment; and because it has been stated that the very opposites of prior and posterior, mutual [difference], spatial location, magnitude, capacity, and conjunction—which are considered absolute non-existences (*atyantābhāva*) down to the son of a barren woman—are in fact existent entities. Therefore, these objects are absolutely real. They might be imagined as "non-existent" only because they are not perceived due to a deficiency in the power of vision, or because other parts are invisible; yet they are not non-existent in the ultimate sense, nor is it the case that they are not seen. For even that "non-perception" does not exist. Why does it not exist? Because it has been established that the cause for the perception of the totality is the nature of a single becoming (*ekabhavanātmaka*). Since it is like that—having the nature of a single becoming just as it was established—and since it has the nature of a becoming whose entire self is established by the aforementioned logic, the distinct parts (the prior, middle, and subsequent portions) of an undivided reality, though imagined through a differentiation of powers, are in fact that very same reality because there is no difference in the substance. Since a part is perceptible, and because the other parts are not separate from it, the perception of one part is indeed the perception of all parts.
For it has been stated that the existent reality is indeed indivisible, and its perception as divided is an error;
therefore, the statement "that very [reality] has passed away" and so forth has already been explained.
Consequently, there is always only seeing, never non-seeing.
"Because one does not see that [other entity] as a different entity," *Bhāṣya*, p.
"Even though objects exist," so it should also be said here:
"the power of the perceiver..."

With the words "tapṛthaya evāti" and so forth, he states the previously mentioned principle as a supporting argument (*jñāpaka*).
The two verses beginning with "That moves, that moves not," etc., are not explained here as they have already been commented upon in that very [section].

However, he extends the application [of the principle] for the sake of recollection, stating the principle along with its divisions: "The Person alone is all this—that which has been and that which is to be;
moreover, He is the Lord of immortality, that which grows by food."
The Ṛgveda 10.8.90 is like that which possesses distinctions among objects and meanings whose various referents have been brought into being.

Furthermore, that which is difference is merely the conceit of difference where no difference actually exists, because that which is non-different manifests sequentially, just like the nature, form, and other qualities of a single substance. Thus, in the twelve spokes [of the wheel of viewpoints],

within the first six— the *dravyārthika-nayas*— such as the *vidhi* (affirmation) and others, the entire passage previously explained regarding how things are conceived according to worldly perception (*yathālokagrāha*) and so forth must be applied here as well.

Regarding the statement "those two verses" (*tannejati*, Praṇava-pṛṣṭha 192, line 3; Tippanī-pṛṣṭha 69, line 1), although it is said there that there are two verses—wherein "that moves" (*tadejati*) and so forth is the first verse—it is not clearly known which second verse is intended here. Nevertheless, it appears that what is intended here must be the *Puruṣasūkta*, beginning with "This whole world is indeed the Puruṣa" (*puruṣa evedaṃ sarvam*).
See page 189, line 5; page 192, line 3.
[The reading] *kārthya* in manuscript *ya* and *kyarthya* in manuscript *bhā*.

The Person alone is all this—that which has been and that which is to be; moreover, he is the Lord of immortality, of that which grows by means of food. (Ṛgveda 10.8.90) Like the distinction between the meanings of "to be cultivated" (*bhāvita*), "many," "object," "substance," and "purpose."

Furthermore, as for that which is difference, it is merely the conceit of difference where no difference actually exists; because that which is non-different is manifested sequentially, like the nature, form, and so forth of a single substance—
thus [ends] the section on the "Twelve Spokes," page 11, line 3.

Furthermore, as for the distinction such as "pot" or "cloth," that is merely a conceit of difference where no actual difference exists. Why? Because that undivided reality manifests sequentially; for the various powers of the potent one, being manifested in succession, appear as if they were distinct entities in relation to the power of the Puruṣa’s perception, but in the ultimate sense, no difference exists.

What is this like? It is like the nature of color and so forth belonging to a single substance (*ekadravyasvatattvarūpādivat*). Just as a single object called a "pot" comes to possess the designations of "color" and so forth according to the specific apprehensions of the eyes and other senses—such that what is grasped by the eye is "color," by the tongue "taste," by the nose "smell," by the ear "sound," and by the skin "touch"—so too, the distinction between a pot, a cloth, and so on, regarding that which is entirely non-different and one, is merely a conceptual construction (*abhimānamātra*).
Thus, first of all, the doctrine of emptiness (*śūnyavāda*) has been refuted by the substantialist doctrine of the self (*puruṣa*) and other substances, and so forth. (Bhāṣya)
The non-apprehension of the person (*puruṣa*),
which is the manifestation of difference— the meaning being the manifestation of differentiated objects— shines forth as accomplished; thus [it is said] in the *Dvayasampattivibhaṅga*.
"Return," thus [ends] the second chapter of the Bhāṣya; thus ends the section on the twelve spokes;
the Prajñāpāramitā is completed.
Oṃ Arhaṃ. Salutations to the true gurus.
Now begins the *Nayacakra-tumba*.
This too is not at all tenable as an absolute [position]; thus, what was previously introduced remains relevant.

Consequently, starting from the *vidhi-naya* (the perspective of affirmation) and proceeding through the sequence of various *vidhi-vidhi* perspectives up to the *dravya-kriyobhaya-naya* (the perspective of both substance and action), one determines the aspect of the substantial object (*dravyārtha*). Beyond that, by introducing the untenability of each successive absolute position regarding the distinctions of the modal aspect (*paryāyārtha*), the untenability of even the absolute position of the *śūnyavāda* (the doctrine of emptiness) is now introduced. Above those, however, the *vidhi* (affirmation) holds that reality is exactly as it is apprehended in the world.

The rule of injunction and restriction (*vidhiniyamavidhi*) is for the purpose of extracting the general and the particular by excluding that [other]; the method of both-and-both (*ubhayobhayanaya*) is for the purpose of negating that; such is the limit. Beyond this, the main body (*tumba*) of the *Nayacakra* will proceed.

Regarding the doubt as to whether that [doctrine] which maintains the absolute reality of the substantial (dravyārtha) is true or false, it is stated: "This too is not tenable as an absolute [position]," as has already been introduced. To the question "How so?", he says: "And therefore," and so forth. And therefore, starting from the perspective of the *vidhi-naya*—which consists of the synthesis of all things—and proceeding through the demonstration of the irrationality of each successive extreme, the matter has indeed been examined within those various sub-sections by way of the inquiry into alternatives such as: "Is the person (*puruṣa*) alone [the reality], or are the states (*avasthā*) alone the person? He thus reminds us of that: through the sequence of one *vidhi* after another, there is a successive establishment of the categories of Person, Necessity, Time, Nature, and Existence (*bhāva*), each subsequent one being established by the refutation of each preceding one. If it is asked: "Beyond that, what is the limit of the refutation of the substantialist position according to the sequence of the order of *vidhi-ubhaya* and so forth? It is said: As far as the *dravya-kriyobhaya-naya* (the standpoint of both substance and action) has been stated, so far the portion of the substantialist view has been determined; beyond that, there follows the division of the modal (paryāya) standpoint. And regarding those divisions of the modal standpoint, by proceeding through the demonstration of the irrationality of each successive extreme, one arrives at the doctrine of emptiness (*śūnyavāda*). Now, even the irrationality of the absolutism of that doctrine of emptiness is being introduced according to the system of the *vidhi-vidhi-naya*.
See *yukta* in the commentary on the end [of the verse],
page 246; the state does not exist in manuscript *ya*.
Successively higher,
successively higher, successively higher; such is the limit.
Regarding the refutation (*dūṣaṇa*):

when there is a refutation, the demonstration of their absolute irrationality is achieved by establishing the mutual connection of the one-sided doctrines (*ekāntavāda*). Having established this connection, one should observe the previously mentioned *vidhinaya* (the method of affirmation) applied to them—individually, in pairs, up to twelvefold, along with their subdivisions. The recollection of that [method] is as follows: the *vidhi* (affirmation) holds that "the object is exactly as it is grasped by worldly convention. By taking up the text beginning with "its arising" (*tadutthāna*) and so forth, there is an indication of the entire [system].
The twelfth [chapter], concerning the removal of the appearance of what is joined with the state of being joined, together with the light.
"Twelve spokes," "with affirmation" (*sapra*), "rule" (*vidhi*), "does not exist" (*nāsti ya*);

[this refers to] "that which is excluded by that," and so forth. Therefore, for the sake of extracting the conceptualized universal and particular that have been excluded by that rule-naya (*vidhinaya*), there is the "rule-and-restriction rule" (*vidhiniyamavidhi*). Then, for the sake of turning those away, there is the "both-both-naya" (*ubhayobhayanaya*). This sequence also continues until this [point] is the limit once again.
[The reading] "bhaya" is also found in the Bhāṣya;
[the reading] "mavidhi" is found in the Ya manuscript.

And just as there is a connection with the position of the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) regarding this doctrine of emptiness, so too is there a connection with the sixfold substantial meaning (dravyārtha).

Just as the *śūnyavāda* (the doctrine of emptiness) is related to those [other doctrines], so too may any of the twelve [doctrines], such as *vidhi* (prescription) and the rest, be related to it according to one's preference; for even the *śūnyavāda* can logically be related to whatever is interposed between them.
In this very way, its name *Nayacakra* (The Wheel of Perspectives) would be significant according to its literal meaning.
Thus, first of all, the emergence of all perspectives from this final one is not contradictory.
And just as it is from this [one], so it is from all [of them];

and just as by this [method]—namely, by the method of injunction (*vidhi-naya*) which asserts that [the opponent's position] is entirely untenable—there is a connection with the status of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣatva*) regarding the doctrine of emptiness (*śūnyavāda*), so too is there a connection for each of the sixfold substantial meanings (*dravyārtha*).

Regarding the phrase "And as by them," etc.: just as the connection of the doctrine of emptiness (*śūnyavāda*) occurs individually with each of the subdivisions of the substantialist standpoint (*dravyārthika*) according to the *vidhi-naya* (the method of affirmation), so too, even when the doctrine of emptiness has been refuted, there immediately follows a connection for all twelve spokes (*ara*)—such as affirmation (*vidhi*) and the rest—as desired. This is because it is logically possible for the doctrine of emptiness to be connected with any one of the other eleven spokes separated by an interval; for it is stated that "by any one" refers to those pervasive spokes, each of which is capable of establishing the nature of the world. Thus, the meaning is that there is no contradiction in a connection occurring through sequence, non-sequence, or both sequence and non-sequence—whether the subsequent spokes connect with the immediately preceding ones, or with those separated by one or more spokes, or whether the preceding spokes connect with the immediately following ones, or with those separated by one or more spokes. Therefore, because of this connection immediately following the exclusion of all entities, the sequence consists of the successive arising of each spoke from the one immediately preceding it, for the purpose of refuting each respective spoke.

In that sequence and through that connection, this entire *Nayacakra* treatise proceeds for the purpose of investigating all the factions of evil heretics and the systems of treatises composed by those with false views; for it demonstrates that all [other] viewpoints (*nayas*) are false views when they disregard the non-absolutism (*anekāntavāda*) that brings about the state of universal unity, since their respective fallacies have been demonstrated here and there, and because all these mutually contradictory positions—following the order of the stated arguments—are shown to be refutations of one another. Thus, by each such [viewpoint] according to its nature as a substantial standpoint (*dravyārthika-naya*), [the others are refuted]. As it is said in the *Tattvārthabhāṣya*: "Just as... [text fragment].
And likewise, if each single such substance were to exist as an object, just as these [are], and if they were to be connected with one another in this way,
then there would be an equality among the vehicles (*yāna*).
By means of the forward order (*krama*), the reverse order (*utkrama*), and both [orders], as well as by means of the forward order, the reverse order, and both [orders],
there is the turning back (*āvartanā*) of the letters beginning with *a* and *bh*.
The arising of the essence;
by the movement of which, the purpose;
the wheel.
Is it the state of being devoid of [defilements], or is it the one who is devoid of passion?
"Thus indeed," and so forth.

And by doing so, this treatise would bear the etymologically appropriate name *Nayacakra*, meaning a "wheel of viewpoints" or a "collection of viewpoints," because it is a collection (*samūha*) of viewpoints (*nayānām*) capable of establishing and refuting both one's own and others' doctrines.

"Viewpoints" (*nayāḥ*) are so called because they lead (*nayante*), that is, they bring about or convey (*prāpayanti*) objects; they consist in the exclusive adherence to one particular aspect of a reality (*vastu*) which possesses multiple natures. Their "wheel" (*cakram*) refers to these [viewpoints].
Thus, it is not contradictory that all systems arise from this final system of the doctrine of emptiness (*śūnyavāda*),
because of its circular nature (*cakratva*);
for this [final] system is the wheel of the first system.
The reading "nayānāṃ cakra" appears correct here; [the variant] "nayanti" does not exist for us, according to the Bhāṣya, nor does it contain dental [consonants], according to the Bhāṣya.

And just as from this [final] standpoint all [other standpoints] arise without contradiction, so too from all [standpoints]; for from every single standpoint, the arising of all standpoints is indeed non-contradictory, because if everything were in contradiction with everything else, dispute would necessarily exist.
Just as from that standpoint... [as previously stated].
In this context, the reading "yathā caitasmān nayāt" is also possible;
for all these methods of the entire teaching, the word of the Blessed Arhat is the foundation.

Of these, there are two root divisions: the method of substantial reality (*dravyārthika-naya*) and the method of modal reality (*paryāyārthika-naya*); their subdivisions are the *saṃgraha* and the others.
The word of the Jina is supportive of them, as follows: "O Venerable One!

Is this Jewel-Luster Earth (Ratnaprabhā-pṛthivī) eternal or non-eternal? O Gautama! In its substantiality (*dravyārthatayā*), it is eternal; in its modalities of color, odor, taste, touch, and shape (*saṃsthāna-paryāyaiḥ*), it is non-eternal. For what reason, O Venerable One, is it said that 'in its substantiality it is eternal, and in its modalities it is non-eternal'? O Gautama! Because of its substantiality it is eternal; because of the modalities of color, odor, taste, touch, and shape, it is non-eternal."
Jīvājīvābhigama-sūtra 3.1.78
Regarding the passage beginning with "of these" (*eṣām*):

if it is asked what is the basis (*nibandhana*) for all these perspectives (*nayāḥ*), it is said: of all these spokes that are the perspectives of the various teachings—wherein the various teachings themselves, such as the Jaiminīya and the Upaniṣads, are the spokes within the wheel of perspectives (*nayacakra*) whose hub is the *syādvāda*—the word of the Blessed Arhat is the underlying basis.
These are merely the waves of the great ocean of the Jina’s teaching.
And thus it has been explained in various places, as the teacher Siddhasena said—
Siddhasena said:

May there be well-being for the blessed word of the Jina, which consists of a collection of right views, which is like nectar, and which is easily accessible to those who are deeply moved and serene. (Sammatitarka 3.69) Thus [ends the citation from] the *Prajñapti*.

And for all these spokes of the teaching, the two fundamental divisions are, in brief, the substance-viewpoint (dravyārtha-naya) and the mode-viewpoint (paryāyārtha-naya); their subdivisions are the [seven] viewpoints beginning with the synthetic (saṃgraha). As it is said: "The substance-viewpoint and the mode-viewpoint are the primary instruments for the collection and specific expansion of the Tīrthaṅkara’s speech; all other conceptualizations are included within them.
(Sammatitarka 1.3)
From such explanations as these:

"The Tīrthaṅkara’s speech consists of the collection [of viewpoints], the specific [viewpoints], the progression, and the root; the substantial standpoint (*dravyārthika-naya*) and the modal standpoint (*paryāya-naya*) are its primary forms, while the remaining alternatives are their subdivisions. (Sammatitarka 1.3)

In this regard, six alternatives concerning the substantial entity (*dravyārtha*) have been stated here in brief, and six concerning the modal aspect (*paryāyārtha*); the word of the Jina encompasses them as follows: when asked, "Venerable Sir, is this Earth of Jewel-Luster (*Ratnaprabhā*) eternal or non-eternal? the response, according to a comprehensive declaration (*samagrādeśa*), is: "It may be eternal, and it may be non-eternal."
Furthermore, for what reason, O Blessed One, is it said: "It is eternal; it is non-eternal"? This is a question for the purpose of providing an explanation.

The answer is given through a partial designation (*vikalādeśa*), which establishes the essential nature of the Ratnaprabhā earth as being of a dual character by way of distinction, as follows: "In terms of substantiality (*dravyārthatayā*), it is eternal; in terms of modalities of color, odor, taste, touch, and shape (*varṇa-paryāyaiḥ, gandha-paryāyaiḥ, rasa-paryāyaiḥ, sparśa-paryāyaiḥ, saṃsthāna-paryāyaiḥ*), it is non-eternal. Thus it was stated in the Prajñāpanā.
Regarding "of those that are impermanent" (*asāsatām*),
see page 3, line 450;
the reading is *asāsatām*.
In this very manner, the following should be noted: in the passage from the *Jīvājīvābhigama-sūtra* cited within the *Nayacakra* on pages 3 and 450, the word "etaṃ" is not found;
therefore, in this context, the reading "bhaṃte evaṃ vuccati" alone appears to be correct.
The phrase *asāsatām iti* (in the Ya manuscript) and *asāsatāt iti* (in the Bhā manuscript) serve the purpose of providing an explanation.
...neither-nor...
(see page 3, line 16; page 450, line 10; page 451, note 1).

The central action is not the means for establishing the function that follows from that [central action]; rather, as it establishes the non-absolutist (anekānta) nature of the self-essence of that Jewel-Light—which possesses the intrinsic nature of both eternal and non-eternal phenomena—by means of the two causes, namely the substantial and modal viewpoints, each having six alternatives, the central action is indeed the means for establishing the function that follows from it.

For example: affirmation (vidhi), affirmation-affirmation (vidhi-vidhi), affirmation-affirmation-affirmation (vidhi-vidhi-vidhi), affirmation-affirmation-negation (vidhi-ubhaya), affirmation-negation (vidhi-niyama), negation-affirmation (ubhaya-vidhi), negation-affirmation-affirmation (ubhaya-ubhaya-vidhi), negation-affirmation-negation (ubhaya-ubhaya-niyama), negation-negation (niyama), negation-negation-affirmation (niyama-vidhi), negation-negation-affirmation-negation (niyama-ubhaya), and negation-negation-affirmation-negation (niyama-niyama)—these twelve modes function in mutual dependence within a single continuum as the true meaning. Sound, characterized by the non-absolutistic doctrine (syādvāda) determined by these modes, is "in some sense eternal," "in some sense both eternal and non-eternal," and "in some sense non-eternal"; for it consists of the manifold non-absolutistic alternatives of being uncreated, created, or both created and uncreated, as determined by the twelvefold divisions beginning with affirmation, just like a jar.

Through the following of the words of the Jina, there occurs this formation of the gourd-vessel (*tumbakriyā*)—the manifestation of the Syādvāda—for the twelve spokes (*arā*) which comprise the entirety of the complete teaching, because all the spokes remain bound to it; otherwise, they would fall apart. As it has been said:
"Because of its function of following that [gourd], it is the means of accomplishment.
(Sādhanabhāṣya / Sādhanaya)
The means of establishing the function that follows from that [substance] is not the activity of the center.

For example: affirmation (vidhi), affirmation-affirmation (vidhi-vidhi), affirmation-affirmation-affirmation (vidhi-vidhi-vidhi), affirmation-affirmation-negation (vidhyubhaya), affirmation-negation (vidhiniyama), negation-affirmation (ubhaya), negation-affirmation-affirmation (ubhayavidhi), negation-affirmation-negation (ubhayobhaya), negation-negation (ubhayaniyama), negation-negation-affirmation (niyama-vidhi), negation-negation-negation (niyamobhaya), and negation-negation-negation-negation (niyamaniyama)—these twelve modes, existing as a single continuous series, function in mutual dependence and possess real meaning. Sound, characterized by the non-absolutist doctrine (syādvāda) determined by these modes, may be eternal, may be both eternal and non-eternal, or may be non-eternal; for it consists of the manifold non-absolutist distinctions of being uncreated, created, uncreated-created, and so forth, as determined by the twelvefold alternatives beginning with affirmation, just like a jar.

"Whichever family is dependent [on you], protect that person with diligence"—this verse was seen by us in a manuscript copy of the *Āvaśyaka-niryukti* written by hand on palm leaves, located within the Khetaravasīpāḍā [monastery] in the city of Anahilapura; however, it is not found in the printed edition.

In the *Hāribhadrī-vṛtti* on the *Āvaśyaka-sūtra*, page 263, it is found as follows: And it says— "Lack of consideration for the meaning of the Sūtras, [neglecting] the teachers, the elders, the novices, and the sick..."
Whether he be a fool or patient, possessed of power or lacking power—
on account of these reasons, the teacher indeed becomes like a gourd.
Service should not be performed for him by the others;
rather, one should carefully protect that person upon whom the family depends, for when the vessel is destroyed, the medicinal juices do not remain.

When a teacher who possesses great power (*ṛddhimant*) arrives, there is a sense of insignificance regarding those who have come for drinks and the like; the same applies to a debater (*vādī*). Furthermore, there is public scandal (*janāpavāda*) that these [monks] are "unruly renunciants. The rest is clear.

However, in the commentary (*vṛtti*) on the *Āvaśyaka-sūtra* composed by Malayagiri, it is found as follows—and thus he says: "Non-reflection upon the meaning of the scriptures... (*suttatthesu aciṃtaṇa...*)
...3 [in the case of] one who has been instructed, a guest, an elder, a novice, one who is ill, as well as a child of tender age, and an ascetic...
...and he says this very thing: "One should protect with great care that man by whom the family is dependent;
for when the vessel is destroyed, the radish-stalks do not remain."

One should protect with care that man upon whom the family depends; for it is said in the commentary on the *Āvaśyakaniyukti* composed by Malaya-giri-sūri, in the description of the practice of the *icchākāra*, that "indeed, when the *tumba* (the main vessel) is destroyed, the *arakas* (the auxiliary vessels) do not remain as *sādhārakas* (supporting) or *sādhāras* (shared)."
"Guard [the vessel],
for when the vessel is destroyed, the medicinal herbs do not remain common property. Thus,
na hi bhā°.

For example—the sequence of means beginning with "prescription, prescription" (*vidhi-vidhi*) and so forth, up to the illustration "like a jar"—in this way, the construction of the *tumbaka* is the means for bringing together into a single statement the twelve-spoked wheel of reasoning (*dvādaśāra-naya-cakra*) along with its conceptualizations (*savikalpa*).

In that regard, there are four initial prescriptions (*vidhi-bhaṅga*), four intermediate dual prescriptions (*ubhaya-bhaṅga*), and four final restrictive prescriptions (*niyama-bhaṅga*); these correspond respectively to the four propositions of permanence (*nitya-pratijñā*), the four propositions of both permanence and impermanence (*nityānitya-pratijñā*), and the four propositions of impermanence (*anitya-pratijñā*).

The first tetrad of propositions (*bhaṅga*) consists of: affirmation of affirmation, affirmation of negation, affirmation of both affirmation and negation, and affirmation of negation; the middle [tetrad] consists of: both affirmation and negation, affirmation of both affirmation and negation, both affirmation and negation of both affirmation and negation, and negation of both affirmation and negation; and the final [tetrad] consists of: negation of negation, affirmation of negation, both affirmation and negation of negation, and negation of negation. These twelve [propositions], functioning through this single continuous sequence in mutual dependence, are true in their collective form—this is the thesis. "Sound" is characterized by the non-absolutist doctrine (*syādvāda*) determined by these propositions, such as: "Sound may be eternal, may be both eternal and non-eternal, and may be non-eternal. Its summary is that the reason (*hetu*) is also threefold, because it consists of the manifold non-absolutist alternatives of being unproduced, produced, or both produced and unproduced, as determined by the twelve-fold options starting with affirmation and so on. Like the thesis, this [reason] consists of a synthesis of the meanings of the propositions previously explained, because it is a single sentence formed from the various perspectives (*naya*) of those views, just like a jar. As for the proof showing the direction of this explanation, it is as follows: the unity of conventional usage (*vyavahāraikatā*)...
emptiness; sound is impermanent; [there is] the unity of conventional usage...

...because of its momentariness, emptiness, and being produced, like a jar; this is the example. Since it has already been explained that the meaning [of the doctrine] is established as consisting of the nature of various non-exclusive (anekānta) conceptualizations—such as the mutual dependence of all systems, the conformity with the consensus of all doctrines, and the inclusion of the eternal, the non-eternal, and the non-eternal, as well as the produced, the unproduced, and the produced-unproduced—the rule is a positive injunction, and the restriction is by means of a positive injunction. (Bhāṣya)
Whether it be "injunction and injunction-restriction" (*vidhi-niyama*),

or "injunction and restriction" (*vidhi-niyama*), or "injunction and injunction-restriction," or "restriction and restriction," or "injunction and restriction," or "restriction and restriction"— all these are to be understood by means of a single primary [category].
Is it "ekapradyadyena" (Bhāṣya) or "ekapraghaṭṭenā" (Vṛtti)?
See page 880, line 7.
The reading "tākṛtakakṛtakākṛtakatvāanekānta" in manuscript Y and "tākṛtakākṛtakatvāanekānta" in manuscript Bhā should be compared with page 878, line 4.
The means for demonstrating the direction of the commentary is as follows: the unity of worldly transaction (*vyavahāraikatā*)...
...emptiness; sound is impermanent; [due to] the oneness of conventional usage...
...because of being momentary, empty, and produced, like a jar; [this is] non-conclusive (anaikāntika) due to the state of being permanent, impermanent, and non-impermanent.
[This is] non-conclusive due to the state of being permanent, impermanent, and non-impermanent. Ya.

The proof for demonstrating the direction of the commentary on this—namely, the proof that establishes the non-unique nature (*anekāntatva*) of the activity of the hub (*nābhi*) mentioned immediately prior—is as follows: this proof serves the purpose of presenting the respective sequential arrangements of the meanings of the twelve spokes (*ara*) that have passed; for example, the presentation of the series of propositions (*daṇḍaka-pratijñā*) beginning with "the unity of conventional usage" and so forth, up to "sound is impermanent because of its emptiness."

The sequence of reasons begins with "because of the oneness of conventional designation" and continues as far as "because of being momentary, empty, and produced," as found in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* (reading:
*evaṃ syād abhāṣye hatyaikatve*).

Regarding the system of conventional truth (*vidhinaya*), the view is as follows: the object is exactly as it is grasped by the world; that is, just as it is accepted by the world through an uncritical acceptance of such categories as permanence and impermanence, cause and effect, unity and plurality—which are impossible to attain and devoid of purpose—it is the mere knowledge of the relationship between action and its fruit, which possesses attainability and purpose, and which is accessible through the impersonal, beginningless, and endless scripture (*āgama*).
This is seen, for example, [in the *Yogācārabhūmi*], see page 11, line 3.
Regarding the "action of the people" (*janatvakarma*):

since even the thorough knowledge of the sentences that enjoin rituals does not escape defects such as being impossible to attain or being purposeless, and because it is illogical—due to contradictions with one's own words and the like—that such knowledge is invariably concomitant with the knowledge of the true nature of reality, [the world] must consist of nothing but a single cause.

And that [single cause] is of the nature of either the Person (*puruṣa*), Time (*kāla*), Necessity (*niyati*), Intrinsic Nature (*svabhāva*), or Being (*bhāva*), since the distinction in conventional usage is merely a difference in states within a single division of the Self.

Since even that [system of] injunction (*vidhi*) necessarily involves the assumption of a distinction between the state (*avasthā*) and the possessor of the state (*avasthāvat*), and because it would entail the undesirable consequence of doctrines such as absolute emptiness (*paramaśūnya*) or momentariness (*kṣaṇika*), the dualistic doctrine—which posits existence as the exclusion of non-existence—is superior. This is because the activity of *prakṛti*, which consists of the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*—characterized by illumination, activity, and restraint—is directed toward the enjoyment of the indifferent experiencer (*puruṣa*). Thus, it is said that "injunction is enjoined and regulated" (*vidhir vidhīyate niyamyate ca*), which constitutes the system of the regulation of injunction (*vidhiniyamanayadarśana*). It is not the case that everything is of a single nature; rather, everything is of the nature of everything else (*sarvaṃ sarvātmakam*).
(The reading *vatabhedo* is supported by the manuscript *bhā.*)
...and the function of the state of proximity and attainment?
See page 261, line 15:
...the pride of this [system]...

Alternatively, this is another formulation of the view that reconciles both the injunctions and the dualistic systems: since the three *guṇas* cannot be established in either *prakṛti* or *puruṣa* individually—because they lack the nature of persistence, origination, and destruction, which would otherwise lead to their non-existence—there exists a duality of entities (*bhāvadvaita*) based on the distinction between the object of experience (*bhāvya*) and the experiencer (*bhavitṛ*). This duality consists of the Lord (*īśvara*) and the one to be ruled (*īśitavya*), arising from the twofold distinction between the independent presiding agent with specific cognition and the dependent object of his governance. (Note: The manuscript reading *īśvaresitadyātmakam* is corrected to *īśvareśitavyātmakam*.)
The reading here might also be "consisting of the two natures of the Lord and the Ruler."

Furthermore, if this primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and the person (*puruṣa*) were not to assume each other’s identities, there would be no connection between action and its fruit, and consequently, neither saṃsāra nor liberation would be possible. Moreover, since even the Lord (*īśvara*) acts under the influence of the actions of the persons he impels, he would lack true lordship. Because every single entity possesses both universality and lordship through the experience of mutual identity via transformation—since all persons are produced by action, actions are produced by persons, and the self itself is both cause and effect of the self—it follows that "the one is all and all is one. Thus, because of being subject to injunctions and constraints, this is the "Vision of the Regulation of Injunctions" (*vidhiniyamanayadarśana*).
This reading is not present in the manuscripts Ya,

According to the *Vyavahāranaya* (*vyamena*), because these four [categories] possess substantiality (*dravyārthatva*), there is an absolute [view] of being uncreated and eternal.

Since it is untenable for either the agent (*bhavitṛ*) or the process of becoming (*bhavana*)—that is, substance (*dravya*) or activity (*kriyā*)—to be primary or subordinate, as that would lead to their non-existence, both injunction (*vidhi*) and restriction (*niyama*) are indeed primary, consisting in the apprehension of both substance and state (*bhāva*); such is the perspective of the *Ubhayanaya*.

In this view as well, if substance (*dravya*) and mode (*bhāva*) were independent and mutually exclusive, their states of persistence, origination, and destruction would be untenable, and they would be non-existent like a flower in the sky.

Therefore, that which is called individual manifestation (*vyakti*) and generic form (*ākṛti*)—namely, substance and so forth—is existent through the relationship of subordinate and primary qualities both from the perspective of another (*parataḥ*) and from its own perspective (*svataḥ*); likewise, existence (*sattā*) and so forth are non-existent from its own perspective but existent from the perspective of another. Thus, these two rules—the rule of affirmation (*vidhi*) and the rule of restriction (*niyama*)—are established; such is the doctrine of the *vidhiniyamavidhinaya*. (From *Nayamārtaṇḍa*, Chapter 6).

Furthermore, for this system which desires the arising of the non-existent, since there is no connection between an existent, a non-existent, or both existent and non-existent things—whether with another existent, a non-existent, or both existent and non-existent—and because it lacks the capacity to produce existence, the arising of the non-existent is illogical. Thus, the view of both perspectives [the universal and the particular] is that a thing, characterized by mutual non-existence in the form of activity and cessation, "becomes" while "not becoming.
(Note: The repetition of *satkaratvābhāvāt* and the corruption *pravṛttirūpa* in the source text are corrected here based on the logical context.)
"Because it becomes, it is existence" (vistv iti); "because it has become, it is existence" (stvit iti).

Since even for this view that [existence] is the negation of another, there is no stability due to the impossibility of specific characteristics of its own nature, and because both [views] are untenable due to defects such as the confusion of non-existence and so forth, the doctrine of the dual regulation is that the agent of becoming (*bhavitṛ*) is primary and the act of becoming (*bhavana*) is secondary.

And among these four types— namely, the *bhāvamata*, the *abhāvamata*, and those two [the former] which consist of both kinds, such as the "produced" and "unproduced" or the "impermanent" and "permanent"— there is the four-membered syllogism based on the production and non-production, or the impermanence and permanence, which is a variation in the explanation of the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the reason (*hetu*).

In this system as well, when difference is primary, there is an absence of continuity because [continuity] is subordinate; and since difference is also inseparable from that [continuity], it too is absent—like the flower of a celestial udumbara tree. Because the various alternatives regarding the predominance or subordination of either the universal or the particular are faced with absolute non-existence, the doctrine of the Niyama-naya is that the state of being "inexpressible" (avaktavyatā)—the non-existence of both identity and difference, like fire and fuel—is superior.

*nyā'nvayā* (bhā॰) *°dagvītvana* (ya॰) (Note: The text provided contains scribal variants for the commentary portion: *nyā'nvayā* appears in the Bhāṣya manuscript, while *°dagvītvana* appears in the Ya manuscript.)

Even this [position]—that "it is inexpressible"—is held [to be untenable], because it does not transcend the state of being expressible, and because it results in a contradiction with one's own words and so forth for one who asserts that the true nature of things is undetermined. Furthermore, there is a restriction [imposed] by one's own words against the following: that a thing is merely a collection of particulars distinct from a location absolutely separate from form, taste, and so on. This is a positive injunction (*vidhi*) [of the restriction]. *Note: The text contains several scribal errors (e.g., *dadhītvana*, *svavāgniro*). The translation reflects the intended philosophical argument as best as can be reconstructed from the context.*

This [view] that "the locus is secluded" (*viviktadeśa*) and "having given" (*pradāya*) is also an unsound doctrine of the *nayā*. For if the exclusion of substance (*dravya*) and mode (*bhāva*) is asserted, what indeed could be called the state of non-difference (*abhedabhāva*) among the constituents of the aggregate? Since conventional constituents lack a nature distinct from arising and perishing, they would result in non-existence; for a thing (*vastu*), by definition, consists of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) that is moment-by-moment absolutely different, characterized by form and so forth, and is inexpressible. Thus, the doctrine of the two *nayās* regarding restriction (*niyama*) is established and regulated.
In wisdom,
there is the state of the destruction of the treasury;
in conventional reality, it is destroyed.

Regarding the [view that things exist] conventionally (*saṃvṛtisat*), this system of logic is also incorrect. For in the etymological derivation of the word *kṣaṇika* (momentary)—as in "that which has a moment (*kṣaṇa*) is momentary"—the suffix *-ṭhan* and the meaning of the genitive case imply a state of coexistence; since such coexistence is untenable, and because [the object] would be a non-existent ultimate reality, it fails due to reasons such as non-establishment (*asiddhi*). Thus, for these four [positions], such as the restrictive rule (*niyama*), the non-restrictive rule (*aniyama*), and the injunction (*vidhi*), there is the conceptual analysis of the reason and the thesis: "because it is produced, it is impermanent. In all cases, the example is "like a jar," which illustrates the meaning already explained.
This single application of the means of proof has been presented by way of summarizing all the topics along with a demonstration of the general direction of the explanation;
this same method applies to all individual sub-divisions as well.

It may be one; it may be both one and many; it may be many; it may be the cause; it may be both cause and effect; it may be the effect; it may be all-pervading; it may be both all-pervading and non-all-pervading; it may be non-all-pervading—because its nature consists of affirmation, negation, and the restriction of both, and because it possesses the twelvefold character of affirmation and so forth, just like a jar. This has already been demonstrated by this *Nayacakra* treatise. And thus, the teaching of the Jina is exclusively true, because its meaning is firmly established through the application of correct and complete proof, [and] because of the nature of its existent and non-existent objects...

"...so too in all distinctions. He extends [this principle] by indicating that it should be applied in the same way to all distinctions of entities, such as single and multiple causes and effects, the omnipresent and non-omnipresent, universals and particulars, subjects and attributes, and so forth. To illustrate this, he states four sets of four alternatives by grouping the twelve alternatives into three groups, beginning with "It may be one," and so on, in that very same sequence.

In that regard, "it may be one" comprises four alternatives condensed into a single position; "it may be one and many" comprises both types of alternatives; and "it may be many" comprises the restrictive alternatives. Likewise, "it may be the cause," "it may be both cause and effect," and "it may be the effect alone";
similarly, "it may be all-pervading," "it may be both all-pervading and non-all-pervading," and "it may be non-all-pervading alone."

Thus, having separately formulated and asserted twelvefold alternatives for each of the following—namely, eternal, single, cause, omnipresent, both, non-eternal, manifold, effect, and non-omnipresent—the reason (*hetu*) is also stated concisely in the same manner: "because of being of the nature of affirmation, affirmation-and-negation, negation, and negation-and-affirmation."

By the mention of *vidhi* (injunction), the four alternatives of injunction are included; by the mention of both *vidhi* and *niyama* (restriction), the alternatives of both are included; and by the mention of *niyama*, the four alternatives of restriction are included—this being due to the grammatical analysis (*vigraha*) as "injunction, and injunction-restriction, and restriction" (*vidhi-vidhiniyama-niyamāḥ*). To clarify this, he says: "because it consists of twelve forms beginning with injunction. The example is "like a jar. The phrase "it has already been explained" refers back to what was previously stated in this very *Nayacakra* treatise, which consists of an extensive exposition of the twelve *nayas*; this is the *tantrayukti* known as *atideśa* (extended application), according to the definition: "extended application is the proof of the subject at hand by means of what has passed [before]."

For a jar consists of a collection of twelve modes of being, such as existence and so forth; in the absence of any one of these, it does not exist, but exists only through mutual dependence. This has been explained at length [in the *Prakaraṇa*], beginning with "In that regard, it may be one," and so forth, following that very sequence. Here, the reading "syāt eka" appears twice in the manuscripts.
Having separately grasped and asserted the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) as being divided into twelve distinct types— this reading should also be considered here—
the [resulting] non-prescriptive rules (*avidhi-niyama*).
And thus, etc.:

when the unity of the text (*ekavākyatā*)—established by the non-dual doctrine (*advaita*) which serves as the hub and foundation for the various treatises such as the *Nayacakra* ending with the *Dvādaśāraśāstra*, as taught in the *Samāptanayacakraśāstra*—and the full extent of the activity of all the scriptures has been set forth in this manner, then that which was asserted by implication (*arthāpatti*) at the outset of the treatise—that the truth of the Jaina teaching is established because it consists of the single essence of the functions beginning with injunction (*vidhi*)—is proven.
