And having summarized that means of proof, this is the formulation: the thesis is that "the teaching of the Jina is exclusively true"; the reason is "because its subject matter is firmly established through the application of correct and well-ascertained proof."

Proper establishment (*samīcīna-samprasiddhi*) is correct establishment (*samyak-samprasiddhi*); it is the realization of the true nature of reality through a mode of operation that does not abandon the mutual relationship between general and particular conceptualizations. This correct establishment is the basis of connection (*upanibandhana*), which is non-contradictory with the conventional usage established by perception, inference, scripture, and worldly consensus. That teaching of the Jina, whose subject matter is firmly established by means of such a basis of connection, is "that whose meaning is established by a basis of correct establishment. Because of that state, it is indeed exclusively true.

The illustration begins with "the existent and non-existent object," and so forth: a treatise consisting of a rigidly one-sided doctrine regarding what is both existent and non-existent has its meaning shattered, because its ultimate purpose is the interruption of the subject matter under discussion, like the sentence "ten pomegranates" (*daśa dāḍimāni*).
This point has indeed been demonstrated by the entire preceding cycle of scriptures on the various philosophical systems (*nayacakra*).

The referent (*artha*) of a word such as "jar" or "exists," which comprises many internal divisions and is of a manifold nature (*anekāntātmaka*), is established through a continuous stream of non-deviant means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—such as perception and inference—by way of the correspondence between the means of knowledge and their objects, and the reality of the expression and the resulting cognition. Thus, the various referents denoted by nouns like "jar" and by verbs like "exists," as set forth in the treatise *Nayacakra*, serve as natural illustrations (*sāṃsiddhikanidarśana*), similar to the meaning of sentences that are either established instructions or occasional utterances.

Since it has its object in the manifold reality of existence and so forth, truthfulness is inseparable from being a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); this has already been clarified because the meaning is firmly established by the application of the well-proven method of exposition.
Thus, the demonstration of the path for stating the proofs that establish one's own position has been completed as the conclusion of the treatise’s subject matter; this is now understood.

The venerable [author] says: "A treatise consisting of any one of these extreme positions, however, has its purpose frustrated, because its ultimate aim is the interruption of the subject matter at hand, like the sentence 'ten pomegranates' and so forth.
This point has indeed been demonstrated by the entire body of scriptures concerning the cycle of all previous *nayās*."
The object of cognition (prameya), the truth (satyatva), valid cognition (pramāṇa), and the words of a reliable person (āptavākya).

Even this demonstration of the direction for stating proofs capable of dispelling the opposing position is performed as a conclusion to the meaning of the treatise—for any composition of a treatise based on one-sided extremes is of ruined purpose.

The meaning of the term *pakṣa* (position) is as follows: these aforementioned systems of doctrine, such as the method of injunction (*vidhi*) and so forth—which possess mutually distinct approaches, have been presented here by synthesizing the views of all scriptures, and which do not transcend the duality of substance and modification (*dravyārtha-paryāyārtha*) through the two categories of existence and non-existence—the composition of any one-sided scripture among them, transmitted through a succession of persons and a lineage of unbroken tradition, such as "only existent," "only non-existent," "only eternal," or "only non-eternal," has its meaning rendered inconsistent [by the other systems]. This is the sense of the term *pakṣa*.

The statement of the *Śāstra* (the treatise) is indeed subject to refutation by the Sāṅkhyas and others; however, this is for the purpose of setting it aside as a mere example, distinct from worldly usage such as "pot" or "exists," so that there may be no confusion between the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the thing illustrated (*dārṣṭāntika*). The reason is that [otherwise] there would be a lack of ultimate purpose due to the interruption of the subject matter under discussion. The subject matter under discussion consists of the determination of the means and the end, and the establishment of the relationship between the goal—namely, liberation from suffering—and its realization through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). An interruption of this subject matter constitutes a contradiction, an obstacle, a deviation, or a failure to carry it through to completion, like a man who sets out with the intent to seize a lotus in a great lake but sinks into the mud before reaching it.

That which is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) of either one of these two—the doctrines of substantiality (*dravya*) or modality (*paryāya*)—is an ultimate reality that severs the subject matter at hand; it is a cause for the subversion of what one intends. Because of its existence—that is, because it is an ultimate reality that severs the subject matter at hand—it has its purpose frustrated.

Like what? Like the sentence "ten pomegranates" (*daśa dāḍimāni*), etc. Just as this [sentence] has its parts' meanings disconnected because it fails to achieve the status of a single coherent statement—its meaning being shattered because its ultimate purpose is the interruption of the subject matter under discussion—in the same way, a treatise (*śāstra-prabandha*) that maintains an absolute alternative (*ekānta-vikalpa*) regarding either the substantial aspect (*dravyārtha*) or the modal aspect (*paryāyārtha*) has its meaning shattered. This point has already been demonstrated by the entire preceding treatise on the wheel of all viewpoints (*naya-cakra*). Thus, by means of this entire section of the text, the following has been stated: Because it lacks the operation of the modes of affirmation (*vidhi*), negation (*niyama*), and their combinations (*bhaṅga*), any teaching other than the Jaina is false, like meaningless speech; whereas the Jaina teaching alone is true, because it consists of the operation of affirmation, negation, and their combinations, like the word "existent" (*bhavati*) or like a "pot" (*ghaṭa*). Alternatively, a single proof (*sādhana*) is capable, through both similarity (*sādharmya*) and dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), of refuting all proponents of absolute views (*sarva-ekāntavādin*) and establishing the position of the proponent of non-absolutism (*anekāntavādin*). Thus, it has been explained according to the initial proposition.
Indeed, [it is] by means of the employment of the very objects to be corrupted;
in reality, [it is] by means of the primary [cause].
Just as that very accomplishment [is obtained] from the person, so too is that [result] produced.
Let it be seen in the *Sūtrakṛtāṅga*, in the second Śrutaskandha, in the first chapter, the Puṇḍarīka;

And thus, the statement regarding "functioning" (*vṛtti*) is intended to demonstrate that even within each individual standpoint (*bhaṅga*), there is functioning, precisely when all standpoints form a single syntactical unity.

The sole functioning, which consists of all the standpoints and standpoints-within-standpoints bound together by the essence of the *syādvāda*, is the truth—like a string of jewels (*ratnāvalī*). Otherwise, there would be no functioning at all, and likewise, the entire process of absolute monism (*ekānta*) would be untenable.

By the very activity of establishing the truth of the Jaina [doctrine] as having a single mode that consists of all perspectives (*sarvanayātmaka*), it is established through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) that all other teachings are incorrect; for if the individual perspectives such as *vidhi* (injunction) and so forth exist in a state of unity, then everything exists, whereas if even one is absent, everything is absent—just as when one speaks of "rain," "the name," or "the rising of the cloud," the meaning of the other components is invariably implied. To explain: this is precisely the intended meaning of the formal argument (*prayoga*). If it is asked, "How can both of these be obtained from a single [term]? it is said: "From the statement regarding its mode (*vṛtti*)."

To explain the cultivation of that [insight], he says: "And having established this, because it is distinct from the breaking of rules and observances,"—this statement regarding the *vṛtti* (mode of conduct) is for the purpose of explaining that even within each individual *bhaṅga* (section), there is a *vṛtti*, provided that all the *bhaṅgas* form a single syntactical unity.

What is meant by this? There is only one true mode of operation (*vṛtti*), which consists of all the various standpoints (*nayabhaṅga*) bound together by the *syādvāda* (the doctrine of manifoldness), just like a string of jewels (*ratnāvalī*). Just as a single "string of jewels" is so called because it is a collection of many gems endowed with a multitude of qualities—such as specific genus, color, luster, essence, purity, brilliance, value, and shape—and not each individual gem separately when placed in its proper position, so too the absolute standpoints (*ekāntanaya*) such as *vidhi* (prescription) and others have their mode of operation bound by *syādvāda*, like the beads on a string. Otherwise, there would be no mode of operation at all. Furthermore, due to the similarity with the example of the wheel (*cakradṛṣṭānta*), and because the title of the treatise *Nayacakra* is indeed literal, there is no need to provide other examples; the same applies to the progression of all absolute positions. Thus, having established this, it follows that all absolute standpoints (*ekāntanaya*) are simply non-existent because they lack validity, as has been demonstrated in various places throughout the work.

And this demonstration of the invalidity of all other teachings is accomplished through *arthāpatti* (presumption) by the very act of establishing the truth of the Jaina doctrine—which consists of the single function that embodies all viewpoints (*sarvanayātmakaikavṛtti*). By demonstrating that invalidity, the demonstration of the truth of the Jaina doctrine is likewise accomplished, because of their mutual inseparability (*anyonyāvinābhāva*). This is because the two meanings—the proof of the truth of the Jaina teaching and the proof of the falsity of other teachings—are established through the presentation of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) via examples of similarity and dissimilarity (*sādharmya-vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*). Thus, since all [viewpoints] exist when one exists—due to the presence of the modes such as injunction (*vidhi*) and so forth—and since all cease to exist in the absence of one, they are mutually dependent.
In this context, it appears correct [to read] "for the purpose of making known the mode of existence" (vṛtti),
rather than "by the very arising" (pra-bhava) or "by the very activity" (pra-vṛtti).
The similarity and dissimilarity of the means of proof [are established] by means of two examples;
the similarity of the means of proof [is established] by means of two examples,
because of the existence of all things as being essentially one with existence.

Regarding the reading *ya* [in the phrase] *°bhāvekasarvabhāvāt*, it appears that either *°bhāve sarvabhāvāt* or *°bhāve vā sarvabhāvāt* is the correct reading. How so? It is like the expression "the rising of clouds called rain," and so forth.

Just as rain is impossible without the rising of clouds, and is thus said to be invariably concomitant (*avinābhāva*), so too, when even one [of the standpoints] such as *vidhi* (affirmation) is stated, the remaining standpoints are also effectively stated because of their mutual inseparability; for in the proposition (*pratijñā*) and other members, the meanings of the other alternatives are non-deviant. Just as when there is a single proposition of "eternal," the propositions of "non-eternal," "both," "inexpressible," and so forth, necessarily follow, so too, because the meanings of the reasons (*hetu*)—which are the properties proving that [proposition]—and the examples (*dṛṣṭānta*) of similarity and dissimilarity which demonstrate their positive and negative concomitance are non-deviant from the meaning, the expression of all twelve [standpoints] is already accomplished by implication. Therefore, it follows that when even a single standpoint is intended to be expressed, since the remaining standpoints are invariably concomitant, the method of proving non-absolutism (*anekānta*) qualified by the word "syāt" and so forth is indeed superior. To this he says: "For instance—this very purpose of the formal argument (*prayoga*) is what we have summarized and stated as the condensed meaning of the treatise, namely 'affirmation, affirmation-and-negation,' etc.; and this reason (*hetu*) is indeed one alone."
And even when only one [of the means] is employed, because of its capacity and because all [the others] are possible, the methods of application occur in relation to whichever means [is chosen].

Among these, there are twelve permutations (bhaṅga) for the combination of each single [factor], sixty-six for the combination of two, two hundred and twenty for the combination of three, four hundred and ninety-five for the combination of four, seven hundred and ninety-two for the combination of five, nine hundred and twenty-four for the combination of six, seven hundred and ninety-two for the combination of seven, four hundred and ninety-five for the combination of eight, two hundred and twenty for the combination of nine, sixty-six for the combination of ten, twelve for the combination of eleven, and exactly one for the combination of twelve.

for each of these, there are likewise four thousand nine hundred and five reasons (*hetu*).
Consequently, the total number of logical permutations (*bhaṅga*) is one hundred and sixty-seven million, sixty-nine thousand, and twenty-five (167,690,025).
Thus, this direction of the doctrine of non-absolutism (anekāntavāda) has been demonstrated;

and this reason is differentiated according to the intention of each individual standpoint (*naya*), because even when any one [standpoint] is employed, everything is possible through its inherent capacity. In that regard, within any given proof concerning any one of the positions such as permanence or impermanence, there are methods of employment—namely, the alternatives (*vikalpa*) or "modes" (*bhaṅga*).
When these twelve modes are combined one by one, there are twelve modes.

In the combination of pairs (*dvikayoga*), there are sixty-six [variations]: *vidhi* (affirmation) and *vidhividhi* (affirmation-affirmation) together constitute one variation; in this manner, *vidhi* is to be joined with each of the eleven [remaining categories]. Likewise for *vidhividhi*, and likewise for *vidhividhiniyama* (affirmation-affirmation-negation), as well as *vidhiniyama* (affirmation-negation).
Thus, through the combination of pairs among all eight remaining variations, there are sixty-six.

By this very method of combination, the Teacher himself has stated the rule for variations starting from "two hundred and twenty" in the case of triple combinations (*trikasaṃyoga*), up to the point where there is only one [variation] in the case of twelve.
Thus, by way of this comprehensive summary, there are four thousand nine hundred and five such propositions (*pratijñā*).
For each one of these, there are likewise four thousand nine hundred and five variations based on the reasons (*hetu*).
And for every single reason, there are that same number of propositions as well, because all the modes of reasoning (*nayabhaṅga*) have been stated through their mutual inseparability.

And so forth; the refutations of the propositions and the refutations of the reasons, when multiplied by one another, result in one hundred sixty-seven million, sixty-nine thousand, and twenty-five refutations.
Thus, without any doubt, this very reason [is established] in any given proof.
And even when only one [of the means] is employed, because of its capacity and because all [the others] are possible, the methods of application occur in relation to whichever means [is chosen].

Among these, there are twelve permutations for the combination of each single factor, sixty-six for the combination of two factors, two hundred and twenty for the combination of three factors, four hundred and ninety-five for the combination of four factors, seven hundred and ninety-two for the combination of five factors, nine hundred and twenty-four for the combination of six factors, seven hundred and ninety-two for the combination of seven factors, four hundred and ninety-five for the combination of eight factors, two hundred and twenty for the combination of nine factors, sixty-six for the combination of ten factors, twelve for the combination of eleven factors, and exactly one for the combination of twelve factors.

For each one of these, there are likewise four thousand nine hundred and five reasons (*hetu*).
Consequently, the total number of logical permutations (*bhaṅga*) is one crore, sixty-seven lakhs, sixty-nine thousand, and twenty-five—1,67,69,025.
Thus, this direction of the doctrine of non-absolutism (anekāntavāda) has been demonstrated; it consists of sixty-six times six [categories],
as well as injunction and restriction.

Thus, the divisions of the twelve-fold dialectical positions (*bhaṅga*) regarding propositions such as "eternal" and so forth have been stated.

In the same way, the divisions of the twelve-fold positions beginning with affirmation (*vidhi*) should be applied individually to propositions such as "the cause is all-pervading," "unitary," and so on.

In this manner, the direction of the doctrine of non-absolutism (*anekāntavāda*) has been shown; who indeed could be capable of calculating the number of this Blessed One’s great ocean of the Syādvāda, which possesses infinite waves of logical perspectives (*nayāḥ*) and whose further shore is difficult to reach?
However, when this direction has been shown by the wise one following that path, the remainder should be understood accordingly;

In this context, there may also be the reading "digupaprada" (bestowing the directions). And thus, there is nothing whatsoever that is not a reason (*hetu*); even grass and such things become a reason for some proposition or other, because everything consists of the nature of all things due to the transformation of the meaning of all substances and modes.

However, he who does not know such a means of proof (sādhana) does not truly know any object whatsoever, because he grasps only a mere portion of it, and because he determines that which is undeterminable—just like one who perceives the true nature of a palāśa tree as being restricted merely to its bark being marked by glowing embers.

When non-absolutism (*anekānta*) is thus correctly observed, there is nothing that is not a reason for a proponent of non-absolutism (*anekāntavādin*). Even something as trivial as a blade of grass becomes a reason for any proposition such as "sound is impermanent," and it is not the case that it is not a reason. Why? Because everything consists of the nature of all things, and there is a reciprocal transformation of all substances (*dravya*) and modes (*paryāya*). Every single substantial aspect (*dravyārtha*) transforms into the nature of every other substance and into the nature of every mode; likewise, every modal aspect (*paryāyārtha*) transforms into the nature of every substance and every mode.

In those various systems of logic, which are skilled in establishing the determination of objects, it has been demonstrated in detail that every single entity consists of the conceptualization of all substances (*dravya*) and modes (*paryāya*).
Therefore, everything is of one nature, and the one is of the nature of all; everything is of the nature of everything, and so forth.
For this very reason, he who knows the one knows all, and he who knows all knows the one.
As it has been said: "He who knows one, knows all; he who knows all, knows one" (Ācārāṅga Sūtra 1.2.6.3). Likewise: "By means of a single cause, [the nature of] grass and so forth... (Avibhāga).
"He who knows one, knows all; he who knows all, knows one" (Ācārāṅga Sūtra 1.2.6.3).
One entity is the intrinsic nature of all entities; all entities have the intrinsic nature of the one entity.
He by whom one entity is seen in its true reality has, by that very fact, seen all entities in their true reality. Thus it is said.

For the proponents of *syādvāda*, because they know all things as having the nature of a single reality, and because they know all things as having the nature of a single reality, any object whatsoever—even a blade of grass—can indeed serve as a logical reason for any given proposition; thus it has been well said.

As for the argument beginning with "by whom such [a proof]... and so forth, it either merely demonstrates the dissimilarity from the truth of *syādvāda*, or it is a proof intended to render fruitless the efforts of the opponent's discourse.

A person who is devoid of the knowledge of reality—which is of a manifold nature (anekāntātmaka) and accessible through such a doctrine of non-absolutism (syādvāda)—is not a knower of the true nature of even a single part of any entity, because he grasps only one portion of it. This is because his intellect is biased toward [asserting] that an entity, which consists of infinite attributes such as permanence and impermanence, is either "only permanent" or "only impermanent," and so forth. He explains this very point: because he is a determiner of that which is indeterminate; that is, because he acts as a determiner regarding that which is unfit for determination such as "this alone" or "exactly thus."

What is it like? It is like one who grasps the true nature of a *palāśa* tree as being restricted solely to its bark being covered in charcoal. For example, suppose someone, regarding a *maitra* tree whose leaves, fruits, and foliage have all fallen away at a particular time, were to say: "These trees are always devoid of leaves, flowers, fruit, and shade," or even during the month of Caitra, seeing an *aśoka* tree with blossoms resembling charcoal—as if surrounded by the garlands of flames from a forest fire—and causing fear to the herds of deer, he might say: "This tree is red at all times."

Because he perceives the true nature of the *palāśa* tree as restricted solely to its specific time and place—something perceivable even by cowherd women whose wisdom extends only two finger-breadths—he, the Blessed One, the Arhat, possesses unobstructed knowledge regarding all that is called "this" [the world], since he is the perfect expounder of its various distinctions as they truly are; just as a friend [is aware] of the true nature of the *palāśa* tree through its various stages, such as being covered in bark or glowing with embers.

Because it lacks the wisdom that extends over a long period of time, it does not know from its own essential nature the various states such as sprout, leaf, flower, and fruit; because its knowledge is diminished by grasping only one particular state among them, the proponents of extremist views (ekāntavādins) likewise lack knowledge of the true nature of reality—just as one who looks at a palāśa tree [and perceives only one part] [is ignorant of the whole].
*sakalapalāśaṃ tamavalokyaya kāntākuru pra*.

The Blessed One, the Arhat, possesses unobstructed knowledge regarding all that is called "name," because he is the perfect expounder of its distinctions as they truly are. Just as a friend [discerns] the true nature of a leaf through its various states such as being covered by bark or scorched by embers, so too the Blessed One, the Arhat, possesses *kevalajñāna* (absolute knowledge)—which is unobstructed, causeless, and unimpeded with respect to the simultaneous transformation of infinite substances and modes—without depending on other causes such as the eye, signs, or words.
Indeed, whatever entities he transforms through natural evolution (*visrasā*) or volitional application (*prayoga*), [he knows them all].
The Arhat understands each of those things in that way; for knowledge does not exist without a sequential process (*aparyaya*).

Because his knowledge functions unimpededly toward all objects and because its scope is not restricted, and because that reality is infinite, he alone perceives the true nature of that reality through a knowledge that functions simultaneously toward infinite objects, and no one else. And since he is none other than the Arhat, it is said: "But the Blessed One, the Arhat, possesses unobscured knowledge regarding all this—meaning that his knowledge is unobscured and unimpeded with respect to every object designated as 'all'."

Because he is the correct expounder of that reality as it truly is in its various divisions—since the word *yathā* has a distributive sense (*vīpsā*), "whatever has become real" (*yad yad bhūtam*) refers to that reality exactly as it is; and since the term "all" (*sarva*) encompasses the infinite varieties and subdivisions consisting of the detailed expansion of specific distinctions, such as being with divisions, having opposites, being eternal, having causes, being one, or being all-pervading—that reality, along with all its infinite parts and divisions, is described through the manifold conceptualizations of the *nayas* within the *syādvāda*. Therefore, his status as the correct expounder of the object of every single division and part of the reality called "all" is established, because *syādvāda* consists of the totality of all *nayas*. Whoever possesses the quality of being a correct expounder of an object that is real in its entirety, including all its parts and divisions, is observed to possess unobstructed knowledge (*nirāvaraṇajñāna*) regarding that object. For example: Maitraka, by specifically describing a *palāśa* tree—which possesses its own true nature through divisions such as being covered in buds—and which is distinguished by place, time, form, and measure as it assumes various states during the seasons of winter, spring, summer, the rains, autumn, and early winter, saying, "This *palāśa* is merely a bud," or "it is budding," or "it has sprouted leaves," and so on, is well known to be one who possesses unobstructed knowledge regarding the *palāśa* in all its parts and divisions. This is not the case for another, such as a Maurya prince born and raised in the middle of Revatīdvīpa who has never seen other lands and speaks otherwise, or a foolish boy who describes only a single state. In the same way, let the Arhat be inferred to possess unobstructed knowledge regarding the reality that is real in its entirety, including all its parts and divisions, as he speaks of it without remainder.

In this regard, because the reason is pervaded by the state of unobscured knowledge (*nirāvaraṇajñāna*) and because it establishes the intended property (*sādhya*), this proof is free from defects such as contradiction (*viruddha*). Furthermore, since everything has been established as a reason for everything through the conventional designation of reasons, the undesirable consequence that the Teacher—who is occupied with delivering the instructions of the Arhat—would be a "non-dual omniscient one" (in a sense other than our own) does not arise; for even the inferer possesses knowledge of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all things.

If it is argued that for the proponent of *syādvāda* there would follow the collapse of logical convention (*nyāyavyavahāra*) due to the collapse of the established distinction between similar instances (*sapakṣa*), dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*), and so forth—[we reply: no, because the establishment of such distinctions as "dissimilar instance" and so on is made with reference to the perspective of another's view (*paramatāpekṣa*), while being within the scope of the intended expression of individual *nayas*. Thus, this proof is indeed free from all suspicion of fault. As it has been said: "Whatever entities [a thing] transforms into, through both natural evolution (*visrasā*) and effort (*prayoga*)... (see p. 182, l. 13; p. 212, l. 19; p. 478, l. 4, note 1).
The Arhat knows each [object] in that way; there is no knowledge in the absence of sequential succession—this he knows through the power of destiny.
*Praśamarati*, verse 145.
Bearing every single limb in its entirety,
yet with [all] defects turned away.
...mānarapiya...

Although there exist treatises on the *nayas* composed by former teachers, such as the *Sanmati* and the *Nayāvatāra*, and although that canonical study, the *Saptatikāranayacakra*, also exists, the venerable Śvetapaṭa Mallavādin Kṣamāśramaṇa composed this *Nayacakra* treatise—a concise work of great significance—to favor those fortunate beings whose intelligence, lifespan, strength, enthusiasm, spiritual urgency, capacity for hearing, and power of retention are daily wasting away due to the force of the defects of the current age of discord (*duḥṣamā*). It was created for the sake of establishing the status of a universal monarch among the disputants of the Jains, just as the wheel-treasure (*cakraratna*) was for Bharata, the universal monarch.
Thus, this very *Dvādaśāranayacakra* (The Wheel of the Twelve Methods) is established; such is the hub of the *Nayacakra*.

Now, however, the purpose of this treatise (*śāstraprayojana*) is stated: Even though there exist treatises on the *nayās* (perspectives) composed by former teachers—such as the *Sanmati* and the *Nayāvatāra*—which follow the study of the *Saptaśatāra-nayacakra* (The Wheel of Seven Hundred Spokes) proclaimed by the Arhat, consisting of seven hundred distinct varieties including the *naigama* and others each numbering one hundred; and even though that scriptural *Saptaśatāra-nayacakra* exists, for those fortunate beings (*bhavyasattva*) whose powers of intellect, lifespan, vigor, enthusiasm, faith, spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), hearing, and retention are daily wasting away due to the force of the defects of this degenerate age (*duḥṣamākāla*), even the mere hearing [of such works] is difficult to obtain. Even having heard them, the comprehension of the truth is difficult; even having understood the truth, the diligence to convince others during the time of practical application (*vyavahāra*) is difficult to find. Even if there is such diligence, the recollection of the meaning of the text, its grasping, and the exposition of the grasped meaning result in extreme exhaustion. Considering this, and wishing to favor those students who are weary from such exhaustion, who fear voluminous texts, and who desire brevity, so that these right-viewed ones (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) might master the *Nayacakra* in a very short time, the venerable Śvetapaṭa Mallavādin Kṣamāśramaṇa composed this *Nayacakra-śāstra*, a concise text of great meaning. This was done out of compassion, thinking: "How might these right-viewed ones master the *Nayacakra* in a very short time? Just as the Cakravartin Bharata—having conquered the entire circle of rival disputants through his own logic and prowess; having conquered the circle of rival kings residing in all of Bharata; possessing the unobstructed *cakraratna* (wheel-jewel) favored by the gods; and possessing vast, pure fame that pervades the world and follows his lineage of sons—created the *cakraratna* for his sons, grandsons, and other kings; so too has this *Nayacakra-ratna* been created for the sake of his sons, grandsons, and other kings. It is like the *cakraratna* for Cakravartins. Thus, this *Nayacakra-śāstra* of many meanings in a concise form was composed by the illustrious Śvetapaṭa Mallavādin Kṣamāśramaṇa.

If one asks for what purpose: it is for the sake of establishing the status of a Wheel-Turning King (*vādicakravartin*) for the Jaina disputants who are intent upon the propagation of the Jina’s teaching—just as [the wheel-treasure] establishes the status of a Wheel-Turning King for universal monarchs. This is the stated purpose for the composition of this treatise, the *Nayacakra*.

Thus, this *Dvādaśāra-nayacakra* is established, firmly grounded, and unassailable; like the wheel-treasure of a universal monarch, it is proven to be endowed with sovereign power that cannot be overcome by others, possessing inconceivable power that is invincible to all else.

The utterance of the names of the Siddhas is auspicious and beneficial; it is worthy of being established through the lineage of disciples and grand-disciples, just like the Siddhas who reside at the summit of the world—those established Siddhas who bring about victory. Thus, its recitation is established as bringing fame. [End of chapter]...recitation...accomplishment...for the sake of the common good.
By hearing this meaning, which is beneficial... [text fragment] ...is established.

Thus ends the *Tumba* (Summary) of the *Nayacakra*, composed by the venerable Mallavādi Kṣamāśramaṇa, whose fame is firmly established. The total number of verses is 18,000. May there be auspiciousness for the illustrious Malla.
After the words "śravaṇa-bhā-yamū-bhavatu," such a praśasti (colophon) is seen in the Bhā manuscript on folio 572:
In the vast *gaccha* propagated by the venerable teacher Āryarakṣita, within the radiant lineage of sages known as the Vidhipakṣa,
there were lords of sūris named Guṇanidhāna, renowned throughout the world for their pure fame.
The sun upon the lotus-throne of his succession, the excellent sūri Śrī Dharmamūrti, shines forth as a boat across the ocean of existence.

He, whose lineage is a jewel-mine of jewels of excellent qualities such as good fortune, prosperity, and excellence, and whose pure conduct is honored by his disciples—by him, for the sake of his own spiritual welfare, this supreme manuscript of the *Nayacakra*, a great vessel of knowledge, has been written. May it flourish! [Therein resides] the son of the minister Govinda, a mass of splendor comparable to a tuft of *muñja* grass.
By the command of the venerable Guru, the wise one thus wrote this scripture. [End of verse 4].
The total number of verses is 18,000. Immediately following this, on folio 309, there is such a colophon in manuscript Ya:
"Just as it was seen in the original book, so has it been written by me."
Whether it be pure or impure, no fault shall be attributed to me.
This scripture, written with great hardship, should be preserved with care from water, fire, thieves, and especially from foolish children.
With his back, hips, and neck broken, and his gaze directed downward, he wrote this treatise with great difficulty; one should preserve it with diligent effort. 2.

This mirror has been composed during the reign of the illustrious Vijayadeva Sūris;
having come together, I shall now reveal their names.
O wise ones, the venerable Nayavijaya are my gurus, and the learned Jayasoma is virtuous.
The wise Lābhavijaya and the Gaṇis known as Kīrtiratna,
as well as the munis Tattvavijaya, exerted themselves here in the act of writing; and together with the wise Ravivijaya, the scholar Yaśovijaya also wrote it down.
Seeing this labor of a book, the virtuous are indeed deeply gratified;
the gaze of the wicked, however, hindered by envy for excellence, does not behold it at all. Homage to them! I praise their virtues, for my devotion toward them is firm.
May there be well-being! This very great treatise, though completed in a single fortnight, has been composed by those who strive incessantly for the purpose of illuminating the words of the Jina.
This pure life-story, an ambrosia for the ears of those with keen intellects, is victorious.
